en: All the water and food previously given runs away ahead of him.
Everything that is done is indeed attained, but never that which is not done;
even the water that has been offered will certainly meet [with its result]. (53)
Having spoken thus, the king, together with his wife, purified the sacred field;
for at that time, the fierce sun blazed intensely in the midst of the sky.
The fierce heat increased, and the queen became thirsty;
her smooth, copper-palmed feet grew hot with distress.
Her hands were as red as coral, and her body was likewise delicate;
she was distressed by the heat of the sun and severely tormented by its intense warmth. (56)
Falling to the ground in a swoon from the intensity of her thirst, that beautiful woman,
as she fell with eyes agitated by distress, beheld the sun.
But as she fell by chance, the Sun was gazed upon with anger;
because of that, the exceedingly radiant Sun became terrified in the sky. (58)
Deprived of his destination, he abandoned heaven and fell to the surface of the earth;
then, devoid of luster, with his complexion faded, he became cold.
In the presence of the devoted wife, the splendor of the sun was dissolved;
King Janaka said, "Protect that which is empty of inherent nature."
For what purpose have you come here to the earth, having abandoned your fiery nature?
What shall I do for the sake of your worship? I pay homage to you, O Bhāskara.
To the king who was speaking thus, Sūrya replied with humility:
"This wife of yours is devoted to her husband; she is merely slightly angry with me."
By the power of her wrath, I fell down unconscious;
there is no woman equal to her in the three worlds. (63)
Oh, what supreme service she has rendered! Oh, what supreme austerity!
Oh, her fortitude! Oh, her power! Her auspicious qualities are indeed like yours.
She is worthy of you, pure, and follows your will;
through her devotion to her husband and her asceticism, this virtuous woman is intent on your welfare.
This [offering] is equal to a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) and is worthy of your worship of the gods;
a worthy vessel has met with a worthy vessel, and the great fruit of merit has been attained. (66)
Whether the desire you have formed be appropriate or inappropriate,
it shall become futile for her through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Make of this field whatever you desire, just as it has been held in your mind;
I shall indeed provide the water, divine and like unto nectar.
I bestow this food, these two most divine sandals,
a parasol, a celestial bed, as well as the wish-fulfilling cow and an auspicious jewel.
"The vessel shall indeed be inexhaustible and always filled with food and other provisions.
Having spoken thus, Sūrya himself created a water-vessel.
Savitṛ, overflowing with affection, gave to that king of Mithilā a pair of sandals, a jewel, an umbrella, a bed, a cooking vessel, and likewise a cow.
He spoke again to the king: "Give [it] to the queen; make her happy.
This field will become glorious, fruit-bearing, and even a granter of desires. (72)
Then that queen, having been revived by the king with water, regained consciousness;
her fear vanished, she spoke thus to the king: ||73||
Tell me here, by whom were given the cool water, the divine parasol, the sandals, the bed, the cow, the jewel, the vessel, and the food? (74)
The king said: "O Queen, out of compassion for you, the Sun himself has come here, leaving the sky, in order to grant all these things. (75)
Having spoken thus, Sūrya was honored; and the two, being treated with hospitality by Sūrya, requested of him: "O Blessed One, what shall we do for you? (76)
Thus addressed, Vivasvat spoke for the sake of his own protection:
"May there always be safety for me from those women who are devoted to their husbands."
"May no affliction ever befall women devoted to their husbands from me.
Having heard the words of Sūrya, the queen replied, "So be it. (78)
"O Sarvanetra, you shall have no fear, just as you have chosen.
Having been addressed thus, the Sun-god went to his own orb in the sky. (79)
This very Janaka lady, devoted to her husband and endowed with beauty,
has obtained everything in the forest through the power of her devotion to her husband.
I too, the son of the Sun, worship her who is devoted to her husband;
O Brahmin, her vow is not [merely] a restraint, for her asceticism is indeed independent.
Neither fasting nor giving gifts, nor even the gods, have power over her once she has passed away from her husband;
for she sleeps only when he sleeps and remains awake when he is awakened. (82)
When her husband has eaten, she who eats herself certainly conquers death;
likewise, when he remains silent, she who remains observant of silence also conquers death.
Single-minded, focused on one vision, and obedient to her husband’s word—of her we all stand in fear: the gods, the daityas, and the dānavas. (84)
That virtuous woman, devoted to contentment and noble vows, was worthy of worship even by the gods;
she never rejected whatever was commanded by her husband. (85)
Though she was rejected by her beloved while engaged in service, she never at any time turned to any deity other than her husband. || 86 ||
A woman who is thus devoted to her husband does not enter the mouth of death;
she who is always thus intent upon the pleasure and welfare of her husband [attains this state]. || 86 ||
She always follows her own husband like a shadow;
she shall never indeed go to the gateway of the mouth of death.
"He is my mother, he is my father, he is my kinsman, and he is my supreme deity;
because she serves her husband in this manner, she always triumphs over me. (89)
Meditating upon her husband, following after her husband,
and grieving for her husband, she does not perceive the door of death.
She who does not hear songs, instrumental music, dances, nor various performances, does not see the gateway of death. 91.
Whether bathing, standing, or even performing her adornment, she who remains present when summoned does not behold the door of death. (92)
But she who, while her husband is worshipping the deities or eating, does not abandon her thoughts of food anywhere, does not see the door of death. ||93||
She who does not look upon another even in her mind does not see the door of death; she who daily sweeps the house before the sun has risen [attains this]. (94)
She who gazes upon the face of her husband, who conforms to the will of her husband, and who conducts herself for the welfare of her husband, does not behold the door of death. ||95||
She whose eyes, body, and disposition are always well-restrained, and who is endowed with purity and proper conduct, does not behold death. ||96||
These deities are seen in the world as belonging to those who possess fame;
even among humans, their wives are seen as deities in heaven. ||97||
Those devoted wives were honored by my father, Āditya;
therefore, I too always honor those devoted wives. ||98||
Thus, those devoted wives always proceed by this path;
having constantly delivered many [beings], they are indeed eternally honored by me. (99)
"They were not obstructed by me, nor was I capable of obstructing them;
for she was Janaka's wife, and she went for half a moment out of a desire for water."
Just as she arrived there, the Sun-god gave her water;
having accepted the worship performed by me, he quickly departed for his own master.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Rūpavatī, the wife of Janaka named Mithi, obtained all prosperity—including fruits, food, water, gold, and more—even in the forest through the power of her devotion to her husband by means of the Sun, along with the narration of the dharma of devoted wives," in the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives within the Solar Cycle (Yāmyacakra) of the first book, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard the dharma of devotion to one's husband from the mouth of Yama, Nāciketa asked Yama about that which is beneficial and brings welfare to all the worlds. || 1 ||
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall speak that which was asked by Nāciketa:
"O Dharmarāja, O mighty-armed one, O you of great asceticism, please explain. (2)
All people desire happiness through asceticism, vows, and the like;
how then can the mind of those who have resorted to such hardships give rise to evil? (3)
Indeed, human beings possess hundreds of diverse vows and means for the sake of the dharma of spiritual welfare;
who is it that performs this sinful act, and who is the one who causes it to be done? (4)
How does the mind arise toward hatred, or how is it produced toward passion?
Who alone draws along the fourfold collection of beings in this world? (5)
Having heard this, the god Yama said: "O Brahmarṣi, listen to that:
human beings were created by Brahmā solely for the sake of their own spiritual welfare."
Those born of other wombs are indeed miserable, whereas humans are truly happy;
having become devoted to the knowledge of Dharma, they are intent upon the highest good through devotion.
"May they attain heaven and liberation through austerity, vows, and gifts"—this [teaching] is for the sake of those possessed by passion to obtain pleasure therein, namely sensual pleasure. (8)
Wealth, wives, and so forth were bestowed upon them, as well as constant tactile pleasures;
they were forever content and satisfied, making remembrance of the Self their primary practice.
They are not drawn back because they turn away from that momentum since they are pleasant;
through enjoyment, craving arises, and its strength is produced.
Abandoning the path of justice, she engages in evil through craving, a mind intent on self-interest, and the mixture of desire, anger, and other passions. (11)
And by that which has the form of a mirage, resembling the loss of objects in a dream, and which is generally fruitless yet results in bondage, one is helplessly enveloped. (12)
The conduct of another is not sinful; it is only the conduct of one possessed by craving.
There is no other agent or instigator except for one’s own craving that exists within.
Upon failing to obtain what is desired, one becomes hateful; upon obtaining it, one becomes full of passion.
Drawn there by craving, the undiscerning one proceeds forward;
he performs both what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and that which is thus accumulated comes into being.
The self causes itself to fall, for it experiences the karma performed by itself.
O Brahmin, one's own past good deeds or evil deeds first attend to one who has arrived;
thus, the self becomes both one's enemy and one's kinsman.
The individual soul (*jīva*), having entered hundreds of wombs, indeed experiences its own suffering created by past actions within this world.
The inner self (*antarātman*), residing in the heart, beholds the entire universe.
Likewise, by means of volition and power, in accordance with the karma of the individual soul. || 18 ||
Knowledge and action manifest at the proper time, whether auspicious or inauspicious; indeed, living beings perform their deeds by means of these two.
Knowledge and action, however, reside in the living being and are dependent upon the living being;
like two wings, they indeed fly forward toward objects and places out of thirst.
One who performs good deeds indeed becomes good and partakes in the merit of heaven and other realms;
one who performs evil deeds becomes evil and partakes in the sin of hell.

Through Māyā, Brahman possesses the nature of the material cause (upādānatva), while through Time and the Great Power (mahāśakti), its status as the auxiliary cause (sahakāritva) is declared. || 22 ||
In that regard, Hari’s role is indeed merely instrumental through his volition;
just as it is with the Lord in the act of creation, so it is with the individual soul in its action.
For when a son is produced, the embodied soul (jīva) possesses the status of material cause;
furthermore, by uniting during the fertile period, it also possesses the status of a cooperative cause.
Moreover, for the soul possessed of desire, there is also the status of a mere instrumental cause.
Thus, in all cases, living beings possess both the status of being the cause and the status of sharing in the fruit.
Therefore, having understood through the scriptures and other means what is beneficial, one should perform that action;
however, one should abandon what is harmful by all means, through both knowledge and effort. (26)
In whatever measure the impurity of people indeed comes to an end, in that same measure their pure intellect increases and proceeds. || 27 ||
He performs auspicious deeds that destroy evil and exhaust the afflictions;
indeed, when pure merit has been acquired, he is honored among the immortals. (28)
Indeed, the attainment of the manifestation of results is brought about by the Inner Controller;
heaven is the attainment of auspicious fruits, and hell arises from sin. (29)
O Nāciketa, listen to that regarding the auspicious path created by yourself,
whether through mind, action, speech, austerity, or conduct.
By relying solely on the auspicious, he is liberated from evils—he who is equal toward all beings, self-conquered, and tranquil in mind. (31)
One who performs service for others turns away from the suffering of others;
he who constantly bestows happiness upon others is liberated from sins. ||32||
He who correctly understands the true nature of reality—the insentient, the sentient, and their qualities—being free from delusion and devoid of worldly attachment, attains the eternal state. (33)
One who fully understands virtues and non-virtues, who possesses discernment regarding the perishable and the imperishable,
and who is devoted to meditation on the Self— that knower is liberated from sins.
One who possesses the vow of non-violence toward his own body and the bodies of others, regarding his own interest as equal to that of others, being wise, shall certainly be liberated from sin. (35)
He who causes no agitation, who is free from craving, anger, and the like, and who follows the path of justice, is liberated from sins. (36)

He who is constantly devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), as well as to concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditation (dhyāna), and whose mind is withdrawn from worldly objects, is liberated from all sins. || 37 ||
He who has no desire for anything whatsoever, who is not greedy for desired objects, and who is eternally content—such a person, upon casting off the body, attains the supreme state. (38)
One who possesses faith, who is devoted to the worship of the gods and the service of ancestors, and who has no desire for the wealth of others, is liberated from sins. (39)
One who is devoted to serving the guru, free from malice, devoid of envy, and not cruel;
one whose conduct is noble and whose character is not mean—such a person shall be liberated from bondage.
But he who performs praiseworthy deeds, who avoids cruelty, and who performs auspicious festivals, is liberated from sins. (41)
He who constantly goes to a sacred ford (tīrtha), always remembering the pure Brahman and leading a sinless livelihood, is liberated from all sins.
Having risen, one should pay homage to the father, the deity, the mother, the preceptor, the twice-born, the virtuous, and the chaste woman; thus, one is liberated from sins. (43)
The giver does not indeed encounter suffering, nor does the striker remain unhappy;
the devotee does not enter the cycle of worldly existence, nor does the seeker of sense-objects fail to attain liberation. 44.
This has been declared as the most excellent and beneficial for all;
nevertheless, I shall now describe the swift means for the destruction of sins.
That which is simple and achievable in an instant, wherein no exertion is required—those who are virtuous people and spiritual teachers are the ones who ferry one across the ocean of saṃsāra. ||46||
The devotees of Hari, the gods, the sages, and the great seers;
those who are truthful, virtuous wives, those whose nature is celibacy, and those who are followers of the Bhāgavata—[all these are purified]. 47.
Placing one's head at their feet, fixing the mind upon their heart, one should abide by their command and remain intent on service. ||48||
In whatever way and by whatever means the virtuous may repeatedly become pleased, one should act accordingly; thus, one is liberated from sins.
By the recitation of the Gāyatrī, one should likewise remember the Moon and the Sun.
By beholding [the deity] with the realization of Brahman, the maker's sin is destroyed.
One should circumambulate the guru, meditate upon him, and worship him thoroughly;
by serving the guru as Hari, one is liberated from all sins.
Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one is released from every sin.
One should meditate on the sun and the moon as being in the eyes, and likewise on that which resides in the heart. 52.
He beholds them complete, stainless, and perfectly radiant;
his sin, whether it be very small or as vast as the ocean, is destroyed.
Having seen the dwarf Brahmin and the Boar arisen from the waters—
One who bows to the lion mounted upon Siṃhikā attains the destruction of all sins.
Cows are pure, auspicious, and the deities even of the gods;
he who serves them with devotion is liberated from all evils.
He who drinks the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) during an auspicious moment is liberated from the sins committed throughout his entire life at that very instant.
The person who receives upon their head the water uplifted by the tail [of the bull] attains the fruit of all sacred fords and is liberated from all sins. (57)
Whoever bathes with cow’s urine during the Rohiṇī asterism by means of a stream of urine—the faults committed through all sins are instantly burnt away; of this there is no doubt. (58)
He who holds and drinks the stream of milk emerging from the udder of a cow at its very head is liberated from all sins. (59)
One should pay homage in the morning to a cow, the sun, a virtuous Brāhmaṇa, and a chaste woman;
by offering curd, unbroken grains, and water, one is liberated from sins.
On the full moon day, one should offer curd, unbroken grains, and water to Soma.
By bowing to Arundhatī and the planets, one is liberated from all sins.
A Śūdra who serves a twice-born man has his sin destroyed;
this applies always during the equinoxes, at auspicious planetary conjunctions (yogas), and at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti). || 61–62 ||
On all days of religious observance and in all festive houses,
a Śūdra who gives milk and curd is liberated from all sins.
Having spread out Kuśa grass with its tips pointing eastward and having likewise established a bull there, [he should offer].
Having paid homage along with the twice-born, one is liberated from all sins.

Having bathed in the southern bank of the river that flows toward the east, one should perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana) and pay obeisance; thus, one is released from all transgressions.
By taking water with a right-spiraling conch shell and pouring it upon his head,
a person surely pacifies the sins committed throughout his life.
Having gone to water flowing eastward and standing in water reaching up to the navel,
a person, having bathed, should offer seven handfuls mixed with black sesame seeds.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
the sin committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
The man who bathes three times with water containing all kinds of jewels and with an unblemished lotus petal is liberated from all sins.
He who performs the vow of the Ekādaśīs, who observes the Dvādaśīs,
and who is a devotee of Nārāyaṇa— sin does not touch him at all.
Those who seize the property of Brahmins, as well as those who kill Brahmins, those intent on betraying their gurus, and likewise those intent on betraying gods and friends; ||71||
Those who are intent on betraying their masters, those who violate the wives of others, those who steal the property of others, and those who consume what is forbidden to eat; ||72||

They were hypocritical, transgressors of the bounds of propriety, revilers of the Vedas and Brahmins, addicted to accepting gifts from the unworthy, and devoted to sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached. ||73||
Those who are violent, those who set snares, those who kill, and those who steal;
those who are rogues, deceitful, and fraudulent, as well as those devoid of virtuous deeds. (74)
If they observe the eleventh and twelfth lunar days with faith,
having fasted upon them and becoming free from sin, they go to the supreme state.
Therefore, there exists no other supreme means for the destruction of evil;
the white [path] should be understood as bestowing devotion, while the black [path] grants liberation. (76)
The Ekādaśī observed by men burns away the sin accumulated through mind, speech, and action during an entire month. (77)
"One must not eat, one must not eat when the day of Hari has arrived;
for he who is unable to fast on the full Ekādaśī," (78)

Therefore, one should perform the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata) by means of eating only at night, or likewise by eating only what is obtained unasked, or by giving a gift consisting of a single meal.
But for those unable to observe fasts, the twelfth day known as Prabodhinī should be observed with a single fast;
it burns away all sin committed during one's lifetime.
By worshipping the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa during that [Ekādaśī],
one obtains all this fruit of the twelve Dvādaśīs.
That which is performed on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with Pūrvābhādrapadā becomes inexhaustible; however, when conjoined with Uttarābhādrapadā, the fruit is ten million times greater. (82)
Everything performed during the awakening [of Hari] shall yield infinite fruit;
likewise for the sleeping, the awakening, and the turning over of Hari. (83)

Having fasted according to the prescribed rule, the observer of the vow shall attain purity on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) conjoined with the moon during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika.
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) conjoined with the Uttarābhādrapadā nakṣatra and the planet Mars is considered to bestow infinite fruit; it yields the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs. ||85||
Therefore, one should observe the fast on the twelfth day with every effort;
they are blessed, they have achieved their life's purpose, and by them alone has a virtuous deed been performed.
O Brahmin, after propitiating the Supreme Lord over thousands of other births,
one attains the status of a Vaiṣṇava when all sins have been destroyed.
For the highly fortunate Vaiṣṇavas purify the entire world;
likewise, by worshipping me, one goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born one, whether remembered, praised, seen, or even touched, [they grant liberation].
Even a Cāṇḍāla who is a devotee of the Blessed One is purified by the will of Hari.
Those high-souled Vaiṣṇavas who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu cross over [the ocean of existence] themselves and cause others— even women, Śūdras, and sinful people— to cross over as well.
O Nāciketa, listen to this supreme secret to be guarded, which is purifying and the great destroyer of even the most heinous sins. 91.

And likewise for those who are utterly impure, those who have fallen from their path, those engaged in [forbidden] actions, as well as for Cāṇḍālas, violent people, and those who consume liquor or commit theft. ||92||
I shall proclaim to you the purification of pervasive sins that cause the intermingling of castes, and the cleansing of those sins that are as indelible as adamantine paste. (93)
Indeed, the water that has washed the feet of virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, as well as the water in which they have bathed, and even the water that they have drunk—[is sacred]. ||94||
Even water that has been touched must indeed be drunk by the sinner;
for when even a single drop of it is drunk, his sins truly burst into flame.
In drinking, bathing, sprinkling, casting water upon the head, anointing the limbs,
and touching the eyes, that water destroys the sins of many lifetimes.
Whatever sins there may be, even those of a sinful nature, are indeed burnt away by the water of the drink of the virtuous who are truly pleasing. 97.
In the sight of the virtuous, even women, Śūdras, and even dog-cookers are purified;
by the touch of the virtuous, even sinners become purifiers through their destruction [of sin]. 18.
The body of one devoted to the service of the virtuous becomes divine and non-material;
the fortune of one devoted to the service of the virtuous becomes divine and bestows liberation. 99.
Those who have bathed in the dust of the feet of the virtuous are partakers of liberation;
that which is a vessel for the affection of the virtuous is remembered as a vessel of Śrī Hari.
The yoga of the virtuous is the Nāciketa fire; it is undoubtedly the yoga of Hari.
My messengers do not go where the messengers of Viṣṇu—the saintly ones—are present.
Those women, men, or eunuchs who have been oppressed by the messengers of Yama,
if they then embrace virtuous people, are quickly liberated from Yama.
For the virtuous, union with all the senses bestows liberation and grants the state of Brahman; there is no divine association with the holy more excellent than this, nor anything else like it.
Through union with Hari, the virtuous indeed become free from qualities (nirguṇa) and embodiments of Brahman; through union with the virtuous, even sinful souls become embodiments of Brahman.
The mere reality, when released by the wise, becomes divine and devoid of qualities;
whether hidden or manifest, all that conduces to becoming Brahman. 105.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have told you the means for deliverance;
go forth, endowed with self-knowledge, and having obtained whatever else has been given.
Having spoken thus, that King Yama rose from his own seat,
performed appropriate worship for me, and spoke pleasant words, O protector of the earth.
The Lord dismissed him with a well-pleased inner self.
O Brahmins, this has been related to you concerning that king in his excellent city.
"Whatever has been seen and heard, and how I have come to be here,
O Lakṣmī"— having heard these words of Nāciketa, the gods on earth [responded].
Recognizing that water to be the most excellent of all, the foremost for the virtuous, and pleasing to behold,
the holy men, who are compassionate toward the distressed, were filled with joy.
Some there were Vaikhānasas, some were Nirāsanakas,
others were Yāyāvaras, and still others were Vānaprasthas.

Some were settled householders (śālīna), while others adopted the pigeon-like mode of life (kāpotī); still others subsisted by gleaning ears of corn (śila) and picking up individual grains (uñcha), being both those who cooked their own food and those who did not cook at all.
Some were performers of various sacrifices, while others had conquered their selves;
some observed the vow of silence and remained in fixed postures, and others likewise dwelt in the water.
Likewise, some sleep on trees; others are like deer in their way of life; some practice the penance of the five fires, while others subsist only on leaves and fruits.
Some subsist on water, some subsist on air, and others likewise subsist on vegetables;
these various ascetics have taken refuge in eternal wisdom.
And having heard this story, the sages of divine luster were struck with wonder upon hearing the majesty of the water, which is the refuge of the virtuous.
Intent on devotion and desiring to drink the water from the feet of the virtuous Nara-Nārāyaṇa, they went indeed to Badarī-āśrama.
The righteous-souled Naciketas, seeing his son honored by Yama and having regained the one whose wealth is austerity, reflected once more upon dharma alone.
Nāciketa also instructed his disciples in the knowledge of the Self and strictly observed the purifying dharma of the virtuous. 1.19.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the water of great power in the western wheel;
it is the means for their upliftment and is most gracious to the virtuous.
And in every way [he dwells] at the Yamunā, the Gaṅgā, and the Gomatī;
and also in every way at the Godāvarī, the Sarayū, and the Revā.
In every way, [the waters] of the Gaṅgā, the Svarṇarekhā, and the Tapatī; as well as those of the Kāverī, the Tāmraparṇī, and all the oceans. || 122 ||
Of all the waters belonging to sacred fords (tīrtha),
the water from the feet of the virtuous is always divine, most excellent, and purifying.
Bestowing all desires, bestowing liberation, and bestowing great fortune—
by hearing or reciting this, the fruit shall be the granting of everything.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Nāciketa’s Cessation after Relating What Was Heard from Yamarāja—Concerning the Causes of Good and Evil Conduct in the First Section on the Kṛta Age of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Means for Liberation from Sin; and the Supreme Well-being Attained through the Service of the Cow, the Ekādaśī Vrata, and the Drinking of the Nectar of the Holy Feet," wherein Nāciketa ceased speaking and the sages departed for Badrī-Nārāyaṇa.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Kṛṣṇa, previously I heard from the lotus of your mouth that at the beginning of creation, you yourself manifested the devoted wife (pativratā).
She indeed exists on earth, in the netherworld (pātāla), in heaven, in truth, as well as in the cosmic egg (āvṛti);
in Vairāja, in Vaikuṇṭha, and in the manifestations of the lords.
In the creation of individual souls and in the creation of the Lord, she indeed abides everywhere;
she is that pervasive Great Power, whose form is your own sovereign capability.
In the beginning, she was born as Mahālakṣmī by the name Kambharā;
you yourself were born as Gopāla, the manifest Supreme Brahman. || 4 ||
The Brahmin named Patnīvrata was himself born as the Great King Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari, the promoter of all dharma.
His wife was Kambharālakṣmī, in whose house the mental son Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa was born— Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself.
She is Lakṣmī and you are Kṛṣṇa; I remember that through your grace.
For the dharma consisting of devotion to one's husband is indeed the dharma of a chaste wife, which bestows liberation.
Bestowing happiness and bestowing heaven, and fulfilling all desires;
being identical with you and identical with me, how could he not deliver people? (8)
The dharma consisting of service to the virtuous prevails above all;
truthful, devoted wives, and saintly women cross over [the ocean of existence] by serving the righteous.
"You are one of virtuous form; indeed, you are one of chaste form.
The dharma of the chaste woman and the dharma of the virtuous man are as difficult to traverse as the edge of a sword."
Having heard that Janaka’s daughter is virtuous and beautiful,
I am filled with a desire to hear specifically about the power of her virtue.

Women, who are objects of enjoyment and subject to the nature of desire, shall cross the ocean of existence upon hearing of the power of the devoted wife, as it is proclaimed through the efficacy of the virtuous Satī.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, cause me to hear of the wonders of the sovereignty of chaste wives, which bestow happiness.
O Keśava, I desire to hear about those beings who have been, those who are being born, and indeed the life stories of the virtuous women whose very nature is the power of Bhava.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that supreme and auspicious matter you desire to know; you appear compassionate toward me, wishing to bring about the welfare of women."
I shall relate many wonderful accounts of virtuous women—
of maidens, of those who have been married, and of women who are lifelong celibates.
[She is] the celestial splendor of virtuous women, of those who have lost their husbands, of generous wives,
of female yogis, and of those established in the state of devotion to the Lord.
I shall relate the wonders of the wives of the Ṛṣis, the consorts of the gods, the women of Brahmā, and the wives of Kṛṣṇa; listen, and be attentive to my words. (18)
She who is Rādhikā in Goloka is Sāvitrī, who is her own partial expansion;
she was indeed created by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for the sake of Brahmā. 19.
When the first creation was accomplished, she remained situated in Śvetadvīpa;
at that very same time, O King, [the Lord] was in Badarikāśrama.
While Priyavrata was performing penance there, Nārada approached him;
seeing the sage in the sky, the king stood up, filled with great joy.
Having offered him a seat and water for his feet, he respectfully asked:
"O Blessed One, is there anything wonderful in this place known as Kṛta?"
"O Nārada, tell me of anything seen or even heard by you in this age.
Then Nārada told him of one marvel exactly as it had been seen.
O Indra among kings, on the day before yesterday I went to Śvetadvīpa;
there I beheld a divine lake adorned with lotuses.
On the shore of that lake, however, was a large-eyed maiden.
Having seen that large-eyed maiden, I was filled with wonder.
O Indra among kings, I questioned that sweet-spoken woman: "Who are you, blessed lady? How do you exist here, and what is your purpose in this place? (26)
"O lady of beautiful limbs, O auspicious one, tell me what must be done.
Thus addressed by me, she, with unblinking eyes, looked at me.
While I remained silent after remembering this, my supreme knowledge was forgotten,
as were all the Vedas, the Saṃhitās, and the fruits [of ritual action].
"O King, as soon as I saw everything, my daughter was carried away in an instant;
thereupon, overcome with amazement, I became paralyzed by anxiety and grief. (29)
Having gone to her for refuge, while I was looking for her once more,
a divine man appeared within her body.
In the heart of that man was another,
and on his chest yet another, glorious one with blood-red eyes, resembling the twelve suns.
Thus, three men were seen here entering the body of the maiden;
in an instant, those three dissolved, and I beheld the maiden alone.
Then I asked that goddess:
"O blessed lady, tell me how my Vedas were lost; explain the cause of their destruction."
The maiden said: "Since you do not know me, the mother of the Vedas, who am Sāvitrī, therefore the Vedas have been destroyed by you. (34)
Having heard this, Nārada asked, "Who are these men?
The maiden replied, "This Ṛgveda within my heart is Nārāyaṇa."
The fire named Viṣṇurūpa burns away sins through the mere utterance of its name;
within his heart is the second [fire], the Yajurveda, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
Within his heart is indeed the third, the Sāmaveda, who is Śaṅkara;
these two, upon being remembered, quickly burn away sins like the sun.
O sage, these three great Vedas are indeed the three gods; O brahmin, accept them and chant the Vedic Gāyatrī dedicated to Viṣṇu. (38)
"Therefore, O Nārada, take up the Vedas and omniscience;
and perform your ritual bath, my son, in this lake of the Vedas. (39)
"O son, by performing this bath, you have remembered that which belongs to another birth;
having bathed, I too have obtained that knowledge which takes a thousand years to produce."
Formerly, there was a twice-born man named Sārasvata in the city of Puṣkara-pattana; I am indeed that very person, the mind-born son of Brahmā, appearing here before you.
Sāvitrī, my mother, then vanished from sight;
however, by means of divine vision, she was beheld by me in Satyaloka. ||42||
The wife of the Creator (Brahmā), renowned for her splendor and devoted to her husband, [was Sāvitrī].
Having created all beings, Brahmā repeatedly cast off his own body;
yet, through the power of her devotion to her husband, Sāvitrī [restored it] from that corpse again and again.
Then, indeed, he created Brahmā by the touch of his own hand.
She brought forth the goat many times after it had died;
when her creation was accomplished according to her desire, she then desisted from further killing.
Having obtained that eternal Brahmā as her husband, she, being devoted to her husband,
shall continue to live and does now live by the power of her devotion to her husband.
Having addressed Death and repeatedly offered Brahmā to Death,
she restored her husband to life through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Having offered the three Vedas as oblations for three generations, she gave them back once more;
by the power of her devotion to her husband, she was my mother, Sāvitrī. 48.
"O King, having performed my ablutions, I have come here desiring to see you;
I shall now go, having paid homage to the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa. (49)
Having spoken thus and bowed to Hari, Nārada departed for Satyaloka.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the great power of wifely devotion been described to you.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vision by Nārada of the Three Vedas as the Three Deities within Sāvitrī, and the Description of how Brahmā’s Body was Restored Again and Again through the Power of Sāvitrī’s Devotion to Her Husband," in the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how the gods in heaven, the Gandharvas, the Maruts, as well as the planets, comets, constellations, and those who are the guardians of the directions [attained their status]. || 1 ||
The Vasus, the Nidhis, the Rudras, the sages, and likewise the Ravis;
the goddesses, the Apsarases, the munis, the female servants, and the male servants. || 2 ||
The elephants Airāvata and others, the elephants of the quarters; likewise the horses beginning with Uccaiḥśravas; and the swans, Garuḍas, and parrots. (3)
The wish-fulfilling cows, the cattle, the dogs beginning with Saramā, the rams, the buffaloes, and even those lions who serve as the vehicles of the gods; || 4 ||
They were all divine, capable of moving at will, and likewise able to assume any form they desired;
they were all endowed with the eight supernatural powers and possessed unobstructed vision.
Their movements are unimpeded and they are masters of all languages;
they are all conversant in the language of the gods and rely upon the merit of the Dharma.
Those peacocks, mice, and snakes who dwell in the houses of the gods enjoy heavenly happiness and possess long lives because they abide by their natural laws. || 7 ||
All of them, assuming forms at will and devoted to their respective duties, dwell there; however, there is one female dog who is a servant of Indra.
Saramā is ever devoted to her husband, faithful to her lord;
the husband of Saramā is named Dyumeya, a servant of Indra. (9)
Devoted to that [task], Saramā was loyal to her own master and did what was pleasing to her husband; she remained obedient to her husband’s command and enjoyed the pleasures granted by her husband.
This glorious one does not take food or anything else anywhere in between;
whatever has been obtained from whichever deities must be offered back to the Lord.
Thereupon, he constantly received his master’s commands and carried them out.
Once, in the heavens, there were two rākṣasas named Vidyut and Suvidyut.
When the Kṛta Yuga had begun, the two most powerful ones suddenly went forth to fight; Mahendra, having been defeated by them, fled. || 13 ||
The male and female servants, the mounts and other attendants, led by Saramā, having fled,
established a secret dwelling in the forest regions of Mount Meru.
The two Rākṣasas, having seized the realm of Mahendra and filled with pride, went joyfully toward Mount Meru for the sake of recreation.
There in that forest, having seen a cave that was pleasant, fulfilling desires, auspicious,
captivating, and excellent, he took his seat upon it and remained there.
Having gone to the city of Indra and returned to that cave,
both Asuras, embraced by many female attendants, took their pleasure.
But the gods, having fallen into distress without King Indraka, deliberated calmly, desiring the position of Indra.
All the armies, being well-armored, gathered together for those two;
then Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, spoke to them there.
Perform the Gomedha sacrifice first to Viṣṇu, the Lord;
offer the pure milk and clarified butter of cows to the one whose form is fire.
Having fed the army and obtained strength, you must again perform sacrifices;
when this is done, victory will be yours, but not otherwise.
"This instruction has been given by me; let it be carried out quickly"—having been addressed thus, the gods then [sought] cows for the sake of milk-rice and other offerings.
Having brought the wish-fulfilling cows to the sacrificial ground in the forest of Meru,
they, constrained by their preceptor, began the performance of the sacrifice and protected the ritual proceedings.
And every morning, they also constantly offer milk, curd, ghee, clarified butter,
and abundant oblations to the sacrificial fire for Viṣṇu and to the gods.
During the day, all those cows go to the grassy lands and to the fearless open grounds for food, for the sake of grazing on grass and other fodder.
Then Indra was urged and instructed there by the gods:
"For the sake of protecting the cows, dispatch messengers constantly. (26)
Then Indra gave Saramā as a devoted wife;
by the power of her devotion to her husband, that virtuous woman became the protector of all. ||27||
They released the cows for the purpose of grazing and gave Saramā to guard them;
the gods performed sacrifices free from anxiety for the sake of attaining strength.
Those cows, though devoid of their divine protector, while being guarded on a grassy plain,
then went to where those asuras were grazing.
But seeing that herd of cows, Śukramūka said to the priest:
"Look, O Brahmin, divine cows are being driven away by this woman who is protecting them."
"Tell us how Indra might be deprived of Saramā so that an obstacle may arise for the sacrifice performed by the gods; instruct us quickly, and we shall act accordingly. (3.1)
Thus addressed, Śukra then replied to the Asuras:
"Let the cows be taken away quickly, O Asuras; do not delay for even a moment. (32)
For cows are the root of sacrifice; they are the bestowers of nourishment upon the gods.
If their flow [of milk] is obstructed, there would be an obstruction of sacrifice, and the gods would experience suffering. (33)
When they were addressed thus, the Daityas then abandoned the cows as they pleased; once those cows had been taken away, Saramā became intent on searching for their tracks.
She saw the cows, the supporters of the sacrifice, being led away by the sons of Diti;
she also saw the bitch, whose path was visible, well-guarded by the Daityas.
Seeing Saramā, they spoke these words to her with conciliation: "O Saramā, by no means should you report this to the gods. (36)
"Do not say that the cows have been stolen by the Daityas; may it be well with you. O auspicious Saramā, the milk of these cows is exceedingly desirable. (37)
Having said, "Drink at your leisure," they then gave her milk;
having given that incomparable milk to her, those leaders of the Daityas [departed]. (38)
"Do not go, O blessed lady; report these words to the King of the Gods.
Having been told this repeatedly by them, she heard it and spoke to the Dānavas: (39)
For one whose food his servants eat, the maintenance of those servants is for his sake;
giving even one's life for their sake brings about welfare, but not otherwise. (1.365.40)
If a servant, having received his wages, does not perform work for the benefit of his master, he goes to the Raurava hell; what then would one receive who acts in the opposite manner? ||41||
"O King, I am certainly not a dog belonging to the gods, nor am I their opposite;
I have been appointed for the purpose of protection, so how could I go toward destruction? (42)
O gods and Daityas, I shall tell you what must be done regarding the cow's disappearance:
I shall never again be either a protector or a devourer. (43)
For one who has eaten even a single grain of food from another, the offering of one's own head is required;
such is the innate nature of dogs that they are not released even from fear.
When food has been digested in the stomach, if a person acts harmfully toward it—becoming a betrayer of his master and a destroyer of dharma—he is slain by all the deities. (45)
There can be no atonement for one who betrays the trust of his master;
we, the protectors of our lord’s wife, enjoy that which we have obtained from him. (46)
Content even with contempt and physical blows, they perceive only virtues; ever devoted to the service of their master through body, speech, and action. (47)
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself directly protects such people who possess true prosperity and are solely devoted to the duty toward their master. 48.
"I shall not drink cow's milk without the command of my master;
nor shall I keep it secret, but will reveal it immediately. (49)
Having spoken thus, she then departed swiftly from that place;
meanwhile, the Daityas rushed toward her with their weapons in order to strike her down.
Saramā said: "O sons of Diti, you ought not to kill me;
for wherever one may be in the three worlds, a wise man never kills a woman. (51)
Although addressed thus, the Daityas, having become dogs and being exceedingly lustful and arrogant, ran there to embrace the female dog.
Terrified, she called to mind the gods and her husband Dyumeyaka;
at that moment, Dyumeya, the servant of the gods, arrived there.
Having bowed to her husband and drunk from the lotus-face of her lord, Saramā, devoted to righteousness, spoke in order to defeat the Daityas. (54)
If I take the food of my master as a token of his grace, may the Daityas indeed be consumed by fire here through that merit. (55)
If I am always established in truthfulness of speech,
by that merit may the Daityas indeed be consumed here by fire.
"If I never forsake my own husband and go to no other man, by that merit may the Daityas indeed be consumed here by fire. (57)
If I am pleased with my own husband and not with another, by that merit may the Daityas indeed be consumed here by fire. (58)
If, even in the service of my master, I have always maintained his favor and been employed [for this task], then let the Daityas be consumed by fire! ||59||
When my husband slept, I slept; when he ate, I likewise ate. Attaining joy in his joy, I transcended sorrow in his sorrow. (1.365.60)
If I am a devoted wife according to my birth for all time, by that merit may the Daityas indeed be consumed here by fire. (61)
When she had spoken thus, the Daityas, assuming the forms of dogs, gathered around her and,
having encircled her with a line, were about to touch that female dog.
At that moment, a most terrible forest fire broke out;
reaching as far as the edge of the Daityas' domain, it completely reduced everything to ashes.
The bitch, having approached Indra and the other deities together with her husband,
related the entire account of what had occurred at the sacrifice.
Having heard this, the gods went there; having taken the cows, they returned to the sacrifice.
Śukra, by means of mantras using *sañjīvanī* leaves, raised the Asuras back to life.
Having taken him, she went to the sacrificial ground for the sake of battle, highly arrogant;
having asked her husband Saramā for permission, she seized Śukra by the head.
Mahendra and the others, having attained nourishment through the power of the sacrifice,
zealously arrayed their armies for the destruction of the Daityas.
By means of the sacrifice being performed, the strength of the deities increased;
and when their strength had increased, Indra spoke to the divine armies: 68.
"Let the gods quickly arm themselves for the task of slaying the Daityas.
Thus addressed, the gods then became armored at that very moment.
With their weapons raised, they rushed forth for the destruction of the Asuras;
those gods fought swiftly and conquered the army of the Asuras.
The asuras, defeated by the gods, those who remained after the slaughter, being senseless and terrified, plunged into the oceans, desiring to live.
Even the king of the gods [Indra] went to the third heaven, as did the world-protectors, the cows,
the planets, the lunar mansions, the stars, the goddesses, and likewise the sages.
Having regained his own heaven together with all the gods,
he ascended to the highest [throne] and enjoyed himself as before, according to his pleasure.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the success born of her own duty and achieved through devotion to her husband caused many demons to burn away, even though she was devoid of divine power. 74.
Whoever in this world hears this *Saramā-dharmasadbala*, that person indeed obtains the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice. (75)
And that king who, having been deprived of his kingdom, listens to this with a concentrated mind, regains his own kingdom just as the lord of the gods regained heaven. ||76||

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how, when the kingdom of the gods was seized by the Rākṣasas beginning with Vidyut, during a sacrifice performed by the gods on Mount Meru for the protection of the cows, the Daityas were incinerated and the cows protected by Saramā—the divine dog—appointed for that purpose through the power of her devotion to her husband, and how the kingdom of the gods was regained by the gods," within the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, concerning the greatness of devoted wives (*pativratā*) in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the most excellent power of the great and truthful Sāvitrī’s devotion to her husband, by which her lord was restored to life.
She who was declared in ancient times by Brahmā to be the mother of the Vedas,
and who was worshipped by the hosts of gods and honored by the assemblies of the learned.
In the first age, the Satya Yuga, she was thus honored by King Aśvapati;
thereafter, that devoted wife was worshipped by all human beings.
In the land of Madra, there was a virtuous great king named Aśvapati;
he had a queen by the name of Mālatī.
The virtuous wife, carrying out her husband’s instructions,
performed worship with supreme devotion to Sāvitrī, following the advice of Vasiṣṭha.
She propitiated the Brahmi Sāvitrī for many years;
yet she did not behold Sāvitrī, nor did she obtain even the slightest fruit.
Her heart was shattered; she became sorrowful and deprived of her enjoyments.
The king, endowed with wisdom, comforted her with soothing words and showed her fortitude.
Having entrusted the queen with the household and handed over the burden of the kingdom,
he went to Puṣkara to perform austerities for the sake of attaining Sāvitrī.
Having become concentrated there, he performed austerities for a hundred years;
then he heard a divine, incorporeal voice in the sky.
"O King, you must indeed perform ten lakhs of recitations of the Gāyatrī.
Having heard this, Aśvapati reflected upon that procedure.
Just then, Parāśara, possessing a divine body, arrived there;
having performed worship, the king bowed to the sage and questioned him.
The sage spoke to the king regarding the procedure for the recitation of the Gāyatrī:
"A single recitation of the Gāyatrī removes the sin committed during the day. (12)
A recitation ten times removes the sin committed during a day and night;
a recitation a hundred times shall destroy the sin committed during a month. (13)
A recitation performed a thousand times shall utterly destroy the sins of a year;
a hundred-thousandfold recitation destroys the sins of an entire lifetime, whether they be dry or moist.
A recitation of one million times destroys the sins of three lifetimes;
a recitation of ten million times will certainly destroy the [sins] from all previous births. 15.
A recitation of ten crores certainly bestows liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having formed the hand into the shape of a serpent’s hood with the fingers pointing upward, one should seal it. (16)
With his head unbowed and remaining steady, the twice-born man should recite the mantra while facing the east;
he should perform the recitation in a temple or at a sacred ford using a rosary made of Tulasī wood.
Or a rosary of one hundred and eight crystal seeds,
strung with gems, gentle in appearance, [placed] upon seven leaves of the Aśvattha tree.
Having established it, one should then bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should bathe it with water from sacred fords or with the meritorious waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having recited the Gāyatrī-śataka, one should indeed cause it to become fit for recitation;
thereafter, perform the recitation of ten lakhs in due order.
You will directly behold Sāvitrī upon the destruction of all your sins;
therefore, always perform the three daily prayers at dawn, midday, and likewise at evening, in accordance with the truth.
One who is devoid of the recitation at the junctions of the day shall partake in the fruits of [worldly] actions;
however, one who performs the three junctions throughout their life becomes as radiant as the sun.
He should be known as one liberated while living, who effects the destruction of the sins of others;
even by the dust of his feet, the earth immediately becomes purified.
Even sacred fords become impure through contact with one who is devoid of Vaiṣṇavism and who neglects the three daily rites of twilight.
The gods do not accept the worship of one who has neglected the Ekādaśī;
nor do the ancestors accept the offerings of water, the funeral cakes, or the ancestral oblations.
One who eats food offered by a monkey, one who touches a corpse and so forth, one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras, and likewise one who approaches a woman in her menses; ||26||

One who lives by the sword, one who lives by ink, one who lives by agriculture, one who eats fish, one who lives off his wife’s earnings, and one who sells the knowledge of his daughter—such a person is not called a twice-born. 27.
"O royal sage, become a Vaiṣṇava and perform your recitation at midday;
on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having become pure, one should be a person observing the vow. (28)
One should perform the vow on the fourteenth day, repeatedly reciting the Sāvitrī mantra;
one should observe this fast for a period of fourteen years.
One should offer an oblation of food consisting of fourteen fruits and fourteen items, along with flowers, garments, a sacred thread, incense, and a lamp. (1.366.30)
Having established an auspicious water-pot filled with fruits, gems, and other offerings,
[he should worship] Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā.
Having worshipped [the preliminary deities], the observer of the vow should worship the principal deity once the jar has been invoked;
the steady observer of the vow should meditate upon the principal goddess Sāvitrī within the image.
Now, O King, listen likewise to the meditation on Sāvitrī at midday, as well as the hymn, the ritual for worship, and the mantra that grants all desires. (33)
Having the excellent color of molten gold, blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
her face bright with a gentle smile, and adorned with gold and jewels.
She was clad in golden garments, the virtuous consort of the Supreme Lord Śrī, who bestows compassion, peace, happiness, and liberation, and grants all prosperity. (35)
I worship the Mother, the presiding deity of the Vedas, who exists in the form of the seed-syllable, the bestower of all intentions, and the giver of wisdom. 36.
Having meditated thus and held the meditation, and having placed a flower upon one's own head,
one should invoke the Goddess into the jar and worship her with the sixteen offerings.
A seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, and likewise water for sipping;
a bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the application of fragrant unguents and the like. ||38||
Likewise, one should offer the consecration, as well as garments for cleansing, clothing,
ornaments, flowers, and articles of adornment.
Incense, the sacred thread and so forth, liquids for the sake of prosperity,
a lamp, food offerings, water, betel leaf, sandalwood paste, and other such items.
The fruit of the nightly lamp-offering, leaves, a comfortable bed, prostrations and the like, massaging the feet, and seeking forgiveness with a divine mind. ||41||
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, he should dismiss that Mother;
the observer of the vow should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin who has arrived.
One should recite "Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sāvitryai Svāhā" one hundred and eight times;
indeed, from a single recitation up to ten million recitations [the merit increases accordingly]. ||43||
One should recite the hymn according to one's ability at midday thereafter;
this Sāvitrī was formerly given by Kṛṣṇa to Brahmā in Goloka. (44)
Brahmā praised her, the mother of the Vedas, who is the very form of Rādhā:
"O Supreme Goddess, you whose nature is the power of Kṛṣṇa, you whose nature is Śrī! (45)
O Nārāyaṇī, O Maheśvarī, you who are the very form of Nārāyaṇa, consisting of splendor, consisting of supreme bliss, and the increaser of the twice-born! 46.
O eternal and ancient Lakṣmī, whose form is all-auspiciousness, who is the very embodiment of all goddesses, O beautiful one, bestower of liberation and happiness! ||47||
O bestower of Brahmanic splendor, O destroyer of the misdeeds of devotees, O annihilator of the sins committed through body, mind, and speech! ||48||
O beautiful maiden, you who were praised by Brahmā and went together with him to the world of truth—O giver of happiness and liberation, be gracious! 49.
"O Aśvapati, recite this hymn and you shall obtain a vision [of me].
Whoever recites this hymn at the three junctions of the day while remembering their mother—"
One obtains the complete fruit of reciting the four Vedas and other scriptures;
[the goddesses] Prabhā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Māṇikyā, Kamalā, and Satī [are attained]. 51.
"Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, she grants her own vision.
Having spoken thus, that best of sages, Parāśara, departed for heaven. (52)
King Aśvapati performed worship with prayers and recitations;
he beheld that Sāvitrī, whose splendor was equal to a thousand suns.
Then, O Lakṣmī, that king worshipped his chosen deity;
she said to him, "I am pleased with you; I know what is in your heart. (54)
"Since your virtuous queen desires a daughter for you, I shall certainly grant her everything she wishes for. (55)
"But you, my son, desire [a son]; in due course, a son shall be born.
Having said this, the Great Goddess vanished and went to the world of Brahmā.
The king, having bowed in that direction, then went to his own abode;
and after not much time had passed, she was born as a daughter. (57)
Resembling the Sun in form and born from the granting of a boon by Savitṛ, she was indeed called Sāvitrī because she was produced with ease. 58.
At the time of his birth, Brahmā arrived together with the gods;
having then showered a rain of flowers, he departed for his own abode. ||59||
For the sake of beholding that young girl, the gods and other celestial beings constantly come with joy to the house of Aśvapati, remaining invisible in form.
The king’s palace shone like Vaikuṇṭha;
and in time, the divine queen, having attained her youth, was resplendent.
In due time, a powerful portion of Brahmā was born as the son of Dyumatsena;
that prince, an ocean of virtues, was known by the name Satyavān. (62)
She chose Satyavān as her boon at the svayaṃvara;
and the king gave her to him, adorned with ornaments made of jewels.
Having led her away according to the rites of marriage, that bridegroom went to his home;
that virtuous woman practiced the duties of domestic life, such as devotion to her husband and so forth.
When the year had passed, Satyavān, by his father’s command,
went to the forest on that fateful day to gather wood for planks.
By the power of her dharma known as devotion to her husband, Sāvitrī, having discerned the time of his death, went after him to the place where her husband had gone.
Satyavān then strove to gather dry wood on the ground;
at that moment, due to a headache, he gave up his life-breaths, and Yama [appeared] to him.
Having bound him and joined him with a subtle body, she went to the abode of Yama;
having preserved that body upon the leaves of trees, the virtuous woman followed after him.
Seeing Sāvitrī, Yama spoke these words consistent with justice:
"Aho! Where are you going, Sāvitrī, a mortal woman yet possessing a physical body?
Or if this virtuous lady desires to come along with her husband,"
"Abandoning this body, come [to me]; for indeed, there is no going with the body. The full time has arrived here for your husband among mortals;
Satyavān goes to my house for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his karma. (1.366.70–71)
The birth of living beings is due to karma, and death also is due to karma;
indeed, they experience pleasure, pain, fear, and grief through their actions. (72)
By action one goes to heaven and proceeds to Satyaloka;
by action one attains lordship, and by action one attains service to Hari.
Through auspicious action, one may attain the fourfold state beginning with Sālokya.
The state of Indra, the state of Vaidhasa, the state of a sage, and the status of the brahmin caste.

The state of being liberated, the state of royalty, the state of a lord of kings, the weighty state of an ascetic, the state of a Kṣatriya, the state of a Vaiśya, the state of a Śūdra, and the state of the lowest caste; ||75||
They attain the state of barbarians, the state of mobile beings, as well as the nature of immobile things;
likewise, the state of mountains, the state of trees, the state of beasts, and the state of birds.
The state of being a worm, or a living creature, or a Gandharva, or a Naga;
the state of being a Rakshasa, a Kinnara, a Kushmanda, or a Yaksha. (77)
The state of a vetāla, the state of a bhūta, the state of a preta, and the state of a piśāca;
the state of a ḍākinī, the state of a daitya, the state of a dānava, and the state of an enemy of the gods (surāri). ||78||
Through their actions, a living being reaches other worlds;
through their actions, a soul becomes meritorious, and likewise, through their actions, it becomes sinful. (79)
One may be handsome, well-formed, and free from disease through one's actions;
likewise, one may be blind, one-eyed, loathsome, or afflicted by a great malady through one's actions.
Truth leads to hell as well as heaven;
likewise, one attains the world of Śakra, the world of the Sun, the world of the Moon, and even beyond.
The world of fire, the world of wind, and also the abode of Varuṇa;
the world of Dhruva, the station of Kubera, and likewise the house of Śiva;
the world of the stars, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Maharloka.
And by their actions, they attain the netherworlds, Vaikuṇṭha, and even Goloka. ||8 3 ||

Furthermore, through their karma, there is both momentary existence and long-lasting existence, as well as life lasting for millions of eons and the like, or even a lifespan that has been exhausted. ||84||
In the womb, death occurs through one's own karma at the mere duration of the soul's transit;
likewise, the death of your husband has arrived through his own karma. (85)
Therefore, Sāvitrī, turning away from my path and according to your pleasure, abandon your desire for your husband and go toward your own home. (86)
Having spoken thus and bowed to Satī, Yama then ceased;
Sāvitrī, however, being devoted to her marital fidelity, did not turn back.
However, O Lakṣmī, he respectfully inquired about that which is to be known— action, inaction, and so forth—
as well as what is auspicious and likewise inauspicious, and the fruit of action.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conversation with King Yama and Other Matters," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives (*pativratāmāhātmya*) in the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. In this chapter, it is related how Sāvitrī obtained a daughter through her worship of [the Sun-god] Sāvitrī from Aśvapati, the ruler of the Madra country; how she was given in marriage to Satyavān; and how, upon Satyavān’s death, Sāvitrī followed the deceased by the power of her devotion to her husband.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, with great devotion, disregarding what was spoken by Yama;
I shall tell you what Sāvitrī asked—understand it from me.
What is auspicious action and what is inauspicious? What is the seed, and who is the giver of the fruit?
By what means and of what nature is action, and what is the cause therein in every respect? (2)
Who indeed experiences the fruit of karma, and who remains untainted? Furthermore, how do virtuous people truly uproot karma? (3)
Who is said to be the agent of action? Who is the body, and who is the embodied one? What is discernment, what is the mind, what is the intellect, and what indeed is the vital breath? (4)
What are the senses and the deities? Who is the enjoyer and who is the one who causes enjoyment? What is enjoyment, and what is its expiation? Who is the self, and who is the supreme Lord? (5)
"O God Yama, if you know all this, tell it to me here.
Having heard this, Yama was exceedingly delighted and spoke to Sāvitrī according to the truth.
Auspicious action, which bestows prosperity and peace as revealed in the Vedas and other scriptures, brings about well-being; that which is contrary to this is certainly not auspicious.
Latent impressions (vāsanā) or even meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) are declared to be the seeds of karma;
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within all, is the one who bestows the fruit.
Through the desire for the auspicious, one performs auspicious action; through the desire for the inauspicious, that very action becomes inauspicious.
Effort is considered the cause of action, while the underlying desire is considered the cause of that effort.
The cause of desire is consciousness, which resides in the individual soul as its objective support;
the cause of knowledge, however, is volition, which is established in the Supreme Lord.
The all-pervading power (vibhvī śakti) joined with Him indeed bestows action and birth;
through the powers of will and knowledge belonging to Hari, the capacities for cognition and action are attributed to the individual soul (jīva).
From those two, all action produced through succession arises;
ultimately, in every respect, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is considered the cause. || 12 ||
The individual soul (jīva) experiences the fruit of its actions, yet the Self (ātman) is not tainted;
indeed, the Inner Controller, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, remains entirely untainted.
The virtuous, being entirely free from attachment to the fruits of their actions,
perform auspicious deeds consisting of service to Viṣṇu day and night.
Whatever is performed without a motive and free from conceptual construction for the pleasure of Hara is indeed of the nature of devotion; it is capable of uprooting all karma. (15)
A devotee of Hari is always liberated; his liberation is considered to be twofold:
liberation while living (jīvanmukti) and liberation into Brahman (brahmamukti), which bestows the state of final extinction (nirvāṇa).
Devotees of Viṣṇu always desire liberation while living in the form of devotion;
virtuous ones desire the supreme liberation of Brahman and service in the divine abode.
That power which impels action is established in Kṛṣṇa;
abiding in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), it unfailingly generates activity.
The body, composed of the five elements, is designated as the gross [body].
That which possesses it—the living being—is always considered to be the knower, conscious, and endowed with knowledge. (1.9)

The comprehension of the twenty-four principles, as well as of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), through their essential natures, qualities, and effects, is called knowledge (jñāna).
Consciousness, which is the seed of all worldly transactions, resides within the Self;
whereas primordial illusion (mūlamāyā), composed of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, is eternally insentient.
She is born in the form of intellect (*buddhi*), in the form of mind (*manas*), and in the form of vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The mind is said to be that which conceives intentions, while the intellect is that which determines. (22)
Breath, vital force, life, function, and abiding together with the principles—
this is proclaimed as the sense-organ (indriya), which is endowed with the power of Indra.
Indra is indeed always declared to be the self (ātman), while the senses are truly many;
for hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell are the givers of knowledge.
The organs of action are indeed speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ;
[their presiding deities are] the quarters, Vāyu, Arka, Pracetas, the Aśvins, Vahni, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Kāma. (25)
The deities were created for the purpose of illumination, and they are the bestowers of power;
the embodied soul is the enjoyer, while Hari himself is the inner self who causes enjoyment.
Experience (bhoga) is defined as the direct perception of pleasure and pain;
likewise, expiation (niṣkṛti), peace (śānti), and cessation (nivṛtti) of karmas are so designated. ||27||
The wise indeed know that ritual acts performed as atonement serve to destroy [the effects of] past actions;
for the rites of expiation are the purifiers of those who came before.

That which is distinct from the subtle body, drawn forth by the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), and experiencing its own state of being while living, is the individual soul (jīvātman), consisting of bliss, existence, and consciousness. 29.
He who is the internal regulator and who abides in the abode of the Imperishable—He is celebrated as this Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (1.367.30)
Indeed, depending upon these five elements— earth, air, space, water, and fire— the living being experiences manifold results.
When he worships Kṛṣṇa, he becomes free from latent impressions;
he becomes free from birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and the like. ||32||
Indeed, there is no other means equal to devotion that is so powerful;
it is the supreme pacifier of all suffering and the bestower of all prosperity. (33)
The Supreme Soul, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari—the bestower of heaven and liberation, the most excellent, who fulfills all prosperity—[is the goal]. (34)
He is the cause of all causes, the lord of the splendors of Rādhā and Lakṣmī,
the master of Pārvatī and Māṇikī, and the sovereign lord of Ramā and Vṛndā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is that Supreme Brahman, the very Śrī Puruṣottama;
devotion to Him must be practiced, for by that, liberation will certainly be attained. (36)
Hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the limbs of Kṛṣṇa’s body, worshiping, praising, serving as a servant, friendship, and total self-surrender. (37)
Thus, yoga in its ninefold form, consisting of devotion, is the bestower of perfect liberation; dharma is like a decoction of medicinal herbs, while dispassion is the purgative. (38)
Awakening is the delightful linctus, and devotion there is the elixir; dharma is the healing medicine that joins one back together, and discernment is the remover of wounds. (39)
Devotion that removes the arrow of pain is the life-giver, as is renunciation;
it is that continuous bond of affection for Hari, preceded by abundant acts of honor.
Devotion should be understood as the giver of liberation; it must always be cultivated by people. One whose heart is free from黏腻 (cikkaṇatva—slime/stickiness) is immersed in intense bliss. 41.
Devotion is to be understood as affection; indeed, that should always be directed toward Hari.
It is an uninterrupted internal state of mind, characterized by a continuous bond of love for Hari. 42.

Devotion, love, attachment, and service toward Hari must indeed be practiced, for they grant liberation; this devotion is of two kinds: that which arises from scriptural injunctions (*vaidhī*) born of the words of the Vedas, and that consisting of the ninefold path beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*). (43)
Endowed with knowledge of His majesty, firm and superior in every respect, attachment, affection, and devotion toward Hari are considered in every way to grant liberation. 44.
Affection for devotees, abandoning hypocrisy toward the image, rejoicing [in their merit], worshiping with a pure mind, and respect for listening to his stories. ||45||
Physical service for that purpose, remembrance of it, and the chanting of its name—these eight are also non-different from devotion and always grant their fruit. (46)
Taking refuge at the feet of the guru, receiving initiation, serving the guru, abiding on the true path through faith, and likewise inquiring about the sublime Dharma. ||47||

The renunciation of enjoyments for the sake of Hari, dwelling in sacred places and other such locations, conducting one's affairs as required, and likewise observing the vow on the day of Hari; ||48||
Hospitality toward deities, trees, and so forth—these ten increase devotion;
as well as freedom from attachment to sons, disciples, and the like, and the avoidance of the company of the wicked. (49)
Abstaining from great undertakings and the like, avoiding ill-founded disputes and such, giving wealth for the sake of Hari, and abandoning grief, delusion, and the rest. || 1.367.50 ||
Not causing distress to others, not censuring gods, gurus, and the like, not committing offenses against the gods, and enduring the censure of the gods. ||51||
These ten should be practiced by devotees for the increase of devotion:
namely, wearing the marks of Kṛṣṇa and the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa’s name within the heart. (52)
Wearing garlands of flowers and the like, dancing, bowing down like a staff, rising up before Hari, and following him when he departs; 53.
Circumambulation, as well as hymn-singing, service, chanting, and recitation;
spiritual realization, the reading of hymns, and tasting the water used for washing the offerings of food (naivedya). (54)
The grasping of the fragrance of the divine grace, the touching, and the beholding of Hari; likewise, the waving of lights before Hari and the witnessing of His festivals. ||55||
Compassion, waiting [for his grace], meditation, remembrance, supreme servitude, friendship, self-surrender, and likewise all activity performed for the sake of Hari; ||56||
The offering of one's dearest [possessions], service to devotees, constant taking of refuge, and the worship of Tulasī, the scriptures, sacred fords, Vaiṣṇavas, and others. ||57||
As is one's wealth, so is one's service; service to the virtuous brings success in livelihood and other matters.
Service rendered in times of distress is the festival of birth for the feet of Hari. ||58||

Through faith comes abundant joy and the supreme savoring of the meaning of the scriptures; association with the virtuous, chanting my names, and always abiding among the virtuous with the virtuous. ||59||
These forty-four qualities, beginning with "abiding in the Self," consist of devotion; they nourish devotion and increase affection. (1.367.60)
One should cultivate the company of the virtuous and always seek the compassion of the virtuous;
likewise, one should have supreme faith in the true dharmas and listen to the virtues of Hari. (61)
The sprouting of the seed of love, taking supreme refuge in the illustrious Hari, the increase of passion for Hari, and the constant manifestation of the vision of Hari’s worship; 62.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the abode of all virtues; constant abiding in dharma for the sake of Hari—these ten qualities, when perfected, cause love to increase exceedingly. (63)
Through the distinctions of sattva and the other [guṇas], and by the divisions of weak, middling, and so forth, there are indeed many subtle varieties of devotion that grant liberation. (64)
Now, that state where no limit to the pinnacle of love exists—that indeed is the eternal devotion which stands supreme above all. (65)
To the extent that the reality of love is nourished by its own nature according to the scriptures, so too is the natural state of embodied beings infinite according to the scriptures. (66)
The reality of love indeed differs in such a way that its number cannot be reached;
therefore, the aesthetic flavor of devotion possesses innumerable varieties and is in full bloom.
The accomplishments of enjoyment, liberation, and so forth, always follow that Great Goddess of Devotion, the Queen, like female servants intent upon her service. (68)
The bliss of Brahmā, multiplied by a hundred million (parārdha), is like a mere atom compared to the bliss of devotion;
indeed, even the joys of Brahmā are but drops in the ocean of the nectar of the bliss of devotion.

For those whose firm devotion, in the form of love, is always directed toward Hari, they indeed become like mere puddles in a cow’s footprint when compared to the one who is overwhelmed by the bliss of divine love.
By practicing devotion attained through the merits accumulated over ten million births, they do not see the destroyer Yama’s abode even in their dreams. (71)
Just as Hari purifies even those who have committed great sins and heinous crimes,
so too enemies, malevolent planets, and Yama’s messengers or Rākṣasas do not cause him any harm.
O spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and others, worship that foremost of gods, the eternal Blessed Lord Hari, who is devoted to his followers. 73.
"Everything you asked has been told; go, my child, as you please.
Having spoken thus and bowed down, O Lotus-born Goddess, Yama indeed ceased speaking. (74)

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Answers Given by King Yama to Sāvitrī’s Questions Concerning Auspicious and Inauspicious Karma and Related Matters, as Well as the Manner and Greatness of Devotion to the Blessed Lord," within the section on the Greatness of the Chaste Wife in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Although addressed in this manner, O Lotus-born One, Sāvitrī did not turn back;
she spoke again to Yama words that were righteous and consistent with the burden of her devotion to her husband.
Having abandoned [all else], where shall I go—[except] to you, my beloved, the Guru who is an ocean of knowledge? A desire to inquire arises; O Lord, grant me the cessation of that [desire]. (2)
O Yama, by what karma does the living being go to which particular womb? By what action does one go to heaven or even to hell, and by what karma is liberation attained? (3)
By what karma does one become healthy or diseased, long-lived or short-lived;
happy or miserable; or have deficient limbs, be one-eyed, blind, or deaf? (4)
By what specific actions is one born as negligent, miserly, deranged, greedy, or a slayer; and by what actions does one indeed attain the supernatural powers? || 5 ||
By what means is the enjoyment of heaven and so forth attained, as well as Vaikuṇṭha and immortality?
And by what means is Goloka, the imperishable [Brahman], and the fourfold state beginning with Sālokya?
How many kinds of hells are there, and who remains in them for how long?
By what karma does such a disease arise in a human being?
"Speak everything as you know it, for it will be of benefit.
Having heard this, Yama spoke this reply to Sāvitrī.
Filled with wonder, Yama said: "O maiden, you are sixteen years of age; from where, O daughter, have you obtained such knowledge?"
