I believe you to be Sāvitrī, the consort of Brahmā,
who in former times attained the status of a mountain-king through asceticism and was united with Aśvapati.
Your knowledge is like that of the ancient sages, the yogis, and the wise;
it is like the Fortune on the lap of the Lord of Fortune, or Lakṣmī upon the chest of Nārāyaṇa.
Just as Rādhā is to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Bhavānī is to Bhava; as Mūrti is upon the chest of Dharma, and Sāvitrī is upon the breast of Brahmā.
She was like Devahūti to Kardama, as Śatarūpā was to Manu;
she was like Aditi to Kaśyapa, and as Arundhatī was to Vasiṣṭha.
As Śacī is to Mahendra, as Ahalyā is to Gautama, as Rohiṇī is to the Moon, and as Rati is to Kāmadeva; || 14 ||
As Svāhā is to the sacrificial fire, as Svadhā is to the ancestors, as Saṃjñā is to the sun, and as the sacrificial fee is to the sacrifice; || 15 ||
Lakṣmī is to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Varuṇānī are to Varuṇa; and as Dharā is to Varāha, so [are they]. || 16 ||
In the month of Kārttika, Devasenā was like Alakṣmī in Uddālaka;
whereas in Patnīvata, she was like the Lakṣmī of a devoted wife in a Brahmin.
Just as Kaṃbharā Lakṣmī resides upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa the cowherd, so too does Jayā reside upon Hari, the Lord of Lalitā and Akṣara. || 18 ||
"O beloved Satyavatī, may you be fortunate and very dear;
thus has this boon been granted to you by me with a gracious mind."
"Choose another boon besides that, O Goddess; I shall grant whatever else you desire.
Having thus seen Yama pleased, the virtuous Lakṣmī spoke to him.
"I choose here that my father-in-law regain his two eyes, so that by Satyavān alone as my son, I may have a hundred sons. (21)
I shall obtain the kingdom, and I shall have a hundred brothers;
this shall come to pass after a hundred thousand years have elapsed, together with Satyavat.
"O Lord, grant me this supreme boon: that I shall go to the abode of Hari.
Furthermore, I wish to hear everything else that I desire to know; please speak of that. (23)
Having heard that, Yama spoke, honoring Sāvitrī greatly:
"O Goddess, everything you desire shall come to pass; so be it. (24)
I shall speak of another matter you wish to know; listen to the ripening of karma.
Whatever I understand, I shall relate to you in brief. (25)
On this earth, human beings here experience the fruits of their auspicious and inauspicious karma, as do the gods, daityas, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and others. (26)
And not all men who generate karma live equally;
all, possessing distinct modes of life, experience the results of their actions within various wombs.
Human beings, in particular, wander through all wombs;
by virtuous action they go to heaven, but indeed to hell by unvirtuous action.
By means of rajasic merit, a human being is born on earth;
by a mass of sattvic merit, one indeed becomes a deity;
and by tamasic sin, one becomes a rākṣasa, a piśāca, or similar beings.
Elementals, ghosts, beasts, birds, trees, and creepers;
insects, moths, snakes, and crawling creatures—these beings are born into eighty-four classes of birth, abounding in suffering. (1.368.30–31)
Those who are predominantly *sattva* are born in the higher realms; those who are *rājasa* arise in the middle; and all those born of inferior wombs are indeed *tāmasa*, arising in the lower regions.
By merit one is born in heaven, and by mere sin, in hell.
Liberation is attained through devotion to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa by means of serving Him with affection. 33.

Through evil action a living being becomes diseased, and through auspicious action one becomes free from disease; through the same, one becomes long-lived or short-lived, happy or miserable—this all arises from the auspicious and the inauspicious. (34)

Those with deficient limbs, such as the blind and others, result from contemptible actions; furthermore, a man becomes blind by injuring another's eyes, or one-eyed (kāṇa) by wounding another's eye. || 35 ||
One who is greedy for hearing the censure of others will certainly be born deaf;
and one who causes distress to others in this world will always be born as a fool.
One who steals another's property shall become poor and destitute;
one who is excessively cruel and a reviler shall be utterly cast down; and one who plunders another's goods and such, having failed to attain the wealth of enjoyments, shall likewise suffer.
This person is born as a killer and a hunter, exceedingly sinful. || 38 ||
One who does not repay his debts certainly takes birth again; there is no doubt about this.
Through the most excellent of rites, one attains accomplishments (siddhi) and other such fruits. || 39 ||
Through charity, a person obtains everything, including the enjoyments of heaven;
through devotion to Viṣṇu, one attains Vaikuṇṭha, and through knowledge, the immortal state.

Through supreme devotion to Kṛṣṇa, one attains Goloka; through the highest knowledge, the Imperishable (Akṣara); and by the grace of Hari, the fourfold states beginning with Sālokya are attained. ||41||
Hell has been described in many ways due to the great variety of karmic actions;
indeed, because the sins are innumerable, the hells are likewise innumerable.
As long as there is sin, the sinner remains there, but upon the exhaustion of that [sin], he does not.

Because they cause suffering to others by burning them from within, diseases overcome that person who inflicts pain upon others. All this has been stated in general; now hear the specific details, O beautiful one. ||43-44||
Among all the human births upon this earth, the birth as a human is difficult to attain;
yet among them, the Brahmins, the virtuous, and the virtuous women are the best—those people who possess devotion.
Indeed, the devotee with desire becomes a practitioner of karma-yoga;
but the desireless devotee, being liberated in Brahman, attains the Supreme. ||46||
There is no returning for those who perform actions free from desire;
however, devotees of Kṛṣṇa go to Goloka on divine two-tusked elephants. Worshippers of Nārāyaṇa go to Vaikuṇṭha on four-tusked elephants.
Those who are devoted to the earth and possess a thousand arms go to that which is called the Immortal.
People established at sacred fords go to Satyaloka, as do ascetics;
those devoted to the Sun go to Ravi, and those who take refuge in Śiva go to Kailāsa.
Those devoted to sacrifice, possessing the latent impressions of their desires, attain the state of Śakra in the heavenly world;
they indeed go to those respective worlds, but return again due to their karma.
Devotees of Hari who are free from desire indeed go to the world of Hari;
for that supreme, imperishable state is from which there is no return.
Deprived of their own dharma and fallen from right conduct, they go to an inferior state;
they undergo the torments of hell and exist among the animal realm. (52)
All those on earth who are devoted to their own duty partake of excellent fruits;
all those devoid of their own duty go to dreadful hells. (53)
The giver of a maiden goes to the world of the Moon for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras;
it is said that the fruit of giving her adorned is twice as great.
Those who give products of the cow, silver, a wife, clothing, grain, fruit, and water,
go to the eternal heaven, enriched with those very things.
But after remaining for a very long time,
those people who give gold, cows, copper, and so forth in this world indeed return again to the earth.
O virtuous lady, they dwell in the world of the sun for ten thousand years;
those who give land and grain dwell in Śvetadvīpa.
One who gives the gift of a house indeed attains the world of the gods;
it is held certain that he shall dwell there for as many years as there are grains of dust in that house. (58)
To whichever deity a person gives a house, he goes to that deity’s world for as many years as there are particles of dust [in the gift], provided it is an excellent one. (59)
In a palace, the merit is fourfold; in a work of public utility (pūrta), the fruit is a hundredfold;
in an excellent one, the merit is eightfold; and in a divine one, the fruit is considered divine.
The builder of a lake goes to Janaloka for ten thousand years;
the fruit for building a step-well is a hundredfold, and for constructing a dam, it is a thousandfold.
A pond measuring four thousand bow-lengths in extent yields a fruit equal to ten ponds when given to a worthy recipient; such is the merit of a maiden [given in marriage].
If one gives [a woman] adorned with ornaments there, the fruit is twofold;
likewise is the fruit when the removal of silt from ponds, wells, tanks, and the like is performed.
One who serves the aśvattha tree and likewise one who plants it goes to the world of Tapas for ten thousand supreme years.
One who gives a flower garden shall dwell eternally for ten thousand years in the realm of Satyaloka;
one who gives a celestial chariot shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of a supreme Manvantara.
One who gives vehicles, mounts, palanquins, or chariots obtains fourfold fruit from a Vaiṣṇava worthy recipient; indeed, it yields supreme happiness. (66)
One who donates swings and other such items shall go to the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of a Manvantara; he who constructs a royal road lined with palaces attains the realm of Indra.
Having enjoyed the earth for ten thousand years, he goes to an auspicious home;
what is given comes back to the giver, and what is not given does not remain with him.
Having enjoyed happiness such as that of heaven, they indeed return again to earth;
here, they obtain birth in an excellent dwelling among superior people.
Whether they be Brahmins, protectors, earners of wealth, or servants,
they always become exactly what they are on earth according to their past actions.
"Whatever has been done here or elsewhere will certainly have to be experienced;
thus I have told you everything. Go, Sāvitrī, do not delay. (71)
Having spoken thus, Yama observed a vow of silence and proceeded slowly ahead;
Sāvitrī also followed slowly behind him, heading toward the abode of Yama.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Auspicious and Inauspicious Destinations According to One’s Karma; Her Own Hundred Sons, the Eyes of Her Father-in-law, and the Obtaining of the Boon that Her Brother Satyavat Would Live for a Hundred Thousand Years," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Seeing Sāvitrī approaching from behind, Yama was struck with wonder;
bowing again to the virtuous lady, he said, "Tell me here, what do you desire?"
Having heard these words of Yama, Sāvitrī questioned him once again; listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you, understand me. (2)
In brief, it should be understood that those possessing merit go specifically to heaven and other worlds by means of such action. (3)
Having asked these questions regarding Sāvitrī, Yama spoke this answer:
"The giver of food is honored in the realm of Indra for nine years."
In this matter, there is no examination of the recipient's worthiness, nor is there any restriction regarding time;
even a person who provides a seat for a god, a Brahmin, or others [is meritorious]. (5)
He rejoices happily for ten thousand years in the world of fire;
for as many sūtras as he has recited, for that many tens of thousands of years he dwells in heaven.
He who gives a milch cow to a god or to a Brahmin is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for as many yugas as there are hairs on the cow's tail.
A gift given on a meritorious day yields fourfold merit; at a sacred ford (tīrtha), the fruit is a hundredfold;
but in the field of Nārāyaṇa, the fruit shall be ten millionfold.
Likewise, one who gives a cow to a Brahmin, to Hari, or to one seeking to perform a sacrifice,
rejoices in the heavenly world of the Moon for ten thousand years.
One who gives a cow that has just given birth to a calf and possesses two faces shall rejoice happily in Vaikuṇṭha for as many years as there are hairs on its body.
One should indeed give a Śālagrāma stone, along with ornaments and other gifts, to its worshiper;
the donor rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the moon and sun endure.
The giver of an umbrella rejoices in the abode of Varuṇa for ten thousand years; the giver of sandals is honored in the world of Vāyu for ten thousand years.
One who gives a bed rejoices in the lunar world (Cāndra-loka), where his lifespan is equal to that of the moon;
likewise, one who gives a lamp to a Brahmin or to Hari, and provides oil or ghee [for it].
For as long as a manvantara, he too is honored in the world of Brahmā;
he shall possess divine vision, and blindness shall never arise for him.
The giver of an elephant dwells perpetually on half of Indra’s throne;
the giver of a horse, O virtuous one, shall indeed remain for a kalpa in the realm of Varuṇa.
One who gives a palanquin is honored in the world of Viṣṇu for a manvantara;
one who gives a chowrie or a fan is honored in the world of Vāyu.

One who gives grain dwells for ten thousand years in the world of Viṣṇu, equal in merit to one who gives a single grain; this person, moreover, who chants the name of Śrī Hari, dwells there eternally.
The great death flees from him, and he becomes long-lived;
that man on earth who swings Lord Hari upon a swing. (18)
He who causes a swing for the Lord to be made during the great festival of the vow,
having enjoyed happiness as one liberated while living, goes at the end to the abode of Viṣṇu.
One shall dwell there in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a hundred manvantaras;
the fruit of [worshipping] Uttaraphalgunī shall be twice that even more.
He shall live until the end of the eon, becoming an abode of all prosperity and virtues; as a giver of sesame seeds, he rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are sesame seeds.
By the gift of sesame seeds in a copper vessel, one shall indeed obtain double the fruit;
the giver of a maiden shall certainly dwell in the world of the Moon for one kalpa.
One who gives a maidservant in the Gāndharva marriage rejoices for ten thousand years;
he also obtains a virtuous wife endowed with good fortune for a thousand births. ||23||
One who plants fruit-bearing trees is honored in the world of Śakra;
on earth, he becomes a wealthy householder, possessed of sons and accompanied by beautiful women.
The giver of fruit dwells for a long time in heaven, which brings great happiness;
the giver of wealth, grain, and houses shall dwell in the abode of Kubera.
Thereafter, for the duration of a manvantara, he is born as a wealthy man on earth,
in a sacred field, to a worthy recipient, as one who has bestowed fields rich with grain upon a virtuous person.
He rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for a hundred manvantaras,
and thereafter he becomes once again on earth a person of great fortune, endowed with prosperity, sons, and wealth.
A woman who possesses cows shall be happy for a hundred supreme births;
moreover, she should give land with offspring and a village to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
For a hundred thousand manvantaras, the donor is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha;
on earth, he is born as the king of a hundred thousand villages for a hundred thousand births. (29)
He who gives a field or a city that is populated, highly cultivated, endowed with crops such as sugarcane, and provided with ponds and wells; || 1.369.30 ||
He is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha for ten lakhs of Indrajīvas; on earth, he is born as a lord of a hundred thousand cities, a king of kings. ||3 1||
He who gives a hundred cities as a gift to Viṣṇu is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of ten million manvantaras.
Then he certainly becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, the earth does not abandon him even for ten million births.
He shall become a great lord of the kings of kings, living for the duration of an eon;
as the bestower of his own authority, he shall obtain fourfold the fruit. ||34||
The giver of Jambūdvīpa shall obtain tenfold the fruit [of other gifts],
as compared to one who gives the earth consisting of seven continents and serves all sacred fords.
Of one who performs all austerities, who observes all fasts, who gives all other gifts, and who likewise possesses all perfections; ||| 36 ||
O wonder! For the devotee of Hari there is indeed no return;
the Vaiṣṇavas behold the passing away of countless Brahmās while they remain. (37)
Those residing in Goloka, those dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, those who have gone to the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāma),
and even those situated in the supreme abode (Para-dhāma)— they all behold this return once again.
But one who worships the mantra of Hari, having cast off the human body and become divine in form like Hari himself, goes to the abode of Hari. (39)
The devotees of Kṛṣṇa residing in Goloka and the Vaiṣṇavas residing in Vaikuṇṭha,
having attained the same form as Kṛṣṇa and also that of Nārāyaṇa— 40.
Those who perform service to these two indeed attain the dissolution of the unmanifest primordial nature;
even the gods, the lords, the perfected ones (siddhas), and all that exists in the universe perish.
The devotees of Hari do not perish; they remove birth, death, and old age.
In the month of Kārtika, one who offers a multitude of tulasī leaves to Hari [attains this]. (42)
He who indeed offers a ghee lamp to Hari during the month of Kārtika rejoices in the abode of Hari for as many years as there are leaves in that lamp.
He rejoices in the abode of Hari for a year equal in measure to a *pala*;
if, by the will of Hari, he returns to the creation, he becomes a devotee of the Lord (*bhāgavata*).
One who is immensely wealthy, possessed of vision, radiant, and full of devotion—whether he be a teacher, an incarnation, or a partial manifestation of Him—shall be a bestower of liberation. (45)
He who bathes in the Gaṅgā or other holy fords at dawn during the month of Māgha rejoices in the abode of Hari by the will of Hari for sixty thousand yugas.

In all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), he becomes a supreme teacher, a devotee, and one who has conquered his senses—namely, he who performs the morning ritual bath in the Gaṅgā at Prayāga during the month of Māgha. ||47||
He too rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a hundred thousand manvantaras;
indeed, at the creation by Nārāyaṇa, he shall become a supreme teacher (deśikendra).
Having cast off that human body, he returns once more to the abode of Hari;
indeed, for one who has gone to the abode of Hari, there is no returning again.
Having attained sā rūpya (the state of having the same form as Hari), he performs service to Hari;
indeed, by bathing daily in the Gaṅgā, he gains at every step the merit born of a horse-sacrifice.
And having attained the fruit [of his merit], he becomes purified; in the presence of that virtuous one, he is born like the sun.
By the dust of his very feet, the earth is instantly sanctified. (51)
He rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha as long as the moon and sun endure;
through the grace of Nārāyaṇa, he shall become an ascetic preceptor upon this earth. ||52||
He who gives water at the beginning of the summer season goes to Vaikuṇṭha for a kalpa;
and he who indeed offers sandalwood paste and other gifts to Hari in the month of Vaiśākha [attains the same]. (53)
For sixty thousand yugas he rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu;
and one who gives parched grain in Vaiśākha likewise rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Then, for a period of years equal in measure to the dust particles of the sesame seeds, by the will of Viṣṇu,
he becomes an ascetic preceptor in the world, the most excellent among those who deliver others.
He who observes the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī in the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādra becomes purified at that very moment from the sins committed throughout a hundred lifetimes.
By the will of Kṛṣṇa, one rejoices in Goloka; likewise, one becomes a devotee of Kṛṣṇa by observing the Janmāṣṭamī of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika.
He who performs [this] with devotion goes to the abode of Hari;
he becomes a servant of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for infinite time. (58)
And he who performs the Śivarātri vow and offers a bilva leaf obtains all his desires when they are offered to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (59)
And for the measure of a pair of yugas, he rejoices in the abode of Śiva;
he becomes possessed of knowledge, sons, prosperity, progeny, and likewise abundant land.
By the will of Śiva, he indeed remains for the duration of seven manvantaras;
having become happy during the great creation, he shall go to the abode of Śiva.
In the months of Caitra and Māgha, one should worship Śambhu and perform dancing before Him for a month,
or half a month, or for ten, seven, or even five days.
He too is honored in the world of Śiva for as many days as there are years;
so it is for the devotee who, as a practitioner of vows, observes the rite of Śrī Rāmanavamī.
He rejoices in the abode of Rāma for the duration of seven manvantaras;
then, indeed becoming a devotee of Rāma, he stands in the position of a teacher.
Through devotion to Rāma, he indeed goes to the second Vaikuṇṭha;
on the full moon day of the autumn season, he performs the worship of Hari and Hara.
He who, as a devoted lord, performs worship endowed with many services, using food offerings, ritual gifts, and likewise incense, lamps, and so forth; ||66||
With dances, songs, musical instruments, and various wonderful auspicious rites,
[the people] shall dwell in the world of Hari and Śambhu for the duration of seven manvantaras.
Furthermore, having become pure and devoted, he shall attain prosperity;
endowed with great power and accompanied by elephants and horses,
he will undoubtedly become a lord of the kings of kings, possessed of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Having reached the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, one should worship Mahālakṣmī.
By means of devotion through the sixteen matters, one goes to Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a kalpa;
thereafter, he shall indeed become a Sāttvata, the sovereign lord of kings upon this earth.
He who performs the Rāsa-maṇḍala on the full moon day of Kārtika, having fashioned two hundred Gopīs and two hundred Gopas out of gold; 71.
Having had an image of Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa made, one should worship it with various offerings as they may be obtained; such a worshipper goes to Goloka. (72)
Having remained there for the duration of Brahmā's lifespan, he proceeds to the creation;
then, having again performed devotion to Kṛṣṇa and obtained a mantra of Hari from him, [he returns].
Having attained a form similar to Kṛṣṇa, he becomes an attendant;
he dwells eternally in Goloka, free from rebirth. ||74||
The observer of the Ekādaśī vow goes to Vaikuṇṭha for as long as the lifespan of the Creator lasts; thereafter, he returns once again to the earth.
Furthermore, a devotee of Hari goes to Vaikuṇṭha and shall not fall again;
so too the person who worships Śakra on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.
For sixty thousand years, he is honored in the world of Śakra on Sundays, at the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), and on the seventh day of the bright fortnight. ||77||
The giver of sacrificial food (haviṣya) goes to the world of the Sun for a kalpa;
returning again to the earth, he shall be free from disease and endowed with prosperity.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship you as Sāvitrī;
he rejoices in the world of Brahmā for the duration of seven manvantaras.
Furthermore, he who worships Sarasvatī on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha shall become endowed with fortune upon this earth and possessed of the perfection of knowledge.
That wise man is honored in Vaikuṇṭha for one kalpa;
furthermore, the giver of cows and gold attains twice the number of hairs on a cow's body in the realm of Hari.
Afterwards, he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha, and then becomes a devotee of Viṣṇu on earth—
a lord of the kings of kings, possessing cattle, and endowed with learning, knowledge, sons, and other blessings.
He who feeds the virtuous, the holy, noble women, Brahmins, and likewise guests,
rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu for as many years as there are hairs on the body of the one who ate.
Having come here, he who gives the name of Hari becomes happy, illustrious, long-lived, and valiant; he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. (84)
By chanting ten million times the name, one attains enlightenment and is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, he attains eternal union with Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha.
A worshiper of Śiva goes to Śiva, who is as vast as the dust raised by Bāṇa;
having remained on Kailāsa for ten thousand ages, he shall become an emperor upon the earth.
The devotee who worships the Śālagrāma and consumes its prasāda is glorified in Vaikuṇṭha; indeed, he shall go there for a hundred cycles of Brahmā.
Furthermore, having become a king on earth, he goes to Vaikuṇṭha and shall not fall;
one who performs austerities, vows, and other observances goes to Vaikuṇṭha for the duration of a kalpa.
Having been a lord of kings upon the earth, he shall indeed be liberated thereafter;
performing the horse-sacrifice, he shall dwell upon half the throne of Śakra.
In the Rājasūya sacrifice, the duration is four times the number of years represented by the hairs on a horse;
in the Naramedha, it is half that of the Aśvamedha; and in the Gomedha, it is likewise seen to be the same.
In the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, however, it shall be half of that; in the Lāṅguleṣṭi, the fruit born of the Gomedha sacrifice occurs;
and in the Vipreṣṭi and the Vṛddhi-yāga, the fruit shall be that born of the Gomedha.
In the Padmeṣṭi, however, it is half of that; in the Viśokeṣṭi, it is born of freedom from sorrow (viśoka);
in the Vijayeṣṭi, it is equal to the lotus; and in the Prājāpatya, it is likewise the same.
In the Ṛddhi-yāga, there is great sovereignty; and in the Viṣṇu-yāga, there is the Vaiṣṇava [attainment].
The devotee shall obtain meritorious status and the eternal world of Viṣṇu. || 93 ||
O beautiful one, the sacrifice to Viṣṇu is the foremost among all sacrifices;
there is no sacrifice superior to the sacrifice to Viṣṇu that bestows such excellent fruit.
The author of that [work] shall live for many kalpas and be liberated in this world;
moreover, by means of knowledge and splendor, he shall even become equal to Viṣṇu.
By a hundred horse-sacrifices alone, the status of Śakra is attained in heaven;
by a thousand, King Pṛthu reached the station of Viṣṇu.

Service to the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is superior in its fruit to visiting sacred fords, performing sacrifices, practicing austerities, studying the Vedas, and observing vows; it bestows liberation.
The description, meditation, worship, chanting, devotion, hymn of praise, remembrance, salutation, and recitation of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa alone. || 98 ||
Worship Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the highest of the high, whose consumption of the nectar-offerings at His feet bestows all that is desired. 99.
"Take a husband, O child; go happily to your own home.
Having spoken thus, O Lotus-born One, Yama remained silent.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Various Kinds of Fruitful Answers Given by Yama to the Questions Regarding the Fruits of Actions Asked by Sāvitrī," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard the greatness of devotion to Hari, Satī again asked Yama: "By what method should Hari himself be worshipped? (1)
Having heard Sāvitrī, Yama spoke these words that grant excellent liberation:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you how Yama spoke to the virtuous lady."
Having risen in the morning, one should remember Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in the heart;
one should meditate upon his form and contemplate it again and again as having a gentle appearance.
During bathing, purification, ritual acts, external and internal duties,
eating, recreation, sleeping, and household chores, one should remember Hari.
With supreme faith, one should joyfully unite all the senses as well as the internal organs toward Śrī Hari in that manner.
While drinking, sitting, sleeping, in slumber, or while waking in succession;
whether in auspicious or inauspicious action, Hari should always be remembered.
The tongue should perform its chanting of his praises; the ear should practice its hearing of him;
the eye should perform its beholding of him; and the nose should experience his fragrance.
The skin should perform the act of touching him; the hand should perform the service of his feet;
the foot should go to his temple; and speech should perform his worship.
The impure vital energy (malamūtrendriya), for the purpose of destroying obstacles, shall attain the state of a quality;
having attained bliss from Śrī Hari, one should practice meditation upon Śrī Hari.
One should perform the determination, the honoring, and the contemplation of Śrī Hari alone;
thus, one should do everything for Hari alone and not for anyone else.
One should perform [this] neither for one's own sake nor for the sake of others, but solely for the sake of Hari;
by doing so, one will before long attain the state of Hari’s abode.
Thus addressed, Sāvitrī, recognizing Yama as the supreme bestower of boons, spoke the eight verses on Yama; listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell them to you.
Formerly, at the Puṣkara tīrtha, Nārāyaṇa performed penance for the sake of the Sun.
I bow to that son Dharmāśa, whom he obtained, the King of Dharma. || 1.3 ||
Salutations to that God who brings about peace for the sake of pacification, having ordained the end of the experience of karma for all living beings.
I bow to that Kṛtānta, who brings about the end of all embodied beings through the proper application of justice for the deeds they have committed. (15)

Salutations again and again to you, the wielder of the rod of punishment, who metes out justice to sinners and bears that rod which bestows purification; salutations to you, the king who applies the principles of policy according to the scriptures.
I bow to that god in the form of Time, who effects the determination of all material affairs and the reckoning of all lifespans. 17.
I indeed bow down to that Yama, who restrains all living beings in every way by the infliction of punishments, bestowing fruits in accordance with their actions. 18.
Just as the action was, so is the giver, neither out of passion nor out of anger;
therefore, I bow to the Friend who brings about purification, the Friend of all. (1.9)
I bow to that Brāhma, who was born in ancient times from the form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and who was produced from a portion of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated before him, and Yama became truly pleased.
For one who recites the *Yamāṣṭaka*, there shall be no fear of Yama.
Through the manifestation of his body, his purification from karmas arises;
he is released from the noose of Yama, so says the King of Dharma.
Yama, having bestowed the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon her, [she] prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa three times, saying: "Oṃ. ||23||
And Yama himself spoke to her regarding the impure ripening of karma:
"By means of evil action, a person goes to hells that are exceedingly terrible. (24)
Furthermore, the pits of the hells are of various kinds;
they are indeed vast, deep, and cause fear and affliction. (25)
There are eighty-six terrible and loathsome pits in Saṃyamanī; learn their names. ||26||
The fire-pit, the boiling-pit, the terrifying pit of decay, the pit of feces, the pit of urine, and the unbearable pit of phlegm. ||27||
The pit of flesh, the pit of burning, the great pit of fat, as well as the pit of semen, the pit of blood, and the loathsome pit of tears. (28)
The pit of impurity, the pit of vigor, the pit of passion, which produces foul odors;
the fierce pit of ear-wax, and the painful pit of nail-dirt. (203)
The pit of marrow, the pit of flesh, and the pit of bones, which bestow suffering;
the pit of body hair, the pit of afflictions, and the great pit of copper and iron.
The pit of sharp thorns, the burning pit of poison, the pit of heat, the pit of heated liquor, and the pit of scorpions. ||31||
There was a pit of boiling oil and a pit of ivory that causes obstacles;
there was a pit of worms, a pit of pus, and a terrifying pit of serpents.
The pit of gadflies and mosquitoes, the pit of sharp-pointed vajras, the pit of arrows, the pit of spears, and the pit of swords which is truly destructive. (33)
The pit of the lizard, the pit of the crocodile, the terrifying pit of the crow, the pit of friction, the pit of powder, the pit of bondage, and the pit without refuge. (34)
The pit of heated stones, the pit of sharp-edged rocks, the pit of saliva, the pit of swords, the pit of powder, and the pit of crushing. (35)

The Cakra-pit (Wheel-pit), the Vajra-pit (Thunderbolt-pit), the Kūrma-pit (Tortoise-pit) which is most formidable, the Jvālā-pit (Flame-pit), the Bhasma-pit (Ash-pit), and the terrifying Pūti-pit (Putrid-pit). ||36||
The heated iron pillar, the sword-blade forest, the razor-edge, the needle-mouthed hell, the pit of lizards, the world-biting hell, and the flattened-helmet hell. (37)
Kumbhīpāka, Kālasūtra, Adhaḥkandhara, Ugraka, Pāṃśubhojya, Pāśakaṇṭha, Śūlaprota, and Sukīlaka. ||38||
The fire-mouthed pit, the blind well, piercing, flogging with a staff, binding with nets, the pulverization of the body, crushing, and causing desiccation—[these are the tortures]. (39)
The pit filled with the flames of serpents, the one blinded by the smoke of venom, the noose of the Nāgas,
the pit of duplicity, and also the salt-pit.
Also Bhaguprapātana, Vaitaraṇīprapātana, Carmotkartanakuṇḍa, and Bhrāṣṭrakaṭāha. ||41||
"O Sāvitrī, these are indeed the pits that purify evildoers;
they cause suffering only to sinners and are guarded by the followers of Yama. (42)
[He was surrounded] by those with staffs in their hands, and those holding tridents, nooses, spears, and lances;
who were intoxicated with pride, characterized by darkness (tamas), merciless, and coppery-brown in hue.
Assuming various forms, they are visible to sinners yet unassailable by them;
they are invisible to those who have performed meritorious deeds, as well as to righteous yogis.
Listen: for whom does residence exist, and where is there a staff-like presence in the bowl?
Through harsh speech and wickedness, he burns his own kinsmen. (45)
He enters a fire-pit whose duration in years is equal to the number of hairs on his body;
having burned away his sins in the fire, he shall obtain three more births as an animal.
He who does not feed a guest who has come to his house, nor likewise one dependent upon him,
shall indeed remain in the Lomamāna Samāstapta Kuṇḍa.
In a desert region of a hot land, he may become a bird for seven births on Sundays, during the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti), on new moon days, or on the day of a śrāddha ceremony. 48.
He who destroys insects residing in cloth by means of alkaline substances during a religious vow indeed goes to the Kṣārakuṇḍa hell for as many years as there were threads [in the cloth]. (49)
O beautiful one, he who seizes a livelihood— whether given by himself or given by another— shall enter the womb of a king for seven births.
For sixty thousand years he goes to Viṭkuṇḍa;
for sixty thousand years he is a worm that feeds on excrement, eating feces there.
He who destroys a pond goes to Mūtrakuṇḍa;
thereafter, on earth, he becomes one who drinks urine for as many years as there are particles of dust in that pond.
For seven births he shall be a lizard dwelling in a wall within a house;
then, eating sweets all alone, he goes for a hundred years to the pit of phlegm.
One who eats phlegm becomes a preta that drinks urine, pus, and the like;
[one who abandons] father, mother, wife, teacher, daughter, son, or friends [becomes such a being]. (54)
He who does not nourish the destitute goes to the Kṣveḍakuṇḍa hell;
there he eats that [excrement] for a thousand years, and thereafter remains a preta for a hundred years.
If one looks upon a guest with a cruel disposition, the ancestors and the gods do not accept the water and the funeral cakes; from that, the destruction of the lineage shall occur.
Furthermore, those slayers are cast into the Pit of Filth (malakuṇḍa);
there they subsist on filth for a hundred years, and thereafter, for seven births, [they remain so].
One becomes poor, miserable, and falls at every step;
for that which was given as a gift to one person is then bestowed upon another. (58)
One who eats fat goes indeed to Vasākuṇḍa for a hundred years;
for three births he becomes a Cāṇḍāla, and for seven births a lizard.
Consequently, that man or woman who commits such a sin shall become poor and short-lived;
they shall [lose] their own semen or menses to one another.
If he makes her drink it out of lust, he goes to the Śukra-kuṇḍa;
and for one hundred years he eats that [semen], remaining a worm in a womb for a hundred years.
Furthermore, he who strikes one worthy of worship, or his teacher, or likewise his parents,
and causes blood to flow, goes to the formidable Pit of Blood.
For a hundred years he becomes a consumer of blood, and thereafter he is born as a hunter;
having committed sins for seven lifetimes, he shall again go [to such a state].
He who laughs at a devotee who is weeping, singing,
or dancing before Kṛṣṇa, becomes a tear-pit (aśrukuṇḍa) by making sport of him.
For one hundred years, he shall subsist on tears and become a Cāṇḍāla for three births;
thereafter, the wicked person goes to the hell Gātramalakuṇḍa for ten years.
He who laughs at, reviles, or even mocks a deaf person as a joke shall become a donkey for three births and a monkey for three births, enduring great suffering.
He goes to the pit of earwax and remains there for a hundred years, feeding upon that;
thereafter, he is deaf for seven births and lacks limbs for seven more.
But he who kills one that provides a livelihood goes to Majjākuṇḍa;
for a hundred thousand years he eats its marrow, and for seven births he is born as a hare. (68)
Seven fish and seven deer are born from that; then one becomes pure.
Those who sell their daughters go to a most dreadful pit of flesh. (69)
Those eaters of flesh, struck down by Yama for as many years as there are hairs on a maiden's body,
being tormented by hunger, devour their own flesh and blood from their heads.
For sixty thousand years he becomes a worm among those who lust after virgins;
then, for seven births, he is a hunter, then a boar, and then a dog.
For seven births, that person who does not have the ritual shaving performed according to the prescribed rules shall become a frog, a leech, and even a crow. (72)
One who eats fingernails goes indeed to Nakha-kuṇḍa for a period of ten thousand years;
likewise, one who eats body hair, having been beaten, goes to Roma-kuṇḍa.
Whosoever worships the earthly Liṅga with its hair shall indeed go to Keśakuṇḍa for a period of one hundred human years consisting of particles of dust.
From that, indeed, a Yavana is born on earth for a hundred years;
one who fails to offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to his ancestors falls into the fierce Ulbaṇa-kuṇḍa.
Furthermore, he who serves a woman in her full menses or one who is pregnant and about to give birth will be lame and utterly destitute for seven lifetimes. (76)
He who eats the food of a woman in her menses remains for a hundred years in a cauldron of molten copper; he remains for a hundred years in an iron cauldron.
Having fallen into the womb of a king’s servant and seven births as a leather-worker,
he is born thereafter as one with great sores and poverty, after which he becomes pure.
And he who applies sweat from his hands, heated by the sun's heat, to the property of the gods, shall indeed remain in the pit of scorching heat for a duration of one hundred years. ||79||
And the drinker of liquor goes for a hundred years into a pit of hot liquor;
thereafter, he becomes a Śūdra, utterly destitute, for seven births.
She who speaks harsh words to her husband falls into a pit of sharp thorns and is beaten there by messengers; she remains there for the duration of four yugas.
Thereafter, one is born as a donkey on earth for seven lifetimes;
indeed, a giver of poison remains in a pit of poison for a thousand years.
One who eats poison and one who kills a human shall be born as a lizard for seven lifetimes;
for seven lifetimes he shall also be afflicted with leprosy, and thereafter he is born purified.
He who, as the controller of that bull, strikes his servant with a staff,
shall remain in a cauldron of boiling oil for the duration of four yugas.
Then, for a year measured by the hair of a cow, he becomes a bull upon the earth;
[he is bound] with a hook, a spear, a tusk, and a stake. (85)
He who kills a bull, or any other embodied living being with iron,
shall indeed dwell in Kuntakuṇḍa for ten thousand years.
From that, the person who eats forbidden food is born with the disease of dropsy in one lifetime;
indeed, such a man goes to the pit of worms.
At the end of a human year measured by his own body hair, a barbarian on earth passes through three births;
due to his sins, he who eats food from the sky goes to the pit of pus for a hundred years.
Then, for seven births, that Śūdra shall bear an intense colic;
as a slayer of snakes, he goes to the serpent-pit and is devoured by a snake.
After consuming snake dung, he is indeed born as a snake upon the earth;
thereafter, having a very short lifespan, he likewise becomes afflicted with the disease of ringworm (dadru).
His death is by a serpent, and his consumption is considered to be by a serpent;
he kills living beings, and that evildoer falls into the hell named Daṃśa. ||91||
Having lived for a lifespan of one year among thousands of small creatures, he is born again and again, and thereafter he will certainly become deformed in his limbs. (92)
A killer of bees, a destroyer of bees, shall fall into a pit of glowing coals;
having remained there for a period equal to his own lifespan in days, he shall attain birth in the womb of a bee.
One who inflicts punishment on those who do not deserve it shall certainly fall into the Vajrakīṭa hell;
having remained there for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall become a worm upon the earth.
A king who acquires wealth through unjust means shall fall into the Kuṇḍaka hell like a scorpion;
having experienced suffering for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he remains a scorpion for seven lifetimes. (95)
Then that person shall become deficient in limbs and afflicted by disease upon the earth;
indeed, a Brahmin devoid of dharma falls thereafter into the Śara-kuṇḍa.
Pierced by an arrow, one remains for a year equal to the number of hairs on one's body and thereafter becomes pure;
likewise, a person imprisons innocent living beings in a prison. (97)
He falls for as many years as there are hairs on his body into a pit of boiling water filled with globules;
thereafter, pierced by insects, he is indeed born on earth as a lowly servant.
The slayer of crocodiles and fish then falls into a pit of crocodiles; having remained there for as many years as there are scales on a crocodile's body, he then becomes a crocodile in the water. 99.
But he who seeks out another's faults falls instead into Kākakuṇḍa;
there, with eyes crushed by crows, he remains for a hundred years of hair-growth.
He who steals gold, copper, or iron becomes impoverished for seven births and is born blind for three births; indeed, such a thief of diamond enters the Vajrakuṇḍa hell.
Even one who misappropriates the property of the gods shall dwell in a pit of vajras for as many years as there are hairs on his body;
struck there by vajras, he becomes a consumer of vajras, his body aflame.
The thief of cows, parrots, or images falls into the pit known as Taptopala for as many years as there were hairs on his body; thereafter, he becomes a crow for three births.

Then he was a swan, then a Śaṅkhacilla bird, and then one afflicted with diseases such as blood disorders; for seven births he had a short lifespan, and even as a thief of water-pots he was of that same nature.

A thief of brass, bronze, and the like, having been cast into a vessel of sharp-edged stones, shall dwell there for a year equal to his own lifespan; thereafter, he shall become a horse for seven births.
From that [sin], one is born with redundant limbs, hunchbacked, and with a diseased foot;
by eating the food of an unchaste woman and living off her, one will certainly fall into the Lālākuṇḍa hell.
One who eats from a vessel made of a child's skull suffers for as many years as there are hairs on his body; he becomes afflicted with eye disease and colic.
One who serves barbarians or one who uses ink as a penance falls into the intensely heated Maṣīkuṇḍa hell.
Thereafter, he shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body; then, for three births, he becomes a black beast, and for three births each, a goat, a serpent, and a palmyra tree.
A thief of grain, betel, bedding, offerings, seats, crops, and so forth, shall indeed dwell for a hundred years in the Cūrṇakuṇḍa hell; thereafter, he becomes a ram and then a cock.
Then, throughout three births, that man shall be afflicted by cough and disease;
he shall be deprived of lineage, impoverished, short-lived, and full of suffering.
One who manufactures wheels, weapons, and the like, however, remains in a pit for a hundred years;
thereafter, through three births, he becomes an oil-presser, diseased, and then deprived of his lineage.
One who is competitive and envious shall fall into the Vajrakuṇḍa hell for a yuga;
for seven births he shall have deformed limbs and be deprived of a wife and lineage.
One who eats the flesh of tortoises and other such creatures shall fall into the Kūrma-kunda for a hundred years;
for three lifetimes, he shall be a tortoise, then a pig, and then a peacock.
Furthermore, a thief of ghee, oil, and other such substances is born as a cat for three successive lifetimes, and [is cast] into a pit of flames or into ashes.
One who drinks oil falls into a pit for a hundred years, and for seven births becomes a fish and then a mouse; after that, one becomes pure.
One who steals substances such as fragrant oils, nurses, or attendants will, after a year, be born as one with foul-smelling body hair in a foul-smelling pit. Thus it is said. (1.16)
For seven births he was foul-smelling, for three births he was musk, and for seven births he was fragrant; thereafter, indeed, he became a pure human being.
The usurper of land shall then fall upon the heated spike and into boiling oil;
thereafter, for seven manvantaras, he shall become a dung-worm for sixty thousand years.
Deprived of his status and rendered poor, he indeed becomes pure after that; however, a killer of a human being shall dwell in the Sword-Leaf Hell for an eon, and thereafter [suffer] again.
If a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa lives for a hundred Manvantaras in a forest of swords,
his limbs will be severed by sword-blades, and he shall become a Cāṇḍāla for a hundred births.
He is born as a pig, a dog, a jackal, a tiger, and then a wolf; thereafter, he is born as a gaṇḍī and a buffalo, each for seven births. (121)

One who sets fire to a village and the like shall fall upon the edge of a razor for three eons; thereafter, he becomes a preta with a mouth of fire, feeding on impurities, and then once again [the same].
For that duration, he becomes a firefly for seven births and then suffers from a great piercing pain; thereafter, having been afflicted with leprosy for seven births, the giver of fire is purified.
One who is defamatory and a slanderer shall dwell in the Sūcimukha hell for three yugas;
thereafter, he shall become a scorpion and a serpent for seven births.
A Vajrakīṭa worm becomes a Saptajana; from there, a Bhasmakīṭa, and then a human being.
One who breaks into houses, a thief, or one who kills cows, iguanas, rams, or goats [attains these states]. 125.
For seven births each, the man shall be diseased and incapable of bearing burdens;
then he becomes a thief of wealth with the face of a crocodile for a yuga, and thereafter he is afflicted by disease.
One who kills a cow, an elephant, a horse, or a human shall suffer three ages of existence as an elephant and a gadfly;
thereafter, they shall undergo three births in those respective species, and after that, they shall become a mleccha.
One who causes suffering to the bovine species certainly goes to the Gomukha hell;
having remained there for a manvantara in the Kṛmitaptodaka hell, he becomes a bull.
Then, for seven births, he becomes a sick man, a pauper, and one of the lowest caste;
likewise, he who has committed the murder of a cow, a Brahmin, or a virtuous person, or who has killed a woman, a friend, or an embryo.
He shall fall into the Kuṃbhīpāka hell for a kalpa and be pulverized by the messengers of Yama;
likewise, he shall be cast for a moment into fire, into a heated pit, into boiling oil, and into water.
He certainly experiences sufferings upon stones and heated iron;
for a hundred lifetimes he is a boar, and for thousands of millions of lifetimes he is a vulture. (131)
For seven births he shall be a crow, for seven births a serpent;
then he becomes a worm in excrement, a low-born man, and one afflicted with oozing leprosy.
Afflicted by consumption, deprived of his lineage, and then bereft of his wife,
he became pure in heart toward Śrī Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa, the Infinite One.

One who creates a sense of duality regarding Vāsudeva, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā should be understood as a committer of the murder of a Brāhmaṇa; for such duality is considered equal to that very murder.
He who perceives a distinction between the Imperishable (Akṣara), Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, the embodiment of Ramā, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Māṇikyā—[is ignorant]. 1.35.
One who creates a division between Lalitā and Jayā, or between one's own guru, one's chosen deity, father, or mother, incurs a fault equal to that of killing a Brahmin. (136)
The perception of duality regarding the hymn to Hari is like the sin of killing a Brahmin;
likewise, one is considered devoid of the merit of offering water used for washing Viṣṇu’s food.
Likewise, he is considered a reviler even if he censures the worship of ancestors, gods, and gurus;
those who slay Brahmins censure Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śivā, and Lakṣmī. (138)

Those who revile the birth-anniversary days of Hari, the lunar day sacred to Śiva, Ekādaśī, and the days of religious vows, are indeed perpetrators of the sin of killing a Brahmin. [Likewise, those who revile] their guru, mother, father, virtuous wife, son, or daughter...

He who does not nourish those dependent upon him is indeed a committer of the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā). He who fails to honor the gods, who strikes bulls and other sacred animals, and who destroys their pasture grounds and so forth, is indeed a committer of the sin of killing a Brahmin. (1.370.140–141)
One who causes suffering to cows incurs the same sin as that born from killing a cow;
likewise, so does he who deprives cows of their livelihood or strikes them with his foot. (142)

One who lives off the wives [of others], who neglects the three daily prayers and other rites, and who destroys the Dharma, is considered a killer of cows if he fails to serve the gods, the ancestors, and guests. (143)
But she who creates a sense of division between her own husband and Kṛṣṇa, and strikes her beloved with harsh words, is considered a committer of cow-slaughter. (144)
He who destroys the pasture, the livelihood, the water, the dwelling, or the shelter of cows shall certainly incur the sin of cow-slaughter.
Likewise [he who destroys] the water, food, or flowers intended for the worship of the gods.
Whoever should step over them with his feet is indeed a committer of the sin of killing a cow.
One who speaks falsely, one who hates his teacher, one who hates the gods, and one who hates his father—even he is to be known as a sinner guilty of cow-slaughter; there is no doubt in this matter.
(147) A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father, and a teacher is a hundred times more venerable than a mother.
And the preceptor who bestows knowledge and mantras is always considered worthy of worship. || 148 ||
The wife of one's guru is even more worthy of honor than the guru himself;
likewise, the wife of one’s chosen deity and the deity itself are to be worshipped.
However, a Brahmin who drinks liquor, eats excrement, or is the husband of a low-caste woman [is not so honored].
And one who eats on the day of Hari shall go to the Kubhīpāka hell, O virtuous lady.
The wife of a guru, the wife of a king, a co-wife, one's mother, a daughter, a son’s wife, a mother-in-law, a pregnant woman, a sister, and a beloved [wife]. || 151 ||
And [he should not approach] the wife of a uterine brother, a maternal aunt, a paternal grandmother, a maternal grandmother, her sister, a [paternal] sister, or a brother’s daughter. (152)
The Lotus-born One declared that a female disciple, the wife of a disciple, the beloved of one's nephew, and even the wife of a brother’s son are women who must not be approached.
A lustful man who has sexual intercourse with these women incurs the sin of killing a hundred Brahmins;
that great sinner goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell, which is extremely difficult to cross.
O virtuous lady, without service to Hari, one cannot obtain the cessation of karma;
one who eats all kinds of food goes to the Kālasūtra hell for a hundred years.
Then a Śūdra shall become exceedingly afflicted, poor, and destitute;
and she who looks upon her husband with a face full of wrath out of anger [shall suffer likewise]. (156)
She speaks bitter words to him and indeed goes toward the Ulkāmukha hell;
moreover, the servant of Yama constantly holds a flaming torch to her mouth.
One should strike her on the head with a staff [a number of times] equal to the number of hairs on her body;
consequently, she shall become a human widow for seven births.
That Brāhmaṇī who was enjoyed by all indeed goes to the Andhakūpa hell;
having suffered there in water heated for purification for the duration of a kalpa, she remains beyond that.
For seven births she becomes a female crow, a sow, a hen, a jackal, a pigeon, a female monkey, and then a Cāṇḍālī woman.
O virtuous lady, a washerwoman and an oil-presser are purified from there;
a prostitute shall dwell in the Vedhakuṇḍa, and a courtesan in Daṇḍatāḍana.
A wanton woman shall dwell for the duration of a manvantara in a fish-net, a harlot in a heap of bodily dust, an unchaste woman in a mortar, and one who has violated her vow in a *kuṇḍa*.
He who, having taken a tulasī plant in his hand, does not fulfill his vow,
or should utter a false oath, shall fall into Jvālāmukha.
But he who, having extended his right hand, does not fulfill his promise,
after having touched a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, a deity, fire, a virtuous man, a chaste woman, and water— (164)
But he who does not fulfill his promise shall indeed fall into Jvālāmukha;
so too the betrayer of a friend, the ungrateful person, and the violator of trust. 165.
Furthermore, one who gives false testimony shall indeed go to Jvālāmukha;
thereafter, he shall dwell as a mute and deaf person for three births throughout a kalpa.
One who betrays a friend becomes a mongoose; one who is ungrateful becomes a eunuch;
a betrayer of trust becomes a tiger; and a false witness becomes a bear. (167)
One who is devoid of vows and fasts, a reviler of the words of the virtuous,
and deceitful, shall dwell indeed in the Haime hell for a hundred years.
Through a succession of a hundred births, one who steals the property of gods and others becomes a fish; furthermore, such a person falls into the Dhūmrāndha hell.
There, as a mouse, he shall dwell for four yugas across seven births;
then he is born among animals, birds, insects, and species of trees.
Then, one who lacks a wife and lineage shall become a Śabara afflicted by disease; likewise, a goldsmith, a merchant, a physician, a trader, or a seller of mercury [shall suffer]. (171)
A fraudulent measure, the serpent-encircled vessel, and the terrible pit—by passing through these one becomes a cowherd; thereafter, O virtuous lady, one indeed attains purification.
O devoted wife, the well-known sacrificial pits have been described;
there are also others that are not well-known, which exist according to the specific ritual action.
There are evildoers who enjoy the fruits in the hells;
thereafter they wander in saṃsāra. This much has been reported to you. (174)
Service to Kṛṣṇa is the most desired, the essential, and the auspicious thing;
it is the means of crossing over birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and suffering. (175)
O auspicious one, it is that which produces the sprout of the tree of devotion, cuts down the tree of karma,
and bestows the states of being in the same world, sharing the same power, having the same form, and residing in close proximity [to the Divine].
Those who serve Śrī Kṛṣṇa do not see the hells, the messenger of Yama, Yama himself, or the servants of Yama, even in their dreams.

Those householders who perform the vow of Hari, those women who renounce worldly attachments, and those who bathe in the sacred ford of Hari and do not eat on the day of Hari—[they attain liberation]. (178)
Those who remember Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and worship Him do not go to my terrible city of Saṃyamanī, the abode of suffering. (179)
Those who abide by the path of the traditional scriptures and logic— whether they be renunciants or householders— who are pure and devoted to dharma, go to the imperishable abode of Kṛṣṇa.
I speak to those messengers of mine who go forth with nooses in their hands:
"Go everywhere, except to the hermitage of the devotees of Hari. (181)
Indeed, Citragupta offers a handful of flowers to the devotees of Hari, and Brahmā always presents them with the madhuparka offering and other honors. (182)
For the virtuous who go beyond my world, Satyaloka, the sins of those embodied beings belonging to Yama are destroyed by the mere touch [of them]. (183)
Those pure devotees of the Lord, being devoid of bodies composed of the five elements,
travel with upward velocity by means of their subtle bodies alone.
Having bathed near the abode of Brahmā and at the Lake of Brahmā (brahmahrada),
they cast off their subtle body within the sphere of Māyā by means of the body of Brahmā in that sacred place.
Those embodied beings who have gone to the world of Yama for the sake of the fruits of their karma rejoice with a sense of self, possessing many powers and lordly senses. (186)
They bear a subtle body for which no destruction ever occurs;
that body shall not turn to ashes even in the blazing fire of the abode of Yama. (187)
It is not destroyed in water, nor is it destroyed by a blow; likewise, it is not destroyed by weapons, missiles, thorns, spikes, or molten metal. || 188 ||
Just as the fruit of an action does not perish even when fashioned upon heated iron or stone, so too one experiences it; there is not even a trace of pleasure [in that experience]. || 189 ||
In the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, not even a trace of suffering exists;
O Sāvitrī, worship Him alone and go to the palace with your beloved.
Having spoken thus, she did not go to her own abode even though Yama urged her;
instead, having brought Satyavat—who was in his subtle body—under her control within her own heart, she remained there. (191)
Desiring to know, she then asked about the dimensions of the sacrificial pit and other details.
"Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you that which was spoken by Yama. (192)

Thus ends the three hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of Sāvitrī’s Eight-Verse Hymn to Yama, the Sixty-four Hellish Pits, Falling into Them According to One's Karma, Great Sins such as Brahmin-slaughter and Cow-slaughter, and the Defeat of Yama by Devotees," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, my dear wife, to that which is beneficial for the worlds—
the description of the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth, as told by Yama to Sāvitrī.
Each sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) indeed has the shape of the full moon's orb;
it is deep and low-lying, bestowing fierce and supreme merit, yet not perishable.
There, the length of the sacrificial fire-pits is indeed measured at one hundred cubits;
for there are indeed millions of these fire-pits, all of which are circular.
The abundance of individual pits should be understood from the great number of sinners;
however, the pit of boiling water measures exactly half a *krośa*.
The pit of boiling caustic water is proclaimed to be one *krośa* in extent,
while the pit of boiling liquid urine is indeed one *gavyūti* in measure.
The pit of phlegm is one *krośa* in extent, the pit of poison is half a *krośa*,
and the great pit of eye-secretions is half a *krośa* and filled with insects.
The Vasākuṇḍa is considered to be a quarter-krośa in extent, and the Śukrakuṇḍa is likewise;
the Durgandhiraktakuṇḍa is equal to a large oblong pond (vāpī), measuring one hundred dhanus.
The pit for eye-tears is half the size of a pond, and the pit for filth is likewise;
the pit for ear-wax is exactly one-fourth the measure of a pond.
The pit of marrow is four hundred cubits [in extent], the pit of flesh is one hundred bows;
the pit of nails, the pit of body hair, the pit of bones, and that of teeth likewise.
Each of these was four *yojanas* in measure and exceedingly terrifying;
there was a copper cauldron shining with ten million heated copper statues.
A pit of molten iron measuring one *gavyūti* in extent,
as well as the Gharma-kuṇḍa, the Surā-kuṇḍa, and a half-pit of iron.
Beneath the Śālmalī tree is a pit of sharp thorns, one hundred thousand paces deep,
one krośa in circumference, and circular in shape.
Thorny spikes, as long as bows, were fixed all around the walls;
there was a pit of poison measuring a *krośa* in extent, and likewise a pit of weapons of equal length.
And there was a pit of boiling oil measuring two *gavyūtis* in extent,
and a pit with beds of weapons measuring a quarter of a *krośa*.
The pit of pus is half a krośa in extent, and the pit of teeth is likewise long;
the pit of cold water measures two gavyūtis.
Likewise, the pit for the gadfly-bite is considered to be half a krośa;
and the pit for the diamond-scorpion is likewise equal to half a vāpī.
The Śarakuṇḍa is for the purpose of a pond, and the Nakrakuṇḍa is likewise elongated;
the Kākakuṇḍa is a hundred thousand bow-lengths, and the Gṛdhrakuṇḍa is similarly elongated.
Likewise, Vājakuṇḍa is long, while Vajrakuṇḍa is a hundred bows (dhanuḥśata) in length;
Taptapāṣāṇakuṇḍa is twice the body-length of a large well (vāpī).
The Lālākuṇḍa is one krośa in extent and contains boiling water;
the Cūrṇakuṇḍa is one krośa, while the Cakraka is a quarter-krośa.
Whirling like a potter’s wheel, it possesses sixteen rims;
there is a pit of flames, a pit for tortoises and other creatures, and a place of wailing.
The pit of heated ashes extends for one *krośa*, as does the darkness;
the pit of burning embers is likewise one *krośa* in extent, and the pit of heated lye is similarly vast.
There is the pool of boiling water measuring two gavyūtis,
as well as the pool of glowing iron images, and likewise the forest of sword-leaves.
The Raktakuṇḍa pit is likewise half a krośa in extent and length;
the terrifying Kṣurāstrakuṇḍa pit measures one hundred dhanus.
The Sūcikuṇḍa, which causes piercing, measures fifty dhanus;
the Godhākuṇḍa, which has the form of a lizard, measures twenty dhanus.
The pit for humans should be shaped like a human face and measure sixteen dhanus;
the pit for elephants should be made with elephant tusks and measure one hundred dhanus.
The Gomukha pit is recorded as being thirty bow-lengths in measure,
while the Kālacakra and Bhrami pits are each two gavyūtis in measure.
And there is the Lakṣamānavakuṇḍa, filled with oil, iron, and stones;
it is heated by fire and measures four gavyūtis in extent.
O beautiful one, however many sinners there are in all the other hells,
four times that number exist in the most terrible Kumbhīpāka.
Kumbhīpāka is proclaimed as the foremost of all pits;
Kālasūtra and Taptatoya are pits measuring twenty bows [in length]. (29)
A hundred bow-lengths away is a pit filled with diseases and ailments;
and another hundred bow-lengths away is a cauldron of hot sand that causes burning.
The Krośārtanāda pit measures twenty dhanus;
likewise, the Śūla pit, containing icy water, measures half a krośa.
The Ulkā-kuṇḍa is proclaimed to measure twenty dhanus,
while the Andhakāra-prakuṇḍa is even greater, measuring one hundred dhanus.
The sacrificial pit for weapons shall be twenty *dhanus* in depth;
the sacrificial pit for the striking with the staff shall be sixteen *dhanus* in measure.
The Jālakuṇḍa is proclaimed to be thirty bow-lengths in measure,
while the Lohavedicūrṇakuṇḍa is one koṭi in measure.
The Mūrchā-kuṇḍa, filled with darkness, measures twenty dhanus;
the Dalana-kuṇḍa is said to measure sixteen dhanus.
The pit of heated sand measures thirty bows in extent,
and the pit of tanned leather is indeed foul-smelling and measures one hundred bows.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a winnowing basket has a measurement of twelve dhanus;
likewise, the Agniśikha pit has a measurement of twenty dhanus. ||37||
Jvālāmukha and Jihmakuṇḍa are proclaimed to be half-moons;
Dhūmrakuṇḍa is a hundred bows long and filled with poisonous smoke and the like.
A hundred bow-lengths [from the center] is the Nāgapūrṇa [pit], and the Nāgaveṣṭana-kuṇḍaka;
these eighty-six pits have been described by me, O virtuous lady. (39)
"O Sāvitrī, speak further if you wish to hear more.
Then Sāvitrī, being satisfied, spoke that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The female species was created by the Ordainer as being devoid of knowledge of reality, yet possessing devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa that is characterized by the nature of a bull among Bhāgavatas. 41.
Tell me here what essential knowledge I should grasp:
for is it the gift of all things, fasting, bathing at sacred fords, religious vows, or austerity? (42)
"Gifts of knowledge do not equal even a sixteenth part of [the merit of] giving knowledge to the ignorant.
A mother is a hundred times more venerable than a father; a teacher is a hundred times more venerable than a mother.
Having heard this, Yama said: "May you have devotion to Keśava."
Even Śeṣa, with his thousand mouths, is not able to describe her. ||44||
Neither Śambhu with his five faces, nor Brahmā with his four faces,
nor even Kārtikeya with his six faces, are capable of describing her.
Sarasvatī, Gaṇeśa, and Sanatkumāra as well; Dharma, Sanaka, Sananda, Kapila, and Sanātana. ||46||
Sūrya, Patnīvrata, and Nārada—the sons of Brahmā—even the Siddhas, the lords of sages, and the yogis are not capable of describing her. (47)
Who else are we, and what are we, in the description of devotion to the Blessed One?
Does anyone truly know even a little of the glorification of the Blessed One's qualities? (48)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, understands a little;
then Gaṇeśa, the teacher of the wise, understands a little.
Śambhu alone is omniscient and knows everything that transcends all;
Lakṣmī alone knows even more than that—of this there is no doubt.
Rādhā, Prabhā, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Jayā, and the others truly know supreme devotion; even the liberated ones know it only to an immeasurable degree. ||51||
By Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, who exists in the form of Puruṣottama,
all knowledge is perfectly preserved within Śrī Kṛṣṇa, his own essential nature.
The supreme knowledge was indeed bestowed upon Śambhu by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, in the exceedingly secluded and beautiful Rāsamaṇḍala in Goloka. (53)
Śiva himself narrated it to Dharma in the world of Śiva;
and Dharma, in turn, related it to Bhāskara at Puṣkara.
The Sun told me of the glorification of devotion to Kṛṣṇa and other virtues;
even he does not know it in its entirety, so what need is there to speak of anyone else? (55)
The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is the inner self of all, the witness of all, the embodiment of all, and the cause of all causes. 56.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees, he assumes a pair of forms—lovely, beautiful, youthful, and possessing a form as dense as a rain cloud. (57)
Possessing the beauty of ten million Cupids, filled with the essence of the erotic sentiment, with eyes having the luster of lotus petals and a face like the full moon. ||58||
Wearing ornaments and jewels, clad in yellow garments, served by Rādhā and others, seated upon a jeweled throne in the midst of the rāsa dance, and holding a flute. (59)
Adorned with a forest garland, the Kaustubha gem, and other ornaments, He is gracious and smiling;
He is worshipped with saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and other fragrant substances.
Adorned with beautiful garlands of campaka flowers, lotuses, and mālatī blossoms,
it shone with the brilliance of his shimmering, delicate, and exceedingly radiant crown that appeared as if naturally adorned.
By His command, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Saṅkarṣaṇa— perform the acts of creation, sustenance, and withdrawal.
By whose grace the wind blows, the sun and moon shine, Indra pours down rain, Mahākāla likewise makes his mouthfuls [of the world], and so forth. (63)
Fire is hot and water is cold—all that has been created by Him;
out of fear of Him the guardians of the quarters protect the directions and the planets revolve.
The trees bear fruit and blossom, and the seasons arrive in their proper succession;
likewise, living beings thrive upon land, in water, and in the sky.
By whose command Yama, the dispenser of justice, the giver of dharma, and the bull [Dharma] himself, fall into blazing fire and into the deep ocean. 66.
Upon the tips of trees, on the points of sharp swords, in the mouths of serpents and other creatures, in battles involving various weapons and missiles, and in perilous conflicts; ||67||
Through whose grace there is protection, and likewise through whose anger there is destruction;
the wind sustains the fire, and the fire sustains the oceans of water.
May He by whose grace the waters, the tortoise, the great tortoise, Ananta the serpent, the earth with its oceans and mountains are sustained—may He be glorified. (69)
Seventy-one divine yugas, along with twenty-eight falls of Śakra, constitute a day and night of Brahmā. 1.371.70.
Thus, thirty nights and days constitute a month, and two such months an *ṛtu* (season). Six *ṛtus* make a year, and one hundred years is the lifespan of Brahmā.
Indeed, upon the passing of Brahmā Vairāja, one day of Mahāviṣṇu occurs;
a hundred years of Vairāja constitute a single day of Mahāviṣṇu.
A hundred years of Mahāviṣṇu constitute a day of Pradhānapuruṣa;
a hundred years of that [Pradhānapuruṣa] constitute a day of Prākṛtapuruṣa.
Every hundred years, the eyelids of that Hari open;
he is this very Hari himself, the Lord of Śrī, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (74)
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara—all are essentially Kṛṣṇa, there is no doubt; upon the closing of his eyes, their dissolution into primordial nature occurs. (75)
Those of material form dissolve into Kṛṣṇa’s navel-lotus;
likewise, Viṣṇu, who reclines upon the ocean of milk and possesses four arms in Vaikuṇṭha, [dissolves there].
They dissolve into the left side of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;
Śiva is absorbed in the knowledge of Hari, and Durgā goes to dissolution in his intellect.
Skanda was hidden within the chest, and Gaṇeśvara within the arm of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
Padmā, Rādhā, and the gopīs attained dissolution into the life-breath of Kṛṣṇa. (78)
Sāvitrī resides in Sarasvatī, she [resides] on the tongue of the Supreme Self;
the cowherds reside in the black hairs, and the winds and other elements reside in the vital breaths. (79)
The sacrificial fire is in the digestive fire of the stomach, water is at the tip of the tongue;
the Vaiṣṇavas [place] devotion and righteousness within the heart upon the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, from whichever form of His lordships arise, and within whose very pores all the universes in their entirety exist— 8.1.
That Supreme Self, by the closing of whose eye there occurs the dissolution of all existing effects, and by the opening of whose eye there is creation; (82)
Thus, O lady of virtuous vows, there is truly no end to the number of creations and dissolutions;
who indeed is capable of enumerating their multitude within the cosmic eggs? (83)
But devotion to Hari is the most important, even superior to liberation;
it must be practiced, O daughter, if you wish to go to the further shore of dissolution. (84)
One bestows the same world as Hari, another bestows a form similar to Hari’s;
yet another bestows proximity to Him, and another still bestows equal power.
But others, who have attained oneness, do not desire even those [other] devotees;
indeed, having abandoned service, there is nothing whatsoever to be desired. (86)
Liberation is devotion devoid of service; devotion increases through service.
This is the distinction between devotion and its application; therefore, one should always practice devotion. (87)
Indeed, the dedication of all actions performed by means of the body, all the senses, and all the internal organs, in every way unto Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, brings about liberation. (88)
O Goddess, a woman should always perform service to Hari by offering herself to a man; with affection, she should do so in every way, for this is the most essential knowledge. 89.
"Go, Sāvitrī, together with your husband, and may you be happy.
Having spoken thus, the son of the Sun (Yama) returned her husband to her.
Having bestowed auspicious blessings upon her, he prepared to depart;
but seeing Yama departing, Sāvitrī bowed down to him.
Making her eyes turbid with tears and placing her head upon his excellent feet, she was overcome by the grief of separation; for the severance from the virtuous indeed causes suffering.
But the compassionate Yama said, "O noble lady, do not grieve;
having enjoyed happiness for a hundred thousand years in every way in this field of merit. (93)
"In the Naranārāyaṇa-khaṇḍa, you will certainly go to Goloka;
having returned home, O auspicious lady, perform that vow just as Sāvitrī did. (94)
Indeed, that bestows liberation upon women for up to fourteen years;
therefore, perform the Sāvitrī vow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha. (95)
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, observe the vow of Mahālakṣmī; this vow lasts for sixteen years, or indeed for one fortnight every year. (96)
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, perform the Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vow with supreme devotion; at the end, you shall go to the abode of Hari.
And on every Tuesday, one should worship the goddess Maṅgalacaṇḍikā;
and every month on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the bestower of auspiciousness.
One should worship Rādhā on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, and likewise her on the full moon of Kārtika;
and every month, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Durgā, the destroyer of difficult distress.
That woman who worships with devotion the virtuous Kaṃbharā, the bestower of happiness,

For the sake of obtaining wealth and progeny, [one should worship] a virtuous woman who has a husband and sons, as well as chaste and pure women, mechanical dolls, and images. 101.
"By worshipping [him], having become happy, one shall attain the Imperishable at the end. Having spoken thus to that virtuous woman and bowed to her, Yamarāja went to his home.
Taking her husband by the hand, Sāvitrī went to her own abode;
Satyavān immediately arose and was restored to life from his deep sleep.
Ānanda arose there in every respect—both in the city and in the house—as Sāvitrī related the account concerning Satyavān in due order. (104)
And he related other [accounts] as well; having heard them, they were filled with wonder.
Sāvitrī’s father obtained a hundred sons in due order.
Her father-in-law, Akṣuṣī, obtained a kingdom that destroyed poverty,

Thus, O Lakṣmī, by the power of her devotion to her husband,

If devotion to one's husband is preserved, it is indeed equal to the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), equal to the celestial wish-granting tree (Kalpavṛkṣa), and even superior to the thought-gem (Cintāmaṇi). || 108 ||
For yogis, through the perfection of yoga, their devotion to their spouse is distinguished;
it cannot be stolen by thieves, it cannot be afflicted, and it is not subject to separation. (109)
That [virtue], firmly established in the self and the eternal Dharma, remained indeed hidden;
yet that great chaste woman, having enjoyed happiness on earth for a hundred thousand years, [attained her goal]. || 1.371.11 ||
Possessing a divine form, she went to Goloka together with her Lord;
praised by the gods, she traveled through the air in a celestial chariot.
In her second form, she is the divine Sāvitrī of the sun,
and she is also the presiding deity of the Sāvitrī mantra of the Vedas.
She herself has become possessed of infinite forms through devotion to Puruṣottama.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this supreme narrative of Sāvitrī has been told to you. 11.3.
Any woman who hears this shall certainly attain the status of a devoted wife;
indeed, she should practice no other primary duty apart from devotion to her husband.
In the image of the Lord, all things—liberation and devotion—are found; and all supernatural powers wait like maidservants upon devotion to the Lord. 1.15
All forms of sovereignty, as well as wealth, grain, and garments;
gold, silver, gems, jewels, and ornaments in every respect.
Prosperities reside in the water from the husband's feet;
great Brahman is in the husband's face; and indeed, all pleasures are in the husband's limbs.
There is great satisfaction in the husband's contentment; there is bliss in the husband's dalliance.
Great fortune resides in the husband's hand; one's own life is contained within the husband's belly. (1.18)
The sacred fords are within the husband's channels, and liberation indeed occurs when the husband's life-force departs;
for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are all established within the body of the husband.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, for the sake of making him my husband, the Supreme Brahman alone is my husband;
Kṛṣṇa is my husband, and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, is my husband.
Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person Śrī Puruṣottama, is the Lord;
likewise, all the gods, the Vedas, sacrifices, prayers, and rosaries [are His]. (121)
The methods for giving sacrificial fees, various forms of knowledge, yogic practices, acts of beneficence toward others, as well as virtuous qualities such as non-violence and the like; || 122 ||
Auspicious deeds should be performed, as well as worship, vows, ritual baths, eclipses, and transits of the sun in every respect. (123)
All days of merit, as well as auspicious festivals, wedding rites, and rituals pertaining to the gods and other such matters [should be observed]. (1.24)
O Lakṣmī, while the husband possesses sovereign power, there are pilgrimages and divine paths;
knowing the husband alone to be the Supreme Brahman, the devoted wife should worship him. 125.
From the reading, hearing, or reciting of this,
