as well as from remembering or honoring it, enjoyment and liberation are held within one's hand.
There is no duty other than that toward one's husband; yet among these, the duty of Satī is distinguished.
The supreme duty is indeed the service of Hari, which constitutes the very essence of Satī’s dharma.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Dimensions of the Eighty-six Hells, the Knowledge and Devotion Spoken by Yama to Sāvitrī, the Restoration of Satyavān to Life, and the Preeminence of the Duties of a Wife," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the sin-destroying life-story of Padmā.
That auspicious [event], consisting of a religious curse, occurred regarding the daughter of Anaraṇya. || 1 ||
In ancient times, while observing her devotion to her husband and abiding by her father’s command,
Padmā caused a decline in dharma according to the distinctions between the ages.
Youth was rendered fruitless by that very [ignorance] as soon as it arose;
after childhood came boyhood, then youth, and thereafter old age. (3)
O Lakṣmī, such things as these were performed by her in the world according to tradition;
that king Anaraṇya was born of the lineage of Manu and possessed great fame. || 4 ||
Long-lived, virtuous in character, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and one who has conquered his senses—
he was the son of Maṅgalāraṇya, born of the lineage of Indrasāvarṇi.
Maṅgalāraṇya was indeed the son of Dharāraṇya.
Being childless, Dharāraṇya went to Puṣkara to perform penance.
Having performed austerities for a very long time and obtained a boon from the Supreme Lord,
he indeed obtained as his son Anaraṇya, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses.
Having given his own kingdom to him, he went to the forest for asceticism;
thereafter, Anaraṇya was [consecrated] by Bhṛgu as his domestic priest.
Having performed a hundred excellent sacrifices, he remained established in the disposition of detachment;
considering even the status of Śakra to be trivial, he did not seek that perishable state.
They had one hundred sons, all equal to their father in virtue;
and they had one daughter, beautiful and charming, Padmā, who was like Lakṣmī, the dweller in the lotus.
He made an effort to search for a suitable bridegroom for her;
meanwhile, in a secluded spot within that penance grove, the sage Pippalāda was there.
Having seen a Gandharva sporting with women, he indeed became filled with desire;
then this lord of sages went to bathe in the Puṣpabhadrā river.
He beheld the youthful Padmā, who was the very incarnation of Lakṣmī; upon merely seeing her, who was so enchanting, he conceived the desire to take her as his wife.
He asked the ascetics standing nearby, "Who is she, and to whom does she belong? And they made this report: "She is a lotus born in the forest."
Having bathed and worshipped his chosen deity Puruṣottama, the sage,
filled with desire, went to the assembly hall of Anaraṇya for the sake of alms.
Upon seeing the sage, the king quickly bowed down with great devotion;
having offered the madhuparka and other honors, he worshipped him with respect.
Being thus requested by the king for a boon as he desired,
the sage Pippalāda then asked for the auspicious maiden Padmā.
Having heard this, the king became silent, unable to say anything in reply;
then the sage said to him, "O best of kings, give me your daughter."
"Or else, I shall indeed reduce everything to ashes in an instant!"—
and thus all the servants became completely enveloped by the ascetic's splendor.
The king and the queen grieved upon seeing the old man afflicted with fever; all the queens also mourned, being at a loss as to what ought to be done.
The girl's mother lamented, reflecting deeply on the suffering of her daughter;
seeing this, Pippalāda enlightened the king.
The daughter of a king, his sons, servants, or likewise daughters—such a girl should be given away either today or on another day. (22)
"O King, give this to whichever Brahmin you please;
I see no worthy recipient other than a Brahmin in the three worlds. (23)
O King, you ought not to give your daughter to anyone other than a brahmin; having given her to me, protect all your prosperity. (24)
"Let not all your possessions, for the sake of a maiden, go to ashes!
Having heard these most formidable words, the beautiful maiden also [spoke]. ||25||
Reflecting upon her father’s welfare, the sage’s respect for asceticism,
and the absence of obstacles to all his prosperity, she said to the king, "Give me away."
Then the king joyfully gave his queen Padmā, adorned with ornaments, to Pippalāda;
having obtained his beloved, Pippalāda was delighted, blazing with ascetic power.
By the power of his yoga, he manifested his own form as a youth suitable for eighteen years— an age fit for a maiden and capable of granting all desires.
The king and others were exceedingly delighted, and the maiden was satisfied within her heart; then the king of sages, taking the dowry and his beloved, departed.
Then Anaraṇya, his mind full, departed for the sake of austerity;
he fixed his mind on liberation there, meditating upon the Lord of Rādhikā.
Having attained Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he indeed went to Goloka;
his eldest son, Kīrtyaraṇya, ruled over his kingdom.
Then the daughter of Anaraṇya served the sage with devotion through her actions,
mind, and speech, just as Lakṣmī serves Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly devoted to her husband, she served Śrī Hari just as she would;
she repeatedly massaged the sage’s limbs and attended to his feet.
Constantly adhering to her duties, she fulfilled his every desire;
having bathed herself, she would bathe her husband, and having fed him, she would eat;
having put him to sleep, she would sleep herself, and she attended to all his activities.
Just as an ascetic, whether old or young, or even a royal sage,
might become pleased, so does the virtuous woman serve day and night,
always considering her own fortune to be superior to the most excellent.
That I have encountered a Brahmin there, a sage and ascetic,
pure and of meritorious form, whose very nature is that of Nārāyaṇa—
a yogi and a knower of the Self— who else is as blessed as I?
I have always been born pure, for I was personally requested by the sage himself.
There is no end to my good fortune, nor is there an end to my merit;
it is through the merits of many births that the Blessed Lord is obtained as a husband.
Thus, this very Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has been obtained by me as my husband;
through service to him alone is liberation attained, and in his satisfaction lies the imperishable state.
Within his heart alone resides Brahman, and from that, Brahman has been attained by me.
In this matter of my liberation, no other means remains for me.

May there be well-being for my father; may there be well-being for Janaka, by whom auspicious things were bestowed upon me; and may there be well-being for my mother, through whom I was born endowed with happiness.
O Pippalāda, lord of sages, everything has been obtained by me here;
the satisfaction of knowledge, the satisfaction of delight, and the satisfaction of enjoyment are attained.
The satisfaction of fame, the satisfaction of renown, and the satisfaction of honor are also attained.
"The burden of sovereignty brings suffering, and the status of a queen is even greater than that. For queens there is no peace at all, just like birds in a cage.
Yet, it is here that dharma, artha, and kāma are enjoyed by me with ease. (44–45)
It is not enjoyed by the queens whose hearts are thus tormented;
rather, whatever auspiciousness has arisen—all that was acquired by me through destiny.
I have not fallen into the hands of a king who consumes liquor and meat.
That very merit shall be my joyful protector here. ||47||
The young maidens do not know that kings cause suffering to kings;
later, having fallen [into hell], they lament, "Where have we gone to this hell? (48)
A husband who is virtuous in character and possesses divine qualities is difficult to find anywhere;
however, a husband who is merely a consumer and a destroyer, like a dog, is found everywhere. 49.
He exhausts the body with enjoyments, destroys merit with sins, and leads one to the realm of Yama; such a husband is easily obtained.
He who is intent solely on his own interest and provides no assistance for the next world is not a husband in the true sense; by union with him, hell is certain.
Therefore, both here and in the next world, the husband protects as if he were half of her body;
in creation and liberation, in happiness and suffering, the husband is her companion. 52.
She who, having obtained such a husband, does not serve him in deed, thought, or word, shall always be a person deceived.
A woman of noble family must by no means preserve her pride before her husband, whether it concerns her lineage, her web of virtues, her beauty, her intellect, or her righteousness. (54)
The body is my husband, the mind is my lord, and egoism is my husband;
the aggregate of causes and effects, as well as pleasure and pain, is my husband. (55)
Food, enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of eating—all objects of experience, as well as trust, the granting of boons, and even the ritual deposit (nyāsa)—all these have me as their Lord. (56)
Wretchedness, excellence, steadfastness, and compliance—my husband is all these.
Vows, righteousness, merit, sacred fords, and charity—my husband is all these. (57)
The recitation of sacred texts, study, and worship, as well as the duties of the twilight devotions—my husband is my festival and my assembly; my husband is my manifestation. (58)
The vehicle, the delightful drama, the dance, the song, and my husband; the palace, the prosperity of the kingdom, the elephants and horses, and my husband—[all these are mine]. (59)
The Guru is Brahmā, Hara, Viṣṇu, and all the gods; he is my lord. The Vaiśvadeva offering and the worship of guests—these are my husband. (1.372.60)
The embryo, the son, delight, joy, the highest good, and my husband;
the abode, the field, the earth, and the kingdom—whatever is my entire possession, my husband is all that. (6.1)
"Both prohibition and injunction belong to me; my husband is one who acts according to his own will.
Thinking thus, and considering it the highest satisfaction, I indeed perform service to the sage. (62)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that princess, satisfied by eternal bliss,
served that best of sages just as she would serve Nārāyaṇa himself.
For the sake of examining her character, Dharmadeva indeed reflected thus.
How indeed does she, devoted to her husband, continue to exist? 64.
Once, Dharma, assuming the form of a king through his illusory power, saw Satī on the road as she was smiling and proceeding to bathe in the celestial river.
Mounted upon a chariot made of gold and jewels, adorned with gold, gems, and other ornaments,
and rich in the beauty of fresh youth, he was like a second God of Love.
Seeing the beautiful and lovely Padmā, he spoke to her through his illusory power:
"Aha! How beautiful is this woman; and where is that decrepit sage? (67)
O beautiful one, you are as radiant as Lakṣmī, worthy of a king, exceedingly brilliant, situated in the prime of youth, auspicious, and the remover of the pride of desire. (68)
Why do you shine in the presence of one who is consumed by old age, who is aged, who is like wood or stone, and whose body consists of nothing but bones? (69)
O Queen of kings, you are worthy of a king; you shine upon the chest of a king, your limbs anointed with sandalwood and aloe, adorned with gold, jewels, and other ornaments.
"O beautiful one, may you be happy, endowed with hundreds of male and female servants!
[Leave behind] this Brahmin, emaciated by asceticism, withered, intent on the Supreme Brahman, and whose life is spent. (71)
Setting these aside, O King, behold the lord of the earth, a hero in love;
behold one like me, enriched with the pleasures of heaven and established in equanimity.
Is there any happiness at all in a hut of leaves? Is there any comfort in a nest of birds upon a branch? And why do you rely upon this sack of bones?
Come, O Cintāmaṇi, here in Acyuta! ||73||
"O Acyuta, may you obtain the jewel of consciousness within me; I choose that you become for me a wish-fulfilling creeper.
A gem set in gold shines with great splendor."
Indeed, it is not on the neck of a beast that is worthy of a conch-shell [ornament]. ||74||
Through merit from a previous birth, one obtains beautiful form;
yet that beauty becomes truly fruitful only through the embrace of a connoisseur (rasika). //75//
"O beloved, as you are so dear, make me—me who am skilled in the performance of love's tasks—your servant; O sinless one, I shall give you everything. (76)
Accompanied by his wife, he wandered in a secluded and beautiful forest, in a wilderness, on a mountain,
by a river, at a stream, in a grove, and in a flowering garden fragrant with scents.
In a celestial vehicle, in a divine mansion, in a sovereign empire, on Mount Malaya, on Mount Raivata,
or elsewhere in a place abounding with sandalwood trees, I shall indeed sport with you.
I am capable of bringing peace to one consumed by the fever of desire;
sport with me and make this birth fruitful. (79)
To the king who had spoken thus and was eager to seize him by the hand as he approached her side, the devoted wife spoke to Dharma.
Go far away, go far away, for you are intent on evil thoughts!
If you touch me with lust, you shall instantly be reduced to ashes. (8.1)
I am a married woman, the beloved wife of the sage Pippalāda;
being devoted to my husband, I do not look upon another man even in my heart. (82)
How can I touch a sinful portion of this king, who is enslaved by women and a libertine?
By the mere touch of one who is unrighteous, all merit is destroyed. (83)
O King, you have exerted yourself here to forcibly violate another's wife; there has never been another sinner like you on this earth.
"I am the wife of a brahmin there; I am the mother of that aged ascetic whom you address to me by assuming a female form. (85)
"Your destruction shall come here from my curse as an assailant;
go to your certain ruin, O King, through your sinful heart and deed. (86)
Having heard the curse of Satī, Dharma abandoned his royal form;
becoming the god Dharma himself, he appeared and spoke to her.
O Mother, know me to be Dharma, the teacher of those who know dharma and the teacher of teachers, who regards the wives of others as his own mother and protects the world. (88)
"O Padmika, I have come here to know you intimately;
O virtuous one, I assumed the form of a king in order to test you. (89)
Nevertheless, people experience the results of their own actions;
thus, I have committed an offense against you through my harsh words. (1.372.90)
"The fruit of that must be enjoyed by me; there is no doubt about this.
My subduing of him here was not improper, but was exactly as it should have been. (91)
"In every way, may there be no death for me; this I always pray for. Punishment for those who have gone astray has been ordained by the Lord. (92)
"Let the instruction composed by you be as it is, provided it is bearable for me.
Padmā then said: "O Dharma, you alone are the witness of all embodied beings. (93)
How was this form of a king assumed by you for the purpose of testing [me], and what was the offense for which I was cursed? (94)
The curse of a virtuous woman never becomes false;
there is no doubt that upon your destruction, the destruction of creation will surely follow. ||95||
Therefore, O Lord of Dharma, listen as I speak according to the distinctions of human types, so that both your life and your curse may become meaningful. (96)
O Dharma, in an age of truth, may you exist in every way as four-footed; O Bull, in an age pervaded by the Tretā, may you exist in every way as three-footed.
O Dharma, when humanity is pervaded by the Dvāpara age, you arise with two feet;
when people are pervaded by the Kali age, you remain with one foot; may your dissolution occur in what remains.
O Dharma, you shall remain concealed among the dull-witted who are like beasts;
may full manifestation be yours among those of sattvic nature, while incompleteness prevails among the rajasic and others.
O Bull, listen as I tell you what place is your support,
especially among all the devotees of Hari and the Vaiṣṇavas.
Among virtuous women, the righteous, ascetics, sages, celibate students, devoted wives, the wise, forest-dwellers, and mendicants; || 101 ||
Among all those of virtuous character belonging to the Vaiśya and Kṣatriya castes, among Śūdras who serve the twice-born, and among those who abide in the company of the righteous; ||| 102 ||
In horses, banyan trees, bilva trees, tulasī, and sandalwood; and in initiations, examinations, oaths, cow-pens, cow-prints, and sacred ground. (103)
And at all marriages, among flowers and species of trees, in temples, at sacred fords, and always in the houses of the virtuous. (104)

In the deliberations on the Vedic scriptures, in those who perform the chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories, in the observance of vows and worship, and likewise in the places where one stands as a witness to sacrifices performed according to the law; || 105 ||
Furthermore, among cattle, living beings, swans, and eagles, as well as among virtuous women, there will be emaciation in every respect in all places of truth. (106)
But listen: there will be scarcity in other places, namely among all unchaste women and in the houses of those who have killed men.
Toward those who are base, foolish, wicked, or intent on reviling others, and toward those who are deceitful;
toward those who seize the wealth of deities, gurus, brahmins, or those worthy of protection;
toward rogues, the unrighteous, the corrupt, thieves, and adulterers— [one should maintain such conduct].
And in cases of gambling, wine, meat, quarrels, and transgressions. || 109 ||
Those who obstruct the service of holy places and fields such as Śālagrāma, those engaged in the most arrogant acts of banditry, and those who live by ink or by the sword; ||| 1.372.110 ||

[One should not give it] to women who revile their husbands, to those who subsist on the slaughter of living beings, nor to those who are devoid of initiation, the twilight prayers, righteousness, and devotion, or who are stained by blemishes. (111)
In men who sell maidens, women, gods, sacred texts, or knowledge;
in those who betray friends or commit ingratitude; in those who destroy truth and trust;
in those who harm those who have sought refuge, the miserable, the blind, or their dependents; and in those who speak falsehoods—[these are excluded from the funeral feast].
Likewise, [this applies] constantly to those whose habit is false speech and to those who seize boundaries. || 113 ||
You cannot remain among false witnesses, nor among kings who practice unjust legal proceedings, nor among all those who obstruct merit.
Dwell forever in four parts among those who are pure, characterized by goodness (sattva), and peaceful; when passion (rajas) increases mixed with goodness, dwell as Trita in three parts.
When rajas is mixed with an increase of tamas, you dwell as Dvāpara with two feet; when the hearts consist of tamas alone, you dwell as Kali with one foot.
In former times, truth, sacrifice, austerity, and charity were your four feet;
today, non-violence, self-restraint, faith, and generosity are your feet.
In the future time, there will be morality, purity, service, and recitation; these are its four feet in order, and thus it dwells even during decline.
Having spoken thus, Dharma ceased; he bestowed blessings upon her, saying:
"Blessed are you, devoted to your husband; may prosperity be yours forever. (119)
"May your husband be young, handsome, and possessed of enduring youth;
may he indeed be long-lived, even more so than Mārkaṇḍeya. (1.372.120)
May you be endowed with wealth and sovereignty, and may you be born with perpetual youth;
may you become the mother of ten sons who live for a very long time.
Having heard this, the virtuous Padmā circumambulated and bowed to the bull, then departed for her own home; Dharma also returned to his own place.
In that assembly, he praised her who was devoted to her vows;
for she, Padmā, though herself a devoted wife, was indeed [praised] by virtue of her own devotion to her husband.
Thus, a woman devoted to her husband becomes possessed of a hundred sons and endowed with all auspicious fortune; she is capable both of destroying and protecting dharma.
"She herself is capable; what other person would dare to overcome her?
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this narrative of Padmā been told to you.
It constantly nourishes righteousness, bestows the power of wifely devotion, grants both heaven and liberation, and likewise bestows all forms of dharma. || 126 ||
This supreme work, which bestows service to a husband and pacifies the cycle of worldly existence, should be heard with devotion by a woman; she shall become firm in her devotion to her husband.
Dharma will surely provide protection for both the listener and the speaker;
for devotion to one's husband and surrender are always two equal virtues.
One may attain everything by means of a single [virtue]; there is no need for a second. O Lakṣmī, when both are present, what more need be said regarding the Self?
Chastity, the duty of a servant, and surrender—these possess the nature of affection;
having attained supreme service and affection, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 1.372.13 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Marriage of the Chaste Padmā, Daughter of Anaraṇya, with Pippalāda; the Curse of Dharma during His Test by Dharma; and the Description of the Gradual Decline of the Four Quarters over Time," within the section on the Greatness of Chastity in the first part, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that story devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity,
which took place in Vaikuṇṭha for the complete destruction of pride.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Hari himself, the sovereign of Vaikuṇṭha,
shone in the midst of the assembly, surrounded by many of his attendants.
The Supreme Lord was served by male and female servants as well as Vaiṣṇavas;
[and] the Great Chaste Lady was born from the chest of the Lord of Akṣara. (3)
The great desire that brings about prosperity, which takes the form of the resolve of Śrī Hari—Lakṣmī beheld her own nature as distinct from those who have attained liberation. || 4 ||
Then, out of modesty, she prayed to Śrī Hari, the Lord of all:
"O Lord, please construct for me a dwelling worthy of my residence. (5)
Just as I served you, the Supreme Lord, through my devotion as a faithful wife,
so too is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa the manifest Supreme Soul and the Supreme Lord.
Having heard the appropriate prayer and knowing that the woman was his own servant,
he fashioned a new and auspicious Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of the couple.
Out of a desire for Mahālakṣmī, he himself became four-armed,
the Supreme Brahman in the form of a husband, possessing the conch, the discus, the mace, and other weapons.
He was eighteen years of age, lovely and exceedingly handsome, with all his limbs endowed with vigor; Lakṣmī was sixteen years old.
She was desirable, worthy of serving her husband, and exquisitely beautiful;
she possessed lovely breasts, a beautiful face, a charming waist, and a golden complexion.
Perfectly endowed with the beauty of all her limbs, she is the refuge of all supernatural powers;
she possesses the great bliss of all sovereignty and assumes whatever form is conceived by will.
She was a passionate woman skilled in the arts of love, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa,
enriched by the splendor of all ornaments, and adorned with divine garments and other finery.
Adorned with the powder and collyrium of all excellent and erotic substances,
Anaṅga remained within her as if inseparable from her body.
To fulfill her resolve, Hari, the four-armed Nārāyaṇa,
took his own four-armed wife Lakṣmī and departed.
Vaikuṇṭha is His self-created abode where there is no other duality except for the pair; there, no third manifest form exists, and that couple alone rejoices.
There, thousands of Siddhis born of mere resolve have indeed arisen;
they are all fifteen-year-old maidens who serve Mahālakṣmī.
For their sake, pleasant palaces as bright as the moon were constructed there;
for his own sake, a divine mansion and a new palace were built.
There, Śrī Hari constructed an exceedingly vast rampart and a city of great length and breadth, along with a multitude of water-lotus ponds.
Rivers, streams, and ponds; groves, gardens, and grounds;
various monasteries, alchemy laboratories, and long oblong ponds.
Likewise, there were dining halls, halls of refreshment, and pleasure grounds;
and in the center of the assembly area was a great, divine throne, higher than the highest.
Having himself fashioned rows of palaces rich with all kinds of articles and furnishings, he and his consort always rejoice there. (21)
When Nārāyaṇa dwells in the home together with Lakṣmī, immersed in love, then the maidservants approach him with devotion.
Endowed with love for the Blessed One and summoned by their passion for the dust [of His feet], they come together for the sake of pastime and embrace the Supreme Lord. (23)
Hari, moreover, assuming many forms, sports with them as well;
and Mahālakṣmī also sports there in her own abode.
Simultaneously, in numbers reaching thousands and tens of thousands, the Lord Hari himself, assuming millions of forms, sports through his manifold nature.
Thus, in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, the fullness of all,
there is no other man who exists apart from Nārāyaṇa.
There are always millions upon millions of female servants and attendants;
and once, while all of them were there, Hari assumed every form.
The Lord indeed provided delight that satisfied ten million female servants;
Mahālakṣmī sported within her own abode with Nārāyaṇa.
She was deeply immersed in great bliss and became as if absorbed in it;
at that very moment, the eternal and liberated Sanatkumāras [arrived]. (29)
Having also realized through the power of yoga that Vaikuṇṭha had been made new,
as well as the true nature of Nārāyaṇa and the true nature of Lakṣmī.
With hearts set on seeing for themselves new palaces in the form of ten million female slaves, they were liberated while still in the form of children.
Those who have not practiced yoga regarding the nature of passion treat women as if they were ignorant; likewise, being ignorant of the union with women, they do not even recognize it as an obstacle.
Exerting themselves for the sake of seeing him, they descended from the path of the sky;
having gone to the area within the enclosure wall, they entered the chamber of pleasure.
Then, seeing Lakṣmī closely embracing Nārāyaṇa,
they went to the side of the two and respectfully carried away their bodies.
All those five-year-old boys, free from any fear, massaged the feet of the two lords and served them. (35)
Having attained joy and served Nārāyaṇa,
the virtuous Lakṣmī became pure and gave food and other provisions to those boys.
Having been fed, honored, seen, touched, and bowed to, they departed;
then Mahālakṣmī spoke to the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa. (37)
O Blessed One, such a vision as this is never appropriate for you;
for children are free from defects and likewise devoid of [mental] afflictions. (38)
But other great souls, sages, gods, and others, having learned of this from the children, became eager for a vision [of him] starting from this point. (39)
"They will always come here again and again for the sake of seeing us;
indeed, there would be constant obstacles for us if we were seen at an improper time."
Maid-servants should be appointed there as guardians at the gate-towers and other such places;
or rather, O Blessed One, do as you wish, according to your desire. (41)
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa appointed the female gatekeepers as was appropriate;
yet even though they were so appointed, in some places and at certain times, due to the excess of their love, they [acted otherwise]. ||42||
Leaving Hari at the gateway, they depart, and even the gateway becomes empty;
yet the seers and sages, perceiving this, come back with devotion. (43)
Then, for the sake of beholding Vaikuṇṭha— that is, for the purpose of seeing Hari—
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was again entreated by Lakṣmī.
"O Blessed One, let the office of doorkeeper be firmly granted to your devotee, so that those friends of yours, immersed in affection, do not remain standing at the door. (45)
"Let those who have exerted effort toward the office of gatekeepers be appointed there.
Having heard this, Hari then called to mind his sovereign powers and excellent qualities.
Possessing sovereign powers and virtues, the attendants, beautiful in form, assumed human shapes with four arms and approached his presence. (47)
Having praised Nārāyaṇa and bowed to Lakṣmī, they spoke these words of instruction:
"O Great King, show us here; we have been born by your will.
Thereupon Keśava spoke of the sovereignty known as Jaya and Vijaya.
"In this matter, my instruction is that you must perform the very duty of gatekeepers.
Thus he appointed Nanda and Sunanda, as well as Puṣpadanta and Sātvata,
and Kumuda and Kumudākṣa, to the city gates.

His attendants, who possess the eightfold sovereign powers, guard the gate-towers; Lakṣmī, accompanied by ten million female servants, serves her husband without hesitation, just as a shadow follows its own body through the dharma of devotion to a husband. ||51||
She recognizes no other man as equal to Nārāyaṇa;
she never beholds any other group of men, not even the gatekeepers.
Lakṣmī does not speak with others, nor does she ever touch anyone else.
She knows no other delight than that of Hari, the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha;
she recognizes no other existence than that of the four-armed Nārāyaṇa.
He speaks of no other qualities except for the qualities of Nārāyaṇa;
he does not meditate upon, remember, think of, or resolve anything else. (55)
"Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord;
Nārāyaṇa is the Seer of all; there is no other Lord higher than him.
Thus, with her whole being, she becomes absorbed therein and remains [in that state].

She who offers responsive speech, who grants happiness to her husband, and who follows her husband—such a woman, devoted solely to her husband, is Lakṣmī herself. Whether during sleep, lovemaking, bathing, reclining, eating, or receiving honor, as well as during recreation and all prescribed duties, she remains ever by his side. ||57-58||
There, on the bed, Narāyaṇī was indeed serving Śrī Hari;
at that moment, the young princes arrived there once again to see him.
Sanaka and the others, the sons of Brahmā who are eternally perfected children,
have likewise come here for the sake of beholding You, O Hari.
Then, leaving the ramparts and the gates from the great sky,
they descended in the form of Brahmā and went into the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
Having performed service as before and having repeatedly offered their salutations,
those five-year-olds departed with joyful hearts, fully satisfied.
When this occasion had thus arisen regarding Mahālakṣmī,
the gatekeepers and others were then commanded to block the passage of those who were moving about.
They should not enter without permission, nor indeed should they do so;
whoever they may be, the duty of gatekeepers must certainly be performed.
Thus commanded by Mahālakṣmī, they became the protectors of all directions;
yet, without the permission of Mahālakṣmī or even that of Hari, they never [acted] anywhere.
Even if Hara and the other gods were present, they would not grant entry;
in this way, Lakṣmī, constantly intent on service, serves Kṛṣṇa.
Free from doubt and exceedingly pure, worshipped by millions of female attendants,
she is eternally devoted to her husband and serves Śrī Narāyaṇa.
After the higher yogic sleep, the lotus-born goddess enters yogic sleep;
while sleeping on her bed, she constantly performs a massage of his limbs.
First abandoning his yogic sleep, Hari gives the water of life and the powder for cleansing the teeth for the purpose of purifying his mouth.
She also provides warm water for bathing and other purposes, along with fragrant sandalwood paste,
clothing, ornaments, and flowers.
For the sake of nourishing the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), she adorns Hari;
she always causes him to enjoy sweet food and the drinking of milk.
The drinking of cool mud, clay, or water yields the fruit of purifying the mouth;
likewise, the offering of betel-leaf and the like results in the cleansing of one's garments. ||72||
One should indeed wash the vessels for Kṛṣṇa’s food and other items with one's own hand,
offer seats and so forth, and perform the preparation of the hair-ornaments, the crown, and other regalia for Keśava.
The offering of musk, collyrium, saffron, unbroken rice, and so forth; the fanning with a whisk to provide a breeze; and likewise the spreading of the bed-clothes. (74)
In this way, that devoted wife performed the various auxiliary rites:
the vow, worship, recitation, fire-offering, as well as reading and hymns of praise. (75)
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, this devoted wife indeed performs all of this;
as Nārāyaṇī, she engages herself in the service of Nārāyaṇa. (76)
Then once, Mahālakṣmī, accompanied by a thousand female attendants, went to a beautiful garden with the desire for recreation. (77)
There, on a soft and auspicious spot covered with green grass, resplendent with rows of trees rich in various branches and abounding in the fragrance of flowers; (78)
She dallied with her friends, praised her own happiness,
spoke highly of that which is worthy of great esteem, and the beautiful woman attained a sense of pride.
O friends, even though the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa is the sovereign of all,
he always carries out his actions only after ascertaining my intention.
"Indeed, by my service, the Lord Mādhava has been brought under my control;
he does not remain in the palace for even a moment without me. (81)
"Let them behold me with gasping breath, for Keśava remembers me;
he will arrive here in an instant, or else let us go to him. (82)
He does not disregard my words, whether they be humorous or factual;
whatever Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa says, He does exactly that. ||83||
By me alone he possesses a home; by me alone he is always graced with splendor;
and by me alone have you all been given to that Supreme Self. (84)
"None other than I am worthy of honor here; I am like her, fortunate and full of pride"—Nārāyaṇa recognized her as she had fallen into such arrogance. 85.
And this Mahālakṣmī, devoted to her husband, having attained an extreme state of pride through her smile, was filled with arrogance and departed from that place along with her female companions. (86)
Having returned home and arrived at the city gate,
Hari, who humbles all pride, entered with Jaya and Vijaya.
Seeking the vast gateway of the Lord, she, surrounded by her female companions,
was stopped at the door by Jaya and Vijaya.
Then, because of those two, Mahālakṣmī was defeated; yet that great virtuous lady, possessed of self-respect, bowed down while concealing her humiliation. (89)
Intent on casting off her body while remembering the lotus feet of Hari,
all the gods then arrived there for the sake of witnessing it.
The Grandfather, Maheśa, Viṣṇu, Dharma, Bhāskara, Candra, Kāmadeva, Vaiśvānara, and the Lord of Wealth; ||91||
The sages, the ascetics, and the Manus, as well as the leaders of obstacles;
Mahendra, Varuṇa, the breath of the world (Vāyu), and the consumer of oblations (Agni). ||92||
Standing at the city gate, they all praised Mahālakṣmī:
"Forgive us, O Blessed Mother, O you of forgiving nature, O Supreme One beyond the supreme! (93)
O you whose nature is pure being, worshipped by the virtuous goddesses;
without you, the entire world is like a corpse and devoid of fruit.
You are the very embodiment of all prosperity, and all women are but portions of you;
those people who worship you, who are worshipped by the entire creation, [attain all success]. (95)
One who is without a wife obtains a wife who is well-disciplined, virtuous, of excellent character, beautiful, charming, exceedingly dear, and sweet-spoken. || 96 ||
A sonless man obtains a son devoted to Viṣṇu who lives long;
and he obtains a grandson endowed with virtues, learned, and illustrious.
One whose kingdom has been lost shall regain his kingdom; one whose fortune has vanished shall regain his fortune;
one devoid of fame shall obtain fame; and one who has lost his wealth shall obtain wealth. 98.
For you are indeed possessed of such great yogic sovereignty;
O Goddess, do not set your heart on death, but be merciful.
Having heard this from the gods, Mahālakṣmī said to them:
"I do not abandon my body now out of anger, nor out of detachment."
Having reflected upon this in your hearts, O gods, listen to this auspicious [truth]:
that in which there is indeed equality toward one’s husband, the true Lord, whether he be like a blade of grass or a mountain.
What is the use of life for me, who am equal to a servant and a wife, yet have been cast out by this doorkeeper, while I am the foremost of Kṛṣṇa’s wives? (102)
That woman who is unfortunate toward her husband is unfortunate in every respect; for her there is no happiness in bed or at the meal, and her life is in vain. (103)
For her who has no affection for her beloved, life is meaningless;
so what is the point of a son, wealth, beauty, prosperity, or even youth?
She who has no devotion for her husband is indeed unfortunate toward her master;
she is impure, devoid of dharma, and abandoned by all sacred rites.
He is the kinsman, the refuge, the sustainer, the deity, and indeed the preceptor.
There is no one higher than the master; there is no preceptor greater than the master. (106)
A father, mother, son, or brother indeed gives only a small amount of wealth;
but the husband is the master who bestows all his possessions upon his wives.
Only a certain woman— born of an exceedingly noble lineage, a great virtuous wife, and an ascetic— comprehends the supreme greatness of her husband.
Born of an ignoble lineage, immoral, and devoid of dharma, she who is wicked and intent solely on her own self-interest reviles her husband out of anger. (109)
That woman who hates her own master, her husband who is equal to Viṣṇu and her guru,
shall fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell for a period measured by one day of Brahmā.
Vows, fasting, charity, truthfulness, merit, and long-endured austerity—all these become ashes and are rendered useless for a woman who is devoid of devotion to her husband. 111.
Therefore, I shall say nothing harsh to my husband;
however, by insulting the servant of Hari, I shall certainly give up my life.
Even when her husband is at fault, a great virtuous woman should not speak harshly to him;
if she is unable to endure it, she may lawfully give up her life.
Service to her husband is the vow of women; service to her husband is the supreme austerity; service to her husband is the highest duty; service to her husband is the worship of the gods.
Service to the husband is the supreme truth; the praise of charity and sacred fords is likewise supreme.
The master embodies all the gods; he is pure and the very embodiment of merit.
The deities always desire the sight and the touch of that virtuous woman who eats the remnants of her husband's meal and always drinks the water used for washing his feet. (116)
"Indeed, all true sacred fords purify sinners from their evil.
Having heard this, Brahmā himself, full of devotion, spoke to Satī.
Neither Jayu nor Vijayu will fare well, for you, fearing the offense against your master, did not curse those two servants. (1.18)
If a most virtuous person does not curse an offender out of forgiveness, his total destruction will surely come to pass; do not delay, O chaste lady! (11.9)
If one is unable to curse and is not empowered to inflict punishment,
then Dharma indeed inflicts punishment upon the guilty person.
"Forgive everything, O Mother; go, go to the presence of your beloved.
For us too, there will be the gain of seeing Hari here. (121)
Then Lakṣmī said: "O gods, if I am indeed devoted to my husband, if I am desirous of the duty toward my husband, and if I am the giver of life for the sake of my husband. (122)
If she is always devoted to her husband and unwavering toward him, and if she always abides by the duties prescribed by me; (123)
"By the power of my devotion to my husband, may Narayana come here;
may my husband come to the city gate to grant me his vision."
"If I am truly the wife of Hari, always the object of his affection,
and have renounced all my possessions for the sake of Hari, then let Hari come here."
"If I am the living wife of this man, devoted to him as his very self and faithful to my husband, then let Nārāyaṇa appear here; otherwise, I shall die."
Having spoken thus, Mahālakṣmī produced fire from her foot;
just as she was about to burn him, Kṛṣṇa arrived.
Holding that Lakṣmī to his chest, he kissed her and embraced her;
saying, "Forgive my cruelty, O Goddess," he became a flowing liquid.
With tears in her eyes, he said to her: "You are truly a devoted wife;
indeed, it is by the power of your devotion to your husband that I have come here to the city gate."
"Come here; do not be angry, O virtuous lady. This was done by me through a servant for the sake of testing you and to quell your pride. (1.373.130)
My equanimity is the same toward my devotee, my wife, and my kinsman;
indeed, my devotee is even more dear to me than my own wife.
My two devotees, your two gatekeepers who expound the meaning of the Katha, are full of devotion; forgive me and them for their transgression. (132)
Having spoken thus to the gods, the Lord of the worlds, having taken delight in their vision and having placed Lakṣmī within his heart, went into the interior of his own abode.
Then Hari, having summoned the gatekeeper, spoke to him comfortably:
"Do not fear, my child; remain at ease. What cause for fear is there while I am present?"
"But who is the teacher for my devotees? Go, child, to your own seat.
I have indeed sown the seed in the worlds for the sake of their departure. (135)
Indeed, human beings shall sing this which was composed for that purpose;
and by means of it, my devotees shall attain liberation through my life-story.
There Hari spoke to the gods: "Let them hear how, in every respect, she is stainless;
through her supreme dharma of devotion to her husband, he has been brought under her control. (137)
Leaving his lion-throne and approaching the gateway,
even though he is the support of all, O gods, it was solely by the power of her devotion to her husband that he arrived.
Therefore, there is indeed no dharma equal to this which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
whether a man or a woman, the devotee serves it with the vow of fidelity.
"He attains my state; O gods, I go toward him.
I dwell in their home and am entirely subject to them."
Having been addressed thus, the gods bowed, offered worship, and went to their own abodes;
Satī became devoted to service, and such is the fruit for both the listener and the speaker. 141.
Jaya and Vijaya, who were formerly the embodiments of Hari’s sovereignty,
became the two attendants of the Lord through their vow, being the sons of the repository of the Vedas in a previous creation.
Due to the curse of Rādhikā, both of them were born as the two sons of Tṛṇabindu;
because of their mutual curse, they performed Marutta’s sacrifice for the sake of wealth.
Those two, Gaja and Grāha, having been born, were sent away from Vaikuṇṭha;
by Hari’s own will, those two attendants were once again expelled.
It should be understood that these two Daityas were born here again and again due to a curse;
and finally, they will become the two attendants known as Aiśvarya.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of Nārāyaṇa’s Attraction toward the City Gate by means of the Chaste Wife’s Lamentation," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the greatness of devoted wives, regarding the destruction of Vaikuṇṭha-Mahālakṣmī’s pride when she was blocked at the city gate.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how the devotion to her husband was so firm in Śacī,
even as fourteen Indras came and went.
Indeed, Indrāṇī’s devotion to her husband remained perfect in every respect toward them alone.
Once, however, Bṛhaspati arrived at the assembly.
And Mahendra, intent on bestowing blessings upon the gods,
was seated by Indra out of pride upon a jeweled lion-throne in the assembly hall.
Seeing his own guru Bṛhaspati, who was most devoted to Brahman, he did not rise;
however, all the other members of the assembly rose and paid their respects.
Having offered those blessings and having disregarded Mahendra,
the Guru, filled with resentment over the insult he had suffered, departed in great anger.
The great sage, being righteous, did not utter a curse, but instead maintained his composure;
for without a curse, Indra’s pride was utterly shattered.
If a great person does not curse one who is guilty and at fault, that fault bears fruit upon him;
for dharma destroys the offender.
If a righteous person, out of anger, should curse a violent man who has committed an offense,
that offender shall perish, but the righteous man becomes possessed of wrath.
All merit performed by one who is angry perishes from its very root;
therefore, he who desires his own welfare should never give way to anger under any circumstances.
Even toward a being who has committed an offense, forbearance should be maintained, for it bestows great merit;
for one whose nature is forbearing, the True Dharma itself provides protection.
By insulting one's own guru, or a Brahmin ascetic, a sin equal to that of killing a Brahmin arises for the offender. (11)
The killing of one who is established [in dharma] is proclaimed as an insult;
by that unrighteous act, Indra indeed incurred the sin of Brahman-murder.
Then that evil-natured one coiled around Indra's head;
he became as if intoxicated, as if insane, and filled with delusion.
Terrified, he abandoned the position of Indra and went to the Puṣkara lake;
there, indeed, he took up residence in secret within the thread of Kāma.
Then, perceiving the kingdom to be vacant, all the gods and sages made the royal sage named Nahuṣa the chief authority, even over Indra.
A king named Nahuṣa, seated beside the throne of Indra,
attained a state of being that corresponded to Indra's own existence and acted like Indra himself.
At that time, he indeed governs the kingdom of the fourteen worlds;
sometimes, at some point, he even occupies half of Indra’s throne.
Out of pride, Nahuṣa used to travel even to Indra’s palace, his vehicle, his chariot, and his mount, as well as to his pleasure gardens for recreation.
Having seen Śacī, who was of excellent form, childless yet beautiful, richly endowed with the splendor of fresh youth, and possessed of many charms; || 19 ||
She was very delicate, possessed of beautiful teeth, and though Indra-less, she was permeated with sorrow;
she was a great saintly lady, a noble queen, bereft of her husband, and captivating to the mind.
Nahuṣa fell into a swoon from desire and youth;
standing before her, he spoke with humility as if she were his own wife.
Alas, the course of the elements is so diverse that it cannot be understood even by the wise;
in one moment one attains the state of Brahmā, and in another, the sovereignty of Indra—thus it is perceived everywhere.
O Queen, enjoy my youth for a moment, for I am like Indra;
how could the great lord Indra abandon a woman such as you? (23)
Among men, he who approaches a woman as if she were a servant-girl when she is actually Ahalyā—such is the mind of one whose heart is set upon the wives of others. (24)
There is nothing surprising in this: desire always longs for the new. Compared to her, who is Rambhā, who is Urvaśī, and who is Tilottamā? (25)
Whether it be Menā, Ghṛtācī, Ratnamālā, or Kalāvatī—
none of these Apsarases, nor any others, are indeed equal to her.
Having praised me thus, Nahuṣa said, "Devote yourself to me with affection;
I have attained the station of Indra, while the former Indra has vanished from sight. (27)
Therefore, O Saubhāgyā, become my abode of bliss upon my chest;
for as a lord, I am capable of conquering thousands of Indras through my mere play.
"O Goddess, take me and enjoy yourself with me, adorned with flowers and sandalwood paste;
for by the boons of Brahmā, I am free from old age and death. (29)
"O blessed lady, make me your husband, for I possess eternal and unchanging youth.
I have no desire for the wives of others; yet, having seen you, my mind has become covetous."
Even there, I shall become Indra today, and you by nature shall be my wife;
become mine today as one who is requested, and certainly not by force.
Having spoken thus, Nahuṣa sought an answer;
then the virtuous Śacī spoke to that human king who was her servant.
Listen, O King, to my ever-justified devotion to my husband:
I was created by Brahmā for as long as fourteen Indras endure. (33)
"I indeed become the wife of the fourteen Indras in succession;
among those fourteen, you truly have not been counted at all."
Therefore, you are by no means suitable to be my husband;
you are a human being, O Great King, and I am indeed a goddess. (35)
"I am not worthy to be your wife; a goddess should not consort with a mortal.
Listen, O Great King, to another matter concerning the very station of Mahendra."
Only the task has been entrusted to you by the gods, not the status of Indra; rather, your state of servitude has been offered to them.
"O Indra, since you are not present, perform for me that which is Indra's task; in this way, the entire task is entrusted to you by virtue of your being the primary agent. (38)
Neither Indrāṇī, nor the throne, nor even the celestial abode, nor likewise the status of Indra has been bestowed upon you by the sages; do not, therefore, indulge in vain pride. (39)
Listen further, O Great King, you who are endowed with the duty of protecting your subjects;
for having attained equality with a father, you are indeed counted as equal to a father.
The status of being the father of the gods shines forth in Indra by virtue of his sovereignty;
likewise, the status of being a father has been attained in you toward one such as me. (41)
"I am not married to you, nor was I intended for your sake;
therefore, I am certainly not yours to enjoy—do not persist with me in vain. (42)
Furthermore, O King, hear the truth:
when the former Indra has passed away, I shall burn my previous body in the form of Satī and assume a new one.
In this way, thirteen times I have fashioned a new body;
I have taken up another Indra as well, and by that means, I am truly devoted to my husband.
O King, if you are capable, then indeed cast off this human body;
take up a new divine one, and thereafter once again the station of Indra.
Obtain a place among the fourteen in the assembly of divine sages;
thereafter, granted by Brahmā and the others, I shall become your beloved. (46)
"O passionate lady, I am not otherwise; I am by no means to be enjoyed by you as long as Indra, together with the Asuras, remains away at Puṣkarābjaka. (47)
And you are indeed the king of the land of action, but not of heaven;
a king should be a protector from fear, the guardian and father of all. (48)
Having fallen from his glory today due to the teacher's wrath, Mahendra has gone to the earth;
you, however, have been appointed to this task, for you are like a father to the subjects. (49)
You have been appointed to the burden of duty; Indrāṇī has not been appointed to you.
Indeed, among the kings on earth, there is no other who is consecrated as king like the former kings.
He shall become renowned on earth as his son and his disciple;
for the wife of the former king is indeed accounted as the queen mother. (51)
"Furthermore, the wife of a newly crowned king is reckoned as a queen;
in this manner, O Great King, I shall become your mother. (52)
"I shall not become your queen; knowing this, do not harbor such longing.
[I am] the wife of a guru, the wife of a king, the wife of a god, and likewise a daughter-in-law. (53)

The sister of one's father or mother, the wife of a disciple, the wife of a servant, a maternal aunt, the wife of one's father, the wife of one's brother, a mother-in-law, a sister, and a daughter; ||54||
The wet-nurse, the chosen deity, and the sixteen mothers of man—among these, you are Nara and I am the wife of the god; indeed, I am your mother in every respect.
"Go, my child, to Aditi to sport with her, if you so desire;
for there is no atonement, my child, for those who approach their mother. (56)
They are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā;
thereafter, they become worms for seven kalpas, and after that, [they attain liberation].
"O King, lepers and barbarians are born for seven lifetimes; thereafter, their sin perishes.
Tell me now, does your mind turn toward the womb of your mother? (58)
There are many apsarases here, if you desire goddesses; yet they dwell in places full of moisture, rich in filth, and abodes of foul odors. (59)
"Even though you have experienced many such things, tell me why you still have this latent impression (vāsanā) in your heart regarding female genitals, which are so common."
O King of kings, since you, a possessor of excellent dharma, have been born as the lamp of your lineage and the lord of heaven,
how can you desire the secret parts of another man's wife?
Even though you have attained heaven, why does thirst not cease here?
O virtuous one, tell me, what happiness do the righteous find within the wombs of women? (62)
The vow of devoted wives is service to their husband, which is their supreme austerity;
for women, this very dharma is that he is their son and their lord over another.
Just as kings protect their subjects like their own biological sons,
so too do kings look upon their subjects and their wives as they would a mother.
Kings, who are protectors of the gods and the brahmins, perform sacrifices;
they also restrain the wicked and provide protection for the virtuous.
Indeed, kings protect virtuous women;
O King, why do you adopt such a contrary course of conduct here?
Having spoken thus, the devoted wife Mahendrāṇī became silent;
then King Nahuṣa, speaking with arrogant words, addressed Śacī.
Listen, Śacī, to this which is consistent with logic; if it pleases you, you should accept it.
Having performed good or evil deeds upon this earth, one takes their fruit [with oneself]. (68)
Elsewhere, a human being enjoys what is taught in the Vedas in heaven and other realms;
having performed great merit upon the earth, the meritorious one goes to heaven.
Having taken all the maidens, he rejoices for a long time in heaven;
the man goes to heaven, leaving behind his human body.
"I have come here in my own body; behold my merit, O beautiful one!
By the merit of many births, I have reached this desired heaven. (71)
By merit even greater than that, he attained the station of Mahendra;
this great merit of mine is my very meeting with you.
For this place of action is not itself the place for one's own enjoyment;
and in a place of enjoyment, the object of enjoyment cannot be abandoned. (73)
But you were the object of enjoyment for Mahendra; I was seated upon his throne.
Now that he is without a master, you have become my object of enjoyment.
You were created for my enjoyment, by which I have attained the state of Indra;
since I am inscribed upon your fortune, I remain established in the position of Indra.
And you, O beloved, are worthy of me as long as I remain Indra;
once the position of Indra is relinquished, I shall indeed never look upon you again.
"Come, beloved, I shall enjoy myself with you within the inner chamber of the house;
cast away this mental hesitation and rejoice, O divine among men! (77)
Having spoken thus, she ceased; and Śacī, having heard this, grieved for him who was senseless, foolish, and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done. ||78||
Today I shall hear what kind of discourse there is for one afflicted by desire; for one intoxicated by passion is like one intoxicated by wind or wine—a person devoid of consciousness. (79)
A lover whose mind is captivated by desire does not take death into account;
indeed, he then spoke this appropriate reply to Nahuṣa once again.
Heaven is indeed a place of enjoyment where the fruits of one's actions are experienced;
yet you have not performed such deeds by which I might become an object of your enjoyment. (8.1)
Ask indeed the King of Dharma, and likewise ask the other teacher;
even flies and small creatures stand upon Indra’s vacant throne.
They are certainly not Indras, nor do I become their object of enjoyment;
Indra alone is my husband, for I am no mere fly or common creature.
But you, O King, being such as you are, do not indeed harbor a false insistence;
listen, O King, to that which must be kept secret: that I am now in my courses. (84)
"O King, today indeed marks the first day of my season;
on the first day of her season, a woman is as impure as a Caṇḍālī. (85)
On the second day she was equal to a washerwoman;
on the third and fourth days, she became pure for the sake of her husband alone. (86)
Thereafter, she becomes fit for rites pertaining to the gods, ancestors, and so forth;
however, he who approaches her while she is in her menses incurs the sin of a portion of the murder of a Brahmin.
On the second day, the eater shall become guilty of the sin of killing a cow;
on the third day, the eater shall become possessed of the guilt of killing an embryo. ||88||
In the fourth month, having bathed, she becomes fit for her husband;
the husband should offer the *ṛtudāna* (gift at the time of the season), according to the rite prescribed by the Vedas. (89)
If a gift is given on nights that are not paired [i.e., odd-numbered], a daughter is born;
but if a gift is given on paired nights [i.e., even-numbered], a son is born.
Up until the end of sixteen nights, there may be the capacity for the retention of the embryo; beyond that, however, there is only cessation, and indeed no retention of the embryo occurs.
In that regard, one must not approach his wife, for it would be a defilement resulting in the destruction of the seed;
such is the established dharma, yet you have indeed abandoned that dharma.
"Today he is overcome by desire; go to your own queen on earth.
O Great King, obtain peace; I shall perform a long vow. (93)
Having heard those words of Śacī, Nahuṣa then laughed and spoke words contrary to dharma, devised out of a desire for enjoyment.
The wives of the gods are eternally pure; menstruation does not exist for them.
The sin incurred by one who is menstruating exists in the world of mortals, but certainly not here in heaven. 95.
"In this world, I am a descendant of the lunar dynasty, Mahendra, who dwells among the ranks of the gods;
I have no affliction from menstruation, so come here, O beautiful one. (96)
"If the sin of [missing] my season should fall upon me, what would you gain by this, O beautiful one?
Prepare a bed for the sake of pleasure; let there be union today. (97)
Having spoken thus, the king ceased, waiting for a response;
Śacī said, "Listen, O King, your intellect has come to ruin. (98)
"Knowing that devotion to one's husband is invincible and that it brings destruction upon the audacious who would violate it, speak first after having indeed reflected upon this. (99)
I curse you if there is no protector for you here;
for the great dharma of devotion to one's husband is the very embodiment of Nārāyaṇa.
Nārāyaṇa, Hara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Vairāja, and the Īśvaras—
even they tremble before supreme dharma, shaken by the power of devotion to a husband.
The sun, the moon, Varuṇa, Yama, Death, old age, and the like—
even Time, Saṃkarṣaṇa, and Rudra— tremble before a woman devoted to her husband.
Clouds, Saturn, Rāhu, Dānavas, and even Rākṣasas;
Daityas, gods, fires, oceans, and likewise mountains. (103)
They tremble indeed because of their devotion to their husbands; therefore, reflect upon this in your mind:
a devoted and virtuous wife truly brings back to life a husband who is dead.
That very virtuous woman alone pacifies the dissolution of waters;
that devoted wife indeed makes the heat of fires cool.
By turning back Mahākāla, the devoted wife indeed remains alive;
the devoted wife indeed causes the obstruction of the paths of the sun and the moon. 106.
A devoted wife indeed causes the abundance of flowers and fruits on trees; by her mere resolve, a devoted wife instantly pacifies even Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana weapon and Brahmā’s world-destroying missile.
A virtuous woman brings about the destruction of the merits of one who has committed an offense;
indeed, a devoted wife is capable of even bringing about the dissolution of the universe. 108.
A devoted wife is capable of turning land into water, water into land, the sky into earth, and earth into the atmosphere; she can turn a woman into a man and a man into a woman.
Do you not know this, O King of Kings? What thought has taken hold of your mind?
"A devoted wife is capable of completely severing the nooses of Yama;
therefore, O King, go to the earth and do not let your mind become troubled.
When this dispute had arisen, Bṛhaspati arrived there.
Because the king was the very embodiment of Indra, Śacī performed her honors with great care;
yet, filled with bashfulness, she went straight into the interior of her own quarters.
Having received hospitality from Nahuṣa and having bestowed his blessing,
he then went to the palace of Śacī; there, upon a beautiful seat offered by Śacī,
the Guru sat down, as the purpose of his visit had been announced by her.
Then, although the Guru was entreated properly by the distressed Śacī, [he did not grant her wish].
Protect, protect me, O illustrious one, for I am submerged in an ocean of grief;
my husband, your disciple, has been driven far away from his own kingdom by you. (115)
While Nahuṣa holds the position of Indra, he has come to my hermitage, which is now desolate,
and is making a violent effort to take me as his wife.
"I am a woman devoted to my husband; I do not desire another husband, O Teacher.
I cannot bring myself to abandon the supreme dharma of devotion to one's husband, O Teacher. (117)
Both the king and the preceptor are always considered worthy of honor and worship;
however, this should continue only so long as there is peace through conciliation before conflict arises. (118)
"A curse must never be uttered by a virtuous woman, regardless of her capability," reflecting thus, I did not cast a curse upon King Nahuṣa;
nor was even you cursed for your offense against your husband, out of respect for you.
"O Guru, if what I have said should not prove true,
I shall curse you and Nahuṣa, and total destruction will follow.
Nevertheless, let there be no haste in my mind regarding the destruction of great beings."
Having said this, she declared: "O Guru, grant peace and happiness, so that my husband Mahendra may return to his own home, and that Nahuṣa may be deprived of his position;
let such a course of action be undertaken."
Having given him the dust of your feet, bestow blessings upon that Mahendra.
Among all gurus, however, the one who gives birth is the supreme guru;
the mother, a hundred times more venerable than the father, is to be honored and saluted as the most weighty.
The giver of learning, the giver of mantra, the giver of knowledge, and the giver of devotion to Hari [are likewise gurus].
The mother’s father is a hundred times more worthy of worship, salutation, and service than the mother herself. || 125 ||
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the applicator of the collyrium of knowledge.
The giver of birth and the giver of food are considered gurus, as are others.
And heavy burdens were forcibly imposed, as well as other weighty tasks.
Likewise, there are those who approach with reverence—both students and even teachers—who are unable to reach the further shore in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra. || 128 ||
One who knows the sciences and mantras, who bestows them, and is skillful in the rites of others—he is capable of uplifting the disciple, for he is a lord, even a lord of lords.
The Guru is Viṣṇu; the Guru is Brahmā; the Guru is the god Maheśvara.
The Guru is Dharma; the Guru is Śeṣa; Keśava, the soul of all, is the Guru.
He is the abode of all sacred fords and is inhabited by all the gods;
he is the divine Hari himself in the form of the Guru, the essence of all deities.
Indeed, when one's chosen deity is enraged, it is the Guru alone who is capable of providing protection.
When the Guru is angry, even the beloved deity is truly unable to provide protection.
When the Guru is angry, the planets are angry, and the gods are entirely angry; even one's fortunes are angered. One should never cause the Guru to be angry. (132–133)
The self is not dearer than the guru, nor even a beloved son;
wealth, wife, austerity, merit, virtue, and truth are indeed not so dear.
There is no teacher higher than the guru, and no kinsman higher than the king.
The mantra, the vidyā-guru, the deity, and likewise the husband obtained previously—
he is to be known as higher than the highest, standing above all.
The mother is venerable, the father is venerable, and a guru such as you is also venerable.

You are the most excellent among the learned Brahmins and the most venerable among ascetics; you are the most devoted to the Veda among those who know the Veda, and the most righteous among all who follow dharma. I have always known you to be worthy of worship by the gods in every respect.
Then I begged for forgiveness, saying: "I shall certainly not curse my guru.
Be pleased, O best of sages; bring Śakra here without delay.
Quickly cast Nahuṣa down from Indra’s abode to the surface of the earth. (138–139)
Having spoken thus, Śacī was inwardly satisfied, yet outwardly gentle; then, maintaining silence with fortitude, she quickly sought the fruit [of her purpose].
Bṛhaspati then said: "O devoted wife, you are blessed!"
"You are indeed capable of cursing me, yet I am protected, as is the king. (141)
"May women become such as Śacī is, who provides protection.
Having said this, he spoke to Indrāṇī: "Everything will turn out well;
by my blessing, you shall immediately regain your husband, Mahendra."
"O beautiful one, you are to me just as Kaca’s wife was;
as a son is, so is a disciple—for there is no difference between a son and a disciple—whether in the offering of libations, the giving of funeral cakes, or in protection and gratification. (143–144)

Just as one who bestows fire is considered a father and a son, so too is a disciple determined to be such; likewise, a father, mother, teacher, wife, child, protector, and kinsman [are defined by their roles]. (1.45)

These are the ones who must be constantly supported by men; this is the eternal dharma. He who directs his human intellect toward his mother, father, and teacher—his infamy spreads everywhere, and he encounters obstacles at every step.
He who, intoxicated by his own excellence, brings about the humiliation of his own guru, [is ruined]. (147)
"Before long, his own total destruction will surely come to pass;
for even upon seeing me in the midst of the assembly, Indra did not rise. (148)
"O virtuous lady, behold now that Indra who enjoys the fruit of those deeds;
O devoted wife, I am capable of granting you liberation. (149)
By the power of your devotion to your husband, even Nahuṣa shall perish;
Indra will come to you quickly, and everything will be as it should be.
O virtuous lady, your power shall be equal to that of Durgā;
your established status shall be like that of Lakṣmī, and your fame shall be equal to her fame.
Her good fortune is equal to that of Rādhikā; her love for her husband is equal to hers;
her honor and respect are equal to his; this is said to be the preeminence of affection. (15.2)
Equal to Rohiṇī, you shall be dear to the heart; equal to Sarasvatī, you shall be worthy of worship; you shall always be pure, forever resembling Sāvitrī. (153)
Having spoken thus, the preceptor there instructed her in protection: "O virtuous one, tell that Nahuṣa [this]: 'If he wishes to enjoy Śacī... (154)
Having mounted an unprecedented vehicle, you shall arrive at night,
having placed your auspicious palanquin upon the shoulders of the Seven Sages.
"Mount it and come; you ought to enjoy Śacī's company.
Then those very words of Śacī were reported to the mountain king.
Laughing, Nahuṣa also spoke quickly to his servant:
"Go, go, go with haste; bring the Seven Sages here at once! (157)
Thus addressed, the messenger departed and quickly brought the Seven Sages;
upon seeing them all, the king bowed and spoke with reverence. (158)
But you are the sons of Brahmā, devoted to the service of others, free from delusion and envy, and devoid of pride and egoism. || 159 ||
May they all, equal to Nārāyaṇa and blazing with the splendor of Brahman,
be truly compassionate for the sake of accomplishing my purpose.
Having heard this, the sages said to him, "Choose what resides in your heart;
we are all capable of granting it for your sake, so do not delay. (161)
There Nahuṣa said to them, "You are indeed devoted to those who seek your help;
now quickly grant me the gift of Śacī, which I desire."
"The great chaste lady Śacī desires this lovely vehicle of the Seven Sages;
therefore, fulfill this very boon of mine today without delay. (163)
Having heard this, the sages laughed at the deluded king;
they placed a palanquin upon his shoulder, and the king proceeded toward Śacī.
"O King, the sages are now worn out and proceed slowly;
let the sages move quickly! Thus he spoke repeatedly to the sages. (165)
Hearing this, Durvāsas became enraged and spoke first:
"Since you said 'let them crawl,' you shall become a serpent, a python. (166)
Thus addressed, the great king immediately became a python;
fallen from his palanquin, he offered praise to the ascetics.
The sages, however, said to the king: "From the sight of Dharmaputra, liberation from the serpent will occur, and you shall go to Vaikuṇṭha. (168)
Having spoken thus, the compassionate sages departed for the truth;
hearing that, Śacī went and bowed with reverence to her preceptor.
Bṛhaspati went quickly to Puṣkara,
upon the lotus fibers where Indra indeed shone, and he summoned the lord of the gods.
"O child, come here; I am your preceptor, Bṛhaspati.
Hearing the subtle voice of his preceptor, Indra abandoned his disguise and approached.
He fell like a staff and placed him upon his chest with affection;
having led him away and caused him to perform a sacrifice, he brought Soma to Amarāvatī.
He bestowed upon her supreme sovereignty, four times greater than that of the former;
Śacī obtained her husband through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the chastity of Śacī has been recounted to you here;
it is the pacifier of the sin of killing a Brahmin and bestows the fruit of the Soma sacrifice. (174)
The sacrificer performed the drinking of *soma* juice for one year;
he subsisted on fruits for one year, and drank only water for another year.

Then the powerful Indra performed a three-year vow; yet he thought, "This sacrifice, though requiring all accomplishments, involving abundant food and great sacrificial fees, is not for everyone. (176)

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Chastity, Beginning with Śacī’s Attainment [of Nahuṣa] while Traveling on the Vehicle of the Seven Sages after Being Sought by Nahuṣa as the Proxy for Indra, when Indra had Fallen from His Position due to the Insult to Bṛhaspati and Taken Up Residence in a Lotus Fiber," in the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives within the first book, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonderful power of the devoted wife Ahalyā.
Ahalyā was the wife of the sage Gautama, and she was a devoted wife.
In that prince’s body, a mass of splendor existed on all sides,
just like the halo surrounding the moon at all times.
The wise sage Gautama lived on the bank of the Gaṅgā at Kāśī,
always in an elevated place within a leaf-hut in Brahmapurī.
Once, upon the snowy mountain, there occurred a downpour of rain with the force of clubs;
the floods of water caused the rivers to abandon their boundaries on both banks.
And terrifying currents rushed along wrong paths;
carrying away villages, hamlets, and market towns, they swept along entire cities. || 5 ||
The waters swelled all around Kāśī,
and the sages, other seers, and the subjects fled to the low-lying ground.
All those who were submerged in the water died, and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose; hundreds of thousands and tens of millions of people residing in the countryside were drowned there.
Mankind, beasts, winged creatures, and likewise forest-dwellers—
as well as Gautama, who was absorbed in meditation— beheld the dissolution and the end.
Emerging from his meditation, he approached and said to his wife Ahalyā:
"O, look at this destruction caused by water, which has ruined all our possessions!"
These waters of the Gaṅgā, though rushing toward your dwelling,
indeed come together with great speed even at this elevated place.
The leaf-hut, as well as I, you, the horses, and the cows—all have been destroyed in many ways; even now, that dissolution does not cease.
"Tell me, O auspicious one, what must be done? The water has reached the steps.
Look, dear child, the heifers are lowing at the sight of the water. (1.2)
Exert yourself quickly so that we may live;
for there is no other place of elevation here besides our house, apart from the house itself.
"How will humans survive by clinging to trees? O virtuous lady, what will be the state of the cows? A great calamity has arrived. (14)
Having spoken thus, the divine Gautama, his eyes filled with tears, lamented;
Ahalyā said to him, "O Lord, whatever is to be, that shall come to pass. (15)
"Having touched my supreme husband, I shall indeed become pure";
having spoken thus, the virtuous woman quickly entered the interior of the leaf-hut.
She kindled the fire and performed an oblation with clarified butter;
by the power of her devotion to her husband, Ahalyā indeed called upon Gaṅgā to mind.
"Come here, O sister Gaṅgā! Why indeed do you cause my destruction?
If you do not come, O auspicious one, I shall surely reduce you to ashes. (18)
Terrified, Gaṅgā arrived in the form of a beautiful maiden;
becoming a servant, she paid homage to Ahalyā, the wife of Gautama.
Ahalyā said to her quickly: "O Gaṅgā, what calamity has been wrought?
Today your waters are bringing about the dissolution of living beings.
O Gaṅgā, withdraw your waters immediately; otherwise, in an instant—"
"I shall perform the funeral oblation for you; once dead, you will surely go to dissolution."
Hearing that, she trembled and spoke dejectedly to Satī:
"What shall I do, O great virtuous lady? No fault of mine is found here;
for Himālaya, the vast mountain, does not indeed obstruct the waters."
Indeed, it does not protect itself; therefore, this ruin certainly exists.
Having heard that, he laughed and said to Gaṅgā: "Stay in my house, O beautiful one;
I shall summon Himavat and employ a means for that purpose."
Having spoken thus, the wife of Gautama, in the presence of the fire, called to mind:
"O Himālaya, come here; otherwise, your oblation shall be consumed. (25)
"I shall do so; do not delay, witness the great slaughter of living beings."
At that moment, the king of mountains trembled and appeared there in embodied form.
Having bowed down to that chaste lady at Kāśyāmahalyā where she was present, he said to her:
"Tell me, O Goddess, how am I remembered here? Direct me quickly."
Behold this deluge of water; why do you not protect it?
Restrain the waters in the forests and upon the mountains. || 28 ||
Then the Himalaya said: "O Mother, I am not capable there;
it is not my fault that the water must always be guarded by me. (29)
I have water upon my peaks, and in my valleys and caves.
And on the belly, on the heights, and even on the plateaus and valleys.
In the wildernesses, in the forests, above, in the rivers, and even on dry land,
I shall maintain water everywhere as far as it is possible.
However, for seven days continuously, there was excessive rain;
day and night, it fell incessantly like a torrent of clubs. (32)
"I am submerged in water; what can I do? I have no power. Today the waters, equal to my own measure, are swelling and overflowing. (33)
Indeed, the clouds do not withhold the rain that brings about dissolution;
for if the clouds were to withhold their waters, all things would go to ruin.
Having heard him, Ahalyā said to him, "Wait; I shall summon a cloud. With a swift mind, she then remembered a cloud by means of a ritual invocation (āhuti).
Agitated by the fear of death, the clouds quickly arrived there.
Trembling, they set forth, and the beloved of Gautama spoke to them.
"O clouds, you are destroyers! Why have you not reflected? Withdraw the waters immediately, or else you shall be dead!
Hearing those terrifying words, they trembled before that virtuous woman.
They said, "O Mother, there is no fault on our part; rather, the fault lies with Indra. (38)
But we are his servants; indeed, by his command we rain down, though we are terrified, exhausted, weary, deprived of water, and even filled with wrath. (39)
Struck down by the thunderbolt, we all rain here; forgive us, for we are always powerless, living only by the command of Indra. (1.375.40)
"O virtuous lady, we are not able to do anything without his command.
Having heard these words of the clouds,
the great satī remembered Indra with a mantra and offered oblations into the midst of the fire.
Then Indra, drawn away by the mantra, fell from his throne;
swiftly traveling through the path of the sky, he landed at the leaf-hut, crying out, "I am dead! I am destroyed! May the hosts of deities protect me! ||42-43||
Speaking thus, he remained in the leaf-hut due to the power of the virtuous woman's influence;
then the great virtuous woman bowed and spoke to Mahendra, the mountain of the gods.
O Indra, why indeed has this great slaughter of living beings occurred on earth because of this rain? Why do you not bring about their destruction? ||45||
"O God, perform the withdrawal of the waters and their immediate obstruction today;
otherwise, O Surasura, I shall perform a fire-sacrifice within the midst of fire."
Thus addressed, he became greatly enraged; however, seeing her to be a devoted wife and perceiving that his own destruction was imminent within a moment, [he desisted].
Having understood that agreement regarding humility, Purandara then said to the clouds: "Make a blockade quickly! (48)
Even though the clouds were gathered there on the Himalayas, there was still no flow of water; then the devoted wife spoke. (49)
"O Indra, O clouds, O Gaṅgā, why indeed do you not descend? Why are the waters of the rivers not seen? Tell me! [1.375.50]
Indra said: "O most virtuous lady, Varuṇa resides within the waters;
