he would cause contraction in the water, and then the rivers would surely become low-lying."
Then that virtuous woman called to mind Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures and the presiding deity of the waters; and at that moment, he too arrived.
Ahalyā said to that Lord of Waters: "You do not even see my husband;
what kind of dissolution has occurred? Indeed, withdraw your waters!"
"Otherwise, your death would occur in fire; there is no doubt about this.
Thereupon, he too quickly bowed down and performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Indeed, due to that agitation, the waters became churned;
the rivers flowed, yet they were constricted on all sides.
Then, having seen her kinsmen and relatives indeed suffering and dead,
the compassionate Ahalyā then asked the Fire-god for the means of restoring them to life.
"Indeed, let a means be told here for those who have died;
[the means are] Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Gaṅgā, the clouds, and the mountain. (57)
Everyone said, "King Yama is considered the bestower of life and non-life.
Ahalyā then remembered him, and Yama arrived there at that moment.
With palms joined in reverence, he said to her, "O virtuous lady, what task must I perform here?
To him, the chaste woman replied, "Quickly [act] here while this dissolution in the waters has not yet passed."
He saw deceased humans— forest-dwellers, householders, and those living in the wilderness—
as well as domestic animals, other living beings, various species of birds, and reptiles.
By my power, restore to life all those who have died untimely deaths;
if you do not restore them to life today, your own death has arrived.
"I shall consume you as if you were a mere blade of grass; quickly restore the dead to life!
At this, Yama, the lord of death, trembled and spoke with a dejected mind.
My existence is always dependent on Rudra, and I am ever a follower of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
indeed, the death of embodied beings, as well as their [destiny] according to their karma, is subject to him alone.
At that very moment, Satī remembered Rudra and Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the two destroyers of Time arrived, and having bowed to Satī, they stood before her.
Satī said: "Let the two Lords restore all the dead to life;
otherwise, by virtue of my devotion to my husband, I shall take away your very lives."
Rudra and Saṃkarṣaṇa have said that creation, nourishment,
and destruction indeed occur here in succession, fashioned by Nārāyaṇa.
In this matter, we are not capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise; the supreme Śrī Hari alone is capable.
Then Satī remembered Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; by the power of her devotion as a faithful wife, Hari arrived there in an instant.
Having bowed down with a mind full of great humility, Satī spoke to Hari:
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Master! (69)
And here, during that great deluge, millions of living beings died—
human beings, animals, species of birds, and likewise other creatures.
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, bring these back to life, for they have met with untimely death.
The Blessed One then said to them, "Make a resolve indeed! (71)
If the dharma consisting of devotion to my husband has been preserved by me, then let all living beings who have died from the force of the rain come back to life. (72)
By this command of Hari, a resolve was made there by her named Ahalyā; at that very moment, all these embodied beings were restored to life.
Wherever their corpses were placed, there they rose up;
as far as the edge of the ocean, all those who were alive at that time [were restored].
At the command of Hari, Gaṅgā, the clouds, Indra and the other gods, Himādri, Varuṇa, Rudra, and likewise Saṃkarṣaṇa [honored her]. ||75||
Nārāyaṇa, Yama, Kāla, and Mṛtyu—the attendants of Hari—having led all [the deceased] back to their former places and their respective homes, [departed]. (76)
By the power of her devotion to her husband, the lords brought her back—
beautiful, highly capable, and lovely in her fresh youth.
Having bowed, all the gods then departed for their own abodes;
those who are born with life are indeed born happy. (78)
Upon seeing Gautama’s wife, who was devoted to her husband, Indra became bewildered; the Lord of the Gods went far away and then returned. (79)
Then, although he had seen her before, the king of the gods did not see her afterwards;
therefore, he departed for heaven in despair, and indeed returned there again after some time.
Even then, he did not see her staying in the leaf-hut;
for one with a defiled heart does not perceive a woman devoted to her husband.
Having returned from there to heaven, he came back after some time;
even then, he did not see her staying in that leaf-hut, though she was indeed present there.
Women devoted to their husbands never come within the range of sight of those who are sinful, impure, and characterized by base qualities. 83.
Thus Indra, though he came and went many times, trembled and fainted even as he sought to violate Ahalyā. (84)
Blinded by desire, he did not recognize the death of himself or others;
then, after some time, he arrived at the surface of the earth during the night. (85)
Where that virtuous and devoted wife Ahalyā, who was composed of dharma, resided, there a great darkness spread all around during the night. 86.
That splendor was seen by Mahendra in the vicinity of Gautama’s hermitage;
he descended upon the earth, beholding that splendor alone.
Just as this orb of the full moon's autumnal radiance [shines], so too he did not see Ahalyā there; then he returned once more to heaven. 88.
She told Candra of her mental agitation, saying:
"I am a divine form full of splendor, long desired as an object of enjoyment. (89)
Candra informed him: "You have assumed the form of Gautama;
I am indeed the cock who announces the hour for Brahmā."
"Let us go to where she dwells; by employing a stratagem, the fruit [of our purpose] may be attained.
If it does not happen, death will occur—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (91)
Having thus deliberated, the cat and the cock then went at the hour after midnight to the vicinity of Gautama's house. (92)
The moon-like cock sang its crowing at the hour of Brahma;
hearing that sound, Gautama then went to the celestial river to bathe.
But Mahendra, indeed, entered the house through Nala in the form of a cat;
assuming the guise of Gautama, he went to his beloveds on the bed. (94)
But Ahalyā, seeing her husband approaching with lustful intent, offered him a kiss, being herself devoted to the desire for sexual enjoyment. (95)
Then, O Gautama, the celestial river suddenly spoke to him:
"O sage, this is not the time for a Brahmin; there must be some deception on your part regarding your home. (96)
"Go quickly and see Satī; having heard this, Gotama will surely return home at once, while Hari remains standing ready to eat. (17)
Gautama beheld Indra, who had assumed his own form and was full of guile; indeed, having perceived that Turāṣāḥ was lusting after Bhaga, he [reproached him].
The sage cursed Śakra, saying, "May you indeed have the mark of female genitals," yet Ahalyā, though she recognized him as someone other than her husband,
did not curse him because he bore the form of her husband’s image; for she was devoted to her husband.
She did not offer an embrace as long as she recognized him as another Gautama;

though she was capable of inflicting a great punishment upon that Gautama who stood before her in his own form and deserved such a penalty, she did not do so because he appeared in the likeness of her husband.
"The husband himself is returning; Gautama knows this personally.
As long as I do not embrace him, he will inflict punishment.
Thinking thus, Ahalyā then became excessively proud of her husband's form.
He did not cast a curse upon Indra, but instead himself meted out a counter-punishment.
Indra, possessed of a thousand vaginas and stained with impurity, departed for heaven;
the Moon, however, being concealed, fled from him, overwhelmed by fear.
Then Gautama said to his wife, "O gentle one, what do you desire?
For a woman who is not exceedingly beautiful brings happiness, yet attachment to women brings suffering. O beloved, you indeed observe the foremost of duties in every way."
I am constantly intent on performing penance; assistance for both [of us] does not grant happiness. If I abandon you out of detachment, you will become sorrowful;
if I keep you by my side, such anxiety as this arises.
"Therefore, tell me, my beloved, what shall I do so that once again I may have no anxiety for you, and there may never again be an obstacle to your dharma.
Having heard this from her husband, the virtuous Satī, devoted to her husband, spoke to him.
"O Lord, I, Pārvatī, always dwell within this vessel as its very self;
likewise,
I dwell eternally upon that stone which serves as your seat, O Lord, having taken refuge in you and being presided over by you."
Because of that, you shall have no anxiety, nor shall there be any obstacle to your dharma;
my devotion to you as my husband shall always be preserved,
and indeed, O Lord, your liberation shall come about through yoga.
Having spoken thus and bowed to her husband, she was quickly consecrated by her lord;
indeed, she became a stone there, forever resting upon her husband's feet.
Then her beloved husband, the Lord Śrī Rāma himself, spoke to her.
He will come right here and find rest in you;
then, O wife, you shall certainly go with me to Vaikuṇṭha.
Until then, I shall always perform penance there according to my heart's desire.
Those who are free from desire possess great peace, both for me and for them here always.
Those possessed of desire are perpetually submerged in the ocean of the sea of suffering;
they never reach the further shore of the latent tendencies of saṃsāra.
O beloved, liberation—which is like a stone and free from obstacles and the like—has been attained by you; your service to your husband has always been as firm as a stone seat.
"I shall remain upon the summit of this rock and perform penance here for a long time;
in the Tretā age, through union with Rāma, we two shall go to the supreme state."
"O virtuous lady, remain forever steadfast in service to me with this second divine form; this is my desire.
Thus addressed, the devoted wife Ahalyā became a stone right there.
But Gautama, her husband, performed austerities upon that rock.
"In the Tretā age, through the yoga of Rāma, those two attained the supreme state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you of the wonderful sovereignty of Ahalyā;
by reading or hearing this, one's devotion to her husband shall become firm. || 121 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Gaṅgā, Himādri, Meghendra, Varuṇa, Rudra, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Yama, Nārāyaṇa, and Others, the Subduing of the Excessive Rainfall, and the Restoration to Life of the Dead through the Power of Ahalyā’s Chastity, as Well as the Liberation of Ahalyā from Her Stone State upon Indra’s Merely Touching Her Genitals," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives, in the first part, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to what the nature of Sītā’s devotion to her husband was;
for the sake of her husband, she gave up her life and endured great suffering indeed from birth.
Having experienced [hardships] in the great forest and in the houses of Rākṣasas and others, that virtuous woman,
though she was the very form of Lakṣmī, finally sank into the earth.
She was the daughter of Kuśadhvaja, born from the womb of Dharaṇī;
indeed, having broken the bow, Rāma married her.
In the city named Sāketa, there was indeed a king named Śatamakha;
his son was Śātamakhī, who became Rāmāditya.
His brother Narāditya was born from Dyutivarṇā;
he was Viṣṇu himself, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who had been entreated by Brahmā.
Vāsudeva, the exceedingly righteous Rāmāditya,
was born on earth during the first part of the Tretā Yuga from a woman of the twice-born caste.
Sent by Viśvāmitra for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas,
he set out together with the Sun among Men (Narāditya) and the sage.
Having seen that Ahalyā, devoted to her husband, who had been transformed into the form of a stone by Gautama, he, possessing divine vision, [beheld her] on his own path.
Then Rāma, the sanctifier of the world, having heard that account of the past, questioned Viśvāmitra regarding the cause [of his arrival]. || 9 ||
Recognizing her through her divine form as one solely devoted to the service of her husband,
he touched her with his toes, and she became a *padminī*.
And she, having offered blessings upon Rāma, departed with her husband by means of a celestial chariot to the supreme world, the Truth, for she was devoted to her lord. (11)
Gautama bestowed auspicious blessings upon Rāmāditya as well;
thereafter, he went to that spot on earth which was purified by the touch of Vāmana’s foot.
Rāma saw it right there and, desiring to remove the dust from her body, he wiped away that purifying dust with his hand out of devotion.
Having gone to the hermitage of Viśvāmitra and slain the Rākṣasa Mārīca, and having gone to Mithilā and performed the breaking of Śambhu’s bow; || 14 ||
And there, O Lakṣmī, the Blessed One took Sītā’s hand in marriage;
having performed the wedding, he joyfully departed for Ayodhyā.
The king, having shown great respect, desired to appoint his son as the monarch;
he quickly brought the water from the heated sacred bathing place for the eminent sages.
Having seen Rāmārka, who had completed his consecration and was endowed with all auspiciousness,
Queen Kalahā, by the power of her previous words, [acted].
He restrained the king from the previously accepted boon—
the exile of Rāma to the forest and the kingship for his own son.
Although he was unworthy and entirely deserving of destruction in time,
the great king, who follows the path of justice, did not wish to grant him a boon.
The wise Rāmārka spoke to that king, who was endowed with righteousness and truth:
"The merit that comes from the gift of a hundred tanks is even greater than that."
O Father, by the gift of a step-well in this world, men obtain merit;
and the merit from the gift of ten step-wells is even greater than that. (2.1)
That happiness which may be obtained by men on earth through a single sacrifice, and that which is even greater than the merit of a hundred sacrifices—[that is attained here]. (22)
By beholding this son here in these lands of action, one obtains merit greater than that which comes from seeing a hundred sons. (23)
O King, by the preservation of truth, a meritorious person attains [virtue];
for there is no dharma higher than truth, nor is there any sin greater than falsehood. 24.
There is no kinsman superior to Dharma; there is no wealth superior to Dharma.
What indeed is higher than truth and Dharma? Protect your own duty with effort. (25)
O King, when one's own dharma is protected, there is constant auspiciousness everywhere, as well as fame, firm establishment, majesty, and supreme honor. (26)
Having renounced the pleasures of home for fourteen years in accordance with dharma,
I shall wander and dwell in the forest for the sake of upholding your truth.
Having made a vow of truth, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
he who does not fulfill it finds his expiation in ashes;
he is cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a day of Brahmā.
Consequently, that person shall become mute and afflicted with leprosy for seven lifetimes. ||29||
Having spoken thus and bowed to his parents, Rāmāditya, accompanied by Nārārkā, took up matted hair along with bark garments and departed for the forest.
Sītā, devoted to her husband, set out together with her lord;
Rāmārka said this to her: "O beloved, stay here, do not go."
In the forest, there are indeed many sufferings at every step;
you, O Jānakī, are unable to endure them all. || 3.2 ||

Sītā said: "The lady with limbs like a young tree, whose life is her husband, who is dear to her husband, a virtuous woman devoted to the duty toward her husband, and a protector of the vow of fidelity. (33)
I have indeed been bestowed by Janaka upon you and not upon anyone else;
my husband’s command must be obeyed by me, for such is my duty. (34)
O Ocean of Compassion, I pray to you: without you, death is certain for me;
here, there will be no refuge for me without my husband. (35)
Death in the forest is better for me than being in the presence of my husband;
for wives, there is no path to the world beyond without their husband. (36)
In this world, there is no destiny whatsoever without a husband;
in his happiness there is happiness, in his suffering there is suffering, and when he is gracious, there is grace. (37)
When her husband is hungry, the virtuous wife should be hungry; when he is satisfied, she should be satisfied.
A wife who is intent on the joy of her own self-interest and is partial [to others] shall go to hell. (38)
By her good fortune, she becomes a virtuous woman endowed with auspiciousness;
yet, even if she lives, she who is bereft of her husband is as if dead, while she who has her husband is truly alive. (39)
A woman is half of her husband's side; such as I am, I belong to you.
I am not fit to be separated from you, for my husband alone is my heaven.
The wanton woman, abandoning her suffering husband, desires pleasure for herself;
yet the devoted wife, the great saintly lady, accepts her share of suffering. ||41||
If by the giving away of all one's possessions the husband may become happy, then a woman should always seek her husband's happiness even at the cost of her life or her body. 42.
A husband must be protected by a woman even by selling her own body in times of distress; having set aside wealth from her inheritance, a virtuous wife must protect her lord. 43.
The Master is one's own Supreme Brahman; Dharma is the Master; Bliss is the Master; the Creator is the Master.
Everything is the Master, and indeed nothing else; how could there be a union with happiness otherwise? 44.
Therefore, as the Lord's shadow-form and his obedient companion, I must always remain with him; I must by no means remain here.
Wherever there is a husband, there are heaven, Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise liberation;
as well as sovereignty, supreme prosperity, great wealth, dharma, and even the aesthetic sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra). ||46||
Without a husband, a home is like the den of a jackal, even a royal palace;
and all objects of enjoyment, in every respect, are equal to poison. (47)
Heaven is not truly called heaven; for a woman, her husband is always her heaven.
A religious vow is not truly called a vow here; for a woman, her husband alone is her vow. 48.
Dharma is not merely called "dharma"; for a woman, her husband is always her dharma.
Likewise, charity, recitation, worship, good fortune, and peace [depend upon him]. (49)
Everything succeeds for a wife who remains by her husband's side, but not otherwise;
one whose husband is absent or whose husband has departed does not obtain the fruit.
Behold, my dear, the misfortune of a woman when her husband has gone to another land:
she becomes devoid of luster and utterly stripped of the power of enthusiasm. (51)
A universal empire devoid of a husband is indeed equal to a mere hovel;
but a leaf-hut accompanied by a husband is superior even to the station of Indra.
For a woman, a forest is not truly a forest, nor is a house truly a house;
a forest with her husband is heaven, while a house without a master is a forest. (53)
A body with its husband is divine; a body bereft of its husband is merely a corpse.
Ornamentation is not said to be true adornment; for the husband alone is indeed the true ornament. (54)
They present her, though she is without a husband, as a courtesan adorned with ornaments; they offer her water, food, garments, auspicious substances, and collyrium. (55)
When joined with a wife, it is full of splendor; otherwise, it brings about corruption.
Therefore, O Lord, a husband should always dwell together with his wife. (56)
For a wife without her husband at her side is destined for destruction;
O beloved, may I not meet my ruin by being separated from you here in this house. (57)
"O Keśava, you alone ought to show such supreme compassion," she said, her eyes filled with tears, wearing garments of bark. (58)
Perceiving Rāma’s inner intent, she indeed prepared for the journey;
Rāma said, "O virtuous lady, hunger will be difficult to endure in the forest."
Sītā said, "O Lord, my hunger will not be appeased at home.
Rāma replied, "O virtuous lady, in the forest, thirst will lead to death."
Sītā said: "At home, my lord, you will kill me with hunger.
Rāma said: "In the lovely forest, you will die at the hands of lions and other beasts. Sītā said: "At home, O beloved, separation from you will consume me."
Rāma said: "O wife, in the forest the heat will take away my life."
Sītā said: "In my home, the fire of separation from Rāma will blaze;
therefore, the forest fire of cold is superior, for it is more cooling than the fire of domestic cold. (6.3)
Rāma said, "O Daitya, someone will one day carry you off in the forest.
Sītā said, "In that case, Rāma must be meditated upon.
Rāma said, "Therefore, he will not take her while she is stained with blemish."
Then Sītā said, "The dharma of the virtuous shall be made manifest."
Then Rāma said, "Afterwards, Satī will undergo separation.
Then Sītā said, "Sītā will attain union in Vaikuṇṭha."
Rāma said: "Happiness has certainly never been seen by me through this body.
Sītā said: "Suffering has certainly never been seen by me without you. (67)
Rāma said, "O Sītā, you will be a source of sorrow in the forest.
Sītā replied, "Having abandoned me at home, you will experience extreme suffering. (68)
Afflicted in the forest and tormented again and again, Sītā, who has her husband as her sole support, will not utter even a sound of distress, not even in her sighing.
Sītā, devoted to her husband, will in the forest practice every form of resolve for his favor and total avoidance of anything contrary to him. (1.376.70)
Protected by Agni and further approved by Rāma,
she shall cast aside the Rākṣasa through her shadow and manifest her devotion to her husband.
Having indeed caused the Rākṣasas along with their letters to wander by means of her shadow,
Sītā, endowed with purity, shall again be united with Rāma.
By the will of her husband, Chāyā indeed became dissolved in the fire;
yet Satī, considering her husband’s words to be for the sake of protecting dharma, [remained].
Sītā, the virtuous wife who does what is pleasing to her husband, will instruct him;
for the forest, being the abode of one’s guru, is as venerable as heaven according to the husband's wish.
Obedience to the husband's word is the supreme duty; the husband is Śrī Parameśvara himself.
Through Sītā, Lord Rāma, having slain tens of millions of rākṣasas, [revealed this truth]. (75)
Desiring to protect her in his heart, he will command his wife;
she is of divine form in Vaikuṇṭha and resides within his heart in Sāketa.
"O Sītā, invisible to people, you must always perform service for me.
Having received this command, she will indeed enter into the earth.
"You ought to take this young Jānakī with you";
having spoken thus, she was filled with enthusiasm to go into forest exile. (78)
Sītā, the illusory guide of the path, assumed a divine form;
she went ahead there, and Rāma then beheld her.
The virtuous woman, with a human form visible, went behind Rāma;
likewise, Narāditya also proceeded in the form of a servant.
Accompanied by Sītā, the sun-like Rāma departed for the forest;
meanwhile, O beloved, Indra abandoned his own body due to grief for his son.
To fulfill his father’s promise, Rāma wandered in the forest;
and after some time in the great wilderness, [he encountered] the sister of Rāvaṇa.
Afflicted by desire, the Rākṣasī Brāhmaṇī beheld Rāma;
Śūrpaṇakhā said to him, "O Rāma, you who are the abode of beauty, accept me! (83)
Rāma said: "I am with my wife; go instead to my younger brother, who is without a wife.
I am devoted to the vow of having only one wife, and taking another would cause me sorrow. (84)
Having heard this, she indeed said to the Sun among Men, "Devote yourself to me.
But the Sun among Men, being a celibate student, spoke thus to that Rākṣasī: 85.
"It is not the time for me to take a wife; go, gentle one, to other people.
Śūrpaṇakhā, becoming enraged, said: "If you two reject me in vain... (86)
"Indeed, a calamity shall befall you both, there is no doubt;
by my curse, this Rāma shall be deprived of his wife. (87)
To her who had spoken thus, "I am a Rākṣasī," the Sun among men (Rāma), in order to make a pretense of slaying a demoness,
cut off the woman's nose with his weapon.
On account of that very cause, Narāditya dispatched fourteen thousand rākṣasas along the path of Yama in battle.
The ascetic Śūrpaṇakhā, having performed penance, became a hunchbacked woman;
she indeed obtained Kṛṣṇa as her husband after attaining him through a boon from Brahmā.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā went to the island named Siṃhala;
there she indeed spoke of the deeds of Hari to King Rāvaṇa.
Rāvaṇa, too, his mind incensed by the words of Śūrpaṇakhā,
resolved firmly in his heart to abduct the virtuous Sītā.
Rāvaṇa was strongly dissuaded by his wife Mandodarī from the violation of that devoted wife,
who was the consort of another man.
"O Lord of Siṃhala, do not go anywhere that results in total destruction!
Even though he was thus entreated, he carried away Sītā by means of his illusory power.
Rāma, aided by Sugrīva, having granted a boon to Hanumān and given him his ring as a token of trust, [established] the lord of the monkeys [in his kingdom]. ||95||
Hanumān traveled through the sky toward Siṃhaladvīpa itself;
there, in the Aśoka grove, he beheld the shadow of Sītā, which appeared sorrowful.
She was without food and exceedingly emaciated, established in the chanting of her husband's name;
she bore a heavy mass of coarse matted hair and was meditating upon her lord, her husband. (97)
Having prostrated before his mother, he gave her a jeweled ring and then recited Rama’s message; he then reduced Siṃhala to ashes.
And that devoted wife, with eyes full of tears, spoke to Rāma’s messenger:
"O, does my Rāma live, having emerged from the terrible ocean of my grief? (99)
Is my protector well? Has the Lord not been overcome by grief?
Has a daughter been born to that master in the forest, one whose very form is sorrow?
How much suffering did that lord of mine undergo for my sake?
What food does he eat, my beloved who is dearer to me than life itself? (101)
"Shall I see that Rāma when he has arrived at the shore of the ocean?
Shall I once again perform service at the lotus feet of my Lord? (102)
The life of a foolish woman deprived of the service of her husband is in vain;
yet, O, my son of dharma lives on like a sun among men! 103.
The brother-in-law of the gods, who was like a god himself, was submerged in the ocean of distress;
then Hanumān, having informed her from the sky that she was entirely free from ailment— || 104 ||
He departed and recounted the story of Rāmāditya and his vow of chastity;
then that monkey, having built a bridge with his monkey armies, proceeded onward.
Having slain the lord of Siṃhala, he effected the liberation of Sītā;
then, together with Sītā, he went to Sāketa by means of the Puṣpaka chariot.
Having celebrated the festival of victory and having placed Sītā upon his breast,
both Sītā and Rāma— the sun— extinguished the flame of their separation.
The two sons of Rāma, the righteous Kuśa and Lava, were born in the hermitage of Vālmīki; auspicious, they became the founders of the Solar dynasty.
Sītā, however, was submerged in the earth at the city of Sāketa;
thereafter, Rāma ruled the kingdom for twelve thousand years.
Then, having established righteousness upon the earth, he departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this supreme account of Sītā’s life.
This life-story of Śrī Rāma, devoted to his wife and afflicted by the cruel rākṣasa of the forest, always bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (111)
No one like Rāma— compassionate, righteous, and pure— has been born,
nor will anyone else be born hereafter, except for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Nor will there ever be a wife equal to Sītā, who lives in sorrow yet remains devoted to her husband; no other woman has ever been born, nor even heard of, who lives for her lord.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Sītā—the Daughter of Janaka and Wife of Rāmāditya—Whose Forest Dwelling, Hardships, and So Forth Were Solely for the Sake of Her Husband, Demonstrating Her Devotion to the Dharma of Chastity," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; Rādhā herself, the beloved of Hari who resides in Goloka, [created] her daughter Lakṣmī, as well as Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, and Padmikā. || 1 ||
She spoke of duties devoted to devotion to one's husband and likewise of auspicious radiance;
"Listen, all you daughters, for I shall declare the eternal duties."
For women, the duty of devotion to their husband is supreme; there is nothing higher than this.
In that lies enjoyment, great liberation, and eternal bliss of the Self. (3)
For all those of the various castes and stages of life, for renunciants as well as householders,
for widows, for Vaiṣṇavas, for the virtuous, and for women in every way.
O sons, for sons, daughters, disciples, and those supported by servants,
devotion to one's husband is the supreme duty for all people in every respect.
A woman who is always purified by meditation performs service to her husband;
she constantly enjoys his favor, having offered everything to Kṛṣṇa in every way.
She shall become an enjoyer of Viṣṇu’s grace, liberated while living, virtuous,
constantly devoted to austerity, pure, peaceful, and endowed with wisdom.
A woman who has resorted to the holy ford of vows is always devoted to her husband;
she takes up the mantra of Viṣṇu and performs service to a true guru.
Having received the blessings of the guru, the disciple becomes devoted to her husband;
the guru’s command must always be obeyed, and everything should be reported to him.
Of all those worthy of veneration, the father is the greatest preceptor;
the mother is a hundred times more venerable than the father, and the deity is a hundred times more venerable than the mother.
In that regard, the true Guru who bestows the mantra is indeed four times superior even to the gods;
the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the manifest Guru, the Supreme Lord himself.
The husband alone is the preceptor and the deity, whose essence is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
he is one's own Guru, the manifest enjoyer, and Janārdana himself embodied within one’s own body.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru himself is Śiva;
all the gods reside eternally and joyfully within the Guru, who is their lord.
When the guru is pleased, Hari is pleased; when he is pleased, the deities are pleased.
By drinking the water from the guru’s feet, a virtuous woman becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred pilgrimage sites.
She is liberated from all sins and becomes destined for the world of Viṣṇu;
she is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices.
If a woman herself performs an ablution with the water used for washing the feet [of the Lord],
that auspicious water of the Śālagrāma is ten times more meritorious than the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Even more excellent than that, the water from the feet of the husband is considered tenfold superior;
the wife who constantly partakes of it is liberated while living and is like a goddess. (17)
The daily duty of virtuous women is to eat only what is given by the grace of their husband,
to worship him with diligence, and to partake of the water from his feet.
O beloved, whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, they all abide within the water used for washing one's feet,
for the sake of attaining the fruit of serving one’s wife at all times.
As long as the earth remains moistened by the water from her footprints,
so long is she, in the form of Mahālakṣmī, worshipped by the gods.
Indeed, she who enjoys the favor of her master sanctifies the earth,
as well as the sacred fords and the subjects, for she is one who is liberated while living.
Walking step by step toward her husband, that virtuous woman, sharing in the fruits of her vows,
obtains at every step the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Purified like fire and wind, and radiant like the sun in her splendor,
she thereafter rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha together with her husband, Hari.
For that Vaiṣṇavī woman who worships the mantra of Viṣṇu and serves her husband,
there exists no other goddess on earth more purifying than she.
A devotee of Hari who is a great saintly woman, devoted to the service of her husband, and who is a Vaiṣṇavī—indeed, from her mouth the name "Nārāyaṇa" shall emerge. (25)
The name of Hari emerges as the very form of a mantra;
even he into whose ear it enters becomes greatly purified.
Even he, having pierced through the entire cosmic egg, shall go to the abode of Hari—
[delivering] seven ancestors, seven descendants, and seven beginning with his maternal grandfather.
A devoted sister rescues her own mother and her mother’s mother;
but a singularly devoted Vaiṣṇava woman can rescue a hundred thousand men.
Even if she is devoid of youth, devoid of knowledge, and entirely devoid of learning; even if she is of low birth and devoid of ritual action—if she is solely devoted to her husband. (29)
She is indeed the most excellent, equal to Lakṣmī, and endowed with ten million virtues;
by the power of her devotion to her husband, that virtuous woman uplifts the worlds.

One who is deprived of youth, as well as one of short lifespan, one devoid of knowledge, and the unlearned; one devoid of learning, one devoid of noble birth, and the fool among fools—the sinner of extreme transgression. (3.1)

One who does not belong to any stage of life (āśrama), one devoid of fame, one who is diseased, one afflicted by illness, one without a lineage, one whose lineage has perished, one deprived of a wife, and one who is impoverished; ||32||
A man who is devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, who has abandoned righteous deeds and the like, who is indifferent, of evil conduct, and even destitute of wealth; ||33||
Through the blessings of a truthful, devoted, and virtuous wife,
one attains heaven, one's own desired goals, the abundance of happiness, worldly enjoyment, and liberation, along with long life and strength.
By the mere acquisition of renunciation, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa; by the attainment of service to her husband, a woman becomes Nārāyaṇī. ||35||
Having burned away her own past karmas and severed the karmas of others,
that virtuous and faithful wife goes to the abode of Hari.
Just as the earth is instantly purified by the touch of the feet of renunciants (sannyāsins), so too is the earth purified by the touch of the feet of virtuous women (satīs). 37.
Sacred fords purify immediately, as does a Vaiṣṇava wife devoted to her husband;
by the word of such devoted wives, offspring become free from sin. (38)
By feeding a devoted wife, one obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice;
by bowing to her with devotion and beholding her, one obtains the fruit of the royal consecration sacrifice.
O sons, the fruit is always equal for renunciants, ascetics, and celibate students, as well as for chaste wives, virtuous women, and devotees of Viṣṇu.
Even if she is bereft of her husband, the Brāhmaṇī woman should always remain free from worldly desire;
eating but one meal at the end of the day, she should be devoted to food fit for an oblation (haviṣya). ||41||
He does not wear divine garments, nor fragrant substances, nor fine oil; nor does he wear garlands, sandalwood, or ornaments such as conch-shell and vermilion. ||42||
She should always be accompanied by her husband and her children, and she should constantly worship Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, she should perform the service of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at all times. 43.
Daughters should always utter his name with devotion;
and from the perspective of the duties of widowhood, they should regard any man as equal to a son.
She should not consume delicious food that increases desire simply for the sake of luxury; indeed, she should enjoy nothing except her husband, who is Nārāyaṇa himself.
She too, equal to a devoted wife, being solely intent upon her husband Kṛṣṇa, should listen to the duties of the virtuous and perform service to her guru. ||46||
A virtuous woman devoted to her husband shall be liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
O daughters, listen; I shall indeed declare what must be done by virtuous women. 47.
A woman should always remain in her heart full of longing for her husband;
with devotion and by his permission, she should drink the water that has washed his feet. 48.
She should perform her vows, ascetic penance, and worship of the deities by the command of her husband;
she should also perform service at his feet, offer praise, and bring him satisfaction. (49)
A devoted wife should never perform any action without her husband's permission;
rather, that virtuous woman should meditate upon her beloved as being truly superior even to Nārāyaṇa.
A virtuous woman should not engage in contact with the passion of other men, nor should she participate in processions, festivals, dancing, singing, or playing. (51)
A virtuous woman should act for the sake of her husband and never for any other purpose;
whatever is the constant food of her master, that indeed is the food for virtuous women.
Devoted to her service, that virtuous woman should not abandon the company of her husband;
a devoted wife should never offer a retort to her lord.
She does not become angry even when struck in anger;
she feeds her hungry husband and gives him drink and food. (54)
One should awaken him while he is in sleep, but never urge him toward worldly activities;
for toward a beloved wife, one should exercise a hundredfold more affection than that felt for a son.
For a woman of noble family, her husband is her kinsman, her refuge, her sustainer, and her deity;
the virtuous wife, her face bright with a smile, beheld her beloved whose countenance was white as nectar.
One who beholds her with a spirit of devotion shall indeed become the bestower of all prosperity;
such a virtuous woman may even deliver a thousand men. (57)
And the husband of those devoted to their husbands is liberated from all sin;
indeed, by the power of their devotion to their husbands, there is no further experience of the fruits of karma for them. ||58||
Together with her, they rejoice in the abode of Hari, free from the fruits of karma;
whatever holy places exist on earth, they are all contained within the feet of a virtuous wife.
The splendor of the gods and the sages resides in virtuous women;
all the austerity of ascetics and the vow of those who observe vows reside in them.
The fruit of giving belongs to the donors; that same fruit is found in those [women].
Nārāyaṇa himself, Śambhu, the Creator (Brahmā), the gods, and others [reside there]. 61.
Even the seers and sages certainly stand in awe of a virtuous woman;
by bowing down to one devoted to her husband, one is released from the bondage of sin.
That chaste lady, possessed of great merit, was indeed capable by her own splendor of reducing the three worlds to ashes in a mere instant.
He is the virtuous husband of faithful wives and always possesses a pure son;
indeed, he has no fear whatsoever from the gods or even from Yama.
Born in the home of those possessing the merit of a hundred lifetimes, she was a devoted wife;
her father, too, was a pure mother of a devoted wife and one liberated while living. (69)
A virtuous wife, having risen early in the morning and discarded her night-garments,
bows to her husband and joyfully offers him praise.
Then, having performed her household duties, bathed, and put on two clean garments,
she should take white flowers and worship her husband with devotion.
Having bathed him with pure water rich in fragrance,
one should joyfully give him a clean cloth and wash his feet.
Having seated him upon a seat, having applied sandalwood paste to his forehead, having smeared fragrant unguents over all his limbs, and having placed a garland around his neck as well; ||69||
Having praised and worshipped her husband with ritual offerings, the virtuous woman should prostrate;
then, having offered incense, a lamp, water, food, and betel leaf—thus it is said.
One should joyfully perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord, who is the essence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
having performed circumambulation and prostration, one should then offer hymns of praise.
Salutations to the beloved, the true husband, whose very form is the parasol over one's head;
salutations to the bestower of all happiness and to him who embodies all the gods.
Salutations to you whose nature is like that of Brahmā, who are as if born from the virtuous and the true;
salutations to you who are worthy of homage, worthy of worship, and the support of the heart.
Salutations to you, whose very nature is the life-breath of Satī, who bestows the glory of good fortune, and who is the embodiment of supreme bliss for your wives.
The husband is Brahmā, the husband is Viṣṇu, and the husband indeed is Maheśvara;
the husband is the god who upholds the lineage—to you, the Self that is Brahman, I bow. (75)
Forgive, O Blessed One, the faults committed through ignorance or lack of knowledge;
O Consort of Your Wife, O Ocean of Compassion, please indeed forgive the faults of Your servant. (76)
Then Rādhā spoke to her daughters concerning their respective husbands: "If you perform such a hymn of praise, it will surely grant you all your desires. (77)
Then, at the beginning of creation, this meritorious hymn was composed by Padmā, and it was also composed by Sarasvatī, Dhara, Gaṅgā, and Ramā. (78)
Then Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, and likewise the wives of the sages sang this song upon having obtained their respective husbands, who bestow all powers. (79)
This hymn, which brings auspiciousness and is the very form of grace, was composed for all devoted wives during the Kṛta Yuga by Kaṃbharā.
Thus it was sung by Mahālakṣmī, as well as by Prabhā and Jayā;
it was proclaimed of old by Māṇikya, Lalitā, and Mohinī.
If a man or a woman hears this, they shall obtain all their desires;
one without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth obtains wealth. ||82||
A woman afflicted by disease shall be freed from illness; one deprived of a husband shall obtain a husband.
By praising her husband, a devoted wife shall obtain the fruit of bathing at sacred pilgrimage sites.
A virtuous woman obtains the fruit of all austerities and the fruit of all vows;
she attains heaven and liberation by pleasing her husband. (84)
He who has no mother in his house and no devoted wife has no home;
by him it must be gone to the forest, for that alone is liberation from hell.
The wicked woman always hates her husband and regards him as if he were poison;
she does not give him food and constantly reviles him. (86)
But that most wicked and proud woman, constantly regarding her husband—who is worthy of worship and equal to a sage—as if he were a blade of grass, treats him with contempt. (87)
Burning with the fire of harsh words, he lives as if dead;
yet, having obtained an unchaste woman, he remains so for as long as his life lasts. (88)
Such a woman is not called a housewife; rather, she is said to be a denizen of hell.
A true housewife, however, is devoted to her husband and honored as a deity by the gods. (89)
Having risen early in the morning, being pure, and having paid homage to her husband and the gods,
she should provide auspicious offerings in the courtyard with cow dung and water.
Having completed her household duties, the virtuous woman, having bathed and returned home,
should bow to the gods, the guru, and her husband, and then worship the deity of the home.
Having fed her husband, she should honor the guests with sincere devotion.
Accompanied by her sons, grandsons, and others, the virtuous woman herself enjoys happiness. ||92||
A devoted wife should never conceive a human-like notion toward her teacher, her father, her husband, her mother, her father-in-law, or even her mother-in-law. (93)
Father, mother, teacher, wife, disciple, son, those who are always dependent, a helpless sister, a daughter, mother-in-law, and father-in-law—[these are the ones to be supported]. (94)
These husbands and brothers are always to be served by the command of the husband;
the female species is truly pure, and all of them are devoted to their husbands. 95.
Indeed, every species was created at the beginning by the Self-Existent One as being of a single form;
all of them are portions of primordial nature (prakṛti), pure and always bestowing happiness. 96.
The best [wife] is devoted to her husband and endowed with the duties toward her husband; the middling one is devoted to her husband, though she also accomplishes her own interests. (97)
The youngest wife, though devoted to her husband, remains attached to her husband who is devoted to her;
the other, however, being intent on desire alone, is united even with another man.
Among those, three lead to Dharma, while the fourth leads to the loss of Dharma; this should always be understood by an embodied being, and having known it, one should marry a suitable woman. (99)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you what was said by Rādhā to her daughters;
and they, having heard those duties devoted to wifely fidelity, attained great joy.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Maintaining the Religious Duties and Conduct of a Devoted Wife as Told by Rādhikā to Her Daughters in Goloka," within the section on the Greatness of the Devoted Wife in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another narrative concerning a house-lizard,
which was narrated in the past and which nourishes the dharma of devotion to one's husband.
King Rukmāṅgada, enjoying his pastimes on Mount Raivata,
mounted upon his horse, beheld the unsurpassed splendor of the mountain.
Dugging up the earth with his own hoof, the horse goes from one dry land to another; indeed, as he tears the ground with his very sharp hoof, [he proceeds]. (3)
Within a certain portion of the ground, a lizard had been cut;
the king, who was devoted to compassion, saw it as it was being torn apart.
O Lakṣmī, he sprinkled her, who had fainted, with cool water; through that sprinkling of cold water, she regained consciousness.
Beholding the king before him, Godhā spoke these words:
"O mighty-armed Ruṣmāṅgada, listen to my actions."
Formerly, in the city of Śākala, I was the wife of a brahmin;
though endowed with beauty and youth, I was not very dear to him.
He was always filled with hatred and spoke harshly to me;
therefore, overcome with anger, I [recited] a mantra for subjugation.
A certain woman went to a female ascetic to obtain a means for bringing all under her control;
there, having bowed down and placed my ring at her feet, I spoke.
Having informed my husband of her insult, I remained steadfast;
then, O King, she instructed me in the ritual application accompanied by mantras.
This powder, endowed with protection, brings all beings under one's control;
you should apply it to your husband, as well as to his drink of milk and upon his head.
"My husband will become submissive and will never harbor hatred;
having taken this protective powder, I have come alone to my husband. (12)
At dusk, protective powder was applied to the head of her husband;
at that same time, at dusk, it was also administered to him for drinking along with milk.
From that very night when her husband had consumed the yellow powder,
he indeed became like one afflicted by consumption, wasting away day by day.
My husband, his splendor destroyed and exceedingly weak, spoke to me while grieving day and night: "O beautiful one, I am your slave. (15)
"Save me, who have come to you for refuge; death is near for me.
Having heard this, I went to the female ascetic and informed her once again.
"My husband has fallen under my control; how can he live and be happy?
She then gave him the medicine, and by it my husband was restored to health.
The burning pain arising from the previous powder was indeed pacified by that medicine;
from that time forth, my husband became submissive and remained obedient to my word.
In time, O King, having died, I underwent the torments of hell;
indeed, I was repeatedly cut into pieces and burned in a glowing copper cauldron.
Born on earth during the age of the Yuga-uttara, she was of a sinful nature;
though she remained here as a *bhūmigodhā*, she was of the same species as a house-lizard (*gṛhagodhā*).
Therefore, a woman who for a thousand years seeks to bring her husband under her control,
being of futile virtue and futile conduct, is burned in a copper frying pan.
The husband is the protector, the refuge, the lord, the deity, and indeed the guru;
how can she who acts under his control ever attain happiness? (22)
She goes through a hundred animal births, afflicted with worms and leprosy;
therefore, O protector of the earth, women must always carry out the word of their husbands. (23)
Devotion to her husband is the supreme dharma, the auspicious deliverer of women;
she should never instill even the slightest enmity toward her husband because of the rivalry with a co-wife. (24)
O King, that wife who acts wickedly toward a husband who is dear to her goes to hell for as long as the day of Brahmā.
She who, out of a desire for her husband's affection, would act with a rivalrous spirit toward her co-wife,
reaps that fruit in the southern realm in the scorching copper cauldron.
A wife should indeed act in such a way that her husband may be happy;
she should behave in a manner that is favorable, beneficial, and pleasing to her beloved husband. (27)
A devoted wife should indeed regard her husband as she would herself;
even by serving one who is inferior, she goes to the third heaven.
She who performs what is pleasing to her husband obtains all enjoyments;
by abandoning the state of envy, she shall attain the station of the Lord of All.
She who always serves her co-wife, observing what is pleasing to her husband, shall attain an imperishable world. ||1.378.30||
Listen, O King, I have seen a courtesan named Padminī who was solely devoted to the service of her husband; I shall relate her story to you. (3.1)
Formerly, by the side of my house, there lived a Śūdra together with his wife;
his name was Bhāluka, and his wife’s name was Māṭulī.
Endowed with beauty and youth, devoted to her husband, the Śūdra woman Piṅgalī was the beloved courtesan of Bhāluka. (33)
The virtuous and devoted wife attended upon that most wicked Śūdra, who had abandoned all sacred rites, while he was engaged in service with a prostitute.
She washes both his feet; she eats the remnants of both;
she sleeps at the feet of both; indeed, she is devoted to the welfare of both.
Though she was being restrained by the courtesan, she remained on the path of virtuous conduct;
thus she continued to serve her husband along with the courtesan.
A very long time passed while she remained devoted to the service of her husband;
then one day, her husband [brought] a dish of buffalo meat accompanied by radishes.
But that man of dull intellect ate flat beans mixed with oil; thus he consumed unwholesome food while showing contempt for his devoted wife. (38)
A severe disease, an anal fistula (bhagaṃdara), arose in his anus.
He was intensely scorched by it day and night, for many long periods.
Then the courtesan, having taken his wealth, indeed departed;
devoted to passion, she gave it with affection to another young man.
Then the Śūdra, dejected in mind and overcome with shame, spoke while weeping: "O beloved, protect me! (41)
"O beautiful one, O devoted wife, for many years I, a sinner, wicked and attached to courtesans, have not done you any service. (42)
That wicked man who, out of pride, does not consent to his wife when she bows down to him, shall encounter inauspicious births for fifteen lifetimes. (43)
Therefore, O wife devoted to the service of your husband, due to my insult of you, I shall obtain a contemptible birth in the house of a Divākīrti. (44)
Having heard these words of her husband, the wife said to him:
"Indeed, it is past misdeeds that give rise to sufferings. (45)
The wise man forgives them; through forgiveness he shall become supreme.
Having spoken thus, she took heart and gave her husband this instruction.
Having brought wealth from Janaka, she performed service;
that virtuous woman regarded her husband as being the very form of Nārāyaṇa.
If one performs the cleansing of hemorrhoids with effort three times every day, it provides both nourishment and wind (vāyu). ||48||
That devoted wife sleeps neither by night nor by day.
Tormented by the suffering caused by her husband, she saw the world ablaze with fire. ||49||
If the goddess Earth exists, and likewise the ancestors and the deities,
let them make my husband free from disease and cleansed of all sin.
"I shall offer a bilva fruit and likewise a buffalo to Caṇḍikā, as well as observe the Navarātra vow for the sake of my husband's health. (5.1)
I shall indeed perform ten fasts with great devotion;
I will sustain my body upon a bed of fine thorns.
I shall not enjoy sweets, nor indeed shall I enjoy clarified butter;
deprived of external and internal massages, I shall remain for many days.
"May my husband live for a hundred autumns, free from disease.
With such a resolve, she served him with the thought that he was Kṛṣṇa.
By the power of her wifely devotion,
her husband also became entirely free from disease, providing daily happiness to his wife.
After a long time had passed, he later became afflicted by a fever born of the three humors;
then, at one point, by the course of time, he was brought face to face with Death.
She gave the three pungent spices (trikaṭu) to her husband with great effort;
yet, afflicted by the cold and trembling, he broke his wife's finger. ||57||
A very firm union of both their teeth was achieved;
even though a fragment of a finger remained in his mouth, the beautiful woman [remained] there. 58.
He served him with supreme affection, yet he indeed gave up his life.
Then, having sold his bangle and purchased a great quantity of wood—
Then, having placed her husband in the center, she prepared a funeral pyre smeared with clarified butter;
and descending [from the tree], she drew the fire toward herself with her arms and feet.
Placing her face against his face, her heart against his heart,
and her hips against his hips,
the auspicious and devoted wife caused her husband’s body to be cremated in his very presence.
Together with herself, she of beautiful limbs entered the blazing fire.
Having suddenly cast off her body, she departed with her husband to the world of the gods,
having purified herself of the accumulation of great sins and other evils.
"Thus, O King, have I personally witnessed the Śūdrāṇikā vow, which bestows heaven and happiness; therefore, one should not hate a wife who is dear to her husband. (64)
A virtuous wife should personally feed her husband’s beloved wife;
for a co-wife indeed gives some food to her rival wife.
O King, that fruit shall be infinite, and the reward shall be endless;
she should be known as a devoted wife who always guards her womb.
For women, service to their husbands; for sons, service to their fathers;
for Śūdras, service to the world; and for kings, the protection of the world. ||67||
And that which is called devotion to one's husband consists in protecting her lord;
for if a husband who has many wives should become miserable, it is due to his wife. (68)
For her who is prosperous yet sinful, a downward course has indeed been declared;
that wicked woman goes to the hell named Pūya for the duration of a Yuga. (69)
Then she becomes a muskrat for seven births on the mountain;
thereafter a female crow, then a female vulture, and then as a monitor lizard, she is purified through her state as a cow.
But she who, for the sake of her husband, does not give away existing wealth, or even her life or her own body, shall become a worm in excrement. (71)
Released from the womb of a worm, one is then born as a *kāṣṭhīlā*.
What was previously spoken by the *kāṣṭhīlā* has been heard by me; I shall tell it to you. (72)
In my youth, however, in my village there was a woodcutter who used to split wood suitable for the hearth and bring it to the house. (73)
There, I saw a wooden doll with a shaven head emerging from a log; its body was as soft as butter, and it possessed the luster of the little finger. (74)
In shape it resembled collyrium in its mouth, yet in size it was like a finger-ring;
seeing it fallen upon the ground, a crow approached to devour it. (75)
Just as he was about to seize it with his beak, I immediately drove away the crow with pellets of iron and clods of earth. (76)
O King, that pearl, pierced by the wound of his beak’s strike, was unable to flee;
trembling and utterly unconscious, she remained there. (77)
Then, having been sprinkled by me with water, she attained her natural composure and consciousness;
thereafter, in human speech, she recounted her previous birth to me. (78)
For there was a daughter of the omniscient sage named Sumantu, who was endowed with virtues and became the highly esteemed wife of Kauṇḍinya. (79)
For I am beloved by my mother, my circle of kinsmen, and my father;
I have been given a dowry by my father and also bestowed upon me by my father-in-law.
And ten thousand pieces of gold were given as the most excellent dowry;
at that time, I became very well-provided with wealth from both my father and my father-in-law. (8.1)
I am endowed with cows, buffaloes, and other livestock, as well as wealth and grain; I am beloved by my parents-in-law and esteemed by the people for my virtuous character. (82)
In due time, my most virtuous father-in-law met his death;
taking her deceased husband with her, his wife entered the fire.
Then, after two months had passed, my husband went to the royal palace for the purpose of accomplishing a sacrificial rite; there he saw some courtesans. (84)
From among those women, who were rich in beauty and endowed with youth, he took two—
the jewels among courtesans— and kept them in his house.
Through their constant indulgence, the entirety of their wealth was brought to exhaustion;
when three years had passed, my husband then became destitute. (86)
He entreated me, saying, "Give me wealth as an ornament for my body.
But I did not give that to my husband at that time, even though he was in distress. (87)
But taking everything with me, I went to my father's house; my husband had sold off the household goods and the like, and they were all exhausted. (88)
Whatever wealth belonged to his father-in-law, wherever it might have been located, all of it—including the land, vessels, and household furnishings—was squandered by him. (89)
Then, having boarded a ship with his mind intent on acquiring wealth,
he traveled by way of the ocean until he had gone a great distance by means of the winds.
Driven by the winds, the ship was brought under their power and shattered;
others died, but by fate, my husband clung to a piece of wood. (91)
By means of auspicious merit, Vāyu reached a small island where there were indeed tens of millions of oceanic gems. (92)
Afflicted by hunger, he rested on that bank for a moment;
having eaten ripe tree fruits and drunk water, he became comforted. (93)
Exhausted, he slept at night at the foot of a *sāla* tree;
then a terrible *rākṣasa* approached, carrying a beautiful maiden. (94)
He abducted from the royal palace the auspicious and virtuous daughter of the Lord of Kāśī, named Ratnāvalī, for his own wife to eat.
The Rākṣasa said to his wife, "A man in human form is indeed staying at the mouth of the cave; bring him here without delay. (96)
Having been told this, she went to the entrance of the cave toward my husband;
she said to my husband, "I have come to make you my husband. (97)
"I give this spear into your hand specifically for the purpose of slaying my husband;
yet, if you do not strike the Rākṣasa with this spear," [98]
That one of dull intellect will undoubtedly devour both you and me;
he shall attain that loathsome destiny which people incur by the murder of a Brahmin. (99)
"If I speak an untruth, I shall surely go to that same fate," she said, and having led the Brahmin toward the cave of the Rākṣasa,
she went there and said to him, "Throw this woman into the *suśaktikā* pit."
Upon hearing this, he immediately released that spear toward the Rākṣasa.
Having reduced the Rākṣasa to nothing but ashes, she ascended into the sky;
then, delighted, she said to the twice-born man: "O my beloved, enjoy pleasures here with me."
My beloved was not killed by me at all, but rather he was liberated from sin;
my beloved has been made a Brahmin, and indeed I have become a Brahmin woman.
"May I not be one who destroys your virginity, nor may your husband be destroyed;
I shall come to where your home is, together with the maiden. (104)
Having spoken thus, the Rākṣasī gathered all the wealth from the cave,
assumed the form of a female elephant, and placed my husband upon her back.
He traveled through the path of the sky toward the palace of the King of Kāśī;
then, along with his daughter, the twice-born one descended from behind the female elephant.
The daughter became a female elephant, while the human wife of the twice-born became Ratnāvalī; she then went to her father’s house and related what had occurred.
Though I was staying on my bed at night, I was carried off by a Rakshasa while in my own city;
yet here I am, alive and unhurt—take heart for my sake.
And I have remained chaste, O father, protected by this Rākṣasī;
the Brāhmaṇa has also been protected—give me to this Brāhmaṇa.
"By this [vow], I have become one who sits on a single seat; therefore, let him be my husband.
Then Sudyumna gave her to that brahmin according to the prescribed rite.
Taking both his wives, including the Rākṣasī maiden, the Brāhmaṇa set out for Mahodayapura, mounted upon an elephant, in an instant. || 111 ||
That husband who was previously abandoned, now accompanied by his two wives, is highly prosperous and renowned; he has even summoned me today. (1.12)
Having returned again to her husband's house, she was honored by him as his principal wife;
he then entrusted all his wealth as well as his two wives to me. (11.3)
Indeed, due to my lack of fortune and my treachery toward my husband, I died after only a very short time; having experienced the hells of Yama, I have now been born upon this tree.
Afflicted by extreme suffering, she became a wooden post; furthermore, she will go to the womb of a beast and undergo births as birds thousands of times again.
That woman of beautiful countenance who does not offer her wealth and even her life to her husband will surely reach such a state as this; of this there is no doubt.
Knowing this, she should constantly protect her husband’s wealth and his life;
for the husband is her mother, father, wealth, life, teacher, and refuge. (1.17)
When the husband is pleased, Padmeśa certainly becomes pleased. But she who deceives her husband even with her life or her wealth [is lost].
Having passed through a hundred births as worms, she is born as a Pulkasī woman; though her lover entreats her for sexual union, that proud woman treats him as if he were mere straw.
That wicked woman who does not restrain [her desires] is certainly born as a wooden post (kāṣṭhīlā), whether it be wealth, the body, a son, or whatever other property there may be. || 1.378.120 ||
And for women, everything would be a humiliation without a single husband;
for his sake, they would abandon wealth and even life itself in every respect. (121)
One should renounce wealth, one should renounce servants, one should renounce wife, life, and home;
likewise, one should renounce country, king, heaven, friend, and teacher. (1.22)
One should abandon the sacred ford, one should abandon dharma, one should abandon that which is most dear;
one should abandon yoga, one should abandon charity, and one should abandon vehicles and meritorious deeds.
A virtuous woman may abandon austerity, she may abandon learning, and likewise she may abandon supernatural powers or even liberation;
yet she must never abandon service to her own husband, for that is superior to all of those things.
Service to the husband is proclaimed as the duty of women according to the Vedas;
whatever the husband says, that should be carried out without hesitation.
One should say that white is white; indeed, service to one's husband is white. Everything else before that is black for the sake of a devoted wife.
Then Kāṣṭhīlā told me her entire life story; having fallen into a painful state that threatened her very life, she spoke for the sake of liberation.
"O sister, take my hand and give me here and now the merit that comes from serving my husband for even a single day. (1.28)
"Give me that merit here, by which I may die from this body and obtain another birth, so that I may again perform service to my husband."
"I shall go to heaven, and after that, I will surely attain liberation through service.
Having been addressed thus, she granted me one day for the service of her husband.
By that very merit which was previously acquired by me, she died;
and having obtained a human birth according to her karma at the proper time, she became a woman. (131)
Having become thus, devoted solely to the service of her husband, she attained the highest good;
O King, I, that earth-lizard, now wish to cast off this body.
O King, listen to what was done by your wife Sandhyāvalī:
the merit arising from serving her husband for a single day, which bestows happiness. (133)
Even when the merit is performed for the sake of one's wife, the husband certainly enjoys its fruit in every way;
what is given by you will indeed be as if given by your wife.
Thus addressed, he who was named Rukmāṅgada then bestowed his merit;
abandoning his body as a lizard, he then went to a radiant state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you how a woman attains merit through the act of serving her husband, as well as deliverance and liberation. (136)
From reciting or hearing this, the fruit of serving her husband shall arise;
the sin committed through treachery toward her husband is destroyed without a doubt. (137)
A sinful woman who serves her husband for even a single day rescues herself;
how much more so one who does so throughout her entire life—what will she not bestow?
Whether the husband is devoted to a courtesan, addicted to vice, or has gone astray, the husband alone is the husband of a woman; there can be no other substitute. (1.39)
There may be a substitute for everything else, but there is no substitute for sexual union;
for men perceive the various limbs of other women as belonging to others.
That part of the womb which is fit for seeing is visible [only] to the husband and not to others;
whether he be intoxicated, old, a beast, or even a demon. (141)
Then the Daitya became untouchable, a Cāṇḍāla, filthy, filled with pus, foul-smelling, smeared with excrement, diseased, and swarming with worms. || 142 ||
Whether he be of such a kind or that kind, he alone is the one who beholds the womb;
for no other god or sovereign is fit for the womb according to the law.
In accordance with the nature of things, that [semen] enters the form of the womb as a subtle essence;
having become subtle and taking on the form of the elements, it is born as the self of a son.
He is a protector in the form of a husband, he will protect in the form of a son; indeed, he is considered the very husband who protects one from falling into the next world.
"Whatever has been performed for her sake all leads to the liberation of the woman.
Knowing this always, O Lakṣmī, one should practice devotion to one's husband (*pātivratya*).
Just as Hari, when worshipped by his devotees, himself delivers those devotees.
Likewise, a husband who is honored by his wife uplifts her himself. || 147 ||
Whether they are filthy or discolored, diseased or filled with pus;
whether they are foul-smelling or misshapen, or even like wolves, dull-witted, and infested with insects. (148)
Whether she be fond of liquor and meat, foul-mouthed, wicked, and full of impurities—whatever her nature may be, she is either a rākṣasī or a piśācikā. (149)
Whether she be a Bhūtinī, a Pretī, a Vetālī, a Ḍākinī, or even a Kālikā—
if she is his wife, the husband indeed desires to sport with her in the home.
Where there is fearlessness and delight, that indeed is the eternal Dharma;
where there is fear and delight, that is proclaimed to be Adharma.
Fearlessness, delight, and the two who cause delight—these deliver one from fear;
thereafter, the vow of the wife and her devotion to her husband are always the means of salvation.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of Chaste Wives," including King Rukmāṅgada’s subjugation of his wife by means of a domestic lizard, the account of Bhālukī, Māṭulī, and Piṅgalī, the account of Kauṇḍinya’s wife Kāṣṭhīlā (the daughter of Sumantu), and the account of the daughter of the King of Kāśī; and how their liberation was attained through the gift of the merit earned by a single day of service to their husbands, as well as the specific excellence of chaste wives toward their husbands. || 378 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate to you the auspicious duties of devotion to one's husband, as told by Menā to Pārvatī, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having performed the marriage with Pārvatī, Menā, the beloved wife of Himavat,
settled her daughter down after instructing her in the supreme duties of righteousness.
O Girijā, listen with great affection to these words which increase righteousness,
which bring joy in this world and the next, and which bestow happiness upon those who hear them.
Blessed is the devoted wife such as you, beloved of Śaṅkara;
she is the purifier of all women and the destroyer of all sins.
That virtuous woman who serves her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with love enjoys all pleasures in this world and, at the end of her husband's life, attains the supreme goal.
Through the dharma of devotion to her husband, a wife attains great honor;
she becomes worthy of respect by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, and is likewise honored by sages.
"You must always serve your husband, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world. O beloved, devoted to your wifely fidelity, you should eat only after your husband has eaten."
A woman should remain in that happiness while her husband remains;
she should sleep when he sleeps, and she should always be the first to wake.
A virtuous wife, whose conduct is free from deceit, should always act for his benefit;
she should never appear before him without being adorned.
While her husband is away on business, she should remain devoid of ornaments;
a devoted wife should never utter her husband’s name here in this world.
Even when reviled, she should not revile in return; even when struck, she should remain serene.
When called, she should set aside her household chores and go to his side.
Commanded by him, she should perform her duties with both mind and body as his beloved;
she should not remain for long at the doorway, nor should she wander about in another's house.
One should not disclose the secrets of the household to others, nor should one hand them over;
furthermore, one should prepare all articles for worship even if they have not been specifically mentioned.
A virtuous woman should never go on a pilgrimage or anywhere else without her husband’s permission;
if she desires to visit sacred sites, she should drink the water from her husband’s feet.
In the water used for her husband’s feet, all sacred pilgrimage sites and holy fields are present;
she should enjoy the favor of her husband, as well as sweet food, water, and so forth.

One should certainly not eat without having first distributed [the food] among the gods, guests, and ancestors, as well as among the circle of attendants, the cows, and the families of mendicants. || 16 ||
With her household utensils well-maintained, joyful, and averse to excessive expenditure,
she should be devoted to her husband and observe religious vows by his command.
She should never rouse her husband from his seat when he is sitting comfortably and at ease;
nor should she revile him when he is distressed, impotent, diseased, or even old.
During the three nights of her menses, a woman must not show her own face at all;
having bathed well, she may look upon the face of her husband, but never that of anyone else.
When her husband is absent, she should look at the sun while remembering him;
she should apply turmeric, saffron, a dot of vermilion, red lead, collyrium, and other such substances.
Betel, the auspicious marriage-thread, ornaments for adornment, the dressing of the hair, the braided coiffure, the bracelet, and the ear-ornament; || 21 ||
A virtuous woman who desires long life for her husband should never cast away her nose-ornament, her sacred thread, or even the substances that bring good fortune.
A devoted wife must never converse with one who hates her husband;
wherever her husband finds pleasure, there she should find the delight of love.
When her beloved is joyful, she is joyful; when his face is dejected, her face is dejected;
in both adversity and prosperity, a virtuous wife remains single-mindedly devoted to her husband.
When ghee, salt, oil, and so forth are exhausted, one should by no means employ [substitutes] for the rites of Viṣṇu, Hara, or Nārāyaṇa, even in times of great distress.
The husband alone is supreme, the truth, and the very embodiment of the Supreme Brahman;
one should not observe fasts, vows, or similar practices without the husband’s permission. (26)
If she gives a reply in anger when spoken to, she would become a female dog (saramā);
if she is contemptuous, she would become a female jackal; and she would become a female monkey. || 27 ||
She should not resort to a high seat, nor should she be full of pride;
O beloved, she should never utter slander, quarrel, or reproach.
In the presence of her elders, a virtuous woman should not speak loudly nor laugh.
Seeing that her husband is returning from outside, the virtuous woman should hasten toward him.
She should please her husband with water, food, fruit, betel-leaf, massaging his feet, and other such services, as well as with pleasant words that dispel his fatigue.
A father gives in measure; a mother, a brother, and a son give in measure.
One should always please the husband, who is the giver of the immeasurable.
The husband is a god, the husband is dharma, the husband is the sacred ford, and the husband is the preceptor;
he bestows happiness both in this world and the next—one should therefore always serve that husband. (32)
Without her husband, she becomes a *tūlūkī* bird that wanders in secret within a tree;
and by striking her husband, she is born as a tigress and a female gadfly. (33)
Another woman who gives sight to men becomes Vakrākṣī Miñjarī; but she who abandons her husband becomes Sūkarī Valgurī. ||34||
She who utters "tūṃ" while addressing her husband is mute and has a small tongue;
she will be filled with hatred for her co-wife, unfortunate, and secretly afflicted by disease. (35)
She who shows her own face to another husband with lustful intent shall become one-eyed, humpbacked, ugly, and foul-faced. (36)
Even a woman of gold, if she is without a husband, is considered equal to a corpse;
blessed is her mother, blessed is her father, and blessed are her kinsmen and relatives. (37)
Blessed is the village and blessed is the country where a devoted wife resides;
she sanctifies three generations on her father’s side, three on her mother’s side, and three on her husband’s side. (38)
By the abundant merits of devoted wives, they indeed become gods in heaven;
the earth marked by the footprints of devoted wives is called Vaikuṇṭha.
Just as the moon, the sun, fire, and wind touch the earth and water with their purity, so too does a sacred ford (tīrtha) become purifying.
A wife is the root of domestic life and the root of bliss; she bestows progeny, is the root of merit in all the worlds, and she is indeed the victory of the home. 41.
She is like the Gaṅgā, purifying, virtuous, and always pleasing to her husband;
she is the goddess who destroys the sins of those who remember her and bestows the supreme goal. 42.
Chastity is difficult to attain even when one exists; it arises naturally from the grace of Śrī.
Having attained the state of a virtuous wife and the true Dharma, one must not destroy them through negligence. (43)
A virtuous woman should always protect her devotion to her husband, even when encountering calamities;
for she has attained this state of virtue through merit, and it is not something she disregards out of atheism.
But that woman who has fallen from dharma becomes unchaste;
whereas she who is devoted to her own duty, truthful, and has conquered her senses [attains the opposite]. (45)
She attains a vast heaven, difficult even for the gods to reach;
therefore, with every effort, a virtuous woman should be devoted to her own duty. 46.
For she who lives for the sake of cows, for the sake of a Brahmin, or for the sake of her husband, indeed preserves chastity (*pātivratya*), which is the cause of all human goals. (47)
She attains her own liberation, earned through service to her husband;
listen, O virtuous daughter, to that which was spoken by Pañcacūḍā. 48.
In ancient times, Nārada questioned the Apsaras named Pañcacūḍā:
"I wish to hear from you about the nature of women; speak of this to me. (49)
There, Pañcacūḍā spoke to Nārada, the best of sages:
"The description of the nature of women turns toward censure. (1.379.50)
O Sage, tell me, how can one woman be censured by another?
For you know women—both who they are and what their nature truly is.
O divine sage, you ought not to command me regarding such a question;
nevertheless, at your command, I shall indeed relate it exactly as it is.
"In this matter, O Nārada, let the fault committed by your speech be accepted upon you.
The sage agreed, saying "Om," and then the excellent Apsaras spoke.
Women of noble birth, those who have protectors, and even those endowed with beauty do not abide by the bounds of propriety; instability is the inherent flaw in women. (54)
Due to their fickleness, they do not strive to protect their own dharma—chastity—which grants a higher destination; consequently, they go to an inferior state. ||55||
"O Lord, this is indeed an unrighteous thing for us women, that we should abandon our shame and consort with sinful men. (56)
Women desire only that man who seeks them out, approaches them closely, and even slightly offers his service. (57)
Out of a lack of suitors and out of fear of their husbands, women—who are otherwise unrestrained—remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands. (58)
There is no one among them who is not to be despised, nor is there any certainty regarding their age;
whether he be handsome or ugly, they enjoy the company of a man.
