Neither out of fear, nor from reproach, nor for the sake of wealth, do they ever act in any other way.
Women do not remain faithful to their husbands merely because of their connection to a family of wise men.
Thus spoke Pañcacūḍā, the best of the Apsarases, regarding the inherent natures of women;
having thoroughly crushed those natures and restrained the mind with effort. (6.1)
Knowing her husband to be the supreme Lord, she should direct her restlessness toward him;
for the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, and the husband alone is the vessel [of all]. (62)
Having understood that service is the supreme vessel for merit, as well as the vessel for dharma and the vessel for liberation. ||63||
He is the vessel for the entire next world as well as for heaven;
he is the vessel of virtuous qualities and the vessel of supreme bliss. (64)
He is a vessel for the fame of his lineage, as well as a vessel for moral discipline;
he is a vessel for the pacification of restlessness, and likewise a supreme vessel for righteousness.
It is a vessel for the pacification of desire, as well as a receptacle for modesty;
it is the cleansing of mental tranquility and the means for the non-arising of misfortune. (66)

A devoted wife should worship her divine husband, who is the very form of Hari, for he is the vessel from which the lineage arises and the vessel that grants heaven, liberation, and other blessings. 67.
The Ender, the Destroyer, Death, the netherworld, the submarine fire, the razor’s edge, poison, the serpent, and fire—these stand on one side, while women stand on the other. (68)
Therefore, having completely dissolved these innate qualities whose nature is that of Anantā and the others,
a virtuous woman must conduct herself in every way toward her husband alone.
A devoted wife who, knowing her husband to be eternally Hari, worships him—her worship of Śrī Hari does not exceed the worship of her husband. (1.379.70)
Knowing this always, my daughter, serve your husband according to dharma;
through your husband's grace, you shall obtain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and whatever you desire. (71)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the duties of wifely devotion have indeed been described by Menā to Pārvatī, and they have been recounted by me to you here in this context. (72)

Thus ends the three hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conclusion of the Duties of Devotion to One’s Husband," following the demonstration of the duties of a devoted wife as spoken by Menakā to Pārvatī and the natural dispositions of women as spoken by Pañcacūḍā to Nārada, within the section on the greatness of the chaste wife in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of a wild doe devoted to her husband, who became the wife of the sage Mṛga at Puṣkara. She was born from a deer. 1.
Just as that devoted wife conducted herself in a human body,
even so did she abide in her devotion to her husband while in the body of a deer.
From the very day the doe, possessed by the nature of desire, embraced the deer,
from that day forth she regarded that single, auspicious deer as her beloved husband.
Having accepted him and taken refuge in him, the devoted wife set out;
she remembered no other deer, nor did she see any other with her heart. (4)
She never touches another nor delights in another;
born again as a doe within a herd of deer, she is indeed in her season.
Then the powerful deer fall after that doe;
yet she, having left her own husband, does not desire union with another.
Then, having been cast out from the herd by other deer who were filled with anger,
she took her husband-deer and left the herd of deer behind.
For the very purpose of protecting the Dharma, he came to a forest interior devoid of wild animals,
to a grassy, fearless spot at the sacred site of Madhyama Puṣkara.
There she constantly serves her husband with acts of devotion;
with the tips of her horns, she truly dispels her master's itching out of sincere affection.
Licking her beloved with her tongue, full of affection,
and touching him with her mouth and other parts, she truly delights that deer.
At river-landing places, among clusters of trees, and on grassy grounds,
wherever there is coolness, neither rain nor the heat of the sun prevails.
There, having reached a spot within the interior of a tree at the base of a shadow,
that doe spent the night together with her beloved.
Having first abandoned sleep while her beloved was still awake, the virtuous woman slowly gazes upon her lover’s face and licks it with her tongue.
But the deer, having regained consciousness and seeing his devoted wife,
would then proceed to scratch his beloved with his horn and his tongue.
Thus, both devoted respectively to their wives and to their husband,
they left the bed and the ground and came outside to an open space.
As long as her beloved does not take even a blade of grass or a tender leaf,
so long will the doe not consume a leaf, grass, or even a sprout.
If a leaf is given by her beloved in the morning, then even the female deer takes only that leaf, and nothing else—not even grass or a sprout. (17)
If her beloved takes up a blade of grass,
then that doe eats only that very grass, born of her husband's favor.
She does not eat even the most excellent and succulent food that her husband has not partaken of;
yet, while she is eating grass and such, if she obtains something fresh, she eats it.
Whether it be sweet, excellent, or soft food; leaves, flowers, fruits, or grass; or even sprouts, tubers, roots, grain, branches, and so forth— 1.380.20.
Then, having summoned her beloved, she gives it to her husband;
indeed, even when drinking water, the deer drinks the water first.
Immediately following that, the doe indeed goes to drink water;
when [the hunter] moves, she always follows after him, and when he stands still, she remains standing.
But as he flees after her, she too flees;
whether threatened or even struck, she takes no account of the pain. (23)
If a deer stands joyfully in the heat of the sun's rays,
then for that long it remains established in that heat, considering it to be its duty (dharma).
When her husband had thus departed, the virtuous woman then awaited his shadow;
she always considered it a blessing to serve her beloved.
While he was living thus in the forest, a drought occurred there as well; because of it, the crops did not sprout due to the lack of water.
The ground also became parched, and the food there was exhausted;
even when searched for, only withered stalks and leaves were found anywhere.
And sometimes it is not found at all; rather, when night arrives, those two who follow their own dharma pass the time hungry from forest to forest.
Then, the herd of deer, filled with nectar, which had previously been abandoned and was wandering through the forest, arrived at the place where that devoted wife resided. 29.
Seeing that the group of kinsmen was suffering from hunger, she was delighted; remembering her husband there, she repeatedly paid homage to the elders.
She said to them, "If I am indeed a devoted wife, then let this forest of mine serve for the honoring of these guests with food. (3.1)
Even without rain, the grassy meadow was lush, adorned with fresh sprouts,
fruitful, and graced by the beauty of excellent crops.
"Let it be here for a moment, even with its grass and water"—
when he had spoken thus, that forest indeed became green once more.
Then, having eaten that delightful food— which was abundant and filled with a variety of delicacies— and having drunk water, all the members of the household departed.
Singing the greatness of the devoted wife, which brings about prosperity, they related that wonderful news everywhere. (35)
Deer, afflicted by hunger, arrived from within the forests;
this devoted wife, having bowed down to her husband again and again, [remained] ever faithful. (36)
He constantly made a formal resolve for the sake of feeding guests;
and thus, even that which was dry would daily become moist for a mere moment. (37)
Then the deer eat the green grass as their food;
having become satiated, they depart for other regions, and the forest dries up once again. (38)
Then, on one occasion, a forest fire broke out in that grove,
resembling the fire of the dissolution of the world, bringing destruction to beasts and birds.
Then, that doe was remembered by everyone for the sake of extinguishing the fire;
having touched her husband's razor and bowed, she spoke indeed to her husband.
O Lord, if service has always been rendered to you by me with devotion, by that merit may this destructive forest fire be pacified. (41)
When he had thus resolved, a fire in the form of a black deer arrived at the place where that doe, faithful to her husband, was staying. 42.
He bowed to that virtuous woman and said, "O Goddess, I am pacified by your fear;
I shall not set this forest ablaze from now on, so let the deer roam in happiness. (43)
"I am afraid of Satī’s curse; forgive me, O devoted wife!
Having spoken thus and bowed to Satī, the forest fire was extinguished. (44)
Then the lions, as well as the tigers, bears, and whatever other predatory beasts there were,
having perceived that the animals had departed, also came to that forest.
Cruel beasts were harming the animals, and there was suffering and lamentation in the forest;
even the animals, having gathered together in fear, arrived there.
When the devoted wife, the deer, was present there at Puṣkara on earth, she then prayed for the auspicious for the sake of destroying their great suffering. (47)
The Great God, the Lord of Deer, arrived there in person.
She said to that Hara, "O Lord, always provide protection for me in the forest. (48)
"Those predators devour our devotees; you ought to protect us.
Then Mahādeva assumed the form of a fierce śarabha.
He wandered through the forest in every direction to put the predatory beasts to flight;
the cruel and violent animals fled far away from that forest.
Then the son of Jamadagni, Paraśurāma, beheld that divine Śarabha,
who was staying at Puṣkara to perform austerities.
Just as he took up his bow and proceeded to strike with an arrow, Śaṅkara himself, in the form of a Śarabha, spoke these words to the god: 52.
"O Rāma, O highly fortunate one! I am the protector of devotees;
I have indeed arrived here through the firm resolve of the devoted wife Mṛgī. (53)
"I am the very form of the hymn to Śaṅkara; do not exert yourself in vain.
Having said this, Hara revealed his own body to him. 54.
The two gods, Rāma and Hara,
embraced each other after showing Śambhu the golden river, the abode of ascetics that bestows happiness.
Then Rāma disappeared; he went there to obtain the fruit [of his penance] and performed a hymn of praise to Kṛṣṇa, by which Hari became pleased. (56)
Keśava went into the presence of that son of Jamadagni and gave him weapons and missiles for the destruction of the multitude of Kṣatriyas.
And Kṛṣṇa vanished; Rāma also returned to Puṣkara, and while arriving for the purpose of bathing and other rites, he saw the virtuous deer-maiden.
By whose power that forest repeatedly becomes green again, and by whose majesty the forest fire there was extinguished. (59)
And by whose power Hara assumed the form of a Śarabha;
having seen that divine female deer, Satī, he was struck with wonder.
Recognizing Rāma as an expansion of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with her divine and noble intellect, the doe bowed to him, offered praise, and performed the rites of hospitality for a guest. 61.
The deer also bowed with affection to that Paraśurāma;
at that moment, a hunter devoted to the chase arrived there.
Thirsty, tormented by the heat, and longing for a drink of water,
he came to the shore of that lake while Rāma was looking on.
The deer and the doe, filled with fear, were drinking water there;
seeing the deer and the doe, the hunter took up his bow for the sake of hunting.
But upon seeing Paraśurāma, he stood with his arrow cast aside;
filled with apprehension and terrified of Rāma, he then reflected.
Having drunk the water and taken refuge in the shade of a tree, the doe,
her mind free from fear upon seeing Rāma, spoke to her husband, the deer.
"O beloved, let us remain right here as long as Rāma is stationed there;
in the presence of this hero, the hunter will not strike us."
"Then, when seen by the sage, he will be reduced to ashes.
The deer said, "So be it; I know this Rāma to be the descendant of Bhṛgu."
It is the supreme [teaching] of Śiva, of Nārada, of Śuka, of the son of Marut (Hanumān),
of Ambarīṣa, of Bali, and of Vibhīṣaṇa.
The excellence of Prahlāda, Rantideva, and Uddhava is supreme;
and among the gopīs, Prabhā, and Pārvatī, it is likewise supreme.
Just as Māṇikya and Lakṣmī possess devotion toward Kṛṣṇa,
so too does this Rāma remain established in austerity while practicing such devotion.
But today, through the sight of this Rāma, the knowledge of our birth has arisen.
Listen, my dear, I shall tell you how we both came to be born as deer. (72)
Formerly, in the auspicious family of brahmins in the Draviḍa country,
my father, named Satrāyaṇa, was born into the Kauśika lineage.
I was his son, Vedasūri, possessed of great devotion, intent upon serving my guru, and dedicated to the study of the Vedas. ||74||
Once, having bathed at Kṛtamālā at dawn, he ascended the mountain;
there, a certain thirsty doe approached him.
Seeing her intent on drinking water, I quickly approached her out of compassion;
she too was full of trust. (76)
Having arrived there, she indeed bowed down at my feet;
just then, a most terrifying tiger arrived at that spot.
A doe fled in terror, and a tiger seized her;
I made great effort for the sake of destroying that tiger. (78)
Nevertheless, for the sake of saving the life of the deer, she was wounded at that time;
having indeed assumed the form of a maiden of fourteen or fifteen years.
Having approached my presence, she fell at my feet;
overcome with wonder, I questioned that young maiden.
"O Goddess, who are you, a maiden in the form of a doe, equal to a goddess? Whose daughter are you, and how have you come to this mountain all alone? (8.1)
Then that maiden said to me: "I am the daughter of Parameṣṭhin;
among the goddesses of the Brahma-lakes, I am named Hariṇī. (82)
"I have indeed become worthy of being chosen as a bride; sent here by Brahmā, I have come to wed Sātrāyaṇi, the sage of the Vedas. (83)
I have come in the form of a doe so that no one else might violate me;
I am a young doe, still intact and not yet having reached my menses. (84)
"I have become fit for the season; may you take me as your wife.
Having been addressed thus by me there, she was wedded according to the Gāndharva rite. (85)
Having kindled the fire right there in the forest and offered fruits and other oblations,
the couple performed a circumambulation and placed a garland of flowers [upon the fire].
Having fully entered into the duties of householders, those two yogins were indeed able to assume any form at will;
sometimes they took the appearance of sages, and sometimes the form of deer.
Sometimes they were of divine form, sometimes indeed birds;
sometimes they were fish in the water, and likewise swans and Garuḍas.
"Having become whatever we desire, let us two dwell as we please in the forest of the mountain;
for you are devoted to the vow of fidelity to your husband, and I too am devoted to the vow of a husband. (89)
Let them remain deeply attached to one another, devoted to righteousness,
remembering their past lives, knowing the three periods of time, and always intent upon virtuous deeds.
On that mountain there were hundreds of thousands of male and female deer;
we remained among them, always sporting together with them so that they would not recognize us as being of the same nature as deer. ||91||
Once, upon a heap of stalks and leaves, on account of the rain, ||92||

"Let us remain on this ground, free from fear, taking refuge at the base of a tree trunk, having separated ourselves from that herd of deer out of a desire for the pleasure of the dharma of our own will. (93)
The night was spent, yet in the morning the rain did not cease;
meanwhile, a certain hungry lion arrived there. (94)
Then, by his sudden intervention, the two deer were saved;
though they had been wounded, they were protected by the doe through the power of her vow-bound dharma.
For when they had met their end, they were both born as deer, remembering their former lives; for whatever one's final thought at the end may be, such will be one's future state. (96)

Through this meditation, after the tiger was slain there, she died and was born as a doe, and I became a deer together with you. Likewise, you remained faithful to your husband's vow, and you were my beloved, devoted to your husband. (97)
By us both, the wicked Bhārgava Rāma was [confronted], who was Hari himself in person. ||98||
"We shall go to the auspicious worlds, reaching which one does not grieve. Having spoken thus, they both sought refuge in Rāma. (99)
Having lived for a thousand years, they both called out to Paraśurāma:
"O Rāma, Rāma! O Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World! (1.380.1)
The deer and the doe, remembering their former births and devoted to their respective duties, have come to you for refuge for the sake of liberation; release them from their bondage.
Having spoken thus, the deer and the doe praised Paraśurāma;
as soon as they touched his feet, a celestial vehicle arrived.
Then, having leaped up, the man and woman became two deer and were pursued by four miraculous, perfected beings who could assume any form at will and move with the speed of thought.
Having bowed at the feet of Rāma, they joyfully ascended [the chariot], having assumed divine bodies marked with the signs of the conch, the discus, and other emblems. || 104 ||
And having gone to the world of Viṣṇu, which is saluted by all the gods,
O Lakṣmī, those who hear or recite this shall attain the state of liberation.

Thus ends the three hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marriage of Hariṇī, the Daughter of Brahmā, with Vedasūri; the Maintenance of Chastity and Wifely Vows while in the Bodies of a Deer and a Stag; the Greening of the Forest without Rain; the Quelling of the Forest Fire; the Arrival of Śiva in the Form of a Śarabha to Destroy the Carnivorous Beasts; the Vision of Paraśurāma; the Narration of Previous Events at Puṣkara; and the Liberation of the Two Deer," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the greatness of devoted wives (*pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story concerning devotion to a husband,
regarding Reṇukā, who was the devoted wife of Jamadagni.
She who, taking her deceased husband, entered the fire of the funeral pyre;
and whose son was Paraśurāma, who remained established in asceticism in the forest.
On the bank of the Narmadā, not very far from Māhiṣmatī,
there was an excellent hermitage belonging to Jamadagni, filled with trees.
Jamadagni, Kāmadhenu, Paraśurāma, and Reṇukā—these were the principal ones; likewise, there were other disciples and other sons.
Reṇukā, who was honored by the gods as a virtuous wife, served her husband with devotion in thousands of ways through the dharma of fidelity to her husband.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to her story in detail, which bestows supreme liberation:
Reṇukā performed a severe penance for the sake of obtaining a son.
During the cold season, the virtuous woman serves her husband day and night;
indeed, at dawn, she performs the worship of Kṛṣṇa with moist garments.
She ate but once a day and performed worship of the Sun;
she also performed worship of the sacrificial fire, of guests, and of cows. || 8 ||
For one year she subsisted on fruits, for one year she lived on leaves;
for one year she fed on water, and for one year the virtuous woman subsisted on air alone.
For a year she wept with tears, and for a year the virtuous woman remained without food;
she chanted the name of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa continuously.
Indeed, she performed service to her husband with a second form as well;
thus, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became pleased with him.
He went directly into her presence and said, "Choose a boon.
Satī replied, "May you yourself be born here as my son and my protector."
"So be it," said Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and he vanished;
thereafter, in due time, Rāma appeared, bearing an axe worn by use upon the wood.
He became renowned in the forests by the name Paraśurāma;
once, having bowed to his parents, he went to the house of his grandfather.
Having bowed to his grandfather Ṛcīka, he sat upon a seat;
devoted to serving him, he dwelt there for several months.
Then he went to the renowned Bhṛgu and bowed to him with humility.
Bhṛgu spoke for the benefit of the worlds regarding the infallible Rāma.
"Go, my son, at my command to the Himalayas for the sake of performing penance;
Śaṅkara, being entirely pleased, will bring about your welfare. (17)
Having bowed to those two, Rāma then went to the Himavat mountain;
having constructed a leaf-hut on the shore of a lake, he practiced austerities.
When much time had passed, Śiva, in the form of a hunter,
being pleased by his ascetic penance, went into his presence and spoke to that ascetic.
Bathe in all the sacred fords and perform severe austerity;
by that merit, O Rāma, you shall obtain all the divine weapons.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished; Rāma proceeded to various holy fords (tīrthas) and went to Kailāsa, where Hara bestowed upon him the Śiva-weapon.
And having given him the axe, he said, "Always slay the enemies of the gods.
Having slain many Daityas, Rāma returned to his own hermitage.
Śambhu, having arrived there, bestowed all the weapons without exception—
the fourfold collection of missiles, along with their methods of employment and withdrawal.
Śaṅkara gave to Rāma the chariot Uttama, which was free from agitation, drawn by white horses, and adorned with a beautiful banner, as well as two quivers containing inexhaustible arrows.
An unbreakable, undecaying, divine bow with a firm string and victory as its name;
and a wonderful, highly precious armor capable of withstanding all weapons.
He bestowed upon Bhārgava both his fierce ascetic power and his own prowess;
then, in the forest, he [beheld] the son of a brahmin who had been slain by a tiger.
This Rāma restored him to life;
having made the son of the sage Śānta his disciple—though he had not performed the traditional salutation—Rāma went to his home.
He prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before Jamadagni and Reṇukā;
then, after some time, the Haihaya king arrived there.
Accompanied by his fourfold army, the king reached the hermitage on the bank of the Narmadā;
having seen Jamadagni, he approached him and bowed his head in salutation.
Then Jamadagni caused that hospitality to be performed by the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu),
[providing] cities, groves, gardens, palaces, and female attendants.
He provided servants, cattle, an abundance of food and drink;
then Reṇukā spoke again to the milch-cow Kāmadhenu.
"This King Kārtavīrya is my guest and your guest as well;
therefore, O sister, manifest all your sovereign power before me. ||32||
Thus addressed, the wish-fulfilling cow said: "O Sovereign Lady, form a resolve;
by the power of your devotion to your husband, I shall bring you the riches of Vairāja."
Then, by the power of those two, that golden city in the forest belonging to the descendant of Bhaga became equal to the palace of the king of the gods.
Through various divine manifestations, it then became of inconceivable form,
with paths radiant with gold and jewels, like a quadrangle of pleasure gardens.
It was endowed with clusters of sand on the waves of its royal highways and the like, and was beautifully adorned with palaces whose peaks possessed the luster of the full moon. (36)
It was resplendent with palaces made of gold, silver, brass, copper, and mercury,
and adorned with gem-studded stones interspersed with crystals and rows of jewels.
It was endowed with the unimpeded radiance of great jewel-lamps, and possessed excellent houses with staircases and altars made of gold resplendent with gems. ||38||
With walls and other structures richly adorned with garlands of jewels, with doors, bolts, and gate-towers; and with thresholds and courtyards graced by golden coverings. ||39||
It was provided with night-quarters, adorned with four-sided pavilions and archways,
featuring divine pillars, variegated walls, and golden lion-thrones.
It was enchanting with couches, various kinds of foods and snacks, countless vessels and drinks, an abundance of food fit for the gods, and beautiful women.
It was adorned with fortresses of gold and jewels, seven-storied storehouses,
and divine moats resplendent with water-channels.
It was equipped with lightning-lamps, long-range machines, mirrors visible from afar,
instruments for hearing from a distance, and vehicles that travel through the air.
It was adorned with long ponds, small lakes, bathing pools, and reservoirs,
and provided various spectacles and dramatic performances to dispel fatigue.
It was filled with wrestlers who exerted great effort, with entertainers and dancers,
with singers and music halls, and it shone with royal assemblies.
It was provided with armories and implements, as well as liberation-halls,
bathing-rooms, service-quarters, and celestial chariots that fulfill all desires;
it was also filled with swans, Garuḍas, peacocks, Cātakas, and beautiful parrots.
It was auspicious, accompanied by peacocks uttering the language of the gods. ||47||
That city was indeed made fragrant with the divine scents of trees, creepers, fruits, and flowers, and it shone with lakes of milk and sugarcane juice. 48.
And there, nectar was prepared in every house and in the lakes;
it was filled with vehicles within the water and adorned with vehicles within the fire.
Reṇukā, Gauḥ, Nirmamāte, Yogyā, Yoṣit, Kumārikā,
and the others were adorned with various garments, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, and cloths.

By means of gestures such as the grace of amorous passion (śṛṅgāra), beauty, splendor, loveliness, and the movements of *hāva* and *bhāva*; and by means of fickleness, brilliance, purity, slight smiles, attraction, and so forth. ||51||
Endowed with qualities such as beauty, their faces were graced with gentle smiles;
they shone with rows of teeth resembling jasmine buds. ||52||
Bearing the full weight of fresh youth, they were beautiful with charming and sweet voices, adorned by side-glances from eyes languid with love. ||53||
With hearts clear and serene with joy, radiant with the splendor of the erotic sentiment and love,
they shone with rows of pearl necklaces upon their chests, as if adorned with the blossoms of the wish-fulfilling tree.
They possessed a divine nature and supreme good fortune surpassing that of the celestial nymphs, and were resplendent with forms that were sweet, endowed with exquisite delicacy and beauty. ||55||
Their slender waists were bent by the weight of their pair of full breasts;
they were also stooped by the burden of their hips, and the palms of their hands and soles of their feet were red.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, neck-threads, and other ornaments, they shone with decorations for the ears, cheeks, forehead, and other parts of the body. ||57||
They were adorned with ornaments for the forearms, fingers, and waists,
and were exceedingly beautiful with floral decorations and graced by lovely braided hair.
Their waistbands, girdles, small bells, and anklets were all tinkling;
they were experts in playful consolation, laughter, the offering of guest-water, amorous play, and song. ||59||
They possess melodious voices and sweet, honey-like speech; their utterances are pleasant and profound.
They are bold in passion, rich in emotion, and experts in the application of love.
Attendants with eyes like lotus petals, endowed with abundant magnificence and wealth, and skilled in the management of household affairs—such were the female attendants. (61)
Then, by the hundreds and thousands, he [provided] household servants and slaves—
cooks, massagers, foot-massagers, and carriers.
They constructed temples, chariots, horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, and many other animals, including cattle, goats, and sheep.
He [addressed] the neighboring kings, the lords of men, the kṣatriyas, the cavalrymen,
the horsemen, the foot soldiers, the army commanders, and the leaders.
And [he appointed] Brahmins and others as chariot-warriors, charioteers, bards,
panegyrists, Māgadhas, Cāraṇas, as well as dancers and actors.
Kinnaras of many forms, courtesans, eunuchs, ruddy geese, swans, ospreys, cranes, and cuckoos; ||66||
[He saw] clusters of white water-lilies, lotuses, night-blooming lilies, blue lotuses, jasmine, and kadamba trees;
as well as mango, priyāla, jackfruit, and madhūka and plantain trees.
Nāgakesara, ketakī, punnāga, mandāraka, kunda, and campaka; karavīra and yūthikā, and all kinds of fruits and flowers. ||68||
The wish-fulfilling cow, Reṇukā, being employed for this purpose, created breezes that were fragrant with the scents of all seasons and spreading very gently.
The king, however, accepted the hospitality and honor usually difficult for gods and others to obtain; he entered the meritorious city that had been prepared for his sake. (70)
The city was a dwelling for all enjoyments, adorned with millions of silken garments, variegated dyes, and woolen cloths, and was brilliantly radiant.
Having entered the city, which possessed such splendor as to bewilder even the inhabitants of heaven, he and his army were struck with amazement; then he understood the cause to be the Earth.
And as the king entered, women positioned at the windows showered him with sandalwood water and heaps of flowers and parched grain.
Seeing the splendor of Brahmā’s asceticism, the king was utterly bewildered;
he praised it with his mind and speech, yet he considered the new glory of the Kṣatriyas to be superior. (74)
Thinking, "My own splendor is not capable of approaching even a hundredth part of this [splendor]," he became possessed by pride and arrogance. (75)
The king received honors such as garlands of jewels and diamonds;
he was ushered in by servants who had formed an army with the aid of the wish-fulfilling cow.
Having slowly passed through three inner courtyards, Arjuna entered the palace, which was brilliantly illuminated by golden lamps.
Honored by young maidens with curds, mirrors, perfumes, flowers, durvā grass, unbroken rice, and other offerings, the king ascended his golden throne.
The matrons honored him with offerings and other services worthy of a king;
together with them, the monarch spent the day as if in heaven.
And in the evening he entered the assembly hall with his ministers, feudal lords, and leaders;
there, entertainment consisting of music was set in motion, accompanied by dance, laughter, and storytelling.
The amorous diversions of the courtesans, including laughter and play, took place;
then, after midnight, he went to the upper palace for the sake of rest. (8.1)
The royal army, finding rest as if in palaces amidst the equal splendor and majesty of the king’s form, became exceedingly joyful.
"The food, drink, and enjoyments for the royal army were all provided by him equally, like those of a king; therefore, let us dwell right here," they said. (83)
Approaching the king as he slept, the bards, panegyrists, and heralds sang aloud with honeyed voices in order to awaken him in the morning.
With eyes wide awake, the king rose and performed his daily rites to the accompaniment of the blended sounds of lutes and flutes, perfectly harmonized with rhythmic beats.
Having approached the treasure-house of asceticism who was being served by celestial nymphs, the sage bowed and said: "Has the night passed happily?"
We are like wild animals, sustained by the forest;
yet kings consider the suffering in the forest to be utterly unbearable. (87)
Thus addressed, the king, free from pride and with his mind overcome by the power and majesty born of the sage’s influence, spoke to the sage while smiling. (88)
"My soldiers, who dwell in comfort, do not wish to go from here;
yet this is not at all surprising for you, O Lord, a yogin perfected through asceticism. (89)
For you, who possess the wish-fulfilling cow, as well as for that devoted wife and for her husband, heaven has been attained right here; what prosperity, then, can there be for a petty king?
"O Brahmin, I shall go home; may you grant me leave.
Having been told "So be it" by the sage, he set out for his own city. 91.
He reflected upon that cow, the most excellent of all those who milk every desire:
"Of what use to me is this entire kingdom, which is indeed like a mere cowrie shell? (92)
The prosperous domain of Indra is not worth even a sixteenth part of a cow;
by a cow heaven was created in the forest, and by a cow it was destroyed in an instant. (93)
Such is the power of that cow; she is fit for a king, not for an ascetic.
Having paid a price in cattle, horses, and other goods, I must bring her back to my city. (94)
Having thus resolved, King Candragupta dispatched his minister;
he said to the sage, "A king is indeed the possessor of jewels on earth. (95)
"Taking these jewels, you ought to give the cow as a jewel to the king;
however, the sacrificial cow must not be given by me to anyone at all. (96)
"I am neither the agent of this purchase and sale, nor am I under the king's command;
yet by seizing you by force, both your life and that of the king will be destroyed. (97)
Thus addressed, the sage Jamadagni became enraged; perceiving the earth [to be his wife], he then dragged her with all his might and obstructed him.
Commanded by the minister, the servants struck the Sage excessively with whips;
they drove the Rishi far away, yet he endured it, while they forcibly seized the cow. (99)
Then, having ascended into the sky and seized the calf, they departed;
meanwhile, the sage died, and Paraśurāma arrived.
Having just returned from the forest, the son heard his mother weeping and crying out "Rāma! Rāma! before him, and he ran forward quickly.
Having set down the load of sacrificial fuel and seeing that his father was dead, he,
with eyes full of tears, consoled his weeping mother.
Then Reṇukā, overcome with grief at the fear of widowhood,
struck her belly three times seven times with both hands.
Then Rāma spoke to his mother with great intensity:
"Indeed, this chest of yours has been struck twenty-one times. (104)
"I shall slay as many Kshatriyas as that number; do not grieve.
Then Renuka, devoted to her husband, spoke to her sons.
"O sons, I am a devoted wife; I desire to follow my father, who has gone to heaven, by igniting the fire with my own body here. (106)
In such a way shall I conduct myself hereafter,
day and night, that I shall become a beloved guest in the world of my father, my husband.
At that moment, a profoundly deep, disembodied voice spoke there:
"O devoted wife, do not commit this rash act; maintain your fortitude."
"O devoted wife, make a firm resolve for the awakening of your husband;
before long, your husband shall regain his senses."
Thus addressed, she led her husband’s body into a small hut;
the virtuous woman then formed a resolve for her husband’s rising and restoration to life.
Just then, the sage Bhṛgu, who is honored by the gods and is an ocean of the science of reviving the dead, arrived there and restored him to life.
Jamadagni rose and bowed to that grandfather;
he asked, "What sin was committed by the king, because of which even I have died? (11.2)
Bhṛgu said: "That king has been cursed by Vasiṣṭha for his destruction;
O fool, because of your offense against a brahmin, your virility shall perish. (11.3)
Therefore, your son Rāma shall slay that Arjuna;
twenty-one times he will rid the earth of the kṣatriya caste.
Having obtained sovereignty from that Atri, a portion of Hari, he lived;
yet today, slain by the weapons of Rāma, he shall depart to the next world.
Having spoken thus and taken the articles of worship, Bhṛgu then went home;
Rāma, meanwhile, made a vow at that time to destroy Arjuna.
And Jamadagni, the twice-born, remembering the dharma of the virtuous, said to him:
"Those who are saintly and highly fortunate are the ones who bring about liberation from saṃsāra."
They do not become angry with anyone, even when reviled or struck;
those ascetics are highly fortunate, self-controlled, and rich in the virtue of forbearance.
And for those who constantly perform virtuous deeds, their worlds are indeed imperishable;
yet he who is struck even with words by wicked people with sticks and other such means— || 11 9 ||
But he who does not succumb to agitation is proclaimed a virtuous man;
he who strikes back at one who strikes him is not virtuous, but is a partaker of sin.
We are virtuous brahmins who have attained the state of being worthy of forgiveness;
therefore, my son, restrain yourself, practice forbearance, and perform austerities.
Thus instructed by his father, Paraśurāma said to him:
"That tranquility which is appropriate for the virtuous and the distressed is never found among the wicked."
"Therefore, the slaughter of this Kārtavīrya must indeed be carried out by me.
To his son who had spoken thus, the son of Jamadagni replied: || 123 ||
"Go from here to Brahmā and act according to what he says.
Having been told this, he went through the sky and bowed down to that Brahmā.
He related the entire account and his own vow in every detail.
Brahmā said, "Listen, my son; go now to Śaṅkara."
He will grant you the divine Pāśupata weapon and the Kṛṣṇavarma;
thereafter, my son, having propitiated Śambhu in every way, you shall be victorious.
Thus, by that command, Rāma went to the supreme Kailāsa of Śiva;
seeking his purpose, he bowed and related everything exactly as spoken by Brahmā.
Śiva gave him the mantra and the armor that bestows victory,
as well as the Nāgapāśa, the Pāśupata, the Brahmāstra, and the Vāruṇa weapon.
The Nārāyaṇa weapon, the Āgneya, the Vāyavya, and likewise the Gāruḍa;
the Gāndharva, the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon, the mace, the spear, and the trident.
Taking up his staff, axe, and a multitude of weapons and missiles, Rāma, filled with great joy, bowed to Puṣkara and set out; he accomplished everything in every way.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with devotion according to the path taught by Agastya, he beheld Kṛṣṇa directly; and Kṛṣṇa spoke to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
"O Bhārgava, destroy Kārtavīrya, who has indeed descended with my discus; endowed with a portion of my own essence, roam upon the earth."
"Having become Rāma once again, I shall take away your splendor," Kṛṣṇa said, and having spoken thus, he vanished; Rāma then went to Māhiṣmatī.
Rāma chose battle with Arjuna; Arjuna set forth for the fight accompanied by many akṣauhiṇīs, but on the way he beheld ill omens.
The quarters of space were covered in dust, the sky was devoid of luster, and the planets and other celestial bodies lost their brilliance;
she appeared with disheveled hair, her nose severed, weeping, and naked.
And he saw a woman dressed in black garments;
one with tattered clothes, one fallen, one broken, one naked, and one clad in saffron robes.
He saw a man with missing limbs who was distressed in mind,
as well as a monitor lizard, a hare, a porcupine, an empty pitcher, and a reptile.
Cotton, a tortoise, oil, salt, and a piece of bone, as well as a jackal making a terrifying howl to one's right. (1.38)
Even upon seeing a sick man, a Pulkasa, a bull, a hawk, and a bear, he proceeded to fight by force, ensnared as he was by the noose of Time.
In battle, Rāma shattered Śatputra, Arjuna, and tens of thousands of Akṣauhiṇīs with his circles of weapons and missiles.
Then he went to Kailāsa for the purpose of seeing Śiva;
however, he was stopped at the gateway by Gaṇeśa, the lord of the Gaṇas, who presented his tusk to the lord of the Gaṇas.
Having broken [the bow] and seen Śivā, Rāma went to his father’s house;
he beheld his parents and fell at their feet.
Having consoled Rāma regarding the killing of Kārtavīrya as a favor, his father then prescribed an expiation for him. 143.
Rāma went to Mount Mahendra and performed an expiation;
having established a hermitage there, he practiced extremely difficult austerities.
Then, on one occasion, other sons born of Sahasrārjuna, accompanied by a fourfold army, went to that hermitage in the forest. (145)
Having carried off the head of Jamadagni, they departed toward their own city.
Seeing her husband slain and fallen upon the ground, Reṇukā—
Having kindled the funeral pyre, she entered it and was reduced to ashes;
yet, as a virtuous wife, she ascended into the sky by means of a celestial vehicle along with her husband.
Worshipped by celestial sages, she then departed for heaven; thereafter, her sons performed whatever funeral rites were to be done immediately following that.
Then, after some time had passed, Rāma returned from the forest to his own hermitage;
he learned of his father’s life being taken away and even his head being carried off.

Having heard of his mother’s death, he set his mind upon the destruction of the Kṣatriyas; having slain the members of the Kṣatriya lineage without exception, he intended to wash away her blood with their blood.
Having resolved, "I shall perform the libation for my parents," he departed;
reaching Māhiṣmatī, Rāma made twanging sounds with his bow.
The sons of Sahasrārjuna and the kings with their fourfold armies, having come together, fought; they were slain by Rāma and fled.
Then Bhārgava discharged the weapon named Kālāgni;
the fire of that weapon utterly consumed the city along with its ramparts.
Having reduced that kingdom to ashes and rendered the earth devoid of kṣatriyas,
Rāma, his mind fixed on asceticism, went to Mount Mahendra.
Having once again made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas after two years,
the twice-born once more produced a sparse remnant of the Kṣatriya order upon the earth.
He struck them down upon the earth until none remained, like Death himself appearing in person; for as the lineage of the Kṣatriyas was repeatedly manifested upon the ground, [he destroyed it]. (156)
Twenty-one times he repeatedly made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas;
thereafter, he again [slain] two thousand six hundred consecrated kings (mūrdhābhiṣiktas). 157.
Having seized him alive, he went to Kurukṣetra;
there, that descendant of Bhṛgu caused five lakes to be excavated. (158)
There, the descendant of Bhṛgu indeed filled those five lakes with the blood originating from the body of the king. || 159 ||
He fully gratified the ancestors and performed the śrāddha ceremony for his two parents;
having returned from there, Rāma went once again to the sacred site of Gayā.
Indeed, that sacred ford Samantapañcaka was located in Kurukṣetra;
by bathing there, a human being becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords.
In Gayā, his ancestors, led by Jamadagni, arrived from the world of the Pitṛs and accepted the worship performed by him.
"O Rāma, they say that by performing this great deed you have satisfied [the ancestors];
however, desist from this slaughter and perform an act of atonement once more. (163)
Having said, "Attain peace; may it be well with you," they vanished.
Rāma, desiring purification, went to all the sacred fords (tīrthas). || 164 ||
Then he went to Mount Mahendra and performed a horse sacrifice;
he gave the earth to Kaśyapa, and Bhārgava practiced austerities.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the marvels of Paraśurāma:
the devotion of Reṇukā to her husband and the filial piety of her son.
The wickedness of Kṣatriyas and even their resulting destruction—by reading or hearing this, the fruit of devotion to each of those [deities] shall arise. || 167 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled “The Description of the Destruction of the Kṣatriyas by Paraśurāma through the Power of the Chaste Reṇukā and the Wish-Fulfilling Cow (Kāmadhenu), the Resuscitation of the Deceased Jamadagni, and the Heavenly Abode of Reṇukā and Jamadagni,” within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of the devoted wife (*pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe to you your supreme devotion to your husband;
you never remain among other people, having ever forsaken me.
Wherever there is a portion of me, there you indeed exist as a portion;
for you abide having firmly maintained the supreme and primary duty of devotion to your husband.
And I too, Lakṣmī, remaining devoted to my vow toward my wife, dwell within you with my whole being— both internally and externally— while guarding [my vow] in my heart.
Formerly, by my will, you were born as Lakṣmī from outside my heart;
thereafter, you were born in Vaikuṇṭha as Satī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
In Goloka, you are always Rādhikā in form, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
and in my unmanifest abode, you exist as Śrī, my dear one.
In Śvetadvīpa you are my wife; in the Ocean of Milk, you are Ramā; and in my abode, Cit-ambaram, you are both Prabhā and Pārvatī.
And Māṇikī, of excellent form, was always my seat;
you were born from the Ocean of Milk, and thus you became Kedāra’s daughter.
Padmā was born as the daughter of Bhṛgu through Khyāti, and she became my beloved; you indeed were born in the house of Anaraṇya from Dharaṇī, and you too are my beloved.
In that same way, you, Kambharālakṣmī, were born in auspicious Saurāṣṭra;
you are that eternal Mother of the World, the inseparable Śrī of Viṣṇu.
O Lakṣmī, you, the invisible and virtuous servant, always abide in the form of Gaurī upon the left thigh of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Just as I am omnipresent, so indeed are you omnipresent;
nowhere am I without you, and nowhere are you without me.
O Lakṣmī, between us there always exists an identity of inseparable establishment;
you are always and everywhere everything, and likewise, I am everything. (12)
"O beloved, may I always be your husband and you always be my wife, through action, mind, speech, body, and the contemplation of virtues. (1.3)
In the states of waking, dreaming, the terrible deep sleep, and even the fourth (turiya);
in the locus, in the Self, everywhere, as well as in the object and its dissolution. || 14 ||
O Lakṣmī, whether in creation or dissolution, in the ether of consciousness or in the realm of the insentient, in effect or in cause, you are always my devoted wife.
Likewise, O Satī, I am eternally devoted to my wife; there is no doubt about this. I and Viṣṇu are always all-pervading everywhere.
There you are the pervasive Goddess, whose very nature is my Śakti;
I am Akṣareśa, and you, my beloved, are Akṣarī.
O Lakṣmī, when I am Mukteśa, you indeed exist as Muktā;
and when you are Jayā and Lalitā, I am likewise Harikṛṣṇa.
I am the meaning and you are Speech; you are policy and I am the method of conduct; I am awakening and you are the intellect; I am dharma and you are virtuous action.
I am the creator and you are the creation; you are the earth and I am the mountain that supports it.
I am contentment and you are satisfaction; I am desire and you are the longing for it.
I am the sacrifice and you are indeed the sacrificial fee; I am the Veda and you are the sacrificial altar.
You alone are the offering of clarified butter, and at that time I am the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
You are the wife's hall, and I become the eastern enclosure.
I am the sacrificial post and you are the altar; you are the fuel and I am the *kuśa* grass.
You are the *udgīti* chant and I am the *sāman*; you are the *svāhā* exclamation and I am the fire into which oblations are cast.
You are Gaurī and I am Śaṅkara; you are radiance and I am the sun.
I am the ancestors and you are Svadhā, the bestower of eternal nourishment;
I am the ether and you are the sky; I am the moon and you are the moonlight.
I am Vāyu and you are indeed Dhṛti; you are the shore and I am the ocean.
You are Indrāṇī and I am Mahendra; you are Dhūmorṇā and I am Yama.
You are Ṛddhi and I am Kubera; you are Gaurī and I am Varuṇa; you are indeed Devasenā and I am Kārttikeya, the commander of the army.
Wherever I am the support, there you alone are my power;
you are the limit, I am the twinkling of an eye, I am the hour, and you are my fraction of time.
You are the moonlight and I am the lamp; I am the tree and you are indeed the creeper.
I am the day and you are the night; you are the bride and I am the groom. (28)
I am the river and you are the form of the river; you are the banner and I am the flag.
I am greed and you are thirst; I am passion and you are considered delight.
Among gods, animals, humans, and others, you are the illusion and I am the magician.
Due to the curse of Durvāsas, you indeed abandoned Mount Mahendra and became completely submerged in the ocean;
yet you have appeared once more.
You are Siddhi, you are Padminī, and by your fame, you are Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu.
On the bank of the Narmadā, you, the daughter of Bhṛgu, possessed of a divine form, became a young woman as soon as you were born; there you performed difficult penance, [vowing]:
"May Nārāyaṇa himself, the four-armed Hari, be my husband."
"Thus, O virtuous lady, you have performed supreme austerity for ten thousand years.
Always appearing sixteen years of age, free from growth or decay,
you remain situated within a circle of light, standing firm upon the peak of Mount Bhṛgu."
For a thousand years you performed severe austerities amidst the five fires;
then, for another thousand years, indeed, you practiced penance subsisting on rice grains;
thereafter, for a thousand years, you were devoted to a diet of fruits.
Then, for a thousand years, you were devoted to eating bulbs;
then, for a thousand years, you were devoted to eating leaves;
and then, for a thousand years, you were devoted to eating withered leaves.
Then for a thousand years you shall subsist on the froth of water;
then for a thousand years you shall subsist on water in some places;
then for a thousand years you shall subsist on smoke and vapors.
Then, for a thousand years, you were devoted solely to subsisting on air;
at the eleventh thousand, having restrained all your senses and reached the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), you entered into meditative absorption (samādhi) upon me.
"Even though you have praised me, I shall not [grant this]," he said for the sake of the marriage;
but when you informed me that you would soon give up your life, I opened the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*) and directed my movement upward. ||41||
At that time, having approached, I placed her back into the opening.
But you then said, "O Lakṣmī, become my wife!"—"In that case, either take away my life or else separate me from her. || 42-43 ||
Smiling, with eyes full of tears, my limbs bristling with joy, my hair standing on end, and my body perspiring, I embraced her; and with my hair thrilled with delight, I said:
"Desist from this most rigorous penance."
"As long as the world of Brahmā exists, so long shall I indeed remain your wife.
Go, Lakṣmī, and tell your father and mother in every way:
'The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is coming for the sake of marriage.'"
Having been addressed thus, you rose up, bowed, and touched my face;
having offered everything [to me], you went to your father’s abode.
And I, having departed for Vaikuṇṭha, then remembered Nārada.

The Seven Sages, Rādhikā, Śrī, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, and Prabhā—all of them having assembled together, questioned me regarding the cause. I then related the account concerning the union with Bhārgavī. || 48-49 ||
On the beautiful bank of the Narmadā, the most excellent Brahmin Bhagu worshipped the Lord Hara for a thousand divine years.
Remaining within the anthill and situated in his southern abode,
he meditates while established in samādhi and likewise prays for a boon.
A great wonder arose for Umā and Śaṅkara;
Gaurī asked Śambhu, "Who is this that is staying within the anthill?"
Śambhu said: "The sage named Bhṛgu, the most excellent among sages, meditates upon, performs penance for, and indeed supplicates Śaṅkara for a boon. (53)
Then Gaurī, smiling, addressed Śaṅkara:
"Your crest has become like smoke; even now you are not satisfied. (54)
"O Lord, you are difficult for me to propitiate; how is it that you behave in this way?
Śiva said, "O Great Goddess, Bhṛgu has been moved by anger. (55)
I shall show you that which is real and I shall do what is pleasing to you;
then, the bull, who is the very form of Dharma, was reminded by the God of Gods.
Upon being remembered by the God of gods, the bull arrived quickly and spoke in human speech: "O Lord, let your command be given. (57)
"O Brahmin, strike him down to the ground while he is covered by anthills!
Then, while he is established in yoga and meditating, strike him down with that [ant-hill]. ||58||
At that moment, burning with anger, he raised his hand toward the bull and spoke:
"O bull, where are you going? (59)
"O bull, today I shall visibly slay you, the embodiment of evil, right here!
For the brahmin was then provoked by that bull who had gone into the intermediate space."
The Brahmin gazed into the sky; this was indeed a supreme wonder.
Then, as Rudra laughed, the seer stood before him, and upon seeing the third eye, he fell to the ground out of embarrassment.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground, he praises the illustrious Supreme Lord.
O Supreme Lord, protect me—me who am joined with false ego, whose power is momentary and fragile, cruel, and fallen upon a wicked path. 63.
"Quickly take away my thirst and grant me the fortune that dwells in the heart;
sever the bonds born of worldly existence and deliver me, O Śaṅkara! (64)
"May this altar become Rudra’s, having the very form of Nārāyaṇa;
if you are pleased, O Lord of the Universe, then grant this to me. (65)
"So be it," Śambhu then said for the welfare of the world;
"Nārāyaṇī Mahālakṣmī shall become your daughter here."
The site of anger shall become Rudravedī and Bhṛgukṣetra;
for there, father and son will not even speak with a single voice.
Having spoken thus, Hara vanished from the house of Bhṛgu;
and a divine daughter, born of his resolve, Lakṣmī, most beautiful, was born.
Khyāti became possessed of a daughter, and a rain of flowers from the dwellers of heaven fell;
there was also a great festival, and the earth became like Vaikuṇṭha itself.
From that time forward, Brahmā and all the other gods, along with the Kinnaras,
have worshipped at Bhṛgu’s Tīrtha, where Maheśvara is pleased.
Where Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, was eternally present as Nārāyaṇī,
she performed most severe penance in order to obtain Nārāyaṇa as her husband.
I, pleased by her asceticism, departed after ten thousand years had passed;
then, I granted her a boon for marriage.
"Indeed, we must go to Bhṛgukṣetra, for it is there that we shall depart from Vaikuṇṭha in a supreme form; O beloved ones, please make yourselves ready. (73)
On Bhṛgutuṅga, the excellent sage Bhṛgu,
whose wealth is his austerity, shines with fame along with eighty-eight thousand Brahman-sages.
Then, at a distance from there on the radiant bank of the Narmadā, at the fifty-yojana mark, we indeed are at Viṣṇutīrtha. (75)
"Having caused Vaikuṇṭha to be constructed as a terrestrial realm by Viśvakarman, we thirty-three crores of dear gods shall also reside there. (76)
Driven by the current, they will remain there at the bank of Devatīrtha;
likewise, the sages will stay at Ṛṣitīrtha and human beings at Cakratīrtha.
At Śuklatīrtha, Kṛṣṇa and all the other supreme lords,
as well as the liberated ones, shall remain at Brahmatīrtha as its great presiding deities.
"In this way, indeed, we shall dwell with devotion in the land of the Narmadā;
and on the full moon day of Kārtika, we shall establish a new Vaikuṇṭha there. (79)
"On the full moon day of Māgha, we shall go to Bhṛgupattana for the purpose of marriage," thus the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa directed them all.
Having summoned the goddess Earth, Acyuta commanded her:
"Make the bank of the Revā empty, extending for a hundred yojanas."
Make it level and beautifully adorned with well-situated gardens; and there, cause halls to be built equipped with every kind of food and drink.
And bring all kinds of things there as well, my dear:
grains, fruits, leaves, tubers, and roots in every variety. (83)
Divine garments, fragrant powders of every kind, delicious and refined foods, and indeed sugar and other such sweets; ||84||
Establish many [treasures] within the depths of your womb;
by my yoga, let the earth become divine, possessing the splendor of Vaikuṇṭha.
Having thus received this blessing, Bhūmi arrived there;
within the interior of the earth, which extends for a hundred yojanas, all riches reside.
Having fashioned it and placed it there, she remained at ease, filled with joy;
then Narayana summoned Varuna, the god of water.
He gave instructions regarding the nectars and other drinks, the milks and the waters,
the curds and the intoxicants, as well as the clarified butters and the juices.
Of honey, of secret waters, and of trees abounding in sap;
of the wealth consisting of the moon-plant, the wish-granting creeper, the celestial tree, and so forth.
He also commanded that streams of juices, drinks, and vast lakes be created and maintained; and he, having gone there, did exactly so.
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa commanded the Sun, the Moon, the lightning, the submarine fire, the great conflagration, and the celestial kitchens. 91.
There were various kitchens and smoke-emitting fire-halls,
constructed there to provide the grandeur of cold and hot bathing pools.
There were the splendors of lamps and torches, with moonlight-like cool radiance;
great expanses of light that, though vast, seemed to create the illusion of darkness.
Keśava commanded that mortars, grinding stones, stoves, water-jars, and brooms be fashioned, all divine and filled with celestial liquids.
Likewise, having summoned Vāyu and the Maruts who are the vital breaths, as well as the fans and palm-leaf whisks that possess a gentle and sweet fragrance. (95)
Hari commanded the winds to become cool in some places and hot in others;
and having summoned space, he then transformed it into the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Having dispatched his divine manifestation there, Hari, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, then made another; Kṛṣṇa said to the clouds, "Let them fashion parasols."
Mādhava commanded Indra to fetch the royal regalia,
and he directed Kubera to bring all the machines rich with every kind of gem.
He said to Yama, "Make your great army march at the front for the sake of splendor," and there he said to Śambhu and his attendants, "Indeed, dance! 99.
He offered the musical instruments to Sarasvatī for the purpose of playing them,
and he assigned Viśvakarman to construct the pavilions.
In order to enhance the splendor [of the city], he dispatched divine artisans;
instructed by Bhṛgu, the Preceptor (Bṛhaspati) examined the auspicious moment, drew up a document, and sent it forth. 101.
He went to his abode, gave gifts to the Infinite One (Bhūman), and had musical instruments played;
he then dispatched Nārada to the three worlds to issue an invitation.
Likewise, Bali and the others residing in the netherworld were summoned, as well as the mountains and so forth, the rivers, and the sacred fords—both the insentient and the sentient. (103)
The sages, the ascetics, the gods, the ancestors, the celibate students, the virtuous women, and all the virtuous Sātvatas were likewise summoned.
The Īśas, the Īśeśvaras, and the Blessed Ones who are lords of the directions;
the guardians of the worlds, the protectors of creatures, the lords of reality, and the supreme lords.
The Brahmās, Viṣṇus, Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus, as well as the Vairājas, Vālakhilyas, the attendants of Yama, the planets, and the stars. || 106 ||
The Ketu-planets, those situated in the coverings, the Īśvaras, the Amṛtas, and the Akṣaras;
those residing in Vaikuṇṭha, the inhabitants of Goloka, and those who go to Śvetadhāma. || 107 ||

Others are devoted to the world of Māyā, while others are devoted to Tejas; there are those who are liberated, those who dwell in the divine abodes, the Śaktis, and the consorts of the Liberated Ones.
The Brahmāṇīs, the Sāṃkhyayoginīs, the Bhagavatīs, and the Devatās; likewise the Īśvarīṇīs, the Ārṣyas, and also the Vedas and the Vedānyas. (1.09)
Likewise, there were male incarnations and female incarnations, the wives of Hari;
all were Mānavīs, Vallikās, Kāśyapīs, and young women.
And there were maidens, as well as married women and others whose husbands were living;
all women, whether insentient or sentient, were summoned together. (111)
For the sake of increasing the joy of the wedding festival of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with Bhārgavī here, let them come to my house at midday. 11.2.
I invoke directly the Lord of Syllables, known as Puruṣottama,
with great love on the eleventh day in my auspicious home.
During the ascent to the pavilion, during the journey, and likewise at the house of the bride's father—may all indeed be my companions; I myself, Hari, am pleased.
"Let them all come here to my imperishable abode together with their households;
we shall all go to Bhārgavapattana on earth."
"O lords, we shall go from here to the beautiful bank of the Narmadā, to Śuklatīrtha, where an hermitage has been established for the sake of Bhārgavī’s marriage. (116)
In this manner, saffron letters were sent to every layer of the cosmic eggs by the attendants; thereafter, auspicious events occurred.
The goddesses, who were abodes of auspiciousness, sang beautiful songs;
they performed the rubbing of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with powdered flour.
Musicians played beautiful instruments on all sides;
the gods and gandharvas sang, and the dancers performed their dances. || 11.9 ||
The great-souled ones assembled toward the abode known as Akṣara;
the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, offered them honor and hospitality.
He caused them to be fed divine, sweet foods that were like nectar,
and he caused them to drink divine waters that were like nectar.
There were vehicles and mounts beautiful with their ornamental attire,
as well as crores of white elephants and likewise crores of Garuḍas.
There were also crores of swans, lions, bulls, and peacocks,
as well as crores of divine horses, śarabhas, gavayas, and other such creatures.
There are Arbudas, Śeṣa-śayyas, and palanquins by the millions upon millions;
there are Paryas with wings, infinite in number, as well as Īśānyas and Pakṣacārikās.
Those who dwell in Goloka, infinite and eternal, were eager for the festival of the wedding and yoked themselves to the bridal procession. || 1.25 ||
Accompanied by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they went to Vaikuṇṭha— countless in number—
those residing in Amṛta, those residing in Hiraṇya, those residing in Āvṛti, and those residing in Virāṭ.
Those established in truth, those beginning with humans, the gods, the crawling creatures, and human beings—
all stationary and moving things— came joyfully to the army.
"Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has a wedding with the daughter of Bhṛgu;
let us go for the sake of seeing it—let all the family members come! (128)
Thus, all of them—beginning with children and ending with the elderly—having been honored and fed, departed with joy; they then gathered together and mingled within the army.
The groom was properly adorned like another Lord of Rādhā, with unbroken grains, saffron, flower garlands, garments, and ornaments. (1.382.13)
He was further honored with blessings by means of jewels, pearls, golden chains, rings, kajjala, fragrant liquids, powders, and other such items.
And at the age of sixteen, he went for the sake of Bhārgavī’s marriage;
indeed, from the world of the Imperishable Brahman, she descended toward the world of Vaikuṇṭha.
That army following the side of the bridegroom became long, resplendent with the throat-sounds of dancing, auspicious musical instruments, and other such sounds. || 133 ||
Counting by arbudas and arbudas, they arrived at Śuklatīrtha;
and at that time, auspicious events occurred throughout all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
In the divine Vaikuṇṭha of ten million levels, on the auspicious bank of the Revā river,
extending for a hundred yojanas and rising a hundred thousand yojanas high.
By the will of Nārāyaṇa, through the desire of Hari, countless world-systems, vast in extent and height, arrived there in that auspicious place.

The supernatural powers (siddhis) are: atomization (aṇimā), magnification (mahimā), extension (prāpti), fulfillment of desires (prākāmya), levitation (laghimā), weightiness (garimā), mastery (vaśitā), and the power of determining the course of things at will (kāmāvasāyitā). || 1.37 ||
But where Hari resides, what indeed is there to wonder at?
For even countless universes exist within the pores of his body.
What wonder indeed could there be even in a space the size of an atom?
Thus did that excellent river arrive at Śuklatīrtha. 13.9.
He rested happily there in his own Vaikuṇṭha with joy;
those who dwell in the abodes of the Lord bathed, were fed, and slept.
Auspiciousness arose everywhere; at that time, the living beings, full of eagerness, came to Śuklatīrtha, [thinking], "This is the wedding of the two lotuses."
Brahmā was accompanied by Sāvitrī, Bhava himself by Bhavānī,
Ananta by Bhoginī, and Dharma by Mūrti and the others.
Bhāskara was with Prabhā, Hutāśana with Svāhā, Kubera with Śrī, and Varuṇa accompanied by Vāruṇī. || 143 ||
Pavana also went with Cāñjanī, and Yama went with Dhūmryā;
the Moon was accompanied by Rohiṇī and others, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra) was joined by Śacī. || 144 ||
The Rudras together with Rudrāṇī and the others, the Ādityas along with Saṃjñā, as well as the Vasus, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Devas, and Dānavas; || 145 ||
They went to Śuklatīrtha for the marriage of the two lotuses;
indeed, having seen it, the gods and others made Vaikuṇṭha new once again.
And having reached the bank of the Narmadā by means of celestial chariots from the sky,
they arrived at a new city near Bhṛgukaccha.
It was adorned all around with rows of jewels such as pearls, rubies, and diamonds, square in shape, and measured one hundred yojanas.
It was surrounded by seven deep moats, sixteen hundred thousand walls, and thirty-three lakes. || 149 ||
It was made fragrant everywhere by the winds carrying blossoming flowers from tens of thousands of flower gardens, which were filled with lotuses and *sarvatobhadra* trees.
It was made fragrant by cool breezes carrying the scent of mild sandalwood,
and adorned with tens of millions of trees, including mango trees.
With coconuts, jackfruits, pomegranates of nine colors, grapes, betel vines, cardamom, and cloves; || 152 ||
With *badarī* trees, *bilva*, *jambū*, and *campaka*;
likewise with *bakula*, *tintiḍī*, *jambīra*, and *ikṣu*. (153)
It was filled with dates, oranges, and myrobalans, as well as other fruit-bearing trees and excellent gardens, and was overspread with lush green meadows. || 154 ||
It was adorned with countless beautiful and exceedingly lofty temples,
embellished by the exquisite paintings of those various sanctuaries and crowned with finials.
It was likewise radiant with divine pillars and clusters of jeweled staircases, and it was adorned with mirrors, fine fabrics, and white chowries. || 156 ||
It was adorned with courtyards made of ruby and other gems, embellished with sapphires, featuring spacious squares and royal highways, and graced by gods and goddesses.
Upon seeing the city of Vaikuṇṭha, they were all filled with wonder;
Viṣṇu, Padma, and Śrī Padmā, as well as Bhṛgu himself, who was their father-in-law. (158)
Wherever the Blessed One, the son-in-law, might be, what indeed could be lacking there?
There were Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Vidyādharīs, Kinnarīs, and Īśikās. (159)
Dancers, singers, musicians, and likewise vocalists; mendicants, astrologers, bards, kings, physicians, and servants. || 1.382.160 ||
Actors, wrestlers, those of many forms, men wearing various costumes, and likewise young men,
full of enthusiasm, arrived there for the marriage of the two lotuses.
At Bhṛgukaccha as well, renunciants, ascetics, and lifelong yogis, summoned by Bhṛgu, arrived for the wedding of the two lotuses. || 162 ||
Sanaka, Sananda, Sanat, and Sanātana likewise arrived with three crores of disciples for the marriage of the two Padmās. || 163 ||
Durvāsas with a hundred thousand disciples, Kaśyapa with a hundred thousand servants, and the marriage of the two lotuses with a hundred thousand disciples of Patnīvat. || 164 ||
Gautama had ten thousand disciples, Vālmīki had ten thousand disciples, and Śukra had ten million disciples; thus was the marriage of the two lotuses [Śiva and Pārvatī] presided over by their gurus.
Bhāradvāja with ten thousand disciples, Bṛhaspati himself with ten million, and Aṅgiras with ten thousand disciples [performed] the marriage of the two lotuses. || 166 ||
Vasiṣṭha had a hundred thousand disciples, and Pracetas likewise possessed a hundred thousand disciples;
Pulastya also had a hundred thousand disciples, and the marriage of the two lotuses [took place]. (167)
Agastya arrived with a hundred thousand disciples, as did Pulaha accompanied by a hundred thousand disciples; Kratu came with a hundred thousand, and Atri arrived with ten million disciples.
Marīci with a hundred thousand disciples and Śatānanda with a thousand came to the house of Bhṛgu for the wedding of the two lotuses.
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga Vibhāṇḍaka was with a thousand disciples, as was Pāṇini; likewise, Kātyāyana was with ten million and ten thousand disciples.
Yājñavalkya [performed the wedding] with thousands, Vyāsa with ten million disciples,
and Garga with his disciples through the joining of their hands (padmayoḥ).
Gālava also [did so] with a thousand, and Saubhari with a thousand.
And there was also the marriage of Lomaśa with Koṭī and Padmā. || 172 ||
Sāndīpani, Devala, Mārkaṇḍeya, Pañcaśikha, Gopāla, and Voḍhu, each with hundreds of thousands of disciples. || 173 ||
Likewise, I am the self-luminous Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa;
Viśvāmitra [performed] a marriage with ten million [brides], as did Padmaja;
Jaratkāru with a hundred thousand, and Āstīka with ten thousand disciples.
Parśurāma [performed] a thousand [marriages]; the marriage of the two lotuses was thus.
Vatsa [performed] a hundred; Dakṣa, three hundred; Kapila, ten thousand; Savarta, with ten thousand disciples and others—the marriage of the two lotuses was thus. (175–176)
Utathya with a hundred disciples, and Bhāguri with another hundred, as well as countless others, arrived for the marriage of the two lotuses.
"We shall go to wed Lakṣmī, the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, who was born to Bhṛgu from Khyāti, for the marriage of two lotuses is [fitting]. (178)
The two gods Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, both brothers-in-law of Meru and the brothers of Lakṣmī, indeed paid them great honor. || 179 ||
Āyati and Niyati were also the two daughters of Meru, devoted to their husbands;
from Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, Mṛkaṇḍu was born as their legitimate son.
Mārkaṇḍeya was the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, and Vedaśiras was his offspring;
likewise, Pūrṇamāsa was born as the son of Marīci.
Tuṣṭi, Vṛṣṭi, Kṛṣṭi, and Āpaciti were the four daughters;
Virajas and Parvata were both the sons of Pūrṇamāsa.
Kṣamā was the wife of Pulaha; their sons were Kardama, Varīyān, Sahiṣṇu, and the youngest, Yayu. (183)
Atri’s wife was Anasūyā, whose sons were Soma, Dattaka, and Durvāsas; likewise, Aṅgiras’s daughter was known by the name Smṛti.
The Vāsiṣṭhas, the Śaktimukhyas, the Vāhneyas, the Kratuputrakas, the Agniṣvāttas, the Bārhiṣadas, the Ājyapas, and likewise the Somapas. || 185 ||
The Vālakhilya sages, the Earth, Meru, the mountain goddess Bhāminī, the mountains, the rivers, the lakes, and the groves; 186.
In this manner, the lineages and genealogies of the sages were recounted there at that great festival,
as they arrived at the house of Bhṛgu for the wedding of the two lotuses.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and likewise the Bull;
Kapila, Vāsudeva, Pṛthu, Datta, and the Lord of Sages (Rāma). || 188 ||
Haṃsa, Hari, Vāmana, Paraśurāma, the Kumāras, Yajña, Rāma, Hyagrīva, Nārada, and the king of kings (Rājarājaka). || 189 ||
Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki, who is Nārāyaṇa himself; likewise Palīvrata and others, disciples who are practitioners of yoga.
The yogic adepts from Mount Raivata in Saurāṣṭra arrived together with their wives, thinking, "This is the wedding of the two lotuses. (191)
Indeed, the Māṇḍavyas on the bride’s side numbered more than a hundred million,
while those on the groom’s side were even more numerous, beyond counting.
On the twelfth day, those honored guests were hospitably entertained with food, drink, and other offerings;
they rested during the night, delighted by songs, dances, and other festivities.
Various auspicious rites and supreme worldly customs were performed;
indeed, all were joyful at heart and became serene and satisfied. (194)

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who was pleased by the penance performed by Lakṣmī—the daughter of Bhṛgu and known as Bhārgavī—for the sake of marriage after having caused Vaikuṇṭha to be established at Śuklatīrtha near Bhṛgukaccha," within the section on the Greatness of the Devoted Wife in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, for Mahālakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, was indeed golden-hued, possessing the brilliance of a campaka flower, radiant, and divine in form. (1)
She was exceedingly beautiful and charming, the most honored among beautiful women; she was endowed with fresh youth and adorned with jewel ornaments.
Rich with the luster of molten gold and adorned by a halo of radiance,
she was Satyaśīlā, a devoted wife whose very nature was pure truth.
She is peaceful, self-controlled, and exceedingly tranquil, endowed with infinite virtues;
she is Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Candranārī, and Rohiṇī.
The wife of Kubera, the wife of Sūrya, Svāhā, Śāntā, Kalāvatī, and others such as Ahalyā and Pārvatī, were all exceedingly radiant. (5)
The celestial women and the wives of the gods, upon seeing her, do not equal even a sixteenth part of Bhārgavī, the daughter of Bhaga. (6)
She was richly endowed with the splendor of the full autumn moon, possessed eyes like autumn lotuses,
was a young woman fit for marriage, and was a virtuous lady whose face was bowed with modesty.
Seeing all those splendors within her form, which was perfectly proportioned to her beauty, they were bewildered; they became motionless, as if dissolved and as inert as wood.
"Aha! By her, Nārāyaṇa himself has been determined as her husband;
in that case, what could be merely figurative regarding his qualities, his form, and his stature? (9)
In the creation of the Blessed One, no such being has ever been produced;
nor does there exist, nor will there ever be, any woman of divine limbs who is destined for such a state.
This Padmā is indeed Nārāyaṇī herself, the daughter of Bhṛgu;
she is worthy of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and he too is worthy of her.
Thus they spoke of this supreme wonder, rejoiced, and gazed upon her again and again;
for, meditating on that maiden as Lakṣmī herself, the daughter of Bhṛgu, they were truly satisfied within their own souls.
And they considered the Lord Nārāyaṇa— who was endowed with excellent youth, virtuous in character, and true to his promise— to be the most worthy suitor.
One who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, a scholar, handsome and auspicious, peaceful, self-controlled, characterized by forgiveness, virtuous, and long-lived. (14)
Born from the family of Brahmā and established everywhere, he is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the perfect Brahman, Śrī Puruṣottama. || 15 ||
Untainted and effortless, the witness of all actions—Him whom the four Vedas and even the virtuous deities do not know. (16)
The lords of the Siddhas, the lords of the Munis, and the gods beginning with Brahmā—
even they, purified by meditation, meditate upon him whom the yogins do not know.
Sarasvatī has become inert, as have the Vedas and whatever scriptures exist;
so too has Śeṣa with his thousand mouths, and Sadāśiva with his five faces. (18)
The four-faced creator of the world, Kumāra, and likewise Kārtika,
as well as the sages and seers, were devoted and supreme Vaiṣṇavas.
Even others do not know who he is, how great he is, or what his qualities are; yet by attaining this excellent descendant of Bhṛgu, the fruit of human birth is fully realized.
Thousands of streams of clarified butter and tens of thousands of streams of honey;
thousands of streams of curd and tens of thousands of streams of milk.
There were lakes of oil, mountains of jaggery, heaps of sugar,
mountains of sweet foods, and likewise mounds of flour.
Mountains of flour made from barley and wheat, as well as heaps of parched grain and piles of side dishes, were seen, appearing as inexhaustible sources. (23)
"Oh, how great is our fortune that we behold with such enthusiasm this marriage of the two lotus-eyed ones! (24)
The palaces are equal to heaven, and rivers of nectar flow there;
there are also vehicles and celestial chariots that travel through the sky in every way. (25)
And there were tens of millions of mounts such as swans, Garuḍas, and elephants, as well as cities all around the mountain at Bhṛgukaccha. (26)
Indeed, Bhṛgu caused new mental [temples] to be constructed,
just as Nārāyaṇa himself had caused a new one to be built in Vaikuṇṭha.
Likewise, by Bhṛgu, a long, radiant shore was created,
extending for a hundred yojanas in width and rising a hundred thousand yojanas in height.
There, the divine city of Bhṛgu was built, and a pavilion for Śrī was constructed;
and the Ocean himself appeared there, bestowing hospitality. (29)
Meru as well as others, the Siddhas, and other Munis, those perfected in the Kalpas, and those from the Kṛta Yuga and other ages, who bestow honor; ||| 1.383.30 ||
On the side of the bride’s party, there were indeed ascetics equal to Kṛṣṇa, and female ascetics equal in splendor to Śrī; there was not even the slightest deficiency therein.
On the thirteenth day, auspicious rites were performed according to the customs of the learned;
likewise, worldly conventions were observed, and [the deities] were worshipped and fed.
During the night, auspicious songs and dances were performed;
and on the morning of the fourteenth day, the women conducted the worship of the deity.
Those auspicious women, accompanied by their daughters-in-law, performed the worship of the goddesses and deities according to the customs of the world. (34)
Having fed the two Nārāyaṇas on the ground on the fourteenth day, he had Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa dressed in fine attire during the night.
Having fully worshipped that which is exceedingly delightful, incomparable, and difficult to find within the three worlds, he caused a most excellent and superior festival procession to be held.
Likewise, Kṛṣṇa and others, as well as Nārāyaṇa and other incarnations, the Vairāja and others who are liberated, and those employed in the creation of Brahmā. (37)
Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, and others; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; their wives, the Gaṇeśas, the ṛṣis, and likewise the inhabitants of heaven. 38.
All the gods and goddesses went to the pavilion at Bhṛgupattana;
there, indeed, were crores and billions of golden lion-thrones.
By him, Sudharmā was created upon that sea of golden sand;
