there were hundreds of thousands of dancers and likewise hundreds of thousands of celestial musicians (gāndharvas).
Kinnara singers, numbering in the tens of millions, stood by;
all this was created by Bhṛgu for the gratification of the Blessed Ones. 41.
Neither what has been nor what is yet to be, neither fashioned nor produced by supernatural power, not even a hundred thousand Vidyādharīs or hundreds of thousands of Apsarases [could equal it]. (42)
That divine city of Bhṛgu, Bhrigupattana, was filled with great palaces;
it was even more resplendent than the palace of Vairāja.
In whose rampart-tower the sun is installed, and within the center of whose interior the full moon is firmly established. (44)
Thus, radiant and eternal structures were built along every street;
there, in Bhṛgupattana, light exists without any external cause.
Indeed, the principles (tattvas) were established in embodied form for the sake of service;
the wheel entered Bhṛgupattana as an excellent procession. 46.
On the morning of the full moon, while the sun was visible, they were honored by Bhṛgu; in that very interval, Bṛhaspati arrived before them.
Accompanied by ten billion rishis, he came before Hari,
having offered auspicious fruit along with a moon-shaped mark and unbroken grains of rice.
Placing a garland of flowers around his neck, she showered Hari with blossoms;
she also performed the auspicious worldly custom of showing him the water-pitcher.
And virtuous maidens performed [ceremonies] near the village gate,
while the sages caused the sounds of the Vedas— recitations for prosperity— to be heard.
Bṛhaspati caused him to enter the city while reciting Vedic hymns;
there were daughters of gods, daughters of nāgas, daughters of kings, and daughters of sages.
The daughters of the sages, smiling, came together to see the bridegroom;
all the women gazed at him with eyes that did not blink.
He is gracious, dark as a rain-cloud, adorned with yellow garments,
his entire body anointed with sandalwood paste, and decorated with a forest garland and other ornaments.
Resplendent, adorned with jeweled armlets, bracelets, and necklaces,
and graced by a pair of jeweled earrings shining upon the regions of his cheeks.
Adorned with tinkling anklets fashioned from the finest essence of jewels, He gazes at a jeweled mirror while smiling, with a flute held in His hand. ||55||
He was served by hundreds of thousands of attendants with white chowries;
he was endowed with fresh youth, and his eyes were like autumn lotuses. 56.
His face is like the full moon of autumn; he fills the hearts of Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and others; his beauty equals that of ten million Cupids; and he is worshipped by Brahmā, Śeṣa, and Īśvara. 57.
The form that brings supreme delight, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons, nourished by the fullness of the potency of desire—[I bow to] the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||58||
She holds a blade of dūrvā grass and a silken thread, a mirror with a core of the finest gems,
a sacrificial knife for the rite to be accomplished, and a shimmering cluster of blossoms from a plantain tree.
Her crest-lock was shaped like the three strides of Viṣṇu and adorned with a garland of jasmine;
she wore upon her head a crown, radiant as a flower offered by a woman.
Upon seeing the Supreme Lord, the excellent youth, the young women fell into a state of delirium;
they spoke their desired words, saying, "Blessed is the life of Bhārgava's daughter; it is praiseworthy! (61)
Khyāti, the beloved wife of Bhṛgu’s descendant,
gazed at her son-in-law with eyes and face bright with joy, never blinking.
Bhṛgu, with a serene countenance, together with the sages and the family priest,
approached Kṛṣṇa Hari and bowed down to him and the gods and brahmins.
He gave a resting palace, a hundred yojanas in extent,
filled with food and drink, and graced by playful female attendants.
Bhūmā performed the auspicious consecration of Hari with mantras,
having fully worshipped all the Mātṛkās and all the deities in person.
Having bestowed a stream of wealth as well as the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other rites,
he fed everyone and caused them to drink the finest flavors;
he had musical instruments played and caused auspicious ceremonies to be performed.
And he caused the auspicious procession for the peerless bridegroom to proceed.
In this manner, the sage Bhṛgu also had a most beautiful and highly auspicious human vehicle prepared for the sake of the wedding.
Through his preceptor, the family priest, he had the ritual performed with sacred mantras;
and [he gave away] jewels, wealth, and the like—pearls, rubies, and diamonds.
He gave foodstuffs, garments, and other gifts to those in need;
he had musical instruments played and caused auspicious rites to be performed.
He had the daughter of Bhṛgu adorned in most beautiful attire, and the goddesses and the wives of the sages performed the customary rites as was appropriate. (71)
Then, when an auspicious moment had arrived, during the supreme rising of Mahendra, at a wedding-appropriate *lagna* conjoined with its presiding deity; ||72||

When the moment is purified by the aspect of benefics, when it is devoid of the views of the wicked, and when the auspicious moment, the auspicious lunar mansion, and the purity of the moon and stars are present; ||73||

Free from defects such as planetary afflictions and devoid of [inauspicious] marks like lines on the palms, it is worthy of bringing happiness to the couple and bestows the bliss of a fruitful marriage. (74)
When this time had arrived, Hari came to the courtyard of the sage Bhṛgu, accompanied by the lords of the gods and other sages, brahmins, and priests.
By the lords and the Blessed Ones, as well as by those with abundance of dharma, devotion, and so forth; by Lakṣmī, the attendants, and likewise by the liberated ones and the sages.
With stationary and moving beings, divine ones, those learned in the scriptures, dancers, actors, singers, garland-makers, and even with vidyādharīs; 77.
The gods, goddesses, and lords, along with their wives, beheld that place [frequented] by apsarases, kinnarīs, female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and others. (78)
With hundreds of thousands of golden plantain pillars adorned with silk threads, and with the tender sprouts of campaka, sandalwood, and mango trees; ||79||
With various kinds of garlands, including yellow, red, and white ones,
and with auspicious jars filled with fruits and sprouts placed all around.
With leaves smeared with musk and sandalwood, radiant with saffron, and adorned with parched grain, fruits, flowers, and dūrvā grass; ||81||
It was inhabited by lords, sages, brahmins, gods, and ancestors;
it was enchanting, furnished with an altar constructed from the finest essence of jewels.
It was honored with offerings of sandalwood paste, blended with musk and saffron,
and rendered fragrant by breezes that were sweet-scented, cool, and gentle.
It was radiant with millions of jewels and brilliant lamps,
and it was made fragrant by various kinds of incense and aromatic substances.
It was made beautiful on all sides by the various delightful works of artisans,
and by the exquisite songs of the Gandharvas and the beautiful dances of the performers.
It was watched by the *vidyādharīs* with their amorous gestures, by the *apsarases* with their beautiful songs, and by the young wives from the windows with melodious voices.
With an auspicious jar, by a learned and excellent priest,
by Bhṛgu with kuśa grass in hand, and by means of gifts consisting of dānava-substances.
Having seen the gods, beginning with Bhṛgu, Brahmā, and Īśvara,
as well as Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Vairāja, and those such as Matsya, in the beautiful courtyard.
Having suddenly beheld them all, Bhṛgu, accompanied by his family,
bowed his head in salutation to the gods, the lords, and the sages who were worthy of worship.
Having honored them with great respect, he seated them one by one in order upon separate and most beautiful jewel-thrones.
He said: "Today my birth has indeed become fruitful, and my life has become the severer of the root of karma for tens of millions of lifetimes. (91)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, is himself the one who descends;
he is the eternal bestower of prosperity, liberation, worldly enjoyment, and heaven. 92.
I am truly unable to behold his lotus feet even in a dream;
yet today that Creator, the bestower of the fruits of all austerities, has appeared in my very courtyard.
To those who delight in their own Self, who are full, and who desire auspicious inquiry—
even by the lords of yogis, the lords of siddhas, the lords of gods, and the lords of sages— (94)

That Blessed Lord Śrī Hari, unseen in meditation, has today appeared in my courtyard—the Death of Death, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Sovereign of the Lords of Incarnations, the Supreme Master. (95)
Having assumed a human form, you have come into the range of men's vision;
you have arrived in my courtyard to make my daughter’s life fruitful. (96)
He who is the inner controller of all, the Lord who grants all desires, whose end cannot be found even in the Vedas—that Hari is today in my courtyard. (97)
He who is the Lord of lords, whose worship is foremost among all—he Kṛṣṇa, the Master of Goloka—has indeed come today into my courtyard by virtue of my good fortune. (98)
He whose beloved wives are indeed Lakṣmī, Anantā, and the others—Nārāyaṇa himself has come today to my courtyard for the purpose of taking my daughter. 99.
The Vairāja gods and others, the ancestors, and those humans who are devotees of the Lord dwelling in the netherworlds—all are here today in my courtyard; I am truly blessed!
They are liberated, never to return, and dwell in the Imperishable;
there are crores of Kṛṣṇa’s wives, as well as all things moving and stationary.
"Today, all the divine host of beings is in my courtyard; I am blessed!
For those sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons of Brahmā who have never been seen before are here."
"O Lord, all of them and my blessed daughter shall come to my house this very day;
oh, until the end of the kalpa, my hermitage has become a sacred pilgrimage site! (103)
The water from whose feet constitutes a sacred ford—that is my pure home.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, they are all contained within the ocean.
Whatever sacred fords exist in the ocean are truly present in the feet of the virtuous;
for as long as the earth endures, it remains moistened by the water from the feet of the virtuous.
To that extent, indeed, the gods and the ancestors remain satisfied on earth;
it is the eradicator of calamities and likewise the bestower of prosperity. (106)
It is the destroyer of diseases, the medicine that removes the sickness of illusion, the bestower of happiness and auspiciousness, the essence, and the nectar from the feet of the divine sages. 107.
Today I shall obtain the nectar of the feet of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
there is no sacred ford equal to the Revā, and no god higher than Keśava.
"Today that very same Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa himself, is present in my home.
Having said this, Bhṛgu prostrated like a staff and praised the Imperishable One.
I am yours; I am your excellent daughter, O Lord.
You truly belong to me, and everything that is mine belongs to you. You alone are the cause of all that is mine.
Grant the supreme state; may it purify my life.
Having placed his own hands upon Kṛṣṇa’s feet,
Bhṛgu joyfully offered water for the feet at the lotus-like feet worshipped by Lakṣmī.
And he offered the *arghya* consisting of water mixed with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
as well as the fragrant *madhuparka* and sandalwood paste for all his limbs.

She placed a garland of *pārijāta* flowers and other blossoms around the neck of her son-in-law, and for the sake of the formal acceptance (*varaṇa*), she placed an ornament on his wrist and gave him the fruit that grants all desires.
He placed upon Kṛṣṇa’s head a crown radiant with jewels,
and offered incense, jewel-lamps, and most enchanting food offerings.
He offered various kinds of flowers and a jeweled lion-throne;
he gave him water from the seven sacred fords for the purpose of sipping.
Excellent betel-leaf, sweet and well-scented with camphor and other fragrances; a delightful bed that brings pleasure in lovemaking; and scented water for drinking. 1.16.
Having thus performed the formal betrothal, he joyfully offered a handful of flowers.
Then, indeed, in the pavilion near the altar, [he worshipped] Śrī Narāyaṇa.
When the full moon had ascended the sky on the day of the full moon,
he caused the customary rites for the world to be performed and worshipped the ruby pillar.
Having bowed to the water-pot, Gaṇeśa, the fire, and his preceptor, Hari,
having performed the auspicious rites, sat upon a beautiful wooden seat.
Then, after the moon had been offered to Hari, blessings were bestowed by the Brahmins with Vedic mantras, as well as by the gods, the lords, and the [manifested] selves.
Bhṛgu, having worshipped the Lord of the Daughter, performed the purification of his body;
meanwhile, there were the sounds of the Vedas, auspicious mantras, and likewise the songs of women.
Likewise, musical sounds of various melodies arose there;
a great festival then took place, such that even Bhṛgu’s joy could not surpass it.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Bridegroom’s Journey from Śuklatīrtha to Bhṛgupattana with his attendants, the auspicious rites and honors, the joyful words of Bhṛgu, and the arrival of the bridegroom at the pavilion," within the section on the greatness of devoted wives in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which was offered from the presence of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as divine garments, ornaments, and so forth for the sake of the bride.
Indeed, all the garments and ornaments that were the manifestation of the splendor of Brahmadhāman,
all of that this daughter of Bhṛgu, possessing a divine form, wore.
Lakṣmī, Śrī, Sāvitrī, Ramā, and the others; Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Jayā, Prabhā, Lalitā, and the rest, adorned her. || 3 ||
Khyāti and the other Mothers also adorned her with great respect;
thus embellished and highly decorated, she shone, endowed with divine splendor.
Wearing garments as pure as fire, adorned with a heavy braid of hair, marked with drops of musk, and anointed with smooth, excellent sandalwood paste. || 5 ||
She is eternally radiant in the center of her forehead with a dot of vermilion;
she possesses the luster of molten gold and a splendor equal to ten million moons.
All her limbs were adorned with moonstones, she was beautified by garlands of *mālatī* flowers,
her eyes were anointed black, and her lips were as lovely as ripe *bimba* fruits.
Her breasts were like orange fruits, her two hands were golden-hued with fingers [of the same color],
and she was enchanting with the various regions of her body where the fine line of hair shone.
Her divine marks were known to be those of one who dwells with Lakṣmī by the lines [on her palms];
the soles of her lotus-feet were adorned with red lac, and her hands were like lotuses.
She was led into the pavilion near the altar by the bridegroom’s garland,
which was beautifully fashioned with jewels, diamonds, gold, flowers, and other ornaments.
Adorned by women holding lamps in their hands in the presence of the bridegroom, she bowed to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and having bowed to the fire and the deities, [she proceeded]. (11)
Having been firmly established on the left side, the cry of "Victory! indeed arose at that time;
and various musical instruments were played during that festival.
Being seen with a smile, Lakṣmī bowed her head to the face of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and her own husband, and scattered a handful of flowers over him.
On Kṛṣṇa’s head and forehead, she applied a crescent-shaped mark of unbroken rice and saffron,
as well as a sandalwood tilaka, and offered fragrant water.
Having placed the garland of choice upon Kṛṣṇa’s neck, she bowed at his feet;
then, having washed her thumb with water from a sacred site, she drank the water.
Having performed seven circumambulations and bowing again to her husband, she [remained there].
He sprinkled the water from the sacred ford, mixed with sandalwood, using sprouts.
Then, having bowed, when Satī sat down on his left side,
the beloved of the world sprinkled his beloved wife, who was tranquil and smiling gently.
Having personally placed a mark of unbroken rice upon her forehead,
the Lord Hari placed his hands upon her head and showered flowers over her.
Then the priest Bṛhaspati, in the presence of Nārada, placed the garland that was around his own neck upon the throat of the bride.
Adorned with a garland of choice flowers, Lakṣmī shone like lightning amidst the clouds;
then, at that moment, mantras issued forth from the circle of sages there.
There, Bhṛgu placed the auspicious hand of his daughter into the hand of Kṛṣṇa;
thus Bhṛgu gave her away with the gift-offering accompanied by Vedic mantras.
Then, at the word of Bṛhaspati, Hari said, "May it be well," and Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa took Lakṣmī as his own beloved.
Then the Lord [bestowed] gifts of jewels, wealth, and likewise cows,
houses, mansions, and even cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Bhṛgu also gave [a gift] there, and Nārāyaṇa likewise gave one;
then Bhṛgu bestowed the city of Bhṛgukaccha upon his daughter.
And the Compassionate One bestowed upon Bhṛgu the state of plenitude, the gift of liberation, the revelation of the light, and the knowledge that is unassailable throughout the three periods of time.

At that time, he also gave gifts of elephants, horses, carriages, and mounts; they bestowed upon the bride and the groom the wealth held in their hands as a dowry. Incarnations of the Lord, sages, and likewise the ancestors [were present].
And the gods and humans, those dwelling on earth and those residing in the netherworld, [were each established] according to their respective order. || 27 ||
Having performed a gift appropriate to whatever kind of prosperity they possess,
he then circumambulated the fire four times.
The couple stood together in the presence of the fire and bowed once more;
they then sat down and performed the fire-oblation with clarified butter and other offerings.
Then Hari gave that very ring to his bride;
placing it upon the tips of her fingers, she offered him a morsel of food.
Kṛṣṇa also offered a morsel of food to her;
having played for a moment with his ring, they both returned delighted.
Then the hands of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa were moistened with perspiration.
The hair on their forearms stood erect with thrill. || 32 ||
Accompanied by Lagnagranthi, the two of them then bowed to Agni, as well as to their preceptor and the deities, and departed from the pavilion.
Feasted by Khyāti and the others, the two rested for a moment in private; then, they were joyfully paraded everywhere through the city filled with elephants and other vehicles. (34)
Honored by the subjects and saluted by the people, those two parents,
having untied the marriage-knot at the Narmadā river so that it was no longer bound, [departed].
Accompanied by Khyāti, the mother of Bhārgava, and by the goddesses Īśanī and the others, as well as by virtuous women who possessed both husbands and sons, she was filled with joy. (36)
Having arrived and performed the auspicious rites such as the washing with saffron and other substances,
he led the couple into a palace constructed of jewels.
Adorned with the splendor of many variegated paintings, embellished with strings of diamonds, and brilliantly illuminated by pearls, rubies, gems, and mirrors; (3)
There, Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa beheld the wives of the gods, as well as the wives of the lords and the liberated ones, such as Ramā and others. (39)
And all those wives of the sages, devoted to their husbands,
were seated upon jeweled thrones and adorned with gem-studded ornaments.
They too, having seen the supreme Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
rose up and joyfully seated him upon a jeweled throne.
The wives of the sages offered praise, and her female friends engaged in jesting;
Khyāti then had the maiden fed together with the bridegroom.
She offered betel with camphor and scented water;
and Śāradā placed a leaf containing verses and other writings into Kṛṣṇa’s hand. (43)
At the command of them all, the goddess said to him, "Read it," and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, exceedingly joyful, read the letter. (44)
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Sāvitrī, Rādhikā, Ramā, Satī, Menā, Jayā, Khyāti, Māṇakī, Pārvatī, and Prabhā. (45)
Tulasī, Pṛthivī, Vṛndā, Arundhatī, Yamunā, Aditi, Gaṅgā, Sītā, Śatarūpā, Devahūtī, and Narmadā. (46)
And these goddesses shall bring about the supreme auspiciousness for the bridegroom and the bride;
and Śrī Kṛṣṇa recited this, and they heard it and laughed.
Her youth is new, her lover is new, and likewise her beloved is new;
may the union of this clever woman with this clever man be ever-new and ever-new. (48)
Mature, beautiful, well-nourished, youthful, burdened with prowess, and strong—
in today's encounter regarding strength and weakness, we shall indeed know whose victory it will be.
Rādhā, Ramā, and other excellent women are yours;
tell us now, what kind of beautiful woman is Bhārgavī in private? 1.384.50.
Thus, for the pleasure of their husband, all the women—Lopāmudrā, Anasūyā, Ahalyā, and Arundhatī as well—laughed for a moment. (51)
Then Kambharā and those wives of the sages impetuously seized the Lord,
as well as the gods who were emanations of the Lord, and all beings, both stationary and moving.
And Bhṛgu honored him and fed him with devotion, saying, "Eat, eat! Let sweet food be given, let it be given! (53)
A sound arose in the city with the auspicious music of musical instruments;
then at dawn, the lords quickly became ready.
He caused the procession to proceed, and Khyāti, having placed her daughter Bhārgavī upon her breast for a moment, wept.
"O daughter, O child, how indeed can I, suffering, live without you?
Tell Nārāyaṇa constantly [to come] for the purpose of residing in the house of Bhṛgu. (96)
"Bhṛgukaccha has indeed been given as a wedding gift by the husband and wife;
establish Nārāyaṇa here in his second form. (57)
Lakṣmī, though devoted to her husband, did not issue such a command to Acyuta;
at that time, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s eyes became filled with tears.
She said to Lakṣmī, "O fair-browed one, why have your eyes become filled with water?
I shall do exactly as my mother-in-law says; I am living here. (59)
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa became twofold;
accompanied by Bhārgavī, he dwelt there eternally in the house of Bhṛgu.
Then a second couple, appearing in human form and accompanied by a dowry of ten million [treasures], went to Śuklatīrtha with countless hosts of armies. (61)
Having entered the beautiful palace, he caused auspicious rites to be performed;
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Earth, played exquisite musical instruments.
All the goddesses and other women who were liberated by Hari gazed repeatedly at Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
They caused him to enter the house and performed auspicious rites,
having fed the people dwelling in the three worlds with the four kinds of food.
Having delighted the great lords, they arranged for exemptions; then, taking their armies with them, they departed for the abodes of those who dwell in various regions.
Then, accompanied by the couple, he went to Vaikuṇṭha itself;
the great-souled ones, their worlds filled with wealth, departed for their own realms.
The earth, water, and other elements brought about the destruction of the fashioned Vaikuṇṭha;
those great ones were fed and honored in the house of Bhṛgu.
Receiving honors and laden with divine jewels and other treasures, they went to the land fashioned by Bhṛgu, extending as far as the ocean, which is the abode of great men.
Then, in a mere instant, Bhṛgu withdrew those supernatural powers;
Kambharā became Mahālakṣmī, and Kṛṣṇagopāla remained as he was.
In the presence of their son, the parents took up residence in Bhṛgupattana for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the descendant of Bhṛgu.
And their parents, possessing divine bodies, always remained in the presence of the couple,
just as Khyāti and Bhṛgu remain worshipful in the city of Bhṛgu.
Having obtained Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in secret, Bhārgavī, devoted to her husband, always serves him with various desires. (72)
Do you not remember, Lakṣmī, how at that time you were born as Bhārgavī?
I was born as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; I remember our marriage. (73)
One such as you shall always be my slave, my wife, my object of enjoyment, and my servant;
my companion, my confidante, my co-resident, my protector, and my devoted wife. (74)

There is no other creator of my happiness than she who is peaceful, endowed with auspicious fortune, residing within my heart in the form of lines, fair-complexioned, and having the form of the Śrīvatsa mark. (75)
"I am you, and you are indeed I; there is not even the slightest difference.
Thus have I spoken to you, Lakṣmī; may you become one possessed of great fortune. (76)
From reading and hearing this, heaven and liberation shall be the fruit;
for women, the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa shall be certain. (77)

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bringing of the Pavilion by Bhārgavī, the Procedure for Giving the Daughter in Marriage, the Departure of the Mahīmānas and the Groom after the Wedding, the Dissolution of the Artificial Vaikuṇṭha and Other Places, and the Dwelling of the Son-in-law in the Second Form in the House of Bhagu," within the section on the Greatness of the Chaste Wife in the first book, the Kṛtayuga-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O devoted wife, what kind of meanings do you understand regarding my names?
Tell me, so that I may be pleased upon knowing your supreme knowledge.
Thus addressed, you, the daughter of Bhṛgu, indeed set forth this etymological derivation:
the word *kṛṣi* denotes the earth (*bhū*), and the syllable *ṇa* denotes fulfillment (*nirvṛtti*). (2)
The supreme Brahman, which is the unity of those two, is designated as Kṛṣṇa;
he is called Kṛṣṇa because he draws away (karṣaṇāt) all miseries and leads beings to his own abode (dhāmni). || 3 ||
The syllable "rā" is always said to be the name for prosperity, while "ma" is declared to mean measurement; Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the measure of prosperity, is thus called by the name Rāma. (4)
He delights with Ramā; therefore he is called Rāma. Kṛṣṇa is said to be Rāma because he is the place of delight for Ramā. || 5 ||
He who makes his dwelling and residence within the assembly of those whose nature is human— that Lord is called Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa.
Nārā means sins, and he is that from whom their destruction occurs;
he is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. || 7 ||
"Nārā" means waters; he dwells therein, and for that reason he is indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Or, "nārā" refers to Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu; he who makes her his abode (ayana) [is Nārāyaṇa]. || 8 ||
Agriculture is my love, and its leader is indeed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
you are my husband, Śrī Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari.
You take away the sorrows of your devotees; you are Hari, the Lord himself.
Endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers, you are always proclaimed as the Bhagavān.
Devotion (bhaga) exists in that devotee; therefore, you are considered Bhagavān. The sprout of the tree of devotion grows through association with devotees. || 11 ||
Likewise, by the sprinkling of the nectar of discourse concerning Hari,
one is [purified] even of a fraction of the flame of the lamp of conversation with non-devotees.
A sprout withers away, but it grows when watered with devotion;
therefore, being vigilant, I indeed abandon the company of those devoid of devotion. 13.
The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies "most excellent," the suffix *ṇa* indicates "true devotion," and *a* signifies "the giver";
thus, you are indeed called *Kṛṣṇa*.
The syllable *kṛṣi* signifies supreme bliss, and *ṇa* signifies the act of servitude to Him;
You, Kṛṣṇa, are the giver of these two, and the daughter of Bhṛgu is the maidservant of Kṛṣṇa. (15)
Agriculture is a source of suffering; through its destruction, Kṛṣṇa manifests within you.
Just as a lotus pierces through the water, so too does the devotee, by taking refuge in you.
By the name Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, you shall uplift [beings] from the ocean of worldly existence;
indeed, you are united with me, Śrī, as Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
O Supreme Lord, I consider my own fortune to be great through union with you;
blessed is that Lakṣmī Kambharā, and blessed is Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (18)
In whosever home you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, eternally reside, and in whosever speech the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa prevails— 19.
Indeed, tens of millions of his great sins are reduced to ashes;
having become divine and being fully liberated, he is not born again.
All the hundreds of thousands of sacrifices, all the vows, all the ritual baths at sacred fords, and all the ascetic penances and fasts—[are not equal to this]. (21)
Thousands of recitations of the Vedas and a hundred circumambulations of the earth are not worth even a sixteenth part of the name "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa."
And may the eternal Śrī—Brahmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Nārāyaṇī, Mahālakṣmī, and Bhārgavī—and their Lord, Mādhava, [protect you]. 23.
May devotion to you, the Lord of all, and service unto you as your servant be mine forever;
and may the worship of your names always abide within my heart. (24)
O Lord, may the service of you alone—through body, mind, speech, action, and all deeds—be my constant desire. (25)
I shall indeed practice that very austerity for his sake, so as to obtain my beloved husband;
and I shall enjoy the eternal bliss bestowed by you.
Having spoken thus before Hari, Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, ceased;
at that moment, her friends arrived to adorn the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Then Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, perceiving the opportune moment,
arose and went to the bank of the Narmadā for recreation with his companions.
Then, all those women of divine form, beloved of Nārāyaṇa,
seated the Goddess upon a beautiful throne of jewels.
Prabhādevī, the wife of Kṛṣṇa, placed a jeweled necklace around his neck;
Pārvatī gave him an auspicious toy lotus in his right hand.
Padmā applied red lac to her pair of lotus-feet,
while her wife Māṇikī gave her excellent, beautiful vermilion.
The beloved Maṅgalā adorned her charming braid, which was joined with sandalwood paste and shone brightly from the parting down to its base. 32.
She adorned Manoharā, who was already graced with garlands of *mālatī* flowers,
by fashioning a braid woven with the petals and blossoms of land-lotuses.
And his beloved Lalitā applied beautiful sandalwood leaf-designs, smeared with musk and saffron, upon her pair of very firm breasts.
Sudhāsakhī gave her a garland of beautiful campaka flowers, enchanting with its fragrance, as well as a full-blown, fresh mallikā jasmine.
Then Jayā, being full of delight, made her— who was adorned with jewel ornaments—
extremely passionate, excellent, and eager for the pleasure of love.
Having adorned her eyes— which possessed the luster of autumn lotus petals and were brilliant with collyrium—
she gave her a very beautiful, new Pāñcālī garment.
Vijayā placed flowers from the Pārijāta tree in her hand, and her friend Amṛtā applied fragrant oil to her body. (38)
Rati reminded the king of the objects of the erotic sentiment with her exceedingly sweet and pleasing words, which were like nectar. (39)
And Kamalā quickly prepared a soft bed of love upon petals of lotuses and campakas, anointed with sandalwood paste.
For the sake of Kṛṣṇa, his beloved Śāradā prepared beautiful campaka flowers and petals of land-lotuses, anointed them with sandalwood paste, and [offered them]. 41.
And she fashioned a beautiful cluster of *kadamba* flowers, as well as a garland of *kadamba* blossoms, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa. ||42||
Kṛṣṇā prepared excellent and beautiful betel-leaf, well-scented with camphor and other ingredients, for Kṛṣṇa's sake, and likewise gave another portion to her.
Menā gave her earrings as a blessing, and Kalāvatī gave the ornament of her forehead and the ornament of her nose to the daughter of Bhṛgu.
Siddhi gave her sandalwood paste for coloring the lips,
while Buddhi gave the daughter of Bhṛgu a charming mark for the cheek.
Hara’s wife, Vasumatī, placed jeweled necklaces around her neck;
and Mūrti gave her a beautiful bodice with the luster of gold. (46)
Sāvitrī gave him an excellent golden sacred thread, and his beloved wife gave him auspicious sandalwood paste for his two sons. ||47||
Śreyasī gave her a girdle made of gold for her waist;
Ṛtambharā gave her an auspicious bracelet for her forearm;
and Bhūriśṛṅgā gave her two excellent armlets for her arms.
Then Rādhyāsā placed a cord upon the surface of her forehead;
Saṃjñā gave her a golden necklace in the form of a garland of mung beans;
and Yatinī gave her a beautiful, well-adorned garland of barley.
Aruṇā gave her a golden garment, radiant as the sun;
Arundhatī gave her two sets of ten golden rings;
and Miṣṭādevī gave her a meditation-band made of gold.
Kambharā gave her a beautiful mirror and an auspicious fan;
Dyuvārṇā gave her an auspicious golden girdle;
and Vikuṇṭhā then gave her two golden anklets.
The female ant offered a finger-ring, the female camel offered eye-salve,
the female tree-spirit offered fragrant incense, the female flower-spirit offered scented water,
and the excellent milch-cow offered a nourishing milk-biscuit.
Tulasī made the daughter of Bhṛgu drink a juice that causes paralysis;
Sarasvatī applied lac-dye to her feet;
and Campā, Mañjulā, Rāmā, Dayā, Śāntā, Jayā, and Anilā [did likewise]. || 55-56 ||
Śānti, Haimī, Ratnā, Muktā, Devī, Pāṇikā,
Mauktikāmodikā, Kānti, Śivā, Maṇi, and Damī—
these and other wives of the Blessed One adorned her thus.
Having thus adorned her with all the elements of erotic beauty, her friends also embellished her.
And for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One, they await the arrival of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rite.
The inner controller Hari, having understood this, left the banks of the Narmadā and arrived before the palace in the vicinity of a Kadamba tree.
Hearing the sound made by the doorkeeper and the word "Victory!", the circle of female companions immediately came outside to pay homage to the Blessed One.
Having offered water for the feet, the respectful oblation (arghya), and drinking water that was most sweet,
he led Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa to the abode of Bhārgavī.
Having released them all and bowed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they went to their respective homes, having granted privacy to the bride and the groom.
With joy, the daughter of Bhṛgu served her husband through the dharma of devotion to her spouse;
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa gazed upon his wife with a steady eye.
She possessed the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, was incomparable and most enchanting;
she had been adorned by her friends for his sake, having been made into a "deluder" (mohinī).
She was beautiful with lovely hair, youthful, with a face graced by a pair of uplifted breasts;
she had firm hips and a shapely posterior, and was a virtuous woman with a gentle smile and beautiful teeth.
Her face possessed a splendor as radiant as ten million moons; her eyes were like autumn lotuses, bright with kohl, and she was adorned with golden ornaments.
Her body was beautifully adorned with colorful patterns, her form perfectly fulfilled all desires;
she was full of aesthetic relish and longing, her mind fixed upon the lap of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Clad in garments as pure as fire, her inner being filled with the intensity of passion,
she shone with a pair of beautiful earrings that illuminated the regions of her ears and cheeks.
She had a beautiful nose and golden locks of hair, wore a fine garland of elephant-pearls,
and was anointed with saffron, lac-dye, musk, and smooth sandalwood paste.
With a nose resting upon the beak of the king of birds, her limbs were delicate and she was most alluring; possessing beautiful cheeks, that lovely woman was like a graceful female elephant. (7.1)
The slender maiden, whose abode was the desire for love, who cast glances like the arrows of the bodiless god of love, bore pārijāta blossoms indeed for the sake of play.
Through action, mind, and speech, both in dreams and in the waking state, it is enriched with the remembrance of the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and filled with love. (73)
She is devoted to the contemplation of the divine essence, pure in her devotion, and faithful to her husband;
she is fair-complexioned, filled with passion, and eternally situated upon the chest [of the Lord]. (74)
Upon seeing Bhārgavī, who was beloved by her lovers, devoted to those devoted to her, and speaking sweet words, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa indeed became infatuated.
On the bed, Bhārgavī saw her husband, the beloved of her life, who was filled with desire, beautifully attired, and smiling, O Lord of Sundarī. ||76||
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, clad in yellow silk garments,
with all his limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, and adorned with jewel ornaments.
He wears a crown of excellent golden *satkargi* and is adorned with a garland of *mālatī* flowers;
his face is bright with a gentle smile, and his very form is for the bestowing of grace upon his devotees.
Quickly placing her beloved husband— the lord of her heart, the lover of desire, who wished to sport— upon her breast, she spoke to the Supreme Lord.
My birth has become fruitful, for I have such a husband;
my life is well-lived, for my beloved is Nārāyaṇa.
Having beheld your moon-like face, my eyes, mind, and five vital breaths have become deeply softened; my joy overflows, finding no room within my body.
O Lord, my face is bathed in the nectar-shower of your glance and filled with bliss;
yet separation from my master is a most terrible forest fire. (82)
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, laid her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon her own seat and performed the massaging of his feet and other limbs.
Fragrant scents, the essence of water, the essence of oil, a mirror, betel-leaf, drinking water, flower garlands, and excellent sandalwood. ||84||
She gave honey, edible sweet fruit, and the *anaṅgabala* pill, as well as nectar (*sudhā*), to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; thereafter, she gave herself [to him]. (85)
The Lord made his enchanting flower-bed fruitful;
he made Bhārgavī, his newly-wedded bride, fruitful within the chamber of love.
Smiling, the lovely Lakṣmī, who was herself tranquil and enchanting, served her beloved—who was likewise smiling and serene—with her whole being upon the couch, as she fainted with bliss. (87)
Satisfied, Bhārgavī spoke to her satisfied husband in accordance with dharma:
"She is a true wife who is devoted in spirit, and he is a true husband who protects his wife. (88)
The happiness of love between husband and wife is indeed difficult to attain through righteousness;
only a devoted wife, a connoisseur of beauty, truly knows a virtuous husband. 85.
Out of greed for honey, the bee flies from afar for the sake of the lotus;
the frog does not know this, and so it places its foot upon its head.
The musician knows the essence of the music, but the instrument certainly does not; nor does the hungry man know the taste of milk, neither the ladle nor the vessel.
Those who enjoy pleasures know the taste of the ripened fruit;
they do not remain forever in one place, unlike those who bear no fruit at all. (92)
Farmers recognize the taste of very cool water [only] when it is in a pond or a jar, not when both are situated in one place. //93//
For those who enjoy [fine food] recognize the supreme, delicious taste of the rice;
yet neither the field nor the vessel in which it is situated possesses that quality. (94)
One who desires sandalwood perceives the scent of sandalwood, not a donkey;
for good fortune, dignity, and love are rare and ever-renewed. (95)
A devoted wife understands what is easily obtained through her service to her husband;
likewise, a husband who is faithful to his wife also attains that which is easily obtained. (96)
O Lord, may my devotion to you be one that grants service unto you;
I choose you, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as my husband, devoted to my wife, as my lord. (97)
"So be it," Hari said to the daughter of Bhṛgu, who was devoted to her husband;
and he revealed to her those forms which indeed belong to Lakṣmī.
Behold, O Bhārgavī, those very forms which were assumed by me; since you remain steadfast in devotion to your husband, you stand together with me.
And I, the Supreme Person, abide in the imperishable Brahman;
therein you exist in the form of the imperishable consciousness and bliss.
In Goloka, Gokula, and Vṛndāvana, you are Rādhikā to me;
I am Kṛṣṇa, the two-armed one in the dress of a cowherd, the husband of Rādhikā.
In Vaikuṇṭha, I am four-armed; eternally, as Nārāyaṇa, I exist in two forms. Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and you dwell with me as your beloved.
You are Lakṣmī, the daughter of the ocean, and at that time the mortal was the Lord of Lakṣmī;
in Śvetadvīpa and in the Ocean of Milk, he was the four-armed Lord of Lakṣmī.
I am the sage Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the eternal Dharma;
you are Śānti, whose very nature is Lakṣmī, and you are a devoted wife unto me.
I am Kapila and you are Siddhi; thus you manifest everywhere.
I am devoted to my wife, and you manifest as a devoted wife.
In Vaikuṇṭha you are indeed Mahālakṣmī and Sarasvatī;
you are Mṛtyulakṣmī and the beloved of the one who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk.
You are the daughter-in-law of the Son of Dharma, you are Peace (Śānti) whose very nature is Fortune (Lakṣmī);
you are the beloved wife of Kapila, and on earth you are the virtuous Bhāratī.
"You shall exist as Sītā, the wife of me in the form of Rāma;
then, in the form of Kṛṣṇa, you will become my beloved Rukmiṇī. (108)
You are Kaṃbharā, you are Mahālakṣmī, the beloved wife of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa;
thus you have become Bhārgavī, and I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
You are Padmā and you are Ramā; you are Prabhā as well as Pārvatī.
You are Māṇikī and you are Jayā; you are Śrī, my beloved Kṛṣṇā.
Haṃsā, Mañjulā, Campā, Haimī, the goddess Ramā, Dayā,
Mauktikā, Jayā, and Śānti— you are the presiding deity of those forms.
Whenever and wherever you have attained birth and exist as my beloved, then,
having performed the marriage ceremony and taken you [as my wife], I shall lead you away with me.
I am always of manifold forms, whether by my own portion or by a fraction thereof;
accompanied by you, O auspicious beloved, I shine everywhere.
I am indeed most perfect, and you are truly most perfect;
wherever and whatever task may arise, there I shall go together with you.
"There is no other woman equal to you in devotion to her husband, nor indeed any other like you;
I am exceedingly pleased, O Goddess, for you remain constant in a single form."
Those women who shall hear of this service to their husband with devotion, and those who shall read it, will indeed obtain me as their husband.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Bhārgavī’s Adornment, Her Service to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and the Demonstration of Her Devotion to Her Husband," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-Santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell another auspicious story that bestows liberation,
which effects the deliverance of a devoted wife from her own husband.
From whose house the gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits depart unhonored as soon as they have breathed within it— no man is more sinful than he.
He whose body and dwelling are struck by the sighs of gods and others—his fortune is entirely destroyed, for he is destined for ruin. (3)
By a virtuous wife, the righteous, virtuous women, the elderly,
the ancestors, the deities, and guests should be honored day after day.
By means of her own meritorious deeds, a devoted wife should always increase the lifespan of her husband and perform auspicious sacrifices.
He who eats without first honoring the sages, the gods, the ancestors, the spirits, and guests,
certainly destroys his own merit.
It is heard that in ancient times there was a famous king on earth named Śatadhanu,
and his wife was Śaibyā, who was entirely devoted to the duty toward her husband.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, endowed with truthfulness, purity, and compassion,
she was intent on serving the elders, peaceful, and possessed of both prudence and humility.
That king, together with her, indeed propitiated me, the all-pervading Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
through supreme meditative absorption.
With devotion, through daily oblations, recitations, gifts, fasts, and worship, with your mind fixed on me and no other thought in your heart.
Once, on the full moon day of Kārtika, that husband and wife, having fasted and bathed together in the waters of the Bhāgīrathī river, emerged from the stream.
Having observed the vow on the eleventh day, those two indeed bathed in the Bhāgīrathī early on the morning of the twelfth day, and thereafter returned home.

The cooked food, condiments, curd, and milk prepared for the purpose of breaking the fast— having failed to offer these to the gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits, he kept them stored in the cooking pot.
Śaibyā was waiting at the gate for her brahmin guest, her guru;
then the brahmin guru himself arrived, known by the name Āpāryaka.

Having himself performed the Vaiśvadeva rite and offered oblations to the sages, the ancestors, and the cows, he will grant us that grace which shall serve as our breaking of the fast; we shall eat that.
Meanwhile, guests arrived at the king's house;
indeed, the time for honoring them passed by for both the king and the queen.
The teacher also arrived and, seeing many guests,
observed that for a moment the husband and wife were intent on their business.
Without having offered food and water to the gods, sages, ancestors, and spirits, Kāla went to his own home; it was past midday.
Likewise, the cooked food remained as it was, while the gods, sages,
and ancestors who had assembled there remained hungry, having received neither honor nor water or food.
Despairing and exceedingly enraged, they departed for their own abodes;
but that devoted wife, having learned that her husband had resorted to the gods, remained there.
She caused her husband to cross over by providing him with food, water, and so forth;
at that time, the food remaining from her husband became the prasāda for his wife.
But that which was previously consumed was not born of divine grace;
through its fault, the husband was tainted, yet the wife was not tainted according to dharma. (22)
The food obtained without the husband's favor was for the husband's sake, while that obtained through his favor was for the wife's sake;
thus, what arose from his displeasure became a source of fault for the husband, whereas for the wife it indeed became a source of merit.
Having fed their honored guests and then having eaten themselves, the husband and wife then remembered their guru, who was a worshiper of the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Having realized that the food they had eaten was not offered to the gods and others,
they performed all the rites, including the worship of Viṣṇu, in the afternoon.
Moreover, as long as the destruction of a fault that has arisen does not occur, it must be experienced either in this very existence or in another existence. (26)
As time passed, the king died, afflicted by fever;
his wife ascended the funeral pyre after her husband, the lord of the earth, who lay upon it. (27)
At that very moment, those two traveled along the path to heaven by means of a vehicle;
meanwhile, the ancestors of the celestial path became enraged.
Suddenly descending upon the celestial chariot,
they indeed obstructed it and glared at the king with cruel eyes from the sky.
Then, due to that previous transgression, the husband and wife fell from that celestial chariot to the earth; the king was born as a dog in the city of Vaidiśa.
The princess, the daughter of the King of Kāśī, became aware of her awakened passion; she was perfected in all branches of knowledge and endowed with every auspicious mark.
Inevitable events come to pass and cannot be averted;
even for a devoted wife, her father’s anger became an obstacle.
When that woman of noble form, devoted to her husband, had become marriageable,
her father desired to give her away to a suitor, but he was dissuaded by her.
Hindered by his daughters, the king desisted from the commencement of the wedding;
through her divine yogic vision, she beheld her husband as a dog.
Taking her father’s command, the daughter set out for the journey;
having gone to the city named Vaidiśa, she beheld a dog as her husband.
Upon seeing his wife, the dog then indeed remembered his former birth;
he wept for a mere moment and was filled with shame for a moment. (36)
Seeing him in that state, she too wept in great distress;
she gave him the favor of the gods, words of honor, and water.
While eating the extremely delicious and desired food given by her, he touched the back, ears, and head of the dog with his hand.
Acting out the playful behavior characteristic of his own species, he offered many endearments;
by him offering such endearments, the young girl was made exceedingly bashful.
O Great King, let that affectionate body of yours, born from the womb of a beast, be remembered— [a body] for which food was not offered to the gods and others, O beloved.
O lord of men, because he was a vessel for his father's anger, he fell from the celestial chariot into the sky and entered the womb of a dog along with me. (41)
“You have attained a contemptible birth; do you not remember that, O Lord?
When he was thus reminded by her, the sage remembered his former birth.
Then, having attained that most difficult-to-obtain detachment, he reflected for a long time;
becoming despondent in mind, he departed from the city. (43)
Protected by the maiden at the boundary and repeatedly sprinkled with water, his sins indeed emerged out from his body. (44)
One was in the form of a jackal, the second in the form of a wolf, the third in the form of a vulture, and the fourth in the form of a crow. ||45||
She saw five peacock forms, each distinct from the others.
The young girl said to them all: "Who are you, and how have you become like this? (46)
Then they said to the maiden, "We are indeed the sins of Śunaḥ;
that which was formerly committed by the king as theft in another kingdom—that am I. (47)
I am he who, like a wolf, devoured the wealth of the subjects; and I am he who, like a vulture, seized the fallen property of the gods that had entered his treasury. (48)
If food obtained through unjust means is digested in his stomach, I become a crow;
if wealth from rivers, pasture lands, mountains, and so forth is released [for his use], I become a peacock. (49)
Thereafter, you shall have five births as the wife of your husband;
by the power of your merit, this King Janaka shall indeed become your husband.
Having obtained him as your husband at the svayaṃvara,
you shall go to heaven when your father Janaka has attained liberation through the śrāddha rites.
Then heaven shall be yours;
go now, O virtuous lady, to your own home, and do not destroy us with your sprinklings.
Thus addressed, that virtuous woman said: "If I am indeed chaste and truly devoted to my husband, then let there be the rescue of my husband in this matter."
If I am a servant of my husband who brings about the liberation of my ancestors, then by that merit, may Yama come here and stand before me. (54)
Having spoken thus, he then took water and sprinkled it all around;
at that moment, Yama himself appeared before the dog’s body in the southern direction.
Having arrived, he said to the virtuous Śaibyā: "How have you remembered me?
Speak, O noble lady; quickly fulfill what is in your heart. (56)
Śaibyā said: "Only after destroying whatever sins exist within the body of the dog can my husband be attained by me. (57)
"Speak quickly here, O King, otherwise I shall reduce you to ashes!
Yama said, "Listen, O virtuous lady; the exhaustion of karmas occurs through their enjoyment. (58)
"O virtuous lady, let it be resolved by you, and let justice also be established;
or else, if you so desire, I shall demonstrate it here—act quickly. (59)
By the power of your righteousness, this shall quickly come to an end;
otherwise, every single person would constantly experience the consequences of their own sins.
Likewise, having stayed here for five days, perform your fast;
for a virtuous woman, by the power of her devotion to her husband, can sustain whatever she must. (61)
O devoted wife, you are capable of doing so here;
therefore, take water today and make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in my presence:
"By this offering of water, may my husband be released from the dog."
For one day, he will become a jackal with the body of a preta.
"Tomorrow morning, he will indeed come into your presence having become a jackal;
by this gift of water, let him be released from his state as a jackal. (64)
Having become a wolf with a corpse-like body for one day, he will return on the following day;
give him water, so that he may be released from his birth as a wolf.
For one day he remains in that corpse of a preta; on the fourth day, having become a vulture, he will come—give him water so that the vulture may be released.
For one day he shall exist as a peacock with the body of a preta;
on the fifth day, O cloud, let this peacock be released.
Furthermore, cast even the body of this [bird] into the waters at the concluding bath of Janaka’s great horse-sacrifice. 68.
The son of Yajña will become your husband, O Janaka;
as soon as he is born, he will be a youth, well-developed, divine, wise, and powerful.
O virtuous lady, by the power of your devotion to your husband, take [this fruit] at your own choice;
thereafter, rule the kingdom for many thousands of years.
Having spoken thus, Dharma vanished after bowing to Śaibyā, the devoted wife;
and Śaibyā joyfully performed everything accordingly every single day.
Even a dog, having likewise become a preta, constantly abandons its body;
in this manner, that prince was reborn on the sixth day.
As soon as he was born, he became a youth, strong and named Rtudhvaja;
then that virtuous woman, having returned to her own home, requested him once more.
Then Śaibyā, with her own mind, chose that very divine being as her husband; thereafter, she urged her father to arrange the marriage.
Śibi also caused her *svayaṃvara* to be held;
when the *svayaṃvara* was performed,
that virtuous and beautiful woman joyfully chose her husband Saṃjñā once again as her spouse.
And the king again enjoyed royal pleasures together with her. ||76||
Having obtained the kingdom in the lands of Videha through his paternal lineage,
he duly performed sacrificial rites for the liberation of his ancestors.
He performed many sacrifices, gave gifts to those in need,
and begot sons after having enjoyed the earth and its sovereignty.
At the end of eighty thousand years, she abandoned her own body;
then that devoted wife,
filled with joy, ascended the funeral pyre according to the prescribed rites alongside her husband, just as before.
Then that king obtained [his desire] together with that princess.
Having transcended the worlds of Indra, one attains inexhaustible worlds that grant all desires, as well as incomparable, eternal heaven and a most rare conjugal union. ||81||
Having reached the realm of Vairāja beyond Satyaloka,
she obtained there the fruit of her merit through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Śaibyā, the Vaiṣṇava queen, together with King Ṛtudhvaja, reached Vaikuṇṭha, which abides in water and light, along with her husband. (83)
Thus, by that noble woman devoted to her husband, her own husband was uplifted, her ancestors were delivered, and they were all made inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. (84)
Sins are destroyed day by day through its own power;
by reciting and hearing this, one's liberation will certainly be attained. (85)

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Husband of Śaibyā, through the Power of His Devotion to His Wife, Attained the Status of Prince Ṛtudhvaja and Liberation in Vaikuṇṭha after Completing Five Days of Births as a Jackal, Wolf, Vulture, and Crow Due to Eating Food Not Offered to the Devas and Ancestors and Other Sins," in the First Section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the Greatness of Chaste Wives (*Pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the beautiful story of a brahmin woman who relied on the power of her devotion to her husband; it increases dharma for those who hear it.
In the Vindhya region, during the first age,
there lived a great sage named Vedaśravas, who was an expert in yoga and devoted to the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa).
Having constructed an auspicious leaf-hut in a delightful place abounding with many trees, on a grassy plain near water, he dwelt constantly in the forest.
Having performed the fire sacrifice, the worship of the gods, the twilight prayers, the honoring of guests and so forth,
as well as the recitation of the Sūrya-mantra and other rites, he subsisted on wild fruits.
Devoted solely to his own spiritual welfare and accompanied only by his wife, he dwelt in the forest; he was a man of virtuous conduct, ever dedicated to his vows toward his spouse.
In some instances, he remained for six days in the meditative absorption of yoga;
his wife, too, being of virtuous vows, was constantly devoted to his service.
There was a yoginī named Suśruti, most devoted to Brahman and faithful to her husband,
who was constantly engaged in virtuous activities such as bathing, meditation, worship, and study.
Having meditated upon Brahmā, bowed to her husband, and performed worship at the very break of dawn,
she considered herself to have attained the highest welfare while still alive.
The Self exists as a ray of the Supreme Brahman, and He is my husband;
the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, for every dharma, O beloved, resides in him.
She who does what is pleasing to her beloved shall always find favor with him; just as a shadow follows the body, so should a wife follow her husband. 1.387.10.
Every kind of duty of a wife rests solely upon the husband;
when the husband is pleased, Hari is pleased, and when the husband is angry, Hari is angry. (11)
She should satisfy her husband with the gift of enjoyments, by providing food and other necessities, through service, by offering sweetness and the like, and by honoring him.
She constantly performed the massaging of his limbs and the rubbing of his body,
as well as shared a bed with her husband during lovemaking and in times of conflict.
Bathing with water and other substances, beautifying with divine articles, perfuming with the essence of flowers and the like, and nourishing with fruits. (14)
Protection through states of wakefulness, delighting through shared play, pleasing through dwelling within His heart, and moving with a single-minded devotion. (15)
Delighting [them] with gifts of garments and satisfying them with gifts of eye-salves. || 16 ||
Sacrifice is performed through the giving of offspring; recitation is performed by uttering "Oṃ";
bathing is performed through the giving of pleasure; and meditation is performed through self-surrender. (17)
Generosity through the bestowing of seasons, Dharma through its various practices, the vehicle together with monasteries, and death through the act of self-surrender. ||18||
"A virtuous and chaste wife should indeed make her life meaningful for her husband"; thus she held other duties devoted to her master in her mind.
Having realized that all phenomena are supreme, she serves her husband in the forest;
the yoginī Suśruti remains at times absorbed in yoga and meditative concentration.
Even among the wild animals of the forests, whatever natural enmity existed between them was indeed pacified as they lived together in her presence.
The sage, moreover, was always accompanied by his virtuous and righteous wife;
through the vision of Brahman, he attained the supreme state, perceiving his wife as his own self.
He did not at all regard his wife as merely a wife; he regarded her as the Supreme Goddess, born from the body of the Supreme Brahman and possessing the very nature of the Supreme Brahman.
Having abandoned his wife, that brahmin did not consume roots, fruits, and the like;
nor did he ever engage in any false exertion for the sake of serving himself. (24)
He considers the body to be perishable and transitory, like a drop of water;
yet, regarding the virtuous Brāhmī as his beloved, he remains ever serene.
Neither in the taste of the tongue, nor in the hearing of the ear, nor in the smell of the nose, nor likewise in the touch of the skin. (26)
Neither attached to his eyes nor to forms, he was free from passion;
for his wife Brāhmī, devoted to her husband, became the very essence of the flavors and other sensory qualities.
The duty toward one's wife is the supreme dharma; liberation comes from serving one's wife.
Through the satisfaction of a devoted wife, the gods and asuras are pleased. (28)
In eating, lying down, traveling, drinking, wandering, in the forest, in pleasure, sleeping, in action, in knowledge, in recitation, and in the worship of the gods; ||29||

In the midst of amorous passion, at a place of festival, in the sentiment of detachment, upon hearing [the teachings], in singing, dancing, and instrumental music, or when resting upon a grassy meadow; ||| 1.387.3 ||| 0 |||

Moving at will and assuming forms at will, they were devoted to the duty of service, considering that through such service they would attain the satisfaction of Brahman, which bestows self-contentment. (36)
Indeed, by the mere sight of whom all evils truly go to destruction—such was the saintliness attained by those two dwellers of the Vindhya forest. (37)
O you two deer, may no man ever see you anywhere; and O you two parrots, may no beast ever see you anywhere. (38)
Just as a bird might not see those two, or as you two might become fish somewhere;
or just as one might not see you two as bulls somewhere, so it shall be. (39)
No one shall suffer defeat because of this; and you two shall become tigers in some places, lions, swans, serpents, and monkeys in various other places.

In that forest, those two were sometimes seen as ascetics with matted hair, and at other times, during the arrival of the rainy season, they appeared in the form of the wish-fulfilling creeper and the wish-fulfilling tree.

Then, at the end of her monthly period, when the chaste wife had bathed after her menses—
In accordance with the nature of desire, the sage, devoted to the pleasures of dalliance, united with her according to human custom for the purpose of bestowing the seasonal gift.
In the vicinity of a hermitage, amidst a dense and spreading darkness, a certain man spoke these words to a woman who was dependent on worldly desires.

having attained happiness in heaven until the end of Brahmā’s day.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the narrative of the Kṛta Yuga concerning the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), [are described] the wonders of Suśruti, the devoted wife of Vedaśravas; the arrival at the hermitage of Vedaśravas and Suśruti by the Rākṣasa who was formerly Kalmāṣapāda, who was infatuated with lust for them; the devouring of Vedaśravas by the Rākṣasa; the curse bestowed by Suśruti; the celestial voice’s narration of the causal circumstances for Saudāsa’s transformation into a Rākṣasa; and [the events] in the presence of Vasiṣṭha.
The three hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure to Heaven by Suśruta and Vedaśravas through the Power of Satī," [ends].
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the conduct of Dharaṇī, the wife of Nanda,
which is filled with wonder and is that of a devoted wife.
There was a king of Jambūdvīpa named Nandasāvarṇi,
whose kingdom had the ocean as its moat on all sides.
He was a devotee of the Lord Vārāha, delighting in the worship of Vārāha;
and in the great sacred field of Vārāha, they were always established on the true path of spiritual knowledge.
Having attained supreme devotion desired by the gods,
the Blessed One himself acted in order to bring back the earth that had been seized by Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having assumed the form of a boar and slain Hiraṇyākṣa,
he brought back the earth and established it upon the waters.
Then, as King Nanda was wandering in his celestial chariot through the sky,

Having descended from his celestial chariot, he then offered this praise to him:
"Salutations to the one whose nature is infinite, who bows down before the Supreme Person;
salutations to the creator of his own world and forest, the Lord of the Earth."
Salutations to you, the abode of all reality and the sovereign of the imperishable. ||8||
Again, let there be my salutation to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
by you, through your grace, the earth has been protected today, and we too have been protected.
O Lord, kings are without support and subjects are without a protector;
for the sake of protecting the subjects, you indeed assume a new form.
You are the abode of all powers; salutations to you, whose self is the form of all things.
Having praised them thus, that king bowed at the feet of Vārāha.
Being pleased, the Boar spoke to the king who was worthy of a boon:

"I shall grant whatever is desired by your mind; I am the one who always grants the wishes of my devotees.

Then Vārāha said to the king, "So be it," and Nandasāvarṇi then worshipped the Lord of the Self, Vārāha.
With leaves, flowers, fruits, water, food, and tubers, as well as with unbroken grains (akṣata), jewels, diamonds, gems, necklaces, sandalwood, and saffron. ||17||

"And let Dharaṇī today become your wife, devoted to her husband.
