Nārada spoke to Upalā, saying, "O virtuous lady, may there be prosperity for you. (84)
"Where is Nanda? And where are the other friends, Paṅkilā and the rest?
When Satī saw that sage, she offered him hospitality, such as salutations and the like. (85)
Having offered the guest-offering (arghya) and other honors, she asked the reason for his arrival;
Nārada then said, "That which I have heard in heaven—"
Whether it be truth or falsehood, I have come here to examine you;
for apart from direct perception, there exists nothing worthy of respect that can be sung by the voice alone. (87)
What has been established by direct perception cannot be set aside, even for a wise sovereign, the universal monarch Nanda. 88.

Since it would be figurative, censurable by those who know the subject, unfit for hearing, and indeed inappropriate, I shall first manifest [myself] directly and afterwards return again to heaven. (89)
In the midst of the assembly of the gods, the deities describe him as one full of compassion:
"Indeed, Nanda performs the worship of the bones of the deceased Dharaṇī. (1.388.90)
And other new women are not such objects of our love as the earth was formerly, nor even as the bone was. (91)
What kind of love does King Nanda have for you, O Vadopala?
And what is the nature of Nanda’s affection for Paṅktilā and the others? (92)
But the king said to the divine seer: "Let me stay for a moment, to eat, to breathe, to sport, and likewise to live. (93)
O divine sage, he is not even able to eat after seeing my face;
such affection as he displays toward me does not exist for others. 94.
The celestial sage said: "If what was spoken by the gods were false, then what was spoken by you would be true;
but if what was spoken by the gods is indeed true, then what was spoken by you must be false. (95)
O virtuous lady, just as the king does not eat without having seen your face,
so too King Nanda does not eat without seeing the bones of the earth.
"Examine how much truth there is [in his words], or where his greater affection lies;
even after seeing it, I shall depart—just look at the objects used for worship! (97)
Having been addressed thus, Upalā quickly went from there to the place of worship;
having seen the articles for worship, she beheld the chest of offerings. 98.
At that moment, a bone was seen there in the form of a tooth;
instantly, she became devoid of luster, her joy shattered and her face withered. 99.
Her face having become copper-red with anger, Nārada spoke to that chaste lady:
"O Queen, do not grieve; this worldly existence is certainly not substantial."
"The gods speak the truth: the king is the worshiper of his wife's bones;
his affection for the bone of the earth is greater than yours, and indeed, it is not even equal to that of her bones. (101)
Co-wifehood is a sorrow that brings an end to peace; you are fortunate to endure it while he is alive.
For an impure bone preserved for worship is indeed like a thing kept in a cemetery.
"Having indeed abandoned you who are equal to heaven, the king frequents the cremation ground.
Keep that cremation ground far away; cast it into the fire so that it may be reduced to ashes. (103)
Having said, "Perform your bath and purification with water," Nārada departed;
Upalā, however, was like a stone herself, consumed by the fire of anger toward her co-wife.
Once it was burnt, she immediately threw the boar's bone into the fire;
by the will of Nārada and the will of Hari, the fire consumed it at that very moment.
In her rage, she even threw his bones and ashes into the river water;
filled with grief and anger, the virtuous woman returned home and took no food.
The king returned in the evening, but Sati did not speak to him;
meanwhile, the monarch remained standing for the sake of worship after having bathed in the morning. ||107||
He saw that the bone used for the worship of the treasury was merely its key;
he grieved for a moment and, with his mind set on death, questioned you. (108)
"O Goddess, tell me where that bone, the cause of all life, has gone," [the husband] asked. The stone said, "That bone has gone into the fire of the hearth. (109)
"Indeed, I never eat without beholding your face;
O King, you boast falsely for the sake of deceiving us. (1.388.110)
The bone of Dharaṇī, who is dead, is being preserved by you for worship, while we—who were valued by you as nothing more than grass—have been treated by you in every way as if worthless. (111)
"O Lord, having yourself become a liar, how can you deceive me?
That bone was cremated, and its ashes were carried away by me into the river. (112)
O King, show affection toward me while my beloveds are still alive; do not show affection for one who is dead, for that creates the bonds of worldly existence. 113.

Thus addressed, that king, greedy for wealth and identifying with that very wealth, [perceived] the aggregates—which are impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self—as being permanent, pure, blissful, and the self. (114)
Crying out "Alas! Alas! as he realized that his eternal consciousness, bliss, and self had vanished, King Nanda died from the complete obstruction of his heart.
Then his wives, who were devoted to their virtuous husband, took him onto their laps; having cremated their bodies, they went to heaven by means of the Vārāha-yoga.
By the power of Dharaṇī, the ocean became the surface of the earth;
from Dharaṇī, Dhanasāvarṇi then became the ruler of the kingdom.
His son was Dharmasāvarṇi, a devotee of Viṣṇu, who became the lord of the earth;
from hearing and reciting this [account], knowledge as well as heaven shall be attained.

Thus, in the first section of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*), it is told how, through the devotion of King Nanda, the Earth was given to him by Vārāha in the form of his wife Kumārikā; how, by virtue of Dharaṇī’s wifely fidelity, she obtained a tooth-bone as a boon; and how, by means of that bone, Nanda established a treasury of wealth in the ocean. Furthermore, after Dharaṇī’s death, Nārada arrived and, having informed Upalā that the king was performing the worship of the bone along with his co-wife, [Nārada gave] the bone.
Chapter Three Hundred and Eighty-Eight: The Reduction to Ashes; and the Account of King Nanda’s Death due to that Blow.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the auspicious story of Merudevī,
the devoted wife of Nābhi, whose son was Ṛṣabha.
Formerly, there was a king of the Āgnīdhra dynasty who was the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa; his son was Nābhi, who, being childless, took refuge in Hari.
Nābhi’s wife was Merudevī, who was devoted to her husband;
she regarded her husband as the god, her husband as Kṛṣṇa, and her husband as the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Regarding her husband as Dharma, as Karma, as armor, as Nārāyaṇa himself,
and as the Supreme Brahman, she serves him always as if he were her own self.
And she was a knower of Brahman among the wives of the Brahman-sages, most excellent in her knowledge of Brahman,
possessed of the knowledge of the Brahma-thread and the Vedas, and devoted to the performance of fire-offerings.
Skilled in the rituals of the ritualistic section (karmakāṇḍa) and devoted to worship and recitation,
she is the very embodiment of the power of Brahman (brahmaśakti), just like the supreme Sarasvatī.
Even while ruling the kingdom, she remained devoted to Brahman and was a purifier;
having bathed in the morning, bowed to her husband, and worshipped the gods with offerings.
Devoted to her husband, that virtuous woman began to perform worship for her lord;
having bathed her husband and adorned him with garments and other ornaments, she then [proceeded].
Having drunk the water from his thumb, she joyfully performed a great worship for her husband,
who was seated upon an auspicious golden throne.
I offer a seat to Viṣṇu, who is my husband;
and I offer water for the hands, water for the feet, and water for sipping to my Lord.
I offer a tooth-stick, a limb that cleanses the teeth, to the Protector;
and I also offer fragrant water from sacred sites for the purpose of rinsing the mouth.
I also give other water for the purpose of purification and so forth to one who requests it from me,
having caused supreme cleanliness through clay and other means, as well as nectar-like foods.
I offer curds, milk, ghee, sweets, and honey to the Master;
I present the water for the consecration to the Master.
"I shall massage my husband with oil made fragrant;
and I shall sprinkle the appropriate water for my mistress's bath. (14)
With a soft cloth, I wipe the water from my body;
[I put on] a garment of golden hue, a washed lower cloth, and a sacred thread.
I offer an upper garment and a sacrificial thread to the Lord, as well as the grooming of His hair through the application of flowers and fragrant oils. (16)
I prepare this sandalwood paste for the pleasure of my Lord and offer it;
I apply a beautiful tilaka and moon-mark upon His forehead. (17)
I apply beautiful collyrium to the eyes of the husband of Satī;
I place a beautiful crown upon his head and auspicious earrings upon his ears.
I give you necklaces of most excellent jewels strung upon threads around your neck, two bracelets for your hands, and auspicious bangles for your arms.
She placed bracelets on her forearms, a girdle upon her waist, beautiful anklets on her feet, flower garlands, and crests.
I offer a garland for the neck, a cluster of flowers for the hand, and auspicious sandals for the feet— all indeed fashioned from gold— for the Lord.
An umbrella and two beautiful chowries, a lion-throne made of gold, incense, a lamp, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, and a golden staff. (22)
I offer this sweet meal as a food offering (naivedya) to the Lord;
it consists of *śaṣkulī*, *laḍḍuka*, and other delicacies presented in a golden vessel. (23)
Milk-rice, side dishes, curd, milk and so forth, fruits; various kinds of food—solid, soft, lickable, chewable, and drinkable—all sweet, as well as water and the like. ||24||
I offer the waving of lights, betel leaf, and cool water from a conch shell to my Lord, whose self is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (25)
I offer circumambulation, a sacrificial fee, and a handful of flowers;
I also offer prostration, the request for forgiveness, and surrender my entire service. ||26||
I perform the massaging of his feet and all other forms of service;
I am a devoted wife to my husband, Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (27)
"I accept the grace of my lord, the god who destroys my sins," thus the virtuous woman always worships her husband every morning.
Then, by virtue of her devotion and conjugal fidelity, that great chaste woman beheld her husband there as the divine Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with four arms.
Thus she served him in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at night;
once, that virtuous woman remained in meditation after having served her husband.
She beheld that great splendor extending as far as the world of Brahmā;
the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari revealed himself. 3.1.
Golden-hued, wearing yellow silk garments, endowed with splendor,
he holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, shield, sword, and sacrificial ladle.
Adorned with a crown, earrings, bracelets, and a waist-band, he is decorated with ornaments for the limbs, such as necklaces, armlets, and anklets. ||33||
Such was Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa whom that chaste and devoted wife honored with offerings of *tulsī* leaves, dūrvā grass, water, flowers, and various gifts. ||34||
O Blessed One, you are the most venerable Arhat, endowed with divine qualities;
may the singing of your virtues and service to you be within the range of my devotion. (35)
"My husband, a royal sage and king of devotees, has long desired offspring;
may he have a son equal to you, so that I may attain happiness. (36)
The Blessed One said: "O virtuous woman, since your mouth is my mouth, may the truthful words requested by you become true; let it be so."
"I shall descend into your house with a portion [of myself] as the Āgnīdhrīya fire," having said this and received due honor, that Supreme Person vanished.
On that day, at nightfall, Narayana entered Merudevi;
then, in the morning, he descended into her house.
As soon as he was born, he was a youth filled with the accomplishment of all knowledge,
and endowed with the manifestations of equanimity, tranquility, dispassion, and sovereignty.
He spoke of that son Ṛṣabha, who was endowed with such fame, strength, vigor, splendor, and virtues, as well as heroism, valor, righteousness, and devotion. (41)
This Ṛṣabha is indeed an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
it was out of rivalry with him that Mahendra did not send rain for three years.
That Lord of Yoga, Ṛṣabha, smiling by means of his yogic power (yogamāyā),
became a cloud and rained down upon his own kingdom, Ajanābha.
Having consecrated his son Ṛṣabha upon the throne, Nābhi himself,
together with Merudevī, attained the great yoga of the supreme self within the individual self.
Having meditated upon Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the couple attained liberation;
Ṛṣabha established the auspicious institution that bestows knowledge and instruction.
For the sake of obtaining instruction in the Dharma, the great royal family of learning—though the king himself became both sovereign and preceptor—instructed [him]. (46)
Indra himself came and gave his own virtuous daughter, named Jayantī, who was like Lakṣmī in form, to the Blessed One Ṛṣabha. 47.
Through the practice of householdership, Ṛṣabha begot upon her a hundred auspicious sons who were a circle of yogis, all equal to himself.
There indeed shone King Bharata, the sovereign of the Bharatas, along with Kavi, Hari, Antarikṣa, Prabuddha, and Pippalāyana. ||49||
Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, and Karabhājana—
these were great devotees of the Lord, practitioners of yoga, and followers of the path of Brahman.
Other sons became kings, such as Kuśāvarta and others;
others became Brāhmaṇas devoted to sacrifice and learned in the Vedas.
The Blessed One Ṛṣabha, compassionate and bestower of peace upon men, moved about when the bull had been conquered, having mastered [the requirements of] substance, place, age, faith, and time. (52)
Once, when the region of Brahmāvarta was crowded with hundreds of thousands of Brahman-sages,
the illustrious Ṛṣabha went there and attained enlightenment.
The kingdom, prosperity, all happiness, and even one's own self are considered as belonging to others; likewise, the body nourished by the king is also regarded as belonging to another. //54//
Having attained that subtle body characterized by moisture through the moistening of food and other such things, as well as the nature of moisture belonging to the animal state,
the acquisition of Brahman is praised.
How can there be purity of being while the body exists and worldly enjoyments are accumulated?
Let the people exert themselves toward the eternal bliss of Brahman. 56.
The virtuous are indeed of the nature of Brahman, the form of Brahman, and the bliss of Brahman; they are yogis and ascetics who should be served by people as great devotees of the Lord. 57.
Houses, wives, children, gardens, cattle, fields, and whatever else there may be— these are indeed bonds that bind me, who am Nārāyaṇa, once I have abandoned them.
If those very [senses] are directed toward me alone by others, placing me at their head, they become like virtuous friends who open the doors to liberation. (59)
He who, abandoning me, is greedy for the collection of senses and always delights here in sense-objects, being ever bound, does not become a virtuous person. (1.389.60)
He whose body— abounding with the self, the senses, the objects, and the internal organ—
is rendered favorable for the attainment of the reality of the Self, is indeed liberated from the bonds.
If one who performs action were endowed with love for Me,
all that would be free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa), bestowing the attainment of My state, and dear to the self.
Since everything directed toward one's own self creates bondage, whereas that directed toward the welfare of others grants liberation,
he who contemplates the state of being male and female residing within the heart as a knot— 63.
Having abandoned delusion, one becomes wise; then the bond loosens, the latent impressions of karma dissolve, and one is liberated by the self within the self.
In the abode of desire, the state of effort arises for one who is not free from thirst;
when the refuge of fulfilled desires is attained, all thirst ceases.
"Having reflected thus: 'I am not the one who brings about the end of all suffering and defects, for I am likewise devoid of effort,' the man of knowledge should take refuge in the Paramahaṃsa."
Having surrendered all actions unto me, through listening to my stories and the like, through association with my holy devotees, and through the chanting of my divine pastimes; ||67||
By meditating upon me as being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), they shall attain liberation;
perceiving me as their own Guru within whatever is seen, heard, or touched.
Having become a person of virtuous conduct, one should indeed attain cessation through yoga,
by means of devotion, compliance, forgiveness, freedom from thirst, and endurance.

Through the perception of faults in illusion, through inquiry, through lack of worldly effort, through my stories, through service, through the vision of equality toward me, and through the desire to abandon [worldly existence]. ||1.389.70||
Through inward awakening, through devotion to joy, through celibacy, through faith, through mastery of the senses, and through the practice of restraints and observances; ||71||
Through cultivation, through knowledge free from negligence and the like, through the practice of yoga, through a mind directed toward sentient beings, and through my gracious compassion; ||72||
Having attained my grace, one should uplift others—
beings who have fallen into the snare of hope and who are carried away by their innate greed— for their own deliverance.
Those who dwell in ignorance, desiring their desires without ceasing, deluded by ritual action, dull-witted by nature, and intoxicated for the sake of a mere fragment of pleasure; ||74||
One should not cause those who have gone astray and are enveloped by enemies to fall into the blind well;
rather, one should employ them toward dispassionate action (naiṣkarmya), for by that there is indeed eternal peace.
A son, a wife, a teacher, a mother, a father, a kinsman, a husband, a sister, a well-wisher, a friend, children, or a caravan companion—he alone is truly such who can liberate one. (76)
Placing the Dharma upon his chest and casting the bull (the ego) behind him,
he who yokes himself with his whole being to Kṛṣṇa is indeed that very Bull and Swan.
By virtue of their dharma, young men are worthy of worship, for they are deities preeminent in merit;
yet the sages, beginning with Brahmā, are preeminent in spiritual power through their powers of Brahman.
Those alone are declared to be true Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with the power of Brahman;
all those Brāhmaṇas who are devoted to Me are highly fortunate and dear to Me. (79)
The virtuous are weighed by my heart; nothing else is equal to them.
Wherever an offering is given with faith, I remain there and accept it.
Indeed, those who possess my own nature are to be served by all creatures;
for at every step they are like fires where an offering has been made to me.
I am he manifest, the embodiment of the virtuous, the conscious preceptor of kings;
I am that supreme one in the form of a swan, bestowing purity upon those of auspicious nature. (82)

Having reached the dissolution of great delusion and severed the noose of Death, the swan-like soul here easily attains liberation through the villages richly entwined by the knots of worldly attachment. (83)
"Let the swan-like seekers grasp the Supreme Swan within their own swans";
having received this instruction and having thus established his disciples as swans, [he departed]. (84)
Clad in the directions [as his garment], a consumer of the Absolute (Brahman), he went alone to the most excellent [state];
like one who is dull-witted, blind, mute, deaf, and mad, he wandered in the forest.
Having surrendered his own nature and the nature of others, he is free from the notion of "I";
blooming with the smile of contentment, he is completely filled with the bliss of Brahman. ||86||
Possessing infinite beauty that fulfills all desires and blazing with his own splendor,
the Lord’s virtue captivates the hearts of mature women.
In a field, a forest, or even in the wilderness, having adopted the lifestyle of a python, he eats, drinks, chews, and even urinates while lying down. (88)
Thus he wandered about with the conduct of a cow, a deer, a crow, and so forth;
he was the sovereign of liberation, absorbed in the great bliss of the Self. (89)
Moving through water, land, and air, and endowed with the accomplishment of all goals,
he did not rejoice even in his heart at the supernatural powers and lordships obtained by chance.
A person should never form a friendship with Hari while his mind is unstable; for that [unstable mind] quickly destroys the long-practiced ascetic merit of one who has placed trust in Him. 91.
Showing only what is sweet and sweet, it casts the yogin into a pit;
it bestows desire, anger, strife, delusion, fear, and wretchedness. (92)
Although he was thus the very form of the Blessed One, displaying his divine sovereignty,
he remained in the manner of an Avadhūta, desiring to cast off his own physical body.
Having made a mouthful of stone, he cast it into the fire born of the bamboo;
at that moment, the incarnations of Hari arrived there to lead him away.

They led the virtuous Ancient Person, whose deeds were gathered for the sake of auspiciousness, with honors, musical instruments, and other offerings, in order to attain the purity of the sacred site.
Having made the people of heaven, austerity, greatness, truth, the Vairāja world, the Stara world, the world of Hiraṇyagarbha, and the earthly nectar his means of purification, he [proceeded]. (96)
He went to the world of Brahman, which is the personification of existence, consciousness, and bliss—
the realm where the gods who are knowers of Brahman abide as perpetual yogis dedicated to the Absolute.
"Even though they are eternally satisfied, they drink the supreme Brahman.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the auspicious account of Merudevī been told to you. 98.
The life-story of Nābhi, whose son was indeed Ṛṣabha Hari, by taking refuge in whom even small creatures will become endowed with life. (99)
Having become swans, they shall go to the world of Brahmā, the state of absolute liberation;
by reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the state of absolute liberation.
O beloved, whatever benefit arises from taking refuge, abandoning the home, receiving initiation, and dwelling in the forest,
that shall belong to him through faithful listening.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnation of the Lord as the Son Ṛṣabha through the Great Worship Performed by Merudevī of Mount Nābhi by Means of the Dharma of Chastity, His Sons such as Yogeśvara and Others, His Instruction, the Practice of Forest Dwelling, the Discernment of the Ancient Tradition of the Paramahaṃsas, and the Knowledge Born of Discrimination," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, listen to this story concerning the world of Vaikuṇṭha,
which arose during the dance at the festival of my birth anniversary.
On the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika,
you manifested on earth in the home of Kambharā and Gopāla.
On account of that, my attendants in Vaikuṇṭha celebrated a great festival;
indeed, Vaikuṇṭha, along with its male and female attendants and devotees, became filled with joy.

Delightful pavilions were constructed, adorned with golden finials, provided with pillars of plantain trees and other materials, and featuring archways made of Aśoka leaves and similar ornaments. || 4 ||
Richly adorned with the splendor of lightning-lamps, resplendent with hearing-instruments and the like,
they possess divine beauty endowed with excellent paintings that delight the heart.
Richly adorned with the splendor of lion-thrones and the like, beautiful with various foods and drinks,
they were filled with sections of dance pavilions and attended by throngs of female dancers.
The circles of divine sages were adorned with excellent musical instruments inhabited by Gandharvas;
there were also various dwellings and constructed palaces.
The divine streets were adorned with ornaments, the roads were well-decorated, all the dwellings were refined, and both men and women were beautifully attired.
The cows were made to flourish with great festivities of food, drink, and other delicacies; they were adorned with ornaments, while the maidens were beautified with garments, jewelry, and the like.
Instruments adorned with rings of powdered ajīraṇi were played in every house during that festival.
And songs were heard from all the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha when the morning sky had become radiant with the golden sun.
The splendors of divine Rāmā, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Pārvatī,
and Śrī [all worship] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, their own Lord and Supreme Sovereign.
Having bathed him with waters of nectar and with fragrant, choice sandalwood,
and having perfumed him with the essence of oils and the like, he adorned him with garments and ornaments.
With necklaces made of jewels, diamonds, gems, and the like; with flowers and various articles; and with crowns, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, chains, and so forth. || 14 ||
The Blessed Lord was adorned with rings, anklets, staffs, earrings, forehead marks, and the like; he was made radiant by his female attendants. || 15 ||
Accompanied by his wives, his attendants by the millions, his daughters, male and female servants, and liberated souls, he entered the assembly hall.
Indeed, shouts of victory arose as they scattered flowers, unbroken grains of rice,
parched grain, blossoms, auspicious substances, gold coins, and other such items upon their beloved.
The cane-bearers produced a sound of their rattles that was enchanting to the ear;
those seated in the assembly bowed down, while the subjects of Vaikuṇṭha gazed upon him.
All the bhāgavatas, the male attendants (pārṣadas), all the liberated souls, the liberated women, the wives of Kṛṣṇa, and the female servants worship [Him] in due order. || 19 ||
All the maidens, the subjects, and the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha [were adorned] with a mark on the forehead and with the offering of darbha grass on the ears.
With a handful of flowers on the head, with a cluster [of flowers] on the hands,
with strings of pearls on the region of the neck, and with water on the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Having bowed with love in his heart to Nārāyaṇa, the Self,
and having worshipped him at the feet in the assembly with offerings, [he spoke].
All remained in their respective places as a wonderful dance commenced;
the Gandharvas sang and the lords played musical instruments.
The singers followed along, and the beat-keepers kept the rhythm;
Nārada and others were present there, as were women such as Vipracitti.
Sages, seers, and gods assembled for the great festival; then, at that very moment, the daughter of the Sāttvata’s attendant indeed arrived there. (25)
Adorned with ornaments and accompanied by a hundred maidens, she who was exceedingly beautiful and sixteen years of age arrived to perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa.
There was a companion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa standing by His side, an eminent member of the Gandharva race named Gandharva Saliladyumna. (27)
Having seen that woman of beautiful hips, he with the flickering eyes was filled with desire;
the maiden, having honored Kṛṣṇa, poured water upon Kṛṣṇa’s feet. ||28||
Holding the remainder in her mouth and remembering only the Gāndharva [Veda], she cursed him:
"Become a fickle human being whose wealth is exhausted! (29)
Gandharva also observed what Sukanyā intended to do;
he cursed her, saying, "O human woman, you too shall have your wealth exhausted."
"O Cañcalā, follow me from this place until we reach Samānava.
Having spoken thus and bowed to him, she went to the home of Nārāyaṇa.
Having fallen upon the earth, he became Cyavana, born not from a womb;
he wandered constantly in the forest and remained even within the water.
Remembering his former births, the sage Cyavana, whose body was worn with age, wandered about;
leaning against a bamboo stalk upon the earth, he performed severe penance.
An anthill grew upon his head, and a bamboo thicket also arose there;
that Sukanyā, the daughter of the Sāttvata, went to the great abode.
That Sāttvata, an attendant of Hari, told all of that to his father;
he consoled his own daughter and spoke to the fair-eyed maiden.
"Do not grieve, my daughter; for your sake, I too shall become a universal monarch on earth in a second form. (36)
"But you, come back later; I shall destroy your sorrow.
Having spoken thus, that Sāttvata became King Śaryāti on earth. (37)
The king was the supreme lord of devotees, most firmly established in Brahman, and beloved by the Brāhmaṇas;
he was a Vaiṣṇava who remembered his past lives and was the sovereign of the earth from sunrise to sunset.
When a moment of Vaikuṇṭha had passed, Sukanyā came to the earth;
Śaryāti became one hundred thousand years old, while Cyavana was two hundred thousand years old.
In the house of Śaryāti, a daughter was born as a mind-born (mānasī) girl;
she was divine, equal to the divine Rāmā, like a resident of Vaikuṇṭha.
She was eternally devoted to Nārāyaṇa, auspicious, a servant to her parents, dedicated to her husband, and possessed of an excellence that surpassed all wonders. (41)
In birth, in memory, in the forest, in the wilderness, at a sacred ford, on the earth, on a mountain,
in the ocean, in the sky, in heaven, in the netherworld, and in battle where armies are arrayed— (he is present).
Moving everywhere through the divine sky, she followed the king;
she remembered the celestial water-born sage Tapana within the lineage.
Accompanied by her, the king set out for the forest together with his army;
and she, joined by her female companions, was indeed gathering flowers.
She went to where the ascetic sage resided, taking refuge in his future service;
and looking toward the south with her flickering eyes, she beheld him.
By the impulsion of fate, the young girl pierced a beautiful and auspicious hole in an anthill, which was shimmering with tiny stars and filled with thorns.
Blood then flowed [from the earth], and there was an obstruction of urine and other excretions for the army;
seeing this, Śaryāti spoke repeatedly to the distressed soldiers. (47)
This must be some divine realm, or perhaps gods, sages, ascetics, or even rākṣasas who dwell here in this excellent forest. (48)
"Surely some offense has been committed here by me and my army;
otherwise, how could there be such an obstruction of urine and other excretions by the troops? (49)
Whatever it may be, in whatever manner, whether it be this or that, or wherever it may be—
if it has been produced by anyone, it must necessarily be made manifest.
"If we were protected from the Lord by means of remedies against that [poison]," then the maiden Sukanyā, who remembered her former births, spoke to her father. (51)
In this bamboo thicket, a pair consisting of light was observed by me; they had been pierced by a thorn within the hollow of an anthill.
Then, O King, blood flowed out; I consider that to be his offense.
Having realized this, the king himself, a follower of the Sāttvata, remembered [the Lord]. (53)
Having heard the words of his daughter regarding Saliladyu, Sukanyā, and the curse at Vaikuṇṭha, the king [remained] in the vicinity of the anthill.
He went and propitiated the sage hidden within the anthill;
the sage said, "Give me Sukanyā, and the obstruction of urine and other ailments will vanish. (55)
"So be it," the king said; and Cyavana rose from the clay, his head shining like a horn upon a bamboo pole.
Right there, his daughter was given to him by Sūryasākṣin;
the army became healthy, and the king went to his own home.
Pervaded by ascetic power, his body with its veins dried up,
the aged Cyavana lived there in that hermitage, emaciated, within a hut of leaves.
Having obtained Cyavana as her husband, who was extremely prone to anger, Sukanyā—
knowing his mind and understanding the proper time— pleased him through devoted service.
The virtuous woman massaged the body of her aged husband with oil, *puṣpasāra*, and fragrant sandalwood and other such substances.
With devotion, he caused him to be bathed with warm water;
he offered him garments and provided them for him every day.
He fed him well with wild fruits, grains, and tubers;
he gave him sweet water brought from a spring to drink.
She caused Satī to lie down on a bed made of plantain leaves,
and having kindled the fire, she performed the Agnihotra sacrifice with excellent juices.
The virtuous woman served the guests who had arrived for an audience,
and she performed the worship of the gods with tulasī leaves and lotuses.
He performed [the rite] according to the prescribed rules with fruits and water and with faith;
he also brought sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the sacred trees growing nearby.
She recited from memory songs, hymns of praise, and sacred knowledge;
thus, by following the sage's lead, that virtuous woman brought him delight.
Having attained supreme devotion to her husband, the virtuous Satī, though devoid of sensual pleasure, once reflected upon her aged husband’s withered frame. (67)
For the sake of the sage’s body, he called to mind the two horse-headed youths;
remembered by Sukanyā, the two sons of the Sun appeared in an instant. (68)
The two physicians, bowing low, said to her: "Speak, O Mother; salutations unto you.
Sukanyā replied: "Tell me how my body may become suitable for a sage. (69)
"Handsome, endowed with youth, strong, and most heroic—thus has my master been granted a lifespan capable of enjoying pleasures. (1.390.70)
Saying "So be it," the two sons of Aśvin, having bowed to Cyavana, chose for themselves a permanent share of the Soma at the sacrifice from him. (71)
The sage said "Certainly" to them, and then he bathed the two of them with elixirs in a pool specially created right there, which was filled with water.
The sage was indeed twenty years of age, a youth who could enchant even goddesses;
he was robust, handsome, and charming, his virility fully matured.
Never before has anyone been seen or heard of who was born through elixirs (*rasāyana*);
even in the past, such a form as his had never been seen or heard of by Sukanyā. (74)
And in order to test the maiden's devotion to her husband,
those two physicians also assumed different forms, having mixed them with an elixir.
United with the young sage, they became equal in form;
as the maiden looked on, the three were seen rising from the vessel.
The men were of similar appearance, wearing earrings and fine garments;
their bodies were permeated with fragrance, and they were oceans of the essence of beauty. ||77||
Wearing divine garlands and possessing splendors like other suns,
that virtuous woman, not knowing her husband, meditated upon him through concentration.
"Which sage here is to be wedded by me, for whom I am a devoted wife? He alone is to be chosen today; the other two must be rejected. (79)
Having reflected thus, Satī produced a great fire from her own body; enveloped by that fire, she went forth to test those three.
He said to Agni, "Kindle these two others instead of my beloved.
Thereupon, the fire blazed up, and those two others indeed burst into flames.
Abandoning their intention to reduce the sage to ashes, the two of them then cried out in lamentation.
With their limbs blazing, they paid homage to the two most excellent physicians.
For the sake of protection, they made a plea, and by that truth, the Fire was restrained; through the power of her devotion to her husband, Satyā offered a garland to Cyavana. (83)
Recognizing her supreme devotion to her husband, the two sons of the Aśvins were satisfied;
having taken leave of the sage and bowed to the virtuous woman, they departed for heaven.
Then the seer Cyavana dispatched his own brother-in-law, Bhūbhṛt,
who was a forest-dweller, to that forest to summon him;
Śaryāti, with a very gracious mind, went to the hermitage of the excellent seer.
Seeing the youth by their side endowed with a different form,
the two queens were filled with wonder, while the king became agitated in mind.
Seeing her father, the daughter rose and offered him a salutation.
Then the king said to his daughter: "Why do you abandon the aged sage and serve a paramour? You are bringing ruin to your husband's and your father's lineage. (88)
Though rebuked by her father, the daughter, with a serene mind, said:
"Father, this sage Cyavana is your son-in-law. (89)
The sage then related the entire account and said to the king:
"Welcome to you; may your sovereignty be entirely free from obstacles in every way."
"O Great King, perform a sacrifice named Soma at my command;
in that rite, grant a portion of Soma to the two Aśvins, who subsist on Soma. (91)
By his own splendor, that King Cyavana performed a sacrifice;
he then caused the two physicians, the Aśvins, to drink the Soma.
Indra, raising his thunderbolt, arrived to slay the sage.
Cyavana paralyzed that arm of Hari along with its vajra.
Then everyone gave their consent, saying, "Let there always be lunar eclipses," since they had previously excluded the two younger physicians, considering them to be such.
Then, after those two had gone to heaven, the king gave abundant sacrificial fees; and Cyavana, having honored the gods, brahmins, and guests, departed for his own hermitage. ||95||
Śaryāti had a son named Ānarta, who was devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
he brought from Goloka a fragment of a jewel given by Kṛṣṇa. (96)
This is that very land of Ānarta, situated on the western shore of the ocean;
from Ānarta was born Revata, who built the city of Kuśasthalī.
From him was born Kakudmin, whose daughter Revatī went with her father to the world of Satya to question the Grandfather.
"But whom shall I obtain as a suitable husband? To her, the Grandfather (Brahmā) replied:
"When twenty-seven [ages] have passed on this earth at this time," 99.
The original and primary kings and others of the four yugas that have passed away, as well as their lineages and the descendants of those lineages— of them too, no sign remains.
"Therefore, give my consent to Baladeva, the brother of Kṛṣṇa.
Having been thus addressed, he approached and gave her to Baladeva. 101.
Kakudmin, however, went to the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa known as Badarī in order to perform penance, and he constantly worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 10.2 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this wonderful account of Sukanyā’s devotion to her husband, which yields merit through both recitation and hearing. 103.
Thus, the destruction of sins, liberation, and enjoyment increase further;
O beloved Kṛṣṇa, one obtains the fruit of service that is exceedingly great in Lakṣmī.

Thus, in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta-yuga, during the festival of *Jayantī* on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja in Vaikuṇṭha, while Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was engaged in dancing and other festivities, the sage Yugāndharva beheld the flickering eyes of Sukanyā, the daughter of Sāttvata. Due to the curse incurred by this glance, they both descended to the earth: he became Cyavana and she became the daughter of Śaryāti. Subsequently, in the forest, when the eyes of Cyavana were pricked by the tip of a thorn, his army suffered from the obstruction of feces, urine, and other bodily functions.

Chapter 390, titled "The Description of Kanyāyāñca, Cyavana’s Household Life, His Attainment of Fresh Youth through the Aśvinīkumāras, the Testing of His Devotion to His Wife, the Two Physicians’ Entitlement to a Share of the Soma in the Soma Sacrifice, and the Marriage of Revatī to Kakudmin—the Son of Śaryāti—by Baladeva," etc.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of service to one’s husband,
hearing which the doubts of devoted wives indeed come to an end.
The husband is Kṛṣṇa in his essential nature, while Śrī Kṛṣṇa exists in the form of the husband;
Hari himself abides in every way for the welfare of his wife.
Her husband performs various actions like an ordinary person;
nevertheless, she is considered to be of the nature of merit because of her devotion to her husband.
For a devoted wife, the highest good indeed resides right there;
for even Adharma, that bull, becomes gracious wherever she may be.
A devoted wife should always act in a way that brings pleasure to her husband;
by acting thus, she attains great joy together with her husband.
Whatever she offers to the gods, to the ancestors, to guests, and whatever she offers to herself— all that a devoted wife should indeed perform for the sake of her husband.
A virtuous wife enjoys half of what has been accomplished solely through her service to her husband;
she always partakes in her husband’s merit and shall dwell for a long time in the world of her husband.
As long as the sun and moon endure, so long shall she, like a goddess in heaven,
remain immersed in great bliss and joy wherever she may be.
I shall now describe the service to her husband performed by a devoted Brahmin woman.
There was indeed a Brahmin named Kauśika, who was highly proficient in Vedic rites. || 9 ||
In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, however, there lived a youth who was an abode of beauty and virtue,
devoted to the narration of stories, and surrounded by many disciples and grand-disciples.
He constantly practices righteousness and performs meritorious acts of charity;
he is devoted to the six duties and likewise carries out the affairs of the king.
He constantly moves about, trusted within the inner apartments among the circle of young women;
he is the instructor of the queens and likewise the teacher of the maidens. (1-2)
Foremost among those skilled in arts such as dancing and so forth, and proficient in the knowledge of reality, he attends the festivals of kings and queens by virtue of his counsel. || 13 ||
On the day of the king's birth, the Brahmin goes to the assemblies by invitation to where there are various dancers, instrumentalists, and singers.
Equal to goddesses, golden-hued, sixteen years of age, and well-honored,
they were commanded by the king to sing, dance, and play musical instruments.
For attachment is powerful, O Lakṣmī; the mind of one in whom attachment arises becomes colored by that [object], just like a crystal or similar substance due to its proximity. (16)
Whatever kind of perception arises, a corresponding desire is set in motion;
and for one who is deluded, an engagement toward the acquisition of objects of enjoyment comes into being. (17)
Previously well-refined, the intellect becomes defiled when possessed by delusion;
for one who is unsatisfied and full of craving, it becomes a servant to the acquisition of gain.
This brahmin Kauśika had a wife who was devoted to her husband;
she was a young woman named Śaibyā, who served the supreme command of her lord.
Considering the supreme scriptural injunction regarding ritual to be the bringer of ultimate welfare, he followed it;
nevertheless, he indeed became happy through his virtuous wife and servant.
O twice-born one, when she goes to the royal assembly characterized by dance, song, and amorous play, there are sixteen courtesans with moon-like faces who are younger than her by thirty-two years.

Beholding those women who were adorned with the beauty of the erotic sentiment and who displayed various gestures and emotions, he became filled with desire; they possessed the luster of the color of golden campaka flowers.
There, the Brahmin indeed prepared one [of his daughters] who was rich in physical beauty and fit for enjoyment;
then, by chance, he arrived home, utterly afflicted by the disease of fever. (23)
Indeed, his blood turned into water within his body;
from that, leprosy of the skin arose, as well as oozing leprosy on his nails.
Thus afflicted by disease, and even more so by the disease of love,
he burned within his heart and did not obtain even a moment’s sleep.
That virtuous wife, being well-disposed, serves her husband with her whole being;
regarding him as the Supreme Self, she feels no resentment. (26)
He constantly washes his nails and other parts with warm water;
he causes him to bathe properly, as well as providing him with clothing and so forth. (27)
A brahmin became the disciple of Atri, and Suśīlā was his devoted wife;
Anasūyā became their excellent disciple, possessing the true wealth of knowledge, virtue, and other such qualities.
Therefore, that virtuous woman constantly gratifies her husband through her body, mind, intellect, actions, speech, and service. (29)
Once, having released a sigh, the brahmin spoke to that virtuous woman:
"Sleep does not come to me; my mind is constantly burning."
"O wife, ever since that courtesan was seen by me in the royal assembly, I have a desire to enjoy her; tell me, what shall I do?"
"The fire of desire, centered on the courtesan, burns within my heart;
my feet are leprous and my hands are severed—being thus afflicted, how shall I obtain her? (32)
O wife, if you lead her [to him], I shall attain a good rebirth;
otherwise, if she dies while still possessed of latent desires, a downward rebirth is certain.
Thus addressed, that virtuous and chaste woman bowed at her husband’s feet and said, "Oh, what great fortune!
Oh, what great fortune! I shall indeed bring satisfaction to my husband. (34)
Just as a husband might obtain a courtesan, so indeed do I act;
she is to be understood as a wife endowed with good fortune and likewise a performer of meritorious deeds. (35)
That which is prescribed by the master for his satisfaction bestows immediate contentment;
that service by which the master becomes pleased is true service, and never any other. (36)
Having spoken thus and having asked her husband's permission, the virtuous woman went to that house;
bowing at the feet of the courtesan, the virtuous woman said, "Do what is pleasing. (37)
"O sister, you are worthy of honor by my husband; day and night he remembers you.
Thinking only of you in his heart, the Brahmin finds no sleep. (38)
"Having become your servant, I shall perform service for you. O most excellent lady, please delight my husband; whatever you desire, I shall give it to you. (39)
Thus addressed, she asked the name and wealth of the Brahmin;
then that courtesan revealed everything to that virtuous woman.
The virtuous woman said: "How indeed can I give my consent to one who is so afflicted?
Nevertheless, out of greed for wealth, I shall please your husband. (41)
"Give me a hundred silver coins every night here;
having brought you to my house, make you my husband upon my bed. (42)
"If you yourself constantly wash clothes smeared with leprosy, as well as hands and other parts affected by it, then I shall grant you the fulfillment of your desire. (43)
"Give him golden ornaments and let him enjoy his desires.
Being thus commanded, she became exceedingly joyful within her heart. 44.
Taking her husband upon her own shoulders, she indeed gives him wealth;
she unites him with Sundarī, her beloved courtesan. (45)
After many days, the Lord was satisfied with Kāmadeva and said to his wife:
"O Satī, may you have an eternal place here in the world of the virtuous."
"Take me tonight, on this final night, and provide me with enjoyment;
afterwards, having become eternally satisfied, I shall have no desire for the house of a courtesan. (47)
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous wife placed her noble husband upon her shoulder and traveled by night along a path shrouded in blinding darkness to the courtesan.
O beloved, listen; meanwhile, a great obstacle arose.
A great sage named Māṇḍavya was staying at night beneath a tree. (49)
Then, by that very same path, the thieves, having stolen much royal wealth, departed;
the king's officers pursued them from all sides.
Having bound him, they took Māṇḍavya and led him to Rājagṛha;
on the way, they impaled him upon a stake, though he was not a thief, out of suspicion that he was a thief.
Having impaled that Māṇḍavya in such a manner upon the stake, the servants returned to their own homes; Māṇḍavya remained in great suffering.
Then the devoted and virtuous wife, placing her husband Kauśika upon her shoulders while he was afflicted by grief, touched that stake of Āṇḍavya which was enveloped in darkness.
As he was traveling along the road,
that brahmin, carrying his husband on his shoulder, caused Māṇḍavya— who was afflicted by extreme suffering— to move.
Enraged by the treading upon his feet, Māṇḍavya said to him:
"His death shall occur at sunrise, by whom I have been moved with his foot. (55)
Having heard that, his wife said: "If I am devoted to my husband and dedicated to my lord, then the sun shall not rise. (56)
"By the merit of serving her husband, may the path of the sun be blocked!
And by her, exactly as it was spoken, that very thing has been brought about. (57)
Then the horses of the sun, though being urged on, became fixed;
having become motionless, they attained stability and could not proceed further.
Then, due to the absence of sunrise, it became perpetual night;
she, however, being virtuous, took her husband and provided him with the enjoyment of a courtesan.
Having caused her husband to be satisfied, she returned again to her own home;
having bathed her husband according to the prescribed rite, she washed away the leprosy from his body.
Having bathed herself, she likewise gratified her husband with fragrant substances and the like;
she presented him with garments, ornaments, flower garlands, incense, lamps, and other offerings.
The virtuous woman gave him milk to drink and performed every act of worship;
yet her husband was satisfied, the household was prosperous, and she herself fell entirely under the power of the courtesan.
Satī then thought of Lakṣmī, and Lakṣmī arrived there;
having been saluted and worshipped by Satī, she then gave her a *cintāmaṇi* jewel.
Having bestowed words of blessing, Lakṣmī departed for her own abode;
Satī, however, fashioned a gateway of wish-fulfilling gems and provided wealth and grain.
All household utensils, ornaments, and rings;
divine juices as well as enjoyments, and the abundance of sweet foods and water. ||65||
Then, when the sun did not rise, the gods were seized with fear;
they sought refuge with Brahmā, and the Lotus-born One spoke to them.
Due to the greatness of a devoted wife, the sun does not rise;
for the splendor of a devoted wife's ascetic heat is superior to the splendor of the sun.
Due to the non-rising of the sun, there would likewise be the destruction of mortal living beings;
furthermore, it would result in the cessation of the twilight worship, ritual offerings, and sacrifices. ||68||
The offering of food to the gods, the best of sages, and the ancestors will undoubtedly be lost if it occurs without the rising of the sun. (69)
Therefore, for the sake of the sun's rising, you must indeed propitiate the virtuous and devoted wife of Kauśika, who is his servant.
Having received this command from Brahmā, the gods, sages,
and seers went to that place where the leper lived with his wife in his home.
Having arrived with dejected faces, they were indeed hospitably received by the woman;
honored, saluted, and questioned as to the reason for their coming. (72)
Having been honored with their own seats, water for the feet, and other offerings for the sake of their comfort,
they all paid homage to Satī again and again, explaining the cause [of her arrival].
O Goddess, the curse of Māṇḍavya has now been cast upon your husband, and your causing the non-rising of the sun—both of these are indeed destructive to the world. (74)
"O virtuous lady, out of compassion, act so that the welfare of the world may be secured; do this so that both purposes may be accomplished. (75)
May the rising of the divine Sun be a bringer of happiness for my husband, and may the word of Māṇḍavya likewise come true. (76)
Then, at that place, Atri’s wife Anasūyā, who was honored by the world and the virtuous wife of Kauśika’s preceptor, spoke to Suśīlā. (77)
Listen, daughter, I shall tell you how the three tasks must be performed:
the gods have come here, and their request is for our benefit. (78)
This must be done by every means, both by you and by me as well.
Speak, and holding water in your hand, let the sun go to its rising. (79)
"Speak, daughter! Let the two physicians of the gods make your husband free from disease;
for in this case, the destruction of the husband's illness should be considered equivalent to the destruction of the husband himself."
"O Lord, this body of yours is considered to be at its end;
may your husband become like a god, a youth of divine form. (81)
"Having caused the rising of the sun, restore my beloved husband who has fallen ill.
Thus entreated, the wife caused the rising of the sun. (82)
She caused her husband to become a new god through two sons of the Sun;
and by thus bringing about the rising of the Sun, she restored her husband to life.
In an instant, Kauśika became possessed of strength, vigor, and power, having been refined by the elixir of the Aśvins and Sukumāra. (84)
She worshipped all the gods and then dismissed them;
she served him who was radiant with splendor and obtained the great bliss of Brahman. ||85||
Māṇḍavya said to King Yama, "Tell me the fruit of my karma.
Yama replied, "While you were playing at the age of five, as a child—" (86)
Out of delusion, you once threw a sharp thorn at a parrot perched on a blade of grass;
as a result, you have now experienced being pierced by a spear here—do not grieve.
Then Māṇḍavya spoke words of righteousness, consisting of reasoned justice:
"In every respect, for a child of only five years who acts according to his own will—" [88]
Corruption, sin, and punishment—none of these exist at all for me, O my consciousness;
yet that sin of my parents remains for ten years as a limit for the sake of their welfare. (89)
"Up until ten years of age, both training and sin may exist;
for me, that sin does not exist—why then was I placed upon the stake? (1.391.90)
Therefore, you must experience that fruit; become a Dharma existing throughout the four ages—one pierced by the Dharma of Tretā and likewise pierced by the Dharma of Dvāpara. (91)
Pierced by Kali and having gone to the earth, you will experience suffering;
for one pierced by the stake of unrighteousness, your status as a Śūdra shall persist day and night. 92.
Having been cursed thus, Dharmarāja removed him from the stake;
he begged for forgiveness and chose freedom from the stake as a boon from the son of the Aśvins so that he might be healed of his wound.
Having joined and filled [the parts] together, he made it just as it was before;
thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this which is devoted to wonders. 94.

O beloved, in this [system], the vow of devotion to one's husband is such that sin gives rise to merit, and unrighteousness attains the state of righteousness, just like the power of yoga and so forth. 95.
Devotion to one's husband is a great dharma that purifies all embodied beings;
yet this very dharma was formerly practiced by this twice-born man, resulting in misery for the wretched woman. (96)
Because of that very act of killing, he was born as a leper in this life;
however, in the past, he had indeed given a gift of three daughters to Gaurī. (97)
By that merit, there shall be a devoted wife in the house of the Brahmin;
and from reciting and hearing this, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and happiness. (98)

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the account of the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā-māhātmya*): the leper Kauśika, a Brahmin who was infatuated with a prostitute, was made to unite with that prostitute by his wife Suśīlā; furthermore, while Māṇḍavya was impaled on a stake, Kauśika met his death before sunrise due to a kick to the foot [by Māṇḍavya], whereupon Suśīlā caused the sun not to rise as a curse; subsequently, at the request of the gods, Suśīlā brought about the cessation of the curse and other afflictions; and as for Dharma—
The three hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of Retributive Punishment in the Ages and the Corresponding Performance of the Duties of Each Age."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahāpadmā Lakṣmī, to this beautiful narrative which destroys sin, brings peace, and grants liberation to those who hear it.
In a former age, there was a king of great prowess named Śatrujit,
who performed sacrifices at which the gods, together with Indra, were gratified.
His son was Mahāvīrya, possessed of divine prowess;
he was renowned as Ṛtadhvaja, a sky-walker and a sovereign among yogins.
Constantly served by supernatural powers, he was an ocean of the qualities of higher knowledge;
there was nothing unknown to him, and his scholarship was supreme in every respect.
Having heard of his supreme fame, the fourteen lords of the stars,
the sages, the seers, and the nāgas indeed come to behold him.
Then, after some time, two Naga sons of Aśvatara came from the world of the Nagas to the surface of the earth.
Concealed in the form of Brahmins, the two youths, who were pleasing to behold,
paid their respects upon seeing him and then departed, only to return once more.
Thus, they two always went forth constantly with great joy;
and that prince attained supreme bliss through them.
Without them, the son neither ate, nor bathed, nor drank wine; he neither took pleasure nor accepted anything whatsoever without those two.
Indeed, for a long time they spent most of their time in the presence of the prince;
once, there in Pātāla, their father [spoke] to those two young Nāgas.
He asked, "By what means does our friendship exist in the mortal world, wherein you two, O good sons, spend so much time? (11)
The two of them said: "The son of Śatrujit was named Ṛtadhvaja;
he was handsome, endowed with uprightness, learned, friendly, and a mine of virtues. (1-2)
My lord is devoted to his guests, and my mind is captivated by him;
therefore, O father, because of separation from him, no happiness arises for us here at all.
The father said: "Blessed is he whose virtues are thus celebrated;
even when absent, the virtuous perform that which makes life blessed. (14)
He whose friends describe his virtues, whose enemies [describe] his prowess, and who is spoken of thus in assemblies—he indeed is a father who possesses a son. (15)
His two sons have accomplished something to satisfy his heart:
whatever gold, jewels, vehicles, or seats there are in my house. (16)
Whatever else may bring him joy, that should be given without hesitation;
for the gods desire the constant prosperity of one who performs acts of service. (17)
And they both said, "O father, whatever jewels,
vehicles, seats, conveyances, ornaments, and garments were in that house," (18)
These exist nowhere in the three worlds; there is no knowledge equal to it elsewhere.
There is one task remaining for him to accomplish, which cannot be achieved through mere principles without a Lord.

Just as fields are indeed made of earth, just as lakes are indeed filled with water and the like,
and just as heavens are indeed composed of light and so forth;
And the vital breaths are the winds; indeed, they do not belong to you. ||57||
Just as you, being conscious, proceed with a noble chariot upon this vehicle that travels many paths, so too do you abide within yourself in the divine sky of consciousness.
In that very same way, there is a driver; remember him as Acyuta.
This body of yours is indeed transitory; those of my father were likewise gone, as were those of his father.
Since it has been so in the past and will be so in the future, therefore, O noble one, obtain an eternal body. (59)
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Rādhikā, Lord of Ramā, Mādhava, Lord of Pārvatī,
Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of devotees, Lord of Prabhā!
O Raṭāṅga, you shall obtain a body that is eternal.
For you there is no sleep, nor is there sloth; for you there is no mother, nor do I have a son. For you there is no childhood, nor do I have old age.
Succession and non-succession do not exist for you in Brahman, nor for me.
Knowing "I am the Self," the servant of the Supreme Self is to be recognized by the heart, the intellect, and the mind,
as one immersed in bliss within direct experience.
He drinks the nectar of Kṛṣṇa and attains satisfaction.
Just as on the earth there are feet that move well while swinging, and feet [fixed] upon the pillars of a swing,
so too do your two feet remain within the space between the cloths.
Worship Him indeed, whose feet dwell within your own heart. ||63||
The Lord, the protector, the giver of liberation, and the God of gods, though formless, stands as if possessed of form;
he alone, the far-sighted one, is both mother and father.
He alone is also named Vikrānta; resort to him. ||64||
You are the Self, you are liberated, you are the eternal Lord; you are Brahman, you are divine, you are ever-blissful;
you are Nara, you are protected by Nārāyaṇa.
You are your own true nature; worship the Lord of the Imperishable.
Discriminative knowledge is said to be "stepping" (krānta), and from that, action is considered to arise.
Since the Self is endowed with both knowledge and action, tell me, O Lord, what is your own "striding" (vikrānta).
Its adversaries are indeed its two wings: volition and power.
Having taken flight with these two wings—volition and power—declare your own true nature.
The letter *vi* is said to be the organ of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), and likewise *kra* is the organ of action (*karmendriya*).
The Self (*ātman*) resides within those two; tell me of your own prowess. (68)
Know yourself to be distinct from the body and the house; know yourself as the Lord who is indeed existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda). Therefore, sorrow shall not touch you.
Thus, by bestowing enlightenment upon her first son,
that virtuous woman liberated him in his childhood, making him a king among yogis who had achieved his life's purpose.
The mother constantly gives her son—who is ever-increasing and a fresh, new awakening—consisting of self-knowledge, during the lullabies and other such activities. //71//
Having attained freedom from egoism and complete absence of possessiveness,
he obtained supreme self-power and realized the knowledge that consists of pure being.
She alone is the mother, the progenitress, by whom the child is thoroughly awakened;
he shall enter the path to liberation and be released from bondage and from worldly existence.
Having attained self-realization through the awakening provided by his mother's own language,
the son was thus enlightened by his mother from the very moment of his birth.
Having transcended physical comfort, he became dispassionate and was no longer struck by sense objects;
even in his youth, he was not of a passionate nature, nor did he harbor hatred toward anything. ||75||
For one who abides in the form of Brahman, no perception of enjoyment arises toward this transient, painful, and perishable corpse, whether in its state as female or male. (76)
Regarding form, taste, as well as smell, touch, and sound, he considered them to be non-self and belonging to another; indeed, he was not bound by them at all.
When the body is nourished and strength is born, that strength is considered to be like a stone; one regards the spheres of the sense organs as being like granaries. (78)
Thus, free from passion, devoid of dualities, established in his own true nature,
and free from the sense of "mine," that wise man did not set his mind upon the life of a householder.
He was free from egoism regarding his own body, devoid of the sense of "I" concerning his kingdom,
as well as toward his field, his elephant, his vehicle, his mount, and his realm.
Devoid of affection, he indeed found no bond of attachment among his male servants and attendants, nor among the female slaves, nor even in his cities. (8.1)
Even amidst palaces, garments, ornaments, and objects of great enjoyment,
his mind did not dwell upon anything at all, just as it was when he had become the foremost of those liberated.
Whether in food, pleasure, drink, or even in all kinds of edible delicacies for the tongue, he appears entirely devoid of the relish of taste, like a supreme ascetic. ||83||
He is free from attachment toward ornaments such as necklaces of jewels, fragrant substances, liquid materials such as oils, and substances such as collyrium. (84)
At the exhibitions of wrestlers, the sports of courtesans, the songs of female dancers, and their dances, he was as if despondent. ||85||

He remains free from passion even in the assemblies of kings, in times of enthusiasm, during festivals of the subjects, in amusements, and even while traveling through forests and on hunting expeditions.
He was indeed dispassionate toward the infliction of punishment, toward violent acts, as well as toward verbal abuse, and toward legal proceedings that were cruel and merciless.
He was always full of enthusiasm for celibacy, as well as for purity, contentment, steadfastness in austerity, the study of sacred texts, and the worship of the gods. (88)
In every kind of truth, in silence, in mental and external honesty, in non-possessiveness, in fortitude, and in the avoidance of desire and the like; ||89||
In serving the guru, in serving one's parents, in honoring the elderly, in welcoming guests, and in looking upon devotees with devotion—he is indeed liberated. (1.393.90)
He remains always full of faith and is in every way a believer; he is an active practitioner, possessed of discernment, rich in liberation, and ever devoted to the practice of Brahman. 91.
He is devoted to serving the virtuous and always intent on the service of Hari; he performs what is beneficial for living beings and is free from causing joy or agitation [to others]. ||92||
Thus, from his very childhood, he became equal to Sanaka;
seeing his son as a great liberated soul, a supreme and equanimous devotee of Viṣṇu.
The mother rejoiced exceedingly, and the father too became filled with bliss;
likewise, the subjects, the servants, and others regarded him as a god indeed. (94)
For him there are: atomization, magnification, heaviness, lightness, as well as reachability, the fulfillment of desires at will, mastery, and the form of lordship. (95)
Śabda, Ūha, Adhyayana, Duḥkhanāśa, Trayas, Suhṛtprāpti, Jñānadāna, Tārā, Sutārikā, and [Tāraṇa]—thus [are the ten]. 96.
All [the gods] bowed at his feet, for he had indeed become the supreme Siddha;
with his desires unimpeded, he shone like one who was liberated while still alive.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of Kṛtadhvaja’s Return to His Father’s Kingdom after Being United with Madālasā in Pātāla, the Birth of His Son Named Vikrama, and the Instruction on Discernment Given to Him by Madālasā," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, Madālasā gave birth to a second son;
his father therefore gave him the name Subāhu.
Madālasā also laughed and said: "In that which is devoid of name and form, name and form are forcibly planted by the world for its own selfish ends."
But this Brahmavidyā indeed instructed that child with coaxing words and the like constantly, just as before, in the stainless state.
Listen, my son: your body has manifested in the form of a child;
it did not indeed belong to you previously, so how can you consider it your own? (4)
For that body, constantly afflicted by cold and heat, repeatedly perishes;
it is perpetually dependent on others and always a betrayer of trust. (5)
The father, ordained by the previously established Creator, entered his body;
having emerged from it, he indeed became the son whose nature was water.
While staying in the womb, his lifespan lasts for ten months;
if he does not remain there, then that lifespan is considered to last but a moment.
In the event of a miscarriage, the life span is less than eight months for one miscarriage, six months for two, or one month for three;
however, if a birth has occurred, the life span is ten months.
Then follows his lifespan associated with ignorance and characterized by delusion;
thereafter, for ten days, it is said to consist of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
At the end of a month, before the rain, the life-span is subject to another's control;
at the end of a year, before three years, the life-span is the mother’s instruction.
Then he is celebrated as a child and a youth until the age of twelve;
thereafter he is gentle, and then mature, becoming a young man preoccupied with anxiety.
Whether solitary or in a group, whether alone, in pairs, or more than that, I am encircled like a jackal, shrouded by the notions of "I" and "mine. (12)
Accumulating enemies, friends, family, fame, gain, and so forth, he came to perceive those things in what was not those things, becoming entirely devoted to joy and sorrow. (13)
Bound by children, grandchildren, and the like, preoccupied with cattle, fields, and so forth, he is rooted in latent impressions (vāsanā) by the snare of the expansion of his lineage. (14)
With a body worn out, he has reached old age; possessed of diseases, incapacity, and the like, he is deprived of the command over his physical frame.
He is a kinsman of wind-diseases and the like, a consumer of unwholesome food and contempt;
he regards insults as honors and is restrained even when desiring to depart. (16)
Once dead and cremated, where was that ghost and where did it go?
Therefore, like a dream, the body and its lifespan are merely a manifestation.
Knowing this, O son, you are always devoid of name and form;
you are designated as Being-Consciousness-Bliss, eternally satisfied and free from desire.
Abide in the state of pure bliss; do not abide in the cycle of worldly existence.
You are eternally pure within this essence-less world; do not carry the burden of impurity upon your head.
"O son, you are always pure; do not allow blackness to enter into yourself.
You are like a clean mirror; do not let defilement settle upon you."

"Kṛṣṇa is my mother," "Kṛṣṇa is my father," "Kṛṣṇa is my elder brother," "Kṛṣṇa is I and am," "Kṛṣṇa is a child," "Kṛṣṇa is self and other"—worship Kṛṣṇa as the Self of all and attain liberation. ||26.1||
The supreme Brahman is light; the supreme Brahman is darkness;
the supreme Brahman is knowledge, offered within the ether of consciousness;
the supreme Brahman is suffering; the supreme Brahman is happiness.
O child, you abide in the Supreme Brahman yourself.
I possess nothing, nor does he possess anything; for that [notion] is merely imagined by the conceited.
There is no union for one who is unattached and free from childishness; you have already crossed over, so always exert yourself within the self. (23)
One may possess only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of one's physical life;
even in that, remain unattached and bring about the desired nectar of Hari’s grace through pleasing devotional practices. 24.
O tree, do not subject your own pure self— which is filled with existence, consciousness, and bliss— to the bonds that bring about suffering; instead, sport according to your true nature.
In the *Samānaka* [section], from the *Tricchidi* up to the *Astika*. ||25||
You have no wife, nor do you have a palace; you have no elephants, servants, or stables;
you have no army, nor any other protector.
Indeed, without Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 26 ||
Just as the virtuous regard association with the body as [mere] contact,
so too should you, O Lord, regard even intense attachment to what is desired as mere contact with Hari. Make it so.
"Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!
(27) Thus, that great queen instructed the boy through playful conversations and other means in the knowledge of the Self, and he, too, became liberated. (28)
He too considered Govinda to be his very arm as his protector;
indeed, Subāhu regarded himself as such because he had obtained Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
But he was not determined to be Subāhu because of his arms being situated on his body;
rather, seeing that he was truly liberated, his mother indeed rejoiced in her heart.
The great virtuous woman considered her own motherhood to have become meaningful,
since she had bestowed upon her son a wisdom equal to her own.
The father Bodhya protects one from evil, and you, O mother, grant us wisdom;
all that which brings satisfaction exists within Queen Madālasā.
Then, after some time, her third son was born;
and the king named that son Śatrumardana.
Then, repeatedly remembering that which is called "excessive laughter," his mother Satī instructed him, who was composed of pure consciousness.
And when she fondly rocks him while protecting him, she gives him milk from her breast, as well as food to be chewed, sucked, and licked. (35)
On various occasions, he would instruct him regarding the ritual sprinkling:
"Listen with your ear, my son; for there is no consciousness in the ear. (36)
Take this excellent drink with your mouth and likewise with your tongue;
yet you are neither tongue nor mouth, for you are eternally pure consciousness.
Speak a word, behold a form, and display a delightful smile; yet you are not sound, nor indeed the eye, nor are you the internal organ.
Behold this stinging and so forth caused by the bite of a fly;
that exists in the body, but it does not exist in you. Indeed, the body is merely dependent upon you.
In that regard, know that what is hot or extremely cold, or scratching, causes blood;
you are neither blood, nor scabies, nor skin, nor bone, nor scratching.
While you remain present, all that is born and dissolves;
yet there is neither decrease through what is born nor increase within you.
Drink, that which is to be drunk, hunger, thirst, food, and what is to be sucked—these are indeed not [needed] by you;
yet while you remain, this body requires them all. (42)
Without you, there is neither body nor the functioning pervaded by hunger and thirst;
indeed, everything would go to dissolution. Therefore, you are supreme over all. 43.
Houses, gardens, and so forth are for the sake of others; water and grain are for the sake of others;
and all that is visible is for the sake of others. He who is "other" is identical with you.
Birth and death are eternally established as residing within the body;
you, however, are indeed beyond all states, being fully supported by the Supreme Self.
Within the body you are He, and whoever exists within you is to be known as the Supreme Lord;
indeed, you are equal to the Supreme Lord—eternally awakened and stainless.
Eternally pure, eternally accomplished, eternally conscious, and transcending worldly existence—this protection is but a dream, and this nurturing as well is but a dream. (47)
May laughter, gratification, and sleep be yours in every way while you are awake;
may the yogic sleep (yoganidrā) of Hari always grant you peace during your union with Him. 48.
Sleep, which consists of the disparagement of enjoyments, is a net of illusion; it does not exist in you. Nor do impurity, decay, or even any excellence in prosperity exist in you. (49)
Indeed, you are not possessed of the stains of malice, envy, jealousy, and the like;
liberated and eternally existent as the Self, you are full bliss, O son.
Just as a new garment is obtained and an old one is forcibly cast off, so too a new day is obtained and the previous one has passed away by force. (51)
The morning has passed, the evening has passed, and the moonlit night has gone;
the night of the new moon, that darkness-born illusion, has also passed away. (52)
If she should come into your presence following the sequence of the jar-rosary, then, O knower of the Self, descend into that divine light consisting of the lightning of the Self. (53)
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and arrogance—these are the enemies to your own awakening; crush them in every way. (54)
Do not grieve for those who have departed; turn away from those who are present;
and do not offer even the slightest hospitality to those who have not yet arrived.
Those internal enemies have been severed by the exceedingly sharp sword of self-knowledge; they neither arise nor flourish, becoming as withered as things deprived of water. 56.
In this world, the enemies of the body are not truly the enemies of the self;
those who create obstacles to the liberation of the self are proclaimed to be the real enemies. (57)
Thus, having become a crusher of your own enemies within the city,
remain devoid of virtue in the nine-gated fortress of the body.
Then his father gave him the name Sārthaka, and his mother called him Śatrumardana;
thus was that third son enlightened by both parents.
From childhood itself he was well-liberated, devoid of fear of the pairs of opposites;
he was indifferent toward pleasant travel, food, and all objects of enjoyment and pleasure.
Free from craving and eternally satisfied, he lived continuously;
obstacles had vanished, dualities had ceased, and for him, saṃsāra no longer existed at all.
The shifting net of illusion has not entered into that which is dear to the heart;
for one who abides on the path to liberation, neither rising nor setting causes any affliction.
For he abides in self-luminosity, in his own bliss, and in the satisfaction of his own Self;
indeed, he appears like a king of yogis, equal to Sanandana.
Seeing him, the mother became joyful; her motherhood was made meaningful.
He does not become colored by water, nor does he undergo agitation from fire. (64)
Neither by celebration does one reach tranquility, nor by poison does one become free from poison;
my son is equal to happiness and suffering, and thus I, the mother of such a son, am truly blessed.
Thus, that virtuous woman Ānandamayī, who was established on the path to liberation, worshipped Lord Hari;
and upon seeing her son liberated, she herself became situated on the path to liberation. (66)
Thus Madālasā obtained three sons who were liberated while living;
through the intoxication of Brahman, she became languid with joy in this world, and so she was called Madālasā.
Thus, with his three sons— who were essentially Brahman and identical with him—
he performed actions free from desire, not for the sake of benefiting the king.
The king, the sovereign of devotees, seeing his auspicious sons who had taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa, were liberated, and had become the very nature of Brahman, rejoiced in them in every way. (69)
He was exceedingly pleased with his devoted wife;
for if one's kinsmen are truly contained within one's son, then what is the use of birth? (1.394.70)
But how can he who is himself shrouded by bonds deliver his ancestors? What is the fruit of birth for one whose wife is the creator of bondage? (71)
That wife who is a deliverer is a true partner who carries one across;
she alone is the one who carries the family across, and through her, the life of the householder is most excellent.
