The son is called Tāraka, and likewise the wife is Tārikā;
the virtuous wife and the saintly son are both considered by you to be deliverers (tāraka).
Blessed am I; blessed is my kingdom, and blessed too are my subjects.
Through association with the virtuous and association with the chaste, we, including the subjects and others, shall cross over [the ocean of worldly existence].
In that kingdom where there are virtuous, truthful, and devoted wives,
and where sons are saintly and liberated, Vaikuṇṭha is present there.
Fie on the man who is the husband of a deceitful wife and the father of a rogue!
Fie on the king who likewise protects a subject who practices deception! (76)
"Victory is always his on earth who has a virtuous wife as his mistress;
by the merit of Madālasā, my victory is complete in every respect. (77)
Heaven and a kingdom equal to heaven; sons who are like gods to me;
a divine wife equal to Lakṣmī—Vaikuṇṭha belongs to me in every respect. (78)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa always dwells among my sons who are free from passion, and Śrī Rādhā indeed ever resides within my Ālasā. (79)
"Lakṣmī always resides in my house and indeed among my cooks;
Nārāyaṇa himself is within me, and there is not even the slightest deficiency in me. (1.394.80)
For him whose wife is devoted to her husband and whose son is a king among devotees, there is indeed a thousand Vaiṣṇava sacrifices performed perpetually. (81)
Where there is no virtuous wife and where there is no son who is a sovereign of devotion,
that house is like the dwelling of jackals belonging to the spirits of the dead.
Thus, truth alone was always seen upon his banner like a flag;
for that reason, the king became truly meaningful as "Ṛtadhvaja" (the Truth-Bannered). ||83||
Then he spoke to his sons for the sake of protecting the kingdom;
and the sons said to their father, "We shall indeed perform a Brahmanical kingship."
It is solely through the grace of our mother and father that we have been rescued from worldly existence;
for this entire earthly kingdom indeed causes one to sink into a state of misery.
A kingdom equal to the kingdom of the Self has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
a happiness equal to the bliss of Brahman has never existed, nor will it ever exist. ||86||
For one who has attained eternal contentment here, the joy of sovereignty is like poison;
for the self free from thirst, there exists no happiness greater than that bliss.
Yogis meditate upon the Supreme Self within their own self;
likewise, the virtuous perceive Śrī Hari within the interior of their hearts. 88.
But we have attained union with that [Reality] through the compassion of our father and mother;
therefore, we do not desire a kingdom that is external, perishable, and subject to decay. (89)
Hearing that they were his sons, he rejoiced again and again, saying, "I have been delivered by my excellent sons; nothing remains to be done."
Thus, after some time, a beautiful son was born to the king who had attained his desire;
he was the fourth son, a repository of virtues, born of Queen Madālasā. (91)
Then that great queen spoke these most auspicious words to him:
"O son, by your great merit, your birth has occurred here. (92)
Though you are unborn, you are born with birth; you were born for the sake of sovereignty.
Though you are not a king, O dear son, through great merit you become a king. (93)
Though childless, you possess offspring for the sake of the kingdom;
though eternally liberated, you are nevertheless bound by the desire to please your father. (94)
Do not consider it a hardship to perform the work for the sake of progeny, according to your mother’s instruction;
nor should you feel weariness toward untruthful matters, even when time is being wasted along with your companions.
You must serve your parents while keeping knowledge well-guarded within your heart;
remain their obedient servant, appearing as if possessed by worldly attachment though you are truly free from it.
Having spoken thus, King Nāma ceased, desiring to act;
he then beheld his virtuous wife, slightly smiling and languid with intoxication.
Filled with curiosity, the king said to her as she was smiling slightly:
"While I am performing the naming ceremony for each one individually... (98)
Laughter arises within you; tell me now, what indeed is the reason for this?
Vikrānta, Subāhu, and the third, Śatrumardana—[these are your sons]. (99)
I believe these names have been fashioned; they are indeed auspicious.
Or rather, some new [insight] appears here as I reflect upon them.
"Tell me, O virtuous lady, what indeed are the names of the good and the bad? O beautiful woman, you must give a name to this fourth son."
Madālasā said to her husband, "I shall give a name to your son;
O knower of dharma, your son will become famous as Alarka."
Where there is no dissolution (la), no destruction (laya), no passion (ra), no expansion (vivṛddhi), and no origination (ka)—
he should be known as Alarka, your fourth son.
No self whatsoever is born, nor does it grow, nor does it perish;
this son of yours, O Arka, is one whose birth, growth, and dissolution are non-existent.
One truly has no enemy by whom one might be crushed;
thus, the so-called "crushing of enemies" would be meaningless.
Therefore, the arm is meaningful for crushing enemies such as desire and anger;
otherwise, it would be merely a limb and not a "good arm" (subāhu), which would be purposeless.
O Kṛṣṇa, he who exists among many is proclaimed as Bāhu;
since he possesses excellent arms (subāhu), that name is therefore meaningful.
Where "krāntiḥ" (striding), "kriyā" (action), and "gatiḥ" (motion) are used as synonyms, it is redundant;
for the all-pervading Self, there is never any motion whatsoever. (1.08)
Moreover, O Blessed One, even if there is no destination found in the world,
your son's name "Vikrānta" (The Valiant) will indeed be meaningful.
Thus, O King, these sons of yours, the Tārakas who bestow liberation, have been born by the power of fortune; may they live for eternal years.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by Madālasā to Her Sons—Subāhu the Second, Śatrumardana the Third, and Alarka the Fourth"—within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, Madālasā, having been joined with the king, instructed her fourth son on the path of spiritual practice.
"Son, grow up and gladden the heart of my husband with your deeds;
bring satisfaction through your actions to all the gods, ancestors, and guests."
"O son, take up the vow of celibacy along with its guiding instructions;
then, from a true guru, receive the knowledge and the statesmanship suitable for a king. (3)
O dear son, uphold the kingdom granted by your father for the sake of dharma;
protect the subjects, and perform the most excellent sacrifices with clarified butter and other offerings in the fire.
Perform sacrifices, give what is requested to Brahmins, the virtuous, and the poor;
from the protection of the earth, happiness will arise and the work of dharma will be accomplished. || 5 ||
By this, you shall attain heaven, divinity, and eternal happiness;
having gone to sacred fords on auspicious festival days, you should offer libations to the gods who dwell upon the earth.
You should fulfill the heart's desires of your kinsmen and their well-wishes;
you should contemplate in your heart the supreme welfare of all living beings.
You should constantly turn away from improper deeds and from evil;
gratify the gods and the twice-born with sacrifices, gifts, recitations, and oblations.
You should strive for the goals of human life known as dharma, artha, and kāma;
you should serve your teachers and bring joy to your friends.
You should protect the virtuous, worship the gods and men,
undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords, and effect your own liberation.
You should observe the duties of a householder, satisfy your virtuous wife, procreate sons, and rely upon the integrity of a trust.
You should strive for liberation and likewise abandon worldly engagement;
you should dissolve yourself into the Supreme Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Akṣara.
Thus, my son, for your sake this path has been pointed out by me;
therein you should take refuge in that which consists of both passion and its renunciation, for that is the highest good.
Being thus addressed repeatedly by his mother,
that auspicious boy Alarka, the son of Ṛtadhvaja, grew up in age.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, he said to his mother: "O virtuous lady, tell me what must be done by me here in this world and whatever pertains to the life hereafter."
Madālasā spoke again: "Now that you have reached an age fit for wisdom, my child, one who has been consecrated in the kingdom must act so as to please the people."
Vices that lead to the destruction of the kingdom must certainly not be indulged in;
one's own self must be protected from enemies, and one's counsel especially so. (17)
One should discern ministers and others through their seating, gifts, and speech;
one should cause spies who know the truth to observe everything everywhere.
A king should never, under any circumstances, place his trust in anyone; rather, he must protect his ability to accomplish his objectives even at the cost of occasional betrayals of trust.

A king should be proficient in place, time, and other such factors, as well as in the various qualities [of his subjects]; he should first conquer himself, then his ministers, then his servants, and after that, [his enemies]. (1.395.20)
Desire and the other passions must first be conquered in every way by kings;
for desire, anger, pride, greed, and arrogance are these destroyers. (2.1)
One should behave like a crow, possess a voice like a cuckoo, gather the essence like a bee, and always wander like a deer. (22)
One should act like a serpent in provoking anger, like a peacock in showing respect,
like a swan in discernment, and indeed like a cock in remaining vigilant.
A king seeking his own welfare should possess the firmness of iron;
he should enter a stubborn enemy slowly and gradually, like a worm.
Having united, the king should seize the enemy like ants;
indeed, he should display his prowess like a spark of fire. (25)
One should observe the rule for the sake of the True Principle (nīti) like the moon and like the sun;
indeed, one should be as untainted among beasts and birds as a harlot is [regarding her own kin]. 26.
Just as a lotus remains unsullied upon the water, standing ever higher and higher, so too does the Śarabha, who possesses the fruit of human endeavor, stand above the host of lions. ||27||
Just as a spear does not fail when piercing its mark, so should one cultivate wisdom;
when a vessel of curd has broken, the cowherd girl does not grieve. (28)
Milk never flows from the breasts of a pregnant woman;
in this same manner, a king should conduct himself and perform the protection of his kingdom. ||29||
Taking water like that of Indra, it should be given at the arrival of the appointed time;
taking water like that of the Sun, it should be given at the union of the seasons.
One should be impartial in the administration of punishment toward both friend and foe, like Yama;
however, one should not always maintain a tranquil mind like the moon in every situation.
Like the wind, he should gather secret information through spies among all social classes;
he who is not dragged down by greed or the group of sensual desires is always happy.
He protects the dharma that leads to heaven and guards the virtuous stages of life;
for him, there is eternal happiness both in this world and in the hereafter.
By establishing the entirety of dharma among his subjects, the king indeed attains his rightful share;
through that, he goes to heaven again and again. (34)
One should engage in the sacrifice of action, the sacrifice of knowledge, and the sacrifice of devotion;
through pleasing Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, one shall attain the eternal abode. ||35||
Truthfulness, purity, non-violence, lack of malice, as well as forbearance, compassion, and freedom from harmful action—these are the qualities that must be protected by people on this earth. (36)
O child, by adopting the householder's life, a person indeed nourishes the world;
and by that merit, he attains the worlds he desires. (37)
The Suras, Daityas, Dānavas, humans, Pitṛs, and Ṛṣis;
sages, insects, moths, birds, animals, and trees—[all these are likewise]. (38)
Householders depend upon him, and through him they attain satisfaction;
indeed, they even gaze at his face, thinking, "Will he give [to us]? (39)

The householder’s life is the nourisher and the support of all; it is like a cow consisting of the three Vedas, in which the entire universe is established, and she is considered the cause of the universe.
Rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* must be performed in every way by the householder alone;
the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā* are considered to have the householder as their support. (41)
The utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance of *hanta*, and even the utterance of *āho* consist of that [Brahman];
he who brings about the destruction of the householder’s life is indeed a doer of evil.
The wise man should support the householder stage of life; he is thus prepared for heaven.
O child, by means of the king or the wealthy man, the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans [are sustained]. (43)
One should nourish all living beings every day as if they were one's own body;
with a concentrated mind, one should perform the libations and *śrāddha* rites for the ancestors at the proper time.
Likewise, one should worship the deities with fragrant flowers, incense, and other offerings.
A householder should give food and other necessities to the distressed, the helpless, and the poor. 45.
One should scatter food on the ground for dogs, for those who cook dogs, and for birds;
likewise for one who has arrived hungry and weary, begging and possessing nothing. (46)
One should offer food and drink, regarding the guest as the Lord Hari;
when he is satisfied, the householder is indeed released from the debt arising from the sacrifice to men (nṛyajña).
If a guest turns away from a householder with his hopes frustrated, he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that host and taking away the host’s merit. (48)
A householder should honor a guest with even the gift of water and vegetables; furthermore, he should give alms to those who beg for them according to his capacity, as often as they request.
The master of the house should always eat only after having fed those who depend on him;
for one who maintains the household in this manner, O son, the state of a householder becomes truly beneficial.
The gods, the ancestors, the sages, the destitute, guests, and beggars; the seers, kinsmen, birds, beasts, and even the minute insects. ||51||
Those who are constantly intent on bestowing blessings indeed become givers of happiness;
they are givers of happiness even in the next world and remain free from obstacles. (52)
Atri himself sang this auspicious verse;
for having given it the name "Vaiśvadeva," one should employ it and not otherwise. (53)
Just as that which is to be done upon the birth of a son, and that which is to be done at a wedding and other such occasions,
so too should expenditure be made on the service of the virtuous and on the day of Hari.
Whatever scattering of food is performed on the ground by humans, by that—even if it be stale—the Piśācas and other spirits attain satisfaction. (55)
Whatever water falls upon the ground from the bathing garment, by that indeed the satisfaction of all those who have attained the state of trees is produced. (56)
But those drops of water which indeed fall adhering to the limbs of the body—by those that have reached the ground, the gods and others truly attain satisfaction. (57)
Even by mere fragments of food from a morsel, animals attain satisfaction; yet those who are burnt [by fire], as well as children who are fit for rites but remain uninitiated, [do not]. (58)
Those who have failed [in their duties] eat scattered food and sweepings; having drunk water from a water-pot, those deceased ones attain satisfaction. (59)
Therefore, one should give during a great festival, one should give at a Śrāddha ceremony, and one should give during a gift-giving rite;
for if a householder gives thus, no one in his lineage shall suffer.
A householder must observe right conduct in its proper manner;
for one devoid of right conduct finds no happiness either in this world or the next.
For a man of evil conduct certainly does not attain long life in this world;
therefore, one who desires a household should practice righteousness for the sake of warding off all sins.
One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon both dharma and artha;
having bathed, one should likewise perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), meditation, and the worship of the gods.
One should avoid idle chatter, falsehood, and harshness of speech;
one should never engage in improper discourse or atheism.
One should bow to the elders and perform the worship of those worthy of honor;
one should offer a seat to the gurus and practice rising from one's seat to greet them and other such marks of respect.
One should respectfully salute one's teacher, parents, and husband as superior;
one should not speak of the teacher's misdeeds, but should appease him when he is angry.
One should never listen to slander of others, nor should one ever engage in it oneself.
One should yield the path to Brahmins, as well as to a king and to one afflicted by suffering.
For the virtuous, for the learned, for one burdened by a pregnant wife, for a younger brother, and for those who are mute, blind, deaf, intoxicated, or insane. (68)
One should avoid joking insults, verbal abuse, and slander directed at the truthful, the enemy, a child, or one who has fallen from grace. (69)
One should never practice hypocrisy, pride, or deceit;
nor should one go to another's wife, if one desires long life.
A woman in her menses must always be avoided by all for four nights;
to avoid the birth of a female child, one should also avoid her on the fifth day. (71)
Then, on the sixth night, one who desires a son should certainly go;
for sons are born from women during even nights, while daughters are born during odd nights.
Indeed, the strength for conception is considered to last up to sixteen nights;
beyond that, the lotus becomes closed and fruitless.
One should not cultivate loving-kindness toward those who are immoral, nor those defiled by theft and the like, nor those who are excessively wasteful, nor the greedy, nor even one's enemies. (74)
Friendship is not formed with those who are powerful, nor with those who are inferior, nor with those who are censured;
it is not formed with those who suspect everyone, nor likewise with those who are devoted solely to fate.
Then, one should cultivate loving-kindness with those of virtuous conduct and goodness, who are wise, free from malice, capable, and devoted to industrious effort in their duties. (76)
One should never stretch out one's feet toward those who are like lords or gurus; O son, one should not dwell where these four are not present.
Where there is a lender of loans, a physician, a learned Vedic scholar, a river with water, and a king who has conquered his enemies and acts as a protector of dharma; ||78||
Wherever the citizens are well-disciplined and the earth is rich with crops, and wherever the people are free from envy, there a dwelling brings about happiness. (79)
"O son, one must not dwell in a place where these three things are always present: those who desire victory, those harboring ancient enmity, and people who are devoid of effort. (1.395.80)
Listen, my son, to how purification and other rites are prescribed for wood, stone, gold, silver, ropes, and garments, according to what is accepted for each. (81)
And likewise for vegetables, roots, and fruits; for split bamboo, leather, gems, diamonds, corals, jewels, and pearls. ||82||
The purification of the limbs of human beings is prescribed with water;
however, the cleansing of vessels that contain oily substances is performed with hot water.
And for winnowing baskets, grain, skins, pestles, mortars, and heaps of cloth, purification is achieved by sprinkling. ||84||
The purification of non-irritating bark garments is desired to be by means of water;
the purification of grass, wood, and medicinal herbs is desired to be by sprinkling. ||85||

The hair of the *ūrṇā* [between the eyebrows] and so forth are pure by means of the wind or a ray of light; likewise, alms-food is pure, as are the hand of an artisan and the merchandise he holds, as well as the face of a woman. (86)
Sacrificial halls, alchemy laboratories, nursing infants, women, pure waters, and flowing streams free from odor and bubbles [are all considered impure]. ||87||
The ground becomes purified over time through sprinkling, smearing, thorough sweeping, scraping, and likewise by rain; such is the purification of earth desired. (88)
The purification of bell-metal is by scrubbing with ashes and water, as well as by fire;
that of other vessels is by earth and water; and that of tin and lead is by alkaline salt.
Dust, fire, a horse, a cow, shade, rays of light, wind, the earth, droplets of water, flies, and the like—these incur no fault through contact with the wicked. (1.395.90)
The goat and the horse are pure from the mouth; so too is the face of a calf and the flow of milk from a mother cow. A bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall.
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, and even the grass on the road are indeed purified constantly by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. (92)
Having scooped out the best portion from abundant food that has been defiled, one should discard it;
for what remains, one should perform sprinkling with water or purification by means of air.
Having touched a corpse, one must indeed perform a bath; purity is considered to result from that.
Upon the discharge of impurities, one should perform a bath along with the cleansing of the hands and other limbs. (94)
Upon the birth of a child, one should observe purity for one month;
however, in the case of death, one should observe the period of impurity for twelve days, as if the child were less than a year old.
Thus, O Alarka, protect this conduct in every way;
one's own purity must always be guarded by destroying the delusions of illusion. 96.
Having been thus instructed with affection by his mother,
and commanded by his father, Tvalarka duly took a lawful wife.
"Accept this worldly kingdom granted by your father, O Ālarka. Then Madālasā spoke these final words to her son: || 98 ||
When you experience unbearable suffering born from separation from beloved kinsmen, or arising from the affliction of enemies, or produced by the loss of wealth and the like; ||99||
Then, O son, having extracted this from my finger-ring which I have given you, you must deliver the command; for it has been written by me here upon this cloth.
Having spoken thus, the mother gave him a golden ring,
and thereafter she bestowed whatever blessings were appropriate.
Having received blessings from his father, Alarka indeed ruled the kingdom;
meanwhile, Madālāsā and Ṛtadhvaja departed for the forest to practice austerities.
Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and having abandoned their material bodies,
they attained a divine form and indeed went to the abode of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the devoted wife Madālasā,
having brought forth sons who were liberated, went to the imperishable abode as a virtuous woman.
By reading or even by hearing this, liberation is attained;
all bonds shall perish, and there shall always be happiness, O beloved.
Alarka also governed his own kingdom according to the law so that no bondage might arise; all the subjects were filled with joy.
The righteous-souled king protected his virtuous subjects like his own sons;
likewise, he procreated sons and performed great sacrifices.
To him were born sons of great strength and prowess,
who were righteous-souled, high-minded, and obstructors of the path of unrighteousness.
He did not entrust the burden of sovereignty to his sons, though they were capable of ruling;
nor did detachment arise within him as he enjoyed manifold sensual pleasures.
To that brother who was thus attached to enjoyments, deluded, and with senses unsubdued,
the forest-dweller was indeed intent on instructing him for the destruction of passion.
An elder brother named Subāhu, a renunciant ascetic,
came quickly to his house and instructed him in liberation.
Remembering again and again that knowledge of the Self and that manifold learning which had been told to him even by his brother, he spoke to him solely for the purpose of destroying his bondage.
Nevertheless, Alarka did not consider the renunciation of his kingdom to be beneficial;
then [the sage], desiring to enlighten him and to make him abandon his bondage, spoke.
But Subāhu, having reflected for a long time, considered battle to be the better course;
he resorted to that enemy and incited a fierce war.
I bring about the highest good for my brother, supreme detachment;
having produced equanimity, I effect his liberation.
Having reflected thus, Subāhu approached the king of Kāśī;
that monarch then made preparations for military force against Alarka.
And he dispatched a messenger with the command, "Let the kingdom be given to your brother.
To that messenger who had spoken thus, he, intoxicated with pride, replied: ||| 1.17 ||
"Let my elder brother come to me and beg for the kingdom out of affection;
I shall not grant it by force, indeed, out of fear of the King of Kāśī."
Then a most terrible battle took place between him and the King of Kāśī;
having fallen into great anxiety, he remembered that ring.
There he saw a leaf given by his mother, with its letters clearly visible:
"Attachment must be abandoned with one's whole being; if it cannot be abandoned, [then one must abandon everything else]. (1.395.120)
One should associate with the virtuous, for the company of the good is indeed medicine;
yet thirst must be abandoned by all means, even if it cannot be relinquished.
That very desire for liberation should be abandoned; let that [desire] itself be its remedy.
Having caused her to recite this and having taken up the desire for liberation, King Ālarka—
Seeking the company of the virtuous and limiting his possessions at night,
he went to the illustrious and unattached preceptor Dattātreya.
Having prostrated and honored him completely, he spoke as follows;
he entreated him, saying, "Grant me your grace for the destruction of suffering and the like."

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Madālāsā Teaching Alarka the Duties of Conduct, Her Attainment of Divine State along with Her Husband, and Subāhu’s Efforts for the Sake of Alarka’s Self-Knowledge," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to the wisdom as it was acquired by Alarka from Dattātreya— wisdom that is difficult even for yogis to attain.
The Guru said: "O King, tell me truly for what reason you have this sorrow;
I shall remove your suffering this very day."
The disciple said: "My brother Subāhu, for the sake of the kingdom alone, has joined with the King of Kāśī and is fighting against me. (3)
"Destroy that supreme suffering quickly, even before morning!
The Guru replied, "But that [suffering] never exists within you."
For one in whose self you do not exist, how can there be your departure?
O Indra among kings, perform this investigation, and may illumination arise within your heart.
"Know for yourself, through my grace, that which is always free from both suffering and pleasure;
O King, take this water and drink even a single mouthful."
"Place [the mirror] likewise upon his eyes and on his head so that he may see Brahman.
Being thus addressed, he did so, and the interior of the heart was indeed opened.
Having thus reflected upon himself, he laughed and then spoke these words:
"All nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas), but I am eternally free from the three qualities."

From primordial nature (prakṛti) arises the sense of "mine" (mamatā); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) is born. Through that [ego], the subtle elements (mātrās)—which are both pleasant and soft—become objects of perception for the grasper.
From the subtle elements come the gross objects of enjoyment; from those arises the body, which is dependent on the qualities.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion—these are the natures of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Their effects are of such a nature that they also come upon those who are like them; for indeed, they do not come upon me, who am unlike them and am not that.
Therefore, neither pleasure nor pain nor delusion exist in me;
nor is there earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air.
Nor am I space; indeed, qualities such as fragrance do not exist in me.
I am not earth, nor is fragrance mine; I am not water, nor is taste mine. (13)
I am not light, nor is form mine; I am not wind, nor is tangibility mine.
I am not space, nor is sound mine; how then could its attributes exist in me?
The five elements, when combined, undergo decrease and increase;
likewise, the decrease and increase of pleasure, pain, and delusion are observed. || 15 ||
Just as the objects of sight and their qualities—such as a jar and its color—are perceived by the eye, so too are pleasure and other such states perceived by the mind. (16)
These perishable things belong only to the visible nature, not to the Self;
for how could that which is imperishable and eternal possess adventitious qualities? (17)
In this way, an insentient fruit such as a mango is to be grasped by the hand;
form is to be grasped by the eye, and likewise, taste by the tongue. (18)

Odor is to be grasped by the nose, and likewise intoxication by the mind; the quality of intoxication in fermented liquors and the like is indeed "mattatā" (intoxication), while in the dhūstūra plant it is "unmāda" (madness).
In buttermilk and other such things, only dullness and so forth are perceived;
these are grasped by the mind, and the mind itself is likewise characterized by those tastes.
The portion of the liberated one becomes even subtler than the mind;
then, dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty reside within that mind.
Since pleasure, pain, and delusion reside in the mind, I am not the mind, nor do pleasure, pain, and delusion belong to me in any way whatsoever. (22)
"I am not, nor is 'I' mine; I am not the intellect, nor indeed the mind.
Happiness and suffering reside therein [in those], so how could they belong to me? (23)
I am not the body composed of earth and the other elements, nor am I the internal mind or the sense organs;
nor am I past karma, latent impressions, or habitual tendencies.
And what do those delusions and sufferings matter to me here? ||24||
The kingdom, the earth, and all the people—this sovereignty is governed by intellect, not by me.
Intellect is the daughter of the Three Qualities; this governance and this kingdom belong to her, not to me. (25)
Let his command be carried out by the intellect of Subāhu, or let it be carried out by the intellect of Nālarka;
for neither the intellect of Nālarka nor the intellect of Subāhu resides within the body, since [the intellect] does not exist in the living soul.
For one who possesses neither hands and so forth under his control, nor flesh, nor bones, nor the distribution of veins—
what need has he for elephants, horses, chariots, and treasuries?
Even a very slight association with such a person exists here for a man. ||27||
Therefore, I have no enemy, nor do I have suffering;
I have no pleasure, for delusion is my city. I have no treasury, no elephants, no horses, no land, and no wife.
They belong neither to him, nor to another, nor to me. ||28||
What belongs to him, that alone belongs to me; what belongs to me, that alone belongs to him.
That which belongs to both is the pure Self.
Tell me here: by whom were suffering and happiness created? ||29||
For the person who perceives correctly, there is neither suffering nor pleasure whatsoever;
for one who beholds the Self, there is no kingdom anywhere except within Hari.
In this way, stability is established and maintained for a long time;
wherever one is attached, one likewise becomes colored by those very qualities. (3.1)
The suffering felt when a domestic cock is eaten by a cat is not equal to that felt for a cakravāka bird or a mouse when they are separated from their mates. (32)

Just as the intellect functions toward the protection of the body, children, and so forth, it does not function in that same way toward a body or even a tiny insect; on the contrary, it functions toward their destruction. (33)
For from the very elements of a single body, various kinds of offspring arise: lice, insects, bugs, as well as legitimate sons and children born of wedlock. (34)

The intellect is not the same toward everything, even regarding nails, hair, and impurities; therefore, that which is produced by the intellect is one's own, while that which is not produced by oneself belongs to another. 35.
Therefore, O Guru, through the realization of truth, I am neither suffering nor happy;
indeed, by your grace, I know that there is no person at all who is deluded.
Having heard these words of his disciple, Dattātreya said to him:
"It is even so, O tiger among men; you know it exactly as it is. (37)
The root of suffering is "mine," while the root of nirvāṇa is "not mine.
And through my compassion, this supreme knowledge has arisen within you. (38)
What was previously commanded by your mother has indeed been reminded to you by me today— that dullness consisting of "I" and "mine" which was cast away through discernment.
For that very person who is bodiless, there is indeed satisfaction in every respect;
[yet] houses, fields, sons, wives, wealth, grain, children, and so forth—[these remain external].

All things are false, yet through false cognition they are made out to be eternal; since they are fallen into the pits of delusive knowledge and the like, how can there be any final liberation for them? (41)
Those people who, through the words of their guru, have severed attachment and other such bonds by means of the swans of association with holy men, have gone to the supreme state. (42)
Having attained the pure forest of the Self— free from duality, devoid of anger,
liberated from delusion, and beyond all limiting conditions— dwell there forever happy.
You are neither gross nor subtle, nor are you composed of causes;
you are not composed of the subtle elements (tanmātras), nor even are you made of ego-consciousness (ahaṃkṛti). ||44||
Therefore, you are the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), distinct from this aggregate designated as the qualities (guṇas),
just as [the observer is distinct from] the water-moss, mud, reeds, fish, mosquitoes, and water.
O King, just as there is distinctness even within oneness, so it is between the field (kṣetra) and the Self (ātman);
[the Self] is eternally pure, eternally awakened, eternally liberated, and stainless.
And you are the Self, distinct from the body; you have indeed gone beyond the mockery of bodily sovereignty, beyond the kingdom of the earth, and beyond the kingdom of possessiveness. (47)
One desiring liberation should renounce attachment, for in its destruction lies the abode of the "mine-ness" complex;
through that, the state of dispassion arises from perceiving the defects inherent in suffering. 48.
The yogi dwells in a state free from passion, having abandoned all enjoyments;
that is his home where he resides, and that is his food by which he lives. (49)
He who is truly without possession shines forth as one liberated while living;
for liberation, knowledge is required, whereas ignorance becomes the cause of bondage.
Listen, O Alarka, to the supreme path that likewise bestows the highest state;
by that path many sages have attained liberation.
For yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, which always bestows liberation;
its fluctuations are indeed right cognition, misconception, conceptualization, sleep, and memory. (5.2)
Valid cognition arising from the means of knowledge is true knowledge; error is false knowledge;
conceptual construction devoid of a real object is non-cognition; and sleep is considered [a state] lacking awareness. (53)

Recollection is held to be produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) such as those of what has been experienced; however, when there is contact with an actual object, it is produced by impressions as a form of recognition (*abhijñāna*). (54)
Even that [perception] is here declared to be nothing other than memory arising from mental impressions (saṃskāra).
In this way, the mental modifications (vṛttis) are to be understood as both known and unknown. 55.
But the complete cessation of these, O King, is called Yoga;
the union of the self with Brahman is considered the most excellent Yoga. (56)
Yoga is constantly applied for the sake of destroying the impurity of the intellect;
those [impurities] are fivefold: ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and fear. (57)
The afflictions (kleśas) abound in the state of being stained; when they are destroyed, the mind is stainless.
For the sake of their destruction, the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas) must be practiced again and again. 58.
The wise person should protect non-violence, speak truth that is beneficial,
guard against theft in every way, and likewise remain a celibate practitioner.
He who is free from possessiveness is indeed liberated from bondage;
he should practice mental purity as well as physical cleanliness appropriate for his state.
One should constantly increase contentment by accepting whatever is obtained by chance,
and one should perform austerity in its proper form, consisting of the restraint of the senses.
One should always perform one's private study consisting of the chanting of the names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and with vigilance, one should constantly maintain focused devotion upon His form.
For one who thus constantly acts with a mind free from defects, hatred and attachment become the two primary faults; therefore, abandon them.
One should make the posture very firm, such as the excellent Svastika and others;
here, the Gorakṣāsana itself is the protector of celibacy. (64)
One should always perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) as required and according to one's strength;
through breath-restraints one should burn away the defects, and through concentration (dhāraṇā), the latent impressions (vāsanā).
Having attained Hari through withdrawal from sense objects, through meditation on the qualities that transcend the Lord,
and through absorption, one rejoices in the imperishable abode.
Indeed, the defects of the senses are burned away by the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
That which consists of twelve counts is light, while that which is double that number is medium.
The third stage is declared to be the best; one should perform it constantly and without weariness.
By the first stage, one should conquer perspiration; by the middle stage, however, trembling.
For with the third [breath], one should conquer despondency, and then the defects in successive order;
once mastered, it destroys the defects just as a trained hawk destroys birds. (69)
The state of freedom from mental impurity arises through breath control (prāṇāyāma);
defects such as desire, anger, and the like are consumed by the restraint of the vital breath.
Wisdom regarding the past and the future arises from the destruction of defects;
and consciousness that awakens the self is born from the restraint of the vital breath.
In that way, a state of mental clarity and gentleness arises;
once you are established in this condition, one should begin the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Having restrained the senses from their objects, as well as the vital breaths and the internal mind, one should cause them to abide within; that is the nature of pratyāhāra (withdrawal). //73//
One should always observe one's own nature through the activities of the senses;
by that means, one perceives the Self within the self, and thus withdrawal (pratyāhāra) also becomes a source of benefit.
O King, after withdrawal (pratyāhāra), one should commence concentration (dhāraṇā).
Twelve prāṇāyāmas constitute the common measure for its duration. (75)
Dhāraṇā consists of two [stages], and dhyāna is the one-pointedness of the mental state upon the form of Hari; when this is accomplished, the masses of defects are destroyed. (76)

And he beholds the Supreme Brahman and the qualities of Māyā as distinct from one another; established in himself, the all-pervading one perceives everything as being within his own self alone. //77//
Likewise, the meditator, always established in his own self, perceives everything within himself—at the navel, in the heart, at the throat, at the palate, on the forehead, and in the two eyes. (78)
One should indeed practice concentration upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa within one's own head;
by thus performing this meditation (dhāraṇā), one attains equality with the Imperishable.

Due to pride in one's status, due to the refinement of one's conduct, and likewise due to the wonder of one's power, one’s capacity for spiritual practice goes to ruin; therefore, one should turn away from those [conditions].
Women, fame, discernment, sovereignty, wealth, capability, divinity, the performance of many sacrifices, and a body made of elixirs (rasāyana). ||81||
Moving without obstruction through space, water, fire, and so forth—these are the obstacles that must be overcome; one should not direct the mind toward them. (82)
One who makes the mind attached to Brahman is not overcome by obstacles;
there arises intuitive knowledge of all things, the power of hearing, and divine hearing. (83)

The power of sight, divine vision, the comprehension of all languages, and the ability to perceive distant objects—these and other such supernatural attainments (*siddhis*) are actually forms of obstacles. (84)
And by means of these accomplishments, O son, the deities remain bound;
they return again and again through calamities and great obstacles. (85)
Therefore, having made yoga his dwelling and having wrapped himself in the *brahmakambala*, he should contemplate the supreme Brahman; thus he shall go to the highest goal. ||86||
The earth would dissolve into water; water would dissolve into fire;
fire would dissolve into air; and air would then dissolve into space.
One dissolves those [subtle elements] into sound, that [sound] into ego-consciousness, that into the Great Principle (mahat), and that into the Primal Matter (pradhāna);
one dissolves the Great Intellect (buddhi) into the Uneven (viṣama), and the Uneven into the Equilibrium of the Guṇas (guṇasāmyaka). ||88||
One should dissolve the three qualities (guṇas) into the one omnipresent [Being] within the single syllable;
the imperishable (akṣara), whose nature is Brahman, [dissolves] its own self into the Supreme Self. 89.
One should unite [the mind] with the Supreme Brahman; that indeed is His supreme state.
For him who has respect for all beings, there is a firm bond [to liberation]. (1.396.90)
Whenever a person feels passion for whatever being, having repeatedly attained attachment to that very thing, he perishes. ||9.1||
O King, the union with the elements returns again, causing obstruction;
yet for one who maintains equanimity toward all beings, that very state is liberation. 9.2
Aṇimā, laghimā, and mahimā, as well as prāpti;
likewise prākāmya, īśitva, and further vaśitva. (93)
Thus, having attained these divine qualities, such as the power of fulfilling desires, which indicate liberation, he is no longer afflicted by the three *guṇas*.
With his defects burnt away, he attains oneness with Brahman;
for he enjoys all desires together with that All-knowing One.
In that way, the self of the master of yoga attains identity with the Supreme Self—both sālokya, sārūpya, and eternal sāyujya. ||96||
And by the power of compassion, he indeed attains equality with me and other such lordly powers, while constantly uttering "Om"—the one supreme Brahman—and remembering me. (97)
O King Alarka, having abandoned his dilapidated home, he went to my abode; having attained constant refuge in me, he acquired supreme knowledge. 98.
Know that through my grace those faults have been destroyed;
there shall be no further bondage for you, and may you always partake in Nirvana.
Merging yourself with the Self, which is Brahman, eternal bliss, and the abode of happiness, become one who possesses perpetual bliss by uniting with the Supreme Brahman.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Alarka’s Liberation through the Possession of Knowledge and Yoga Bestowed by Dattātreya," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having thus received these auspicious blessings and experiencing his own nature as Brahman within himself, Alarka spoke to the Lord Hari, his spiritual preceptor.
O Blessed One, I desire to hear in every way about the conduct of a yogin; by what distinctive marks is one recognized as following the path of Brahman? (2)
The Guru said: "Listen, O Lord of the Earth! His modes of conduct are indeed contrary to worldly behavior; they are boundless and unimpeded. (3)
These two—honor and dishonor—which cause joy and agitation to men, are the very opposites for a yogi; to him, they are poison and nectar respectively.
He generally resorts to silence while repeatedly chanting the name of Hari;
desiring solitude, he should not go to functions such as welcoming guests, sacrifices, or pilgrimages.
When the people have all finished eating, when the fire has subsided and the embers are scattered,
he should wander for the sake of the pilgrimage of the gods, content with whatever is obtained by chance.
Or rather, having indeed adopted the lifestyle of a python (ajagarī-vṛtti),
he should subsist on whatever fruits, roots, leaves, bulbs, or grains he may happen to obtain from a householder.
Having entrusted that [work] to the gods, one should employ it without defiling the path of the virtuous;
one should take from it only what is essential according to need, and never anything more.

The staff of speech, the staff of action, and the staff of mind—these three are his who has them fully restrained; he shall be a true bearer of the triple-staff (tridaṇḍin), the supreme king of yogis.
Constantly engaged in yoga upon the form of Kṛṣṇa and muttering "Kṛṣṇa," he remains eternally immersed, upholding the highest state of existence.
One should practice the chanting of the Lord’s name with a loud voice;
for the lord of yogis, intent upon that, shall attain absorption into the Blessed One. 11.
Just as the moonstone releases water through contact with the rays of the moon, yet does so without being prompted by anyone else—that is remembered as the simile for the yogin. 12.
Just as the sun-gem produces fire through contact with the rays of the sun,
and not by itself— this is recorded as the analogy for the yogin.
Ants, mice, rats, house-lizards, and francolin partridges dwell in a house just like their master; when it is destroyed, they depart from there to another place.
Just as there is indeed no suffering for those [servants] when the master’s house is destroyed, so too should the yogi be, truly unenveloped by suffering. 15.
Just as an anthill insect builds up a mound of earth with its tiny mouth, so too should one cultivate yoga.
Just as leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, along with the trees themselves, are plundered by beasts, birds, humans, and others, so too must everything be plundered by the yogin. 17.
And observing the tip of the horn of a young ruru deer as it grows,
the yogi increases in yoga and then attains perfection.
That house is where one dwells; that is food by which one lives;
and that wealth is by which one prospers—this is happiness; what attachment can there be to these?
Whether food is sweet or not sweet, pungent, alkaline, or bitter, the yogi does not experience it; even though he knows it, he does not speak of it.
He has indeed completely conquered the tongue, taste, and flavor—whether soft or hard, dry or mild, oily, rough, or coarse. (21)
Knowing that [the fire] is sharp and burning, yet not being joined with suffering, he has completely conquered this skin and its pleasant touch. (22)
Sweet, auspicious, and melodious, the song was delightful and soft;
it brought forth jesting and laughter, as well as provoking anger and bestowing honor. (23)
Having understood the sound, he indeed does not perceive pleasure or pain therein; he has completely mastered both the speech and its meaning. (24)
It may be beautiful, well-constructed, like gold, full of brilliance, auspicious, white, variegated, or otherwise smooth or even sharp. ||25||
Having seen a form, he who does not conceive of pleasure or pain in his mind has completely conquered form; such a one is a king among yogis, with his eye fixed on the visible. (26)
Upon encountering a pleasant fragrance, the nose does not expand;
upon encountering a foul odor, the nostrils do not contract. (27)
That yogi has naturally conquered both odor and the sense of smell;
even when a pungent smell is encountered, or if there is some agitation in the skin.
He does not even touch his ears, nor does he conquer his skin;
yet with his feet he goes to the abode of Hari and performs circumambulation.
Victorious in his conduct, he undertakes pilgrimages and virtuous journeys;
with both hands, he should perform service to the gods, his preceptor, and the virtuous.
One should perform the vocal glorification of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; one should dance before the Lord and engage in sacred discourse with the virtuous. (3.1)
He performs song for his devotees, meditation upon the forms,
and indeed carries out contemplation, salutation, and hymn of praise toward the Supreme Self.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa here and there, she bows down, laughs, and calls out in every direction, manifesting her joy.
In one place he becomes invisible; in another he dwells among the trees;
in some places he is in a body of water, and in others he is even on the battlefield. ||34||
In some places, in deep pits or among thorns and the like; in some places, in market-towns, cities, villages, and so forth; and in forests, wildernesses, and desolate regions. (35)
Whether on a spot of ground conceived by the mind, or even upon the surface of the sky,
one dwells indeed as one desires and according to one's very resolve.
Sometimes holding a piece of stone in her mouth, she eats it as if it were a sweet;
she also throws collyrium, mud, or dust upon her body.
Thinking sandalwood to be cool, one desires to take it again and again; yet an object that is inaccessible and situated in a distant land cannot be held in the hand. (38)
And he describes, exactly as it happened, an event occurring in another land within the assembly of people, just like Satīśa in some instances. (39)
Sometimes he sleeps on the roads, sometimes he leaps among the people;
even among animals, free from anxiety, he sleeps like one intoxicated, as if possessed by fear.
With his limbs greyed by dust, he rejoices in his mind at times;
sometimes he goes about naked, and sometimes even with leaves for clothing.
In some places he was clothed only in tree-bark, and in others indeed in ashes;
sometimes amidst torrents of rain, and sometimes amidst the fires of the sun's heat.
In some places he stays by shrines, water, or mud;
in some places his limbs are smeared with filth and the like, while in others his body is clean. ||43||

In some places there is the foul odor of urine and the like; in others, the merciless spitting and such; in others, [the smell] clinging to the nostrils; and in others, the lack of bodily cleansing. ||44||
Delighting in the self, like the very nature of Brahman, possessing a divine form, moving about without obstruction, he shines as both man and woman. ||45||
Fearless among beasts, birds, grass, creepers, thorns, and the like,
he is endowed with the realization of Hari, yet remains free from the perception of a physical body and so forth.
That which must not be forgotten and that which must not be abandoned here—one who possesses attentiveness neither abandons nor forgets it. (47)
Sometimes he behaves like a child, and at other times like an old man;
sometimes he acts like a crow, a crane, a cat, or an owl.
In some cases he abides in love like a peacock, a parrot, or a swan; in some cases he follows the "bee-like" mode of life, and in some cases the "monkey-like" mode. (49)
In some places he lives adopting the behavior of a lion, in some that of a wretched beggar, in some that of a hawk, and likewise in some that of a fish.
For that yogi of Brahman, the passing of days occurs with his mind fixed on Śrī Hari in one state, and devoid of mind in another. 51.
In some instances of mental worship, Dhruva feeds Hari;
having offered water and performed obeisance, he dismisses Him with a gesture.
At other times, having fashioned a couch out of dust, he establishes the Lord there.
A leaf, a flower, a petal, a blade, a fruit, or even a grain of rice or a blade of grass. ||53||
Having offered tulasī and lotuses, he sometimes delights Hari;
such is the conduct of the yogin, free from all constraint. (54)
Divine, possessing a divine nature, and initiating a divine course;
composed entirely of divine reality, she bestows the supreme good upon all. ||55||
A yogi who is always like a mad dog indeed knows another yogi;
Sanaka and others, Ṛṣabha and others, as well as Śuka and others, became just so.
The Siddhas, Nāthas, Tīrthakaras, Haṃsas, Aghoravartanas, Sādhakas, Yogins, others, as well as the Jaḍas, Bhairavas, and so forth—[all these are included]. ||57||
Śaṅkara, the circle of Yoginīs, and likewise other Avadhūtas; the Satyas, the Sādhvīs, the Dāsīs, and the Vaiṣṇavīs who have attained meditative absorption. ||58||
They indeed attained the supreme Brahman, their actions being unlike those of the world;
what more need be said here? For the yogi, emboldened by yoga, [attains this] through speech alone.
Within his heart, he perceives nothing else whatsoever apart from Brahman;
for him, the Self exists everywhere, and in whom the abode of the Universal Self resides.
Just as a thread remains within a jewel and a jewel within a thread,
so too he who has attained stability therein has attained the most perfect bliss, being filled with that intoxication.
Who is capable of scrutinizing the equanimity of that yogi, who remains active and alert in his movements yet is wise and composed in his intellect? (62)
In speech he conducts himself as a virtuous man, for in his conduct he is indeed peaceful;
in his heart he conducts himself as one who is contented, and in his body he conducts himself as one free from fear.
The fool functions through the qualities (guṇas); the affectionate one functions with the mouth;
the passionate one functions in Brahman; the angry one functions in the illusory (māyika). 64.
The greedy man behaves with cruelty in solitude, yet he behaves with compassion among people;
and in the rites for the gods, the ancestors, and the yoga of Hari, he behaves with faith.
In the matter of bodily functions, he is indeed distracted; but in his own true work, he is possessed of a steady mind;
and regarding the supreme beatitude, he proceeds endowed with all his strength.
In worldly transaction this [yogi] is diverse, yet toward the Supreme Lord he possesses consciousness;
endowed with such characteristics, the yogi should conduct himself at all times. (67)
In some places he displays many and manifold wonders within himself; in other places, like a forest-dweller, he exhibits sheer folly. (68)
Having recognized such a person who repeatedly displays various activities,
one should know him to be a great lord of yoga, whose very nature is Brahman.
Now, having recognized the signs for himself, the yogi abandons the body;
listen, I shall describe the portents so that, at the time of departure, he does not fall into the state of existence.
He who does not see with his own eyes the path of the gods, Dhruva, Śukra, the shadow of the moon, and Arundhatī— for him, death is within a year.
He who sees with his own eyes the orb of the sun devoid of rays, or fire accompanied by rays, will face death within a year.
If one sees urine and feces as equal in value to gold,
even in a dream, he shall live for ten months.
Having seen pretas, piśācas, and the like, as well as cities of the gandharvas and trees with golden foliage, he lives for nine months.

If one who was stout suddenly becomes emaciated, or one who was emaciated suddenly becomes stout, repeatedly and without cause, and experiences dizziness in the head due to wind (vāyu), his lifespan is only eight months. (75)
If, upon placing his foot on the ground, his heel is broken against a serpent’s hood, or if he is covered by dust, mud, or soil, he shall live for seven months. (76)
If a vulture, a dove, a raven, a crow, a carnivorous bird, or a blue bird alights upon one's head, it indicates that one has six months of life remaining.
If one is struck by a flight of crows or by a shower of dust in a dream, or if one sees one's own shadow distorted, such a person lives for four or five [days]. ||78||
One who sees lightning in a cloudless sky will go abroad to the south;
one who sees Indra’s bow at night shall live for two months.
He who sees his own body without a head in ghee, oil, a mirror, or water,
does not live beyond a month.
He whose body has a smell like that of a goat or even like a corpse,
his life should indeed be known to last for only half a month.
But he whose heart, hands, and feet become parched and whose throat dries up immediately after bathing survives for ten days.
If, by the force of his breath, a fracture of the staff occurs, then Death has arrived; he will surely die within a moment. ||83||
If one travels toward the southern direction while standing upon a vehicle drawn by bears, monkeys, goats, camels, donkeys, jackals, or similar animals, he will die.
If a woman wearing red and black garments leads a man toward the southern direction while singing and laughing in a dream, he shall not live.
Upon seeing a naked ascetic, or a Rākṣasa, or even Kāla himself laughing and leaping about, one should contemplate death. (86)
One who perceives oneself as entirely submerged in mud will die; likewise, one who sees fire in their hair, a serpent, ashes, or a dried-up river [will meet the same fate]. (87)
Having seen [this] in a dream, one will die within ten days; of this there is no doubt—[being struck] by terrifying men with weapons and the like, or with stones and the like.
Even he who has killed or struck him will die, there is no doubt;
for one whose teeth have become fixed, death will occur, there is no doubt. (89)
If at sunrise a jackal approaches someone from the front,
whether moving in its natural direction or the opposite, that person meets with immediate death.
He who, immediately after eating, is again oppressed by hunger, and who does not perceive the scent of a lamp, has reached the end of his life; of this there is no doubt.
One does not see one's own reflection in the eyes of another;
at night one sees Indra’s weapon (the rainbow), and by day one beholds the planets. 92.
He whose nose is crooked and whose ears are sunken or protruding, and whose left eye constantly weeps—for him there is no life at all. 93.
The face becomes red, the tongue dark, and the teeth black;
there is no sound heard from the ears, and likewise, the light of the eyes fades away. (94)
For one who has gone to a pit and whose opening is closed by stones, death occurs a moment later, as does that of one who is placed in fire in a dream. 95.
Death arrives through entering water or being struck by spirits;
there is also a reversal of one's natural disposition and a transformation of one's fundamental nature. (96)
Receiving honor, criticism, contempt, and so forth, are considered forms of death;
therefore, on that day, one should practice yoga for the destruction of death. (97)
Or rather, one should yoke the self to Brahman and certainly not remember anything else;
united with that Kṛṣṇa, he goes to that supreme state. (98)
This is absolute liberation, for that is indeed the absolute end of death;
and that is the fruit of the practice of yoga: the worship of the feet of Hari in the Imperishable.
His birth is meaningful, and likewise his death is meaningful;
his exercise of kingship is meaningful, for he has attained the feet of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard the word "Alarka," he bowed at the feet of his guru;
indeed, in that very hour of midnight, he attained both knowledge and yoga.
The blessed Dattātreya, having been repeatedly honored and saluted,
spoke with great satisfaction, his body covered in horripilation.
By good fortune, he who came here for your sake— having been threatened by the vast army of the Lord of Kāśī— is now within my reach through association with you.
Blessed is my brother Subāhu, by whom he has been well-established in knowledge;
and by good fortune, I have likewise read the letter sent by my mother.
By good fortune, I have thus served the pair of your feet;
by good fortune, all your words are firmly established in my heart.
By good fortune, knowledge has arisen in me through my meeting with you, O holy one;
by good fortune, compassion has been shown toward me by your blessed self.
Thus, through your grace, my fires of "I" and "mine" have been utterly consumed;
I shall indeed strive to proceed toward the abode of Brahman by renouncing the conduct of kingship.
Then Dattātreya said to his disciple: "Go, may you be happy;
conduct yourself for the sake of liberation, free from possessiveness and free from ego."
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to him and went home at nightfall,
to where the king, the lord of Kāśī, as well as his elder brother Subāhu, were.
Having gone there, he said: "Enjoy this powerful kingdom;
or, as it pleases you, bestow it upon Subāhu."
Then the King of Kāśī said, "Why was the battle abandoned midway?
Alarka replied, "My knots have been destroyed by my preceptor. (111)
By the grace of Dattātreya, the sense of duality was dispelled;
having fixed the mind upon Brahman, supreme victory is won in its conquest. 11.2
Subāhu said: "That purpose for which I came to fight you has been entirely achieved by me; I have no further need for the kingdom. (11.3)
The King of Kāśī spoke thus for the sake of knowledge and dispassion:
"O Alarka, I have declared war against you for the purpose of your liberation."
Therefore, that knowledge and dispassion have arisen within me; I am departing. My own kin, relatives, and friends are being neglected as they sink into despair.
He is not called one's own kin or the like; rather, he should be regarded as such by people.
Indeed, the company of the virtuous is said by you to be the mother that bestows fruit.
"O King, you should strive for your own welfare by attaining the knowledge born from that [instruction].
Having spoken thus and performed a festival, the King of Kāśī departed from there.

Subāhu, having achieved his purpose, returned once more to his own forest; but Alarka, having emerged [from the water], sang this verse: 1.18. Subāhu, having accomplished his goal, went back to his own forest; but Alarka, having emerged, sang this song.
"Alas, what a wretched kingdom I have governed out of pride! Through the grace of my guru, I have attained realization; there is no happiness higher than yoga. (11.9)
Having spoken thus and consecrating his own son as the lord of men,
he departed for the forest, having abandoned all attachments, for the sake of liberation.
Then, after a long time, he attained the nirvāṇa of Brahman;
by hearing and reciting this, one shall attain union with Brahman (brahmasāyujya). || 121 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct of Liberation, the Signs of Death for Yogis, and the Forest Dwelling of Alarka," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Long ago in the Age of the Gods (Devayuga), O Lakṣmī, the most excellent sage Nārada went to the peak of Mount Sumeru and beheld the abode of the Creator.
To the north of that [tree] is a divine pavilion beneath a Pippala tree,
adorned with thousands of pillars made of ruby gems.
It was adorned with auspicious svastika symbols, beautified by divine archways,
featuring great gates of topaz and seven-storied gate-towers.
Having entered, he beheld within a celestial pavilion made of pearls;
in its center was an altar, adorned there with eight lofty pillars.
And in the center of that was a lion-throne with a thousand-petaled lotus; upon it sat one of beautiful form, having the appearance of a man.
He beheld Puruṣottama, who had four arms, was white in complexion, and had the face of a boar; he held a conch, a discus, and displayed the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
The god who wears yellow garments, whose eyes are as long as lotuses, whose face is as pleasant as the full moon, and whose radiance is brilliant with a crown; (7)
He whose voice is the Sāman chant, whose form is the sacrifice, whose snout is the *sruk* ladle, and whose nose is the *sruva* ladle;
he who is resplendent with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest and adorned with the shining sacrificial thread (*yajñasūtra*).
Hari, who shines with the splendor of the Kaustubha gem, adorned with golden ornaments, and radiant with bracelets, armlets, bangles, and earrings; (9)
Having offered praise to him, Nārada stood in the presence of the Lord;
in the meantime, O Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī arrived there as well.
Accompanied by her two friends, Ilā and Piṅgalā,
that young woman, joined by her companions, was enriched with the splendor of all her ornaments.
She bowed at the feet of Śrī Hari, scattering many fragrant flowers upon his head, and remained standing with her palms joined in reverence.
Śrī Varāha, having embraced that goddess and placed her upon his lap, inquired after her welfare as well as the reason for her arrival.
The Earth said: "O Blessed One, by your grace all is well with me;
indeed, I have heard this from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa reclining upon Śeṣa. (14)
O Mādhava, I desire to behold that great sacred site on earth where Vedavatī formerly dwelt by the will of Lakṣmī. (15)
Having heard that, Nārada said: "O Vasuṃdharā, that is indeed true;
for I heard this very thing in the assembly of sages regarding Truth. (16)
Having spoken thus and bowed to Hari, Nārada went to Badarī.
Dharaṇī said: "O Blessed One, show me that place;
if you have compassion for me, I wish to behold the Padminī."
Saying "So be it" to her, Varāha called to mind the bird.
Vainateya arrived before him with his divine body;
likewise, the Lord Vārāha himself had previously lifted the earth along with it.
He mounted Garuḍa and proceeded to Janisthala;
there he beheld Padminī, the daughter of Viyadrāja, who was like a shadow.
Having beheld Nārāyaṇapura, he went to Nārāyaṇācala,
where there is the mountain Śeṣācala, which is supremely purifying.
There is Aruṇādri, also known as Hastiśaila, and the river Suvarṇamukharī;
and on its northern bank is the lake named Kamala. 22.
On its bank sits the Lord Hari, the granter of boons to Śuka;
on the northern side of the lake, he is adorned with yellow sandalwood trees. ||23||
The mountain named Śrī Veṅkaṭācala is the abode of Vāsudeva;
the hill extends for two yojanas and rises half a yojana in height.
The hosts of deities beginning with Indra, the lords of sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, the Siddhas, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vaiṣṇavas who are dear to the Lord. ||25||
Hosts of apsarases, such as Rambhā and others, always dwell there with self-restraint;
likewise, nāgas, garuḍas, kinnaras, and others perform ascetic penance. (26)
O Lakṣmī, on Mount Nārāyaṇa is the auspicious Svāmipuṣkariṇī;
on its western bank resides Vārāha together with Dharaṇī.
Having descended from Garuḍa, Hari made his dwelling there;
Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Universe, resides on its southern bank. ||28||
O lotus-born one, I dwell there together with Śrībhūmi;
in the Kṛta age it was called Añjanādri, and in the Tretā age they called it Nārāyaṇagiri.
In the Dvāpara age they call it Siṃhaśaila, and in the Kali age, O gods, they speak of that mountain as Śrī Veṅkaṭācala, the abode of the Supreme Self.
On the western bank of Svāmipuṣkariṇī, honored by the world,
he dwells with the face of a boar on Śeṣādri, at Vṛṣabhācala.
Having found rest there on Nārāyaṇagiri,
the Earth, accompanied by her companions, [beheld] the Lord in the form of a boar.
Beholding the shadow of Lakṣmī, she asked with supreme affection:
"Is Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of the Universe, present on the great mountain named Veṅkaṭa? (23)
"When will the Lord Śrī Varāha, accompanied by Śrī Bhūmi, come within the range of my vision? O beloved, listen to the account of what occurred in the past. (24)
Formerly, in the Kṛta age, having beheld the great austerity of Vāyu here,
the Lord Śrīnivāsa indeed arrived accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
On this most meritorious southern bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī,
Hari, who brings delight to Vāyu, resides in the celestial chariot named Ānanda.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is Vaikuṇṭha, remains invisible within this celestial chariot until the end of the kalpa. ||37||
Dharaṇī asked, "When and how might Kṛṣṇa be seen?
If you have the inclination, O Agastya, king of sages, you should entreat him."
"Then the Lord of Śrī would become an object for the eyes of everyone.
Having heard this, Dharā called Agastya to mind, and he too arrived.
Having propitiated the Supreme Soul and pleased him again and again, you requested for the sake of the world's welfare: "May You become visible. (1.398.40)
Thus addressed, the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, that abode of compassion, indeed became visible to the eyes of them all. 41.
Having beheld that sight, the sage departed for his own hermitage filled with joy;
yet the celestial chariot remained present, though it was never seen again.
Thereafter, the four-armed Lord remained constantly visible;
having beheld him, the Earth felt her purpose was fulfilled. (43)
Then, born of the Lunar dynasty, the great chariot-warrior Mitravarmā became the king in Nārāyaṇapura within the district of Tuṇḍīra.
While Mitravarmā ruled the world of mortals with righteousness,
the earth yielded crops without being ploughed and was endowed with all kinds of grain.
All the people became free from disease and were filled with devotion;
his wife was the charming Pāṇḍya princess Manoramā.

He said, "Daughter, what is dear to you? Tell me so that I may do it.

That which is delightful to the eyes in this world, pleasing to the minds of the virtuous, the brilliance of even all briliancies, and the deity even of the gods. (1.399.60)
It is attainable here by the virtuous devotees, but never by those who are not devotees;

Those who bear the name of Śrī Hari on their tongues, the image of Hari in their hearts, who are devoted to worship and recitation, who speak the truth, and who are free from malice; ||64||

Those who always associate with the virtuous and are ever-peaceful are proclaimed as Vaiṣṇavas;

O Mother, from birth itself my mind has longed for the attainment of Him;

While the earth was being investigated in this manner, all the female servants gathered there and, filled with anxiety, asked about her whereabouts. (71)
"How does that which consists of reflection exist? Tell us so that we may bring about what is beneficial and pleasant.

Once, having mounted a horse as white as a swan and swift as thought,

Having seen a certain elephant in the forest, he then leaped onto its back;

There in the forest, he was performing austerities and worshiping Janārdana—
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa together with Śrī and Bhūmi— with devotion.
Having dismounted from his horse, Narāyaṇa, appearing in the form of a king, beheld King Śaṅkha on the shore of the lake of the Śaṅkha serpent. (78)
He asked, "Tell me, what is being done here in the forest of Veṅkaṭādri?
Then Śaṅkha said to Viṣṇu, "I am born in the Haihaya country. (79)
I am the king of Śvetanṛpati; for the propitiation of Mahāviṣṇu, I have repeatedly performed all sacrifices in order to behold Hari.

consequently, I became despondent, whereupon the Sarasvatī of the sky [spoke]. (81)
Śāntidā said, "O King, you have not attained my vision here;
go to Nārāyaṇagiri, perform penance, and perform recitation. (82)
"By propitiating me there, you will obtain my vision;

"By acting according to the method thus described, you shall indeed attain supreme liberation. Having been told this, I abandoned that region and came to Vaikuṇṭha. (84)
In the forest, I constantly worship Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, I adore Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa together with Śrī and Bhūmi.

having bowed down to Viṣvaksena, who is seated at the foot of the banyan tree. (87)
Having gone to Svāmipuṣkariṇī and bathed,

for there, in that very place, Hari known as Śvetavarāha wanders.
"You shall see him somewhere in an anthill by the power of your merit," having thus instructed Śveta, he reached the Araṇī river.
When Hari, having dismounted from his horse, was wandering along the bank,

and then that lord gazed upon the elephant and his companions.

Seeing her, Hari’s mind became attached to that lotus pond;

Having been insulted by you with force, that Viyadrāja,
upon hearing this, immediately mounted his horse and went to the Venkata mountain.
Sent by her very self, I, the maidservant Bakulamālikā, am going to the earth with beautiful maidens to obtain Padminī for Hari. (96)
Having spoken thus, that maidservant of Kṛṣṇa approached you and indeed requested your daughter for Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (97)
"O Mother, having reflected with Viyat and the others, do what is appropriate;
for there is indeed a worthy gift to be given to this most worthy Supreme Self. (98)
The lotus-like Ramā should be given to Rāma, who has eyes like lotuses;

"Divine women must certainly be given to the divine Lord as his devotees.

Through Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my longing has been fulfilled; today grace has been bestowed, and my heart's desire is complete—surely it shall be so for others as well. (102)

"This incomparable daughter of yours shall sport together with Śrī."
Let this spring, endowed with splendor, be offered to the Supreme Lord who dwells on the Veṅkaṭa mountain; may auspiciousness be swiftly ordained.

Having examined the birth [ascendant] as being in Mṛgaśīrṣa for Kanyā and the asterism Śravaṇa for the deity, the Guru declared the lagna accordingly. || 106 ||
Uttaraphalgunī is approved for the increase of happiness for those two;

"Having received your command once more, we shall become full of enthusiasm.

"O Lord Keśava, show favor to me and to Padminī as well.

Rivers, streams, and oceans; heaven, the netherworld, and the earths;

The second great and meritorious region of heaven, consisting of delusion,
