Thus ends the three hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sending of Bakulamālikā by the Blessed Śrīnivāsa to Padminī, Sītā’s Shadow Vedavatī Being Born as Padminī, Bakulamālikā Going to the Subterranean Dwelling of Dharaṇī, the Signs Indicating Padminī’s Status as a Wife of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Decision that She Should Be Given to Nārāyaṇa, the Sending of the Marriage Proclamation, and the Commencement of Wedding Preparations," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of devoted wives.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī: Śrīnivāsa, having summoned his beloved Śrī, Lakṣmī, as well as her other female companions on the Veṅkaṭa mountain, spoke to them.
"Tell me, Lakṣmī, what must be done? O Śrī, [command] your circle of female friends as well; give orders for everything that is required for the sake of the wedding. (2)
"Let all of you, gathered together, perform what is auspicious, such as providing encouragement.
Having heard Kṛṣṇa's words, Lakṣmī summoned all her female companions.
The friend Prīti, commanded by Śrī, took fragrant oil;
the friend Śruti arrived bringing silken garments. || 4 ||
Smṛti stood before her, having taken up her companions and ornaments;
Dhṛti held a brilliantly shining divine mirror. || 5 ||
Then Śānti held the excellent musk of a fragrant deer as her companion;
and the companion Hrī stood before her, holding yakṣakardama.
Kīrti held a golden fillet adorned with jewels,
while Indrāṇī held a parasol and Sarasvatī held a fly-whisk.
Gaurī held the fly-whisk, while Vijayā and Jayā held the fans;
then the Lord was consecrated with a ritual bath by Śrī, becoming the illustrious Parameśvara.
Taking fragrant oil, the maidens anointed the god,
and having rubbed his body with scented powders, they wiped it clean.
Taking up each of the hundred golden water-pitchers that had been brought by the elephants, Ramā and the others consecrated him.
Having perfumed her hair with incense and having groomed it with a comb,
Śrī bound her curls, which were beautifully radiant at their tips.
Having smeared her limbs with fragrant yellow-colored paste,
she put on yellow garments and fastened a beautiful golden girdle around her waist.
Indirā adorned her with ornaments and garlands of flowers;
and Dhṛti presented a mirror, the source of auspiciousness.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra);
thus adorned with ornaments, the Blessed One himself shone resplendent.
Then the lords arrived as guests at the house of Kṛṣṇa:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, Virāṭ, and the lord Sadāśiva.
Bhūman, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vāsudeva and the others, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the guardians of the worlds and so forth. || 16 ||
The ancestors, the sages, the gods, the seers, the guardians of the directions, the planets beginning with the Sun, as well as the Vasus and the treasures; || 16 ||

The guardians of the quarters, the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the Manus, Vāsava and the others, the lunar mansions, the principles (tattvas), the qualities (guṇas), and likewise the Maruts; || 18 ||

The Vālakhilyas, the Kalās, the rivers, the streams, the sacred fords, the mountains, the oceans, as well as the moats, the shrines, and the elements beginning with earth, and the trees and so forth; || 19 ||
The subterranean fire, the wind, the clouds, nights, days, and so forth—
both the insentient and the sentient— are pervaded by Nārāyaṇa’s seal.
On Mount Veṅkaṭādri, millions and billions of great beings assembled:
Satyas, Detyas, Muktānyas, Īśānyas, and the wives of the gods. (21)
The human women born of Kaśyapa, the mothers of the three worlds, arrived at Śrīnivāsādri by means of celestial chariots, elephants, and swans. 22.

By means of horses, lions, and the best of birds, as well as through yogic breath-control (kuṃbhaka), the virtuous, the saintly, the steadfast, the devotees of Viṣṇu, and those free from passion [attain their goal]. || 23 ||
Sannyāsins, excellent celibates, and renunciants arrived; likewise, twenty-four in number came even to the celestial mansion. (24)
The Puruṣas consist of the principles (tattvas), as do the divine beings beginning with Earth; likewise, there are creepers, rivers, great plateaus, lands, the heavens, and excellent forms. (25)
The gods and goddesses arrived together, full of eagerness and longing for a vision [of him];
they were provided with food, honor, lodging, drink, and comfortable seats. ||26||
Both parties performed the giving of appropriate honors;
auspicious ceremonies took place there on Mount Veṅkaṭa, which was like a celestial palace.
They arrive at the wedding of Śrī Padminī and Śrīnivāsa;
Hari, Kṛṣṇa, having mounted Garuḍa, is accompanied by Śrī Lakṣmī.
He is served by Brahmā, Śiva, Vajrin, Varuṇa, Yama, and Yakṣeśa, as well as by the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha, and by yogis such as Sanaka and others. ||29||
He was magnified by the devotees of the Lord, the virtuous ones such as Nārada, Sanaka, and others,
as well as by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, and Hiraṇyagarbha.
Adorned by the lords, Viṣṇu went to the city of Nārāyaṇa;
the Gandharvas sang his glory and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The celestial drums resounded and the divine damsels sang songs;
the women were filled with wonder, and the forest deities beheld him.
The birds scattered flowers over the forests and sang of victory;
the sages followed along, chanting hymns of auspiciousness.
The Lord was accompanied by hosts of gods, his disciples, and his attendants such as Viṣvaksena, as well as by female companions seated upon chariots, elephants, and vehicles. ||34||
Accompanied by all those who possessed great majesty, numbering in the tens of millions and more,
the excellent one reached the well-adorned city of Viyadrāja.
In the outer garden of the city, which extended for many yojanas and was completely pervaded by the path of the sky, the glorious Blessed One stayed for a moment.
According to worldly custom,
the lotus-lake, mounted upon the elephant, went around the city in circumambulation and returned to the gateway.
She remained standing, intent on awaiting the Lord face-to-face;

The Lotus-born [Brahmā] then kindled the Āhavanīya fire, while verses of benediction and auspicious hymns were being sung. 47.
Having adorned Padminī with garments, ornaments, and necklaces obtained through the boon,

Then they both engaged in swallowing each other's morsels, as well as playing with a golden ring in the water of the arena. (51)
Then they also threw clusters of flowers at one another,

There, surrounded by auspicious Brahmins who were well-versed in the Vedas and possessed of true passion,

Then the bride’s party gave the dowry into the hand of the bride, while the groom’s party gave much gold and wealth into the hand of the groom. (55)
And jewels, gems, necklaces, pearls, and ornaments;

They gave divine objects such as fragrant substances and the Brahmavallī creeper;

Having performed the marriage rites up to the end of the *lājā-homa* (the oblation of parched grain),

On the fourth day, the Four-faced One completed everything:
King Viyat’s ever-new and eternally fresh meal of cooked food.
With true devotion, he caused [the temple] to be built for the Vaiṣṇavas, who were dearer to him than his own life;
and for each of their bodies, whatever food was naturally produced, that he provided.
Having given them various things in such a manner, he caused them to attain supreme satisfaction; he also served diverse drinks, both sweet and sour. ||62||
Likewise, he gave betel and other means for cleansing the mouth;

The monkeys numbered in the millions, as well as celestial sages, hermits, and humans—gods and goddesses alike—were delighted by the male and female servants and attendants. (64)
Then Brahmā, having obtained the permission of Viyadrāja as well as Dharā,
placed Hari, together with Śrī Lakṣmī and Padminī, upon Garuḍa.
Then, accompanied by Mahīmāna, Viyadrāja, Dharaṇī, and Vasudāna, he proceeded to go toward the eyes [of the Lord]. 66.
Thus, for a moment, they became filled with tears born of separation from their daughter;

Having said, "You must come," and having embraced her to her chest, she then departed again on Garuḍa; at that moment, there arose a cry of victory.
There was a great sound of musical instruments, as the bards, heralds, and panegyrists uttered cries of victory; and the kettledrums resounded in the sky.
Thus Varātikā went to Śrī Veṅkaṭācala for Viṣṇu;
they all rested at home, refreshed by water and food.
Then, desiring to depart, Śuka and the other hosts of sages, as well as the groups of deities headed by Brahmā, praised Puruṣottama.
And a magnificent golden throne sent by King Viyat,
as well as grains of rice from a golden granary, were sent for the pleasure of the two sons of Viṣṇu.
Many bowls of mung beans and tens of thousands of jars of ghee, as well as divine fruits such as mangoes, plantains, and coconuts. ||73||
Emblic myrobalans, pumpkins, and plantains;
boxes of sugar, jewels, pearls, and likewise cows by the millions.
There were horses as white as swans or the moon, four-tusked elephants, and many women from the inner apartments as well as numerous female attendants. (75)
Whatever was mentally resolved by him in this pavilion after the giving away of the daughter—
all that was sent by him at that very moment.
With his heart, he always sought the favor of Hari—service at His feet and devotion—and nothing else, such as worldly happiness or the like. (77)
And those guests who belonged to the bride's party were fed and honored;
then, with the permission of King Viyadrāja, they returned once more to their own worlds.
Then the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha, having indeed worshipped the gods and others, and having honored the supreme lords, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Bhūman; 79.
He then granted permission for Virāṭ and the other ṛṣis, the ancestors, and human beings—both sentient and insentient—to go to their own respective worlds; and so they departed.
Having bowed to Hari, all the male and female servants departed;
for all creations sing the glory of the Blessed One and the good fortune of the lotus-born Lakṣmī. 8.1.
That shadow which was Vedavatī indeed attended upon Sītā;
though she was not lotus-born, she became lotus-born, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (82)
Those who practice devotion by surrendering their very lives are born as lotuses; for the devotees of Kṛṣṇa are indeed eternal. ||83||
When they had all departed, the Blessed Lord, ever endowed with the splendor of Padminī, along with Lakṣmī and Ramā, continued to enjoy himself. 84.
And Kṛṣṇa always resides on the bank of the Svāmipuṣkariṇī on the Veṅkaṭa mountain; at times, he is also present in person within the divine temple.
In some places the Lord was accompanied by Padminī; in some places the Master was accompanied by Śrī; and in some places he was accompanied by Lakṣmī and Ramā. ||86||
In some places on Mount Veṅkaṭa, the Blessed Lord Hari, Svāminārāyaṇa, indeed sports with Bakulamālikā and others. (87)
All those wives were devoted to their husbands and always dedicated to the Blessed One; they served Kṛṣṇa with their hearts, their bodies, and their actions. (88)
The lotus-lake, having obtained you as her lord who dwells within the lotuses, serves you;
rising early every morning, she constantly attends upon Kṛṣṇa.
She performs the massaging of his feet and the rubbing of his limbs,
and she truly pleases Śrīnivāsa on the bed through her service.
He indeed gave her embraces and kisses at will, granting whatever his beloved desired;
then, rising from the bed, he washed his hands and face. (91)
He indeed makes the water warm for the sake of purifying the Lord’s bath;
having bathed, he offers pure water for the purification of his own hands and face.
Having given a moist tooth-stick, fresh and liquid milk-rice (pāyasa), and fragrant powder, he gives a water-pot. ||93||
Having performed his purification and other rites, and having washed his hands with clay,
Hari rinsed out his mouth and bathed upon a golden slab.
The lotus-like Padminī ground fragrant powders upon the limbs of Śrī Hari, as well as sesame paste, the essence of flowers, scented oils, and so forth. (95)

In the lunar dynasty, there was a son of King Nanda named Dharmagupta,
who was devoted to righteousness and dedicated to statesmanship.
He worshipped with various kinds of sacrifices and gave gifts manifold;
the subjects were devoted to righteousness, and the women were devoted to their husbands.
Then once, having mounted his horse, Dharmagupta went to the forest;
while he was pursuing the hunt, night fell, and he then [took shelter] under a tree.
Having climbed up, the bear who had arrived there rested;
pursued by the lion, that bear then climbed a tree.
Seeing the king, trembling with the fear of death, he said:
"O lord of men, do not be afraid; we two shall dwell here for the night. (23)
A terrifying lion has arrived here at the foot of this tree;
enjoy sleep for half the night, being protected by me and remaining at ease. (24)
"Therefore, O excellent protector, protect me while I am fast asleep for half the night.
Having heard this, when Dharmagupta had fallen asleep, the monkey spoke to the bear.
"We are all forest-dwellers, four-footed beings, not human beings. Why should we concern ourselves with a human? Let this king be abandoned by me. (26)
"Let that which will become my full meal be offered up.
Then the bear spoke to the lion in words consistent with dharma and excellent policy: ||27||
In this world, those who betray trust are considered to face a great downfall;
[even] men, animals, insects, birds, children, and women [are subject to it]. (28)
Wild animals as well as those from the village and the forest dwell with confidence;
they live trusting in their refuge, so being four-footed is not the cause [of fear]. 29.
Whether it be my status as a biped, or my possession of wings, or even my livelihood based on trust—trust indeed is the supreme dharma; how then could I ever abandon it? (1.402.30)
"One who seeks their own interest, having abandoned the dharma of trust, becomes a destroyer.
I must not do that; go, abandon this waiting. (3.1)
The sin of those who betray their friends cannot be destroyed even by ten thousand sacrifices;
for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, there may sometimes be an atonement. (32)
The sin of those who betray trust can never be destroyed;
Mount Meru does not become heavy as long as there remains the weight of the betrayer.
Violence is the supreme form of unrighteousness and brings about destruction;
therein, the betrayal of trust is a sin greater than the greatest of sins. (34)
"Therefore, go from this forest to another forest, and food will meet you there.
Having been addressed thus, the king of the forest remained silent and stood still. (35)
When midnight had passed, the prince awoke;
meanwhile, the monkey, full of confidence, slept soundly upon the branch. (36)
The lion said to the king: "O King, what use have you for this tree? You are surely protecting my prey; you must indeed be a sinner. (37)
Just as you are to your subjects, so am I a forest king;
for all subjects have been ordained by law to be consumed by kings in every way. (38)
"This wild deer has today presented itself as my food;
for it was by taking refuge in you that the bear climbed the tree. (3.9)
"Today, you have indeed become my king, acting as an obstacle to my meal.
What use have you for this bear? Release my food! || 1.402.40 ||
Otherwise, I shall devour him this very morning or during the day;
likewise, I shall summon others like you and devour them as well.
Thus addressed by the lion, the king then released that bear from the tree; it was sleeping unsuspectingly with its head resting upon the king’s own lap.
Having performed circumambulation, he climbed by the power of merit to the upper part of that very tree branch and wept.
Both the king and the lion asked him, "Why indeed do you weep? (43)
"O monkey, tell me, has the fear that dwelt in your heart departed today?
The bear replied, "O Lord, I am not afraid; I do not weep for my own sake. (44)
For many wild monkeys dwell with confidence in the forest;
yet, having encountered such a king—a treacherous and deceitful man—they have been destroyed. (45)
"Thinking that they will be slain, O lion, I weep;
may death come to us facing our enemy, and may there be no sudden, untimely death for us. (46)
"O King, I am not a monkey; rather, I am a sage born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, known by the name Dhyānakāṣṭha, who can assume any form at will while dwelling in the forest. (47)
"O King, why have you abandoned me, who am innocent and asleep? Because of my curse, become utterly insane and wander upon the earth! (48)
Having thus cursed him, you then struck the lion, O sinless one; for in former times you were the minister of Kubera, preceded by a circle of friends. (49)
While wandering on the Himalayas, he happened by chance to go to the hermitage of Gautama;
upon seeing you naked, Gautama uttered a curse.
"Naked and practicing the behavior of a beast in the vicinity of my hermitage, how indeed do you roam about so wickedly? Be a wicked one, O most cruel one! (51)
"O you who are truly devoid of hair and the like, become a naked lion here!
By this curse, you became a lion; yet, being pleased, you spoke to the sage again and again.
And he said: "When [the tree] of King Dharmagupta..."
Indeed, through the good fortune of the wood for meditation, a vision shall truly occur. || 53 ||
Then your liberation from the curse will surely come to pass; do not grieve.
You are indeed named Bhadra, my servant; for I know this through meditation.
Thus addressed, he bowed to that best of sages and likewise to the king;
and instantly casting off his lion-form, he assumed the appearance of a yakṣa.
Then, remembering his past lives and having understood everything through the power of the sage's compassion,
he departed for heaven in a divine celestial chariot that had arrived.
The sage had gone to his own forest, and the king became intoxicated in the woods;
wandering like a beast, he roamed about, and the subjects went forth to search for him.
Wandering in the forest like one mad, they brought him to the bank of the Narmadā.
Having reached the presence of Jaimini, they confessed their transgression.
Upon hearing this, Jaimini said to them: "On the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, on the Veṅkaṭa mountain, at the exceedingly purifying holy site of Svāmipuṣkariṇī..."

"Let them bathe the king; by that, he will be released from the curse. Having gone there, the people residing in that kingdom did exactly so. Dharmagupta became restored to health and bestowed wealth, jewels, and other gifts.
He bestowed grain-fields and jewels upon Veṅkaṭeśa.
Thus the king was liberated from the curse and ruled his kingdom.
In this manner, the holy site of Svāmipuṣkariṇī remains a bestower of wealth.
It bestows dharma, fulfills desires, grants liberation, and destroys suffering;
through its water, the madness caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and the like is destroyed.
By bathing in it, drinking it, touching it, seeing it, or even bowing before it, [these afflictions are removed].
O Lotus-born one, even by mere remembrance, sins are destroyed.
O beloved, men who have bathed and recite three times, "Svāmitīrtha, Svāmitīrtha, Svāmitīrtha," likewise obtain the fruit of bathing at Svāmitīrtha.
They indeed attain the most excellent station of Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
By hearing and by reciting this, one obtains the fruit of bathing there.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story concerning the Brāhmaṇa Sumati.
In Mahārāṣṭra, there was one named Sumati, the son of Yajñadeva. || 67 ||
Having abandoned his home, he went to the land of Oḍhra due to association with the wicked.
There, upon seeing a certain Kirāta woman, he became infatuated and stayed in her house.
He took pleasure with her, ate, committed theft, and drank liquor.
Then, at midnight, he struck a certain brahmin with his sword.
Taking the wealth of the Brahmin, he went to the abode of the Kirātī;
then the terrifying, dark-complexioned personification of Brahman-slaughter (brahmahatyā) pursued him.
Driven mad by that, Sumati set out toward his own home; crying out, "Save my father! Save him! he went to him for refuge. (71)
Then Brahmahatyā spoke the truth to her progenitor:
"This man is a drinker of liquor, a thief, a slayer of a Brahmin, and a perpetrator of the most heinous crimes. (72)
A traitor to his mother, a traitor to his father, a deserter of the law, one who has abandoned the bull [the god Śiva],
and one corrupted by association with Kirātīs— release this wicked-souled man!
If not, I shall devour you, your wife, this son of yours, as well as others and your entire lineage; do not destroy your family.
Saying, "Abandon one [of us] and protect the family," he seized him by the neck;
at that very moment, Durvāsas arrived there by chance.
Praised by them, he said to his father: "Bathe him in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī; he shall be liberated from the sin of slaughter—of this there is no doubt. (76)
Then, together with Durvāsas, he went to the waters of Puṣkariṇī;
having bathed there, the Brahmin was purified and freed from the sin of killing a cow.
Such is the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), which acts as an axe to the tree of sin;
it bestows the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice upon those who hear of it or recite it.
By bathing at Veṅkaṭa and Kṛṣṇatīrtha as well, one is liberated from sin;
even those of wicked intent who show contempt for their fathers, mothers, and teachers [are so purified]. (79)
They too are indeed purified by merely bathing in this Kṛṣṇatīrtha.
A certain sage named Kṛṣṇa performed auspicious penance here.
On Mount Veṅkaṭādri, another sage named Rāmakṛṣṇa, who was devoted to liberation, meditated upon Hari and established an excellent sacred ford (tīrtha). ||81||
He performed severe austerities for many hundreds of years;
even though his body was covered by an anthill, he did not move from his place.
Vāsava sent down a rain of clouds for seven days,
and indeed, a great thunderbolt fell upon the top of the anthill.
The summit of the anthill was destroyed, and the sage remained as nothing but bones;
then Mahendra beheld that Mādhava for the sake of his protection.
The great lord Kāṃbhareya himself appeared as the cowherd boy Gopāla,
equipped with the conch, discus, and other [emblems], and he spoke to him.
Arise, may it be well with you; O devotee, I have been gratified by your austerity.
For whatever person is at this sacred ford when the sun is situated in Capricorn— ||86||
Whether one bathes on the full moon day or on the very day of my manifestation,
my attendants— possessing the radiance of ten million suns— lead such a person to my own abode.
"And by your name, this excellent holy place shall attain supreme renown.
Having spoken thus, Śrīnivāsa vanished right there.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa went to the abode of Hari together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, by reading or even hearing this, it bestows liberation as a sacred ford (tīrtha). ||89||
The gift of water, the gift of food, the gift of clothing, and the offering of wealth should be performed at the Vaiṅkaṭa Tīrtha; indeed, that shall become eternal.
There was a royal sage named Hemāṅga, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
he bestowed gifts of cows, gifts of land, gifts of gold, and so forth. (91)

Therefore, O beloved, if one gives even a single drop of water that was not given [by another], with the thought that it is easily obtained—since it is priceless and obtainable from everywhere—what fruit could there be for the donor? (92)
He reasoned that merit would arise from giving to those who could not receive [in return],
and thus he honored the wretched, the deformed, the poor, and those distressed for lack of livelihood.
He did not honor the Vedic scholars, the virtuous Brahmins, or those who discourse on the Absolute;
yet all people, full of zeal, continued to worship those who were renowned. ||94||
"I am the refuge of the poor; therefore, they are the objects of my compassion.
Thinking thus, he gave [gifts] to wicked recipients; because of that, indeed, for him— (95)
I was born as a cātaka bird for three lifetimes, then as a vulture for one birth, and as a dog for seven births; thereafter, I was born in a human household.
A female house-lizard, indeed a devourer of flies, was born;
meanwhile, Śrutadeva arrived at the palace of the lord of Mithilā and other cities.
Indeed, that king, who had lived for eighty-eight years, was seen by the sage;
having fully honored Śrutadeva, he [drank] the nectar of his feet.
Then, although she was sprinkled with drops falling from his head, she immediately became one who remembers her past lives and cried out, "Save me! Save me! (99).
I was born in the Ikṣvāku dynasty and became a king named Hemāṅga;
I showed partiality toward giving gifts, yet I did not give water in such a manner.
Likewise, having cast away the worthy recipient, I have bestowed [this gift] upon an unworthy one;
it is as if, having cast away a blazing fire, I have offered my oblation into mere ashes.
Having cast aside the Tulasī plant, a poisonous creeper has been watered;
for those who are lame or otherwise helpless are indeed the sole objects of compassion.
Those who take refuge in austerity, wisdom, and true knowledge, and who possess the very nature of Viṣṇu—such wise ones are always dear to Viṣṇu and worthy of worship. || 103 ||
Therefore, the man of knowledge is always worthy of worship; one should give to him for the attainment of the fruit.
He is even more worthy of worship than the object of worship itself, and he shall be the bestower of heaven and liberation. || 104 ||
"Indeed, no water was given by me, nor were the virtuous ever served;
because of that, this miserable state has arisen for me, even though I have gone to heaven. (105)
Having heard this fruit of bathing at the holy ford on Mount Veṅkaṭādri, the sage gave it to the iguana; and she, too, by virtue of the merit of a single day [of bathing], attained it.
Assuming a divine form and seated upon an excellent celestial chariot,
he, endowed with the fruit of giving water, departed for the heavenly world after offering praise.
From that [merit], one attains water in heaven; therefore, the gift of water and other things must always be performed on earth by men with true devotion. (108)
Then, after some time, he became the lord of the earth named Kakutstha;
having become the ruler of the seven continents, he attained union with Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supreme majesty of the worthy recipient,
as well as the merit of giving water and other gifts, and the fruit that comes from hearing this.

Thus ends the four hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of King Toṇḍamān on Mount Veṅkaṭādri, of King Dharmagupta who betrayed the bear, of the Brahmin named Sumati, of the sage Rāmakṛṣṇa, and of Hemāṅga," within the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, concerning the majesty of devoted wives (*pativratā*) in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: There, Śrī herself appeared in the form of Sītā as her shadow-form,
while Vedavatī manifested as the very embodiment of Lakṣmī.
Who indeed is able to describe the supreme majesty of that sacred field, by taking refuge in which Veṅkaṭādri exists as the very embodiment of the abode of Brahman? || 2 ||
Where Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, the self-effulgent Lord, shines resplendent;
where the Blessed Lord Varāha truly manifests himself again and again.
Where devotees are born who are Vaiṣṇavas and saviors of the world;
where even a tiny particle of dust from that land is a savior for this world.
This auspicious place, consisting of land, water, and so forth, destroys great sins;
it directly bestows the abode of Brahman and grants the status of Kṛṣṇasvāmī.
There dwell devoted wives who have attained liberation— greatly virtuous Vaiṣṇava women, solely intent on the service of their husbands.
For they are considered the wives of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, devoted to their husband;
all of them are equal to Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and equal to Pārvatī and Māṇikī.
For those [goddesses] such as Jayā and Vijayā are indeed equal to Prabhā and Ramā; by whomsoever Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, joined with Ramā and the others, has been worshipped. || 8 ||
O beloved, by my grace they have indeed attained the eternal heaven, the state of liberation from which there is no return; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever holy places exist on earth and within the cosmic egg,
they all reside upon the Veṅkaṭa mountain in the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
For the sake of serving that god, there were sages, lords, gods, seers, perfected beings (siddhas), yogis, and ascetics as well. || 11 ||
Virtuous women and virtuous men, wise ones, and the lords of the gods and others,
come every day with their families for the purpose of service.
Then, by Brahmā, the great festival of the banner of Veṅkaṭeśa was established in Kārttika;
consequently, the lords of Satyaloka arrive every year.
O beloved, at Svāmisarovara and at Vaikaṭeśvara to its south,
an immeasurable merit is produced for those who perform pilgrimage rites;
indeed, the merit that is earned during ten years in the Kṛta Yuga is attained there in a single day.
In the Tretā age, that merit is accomplished by people in one year;
in the Dvāpara, in five months; but in the Kali age, it is attained in a single day.
Yet, the fruit of beholding Śrīnivāsa is ten million times greater than that.
O Lakṣmī, at every moment it is born; of this there is no doubt.
Even by a particle of dust, liberation is attained in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
Those who glorify Śrīnivāsa, Mahādeva, Veṅkaṭeśa, and Nārāyaṇa within their hearts are liberated from the cage of worldly existence.
Of what use are gifts, vows, other holy places, penances, or sacrifices?
What is the use of Kāśī, what of Gayā, and what fruit even from Prayāga?
What need is there for Śambhu, the creator of the universe, or for Śakra and the other gods,
when Nārāyaṇa Veṅkaṭeśa has been beheld with supreme devotion?
One should practice the eightfold devotion toward the Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara, including the honoring and worshiping of His devotees to their complete satisfaction. (21)
Contentment through the worship of the gods, bodily exertion for their sake, listening to stories of their majesty, and likewise hearing of their heroic deeds; ||22||

Devotion characterized by the emotion of longing for his dance, meditation upon Veṅkaṭa, and subsisting on the livelihood provided by residence on the Veṅkaṭa mountain—these are the givers of liberation. 23.
Such devotion is to be understood as being possible even without hearing the Vedānta;
Veṅkaṭa and Veṅkaṭeśa are both the very essence of Nārāyaṇa. (24)
One should pray to Veṅkaṭa, who bestows the meritorious state of Nārāyaṇa;
O best of mountains, I would otherwise tread upon you with my feet. (25)
After bathing first in the Pāpanāśana Tīrtha at Svāmipuṣkariṇī, show me Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who has made his dwelling upon your head.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should bathe for the destruction of sin.
In ancient times, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Sumati who followed the conduct of a Śūdra.
Seized by a Brahma-rākṣasa due to the fault of wearing a garland, he wept, wandered about, stumbled, was bewildered, rambled on, and laughed. (28)
Constantly crying out, "Alas! Alas!", he completely lost his auspicious intelligence;
his father, having taken him to the Veṅkaṭa mountain, caused him to perform an ablution.
For three days he drank water at that sin-destroying holy site;
by that means, his son was there liberated from the Brahma-rākṣasa.
Having been happy for a long time, at the end of his body he attained liberation; through the drinking of water at that holy ford, the Brahmarākṣasa [was released]. ||3 1 ||
O Lakṣmī, even he attained liberation at that very spot through my yoga;
likewise, another brahmin named Bhadramati, who was possessed by poverty, [attained it there]. ||32||
He was indeed a knower of the scriptures and righteous, served by six wives;
yet his sons and their descendants became afflicted by hunger. ||33||
Beholding them, Bhadramati, his senses agitated, lamented:
"Fie upon this life, devoid of fortune and destitute of wealth and fame! (34)
Fie upon a birth devoid of hospitality! Fie upon one who lacks both knowledge and right conduct! And fie upon that which is bereft of effort, happiness, fame, kinsmen, renown, and the like! (35)
Fie upon such a birth that is devoid of sovereignty and burdened with many offspring!
Alas, [how great are] virtues, gentleness, learning, noble lineage, and the like! (36)
For one devoid of wealth, even all of these—sons, wives, grandsons, kinsmen, and brothers—do not shine, however excellent they may be. (37)
Disciples, servants, and mothers abandon one who is destitute of wealth;
whether he be an outcaste or even an ascetic, it is the wealthy man who is honored on this earth. (38)
A corpse is counted as empty, yet one who has accumulated wealth is counted as rich;
a meritless fool is counted as virtuous and as a scholar.
A man devoid of righteousness is counted by people as one who possesses true righteousness if he is wealthy;
therefore, poverty and hope are considered more painful than pain itself. (1.403.40)
Those who give with hope are always afflicted, while the one who hopes for service prospers in happiness;
the one seized by the great crocodile of poverty stands at the very brink of the mouth of death. (41)
"Alas, what suffering! How indeed is this to be crossed by one such as I?"—while he was thinking thus, his wife, named Kañcana, [spoke]. (42)
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, always regarding her husband as a deity, and endowed with all the virtues of a virtuous woman, she replied to that husband.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, treasury of the knowledge of all purposes, my beloved, ever worthy of worship, listen; I speak, so please do as I say. (44)
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī lies the purifying Veṅkaṭācala;
and there is a supreme holy site there known by the name Pāpavināśana. (45)
Merely by bathing there, it burns away sins, bestows wealth and merit, pacifies all sufferings, and grants all forms of prosperity. ||46||
Nārada also declared in ancient times that this bestows sovereignty over the Dharma;
one should perform the gift of land there, for it grants the fruit of all desires. (47)
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of land;
the giver of land attains supreme Nirvana—of this there is no doubt. (48)

By giving even a very small amount of land to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to a twice-born brāhmaṇa, or to a virtuous person for the purpose of maintaining the sacred fire (agnihotra), one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. ||49||
The giver of land is declared to be a giver of everything; through that, indeed, liberation shall come.
By giving even ten cubits of earth, one is released from all sins.
One who bestows land upon a worthy recipient indeed obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
[The earth] is adorned with fields of sugarcane, wheat, betel-nut groves, and dates. (9.1)
He by whom land is given shall indeed become a Vaiṣṇava in the Imperishable;
the giver of land for the sake of the gods becomes eternally liberated. ||52||
One who bestows a *droṇa* of land on the bank of the Gaṅgā partakes in the fruit of horse-sacrifices;
[the merit] of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of *vājapeya* sacrifices [is attained]. (53)
"The giver of land, even if it be as small as a burden, indeed partakes in the fruit of those who have performed meritorious deeds on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Having heard these words of his wife, Bhadramati then departed. (54)
In that city of Suśālī, he requested five cubits of land from the eminent brahmin Sughoṣa, and he too gave it to him with joy.
He said, "I have achieved my purpose; my birth has become fruitful;
my lineage has become meritorious, since you, a brahmin, are the one who asks of me. (56)
The earth is indeed sacred to Viṣṇu; the earth is protected by Viṣṇu. It is given to a worthy recipient; may Janārdana be pleased with me. (57)
That devotee of Hari, having indeed accepted that earth,
then went to the Veṅkaṭa mountain where the Svāmisarovara lake is located.
Having bathed there and then bowed to Śvetavārāha, the upholder of the earth,
he went to Veṅkaṭeśa, the supreme lord Śrīnivāsa.
Then he went to the supreme holy place named Pāpanāśana;
having bathed there, he gave a gift of land to a Vaiṣṇava who was well-versed in the Vedas.
At that moment, the Blessed One appeared there visibly;
Bhadramati offered praise: "Salutations to you, O Nārāyaṇa! (6.1).
Salutations to you, the cause, the protector, the end-maker, and the leader;
to the purifier, the gracious one, and the bestower of prosperity.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Śrī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Upholder of the Earth, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Prabhā, and the Lord of Māṇikī. ||6 3||
Salutations to you, the Lord of Pārvatī and the cowherd boy;
salutations to you, the omniscient one born from the lap of Kaṃbhārā. ||64||
Homage to you, the supreme person, whose marks include the discus, lotus, and other signs;
who dwells in the ocean of milk, and who is served by Śrī Lakṣmī.
Salutations to you, the bestower of desired happiness, who took the form of a sacrificial boar;
salutations to you, the beloved of Kamalā, and salutations to you, the beloved of Padmā. ||66||
O Kṛṣṇa, obeisances again and again to you, the Lord of the Lotus Lake, the destroyer of the poverty of your devotees, who possesses a virtuous form. ||67||
Having heard this, Hari said: "I am pleased, O best of brahmins;
endowed with all enjoyments, you shall attain liberation at the end of your body. (68)
Having thus granted the boon, he vanished right there;
that twice-born man, having bathed at the Pāpanāśana Tīrtha, went home.
Thereupon, the merchant became possessed of an abundance of gold, wealth, and grain;
by the power of his gift of land, he was like another great Indra.
Furthermore, there exists another great holy site that bestows liberation upon men;
it is renowned as Ākāśagaṅgā, and I shall describe its majesty to you.
A certain twice-born man named Rāmānuja, who was solely devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu,
performed penance while standing amidst five fires, chanting the eight-syllabled mantra.
Even while standing in the rain or in water, he remained free from the touch of dualities;
for a long time, he subsisted on withered leaves, or took only water as food, or lived on air alone.
Devoted to penance, he remained steadfast; and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, who is affectionate toward his devotees, being pleased with him, arrived there to inquire after his welfare.
His body adorned with golden ornaments, served by Ramā, Rādhā, and others, and accompanied by Viśvaksena, Sunanda, and his attendants—such is the glorious Lord of Ramā. (75)
The Lord, clad in yellow garments, was accompanied by Nārada and others,
with Sanaka and other great yogis attending at his two sides.
The twice-born ascetic praised that compassionate Veṅkaṭeśa:
"Obeisance to Rāma, the Great One who bears the discus and other weapons; obeisance! (77)
Salutations to You whose nature is eternally pure; salutations to the remover of the distress of devotees;
salutations to You who exist as the supreme, the manifest, and the empowered forms, and in the form of the images for worship.
Salutations again and again to You, who pervade the self as the inner controller;
salutations to You, the illustrious Kṛṣṇa, the Great Being, Nārāyaṇa. ||79||
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha and to Vairāja, the creator;
salutations to Sadāśiva, to Kānta, to Viṣṇu, and to Brahmā.
Salutations to the Lord of lords, the Sovereign, whose eyes are like flowers;
who is beyond name, genus, and the like, yet whose form consists of name, genus, and so forth. ||81||

Salutations again and again to You, the son of Kambharā, to Kṛṣṇa, who performs the *rāsa* dance with the circle of cowherd girls, the son of Gopāla, who is affectionate toward the service of the cows. ||82||
Salutations to you, who are to be known through the Vedānta and Nyāya, the author of the Bhāṣya, the well-gone one (Sugata) within the Āgamas, and the protector of the world. ||83||
To him whose true form is the sun of Saurāṣṭra, who dwells on Mount Raivata, who is the lord of the land of Aśvapaṭṭa, and who possesses the Puṣkara forest; 84.
"Obeisance to you, the Lord of Kāśī, who are worshipped with saffron and other offerings.
Having thus praised Śrīnivāsa, Rāmānuja attained peace. (85)
Veṅkaṭeśa, having embraced Rāmānuja, said:
"Pleased by this hymn and your penance, choose a boon quickly."
Then Rāmānuja said: "O Śrīnivāsa, O Lord Hari!
By the sight of you, I have achieved my life's purpose; what more could there be for me than this sight today? (87)
Neither the gods, the ancestors, the sages, nor those established in lifelong vows, nor the performers of ritual action, nor even the yogis skilled in knowledge, perceive Him or know Him. ||88||
I know him and I see him even today; what indeed could be greater for me than this?
By means of this seed of liberation, I have in every way achieved my life's purpose. (89)
"May my devotion to the pair of your lotus feet be unwavering.
Having heard this, Hari said, "May your devotion to me be firm."
Those people who, having come here to this place of my asceticism, shall bathe in the celestial Gaṅgā, will go to my supreme abode. (91)
And you, at the end of this commenced body, shall attain my own nature;
as for all those excellent devotees who have bathed in the celestial Gaṅgā, [they shall likewise attain it].
O best of devotees, listen to the characteristic mark of the Bhāgavatas—those who, through their actions, mind, and speech, are absorbed in the conduct of the Blessed Lord. 93.
Those who perform all their duties for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, who are contemplative of Kṛṣṇa, who possess knowledge, are free from desire, and are peaceful—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (94)
Those who perceive Kṛṣṇa in all things, who are devoted to the sacred stories of Kṛṣṇa, and who are devotees of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet—they are the best of Bhāgavatas. (95)
Those who are devoted to the service and care of their parents, whose bodies are dark with age, and who are filled with the weight of supreme joy in the worship and adoration of the gods; 96.

Those who are devoted to serving the virtuous, who bestow honor upon the virtuous women, and whose conduct is centered on the Supreme Lord—they are the most excellent among the great bhāgavatas. ||97||

Regarding all beings as themselves, possessing vision like that of Bhāgavatas supreme, they are knowers of the scriptures, upholders of dharma, speakers of truth, and the best among the virtuous. (98)

Those who delight in the stories of Kṛṣṇa, who feel affection for the narrator of those stories, who love sacred pilgrimage sites, and who serve the wish-fulfilling cow—these indeed are the best of virtuous men. 99.
Those who are joyful at the rising of any [auspicious occasion], who are devoted solely to the name of Kṛṣṇa,
and who dig wells for the sake of Kṛṣṇa— they are the best among the Bhāgavatas.
Those who build temples for the gods, those who perform the japa of the Deva-gāyatrī, those whose joy is devotion, and those who are immersed in Hari—they are the best among the Bhāgavatas. 101.
Those who worship Tulasī bow down to Vṛndā;
they carry Tulasī in their hands, wear garlands of Tulasī, and are adorned with Tulasī-sandalwood paste.
Those whose bodies are made of Tulasī soil are indeed the best of Bhāgavatas;
they are the perceivers of Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa within the Vedas and other scriptures. (103)

Those who are constant contemplators of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa alone during hospitality and other rites, who possess knowledge of the true principles, who awaken others to Brahman, and who are of virtuous conduct; || 104 ||
Those who correctly grasp all virtues and other qualities are indeed the best of Bhāgavatas;
they observe vows such as Ekādaśī and perform actions for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Those Vaiṣṇavas who, upon seeing Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Śrī, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Māṇikī— who are my own portions and female forms— bow down to them,
always perceive with their hearts that they are of my very nature and presided over by me.
Those who [behave] toward a fool as they would toward a young girl are indeed the most excellent devotees of the Lord.
Likewise, O sinless one, those women among men who behold me, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, are truly called great Bhāgavatas by me.
All men are of the form of Kṛṣṇa, and all women are of the nature of Rādhā and Ramā;
those who possess such knowledge of the Bhāgavata are the best of devotees.
In brief, I declare that all men, women, and even animals who abide entirely for my sake are the most excellent devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatottama).
O Rāmānuja, you alone are indeed the supreme devotee;
I am pleased with you, O beloved one, because of your constant abiding in unwavering devotion.
There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) named Ākāśagaṅgā, which delivers one from saṃsāra and leads to the further shore of existence;
for those who bathe there, it bestows liberation and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and emancipation.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa then vanished;
by reading or hearing this, devotion and liberation are placed within one's grasp. 113.

Thus ends the four hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of Sumati, Bhadramati, and Rāmānuja—who were protectors of their husband’s devotion—along with other matters, at the most excellent holy site," in the section on the Greatness of Devotion to the Husband within the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe to you the worthy recipient of gifts, who is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha). Nārāyaṇa is the highest tīrtha; indeed, one should give to this wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
What is given to one who is virtuous, of righteous character, possessed of learning, high-souled, generous, and a knower of Brahman, becomes inexhaustible. (2)
That which is given to a virtuous woman who is devoted to enjoyment, to the wife of Hari-Kṛṣṇa, to Nārāyaṇī, the Great Lakṣmī, becomes eternal. || 3 ||
And to Satī, the servant of Hari who is devoted to virtuous deeds and the wife of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, this eternal [gift] was given. || 4 ||
What is given to the protectorless, to the devotee, and to the Yoginī is inexhaustible;
likewise, what is given to the devotee, to him who is of the nature of Brahman, to Brahmā, the knower of the Vedas. || 5 ||
Salutations to the teacher who is the very embodiment of the form of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the brāhmaṇa who is a disciple of the Lord and a performer of virtuous deeds. || 6 ||
What is given to one who seeks peace becomes inexhaustible;
what is given to a cow, to a child, to a maiden, or to one's parents, is inexhaustible.
That which is given to one's wife, sister, daughter, virtuous grandson, sister’s son, or disciple becomes inexhaustible. (8)
That which is given to the guru, to the guru’s wife, to the learned son of the guru, and to one who propagates the Dharma, becomes inexhaustible. || 9 ||

Indeed, that which is given to an expounder, to a giver of knowledge, to a teacher, to a learned man, to one qualified for learning, and to a worthy recipient of knowledge, becomes inexhaustible. 1.404.10.
Indeed, [this] should be given to one who is destitute of livelihood, to a poor householder,
to a worshiper of the deity, and also to one who performs service for others.
It should be given to the teacher; it should be given for the sake of the country;
and it should also be given to the protector for the purpose of prosperity.
That which is given in the presence of Nārāyaṇa becomes inexhaustible;
it should be bestowed upon a Vaiṣṇava, by whom indeed I am pleased.
But that which is given to one who acts with hypocrisy, to a thief, to an enemy, to a slanderer,
or to one intent upon the wealth and wives of others, is indeed fruitless.
That which is given to an ungrateful person, to a fool, to one whose heart is possessed by envy, to a violent person, or to a seller [of sacred things], becomes fruitless. (15)
Of one who causes suffering to others, an atheist, a fool, a wicked person, one whose nature is deceitful, and one who violates the boundaries of social conduct. || 16 ||
But for one who is heretical, deceitful, dishonest, living unrighteously,
quarrelsome, and of fierce disposition, it is indeed fruitless.
At the sacred ford on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī, gifts should especially be given;
for in matters of charity, the unsurpassed Cakratīrtha is the most meritorious of all sacred sites.
Formerly, Padmanābha, a bull among the twice-born belonging to the Śrīvatsa lineage,
performed severe penance on the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī.
For several years he subsisted on withered leaves;
for some time he lived on water, and for many years he sustained himself on air alone.
Thus, at the end of the twelfth year, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhā and Kamalā, being pleased, appeared before his very eyes.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa, the abode of Śrī, he began to offer praise to Viṣṇu,
who is in the form of Gopālakṛṣṇa and the son of Kaṃbhārī.
Salutations to You, Veṅkaṭeśa, who dwells upon Śeṣādri;
salutations to You, Śrīnivāsa, who dwells upon Nārāyaṇādri. ||23||
"Salutations to you, the beloved of devotion, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of the Lotus!
Thus praised, Śrīnivāsa, who is dark as a rain cloud, was indeed pleased.
Padmanābha spoke to the twice-born one here at Cakratīrtha:
"O best of devotees, my dear one, dwell here and worship me for all time until the end of the kalpa."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa vanished right there;
Padmanābha remained there for a time, intending to devour him.
Then a Rākṣasa arrived there and seized the Brāhmaṇa;
he cried out repeatedly, "O wielder of the discus, protect me! Protect me! (27)
O Veṅkaṭeśa! O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lord!
O son of Kaṃbhari! O Lord of Mercy! Protect me, protect me from being seized by the Rākṣasa! 28.
While he was thus offering praise, the wielder of the discus dispatched his own discus to the bank of the Cakrapuṣkariṇī for the very purpose of protecting him. (29)
Seeing Sudarśana with its great blaze, the Rākṣasa fled;
the Brahmin cut off his head and praised the Discus.
O Discus of Viṣṇu, salutations to you, who are consecrated to the protection of devotees;
salutations to you, the ornament upon the lotus-hand of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 31 ||
Be established here at all times; be my protector for my sake.
Salutations again and again to the one whose nature is Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of liberation. ||3 2||
To his devotee Padmanābha who had thus petitioned him, Sudarśana said:
"O devotee, this Cakratīrtha established by you must be known by my name."
"I shall dwell constantly at Cakratīrtha out of a desire for you;
from now on, there shall be no suffering for people caused by Rākṣasas and other such beings."
"Those who bathe here, cleansed of sin, shall go to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Having spoken thus, he entered the radiant Cakrapuṣkariṇī.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, by the power of the devotion and chastity of his wife, that holy site (tīrtha) situated at Cakrāśrita became a bestower of liberation and a destroyer of sins. Now listen to how even that Rākṣasa who has just died came to be.
Formerly, in Śrīraṅgapurī, there were indeed Vaiṣṇavas such as Vasiṣṭha and others. ||37||
They waited upon Śrī Raṅganātha with a desire for liberation.
Once, a Gandharva named Sundara arrived there. (38)
While the young women were performing their ablutions in the water,
Vasiṣṭha engaged in various kinds of play for that very duration.
Having gone to bathe, he saw him naked and cursed the shameless one:
"O handsome one, even upon seeing me, you do not put on a garment; therefore, [you shall suffer]."
By those [curses], he immediately attained the state of a Rākṣasa and became a Rākṣasa;
then the young women, having bowed to the illustrious Vasiṣṭha, begged for his forgiveness.
O ocean of compassion, beholding us, you ought not to be angry;
for indeed, the husband alone is considered the supreme ornament of women. (42)
A woman who is bereft of her husband is not auspicious even if she has a hundred sons;
being a widow, she is inauspicious, and therefore her birth is meaningless. (43)
"O Lord, our beloved, one offense should be forgiven; be gracious!
Thus praised, Vasiṣṭha said to them, "My curse cannot be fruitless."
The Rākṣasa shall remain so for sixteen years, after which he will attain the state of a Gandharva;
at Cakratīrtha, through separation from Padmanābha, he will be liberated.
By means of the Sudarśana discus, his liberation will come about;
the handsome husband will once again delight him in the third heaven.
Having spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha indeed departed for the temple of Śrīraṅga;
the Rākṣasa became handsome, yet possessed of great fangs and terrifying.
Seeing him, they were overcome with fear and went to the triple heaven;
while the Rākṣasa wandered on the mountain, sixteen years passed away.
Then, having been liberated by Sudarśana through the power of a brahmin, Sundara became truly beautiful and ascended to heaven in a celestial chariot. ||49||
The discus resided there eternally; therefore, it became known as Cakratīrtha.
By hearing this, the destruction of the multitude of sins certainly occurs.
O Lakṣmī, listen to the majesty of Jābālitīrtha; I shall describe it to you.

A brahmin named Durācāra, who resided on the banks of the Kāverī, was constantly associated with evildoers; having lost his Brahmanical rites and virtues, he was seized by a powerful and terrifying Vetāla. ||51-52||
After wandering for a very long time, he reached Mount Veṅkaṭa;
there, while he was submerged in the water, he was released by a vetāla.
At the very spot in the water where he was liberated, the sage Jābāli was present.
He dwelt at that great holy ford, which is called Jābālitīrtha. Formerly, there was a great atheist who was a Brāhmaṇa;
because he reviled the gods and the virtuous, he fell into the state of a Vetāla. ||54-55||
By the power of that sacred ford, he too shall attain human birth once again.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supreme Jābāli-tīrtha.
Now listen, my beloved, as I describe the Tumburu-tīrtha here as well.
Indeed, all sinful men bathe repeatedly in these [rivers] during the Amāvāsya.
Having cast off the nets of sin, those people become purified;
how may our nets of sin be destroyed on all sides? (58)
Having reflected thus, they went to the holy fords (tīrthas) on the Veṅkaṭa mountain; there, at Tumburu, they bathed in the waters of Svāmipuṣkariṇī,
and on the bright lunar festival day under the Uttarāphālgunī constellation, they bathed in that sacred ford.
Their sins were destroyed and returned to their respective abodes.
One who is devoted to great sins, cruel, devoid of charity, the destroyer of his lineage,
a killer of animals, a perpetrator of treachery, a slanderer, and a person of untruth— [these are those who should be avoided].

One who betrays a friend, one who is ungrateful, a killer of an embryo, one who goes to another's wife, a betrayer for the sake of others' wealth, one who betrays his master, and one who turns away from the gods—[these are those who fall]. (62)
One who is deceitful and fraudulent, an obstacle to the Dharma, a divider of families, and a destroyer of gardens and trees endowed with fine foliage and fruit. (63)

One who sets fire [to a dwelling], one who administers poison, a sinner, a betrayer of trust, a wicked person who harbors hatred toward his guru, and one who causes discord between husband and wife—[these are not to be accepted]. (64)
O Lakṣmī, this supreme Tumburu-tīrtha purifies all these [beings] through bathing, drinking, and other such acts, and it bestows both heaven and liberation. (65)
In former times, a gandharva named Tumburu said to his wife:
"Perform, along with me, the bath that removes impurity during the three months of Māgha."
In the month of Māgha, when the sun has risen, perform the smearing with cow-dung,
using colored streaks and the like, as well as white lotuses and svastikas made of mineral pigments.
"O beloved, make the place for the worship of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa pure;
prepare a fragrant lamp illuminated by a wick of ghee."
Having become pure, offer cooked food to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and serve Him along with me through circumambulations and prostrations. (69)
Constantly perform service to the Lord and practice listening to His sacred narratives;
O Vaiṣṇavī, always accept food and water through the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O son of Kaṃbhara, O Janārdana!
O Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Govinda, O Lord of Ramā-Rādhā, O Master! ||71||
O Lord of Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Pārvatī; O Master of the luster of the ruby;
O Inner Controller and Bestower of Liberation—thus praise me always. (72)
Abandoning anger, envy, greed, and the like, observe the vow;
by that very means liberation arises, and the world of Viṣṇu is indeed attained. (73)
Having heard these words of her husband, the passionate woman became enraged and then replied to her beloved, as if afflicted by the pain of cold: 74.
"O Lord, why do you hold bathing in Māgha—which takes away life—to be so highly esteemed?
I will not bathe; if I die, let you be my protector here. (75)
Dharma should be practiced by people as long as it can be performed gently;
one should not practice that dharma which causes suffering and brings about destruction—I shall not do that.
"And the rites for Viṣṇu cannot be performed by me at dawn.
To her who had spoken thus, Tumburu cursed that woman who spoke unpleasantly. (77)
"On Mount Veṅkaṭa, at the Ghoṇatīrtha, within the hollow of a Pippala tree—there, O fool, in a place devoid of water, become a solitary female frog. (78)
Having heard this, she entreated her beloved;
her husband said, "One day Agastya was in your presence together with some sages. (79)
Having stayed there, he will indeed then proclaim the greatness of Ghoṇa;
having heard it from afar, you shall truly be liberated from the body of a female frog.
"Having returned, you shall sport with me in my abode.
Having spoken thus, the virtuous wife, devoted to her husband, then became silent. (81)
Having assumed the body of a frog due to her husband’s most terrible curse,
after many years had passed, Agastya arrived there.
Having bathed in Svāmipuṣkariṇī and bowed to Lord Varāha, one should behold Veṅkaṭeśa Śrīnivāsa in the vicinity of the Pippala tree. ||83||
Having arrived, she told the people of the greatness of Ghoṇatīrtha;
then that Maṇḍūkī was liberated and shone in her former form.
Out of compassion, he said to me, "Protect me, for I have acted in opposition to my husband's word.
By my husband's curse, I was born as a female frog; I have been liberated by you. (85)
Then Agastya said to her: "Listen to the power of wifely devotion;
your husband, who is well-versed in righteousness, has indeed cursed you truthfully. (86)
Indeed, a curse is entirely appropriate for one who contradicts her husband's word;
for she who disregards her husband's command acts according to her own will. (87)
That wife falls into a miserable hell for an entire kalpa;
indeed, a woman must never transgress the word of her own husband.
Through the merit of devotion to their husbands and through service to their lords, women go to the abode of Viṣṇu, and not by any other virtuous vows. (89)
The husband is the mother; the husband is Viṣṇu; the husband is Brahmā; the husband is Śiva;
the husband is the guru; the husband is the sacred ford; the husband is considered the supreme liberation.
But she who, having set aside her husband's reply, acts according to her own will, does not obtain the fruit [of her actions], nor indeed does she become pure. || 91 ||
Even if she abides by the command of her guru, if she does not carry out the command of her husband,
she shall never become pure nor meritorious.
By her husband's command, she should likewise perform religious vows and other duties;
and with the understanding that he is her husband, she should always perform service and other acts for Hari.
She who has bathed in the sacred water of the lotus-feet of the Lord is beloved by Hari;
she has, without a doubt, bathed in all the holy fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
You have experienced the fruit of suffering; you have been born again just as before.
Go now to the abode of Tumburu and be happy in every way. (95)
This very place is Tumburu-tīrtha; it has attained renown because of him.
Those who bathe here on the full moon day partake in the fruit of sacrifice.
Day by day, one obtains the merit arising from the gift of a thousand tawny cows;
day by day, one obtains the merit arising from the gift of ten million jewels. || 97 ||
O fair-browed one, by bathing in Ghoṇatīrtha, one indeed obtains the fruit that arises from the gift of a thousand elephants and ten thousand horses in a single day.
The fruit obtained from bathing at Ghoṇā is equal to that of giving away ten million maidens in marriage, or that born from the gift of a thousand pieces of gold at Kurukṣetra. || 99 ||
One obtains that fruit by bathing at Tumburu-tīrtha which belongs to him who would sacrifice his body for the sake of a guru, for the sake of the virtuous, or for the sake of his master.
Whatever fruit one obtains by sacrificing the body for the sake of a devoted wife, for the sake of a virtuous woman, or for the sake of Hari— that same fruit one attains by bathing in Ghoṇatīrtha.

Whatever merit belongs to those who remove the suffering of the afflicted, who are devoted to serving sacred fords, and who are firm in their vows of truth—that very merit indeed arises from Ghoṇatīrtha. || 10.2 ||
Whatever fruit is obtained at the Gaṅgā, the Narmadā, the Sarayū, the Candrabhāgā, the Svarṇavatī, and the Yamunā, that same fruit shall be attained here.
Having heard this and drunk the water, she went to the house of Tumburu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this excellent Tumburu-tīrtha been described to you.
Having heard which, a person may attain the great fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice,
as well as the supreme heaven, the world of Viṣṇu, and the eternal state.

Thus ends the four hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worthy Recipient of Gifts, the Majesty of Chaste Devotion at Cakratīrtha and Jābālitīrtha, and the Power of the Sacred Fords," within the first section, the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, there are six principal holy bathing places (tīrthas) on Veṅkaṭādri;
they are Svāmipuṣkariṇī and Viyadgaṅgā, which is superior even to that.
Furthermore, there is Pāṇḍutīrtha, the supreme destroyer of sins,
as well as Kumāradhārikātīrtha and Tumburutīrtha.
When the conjunction with Maghā occurs on the full moon day in the Aquarius ascendant,
all the sacred fords from every direction go to Kumāradhārī.
From bathing there, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and liberation in the abode of Viṣṇu;
food should be given as a gift, and eternal fruit is thereby attained.
On the full moon day conjoined with the asterism Uttarāphālgunī,
when the sun is in Pisces, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) go toward Tumburu from every direction.
By merely bathing in the afternoon, rebirth no longer exists;
[one attains] the sacred thread, the vow of Brahman, and the auspicious moment for marriage.
He who causes [this] to be made after giving wealth gains infinite merit,
especially when the sun is in Aries, under the asterism Citrā, or on the full moon day in every respect.
Indeed, the purifying holy places (tīrthas) come to the celestial Gaṅgā;
by bathing there, a human being obtains the merit of a hundred sacrifices.
The gift of gold, the gift of food, and especially the gift of a daughter in marriage,
should be bestowed by one who desires the highest heaven or a [prosperous] home.
On the twelfth lunar day, on the day of the Sun in Taurus, at the commencement of a vow, or on a Friday,
people come from all directions to Pāṇḍutīrtha on the Gaṅgā when it is joined with Mars.
Having bathed and given a milch cow as a gift, one is liberated from tens of millions of sins on the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight when the sun is in Aśvinī and it is a Sunday.
When the sun is conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā and the moon is in Uttarābhādrapadā,
on that twelfth lunar day, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) that destroys all sins.
Having performed the gift of a Śālagrāma stone and bathed, one is liberated;
this occurs at dawn on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Dhanus. || 13 ||
Tīrthas from all directions come to the Svāmipuṣkariṇī tīrtha;
only he whose merit has been earned over thousands of births may attain it.
The bath there belongs to him alone, and certainly not to anyone else who has not performed meritorious deeds;
having bathed, one is liberated by giving gifts according to one's ability. || 15 ||
One should especially give a Śālagrāma stone and a wish-fulfilling cow there;
one should perform the gift of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
By the gift of this [text] in Saurāṣṭra, one will certainly attain Goloka.
By giving her as a gift to the south, one shall attain the station of Vairāja.
By making a gift at Prāgjyotiṣa, one attains the world of the Sun;
by making a gift at Jālandhara, one attains the world of Varuṇa. || 18 ||
By giving this [gift] in Uttarakuru, one shall attain the state of Brahmā;
by giving in the seven continents, one shall become the lord of the seven continents. || 19 ||
Those who always hear the story of Viṣṇu, which purifies the world, are considered liberated while living; they are my devotees, the great Bhāgavatas.
Whether for a moment, half that time, or even a single instant on Veṅkaṭācala,
the man who listens with devotion to even a single chapter of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā shall attain eternal liberation.
Whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices and whatever fruit is found in all acts of giving—
that fruit a person attains by hearing the Saṃhitā even once.
Hearing the Saṃhitā is the glorification of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Both indeed bestow the merit of the wish-fulfilling tree upon human beings;
yet one alone, by drinking the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories, shall become ageless and immortal in this world,
and the entire family shall likewise become ageless and immortal through drinking the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories.
I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, always dwell within the speaker.
One should know my form to be the speaker, the embodiment of thought that bestows awakening.
I am the Lord manifest as the speaker; Lakṣmī, my beloved, is the listener.
Thinking thus, one should always worship both the listener and the reciter;
for without my entry, who would be capable of being either a listener or a reciter? (27)
O Lakṣmī, whether for the purpose of hearing or speaking, wherever this Saṃhitā exists within the inner core of a divine narrative, there I, possessing a divine form,
will certainly manifest, surrounded by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others.
He was then accompanied by his attendants and joined by those who were participants in the discourse.
Those with divine vision behold [this], but not people with the eyes of flesh;
while this story exists, I shall abandon those very lives.
I lead him by means of a divine vehicle to Vaikuṇṭha, the imperishable realm,
as well as to Goloka and the immortal abode, according to whatever the devotee desires.
Whether he be a child, a youth, or an old man; whether poor or even unfortunate—a narrator of this sacred story is always worthy of honor, for he is the very embodiment of the Supreme Self.
One should never entertain a low opinion of one who knows the Saṃhitā.
From whose mouth arises speech that bestows liberation and heaven upon men.

The observer of the vow of the sacred narrative bestows the gift of fearlessness upon all living beings, who have repeatedly perished after being born again and again throughout the fields of infinite births.
Vyāsa is the bestower of knowledge; what teacher is higher than he who occupies the seat of Vyāsa?
Until the completion of the narrative, one should not bow to any other teacher. ||35||
The king, the sovereign, the universal monarch, the great teacher, the guide, or even the god—all these are proclaimed by Vyāsa to be inferior [to him]. (36)
The Vyāsa-seat is always considered higher than the seats of these [others]. Upon their arrival, the Vyāsa should never rise from his own seat. (37)
In a temple, at a crossroads, or on ground where five streams meet;
in a house, at a sacred ford, in an auspicious field, or at a holy site—one should recount the meritorious narrative. (38)
Those who possess faith and devotion, who are restrained in speech and steady-minded,
who are undistracted, believers, self-controlled, and listeners— such people are vessels of merit.
One should honor the discourse and the speaker with all necessary offerings;
the fruit of their merit shall eternally bestow fortune, prosperity, and wisdom. (1.405.40)
But those who, drawn by greed, listen to the Saṃhitā without having made an offering, shall have no merit nor fruit; they shall suffer poverty in birth after birth. (41)

Those who create obstacles for the discourse, the talkative, the mockers, those who compose other verses, and those whose intellects are intent on childish play and the like—[these are the adversaries]. (42)
Those who cause distraction during discourse or meditation and those who interrupt the sacred hearing (śruti),
their enjoyments, wives, wealth, and prosperity perish.
And those who are seated on high thrones, or likewise established in the vīrāsana posture, or seated upon lion-thrones, placing one foot atop the other; ||44||
But those who listen [to such teachings] are born as crows or trees; and those listeners who do not bow down are born as poisonous trees. ||45||
Moreover, those who listen while lying down are indeed like pythons; and those who sit on the same seat as the speaker become difficult-to-answer critics. (46)
Those who create obstacles are born for a hundred lifetimes as dogs, donkeys, lizards, and even pigs. (47)
Those who praise the discourse attain the eternal state;
as listeners of the discourses, they go to the eternal abode of Brahmā. (48)
One should give blankets, skins, garments, and an excellent seat;
such a giver of wealth shall indeed go to the heavenly world, the abode of Brahmā.
One who gives an auspicious cloth for a book shall become a partaker of happiness;
those who have committed great sins become purified through the attainment of knowledge. ||1.405.50||
Having thus heard the greatness of the act of listening to this narrative,
the gods, sages, perfected beings (siddhas), seers (ṛṣis), and likewise the ancestors (pitṛs)— [51]
The guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, the rivers, the streams, and the forests;
the principles (tattvas) and the earthly worlds—all reside on the auspicious abode of Veṅkaṭādri.
The women and men heard from the mouth of Śvetavārāha the most purifying narrative of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. (53)
To provide food for them, the cooks of Veṅkaṭeśvara guarded large cauldrons of sweet delicacies in the kitchens. (54)
Having fed countless gods, goddesses, and embodied beings,
that purifying sacred ford became known as Kaṭāhatīrtha.
Mahādeva alone understands the majesty of that sacred ford (tīrtha),
as do others established in the system of castes and stages of life, as well as even animals, birds, and the like.
By residing at the Kaṭāha-tīrtha, one attains the supreme state;
through the service of Kaṭāha, there is the destruction of sins for which no other expiation exists. (57)
By partaking of this water, the suffering of the afflicted shall be destroyed;
it is equivalent to bathing in Svāmipuṣkariṇī and beholding Varāha and Śrīśa. (58)
At Varāhatīrtha, one should always partake of food and drink that water, and listen to the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā. (59)
Constant service to the virtuous—these six are difficult to find even in the three worlds;
at the commencement of the narration of this Saṃhitā, the Lord Vārāha himself [spoke]. (1.405.60)
The four-armed Lord Hari emerged from the hollow of the earth;
O beloved, that sacred site known as Bhūkaṭāha exists right there.
Those who listen to it are satiated by that water which is nectar;
immersed in the narrative of the Saṃhitā, they are not overcome by ignorance.
Having heard this for a month, all the deities departed to their own abodes.
Then there was a brahmin named Keśava who had killed another brahmin.
Overcome by the sin of killing a Brahmin, he went to the Kaṭāha Tīrtha;
having bathed and drunk the water, he became pure through the power of that sacred site.
On the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā, his residence was in Vedagrāma;
there were thousands of Vedic Brahmins who were experts in the scriptures. (65)
This Keśava, a recipient of land-grants, was deceived by a wanton woman;
he abandoned his mother, his father, and even his devoted wife.
He remained devoted to unchaste women and lived in their houses;
after a long time had passed, Keśava was indeed abandoned by her because he had fallen ill.
And being hungry, he committed theft at the house of a brahmin;
having taken gold, he killed the brahmin with a sword.
Having taken wealth from her, he went to the house of that unchaste woman;
but being beaten and cast out by her, he went to his father's home.
The sin of killing a Brahmin clung to her back, and that Rākṣasī said:
"Having slain this Brahmin, he gave the wealth to an unchaste woman. (1.405.70)
The paramour she had cast out—a wicked soul who mocked his father and mother and abandoned his wife—has now returned to his father’s house. (71)
O best of the twice-born, you must indeed consider this one as no son;
abandon this killer of a brahmin, for if you do not abandon this son, [you will suffer]. (72)
"O twice-born one, I shall devour his wife, his wife, you, this son of yours, and your entire lineage; therefore, release this evil-minded man! (73)
I myself am the very personification of the murder of a Brahmin; I will not release him under any circumstances.
You ought not to destroy an entire lineage for the sake of a single individual. (74)
Having spoken thus, that Brahmahatyā coiled around her son Keśava;
intent on devouring his life-breaths, she became like a Rākṣasī.
Then all the family members wept with distressed minds;
at that moment, the sage Bharadvāja arrived there.
Having offered praise, the twice-born Padmanābha repeatedly begged for refuge:
"O portion of Kṛṣṇa, protect my son so that this act of slaughter may come to an end. (77)
"I have but one son; if he dies, there will be the destruction of my lineage, the cessation of the ancestral offerings to the ancestors, and the fall of these twice-born men into hell. (78)
"O Brahmin, extract that [mantra]; it will yield great merit.
Then Bharadvāja, who was a portion of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, spoke thus. (79)
"O Brahmin, this son of yours [resides] on the great mountain Veṅkaṭādri,
the enchanting abode of Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā."
"Having bathed in the waters of the Kaṭāha-tīrtha, one shall go to the abode of Hara.
Having taken these words to heart, the twice-born Padmanābha [spoke] to his son. (8.1)
Having led [him] to Veṅkaṭādri, he bathed in the waters of the Puṣkariṇī;
having bowed to Lord Varāha, he beheld Śrīnivāsa.
Having bowed to that divine celestial chariot, he went to the Kaṭāha-tīrtha;
there, together with his son, he drank the water and bathed in the water. (83)
At that moment, the slaughter was dissolved and the Blessed One appeared;
having arrived at this sacred ford, he said: "Those people who shall drink the water here—" (84)
"For them, both enjoyment and liberation shall indeed always exist.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa described his own majesty to him. (85)
This Veṅkaṭācala has been brought by me from the abode of Goloka;
there, Brahmā was thoroughly pleased with the sage Agastya as he performed penance.
He said, "O son, choose a boon; I shall grant whatever is in your heart.
Agastya then spoke to the Creator on the great mountain named Veṅkaṭa. (87)
"I must bring the Gaṅgā, who is eternally the purifier of the worlds.
As soon as she was remembered by Brahmā, the Gaṅgā arrived there immediately.
Agastya went forth from the peak;
the river followed him, making that region golden and resounding with the cries of cattle.
Then, awakened by the wind named Suvarṇamukharī,
she spread across the low-lying lands of Veṅkaṭādri and entered the ocean.
Agastya, having shown her the way to the place of his asceticism, dwelt happily there with that second river, which was a portion of the Gaṅgā.
There dwells the illustrious Veṅkaṭeśa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Lord of Śrī Rādhā, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Padminī, and Māṇikī. ||92||
He is the Lord of Padmā, who sports upon the banks of the Prabhāsa river;
accompanied by his friends, he constantly bathes and drinks water there. (93)
The gods, the liberated ones, and virtuous women bathe in these sacred fords on festival days;
she originates from the mountain of Agastya and flows toward the southern ocean.
Indeed, by taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, one purifies the regions;
even a niṣka-measure of water, when drunk, destroys mountains of sin. (95)
One who desires purity, security, and auspiciousness should constantly remember, bow to, praise, and worship the Suvarṇamukharī in his mind. (96)
Summoned by Brahmā and brought down to earth by Agastya, she is the goddess Suvarṇamukharīśvarī, who exists in personified form as a second manifestation. 97.
On its bank, by making a gift of land, a gift of wealth,
or the offering of a daughter according to the prescribed rites, an embodied being goes to the eternal Brahman.

Recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, austerity, charity, rites for the ancestors, and worship of the gods—whatever is performed on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī becomes a hundredfold more meritorious. (99)
Those partakers of merit who perform their ablutions in this [river] during the month of Agastyodaya shall dwell for a kalpa in the abode of the gods.
Those who give golden images of Agastya indeed go to the eternal Brahman;
Agastya, born from a pitcher, is the leader of Govardhana.

May the Lord, who brought the Vindhya mountains to a standstill, who possesses the power to turn the ocean into a mere mouthful, and who has the capacity to purify the waters while carrying the Suvarṇamukharī river,
attain great joy through this gift of mine.
Having spoken thus, he should give an image adorned with matted hair, a deer skin, and so forth.
One should give [an image] endowed with a staff and a water-pot, seated in the svastika posture,
wearing bark garments, holding a rosary in her hand, and most beautiful,
together with Nārāyaṇa, for the purification of sins.
One should remember all the sacred fords (tīrthas) at the time of giving; listen, O beloved.
At its base is Agastyatīrtha and Śaṅkara as Agastyeśvara;
one should enter the water there during the northern transit of the sun (uttarāyaṇa).
The fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices, which bestows heaven, is obtained there;
the sacred ford (tīrtha) extends one krośa downward and is named after the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Having bathed there, a person becomes liberated from the three debts.
