Beyond that, at a distance of two yojanas, is the excellent confluence of the river Veṇā.
There, the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices is obtained by bathing.
Four yojanas from there to the east is the excellent Liṅga known as Astyeśvara.
Half a yojana from there, indeed, is the confluence of the Vyāghrapadā;
there, at Śaṅkhatīrtha, Śiva as Śaṅkheśvara shines resplendently.
Formerly established by the sage Śaṅkha as a destroyer of sins,
the Kalyā river, which also destroys sin, flows there into the low-lying ground.
Where the beautiful Brahma-śilā indeed stands in the middle of the river,
half a yojana to the north of that place, the Vaikṭa mountain shines resplendent.
Surrounding that very mountain, which is one krośa in height, there are other mountains as well:
Añjana, Ananta, Vṛṣabha, Nīla, Varāha, and Kesara. (113)
He took up residence on Nārāyaṇācala, the venerable Veṅkaṭādri;
because the Boar (Vārāha) dwelt there, that mountain is called Vārāhakṣetra.
On the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī, on Mount Veṅkaṭa,
the Blessed Lord Hari dwells, accompanied by Śrī, accompanied by Bhū, and accompanied by Padminī.
He was endowed with victory, grace, the *bakula* flower, and splendor;
he was joined with Pārvatī, radiance, Lakṣmī, ruby, and playful charm.
It is served by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Munis, Mānavas, and Dānavas;
indeed, the desires of those who remember it are surely fulfilled.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this auspicious circle of sacred fords has been narrated to you;
by hearing or reciting it, both heaven and liberation shall indeed be attained.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Six Holy Tirthas on Mount Veṅkaṭādri, the Worship of Vyāsa named Śveta—the Narrator of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā—, the Liberation of the Brahmin Keśava from the Sin of Brāhmaṇa-Slaughter, the Bringing of the Gaṅgā-like Suvarṇamukharī River, and the Enumeration of Other Tirthas," within the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of devoted wives in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord of Śrī Ramā Kamalā, on the highly meritorious Veṅkaṭādri, how did you first manifest? Tell me all that wonder.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe his majesty in brief.
Of all beings indeed, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa am I, the source.
In Goloka I am named Kṛṣṇa; in Vaikuṇṭha I am Nārāyaṇa;
in the immortal abode I am Vāsudeva; and in the infinite, unmanifest realm I am Bhūman.
In the supreme, imperishable abode, I am the Supreme Person;
I am Hiraṇyagarbha, Vairāja, and Sadāśiva.
I am the blessed Mahāviṣṇu with a thousand heads, and I also become Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with a single head upon the earth. (5)
By my light the entire world shines; I am the sun.
By my knowledge indeed is creation pervaded, and I am that as well.
I indeed dwell as the Inner Controller, present within the hearts of all;
I am Hari, Sadāśiva, Brahmā, Kāṃbhareya, and Janārdana.
I alone am these various manifestations; thousands of forms arise from me.
Whenever I desire to perform a virtuous deed, then I descend to the surface of the earth.
I create this through the quality of passion (rajas), and I sustain it through truth (sattva);
I withdraw it through darkness (tamas) alone, and I sleep through the power of slumber (nidrā).
In the past, I assumed the form of a boar by my own will as a mere sport, in order to bring back the earth that had sunk into the depths of the water.

Having reduced them to a state of mud by means of the supernatural powers of my fangs' tips, I gathered them together and brought them here to establish them upon the water so that they might have a place to stand.
Just as water, when confined, does not destroy the earth,
so did I establish the elephants of the quarters and Śeṣa as a tortoise for the sake of providing a support.
By my command, Brahmā fashioned the universe as it was before;
and in every kalpa, for the sake of protection, I sport upon the surface of the earth.
Assuming the form of a boar, I then went to Mount Veṅkaṭa and dwelt at the holy site of Svāmipuṣkariṇī together with Brahmā.
O beloved, having been thus entreated by the one in his original form, I became invisible to him;
for there was indeed a king named Śaṅkha, born of the Haihaya lineage.
The king was a supreme Vaiṣṇava devotee who constantly engaged in the ninefold worship; he always listened to the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Nevertheless, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa did not appear before him directly;
therefore, with a mind unsatisfied, he reflected upon this repeatedly. (17)
"How indeed might the Blessed One come within the range of my eyes?"—
as he was thinking thus, the glorious Blessed One spoke within his heart.
"Go to Śrī Veṅkaṭādri and worship [the Lord] for a thousand years;
remaining invisible, I shall become visible to you and to Agastya.
Having propitiated me through your steadfastness in austerity, you both shall obtain my vision."
Having entrusted the kingdom to his son Vajra, Śaṅkha went to Śrī Veṅkaṭa.
Agastya also approached that mountain, surrounded by hundreds of sages;
he performed a circumambulation of it, which was inhabited by gods beginning with Brahmā.
All the gods and the sages, such as Sanaka and others whose wealth is their austerity,
await the direct vision of Hari just like the Pot-born Sage (Agastya).
Having gathered together, they went to where Śaṅkha, the king of devotees, was;
on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī, they beheld King Śaṅkha.
Seated there, they all honored one another with great eagerness, being devoted to the chanting of Govinda and having Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as their very soul. (24)
And at the end of the third watch of the night, they saw a dream:
the Lord himself, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, accompanied by Padminī.
They beheld Hari, who had arrived to grant a boon;
then, having bathed in the lotus pond at dawn, they praised the Imperishable One.
The eight-syllable mantra "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa" appeared before them as a single, most wonderful radiance.
Having seen Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa there, they praised him with reverence:
"Victory to you, O Viṣṇu! Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa! Victory to you, O Śrīkṛṣṇa Keśava! (28)
Victory to you, O Upholder of the Earth, Govinda, Lord of Veṅkaṭādri! Victory indeed!
All have truly been made successful by the granting of this divine vision. 29.
O Lord, bestower of grace upon devotees, always make your dwelling here;
and make this Suvarṇamukharī river the purifier of the three worlds.
"Always remaining on this mountain, grant the fulfillment of our desired aims.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa spoke these pleasing words: "So be it."
By him, Kṛṣṇa, the Suvarṇamukharī was made his own abode,
and the mountain Vaikuṇṭhaśaila was made his eternal dwelling place.
"O beloved, Hari has been born as the bestower of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Kṛṣṇa Hari said to Śaṅkha: 'I am pleased with your devotion.'"
Remaining in the world of Indra for an eon, served by hosts of apsarases and having enjoyed manifold pleasures, you shall thereafter come to my own world.
Having thus granted the boon to the gods and bestowed upon them their eternal abode,
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Kamalā, vanished right there.
Thus, having assumed a gentle form, Kṛṣṇa dwells on Veṅkaṭa;
likewise, he resides at Nārāyaṇa, Veṅkaṭādri, and Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
By remembering sacred sites such as Kaṭāha and others, they indeed become pure;
they shall attain Puruṣottama, the Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, Bhū, and Padminī. ||37||
Listen, Lakṣmī: formerly, a certain virtuous woman named Añjanā, who was a great devotee of Viṣṇu, being childless, began to perform penance. (38)
A certain sage named Mataṅga spoke to her as she remained engaged in asceticism:
"Tell me, O beautiful one, what do you desire with this severe penance? (39)
"Añjanā said: 'My father, Kesarī, a rākṣasa by birth, performed a severe penance, meditating upon Śiva for the sake of obtaining a son.'"
Śiva and Śivā, seated upon their bull and acting as bestowers of grace, arrived;
and Śiva said, "In this birth, we shall not grant you a son. (41)
But by my merit, I grant you a daughter renowned throughout the worlds;
through her son, you shall consider yourself to have a son and be happy. (42)
Having thus granted him the boon, Hara vanished on that very spot.
Thereafter, my father, the Rākṣasa, being satisfied, went home.
In due time, I was born to his wife and was married.
In the great city named Kiṣkindhā, by her husband known as Kesarin,
the vows of the month of Māgha, the vows of the month of Kārttika,
the vows of Vaiśākha, and the Cāturmāsya vows were observed. || 44 || 75 ||
She performed the ninefold devotion to Nārāyaṇa,
as well as the offering of food at Śālagrāma, the gift of cows, the offering of lamps,
the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of clothing, the gift of land, and the gift of water.
Out of a desire for the fruit of having virtuous sons, I have performed the offering of fruits and flowers;
yet, despite performing every kind of meritorious deed in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
I have still not obtained a son, and for that reason I remain engaged in ascetic penance.
Then Mataṅga said to that virtuous female ascetic, "To the south of here is the mountain Ghanācala, the dwelling place of Nṛsiṃha.
It is ten yojanas away; ten yojanas further to the east of that [is the place]."
There is the river Suvarṇamukharī, and upstream from it is Vṛṣabhācala. At its summit lies the beautiful lake Svāmipuṣkariṇī.
Go there, bathe according to the prescribed rites, and behold Keśava in the form of Varāha.
"Having paid obeisance to Veṅkaṭeśa, proceed to the celestial Gaṅgā;
and there, O Vaiṣṇavī, perform penance directed toward Vāyu.
Having heard this, that ascetic woman indeed went to the Veṅkaṭa mountain.
He duly visited sacred fords and performed most rigorous penance.
Then, on the bank of the celestial Gaṅgā, the Wind-god appeared before him;
for the purpose of granting a boon, he said, "O son, choose [a gift]," and she (the goddess) spoke thus.
Having said, "I shall become your son here," the Wind-god vanished.
Then the great sages, having taken up the seed of Śaṅkara, assembled there;
and at that time, Vāyu assumed the form of a lion.
He took him into his ear and gave him to Añjanī; from her he was born as a son.
As soon as he was born, he was a youth, possessed of the memory of his past lives, and surpassing the wind in strength;
he became Hanumān, the excellent son of that ascetic woman.
On the fourteenth lunar day, when the sun was in Aries and in conjunction with the Citrā asterism,
the Wind-god himself appeared on the banks of the Suvarṇamukharī.
At that time, whatever bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites performed here become inexhaustible.
The gift of food, the gift of clothing, the gift of gold, and the offering of a daughter;
the gift of a Śālagrāma stone, the gift of a cow, the gift of land, the gift of a water-shed, the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of grain, and the offering of a house. || 1.406.59-60 ||
To that person who gives there scents, campaka flowers, and the like; umbrellas, fans, and chowries; betel, camphor, and so forth; household utensils;
and a thousand divine garments—
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures, he shall be a possessor of enjoyments even in the heavenly world;
thereafter, becoming a sovereign emperor and then a Brahmin, he attains liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I described to you the wonders of Veṅkaṭādri.
From hearing and reciting this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.
Listen now to another divine narrative centered upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (64)
Out of affection for you, I shall tell [the story] of her who was devoted to her husband:
once, Śrī Veṅkaṭādri thought of going to Meru. (65)
As soon as he flew up from the earth with his two wings,
a great earthquake occurred, leading to the destruction of many living beings.
All living beings cried out and went to the Boar for refuge, saying:
"O Blessed One, we are perishing through this rising of the sun, left without a protector."
"O Lord of the Earth, grant us protection; O Master, establish us properly. Thus entreated, the Lord Varāha was indeed Nārāyaṇa himself.
He comforted the living beings and reassured Indra, who held his thunderbolt;
meanwhile, Indra, the slayer of Paka, arrived with his vajra raised high.
Upon seeing Indra, Veṅkaṭādri became terrified and trembled;
he then went for refuge to Viṣṇu in the form of the Boar.
Fearing death, he offered praise; the Blessed One himself said to him:
"If ever you should go through the path of the sky on your two wings, do not come to me. (71)
"Then I shall provide protection; remain steadfast here, O Mountain.
Thus addressed, he bowed and became motionless and very firm. (72)
The boar became invisible, and Mahendra went to his own abode;
by resorting to the boar, his wings were not cut off by Indra.
Then, on one occasion, that mountain indeed reflected in his heart:
"I have indeed come from Goloka and have dwelt here for many years."
"Indeed, I shall go into the presence of Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of beholding Goloka.
Having thus reflected, he [set out] on the earth on the occasion of Kṛṣṇa-janmāṣṭamī.
Indeed, all the holy fords gathered at Kuśasthalī on the Gomatī to bathe;
all the sages, rivers, streams, and deities went there as well. (76)
Agastya and the others went to the confluence of the Gomatī;
then, seeing that place to be secluded, they set their minds on departing.
There the earth trembled, and living beings perished from that shaking;
at that moment, there was a certain poor female ascetic present there. (78)
The Brahmin woman was constantly devoted to the service of Brahmins and remained faithful to her vows;
she was named Suvarṇarekhā, and Hiraṇyā was likewise her sister.
Hiraṇyā was a great and virtuous maiden, an ascetic;
Suvarṇarekhā was her husband, whose name was Nārāyaṇa.
Having drunk water from the feet of the twice-born Nārāyaṇa, she spoke to him.
"Veṅkaṭādri has wings, yet he was prevented from flying away in the past.
If he were to fly up again, our death would surely follow; therefore, by my husband's command, I shall certainly paralyze him in every way. (81–82)
"Then Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa and the others will surely become angry and bring us suffering;
therefore, O Lord, tell me what must be done here.
Thus addressed, he said to his beloved, "O beautiful woman, do as you wish."
"O people here, if your devotion to your husband is indeed firm, then all shall meet with defeat before him.
Do not fear, O virtuous lady; rather, instruct the mountain. || 84-85 ||
Having received these words from her beloved,
the virtuous woman then said: "If I am indeed established in my duty as a devoted wife,
then let the king of mountains here have wings within the earth."
"May they both remain forever rendered inert, deprived of the power of their wings,
and having attained oneness with the earth, so that they can never fly again.
As soon as these words were spoken, those two birds became motionless and paralyzed.
Deprived of their power, they were stationed within the earth;
then Veṅkaṭādri, with humility, repeatedly begged for forgiveness.
Satī said, "This place has always belonged to Nārāyaṇa as well as to me."
"Therefore, our residence is not yet determined; we shall go to Mount Raivata.
You must always remain inactive; do not be a fickle mountain, O Cañcalaparvata, otherwise the Lord will surely bring about your destruction."
"O winged one, remain always thus; let there be no more flying.
Out of compassion, I grant life to your wings; do not grieve any longer. (92)
"Crores of locusts and parrots shall appear upon your two wings;
empowered, they will fly up into the sky. (93)
In the grassy glades, forests, and wilds here, locusts and parrots,
having consumed the medicinal herbs, shall attain dissolution within their wings.
Thus, I grant you indeed the state of being endowed with life within those wings.
Having spoken thus and having made Veṅkaṭa firm, the twice-born Nārāyaṇa departed;
the devoted wife Svarṇarekhā went to Mount Raivata.
The eternally devoted wife Svarṇarekhā became a river. || 95-96 ||
Nārāyaṇa became a lake and dwelt eternally on the mountain;
thus Nārāyaṇa and Svarṇarekhā were indeed husband and wife.
Indeed, those two divine ones, appearing in the form of holy fords (tīrtha), made their abode on Mount Raivata,
where even Viṣṇu, as Dāmodara, remained devoted to his wife.
"Indeed, the śrāddha performed gave supreme satisfaction to those conscious beings.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this wondrous account been told to you. (99)

Thus ends the four hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Varāha through Agastya and Śaṅkha on Veṅkaṭādri, the Attainment of a Son as Hanumān by Tapasvinī there, the Paralysis of the Wings of Veṅkaṭādri, and the Arrival of Tvaritā, Rekhā, and Nārāyaṇahṛdaya at Raivatācala," within the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga and the majesty of the devoted wife in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious story of Jayantī, the daughter of Indra,
who performed the service of penance for the sake of Śukra’s devotion to his wife.
In the battles between the gods and the Dānavas, whenever the gods were accompanied by their armies,
the host of Dānavas was impossible for the Daityas to conquer.
He praised Śukrācārya in such a way that the victory of the Daityas would be achieved;
then Śukra, perceiving the agreement that brought about the refuge of the gods, [acted accordingly].
Having abandoned all the Daityas, Śukra approached the gods;
then the Daityas challenged Śukra, who had gone over to the side of the gods.
"Why have you abandoned us while we looked on and taken refuge with the gods?
We are unable to remain upon the earth; we shall enter the netherworld (rasātala). (5)
"Without you as our protector, O Guru, how shall we remain?
Thus addressed, he spoke to the dejected Daityas, consoling them with his voice: || 6 ||
"Do not fear; I shall protect you with my splendor stationed there.
Indeed, the powers of mantras, herbs, wealth, supernatural attainments, and elixirs abide in me."
Whether that [wealth] exists among the gods or not, a fourth part of it in its entirety shall belong to me;
I will bestow it upon you, and by means of it, you shall be protected.
Having thoroughly understood this conduct, the gods, desiring to seize him entirely,
held a consultation to bring him under their control through the power of counsel.
The gods commenced their studies in the presence of Śukra;
he gave them a little here and a little there, yet even that remained incomplete.
As long as Śukra did not teach this [knowledge] to the Daityas,
the gods, having slain the Daityas, sent them indeed to Pātāla.
Then the Daityas, being dejected in spirit, fled toward Kāvya;
even then, the gods pursued the Daityas without hesitation.
Then Śukra was unable to perform a protection ritual or provide the mantras;
however, he spoke thus to the Daityas: "It is my opinion that there should be no war. (1.3)
"O gods, since you are now powerless while I am currently most powerful, wait for the proper time; as for me, I shall go to perform austerities."
"O Mahādeva, having obtained from the god Maheśvara these supreme mantras that are irresistible and bring victory, I shall go to him for the sake of a boon. (15)
"When we fight the gods, then you shall indeed attain victory. Then the Asuras, abandoning their scriptures, spoke to the gods at that time.
"We shall practice austerities, peaceful and clad in bark garments in the forest.
Having heard this, even the gods desisted from their assault upon him.
Then Śukra said to the Daityas: "Go, you, to the netherworld (rasātala);
for the sake of your purpose, remain there engaged in asceticism for some time. (18)
Having spoken thus, the preceptor of the Daityas went to Śambhu on the Himālaya;
there he performed a severe penance for a full thousand years.
With his head downward in the pit of the earth and his feet in the sky,
he became a celibate student and performed severe penance.
Remaining motionless and even without food, he mentally recited the Śiva-mantra.
Then, after some time, the Daityas arrived, intending to remain upon the earth.
Then, struck by the gods, they went to the mother of Kāvya for refuge;
she said to them, "May there be eternal fearlessness for you."
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas! For you who dwell in my presence, there shall be no fear; this I declare."
The gods went there again to strike down the Daityas by force;
Khyāti, becoming enraged, said to the gods, "I shall destroy you and Mahendra!"
Having done this, that yoginī, whose wealth was her asceticism, paralyzed Mahendra with a spell and immobilized him through a malevolent rite.
Then the gods fled upon seeing Indra brought under control;
thereupon Viṣṇu, having instantly drawn Mahendra back into his own form, [departed]. (26)
As he was leading her up to heaven, Khyāti, filled with rage upon seeing that she had been protected by Viṣṇu, spoke these words there: || 27 ||
"O Maghavan, I shall now forcibly burn you along with Viṣṇu;
at that very moment, Viṣṇu seized his discus for the sake of his own protection in this calamity. (28)
Then, having understood that Khyāti’s cruel intent was to bring about the end of his life,
Sudarśana, out of fear of her, indeed severed Khyāti’s head.
Seeing that murder of his wife at that time, Bhṛgu became enraged and then cursed Viṣṇu, the slayer of his wife Khyāti.
"Since you, though knowing the Dharma, have slain this woman who was not to be killed, therefore you too shall suffer the death of your head at the beginning of the kalpa. (31)
Thus, having become Kṛṣṇa due to that curse, he was indeed Gaṇeśa;
and by the hand of Śaṅkara, he obtained the severing of his head.
Then Bhagunā quickly placed her head upon his body and said, "O Goddess, you have been slain by Viṣṇu; I shall restore you to life. (33)
If I have fully observed the religious vow of a devoted wife, by that truth, and if I speak the truth regarding Jīva, [may my head not split]. (34)
Having sprinkled her with cool water, he said, "Live!
As soon as he uttered the word, "Arise," Khyāti was restored to life.
"Excellent! Excellent! the gods and others cried out in every direction;
however, Indra did not find peace because of his fear of Śukra’s fame. (36)
Having deliberated on how to create an obstacle to Śukra’s asceticism, Indra said to his daughter Jayantī:
"O daughter, you have been entrusted by me to Śukra. (37)
"Go; you have been given to him, so exert yourself for my sake.
Śukra is performing a severe penance for the purpose of propitiating Śambhu. (38)
He strives intensely for the sake of the gods' destruction and for the sake of [evil] spells; go and subdue him by means of removing his fatigue and other such comforts. (39)
With various such services, including beds and other comforts that were pleasing to his mind,
Jayantī, having been thus addressed, remained steadfast in her father’s command.
She went to that mountain where he was engaged in terrible asceticism;
there the lovely maiden stood before him as he sat with his head downward, absorbed in poetry.
Saying, "I am your bride," she attended upon him with pleasing words and by massaging his limbs and other such services.
At the appropriate times, she spent many years serving her skin with pleasant things such as desired objects, all of which were conducive to the practice of her vows. 43.
When a full thousand years had passed, that virtuous woman, devoted solely to her husband, remembered Śaṅkara, wondering, "How can he not be pleased? (44)
"If Śambhu is indeed not pleased, I shall surely consume him here with a curse"—
as she fell into such a rage, Hara arrived at that very spot.
Your husband has declared that he will perform fierce austerities for the destruction of the gods; therefore, I do not come into his sight.
"But, drawn by your exceedingly powerful devotion to your husband, I have come to grant you a boon; tell me what I shall do for you. (47)
Jayantī said: "She was entrusted to me by my father for his own purpose; indeed, that task must be performed, as well as the task of my husband. (48)
She should practice the dharma of him to whom she has been given;
that which is his benefit, his welfare, and indeed his prosperity. (49)
The husband is said to be the entire possession of women who have taken refuge in him;
surely, when there is opposition to him, no good can ever come to a woman.
Therefore, becoming well-disposed toward your husband, perform all that is appropriate as I have instructed;
for a daughter who seeks her father's welfare should never cause suffering to her husband. ||51||
O Śambhu, act appropriately so that the welfare of both may be secured;
for I have performed service toward this poem, filled with devotion. (52)
However, no obstacle was indeed created for his austerity or celibacy, because I have become his lawful wife, granted by Indra. (53)
"How can I create an obstacle to his asceticism through desire? Therefore, having restrained my passion, I truly did not give way to delight. (54)
The perfection of his asceticism has been attained, since it serves for my own welfare;
indeed, I have maintained my devotion to my husband and have never done anything undesirable.
"By that very devotion to her husband, she shall fulfill the desire of your heart.
Having spoken thus to Kāvya, that object of his love fell silent. (56)
Then Mahādeva, being pleased yet startled, said to Śukra:
"O Śukra, such is this maiden for whose sake you have surrendered your life. (57)
Indeed, for a full thousand years you have stood constantly at my side;
even so, you have not abandoned your vow of celibacy.
Even by that devoted wife, her unsteady mind was restrained;
for though she has always been sixteen years of age, even now she remains as if playing.
This unharmed woman, devoted to her husband, is truly blessed and remains under your protection;
may they too enjoy the reputation of being blessed, for you have in every way reached the further shore.
This vow has been performed by you alone and by no one else;
therefore, indeed, by means of your austerity, intelligence, sacred learning, and strength, [you have attained this]. 61.
And by your splendor alone, you shall surpass all the gods,
through the power of your wife’s devotion to her husband and her lifelong celibacy.
You shall attain everything you desire; this must not be told to anyone.
The couple shall go happily to the lordship over subjects and the lordship over wealth.
"Accept invincibility and the Sañjīvanī [science] of true knowledge.
Thus addressed, the god Śukra, remaining with his head hanging downwards, offered praise.
Salutations to you who possess the form of Brahmā, the fulfiller of the desires of your devotees;
salutations to you who are instantly gratified, and salutations to you who are eternally contented.
Homage be to you who are eternally satisfied, to you who are clad in the directions;
homage to you, the formidable Rudra, the Great God. 66.
Salutation to the fierce one, the wielder of the Pināka bow, to Śambhu;
salutation to you, the hunter of deer, the ascetic, and the Kirāta. ||67||
Salutations to the three-eyed one, whose forehead is marked by the moon, who has the form of a *liṅga*;
salutations again and again to Sadāśiva, to Śarva, and to the Lord of Bhava.
Salutations again and again to you, the gentle one, the witness, the husband of Satī;
to the blue-throated one, the fierce one, the one born in an instant, the wielder of the trident.
Salutations to you, the Sovereign, tawny-hued, clad in animal skins;
salutations to you, the Lord of beasts and the Lord of all beings.
Salutations to the one with eight-fold stature, whose essence is Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
salutations again and again to you, the husband of Pārvatī, the radiant Lord.
Salutations to you from all sides, O Lord, who are present in all directions and in all beings;
salutations again and again everywhere to the giver of fruit and the creator of bliss.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu ceased; he said, "Your penance has become complete; arise and choose the boon you desire. (73)
Nevertheless, Śukra did not rise, and Śambhu vanished from sight;
seeing this, Jayantī spoke to him as the occasion required.
O Lord, why do you not arise? Why do you remain indifferent?
Why indeed do you pay no heed at all to the words of Śambhu? (75)
As soon as the ascetic rose from the ground upon hearing the sound made by his wife,
he no longer beheld Śambhu, for the Lord had vanished from sight.
He fell into extreme distress and experienced intense grief, for once that which has arrived is abandoned, union with it again is indeed difficult to obtain. || 77 ||
Having been thus informed by the celestial voice, that Kāvya,
having respectfully taken Jayantī along with the merit of his austerities, set out toward his home.
Śukra went to his wife’s house and remained there entirely hidden for ten years,
enjoying pleasures with Jayantī in the palace.
Devayānī, the daughter of Yayāti, was born of her;
then all the sons of Diti, knowing that Śukra had achieved his purpose, [approached him].
Desirous of seeing their own preceptor, they went to his house;
not finding him there, they then returned to their respective homes, while Bṛhaspati remained.
For ten years, for the sake of her satisfaction and out of a desire for her welfare,
he assumed the form of Śukra and challenged the asuras.
He said to those who had arrived, "I shall give you the sciences (vidyās) spoken by Śaṅkara.
Delighted, they approached him for the sake of the sciences for ten years.
Indeed, you have been taught various things and deceived by your teacher;
Nala shall see his own priests ten years hence. (84)
Having been seen by his preceptor in his true form, they were confounded;
but when they had been thus deceived by Kāvya in the form of a poem, Kāvya then spoke to them.
"Know me to be Kāvya; this Bṛhaspati is not Kāvya.
Then Bṛhaspati said, "I am Kāvya; he is certainly not he. (86)
"However, for the sake of deceiving you, my preceptor has returned from my country after ten years; let it not be thought that this man is Kāvya. (87)
Having heard these words of the two who were identical in form,
the Dānavas gazed upon them both and then became utterly bewildered.
The wood held by Hālala will not be released until death;
it is impossible to alter this, for destiny is indeed most powerful.
Although they were awakened by Śukra, they did not heed his words at all, saying:
"He who has been our lord and ruler for ten years without ceasing—" || 1.407.90 ||
"This Kāvya is indeed our guru; he is certainly not a newcomer.
Having thus resolved, those Daityas were deluded by their long-standing habituation. || 91 ||
They said, "Go quickly, O mind; our teacher is the instructor.
Whether he be Bhārgava or Āṅgirasa, this Blessed One is our guru. (92)
Then Śukra became enraged and cursed the Dānavas:
"All of you shall indeed have your splendor destroyed and shall experience great suffering. (93)

Cursed by Śukra, the Asuras were defeated, while Bṛhaspati achieved his purpose. Then, O Lakṣmī, they vanished from that place; thereafter, those Asuras became utterly bewildered and said, "We have been deceived."
Placing Prahlāda at their head, they went to the house of Śukrācārya.
They said to him, "Forgive us; show us favor, O Bhārgava! If you do not grant us your favor, we shall enter the netherworld (rasātala). || 96 ||
Kāvya reflected: "Even without a patron, I have falsely [claimed] to be so;
therefore, I must protect them, for I am honored and served by them. (97)
Then he said to them: "You must not fear, nor must you go to the netherworld (rasātala).
When your light has vanished today, you shall regain it once again."
"Having conquered the gods but once, you shall enter Pātāla.
Thus addressed, the Asuras, filled with joy, set out to conquer the Suras. || 99 ||
At that time, a terrible battle indeed took place between the gods and the asuras;
the asuras defeated the gods, and the gods, in turn, held a consultation.
"By inviting those two preceptors of the Daityas, Śaṇḍa and Marka, to the sacrifice, we shall take refuge in them, honor them, and worship them; thus victory will be ours. (101)
Summoned by the gods, the two were told: "O twice-born ones, abandon the asuras;
we shall serve you once we have conquered the dānavas."
Having thus made this secret agreement, the gods indeed waged a terrible war;
the Dānavas, abandoned by Ṣaṇḍa and Marka, were utterly defeated.
Overcome by the curse of Kāvya, those Dānavas entered the netherworld (rasātala);
thus were the gods rendered devoid of effort, leaving the Dānavas in a state of distress.
Jayantī, who causes delusion, constantly served her own husband; Śukrācārya, for his part, forgot even the prosperity of the Daityas.
Thus was Indra’s task accomplished by Jayantī, who is victorious by nature;
and indeed, the powerlessness of the Daityas was brought about by her through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Through her vows, the maiden established her husband’s invincibility against Mahendra and others, his victory over them, and the inferiority of the Daityas.
Nārāyaṇa, though established in the supreme Brahman, the imperishable abode,
assumes a body characterized by righteousness at the proper time and performs the work of protection.
In the first [kalpa], he was known as Patnīvrata, the one who dwells in Goloka; thereafter, Kṛṣṇa was born as Nārāyaṇa on Mount Himavat, joined with Nara.
Again he became Yajña, the son of Dharma, that very same righteous one;
he became Narasiṃha, and he also became Vāmana.
Dattātreya, Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Āditya, Vāsudeva, Vedavyāsa, and likewise Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa appeared. (111)
Likewise, Kalkī, the son of Kambharā, is that very Blessed One himself;
he is born at the turn of the age (yuga) for the protection of the dharma of the gods.
I am indeed that very one, and my portions are born by the thousands day after day; they arise in hidden forms, bestowing happiness. 113.
They bear the marks of a bow, a discus, a banner, a fish, and a svastika on their hands;
they have lines rising above the three ankles, and their feet possess the half-moon, the wheel, and the lotus.
By serving whose feet embodied beings become virtuous;
they become like gods, bestowing liberation, and are indeed liberated—of this there is no doubt. (115)

Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supernatural powers of the renowned Jayantī, which, when performed through devotion to one's husband, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon reading or hearing them. (116)

Thus ends the four hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Stupefaction of Indra and Others Caused by Khyāti’s Devotion to Her Husband, the Destruction of Khyāti’s [Pride] by Viṣṇu, the Restoration of Khyāti by Bhṛgu, the Austerities of Śukra, the Giving of His Daughter Jayantī to Śukra by Indra for the Purpose of Obstructing Him, Her Daughter Devayānī, the Interruption of His Penance, the Defeat of the Asuras, and the Greatness of Devotion to One’s Husband," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the great power of devotion to one's husband,
as demonstrated by Mālavatī, the wife of Upabarhaṇa.
When Brahmā, having fashioned the creation, created Nārada, he spoke to him for the sake of continuing the flow of creation; however, Nārada forbade it.
The father is declared to be the giver of liberation, and the son is considered one who attains liberation;
the brother, mother, husband, and wife are always auspicious bestowers of devotion.
Those householders who bestow the bonds of illusion are not worthy of enlightenment;
yet you yourself, O Brahmā, though possessed of knowledge, employ me in that which is illusory.
"I shall not grasp at illusion, nor shall I even create;
I shall worship the supreme Brahman and deliver you and the others. (5)
"I shall make your sonship meaningful; do not harbor grief, O Creator of the Universe.
Having been addressed thus, Brahmā, his eyes copper-red with rage, cursed Nārada:
"After you have met your death, become a servant accompanied by a wife."
O Nārada, you shall repeatedly become a burden of karma, devoid of knowledge.
Then Nārada said to him, "O Lord, my son, do not act thus;
for you too shall never attain honor anywhere in this cycle of existence."
Thus addressed and entreated by Sanaka and the others, Brahmā then spoke again to his son: "Indeed, you shall obtain me once more in the fourth [birth]."
O son, you will always be devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya) there;
for that long, you will undoubtedly be occupied with a wife and a home.
Having spoken thus, Nārada vanished; he then became Mārīca and attained the status of being the son of Viśvāvasu, the king of the Gandharvas.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I tell you: in ancient times, there was indeed a Vaiṣṇava Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa, who was Viśvāvasu. (1-2)
Deprived of a son by his past actions, he performed penance for Śambhu;
Vasiṣṭha then bestowed upon him the twelve-syllable mantra.
He recited this for a hundred years at Puṣkara,
and for exactly that long he beheld Śiva before him, with a gracious countenance and mounted upon his bull.
"Choose a boon," Śiva said to him; thereupon, O son, he requested supreme devotion to Śrī Hari from that most devoted Vaiṣṇava.

Śiva said: "I am pleased; let it be so for you, may there be auspiciousness. You have achieved your purpose through this one boon; anything else would be merely chewing over what has already been chewed."
O child, he whose devotion to Hari is very firm and auspicious in every way is capable of protecting and creating the entire universe by his mere play.
If a virtuous man has a son who is a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu,
they indeed deliver ten million ancestors of his lineage with ease.
A man who has achieved his purpose through one boon—alas, why seek a second? Is there no satisfaction for a person even with a second boon in this auspicious occasion?
Devotion to Hari, service to Hari, a son who is a supreme Vaiṣṇava,
long life, virtuous character, and perpetual, stable youth.
"Obtain this boon: a wise, handsome, excellent teacher who is devoted to his guru and has conquered his senses"; having said this, Śambhu vanished.
Viśvāvasu went to his home on Mount Gandhamādana;
there, Nārada obtained an auspicious birth from his wife. 22.
The preceptor Vasiṣṭha gave him the name Upabarhaṇa.
In this context, the prefix *upa* signifies "superiority," while *barhaṇaḥ* is a masculine noun meaning "one who is worthy of honor.
Thus, because the child was superior among those worthy of honor, he was named Upabarhaṇa.
Upabarhaṇa also performed difficult austerities for a long time.
Then, having reached the bank of the Gaṇḍakī, the fifty Gandharva maidens beheld him, who possessed eternal youth, and they chose him as their husband.
Having taken them, that lustful youth enjoyed with them for two hundred thousand years.
Once, he went to the assembly of Brahmā and sang a story.
Then, beholding Rambhā, he became repeatedly agitated;
he quickly abandoned the musical performance and fell into a swoon upon the floor of the assembly hall.
The gods laughed aloud, and Brahmā, out of anger, cursed him:
"Go to the womb of a Śūdra and cast off this Gāndharva body! (28)
"In time, through association with a Vaiṣṇava, you shall become my son;
that Gandharva Upabarhaṇa then cast off that body. (29)
Having pierced the six centers— the mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddha, and ājñācakras— she emerged from her body.
Through yoga, he attained Brahman while remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa in his mind;
and all the wives and kinsmen, having lamented, wept bitterly.
Then, in the midst of fifty women, the virtuous Mālāvatī wept loudly and intensely, placing her beloved upon her breast.
The daughters of Citraratha and his wives wept;
Mālāvatī lamented: "O Kṛṣṇa, you are the Lord of the worlds! (33)
"I am not outside the world; O Lord, why do you not protect me? O gods who consume the sacrificial offerings, you are capable of consuming ghee on this earth! (34)
In an instant, by virtue of my chastity, I shall deprive them of their share in the sacrifice;
O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of the world, I am not outside the universe. (35)
"If my devotion to my husband is indeed complete and unbroken, then quickly restore my beloved to life; otherwise, I shall curse you. (36)
"O Prajāpati, due to the curse of your son, you shall be unworthy of worship on the surface of the earth;
I myself shall bring about your lack of authority here in this act of creation. (37)
"O Śambhu, I shall indeed cause the loss of your knowledge through a curse;
and I shall surely cause the loss of Dharma's merit in an instant.
Furthermore, I shall cast Yama’s authority far away; of this there is no doubt."
By truth, I shall curse Time and the most cruel Daughter of Death.
Here and now, I curse them all to be without old age and disease;
for my husband has never experienced death through either disease or old age.
Having spoken thus, she went to the bank of the Kauśikī river specifically to curse them.
Seeing her prepared to utter a curse, Brahmā, preceded by Śambhu,
and the other deities went to the shore of the Ocean of Milk to seek refuge with Hari.
Having bathed there, they praised the Supreme Self, the Lord Viṣṇu, the beloved of the world; then Brahmā spoke to him like one afraid.
That maiden, the wife of Upabarhaṇa and the daughter of Citraratha, [also spoke]. || 42-43 ||
O Mādhava, protect me so that she does not curse the gods for the sake of her husband;
virtuous and saintly people remember the Supreme Lord even in the midst of great calamities.
O You who are solely devoted to the protection of those who have come for refuge and those who are distressed and miserable!
"Protect, protect us, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who have come to you for refuge!
Mālāvatī indeed sustains me, though I am devoid of authority;
all my great Brāhmī prosperity shall surely depart from me now. (45-46)

He said to Śambhu: "O Nārāyaṇa, you have bestowed upon me this great knowledge so difficult to attain, which was formerly acquired by me at Puṣkara through the fruit of austerities performed for a hundred manvantaras;

"Indeed, this jewel of knowledge of mine departs from me because of a woman's curse.
Alas! The splendor of a devoted wife is supreme among all splendors;
O Lord Hari, protect and save me, for I am consumed by the fire of that splendor."
Dharma said: "O Lord, Dharma alone is the great jewel and the eternal one;
yet I, who am that very Dharma, shall meet my destruction through the curse of a woman, O Supreme Lord, as a result of my penance performed for seven manvantaras."
"The Dharma you attained has now been destroyed by a curse.
The gods said: "We were made consumers of clarified butter at the sacrifice by you;
yet everything is being brought to ruin by the curse of a woman—please show us mercy! (51-52)
While they were thus praising him, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"Go there yourselves; for I shall go myself to protect her.
Hearing this, the gods were delighted and departed for Mālavatī at that very moment.
Seeing the gods, the devoted Mālāvatī bowed down;
O beloved, she wept while establishing her husband in the presence of the deities.
In the meantime, a certain young Brahmin boy was there. ||54-55||
Clad in white garments, adorned with five-fold leaf-patterns and a tilaka mark, he arrived and,

Having bowed to him as he was speaking thus, Mālāvatī said:

Suddenly, due to a curse from Brahmā, my husband gave up his life;

Whatever lies within the domain of the gods, that alone they grant and nothing else—not strength, nor beauty, nor sovereignty, nor wealth, nor a son. (65)

Knowledge, wisdom, skill in poetry, sons, grandsons, supreme prosperity, strength, wealth, valor, and even great sovereignty—[all these he obtains]. (68)
From the worship of Brahmā, one obtains supernatural powers (siddhis), knowledge, prosperity, and likewise progeny;
from the worship of Sūrya, one obtains knowledge, health, wealth, and sons.
From the worship of Gaṇeśa, one obtains the destruction of obstacles, the status of being worshipped at the forefront of all,
supreme bliss, sovereignty, a son, knowledge, wealth, and progeny.
Through service to Viṣṇu, one obtains liberation, austerity, righteousness, fame, and prosperity;
and by the practice of righteousness, one shall also obtain peace, happiness, and wealth.
Whichever deity one worships with devotion, one attains that [deity] through the qualities of goodness (sattva) and so forth;
later, in due course, one shall attain the supreme state of Kṛṣṇa together with Him.
He who worships Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond material nature, the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the eternal Lord. (73)
The Lord is both with form and without form, the light consisting of His own will,
all-pervading, the support of all, the sovereign of all, and the Supreme Bliss.
Untainted, in the form of a witness, and an embodiment of grace toward devotees—he is truly liberated while living; indeed, he certainly does not desire any boon.
He considers all four states— residing in the same world as the deity and so forth,
as well as the status of Brahmā and immortality— to be as worthless as a clod of earth when [the Supreme Reality] exists.
He considers sovereignty to be equal to a clod of earth and transitory;
he knows that everything is indeed perishable, like a bubble on the water.
One should not seek the supreme abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa without servitude;
for whether in dream or in waking, one constantly desires service alone. (78)
He who remains steadfast and constantly serves the most perfect Brahman effortlessly rescues,
by his own power, a hundred crores of his ancestors, a hundred of his maternal grandfather's lineage,
and a hundred of his father-in-law's ancestors.
A devotee of Kṛṣṇa indeed delivers even a hundred generations— including male and female slaves, mothers, wives, and sons— and goes to the abode of Goloka,
provided that the mantra of Viṣṇu enters his ear from the mouth of a guru.
At that moment, out of fear, Yama drew far away from the writing;
and Brahmā, having assigned the madhuparka and other offerings for his sake, [departed].
He goes toward Satyaloka by this path;
casting off his human body, he proceeds fearlessly to Goloka.
Whatever ancient karma he has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious—
Kṛṣṇa constantly cuts [them] with his sharp-edged discus. ||84||
Leaving him behind, Old Age and Death depart out of fear of the Discus;
otherwise, the Sudarśana would indeed shatter them into a hundred pieces.
Having gone there and assumed a divine form, she then serves Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
As long as Kṛṣṇa remains in Goloka, so long shall the devotee dwell there forever.
A servant considers even a single moment of Brahmā’s lifespan to be perishable;

"O virtuous lady, by what disease has your beloved now died?
As a physician, I know the treatment for every ailment. (88)
"Having brought King Death, Yama, Time, and Disease before you, I am capable of binding them and delivering them up, just as a hunter binds and delivers a beast. (89)
Or whoever, through yoga or through exhaustion, effects the abandonment of the body—

Having heard the words of the brahmin, she who was devoted to her husband spoke to him:
"O best of brahmins, if you are indeed capable of accomplishing everything... (91)
"Bring Kāla, Yama, and the Daughter of Death into my presence.

She had six arms, was endowed with compassion, and was accompanied by sixty-four sons;
then the virtuous lady beheld Kāla of terrible form standing before her.
He has six faces, sixteen arms, and twenty-four eyes;
he has six feet, is black in color, wears red garments, and is most excellent. (95)
Satī beheld before her a host of diseases, exceedingly difficult to conquer, possessing a brilliance equal to the summer sun and appearing as the very embodiment of universal destruction. 96.
Satī beheld Yama, who was most righteous and dark-complexioned, as well as the slayers—both young and old, and those exceedingly advanced in age. (97)
Then Mālāvatī, skilled in reasoning, questioned Yama— the teacher who knows how to discern dharma and adharma, and the preceptor of sinners.

Yama said: "O virtuous lady, one whose time has not yet come never dies;
without the command of the Lord, I do not indeed take away even an immortal."
I am Time, the Daughter of Death, and the diseases that are so difficult to conquer; we shall indeed carry off at that very moment him by whom we were created during the consecration. 101.

In the act of severing life, I withdraw [the senses] according to my power.
Impelled by Time and residing together with the seminal discharge (niṣeka), I constantly take away life; there is no fault in this on my part, my dear.
If there were some radiant woman among virtuous women who was capable of reducing even me to ashes, then indeed the entire world—
deprived of the Daughter of Death— would truly become immortal; but not otherwise.
I abide even within the womb, in the very essence of the bodies of embodied beings.
Day after day I am constantly withdrawing [the world], yet people do not perceive it at all;
that which is born today is regarded as "grown old" by tomorrow. 108.
That which is newly born later becomes worn out and is called "old";
indeed, old age constantly and perpetually prevails everywhere. (109)
Foolish people rejoice, thinking, "I am young," or "I am a child," or "I am not old"; thus, through ignorance, they do not recognize their own state of old age.
For growth is said to be the state of increasing; the infused seed always grows, it grows constantly in the womb, and it continues to grow during infancy and the subsequent stages.
It increases constantly and never diminishes;
likewise, my sons, the diseases, are impelled by the arrival of time. (112)
We perform our duty at every moment; there is truly no fault on our part while you are present.
Ask the Great-Souled Time, and he will do what is appropriate.
Then Satī said: "O Lord, you are indeed the witness of all actions;
O Master, why do you take away my beloved while I am still alive?"
Having heard of Mālāvatī’s suffering, Kāla then said to the virtuous woman: "Who am I? Who is Yama? And who is the Daughter of Death, as well as these mental agonies? (115)
We wander about as the protectors of the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she whose left side is the primordial nature (Mūlaprakṛti), and in whose womb reside Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Brahmā. 116.
The deities abide by his command, and even Dharma is indeed under his control; the planets, the zodiac signs, and the guardians of the quarters are likewise under his sway.
For this Time is indeed a portion of him, as are Death, the Son of Death, and the afflictions;
impelled by him, we all perform the severing of yoga.
Ask Kṛṣṇa, for you are his ruler; how can your master be dead?
Having spoken thus, Kāla ceased; the Brāhmaṇa then said to her:
"Kāla, Yama, Mṛtyukanyā, and the hosts of diseases have all been questioned.
What doubt do you still have now? Ask that again, O maiden. (1.408.120)
Then Mālāvatī said: "O Brahmin, whom shall I ask now?
My husband has abandoned his life through yoga on account of a curse. (121)
"Now, if you have compassion, give me back my beloved, the lord of my life;
having bowed before you along with my husband, I shall go toward my own home."
"O Kṛṣṇa, where shall I search here? For Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Brāhmaṇa;
whatever the Brāhmaṇa does, Kṛṣṇa follows that twice-born one. (123)
Having heard these piteous words, the Brahmin, standing in the midst of the gods and moved by compassion for them, spoke this supreme truth to the deities.
This wife of Upabarhaṇa and daughter of Citraratha has come for refuge with her husband and entreated him for the gift of life. (1.25)
Therefore, tell me, O gods, what beneficial course of action should be undertaken here;
for I have restrained Satī, who was desirous of cursing all the gods.
What is the use now of these many idle words? Why this delay? Viṣṇu was entreated by you, yet he has not come to Śvetadvīpa.
Then a voice from the sky arose: "Keśava is coming."
But that which has arisen is contrary [to what is desired], since Keśava does not come. || 128 ||
Brahmā said: "At that time, this Nārada, my own son, became the Gandharva Upabarhaṇa due to my curse at an improper time."
By means of yoga, he indeed relinquished his vital breaths even though his allotted time had not yet expired;
nevertheless, he still possesses a lifespan of one thousand years at this present moment.
Two hundred thousand [verses] have been traversed by him; I shall now proclaim that which remains, so that the curse may not touch him and the gods may be free from fear. (131)
Hari exists everywhere; he has not come from elsewhere, nor does he not exist. That Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa exists in the form of both the visible and the invisible.
"Does Kṛṣṇa not come? Even the voice of the sky is surely false!"—O twice-born one, do not utter such reproach against Hari in the assembly.
Of which Lord of Sages are you a disciple? Who are you by name, O twice-born one?
Where is your residence, from where have you come, and from what lineage are you born? (1.34)
You mock the gods as well as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with these words: "Even now Viṣṇu has not come to the assembly. (1.35)
What you have said—that which is of a censuring nature regarding the Supreme Self—should not be heard.
Viṣṇu is all-pervasive; indeed, as far as the term *viṣi* (pervasion) extends, so far does Viṣṇu pervade everywhere.
Thus, for all beings indeed, where could there be coming and going? Where great censure occurs, the virtuous person does not hear it at all. (1.37)
The reviler, together with his listeners, shall go to Kumbhīpāka for a yuga;
indeed, the reviling of Viṣṇu is threefold, consisting of the form of destroying [his] images.
And that which consists of non-existence and has the nature of equality with the individual soul—
for it, there is no atonement here until the end of a hundred Brahmās.
That lowest of men who reviles his guru or reviles his father goes to the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Having heard that, the Brāhmaṇa then spoke to the gods:
"O gods, who are pillars of righteousness, what indeed has been done as a censure of Viṣṇu? (141)
"Harir has not come here"—this was empty talk regarding the sky;
thus it was spoken by me for the sake of auspiciousness, and it was certainly not intended as a reproach. (142)
"You are indeed destined for greatness; speak! Is Viṣṇu the all-pervading Lord?
If so, then how did you go to Śvetadvīpa and [attain] the boon? (143)
If there is no difference between the part and the whole, then how is it that the wise, setting aside the *kalā* (limited power), worship the Supreme Lord who is the most perfect (*pūrṇatama*)? 144.
Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of all parts, his form being for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees;
and indeed, Vaikuṇṭha, which is situated above the entire cosmic egg, is truly eternal.
And in Vaikuṇṭha is the eternal beloved of Lakṣmī, possessing four arms;
fifty crore yojanas above that is Goloka.
In Goloka, Kṛṣṇa is two-armed, the eternal beloved of Rādhā;
beyond that is the all-pervading world, whose nature is the imperishable Brahman and which transcends it.
The supreme Brahman, most perfectly complete, shines forth there;
tell me, how could it not be present here today? (148)
The virtuous Vaiṣṇavas meditate upon Him,
and the virtuous Bhāgavatas serve His divine form, as do chaste women, without ceasing.
"He from whose lineage I am born and whose young disciple I am—he, having become a brahmin, speaks; O hosts of gods, listen! (1.408.150)
"O Lord of Gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, revive the Gandharva quickly!

Having spoken thus, the young brahmin then became the four-armed Lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, united with Ramā.

nevertheless, the corpse did not rise, remaining just as it lay, like one who is inert. || 156 ||
Brahmā said: Then we, having accomplished our desires, shall honor that virtuous lady;
thereafter, having bathed, remember Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in your heart. 157.
"Without him, there is truly no revival; he alone remains as the living reality.
By these words of Brahmā, the virtuous woman, being satisfied, praised the Supreme Lord.
I bow to that Supreme Self, the cause of all causes, without whom all living beings, though possessing breath, are as good as corpses and utterly devoid of purpose. (159)
Since it is through that [divine] possession that beings become endowed with life, activity, and consciousness,
even such service and meditation are not possible without a physical form.
Such was the divine form of the all-pervading Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, situated in the midst of a circle of splendor and surrounded by millions of hosts of gopīs.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how Nārada’s Death Resulted from a Brahmin’s Curse in the First Kṛta-yuga Lineage, and his Subsequent Rebirth as the Gandharva named Upabarhaṇa, followed by his Second Death there, whereupon his wife Mālavatī, through the power of her devotion to her husband, summoned Viṣṇu along with the gods and Kāla and others, and thereby restored her husband to life," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate a most wonderful story concerning a woman devoted to her husband, which took place in a former age.
The daughter of King Viśāla was a heroic woman devoted to righteousness;
she appeared at the svayaṃvara arranged by Viśāla, which was graced by the presence of kings. ||re||
Karandhama’s son, Avikṣit, indeed conquered the Svayaṃvara;
then, alone in battle, he was overcome by many hosts of kṣatriyas.
Having been defeated, that maiden was then offered as a sacrifice by the royal families;
hearing this, Karandhama set out accompanied by a hundred thousand troops.
Having slain the kings and taken his son and daughter-in-law, he returned home once more;
Avīkṣit said to his father, "What glory will remain for me? (9)
"O father, I will not take her, nor any other woman,
as long as I have been defeated in battle by others while she was looking on."
Since I have been defeated by others, I am as weak as a coward;
what is the point of my human nature while remaining in a state of dependence?
"Through this woman, my reputation has been destroyed by my enemies here;

Cāvīka took her hand in marriage in the midst of the forest;
then the gods arrived there and showered flowers.
Divine musical instruments resounded, and throngs of apsarases danced;
the gods and gandharvas sang, and the forest deities were filled with joy. (48)
There, sages, gandharvas, and kinnaras presented them with excellent food, ointments, garments, garlands, drinks, and other such things. 49.
He took delight together with that slender maiden, and she, unobserved by him, went to her own father’s palace; there was a great festival for her parents.
Then the parents gave all kinds of gifts for the sake of their grandson;
thereafter, he went through the sky with his wife to Mount Meru.
And while that hero was sporting with that beautiful woman in the world of the Gandharvas, that virtuous lady gave birth to a son.
When the son was born, there was a great festival among the Gandharvas;
some sang, while others likewise played mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, and ānakas.
They played musical instruments such as flutes, lutes, and mayūrakas,
and many hosts of apsarases danced for that festival.
Clouds that released showers of flowers thundered with gentle sounds;
and there, Tumburu himself came, having been summoned by the couple.
Then, with a mind full of exceeding joy, he performed the birth-rites;
he offered a benediction for that child, preceded by hymns of praise. (56)
May the universal monarch, of great heroism, mighty arms, and great strength, the teacher and lord of virtuous women, be the bringer of well-being to the entire earth. (57)
May all these world-protectors, beginning with Śakra, as well as the ṛṣis, grant you well-being, O hero, and may they bestow upon you the prowess that destroys your enemies. (58)
May the eastern wind blow auspiciously for you, Marutta, which does not stir up dust; may your southern wind be pure, inexhaustible, and free from turbulence.
May the western Marut bestow supreme valor upon you;
and may the northern Marut likewise grant you preeminent strength.
Thus did the Guru speak for the sake of Marutta’s well-being;
indeed, he became known as Marutta, the son of the great seers.
Taking Marutta with them, the couple went to their own home,
along with the Gandharvas, gods, and sages, into the presence of the king.
Having placed the child before their father and bowed down, they reported his entire conduct in every respect;
and the king, too, [rejoiced] from the sight of his grandson.
"O, how fortunate I am! he said, praising himself again and again;
and the queen too, seeing her grandson's son, rejoiced with great delight.
Then there was great joy in the city and in the houses of the citizens;
the king also gave away precious gems and ornaments for the cows at that time. (65)
Having consecrated his son in the kingdom, he entered the forest together with his wife;
there, for a thousand years, he indeed performed severe penance.
Having abandoned his body, the king attained the same world as Śakra;
his wife, after remaining for a hundred years, obtained that very same husband in heaven.
Then Avikṣita performed many sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees;
his unimpeded wheel [of dominion] extended over the seven continents.
His son Marutta also performed sacrifices numbering ten million;
from there, the golden mountain named Muñjavat was brought.
Gold was given in every way and relinquished with satisfaction by the gods of the earth;
indeed, everything in his sacrifice, such as the temples and other structures, was made of gold.
The gods were indeed the servers for the brahmins; they were present there at that time. For all the Viśvedevas were the members of the assembly on the sacrificial ground. ||71||
The Sādhyas, Maruts, Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas,
as well as the Nidhis and the Ṛṣis, then became his servants in his ritual activities.
At that time, his officiating priest was Saṃvarta, the son of Aṅgiras,
a brahmin who was the elder brother of Bṛhaspati and the foremost among the gods.
Then, at the excellent hermitage of the seer Aurva, the king of serpents caused a disturbance;
for the purpose of his destruction, he seized the bow.
Likewise, out of anger, he brandished the great weapon Saṃvartaka;
and by it, Marutta brought about the crushing of the serpent kings.
He returned once more to his own kingdom and ruled over the earth;
meanwhile, his virtuous mother Satī and his father Vīkṣit had both departed for the forest.
Having attained heaven, they were rescued by the power of their devotion to their husbands and their vows as wives:
Marutta’s wife and Prabhāvatī, the daughter of Vidarbha.
Suvīraputrī Sauvīrī was the second beautiful woman;
Ketuvīrya’s daughter Keśī was the third beautiful woman. ||78||
The daughter of the King of Madra was there, and Kekayī was the fourth;
the daughter of the King of Sindhu, Saurandhrī, was indeed the fifth wife. (79)
And the daughter of the King of Cedi, Sulocanā, became the sixth wife;
those devoted wives had eighteen sons.
The eldest and foremost among them became King Nariṣyanta;
all these queens were auspicious and truly devoted to Viṣṇu.
The lineage of great devotees, devoted to their respective duties, took refuge in the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari. (82)
She did not indeed enjoy wealth or her husband without first offering them to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she offered everything to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, including her very self. (83)
Perceiving Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who has appeared in the form of their husband, the goddesses, as well as Lakṣmī and his other wives, perform service to him.
In this way, those rulers of the earth were indeed equal to Viṣṇu, and the royal wives, the consorts of the kings, were equal to Lakṣmī. ||85||
Once, while King Samaruttaka was absorbed in meditation during the worship of Mahāviṣṇu,
Rudra arrived there.
Since Rudra had not received such honor despite this being the case,
he became enraged with extreme vehemence and hurled his trident to kill him.
Having pierced the heart of the king, that virtuous daughter of Vidarbha, Prabhāvatī, then remained there, having entered his very heart and taken away his life-breaths. 88.
Taking water in her hand, she said: "If it be true that throughout my life I have served my husband and remained devoted to him as a faithful wife," 89.
"By that truth, may this Rudra meet death again and again, if indeed the gods have been worshipped and guests have also been honored. (1.409.90)
If she serves her mother-in-law and father-in-law with great devotion, her husband will always be pleased, and his malady will gradually subside and move far away. || 91 ||
If I am always devoted to the duties of the household and regard my husband as a god, the family of my lord will be propitiated and his heart will be won over. (92)
If my husband, devoted to his wife, remains alive, let him be dear to me; provided that my co-wives are always honored and satisfied as if they were my own sisters. (93)
They were honored like mothers and protected like daughters;
by that merit, may my sin indeed not exist, through the destruction [brought about] by Rudra. 94.
When she had spoken thus, everything was overturned;
there was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! as the unbearable destruction of Rudra took place.
Then that virtuous and passionate woman was consoled by Marutta;
for the sake of reviving Rudra, Śāntā then spoke to her husband.
O Lord, revive the god Rudra, who is indeed a Vaiṣṇava;
for those Rudras who are not Vaiṣṇavas exist only during the period of the world's formation at the beginning of a Kalpa.
"Those born from the Brahmamālā will certainly meet their destruction"—this was the curse repeatedly pronounced by me against Rudra at the beginning of every kalpa. (18)
During the discharge of the fierce Rudra, he will touch them again and again;
however, the Vaiṣṇava Mahārudra will certainly remain there—of this there is no doubt.
Having addressed the water, he shall turn that very moisture into ash;
thus this Lord Marutteśvara will become fully restored to life.
Thus addressed by his wife, Maruta took up water and said:
"If I have indeed been devoted to my vows toward my wife throughout my life..."
I am a follower of the dharma of subjects, fallen from the dharma of kings, yet always a Vaiṣṇava; even if touched by the unrighteousness created by many transgressions, it shall never affect me.
By this merit, may this Rudra, a devotee of Viṣṇu, indeed live,
provided that his wife Satī becomes his spouse just as Prabhāvatī is mine.
Likewise, there were other wives who were indeed full of devotion to their husbands;
I treated them all equally and did not show partiality toward any of them.
"By this merit, may this Rudra, together with his trident, live!
Having said this, he poured water upon the ashes. || 105 ||
Then that gentle Mahārudra became alive again before him;
he was saluted, worshipped, and repeatedly asked for forgiveness.
Even by Rudra, the virtuous Satī was propitiated;
Prabhāvatī was also propitiated, and the king too was propitiated, honored, and saluted by the king.
Hara remained in that palace in the form of Marutteśvara,
while Śaṅkara then departed for Kailāsa in his divine form.
Pārvatī realized the greatness of devotion to her husband;
thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this vow which bestows great merit. 109.
From hearing and reciting this, the fruit of all sacrifices shall be obtained;
and even from remembering this narrative, the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained.

Thus ends the four hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Rākṣasa and the Resuscitation of Rudra through the Miracles of Chastity by Vīrā, the Wife of King Avīkṣita, and Prabhāvatī, the Wife of Marutta," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the prowess of Śakti’s wife.
Vasiṣṭha is a portion of Brahmā, a seer (ṛṣi) made the beholder of the Vedas. || 1 ||
Arundhatī was his virtuous and chaste wife, devoted to her husband;
in her the blessed Vasiṣṭha begot a hundred sons.
There, indeed, was an eldest son named Śakti;
in whose wife the sage Parāśara was born, and from him I was born under the name Vyāsa.
I became my son, Brahmā Śuka by name,
whose glory is sung in every way for the sake of attaining liberation.
A Rākṣasa named Rudhira devoured the son of Vasiṣṭha;
hearing that, Vasiṣṭha was deeply distressed.
And eighty-nine sons were devoured by the blood;
having heard that, Vasiṣṭha then set his mind upon dying.
Then his daughter-in-law said to the great sage, the husband of Śakti:
"O Blessed One, O best of Brahmins, this auspicious body of yours—"
Protect him, O Lord, so that I may see my own son, your grandson;
for he, born of Śakti, shall accomplish all my purposes while still remaining in the womb.
Then the child within the womb indeed spoke a verse with his voice;
hearing that, Vasiṣṭha was filled with wonder, wondering how and from where it could have come.
At that moment, Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa appeared visibly in his courtyard and said,
"Vedic verses have issued from the mouth of your grandson."
"This grandson of yours, born of Śakti, shall be equal to me and possessed of power;
by the gain of such a worthy grandson, your lineage shall cross over [to salvation]. (11)
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa vanished;
Vasiṣṭha then affectionately touched her womb with his right hand.
He performed the protection of the fetus for Adṛśyantī, the wife of Śakti;
at that time, Adṛśyantī was a virtuous and chaste woman, devoted to her husband.
She cursed Kāla, Rudra, Yama, Viśvāmitra, and the Rākṣasa:
"O Śakti, O husband of Śakti, I am devoted solely to my husband. (14)
If I am a most virtuous wife who has dedicated my life for your sake, and if my mother-in-law and Arundhatī are chaste wives equal to Lakṣmī; (then may I attain that state). 15.
Then let Kāla, Rudra, Viśvāmitra, Yama,
and the Rākṣasa— all of them— become inert stones.
Wherever they may be, let them remain in the form of stones—
insentient and devoid of consciousness— until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus cursed, wherever they were at that time,
they became stone-like in form and shall remain so for the duration of a Brahmā's life.
In whatever place, such as the earth and so forth, time existed, there indeed stones of black color were produced; for they consist of the very essence of the surface of the earth.
When the clay that serves as their support was produced from the form of Time,
then Rudra became the stone, while the magnetite appeared in the west.
That stone is called Raudrī, the image from the cave of Śiva;
it draws all clods of earth toward itself, even across the ocean.
The ocean will eventually submerge that land which Viśvāmitra once inhabited in the western desert.
From that very place where he was born in the form of a stone,
the river Viśvāmitrī indeed arose from his sweat in Gaurjara.
In time, the stone will submerge, and its form will remain upon the earth;
and at that time, Yama indeed became dark-complexioned on Mount Raivata.
Mounted upon his buffalo vehicle and having come for refuge out of fear,
Yama was present there together with his buffalo in the presence of Dāmodara.
The mountain Māhiṣa indeed became the form of a black stone;
that Rākṣasa then fled in fear, running toward the southern direction.
By that curse, he fell into the ocean and then became a mountain on the bridge;
indeed, that mountain which had obstructed the sky during Hanumān’s journey became fixed there.
The dull-witted one fought against the massive-bodied Hanumān;
then the entire world, rendered senseless, broke out into cries of "Alas! ||28||
Without Rudra, without Kāla, and without Yama and Viśvakarman,
all the gods, being distressed, approached Brahmā.
Accompanied by Viṣṇu, they all went to where Satī was staying—
where the gods found the wife of Śakti, Vasiṣṭha, and Arundhatī.
Distressed, they reported their destruction to the world-protectors and earnestly entreated the guardians for their lives.
"O Mother, revive the protectors of the worlds so that there may be well-being.
Adṛśyantī then said: "If [you will revive] my husband and brothers-in-law..."
"Then bring the gods back to life; I shall restore them, and not otherwise.
Brahmā replied, "Śakti and the others have been devoured by the Rākṣasa. (3.3)
Only ashes, bones, skin, and their dust remain; nothing else is found, by whose refinement they might today be restored to their bodies. (34)
Wherever a corpse’s bones, flesh, ashes, or even soil are found, there he is restored with his body by means of water consecrated with mantras. (35)
"Without flesh and bones, it is impossible to bring back to life even my hundred sons, Śakti and the others; tell me, what would happen in this situation? (36)
Then Adṛśyantī said: "If my husband's brothers cannot produce offspring, nor can they restore them to life," (37)
"Even the gods, beginning with Rudra, cannot be incited by me;
however, if I obtain a husband and so forth, you, the guardians of the world, will also obtain your gain. (38)
"I consider it a matter of justice that the response should be of such a kind as the offense;
Brahmā said, 'If you have the power, I shall grant you divine [boons] and so forth. (39)
Then Satī spoke of the Videhas as being subtle in form and devoid of gross existence; and Vedha said that he himself was likewise.
I bestow and indeed awaken those such as Kālarudra and others— devoid of grossness, possessing subtle forms, and transcending the state of being like a stone.
By the second subtle form, let Kāla, Rudra, Yama,
Viśvāmitra, and Rākṣasa perform the work pertaining to creation.
"Indeed, let not the stones remain forever in their gross form.
Having heard this, Śakti and the others were then addressed by the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Possessing divine and subtle forms, they were brought from heaven and presented;
those minute-bodied beings exist both in heaven and on earth.
At that time, even Adṛśyantī, as well as Kālarudra and the others,
were likewise made into minute entities (aṇu) and appointed to their respective offices of action.
Taking water in her hand, she who considered herself powerful spoke:
"Just as is the form of my husband, and as is that of the gods... (46)
"Let such consciousness become the embodiment of Time and the other [principles].
Thus were Time and the others made her subtle presiding deities (adhikārin). ||47||
Then the gods went to heaven; truly, they do not offend virtuous women.
Even though they are powerful, they tremble before the majesty of devotion to their husbands.
The sun, the moon, Mahendra, Viṣṇu, and other deities indeed tremble at the mere name of a virtuous woman; what then need be said of others? (49)
The dharma of a virtuous wife is the supreme dharma; it has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again, such as the state of dependence that Brahmā has ordained for a woman.
Supreme and great splendor, as well as sovereignty, were bestowed upon her through her devotion to her husband; just as a woman serves [her lord], so too does she serve the Supreme Lord. 51.

Sabalā also always conducts herself according to the duty of devotion to her husband. As she was thus living her life, a child— a sage endowed with great wisdom— was born in due time from that woman of invisible power.
That very sage Parāśara became renowned on earth by that name. ||53||
O virtuous lady, when the Blessed Lord, who is my son in the form of Vyāsa,
was born, the ancestors sang and the grandfathers danced.
And when Parāśara had descended, all the great-grandfathers and the sky-dwellers, beginning with Puṣkara, showered a rain of flowers.
When Parāśara arrived, there was a supreme and great radiance everywhere;
the boy beheld his divine ancestors and brothers who had assembled there.
As soon as he was born, the one of great wisdom spoke and bowed to them;
growing day by day, he brought joy to everyone. 57.
While he had not yet reached his youth, he sang the narrative of Viṣṇu, which contains all accounts of the past, future, and present, and bestows excellent liberation. ||58||
Whoever should cause this to be heard with devotion, or likewise listen to it with faith, and should also remember Parāśara, shall indeed attain his own desired object. (59)

Thus ends the four hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of how Kālarudra, Yama, Viśvāmitra, and the Rākṣasa were cursed by Adṛśyantī—the wife of Śakti—after the sons of Vasiṣṭha, including Śakti and others, were destroyed by the Rākṣasa; how they subsequently became mountains in the form of stones; how Śakti and the others were restored to life by Brahmā and others, while Kāla and the others were revived by Adṛśyantī in a subtle form; and how Parāśara was born as the son of Śakti," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the majesty of the devoted wife (*pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this most excellent narrative, which destroys the sins of those who hear it, and which bestows liberation and one's own desired goals upon virtuous Vaiṣṇava women. || 1 ||
Wherever the Vaiṣṇavī woman resides, there Nārāyaṇī is established;
there Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa are also present.
When Hari is being praised, he whose hair stands on end repeatedly, and in whom trembling, perspiration, and drops of water are seen upon his eyes; || 3 ||
Seeing those women devoted to Viṣṇu, she felt joy arise in her heart;
rising up, she performed worship to Vāsudeva just as Satī did.
She is a devotee who nourishes righteousness; she alone is a devoted wife who, ever intent on her marital fidelity, serves her own husband, Hari.
Thinking that "all this belongs to Hari," that virtuous Vaiṣṇavī indeed maintained all things, including perfumes, flowers, and the like, in a pleasing manner.
Filled with affection, she performs only auspicious deeds in the field of Hari;
and she constantly worships the image of Hari just as she would her husband.
Whether through action, mind, or speech, while awake or even in sleep, she is indeed a great devotee of the Lord because of her identity with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (8)
She who performs all service for the sake of food according to her ability—that virtuous woman is an eightfold servant of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. || 9 ||
Having seen her splendor and power, the deities were indeed struck with fear;
bowing down to her who is devoted to Vāsudeva and faithful to her husband, they departed.
A Vaiṣṇava woman excels thousands of other women;
a woman devoted to her husband excels thousands of devotees of Viṣṇu.

A virtuous woman who regards her husband as her deity surpasses thousands of women devoted to their masters, for she possesses a husband who is a devotee of Viṣṇu; thus, she is distinguished above all others.
She whose sons, daughters, grandsons, brothers-in-law and others, two sons-in-law, father-in-law, parents, kinsmen, and so forth [are present]. (1.3)
Compared to co-wives, female slaves, friends, those of her own household,
