and even other Vaiṣṇavīs who are devotees of Viṣṇu, she is distinguished as superior.
She was Triśaṅku’s beloved wife, adorned with all auspicious marks;
she was the mother of Ambarīṣa, a most exalted devotee of the Lord and a virtuous woman.
Constantly devoted to her master, a servant of her master, and a handmaid of Hari, that virtuous woman serves him, regarding her husband Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Brahman.
Triśaṅku, having bathed daily in the Sarayū, worshipped Hari;
she too, devoted to his service, attended upon her husband in the morning, at midday, and at night.
Likewise, at the time of worship, she served Kṛṣṇa with excellent articles:
sandalwood paste, lamps, incense, and likewise an immersion in the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). || 18 ||
She performs [her tasks] only with her two hands, never by means of servants or others;
thus, she constantly remains intent on service, as if she were liberated.
He constantly worshipped Nārāyaṇa, the four-armed one who reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa, through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
She performed everything herself, including the offering of garlands and so forth,
as well as the grinding of perfumes and the like, and likewise the cooking of the sacrificial oblations.
That queen, Padmāvatī by name, who was [in truth] Nārāyaṇī in speech, personally performed the smearing of the ground and other such tasks. (22)
Constantly uttering only the name "Śrī Kṛṣṇa," that devoted wife remained for ten thousand years with her inner self entirely absorbed in Him.
She constantly worshipped Govinda with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
as well as the devotees of Viṣṇu, the Bhāgavatas— both men and Vaiṣṇava women.
He constantly gratified her with gifts, honors, worship, wealth, and jewels;
then, on one occasion, that goddess, having indeed fasted on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), [spoke].
The highly fortunate lady slept before Hari together with her husband;
meditating upon her husband as Nārāyaṇa, she served him according to the duties of domestic life.
There, the god Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, said to her:
"O blessed lady, O beautiful woman, what boon do you desire from me? Speak. (27)
She chose a boon from Kṛṣṇa: "May my son be a devotee of Viṣṇu, a sovereign emperor of great splendor, and one whose devotion consists of the total surrender of all his possessions. (28)
Saying "So be it," Janārdana gave her a single fruit.
Seeing the fruit manifest before her eyes, she reported everything to her husband.
Beholding it, she ate that fruit with her mind fixed upon it;
then, in the course of time, Padmāvatī gave birth to a son who would uphold his lineage.
She gave birth to a Vaiṣṇava devotee who was solely devoted to Vāsudeva,
endowed with the characteristics of a devotee, and whose body hair was marked by the discus.
The father performed all the birth-rites for that supreme devotee of the Lord, who was endowed with divine marks and was an abode of virtues; and he grew up.
He became known by the name Ambarīṣa, liberated from qualities and the like;
though consecrated to the kingdom by his father, he performed severe austerity.
For a thousand years, he chanted the name of Nārāyaṇa Hari,
the Lord of Rādhā, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Māṇikī.
He who has the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, the Lord of Vṛndā and the lotus-like Śrī, the husband of Padmā, Tulasī, Vijayā, Lalitā, and Mañjulā. 35.
The goddesses Haimī, Dayā, Śāntā, Śānti, Campā, Supuṣpikā,
Haṃsā, Ārambhā, Savitrī, Muktikā, Muktā, Jayā, and Aparājitā [honored] the Lord.
The king always worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama;
consequently, the Blessed Lord, whose palms were marked with the discus and the lotus, became pleased.
Having made Garuḍa into an elephant, Indra himself came from heaven;
Hari said to Ambarīṣa, "I am Mahendra; choose a boon. (38)
"Tell me, what great fruit of your asceticism shall I grant you here?
Ambarīṣa then replied, "Indeed, I do not perform penance for my own sake."
"I shall take what was given by you; go, O Indra, as you please.
I do not desire your perishable enjoyments, even those pertaining to the highest state."
Indeed, the Vairāja, Vaiśvara, and Niraya hells, which are accumulated through the power of desire, [do not exist] except for the state of servitude to the lotus feet of Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa. ||41||
Then, laughing, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself assumed his own form as the four-armed beloved of Lakṣmī.
Seeing his Guru seated upon Garuḍa, Ambarīṣa bowed down to him and praised him, saying:
"Be gracious here to me, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (43)
O Mahāviṣṇu born of Kambharā, child of the cowherd clan, primordial deity Śrī Vyāsa, Lord of Kamalā, you who are devoted to your wife! 44.
Having entrusted the performance of all ritual actions to you, who are the Supreme Self, I have taken refuge in you, O beloved of devotees, O bestower of shelter. (45)
And the Blessed One, smiling, spoke playfully to Ambarīṣa:
"Speak, O devotee; I have come here for the sake of granting your desired boon. (46)
Ambarīṣa said to Hari: "You alone have been chosen by me;
I shall practice devotion to you constantly, according to my understanding. (47)
I shall protect the earth, having indeed made the world Vaiṣṇava;
and by means of sacrifices, oblations, and worship, I shall gratify those who abide among the gods. 48.
I shall protect the Vaiṣṇavas, I shall slay my heart-enemies,
I shall perform worship unto You, and I shall lead many to the Imperishable.
Having said, "So be it," and having given the Sudarśana discus,
he vanished in order to destroy the torment caused by curses, diseases, and other afflictions.
Having placed the discus upon the lion-throne and fashioned the form of Viṣṇu, Ambarīṣa and his mother Padmāvatī worshipped it. (51)
Cakra always accepts the offerings made by his mother and son;
once, on the slopes of the Himalayas, there occurred a terrifying rainstorm.
There, the destruction of the Sāketa region was submerged;
then the beautiful Padmāvatī, having worshipped the Discus, spoke to Hari.
O Blessed One, protect in every way your own subjects who are devoted to Viṣṇu;
a calamity has arisen because of the rain—protect them, save them, and show mercy! 54.
If I am devoted to my husband and intent upon seeking refuge in you,
by that merit and through devotion to you, may the water and the cloud perish.
Sudarśana, having laughed, became terrifying with garlands of flames;
reaching the sky, he utterly destroyed all the clouds.
Having effortlessly withdrawn all the waters and protected the subjects,
the Discus returned and settled upon its own place.
Now, King Ambarīṣa had a daughter named Śrīmatī, who was auspicious and radiant.
Seeing that it was the time for Śrīmatī’s marriage, the king [consulted] Nārada.
Having prostrated before the guest, he requested a boon;
then, upon beholding her beautiful form, Nārada desired her.
Parvata also arrived and desired her; he wooed her repeatedly.
Then the king said to both of them: "How indeed can I [give] only one daughter?"
"I am indeed giving her to both of you who are requesting her;
nevertheless, if she should choose one of you two," (6.1)
"I shall give my daughter to him; otherwise, I have no power [to do so].
Having said, "So be it," they then added, "We shall go tomorrow."
The two of them went to Viṣṇu and bowed down in a secluded place;
Ambarīṣa desires to give his daughter, named Śrīmatī, in marriage.
O Nārada, you ought to act in such a way that you might give [this] to me,
so that the face of the mountain may shine like the face of a monkey.
"Do so," Hari said, and "So be it," he replied and departed.
Then Parvata also arrived and said to Hari, "Let him deliver [the gift] to me."
"Just as Nārada is seen there with the face of a monkey, so do it," Hari said; "So be it," he replied, and he departed.
The king himself adorned the site of the assembly for the *svayaṃvara*,
which was filled with princes and gods and resembled the site of the assembly in heaven.
Having led the adorned maiden away, Ambarīṣa entered;
meanwhile, those two, the celestial sage and the Siddha, both of beautiful form, remained there first.
All became free from desire and abandoned their longing for the maiden;
then the king spoke to his lotus-eyed daughter Supadminī.
"O blessed lady, whichever of these two you desire in your heart here, give this garland to him; let the maiden look upon them both."
Then, seeing Nārada and Parvata with the faces of monkeys, she, being terrified, said to her father: "Who are these two, a man and a monkey? (7.1)
Thinking thus, she went away slowly and slowly, trembling behind them;
meanwhile, between those two, there was a boy of less than sixteen years of age.
Resplendent with all ornaments, surpassing the beauty of a land-lotus,
with long eyes like red lotuses reaching to their corners, he was more beautiful than ten million gods of love.
She beheld Acyuta, who was exceedingly handsome, smiling with rows of teeth that closely resembled jasmine buds.
Upon seeing the maiden, the king was greatly deluded and said, "Give me the garland.
Then Nārada and Parvata looked at each other's faces. (75)
Seeing this monkey-like face in the mirror, the two became exceedingly ashamed;
and all the other kings laughed at those two who had monkey faces. (76)
Thereupon, both of them spoke forcefully to the king: "Let her choose one of us two; do not delay. (77)
Then that intelligent maiden, having bowed to her chosen deity, took up an illusion (māyā) and stood there in the middle for the sake of protection.
She offered a garland to her beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
immediately thereafter, that maiden was no longer seen by men or gods.
Then a cry arose in the assembly, "What is this?
Taking her with him, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, went to Vaikuṇṭha.
The assembly having been dismissed, Nārada and Parvata likewise departed;
they went to the primordial Vaikuṇṭha and beheld Nārāyaṇa.
They beheld his wife, Śrīmatī, seated comfortably upon his lap;
overcome with great wonder, they addressed the Supreme Lord.
O Blessed One, how is it that after granting us a boon and causing us to be deluded, you have led us away from our purpose by promising the acquisition of a maiden? (83)
Therefore, in another birth, due to delusion regarding women, your state will be one of great suffering;
there you shall wander among the monkeys.
The Blessed One said, "Ome! O Sudharmadhṛk, you have accepted it thus.
He then consoled those two sages: "Listen to the reason for this. (85)
"How was this illustrious lady brought away by you after entering into our midst?
There are many Rākṣasas who follow the way of deceit, like Rāhu. (86)
Just as there was [joy] upon drinking the nectar, so it was here for the Krouñca Rākṣasa, who, infatuated by the maiden’s form, waited in the midst of you two. (87)
I remained there, having come as a mediator for the sake of that Vidūra;
however, you two have instead agreed upon a monkey-faced one. (88)
For it has indeed come to pass exactly so through the very request of you two;
there is not even the slightest fault of mine in that matter, O bulls among sages. (89)
Indeed, you two were delivered by me even though you were deluded by my illusory power;
however, O Brahmins, listen to something else regarding [your] daughter in a previous birth.
Austerity was indeed performed for my sake by her for many years;
she was formerly a great virtuous woman who had practiced celibacy from childhood.
That virtuous maiden was the mind-born daughter of the great seer Mārkaṇḍeya, serving as a companion to Mahālakṣmī, known as Kambharā, at her place of penance. (92)
Known by the name Śrī, she performed penance for a thousand divine years with the purposeful desire:
"May Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my husband. (93)
When Mādhava arrived through the path of the sky to grant the Sudarśana [discus] to Ambarīṣa, he then beheld Nārāyaṇa.
Filled with joy, she desired Kṛṣṇa and, abandoning her asceticism,
suddenly flew up into the sky through yoga and followed Hari.
Having entrusted the Sudarśana discus to King Ambarīṣa in his palace, Nārāyaṇa then indeed became invisible.
Indeed, the mind-born daughter of Ambarīṣa became a rememberer of her past lives;
born as a Vaiṣṇavī for my sake, she awaits my arrival.
"Driven by me alone, who remained within you, you two went into her presence and returned deluded by me. (98)
Taking your fish and in order to fulfill your desire,
the Four-armed Lord himself came to the house of Ambarīṣa.
But then, standing between you two, I took that beautiful garland from the hand of the maiden; she, the illustrious one, became my beloved.
"She is here on my lap, laughing with those two monkey-faced ones.
When addressed thus, the two best of sages bowed and departed in anger.
Having approached Ambarīṣa, both those sages reproached him, saying:
"After inviting us, you have subsequently given the maiden to another."
"Therefore, through the power of illusion, darkness shall indeed overcome you. When this curse had been pronounced, a mass of darkness then arose.
Then the Sudarśana discus struck the king;
having swiftly destroyed that mass of darkness, it returned to the backs of the two sages.
Running toward the far shore of the Lokāloka mountain, afflicted by fear, the two of them reached Govinda, the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, crying out, "Save us! Save us! (105)
Save us both, O lotus-eyed one; you are our protector, O Supreme Person.
How is it that the maiden has been won by you, while the discus has been placed upon our backs? (1.06)
Having heard this and having laughed, the Blessed One then turned back the wheel;
the Sudarśana, being obstructed there, remained just as it was before.
The two best of sages, having bowed before Hari and made a vow in his presence, said:
"From this day forward until the end of our bodies, we shall not take a wife."
Having resolved, "We shall not do so," they were both devoted to meditation;
Ambarīṣa, having meditated upon Hari, went to the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa.
She always serves Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the world of Viṣṇu;
she serves Him like Śrīmatī, like Lakṣmī, and like Ramā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this former account of the birth of Śrīmatī;
whoever—whether a man or a virtuous woman—should read it, hear it, or cause it to be heard, [shall attain great merit].
All those Vaiṣṇavas go to my Vaikuṇṭha, indeed to me alone.
One who constantly recites this meritorious [text] shall attain union with Viṣṇu. 11.2.

Thus ends the four hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Ambarīṣa from King Padmāvatī of Triśaṅku, the Monkey-Faces of Nārada and Parvata during the Marriage of His Daughter Named Śrīmatī, the Attainment of Vaikuṇṭha by Śrīmatī through Nārāyaṇa, and the Power of the Chastity of Padmāvatī and Śrīmatī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the greatness of devoted wives (*pativratā*).
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the story of Duḥsaha, the son of Adharma, who was devoted to his wife's chastity. || 1 ||
Adharma was born from behind Brahmā;
he had a son named Duḥsaha, a mental offspring who followed him wherever he stayed. || 2 ||
In various places, even among living beings, a state of unbearable suffering arose;
he had four wives, and their names were Poverty and the rest. (3)
Hunger, quarrels, and impurity— these afflict those devoted wives where the unbearable god resides, even as they dwell there.
Family members, friends, and even neighbors—those who are in the country, those who are in the city, and those who have come within the range of one's sight; || 5 ||
Upon seeing prosperity, they cannot endure it and burn with envy;
for their minds are always filled with jealousy, malice, and hatred.
The Grandfather Brahmā himself granted a dwelling to Duḥsaha;
then there was born from Adharma’s mind a son who was a mixture of castes.
To that Confusion were born four daughters— Poverty,
Hunger, Quarrel, and Impurity— who were then given in marriage.
Given over to unbearable companions through such confusion, those women devoted to their husbands appeared devoid of luster, as if poverty itself were their very form.
She was hunger, misshapen and quarrelsome, possessing a cruel form;
she was filth, covered with flies and the like, and smeared with excrement.
Deprived of the merits of bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation, and so forth,
he took up residence in the forest, having taken hold of unbearable hardships.
Failing to find a livelihood there, he entered the city of Udyama and established himself in a mansion amidst enterprising merchants, brahmins, and others.
He took up residence there with his wife; for he cannot endure the prosperity of others, and wherever that prosperity cannot be endured, he goes to that person's house. (13)
And having entered among the household members, they incited mutual blame and contempt toward both elders—even those who were virtuous and righteous—in every way. (14)
One performs or causes to be performed [an action] that is obstructive to wealth, as well as that which increases it, and likewise that which causes the loss of profit. (15)
Once, while Mahendra was failing to worship his preceptor,
Śakra could not endure the garland offered by Durvāsas due to its power.
Then that garland was thrown by him onto the forehead of the elephant; however, the elephant, having seized it with its very trunk, crushed it with its own foot.
At that time, Duḥsaha also entered into Durvāsas;
Durvāsas then cursed him, saying, "May you indeed be deprived of all prosperity."
Consequently, these riches met their destruction in the waters and other elements; and instantly, Indra’s palace was joined by the wife of poverty.
Duḥsaha, being constantly delighted, indeed made his own residence [his home];
then, due to the fault of poverty regarding Śacī, he performed acts such as giving and honoring.
Having withheld [the food] from the gods, brahmins, sages, ancestors, and others worthy of worship, as well as from guests and travelers,
he then entered that [house] while hungry.
From whatever place, whether from a god or likewise from a human, that which is to be grasped must be grasped and brought together; there is nothing whatsoever that should be avoided. 22.
Everything that is to be grasped she indeed seizes out of hunger;
the great king Nahuṣa, a universal monarch, has come within her sight. (23)
Being well-provided with wealth, she desired Śacī; therefore, she requested prosperity as well as gifts from the king, and having summoned him, she asked for an excellent jewel.

The king, too, beholding her—who was worthy of being honored by the gods—fallen into such distress, [gave] that which was his own, that which belonged to his son, and that which was acquired in other worlds. (25)
Even though she was being destroyed by the curse of Durvāsas, he gave her back;
for Śacī always desires a fresh gift whenever she is overcome by hunger.
Having obtained the consent of the gods, he was established in the command of Indra;
the king realized, "I have been made hungry by those who were supposed to provide me with sustenance. (27)
"Once she is satisfied, she will eternally be my object of enjoyment;
however, she shall remain at the disposal of Nahuṣa for the sake of sexual pleasure. (28)
Meanwhile, having lived with King Nahuṣa, Śacī was distressed; Mahendrāṇī became afflicted because Nahuṣa used the vehicle of a sage.
The serpent fell down, while Śacī went to Puṣkara;
thus, impurity resided in the serpent, in Mahendra, and in Śacī.
For many thousands of years, he remained thus unbearable everywhere;
meanwhile, his four wives lived among all the subjects in every way.
Then everything became filled with cries of "Alas! Alas! and afflicted by great suffering;
Udyogapattana was ruined, and the merchants fled to the forest. (32)
Lakṣmī went to the ocean, and even prosperities met their end;
wherever he was looked upon, there indeed was unbearable suffering accompanied by the three [poisons].
Without their husband, those four women, observant of their vows, did not remain;
they rejoiced, laughed, and danced in every house. (34)
Duḥsaha, however, takes the mṛdaṅga drum by the throat and plays it;
and Poverty performs a powerful, frantic dance. (35)
Driven by hunger, she wanders about the sides and even begs for ladles;
when something is thrown at her by someone, she seizes it by force. (36)
If someone gives her food, whether it be dry or fresh fruit, she immediately seizes it and eats it; indeed, she does not give any of it to another.
And if another woman takes her own share, she immediately begins a quarrel, uttering insults and slapping her forehead. (38)
If more than what is needed for his own satisfaction should remain, he gives it to another woman; he does not even take a mouthful of water, nor wash his hands, nor cleanse his face. (39)
In this dance, one woman, though soiled, cleanses the house, the door, the courtyard, the water-place, and the drain. (1.412.40)
The entire site of the Rasaśālā and its embankment was covered in filth;
what more need be said of the chests, the carpets, and so forth? (41)
The house walls, as well as the garden and even the crystal throne—the face, the eyes, the skull, and the forehead—all are covered with impurities. (42)
Everywhere in the world, beauty became uniform, and form turned into ugliness; brilliance lost its luster and was enveloped in thick darkness.
Thus, having witnessed that *tāṇḍava* dance, the gods, Nārāyaṇa and the others,
performed the churning of the ocean and [beheld] the auspicious Primordial Person.
Hari spoke to the virtuous Udārākhyu, who was born of dharma:
"Take these jewels as you desire; depart now. (45)
Wander everywhere throughout all the worlds together with contentment and the woman named Serenity; do not delay in your departure.
Then that son of Dharma, indeed possessed of a serene countenance, noble, and accompanied by his younger brother, was filled with contentment. ||47||
He moved swiftly among the subjects and took up residence in house after house;
seeing that, the unbearable one became enraged and went toward the gods.
Being driven out from all sides, he indeed begged along with his wife:
"O gods, let a place be granted to me for the sake of dwelling and for the sake of my livelihood. (49)
If I do not attain dispassion, I shall die; of this there is no doubt.
And my wives, devoted to their husbands, will enter the fire.
O Truth, when all these worlds reach a state of worthlessness upon my back,
I alone shall remain as the essence in this cycle of birth and death.
Without me, the court of King Yama would not function;
without me, the portions of Śrī Hari will by no means come into being. (52)
"As long as I exist, even unrighteousness everywhere receives constant nourishment;
indeed, fierce Asuras come into being only while I remain. (53)
"Let them do as they please; what is the use of saying more here?
Having said this, he ceased speaking, and at that moment his wives [spoke].
Deprived of food, reviled, and treated with contempt by their subjects, they went there before the gods, hungry and thirsty. ||55||
Where their husband resided, they then became enraged; they wept, beat their own breasts, and their heads burst asunder.
They uttered loathsome cries and raised a great clamor, saying:
"O, O, O! Where shall we go? We are thirsty and hungry! (57)
There is no field that yields food, nor likewise any dwelling house;
there is no tree bearing fruit, nor even any place of refuge to be found. (58)
"She was indeed given by Janaka to one who is devoid of qualities and has no fixed abode!
Oh, what fortune! We shall surely perish in the forest without food and water. (59)
There is no hearth, there is no house, and likewise no clothing or such things;
there is neither flour, nor sweets, nor even what is ordained—what indeed remains to be done?
What shall we eat, what shall we drink, and where shall be our dwelling place? Shall we indeed cut off our own feet and burn them in the hearth for lack of fuel? (6.1)
O Lord, why should we cut up our own children into pieces and eat them?
What is to be poured into a lamp here, if not oil—what need is there for blood? (62)
Beating the earth with their feet, clutching their hair with their hands,
and shedding tears from their eyes, they wept with distressed minds.
And those women raised a cry of lamentation filled with great sorrow;
then Dharma, Yama, Sūrya, Indra, Śambhu, and likewise Hari [appeared].
Seeing this, the world-protectors and the goddesses were overcome with compassion;
they consoled her and, after due consideration, granted her dry land.
Where husband and wife are mutually antagonistic; where teacher and pupil, guest and host, the twice-born, and even cows, are in conflict. (66)
O Duḥsaha, you should dwell specifically in their house with your wife,
where there is censure of the gods, the gurus, the masters, and Śrī.
Dwell there where there is censure of women, the elderly, and one's parents,
and where recitation, fire-offerings, charity, and worship are not practiced.
And enter among those who are devoid of helping others and who live with their wives, where there is no discourse on Hari and no honoring of the guru. (69)
And enter those houses where mutual quarreling occurs night after night,
and which are devoid of the libations offered to the ancestors, along with their wives.
While the children were looking on, you took and ate edible things there without giving any; enter that place, full of joy, together with your wife. (71)
Do not dwell in that house or even in that country where sinful people, devoid of compassion and devoted to acts of violence toward one another, reside. (72)
"Enter together with your wife into the house of one who has a crow's nest in a neem tree, or in a grove, or even in his own home, or always in the house of a shaven-headed woman. (73)
Enter that house where there is one female slave, three oxen, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants—there you shall dwell together with your wife. (74)
Where the wife is a mantra-practitioner and the husband is a *ḍāka* or *ḍākinī*, and where there is the dwelling of a *piśāca*—enter that place together with your wife. (75)
Where a maiden is pregnant, a young girl has reached puberty, and a widow is attached to another man—enter that assembly along with your wife. (76)
Enter those places where men are revilers of the virtuous and harborers of hatred, smelling like the onion species, along with their wives. (77)
Enter that place where virtuous women reproach ascetics, the righteous, husbands, the elderly, and Brahmins along with their wives. 78.
Where there is no bathing after sexual intercourse, there is no purity at all;
nor is there purity after the menstrual period, nor is the impurity of birth (sūtaka) observed. || 79 ||
And enter among those who are devoid of wisdom and auspiciousness, along with their wives;
they have soiled faces and dirty teeth, and subsist on wine and meat.
Enter wherever you find women who are devoid of twilight prayers and meditation, addicted to gambling and prostitutes, and delighted by harlots and the like. (81)
Enter the house of those mortals where animal-like passion prevails and human beings act like beasts, who vainly seek to extract the essence from the elements. 82.
Where thorny trees and hungry cattle and other such creatures are constantly struck by those who have let out their breath, dwell forever upon their shoulders. (83)
Even in a place that is pure and fit for dwelling, there exist those who produce impurities and the like;
though they possess power, always dwell upon their shoulders. (84)
Those who violate the scriptures, those who transgress the laws of the kingdom, and those who have fallen from the path of the world—dwell always in their house and upon their shoulders. 85.
Those who are opposed to the act of giving and hostile to the pursuit of happiness, and who destroy the affection between husband and wife—dwell there with your wife. (86)
Thus addressed, Duḥsaha bowed to the gods, headed by Viṣṇu,
and went to dwell wherever that place could be found everywhere.
On the thirteenth, the fourteenth, during the Festival of Lights, and on the first day of the lunar fortnight—all those four unbearable women roam the streets. (88)

In the courtyard, at the gate-tower, on the wall, at the threshold, in the quadrangle, and outside—by the offering of lamps, by filling the svastikas, and by means of beautiful archways (toraṇas). ||89||
Furthermore, by means of colored streaks and the like, by the sweeping away of dust,
by making them clean, or even by the offering of curd, those [lines] are established.
Where noble women are devoted to their husbands and husbands are devoted to their wives,
where both are intent upon Kṛṣṇa, and where the people are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
O beloved, those [demons] do not go where there are virtuous disciples who grant perfect satisfaction, where there are saintly women dear to Hari, and where Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa resides. (92)
Where there shall be the worship of Lakṣmī as well as the worship of Śāradā, where there shall be the worship of Gaṇeśa and various kinds of gifts; || 93 ||
Having bowed, they all return; indeed, they do not come again for a year.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the procedure for averting poverty and other such misfortunes. 94.

Thus ends the four hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Residences of the Chaste Wives—Duḥsaha’s Sons of Adharma—Known as Daridratā, Bubhukṣā, Kalaha, and Amlinatā," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to an ancient account that took place in the assembly of Brahmā,
in this world created by Brahmā and protected by the celestial sages.
Sages, seers, gods, ancestors, humans, birds, those dwelling in the netherworld, trees, gandharvas, kinnaras, and kings. || 2 ||
The Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the Vasus, the leaders of the gods;
as well as ascetics devoted to celibacy and yogins absorbed in meditation. || 3 ||
Vidyādharas, numerous Kimpuruṣas, and various classes of divine beings;
Apsarases from the Brahma-lake, virtuous women, and truthful maidens. || 4 ||

There were female servants and handmaidens who accomplished the purpose of service; they were women who could act according to their will, assume any form at will, and bestow pleasure as desired. || 5 ||
Equal-minded, equal-bodied, beautiful, and sixteen years of age— Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created them there specifically for the sake of wives.
He gave Śacī and other daughters born of his mind to the gods and others;
their duties as devoted wives were those of women accepted by their husbands.
Indeed, when undertaken with devotion to their husbands, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
thus were they described by Brahmā to the wives of the gods and to his daughters-in-law.
They were instructed in the duties devoted to their husbands, which are the means for attaining liberation;
and they listened with great respect to the teachings known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Those women were accepted in every way as auspicious and were satisfied;
however, though they were in the form of maidservants, they heard all the religious teachings in their entirety.
Reflecting on what indeed was the duty of us female attendants, [they thought]:
"We were created by the Grandfather (Brahmā) as maidservants subject to another's will. (11)
We shall become the female servants of the gods and likewise of the divine wives;
we shall be concubines, devoid of devotion to a single husband. Under slavery, the state of having only one master can never be maintained with proper protection.
And service is dependent on others, having the satisfaction of the master as its support. (13)
There may be many masters, and no single duty remains firm;
for through service to many, the life of a slave indeed unfolds.
In that regard, through many such attachments, misconduct arises;
consequently, due to the fault of that ill-deed, one's destination will indeed be hell. || 15 ||
Therefore, servitude for women can never bestow ultimate welfare;
such service should not be performed where there is no supreme goal. 16.
She serves all kings and wealthy men with a lustful disposition;
she dances for the sake of a fee and conducts herself as a courtesan. (17)
If it were harmful, then it should certainly not be accepted in any way;
therefore, just as all the celestial women were made to be married. (18)
We are the daughters of the lake of Brahmā, married in that same manner;
we are indeed Apsarases who have been taken as handmaidens by the gods and others.
We shall indeed always remain auspicious, devoted to the dharma of fidelity to our husbands,
toward sages who are like Brahman, toward gods, and even toward men.
Among the Nāgas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and even in the forests,
those women devoted solely to their husbands remained with their husbands through marriage alone.
We shall indeed conduct ourselves by fully upholding the duties toward a husband;
for the duty toward a husband is the supreme dharma, bestowing virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. (22)
The husband is the supreme consecration (nyāsa), bestowing sons, wealth, and happiness;
he is the supreme protection, the supreme refuge, the supreme deity, and the supreme teacher. ||23||
Without the rite of marriage, the status of a slave-girl is considered to be like that of a mere gem:
unstable, perishable, providing no security, and acquired through deception and the like. ||24||
It brings no satisfaction, causes constant agitation, and always bestows suffering;
therefore, indeed, we have all gathered together before Brahmā.
"We shall indeed request the Apsarases for marriage through the rite of giving";
having thus deliberated, all those Apsarases [spoke] in the assembly of the gods.
They entreated Brahmā again and again for the sake of marriage;
and then, for the sake of dharma, Brahmā [bestowed them] upon his own daughters.
These very dharmas, which bring about liberation, bestow happiness, grant heaven, and cause the destruction of evil deeds, are for those who have become daughters-in-law. ||28||
These have been taught for the sake of happiness as well as for the ultimate good.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the commercial laws which provide a basis for happiness. (29)
Whether she be a maidservant dependent on others, a maiden, a married woman, one without a husband, or one who remains in servitude, she is subject to the laws of the king. ||1.413.30||
Or she who has many masters, or whose master is unknown;
or she who is greedy for sensual pleasures, or for whom there is no other recourse. || 31 ||
By that [virtue], kings would become equal to their master, or even charioteers would become equal to them;
indeed, they would be worthy of service, for such was their very good fortune.
Whoever are the givers of livelihood or even the givers of wages, they are known as protectors for life, as saviors, and as lords. ||33||
Indeed, by serving them with heartfelt devotion, these maidservants cross over [the ocean of existence], even when their paramour gives them his fee, provided they remember me, Hari Nārāyaṇa. (34)
Those women who shall perform service equal to that of Nārāyaṇa will, by the power of Hari, cross over [saṃsāra] through such conduct free from hypocrisy.
He was attended with the thought that he was Hari, like a guest who has arrived;
indeed, it was not out of craving, nor by a greedy disposition, nor through deceit. (36)
Considering even one's husband to be momentary, he should be served like Hari when an auspicious day for the ancestors and the gods has arrived. (37)
Gifts of cows, land, and gold should be given according to one's capacity, as well as the blessings of gurus, virtuous people, and divine beings. (38)
Those [days] should be attained for the sake of prosperity, and their words should be observed;
when the sun is in the asterisms of Hasta, Puṣya, or Punarvasu. (39)
A courtesan should perform a bath with all medicinal herbs using a paste of *dhātrī* fruits and sesame seeds, along with *apāmārga* and *tulasī* leaves.
One should bathe with auspicious rice grains and water mixed with the water from the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, and likewise worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who can assume any form at will.
Having established Rati and Kāma, and Rādhā and the golden Kṛṣṇa, she should install and worship Lakṣmī and the golden Nārāyaṇa. ||42||

Having worshipped the feet for the sake of desire, the shanks indeed for the cause of delusion, the penis for the treasury of passion, and the waist with "Salutation to the one possessed of love. (43)
The navel to the ocean of bliss, and likewise the belly to Rāma;
the heart to the Lord of the Heart, and the two breasts to the one who causes delight.

To Vaikuṇṭha, who causes longing, [he offered] the face; to the one who bestows bliss, [he offered] the left side; to the flower-bowed one, [he offered] the right side; and to the one with flower-arrows, [he offered] the right side. (45)
"To Mānasa" [he offers] the crest-jewel; "to Vilola," the hair on the head; "to the All-Self, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Self, the one who flows forth. (46)
Salutation to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self, who possesses a beautiful form, who bears the discus and other [emblems], and whose essence is the god of love. ||47||
Salutations to you, the father of desire and the abode of the god of love;
salutations to Hari, the bestower of desire and liberation, the remover of suffering. ||48||
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, salutations to You, the builder of the prison of desire, the remover of the bonds of desire, and the bestower of liberation. ||49||
"O Kṛṣṇa, you are our husband; there is no other husband like you. Other husbands are seekers of their own self-interest, and we women are likewise seekers of our own self-interest. (1.413.50)
O Supreme Being, O Supreme Brahman, take us into your own hand;
let our devotion be fixed upon you alone, and never for even a moment upon others, O Giver of Night.
O Lord, you alone abide within all states of existence; you alone are our master.
O Lord, ferry us across the ocean of worldly existence and lead us, O Master, by means of the vehicle of Kṛṣṇa.
Women were created for the sake of desire, and you are indeed our embodiment of desire;
Kṛṣṇa Hari is considered the form of the seed, while you are regarded as the form of the child. (53)
For we consider you alone to be the form of love and the form of the *liṅga*;
let there not be any neglect toward us, your female devotees and servants. (54)
And if we, your beloveds, should ever touch you while you are for sale, let us—standing on your left side—perform that auspicious act which brings happiness. (55)
"O Lady, we offer even that which is devoid of merit; let it be withdrawn.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the offering to Kṛṣṇa is to be performed by a woman on the day of her husband. (56)
Likewise, courtesans and female servants should indeed perform that service as an offering to Kṛṣṇa;
then, regarding Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, and Rati, one should worship them. (57)
Salutation to Puṣṭi, salutation to Tuṣṭi, salutation to the accomplishment of all aims;
I bow to the mother of Anaṅga, salutation again and again to the wife of Kāma. ||58||
Salutations to you, Sundarī, whose essence is desire and who possesses the luster of Kṛṣṇa;
salutations again and again to you, Tāriṇī, whose form is the nature of bliss. ||59||
Thus, every morning, the courtesan should always worship Śrī Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī, as her husband with the feeling of devotion to a master, and she shall attain liberation.
With perfumes, garlands, incense, food offerings, water, and lamps,
as well as with lovely women and celestial nymphs, one should worship Śrī Janārdana.
One should give gifts of food, clothing, and wealth to the twice-born,
and one should also give to the virtuous, to those of Brahmanic character, and to the student (brahmacārin).
"I offer this to that Kṛṣṇa; may Śrī Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me.
With these words, the virtuous woman should either have the worship performed or perform it herself, which bestows merit. (63)
Kṛṣṇa indeed delivers such a beloved and devoted woman;
one should hold this Kṛṣṇa to be none other than the god of love himself. ||64||
And she who is absorbed in Kṛṣṇa should offer herself with her whole being;
then she would not be tainted by faults, whether she be a courtesan or a servant. 65.
One should perform the gift of a prastha of rice on Sundays,
during the months of Kārttika, Mādhava, and Māgha, and on the day of the Cāturmāsya vow.
One should practice the ninefold devotion; thus a courtesan becomes purified.
One should give a very beautiful bed, provided with all household utensils, to a Brahmin.
Provided with a pillow for rest, furnished with a rug and a coverlet, auspicious, and equipped with a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, wooden shoes, and a seat; ||68||
One should indeed give the gift of a bed at the temple of Kṛṣṇa, for it is purifying;
as well as golden threads, ornaments, necklaces, and beautiful garments. (69)
And [he gave] rings, girdles, bracelets, and various articles;
likewise, an image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and a statue of Kāma.
And one should present an image of Rati as a gift to a learned Brahmin;
it should consist of a copper vessel, a golden thread, and a pearl for her eye.
One should give to a twice-born man a stalk of sugarcane, a jar of molasses, incense, garlands, ointments, fragrant oil, and food.
Likewise, one should give a milch cow and, in the presence of the cow, say:
"Just as I never perceive any difference between Kāma and Keśava... (73)
O Kṛṣṇa, O Keśava, may I likewise always attain all my desires, so that Lakṣmī never departs from my body as she does not depart from yours. (74)
"O Lord of gods, O Master, place me likewise within your own body.
Then, having circumambulated the brahmin, the virtuous woman should bid him farewell. (75)
In this very way, one should worship the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; or, one should fully satisfy a brāhmaṇa, or any other man who has arrived as a guest, as if he were Kṛṣṇa himself. (76)
She should satisfy him according to his desire; when he is away on a journey, she should please another [relative];
and she who is dear to her husband should delight one who has arrived unexpectedly by chance. (77)
Even when this has been done, if the embryo should desire [to remain], one should protect that which is auspicious;
if there is no desire, then after sixteen days from the onset of the menses, [one may approach] a man.
She may touch him for the sake of pleasure or for the sake of offspring; likewise, she may dwell with him even without desire, if she is under another's control and lacks her own will.
For otherwise, the consequence of being pregnant would follow; yet one should employ metaphorical designations.
Indeed, this was previously told by the Creator to the Apsarases.
Therefore, this would not be unrighteous in any way for courtesans;
for it was said by Indra in ancient times regarding the daughters of the Dānavas: ||81||
As it was declared in former ages regarding beasts, birds, and women, so now all of this applies to you as well. (82)
By my command, every action performed as an offering to Kṛṣṇa—which pacifies all sins and bestows the attainment of Kṛṣṇa—shall become free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa). 83.
"O excellent women, do that which has been told to you, O auspicious ones.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, all the Apsarases acted according to his word. 84.
They spread among the gods, the sages, and human beings;
then, for the sake of destroying their sins, the gods spoke repeatedly. (85)
And those female slaves who are under the control of others, female servants who are without support, laborers who abide by orders, messengers, and women who are bondsmen; ||86||
May those noble women who are pure and without husbands become goddesses;
likewise may the courtesans, dancers, instructors, and female attendants [become so]. (87)
And may all those secondary wives always remain pure;
for men have always taken refuge in [the thought], "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! (88).
Being honored and existing [in this world], they shall be worthy of worship by the gods and will go to the city of Hari;
they are knowers of the good deed, and I am the witness for women. 89.
"Indeed, for those women whose vow is that their menstrual flow occurs month after month, all such women become pure through their season; so has Aja declared."
The vow of Ṛṣipañcamī, observed with fasting, is considered supreme;
by it, beautiful women are purified, and there shall be a dissolution of all defects. (91)
With devotion to Kṛṣṇa, all those women devoted to their husbands serve men;
Kṛṣṇa is the husband who is the Supreme Brahman, and those who observe that vow are truly devoted to their husbands.
Kṛṣṇa attains satisfaction when established in the self of man; Hari attains satisfaction when established in the self of woman. ||93||
Thus, a devotee whose nature is devotion does not deserve censure;
in this same way, the duty of a devoted wife has been illustrated by the example of courtesans.
This was proclaimed in the beginning during the Kṛta Yuga, and the celestial women practiced it; [but now] at the end of the age, when the mind is corrupted and devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. (95)
When the time has come, there is indeed a fault in excessively indulging one's desires;
no merit will arise, and the austerity already performed will surely perish.
Therefore, it is not fitting for a woman to behave as a commodity;
nor is it fitting for a man to behave as a paramour. (97)
In purity, the quality of purity is the dharma; in impurity, sin is considered the stain.
Therefore, the dharma of attachment is held to be superior to the dharma consisting of mere trade.
In truth, listen to all this: it is indeed excrement and urine, impure, with an unbearable stench, base, inauspicious, and always filthy. ||99||
Indeed, "mala" (impurity) should be understood as sin; "nirmala" (pure) is that which is devoid of sin.
Impurity flows out through the nine gates in various forms.
The dwelling in the womb is declared to be impure; urine is a liquid substance consisting of waste.
That indeed should be understood as a place of sin, and union with it is called sin. (101)
Yoga, however, is in every respect a sin in the case of both the means and the goal;
whether those two are joined together or even when they are not joined. (102)
Marriage is declared to be a religious observance (niyama), and that observance is always endured; however, non-marriage is not an observance, for it is certainly not endured by people. (103)
Impurity is evil action; it is either endured or not endured.
Since it is endured therein, it is certainly not the case that it lacks the nature of evil. (104)
Sexual intercourse is in every way sinful; no meritorious act exists therein.
Desire is in every way a fault, for it is indeed a lineage of unrighteousness.
If one is offered as divine through union with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, then that indeed consists of total self-surrender and bestows the grace of Hari. (106)
The favor of Hari should be sought through both one's own wife and another woman as well;
for desire, which is a source of sin, has been restrained by the elders through the rite of marriage.
For Apsarases, however, the Gandharva marriage was ordained by Brahmā;
for female slaves and women who have been purchased, that same Gandharva rite is merely momentary.

Whosoever is fit to be embraced by means of a bride-price with respect to a woman, he is designated as a "veśya" (a man of the courtesan class), and she is indeed a "veśyā" (a courtesan) for that very reason.
If men tolerate such a union between those two, it may be endured as if they were married; yet, by that alone, it is not considered righteous conduct.
However, that which is agreeable in thought and action is figuratively designated as "dharma";
having offered that to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, one should practice dharma according to its true meaning. (111)
Thus has the truth regarding courtesans been told to you, O beloved; likewise, for wives devoted to their husbands, duty is considered by rule to consist in equal action. (112)
But the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is itself a hell, for it leads only to the infernal realms;
whether with one's own wives, courtesans, prostitutes, or the wives of others. (113)
And the great sage named Dālbhya formerly declared the truth to women:
"Whatever action is performed through the senses that is devoid of remembrance of Kṛṣṇa... (1.14)
For all that consists of evil—desire, anger, muttered prayers, and vows—as well as all the realms beginning with heaven and the hells, exist within Kṛṣṇa. 1.15
The multitudes of enjoyments beginning with desire are hells within Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, having made Kṛṣṇa the supreme beloved and having propitiated that Lord, [one should remain]. 1.16.
Having served Nārāyaṇa, the true Lord, one becomes a Nārāyaṇī;
yet, the enjoyment of desire does not arise for the sake of the body's desires.
The Unborn One experiences the enjoyment of desires solely for his own pleasure;
yet these enjoyments of desire do not exist for the sake of the senses.
Even sensual enjoyments exist solely for the sake of the bliss of the Self residing within;
nor does the Self engage in desire independently, for Hari dwells within it.
Therefore, these who desire the Self do so only for the sake of Hari;
for if Kṛṣṇa were not there, the Self within the self would be purposeless.
Therefore, desires indeed become givers of bliss through union with Kṛṣṇa;
thus, by propitiating Kṛṣṇa, the fruit of one's desires is to be attained. 121.
"O Lotus-born One, that alone is declared to be the duty of devotion to one's husband even for courtesans.
Having heard this supreme dharma and considering it their own, the hosts of Apsaras [were filled with joy].
They proceeded according to the command of Brahmā, being devoted to the practice of *śulka*;
the master was honored with a fee (*śulka*) until he attained a state of complete satisfaction.
By performing service to him alone, they shall attain that supreme state;
and through reading and hearing this, the true nature of Dharma is awakened.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotion to the Lord among Slave-Women and Prostitute Women Who Are Without Husbands," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, how devotion to the husband (pātivratya) toward the Supreme Soul is to be practiced;
it was told by Hara to Nārada and by Kṛṣṇa to Śaṅkara.
I shall relate to you that which was told to Brahmā and Sanatkumāra;
it has been spoken by me and by my devotees, handed down through successive tradition.
What was said by you to Kambharādevī, I speak to you again after remembering it:
one must apply the mind to the self-surrender to Kṛṣṇa; he alone is to be served.
She should propitiate the Lord, who is the embodiment of the Master, together with Śrī;
for women, the husband alone is Hari, and she should conduct herself toward him with the attitude of a maidservant. || 4 ||
That woman who serves Nārāyaṇa even in the state of a maidservant delivers twenty-one generations of her own family.
That very day is blessed; blessed are the mother and the kinsmen;
blessed is the father, blessed is the husband, and blessed is the entire family.
By her who has served Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, with the realization that he is her husband,
the sins committed over many lifetimes are entirely destroyed.
The Supreme Goddess, whose nature is Lakṭhmi, became a purifier;
in ancient times, Śambhu spoke of devotion to her husband to Satī, the Supreme Sovereign.

O beloved, listen to what was thus spoken by Gaṅgādevī, which is worthy of being heard: "Devotion to one's husband and supreme affection are directed toward the master alone, and not toward others. (9)
Just as a woman’s love for her husband is directed toward him as being Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, so too have you meditated upon me, Śaṅkara, as your husband.
In this way, O beautiful one, Hari was meditated upon by me in all circumstances;
he alone is the protector, the nourisher, and the lord of all embodied beings.
Truth and lordship abide in Kṛṣṇa among those who possess bodies;
just as one afflicted by thirst longs for water, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
Just as one overwhelmed by cold remembers fire, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
Just as a devoted wife [remembers] her husband, so do I remember Mādhava.
Just as one dwelling afar remembers his home, or as the cātaka bird remembers the rain-cloud, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa, the knower of Brahman, through the knowledge of Brahman.
As swans desire Lake Mānasa, as sages [desire] Hari in Mānasa, and as devotees desire devotion, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa. || 15 ||
Just as Vaiṣṇavas desire purity, as cattle desire grass, and as the virtuous desire forgiveness, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa. || 16 ||
One who is addicted to vice is attached to vice; one who is attached to the body is indeed a non-knower of the Self; and one who is thirsty is attached to life—likewise, I remember Keśava.
Just as bees long for a flower, as ruddy geese long for the sun, and as one longs for the beloved of one's own heart, so do I remember the All-pervading Lord. (18)
Just as those dwelling in darkness long for a lamp, those afflicted by fatigue long for rest,
and those who are awake long for sleep, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa.
Just as elephants devoid of the lethargy of ignorance [seek] the wild forest land, and lions [seek] deer and other such animals, so do I remember Kṛṣṇa. || 1.414.20 ||
Just as fire arises from the sun-gem through contact with the sun, or as water is produced from the moon-gem through contact with the moon; ||21||
Just as the night-lotus bed blossoms with flowers upon seeing the moon, so too does Kṛṣṇa shine forth through association with Satī. 22.
Just as a female bee inside a lotus stalk at night might remember its protector, or else, having entered the stalk, might abandon its life-breaths and attain extinction; ||23||
Likewise, a virtuous wife’s maidservant should remember Kṛṣṇa as her protector; indeed, Kṛṣṇa was remembered by the gopīs in every way solely with the thought that he was their lover. 24.
I remember Kṛṣṇa as having attained union with Him;
likewise, some [remembered Him] with a wicked disposition, and some with a deceitful disposition. (25)
Some [attain it] through greed, others likewise through a state of dispassion;
another through affection, through devotion, through hatred, and yet another through the state of being a lover. ||26||
By means of her knowledge, a certain virtuous woman, having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janārdana, enjoyed happiness in this world and then departed for Goloka. ||27||
Even a spontaneous remembrance of the devoted wife bestows liberation;
by her singular devotion to her husband, she is seen in [his] presence in an instant. (28)
Without mutual affection, a wife is no wife, and without a wife’s affection, a husband is no husband;
though standing in close proximity, they remain as far apart as collyrium is from the eyes. (29)
Devotion consisting of fidelity to her husband was attained, and then Hari was obtained;
whereas Indra and the others, though they obtained the nectar, remained miserable because they lacked such devotion.
Having obtained the nectar of devotion to the Lord, suffering does not arise again;
just as swans leave the water behind and drink only the milk, and nothing else.
Abandoning illusion and abiding in truth, they drink in Kṛṣṇa with their eyes;
for a cloth pouch is not capable of binding water.
A magic pouch would not be capable of uniting one with Kṛṣṇa;
without devotion to her husband, a woman cannot desire Kṛṣṇa as her beloved. (33)
And how will Kṛṣṇa come without the offering of her devotion to her husband? A woman must always spontaneously practice devotion to her husband as devotion to Kṛṣṇa. (34)
Just as a fool desires to cross the ocean with his two arms, so too, O Kṛṣṇa, does she desire to cross the ocean of saṃsāra without a husband. (35)
As a poor man has longing for gold, so do I have longing for Hari;
as a woman has longing for a man when passion arises, so do I have longing for Kṛṣṇa. (36)
Even a tiny fire, if constantly nourished, consumes entire forests;
likewise, even a speck of dust of devotion to one's husband, O Kṛṣṇa, [destroys all evil]. (37)
One should worship the Lord, remembering: "Kṛṣṇa is my husband; my husband is Kṛṣṇa. This reduces to ashes the mountains of sins accumulated over thousands of previous births. (38)
Devotion to one's husband is heard of among hundreds of women through their association with the virtuous;
it is perceived by thousands of women, yet it is never actually maintained.
In this world, women of many kinds will impart their understanding to others;
yet that woman who practices it herself is seen but once in ten million.
Just as a boat [is used] in the ocean, or a small wooden trough for watering a well,
so too does the Dharma manifest itself according to the nature of the recipient.
Water poured at the root of a tree goes to the leaves and branches;
likewise, flowers, fruits, and seeds come into being in due succession. (42)
Likewise, service rendered to the husband increases one's sons, grandsons, and so forth;
it bestows heaven and even liberation—of this there is no doubt. ||43||
Just as a woman drawing water directs her mind toward the jar, the well, her feet, and her hands, so too does she direct her mind toward herself, her husband, and even Lord Hari.
Just as a child, having eaten jaggery, asks his mother for more,
so too a virtuous wife, having enjoyed her husband, likewise asks for Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Just as water is mixed with water, milk with milk, and ghee with ghee, so too is Kṛṣṇa merged in her husband; Satyā must indeed perceive him in that way. 46.
Just as the sun is omnipresent through its radiance and its rays, and just as fire is omnipresent through its digestion and its internal heat; ||47||
Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as well as Hari who is the very self of the husband, is omnipresent, O Queen of Devas; therefore, one should practice devotion to the husband. 48.
Sacrificial stones situated in the midst of water are not stained by the water even slightly; likewise, women devoted to their husbands are not defiled by other embodied beings. 49.
For the moonlight is indeed a giver of happiness, and the beloved husband is likewise a source of joy; just as ripe fruit is always sweet, so too is Kṛṣṇa the husband of a woman.
The frog dwells in the water, while the six-legged bee indeed resides within the forest; the bee perceives the fragrance of the night-lotus, but the frog does not. ||51||
Some dwell on the banks of the Gaṅgā, while others do so for a hundred yojanas;
yet only a few truly know the fruit of the Gaṅgā, as does Kṛṣṇa’s devoted wife.
A camel constantly carries a load of camphor and agallochum, yet it does not perceive their fragrance; being absorbed in its own nature, it knows no joy therein. //53//
Likewise, a wife who merely bears the burden of her husband, lacking devotion to her husband (pātivratya), never perceives even the fragrance or the bliss of her husband, Kṛṣṇa. 54.
Deer seeking the scent of musk smell the *śāla* tree; yet women, without devotion to their husbands (*pātivratya*), do not recognize that which resides within their own navels. 55.
For instruction given to fools results in the opposite effect;
likewise, the command of a husband becomes poison for an unfortunate woman. (56)
Just as milk drunk by a snake turns into venom through the application of poison,
so too does a husband become like poison for a woman who is devoid of devotion to her husband.
Even the instruction on wifely devotion becomes like poison when it is so intense;
it is like a lamp without eyes, or like a mirror [without eyes] for a jar. ||58||
One does not perceive existence in that way without perceiving Kṛṣṇa;
fire appears copper-colored with smoke, and the mirror is obscured by breath. (59)
In the same way, one whose soul is devoid of love and is struck by impurities does not perceive Him;
just as a fetus is enveloped by the amnion, so Hari resides within the husband.
Just as clarified butter resides in milk and oil always resides in sesame seeds, so Kṛṣṇa resides within all things moving and unmoving; he who knows him thus shall become his very self.
Just as many clusters of jewels are strung upon a single thread, even so are men and women woven together in Śrī Nārāyaṇa. (62)
Just as fire residing within wood is obtained by one who knows it through exertion, so too Viṣṇu residing in the husband is obtained by her who knows him through worship. 6.3.
The primordial Great Hari is the lamp; from that lamp, the lords such as the Sun and others were created as lamps. One should take refuge in that original lamp.
Among all lamps, the lamp of the Master is the foremost; therein one should kindle Kṛṣṇa, just as at the rising of the sun, light spontaneously pervades everywhere.
Likewise, when her husband has risen as Kṛṣṇa, her own light shines forth;
and the wind always carries fragrance by its very nature. (66)
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa indeed carries the fragrance of love, yet his water becomes like that which is mixed with sugar and poison. 67.
And such a husband becomes one who is infused with the essence of cultivation;
like the earth joined with seed, he gives birth to offspring in the form of various trees.
Just as water is made rich with its own essence by means of a seed,
so too is the Lord Kṛṣṇa born endowed with the essence of all states of being.
O Lakṣmī, her who thus beholds me as Śrī Kṛṣṇa while her husband is present—her, O Lakṣmī, I make into my own beloved Kamalā. (1.414.70)
She who knows me thus in her husband is my devotee and a faithful wife;
I am one, yet I exist in many ways, appearing in the form of the husband of all women. (71)
When name-and-form have been bestowed by me,
it is indeed by abiding in their true form that the eye is illuminated by the sun, and not merely from the sight of heaven.
In this way, O beloved, through Kṛṣṇa both wisdom and affection always increase;
yet, without Kṛṣṇa as her husband, affection does not increase.
"The Supreme Self and likewise I am present in every body—whether in a woman or a man, in every single pot. Let that devoted wife perceive Me as such. (74)
Just as all things, such as wood and the like, possess power through Nārāyaṇa, so too all things, such as husbands and the like, possess power through me, Kṛṣṇa. (75)
Just as various forms of gold arise from the work of a goldsmith,
so too do sons and other offspring take on the form of their husband through the wearing of Kṛṣṇa’s cloth.
When one does not perceive the Self as the Lord, then bliss turns into sorrow;
just as fools consider the sun to be lusterless when it is shrouded by clouds.
Likewise, just as a wife recognizes her husband even without his physical presence,
so too is that woman a devoted wife whose very nature has arisen from me as my sattvic manifestation.
The beloved of Hari recognizes me as her husband, appearing in the form of a husband;
yet she, deluded by karma and relying solely on desire, does not recognize me. (79)
But how could one who is deluded by ignorance conceive of me with such a mind?
Being inert from her past actions and a proponent of nihilism, she views me as if I were her own husband.
A wife should not be like an elephant's tusk, but rather like its trunk;
a husband should not be like the sky, but rather like a parasol. (81)
The two must always be cultivated together with one another, like water and milk; when they are heated by the fire of austerity, they act as mutual aids to each other. (82)
O Lakṣmī, when the essence of service is known, then Hari himself is attained by one's husband in this very life; for he is indeed easily won through service. 83.
The Knowable, the Supreme Brahman, is attained through the states of the heart within one's own [practices] and others;
indeed, among all states of being, the purity of state is preeminent. (84)
Sisters' sons, daughters, mothers, children, other women, female slaves, mistresses, attendants, and so forth are touched; according to the nature of the relationship, so is the result. (85)
Relatives, sons, enemies, the sons of friends, companions, and others are touched [by fortune];
as is the nature of the husband, the Brahmin, the guru, or the most eminent, so is the fruit. 86.
The beloved is the form of Nārāyaṇa, and the beloved wife is the image of Ramā;
indeed, through purity of intention, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is attained therein. (87)
Just as a stone image is worshipped with purity of heart, so too is Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa served within the beautiful form. 88.
As a beloved is embraced, so is the fruit according to one's inner disposition;
for indeed, one whose feet are shod with sandals perceives the earth as the Carmaṇvatī river.
According to the nature of one's intellect, so is one's manifestation made manifest;
indeed, through the intellect one returns to primordial nature, and through one's inner disposition one undergoes transformation.
A neem tree sprinkled with milk indeed does not abandon its bitter nature;
however, if it is sprinkled with salt, it gives up its life. ||91||
Just as a fruit may attain a sweet state through cooking, so too does the Lord bestow the cycle of existence through the nature of māyā. (92)
One should always distance oneself from saṃsāra through the alkaline nature of dispassion; for the Lord, having ripened [the soul] through the heat of the dark [stage], shall bestow immortality. 93.
Having cut down the mango tree, how indeed could one obtain its fruit or leaf?
Having abandoned the Lord Kṛṣṇa, while he is one's own master, how could a virtuous wife obtain her reward? (94)
How indeed could one prepare a golden plow for the cultivation of the *arka* plant?
Having cut down the *karpūra* and bamboo, from where could one protect the *kodrava* weeds? (95)
Having abandoned her husband Kṛṣṇa and forsaken a human being, how could she act so fruitlessly?
Indeed, how could a goat’s neck be roasted in a vessel made of lapis lazuli? (96)
Having abandoned the householder who is a treasure-trove, how could one practice the service of a mere oyster shell?
Having abandoned Śrī Hari who resides in the husband, how could one wander elsewhere in vain? (97)
Having abandoned the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) in one's own home, how could one resort to a mere cowrie shell?
When the husband is indeed the very form of Kṛṣṇa, how can meanness be conceived? 98.
Having abandoned the worship of Narasiṃha, how could one serve a dog? Having abandoned the beloved Lord of Ramā, how could one take pleasure with the lover of Death? 99.
If the bracelet is already on one's own wrist, what need is there for a shop?
When Lakṣmī is a servant in one's house, how can one's sovereignty even be described?
That Śrī Kṛṣṇa always resides with his Lord; let him not go elsewhere.
How can one perform meditation there on a formless Kṛṣṇa? (101)
"Having meditated upon Him with His form and His beautiful appearance, one shall go to the supreme state.
Thus, a virtuous wife should always remember Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her husband. (102)
When the body is covered in horripilation through the joy of remembering Kṛṣṇa,
then tears of bliss from the eyes shall become the handmaid of liberation.
The sin of speech is indeed destroyed by [the act of] cutting [the tongue], mental sin by remembrance [of Kṛṣṇa], and the evil of action perishes through the service and worship of Kṛṣṇa. 104.
Abandoning her duty toward her husband, she should certainly not practice severe austerity;
the dharma consisting of service to her husband is superior, for there is fear from another's bull (a paramour). 1.05.
Having left the hermitage of Kṛṣṇakāntā, how could she enter the hermitage of a wandering ascetic?
Having purchased Kṛṣṇakānta with her husband’s wealth, she should satisfy him. (106)
One should give pure white substances of excellent quality as a gift to a Brahmin or to Lord Hari;
one should give materials full of affection and imbued with faith to a married husband.
The great merit that comes from such giving is indeed beyond counting;
one should not take pleasure in any other object, but should find delight only in the husband who wields the Śārṅga bow.
For one who possesses such conduct, suffering indeed does not arise;
even if it should occur, one should not feel distress, for that was produced by past actions.
For animals are bound by ropes, and likewise living beings are bound by their karma;
having become devoted to the Supreme Lord (Patikṛṣṇa), one should joyfully sever that bond.
The male monkey wanders from tree to tree in the forest with longing, and the female monkey wanders from house to house in the city with longing. (111)
If that craving is offered as an oblation into the glorious fire of one's own husband, Nārāyaṇa,
the virtuous wife, having drunk the nectar of eternal immortality, shall obtain happiness.
Just as a ball exists for the sake of play, so too does the body exist as a sport;
therefore, a virtuous woman should please Kṛṣṇa, who is her husband in essence.
By their former karma, living beings are led through many wombs;
even the gods are subject to karma in heaven, and the sages are bound by truth.
Even the serpent residing within the body of Śambhu is indeed poisonous due to his past actions;
likewise, Aruṇa is lame in the chariot of the Sun. Karma is a most powerful source.
The entire world is dependent on karma and was created by me through Viṣṇu;
by my name and by service [to me], all karma is destroyed. (1.16)
There is one water, O Devadatta, and another is that which remains in the jar;
liberation comes from what is offered to the gods, and likewise, O beloved, from offering it unto me.
Thinking, "I am the wife and this one is the husband, both of us have taken refuge in Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa," one should perform the offering of everything as an offering unto Śrī Keśava.
One should cultivate the sense of "I" in Hari, and one's duty must be surrendered to Him; one should experience the fruits of past karma, yet by offering everything to Kṛṣṇa, one is not tainted.
They praise the seizing of spirits, ghosts, and piśācas; they praise mantras, medicinal herbs, success, valor, intelligence, exertion, daring, and strength. (1.414.120)
Some praise policy, others fortitude, and still others praise the line [of conduct];
yet he praises his husband as Dharma and Hari as Dharma, not out of delusion.
They do not praise the vow of a devoted wife, nor virility, nor good character, nor devotion;
likewise, due to their folly, they do not take refuge [in these], being deceived at home by rogues. (122)
When a living being is absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, then no sin exists;
whatever merit or happiness there may be, one should offer it to the Lord Kṛṣṇa.
Then one attains the union of the couple, the state of bliss;
when one performs external actions with the body but has no longing for them in the mind.
O beloved, that renunciation which is performed with a desire for offering to Kṛṣṇa is the highest;
some renounce everything out of anger, while others renounce it out of distress.
Others abandon [their vows] when they do not obtain [the goal], but renunciation for Kṛṣṇa is considered supreme; even if a woman devoted to Kṛṣṇa is moved by worldly action, [she remains steadfast].
Constantly devoted to the service of her husband, that virtuous woman goes to a happy rebirth, even in the home of those who are pure, prosperous, wise, and yogis. (127)
A virtuous woman devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa is reborn as a daughter; through the yoga of devotion, she attains the fruit of serving her husband with very little effort.
Through my grace and by means of devotion, one attains the state of consciousness and bliss;
by the very act of total self-surrender, one attains liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Just as mud cannot be washed away by mud, nor blood by blood, how can an action of a violent nature ever be capable of cleansing another action? 1.414.1–30.
Without the Lord Kṛṣṇa, how can there be the destruction of karma through action?
Through the Lord joined with Kṛṣṇa, the destruction of all karma occurs. || 131 ||
Eternal happiness is to be found in Hari, not in heaven nor through ritual acts;
nowhere does that eternal happiness exist for them without devotion to Hari.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, a woman devoted to her husband should always act in this manner toward her husband;
she bestows both happiness and liberation, and I am the witness to that in every respect.

Thus ends the four hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Divine Wifely Devotion as Taught by Śaṅkara to Kṛṣṇa, Who is Essentially the Husband," within the section on the Greatness of Chaste Wives in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī; though I have told you this again and again, I am not yet satiated. O beloved, listen as I explain the reason for my faith in this matter.
By observing the great duties of devotion to their husbands, virtuous women and others likewise attain certain liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. || 2 ||
Even though pleasures may be many, they are impermanent;
there is never any permanent happiness among them without service to Hari. (3)
Whether it be the happiness of a universal monarch, or even the happiness of Virāj, or any other divine happiness whatsoever, it should certainly not be desired as a final goal.
For a pressing-stone may be broken by metals, but a diamond is never broken;
likewise, devotion to one's husband and devotion to Hari can never be broken by anything.
Just as a crane eats aquatic creatures while avoiding frogs and the like,
so too Yama, the destroyer of all, avoids the servants of Kṛṣṇa.
Every morning, having bowed to her husband in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, she should say:
"Take this maidservant, who is burdened with hundreds of offenses, back to her own place. (7)
O Kṛṣṇa, show mercy to me who am unaware of my wifely devotion;
for even though the gatekeeper is present, if the master desires it, [he may enter].
Having prepared [the offering] by any means whatsoever, she should give it to one authorized by her affection;
that virtuous woman obtains the fruit, provided she remains steadfast as a devoted wife within.
Thus, O Lord, even though she is a servant stationed far away and situated outside, please protect her and bring her close to you, O Master.
Others have indeed not attained liberation, yet Kubjikā has been delivered by you;
that which is difficult for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain even in a dream is easily obtained in the house of the cowherd woman.
The cowherds, having enjoyed your grace, have gone to the world of Brahmā;
likewise, grant me your grace, deliver me, and lead me to your own state.
O Keśava, so that I may obtain you, the Lord of Śrī and the descendant of the Pāṭhya lineage, as my husband, and so that you may be gracious toward me, place me under your protection. (13)

Just as the two thorns of the Badarī tree—one crooked and one straight—both act as obstructions, so too does the crooked one, by assuming the guise of a cloth or similar object, obstruct the traveler. (14)
The straight arrow, having pierced the skin, burns the embodied being;
the crooked one, Nārāyaṇa, [pierces] the body, while the lord alone is truly straight.
O beloved, without Nārāyaṇa, the Lord is a burner through the objects of the senses and so forth; but He alone, when united with Kṛṣṇa, is a restrainer and the giver of liberation.
Just as a slight contact with fire causes gold and other metals to become heated, while an intense union with fire becomes their purifier and liquefier; || 17 ||
Likewise, the union with a mere child or the like produces only the state of being an object [of attachment];
that very same union with the great fire of Śrī Kṛṣṇa bestows liberation. 18.
Just as a machine would be useless without its operator, so too the machine that is the husband is useless without Kṛṣṇa. 19.
Just as a maiden without hair does not grant peace to the beholder, so too, O Satyabhāmā, the Lord without Kṛṣṇa does not bestow eternal bliss upon us. || 1.415.20 ||
Just as a deer dwelling in the forest never leaves its circular range, so too a doe remains with her mate; she does not abandon Hari who dwells within her heart.
Just as a lion, while moving through the forest, repeatedly looks back behind him, so too Hari is always to be seen by his wife as she goes to her husband's house. 22.
Just as a full river flows down toward lower and lower ground, so too does she who is full of the dharma of devotion to her husband proceed toward her husband, Kṛṣṇa. ||23||
The cloud always moves through the sky and releases its water upon the ground below;
likewise, a virtuous wife should always remain faithful to her husband and love Hari who dwells within her heart. 24.
Just as there are indeed minute plantains within the trunk of a plantain tree, so too are pleasures minute within Kṛṣṇa, who is the inner self of all beings. (25)
Just as the syllable 'A' exists as the imperishable inner self within all letters, so too does Kṛṣṇa exist as the imperishable one within the husband, the wife, the son, and so forth. (26)
Without a door, a very strong chain is useless;
likewise, without Kṛṣṇa, the firm dharma of devotion to one's husband is fruitless. ||27||
A marriage performed properly is in vain without seed, and a husband is in vain without Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as that seed. ||28||
In the summer, without water, coolness that brings satisfaction does not arise;
likewise, in the forest fire of worldly existence, Kṛṣṇa alone is the Lord who grants peace, and no other.
The Earth, the wife of all, was indeed lifted up by the Boar; Govardhana, common to all, was lifted up by Kṛṣṇa.
The Gopīs, women who were under the control of cowherds, were uplifted by Kṛṣṇa through their devotion;
indeed, Kṛṣṇa will certainly uplift a virtuous wife through her devotion to her husband. 31.
Likewise, even female servants who are devoted to Lord Kṛṣṇa as their master and are dedicated to the virtue of devotion to their husband undoubtedly uplift themselves; of this there is no doubt.
Just as a bird has confidence in its egg regarding the chick, so should a wife place her confidence in her husband regarding Mādhava. ||33||
Just as a lineage resides in a son, a tree in its seed, and desire within embodied beings,
so too does Hari dwell in both husband and wife, bestowing all desires and bliss.
Milk mixed with a small amount of buttermilk bestows fresh butter;
likewise, the Lord mixed with Kṛṣṇa grants liberation, without a doubt. (35)
Just as a moth beholds the forest glade by its own radiance,
so should a devoted wife behold her life through Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within her husband.
The celestial chariot of a Vaimānika moves with speed; it proceeds in every way by means of the eye of that [rider] and by the Kṛṣṇa situated within it. (37)
Just as a large water-wheel, causing the buckets to revolve repeatedly,
returns them to their respective places again and again, so too should a faithful wife go to the place where her husband is.
Just as strength increases in the horns of a young calf, so too does strength increase in a woman toward her husband. (3.9)
Just as a boat made of wood certainly carries the wood across,
