so too a wife created by the elements shall carry her husband across by means of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as flowers that were hidden bloom when their season arrives, so too will Hari, who remains concealed, be made manifest through devotion when the Lord has arrived. 41.
Just as joy arises when long-absent family members return home, O Kṛṣṇa, so too may it arise for you when your husband returns. 42.
Just as a verse, even if its meaning is already known, shines forth when it is present in the heart, so too does Kṛṣṇa shine within the heart of the wife through her devotion toward her husband. 43.
Radiance is eternally situated in the sun, and blackness is established in Rāhu;
Kṛṣṇa is eternally present in his husband, and he does not shine in atheism. 44.
All those activities of the Lord are indeed the activities of Kṛṣṇa and none other, because they are divine, bestowing liberation, and conceived within the Supreme Brahman. (45)
Desire for her husband, his ritual acts, his efforts, sleep, dalliance, and the act of pressing him—all she considers as divine and consisting of Kṛṣṇa; such is the devoted wife. 46.
Having become divine and most divine, like the splendors of Ramā, Rādhā, and Prabhā,
she leads her husband to heaven and goes to that place called Apunar-māra.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge of the Chaste Wife’s Worship of Hari as Embodied in Her Husband," within the section on the Greatness of Chastity in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga, in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the most excellent duties that bring about the attainment of a husband; by observing which, a woman obtains a husband equal to Kṛṣṇa.
Ananta was the son of Kadrū who was born from Kaśyapa;
Nāgalakṣmī became his wife, and she was devoted to her husband. || 2 ||
Ananta supported the circle of the earth upon the tip of his own hood;
then Nāgalakṣmī respectfully questioned her husband Ananta.
"O Blessed One, you must go upon the earth together with Viṣṇu;
whenever that time comes, I too shall remain there together with you."
"In what form and where [did he appear]? Tell me, O Treasure of Compassion!
Then Ananta spoke to his beloved Śrī.
"O beautiful one, you must indeed remain steadfast in devotion to your husband during the asterism Revatī;
for in a previous birth, she was a virtuous maiden named Jyotiṣmatī."
The daughter of Cākṣuṣa Manu was born from the sacrificial fire-pit;
as soon as she was born, she became mind-born (mānasī) and possessed the memory of her former births.
The auspicious sister of Sudyumna, a woman of excellent complexion and noble form, was a knower of the Vedas who obtained the fruit of sacrifice; she became a young woman as soon as she was born.
Once, Akṣuṣa asked his daughter: "Tell me, daughter, what kind of husband do you desire? I shall indeed make such an effort."
She then said, "May he who is the strongest among all become my husband.
Having heard that, Cākṣuṣa, knowing Indra to be preeminent in strength, [chose him].
He respectfully summoned Bali, the strongest, who was nearby;
and as the wielder of the thunderbolt arrived immediately and stood before him, he spoke to him.
"I know you to be the strongest; tell me, if there is anyone stronger than you. Indra said, "O Cākṣuṣa, there is one stronger than I: the Wind."
"By whose assistance I accomplish even tasks that are difficult to conquer"—
having spoken thus and received honors, Indra departed for his own abode.
Then Cākṣuṣa summoned Vāyu and said this:
"I know you; I am stronger than you, so name someone else. (14)
Vāyu said, "O Cākṣuṣa, the mountains are stronger than I am.
Having spoken thus and received due honor, Vāyu departed for his own abode. || 15 ||
When the wind had departed, Cākṣuṣa summoned the mountains there and asked them, "I am indeed counting all of you who are most powerful. (16)
"If there is another who is stronger than you, tell me here," they said;
then the mountains replied, "A fragment of the earth is more powerful. (17)
"Wherever we remain, we shall always be supported by you.
Having spoken thus and received due honor, the mountains then departed.
Having summoned Bhūkhaṇḍa Cākṣuṣa, the king asked them:
"I know you alone to be powerful, and no other."
"If there is anyone, speak; is there a Khaṇḍa who is powerful and world-renowned?
Thus addressed, Khaṇḍa himself replied: "O King, there is one superior to me in strength."
The Blessed Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the sustainer of the cosmic egg, possessing infinite qualities and a thousand coils, exists as an expansion (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu. ||21||

He was auspicious, radiant with white light, possessing the brilliance of the sun, youthful, and powerful; he possessed the loveliness of ten million Cupids, had lotus-like eyes, and a beautiful face. ||22||
Wearing a forest garland, he is praised by the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas;
his lotus feet are meditated upon by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Sādhyas, and others. || 23 ||
By whose name the heap of sins and the like is dissolved and liberation is attained—such is the power of the Blessed One, the cause of all causes. (24)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is manifest; he is not inferior, for his very nature is that [of the Supreme].
Possessing inexhaustible power and the Lord of all, he is established at the root of Rasā.
Having spoken thus, Khaṇḍa departed; then Cākṣuṣa said to the maiden:
"Daughter, one shines by placing one's foot upon the heads of the powerful. (26)
Ananta, who is indeed Śeṣa, upon whose head rest millions of cosmic eggs—he is determined as your husband; he cannot be obtained without ascetic penance.
"If you desire that your wish be fruitful, perform the means for the sake of the fruit.
Thus instructed by her father, she went to the Vindhya mountain.
Bathed in the command of her father-in-law,
that devoted wife performed most rigorous penance, remaining engaged in asceticism for a hundred thousand years.
In summer she was scorched by the five fires; in the rainy season she endured the downpours;
in the cold season she remained submerged in water up to her neck, sleeping upon the bare ground.
Then, while the forest goddess was without food, dwelling alone in the wilderness,
other forest deities approached her for the sake of service.
Standing all around her as she chanted "Rāma Kṛṣṇa, Rāma Kṛṣṇa," they gave her dry leaves and pure, wholesome fruits.
In various places, she gathered bulbs, roots, and leaves—appropriately and as they were to be taken—so that there might be no obstacle to her ascetic practice. (33)
In this manner, half a hundred thousand years passed;
then that virtuous woman subsisted on water, and after that, she subsisted on vapors.
Then she became one whose food was breath, and subsequently entered the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Thereupon, an anthill adorned with bamboo and other plants arose at the front of her body. (35)
Having joyfully made a hole in the body of an ant and dwelling there, she—
consisting of Brahman, having the body of Brahman, and manifesting in the form of Brahman— remained.
Those divine women, free from the pairs of opposites, indeed became [manifest] for the sake of attaining power;
then, on one occasion, they arrived, having been deprived of their fortitude by asceticism. (37)
The gods Śakra, Yama, Sūrya, Varuṇa, Agni, and Dhanādhipa; Soma, Maṅgala, Guru, Budha, Śukra, Śani, and Rāhu. ||38||
Having arrived there for the purpose of examination, where she was established in austerity, they said: "Who are you? How is this? For whose sake do you perform this austerity? (39)
"You are too delicate to perform austerities; tell us, what do you desire?
We shall grant you everything. Having heard this, Sundarī spoke thus: [40]
"May he who has a thousand faces and is infinite be my husband"—thinking thus, I am performing penance for his sake; having heard this, they then laughed.
Indra spoke previously to the virtuous maiden Jyotiṣmatī:
"O auspicious one, why do you practice penance in vain when the King of Serpents is the intended groom? (42)
"Choose me, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, who have come to you of my own accord;
I shall grant you all the most excellent enjoyments—accept the fruit of your asceticism."
Yama said to the great king, "Choose me alone as the wielder of the rod of punishment;
become the sovereign of the world of the ancestors under the Lord of the Three Worlds. (44)
"O daughter of Akṣuṣa, you shall be my most excellent wife and always my beloved;
for I am Sūrya, the eye of the world," he said. (45)
"O auspicious one, become worthy of worship through your radiance; O excellent one, adorn heaven and grant me your favor.
You shall yourself become a divine golden-colored vessel, well-fashioned. (46)
Varuṇa said to the Lord of the World: "O Lord of the hosts of aquatic creatures, grant me, the bearer of the noose, the sovereignty over the seven oceans."
Agni said: "I dwell within the mouths of all sacrifices, gods, and brahmins;
I am golden-hued, invincible, worthy of worship, and possessed of great strength. (48)
"Serve me, the youth who fulfills all desires; become my most excellent wife, Svāhā!
Kubera said to the auspicious one, "O Queen of Queens, [serve] me, the lord of the treasures. (49)
O ocean of joy from enjoyments, comforts, garments, and ornaments, worship me today;
I shall make you a mistress of wealth, so give gifts at all times.
Soma said: "Eat the nectar; eat the most excellent, fresh herbs.
I am indeed the bestower of strength to women, the radiant creator of the moon. (51)
Worship me, the king of the twice-born, the lord of the constellations, the husband of Rohiṇī;
become my first great queen, honored by the twenty-seven [stars]. (52)
Maṅgala said: "I am red; you are red, O Dhruvā, who are powerful and nourished.
Therefore, accept me as your lover and become a beloved equal to Śrī Lakṣmī. (53)
The earth is my mother, and Sadāśiva himself is my father;
becoming my beloved, enjoy all auspicious things. (54)

The Guru said: "I am the one to be worshipped by the gods; O Goddess, go to the state of being worthy of worship. By becoming the wife of the preceptor of the gods, you shall obtain the joys of heaven. (55)
"I am composed of all branches of knowledge; honor me, O auspicious one," said the wise man, who was always well-nourished and possessed great strength and vigor.
Embracing me, O mistress of desire, take your pleasure with me;
enjoy my divine delights, for you are one who knows the essence of passion.
Śukra, the great poet, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the bestower of life, the knower of the true sciences such as Sañjīvanī, and the possessor of a body at will, spoke. (58)
I am exceedingly radiant, proud of my prime youth; I possess all supernatural powers and knowledge of all bodily arts, such as the *kalpas* and others. (59)
Under whose control the Daityas and Dānavas always dwell,
as do Bṛhaspati and others, and even the lords such as Mahendra and the rest.
Out of fear of me, they remain in my service; therefore, O Bhavānī, be dear to me.
Śani, the highly wise one, said: "I am the bestower of all fortune."
I am the one who reduces the world to ashes, and I am the eternal sovereign of the sky;
I stand above the gods, and my riches are likewise beyond counting.
Enjoy pleasures; become the great mistress of the daughters of the Dānavas.
I shall place heaven in your hand for as long as the moon and sun endure.
Having heard this, Jyotiṣmatī,
who was virtuous, for a moment directed her eyes, copper-red with rage, toward all those slaves who had made their request at an improper time.
And having remembered Ananta, the devoted wife spoke to them all:
"Since you are all gods, the best of deities, you are worthy of worship. (65)
O lords of the gods, noble women are not objects for my reproach;
indeed, I desire only the infinite, supreme boon, and nothing else.
Since this has been determined thus, may the gods not act as obstacles to me;
rather, let that ascetic woman, who is virtuous, be honored with blessings by the deities. (67)
"It is certainly not appropriate to go back to your own hermitages in such a contrary manner.
O gods, I bow at your feet; I am indeed the maiden Cākṣuṣī."
Having heard her words spoken in such a manner, they laughed among themselves;
then Jyotiṣmatī realized that those gods were indeed acting in jest.
He cursed those who were in a state of playful jesting: "May you, in this world, soon become objects of ridicule for women and suffer great misery on account of women. (1.416.70)
Then, overcome with terror, they all repeatedly bowed to Satī, propitiating her so that the end of the curse might occur at another time. (71)
Having received your word, the gods remained silent for a moment;
for by her curse, when Saṃjñā had become a mare for Sūrya, [they stood thus]. (72)
Due to separation from his wife, the Sun became a horse in order to regain her;
Indra fell into reproach through his lust for the wife of Gautama. (73)
Separated from Śacī and repeatedly tormented by others, Yama, the lord of the realm of hell, is constantly censured by the denizens of hell. (74)
Varuṇa is insulted by women during their bath when they are naked;
Agni is insulted by women at the hearth with their hissing breaths. (75)
Kubera was beaten by the rākṣasīs and driven into exile;
and Candra, having desired Tārā, indeed incurred reproach. (76)
Maṅgala, having the face of a monkey, was indeed censured by the female monkeys;
Bṛhaspati was reviled by Tārā and is called powerless.
The wise one is not seized by women for an auspicious task; he is censured.
Śukra was held in the womb by Śambhū, who had accomplished her purpose in battle. 78.
Śani was born as a woman herself, and Hanumān was afflicted by the crushing of his feet;
thus, through the power of their curses, they fell into contempt over time.
The fruit of their jesting will be obtained by them in another kalpa; endowed with those respective dispositions, they shall exist according to their established nature.
Then the gods cursed Jyotiṣmatī while she was healthy and dwelling within an anthill:
"Even though you have obtained a husband, you shall remain childless. (8.1)
She performed severe penance, and Brahmā arrived there in the form of a swan,
accompanied by Marīci and other Brahmins who were knowers of Brahman.
Standing in the sky, he said to that Jyotiṣmatī, the daughter of Akṣuṣa:
"O creator of the universe, I have come to ensure that your penance bears fruit. (83)
"I am pleased; choose a boon, for you have attained perfection through your asceticism, my daughter.
Having heard this, she emerged from the water up to her neck and, having prostrated before the Unborn One (Aja), [spoke]. (84)
Having praised him with palms joined in reverence, she said: "You are indeed pleased with me here;
you are my lord, the thousand-faced Ananta Saṃkarṣaṇa. (85)
"May it be so! Grant me a boon; I certainly request a boon.
Having heard this, he replied, "This desire of yours is difficult to attain. (86)
Nevertheless, I shall fulfill that desire at the end of the twenty-seventh Dvāpara age of Vaivasvata Manu.
"O daughter, Saṃkarṣaṇa Ananta shall be your husband.
Having heard that, the virtuous Jyotiṣmatī spoke to Brahmā:
O God of gods, how indeed may this great time be spent by a woman?
Grant me your grace so that my heart's desire may be swiftly fulfilled. (89)
Having heard this, Brahmā reflected for a moment and said to the ascetic woman:
"Become today the daughter of King Ānarta in Kuśasthalī."
"O daughter, become a maiden named Revatī, the daughter of Revata; and having taken you with him, O daughter, your father will truly go to his own world. (91)
When he comes for the sake of obtaining a worthy bridegroom,
the period of twenty-seven ages will pass away like a single moment.
Having thus granted her the boon, he vanished on the spot;
then she [was born] in the land of Ānarta, in the house of the lord of Kuśasthalī.
Indeed, Jyotiṣmatī Revatī took birth from his wife;
that virtuous maiden, endowed with beauty and loveliness, grew up. (94)
Revata asked his accomplished daughter, who was fit for marriage:
"Daughter, tell me what kind of husband you desire; I shall provide him. (95)
Then Revatī said, "May I have a powerful husband.
Having heard this, the king, together with his wife and daughter, [departed] by means of a divine chariot.
To question Brahmā— the long-lived one and the foremost among those possessing strength that surpasses all— he went to Satyaloka and remained there for a moment.
In a mere moment of time, twenty-seven Dvāpara ages have passed upon this earth; today, only an infinite portion remains for the sake of your daughter. (98)
"Give the maiden indeed to Bala, the elder brother of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
she, being an incarnation of Revatī, has always been Jyotiṣmatī. (99)
Having obtained Saṃkarṣaṇa as her husband, Revatī, who was the Nāga-lakṣmī,
remained ever devoted as a virtuous woman, radiant and of divine form.
Because his father, standing upon the hump of the bull, conquered the surface of the earth,
he became famous on the face of the earth by the name Kakudmin.
O Lakṣmī, that ascetic woman devoted to her husband has been described to you;
by reading or hearing this, the fruit of wifely devotion shall be attained. (102)

Thus ends the four hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Curse, Power, and Other Matters Concerning Jyotiṣmatī, Also Known as Nāgalakṣmī," in the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives within the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. This chapter describes how she, who was devoted to her husband, was tempted by hosts of gods despite her asceticism, yet remained in the form of Revatī and was wedded only by Baladeva.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you about my wives and daughters—
the five principal ones who reside in the abode of Goloka, who are truthful and devoted to their husbands.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, Śivā, and Rādhikā—these are they.
Rādhā is the daughter of Karṣṇa, the mother of Śiva, Lakṣmī, and she who is Nārāyaṇī.
She indeed generates noble effort, is the very nature of the perfect Brahman,
and bestows fame, auspiciousness, righteousness, prosperity, truth, and merit.
She bestows the joy of liberation and destroys grief, suffering, and affliction;
she is solely devoted to the protection of the distressed and the miserable who have come for refuge.
Siddheśvarī, she whose form is perfection, the giver of success, the sovereign of the attainment of success;
she is intellect, sleep, hunger, thirst, shadow, lassitude, compassion, and memory. || 5 ||
Birth, patience, peace, splendor, delusion, volition, contentment, nourishment, as well as fortune, conduct, the mother-form, and supreme intellect. (6)
May these women, who are the very embodiment of Lakṣmī and devoted to their husbands, remain here;
for Lakṣmī is the essence of all crops and the means of livelihood.
In Vaikuṇṭha she is Mahālakṣmī, devoted to the service of her husband;
in heaven she is Svargalakṣmī, and among kings she is Rājalakṣmī.
She is the household fortune in the home, the fortune of beauty in embodied beings,
the fortune of affection among the meritorious, and she is the fortune of splendor in kings.
The merchant exists for trade; among the wicked, she is quarrelsome;
she is the goddess of compassion toward devotees, and the fortune of prosperity among the fortunate.
O beloved, she exists in the form of substance, consisting of gold, gems, rubies, and pearls; without her, the entire world would be as if dead while living.
And Sarasvatī is the consort of Brahmā, the embodiment of all sciences;
she is the presiding deity of speech, intellect, learning, and knowledge—the virtuous Śāradā.

Subuddhi (good intellect), kavitā (poetic power), medhā (retentive memory), pratibhā (inspiration), smṛti (recollection), as well as kalpanā (imagination), bodhinī (awakening power), vaktṛtā (eloquence), and likewise granthikā (the power of composition). || 13 ||
Chanting, rhythmic clapping, the union [of melody], and speech in the form of exposition—without these, the entire world would be mute, as if dead. (14)

She is Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Vedas, Brāhmī, and she who takes the form of the Sandhyā and other rites; she is the embodiment of mantra, the embodiment of tantra, the embodiment of japa, and the ascetic woman.
Gāyatrī, the beloved of Brahmā, is the embodiment of the Brahminical splendor, the form of all sacred rites, the purifier, and the personification of holy pilgrimage sites.
She is the progenitor of all splendor, whose form is the light of Brahmanic luster;
without her, the entire world would be blinded by ignorance, like one who is dead.
She is Śivā, Śaivī, Raudrī, Durgā, Kālī, and Caṇḍikā;
she is the embodiment of all powers and the destroyer of all Asuras. || 18 ||
Devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), possessing the form of Brahman, and endowed with the quality of purity (sattva);
she consists of all spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) and is Jaya, Vijayā, and Prahāriṇī.
She is the withdrawer and the destroyer, the protector and the devoted wife;
without her, the entire world would be powerless, as if dead.
Rādhā, the consort of Kṛṣṇa, the Great Illusion, the most exalted devotee, the virtuous one;
the goddess of love, equal to his very life, dearer than life, and the foremost of beauties. (21)
The supreme Śakti, the bestower of good fortune, proud and endowed with dignity,
is in every respect equal to Kṛṣṇa in her qualities, splendors, and sovereign powers.
She is the supreme and the inferior, the mother of all, blessed, venerable, and worshiped;
she is the presiding deity of the rāsa-dance of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. ||23||
Born from the circle of the *rāsa*, she is the embodiment of bliss for the connoisseurs;
she is the cowherd girl dwelling in Goloka, whose form consists of both contentment and indignation.
Bestowing all service upon Kṛṣṇa, her essential nature is one of detachment;
she grants the singular state of servitude to the devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and all forms of prosperity. (25)
She possesses a splendor graced by the light of ten million moons, her form is composed of devotion, and the earth is purified by the touch of her lotus feet. 26.
The very essence of the jewel among women, she rests upon the chest of Kṛṣṇa;
in ancient times, Brahmā performed austerities for sixty thousand years [to attain her].
Even in a dream, the lotus feet of that Best of Men have not been seen for the sake of beholding them or for the purification of one's own self;
what then need be said of seeing them directly before one’s eyes? 28.
In that very same way, she was seen again in the forest of Vṛndāvana through her ascetic penance—Rādhā, rich with longing for Kṛṣṇa, her form being entirely absorbed in Kṛṣṇa. (29)
Thus, these five natures of Brahman, the Supreme Self, are considered to be the fivefold goddesses who are most perfectly complete. 1.417.30.
All other women are of the nature of parts, sub-parts, and further subdivisions;
I shall describe the principal ones—listen, O daughter of the ocean! (3.1)
The Gaṅgā, born from the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, is liquid in form;
she bestows liberation through being seen, touched, bathed in, and drunk.
The beloved Dhavalā is like a ladder or staircase to liberation;
furthermore, another virtuous woman was created, Tulasī, who bestows liberation.
She, the virtuous beloved of Nārāyaṇa, was the very ornament of Viṣṇu;
by the touch of whose lotus feet the earth was instantly purified. (34)
Without her, every action among all beings is fruitless;
she is the giver of liberation, appearing in the form of a tree, yet possessing the nature of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
And [there was] the beloved disciple of Śaṅkara, who was mentally the daughter of Kaśyapa;
then another was a daughter of the Nāgas, the sister of Ananta-bhogin. (36)
She is considered the sovereign of the Nāgas, the mother of the Nāgas, the virtuous Jaratkārvī;
she is a devotee of Viṣṇu, the mother of Āstīka, and the beloved of the sage Jaratkāru. (37)
For three hundred thousand divine years, she performed penance for the sake of Hari;
established in yoga, she was of the nature of Brahman, devoted to Kṛṣṇa and Śambhu as her supreme vow.
Then there was another divine army, the sixth goddess, devoted to her husband;
she was Mātṛkā, the youthful wife of Kārtikeya. ||3.9||
She is indeed the protectress of children throughout the universe,
the bestower of sons and grandsons, and the nurse of the worlds.

It is fitting that this Yoginī, who appears in the form of an aged woman, should be the supreme object of worship for children; indeed, her worship should be performed by the sixty [deities] throughout the twelve months.
And worship in the lying-in chamber on the sixth day after the birth of the child, as well as on the twenty-first day, brings about auspiciousness. (42)
She is the form of a mother, the embodiment of compassion, and the eternal protector;
she dwells in water, on land, and in the atmosphere, appearing in the dreams of children. (43)
Then there is another great goddess, Satī Maṅgalacaṇḍikā, who was born from the mouth of Prakṛti and always bestows auspiciousness upon creation. 44.
In the process of withdrawal she takes a wrathful form, and on the day of Maṅgala she is worshipped with the fivefold offerings by women throughout all the worlds.
She bestows sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, fame, and auspiciousness.
She is the destroyer of grief, torment, sin, extreme suffering, and poverty. ||46||
When pleased, she fulfills all the desires of every woman;
when enraged, she is capable in an instant of destroying the entire circle of the universe. 47.
Now there was another Mahākālī, the devoted wife of Śambhu, born from the forehead of Durgā, who destroys both auspiciousness and inauspiciousness in battle. 48.
She is the foremost of all powers, excellent, and truly mighty;
she is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, equal to Kṛṣṇa in splendor, valor, and virtues. (49)
Constantly contemplating Kṛṣṇa, she is eternally dark-complexioned;
she is capable of destroying the entire universe with a mere breath.
Then there was another Vasundharā, who was the primary form [of the earth], serving as the support for all things and the source of all crops. (51)
A mine of jewels, containing jewels within, the foundation of all sources of jewels; she whose form is that which sustains all, and who bestows every prosperity. ||52||
Without her, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings would be without support;
she is the goddess Vasundharā, the devoted wife of Varāha. 53.
The goddess Svāhā, the wife of Agni, is devoted to her husband and well-honored;
without her, the gods are not capable of accepting the oblation offered. (54)
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the wife of the sacrificer, and the consecration (dīkṣā) are honored in the sacrifice;
for without her, all ritual action in all the worlds is fruitless. (55)
Svadhā is the wife of the Pitṛs, devoted to her husband and well-honored;
without her, the ancestral offerings made at śrāddha and other rites become fruitless. (56)
The goddess Svasti, the wife of Vāyu, is worshipped among all the Viśvedevas;
without her, both taking and giving are fruitless. (57)
Puṣṭi, the wife of Gaṇapati, is honored and devoted to her husband;
without her, both men and women become utterly emaciated. (58)
Anantapatnī and Tuṣṭi were always worshipped and saluted;
without her, all the worlds everywhere were not contented. (59)
The consort of Īśāna is prosperity, worshipped by gods and men;
without her, all worlds and all beings would be destitute. (1.417.60)
Dhṛti, the wife of Kapila, is honored by all everywhere;
indeed, all the worlds would be devoid of fortitude without her throughout the universe. (6.1)
She was the wife of Yama, patient, virtuous, well-behaved, and honored by all;
yet without her, everyone became deranged and filled with fear.
She is the presiding goddess of play, the virtuous Rati, the consort of Kāma;
indeed, all the worlds are devoid of sport and delight without her. (63)
Mukti, the devoted wife of Truth, is honored by the worlds and beloved by all;
without her, the world would be devoid of the sentiment of friendship.
Compassion is the wife of delusion; she is virtuous, honored, and beloved by the world.
Indeed, all living beings in this world would become cruel without her.
She is the meritorious wife, the foundation, the purifier, and honored by all;
without her, the entire world is seen as dead while still alive. (66)
Fame is the wife of good deeds; she is blessed, honorable, and worshiped, for without her the entire world is devoid of glory, as if dead. (67)
For action is the wife of exertion, honored and associated with all things;
without her, O Lotus-born One, the entire world would be as if extinct. (68)
That false wife of Adharma was honored by all beings;
without her, the conduct of the rogue, ordained by fate, would have been cut off. (69)
In the Kṛta age, it was not seen; in the Tretā age, it was seen only here and there;
in the Dvāpara age, it appeared among those devoid of shame; and in the Kali age, deceit exists in every house.
Accompanied by his brother Deceit, he wanders indeed from person to person;
Peace and Modesty are his two highly honored wives, Suśīla. (71)
Without Yāmyā, the entire world becomes as if insane;
and Jñāna has three wives, all of whom are devoted to their husband.
Buddhi, Medhā, and Smṛti—without whom the world would be as if dead and deluded;
and Mūrti was the wife of Dharma, lovely in form and enchanting. (73)
She is the mother of the Supreme Self, without whom the universe would be without support;
she is Lakṣmī herself, the very embodiment of all beauty, existing in personified form. (74)
She is Śrī, she is Mūrtirūpā, she is honored, blessed, and worshipped;
she is the consort of Kālāgnirudra and the sleep of the perfected yogis. 75.
That which causes all people in the world to become inactive during the nights is the terrible, tamasic sleep that brings about their cessation.
Time has three auspicious wives— dawn, night, and day—
without which the Creator himself cannot calculate.
Hunger and thirst are the two wives of greed—worthy, honorable, and highly esteemed—by whom the entire world is pervaded, and for whose satisfaction one always strives. (78)
Light and heat are considered the two wives of fire;
without these two, the entire world would not undergo transformation through ripening. (79)
The two daughters of Time, Death and Old Age, are the two beloved wives of Fever; by means of them, the world indeed goes to its destruction in successive stages.
And the daughter of Sleep, named Tandrā (Drowsiness), and Prīti (Affection), who are fond of pleasure;
by these two the entire world is pervaded and finds rest for a moment. (81)
But detachment has two honored wives, faith and service, by means of which the entire world is constantly seen as liberated while living. (82)
Lāḍitī is the mother of the gods, Surabhi is the progenitor of cows, Diti is the mother of the Daityas, and Kadrū is the mother of the Nāgas. ||83||
Vinatā, the mother of Garuḍa; Danu, the mother of the Dānavas; and all those devoted wives who were employed in the process of creation—[all these] are but portions [of her]. (84)
Rohiṇī is the wife of the Moon, and Saṃjñā is the beloved of the Sun;
she is Mahālakṣmī, known as Kambharā, the consort of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. 85.
Śatarūpā was the wife of Manu; Śacī is the consort of Indra;
Tārā is the wife of Bṛhaspati; and Arundhatī belongs to Vasiṣṭha. (86)
Ahalyā was the beloved of Gautama; Anasūyā was the beloved of the sage Atri; Devahūti was the daughter of Kardama; and Prasūti was the wife of Dakṣa. (87)
Asiknī and Paliknī were likewise the two beloved wives of Dakṣa;
and Menā, the mind-born daughter of the Pitṛs, was the mother of Pārvatī.
Likewise, Lopāmudrā and Hūti were the devoted wives of Kubera;
Varuṇānī was the wife of Yama, and Vindhyāvalī was that of Bali. (89)
Likewise, Kuntī was the wife of Pāṇḍu; Damayantī was the beloved of Nala;
Yaśodā was the wife of Nanda; and Draupadī was the beloved of the Pāṇḍavas.
Devakī was the virtuous wife of Vasudeva and beloved of Hara;
Gāndhārī was the wife of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Sāvitrī was the beloved of Satyavān. (91)
The beloved of Vṛṣabhānu, the virtuous Rādhā’s mother Kalāvatī, Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Jayā, and Lalītikā. (92)
The wives of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa are bestowers of auspicious nectar;
Mandodarī is the wife of Rāvaṇa, and Kauśalyā is the mother of Rāma.
Subhadrā, Satyabhāmā, Kālindī, and likewise Lakṣmaṇā; Mitravindā, the daughter of Nagnajit, and the virtuous Jāmbavatī. (94)
Lakṣmaṇā, Rukmiṇī, Sītā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Padmāvatī, and Padminī are indeed the beloved consorts of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||95||
Vṛndā, Śrī, and the great saintly women who are dear to the glorious Nārāyaṇa; Satī, Yojanagandhā, and the devoted wife who was the mother of Vyāsa. (96)
Likewise, Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇa; Khyāti, the devoted wife of Bhṛgu;
and Reṇukā, the chaste and devoted wife of Jamadagni. 97.
Rohiṇī is the mother of Baladeva; Durgā is the beloved of Hara;
Ekānaṃśā is the beloved of Durvāsas; for she is indeed the sister of Kṛṣṇa. (98)
Whichever village goddesses there may be, they are all portions of Prakṛti; these women in every world-system have arisen from the minute subdivisions of those portions. 99.
Those women who are devoted to their husbands, virtuous, truthful, and deliverers from the cycle of worldly existence—
by whichever devotee they are honored, Puruṣottama himself is honored.
All those with a preponderance of *sattva* are excellent, virtuous, and devoted to their husbands;
those with a preponderance of *rajas* are middling, longing for enjoyments, pleasures, and the like. (101)
The base portions of *tamas*, such as the *dānavīs* and others, were dear to their husbands;
then Lakṣmī was previously worshipped by Rāmāditya with various offerings.
In the beginning, the goddess Sarasvatī was worshipped by Brahmā;
thereafter, Sāvitrī was first worshipped with devotion by the gods.
Formerly, Śivā was worshipped by King Suratha;
formerly, Rādhā was worshipped by Kṛṣṇa in the pavilion of the Rāsa dance.
Indeed, in Goloka, by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow accompanied by the cowherds and cowherd-maids,
the powers residing in the left side of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s body are then worshipped by the worlds.
They are indeed incarnations in the form of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
[they grant liberation] through being seen, touched, served, and likewise through being saluted.
O virtuous ones, because they are of the nature of Kṛṣṇa, these women grant liberation through salutation and worship;
they are not of inferior bodies, but possess divine forms. (107)
They were performers of the world's welfare, protectors of the dharma of virtuous women, establishers of the bull-emblem of the virtuous, ascetic women devoted to their husbands.
These preceptoresses are indeed the wives of Brahmā, possessing the very form of Brahman;
they are givers of mantra, givers of knowledge, givers of dharma and honor, and protectors of all.
All these were manifested by Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of His own descent;
they were all sustained by Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa Himself is eternally withdrawn within them.

The right half is Kṛṣṇa, while those on the left are his Śaktis; they are considered to be the sovereign powers (aiśvaryas), the supernatural accomplishments (siddhis), and the female generative organs (bhagas). 111.
By him who honors a virtuous Brahmin woman who has a husband and sons,
all [Brahmin women] have been honored by him with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste.
By him who worships an eight-year-old maiden with a sattvic disposition, all of them have been worshipped with garments, ornaments, and sandalwood paste. (113)
By whomsoever a virtuous woman, a chaste wife, a female yoginī, one who observes celibacy, an initiated woman, or an ascetic woman is honored, she is thereby honored as one's own mother. (1.14)
By whomsoever Surabhi is worshipped, by him indeed those [goddesses] are worshipped;
for on this earth, Rādhā was first worshipped by Suyajña.
Then, O beloved, as instructed by Śaṅkara, the gods and others [established the name];
"Śak" denotes sovereignty, and "ti" denotes prowess.
She who bestows penance and whose nature is that very [penance] is considered the Śakti Ṛtā;
Bhaga is the designator of prosperity, intelligence, wealth, and fame. 1.17.
Therefore, the Goddess Śakti and the Lord Hari joined with her are Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master who governs his mistresses.
Lakṣmī was first worshipped by King Maṅgala;
you alone, O Mahālakṣmī, abide here in my presence.
I am Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and I am Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa;
I am Śrīmannārāyaṇa, and I am Naranārāyaṇa.
I am Prabhā-Nārāyaṇa; I am Pārvatī-Nārāyaṇa;
I am Jayā-Nārāyaṇa; I am Māṇikī-Nārāyaṇa. || 121 ||
I am Ramā-Nārāyaṇa; I am Lalitā-Nārāyaṇa;
I am Padmā-Nārāyaṇa; I am Padminī-Nārāyaṇa.
I am Virāṭ-Nārāyaṇa, and I am Padmāvatī-Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, O beloved, I am always Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa and Sītā-Rāma.
I am Balanārāyaṇa, and I am Brahmanārāyaṇa;
I am Rukmiṇīnārāyaṇa and Vāsudevanārāyaṇa.
I am Nārāyaṇa of the swans, I am Nārāyaṇa of the beautiful ones;
I am Nārāyaṇa of the liberated, and I am Nārāyaṇa the witness.
This family of Brahmins, devoted to fidelity toward their husbands, will remember this;
whoever hears it or recites it shall become destined for liberation.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Lakṣmī and Many Other Chaste Women from Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī; I shall speak from my heart before you.
O beloved, there is nothing whatsoever that I must conceal from you in any way.
I am Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, possessed of unfailing virility;
there is no end to my wives, and they are all devoted to their husband.
Those who perform what is beneficial for others, who have directed their contemplation toward me, and who have created [this work] for my sake, were previously revealed by me. (3)
Innumerable are my beloved ones who abide in the abode of the Imperishable Brahman;
twelve thousand are my most excellent beloveds who have reached the supreme abode.
Some were residents of Goloka, some were indeed gatekeepers; some were collections of ornaments, and some were attendants at the bedchamber.
Some of her beloved female attendants were protectors of Śrī Vṛndāvana;
some resided on Govardhana; and some were creators of forest groves.
Dwelling in the groves of Maninikūṭa, they were in numbers of arbudas upon arbudas;
some belonged to the herd of Yamunā, while others belonged to the herd of Jāhnavī.
Others belonged to the troop of Ramā, others to the troop of Madhumādhavī,
those belonging to the troop of Virajā, and likewise those belonging to the troop of Lalitā.
Also those belonging to the herd of Viśākhā, as well as those belonging to the herd of Māyā;
likewise the Śrutis, the Ārṣyas, the Maithilas, and the Kauśalas.
Likewise, the women of Sāketa, Sītā, and the Pulindas are dear to me;
through my yoga, they are eternally divine and devoted to their husbands.
It is impossible for me to enumerate those wives of mine from former births;
remembering them, I tell this to you, so that upon hearing it, you may rejoice along with your sisters.
And in the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), the Śrutis formerly praised me, the Lord, with resonant words; at that time, I became pleased.
Choose as your boon that which is desired by my mind for you;
for the Śrutis declare that your essential nature consists of nothing but bliss.
"If a boon is indeed to be granted to us, then show us that divine realm.
Having heard this, he showed them his own world and the imperishable Brahman.
There, the virtuous husband showed all his wives, the consorts of Brahmā;
in their midst was Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable Abode. || 15 ||
Having revealed them, he said, "Tell me, what shall I do for you? And then the Śrutis replied, "Our minds are fixed upon you once you have been seen."
O Lord, we have undoubtedly become filled with the thought of being beloved women before one whose beauty is like ten million Kandarpas; please accept us, who have been cast aside by Smara. 17.
"Having approached you, our delight, we worship you; make this fruitful.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said, "This desire is difficult to accomplish. (18)
Nevertheless, within the cosmic egg of Trivikrama, on the banks of the Yamunā,
upon the earth in Vraja, my sacred field, you shall become gopīs.
"In Vṛndāvana, I shall indeed become your beloved husband in the rāsa dance;
by serving me with the fulfillment of your desires, you will have accomplished all that is to be done."
Thus, all those Śrutis were my devoted wives.
Now hear of others, O Lakṣmī, in the former age of Rāmāditya. (21)
And when I, Rāma, strong and young, carried off Sītā after the breaking of the bow at her svayaṃvara, the Maithilas were there. (22)
Millions of women arrived, and upon seeing me, they were struck with wonder;
perceiving them through my nature as the Inner Controller, I assumed ten million forms for their sake.
At that very moment, he granted his vision to each of the ladies;
and those ladies said to me, "O granter of desires, become our husband! (24)
I, Rāma, said to them: "Perform for my sake pilgrimage, charity, austerity, the kṛcchra penance, recitation, and constant remembrance. (25)
Therefore, through supreme faith and devotion, I shall become Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, your beloved, at the end of the Dvāpara age, and fulfill your heart's desires.
"Having become your husbands, I shall fulfill [your desires]; O gopīs of Vraja, you shall become [my wives]. By serving me with the dharma of desire, you shall have accomplished your purpose. (27)
Then, having conquered Bhārgava and taken that virtuous Sītā, I set out for Kosala;
on the way, the women of Kosala followed me.
Seeing him as a handsome youth, they chose him as their husband with their hearts;
then, assuming ten million forms, he gave them a divine touch.
And I have granted you this boon: "By performing my recitation with devotion, O gopīs, you shall become [my consorts] in Vraja; I shall fulfill your heart's desires."
"Having served me with the dharmas of desire, you shall have accomplished your purpose.
Then, having seen him in the city of Sāketa, the women of Sāketa [beheld him]. (3.1)
At that moment, having fallen into a state of delusion, they performed austerities while maintaining their vows,
certain that they would attain Rāma in his beloved form.
And Rāma said to them through a voice from the sky: "Your heart's desires shall become true and fulfilled on the bank of the Yamunā at the end of the Dvāpara age. (33)
"By serving me through the objects of desire, you shall have fulfilled your purpose.
Then, O beloved, when I have gone to the forest in the form of Rāma... (34)
The cowherd women of the Daṇḍaka forest were infatuated with me out of desire;
the Kirāta women and the ladies of the forest were infatuated with me and chose me as their husband. (35)
I have granted a boon to them: "At the end of the Dvāpara age, you shall become Gopīs; I will surely fulfill your heart's desires, for I shall be your husband. (36)
Then he, in the form of Rāma, indeed went to Pañcavaṭī;
meanwhile, the Pulinda women, overwhelmed with love, were tormented by the fever of longing for the sight of me.
Having touched the dust of Rāma’s feet, they approached Rāma, who was embraced by them;
Rāma then spoke to those women of broken hearts concerning his vow of fidelity to his wife.
And he spoke again: "O beloved, in Vṛndāvana your heart's desires shall once more be fulfilled when the end of the Dvāpara age has arrived and I am present."
"By serving me with the objects of desire, you shall have fulfilled your purpose.
Then, having seen Rāma on the island of Rāvaṇa, the wives of the twice-born [spoke].
Filled with devotion, they became bewildered and chose [him] in their minds;
then he granted them a vision in a dream and spoke to them.
"I shall act in every way on the banks of the Yamunā in a beautiful form;
thus, your heart's desire, which bestows the bliss of love, will then be fulfilled. (42)
"Having served me with the dharmas of desire, you shall have accomplished your purpose.
Then, having arrived at the city of Sāketa, he performed many sacrifices.
And women who had arrived there from various regions and foreign lands, upon beholding Rāma, chose him as their mental husband. (44)
Then Rāma granted them a boon: "O beloved ones, you shall all become my cowherd wives; I shall fulfill your heart's desires. (45)
Do not consider yourselves to have accomplished your purpose by indulging in the objects of desire.
Furthermore, after the abandonment of Sītā, [there shall be] golden [images] in the sacrifices. 46.
A collection of those [gopīs], each having been created for every sacrifice, came to be in the abode of Hari;
and they, becoming dense with consciousness, arrived to sport with Rāma.
Rāma said, "I do not accept them, for I am devoted to the vow of having only one wife.
Then they asked, "O Lord, why do you not accept these women as yours?"
At times of half-yearly sacrifices and other rituals, you constantly take taxes while claiming they accomplish the necessary work; therefore, you shall incur sin. (49)
Rāma then said: "Sītā, whose very nature is truth, is my beloved; she alone exists and there is no other, while you all are indeed her shadow."
Then, in another birth, at the end of the Dvāpara age, I shall fulfill your heart's desire; you shall be born in Vṛndāvana on the banks of the Yamunā.
Thus those cowherd girls were born as Yajñasīs, who are dear to me.
Now, O Lakṣmī, hear of my other wives belonging to the next world.
The Ramās who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, the companions of Śvetadvīpa, those who reside in Urdhva-Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise those who have taken refuge at the feet of Ajita; ||53||
The illustrious companions who dwell on Lokācala and those born from the ocean shall indeed become my beloved gopīs in Vraja. (54)
Then all the other deities gathered together in Vṛndāvana;
they became my wives, numbering in the hundreds of millions and billions.
All the creeping medicinal herbs performed penance on the bank of the Yamunā;
they became women who had fallen into a state of infatuation and arrived at the Rāsa dance. ||56||
Then all those women of Jālandhara, having fulfilled their desires through the dharma of passion, [saw] me, the husband of Vṛndā, at that time.
Having beheld him, they chose him as their beloved; then Viṣṇu said to them:
"Becoming women in the forest of Vṛndāvana, you shall worship me, my dear ones."
The daughters of the ocean, having seen the glorious Fish-Hari, were utterly enchanted;
by virtue of the boon granted by the glorious Fish, they became my beloved gopīs.
Those women who were enchanted upon seeing both Pṛthu and me in the kingdom of Pṛthu have now become the beloved cowherd girls (gopīs) of the earth, milking Lord Kṛṣṇa as their husband.
And by the command of Nārāyaṇa, those divine hosts of Apsarases were manifested from the thigh of Nara for the purpose of deluding the army of Kāma.
Upon seeing the excellent Nārāyaṇa, they were then bewildered;
Hari said, "On the bank of the Yamunā, you shall become gopīs."
"Having served me with the objects of desire, you shall have fulfilled your purpose;
remaining in the world of your sons and daughters, you women will be deluded upon seeing Vāmana.
Having obtained that boon from him, those cowherd girls remained on the bank of the Yamunā.
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa with devotion and a desire for his favor, the daughters of the Naga kings entreated him most fervently; and those Gopīs on the bank of the Yamunā,
having served him according to the law of passion, were women who had fulfilled their purpose.
Seeing me as a celibate student even though I was the son of Anyadatta and Kapilā, those women who were infatuated with me became my lawful wives;
all of them were virtuous, devoted to their husbands, and the wives of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Through union with Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they became divine like Rādhā and Ramā;
eternally devoted to their husbands and having taken refuge in my dharma, they numbered in the hundreds of millions, billions, trillions, and quadrillions. ||67-68||
O beloved, there are always countless eggs within the pores of the skin of my husband Vairāja;
and within each of those eggs, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara come into being.
Indeed, being of my own nature, she is appointed thus throughout millions of cosmic eggs.
There, millions of my beloveds, each possessing individual splendor, reside.
Behold, O Lotus-born one, I grant you a supreme divine vision here.
Thus, the gaze bestowed upon her by Viṣṇu, who is the Great Divine One,
beheld her husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa for that long.
In every egg [of creation], he is the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Ramā, the Beloved,
the Master of Pārvatī, the Lord of Prabhā, and the Lord of Śrīmāṇikī.
To Hari, the Lord of Rādhā; the Master of Padmā; the Lord of Kambharā;
the Lord of Padmāvatī; the Lord of all virtuous women; the Lord of Rukmiṇī. ||74||
The Lord of Māyā, the Sovereign, the Lord of Nārāyaṇī, the Lord of Vaiṣṇavī, the Lord of Yatinī, the Lord of the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, and the Lord of Kanyakā. ||75||
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa, the great king and lord of the Vedas, she rejoiced;
quickly averting her gaze, she fell at Kṛṣṇa’s feet. (76)
Indeed, by merely beholding the majesty of the Lord a hundred million times,
and by hearing and reciting this, one shall attain the state of being a servant of Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighteen chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Names of the Innumerable Devoted Wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," within the section on the Greatness of Devoted Wives in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the duties of a virtuous wife which bestow heaven and liberation;
these duties of a wife must always be observed on earth with the same reverence as the duties of a husband.
In the tiger-infested forest of Saurāṣṭra, on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake at Kuṅkumavāpī, there was once,
at the beginning of creation, a twice-born man named Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Then, having departed for the forest for the sake of asceticism,
his devoted wife Kambharālakṣmī joyfully prostrated herself before her husband.
The husband said: "O beloved, I am going to the forest to perform penance;
you shall remain here in this leaf-hut in the presence of the families of the sages."
"Stay until I have desisted from my ascetic penance;
then that devoted wife Kambharā, her eyes filled with tears... (5)
Then that virtuous woman spoke beneficial words with humility to her own husband:
"O son of Brahmā, father, mother, brother, son, and likewise daughter-in-law—" (6)
Enjoying their own merits, each person experiences their own fortune;
however, it is the married wife alone who attains the fortune of her husband.
Therefore, I shall go with you to the forest by all means;
for neither father, nor son, nor one's own self, nor mother, nor friends matter [in the face of death]. (8)
In this world and after death, the husband alone is always the refuge for women;
yet you are departing for the difficult forest inhabited by ascetics.
I go before you, enduring the sharp *kuśa* grass and thorns;
O Lord, lead me with confidence, for no sin exists in me. (1.419.10)
Whether from the top of a palace, from celestial chariots, or traveling through the air,
the shadow of the Lord’s feet is superior in every situation.
I shall dwell happily in the forest, which is adorned by my husband’s footprints,
not thinking of the three worlds but contemplating my devotion to my husband.
Constantly serving you, self-restrained and observing the vow of celibacy,
O Brahmin, I shall enjoy myself with you in the forests fragrant with honey.
I shall always subsist on fruits and roots; of this there is no doubt.
Dwelling with you forever, I shall never cause you any distress.
I will go before you; I shall eat only after you have eaten.
Devoted to you, I will perform the consecration together with you.
I shall not tolerate any transgression where you, indeed, are my heaven;
without you, I do not find even that great heaven pleasing.
Wherever heaven may be for you, there my home and forest shall be without you;
I shall go to that forest which is unbearable to others, yet perfectly tolerable to me.
At that time, the Brahmin Dharmabhusura, remembering the sufferings in the forest, did not set his mind on taking the virtuous Kambharā, who was thus resolved, away with him.
He said: "O virtuous wife, ever devoted to righteousness, my dear one;
practice dharma here in such a way that there is happiness for my mind."
In the forest there is indeed abundant suffering; the forest is always a place of hardship.
Encounters with predatory and wicked creatures in the forest are painful.
The waters were indeed infested with crocodiles, and likewise the rivers were filled with mud;
they were painful for bathing and crossing, and during the rains, they were terrifying.
Where there are intoxicated elephants, wild beasts, and distressing rākṣasas and the like,
where there are creepers, thorns, and stones— that indeed is a forest. There, one sleeps on beds of leaves upon the ground during the nights in the wilderness.
Satisfaction should be provided with leaves, fruits, petals, and roots. ||23||
In some cases, even fasting must be observed without any food;
one must wear a mass of matted hair and don garments of bark.
The forest, with its contact with cold and hot water, causes hardship during bathing and other activities;
therefore, one should practice contentment with whatever is obtained, whether it be wet or dry. (25)
Excessive wind, darkness, and constant hunger arise;
indeed, even great terrors that cause suffering are produced. (26)
There are many reptiles, forest-dwellers in various guises, and rogues who dwell by the rivers; therefore, the forest is even more painful than that.
Flies, scorpions, insects, gadflies, and mosquitoes constantly harass the weak in the forest; everything in the forest is more painful. (28)

There are thorny trees such as the small jujube and barbara; there are also [trees with] branches like kusha grass that must be stepped upon with the feet; therefore, the forest is even more painful than that. (29)
There are many bodily afflictions and various fears;
one must abandon desire and anger, and set one's mind upon austerity.
Having heard these words from Gopālakṛṣṇa, the virtuous Kambharā, her face bathed in tears, spoke these words softly. ||3 1||
Those faults which you have enumerated regarding dwelling in the forest,
I recognize them only as virtues when preceded by devotion to my husband.
Deer, lions, elephants, tigers, leopards, śarabhas and others, yaks, sṛmaras, and other wild animals, as well as predatory humans; || 33 ||
Or else, being cruel or obstructive, they might depart due to my Brahmanic luster;
for, O Kṛṣṇa, separated from you, my life must indeed be abandoned.
O Lord, no one at all would be able to violate me while I stand in your presence, for I am well-protected by my devotion to my husband. (35)
A woman who has lost her husband will truly not be able to live;
therefore, O Lord, your command must now be received from your own lips. (36)
Having received your command, I shall go with you;
forest life always pleases me, and it would surely be a source of happiness.
For me, who have lived a life of tranquility as a nun, there would be even greater happiness in following my husband; for the husband is indeed the supreme deity.
"Even in the life hereafter, may my meeting with you in the forest be auspicious;
O lady of the brahmins, this is especially so for women of the excellent circle of brahmin wives. (39)
In this world, whatever woman has been given by her father to a twice-born man according to his own dharma with the offering of water, she belongs to him even in the state after death.
Thus [spoke] the brahmin to his own wife, who was well-conducted, devoted to her husband, faithful, virtuous, and equanimous in both happiness and sorrow. (41)
O best of Brahmins, you ought to take me with you, for I share equally in joy and sorrow;
yet if you do not wish to take me, your own handmaid, to the forest— [42]
For the sake of death, I shall resort to poison, fire, water, or a noose—[I who am] devoted to Satyavān, the heroic son of Dyumatsena. (43)
Know me to be like Sāvitrī, subject to your will in this forest;
therefore, it is not fitting for you to go to the forest for the sake of asceticism without taking me with you. (44)
Whether it be asceticism, the forest, or heaven itself, let it be with you;
for in the forest, even predatory creatures would become great devotees of the Blessed One. (45)
Thorns, pebbles, and muddy grounds are pleasant to me in the forest;
all things such as the great wind and even dust are like sandalwood in the forest. (46)
O Lord, with you, even the grassy grounds are pleasant to me;
in the forest, even a small amount of leaves, roots, fruits, and water becomes abundant. (47)
If you will grant me your grace, that would be like the essence of nectar to me;
enjoying the seasonal offerings, I shall always serve my husband. (48)
You shall have no grief on my account, nor shall I become a source of sorrow for you;
for that which is with you is heaven, and that which is without you is hell.
"Either I must die without you, or I must live with you; this is my firm resolve, O virtuous lady. Be gracious, O Mādhava."
O Lord, I cannot endure separation from you even for a moment;
O Lord, once abandoned by you, death would be better for me.
Having heard these affectionate words, the husband spoke to his beloved:
"Follow me, O Goddess; be my partner in the practice of dharma. (52)
"O virtuous one, O beloved, you have undertaken an undertaking that is in every way worthy of yourself and of my family; it is most excellent. (53)
"O Kambharā, now heaven itself does not please me without you;
set out for the sake of the forest, wherever it may be, for that is most auspicious. (54)
O Kambharā, for one who is truthful, there is no fear whatsoever from the forest or from wild beasts;
indeed, you were created by me together with [my son] for the sake of dharma and worldly prosperity.
I am unable to abandon my beloved wife, who is devoted to her husband;
for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself is the most excellent dharma for me. (56)
He declared the vow of the wife to be supreme; he made me a portion of that.
O Goddess of gods, through your yoga, women have become devoted to dharma.
Even forest-dwelling female ascetics will become exceedingly devoted to their husbands;
yet there will be neither truth, nor charity, nor honor, nor sacrifice accompanied by the distribution of sacrificial fees.
Likewise, such dharma as consists of devotion to one's wife brings strength; it likewise brings heaven, wealth, grain, knowledge, sons, and happiness. (59)
Due to your devotion to your husband, nothing is difficult for you to attain—
not even the worlds of the gods, the Gandharvas, Goloka, Brahmaloka, or other higher realms.
Virtuous and noble women, devoted solely to the service of their husbands, attain [these rewards].
Follow me, O beloved; be my partner in the practice of dharma.
Having spoken thus, that great virtuous lady Mahālakṣmī Kaṃbharā went together with her husband to the Siṃhāraṇya forest for the sake of performing penance.
The highly fortunate brahmin Gopālakṛṣṇaka, devoted to his wife,
went with his wife to Siṃhāraṇya for the sake of attaining success through austerity.
On the eastern bank of the Hiraṇyā, he performed most severe penance for a full thousand years, remaining without food together with his wife.
Then the divine Lord Puruṣottama himself, accompanied by Dharma and Bhakti, and joined by Lalitā, Śrī, and Jayā, [emerged] from that abode. ||65||
He granted them direct vision of Himself and said, "Choose a boon.
Then the husband and wife spoke to Kṛṣṇa: "O Blessed One, if [this is so]... (66)
"You are always gracious; please remain in our home in this manner.
O Lord, the protection of dharma must be performed by you for us in every way. (67)
O Kṛṣṇa, remain ever before our eyes; be the bestower of happiness.
O All-pervading Lord, do not abandon us in accordance with the dharma of this age. 68.
"I am a brahmin devoted to my wife, and she is a virtuous woman devoted to her husband;
first, let us observe the time of truth, and only after that. (69)
Through yoga and meditative absorption, through austerity and celibacy, and likewise through your grace, [I shall overcome] the laughter of Time and that which is yet to come.
O Ocean of Compassion, I reflect: grant me the fruit of my ascetic penances such that I may never again experience this destruction of the Dharma. (71)
"So be it," he then said, and likewise spoke the account of Kāla;
and those two foremost ones, the husband and wife Kambharā and Hari, heard it. (72)
Hari proclaimed the divisions of time, the characteristics of the ages, and the decline of righteousness;
and at each such time, for the sake of protection, I assume the state of being the excellent sons of the two of you.
"I shall always abide as a divine presence in your vicinity," having said this, Kṛṣṇa became invisible; the husband and wife then entered their residence.

Thus ends the four hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Kambharā’s Journey with Lakṣmī and Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa for the Purpose of Performing Austerities, Her Accompanying Them by the Power of Her Devotion to Her Husband, the Vision of the Lord during the Penance, and the Granting of the Boon: 'I shall appear in the form of a son in age after age,'" in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
What are those dharmas, and how were they proclaimed? And how indeed does the diminution of time occur?
When was Kṛṣṇa [born], and when did the divine Lord become invisible? (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall now declare those divisions of time and the laws of time that I previously mentioned, as well as how protection was provided by me.
O Lakṣmī, in the Kṛta Yuga, people, taking refuge in virtues such as truthfulness,
indeed consume food produced from the essence of the earth, which is known by that name.
Those creatures moved according to their will, established in mental perfection;
neither merit nor demerit existed for them, and those creatures were devoid of distinctions.
In that Kṛta Yuga, their lifespan, happiness, and physical form were equal;
at the beginning of the Kalpa, during the Kṛta Yuga, dharma and adharma did not exist for them.
In the Kṛta Yuga, they were born with their respective individual offices;
[the lifespan] was four thousand years according to divine reckoning.

They say the first age is the Kṛtayuga, which consists of one hundred and eight periods of twilight (sandhyā); thereafter, even as those progeny became widely multiplied by the thousands, [the other ages followed].
For them there is no obstruction, no duality, nor even fatigue;
for they dwell upon mountains and oceans, having no fixed abode as their refuge.
Free from sorrow, abundant in virtuous beings, and with their offspring always happy, they indeed live without desire and are ever joyful in mind.
The time was one of every sensual pleasure, for there was no excessive heat or cold;
their desires were fulfilled by the mind, and they were present everywhere and at all times.
Indeed, they arise upon the earth, and by them, those who are meditated upon become overflowing with essence;
their accomplishment bestows strength and complexion, and it is the destroyer of disease.
With bodies that required no refinement, those subjects possessed perpetual youth;
from their pure volition, offspring were born in pairs.
Their birth and form were equal, and they died together;
at that time, truth, freedom from greed, forbearance, contentment, happiness, and self-restraint prevailed. (13)
All of them were indeed indistinguishable in terms of appearance, lifespan, conduct, and behavior; the way of life of the subjects arose spontaneously, without being preceded by conscious intent.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was no engagement in actions, whether auspicious or sinful; there were no regulations for the castes and stages of life, nor was there any intermixture at that time.
Free from desire and aversion, they dwell together with one another;
all are equal in form and lifespan, devoid of the distinctions of inferior or superior. (16)
For in the Kṛta Yuga, beings are born for the most part happy and free from sorrow;
they have minds that are eternally joyful, and they are great-souled and possessed of great strength.
For them, gain and loss, friends and enemies, and the pleasant and unpleasant did not exist;
for those who were free from desire, the objects of the senses proceeded only as mental constructs.
In the Kṛta age, they did not desire one another's possessions nor did they seek to favor one another; however, in the Tretā age, meditation and knowledge became predominant.

Sacrifices prevail in the Dvāpara age, while charity is practiced in the Kali age; goodness (sattva) characterizes the Kṛta age, passion (rajas) the Tretā, and both passion and darkness (rajas-tamas) the Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, indeed, darkness is to be recognized by virtue of the progression of the ages;
at that time, all the accomplishments of the Kṛta age became diminished by one quarter.
When that accomplishment had vanished upon its fulfillment, another accomplishment came into being:
the subtlety of the waters then returned to the earth in the form of clouds.
When the release of rain had begun from the thundering clouds, and the surface of the earth was once again joined with that rain; ||23||
Then trees appeared, situated as their dwellings;
from them, all their various articles of enjoyment were produced. (24)
For at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, those beings brought forth offspring from them;
then, after a long time, there occurred a reversal of those very same [beings].
At that time, a state consisting of passion and greed arose quite spontaneously;
for that which occurs to women at the end of their life is then [manifested as] the menses. (26)
Then, while they were engaged in that very same practice,
those women approached their husbands month after month, as was appropriate for that time.
Indeed, at that time which was to come, there occurred the appearance of menses and the conception of embryos out of season,
due to the reversal of their natural order.
Then all those trees situated within the house perished;
when they had perished, [the inhabitants] became bewildered, their senses agitated. ||29||
Then those who meditated with truthful intent longed for that perfection;
and those trees appeared for them, established as their dwellings.
And from them are produced garments, fruits, and ornaments;
within those very things, their [fruits] arise, endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor.
In that Tretā Yuga, they made their livelihood from honey that was free of bees, possessed great potency, and was collected pot by pot; thus they lived in happiness at that time.
Delighted and satisfied by that accomplishment, the subjects were indeed freed from their distress;
yet, after a further interval of time, they were once again shrouded by greed.
They forcibly seized those trees, taking the honey of the bees;
indeed, because of that misconduct on their part, which was brought about by the Creator of the World, [the following occurred].
In some places here and there, the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) have perished along with the honey,
as that very [world] remains but slightly diminished due to the power of the time of twilight.
Then, pairs among them began to arise;
due to intense cold, wind, and heat, they became exceedingly distressed.
Afflicted by pairs of opposites, they constructed shelters;
having provided remedies for these pairs, they indeed took refuge in dwellings.
I dwelt in those dwellings according to what was appropriate and pleasing—
among the desert wastes, in lowlands, on mountains, and by rivers.
And they take refuge in fortresses, in arid wastes, and in places with perennial water, as is appropriate and according to their desire, whether on level ground or in difficult terrain. (39)
They indeed began to construct dwellings to ward off the cold and heat;
thereafter, they established hamlets and cities.
He likewise [assigned] the villages according to their respective shares, as well as the inner apartments;
he [determined] the lengths and breadths of those [palaces], as well as the intervals between their sites.

Then, having measured with their own fingers according to their wisdom, they established the various objects of the mind as standards of measurement, or rather, they created them from that very [source].
Having reflected again and again, they set about acting in such a way that those trees which had previously been situated as houses would indeed become so once more. 43.
They constructed beautiful dwellings among the branches of the trees;
having resolved those conflicts between pairs, they considered the means for their livelihood.
When the wish-fulfilling trees had perished along with the honey,
those subjects, overwhelmed by despair and characterized by thirst and hunger, were indeed distressed.
Then, in the Tretā Yuga, the power of bestowing food appeared for them;
moreover, another means of livelihood, which accomplishes the goals of worldly affairs, arose for them according to their desire.
The waters of the rain became downward-flowing streams and rivers;
at that time, the low-lying areas took the form of lakes and ponds.
Those [elements] always became conducive to the growth of crops; then, through the union of water and earth, medicinal herbs appeared within them.
Then there arose medicinal herbs that produced flowers, roots, and fruits;
they required no plowing and were not sown, yet they yielded flowers and fruits according to the seasons.
At that time, during the Tretā Yuga, living beings subsisted on medicinal herbs;
thereafter, passion and greed arose among them in every respect.
Then they seized the rivers, fields, and mountains, as well as the trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, by force according to their strength. ||51||
There, some take hold of others and cause them to suffer;
some are peaceful, while others are harsh and cruel. (52)
Those who were malicious became powerful through their deeds, and the radiant ones became weak; at that time, those who acted according to the will of the radiant ones became powerless.
While they were thus engaged in mutual conflict and had fallen into it,
those medicinal herbs were then destroyed as they were being carried away.
Then, when those [creatures] had perished, as the waning of the Tretā age approached, the subjects, desiring to obtain a means of subsistence, went to Prajāpati.
Then, having fashioned them by his mind, Brahmā indeed cast the seeds upon the earth; from that, the medicinal herbs were born.
And the crops ripened on plowed land in every way;
moreover, those powerful Brāhmaṇas sustained themselves by means of them.
They protected other Kṣatriyas who had sought refuge,
as well as Vaiśyas of the merchant class and servants who provided their livelihoods during the dissolution of the Yuga;
those Brāhmaṇas acted thus, approved by Brahmā himself.
Brahmā, however, ordained their respective duties and laws once again.
The subjects likewise protected those laws with reverence; living according to the duties of their castes, they lived in mutual harmony. || 1.420.60 ||
Brahmā, having understood that matter, as well as the Vedic duty of the Brahmins,

established officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts as their third means of livelihood; he likewise ordained strength, punishment, warfare, and combat as the livelihood for the Kṣatriyas.
And he assigned cattle-rearing, trade, and agriculture to the Vaiśyas.
The Lord established the livelihood of crafts and wages for the fourth [class];
then, having assigned them a livelihood based on labor, he granted them their respective stations.
Indeed, for those devoted to their respective duties in other worlds, it is as follows:
the realm of Prajāpati for Brāhmaṇas, and that of Mahendra for Kṣatriyas. (64)
The station of the Vaiśyas is that of the Maruts, and that of the servant is indeed that of the Gandharvas;
then Brahmā himself established the stages of life (āśramas) according to dharma.
In former times, the householder stage of life was declared to consist of the four social orders; it is the foundation and indeed the source of the other three stages of life. (66)
Wife, sacred fires, hospitality, sacrifices, ancestral rites, and progeny—this, indeed, is the summary of the duties of a householder. (67)
Carrying a staff, wearing a girdle, sleeping on the ground, and likewise having matted hair,
the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should practice service to the teacher and subsist on alms;
he may wear rags, leaves, or skins, and his food shall consist of grain, roots, fruits, and herbs.
For those dwelling in the forest, there is immersion in both twilights and the performance of fire-offerings;
begging for alms at midday and thereafter, as well as non-stealing, purity, vigilance, celibacy, compassion toward all beings, and forgiveness.
Absence of anger, service to the teacher, and truthfulness— this tenfold dharma is the bull [of virtue].
Indeed, for a person whose inner disposition is corrupted, none of their external actions will succeed,
even if they exert great effort.

Even if one were to give away all one's possessions with a defiled inner self, one would not partake in the merit through that act; indeed, the internal disposition (*bhāva*) alone is the cause here. Furthermore, in the latter part of the *tretā* age, at the time of twilight, [one should perform] the entire ritual beginning with the bull-sacrifice (*vṛṣotsarga*).
Furthermore, [the world] was lost due to the afflictions of the subjects and through mutual violence.
Then there arose kings, Manus, emperors, and likewise restrictive laws.
The existence of things among the worlds—among humans, animals, and birds—[was established].
In fields, in occupations, and in all means of livelihood. ||75||
And everywhere, O Lakṣmī, the dharmas existed according to their original form: truth, charity, compassion, sacrifice, and recitation—all these were present in their entirety. (76)
At that time, the Dharmas proceeded on foot, while the Asuras were unrighteous and especially characterized by darkness (tamas). ||77||
And in the Dvāpara age, O Lakṣmī, the subjects were primarily devoted to sacrifice;
there, the Smṛtis and rules were composed by the sages for their ease.
Therein were established the livelihoods of the gods, the livelihoods of brahmins, the livelihoods of servants, and the livelihoods of the foremost artisans such as craftsmen and others. (79)
The existence of marriages and other rites for women was firmly established there,
and the right of legitimate sons (aurasa) to inherit property was made secure.
The entitlement to inheritance for disciples and maidens has been divided;
likewise, that of kings over the earth and their subjects, both in general and in particular. (81)
In this world, the means of livelihood and occupations are determined;
the referents of words such as "father" and "son" are applied to individual persons. (82)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how these things have been set forth in the world:
the father is said to be the provider of the seed, and the mother is the bearer of the embryo. (83)

One who is childless is proclaimed a *mātṛpati*; likewise, one who has given birth [to a son] is proclaimed a *upamātṛ*. One who does not bear a fetus is a *pitṛpatnī*, and she is also proclaimed an *upamātṛ*. (84)
The grandfather is the father of one's father; his father is the great-grandfather. The maternal grandfather is the father of one's mother; his father is the great-maternal grandfather. ||85||
The father’s mother is the paternal grandmother; her mother is the great-grandmother (prapitāmahī); and her mother is to be known as the great-great-grandmother (vṛddhaprapitāmahī). ||86||
The mother’s mother, who is honored as equal to one’s own mother, should be known as the *pramātāmahī*, the beloved wife of the maternal grandfather. (87)
The mother of one's paternal grandfather is to be known as the *vṛddhamātāmahī*, as is the wife of that [grandfather].
The brother of one's father is the paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*), while the brother of one's mother is the maternal uncle (*mātula*). (88)
The father’s sister, the father’s mother’s sister, and the mother’s sister are recorded [as maternal relatives].
Furthermore, *sūnu*, *tanaya*, *putra*, *dāyāda*, and likewise *ātmaja* [denote son]. (89)
The one who shares in the wealth and is born of valor exists in the son (puṃsi) and the progeny (janye);
while in the female progeny (janyāyām), the daughter and the maiden are proclaimed as the offspring (ātmajā).
A son’s wife is to be known as a daughter-in-law (*vadhū*); a daughter’s husband is a son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*).
The term *pati* signifies a beloved, a supporter (*bhartṛ*), and a master (*svāmī*), and it is used for a husband (*kānta*). ||91||
The husband's brother is the *devara*; the husband's sister is the *nanāndṛ*.
The husband's father is the *śvaśura*; and the husband's mother is the *śvaśrū*. (92)
*Bhāryā*, *jāyā*, *priyā*, *kāntā*, *strī*, and *patnī* are proclaimed as synonyms for wife. The brother of one's wife is called *śyālaka*, and the sister of one's wife is called *śālikā*. (93)
The wife, mother, and mother-in-law are likewise remembered; the father and father-in-law are so designated.
A brother born of the same womb is known as a *sagarbha* (uterine) brother, and a sister born of the same womb is known as a *sagarbhā* (uterine) sister. || 94 ||
The sister's son, the nephew, the brother's son, and the brother's son;
the father-in-law, the sister's husband, and the sister's husband as well. ||95||

O Sage, the husband of one's sister-in-law and one's own brother are to be regarded as a father-in-law due to the same status of being a father-in-law; however, the biological father is to be known as equal to the giver of birth.
The giver of food, the protector from fear, the husband who protects his wife, the giver of knowledge, and the giver of birth—these five are the fathers of men. (97)
The mothers who give birth, those who nourish with milk, and those who bestow knowledge are the true mothers of men;
likewise, the wife of one who gives food, a sister, and the wife of one's teacher [are to be honored]. (98)
One's mother and her co-wife, as well as one's daughter and one's son’s wife;
likewise, one's maternal grandmother, one's paternal grandmother, and one's father-in-law’s sister. (99)
The paternal uncle’s wife, the maternal uncle’s wife, and the mothers—these are the sixteen [types of women for whom one must not eat].
Furthermore, the grandson is [the son of] the son’s son, and the great-grandson is likewise [the son of] that grandson’s son. (1.420.100)
His sons and others who are of his lineage are proclaimed as *kulaja* (kinsmen of the family); the daughter's son is the *dauhitra*, and his sons and others are the *bāndhava* (relatives). 101.
The sons of one's sister and so forth are remembered as *puruṣa* kinsmen;
