the sons of one's brother’s son and so forth are further remembered as *jñāti* kinsmen. || 102 ||
The teacher’s son, as well as his brother, are to be supported as supreme kinsmen;
likewise, the teacher’s daughter and one’s own sister are to be supported like a mother. (103)
The father-in-law of one's son is considered a teacher, a brother, a dependent, and a very affectionate kinsman; likewise, the brother of one's son's wife is remembered as a relative by marriage.
The relationship of the daughter with her father-in-law is thus proclaimed;
and the brother of the daughter is a most affectionate kinsman to the preceptor. || 105 ||
One who is equal to a preceptor is proclaimed to be [the equivalent] of a teacher, a father-in-law, or a brother;
and he with whom one shares kinship is proclaimed to be a friend. 106.
A friend should be known as one who bestows happiness, while an enemy is said to be one who gives suffering.
A kinsman may give suffering by chance, whereas one with no connection at all provides nothing but unhappiness.
In this world, on the surface of the earth, all relationships are declared to be of three kinds:
those born of learning, those born of birth, and those born of affection. || 108 ||
A friend born of affection should be known as a relationship that is very difficult to find;
a friend’s mother and a friend’s wife are equal to one’s own mother, without a doubt. (109)
A friend’s brother, a friend’s father, and one equal to a brother’s father are [considered kin] for men;
the fourth type of relationship among men arises everywhere through the connection of names.

A *jāra* is a paramour; one who is corrupted by kinsmen is a *bandhuduṣṭa* when engaged in sexual union. A *preyasī* is a beloved mistress who captivates the heart, yet she is not to be treated with disrespect. || 111 ||
"The paramour is equal to the husband, and the housewife is equal to a new bride"—
such words, born of worldly conduct, came into use during the Dvāpara age.
In every age, the practices of those who are more powerful do not constitute a fault;
therefore, at the transition of the Dvāpara age, I became Kṛṣṇa, the protector.
I became a protector of the Dharma, a destroyer of Daityas, and a lion for the female ascetics;
for in the Kali age, many afflictions indeed arise against the Dharmas.
The Gaṅgā and other rivers, as well as the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the deities,
will likewise depart from the earth when four thousand years of the Kali age have passed.
Then indeed the son of Kambharā, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, will go to the divine world and establish Dharma upon the earth.
This teacher is the Lord himself, the son of Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa;
he is the beloved of the lotus-like Śrī Rādhā and the husband of Kamalā and Pārvatī. 1.17
Māṇikīśa, the Lord of Prabhā-Lakṣmī and Amā, the Supreme Sovereign,
having established the Bhāgavata Dharma in the world, will indeed depart for the forest.
Then, after a hundred by a hundred periods of time have passed, Dharma will reach destruction once more, and the bridges of righteousness that were established will perish. (11.9)
The Śālagrāma is the form of Hari, and the story of Jagannātha;
within a thousand years, all shall go to the abode of Śrī Hari.
The Vaiṣṇava Saṃhitā texts, conch shells, the Śrāddha rites, the Tarpaṇa offerings,
and even the rituals prescribed in the Vedas will likewise go to their dissolution.
The worship of Hari, the name of Hari, the glorification of Him, and the chanting of His qualities—
the Vedas, the scriptures, and the codes of dharma— will all naturally go to ruin.
Virtue, truth, goodness, divinity, and the village deities,
as well as vows, austerity, and fasting, shall go to the abode of Śrī Hari.
Thereafter, all will be devoted to left-handed practices (vāmācāra), possessed of falsehood and deceit,
and entirely devoid of Tulasī.
Thereafter, they will be devoid of the Ekādaśī vow, abandoned by all righteous duties, and turned away from devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Thereafter, all will become deceitful, cruel, hypocritical, and possessed of great ego; they will be thieves and violent oppressors.
From this time forward, there shall be no distinction between men and women, nor marriage, nor legal disputes, nor the distinction between property and its owner.
All people were under the sway of women, and in every house there were unchaste wives who constantly struck their husbands with threats and reproaches.
The mistress of the house and the housewife are superior to the master; the servants are inferior.
The female servant is equal to the male servant; likewise are the daughters-in-law, the mother-in-law, and the father-in-law.
Adulteresses, those who rule kingdoms, and kings related by birth are powerful agents in this world;
indeed, kinsmen related by birth are the most influential in the world.
There is no conversation with the wise, nor internal friendship with fools;
for a man, all actions are rendered fruitless without the command of women. 13.111.
The sacred thread will be lost from sight, there will be no recognition of birth,
and all castes and stages of life will then adopt the conduct of barbarians.
They will study the scriptures of the Mlecchas and subsist on the food of the Mlecchas;
at that time, all the social classes (varṇas) will become servants of the Mlecchas.
Women will become cooks, leather-workers, and makers of skins;
all people will be devoid of truth, and the earth will be devoid of crops. 1.34.
Trees devoid of fruit, women devoid of offspring, cows devoid of milk, and milk from which the clarified butter has been extracted; ||| 1.35 ||
Husbands and wives will be devoid of affection, householders will be bereft of happiness, kings will lack majesty, and the subjects will be oppressed by taxes. (136)
Rivers and streams were devoid of water, as were the ponds and mountain caves; likewise, the castes were devoid of righteousness and merit, and thus became devoid of their proper characteristics.
Beyond that, among hundreds of thousands, not a single meritorious person remains;
instead, there are men, women, and children who are despicable and deformed in appearance.
Thereafter, false rumors and wicked paths will prevail; some villages and cities will be on the verge of destruction and difficult to traverse.
In the Kali age, the forests will become devoid of men, devoid of people, filled with only small huts, and haunted by jackals.
All people living in the forests will be oppressed by taxes, while the crops will grow only in ponds and rivers. (141)
Fields will be devoid of crops; the wealthy will be destitute of goods;
thieves will become affluent; and those endowed with physical strength and pride will be preeminent. (142)
In the Kali age, those born of noble lineages will become base;
rogues and scoundrels will speak falsely, while the truly honest will be regarded as deceitful.
Sinners and the meritorious, the uncultured and the cultured alike;
those who have conquered their senses and the lecherous, unchaste women and devoted wives. (144)
Ascetics and sinners, devotees of Viṣṇu and non-devotees of Viṣṇu, those who inflict harm and those endowed with compassion, thieves and murderers of men—[all these attain the same state]. (145)
Wicked men wearing the garb of monks revile and mock [the virtuous];
they are skilled in catering to the bodies of people and likewise cause delusion among them. (146)
They will become worshippers, deceivers, and weak in knowledge;
men and women everywhere will be dwarfish, diseased, and emaciated. 147.
In the Kali age, people are short-lived and afflicted by old age even in their youth;
dharma consists of the conduct of cattle, and the primary concern is the connection of one's birth.
Moreover, the state of motherhood will be lost during that Kali age;
indeed, it will happen again and again upon the passing of five thousand years.
Then, in the Kali age, I shall become a Brahmin in Camatkārapura, a great yogi perfected by birth, known by the name Bṛhadvrata.
And I shall indeed establish devotion to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by means of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā at that time.
By means of the words taught by me, men shall attain liberation;
their minds shall become purely *sāttvika* through taking refuge in me.
From this time forward, all men and women—even those who are *cāṇḍālas*—[shall do so].
Those with grey hair at sixteen years are considered "greatly aged" at twenty. || 153 ||
A young woman of eight years who has reached puberty and becomes pregnant gives birth at the end of the year; such a woman is possessed of old age at sixteen. (154)
Among these, in every house among thousands, there are some who are barren, as well as those who sell their daughters and those for whom their own daughters have become husbands. (155)
They were intent on procuring paramours for their mothers, wives, and daughters-in-law;
they lived by procuring paramours for their daughters and sisters. (156)
Then, those who sell the names of Hari—those sellers of merit—will give a gift for the sake of fame for a moment, and then take it back again. (157)
He will forcibly seize the livelihood of gods, teachers, and Brahmins; he will be one who approaches virgins, mothers-in-law, daughters-in-law, sisters, co-wives, and mothers.

In the Kali age, there are those who approach women who should not be approached, such as the wives of brothers and others; and in the Kali age, there are those who approach goats, cows, female donkeys, female camels, and female deer.

In the Kali age, there will be those who engage in sexual intercourse with female gavayas, female garuḍas, female dogs, and female peacocks, as well as those who consort with female pigs, female monkeys, female horses, and other such beings.
Abandoning their own wives, they will roam about everywhere;
in the Kali age, there is no fixed rule for either wives or husbands.
Regarding subjects, objects, and especially villages, all will be speakers of falsehood, and all will be greedy for wealth through theft. 162.
They were all mutual destroyers and slayers of men; at that time, women were united with all kinds of animals, kinsmen, and men.
In the Kali age, they will be protected by outcasts (vṛṣala), devoid of clothing,
bereft of sacred threads, and lacking purity through meditation.
Prostitutes, usurers, warriors, procuresses, and women in their menses shall all become cooks in the kitchen of everyone. (165)
There is no certainty regarding foods, nor is there any certainty regarding wombs; there is no certainty at all regarding sons—all are Mlecchas in the Kali age. 166.
When the terrible Kali age has set in, at its conclusion upon this earth,
there a maiden of five years shall become a mother.
At that time, women ten years of age were like the aged standing at the threshold of death, and men twelve years of age were indeed destined for death. 168.
When the entire Kali age has passed, everything will then become diminished;
trees will be only the size of a cubit, and humans will be the size of a thumb.
All four-footed creatures had a lifespan of two years, those with four feet a lifespan of one year;
the male and female elephants were like cats, having a lifespan of only one month.
In the Kali age, people will be satisfied with the handfuls of grain given by mice;
women will give birth to children who have the appearance of being born from mice.
At that time, people will dwell upon the earth with no houses or such dwellings;
there will be only one rainy season, and the rain will fall in drops the size of a thumb-joint. (172)
Thus, when all time has passed in the final portion of the Kali age,
Kalkī will be born as the son of the Brahmin Viṣṇuyaśas.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am that Nārāyaṇa, holding a sword in my hand and mounted upon the white-horsed chariot given by Kṛṣṇa, traveling through the sky.
Having circumambulated the earth three times in three nights,
he made the entire circle of the atmospheric region round by the touch of his own limbs.
"Afterwards, I shall perform a purifying act by making the Mlecchas well-disposed;
having slain others who are exceedingly wicked, I shall make them refined. (176)
I shall establish the Kṛta age, restoring men worthy of the sacrifice of truth,
once the invincible Kali age has passed and the Kṛta age has fully commenced.
Dharma, joined with austerity and truth, will become complete;
at that time, the Brahmins will be ascetics, purified, and truly Vaiṣṇavas.
The disciples of Kalki will be most righteous, illuminators of the knowledge of the Vedas;
likewise, women will be devoted to their husbands and true, while men will be devoted to their wives.
Furthermore, the duties of the social classes shall find their proper place and manifestation;
indeed, sacrifices, gifts, ritual acts, and a sense of shame shall exist among human beings.
All will be devoted to Viṣṇu and become Vaiṣṇavas;
indeed, there will be no trace of unrighteousness in this Kṛta Yuga, which is filled with dharma.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be celestial vehicles everywhere, powers of hearing from afar, and means of travel for going to heaven.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be those possessing the yoga of far-sight, those who travel upon the surface of the waters, and those who move through lightning, fire, and wind.
In the Kṛta Yuga, the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, which consist of power and bring about dissolution, destruction, and manifestation, will exist among material beings.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be no distinction between the world of mortals and the world of heaven;
in that age, women will appear like goddesses and men like gods.
In the Kṛta Yuga, mantras, tantras, and yantras were fruitful;
in every house there were channels of light, channels of water, and channels of sound.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there shall arise a detailed knowledge of the sixty-eight arts, of the grasping of reflections, and of the analysis of the body's constituents.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there will be rules regarding conception and non-conception, as well as the powers of transformation into male or female forms, and the granting of death or life. (188)
This divine ritual concerning the trees of the forest, which is a transformation of elixirs (rāsa-āyana),
will quickly fulfill all desires and become effective when the Kṛta Yuga has arrived.
The great vidyā Sañjīvanī, as well as the power of invisibility,
and the movements such as divine possession, will come into being during the Kṛta Yuga.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there shall be only divine measuring instruments, such as those for perceiving the Śakti-tattva and others, as well as those produced from the elements and their derivatives.
Having thus established the Dharma as a new Kṛtayuga, the Blessed One,
having made the earth like heaven, will pass into disappearance.
Dharma is said to have three feet in the Tretā age and two feet in the Dvāpara;
when the Kali age has begun, it consists of only one foot, and after that, there is the total disappearance of everything.
O Lakṣmī, my devotees indeed wander everywhere as purifiers;
by the touch of the dust of their feet, the earth is always of the nature of a sacred pilgrimage site.
Rivers, trees, and mountains have been purified by my devotees;
appearing in the form of sacred fords (tīrtha), they indeed wash away the sins of people.
So too do the virtuous ones with meritorious bodies and the saintly women who take refuge in Hari.
For sacred fords purify only those who possess volition, day after day.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, as well as sinful men and others—
gods, humans, animals, living beings, both stationary and moving— [are all contained therein].
"And they shall become purified by the touch and sight of my devotees.
Thus, O virtuous lady, have the widely renowned dharmas of the ages been described to you. (198)
In whatever age women who are devoted to their husbands shall exist,
there will always be heaven, happiness, wealth, and so forth.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you my birth as it arose in this context;
by reading or hearing this, one shall become a dweller in Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the four hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Four Yugas," within the section on the greatness of devotion to one’s husband, in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder at Prayāga, the king of holy places,
concerning Bharadvāja as he dwelt there with his wife Triveṇī.
The daughter of Brahmā, born from his mind, was a great virtuous woman as soon as she was born;
in beauty she was like a hundred moons, a young woman devoted to her husband.
She was foremost among the assembly at Brahmasaras, born from a portion of the three rivers;
she approached Bharadvāja, who had been practicing austerities for a hundred thousand years at Prayāga.
During the ritual bath with the water-pot (kumbhasnāna), she saw him who had come from the world of Brahmā, exclaiming:
"Aha! A divine sage worthy of choosing as a bridegroom shines here!"
Having reflected thus, she remained in attendance upon him like a shadow;
thereafter, Brahmā performed his ablutions at the time of the water-pot (kuṃbha).
Having recognized Mānasa as the confluence of the three rivers, it was offered to Bharadvāja;
for it was indeed a portion of the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī.
Having offered that maiden, named Triveṇī, to Triveṇī and having praised her after making the offering to the sage, Brahmā went to Satyasthala.
Triveṇī always serves the ascetic Bharadvāja with devotion through her wifely fidelity, for the sake of increasing that very fidelity.
By means of daily morning ablutions and the like, by massaging his feet, by offering articles for worship, and by always presenting food; || 9 ||
And through the knowledge of Brahman, by the constant performance of the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana),
and even by her service upon the bed, that devoted wife serves [her husband].

Where the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) always resides and the wish-granting tree (Kalpavr̥kṣa) is ever present, there the moon-creeper (Somavallī) is always found and the wish-fulfilling gem (Cintāmaṇi) rests in the hand.
Wherever there is a virtuous woman devoted to her husband,
there the presence of all jewels manifests itself.
Once, Bharata, the lord of Sāketa and Kosala,
came there with his army for the sake of performing the rites of the sacred ford (tīrtha-vidhi) as an ascetic during the month of Māgha.
Having stationed the army at a distance,
he then went to visit his preceptor Bharadvāja, the most eminent among sages.
With joy, Bharata prostrated himself like a staff at his feet,
and he likewise bowed at the feet of Bharadvāja’s wife.
Then, having offered that water of honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and fruits to Bharata,
the knower of dharma inquired in due order after the welfare of his family.
In Sāketa, Bharata also inquired about the welfare and other matters concerning Bala, the treasury, his friends, and the ministers, as well as regarding Bharadvāja.
Having promised "So be it" regarding his own body, the sacrificial fires, his disciples, the trees, and the beasts and birds, the highly illustrious Bharadvāja [departed].
Being pleased, he said right there: "Dwell here in this hermitage during this festival; welcome to you, and receive hospitality and service according to your merit."
"O bull among kings, I shall dwell at this sacred ford as long as you remain;
for there is the proper conduct toward one's guru, self-restraint, and the practice of following the path of the virtuous."
"All virtues reside in you; dwell here in my hermitage.
Thus addressed, Bharata replied to him, "So be it."
Then that sage invited Bharata, who was equal to a seer, to dwell right there with the hospitality due to him, as he had already made up his mind to reside in that very place.
Bharata said to him: "Surely this has been prepared by you—the water for the feet, the guest-offering, and hospitality as is available in the forest. (23)
Then Bharadvāja spoke to Bharata as if smiling: "I know you are filled with affection; I shall satisfy you according to your desire. (24)
I wish to perform an act of hospitality for your entire army, such as my affection merits, and such as you, O King of Sages, deserve. (25)
And for what purpose have you come here, leaving your army far behind? O King, sovereign of those devoted to you, why did you not arrive here accompanied by your forces?
Bharata, with palms joined in reverence, replied thus to that ascetic:
"O Blessed One, I have not come with an army out of fear of you. (27)
For a king, O Blessed One, who is constantly engaged in the administration of the kingdom, ascetics must be diligently avoided within his domain. (28)
O Blessed One, excellent horses, men, and rutting, choice elephants follow me, covering the vast earth. (29)
Thinking that they might not harm the trees, the water, the ground, the hermitages, or the huts, I therefore came here alone.
Commanded thus by the supreme seer, "Let the army be brought here," Bharata acted accordingly and brought the army forward. 3.11.
Then the sage said to his virtuous wife Triveṇī, "O beautiful one, having constructed a magnificent city through the power of your devotion to your husband, O righteous lady. (32)
"O beloved, provide him a welcome and hospitality equal to that given to the King of Kuru.
Having been thus addressed, that virtuous wife bowed to her husband, who had bestowed this favor upon her.
Then, having entered the fire-hall, drunk water, and wiped his mouth,
he summoned Viśvakarman for the purpose of performing the rites of hospitality.
"I invoke Viśvakarman and Tvaṣṭṛ here;
I desire to perform the rites of hospitality, so let them be prepared for me.
I invoke the three world-protectors, the gods headed by Indra."
I wish to offer hospitality; please make the necessary arrangements for that.
May the rivers that flow eastward and those that flow crosswise,
both upon the earth and in the intermediate space, come together from all sides this very day.
Let other [streams] flow with milk and other sweet drinks to be consumed; and let others flow with cool water resembling the juice of sugarcane stalks. (38)
I summon the divine gandharvas Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū,
as well as the apsarases and all the divine gandharvas from every side.
Then [he saw] Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Miśrakeśī, Alambuṣā,
Nāgadattā, Hemā, Somā, Adri, and Kṛtasthalī.
I summon all those beautiful women who attend upon Śakra and those who attend upon Brahmā, together with Tumburu and their entire retinues. 41.

That divine forest among the Kurus, which has garments for its foliage and ornaments for its leaves, and which eternally bears celestial women as its fruit—that forest belonging to Kubera is indeed right here. 42.
"O Blessed One, let Soma here provide for me excellent food—abundant and diverse kinds of what is to be chewed, eaten, sucked, and licked. (43)
And various garlands fallen from trees, as well as juices and other drinks, and various kinds of foods. ||44||
Thus endowed with concentration, that radiant and devoted wife meditated upon the fire; she remembered them all, and they each arrived individually. (45)
Having touched the sandalwood mountains, the auspicious wind blew—driving away perspiration, very dear to the soul, pleasant, peaceful, and filled with fragrance. (46)
Showers of celestial flowers created by the gods, which bestow divinity, fell down in thick droplets of sandalwood paste. 47.
Then the sounds of divine drums and the hearing of auspicious proclamations were heard upon the earth, and throngs of apsarases danced there.
The gods and gandharvas sang, the lutes emitted their notes, and musical instruments were played for the sake of a welcome. ||49||
Bharata, having taken his army, arrived full of curiosity;
he beheld that army of his, which was a masterpiece of Viśvakarman’s craftsmanship.
There, a great expanse of land was created extending five yojanas on all sides, covered with abundant meadows resembling blue lapis lazuli. || 51 ||
There, bilva, kapittha, panasa, and sahakāra trees, as well as āmalaka and kharjūra trees, were adorned with fruit. (52)
And from the Northern Kurus, a forest possessing divine enjoyments arrived, along with a river endowed with trees, creepers, and fruits. (53)
There were bright four-sided pavilions, halls for elephants and horses, and auspicious gateways joined with mansions and palaces.
The royal palace, with its beautiful archways, resembled a white cloud;
it was adorned with white garlands and permeated with divine, sweet fragrances.
It was quadrangular and spacious, provided with beds, seats, and vehicles;
it was endowed with all kinds of divine jewels, as well as divine food and clothing. (56)
With all kinds of food prepared, with vessels washed until they were spotless, with every seat arranged, and with a magnificent, excellent bed well-spread; ||57||
The great devotee Bharata entered that jeweled palace, followed by the ministers and the family priests of the army. (58)
And Vasiṣṭha and the others, having seen the palace, were filled with joy;
there was a divine royal throne, as well as a fan and a parasol. (59)
Accompanied by his ministers, Bharata approached like a king;
he graced that divine throne, which was indeed worthy of a god.
Then all the ministers and priests sat down in order of seniority;
after them, the commander-in-chief and the chief justice sat down.
Then, in that very moment, by the command of Triveṇī, rivers with mud of milk-rice appeared there before Bharata.
On both banks of these rivers,
there are delightful and divine dwellings plastered with white clay, produced from the grace of the Triveṇī.
And at that very moment, twenty thousand women, adorned with divine ornaments and sent by Brahmā, arrived.
Adorned with gold, jewels, pearls, and coral,
twenty thousand women sent by Kubera arrived.
And by those [graces] favored, men shall possess divine bodies;
twenty thousand hosts of Apsaras shall come from the Nandana grove.
Nārada and other Gandharvas, equal to the sun in splendor,
went there and sang before Bharata with their musical arts.
Alambusha, Mishrakeshi, Pundarika,
and Vamana danced before Bharata at the command of Bharadvaja.
Whatever garlands exist among the gods and whatever are found in the Caitraratha grove,
all those were then seen at Prayāga by virtue of the splendor of the Triveṇī.

At that time, by the splendor of Triveṇī, the Bilva trees became drummers, the Śamī trees became cymbal-players, and the Vibhītaka trees became dancers; likewise, the Aśvattha trees became dancers. || 1.421.70 ||
Then the Sarala, Tāla, Tilaka,
and Tamāla trees arrived there in great joy, having assumed the forms of hunchbacks and dwarfs.
The trees—śiṃśapā, āmalakī, jambū, navaraṅga, and others—dwelt in the hermitage of Bharadvāja, serving as providers of fruit. (72)
Grapes, cirbhaṭikā, betel vines, somā, and other such creepers;
sweet sugar-canes and whatever other creepers exist in the forest. (73)
Assuming the forms of young women, they dwelt in the hermitage of Bharadvāja, saying, "O servants, drink sweet wines as you desire! (74)
Let milk-rice and choice foods be eaten by those who are hungry;
give fruits fit for eating, and let them be consumed by the leaders of the army.
After applying fragrant unguents once, those women— seven or eight of them— would bathe each individual man on the lovely riverbanks.
As he was massaging her, large-eyed women emerged;
those excellent ladies took his hands and made him drink honey and other such drinks.
The keepers of the mounts fed the horses, elephants, donkeys, camels, bulls, and excellent mules their respective fodder according to their needs. (78)
They fed the mounts with sugarcane, honey, and parched grain;
then the army shone forth, intoxicated, exhilarated, and joyful.
Satisfied with all their desires, honored with red sandalwood,
and cheered on by the Apsarases, the soldiers then raised a great shout.
"Oh, what palatial buildings! Oh, what treasures! Oh, these handmaidens and female servants!
Oh, what wish-fulfilling creepers are here! they exclaimed, "This is heaven! (8.1)
Dancing, laughing, and singing, the soldiers,
as well as thousands of men and women, shouted with great joy.
Thousands of Bharata’s followers, adorned with garlands, satisfied and filled with wonder, paid homage to Bharadvāja. (83)
Blessed is this king of sages, whose beloved wife is Triveṇī;
she is a virtuous woman who grants all perfections, and by her power this auspiciousness has come to pass. (84)
Even if one should dwell in the forest, if his wife is devoted to her husband, heaven resides in the palm of his hand; what need has he for the splendors of sovereignty? (85)
That noble wife who, having drunk the water used for washing her husband's feet, stands near the fire and desires great divine powers, attains them at that very moment.
Do they ever fail to attain heaven or even higher states?
Therefore, let virtuous women devoted to their husbands prevail everywhere. (87)
Likewise, may their husbands be men comparable to Bharadvāja, devoted to their wives, for whom heaven is always within reach. (88)
Thus spoke all the soldiers by the thousands, as well as the inhabitants of the district of Sāketa, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, who were full of pride. ||89||
Then, tens of millions of other non-Buddhist ascetics arrived at the Kumbha festival,
having beheld that divine heaven created by Bharadvāja.
And [he saw] Kambharā, Mahālakṣmī, and the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa;
there he beheld the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa seated upon a leaf-throne.
And [he saw] Triveṇī in the form of a river, as well as crores of sacred fords (tīrthas),
and the youthful Triveṇī, the beloved wife of Bharadvāja.
Having beheld him and received his sight, they were purified and attained divinity;
then, as they ate that food which was like nectar, [they were satisfied]. (93)
Beholding divine foods, his mind became intent on eating them; so too did the male servants, female slaves, daughters-in-law, soldiers, and the local inhabitants. (94)
The male and female servants, as well as the male and female attendants, were numerous;
they all became exceedingly joyful and likewise dressed in new garments. (95)
Elephants, donkeys, camels, cattle, horses, wild animals, and birds became satiated; they indeed sought nothing other than grass and such at that time.
At that time, no one there was dressed in white garments, nor was anyone hungry;
they were provided with fruits and other delicious juices, soups, boiled vegetables, and milk-rice porridges.
For there were lakes full of cooked rice, as well as mountains of it;
and by the side of the hermitage, there were wells with mud made of milk-rice.
And those cows were wish-fulfilling, and the trees exuded honey;
there were ponds filled with wine and crores of golden vessels.
At that time, there were silver vessels, ten million copper ones,
thousands of bowls, and hundreds of thousands of cooking pots.
And there were tens of millions of vessels made of gold, as well as cooking pots, jars, and bowls, all well-prepared and filled with curds. (101)
There were heaps of fresh butter, jars of buttermilk,
lakes full of sweetmeats (*rasālā*), and powders of bitter, sour, and pleasant flavors.
In that hermitage, there were heaps of parpaṭas, mountains of polikās,
and great peaks of sweetmeats.
There were heaps of condiments and sugar-candies,
as well as powders fit for smearing and various kinds of bathing unguents.
People at the riverbanks saw vessels containing heaps of white, radiant tooth-sticks.
White sandalwood pastes were kept in covered caskets,
along with excellent mirrors and a great abundance of variegated garments.
There were various kinds of mouth-fresheners, powdered betel, and betel leaves for chewing,
as well as thousands of pairs of wooden sandals and leather shoes.
Collyrium-sticks, combs, brushes, toothpicks, umbrellas, and chowries; various armor for protecting vital parts, as well as beds and seats. || 108 ||
They plunged into ponds full of water for the drinking of donkeys, camels, elephants, and horses, and into lakes with excellent landing-stairs that were filled with blue and white lotuses.
[They saw] ponds resembling the color of the sky, with clear waters, providing pleasant immersion;
some were the color of blue lapis lazuli, and others were covered with soft carpets.
They saw there, on all sides, bears devouring the animals,
and various beautiful swings in every chamber.
There were delightful wind-machines, thousands of electric lamps,
pools of cold and warm water, and likewise gambling houses.
Even the celestial palaces and mansions are vehicles for traveling to heaven;
they are also excellent watercraft and instruments for hearing from afar. (113)
There were television sets and pastime projectors,
as well as numerous arenas for games such as those of actors, dancers, and jesters.
Those men were filled with wonder at that marvelous hospitality, which was like a dream and even greater than that of Mahendra.
For that new heaven was indeed created by Bharadvāja and Triveṇī;
in the hermitage of Bharadvāja, a day and night passed happily.
Then, having performed their morning ablutions, Bharata and the others again completed the rites of eating and so forth, and worshipped the sage Triveṇika.
Having given many gifts, they went to the city of Sāketa;
and all those Gandharvas and beautiful women returned.
All those who had been summoned there by the command of the Lord of Triveṇī returned;
that entire artificial creation vanished from sight.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, dear one, this majesty of the bull of wifely devotion has been told to you, which is indeed renowned throughout the fourteen worlds.

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Triveṇī, the Wife of Bharadvāja, Created a New Heaven for the Sake of Bharata at Prayāga through Her Chastity," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of Śabarī, the purifier of the world;
she was the beloved of Brahmā, known by that name, who was the wife of Kṛṣṇa in his abode.
When indeed Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, and Sarasvatī were spoken to with anger by Rādhā regarding their departure from the earth, then a friend of Brahmā’s beloved [spoke]. || 2 ||
Having bowed at her feet, he said to Rādhā: "O auspicious one, do not speak thus;
show forgiveness toward your co-wives, for forgiveness is befitting of you, O Mother."
Then Rādhā said to her: "Go with Ramā;
having taken birth as a group of maidservants on earth, dwell upon the surface of the world."
Then another friend of Rādhā named Pampā was there;
she bowed to Rādhā, and Rādhā said to her, "Do not speak. || 5 ||
Rādhā said: "Go to the earth, accompanied by ten thousand beloveds of Brahmā;
dwell in the great forest of Mahāpampā, and go near the Jaḍa."
When this was said, they performed a foot-massage for Rādhikā;
then Rādhā became pleased and spoke regarding the release from the curse.
If any of my friends should sport with Kṛṣṇa in the absence of Rādhā, I shall send them all down to the earth.
Having enjoyed the time limit of a ghaṭikā in Goloka at both Brahmapriyā and Pampā on earth during the reigns of many Manus, after that—
Having obtained here the excellent Kṛṣṇa in the form of Rāma, you two shall return again;
meanwhile, as knowers of Brahman, you two shall practice devotion to Hari on this earth.
Possessing the virtues of those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) and always bestowing welfare upon the world,
you two goddesses shall exist on earth endowed with divine and long-lasting lifespans.
Having thus received this grace and by the command of Kṛṣṇa,
those two indeed arrived together with Lakṣmī upon the surface of the earth, in the southern region.
Lakṣmī was born as Vedavatī, the daughter of Kuśadhvaja;
and that virtuous woman, having performed severe penance in the hermitage named Badarī, [became his daughter]. (13)
And on earth, Sītā, the daughter who delights Janaka, was born as Bālikā;
and at that time, Kuśadhvaja’s servant became a forest-guardian.
There was indeed a potter named Bhīma who resided on the auspicious Veṅkaṭādri;
he had two daughters born of his mind: Pampā and Brahmapriyā. || 15 ||
Once that divine pair, who remembered their past lives and were dear to Hari, had been born,
they departed for the forest immediately after birth in order to perform ascetic penance.
Then those two maidens entered the great forest, which was adorned by Mount Ṛṣyamūka and began from Krauñcāraṇya. 17.
They performed fierce austerities in that solitary place of divine nature;
there were monkeys born of the solar dynasty and those who were beasts.
Powerful, performers of cruel deeds, and devoid of the traditional teachings of dharma, they were there in various parts of that forest; yet those two maidens were practicing asceticism.
They tormented her excessively with cries like those of cattle;
then Pampā, having reflected, became a lotus pond filled with water.
Taking the form of a river, she performed austerities to attain Hari;
there, she became the beloved of Brahmā, aged and extremely ugly in appearance.
With a body consisting of nothing but bone, emaciated, yet bearing a bow,
she was Śabarī— of cruel appearance, exceedingly pitiless, and terrifying.
Seeing her, those monkeys were struck with fear as if she were a Rākṣasī;
thus, both beloved women remained there, performing their ascetic penance.
And you two must constantly worship your husband Kṛṣṇa with devotion in the forest of Mount Ṛṣyamūka, which is densely crowded with fruit-bearing trees.
With *jambū*, *priyāla*, and *panasa* trees; with *nyagrodha*, *plakṣa*, and *tinduka*; and with *aśvattha*, *karṇikāra*, *tilaka*, and *naktamālaka* trees. ||25||
With *nāga* trees, mangoes, *aśoka*, and *karavīraka*; with *pāribhadra*, *kadamba*, sandalwood, and *nāraṅga-khārika* trees. ||26||
It was filled with fruit-bearing trees such as date palms, bilva, and coconuts;
there, the trees bore fruit in all seasons and exuded sweet juices. (27)
And all the seasons there produce fruits and flowers;
where the waterfalls shine, as do the amṛtakanda and other such plants.
That lotus pond Pampā became filled with water;
it was free from gravel, free from treacherous places, possessed level landing-stairs, and was devoid of water-moss.
The river was adorned with fine sand and beautified by lotuses and water-lilies;
it was frequented by swans, cranes, frogs, ospreys, *cātaka* birds, and parrots.
Repeatedly resounded by peacocks, wild cocks, and water-fowls, that maiden of beautiful form rejoices at night together with Śabarī. 31.
By day, Pampā takes the form of water where Śabarī rejoices; when living beings are asleep, the two maidens take their delight there. (32)
The excellent Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Rādhā,
joined with Pārvatī and Prabhā, and united with Śrī and Māṇikī.
Accompanied by Padmāvatī, Padminī, Mālatī, and Jayā, together with Mohinī and Vṛndā, and joined by Tulasī and Padmā. (34)
With joy, [they beheld] Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Mālatī and Durgā, as well as Sarasvatī and Gaṅgā, and joined by Lalitā. 35.

At a moment free from the presence of living beings, they both worshipped their husband—who was endowed with the dharma of devotion to his wife and with innate goodness—using auspicious materials. (36)
The fragrance of sandalwood spreads there in every direction, and at that time,
the sounds of musical instruments arise there, bringing delight.
Then forest goddesses arrive and sing songs;
trees, creepers, grasses, and shrubs come in embodied form for the worship.
The wish-fulfilling cows yield milk as offerings of fruit and flowers;
likewise, the celestial elephants are white and the Garuḍas are pale.
During worship, the swans of heaven and the golden fish come there in embodied form;
indeed, rivers, streams, and oceans bring their jewels to that place.
Mahālakṣmī, known as Kambharā, and the Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa arrived and accepted their worship during the latter part of the night.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by his twenty wives beginning with Lakṣmī,
accepted the worship performed by the two maidens and embraced them to his chest.
Having delighted her and bestowed all happiness born of his grace, Hari then kisses her and thereafter becomes eternally invisible. ||43||
Furthermore, Pampā is composed of water, and Śabarī is aged;
thus, one's penance always proceeds without obstacle from these two sources. ||44||
Thus, having heard of the new lotus pond Pampā, the sages who were disciples of Mataṅga and dwellers of the mountains and forests indeed [arrived]. ||45||
Then those who were residing nearby arrived there to see it;
and having seen that divine lotus pond, they were thereafter filled with joy.
Having constructed numerous leaf-huts on the banks of the Pampā, they settled there;
from the bodies of those practitioners of austerity, drops of perspiration [began to fall]. (47)
Those [tears] which fell to the earth indeed became flowers;
born from drops of perspiration, those flowers do not perish.
On that ground suitable for their dwelling, that Śabarī, a wandering female ascetic (śramaṇī) devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa, was always traveling on foot. 49.
He awaits that moment: "When will Sītā be reunited? When, as Rāma departs for the forest, will he grant us liberation? (1.422.50)
In the meantime, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa appeared;
they reached the western bank of the Puṣkariṇī lake. 51.
While searching for their beloved, who had been abducted by Rāvaṇa during their forest exile,
the two of them came upon the beautiful hermitage of Śabarī.
Beholding that most delightful place, crowded with many trees and beautified by the Pampā lake, they approached Śabarī.
Seeing them, the Siddha woman then rose up with palms joined in reverence;
she grasped Rāma’s feet and bowed down to Lakṣmaṇa.
He offered her water for her feet and water for sipping, everything according to the prescribed rites;
then Rāma spoke to that female ascetic who was firmly established in dharma.
O beloved of Brahmā, do you not remember Rādhā’s words which bestow the fruit of penance:
"I am Rāma; I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the giver of liberation to you"? (56)
Hearing that voice, Pampā then appeared in the form of a maiden;
bowing at Rāma’s feet and falling prostrate, she shed tears. (57)
Rāma inquired after their welfare and well-being, preceded by questions regarding their circumstances:
"I hope that your obstacles have been overcome, and I hope that your ascetic penance is increasing? (58)
O you whose wealth is asceticism, is your anger and your food restrained? Have your observances been successfully attained, and is there peace in your minds? (59)
"Is your service to your elders bearing fruit here?
Thus was asked by Rāma to the two female ascetics, who were perfected beings honored by the perfected ones.
The aged Śabarī and Pampā both proclaimed to Rāma:
"O Lord, through the sight of you today, the perfection of your asceticism has been attained."
Today our birth has become fruitful, and our guests have been honored;
today our ascetic penance has borne fruit, and the eternal state of heaven is ours. (62)
O Lord Kṛṣṇa, since You have become our protector— being honored, saluted, served, and fed— all the fruit has been obtained.
"O Protector, when our eyes have been purified and attained divinity, we shall go to our own Goloka by your grace, O dear Lord. (64)
When you reached Citrakūṭa,
those whom we had served here ascended to heaven from this place by means of celestial chariots of incomparable splendor.
When this had been said by those highly fortunate sages who were exceedingly learned in the Dharma, [they declared]:
"That Rāma shall come to this meritorious hermitage of yours."
That Śrī Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by His younger brother, is to be served by you as a guest;
upon seeing Him, you two shall go to your own world, Goloka.
When this was said by those illustrious ones, O Kānta and Keśava,
we both brought together various forest-grown fruits and other provisions that we had gathered.
O Beloved of Kamalā, for your sake, accept this water-offering (arghya) produced on the banks of the Paṃpā and presented by Śabarī with the waters of the Paṃpā. 6.9.
Having spoken thus, they seated him upon a seat of kuśa grass and performed the washing of his feet; that water was the destroyer of sins.
Having borne it upon their heads and having drunk [the water], they worshipped [him] with wild flowers, as well as with well-ripened fruits and sweet roots. (71)
Having personally tasted its sweetness, examined it, and consumed it,
Śabarī then offered it to the Giver of Life.
The two of them ate the ripe jujube fruits and other fruits;
then Rāma, remembering her, spoke to the virtuous Śabarī, his servant.
In ancient times, the Dānavas indeed performed a great sacrificial festival here;
even today, the altar remains and the fire shines forth there.
"O beautiful one, I wish to see this place which is full of wonders.
Having been addressed thus, she led Rāma away to a distant part of the forest. (75)
Śabarī showed them both that great forest:
"Behold it, resembling a dense mass of clouds and teeming with beasts and birds. (76)
This very place is renowned as the Mataṅgavana forest, inhabited by sages;
here, O dear one, my gurus have purified their souls. (77)
They offered oblations in the nest with mantras, honoring it with sacred formulas;
this very spot facing west is the altar where the Dānavas always reside.
Day after day they offer floral oblations to the deities;
behold even now, O Janārdana, the power of their asceticism! (79)
Illuminating all directions with her splendor, she possessed an incomparable radiance upon the sacrificial altar;
and those who were emaciated by fasting were unable to proceed further toward her.
Indeed, seven oceans intended for his ablutions remain here;
by those who have performed their ritual baths, bark garments have been hung upon the trees in this place. (81)
Look here: even today they have not dried up in this place, for these were indeed worn by those performing the rites of the gods.
"Even delicate flowers do not wither here;
indeed, Rāma saw this very thing while those ascetics were present. (83)
All those born of the lineage of Danu, possessing divine forms and devoted to Viṣṇu, arrived there as disciples of Mataṅga. (84)
Having fallen at the feet of that Rāma, they washed his foot;
for in their previous birth, all those sages had drunk [the water from it]. 85.
Having abandoned their demonic wombs and ascended a celestial chariot,
they were all led by the attendants and went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then the maidservant said to her beloved Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"This entire forest has been seen by you, and what was to be heard has been heard. (87)
Therefore, having been granted permission, I desire to cast off this body;
for when the Yuga is complete, O Hari, Pampā wishes to go to Goloka. (88)
"O Lakṣmī, where is the fortune of our sister? O Śrī, tell us; show us mercy!
Hearing this, Rāma wept, and they both then granted him courage.
Having learned the news concerning Sītā, they fell into deep reflection;
then, indeed, through the grace of Rāma, they attained supreme composure.
Then, summoning her courage, Pampā arrived there to see him and begged for his release so that he might cast off his body. ||91||
Rāma also, having looked upon her there with compassion,
spoke to Śabarī, who had adopted the lifelong vow of asceticism at Pampā.
"O Śabarī, you who have remained steadfast in the vow of celibacy throughout your life and who are dear to the illustrious Hari—
since I have been honored by you, O Pampā, go now to my abode."
Just then, a celestial chariot joined by Kṛṣṇa arrived there,
accompanied by Lakṣmī and attended by his attendants, carrying the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Having bowed, meditated, and placed [Rāma] in her heart, Pampā and Śabarī were then granted leave by Rāma; she then produced fire from her foot.
Having reduced her body to ashes, the Gopī became a resident of Goloka;
just as she was beloved by Kṛṣṇa, so too did Pampā become beloved by Brahmā.
Resembling blazing fire and equal to Rādhā and Lakṣmī, the two divine maidens, having come into being, sat down by the side of Kṛṣṇa. ||97||
Adorned with divine ornaments, anointed with divine unguents, and wearing divine garments, they both appeared beautiful there. (98)
Shining like two streaks of lightning at the side of Kṛṣṇa, those two indeed traveled to eternal Goloka by means of that beautiful vehicle. 99.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account of the life of Brahmapriyā;
by hearing or reading it, a woman or a man shall indeed go to Goloka.

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Descent of Pampā and the Consort of Brahmā from Goloka due to Rādhikā’s Wrath, Their Return to Goloka through the Yoga of Rāmacandra, and the Nature of Chastity," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity,
which concerns a maidservant of Kṛṣṇa from Goloka who bestowed the name Citralekhā upon you.
Formerly, I was born as Ṛṣabha, an incarnation who practiced righteousness;
having renounced the life of a householder, I placed the burden of responsibility upon my own son, Bharata.
Having renounced his state and attained the condition of a wandering mendicant, he established the bull of the highest ascetic order upon the earth and departed for Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Bharata had a powerful son named Śataśṛṅga;
he had eight sons and one daughter, making nine children in total.
Indradvīpa, Kaseru, Tāmradvīpa, Gabhastimān, Nāga, Saumya, Gandharva, Varuṇa, and Kumārikā. (5)
Having been a maiden, she became an eternal companion in Goloka;
by the name Citralekhā, she took birth there due to Rādhā’s anger.
There, a maiden became renowned by the name Harivratā;
from the moment of her birth she remembered her former lives, and as a young woman she was a speaker of Brahman.
Devoted to ritual bathing and the twilight prayers, she recited the Vedaprasū mantra for three years;
she constantly served with faith the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
A Vaiṣṇava tulasī garland always remained upon her neck,
and with a wreath of vṛndā flowers in her hand, she chanted the name of Hari as her husband.
In lying down, in waking, in action, in rest, in eating,
in acquiring, in drinking, in bringing objects, in bathing, and in adorning the body.
In recitation, in ritual accomplishment, in anointing, in washing, in seeking, in cooking, in bathing, in purification, in laziness, in playing an instrument, and in praise; || 11 ||
In hearing, in chanting, in the gathering of firewood, in joy within the mind,
in passion, in looking, in conduct, in movement, and in hunger.
In thirst, in fever, in summer, in cold, during a festival, in the forest, upon a tree, upon a creeper, in a house, and in the circle of her friends; || 13 ||
She chants the name and meditates upon her Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
she laughs, dances, cries out, runs about, and sheds tears. || 14 ||
She attains a divine state and travels through the sky to the interior of the forest;
she enters the interior of the house of Kṛṣṇa with unimpeded gait.
Food, water, fruit, leaf, flower, seed, liquid, milk, the sweet, the dry, clothing, the arghya offering, incense, and a lamp—each of equal value. (16)
Having given her daughter to the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
she enjoys what is offered by Him, having made it prasāda, while being devoid of any other enjoyment.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself eats what was offered by the maiden;
he indeed sports with her for a moment in a charming game of dice.
Thus, the young maiden, eternally devoted to her fidelity to Kṛṣṇa, propitiates her husband and lord, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Her face, moreover, had the appearance of a goat's head;
hear the reason for that, O Lakṣmī, when Rādhikā was in Goloka.
Then, having become enraged, Citralekhā caused her face to hang down;
she made her lips long and her tongue loll outwards.
At that time, this very distorted face was shown to Rādhā;
having seen the face painted on the canvas, she perceived it as being engaged in a distorted imitation.
Rādhā said to her: "O Barkarikāmukhī, become long-faced!
You show your face just like a she-goat by nature. (23)
"Therefore, having become a she-goat, roam upon the circle of the earth.
Thus addressed, that friend, a servant of Rādhā, spoke with humility: ||24||
The fruit of service to the great becomes vast when obtained through a maidservant;
this is so, O Rādhā, if you are indeed the Great One, the Sovereign of the Queen of Queens. 25.
And then bestow upon her a most great fruit corresponding to herself;
if you are mean, O Kṣudrikā, give a mean fruit to your servant. (26)
The gift of objects such as rewards proclaims to the worlds the superiority or inferiority of the giver, according to the nature of the gift bestowed. (27)
Having heard this, the great queen Rādhā became delighted and, smiling, then said to Citralekhā: "Become a sovereign queen upon the earth. (28)
"O child, for a moment become a female barkarikā, the daughter of the black bull; remain thus on this mountain, for he will arrive here in an instant. (29)
Having been addressed thus, that divine maiden Citralekhā descended from the path of the sky at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.
Seeing her, who was radiant with beauty, the ocean was agitated in his mind for a moment;
becoming a youth adorned with jewels, he approached with a desire for union.
Then that girl became invisible in the forest as a she-goat; [the king thought:
"Is she the Great Siddhi, or the Goddess, or an Apsaras? ||32||
When, having reflected with a tranquil mind, he went behind her to question her, she became terrified and fled into the depths of the forest. (33)
Overwhelmed with distress, she wandered through that difficult terrain near Stambhatīrtha, which was overgrown with thickets, shrubs, and creepers.
Wandering here and there, afflicted by hunger and thirst, she then fled toward the shore of the earth, O beloved. (35)
Having reached a trench in the water ten cubits or more in length, he leaps and bounds across it until he falls upon the excellent bank ahead. (36)
On that bank, adorned with nets, trees, branches, and the like, she fell among the wooden frames of the nets, desiring concealment. (37)
But her head there had fallen under the power of the noose of the branch;
indeed, she experienced fear from behind and even fear for her throat. (38)
The fear of hunger and thirst, the fear regarding enjoyments, and the fear of falling into an unfamiliar land—she is indeed [afflicted] by these five fears. (39)
She died in that very moment, her body falling into the water;
her head remained on the branch of the Jāli tree, about a span's length above [the surface].
There he clung to the bank, not submerged within the water;
his head was above the water, while his body remained between the earth and the water. (41)
Thus, by the power of the holy ford, the maiden became a beautiful human being in body, though her head remained like that of a goat.
Thus, that beloved of Hari was born as the daughter of King Śataśṛṅga among the Siṃhalas, with the face of a she-goat. 43.
Divyanārī, of auspicious form, shone with a beautiful remaining body;
she was like a hundred sons to King Jyeṣṭha, who had no son, being full of affection for him. (44)
A daughter was born who increased the joy of her kinsmen with great delight;
seeing that girl with the face of a goat, the kings were filled with wonder. (45)
The king, accompanied by his inner apartments, fell into extreme despondency;
likewise, the subjects and all the people who beheld that virtuous woman were distressed.
"What is this?"—thus did all men everywhere say in wonder;
for she possessed a divine form, with a radiance exceeding that of the moon. (47)
Having recognized Mahāmāyā as Ajāmukhī, they worshipped her with devotion—
she who is the single unborn one, red, white, and black, the very form of the primordial source.
Having understood her to be the power (śakti) and primordial nature (prakṛti) of Hari, they worshipped her with reverence;
yet even the Unborn (Aja), failing to obtain her for his own desire, desisted.
Then, as soon as she was born, that young woman became an awakener of the Vedas;
like the goddess Sarasvatī herself, she possessed the true resonance of knowledge.
Having seen her own face in the mirror, she constantly remembers that sacred ford in the form of the Mahī river where it meets the great ocean.
Pregnant with wisdom, she spoke to her mother, father, and subjects about her own self, who resides in Goloka and exists in the form of Citralekhā.
Do not be astonished at this; it is the fruit earned in a previous birth.
My head is located here within the Jāli tree on the bank of the Mahī river.
"If I were to fall to the earth from there, my face would become human," she said, and having spoken thus, she resolved to go toward that place. (54)
Then his father gave him servants, boats, foods, jewels, female slaves, and various kinds of wealth for the purpose of giving. (55)
Then, having reached Stambhatīrtha together with her husband and wealth,
she gave abundant gifts there, offering her entire possessions as the sacrificial fee.
Having searched within the thicket of creepers for the skull, which was the bone of his head,
he burned it in the presence of Saṅgama and cast the bone and other remains into the sacred ford.
By the power of that sacred ford (tīrtha), through its full capacity and splendor,
the human face indeed became completely enveloped by a halo of radiance.
Neither among the daughters of the gods, nor among the wives of the nāgas, nor among mortal women is there such a truly auspicious face as hers. (59)
The gods, asuras, humans, and others were infatuated by her beauty;
they entreated him in many ways, yet she did not desire a husband.
Thereupon, she undertook the most excellent austerity, which was difficult for others to perform;
indeed, when the year was complete, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became her Lord.
Having become visible to her, he said, "I am the giver of boons.
And having honored that former husband, the virtuous maiden spoke to him.
O Lord, if you are well-pleased and a boon is to be granted to me,
then remain present with me, O Lord, and lead me thereafter to Goloka.
Having been told by Kṛṣṇa, "So be it," the young girl was delighted;
then, after honoring Kṛṣṇa, the maiden spoke to Janārdana. (64)
Let this sacred ford (tīrtha), consisting of the waters of the Gaṅgā, indeed bring well-being here;
and let the cremation of those who die here take place in the vicinity of Barkarīśvara. (65)
From that, O Mādhava, let there be liberation for them;
O Hari, let people attain liberation after bathing in the waters of the ocean and the earth.
"So be it," Hari said, and he departed once more, becoming invisible.
Then, having heard of this supreme marvel from Pātāla, the one named Svastika—
The Naga king emerged from his hole there in order to see him;
that well, named Svastika, then attained the fame of being a sacred tirtha.
Likewise, a Nāga installed the Barkarīśa Liṅga,
and he also installed the auspicious Liṅga known as Svastikeśvara.
Having had a magnificent temple constructed there by that maiden,
she herself installed the Lord Ajāviṣṇu as her own husband.
She serves Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in personified form;
moreover, whoever bathes there in that well on the fourteenth day of the month of Kārttika [attains great merit].
He who offers libations to his ancestors saves twenty generations;
thus that divine maiden, having established a sacred ford, went to her home.
In Siṃhala, he reported everything to his father Śataśṛṅga;
having heard this, the king, accompanied by his subjects, arrived there for the sake of visiting the sacred ford.
He gave gifts and provided a livelihood at his daughter's residence;
the king attained fame through his daughter, for blessed is he whose daughter is virtuous. (74)
Then, having returned to his own city, he held a great festival; and although the maiden was unwilling, O Lotus-born One, he chose her as his bride and received wealth as well.
Having divided his own portion of the navel-region into nine parts,
the father gave eight to his sons and gave the ninth to Ajā.
In the southern region of Kanyākumārikākhaṇḍa, the king and the great virtuous maiden Kumārikā, who observed the vow of Hari, established a kingdom. (77)
That illustrious maiden exists at Stambhatīrtha on the shore of the earth in a divine form, and she always dwells within the kingdom as well. 78.
In the navel of the nine-fold continent,
there are indeed ninety-six crores and seventy-two lakhs of cities.
Having thus made these arrangements for that supreme field of Kumārī and having established Mahākāla as its protector, the virtuous lady then departed from there.
Having gone to Badarikāśrama to perform penance in the abode of Hari,
Citralekhā became an ascetic at Badarikāśrama.
"When I become Kṛṣṇa and sport in Vṛndāvana, my son Aniruddha shall then be the excellent husband of Uṣā. (82)
By means of which, having had him painted in a picture, he will become visible in dreams;
that [knowledge] shall then appear on earth after five thousand years have passed. ||83||
The wife of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa will be born in Saurāṣṭra;
having served her husband Hari with a visible form equal to Śrī, she will remain so. 84.
"She shall go indeed to the Goloka of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I told you of the divine, virtuous Citralikhā. 85.
By reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of Kanyātīrtha;
one will possess wealth, daughters, sons, wives, and prosperity—of this there is no doubt. (86)
The beautiful Citralekhā, though invisible, has become visible;
she too is remembered as the bestower of liberation, for she is as dear as Kṛṣṇa himself. (87)

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Citralekhā from Goloka into the Lineage of Ṛṣabha; Her Transformation into a Barking Goat through Delusion by the Ocean in the Form of Barkara; The Display of Miracles at the Holy Site of the Confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean, including the Renown of the Kumārikā-khaṇḍa; and the Attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by her in the Form of Mañjulā," in the first section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of a Brahmin named Bhikṣu and his wife Kalahā, who lived long ago in the shade of Mount Revatācala.
This story, which counters opposing views and awakens one to the greatness of the Lord, is as follows:
In the city of Karavīra, there was a Brahmin named Dharmadatta.
Devoted to bathing, the twilight prayers, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and the chanting of mantras,
that great devotee constantly served virtuous people.
Having gathered all the people residing in the village onto the surface of the ground,
he constantly performs the chanting of the Name preceded by song;
he dances in the presence of Kṛṣṇa and recites sacred stories.
With devotion and sincerity, he performs many festivals;
especially on the days of vows and the like, he causes them to be celebrated by the guild-leaders.
That twice-born man gratifies his guests with welcoming words day and night.
Performing his recitation with beads of a garland for Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and constantly chanting "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya Oṃ," he goes to the temple for the purpose of performing the worship of Nārāyaṇa.
Having bathed well in a river during the Brāhma-muhūrta while taking up his residence, || 8 ||
On his way to the temple, he indeed beheld a Rākṣasī who was terrifying,
hungry, cruel, with protruding fangs, and naked.
"Thick as a black mountain, with a lolling tongue and carrying a skull-fragment, I eat and devour while uttering a gurgling sound. (1.424.10)
Leaping up with great speed, she was difficult to seize;
and Dharmadatta, seeing her, fled in terror while crying out. (11)
She too ran after him on his back to seize and devour him voraciously;
but as she drew near, Dharmadatta became utterly distraught.
Intent on protecting his life from the cause of her removal, he cried out:
"O Hare, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, Mādhava, protect me! (1.3)
O Lord of Śrī, O Master of Māṇikī, O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of Prabhā!
O Lord of Lakṣmī and Rādhā, O Lord of Pārvatī, O Lord of Kamalā! || 14 ||
O Lord of the Swan of Peace, protect me—just as Jayā, Ādyā, Ramā, and Campāpate protect Muktāpate—who am lovely and charming. 15.
Reciting, "Oṃ, O Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Sudarśana, protect me here," he cast two Tulasī leaves and water [into the fire]. 16.
And in the Rākṣasī [language], the articles for the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa are:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, protect, protect!"—thus he should speak. (17)
If you touch me, O Brahmin, may the curse of Rāma fall upon you! If you touch me, O wretch, may the curse of Caṇḍikā fall upon you! (18)
"If you touch me while naked, let there be the curse of the Queen of Yoginīs upon you! If you touch me, O slut, let there be the curse of Durgā upon you!"
If you touch me for a wicked purpose, let there be a curse upon you from Rudra;
if you touch me, O Kṛṣṇā, let there be a curse upon you from Kṛṣṇa.
If you touch me at night, let there be a curse upon you from Māyā;
if you touch me, O wicked woman, let there be a curse upon you from Kāla.
Speaking thus, he struck Kṛṣṇa with stones in his rage;
yet with the water and tulasī leaves used for worship, he burned away all sins.
Having regained her auspicious composure and remembering her previously committed sin,
she recalled the web of her misdeeds and spoke to Dharmadatta.
In a previous birth, in Saurāṣṭra near Mount Raivata on the banks of the Bhadrā,
there lived a Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa named Bhikṣu.
His wife was cruel and acted in opposition to him; what was her character, what was her speech, and what was her contentiousness that caused such great suffering? (25)
My Kali resides in my heart, my tongue dances with insults at its tip, cruelty dwells forever in my eyes, and the nature of tamas is ever-present in my mind. (26)
A fierce disposition resides in my forehead, great anger on the slope of my nose; contempt dwells in my two lips, while strife is situated in my speech. (27)
In his breathing, he dwells in what is undesirable; agitation resides in his actions;
shame is always cast behind him, while shamelessness is maintained before him. (28)
Insult and beating are held in the palm of my hand;
thus living constantly, I dwell in the house of the twice-born. (29)
In the land of Saurāṣṭra, in every region, in whatever house, wherever it may be,
if a dispute should arise between a husband and wife, then [I am there].
"Is it remembered by name? A quarrel has arrived here—phat! Thus am I known by name as one who always causes distress to my husband. (31)
Just as one remembers having eaten in the morning but does not obtain it [when hungry], so too was I formerly a sinful wife of a monk. (3.2)
I cause my own husband to perform the massaging of my feet, as well as the washing of my clothes and even the sweeping of the house. (33)
I even had a monk prepare my cosmetics and ointments;
at that time, I was the embodiment of such a great mass of evil.
I do not give food or water that grants happiness to my husband;
rather, I indeed give him the opposite of what he requests. ||35||
Even that which was joined with the *gālikā*—lost and fallen—I give away;
and thus I speak: "O woman, eat the fruit of passion! (36)
My lover was constantly agitated and never spoke sweetly;
he performed no auspicious deed for me at all, and even the courtesan gave me no happiness. (37)
"O Brahmin, though I am a harlot, I grant contentment and never engage in quarrels;
thus, even though I am wicked, I have become a source of happiness for you through my magic power. (38)
"Even a concubine can grant happiness, whereas I, though married, do not;
thus deeply distressed, the mendicant went to the Raivata forest. (39)
Enraged and intent on inflicting suffering, I went there to that forest region;
seizing him firmly by his topknot, I brought him to my own home.
Though she was afflicted by passion, devoted to her own sensual interests, and engaged in animal-like conduct, even then that twice-born man never killed me nor did he ever strike me. (41)
Then, on one occasion, moved by compassion, I wept after a quarrel;
however, at another time, I requested a drink of water from a Brahmin. (42)
While she lay on her bed for a day in vain, being exceedingly angry,
she gave me water that was lukewarm and kept in a pitcher.
The clay vessel was indeed empty; there was no cold water to be found.
Then, becoming enraged, she seized a pestle and rose up.
A great sound was heard by the neighbors as he was being beaten;
they came and said to the brahmin, "Drive this woman out of our house."
"O monk, take another wife and abandon this *kṛtyā*. We shall even give you wealth; live happily, O Brahmin! (46)
The brahmin, having made his decision,
went elsewhere to marry a second maiden who had previously been requested for that purpose.
Then I consumed poison and immediately gave up my life;
bound with nooses by the messengers of Yama, I was led toward the abode of Yama.
At that time on the road, I experienced great suffering from being beaten and the arrows of harsh words, as well as the distress arising from walking upon fire and hot sand. (49)
Enduring hunger and thirst, their bodies torn asunder, and falling into fainting fits—
thus they reach the abode of Yama, being slaughtered again and again.
Having observed me, Dharmarāja questioned Citragupta: "What kind of sin does she have? Examine her deeds, both auspicious and inauspicious. (51)
Upon seeing her, the fruit of karma appears exceedingly evil;
then Citragupta, having quickly perceived that most dreadful deed, [acts accordingly].
Addressing that wicked, sinful, and most evil harlot, he said:
"Nothing auspicious whatsoever has been done by this sinful and wicked woman. (53)
She always gave insults and administered beatings to her husband; she never once fed him anything sweet while she herself was eating. (54)
By that sin, may she furthermore become a female crow that eats excrement;
may she become a bat, always eating her own excrement with her face turned downwards. (55)
But because she struck her husband with that sin, she became a female donkey;
furthermore, may she become a sow that eats excrement while cooking food in a pot. (56)
"May she therefore always be a female cat who hates her husband;
because she committed suicide, may she become a preta wandering in the desert. (57)
Then, having become a Piśācī and the beloved of many Piśācas, she shall thereafter become a wicked Rākṣasī, a doer of evil. ||58||
Having heard this reasoning from another, King Yama, having assigned me to various deeds, repeatedly granted me those respective births. (59)
Having completed all of that, I became a sorrowful ogress;
there is no end to my karma, and evil arises again and again.
Constantly defiled by sin, I am a rākṣasī in the forest;
I devour beasts, the best of birds, and humans in the woods. (6.1)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? There is no end to my karmas. Thus she was filled with grief and exceedingly tormented by hunger and thirst.
I leaped up and indeed entered the body of that merchant;
together with him, I went to the auspicious southern country.
That merchant drank water at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and Veṇī;
while he stood there, exhausted, the gods remained on the bank.
They struck me repeatedly, and I fled far away;
afflicted by hunger and thirst, I again sought a merchant-like vessel. (65)
"I have seen you and I am satisfied; my hunger shall be appeased.
For this purpose, I have come quickly and joyfully to take [you]. (66)
In the meantime, you have indeed caused me to hear the most purifying name of Hari, and you have sprinkled water joined with *tulasī* leaves, which is like a sacred bathing place. (67)
The sight of an excellent devotee such as you is purifying for me;
indeed, I am especially sanctified by the dust of your lotus feet. (68)
I truly consider all my karmas to have reached their end;
all my sin has gone to destruction, and now my merit increases.
Peace has arisen in my heart and satisfaction from this sprinkling of water;
all delusion and every internal fire of negligence have departed.
"O dull-witted one, I believe that the sin which caused my husband's suffering has been destroyed here at this sacred ford through your power; O twice-born one, grant me liberation. (7.1)
Whether I am a servant girl, an outcaste woman, or a dog-cooker;
whether I am wicked, a widow, or base—I am indeed a vessel for your compassion. ||72||
Through compassion, a living being here overcomes terrible sin;
the compassion of the virtuous is the supreme merit, the root of all wholesome deeds. (7.2)
Without the compassion of the virtuous, even another well-performed deed becomes a misdeed.
Compassion is merit; compassion is liberation; compassion is heaven, happiness, and wealth.
The compassion of the virtuous and service to one’s husband are obtained only through great merit.
She who has no service of a lover must always serve the virtuous. ||75||
Everything has been ruined by her, whose service is not performed by the virtuous;
he alone is the master to be served, the husband to be served, and the Supreme Lord himself. (76)
In the end, she must repeatedly pray to him and seek his forgiveness;
for the husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, and he is eternal merit itself.
The husband is always the giver of life, the giver of sons, and the giver of worlds;
Lord Hari, the husband, is the giver of heaven, the giver of happiness, and the giver of bliss.
She removes the suffering of her husband and herself endures it in his stead;
she bears the hardships born of the body and bestows half of her merit upon him. (79)
He bestows his own earned wealth, merit, strength, and seed; who else in this world can be understood as superior to him, the Supreme Lord? (1.424.80)
For the husband alone is the supreme deity for women;
therefore, the husband is to be served, the husband is to be honored, and the husband is to be attained by those who excel in austerity.
"Otherwise, it is the established rule that women would become *rākṣasīs*.
Having said this, the *kṛtyā* spoke again: "Tell me how my deliverance may come about. (82)
The destruction of the remaining water-stalls shall likewise occur;
therefore, O Brahmin, bring about liberation, and prosperity shall be yours.
"The deliverer of the helpless shall himself be delivered.
Thus addressed, the compassionate Dharmadatta, with a humble mind, [spoke]. (84)
Having reflected, he spoke to Kalahā that which bestows happiness:
"Listen, O beautiful one; through vows, sacred fords, and gifts, one becomes a dweller free from sin. (85)
The destruction of both *prārabdha* and accumulated (*sañcita*) karmas occurs through meritorious deeds;
furthermore, you are a female demon and a ghost, and thus have no entitlement to the first [category] of the wretched. (86)
A preta has no entitlement to sacred fords, gifts, vows, and the like;
nor is the karma that bestows the state of a demon or preta exhausted by others. (87)
However, I have observed this vow dedicated to the devotion of Hari;
from the time of Kārtika’s birth, I shall give half of it to you. (88)
"The merit of devotion to Hari destroys the sin of unchastity.
Having said this, the Vaiṣṇava Dharmadatta took up water.
He sprinkled that water mixed with *tulasī* over her,
uttering "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Oṃ."
Having thus acquired merit, she was indeed freed from her state as a preta;
she became a divine maiden, twelve years of age, adorned with every beauty.
Clad in fire-like garments, equal to the moon in splendor, and radiant with tranquility,
she bowed to the brahmin and, filled with great joy, spoke to him.
Through even a slight fragment of your compassion, I have been graced, refined, and delivered from affliction by you; I go now to the state of the Blessed One. (93)
When this had been said, a divine celestial chariot arrived,
resplendent with two attendants and accompanied by a multitude of female attendants.
Summoned by the two attendants, the maiden ascended quickly;
then Dharmadatta paid homage to those two attendants of Kṛṣṇa. (95)
When asked, "Who are you two? Śreṣṭha replied to him; Puṇyaśīla, being approved by Suśīla, recounted his previous births and other details.

Thus ends the four hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Loss of Purity through Unchastity of Kalahā, the Wife of a Mendicant, in Saurāṣṭra during the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā, and Her Liberation upon the Destruction of Her Sin by Means of the Brahmin Dharmadatta, the Chanting of Names, Tulasī, Water, and so forth."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious account of Puṇyaśīla, which he related concerning two [others]—
an account devoted to devotion to Viṣṇu and bestowing the status of being an attendant.
"O Brahmin, I am Puṇyaśīla, residing in a celestial chariot and devoted to the service of Viṣṇu; this second one is Suśīla. || 2 ||
O Brahmin, you have done what was fitting; she has been delivered by means of great merit.
The sin arising from hundreds of her previous births has gone to its destruction.
She shall be led to Vaikuṇṭha and will become a servant of Viṣṇu;
and you, O brāhmaṇa, having observed the Kārtika vow along with your two wives, [shall attain the same].
In time, through great merit, you shall go to the abode of Hari;
for the vow of Hari performed by a devotee is like the vow of a devoted wife.
This vow is indeed a bestower of merit and liberation; there is no doubt about this.
Having enjoyed its merit here on earth for many thousands of years, [one attains the ultimate goal].
"You shall become King Daśaratha, born of the solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa),
together with your two wives who have been married to you."
This third Kali, who shall share half of your merit, will then become your wife; and Viṣṇu shall come to your home.
Having performed the work of the gods, he will depart to his own abode;
this very Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shall become known by the name Rāma.
But those people on earth who shall seek refuge in Rāma,
they too shall attain liberation through the majesty of Vāsudeva.

Cultivation (bhāvanā), love (prema), devotion (bhakti), affection (sneha), and even tenderness (ārdratva)—these are distinguished from the ritualistic section (kriyā-kāṇḍa) regarding Hari; such is the established conclusion.
Knowledge is superior to action, and meditation is likewise supreme to knowledge;
cultivation is better than meditation, and affection is highest of all cultivation. (3.2)

Since desireless affection is indeed superior to affection accompanied by desire, humility is superior to affection; its very nature is that [humility], and its essence is the state of being that [humility]. 13.
O Brahmin, there is nothing whatsoever superior to that [devotion] toward Hari at all times;
listen to a beautiful story regarding this: devotion is distinguished as being superior even to charity. 1.4.
In ancient times, there was a king named Cola in the city of Kāñcī; he was a performer of vows, a devotee of Viṣṇu, a giver of gifts, a protector of his subjects, and one honored by all. || 15 ||
