O Lakṣmī, he indeed performed service to that yogi Trita;
for service to the virtuous is worthy and burns away the sins of one's birth. (38)
The sight of the virtuous is meritorious; saluting them destroys sin;
their graciousness bestows good fortune; and finding satisfaction in them grants a lineage like that of a son. (3.9)
Service at the feet bestows prosperity, while total surrender bestows liberation;
indeed, pleasing the virtuous bestows everything, for the virtuous are to be pleased.
The water from whose feet destroys such acts as the killing of a Brahmin,
and the auspicious dust from whose feet utterly annihilates the sins of the wicked.
The worship of those [gurus], including offerings of food and all else, always provides protection;
and their well-formed blessings protect one throughout both place and time. (42)
According to one's capacity, according to one's resources, and according to one's state of being—just so should the virtuous always be served; for they are divine, being the very forms of Hari. (43)
Devoid of qualities and free from bonds, they truly deliver their servants;
O Lakṣmī, by service to Trita, even the sin of killing a Brahmin went to its destruction.
Then the prince Dānaka, filled with wonder, repeatedly thought that the meeting with the virtuous man was the cause of her destruction. (45)
Just then, Dānaka beheld the most terrifying messengers of Yama arriving there to take him away.
By the merit of her service, she remembered the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—the Lord of the gopīs, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Master, and the Lord of the worlds. (47)
Nārāyaṇa himself quickly spoke to his own attendants:
"Go for the sake of protecting Dāni and ward off the followers of Yama. (48)
Thus commanded, those attendants arrived at the hermitage of Trita;
seeing those terrible messengers from afar amidst the trees, [he spoke]. (49)
Having humiliated and put to flight his devoted servants with insults,
they led Hari, the donor, along the path of the celestial chariots.
Hari said: "Service rendered to this sage bestows great merit;
he is my devotee, profoundly peaceful, self-controlled, and long-lived. (51)
Therefore, let them establish this one of great strength upon the burden of the kingdom;
he shall become a servant of the virtuous and a great devotee of Viṣṇu.
"He shall become a great devotee who has dedicated his own self for my sake.
Thus addressed, the donor then spoke to that Supreme Lord. (53)
Neither the sovereignty of the earth, nor birth, nor even heaven is desired;
rather, your constant service to Him who is accompanied by Rādhā and Lakṣmī is indeed what is desired.
Hari said, "So be it; go, my child, as you please.
O auspicious ones, Rādhā and Lakṣmī shall dwell with your two sisters and with me."
"I, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, shall dwell in your house;
I will bring you happiness and grant you liberation. Go now, together with your attendants. (56)
"I shall dwell in your fortress; may it be well with you, O servant," thus commanded by the Blessed One, he departed toward his own city. (57)
Devoted to the duties of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, he performed religious acts; intent on serving the virtuous, he was a worshiper of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||58||
Causing every festival and offering all his possessions as sacrificial fees to Kṛṣṇa, he flourished with all kinds of prosperity in a home resembling Goloka. (59)
Having caused [the image] to be made and having installed Kṛṣṇa there along with Gopikā,
he enjoyed all pleasures and became eternally liberated while living.
The Lord of the virtuous, the Sovereign Nārāyaṇa, the Master Janārdana,
took up his residence in that house exactly as described.
Thereafter, both Satī and Jīvantī, endowed with devotion to their husband, became possessed of beauty and divine sovereignty. ||62||
While Śrī Rādhikā was still living, an infusion of her artistic grace occurred in Lāvaṇyavatī; likewise, an infusion of Lakṣmī’s grace occurred in her.
While she was still alive, endowed with beauty and youth, she practiced unceasing devotion to her husband,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Gopīs.
The Blessed One, the possessor of Dharma, is present every day before the three [of us]:
at the meal, at rest, on the walkway, and during recreation and festivals. (65)
He always travels by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) among the various worlds together with those liberated gods, and being honored by them, he returns to that [same] house.
Hari himself enjoys that which was offered by the living Lāvaṇyavatī;
yet to Śrī Hari, who gave it to the living Lāvaṇyā, [she remains devoted]. (67)
And his own mantra, which destroys the house of worldly existence, was bestowed upon him:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (68)
Having thus received this mantra, they repeatedly recited it;
hearing that, all living beings went to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (69)
Once, having gone to the exceedingly terrible path of Yama,
Dādaka stood at the gate reciting a mantra and caused the denizens of hell to hear it.
All the denizens of hell became purified and went to the imperishable abode of Hari; the realm of Yama became empty through the hearing of Kṛṣṇa’s glories.
In an instant, as people remained steadfast in their own duties and proceeded toward the abode of Viṣṇu,
all the hells became empty, being utterly devoid of sinful living beings.
In Vaikuṇṭha, Nārada, having suddenly perceived the arrival of Vaiṣṇavas, asked them: "From where indeed do all these Vaiṣṇavas come? (73)
They said: "In that realm of Yama, one named Dādaka, having caused the mantra of Hari to be heard, made the denizens of hell drink it. (74)
"O Sage, those who were hell-beings have now become us.
Having heard this, Nārada quickly went to see the realm of Yama.
Honored by Yama, the sage arrived at the realm of Dharma;
he asked the King of Dharma, "How indeed has your sacred field become empty? (76)
Then the King of Dharma said: "This giver is the foremost among devotees;
he is exceedingly devoted to Hṛṣīkeśa, the Ancient Supreme Person. (77)
Indeed, the mantra of Kṛṣṇa’s name awakens those in hell;
they all go to the eternal world of Viṣṇu-Brahman. ||78||
Whether this devotee has been brought here by me or by you from the realm of Yama, he must certainly be sent far away with humility and due honor. //79//
Having reflected thus, the celestial sage Nārada and the wrathful Yama both said to him:
"O King of Devotees! Indeed, by the hearing of your kīrtana, [the sins of] the sinful have been destroyed."
Leaving behind even a ground that is fit for punishment, they go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
O sinless one, you must not act unjustly in this matter.
There shall be no loss of Dharma, nor shall there be any loss of ritual action;
therefore, O devotee, you must act accordingly and go toward your own city. 82.
Then Dānaka said: "Liberation must be granted; this is my vow.
Devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma, for it is indeed the very essence of Kṛṣṇa. (83)
For the sake of attaining that, I perform here the recollection of His name, which destroys the sins of sinful living beings; this indeed is my dharma. (84)
I shall not go; my own place is where I dwell, for it pleases me here as the means to liberate those in hell from their intense sufferings. (85)
"Having been told this, he will not return to his own home;
having reflected thus, Yama and Nārada departed by means of their celestial chariot. (86)
They attained the abode of Śrī Hari known as Brahman, which is the welcome of Hari;
they worshipped Him, bowed down, and sat before Hari. (87)
Then Yama said to that Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World:
"O Master, in this field full of sin, Dānaka is indeed your devotee. (88)
Having come together, he repeatedly performs the chanting of your names;
by him, the entire field of Yama has been made empty and utterly deserted.
My authority has become meaningless because of that excessive boasting;
thus, the insignia of your rod of punishment has become useless.
One who is appointed does not perform his duty merely because he is engaged in the task;
if he consumes the wealth of his master, he becomes a wood-worm. (91)
One who, out of greed, steals wealth and does not turn back from his task, attains birth in the animal realm for the duration of an entire kalpa. ||92||
But he who earns a salary yet performs his duty with laziness is born in the middle of a forest as a crow for a hundred years. (93)
One who seeks only his own interest and neglects the master's business is born as a mouse in the forest;
such am I, for I have become useless while I still remain in my own place. (94)
Therefore, O Janārdana, remove him from my field;
O Lord of the worlds, this pure Dānaka must be subdued by you. (95)
"Otherwise, that staff-cloth shall be presented by you at our feet;
what is the use of carrying this in vain, and indeed, what is the use of this useless wages? (96)
Having spoken thus, Hari ceased; then he said to Yama:
"What wonder could there be in this recitation of my names? (97)
For one upon whose tongue-tip the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside, there is the destroyer of all sins for the wicked, as well as the bestower of heaven and liberation. (98)
He upon whose ears the name "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa" has fallen attains union with Kṛṣṇa; Hari is the one who effects the liberation of even the sinful.
My devotees wander at will from place to place for the sake of uplifting sinful living beings; they deliver them through the path of total surrender.
I am always pleased with those who utter my name;
they deliver the sinful and proclaim my story.
Those men and women who maintain their devotion to their husbands, who hold Me in their hearts, and who live for My sake, are considered by Me to be truly Mine.
For they perform my work and have renounced their lives for my sake;
and I, with a gracious soul, am always present as their helper.
Whatever one performs, O Yama, that very act is excellent and brings about liberation, for an agent exerts himself to the best of his ability in the tasks of his master. 104.
To that extent he shall have accomplished his purpose and will certainly not go to hell;
when his capacity for the task has been fully exerted, he should indeed report it to his master.
By that much, the servant becomes free from debt and the official enjoys happiness;
therefore, for one who has reported the matter as it is, there is neither debt nor sin.
When one has exerted effort in what ought to be done by oneself, there is no fault on the part of the embodied being;
therefore, you should not grieve over this impossible task.
I shall renounce even Lakṣmī, or my life-breaths, or even my body;
or else the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha gem, and the Vaijayantī garland.
Neither Śvetadvīpa nor Vaikuṇṭha, nor even the Ocean of Milk, nor Śoṣa nor Garuḍa— O devotee, I am unable to abandon you.
Having renounced all enjoyments for my sake and having sacrificed their very lives,
how could I bear to abandon these illustrious ones who are my very self?
Therefore, O King, I am going myself by means of a vehicle to grant you the gift of a vision of Hari while he partakes of the excellent food, and to lead him back again.
"Go to the realm of Yama, and after you have gone, I shall come, O Yama;
tell him that I have sent this man to you, drenched with water by my command. (11.2)
If he abandons my chanting and performs laughter and dance instead,
I shall grant him a vision of myself at that moment and take him up into a celestial chariot.
"I shall go from the realm of Yama after having accomplished your task.
Having been addressed thus, Yama departed from there exceedingly joyful.
He announced the arrival of Kṛṣṇa to that donor;
he too, filled with love for the Lord, performed dances and other such acts.
At that moment, a divine celestial chariot indeed arrived for Nārāyaṇa Hari;
and Dānaka, having beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with four arms, [was filled with wonder].
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, he ascended the celestial chariot, crying out repeatedly:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord! (1.17)
Dancing and meditating upon Kṛṣṇa, he then became immersed in love;
the Blessed Lord Hari accepted the worship offered by Dharmarāja.
Accompanied by Rādhā and Ramā, the Lord went to the house of Dāni in Durgā;
having set down his supreme devotee, the Master himself remained there for the night.
Having accepted the service of that beautiful woman while she was still alive— a service characterized by her devotion to her husband— and having obtained food, he granted her his divine vision.
For the sake of Abhaya’s family and for the preservation of his wife's devotion,
he took a portion of Rādhā while she was still alive, as well as a portion of Śrī for her own beauty.
Having granted you permission to dwell there as a portion [of yourself], just as in the case of Chāyātmaka,
he made those two maidens yours and purified your homes.
Having bathed in the water of Unmattā and drunk that purifying water there,
she went to her own abode by means of a divine celestial vehicle.
Having learned of that event, the Gopīs, possessing divine forms, departed from the region of Mathurā as well as from Dvārakā to where Kṛṣṇa’s wife was. 124.
This sacred field, a city characterized by fortitude, became the dwelling place of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and the abode of the cowherd women and the wives of Kṛṣṇa. 1.25.
Due to the residence of Śrī Hari there, that place indeed became like Goloka;
it became divine, equal to the abode of Brahmā, supreme, and a bestower of liberation.
Through seeing, touching, drinking the water of the river, bathing in it,
and by wearing its dust upon the body, there occurs the destruction of sins and liberation.
By the power of Rādhā-Lakṣmī, by the virtue of her devotion to her husband,
and by the vow of Sāṃkhya-yoga, she [governs] the countless maidservants.
It bestows the fruit of ten million sacrifices upon one who takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
it grants the state of the supreme imperishable syllable to the listener, the speaker, and the pilgrim.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the devotion of a husband and wife: during King Dādaka (or Dānaka) of the Saurāṣṭra and Pañcāla regions’ pilgrimage to Talaśyāma, he was struck by a sage in the form of a lion. Consequently, the sin of *brahmahatyā* arose; however, through the service of the sage Trita, that sin was destroyed. Subsequently, the messengers of Yama arrived, but they were repelled by the Lord’s attendants (*pārṣadas*). By the worship of Hari, the inhabitants of Yama’s realm and the denizens of hell were liberated. Finally, in the city of Durga, King Dādaka received the blessings of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Nārāyaṇa.

The four hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Jīvantī and Lāvaṇyavatī as Portions of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, the Abode of Hari, and His Residence in the Sacred Field of Durga," etc. ||430||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the most excellent vow of a devoted wife;
her husband is Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, and that vow is the "pativratam" (the vow of devotion to the husband).
As long as she strives for the sake of her husband through actions that employ the intellect,
the wife is so ordained that her husband may be praised.
Whether devoid of qualities, possessed of qualities, or even possessed of bad qualities, a man is praised by a woman’s tongue and mind in every way, just like a lord. (3)
O Lakṣmī, that vow is considered the foremost and the highest form of devotion to one's husband;
it is praised in every way by all living beings as being like sugar.
That which is most sweet is experienced as the sweetest everywhere, just as parents rejoice through the praise of their son. (5)
Sons rejoice with great joy through the praise of their father;
likewise, a husband rejoices greatly within himself through the praise of his wife.
Through praise of the merchant, the servant rejoices; through praise of the king, the subjects rejoice;
and through praise of the bull, even the bull-driver rejoices. (7)
Through praise of his disciple, the teacher is honored; through praise of the teacher, the follower is honored;
through praise of the country, the native is honored; and through praise of the scripture, the believer is honored. (8)
The praise of that which exists for the sake of something else belongs to the future;
it is the abode of joy and delight, bringing forth enthusiasm and celebration.
O Lakṣmī, a devoted wife always remains truly pregnant with the fame of her husband upon hearing news of her beloved who is staying in a foreign land. 1.431.10.
At that very moment, she becomes filled with a joy exceeding even the festival for a son;
such is that vow of wifely devotion, accessible through the mind and bringing forth delight. (11)
Others indeed do not understand the affection residing in the heart of the Supreme Self;
for the qualities of the Supreme Self are by no means directly manifest in every way.
Because the cause— the conjunction of one's own self and mind— is not present there,

[these states] appear to others as if they were perceptible through the application of activities such as possession (*āveśa*), due to a continuous succession of influence; however, they are not real.
Devotion to one's husband is always affectionate, whether it be without cause or with cause.
Whether for her own sake or for the sake of another, it is her own interest that is experienced;
a woman’s persistence is simply this: "How might my husband become famous? (15)
Indeed, you must always remain mindful of your devotion to your husband;
for just as you feel such joy and eagerness when listening to stories of your husband. (16)
In the same way, for one who possesses intense longing for the understanding of Kṛṣṇa’s stories, or even for hearing, chanting, or praising them; (17)
For the devoted man and the devoted woman who are always virtuous and truthful toward Hari,
their eternal fidelity shines forth from that.
Service to the husband is the highest form of devotion, auspicious and bestowing grace;
however, listening to the sacred narrative is considered even superior to that devotion.

The narration of this story is the practice of devotion to one's husband; even more excellent than that is the constant singing of the glory of one’s own lord, which is indeed difficult to attain. (1.431.20)
Constantly singing the praises of her husband’s virtues with a sense of non-difference from Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the supreme devotion of a wife to her husband. (21)
Devotion to the husband consisting of the stories of Hari grants the world of the virtuous Lord;
there is no doubt for either the listener or the speaker. I, Janārdana, am well-pleased. 22.
I lead that virtuous woman to the great heaven and likewise to the world of the Satīs;
and those who are free from desire, I indeed send to my own abode, my supreme state.
For by means of my stories, devotion to me has been continuously instilled in the hearts of millions and tens of millions of living beings. (24)
By whomsoever among embodied beings the sprout of the word "my servant" has been uttered toward me—that is my vow, my service, my worship, and my honoring. (25)
My recitation, my devotion, my mindfulness, and my refuge;
my will, my realization, my meditation, and my exertion—[all these are mine]. (26)
My yoga, my desire, my offering, my grasping;
my concentration, my placement within me, my dwelling in me, and my prayer—[all these are for you]. 27.
Non-difference from me, affection for me, desire for me, and delight in me;
the giving of all one's possessions to me, and living or dying for my sake. (28)
Acquisition for my sake, performing services for my sake, giving gifts such as helping others, and observing vows and meritorious deeds—all are for my sake. (29)
Going to my abode at the end, and the constant acceptance of service to me—these were brought about by him through his discourses within the hearts of people. (1.431.30)
Such a speaker of my stories and bestower of knowledge of the scriptures upon me is he who increases my greatness and nourishes my devotion. (3.1)
O Lakṣmī, his devotion to me is considered ten million times greater than that of others;
for the devotion to the speaker is indeed eternal, being the most excellent among the excellent. (32)
I have not reached the end of the merit from reciting this narrative,
which [is performed] with devotion to Viṣṇu for the sake of countless species of living beings and their lineages.
The teacher who recites this narrative is indeed the savior;
he is the Fish-form [incarnation] without a doubt, and he is superior even to you, O Lotus-born One.
The mother is ten times more venerable than the father, and the teacher is ten times more venerable than the mother;
for the father is the provider of the seed, while the mother is the giver of birth. (35)
The Guru is said to be superior to all because he bestows liberation;
the husband is superior, the Guru is superior, but the Guru is even more superior than those two. (36)
The father, the husband, and the teacher are excellent; among them, the teacher is the most excellent.
The self is excellent, and Hari is the most excellent of those two; Hari is the most excellent of all. (37)
The self is Hari, and the guru is superior; among them, the guru is the most excellent.
For it is by taking refuge in him that one attains Hari, and without him, Hari is difficult to reach. (38)
The giver of land, the giver of livelihood, and the giver of life are always excellent;
yet, compared to them, the giver of liberation through knowledge is supreme. (39)
Knowledge of Kṛṣṇa and devotion to the husband are known as *pātivratya*; he who bestows that is remembered as a good husband.
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa and duty toward one's master are always considered the true dharma of a wife; he who bestows that is always a good husband. (1.431.40)
One husband is merely the bearer of a name, whereas the other is the husband who is true to his name and bestows devotion;
knowing this, O beloved, one should always maintain devotion to Hari as one's husband. (41)
The singing of Hari’s virtues, the contemplation of Hari’s form, the exposition of Hari’s stories, and devotion to one's husband—these are the highest forms of virtue. 42.
Wherever there is discourse [on Him], there are the devotees, the gods, the sacred fords, and Acyuta;
there are the goddesses, the sages, the ancestors, liberation, devotion, Dharma, and so forth. ||43||
The perfected ones, ascetics, the truthful, the virtuous, and likewise the yogis;
the ages, the scriptures, the Vedas, the sacred fields, and the forests. ||44||
The Vyāsas, the principles of reality, and those who are liberated— all of whom are characters in the narrative—
come and constantly listen to that story, overflowing with devotion.
Some were embodied and some formless; likewise, some were invisible and others visible.
All of them, devoted to their husbands, were indeed listening to the story of Hari.
Having heard again and again of their own respective fame, the glory of Hari, and the narratives concerning his devotees, they rejoice and offer their blessings. (47)
Likewise, those who listen—the assembly of disciples—indeed pay homage to the reciter, their teacher. ||48||
Therefore, the one who causes [this] to be heard is the most excellent among all, for he bestows devotion to the Guru;
he should be understood as equal to Nārāyaṇa, being the enlightener of wifely fidelity. 49.
Having bowed down to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and having heard the auspicious narrative of Hari,
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Long ago, on the banks of the Godāvarī, a wonderful story unfolded; indeed, there was a complete recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. ||51||
It destroys sin, purifies, bestows heaven, grants knowledge, and grants liberation.
There was a mendicant disciple of the sage Durvāsas named Satyavrata. (52)
Devoted to Brahman, free from expectations, subsisting on mere alms,
he dwelt there in a cave, observing the vow of non-possessiveness.
Wearing a garland of tulasī and chanting the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he would daily recount His stories every evening, O beloved. (54)
Having meditated upon, remembered, and caused others to remember his lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
and having offered salutations and caused others to offer them, he engages in the narration of Kṛṣṇa’s stories.
Even when there are no listeners and no teachers have arrived, Satyavrata constantly narrates the stories of Śrī Hari. (56)
Having performed his own daily obligatory duties, he indeed engages in the narration of Hari;
if there is anyone who wishes to hear, he explains it to them day and night.
If there is no listener on dry land, he tells the story even in the water;
or if someone else explains the meritorious story of Hari, then he does so as well. (58)
Abandoning his own duties, he listens to the stories of Śrī Hari; devoted to the exclusive loyalty toward Hari, he delights in hearing His stories. (59)
Abandoning the holy fords of the deities and even their temples,
he also abandoned other activities that were contrary to the sacred narratives.
He always listens to the divine narrative when there is a speaker;
when there is no speaker, he himself explains the excellent narrations of Kṛṣṇa.
Without discourse, she does not know the supreme dharma of devotion to her husband;
yet, both in the public square and in her own home, she herself explains it with heartfelt sincerity. 62.
Necessary duties are indeed no more than the [sacred] discourse;
the most excellent of necessary duties is that which consists of the discourse and is preeminent. (63)
When discourse has ceased, there is indeed the predominance of other duties; O Lakṣmī, for one who listens to a discourse with devotion, no bondage of karma exists.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, and I shall relate to you a divine marvel concerning one devoted to her husband, which destroys the heat of sin.

May your mind be intent upon his feet; may your speech be engaged in the glorification of his virtues;
may your eyes be fixed on the sight of him; and may your ears be devoted to the hearing of his stories.
May my tongue be for your grace; may my nose be for the fragrance of your form;
may my skin be for your touch; and may my two hands be for the sweeping of your temple.
May my feet be for traveling to your sacred field, and may my other limbs be employed for your sake;
may my head be for bowing to you, and may every desire be directed solely toward you.
May your mind always be fixed upon the Buddha, his teaching, and the Sangha;
may the sense of "I" reside within me, O beloved, and may my life be offered unto you.
May the days of the virtuous be spent in service with a spirit of love;
may there be association with the good, and may liberation be their service at Your feet. 1.24
"I desire no other glory anywhere except for the Lord of Glory (Śrīpati)"—
thus praised was Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Mañjuleśvara.
Hasan said to him: "I grant you a boon: ten thousand years of supreme longevity, provided that you practice devotion to me, serve as my servant, and observe the vow of fidelity. (126)
Accompanied by your own family, you shall attain union with me alone;
on the third day, which is imperishable, my worship shall be performed just as it was by you.
Those people who perform bathing, giving of gifts, and worship of me shall certainly go to my abode; indeed, so shall those subjects who perform these acts.
"I shall lead men and women to my imperishable abode.
Having granted this boon, Kṛṣṇa vanished right there.
The king took up residence among the virtuous, listened to sacred discourses,
and, together with his family, practiced devotion to Kṛṣṇa characterized by supreme fidelity to his wife.
Having enjoyed sovereignty for ten thousand years, he went at the end to the abode of Hari;
and by hearing or reciting this, others shall go to the abode of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Hemanta of the Pañcāla Country in Saurāṣṭra Losing His Kingdom Due to Past Karma, His Regaining of the Kingdom through the Dharma of Devotion and Chastity to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as instructed by his Guru, and His Vision of Śrī Hari and Liberation," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 432.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to how Urvaśī was born from the Lord Nara-Nārāyaṇa through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Formerly she was a bitch, and even earlier than that, a Brāhmaṇī woman from the land of Kaśmīra— wicked, treacherous, and one who bore hatred toward her husband.
The daughter of Devavrata, named Mālinī, was of beautiful form;
she was the wife of a Brahmin named Satyaśīla, yet she was not at all devoted to her husband.
Accompanied by her, the husband went somewhere to the land of Yavana;
she, however, filled with anger toward her husband and greedy for the power of subjugation, [remained behind].
He asked many Yavana women for a medicine to bring her under his control; they pointed out to him a certain rogue woman who prepared medicinal herbs.
"She will give you a medicine by which your husband shall become like a slave. And the Brahmin woman, being cunning, went to the house of the harlot with eager longing.
She saw her hut, equipped with a skull-bowl and other items,
along with many medicinal herbs, excellent vessels, a hearth, and so forth.
It was adorned with the seats for the practice of mantra-sciences,
resplendent with yantras, mantras, sacred ash, knots, and blue garments.
It was filled with the essence of yoga practice through its bones and altars,
and it was brilliantly illuminated by long-haired female disciples who shone with auspiciousness.

Seeing the hut equipped with an incense burner and containing a staff-bearing mendicant woman, who was being propitiated by many distressed women for the sake of obtaining their desired ends; 1.433.10.
The Brahmin woman bowed with supreme devotion to the illusory yogini, who was smeared with ashes on her body and adorned with sectarian marks like a true yogi.
Then that deceitful harlot reported her suffering;
she performed a cleaning for her with a peacock-feather broom.
He performed the consecration upon that body with ashes blown forth [from his mouth];
he made a crescent moon on the forehead with ashes and offered water into the hand.
Having placed a black armlet and a rosary of rudrākṣa beads upon his shoulder,
he caused the brahmin woman to hear the subjugation mantra three times.
"Obeisance to the goddess Kāmākṣikā; bring [his] husband under control, svāhā!"—thus she gave her this mantra and gave her a substance for the ring.
She gave him a red golden bracelet inlaid with rubies for the purpose of subjugation,
as well as a red woolen cord to bind upon his arm.
He gave him a medicinal powder, auspicious and endowed with protective power, and said:
"Indeed, this powder is a great bringer of subjugation. (17)
Through the practice of this [mantra], even those who are powerful like the wind constantly become subject to their master, just like monkeys. 18.
You should always consume a very small amount of this powder at the beginning of meals and other times;
furthermore, you must certainly wear the protective cord around your neck. (19)
O beautiful woman, bind this red cord upon your own arm;
your husband will become submissive, so recite the mantra while lying on your bed.
"Give me consecrated food, and likewise consecrated water;
give me a consecrated bed—give everything well-consecrated. (21)
"In a very short time, your master will come under your control.
If there should be any task to be done, come to me quickly. (22)
Having been addressed thus, the Brahmin woman gave the sacrificial fee and went to her own home;
she prepared the medicinal herb in milk and offered it to her husband in his meal.
She gave the consecrated water, garment, and bedding to her husband;
in this manner, day after day, she gave the powder, and as she did so, [the effect increased].
Her husband was extremely afflicted by asthma, cough, phlegm, and consumption; moreover, there was excessive heat in his urine and other secretions. (25)
Within his body, red eruptions broke out like blossoming flowers, causing extreme itching;
within a few days, the master became as if dependent on others. (26)
Incapable, afflicted by the pain of disease, and filled with fear of death, her husband, his vitality destroyed, then spoke to the Brahmin woman in great agitation: (27)
"I am yours here like a slave; protect me, O beautiful one!
O beloved, I desire no other woman whatsoever besides you. (28)
I shall abide by your command; from now on, I am forever your servant.
When your work is to be performed, I shall not offer any opposition. (29)
Then that lustful woman, intent on her own interests, thought: "While the husband is alive, ornaments and such must certainly be worn, and enjoyments must be experienced. (1.433.3)
Thus, having spoken, she then went quickly to the practitioner of sorcery as if terrified, thinking:
"My husband has fallen under her control; he will certainly die."
"My own self-interest would be destroyed; therefore, O auspicious one, let him live.
Having understood this, the rogue reported everything to the other [king]. (32)
She gave him a medicine that destroys suffering, burning sensations, and other ailments;
as soon as that medicine was administered, her husband became healthy at that very moment.
She became exceedingly devoted, and her husband remained under her influence;
moreover, she did not speak even the slightest word to him regarding his association with other women.
The husband-in-law stays at home under the pretext of household duties; the husband himself does not say anything at all, in any way whatsoever. (35)
Then that wicked Brahmin woman, who had harbored hatred for her husband, gradually became afflicted with disease in her body, and worms were born within her. (36)
Because of that, she met her death and underwent the torments of hell;
for many years, she was cast into a seething cauldron of molten copper.
Then, for a hundred times, she was born as a bitch, afflicted by ringworm, with limbs oozing and lame, and beaten from house to house. (38)
In her final birth, however, she was born in the house of a brahmin named Padmabandhu in the land of Sauvīra as a diseased bitch belonging to a maidservant. (39)
When she, her limbs covered with worms, stood upon the stone used for washing feet in the courtyard of the Brahmin’s house, [she was seen]. (1.433.40)
Then, by chance, the son of a brahmin, remembering Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, chanting the Gāyatrī mantra, and having performed the worship of Kṛṣṇa within his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), [acted]. 41.
Having taken the water produced from [the Lord's] grace, with which Viṣṇu had been bathed and which was joined with *tulasī*, he arrived home while still on the steps. (42)
The courtyard of the house was indeed elevated by only five steps;
he ascended it until his foot reached the very last step.
By the turn of fate, as she stood upon a low-lying rocky ledge at her side, the water-filled water-pot slipped from her hand and fell. (44)
All the water that had fallen from the water-pot into an empty place was then, by the power of fortune, bathed in and drunk by a female dog. (45)
Then, by her good fortune, she ate a sweet offering that had fallen;
by that merit, O Lakṣmī, her sins were utterly destroyed.
Remembering her past lives, she spoke to the twice-born man at that moment:
"O divine Brāhmaṇa, save me, a great sinner; save me, O twice-born one! (47)
"O Brahmins, in the past I was always one who hated my husband;
I gave poison to my husband and likewise employed mantras for subjugation. (48)
A giver of suffering, extremely wicked, and one who causes intimacy with others—because of that sin, she was cast by the agents of Yama into the cauldrons of molten copper. (49)
O twice-born one, I have been born as a dog afflicted with ringworm a hundred times;
this is my final body, consecrated by you with water.
By divine providence, I have become one who remembers my past births; I recall what was produced over a hundred lifetimes.
The extreme suffering I endured cannot indeed be fully described.
A woman who harbors hatred toward her husband is cooked in molten copper;
being of wicked conduct, she is then forced to embrace glowing iron images by those filled with lust.
The husband is the protector, the husband is the teacher, and the husband is the supreme deity;
how could she be happy after committing an offense against him? (53)
She goes to a hundred animal births, filled with worms and terrifying;
therefore, a noble woman should always perform service to her husband in accordance with his word. (54)
Devotion to one’s husband is the supreme dharma; indeed, serving the husband is merit.
For the sake of a woman’s liberation, Hari himself resides within the husband.
Lame, one-eyed, maimed, squint-eyed, and eight-faced;
beautiful with collyrium on his body, deaf, dwarf, and emaciated. (56)
One who is diseased, a leper, or mentally deranged; one who is cruel, or possessed by excessive lust; one who is addicted to sensual objects, or habitually intemperate, or a talkative liar; ||57||
Such a portion of Kṛṣṇa was himself fashioned by Brahmā for the sake of a wife;
by him alone, and no other, shall the wife be redeemed, he who possesses the splendor of the sun.
Whether he be such or such—blue, black, or having the appearance of collyrium—one’s husband, the lord, should be served once one has encountered him through the power of desire. 59.
If her husband is fully satisfied by desire through the giving of pleasure, then Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself is satisfied by her; such is the bull-like virtue [of the wife]. (1.433.60)
Thus, a husband should always be served by a woman:
with devotion when he is ill, with tranquility in his happiness, and likewise with fortitude in times of misfortune.
When hungry, she gives food; when thirsty, she gives satisfaction; on the bed, she is beloved;
in affairs, she is a helper; while traveling, she goes along; and in the home, she is virtuous.
In worldly affairs she acts as a friend, and in her protection she is like a mother;
that woman enjoys ten thousand heavens—of this there is no doubt. (63)
Even if one does not possess a handsome husband in this life,
a virtuous woman (satī) is capable of making him equal to a god through her devotion to her husband.
Kālī was the daughter of Himagiri, yet she became Gaurī through her ascetic penance;
formerly, by association with Kṛṣṇa, Kubjā became equal to Rādhā.
Through union with Rāma, Śabarī likewise became four-armed;
formerly, through union with her Lord, the Yavanī was liberated and became divine. (66)
Through union with Rāma, Jaṭāyū became auspicious and four-armed;
through union with Viṣṇu, the elephant and the crocodile were liberated and became divine.
Arundhatī was a dog-cooker (outcaste woman), yet she became the wife of a sage by resorting to cows; Saramā was a divine bitch, yet she was liberated through service to Surabhi.
The Vṛndāvana and Tulasī trees, through their union with Kṛṣṇa, become identical with Him; though insentient, they become as if sentient through their connection with Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 6.9.
The divine Sūta Paurāṇika became worthy of worship by Brahmā;
indeed, the flower rejected by Indra brought about the destruction of Lakṣmī’s fortune.
Furthermore, that which was offered by him in the Ocean of Milk bestows prosperity;
likewise, if any object—whether a man or a woman—is beautiful, [it should be offered]. (71)
Through austerity, that place becomes delightful; of this there is no doubt.
Through austerity, both bad qualities and good qualities are always produced.
Whether it be a hunchbacked woman or a hunchbacked man, they should be protected with the thought that they are the Blessed One;
they should be served through one's own austerity, devotion to the Master, and the realization that they are a virtuous wife.
Having acted thus, regarding Hari as their husband and Sati as their wife, the couple served him, having attained endurance and forgiveness through the attainment of happiness. (74)
I served the Brahmin, never disregarding him, yet he brought me under his control;
because I was distressed and oppressed by him, I have become miserable in the ocean of existence. (75)
O Brahmin, deliver me now by offering the fruits of your worship of Kṛṣṇa;
otherwise, my rebirth in wicked wombs will surely be seen again. (76)
Thus addressed, the brahmin then felt compassion and [expounded] the fruit of the Ekādaśī as well as the worship and other rites of the Dvādaśī.

He gave her all his merit, which was considered to yield inexhaustible fruit—whatever had been performed as austerity, given as charity, offered in sacrifice, or as the worship of the gods and so forth. (78)
The brahmin bestowed upon her everything in the form of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, and said to her:
"O highly wicked woman, you are not worthy of compassion."

She who harbors hatred toward her husband, who hates virtuous men, and who reviles the gods—she is certainly not said to be a fit object of compassion; nevertheless, she is [to be protected] because she has taken refuge in me.
"Having recognized me as a wretched servant, you have shown compassion toward me;
for those who are to be supported by a high-souled householder indeed exist. (81)
Thinking, "Their deliverance must be accomplished," the Caṇḍālas, crows, and even the dogs were raised up as his servants.
Male and female slaves, as well as servants, mongooses, parrots, and mainas;
rabbits, deer, swans, and whatever other creatures feed upon offerings. ||83||
For householders, infants and young girls who are without protectors are objects of compassion; likewise, women without husbands and those who are always ill and without refuge. (84)
All those who are to be supported must be diligently uplifted;
if a householder does not support those dependent on him, he will undoubtedly fall into a lower state. (85)
Devotion to the husband is supreme; the husband is the Supreme Lord.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the Master, and his command is the nourishment and protection [of the wife]. ||86||
He who abandons the protection of those dependent on him and proceeds according to the designs of others becomes a traitor to his husband; in this world, he goes to the house of the god of death.
Benefiting others is dharma; it is the bull [of virtue], the liberation of servants, and the great gift that grants liberation, being solely intent upon the attainment of Kṛṣṇa. ||88||
The Lord Hari is always pleased with her there; for her, supreme liberation is attained through the perfect practice of devotion to her husband. (89)
In this world, helping others is liberation; that must certainly be bestowed by the man of knowledge.
Likewise, it should be bestowed upon another by one possessed of devotion, in accordance with the command of her husband.
The moon, the sun, the wind, day, night, water, the earth, sandalwood, trees, and virtuous people—all remain dedicated to the service of others. (91)
It was Dadhīci who gave his bones to the gods, and it was Śibi who offered the flesh born from his own body to the pigeon. (92)
Formerly, the compassionate King Jīmūtavāhana also offered his own long-lasting life to Garuḍa. (93)
Dharmāṅgada offered his head to Mohinī for the sake of a vow;
likewise, Brahmā has repeatedly offered his bodies for the sake of creation. ||94||
For the sake of liberating the worlds, the Gaṅgā and other rivers came into being;
Viṣṇu became the Śālagrāma stone, and Śaṅkara took the form of the Liṅga.
Lakṣmī, in the form of Tulasī, exists for the sake of liberating the world;
likewise, Kṛṣṇa assumed the state of a cowherd as well as forms such as the Fish and others.
Everything has been performed by those of old and even more ancient times for the sake of benefiting others;
like the rain-cloud, the moon, and the sun, they are equal toward all living beings. 97.
Thus, by you, the compassionate one, who were endowed with equanimity, merit was bestowed upon me, a servant, while I was empty [of virtue];
thereby, all my impurities have been washed away. (98)
O Guru, may there now arise on this earth those like you who grant liberation;
for the virtuous are indeed devoted to helping others and are as faithful to their vows as a wife to her husband.
"Give me permission to go to the abode of Hari; I am going to that dwelling of bliss.
Thus addressed, the brāhmaṇa repeatedly gave her the mantra of Hari.
Oṃ, salutations! O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, deliver Kukkurī!
Go to Goloka, the realm of Kṛṣṇa; O dog, may you become meritorious. 101.
Having heard this, she became Pūrṇā, divine and beautiful of form;
abandoning her canine body, she became as radiant as the auspicious sun.
Just then, a divine celestial chariot belonging to the world of the sun arrived there;
she ascended it, illuminating the expanse of the sky from above.
She became a divine goddess with a moon-like face, adorned with ornaments;
having dwelt for a kalpa in heaven, she enjoyed pleasures upon the earth.
From the god Nara-Nārāyaṇa, a beautiful woman named Urvaśī was born; she was a Vaiṣṇavī, beloved by the gods.

Though endowed with the nature of an Apsaras, she was always devoted to her husband Kṛṣṇa; being supremely dedicated to her marital fidelity, she became the bestower of liberation upon those who take refuge in her.
Having gathered mango blossoms while a man was trampling them under his thigh,
she manifested as a great divine being who bewildered the army of Mahendra.
When Indra, who had come to create obstacles for the ascetic penances of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
departed from the region of Nārāyaṇa, she remained there in the abode of Indra.
That illustrious Vaiṣṇavī is active there;
she constantly serves Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her husband.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this entire auspicious teaching, which destroys sin and suffering,
is devoted to the virtue of wifely fidelity, grants liberation, and is the means of salvation.

Thus, in the first section, the account of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, [it is told] how a Brahmin woman of Kashmir who hated her husband became a bitch for a hundred births; how she was then liberated from that state as a bitch by a Brahmin of the Sauvīra country devoted to devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and attained divinity; and how she subsequently became Urvaśī from the thigh of Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
The three hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "Nirūpaṇa."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, listen as I tell you once more of a certain wonder:
there was a Vasu named Vidhūma, and his wife was the excellent lady Alambuṣā.
In ancient times, they both attained human status on earth due to a Brahmin’s curse;
through their devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, they were liberated from that Brahmin’s curse.
Formerly, having gone to Satyaloka, Brahmā convened a great assembly of exalted beings in the hall known as Sudharmā on the festival day of Viṣṇu.
There, upon a beautiful central seat, the four-armed Lord sat down,
resplendent with Sāvitrī and Sarasvatī by his two sides.
He was adorned by Gāyatrī, the four Vedas, and Mohinī,
as well as by Sanat, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanaka, and Nārada.
Accompanied by Dakṣa and others, the Vālakhilyas, Dharma and the other Pitṛs, as well as the clouds, sages, and goddesses, the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) was present.
By Indra and the other world-protectors, by the guardians of the directions, by the planets and stars, by the Siddhis, the Vasus, the Nidhis, and likewise by the Ṛṣis; || 7 ||
He was likewise served by the quarters, the Rudra deities, the Ādityas, the spheres of Kāma, as well as by the Manus, the lunar days (tithis), and the Kalās.
It is well-served by the principles (tattvas), the best of constellations, the hosts of gods and demons,
the qualities (guṇas), the winds (maruts), the castes (varṇas), enjoyments, and sacred fords (tīrthas).
Indeed, the Unborn One is praised by the inhabitants of the realm of desire,
by those of the nether regions, by those of the subterranean mines, and by embodied beings belonging to the aerial, terrestrial, and subterranean worlds.
The Grandfather was indeed honored by those moving in the sky and those born in the water,
as well as by the Kinnaras, the Kimpuruṣas, the Sādhyas, and the Gandharvas who serve as ornaments.
He was honored by the Urvashis, who were experts in the great art of dance;
[he witnessed] the captivating dance of the Apsarases accompanied by musical instruments.
Beholding [the assembly], Brahmā himself shone forth in that gathering;
and gradually the celestial women danced, delighting the assembly.
The sound of lutes, flutes, and drums became sweet,
and various melodious notes issued forth from the celestial women.
Alambuṣā and Madayantī danced most beautifully;
they repeatedly tossed their principal limbs, which were captivating to the mind. (15)
There she smiled very gently, looking at him again and again;
with eyes filled with love, she also cast glances at him.
She gently shook only her breasts, only her hips,
only her cheeks, and only her thighs.
Thus, having repeatedly beheld her dancing,
the Vasu named Vidhūma became filled with desire for her and was utterly infatuated.
Displaying his desire for her, he laughed again and again,
repeatedly expressing his longing with his unblinking eyes.
While the members of the assembly were looking on, Vasu indeed revealed himself;
and Brahmā, perceiving the fickleness of Vidhūma there, [acted accordingly].
He said: "O Vasu, such fickleness is not fitting for you on the stage of dance;
you have acted in a manner that is by no means appropriate for an assembly. (21)
"Since there has arisen a disruption of the dance, a disturbance of the stage, and a distraction, go on account of that fault and become a human being upon the earth. (22)
"Human beings on earth are fickle and devoid of the binding rope; let your dwelling be among them in the mortal world, and depart from here. (23)
"Alambuṣā shall indeed become your wife; go, do not delay.
Thus commanded, Vidhūma fell at the feet of Brahmā.
He prayed repeatedly for the sake of destroying the curse and for his own protection;
then Brahmā said, "Everything will happen exactly as you have said, there is no doubt."
In the city of Kauśāmbī, you were indeed born as a young prince to Viṣṇumatī, the devoted wife of King Śatānīka.
Having thus become a king, he then begot a noble son upon Alambuṣā; and having consecrated that son in the kingdom by the Southern Ocean, [he departed].
As soon as you bathe at Cakratīrtha accompanied by your wife,
you, possessing a divine form along with your wife, shall attain your own world.
Thus addressed, Vasureva truly fell upon the earth;
born in the house of Śatānīka, he became a prince of great discernment.
Śāṇḍilya gave him the name Sahasrānīka;
for Alambuṣā was the daughter of King Kṛtavarman of Ayodhyā.
In the house, a daughter named Mṛgāvatī was born, endowed with the qualities of a goddess;
from birth she was a Vaiṣṇavī, devoted solely to the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Though she was young, she was wise and devoted to her husband;
she repeatedly performed the chanting of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||32||
Then Śatānīka was invited by Indra to fight with the Daityas;
having gone to heaven after dying in battle, his corpse was handed over to his son.
Sahasrānīka himself performed the funeral rites for him;
having recovered the corpse, Viṣṇumatī lamented and spoke. (34)
O Lord! O Lord of my life! Come, O you who are dearer than my very breath!
O God presiding over my life-breaths, my life-departures will flee without you. (35)
A woman's pride increases day by day through her husband's good fortune; therefore, if he is wealthy and happy, one should honor him in accordance with dharma.
The husband is the kinsman of noble women, their presiding deity, and their constant refuge;
he is the supreme embodiment of prosperity and the personification of happiness.

He is the giver of Dharma, the giver of happiness, the eternal giver of joy, and the giver of peace; he is the bestower of honor, the giver of respect, the one worthy of honor, and indeed the crusher of pride.
The master is the essence of essences, the increaser of his kinsmen;
indeed, among all kinsmen, no relative is seen who is equal to a husband. (39)
He is called "Bhartṛ" (supporter) simply because he supports, and "Patī" (lord) because of his protection;
he is the "Svāmī" (master) because he is the lord of the body, and he is truly the "Kānta" (beloved) because he grants all desires.
He is indeed a kinsman because he binds one with happiness; he is most dear because he bestows affection;
he is a lord because he grants sovereignty; and he is the leader of life because he is the master of the vital breaths. ||41||
He is called "Ramaṇa" because he gives pleasure; there is nothing dearer than what is dear.
Furthermore, a son is born from the master's seed (śukra); therefore, he is dear. ||42||
A husband is always dearer than a hundred sons to women of noble birth;
however, those born of an ignoble family are indeed incapable of understanding their beloved.
It is indeed equivalent to bathing in all sacred fords, giving the sacrificial fee at all sacrifices,
circumambulating the entire earth, and performing all forms of austerity.
All vows and the like, whatever great gifts there are, meritorious fasts, and all other such things in every respect; ||45||
Whatever service is rendered to gurus, Brahmins, and deities, and so forth, does not equal even a sixteenth part of the service rendered to the feet of one's own master. 46.
Among gurus, Brahmins, and beloved deities, the husband is the most venerable for all;
yet for women of noble birth, the giver of knowledge is as dear as he.
"All my fortune has vanished; my parasol-like head is gone," she said to her husband, and then, with deep devotion, she meditated upon his body there. (48)
Viṣṇumatī, a virtuous wife devoted to her husband, having produced fire from her big toe due to her chastity and having bowed to the great people, [spoke]. (49)
Burnt by that very fire, she died along with him;
her son Sahasrānīka then performed the funeral rites for them.
Vasu Sahasrānīka ruled his kingdom according to the law.
Once, at a great festival in the Nandana grove in heaven, Indra was present.
Invited, Prince Sahasrānīka went to heaven;
there, in the abode of Indra, he likewise heard of his own status as a Vasu.
Then Vasu heard that Alambuṣā was his own wife;
having come to the earth, he [sought] Alambuṣā, the daughter of the king of Ayodhyā.
Having married Mṛgāvatī, he rejoiced with her;
she conceived a child from him and shone as if washed with nectar.
During the festival of the flower-swing, the queen and the king [were seated] in water within a pond that was reddened with saffron, filled with filaments and the like, and richly colored.
Having bathed, both of them, exhausted, stood on either side;
they were red-hued, golden-hued, beautiful, and exceedingly pleasing. (56)
Then the king, overcome by fatigue, fell into a momentary sleep;
the queen, however, went again to the bathing pool by the side of the arena to bathe. (57)
Desiring satisfaction and happiness from bathing in the water, the virtuous lady, who was red in complexion, respectfully performed her bath in the colored waters. (58)
Then, perceiving that very large fish moving within the water and moistened by the colored water, he [perceived it] from the sky with the thought that it was meat.
A certain bird born of the lineage of Suparṇa, formidable with a great roar, fell with speed and flew away, seizing the sky with its beak.
Realizing that she was merely some human woman, he left her in a cave on the mountain of sunrise and departed elsewhere through the sky.
Terrified, she wept and shed tears again and again, crying out:
"Alas, my lord! I am ill-fated; I have performed my bath without my husband. (62)
Afflicted by that sin and by the swift separation from you, what is my fate? Where indeed shall I go? When shall I behold your face again? (63)
Having spoken thus, she stood before the elephants and lions, desiring death;
though abandoned by all those cruel beasts, she did not meet her end there.
In times of calamity, death does not indeed seek friendship from men;
thus did the noble son of Jamadagni [behave] toward the weeping woman among the forest trees.
The compassionate man, having taken her, presented her to the sage;
consoled by the sage, the queen was nourished and protected in the hermitage.
In due time, she gave birth to a boy named Udayana;
he grew up and became a disciple of Jamadagni, well-versed in the Vedas.
Once, a certain forest-dwelling hunter arrived at the hermitage of Jamadagni and [found] a serpent inside a basket.
Holding the serpent, she entertained him solely for the sake of alms;
having given him alms, she gave him her bracelet and released the serpent. (69)
Then the hunter went to King Sahasrānīka himself to sell that bracelet of the queen; it was the king's own name-bracelet.
Having seen him, the hunter asked about his story, and he related everything.
Then, having given wealth to the hunter, the king went to that hermitage.
Seeing the sage engaged in ascetic penance, he bowed his head in salutation;
the sage received the king with a blessing.
He worshipped him according to the prescribed rites with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and water for sipping;
then he addressed the protector of the earth with words consistent with dharma and artha.
"O Lord of Men, this son born to you from Mṛgāvatī shall be the conqueror of the quarters; indeed, he has been named Udayana. (74)
This wife Mṛgāvatī is devoted to her husband;
she is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, a follower of the Bhāgavata path, and a virtuous woman. 75.
"Behold her who has endured sufferings for your sake, as pure as Renuka;
O Great King, accept her along with her son without delay. (76)
Having heard this, the king bowed to the sage, accepted her, and bestowed wealth upon her;
accompanied by his beloved wife, the monarch returned toward his own city.
Remembering the words of Śakra and disparaging his human birth,
he gave the earth to his wise son Udayana.
Then, together with Mṛgāvatī, the king went to Cakratīrtha;
standing on the shore of the ocean, he performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites.
Having become a sage, King Vidhūma Sahasrānīka made his dwelling among the forest trees and sustained himself solely on wild produce.
And Mṛgāvatī, devoted solely to the service of her husband in the forest, ate only once a day, subsisting on fruits, and never partook of anything else. (81)
She drinks only the water used for washing her husband's feet and never any other drink;
she makes her dwelling by her husband's side and never dwells elsewhere. (82)
She who bathes with the water used for washing her husband's feet never bathes with any other;
she who meditates upon her husband as Lord Hari never meditates upon any other—she alone is a true *satī*. (83)

That virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, delights in massaging his limbs; she finds no pleasure in the touch of another, not even through delusion, other than the joy derived from her husband, who is as dark as Kṛṣṇa. (84)
Constantly devoted to worship and dedicated to the service of her husband, she herself attained a state of detachment for the sake of her husband, being ever fond of auspiciousness. (85)

Considering the speech composed by the Vedas to be the command of her husband, the supreme Lord, that virtuous woman conducts herself according to his word; she is indeed an Apsaras, for she does not act like a mere celestial nymph.
Fickleness regarding the subject of liberation became something else—that is, it turned into a state of attachment;
yet even that desire for desirelessness, when directed toward liberation, resulted in liberation itself.
The state of having a body was transformed into bodilessness for the queen;
her physical eye became a divine eye, and she assumed the form of Brahman.
And the objects of the senses, being free from excess and moderate in measure, became natural to Mṛgāvatī and brought her happiness through her husband. (89)
She constantly honors Kṛṣṇa as she would her own husband; having perceived everything as consisting of Kṛṣṇa, she offers all virtuous deeds to her husband.
Indeed, that [devotion] consists of the section on ritual action, the section on recitation, and the section on meditation directed toward Hari;
it consists of the section on the body and the section on the functions of the senses directed toward Janārdana.
She offered oblations eternally only to her Lord, Hari Nārāyaṇa;
thus meditating upon Hari Nārāyaṇa as her husband, she served him.
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, the sacred ford of Hari, and at Patitīrthaka,
she herself likewise made her husband divine by the mere act of bathing him.
Having become divine, possessing a form as enchanting as a hundred moons,
she indeed went to heaven with her husband by means of a celestial vehicle.
Having remained there for ten thousand years, they constantly worshipped Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, their Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (95)
Those men and women who have gathered at Cakratīrtha for the purpose of a pilgrimage, as well as those whose actions consist of devotion to the Lord; ||96||
From all of them indeed, this most fortunate Satī heard: "Obeisance to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (97)
With a resonant voice and the rhythmic clapping of her palms, she,
filled with intense joy, repeatedly caused the hymn of praise to be heard.
Having thus made countless embodied beings devotees of the Lord,
she went together with her husband to the true city of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this divine account which bestows great merit;
by reading or hearing it, the fruit of the world of Brahmā shall be attained.

Thus ends the four hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Vidhumavasu and Alambuṣā, the Apsaras, by the word of Brahmā, attained the status of King Sahasrānīka on earth and Queen Mṛgāvatī respectively, and how, after becoming disciples of Jamadagni, they regained their places in heaven through the dharma of conjugal fidelity. from the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen with your mind as I relate this most wonderful tale, O beloved daughter of the Lotus; even the ignorant rejoice upon hearing it.
Long ago, in a mountainous region of the desert land, the sage Gālava was indeed constantly remembering the Supreme Brahman, Hari Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He performed austerities on a mountain in his own hermitage, which was endowed with trees and water;
he had a daughter who was exceedingly beautiful, a virtuous woman named Kāntimatī.
Devoted to her husband Kṛṣṇa, faithful, virtuous, pure, and a supreme Vaiṣṇavī,
she constantly wears a dark garland of Tulasī around her neck.
Holding a rosary in her hand, that virtuous woman, endowed with beauty and youth, constantly performed the recitation, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa."
Abandoning no other husband, she indeed desires none but Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
knowing her husband to be the supreme and true Kṛṣṇa, she is a devoted wife to Kṛṣṇa.
Whether on her bed, while eating, traveling, wandering, at her hermitage, by a tree, while drinking, or even in the performance of bodily functions, she did not forget that husband.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed became manifest to her in secret on one occasion;
then, at another time, the Blessed Lord himself performed a test.
Just as that young woman constantly performed the sweeping of the altar and other such tasks,
she likewise brought flowers and sacrificial fuel for the sage’s offerings.
In that same manner, on that day,
the virtuous woman set out to gather flowers for the purpose of making an offering as a bali-oblation to Kṛṣṇa.
Near the hermitage, that young girl went to a cluster of flowering trees,
gathered beautiful flowers, and placed them in a basket.
Having done so, he turned back; meanwhile, as he was departing by means of a celestial vehicle, a young Vidyadhara saw her, who was in the full bloom of youth.
Having seen her, the one named Sudarśana, overcome by the delusion of desire and longing to sport with her, descended from the top of his celestial chariot.
Showing his affection with tender words, he said to the maiden:
"O maiden, if you do not belong to another, I desire you."
If you consider it appropriate here according to the Gāndharva rite,
I am the son of a Vidyādhara named Sukaṇṭha.
And you, named Sudarśanā, speak what is in your own mind; O blessed lady, accept me who have approached you as one devoted to you.
Then Kāntimatī said: "I am indeed the maiden of Gālava; I am unmarried, devoted to Viṣṇu, pure, and intent upon the service of my father. (17)
"Devoted solely to the service of my beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, I do not desire any other husband; my father will be angry [if I do]. (18)
"O Vidyādhara, go quickly with the flowers; do not delay.
A maiden is always dependent upon her father and is never independent."
"I, an ascetic devoted to Viṣṇu, do not desire even a husband. Having been addressed thus, that Vidyādhara went to her side according to his desire.
But as he seized her by the hair, the young girl cried out loudly and suddenly to the Vidyadhara: "O Janaka, save me! (21)
At that very moment, Gālava and the others standing nearby,
having heard this, arrived quickly and beheld Sudarśana.
As he was fleeing swiftly through the sky after abandoning his daughter out of fear, Gālava cursed him thus: "Become a wicked human! (23)
"Fall here from the path of the sky; go and experience for a long time the fruit of your insolence, enduring reproach, and then turn into a Vetāla! (24)
"May you become a consumer of flesh and blood and suffer in the great forest!"—
as soon as he was addressed thus, that celestial chariot fell to the earth.
The Vidyādhara fell from that celestial chariot, which then ascended to heaven;
by the power of his karma, he became a long-term resident on the bank of the Yamunā.
A boy named Vidyādhara was born to Govindasvāmin’s wife;
and his father, the twice-born, gave him the name Vijayadatta.
For he too became one who remembered his births and recalled his past deeds;
as a youth, he went to the city of Kāśī for the purpose of pilgrimage.
Accompanied by his son and wife, Govindasvāmī proceeded very slowly;
having performed his ablutions at Prayāga, which he encountered on the way, he then [continued on]. ||29||
Having heard of a certain yogin there who wore a garland of skulls,
and having heard what he said— that the destruction of your son would soon come to pass— [you acted].
Having heard this, Govindasvāmī quickly departed toward Kāśī;
however, on the way, a violent and intense cold wind suddenly arose.
A son blew [the fire] with cold breath, yet the fire was not attained;
meanwhile, the villagers were there nearby on the bank of the Gaṅgā at the corpse.
The other villagers arrived to cremate him;
his son went there to dispel the cold with the fire of the funeral pyre.
Standing at his side, Vijayadatta held the torch;
at that moment, the cremator took up the bamboo pole for the corpse. (34)
And he cast the head portion into the fire upon a bamboo pole for the purpose of burning;
at that moment, the head was split in two by the bamboo pole.
And by the application of fire, the blood [of] Vijayadattika was expelled with force;
having come to his mouth, it adhered there for only a moment before falling away completely.
That Vijayadatta, having arrived, became a vetāla;
with sharp fangs and a massive body, he became exceedingly terrifying. ||37||
Licking the marrow of corpses, he drank it there again and again;
by the sound of his boisterous laughter and the dancing of the vetālas, [the world was shaken].
The cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the sub-directions seemed to burst asunder;
then, from the sky, he rushed toward his father and others to slay them.
Terrified, they all fled from the cremation ground in every direction;
having devoured the corpse, that Vetāla then became powerful.
Having joined with the Vetālas who dwell in cremation grounds, he took up residence there;
at one time, indeed, a battle took place between the Vetālas and the Gandharvas.
Indeed, on the Vindhya mountain there was a terrible [battle], where he achieved victory;
he became a king of the Vetālas and ruled over the Vindhya range.
Then, having abandoned that form of a vetāla, the brahmin, together with his wife, set out for his son and went to the city of Kāśī.
There, his second son was born, whose body was like a diamond;
devoted to Kṛṣṇa, he made his residence in Kāśī along with his sons.
In the meantime, a certain powerful wrestler approached the king named Pratāpamukuṭa, who was the ruler of the land called Kāśī.
Then, at the instruction of the King of Kāśī, the twice-born Vajradeha struck that great wrestler in a wrestling match until he was deprived of life.
Five villages were bestowed upon a brahmin by the King of Kāśī.
Once, the King of Kāśī was accompanied by the son of a twice-born man.
He wandered for some time in a secluded place during the twilight;
then, from afar, he heard a piteous and miserable voice.
Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! Under the rule of the King of Kāśī, for even a slight offense, there is indeed the most dreadful impalement upon a stake. (49)
"Alas! My life-breaths do not depart; rather, it is thirst that afflicts me.
Hearing this, the Lord of Kāśī quickly went there along with the Brahmins.
Just as Vajrāṅga was going there to drink, taking water with him, he indeed saw the householder’s wife standing there. ||51||
That devoted wife also stood ready at that time to follow her deceased husband;
she said to him, "I am short of stature and cannot wade across to offer the water."
Then Vajrāṅga, endowed with compassion, said to that bride:
"Mother, climb upon my shoulder and give him cool water. (53)
Thus addressed, that Vetālī, seated upon the shoulder of Vajrāṅga,
took up water and [sprinkled] the Vetāla who stood upon the stake in a magically assumed form.
His wife made him drink water while he was lying on a false bed;
then the son of the twice-born asked, "Who are you, and who indeed is this person belonging to you? (55)
"How did you come to be under this punishment? Tell the truth, O fair-faced one.
Vaitālī said: "In former times, this master of mine was a brahmin. (56)
The son of Govindasvāmin was named Vijayadatta;
previously, however, he had been the Vidyādhara Sudarśana. (57)
For a moment he violated Gālava’s virtuous daughter in the forest;
then, by the sage Gālava, he was cursed to such a state.
"I am his wife; rescue us two, O Vaitāla!
This stake and so forth were made for the purpose of our deliverance, yet they are false in nature. (59)
The purifying water reached your hand under the pretext of the trident;
by that, this being has been purified, and likewise I, a living being, have been purified.
"O Brahmin, grant us liberation; let there be the fruit of all gifts [offered] at the Rājasūya, Vājapeya, Gomedha, and Naramedha sacrifices. (61)

In the horse-sacrifice, the ploughing-rite, the Viṣṇu-sacrifice, the sacrifice for fame, the sacrifice to the Giver of Wealth, the sacrifice for land, the Phalgu-sacrifice, the sacrifice for sons, and the elephant-sacrifice; (62)
In the iron sacrifice, the gold sacrifice, the removal of eye diseases, the Śanuyajña, the Rudrayajña, the Śakrayajña, and in the rite for binding; 63.
In the sacrifice of Varuṇa, in the ritual of the ball for crushing enemies, in the sacrifice of purity, in the sacrifice of dharma, in the emission, and in the liberation from sin; ||64||
In the Bandhana sacrifice, the Karmayoga, the auspicious Maṇiyāga, the Śyenayāga, the Vājapeya, the Sāvitra, and the Kamalakratau; ||69||
Whatever fruit is obtained from the sacrifice of recitation, the sacrifice of knowledge, and the sacrifice of discourse—
that fruit shall certainly be yours through the liberation of the Vaitālas.
Having heard this, the twice-born said to his own king: "O King, these beings in the form of ghosts exist in your kingdom and in the kingdom of Kāśī, suffering in misery. (67)
"That liberation should be achieved by the offering of water from the Gaṅgā.
The king said, "In the past, this Vetāla was your brother."
Water was given to him to drink by you, and thus his sin has been destroyed;
however, something else must be done for him that will bring about his liberation. (69)
Having spoken thus, the king asked that spear-bearer:
"Tell me, by what action here might your liberation be achieved?"
The preta said: "Liberation from the sage's curse cannot come from any other source;
my liberation will occur only through the grace of the sage himself. (71)
"The King of Kāśī, as well as my father Govindasvāmin and his younger brother, and my mother—you all must go indeed to the sage Gālava. (72)
"By the method he has described, there shall be deliverance from my suffering.
Then, having heard this, they all went to where Gālava was.
Having bowed to the sage who was accompanied by ten thousand maidens, they paid homage again and again;
then, being honored by Gāvalgaṇa, they related that very account.
The sage said: "My daughter is a virtuous and chaste woman, devoted to the Supreme Lord;
she is composed of all spiritual perfections, a great devotee of the Blessed One, and truly a faithful wife. (75)
She is the compassionate protector of living beings who have come for refuge;
she is devoted to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and is endowed with sovereign power. ||76||
Divine, clinging to Nārāyaṇa, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
endowed with the vow of celibacy, she was a devoted wife whose very soul was Kṛṣṇa. ||77||
In an instant, that Goddess is capable of burning away even the sins as vast as Mount Meru, and likewise, she is able to grant liberation to ten million vetālas and bhūtas.
The sovereign Prakṛti, who is a portion of Kamalā belonging to Viṣṇu, exists as the power capable of creating infinite Brahmās; may they propitiate that virtuous lady. (79)
That Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa and possessor of beautiful luster, being truly pleased,
will deliver the Vetālas by the bestowal of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra.
Thus addressed, the King of Kāśī and all the others [praised] the maiden, the mother of the worlds, Lakṣmī, the radiant one, the beloved of Hari. 8.1.
They bowed, offered hymns of praise, fell at his feet for refuge, and paid their respects;
having learned from them the account regarding the liberation of the Vetāla, [he departed]. (82)
The maiden spoke of the duties of Kṛṣṇa’s vow, which bestow all happiness:
[they remove] pleasure, pain, fear, sorrow, joy, and even misfortune. (83)
Prosperity and adversity—all comes about through actions;
by action one becomes a daughter of Brahmā, and by action one is born into a low lineage. (84)
By action one possesses beauty, and by one's own action one is constantly diseased;
by action one becomes the son of a charioteer, and by action one becomes long-lived.
By action one becomes possessed of qualities, and by action one suffers physical deficiency;
by action one becomes elemental spirits or vampires, by action one becomes deities, and by action one becomes human beings. (86)
When auspicious deeds are performed, the worlds are auspicious; when inauspicious, people are humiliated.
By that very auspiciousness, he attained the status of a Vidyādhara. (87)
And his impurity was indeed caused by that very act of wicked intent, even though there was a devoted wife and a pure maiden [present]. (88)
Those who employ evil eyes indeed become born blind;
they likewise become afflicted with leprosy, one-eyed, lame, maimed, and crippled. (89)

Those who possess evil dispositions through corrupt mental cultivation are wicked and suffer due to the fruits of their actions; those who possess virtuous dispositions through the cultivation of goodness are endowed with noble qualities and partakers of happiness.
Indeed, the breaking of those who observe rules is certainly a violation of dharma;
those who proceed without restraint shall surely be punished by the king.
They alone are subject to the rod of Yama and subject to the black rod;
they are subject to every rod in the world, for there is no other path than that. 92.
The vow of devotion to one's wife is the supreme dharma; it always bestows happiness and peace.
O twice-born one, in ancient times, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself established this vow of devotion to one's wife.
All the Brahmins of that lineage, as well as the Ṛṣis and Munis,
were entirely devoted to their wives and endowed with the household vow of Brahman.

The elements produced from food, which reside within the bodies of embodied beings, cross over [suffering] themselves and cause others to cross over as well, for they maintain their course through the application of discipline. 95.
Restrained celibacy is the form of dharma; it brings happiness. In the absence of restraint, there is a loss of dharma, which results in the suffering of dwelling in the womb and so forth. //96//
Having abandoned the bliss of the Self and resorted to the bliss of scratching, he who is deprived of the bliss of Brahman experiences the suffering of scratching. 97.
If there is scratching [of the skin] during the Dadrucandra period, there will certainly be a burning sensation later on;
likewise, if one indulges in unrighteous sexual pleasure, a constant burning sensation will surely occur in the southern part of the body.
Therefore, desire has been restrained by marriage;
touch has also been restrained, as have sight and speech. (99)
Who possesses what, and what is to be enjoyed by whom? Everything has been ordained by those of old. This very restriction is indeed dharma; it is the vow of a wife, to be observed in her youth.
Likewise, he who is devoted to his wife is surely always a bestower of happiness;
yet by him that [virtue] was violated, since he committed the assault upon the maiden. (101)
Even for one who does not desire it, contact consisting of fire arises;
yet that [fire] becomes extinguished by the application of the "black" [remedy]. 102.
If you desire the swift liberation from that spirit, [recite]:
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord. 1.03
Having thus received the mantra and wearing a garland of *tulasī*,
[he should consume] the water, food, leaves, and other offerings that are the remnants (*prasāda*) of Kṛṣṇa’s worship.
"Take me there where that preeminent Vetāla resides;
and take him, along with his thousand Vetālas, to the ocean."
On the shore of the southern ocean, in the vicinity of Cakratīrtha,
at the Vetālamuktikṛt-tīrtha, there is the supreme Vetāloddhāraka.
"Bathe thousands of Vetālas there in that water;
then, repeat three times again and again the mantra spoken by me. || 107 ||
Having offered water, food, and leaves produced from pure faith for their meal, perform their liberation; there is no other path that bestows happiness.
Having heard this, they all at that very moment [uttered] for Kāntimatī:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord."
Having taken this mantra, and having received the food, water, and so forth,
as well as the leaf-plate given by her, they offered praise and departed for him.
Having gone toward the Vetāla and having taken those thousands of Vetālas with them,
they departed from Cakratīrtha to the southern shore of the ocean.
