Those belonging to the Upamanyu gotra are endowed with three pravaras:
Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, and Indrapramada—these are they. (29)
For those born of Gārgya’s lineage, there are indeed three pravaras:
Aṅgiras, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva as the third.
At that time, Mauṣaka’s lineage was not independent,
nor indeed was Mudgala’s lineage independent.
In the lineage of Gāṅgāsana, however, there are exactly five pravaras:
Bhārgava, Āvanāpnuvāna, Aurva, Jāmadagnya, and [the fifth]. || 32 ||
Ātreya, Arcanānasa, and Śyāvāsya—these three are all [descendants] of Gaṅgā; in some cases, these three also constitute the *pravara* lineages.
O Lakṣmī, in former times, there were no independent *pravara* lineages within the clans of Kauṇḍinya, Puṇyāsana, and Parāśara. (34)
Now I shall tell you of five others belonging to Jamadagni:
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagnika.
In the lineage of Māṇḍavya, there are five pravaras as follows: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Ātreya, Apnavāna, and Aurva. (36)
Those belonging to the Vātsyāyana lineage are endowed with five *pravara*s:
Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnuvāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni. (37)
There are others in the Kaśyapa lineage who are endowed with three *pravara*s:
the renowned triad consisting of Kāśyapa, Āpavatsāra, and Raibhya. (38)
Those born among the Śaunakas are endowed with three *pravaras*:
Bhārgava, Śaunahotra, and Gārtsyamada—these three. (39)
They were born in the lineage of Aṅgiras, endowed with three *pravara*s:
namely, the three—Āṅgirasa, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva.
Now, in the Patnīvratagotra, there are Devānīka, Dasāyaka, and Santaka; these are the ancestral sages (pravaras) who were devoted to great acts of charity. ||41||
O twice-born ones, their branches and sub-branches— sons, grandsons, and so forth—
were born in great numbers in the world, adhering to new schools of thought.
The three ancestral sages (pravaras) belonging to the Dharmasāvarṇi lineage were indeed Vaitahavya, Sāvetasa, and Bhāradvāja. ||43||
And having abandoned these [ancient paths], O Brahmins, those who follow new and superior ways will come into being when time has passed; everything will then be a mere mockery of time.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to these twice-born ones in Dharmāraṇya and other lands;
at that time, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and others will indeed cause them distress. (45)
There was a yakṣa named Jṛmbhaka near Dharmāraṇya;
he constantly tormented those dwelling in Dharmāraṇya. (46)
That suffering was reported by those foremost of the twice-born to the gods;
having placed their vow of devotion to their wives at the forefront, the deities went to the assembly of Brahmā. (47)
Brahmā went to Goloka and spoke to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
at that time, hundreds of thousands of gopīs were sent there by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Those divine wives of Kṛṣṇa, who act according to Kṛṣṇa’s command, are beloved; they are immersed in the dharma of devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as their husband. ||49||
Truthful, serene, and possessing divine limbs, those daughters of Ayurvedha arrived at his home;
and by the command of Brahmā, they all went from there to heaven.
There, in an instant, the daughters of Viśvāvasu became Mānasīs—young women who remembered their former births and were beautiful in every limb. (51)
The wives and daughters of Kṛṣṇa, devoted to the dharma of celibacy,
[did this] for the sake of protecting the Brahmins and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The yoginīs were established by gods and gandharvas in the grounds of the Dharma;
likewise, each individual yoginī was established according to her respective lineage. (53)
Whatever power a lineage possesses that is capable of its protection and preservation,
that indeed became manifest there as its family deity.
O Lakṣmī, listen; Śrīmātā and the others are all twelve years of age:
Śrīmātā, Tāraṇī, Āśāpurī, and Icchārtināśinī. (55)
Pippalī, Vikarāvaśā, and Jaganmātā as the seventh;
likewise Mahāmātā, Siddhā, Bhaṭṭārikā, and the Kadambikās. ||56||
Vikarā, Miṣṭā, Suparṇā, Mātaṅgī, Vasujā, as well as Mahādevī, Vāṇī, Bhadrī, and Mukureśvarī. ||57||
Saṃhārī, Mahāśakti, and likewise Mahābalā, as well as the great goddess Cāmuṇḍā—these are the Mothers of the Lineage (gotramātaraḥ). ||58||
Established by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others for the protection of the Brahmins,
the foremost of Brahmins worship those Vaiṣṇavī goddesses, who are the chaste wives of the Lord.
Then, during the sacrifices for the sake of obtaining cattle, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, remembered Kāmadhenu; and Kāmadhenu arrived.
Brahmā spoke to her for the sake of the twice-born:
"O Mother, be gracious to me; grant a wish-fulfilling cow to each and every brāhmaṇa."
Having said "So be it," Kāmadhenu brought forth female calves;
hundreds of thousands of white Nandini cows appeared, all in the full bloom of youth.
By mere thought, auspicious cows that yielded milk along with their calves and bestowed all desired objects began to flow; the gods were satisfied by the excellent milk-porridges.
Then, ten thousand merchants of the Brāhmaṇa varṇas,
who were twice-born servants created mentally by the Brāhmaṇas, were produced there.
Wearing sacred threads and topknots, they were experts in all principles;
devoted to the twice-born, they were of virtuous conduct, youthful, and endowed with austerity.
For each individual brahmin, two attendants were indeed assigned;
whatever was the lineage (gotra) of the brahmin, that same lineage belonged to his attendant.
Indeed, Brahmā has instructed them to be your disciples for your benefit;
follow their words and grant them whatever they desire.
"Bring fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and other such items day after day;
conduct yourselves according to their instructions and never show them disrespect anywhere. (68)
Thus conducting themselves, devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), all those Vaiṣṇavas, distinguished by their vows, served the Brāhmaṇas. 69.
For their sake, indeed, the Creator and Vṛṣa have provided beautiful Gandharva maidens as wives there for their enjoyment.
Those daughters of Viśvāvasu, devoted wives of Brahmins,
then became sixty thousand daughters-in-law in the form of his granddaughters.
Likewise, O beloved, there were others in the form of mothers-in-law, as well as mothers and wives of Brahmins;
there were forty thousand maidens.
Then there were the Śreṣṭhā-devīs, the Yoginīs, and the protectors in the form of Mothers;
in Dharmāraṇya, there were hundreds of thousands of such women who were devoted wives to Kṛṣṇa.
Thus they became householders, with an abundance of sons, grandsons, and so forth;
all the women were devoted to their husbands, and all the men were devoted to their wives.
While the forest-dwelling brahmins were living in this manner,
the rakshasa Lolajihvaka caused them great distress.
Having large fangs, a massive body, and a tongue like lightning, he was terrifying;
yet the goddesses, intent on protecting the brahmins, were determined to destroy him.
Some bear the excellent trident, others are endowed with the conch, discus, and mace;
still others are equipped with the whip and sword, as well as the noose and goad.
Some with axes in their hands and others bearing divine weapons fought the Rākṣasa here, and they called to mind Nārāyaṇa.
Viṣṇu arrived and slew the Rākṣasa with his discus;
meanwhile, the Brahmins, having united, took up residence in a single city.
Formerly, that city of Dharmāraṇya was the town of Satyamandira;
it was a divine city where Brahmins resided, truly equal to heaven.
Other Yoginīs were established for the purpose of protecting the city, such as Śrīmātā in Madārikā and likewise Śāntā in Nandāpura. (81)
Sāvitrī, Jñānajā, Gātrāyī, and likewise Pakṣiṇī;
Chatrajā, Cūṭikā, Dvāravāsinī, and likewise Pippalā. ||82||
Śīhorī, Śāpurī, Cetā, Raktavastrā, and Bhayaṃkarā; Ānandā, likewise Oṃkārā, and likewise Dharmaputrikā. ||83||
And Śyāmalā—these [goddesses], having taught the Dharma, provide protection.
Now, there was a Rākṣasa named Karṇāṭa who oppressed Brahmins. ||84||
Yogamālinī drove him away toward the south;
that region became famous by his name as Karṇāṭaka. (85)
By her, however, these cruel ones were produced while they were still celibate students:
Śākinī, Ḍākinī, Kākinī, and likewise Hākinī. (86)
Ekinī, Lākinī, and these other Śaktis, who destroy the Daityas, were stationed by Dharmadeva for the purpose of guarding Dharmāraṇya. (87)
All these women were devoted to their husbands and were servants of the beloved of Rudra; they were constant protectors of the Brahmins and guardians of the lineage of virtuous wives. 88.
By her, Lakṣmī was produced, as well as other devoted wives,
great goddesses observing the vow of Rudra, who took refuge in Dharmāraṇya.
These maidens, who observe the vow of celibacy, are the family deities; by them the lineages of Brahmins on this earth are protected at all times.
Bhaṭṭārikī, as well as Chatrā, Auvikā, Jñānajā, Bhadrakālī, Māheśī, Siṃhorī, and Dhanamardinī. ||91||
Gātrā, Śāntā, Śeṣadevī, Vārāhī, Bhadrayoginī, Yogeśvarī, Mohalajjā, Kuleśī, and Śakulācitā. 92.
Tāraṇī, Kanakānandā, Cāmuṇḍā, Sureśvarī,
Dārabhaṭṭārikā, and others— each of these is further divided into a hundred forms.
All powers that had arisen, having the forest of Dharma and other places as their support, were then employed by Dharmapitā for a great sacrifice in the Forest of Dharma. 94.
There, the gods, the ancestors, the seers, the sages, and men—the fourteen lords of the worlds beginning with Manu—all arrived. (95)
There, he appointed Mārkaṇḍeya, the descendant of Aṅgiras, as the Ācārya;
and he likewise appointed Atri and Kaśyapa as the Hotṛ priests. ||96||
He appointed Jamadagni and Gautama as the Adhvaryu priests, and he appointed Bharadvāja and Vasiṣṭha as the Pratyadhvaryu priests. ||97||
The King of Dharma also fashioned Nārada and Vālmīki as his inspirers, and he established Brahmā upon the Brahma-throne. 98.
Then, after the gods had constructed a beautiful altar measuring four *krośas*, all the twice-born were summoned—both those who recite prayers and those who read the scriptures. (99)
Gaṇeśa, Skanda, and Indrajayanta were appointed as gatekeepers;
thereafter, oblations were offered into the sacrificial fire with a mantra that destroys Rākṣasas.
Then, O Lotus-born One, those gods offered oblations with Vedic mantras,
consisting of sesame seeds mixed with barley and well-blended with honey and clarified butter.
Then, after having offered the two āghāra oblations and the two ājyabhāga portions,
[he should offer] grapes, sugarcane, betel nut, orange, citron, and pomegranate.
To the north, one should place a coconut and a pomegranate in due order,
along with honey and clarified butter mixed with milk, and rice cooked with sesame (kṛśara) combined with sugar.
Having performed a sacrifice with rice grains and lotuses accompanied by ritual fees,
they then sang the most excellent and auspicious Vaiṣṇava hymn of praise.
He gave food without restriction even to the wretched, the blind, and the miserable—
rice-pudding mixed with sugar, accompanied by ghee and vegetables.
Maṇḍakas, vaṭakas, pūpas, as well as auspicious veṣṭikas, a thousand modakas, pheṇikās, ghurghuras, and so forth. (106)
Likewise, there is boiled rice (odana), as well as dal made from adzukis and other grains;
similarly, there is mung-bean dal, as well as thin pancakes (parpata) and medicinal boluses (vati).
Long pepper, cloves, black pepper, and red arsenic; as well as half-cooked grains, *vellaka* seeds, and auspicious, tender *vālaka* grass. 108.
Karkariṭas and fresh ginger combined with black pepper, various excellent vegetables, and likewise diverse kinds of cooked dishes. || 109 ||
Having fed thousands of twice-born brahmins with milk-rice, sugarcane products, wheat preparations, sweet foods, and chickpea dishes, the bull [attained his goal]. (1.440.110)
Having performed the purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) after [offering] eighteen *lakṣas* and likewise other people by the millions, he obtained the fruit of the sacrifice.
Having performed the sacrifice, all those embodied beings went to their respective abodes;
by hearing or reciting this, the fruit of a sacrifice to Viṣṇu shall be obtained.

Thus ends the four hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Circle of Family Deities of the Chaste Maidens of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Who Became Gandharvas in Dharmāraṇya during the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," as well as the Gotras and Pravaras of the Brāhmaṇas and others, the destruction of the Rākṣasa Lolajihva by the Goddess, the establishment of the Yoginīs, and the sacrifice performed by Dharmadeva. || 440 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how women may worship Kṛṣṇa;
I shall proclaim that dharma by which liberation may also be attained. || 1 ||

A wife who has been wedded according to the Dharma, who is free from the ten defects, who is neither impotent nor deformed, and who is not afflicted by major diseases or other such ailments, is highly commended. (2)
Blameless, possessing auspicious qualities, free from eye diseases, devoid of deafness, steady, and sweet-spoken—such is the maiden. || 3 ||
When she has been married by men according to the prescribed rite, being free from the ten defects,
she is known as a lawful wife, a mistress of the household, and a virtuous woman.
In all meritorious deeds, she stands foremost;
when Dharma is well-established by her, it becomes a bestower of complete fruit. || 5 ||
Women should always perform the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) while constantly remembering Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, they should perform bathing, libations, fire-offerings, and the worship of Acyuta.
And the hospitable reception of guests—one should not abandon these five sacrifices;
for by these five sacrifices, the ancestors and the deities become satisfied. (7)
For a devoted wife, through her joyful service to her husband,
the ancestors and the gods become satisfied when Hari, who is identical with the husband, is pleased.
Indeed, all the gods dwell within the body of a devoted wife; therefore, through her union with her husband, there is the arrival of dharma.
When there is unity of mind between the two, the ancestors and the deities are satisfied;
all undertakings reach successful completion, and auspicious fruit is attained.
A wife born of the same caste should be married;
her husband shall be her partner in all religious duties in every respect. (11)
She possesses authority over half of his body; therefore, she is the bearer of half of his dharma.
And the husband is the bearer of half of her dharma—this applies to both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
O beloved, that virtuous and highly faithful woman who follows her deceased husband through great austerity is to be known as one by whom the family is uplifted. (13)
Whether she was previously married or already widowed,
any woman who maintains her vow rescues that husband by means of the path of Vaiśvānara.
Just as a savior rescues one who is drowning from the water, even so does the virtuous wife who follows her husband rescue him. (15)
That maiden who, having herself exerted effort, is given by her father to the bridegroom and wed according to the marriage rite, accomplishes the welfare of the ancestors and the gods. 16.
Marriages are said to be of ten kinds; she who, having obtained a husband through any one of them, supports him, uplifts her entire lineage. (17)
Even she who has been remarried is a virtuous wife if she protects the family;
however, if she is purchased for a price, she is a slave, even if she has been married.
A woman who is virtuous and endowed with righteousness uplifts her family;
even if she is born of a lowly lineage, if she is wedded according to dharma and is a faithful wife, she purifies her kin.
She purifies her entire family through the power of her devotion to her husband.
Among the forms of marriage, those of Prajāpati, Brahmā, Daiva, and Ārṣa are the most excellent.
The Gāndharva, the Āsura, the Rākṣasa, the Piśācaka, the Prātibha, and the Ghātaka—these are said to be the ten forms of marriage. ||21||
The legitimate son (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the given son (datta), the made son (kṛtrima),
the son secretly born (gūḍhotpanna), the cast-off son (apaviddha), the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son of a pregnant bride (sahoḍhaja),
the bought son (krīta), and the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava)— these are considered the ten kinds of sons.
In this way, [the grief of] sons, daughters, wives, husbands, fathers, and family members [is described]. || 23 ||
By virtue of devotion to their husbands, virtuous women cross over [the ocean of existence] through service to Kṛṣṇa;
truthful women devoted to their husbands sport like gods in heaven. 24.
O Lakṣmī, for all women, devotion to Kṛṣṇa is always auspicious;
service to a true guru and the worship of the guru are ever-enjoined for the sake of purification. (25)
Service to one's husband for the sake of heaven is always proclaimed as the worship of the Lord;
however, for women, the dedication to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is for the sake of liberation. 26.
Thus, in ancient times, by relying on this dharma, the Śūdra Paijavana went to the world of Kṛṣṇa together with his virtuous wife.
He was devoted to righteousness, a worshiper of Viṣṇu and the brāhmaṇas; content with wealth acquired through righteous means, he lived with his wife as a servant of the virtuous.
He was a speaker of truth and a devotee of Viṣṇu; his wife was Sundarī, a virtuous woman of equal lineage, wedded according to the prescribed rites.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and intent on the welfare of the gods and the twice-born,
she was born as a maiden in Kāśī and married in Vaijayantī.
Skilled in the practice of dharma and observing the vows of Vaiṣṇava, she,
knowing her husband to be Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, serves him with devotion.
The attainment of wealth through his virtuous merits always increases in the house of this husband of a chaste wife,
by means of successful trade and business.
In this manner, many sons were born to that seer of Dharma; and there were also two daughters, O Vaiṣṇavas. (33)
The devotees of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa are devoted to the service of their parents;
they are intent on attending to their parents, and their wife is always faithful to her husband.
Having remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they all perform worship, service, and other honors for their guests as well. || 31 ||
Their abode is endowed with supernatural power and filled with wealth and grain; never does one who has entered their house depart disappointed. (36)
In the cold season they gave wealth; in the hot season, they were givers of water and food; in the rainy season, they were givers of clothing; and they were always givers of food. (37)
Established in the vow of devotion to Kṛṣṇa, they cause step-wells, wells, tanks, water-stations, temples, and houses to be constructed at the appropriate time. (38)
There was no distinction of seating order in their home, for they were satisfied with equal shares;
while they lived in this manner at home, the sage Śrī Gālava [visited them].
Accompanied by many devoted disciples,
together with Sundarī, and joined by his sons and others, Paijavana arrived.
Having welcomed him with rising from his seat and other marks of respect,
he was filled with great joy there as he drank the water from [the sage's] feet.
Honoring his own family as one who had accomplished their purpose, he said:
"Today my birth has become fruitful; today my life has become supreme. (42)
Today my dharma has become fruitful, and my lineage has been uplifted by you;
O Sage, thousands of my sins have been consumed by your very sight. (43)
Hari, Nārāyaṇa, and Kṛṣṇa—Gālava has come to my home;
my house, as a householder, has been purified by you, O Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard this, Gālava, his fatigue from the journey dispelled by great devotion and being well-pleased, inquired after the welfare of the Śūdra at length. (45)
"Is all well with you, gentle one? Does your mind proceed toward the Dharma? And as for your wife and children, whose every possession has been taken by Kṛṣṇa—are they well? (46)
Do you possess devotion preceded by generosity toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa? And is your mind indeed full of affection for virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation? (47)
Does she indeed always bear upon her head the water from Viṣṇu’s feet? Is she truly Satī, entirely devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa, her beloved? (48)
Indeed, everything is sustained by truth; likewise, everything is protected by truth.
Through truth one crosses over suffering, for truth is the means for attaining happiness and other such goals. 49.
Thus addressed, Paijavana replied: "Your compassion toward me is such that everything remains as it was; this special favor of yours is extraordinary."
"Consider me your servant and instruct me; consider this virtuous woman your female servant, and these sons your servants—[instruct us all] regarding the purpose for which we have come. (51)
Gālava said to them: "He whose devotion is always fixed on Acyuta, and whose wife is a virtuous, chaste woman devoted to her husband as her god—[he shall attain success]. (52)
He whose sons are servants of Hari, whose daughters are female servants of the virtuous Hari,
and whose family members, kinsmen, and others are purifying Vaiṣṇavas.
At the holy confluence of these rivers, liberation is nowhere difficult to attain;
for this auspicious physical body is indeed a Vaiṣṇava family and a portion of Brahman.
By the very sight of you, who are united with the attribute-less Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, even a sinner becomes purified. (55)
Everything has attained a state devoid of qualities through the dual nature of devotion and the duty of a servant;
even for virtuous women, there exists this dual nature of devotion and the duty of a servant.
The dharma of love for Hari arose in the cowherd women and in Śabarī;
the dharma of love in Piṅgalā became purifying and bestowing liberation. (57)
O Śivā, the daughter of the Black and White Mountains attained the nature of love;
by means of that, at the end of a thousand years, she reached Maheśvara.
O beloved, Pārvatī’s, Prabhā’s, Lalitā’s,
Lakṣmī’s, Jayā’s, and Māṇikyā’s affection has reached its ultimate limit.
They obtained Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as their husband;
and the marriage between Vṛndā and Tulasī was rooted in mutual affection.
Through the worship of Kṛṣṇa with Tulasī leaves, liberation will certainly be attained;
it is held that liberation in Hari is rooted in devotion, just as it is for a wife toward her husband.
Vṛndā and the others also became saviors of the worlds on earth;
listen, O devotee, for once in a former age all of them were indeed ancestors.
Then, for the sake of satisfaction through food, they went to Brahmā for refuge;
likewise, for the sake of satisfaction, they sought whatever auspicious water was presided over by Varuṇa.
However, without libations (tarpaṇa), it should not be accepted at all by the ancestors;
for when it is given by anyone [else], that [gift] becomes acceptable and brings satisfaction.
"Therefore, O elder brother, ordain something for our satisfaction.
Thus entreated, Brahmā then sought refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, for the sake of satisfying the ancestors and providing them with water,
he made a request to the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having reflected for a moment, he said: "I am the Blessed One, the Self of all;
I am the one who brings satisfaction to everyone, and no other is like me. (67)
Therefore, I must certainly act so that they may be satisfied;
for where will all these people find me, who possess a divine form? (68)
Therefore, for the sake of offering libations of water, I shall maintain this auspicious form; may it bring about the welfare bestowed upon all living beings in the world. (69)
Having reflected thus within himself, Kṛṣṇa indeed became the form of the Aśvattha tree;
Janārdana, assuming a physical body, became the Pippala tree with a divine form.
On Mount Revata, at the site of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Dāmodara,
a Śrāddha was previously performed by two [brothers] there in the Nārāyaṇa lake.
Then, at the foot of the Plakṣa tree, he stood with the two Kṛṣṇas according to the mantra;
water from the sacred ford was offered, and consequently, his ancestors were satisfied.
Thus, in a former age, the glorious Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself assumed the Plakṣa incarnation on Mount Raivata. (73)
Now, the sages have always performed the gift of water at the Pippala tree;
the water offered at the Pippala is obtained by those who have gone to the three worlds. (74)
Then the gods, headed by Mahendra, as well as those headed by Śiva and the Vaiṣṇavas,
went there to the Nārāyaṇa lake in order to behold Kṛṣṇa.
In the forest on the banks of the Svarṇarekhā river, Kṛṣṇa was searched for;
indeed, Hari was sought there by some through his illusory power.
Indeed, the Blessed One was perceived neither as a tree nor otherwise;
then the gods said to Bṛhaspati, "The Blessed Hari [is here]. (77)

"How indeed can he, who has become united with a tree, be seen? Then Bṛhaspati said: "If you wish to see him as a tree, then Hari, in the form of a tree, shall come into direct perception through the eyes of trees."
Thus addressed, all those gods [remained] near the lake of Nārāyaṇa.
Then they were born assuming the forms of trees in order to behold Kṛṣṇa;
there, Śrī appeared in the form of Tulasī, and Pārvatī was born from the sectarian mark on his forehead.
There arose a great tree known as the Bilva, and Pārvatī appeared there in the form of a Bilva; at that time, Brahmā likewise became a Vaṭa tree. 8–1.
Sāvitrī became known as Tilagulmā and was accompanied by sesame;
Mahendra became a barley tree, and the lords of progeny became mango trees.
The Gandharvas are the Malaya trees, Aguru is the Lord of the Gaṇas;
the oceans are the reed trees, and the Yakṣas are the Punnāga trees. ||83||

At that time, the Nāgas were the *nāga* trees, the Siddhas were the *kaṅkolaka* trees, the Guhyakas were the *panasa* (jackfruit) trees, and the Kinnaras were the *marica* (black pepper) trees. ||88||
Yaṣṭimadhudru is Kandarpa; Vahni is the Raktāñjanadruma;
Yama is the Vibhītakavṛkṣa; and Nirṛti is the Bakuladruma. ||85||
Varuṇa is the date-palm tree, while Māruta is the betel-nut tree;
Dhanada is the walnut tree, and the Rudras are the jujube trees. ||82||
The seven sages became great palm trees, the other gods became cardamom trees, the clouds became rose-apple trees, and the lightning flashes became *aśoka* trees. ||87||
The Vasus were born from the Priyāla trees, while the Ādityas arose from the Japā trees;
the two Madanas then became the Aśvinīkumāras.
The Viśvedevas became Madhuka trees, the Rākṣasas became Guggulu trees;
Sūrya became the Arka tree, and the Moon became the Palāśa tree. (89)
Maṅgala was born as the Khadira tree, Budha became the Apāmārga, Bṛhaspati was then the Aśvattha, and Śukra became the Udumbara.
Śanaiścara became the Śamī tree, Rāhu became the Durvā grass,
and Ketu likewise took the form of Darbha grass as well as a fruit-bearing tree.
Then those wives of the gods became creepers;
Viṣṇu took the form of a *śāla* tree, and the *apāmārga* was his vehicle.
Śrīvatsa became the Kalpa tree, Kārtika became the Campaka, Nārada became the Pārijāta, and Gaurī then became Vṛndā. (93)
Lakṣmī was born as Mālatī, while Sarasvatī became Dhātrī;
then, in another part of that very forest, he assumed many forms.
The Lord Viṣṇu was born in the form of the Aśvattha tree, assuming a beautiful appearance;
Rudra became the Vaṭa tree, and Brahmā assumed the form of the Palāśa tree.
At that time, Nandin was seen as a white [tree], Śambhu assumed the form of a bilva tree, Indra became a śirīṣa tree, and the Sun became a nimba tree. (96)
Śiva and Aśvinī are the two Bilva trees; Śivā is Vṛndā in her true form.
Brahmā and Rudra are the two Vaṭa trees; Brahmā possesses the form of the Palāśa tree. || 97 ||
The Moon became a *palāśa* tree, while Nimbārka were both in the form of the Sun;
and Viṣṇu and Bṛhaspati were both in the form of the *aśvattha* tree—thus indeed [the deities] were twofold.
At that time, those two were considered to belong to specific sub-species within their respective trees;
these tree-bodied ones gazed at Kṛṣṇa with their tree-eyes. (99)
The Aśvattha tree, endowed with large leaves, was seen in the Nārāyaṇa lake;
Kṛṣṇa, in that very form, [emerged] for the purpose of taking water from the water.
The Compassionate One remained there for the sake of attaining satisfaction for his ancestors;
at its base were also Brāhmaṇas and two Nārāyaṇas. || 101 ||
The water of the celestial river offered by the god who is devoted to his wife—
all that, when offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, reaches the ancestors and becomes a provider of satisfaction; therefore, one should worship the Pippala tree.
And by its power, those trees shall remain, bestowing food and liberation.
As long as the black *pippala* tree stands upon the earth until the dissolution of the world,
these celestial trees, when well-worshipped, grant liberation to all; indeed,
through their service, they bestow liberation even upon women and those of other castes.

Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa took water and offered it to the ancestors; then, in his original form, he went to his own realm, Gosthala. The gods, devoted to Kṛṣṇa-bhakti, each departed for their own world.
This was heard from the mouth of Gālava by the wife of Paijavana;
and then Sundarī repeatedly resolved upon the vow of devotion to her husband,
just as this Gālava reveals the deities.
If those gods and others were truly of the nature of trees, [then... (108)
"O Lakṣmī, if I am indeed devoted to the duty of a wife and solely dedicated to my husband, may I behold all those [husbands] according to their respective true forms.
When she had thus resolved, O Lakṣmī, all the gods arrived.
She saw trees and creepers that were of the same nature as herself.
Then Sundarī formed another resolve there: "May I be a devoted wife, and may there be meals for the disciples of Gālava."
In that place, O beloved, there were mountains of most delicious food;
having eaten, Gālava together with his disciples went to his own hermitage, O beloved.
The deities, honored and restored to their own forms, departed for their respective abodes.
From that time forward, virtuous noble women have repeatedly honored trees. || 113 ||
In sacrifice, those divine trees, which are of the nature of purifiers and bestowers of great merit, are offered as oblations;
they grant heaven, bestow liberation, and confer prosperity.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the worship of trees and other such rites for women;
by reading or even hearing this, one obtains great merit, leading to heaven and liberation. 115.

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Various Trees such as Tulasī as Incarnations of Deities and Others, and Liberation through Their Worship," within the section on the Kṛta Yuga in the first book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the straightforward means for the liberation of women demonstrated by Gālava.

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the vow dedicated to Lord Kṛṣṇa, which bestows liberation, is purifying, and is cherished by Kṛṣṇa’s devotees; it is indeed a supreme Vaiṣṇava rite known as Suyajña.
The son of Brahmā was indeed Svāyambhuva Manu;
his son was Uttānapāda, and his son was named Dhruva.
The son of Dhruva was Utkala, who was solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
he performed a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices at Puṣkara.
Brahmā himself bestowed upon him the name Suyajña;
he was a giver of food and a giver of jewels and all forms of prosperity.
Filled with joy, he also constantly gave away one million cows adorned with jeweled horns, as well as twelve lakhs of cows possessing the auspicious marks.
And he fed six crores of Brahmins daily,
making them thoroughly satiated day after day with foods to be sucked, chewed, licked, and drunk.
Thereafter, he fed thirty-six million crores of cooks on that day at the conclusion of the Suyajña sacrifice.
O beautiful one, the brahmins partook of excellent food and were thoroughly satiated;
yet, having taken the jewels, they were unable to carry them to their own homes.
To whomever they gave, even many times, and whomsoever they left behind on the road— to all those brahmins as well, they gave food.
Nevertheless, a thousand heaps of men remained there.
Having thus performed that auspicious sacrifice in the assembly of kings, Suyajña—
He sat upon a beautiful throne fashioned from great jewels,
adorned with silk cloths and perfumed with excellent sandalwood and other fragrances.
It was beautifully adorned with full water-pots joined with branches of the *ramā* tree,
and refined with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, camphor, and vermilion.
It was filled with Vasus, Vāsava, Candra, Indra, Rudra, and the Ādityas;
it was attended by sages such as Nārada and Manu, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
In the meantime, a certain brahmin arrived there;
he was coarse and wore soiled garments, yet he offered auspicious blessings to the king.
The king bowed to him but did not rise from his own excellent seat; the members of the assembly likewise did not rise, yet they laughed slightly at him.
Enraged by that, the twice-born man there cursed the king:
"May you now be deprived of your kingdom, afflicted with oozing leprosy, and devoid of intellect. (16)
At that moment, the members of the assembly bowed down, and the Brahmin rose up;
the king also abandoned his anger and fell at his feet.
There the sages— Pulaha, Pulastya, Pracetas, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras— offered that eminent brahmin an excellent and auspicious seat.
Marīci, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Kratu; Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Durvāsas, and likewise Lomaśa.
Gautama, Kaṇāda, Kaṇva, Kātyāyana, Kaṭha, Pāṇini, Jājali, as well as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and Vibhāṇḍaka.
Taittiri, Āpiśali, Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism, Sanaka, Sananda, Voḍhu, Paila, and Sanātana. || 21 ||
Sanatkumāra, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Parāśara, Jaratkāru who was devoted to his wife, Saṃvarta, and likewise Karabha. || 22 ||
Bharadvāja, Vālmīki, Aurva, Cyavana, Agastya, Atri, Utathya, Saṃkṛti, Tīrtha, and Āsuri; ||23||
Śilāli, Lāṅgali, Śākalya, Śākaṭāyana, Garga, Vatsa, Pañcaśikha, Jamadagni, and Devala. ||24||
Jaigīṣavya, Vāmadeva, and the Vālakhilyas by the hundreds of thousands;
Śakti, Dakṣa, Kardama, Praskanna, and likewise Kapila. ||25||
Viśvāmitra, Kautsa, Ṛcīka, Aghamarṣaṇa, Svayaṃprakāśa, Brahmiṣṭha, Śatānanda, and Suvrata; ||26||
These and other sages, the ancestors who delight in the oblation of fire,
and all the guardians of the quarters and deities, spoke in turn to the brāhmaṇa.
O best of Brahmins, by your curse the destruction of the king's fortune shall come to pass;
for the heart of Brahmins is always tender due to their asceticism. (28)
Forgive me; bestow your blessing and make that house pure.
For from whosever home a guest returns with his hopes frustrated, [that house is defiled]. (29)
The ancestors, the gods,
and the fire depart unsatisfied from him who looks upon a guest who has come to his house with a crooked glance.
Having given his own sin to him, he departs taking that man's merit;
the king did not rise due to the fault of his own pride, so please forgive him. (3.1)
The Brāhmaṇa who disregards another because of royal splendor or learning shall immediately be deprived of his prosperity, being excluded from his vows and his offerings. ||32||
His initiation shall become fruitless; he shall be destitute of wealth, sons, and so forth, and he shall even be deprived of his wife. Forgive this transgression of his. (33)
He who treats a guest, his parents, a deity, a learned man, a Brahmin, or a guru with contempt will certainly fall away from devotion in this world. (34)
He who, upon seeing a guest who is a Brāhmaṇa, does not rise to greet him, enters the womb of an elephant in the forest for seven births. (35)
Having quickly shown compassion, bestow auspicious blessings upon the king—whether he be a preceptor, a brahmin, or even an image of a deity. (36)
Having seen him, one should not fail to bow quickly; he would become easy to manage on this earth.
"Forgive us everything and accept our hospitality. (37)

One who shows disrespect to a guest shall share in the sin of those who kill women, those who kill cows, those who are ungrateful, those who violate the wives of their teachers, and likewise those who kill Brahmins. (38)
Having heard these words of the sage, the king questioned those sages:
"O best of yogis, tell me, what is the sin of those who kill women and others? (39)
Vasiṣṭha said: "O Indra among kings, listen; for that [penance] arises from the killing of a cow.
O King, in the case of intentional cow-slaughter, a man should wander to sacred pilgrimage sites for one year."
Subsisting on barley and barley-gruel, he should drink water from his hand;
thereafter, he should give a hundred divine cows along with sacrificial fees to the Brahmins.
One may indeed be released from sin by giving gifts or by feeding a hundred twice-born brahmins;
however, even when a penance has been performed, one is not released from all sins.
Due to the remainder of his evil deeds, he becomes miserable and is indeed a Cāṇḍāla;
the sin incurred by killing a woman is certainly twice that of killing a cow. (43)
He shall indeed dwell in Kālasūtra for sixty thousand years;
thereafter, he shall become a pig and a snake for seven births.
The sin incurred by one who commits the murder of a Brahmin is twice that of the murder of a woman;
indeed, he shall dwell for a hundred thousand years in the most terrible hell, Kubhīpāka.
O King of kings, the ungrateful person becomes a worm in excrement for a hundred years and a serpent for seven lifetimes;
the fault of an ungrateful person is four times that of killing a Brahmin.
O Indra among kings, no atonement has been ordained for those who are ungrateful.
O Indra among kings, it is certain that there are sixteen kinds of ungrateful people. (47)
When the Kṛta age, truth, merit, one’s own duty, austerity, commitment, generosity, and the protection of one’s own community are firmly established; ||48||
In service to the guru, in service to the gods, in rites for desired goals, in the worship of the twice-born, in daily obligatory duties, in trust, and in the bestowing of supreme dharma. ||49||
The most wicked person who kills these is remembered as ungrateful;
for various types of ungrateful people, there are likewise various hells.
Having made a vow in the form of an oath, he who kills truth and does not protect it is ungrateful;
he dwells indeed in the Kālasūtra hell for the duration of four yugas.
For seven births he was a crow, for seven births an owl;
thereafter he was a Śūdra afflicted with a great disease, and after that, he became pure.
Having performed a meritorious deed, he speaks only for the sake of increasing his fame;
that ungrateful person dwells indeed in the Taptakuṇḍa hell for three yugas.
In five births he was a frog, in three births a crab;
thereafter he was mute and greatly afflicted, and thereafter poor, and finally pure.
He who, having performed his own duty, destroys it by obstructing the practice of the *sandhyā*;
he who reviles the worship of Viṣṇu, the recitation of mantras, the offering of food (*naivedya*), and religious observances (*vrata*). ||55||
Devoid of devotion to the gods and other virtues, and shunning ancestral rites and the like,
that ungrateful person dwells in the Kumbhīpāka hell for the duration of an entire kalpa.
For seven births he becomes a Cāṇḍāla, for a hundred births a vulture, for a hundred births a pig, and thereafter he becomes a Cāṇḍāla once more. (57)
Furthermore, having gone to Raurava, he becomes a donkey for five births;
then, after that, a cat and a frog for five births each.
Having become a carrier of bulls, a Brahmin undergoes sufferings;
whether by means of a servant or even personally, that Brahmin who acts as a bull-carrier [reaps these consequences]. (59)
He should be understood as ungrateful, for he is considered a destroyer of merit;
the sin in constantly striking a bull is equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
By making a bull carry a load on its back, that sin becomes twofold;
so too for one who makes a bull, hungry or thirsty, pull a cart in the heat of the sun.
One incurs the sin of a hundred murders of Brahmins; of this there is no doubt.
One dwells indeed in Lālākuṇḍa for as long as the moon and sun endure.
There, he shall always have to consume excrement and drink urine;
furthermore, at the three junctions of the day, a servant of Yama shall strike him with a trident.
He who places a torch in his mouth or constantly cuts with a needle shall be born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Then the crow likewise became a crane for five births;
he was a vulture for five births, and a jackal for seven births.

Then [the fifth] is the poor Śūdra, and then the pure one who is severely ill; the unchaste noble woman, the violator of dharma, and the ungrateful person are proclaimed [as the remaining ones]. ||66||
That twice-born man who is the master of a low-caste woman, the master of an unchaste woman,
or is ungrateful is considered to dwell in Kṛmidaṃṣṭra for as long as fourteen Indras endure.
He constantly embraces that image made of heated iron;
consequently, that Śūdra shall remain miserable for a thousand years.
One who destroys the merits of those who have performed austerities is called ungrateful;
one who destroys the austerities practiced by others is called ungrateful. ||69||
For one who destroys a vow and for one who is ungrateful, there is the Kumbhīpāka hell for ten thousand years;
likewise for one who, having made a promise regarding a task, betrays the highest trust.
He who breaks his own promise is indeed ungrateful;
the Lord casts him into a heated iron cauldron and causes him to burn there for an eon.

Whatever various kinds of giving there are—whether the gift of a word, the gift of a material object, the giving away of a daughter, or the imparting of knowledge—he destroys them all through deceit. (72)
That person who, having made a promise or given his word, breaks it or destroys a social gathering, shall certainly dwell for ten thousand yugas in the Kālasūtra hell. (73)
One who neglects his duties, one who destroys social gatherings, one who strikes a guru, and one who beats a guru must remain in the Pāśakuṇḍa hell for ten thousand years.
That ungrateful person who kills his guru shall dwell for ten thousand years in a pit of fire;
one who seizes the property of a deity during a rite for the gods is called ungrateful.
One who seizes the means of subsistence belonging to gods or others, whether given by himself or by another,
shall remain impaled upon a stake for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the body.
He must consume glowing coals as food and drink heated urine;
he lies upon burning coals and is beaten by the servants of Yama. (77)
Then, having become a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years, he will thereafter be poor, wretched, and deprived of both land and offspring. (78)
A Śūdra who performs such acts becomes diseased and censurable; thereafter, after a period of time, he becomes pure.
He is excluded from rites performed for specific desires and is a destroyer of his own and others' wealth.

That lowest of men who destroys the fame of others as well as his own is ungrateful, and he is one who causes the destruction of the merit derived from sacrifices, charitable works, and other religious duties performed in the Kāmyaka forest.
Indeed, he shall dwell in a most terrible blind well until the end of the kalpa,
being devoured by mongooses, vultures, worms, and the like, and drinking heated alkaline water.
From this point on, he shall be a serpent for seven births and a crow for five; thereafter he becomes pure.
He who destroys the worship of the twice-born is considered a great ungrateful person.
He who seizes the property of a Brahmin, the property of a teacher, or even the property of a deity—
even such an ungrateful person shall dwell in a pit for an entire kalpa.
From that he becomes a drinker of spirits, from that a Śūdra, and from that pure;
yet he who destroys his daily duty is a greater ingrate than those.
Lacking devotion, he would not support his father, mother, or teachers; he would never bow to them even in the morning, and would repeatedly strike them with his words. (85)
Likewise, that unchaste woman who strikes her own husband with words—those who neglect the worship of those worthy of worship are proclaimed to be ungrateful. (86)
They shall dwell indeed in the fire-pit as long as the moon and sun exist;
thereafter, they become water-creatures for seven births, after which they become pure.
He who gives false testimony out of desire, anger, or likewise fear, commits the greatest sin; such an ungrateful person brings about the destruction of the entire world.
In the assembly, the ungrateful destroyer of merit speaks partiality;
indeed, he does so everywhere regarding the good deeds performed by everyone.
The act of killing for the sake of enjoyment is proclaimed as ingratitude; those who destroy merit are called destroyers of what has been done, for merit is always perishable.
Therefore, there is no ingratitude toward the eternal one known as Kṛṣṇa’s grace;
for that which is eternal is indeed worthy of merit, whereas that which is perishable is not worthy at all. 91.
A false witness, one who sides with a faction, a betrayer of trust, and those who destroy merit—
such a person will certainly dwell in the Sarpakuṇḍa for as long as a thousand Indras.
One who has been bitten by snakes eats their excrement and urine;
indeed, one who has been struck [by them] is born as a frog or a chameleon for seven lifetimes. (93)
Then, in the forest, [he becomes] a Śālmalī tree; then a mute Śūdra; thereafter he is pure.
[This refers to] approaching another's wife and so forth, and the non-mixing of the duties of others. 94.
Indeed, the practice of another's dharma is reckoned as ingratitude;
it is the obstruction of one’s own appropriate duties and the resorting to the duties of others. (95)
Ungratefulness indeed exists; such a person is like a *caṇḍāla*, for he shall dwell in the Kumbhīpāka hell until the end of a kalpa. (96)
Afterwards, he who approaches one who should not be approached becomes a eunuch; then, for seven births, he is afflicted with wasting leprosy, and thereafter he becomes a Śūdra, and finally pure.
He may even fall into a red-hot iron pin, and from that state become a eunuch;
having then become a Cāṇḍāla, and then a Śūdra, he finally becomes pure.
Having performed a distinguished gift, such as the giving away of a daughter or the bestowing of gold and other riches, he who destroys that gift is proclaimed to be ungrateful (kṛtaghna). ||99||
One who destroys what has been done for him and does not acknowledge what was performed for him is ungrateful;
O King, such a person is said to be ungrateful in sixteen ways in every respect.
Through the dishonor of a guest, ingratitude is born;
therefore, for the sake of removing that fault, you must honor the guest. 101.
Having brought him into the house, let him be honored and let his lotus-feet be served; let his grace be accepted and let the *pajjala* be drunk. (102)
Let the blessing of the guest be earned and likewise let the fault be wiped away;
then let you go to the forest, and thereafter let auspicious prosperity be regained.
Let the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Śrī, be remembered;
the infallible One will grant you once again auspicious prosperity and liberation.
Having spoken thus, all the sages departed for their own abodes;
Suyajña first bowed to that twice-born one and conducted him to his home.
Having propitiated him with repeated worship, he asked about his name, lineage, and so forth;
the sage replied that his own name was renowned as Sutapas.
His father was named Virūpa, and his father was Viśvarūpa;
Tvaṣṭṛ was his father, and Kaśyapa was his father as well.
His father was Marīci, and his father was Viśvasṛj himself;
O Lord of the Earth, I am the seventh person from Brahmā.
Mahādeva is my guru, the giver of knowledge and the bestower of excellent counsel;
the beloved deity Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my husband, lord, and master.

I meditate upon that lotus-foot; I have no desire for worldly prosperity, nor even for the states of living in the same world, sharing the same power, having the same form, or being in the proximity of the Lord of Rādhikā.
"I do not accept what is given by him without serving at his feet.
O King, having heard this from Suyajña regarding the arrival of the sages for his sacrifice, [he went to them]. 111.
I have come to cause you to attain a longing for devotion to Viṣṇu;
you have been solely favored by me, and have not been cursed by me now.
And though he was uplifted, he fell again into the terrible, deep ocean of worldly existence;
for holy places do not consist of water alone, nor are the gods made of clay or stone. (11.3)
Furthermore, O King, those devotees of Kṛṣṇa purify themselves merely by being seen, whereas others do so only after a long period of time;
therefore, depart from this house and bestow the kingdom upon your son.
Worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Rādhā; abandon everything else as perishable. O sinless one, by my curse, may you forever renounce your great kingdom.
Make this decaying body remain upon the earth through austerity;
be completely detached from the mind that is rich in the illusion of royal pomp.
By the command of the brahmin, the king adopted peace and renunciation;
with intense spiritual agitation, he inquired about the means of attaining Goloka.

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of King Suyajña’s Curse due to His Disrespectful Treatment and Harassment of an Ascetic Brahmin at the Conclusion of his Rājasūya Sacrifice; Furthermore, the Greatness of the Guest, the Sixteen Types of Ingratitude, and the Instruction Given by the Sages," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which Suyajña then said to Sutapas:
"O sage, tell me here: how and when is everything perishable? || 1 ||
"And likewise, tell me the supreme means for liberation that is intensely effective.
Having heard these words of the king, Sutapas, the knower of reality, spoke.
Listen, O King, to how everything born of nature is indeed perishable:
a vessel made of six palas of metal, deep and four finger-breadths wide. (3)
A vessel made of one māṣaka of gold, with holes [drilled] at intervals of four finger-breadths,
takes as long to become submerged in water as the time defined here as a *daṇḍa*.
Two *daṇḍas* make one *muhūrta*, and four of those make a *yāma*.
A day consists of eight *yāmas*, and a fortnight (*pakṣa*) consists of fifteen of those [days].
A month consists of two fortnights, and a year consists of twelve months;
indeed, what is a month for humans is a day and night for the ancestors.
The dark fortnight is declared to be the day, and the bright fortnight is proclaimed to be the night;
indeed, for humans, one year is the day and night of the gods.
O King, the northern course is day and the southern course is night;
and the lifespan of humans and other beings conforms to the sequence of the Yugas.
The Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali constitute the four yugas;
they consist of four, three, two, and one thousand [divine years] respectively, beginning with the Kṛta.
The transitional periods (sandhyāṃśaka) for these [ages] consist of eight hundred, six hundred, four hundred, and two hundred years respectively;
those [four ages] together comprise twelve thousand years.
Four yugas constitute a manvantara, which is seventy-one yugas;
these fourteen Manus belong to a single day of Brahmā.
As it is by day, so it is by night; thus the time of the Creator passes away, since twenty-eight Manus constitute a single day and night of Brahmā.
O King, the first Manu was Svāyambhuva, the son of Brahmā;
having received from Śaṅkara the knowledge of the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which is very difficult to obtain.
Having attained the service of Kṛṣṇa, he indeed went to Goloka;
so too did Svārociṣa Manu, the second son of Vahni.
Those two, Priyavrata’s sons, were the third and fourth Manus;
Raivata was born as the fifth, and Cākṣuṣa is declared the sixth.
Śrāddhadeva, the son of Sūrya and a devotee of Viṣṇu, is the seventh Manu;
Sāvarṇi, the son of Sūrya and a devotee of Viṣṇu, is the eighth Manu.
The ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi, who is devoted to the vows of Viṣṇu;
the tenth is Brahmasāvarṇi, who is proficient in the knowledge of Brahman.
And thereafter, Dharmasāvarṇi is remembered as the eleventh Manu;
and Jñānin Rudrasāvarṇi is remembered as the twelfth Manu. || 18 ||
This thirteenth Manu is Devasāvarṇi, whose nature is righteousness;
the fourteenth and final one is Candrasāvarṇi, the possessor of great knowledge.
As long as the lifespan of the Manus lasts, for that same duration do the Indras exist;
fourteen such Indras constitute one single day of Brahmā.
O King, that is one night of Brahmā; it is called the Brāhmī night. During that night of Brahmā, what is known as the minor dissolution (kṣudra-pralaya) occurs.
In this [period], ten worlds—including the gods and the Manus—are indeed destroyed;
thus, thirty such days and nights constitute a single month of Brahmā.
O King, a year of Brahmā is born from a thousand kalpas;
thus, the maximum lifespan of the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) extends to one hundred such years.
Upon the dissolution of Brahmā, there shall be one Vairāja Kalpa;
the lifespan of a Vairāja is one hundred years, after which his destruction occurs. (24)
That day belongs to Mahāviṣṇu, and he too has a duration of a hundred years;
thereafter, this very day of Pradhāna-Puruṣa comes to an end.
When one hundred years of that primordial person (prakṛtipuruṣa) have passed, it becomes a single day; indeed, after another hundred years, there is dissolution (laya).
Dissolved into the imperishable Brahman along with Māyā, this is the dissolution pertaining to Prakṛti;
she is called Rādhā-Prakṛti. (27)
"O King, liberation is the absolute dissolution [of the self], and that is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Having heard this, Suyajña quickly asked about the means of attainment. (28)
"What bestows liberation by which I may go to the eternal abode of Goloka?
Suyajña replied, "O one of great austerity, worship Rādhā, the beloved of Hari. (29)
Even Kṛṣṇa considers her words to be filled with love for Kṛṣṇa;
by serving her with grace, you will quickly go to Goloka.
By propitiating Śrī Kṛṣṇa, devotees go to the divine realm of the cows after a long time;
however, by serving Kṛpārādhā, they indeed go there without delay.
She who is a portion of Rādhā and your wife, known by the name Rāseśvarī,
that illustrious and devoted wife is your hidden Rādhā here.
Having performed the supreme vow of devotion to your wife and protected those virtues,
you shall conquer great death through the power of her who is a portion of Rādhā.

O King, it is especially because of my scriptural authority that I say this to you: worship according to dharma Rādhā, your wife, who is the Mistress of the Rāsa dance and a portion of [the Supreme]. 34.
"Behold this virtuous woman as she exists, with your divine eye.
Having said this to the king, he touched his eyes at that very moment.
He beheld his virtuous wife, devoted to her husband, in the form of Rādhikā;
becoming struck with wonder, he obtained the mantra of Rādhā.
"Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Rādhikā, the Queen of the Rāsa-dance.
Then he heard the duties of a husband devoted to his wife from Sutapas. (37)
As is Kṛṣṇa, so is Rādhā; the portions of Rādhā are the very forms of Kṛṣṇa.
Just as devotion to her husband is considered the highest ideal for a woman's body, so it is toward Kṛṣṇa. (38)
Likewise, regarding the duty of a devoted wife toward one born from portions of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā:
having risen in the morning, a true devotee should repeatedly remember Rādhikā. (39)
One should bathe him, worship him, adorn him, and feed him well;
one should serve him, satisfy him with desired gifts, and please him repeatedly.
One should perform the lustration ceremony, offer hymns of praise, perform the ritual sleep-induction, and perform the invocation;
thus, ever devoted to the vow of a faithful wife, one should worship Rādhā, whose very essence is Kṛṣṇa. ||41||
A house is not called a "home"; it is said that the wife is the home.
When enriched by her, who is a portion of Rādhā, it shines with splendor.
A housewife is indeed the fortune of the home; without her, the house is a mere cave.
But with a housewife, even a house pervaded by darkness shines brightly.
Even a dog, when joined with a mate, becomes a "lion of the village";
even a pauper, when with his wife, is counted as a member of a family.
Even a king, deprived of his beloveds, will be driven out from his home by a woman;
yet even a servant, when accompanied by his wife, is protected within the house.
He who has no virtuous wife at home who speaks kindly must go to the forest; for him, the house is just like the forest.
Alas, that house where there is no virtuous and beautiful wife should be considered a forest; for such a person, the forest is as good as home. (47)
For one who has no devoted wife, well-disciplined and capable of accomplishing her husband's tasks, the home is parched and devoid of affection, even if it be full of kinsmen and wealth. (48)
A house devoid of a wife is like a forest; a house with a wife is a true home.
Indeed, in rites for the gods and ancestors, it is the housewife who bestows merit upon the household. (49)
O King, all religious rites have their root in the wife; likewise, homes have their root in the wife.
All happiness for those living as householders in the home has its root in the wife.
Joy always has its root in the wife; auspiciousness has its root in the wife;
worldly existence has its root in the wife; and fragrance has its root in the wife. (51)
For householders, the jewel of women is indeed the foremost of all jewels;
as a lotus cannot exist without water, so a home cannot exist without a wife. (52)
O King, that wife of yours resides in your palace;
she is a portion of Rādhā, devoted to her husband, virtuous, chaste, and a beloved who enjoys all pleasures.
Rādhā has been honored by Kṛṣṇa through the dharma of devotion to his wife;
likewise, you too have been praised, so please perform worship with respect. (54)
When she is satisfied, she will indeed soon bestow heaven, liberation, and the divine abode.
Suyajña, the bull among sages, who had heard much, spoke in many ways concerning the devoted wife.

"O King of kings, what is the nature of one devoted to his wife? I wish to hear this; please tell me. Sutapas replied, having visualized his wife as the sovereign power (Īśvarī): 56. "What kind of person is a bull among those devoted to their wives? Tell me, for I wish to hear it. O Indra among kings, Sutapas spoke thus, having meditated upon his wife as the Sovereign Goddess.
Every morning one should constantly remember one's wife; one should meditate upon the wife who is dear to Hari.
In the morning, one should look at the face of one's wife, and only afterwards look at others.
One should have the wife bathe with auspicious waters and dress her well;
one should have her hair styled by female servants and others.
Or else, the husband himself should groom her hair and other features;
he should adorn her with perfumes and the like, bestowing upon her beauty and the marks of good fortune.
One should provide ornaments and apply a drop of collyrium;
one should feed them with water for drinking and the like, and offer and present betel-leaf.
Whatever she desires, he should give all of that and always please her;
he should massage her body and remove the woman's fatigue.
One should wash away her impurity and likewise massage her limbs;
one should reveal knowledge to her by reciting sweet stories and narratives. 62.
One should practice the ninefold devotion toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul;
one should provide a comfortable bed and delight the virtuous lady with amorous pleasure.
One should not speak with another woman, nor should one ever touch another;
one should certainly not look at the face of another, nor should one engage in conversation with another.
One should never think of another woman anywhere, nor should one have a mind attached to another;
one should not take the scent of another, nor hear the voice of another.
One who observes the vow of a wife should not look at the dancing and other performances performed by others; nor should he ever look at the bodies, breasts, or other limbs of another woman.
One should never accept water, food, or anything else taken by another;
nor should one wear clothes, oil, or similar items that have been touched by another.
One should not consume flowers and the like offered by another, nor even milk and such;
one should never sit with another woman in a vehicle or similar conveyance.
One should not walk along a path or similar places with another woman even for the sake of some purpose;
nor should one lie down together with another woman in a field, a garden, a marketplace, or the like. ||69||
A person devoted to his wife should not perform any task with another woman;
he should certainly not engage in union with another in places such as public assemblies, festivals, or halls.
One should never consume anything whatsoever that has been given by another;
one should never even stand upon grounds belonging to others.
One should not go for the purpose of bathing and so forth to another's bathing grounds or similar places;
one should neither look upon nor contemplate the beauty of another's form. ||72||
One should never consume food cooked by another;
one should not go outside at night, nor should one enter the house of another. (73)
O King, he should not stand on paths frequented by women or at crossroads;
nor should he listen to the music played by a woman during another's festival.
One should never cast a sidelong glance at another woman, nor should one indicate a secret rendezvous;
one should not praise another, nor should one sing of her virtues. (75)
In this way, indeed, one should practice renunciation of all one's own unjust ways;
that is truly the vow of a devoted wife, which, when fully realized, bestows liberation.
One should never eat before one's own wife, nor should one ever strike her;
one should never cause her to hear harsh words, nor should one treat her with anger or contempt. (77)
Having produced wealth through exertion, effort, occupation, other labor, agriculture, and the performance of service, [one should acquire] that which is ethical.
One should nourish one's own wife and not create any division regarding food;
one should fully satisfy her in amorous dalliance, adornment, service, and play. (79)
One should praise and eat with affection the water, food, and other offerings given by one's wife;
one should never take account of defects such as an excess of saltiness.
Thinking of it as nectar, one should indeed accept it and not treat it with contempt;
one should never coerce a woman who is unwilling, nor should one ever abandon a woman during her menses.
One should never awaken a sleeping woman, nor act with disregard toward one who is desirous; nor should one ever cause her distress, whether out of greed or by force.
In whatever manner she may become pleased, in that very manner the observer of the vow should act;
he should entrust all household property without exception to his wife.
One should offer oneself to her and always practice respect toward her;
one should well preserve the honor of the wife and must never speak with a term of endearment.

One should never oppress [them] by means of one's own powers, nor should one insult them through injustice; one should never revile them, transgress against them, or ever disregard the words of one's wife.
Always regarding his wife as the Great Goddess (Mahādevī), he should offer salutations;
he should bestow all objects of enjoyment upon her and must never say, "I have nothing. (86)
In the practice of service and at the beginning of the ritual sequence, one should not fall into a state of mental indifference;
just as Nārāyaṇa never enjoys anything at all without Lakṣmī. 87.
Just as Kṛṣṇa never eats anywhere without his chaste Rādhā, so too a man observing the vow should never eat anything at any time without his wife. 88.
Except for his own private parts and so forth, nothing should be looked at by another woman;
nor should even his own cheeks, face, and so on be kissed by another. (89)
His heart shall never be drawn away anywhere by another woman, nor shall he behave toward her in such a way;
even in a dream he shall not touch another, nor shall he look upon another.
One should perform rites for the gods and ancestors, such as those pertaining to the Dharma, together with one's wife;
one who is devoted to his wife should never conceal household affairs from her. (91)
Having informed his wife, he should indeed perform whatever task is to be done, but not alone;
nor should he practice religious vows and the like without the consent of his wife.
One should always be under the authority of one's wife for the sake of spiritual welfare, not for the sake of hell;
one should be dependent on her for the sake of liberation, but never for the sake of hell. (93)
One should always honor [the teacher] for the sake of happiness, never for the sake of affliction; one should place trust in a worthy vessel of confidence, not in unchaste women or the like. 94.
A husband should bestow his life, wealth, jewels, and so forth at the wife's disposal;
for the wife is always half of the husband, and likewise, the husband is half of the wife. (95)
Her husband is born within the cavity of her womb in the form of a son;
thus the wife is the one who consumes, the progenitor, the mother, and the nourisher. (96)
She must always be protected, always nourished, and always guarded with excellent things;
for in the wife lies the satisfaction of desire, and in her indeed is the purity of one who voids urine. (97)
Service to the wife is the highest austerity; through her, one obtains the nectar of conversation.
Indeed, for the husband, the mere presence of the mistress of the house is a form of meditative concentration.
Non-violence is the absence of malice; truth is not concealing that [truth];
being of one heart with one's wife is non-stealing, which is indeed never deception. (99)
The pursuit of desire for one's wife as much as desired, practicing celibacy while residing in the householder stage,
and the non-acceptance of all things for the sake of a wife constitute non-possession.
When she is asleep, he should be deeply asleep; when she is awake, he should be alert. When she has bathed, he should be pleased to bathe; when she has eaten, he should be fond of eating.
When she is yellowed, he is intoxicated by drinking; when she is sporting, he is a playful companion;
when she is adorned, he is rich in splendor; and when she is distressed, he is deeply sorrowful. (102)
When [the reflection] is unclear, he is not very bright; when she is happy, he is endowed with happiness;
when she is ill, his mind becomes dull; and when she is in full bloom, he is blossomed. (103)
When she smiled, her husband smiled beautifully; when she was satisfied, he was satisfied;
when she thought of him, his mind was broken; and when she observed her vows, he was likewise devoted to his vows.

If she remains steadfast in austerity, he should be devoted to austerity; if she performs virtuous deeds, he should be a performer of good deeds; and if she has died, he should follow her in death by ascending the funeral pyre and burning along with her.
Thus, a husband devoted to his wife may deliver his family;
likewise, he uplifts one hundred and one generations of himself and his wife.
O King, always worship Rādhikā, the mistress of the rāsa dance and my wife, who is a portion of me;
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇī, may there be obeisance to you, my wife.
Thus bowing and practicing the vow of a wife to a universal sovereign,
and uplifting the entire world, he goes at the end to the imperishable Brahman.
Having drunk the water from the hand of his wife, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
having obtained a son who has entered his wife’s vessel, he is honored by the ancestors.
By attaining the supreme vehicle of the Consort, the highest state is reached;
indeed, as many water-tirthas as there are born of the earth, forests, and mountains—
All these—dharma, vows, austerity, burnt offerings, recitation, Vedic study, and humility—indeed rest upon a wife who is devoted to her husband. (111)
Generosity, merit, assistance, service, and even blessings—all these exist within the body of one's wife, provided she is served with sincere devotion. (11.2)
She is said to be the savior of her husband, and he is the savior of her;
those two are the saviors of their entire lineage from the bondage of worldly existence. || 113 ||
Therefore, the vow of a wife must be observed; for that alone is true celibacy (brahmacarya), since it eternally brings about the attainment of Brahman and bestows the abode of bliss.
All the gods, sages, goddesses, and virtuous wives devoted to their husbands dwell within the body of the wife; and there, Brahman dwells as well.
And a man who observes the vow toward his wife is undoubtedly a form of Viṣṇu;
just as Kṛṣṇa is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa) and the presiding deity of all living beings. 116.
He is the savior of all and remains untainted by actions;
likewise, the Supreme Lord is another who is devoted to his wife and is the deliverer.
Upon merely beholding him, the fires rise up with devotion;
so too do the supernatural powers, the efficacy of yoga, and all lordly powers without exception.
In her resolve, all things always become fruitful, just as with Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa himself, devoted to his wife, dwells within the vow of a chaste woman.
O King, worship the virtuous Rāseśvarī, the beloved born from a portion of Rādhā,
just as Dharmadeva, devoted to his vows, worshipped his beloved wife Mūrti.
"O beloved Kamalā, just as Manu enjoyed Śatarūpā, so too should you honor him who is devoted to his wife"; having spoken thus, that one of great austerity fell silent.

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of King Suyajña’s Instruction on the Dharma of the Vow of Devotion to His Wife by the Sage Sutapas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said: How did that King Suyajña, devoted to his wife, attain liberation after chanting this hymn? Tell me what kind of austerity he performed. (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: That Suyajña, devoted to his wife and fond of austerity, went to Puṣkara accompanied by his wife and received the mantra of Rādhikā, which he then recited.
The king constantly recited the mantra "Oṃ rādhāyai svāhā," meditated upon Rādhā, and performed her worship with great devotion.
She has the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, with a radiance equal to ten million moons; her face is like the full moon of autumn, and her eyes are like autumn lotuses.
Her lips are like a ripe bimba fruit, she is resplendent with a row of pearl-like teeth,
her face is bright with a gentle smile, and she is adorned with necklaces of jewels and other ornaments.
She wears garments as white as fire, adorned with grace for the sake of favoring her devotees;
she is graced with jeweled armlets and bracelets, and resplendent with jeweled anklets.
Her ears were beautifully adorned with silver ornaments shining like jeweled earrings;
her cheeks possessed the luster of the sun’s radiance, and she was resplendent with a halo of brilliance.
Adorned with jeweled necklaces, radiant with a crown and diadem, beautiful with jeweled rings, and graced by jeweled bracelets; || 8 ||
She was adorned with a heavy braid of hair woven with garlands of *mālatī* flowers;
her limbs were in perfect proportion to her beauty, and she shone as the most excellent of all embodied beings. || 9 ||
Her forehead was adorned with a tilaka made of musk, and she was worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
she was radiant with the splendor of her auspicious fortune for Kṛṣṇa, and her very nature was the life-breath of Kṛṣṇa.
I worship the Queen of the Rāsa dance, who bestows devotion to Kṛṣṇa, who is peaceful, who belongs to Viṣṇu, who is affectionate toward Kṛṣṇa, and who is seated upon a jeweled throne in the Rāsa.
Having meditated thus, he indeed offered her the sixteen services:
a seat, clothing, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), perfumes, and unguents.
Incense, a lamp, beautiful flowers, bathing water, jeweled ornaments, fifty-six varieties of excellent food offerings, betel leaf, and scented water. (13)

The king of devotees, with heartfelt devotion, offered the honey-mixture (madhuparka) which is equal to jewels, along with the sixteen types of services, as well as one hundred and eight [other offerings].
"O worshiper of Kṛṣṇa, grant me devotion to Kṛṣṇa and service to Kṛṣṇa. Having thus offered this plea for exemption, she bowed down to the Supreme Goddess.
By worshipping that Supreme Goddess on the full moon day of Kārtika,
one attains immovable prosperity and obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
A woman who meditates upon her with devotion shall attain the good fortune of her husband;
she goes to Goloka and is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. (17)
Thus Suyajña constantly chanted his prayers and performed worship;
he offered praise and meditated, repeatedly reflecting upon the names and their meanings. (18)
"Rāṃ indeed bestows prosperity; Dhāṃ leads to steadfastness at the feet.
'I bow to Kṛṣṇā, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation'—thus he meditated. (1.9)
Having subsisted on leaves, flowers, and fruits, the lord of men performed most difficult penance;
for a hundred years, he made everything consist of Rādhā.
Rādhā, being pleased, appeared visibly before the king;
then the Queen of the Rāsa dance spoke appropriately to him, Suyajña.
O King, you have always observed the vow of a devoted wife like Kṛṣṇa;
you have served me constantly, and I have been exceedingly pleased by your devotion. (22)

The Mistress of the Rāsa dance has been constantly worshipped, saluted, and meditated upon by you; likewise, the vow of devotion to your wife has been preserved by you without break, just as it was by Kṛṣṇa.
Always regarding her as equal to a flower in her delicacy,
you protected her and fully satisfied her with garments, ornaments, cosmetics, and other such articles.
She was constantly nourished by gifts of food, drink, and excellent enjoyments;
and perceiving her state of pregnancy, she was protected by the granting of her heart's desires. (25)
She was gazed upon without obstacle during states such as childbirth and the like;
yet she was perfectly delighted by all beings even amidst conditions such as royal power and the rest. ||26||
Maintaining patience while shrouded in darkness, she was consoled by being held upon his lap;
even in the presence of conditions such as fever, she was not separated from him for even a moment. (27)
O King, even in times of calamity, you did not abandon me from your side;
indeed, having endured all that was most terrible, you were never truly joined with misfortune.
Never have you caused me to fall from righteousness during times of impurity or the like;
nor have you ever joined me with futile desire while I was pregnant. (29)
Never, even when she was with her children, was she ever deprived of her possessions by you;
nor was she ever subjected to hardship when her beloved was hungry or thirsty. (1.444.30)
She was never distressed by any confusion or excessive anxiety;
she was honored with her whole being at the proper time and with appropriate materials. (3.1)
O King, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was thus pleased by my service—he who is saluted, gratified, and propitiated everywhere by the giving of happiness. (32)
Sent by her very self, I, Rādhā—the mistress of the rāsa dance who bestows the fruit of the Pannīvratam—have come to lead you away. 33.

Whatever has been caused to be done for my sake, or whatever has been done [by me], it bestows its fruit; whether performed with goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), or even darkness (tamas), it is offered unto me.
Through the yoga of Kṛṣṇa, I render all that devoid of qualities (nirguṇa):
desire, anger, as well as relish, affection, greed, pride, and so forth. (35)
They were born and even fashioned for my sake, yet they are devoid of qualities, because I, indeed, am the quality-less wife of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (36)

Then, through the play of Kṛṣṇa, the entire world—including myself who have attained union with Him, as well as the virtuous Pativratā and those devoid of qualities—becomes truly active once more. 37.
If Kṛṣṇa did not act, the world would be devoid of ritual activity;
for all the rites of husband and wife originate from Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. (38)
Even those who appear similar may be devoid of virtue and merely shackles;
likewise, Brahmā, though joined with Brāhmī, creates the world from the beginning. (39)
Day does not exist without night, nor indeed does the self exist without the intellect;
Brahman does not exist without the Brāhmī, nor indeed does Kṛṣṇa exist without Kṛṣṇā.
Sound does not exist without power, nor indeed do attributes without devotion;
Kṛṣṇa does not exist without Rādhā, and being-consciousness does not exist without bliss. 41.
O Indra among kings, since you have been purified in every way by my vow,
come now with your wife to the black Goloka by means of a celestial chariot.
O best of kings, I was propitiated by you through all my vows when this Rāseśvarī was overcome by fever. (43)
Previously, she did not take water or food for one month;
nor did you yourself consume water or food for that same single month. (44)
Even though you were healthy, you maintained your vow of devotion to your wife;
yet whenever there was fine food to be eaten at the time of childbirth and other such occasions, it was abandoned by your wife.
Furthermore, O King, whatever else was enjoyable and so forth has already been abandoned by you, whether in times of prosperity or adversity, and in whatever situation you may find yourself.
Having left his wife and not entrusted her with anything, he made no use of it;
O King, you conduct yourself like a virtuous man, having placed everything under the care of your wife.
The inexhaustible merit of your giving and other virtues performed through the agency of your wife—that very merit has been made by me to bear eternal fruit for your sake alone. (48)
When the Cāturmāsya vow was observed by your wife, the Queen of Rāsa,
you never ate anything at all without first informing her.
Indeed, whatever difficult vows were observed by your wife during the months of Kārtika, Śrāvaṇa, Māgha, and Vaiśākha— 50.
And whatever was given away there by the Queen of the Rāsa dance was likewise never accepted by you, who are entirely devoted to your wife.
Whatever restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) were practiced by your wife, those same ones were practiced by you as well for that same duration of time. ||52||
The baths, gifts, recitations, and fire-offerings performed by her have been performed by you;
whatever was intended by her has all been determined by you as well. (5.3)
