No other woman has been touched by you out of desire, nor has one been looked upon with lust;
even the maidservants and laborers have been protected by you like daughters. (54)
The subjects—both maidens and young women—were looked upon like disciples;
daughters-in-law, wives, and mothers were honored like goddesses. (55)
You have paid homage to the virtuous, truthful, and auspicious women endowed with yoga;
you have protected the helpless widows and female mendicants like a father. (56)
The female dancers are traditionally considered to be the many-formed Heroines;
they are worshipped like the wives of the Gurus, being Vaiṣṇavīs and Sāṃkhya-yoginīs. (57)
Student women were always regarded as equal to Sarasvatī;
indeed, those observing the vow of celibacy were seen as purified by sacred fords like the Gaṅgā. (58)
Thus, O Suyajña, all those women were permeated by the nature of Brahman;
they were beheld by you, O King, while you were a mountain-king devoted to the vow of fidelity to your wife.
Others were freed from their debts, and others were well-delivered from their transgressions; others were removed from suffering, and indeed, other women were made devotees of Viṣṇu.
"You are always blessed, O King; blessed is the beloved Rāseśvarī;
and blessed is my own partial incarnation (aṃśasvarūpa), by the attainment of which you have reached liberation. (61)
He has placed in me his trust, his choice, his entrustment, his humility, and steadiness of mind; he has shown favor toward me, free from all hostility.
No one else will ever observe such a vow as mine;
this vow of mine regarding my wife, which bestows liberation when observed, has been fulfilled by you.
O King, your ancestors have been delivered, and your subjects have been delivered by you;
indeed, everything—whether animate or inanimate—in both the kingdom and the forest, has been delivered.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Rādhikā, the Queen of the Rāsa dance, took Suyajñaka and [her consort], both possessing divine bodies, upon her celestial chariot and departed for Goloka. (65)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the vow of the wife has been clearly explained to you.
By reciting or hearing this, the observer of the vow shall attain Goloka. (66)

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Chastity," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning how Rādhā, the Queen of the Rāsa dance, took King Suyajña—the protector of the dharma of chastity—and his wife in a celestial chariot and departed for Goloka.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of Tārā, the wife of her guru, who was devoted to her husband;
though she was forcibly enjoyed by the Moon against her will, she did not fall from her chastity due to her devotion to her husband.
Atri was the son of Brahmā, and his son was Niśākara;
having performed the Rājasūya sacrifice, he indeed became the Moon.
Once, the Moon, intoxicated by his own excellence, went to the bank of the Ganges;
there he beheld Tārā, the wife of his preceptor, who was devoted to her husband and firm in her virtue.
Well-bathed, beautiful, and charming, with full and elevated breasts, slender-waisted, handsome, with beautiful teeth and a delicate form. || 4 ||
She was a young woman dressed in fine garments and adorned with golden ornaments,
with a drop of musk together with a drop of sandalwood paste below it.
She is radiant with a beautiful forehead-mark in the center of her brow by means of a drop of vermilion;
she is white as the moon, yet possesses a golden luster, with red eyes and a heart filled with passion.

Having bathed, she was going to her own home— she whose face was like the full moon of autumn, whose lower lip was like a ripe bimba fruit, who was virtuous, and who moved with the gait of an elephant in rut.
Seeing her in that solitary place, he was instantly afflicted by love;
casting aside shame and blocking her path, he spoke to her.
Salutations to you, O beautiful Brahmin lady, of lovely form and divine nature!
Stay for a moment, O most excellent one; I bow down at your feet.
Indeed, through union with virtuous women such as you, there is the destruction of sin;
know that good fortune will arise and that this is the inner intent of my mind.
"O virtuous lady, if my mind has reached a state of overflowing passion, I desire to make you my companion while we lie upon our beds at night. (11)
If you are indeed able to bring peace by granting me sexual pleasure even once, then I shall abandon you and depart; act accordingly.
"If you do not give me the gift of love, I shall take you away;
having indeed carried you off by force, I will certainly depart. (1.3)
"Aha! You have been appointed by the ascetic preceptor of the gods;
how could that pleasure of sexual union bring you peace? (14)
"I am Candra; my kingdom is visible directly in heaven.
Either come there, or remain here for twenty-two years. (15)
Your youth passes fruitlessly with you as an aged master;
Bṛhaspati remains lost in thought, both in sleep and in waking.
Moreover, your mind's desire is one thing, while the preceptor's intended action is another;
when the objects of two are so different, what joy can there be in their union? (17)
Or rather, let the fortunate young woman rejoice right there upon a bed of vāsantī flowers, anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste. (18)
Having spoken thus, intoxicated by passion, he fell again at her feet;
but the devoted wife, her path blocked by the moon, spoke to him.
"You are my disciple; Tārā, the wife of your guru, shall be like a mother to you.
O lustful one, are you not ashamed to speak thus? How is it that you have become blind?"
"O Moon, I am not a lustful woman; I am a virtuous ascetic.
O wicked son, I shall become your pure and purifying mother. (21)
"You have twenty-seven wives; what more do you need from me? Give me your heart and go in peace; what use have you for a virtuous wife? (22)
"Due to your misfortune, you were born here; your birth and life are in vain.
Shame on you, who thirst for the beloved of another! All your meritorious deeds are rendered useless. (23)
"I am a wretched ascetic who has taken refuge with wicked ascetics;
that king of yogis, Bṛhaspati, is worthy of me and shall grant me liberation. (24)
If you, who are like a paramour and conquered by base desires,
destroy my chastity, you shall become seized by consumption.
Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of the pride of the wicked, will destroy your pride.
Abandon your resolve toward me; truth shall bring you well-being.
Having spoken thus, as Tārā was departing from his side, the Moon seized her by force by the hand, took her to his chariot, and went to heaven.
Tārā wept and wailed aloud; she made the sun her witness, as well as Dharma, Vāyu, Earth, Fire, Space, Aja, Water, and Acyuta.
Taking the water contained in the jar in her hand, the chaste Tārā, devoted to her husband, strove with rage to turn the moon into ashes. ||29||
"At this moment, you must not reduce me to ashes by the voice from the sky;
everyone experiences the fruit of their actions, and thus has the fruit come to you."
Listen, O virtuous and chaste girl; you have done this unknowingly. When you were ten years old and living in your father’s house, at that time— (3.1)
At that time, a pair of dogs and a pair of humans were seen by you in your hermitage embracing one another;
they were then struck by you with both a staff and a stone.

"Since you did not attain the cessation of desire, but were instead separated and driven away by the insatiability of desire, you have now been cursed by that void [state] with its corresponding speech. (33)
"O wicked woman, just as you cause this separation from my husband, so too shall there come to be a separation for you from your own husband. (34)
Just as another dog will bite me, so too will it bite you;
like another dog, this calamity will certainly fall upon you.
Two small insects, or two animals, or two birds, or even two humans of different castes who are attached to sensual pleasures must never be separated from one another. (36)
Whether they are righteous or unrighteous, those who do not obtain satisfaction of their desires should never be separated from that satisfaction by the wise. (37)
For those who create obstacles to pleasure, there will be the loss of a wife or the loss of a husband;
or else separation or a great disease shall arise—of this there is no doubt. (38)
The fire arising from insatiable desire reduces obstacles to ashes;
likewise, O Tārā, you have performed this deed—indeed, experience its fruit. (39)
Otherwise, that action of yours will not be well-done; for he who gives suffering to another in every respect performs no good deed. (1.445.40)
The Teacher Nārāyaṇa himself gave suffering to him;
listen further, O Tārā, to what was done for you by your Lord in the past. 41.
Bṛhaspati, Utathya, and Saṃvarta—these three were all sons of Aṅgiras, and they had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. ||42||
Bṛhaspati gave no portion of the inheritance whatsoever to his youngest son Saṃvarta, because Saṃvarta was a mendicant.
O Bṛhaspati, this household fortune of his has been consumed by his sighs;
it is being carried away by another who possesses a form like yours. Do not grieve over this.
Out of lust, Bṛhaspati seized Satī, the pregnant wife of Utaṅka Madhyama, who was his brother’s wife.
He who, out of lust, would take the wife of his brother—whether she be willing or unwilling—obtains the sin of a thousand murders of Brahmins following his death. ||46||
He surely goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell for as long as a kalpa;
thereafter, he is born again as a worm in excrement for thousands of millions of years.
Then he becomes a worm in a vagina, then a vulture for a hundred births, then a dog;
and after that, having become a pig, he is born as a man devoid of women. 48.
An acquired karma that has not been experienced does not perish; it must simply be endured, as was the sin of Bṛhaspati’s abduction of Utathya’s wife. 49.
"There must be a reason for your seizing him; do not reduce Candra to ashes!
If you do so, you will incur a second sin of Brahman-murder."
"Therefore, O Tārā, may it come to pass according to destiny; bring about peace.
Having been addressed thus by the voice from the sky, she ceased speaking and did not utter a curse. (51)
The virtuous Satī, devoted to her husband, forcibly took refuge with Candra;
though she was unwilling, the Lord of Night repeatedly enjoyed her by force. ||52||
In heaven, which is full of bliss, in the beautiful Puṣkara, in the Puṣpaka forest,

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

For ten thousand years, King Candrāṅgada enjoyed many worldly pleasures together with his wife Sīmantinī.
She gave birth to eight sons and one daughter of beautiful countenance;

Day by day she attained good fortune from the lunar day (Induvāsara);

Whether in heaven, in the true world of Brahmā, in the netherworld, or among women,
if devotion to one's husband is preserved, it brings about all perfections.
Always regarding her husband as the very form of Kṛṣṇa and meditating upon him,
the virtuous woman should practice the duty of devotion to her husband, which is equal to the wish-fulfilling tree.
Indeed, for women who are dependent on others and whose lives are devoted to desire, their bodies are the abode of sin; yet they bestow even greater merit than that. (85)
Evil is an excess of desire, while merit is service at every step; service to one's husband is service to Kṛṣṇa, as is the practice of vows, giving, and other such duties. ||86||
Service to guests, service to the virtuous, service to cows at every step, and service to sinless offspring who are of the nature of Brahman—[these are the highest duties]. 87.
Protecting the household, service, cooking food and other items over the fire, performing the Vaiśvadeva ritual, and feeding the destitute, dogs, and others—these indeed constitute service. ||88||

Dependent on her husband and free from worldly desire, she is beautifully adorned by virtuous qualities and the like; through such service, a woman always gains infinite merit.
Therefore, one should practice devotion to one's husband, for it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how Candrāṅgada’s husband, though submerged in the Yamunā and carried away to the netherworld by Nāga maidens due to the miraculous power of his wife Sīmantinī—a devoted wife of Kṛṣṇa—was recovered once again," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Kṛṣṇa is always pleased by the dharma of devotion to one's husband;

This being so, even that which is inconceivable arises through the power of truth;

Thus ends the four hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Sāmavān, the Son of the Sārasvata Brahmin, Who Went to the King of Vidarbha Out of a Desire for Wealth for the Expenses of His Marriage; How He Was Honored by the Chaste Sīmantinī, Thinking Him to Be a Girl Disguised as a Beggar, and the Attainment of Another Son by His Father," in the first section on the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of Pārvatī’s devotion to her husband for the sake of a son,
which Satī herself manifested in the midst of the gods at the conclusion of her vow.
Himālaya gave his daughter Pārvatī to Śaṅkara;
Hara then took his pleasure with Śivā upon a couch on the bank of the Narmadā.

they stood at the door just before the moment of the emission of semen.
Those gods, who were destroyers of pleasure, invoked Mahādeva;
as Maheśa was rising up, his seed fell upon the ground.
Indeed, gold and silver were produced there from that [seed].
Then, because her seed had not reached the womb, Satyā grieved over it.
"Since the gods have created this obstacle, therefore may all the gods also always be destroyers of pleasure and possess fruitless virility. || 7 ||
Having spoken thus to Śaṅkara, she, distressed by the interruption of her pleasure, said: "The breaking of sexual union is one sorrow, and the second is the spilling of semen. (8)
But the third sorrow, which is a sorrow exceeding all others, is childlessness;
therefore, O Śaṅkara, act in such a way that I may have sons. (9)
Having heard that, Śaṅkara said: "O beloved, always endowed with devotion to Hari, perform for one year the meritorious vow known as Puṇyaka."
"Therefore, the fruit of a son will certainly be yours here;
that vow is merit-bestowing, a giver of happiness, and like a wish-fulfilling tree. (11)
As the Jahnavi is among rivers, as Sri Hari is among the gods,
so am I among the devotees of Vishnu, and as you are among celestial women.
Just as Lakṣmī is among riches and gold is among things called wealth, so too is this vow of merit the foremost among vows of virtuous conduct. (13)
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is among the castes, Badarīvana is among sacred fords, the Pārijāta is among flowers, and the leaf of Tulasī is among leaves; 14.
Just as the eleventh day is foremost among lunar days and the Sun among the weekdays, so too is Mārgaśīrṣa among the months and the spring among the seasons. || 15 ||
He is like the year among years, like the Kṛta age among the ages;
he is like the teacher of knowledge among those worthy of honor, and like one's own mother among all gurus. || 16 ||
She was like a virtuous wife to those who have attained [their goal], like the heart to the trusting,
like a jewel among riches, and like a husband to those who are dear.
He was like Suta among kinsmen, like the wish-fulfilling tree among trees, like the mango fruit among fruits, and like Saurāṣṭra among countries. || 18 ||
Vṛndāvana is among forests as Rādhikā is among women;
as Kāśī is among cities, so is Kaṃbharā among Lakṣmīs.

Just as the sun is among the luminous bodies, as the lotus-born Brahmā is among the lords of the quarters, as the moon is among the rulers of the night, and as the god of love is among those who cause infatuation; ||| 1.450.20 ||
Just as the Vedas are among sciences, as Kapila is among the virtuous, as Hanumān is among monkeys, and as the face is among the fields of the senses; 21.

it is like falsehood among sins, and like a mother among sinners. (24)
Just as the dedication of one's merits is the best among all tasks, and service to the virtuous is the best among duties;

Just as clarified butter is among products of the cow, as the tree is among ascetics, as nectar is among edible things, and as rice is among grains; ||26||
Just as water is among purifiers and fire is among cleansing agents, so is the female form among all forms, and sweet speech among pleasant things. (27)
Vainateya is the foremost among birds, Airāvata among elephants, Sanatkumāra among yogis, and Nārada among the celestial sages (devarṣis). ||28||
Just as Citraratha is the preceptor of the Gandharvas, as he is among the wise, so is Śukra among the poets, and the Saṃhitā among poetic compositions. ||29||
As the ocean is among those possessing currents, as the earth is among those who endure, as liberation is among fruits, and as peace is among all prosperities; ||1.450.30||
Just as the syllable Om is among purifiers, so is the Vaiṣṇava among castes;
and just as Prakṛti is among nourishers, so is the mantra of Kṛṣṇa among mantras.
As Sarasvatī is among the learned, as Gāyatrī is among the meters, as Kubera is the foremost of the wealthy, and as Vāsuki is among the serpents; ||32||

The gods said: "Protect righteousness, O faithful one, and fulfill your vow. (75)
"We shall make you full-hearted once your vow is completed," the sages said to her; [and she replied,] "O Śambhu, grant a sacrificial fee to the brāhmaṇa."
"O knower of dharma, while I am present, no misfortune shall befall you.
Sanatkumāra said, "Give me the auspicious sacrificial fee. (77)
"If you do not [grant] the entire fruit of my vow, I shall abandon it; I myself shall obtain the fruit," Śivā said, whereupon the priest began to carry away her husband. (78)
O gods, what would I gain from that vow, or what from sacrificial fees, or even from a son or from dharma, when everything is being led away? (79)
Whence can there be fruit, and whence a tree, if the seed does not exist?
That earth is indeed fruitless; without a seed, it cannot yield a harvest.
Just as all annual cultivation is fruitless without seed, what is the purpose of the body after one has exerted effort and cast off the vital breath? (81)
O lords of the gods, what is the use of eyes devoid of the power of sight? To virtuous women, however, a husband is superior even to a hundred sons. (82)
If the husband is to be given away for the sake of a vow, what is the use of that vow or even of a son?
For a son belongs to the lineage of the husband; he always has the husband as his root. (83)
Where the root has become corrupted, its activity brings about loss;
regarding this, Viṣṇu said to Satī: "In that case, the husband is always superior to the son. (84)
"The supreme duty belongs to the master; when he is lost, what is there for the master?
Brahmā said: "O daughter, it is true that the supreme duty indeed belongs to the master. (85)
There is no duty higher than dharma; truth is considered the highest vow.
Truth is action accompanied by sacrificial fees; do not let your vow fall away.
And Śivā said: "In the Vedas, the word 'sva' denotes wealth;
he who possesses that is the owner, and he is called wealthy. (87)
In this world, wealth is indeed the highest dharma, and from that comes the vow of truth;
superior to those is the husband, the master, for his lordship therein is eternal. (88)
Therefore, for those who possess wealth, a guest is the supreme master;
I am indeed his wealth, having been offered by my father in the past. (89)
"I am of the nature of a gift and possess the ownership of Śiva; yet Śiva does not belong to me.
How can there be a gift without ownership?"—thus do the gods and others speak in this matter. (1.450.90)
Dharma said: "A wife is always considered the half-body of her husband;
the couple is but a single form, and by oneself, one can offer oneself. (91)
Satī said: "Mastery over me has come to pass, as well as lordship;
yet the cessation of lordship would be capable of bringing about the end of that mastery. (92)
Therefore, I am not fit to hand over my husband here;
for it has never been heard in the sacred tradition that a husband is given away by a woman as a gift.
The gift of a daughter is prescribed in the Vedas as the proper sequence for the son-in-law;
how then could there be any order for giving a boon to the father of the eldest when he is the one seeking the bridegroom? (14)
The gods said: "O wise one, we have indeed placed our trust in you;
perform your duty by accepting this master's fee prepared for the merit-rite. (95)
"That which is heard in the Śruti is indeed Dharma, while that which is contrary to it is Adharma.
To this, Satī replied: "Without the conduct of the world, the Veda is utterly powerless. (96)
"In the Vedas, it is said that among Prakṛti and Puruṣa, Puruṣa is the superior Lord. How then can I give away my Lord? I am but a girl; what shall I say? (97)
Then Bṛhaspati said: "Creation is fashioned from both;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the creator of both, for Prakṛti and Puruṣa are equal. (98)
Satī said: "He is indeed a portion of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
women, however, are portions of Mūlaprakṛti (the primordial nature). Therefore, the male is the superior. (99)
"But as for a man here, my husband is Sadāśiva, the Supreme Brahman.
How can a husband be given away by me? Let the deities speak on this matter."
While this discourse was underway, a celestial chariot radiant with gold arrived; then the four-armed Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, appeared there.
Having descended and stood in the midst of the assembly, he was honored by everyone;
he said to Gaurī, "O Satī, what you have spoken is indeed just."
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the wife of the sacrificer are given by the patron;
in that regard, it is indeed a price paid to the Brahmin, not something dear to the sacrifice itself.
The wife of another is never given by one person to another;
whatever gold, silver, or wealth is given for that purpose is given solely for the sake of money.
In the giving of a wife, the giving of a son, the giving of oneself, or the offering of oneself to a husband, only by performing the gift of a cow does the rite become complete. || 105 ||
As cows are the body of Viṣṇu, so too is Śiva the body of Viṣṇu;
and Dakṣiṇā, being the very essence of value, is given as the body of Viṣṇu.
O Śivā, when the vow is completed, give an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
then, having given the appropriate price once more, you shall take back your Lord.
Having been addressed thus at the conclusion of the oblation, she gave Śiva the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Saying "May there be well-being," Kumāra accepted it in the assembly of the gods.
Satī said: "O Brahmin, take this wealth—a hundred thousand cows—or whatever else you desire;
give back my husband, and then I shall indeed bestow gifts."
"Indeed, without my husband, I am not capable of performing any other ritual act;
furthermore, Sanatkumāra told me that I have no need for cows."
What use have I for jewels or wealth, or for the virtuous? My purpose is that of a disciple, one who has renounced all and is a wandering ascetic (avadhūta).
"But since that has been obtained by me from you, I will not give Śaṅkara to you;
for the desired fruit belongs only to the performer of the rite, and one has independence over one's own property. (1.12)
Let others say whatever they wish; I have no need for cows.
Placing the naked one before me, I shall wander through the three worlds. (11.3)
"This is the cause of the smiles of the groups of boys and girls.
Having said this, Sanat indeed caused Śiva to sit down by his side.
Then Pārvatī rose up, overwhelmed with grief, and said:
"My husband has not been regained; the fruit of my vow has not been attained. (1.15)
"Being a virtuous woman, I shall produce fire from my body here.
At that, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there, and the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself appeared.
Suddenly, the Lord appeared in person and, embracing her, restrained her;
and Satī, having seen the Blessed One, descended from her celestial chariot.
Having warded him off, she shone as she was gazed upon in the midst of the assembly;
Pārvatī, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the gods, praised him within her heart.
O Kṛṣṇa, you have restored me to life; O Śambhu, grant me Śambhu [Śiva] as my husband; O Lord, grant me the fruit [of my devotion]: a son such as yourself. || 1.1.9 ||
Thus addressed, Śrī Hari caused Śaṅkara to be bestowed upon Satī;
he gave wealth to the family priest and likewise sacrificial fees to the Brahmins.
Having completed her vow and then fed everyone,
she thereafter ate together with her husband and then offered him betel.
Then all the gods and others, having been honored, departed for heaven;
meanwhile, Satī took her pleasure with Śambhu upon the couch, while he had assumed the form of a brahmin.
Kṛṣṇa arrived there, and an old mendicant said:
"O mother, give me alms," and he spoke thus again and again. (123)
Śambhu, having risen quickly from the bed after emitting his seed, went swiftly outside;
however, it fell upon the body of Satī.
The mass formed from that energy became black;
Satyā quickly became a child who appeared just like Kṛṣṇa. || 125 ||
Thus, although Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself had attained the status of Gaṇeśa,
Durgā, by virtue of her devotion to her husband, never abandoned him.
The husband is a god, the husband is a nourisher, and the giver of the next world;
the husband is the supreme lord, the very root of the lineage consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth. (127)
Even at the loss of her own life, she did not abandon her beloved husband;
though he had been seized for the sake of a sacrificial fee, once captured, he was never released.
In this way, a virtuous wife who is dear to her husband obtains a son like Kṛṣṇa through the grace of her husband; O Lotus-born One, what more need be said? 129.
Whoever hears or even reads this narrative of Satī’s vow and her steadfast devotion to her husband shall obtain a son and good fortune.

Thus ends the four hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Pārvatī’s Meritorious Vow, the Power of Her Chastity for the Sake of Śambhu’s Dakṣiṇā, the Dialogue, and the Attainment of a Son through Gaṇeśa," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the story of Śabarī’s devotion to her husband, which is filled with all manner of wonders; for what cannot be accomplished for the sake of a husband? (1)
She who is virtuous and entirely devoted to the satisfaction of her husband and other duties always triumphs in this world; for dharma, when protected, protects.
There was a servant of Siṃhaketu, the king of the Pañcālas, named Caṇḍaka, who was a Śabara; in his house lived a devoted wife.
Śabarī was devoted to her husband, regarding him as the Supreme Lord;
she served her husband with constant devotion so that he might attain complete satisfaction.
Whether at the beginning of a meal or while wandering about, in tasks such as industrious labor, in service, or in household chores, she never experiences any distress. (9)
She is always very gracious, her face smiling, and she is a servant;
whether the food is dry, parched, stale, oily, sweet, or even unpalatable.
Whether it be bitter, burnt, uncooked, fried, boiled, prepared, steamed, or whatever else it may be—of such a kind it might be. (7)
The Śabara feels no anger, and the Śabarī is not distressed;
the Śabara is always the object of her love and the bestower of perfect peace. (8)
Śabarī, remaining under the control of her Lord, gives herself to her beloved and eats;
always regarding her beloved as Viṣṇu, the virtuous woman performs service to him. (9)
Placing the duty of a Śūdra foremost, the husband and wife always conduct themselves without guile or deceit, devoted solely to the path of truth.

They are servants of the virtuous, who have obtained a righteous livelihood through the path of justice; they find contentment in whatever food and other provisions are received through their service. (11)
When a task arises, the Śabara asks his wife and performs it;
the Śabarī also asks her husband and performs what is appropriate.
Even if it should cost him his life, he does not abandon his husband’s command;
for even a Śabara does not do that which has been forbidden by his Śabarī wife.
Śabarī also did not do that which was forbidden by her master;
where there is indeed oneness of mind, that is Vaikuṇṭha, that is heaven itself. (14)
Where there is truth, sincerity, and mutual respect, there dwell Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Śivā, and Śrī. (15)
There was prosperity, auspicious gain, success, protection, and freedom from disease.
Once, that Siṃhaketu, having fully embraced the duty of a warrior (kṣātradharma), [acted].
Accompanied by his servants, he went to the forest filled with deer for the purpose of hunting;
in that forest, the Śabara saw an ancient temple of a deity.
There, seeing a linga that was slightly detached from its broken pedestal, he took it and said to the king: "Behold this beautiful Shiva. (18)
"I shall worship him with devotion according to my means;
tell me the procedure for his worship so that Śaṅkara may be pleased. (19)
Thus questioned, the king laughed and spoke to him truthfully:
"Indeed, you are not capable of performing such a rigorous act of worship toward him."
One should always perform the consecration with fresh water through mental resolve,
having seated [the deity] upon a pure seat with auspicious, fresh fragrances and unbroken rice grains.
One should worship with wild leaves, flowers, incense, and lamps;
first, one should offer an oblation of funeral pyre ashes.
One should always prepare the food offering with the same rice that one eats oneself;
furthermore, one should arrange the services such as incense, lamps, and so forth. ||23||
One should appropriately imagine dancing, instrumental music, singing, and so forth; one should perform prostrations and thereafter maintain a state of serene devotion.
This common procedure for the worship of Śiva has been declared to you;
Śaṅkara is immediately pleased by the offering of funeral ashes. (25)
One should say, "Salutation to Śiva, salutation to the Lord of Pārvatī";
uttering this, one should worship the God together with his family.
Thus addressed, the terrified Caṇḍaka accepted those words with his head bowed;
then, having reached his own abode, he beheld Sadāśiva in the form of a *liṅga*.
Having established [the image] upon a four-legged stand made of *pippala* roots atop a Vedic altar,
he worshipped it daily, offering oblations of funeral pyre ashes.
Whatever object is dear to oneself and whatever is dear to one's wife—be it perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, or sweet food, or even a mere grain of rice. (29)
Having offered it daily to Śambhu, he then consumed it himself;
in this manner, he worshipped Sadāśiva with devotion along with his wife.
Āśutoṣa was pleased with him and bestowed upon him happiness, wealth, and so forth—
food, clothing, a house, property, a milch cow, and likewise fame.
Everything is obtained from kingship, and wages are received through the duty of service;
yet it is upon truth and Śiva as its foundation that happiness is attained by the householder.
In whatever way he became fearless, happy, and possessed of the means for practice, he performed worship constantly and repeatedly offered honors according to the rule. (33)
Having gone himself to the cremation ground and other such places, he took the ashes of corpses and performed the worship of Śiva constantly, even during rain and other such times. (34)
Once, when the best of Śabaras had set out for the worship of Śiva, he did not see the funeral ash that had been kept in his vessel. (35)
During the night, due to rain, a stream of water fell through a hole into the vessel;
all the ashes were washed away and carried off by the current. (36)
Having thus observed that the vessel was empty and that not even a trace of ash remained therein,
he then departed for the cremation ground located at a great distance.
Because the cremation ground had been washed away by the rain,
not even a trace of ash was found there, despite his searching everywhere with great agitation.
Then, exhausted, empty-handed, and hopeless, he returned home, thinking:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go for ashes today upon this earth? (39)
Rain has fallen everywhere in abundance, and it continues to fall in great measure;
even within the villages, the ground has been washed clean everywhere by the king of jackals.
Today ashes alone would be obtained, and no worship whatsoever would take place;
consequently, there would truly be nothing for me today—not even food and such. (41)
When the rain has ceased following the death of someone, or at the end of a month, one should take that ash and go to the Lord Hara. 42.
"Then, after performing worship, I shall take food together with my family.
Having reflected thus, the Bhila summoned his wife and said, "O beloved," 43.
"I have not obtained the ashes from the funeral pyre; tell me, my beloved, what shall I do?
A great obstacle to my worship of Hara has arisen for me today, one that is difficult to overcome. (44)
I have not obtained any funeral ashes washed away by the rain from the cremation ground;
I see no means here for procuring the requisites for worship.
Without worship, I cannot endure to live for even half a moment;
let my fasts be rendered in vain without the honoring of the sacred ashes.
Seeing him thus distressed, that virtuous Śabara woman constantly thought: "We are always happy because of Śiva. (47)
Śiva is the bestower of happiness, the bestower of prosperity, and likewise the bestower of liberation;
indeed, nothing inauspicious can ever befall the devotees of Śiva. 48.
Whatever is performed for the sake of Śiva shall grant all that to one—be it wealth, a home, fame, clothing, food, or even water. (49)
Everything prepared for the sake of Śiva becomes divine and auspicious;
by Śiva this beautiful body was given and by him it was nourished.
For the sake of a husband and for the sake of Śiva, may my female body become auspicious;
what further gain is there beyond that by which my liberation might be attained? (51)
Having reflected thus, Śabarī said to her beloved, "Do not fear;
having burned this very house, which is reinforced with old wood—" (52)
"I shall enter the fire, so that my body may become funeral ashes;
with those, O beloved, perform the worship, for no other task remains for me. (53)
And upon the separation from your body, I shall reach Kailāsa;
I will come to lead you there along with Śambhu, so do not grieve.
Having heard those affectionate words, the Śabara said to her:
"The body is the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (55)
How can you abandon that body, which bestows happiness and is in the bloom of youth?
Now you are childless, yet you are repeatedly worthy of enjoyment. (56)
"How can you wish to burn one who is firm, well-nourished, and most powerful?
Śabarī said, "O beloved, this is the fulfillment of my life! (57)
She gave up her life for the sake of her husband—for the sake of Śiva—how much more so for herself!
What terrible austerity must she have practiced, or what gift must she have given in the past? (58)
What worship of Śambhu was performed by my father in hundreds of previous births? What merit belongs to my mother, and how has she achieved her purpose? (59)
"Since I am casting off this body into the kindled fire for the sake of Śiva, the time has come for me as a Śabarī; this liberation is now unfolding."
"How can I, a low-born woman, fall into delusion and render fruitless that which has not been attained by women even through many lifetimes? (61)
I consider all sacrifices, gifts, sacred fords, and austerities to have been born from me, since the ashes of my body were offered to Śaṅkara.
Having thus observed her steady resolve and her devotion to Śaṅkara,
the Śabara also set his mind upon giving his own sacred ash to her.
He said to his wife Śabarī, "Live, O beloved, for a hundred years;
having reduced me to ashes, you shall attain liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to achieve. (64)
Due to the sins of many lifetimes, I am a Śabara, most base;
having reached the true gateway to liberation, how could I bear to abandon it? (65)
O beloved, Śambhu should always be worshipped by you with my ashes; for Satī brought her dear husband back to life from ashes. (66)
In ancient times, Sāvitrī indeed restored Satyavān to life;
or else, as Satī herself, having produced fire, [performed the sacrifice] together with her husband.
"O beloved, you must act in such a way that I may go to heaven;
thus addressed, she said to her husband, 'O Lord, after your death...'"
Death is certain for me in every way according to the laws of nature;
between the two deaths [that would occur], death here for my own sake is better. (69)
A virtuous woman who dies by the hand of her husband out of devotion to him attains the fulfillment of her birth for the sake of her husband and for the sake of Śiva.
May she be the one who upholds the lineage of the hundred and one [Buddhas];
may that attainment be mine here, and may there be such compassion toward me. (71)
Seeing her resolve thus firm and her words both righteous and beneficial,
the Śabara, his determination strengthened, honored her reply, saying, "So be it."
Having obtained her husband's permission, she bathed, purified herself, and adorned herself;
then, having set fire to the house, she circumambulated that fire with devotion.
Having paid homage to her own guru and meditated upon her husband as Śiva, she, facing toward the entry into the fire with palms joined in reverence, spoke this: (74)
May my senses be the flowers, my body agallochum incense, my heart a splendid lamp, and my vital breaths the sacrificial oblations. (75)
"O Śambhu, may my senses remain unimpaired; I worship you.
I do not desire great sovereignty, nor heaven, nor even the supreme state. (76)
O Śaṅkara, I desire to serve you along with my husband;
O Lord of my heart, may my mind always abide in you—salutations be unto you! (77)
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, Śabarī, with a joyful countenance,
entered the blazing fire and was reduced to ashes in an instant.
The Śabara, however, having carefully collected that ash,
performed the worship of Hara with a concentrated mind near the site of the burnt house.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, he remembered his beloved wife, who was accustomed to receiving his favor, who always came before him with joined palms and full of humility.
As soon as he thought of her, he then beheld her arrived and standing behind him—
possessing her former form, appearing as was fitting, beautiful in appearance, and bowed with devotion.
Seeing his wife thus rendered into ashes, yet standing there with joined palms as if full of laughter and remaining exactly as she had been before, the Śabara [was amazed].
For a moment, overcome with wonder, he reflected within his heart:
"Fire burns with its splendors; the sun burns with its rays. (83)
A king burns with his rod of punishment; a brahmin may burn with his mind;
an enemy burns with the loss of wealth and other such means; but an unchaste woman burns with the lashings of her words. 84.
Poison burns because of its heat; the wicked burn by their very sight;
anxiety burns because of its worthlessness; and snow burns because of its coldness. 85.
Thirst burns because it is never satisfied; a virtuous person burns away sins through a curse; and a holy man burns away evils by mere touch—of this there is no doubt. (86)
And how is it that she is not seen here as burnt, according to the facts?
Is this a dream, or is it an illusion created by a magician? (87)
Thus, bewildered by amazement, he questioned his wife:
"O lady, how is it that you remain alive even though you have been reduced to ashes?"
Hearing that the burnt house had once again become as it was before,
the devoted wife, her face bright with joy, spoke to her beloved husband.
When I entered the blazing fire after setting the house on fire,
I was no longer conscious of myself, nor did I see the fire.
Then I saw Śambhu, smeared with nectar, standing by my side;
he was making me drink the nectar and touching me with his own hand. 9.1.
Not even a trace of heat remained for me, as if I had entered into water;
like one who has slept soundly, I was awakened again in half a moment. (92)
Until now, we have seen this palace standing firm as if it had not been burnt;
now, at the conclusion of the worship of the deity, we have come to receive your favor. (93)
"Grant me your favor, my beloved; what excellent thing shall I bring for you?
Having been addressed thus, she took water and gave him fruit as well as unbroken grains (akṣata). 94.
In this manner, those two worshipped [the deity] with devotion every day; and hundreds of thousands of people, having heard of such a marvelous and wonderful miracle, [did likewise]. (95)
They gathered for the purpose of seeing those two and Śaṅkara as well;
thus did the couple continue to dwell in mutual love. (96)
By a mere fragment of Śaṅkara’s grace, happiness has lasted for a hundred thousand years;
[he possesses] sons, grandsons, wealth, houses, fields, cows, servants, and wives.
Having received a mantra from Śaṅkara, those Vaiṣṇavas became householders;
then, at the end of their bodies, that couple of devotees attained a divine and wonderful [state]. (98)
And a celestial chariot appeared there; standing upon it, the couple, through the touch of the hand of Śiva’s messenger, became possessed of divine bodies and visible forms. (99)
Having become [one with] Śiva, they went to his abode, the supreme beyond the supreme.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme vow of wifely devotion been recounted to you.
The vow of devotion to one's wife is likewise excellent, as is the vow of offering everything to Śambhu;
indeed, the vow of self-surrender is distinguished above all other vows. (101)
Even a Śūdra who might read or hear this narrative shall go with devotion to the world of Śiva or the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
Even after understanding the vow of a wife—that is, devotion to her husband—one should practice it accordingly;
from that, O beloved, one shall obtain enjoyment in every way and liberation at the end.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Marvels of Chastity, including the Revival of the Śabarī Woman through the Offering of Ashes from the Funeral Pyre by her Devoted Consort, for the Purpose of Śiva-Worship Performed by the Śabara Couple," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen again, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of devotion to one's husband;
she by whom the husband, the preceptor, and Śiva—the three gods—are regarded as divine.
Constantly worshipped, served, and saluted by the beloved of Kṛṣṇa,
even her falsehood becomes truth, and what is contrary yields excellent fruit.
There may also be suffering and happiness, childlessness and having children, widowhood and being a wife with a husband, misfortune and excellent fortune. (3)
Even misfortune becomes auspiciousness, and adversity becomes favorable, when the husband, the preceptor, and Śivā are pleased. (4)
In the region of Ānarta, there was a certain twice-born man named Vedaratha who lived in Camatkārapura, possessed of sons, a wife, and a household.
His daughter, named Śāradā, who was ever as virtuous as a lotus, [was given] from birth to her husband, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; salutations to him! (6)
Thus, due to the impressions of her previous lives, she always spoke clearly;
hearing this, the people were struck with great wonder and paid homage to the virtuous woman.
Having daily paid homage in the morning to Kṛṣṇa, Śiva, Hāṭakeśa, her guru, and her parents, Satī would always perform whatever else remained to be done thereafter.
Thus, having become twelve years of age, she was filled with the bliss of devotion;
then a Brahmin named Padmanābha, honored by the king, made a request to her.
The father gave that maiden to the peaceful Mahādhan;
having performed the marriage, the twice-born man went to the river in the evening to perform the twilight rites.
Then, bitten by a serpent on the road, that brahmin died;
his kinsmen wailed, as did his wife, who cried out to her parents-in-law.
Once the funeral rites had been performed by her kinsmen, Śāradā,
the Brāhmaṇa woman who had attained widowhood, remained in her father’s own house.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisance!"—thus the young girl always spoke, and she likewise chanted the mantra "Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa. (13)
Knowing that Kṛṣṇa alone is the Lord and no other, he worships Mādhava;
he constantly serves his parents, who are the very embodiments of Śiva and Śivā. 14.
The yoginī beholds Lakṣmī in Nārāyaṇa and the woman in the man;
Śiva is the master, Kṛṣṇa is the husband, and Hari is the teacher, the god, and the father. 15.
Lakṣmī is my mother, the Goddess is my friend, and the assembly of the virtuous is my family; devotion to Kṛṣṇa is my bed, and meditation on His form is my auspicious happiness. 16.
For her, fortune, righteousness, action, service, and rest consist in the remembrance of the Blessed One;
all her activities are devoted to the Lord, divine, and composed of truth.
Even in widowhood, she remained auspicious through the power of merit acquired in the past;
she whose husband was Kṛṣṇa as her beloved, and whose service was the very mother of the virtuous.
In that state, while she remained in her father’s palace, fortune alone persisted, yet widowhood was ever present.
Once, an aged and virtuous man named Naidhruva arrived;
blind and holding the hand of a disciple, he said, "Give me alms."
Seeing the virtuous one like Viṣṇu, she gave him this excellent command:
"Welcome to you, O most worshipful one; please sit down upon this seat. (21)
Having spoken thus, he established devotion, performed the washing of the feet,
fanned him, offered water, and worshipped him with flowers and sandalwood paste.
He respectfully fed him with the finest and most desired foods;
and the blind sage, being satisfied, bestowed upon her a supreme blessing with great joy. (23)
Having lived happily with your husband, having obtained a son preeminent in virtues, and having attained great fame, may you become one who is favored by the gods. ||2||
Having heard those well-spoken words, she was struck with wonder and replied to him:
"O virtuous one, your speech is true; how could it be otherwise for one as dull-witted as I? (25)
Just as good rain upon a stone, or a hospitable reception for a dog,
even a virtuous blessing bestowed upon a widow is indeed fruitless.
"I have become a widow; how can I be a recipient of your blessings?
The virtuous one said to that goddess, "What I have spoken shall come to fruition. (27)
Kṛṣṇa himself shines forth in the words of the virtuous;
Śambhu and the gods become his helpers when the words of the good are spoken. 28.
Impelled by the power of Śivā-Lakṣmī, O virtuous daughter, I have come here; through your devotion, good fortune shall be yours.
"Thinking that this devoted young woman should not remain in sorrow,
I, the Lord Viṣṇu, have indeed come here in the form of a virtuous man for your sake."
Worship Kṛṣṇa and Śiva, as well as Lakṣmī and Śivā, and your parents always; O daughter, observe the single vow known as Umā-Māheśvara.
"As I have said, you shall possess all good fortune;
but how can I endure widowhood, O fair daughter, while I remain devoted to my husband?
Come, I shall tell your parents exactly as it is."
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Viṣṇu brought her into the presence of his father.
Hari recounted the account of the blessings he had granted, as well as her good fortune and the vow;
he spoke of everything that was yet to happen, and then he vanished from sight.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the vow of Umā-Māheśvara which bestows good fortune;
it was formerly told by me to Śāradā, and she performed it. (35)
In the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa, on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight,
or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, or even on both the full and new moon festivals (36).
By the command of her guru, the virtuous and auspicious woman should undertake the vow;
having performed the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) according to the rules, she should perform her morning bath. ||37||
Having gratified the ancestors, the gods, and others, one should construct an auspicious pavilion;
in its center, one should draw a lotus with powders of five colors.
With fourteen petals on the outside, twenty-two in the middle, sixteen within that, and eight within that as well. (39)
Then one should make it square, with a circle within;
in the center, a tuft of grass, and around that, heaps of rice and grain.
Then, having prepared a vessel filled with water upon a grass mat,
one should place a multicolored cloth over the jar and install Śiva therein.
One should install Śivā and worship her with the sixteen offerings;
one should bathe her with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then bathe her with water.
Having recited "Rudra" eleven times and [the mantra] one hundred and eight times,
and having said "Salutation to Śiva," one should worship the image upon the pedestal.
Having performed breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) according to one's ability, one should then form a formal resolve:
"I worship you for the sake of destroying the sins committed in previous births. (44)
For the increase of good fortune, victory, health, dharma, and sovereignty, and for the sake of attaining sons, wealth, heaven, and liberation, I worship you both. (45)
Then, having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should meditate upon Īśa and Pārvatī;
one should meditate upon Śaṅkara as the Yogi, and one should meditate upon Satī as the devoted wife.
He saw Tryambaka with his matted locks and hair, as well as Tryambikā;
he was lovely, adorned with serpents, while the virtuous Satī was endowed with golden ornaments.
I meditate upon the blue-throated one with a sweet voice, who has two arms and eight hands;
he is absorbed in meditation while she, red in hue, is absorbed in him. 48.
Having meditated thus, one should commence the invocation and other rites upon the image;
namely, the invocation, as well as the water-offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should offer incense, a lamp, food offerings, water, and betel leaf;
with the mantra "Obeisance to Śiva," one should perform one hundred and eight oblations.
Then one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer salutations, and ask for forgiveness;
thereafter, having honored them with ritual services, one should feed the devoted couple.
In this manner, one should perform the worship in the evening and eat milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should continue doing so for a year, and thereafter perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having caused the recitation of the Śatarudrādhyāya to be performed, one should worship;
one should offer clothing, gold, a water-pot, and an image to the preceptor.
One should feed virtuous Brahmins and give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
thereafter, one should receive the sacred remains (prasāda) and perform rites such as the gift of a cow.
Thus, the performer or female practitioner of this vow shall obtain their desired happiness;
they shall attain lineage, good fortune, wealth, prosperity, and liberation. ||55||
Before reaching liberation, she attained the state of Śiva, which is the state of Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, this great vow was both spoken and performed by that virtuous woman.
At the end of the year, that virtuous girl, having fasted, performed the concluding rite for that vow and chanted the mantra every day.
Śivā and Śiva arrived together, auspicious and assuming divine forms;
everything was exactly as Viṣṇu had described, and it was indeed full of good fortune.
"May you obtain the happiness of a husband right here in this very body!"—with such words of blessing, both of them indeed delighted the young girl. (59)
Śambhu said: "O dear girl, O child, summon your parents, kinsmen, and others here; I wish to tell you of your former birth."
Having been addressed thus, Śāradā summoned them all into the presence of Śiva;
while everyone was listening, Śambhu said to Śāradā, "O daughter! (6.1)
In a previous birth in Draviḍa, you and another woman were both the wives of a Brahmin;
there, your husband was constantly infatuated with you.
"Never once did you bestow upon your co-wife Jyeṣṭhā the happiness that you, O beloved, created for her; therefore, Jyeṣṭhā has indeed died from grief. (63)
"By that sin, you have now become a widow;
for those women in this world who cause discord between husband and wife [reap such a fate]. (64)
For them, lifelong maidenhood and widowhood will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
But by you, Kṛṣṇa has been propitiated and an auspicious vow has also been performed. (65)
By that great merit has been produced, and by that merit your husband—
that Brahmin from your previous birth— will grant you pleasure in a dream.
"Therefore, a son equal to Viṣṇu shall be born right here.
As Śambhu was saying this to her, that best of brahmins appeared.
At that moment, the young lord of the eastern quarter indeed appeared there;
seen by all according to the word of Śiva, the garland was offered by her.
Her beloved applied vermilion powder to her forehead and hair,
placed bracelets upon her forearms, and applied collyrium to her eyes.
Having given all the articles of auspiciousness, the Brāhmaṇa husband then touched her head with his hand for as long as it took.
For that long, his hair grew black and was well-adorned; he fashioned a braided topknot and wore a golden-bordered garment. (71)
Having bestowed auspicious blessings there, Śambhu remained for a moment laughing, having offered his benediction by the touch of his hand.
He too became invisible, and her husband likewise vanished from sight;
through the merit of her vow, a great festival took place for that maiden.
Listen, Lakṣmī: Viṣṇu himself became the bestower of the vow;
he, being summoned here by Śambhu, became the bridegroom. (74)
And likewise, for the sake of convincing the maiden as well as the householders, Mādhava assumed the form of her beloved from a previous birth. (75)
That very Lord Kṛṣṇa, becoming her husband, always at night grants eternal satisfaction of desire within the mind of his devotee. ||76||
In some places he has the form of Kṛṣṇa, in some places the form of a Brahmin;
in some places the form of Śiva, and in some places the form of a holy man. ||77||
The Blessed One accepted her and always took delight in her residence;
she too became radiant with the splendor of her beauty and good fortune, like the goddess Śrī herself. (78)
Thinking herself liberated, the virtuous woman did not reveal [her condition];
thus, as the days passed, that young girl [remained so] at every moment.
By virtue of the boon granted by Śiva and Śivā, Śāradā, whose vows were pure, obtained a meeting with her husband at night that increased her happiness.
By the power of experiencing union with Kṛṣṇa even in a dream, she conceived a child;
yet people, unaware of the truth, called the maiden pregnant and unchaste.
An assembly of the village dwellers was convened there by them without their knowledge;
the learned men who had gathered there were questioned regarding the payment of the fine. (82)
Among them, Kṛṣṇa himself arrived having become a brahmin;
Śiva also came to Kāśī, having become a great scholar.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to what happened then for the sake of Śāradā:
having summoned the pregnant Śāradā, the elderly men [spoke]. (84)
Then they asked, "From where did this pregnancy come? Śāradā and her father replied, "From the union with a lover in a previous birth, acquired through the merit of our vows. (85)
"By obtaining the seed in a dream, this embryo is not at fault";
then everyone laughed, disregarding the family. (86)
Highly enraged, some reviled them and turned their faces away;
they all consulted together, saying, "What shall we do? (87)
Some said, "This woman is a sinner who has brought ruin to both families;
let us shave her head, cut off her ears, and her nose. (88)
And let them banish him from outside the village, as one excluded from his own lineage.
Then Viṣṇu, the learned one, spoke thus to all the men there: ||89||
"Previously, I heard that the Umā-Māheśvara vow was performed by her;
by that merit, she has always obtained a husband in her dreams."
There is no doubt that the fetus in her dream was not actually produced; no punishment should be inflicted upon her, for this woman is of virtuous conduct. (91)
The tongues of those who spoke of her misconduct split in two;
upon hearing this, her mother, father, and the others were filled with joy.
Then, for a moment, the village elders maintained silence out of fear;
among them, some who were untrustworthy spoke falsely of a dream. (93)
Their tongues split in two and they vomited blood;
terrified, they all spoke nothing contrary [to what they had heard]. (94)
Then Śambhu Paṇḍita said to Viṣṇu Paṇḍita:
"Even a fetus occurs in a dream; such is the course of destiny. (95)
This entire universe, whatever is seen and heard, is composed of illusion; what in this world created by Kṛṣṇa is real, and what is unreal? (96)
That which is unascertainable and unreal sometimes becomes reality;
everything is under the control of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—who knows his activity? (97)
It is said that the seed of the royal sage Yūpakeśu fell into the water;
having drunk that water containing his seed, a maidservant conceived a child. (98)
Having drunk the semen of the sage Vibhāṇḍaka along with water,
a female deer became pregnant and gave birth to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga.
Likewise, the doe of King Saurāṣṭra, having been touched by his hand,
became pregnant at that very moment and gave birth to a sage-ascetic.
Likewise, the woman Satyavatī was born from the womb of a Śapharī fish;
and in the same way, Mahiṣāsura was indeed born from the womb of a buffalo-cow.
In ancient times, even by merely eating fruit, women who were pregnant became mothers of sons,
and women conceived in their minds became mothers of sons.
The club was born from the womb of Sāmba due to the curse of the sages;
through the power of the sages' mantras, it became the embryo of Yuvanāśva.
O people, the seed exists in every way within both woman and man;
however, transformation occurs through the word of the yogis. 104.
Ahalyā became a stone by the very word of Gautama;
yet it is seen that through the touch of Rāma, she became a young woman again. 105.
Thus many Maruts were born, created by Indra as their weapon;
and at the word of Rādhā, Gaṅgā manifested herself in the form of water.
From the churning of the ocean, Lakṣmī was born, and from the earth, Sītā indeed arose;
thus, in many ways, creation is produced by yogis.
By the grace of Vasudeva, he was conceived as a fetus in Rohiṇī;
and from the matted locks of Śaṅkara, Vīrabhadra was also born.
Surely this auspicious lady [is so] by the power of her vow,
by the majesty of serving the virtuous, and by taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa.
"The blameless woman bears in her womb a seed consisting of a blessing.
Thus addressed, O best of assemblies, her kinsmen and relatives offered their praise.
"Excellent! Excellent! they cried; with tears falling from their eyes, the joyful women of noble family comforted her as they spoke to her.
Nevertheless, for the sake of dispelling the doubt of human beings, Śiva and Hari both became two Brahmins there for a mere moment. (11.2)
Viṣṇu assumed the form of a Brahmin; placing Śāradā upon his lap, he showed them all his own beautiful self and his beloved Śāradā.
Seeing them in the form of a husband and wife, they attained the highest wonder;
then Kṛṣṇa vanished, and Śiva also disappeared.
Then the people residing in Camatkārapura honored her, who was embodied as Śrī, and each went to his own home.
Then, in an auspicious time, the virtuous Śāradā gave birth to a son;
he was named Śāradeya, and being learned, he became equal to Kṛṣṇa.
Having performed service to Kṛṣṇa for many years and having established her lineage in the world, the virtuous Śāradā [attained union] with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
By means of a divine vehicle, she went to Goloka, the eternal abode.
Thus has this meritorious narrative of Śāradā been described. 118.
It bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those who read it and listen to it correctly;
for women, it grants auspiciousness, good fortune, progeny, prosperity, and long life. (11.9)

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Miracles of Chastity," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It concerns the widowhood of Śāradā of Camatkārapurī in the Ānarta country, her restoration of good fortune and the birth of a son through the blessing of a saintly man, and the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa in the form of a Brahmin for the sake of inspiring public faith, as well as the attainment of Goloka by that Brahmin-form of Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the wondrous story of a courtesan who was devoted to me and whose mind was fixed on Nārāyaṇa.
O Hari, formerly in Nandigrāma there was a devoted woman named Mahānandā, whose form was graceful with ornaments.
Though she was a courtesan, free from family ties and independent by her own will, she was a servant of Śiva; yet, being virtuous, she was entirely composed of Kṛṣṇa.
He bathes daily and worships Hari Viṣṇu with supreme devotion;
he also performs dancing and singing in the presence of the God.
To those spectators who come for dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the like,
[he offers] pleasing water mixed with tulasī leaves as their fruit.
For the sake of purification, she indeed offers everything that arises for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
she constantly worships Govinda as a human being through the contemplation of Kṛṣṇa.
Having offered everything as an oblation to Kṛṣṇa, she performs the duties of her body;
[she possesses] a parasol resembling the full moon and a vehicle resplendent with gold.
Chowries with beautiful handles, golden sandals,
variegated garments, and a golden couch.
She protects a bed resembling moonbeams for the sake of Kṛṣṇa;
she possesses cows, female buffaloes, milch-cows, lamps, ornaments, male servants, and female slaves.
Trusting her words, they worship Hara and Hari with most precious ornaments resplendent with the nine gems.
Anointing with perfumes, saffron, musk, camphor, and agallochum;
variegated garlands and ear-ornaments; and delicious food as desired. (11)
A house known for its various colorful canopies, filled with diverse grains, and abounding in thousands of jewels as well as wealth such as gold and silver. (12)
Everything was always done by her for the sake of Hara and for the sake of Hari;
thus, that courtesan was possessed of great wealth and was devoted to the dharma of truth.
Devoted to the service of her husband, she was intent on the worship of Kṛṣṇa and Śiva;
she constantly listened to discourses on the scriptures and was dedicated to the chanting of the Name. || 14 ||
For the sake of diversion, in the midst of the dance pavilion before the gods,
he adorned one monkey and one cock with rudrākṣa beads.
Adorned with armlets, earrings, and ornaments made of Rudrākṣa beads, he himself constantly causes [them] to dance with rhythmic clapping and songs.
Through her instruction, the monkey always danced like a child;
and a cock, with rudrākṣa beads tied upon its crest, danced together with the monkey.
The dancer, skilled in his art, danced for a long time, bringing wonder to those who watched.
Once, a certain merchant accompanied by his servants arrived at her residence. (18)
A true devotee, wearing a bracelet, came for the purpose of seeing the dance;
seeing the jeweled bracelet situated on his forearm, he said to him: ||| 19 ||
"This bracelet set with great jewels that rests upon your hand captivates my mind, O devotee; it is worthy of the ornaments of celestial women."
Seeing her looking on with longing, the merchant then said to her:
"If this bracelet, my own ornament, pleases you... (21)
"Take this auspicious ornament of mine; what price will you give for it?
Then that courtesan laughed and spoke clearly to him: (22)
"For one who has come as a guest, there is always the duty of service toward the body;
however, regarding you as the very form of Nārāyaṇa, I indeed perform this service. (23)
"If you give me this hand-ornament inlaid with jewels, I shall become your wife for three days and nights. (24)
A woman of the courtesans' quarter can never be the devoted wife of one man,
just as the apsarases in heaven do not have a single, fixed husband.
"So be it," the merchant said; "the moon and the sun are my witnesses. Having spoken the truth three times, they touched one another's chests. (26)
"Having become husband and wife for three days and nights, let us both practice our dharma together"—thus they spoke words that touched the heart. (27)
Then the merchant-chief gave her a jeweled bracelet;
the couple spent that night happily according to their desires.
Then, on the second night, within the dance pavilion, a fire suddenly broke out by chance from the wick of a lamp. (29)
The monkey and the cock were both released from their bonds and set free;
so too were the other male and female slaves, as well as the cattle, buffaloes, and the rest.
Free from all bonds, they both emerged and departed from there;
at that moment, the Śiva-liṅga and the form of Hari were reduced to ashes in the fire.
Remembering that, the couple fell into boundless sorrow.
The merchant said, "O beloved, through my union with you, everything has been consumed by fire."
"Śiva and Viṣṇu have appeared before me in embodied form, blazing with splendor according to my sacred tradition;
yet, having come here, I have acquired a great and terrible sin. (33)
"O virtuous one, I truly find no peace; O beloved, I am dying from this unbearable sorrow.
Having spoken thus, the merchant drew in his life-breath and fell upon the earth.
Since that young woman had been his lawful wife for three days,
she became exceedingly distressed, remembering her duty in the presence of the supreme witness.
Having summoned everyone there, she spoke these piteous words,
taking up a jeweled bracelet as witness before the sun and the moon.
"For three days, I have become his wife according to dharma; indeed, it is by dharma that I must enter his funeral pyre. (37)
Having heard these words of hers, the merchant’s servant said to her:
"Do not say so, do not say so, O gentle lady; this man is not married. (38)
She who has been taken by the hand by her wedded husband, with fire as witness, is proclaimed a wife. (3.9)
But you are not such a wife devoted to infidelity;
out of great greed for the sake of the bracelet, you boast under the name of "wife."
Just as there is hell for one who lives with you while burning him, so too is there for one who has lost his way in the house of a woman of loose conduct through the hand of such a woman. 41.
Burning with one who is promiscuous brings no benefit to the virtuous;
go far away, O ever-wicked harlot, you who lead men astray! 42.
I shall likewise perform the cremation of my master’s corpse;
following the duty of a servant, I will enter my master’s funeral pyre and die. (43)
I am a servant of long standing who serves you without interruption;
indeed, without my master, my life-breaths are truly unable to remain here. (44)

The provider of food, the provider of livelihood, the protector, the giver of knowledge, the one who performs the initiatory rites (*niṣeka*), the teacher of mantras, and the one who saves from calamity—these are remembered as fathers. (45)
In this world, a servant without his master is considered as good as dead;
having caused my master's destruction, how could I show my face? (46)
"I am your servant, I am like a son to you, and I am always to be supported by you according to dharma;
after giving you the gift, I shall indeed enter the fire. (47)
"My worlds shall be eternal together with my lord," he said,
and having spoken thus, he gathered wood and prepared the funeral pyre in every way.
The merchant, however, gave some wealth as well as other items such as chains and so forth as gifts to worthy recipients, having placed the corpse upon the funeral pyre.
Just as he was about to enter, that beautiful woman rushed forward, seized his hand, and cried out to him, "Do not! Do not! Do not! (1.453.50)
"O servant, do not act thus; O son, live forever on this earth!
Though addressed by all the people in this way and though restrained by them all, he nevertheless entered.
When the servant had fallen upon the funeral pyre, his lawful wife, a virtuous woman, then spoke while the assembly was listening: "I am the wife of this man. (52)
His highly esteemed wife, a fellow-practitioner of dharma, was in my house for three days; through my yoga, this husband of hers was indeed made dead. (53)
Therefore, I shall enter the fire along with him;
for by truth, the gods who are the lords of the three worlds attain satisfaction. (54)
Truth is indeed the supreme dharma; everything is established upon truth.
Through truth one attains heaven and liberation, but through untruth there is no higher goal.
Therefore, relying upon truth, I shall enter the fire;
purified by the yoga of devotion, I shall become a sanctifier.
O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Viṣṇu, O Śiva, be the bestower of auspiciousness! Om, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations! ||57||
"Obeisance to Śiva, to Kṛṣṇa, obeisance to the Lord of Śrī Rādhā.
Thus he performed the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and gave many gifts. (58)
Having given away all her possessions to virtuous devotees, and having meditated upon Hara and Hari,
the chaste woman bowed to all and, meditating on her husband, [entered] the fire of her husband's funeral pyre.
Her devotee, having circumambulated him three times, stood facing the entrance;
she was about to leap into the kindled fire, her mind fixed upon his feet.
Seeing those two gods of gods, Śiva and Acyuta, who had manifested there with a splendor exceeding ten million suns, she [the demoness] tried to ward them off.
As she was being born, she remained as if paralyzed, as if terrified, and as if insentient;
the two Blessed Ones, treasuries of compassion, comforted her and spoke to her. (62)

I have come to behold your truth, your righteousness, your fortitude, and your devotion toward the Supreme Lord who dwells within men—the auspicious Śiva and Acyuta, both of whom are present in this image. (63)
Having produced fire through illusion, they burnt the beautiful pavilion;
having set both images on fire, Śiva himself, his servant, was filled with joy.
To demonstrate my devotion as a servant, I have entered the fire here;
though appearing in the form of a merchant, O Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, I am indeed your husband.
I have come to test you and to offer my final service;
for courtesans are deceitful, wanton, and deceivers of people. (66)

Since you, O most excellent one, have entered the fire together with your followers while recollecting the truth, I shall grant you your desire; speak, therefore, that which is most supreme among the supreme.
Having heard this, she said: "I have no desire for enjoyments apart from your feet;
these servants, maidservants, and whoever else are my kinsmen. (68)
All these people are intent upon worshipping you and have surrendered their livelihoods to you;
lead all of them, along with me, to your imperishable abode.
"Always protect me in my service, which is filled with eternal bliss.
Nārāyaṇa, having welcomed her words with "So be it," [departed].
He led them all together with her to the state beyond death; as for the cock and the monkey, they met their end in due course of time.
By virtue of his merit, Kukkura became the prince of the kingdom of Kaśmīra;
at that time, the monkey became the prince of its chief minister.
Having become great devotees of Śiva and Viṣṇu and having ruled the kingdom for a long time, those two,
at the end of their bodies, went to the imperishable abode where that Satī resides.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this which grants liberation from great sins;
by reading or hearing it, the destruction of one's sins shall occur. (74)
Even a sinful courtesan, through hearing [the teachings], through practicing them, and likewise through serving the virtuous, is instantly liberated; others are liberated in the same way.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of How Śiva and Acyuta, having become a servant and a merchant respectively through the devotion of a courtesan who offered her all to them, underwent a test by the fire of her conjugal fidelity and granted her liberation," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O beloved Mahālakṣmī, to this devotion to the husband that transcends all people;
it is certain that dharma and adharma consist primarily of the master’s word, and nothing else. (1)

If a virtuous wife should render her husband’s words—which might otherwise be like nectar—dull; or if she should render her husband’s words—which might otherwise be harmful—as meritorious; [then she is truly virtuous]. (2)
If her husband should speak of theft, a virtuous wife, considering it right, would carry it out; and if commanded by her husband, she, regarding sexual union as her duty, would perform it. (3)
The husband alone is the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself;
whatever he may ordain, whether auspicious or inauspicious, the virtuous wife should carry it out.

A virtuous wife who is obedient to his word shall obtain the fruit of her devotion to her husband; however, if the husband should command something inauspicious, he himself shall be the one to experience that result.
In this matter, since the unwholesome speech is not dependent on her, the virtuous woman,
being its possessor, would instead perform a wholesome deed through her power, even if it were an unwholesome task.
She transforms that which is undesirable and painful into that which bestows happiness;
by the mere power of her true resolve, she turns death, time, Yama, and fear into nothingness.
Indeed, all unrighteous acts bring about suffering, whereas those that grant happiness truly come into being through devotion to one's husband;
devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma, and devotion to one's husband is the supreme strength.
Even sin becomes a bestower of merit at the feet of the bull-like husband;
suffering takes on the nature of happiness through the propitiation of the husband, who is Kṛṣṇa himself.
In this regard, O beloved, listen as I relate an ancient event: how a man, honoring the words of his husband, [acted] toward his own wife while she was engaged in sexual union.
Everything became meritorious in nature, just as it brings satisfaction to the gods,
in the village named Bāṣkala in the middle of the Deccan.
The subjects were unrefined, devoid of knowledge and detachment; both men and women were engaged in agricultural labor, subsisting like forest-dwellers. || 1-2 ||
There was a certain twice-born man named Vidura who was devoid of righteous conduct; he was a protector of agriculture and had formed friendships with Śūdras and others. (13)
He is constantly occupied with agricultural work through his female laborers;
he is not at all aware of the fault of consorting with other men's wives and the like.
Having once united with a Śūdra woman out of desire during some business or other,
that wretched woman now begs Vidura for food and wealth.
Overcome with compassion as well as by the influence of desire, Vidura would indeed give something here and there to the Śūdra woman for the sake of her sustenance.
Even though he had a wife, he did not treat his virtuous spouse Bandulā with disrespect;
he gave the wealth and food remaining in the house to the Śūdra woman.
For the sake of her husband, Bandulā, though in the bloom of youth, endured everything;
she even accepted the wealth and food that had been reduced to ruin and offered by her master to a Śūdra woman. (18)
Vidura, however, entreated his virtuous wife: "Give me wealth;
give me food; give me clothing; O beloved, give for the sake of the Śūdra."
Thus addressed, that virtuous woman said: "O Lord, let whatever is found in the house be taken; the home is always under your control."
With you as my protector and being well-disposed toward me, everything shall become a source of happiness for me;
however, I have no wealth before me, so I shall do exactly as you have said. (21)
Vidura said to that virtuous woman: "Go, serve others;
having served wealthy men, bring wealth and give it to me. (22)
A virtuous wife, like a trusted servant to her husband or a devoted attendant to her lord,
performs service for him, whether as a slave or as his very own consort.
She brings wealth at her husband's command and gives it to him;
the husband alone is the supreme dharma, and the husband’s word brings happiness. (24)
Thinking thus, she became intent on serving the desires of other men.
While that couple was thus engaged in such wicked conduct, (25)
By the turn of fate, a certain Brahmin storyteller arrived in a village and, in accordance with the Dharma, recounted the narrative of the Saṃhitā.
All the villagers heard the ancient compendium of dharma;
having completely abandoned the wrong path, they took refuge in the path of righteousness. || 27 ||
The people indeed took up the Vaiṣṇava mantra, worshipped Acyuta,
and honored the Brāhmaṇas, abandoning all improper conduct.
They felt remorse for their own deeds and remembered Hari;
thereafter, Vidura abandoned his association with Śūdras.
He was born exceedingly righteous and observed the practice of eating only once a day;
he performed ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation of mantras, worship, offering of food, and beholding the deity.
Having prepared it, he would always eat in this manner, and his wife did likewise;
thus it continued until the end of Vidura’s life.
Then the messengers of Yama arrived to lead him to the city of Yama;
seeing those messengers, he cried out, "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! (32)
Having heard that, his wife said to him, "O beloved, why this reproach?
And he said to her, "The messengers of Yama have indeed arrived to take me away. (33)
Then the virtuous wife, taking water in her hand, spoke:
"If I am a beloved wife to my husband, always doing what is pleasing to my husband... (34)
Abiding by my husband’s command and devoted solely to my husband Kṛṣṇa, by that truth may those messengers go far away to the abode of Yama. (35)
Having said this, she threw that water toward her husband;
at that moment, the messengers fled from afar, leaping down from that dry land.
Then the husband, having recovered his health, related the matter exactly as it had happened;
his wife, in turn, spoke to her beloved about the fruit obtained through service to her master.
"I give this to you, my beloved; by this, may you attain a good state.
