Just then, the attendants of Viṣṇu arrived joyfully. 38.
Beheld by his wife at that very moment through the fruit of her vow of devotion to her husband,
they were honored and saluted, and led her husband to the supreme state.
Bandulā, having placed her husband on her lap, wept for a moment;
then she reflected: "If I am one who delights my beloved..."
Then, at that very moment, may my life-breaths depart along with my beloved;
for having fallen into a swoon, that virtuous woman immediately gave up her life.

Endowed with a beautiful form, she departed together with her husband who possessed a divine body; possessing a celestial body and seated in a celestial chariot, she was honored by the attendants of Viṣṇu. ||42||
That radiant splendor and the celestial chariot were seen by the listeners;
and that Brahmin, along with his true devotees, performed the funeral rites for those two.
He caused [the rites] to be performed according to the prescribed rules and fed the Vaiṣṇavas;
he gave the instruction of Kṛṣṇa and bestowed the dharma of the vow of devotion to one's wife.
The twice-born one himself bestowed upon his subjects the duty of devotion to their husbands;
indeed, all the men and women everywhere became Vaiṣṇavas. ||45||
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisance!
Having received this mantra, they worshipped the infallible Kṛṣṇa. (46)
They constantly performed worship and listened to the stories of Śukakarīśa;
moreover, the Brahmin who recited those stories appeared to them in a dream. ||47||
From both men and women, Nārāyaṇa appeared with four arms,
adorned with necklaces, armlets, a crown, yellow garments, and the Sudarśana discus.
Accompanied [by his followers], he appeared truly captivating as he was served by Lakṣmī;
at the conclusion of the discourse, he was honored by all, and having accepted that worship, he then [proceeded]. ||49||
Having observed the supreme virtue of Bandulā’s devotion to her husband, He whose form is the embodiment of grace toward His devotees instructed them all in that highest dharma of wifely fidelity.
"I am Nārāyaṇa; for her welfare, I have come in the form of a twice-born man as the author of this narrative, and thus you have been delivered. (51)
Having heard the narrative, they became Vaiṣṇavas and devoted themselves to me;
worship me constantly and listen to the story of Hari. (52)
Men must observe the vow of devotion to their wives, and women must observe the vow of devotion to their husbands;
both together must observe the vow of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which is the means of liberation.
One should constantly listen to sacred discourses, which grant supreme liberation;
through the narration of Kṛṣṇa’s deeds, the mind attains the highest purity. (54)
Through discourse, meditation is perfected; from meditation comes supreme liberation.
The hearing of noble discourse is considered the seed of all that is auspicious. (55)
Lust, anger, greed, as well as pride, arrogance, and other such vices—
the offspring of unrighteousness— flee far away upon hearing the narration of Hari.
Violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, and likewise sexual misconduct—these are the sons of Desire; they flee far away at the mere mention of their names. (57)
The killing of a father, the killing of a mother, and even the murder of a Brahmin—these sons of anger perish from merely hearing this story. (28)
The seizing of a deity’s property, the seizing of a Brahmin’s property, and the theft of gold—these are the sons of Greed; they flee far away at the mere mention of its name. (29)
Both lack of faith and dullness of intellect are indeed born of ignorance;
they both depart far away from hearing the stories of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

This auspicious narrative, which bestows immediate liberation upon those bound to the cycle of worldly existence—including women with dust-covered feet, male servants, and the wives of servants—is now told. (61)
The story of Hari is like a lamp for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance;
it is the supreme medicine to be well-served by those afflicted by the disease of worldly existence. 62.
The discourse on the mountains of great transgressions is considered to be like a thunderbolt;
it is the parching of the seeds of karma and the means for attaining all prosperity. (63)
O sages, the dust from the feet of those virtuous ones who hear and likewise glorify the stories of Śrī Hari is itself said to be the sacred bathing places (tīrthas). 64.
Even if one is incapable, one should listen day by day for even a moment—
a ghaṭikā, or half of that, or even a kṣaṇa— to this purifying narrative.
For those intent upon gross effects and possessed of gross intellects, there is no other path as pleasant as this discourse, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree; no other way is so easy.
By drinking nectar alone with effort, one individual may become free from old age and death;
but the nectar of this narrative, when drunk, shall render the entire lineage free from old age and death.
Hari is the speaker of the narrative, the direct teacher of all teachers;
he is the supreme guru, the bestower of liberation, the giver of merit, and the lamp of knowledge. ||68||
Even those people who praise this discourse and its expounder go to the eternal, supreme state, even if they do not listen to it themselves. (69)
Those people on earth who provide assistance by listening to the discourse remain in the abode of Brahmā for more than a hundred crores of kalpas.
Through the attainment of awakening by means of sacred discourse, may there be remembrance of Hari;
through the yoga of constant remembrance, may there be the destruction of latent impressions.
If that were so, there would be dispassion; in the absence of passion, there is supreme happiness.
However, the bliss of the destruction of craving acts as an auxiliary to the arising of the bliss of the Self.
When passion is destroyed, its opposite, hatred, is also certainly destroyed. For one in whom both passion and hatred have perished, there is no further engagement with defects. 73.
Indeed, neither the auspicious nor the inauspicious arises as the bestower of birth and death;
through the absence of even worldly activity, there would always be an absence of experience. (74)
Immersed in the essence of devotion through the state of being one with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he enjoys his own self—which is eternal bliss, the bliss of consciousness, and perpetual bliss. (75)
Eternally satisfied in my form, perpetually immersed in my own Self,
and consisting of the bliss of Brahman in my abode, he enjoys the happiness of the unconditioned.
Thus, from hearing this discourse, there shall arise merit that bestows liberation;
for I am truly pleased wherever my nectar-like discourse exists. (77)

Sins such as those involving adamantine glue (vajralepa) and the like are entirely reduced to ashes through the application of my own discourse and by means of the knowledge of my propitiation. //78//
The virtues of a husband are worthy of being heard; this is the eternal dharma.
I am the husband who is the Supreme Brahman; one should listen to my auspicious story. 79.
For a devotee who is unable to perform charity, sacrifice, pilgrimage, expenditure of wealth, or festive celebrations, my stories must certainly be heard. 1.454.80.
The chanting of my names and those of my Lord must be performed daily, both at dawn and at night;
worship must be offered on my behalf, and the food offering must be consumed. (81)
One should consume leaves, flowers, water, food, and everything that is pleasing;
by that, there shall be purification of the being and eternal mindfulness of the Deity. (82)
Through the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, even liberation (mokṣa) is attained;
however, the cause for such remembrance is, in every respect, the hearing of the glories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (83)
The attainment of heaven through one's own performed merit is indeed not certain;
however, by devotion to hearing this narrative, one goes to the eternal abode. 84.
The story of Śrī Hari is superior even to the gift of thousands of crores of gold, and it is more excellent than a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices. (85)
Discourse is more beneficial than vows, observances, and recitations, wherein [I reveal] myself to the virtuous, the devotees, and those women devoted to yoga. (86)
The wonders of virtuous and faithful women have been described, and their most divine and radiant deeds have been recounted. (87)
All of these are givers of prosperity and liberation;
for the sake of your own liberation, through service to the true nature of reality, they shall become so. (88)
Indeed, for the sake of your deliverance, I have assumed the form of a brahmin;
now I shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, while you continue the service of the virtuous. (89)
May you all constantly listen to my discourse and practice meditation upon me; through my service, you shall all attain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and union with me.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin reciter, becoming Nārāyaṇa and served by his devotees, departed for Vaikuṇṭha in a brilliantly radiant celestial chariot.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described the fruit of obeying the command of one’s beloved;
from hearing and reciting this, enjoyment and liberation will surely be attained. 92.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Bandulā, devoted to her husband, attaining the abode of the Lord through the acquisition of divine stories despite the non-faultiness of sexual union while obeying the command of her own husband, the Brahmin named Vidura," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O beloved, listen to the power of Agastya’s dear wife,
Lopāmudrā, that divine woman who was the most excellent of those devoted to their husbands.
Once, O Lakṣmī, having bathed in the waters of the auspicious Narmadā and while proceeding toward the venerable Badarīśvara, Nārada gazed upon the Vindhya mountain.
It was an abode of flavors, adorned with trees, creepers, pillars, crops, and the like;
it was expanding within the great space, beholding all things on every side.
Having seen him, Nārada stood for a moment in the sky itself out of curiosity;
Vindhya also beheld him in the heavens, resembling the sun and illuminating the firmament.
Seeing Nārada from afar, he went out to meet him with affection;
for even a hard-hearted man assumes gentleness upon seeing a saintly person. || 5 ||
Having bowed to the Sage, he offered water for the feet, the guest-offering, a seat, and honors;
he massaged his feet and, bowing low, the Mountain spoke.
Today, by the dust of your feet, my passion and ignorance have been destroyed;
through your arrival, may my status as a bearer of the earth among mountains be honored.
Having heard this, Nārada sighed slightly and remained silent; thereupon Vindhya, the king of mountains, said: "O lord of sages, tell me the cause of your sighing."
"I do not count the Himalayas as mountains or even as bearers of the earth;
tell me some task, and I shall perform it for you, provided you are intent on service."
Then Nārada said to him, "Meru disregards you.
Having spoken thus, Nārada departed from there for Badarikāśrama.
Vindhya Mountain fell into great anxiety: "Fie upon my life here, for I am defeated by my kinsmen and devoid of all effort! (11)
How does he eat by day, and how indeed does he sleep at night—how can there be any private happiness for one who suffers the humiliation of his kinsmen? 12.
It has been rightly said by those who know the past: "Anxiety is a terrifying sorcery;
this dreadful state is not pacified by any means, for it robs one even of sleep and strength. (1.3)
The fever of anxiety is most intense and grows anew every day:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How shall I conquer Mount Meru? (14)
"I shall go for refuge to Viśveśa; he will grant me my intellect.
Having reflected thus, the mountain grew great in the vast sky. (15)
Having blocked the path of the sun on the right, he stood firm;
then neither the horses of the sun nor Aruṇa were able to proceed further.
The Great Vindhya mountain, having blocked the sky and remained there, spoke to the Sun:
"He vies with Meru, desiring the circumambulation granted by you. (17)
He who, being occupied with seizing Rāhu’s arms, does not remain still for even a moment,
[traverses] two thousand yojanas, two hundred yojanas, and two yojanas.
Even he, who travels a yojana in half a blink of an eye, remained there for a long time;
that [stopping] was caused by the obstruction of the sun's motion.
The people wept and fled as they measured out the time for the task;
then all the gods and others went to Brahmā for refuge.
They paid homage, offered praise, and cried out, "Protect us! Protect us!
Seeing the gods thus distressed, Brahmā replied to them.
"I shall grant all your desires; listen to this supreme boon! Remain at ease, O you all; why are you so agitated regarding the truth? (22)
These Vedas, all branches of knowledge, truth, dharma, austerity, sacrifice, Indian celibacy, as well as the Śrutis and Smṛtis—[all these have originated from him]. ||23||
Ascetics devoted to Brahman, those observing vows and fasting, women dedicated to their husbands, and others who are celibate students; ||24||
They were always devoted to their mother and father, devoted to cows, and servants of the gods;
they were faithful to their wives, honorers of guests, and performers of meritorious acts of charity. ||25||
"All of you are here in my world of truth and are always happy. Tell me what you desire; I shall surely do that which brings you happiness. (26)
The gods said: "Mount Vindhya vies with Meru in the heavens;
obstructing the path of the sun, it grows ever higher toward your abode. (27)
The activities supported by the sun are obstructed; therefore, dissolution will occur.
Hence, you must by all means keep the solar path free from obstruction. (28)
Having heard this, the great sage named Agastya, the creator of the universe, said:
"O gods, go and beg that sage who is performing fierce penance in the sacred field of Kāśī."
That sage, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, the husband of Lopāmudrā,
and the devourer of Vātāpi and Ilvala, will accomplish your task.
Thus addressed, those gods and others went to Agastya at Kāśī;
having bathed in Maṇikarṇikā, the gods beheld the city of Kāśī.
It was presided over by the marks of true saints visible to learned men, and it was shimmering with a multitude of circles formed by tens of millions of people dwelling at the holy ford.
With thirty million temples, ten million residential houses, thousands of excellent gardens and fields, and thousands of royal palaces; ||33||
With hundreds of thousands of women from Vārāṇasī and hundreds of thousands of celestial women, and with tens of millions of celibate students and men from various regions. ||34||

With hundreds of millions of crores of sacred fords, with rivers such as the Gaṅgā and other streams, with celestial chariots, vehicles, and modes of transport, and with great cities of sacred books; ||35||
It was beautifully adorned with halls for Dhanvantari and others, with thousands of food-distribution centers, and with thousands of mendicants, the wretched, and the helpless.
Having thus seen that city and visited numerous sacred fords, as well as Viśvanātha, Annapūrṇā, and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; ||37||
Having seen Śrī Bindumādhava, the god of Dharma, they bowed down to him;
having worshipped him and washed his feet, they received the nectar.
They went for the sake of helping others to where Agastya was staying;
and having fashioned the Agastīśvara Liṅga and a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front of it, [they remained there]. ||39||
Chanting the Śatarudrīya Sūkta, the sage shone resplendent;
seeing him radiant as the sun with his splendor, the gods smiled.
Oh, having taken refuge in this Brahmin body, all splendors cultivate the supreme, peaceful abode for the sake of attaining the state of peace! 41.
In whose hermitage here even predatory creatures, dwelling together on all sides, have abandoned their innate enmity toward all living beings. (42)
All dwell together—both the cruel and the peaceful, those characterized by passion (rājasa), as well as all beasts, birds, wild animals, and reptiles. (43)
Seeing even the animals dwelling in the hermitage as if they were sages,
all the gods realized that this was the power born from the soil of Agastya.
"Indeed, where Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa move about in embodied form"—seeing this, the gods beheld the hermitage of the sage. (45)
Rich with the fragrant smoke of burnt offerings, surrounded by many young students,
and filled with the splendor of Vedic study by women devoted to celibacy.
It was graced by gentle hermit maidens with moon-like radiance,
and adorned with moist bark garments and loincloths hanging from the branches of trees.
It indicated the dwelling places of the excellent sages, which bring about clarity of being,
by means of the footprint-mark of Lopāmudrā, the crest-jewel of devoted wives.
Seeing him sealed [in meditation] in the courtyard of his leaf-hut, the gods bowed down to him as he emerged from his samādhi,
holding a rosary of beads upon his ears and eyes.
Beholding Agastya seated before them upon a cushioned seat, endowed with splendor equal to that of the Creator, all the gods, including Indra, [were struck with wonder].
With joyful faces, they cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory!
Then the sage, having seated them all, asked the reason for their arrival.
The preceptor of the gods spoke to him regarding the reason for the arrival of the gods:
"You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you are worthy of honor even by the great. (52)
Are there not virtuous men in every hermitage, at every mountain, and in every forest, O you whose wealth is asceticism? Or is your state with Agastya something entirely unique? (53)
The splendor of asceticism resides here in you; the Brahmanic luster is firmly established in you;
the supreme glory of merit is in you; and wonders abide in you. (54)
This auspicious Lopāmudrā is devoted to her husband and shares his dharma;
she is like the very shadow of your body, for even her story brings merit. (55)
Arundhatī, Sāvitrī, Śāṇḍilī, Śrī, Satī, Anasūyā, Mahālakṣmī, Śatarūpā, and Menakā. ||56||
Sunīti, Kamalā, Svāhā, and Saṃjñā were devoted wives;
yet none of them was as excellent as she is described here. (57)
O Sage, when you eat, he eats; when you remain, he remains;
when you are sound asleep, he sleeps, yet he awakens first.
She never shows herself unadorned to you;
yet, when you have gone away for the sake of business, she does not wear her ornaments.
For the sake of increasing your lifespan, she does not utter your name;
except for Kṛṣṇa, she never speaks another man's name at any time.
Even when reviled or punished, she does not revile in return but remains serene;
when commanded, "Do this," she performs it immediately and swiftly. (6.1)
When addressed with "You shall do it," she says, "Certainly, my beloved";
and when summoned by you, she abandons all other duties and comes to you in great haste.
"Command me, O Ocean of Compassion! He says that his task is finished;
he does not remain at the door of the courtyard on the path to the inner chamber. (63)
Without having asked you, she does not give even a mere object, or even a blade of grass; indeed, without your permission, she gives nothing whatsoever to anyone.
He himself brings the materials for worship, even when prompted,
including water, darbha grass, fruits, leaves, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth.
That virtuous woman accomplishes her purpose at the proper time even without being commanded;
she never becomes agitated anywhere, nor does she cause agitation in others.
She attends upon him at the proper time and in a fitting manner, and she partakes of her husband’s favor—water, food, fruits, and so forth. (67)
Considering that gift bestowed by his master to be a great favor,
he always desires to support the gods, the ancestors, guests, dependents, the destitute, and virtuous women.
Having given away her slaves, cows, and female servants, she eats her own portion after it has been divided;
with her household utensils kept in order, she is seen in the morning to be averse to expenditure.
Acting according to her needs and expenditures, and always maintaining what is appropriate, she does not perform the vow of fasting without your command. (1.455.70)
Without your permission, she does not go to see this assembly, festival, exhibition, wrestling match, dance, drama, or art gallery. (71)
She did not go to see her husband on pilgrimages or at weddings without his permission;
she lived happily with her husband whether he was seated, enjoying himself, or asleep.
Even when there is a most urgent matter, she never rouses you;
and out of passion, she does not serve you even against your will for the sake of her own interests.
During her menstrual period, she does not show her face for three days;
nor does she utter her own words before she has become pure through bathing and other rites.
On the fourth day, she beheld her husband’s face as the sun, Hari;
meditating upon her beloved’s form as the form of Kṛṣṇa, this devoted wife remained steadfast.
Devoted to you, she constantly wears the signs of good fortune:
the adornment of her hair, her braided tresses, and the ornaments for her hands, ears, and other limbs. (76)
Turmeric, saffron, camphor, vermilion, collyrium for the eyes, a bodice, a bodice-fastener, a lute, anklets, and likewise a waist-belt; ||77||
Devoted to you, she wears a chain, a ring, a necklace, golden earrings, and a garment;
she also applies fragrant Viṣṇutaila.
One should not form an attachment to these women: to an atheist woman, nor to one who is untouchable, nor to an unchaste woman, nor to a heretical woman. ||79||
This virtuous woman does not converse with an impure woman, nor with a lustful woman devoid of dharma, nor with a woman who hates her husband. (1.455.80)
She does not go outside alone, nor does she ever bathe naked;
she always sits on low ground, never on level ground in the presence of her husband. (8.1)

Neither on the grain-pounding mortar nor on the grinding stone, nor on the hearth nor in the water-jar; neither in the gargari vessel nor in the cauldron and such, nor on the pestle nor on the surface of a stone slab. (82)

She should not grind [grains] on a grinding stone, nor with a broom, nor indeed with a mortar and pestle; she should not turn her back upon the threshold, nor upon a worthy recipient, nor upon her teacher or husband. (83)
In some places she sits even after removing her bodice, yet she does not reveal herself to you;
likewise, she conducts herself so that no one may behold her breasts or her hips. (84)
In the absence of the time for sexual union, she maintains her boldness;
wherever there is satisfaction for her husband, there she exerts her desire. (85)
Considering the supreme Dharma, the most excellent vow, and the highest worship of the gods to be the observance of her husband’s word, she never transgressed it. (86)
A devoted wife [should not abandon] a husband who is a child, powerless, unwilling, diseased, in a difficult situation, impotent, observing a vow, aged, or afflicted by illness. (87)

Whether he is well-established or poorly situated, whether he is beset by calamities or impoverished, whether he is a thief or excessively addicted to desire—the virtuous woman always serves him. (88)
Moreover, she always attends upon you, the ascetic free from desire;
she is ever joyful when you are joyful, and filled with grief when you are dejected. (89)
Your beloved remains constant toward you in prosperity and likewise in adversity;
even when the food, household goods, and fine garments in the home have been exhausted.
He accomplishes [his tasks] by your command and does not even say "it is not so";
out of devotion to you, he drinks the nectar of your feet constantly. (91)
She considers her husband to be superior to Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and Śambhu;
yet she strictly maintains the self-restraint of worshipping her husband’s feet.
He never utters words that are shameful, slanderous, painful, provocative of strife, false, mocking, or abusive. ||93||
She recognizes the god, the guru, the vow, the sacred ford, and the Dharma as her husband;
like your own shadow, she remains here as your servant. (94)
"You are blessed, O best of sages, and blessed are your parents as well;
blessed indeed are her parents, since she is such a devoted wife. (95)
Wherever the foot of a devoted wife touches the ground, that ground shall always be a sacred ford (tīrtha), purifying and salvific. ||96||
Only through devotion to the Supreme Lord does a woman become devoted to her husband;
you are truly a householder, for you possess a wife devoted to her husband. 97.
Even by the mere sight of a devoted wife, a sinner becomes pure;
there is no difference between her and the Gaṅgā for a woman who regards her husband as a deity. (98)
Indeed, this fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā has arisen from the sight of you;
and the sight of your wife has also occurred for us through our great merit. (99)
You are the *praṇava*, and this is the Veda; you are patient, and you are austerity itself.
This is the virtuous rite, and you are its fruit; you are blessed, O great sage!
This is the splendor of devotion to your husband, and you yourself are the supreme splendor of Brahman; even so, what is this splendor of your asceticism that is most difficult for you to accomplish?
Nothing is unknown to you; nevertheless, I shall speak.
O Sage, listen here to the purpose for which the gods have come.
This is the glorious Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices; this is Agni, the lord of the world;
as well as Dharmarāja, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Śrī, Īśa, Śiva, and the others.
These petitioners are here, and you yourself must be entreated for the sake of the world;
that benefit for the universe is achievable by you through a mere effort of speech.
The Vindhya mountain is growing out of rivalry with Mount Meru; restrain it, for it is now ascending upwards, obstructing the path of the sun. (105)
But those who are cruel by nature, those who obstruct the path,
and those who compete for the sake of growth— their very growth is always a cause of ruin.

Having heard this and reflected for a moment, the great sage Agastya said, "So be it," dismissed the deities, and spoke these words to Lopāmudrā: śrutvā dhyātvā kṣaṇaṃ tathetyuktvāgastirmahāmuniḥ | visṛjya devatāḥ prāha lopāmudrāmidaṃ vacaḥ || 107 ||

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gods' Journey to Sage Agastya and the Account of Lopāmudrā’s Devotion to Her Husband," in the first section on the continuity of the Kali Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the obstruction of the sun's path by the expanding Vindhya mountain.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having reflected upon everything in meditation, Agastya spoke thus to his devoted wife Lopāmudrā; listen, O Lakṣmī, to this which is for the welfare of the world.
Look, O lady of excellent hips, what is this that has arisen?
Where is that task, and where are we, who follow the path of the sages? (2)
Obstacles may arise by chance for those dwelling in the sacred field of Kāśī;
however, the field of Kāśī must never be abandoned under any circumstances by those seeking liberation.
"O auspicious lady, this great obstacle has presented itself before me;
nevertheless, for the sake of the mission of the gods, I shall depart—may Śrī Śiva protect us. (4)
Having uttered this and bowed to Śiva, the sage— accompanied by Lopāmudrā— touched the auspicious water of the sword and [proceeded] through yoga and austerity.
By means of the divine path through the sky, he indeed went to heaven in half a moment;
looking ahead, he saw the Vindhya mountain, which obstructed the heavens with its height.
Upon seeing that sage Agastya standing before him,
accompanied by his beloved and the enemy of Vātāpi and Ilvala, the mountain quickly trembled.
Having held Govardhana in his hand, he established it upon the earth;
before him, who was like fire, Vindhya became dwarfed out of fear. || 8 ||
"Grant me your command; I am your servant," he said.
Agastya replied, "O Vindhya, you know me as I truly am."
"If you are to return to me, then become even shorter," having said this,
the sage departed for the southern direction together with his beloved.
Vindhya gazed on with longing, thinking, "Since he was not cursed by Agastya,
he is more fortunate than I am," and he rejoiced.
"Today, tomorrow, or even the day after, the sage will surely arrive"—
with such great burdens of anxiety, the mountain remained thus diminished.
"Even now the sage does not arrive; even now the mountain has not grown large.
Yet at that very time, Aruṇa, who knows the proper moment, urged on his horses."
The world attained great well-being once more through the movements of the sun as before;
yet that base man, harboring intense malice, desired to cause its decline.
News of its growth is far off; even before it grows, there is doubt.
Desires will not be fulfilled, and even if fulfilled, they will certainly perish.
Without recognizing the capability of another, he who displays his own capability meets with derision; so too does this mountain here.
Then the lord Agasti went to the bank of the Godāvarī;
there he beheld before him Mahālakṣmī, standing for a very long time with a smile upon her face.
Having praised that Blessed One, Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari,
the sage, accompanied by his wife, prostrated himself like a staff with all eight limbs touching the ground.
Lakṣmī said to the sage and to the devoted Lopāmudrā:
"I am pleased having beheld you; choose whatever resides in your heart."
"O illustrious princess, O pure one, sit here;
I have come here for the purpose of destroying the demon Kola."
"By these auspicious marks upon your body and by your most purifying vows, I desire to cool this body of mine, which has been scorched by the weapons of the Daityas. (21)
Having spoken thus, the beloved of Hari embraced that wife of the sage and,
with great affection, adorned her with many auspicious ornaments.
Lopāmudrā also served that Lakṣmī with gentle touches;
she massaged her body, and the heat of Śrī’s affliction was stilled.
Then the virtuous Lopāmudrā, having grasped the feet of Śrī, bowed with reverence;
Lakṣmī then offered salutations and performed a hymn of praise to her. (24)
Listen to that hymn of praise by which those who offer praise may become dependent on wealth—those endowed with manifold prosperity who have been looked upon by you with favor. (25)
O Mother, I bow to you, O Kamalā, Padmā, whose eyes are long;
O Mother of the Universe, who dwells in the lotus-heart of Śrī Viṣṇu, salutations be unto you! 26.
O true daughter of the milk-ocean, O beautiful one with the luster of the interior of a lotus, O Lakṣmī, be ever gracious; O Mother of the Universe, homage be to you! (27)
In the abode of Mahendra you are Śrī; you are Rukmiṇī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa;
you are the moonlight in the moon and the radiance in the sun—O Mother of the Universe, obeisance be to you! 28.
O Mother of the World, with a smiling face, O Refuge, O Increaser of Happiness; O Jātavedas, O Consumer, O Mother of the Universe—salutations be unto you! (29)
O Mother of the Universe, you are the creative power in Brahmā, the nourishing power always in Viṣṇu, and the power of dissolution in Śiva; salutations be unto you!

O Mother of the Universe, you are the heroic, the virtuous, the wise, the blessed, the honorable, and the one of noble birth; you are enriched with a multitude of arts and good character—salutations be to you! 3.1

To you, O Mother of the Universe, who regard an elephant as a horse, a woman as straw, a lake as a mere puddle, a temple as a dwelling, and a god as a grain of dust—you who are most excellent—salutations be unto you! (32)
By you, O Mahālakṣmī, Mother of the Universe, the bird, the animal, the bed, the jewel, the earth, the man, and the bride are made excellent and pure; salutations be to you! 33.
O Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Padmā, Ramā, O you who are born from the lotus, O virtuous one, O daughter of the ocean, O consort of Viṣṇu, O beloved, be forever gracious! 34.
Thus praised and gratified, Śrī said to the devoted wife:
"O Lopāmudrā, O sage, I know the cause of the distress in your hearts. (35)
The fire born of separation from Kāśī surely torments even one who possesses consciousness;
yet, having reached Vārāṇasī, you two shall attain your desired perfection.
Those who shall recite this hymn of mine, which destroys suffering and poverty, bestows desired prosperity, and brings about victory and continuity, [shall attain these blessings]. (37)

It shall grant me its presence, destroy diseases such as those caused by child-seizing spirits (bālagraha), and likewise bring about my liberation through the attainment of my own form (sārūpya) and other states. ||38||
Having thus received the blessings for the bestowal of prosperity, the couple bowed to her and departed for Śrīśaila, the abode of Kamalā, which was not very far away.
Accompanied by his wife, he beheld this and attained supreme joy;
for in the hearts of the virtuous, the impulse to assist others remains ever awake.
Their misfortunes perish and prosperity attends them at every step;
that purity is not attained by bathing in sacred fords, nor is that fruit gained by manifold gifts,
nor is it reached through fierce austerities— that which is obtained by performing a service for others.
There is no dharma higher than helping others, and no evil greater than harming them. (42)
The fruit of assistance is the sight of Lakṣmī and the sight of the mountain;
thus was Śrī Veṅkaṭādri beheld by Lopāmudrā and the Sage. 43.
Then the sage, with a joyful mind, spoke these words to his wife:
"Listen, O lady of excellent hips; I shall indeed tell you the truth."
While there are many places of liberation upon the earth, [the foremost are] Prayāga, the king of holy sites, as well as Kurukṣetra and Naimiṣa. ||45||
Avantikā, Haridvāra, Ayodhyā, the city of Mathurā, Dvārikā, Amarāvatī, and likewise Kuṅkumavāpikā. ||46||
The confluence of the Sarasvatī and the Sindhu, the meeting of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Kāñcī, Tryambaka, and the banks of the seven Godāvarīs; ||47||
Kālañjara, Prabhāsa, Badarikāśrama, Raivata, Mahālaya, as well as the sacred field of Oṃkāra and Pauruṣottama. ||48||
Gokarṇa, Bhṛgukaccha, Bhṛgutuṅga, Puṣkara, Śrīparvata, Mānasa, Dhārātīrtha, and Bhautika; ||49||
The internal sacred sites, such as compassion, affection, and the like, are indeed the givers of liberation; there is not even the slightest doubt about this.
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford, compassion toward all beings is a sacred ford, and uprightness is also a sacred ford. (51)
Generosity is a sacred ford, self-control is a sacred ford, contentment is said to be a sacred ford;
celibacy is the supreme sacred ford, and kind speech is also a sacred ford. (52)
Knowledge is declared to be a sacred ford, fortitude is a sacred ford, and austerity is a sacred ford;
yet the supreme ford among all sacred fords is that purity which is always mental.
Purification does not come through water; rather, the mind is always pure when it is virtuous.
There is no purity from merely removing the impurities of the body, for the body is never stainless.
The desire for the attainment of worldly pleasures is indeed the impurity of the mind; detachment from those very things is declared to be perfect purity. (55)
But when the internal state has become pure, even desire and the like become pure;
and defects turn into virtues by relying on the excellence of the sattva quality. (56)
Wherever a person may dwell whose collection of senses is restrained, there for him are Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes. (57)
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford, purified by meditation and filled with the water of wisdom that removes the stains of passion and hatred, attains the supreme goal. (58)
This mental holy site (tīrtha), which is frequented by the virtuous, has been described to you.
Now hear how the external holy sites—those of the earth and those of the water—are constituted.
Just as the bodily parts beginning with the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) are most pure, so too are the portions of earth and water pure; they are indeed sacred fords (tīrthas).
Some merits are self-born, some are born of the gods,
and some are produced by the dwellings and other [associations] of virtuous men.
Through the wonders of the dwellings and other [signs] of devoted wives, through the favors of virtuous women, and likewise through the asceticism of chaste ladies; 62.
Indeed, holy places arise from the performance of duties toward one's wife;
however, the "self as a holy place" (ātmatīrtha) is declared to be great—Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is greater than the great.
The pure ford consists of the nature of the intellect; the senses are also stainless, and the physical bodies are purified by austerities.
Even impure things such as bones and skin become purifying for the virtuous; indeed, through the power of Kṛṣṇa’s ascetic penance, they become truly divine sacred sites (tīrthas). 65.
The essence of discourse is the most excellent sacred ford, the highest among all supreme fords;
it is the great sacred ford consisting of pure being, the sacred ford of affection, and the source of merit.
Saluting the elderly is considered a sacred ford that bestows the world of Brahmā;
the sacrificial ground is a great ford, as is the water where cows have bathed and the place where Tulasī has been crushed. (67)
The Ekādaśī and other sacred observances certainly deliver one from bondage;
however, faith is the supreme sacred site, bestowing both merit and its fruit.
Therefore, O beloved, just as one possesses the perception of divinity toward terrestrial and aquatic sacred sites, one should likewise maintain that same perception toward embodied beings.
In temples, toward the gods, in sacred images and idols,
and toward virtuous women and holy deeds, one should always diligently acquire merit through good actions.
Whatever person bathes in internal or external sacred fords,
that devotee who has entered the assembly of Kṛṣṇa attains the supreme goal.
Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, fire-offerings, libations, shaving the head, serving the virtuous, and beholding Hari—all these become inexhaustible. (72)
Kāśī, Kāñcī, the one called Māyā (Māyāpurī), Ayodhyā, Dvāravatī, Mathurā, and Avantikā—these are the lands of the Lord that bestow liberation. (73)
Nevertheless, O devoted wife, no other city pleases my mind today as much as Kāśī does, which is the dwelling place of all the gods. (74)
Śaṅkara himself bestows the liberating knowledge, mantras, and so forth;
he constantly wanders from house to house in the form of a mendicant. (75)
This king of great Vaiṣṇavas, the Lord, sends his devotees to Vaikuṇṭha, as well as to Amṛta, Goloka, and Kailāsa.
O beloved, the path of Yama is forever blocked for those who dwell in Kāśī;
Avimukta is the great sacred field, the supreme among the supreme even for Śiva and others. 77.
I desire to dwell in that city of Kāśī for as long as I live;
indeed, by residing in Kāśī, virtuous women attain the world of Brahmā. (78)
"Those women go from this world to the supreme realm, Vaikuṇṭha.
Having heard this, Lopāmudrā respectfully questioned the sage. (79)
"Where is that city of virtuous women and celestial nymphs? Tell me, O mistress of my life, so that I may become free from doubt."
Having said "Om," Agastya spoke to the virtuous woman:
"Listen, O noble lady; it is taught that the world of Vāyu is superior to the world of Bhūmi. (81)
It is the abode of Piśācas and others; therefore, it is the circle of the Guhyakas.
That world of the divine Guhyakas is filled with prosperity.
Beyond that is the world of the Gandharvas, where the Gandharvas and Cāraṇas dwell; beyond that is the world of the Vidyādharas, for it is there that the Vidyādharas reside.
From there, one reaches the delightful Dharmapurī, where the righteous dwell as if in heaven;
from there, one reaches heaven, the abode of those possessing great merit, which is ever-blissful.
Beyond that, the world of the Apsarases is situated above in heaven;
these Apsarases are of great truthfulness and bring delight to those who partake in the sacrifice.
And they dwell in the world of the Apsarases, serving the guardians of the world—auspicious young women who are treasuries of beauty, charm, and good fortune. (86)
With firm knots upon their hips and beautified by divine ornaments, they bestow divine enjoyments and are highly skilled in song, dance, and instrumental music. (87)
They were skilled in the arts of amorous play, proficient in the science of gambling, connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, perceivers of inner emotion, and clever in appropriate speech. (88)
They were knowledgeable regarding the specificities of various regions, well-versed in various languages, experts in signs and news, independent, and pleasing to the deities. ||89||
Expert in playful jests and skilled in eloquent speech,
all these daughters of the Ocean of Milk were created by Nārāyaṇa.
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Candralekhā, Tilottamā, Vapuṣmatī, Kāntimatī, Līlāvatī, and Upalāvatī. (91)
Alambuṣā, Guṇavatī, Sthūlakeśī, Kalāvatī, Kalānidhi, Guṇanidhi, Karpūra, Tilaka, and the excellent Urvarā. 92.
Anaṅgalatikā, Vidyullatā, Madanamohinī, Cakorākṣī, Candrakalā, Maṇiprabhā, and Manoharā. (93)
Grāvadrāvā, Tapodveṣṭrī, Cārunāsā, Sukarṇikā, Dārusañjīvanī, Suśrī, Kratuśulkā, and Śubhānanā. ||94||
Himāvatī has austerity as her bride-price, the sacred ford as her bride-price, and charity as her bride-price;
Prabhā possesses the knowledge of fifty horse-sacrifices and desires the Rājasūya sacrifice. (95)
Aṣṭāgnihomikā, Mādhvī, Vājapeyaśatodbhavā, Acchodā, Mohinī, Campā, Lalitā, Jayā, and Ramā. (96)
Vardhinī, Padminī, Mañjukeśī, Hemnī, Mañjulā, Miśrakeśī, Devikā, and Śāntikā—these constitute the sixty thousand [goddesses]. 97.
There is another residence for the Apsarases; there are also women here in this world who possess ever-unfailing beauty and ever-unfailing youth. (98)
Clad in celestial garments, wearing divine garlands, and anointed with divine perfumes and ointments,
they were fully endowed with celestial enjoyments and could assume forms at their own will.
Having performed month-long fasts, they may stumble from their celibacy—
either once, twice, or thrice— due to the influence of fate.
These celestial enjoyments, perfect in beauty and charm, dwell in the world of the Apsarases, endowed with every object of desire. (101)

Having performed their desired vows along with their ancillaries according to the prescribed rules, they become capable of moving at will; having come here, they become objects of enjoyment for the gods.

These noble women, who uphold their devotion to their husbands, though held by force by one more powerful than they, take delight with the thought that he is their husband; thus, at times, these beloved ones remain so.
Those women who, while their husbands are away, always observe the vow of celibacy, yet happen by chance to violate it even once—these are the ones called "beautiful-eyed" (vāmalocanā). 104.
Having honored a brahmin couple with gold, fragrant substances, a thousand [pieces of gold], a bed, ornaments, food, and many wonderful objects; 105.
Or at the time of a solar transit or during the Vyatīpāta yoga, that woman of excellent complexion should give [the gift], saying: "May the God who can assume any form at will be pleased."
Who gave? To whom did he give? Desire gave; it was given to desire. Desire is the giver; desire is the receiver. O Desire, this is yours.
With this mantra, if a woman gives [the gift] according to her ability and with desire, she shall dwell among the most excellent Apsarases for a kalpa in this world. (108)
A certain woman, assuming the form of a maiden, was enjoyed by someone somewhere;
from that time forward, she remained a celibate ascetic in the form of a deity.
Meditating upon that conduct, she passes away in due time;
assuming a divine form, she is born here as one who partakes of divine enjoyments.
Having thus informed his wife, the great sage Agastya, born from a jar and begotten by Mitra and Varuṇa, remained silent before his wife named Lopāmudrā.
Then, in Kāśī, the goddesses Śivā and Durgā, who are fond of the vow of Brahman,
went in the morning to the hermitage of Agastya, where the devoted wife was present.
He went to see Lopāmudrā, the great virtuous wife worthy of worship by the goddesses;
but not seeing her there, nor finding her returning, the entire circle of the hermitage was empty.
Having meditated and understood [the situation], they went quickly to see her stationed on the Veṅkaṭa mountain;
they bowed, embraced one another, and spoke words to each other.
Requested by the goddesses,
that virtuous woman, together with them and with Agastya, arrived at her own hermitage in Kāśī.
Having obtained the devoted wife, the great virtuous Satī, the celestial women residing in Kāśī attained happiness; for association with the righteous is difficult to find.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you the growth of the Vindhya mountain,
as well as the marvel of Agastya and the hundred virtuous wives of Lopāmudrā.
Any maiden who hears this or recites it shall become devoted to her husband; she will undoubtedly become a virtuous, chaste woman, equal to Śrī herself. || 1.18 ||

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Agastya’s Obstruction of the Vindhya Mountain which had stood blocking the Sun’s Path, Agastya’s Vision of Mahālakṣmī, the Hymn to Mahālakṣmī, the Diversity of Holy Places (Tīrthas), the Praise of Holy Places, the World of the Apsarases, the Causes for Attaining the State of an Apsaras, and the Return of Lopāmudrā and Agastya to Kāśī by the Goddesses of Kāśī," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: King Kārtavīryārjuna was a true disciple of Atri’s son Datta;
he was constantly [instructed] by his devoted wife named Manoramā.
Though protected and though awakened, he did not heed the words of his beloved;
disregarding them, he went to the presence of the son of Jamadagni for battle.
Then the body was abandoned by the woman named Manoramā;
thereafter Kārtavīrya died—listen now to that story, O Lakṣmī. (3)
In the city of Māhiṣmatī, that great king Arjuna Kārtavīrya was the ruler;
once, he went out for a hunt in the forest.
Hungry and exhausted at night, he went to the hermitage of Jamadagni;
by the power of Kāmadhenu, the king was fed along with his army.
Having killed Jamadagni, he seized the wish-fulfilling cow;
then Reṇukā, following her husband, entered the fire and perished.
Filled with wrath, Paraśurāma made this vow:
"I shall rid this earth of kings twenty-one times."
Having given wealth to the Brahmins, he went to the world of Brahmā;
he then related his vow to Brahmā, and Brahmā spoke to him.
"Go to the world of Śiva, my child; seek refuge in Śaṅkara.
Receive from Śaṅkara the armor-mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
Having heard that he would conquer the rare Vaiṣṇava splendor as well as that of Śiva and Śakti,
and having bowed to the Creator (Brahmā), he departed for the world of Śiva.
He bowed his head to Śambhu and related that account to him;
Śaṅkara, being pleased, granted him the excellent mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The armor of Trailokyavijaya, as well as the auspicious hymn of Hari;
Prajāpati is the seer of this Trailokyavijaya armor.
The seer is [the same], the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is the Lord Rāseśvara;
this is always considered the application for attaining victory over the three worlds. (13)
May the Praṇava protect my head; may that which consists of the five syllables, "Obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Svāhā," always protect my skull. (14)
May "Kṛṣṇa" protect my eyes, may "Kṛṣṇaḥ Svāhā" protect my pupils;
and may "Haraye Namaḥ" always protect the creeper-like eyebrows of mine. (15)
Oṃ, may "Govindāya svāhā" always protect my nose;
O Lord, may "Gopālāya namaḥ" protect both my cheeks on all sides. (16)
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the cowherd women; may he always protect my ears. Oṃ, salutations to Kṛṣṇa; may he eternally protect the pair of my lips. (17)
Oṃ govindāya svāhā—may this always protect the row of my teeth.
Kṛṣṇāya—may it protect below the teeth; klīṃ—may it always protect above the teeth. (18)
Oṃ śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā—may this protect my tongue forever. Rāseśvarāya svāhā—may this protect my palate forever. || 19 ||
"Obeisance to the Lord of Rādhikā, svāhā"—may this protect my throat forever. "Obeisance to the Lord of the cowherd women," may this protect my chest forever. || 1.457.20 ||
"Oṃ gopeśāya svāhā—may this protect my shoulder forever!
Namaḥ kiśoraveśāya svāhā—may this always protect my back! (21)
May my belly be protected eternally; salutations always to Mukunda!
Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā—may this protect my hands at all times. (22)
Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu; may he always protect my pair of arms.
Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the Blessed One; may he always protect my nails. (23)
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa; may he always protect the cavities of my nails.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, may Padmanābha always protect my navel. (24)
Oṃ, svāhā to the Lord of All; may this protect my head at all times.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Beloved of the Gopīs; may this always protect my hips. (25)
Oṃ, may the feet of the Lord, the Beloved of the Gopīs, always protect me.
Oṃ hīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to the Lord of the Rasikas; may everything always protect me. (26)
"Oṃ keśavāya svāhā"—may this always protect my hair.
"Namaḥ kṛṣṇāya svāhā"—may this always protect the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*). ||27||
Oṃ, may [the mantra] "svāhā to Mādhava" always protect my body hairs;
Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may "svāhā to Ralikeśa" always protect everything. ||28||
May Kṛṣṇa, the most perfectly complete, protect me always in the eastern direction;
may he himself, the Lord of Goloka, protect me in the south-eastern direction. (29)
May He whose nature is the perfect Brahman always protect me in the south;
may Kṛṣṇa protect me in the southwest, and may Hari protect me in the west.
May Govinda protect me eternally in the northwestern direction at all times;
may he, the crest-jewel of the connoisseurs of rasa, always protect me in the north.
May He who sports in Vṛndāvana always protect me in the northeast;
may the Lord of the life-breath of Vṛndāvanī protect me from above. (32)
May Mādhava, the receiver of offerings and possessor of supreme strength, protect me always;
and may Nṛsiṃha protect me evermore in water, on land, and in the atmosphere. (33)
May Mādhava always protect me constantly, both in sleep and in waking;
may Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the soul of all, protect me from every side. (34)
Thus has this most wonderful armor, the Trailokyavijaya, been declared to you;
by wearing it on the neck or the right arm, there is always victory.
He who recites this ten lakhs of times shall possess an accomplished armor;
one desiring success as wished should perform a fire-oblation consisting of one-tenth of that number.
Oṃ śrī namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇāya paripūrṇatamāya svāhā.
This seventeen-syllable mantra becomes perfected by five hundred thousand recitations. (37)
Now hear this divine hymn of praise, which brings supreme and immediate satisfaction;
it is the celestial hymn of Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, proclaimed by the Creator. 38.
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the subtlest Lord of the Imperishable, who is both devoid of qualities and possessed of qualities, and who is both formless and possessed of form. ||39||
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa—Hari, the support of all, the independent, the desirable, the all-pervading, the witness, and the bestower of the fruits of karma. ||1.457.40||

I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the creator of the birth and other states of the universe, who is existence-consciousness-bliss, who is the ultimate reality, and whose nature comprises female, male, and neuter. ||41||
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the savior, the sustainer, the cause of all causes, the seed, the Brahmin, the sun, and the moon. 42.
I bow down to Śaṅkara, to Śeṣa in his form, to Brahmā, to the sage Kapila, to Sanatkumāra, to the Lord of Rādhā, and to Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||43||
I bow down to Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Manu, the devotee, Vasanta, Mārgaśīrṣaka, Ekādaśī, Sāgara, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||44||
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the Himalaya mountain, the earth, Vṛndāvana, sandalwood, the wish-fulfilling tree, the grain, and the Pārijāta flower. ||45||
I bow down to Airāvata, Vainateya, the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu, as well as nectar, gold, barley, the lion, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||46||
I bow down to Bṛhaspati, Kubera, Veda, Indra, Sarasvatī, the letter 'A', the Ganges, the mind, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||47||
I bow down to Sudarśana, the splendor of Brahman, the beloved, Time, Strength, the Guru, his mother Viśvakarmā, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
I bow down to the devoted wife, the father, the Śālagrāma stone, the son, the king, the Sāmaveda, the bull, the coolness, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||49||
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is fragrance, sound, the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Gāyatrī, the purifier, milk, the one residing in the beautiful picture, praise, and the sacred darbha grass. 1.457.50.
I bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa—the peaceful, all-pervading, intelligent, and wondrous one; the dark-complexioned Lord of the cowherd girls, the beloved who wears divine ornaments. ||51||
I perpetually bow down to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the lover of Rādhā, the captivating one who dwells in bliss and relishes the divine rasa. 52.
"By this hymn, victory shall always be yours throughout the three worlds.
Go, accomplish it, fulfill your vow; victory is yours. (53)
Rāma, having gone to Puṣkara and prepared himself, set out for battle;

The sounds of "Hari" and "Siṃha," the ringing of bells and drums, and celestial songs of melody shall indeed proclaim: "Victory be yours! (55)
He beheld before him auspicious gestures, the sound of clouds bringing victory, and Brahmins, panegyrists, astrologers, and mendicants. (56)
In front, he saw a lamp, a virtuous woman accompanied by her husband and sons,
Śiva and Śivā, a full water-pot, a bow, and likewise a mongoose.
The black antelope, the elephant, the lion, the horse, the rhinoceros, the elephant, the yak, the royal swan, the ruddy goose, the parrot, and the cuckoo. ||58||
The peacock, the wagtail, the conch-bird, as well as the cakora, the pigeon, the crane, the kāraṇḍava, the cātaka, and the sparrow; ||59||
A flash of lightning, a rainbow, the sun, auspicious sunlight,
fresh meat, a living fish, a conch shell, and gold.
Ruby, silver, pearl, the lord of gems (sapphire), and coral;
curd, parched grain, white grain, white flowers, and saffron. ||61||
A leaf, a banner, an umbrella, a mirror, a white chowrie, a cow with its calf, and a king seated upon a chariot equipped with weapons; ||62||
Milk, clarified butter, betel nut, nectar, auspicious milk-rice, a Śālagrāma stone, ripe fruit, a svastika, sugar, and honey. (63)

Musk, a fan, water, turmeric, clay from a sacred ford, white mustard seeds, black mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, a lock of hair from a brahmin, and a young maiden. ||65||
A deer, a courtesan, a bee, camphor, one clad in yellow garments, cow urine, cow dung, the dust raised by cows, and the impression of a cow's hoof. ||66||
A cow-pen, the path of cows, a beautiful cow-stall, the movement of cows, as well as an ornament, a divine image, a blazing fire, and a great festival; 67.

Having received auspicious blessings from the Brahmins and inhaling the fragrant breeze,

There, beneath the Akṣaya-vata tree, he fell asleep at night;
when the night had passed, he beheld various dreams.
That which is not conceived by the mind, nor produced by wind, bile, or phlegm, appears [as illusions] in elephants, horses, mountains, palaces, cows, trees, and their fruits. (7.1)
One sees oneself being mounted [into hell], weeping and devoured by worms;
then one sees oneself being mounted upon a boat, anointed with sandalwood paste. ||72||
He was wearing a garland of flowers and beautifully adorned with yellow garments;
yet all his limbs were drenched in feces and urine, and smeared with fat and pus.

he saw himself on the riverbank, adorned with broad lotus petals.
Having consumed milk-rice mixed with curd, ghee, and honey, and having eaten betel-leaf, he receives the blessings of the Brahmins. ||75||
And he saw himself beholding lamps made of fruit and flowers, as well as ripe fruit, milk, and hot food mixed with sugar. (76)

Then she saw herself within the mandala of the moon and the sun; thereafter, she saw a woman accompanied by her husband and son, smiling.

He saw himself beholding a tree laden with fruit and flowers, a statue of a deity, and a king seated upon an elephant or mounted on a chariot. (81)
He saw himself entering his own house, beholding a Brahmin woman dressed in yellow garments and adorned with jewel ornaments.

Parśurāma beheld an elephant, a bull, a serpent, a white [horse], a white chowrie, a blue lotus, and a mirror. 84.
In a dream, Rāma beheld himself seated upon a chariot rich with the nine gems, adorned with garlands of jasmine, and resting on a jeweled lion-throne.
In his dream, Rāma beheld a row of lotuses, a lotus-pitcher, curd, parched grain, ghee, honey, a leaf-parasol, and a person holding a parasol.
In a dream, Rāma beheld a row of cranes, a row of swans, and a row of maidens observing vows, all worshipping a bright water-jar.

In a dream, Rāma beheld a rain of nectar, a rain of leaves, a rain of fruits, the arrival of cows, and a rain of flowers and sandalwood.
In a dream, Rāma beheld fresh meat, a living fish, a peacock, a white wagtail, a lake, and sacred pilgrimage sites.
In a dream, Rāma beheld a pigeon, a parrot, a bow, a conch shell, a hawk, a cātaka bird, a tiger, a lion, and a cow.
In a dream, Rāma beheld yellow orpiment, turmeric, a heap of auspicious white grain, a blazing fire, and likewise dūrvā grass.
In a dream, Rāma beheld a multitude of temples, a worshipped Śiva-liṅga, and an honored earthen image of Śiva. (93)
In his dream, Rāma repeatedly saw himself eating various foods made from the flour of barley and wheat. ||94||
In a dream, he enjoyed women adorned with divine garments and ornaments;
moreover, Paraśupradhi committed an act of incestuous intercourse in his dream.
He saw a dancing courtesan and drank blood and wine;
indeed, he beheld his own self with all its limbs smeared with blood.
O Lotus-born One, Rāma joyfully ate the flesh of yellow-colored birds and humans in his dream at the break of dawn.
Seeing himself suddenly bound with fetters and wounded by a weapon, he was bewildered;
then, at dawn, he arose while remembering Hari.
In his mind he thought, "I shall certainly conquer all my enemies";
then Kārtavīryārjuna beheld ill omens during the night.
He saw himself anointed with oil, mounted upon a donkey,
wearing a garland of *auḍra* flowers and smeared with red sandalwood paste.
Clad in red garments and adorned with ornaments of iron,
he was playing and laughing with a heap of extinguished charcoal.
He saw the earth covered in ashes, the ground strewn with *jaya* flowers,
and the sky devoid of the moon and sun, filled with a crimson twilight.
And he saw a widow with disheveled hair dancing, her nose severed,
dressed in red garments, and laughing with a loud, boisterous laugh.
He beheld a funeral pyre provided with arrows yet devoid of fire, accompanied by ashes;
he saw a rain of ashes, a rain of blood, and a rain of fire.
He also beheld the earth strewn with ripe *tāla* fruits, covered with heaps of bones,
and filled with multitudes of skulls along with severed hair and nails.
At night, he beheld a mountain of salt, heaps of cowrie shells, and a cavern filled with powders and oils.
He beheld a flowering tree of both the Aśoka and Karavīra;
and he saw a palm tree laden with fruit, from which the fruits were falling.
A full pitcher fell from his own hand and shattered;
he also beheld the orb of the sun falling from the sky.
Thus he beheld the lunar orb falling from the sky,
the falling of meteors, comets, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
And Arjuna saw in his dream a man of deformed appearance with a hideous face, naked, approaching right before him.
In a dream, he saw a twelve-year-old girl, adorned with clothes and ornaments, departing from her own home in great anger. || 111 ||
Arjuna saw in a dream that his beautiful wife Manoramā was requesting him to go alone into the forest. || 11.2 ||
An angry Brahmin cursed him, as did a renunciant, an ascetic, and his guru;
he also saw painted dolls on the wall dancing.
He saw himself being tormented by vultures, crows, and buffaloes,
and being crushed in an oil-press, whirled around by an oil-maker.
He saw himself held by naked men with nooses in their hands;
all the singers were dancing and singing songs in his house.
At night, Arjuna indeed beheld the leaders of the worlds sporting in marriage, experiencing supreme bliss, and even engaging in hair-to-hair combat.
At night he beheld a battle between crows and dogs,
as well as *moṭakas* and funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) in a cremation ground filled with corpses.
At night, Arjuna saw a woman wearing red garments and another wearing white;
she was dressed in black clothes, dark-complexioned, naked, and had her hair disheveled.
Arjuna saw in his dream that a widow was embracing her own husband,
and that a barber was shaving a bald man’s head and the rows of beard upon his chest.
In a dream, Arjuna beheld his chest torn open by claws;
in that same dream, he saw a heap of sandals and leather thongs.
He saw a wheel revolving on the ground belonging to a potter,
and a withered tree that had risen up, being whirled about by a whirlwind.
In his dream, Arjuna beheld Pūrṇamāna and Kabandha,
as well as a string of skulls being ground to powder by a whirlwind.
In his dream, Arjuna beheld terrifying spirits and ghosts with most dreadful teeth, vomiting forth fire.
In a dream, Arjuna beheld a scorched soul, a burnt tree, a man seized by disease, one who was maimed in limb, and a low-born man.
Arjuna beheld in his dream the sudden falling of trees on the mountain peaks, as well as the repeated descent of thunderbolts.
He repeatedly heard the howling of dogs and jackals;
[he saw one] with head downward and feet upward, with disheveled hair and naked.
At night, Arjuna saw one wandering and moving upon the ground,
and he heard the sound of a distorted cry and the weeping of a deity at the edge of the village.
Having heard this, King Kārtavīryārjuna woke up at dawn;
while sneezing, he rose from his bed and stumbled against his devoted wife.
Seeing her beloved husband, the lord, at night, the virtuous and faithful Satī, who was deeply distressed by having seen a wicked dream, [approached] Manoramā.
She performed her final service by placing her husband upon her lap,
for to virtuous women, a husband is indeed dearer than a hundred sons.
However, having perceived through evil omens my impending destruction,
my husband was indeed united with a Brahmin who was a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Knowing she was about to go forth to battle, she restrained all her vital breaths;
having pierced the six cakras, she entered the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra). || 1.32 ||
That woman of divine form quickly departed for the world of the virtuous (Satyaloka).
Then Arjuna went forth to fight, and he beheld many inauspicious omens.
Satī, having ascended her chariot, went to the battle with her husband in his divine body, while her companion remained invisible by her side.
At the gate, Arjuna saw a widow who was ill-favored and had a severed nose; she was dressed in black garments, weeping, shaven-headed, and wicked.
He saw another unchaste woman who was corrupt in speech, corrupt in her private parts, afflicted by disease, a procuress, and bereft of husband and sons. (136)
A potter, an oil-presser, a hunter, one who lives by snakes, one with tattered clothes, one with very coarse limbs, one who is naked, or one dressed in saffron robes. || 1.37 ||
One who has burned a corpse on a funeral pyre, one who has extinguished the embers of a fire, a seller of fat, and likewise a seller of a daughter; || 1.38 ||
A man bitten by a snake, a snake, a monitor lizard, a hare, poison,
the food prepared for a śrāddha, a funeral ball (piṇḍa), a moṭaka, and likewise sesame seeds— || 139 ||
A Brahmin who eats the food of a Śūdra, a temple-priest, a village-priest, one who makes grass effigies, and one who performs the cremation of a corpse; ||| 1.457.140 ||
An empty jar, a broken jar, oil, salt, and bone; cotton, a tortoise, powder, and a dog that makes noise. || 141 ||
On the right, however, [he sees] a jackal making a terrifying sound, as well as a cowrie shell, a razor, shorn hair, a fingernail, and filth. (142)
One should avoid quarreling and lamenting, as well as people who cause distress, inauspicious things, weeping, and people who are crying out in grief. || 143 ||
One who gives false testimony, a thief, a murderer of a man,
the husband of an unchaste woman, the son of an unchaste woman, and one who eats the food of an unchaste woman— (144)
One who steals the property or wealth of deities, gurus, or brahmins;
a thief who misappropriates what has been given; a robber; a violent person; a slanderer; and a wicked man—[these are those who must be avoided]. 145.

One who is disaffected toward his father and mother, one who harms twice-born men or the holy fig tree, one who destroys the truth, one who is ungrateful, one who is wounded, and one who betrays trust—[these are excluded]. (146)
One who reviles his guru, the gods, or the twice-born; one who is devoid of good conduct;
as well as a eunuch, a leper, one who is one-eyed, or even one who is deaf—(147)
A Pulkasa, one whose linga has been severed, one who is bald, one who is devoid of facial hair, one intoxicated by liquor, liquor itself, a widow, a fist, and a buffalo or a donkey; || 148 ||
He saw a crow vomiting blood,
as well as urine, feces, phlegm, a withered corpse, and a human skull.
Fierce winds, rains of blood, evil omens, the felling of trees,

An iron chain, dry wood, a crow, sulphur, one who lives by black magic, a quack physician, chaff, and likewise medicinal herbs; || 151 ||
Kārtavīrya beheld a red flower, news of death, a Brahmin’s curse, sneezing, as well as the falling of his staff and crown.
The throbbing of his left limb, a numbness in his body, the sound of chariots, horses, and cattle, the harsh rattling of chariot wheels, and a sense of terror arose within his heart. (153)
Nevertheless, the king entered the battlefield without hesitation;
having bowed to Paraśurāma, he bestowed wealth upon the brahmins. (154)
War-drums were sounded and both armies arrayed themselves for battle;
then Paraśurāma spoke to Arjuna in a manner that was heard by all and consistent with justice.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Abduction of the Wish-Fulfilling Cow (Kāmadhenu) by Jamadagni under the pretext of recovering it, the Chastity of Reṇukā, Parśurāma’s Acquisition of the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa Mantra, Kavaca, and Stotra from Śakra, the Omens for Parśurāma in Dream and Wakefulness, the Ill Omens for Sahasrārjuna, the Chastity and Devotion of the Virtuous Wife Manoramā, and the Arrival at the Battlefield," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. ||457||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; Parśurāma, who is a portion of Mādhava, spoke these words to Kārtavīrya, the upholder of dharma, in the midst of battle.
Listen, O Indra among kings, most righteous one born of the Lunar dynasty;
you are the disciple of the wise Dattātreya, who is a portion of Viṣṇu.
O evil-minded one, why have you insulted this aged Brahmin? His virtuous wife, tormented by grief, has gone away together with her husband. (3)
O King, what will become of you in the next world from the slaughter of these two?
Where has that Kapila of yours gone, and what will the state of the bank be like? (4)
O King, that which has been accomplished by you, a plowman will not perform;
thus both your good fame and your ill repute shall remain as nothing more than a mere story. (5)
A most terrible injustice has been committed by you; receive its fruit!
O Indra among kings, give an answer in this assembly at the head of the battlefield.
Having heard this, Kārtavīryārjuna began to speak:
"Listen, O Rāma; you too are a portion of Hari, of this there is no doubt."
He who, through right understanding and action, cultivates the realization of Brahman,
being pure and devoted to his own duty— he is proclaimed a Brāhmaṇa.
Because he reflects both internally and externally, he performs fruitful action;
the silent sage who always speaks at the proper time for the sake of others' welfare is called a *muni*.
Whether toward gold or a clod of earth, a house or a forest, mud or highly fragrant sandalwood,
the yogi whose conduct toward Rāma is one of equanimity is called "one who acts according to reality."
He who contemplates Viṣṇu with an attitude of equanimity toward all living beings,
and who practices devotion toward Hari— he is called a devotee of Hari.
For Brahmins, sages, and likewise for yogis,
as well as for the devotee of Hari who is a brahmin, these [sacred sites] are the wish-fulfilling cows of asceticism.
Kṣatriyas always desire sovereign power and always long for jewels;
however, a Kṣatriya’s longing for asceticism is exceedingly ill-regarded.
In disputes among Brahmins, one who is excessively desirous is greatly censured;
one who is passionate performs rajasic actions out of attachment to worldly deeds. || 14 ||
One who is blinded by passion and characterized by the quality of rajas is proclaimed a king;
O Sage, it was out of such passion that I indeed requested the wish-fulfilling cow.
"O Brahmin, tell me, this transgression was indeed committed by your father against my armies; what fault is there here for me, who am full of passion? (16)
"An army of thirty akṣauhiṇīs has risen up to destroy me;
there is no fault in killing an assailant who is intent on slaying. (17)
And you too, having become an ascetic, have made a vow devoid of the dharma of a brahmin; tell me, is this not an injustice? 18.
"However, for the sake of both your parents, you intend to rid the earth of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times; tell me, O brāhmaṇa, is that right? (1.9)
Having heard these words of pride, Paraśurāma,
his wrath overflowing, struck his own bow with a twang in an instant and released his arrows.
With floods of arrows, she covered Arjuna, his chariot, and likewise the sky;
the beautiful, divine, and virtuous wife remained stationed upon the chariot.
Then the Goddess, accompanied by Mahālakṣmī, protected her husband;
meanwhile, the king also cut down the volleys of arrows with his own shafts.
All the other four brothers of Rāma, acting as his disciples, slaughtered Arjuna’s army with sharp weapons and swords in their hands. ||23||
The lord of kings warded them off with a net of arrows,
and then the sons of Jamadagni cut through that net of arrows as well.
The king discharged a divine weapon, but the sages cut it down;
with divine weapons alone, the sages severed his bow along with its arrow.
The virtuous Manoramā, of divine form, protected her husband— the chariot, the charioteer, and even the king’s armor.
Seeing the king with his weapons laid aside, the sages were overwhelmed with joy;
they seized the tridents of the wielder of the trident (Śiva) with the desire to slay the king of the Matsyas.
At the moment the trident was being set down, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O best of Brahmins, cast away the trident; for that [trident] of Śiva is indeed unfailing. (28)
This divine armor of Śiva protects all its limbs;
it is on the neck of the King of Fish—ask the king for this armor.
Having heard this, Rāma became an ascetic and begged the king for his armor;
the king then gave him the armor for the sake of victory over the universe.
Rāma struck him with a trident, and Arjuna fell into a swoon; meanwhile, the virtuous Manoramā, through her ascetic vows and yogic powers, [protected him]. || 3.1 ||
Then, at the hands of her own husband, that beautiful woman protected her life-breaths in her head;
at that time, the virtuous and chaste lady spoke to the kings like the sky.
Bṛhadbala, Somadatta, Vidarbha, the lord of Mithilā, as well as the sovereign of Niṣadha and the sovereign of Magadha; ||33||
"Let those who are as dear to me as my own life hear: I shall now perform the funeral rites for Prāṇa;
you, however, must go to battle and fight fiercely. (34)
War is the duty of Kṣatriyas; death in battle is not censurable.
"Svāhā" in battle is for Brāhmaṇas; in this world, it is a mockery in the Veda.
For Kṣatriyas, strength is the weapon; for Vaiśyas, however, strength is their occupation.
For mendicants, strength is alms; for Śūdras, service is strength. (36)
Devotion to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the strength of devotees; Hari is the strength of ascetics;
and the subduing of the wicked is indeed the strength of those who practice austerity. (37)
For women, dress is indeed their strength; for housewives, youth is their strength;
for kings, the army is indeed their strength; and for children, weeping is their strength. (38)
Truth is the strength of the virtuous, while forgiveness is the strength of the holy;
falsehood is the strength of the wicked, and fortitude is the strength of the reckless. (39)
Knowledge is the strength of the learned, while wealth is the strength of the wealthy;
discernment is the strength of the noble, and unity is the strength of the subjects.
For those possessing qualities, virtue is strength; for virtuous women, service to their husbands is strength;
for the gods, worship is said to be strength; and for disciples, service to the guru is strength. (41)
Strength for householders is their wife; strength for servants is pleasing their master;
strength for renunciants is freedom from desire; and the great vow of Brahman is indeed their strength. 42.
Merit is the strength of those who perform good deeds; water is the strength of aquatic creatures;
tranquility is the strength of Brahmins; and power is the strength of Kṣatriyas. (43)
"Let all the Kṣatriyas with their armies wage war against the Brahmins!
Having spoken thus, that virtuous Manoramā [beheld] Arjuna unconscious. 44.
"If I am in every way a devoted wife to my lord of life, then let me serve him with various offerings that grant great power. (45)
"May my lord regain consciousness," said the devoted wife;
at that moment he regained consciousness and rose up for battle.
Then Rāma struck Somadatta with a trident,
Bṛhadbāla with a mace, and Vidarbha with a lance.
He struck the King of Mithila with a mallet, the King of Niṣadha with a spear,
the King of Magadha with sharp iron arrows, and the soldiers with a multitude of weapons.
Having slain all the kings, he rushed toward Arjuna;
meanwhile, the virtuous Manoramā remained standing nearby. ||49||
"O base Brahmin Rāmarāma, you shall be reduced to ashes if you resort to injustice and kill my protector."
Having heard [of Satī] and seeing her before him, Rāma turned back out of fear;
likewise, there were hundreds from Kānyakubja and hundreds from Saurāṣṭra.
Hundreds of Rāṣṭrīyas, as well as Mahārāṣṭras, Vangajas,
Gaurjaras, and Kaliṅgas, were rendered lifeless by Rāma.
Rāma slaughtered twelve akṣauhiṇīs day and night;
yet King Kārtavīrya held the Śrīlakṣmī-kavaca in his hand.
Having girded himself and being fully equipped with weapons and missiles, he mounted his chariot and advanced;
he fought with various missiles and slew many Brahmins. (54)
Parśurāma, assuming the form of Time (Kāla) and bearing his axe, rushed forward to sever the head; at that moment, Viṣṇu assumed the form of a Brahmin.
Saying "Do not go," he seized her hand and restrained her, speaking at that very moment because she had held the armor of Śrī Mahālakṣmī upon her arm.
"The king will not die; remain firm," said [the messenger].
Then Viṣṇu, in the form of a Brahmin, came to that king to make this request. (57)
Having become a Brahmin, the Blessed One himself requested the armor;
at that time, Manoramā, the female bird who was his mate, was seized with terror.
Arjuna wished to give those delightful things, but Lakṣmī restrained him,
saying, "O King, as long as the armor of Lakṣmī remains upon your arm," (59)
"As long as I am Lakṣmī herself, I am able to protect you.
Though he was told repeatedly, "Do not give it," the king nevertheless gave it.
For a moment, Manoramā, her beauty radiant, bowed to her husband and wept;
then, intent upon that [task], she was unable to go along with the armor.
Then Satī performed a test of Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu, taking up his armor, approached Rāma.
O beloved, listen as he gave that mantra with its ritual formula to Paraśurāma;
then he bestowed the mantra: "Oṃ śrīkamalavāsinyai svāhā. (6.3)
Prajāpati is its seer (ṛṣi), its metre is Bṛhatī, and its deity is Padmālayā; its application is to the four aims of human life.
Oṃ śrī kamalavāsinyai svāhā—may this protect my head. Oṃ śrī—may it protect my skull; śrīṃ śriyai namaḥ—may it protect my eyes. ||65||
"Oṃ śrīṃ śriyai svāhā"—may this indeed always protect the pair of ears.
"Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mahālakṣmyai svāhā"—may this protect my nose. (66)
Oṃ śrīṃ, may [the goddess] Padmālayā always protect the teeth; au śrīṃ, may Kṛṣṇapriyā always protect the cavities between the teeth. ||67||
Oṃ, may the mistress of Śrī Nārāyaṇa always protect my throat;
Oṃ Śrīṃ, may the beloved of Keśava always protect my shoulders. ||68||
Oṃ śrīṃ, may she who dwells in the lotus protect my navel forever;
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, may the Mother of Saṃsāra protect my chest forever. (69)
Oṃ śrīṃ mo kṛṣṇakāntāyai svāhā—may this always protect my back.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śriyai svāhā—may this always protect my hands.
Oṃ, may she who is the beloved of Śrīnivāsa always protect my feet;
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, svāhā to Śrī, may she always protect all my limbs. ||71||
May Mahālakṣmī protect me in the east; may Kamalālayā protect me in the southeast;
may Padmā protect me in the south; and may Śrī, the beloved of Hari, protect me in the southwest.
May Padmālayā protect me in the west; may she herself protect me in the northwest. May Kamalā protect me in the north, and Sindhukanyakā in the northeast. (73)
May Nārāyaṇī protect me above, and may Viṣṇupriyā protect me below; may she who is dearer to Viṣṇu than his own life-breath protect me constantly and from every side. (74)
Wear this armor, which bestows all sovereignty, well upon your arm;
you will certainly become invulnerable to both the lords of the gods and the lords of the asuras.
Having spoken thus and given him the armor, Acyuta departed for Vaikuṇṭha;
at that moment, Manoramā, a mere fraction of Lakṣmī, indeed left Arjuna.
She went to Vaikuṇṭha together with Viṣṇu, having been carried away by Viṣṇu;
Arjuna said, "O wife, O beloved, do not go, leaving me behind! (77)
But Manoramā said to him: "The connection has reached its end;
slain by the weapon of Paraśurāma, you shall follow after me. (78)
"O King, slain by the hand of a Brahmin, you will swiftly attain liberation;
for your sake, Vaikuṇṭha—where my own abode is certainly established—will be yours. (79)
Having spoken thus, the goddess departed; the king fought fiercely.
