O Padmaja, his army of two hundred thousand fought together with the Brahmins.
The king hurled weapons, and the disciples of Rāma fled;
but Rāma then discharged the Āgneya weapon, and the battlefield became filled with fire.
The king extinguished it with the highly powerful Vāruṇa weapon;
Rāma then discharged the Gāndharva weapon, which consisted of ten million mountains, serpents, and other such things.
Arjuna indeed warded off that terrible [weapon] with the Vāyavya weapon;
Rāma discharged the Nāga weapon, and the king discharged the Gāruḍa weapon.
Rāma discharged the Māheśa weapon; the king discharged the Vaiṣṇava.
Rāma discharged the Brahmāstra; the king countered with the Brahmāstra.
While he was thus meditating, Dattātreya, the preceptor of Arjuna, arrived;
he indeed gave a trident to Rāma for the purpose of destroying Kṛṣṇavarmā.
The king seized that trident and hurled it at Rāma's neck;
Rāma fell into a swoon and collapsed while remembering Śrī Hari.
At the command of Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu restored the Brāhmaṇa to life;
and once he had regained consciousness, Rāma received the Pāśupata [weapon]. (87)
But Arjuna, having been granted the perfected weapon by Dattātreya, paralyzed him right there;
indeed, Rāma himself was rendered motionless.
And Kṛṣṇavarmā saw the king protected by Śrīkṛṣṇa;
he also beheld the Sudarśana discus, which was wandering about as a protector against the enemy.
In the meantime, an incorporeal voice arose there, saying:
"O King, that supreme armor of Kṛṣṇa is upon your arm."
Śambhu protects that king; therefore, beg for it as alms.
Then this Bhārgava will be able to slay the king. (91)
Then Śambhu, having restored consciousness by means of perfected mantras and having removed the paralyzing spell, Rāma seized his own axe.
Holding a *pāśupata* weapon in one hand and likewise an axe in the other, he remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; at that moment, He arrived.
Śambhu himself, having become a brahmin, begged that very armor from Arjuna;
Śambhu then delivered the armor given by the king to Rāma.
Sudarśana, the armor, and the three forms of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa approached Rāma’s side and said, "Now you shall be victorious."
The Pāśupata weapon of Śambhu is the most excellent, as is the Sudarśana of Hari alone;
these two are indeed the foremost among all weapons in the three worlds. (96)
Having donned that supreme protective armor, the twice-born said to him:
"O King, engage in battle quickly; for victory and defeat depend upon the timing. (97)
"By you much has been studied, much has been given, and the earth has been ruled;
yet here in this very place, I have been rendered motionless by you and utterly stupefied. (98)
All the kings were conquered, and Rāvaṇa was defeated with ease;
I was conquered by Śambhu when he gave me the trident, yet I have been restored to life.
"Act quickly; this is your moment. Upon hearing this, he replied:
"O Rāma, what has been studied? What has been given in charity? And who has been instructed?"
How many kinds of kings, my best ones, have passed away, consumed by Time?
[They were] Intelligence, Splendor, Valor, Victory, and likewise Triumph;
Fortune, Sovereignty, Wisdom, Generosity, Prestige, and Supreme Austerity.
Pride in learning, as well as honor and even universal sovereignty—these too [are obstacles]. || 102 ||
In an instant, everything belonging to me passed into the possession of Manoramā;
she was Lakṣmī herself, a virtuous woman devoted solely to her husband.
"My protector has died, and I have gone with her;
O Brahmin, why do you merely watch the first battle? (104)
"The grief that my former battles were not witnessed is the first; now, even the second is my death at the hands of a Brahmin. (1.05)
The grief caused by the loss of aged parents is exceedingly cruel;
for at the proper time, a lion may kill a jackal, or a jackal may kill a lion.
At the right time, a deer kills a tiger, and likewise a lion kills a lordly elephant; at the right time, a fly kills a buffalo, and likewise a snake kills Garuḍa.
The king praises his servant, and likewise Mahendra praises a mere mortal;
O Brahmin, all is wrought by Time, for Time is indeed insurmountable.
The killing of a Brahmin brings about my total destruction;
the death of a devoted wife results in the ruin of the Brahmin woman.
O twice-born one, when my devoted wife died, I too died in every way;
for she was the very form of Lakṣmī, and that agreement had indeed been made by Acyuta.
I entreat you, as well as the gods and all my gurus, with devotion:
may you forgive whatever offenses I have committed against you, so that hell may not await me in the future. (111)
Having spoken thus and causing his bow to twang repeatedly,
he became like the Destroyer of Time himself and rained down many arrows by the hundreds of thousands.

Crying out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! and addressing him as "O charming one," the king discharged thousands of crescent-headed arrows, spears, javelins, and swords from his bow at the brahmins there when their lifespans had come to an end.
Rāma, having assumed a twofold form, fought with that mountain.
But assuming an artificial form and holding an axe in his hand,
he ran toward him, went before him, and severed his circle of arms.
With his second form, he seized the most formidable weapon,
the Pāśupata, along with its mantra, and discharged it at the king as if in play.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, for Kārtavīryārjuna had been slain;
likewise, those other warriors who were capable of seizing the living were killed by the brahmins in battle.
Others likewise fled and established their own respective kingdoms;
then Rāma gave Māhiṣmatī as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the brāhmaṇa.
And he also gave the kingdoms of others as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin—
the gods, the sages, the goddesses, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras.
And all the lotus-born ones showered a rain of flowers upon the head of Rāma;
in heaven the kettledrums resounded and a cry of joy arose.
Thus, twenty-one times he cleared the earth of the kṣatriyas;
and by the fame of Paraśurāma, the entire world was filled.
Rāma gave the kingdoms to the Brāhmaṇas and desisted from his task;
indeed, all the Kṣatriyas were slain, as well as those in the womb and the young children.
O beloved, some Kṣatriya women were devoted to their husbands—some young, some middle-aged, some old, and even some who were still nursing at the breast. (123)
The goddesses, possessing divine movements and remaining concealed, went to the Himalayas;
dwelling in the mountain caves, they nurtured their own children.
The Kṣatriyas born of his lineage once again established kingdoms;
meanwhile, Paraśurāma, having fulfilled his vow on the field of the Kurus, [departed].
Having prepared five sacrificial pits at Syamantapañcaka filled with the blood of Kṣatriyas, he offered handfuls of water to his father, mother, and the Brāhmaṇas.
Then he performed the śrāddha ceremony and brought satisfaction to the ancestral deities;
thereafter, he himself partook of the water and food with a sense of peace.
But upon the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, those who were weak and indeed disliked by the living,
speaking falsehoods, performed the protection of the living beings.
Various other types of births have arisen, and distinct castes have emerged;
those who are not of the Kṣatriya lineage, being devoid of Kṣatriya duties, are indeed nothing but Dasyus.
O Lakṣmī, there were others on earth who were kṣatriyas by birth but lived in secret, engaging in various occupations such as servitude and agriculture. (1.458.13)
Then, having fulfilled his vow, Rāma went to the preceptor Śiva at the divine gateway of Kailāsa in order to worship him.
Obstructed by Gaṇeśa, Rāma then struck that Lord of the Gaṇas, Gaṇapati, on the tusk with his axe in a fit of rage.
Having had his tusk broken, he is then called Gaṇeśa, the Single-Tusked;
having made his trunk very long with its tusk broken from the root to the tip. (1.33)
Held by Gaṇeśa on his trunk, the elephant grew to a great size;
having whirled him around the three worlds, he threw that Rāma into the ocean.
Having again rendered him inert, he was cast down into Goloka for the purification of his sins at the lotus feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having raised the purified Rāma, the illustrious Lord Gaṇeśvara cast Paraśurāma into the presence of Śaṅkara.
Having approached Śaṅkara, he beheld him and received his blessing and favor;
and having propitiated the illustrious Gaṇeśvara, he likewise received the grace of both Śaṅkara and Śivā.
He offered praise to Śiva and Śivā, and Śiva said to him, "May you be auspicious!
O son, may you be immortal; my child, attain steadfastness."
Through every act of devotion, may victory be yours forever;
may the Blessed Lord Hari, the inner soul of all, be eternally pleased.
"May you have devotion to Kṛṣṇa, to Śiva who bestows auspiciousness, and to your guru, O Śiva.
Śambhu said: 'O disciple, may you live long and remain steadfast.'"
Thereafter, that Paraśurāma went to the earth for the sake of asceticism;
staying on Mount Mahendra, he performs eternal penance. || 141 ||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you of the destruction of Kārtavīrya,
as well as the power of Manoramā’s devotion to her husband.
By reading and hearing this, one obtains the strength of devotion to her husband;
by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, she shall obtain worldly enjoyment, liberation, and service to Kṛṣṇa.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of How Sahasrārjuna was Protected by the Divine and Chaste Manoramā During His Battle with Paraśurāma, How Manoramā’s Separation Occurred Due to Lakṣmī’s Armor Being Removed, the Subsequent Death of Arjuna, and the Single-Tusked Nature of Gaṇeśa," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Beyond the world of Indra, O Lotus-born one, there is a beautiful city named Arciṣmatī; it is the city of Vītihotra, situated in the highest heaven.
Those who are devoted to Jātavedas dwell here, firm in their vows;
those of steadfast resolve and conquered senses who enter the fire [also dwell here]. || 2 ||
The men and women there all bathed in fire and were radiant like fire;
likewise, the brahmins were devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice and lived as celibate students of the sacred fire.
The devotees who observe the five-fire vow, the Brahmins who worship the sacred fire,
and those who provide fuel, wood, and kindling for the fires, are themselves the very form of Agni.
Indeed, those who perform sacrifices dwell in the radiant flame of Agni,
[offering] incense, lamps, food offerings, milk, curd, ghee, and sugarcane juice.
All kinds of gods dwell at Vahnibhakta,
belonging to the brahmin Viśvānara who resides on the banks of the Narmadā.
Sucintana was the son of the presiding deity of Narmapura, who was devoted to the sacrifice to Brahman,
possessed of Brahmanic luster, and belonged to the Śāṇḍilya lineage.
"Of these four stages of life, which one is most conducive to the supreme good for the virtuous?
Having reflected thus, Viśvānara praised the householder's life.
The householder is indeed the support of all; he is depended upon by all embodied beings because he abstains from the wives of others and is contented with his own wife.
"By approaching his wife only during her fertile season, a householder is always a celibate.
Having thus resolved, that Brahmin Viśvānara [approached] his devoted wife.
According to the prescribed rites for taking a wife, he took a maiden of his own caste;
devoted to the service of the sacred fire, he was intent upon the performance of the five great sacrifices.
He was one who fully honored the gods, ancestors, guests, the helpless, cows, and others;
while he lived in this manner, a great deal of time passed away.
His wife, named Śuciṣmatī, was devoted to her vows and served her husband;
yet she did not see even a sprout of progeny, which is the means for attaining heaven.
Considering her husband to be Kṛṣṇa and her husband to be Viṣṇu, the devoted wife said:
"O Blessed One, there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to obtain for you who are compassionate."
"Grant me a son who resembles Maheśa and increases my lineage.
Having heard this, he, remaining steadfast in his vow of devotion to a single wife, spoke to his wife.
"So be it," the brahmin then replied; he departed quickly for the sake of penance. Having reached Vārāṇasī, he bathed in the Gaṅgā and beheld Śaṅkara.
Having gone to that land of Vīreśvara, where he attained steadfastness through his desire for a son by means of austerity, he undertook a noble vow.
For one month he took food once a day; for one month he ate only at night;
for one month he subsisted on unsolicited food; and likewise for one month he abstained from food entirely.

For one month he observed the vow of consuming only milk; for one month he subsisted on vegetables and fruits; for one month his food consisted of a handful of sesame seeds; and for one month he lived on water alone.
For one month he subsisted on the five products of the cow; for one month he observed the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
for one month he consumed water from the tips of Kuśa grass; and for one month he lived on air alone.
Then, in the thirteenth month, having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā at the very break of dawn, the twice-born brāhmaṇa arrived before Vīreśa.
Then, within another liṅga, he beheld a beautiful child of eight years,
with tawny matted hair and long eyes, white-complexioned and adorned with sacred ashes.
Beholding him, Viśvānara, filled with exceeding joy, offered this praise:
"That which is the Supreme Brahman, the highest of the high, one alone without a second. (23)
O Śiva, salutations to you who are known as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of auspiciousness;
you are the creator, the nourisher, and the destroyer, your splendor having assumed manifold forms. (24)
Salutations to You, the Child, from whom proceeds that sovereignty consisting of fire and other qualities, as well as fragrance and the like, which resides in even a single part of matter;
salutations to Him who is the internal grasper, the mover, the seer, the supporter, and the controller.
"Salutations to you, the bestower of all desires; homage to you, that child!
Having thus praised him, Viśvānara fell at his feet.
With a smiling face, the Child said to him, "Choose a boon."
Viśvānara replied: "Since you are the bestower of all things, grant me a son such as yourself; I bow to you again and again. (28)
The boy said, "So be it; before long your desire shall bear fruit, for I shall become your son through Śuciṣmatī."
Having said, "I shall become your son, a householder known by name as Śuci, beloved by all the immortals," he vanished from sight.
Then Viśvānara quickly went to his own home and told this to Śuciṣmatī; O beautiful lady, it was not long before she [learned of it]. (31)
She conceived and in due time gave birth to a son;
all the purificatory rites, beginning with the impregnation ceremony (garbhādhāna), were performed by her preceptor.
Upon the birth of the son, the gods and others showered flowers and other offerings; the celestial drums resounded, and indeed, a great festival took place.
In the abode of the brahmin, there were the beautiful dances of apsarases, as well as thousands of vidyādharīs, kinnarīs, and goddesses. (34)
Gandharvas, serpents, and trees, as well as beautiful women and maidens, brought gifts of jewels and gems, appearing most radiant with their ornaments. 3.5.
Accompanied by various auspicious objects and possessing the beautiful luster of the moon,
they went to the house of Viśvānara, singing charming songs.
Hundreds of sages, beginning with Marīci, as well as thousands of world-protectors and ascetics, arrived at that house. (37)
All the gods, beginning with Viṣṇu, as well as the nāgas, humans, and others, and all the sacred fords and holy sites, as well as the ancestors, arrived there. || 38 ||
Stationary beings arrived by the thousands, having assumed mobile forms;
the divine Grandfather himself performed his birth-rite (jātakarma).
Having reflected upon the Veda, which is of that same nature, this householder gave him the name "Śruti," a name which is to be bestowed on the eleventh day.
The householder is the master of the household, the best finder of wealth for his progeny.
O Agni, Lord of the Household, grant me food, glory, and strength. 4.1
Having praised him with the thought, "He is indeed the Unborn (Aja)," Satya then departed;
and all the gods and others likewise went away, praising his radiant son.
Therefore, those dwelling in the householder stage of life desire a son;
for through a son, and especially through one who is devoted, one conquers the worlds. ||43||
The house of one without a son is empty; the earnings of one without a son are in vain;
the lineage of one without a son is severed; for there is nothing more impure than being childless.
There is no gain greater than a son, and no happiness greater than a son.
Nowhere, neither in this world nor in the next, is there a friend superior to a son. (45)

The legitimate son (aurasa), the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), the purchased son (krīta), the given son (datta), the son received (prāpta), the son of a daughter (sutāsuta), the son protected in times of distress (rakṣita), and the pupil (śiṣya)—these are considered the eight kinds of sons. 46.
Viśvānara taught him the Sāman according to the proper method;
in his ninth year, Nārada went to Vaiśvānara. ||87||
The king of sages inquired after the complete welfare of his son, saying:
"O illustrious Viśvānara, O Śuciṣmatī of auspicious vows! (48)
Does the young householder follow the word of you two?

For a son, there is no other sacred ford, no god, no teacher, and no act of merit—nothing else at all—that exists apart from the command of his parents. Indeed, there is no other duty for a son than this.
A mother is more venerable than a father because of her bearing and nourishing [the child] in the womb.
A father is worthy of worship, an ascetic (yati) is worthy of worship, and a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) is also worthy of worship;
yet by all of them, the guru is to be worshipped, and among them, the mother is always to be worshipped.
This alone is the most intense austerity, this alone is the supreme vow, and this alone is the highest dharma:
that which brings satisfaction to one’s parents.
This is declared to be the vow of filial duty; one should serve them just as one would serve Kṛṣṇa.
This is declared to be the vow of a mother; one should serve her as if she were Lakṣmī herself.
"O Vaiśvānara, come hither; sit upon my lap, sir!
I shall examine your marks; show me your right hand. (53-54)
Thus addressed, that householder sat upon the lap of Nārada.
Then the sage, having observed the palate, tongue, and teeth of the boy,
brought a thread dyed with saffron and tripled it.
He measured from the crown of his head down to the soles of his feet;
in height, he was equal in measurement across and upwards, measuring one hundred and eight finger-breadths.
Such a person shall become a protector of the earth, just as this boy is.
He possesses the thirty-two marks: five subtle, five long, seven red, six elevated, three broad, and he is light and deep. (58)
The skin, hair, fingers, teeth, and the joints—these five are indeed his subtle parts; one who possesses these becomes a partaker of the rank of a world-protector (dikpāla).
Furthermore, his two arms, eyes, jaw, knees, and nose are truly long.
By this, he shall indeed become long-lived and a wanderer through the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, the corners of his eyes, the palate, the tongue, and the upper and lower lips—
these seven being reddish-brown, along with his nails, bestow the happiness of sovereignty.
His chest, belly, forehead, shoulders, hands, and face—the six parts—are prominent;
such a person is seen to possess indeed great sovereignty. (6.2)
One who has a broad forehead, waist, and chest will become a king;
one who has a short neck, shanks, and private parts will be short in stature but possess great enjoyments.
His voice, heart, and navel are deep, and he always experiences happiness;
his hands are as firm as the back of a female tortoise and as soft as a leaf.
The feet of this infant, as tender as lotuses, are the cause of his sovereignty;
likewise, his lines extend across the entire forefinger without being broken. (6.5)
If [the lines] emerge from the back of the little finger, one should declare long life;
the feet are well-fleshed, red, even, fine, and very beautiful.
Those with ankles that are even, free from perspiration, and glossy are indicators of sovereignty;
one with very few lines on the palms, which are slightly reddish, is always happy. (67)
By his physical marks, he will become a king of kings; his hands are slender, and his buttocks, ankles, and navel are well-rounded. (68)
The single channel that flows to the right, which is reddish and indicates great sovereignty, is called "dakṣiṇāvartinī" because it urinates while turning to the right.
And the fragrance of fish and honey resides in his secret virility;
his buttocks are broad, fleshy, smooth, and accustomed to comfort.
His two arms, curling to the left and extending gracefully, are fit for the protection of the quarters;
he bears the Śrīvatsa, the thunderbolt, the discus, the lotus, the fish, the bow, and the staff.
The lines on his palms were such that he would become the lord of the three worlds;
he possessed thirty-two teeth and a neck marked by three folds like a conch shell.
His voice possesses the resonance of the *krauñca* bird, the kettledrum, the swan, and the clouds; he is superior even to the Lord of All.
His eyes are tawny like honey, and Fortune never abandons him at any time.
One who has five lines on the forehead, as well as a lion-like belly, is auspicious;
one whose feet are marked with upward lines, and whose breath carries the fragrance of a lotus, is likewise blessed.
This man has unblemished hands, beautiful teeth, and possesses the great marks of excellence;
nevertheless, in his twelfth year, there will be an obstacle caused by lightning-fire.
"O Blessed One, he must be protected with great effort; I fear for him.
Having said this and taken the image, Nārada indeed departed.
For a mere moment, the couple both grieved and rejoiced;
then, at that time, the child was destined to become long-lived for the sake of his parents. (77)
He made a vow: "Listen, if I am indeed your son, I shall perform such asceticism that even Vidyunmālin will tremble with fear. (78)
In order to propitiate Mṛtyuñjaya, the Destroyer of Time,
the son obtained his parents' permission and went to the city of Kāśī.
He bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā and beheld Śambhu and Annapūrṇikā;
then, having gone to the earth at Matsyodarī, he stood there for a moment thereafter.
Having installed the Liṅga on a site free from obstacles, the son performed penance, bathing Śambhu every day and offering blue lotuses. ||81||
He muttered the mantra: "Obeisance to you, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-Śiva.
For six months he performed austerity, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits.
Likewise, for six months he practiced austerity by eating withered leaves;
for six months he subsisted on air, and for six months he consumed only drops of water. ||83||
Thus, when two years had passed and the twelfth year from his birth had arrived,
the wielder of the thunderbolt indeed approached, intending to bring about the obstacle.
"Choose a boon," he said to him; having heard this, the son spoke to Vāsava:
"I do not choose a boon from you, for Śaṅkara is my granter of boons. (85)
"Go, you wicked husband of Ahalyā! Having heard this, Śambhu became enraged and hurled his own vajra; as it was thrown, he caught it effortlessly in his hand. (86)
Śaṅkara became manifest before his eyes, and Mahendra departed for heaven;
Śambhu, however, granted him the supreme boon: "May you live long. (87)
May you become the mouth of all the gods, embodied as the sacrificial fire; may you become the digestive fire within living beings, and may you attain sovereignty as the lord of the quarters. 88.
"Let this Malliṅga installed by you be known by the name Agnīśvara.
Having spoken thus and having bestowed a Vaiṣṇava mantra, Śambhu departed. (89)
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Master.
Vaiśvānara went to his own home, where his wife was devoted to her husband. (1.459.90)
And Janaka too rejoiced upon seeing the son of Arciṣmatī;
with joy, he celebrated a festival, having summoned the gods and others.
Seeing Indra arrived there, the king of fire became enraged;
Indra, for his part, hurled the thunderbolt once more at Vaiśvānara.
The boy fell into a swoon; his mother, placing him upon her lap, said:
"If my devotion to my husband be true, let Indra fall to the earth! (93)
If I am firm in devotion to my husband, then Indra’s thunderbolt shall be useless;
may it be so in every way that my son may come to life.
When she had spoken thus, the thunderbolt turned into black mud;
Indra fell to the ground and realized that you were his son, born from a lotus.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose indeed through the power of her devotion to her husband;
the Goddess, moved by compassion, was entreated by Mahendra for the sake of forgiveness. 96.
She said to that Mahendra: "Arise and be firm;
take up the thunderbolt, but never employ it against fire. (97)
"Upon those who betray their mother, father, guru, or Kṛṣṇa, and upon those who betray a virtuous wife—by my boon, let this thunderbolt hurled by you take the form of lightning. (98)
Upon those devoted to Kṛṣṇa, upon the devotees of your parents and your guru, upon ascetics, and upon the devotees of virtuous women—upon them let your thunderbolt turn into mud. (99)
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to Satī, and likewise to Vaiśvānara;
bowing again to Viśvānara, he went to heaven, as the gods departed.
By the power of Arciṣmatī and by the virtue of his devotion to his wife,
he was protected from death, even though it was imminent, through the grace of Śambhu.
"As long as he remains a Brahmā, so long shall he be Vaiśvānara.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this account been told to you, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and supreme liberation.

Thus ends the four hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Longevity of Gṛhapati, the Son of the Brahmin Viśvānara, through His Austerities, and the Destruction of the Obstacle to His Death Caused by Indra’s Thunderbolt through the Power of His Mother’s Chastity," in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the wonder of Jñānoda;
it occurred long ago in the Age of the Gods within this beginningless cycle of worldly existence.
The guardian of the quarter named Īśāna, while wandering, arrived upon the earth;
at that time, in the Kṛta Yuga, true dharma existed by mere intention alone.
When the clouds did not rain and the rivers did not flow, when there was no desire for water for such activities as bathing and drinking; (3)
While the earth was being traversed here and there by wandering sages,
he entered the field of Ānandakānana, which had become like saline soil.
He beheld the Linga composed of Brahmanic splendor which had emerged from the Imperishable; it was that which, known as "Kiraṇa," had come forth from Viṣṇu and Brahmā.
At that time, there arose a state of competitive striving for superiority;
then, Īśāna beheld a small patch of saline wasteland.
It was like gold, beautiful, radiant, divine, and utterly enchanting;
then the desire arose in Īśāna: "I shall bathe it with waters."
And with his trident, he dug near the vicinity of the southern quarter;
there, in that pit, was divine water born from the body of Nārāyaṇa.
A most purifying stream, connected to the obstruction of water, appeared;
with those waters, he bathed the linga which resembled gold.
Sweeter than nectar, untouched by other embodied beings, and captivating to the minds and eyes of those who had never before seen such worlds; || 1.460.10 ||
Then Hara, the Lord Īśāna, the sovereign of the quarters, being pleased, bathed him a thousand times with jars possessing a thousand streams.
"Choose a boon from me; I shall grant you one that is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Īśāna said to Viśveśa, "Let there be a sacred ford (tīrtha) named after you."
Then Viśveśvara, possessing a beautiful form, said, "So be it";
having become the very nature of the Liṅga, that Maheśvara remains present there.
The *liṅga* makes the hidden meaning understood and bestows knowledge;
without its rays, that support could never come into being. (14)
The substratum, however, is the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord Puruṣottama;
His sign that bestows knowledge is the Liṅga, which is considered to be His radiance. || 15 ||
The step-well belonging to that Suvarṇarūpa, intended solely for the purpose of bathing, is indeed the Jñānavāpī; it is the water of knowledge, the essence of knowledge, and a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Knowledge is of the nature of fluidity, and the lake of knowledge is the abode of Śaṅkara;
by its touching, drinking, sipping, bathing, sprinkling, and so forth— || 1.7 ||
One shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, satisfaction of the ancestors, and whatever fruit one desires;
for I myself am here in the form of knowledge, having assumed a liquid form.
"I shall effect the destruction of dullness and I shall provide instruction in knowledge"—
having granted this boon, Śambhu vanished within the liṅga.
And Īśāna, having bowed, departed toward his own quarter, O Lotus-born One;
meanwhile, there in Ānandavana, there was a Brahmin named Harisvāmī.
She had a daughter who was endowed with virtue, beauty, and good qualities; she was skilled in the entire range of arts, possessed a sweet voice, and was exceedingly beautiful. (21)
A devotee of Kṛṣṇa who regards Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as her supreme deity, she was named Suśīlā; she would always bathe in the Jñānoda-tīrtha.
In the temple of Viśveśvara, the virtuous woman performed sweeping and other services;
she joyfully sang, "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Śiva, Śambhu! ||23||
That maiden Sulocanā did not look at the face of anyone; for that girl Suśravā did not take to heart the words of anyone. (24)
Though she was entreated in secret by those whose minds were fixed on her, Suśīlā— endowed with virtue and devoted to the vow of Kṛṣṇa— did not harbor any desire for them.
Her father was sought after by many young men for his wealth; yet, despite his great prosperity, he was unable to give away that virtuous girl of exalted beauty. (26)
By resorting to the sacred ford of the flood of knowledge, that virtuous maiden then beheld the entire world, both within and without, as being composed of Kṛṣṇa. (27)
Then a Vidyadhara, who had come there out of a desire to see Śambhu,
beheld her endowed with beauty and grace, and he lusted after her.
Having taken Satī as his wife through the Gāndharva rite of marriage, he departed;
she, for her part, constantly served that husband on the Malaya mountain.
There, that virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, constantly remembered her lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, her own master and her chosen deity.
Then once, while her husband was wandering in the Malaya mountains,
a great being suddenly struck him from the path of the sky with a trident.
And by that devoted wife, water was quickly held in her mouth;
she released it, and that virtuous woman reduced the Rākṣasa to ashes and gave up her life.
Then, having taken his corpse and prepared the funeral pyre, Sundarī,
meditating upon her husband Kṛṣṇa, cast her body into the fire of the pyre.
Having enjoyed the heavenly realm for a hundred thousand years,
that couple indeed obtained birth as a Vidyādhara from King Malayaketu.
A most noble Vaiṣṇava devoted to the service of the virtuous, that chaste woman Suśīlā obtained birth in the city of Karṇāṭa. (35)
In due time, the son of Malayaketu married her;
those two, husband and wife, were devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa and possessed the memory of their former births. (36)
They were both renowned by their names as Mālyaketu and Kalāvatī.
Having obtained Mālyaketu as her husband, Kalāvatī became devoted to her husband.
Enjoying an abundance of divine enjoyments, he obtained three offspring.
Once, a certain man from the north approached King Mālyaketu.
Then the painter displayed a variegated picture-scroll;
the king presented that picture-scroll to Kalāvatī.
Pointing with his finger, he recalled the place of his former residence;
remembering the northward-flowing Gaṅgā and repeatedly recollecting Maṇikarṇikā, he understood it.
And [he visited] Pañcagaṅgā, Goghāṭa, as well as Prahlādakeśava, the one named Balikeśava, and Viṣṇu known as Nāradakeśava. ||41||
[He saw] Kṛṣṇa named Ādikeśava, Ādityakeśava, Bhīṣmakeśava, and likewise Vāmanakeśava. ||42||
[He saw] the one named Bhṛgukeśava, as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the one named Gopīgovinda, and Yajñavārāha-Keśava. ||43||
That devoted wife remembered the one named Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha, the one named Śeṣamādhava, and the one named Śaṅkhamādhava.
He meditated upon Śrī Bindumādhava Kṛṣṇa, the Lord himself, the husband of Lakṣmī, as well as the glorious Maṅgalāgaurī, the wellspring of dharma. 45.
The Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha, the supreme beloved Jñānavāpī, Viśveśvara, and likewise Hari as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇeśvara; 46.
Kalāvatī, looking repeatedly at the painted canvas in this manner,
again beheld the Ocean of Knowledge upon the ground of the venerable Viśveśvara.
When her two beautiful eyes became clouded with tears of joy,
her creeper-like body grew rigid and her face attained full bloom.
Then his voice became faltering upon beholding the Jñānavāpī;
seeing Satī, the king said, "O beloved, do you remember this place? (49)
She quickly became bowed down with shame and then spoke:
"O Lord, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—these are the goals of human life."
A person must strive to achieve liberation, which is the primary goal of human existence; a birth devoid of that [liberation] is considered as worthless as a bubble on the water. (51)
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish;
yet in your palace, there is an abundance of slave-girls like me. (52)
Nevertheless, my lord’s love for me is seen to be exceedingly great;
even your maidservant is rich in enjoyments, so what need be said of one who dwells upon his lap? (53)
Even there, there is no other such perfection as having a husband under one's own control;
therefore, a wise man should accumulate wealth for the sake of performing the rites of *iṣṭāpūrta*.

O King, your lifespan for the sake of austerity has been secured free from obstacles, and your wife is obtained for the sake of obtaining progeny; all this has come to pass for you, so now set your mind upon detachment.
For those who desire various kinds of food, there is no end except through death;
yet death should be brought about through knowledge—that is not the death of the body.
I wish to undertake a pilgrimage to Ānandakānana, which bestows liberation;
my desire must be fulfilled so that this human birth may become fruitful. (57)
Having heard that, the king said to her at the appropriate time, "This is well-remembered;
she alone is the virtuous and chaste wife, Lakṣmī, Śrī, the beloved of Hari. (58)
Even she is truly devoted to her husband who, at the end, causes Hari to be remembered as her lord;
for they do not call a kingdom a true kingdom, but rather that royal fortune which is devoted to her husband.
Even an empire consisting of seven limbs is treated as mere straw if it is bereft of her,
provided that the wife herself causes her husband to fall from righteousness.
Furthermore, she is not a wife at all, but a *kṛtyā*, an illusion, a female *rākṣasa*;
she herself goes to hell and leads her husband and sons there as well. (61)
Moreover, she causes even entire families to fall from heaven through their sins and other transgressions—
she who does not cause one to remember devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
She is called a virtuous woman who, when wealth and prosperity are present, reminds [her husband] of dharma, pilgrimage sites, vows, merit, charity, and Hari. (63)

That beloved woman indeed causes one to perform pilgrimages, festivals, and worship of the Guru, the parents, and the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow; she causes one to serve the virtuous and to practice devotion as a servant of Hari. 64.
The self is dearer than the dear; for him, Acyuta is most dear;
and liberation is exceedingly dear—thus should the devoted wife cause him to remember.
O virtuous lady, through your power I have enjoyed a kingdom free from thorns;
my senses have been satisfied with their objects, and incomparable merit has also been performed.
"Even though children have been born, what remains for me to do here?
We two must certainly go to the city of Vārāṇasī."
Having thus resolved and having entrusted the kingdom to his son,
the king gave many gifts and set out toward Kāśī.
Having beheld Viśveśvara and Jñānavāpī, the sacred site of their own city,
those two who sought the feet of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa rejoiced.
Having bathed, he gave various gifts and gold;
with joy, he gave golden and silver jars as well as milch cows.
Taking various fine garments and articles for worship,
he went with his wife to the pavilion of liberation or to the funeral pyre there.
Having offered a sacrificial fee and excellent wealth, he listened to the sacred narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* and performed the evening worship of Śiva.
Having caused Jñānavāpī to be constructed according to the prescribed rites,
the king then went there with Kalāvatī and bathed joyfully.
There, having offered funeral cakes and satisfied the ancestors with faith,
he then gave gifts to the poor, the helpless, virtuous women, and the righteous.
The couple then ate their meal after dividing it between them;
thereafter, Kalāvatī joyfully [gazed upon] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa again and again.
The ascetic woman performed penance with supreme devotion;
she observed fasts on alternate days and sometimes undertook vows lasting three days.
Furthermore, by eating only every sixth mealtime, by the observances of half-months, by fasting for the duration of a fortnight, and by month-long fasts and the like; || 77 ||
Through the Cāndrāyaṇa vows, through penances (kṛcchras), and even through service to her husband,
that virtuous woman passed the remainder of her life as if it were a mere moment.
Once, when the two of them had bathed in the morning at Jñānavāpī and were seated there,
a certain matted-haired ascetic arrived and greeted them with blessings.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Master!
Having bestowed this mantra, he, with a gracious countenance and wearing a garland of tulasī, [spoke]. (1.460.80)
Arise and direct your supreme mind toward liberation;
meanwhile, a celestial chariot has arrived, adorned with clusters of tinkling golden bells.
It was joined by divine four-armed devotees of Hari along with their attendants,
and it was beautifully adorned, pervaded by the splendor of the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Lakṣmī herself descended and, having bestowed the supreme, transcendent,
liberating knowledge that grants emancipation, she led those two, who possessed divine forms.
O beloved, by means of a celestial chariot, those two, possessing four arms and divine bodies, went to the abode of Kṛṣṇa together with Mahālakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you the auspicious vow of Kalāvatī;
it bestows liberation, O virtuous lady, whether through its recitation or its hearing in every respect. (85)

Thus ends the four hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Kingdom in a Future Birth by the Couple Following their Gāndharva Marriage, and their Liberation through the Power of Chastity, Belonging to Suśīlā who was established in the vows of a virtuous woman at Jñānoda-mahima in the field of Ānandavana," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
I have heard from your mouth and understood that devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma;
yet, is the purity of a woman’s body eternal or is it artificial? (1)

"O beloved, tell me truly which is conducive to the prosperity of religious duties and other matters: that which is considered to be obtained through sacramental rites (saṃskāra), or that which is deemed to be matrimonial?"
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Women are eternally pure; they are never defiled by anything. Month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
In former times, women were enjoyed by the gods—Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
men enjoy them afterwards, yet they are not defiled by anyone.
Soma bestowed purity upon women, and Pāvaka (Fire) bestowed the state of being entirely pure;
the Gandharvas bestowed auspicious speech. Therefore, women are always pure.
Fire consumes a maiden during her menstrual period, and the Moon [consumes her] upon the appearance of body hair.
When the breasts have begun to develop, the Gandharvas [take possession]; therefore, she should be given away even before that.
By giving away a maiden who has not yet been enjoyed by the Moon and other [planets], one obtains great fruit from the gift.
Therefore, one who desires the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage should give her away while she is still pre-pubertal.
The appearance of pubic hair, body hair, and the budding of the breasts are the indicators of youth.
A girl of eight years is Gaurī, while one of nine years is Rohiṇī. (8)
A girl becomes a maiden at ten years of age, and from that point onward she possesses menses;
the giving away of a maiden in marriage is declared auspicious when she has reached fourteen years.
Beds, seats, vehicles, a corpse, the face of a woman, kusha grass, and all sacrificial vessels—these are indeed never defiled.
A calf is pure when it causes milk to flow; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall.
Women are pure during sexual union; a dog is pure when seizing game.
The mouth of a goat and a horse is pure; cows are pure on their backs;
those who know the Veda are pure at their feet; and women are pure in every respect.
Whether she has been enjoyed by force or has fallen into the hands of thieves, a beloved woman must not be abandoned; she was created by Medhyāja as a means of subduing others.
The virtuous are purified by red ochre, and women are purified by their menstrual flow;
the entire world is purified by Kṛṣṇa, and the couple is sanctified by their marriage ceremony.
Semen is always purified by the womb; an infant is purified by birth; disciples are always purified by mantras; embodied beings are purified by initiation;
the virtuous are always purified by their vows; and a wife is purified by her husband. (19)
The milk is always purified by the living being; the teeth and other [faculties] are purified by their respective locations. || 16 ||
A girl—whether young, youthful, or even aged—is always pure by nature;
water is pure by its very nature, and fire is pure by its very nature.
Fire, water, wind, and women born of noble lineage are always pure.
Therefore, those women who have not yet borne children should always be honored with ornaments, clothing,
and food by men desiring prosperity, both at virtuous rites and during festivals;
for the deities delight there, and there all ritual actions become fruitful.
In that household where the wife is pleased with her husband and the husband is pleased with his wife, there prosperity shall accrue at every step.
If one's wife is hostile, what does it matter even if one is in hell? But if she is capable, fertile, virtuous, sweet-spoken, and submissive—[what more could one desire]? (21)
That divine Śrī, assuming a female form, follows after every breath;
if a woman possesses auspicious marks, the householder always enjoys happiness through her. (22)

The physical form, the scent of the body's folds, the complexion, the temperament, the voice, the gait, and the color—these eight are to be understood as the grounds for the characteristics of women. (23)
Sixty-six are the wombs that are mines of the marks of beauty:
first, the soles of the feet with their lines; then the thumbs, the toes, and the nails;
the backs of the feet, the two ankles, the heels, the calves, the body hair, and the knees.
The thighs, the waist, the hips, the buttocks, the private parts, the loins, and the bladder. || 25 ||
The navel, the two sides of the belly, the flanks, the abdomen, and the three folds;
the line of hair, the charming chest, the pair of breasts, and their nipples;
the collarbones, shoulders, armpits, arms, wrists, and the two hands. || 26 ||
The back of the hand, the palm of the hand, the lines, the thumb, the fingers, and the nails;
the back of the neck, the nape of the neck, the throat, the chin, and the two jaws; the cheek, the mouth, the lower lip, the upper lip, the teeth, and the tongue. || 27–28 ||
The uvula, the palate, the smile, the nose, the sneeze,
the eyes, the eyelashes, the eyebrows, the ears, the forehead, the crown of the head, the parting of the hair, and the hair itself—
listen, my dear, women are indeed examined in these parts.
The soles of women's feet are glossy, fleshy, soft, and even.
That which is sweatless, warm, and reddish is known to be fit for great enjoyment;
whereas that which is dry, discolored, rough, with a broken reflection,
shaped like a winnowing basket, and parched, indicates suffering and misfortune.
It is marked with a wheel, a svastika, a conch, a lotus, a banner, a fish, and a parasol.
She on whose sole of the foot there are lines shall indeed be the wife of a king;
a vertical line extending to the middle finger bestows great enjoyment and excessive luxury.
Lines resembling a serpent or a mouse, however, bring about poverty and suffering.
A thumb that is well-nourished, elevated, auspicious, and rounded bestows great enjoyments. || 34 ||
A thumb that is short, crooked, or flattened destroys good fortune;
one with a broad thumb becomes a widow, while one with a long thumb is unfortunate.
Fingers that are soft, elevated, thick, and rounded bestow prosperity.
Those with long fingers are unchaste women; those with thin fingers are destitute. || 36 ||
Women with short fingers and short life-spans, those with crooked fingers, are considered deceitful;
those with flattened fingers become maidservants, while those with widely spaced fingers are poor.
Furthermore, women whose toes overlap one another [are likewise ill-fated].
They are considered widows and the wives of others many times over.
She from whose back dust rises as she walks along the road brings about the destruction of the families of her parents as well as her husband. (38–39)
That woman whose little toe does not touch the ground as she walks shall slay her husband and take a second husband. || 1.461.40 ||
If, while walking, her ring finger does not touch the ground,
she will surely slay two husbands and then take a third as her husband. If, while walking, her middle finger does not touch the ground at all, [the same fate awaits her].
Having slain three husbands, she makes a fourth her husband. ||40||
If the ring finger and middle finger are excessively short, one will be separated from her husband;
if the index finger is always joined with the thumb, it makes one unchaste. ||43||
The auspicious toenails are glossy, elevated, copper-colored, and rounded;
likewise, the instep of the foot is elevated, smooth, soft, and fleshy.
If it is free from sweat and not rich in visible veins, she will become a queen; of this there is no doubt.
A foot-arch that is depressed in the middle always indicates poverty. (45)
A woman's hand that is veiny, marked by travel lines, covered with many hairs, or devoid of flesh should be understood as bestowing great misfortune. (46)
Ankles that are hidden, round, free from visible veins, and give comfort are auspicious;
however, those that are low-lying, flaccid, or turned outward bring misfortune to women. (47)
A heel that is even brings great fortune; a broad heel, however, brings ill-fortune.
A raised heel belongs to an unchaste woman, while a long heel causes much suffering. (48)
The shanks of a queen are considered auspicious when they are hairless, free of veins, smooth, tapering gradually, beautiful, well-red, and pleasing. (49)
A woman with a single hair [per pore] shall become a queen; one with two hairs shall be a partaker of happiness; one with three hairs in her pores will undoubtedly become a widow. (1.461.50)
The knees of the wife of Dharma are round, fleshy, and well-nourished; those of a woman who acts according to her own will are fleshless; and those of a poor woman are pendulous. (51)
The thighs are shaped like plantain trunks or the trunk of an elephant, smooth, white, and firm;
they are rounded, soft, hairless, without veins, and auspicious. (52)

The woman with *bhūpa* [on her forehead] will be a king's wife; she who has *sudhana* [on her forehead] will be a wealthy woman; she who has *viduṣī* [on her forehead] will be a learned woman and devoted to her husband.
She who has *saramoru* [on her thighs] will indeed be a widow, and likewise, one with *paraga* [on her thighs] will go to another man.
A woman with flat thighs will be unfortunate and always filled with suffering; one whose thighs have a gap between them will be a partaker of misery and suffer from headaches. (54)
The waist, which is characterized by firm skin and great intelligence, is always pervaded by poverty;
it measures twenty-four finger-breadths and possesses a circular dimension. (55)
A waist that is elevated by prominent hips and square-shaped is auspicious;
however, one that is sunken, bent, flattened, withered, or elongated brings suffering. (56)
A short waist covered with hair portends widowhood;
however, hips that are elevated, well-developed, broad, firm, and fleshy are auspicious. (57)
The two [labia] that increase pleasure and enjoyment are like the fruit of the wood-apple (kapittha);
the vulva is auspicious when it is as wide as a tortoise and elevated like the frontal globes of an elephant. 58.
If the left side is elevated, she gives birth to daughters; if the right side is elevated, she gives birth to sons.
She whose body hair and pubic hair are coarse, whose waist is concealed, and who is broad [is likewise auspicious]. (59)
Firmly bound, with firm and elevated banks, as broad as the leaf of a Plakṣa tree,
lotus-colored, and only slightly diminished by drying— such a river is excellent and increases good fortune.
That which has the shape of a deer's hoof, is circular like a hearth,
covered with hair, and has its mouth wide open, is considered the lowest type, resembling a hanging parrot.
A vulva shaped like a conch-spiral is fit for bearing a fetus; it does not become flat or shaped like a skull-fragment, which always brings about servitude. (62)
A vulva that resembles the leaf of a bamboo or reed, is covered with long, upright hairs, and is excessively elevated and thick, does not bestow auspiciousness. (63)
A vulva with firm, elevated rims, a clear reddish luster, a narrow middle, and an inner ring always bestows happiness. (64)
The female organ, covered with flesh, protected by upward-pointing bones, moistened by sinking fluids, and surrounded within by flesh, always bestows pleasure. (65)
A cave that is formidable, crooked, deep, vast, and dilapidated, with its interior moistened by dripping flesh, never provides any comfort. (66)
The vulva, the hips, and the loins should be broad, elevated, and fleshy;
they should be soft, rich with fine hair, and excellent when spiraling to the right.
A waist that spirals to the left, is fleshless, or crooked indicates widowhood;
a hip resembling that of a pregnant woman or one with a protruding belly does not grant peace.
The hips are dry, shriveled, sunken, bony, and cause suffering;
the bladder situated at the sides of the hips is soft, expansive, and delicate. (69)
A line that is somewhat elevated and excellent is one that grants vehicles and conveyances;
however, a line that is hairy, veiny, or marked with lines is not at all praised.
The navel should be deep and spiraling to the right, bestowing happiness;
one that spirals to the left, is flat, or has distinct ridges is not praised. (71)
A woman with an expansive belly indeed gives birth to many sons;
a virtuous woman whose belly is like that of a frog gives birth to a son who becomes a king. (72)
A woman with a protruding belly becomes barren; one with a wrinkled belly becomes a virtuous wife; one with a whorled belly becomes a slave, a servant for as long as she lives. (73)
With symmetrical, fleshy, and soft sides whose bones are not prominent, she shall possess the fortune, joy, excellent qualities, sovereignty, and happiness of a virtuous wife. ||74||
With visible veins protruding like lakes and sides emaciated, she will be ill-behaved, childless, and immersed in an ocean of suffering. (75)
The belly that is very small, headless, soft-skinned, and indicative of enjoyment is indeed difficult to fill, like the bellies of a water-jar, a drum, or a pumpkin.
One with a protruding belly is a killer of her father-in-law; one with a broad belly is childless;
but one with a slender waist, three folds, and who is fortunate, bestows sexual pleasure. (77)
She whose line of body hair is straight and slender brings protection and joy;
she whose line of body hair is tawny, crooked, thick, broken, and devoid of a husband [brings misfortune]. (78)
A woman whose heart is hairless and elevated, who always bestows affection upon her husband, and whose heart is expansive, would never become unchaste or merciless. (79)
A woman whose heart-hair is bristling certainly becomes the mistress of her husband;
she whose broad chest is eighteen fingers wide and full [attains the same]. (1.461.80)
An elevated [forehead] is said to bestow happiness; one that is fleshy, beautiful, and excellent is likewise auspicious.
However, one that is hairy, uneven, or broad will indeed bring about suffering. 8–1.
Breasts that are dense, rounded, firm, full, and symmetrical are praised;
those with thick tips, sparse nipples, or that are withered and hard do not bestow happiness. (82)
A woman whose right breast is elevated, firm, and full will have sons;
one whose left breast is elevated will give birth to a daughter who is beautiful and endowed with good fortune. (83)
The two breasts, resembling the buckets of a water-wheel, indicate immoral conduct;
being swollen at the nipples, separated by a wide space between them, and broad at the edges, they are not beautiful. (84)
Those breasts which are thick at the base, gradually tapering, and sharp-tipped, give pleasure at first but later bestow sorrow and cause suffering. (85)
When the nipples are beautiful, firm, dark, round, and auspicious, they are favorable;
however, when they are sunken, long, or thin, they indicate suffering. (86)
A bride with thick clavicles will possess wealth and grain;
however, one with loose, sunken, and uneven clavicles will be poor. (87)
Shoulders that are not bound together, not drooping, not long, not thin, and auspicious;
yet those that are crooked, thick, and covered with excessive hair, indicate servitude and widowhood.

Shoulders with well-concealed joints and drooping tips are auspicious, while those that are well-knit and elevated at the tips bring widowhood; those that are devoid of flesh cause extreme suffering. (89)
The armpits are auspicious when they have fine hair, are elevated, smooth, and well-fleshed;
they are not auspicious when they are perspiring, deep, or veiny.
The hands of virtuous women are red, fleshy, and without prominent veins; their bones are hidden and they are tender, hairless, bright copper-colored, and straight. (91)
Thick-haired eyebrows lead to widowhood; short ones cause misfortune;
those with visible roots, as well as rough and black ones, are considered to bring about suffering.
The two hands of virtuous women, joined together with the thumbs and fingers facing each other in the shape of a closed lotus bud, indicate the attainment of great enjoyments. (93)
The palms of the hands should be soft, moderately elevated, red, and without cracks; they are praised when endowed with auspicious lines, and possessing few lines brings good fortune.
A widow is indicated by many lines, while a lack of lines signifies poverty; one who has veins on the palms of her hands is a beggar, which portends a state of world-weariness.
If the lines on the palms are hairless, without veins, auspicious, and well-raised; yet if they possess hair, lack flesh, or have visible veins, women will become widows. (96)
Red, distinct, deep, glossy, full, and circular—the lines on the hand, such as the line of fortune (*bhāgyarekhā*), are considered praiseworthy for women. (97)
With a fish [mark], she is fortunate and virtuous; with a svastika, she bestows wealth;
with a lotus, she becomes the wife of a king and the mother of a monarch. (98)
On the hands of the wife of a universal monarch (cakravartin), there are clockwise svastikas;
on the left [hands], there are conch shells, umbrellas, tortoises, banners, and parasols. (99)
Tulārekhā, Vaṇikpatnī, Baddhakośā, and Vaṇikpriyā;
likewise, elephants, horses, bulls, palaces, and wagons are on the left.
If there is the mark of a yoke on the left, she will indeed be the wife of a Vaiśya;
if she holds a chowrie, a goad, and a bow, she is declared to be the wife of a king.
If a line emerging from the base of the thumb goes to the little finger,
she shall be a killer of her husband, a slayer, and a bringer of suffering.
A woman who has a line shaped like a trident, sword, mace, spear, or drum will be a giver of gifts, renowned, and devoted to her husband.
A crane, a jackal, a frog, a wolf, a scorpion, a serpent, a donkey, a camel, and a cat—these, when held in the hand, bring suffering to a woman. 104.
She whose teeth are black, whose tongue is long,
whose face cries out repeatedly, who is lame, and who walks crookedly.
She whose feet are like black campaka flowers, whose face hangs down from her jaw, and whose belly-jars are broken at the back, destroys one's place of fame. 106.
The thumb is auspicious when it is straight, rounded, with rounded nails, and soft;
the fingers are also auspicious when they have well-formed joints and are long, rounded, and slender.
Those that are flat, rough, and dry; those with hair on their backs; those that are inauspicious; those that are excessively short, emaciated, crooked, or sparse—these are causes of misfortune.
Fingers endowed with many joints always bring misery;
however, nails that are reddish, possessed of crests, prominent, and rounded are auspicious. (109)
Nails that are sunken, discolored, resembling mother-of-pearl, or yellow indicate poverty;
white spots on the nails portend a life of unchastity.
If the backbone has its vertebrae deeply sunk and the back is fleshy and auspicious, it is so;
however, if the back is covered with hair, it indicates widowhood. (111)
A back that is bent, curved, or has prominent veins causes suffering;
one that is straight, with a raised nape and even flesh, is always beautiful. (11.2)
A neck that is dry, veiny, hairy, broad, crooked, and inauspicious is unfavorable;
one that is fleshy, round, four finger-breadths in circumference, and well-proportioned is praised. (113)

A neck marked with three lines, taught [as auspicious], is one where the bones are not prominent and it is well-knit; however, one that is fleshless, flat, long, or withered does not bestow good fortune. (1.14)
A woman with a thick neck is a widow; one with a crooked neck is a servant;
one with a flat neck is barren; and one with a short neck is childless.
A chin measuring two finger-breadths is praised; it should be rounded, full, and very soft.
A thick chin that is divided into two parts or is covered with long hairs is not auspicious. (116)
The jaw that is joined to the chin, hairless, and very dense is auspicious;
one that is crooked, thick, thin, short, or hairy does not bestow good fortune.
Cheeks that are plump, round, elevated, and well-filled are auspicious;
those that are sunken, rough, hairy, and fleshless do not bestow happiness. (1.18)
The face of a virtuous woman is like the reflection of her father’s face; it is fragrant, round, symmetrical, glossy, beautiful, well-fleshed, and full. (119)
A lower lip that is reddish, round, glossy, adorned with a line in the middle,
and gradually thinning from the center toward the edges, bestows sovereignty.
A lower lip that is thin, drooping, cracked, or rough indicates misfortune; one that is thick and brownish brings the suffering of widowhood. (121)
The lower lip that is slightly raised in the middle, hairless, and glossy brings wealth;
and the upper lip, marked with lines in the shape of a bow, bestows fortune.
The teeth of virtuous wives of dharma are white, resembling pomegranate seeds, glossy, even on both sides, and slightly elevated. (123)
Teeth that are yellowish, dark, thick and long, resembling mother-of-pearl, sparse, rough at the base, uneven, or arranged in two rows belong to those devoid of fortune.
A woman with a sunken lower lip is considered to bring about the destruction of her mother;
one with protruding teeth becomes a widow; one with uneven teeth becomes unchaste; and one with widely spaced teeth likewise [brings misfortune].
A tongue that is reddish, soft, and white, and which enjoys sweet and desired foods, is auspicious;
however, one that is contracted in the middle and broad at the tip brings suffering. (126)
A white woman brings death by water; a dark woman causes quarrels;
a fleshy woman bestows poverty; and a pendulous one eats what is unfit for food. (127)
A broad tongue is considered to be constantly awakened by heedlessness;
a very smooth palate, the color of a lotus petal, is praised as being soft. (128)
If the palate is pale, widowhood occurs; if it is yellow, it belongs to renunciants. If it is black, she is childless; if it is dry, she has many dependents.
The bell situated within the throat should be sharp, red, and circular;
it should not be hanging down, but rather auspicious and thick. However, one that is thick and black brings suffering.
A woman's smile is praised when her teeth are slightly visible, her temples are somewhat blooming, and her eyes are not fully closed. (131)
A nose with symmetrical nostrils and small openings brings good fortune;
one that is thick at the tip, depressed in the middle, or elevated is not praised. (132)
A nose with curved edges like the tip of a parrot's beak is excellent;
however, a nose that is short at the tip and reddish at the end brings about widowhood.
A flat nose like that of a servant-maid is inauspicious; one that is too short or too long is fond of strife.
For a woman, eyes with red corners and black pupils are praised.

One whose eyes are white, wide like a petal, very glossy, and have black lashes is long-lived; one with upturned eyes is considered to be unchaste, while one with round eyes is regarded as an adulteress.
A woman with eyes like those of a ram, a buffalo, or one with flattened eyes is not praised;
however, she who has eyes like a cow or a tawny monkey may possess the impetus of desire and become the resort of many enjoyments. (136)
A woman with eyes like a pigeon's, one of bad character, red-eyed, or a killer of her husband; one who is wicked, with sunken eyes, or elephant-like eyes—is not praised. 1.37.
A woman with a crooked left eye is unchaste; one with a crooked right ear is barren;
a woman with honey-colored, tawny eyes is a delight and possesses an abundance of wealth and grain.
One who possesses eyelashes that are thick, fine, glossy, and black enjoys good fortune;
one whose lashes are tawny, sparse, and coarse is considered a performer of blameworthy deeds. (139)
The eyebrows are well-rounded, glossy, black-edged, and situated separately; they are praiseworthy, with soft hairs, very sharp, and shaped like a bow.
Eyebrows that are coarse-haired, wide-spreading, long-haired, tawny, joined together, or scattered are not auspicious for an excellent woman. (141)
A woman’s ears that are long, with auspicious whorls, soft, and pleasant are auspicious;
those lacking earlobes, veiny, crooked, or thin are censurable. (142)
A woman’s forehead that is free of visible veins, hairless, resembling a half-moon, and measuring three finger-breadths without being sunken, bestows good fortune, health, and happiness. (143)
A forehead with clearly defined svastika lines bestows sovereignty;
a woman with an elongated head will become a slayer of her husband.
A woman whose head is elevated by prominent veins is considered sickly;
a straight parting of the hair is excellent, as is a well-elevated crown of the head. (145)
A head that is rounded like an elephant's frontal globe indicates good fortune and sovereignty;
a pot-shaped head makes one a widow, while a protruding head makes one unchaste.
Indeed, in this world, a large-headed or double-headed woman becomes unfortunate.
The hair is black, soft, fine, glossy, and curled at the tips.
Long, straight, and lustrous [nails] indicate devotion to one's husband;
whereas those that are rough, cracked at the tips, tawny, light, and coarse [indicate otherwise]. (948)
Moles that are sparse, large, and hard are considered givers of suffering and poverty;
however, a mole between the eyebrows or on the forehead is held to bestow sovereignty. (149)
A red mole on the left cheek bestows sweet food and drink;
likewise, a clockwise tilaka-mark, or a garland, or even a bee [on the right cheek] does so.
A sesame seed, a moon, or a mole on the right breast are signs that grant the fortune of sovereignty;
she who has a drop of blood or a sesame seed there shall be a mother. (1.5.1)
She was the virtuous mother of four daughters and three sons;
on her left breast there was a red mole, and she was the sole mother of her children.
Then that virtuous and faithful woman shall attain widowhood;
but if she is skilled in secret matters and possesses sesame seeds, that faithful woman shall become the mother of a king.
That royal lady on whose nose-tip there is a red mole—
if that [mole] were black, she would indeed be a killer of her husband and a wanton woman.
A mole or a freckle below the navel belongs to a woman devoted to her husband;
a freckle or a mole on the region of the ankle, however, causes poverty.
If there is a mole, a freckle, or even a mark on the left side of the neck, the hand, the arm, or the cheek, it shall be the first sign that brings the gift of a son. (156)
If there is a trident-mark on the forehead, she becomes a queen and a teacher;
if she speaks while asleep and grinds her teeth, she is ill-omened for the family.
Hair on the hand that curls to the right is always a bringer of dharma;
however, hair on the hand of a woman that curls to the left shall be a giver of suffering. (158)
A clockwise whorl at the navel, the ear, or the heart is indeed auspicious;
a clockwise whorl on the right side of the back bestows great happiness. (159)
A clockwise whorl on the spinal column bestows long life and sons;
a clockwise whorl at the head of the vulva indicates the status of a queen.
If it has the shape of a cart, it bestows happiness through many children and other blessings; however, if it begins at the vulva and ends at the waist, it causes the destruction of sons and husband.
A belly-tail and a back-whorl that are pendulous do not bestow peace;
one of these makes a man a slayer of his lord, while the other makes him a libertine.
A clockwise curl situated on the neck is considered to bring the suffering of widowhood;
one at the beginning of the hairline on the forehead or in the braid brings the hardship of wind-related ailments.
She who has a whorl of hair at the nape of the neck or in the hollow [of the throat], whether it curls to the left or to the right, shall become a widow. (164)
If there be one or two on the left side of the head, she will be a killer of her husband until the tenth day [of her life]; but if there be a whorl at the waist, she is an unchaste woman.
A woman with hair-whorls on her back is a killer of her husband; one with hair-whorls at her navel is devoted to her husband.
Even if she possesses ill-omened marks, if she is truly devoted, she is considered a virtuous woman who is devoted to the gods.
Devoted to sacred fords, vows, austerities, fire-offerings, recitations, and charity, these women of auspicious marks became devoted wives through the grace of the virtuous and of Hari. || 167 ||
Virtuous noble women endowed with auspicious marks can transform even a short-lived beloved into one of long life, and they deliver their entire lineages.
Chastity toward one's husband is the supreme virtue and the foremost of all auspicious marks;
if that exists, then indeed all other marks become truly bestowers of happiness.
O beloved, these characteristics have been declared by me for the happiness of householders;
by reading or hearing this, one's own knowledge shall become a giver of happiness.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Results of the Marks, Lines, Limbs, and Minor Parts Indicating Female Purity and the Auspicious or Inauspicious Nature Residing in the Body of a Woman," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you a story concerning the future;
it was spoken by the Blessed One and describes events pertaining to all three periods of time.
Everything within the range of the Blessed One is true to reality and uncontradicted;
yet in every eon, there is some [manifestation] that, though distinct, resembles its own kind.
O beautiful one, a conversation concerning Viṣṇu, myself, and you also has arisen;
listen, my dear Lakṣmī, for Hara himself is five-faced.
Having become fivefold upon the earth, Śiva performed the act of withdrawal at the sacrifice;
and Umā, the sustainer of the world, [became the daughter] of King Drupada.
From the sacrificial fire-pit, that beautiful maiden appeared;
and all five sons of Pāṇḍu were there in person, possessing the very form of Indra.
They descended here from heaven to remove the burden of the earth;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa also took birth as their helper.
On the earth of the world, the whirlpools of wandering through prosperity and adversity are natural;
indeed, for those born upon this earth, there arise the cycles of rise and fall, and so forth.
On one occasion, those great heroes resorted to the practice of forest-dwellers, which was fraught with calamity, having been imposed upon them by their kinsmen.
That queen, the daughter of Pañcāla, went to the forest region with them;
devoted, chaste, and virtuous, she always worshipped them.
Devoted to her husband, virtuous, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and a friend of Hari,
Indrapatnī, a female ascetic, propitiated the Sun-god.
Devoted to the celibate life and subsisting on forest fare, she served her husbands;
indeed, during the remaining time, she remained unrestrained and intent upon meditation on the Sun.
Having meditated [on him] from the tips of the nails to the ends of the hair, and having invoked him into the *arka* tree,
he worships him with true devotion by offering many articles.
That virtuous woman offered with devotion water, flowers, wild leaves, fragrant fruit fit for eating, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and a lamp.
Bowing, recollection, praise, circumambulation, and the request for forgiveness—these the devoted wife performs, along with the offering of handfuls of flowers and the ritual dismissal. (14)
Then, having been propitiated, the Sun, the progenitor, granted her his vision;
he spoke to that great goddess: "Tell me, what is it that you desire?"
I am the Sun with a dark body, and you are Kṛṣṇā, born from sacrifice;
I know the oneness of our two bodies, for what is mine is yours as well.
Draupadī said: "O Lord of Gods, in the forest indeed, without means of procurement, even the food and other necessities for many cannot possibly be sufficient. (17)
Occasionally, thousands of guests would arrive;
for they had heard of the Pandavas' forest dwelling in the woods. || 18 ||
O Blessed One, grant them that wealth which is free from affliction, so that for their sake there may arise a full and worthy honor as before.
O Arthadā, grant me assistance for my dwelling in the forest, so that I, like a river, may not lose my devotion to my husband nor my renown as his wife.
A seat, water, forest fruits and food, and sweet speech, as well as the oil for the eyes of guests—these are the means for producing favor. (21)
Blessings arise from a heart full of serenity;
however, curses arising from a tormented heart are considered to be merely ashes.
"Service to my husband is my supreme gain here in the forest; O Lord, my life is sustained by food and other offerings through service to guests who are equal to my husband. (23)
Having heard this from the princess of Pañcāla, the Lord Bhāskara was pleased and gave her an inexhaustible vessel along with a ladle and a lid.
With a tranquil soul, he spoke to that virtuous body which was his own:
"By means of this vessel, [provide for] as many people seeking food as there are in this highly meritorious place. (25)
They shall attain satisfaction only so long as you do not eat;
once you have eaten, this vessel, though empty, will become full of food.
A treasure-house of flavorful side dishes that provides whatever food one desires;
as long as you dwell in the forest, she shall remain under your control.
Constantly serve by the hundreds of thousands the lords who dwell in the forest;
O Goddess of gods, acquire merit, and may all that is auspicious always be yours. (28)
You are Lakṣmī, you are Satī, you are Śrī; you are Prabhā and you are Māṇikī.
You are Pārvatī, Jayā, Rādhā, Ramā, Padmā, and Mohinī. (29)
You are Padmāvatī and Rudrāṇī; you are Campā, Śāradā, and Śivā;
you are Tulasī, Mahālakṣmī, Vṛndā, Sītā, and Rukmiṇī.
"O Queen of the Gods, you do not know that I am endowed with human playfulness;
I know you well, O virtuous lady, for you are in every way the beloved of Kṛṣṇa."
Arjuna is your husband in human form, and Kṛṣṇa is half of your lord.
O Kṛṣṇā, you possess devotion to your husband; you are Kṛṣṇā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
O Daughter of Sacrifice, making you alone the cause, Kṛṣṇa desires to rid the earth of its burden of demons by means of the five heroes.
Your own essential nature and my vessel—both of these grant inexhaustible fulfillment;
from you all the arts (kalās) are true, but from my vessel they are true sacrifices.
Those who have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa will indeed exist and will continue to exist;
for there has never been, nor will there ever be, a virtuous woman as tender as you who carries out the word of Kṛṣṇa.
That sattvic state, pervaded by forgiveness, will exist even without wealth;
for that very word of Kṛṣṇa is your vow, your vow of devotion to your husband.
Dharma and adharma, as well as bondage and liberation, are under the power of Kṛṣṇa’s word;
pleasure and pain reside in the form of Kṛṣṇa; and the Pāṇḍavas are themselves forms of Kṛṣṇa. ||37||
May you always have well-being; may you not experience the suffering caused by dwelling in the forest.
Consider yourself to be in a state of happiness, and remember Hari and me during times of distress.
"I shall serve them at the proper time and I shall also give my assistance"—such a thought would cause great distress to noble women; what then could be said of those who are base? (3.9)
On this earth, Kṣatriyas rule kingdoms with the edge of a sword;
for those who are like jackals, even their own small field would not remain theirs.
She who endures the hardship of fire becomes adorned with the splendor of fire;
indeed, she becomes the wife of Agni, possessing the brilliance of ten million suns.
A female frog is not the mate of a lion; a female crow is not a swan; a maidservant is not the wife of a king; and paupers are not lords of the god of wealth. 42.
By you the entire world is made prosperous; without you it appears lusterless.
O Draupadī, remember Govinda, who dwells within the heart and resides as the Master. 43.
Having spoken thus, Sūrya departed after bowing to her; she too bowed to him.
Draupadī, in the midst of the forest, serves Śrī Hari and her husbands. 44.
Duryodhana sent Durvāsas, who was served by ten thousand disciples, with the intent of seeking an opportunity for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas. ||45||
"There will not be enough food for the guests; therefore, the Rishi will curse the Pāṇḍavas, and they shall then meet their destruction. (46)
Having intended this, Durvāsas, who had been summoned, went to that forest; there he was honored by the Pāṇḍavas and invited to take his meal.
Just as he went for the purpose of bathing, Satyā would not give him food, even though the sun-dish had been washed and set out at that time. 48.
But after the period of restriction has ended, one should not increase the amount of food, for the King of Sages, being enraged in the absence of food, will certainly pronounce a curse. (49)
Then, remembered by Satyā, that woman dear to Kṛṣṇa,
Kṛṣṇa himself— the abode of mercy— arrived in his own divine form.
"Tell me, O Goddess, why did Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa say this when remembered?
Satī replied, "What food shall I give to the son of Atri? (51)
Everything has become empty; even my alms-bowl has been consumed.
Having washed it, I have set it aside in its place; there is no food left, O Kṛṣṇa, O Mādhava. (52)
Kṛṣṇa said, "Bring the worthy recipient so that I may examine him.
When he was brought there, a betel-leaf fragment was found clinging to his side. (53)
Kṛṣṇa saw that leaf placed within his own mouth;
may the Lord of the Universe be pleased, and likewise may the universe be pleased. (54)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa ate that auspicious leaf;
he then drank water and belched again and again. (55)
"Oh! Satisfaction has arisen for me, and indeed the three worlds are satisfied; and ten thousand disciples of Durvāsas are likewise satisfied. (56)
The bellies of all beings indeed become full by the act of Hari alone;
he in whose house Hari eats, for him the three worlds eat.
In whosever house Hari is satisfied, for him the three worlds are satisfied;
Durvāsas, along with his disciples, having attained great satisfaction, was filled with fear.
"What could possibly happen? We shall simply eat it; let us be cursed by the woman.
We will perish there anyway, so we must certainly go from here. (59)
Thinking thus, they all, including the disciples and the wrathful sage, suddenly and swiftly departed from the bathing place, intent on flight.
The Pāṇḍavas became at ease, and Draupadī was free from anxiety;
moreover, Hari, the protector, was served by all of them in the forest.
"Whenever calamity should arise, you must remember me," having said this, the Lord departed.
"O virtuous lady, this is the dharma of a devoted wife, which consists of Kṛṣṇa as one's husband. (62)
All desire a husband who is fortunate, handsome, endowed with youth, wealthy, prosperous, possessed of power, and a bringer of fame. (63)
Having encountered such a Kṛṣṇa, what handmaiden would not serve him?
And what devoted wife would not indeed make her own birth fruitful? 64.
