The goddesses, the Gandharva women, the Asura women, the wives of the Nāgas, the beloved wives of the sages, the creepers, the rivers, the Earth and others, and the Kinnara women; ||65||
The daughters of Manu, the wives of the Kiṃpuruṣas, the Vidyādharīs, and others—
whosoever were infatuated with Kṛṣṇa— all of them attained the supreme state.
For their sake, Kṛṣṇa is born into the world through his birth as one who brings happiness;
that birth and his divine activity are not brought about by ritual injunctions, but are seen as such.
The births of Śrī Hari, Harikṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and indeed those of Rādhā and others, as well as Ramā and others, are not born from a womb.
Whenever Kṛṣṇa himself desires to descend, he gives the command to the god Vāyu: "Dwell steadily within the womb."
Just as the visible womb of a woman, containing the embryo, becomes auspicious after remaining stable for nine months when the tenth month has arrived; ||1.462.70||
"At the time of birth, you must emerge from the womb like a child;
I, for my part, will then fashion myself into the form of that infant son. (71)
I shall fall upon a portion of the earth, for people would surely know me as one born;
thus my birth will in every way be such that it is not from a womb. (72)
For all my incarnations, my birth is not from a womb;
[my consorts are] Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Śrī, Prabhā, Kānti, and Śāradā.
Māṇikī, Pārvatī, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Satī, Jayā, Padmāvatī, Lalitā, Kambharā, and others—these were not born from a womb. (74)
Whenever they are born, the wind becomes established in the womb;
when the tenth month has arrived and the time has come, the wind itself [acts].
Having indeed assumed the form of a child for a moment, he then emerges from the womb;
at that time, the goddesses likewise become children.
They become like children so that others may not recognize them;
then ignorant people say of them, "These women are born from a womb. (77)
But those women who have surpassed divine vision behold Him as unborn;
this is the divine birth of that Kṛṣṇa and of His wives.
The creation of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is indeed like a creation born of mere volition;
desire, semen, pleasure, and the embryo—all are visible only through his glance. (79)

But the world perceives His play as being like that of the world, and His liberation also as being like that of the world; however, the gods, possessing divine vision, perceive it as being like that of the gods.
The lords see that [Supreme Lord] as the Lord, and the liberated see Him as the liberated; just as one sees one's own reflection, Śrī Puruṣottama beholds His own self. ||8 1 ||
Therefore, all actions performed for Kṛṣṇa are divine and bestow divinity;
such are the duties, the duties of Kṛṣṇa, which have Kṛṣṇa as their supreme goal. (82)
Having obtained suitable husbands who are devotees of Kṛṣṇa, those devoted wives acquire heaven, liberation, virtue, desire, and wealth. (83)
They acquire sons, daughters, happiness, and divine bliss;
having performed everything for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, they worship Mādhava. (84)
Having always observed the vow of Kṛṣṇa and having served their husband Mādhava,
they offer their own bodies to their husband and attain the abode of Hari.
What need is there to say, O beloved Lakṣmī? You surely know this kind of vow;
my vow and your vow are entirely auspicious, consisting of the duties of a married couple.
O my beloved, I have told you that which is devoid of qualities, which bestows supreme nirvāṇa, which is the guide to my state, and which is the most excellent among the excellent. 87.
Whatever woman there may be—whether born of a low lineage or a noble family—who finds her delight in me, whose life is dedicated to me, and who has surrendered her existence for my sake; 88.
This devoted wife, who serves me while remaining undisturbed by the states I have described,
and who is intent upon Hari, shall indeed attain her husband at the end.
She who listens to this chapter, she who performs its rites, and she who constantly honors me—she who is virtuous shall indeed attain me. (1.462.90)

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of how Draupadī Protected Durvāsas and His Disciples Who Arrived at Mealtime in the Forest by the Power of Her Chastity and Fidelity as a Satī, and How Kṛṣṇa Provided Them with Tāndūla Leaves," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, Prabhe, Pārvatī, Padmaje, Sarasvatī, Rame, Kṛṣṇe, Māṇikī, Kambharā, and Sati!
O Durgā, Rādhā, Śāradā, Vṛndā, Tulasī, and she who is born from the ocean;
O Padmāvatī, Queen of Pāṇḍava, Sāvitrī, beloved of Rukmiṇī! || 2 ||
Likewise, [he told] the story of Vinatā and Kadrū regarding their former birth and their wager;
how Kadrū and Vinatā were given to Kaśyapa by Dakṣa.
O you two devoted wives, great saintly ones, solely intent on service to your husband, devotees of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, auspicious ones who can assume any form at will! || 4 ||
And while we two were performing austerities for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, desiring offspring,
the serpents were born as the sons of Kadrū— auspicious beings capable of assuming forms at will.
Those hosts of Kadraveyas were indeed black, red, and green;
they were tawny, yellowish-red, brown, and variegated as well.
White, blue, as well as subtle, medium-sized, long, and very long;
these were the snakes and reptiles, the sons of Kadrū, who possessed the form of Kadrū.
There were also dark-colored, variegated, white, and smoke-colored serpents;
of mixed colors, resembling scales or lotuses, there were millions of species of nāgas.
Then Vinatā gave birth to her sons, Ulūka, Tārkṣya, Aruṇa, and others;
and because he was the eldest, Ulūka subsequently obtained the sovereignty over the birds.
And because he was devoid of all virtues, he was deposed from the kingdom by them all;
he was cruel-eyed, blind by day, always having crooked claws, and inauspicious.
But his speech is so terrifying that he is not fit for kingship;
moreover, in a kingless kingdom, people act according to their own whims.
Then Vinatā, longing to see her son for the sake of the king,
crushed the middle egg.
When the thousand years had reached completion, that which was indeed cooked burst forth out of eagerness from that egg during the eighth hundredth year.
Indeed, at that time, all the limbs were not yet fully formed.
But that embryo became enraged at the interruption of its attainment of half-growth;
for, without reflection, the mother had been cursed by the child out of anger.
I curse you, who act for the harm of your son, once all my limbs have been fully formed by your teeth, having split open the embryo contained within half of your mother’s body. 16.
Since, upon seeing the sons of Kadrū being caressed by their mother’s lap,
this egg of mine was burst by you out of impatience under that very pretext.
"O bird, if out of desire you quickly obtain a son and fondle him on your lap, then you shall indeed become a slave to your co-wife. (18)
Having heard the curse pronounced by her son, the mother, overcome with grief, said:
"O Anūru, tell me the end of this curse; my son, act for our welfare."
Anūru said, "Do not pierce the third egg, which is not yet full;
he who is to be born from the third egg will ward off the curse."
Having spoken thus and bowed to his mother, Uḍḍīyānurū went to the forest;
there, having propitiated the Sun through austerity, he obtained boons from the Prabhākaras.
Protected by the Sun, he drives the horses of the Sun in the machine;
thus, the rising of Aruṇa was made first, and the rising of the Sun afterwards.
Then, when a thousand years were complete, the third egg split open by itself; from it was born Garuḍa, resembling the sun.
Even the grasshopper, having emerged directly from the egg as a young one, being hungry, said to his mother: "Let food be given to me. (24)
The mother, though delighted, said to the hungry and mighty Garuḍa:
"O son, I am ultimately unable to satisfy your hunger. (25)
Your father Kaśyapa is on Mount Meru; go to him.
He will give you food, and your hunger will be appeased.
Having heard his mother’s words, the bird went to where Kaśyapa was;
bowing with his head, he spoke these words to his father.
"O Father, you have heard that I am Garuḍa, sent by my mother Vinatā;
I am tormented by hunger, O Lord, so let food be given to me. (28)
Having learned of that son, Kaśyapa, bowing down out of affection, said:
"The Niṣādas, numbering many hundreds of thousands, [dwell] by the ocean, the storehouse of waters. (29)
Fish-eaters dwell on the banks; eat them and be happy.
Without a Brahmin, maintain your livelihood among the Niṣādas.
Thus addressed, he went there and ate them;
though he was a Brahmin, he remained unobserved as he was swallowed by that bird.
Then, as soon as he was born, fire blazed up in his throat down to the middle of his neck;
that king of birds was unable either to vomit it up or to swallow it.
Having gone, he then said to his father: "O father, fire is constantly burning within my throat; some person who brings about my end has become attached to me. (23)
Kaśyapa said, "O son, it would be otherwise if he were a Brahmin.
Having spoken thus, Kaśyapa summoned the Brahmin from outside.
The Brahmin said: "O father, I will not go out leaving these behind;
some dear friends and kinsmen have already been swallowed. (3.5)
"I shall go with these to hell or to the blissful Hari.
Having heard this, Kaśyapa was struck with wonder and spoke to the fallen twice-born man.
Because you have formed a connection with the Niṣādas, you shall therefore go to hell; for, through association with the wicked, you yourself have become a sinner.
If, out of ignorance or delusion, one has committed a most terrible sin,
yet thereafter practices righteousness, he shall indeed attain the supreme goal.
One who commits evil should not perform a *vṛṣotsarga*; if he should do so, he will commit evil once again.
His destination is such that he sinks into a most terrible hell. (39)
"Either depart or go to your death; do not remain at my throat, O Brahmin! Having heard Kaśyapa’s words, that twice-born man, who was bound by his vow regarding his kinsman, [remained silent].
He spoke clearly to Kaśyapa: "Listen, dear father, to what is for my benefit:
although I am a twice-born by birth, my beloved wife is a Niṣādī. (41)
My brothers-in-law, my father-in-law, and others as well—these Niṣādas were swallowed by Garuḍa and died within his stomach. (2)
By the yoga of the Purifier, even that which is impure becomes purified;
yet all those [others] are devoid of such union, whereas through your yoga they become purifiers. (43)
They have been especially purified by the Garuḍagarbha yoga;
and I am devoted to my kinsmen’s vows and dedicated to my wife’s fidelity.
O my father, if they were all released and restored to life, then I would depart from your throat; otherwise, death is certain. (45)
"Either the bandhujīva flower or the end of my life—this is my firm resolve.
Having heard this, Kaśyapa spoke to the bird for his own welfare.
"Vomit them out, along with the Vipras and all the Niṣādas as well.
Thus addressed, Garuḍa vomited out those Niṣādas.
Indeed, those birds that dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions are predators;
they devour eagles, cocks, swans, pigeons, and other such creatures. ||48||
In the Kali age, all the people will gather together for a single meal; when there is no distinction of caste whatsoever between those who eat and those with whom they eat. (49)
Then, overcome by hunger, he begged for excellent food;
commanded by Kaśyapa, he went to the vicinity of the ocean.
There, seeing the two great beings— the tortoise and the elephant— whose bodies were many yojanas in length, the victorious one pierced them with his claws and leapt up into the sky.
Seeing my great Jambu branch, the elephant and the tortoise sat down; then, seizing the broken branch, they flew up into the sky.
He went to Satyaloka, the abode of Brahmā, where Mādhava—Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu—had arrived after being praised there. ||53||
Hari said: "O Lord of Birds, why do you wander in the sky, holding up this great branch along with the massive elephant and tortoise?"
Then Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā and descendant of Kaśyapa, said to Hari:
"I am Garuḍa; having seized the elephant, the tortoise, and the Jambu tree... (55)
"That Meru-tree has gone; it is broken. Where indeed shall I stay?
I am hungry and wish to eat; tell me, O Lord, where shall I go? (56)
Neither trees nor other such things can endure my weight or my speed;
even the mountains tremble, and the planets are agitated in the sky. (57)
Thus addressed, the Blessed One said: "Stay here indeed upon my arm;
appease your hunger by eating these two, the elephant and the tortoise. (58)
Thus addressed, Garuḍa then alighted upon the arm of Śrī Hari;
leaving the branch behind, he devoured the elephant and the tortoise in the great ocean.
Nevertheless, his hunger was not appeased; therefore Hari said to him:
"Eat my flesh; by consuming it, you shall become happy."
Having been addressed thus, he ate the flesh of his own arm and attained satisfaction;
yet, seeing that no wound had appeared on his arm despite this, he [was amazed].
He said to Hari, "O Lord, tell me what I shall do for you, my beloved.
Hari replied, "Become my vehicle for all time."
May you be invincible among all beings, and may you be free from old age and death;
may you have access everywhere, and may your power and energy be equal to mine.
"You shall obtain a full meal from the one who causes the destruction of his mother's rival," having been told this, the bird went toward his father, Kaśyapa.
With a joyful heart, he spoke to his father to ask for permission and receive his command; and Kaśyapa, in turn, addressed these virtuous words to his son.
I am blessed; my mother is blessed; blessed is the family that possesses such a good son—a devotee of Viṣṇu who brings liberation to ten million generations of his lineage.
Upon the exhaustion of all sins, one shall attain the status of a servant of Viṣṇu;
he with whom Viṣṇu is pleased shall himself become the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He who possesses a son, a wife, a daughter, and a cow for the sake of Kṛṣṇa is a blessed embodied being here, whose family is purified. (68)
Viṣṇu cannot be attained even by the gods through manifold austerities, religious duties, or various kinds of sacrifices; yet that very Hari has indeed been attained by you.
"Having served your mother, go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having received this command, he went quickly to his mother.
Having bowed to his mother, that boy, assuming a form at will, took delight and rejoiced in her presence with his diminutive body.
Seeing his mother standing there having become a servant to Kadrū,
Garuḍa asked, "O Mother, tell me the reason for this."
The mother said: "Listen, my son; I shall tell you what happened previously. Understand from me the wager that was made with Kadrū. (73)

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Serpents as the Progeny of Kadrū from Kaśyapa, the Birth of the Owl, Aruṇa, and Garuḍa from Vinatā, the Consumption and Vomit-ing of the Brāhmaṇas and Śabaras by Garuḍa, the Eating of the Flesh of Viṣṇu’s Arm, and the Granting of Boons to Viṣṇu as His Vehicle," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In ancient times, Kadrū and Vinatā, the two daughters of Dakṣa and lawful wives of Kaśyapa, were once sporting together, O auspicious ones.
In the house of Kaśyapa, they engaged in discussion, wondering: "What will the horses of the Sun be like—will they be the high-spirited Uccaiḥśravas, or brindled, or perhaps white? (2)
Kadrū said: "O Vinatā, your movement through the sky is unimpeded;
therefore, you know everything. Tell me, then, what is its form like? (3)
"Make a wager, O auspicious and sinless one, on whatever pleases you.
Vinatā said: "O auspicious daughter of Dakṣa, what is the use of a wager here?"
"In a wager, there is no happiness for both parties; a wager causes suffering for one or the other.
Knowing this, one should never enter into a wager that causes the loss of affection. (5)
What loss would there be for me in your victory, and what injury to you in my victory?
For when one is certain to be victorious, the other must inevitably suffer defeat.
"In this very same way, O sister, I shall speak without a stake.
Kadrū replied, "In the game of dice, one always plays without a stake. (7)
No mental relish arises, nor does any flavor at all;
therefore, those who engage in play take delight by setting a wager before them. (8)
Even children make false bets and laugh; they play for the sake of passing the time. Therefore, make a bet and speak!
Vinatā said, "Since your pleasure lies indeed in this matter," then Kadrū, deceitful and cunning, proposed a wager.
She who is defeated by the other shall become her slave;
and in this wager, all these friends of ours shall indeed be witnesses for both of us.
Having thus made a wager, Kadrū spoke of a dappled horse, while Vinatā spoke of a white one; thereafter, they both went to their own abode.
Kadrū, having summoned her sons, the black serpents, made her life the wager;
she said, "O virtuous sons, go quickly at my command."
"O sons, gallop toward that white horse, leaping over every hair;
let a black spot be visible everywhere so that it may appear stained. (14)
Having heard these words of their mother, some said to their own mother:
"We shall certainly not go, being filled with fear of the fault of falsehood. (1.5)
Others also have spoken thus; however, falsehood is a fault that destroys trust and is the gateway to hell—a fault we shall not commit.
Others also, placing their affection for their own kinsmen and likewise for their maternal aunt before them, acted in accordance with that purpose while remaining guided by sound policy.
Kadrū, a repository of wrath, cursed all those serpents:
"May those who oppose my words always become food for Tārkṣya."
Thus, consumed by the curse, they went to Pātāla as their refuge;
meanwhile, there were other boys who were overwhelmed with affection for their mother.
Having understood their mother’s words, they went into the sky after the horse of the Sun;
they galloped around the horse and made it dark blue and variegated.
Then, scorched by the heat of the sun, they went home;
Kadrū then told her mother Rāhukī everything that had happened.
Having summoned and honored him who destroys the heat of the sun,
he commanded Suyojana to cover [the moon] with Rāhu during the lunar festival.
Having gone to the sun, the serpents cried out from all sides when Kadrū,
having mounted the back of Vinatā, ascended to heaven.
By those two, a dappled horse of dark-blue color was seen;
Vinatā said, "I have indeed repeatedly beheld one that is white. (24)
"By the rise of your good fortune, a dappled horse is seen today.
Let it be as it shall be; who can ward off destiny? (25)
In all cases, destiny is more powerful, such that even what is white appears as blue;
for whatever kind of experience presents itself in a given place as an object of enjoyment, so it must be according to unseen fate.
"That which is adverse may quickly become favorable," having seen this regarding the dark horse, the female bird was indeed defeated.
Remaining constantly in Kadrū’s house, he always performed service for her;
Garuḍa, seeing his own mother in such a state as a slave, [was filled with grief]. (28)
She said, "O mother, how is it that this servitude is being imposed upon you?
Fie on those sons who are so powerful, since their mother has become the servant of another! (29)
The birth of a son indeed has that purpose which consists in nourishing one's parents;
a mother who is not supported by her sons is equated with a she-ass.
While seven sons were alive, the donkey was the one carrying the burden;
fie on those sons, that their mother remained miserable while they lived! (3.1)
It would be better for her to be barren than to have sons who perform the deeds of the barren;
for they cause their mother’s womb to suffer, so that she finds no joy.
Lakṣmī is the mother who grants birth and bestows her own self-ownership;
for those by whom she has not been rescued from suffering, their birth is useless.
If my mother is in extreme distress while I am strong and capable, what strength is truly praiseworthy for me? That strength is indeed remembered as being hellish.
Even if sons have committed evil deeds, if they protect their mother,
they cross over [the ocean of existence] by means of the "mother-tirtha," through service that has been rendered pleasing to her.
Neither sacrifice, nor vow, nor recitation, nor gift, nor even sacrificial fee ever attains even a hundredth part of the service rendered to one's mother. (36)
Indeed, even thousands of obstacles and tens of thousands of messengers of Yama flee far away simply through the service and blessings of the Mother. (37)
Having heard these words of her son, Vinatā said to her devoted child:
"In former times, I indeed entered into servitude to Kadrū on account of a wager."
Then I stated that the horse of the Sun was white,
and by her it was called "spotted," and subsequently indeed by her sons.
Having gone there, the horse was painted black and I entered into slavery;
for at that time, I would give her whatever wealth she desired.
"Then I shall attain freedom from servitude; ask the female serpent.
Having bowed to Vinatā and having bowed again and again to Kadrū, Garuḍa [departed]. (41)
He questioned Kadrū, who grants liberation from the state of being a mother's slave;
Kadrū replied, "Give me nectar, and there will be release from slavery. (42)
Having heard that, Garuḍa took leave of his mother,
remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and went to Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapa spoke to him regarding his own journey for the sake of nectar:
"It is indeed a treasure-store above the world of heaven, the food of the gods. (44)
The nectar remains protected by the wheel and the servants of the gods.
Go quickly; by remembering Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, victory shall be yours. (45)
At his father's command, Garuḍa entered the sky and departed;
seeing where that storehouse of nectar was located, the king of devotees rejoiced.
Having remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, that powerful one saw the treasury officials;
shaking them all on every side with the wind of his wings, he [overwhelmed] them completely.
He beheld a scissor-like machine situated above the nectar, whirling with great velocity, vast and resembling the Sudarśana discus. 48.
Even one who touches it, Garuda, having reflected for a moment, is surely shattered into pieces as he attains the state of a subtle atom. (49)
If I am devoted to my mother and a follower of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
then may the Blessed Lord himself grant me protection here.
For one whose parents are aged, who has young children, who is destitute, and who has a virtuous wife, there is no fault even in performing an improper act for their sustenance. (51)
For the sake of saving the life of one's mother, a Brahmin, a child, a cow, a wife, or even a teacher, there is no fault in committing an act that would otherwise be forbidden.
Having done this, and having beheld the nectar situated beneath the wheel, he filled a vessel with it and drank that which destroys death. (53)
Then, by the power of yoga, having uprooted the wheel from its pin with a brush, and having made it steady—free from rotation and with slow velocity—for as long as it takes; ||54||
Just as he was rising up together with the jar of nectar,
the guards, upon merely seeing him, fled with nooses in their hands.
Having violently fainted them all with the wind from his wings, he emerged from that treasure; at that moment, the Lord of the Gods and the others arrived.
Remembered as messengers there, they quickly approached for battle in fury; Mahendra, along with his weapon, said to him: "Who are you, this stealer of nectar? (17)
"Stay! Stay, O mighty-armed one! I shall indeed destroy you with my thunderbolt!
Upon hearing these words of Hari, Garuḍa then became enraged.
"Show your prowess; I shall carry you to the nectar, O Garuḍa!"—having been addressed thus, Indra indeed struck him with his thunderbolt.
Even upon the falling of the thunderbolt, the one of great strength was not at all shaken;
seeing his own thunderbolt rendered futile, Indra became afraid and said this to him: ||| 1.464.60 ||
"O mother of the serpent, O bird, if you grant this nectar now,
then all the serpents shall indeed be made into immortals by you."
Your vow would be destroyed and you would indeed have no food;
therefore, do not give that nectar to her, and do not make Kadrū immortal.
Having heard this, Garuḍa said: "O King of the Gods, I shall bring the nectar;
I will give Kadrū to you, so that thereafter she may no longer be my mother as a slave."
"You must strike quickly; let not the nectar be swallowed.
"So be it," said Hari, and the king of birds departed for Kadrū.
Having given [the boon] and shaken off his servitude to his mother, he became free from debt;
then the King of Birds himself spoke to the serpents and Kadrū.
If it is impure, the nectar must not be drunk, for it would become impure;
it would be devoid of the power of mercury. Therefore, having bathed, drink it.
Having been told this, they went to bathe; Śakra seized that nectar.
Upon their return, the serpents did not see the vessel of ambrosia at all.
At Kuśastamba, the vessel had indeed been placed there;
as they licked it from all sides, their tongues were split in two by the kuśa grass. (68)
Then the serpents, becoming exceedingly agitated, cried out for the sake of the nectar;
however, Indra had at that time prepared another, artificial jar.
Where poison had been secretly placed, appearing as nectar, they all took it and drank a single drop each in their respective portions.
The Mother said to those sons: "O sons, may drops always remain upon your faces; let there never be a loss of them at any time. (71)
Having thus received this blessing, those serpents went to their own home;
then those Nāgas were thrilled and exceedingly joyful, under the delusion that it was nectar.
Then the powerful Garuḍa, being hungry, devoured those various [serpents];
but those serpents who had fled took refuge in mountains and other places.
Thus that Garuḍa, having liberated his mother from the state of servitude and having received the benedictions of his parents, [departed]. (74)
He went to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha and became a carrier for Hari;
having attained eternal service to Hari, he reached a state of worshipfulness like that of Viṣṇu himself. ||75||
And because his mother Vinatā was devoted to her son and gave birth to him,
she was always honored by Kaśyapa, for she remained established in truth.
The sons of the virtuous woman Vinatā were the givers of nectar (amṛtadaḥ),
while the sons of the deceitful Kadrū, whose face was like poison, were themselves deceitful.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, you must always protect my devotion to my husband, Hari;
by my own power, I shall indeed drive away that which is difficult to overcome for them.
Devotion to one’s father, devotion to one’s mother, and devotion to one’s guru are deliverers;
devotion to one’s husband, devotion to one’s son, and devotion to a chaste wife are excellent deliverers. (79)
Devotion to servants, devotion to the gods, and devotion to one's wife are deliverers;
devotion to the virtuous and devotion to Kṛṣṇa grant liberation in my abode.
"I am eternally present within all embodied beings along with your power";
thinking thus, embodied beings should practice devotion toward me through their devotion toward those embodied beings. 8.1
The devotee should offer everything performed back to me alone, who abide within;
considering it to be of the nature of my grace, he should partake of it, and not otherwise.
Whether in a woman, a man, an animal, a tree, a creeper, or in that which is insentient or sentient, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa alone is the enjoyer and he is everything that is to be enjoyed. (83)
Thinking thus, whatever that embodied being eats is indeed devoid of qualities;
this is declared by me to be devotion to the husband (pātivratya) with my whole soul. 84.
Having performed it thus, grant the vow; one is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
By reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of wifely devotion (*pātivratya*).

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Garuḍa Eradicated Vinatā’s Servitude through Deceit," within the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the wager between Kadrū and Vinatā regarding whether the horse of the Sun was spotted or white.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the great virtuous Līlāvatī, who was beloved by her husband, the wife of Divodāsa, the king of Kāśī, and firm in her vows. 1.
Divodāsa became an attendant of Kṛṣṇa and established a dwelling for Him on this earth by the command of Kṛṣṇa, for the purpose of promoting devotion. || 2 ||
O beloved, he became a human king, a great devotee of the Lord;
his devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was always pure.
Līlāvatī, the wife of Hari, was indeed free from desire and the bestower of grace upon Kṛṣṇa; she was his servant and a resident of Goloka.
The virtuous and chaste Lakṣmī, who was always by the side of Kṛṣṇa and desired him as her lover, became the daughter of the King of Surāṣṭra by the command of Kṛṣṇa. || 5 ||
At her birth, the lords of the gods, sages, ascetics, women,
goddesses, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, the Īśas, and likewise the Manus [were present].
They arrived at his house and bestowed auspicious blessings;
then the gods showered flowers and the women sang.
The Apsarases danced, and a magnificent, auspicious festival took place;
for as soon as she was born, that beautiful girl possessed four arms for a moment.
The beautiful woman of excellent limbs appeared like Kamalā;
in an instant she became a maiden, born lying upon her confinement bed.
Then, when [the boy] had reached a suitable age, King Pṛthivījit, the great monarch, performed his marriage; at that time, indeed, the attendants of Viṣṇu were present.
All the crores of Gaṇas and others belonging to Śaṅkara, residing in Kāśī,
arrived from all sides for the wedding of this Līlāvatī.
And those gods and goddesses, exceedingly joyful, bestowed their blessings;
then the virtuous lady, accompanied by Divodāsa, went to Kāśī by means of a celestial chariot.
Then the gods showered flowers upon the top of the celestial chariot,
and Śaṅkara, the Vaiṣṇavas, and others offered blessings to the couple.
To the couple was born a son named Samarañjana;
thereafter, there were five hundred sons who lived according to dharma.
Having consecrated his son Samarañjaya as king, the highly intelligent Divodāsa, the lord of kings, departed for the conquest of the quarters. || 15 ||
Having taken the great chaste lady Līlāvatī, who was devoted to her husband, upon his chariot,
he conquered the kings of the south through the power of Līlāvatī.
Having conquered the kings of Prāgjyotiṣa, as well as those dwelling on the Himālaya mountains,
he defeated those situated in the north and the west, and then indeed proceeded to Kāśī.
Having crushed his enemies in battle, he caused a palace to be built on the western bank of the celestial river, using all the wealth that had been acquired.
The king had temples constructed for that many [deities],
wherein the entirety of the king’s fortune was invested.
In the center of that, the auspicious image of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was installed;
Śambhu was installed on one side, and Brahmā on the other side as well.
Other deities were also installed by the king for the sake of propitiating Satī, and he likewise caused a temple for Mahālakṣmī to be built for Līlāvatī. (21)
O beloved, listen as I tell you of the wonder of Līlāvatī:
having bathed at dawn, Līlāvatī performs the worship of the gods. (22)
She always performed the worship of her husband according to the prescribed rites;
once, however, she reflected: "Whose worship should come first? (23)
"What must be done by a devoted wife in the very early morning?"—
having fallen into this doubt, she remembered the Lord of Kamalā.
The Lord of Lakṣmī, together with Lakṣmī, departed, brilliantly radiant;
he was honored, saluted, worshipped by the Goddess, and even questioned as follows. (25)
"O ocean of mercy, whom indeed should I worship first?
Thus urged by Śrī, the Blessed One quickly spoke to the devoted wife.
Devotion to one's husband is the supreme duty; the worship of the husband is preeminent.
O beautiful one, the husband is twofold: both of the body and of the self. (27)
O virtuous lady, you previously honored the excellent lord of both [worlds];
thereafter, Līlāvatī became pleased and conducted an examination.
Who is the master of the body, and who indeed is the master of the self?
Who truly is the master of both? Listen to this, O Lotus-born One! (29)
The husband is the sustainer of the wife's body; he protects and guards her body.
When his own elements (dhātus) decline, hers likewise declines; thus, guarding him is the vow of a devoted wife.
O Lotus-born One, through this celibate conduct and through a woman’s devotion to her husband— by means of this Brahmanic virtue and conjugal fidelity— (3.1)
Those people who observe virtuous vows go from the world of Brahmā to the world beyond—
namely, renunciants, ascetics, those who have renounced worldly attachments, and celibate students.
It is likewise a vow for maidens, children, the elderly, men and women, as well as for the young and for married couples, to protect the Creator.
In such a way that protection is ensured, that offspring may be born, and that there is no expenditure in vain—that indeed is always true conjugal fidelity. (34)

The vow of devotion to one's husband (pātivratya) should be known as the second; it bestows liberation, perpetuates the lineage, grants heaven, and provides nourishment even for the body. Listen now to that as well. (35)
That food which always protects the body through nourishment should be regarded as its lord;
from food all beings are born, they live by it, and they enter into it. (36)
One should know that food is Brahman, which is to be worshipped through the five sacrifices;
having shared it, it should be given away, and thereafter one may eat from it. (37)
Whatever food is fit for censure, one should first offer that here to the deity;
thereafter, to the sages, the ancestors, the cows, and the servants. (38)
One should offer food that satisfies both the husband and the master as Brahman;
for the husband is his vow, and devotion to the husband is his eternal vow. (39)
Chastity toward one's husband is indeed a sacrifice of food; through it, heaven and liberation are attained.
O Lakṣmī, even when food is being eaten, if the life-force does not remain present, [the merit is lost].

Then the body becomes a corpse; therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa) is said to be the third [element], always appearing in the form of a husband. One should practice the vow of the vital breath. ||41||
When elders and those worthy of honor arrive at one's own home,
one should rise, go near them, and likewise bow down to them.
If one does not exert oneself, the vital breaths indeed rise up by force;
likewise, there would be a depletion of life-span. Therefore, one should well protect the vital breaths.
That which is always honored by the elders is known as the "vow of life" (prāṇavrata);
indeed, for the sake of her husband, a wife should observe that very vow of life, namely, devotion to her husband (pātivratya). ||44||
[One should not look at] the mother-in-law and father-in-law, one's parents, a master, ascetics, the learned, the best of men who have renounced, and the wife of a guru. (45)

Not to show disrespect toward kings, gods, virtuous women, or those endowed with good qualities—this is declared to be the vow of life; indeed, such devotion to one's husband is the highest form of wifely fidelity. (46)
A virtuous woman should always protect that; heaven and liberation are then in her hand.
Now hear the fourth, O Lakṣmī: it is the mind, which is always the heart. (47)
Scattered by millions of latent impressions (vāsanā), filled with desire, anger, and the like;
constantly laden with attachment and aversion, and presided over by greed, delusion, and so forth. ||48||
If that mind is indeed characterized by sattva, it protects and guards the embodied being;
if his mind remains in its proper place, his fame arises everywhere. (49)
If the mind of that heedless person becomes distracted, its destruction occurs;
yet the mind, like a horse standing on the right path, bestows both heaven and liberation.
In this cave, he alone is declared to be the protector and the Lord;
therefore, the mind, when restrained, is thoroughly protected by him who is the very form of the Lord. (51)

That vow is indeed the state of devotion to one's husband (pātivratya), which consists of the avoidance of passion, hatred, and the like, as well as the avoidance of illusion, latent tendencies, and false desire. ||52||
Chastity is the fourth; it is the mind’s worship of Brahman.
One should know that the mind is Brahman and should practice the vow of the mind.
Now hear, O Lakṣmī, about the fifth: knowledge protects the embodied being;
knowledge protects the body, while realized wisdom (vijñāna) is the protector of dharma. (54)
Knowledge bestows wealth and desire, while higher knowledge (vijñāna) awakens the self;
higher knowledge is the protector that guards one even in a place of sorrow. ||55||
As long as there is a body, consciousness alone is its protector;
O beloved, living beings do not protect themselves within that very consciousness.

Therefore, even in the case of a suckling infant, the husband must ensure that the vow of knowledge and the devotion of a faithful wife are well-protected, even through the course of casual conversation. (57)
The tasting of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s stories is her vow of devotion to her husband;
her husband is the Lord, her husband is Kṛṣṇa, and the knowledge of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is her husband. (58)
One should always perform worship accompanied by the adoration of the deity;
for that vow of devotion to one's husband is supreme, bestowing both heaven and liberation. (59)
Listen, Lakṣmī, likewise to the sixth vow known as Ānanda;
[by it] all—whether those of great wisdom or those of little knowledge, even grass and the like—are always [blessed].
Living beings desire joy, happiness, affection, delight, festivity, and enthusiasm; by these they live. (6.1)
Indeed, all beings are born through bliss;
they live by it as well, and even unto death they go for the sake of bliss alone. (62)
Therefore, the Lord, who is eternal bliss, indeed protects all living beings;
one should know that this bliss is the Supreme Brahman, the supreme Lord.
In bliss, however, even yogis remain forever liberated;
that bliss is the Supreme Brahman, and it is both the Lord and the devoted wife.
O Mahālakṣmī, having understood this nature of devotion to one's husband (pātivratya), one should practice it;
for these [husbands] are indeed masters of the body, but only to a slight degree in the self.
In this body composed of the five elements and consisting of your beloved, they always abide, as does the innate devotion to their husbands inherent in every woman. (66)
These [qualities] abide likewise in the wife of the master and in one's own self as well;
having understood this very nature of dharma, one should perform the vow.
Now listen, Lakṣmī, regarding my own devotion to my husband; I shall tell it to you:
hearing, chanting, remembering Kṛṣṇa, and serving Kṛṣṇa. (68)
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, self-surrender, trust, acceptance, renunciation, humility, and unwavering intellect. (69)
May there always be conformity toward Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, Mādhava;
for He alone—Hari—is the protector, the savior, the one who grants bliss, and the refuge.
That vow consists entirely of the surrendering of oneself, having the nature of surrendering everything;
there is no other such vow that bestows either heaven or liberation.
It bestows heaven and accomplishes all things, wherein no residue remains;
wherein there is no injury whatsoever, and wherein no bondage exists. (72)
Where there is no loss whatsoever and indeed no lack of gain, O beloved—
having performed this vow of devotion to their husbands, countless souls have gone to heaven.
Other men, women, and others indeed have gone and will go [to that state];
this very Self is Brahman, the Lord, endowed with the vow of the Supreme Brahman.
"He is one who observes eternal vows and is devoted solely to his wife's fidelity.
Thus, O Satī, have all aspects of wifely devotion been described to you in every way. (75)
Having heard what was spoken by me to Līlāvatī, she, filled with wonder and pride,
reflected for a moment and understood that her own beloved had indeed been married.
That virtuous woman always maintained her devotion to her husband in two ways toward Divodāsa:
first, she practiced celibacy, and then she practiced devotion to her husband. (77)
The second act of devotion to her husband was the offering of food to Divodāsa;
the third act of devotion to her husband was the offering of her own life to Divodāsa. ||78||
The fourth [chapter] is the dedication of the mind to Divodāsa; that is the vow of devotion to one's husband.
The fifth is the mere knowledge of Divodāsa; that is the vow of devotion to one's husband. (79)
Having protected Ānanda, Divodāsa, and her sixth husband who was devoted to his wife, the virtuous Līlāvatī honored her husbands.
Indeed, the devotion of the body to Divodāsa was [the highest] for him;
but when Śrī Hari resides within the self, the devotion of one's own self is the true devotion to the husband. 81.
That virtuous woman protected him and honored her husband;
she indeed offered all sixteen types of ritual services to her lord.
She offered her very self to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) who abides within the self, through a state of complete absorption. (83)
With devotion he offered [himself], and there he beheld that Hari;
in Divodāsa, he saw the divine-formed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord. (84)
Then, seeing her supreme husband, the virtuous Satī rejoiced;
she immediately beheld her own lord as the manifest form of Kṛṣṇa. 85.
With her physical eye she beheld Divodāsa,
but with her divine inner eye she beheld that Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, having attained that supreme divine vision, Līlāvatī always [attained] through the dharma of devotion to her husband both yoga and eternal perfection.
By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, she attained that which is unattainable even for yogins;
in the end, she reached the imperishable state with that very same divine body.
Together with her husband, her lineage, and likewise her virtuous offspring—thus, O Lakṣmī, has this divine and auspicious account of a devoted wife been told to you. (89)
Having thus offered themselves completely and attained the imperishable state, they all undoubtedly obtain Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as their husband.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Queen Līlāvatī, Consort of King Divodāsa of Kāśī, Attaining Service at the Feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through the Miracles of Her Various Divine Devotion as a Chaste Wife," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the most purifying story of the wife of Dharma, who was devoted to her husband,
which describes how she made the five Gaṅgās at Kāśī into sacred bathing places.
The Blessed One himself resided at the holy ford Pañcanada in Kāśī;
among all regions of the earth, the intermediate space, and heaven, Pañcanada is the supreme sacred site.
Kṛṣṇa himself was present there at that supreme Pañcanada Tīrtha;
formerly, there dwelt a great ascetic named Vedaśiras who was devoted to rigorous self-restraint.
There was a sage of the Bhṛgu lineage who was always devoted to ascetic penance;
seeing him as a youth, the most excellent Apsaras named Śuci [was struck with desire].
She, being pure, drank that which had been spilled by that rishi;
Vedaśiras declared her to be pure, righteous, and free from fault.
Listen, O virtuous lady, the transformation of youth arises in all embodied beings;
it does not become a fault for an embodied being who is free from desire.
The natural state of the elements is subject to occasional lapses;
these do not lead to a failure of asceticism, nor is purification through ritual bathing required. (7)
However, there was a mental conception in my mind for the sake of obtaining seed; therefore, semen was emitted by me even without sexual intercourse. (8)
Therefore, O beloved, bear in your womb that which you have drunk; for as a wife of a god, you are indeed able to do exactly as you wish in every way.
O my beloved, from my seed, the sages shall have fruitful offspring;
indeed, from your seed, there shall arise a jewel of a daughter, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to her husband.
Having been addressed thus, she remained in his hermitage with the desire for childbirth;
then, in due time, she gave birth to a jewel of a daughter, a celestial woman.
Having given away her daughter— a treasure-house of beauty, exceedingly radiant and a source of delight to the eyes— the excellent Apsaras named Śuci went to heaven.
The sage Vedaśiras nurtured that girl with affection,
nourishing her with the milk from the udders of Hariṇī, who resided in his own hermitage.
The sage gave her the meaningful name Dhūtapāpā;
then, seeing that the girl was more than ten years old, the sage questioned her.
"To whom shall I give you as a bridegroom? You yourself choose him, O auspicious one.
Having heard her father's auspicious words, she, with a devoted mind, spoke.
He who is the most pure among all, he who is saluted by all, whom all desire, and from whom the arising of all happiness comes—[to him]. (16)
That which never perishes at any time, which always persists, and which, possessing its own essential nature, protects one from great calamities both here and in the hereafter; (that alone is real).
Since all my heart's desires are fulfilled through him, and my great good fortune increases day by day by serving him. (18)
In his presence, there is no fear for me whatsoever due to its continuity; and by the mere utterance of his name, even the most intense afflictions dissolve away. (1.9)
I offer myself to Him for my well-being, in whom such qualities as these reside— the support by which even the cosmic eggs endure throughout the creations.
Having heard this, the sage was exceedingly pleased and attained great joy, saying:
"I am blessed, for in my house there is a virtuous daughter who delivers her family."
This blessed one, named Sārthā, has shaken off all evil and is a treasure-house of knowledge;
who indeed in this world could possibly describe the arising of her excellent qualities? (22)
I consider that one named Dharmadeva to be the better choice; I shall give her to him.
However, he is not easily obtained through mere pleasure, for he is adorned with every excellent virtue.
"She can be purchased by the price of asceticism, or perhaps by great merit;
having reflected thus, he said to his daughter: 'O girl, there is a bridegroom such as that. (24)
O maiden, he is not easily obtained by means of wealth, nor by noble lineage, nor even by the power of sovereignty, nor by intelligence, nor by valor. (25)
Through purity of mind, purity of the senses, austerity, and self-restraint, that highly wise and peerless husband is obtained; not otherwise. (26)
Having heard these words of his father and having prostrated before him,
and having obtained his father's permission, he performed most rigorous penance.
Having perfected her body through the harsh showers of rain, she remained upon the rocks amidst the Himalayan winds without trembling even slightly. (28)
Even while performing the five-fire penance in the forest of asceticism,
the young woman, though longing for water, did not drink any water at that time.
Having cast off contact with worldly enjoyments and subsisting on air alone, she became emaciated; yet, through her intense asceticism, her body shone all the more brilliantly.
Brahmā, having approached her, said, "I am pleased; choose a boon.
Dhūtapāpā, having offered salutations, spoke to the illustrious Parameṣṭhin.
"O Grandfather, make me more purifying than even the purifiers.
Brahmā, being pleased, said to her: "Whatever things are indeed purifiers—"
O Kanyakā, by virtue of the granting of this boon, it has become even more supremely pure than those;
there are thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas) here.
Among them, there are sixty-eight principal and most excellent ones;
indeed, all those sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in reverse order within your body.
Dwell here at my command and become the purifier of all;
in another kalpa, you will indeed become a divine form—of this there is no doubt. (356)
"Dharmadeva’s beloved wife is indeed the mother of Hari, born from Dakṣa.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā vanished, and she too went to her father's house.
Having understood everything through his constant austerity, Vedaśiras was repeatedly gratified;
she too constantly fashioned a four-armed embodiment of Dharma.
Every morning, she constantly worshipped the Divine with sixteen types of offerings;
through her virtue of devotion to her husband, she dedicated everything to Lord Viṣṇu.
Having shaken off her sins, she constantly beheld Dharma in her dreams;
once, that god Dharma himself came in person to that sage.
The sage requested a suitable maiden, and he then gave her to him;
she was a girl as radiant as the moon, full of luster, and devoted to righteousness.
Then, in that great field, the great virtuous woman Dhūtapāpā shone within the temple of Dharma in her invisible true form. ||41||
By her second form, having herself become a moonstone (candrakāntamaṇi), that ascetic woman shines within the waters of the Gaṅgā. ||42||
Moreover, Dharmadeva, having become the river Dharmanadī within the waters and joined with moonstone (candrakānta) rocks, shines indeed day and night. || 43 ||
In the temple of Dharma, he shines even with a divine form;
thus, in Kāśī, by the Gaṅgā, Dharma became the Dharmanada.
The river, though small and joined by tributary streams, became cleansed of sin;
then the Sun arrived and performed fierce ascetic penance.
From the rays issued forth a great succession of perspiration;
from that, the river named Kiraṇā was born, which is exceedingly purifying.
Then the great and virtuous Sarasvatī arrived there;
the purifying Yamunā, joined by the Gaṅgā, remained there.
The Kiranā, Dhūtapāpā, Yamī, Gaṅgā, and Sarasvatī—these five rivers are truly great; the river is called Dharmanadā. (48)
All these [five rivers] having merged together, that sacred ford consisting of the five rivers became universally renowned by the name Pañcagaṅgā.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, one is released from all bonds;
having given gifts at Pañcanada and performed the libations for the ancestors.
By worshipping Bindumādhava, one shall not undergo birth again;
for that purity which is proclaimed as resulting from drinking the fivefold *kūrca* [mixture] has been declared. (51)
That purification was attained by drinking a drop of water from the Pañcanada river— formerly named Dharmanada and later known as Dhūtapāpaka— while remaining full of faith.
From that indeed comes the Bindu-tīrtha, and from that the one called Pañcanada;
[therein lies] the merit of cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, horses, garments, food, garlands, and ornaments.
Whatever one gives here at Bindu-tīrtha, one obtains that as inexhaustible.
Having come there, Vahnibindu performed most rigorous penance.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself came and said, "Choose a boon.
Agnibindu said to Hari, "Dwell here in my presence."
"So be it," Hari replied, and he joyfully established his residence there.
"O lotus-born one, I dwell there under the name Bindumādhava. (56)
In the temple of Dharmadeva, I dwell eternally as a divine being known by the name Bindumādhava, O son of Dhūtapāpā. ||57||
My mother is Dhūtapāpā, and Dharma is my father, O beloved;
I am Mādhava in form, and we dwell together at Bindutīrtha.
Lakṣmī, whose nature is that of the Vasus, who is known as Nirvāṇa, stands at the side of Dharma; she is in my heart, and I too am in Pañcanada.
When the body has been thoroughly purified by vows, Dharma dwells there eternally;
and Kṛṣṇa, Dhūtapāpā, and Śrī likewise dwell therein in every way.
There, Artha and Kāma, together with Nirvāṇa, dwell forever;
I am there as Ādimādhava, and thereafter as Anantamādhava. (61)
Known as Śrī Damādhava, and then indeed as Bindumādhava—
in these names I, the Lord of All, shall reside in Ānandakānana.
My mother is a lawful wife, cleansed of sin and devoted to her husband;
dedicated to the virtue of wifely fidelity, she constantly serves the holy Dharma.
In that field, at the Pañcanada—a place of great merit and divine Śrīdharmamandira—men and women, having bathed and performed the worship of the Bull (Vṛṣa), [attain their goal]. (64)
Having performed the worship of Dhūtapāpa and my own worship as Mādhava,
and having made a vow of righteousness, one should undertake the Cāturmāsya fast and other observances.
Having performed the Kārttika-dāna and other rites, the observer of vows shall attain liberation;
likewise, virtuous wives dwell there in the practice of dharma.
In their second form, they are all the Mothers of the universe:
Śraddhā, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Medhā, and Kriyā. ||67||
Intelligence, modesty, physical form, tranquility, accomplishment, and fame—these thirteen, all remaining together, indeed practice the service of Dharma. (68)
Wherever dharma resides, there all women are devoted to their husbands;
having especially shaken off their sins, they serve their husband as Lord Śrī-Vṛṣabha.
Having bathed in the morning, that goddess bathes the Bull in the morning with garments,
ornaments, musk, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and saffron.
Having worshipped him, the goddess Satī then performed the lustration rite for her husband;
having offered circumambulation and praise, she bowed at his feet.
Having washed both feet with the water of the Gaṅgā for the sake of Dharma,
and having drunk the pure nectar of the ritual sipping (ācamana), he offered a handful of beautiful flowers.
Then, for the sake of Dharma, she, his beloved, provided fifty-six delicious foods at the meal—dishes with various condiments, accompanied by savory drinks and the like. (73)
He offers betel-leaf, performs body-massage, dances before the Dharma, and proclaims the glory of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (74)
She composes the Nara-Nārāyaṇa Gāthā for the teaching of the Dharma; thereafter, she performs service toward her co-wives, who are the personifications of faith and the other [virtues]. (75)
He also performs devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by the command of Dharma.
Once, the illustrious god Dharma was established in the Cāturmāsya vow.
He constantly recited the auspicious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* for its complete study at the holy site of Pañcanada and in his home. (77)
Sages, seers, gods, ancestors, humans, and women—
the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds— also arrived there for that festival.
Dhūtapāpā indeed made all the rivers, streams, holy fords, and various sacred fields excellent dwellings and the like.
Having shaken off her sins, Satī said: "If I am a practitioner of dharma, a lawful wife, a sustainer of dharma, and one who seeks devotion to my husband in accordance with dharma," [1.466.80]
Then there was a divine and excellent city, fifty *krośas* in extent,
wherein indeed resided all the riches belonging to those headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Śambhu.
Furthermore, in my palace, I indeed possess abundant foods and drinks, as well as vehicles, conveyances, objects of enjoyment, beds, and articles of adornment. (82)
May there be bowls, savory foods, and various beautiful sights, as well as garments purified by fire and other such things, in the excellent home of my husband. (83)
May there be streams of curd, streams of ghee, streams of honey, and mountains of sugar;
likewise, may there be rivers of milk, and may male and female servants be by the hundreds of thousands.
Having remembered the lotus feet of Dharma as they had been envisioned, at that very moment, various kinds of divine prosperities appeared instantaneously. (85)
Ornaments of gold and jewels, as well as collections of gems such as diamonds and the like, arose near that river from the power of the vow of Dhūtapāpa. (86)
O beloved, in an instant a divine assembly hall like Sudharmā appeared;
Durgā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, Rādhikā, and Dayā were there. (87)
Jayā, Lalitā, Māṇikyā, Ramā, Padmā, and Pārvatī; Prabhā, Haṃsā, Manasā, Mañjulā, Śrī, and Padminī. ||88||
Śānti, Śāntā, Hemalatā, the goddess Muktā, and Mauktikā were indeed the attendants there at that festival of storytelling in the House of Dharma. (89)
For those who listen to the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, they shall provide hospitality and other great services, as well as food and drink. (1.466.90)
And in the month of Kārttika, on the Prabodhinī day, at the conclusion of the narration, a supreme and great worship of Dharmadeva was performed by all of them and with all [offerings]. (91)

Filled with joy, he bestowed upon them all manner of gifts—bestowing infinite merit—consisting of jewels, gold, diamonds, and other precious objects; indeed, he gave them every kind of sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
He bestowed immense wealth upon the gods, the assembly of listeners, and the brahmins;
at that sacrifice, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, arrived there.
Then Kambharā and Mahālakṣmī, along with Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa,
arrived by celestial chariot in the presence of all while Puruṣottama was visibly manifest.
A divine rain of flowers was showered and cries of "Victory! arose repeatedly;
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with his parents, [was honored] at the great sacrifice.
He performed the offering of the tenth part [of the oblations] with great devotion by the command of Dharma;
having completed the sacrifice according to the rules, he performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Dharmadeva gave divine sacrificial fees to the twice-born;
likewise did the King of Kāśī, the Lord of Mithilā, the Lord of Sāketa, and the King of Kaliṅga.
The lord of Saurāṣṭra, the lord of Maru, the king of Sindhu, the king of Nipāla, the lord of Kurukṣetra, the king of Śveta, and the king of Prāgjyotiṣa paid him honor. (98)
They gave gold, diamonds, silver, garments, and sacrificial fees by the thousands to Dharmadeva, to the Brahmins, to virtuous men, and to virtuous women. ||99||
Then Dharmadeva, having fed and honored them all, dismissed them; and Satī, by her own splendor, granted them exemption from taxes.
Having shaken off his sins, he joyfully took water in his hand and made this resolve:
"May I know the Dharma of my Lord, the God, for His complete satisfaction. (101)
"Then, by the power of my devotion to my husband, let all this—palaces and the like—become invisible to me, yet remain abundant within my mind. (1.02)
As soon as he had thus resolved, everything instantly vanished in an instant;
millions of people, including the gods and others, were filled with wonder.
Having recognized the power of her devotion to her husband,
the goddesses respectfully praised that virtuous lady, the sovereign who was cleansed of all sin.
Thus, the Pañcanada Tīrtha, consisting of the hermitages of the Dharmadevas,
is purifying for all the gods by virtue of its power to wash away sins.
O beloved, the power of the vow of the chaste wife that purifies sins has been told to you;
by reading or hearing this, both liberation and worldly enjoyment shall be attained.
The dharma consisting of devotion to one's husband is indeed firm, bestowing liberation;
it grants all prosperity and likewise bestows devotion to righteousness.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Maiden named Dhūtapāpā from the Apsaras named Śuci to the Sage Vedaśiras in the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*; her attainment of the status of a Mūrtidevī through union with the god Dharma; the construction of a city across fifty *krośas* by the power of her conjugal fidelity during the discourse on the *Saṃhitā* at Pañcanada; the arrival of gods, kings, humans, and others; the performance of the sacrifice and its concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*); and the marvel of the subsequent disappearance of the prosperity of that new city. || 466 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the most excellent power of Kalāvatī, the wife of Vṛṣabhānu; I shall proclaim the prowess of that devoted wife.
Kalāvatī, a mental daughter of the Pitṛs and a partial incarnation of Kamalā,
was the beautiful wife of Vṛṣabhānu, devoted solely to her husband.
She whose daughter Rādhā is dearer than her own life to Kṛṣṇa,
born from half a portion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, and equal to him in splendor— (3)
In ancient times, three daughters were born from the mind of the Pitṛs:
Kalāvatī, Ratnadhanyā, and Menakā, on successive days.
Ratnadhanyā chose the mountain king as her father,
while Menakā chose Himācala, who was a portion of Hari, as her father.
Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, the wife of Rāma, was devoted to her husband;
likewise was Satī, the daughter of Menā, the wife of Śambhu, who became Pārvatī.
Both Ayonisambhavā and Pativratā were auspicious and devoted;
however, Kalāvatī chose Sucandra as her virtuous husband.
Having obtained the sovereignty of the kingdom for a thousand years under a king of Manu’s lineage,
the king then became truly detached from worldly life.
He went with his wife to the Vindhya mountain for the sake of penance;
having reached the hermitage of Pulaha, he performed most rigorous austerities.
Desirous of liberation, the king remained without food for a thousand divine years; meditating upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, he attained samādhi.
Seeing her husband motionless, his body devoid of the movement of breath, she cast far away the anthill that had enveloped his limbs.
Seeing that body devoid of flesh and blood, a mere collection of bones,
Queen Kalāvatī was overcome with grief and wept.
Uttering "O Lord of Lords," she was devoted solely to her husband;
hearing her weeping, that abode of compassion moved with pity. (13)
The unborn Grandfather of the worlds appeared in person;
and upon seeing her and the king as well, Brahmā was indeed filled with grief.
Then, having sprinkled the king's body with water from his water-pot,
that creator of the universe transferred the life-force by means of the power of Brahman.
But the king, seeing him before him as the very sustainer of the world,
prostrated and praised him, whose face and eyes were serene.
Brahmā said to the king, "Choose a boon as you desire.
The king, however, chose Nirvāṇa, the supreme state of eternal liberation. || 17 ||
When Brahmā, having heard this, was prepared to grant a boon,
the great virtuous Kalāvatī spoke respectfully to Brahmā.
O Lotus-born One, if you grant liberation to the lord of men, then,
O Brahman, what will be my fate as a helpless woman without my husband?
Without a beloved, what beauty can there be for women upon a widow’s person?
For a devoted wife, her husband alone is considered her vow according to the sacred scriptures.
The guru is indeed her beloved deity; the husband is her lord, composed of austerity and dharma; all kinsmen are truly excellent, yet for women, there is none equal to the husband. (21)
Indeed, for all, no kinsman is dearer than one's own husband;
O Brahmin, service to the husband is superior to all duties and is exceedingly difficult to attain. (22)
Whatever vows, charity, austerity, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth she may perform, all that shall be fruitless for her who is devoid of service to her husband. (23)
Bathing in all sacred fords, as well as circumambulating the entire earth, initiation into all sacrifices, and indeed the vows of great gifts—[all these are equal to this]. (24)
The recitation of the Vedas, as many ascetic practices as there may be, feeding those who are virtuous, the worship of Brahmins, and the service of the gods; ||25||
Likewise, the Cāturmāsya penance, the Kṛcchra, the Cāndrāyaṇa, and so forth—these do not equal even a sixteenth part of service to one's master. (26)
Those women who, devoid of service to their master, speak harshly to him, fall into the Kālasūtra hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. (27)
And there, serpents and worms bite them day and night;
they cause them to consume urine, phlegm, and excrement. (28)
The servants of Yama thus place flaming torches into their mouths;
having experienced such torments, they indeed enter the womb of worms.
They consume impurity there, and from that they return to the human state;
this has been heard by me from the virtuous and from the words of the Vedas. (1.467.30)
What shall I say, O Sustainer of the World? For I am but a weak woman and do not know;
you are the father of the worlds, the Creator, the Yogi, and always the Guru of the virtuous.
O Omniscient One, what more can I tell you? O Father, do not separate me from him!
This beloved of mine is dearer to me than life itself; what if he has indeed been released? (32)
O Brahmin, who is the protector of my dharma and my youth? In childhood, my father was my protector; having given me away to a worthy recipient, he is now liberated. (33)
A woman is protected by her husband as long as he lives; in his absence, her son shall protect her. These three are traditionally remembered as her protectors. (34)
If she is left without a protector, even though she be virtuous, she may seek refuge with another;
being dependent upon him there, her devotion to her husband would come to an end. (35)
At that time, the merit accumulated over many births perishes for a virtuous woman—whether in childhood, youth, or even in old age. (36)
A devoted wife’s desire for her own husband is equal at all times;
yet the affection of mothers for their son is indeed the greatest of all. (37)

The affection of sons does not equal even a sixteenth part of the devotion of virtuous wives; it ends with the child's weaning from breast milk, while hers continues until the end of their enjoyment of sweet foods.
The affection of those seeking their own interest ends with the attainment of that interest and is not enduring;
but the affection of virtuous women for their beloveds is constant, whether in dream or in waking. (39)
The end of mindfulness is the severance of kinsmen, but for sons it is even greater;
there is no suffering more terrible than this for a woman from her husband.
Just as one who is unskilled is consumed when swallowing poison over a blazing fire, so too is the unskilled woman consumed by the fire of separation from her lord. 41.
Virtuous women have no thirst for food, no thirst for water, and no craving for enjoyments such as clothing; they have no longing for their home, fame, or beauty, except for their husband. (42)
In the fire of separation, the mind is burnt, and likewise the face is burnt;
food is burnt, wealth is burnt, just as grass is consumed in a fire. (43)
There is no kinsman greater than the beloved; there is no one dearer than the beloved;
there is no deity greater than the beloved; there is no teacher greater than the beloved. (44)
For there are no life-breaths higher than the beloved; for a woman, there is nothing higher than the beloved;
there is no dharma higher than the beloved; and there is no wealth higher than the beloved. (45)
Just as the minds of the virtuous are immersed in Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and just as a mother’s [mind is immersed] in her only son, and just as the minds of the wretched are immersed in wealth; 46.
Just as [the mind functions] for those terrified by dangers, for the learned in their treatises, for infants in suckling at the breast, and for artisans in their crafts. (47)
O Brahmin, my mind is as intent upon my beloved as women are upon their lovers; indeed, it is not possible for me to live even for a single moment without him. 48.
For those virtuous women who are deprived of their husbands and whose hearts are filled with grief, death is better; for them, life itself acts as death. 49.
The grief caused by others may be kept at a distance by means of drinking, eating, and play;
yet the grief for one's beloved truly increases even through drinking, eating, and play.
A virtuous woman ought never to be separated from her husband;
she is the embodiment of her husband’s merit and remains perfectly united with him alone. (51)
A devoted wife is the fruit of the merit accumulated by her husband;
since the enjoyment of that fruit belongs to the husband, how can a virtuous woman be separated from him? (52)
In separation, she did not enjoy the fruits [of her husband's absence], nor was her husband’s effort rendered fruitless;
therefore, a virtuous and auspicious woman always remains united with her lord. (53)
Others indeed perish by their very nature upon the destruction of the body;
but for a woman, her form is the fruit of karma, and she is meaningful in birth after birth. (54)
Therefore, O Brahmin, if you release my husband while I am still here, I shall curse you and then forcibly deliver you over, for the killing of a woman is indeed a sin. (55)
Having heard Kalāvatī’s words, the Prajāpati was struck with wonder;
filled with apprehension, he spoke in such a way that it would be for Satī’s benefit.
"O child, I will not grant you liberation as long as I am without my lord;
likewise, your merit perishes through the enjoyment of heaven. (57)
"I am not currently able to grant liberation to you along with him;
for a daughter, liberation is difficult for anyone to attain without the enjoyment of merit. (58)
The possessor of dharma attains the state of nirvāṇa through the destruction of enjoyment;
therefore, for a long time, enjoy the pleasures of heaven together with your husband.
And thereafter, your birth shall take place on the bank of the Yamunā;
when that virtuous girl Rādhikā herself comes into being, you two shall be born.
Upon liberation while living, you two shall go together with her to Goloka.
She is indeed a virtuous woman endowed with goodness; you ought not to curse me. (61)
"Being liberated while living, they remain equanimous and devoted to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed for his own abode, and those two also went their way.
Having enjoyed the heavenly realm, Sucandra was indeed born as Vṛṣabhānu from the womb of Padmāvatī by means of the seed of Surabhānu.
Remembering his past births, a portion of Hari, whose mind was fixed on the lotus feet of Hari,
he was the kinsman of Nanda, a great yogi, a supreme and exalted Vaiṣṇava.
In Kānyakubja there was Kalāvatī, born not from a womb;
a great saintly woman who remembered her past lives, she was the excellent daughter of Bhaṇḍa.
Having obtained her, who possessed the luster of fine gold and had arisen from the sacrificial fire-pit,
she gave her to her wife Mālāvatī, who reared her with great joy.
King Bhavaṃdana celebrated a very great festival for her, named Kalāvatī,
and bestowed her upon Vṛṣabhānu.
Vṛṣabhānu, an incarnation of Hari who remembered his past lives, took her as his wife;
from her was born Rādhā, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 68.
Brahmā arranged her marriage at the Bhaṇḍīra banyan tree;
Rādhā attained happiness with Kṛṣṇa, and she who excels Rādhā (Atirādhikā) attained supreme bliss. 69.
Once, on the birthday of Kṛṣṇa, the beautiful Satī Rādhā bathed Kṛṣṇa in a secluded place within Vṛndāvana.
There, with the water of Yamunā, she remembered her own herd of cows;
by the mere act of her remembering, the cows returned from Goloka.
Sunandā, Sumanā, Suśīlā, and Surabhi,
with Kapilā as the fifth, were accompanied by the extensive lineages of their own clans.
By the glance of Kṛṣṇa’s affection, their udders overflowed;
those clouds (the cows) rained forth floods of milk from their udders.
Kṛṣṇa was bathed by them and adorned with ornaments by Rādhā;
having been honored by Kṛṣṇa, they then departed for Vārāṇasī.
Rādhā fed her husband and delighted him;
having celebrated the joyful festival of his birth, Kṛṣṇa went to his own home.
In Vārāṇasī, those cows [offered] milk to Śaṅkara, the supreme Lord, with unceasing torrents that destroy sins. (76)
They crushed it excessively until it became a lake,
where Śambhu had previously stayed and bathed in milk.
Out of affection for the cows that had returned, he went out onto the dry land;
that spot became famous as the Kapilāhrada itself. ||78||
At that sacred site of Kapiladhārā, by means of a śrāddha rite performed with milk-rice (pāyasa), the Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣads, Ājyapas, and Sāmapas [are gratified]. (79)
Even ancestors of other lineages attain eternal satisfaction through reading and hearing this; O Lakṣmī, it has been declared to you as the bestower of liberation.

Thus ends the four hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of how Kalāvatī, the wife of Vṛṣabhānu and mother of Rādhikā, was born on the banks of the Yamunā in the forms of Vṛṣabhānu and Kalāvatī due to her wifely devotion and the penance of her husband in a previous birth as the wife of Sucandra; and how their daughter Rādhikā bathed Kṛṣṇa with cow’s milk during the festival of His birth," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the auspicious story of a devoted wife who was an actress—a dancer of low birth—yet whose soul was characterized by fidelity to her husband. 1.
Formerly, there was a dancer of Śambhu named Kalāvatī;
she was devoted to celibacy and was highly skilled in the meaning of dance and drama.
Once, during the dark fortnight of Phālguna on the night of Śivarātri, he performed a vigil in a temple of Śiva, danced, and sang a song with a beautiful voice.
She herself played musical instruments and danced, saying:
"Kṛṣṇa is my husband, Śambhu is my husband, and Nārāyaṇa is my husband."
The divine Lord has been known by me; the god as my husband has been found by me.
Hari is my sustainer, my protector, my guardian, and my source of bliss.
"O Lord, I have no need here for any other master," thus she sings,
speaks, dances, and rejoices.
She constantly bathes Śambhu and adorns him with devotion;
she feeds him excellent, delicious food and makes him drink auspicious milk.
She performs the lustration ceremony at twilight, meditates upon Śaṅkara at night,
and, regarding Śambhu as her husband, she worships him always and in every way.
Thus, that dancer, devoted to Śambhu’s wife and endowed with merit,
passed away when she, that dancing devotee, fell under the power of the law of time.
She was the daughter of Vasubhūti, the king of the Gandharvas;
she was named Ratnāvalī, delightful and endowed with beauty and charm.
Skilled in the entire range of arts, speaking with sweet conversation,
she was a daughter who constantly brought joy to her father Vasubhūti.
She was skilled in all the arts of music and a great mine of the jewels of virtue;
she had three female companions who were vessels of exquisite cleverness.
O dear one, that [city] also belonged to Hari, who was endowed with the dharma of devotion to his wife;
it had three daughters known by the names Śaśilekhā, Anaṅgalekhā, and Citralekhā.
The Goddess of Speech was cultivated by those three together in one place;
being thoroughly pleased, Sarasvatī bestowed all the arts upon them.
Having regained her memory of past lives, Ratnāvalī repeatedly undertook the supreme vow of Śaṅkara.
"Having performed the daily visitation of Kṛṣṇeśvara in Kāśī, I shall indeed perform another task; I shall even speak words from my own mouth. (16)
Thus, that virtuous daughter of the Gandharva remained observant of her vows;
accompanied by those friends, she constantly beheld Śambhu.
Once, she worshipped Śaṅkara as Kṛṣṇeśvara; that young girl delighted him with a beautiful series of songs.
When the friends went to circumambulate Kṛṣṇeśvara,
Śaṅkara himself was personally pleased by Ratnāvalī’s songs.
Praising Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with all the Vaiṣṇava marks, He appeared before her and said, "O Sukanyā, choose a boon."
The maiden said: "O Lord Śambhu, you are extolled as Brahman;
I know you, Mahādeva, the Supreme Person, higher than the highest. (21)
O Lord, for whom is this worship being performed by you with a garland?
Whose is this tilaka upon your forehead? And whose moon is this, O Śaṅkara? (22)
"By whom is this garland of *tulasī* worn upon the neck?
Having heard these beneficial and sweet words that bring the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, Śambhu spoke. (23)
"Blessed are you, O blessed girl, that you inquire so well of me;
Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari himself, is my chosen deity. (24)
I wear upon my forehead a tilaka made from the footprint of her foot; a crescent moon made of saffron is worn by Lakṣmī. (29)
Tulasī is the wife of the Lord; her leaf is pleasing to Hari. O child, a garland made from it is worn for the purpose of chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa. 26.
He who always wears the garland of Vṛndā upon his hand or neck is indeed the best of devotees, a supreme Vaiṣṇava for all time. ||27||
Having heard this, the maiden said: "O Lord, he by whom this garland is being recited by you shall become my husband, my protector, my beloved, and my excellent lord. (28)
"O Maheśvara, grant me this boon, which is indeed the most excellent among boons.
"So be it," Hara replied, and then he spoke what was highly beneficial.
Tonight, Kṛṣṇa himself will take delight with you;
pleased by your devotion, he shall become your husband.
"These friends shall become servants of Kṛṣṇa along with you.
Having received this boon, they all then departed for their homes.
Her friends, laughing, said to Ratnāvalī: "Listen!
If that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa comes to you tonight today—"
The thief must be bound with the nooses of our vine-like arms with great effort,
so that he, the Lord of Rādhikā, may be brought within our range.
Oh, how great is the rise of your fortune today! How great is the rise of your merit!
Truly, you have achieved success for yourself alone, and yet it has been attained together with us.
Thus conversing, they passed the night according to the facts;
then, having risen in the morning, they gathered together once more in one place. (35)
In the morning, Kalāvatī, having bathed and worshipped Hara,
was questioned persistently by her companions and spoke.
The grace and blessings of the guru indeed bear fruit with certainty;
service to the guru is austerity that swiftly bestows supreme bliss. (37)
Today, having placed Kṛṣṇa in my heart, I quickly entered the bed;
with eyes overcome by sleep, I was longing to behold him. 38.
In an instant, I fell into a dream-like state due to the weight of what was to come;
thus, two causes for my self-forgetfulness arose within me. (39)
The touch of Kṛṣṇa’s limbs was like languor, robbing me of my consciousness;
through that languor, I became subject to another's will, and by his touch as well.
I am submerged in a treasure-trove of bliss and do not know myself nor that Lord;
while he desires to depart after having granted me happiness, I strive only to hold him back. (41)
