"By my blessing and through devotion to Hari, let all these who have come for refuge, including this brahmin, likewise become free from fever while remaining on Kailāsa. (92)
"May Durvāsā, the devotee of Viṣṇu, quickly be freed from his fever," having spoken thus out of compassion, Śivā and Śiva fell silent. (93)
Sudarśana remained for a moment, waiting repeatedly for the sage;
the sage, having bowed to those two gods, went to Vaikuṇṭha for refuge.
Having beheld Sudarśana, he then fell at the feet of Hari, crying:
"Save me, O Beloved of Kamalā! Save me, O Ocean of Compassion! (95)
O Great Viṣṇu, friend of the distressed, save me from the ocean of calamity!
O Blessed One, protect me who am afraid; guard me in the sea of worldly existence. ||96||
"What shall I praise? Protect me, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; salutations be unto You!
Having spoken thus, he drenched his lotus-feet with the tears from his eyes. (97)
Nārāyaṇa, however, said to him: "Arise and be firm;
listen to my words, O gentle one, and there shall be well-being and happiness for you. (98)
Others may acquire knowledge by hearing the scriptures from the mouths of the virtuous;
but the scriptures are my very forms, and the virtuous are the embodiments of the scriptures. (99)
For the virtuous indeed wander about as the scriptures incarnate; what they have spoken is the scripture itself, and what I have spoken is that very truth within my heart.
The virtuous are always superior to both the Brahmins and the Vedas in my view; even more excellent than I am the holy ones, and I always worship them within my heart.
I am indeed the life-breath of the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Vaiṣṇavas are my very life-breaths;
he who hates them hates me, for he is a destroyer of my life-breath.
Having abandoned sons, grandsons, wives, kingdom, and prosperity, those who constantly meditate upon me—who is dearer to me than they? || 103 ||
My life-breaths, nor Lakṣmī, nor Śaṅkara, nor Bhāratī, nor Brahmā, nor Durgā, nor Gaṇeśvara are dearer to me than my devotees. (104)
There were no brahmins, nor the Vedas, nor the supreme mother of the Vedas;
there was no Rādhā, nor the cowherds, nor the cowherd girls who are dearer than life. 105.
Just as the virtuous are dear to me, so too are they worthy of my worship;
all this that I have spoken is true, essential, and real.
I do not hold those in high esteem; they are dear to me even more than my own life.
But those who hate my devotees, who are dearer to me than life itself—[they are otherwise]—107.
I am their teacher, Pūrṇa, their swift lord who metes out punishment;
independent in all principles, yet dependent upon the virtuous.
Whether in Goloka or Vaikuṇṭha, as two-armed or four-armed,
my form in the imperishable realm is indeed eternally that very form alone.
O sinless one, my life-breaths reside entirely within my devotee;
therefore, water and food given by a devotee must indeed be consumed by me.
Even if food that is unfit to be eaten were given by another, it was like nectar to Ambarīṣa,
the best of kings, who was free from desire and non-violent.
How can you slay one who is compassionate by nature, virtuous, and devoted to the welfare of living beings—
those holy ones who constantly exercise compassion toward all creatures?
But those who worship me with devotion, who possess my fortune, and who abide in me— [1.12]
But those fools who hate them—of them, I alone am indeed the slayer.
I am unable to protect you from this enemy who harms my devotees;
go to the abode of Ambarīṣa, for he is capable of protecting you.
May you perform the breaking of the fast there for the pleasure of the king;
for a full year, being afraid, you have wandered from place to place.
That lord of kings, together with his wife, remained fasting and filled with grief;
therefore, I too remained fasting for the sake of my devotee’s fast.
By my blessing, Durvāsas, you shall be free from distress;
moreover, my discus shall never cause you harm on the road.
Today, free from anxiety, I shall certainly enjoy with pleasure the food offered by my devotee for the breaking of my fast, treating it as if it were nectar. 1.18.
"Even wealth given by Lakṣmī, I am not even able to enjoy it,
as long as my devotee remains fasting— he is dear to me."
"Go quickly, O sage, and prepare a meal for Ambarīṣa.
Thus addressed, the angry sage departed swiftly with his discus.
Having observed the fast for a year, the king awaited the lord of sages;
seeing that he had arrived, he bowed to him and fed him with excellent food.
Then the king himself enjoyed [the meal] and worshipped the discus;
the gratified brahmin also bestowed the highest blessing upon the king.
He went quickly to his own abode and praised again and again the supreme majesty of the virtuous Vaiṣṇavas, which is the best in every respect— oh, how wonderful!
Then, after performing austerities for some time, the wrathful sage again obtained Ekānaṃśā, the daughter of Vasudeva, as his wife.
Served by his devoted wife out of a desire for spiritual merit,
the irascible sage Durvāsas now shines in Satyaloka together with his consort.
O Lakṣmī, by hearing this, one's devotion to the husband becomes firm;
and having understood that service to the devotee is the supreme dharma, a virtuous woman becomes a true devotee.
Having become a devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, a chaste wife devoted to her husband Kṛṣṇa, she should not commit any offense against her devotees or her lord. 127.
A virtuous wife should endure all from her husband, just as the patient earth endures everything;
she should be as cool as a plantain tree and thus bring happiness to her lord.
Indeed, the story of Kandalī was narrated for the sake of my awakening;
may women likewise become like Kandalī, who gave me such harsh rebukes.
"May men not become like Durvāsas, full of wrath;
by reciting or hearing this, O beloved, one shall attain both enjoyment and liberation."

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Durvāsas Seeing Nārāyaṇa in the Form of a Young Brahmin, the Transformation of Kandalī into a Plantain Tree, Durvāsas Becoming Durvā Grass through Mud, the Arrival of Great Fear Caused by the Offense of Ambarīṣa due to Aurva’s Curse, the Firmness of Devotion to Her Husband, and the Marriage of Durvāsas with Ekānaṃśā, the Daughter of Vasudeva," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the sin-destroying narrative;
how Viśvakarman practiced devotion to his guru and its auspicious fruit.

Devotion to one's husband, devotion to one's father, devotion to one's mother, and devotion to one's guru bestow heaven and liberation; furthermore, they unfailingly grant whatever else is desired. || 2 ||
In former times, Viśvakarman was another body of Brahmā;
he was the son of the Prajāpati Tvaṣṭṛ, naturally skillful and intelligent.
Having undergone the initiation ceremony, the boy, dwelling in the teacher’s household as a religious student,
performed service to his guru, subsisting on food obtained through alms.
Once the Guru said to him: "Build a hut for my sake, so that the heat may not afflict me as the stream of water provides coolness. (5)
Just as there may be no aging for it, nor its destruction,
so too there may never be any transformation of it.
"O son, where is that hall which provides comfort in all seasons and is intended for my sake?
"So be it," the son said to his father, "I shall do so by your grace."
Then he was also commanded by the teacher’s wife:
"O Lord, please make for me a bodice that is suitable, soft, and equal in brilliance to the sun and fire."
Neither too tight nor too loose, his most beautiful bark garment,
when worn, does not require the wearing of any other cloth.
Then that auspicious servant said to her, "Om," and having been commanded by the preceptor’s son, he said, "Prepare the sandals for my sake."
When I have mounted that which is free from leather straps and the like, eternally close [to me], and bestowing bliss—then my movement occurs in mud, water, on land, and in the air. (11)
He said "Om" to him, and then the preceptor’s daughter said to him:
"I have earrings suitable for my ears, but bracelets suitable for my hands. (12)
There were also toys for young girls made of ivory,
as well as household utensils such as pestles, mortars, and the like.
There were also seats, bowls, and bright cooking pots,
such that the fingers would not be burned and the cooking would be auspicious.
"She is a mansion with a single pillar, and her body is supported by the wind";
thus she spoke, and her companions likewise sang of him.
O beloved, he spoke to them all in the presence of everyone, saying, "Create each your own desired object," and they promised, "So be it. (16)
He did not know how to do anything at all, and because of that, he became lost in anxiety;
for having accepted the word of his guru, if one does not act upon it, he shall fall into hell. (17)
Service to the guru is the constant duty of those living the life of a student;
indeed, by carrying out the words of their gurus, their heart's desires are fulfilled. || 18 ||
Having reflected thus, he went to the forest and indeed beheld someone there;
he asked that ascetic, "Who are you? Salutations to you. (19)
The ascetic said to that son of Tvaṣṭṛ: "Who am I? Tell me what you desire here.
The son of Tvaṣṭṛ replied: "I wish to learn the arts and crafts from your mouth."
The ascetic said to Viśveśa Śaṅkara: "May you propitiate Śambhu through your austerity; he will grant you whatever is desired in your heart. (21)
Having spoken thus, the ascetic then vanished from sight;
thereafter, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ performed intense penance with devotion for three years.
At that moment, the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the husband of Pārvatī, appeared suddenly in all his grace and bestowed upon him a boon consisting of every artistic skill.
All the arts shall reach full blossoming within your intellect;
receive from my mouth the mantra for the sake of purification and for the sake of becoming a fit vessel. (24)
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!"—O son of Tvaṣṭṛ, always recite this auspicious mantra which bestows all prosperity. (25)
Take this merit-bestowing tulasī garland for your neck and hand;
take this auspicious mark, consisting of a digit of the moon, for your forehead. (26)
Having said this, Hara spoke: "And may the spiritual knowledge you desire be yours, augmented by ninefold skill through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (27)
You [are the source] of gold and other minerals, as well as of woods and stones, and even of gems, jewels, flowers, and cloths. (28)
Of substances fragrant with camphor and the like, as well as of waters, of bulbs, roots, and fruits, and also of the inner fibers and barks of trees; ||29||
You shall come to know the excellence of craftsmanship among all classes of objects;
you shall learn how to create desired works according to the tastes of your masters.

"You shall know in truth all the arrangements for the dressing room, all the preparations of soups and other dishes, and also the entire art of the triple symphony (song, dance, and instrumental music). (31)
Machines, weapons, water-reservoirs, fortresses, the arts of weaving, and so forth; sorcery, fascinating knowledge, and the arts pertaining to other worlds—[all these are included]. (32)
And you shall know everything that is even beyond the world from its very root;
always worship Kṛṣṇa, for he will swiftly bestow knowledge upon you. (33)
"O Blessed One, when King Divodāsa comes into being by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he shall address you by the name Viśvakarman. (34)
"Then you shall construct a palace for me in Ānandavana;
the king, having spent the wealth, will cause the mansion to be built. (35)
"O Viśvakarman, go; abide by the command of your preceptor and do that," having said this, Śambhu vanished, and the son of Tvaṣṭṛ went to the house of his preceptor.
And those who were addressed with "Om" in whatever craft they practiced were satisfied by him;
having bestowed those desired things upon them and received their blessings, [they departed]. (37)
She delighted them all with her works of artistic skill;
then, in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, she remembered her beloved helpers.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa manifested himself, and by Kṛṣṇa’s will, the divine powers of his own form were then born as maidens from his left side. (39)
Sixty-four divine arts, celestial, beautiful, and in the bloom of youth,
devoted to their husbands, followed the son of Tvaṣṭṛ at the command of Kṛṣṇa.
They served him, their husband, who was the very form of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ;
they performed the silent recitation: "Obeisance to Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||41||
They performed meditation, worship, and service to Kṛṣṇa in the month of Bhādrapada;
and within that interval, Kṛṣṇa appeared in their presence.
Pleased by their devotion to their beloved, he granted them a boon:
"Having enjoyed every happiness here, you shall come to me at the end of creation. (43)
For you there is no other duty than the service of your beloved;
and as for the beloved, I am that beloved, and it is I who am proclaimed as the beloved by me. (44)
Where there is neither I, nor that beloved, nor that beloved without me—
by my devotion to her, O beloveds, you shall attain liberation from that place.
Indra and the other guardians of the world, the Viśvedevas, the hosts of Maruts, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Vidyādharas, and Uragas; ||46||
The ṛṣis, apsarases, yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas—all these consist of my own self; I alone am Viśvakarman as well. 47.
His auspicious wives, having always propitiated me in the form of their husband,
attain liberation at the end of every kalpa by taking refuge in me.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa then vanished;
those divine women, who were of the nature of his portions (kalās), continued to serve their husband, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
By reading or hearing this, one shall attain skill in the arts;
O Lakṣmī, the auspicious fruit for a devotee of the Lord of Gurus has thus been told to you.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Artistic Skill of Tvaṣṭṛ’s Son through Devotion to His Guru by Means of Śambhu’s Boon, the Attainment of a Wife Possessing the Sixty-Four Arts through Devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and Their Wifely Fidelity," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the auspicious life-story of Vyāsa,
who dwells eternally in Ānandakānana as a treasure-house of the scriptures.
Once he spoke to his disciples: "Recite this verse:
'Kāśī is indeed the refuge of all sciences; Kāśī is the supreme abode of Lakṣmī. (2)
This Kāśī is the field of liberation; this Kāśī is entirely composed of the three Vedas.
Furthermore, Ka is Brahmā, Śa is Śambhu, and A is Viṣṇu—these three indeed reside here.
Brāhmī, Brahmā, and Parabrahmā—these three indeed reside in Kāśī;
and here all three are attained: worldly enjoyment, liberation, and service. || 4 ||
In this very forest, a human being indeed attains action, knowledge, and devotion;
having heard of its purity, Vyāsa [resided] there in such a forest. || 5 ||
He wandered in every direction throughout Kāśī for the sake of alms;
when he did not obtain any alms, he cursed Kāśī out of anger.
"Since the people here are so arrogant that they do not give alms, may our learning not last for three generations, and may our wealth not last for three generations. (7)
"Let there be no liberation for three generations among the people dwelling in Kāśī.
Having uttered this curse and cast down his alms-bowl, he departed.
Then, as he was going along, he was entreated for alms by the Great Goddess, who was seated at the door of her house in the form of an ordinary woman.
"O monks, the Blessed One has not been seen anywhere today;
having disregarded his guest, my Lord will never eat again."
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, he always awaits a guest;
therefore, O twice-born one, you shall be my guest today, for you are my master.
That householder who consumes food alone, without a guest, [incurs sin].
The householder, together with his ancestors, experiences the evil karma.
Therefore, come, O best of Brahmins; fulfill the desire of my husband.
Make the household life of both myself and my husband fruitful through your acceptance of alms.
Having heard this, Vyāsa was filled with wonder and questioned that compassionate lady: "O blessed one, who are you? You are an embodiment of dharma and a bestower of peace. (14)
Beholding you, my inner self becomes serene; are you Śivā?
Or perhaps you are Lakṣmī dwelling in the lotus, or Rohiṇī residing in the moon? (15)
Is it that Vārāṇasī is present, or that the Goddess who bestows liberation resides here;
or is it compassion itself, or perhaps my own fortune that has taken the form of this woman? || 16 ||
Whether you are devotion, or the consort of Śiva, or the giver of food, or the beloved of Hari—in every way you are not a mere woman; you are his chosen deity.
"What is this anxiety of mine here, or rather, what need have I for it? O beautiful one, become [my guest]; if you would speak of yourself, I shall accept alms from you with devotion. (18)
Thus addressed, she said: "I am the wife of a householder residing right here;
I see you constantly moving about, surrounded by a multitude of disciples."
"You alone do not know me, whereas I know you;
O ascetic, fulfill the hospitality due to my masters through you."
Vyāsa said: "I have a certain rule that must be fulfilled;
I shall indeed accept only one alms-offering at a time, and never more than that. (21)
Satī spoke without hesitation: "Tell me what is lacking here.
Vyāsa replied: "I choose a row [of seats] together with ten thousand disciples. (22)
Satī said: "Without delay, you and your disciples form yourselves into rows;
everything is prepared through the majesty of my husband, and the food is ready. (23)
I am not such a woman who brings disgrace upon her husband;
as soon as a guest arrives at the house, the meal is prepared. (24)
All the halls were filled, all their desires were fulfilled, and everything in the house was complete through the grace of the husband’s feet. (25)
Thus addressed, he and his disciples became joyful and sat down in rows;
meanwhile, food, water-vessels, and sandalwood were placed in their bowls.
Simultaneously established from the sky according to the prescribed rite,
they all began to eat the food served by Vidhi.
Having eaten those divine preparations of cooked food, they attained satisfaction; and once they had sipped water for purification and were honored, they prepared to depart. (28)
Then Satī questioned him: "What is the bull here at this sacred ford?
Let us conduct ourselves at this tīrtha in accordance with that. (29)
Having heard this, Vyāsa said to Satī: "This is the duty of those who dwell at sacred fords;
there is no other duty than that which is being practiced by you."
You alone know the dharma, being devoted to the service of your husband,
by which means this long-standing husband of yours attains satisfaction.
Satī said: "That indeed is the dharma which is protected by me day and night;
ask about those duties common to all, and tell them to me. (32)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O virtuous lady; one should never cause agitation to any living being, whether by thought, word, or deed. (33)
Upon seeing the excellence of others, one should cultivate a serene disposition in the heart;
everything should be undertaken after due reflection, so that there may be auspicious success. (34)
Then Śambhu said to Vyāsa: "Tell me, who among these is like you?
You have uttered a curse out of anger against the residents of Kāśī. (35)
That indeed produces agitation, for the excellence of others cannot be endured;
for that was not done after due reflection, whereby auspicious prosperity might have arisen. (36)
The rule you yourself proclaimed has been broken by you alone through the giving of this curse;
for one behaving in such a manner, Kāśī is certainly not suitable for you.
"Go outside always, Vyāsa; there is a dwelling place for you here," thus addressed, he went to the eastern bank near the river.
Having established an auspicious hermitage, Vyāsa indeed dwells there eternally;
and wherever Vyāsa went, the goddess Sarasvatī followed him there.
In Kāśī, people were born liberated, including men from children to the elderly;
all were forms of Viṣṇu, sages who had mastered the Vedas.
All the scriptures went to the auspicious hermitage of Vyāsa;
at that moment, Śaṅkara and all the others indeed became mute for an instant. (41)
Having understood that the cause there consisted of the expulsion of Vyāsa, Śaṅkara, accompanied by Pārvatī, then went to Vyāsa’s hermitage. 42.
Having bowed to Vyāsa and honored him, Hara offered this praise:
"Forgive my transgression, O Vyāsa, Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (43)
"O Lord of Gods, destroyer of pride, my city is indeed mute, for it is entirely devoid of Sarasvatī, as well as Vyāsa and all the Śāstras. (44)
Where the Vedas do not exist, where the scriptures are not found, and where the mantras are not present—there the Brahmins are indeed like the mute. (45)
Where the Sarasvatī river is not present, and where there are no learned scholars, that place is said to be "laya" (dissolution); today, Kāśī is more desolate than that. ||46||
O Acyuta, O Lord of Compassion, forgive me for what I said out of ignorance, delusion, or pride; I have been brought back to life by you, Kṛṣṇa.
I dwell in the eternal city by you, the all-pervading Lord;
come, O ocean of compassion, and drive my muteness far away. (48)
Thus requested then by him, the lord Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana spoke to Śaṅkara and Pārvatī, saying, "Let there be silence then. (49)
O Śambhu, if you, along with your attendants, reside near Sarasvatī on every full moon day, let her dwell in your presence.
"Come here at dawn and perform a great worship for me;
then, by my command, Sarasvatī will arrive there. (51)
"Build a temple for Sarasvatī to the east, in your presence;
she shall dwell there eternally."
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara, accompanied by Śivā, said, "So be it.
Then Vyāsa, the Vedas, Sarasvatī, and likewise the excellent scriptures [appeared].
The sages and brahmins departed and dwelt in Kāśī according to their respective places;
everything became silent, and even Viśveśvara rejoiced.
In the palace offered by Śaṅkara, the mother Sarasvatī remained;
Vyāsa, having bestowed upon her the state of silence, returned once more to his own hermitage.
Śambhu, Śivā, and likewise the gods perform their monthly pilgrimage on the day of the full moon at that very place where the hermitage of Vyāsa is located.
All the gods, along with Śaṅkara, the sacred fords, and all living beings,
go for the sake of worshipping Vyāsa and for the attainment of freedom from muteness.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described the power of Śaṅkara, the devotion of Pārvatī, and the supreme sovereignty of Vyāsa. (58)
O Kṛṣṇā, Śaṅkara’s supreme devotion to his wife is ever-present,
and that same devotion exists in all the gods toward Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
O Lakṣmī, by hearing or reciting this supreme devotion to one's husband, there shall be enjoyment and liberation; one shall attain whatever happiness is desired.

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Vyāsa’s Failure to Obtain Alms in Kāśī during the Kṛta Yuga Lineage, the Curse Resulting Therefrom, the Hospitality Rendered to Him by Pārvatī, Śambhu’s Causing Vyāsa to Dwell Outside, the Water Brought by Sarasvatī and Others, the Deafness of the Citizens of Kāśī, Śambhu’s Return and Bringing Back of Vyāsa and the Others, the Cessation of the Deafness, and the Instruction that Vyāsatīrtha Must Be Established on the Full Moon Day," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the auspicious story of Vālmīki.
There was a brāhmaṇa named Sumati, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu. || 1 ||
His beloved wife was Kauśukī, endowed with beauty and youth;
from her a son was born, named Agniśarman.
Although he was urged by his father, he did not engage in the study of the Vedas. Then, on one occasion, the people were severely oppressed by a drought.
Sumati, indeed, having established a hermitage in the forest, lived there with his family;
Agniśarman, however, came to associate with Ābhīra bandits.
Furthermore, Agniśarman, a man of cruel deeds, slays those people who go out along that path in the forest and seizes their wealth.
The seven sages of virtuous vows arrived by that path;
and Agniśarman, desiring to seize her, beheld those seven.
He said: "Release all these garments, umbrellas, fans, and so forth; otherwise, I shall kill you."
Having heard these words of his, Atri spoke to the one named Agni:
"How indeed can there be such a sinful act, which causes us distress, in you, a Brāhmaṇa?"
"We have set out on a pilgrimage as ascetics," they said;
then Agniśarman replied, "My mother, father, and sister—"
"My wife and sons are indeed hungry; I must support them. Without some act of seizure, how indeed could there be sustenance here in this forest? (10)
"Therefore, I shall commit sin, disregarding both good and evil.
To him, Atri said: "Listen to that which is true, beneficial, and auspicious. (1.1)
Ask your father and others concerning that which is earned by one's own karma;
tell me, to whom can the sin committed for your sake be ascribed?
If they do not tell you, or if they do not acknowledge [the truth],
and if they should say that the sin belongs to you alone— then do not kill living beings falsely.
Then Agniśarman said: "I have never asked you before;
at your word, I shall go and inquire into the disposition of my family members."
"I know how you all remain here;
I shall return to you again," having said this, he went quickly to his father. || 15 ||
He asked: "By the destruction of dharma through acts such as the harming of living beings, a very great sin is produced; tell me, to whom does this belong? (16)
He questioned his mother as well, and his parents said to him:
"O son, this sin shall belong to you alone; it is not ours. Then... (17)
"What was done by you must be enjoyed by you; provide for the maintenance of us both.
Then she spoke thus to her husband: "That sin is yours alone. (18)
Then he spoke to his sons and daughters, and they spoke to him;
they said, "The sin is yours alone; not even a trace of it belongs to us.
Thus, perceiving their self-interest, he was filled with world-weariness.
Bowing at the feet of the sages, the twice-born man spoke to them in sorrow:
"I have no mother, nor father, nor wife, nor son;
I have neither daughter nor sister, for they are concerned solely with their own interests. (1.479.20–21)
"Sirs, you ought to protect him who has come for refuge from that sin.
Atri, standing beneath a tree, said to him: "Practice meditation;
destroy the mass of sins through the form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa."
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord. || 23 ||
Chant [the mantra] constantly with faith while holding a garland of tulasī in your hand;
for Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself will effect your liberation here. (24)
Having spoken thus, they all departed, and he too became intent on meditation;
established in that meditation, the yogi remained for thirteen years.
Remaining constantly in meditative absorption, he indeed recited the mantra with its proper phonetic intonations;
meanwhile, an anthill grew up over him, constructed by female termites.
Remaining motionless there, he meditated and recited that [mantra] accordingly;
he neither rose, nor drank water, nor ate anything at all.
Then those sages emerged from the vicinity by that path;
they heard the sound of that mantra-recitation and were filled with wonder.
Seeing them as mere anthills, like inert matter situated within,
those lords consecrated them with the waters of the Gaṅgā and caused them to rise.
Having slowly risen from that state, he paid homage to the lords of sages and said:
"I have been delivered from sin and from this world of terrible karma."
I recite that mantra of Kṛṣṇa which was extracted by the compassionate ones;
through your grace, I have likewise acquired true knowledge. (3.1)
"May I go to the state of liberation; please show me favor.
Having said this, he drank the water used for washing the feet of the sage. (32)
The sages addressed him by the name Vālmīki;
those sages departed for the truth, while Vālmīki remained devoted to Hari.
Having attained knowledge of the three periods of time, he composed the Rāmakāvya,
by which countless embodied beings shall attain liberation.
For as long as he lived, that king of devotees, protecting his vow of celibacy, maintained his eternal devotion to Kṛṣṇa. ||35||
In the morning he performed his bath and observed the twilight devotions with devotion;
[he worshipped] Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇapati, Pārvatī, Agni, and the Sun.
Every day the sage worshipped Rāmāditya and the seven deities with sixteen excellent articles and auspicious inner dispositions. (37)
He constantly offered as an oblation wild fruits, roots, leaves, seeds, and the like,
as well as water from the well.
He offered incense and lamps made from wild sandalwood wood,
and he presented garments such as bark-cloth to Rāma during the worship.
With devotion, she offered flowers brought on the fibers of creepers;
she gave sweet honey, raw honey, and seasonal fruits and the like.
With joy he gave rice that ripens without being ploughed, which was cooked by the sun;
likewise, he gave seeds such as *śigru* and others, cooked by fire.
Deer, birds, and other animals, freed from fear and seeking liberation, come there upon hearing the name of Rāma.
They remain there with steadfastness as long as the worship continues;
at night, they dwell in that very place, eager to hear the name of Rāma. ||43||
Having given them the grace of Rāma in the form of leaves, flowers, fruits, water, bulbs, grains, and so forth, he then eats with great joy. (44)
Sometimes, by the power of fate, forest-dwellers happen to arrive as guests;
perceiving them to be forms of Kṛṣṇa, she serves them with the utmost reverence. (45)
He did not forget the chanting "Rāma, Rāma" for even a moment;
through the power of his recitation, he attained a perfection of speech that is difficult for others to obtain. (46)
Indeed, the jewels desired by Vālmīki appeared before him.
Once, during the summer season, in a forest that was parched and intensely scorching, [he stayed].
When the fruits, leaves, and petals had perished and he could find no fruit or the like, he lamented: "What shall I offer as the eternal *naivedya* for Śrī Hari? (48)
"There is no leaf or other edible offering to dedicate to Kṛṣṇa; what can I give?"—thinking thus in his mind, he remained standing near the hut. (49)
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Rāma, Hara, and Vibhu!
Having swallowed my mental constructs today, be satisfied, O Keśava! (1.479.50)
While he was speaking thus, a certain cowherd arrived right there, accompanied by a milch cow and separated from her calf. ||51||
He said to him, "O sage, I wish to stay here for a moment;
having rested for a moment in your hermitage, I shall go to another forest. (52)
Having spoken thus, he stood for a moment in the shade of an *aśvattha* tree together with the cow;
he milked her into a leaf-cup and joyfully gave the milk to him. (53)
Vālmīki, being exceedingly delighted, took that [portion] for worship;
having offered it to the gods and having distributed it with graciousness, he shared it out.
He drank that which was purified by being offered to Kṛṣṇa and likewise gave it to him;
at that moment, the light of the imperishable Brahman arose within his heart.
Divine vision arose within him, its true radiance unobstructed;
with it, he beheld that cowherd, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the husband of Rādhikā.
Accompanied by the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and having arrived for the purpose of offering food oblations,
he again beheld this very Gopāla through the illusory power (māyā) of Hari.
Filled with this great weight of wonder, he praised the Supreme Lord;
indeed, his eternal satisfaction was produced by that milk. (58)
In an instant, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa became invisible;
Vālmīki, repeatedly remembering that divine form, danced indeed.
He constantly remembered that divine Kṛṣṇa, who is compassionate toward His devotees;
indeed, He was perceived within the anthill in the form of Rāma.
He showed him his entire future life as if it were already in his hand;
he constantly engaged in the contemplation of Rāmāditya.
He went before to the abode of Hari, the eternal station of Vaikuṇṭha;
for indeed, there is no evil destiny for those who commit sins if they are devotees of Kṛṣṇa.
The devotees of the Blessed One are capable of performing even the extraction of anything else:
desire, anger, the mind, the vital breath, the senses, and latent impressions.
They indeed exist in that very form, yet through union with Kṛṣṇa, they become divine in form and bestow liberation upon all. ||64||

Thus ends the four hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Agniśarman’s Attainment of the State of a Vālmīki, Omniscience, and Liberation through the Penance of Chastity; His Becoming a Rishi through Association with the Seven Sages; and His Vision of Kṛṣṇa in the Form of a Cowherd and a Cow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Pṛthvī, to the auspicious and delightful city of Avantī, where the river Śiprā flows; once, Rāma went there.
Together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he offered libations to his ancestors;
then he commanded Lakṣmaṇa to fetch water from the Śiprā.
Disregarding those words, Lakṣmaṇa said to Sītā:
"Tell me now, what will Sītā do even if I were to bring her here by force? (3)
"O Rāma, I shall not remain in a state of servitude to you at all times;
for she is well-nourished, very firm, and indeed more robust than even I."
"Speak, O Rāghava! What will you do with this Sītā?
Having heard those unprecedented words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma [addressed] Jānakī.
The two of them remained there dejected; Sītā indeed took up water, and having drunk and eaten there, they went to Mahākāleśvara.
Having spent the night there, Rāma said to his younger brother at dawn:
"Arise, dear son Saumitri; let us go to another forest region."
The son of Sumitrā, filled with rage, said: "I will not go by any means;
you yourself go along with this beloved wife of yours."
"I shall never go to the foremost forest, nor indeed to Ayodhyā.
To the son of Sumitrā who was speaking thus, the Blessed One himself replied: (9)
"Come slowly, O son of Sumitrā, along with Sītā, my younger brother.
How indeed do you fare in your anger, or how did you depart together with her?"
"Since you, an ascetic, must proceed slowly and gradually," Lakṣmaṇa replied, "If that were so, I would not follow your word."
"I will not perform service for you; then I shall go to the forest together with you.
"So be it," said Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa departed slowly.
Then he spoke again: "I will certainly not go to the forest with you.
Having said this, Rāma sat down, even as he continued to move forward and forward.
Then, having risen and made his bow ready,
he fixed an arrow upon it and deliberated whether to kill Rāma or Jānaki.
I shall bring them under my control while living as an ascetic in the forest, always happy;
Rāma will surely depart quickly, and Sītā too will go with speed. (15)
Lakṣmaṇa, having fixed an arrow to his bow, was unable to release it, thinking:
"Alas! How can my brother be slain? For here is my mother, Jānakī! (16)
"How can she, who is worthy of worship, be brought under my control? What indeed is this delusion of mine?
Even after reflecting thus once more, her mind remained once again dependent upon the arrow.
Then Rāma, his heart full of compassion, saw a Plakṣa tree before him; having gone there, he sat down upon its ground.
Sītā also arrived and rested; Lakṣmaṇa likewise departed slowly.
Rāma said, "O brother, why indeed have you taken up the bow with an arrow?"
Lakṣmaṇa stood bowed with shame for a mere moment;
then Rāma, perceiving his inner state, spoke regarding the condition of the earth.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, this is not your fault; rather, it is the behavior of this field.
In this field, there is no brotherly affection, for everyone is intent upon their own self-interest. (21)
Devoted solely to their own self-interest as the primary motive, they do not respect one another;
sons do not listen to their father, nor likewise does a father to his sons.

Neither does the disciple [act] out of regard for the teacher’s word, nor the teacher out of service to the disciple; affection is merely bound up with one's own self-interest—no one is truly dear to anyone else. (23)
Such power as this belongs to this earth, my younger brother;
there is no fault on your part in this, so do not feel ashamed, O sinless one.
Having heard this and bowed, the son of Sumitrā said: "How has such a place come to be, which, though insentient, afflicts us who are sentient? (25)
Rāma said: "Formerly, there was here a Rākṣasa named Ghorakhana, who was very well-nourished and measured seven palm trees in height."
Assuming any form at will, he would fly through the sky into cities and houses, and by force seize people and other things to devour. (27)
That wicked man, having established a hermitage in the forest within a single *gavyūti* of land, would cruelly carry off children, women, and bulls.
Moving about in an invisible form, he devours birds and other creatures;
sometimes he becomes a tiger, and sometimes a deer or a gayal.
In one place he is a king, in another a brahmin, and in another a woman of beautiful form;
in one place he is a serpent, in another a monkey, and in another he even becomes harsh.
In whatever form one may be fit for a particular purpose, one becomes possessed of that very form; having come together, having dwelt together, and having arranged for a joint journey. (3.1)
He inflicts violence upon them and devours them all;
at times, however, he creates an artificial, delightful city or a beautiful town.
He displays a spectacle adorned with offspring, like a magician’s trick, wherein new undertakings are seen in the marketplaces of merchants. (33)
The princes had auspicious halls, gardens, and groves;
there were most delightful palaces and a very great royal army.
In this way, he indeed causes a city of the Gandharvas to appear in some place;
then once again, Śrī Gopāla, together with his wife Kambharā— 35.
For the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites, Śrīgopāla, an incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, emerged along that path, accompanied by the virtuous Kambharā, who was an incarnation of Lakṣmī. (36)

In the forest, while they were traveling on the path, two extremely radiant beings, possessing a beautiful luster and the brilliance of the sun, were seen by a rākṣasa who was digging a terrible hole. ||37||
However, having gained their trust through appropriate actions, he set his mind upon them;
for the Rākṣasa thought: "Since these two have been favored by destiny, they shall be mine. (38)
Having prepared a beautiful city favored by fate and filled with festivities,
they honored those two excellent eaters according to the rites of hospitality.
Having reflected thus, he created a divine city inhabited by celestial beings,
adorned with royal implements of the gods and beautified by sacrificial halls and other structures.
Having himself become the lord of the city and having offered water for honor before them,
he went a great distance to show them great hospitality and brought them home.
Then that couple experienced supreme wonder, having been honored, fed, massaged at their feet, and fully satisfied. || 42 ||
Having rested, they became as if fast asleep;
meanwhile, that Rākṣasa went forth to seize his formidable weapon.
At that moment, for the purpose of slaughtering the couple, Gopālakṛṣṇa spoke to the virtuous Kambharā: "Behold that deceitful servant! (44)
To bring back Kambharālakṣmī, he has gone with his sword;
this Rākṣasa is extremely wicked and devours many by means of deception in the forest. (45)
"I must bring about his destruction; for that purpose I have come.
Be at ease for a moment, O virtuous lady, and watch my deed for a moment. (46)
Just as the Blessed One was thus reporting his wife,
he arrived, having seized a very sharp sword.
Then, having risen quickly, Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa himself,
together with his wife, went to another place in an invisible form.
And as soon as he had moved away from the bed and was seen just as before, [the king],
thinking him to be on the bed, struck him with a sword for as long as it took.
Then the sword, struck against the bed, broke in two;
one half remained in the hand of the Rākṣasa, while the other half fell at his feet.
He cut off his two forefeet;
that half-portion which was the tip flew up and became fixed, with its sharp point, upon his throat.
His throat was severed and the Rākṣasa fell down, unconscious for a moment;
then Lakṣmī, endowed with compassion, went toward him to give him water.
Out of a sense of enmity, he held [the snake] with his two arms as long as he was about to die;
meanwhile, out of a desire to eat, he wished to swallow it.
Then she cursed him: "O Rākṣasa, go to your death!
You act with such deceit everywhere in this city. (54)
O you whose nature is deceitful, you deceive; therefore, your stages are always characterized by guile, deceptive in essence, delusive, and joined with hypocrisy and cruelty. (55)

May there always be [only] those of cruel nature residing here, and may others on this earth likewise possess the qualities of deceit, cruelty, and the like through their connection with this place. (56)
There is no doubt that they will become friends as well as enemies—both one's own and those belonging to others—due to the fault of association with Rākṣasas. (57)
But because of that evil, they shall again become experiencers of hellish suffering; all of them, the lowest of men, shall fall to the earth. (58)
As soon as the Rākṣasa was thus cursed by the goddess, that cruel one gave up his life and the city went to ruin. ||59||
That ground became a solitary wilderness, a mere stretch of land;
at that time, Kambharā-lakṣmī was overwhelmed by extraordinary wonders.
He asked the God of gods, "What indeed is this net? Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa replied, "It is the sorcery of the Rākṣasa. (61)
"O beautiful one, everything was indeed already known by me beforehand, since this Rākṣasa has died by his own hand once again. (62)
He shall indeed enter the womb of a Rākṣasa once again by the hand of Rāma;
he shall die as a result of the fruit of his service and sight of us two.
Then he will attain liberation; meanwhile, when Rāma dwells on the southern island, he will go there and slay him.
Having spoken thus, the two of them departed; for that land was formerly a Rākṣasī who had been cursed by him through that yoga, O Lakṣmaṇa, and here your mind [is troubled].
There is not even the slightest fault in you for having engaged in improper reflection;
for place, time, action, association, mantra, meditation, and the sacrificial fee [are all essential factors]. ||66||
And as these gurus may be, so do they bear fruit for the disciple;
indeed, by the dwelling of the Rākṣasa, that land became cursed.
"O son of Sumitrā, it was through contact with the earth that your mind became cruel;
but that state of the earth has passed, brother, so be at ease and filled with happiness. (68)
By the power of Sītā’s devotion to her husband, my mind indeed did not undergo any transformation;
nor indeed did my mind undergo any change.
For those whose vow as a wife is constant and whose devotion to their husband is firm,
no attachment to the earth or other worldly objects ever takes root in their minds.
And you too, O brother, remain a celibate student and a great ascetic;
therefore, even now, your fortitude remains well-established despite the agitation of your heart. (71)
But others might certainly provoke a quarrel in such a place;
they would obtain the fruit of destruction—of this there is no doubt. (72)
By the dharma of devotion to her husband, people become happy;
for their husband is Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the Lord. (73)
"Because Sītā is devoted to her husband, I have found joy even in the forest;
such is my brother, a keeper of his vows who has spoken these words here. (74)
There is no suffering for three who dwell together in the great forest;
heaven, liberation, home, and sovereignty all exist together for me in the woods. (75)
Thus has this power of the earth been described here, which was previously well-consecrated;
our touch of foot has occurred here, therefore [proceed] very slowly.
The power of the earth, its cruelty, and its form will, in the course of time, go to destruction;
the great region of Avantī shall become a sacred site (tīrtha) of auspiciousness.
Having spoken thus, those forest-dwellers departed ahead into the woods.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this account of the curse upon the devoted wife been told to you. (78)
Furthermore, the power of devotion to one's husband, when not overwhelmed by place and other factors, shall result in a pure intellect through the recitation and hearing of this [text]. (79)
Defeat encountered due to place, time, and other such factors should not cause one distress;
rather, the mind should become nourished in dharma and pure in its commitment to vows and the like.
Indeed, the mere remembrance of this [mantra] shall grant one's desired fruits and bestow peace;
it shall grant heaven, liberation, and eternal bliss. ||81||

Thus ends the four hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ground Consecrated by the Destruction of the Rākṣasa Ghorakhana through the Efforts of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa Following Lakṣmaṇa’s Change of Heart during the Avantī Pilgrimage, as well as Lakṣmaṇa’s Mental Impurity and Sītā’s Devotion to Her Husband," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
I shall further describe the vow performed by the wives of the sages;
listen to that which has been narrated by me, which is purifying and destructive of sin.
The seven wives of the seven sages, who were devoted to their husbands, went to the Gaṅgā to bathe; there, at Kuśasthala, they saw the Fire-god.
Trembling from the cold, they went near a fire to warm themselves;
however, that was not a real fire, but one thrown there by Gaṅgā.
The son of the Creator Śaṅkara was radiant like fire;
resembling a flame, he was placed by Agni within a clump of reeds in the waters.
That very element, mixed with fire, having seen those devoted wives who had bathed,
was instantly impelled by the fire and entered into them.
They became pregnant and were recognized as such by the sages;
thus, fallen from their divine state, they were indeed defiled by fire.
Abandoned by the sages, they wandered from forest to forest;
thus, after much time had passed, Nārada, the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu, [arrived].
Desiring their welfare, that great sage, firm in his vows, arrived within the forest; there he was hospitably received by them.
Seated there, he spoke words appropriate to the time and place:
"What is this being done? An insult has been inflicted upon you."
"Why indeed were those women, devoted wives and mothers of the world, abandoned by the sages?
They replied, "We have been abandoned on account of Kārttikeya."
The great power of Śaṅkara was present upon the kuśa grass in the fire;
knowing this, when we had bathed and went there to perform our austerities, [we encountered it]. || 11 ||
Agni, having touched us, entered our bodies in a concealed form;
he became attached to the region of our womb within the circle of the birth canal.
"Because we were born from him and are his uterine siblings, it is established that we are wicked;
and by those performers of sacrificial rites, we have been abandoned, left in great misery. (13)
Whatever sin has arisen by the power of fate from public censure—what can we do, where shall we go, what austerity, or what deity [can help]? (14)
O Brahmin, having ascertained this— that by the merit of propitiating whom we may again attain purity— tell us the truth regarding this matter.
Thus questioned, Nārada reflected and spoke these beneficial words:
"Listen, O you of excellent austerity, to that which is the true cause of your happiness. (16)
Gayātīrtha is most excellent and is situated in Mahākālavana;
having gone there to the Akṣayavaṭa tree, you shall be cleansed of all sins.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, those devoted to fasting should perform this most purifying vow accompanied by a night vigil.
Having heard the words of Nārada, the wives of the sages were greatly delighted and went to Mahākālavana, where the sacred site named Gayā is located.
There, having beheld the banyan tree and bathed, they performed meritorious rites such as giving gifts during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādra.
Having fasted on the fifth lunar day and kept a vigil for a single night,
they became then free from the fault of contact with another man.
Their anger toward their husbands having subsided, they immediately went to their own homes;
the sages, with their visionary insight, offered them a welcome just as before.
From that time forward, that lunar day has been known in this world as Ṛṣipañcamī;
it was indeed established by Nārāyaṇa for women to obtain the merit of their vows.
And with Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Gaurī, Prabhā, Jayā, as well as Pārvatī, Padmā, Mañjulā, and Māṇikyā. ||24||
Having heard from the mouth of Nārada about that vow consisting of the "Five Sages" (Ṛṣipañcamikā), which had been performed by Sāvitrī, Saṃjñā, Śacī, and Menā.
Whatever sin a woman incurs from contact with another man during all twelve months—whether arising from desire or lack of desire, or from intentional or unintentional association—[is removed]. (26)

Whether it be very small or even great, whatever arises from the enjoyment of pleasures, or that which is produced by contact with a woman in her menses, or [impurity] such as birth-impurity (sūtaka) and the like; ||27||
Impurity is that which is produced by contact in household utensils and the like, in water vessels and food containers, and in all objects on dry land. (28)
Whatever fault may arise from menstruation, or that which is produced by physical contact, as well as any [fault] occurring among children, the elderly, or those who are dependent on others; ||29||
All defects born of physical contact, as well as those born of sexual desire, perish for women through the Ṛṣipañcamī vow. (1.481.30)
By observing the vow of Rṣipañcamī, women become pure in every respect; they indeed remain sanctified throughout their menstrual period. (3.1)
A man, having become pure, should subsist on wild rice;
for those two, no misfortune or suffering shall ever arise at any time.
There shall be no misfortune for women, nor separation from their husbands;
nor shall there be any separation from sons or from wealth. (33)
In Avanti, there exists such a sacred ford that destroys sins;
by performing acts such as giving gifts here, one obtains imperishable merit. ||34||
Whoever, relying upon the prescribed observances, listens to this discourse on a sacred festival day or constantly, he too shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice. ||35||
By observing the fifth lunar day, a wife shall obtain the fruit of devotion to her husband;
thereafter, she shall attain the imperishable abode of Hari together with her husband.
Whether she be a virtuous wife or one whose husband is deceased, she may perform this supreme vow with the desire for purity, in order to please Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The glorious and compassionate Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, having purified the virtuous people, will protect them for their service at his own feet. (38)
To those two by whom a vow has been sincerely offered to Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa will certainly become their husband, lord, and protector. 39.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the context of Kārttikeya, the *Ṛṣipañcamī* vow has been described for the purpose of warding off the defect arising from contact with fire; this concludes the four hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Chastity. || 481 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the deeds of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa,
as well as his prayer for desired objects on the bank of the Narmadā, which bestows excellent liberation.
In former times, there was a most excellent sage named Parāśara;
he performed severe penance for ten years in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the retention of air (kumbhaka), he entered the waters of the Ganges;
then, when twelve years were complete, he emerged.
He went to the village for the sake of alms, and there he saw a boat standing right there; in it was a beautiful young woman, uninjured and in the full bloom of youth.
Seeing her, he was overcome by the god of love and spoke these sweet words:
"O fair-browed one, do not take delight today; you are the agitator of my heart."
Having been addressed thus, she bowed to the sage and said: "Where indeed am I, a fisherwoman, and where are you, a great and virtuous sage? A union between us is not fitting."
The sage, having meditated, said to the girl: "You are not the daughter of a fisherman;
you are a princess. Listen, I shall tell you of your birth.
There was once a powerful king named Vasu in the Lunar dynasty."
O maiden, he is the lord of Jambūdvīpa and indeed the husband of many wives.
That devotee of Viṣṇu, being devoted to his guru, ruled the kingdom according to dharma;
the Mlecchas dwelling in Śākadvīpa were in opposition to him.
For their victory, he indeed set out accompanied by his servants and sons;
a great battle then took place with Vasu, the upholder of the earth.
The Mlecchas have been conquered and made to pay tribute along with their local chieftains;
meanwhile, his chief queen remains in her own palace during her menstrual period.
Once born, she indeed dispatched a messenger to the presence of the king;
that messenger was in the form of a parrot, and he spoke just as a human would when instructed.
Having seized the written letter with her beak, she flew through the sky:
"Without you, this chief queen lives even during her fertile season."
Thus was written upon a birch-bark leaf in auspicious characters that very letter which the bird Vasu had carried there, having been sent by Satyabhāmā.
King Śuka gave the letter and read it at that very moment;
having displayed his own prowess, he placed it inside a firm casket.
And he entrusted it to the parrot, saying, "Go and give that to the queen.
Having bowed to the king, the parrot took the seed-pod in its beak.
He flew up over the ocean and approached with great speed;
imagining the parrot to have meat, the hawk also rushed toward that spot.
Struck by the blow of a beak, that vessel of valor fell down;
swallowed by a fish in the water, he became two offspring there. (18)
As soon as the fish was caught and pulled up by the fishermen,
they saw within its womb a pair [of infants] possessing a radiance equal to the moon and the sun.
Delighted upon seeing the boy and the girl,
those fishermen gave the son to the king and continued to care for the daughter.
"You are such a maiden, O lady of excellent hips; you are certainly not the daughter of a fisherman.
Having been addressed thus, she indeed gave herself to Parāśara.
"If I am indeed a princess, let this fishy odor be removed!
Thereupon, by means of his ascetic power, Parāśara made her fragrant right then and there.
And when the sage touched her while on the boat during the day, she said, feeling ashamed, "The people are looking; please cover yourself. (23)
Then, by Parāśara as well, that Tāmasī was meditated upon;
she took the form of darkness and was filled with the waters of mist.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Vyāsa from Parāśara in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Part of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Account of the Birth of Matsyagandhā; and Vyāsa’s Pilgrimage, His Residence on the Banks of the Narmadā, and the Chastity of the Narmadā. || 482 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe Anasūyā, the devoted wife;
her husband was named Atri, indeed a son of Brahmā. || 1 ||
She was constantly devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, honoring the deities and guests; free from malice, she held her husband as her very life and was intent on his welfare and well-being.
The devoted wife served her husband just as she would serve Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
yet, as time passed in this manner, no offspring was born to the couple.
Seated comfortably, they spoke of the joys and sorrows resulting from their past actions;
then Atri said, "O dear beloved, in these three worlds with all things mobile and immobile," (4)
There is no woman in the world equal to you, who is ever devoted to my welfare;
a wife who loves her husband and children conquers even the worlds that are difficult to cross.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a son one attains the supreme goal.
No kinsman equal to a son is seen upon this earth.
A virtuous son protects one who is falling into the southern Asipatravana hell,
even during famines, times of misery, and in old age.
"But without a son, O blessed lady, what is the use? Or is even an ascetic a true son, my dear? (8)
Driven by a sense of local shame, he indeed delivers his parents;
for how can there be happiness in this world or the next for one who is childless? (9)
Thinking of this day and night, I wither away and find no peace;
Anasūyā, having heard that, said: "I too grieve for that."
O Lord, that which causes you distress also causes me distress;
therefore, [grant that] by which I may have sons and by which Prajāpati may be pleased.
Atri said: "O blessed lady, O beloved, I have performed most rigorous penance through vows, fasts, restraints, and subsisting on vegetables and the like."
My body is worn out and I am incapable; having been an ascetic since birth, old age is now visible in my body, and the departure for the next world is at hand.
"The truth has been reported to you; it is not seen as being far off here.
Anasūyā said to her husband, "I am a devoted wife to you. (14)

I am the means for accomplishing the three goals of life and the one who increases my husband’s lineage through sons; yet, by your command, having performed austerities, I shall become a mother of a son. (15)

The teachers who protect the world declare that for a devoted wife, her very devotion to her husband constitutes recitation of mantras, austerity, pilgrimage, sacrifice for a son, and the accomplishment of mantras. (16)
And having been granted permission, I shall perform severe austerities in this world of suffering;
desiring a son, I have been practicing them for many days and am now approaching Viṣṇu.
Atri spoke these appropriate words, which brought me great satisfaction:
"O blessed lady, permitted by me, perform austerities for the sake of a son."
Having discharged the three debts, one should apply the mind to liberation;
discharge your debt to the gods, to human beings, and to the ancestors.
No other vessel is considered a better savior than a wife;
indeed, the gods do not praise a home devoid of a virtuous wife.
Indeed, another happiness, when deprived of a wife, becomes parched;
she comes face to face when things are favorable, but turns her back when they are adverse. (21)
Therefore, O devoted wife, O highly fortunate one, O you who always act for our welfare, you are the object of praise for householders. (22)
"Perform fruitful penance that shall grant me a son at my command;
O beloved, may the husband's command and the word of Viṣṇu bear fruit in you."
"May the Lord quickly bring that desire of yours to fruition as well.
Having thus received the favor of her husband, the devoted wife [spoke]. (24)
Having become empowered in her own task, she prostrated with eight limbs and said:
"O best of Brahmins, by your grace, may all this be attained. (25)
Endowed with blessings, the devoted Anasūyā,
moving with the graceful gait of a swan, reached the bank of the Narmadā.
On the northern bank of the Narmadā, she lived subsisting on leaves;
remaining constantly established in her observances, she occasionally took only vegetables as her food.
Devoted to hymns, she remained self-restrained, praising the gods in her heart with auspicious chants;
during the summer months, she stood in the midst of the five fires under the scorching heat of the sun.
During the rainy season, that virtuous woman remained outside and performed the Sāvarṇya and Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
in the winter, she dwelt in the water and observed the three daily ablutions.

The satiation of the gods, their worship, as well as the fire-oblation, the offering of food with festive rites, the handful of flowers, the hymn of praise, and the prayer for forgiveness. ||1.483.30||
She lived thus in the forest, constantly accompanied by female deer and other creatures;
and when a hundred years had passed in this manner, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pitāmaha [appeared].
Knowing her to be an ascetic woman emaciated by hunger and desiring a son,
those gods arrived at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī in the guise of brahmins.
Having arrived at the place of austerity, they recite the Vedic mantras;

Looking back toward that direction again and again, she rose from the ground;

Having washed their feet, he drank [the water] and placed it upon his head, saying:

Today my undertaking has become fruitful through the sight of this brahmin;

Having spoken thus, he bowed at his feet and performed circumambulations many times;

Today I shall satisfy you with divine roots, tubers, and fruits;

Having heard this, those brahmins said to that virtuous female ascetic: "O lady of excellent vows, by your intense austerity and by your truthfulness... (39)
"We are satisfied by the sight of you through the dharma of devotion to your husband;

"O virtuous lady, what do you desire through this difficult penance—is it heaven, the prosperity of the world, liberation, or something else? (41)
Through austerity one attains heaven; through austerity, indeed, the supreme goal is reached.
Through austerity, the abundant fulfillment of all desires comes to pass. 42.
In youth, one should always enjoy those pleasures desired by the mind;

But Anasūyā, having heard that, spoke to the foremost of the gods:

"The birth of sons occurs in youth, while everything is unpleasant in old age.
Having been addressed thus, those best of gods exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! ||45||
Having manifested in the forms of Brahmins, the triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara appeared before him in person and said, "Choose a boon."
"Whatever you have desired, we shall grant it all; speak now.
[Become] Vāsudeva with four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace."
Accompanied by Garuḍa and accompanied by Śrī,
Brahmā, adorned with four faces, appeared with a serene countenance.

Having seen these gods— who have five faces, three eyes, and are endowed with ten arms— the female ascetic [worshipped them].
She became joyful instantly; having seen and bowed to them, she said to them:

"Therefore, O compassionate one, I wish to hear this; please speak.
Brahmā said: "The rainy season has arrived, and I am water. (52)
"I am the cloud that pours down rain, and I am the eastern twilight," Viṣṇu said. "And I am the winter season that nourishes all things in every way. (53)
"The entire world must be protected; this is my supreme duty.

"O blessed lady, I shall give you those sons, whose prowess is equal to that of the gods, who are endowed with virtues like their father's, and who are performers of Soma sacrifices and deeply learned. (59)

"It must not be done otherwise; you shall dwell within my belly this very day.
Viṣṇu said to that goddess: "Indeed, we [do not desire] dwelling in a womb."
"However, Vāyu shall remain within your womb like an embryo; indeed, Vāyu will make your belly appear pregnant. (62)
After a period of nine months and more, we shall come to your auspicious home, accompanied by sovereign power, at the time of your delivery.
At the time of Vāyu’s departure, we three shall become sons in the form of children, born not from a womb.
"The gods, who have auspicious abodes, never go to a place of birth (yonivāsa).
Having said this, they were seen for a moment in the form of children. 65.
Then, mounted upon their divine vehicles, they departed for their own abodes;

When asked about her welfare, she spoke out of compassion: "Endowed with fruit and free from obstacles, I have indeed come here for service, having received a boon. (68)
And when cultivated with skillful means, the trees of one's desires bear fruit;

The fruit of service to the feet of the Blessed One has indeed been attained after a long time; a husband, difficult for other women to obtain and exceedingly rare, has been secured. ||1.483.70||
"Therefore, I shall grant you sons who are ṛṣis rich in asceticism.
Having been addressed thus, she was filled with joy and became entirely devoted to the service of her husband. (71)
She gazed at her beloved husband, and she was gazed upon by her beloved;

It is rootless and has long roots; it possesses three parts and is auspicious like a sphere.
It consists of light and is enveloped by a network of thousands of rays.
In its center, three deities indeed shone forth in an instant;
commanded by the gods, Vāyu dwelt perpetually within the womb.
Anasūyā became radiant with splendor as she conceived;
then, when nine months had passed, it was as if the tenth had arrived.
At the auspicious moment, the virtuous woman entered the lying-in chamber;
the wind issued forth from the womb, and the gods became the infants. (76)
The first son, golden-hued, became Brahmā, the Grandfather;
the Moon, possessing sixteen digits, was Soma, the bestower of nourishment. ||77||
And this first son was the delight of Anasūyā;
the second, however, was the highly fortunate Maheśvara himself in person.
That portion which effects creation and destruction became known by the name Durvāsas;
the third son was Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (79)
Dattātreya is the great yogi, the Blessed Lord, the Master,
the all-pervading one, the Lord of the universe, the God himself, Janārdana.
Thus, having obtained these three excellent sons, that chaste and devoted wife became one who had fulfilled her purpose,
and the sage Atri likewise did so.
O beloved, as soon as they were born, those three became youths; Satī, Lakṣmī, and Sāvitrī arrived there from the divine realm. ||82||
Having bowed to Anasūyā for the sake of serving their husbands,

Those three, possessing divine forms, granted a vision to their parents;
indeed, the house of Atri was always made by them to consist of every kind of prosperity.
Gods, sages, perfected beings, and seers whose wealth is austerity, as well as goddesses, attendants, and hosts, come constantly to behold [him]. (85)
Atri’s hermitage is filled with tens of millions of deities;
sacrifices are performed there constantly, as are festivals day after day. (86)
Then these three gods spoke respectfully to the two parents:
"We wish to perform austerities; therefore, we shall go to another forest. (87)
Hearing this, the mother, longing for her son, became submerged in grief and said:
"Since I have performed penance for the sake of my sons' happiness... (88)
Indeed, for the sake of nourishment, protection, and happiness—for these three purposes alone—I have made the gods my sons, as well as for the sake of their vision and service. (89)
"How can you, O infallible ones, depart for asceticism and leave us behind?
He will not endure our separation; therefore, we must certainly go with you."
Having heard this, the three gods then assumed two forms for their mother;
with their divine forms, they went to another place to perform penance.
Durvāsas went to his own Kailāsa in the presence of Śiva;
Candramas went to Satyaloka, and Datta departed for another island.
Then, having assumed the forms of children, those three remained in their own home,
playing in their mother's lap like ordinary mortals.
Playing on their father’s lap, they sported in the hermitage together with the fawns of the deer and even with the young of the wild animals and birds. (94)
They associate with ascetics like common children, engaging in childish play, the worship of deities, and the propitiation of ancestors. (95)
Those sons of the sage, who bestow happiness upon their mother and father, pass their days;
thus indeed were the three gods obtained through austerity. ||96||
Having taken up the sacred thread and engaged in the study of the Vedas,
those three sons of Atri constantly performed sacrificial rites here.
And by those eminent Vaiṣṇavas, the mantra consisting of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was indeed received from Atri himself, as was the garland of *tulasī*.
Those three long-lived ones, who provide a refuge for all the worlds, exist as divine stars—the Vaiṣṇavas who are the saviors of their lineage. 99.
O Lakṣmī, this supreme and most auspicious divine narrative has been told to you;
it is considered to bestow both heaven and liberation through its reading and hearing.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of how Atri’s wife Anasūyā obtained the sons Somadatta and Durvāsas from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa through her penance, as well as the power of her wifely devotion," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the supreme penance performed by Rohiṇī in the past,
by which that virtuous woman forever attained preeminence among the wives of the Moon.
Desired by all women and especially by her husband,
that devoted wife once resolved to practice asceticism.
Having gone to the bank of the Narmadā, he performed extensive penance for one night,
two nights, six nights, and likewise twelve nights with others.
With her body emaciated by fortnightly and monthly fasts,
she was constantly devoted to the worship of Hari, whose guru is Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly bathing again and again in the waters of the Narmadā,
she who was devoted to Hari worshipped the Lord Govinda, the husband of Nārāyaṇī.
The blessed Lord Nārāyaṇasvāmin, Nārāyaṇa himself, being pleased, said: "I am pleased with you because of your vow and your observances."
"I grant you today the boon you desire; choose it, O great virtuous lady.
Having heard these words of his, she bowed and worshipped him with devotion.
Having drunk the water from her feet and become purified by the sight of her, Rohiṇī chose this boon: "May I be your servant at your lotus-feet."
First, grant me that boon: may my devotion toward you be preeminent.
And as for the second boon, may I always reside in the world within the abode of the Moon.
"Among all my co-wives, the beloved of the Moon is superior;
O Bhavānī, by your grace, act so that this may indeed come to pass without delay. (1.484.10)
Hari said: "By our grace, maintain two forms:
go to Vaikuṇṭha with one, and dwell here with the second."
By means of your second form, become the beloved of the Moon;
be his devoted wife, the foremost among all his consorts.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa took that virtuous woman with him and departed for his own Vaikuṇṭha by means of a celestial chariot through the sky.
She, assuming a second form, went to the abode of the Moon;
from that time forth, she became the most eminent of all women.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the supreme fruit of penance—delightful, bestowing both heaven and liberation, and consisting of my own propitiation. (15)
Now I shall tell you another deed of mine that bestows liberation:
there was a daughter of Dakṣa, renowned by the name Kumudā.
Having given them to Soma, Dakṣa attained supreme joy;
upon her he begot a son named Amṛta.
Then, having learned [of the situation], the gods, desiring the fruit of the sacrifice, went to him;
and the Daityas, having learned that they had drunk the nectar, departed from there.
And they said to the Moon, "Give us the supreme nectar for the purpose of drinking;
otherwise, we shall surely devour you."
Since Candra was unable to give them the nectar,
they seized him and cast him down from the sky.
A great cry of lamentation arose; his beloved wife Kumudā, through her virtue of devotion to her husband, then took water in her hand. ||21||
She said: "I am devoted to my husband, faithful to my husband, and established in my husband;
by the power of my devotion to my husband, let these Dānavas go to their destruction. (22)
Having spoken thus, he then cast water upon the Dānavas;
they were instantly reduced to ashes, while the survivors fled toward Śukra, their preceptor.
They went and reported the reduction of the Daityas to ashes;
Śukra, arriving there, restored the Asuras to life.
Śukra bowed down, the Daityas prostrated and went home,
and Candra was raised from the earth by the power of Kumudā herself.
Then, having been brought by Brahmā, Maheśa, and the others, he was restored to peace; once re-established in heaven, the gods became free from their feverish distress.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the great power of devotion to one's husband, which bestows all prosperity, removes obstacles, and increases good fortune. (27)
Now I shall speak of another marvel; listen, O beloved!
On the Narmadā, at the confluence of the four, there stands Yajñaparvata.
O Lotus-born one, in ancient times the self-existent Brahmā performed the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice there; likewise, Maghavan performed the horse-sacrifice at that very spot.
Emerging from that mountain, the great river Catūrnāmā fell into the Narmadā at their confluence on Yajñaparvata.
There was a sage named Suparṇa Jābāli, born from the seed of Brahman;
Puruhūtā was his wife, his lawful spouse, devoted to her husband. (3.1)
Having become negligent, she spoke these words to her own husband, Puruhūta:
"O great sage, enjoy me during my fertile period on the auspicious lunar day. (32)
May a son be born to me who shall purify my entire lineage;
for through a son one conquers the worlds, and the ancestors and deities are satisfied. ||33||
"There is no destination for one who has no son; therefore, you have procreated a son.
Having heard this, Suparṇa said to her: "Today is the new moon day. (34)
O wife, Kāmadeva must always be avoided on a festival day;
he should not be worshipped during a meritorious vow or even on the lunar day dedicated to the ancestors.
O beautiful lady, when a husband and wife engage in sexual intercourse even during the fertile period,
the ancestors of that man who approaches his wife at such a time consume his very flesh.
For a thousand divine years, I have performed difficult austerities;
yet all of that might be utterly destroyed by meeting you on this sacred festival day.
Behold, O beloved, how after bathing here at this confluence for merely a moment, a Cāṇḍāla is now departing by way of a celestial chariot to heaven, having surpassed me! (38)
"I perform penance constantly; how could it be that because of this I am censured?"—thus, O beloved, I am consumed with anxiety. (39)
"Tell me the reason for this, O virtuous one; why indeed was he censured by him? Later, O chaste lady, I shall bestow righteousness upon you, if you so desire."
O beloved, if the ritual gift at the time of a festival were indeed dharma,
then at that moment a certain Niṣāda woman arrived on the bank of the Narmadā.
Having heard that reproach, she said to the seer for his sake:
"There is no ascetic equal to you, whose soul is deluded by egoism. (42)
Neither bathing, nor recitation, nor fire-offerings, nor self-study of scripture, nor worship of Acyuta, nor even the practice of your prescribed mantra has been performed by you. (43)
You have undergone fruitless hardship, subsisting on air without any support;
your asceticism, meditation, and yoga are indeed fruitless and do not grant heaven.
Then he spoke repeatedly to that Niṣāda woman with humble words:
"Who are you, who have come to this sacred ford while assuming the form of a Niṣāda woman? (45)
Umā, Sarasvatī, and Gaṅgā have come to me desiring to know;
I consider this a favor—speak the eternal Dharma.
The Niṣāda woman then spoke to him with joy regarding eternal dharma:
"O Brahmin lady, I am a Brahmin; my husband was a Brahmin in the Naimiṣa forest. (47)
Constantly established in austerity, he did not touch me during my monthly period;
for though I, afflicted by desire, had bathed after my menses, I entreated him.
On the day of the new moon, I begged my husband for the sake of obtaining a son.
"Because I begged at an improper time, I was cursed by that high-souled one. (49)
"Since you ask for what is unrighteous, become a Śūdra born of a Niṣāda!
Cursed by me, become a Caṇḍāla wherever I am. (1.484.50)
Thus, overcome by the curse, the couple, having heard the narrative concerning the origin of the Narmadā together with Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, [attained peace]. (51)
The supreme, divine majesty [of this place] is such that liberation is attained merely by bathing;
my husband, though he was a Cāṇḍāla, has reached heaven. ||52||
"I am a Niṣādī woman, O Brahmin; having bathed, I shall go toward liberation.
Therefore, you too should always worship Govinda with austerity. (53)
Everything of yours shall be meaningful; otherwise, it will be fruitless for you.
Perform indeed actions such as fire-offerings and recitations for the sake of Hari.
"You, however, shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, which is presided over by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, she bathed on the banks of the Narmadā and indeed departed for heaven.
She followed by the same path by which her husband had gone;
having heard this, the virtuous woman [sought] Suparṇa, her own husband, from Jābāli.
Having prostrated herself before Puruhūta, she then begged for forgiveness,
recognizing that this was a violation of eternal dharma, occurring both on a sacred festival day and during her fertile season.
Sexual union for a married couple is indeed not appropriate in any way whatsoever;
having thus understood this supreme dharma, those two Vaiṣṇava spouses— ||58||
Having performed daily worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, their Lord, and having performed the recitation of mantras, the husband and wife remained faithful to each other. 59.
Devoted to the practice of recitation and righteousness, they went to Vaikuṇṭha in the course of time.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this knowledge of dharma concerning the sage and his wife.

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Rohiṇī Kumudā’s Austerities, the Liberation of Puruhūtā through Bathing in the Narmadā, and the Dharma of Bestowing and Receiving Gifts During Festivals," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Lakṣmī, listen to another ancient narrative;
the great sage Dīrghatamas attained liberation along with his entire family.
There was a king of Kāśī named Citrasena;
in his city, called Kāśī, the sage Dīrghatamas always resided.
To the north of Kāśī, there is a place named Mandārārāma, abounding in trees and creepers; there dwells the sage Dīrghatamas.
