He performs intense austerities while remaining together with his wife and son;
likewise, all five of his sons as well as the others attend upon him with service.
His son was Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, who, though the youngest, was an ascetic,
a yogi, a celibate student, and devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, he dwells in the form of a deer;
living constantly among the deer, he performs the rites of homage for his parents.
In the morning and evening he would come among the deer and then depart again;
then King Citrasena, the lord of Kāśī, [arrived] together with his people.
Having mounted his horse for the sake of hunting, the king beheld there a most magnificent grove of Mandāra trees, where he saw a great herd of deer.
The deer fled in fear toward the ten directions, and the king also,
remaining alone, pursued the deer into the dense forest.
Midday had already arrived, and the king was disoriented;
afflicted by hunger and thirst, he took refuge in the shade on the bank of the lake.
Having remained for a moment in the water, he performed his ablutions; then, taking lotuses and offering libations, he drank as much water as he desired.
The great ascetic Rishyashringa, a yogi, was staying in the midst of the deer;
meanwhile, the king, desiring to eat the deer, took refuge at the foot of a tree.
Taking up his bow with the tip of his hand, he discharged that arrow at the deer;
pierced by the arrow, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga cried out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! || 13 ||
Whose evil thought has arisen that I, though standing in the midst of deer, have been struck down here by someone, even though I am without any fault? (14)
Having heard those human words, the king went near him;
seeing that Brahmin slain, he cried out "Alas! Alas! and wept.
The Brahmin said: "O King, there is no success for you;
rather, upon my destruction, the slaughter ordained for you has been reflected back by you. (16)
"My mother and father are aged, and my two brothers are ascetics;
O King, upon hearing of my destruction, they will surely die. (17)
"These will become murders; how can there be purification for you?
I shall tell you a means; do it, if you so deem fit. (18)
Taking me with you, go to the holy hermitage where my parents dwell,
and announce yourself as one who has come having slain their son.
Seeing me, they will surely show compassion toward you,
or they will devise a means by which peace shall be established.
But Citrasena, having heard that,
and seeing the Brahmin being carried on his shoulder, unconscious and lifeless on the road, O King—
In that forest, at the foot of a banyan tree, he had the Brahmin cremated;
then, overcome with intense grief, he both wept and rejoiced.
Seeing the king who had come to the vicinity of the hermitage having taken the bones of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the sage Dīrghatapas then [spoke to him].
With affection, he offered the king a seat, honey-mixture, and other honors;
the king said, "O Brahmin, I am not worthy of such worship, for I am a sinner. (24)
"O Brahmin, standing in the midst of the deer, your son was killed by me.
Punish me, O Brahmin, as a slayer of a son; chastise me with a severe penalty. (25)
"O Lord, that brahmin was killed by me through the delusion that he was a deer; that was a wicked deed.
Upon hearing this from Mātāyā, the kinsmen and others wept.
Having reflected thus, Dīrghatapas went to that place weeping;
he said to the king, "O King, the intellect follows the course of one's past actions. (27)
For such an understanding arises among men;
yet, O King, although you have committed this slaughter, it shall truly not be yours.
We—the father, likewise the mother, and the brothers—have abandoned our bodies through grief and yoga for the sake of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga. 29.
"O King, we shall become so in an instant; taking our bones made of Narmada wood, go to the holy site of Śūlabheda and cast those bones into its waters."
"You shall be liberated from all sins by my word; there is no doubt.
I shall carry out your command," said that best of kings to him. (31)
O twice-born ones, through grief for Ṛṣyaśṛṅga and by means of yogic concentration, his family perished; having been consumed by fire, they were then cremated by the Brāhmaṇas and the people.
Having collected the king’s bones and purified himself, that monarch went to the Narmadā river after inquiring about that sacred ford (tīrtha), and he arrived there in a short time.
Having come to the very purifying Śūlabheda on the southern bank of the Narmadā and having gathered the bones upon the ground, he then bathed and became pure.
Having gratified his chosen deity with water mixed with sesame seeds,
he should cast his bones into the water while looking toward the sky.
Then he beheld all of them, auspicious and bearing divine forms,
clothed in celestial garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
Beholding them ascending in divine golden celestial chariots frequented by Kṛṣṇa and the Ṛṣis, the king was filled with joy.
The Ṛṣi, having ascended the celestial chariot, then spoke to Citrasena:
"O King, by your grace, a divine state has indeed been attained by me today. (38)
"O King, by my word you shall become free from sin.
Having spoken thus, all those people of long austerity departed for liberation. (39)
Remembering Śambhu, the king prepared there to give up his life;
but Śaṅkara, arriving there, forcibly restrained the monarch.
"O King, you are still young; death is not fitting for you.
Go to your own place and enjoy your kingdom for the time being; thereafter, [death will come]. (41)
Having ruled the kingdom of Kāśī for a long time and having meditated upon me, Śrī Śaṅkara, you shall become my attendant named Nandin at the end of this body. 42.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu departed; the king went to the city of Kāśī, and at the end of his body, having meditated upon Śaṅkara, he became a Gaṇa named Nandin. (43)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this auspicious and purifying life-story, by hearing which, O beloved, the sins of men go to their destruction. (44)

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, who had taken the form of a deer, attained liberation after his death by the arrow of King Citrasena of Kāśī through the casting of his bones into the waters of the Narmadā by his father Dīrghatapas and others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the region of Ānarta, within Saurāṣṭra, near the city of Camatkārapura,
there exists to the east an auspicious river named Nāgamatī.
O Lakṣmī, at that place where men are liberated and become freed by bathing,
there was a certain doe afflicted by the arrow of a hunter.
He descended into the water and gave up his life-breaths within the waters on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, at midday, under the constellation presided over by Aryaman.
On that Sunday, by virtue of that merit, she became an Apsaras named Menakā, belonging to the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods; she was beautiful in form and devoted to her husband.
Once, the king of sages, Viśvāmitra, arrived there;
for the sake of visiting holy sites, he bathed in the Nāganadī river to the east of the city.
Where that Menakā used to come daily, desiring to bathe;
and having beheld the sage, who was handsome, divine, and robust, as he was bathing— (6)
Afflicted by desire, she sought to make her husband young again; full of joy for the sake of sexual union, she approached him.
He bowed at her feet and praised her with most enchanting words;
yet, remaining steadfast, that sage indeed regarded her as a mere city-dwelling woman.
Having offered his blessings with a joyful inner soul,
he spoke to that goddess, inquiring especially about the duties of women.
May you obtain auspiciousness through thought, deed, and speech;
may your eternal devotion toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa ever increase.
I hope you fare well, O young woman, devoted solely to your husband, endowed with virtuous conduct and humility, and always speaking sweetly? (11)
I hope you are always beloved by your husband; and that you honor his kinsmen and circle of friends, whether in his presence or behind his back, with gifts. (12)
I hope that when your husband has fallen fast asleep, you too fall under the power of sleep;
and that you rise at the hour of Brahma before he has awakened. (13)
I trust that, having risen early in the morning, you attend upon your husband;
and thereafter, having swept the house, you perform your adornment and other such duties. || 14 ||
Having bathed and caused your husband to bathe, having honored him with devotion, and having cared for your young children, do you abide as one whose yoga is characterized by devotion? 15.
I trust that you sustain your life by first paying homage to the gods, your teacher, the cow, and likewise your husband, and by giving food and water according to your ability. (16)
Do you serve food to guests at the time of midday? Do you indeed give food to those who have come to your house seeking refuge? (17)
I trust, O beautiful lady, that you do not eat food after the sun has set, without having first given it to your own servants and especially to the virtuous. (18)
Do you drink water that has been strained with a cloth and consecrated with *surā*?
And having become compassionate, do you protect even the lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and other such creatures that cause affliction to the body, as if they were your own children? (19)
Do you constantly practice the dharma of Kṛṣṇa with true devotion toward virtuous people?
O auspicious lady, you listen with devotion and you practice devotion with respect;
having heard [of this], do you perform vows and other meritorious acts on that holy day? (21)
You honor the guru, the ācārya, or the Lord who has arrived, as well as the speaker of the scripture and especially its commentator. (22)
Do you bestow beautiful scriptures upon the virtuous?
And having heard a discourse, do you provide a fee for the reciter? (23)

Do you perform dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the chanting of sacred hymns in the temple of Kṛṣṇa, as well as the offerings of oblations, worship, and gifts, according to your ability? (24)
Do you give garments and coverings to the virtuous? O beautiful lady, do you not wander in vain from house to house? (25)
I hope that you do not eat before your husband has eaten; and I hope that you never disobey the command of your husband. (26)
O lady of virtuous vows, I hope you do not yield to anger when your beloved is provoked;
and I hope that when you are angry with your husband, you do not offer him harsh retorts. (27)
Now, do you speak pleasant and heart-pleasing words for the sake of appeasing his transgression?
And when your beloved is away on a journey, do you wear soiled garments? (28)
Are you perhaps distressed, with a pale face and emaciated? Do you perhaps dispel the gloom of the household through your service? (29)
I hope you do not keep a broken vessel or one that has been used for leftovers in your home;
and I hope you do not go out at the beginning of the night or to other places during festivals.
I hope you never cultivate friendship with unchaste women;
and being the delighter of your husband, I hope you maintain the signs of good fortune.
I hope that no obstacle whatsoever arises to your devotion to your husband;
O beautiful lady, I trust you remain virtuous, blessed with both husband and son. (32)
Thus addressed, she spoke to the sage who had instructed her in the duties of devotion to her husband:
"O Brahmin, those other women are different for whom the duties you have proclaimed are intended. (33)
We are indeed the celestial nymphs of heaven who move according to our own will; we are without husbands, independent, and enchanters of the minds of sages. (34)
Always unblemished and pure, devoted to loving service, these maidens assume ever-new forms and are intent on the joy of service. ||346||
With a mind free from desire, let us perform service for the ascetics who strive in penance, or for the virtuous householders who recognize our hospitality. (36)
Having delighted him in many ways, we then obtained his blessing;
by that merit, heaven indeed exists eternally for us. (37)
We consider that there is no merit equal to the enjoyment of desire, nor is there any other curse-bestowing sin on earth equal to the frustration of desire. (38)
O Sage, the destruction of happiness is a great sin that consumes all one's possessions;
the gift of happiness is a great gift, given through food, service, and clothing. (39)
Through constant massaging of the limbs, such as the rubbing of the feet, and through dancing, chanting, and praising, merit is attained. (1.486.40)
For those by whom others are delighted, the worlds beyond bestow happiness;
for those by whom others are made miserable, the worlds beyond indeed bestow suffering. ||41||
For the sake of happiness in the next world, we shall serve people;
indeed, we shall perform acts of benefit for others by means of all kinds of gifts given according to their wishes. (42)
We give wealth, clothing, ornaments, food, and even our very bodies;
we give all this for the sake of supreme bliss, which is the fruit we seek to attain. (43)
Food is given by people with the tongue for the sake of one's own satisfaction;
likewise, touch is given with the skin for the sake of one's own satisfaction. (44)
The hearing of songs provides satisfaction to the ears, while the sight of beauty, adornment, and the like bestows pleasure upon the eyes. (45)
In this same way, with our other senses as well, we offer this supreme gift for the sake of self-satisfaction, for the sake of merit, and to please Lord Hari. (46)
When there is satisfaction of the self, there is satisfaction of Hari; by that, the self-offering is maintained.
We always protect this great fruit offered to Kṛṣṇa.
The Creator fashioned three kinds of women who serve the cycle of worldly existence:
those who are married, those who are ordinary, and likewise those devoted to celibacy.

The duties of married women, which consist primarily of service to their husbands—those which you have described under the guise of excellent questions, O carriers of the pair—[are now understood]. (49)
Those who are common [to all] are the Apsarases; we belong to them.
Therefore, our duties are distinct from theirs, as we are devoted to the service of all.
But those who are devoted to the practice of celibacy become virtuous women;
having abandoned the nature of desire, they are dedicated to excellent conduct.
Those established in their own dharma go to heaven; following the dharma of others brings fear.
We are servants devoted to service, always considered as handmaidens.
For we are divine goddesses, whether as maidservants or as concubines, since through service to sages such as you, we have realized our purpose in life. (53)
"Speak, O best of Kṣatriyas, you who are a heart-pleasing ascetic;
for the sake of satisfying my mind, O sage, if you possess dharma. (54)
Accept me, who have come to you devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
considering you to be Nārāyaṇa himself, I shall serve you without fault. (55)
Then Viśvāmitra spoke these beneficial and righteous words to the ascetic woman:
"O fair-browed one, I am one who observes vows and is devoted to the life of celibacy. (56)
Celibacy is declared to be the root of all those who observe vows;
let alone your association, even your touch or conversation [is forbidden]. (57)
"Go far away, O Goddess of Heaven; I have no need for you.
For those observing vows, attachment to women brings sin and destroys merit. (58)
A woman who has entered the marriage pavilion certainly reveals her husband under the pretext of circumambulating the fire during the wandering of saṃsāra. (59)
Therefore, one should avoid association, touch, and union with women;
for a woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter.
Through lack of touch it attains firmness; through contact with that [touch] it dissolves.
Women are the root of misfortunes and the obstruction for those destined for heaven. 6.1.
Even women of noble birth, possessed of heroic husbands, and having protectors,
if they remain contented with only one husband, they go to heaven.
Having encountered the company of women, a man wanders in saṃsāra;
having encountered the company of men, a woman wanders in saṃsāra. (63)
For I have abandoned cyclic existence, yet you have appeared as its seed;
thus, the suffering of the realms of Yama shall belong to me, and it shall also belong to you.
"Therefore, I must certainly not accept you; go elsewhere and be my beloved.
Thus addressed, Menakā said, "Listen to the words of Viśvāmitra. (65)
Knowing that Nara and Nārāyaṇa were indeed performing supreme and fierce penance on Himācala, Mahendra, accompanied by hosts of Apsarases, [approached].
Accompanied by the arrows of Kāma and Vasanta, he proceeded swiftly;
for the purpose of destroying his asceticism, he began a dance and song.
Nārāyaṇa said to Nara: "Bring mango blossoms;
rub my thigh and produce a most excellent Apsaras."
Having gathered flowers, Nara caused Urvaśī to appear;
she was so exceedingly beautiful that, in her presence, all others seemed as if their skin were shrouded in darkness.

Seeing them from that lake of Mahendra, Indraka spoke these words with wonder in the hearing of the gods: 70. "Beholding them from that lake of Mahendra, Indraka spoke this with amazement while the dwellers of heaven were listening."
"Hundreds of Apsarases have been eclipsed by my splendor;
how could I possibly succeed in bringing down her lord? (71)
Thus, having abandoned his pride, he fell at the feet of Hari;
he begged for Urvaśī from Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇa granted her to him.
Then that daughter of Nara entreated Mādhava:
"O Blessed One, I am indeed the maiden of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (73)
"O Lord, being not born from a womb, virtuous, devoted to the practice of celibacy, an ascetic, and the daughter of the Blessed One—how can I go to heaven? (74)
"Having become a mere common woman, how shall I conduct myself toward those gods?
What, however, are the duties of the Apsarases? Proclaim them to me according to the truth. (75)
Thus addressed, Śrī Hari informed her of his boons:
"One must always remain like a maidservant toward the gods residing in heaven. (76)
Dancing, singing, and service must be performed by the celestial woman;
indeed, all the gods in heaven are to be served equally in the form of her husband.
Whether they be men, sages, or ascetics, they shall be served by you in the form of husbands; go, or stay, as you please.
Having heard this, the virtuous Urvashi spoke to her father:
"Through association with other men, one goes to a hell characterized by torment. (79)
"Therefore, it would have to be enjoyed by me; thus, heaven is not desired by me.
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke regarding the celestial nymphs of heaven: [1.486.80]
For your sake, O daughter, there shall indeed be no torments of Yama;
the Creator himself fashioned these Apsarases from the merit of the gods. (81)
"Brahmā declared long ago that there is no sin whatsoever for them;
it is the same for you too, my daughter, by virtue of serving the innumerable gods. (82)
"Even for one who is joined with the dharmas of desire, there shall indeed be no sin";
thus did Brahmā and likewise Nārāyaṇa declare this to be sinless in the past. (83)
"For us women who are entirely servants of the gods, [this is our nature];
therefore, O Viśvāmitra, accept me and abandon your obstinacy. (84)
"As long as we courtesans possess even the bond of speech, we remain devoted wives; therefore, be forever my husband. (85)
Having spoken thus, she stood there firmly facing him;
then Viśvāmitra, abandoning that spot, departed elsewhere. 86.
Afflicted by the frustration of her desire, she cursed that best of sages:
"O evil-minded one, become wrinkled and grey-haired this very day! (87)

Thus addressed, the sage, who was already overcome by old age, became like that [in appearance] due to the curse; he said: "O sinful one, no sin shall accrue to you, but rather sin shall befall me. ||88||
Therefore, having abandoned him, I shall go elsewhere; for that reason, it pleases me.
So you too, O lady whose limbs are withered by old age, should depart quickly. (89)
By his word, she too immediately assumed such a form;
then, for the sake of pacifying his anger, that virtuous woman [remained] in Nāgavatī.
The beloved young woman bathed as before and duly assumed her former form;
thereafter, Viśvāmitra bathed in the river water.
He too became his former self, and their mutual curses were destroyed.
Such a great holy site exists on the Nāgā River,
where men and women, having bathed, become endowed with youth.
The women were like the goddesses of heaven, and the men were like the gods of heaven. ||93||
Then that Menakā, having bowed to the sage, departed for heaven of her own accord;
the rishi, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, performed supreme austerity. (94)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this secret propagation of Dharma, by the knowledge of which practitioners attain both heaven and liberation. 95.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim that which shatters the pride of Mahendra; hear about what occurred in Camatkārapura, which bestows intelligence. (96)
In former times, having joyfully performed a hundred sacrifices out of pride, Śatamakha became the presiding lord of all the gods, endowed with great prosperity.
Day by day, his sovereignty increased as the fruit of his austerities;
and Bṛhaspati indeed bestowed upon him at Puṣkara a mantra that grants success.
He muttered the mantra "Oṃ, salutations, salutations to Rādheśvara," and having chanted it for a hundred years, his heart's desire was fulfilled.
The deluded one did not recognize Prakṛti, who is of the nature of Brahman;
thereafter, Prakṛti, both inert and divine, cursed him.
Seeing his guru, he rose up but did not bow with joy;
the guru, out of anger, cursed him, saying, "May you lose the fortune of Hari."
Thus, with his mind corrupted, Indra, having beheld Ahalyā,
assumed the form of Gautama and, desiring her, took his pleasure with her.
Gautama beheld him and, rebuking him, cursed him:
"Indeed, let a thousand wombs be formed within your body here."
And for a full year, you shall constantly experience the odor of the female reproductive organ;
thereafter, having propitiated the Sun, you will become thousand-eyed.
"By my curse and by the curse of your preceptor, may you now be deprived of your fortune.
Thereupon, Indra departed for the holy site of Puṣkara to perform austerities.
Having then made arrangements for atonement, he returned home;
meanwhile, Indra, having abandoned his preceptor, by chance went to Brahmā for refuge.
At his command, he appointed Viśvarūpa as the domestic priest,
knowing him to be the grandson of a Daitya and thus a partisan of the Daityas.
While he was giving that most excellent sacrificial offering to the Daityas at the sacrifice,
[Viṣṇu] then indeed severed his head with a sharp arrow.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the father of Viśvarūpa, was instantly enraged upon hearing this;
saying, "O enemy of Indra, grow strong!", he prepared a supreme sacrifice.
From the sacrificial pit arose a great asura named Vṛtra;
Indra indeed struck Vṛtra, that thorn in the side of the gods, with his thunderbolt.
Brahmahatyā appeared, wearing red garments, seven nālikas in height,
with teeth as long as plow-poles, and holding a sword in her hand.
Running after him as he ran, she went toward that Mahendra;
Indra fled and entered the lake known as Mānasa.
She remained on the bank of the Vaṭa tree, indeed as thin as a lotus fiber;
meanwhile, Nahuṣa became Indra and, driven by desire, begged for Śacī.
Śacī indeed went for refuge to her preceptor, and the preceptor protected her;
thereafter, Bṛhaspati himself departed for the lake named Mānasa.
To protect his own disciple, he summoned the Lord of Śacī;
having recognized Bṛhaspati’s voice, Indra came out to meet the Guru.
Having bowed down, he then fell at the feet of his guru and praised him:
"Forgive this fault, O Blessed One; have mercy, O treasure-house of compassion! (1.16)
A true lord never takes account of the constant transgressions of his wife, his disciples, his servants, or his sons.
Having heard this, the Guru said: "Go and rule the kingdom of heaven;
with my grace, go and see Śacī, whose enemies have been slain."
"Next, take this armor that conquers saṃsāra;
then reduce the killing of a Brahmin to ashes and go with me."
Having done this, Mahendra then returned once more to heaven,
to his own capital city, which had been destroyed by the Daityas and was now restored anew.
He caused the city named Amarāvatī to be constructed;
however, upon seeing it built by Viśvakarman, the Lord of the Gods was not satisfied.
Viśvakarmā was unable to go to the house without permission;
Viśvakarmā then remembered Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Kamalā.
Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a brahmin, came to that city;
being extremely short in stature and a Vaiṣṇava, he offered his blessings to Śakra.
Having offered the honey-mixture and other honors, Śakra performed a formal reception and asked the young Brahmin, "Tell me, for what reason have you come? (124)
But the Brahmin boy said to him: "I have come to see your new city and to ask about the matter I desire."
Having heard of this wonderful and marvelous construction of your city, for how many years have you been intent upon its creation? (1.26)
Perhaps Viśvakarman will fashion it as a mere construction;
yet such a creation has never been fashioned by any Indra whatsoever.
"Even Viśvakarman, the supreme craftsman, is not capable of such a perfect creation.
Having heard the boy's words, that lord of the gods laughed.
And again, being completely intoxicated with wine, he asked the boy:
"How many hosts of Indras have been seen or heard of by you?"
"O child, tell me now how many kinds of Viśvakarman there are.
Having heard the words of Śakra, the young brahmin said to him:
I know Kaśyapa, O dear one, as your Prajāpati;
likewise, I know the sage Marīci, your father, as the Creator (Vedhas). || 131 ||
I know in every way the various kinds of kalpas and pralayas,
as well as Brahmā Janaka, Vairāja, and his father Hiraṇmaya.
I know how many kinds of cosmic eggs there are, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; and I know in every respect how many kinds of sleepers exist within those cosmic eggs.
O Lord of the Gods, even if there were a number for the dust particles on the earth, there would still be no number for the Indras; what more can I say to you? (134)
The lifespan and authority of Śakra last for seventy-one yugas;
when twenty-eight Śakras have fallen, it constitutes one day and night of Brahmā.
The lifespan of Vidhi is measured at exactly one hundred and eight years; but what is the number for the lords of the gods? Even for Vidhi, there is no fixed number.
Within a single pore of Mahāviṣṇu, there are countless Vairājas;
within a single pore of a Vairāja, there are countless beings beginning with Brahmā.
Thus, by the measure of a single hair, there exist innumerable universes;
and within each universe, how many gods indeed exist who are equal to you? (1.38)
While the brahmin boy was speaking thus,
a long line of ants, extending for a hundred bows' length, then emerged from his side.
Having gazed at them one by one, the young brahmin laughed loudly;
yet he said nothing, remaining silent and profound like Śiva accompanied by his attendants.
Indra said: "O young Brahmin, tell me, why do you laugh at me? The young Brahmin replied to Indra: "Have you seen ants? (141)
A swarm of ants was created by me one by one in succession;
all of them, in turn, were Indras, beginning with those who were my ancestors.
Now they have indeed attained the species of living beings as ants; by their karma, living souls gradually pass through the states of insects, humans, and gods. (143)
Through karma they attain the state of trees, as well as the state of yakṣas and nāgas; likewise, they attain the state of birds, the state of animals, the state of women, and the state of men. (144)
The state of a preta, the state of a god, and likewise the state of a seer are attained through karma;
even the state of Brahmā and the state of the king of gods are indeed obtained through karma.
Death, however, always dwells upon the head of everyone;
O Śakra, everything perishes constantly like a bubble on the water. (146)
"The deluded are bewildered in this world, but the wise are not bewildered at all.
Having said this, that young brahmin stood there with a smile.
The lord of the thirty gods was struck with wonder and became divested of his pride;
in the meantime, a person who was an ascetic arrived there.
The great yogi was extremely aged, wearing matted hair and a deer-skin;
his entire chest was covered with circles of body hair.
In the middle, having removed some hair so that it was entirely shaven,
he placed a circular, long-tailed tuft upon his head.
Having arrived, he stood between the Brahmin’s son and Mahendra;
Mahendra offered him, who was in the form of an elder, the madhuparka and other honors.
Then he prostrated and asked: "From where have you come?
What is your name? Where is your home? And how did you arrive here? (152)
How is it that you have a hand upon your head and a circle of hair upon your chest?
How is there a hollow space in your midsection produced by the plucking out of body hair? 153.
The old man said, "Today I am coming from Vaikuṇṭha;
I am a sage named Lomaśa, and my purpose is to go on a pilgrimage."
"O Indra, because my life is short, I have not established a household anywhere; nor have I married, for I now subsist on alms. (155)
As long as this mat upon my head remains for the purpose of pacifying the heat of the rain, I shall have a lifespan lasting as many kalpas as there are hairs upon my chest. (156)
O Indra, when one eon has passed, I pluck out a single hair;
the number of eons that have perished before me is equal to the number of hairs thus plucked out. 157.
Once born, it was only the size of a finger, circular, and hairless;
as for all the hairs on the chest, they became one hair each during every kalpa.
When those [eyes] have been plucked out, then my death shall occur;
when one hundred and ten Brahmā-years have passed, my death will take place. (159)
Countless ways of existence will perish in this creation, even those who have already died;
what purpose, then, is there in a wife, a son, or a home?
The blinking of an eye for Hari occurs at the falling of a Vairāja kalpa;
I constantly contemplate the feet of Śrī Hari at every place. (161)
Service to Śrī Hari is difficult to attain; devotion is superior even to liberation.
All worldly sovereignty is like a dream and acts as an obstacle to that devotion.
Having spoken thus, the elderly brahmin vanished;
then the young brahmin, having rendered Indra devoid of pride, [proceeded].
Having quickly vanished from sight, Indra attained a state of world-weariness;
he entrusted everything to his son and abandoned both the royal splendor and Śacī.
Out of devotion for Hari, Bṛhaspati became eager to go to the forest; at that time, he indeed instructed his own disciple.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord.
Thus, perform daily the recitation of this mantra along with meditation upon the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. 166.
"Therefore, you must strive for liberation; do not go to the forest otherwise.
Having been addressed thus, Bhajamāna became a great devotee of Viṣṇu.
The most righteous one ruled the kingdom and in the end attained liberation;
by reading or hearing this, a person becomes possessed of knowledge. || 168 ||
Faith increases for the devotee, and pride in devotion perishes entirely;
vain conceit goes far away, and in the end, one reaches the abode of Hari. 169.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you this auspicious knowledge which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
for the purpose of destroying pride and for the increase of devotion.

Thus, in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, [is described] the inquiry by Viśvāmitra regarding the virtue of wifely devotion (pātivratya) directed toward Menakā; how the Apsarases incurred old age through mutual curses due to their deviation from dharma; and how that curse was averted by bathing in the Nāgamatī river, and so forth.

Likewise, for the purpose of destroying Indra’s pride, there was the curse of Prakṛti, the curse of his preceptor, and the curse of Gautama; the destruction of his prosperity through a curse due to his insult of his preceptor; the slaying of Vṛtra; the sin of Brahman-slaughter; the destruction of that sin of Brahman-slaughter through the grace of his preceptor; the construction of a new palace; the obstruction of Viśvakarman; the arrival of Nārāyaṇa in the guise of a young Brahmin boy and his observation of a swarm of ants; the arrival of Lomaśa; and Indra’s renunciation upon determining that his life span would end with the falling out of his hair, as well as [the departure] of Viśvakarman.
Chapter Four Hundred and Eighty-Six (486), titled "The Determination that Indra’s Pride was Destroyed by Persistence."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Now I shall relate the account of how Dhanvantari’s pride was previously humbled; listen, O Lakṣmī, sovereign of the gods.
The great Lord Dhanvantari himself, an emanation of Nārāyaṇa,
arose in ancient times from the great ocean during its churning.
He was proficient in all the Vedas, an expert in mantras and tantras,
a true disciple of Garuḍa, and a grand-disciple of Śaṅkara.
Once, accompanied by a thousand disciples, he was traveling toward Vaikuṇṭha when he saw on the path the terrifying Takṣaka, licking his lips.
Surrounded by lakṣaṇa nāgas, he had come from the netherworld (pātāla) to wander upon the earth with auspicious intent, desiring to visit sacred fords (tīrtha).
Dhanvantari, filled with pride, discharged poison-mantras;
Takṣaka, overcome with rage, rushed toward the physician to devour him.
At that time, a disciple of Dhanvantari named Dambhi recited a most terrible poison-mantra and brought Takṣaka under his control.
Having caused him to yawn by means of a mantra, he rendered him free from poison;
he then seized the priceless jewel situated upon his head.
Having whirled him around with his trunk, he flung him far away;
Takṣaka fell and lay there as if dead, while his attendants then [fled].
They made their report to Vāsuki; Vāsuki arrived, bringing thousands of five-headed serpents whose venom was most virulent.
Beholding Droṇa, Kālīya, Karkoṭa, Puṇḍarīka, and Dhanañjaya,
the hosts of Dhanvantari’s disciples were struck with fear.
Bitten by the venom of serpents, those servants lay upon the surface of the earth; Dhanvantari restored them to life with the nectar of his mantras.
Blazing with rage, he caused the host of serpents to yawn by means of mantras;
Vāsuki, however, then mentally remembered Gaurī, who is known by that name.
O Manasā, come hither; protect the Nāgas from this great peril.
O highly fortunate one, worship shall be yours throughout the three worlds.
Having arrived instantly by means of his mind, he said: "I am going to the field of battle;
I shall slay that enemy and conquer him, without a doubt. (15)
My preceptor, the blessed Śeṣa, gave this armor to me;
having reduced the cycle of worldly existence to ashes, I am now capable of creating it anew.
"I am a disciple of Śambhu in the mantra scriptures, O Blessed One;
yet I do not hold even the slightest regard for Garuḍa, who is himself a disciple of Śambhu. (17)
"Dhanvantari is but one among his disciples; how can I even count him?
Having said this, he remembered Śrī Hari, Śeṣa, and Śambhu, and bowed down to them. (18)
At that very moment, he went to where Dhanvantari was staying;
there, with ease, he restored to life the serpents who had been paralyzed by mantras.
With poisonous mantras, she rendered the enemies' disciples motionless;
even Dhanvantari was not able to revive them despite his efforts.
Laughing within his mind, he said: "Abandon your pride in having attained perfection!
Speak, O Siddha; what do you know? You are indeed a disciple of Garuḍa. (21)
Both I and Garuḍa are renowned as disciples of Śambhu;
we have studied there until the end of the kalpa—what need is there to mention you?
Having said, "I cast forth this consecrated lotus; remain firm," he threw the consecrated lotus, which was like the sun.
By the hissing blasts of Dhanvantari, that [city] was then reduced to ashes;
the Goddess seized a most terrible spear, rich with mantras.
Dhanvantari, however, shattered her into pieces with his trident;
then, he mentally hurled a consecrated serpent-noose.
At that very moment, Dhanvantari discharged the formidable Gāruḍa weapon against the terrible [enemy] accompanied by hundreds of thousands of nāgas;
by it, the nāga-weapon was consumed.
Having thus acted with ease, he then mentally took up the trident granted by Śiva, which was fruitful and possessed a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Just then, Brahmā and Śambhu arrived swiftly for the sake of protection;
Garuḍa and the physician bowed mentally to the two gods. (28)
Brahmā said to the physician, "Perform the worship of Manasā;
for there is no equality with Dhanvantari, and your battle shall be with Durgā. (29)
This Prabhāvatī is capable of reducing the three worlds to ashes with her trident;
perform a hymn of praise to Manasā, for being pleased, she will grant you a boon.
Having become pure, Dhanvantari worshipped her with white flowers—
she who possessed the luster of a beautiful campaka flower and was enchanting in every limb.
Having meditated upon the Goddess who is borne by the king of serpents and is proficient in all branches of knowledge,
and having offered the sixteen articles, he indeed composed a hymn of praise.
Salutations to her whose nature is perfection; salutations again and again to the bestower of boons.
Salutations to the daughter of Kaśyapa; salutations again and again to Śaṅkarā. ||33||
Salutations again and again to Nāgadevī, the protector of children; salutations again and again to you, Jaratkārū, the mother of Āstīka. ||34||
Salutations again and again to you, the ascetic, the yoginī, and the sister of the Nāgas;
salutations to you, the virtuous woman whose very form is penance, and the disciple of Śambhu. (35)
Thus praised, Śāntā, who bestows happiness, became manifest in his mind;
saying "May it be well," she bowed and departed for her home, while Brahmā and Maheśvara [remained]. (36)
The gods, the physician, Garuḍa, and the serpents all returned to their own abodes.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the great power of Manasā. 37.
The pride of Dhanvantari was shattered; there is indeed no fear of serpents from hearing [this];
for those born of the lineage, there is no fear of snakes merely by hearing it. (38)

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Application of Mantras by Dhanvantari among the Nāgas and the Destruction of Dhanvantari’s Pride through the Application of Mantras by Manasādevī," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the autumnal Rāsa-maṇḍala; please listen [to me] as I describe the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and the gopīs. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, I shall describe to you that supreme Rāsamaṇa (the delight of the Rāsa dance),
performed with nine hundred thousand gopīs and nine hundred thousand Mādhavas.
On the full moon day of autumn, that youth became a young man;
O beloved, young men and young women took delight with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having reflected thus, Śrī Hari went to the forest of Vṛndāvana at night, when the auspicious moon had risen, in order to fulfill the desires of all the gopīs. || 4 ||
There, out of curiosity, he produced the playful sound of his flute;
hearing that, Rādhikā quickly emerged from her house.
And thirty-three companions, headed by Suśīlā, went forth with joy;
they were equal in dress, age, appearance, and virtue.
Other nine hundred thousand gopīs departed, abandoning their homes and possessions;
they all gathered together in one place, some holding garlands in their hands.
Some held beautiful sandalwood in their hands, and some held white chowries; some held musk in their hands, and some carried saffron.
Some carrying betel-boxes, some wearing golden garments, and crying out "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa!", they beheld the circle of the Rāsa dance.
In that secluded place, blossoming and perfumed by flower-laden breezes,
they heard the sweet humming of bees and the song of cuckoos.
Rādhā and the gopīs entered the beautiful Rāsa-maṇḍala;
and beholding Rādhā and the gopīs, Kṛṣṇa also appeared, smiling.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with jewel ornaments,
he was captivating and radiant with a beauty surpassing ten million gods of love.
With the corners of her eyes, she gazed repeatedly at the cowherd girls,
as well as at the nine hundred thousand Gopīs and the same number of Kṛṣṇas.
In the circle of the rāsa dance, there were indeed eighteen crores of couples;
He enjoyed the rāsa with songs of praise, rhythmic beats, and frequent leaping. || 14 ||

By the clashing of hands, the giving of rhythmic beats (tāla), the contortions of facial expressions, the striking with staff-like arms, the joining of shoulders, kisses, and the pressing of palms; || 15 ||
Having thus sported in the Rāsa dance, they sat down, exhausted and looking up;
they honored their beloved, their lover, and offered him excellent betel.
Filled with passion, they took betel from one another’s mouths;
Kṛṣṇa himself, assuming a form of love, truly understood their inner thoughts.
With amorous intent, he took hold of them all and kissed them,
as well as engaging in the eightfold erotic union with their limbs.
The Lord of Rasikas indeed delivered appropriate blows with his nails, teeth, and hands,
and also performed the eightfold kissing.
He joined limb with limb and minor member with minor member;
he embraced those lustful women, bringing them pleasure.
At the site of the nine hundred thousand [sacred spots], Kṛṣṇa shines forth, intent upon his beloveds;
yet, having granted them satisfaction through amorous play, he himself remains a master of upward-directed vital energy (ūrdhvaretas).
Having thus engaged in sports on land, they came for water-sports;
nine hundred thousand couples took delight in the waters of the Yamunā.
Both clothed and unclothed, they took delight for the sake of satisfying their desires;
they kissed their lord and reached a state of swoon within the ocean of bliss.
They firmly embraced their beloved, pressing him against their chests;
in this way, the Lord Kṛṣṇa gave them satisfaction even in the water for a very long time.
Then, having gone out, they eagerly put on their garments;
thereafter, each one sported separately with his own beloved.
Proud of themselves, they performed various amorous gestures for Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa, however, created ever-new adornments for their braided hair and other parts of their bodies.
One woman, placing her beloved in front of her, performed the grooming of her hair;
another placed an excellent peacock feather upon her crest.
One woman gave collyrium for her eyes and forehead-saffron;
another wound a garland of guñjā berries around her crest.
One gave a fine garment to her husband as an upper cloth,
and another placed a beautiful garland of flowers around his neck.
One applied a tilaka mark; another placed a crescent moon ornament;
one applied red lac to her hands, feet, and nails.
One gave a flute into his hand; another offered betel-leaf;
yet another showed him her beautiful face in a lovely mirror. || 3.1 ||
One joyfully massaged Kṛṣṇa’s feet;
another offered water, while yet another gently provided a fine breeze. (32)
One woman applied sandalwood paste to the dark-bodied one;
another, taking his hand, loosened the knot.
Another indeed performed a massage of the calves and thighs;
some danced and sang, while others, full of longing, kissed [him]. (34)
One woman, taking Kṛṣṇa with her, went into a bower;
another, placing him upon her bed, joyfully took her pleasure in love.
A certain woman indeed made him dance by force, while he,
in turn, fashioned a beautiful braid for another woman.
She applied vermilion on his forehead along with dots of musk,
and out of affection, she placed a very fine mark of sandalwood paste below it.
She drew a beautiful row of leaf-designs upon her lovely cheeks;
having applied lac-dye to her feet, she gave them a beautiful appearance.
She adorned herself with ornaments and removed the sandalwood paste;
she placed a rare elephant-pearl in the middle of her nose. (39)
In this way, Kṛṣṇā and nine hundred thousand gopīs adorned one another, sporting with amorous gestures as they took delight.
Having assumed many forms, the supreme teacher of yogis again manifested amorous passion, bestowing the bliss of desire upon the cowherd maidens.
Constantly overwhelmed by the bliss of passion, they fell into a state of swoon;
thus the women, having been delighted, made the night last for six months.
Having brought long sleep to the earth and having made the course of the sun stable,
the Supreme Lord, whose semen is drawn upward, bestowed supreme satisfaction of desire.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the remover of desire and pride, remained unshaken;
he went once more to the pavilion of the rāsa dance for the rāsa play. 44.
Then, through many wanderings and various hymns of praise, all the gods and others, together with their wives and offspring, remained stationed in the sky. (45)
They showered a rain of flowers and beheld the circle of the Rāsa dance;
the lords of sages created showers of musk, sandalwood, and other fragrant substances.
Having offered cries of victory and praise, they went to the bank of the Yamunā;
and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having rested, again delighted them there. 47.
He dwelt everywhere as he pleased, even in solitary places, in delightful flower gardens, and on the beautiful banks of lakes. (48)
In every delightful cave, by the streams and even the rivers, and in all the thirty-three forests desired by women. (49)
In the delightful Bhāṇḍīra forest, in the beautiful Śrīvana, as well as in the Kadamba grove, the Tulasī grove, the Kunda grove, and the Campaka grove; ||| 1.488.50 ||
In the Nimbā forest, in Madhuvana, and likewise in the Jambīraka grove;
in the coconut forest, in the betel-nut forest, and in the plantain forest. ||51||
In the Badarī forest, in the Bilva forest, in the Nāriṅga forest, in the Aśvattha forest, in the Vaṃśa forest, and in the Dāḍima forest. ||5 2||
In groves of Mandāraka trees, in groves of palm trees, and likewise in groves of mango trees;
in groves of Ketakī flowers, in groves of Aśoka trees, and in groves of date palms. ||53||

In the forest of *āmrātaka* trees, in the forest of *jambū* trees, in the beautiful forest of *śāla* trees, in the forest of *kaṭā* trees, in the forest of lotuses, and likewise in the forest of *jāti* trees; ||54||
In the delightful thicket of banyan trees, as well as in the forest of sandalwood and the grove of excellent *kesara* flowers,
he enjoyed himself for six months' nights.
Just as the desire of amorous women increases through the erotic sentiment, even so did Hari, the bestower of bliss upon them, take delight with them. 56.
Nevertheless, the hearts of the amorous women were not entirely satisfied;
thus, throughout the morning, Hari bestowed the pleasure of love during the rāsa dances.
And when all of them had become satiated with desire, he released them;
thereafter, he went to the Yamunā to sport in the waters.
Kṛṣṇa became invisible, and the gopīs returned to their own homes;
all these cowherd women no longer regarded their husband as their lord. (59)
Driven by lustful passion, those women indeed regarded him as a hero in love; nevertheless, with their minds fixed on Him alone, those beloved wives attained the divine state.
Through divine yoga, even that which is inert attains a divine state;
indeed, a black clod of earth attains the nature of fire through contact with fire.
Then, from the most excellent Rāsa, there arose auspicious, artificial, divine pavilions fashioned by Viśvakarman, extending for a hundred yojanas.
In a mere moment, Viśvakarman made nine hundred thousand beautiful couches with nine hundred thousand seats disappear from sight.
Then, as this young Śrī Kṛṣṇa was going alone toward his own home,
the best of sages saw him on the way.
Aṣṭāvakra was dark-complexioned, naked, and possessed of matted locks;
his nails and beard were very long, and he was peaceful with his neck bowed in reverence.
Having bowed down to Govinda, that bull among sages offered praise;
then, falling at his lotus feet, he abandoned his life-breaths through yoga.
That splendor rose up to the height of seven palm trees and,
having become a most divine person, stood near Kṛṣṇa.
Seeing the sage dead, Kṛṣṇa prepared to perform the funeral rites;
the sage had remained without food for sixty thousand years.
Deprived of blood, flesh, and bone, that body became filled with ashes;
having extracted it, Kṛṣṇa placed it upon the funeral pyre mixed with the ashes.
In the meantime, a chariot arrived from the sky,
accompanied by excellent attendants who were like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
Having bowed to Śrī Hari and led that divine person,
Aṣṭāvakra, whose body was liberated, the attendants went to the supreme Goloka.
Listen, Lakṣmī: Pracetas was the son of Brahmā, and his son was Asita;
being destitute of offspring, he performed penance for a thousand years.
When, despite having a wife, he did not obtain a son even after many years,
he then indeed became intent on giving up his life.
Then, in order to awaken him, an incorporeal voice spoke the truth:
"Why do you abandon your life? Go to the presence of Śaṅkara. (74)
"Having received the mantra from the mouth of Śaṅkara, accomplish its success;
by the boon of your chosen deity, he shall certainly become your son. (75)
Having heard this, he went to Kailāsa with his wife and said to him:
"O Mahādeva, ocean of compassion, grant me a son; I bow before you. (76)
Hara said: "A son shall be born to you who will be equal to me and a portion of myself;
chant this mantra for Rādhikā: 'Obeisance to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (77)
Indeed, by means of the Rādhā-mantra, she became manifest after more than a hundred years;
having said, "Be possessed of a son," Rādhikā vanished from sight. (78)
From Asita, there was then a son named Devala;
he married the daughter of King Suyajña, known as Ratnamālāvatī. (79)
And after one hundred years had passed, he took her in marriage;
yet, becoming detached, he abandoned her on the bed and went to the forest himself.
For a thousand years, the twice-born one performed austerities on Mount Gandhamādana; through his body, he became divine like the sun. (81)
Once, having seen Devala, Rambhā was deluded by passion; as she approached for the purpose of breaking his asceticism, Devala did not accept her.
Enraged and filled with inner grief, the virtuous woman, afflicted by the pain of unfulfilled desire because he would not accept her, uttered a curse out of anger: "83"
May you become hunchbacked, eight-faced, decrepit, blue and deformed, devoid of austerity, ugly, and despised by women. (84)
Having cursed Rambhā, the sage named Aṣṭavakra went to heaven;
he became renowned as Devala and departed for the Malaya mountain.
He performed penance again for sixty thousand years;
having now understood the Rāsa-sport, he has arrived here to behold it. (86)
Absorbed in meditation and procrastinating, he did not attain the sight of the Rāsa dance;
yet through union with Kṛṣṇa, the devoted sage went to his abode, Goloka.
Then Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu went to the house of Nanda;
at dawn, all those women, transformed and absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, remembered him.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the supreme Rāsa-maṇḍala has been described to you;
by reading or hearing this, the attainment of Kṛṣṇa will certainly come to pass. (89)

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Kṛṣṇa’s Deeds with the Gopīs in the Rāsa-maṇḍala through the Emotion of Desire during the Lineage of the Kṛta-yuga in the First Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, as well as Devala’s Transformation into Aṣṭāvakra due to Rambhā’s Curse and His Liberation."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this delightful narrative originating from Camatkārapura;
it is auspicious, devoted to truth and righteousness, and brings about liberation even for those born of animal wombs.
Two yojanas to the south of that bank of the Nāga river,
there lies a long lake five yojanas in width.
Then, after some time, having bathed in that lake,
the eminent sage Durvāsas went to the house of King Kalaśa.
Hurrying, he spoke to that Kalaśa, the lord of Camatkārapura:
"I am observing the Cāturmāsya vow and I desire to perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa)."
Therefore, O King, whatever food has been prepared for you in your house, give that to me for my meal; my hunger is increasing exceedingly. (5)
The great king named Kalaśa [offered] the prepared food,
consisting of sweetmeats, side dishes, foods to be sucked, drinks, foods to be chewed, and likewise meat.
He himself indeed gave everything for the sake of his meal;
then that brahmin ate the soup accompanied by meat broth.
The Brahmin, having eaten unknowingly, realized that the food was mixed with meat;
due to the fault of violating his vow, he became enraged and cursed him.
"Since you have caused a breach of my vow by giving me meat,
therefore you shall become a flesh-eater, a tiger in the forests and other wild places."
The king, speaking with humble words, said: "Show favor to me, your servant who is marked by your command, devoted, and submissive. (1.489.10)
Then Durvāsas said to him: "O King, when the cow Nandini shows you Bāṇa standing upon the surface of the earth..."
"Then you shall be liberated," having said this, the sage departed;
[the king] became a forest-dweller in the form of a terrifying tiger.
Then, in the course of time, a herd of cows came there for the sake of grass,
where the cow Nandini resided— she who was the color of a swan and whose udder flowed like a jar.
Having gone to the edge of a bower for the sake of grass, she saw the linga of the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva),
hidden among shrubs and the like, and covered by grass, grain, and other vegetation.
Then, standing upon him, she poured forth a great quantity of milk;
there, by chance, that tiger indeed arrived, wandering about in haste.
Seeing that Nandinī, the tiger then seized her;
she, however, [ran toward] her own calf tied in the cow-pen, who was not eating grass and was intent only on milk.
Remembering this, distressed and dejected, she lamented piteously:
"Alas! By what sin have I been abandoned, leaving my infant behind at the cow-pen? (17)
May Śaṅkara protect her who has fallen into the mouth of a tiger for the sake of death,
by that same truth and devotion with which she offered even grass for his bathing.
"By that truth, may I have reunion with my son.
Having heard her, the tiger said to her: "Abandon these vain lamentations."
"Remember your chosen deity, the giver of heaven; from that, happiness shall arise.
Death is certain for you, since you have come under my power."
The cow said: "Listen, O tiger; I do not lament for myself, because death following the performance of Śambhu’s worship bestows liberation upon me. (2.1)
"My calf, tied in the cow-pen and remembering my arrival, remains there subsisting on milk; how will he fare without me? (22)
Therefore, O great tiger, release me today, for I am devoted to my son;
having delivered him to my circle of friends, I shall return to your presence. (23)
The tiger said: "She who, having emerged from the mouth of death, goes forth, shall never return again; therefore, I shall devour you."
Nandinī said: "I shall come into your presence by means of oaths;
[may the sin] that lies in the killing of a Brahmin or in the deception of one's mother and father [be mine]. (25)
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin as one who deceives a virtuous guru, or as a chaste wife who deceives her husband. (26)
Whatever sin belongs to those who betray trust, to the ungrateful, to those who cause the breaking of vows, and to those who destroy the images of the gods; ||27||
Whatever sin may belong to those who revile me and those who deprive me of my livelihood, by that sin may I be tainted if I do not return again. (28)
Having heard these oaths, that tiger spoke with amazement:
"If it be so, then go home and look for your own son. (29)
"Entrust her to your friends and then return," she was told;
and weeping, she departed for Vatsa with great haste. (1.489.30)
Then, seeing his mother crying out as she had arrived at an improper time, the calf asked: "O mother, why have you come today at such an unseasonable hour?"
"Why is your mind so bewildered? Why is your face drenched with tears?
The mother said, "Drink some water first; afterwards I shall tell you."
The calf drank the full milk, being repeatedly sniffed on the head by her;
he was gently licked and told the entire account of the tiger.
Today I went into the forest and was forcibly seized by a tiger;
that claw-armed tiger, even as he was devouring me, was entreated by me. (34)
"I would have returned to the cow-pen after seeing the boy, having sworn oaths;
but I, O son, have been released from those oaths for your sake. (35)
Then I shall go there after giving you away to another cow;
live happily, dear child, having been fed, seen, and spoken to. (36)
My child, I too shall go to that very place where you are going;
for now, death in the presence of my mother would be truly praiseworthy for me. (37)
"You must die alone, deprived indeed of me;
for I must die before you, and that will grant me heaven. (38)
O mother, if the tiger should devour me along with you, that destiny which belongs to those devoted to their mothers will surely be mine. (39)
Or else, I shall depart under oaths while you remain here;
for there is no kinsman equal to a mother for children who subsist on milk.
There is no protector equal to a mother; there is no refuge equal to a mother.
There is no one worthy of worship equal to a mother; there is no friend equal to a mother. (41)
There is no deity equal to a mother, both in this world and in the next;
thus, one should always perform service to one's mother with supreme devotion.
Those sons who practice the supreme dharma of serving their mother attain the highest state, marked by their mother’s blessings. (43)
Therefore, I shall depart; you, however, remain here in this cow-pen.
Without a doubt, I shall protect your life with my own life.
Having heard her son’s words, which were consistent with dharma, Nandini said:
"Death has been ordained for me alone, not for you, my son, on this day. (45)
So how can you protect my life with your own vital breaths?
Having carried out your mother’s command, do not act with such negligence.
From greed arises destruction both in this world and in the next;
indeed, a person is bound by these three: greed, negligence, and misplaced trust.
Therefore, my son, you must not harbor the desire to go;
rather, my son, you must always protect yourself with every effort. (48)
"O Lakṣmī, one should never go anywhere alone, having abandoned one's own herd.
Having spoken thus to him and repeatedly licking him, [she departed]. 49.
Overwhelmed with tears of grief, she stood for a moment in the midst of her companions and spoke to Bahulā, Campā, Vasudhārā, and Ghaṭasravā: [1.489.50]
O Haṃsanāda, Śriyānanda, Śubhakṣīra, and Mahodaya, as well as all other cows, having heard this, may you carry out my word! (51)
"Today, I was seized by a tiger nearby for the sake of food;
I have come here for the purpose of seeing you and to see my son. (52)
"Having been brought here with difficulty through oaths, this wicked son has been well-admonished by you and has now been returned to me as my son. (53)

Whatever misdeed has been committed by you through ignorance or lack of knowledge, O beloved ones, forgive it; this child, who is like milk to me and is without a protector, must always be protected. (54)
Tormented by grief for his mother, he must be protected by all of us;
I shall go there, to where that tiger is.
"This is my final prostration to you all," she said.
Upon hearing this, the cows replied, "O Nandinī, you must not go! (56)
In matters concerning times of distress, one must indeed utter a false oath;
for there is no sin in speaking falsely when the loss of life is imminent. (57)
In marriage, in jest, regarding a woman, in a life-threatening crisis, or in a financial crisis—falsehood does not lead to sin; it is declared that such a rule is a protector.
"Protect your own son; come with us to our own home.
Hearing them, Nandinī spoke regarding the protection of another's life: ||59||
For the virtuous, even the five kinds of falsehood are not a righteous act when it comes to protecting one's own life;
for the righteous, truth alone is the dharma that effects deliverance.
The world is established in truth; Dharma is established in truth.
Having given the earth to Viṣṇu, Bali remained steadfast in truth.
If, having made a promise, one should fail, he would indeed be a destroyer of all;
then the cows said, "In every way, you are worthy of our salutation."
Since you, who possess truth and righteousness, do not even count your own life, what can we say of you, O Bull, who stand firm in truth and are worshipped by the gods? (63)
Therefore, go, O lady of great merit; your son is not to be grieved for by you.
May your victory be auspicious, and may Dharma protect Nandinī. (64)
Having spoken thus and bowed to her circle of friends, Nandini said slowly:
"May all the presiding deities of the forest protect my little son. (65)
Thus bellowing, that cow went toward Vyāghrasthala;
meanwhile, the tiger sat with mouth agape, watching her path.
Having bowed to him, Nandinī said: "O forest-dweller, I have come here relying upon truth and righteousness; indeed, satisfy yourself and eat. (67)
The tiger said: "Abiding in truth and free from obstacles, by seeing you today I have become greatly meritorious and exceedingly pure. (68)
For nothing inauspicious exists anywhere for those who possess truth;
yet I, O blessed lady, am indeed ill-behaved, a doer of harm, and a treasure-house of sin. (69)
Having caused you, who are most righteous, to be slain, what destiny indeed shall I attain?
Therefore, you ought to show me the favor of granting the gift of knowledge.
"Having obtained the fruitful company of the virtuous, may my destiny become auspicious.
The cow said: "In the Kṛta age, penance is the means; in Tretā, meditation alone. (71)
In the Dvāpara age, sacrifice and charity [are meritorious], but in the Kali age, charity alone is auspicious;
however, at the end of the Kali age, the name of Hari shall be the sole means of liberation.
Indeed, the gift of fearlessness is the supreme among all gifts; it does not belong to those who are violent. Therefore, one should engage in the glorification of Śrī Hari. 73.
Service to Śrī Hari, or to Śambhu, or to the Lord of Rādhikā—such action shall lead to liberation; therefore, you should always perform it. (74)
"O tiger, in this dense forest there exists here the abode of Hara;
it is a Śiva-liṅga covered by grass. Worship it every morning. (75)
"Perform circumambulations, prostrations, and so forth; liberation will come to pass.
Having said this, Nandinī, the daughter of Vyāghra, revealed the Liṅga. (76)
Having seen [the king], he quickly became like the tiger of old;
released from the curse of Durvāsas, he remembered and spoke to Nandinī.
"I am a king named Kalaśa, born of the lineage of the Haihayas;
due to the curse of the sage Durvāsas, I have fallen into the state of a tiger. (78)
"Through the practice of the Nandinī-dhenu, there will be liberation from the curse;
by the sight of Śaṅkara, you shall become a king once again. (79)
"Thus do I remember my former history today, O Śucitvada," he said;
having spoken thus, he bowed to the Earth and prostrated before that Śiva.
With supreme devotion, Gauḥ worshipped Śiva and bathed him with milk;
then Śambhu, manifesting himself, spoke.
For those who are always pure in devotion to me and who joyfully worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord Hari, for the sake of liberation— 82.
Having spoken thus, they offered salutations to their lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
then, having received the mantra, they both departed for their respective homes. (83)
At that time, having attained joy for both their families and so forth, they took refuge in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and after some time attained liberation. 84.
By means of a most divine celestial chariot, those two went to the abode of Kṛṣṇa.
By reading or hearing this, one shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, and merit. (85)

Thus ends the four hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of King Kalaśa of Camatkārapurī Attaining the State of a Tiger Due to the Curse of Durvāsas, His Liberation through the Contact with the Cow Nandinī and the Vision of Śiva, and the Power of Satyavrata," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another story that bestows the wealth of true fortune. There was a king named Vṛka, born of the Lunar dynasty (Somavaṃśa). || 1 ||
He had a virtuous wife devoted to her husband;
in their later years, a daughter was then born to them.
Having examined the birth ascendant, the astrologers said to the king and the queen:
"When the sun was situated in Citrā, on the fourteenth lunar day, and the moon [was in its place]... (3)
A maiden who may be born [under such conditions] shall be a poison-maiden (viṣakanyā);
the one who takes her hand in marriage shall meet his death within six months.
O King, that girl who has been born in your house shall be devoid of prosperity; she is such a poison-maiden (viṣakanyā).
She will destroy both her father’s and her father-in-law’s households;
therefore, O King, abandon her and always remain happy in your kingdom.
Or, if she should become a virtuous female ascetic, a practitioner of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, then she will effect the upliftment of both families; of this there is no doubt.
Even for those who are unfortunate, fortune transforms when there is renunciation; for even an ascetic covered in ashes becomes like a medicinal powder for one's welfare.
Wherever they may have originated— a mendicant, a jewel, a pearl, gold, a maiden, or a medicinal herb— all attain a divine state through initiation.
"Therefore, O King, you may do as you wish, whatever pleases you.
Though addressed thus, that royal sage, reflecting upon his own past karma, [remained silent].
Though it was impossible to cleanse her, he, being full of affection, did not indeed abandon her;
for whatever action a person performs with whatever body, [that body remains bound by it]. (11)
In whatever state one may be, and from whatever momentum, one experiences that very thing through that [cause] in that [state]; nowhere is what has not been done ever obtained.
These five things are created here for the embodied being while still in the womb:
lifespan, action, wealth, knowledge, and death itself.
Just as fruits and flowers on trees and creepers do not bypass their own appointed time, so too does karma performed in the past.
Just as a calf finds its mother among thousands of cows, even so does the action find the doer situated in the midst of ten million others. 1.5.
No embodied being on earth is capable, by means of either strength or wisdom, of altering the karma previously performed by oneself. (16)
The happiness and suffering of embodied beings arise from their own actions;
he who clings through the notions of "I" and "mine" is bound. 17.
One's own karma runs very swiftly after one as one runs;
it lies down with one who lies down and stands by one who stands.
Wherever a man is destined to experience either happiness or suffering, he is led there by force, as if bound by a rope. 19.
Whether they are awake or sleeping, speaking or walking, desiring to accomplish an action or even in the process of performing it— ||1.490.20||
For those who offer their entire being, [the goal] necessarily presents itself;
just as a lamp reaches extinction when its oil is exhausted. ||21||
Upon the exhaustion of karma and the exhaustion of latent dispositions (āśaya), one attains nirvāṇa;
for that which has its root in the afflictions (kleśa) is called the latent impression (vāsanā), which is the storehouse of karma (karmāśaya). //22//
The fruit produced by that is experienced in both the present and future lives;
neither mantra, nor austerity, nor charity, nor a sacred ford, nor even a refuge [can prevent it]. (23)
Living beings are not capable of protecting themselves from the flow of their past karma;
food and drink are digested day and night. (24)
How indeed is it that the embryo does not decay within that very same belly?
Therefore, an action equal to the embryo is not destroyed without its fruit being experienced. (25)
Whether it be auspicious or evil, people experience the results of their own actions;
likewise, this daughter of mine has arrived here according to her karma. (26)
A poison-maiden was inscribed upon my destiny by my past actions;
let it be so, for that which is granted by fate must never be disregarded. (27)
"Let that which has appeared for the sake of enjoyment come toward me;
for when there is prosperity, there are many enjoyments, and upon its destruction, there remains only the state of an ascetic. (28)
In both cases, I have gained a profit, for Nirvana is attained by its very nature; if, moreover, that which is granted by fate should meet me, what gain could be more supreme than that? (29)
This daughter of mine shall be the instrumental cause for my dispassion;
and when I am liberated, her liberation shall also come to pass.
By fate one remains unprotected, and by fate even that which is guarded perishes;
by fate even the helpless lives, and by fate even the one with a protector perishes. (3.1)
"For the sake of the happiness of my extreme old age, my daughter is my support;
whether she be poisonous or the destroyer of all, how can I abandon my own child? (32)
Having abandoned this helpless, unprotected woman, how could I become a killer of an embryo on this earth?
Having committed the desertion of one who must be supported, how could I go to the realm of Yama?
A daughter is like a son; for her sake, one would renounce the earth. She herself is Lakṣmī; this young girl has come to me through my good fortune. (34)
"Let all these people, intent on their own interests, say whatever they desire in their minds;
however, I must protect my daughter for the sake of detachment and renunciation. (35)
I have ruled a kingdom for many years and experienced endless enjoyments;
now, under the pretext of my daughter, I shall make a firm resolve to worship Hari.
May everything that obstructs my purpose perish quickly; may my own self-interests perish.
But let not my devotion, liberation, progeny, peace, and virtuous conduct ever perish. (37)
Having made this resolve, he did not abandon his own daughter;
and Śarmavatī, for her part, remained constantly possessed by a spirit of renunciation.
Therefore, she was given the name Śarmavatī by her father, as she bestowed happiness;
then, having reached youth, she [worshipped] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa constantly.
Having bathed in the morning, she would worship; she would bow at her father's feet;
and regarding it as unsurpassed merit, she would serve her virtuous mother. (1.490.40)
Then, due to destiny resulting from past actions, enemies surrounded the city of King Vṛka and besieged it for many days without engaging in battle.
When Vṛka was killed in battle by fate on the tenth day, the people then said:
"By this poison-maiden, the king's entire kingdom has been lost and the king himself has been slain in combat. (42)
Although the astrologer had previously spoken thus, the king did not abandon her at all. ||43||
Now let her be executed and led out from this city;
otherwise, there will be protection for those who remain, but surely total destruction. (44)
Having heard the voice of Prajāpati, the virtuous maiden went forth at nightfall;
having reached the sacred field of Śambhu Hāṭakeśvara, she stood there for a moment. (45)
Having bowed to Śambhu, she, immersed in grief, indeed contemplated death;
then, a memory arising from her previous birth occurred to her.
"In my previous life as a caṇḍāla, I quenched the thirst of a single cow;
by the merit of that act, I have been born as a princess in this abode of wolves. (47)
In a previous body, I was a Caṇḍāla woman with many sons;
I was despised, tormented by poverty, and afflicted by hunger. (48)
Though afflicted by thirst, I gave abundant water to a cow;
by that merit, I have indeed been born as the daughter of a king. (49)
But at that time, while she was the daughter of a Caṇḍāla, she stole the golden Gaurī and shattered her into pieces with stones.
Having emerged from the temple, as soon as I had gone to the great marketplace for the purpose of selling [the goods], I was seized by the king's officers. (51)
Beaten, punished, and cast into prison, she then died;
through the breaking of the image of Pārvatī, she was reborn as a poison-maiden (viṣakanyā).
I must certainly experience my own karma, which is indeed evil;
however, I have obtained the auspicious merit resulting from the gift of water. (53)
Then, having constructed a hut there, I performed supreme austerity, offering water and fruit, and serving according to my ability. (54)
Through service to the virtuous, to ascetics, to the holy, to cows, to righteous women, to children, and to those devoted to the gods, liberation shall come to pass. (55)
Having resolved thus, she performed penance after installing Gaurī with devotion;
she undertook the vow for Gaurī and, having bathed, performed worship and other rites.
She constantly gratified him with fasts on alternate days and enchanting dances and songs; in the summer, she practiced the penance of the five fires.
In the winter she stayed in the middle of the water, and during the rains, amidst the falling showers;
previously she subsisted on fruits, and thereafter on leaves.
Afterwards, she subsisted on dry leaves and such; then she became one whose food was water;
thereafter she became one whose food was air; and after that, she became one who delights in the Self.
Sleeping in the open air, having abandoned her hut, and clad only in the directions,
she became submerged in dust upon the earth as if she were the very ground itself.
A long time passed for that yoginī through the practice of yoga.
Her face was overcome by wrinkles and her head was marked by grey hair;
yet, even while she remained in the state of a maiden, Gaurī became pleased.
Then, for the sake of testing her, Pārvatī became Śacī.
Mounting a white elephant, the Great Queen arrived,
wearing a crown upon her head and being attended by throngs of apsarases.
With a serene countenance, she spoke respectfully to Śarmavatī:
"Choose a boon as you desire, O dear ascetic woman; I shall grant it to you."
I am the wife of Sureśa, known by the name Indrāṇī;
having personally shown compassion, I have come here to bestow upon you the fruit of your ascetic penance.
"O daughter, Bhavānī is stern; she does not look upon you even now.
Hearing this, she shook the dust from her body and joined her palms in reverence.
Having paid homage, he said: "O Śacī, I do not think of your favor;
I desire no boon from you, nor from any other divine women. (67)
I choose as my boon that goddess who is the beloved of Śiva,
she by whom penance was indeed performed for the sake of Śiva for thousands of years.
I choose a boon from her who is Prakṛti, born from the left side of Kṛṣṇa, who is eternally auspicious, and by whom all this is pervaded. (69)
Śacī said: "I am Śacī, the daughter of Vajradhara;
I am the mistress of the gods and the virtuous sovereign of the goddesses."
"O maiden, by the boons granted by me, all goddesses become [such];
why then, O ascetic woman, do you not accept a boon from me? (7.1)
"Surely I shall crush your head with a blow from my thunderbolt!
Hearing this, the steadfast maiden spoke to the Queen of the Gods: ||72||
"You are the mistress of both the gods and the goddesses; that is the truth.
I shall propitiate her from whom this sovereignty of yours was obtained. (73)
Welcome to you, O one equal to my mother; I honor you, the worshipful one, with excellent fruits.
O Great Goddess, I shall not commit even the slightest offense against you.
"Nevertheless, you consider me worthy of death; cast down your weapon!
Having spoken thus and meditated upon Śivā, he descended into the expanse of his heart.
And he reflected in his heart: "Either death or a vision must be obtained here; one or the other shall surely come from Śacī or from the wife of Śiva. (76)
"Otherwise, I shall resort to fire, which is fit for burning;
meanwhile, Airāvata has appeared there in the form of a lion. (77)
Śacī was born in the form of Śivā, while the Apsarases became her attendants;
they were Rudrāṇīs with the crescent moon on their foreheads, holding tridents in their hands and possessing auspicious faces. ||78||
Having seen Pārvatī in her heart— white-complexioned, seated upon a white bull, and clad in white garments— Śarmavatī opened her eyes and gazed before her.
The Poison-Maiden, having prostrated herself with a faltering voice, offered this praise:
"Salutations to you, O Śāṅkarī, O Protectress, O Beloved of my very life! (1.490.80)
O Satī, who bestows all desires, who dwells in the heart of your devotee;
salutations to you, O Satī, who possess the sovereignty of the eightfold qualities! Salutations again and again! ||81||
Yogis meditate upon you and worship you with objects of affection;
O Maheśvarī, I worship you with flowers consisting of perfect devotion.
Having spoken thus, Pārvatī then bowed down to her, and she said to her:
"I am well-pleased with you, my daughter; ask for the boon you desire. (83)
Then the Poison-Maiden said: "O Sovereign, you know everything;
for the sake of my husband, I have undertaken all this effort of asceticism. (84)
What shall I do with that now, being enveloped by old age?
Dwell here forever, O Pārvatī, and be the bestower of auspiciousness upon maidens. (85)
Having been addressed thus, Pārvatī then said, "So be it," and she touched the maiden with her hand, making her attain fresh youth.
He spoke to that divine girl, who was sixteen years of age and resembled a campaka flower: "Tell me, O maiden of beautiful hips, what is desired beyond this? (87)
The maiden said, "O mother, cause me to have a vision of the Lord Śambhu.
Satī replied, "Come to Kailāsa, seated upon the lion. (88)
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous Śarmavatī went to Kailāsa itself;
and having beheld Śaṅkara, she received a Vaiṣṇava mantra. (89)
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations! Having thus spoken, the Sāttvatī then took a garland of *tulasī* around her neck. (1.490.90)
She became a Vaiṣṇava maiden, solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
in the end, having obtained Nārāyaṇa as her husband, she attained liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told the auspicious and pure life-story of the female ascetic Śarmavatī, which is the supreme penance of the poison-maiden. 92.
Having obtained a vision of Śambhu through her devotion fixed on Pārvatī,
