The husband is a sacred ford, the father is a sacred ford, and the devoted wife is a sacred ford; a virtuous woman is a sacred ford, a cow is a sacred ford, and the virtuous are the most excellent sacred ford. (29)
The guru is a sacred ford, Hari is a sacred ford, and the gods are always sacred fords;
knowledge is the supreme, pure sacred ford, and devotion is the sacred ford beyond that.
Service is the best of holy places; service is the holy place superior to the most excellent.
Through service, all goals of human endeavor, which are otherwise very difficult to attain, are obtained. (3.1)
Service to Hari and service to the virtuous are the most excellent of all sacred fords;
indeed, whatever other sacred fords there may be, they have their root in those two.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Thus, this recitation is the supreme sacred site that makes one a great Vaiṣṇava. (33)
"Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa alone is my master; no other is considered my master.
In this way, the dedication and the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) of one's own self are proclaimed. 34.
Indeed, the offering of all things—gross, subtle, and intermediate—is service to the sacred ford;
whatever is done so that Kṛṣṇa may be pleased is truly the sacred ford itself. (35)
Dancing is the sacred ford for the Apsarases by which Janārdana is pleased;
and singing is the sacred ford for women by which Mādhava is pleased. (36)
The Gāndharvas' bathing place for instrumental music is that by which Nārāyaṇa may be pleased;
the Gopīs' bathing place for desire is that by which the Lord of Vraja may be pleased. (37)
Meditation is the sacred ford for those possessed of yoga, by which Keśava is pleased;
thus, considering meditation to be the supreme ford and knowing Śrī Kṛṣṇa to be the bestower of desired boons—38.
Having surrendered everything to Him alone, the wise person should accumulate merit for liberation;
by reading and hearing this, the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites shall be attained. ||39||

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled “The Description of the Enumeration of the Sixty-eight Holy Places and Other Spiritual Pilgrimage Sites,” in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this wonderful narrative concerning the Brāhmaṇas.
The king, the lord of Ānarta, being well-disposed, granted boons to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having summoned him, he spoke after prostrating himself again and again:
"Gold or elephants and horses [should be given] at the transit of the Sun into Capricorn."
Whatever anyone desires to give, I am willing to grant even the earth; please show favor to me, who am humble and prostrate before you. (3)
The Brahmins said: "We are always of the nature of non-possessiveness;
we are ascetics who subsist on alms—what use have we for elephants, horses, and gold? (4)
King Camatkāra said: "O purifiers of the world, you holy ones, please accept this gift for the sake of purifying the royal fortune."
And seventy-two Brahmins dwell here on the riverbank,
having constructed leaf-huts, traveling through the path of the sky.
By the power of their austerity, they always go with devotion to various sacred fords;
having performed recitation, ritual bathing, and libations, they indeed return once again.
In Vārāṇasī or Prayāga, in Puṣkara or likewise in Naimiṣa;
in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, in Prabhāsa, and likewise in Kedāraka.
In some places they go during the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), and they also go during the Cāturmāsya;
and here, O twice-born ones, they go during the transit of the sun on the bank of the Nāgavatī in this year.
"Accept my gift and indeed purify us!
Though addressed thus, those brahmins, being free from worldly attachment, departed for Puṣkara.
When the sun entered Capricorn at the time of the transit, for the purpose of staying for five nights,
the king, having learned all of that, then [sent] his beloved Damayantī.
He said: "Taking gold, ornaments, garments, and excellent wealth, go to the bank of the Nāgā river where the wives of Brahmins reside."
"Give them whatever objects they desire, such as ornaments and the like; their husbands do not accept gifts from us. (1.3)
Women will certainly accept gifts such as ornaments and the like;
for whatever kind of ornament a woman wears, [she will surely take it]. (14)
Having promised "So be it," she gave many ornaments,
as well as gems, pearls, corals, and beautiful earrings.
Likewise, there were necklaces as radiant as the moon, and large anklets inlaid with sapphires,
great lapis lazuli, and cat's-eye gems.
With rubies, as well as diamonds and enchanting māṇikya gems, and with divine armlets, bracelets, chains, and golden threads; ||17||
Having taken [these items], she indeed arrived at Nāgavatī on the occasion of the Saṃkrānti festival to bathe,
bringing sesame seeds and large quantities of desirable foods.
Having bathed and established this mountain of great ornaments on the bank,
he awaited the recipients for his gift on that riverbank.
In the meantime, the female ascetics arrived, filled with curiosity,
having learned that Damayantī, the beloved of the king, had come for the purpose of giving gifts.
"What kind of queen is she? What is her form and what are her ornaments?"—filled with such curiosity, the wives of the brahmins gathered together. (21)
When they arrived, the queen paid them homage and spoke charmingly:
"This collection of ornaments was intended by me for the one whose banner is Garuḍa."
"Today, on this day, a gift given to Brāhmaṇa women yields fruit;
therefore, let the female ascetics accept these things offered by me according to their desire. (23)
"There are indeed many ornaments; please grant me a favor.
Then one among them said to her, "This pearl necklace is for me. (24)
Having heard this, the queen herself washed his feet and gave him a string of pearls together with divine garments. (25)
Likewise, perceiving that another desired a necklace, she gave her a necklace;
and knowing the mind of a third, she gave her earrings. (26)
Then the remaining female ascetics joyfully accepted whatever ornaments she gave to each of them.
The more those female ascetics took up the ornaments,
the greater the joy that arose within this Damayantī.
She threw out hundreds and thousands of others as well;
having said, "Let them take [these]," the king’s beloved remained silent.

Even after all [the gifts] had been accepted by the female ascetics from there, they still felt no satisfaction; then the queen spoke to them again: 30. "Even after all [the gifts] had been accepted by the female ascetics from there, they still felt no satisfaction; then the queen spoke to them again: (1.498.30)
"Be satisfied; I shall go and bring them back again and again.
Having said this, he departed quickly and returned swiftly with them.
For five days, he repeatedly gave infinite ornaments, garments, and wealth to the Brahmin women.
The female ascetics also, filled with longing and joy, placed those various garments and ornaments upon their bodies.
They constructed huts filled with wealth, garments, and ornaments;
then there were four Brahmin women, adorned with bark garments and deerskins.
Not wishing to accept gifts, they did not come near her;
however, on the fifth day, the queen [approached] for the sake of obtaining their gifts.
Taking those highly precious ornaments, she departed quickly;
the queen said to them all, "Let this favor be granted. (36)
"Let these ornaments indeed be accepted for the sake of adornment; for ascetic women are dispassionate, always following the will of their husbands. (37)
Devoted wives said: "The minds of husbands are not [on such things];
without her husband's command, a wife adorns her body. (38)
She would incur sin because of that; therefore, we do not accept yours.
We have no need for ornaments; we are adorned by bark garments.
While they were thus conversing with her at that very moment,
four husbands arrived at the hermitages by way of the sky.
Then Śunaḥśepa, Śākreyabodha, and Dānta as the fourth—these alone remained;
all the others, having suffered a loss of their spiritual state, resorted to the path of worldly existence. ||41||
Due to their greed for their wives and the fault of accepting gifts of ornaments, those four [took] the wives of sages and adorned maidens. (42)
Seeing this, they were overcome with agitation and cried out, "What is this? What is this? By whom have these ornaments been given, that the female ascetics have been thus mocked? (43)
Having given us wealth and garments, he has transformed this hermitage;
then indeed the ascetics spoke thus to King Camatkāra. (44)
"This queen Damayantī is present here now;
by her, all the ornaments and garments have been bestowed upon every [one of us]. (45)
"This very [gift] has come to us as well to be given; it was standing ready.
It was not accepted by us, and she was forbidden and turned back. ||46||
Having heard this and having seen her, the brahmins, due to the exhaustion of their ascetic merit, cursed her after making her hear [the curse]; listen, O Lakṣmī, to the power of asceticism.
"O Queen, seventy-two of us went to Puṣkara for the purpose of bathing by way of the sky, through the power of our asceticism, with a speed like that of thought or the wind. (48)
These four have arrived, whose wives have been taken;
others have not been made [to come], for they have fallen from the path of the sky and into the lotus-pond.
For virtuous women, the power of their chastity is indeed great;
yet that celestial power has been lost through the act of giving and receiving [the gift].
"This hermitage of ours has been deceived by you with austerities, wealth, and gifts such as ornaments; therefore, you shall indeed become a stone here. (51)
Then that queen praised them for the sake of liberation;
and there they spoke [to her], saying, "O Mādhavī, daughter of Śāṇḍilī, you who are born from a portion of Kamalā."
A maiden from a noble family will come and effect your deliverance;
in no long time at all, that Mādhavī shall arrive.
She, in the form of Lakṣmī, shall indeed remain upon a stone on the riverbank;
she will become a stone in the likeness of a maiden, just like Ramā.
Listen, Lakṣmī, regarding that girl Śilā who was born at that very moment in the presence of the Brāhmaṇa; having learned that very account. (55)
The king quickly arrived there and grieved for his wife;
meanwhile, the four Brahmins had taken the family away through the path of the sky.
The ascetics went to the Himalayas, a place free from obstacles;
the king, however, touched a stone and repeatedly remembered the virtues of his beloved.
The king lamented for a moment, performed the śrāddha rite for his devoted wife,
and had a mansion constructed upon her [remains].
He himself performed worship daily with camphor, incense, and other offerings, as well as with garments, saffron, and sandalwood; he also caused the brahmins to perform the worship.
Then, having traversed the earth on foot, those sixty-eight auspicious twice-born ones arrived at the bank of the Nāganadī, exhausted from traveling such a great distance.
Having seen them adorned with ornaments and having learned this account as well,
they understood that the cause of their fall from the sky was the withholding of gifts.
Having learned of Damayantī’s transformation into stone,
they then took up water for the purpose of destroying King Camatkāra and his kingdom.
Since our movement in the sky was destroyed by greed for the gift, the minds of the Brahmin women became passionate and filled with attachment. (63)
"Let the fruit of that go to the king and the kingdom"—thinking thus, the wives of the brahmins began to utter a curse. (64)
They restrained him excessively, saying, "A curse must not be given under any circumstances, for we have been adorned by the wife of this lord of men. (65)
With divine garments and ornaments, and with a mind purified by faith, we have been drawn into your house due to the affliction of poverty. (66)
But the happiness arising from clothing, ornaments, and the like is not attained by mortals;
for ascetics alone is the next world a source of happiness.
For those of low birth who remain in the objects of the senses, there is only pleasure in this very world;
but for householders established in austerity and dharma, there is constant happiness in both worlds.
Therefore, we, abiding in the Dharma, should enjoy happiness here;
thus, having always partaken of the pleasures of garments and ornaments, we [shall remain]. (69)
Having fully observed the duties of a householder, and having practiced service to our husband and worship of the gods,
we shall attain the two unsurpassed worlds.
Therefore, O Brahmins, you should take possession of land here from the king, and having accepted both a livelihood and beautiful houses, [dwell here]. (71)
Then, having accepted [this], behold the arising of sons and grandsons, as well as the happiness of the daughters and especially that of your kinsmen. (72)
If you do not carry out these words spoken by us, we shall all give up our lives; of this there is no doubt. (73)
"Endowed with the sin of killing a woman, you shall go to Raurava.
Having heard this, water was held upon the surface of the earth for the purpose of pronouncing the curse.
They abandoned her because of the words of their wives; she became addicted to the pleasures of the earth.
Then, having heard that news, the king rejoiced and arrived.
At the word of the brāhmaṇas, the king had a city constructed for the purpose of bestowing upon the brāhmaṇas wealth, lands, and treasures. (76)
Adorned with walls and moats, and beautified by gate-towers and rows of palaces,
that city was named Camatkārapura.
The king caused sixty-eight Brahmin householders to dwell there and provided them with a means of livelihood.
After that, Lakṣmī, Mādhavī, and Śāṇḍilī indeed arrived before long at the city on the Nāganadī river to see the town.
Having bathed, that virtuous woman Damayantī then sat for a moment upon the stone; she appeared like a woman restored to her former female form, as if born again.
Having paid homage to the Brahmin women, she departed for Rājagṛha as if just awakened from sleep, filled with joy; and the king held a great festival.
O beloved, he gave as a gift sixty-eight villages that bestow happiness,
as well as four other lineages of Brahmins.
And sixty-four remained there; they went to the Himalayas and properly performed sacrifices with abundant oblations and excellent sacrificial fees.
When the sacrifice was completed, the king became severely afflicted by a disease;
the cause of that was indeed a certain brahmin.
The offering of a substance touched by one born of three castes yields cruel results;
for the purpose of testing one born of three castes, water sanctified by fire is used as a divine ordeal.
A pit was shown there; he who experiences an eruption upon bathing therein should be recognized as a *trijāta*, for that is his lot. (86)
Having thus examined him, that brahmin was expelled and went to the forest;
there he performed penance while remembering Hara, and Hara became pleased.
"Choose a boon," Hara said; the Brahmin spoke to Śaṅkara:
"Having removed the defect of being born three times, grant me the highest and most exalted status. (88)
And Śaṅkara gave him the mantra "na garaṃ na garaṃ," by the mere utterance of which serpents likewise became devoid of poison. (89)
"They may even meet their death; therefore, take this mantra and go to that place.
Having taken this mantra, the twice-born man went to the city.
At that time, the twice-born residing in the city were indeed tormented by serpents;
however, those brahmins were protected on all sides by means of the mantra consisting of the three births.
All those Nāgaras who were present there—the Trijātas and others, the most excellent—were all devoted to Kṛṣṇa and were worshippers of Hāṭakeśvara. ||9 2||
Then they received the mantra from the god Hāṭakeśvara:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (9.3)
Men and women always performed worship and japa;
others went to Goloka, O beloved, and through such devotion they continue to go.
Thus has this marvel been narrated for the sake of ascetic brahmins;
by reading or hearing it, one's desired fruit shall be attained. (95)

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fall of the Sky-traveling Brahmins due to the Acceptance of Gifts of Jewels, Gold, and Other Valuables by Damayantī, the Wife of King Camatkāra; the Transformation of Damayantī into Stone through a Brahmin’s Curse, and Her Return to Royalty and Residence in the City upon the Touch of Mādhavī," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the divine and heart-pleasing story of Bhadrikā;
and listen to me as I relate the divine story of Revatī. || 1 ||
In Camatkārapura, the Nāgas, out of devotion to Hāṭakeśvara,
indeed come from Pātāla and dwell here and there.
Once, a brahmin named Kratha struck a young elephant called Rudramāla with a club in the water for no reason.
"Alas, I am destroyed! cried that serpent, his mother, at that time;
likewise, other serpents arrived, assuming human forms. || 4 ||
That boy gave up his life; the serpents, enraged and terrifying, ran away for the sake of destroying the brahmin, and the brahmin fled toward the hermitage.
The fierce nāgas went and devoured him along with his family;
the sister of that brahmin was distressed by the sorrow of widowhood from her childhood.
Then the virtuous female ascetic named Bhadrikā, devoted to celibacy and dedicated to devotion to Kṛṣṇa, cursed the Nāginī.
"O Revatī, mother of the Nāgas, may you and your entire lineage meet with destruction!
Having received this curse, Revatī propitiated Pārvatī. (8)
Then, after a few days had passed, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, being pleased with her,
said, "I am a granter of boons," whereupon Revatī requested a boon.
"Bhadrikā prayed, 'May my curse be destroyed,' but Pārvatī said, 'The destruction of the curse shall never occur.'"
But that serpent Takṣaka shall indeed become King Raivata in Saurāṣṭra;
he will be born in the region of Ānarta, and Kṣemaṅkarī will be his beloved wife.
A daughter shall be born to the two of them, and you will become human;
at that time, Śeṣa himself will become your husband there.
For the sake of obtaining a boon for you, my departure toward Brahmā will last but a moment; indeed, it is there that the expansion of your lineage shall take place.
Thinking thus, "He will meet his destruction," the lineage will come to an end;
yet, your marriage with Balarāma will take place once more.
Furthermore, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa will bring about the destruction of his own lineage.
Indeed, by the curse of Kaṇva, the curse will bear fruit there in this very manner.
Having been addressed thus, Revatī departed for Pātāla itself and reported the remainder of the events that had occurred on earth to Śeṣa.
Then there was a certain widow, a virtuous woman named Bhadrikā.
He heard discourses on the scriptures from the mouth of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He undertook pilgrimages to sacred fords and showed devotion to Nārāyaṇa.
Then, on one occasion, Takṣaka arrived upon the surface of the earth.
Having seen the beautiful Bhadrikā on the bank of the Nāgavatī,
he led her to Pātāla in human form, and Bhadrikā likewise led him there.
"Having become human, you shall experience suffering that brings about the destruction of your lineage along with your wife and children.
Takṣaka, overcome by fear, then offered praise to that auspicious lady.
Bhadrikā said, "Lead me back to that spot on the earth.
Then she was brought by Takṣaka toward Camatkārapura;
subsequently, due to public scandal, she entered the funeral pyre.
While the elders of the people were looking on, when Bhadrī was not burned, the horse Romaśa was likewise unharmed; the people were struck with wonder. (23)
The fire indeed became cool because that auspicious lady was pure;
then, a great rain of flowers fell from the surface of the sky.
The gods said: "O Subhadrā, you abide in supreme purity;
there shall be no other virtuous woman equal to you.
There are thirty-five million hairs upon a human being."
Among them, O virtuous lady, not even a single one of them ever committed a sin. ||26||
And you, having become a virtuous and chaste wife devoted to your husband Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, became a renunciant goddess who took refuge in Sāṃkhya and Yoga. 27.
"Serve the virtuous, perform meritorious deeds, and worship Keśava.
Having heard this regarding Lord Janārdana, Bhadrikā made her request;
at that moment, Kṛṣṇa, having assumed the form of a brahmin, descended to the surface of the earth.
He gave her the auspicious initiation and placed a garland of *tulasī* around her neck.
Having uttered the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ" three times into her ear, the twice-born sage vanished from sight.
Bhadrikā constantly worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
there she performed supreme penance, subsisting only on food obtained through alms.
And on the Nāga River, there arose an excellent holy ford (tīrtha) named after him called Bhadrikātīrtha;
it is wondrous, for by bathing there, one becomes free from sin. ||32||
Then that Bhadrikā, having reached her end, became possessed of a divine body and went to the abode of liberation, the realm of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||33||
O Lakṣmī, when this is so, the power of truth bestows liberation and destroys sin;
it certainly arises through devotion to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—of this there is no doubt. (34)
O Lotus-born One, by reading, hearing, or even reciting this, one shall obtain enjoyment, liberation, excellent prosperity, health, and lordship. (35)

Thus ends the four hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mother of the Nāgas becoming Revatī due to the curse of the Brāhmaṇī named Bhadrikā, Takṣaka’s attainment of human form, and the liberation of Bhadrikā through devotion to Kṛṣṇa," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of Karṇotpalā, the wife of Brahmā. In ancient times, there was a lord of the earth renowned as Satyasandha.
He had a daughter named Karṇotpalā who protected the dharma;
she was a partial incarnation of Lakṣmī, equal to Kamalā by her marks and lines.
Seeing that young woman who was worthy of being chosen as his bride, the lord of the earth reflected repeatedly: "To whom shall I give her?"
"There is no suitor equal to her here upon the surface of the earth, nor in heaven, nor in the netherworld; therefore, I shall go to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
In this matter, Brahmā will certainly show me the one who is the suitable groom."
I shall give my daughter to him alone, and certainly not to anyone else under any circumstances.
Then, taking his daughter with him, he went to the world of Brahmā;
and for a moment, Brahmā, the Lord of the World, became intent upon the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
At the conclusion of the worship, that king, true to his promise, having respectfully prostrated before Brahmā along with his daughter, spoke with humility: || 7 ||
"O father, I have arrived from the mortal world into your presence;
I am the king Satyasandha, renowned throughout the land of Ānarta. (8)
"This daughter of mine, named Karṇotpalā, is a portion of Kamalā;
a husband worthy of her is not to be seen anywhere else in the world."
"Therefore, tell me her husband, so that I may give her to him.
Having heard this, Brahmā said to him: "Listen, O King, regarding Vṛṣa."
A daughter should be given in every way to one born of a noble lineage, who is senior in age,
for the sake of dharma, fame, and the prosperity of the family.
This daughter of yours, having attained the status of the eldest among mortals, has brought about the old age of all the rulers of the earth; hear now the reason for that.
Three ages have passed for you who have come into my presence,
O King— those mortals on earth whom you previously beheld.
Another creation has now arisen upon the surface of the earth;
however, those great sages who abide here in my world of truth (Satyaloka), [remain]. || 14 ||
Indeed, they do not by any means make a human woman their wife, for she is a most contemptible receptacle for phlegm, urine, and excrement. (15)
If this maiden, through her ascetic penance, effects a change of body,
Kāmadeva will take your daughter, who possesses a divine form.
"O Indra among kings, go therefore from here to the world of mortals with your second wife, named Prīti, who has attained even greater delight than Rati."
"Your daughter must be given to Kāmadeva at the appointed time. Having been told this, he returned to the earth together with his daughter. (18)
As he looked, he saw reservoirs of water in places where there should be dry land,
and various wonderful masses of dry land produced in places where there should be water.
Even when questioning others about other worlds and the dharmas established in that region, he does not understand his connection with anyone.
Sons, grandsons, as well as servants, elephants, horses, and so forth—all those kinsmen have met their destruction in another age. (21)
Then, at that very moment, touched by the mortal wind,
both that lord of the earth and the maiden became seized by old age, with their hair turned white.
With broken teeth, covered in wrinkles, deformed, and withered in body; they had become utterly unattractive, with sunken eyes, and were ancient in appearance. ||23||
But that king, being in such a state and trembling at every step, asked his attendants: "What country is this? What city is this? (24)
Then the people said to him: "The country is named Ānarta;
there resides a king called Bṛhadbala, and the city is Prāptipura. (25)
"This river is named Śubhramatī, and this bathing place is called Gartātīrtha"—
hearing these other names, the king was filled with wonder.
After bathing in the river, that king grieved for a moment and then set out toward Bṛhadbala, who was present there, accompanied by his daughter.
Satyasandha said to him, "O King, understand my conduct:
in former times, I was known as Satyasandha, the lord of Ānarta. (28)
I have a virtuous daughter named Karṇotpalā;
she dwells with me, equal to Lakṣmī and a portion of Ramā herself. (29)
Therefore, for the sake of giving her away, I have come from here to Satyaloka;
having gone there, I stood for a moment before the divine Grandfather (Brahmā).
O King, many more yugas have indeed passed here while I remained in Satyaloka until I beheld the surface of the earth.
All water has turned into land, and forests have become cities;
everything appears as if unknown to me, yet it is perceived by men. (32)
O Lakṣmī, having heard your name as it was bestowed upon you and your lineage from former ancestors, King Bṛhadbala has come into your presence.
Having heard that he had arrived there and having seen him come, he became extremely overwhelmed;
with eyes filled with tears of joy, he fell at his feet. (34)
He said, "Welcome, O King; a most hearty welcome, O Father!
This kingdom, which was once my own, has been protected by me as your servant. (35)
"O father, give gifts according to your will and rule your own kingdom.
Then that king, having embraced his own descendant, [spoke to] the prince.
Smelling him on the head, he sprinkled him with eyes full of tears and said:
"The kingdom has been enjoyed by me; much charity was given in the past. (37)
I have performed sacrifices, foremost among them the horse-sacrifice, with complete sacrificial fees;
therefore, I shall practice penance together with this daughter of mine.
Bṛhadbala said to him: "O King, do as you wish!
This great kingdom is yours alone; either take it or practice asceticism. (39)
O Indra among kings, I have heard all this through tradition:
the king Satyasandha departed, taking the maiden with him.
Furthermore, after he had not returned for a long time, his son named Suhaya was consecrated as king by his excellent ministers.
I am the seventy-seventh descendant of his lineage; I am that person who shall be your deliverer. Blessed am I by the sight of you! (42)
O Grandfather, perform penance at the Garta-tīrtha together with my daughter, so that I, along with my attendants, may eternally serve your feet. (43)
"I shall undoubtedly attain the highest good; let favor be granted.
Then the subjects, the brahmins, and the men and women born in the kingdom [spoke thus].
Filled with curiosity, they came to see him who is true to his promise;
offering their blessings, they honored him with joy.
Then the king and the maiden, having reached the riverbank,
constructed a leaf-hut there and both performed supreme austerity.
Having installed Gaurī there, Karṇotpalā constantly worshipped her with devotion, and then the king likewise worshipped Śaṅkara.
Mahādeva himself, satisfied and with a gracious countenance, arrived;
he said to the king, "By means of austerity, merit increases exceedingly. (48)
"Tell me, what shall I give you here? The king chose liberation;
Śambhu replied, "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself [grants] supreme liberation. (49)
The Lord will give you; take this garland of *tulasī*.
Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Master.
Having said, "Accept the mantra," Śambhu gave him the mantra and a rosary;
then he vanished, and the king worshipped and chanted the name of Mādhava.
Then King Vṛhadbala met his death;
meanwhile, Satyasandha had bestowed means of livelihood and other provisions upon the brahmins.
When the day had passed in this manner, Gaurī became pleased with the girl and spoke to her directly: "O daughter, I am satisfied; tell me what you desire."
Karṇotpalā said: "For my sake, my father has undergone great suffering;
he was deprived of his kingdom and his family while searching for my husband. (54)
Through dispassion I performed austerities and became an old maiden;
then, O Gaurī, out of compassion for me, you made me young and fresh again.
"Act so that I may become beautiful, endowed with form and youth;
likewise, let my husband be some most excellent among the best of gods. (56)
"O Mother, act in such a way that my father may be satisfied, so that I may be endowed with beauty, youth, and the like, and live for a long time. (57)
Gaurī said: "On the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, on a Saturday, under the asterism presided over by Vasu, one attains youth. (58)
O beautiful one, while you were bathing in the river after having mentally envisioned a form,
you then became possessed of a divine body, endowed with fresh youth.
You will become [liberated], there is no doubt; worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord. (1.500.60)
Always recite this mantra and likewise perform meditation on Hari;
through penance and devotion you shall obtain everything desired—spend but a moment [in this].
Having spoken thus and having given the mantra of Kṛṣṇa along with a garland of tulasī, Gaurī vanished; and the maiden acted exactly as she had been instructed.
On the third lunar day, conjoined with the yoga of Śani and associated with the constellation of Vasudeva,
one should meditate upon [the deity] who possesses a form identical to his own, as well as fresh good fortune and youth.
At that very moment, as she entered the water at midnight,
she emerged from the water, endowed with the beauty of fresh youth.
Then, indeed, Kāmadeva himself, commanded by the illustrious Brahmā and filled with affection, came for the sake of a wife and spoke to her: ||65||
Sent by Brahmā and endowed with the form of fresh youth,
and permitted by Pārvatī, I have come here for your sake.
"I am indeed Kāmadeva, the long-lived lord of Rati;
my wife is named Prīti. Become mine forever; do not delay. (67)
"Karṇotpalā said: 'Go, my dear, and entreat my father himself for me;
for a maiden never has her own will in the presence of her father. (68)
"There, having gone ahead, I shall remain as a beautiful maiden;
and you, arriving afterwards, will joyfully entreat me. (69)
Having spoken thus and prostrating before him, the maiden departed to her father.
Then her father, beholding his daughter in the full bloom of youth, [reflected].
Filled with wonder, he asked the cause of her beauty and youth.
The maiden said, "O father, by the grace of Gaurī, through the mere act of bathing. (71)
Having obtained a beautiful form in the river, as well as youth and a fresh body,
she likewise worshipped her beloved Lord Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The Goddess has obtained everything, and by Brahmā, a husband has been secured for my sake—one adorned with beauty, charm, splendor, and youth. (73)
That Sundara, bearing flower-arrows, has also been sent to your presence;
seeing him arrive, accept me and be happy. (74)
Thus addressed, the father, beholding his daughter who was like Kamalā, said:
"O daughter, today the fruit of my ascetic penance has been realized."
In the meantime, Kāma approached the king;
having bowed, he said: "O King, give me your beautiful daughter. (76)
Commanded here by Brahmā and likewise approved by Pārvatī, I, Kāmadeva, have come in person for the purpose of choosing [you]. (77)
Then he offered that maiden into the presence of the Fire;
and she, through her devotion to Rati, became his beloved named Prīti.
Having taken her away, Kāma went to the world of Kāma, which is like that of the gods;
Satyasandha too, his heart rejoicing upon seeing his daughter filled with happiness, was himself endowed with bliss. (79)
United with her beloved husband, she indeed became one who had accomplished all that was to be done;
the knower of yoga, having firmly established the lotus posture, [attained success] through the aperture of Brahma.
He drew his self out from the body together with Brahmā and went to where that beautiful daughter, the maiden, was located in the world of Kāma.
Therefore, having taken that second maiden who possessed a beautiful form and other qualities,
and having given her as a single form to Kāma, he [assumed] another body.
The king, having been liberated, took his daughter Muktā along with his attendants and, together with the liberated associates of Hari, attained the eternal abode of Goloka. ||83||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Karṇotpalā, through devotion and likewise through austerity, became the personification of love, the wife of Kāma, and was liberated, attaining liberation. (84)
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Mādhava, was propitiated by the queen of Bṛhadbala in the form of a brahmin for the sake of obtaining a son.
Having approached, she bestowed upon him a mental conception in an instant;
the son born from Nārāyaṇa became one who remembered his former births. ||86||
Though his lifespan was only twenty years, he was equal to Nārāyaṇa in virtues; he was a treasury of wonders such as mastery in archery, the Vedas, and other branches of knowledge. (87)
There was a king of Camatkāra named Aṭacandra;
whoever should hear this, or likewise cause it to be heard with a spirit of devotion, [shall attain success]. (88)
One attains the complete accomplishment of the fourfold aims; of this there is no doubt.
A maiden or a woman likewise always obtains good fortune and remains full of joy. (89)
One obtains enjoyment, liberation, prosperity, a son, grain, wealth and the like, good fortune, and a mass of merit; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the five-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of King Satyasandha’s Daughter Karṇotpalā—Who is a Portion of Kamalā—Traveling to the World of Brahmā to Seek a Husband, and Then Returning to Earth to Become the Wife of Kāmadeva under the name Prīti, and Her Liberation in a Second Form," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the captivating story of the sage Yājñavalkya.
There was a tiger among Brāhmaṇas, renowned as Śākalya. || 1 ||
Born in the lineage of Bhṛgu, a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
he resided in the city of Vardhamāna within the Dharmāraṇya forest, accompanied by his disciples and grand-disciples.
He was a constant giver of the gift of knowledge, adorned by the attainment of yogic powers and other such qualities;
Yājñavalkya became his disciple, devoted to his service.
And Śākalya was indeed the family priest of King Vardhamāna;
he performed the duties of the priesthood in all the king's affairs.
And at dawn, he urges Yājñavalkya, his most excellent disciple, to bestow blessings; and Yājñavalkya, too, does so constantly.
Filled with joy, he would go in the morning after bathing for the purpose of bestowing blessings;
however, on one occasion, he went without having bathed, clad in soiled garments.
At dawn, the teacher Yājñavalkya was indeed present;
he said this to Yājñavalkya: "Go quickly to the king. (7)
Thus he engaged him for the sake of peace in the royal palace;
Yājñavalkya then departed after performing the recitation for peace following his prayers.
He went toward that king to offer the water of pacification;
the king, too, became apprehensive upon seeing the sage without his bath.
On that day, he neither took water nor accepted words of blessing;
and the king spoke an untruth, saying, "O best of the twice-born, I have not bathed."
"Since you are unable to speak the truth regarding the sage who has not yet bathed,
pour this water upon the piece of wood here in the hall."
Yājñavalkya, having understood the reason for his own lack of bathing and recognizing it as an insult directed at himself, threw water upon the wooden post.
At that very moment, by the power of the touch of the water, the wood became covered with sprouts and was instantly endowed with branches and fruit. (13)
Having witnessed this wonder and having felt remorse, the king spoke these words again: "O Sage, it is true that I have bathed, but [only] in your [words]. (14)
Seeing that very filth [of yours], he did not take it out of fear;
therefore, O Brahmin, perform my consecration so that I may have a son.
Then Yājñavalkya said: "O King, you are full of doubt;
at present, you are unworthy of receiving my consecration. (16)
O King, spiritual preceptors are always pure, as are virtuous Brahmins, whether they have performed ritual ablutions or not; for they are the very body of Lord Hari.
Even there, if there are wise men, or those possessed of sovereign power, or perfected beings (siddhas), or Brahmins, or gods, or radiant celestial dwellers; || 18 ||
Even those who have attained mastery over mantras, mastery over Brahman, or mastery through austerity are not purified by bathing, if they have engaged in sexual union with women.
In that regard, one should never perceive purity in a guru, a saintly person, a deity, Lord Hari, a father, a mother, a husband, a virtuous woman, or a cow. (1.501.20)
Desire, anger, greed, harshness, latent impressions, and passion—all these are to be understood as divine there; for one who is capable, there is no fault. ||21||
For the earth, though defiled, becomes purified by his touch;
even the water of the streets, when mixed with the Ganges, destroys sin like the waters of the Ganges themselves. 22.
One who eats only what is granted by the grace of Viṣṇu is indeed considered a Guru liberated while living;
he is constantly devoted to austerity, pure, peaceful, and learned in the scriptures.
The guru is the purifier of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
the father is considered the most venerable among all those worthy of worship. (24)
The mother is a hundred times more venerable than the father; the deity (or spiritual teacher) is a hundred times more venerable than the mother;
and the giver of mantra and the giver of tantra is four times more venerable than the deities.
The Guru is supreme, the destroyer of heaps of sins and the bestower of liberation;
indeed, the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself should be regarded as the Guru. (26)
And here, the Lord Īśvara himself becomes the savior and the master;
it is heard in the Śruti that he is designated as "the god" (surāya). 27.
The embodied Janārdana himself is one's own guru, the direct enjoyer;
the guru is Brahmā, the guru is Viṣṇu, and the guru is indeed Śiva himself. (28)
All the gods and others always reside joyfully in the guru;
when the guru is pleased, Hari is pleased, and when he is pleased, the deities are pleased. (29)
Purified like fire and wind, equal to the sun in brilliance,
a worshiper of the mantra of Viṣṇu— such indeed is the Vaiṣṇava brahmin who is a guru.
Upon seeing a radiant guru, one should indeed receive everything—
mantra, water, prasāda, and blessings— without any hesitation.
The Guru, who is the exclusive deity for men, can uplift a hundred thousand;
he whose auspicious and inauspicious actions have been offered at the feet of Viṣṇu. (32)
Merely by receiving the mantra, one becomes liberated while living;
having shattered the entire cosmic egg, one reaches the abode of Hari.
"O King, you have been deceived today by my artifice and are suspicious of me;
therefore, water shall not be given to you again while you remain in such suspicion. (34)
Especially when one begs after seeing a gain for one's own sake, the sages must not give to such a self-interested person or to an atheist. (35)
Therefore, O King, you are no longer a fit recipient for the bestowal of consecration;
I shall go to that very place where my guru resides. (36)
The king said to Yājñavalkya: "If you grant me the consecration, I shall give you garments, vehicles, and riches. (37)
The sage said: "Indeed, that mantra does not flash forth for me at the conclusion of the fire-oblation;
therefore, water of such power is never produced again. (38)
"I am going home, O King; what you desire cannot happen today.
Having said this, the best of sages quickly departed for his own abode. (39)
And on the following morning at dawn, Śākalya himself went to bestow his blessings upon the king; then the monarch [received him].
Having prostrated before the sage, he said: "That disciple who was previously sent by you should be sent again to my house for the sake of peace."
Having replied, "So be it," the Guru took the offerings of worship, summoned Yājñavalkya, and spoke to him again with respect. ||42||
Even now, go to the palace for the sake of the king's peace;
especially, my son, you have been summoned by the lord of kings.
Then Yājñavalkya said: "O King, there is a certain twice-born man who is an atheist;
he is full of pride. Therefore, I shall certainly not go there again."
When I raised the water for his consecration, that evil-minded one said, "Pour that water on a piece of wood! (45)
I too quickly threw water upon the wood, and then the wood immediately sprouted new leaves; seeing this, the king fainted.
Śākalya said: "Having observed your capability, that king is calling for you again; go to him with honor."
Kings who follow [the path of righteousness] must always be supported and never disparaged;
for servants will eventually mount even a king who shakes them off, albeit slowly. 48.

One who understands the minds of others, who always knows the proper time for both honor and dishonor, who is all-enduring, patient, and wise—such a person indeed becomes a favorite of the king. ||49||
"My command must also be obeyed by you; go, my son, toward the king.
Yājñavalkya then replied, "I will not go before an atheist."
O true Guru, listen: the destruction of the Dharma occurs here in four ways.
O Guru, there is indeed a sequence for which disciple it applies today. (51)
The refutation of that [proposition] is the first fault; the second is the fault of violating the proper order; and "I shall not go" is the fault consisting of the negation of my own statement. (52)
"The third [fault] that arises here for me is the defect of failing to fulfill the king's desire;
the fourth consists of the defect regarding the fruit. Therefore, that must not be done by me. (53)
Thus, if you should force me toward him by compulsion, I shall abandon you and go elsewhere; I will not go toward him.
Thus addressed, Śākalya became filled with anger and spoke to him:
"Having understood not even a single syllable from my teacher, you have gone beyond me! (55)
There is no fee on earth by giving which a disciple may become free from debt;
therefore, either obey my command or abandon my science.
"If I do not give [it], I shall cast a curse upon you; go elsewhere as you please.
Having been addressed thus, Yājñavalkya then disgorged that knowledge.
Having bowed to her teacher, she said: "Behold the knowledge I have vomited forth;
not even a single syllable of yours remains within my belly. (58)
Therefore, I am not your disciple, nor do you stand as my guru.
Now, by my own will, I shall depart elsewhere; salutations be to you! (59)
Having spoken thus, he indeed came to the field named Hāṭakeśvara, which bestows spiritual perfection, and there he propitiated the Sun-god.
Restrained, restricted in his diet, and devoted to the life of celibacy,
he performed difficult austerities after having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Gāyatrī.
The Sun, being pleased with that mortal, spoke to him at the end of a year:
"O Yājñavalkya, choose whatever you desire; the Sun will grant it all to you. (62)
Yājñavalkya, having prostrated himself, requested the Vedic knowledge,
as well as other forms of knowledge pertaining to mantras and tantras, the knowledge of Brahman, and the supreme knowledge.
The Sun said, "I shall indeed grant you the supernatural power of levitation (laghimā-siddhi).
Having become light, enter into the vicinity of my horses' ears and remain there. (64)
"Quickly undertake the practice of the Vedic sciences from me.
Thus addressed by him, he then took refuge at Vājikarṇa.
While the Vedas were not being recited from the Sun,
that sage taught them to the assembly of Janaka and bestowed the knowledge of Brahman upon his two wives.
Maitreyī was the first and eldest wife, and Kātyāyanī was the second;
Yājñavalkya had these two wives, and his son was Kātyāyana. (67)
In the end, she taught all branches of knowledge to Kātyāyanī;
once, Śāṇḍilī bestowed auspicious wisdom upon her.
On the bank of the Nāga river, she attained detachment;
that virtuous woman neither bathed nor ate, nor did she engage in laughter.
With her eyes filled with tears, she simply sighed;
and Śāṇḍilī gave her instruction every day.
Listen, O virtuous lady: my father was Śāṇḍilya, the best among sages;
I am his only daughter, born as a girl named Mādhavī. (71)
I perform the appropriate service for my father at the time of the fire-oblation;
I also regularly bring wild rice and other grains. (72)
Then, after some time, the sage Nārada arrived at my father’s hermitage; being weary, he was attended to by me.
Having been bathed, fed, and massaged with great devotion, he sat upon his seat and was then questioned by his mother with humility. (74)
"O Sage, this one daughter of ours remains in our old age;
therefore, quickly proclaim for her a husband who brings about great happiness. (75)
"Whether it be a vow, a restraint, austerity, a fire-oblation, or recitation;
or a mantra—by the performance of which a husband may become gentle and endowed with excellent qualities. (76)
Affectionate, with a serene countenance, speaking kindly and indifferent to his own pleasure or displeasure,
the venerable Nārada, having heard this, spoke of the supreme worship of Gaurī.
"Having gone to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara, let your daughter perform [the rites];
by the blessing of Gaurī, your daughter will obtain a husband. (78)
There, Gaurī first went to the auspicious place out of jealousy toward Gaṅgā;
then she reflected: "Which goddess shall I worship? (79)
Thinking, "So that other women may always worship me for the sake of good fortune," she worshipped herself with devotion. (1.501.80)

Having fashioned his own image out of clay and placed it upon a single seat in one location, he [should worship] with the Ātharvaṇa mantras pertaining to the self, the vital breaths, and the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra). ||81||
Having joined herself with these— the earth, water, fire, air, and space—
in embodied form, that female ascetic remained firm in her vows.
He worshipped Gaurī with flowers, incense, and unguents;
indeed, Śaṅkara, his mind drawn by her mantras, went there with haste.
"O Goddess, drawn by your power, I have come as Gaurī;
why do you perform this worship of your own form? (84)
Gaurī forcibly draws me into your presence;
therefore, come to Kailāsa and tell me if there is any fault in me. (85)
Pārvatī said: "You carry Gaṅgā on your head together with her husband;
therefore, I will not go until you abandon your beloved. (86)
Śambhu said: "King Bhagīratha, having performed most rigorous penance, indeed entreated me for the sake of bringing down the Gaṅgā."
Perceiving me as I fell from the sky toward the surface of the earth with the force of the Gaṅgā,
and destined to go to the netherworld (pātāla), he employed me.
Right here, for the sake of the Gaṅgā’s abiding, she was thus supported by me;
then, resting upon my head, that auspicious river gradually reached the Himālaya, her blessed home.
She will certainly go to Bhārata for the purification of embodied beings;
having made her into the form of water, I shall give her to you, my father.
"Come to me, my dear, beloved; may you always possess good fortune.
You need not fear rivalry from co-wives, for she has not been married by me. (91)
Neither a wife, nor a female slave, nor any other woman who might be considered my spouse has taken refuge here; therefore, come to my very home.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva caused Śivā to mount the bull;
then, having mounted it himself, he departed for Mount Kailāsa.
Let him quickly propitiate this Gaurī, your daughter;
then he shall obtain a virtuous husband who brings him joy and fulfills his every desire.
Having spoken these truthful words, Nārada then departed for the higher world.
By me and by Kumārī, Gaurī was worshipped with devotion during the vow.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, by means of food offerings, perfumes, and unguents, this Brāhmaṇa Jaimini attained lordship through its power. 96.
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too should worship her with a concentrated mind;
O beautiful lady, you will attain great good fortune equal to that of Maitreyī.
Having heard everything that was proclaimed by Śāṇḍilī, Kātyāyanī performed the vow of Mārga-tṛtīyā and the worship of Gaurī. ||98||
Then her husband, having arrived and taken her by the right hand, led her to his own home with great honor. (99)
Thereafter, he always lived with her joyfully,
even more so than with Maitreyī.
Kātyāyanī gave birth to the excellent son Kātyāyana;
and the son of Kātyāyana was Vararuci, who was an abode of virtues.
O Lakṣmī, listen to the power of Kātyāyana as I tell it to you: long ago, there arose from the earth a certain moving being composed of living breath. (102)
He was unprecedented, fierce, dark-toothed, and terrifying;
he had spike-like ears, a thin face, upright hair, and was ravenous.
Drawn by the powerful king with mantras, that great and mighty being then rushed again and again toward the gods to devour them.
Abandoned by Bali and repeatedly struck by the gods,
it nevertheless suffered no injury even when cast down upon the surface of the earth.
Then the gods, having become his attendants, sat down all around him;
Brahmā entered his belly, while Śakra and the others stood at his sides.
At that time, commanded by Śukra, the Daityas arrived with their wings spread in order to slay the gods;
meanwhile, Viṣṇu himself, the Lord, [appeared].
He spoke the truth: "Listen, O Bhūta, for your sake; a battle between the gods and the Daityas will take place here, and that indeed shall not be auspicious."
"May the gods and the Daityas abide in you as a living being, like friends. I shall thus perform your worship; you are considered by name to be Vāstu.
Therein, I offer you food; please accept it with devotion."
Then, with an unwavering mind, he made this vow:
"And it was said: 'Any human being whatsoever who shall not offer me worship on this new ground, he shall become my food.'"
When he had said, "So be it," Viśvakarman performed the ritual;
Kātyāyana then constructed the house and worshipped the site (vāstu).
Kātyāyana performed the entire Vāstupūjā;
thereafter, the worship was established in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara. 11.3.
In that way, one shall not incur any defect whatsoever from [a house] built on a site born of a stone, or born of a bad spot, or even born of a bad foundation. 1.14.
In ancient times, on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, there was a worship of Vāstu;
at that time, the house of the one who performs this worship becomes equal to a kingdom. 115.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have narrated to you this most excellent of accounts, which bestows enjoyment, liberation, great good fortune, a husband, sons, and more. (116)

Thus ends the five-hundred-and-first chapter, titled "The Description of Yājñavalkya, the Disciple of Śāṇḍilya, Turning Dry Wood into Sprouts; the Emission of Knowledge; the Marvels of Yājñavalkya and his Son Kātyāyana; and the Worship of the Vāstu-Puruṣa," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 501 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, in ancient times there was a sage named Hārīta;
he was a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and his wife was named Pūrṇakalā.
Seeing that virtuous and devoted wife, who was adorned with beauty, nobility, and youth,
and who resembled Lakṣmī herself, the god Kāmadeva became infatuated.
Seeing the two women bathing naked and having abandoned their joy and passion,
he considered that place secluded and slept for a moment on the bank.
Sighing repeatedly,
he displayed great longing as he stood within her sight, like a person who is sick and dejected.
She too, perceiving a certain auspicious, destitute beggar in such a state, approached his side to give him some fruit and a meal.
At that time, Kāma stood in the prime of youth, radiant like fire;
his eyes were filled with passion, he was firm, and beautiful in every limb.
In a mere moment, he became full of passion and affectionate;
and Pūrṇakalā, seeing him thus impassioned in that secluded place, [was likewise moved].
Her body trembling from the exertion caused by the act of biting,
she was quickly pierced by his arrow and became filled with longing.
Having touched him and laughing repeatedly, that devoted wife sat down by his side,
being especially struck by the arrows of love.
Gazing at his lotus-like face, she traced the ground with her finger;
evening had arrived, yet Hārīta had not come.
Having learned this, he went for a long time to search for her where that virtuous woman was staying; yet even then, she did not grant him union.
Hārīta, seeing that virtuous and devoted wife thus deluded,
spoke to him who was causing her to be infatuated and was filled with passion.
Having understood the state of Kama's heart, he spoke out of anger:
"O wicked one, since my wife has been thus tormented by your arrows... (13)
"Unaware of this, that virtuous woman, devoted solely to her husband's duty, is being deceived;
for though he is handsome, he desires to enjoy my beloved. (14)
Therefore, afflicted by the disease of leprosy and having an unpleasant appearance, you will undoubtedly be abandoned even by your own wife. (15)
Thus addressed, he prostrated himself and spoke this reply to Hārīta:
"O Sage, I indeed saw your wife through mere delusion."
I have neither eaten [forbidden food] nor committed any misconduct now; therefore, I am not a fit object for a curse. Grant me forgiveness, O treasure-house of compassion! (17)
Sin is threefold—mental, vocal, and born of action;
may that mental sin which has entered me depart through remorse of mind.
But verbal [sin] perishes through mere recitation or simply by means of praise; it is destroyed precisely by propitiating him (the deity) in whom that [sin] was committed.
Through the prescribed expiations, one may go beyond the sin born of action;
that which is born of action includes what has been done, as well as that which is mental or verbal.
"By your grace, may [this] perish; be gracious in every way.
Hārīta spoke thus to Kāma, on account of the power of his own physical body.
First, everything is conceived by the mind; immediately thereafter, it is articulated by speech and then performed through action. (22)
For the mind is indeed the first [cause] in all actions and is therefore faulty; thus, its restraint here has also been effected by me. (23)
"By the very propitiation of the Sun, your leprosy shall depart;
this stone fragment here shall become my wife for a moment. (24)
"By the merit of worshipping the Sun, she shall become your virtuous wife.
Having said this, the sage Hārītaka departed for his own hermitage. (25)
Pūrṇakalā became a stone, and Kāma consequently became afflicted with leprosy;
he then performed worship on the bank of the Nāganadī while meditating upon the Sun.
At the end of the month, the Sun arrived and destroyed his leprosy caused by lust;
having touched the stone and restored his virtuous wife to her former state, he remained as he was before.
He gave the Nārāyaṇa mantra and the Sun departed toward heaven; Kāma went to the abode of Kāma, and Satī went to the house of Hārītaka.
Having then prostrated before her husband—who was in truth the purifier—the virtuous woman served him with devotion and took refuge in Nārāyaṇa Hari. 29.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
She constantly chanted this mantra and became a divine Vaiṣṇavī. (1.502.3)
Then, indeed, a maiden named Dīrghikā would constantly come from within the house into her presence for the purpose of service.
And that leaf-hut exists in close proximity;
thus, with this thought, he constantly remains at the foot of the tree in the courtyard, near Pūrṇakalā.
And on the altar within the hall, he recites the mantra of Śrī Hari:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye namaḥ* (Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance).
Thus, by the power of her recitation, the maiden indeed attained a divine body;
she became a traveler of the sky, possessing unobstructed siddhi. (34)
She became the daughter of the sage Vīraśānta, named Dīrghikā;
she was exceedingly tall in stature, causing laughter among the people. (35)
Seeing her to be exceedingly tall, with excessively short hair, yet also very tall and dwarfish, no one chose her as a bride.
He who performs the marriage will meet his death within six months; taking this as the reason, people do not accept her. (37)
Then, having attained dispassion, she performed most severe penance;
likewise, she repeatedly practiced the Cāndrāyaṇa and Kṛcchra vows. ||38||
She performed the Pārāka penances as prescribed, as well as the Sāntapana penances;
thus, while she remained established in her vows, her splendor increased greatly.
By the power of her asceticism, the capacity to travel through the sky was manifested;
consequently, she would go to the assembly hall of Mahendra during festivals and other such occasions.
When she departs from the assembly of the gods for her own home, the servants of Indra then perform the sprinkling of her seat with water. ||41||
Having seen this, she asked Purandara:
"O Śakra, perceiving what fault of mine is my seat being sprinkled by you?"
Indra said: "In you, though you have been born, there is indeed a physical defect;
for although you are a maiden, you have reached the censurable time of menstruation. (43)
And yet you are still unmarried; that impurity remains within you.
For women, union with a husband during the fertile period is indeed what brings about purification. 44.
"Therefore, choose as your husband one by whom you shall attain purity.
Having heard that, she went to the earth and [searched] at crossroads and triple-junctions.
Raising her right hand, she spoke for the sake of a boon:
"If there be any twice-born man by birth, let him take my hand. (46)
"I shall now give half of my ascetic merit to him.
As she spoke thus, the people laughed and joked with one another. (47)
A certain leper Brahmin said to the Dīrghikā:
"I shall marry you and take you as my wife. (48)
Then he took the hand of that maiden, and she then said to her husband: "Tell me, my lord, what service shall I perform for you? (49)
The husband said, "I intend to go to the sixty-eight holy places;
if you are able, do so with me as your companion."
Thinking, "Oh, what good fortune!", that devoted wife then quickly had a beautiful and easily accessible bamboo hut constructed.
Then, provided with a seat of soft cotton, she said to her husband:
"O Lord, mount me upon the top of this chest-like seat."
"I shall lead you to all the holy fords and auspicious sacred fields.
Thereupon, the leper, filled with joy, sat down in his small hut.
Placing him upon her own head, she wandered at her pleasure through all sacred fords and all holy fields, bathing her own husband.
From bathing at the sacred ford and through union with a virtuous woman, her husband’s leprosy was cured;
a constant reduction of the leprosy was observed, and his splendor increased. (55)
Thus, at the onset of night, she reached the field of Hāṭakeśa;
there, on the bank of the Nāgavatī, she took refuge in the shade of a tree with her basket. (56)
Having set her down, her husband rested on the riverbank;
and rising slowly in the morning, the one known as Māṇḍūkyi went to bathe.
As he moved along, leaping over a cluster of leaves with his staff, the king of sages, Māṇḍavya, was sleeping upon those very leaves. (58)
Touched by the foot of Māṇḍūkeya with a staff while he was staying between the leaves,
Māṇḍavya remained awake, being unaware of the path of his movement.
He said, "Who is this great fool who strikes me here with his foot and staff?
This sinful man causes the interruption of my sleep."
"May your death indeed be certain to occur even before sunrise!
Having heard this, Māṇḍūkya bowed down to him again and again. (61)
Nevertheless, this son of Māṇḍavī did not attain satisfaction;
however, the son of Māṇḍūkya, having bathed quickly, returned to the vicinity of the tree. (62)
He said to his wife: "Perform service as it has occurred; likewise, perform the final rites.
Due to the curse of Māṇḍavya, I shall die before the sun becomes visible. (63)
Then Dīrghikā said: "If my devotion to my husband is true—if I have performed pilgrimages according to the rules and served my husband with sincere heart—" (64)
"If all my vows of truth are true, may there be no sunrise here!"—
having spoken thus, he brought about the paralysis of the sun's horses in the expanse of the sky.
Suddenly, because of him, the sun did not rise;
a great night ensued for everyone in the absence of the rising of the sun.

All sacrificial rites and other ceremonies were obstructed and fell into extreme distress, as did the ancestral offerings, Vedic studies, acts of charity, and whatever religious duties there may be. (67)
All the supports of the sun were especially obstructed;
all the gods, intent on heaven, were deprived of their shares of the sacrifice.
Born, they were all distressed and went to where the Sun was;
they said, "O Lord, O Master, why indeed do you not rise? (69)
"Without you, this entire world has fallen into turmoil;
the Sun declared out of fear of her devotion to her husband: 'There shall be no rising for me.'"
Therefore, let all the gods go and speak to her on my behalf, so that by following their words I may attain prosperity and happiness. (71)
Otherwise, that devoted wife would surely curse me in her anger;
for that queen of the gods lives by the power of her devotion to her husband and her ascetic penance. (72)
Who would be able to act otherwise than according to her word?
For this reason, being afraid, I do not emerge at all. (73)
A woman who has attained the state of devotion to her husband realizes that fruit;
indeed, it is the very fruit that arises from a thousand horse-sacrifices. (74)
"Thus, because of her supreme application of asceticism, I am afraid of that woman devoted to truth.
Therefore, let the gods go quickly to where that faithful wife resides. (75)
Then the gods arrived and said to Dīrghikā:
"O devoted wife, since the sun, the maker of day, has been restrained by you."
"O auspicious lady, that which was beneficial has not been done; the rite dependent on the sun has failed.
Therefore, O wise one, let the sun rise at your word. (77)
"O auspicious one, from whom do sacrificial rites, recitation, and burnt offerings proceed?
Then Dīrghikā spoke out of anger toward Māṇḍavya: 78.
"My husband has indeed been cursed; he would die at sunrise.
Therefore, I have obstructed the sun from rising. (79)
Without my beloved, I have no need for the rising of the sun;
I have no need for funeral rites, acts of charity, or any other such duties.
Then those gods, having deliberated, spoke with humility:
"O auspicious lady, let the sun rise; he shall be this beloved husband of yours."
Having obtained a body free from deformity, he lived once more at that very moment, appearing like another Kāmadeva twenty-five years of age. (82)
And you, having become a fifteen-year-old maiden, shall behold this;
thus you will achieve the most excellent happiness in the world according to your own desire. (83)
At sunrise, your husband’s body has met its end;
we shall restore it to life again, so grant us the rising of the sun. (84)
Having been addressed thus, Satī agreed, saying "So be it," and spoke again:
"Just as the gods declare that the youth of a husband and wife is ever new. (85)
"By that truth, O Udaya Bhāskara, they shall bring about our rising.
As soon as this was said, the eastern quarter instantly became bright with dawn.
The entry of the dawn was visible upon the mountain of dawn;
at that moment, sunrise occurred, and the keeper of the lotus pond was killed.
Touched by the hands of the gods, he rose up once more,
twenty-five years of age, able to assume any form at will, and exceedingly beautiful.
Dīrghikā also became exceedingly beautiful at fifteen years of age;
she was divine, like a goddess, with a touch like that of a god, and equal to Kamalā. (89)
The gods spoke respectfully to that devoted wife who was with her husband:
"Choose a boon, O virtuous lady; there is nothing that cannot be granted to you."
She said: "From this day forward, let it be known throughout the three worlds and in the world by my own name as 'Dīrghikā,' the river-tirtha. (91)
"May I attain the abode of Hari, the imperishable place of liberation, together with my husband. "So be it," the gods said to her and departed. (52)
Then, having indeed enjoyed happiness for a long time, that devoted wife,
when she had reached her later years, beheld her beloved husband dead.
Together with him, this devoted wife went to the world of Brahmā.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this supreme Dīrghikā-vrata been described to you.
Through reciting, hearing, as well as by repeating and practicing it, both woman and man shall obtain worldly enjoyment and liberation; there is no doubt in this matter. (95)

Thus ends the five hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of how Kāmadeva was afflicted with leprosy when deluded by Pūrṇakalā, the wife of Hārīta; how Pūrṇakalā became a stone and was subsequently liberated; and how Dīrghikā, through the merit of serving her husband, paralyzed the sun and attained liberation along with him in fresh youth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the sage Jābāli, which brings about liberation.
Jābāli was the son of Jabālā, the servant-maid of a seer. || 1 ||
He was indeed born from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa,
by whom asceticism had always been practiced through lifelong celibacy since youth.
By performing the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and Pārāka penances gradually,
he has indeed brought the gods within the range of his fear.
Then the gods assembled and held a consultation regarding the obstacle; they dispatched Rambhā, who was capable of destroying his vow of celibacy.
Celibacy is rooted in austerity and is a great means for accomplishing perfection;
Jābāli has been a celibate since childhood and is great in his spiritual luster.
He who avoids union with women does not know the nature of desire;
and for the sake of disturbing him, the god Spring appeared likewise equipped with his weapons.
At the command of Indra, all the lords went to the land of Hāṭakeśvara and dispatched Kāma, Rati, and Prīti. || 7 ||
In the vicinity of Jābāli’s leaf-hut, Kusumākara suddenly brought about the great beauty of an Aśoka tree with a profusion of blossoms.
The Tilaka and mango trees attained supreme beauty through their clusters of blossoms and the like, while the lotuses on all sides reached a state of full bloom.
And a fragrant southern breeze, which kindles desire, began to blow;
in the meantime, Rambhā approached the presence of that sage.
The sage watched her as she, having cast off her garment,
entered the nearby water to bathe.
Beholding her unclothed, he fell under the sway of desire;
his entire body became covered with horripilation, and he was thereafter deeply agitated.
Rambhā, having emerged from the water and covered herself with half a garment,
approached the sage in her wet state and bowed down with a smile.
"O Brahmin, is all well in the hermitage? he asked sweetly.
The sage replied, "I am always well, and my welfare is secured by your arrival."
"Who are you, goddess or human, who increases my passion?
Rambhā replied: 'How is it that there is perspiration on your body and such a transformation? (15)
The sage said: "From the sight of you, sweat born of love has arisen within me, even though I am devoted to celibacy and abide in the great vow."
Rambhā said: "If it is so, then enjoy me as you please;
there would be no fault in this, since I am approaching you of my own accord. (17)
"I am an Apsaras, the wife of a celestial being; accept me, who am devoted to you.
For he who would reject a woman who has come to him of her own accord, tormented by desire—" (18)
"Consumed by the sighs of women, that person is utterly ruined.
Having spoken thus, she embraced the great sage.
Thus he took his pleasure with her until the end of the day;
then, having reached the time for departure, he dismissed her from there.
Having gone there, she said to the gods: "The great sage has indeed been agitated;
his entire ascetic merit has been destroyed. O Indra, may you become a partaker of happiness. (21)
Then she conceived the sage's child and gave birth to a girl;
and she departed for that place where the sage was once again performing penance.
Having led away the lotus-petal-eyed maiden whose face was as radiant as the moon,
he went before the rishi in his hermitage, released her there, and spoke these words.
Obeisance to you; please protect this divine daughter of yours, a maiden born of your own prowess whom I have conceived in my womb. (24)
Dwelling in heaven is not possible for humans in any way whatsoever;
for this reason, having given [this] to you, I shall go back to heaven once more. (25)
Having spoken thus, Rambhā departed, and Jābāli, filled with affection,
nurtured that girl with juices produced from sweet fruits.
He grew up together with the deer and played with the birds;
he also rendered assistance to that ṛṣi in all his tasks.
She constantly brought firewood, *kuśa* grass, and other materials from the forest;
once, she went far from her own hermitage for the sake of fruit. (28)
Then, a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, seated in a celestial chariot, emerged from the sky; having seen her, he descended and spoke to her.
"Who are you, O young maiden, that wanders alone in the forest?
The girl replied to Jābāli: 'I am indeed the maiden Phalavatī.'"
"Having come for the sake of fruits and flowers, my father is nearby.
Then Citrāṅgada said: "Your father is here without his wife."
"How indeed did a celibate youth bring you forth?
The maiden replied: "My mother was Rambhā, the most excellent of the Apsarases. (32)
Having attended upon the sage through that means, her father then obtained a daughter;
Jābāli is my father, and I was nourished by him with excellent flavors.
Then Citrāṅgada said: "O lady of beautiful hips, accept me;
I am a Gandharva named Citrāṅgada, a dweller of the third heaven. (34)
The maiden said: "I am a virgin and likewise remain under the authority of my father;
therefore, entreat my father, and he will bestow me upon you. (35)
"It is also pleasing to my heart that you are young and handsome.
Citrāṅgada said, "I am certainly not able to request such a thing."
"Who indeed knows what form that mind will take?
The maiden replied, "If this is so, what can I do without your command? (37)
"If my father should learn of you, he will surely consume both you and me as well"—as she was speaking thus, the impatient Citrāṅgada [replied]. (38)
The powerful one took her onto his lap and sported with her at the forest tree;
she too, pervaded by desire, delighted him repeatedly.
Having abandoned her divine nature and resorted to a state of passion,
she did not perceive that the day had passed and evening had come.
Then Jābāli, immersed in thought and overcome with grief,
realized at the onset of night that his daughter had not returned and was in distress.
He wandered everywhere through forest after forest, searching:
"Alas! Has she been devoured by tigers, or has she perhaps fallen from a tree? (42)
"Or was she submerged in fathomless waters, or perhaps forcibly taken away by another?
Thus lamenting, he wandered about, emaciated by grief.
Hearing a certain sound and thinking it was the girl, he went toward it;
then, at the foot of a tree, he heard a voice produced by the maiden.
Arriving there quickly, he saw his daughter along with the man;
overcome with rage, he seized a wooden staff and rushed toward that man.
"Fie, fie upon you, O sinful one! You have defiled the maidenhood of my daughter in the forest; O daughter, you have brought disgrace upon me in the world. (46)
Speaking thus, "Therefore, I shall destroy both him and you," just as he was about to hurl a blow, Citrāṅgada [appeared] in the sky.
And that maiden became invisible, naked and deprived of her power;
trembling with fear of her father, she sat down right there. (48)
The sage, having struck her with a blow of wood so that she fell to the ground, and thinking her dead, released her; and as he looked up into the sky—
Just then, Citrāṅgada was seen departing for heaven in a celestial chariot;
he was immediately cursed by the sage: "Become a leper and fall down here!"
But Gāndharva fell upon the earth and instantly became a leper;
he then said, "Grant me forgiveness; be compassionate toward my daughter. (51)
"That which has occurred is indeed as it is; for anger toward the virtuous is truly slight.
Then Jābāli, having considered him worthy of punishment, spoke to him.
Just as my daughter, so too shall you always remain without clothes;
both of you shall indeed always stay naked here upon the forest tree. (53)
"If you two had come elsewhere, your heads would surely have burst asunder.
Thus did those two receive the curse at the sacred field of Śrī Hāṭakeśvara.
Having thus restrained them right there, the sage went to his own hermitage;
meanwhile, at midnight during the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the Blessed Lord Hara [arrived].
By chance, he arrived in that forest to sport with the yoginīs;
at that time, both of them were likewise naked while singing.
And he performed a dance again and again with joy for the sake of Śambhu’s favor;
Śambhu, being pleased, then made this Gandharva free from disease.
Hara bestowed upon her the power of traveling through the sky and the status of being a member of his retinue;
she, for her part, accepted the state of a Yoginī and the ability to travel through the sky.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance!"—thus he gave this mantra to them and gave them a garland of tulasī. (59)
Through devotion, those two became Vaiṣṇavas at the Hāṭakeśvara Tīrtha;
and Jābāli, having been cursed by Citrāṅgada, was left naked.
"May you become like me, eternally an object of public derision!
Burned by this curse, he censured the woman. (61)
Alas! For sinful men, attachment to women indeed arises;
for what kind of suffering has come upon me through this single instance of association with a woman? (62)
"From birth until death, I have committed naked sin;
what then will be the destiny of those who are addicted to women?"—thus he reflected. (63)
While he was speaking thus, his daughter, a yoginī, said:
"This auspicious universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, is sustained by women. (64)
"How can you revile her, O father? One who reviles his father shall incur suffering.
The father replied: "Women are a constant source of misery in all circumstances. (65)
"In this world and even in the next, no happiness is obtained from them.
The daughter said to her father, "Indeed, you have neither wisdom nor self-restraint. (66)
How could even an outcaste perform such an act as you have done?
I have been struck by you repeatedly with blows from a wooden staff. (67)
No thought occurred to your heart regarding the sin arising from the killing of a woman, especially that of a daughter; what will become of your fate? (68)
"I am cursed that I shall always remain naked, and your sin shall be ever-renewed and exceedingly great, born from my sighs. (69)
"Even at the end of a kalpa, no end to it shall come for you;
therefore, O father, you must continue to eat in this very way due to the curse of the Gandharva."
Henceforth you will likely no longer censure them, nor will you strike them; all women are beyond reproach, for they can never be found at fault. (71)
"Indeed, month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their evil deeds.
The father said: 'Women are sinful; they are never purified. (72)
The daughter said: "It is certainly not so; listen to the injunction declared in the Vedas:
'Brahmins are pure from their feet, but cows are pure from their tails. (73)
"Goats are pure in their mouths, and women are pure in every part";
thus did the father speak, having set aside the fabricated scripture.
Brāhmaṇas are pure in every respect, and cows are pure in every respect;
even goats are pure in some instances, but women are never pure.
The daughter said: "In the house of one who has a loving wife, there is the wish-fulfilling gem and the desire-granting tree; Kubera himself is his servant. (76)
The father said: "All suffering resides in the home of that man who has a wife;
indeed, for him who has a lustful woman in his house, there is hell right here. (77)
The daughter said: "In this world, whatever pleasures and objects of enjoyment there are—those arising from dharma, artha, and kāma—they indeed come from women. (78)
The Father said: "Whatever sufferings and whatever hardships there are for embodied beings due to their sins, they indeed arise from women. (79)
The daughter said: "Through marriage and by circumambulating the sacred fire, a woman makes it certain that dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are attained."
The father said: Through marriage, a woman makes known through her delusions the wanderings in saṃsāra throughout birth after birth. (8.1)
