The daughter said: Having obtained a virtuous wife who accomplishes all goals, what embodied beings indeed would not be filled with passion—even those possessed of knowledge? (82)
The father said: "Those who are free from passion do not become attached, for they are established in the Self;
the deluded fall into them like moths into a flame. (83)
The daughter said: "The breasts, the hips, the loins, and the orb of the face are enjoyed by those who possess merit; others, however, are deprived of such fortune. (84)
The father said: "A line for destruction is visible upon his forehead;
those who possess such a mark must serve him, while others are the truly meritorious. (85)
The daughter said: "The touch, the sight, the arrangement, and the embrace of a woman are in every way givers of pleasure and destroyers of fatigue. (86)

The father said: "The touch of women and other such things are like sweet poison; attachment and the like grant only suffering in this creation, and they are the destroyers of the virtuous stages of life. (87)
The daughter said: "What woman is not wicked? Who is happy? Who is virtuous?
Indeed, who is not most desirable? And what group of women does not have a lover? (88)
The father said: "Is there no sinful man who, seen by a woman, would suffer? And who would not be held in contempt, he for whom a woman is dear? (89)
The daughter said: "Even for an insect, union with a woman is pleasing;
how much more so for a human, a god, and even for one possessed of knowledge?"
The father said: "To a worm, this impure body is pleasing because it is its own filth;
likewise, it is pleasing to a lustful man, but certainly not to any other virtuous person. (91)
The daughter said: How indeed did Brahmā himself create this noose in the form of a woman, which Brahmā himself experiences? 92.
How was Rambhā enjoyed by you? How was I, your own daughter, protected?
And how was she, who was betrothed to another, cursed—if indeed no price was considered? (93)
And how were you obtained by your mother through the service of Jabālā?
Behold then the price of a woman even in the hermitages of the sages! 94.
When you were being questioned by Yājñavalkya during his recitation, "Whose son are you?", you instead asked about your mother; at that time, she was your price. (95)
"Where indeed has that knowledge shown by the woman gone now?
You are truly the son of your mother; you are certainly not the son of your father. (96)
"O Father, those like you who revile a woman whose father is unknown always suffer in the Kālasūtra hell, for they are revilers of women. (97)
"O father, thinking that parents are always to be honored, you were not cursed by me; nevertheless, for this reason, you have been cursed here by means of a *gāndharva* [rite]. (98)
The fruit of our own actions has been obtained by you as well as by me;
a daughter should be given at the proper time to whomever she may be destined for. (99)
"By the turn of fate I have arrived here; what harm is there in following the Gandharva rite?
For I am an Apsaras maiden who has resorted to the Gandharva way. (1.503.10)
"What loss is there in this connection, or what gain indeed is there in a curse?
He acted without reflection and was filled with anger, being weak in wisdom. (101)
"Forgive my excessive words, for I am indeed to be conciliated.
Having said this, with eyes full of tears, she prostrated at his feet.
But the father, having become ashamed upon observing his daughter’s knowledge, said:
"Indeed, today I consider myself most blessed. (103)
"Since you, my daughter, have been born to me as one so expert in the scriptures, therefore my anger has now been appeased; O daughter, be happy."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed quickly toward his leaf-hut;
there, situated among the female yogis, he performed penance as a daughter.
Then, after some time, Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, arrived;
having assumed a divine form, he brought about her liberation.
The virtuous wife, devoted to her husband Nārāyaṇa, became four-armed;
Citrāṅgada went to his own hermitage in the world of the Gandharvas.
Then Jābāli, worshipping Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through his ascetic penance,
was liberated from the curse by the power of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
By the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace, she went to the supreme abode of Goloka;
what indeed is difficult to attain that one who has surrendered the self does not accomplish? (109)
That which is uncuttable, indestructible, invincible, and eternal—
he, having turned it back and made it new, bestows it upon those who have attained the state.
Even fortune as firm as a diamond it certainly renders lax;
yet devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa creates new fortune.
O Lakṣmī, all this has been told to you, which fulfills every desire for those who read it and listen to it, both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the five hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of how Phalavatī—the daughter produced by Jābāli through Rambhā—was turned into a naked Yoginī due to her father’s curse while enjoying the company of the Gandharva Citrāṅgada; how she remained near her father; her subsequent liberation through penance; and the dialogue and dwelling of the two on the Lotus Stone," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga lineage, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 503 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Lakṣmī, the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the two Aśvins, who are the lords of the gods,
should always be worshipped, for they are indeed the providers of acquisition and preservation.
Varuṇa, as well as Sūrya, Bhānu, and the scorching Pūṣan;
Indra, Aryaman, Dhātṛ, and likewise Bhaga. || 2 ||
Gabhasti and Dharmarāja—these are the ten Ādityas, plus two more:
Dharo, Dhruva, Soma, Makha, Anila, and Nala. (3)
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are indeed the eight Vasus by name;
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Mṛgīvyādha as the third.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the sixth; likewise Dahana, Kapālin, and Raivata as the ninth.
Vṛṣākapi and Tryambaka—these are the eleven Rudras;
and Nāsatya and Dasra, these two are the sons of Aśvinī.
These thirty-three are proclaimed as the leaders of the gods,
as well as of the Dānavas, the gods, and embodied human beings.
By him they should always be worshipped, and thus untimely death does not occur;
O beloved, on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, the Rudras should always be worshipped.
On the tenth day, the Vasus are to be worshipped, especially during the bright fortnight;
likewise, one should worship the Ādityas on the seventh and the sixth days.
Likewise, the two sons of Aśvinī should be worshipped on the twelfth lunar day with sixteen and other offerings;
the Rudras, being gratified, grant protection as well as the supreme state.
When worshipped, the Vasus indeed bestow luxuries and the like,
while the Ādityas, when propitiated through worship, truly grant sovereign power.
The two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, when worshipped, destroy all ailments;
they are the scribes who record the praises of the virtues of all beings, including the deities.
Vyāsa, however, is always to be honored as the Guru who bestows knowledge and liberation;
for even his son, named Śuka, was born of a parrot (śukī) and became Brahman.
Vedavyāsa indeed once had the desire for a wife;
therefore, he [sought] sons who would be capable leaders in the field of Vicitravīrya.
At the command of Satyavatī, that lord begot the Kauravas— Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vidura.
While remaining even in the stage of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he expanded his lineage;
then he reflected, "Today I shall take a wife."
Then he requested Jābāli, the bull among sages,
for his second daughter, the auspicious parrot named Ceṭikā.
Jābāli, however, gave him his own auspicious daughter as a maidservant;
she too became pregnant, yet the fetus would not come forth.
Twelve years have passed, yet he indeed does not emerge;
whatever the son hears while remaining within the womb, he hears it all. (19)
That Śukī shone with the splendors of her embryo like a source of the Vedas;
the embryo, too, held within its heart all knowledge and reflection.
By him the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, were heard as they were taught while still in the womb;
likewise, the Smṛtis, the Saṃhitās, the treatises on liberation, and the sciences of ethics were mastered.
Even the study of the Veda, as well as the soulful explanatory narratives—whatever has been heard in the womb and whatever has been studied thereafter, all that [remains]. ||22||
Just as the son grows while remaining within the womb, so too does the mother become heavy, and from that, the father experiences pain. (23)
Vyāsa asked: "Who indeed are you who have entered here assuming the form of an embryo?
Why do you not come outside? Tell me everything exactly as it is. (24)
The embryo said: "I am a Piśāca, and I am a Rākṣasa, and I am a human;
I am a god, and I am a horse, and I am an elephant, and I am a cock. (25)
"I was a goat, I was a prince, I was a tree, and I was a young boy;
indeed, I wandered repeatedly through eighty-four hundred thousand wombs. (26)
"I have arrived; how could I know? Who am I? To whom do I speak, and who am I?
Though I am the stainless one, I have entered here into a human womb. (27)
"Having attained the knowledge born of the Vedas, I shall here accomplish yoga;
I am weary of worldly existence and await the eternal path to liberation. (28)
Indeed, wandering in this terrible cycle of existence does not appeal to me;
I shall not go outside the womb, but shall contemplate Brahman right here.
"Then, by the power of your grace, I shall act and I shall go to liberation.
Vyāsa said: "Listen, O son, for you are the stainless Self."
Tell me, how can you take pleasure in dwelling within this womb-cavity so foul with stench?
O wise one, emerge from that loathsome pit of urine!
"Come outside and acquire auspicious yoga or knowledge!
The womb declares that neither new knowledge nor new yoga is desired. (32)
Knowledge, detachment, and likewise the recollection of former births remain with me only as long as I am situated in the womb; indeed, my desire for liberation lasts only so long.
If a living being, having emerged from the womb, is touched by the external wind, all the knowledge pertaining to the womb and the yogic radiance perish. (34)
Therefore, I shall by no means depart from my duty;
it is my firm resolve that I will attain liberation even from within the womb. (35)
Vyāsa said: "O Ātman, the noose of Vāyu shall not ensnare you;
all your knowledge and yoga will certainly remain steadfast and true. (36)
"Mayā does not afflict you at all, whether within the womb or outside;
therefore, show me your face, and I shall discharge my debt. (37)
"Your ancestors shall quickly be fully satisfied by the mere hearing of your birth.
The fetus said: 'If you protect me with Viṣṇu as my witness. (38)
"Then I shall go outside; quickly do what is appropriate there.
Having heard that, Vyāsa remembered the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (39)
The Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa arrived there swiftly;

"I shall be your guarantor today for all your knowledge and so forth;
it will surely remain [with you]. Go outside and depart for the sake of yoga. (41)
The illusion created by the touch of the wind pervaded me; it could not affect you.
Then the fetus emerged by the will of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Twelve years of age and approaching the prime of youth, he was like a king of yogis from birth, possessing the consciousness of one who remembers his past lives. ||43||
Having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa, his mother, and his father, that boy immediately set out for the forest; Vyāsa then said to him, "Wait! (44).
"I shall perform for you the purificatory rites, such as the birth ceremony; be firm!
The son of a maidservant replied: "Purificatory rites must be performed at every birth. (45)
Thousands and tens of millions of times have I been born in the ocean of existence, by which forms of bondage I have been encompassed within various wombs. (46)
Then the venerable Vyāsa himself conceived Śuka;

O son, he who abandons his father and goes to the forest for the sake of yoga goes to hell; do not go, but dwell at home.
Śuka said: "Just as I am your son in this present existence, so you were my son and I was your father in that [other] state; such is the teaching therein. (49)
"O Vyāsa, if this establishment of dharma is to be protected by you,

Vyāsa said: Having obtained birth in the house of a twice-born, he who undergoes the sacraments prescribed in the Vedas is preeminent. (5.1)
And Śuka said: "Liberation of the self through mental refinement is not certain;

Vyāsa said: "O son, one should first be a student (brahmacārī), then a householder (gṛhī);
thereafter, having placed renunciation (tyāga) foremost, liberation (mukti) shall come to pass."
Śuka said: "If liberation comes from celibacy, then a eunuch would attain it;
and if liberation comes through the householder's life, then the entire world would attain it. (54)
If liberation were to come from dwelling in the forest, it would indeed belong to the deer and other such creatures;
if liberation were superior through renunciation, then it would belong to the poor as well. (55)

Vyāsa said: By taking refuge in the true path through the sequence beginning with the householder's stage, one bestows bliss both in this world and the next; by that means, liberation becomes the ultimate fruit.
Śuka said: One who is attached to household life, fallen under the sway of delusion and passion, and bound by the fetters of latent impressions (vāsanā), shall reap the fruit of the path of Yama.
Vyāsa said: "One should perform rites for the ancestors and the gods without attachment. Śuka said: "One should perform rites for the ancestors and the gods without devotion. (58)
Vyāsa said: "Always perform devotion toward your ancestors and the gods at home.
Śuka replied: "My own Self is my home; therein I shall perform it. (19)
Vyāsa said: "Without a son, the hell named Put is certain;

Śuka said: "If it were so, then donkeys, monkeys, and pigs would also possess sons and cross over; what then is the distinction here for a human being?"
Vyāsa said: "If even they possess knowledge and liberation," Śuka replied: "O Father, that was indeed acquired by me while still in the womb."
"I shall go with devotion to Keśava, who has arrived as liberation;
for having obtained the wish-fulfilling gem, how could one take up a mere pebble? ||63||
Having first cast out the nectar, how indeed could one swallow a fly?
And when the essence of gold has been obtained, how could one trample upon mud before it?
Having abandoned the sight of the sun, how could one look upon Rāhu? Having discarded the divine lamp, how could one seek out a smoky meteor? (65)
When one has been liberated from the first prison, how could one fall into a second?
And when the path of Brahman has been realized, how could one proceed by a trivial way? (66)
Having abandoned the superior one who has arrived, one should not take refuge in the inferior;
having rejected the truth when it is attained, how could one embrace what is artificial? (67)
If one should find honey right here on the branch, why would he go to the mountain?
When a desired object is already accomplished, what wise person would exert effort? ||68||
Having spoken thus, he respectfully bowed to his father Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana who resided in his heart, and to his mother, the maidservant who was the power (śakti) of Kṛṣṇa.

At the command of his parents, the great yogi Kapiñjala took up the life of a householder and married the beautiful daughter of Bharadvāja.

He went to the mountainous region of Prāgjyotiṣa;
then, returning once more, he went to the mountain named Navalakṣa.

By the power of his asceticism, the king became the preceptor of the mountain-dwelling subjects;
consequently, the mountains thereafter came to be known as Kāmarūpas.
Men became few and women were many due to the desire for chastity;
indeed, hundreds of women would serve a single man. (81)
Then the lord of yogis, Bālava, dwelling on the bank of the Brahmaputra, performed severe penance like a child, free from delusion. ||82||
Then they prayed for those [plants] for the prosperity of human beings:
"By my boon, may they all be oriented toward the birth of sons. (83)
Let the number of girls be equal to that of the men;
in the event of equality or a surplus, the mothers of the girls and boys [shall be treated] equally. (84)
"You shall become as you are worthy," and they became so;
thus, O Lakṣmī, has this ancient account been told to you, occurring age after age.
In existence, it is born again and again as ever-new, like a magical creation;
likewise [are] Kāmarūpa, Tīrtha, and Bālavākuṇḍaka. (86)
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is most excellent even through recitation or hearing, grants all desired objects, and indeed bestows the perfection of mantra. (87)

Thus ends the five hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa had two sons, Śuka and Kapiñjala, by Śukī; how Bharadvāja was the son of Kapiñjala and Taittira was his son; and how, due to the boon granted by Bālava Yogī, men were born in the land of Kāmarūpa in equal numbers to women," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Brahman, Blessed One, ocean of compassion!
By meditating upon Your form, Your devotees attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana,
and Sanatsujāta— these five are equal to you and bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śaṅkara, Lomaśa, Mārkaṇḍeya, Yājñavalkya, Dharma, Śeṣa, and Vṛṣa were likewise the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas. || 3 ||
The Vedas, the eternal Vaiṣṇavas, Bali, Bāṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanumān, Jāmbavān, Aśvatthāman, Prahlāda, and Āsuri; || 4 ||
Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Divodāsa, and likewise Ambarīṣaka; Uddhava, Śaśin, Sūrya, Anila, and also Hutāśana. || 5 ||
These are your eternal devotees and your obedient sons;
having always performed meditation upon you, they remain alive for a long time.
And how is it that Śaṅkara is your son, yet he has five heads? Furthermore, why is he distinct from your own nature? Tell me the reason for this.
The son of the one-headed god has five heads;
this is a great marvel—dispel my doubt regarding it.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Formerly, the Lord Aja, having performed an extensive creation of four kinds consisting of men and women, which was auspicious and lasted for a long time— (9)
Then he reflected upon female forms in every respect— those enchanting objects of delusion that had been fashioned even more so than before.
"Even for women, there may be delusion [regarding such things]; therefore, I shall fashion an image endowed with a collection of all beautiful forms," having thus resolved, he [created it]. (11)
Having taken a single divine apsarā, more radiant even than the goddesses,
by gathering the luster of all the celestial dwellers bit by bit, like sesame seeds.
He fashioned a wonder of beauty, surpassing all other forms,
such that upon seeing it, even the Grandfather himself was struck with agitation.
Then he indeed sent her to the yogi Śaṅkara for the purpose of thoroughly testing his fortitude; she, too, went to Kailāsa.
In that solitary place, she beheld Śaṅkara immersed in meditation upon Kṛṣṇa,
just as the devoted Satī, ever remaining there, was herself engaged in meditation.
Standing nearby, she performed the japa of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
from her body issued forth something as sweet and cool as ten million moons. || 16 ||
A fierce and wonderful circle of golden light issued forth;
that radiant orb, having reached the eyelashes of Śaṅkara, [vanished].
And that which has the nature of light, having entered the eye,
reached the interior of the heart through the gateway of the rays, where the king of yogis resides.
Having united himself with his own self within the sun, the abode of splendors,
Śambhu beheld there that beautiful radiance.
In Samādhi, a twofold manifestation has arisen, wherein the real and the unreal are equal;
indeed, it was for the purpose of perceiving the unreal that this state of Śaṅkara came to be here.
Having dismissed Satī, he came outside out of curiosity;
and as soon as he opened his eyes and looked before him, he beheld Sundarī.
Having attained a state of supreme wonder, he forgot his embodied form;
perceiving through his own disposition that he was captivated and longing for a vision [of her], he became absorbed in her.
She too, fearing that he would be reduced to ashes upon the opening of his third eye,
left him as he gazed charmingly at her and departed from that former place.
Under the pretext of circumambulation, she bowed with palms joined in reverence;
then, while Śambhu’s head remained motionless, she moved to his right side.
Desiring to see her, he approached with great passion from his heart;
at that very moment, a beautiful southern face emerged.
Then, overcome with fear, she fled toward the western direction; Śambhu, though his inner being was drawn by her true form, also went westward.
He created a third face, beautiful and new, for the purpose of seeing;
then, overcome by fear, she went to the northern side.
And in order to see her, she fashioned a northern face and beheld her;
then, having gone into the sky, she beheld her with a fifth head.
There, Śaṅkara made her move through the sky and beheld her;
he laughed out of affection and became absorbed in her beauty.
Endowed with the power of yogic practice, he did not move his neck;
in the meantime, the divine Nārada [approached] Pārvatī.
He reported everything and spoke of Śaṅkara’s deed:
"Having seen that beautiful woman, he has made himself ever new.
Because of her, Śaṅkara indeed came to have five faces."
I know that there is no other woman anywhere who is equal to you. || 3.2 ||
And how will you, being so deluded, become an object of laughter? O Pārvatī, today you shall surely fall into the path of ridicule.
He who himself, as a lord of yogins, reduced Kāma to the form of ashes—
today he has fallen into delusion regarding a celestial woman through the illusory power of Viṣṇu.
You are worthy of worship by all the wives of the gods, as is your husband;
behold how his heart has become filled with affection for this servant of the gods.
He will immediately take her and place her upon his own lap;
he will set the price of an apsarā as a price far exceeding yours.
"Quickly effect his suppression before he makes his mark!
Having heard this from Nārada and seeing her five-faced husband, [she acted]. (37)
Beholding him thus transformed, that Yoginī entered into his eyes;
indeed, she blocked all the eyes of Śambhu.
In the meantime, all splendors were extinguished;
everything was filled with darkness, and the two suns were deprived of their light. (39)
The onset of universal dissolution occurred, along with the arrival of the Night of Doom;
earthquakes then broke out, and all embodied beings were struck with terror.
When this agitation of the entire creation had thus arisen, all the Gaṇas, Nandin and the others, bowed to Satī and praised her again and again. ||41||
Release them, release them, O best of goddesses; indeed, release the eyes of Śambhu!
Let the eyes of Hara see [the world], and let blindness spread over the universe! 42.
Although addressed in this manner, that goddess did not release her eyes;
then Hara discharged the supreme eye situated upon his forehead.
"By him who, filled with compassion for the worlds, provides their protection—I am not able to restrain the Goddess, who is dearer to me than life itself. (44)
Then the Goddess, having abandoned the act of looking from that point and becoming perfectly composed,
spoke to Tilottamā with anger in the presence of Hara.
"O sinful woman, because my beloved has been mocked by you through [the imitation of] his form, therefore you shall be devoid of beauty, with matted hair and a protruding belly. (46)
"May you have flattened eyes, large teeth, and a broken nose!
Then, at that very moment, Tilottamā was born with an ugly form.
With palms joined in reverence, he praised Pārvatī and begged for her forgiveness, saying:

Then Pārvatī said, "Come with me. 49.
From Śaṅkara, receive here this auspicious mantra that removes sin:

"Therefore, go with me to the holy site of Śrī Hāṭakeśvara;
bathe in the Rūpa-tīrtha at the Nāga river for the sake of ending the curse. (51)
Having thus received the mantra and having taken a garland of *tulasī*, she went to the Nāgamatī river and bathed; indeed, she became beautiful in form.
Having bowed down, Pārvatī, who was exactly as she had been before in every particular, went to the Grandfather in Satyaloka. 53.
She reported everything, beginning with her ascent upon the five-faced one; Brahmā said, "O daughter, it shall be so for every creation."
Having encountered you as its cause, Hara will repeatedly become five-faced;
and your fame shall forever endure in the world. (55)
Having spoken thus, he gave her blessings: "Be firm in creation;
be one who accomplishes the work of the gods and makes your dwelling in Satyaloka. (56)

Thus ends the five hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Śaṅkara’s Five-Facedness on Account of Tilottamā, the Curse of Pārvatī upon Tilottamā, and the Removal of that Curse by the Bathing of Nāgavatī," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how Sarasvatī was formerly brought forth by the red waters; I shall relate to you that purifying account.
Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha became despondent;
Viśvāmitra was repeatedly exhorted by Brahmā and by the Brahmins.
"This one is a Brāhmaṇa, this one is a Brāhmaṇa, and even this one is a Brahmarṣi and a Kṣatriya"—why Vasiṣṭha did not say this, listen to the reason for that, O beloved. (3)
In ancient times, there was a great sage named Ṛcīka, the son of Bhṛgu;
he was perfected in his vows and studies, and at one time he was devoted to ascetic penance.
In the course of his pilgrimage to sacred fords, he went to the city of Bhojakata,
where the river Kauśikī flows and where King Gādhi resided.
Having bathed in it and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, he recited prayers;
at that moment, a princess arrived there on the bank for the purpose of bathing.
A young woman, endowed with beauty and radiant in all her limbs, arrived there; and upon seeing her, the sage was infatuated by desire.
He asked the people, "Whose daughter is this?
and those people replied, "She is the daughter of Gādhi, and she is devoted to the worship of Gaurī."
Desiring an excellent husband, she observes a vow that subdues her passion;
having recited the sacred prayer (*brahman*) here and performed worship in due order. (9)
Having offered various kinds of food-oblations to Gaurī, he daily performs singing,
dancing, and instrumental music for the constant gratification of Gaurī.
Having heard this, that king of sages returned to Gādhi with great longing;
and seeing that Ṛcīka had arrived, the king performed the rites of hospitality for him.
Having offered worship to the sage with palms joined in reverence, he asked him with devotion:
"O Brahmin, what is the reason for your arrival, even though you are free from desire?"
"Tell me what you desire; I shall give it all to you.
Out of delusion, Ṛcīka then requested that beautiful maiden.
He said, "Give her to me in accordance with the Brāhmaṇa form of marriage," and she replied, "She has been seen by me during the worship of Gaurī. || 14 ||
Having heard that, Gādhi—the best among the wise—was terrified with fear;
considering him to be poor and aged, he spoke words imbued with political wisdom.
"O best of the twice-born, there is a bride-price for the giving of our daughter;
if you pay that, I shall give her to you without a doubt. (16)
Ṛcīka said: "O King, tell me here the bride-price for the maidens;
I shall quickly give you everything, even that which is difficult to obtain, O Golaka."
Gādhi said: "O twice-born one, give me seven hundred horses with one ear black, and also white ones from every direction. (18)
Having promised "So be it," Ṛcīka, blazing with ascetic power,
went to the bank of the Gaṅgā and indeed muttered the mantra *āpohiṣṭhā*.
He indeed employed the hymn of Varuṇa consisting of sixty-four verses;
when that recitation was completed, the god Varuṇa arrived there.
Then, together with him, the horses emerged from the water;
they were all white, swift, auspicious, and had one dark ear.
Accompanied by as many men numbering seven hundred,
Ṛcīka then took [the horses], bowed to Varuṇa, and departed.
Having seized the horses with his men, he went quickly to Gādhi and presented those excellent steeds to him for the sake of the maiden.
Gādhi, however, having accepted all of them for the sake of the horse-sacrifice,
gave his daughter to him according to the prescribed rites, with the Brahmins and the fire as witnesses.
Ṛcīka became free from desire together with his lawful wife;
after some time, he spoke to Satī, who was devoted to her husband and serving him. (25)
"I shall go to perform ascetic penance; choose a boon, and I shall grant it to you.
Then, having heard those words of the sage who was devoid of self-interest, she [replied].
Overwhelmed by grief, she told her mother the whole account;
her mother said to that daughter, "O daughter, choose a husband for the sake of your son."
"O daughter, choose for my sake a son endowed with Brahmanic qualities;
and choose for my sake a son endowed with Kshatriya splendor. (28)
Having prostrated before her husband, she related in detail what her mother had said:
"Ṛcīka prepared two portions of sacrificial porridge for the sake of the gods and the sacrifice. (29)
Having performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice according to the rules and having divided the sacrificial oblation (caru) into two parts,
he infused the entirety of Brahmanic splendor and glory into one of them.
Then he infused his entire kṣatriya energy into the other [portion],
and he gave the sacrificial porridge (caru) endowed with brahmanic energy to his wife.
He said, "Feed him this and embrace the holy fig tree (aśvattha);
then you will obtain a virtuous son endowed with Brahmanic splendor."
And he gave the second *caru*, intended for a son, to his wife’s mother;
having given her that which was composed of Kṣatriya splendor, he said, "Having consumed this *caru*... (33)
"By embracing a banyan tree, you shall obtain a son who is a kṣatriya.
Then, in private, the mother spoke to her daughter, who was inspired by what was to come.
"O daughter, for all the world, excellence lies in one's own interest and meanness in the interest of another; yet, in comparison with my porridge, yours shall possess superiority. (35)
Having heard this, the daughter, who was as devoted to her mother as a calf to its dam and desiring preeminence for her brother,
indeed made an exchange between the tree and the sacrificial porridge, O Lotus-born One.
Then, during the *puṃsavana* rite, those two auspicious women, overwhelmed with love, bathed; one of them conceived a child through the splendor of the Kṣatriya lineage. || 37 ||
Constantly appearing pregnant, she set her mind upon royal pleasures and engaged in talk of war, such as the mounting of elephants and horses. (38)
Having brought from her father’s house red garments, excellent ornaments, saffron, and unguents, she prepared herself for adornment. (39)
Having seen this conduct of his wife, Ṛcīka then said to her: "What is this, my dear? Has there been a reversal of the sacrificial cakes, or likewise of the two trees?"
"By your behavior here, it is known that who could transgress destiny?
Devoid of the conduct of the twice-born, your son will certainly be such. (41)
Your mother, however, is always seen to be established in tranquility and devoted to recitation and burnt offerings, devoid of the active conduct of the kṣatriya dharma. ||42||
"By listening with faith to the narrative of the pilgrimage to sacred fords, that younger brother of yours will become equal to Brahmā through the spiritual power of a Brāhmaṇa. (43)
Whatever longings exist in pregnant women, such characteristics reside in their sons. (44)
At the time of the father's infusion of seed, whatever kind of activity exists in the pregnant woman, that is reflected in the embryo. (45)
Then the wife said to the sage: "Forgive that injury of mine;
O Lord, O Master, since this transgression was committed, please show mercy once again. (46)
"May my son be a Brāhmaṇa and my mother’s son be a Kṣatriya.
Ṛcīka said, "It cannot be so; that which has already been born remains exactly as it was. (47)
"But by my boon, your sons of the Kṣatriya lineage shall attain the state of grandsons;
thus indeed do I show mercy, so let your son be a Brāhmaṇa. (48)
Thus, by the granting of that boon, Jamadagni became his son;
and from Jamadagni was born Parśurāma, who followed the lineage of the Kṣatriyas.
He waged war on the earth twenty-one times against various kings;
thereafter, Gādhi’s housewife conceived a child.
Conducting herself like a Brāhmaṇī woman, she gave birth to an excellent son, a Brāhmaṇa by his actions, who was devoted to yoga, the twilight prayers, and meditation. (51)
