Having been addressed thus by the boy, Nārada went to heaven;
and having been honored, he departed for Satyaloka. Then that boy [proceeded].
She was brought into the presence of Yājñavalkya by the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī. || 1.13 ||
The boy was both entrusted and brought forward by Yājñavalkya to Pippalāda,
the wondrous lord of yogis and a seer learned in the Vedas.
He became one of great heroism, a benefactor of the world.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account which destroys sin.
Whoever reads or hears this meritorious narrative, the sin of approaching those who should not be approached shall undoubtedly come to rest. (116)
When the danger from the calamities had arisen,
his flood subsided gradually and without doubt, by the power of Pippalāda’s words.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Sābhramatī River, the Birth of Pippalāda from Yājñavalkya’s Sister, Bṛhaspati being Born as Pippalāda, the Worship of Śanaiścara, and Other Matters," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī; formerly you worshipped Gaurī Pañcapiṇḍikā, and by that act, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was obtained as your husband.
By the mere sight of Gaurī, a woman shall attain good fortune;
on the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, when the sun is situated in Taurus, she should offer water to her.
She who performs this daily with the water-mantra shall obtain auspicious good fortune;
she shall never remain barren, nor even one whose children die in infancy.
One shall never encounter misfortune anywhere, even throughout hundreds of future births;
[one attains mastery over] earth, water, fire, air, and space as well.
One should fashion Gaurī with five [lumps]; she is called Pañcapiṇḍikā.
In the worship of the five lumps, the merit is a thousandfold.
In former times, there was a powerful king of Kāśī named Jayasena;
he had a thousand wives, among whom one was his most beloved.
Amānāmnī was the daughter of Viśvaksena, the king of Madra.
Rising early in the morning, she performed her auspicious ablutions on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having fashioned Gaurī from clay, consisting of five lumps,
Satī then worshipped her with the sixteen articles of offering.
Then, having dismissed that goddess and given gifts, she would always go home; and her good fortune increased constantly.
Beholding her beauty, youth, the affection of her beloved, and her blessed renown, her co-wives then became sorrowful.
Having learned that Gaurī’s worship was rooted in that, they went to see it;
there, she who performed the five-piṇḍikā rite was worshipping Gaurī.
Rising early, she honored them there and offered them seats;
they then asked her the cause of her constant increase in good fortune.
With a gracious mind, Amā spoke to her co-wives regarding what had been done in the past.
In former times, I was a Śūdra girl, the daughter of Vīrasena.
At that time, my marriage also took place in the city of Kusuma;
from the mouth of a Brahmin, I heard of the worship of Gaurī, which bestows good fortune.
Nowhere should even water be drunk without having performed the worship of Gaurī;
for by means of that worship and its merit, one’s desired object and what is sought after are attained.
Then, I performed worship there constantly;
having worshipped Piṇḍagaurī, I always cast [the offerings] into the water. (16)
Then my beloved departed for Dvārakā for the sake of visiting sacred fords;
taking me with him, he reached a waterless desert region.
The sun blazed fiercely while the bull stood in the constellation Raudra, causing excessive thirst;
the caravan became afflicted by thirst, perceiving as water the mirage born of the desert sands.
That which is seen as real is indeed false; the water reached there is not present on dry land.
I became distressed with thirst, and then Gaurī was remembered by me.
I was well-fashioned from five handfuls of heated sand;
Gaurī was worshipped by me with speech and heart, and then indeed I died.
By that merit, I became the auspicious daughter of the lord of Daśārṇa;
I am the youngest among you, while I am the eldest due to my worship of Gaurī.
I have become one who remembers my past lives; remembering that, I constantly worship here by fashioning that five-lump image with clay.
Because of that, my various forms of good fortune increase perpetually here.
Divine merit increases, which bestows a divine state.
You are all my sisters, and I have no sense of envy;
you too should worship, and you will certainly obtain good fortune. ||23-24||
"By this truth, may Gaurī grant my desire;
may that beloved of Hara grant you all your desires.
Having spoken thus, those co-wives then worshipped Gaurī.
Those worship-mantras were given by that virtuous woman to them at that very moment:
"O Mahālakṣmī, those which were previously uttered by you during worship—'Salutation to the Earth, O Mistress of Forbearance; salutation to the Auspicious One composed of Water. (26–27)
"O Tejasvinī, salutations to you; salutations to you who have the form of wind;
salutations again and again to you who possess the nature of space, O you of fivefold form!
O Lakṣmī, by means of these mantras, the five *piṇḍikās* were worshipped by you."
By that [merit], you have attained the kingdom of Vaikuṇṭha, which is very difficult to reach.
Thus, whatever woman worships Gaurikā Pañcapiṇḍikā with the sixteen types of offerings, she shall immediately become beloved by her husband.
Listen, Lakṣmī; thereafter Āmā indeed reflected in her heart:
"I have obtained supreme good fortune, which is difficult for all women to attain;
yet no offspring has been born to me, and because of that, I am truly consumed by grief again and again. (31)
Then, while things were proceeding in this manner, Durvāsas arrived in haste.
King Jayasena offered a welcome and gave him a seat;
having presented the *arghya* and the *madhuparka*, he then questioned that sage.
Having made me your disciple, you have purified me, a worthy recipient of your compassion.
Today, along with my entire family, I have become most blessed by your arrival.
Therefore, O Sage, tell me what I may do for you now that you have come to my home.

Durvāsas said to the king: "Dwelling in your palace, I shall perform the Cāturmāsya rites with ease. From the taking of the sacred clay until their completion, let service be rendered unto me. (35–36)
Having said, "So be it," the king performed that service;
by the king's command, he remained constantly engaged in excellent service every day.
When the four-month period had passed and the sage was about to depart,
he spoke with satisfaction, "O King, what shall I do for you?
The king said to that sovereign of sages, "O Sage, [grant me] progeny."
Therefore, always treat her as a mother to your son. 39.
The sage said: "Listen, O Lord of the Earth! Indeed, in a previous birth, at the time of death, she fashioned an image of Gaurī out of heated sand and worshipped it;
by that merit, this virtuous woman has obtained sovereignty here."
For this Gaurī has been fashioned by her from sands joined with the heat [of her asceticism]. || 41 ||
And the fruit of that [merit] is her constant anxiety for the sake of a son;
for no god exists in wood, stone, or clay.
Indeed, a god exists in the heart when it is endowed with devotion to the mantra and other such qualities.
Having fashioned this very Gaurī from clay into a five-lump image, || 43 ||
If one goes to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara and worships there,
one should offer an unbroken stream of water when the sun is situated in Taurus.
Furthermore, by the power of the sacred field, there will arise an increase of merit;
and just as coolness shall emerge from the water of Gaurī,
so too her burning fever shall be pacified day and night.
At the end of the burning, there will be a conception; from that, she shall obtain a son. || 46 ||
Now, there is a meritorious vow that brings supreme satisfaction to Gaurī, by the performance of which a woman indeed attains the state of a goddess. (47)
The Great Goddess known as Gomayā should indeed be fashioned from cow dung.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada, one should clean one's teeth in the morning.
One should undertake the observance of the fast while remembering Gaurī;
at the arrival of night, four clay images of Gaurī must indeed be fashioned.
A single Gaurī should be fashioned with five lumps as prescribed;
when each watch of the day has arrived, one should perform worship upon them.
O Goddess, beloved of Śaṅkara, you were born in the home of Himācala; having emerged from the womb of Menā, accept this worship. Homage to you!
[I offer] incense, camphor, a red wick, and a lamp of ghee.
One should offer jasmine flowers as an oblation and present sweetmeats as the respectful gift.
"Accept this arghya enriched with citron flowers; salutations to you.
At the end of the second watch, one should worship Ardhanārīśvarī. || 53 ||
One should then offer incense of aguru and sandalwood, along with an offering of guḍa (molasses) and coconut, while reciting the mantra for the arghya:
"O Gods, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, please accept this arghya from me."
When the third watch has arrived, one should worship with a hundred-petaled lotus. || 55 ||
Guggulu incense, an offering of food (naivedya), arghya water with jasmine flowers,
incense made from granthi powder, and its own arghya consisting of madana fruit.
Then, when the fourth watch has arrived, one should again offer [the gift] and worship that five-lump Gaurī with Bhr̥ṅgarāja. || 57 ||

May Gaurī, who consists of the five elements, accept the arghya offered by me; one should likewise offer the food oblation, incense, lamps, and other offerings, as well as the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). ||58||
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), offer prayers for one's desired goals, and keep a vigil;
with great effort, one should engage in dancing, instrumental music, and devotional singing amidst the festivities.
At dawn, the observer of the vow, having bathed, should worship a pair of Brahmins;
he should cause a female elephant or a mare to carry four Gaurīs.
With the sound of festive music and the like, one should encircle her by a river or similar body of water:
"O Goddess, you have been invoked by me; O auspicious one, you have been worshipped by me. (6.1)
"Go as you please so that I may grant you good fortune"—
thus was the worship previously performed by Lakṣmī, and especially so by Gaurī.
On the third day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, during the four watches of the night,
she saw in the morning four white cows adorned with the luster of jewels.
And they said to Mahālakṣmī, "Do not carry us away into the water;
instead, have a temple constructed here in the holy field of Hāṭakeśvara. (64)
"Establish us here for the sake of the vow, we who bring happiness to women.
Thus were they installed there by Lakṣmī as bestowers of fortune and sons. (65)
O King, this is your wife; likewise, there is a set of four Gaurīs, as well as a Gaurī made of cow-dung consisting of five lumps.
Having performed this, one should worship with it; thereby one shall obtain the good fortune of having a son, and likewise, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself shall become one's husband.
Having spoken thus, Durvāsas departed quickly;
then that virtuous woman, named Amā, went to the sacred field known as Hāṭakeśvara.
Having performed everything according to the prescribed rite, she became the Mother of Sons;
after a long time had passed, she indeed became the very form of Lakṣmī.
Having attained a divine body, she went to Vaikuṇṭha and became a maidservant of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I told you of her and that vow of Māyā.
Whoever recites this with devotion shall obtain the fruit of the worship of Gaurī;
she shall never be separated from prosperity, nor shall she encounter misfortune. ||71||

Thus ends the five hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Five-Piṇḍikā-Gaurī-Vow performed by Amayā, the wife of the King of Kāśī, in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, wherein she obtained a son, good fortune, and the state of being Lakṣmī."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; once in the Satyaloka, Nārada, having wandered through the three worlds, went to see Brahmā and bowed down before him.
Brahmā asked, "Son, from where have you come? Tell me.
Nārada replied, "Having surveyed the circles of mortals... (2)
"O Father, I have come to inform you of what is in my heart regarding the performance of your worship; having heard it, do as is appropriate. (3)
For the strength of the Daityas prevails everywhere in this world,
as do sacrifices, truth, righteousness, and all kinds of virtuous deeds.
By force they are being destroyed by them; the gods and the devotees are suffering.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to perform what is beneficial as you see fit. (5)
Having thus made his report, and having bowed down and performed worship, Brahmā departed; he indeed reflected upon an auspicious ground for the sake of the sacrifice.
In order to ascertain where that place free from obstacles was located, he spoke to the lotus flower held in his hand: "Fall upon the sacred ground."
Then he cast that flower, which, having wandered through all the worlds on every side,
fell into the most sacred field born of Hāṭakeśvara.
In the meantime, his grandfather, the great-grandfather, arrived later;
having seen the field, he became delighted for the sake of the sacrifice.
Then he commanded Vāyu: "Bring Purandara here, together with the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the hosts of Maruts."
"Let the Gandharvas, the world-protectors, the Siddhas, and likewise the Vidyādharas—whoever may be my assistants—be present at this entire sacrificial rite. (11)
Vāyu brought Indra, accompanied by the hosts of gods;
and on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, Brahmā spoke to Mahendra regarding the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
"I intend to perform a sacrifice here; indeed, bring together the necessary materials, as well as Brahmins worthy of it and suitable implements."
Indra brought those materials and the best of the twice-born;
then the Great-Grandfather commenced the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.
Śambhu arrived at that sacrifice together with the hosts of gods;
Brahmā then spoke to the gods, "Stay each in your own respective places."
O Viśvakarman, construct the sacrificial pavilion, the sacrificial altars,
the wives' hall, the assembly halls, and the necessary fire-pits.
Have the sacrificial vessels, the domestic cups, the ladles, the sacrificial posts, the pits for the couches, and the altars prepared. (17)
"O Bṛhaspati, have a beautiful golden image of the Supreme Person fashioned; and you must bring all the officiating priests worthy of the sacrifice."
"O King of the Gods, perform service for as many as sixteen [brahmins];
and Kubera, you must provide the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) appropriate for the occasion."
O Creator, you must perform an examination of what ought and ought not to be done;
likewise, let the world-protectors, Indra and the others, protect the directions.
"Let there be no entry for bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, daityas, or rākṣasas; therefore, let an excellent gift be given through this sacrifice. (21)
May the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts be the servers for those people who desire to eat.
Let the Brahmins worthy of sacrifice stand in the sacrificial pavilion—Maitrāvaruṇa, Cyavana, Atharvāka, and likewise Gālava. (23)
Marīci and Mārkava—these two are experts in all ritual acts;
let Pulastya stand there as the Adhvaryu priest who initiates the departure.
Let the sage Raibhya remain as the Unnetṛ priest in the sacrificial pavilion;
let Nārada be the Brahmā priest, and Garga be the supervisor of the sacrifice. || 25 ||
The three Hotṛ priests were Agnīdhra, Bharadvāja, and Parāśara;
likewise, the Ācārya Bṛhaspati was the Udgātṛ, as was the sage Gobhila. ||26||
Śāṇḍilya shall be the Pratihartṛ and Aṅgiras the Subrahmaṇya;
may these sixteen priests be present for the successful accomplishment of this sacrifice. ||27||
Brahmā, having been initiated by them, honored them; as the creator of the universe, he became the patron of the sacrifice, and thereupon the sacrificial rite was set in motion.
And Brahmā said to Nārada, "Bring Sāvitrī quickly," while musical instruments were being played by the Siddhas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas.
Accompanied by Gandharvas playing musical instruments and by Brahmins intent on chanting, Pulastya took up the fire-drill and spoke these words: ||1.509.30||
"Patnī! Patnī!"—thus the lords of the Brahmins cried out loudly there;
meanwhile, Brahmā quickly signaled to Nārada with his hand.
He sent her home, saying, "Let your wife be brought back.
He too went and said to Sāvitrī, "I have been sent by my father. (32)
"Come to the pavilion, O Goddess; the sacrificial rite is proceeding. How is it that you are seen alone in this assembly, and what is your appearance? (33)
"Then let the goddesses be brought; surrounded by them, you shall depart.
Having said this, Nārada went to the sacrifice and spoke to the Unborn One (Brahmā).
Sāvitrī will arrive at an auspicious moment together with the goddesses;
then Brahmā sent him back, and Nārada departed.
"O Mother, come quickly, surrounded by the goddesses.
Then Sāvitrī said, "I shall go only after I have dressed my hair."
Then Nārada, having groomed his hair, spoke to the Unborn One (Brahmā), saying, "I am indeed coming from there with haste, as only a short moment of the Soma-drinking hour remains. (37)
Pulastya also went there, for Sāvitrī was indeed alone. "O Goddess, why do you appear so languid? Go quickly to the site of the sacrifice. (38)
Sāvitrī said: "Tell him that he should wait for a moment, until Śakrāṇī, Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and the others arrive. (39)
"I shall come to this assembly joined by those celestial maidens.
Having gone quickly, he spoke thus to Brahmā, who was oppressed by the weight of the Soma.
She said to me: "In this sacrifice, I shall indeed go together with the goddesses;
I will not go alone by any means. (41)
Knowing this, O best of gods, do whatever pleases you;
for the time characterized by the opportunity for sacrifice is passing away. (42)
Having heard this, Brahmā spoke to Mahendra; she, being of a fickle nature, said:
"The sacrifice shall not be performed at all unless it is done with another wife. (43)
By the command of Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods beheld a certain maiden wandering about—
moon-faced, born of a cowherd family, slender, with her head intent upon a water-pot.
He asked the young and delicate maiden, "Who are you, O girl? She replied, "I am a cowherd's daughter; I have come here to sell buttermilk. (45)
"If you will accept the buttermilk, give me the price quickly.
Indra took that cowherd girl along with the buttermilk. 46.
Having caused it to enter through the cow's mouth, he then drew it out with urine;
having thus rendered it most pure, he bathed it with auspicious waters.
Having dressed her in beautiful garments and led her into your presence, O Brahmin, she has been brought for your sake—she who is indeed endowed with every virtue. (48)
The lineage of cows and the lineage of Brahmins are one and the same, though divided into two; in one part the sacred mantra resides, and in the other the sacrificial oblation resides. 49.
Having emerged from a cow-pen, she has been brought to the state of twice-born status;
take her hand in marriage and perform the drinking of the sacrificial soma.
And Rudra said: "She has indeed emerged from the cow-pen;
let her, named Gāyatrī, be your wife here at this sacrifice forever."
Then the Brahmins said: "Let this be the best of Brahmin women;
perform the marriage ceremony with her, excluding those of the cowherd caste. (52)
Brahmā took her hand and began the auspicious rite;
Gāyatrī too, with joy, placed that fire-drill upon her head.
While musical instruments were being played, they arrived at the sacrificial pavilion;
thereafter, Vidhi performed the rite of shaving his own hair.
Viśvakarman indeed fashioned the nail-clippers for the Gāyatrī;
then Paulastya gave a staff made of Udumbara wood to Brahmā.
Likewise, he gave him a hide equipped with a deer-horn along with the sacred mantra;
and having taken his wife Śālā, who was observing silence and reciting the Gāyatrī, [he departed].
He placed another auspicious girdle made of muñja grass around his waist;
then Brahmā, together with the officiating priests, performed the sacrificial rites.
And as the rite was being performed, a great marvel occurred there:
someone wearing the form of a fool, naked and with a deformed face, appeared. (58)
Carrying a skull in his hand, he arrived, saying, "Let food be given!
Although forbidden by the Brahmins, he entered the sacrificial pavilion.
But the members of the assembly rebuked him, saying, "Who are you, a sinner who has arrived here—a skull-bearer, naked in form, and carrying an impure bowl? (1.509.60)
"The sacrificial ground would become impure; go quickly away from here!
The fool replied, "How am I impure? For I am a mendicant observing a vow. (61)
Having understood this Brahmayajña and having become pure after bathing, he arrived;
she, however, was a cowherd’s daughter, a Śūdrī of impure birth, who was constantly [present]. (62)
"Has that pure one been established here? Am I not a Brahmin, a purifier?
Just then, an old Brahmin arrived there.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed spoke this reply to her: "Listen, my dear;
O fool, she is not a Śūdra woman; by birth, she is indeed a Brāhmaṇī. (64)
Listen; I know that account, for others who do not know this do not.
Long ago, at the commencement of creation, by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self— ||65||
For Sāvitrī was indeed his own partial incarnation, manifested from his own form;
then a second daughter was created, named Pativratā.
Then the Brahmin named Patnīvrata was made into a youth;
Brahmā was fashioned from the body of Vairāja and entrusted to him.
Sāvitrī and Śrī Hari themselves are present right here in Goloka;
now, for the sake of the continuous flow of sacrifice, Brahmā shall perform the sacrifice.
On earth, in the form of a mortal, there she shall exist in human body as the wife of Yajña, required for the sake of his purpose.
For this reason, O Kṛṣṇa, Sāvitrī was then commanded:
"You must indeed go there in your second form."
Long ago, on the surface of the earth, for the sake of Brahmā, Sāvitrī took the form of a maiden and said to Śrī Kṛṣṇa: "Where are my parents there? (7.1)
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa revealed those two auspicious ones:
this brahmin devoted to his wife, and this brahmin woman devoted to her husband. (72)
My two portions, identical to my own nature, born not from a womb and possessing divine forms,
[shall appear] on earth at the Kuṅkumavāpī in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasāra.

At the beginning of creation, two extremely purifying beings in the form of Brahmins shall exist, accompanied by cows for the sake of the oblations and other offerings in sacrifices such as the Vaiśvadeva. (74)
And when Brahmā shall assemble in Saurāṣṭra for the sake of sacrifice,
prior to that, they shall be known by the names Gobhila and Gobhilā.
Having become cowherds, they will go to the land of Ānarta, where the Ābhīras dwell, assuming their dress and occupations. (76)
"Because of that [destruction] caused by the Daityas, it would certainly not happen for those two while they remain concealed.
For this reason, out of fear of the affliction caused by the Daityas, those two [performed] the sacrifice first. (77)
By the command of Śrī Hari, those two Brahmins were born in Ānarta in the form of cowherds; they were indeed the protectors of cows, and they were your parents. (78)
"In reality, both are Brahmins; they must indeed assume the dress of cowherds there. O Sāvitrī, you too, as their second form, shall become portions of my own self. (79)
One must become a daughter born not from a womb, a divine woman;
then one should go to that place as a seller of curd, milk, and other such goods.
When a sacrifice takes place there, then, remembering [this] through excellent yoga, you shall perform the rite as a human woman with a new bridegroom. (81)
Having entered into a state of coexistence, Brahmā, you shall become Gāyatrī, the hidden daughter of two Brāhmaṇas living among cowherds. (82)
Then, having become Brahmāṇī, you shall go to Satyaloka;
thereafter, the Brāhmaṇas who have returned to the mortal world will recite prayers for you.
Thus, while being born as this Gāyatrī, daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, she exists in the guise of a cowherd; for she is indeed not impure by birth. (84)
When that rogue had been thus answered by Kṛṣṇa, at that moment Gobhila and Agobhila arrived there with joy. 85.
Our daughter has great fortune, for she has been wedded by Brahmā; ours too is great fortune, as the affliction of the Daityas is being warded off. (86)
"By means of the sacrifice, for the sake of the gods, the brahmins, and the virtuous.
Having spoken thus, those two abandoned their cowherd attire and assumed the forms of brahmins. (87)
For the two grandfathers of those high-souled brahmins were well-known;
they were both born there as divine and earth-dwelling ancestors of them all. (88)
Then Brahmā and the others bowed down and respectfully offered him honor;
and all the gods and other beings, filled with joy, established him at the sacrifice.
Having honored Brahmā with garlands, saffron, unbroken grains, flowers,
and other offerings, they gave their daughter there in the sacrificial pavilion.
An aged brahmin indeed assumed a dark form there;
saluted by all, the gods and others exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (91).
Upon seeing Kṛṣṇa Hari as well as Gāyatrī and her father, the wretch bowed down with devotion and said, "Give me alms. (92)
"I am hungry, O best of Brahmins; let the twice-born not reproach me.
It is said that a sacrifice is complete when all the poor, the blind, and the wretched have been satisfied. (93)
Otherwise, even this sacrifice performed by you would lead to destruction; for a sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom, while one lacking mantras consumes the officiating priests. (94)
"A sacrifice devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is no sacrifice at all; there is no enemy equal to a sacrifice.
Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa said, "O wretch, give them food! (95)
The Brahmins said: "Your begging bowl is impure; therefore, go outside. We shall give alms to you at the side-kitchen. (96)
In this food-hall, ascetics, the wretched, the blind, the miserable, and likewise brahmins emaciated by hunger eat. (97)
"Your skull-cup is indeed impure; take another pure vessel and cast this skull far outside the sacrificial ground. (98)
Thus addressed, that rogue, out of anger, threw his skull-cup into the middle of the sacrificial pavilion and himself vanished from sight. 99.
All the brahmins were struck with wonder; they threw their water-pots with sticks outside, and immediately a second one appeared.
When that too was surrounded, a third [enclosure] came into being;
in this way, hundreds of thousands indeed came into being at that time.
The Brahmins were exhausted and the sacrificial enclosure was filled with distress;
at that time, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from all sides everywhere.
Brahmā, bowing repeatedly toward that direction, indeed requested:
"O Lord, what is this? Is it fitting that there should be such a failure of the ritual in this sacrifice? (103)
Therefore, O Maheśvara, withdraw all these skull-bowls;
let there not be a disruption of the sacrificial rite now that you have arrived.
Then a voice arose from the sky: "My vessel is indeed pure;
these are my vessels for eating. Why do these Brahmins revile them? (10.85)
Likewise, O Vidhi, they did not offer oblations into the fire specifically for my sake,
nor did they do so for other deities as they did for the sacrificial offering purified by mantras.
Therefore, having dedicated this specifically to me here in the sacrificial fire, the oblation must be offered;
only then will the sacrifice reach its completion.
Then Brahmā spoke this reply to him from the sky:
"O Yogi, your forms indeed become innumerable."
As long as the skull remains within the pavilion,
for that very duration there should be no ritual use of a cup (camasa) here, nor indeed a bowl (khappara).
That is not declared to be a sacrificial vessel, for it is indeed always impure;
whatever the form of the vessel, and whatever its nature, such is the ground for the ritual act.
Such a thing should be employed there; this [vessel] is not suitable for that purpose. It is held that in a ritual sacrifice, the oblation is to be cooked in earthenware potsherds.
Therefore, let this skull be taken far away so that it may serve as a sacrificial vessel;
for you have indeed displayed here such a form as that of a skull-bearer.
In this sacrifice, let that form alone have the right to the sacrificial cake;
moreover, accept alms and attain satisfaction.
From this day forward, O Lord of Gods, the Śatarudriya, consisting of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), must be offered by the twice-born in sacrifices dedicated to you.
Especially among all sacrifices, this should be recited with particular care;
for whoever, having commenced a sacrifice here, shall worship you first— || 1.15 ||
"His sacrifice will proceed without obstacle and reach completion.
When this was said, O Padmaja, a marvel occurred; listen to it.
And whatever skull-bowls there were, from all of them at that very moment,
thousands of goddesses known as Rudrāṇīs and Annapūrṇās were born.
All those women were forms of Pārvatī, identical with Annapūrṇā; without them, the giving of alms would not even be possible.
Meanwhile, the illustrious Śaṅkara, with his five faces, being greatly delighted,
reached the sacrificial pavilion and stood near the altar.
The Brahmins, sages, and gods likewise paid homage to Hara;
they worshipped the Rudrāṇīs and commenced the performance of the sacrifice.
By the thousands, divine women, the consorts of Śiva, sat down at the sacrifice;
and other celestial women, accompanied by Śiva, arrived by the millions.
In this manner, Śambhu established his share at the sacrifice for all time;
by reading or hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.

Thus ends the five hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Brahmā’s Commissioning of the Construction of the Pavilion and its Appurtenances with Full Materials through the Agency of the Devas and Others at the Hāṭakeśvara Kṣetra on the Banks of the Nāgavatī for the Purpose of Sacrifice in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Arrival of Śaṅkara in the Form of a Jālmaka; the Account of Gāyatrī’s Birth into the Brāhmaṇa Caste; the Nature of the Skulls as Being the Goddess Annapūrṇā; and the Station of Śaṅkara in the Sacrifice. || 509 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, as the Brāhmaṇa was performing the sacrifice at that time,
ten million sages dwelling in the southern region arrived.
Then, crores of those dwelling in Siṃhāraṇya, those residing in Naimiṣāraṇya, and those situated in other regions assembled together.
Having heard of the sacrifice of the Grandfather, they were filled with curiosity:
"What kind of sacrifice will it be, wherein the Lotus-born One is consecrated? (3)
Having bathed at the Rūpa-tīrtha on the Nāga-nadī, those sages, possessing divine forms,
went to the sacrificial ground and bowed to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Seated and weary, they were honored with a welcome and engaged in divine conversations concerning the performance of the sacrifice.
They engaged in mutual debate regarding the drinking of the soma;
thus, between the Udgātṛ and the Adhvaryu, there arose a discussion concerning the truth.
Then, having all eaten, they spent the night in comfort;
when the second day arrived, on the twelfth lunar day, for the performance of the sacrifice.
O Lotus-born one, listen to the curious event that occurred when the officiating priests had begun their work: a certain mischievous young brahmin placed a water-snake on the sacrificial ground.
Then, laughing, he quickly hurled it into the presence of the Creator;
that *ḍuṇḍubha* snake, as it whirled around, approached the side of the Hotṛ priest.
He enveloped the Hotṛ priest Bhṛgu; nevertheless, Bhṛgu did not move from his own place due to the fear of [the need for] expiation.
Then, indeed, there arose a slight agitation and anxiety among everyone;
the sage Cyavana beheld his father enveloped by a serpent.
He cursed the boy who had thrown the snake and caused such agitation:
"O wicked one, O evil-minded one, since you have thrown a snake into the assembly... (12)
"Therefore, become a snake quickly! Having heard this, the boy then said to him:
"In jest, I released this water-snake here as a mere play. (13)
"Why do you cast a curse upon me, targeting the Hotṛ priest?"—
speaking thus, he attained the state of a serpent in that very moment.
The young student, the son of the sage Sanātana, grieved repeatedly;
taking his own *duṇḍubha* snake with him, he went to Bhṛgu and spoke to him. (15)
I am the son of Sanātana and the grandson of Parameṣṭhin; I have been cursed by your son, the high-souled Cyavana.
"O Sage, protect me, a brahmin boy who has come to you for refuge from this curse!
Hearing this, Bhṛgu was overcome with compassion and said to Cyavana, "O son! (17)
This which you have commanded regarding this young brahmin is improper;
even a serpent full of poison would not be able to overpower you. (18)
How much more so this water-snake, which is poisonless and resembles a rope?
Grant him release from the curse; let the young Brahmin become happy.
Cyavana said, "O father, my curse shall not be in vain.
Brahmā, having heard that, then said, "Everything has come to pass by my will."
"Formerly, I desired to unite with the ninth lineage of the Nāgas;
therefore, from you, your lineage shall indeed exist upon the surface of the earth."
The Naga Karkotaka will give you his own beloved daughter;
your lineage shall expand and take up residence in the world of mortals.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, people will perform the worship of that lineage;
thus your residence shall become renowned as Nāgatīrtha.
While the unborn one was speaking thus at the sacrifice, the nāgas arrived;
Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and Kṛṣīhara had been invited.
Puṇḍarīka, Kambalāśvatara, Kālapara, Bala,
Śeṣa, and the others, having bowed down, spoke to the god Pitāmaha at the sacrifice.
"O Brahman, grant us the service appropriate for this sacrifice at all times.
Brahmā said: "In this matter, you are auspicious ones capable of assuming any form at will. (26)
Let those who dwell at the Nāga-tīrtha and those who harbor malice toward this sacrifice, as well as those who desire to create obstacles, be kept away from my sacrificial rite. (27)
"O Nāgas, this is my most important duty: the protection of my sacrifice.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, you shall receive worship from the people. (28)
Having said "So be it," they all, accompanied by the son of Sanātana, resorted to the Nāga-tīrtha, which was the perpetuator of Sanātana’s lineage.
He married the daughter of Karkoṭaka, who was in the bloom of youth;
from that time on, his lineage became widespread upon the earth in every way.
Those who bear upon their hoods a square tilaka-mark joined with a bindu,
and which is devoid of a staff above— that are born of your eternal lineage.
The Vaiṣṇavas were of many forms; they became white, tawny, pale, red, black, and green according to the difference in time.
Then, due to that intermixture, they became variegated and likewise venomless;
there were water-snakes, land-snakes, and those capable of assuming any form at will.
Then, on the evening of the thirteenth day, those very officiating priests prepared the food offerings and so forth, and held a vigil throughout the night. (34)
Having reached the morning libation and being fully engaged in the sacrificial rites,
no sound was heard there once the sacrifice had commenced, for not even a moment's pause occurred.
"Let it be given, let it be given! Let the desired be eaten, let it be eaten in abundance! Let the gift be taken, let it be taken; indeed, let it be four times more than what was wished for. (36)
There were mountains of cooked foods as well as heaps of wealth;
there were rivers flowing with ghee and milk, and lakes of sweet drinks.
At that time, they were multiplied a thousandfold, providing satisfaction to millions;
in the meantime, a certain wise man arrived there. (38)
Having paid homage to Brahmā, who knows the three periods of time,
he sat down and then related his entire personal history.
The officiating priests asked him out of curiosity about his own past deeds;
he recounted them to them, and they were filled with wonder.
They asked: "Tell us, why indeed do you possess such supramundane knowledge? Tell us, O wise one, who is your guru—is it Brahmā, Hara, or Hari? (41)
The Knower said: "These six are my gurus: Piṅgalā, Kurara, Sarpa, Bhramara, Iṣukāra, and Kumārikā. (42)
Through their conduct, O twice-born ones, I obtained this most auspicious and supreme knowledge; the lord of Saurāṣṭra had a hundred women. (43)
In his inner apartments there was also a lady named Piṅgalā;
deprived of her husband and free from desire, she slept peacefully at night. (44)
But hundreds of other wives, out of lustful desire, bring beautiful incenses, ointments, and flowers during the night.
With excellent unguents and fine garments, they were filled with the excitement of love and possessed a thrill of horripilation. ||46||
One knows me on the bed and will surely call out for me;
another knows me as well, but the third knows neither me nor the other. (47)
Then they vie with one another, look on, and wait for the king;
he calls one of them, or the second, or the third. (48)
On the fourth, the fifth, or sometimes for ten nights,
the remaining ones, having fallen into grief, sigh and sleep.
Those who have fallen into the suffering of hope do not obtain even a moment of sleep;
for hope is the supreme suffering, and freedom from hope is the supreme happiness.
Having turned hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace;
she no longer engages in amorous dalliance nor in any kind of rivalry whatsoever. (51)
Piṅgalā did not fall into distress; she slept happily, even though I was constantly appointed to the service of the harem. (52)
Having observed this, I then abandoned all hope and even fell asleep;
for those who sleep happily at night, their digestive fire remains active. (53)
When food is ignited, it takes up [the fuel] and attains nourishment;
this very cause has arisen such that nourishment increases knowledge. 54.
Listen to the knowledge I have obtained from the osprey, just as I shall tell it:
I possessed abundant wealth, a great inheritance from my father and grandfather. (55)
For the sake of wealth, my sons, grandsons, heirs, kinsmen, and relatives likewise harass me day and night. (56)
"He whom I do not grant [his desire] constantly torments me;
indeed, he alone strives perpetually to take my life in my very presence. (57)
Another begs while employing force and instilling fear;
a third begs with conciliation, and yet another likewise with praise. (58)
One [type of person] seeks wealth through separation, while another likewise does so by means of bestowing victory;
and at the end, having become wretched, he indeed repeatedly begs for riches.
Thus, I do not obtain happiness anywhere from their presence;
by day or by night, I find neither comfort, nor sleep, nor peace at all.
Then one day, a kurara bird was seen in the sky carrying a piece of meat, being attacked from all sides by other birds for the sake of that meat.
The meat that had fallen from his beak was followed by those birds;
and the osprey, abandoned by them, became happy.
"By the renunciation of material wealth, the osprey prospers in happiness;
for I have indeed divided and bestowed my property, including my sons and others. (63)
From that time forth, released by them, I have lived happily and in full vigor.
The attainment of wealth leads to delusion, and delusion leads to hell.
Therefore, one who seeks liberation should abandon both profit and loss from afar;
just as bait is devoured by fish in the water and by beasts of prey on the ground.
Just as birds fly everywhere in the sky, so too does the wealthy man go everywhere;
even if he is free from fault, the wealthy man is repeatedly punished by kings.
A poor man is generally abandoned by people even if he has committed no fault;
though constantly surrounded by others, they stumble at every step.
The wealthy speak incoherently, like those intoxicated by wine; they harbor hatred for what is beneficial and affection for what is external, finding pleasure even in that which is trivial. (68)
But for the wealthy, there is constant bitterness in their mouths, as if they were suffering from a fever;
for the sake of wealth, this world of living beings frequents even the cremation ground. (69)
Even sons abandon their own father if he is destitute;
indeed, friendship lasts only so long as there is no application for wealth.
When a connection with wealth arises, enmity follows of its own accord; therefore, having abandoned riches, I remain at ease like a kurara bird. (71)
I shall relate how knowledge was obtained from a snake in the past, just as a snake, having entered a dwelling made by another, enjoys happiness. (72)
Having dwelt there in happiness, he departs for another region after abandoning it; he feels no sense of ownership at all, neither toward himself nor toward anything else. (73)
The undertaking of building a house leads only to suffering and never to happiness;
through the construction of a house, the sense of possessiveness persists until the time of death.
Once a house is built, a wife is acquired, and from her come sons and daughters;
for their sake, one performs both what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, remaining thus once more for the sake of worldly enjoyment. (75)
Like a silkworm that has enveloped itself in its cocoon, one does not perceive oneself at all;
bound by the notions of "I" and "mine," living beings who are thus attached sink into ruin. (76)
Immersed in the ocean of the mire of attachment to sons, wives, and wealth, ignorant men perish just like intoxicated elephants. //77//
A servant commits sins, yet the master enjoys the wealth;
the enjoyer is released from that sin, while the doer alone is tainted by the fault. (78)
Therefore, I have abandoned this mansion that serves as a bolt upon the path to liberation;
a virtuous person should never become a giver of suffering to householders. (79)

One should dwell constantly anywhere at all, taking refuge under trees while avoiding inhabited places; one should practice the "bee-like" mendicancy for alms, avoiding those who cause harm, in a place free from smoke.
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa and constantly chant the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; indeed, neither attachment nor aversion should be entertained, nor enmity nor friendship. 8.1
For one to whom clods of earth, stones, and gold are equal, and for whom honor and dishonor are the same, there is never any distinction between "one's own" country and another's. (82)
Whether it be the earth, one's family, or even the family of Brahmā;
the twenty-four principles (tattvas) constitute the house and the family, which are all unstable. (83)
The latent impression (vāsanā) is always carried along with [the self] and not in another's house;
for when there is a whirling with speed here, it is like the wheel of a potter. 84.
He will indeed attain peace once he has acquired the jar of liberation;
such knowledge, which bestows liberation, was obtained by me from the serpent. (85)
By its power, my great splendor and happiness always endure;
nevertheless, I shall now declare the essential knowledge obtained from the bee. (86)
Once, on a certain tree, I saw a bee that had previously made its dwelling by taking refuge at the tip of a branch. (87)
In spring, among the blossoms of the trees and even among the fragrant fruits upon many wild trees, he perceived the most excellent essence.
Having taken it, he constantly employed it in his own dwelling;
free from agitation, he filled many baskets with the finest honey. (89)
By that, many others, like bees, attained satisfaction;
and by me, the auspicious essence of the scriptures has been extracted, like honey.
Men accept those well-composed treatises, and others indeed subsist upon them, just as bees do from flowers. ||91||
By that merit, I am always radiant with splendor and endowed with knowledge;
likewise, the sages, who delight in the Self, are entirely free from the thirst for worldly enjoyments.
Those who are fully satisfied by the essence of the honeyed liquor become possessed of great splendor;
those who are possessed by greed and delusion indeed become devoid of splendor.
The Vedas and the Shastras were created by me for the benefit of the worlds; having extracted the essence from all of them, I have indeed bestowed it and am at peace. (94)
I shall proclaim that knowledge which was obtained from the arrow-maker;
for the sake of perceiving the Self, I have questioned thousands [of teachers]. (95)
Those renowned for their vision of the self have said that what was taught by them has been accomplished through knowledge, through yoga, and through the study of inner science. (96)
And through divine vision gained by practice, I have become absorbed in that;
yet I have not seen the Self, and therefore I am possessed of dispassion.
I wandered upon the earth seeking such a teacher who would demonstrate the goal of the guru;
yet, I did not find such a teacher anywhere. (98)
Then I stood on a secluded spot by the royal highway,
where a certain practitioner was shooting at a target.
With his mind one-pointed, he indeed pierced the target with an arrow again and again; standing by its side, he struck it alone and perceived nothing else at all.
Accompanied by that army on its path, the king proceeded;
then, in another moment, he was seen by me after someone had approached him.
This archer, skilled in hitting the mark and having devoted his mind to practice, was asked:
"How much time has passed since the king departed? (102)
The arrow-maker did not hear; he questioned him again in that same manner, yet even by her [the voice] he did not hear at all, having become absorbed in the target.
Having touched him again and shaken him, the young man indeed questioned him;
then he said, "I did not see anyone who went away from here with an arrow."
"I have not seen the army depart from here; ask someone else if it has gone.
My mind was entirely absorbed in the practice of aiming at targets with arrows, so I did not look around. (105)
Having heard that, I then reflected there with one-pointed mind upon the means for seeing my own self— that which brings about the vision of one's own soul.
Knowledge of the Self, which is the science of Brahman, does not arise anywhere without the cessation of the mind; nor is there any vision [of truth] without practice.
"I have attained this knowledge; therefore, I shall practice its cessation.
I meditate constantly upon Hari, who dwells within the lotus of my heart. (108)
I indeed bear within my heart and contemplate again and again Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who possesses a universal form and a beautiful appearance.
Then, in all directions and their extremities, in the sky and on the surface of the earth—
in men, children, cows, trees, women, creepers, and mountains— [he was seen].
Through practice, I perceive Hari in front, behind, and in every reality;
I see Him alone as such, and nothing else whatsoever apart from Hari.
"By that very splendor, I am thus illuminated today and always;
from that, knowledge has been obtained by me in every way through the practice of meditation. (11.2)
Now I shall speak of the knowledge obtained from the maiden:
formerly, on the road, my wife went out behind me. (1.13)
A woman who has sons and daughters spoke to her husband and me:
"Perform your religious duties at home; liberation will surely come about, there is no doubt."
Becoming a celibate ascetic, remain self-restrained even while living at home;
for if you were to abandon me and go elsewhere, [it would be a great loss]. || 115 ||
Therefore, I shall die, and your child shall also die;
the young girl too shall die. Therefore, O Lord, have mercy!
Do not go to any other sacred ford, having abandoned the sacred ford of the home,
for the sacred ford born of Hāṭakeśvara grants liberation through mere remembrance.
Having constructed a leaf-hut at the command of my wife,
I indeed dwell not far from the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
"The daughter of a forest-dweller is playing in my hermitage, her forearms adorned with many jingling bracelets. (11.9)
In the task of carrying wood, sometimes by the striking of the wood,
one ring at a time is broken into pieces here and there.
When time has passed in this manner, two bracelets remain;
then a sound arises, and after that time has further elapsed, [the same occurs again]. (121)
Now, however, there is but one bangle on each forearm;
for being alone, neither friction nor sound arises. (122)
Having reflected upon that, I attained knowledge and abandoned that stage of life;
for there is constant quarreling with many, as well as rivalry between two.
I shall wander alone like a maiden’s bracelet;
therefore, having abandoned my wife, daughters, and sons, I shall roam.
Wherever I sleep at sunset, and whatever food I have obtained and eaten, I always remember Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, free from all bonds.
Thus was this knowledge obtained by me through reflecting upon various [sources].
Whomever from whom that knowledge may arise, he shall likewise be your guru. (126)
Through these, I have obtained knowledge of the worlds beyond and self-knowledge as well;
this has been gained even more abundantly through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
"By hearing this, one also attains such knowledge as this.
Having spoken thus, that wise Jñānātithi then fell silent. (128)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, residing at Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ, has arrived for the purpose of this command: "He must be honored as a guest at the sacrifice. (129)
Having recognized Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa through meditation, the learned Śrī Hari, honored by the officiating priests, sat down among the ṛtviks.

Thus ends the five hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Arrival of the Son of Sanātana in the Form of a Boy at the Sacrifice for the Purpose of Throwing a Snake, and Subsequently the Arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in the Form of a Guest for the Purpose of Bestowing Knowledge upon His Teacher and Others, as well as the Exposition of that Knowledge," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. ||510||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī; then those brahmins situated in the pavilion questioned this guest, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, who was in the form of a brahmin.
"Having abandoned your home, where have you gone and how much time has passed for you? Tell us what is appropriate for the sacrificial rites of these assembled ascetics. (2)
Then the guest said: "I have wandered through the three worlds—the world of Brahmā, the world of Īśa, and the world of living beings—again and again."
There are hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, lakhs, and arbuds of continents, earths, and Golokas.
Wherever I lie down at sunset, having performed my bodily sustenance,
I dwell there as if in my own body, for I generally abide in the fundamental principles (tattvas).
I dwell everywhere in sacrifice, and I dwell even in the dissolution;
indeed, years beyond all calculation have passed for me.
There is no counting the number of ages; my lifespan is considered eternal.
Wherever I go, the sacred fords (tīrthas) come into existence simply by my arrival.
Having performed those endless rites for you at the sacrifice of the gods,
and having wandered through islands, regions, and all sacred fords—
namely the southern, the eastern Jyotiṣka, the snowy mountain [Himalaya], and likewise the northern ones— I have now returned.
Śvetadvīpa, Kṛṣṇadeśa, Siṃhāraṇya, and Raivata; || 9 ||
Having visited Sārasvata, Gāṅga, Vārāṇasī, and Puṣkara,
he heard of the universal sacrifice of the Grandfather in the western region.
"I have come here to accept hospitality, if it is granted to me.
Brahmā and the other gods say to you: 'O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, choose a boon! (11)
Accept as hospitality whatever you desire, whether it be material or spiritual;
we shall certainly bestow that upon you, the knower who is our inner self.
The guest said: "I am always to be regarded by you as one who has offered himself; likewise, I am a seeker of refuge, and my desire is the offering of everything. (1.3)
Even if Brahmā and the other gods were to perform a sacrifice for me without having first given [to others],
they would not obtain their desired fruit, for they failed to give to the guest.
I pray for my share of the sacrifice, the portion of the gods, and divine status;
likewise, may they grant me both inner and outer states.
Thus addressed, the deities said: "A guest has arrived from afar;
you are a vessel of truth, O best of Brahmins, and everything shall be given to you at this sacrifice."
Hari is remembered as the lord of this sacrifice that is being performed;
for this reason, that God is called Yajñapuruṣa (the Person of Sacrifice). || 17 ||
You reside at Kuṅkumavāpī in the sacred field as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
the beloved Kamalā of Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa is Kambharā. 18.
Through austerity, you obtained the mind, and that which is established in the self, your own offspring;
you are Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Lord of Śrī Pārvatī.
You are Prabheśa, Māṇikīśa, Jayeśa, and Śrī Hari himself;
you abide as the soul of sacrificial rites, the bestower of the fruits of actions.
He is the Lord of the mind, the Lord of Maṅgalā, the Lord of Rādhā, and the Sovereign of the Imperishable;
He is the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of the liberated, and the Supreme Self dwelling within.
"Under your name, the fruit of a complete sacrifice shall always be granted;
likewise, whoever worships you during a śrāddha for the ancestors or a rite for the gods," (22)
Endowed with the name of Viṣṇu, that [merit] shall be inexhaustible;
indeed, when Kṛṣṇa is gratified, all the gods become gratified.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Dharma, Śeṣa, Śiva,
and the others indeed gave everything to the guest Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
From that time forward, worship arising from guests was established.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, worship of the guest should always be performed at an auspicious moment;
for householders, there is no higher duty than the honoring of guests.
There is no god higher than the guest; one should never bypass a deity. || 26 ||
When a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated, he departs having transferred his own misdeeds to that person and taking away their merit. (27)
Truthfulness, vows, austerity, study, charity, and sacrifices performed for a hundred years—all that becomes lost for him who does not honor a guest. (28)
He in whose house guests indeed remain well-satisfied is truly a householder; others, however, are merely guardians of the home.
In this world, for those people who have previously performed meritorious deeds, these three things come to them: the ancestral rite (śrāddha), charity (dāna), and auspicious speech.
When the guest is satisfied, all the deities of the householder are satisfied;
when he turns his face away, they all likewise turn their faces away—of this there is no doubt. (3.1)
He—Nārāyaṇa, the deities, the goddesses, guests, and the teacher—must indeed be satisfied even by the offering of one's own self. (32)
A virtuous woman, an orphaned maiden, a female mendicant, and a guest are considered [worthy recipients]; so too is he who arrives at the time of the meal during a paternal *śrāddha* ceremony.
One who arrives exhausted from a long journey, or one who approaches at midday after having already eaten, or one who comes during the night—[these are not to be refused]. (34)
These are declared to be guests; one who arrives first is not a guest, whether he be a friend or an enemy, a fool or a scholar. (35)
A householder should indeed provide food according to his capacity, as well as a seat, water, a kind disposition, pleasant speech, and a loving glance. (36)
These, however, are never cut off in the house of the virtuous;
indeed, through the welcome of a guest, the ancestors truly become satisfied. 37.
Likewise, satisfaction arises for Brahmā from providing a seat for a guest;
through the offering of the arghya water, Śambhu is pleased, and by the offering of water for the feet, the gods are gratified. (38)
Through the gift of food, Viṣṇu attains eternal satisfaction;
therefore, he should always be honored according to one's ability, and especially fed. (3.9)
Having spoken thus and performed the ritual procedures for the sacrificial work, the gods then provided exemptions and fed the lords.
They passed the night with festivities and expositions on the supreme Lord;
on the fourth day, they commenced the sacrificial rites as prescribed.
The drinking of soma and all other such rites, as well as the sacrificial materials and so forth, proceeded there appropriately until he arrived. (42)

Formerly, there was a twice-born man belonging to the Sāmaveda named Chāndogya;

On that very day when he was born,
a daughter was also born to the lord of Ānarta.
The king indeed gave her the beautiful name Ratnavatī;
for a friendship arose between Ratnavatī and the daughter of the Brahmin, Śubhākṣayā.
Sharing a single seat, as well as a single bed and eating from a single meal, the Brahmin reflected even when the appropriate time for his daughter's marriage had arrived. (5)
However, that maiden, distressed by the prospect of separation from her friend, went and spoke at great sorrow to the king's daughter. (6)
"Friend, my father will now arrange my marriage;
by that, our friendship would perish and we two would be separated. (7)
Having heard this, the king’s daughter placed it around her neck and wept;
hearing her cries, Queen Mṛgāvatī came there in great haste.
Having understood the cause of her weeping, he spoke to the fair-eyed woman:
"Daughter, I now determine that you and my daughter are friends."
"I shall give you to my daughter as her beloved friend.
Having summoned the Brāhmaṇa, the queen said, "O Vipra, this is your daughter."
For she is indeed my daughter’s very affectionate and beloved friend;
therefore, do as I say and give your daughter to me.
Alternatively, your daughter should be given to that brahmin who is the family priest of the king to whom my daughter is to be given. (12)
When two people remain in one place, there will always be the happiness of friendship;
for [the sage], having indeed understood the intention of his daughter Chāndogyā— ||| 13 ||
The king gave that princess, who was devoted to a life of celibacy, to the queen; she then took up residence together with Ratnavatī, the daughter of the Brahmin.
Born in the king's palace, she became an exceedingly beautiful young woman;
and the king desired to give his daughter to a most worthy bridegroom.
He indeed caused the Brahmins to search for him throughout the earth;
the king who was the lord of Daśārṇa was chosen by her as her husband.
That king Bṛhadbala had arrived for the purpose of the marriage of the Brahmin Viśvāvasu and the royal priest. || 17 ||
At that time, there was a young man named Parāvasu;
he too, along with the royal priest, arrived there together with the king.
At the auspicious moment of the wedding, the king arrived there in the pavilion in the presence of the sacred fire, and the maiden arrived accompanied by her friend, the daughter of a brahmin.
Led by her parents to the presence of Heḍī, she was brought there to be given away in marriage along with other women; a great marvel occurred there.
The maiden was a rememberer of her past lives, devoted to celibacy, and born from a portion of Śiva;
produced by a digit of Pārvatī, she became a yoginī from birth.
That virtuous Brahmin maiden was likewise capable of assuming any form at will; she was composed of all spiritual perfections and was entirely devoted to the practice of celibacy.
Through the power of Gaurī, those two accomplished a manifold manifestation of bodies;
they attained all supernatural powers and likewise conquered Kāmadeva. (23)
A Vaiṣṇava mantra, which reveals the secret, was indeed given to them both by Pārvatī:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (24)
And Śrī Pārvatī said to you: "No one other than Kṛṣṇa is the husband; the devotion to the husband (pātivratya) must always be maintained toward Hari alone, and never toward anyone else."
He bestowed yogic perfections upon the two of them; through those perfections, they became endowed with divine majesty and filled with wonder within the pavilion.
There, a princess appeared in the form of Siṃhikā—
fearsome, with a lolling tongue, wide-open eyes, and a roaring voice.
Then, in an instant, the daughter of the Brahmin became a cruel tigress;
seeing her, all the people were terrified and fled outside the pavilion.
Except for the two maidens, everyone indeed fled from the pavilion;
a great clamor arose in the village, the kingdom, and among the subjects. (29)
Then Bṛhadbala, having left them behind, departed for his own city;
later, even when restrained by his parents, he maintained only the form of Pārvatī.
When they had thus been sustained, peace indeed arose among the people;
and the two Pārvatīs, possessing divine bodies, were worshipped by the world.
Those two maidens, accompanied by Śaṅkara, were like a hundred moons.
Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance! (32)
While the two Vaiṣṇava women were thus chanting, those two maidens were born;
seeing them endowed with their former forms, the onlookers were filled with satisfaction.
News of that very same pair of Pārvatīs spread everywhere throughout the worlds;
indeed, a pair of goddesses existed in every single household. (34)
The people always worship, behold, and bow down to [it];
and they constantly perform the *ārātrika* ceremony in Camatkārapura. (35)
Thus, after some time had passed, a supremely purifying holy ford (tīrtha) consisting of two goddesses arose in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara.
Ratnavatī remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa repeatedly:
"I have offered my very self to you; therefore, lead me from here to the state of Kṛṣṇa. (37)
The Brahmin maiden also said this: "Wherever you are, there shall I also be;
for a female friend never goes to another place, having abandoned her friend. (38)
Then the goddess Durgā was remembered by them and she arrived quickly;
she gave them both instructions for their penance when they set forth.
Then Queen Mṛgāvatī, overcome by delusion and infatuation, her eyes filled with tears and her spirit dejected, spoke thus to her daughter: ||| 1.513.40 ||
"O daughter, you must not under any circumstances act rashly for the sake of asceticism;
you are but a young girl with delicate limbs, always accustomed to comfort. (41)
"How, O blameless one, are you able to perform ascetic penance, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, and wearing garments of bark and rags? (42)
Therefore, I shall give you to some preeminent king;
this Brahmin woman named Sakhī is your most esteemed companion.
Adopting the state of maidenhood, she will indeed go with you to the palace of that king to whom you shall be given in marriage. (44)
And Ratnavatī said to her: "Mother, if you wish to protect my life, you must never speak thus again on my behalf. (45)
If you create an obstacle for me by force,
then I shall abandon my body through the application of poison, having first chewed my tongue.
"Either I shall enter the fire or I shall obtain Śrī Hari as my husband;
I will not take another husband—this is the resolve I have made. (47)
I shall practice austerity, observing the vow of lifelong maidenhood;
I shall attain the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as my husband, the true lord.
Kings speak but once; twice do the twice-born speak;
thrice do they utter the truth; these things are purchased only once each.
A task is first conceived by the mind, then it is proclaimed by speech, and afterwards it is carried out through action; being virtuous, I act in that same manner.
Having thus spoken to her mother, the beloved of Hari ceased;
then the queen spoke to her friend, the Brāhmaṇī.
"My daughter does not desire a husband nor even marriage, O daughter;
you must be married, so go to your father's palace."
"Or rather, I shall have your marriage performed according to your desire;
forgive those bitter words that I may have spoken to you at any time. (53)
"Or whatever was said by you at any time, all that has been forgiven by me,
my daughter," the Brahmin woman then spoke these words of righteousness to the queen.
An eight-year-old girl is Gaurī, a nine-year-old is Rohiṇī, and a ten-year-old is Kanyā; the giving away of a daughter in this manner is highly praised.
Furthermore, it is heard that as long as [the bridegroom] is not yet visible above [the horizon], the gift of a maiden indeed bestows full merit. (56)
My maidenhood has indeed perished, and my youth is passing away;
once the sixteenth year has elapsed, I shall surely become subject to the nature of women.
He who marries a maiden while she is in her menses, his offspring will indeed be joined with sin and cause ten others to fall as well. (58)
Furthermore, the father who gives away a daughter while she is in her menses causes ten ancestors and ten descendants of his own lineage to fall. (59)
Therefore, I shall perform supreme austerity together with my friend;
I have no need whatsoever for my father, mother, or even you.
"Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord and Master, has arrived.
Having spoken thus, the two maidens, endowed with the knowledge of yoga, [prepared themselves]. (61)
Having bowed down, received the command of their parents, and prostrated before the Lord of the Gaṇas,
they both traveled by way of the sky to the sage Bhartṛyajña in the forest.
And they beheld that auspicious, sattvic hermitage,
where, by the power of the sage’s asceticism, even those things that are mutually antagonistic [coexisted].
A meeting always exists where enmity is not seen;
having approached and bowed to Bhartṛyajña, the Vaiṣṇava, they both stood there. (64)
Both of them, endowed with humility and with palms joined in reverence, said:
"We have come to you for the sake of asceticism; therefore, tell us the method of that asceticism."
The great yogi Bhartṛyajña proclaimed the rule for austerity, by which liberation is attained—how much more so the abode of the gods! ||66||
The Cāndrāyaṇa fasts, the Kṛcchra penances, as well as the Sāntapana rites—all these gateways to austerity, and the vows dedicated to Kārttikeya. ||67||
Freedom from passion and hatred, universal non-violence, truthfulness, celibacy, non-stealing, and the acceptance of Kṛṣṇa [as the sole object]. (68)
Contentment, self-purification, as well as the restraint of the vital breaths, meditation upon Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and the offering of everything to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa—[these are the means]. (69)
Likewise, one should cultivate loving-kindness toward those who are happy, compassion for those who suffer,
sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit, and equanimity toward those who lack merit.
One should perform service to the virtuous in every way, as well as the worship of the Divine;
one should daily practice the propitiation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Through the three bodies within their respective states, one should offer the three qualities to Him.
Attachment to the body is merely for its sustenance; love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa is eternal. ||72||

Action, conceptualization, meditation, dreaming, and its manifestation—these are the offerings [of the mind], whether through the quality of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), or even darkness (tamas). ||73||
Whether bodily or mental, performed with desire or without desire, he taught that offering [of all actions] as well as chanting, remembering, glorifying, and performing [devotional acts]. (74)
Beholding, speaking, touching, approaching, grasping, and releasing—all these actions must be performed as being of the nature of Kṛṣṇa; this is considered the supreme austerity.
Whatever action— whether of the path of worldly engagement (pravṛtta) or the path of renunciation (nivṛtta)— by which Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa may be attained, that action is the highest austerity (tapas).
For everything else might indeed be obtained, were it not for Kṛṣṇa being attained;
without Kṛṣṇa, that [attainment] is merely hell—therefore, that is not considered true austerity.
When oneness arises between the object to be grasped, the object to be held, and likewise the Self—[all] being "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa"—then one shall attain liberation. ||78||
Service to Kṛṣṇa and devotion to Kṛṣṇa are said to be the supreme austerity;
having attained a human birth through the austerity of many lifetimes, [one should practice them]. (79)
If there be devotion to Kṛṣṇa, human birth is fruitful;
his life is fruitful as he performs actions that bear fruit.
He certainly [delivers] thousands of his own paternal ancestors, as well as his mother,
hundreds of his maternal grandfathers, and his uterine brother.
O two daughters, even for a kinsman, a wife, teachers, a disciple, or a servant, that action is auspicious which consists of surrendering everything to Kṛṣṇa. (82)
That alone is true austerity, that is auspicious action, since it brings satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa;
that alone is the vow, that is true penance, that is truth, and likewise that is devotion and worship.
The fast undertaken with that as its objective bestows the service of Hari;
it is equal to the gift of the entire earth and likewise to circumambulating the world.
It is equivalent to bathing in all sacred fords, performing every vow and austerity, conducting all sacrifices, and likewise obtaining the fruit of all gifts. ||85||
The recitation and teaching of all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, as well as the protection of the frightened and the bestowal of supreme knowledge; ||86||
The honoring of guests, the protection of those who seek refuge, the worship of all the gods, as well as salutation and the chanting of the mantra. (87)
Feeding the Brahmins and the gods preceded by the *puraścaraṇa* rite, service to the guru, devotion to one's parents, and the nurturing [of dependents]. (88)
All these do not equal even a sixteenth part of Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa;
therefore, O two daughters, worship the Lord Kṛṣṇa with great effort. (89)
Indeed, [she sought] the eternal Lord of beings, the divine Supreme Self,
the ever-present Truth, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, as her husband.
To Hari, who is most perfectly complete, pure, untainted, and the witness; who bestows devotion and servitude, and grants his own state of innate perfection. ||91||
Worship the Lord, the beloved of the inner self, who is supreme bliss;
for what is water and what is land, or likewise, what is night and what is day? (92)
What vow, or what austerity, or what food, or even what drink? What body, or what mind? Having forgotten all these, worship Hari. (93)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Beloved Kṛṣṇa!
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, inner soul of all, grant me service at Your feet, O Lord of my beloved! 94.
Through love, devotion, praise, worship,
and even through self-surrender, [she beheld] Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, her inner husband, residing in the heart of her son.
Worship the protector who bestows happiness. ||95||
O daughter, worship the foot of Kṛṣṇa, which is honored by Ramā and Padmā, served by Lakṣmī, graced by splendor, and kissed by Māṇikī.
It is constantly sung by Śambhu, meditated upon in the heart by Pārvatī, and contemplated by the virtuous Sanaka brothers; worship that state of Hari. 97.
He who chants the lotus feet of Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa during his sleep, O son, is liberated from the sins committed in a hundred lifetimes; of this there is no doubt. (98)
That vow, that austerity, that truth, and that merit, as well as that worship, becomes fruitful when connected with Kṛṣṇa, since it destroys the cycle of rebirth. 99.
"O daughter, what would be the use of performing penance if one abandons that Śrī Kṛṣṇa?
Indeed, one attains the fruit of all penances simply by remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa."
Since devotion does not arise toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, that guru is the supreme enemy; he renders one's birth fruitless.
Saying "So be it," they received that supreme and auspicious knowledge consisting of devotion;
having bowed and gone to the shore of the lake, they performed the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances.
For three autumns, they indeed subsisted on food taken at the sixth mealtime;
during the winter, they dwelt in water, and in the summer, they practiced the penance of the five fires.
And during the rainy season, while staying without shelter, the two beloveds of Hari remained meditating day and night, chanting the name of their husband, Śrī Hari.
Then for a hundred and fifty years they remained without food;
for that same length of time, they also subsisted on withered leaves.
Thereafter, they remained subsisting on water for six hundred years,
and they subsisted on air for a thousand years.
While both of her two friends remained constantly engaged in austerity there,
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe, himself became pleased.
Young, handsome, and dark-complexioned, he arrived together with Garuḍa;
his splendor pervading every direction, he spoke indeed to the two female ascetics.
"Open your eyes and look; I have come to grant you a boon.
Hearing this, they opened their eyes and beheld the Lord.
The true lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved and enchanting one,
whose limbs are proportionate to His form, the worthy one whose lotus feet are to be served.
Abandoning their asceticism, they fell at his feet and said, "O Lord, accept this pair of handmaidens; grant us service and become our master."
With tearful eyes and deeply distressed, they both embraced Kṛṣṇa around his neck;
Kṛṣṇa, perceiving their inner feelings, kissed them and touched them with his hand.
Having covered and led away those two of divine form, who were equal to Rāmā,
you placed them upon your own lap, resting them above your thighs.
Having carried them on his two arms to the side, he went to the sacrificial ground of Bhartṛyajña;
and having placed their Vaiṣṇava preceptor upon the back of Garuḍa, he departed.
Those four went to the abode of Goloka by means of Garuḍa;
having learned of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s arrival, the sages went to that place.
As he was traveling through the sky, they bowed and worshipped the Lord;
that lake of the Nāga river was also known by the excellent name Ratnasaras.
At that time, it became truly renowned as a bestower of liberation through bathing;
moreover, those two maidservants of Kṛṣṇa were born as attendants of eternal bliss.
When the goddesses arrived in heaven and requested that he remain there, it was then said:
"For the welfare of the goddesses, you must indeed remain in heaven."
Although those two Tārakas were established by Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
they are merely shadow-forms that grant liberation through reading or even hearing them.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lioness and Tiger Form Assumed by the Two at the Time of the Marriage of the Princess of Camatkārapurī and the Brahmin’s Daughter, Their Residence in the Hermitage of Bhartṛyajña, Their Difficult Penance, and Their Attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa along with Bhartṛyajña and Subsequent Departure for Goloka," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which destroys all sins in the mortal world—the three sacred fields (kṣetra), the three forests (araṇya), and likewise the three cities (purī). || 1 ||
Likewise, there are three forests, three villages, and three supreme holy sites;
as well as three mountains and three rivers that bestow all fruits.
By visiting Kurukṣetra, Hāṭakeśakṣetra, and Prabhāsakṣetra according to the prescribed rites, a person is liberated from sin.
First is Puṣkarāraṇya, and Naimiṣāraṇya as well;
Dharmāraṇya is the third, bestowing all desired fruits. || 4 ||
Vārāṇasī is the first city, the second is Dvārakā, and the third is Avantikā; each bestows its desired fruit.
Vṛndāvana, Dvaitavana, and likewise Khāṇḍavavana grant heaven and liberation through bathing and residence; they are the destroyers of sin.
Kālagrāma, Śālagrāma, and Nandigrāma as the third;
these are the destroyers of the thirst for the collection of sense-objects and likewise bestowers of liberation.
Agnitīrtha, Śuklatīrtha, and Pitṛtīrtha as the third;
by bathing there, a human being certainly attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Śrīparvata, Arbudādri, and Raivatācala as well—
one who undertakes a pilgrimage to these shall enjoy heaven and subsequently attain liberation.
The river Gaṅgā, the river known as Narmadā, and the river Sarasvatī—
through bathing in them, one gains enjoyment as well as liberation, and they grant all that is desired at all times.
Jñānavāpī, Kuṅkumavāpī, and Rohaṇavāpikā—
by drinking the water of these three purifying step-wells, liberation shall be attained.
The Nārāyaṇa lake, the Indra lake, and the Mānasa lake—
by bathing in these three lakes, even the granting of worldly enjoyment and liberation occurs.
Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Jayā, Ramā,
Rādhā, and Padmā— these eight names shall deliver one from the ocean of worldly existence.
Vastrāpatha, Uttarāpatha, and Dakṣiṇāpatha—these three alone grant liberation here through pilgrimage; of this there is no doubt. (14)

Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, eating the food of those of other castes and so forth, dwelling in the house of a Cāṇḍāla, and the consumption of liquor and meat—what need is there to say more? (16)
By bathing in the Nāganadī, everything is purified in every way;
therefore, Nāgalīlā is indeed a maidservant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In the presence of Kṛṣṇa, she indeed loosened and disheveled the braid of Rādhikā’s hair with her own hand as a playful jest.
Again, Rādhikā wound her hair into a braid;
Nāgalīlā, however, with her intellect, once more fashioned it into a loose, flowing knot.
In Goloka, there was a knotting together and a constant untying of those two;
through their playful companionship, Rādhikā was born from that.
Enraged, she said: "Go, O Nāgalīlā, to the surface of the earth!
Go to the house of an Ābhīra and be held by an Ābhīra!"
Having spoken thus, that friend offered praise to Rādhā for her release from the curse;
Rādhā said: "When you shall be held by the cowherd... (21)
Then you shall move about in the form of water as a purifier;
you will be ungraspable except by Kṛṣṇa, of this there is no doubt.
"When Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa comes there, you shall become a maiden and come with me to Goloka. (23)
To that extent, it always bestows liberation, washes away sins,
grants purity, and purifies even those men who have fallen from their caste, such as the outcaste dog-cookers (śvapacas).
"By merely bathing, you shall indeed become the bestower of purity.
Having been addressed thus by Rādhā, she bowed and then departed for the earth. (25)
