For this maiden was born in the house of Śyāmasura, the best of the Ābhīras from Ānarta; his name was Nāgalīla. (26)
Jātismarā called out to you, as did her mother Rāṇikā;
she rejoiced at having obtained a daughter who was radiant and possessed a divine form.
Always during the day, she would go to the shore of the lake and gather cow dung; seeing her wandering among the herd of cows, a young cowherd boy [watched her]. ||28||
The youth assailed that beautiful young woman;
remembering Rādhikā’s curse, she indeed turned into the form of water.
That river became known as the Nāganadī, the beloved friend of Kṛṣṇa himself;
by bathing in it, even the wife of a Cāṇḍāla becomes a Brāhmaṇī.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in the city of Vardhamāna, there was a Caṇḍāla of the lowest caste named Kumbhaka; he had a son, his own offspring.
Known as Ghūkakarṇa, who was handsome, he arrived at Camatkārapura while on a pilgrimage to sacred sites, having assumed the form of a twice-born brahmin.
He bathes in all sacred fords, subsisting on food obtained through alms;
he conducts himself constantly like a twice-born man, performing the rites of the twice-born due to living with them.
In that city of Camatkārapura, in the lineage of the Brahmin Subhadra,
there was indeed one daughter who possessed double the number of teeth.
She was endowed with three breasts, possessed a large belly, and was terrifying;
if anyone were to become her husband, he would meet his death within six months. ||35||
No one accepted her for alms while she was eighteen years old;
meanwhile, that man of the lowest caste went to her house to beg for alms. || 36 ||
Ghūkakarṇa arrived; seeing him, she fainted, and her father, beholding his handsome form and his guise as a twice-born, [was amazed]. (37)
Then he asked about his lineage, caste, family name, and so forth; Ghūkakarṇa said to the brahmin, "My place is in the land of Goḍa."
In the village of Bhojakata, I have a father, the Brahmin Madhavabhusura;
he belongs to the Vashistha lineage, and I am his son, named Candraprabha. (39)
In my eighth year, my father indeed passed away;
having studied for only a short while in Vārāṇasī, I had performed some auspicious rites.
"Having wandered among the sacred fords (tīrthas), I have arrived here; from here I shall go to the Gomatī, then to Prabhāsa, then to the Śukla-tīrtha, and after that, home again. (41)
Having heard this and thus understood his daughter's conduct, the father of the daughter said:
"If you will accept my daughter here, I shall give her to you."
Having said "So be it," the Cāṇḍāla then accepted her according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, after the marriage was concluded, he engaged in many amorous diversions.
With foods, drinks, fine garments suitable for the twice-born, and great festivities, he generally proceeds by whatever path leads to the Supreme. (44)
Dogs bark at him and follow behind him;
and if he should ever utter a Vedic verse when separated [from his wife], [he is likewise afflicted].
At that very moment, blood fell from the mouth of that evil-minded one;
and in his dream, he spoke of performing the act of discharging filth.
Thus, suspected by people to be some sort of outcaste because of these signs, she required divine purification to destroy their suspicion. (47)

Just as the suspicion regarding purity is removed by holding heated iron in one's hand, so too must you act this morning; for if you are not consumed [by the ordeal], O twice-born one, then indeed you are pure.
"If there were a certainty that he who was burnt belonged to another caste, then at night he spoke to his own wife, saying: 'I am certainly not a twice-born. (49)
"I am of the lowest caste and am known and suspected by the people;
I shall go to another country—come with me. (1.514.50)
The wife said: "Indeed, by my ill fortune, everything pertaining to the fire has become wicked;
my entire family and even my own body are utterly defiled by sin. (51)
"Go outside at night, otherwise you will not attain the great state.
Having been told this, he indeed went to another country at night out of fear. (52)
At dawn, her daughter, with tears in her eyes, said to her mother:
"Mother, it was my own past sin that I was given to an outcaste. (53)
Having announced his own lineage at midnight, he set forth, saying:
"For me, there is only the ablution by fire; there is no other purification on the surface of the earth. (54)
The father, having learned of this, grieved intensely, and others as well fell into sorrow; all the brahmins assembled and determined an expiation that would bring purification. (55)
Then they spoke of the maiden's entry into the fire, and of the vows for others who had come into contact with her. (56)
Then, having taken wood and applied fire, the maiden,
having bowed to her ancestors and called upon the gods, was just as she was about to ascend [the pyre].
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations! Reciting this very mantra, she placed her foot upon the fire. (58)
The fire remained cool and did not burn her, out of its compassion;
therefore, she is without fault and is purified by her menstruation. (59)
Then, at that very moment, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa arrived;
he was dressed as a holy man, a Vaiṣṇava, and a scholar well-versed in the Dharmaśāstras and other scriptures.
The Lord of Lakṣmī himself, Śrī Puruṣottama, who knows the three periods of time, said:
"What is this that is being born, and how does it burn in the fire? (61)
Then the people reported the news concerning the elephant;
thereupon, the compassionate Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa spoke to them.
Formerly, I heard that in the city of Camatkāra in heaven,
there is a river named Nāgalīlā, the wife of Kṛṣṇa, who has come from the abode of Goloka.
For the sake of purification, it exists for those who commit sins through contact with outcastes and others;
by bathing in that water, outcastes and the like become pure. (64)
"Therefore, go there and by all means perform your ablutions.
Having heard this, Vahni said, "So be it," and then they all went to the river.
A certain maiden, having seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, approached Him;
bowing down and joyfully taking His hand, she spoke to her Lord. (66)
"O lords of the twice-born, there is indeed a sacred pool not far away that destroys the sins of the lowest castes; come and perform your ablutions there."
Instructed by her, they went with her and bathed while still wearing their clothes.
When the brahmin girl had finished bathing, [something emerged] from her body.
The dog-cooker woman, who was black in color, emerged [from her body] merely by means of bathing;
likewise, crows, owls, and ants emerged from the bodies of the others as well. (69)
Emerging with a dark complexion, they went to the western region,
across a thousand yojanas on that uncovered surface of the earth.
These Brahmins are purifiers, and the Brāhmaṇī has attained purity;
thus they all returned to their own respective hermitages in the city. (71)
Thereafter, that virtuous and chaste Brahmin girl, devoted to celibacy and faithful to her husband Kṛṣṇasvāmī, remained steadfast.
Then she would always go to the river Nāgavatī for the purpose of bathing;
indeed, she would constantly become a young maiden in the house of a Brāhmaṇa woman. (73)
And she set out for the sake of beholding Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
when the end of the Brāhmaṇa’s daughter's life arrived, Hari [appeared]. (74)
Having transformed both that river and the Brāhmaṇī woman into divine forms,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa led them both to Goloka.
Having reached their lord Kṛṣṇa by means of a celestial chariot, well-bound with divine jewels and possessing the radiance of ten million suns, they both departed with joy.
Goloka is that eternal abode, adorned by Rādhā, Ramā, and others;
yet even Brahmā, due to the curse of an unchaste woman, was here at this excellent holy place.
"Indeed, in ancient times, he was liberated from the curse of a wanton woman;
thus, O Lakṣmī, has this most excellent and purifying holy site been described. (78)
Indeed, by bathing there, all impurity reaches its end;
moreover, by reciting or hearing this, a human being is always purified. (79)
Having received the mantra and bowed to the guru, he who bathes with a concentrated mind in Nāgavatī shall become pure like Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the five hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how Nāgalīlā’s Friend became the River Nāgavatī in Goloka due to Rādhikā’s Curse in the First Section on the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; and how, by bathing in that river, the Brahmin girl who had been married to Ghūkakarṇa the Cāṇḍāla, as well as the Brahmins themselves, attained purification; thereafter, both the Brahmin girl and the River Nāgavatī became divine maidens and went to Goloka along with Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||514||
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
When was Brahmā cursed by the unchaste woman, and for what reason? And how did the Creator of the Universe become purified after bathing in the Nāga river?
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, tell me that story here.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa related that story to Lakṣmī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī, in ancient times Brahmā begot a daughter;
he himself made that mind-born Māyinī an Apsaras.
She then became the common wife of all the gods;
then, on one occasion, having seen Brahmā, she indeed became infatuated with him.
And having forgotten his father, he engaged in the pursuit of sensual desires;
in the Manvantara of Raivata, there was a king named Sucandra who was a devotee of Viṣṇu.
He went to the valley of the Malaya mountain for austerities for a thousand years;
seeing his body covered by an anthill, the Creator (Brahmā) approached him.
"Choose a boon; I am well-pleased," said the Father of the World to him.
He chose devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and the state of being His servant.
Brahmā indeed sprinkled water from his water-pot and drenched him;
the king, with his body composed, bowed down again and again.
Saying "So be it," Brahmā then granted him the boon; the king ascended that divine and excellent chariot which had come from Goloka.
Having assumed a divine form, that attendant went to the feet of Kṛṣṇa;
Brahmā saw him on the way as he was departing for Satyaloka, along with Mohinī.
Then, upon seeing him, that woman with the curved eyes immediately became infatuated with the desire to sport in that secluded place; she protected her face with a smile.
With all her limbs covered in horripilation and tormented by the force of desire,
she slowly sat down on the ground before the feet of Brahmā.
Brahmā, having gazed upon his daughter, did not undergo any transformation;
like a father, he comforted her and departed for the world of Brahmā.
Then she became filled with desire, yet hopeless and deprived of her senses;
day and night she was lost in thought, seeing the Four-faced One in both her dreams and her waking consciousness.
Whether sitting, standing, or even for a moment lying down on her bed,
she wanders along the road just like grain in a heated vessel.
Having obtained Kāma as her companion, the deluding woman went with him to the world of Brahmā; there, in a secluded place, she beheld the Unborn One.
Standing before him, she began to delude that very man;
for a moment she danced beautifully for a long time, and for a moment she sang.
Upon hearing that melodious voice, the Creator was overcome with emotion and his eyes filled with tears;
seeing him thus enchanted, he displayed all his artistic skills in a dance.
Having thus given him a reward, he departed, having desisted from his effort.
But she, her exertion frustrated, said: "O God, as you desire, let there be salutation unto you."
"O Kāmadeva, discharge your own arrows at the Creator";
then Kāma, standing in the sky, joyfully launched his great weapon.
Brahmā became restless and gazed repeatedly;
then, having approached Mohinī and reflected upon her, he spoke to Mohinī.
"You are fickle and enchanting; I am not fit for this deed.
Go, my daughter, you are no longer to be grasped by me; sport elsewhere as you please. (22)
Whoever trusts a unchaste woman will meet with calamity at every step. O child, go far away, leaving me, your father, behind. (23)
"O Mohinī, behold a supreme, youthful god worthy of you.
Mohinī replied to the Creator: "Because my mind is not steady. (24)
Indeed, it was real that you were seen by me as particularly fickle;
oh, even though I was rebuked by you, I am unable to go away. (25)
Have mercy, O ocean of compassion; you ought not to kill me.
The virtuous, who are dedicated to helping others, do not indulge in pride. (26)
One virtuous woman, having obtained a husband, remains devoted to her wifely fidelity;
another, however, enjoys a man by means of her own actions, having sold her body.
O Brahmin, just as my dharma would result in satisfaction after enjoying a man who is the object of my heart's desire, so too must the service of such a man be performed. (28)
"By that, there is satisfaction and the annulment of [past] actions; for us, this is indeed Dharma itself.
Therefore, I have come because I am capable of making your action otherwise. (29)
Through constant service to the great, women shine with glory;
yet whether he be a householder, an ascetic, or a seeker of pleasure, one may abandon a woman who has approached him.
Having his merit destroyed by his sighs, he shall here become a vessel for curses;
likewise, his fortune shall perish, his beauty shall fade, and his intellect shall be ruined.
O Brahmin, by the curse of a woman, he immediately becomes impotent;
and by the power of that curse, he always becomes distressed and unhappy.
Arise, O Lord of the World, and bring me across the ocean of passion; purchase me, your handmaiden whose mind is ever fixed on you, with your respectful favor. (33)
Having spoken thus, the deluding goddess indeed pulled at the garment of the Creator;
Brahmā, maintaining his composure, spoke these essential words to his daughter.
"O Mother, abandon me, for I am old and free from desire; look instead upon another. I have no bond with you, nor any trace of passion. (35)
"The lines drawn by past karma grant a husband to a woman. Release my garment, my daughter, and take courage for a moment. (36)
In the meantime, lords in the form of obstacles arrived:
Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Vasiṣṭha, Kratu, and Aṅgiras. (37)
Bhṛgu, Marīci, Kapila, Voḍhu, Pañcaśikha, Ruci, Āsuri, Pracetas, Patnīvratas, and Bṛhaspati. (38)
Śukra, Utathya, Karaka, Kaṇva, Gautama, Kaśyapa, Sanaka, Sananda, Kardama, and Sanātana. || 39 ||
Sanatkumāra, Pippala, Śaṅku, Śukra, Parāśara,
Śātātapa, Lomaśa, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Vibhāṇḍaka.
Mṛkaṇḍu, Cavana, Jaratkāru, Āstika, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Bharadvāja, and Nārada; ||41||
Vāmadeva, Durvāsas, and Svayaṃprakāśa—these [sages] then abandoned the Creator out of shame upon seeing Mohinī. ||42||
Brahmā ascended his throne and Mohinī stood by his side;
the sages bowed to him, and Brahmā bestowed auspicious blessings upon them. ||43||
The sages asked the Lord, "How is it that she dances and sings such unprecedented songs in your presence? Brahmā replied, "It has been thus for a long time."
Since she has come here to show herself and stands there exhausted from her efforts, the sages laughed there at her in every respect as if she were an unchaste woman. 45.
Then, rising up immediately, she became enraged and said to the Creator of the Universe:
"O Vidhi, all these elders, being unrestrained, are laughing at me."
They too will become objects of ridicule among people because of their respective actions,
since you do not accept me even though I am devoted to you.
O Brahmin, you do not restrain them; therefore, you shall become an object of ridicule.
You shall be everywhere unworthy of honor, despised by women. (48)
Your wife will surely rebuke you for your actions;
having failed to perform the worship of the goat, that deluding woman went to heaven. (49)
For a moment, Brahmā and the sages lamented for their release from the curse;
then Brahmā, having reflected, [went] to the vicinity of Camatkārapura.
He arrived at Nāgavatī for the sake of purification and the removal of the curse: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (51)
Having received the mantra from Kṛṣṇa, he bathed in the sin-destroying holy ford;
then, on the bank of the Nāga river, Brahmā cast off that body which had been cursed.
Therefore, thousands of Vṛndalas were born there from him;
having settled in that city, they remained there, and Brahmā went to heaven.
Bearing a divine form, yet remaining in their former bodies due to a curse, they were always despised by Vṛndalā in the world; consequently, they became unworthy of worship.
Constantly reviled by women, they were mockeries of female form; they were deluders like enchantresses, yet devoid of passion and lacking in virility.
They are neither men nor women, being devoid of sexual organs;
they possess only a minute opening for urine, and nothing beyond that. (56)
They performed a libation in the water dedicated to Brahmā;
Brahmā arrived there, and they offered prayers to the Creator.
Then Brahmā spoke to them for the sake of destroying their state of being neuter:
"Perform penance constantly, directed toward Mohinī."
"She will indeed bring you across and bestow welfare upon you.
Thereupon, they performed penance without interruption on the bank of the river.
Obeisance to you, O Mother Mohinī, who removes the thicket of worldly existence;
O Svāhā, beloved of Kāma, grant us deliverance here in this world.
Thus praying, those hosts of Vṛndalās then beheld Saubhāgyasundarī on the bank of the Nāga river.
She, whose nature is manifold, was clad in a red bodice,
endowed with a red lower garment, possessing the hue of fire, and adorned with ornaments.
She was well-nourished, with full breasts and a full hip, yet slender-waisted;
she was beautiful, with eyes like lotus petals, adorned with a braided mass of hair.
She was adorned with a beautiful braid of hair and a leaf upon her forehead; her hands were graced with bracelets, armlets, rings, and other ornaments.
She was adorned with a girdle, graced by excellent anklets,
and decorated with ornaments for the ears, nose, arms, neck, and forehead.
Her breasts were budding, her hips broad, and her cheeks rounded;
her teeth were like the finest jasmine buds, and her auspicious lower lip was red as the bimba fruit.
She whose face is like the autumn moon, who possesses a sweet voice and a smiling countenance,
a well-nourished maiden overflowing with love and eager to bestow grace upon her devotees.
Seeing her in the sky, free from sensual desires, devoid of menstruation, and assuming any form at will, all [the gods] became eunuchs.
At that moment, their eyes were momentarily blinded by her splendor;
she then descended to the surface of the earth on the bank of the Nāgavatī.
She was saluted by all, honored, gratified, and petitioned;
likewise, she was massaged and rubbed on all her limbs.
She said to them, "I am pleased; I shall endow you, who have taken refuge in me, with boons.
Choose indeed whatever you desire, and do not delay. (71)
Then the Vṛndalas said, "Have mercy for our deliverance!
For the destruction of this impotence, they praised him again and again. (72)
Then the Goddess said to them: "In the past, I was Mohinī; because of my disregard for Prakṛti, you were born from the body of Brahmā. (73)
Indeed, all those born as eunuchs arose from the sin of reviling women;
men were created by Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of satisfying the desires of women. (74)
During the monthly course of women, the fire of desire increases;
yet the wife desires its pacification together with her husband alone. (75)
She who has no husband may go to her own desired [lover] for the sake of peace;
for women, the rite of pacification is their duty, which bestows peace upon men. (76)
Those who honor you when you honor them are the ones worthy of blessings;
whereas those men who treat with contempt a woman who has come to them, tormented by desire. (77)
They should be known as destroyers of their own souls and slayers of their female attendants;
by that sin, they enter into a state of impotence in every birth. (78)
Even those who create obstacles for one engaged in sexual acts become eunuchs;
all such impotent ones become castrated by a curse. (79)
Even those who forcibly enjoy [another's] property certainly deserve punishment;
likewise, if a woman who is bereft of her husband should become tormented by desire.
One who does not accept [her] would be at fault, for the fruit [of such rejection] is indeed impotence;
therefore, men should always honor and serve women according to their wishes. 81.
Sirs, for the sake of removing your impotence, become initiated;
be shaven of beard, wearing women's garments, and adorned with women's ornaments. (82)
My devotees, those who worship me, those who chant my name, and those who uphold my lineage shall be liberated; you shall no longer be subject to impotence.
Having said, "O Bahucarā," she gave him her own mantra:
"Oṃ, salutation to Bahucarā, the Enchantress, who dwells in desire. (84)
"O Mother, remove my impotence and grant me the highest welfare!
Having bathed him in the Nāganadī with this mantra, she bestowed auspiciousness upon him. (85)
"Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kāmadātryai svāhā"—this ten-syllable mantra he gave as the second for the sake of accomplishing all desires. (86)
In that place where her vaginal opening was only the size of a chickpea,
the Goddess made that vulva full during the initiation ceremony.
Because the mark of the linga there was like a young monkey, she drew lines upon that full linga, which had two testicles, to make it appear variegated. ||88||
By the gift of vermilion and liquid [offerings], for the sake of attaining the fulfillment of all desires, one may become a woman or a man marked by those [auspicious] lines in another birth. (89)
A fine silk garment, a bodice, a water-pot, a waist-cord,
as well as a tooth-stick, vermilion powder, cinnabar, and even the mantra.
Then the Goddess gave them consecrated water, an affectionate kiss,
and she touched all the eunuchs upon their breasts.
On the cheeks, the forehead, the temples, the hair, the eyes, the back, the hips, the front of the body, the thighs, and likewise on the belly; 92.
He sprinkled them on their navels, thighs, feet, and heads, saying to them, "May the sin of being a eunuch be destroyed. (93)
Having thus received initiation, they then worshipped Devikā;
and she, having accepted the worship, departed indeed toward the northern direction.
Thus, the virtuous Bahucarā Hiṅgulājā, who dwells eternally on earth, bestowed initiation in order to bring about the cessation of his impotence. 95.
And as for why Brahmā did not accept her even though she was devoted to him, I shall tell you the reason for that; listen, O Lakṣmī, to what occurred in the past.
In the past, having performed penance upon his own lotus and having heard the voices from the sky, Brahmā commenced the entire creation and again remembered Śrī Hari.
He beheld Nārāyaṇa before him and requested a boon:
"May your Māyā, in the form of a woman, not afflict me. (98)
"Likewise, grant me a blessing, and then I shall indeed bring about creation. To the Creator there, Nārāyaṇa said, "So be it. (99)
Fashion the creation of the four ages, consisting of women and men,
in such a manner that it is appropriate for each respective time.
"Even if you should ever take up desire, anger, greed, delusion, or deceit, I shall protect you who remain untainted; therefore, perform the act of creation."
May you always be a reciter of the Dharma; may you always be free from passion.
May I always possess mindfulness, and may I always be liberated while living. (102)
Dharma and adharma always arise from your own will and from your body;
by my desire, may you yourself become the bestower of the fruits of actions.

O Lotus-born One, even while action is being performed, you are indeed a non-doer; and even amidst an ocean of enjoyments, you are a non-enjoyer—both unstained and yet appearing stained, you are forever such, O Lotus-born One.
For this reason, by the grace of Hari, Brahmā Prajāpati,
being free from delusion, did not at all accept Mohinī through his own will.
The devotees of the Blessed One never take up sense objects at any time,
having abandoned devotion to Hari, which is purifying and destroys bondage.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have told you of the intense delusion wrought by Mohinī,
as well as the cause of the curse, the liberation, the state of eunuchism, and likewise the initiation.
Whoever hears this with devotion or recites it, all defects caused by desire and worldly attachment are surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt. (108)
In Nāgavatī, this Pratāpa has been made a companion to Nāgalīlā;
he is the destroyer of the wicked and likewise the savior of all living beings.
By whose service, drinking, bathing, and likewise by ritual ablution,
there arises enjoyment and liberation— the fourfold goals of human life in their entirety.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Apsarā Mohinī became infatuated upon seeing Brahmā but was not accepted by him; how she then cursed him; how Brahmā was purified in the Nāgavatī river; the birth of those who abandoned their bodies as eunuchs; and the liberation of eunuchs through the initiation of Bahucara, Hiṅgulāja, and others," in the first section, the Kṛta-yuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-nārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*. || 515 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this beautiful and auspicious narrative concerning the demon Vṛka.
In ancient times there was a Daitya named Vṛka, who performed supreme penance.
For a hundred years, Hara remained pleased with him in the field of Kedāra;
he went there daily to grant a boon, yet the Asura did not accept a boon.
The Daitya did not accept any of the universal sovereignty, any supernatural power, worldly enjoyment, liberation, or the abode of Hari from the wielder of the trident who stood all around him.
Seeing him, Śambhu wept, enveloped by the noose of love;
and from hearing his weeping, his meditation was indeed broken.
He beheld before him Śambhu, the bestower of all prosperity;
and having bowed down with devotion, Vṛka chose a boon from him.
And as he placed his hand upon [the demon's] head, saying, "He shall become ashes," the preeminent Daitya rushed toward him as he was departing with the utterance of "Om.
The drum of Śambhu and the tiger-skin fell to the ground.
And he did not kill the Daitya with compassion, even though the latter was running behind him.
A virtuous person never follows the wicked;
indeed, the virtuous will slay even a servant, a son, or a beloved wife if they strike them.
Śiva, free from egoism, came to me for refuge as I was overwhelmed by fear, chanting, "O Hari, protect me! Protect me! (9).
Then I assumed the form of a woman, and the Daitya was deluded;
having made that bull among Daityas place his hand upon my own head—
Having reduced him to ashes, Śaṅkara became free from his fever;
nevertheless, Śaṅkara remained filled with pride toward me as my devotee. || 11 ||
Viṣṇu always performs my work even in times of great calamity;
thinking "I am the destroyer," he was prepared to slay Tripura.
Thinking, "Who is this Daitya that he has come to battle like a moth," he cast aside the spear given by me as well as my own armor. (13)
The battle continued for a long time, day and night, for one full year;
he even shattered Śambhu’s chariot and seized the weapons from Śaṅkara.
Having lifted up Śiva as he lay there, he threw him to the ground;
then I quickly assumed the form of a bull by means of my creative power (kalā). || 15 ||
Seizing the wide-striding Śaṅkara as he lay down with his two tusks,
Hara struck Tripura with the trident given by me.
The lord of the Daityas fell instantly to the ground, pulverized;
the deities praised Śambhu, and Śaṅkara abandoned his pride. ||17||
Therefore, in the form of a bull, I carry Śiva for the sake of my devotees;
there is no one dearer to me than Śiva throughout the three worlds.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this beautiful ancient story of Hara:
having performed penance for sixty thousand yugas, Maheśvara—
Then he ceased, and before him he beheld Narayana,
a youth with exceedingly beautiful limbs, dark and handsome.
The three-eyed Lord did not become satiated with his two eyes;
gazing without blinking, he wept, overwhelmed by love.
"How indeed can I praise Śrī Puruṣottama with only one mouth?
Thus he mentally fashioned a head in four ways.
And at every moment of conceptualization, his head became ever new;
thus, that four-faced one, together with the previous one, became five-faced.
Each individual face shone with three eyes;
thus, he who had five faces and three eyes became exceedingly beautiful.
Śiva’s affection for me is greater than his affection for praise;
therefore, he truly came to possess many eyes in this manner. (25)
The eyes possess the three qualities, and the third is the one of withdrawal;
that all-pervading Lord has a body of ashes from the consecration of Satī.
Out of a spirit of love, he wears her garland of bones and her ashes;
for others, those whose bodies have been withdrawn, he wears a garland of skulls.
Out of discernment, the yogi still wears his matted hair from the time of his asceticism;
he has no desire for the grooming of his hair or for personal adornment. (28)
Equanimity toward sandalwood paste, mud, a clod of earth, a jewel, a gem, and wealth—[exemplified by] the serpents who, out of enmity toward Garuḍa, went for refuge to Śaṅkara. (29)
Out of compassion, He bears those very ones who have come to Him for refuge upon His own body; I am but a bull-shaped vehicle, incapable of bearing anything else for you.
Having entrusted fragrant flowers such as the pārijāta and scents such as sandalwood to me, they never have any attachment to those very things. (3.1)
He always finds delight in the thorn-apple tree, in the application of bilva leaves as an ointment,
in fragrances devoid of scent, in the mouth of a camel, and upon a tiger skin.
That mind of mine does not dwell upon the divine world, nor on a celestial couch, nor among the masses;
rather, it meditates on me day and night, intensely and in solitude, within the cremation ground.
He bears the trident that conquers death and is endowed with my own splendor;
he carries water day and night for the purpose of quelling poison and for its cooling nature.
And for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, he maintains as his wife Pārvatī, a yoginī given to him by me, who is devoted to her husband and acts for the sake of instructing the world. (35)
Śaṅkara, the Supreme Self, is dearer to me than even my life-breaths; O Tryambaka, my mind is eternally devoted to Śiva, and there is none dearer to me than Bhava.
I do not dwell in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor upon your chest; I am forever bound by the noose of love within the heart of Śiva. (37)
Śaṅkara, having composed this with his five faces, constantly sings my song by its own inherent power; therefore, I am near him. (38)
He alone is capable of granting me devotion, service, liberation, all prosperity, and all perfections; there is no giver superior to Śaṅkara. (39)
With his five faces, he sings my name day and night out of love;
he constantly meditates upon my form—there is no devotee superior to Śaṅkara.
Due to devotion, or due to his own majesty, or because of the difference in the recipient, or after a moment,
or even after a Manvantara, Hara assumes different forms, actions, and movements. "I am Sudarśana, and we are equal in splendor to Śambhu."
But Brahmā, the creator, is equal to us through yoga, not through his own splendor. ||42||
Once Sanatkumāra went to Vaikuṇṭha and beheld me, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, having indeed finished my meal.
With a joyful heart, I gave him whatever remained;
as soon as he received it, he consumed a portion right there.
He saved a portion for his kinsmen and set aside what was difficult to obtain;
he gave a portion to Śaṅkara, but everything was consumed by Śambhu. ||45||
Having received and consumed it with an outpouring of devotion, he danced with joy, his entire body covered in horripilation and his eyes filled with tears. 46.
With devotion, the sweet-voiced one sang my virtues from his five mouths, beautifully attuned to various musical modes and measured by rhythmic beats. 47.
The hand-drum fell from his hand, as did the horn and the tiger-skin;
then, having fallen down himself, he wept and fell into a swoon.
Meditating with a one-pointed mind on that exceedingly beautiful form,
he beholds me situated within the thousand-petaled lotus of his heart.
In the meantime, the goddess Pārvatī, the supreme sovereign,
arrived there quickly with joy, her face and eyes radiant with serenity.
Seeing him weeping, fainting, and fallen down out of devotion,
she laughed and questioned the serpent standing beside her about the matter.
The King of Nagas, with palms joined in reverence, related everything to that devotee of Viṣṇu, who could assume any form at will and was seated upon Skanda's shoulder.
Overwhelmed with love by partaking of the grace of Nārāyaṇa, Śaṅkara has attained such a state of perfect meditative absorption. (53)
Hearing this, she became enraged at me: "Why was favor not granted?
She cursed that food as unfit for consumption, even for the wise. (54)
She said to Śambhu: "How can you, the nourisher, act so improperly?
I am always to be protected by you, to be nourished, and I am your devoted servant. (55)
"O Lord, I have been deceived by you regarding the consumption of Hari’s prasāda;
for you are the vessel of Hari’s prasāda and the foremost devotee of Hari. (56)
O Pārvatī, I am the beloved of your grace;
I, the sovereign lady, am the recipient of the favor of both Hari and Hara. (57)
Today you have been deceived by not giving [the offering] while consuming the remains of Śiva's garland;
today you have been deceived by not giving while consuming the grace of Hari. 58.
Therefore, O Śiva, accept from me this fruit born of deception;
from this day forward, those people shall no longer consume your sacrificial offering. (59)
"They shall certainly be born as dogs for one lifetime in every way.
Having said this, Pārvatī wept there for a moment before him.
Śiva wiped away the water from his eyes with his hand;
placing him upon his chest, he comforted him with kind words and consolations.
Being thoroughly satisfied, that goddess spoke to her husband:
"I shall cast off this body without the offering (naivedya) of Hari."
I constantly bear this body that increases your good fortune;
how indeed could I carry a frame devoid of such fortune? (63)
"Your unprecedented offering, which removes birth, death, and old age, has been cursed by me; it has been made wicked and shall grant the birth of a dog. (64)
"If I were to eat [her], I would become a female dog; yet if I do not eat her, I am deceived by my husband's favor. (65)
"How indeed can I live, devoid of the dharma of devotion to my husband?
Therefore, having abandoned this body, I shall go to Goloka itself. (66)
To Pārvatī, who had spoken thus, Hara himself granted courage, saying:
"Listen, O Goddess; prepare the cooking and offer the food-oblation to Viṣṇu."
"Having enjoyed that prasāda, I shall give it to you; remain steadfast.
Let the words 'the prasāda of the Liṅga is not to be accepted' be the fruit of your speech. (68)
Every grace (prasāda) from the image shall indeed be accepted;
even that which is mixed with the liṅga of the image shall be entirely acceptable. ||69||
"Accept this gift from me, remaining forever established in devotion to your husband;
by doing so, you shall certainly not be reborn as a dog."
And regarding the authority over the grace of the mere *liṅga*, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa have been appointed by me; they are my two devoted attendants (*gaṇas*) who are ever-present with me. (71)
Having been addressed thus, Pārvatī prepared the cooked food and gave it to Śrī Hari;
she then gave that which remained to Śaṅkara and, being virtuous, she herself ate it.
Thus, O Rame, the unacceptability of one who possesses only the marks [of a renunciant] has been declared.
Then the Goddess [offered] various kinds of sweet food to Mahādeva at all times. 73.
Having manifested her favor toward me, that virtuous woman, out of devotion, fed me fifty-six varieties of cooked foods and side dishes.
Having performed my rites on the day of Kṛṣṇa’s birth and having prepared my prasāda, he would respectfully feed that prasāda of mine to me constantly. (75)
When Śaṅkara, a devotee of Viṣṇu, began to feed [the guests], he then said to the Goddess: "Listen, today a crisis regarding dharma has arisen. (76)
On the day of one's desired vow, food must certainly not be accepted;
the grace of Kṛṣṇa must not be abandoned, for in abandoning it, there is more than a hundredfold sin. (77)
"Tell me what should be done here; I shall do it provided there is no objection.
At that moment, Pārvatī entered within her own heart for a brief instant. (78)
There, Hari himself remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
having arrived, he said to the Queen of the Gods, "O Pārvatī, look at me."
Śaṅkara is my very own form; indeed, no difference exists here. One should eat with my own nature as one's essence; then no fault shall arise.
In this vow, one must certainly not eat in the form of food;
it should be eaten as my own essential nature—therein no fault is found.
O Goddess, speak to Śaṅkara, who is devoted [to you], so that he may abandon his current form and, assuming the form of the Blessed One, partake of the meal. (82)
Having been addressed thus, that virtuous woman quickly bowed to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, went outside, and spoke to her beloved husband with devotion exactly as she had been told. (83)
"Abandoning the form of a devotee here, assume the form of the Blessed Lord;
then partake of the food in the omnipresent Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. (84)
Śambhu said: "O Goddess, how could my eternal state of being devoted to you ever be abandoned?
Tell me this matter now, for there would be great fault in such an abandonment. (85)
The water and food of one who is not a devotee should not be accepted, nor should he ever be accepted again;
such a non-devotee must be avoided in every way by Vaiṣṇavas and by the gods and others.
Pārvatī said: "O Lord, I am a woman devoid of intelligence;
nevertheless, I shall speak for the sake of this debate—please act accordingly. (87)
"If I am your devotee and never a devotee of another, then let there be the successful fulfillment of this prepared food; do so. (88)
Become one who possesses these three forms: Kṛṣṇa, Śambhu, and a Sannyāsī;
indeed, in the form of Kṛṣṇa, enjoy all this prepared food here from me.
"Enjoy that very nature of His grace through the form of a renunciant;
for the grace of a virtuous renunciant shall be the accomplisher of my purpose."
At your command I shall accept it; otherwise, I will not touch even water, fruit, flowers, medicinal herbs, milk, or any other liquid. (91)
"The word of the guru is the word of the Lord; never, O observer of vows, should it be disregarded.
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara there assumed three forms.
In the form of Kṛṣṇa, he consumed all the food prepared by Pārvatī;
[likewise], devotees enjoy [the fruits of their actions] in the divine abode according to their own forms and their state of likeness [to the Divine].
"Furthermore, for one who has renounced and attained freedom from action, there is no fault even in eating";
thinking thus, Śaṅkara himself, as a renunciant, partook of food. (94)
The virtuous goddess Satī, having assumed the form of a female ascetic by the command of Śaṅkara, partook of the food of Hari through his grace. (95)
The devoted lady, who was the very embodiment of Satī, performed tasks such as wiping the vessels;
then Pārvatī and Parameśvara withdrew those forms.
They both regained their former forms and became devoted;
such indeed, O Lakṣmī, is the devotion found among my devotees.
Who indeed, other than him, knows that subtle essence of the entirety of Dharma?
That Śaṅkara, however, wandered joyfully through the three worlds as a renunciant. 98.
He performed devotion to me and indeed caused the Vaiṣṇavas to do so;
likewise, Śiva, having become such at every season, performs devotion unto me. ||99||
Śivā also, having become an ascetic woman, likewise offers devotion to me; Śambhu, the author of the scriptures, is my teacher and the refuge of my knowledge.
He is the savior of those whose lives are bound, the bestower of knowledge and devotion;
for holy places are not merely made of water, nor are the gods made of clay or stone.
Virtuous sacrificial forms, vows, fasts, various austerities, diverse acts of charity, and the worship of Brahmins and deities—[all these are included]. (102)
The virtuous purify everything merely by being seen;
for those who are truly saintly devotees of Viṣṇu, [everything is purified] by the mere touch of their dust.
By the mere touch of his purified lotus feet, the earth was instantly sanctified,
as were the holy fords, the oceans, and the mountains.
The Suras desire the sight of the virtuous who destroy all sins;
yet that ignorant one did not recognize the saintly man in his human form.
Just as one does not perceive the supreme sweetness of milk or likewise its curd,
so too one does not perceive the virtuous people who are being born from the virtuous.
Through the knowledge of others, one truly does not recognize one's own home;
this alone is the supreme gain for Vaiṣṇavas—the grace of the virtuous.
In crossing the ocean of worldly existence, the virtuous are indeed the sailors;
the Brahmins are the teachers of the world, and among them, the virtuous Brahmins are the most excellent of teachers.
The great saints, Sanaka and others, who are renunciants of supreme purity,
purify the worlds from the impressions accumulated over long periods of time.
Thus that Śaṅkara became a devotee, and likewise Śivā became a devotee to me; assuming the forms of a virtuous man and a virtuous woman, they both appeared for the sake of my grace.
O Lotus-born One, what is impossible for my devotees to accomplish for my sake?
For the sake of attaining me alone, they renounce every obstacle.
Thus I have previously told you this auspicious matter, and now it is reminded to you once more: my service to Hari, to the Goddess, and to You, who are the supreme among the supreme.

From hearing this, from reciting it, from reflecting upon it, and likewise from practicing it, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and my own service; all this shall come to pass, of this there is no doubt. (113)

Thus ends the five hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Removal of Śaṅkara’s Arrogance, His Excess of Devotion, His Possession of the Dharma of Surrendering All to the Supreme Bhāgavata, His Assumption of the Form of a Sannyāsī, His Eating of the Lord’s Grace, and Other Matters," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, in ancient times there was a great king named Hiraṇyakaśipu.
To him two sons were born: Prahlāda and Andhaka.
When Hiraṇyakaśipu had departed for the other world by the hand of Hari,
Prahlāda was appointed by his ministers to the ceremony of consecration.
But he did not desire that kingdom because of his hatred for the Dānavas;
consequently, Andhaka was consecrated in the kingdom by the foremost of the Dānavas.
Andhaka also, having propitiated Brahmā, became immortal;
for as long as a kalpa, nourished by that boon, he then conquered Śakra.
He made Amarāvatikā his own capital;
Indra, having propitiated Śambhu, chose a boon for the sake of the gods.
The entire sovereignty of the gods, including the sacrifices and so forth, as well as all sacrificial portions and the like, has been seized by Andhaka; restore this kingdom to me.
Śiva said, "So be it," and dispatched his own messenger Vīrabhadra toward him; having gone there, he spoke to Andhaka.
"By the command of Hara, abandon heaven and go to the surface of the earth;
rule over the kingdom of your father and grandfather upon this world."
"If you do not [submit], Śaṅkara will destroy your entire abode.
Andhaka said to Vīrabhadra, "Tell Hara [this]."
"Who are you that dwell in a cremation ground? In my presence, you are not even counted among my attendants. Hand over Kailāsa to me, and go from here to a cremation ground in Kāśī!"
"O Śaṅkara, if you do not take away my life along with that of Indra, [I shall continue my attack].
Having heard this, the heroic Prabhadraka rebuked him and went toward Hara.
He spoke those words, and Hara became prepared;
joined by his Gaṇas, the gods, and other armies, he marched toward Amarāvatī.
Upon seeing that army approaching, the foremost of the Daityas were struck with terror;
meanwhile, Andhaka beheld a most dreadful and ominous nightmare while asleep.
Overwhelmed by agitation and fear, and deprived of the will to eat, Andhaka said to his sons, friends, and others: "Everything is a portent of death."
Today at midnight, I beheld a most terrifying bad dream:
[a man] wearing a garland of red flowers and red sandalwood paste. (15)
Clad in red garments, holding a sharp sword and a terrifying skull-bowl, she lets out a natural, loud guffaw; her tongue lolls out, making her fearsome.
In this city, an exceedingly old woman with a dark body dances;
she has disheveled hair, a severed nose, and is dressed in black garments.
That widow, a Mahāśūdra woman, was desirous of embracing me;
she wore a piece of soiled cloth and had coarse hair.
Applying a powder-mark upon my cheek and placing it upon my breast, she laughs, displays her cruelty, and kisses me again and again. (19)
Indeed, dark-colored, ripe tāla fruits, severed and split on all sides, fall down while constantly making loud sounds.
Clad in rags, deformed in appearance, and indeed a barbarian with coarse hair, he gives me for ornament broken and worn-out cowries. ||21||
And a divine woman, highly enraged and accompanied by her husband and sons, broke the full water-jar while repeatedly uttering curses. (22)
And the brahmin, being exceedingly enraged and having indeed uttered a curse, gave me a garland of withered heads smeared with red sandalwood paste.
For moment after moment, a rain of embers and a rain of ashes fall, and for moment after moment, a rain of blood arises within my city. (24)
I see a monkey, a crow, a dog, a bear, a boar, and a donkey—of hideous form and making a harsh noise. (25)
At the time of sunrise, I see a heap of dry wood, unsoiled soot, and monkeys with their claws severed. (26)
Clad in yellow garments, anointed with white sandalwood paste, wearing a garland of jasmine flowers, and adorned with jeweled ornaments. || 27 ||
With a play-lotus in her hand and adorned with a dot of vermilion, that virtuous woman, having cast a curse upon me in her anger, departs from my palace. (28)
And I see terrifying men with disheveled hair and nooses in their hands, exceedingly harsh, entering my city. (29)
In every house, I constantly see a naked woman with disheveled hair, dancing and always smiling, her form exceedingly distorted.
With her nose cut off, a widow, a great Śūdra woman, naked as the sky—she, most terrifying, anoints me with oil. (31)
At the time of early dawn, I see them—wearing the charcoal of nirvāṇa, covered in ashes, naked, variegated, and smiling. (3.2)
And I see a wedding ceremony, enchanting with dance and song, and men dressed in red garments with red hair. (33)
I see a man vomiting blood, dancing naked and grotesque, running, lying down, and likewise smiling.
And I beheld at one and the same time in the sky the orbs of both the moon and the sun eclipsed by Rāhu, swallowed entirely in a state of darkness. (35)
Standing upon the earth, I behold the falling of meteors, comets, earthquakes, and the upheaval of the kingdom; I see violent winds and great portents. (36)
I see great trees with severed trunks being whirled about by the wind, as well as fallen mountains upon the surface of the earth.
And in every house, I see a man with a severed head, dancing, naked, and uplifted, holding a garland of skulls, and appearing terrible. (38)
I see everywhere that the entire hermitage has been burnt, filled with ashes and thick with embers, with everyone crying out "Alas! Alas! on all sides. (39)
I went to the river to bathe, but it dried up in an instant;
and the forms of the deities, when seen, had vanished into dissolution.
I repeatedly beheld for a long time a donkey and a horse harnessed to a cart traveling toward the south, and I saw myself standing there upon that very cart. (41)
It appears to me that I shall indeed go elsewhere, toward another world;
for I myself have seen my own marriage with this woman.
"I saw that the head of Gāgareśa was severed from the shoulders and burnt; 'I [saw it] in the river,' [I thought], and in an instant I became wide awake. (43)
It was observed that the camel, having eaten the bhūphalinī fruits, was returning toward me;
however, although prepared foods were seen, they were indeed not eaten by me. (44)
In my dream, a great quarrel with one another was witnessed;
and in the dream, I repeatedly had my own head shaved. (45)
I have seen the broken branches of green trees;
I have seen a certain kinsman of mine drowning in the ocean. (46)
I observed that blood had issued from the private organ of a certain man,
and I saw that a Brahmin, being exceedingly enraged, was pronouncing a curse.
I observed that the worn-out garment I wore on my body had been lost and fallen away; as soon as they saw me, dogs began to bark at me. (48)
And dry pieces of wood were split in two by me with my hands; I looked for a sawing machine for the purpose of cutting. (49)
A great serpent with its hood expanded was seen, and even though it was dead,
Bālaka, the son of Vyomasetu, leaped up to fall into the water.
Leaving the water and falling by mistake onto a stone far away,
he saw another's empty cow-pen turned upside down in his house.
And a wild cat was seen by me in the forest;
a person dressed in black garments indeed reviled me with a sound like "dhūṣ-kṛt. (52)
He perceived that she had intended to kill me after circumambulating me;
thus, having been rendered empty by me, she was reviled and split asunder before those people. (53)
A cow with her calf has gone out from my hermitage during the night, and the banner of the palace has also been seen fallen. (54)
The key to the treasury for the sake of the *satkārya* was not seen at all;
the Brahmins, intent on receiving blessings, departed elsewhere, leaving me behind. (55)
Thus was everything seen by me today at the end of the night in a dream;
I do not know whether, through the turn of fate, it might prove otherwise. (56)
Having thus described how Andhaka grieved,
he spoke of that evil dream which his beloved wife had seen during the night.
Listen, O King, for even today at the end of the night, while I was asleep, certain portents appeared to me; indeed, because of them, I am filled with fear. (58)
"Oh, my lord, come here; I shall place you upon my own breast.
As for the ultimate consequence, I do not know what the Ordainer will do. ||59||
O Lord, while I was seated upon a jeweled throne and holding a jeweled parasol,
that enraged brahmin seized that very parasol from me.
And he impelled me alone, though I am weak, into that ocean which was like collyrium, most terrible, difficult to cross, and deep.
There, afflicted by grief, I wander again and again in that current,
distressed by the force of great waves and crowded with crocodiles.
"Save me! Save me! O Lord, thus I speak to you regarding my deceased husband;
not seeing you, I am greatly terrified and weep profusely. (63)
O Lord, as I was sinking there, I saw the orb of the moon falling from the sky in a hundred fragments upon the earth.
In another moment, I saw the sun broken into a hundred fragments upon the earth;
at that same time, there was a seizing of both [the sun and moon], and the orb of the sky turned black.
In another moment, I saw a radiant brahmin who,
filled with rage, shattered the jar of nectar held in my lap.
In another moment, I beheld a Brahmin in a great rage,
who was walking along while grasping my husband by the side.
O Lord, the staff of skulls used for play passed from hand to hand and suddenly broke into pieces along with its handle.
Suddenly, from hand to hand, the mirror and the bracelet became stainless yet took on the appearance of soot, breaking apart into fragments.
My necklace of precious gems, having broken from my chest,
fell upon the surface of the earth along with an exceedingly soiled lotus.
All the puppets in the palace dance and laugh;
they clap their hands, sing, and weep from moment to moment.
I beheld a large, black-hued trident, a great weapon, appearing in the sky—whirling, falling, and leaping upward. (72)
The Puruṣa, the presiding deity of the vital breath, having emerged from within me, said to me: "O beloved, grant me leave; I am departing. (73)
And now, in a dream, I see a dark-complexioned image embracing and kissing me, dressed in black garments. (74)
O beloved of my life, seeing this very reversal, my right limbs dance and my vital breaths tremble. (75)
They weep out of grief and their minds are deeply distressed;
moreover, I observe the trembling of your left limb again and again. (76)
"What is this? What is this, O Lord? Will there be some calamity?
Having said this, she embraced him and for a moment found happiness. (77)
Andhaka embraced her and repeatedly gave her courage;
drawing the slender-limbed woman toward him with love, he clasped her and kissed her. (78)
At that very moment, auspicious dreams indeed appeared to Mahendra; therefore, with a joyful mind, he was gratified.
First, he beheld a young Brahmin boy with lotus-like eyes,
adorned, smiling, and radiant with flower garlands and sandalwood paste.
Then he saw a beautiful, virtuous woman who had sons and a husband, with her hair tied in a topknot and a tilaka mark on her forehead, chanting the Mother of the Vedas.
Clad in golden garments, adorned with jewel ornaments,
holding a blazing lamp in her hand, and bearing white grain in her other hand— she is most excellent.
Then he beheld her, auspicious, smiling, bestowing boons, and resembling the autumnal moon;
and thereafter, he saw the brahmin pronouncing auspicious blessings.
He beheld a white lotus, a royal swan, a horse, and a lake; he saw them beautifully depicted, auspicious, with fruits and flowers in full bloom. ||84||
One sees oneself biting mango, neem, coconut, aguru, arka, and banana trees, as well as a white snake, while standing upon a mountain. (85)
He saw him standing on a tree, standing on an elephant, standing on a boat, and standing on a horse;
he saw him playing the lute and eating sweet milk-rice.
He offered his desired food, mixed with curd and milk and placed upon a lotus leaf, while his body was smeared with white sandalwood paste and covered with worms and excrement. (87)
Then he saw one with white grain and flowers in his hand, standing upon a palace overlooking the ocean;
there he beheld silver, bright gems, and gold.
Pearls, māṇikya gems, and water from a full, auspicious pitcher;
a fragrant cow with her calf, a lordly bull, and a peacock—[these he should present]. (89)
A parrot, a crane, a swan, a hawk, and even a wagtail;
betel, flower garlands, a blazing fire, and the worship of the gods.
He fashioned an image of Pārvatī in the presence of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as well as a radiant Śaṅkara-liṅga and the divine preceptor Bṛhaspati. (91)
A Brahmin girl, a fruitful harvest with ripe fruit, a sacred site, a lord of kings, a lion, a tiger, an elephant, and a sage. (92)
Having seen the dream, he arose and performed his desired daily rites;
he then related that entire account to Śaṅkara.
Then Śaṅkara also spoke to Mahendra regarding those omens which he had seen on the road, all of which were entirely auspicious.
Indeed, all these are bestowers of victory and indicators of auspiciousness:
a Brahmin on the left, a female jackal, a full water-pot, a mongoose, and a blue jay. (95)
A virtuous woman who has sons, adorned with divine ornaments,
white flowers, garlands, grain, and an auspicious wagtail bird— 96.
On the right [he saw] a blazing fire, a brahmin, a bull, and an elephant;
a cow with her calf, a white horse, and a royal swan. ||97||
A courtesan, a garland of flowers, a banner, curd, milk-rice, a jewel, gold, silver, pearls, rubies, and whatever else is desired. (98)
Wine, meat, sandalwood, honey-wine, excellent ghee, the black antelope, fruit, parched grain, prepared food, and likewise a mirror. (99)
He saw a decorated celestial chariot and a brilliantly radiant image,
as well as white lotuses, a forest of lotuses, a conch shell, a cilla bird, and a flower bud.
He heard the auspicious sounds of a cat, a mountain, a cloud, a peacock, a parrot, and a crane, as well as the tones of conch shells, cuckoos, and musical instruments. (101)
He related in every way how he had seen such an auspicious sight: the diverse music of the Kṛṣṇas, the sound of the word "Hari," and the roar of victory.
Then indeed the kettledrums and conchs were sounded in the army of Śaṅkara;
and Andhaka, having learned of this, set out for the battle accompanied by his troops.
First appeared a naked widow, wearing a tattered cloth,
filthy, deformed in appearance, with a severed nose and hair standing erect.
The donkey, the buffalo, the camel, the pig, and the dog; the bear, the crow, the vulture, the monkey, and the heron; and dry grasses. (1.05)
The potter, the oil-presser, the barber, and likewise the washerman;
burnt wood, one suffering from trickling leprosy, a low-caste man, and a quarrelsome Brahmin. (106)
An angry monk, a shaven-headed woman, and likewise a shaven-headed man, a beggar, the sound of hunger, the falling of weapons, and the falling of chariots and crowns. 107.
The falling of the banner and the mirror, the bending of the knees of the horses, a pair of empty jars, and a terrifying black serpent [are inauspicious omens]. (108)
And the sight of an owl—
these signs that indicate death were indeed observed by Andhaka as they closed in upon him.
The wind blows with excessive force against him, causing him distress;
the mechanical wheel is shattered, and the elephant has fallen into a state of madness.
Having realized this, he was terrified in battle; though outwardly maintaining composure, he was filled with ostentation within, his mind certain of death. (111)
Andhaka, with an army of ten million, approached the presence of Hara;
he beheld the hosts of the gods upon the earth, in the sky, and even in the water.
The armies of the Dānavas stood ready for the counter-attack,
and musical instruments were sounded among the Asuras and others to mark the commencement of battle.
The banners, bearing the emblems that signal the commencement of battle, shone in the sky;
then the Daitya, having bowed to Śaṅkara, released hundreds of arrows.
Śaṅkara, having cut those arrows with crescent-headed shafts, released his own missiles;
the Daitya, for his part, sliced those hundreds of feathered arrows.
Thus the battle took place between the gods and the Dānavas,
along with the hosts of hideous appearance, which was terrifying to the Dānavas.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Evil Dreams and Other Inauspicious Omens of the Asura Andhaka and His Wife, the Auspicious Omens of Indra, and the Battle of Andhaka with Śaṅkara," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how at that time in the battle between both armies there occurred a terrible,
immeasurable, and life-consuming conflict.
He became terrifying everywhere—in the sky, on the earth, and even in the water.
In the meantime, there was one named Bhadra who possessed great strength.
The powerful great chariot-warrior, the commander-in-chief of Andhaka,
having reviled Śaṅkara, Kārttikeya, and likewise the lord of the Gaṇas...
He indeed hurled an arrow, resembling the fire of universal destruction, at Śrī Gaṇeśa;
but the Lord of the Gaṇas cut that arrow down with a crescent-shaped shaft.
Bhadra, filled with rage, hurled a spear radiant as the sun at Skanda;
Kārttikeya, however, then struck it down with the Vaiṣṇava weapon.
But Bhadra discharged the Nārāyaṇa weapon at the head of the battle;
Kārttikeya, however, having offered his salutations, lay down prostrate upon the earth.
The weapon, possessing a brilliance equal to a hundred suns and capable of effecting the destruction of the universe, roamed upwards and then dissolved into the sky.
When the weapon had departed, Kārttikeya, seizing his own firm mace,
shattered Bhadraratha’s chariot and slew his horses and charioteer.
Then the army commander of Andhaka fled toward Kārtika;
but Kārtikeya, filled with rage, struck that Bhadra with his spear.
Split in two, he fell and died upon the field of battle;
when Bhadra was slain, Dhūmra, the son of Andhaka and possessed of great prowess, [advanced]. 1.518.10.
He discharged a hundred arrows at Skanda at the forefront of the battle;
Kārttikeya, for his part, consumed the floods of arrows with his fire-missile.
Seeing this, the son of Śambhu quickly discharged the Brahmāstra, which causes both creation and destruction, accompanied by its seed-syllable and preceded by the appropriate mantra. || 12 ||
With the Brahmāstra itself, he suddenly withdrew [the weapon] with ease;
meanwhile, Dhūmra repeatedly struck Kārtika with sharp-pointed arrows.
But Kārttikeya, seeing that [weapon] equipped with a multitude of bows and arrows,
quickly released the Jṛmbhaṇa weapon in battle against that great chariot-warrior.
Dhūmra became inert and motionless at the forefront of the battle;
Dhūmra then discharged the sleep-weapon (nidrāstra), and he fell asleep.
Meanwhile, Andhaka awakened him with the weapon of awakening;
then Skanda struck that asura Andhaka with a hundred arrows.
Andhaka also struck Kārttikeya with a trident,
and with a mace, he shattered Kārttikeya’s chariot made of jewels.
Enraged, Kārtika shattered Andhaka’s chariot with his mace,
while Andhaka effortlessly [struck him] with a razor-sharp crescent-headed arrow.
Kārtika, having discharged a bhalla-weapon, cut the bow;
then Kārtika, approaching with a mace, struck Andhaka on the back.
Then Andhaka fell into a swoon; after a moment, Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, Kārtika, and likewise the Bhairavas [arose].
Kālya and Raṇacaṇḍya fought with the Dānavas;
the Dānavas were Śaṅkukarṇa, Māhiṣākṣa, and Vṛkāsya. || 21 ||
With the Vindhya as his jaw, Yama as his shoulder, the bull as his horn, and a cave as his mouth,
he whose stride was cruel and whose eyes were in his belly fought with the gods.
Then Śaṅkara, seizing his trident, made an effort to slay the demon Andhaka and blew his great conch shell.
Śambhu himself, the agent of destruction, stood in the middle of the chariot,
accompanied by hundreds of thousands of great car-warriors and thirty million chariots.
With three crores of lordly elephants and three crores of wrestlers, with ten billion horses and four times that number of shield-bearers. (25)
Those with swords [are equal] to seven times that number, and those with bows are twice that;
there are also eight guardians of the directions and ten million Bhairavas.
Clad in armor, they fought with hundreds of millions of Dānavas;
so too did Unmattabhairava and Saṃhārabhairava.
Asitāṅga and Bhairava, as well as Rurubhairava;
he who is known as Mahābhairava, and then Kālabhairava. ||28||
Pracaṇḍabhairava and the fierce Krodhabhairava, all accompanied by their Śaktis, fought upon the field of battle. ||29||
Ugracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍināyikā, Caṇḍeśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍī, and Caṇḍakapālikā. ||1.518.30||
Koṭarī and others, as well as others, fought on the field of battle;
likewise Candrāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Śāntā, Brahmāṇī, and Brahmavādinī.
Kaumārī, Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī of formidable form, Māheśvarī, Mahāmāyā, Bhairavī of terrifying appearance; ||32||
Then all those women standing in chariots fought with the asuras;
and the rakshasis, who were like mountains, waged war by the millions.
Andhaka, having prepared a divine weapon to slay Śaṅkara, took up his strung bow and discharged an arrow at Hara. (34)
Hari discharged the divine weapon named Añjana, which resembled the sun in summer, and the divine weapon Dhāvalya, which was like the moon. (35)
And Andhaka hurled a fire [missile] at Hara; he indeed extinguished that blazing [fire], which was as large as a palm tree, by means of the Vāruṇa [weapon]. ||36||
Andhaka hurled a wind, and Hara hurled a mountain;
then Andhaka indeed hurled the Nārāyaṇa weapon at the forefront of the battle.
Śambhu, the most excellent among the descendants of Bhṛgu, bowed down to that Nārāyaṇa;
meanwhile, Andhaka hurled the serpent-weapon (nāgāstra) at Śrī Śaṅkara.
Śaṅkara indeed seized Garuḍa in an instant;
Andhaka, for his part, hurled a crescent moon at Śaṅkara.
Śambhu hurled a terrifying mace at Andhaka;
Andhaka’s chariot was shattered, as was his charioteer.
Then Indra hurled his thunderbolt, which reduced Andhaka to ashes;
it was swallowed by Andhaka's mouth like water in the form of lightning.
And then Andhaka hurled the Brahmā-astra specifically to slay Indra; Śaṅkara, however, neutralized that [weapon] with his own Brahmā-astra.
Then Andhaka, with the intent to kill Śambhu, rushed forward swiftly with his sword amidst the army; at that moment, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose.
Desiring death, he went into the presence of Maheśa;
there, with exceeding strength, he struck Śaṅkara upon his matted locks.
The matted locks were instantly split in two, and likewise the sword was split in two;
and the mace was struck by Vīrabhadra along with his own mace.
At that time, Andhaka entered halfway into a fissure in the surface of the earth.
Embracing the iron mace held by Vīrabhadra,
Andhaka emerged from the palm of his hand along with that drawn-up mace.
Being separated [from his chariot], he seized an iron spear to slay Hara;
Śambhu, taking up his trident, hurled it at the chest of the Asura.
Although that great asura was himself pierced by that trident,
he was not deprived of his life due to the power of Brahmā’s boon.
The supreme fruit of his austerity protected him again and again:
for a hundred years he subsisted on fruits, and for a hundred years he ate leaves.
For a hundred years he subsisted on roots; for a hundred years he ate only *sumādana* flowers;
for a hundred years he subsisted on bulbs; and for a hundred years he lived on alms without asking.
For a hundred years he subsisted on water, for a hundred years he drank only vapors,
for a hundred years he fed on air, and for a hundred years he remained without food.
Then, remaining for a thousand years situated within the water,
the water was indeed dried up by the fire born from his ascetic heat.
But there the earth appeared beautiful;
thus, the third thousand years passed away at that time.
A very large anthill grew up, situated over the bamboo stalk;
the gracious Creator of the Universe said to him, "Choose a boon. ||55||
And he chose: "Neither from your hand, nor from the hand of Śaṅkara, nor even from the hand of Viṣṇu, nor from the goddesses or other deities shall it come to me. (56)
In your creation there shall be death, yet I shall become long-lived;
indeed, with this very body, I shall attain divinity and enter the state of renunciation.
Having heard this, the Creator said to him, "So be it; let it be so.
Thus, by the granting of that boon, the great asura attained a divine body.
He did not meet his destruction; on the contrary, rising up again, the powerful one, filled with rage, slaughtered many hosts with particular ferocity.
He struck Śaṅkara repeatedly with blows from his mace;
thus did the battle continue for a long time in heaven against the wielder of the Pināka bow.
When that Daitya did not meet his death even though pierced by the trident,
the powerful one rose up again and again and struck him in anger with blows.
Śaṅkara, having carefully examined him and found him to be spared by death,
then pierced him with the tip of his trident and hurled him into the courtyard of the sky.
He held it like an umbrella, hanging down with its opening facing downward,
as blood flowing from his limbs— produced by his body— streamed onto the ground.
He kept him fixed there for a long time with that very spear;
then, after some time, through the combat, he was reduced to mere skin, bone, and sinew.
Possessing three elements but having lost four elements, Andhaka was thus deprived of strength; like one in distress, he offered praise.
I did not know you were a god, I wicked-souled one corrupted by speech;
since you are endowed with such prowess, what you have done is justified.
It is only fitting for one blinded by pride and devoid of discernment, who, having attained wealth, learning, and even sovereignty, remains ill-behaved. (67)
I, intoxicated with pride, do not remain for a long time as I am;
I am sinful, I am a performer of evil deeds, I am of a sinful nature, and I am born of sin. (68)
Save me, O Lord, O Īśāna; wash away all my sins!
I am suffering, I am wretched, I am miserable, and I am devoid of power. (69)
O Lord, you ought to protect me, who have approached you and stand for refuge;
O Śambhu, my mind has been born toward you, the destroyer of all sins.
By merely uttering your name, even a doer of evil attains liberation;
for those devoid of your worship, their days are rendered fruitless. (71)
Therefore, knowing that your form is devoted [to me], liberate me here;
indeed, make me your own divine attendant with this very body, and not otherwise. (72)
O Lord, my disposition as a Dānava has departed; likewise, O Master, the kingdom has been renounced by me.
Today, indeed, sons, grandsons, and all my riches have been abandoned by me. (73)
Having heard those words of his, Śambhu slowly removed the Daitya, who was free from sin and possessed of humility, from the stake.
Then the Lord gave him the name Bhṛṅgiriṭi and said,
"You shall always be my beloved."
"Remain with gentleness among all my hosts, having taken refuge in me"—having thus performed the consecration with water for that new-formed body, [he spoke]. (76)
Śambhu led [her] to Kailāsa, and the gods and others returned to their own homes; they once again obtained their respective celestial kingdoms as was fitting. (77)
Then the wicked son of that Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas named Vṛka,
who was exceedingly cruel, entered the waters of the ocean.
Indra went to the beautiful city named Amarāvatī;
the Sudevās regained their sacrificial shares upon the surface of the earth.
Vṛka performed penance standing on one foot for thousands of years;
for five thousand years, he remained stationed with his body the size of a thumb.
And he obtained from Brahmā the granting of a boon, being exempted from old age and death;
thereafter, he went to Mount Revata in Saurāṣṭra.
Then he went to heaven and indeed conquered the station of Indra;
having received the consecration from Śukra, he himself became Indra.

Therefore, all sacrificial rites and other duties toward the gods, as well as recitations, burnt offerings, and other ancestral rites, and the honoring of Brahmins—[all these are accomplished by him]. (83)
Everything that one has done, such as the offering of one's own hands and so forth, is thus destroyed;
he alone is the enjoyer of the sacrificial portions, and never anyone else. (84)
"And one who ordains sacrifices and such acts is certainly to be punished; there is no doubt.
In this manner, he issued a decree that was opposed to righteous conduct. (85)
That demon Vṛka went to Sāṃkṛti, who was a full treasury of ascetic power, and killed him there; for weapons were of no use against him at all.
His sword touched him and broke into a hundred pieces; then Sāṃkṛti cursed him, saying, "O Asura, may your destruction come quickly! (87)
And Śaṅkara slew that wolf; this has been told to you. O Lakṣmī, in the course of this narrative, listen now to another story. (88)

Thus ends the five hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Asura Andhaka was Pierced by Śaṅkara with His Trident in Battle and Made into the Gaṇa Bhṛṅgīṛiṭi, and How His Son Vṛka was Also Slain by Śaṅkara," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||518||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, kings, gods, Daityas, and others likewise,
having embraced the delusion of Māyā, take delight in the gambling for their very lives.
When all have gone to the state of the five [elements], he who is free from the five must himself go elsewhere;
yet, in that state of the five, he attains oneness with the five.
For Māyā, being perishable by nature, has never been destroyed along with any of the individual souls (ātman),
even by those who have lived for arbudas upon arbudas of years.
Listen, O King: in former times there was a ruler renowned as Indradyumna;
he was devoted to the Brahmins, a protector of those seeking refuge, and a guardian of the virtuous world.
He was a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, skillful, and devoted to the welfare of all beings;
there was neither famine nor disease, nor any fear caused by thieves.
Indeed, there was no deficiency whatsoever among his subjects regarding any object of enjoyment;
moreover, he performed innumerable sacrifices accompanied by complete sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atirātra, the Uktha, and likewise the Ṣoḍaśika; then the Sautrāmaṇī, the animal sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya, and the Vrata-kratu.
The Vājapeya, Aśvamedha, Rājasūya, and Soma sacrifices;
the Puṇḍarīka, Putreṣṭi, Sasyeṣṭi, Rudra, and Vaiṣṇava sacrifices. (8)
He performed sacrifices such as the Kārīrī and the Vaiśvadeva;
there was no city or town on the surface of the earth that he did not reach.
Whether at a sacred ford, a hall, a forest, or a pond, there was indeed no place where his sacrificial session did not exist;
everywhere, the lords partook of the food of Indradyumna.
Gods, sages, servants, seekers of knowledge, and Brahmins;
ascetics, virtuous men, virtuous women, and even female practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga—[all these came]. (1.1)
Brahmacārins, forest-dwellers, renunciants, those who have renounced all possessions,
the destitute, the wretched, and others likewise partake of his sacrificial feast.
No such sacred ford exists where his divine power is not present;
therefore, the gift of tens of millions of maidens is considered supreme by him.
Whatever has been done or caused to be done, the virtuous are always well-honored;
on the tenth day of his reign, he indeed rides upon the back of an elephant.
The drum, being beaten, resounded throughout the entire city:
"In Ujjayinī, tomorrow morning will be the auspicious day of Hari. (15)
By means of that very same body, he went himself to the world of Brahmā;
then, at the end of a thousand kalpas, he was addressed by Brahmā himself: || 16 ||
"O Indradyumna, go to the earth; you must certainly not remain here, for today the destruction of your fame has occurred upon the surface of the earth. (17)
As long as one's fame remains upon the surface of the earth, so long shall that person dwell in heaven;
for this reason, people write down their names.
Go quickly to the surface of the earth— to places such as ponds, wells, tanks, and temples— and renew your own fame.
"When my fame becomes true, you shall indeed behold the truth.
Thereupon, he departed for the earth toward the city of Kāmpilya.
Then he asked: "What is the country? What is the city? And what are the people there?
They replied: "This region is Ānarta, and the city is indeed [Kuśasthalī]."
"Who are you that enters Kāmpilya here unrecognized?
The king replied, "In former times, I was King Indradyumna. (22)
"In the land of Vajrahaka, in the city called Rocaka, there is a sovereign;
where is that land, where is that city, and must I indeed dwell there? (23)
The people said, "We do not know that king, nor the country or the city.
The king said, "O people, show me one who is long-lived. (24)
If anyone here were to know that lord of the earth, people would say: "That sage who has taken refuge [there] lives for ten kalpas. (25)
"In the Naimiṣa forest, ask Mārkaṇḍeya; he will speak.
Having traveled by way of the sky, the king went and questioned that lord of sages. (26)
"O Indradyumna, has this king been seen or heard of by you here?
The sage replied, "Neither have I seen him, nor even heard of him. (27)
Having heard those words of his, the king fell into despair.
The sage said, "Come with me to the Himalayas. (28)
"And there dwells a sage named Baka, who is more ancient than I.
Having said this, the two of them traveled by way of the sky and, bowing down, questioned him. (29)
"Have you seen King Indradyumna, or have you even heard of him?
The crane replied, "Twenty kalpas have passed for me."
At that time, I did not know at all who that king was there before me.
Indradyumna said to Baka: "How is it that you possess such long life? (31)
The crane said: "Formerly, O twice-born one, I was Viśvarūpa.
Then, at a certain time, during the transit of the sun into Capricorn," (32)
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was bathed by me with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
and Śaṅkara was bathed there with the water of Hari’s grace.
Then I attained the status of a prince on the western land;
remembering my past births, I always [worshipped] Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa with the five nectars.
In this manner, I worshipped Śiva for a thousand years in the morning;
by the power of that merit, I have indeed become long-lived and steadfast. (35)
Thereafter, I indeed rendered service to Śambhu on Kailāsa;
then, having gone to the hermitage of Gālava, I engaged in the study of knowledge.
His wife, having bathed after her menses, was touched by me with a change of heart;
she then cursed me, saying, "O rogue, become a crane dwelling in the forest. (37)
Therefore, I am in the form of a crane, a sage who assumes a form according to his will;
I dwell here in this great forest, always pure, in the shape of a crane.
"Being one who remembers his past births, the crane always worships Śrī Hari here.
Mārkaṇḍeya, however, said to him: "Do you know anyone even more ancient than yourself? (39)
"If you show me anyone, I shall ask him about that. The crane said, "Come with me; there is one even older than I."
"Where my beloved is," said Ulūkarṣi, remaining there for a long time;
those three then went to that peak of Kailāsa which belongs to me.
Having seen his friend the crane, he greeted him with a welcome;
the crane then questioned the owl concerning King Indradyumna.
"Tell me, friend, if you know, when was that king born? The owl replied, "Forty kalpas have passed since my birth. (43)
"King Indradyumna has passed away; he has not been heard of nor seen.
But Indradyumna said to him: 'How indeed have you become an owl?'"
The owl told his own story: "Formerly, on this earth, there was a Brahmin who was a celibate student (brahmacārī) devoted to Hara, worshipping him with bilva leaves. (45)
Then, at the end of a thousand years, Hara granted me his vision;
he gave me the Vaiṣṇava mantra, "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa."
Śambhu became invisible, and I, though deformed, reached the auspicious hermitage of that descendant of Bhṛgu.
