The wife of Bhārgava was the virtuous Sudarśanā by name; she was the daughter of Gālava and was devoted solely to her husband. 48.
In that city, however, there was a single beautiful young maiden of the Bhṛgu lineage;
she was then requested by me in marriage and subsequently wedded.
Always regarding me as ugly, the maiden said to her mother:
"I have been given away to an ugly man; I have no desire to live. (1.519.50)
"I shall either consume poison or enter the fire.
Then Bhārgava said to her, "Become firm for him to whom you have been given. (51)
"That alone is the Vedic dharma: one should remember Nārāyaṇa as the husband.
By serving your own husband, you shall indeed go to heaven. (52)
"Therefore, serve that Lord and make your birth fruitful.
Though instructed in this way, she did not at all accept what was for her own benefit. (53)
She did not attend upon me at night;
therefore, I forcibly carried her from her father’s house to my hermitage at midnight. (54)
At dawn, the Brahmin father and likewise his mother woke up;
"Where is that daughter of ours? they asked, as they wandered through my hermitage. (55)
Having arrived, they beheld her, and she too wept upon seeing them;
then that descendant of Bhṛgu, his soul overcome with anger, spoke to me.
"Since my daughter was carried off by you as your wife during the night, by this curse you shall become a night-stalker (niśācara) and an owl. (57)
For I was born as an owl, remembering my former births at all times;
I am able to assume any form at will and I dwell here upon this mountain. (58)
My wife, remaining in her father’s palace and taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, attained the state that bestows the service of glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (59)
"O Kauśika, in this manner my status indeed arose here on this mountain;
the fruit of worship with unbroken bilva leaves is supreme."
"But as for my long life and my possession of a divine form," the crane said to another,
"if you know anyone who is long-lived..."
"Speak; let us go there and question that king.
The owl replied, "Indeed, come here along with me."
On the peak of Gandhamādana dwells the great vulture-sage;
if he is long-lived, he may know that king as his ancestor.
Having spoken thus and taking them with him, the owl approached the vulture;
seeing them there, the eminent vulture was delighted and went out to meet them.
Having welcomed him and inquired about his well-being in the hermitage,
the owl said, "This is my friend Baka Nāḍījaṅgha."
He whose friend is Mārkaṇḍeya has this king as his well-wisher;
and this King Indradyumna has come here to inquire about him.
"Whether he existed or not, I have come here to know this," [the king said].
But the vulture replied, "Indeed, eighty eons have passed for me. (67)
"No one has ever seen or heard of King Indradyumna anywhere.
Having heard those words of his, that king also became deeply dejected.
Having resolved upon death, he reflected in his mind and asked the vulture: "Tell me, how is it that you have become so long-lived? (69)
The vulture said: "In former times, I dwelt happily in a sacred tree (caitya-vṛkṣa).
And during the spring, people would worship that fruit-bearing tree."
There, the amorous women tied an excellent swing to the tree;
having placed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon it, they [shook it] again and again.
All the maidens as well as the married women caused [the image] to sway;
I, however, filled with curiosity, remained there myself during the night. ||72||
I would swing with them, take my pleasure, and then cease;
seen by people and beaten by them, I subsequently met my death. ||73||
I became a king known by the name Kuśadhvaja, endowed with the memory of my past lives;
I constantly swing Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as I did before. (74)
On Śivarātri, I repeatedly swing Śambhu,
and likewise on Janmāṣṭamī, having installed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa there.
I constantly invoked Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
while I was doing so, the illustrious Śambhu became manifest before my eyes. (76)
"I am the bestower of boons to the Vaiṣṇava; choose a boon," Hara said to me, and I likewise requested one from him. (77)
Grant me a dwelling on Kailāsa during the assembly of Vaiṣṇavas;
I shall always perform excellent service for you, a devotee of Viṣṇu.
Having been addressed thus, Mahādeva led me to Kailāsa;
and after some time, he went by his own will in a celestial chariot.
And while wandering about, I saw the daughter of Agniveśya, accompanied by many female companions, having entered the water for the purpose of bathing. (1.519.80)
Having descended, I then requested that young woman for the sake of a wife;
however, out of lustful intent, she did not even look toward me.
Having rescued her from the water, I forcibly brought her to the celestial chariot;
then, hearing her weeping, her father cursed me.
"Since you touched that girl, who is devoted to her virtuous vows, like a vulture, therefore become a vulture here, and let your celestial chariot perish. (83)
At that time, I was born as a vulture and my celestial chariot vanished;
that young girl, having not yet experienced enjoyments, went back to her father. (84)
O friend, this entire reason for my transformation into a vulture has been told;
through the grace of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, I have attained long life upon this earth. (85)
"I do not know Indradyumna; tell me, what can I do for you?
Hearing this, the king became despondent regarding the fire.
If he desires entry there, he wishes to bring about his own death;
then the vulture said to him, "O King, do not enter the fire. (87)
I shall proclaim it to you; for I too possess one who is ancient.
He will recognize my old friend, Indradyumna. (88)
We shall go there where Kamaṭha Māntharaka resides,
who is famous for having made his dwelling right there in Lake Mānasa.
They all went to that tortoise, which was basking in the auspicious sunlight on the shore of the lake; then they descended from the sky there.
Then that tortoise quickly went beneath the water;
and the vulture said to his friend, "O sir, why are you departing? (91)
Seeing a friend, why do you depart as if afraid?
Even one who is very lowly becomes most worthy of honor by the virtuous once he has reached their home. (92)
Then the tortoise, with only his head protruding from the midst of the water, replied to his dear friend: "I offer you a welcome. (93)
Likewise, there is honor for your friend and for his friends and so forth;
however, this king who is seen here as the fifth is someone else entirely. (94)
Out of fear of that one named Indradyumna, I am going to another body of water;
for in former times, my back was scorched by him with the sacrificial fires. (95)
Even now, that wound on my back has not yet healed;
for whenever I see this Yajñakīrti, I am reminded of that injury to my back.
"I flee into the water, O friend, yet I offer you a welcome;
for there is the great renown of the royal sage Indradyumna. (97)
By the king, all sacrifices have indeed been performed in the number of a thousand;
yet even today, the fame and merit of this monarch do not diminish.
Fifty-one hundred kalpas have passed for me here in this water;
prior to that, I was then in a city named Rocaka. 99.
"Out of fear of him, I have abandoned that place and am dwelling here in this lake.
Having said this, he went outside and offered him great honor.
The tortoise, who remembered his former births, could assume any form at will and possessed a divine appearance; he engaged in various conversations with them concerning other kalpas.
At that very moment, Indradyumna prepared hospitality, including food and other offerings;
filled with joy, he then questioned the tortoise.
How do you possess such long life? Was it even before Rocaka?
Where was your residence, where was your birth, and what is your vow? (103)
"Tell me, for great joy arises from the sight of a friend.
Having heard this, the tortoise said: "Listen, O King, to what occurred in the past."

Thus ends the five hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of King Indradyumna’s New Fame Established on Earth by the Sages Mārkaṇḍeya, Baka, Dhūkarṣi, Gṛdhra, Kamaṭha, and others, as well as his Former Births as a Baka and Other Creatures, and His Longevity Resulting from Meritorious Deeds," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī! That tortoise related his own previous birth;
O Great King Indradyumna, listen to what was seen by me.
Residing in the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, I was an attendant of Nārāyaṇa,
named Vasuhārīta, four-armed and enchanting.
He was appointed to gather lotus flowers daily from the eternal lake within the golden enclosure.
A garland made of *lakṣmī* flowers is offered daily upon the neck of Śrī Hari;
however, I, having brought flowers myself, offer them daily to Śrī.
Once, while immersed in a bath, I was searching for lotuses;
I remained there for a very long time, delighting in the immersion in that lake.
After that time had passed for Mālā, Lakṣmī herself arrived there and said to me, "What are you doing, you? (6)
"O evil-minded one, you have been submerged in water for a long time during this worship;
remain forever in the water, for I have no need of you."
"You act like a tortoise; always remain as a tortoise.
Thus addressed, he attained the state of a tortoise in the lake of Vaikuṇṭha.
When the creation was coming into being, Gaṅgā arrived at Satya;
therefore, that is indeed the Brahma-lake, and because of it, I have come here.
Then another attendant there, appointed for the sake of the lotuses, was named Anantaśīla; once, while he was in the midst of the water, [he saw a vision].
Advancing toward Satyaloka, he arrived together with the waters;
perceiving him to be Viṣṇu in form, Brahmā honored him with joy.
There, Anantaśīla said, "I am pleased; choose a boon.
Brahmā replied, "As long as there are tens of millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas)..."
"O Lord, always uphold those [deeds] which are performed as equal to a mustard seed.
He then said, "So be it," but added, "However, give me a sacrificial altar."
Abiding there, I maintain the firm sphere of the universe;
thus, I am indeed present both in Satyaloka and in the Gaṅgā. || 14 ||
I was right there in the Gaṅgā when Brahmā then said to me: "O Tortoise, you shall carry Ananta; indeed, I shall grant you your desired wish."
And I said: "O Brahmin, act in such a way that I may become a servant of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; I shall be one of His attendants. (16)
The Creator replied, "So be it," and by me Śeṣa was supported;
he, named Ananta, is upon my back, and by Ananta, in turn, [the world] is held above his hoods.
The cosmic eggs are indeed born and cease;
yet Brahmā performed penance for the sake of attaining me.
Then, at the end of the year, Śrī Hari approached Brahmā and, standing face-to-face with him, spoke for the sake of attaining the state of servitude to Nārāyaṇa.
"Choose a boon—blessings upon you! Tell me how I am remembered.
Brahmā said: "O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of the Universe! (1.520.20)
I have obtained this attendant of yours named Vasuhārīta,
who, by the curse of Lakṣmī, assumed the form of a tortoise.
I requested your infinite and most excellent chief attendant;
for the purpose of supporting the cosmic eggs, he requested a splendid seat.
Then that tortoise was indeed properly offered by me as a support for Ananta; and the tortoise chose Nārāyaṇa as his refuge.
Therefore, grant us the state of servitude;
O Lord, show Your mercy likewise toward both of Your devotees and attendants. 24.
Then Nārāyaṇa said again and again,
"So be it," after having destroyed the hosts of Asuras, beginning with Andhaka, within a moment.
Then, for the sake of dispelling his fatigue, he made the back of the tortoise Śeṣa into a ball in the Ocean of Milk.
"I shall always be your servant there, as will Kacchapa and Ananta.
Having granted this boon, saying "So be it," Nārāyaṇa vanished.
Śrī Hari arrived there, taking Lakṣmī with him to the ocean, where I, as a tortoise, eternally reside in the great waters. (28)
The serpent Śeṣa, Ananta, became my couch and pillow upon my back;
there lies the Lord of the World, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (29)
There, eternal servitude was obtained by both at the feet of Śrī Hari;
then, once a hundred Brahmās had passed away, the sage Lomaśa [appeared].
Having come to the Ocean of Milk to behold Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
he was seen by me and questioned regarding his welfare.
He replied, "O tortoise, my home and other comforts remain, but ten Brahmins have perished in my presence. (32)
When a hundred Brahmās have perished, I too shall die in a mere moment;
how then could one of such short life build a house that perishes in an instant? (33)
Then, by the command of the Sage as well as the command of Śrī Hari,
I assumed a second form, indeed quite small, measuring only one hundred yojanas.
I went forth for the purpose of a pilgrimage to behold the interior of the universe;
thus, together with the sage Lomaśa, from the subterranean realm, [I traveled].
As I ascended higher and higher, my body was likewise affected by the wind and underwent extreme contraction due to its own nature.
On earth, in the land of Kṛṣṇamaṇi, in Saurāṣṭra, and in Aśvapaṭṭaka;
in the excellent Vyāghrāraṇya forest, and indeed at the lake Miṣṭoda. (37)
On the bank of the Lomaśa hermitage, five yojanas in extent,
in the eastern part relative to Raivata, I obtained a moment's rest.
There, at Kuṅkumavāpī and in the temple of Kambharā-Kṛṣṇa, a Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to his wife and is a portion of Kṛṣṇa resides eternally. (39)
Śrī herself is Kambharā-Lakṣmī, and Kṛṣṇa is Gopāla-Kṛṣṇaka;
where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa always resides in that temple.
Likewise, there are eleven Rudras, eight Vasus,
twelve Ādityas, and always the two physicians of the gods.
And those thirty-three gods remain ever anew in every kalpa at that auspicious and most excellent sacred ford where its gate stands.
I beheld that Brahmin, devoted to his wife, who possessed a lifespan equal to that of Mahāviṣṇu; he was honored by Lomaśa, and at that time, he was likewise honored by me.
In whose presence millions of Brahmins have attained dissolution, and whose lineages are considered Brahmins throughout the fourteen worlds. (44)
In every other creation as well, those Brāhmaṇas have always belonged to his lineage;
having obtained a vision of him, I dwelt in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
At that time, there was a great king named Indradyumna here on this earth,
a sovereign ruler of the lands consisting of the seven continents and oceans.
In the capital city of Rocakā, in the vicinity of Mount Raivata,
he was born in the eastern direction, upon the grounds of the Vyāghra forest.
The second capital was in Mahākālavana, and the third was likewise located in the glorious city of Puruṣottama. 48.
When forty years of the current era of Vedhas had passed,
there was indeed a king on the surface of the earth named Indradyumna.
And he saw me, a tortoise of massive body, perfectly circular and half a yojana in size, in his own sacred bathing place, the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Knowing that she was under Lomaśa’s authority and realizing she had reached her fertile season,
the king chose me from Lomaśa for the purpose of the supreme sacrificial altar.
Having agreed to it in that manner, Lomaśa gave me as a gift;
thus, I have been carried on the back of this mountain continuously for many years. (2)
However, the sacrifices performed by him were promoted by Lomaśa;
consequently, my back was scorched, and I entreated the sage for relief.
The very compassionate Lomaśa said to me, "Go to Lake Mānasa at the edge of the Himālayas"; it was from there that I have come here.
O Bhava, five years of Brahmā have indeed passed for me here;
now listen to those kalpas of Brahmā that have passed for me here.
Eighteen thousand and twenty-five kalpas have passed here in this Mānasa; I remember them exactly as they were.
And by my second form, I always remain here;
my back has become perfectly free from pain due to its resting upon the Himalayas. (57)
"Lomaśa Ṛṣi is my preceptor; go to his auspicious hermitage there.
O King, you should first go to the excellent city of Puruṣottama."
"Go from there to Mahākālavana, where your own home is located, O Lord of the World, where formerly you yourself placed [the image] with your own hand. (59)
Then go to Surāṣṭra, where the Aśvapaṭṭa lake is located,
where Kuṅkumavāpikā is, and where the sage Lomaśa resides.
Where indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the husband of Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Rādhā, and Prabhā, the Supreme Person, resides; ||61||
Hari shines resplendent in a divine seven-storied palace;
go there, O King, and having performed service, proceed from there to what follows. (62)
Then, at the end of the kalpa, you shall behold me again in Satyaloka;
together with these sages, your fame shall remain unimpeded upon the earth.
Having heard that true and beneficial word of the tortoise, you will certainly go toward that island, having accepted his sweet speech. (64)
Having departed from that place, they returned to their respective abodes;
Indradyumna, in due course, arrived before Lomaśa.
Indeed, for him on whose four sides, throughout the four directions and across the earth for four yojanas, there is no illusion, nor passion or hatred; how then could there be any latent tendencies?
Having reached the hermitage of Brahmarūpa and having heard everything from the mouth of Lomaśa regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the king then became satisfied.
Having worshipped Kambharā-Lakṣmī, the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa,
and the thirty-three gods, he dwelt there for a year by their command.
There, he constantly heard ever-new and virtuous discourses from the lotus-like mouth of Lomaśa, concerning the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā. 69.
There he heard from Lomaśa about the sacrifices he had performed himself,
as well as the auspicious installation of the illustrious Jagannātha that he had carried out.
Likewise, everywhere there were sacrificial sessions, feasts for those bearing your name, and gifts of elephants, cows, horses, gold, jewels, and women. (71)
Whatever objects exist upon the earth, for all of them he has performed acts of giving, recitation, worship, and so forth, having heard [the teachings] from the mouth of his guru. (72)
He obtained from the mouth of Lomaśa all knowledge— which bestows the self, bestows heaven, and likewise bestows liberation— as well as the vision of the Self.
O Lakṣmī, listen; I shall tell you that which was heard by Lomaśa from the mouth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—this method suitable for a devotee. (74)

Thus ends the five hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Narration of Events such as the Residence, Lifespan, and Sacrifices of Indradyumna at the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara in the Lomaśa Hermitage in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpī," following the account by the tortoise residing on the Mānasa lake regarding his own and Śeṣa’s status as attendants of Viṣṇu, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; Indradyumna once questioned the sage Lomaśa:
"O Sage, tell me how that knowledge which brings about peace may arise. (1)
Without the peace of the self, everything is considered a web of agitation;
tell me, there is no other gain equal to the peace of the self. (2)
Lomaśa, having remembered Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, spoke to him:
"Listen, O King, I shall speak; keep Śrī Hari in your remembrance. (3)
The Imperishable Brahman is the supreme abode, all-pervading and most excellent;
there, the eternal one, higher than the highest, is to be served by those who are liberated through their realizations.
The glorious Lord Hari shines forth as the illustrious Kṛṣ�ṇa-Nārāyaṇa; He is divine, eternally youthful, exceedingly powerful, and a treasure-house of every form of beauty.
The splendors of millions upon millions of suns always shine forth from every atomic portion of him, who pervades all created beings and is served by the liberated ones.
He is indeed the glorious Puruṣottama, the bearer of infinite forms;
He is Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all things, beginning with the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Transcending all syllables, he is indeed the two-armed one of divine form;
the Lord Śrīpati is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. (8)
Her eyes, beautiful with collyrium, were as long as lotus petals and reddish; they were ever steady with love, filled with inner emotion, and intensely captivating.
And in that exceedingly beautiful place, resplendent with rows of golden hair,
offer from your heart the entirety of your being with devotion.
With eyebrows that pierce with the arrows of ten million Cupids,
filled with self-bliss, affectionate, and imbued with aesthetic flavor for those who possess such taste.
O you who bestow the nectar of the drinking of the stars, O you as tremulous as a fish, whose outer corners reach to the ears, and who are filled with skill in the corners [of the eyes]! 12.
It is white, marked with red lines, radiant with crystal on all sides, endowed with the reflections of all visible things, and beautiful to meditate upon. (13)
Their noses were like sesame flowers, their lips resembled ripe bimba fruits,
and they were adorned with thin lines and a beard that produced a wondrous brilliance.
Then one should clearly visualize the chin as slightly depressed and elevated;
the cheeks as having the luster of the sun and moon, and the forehead as adorned with a dot (bindu). 15.
One should remember Him with a tilaka-mark, exceedingly radiant, and marked by a single line;
and His beautiful, glossy, curved, black, and tawny locks of hair.
One should remember his ears, adorned with jeweled and diamond earrings, shining with long rays of light from the brilliance of his crown and beautified by their earlobes. 17.
One should meditate upon the Lord’s face, pervaded by a halo and radiant with splendors, adorned with the beauty of ten million Cupids, and captivating to the heart.
One should meditate upon his charming, conch-like neck and his firm, well-developed shoulders;
his two arms, resembling the coils of a serpent, are as radiant as golden campaka flowers. (19)
His two hands resemble the trunks of elephants, and the palms of his hands have the luster of lotuses;
his nails are like the rays of the moon—white, beautifully rosy at the edges, and well-raised.
One should meditate upon [the Lord's] chest as being elevated and marked with the signs of Lakṣmī, with all the fingers possessing lines and the thumbs and forearms likewise adorned. (21)
One should meditate upon the broad chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, the hair curling to the right, the pair of breasts, and likewise the belly adorned with three folds.
One should meditate upon the deep navel, the hips, the two sides which are brilliantly radiant, the waist equal to that of a lion, the generative organ, and the two buttocks. (23)
One should meditate on the thighs, which are like the trunks of elephants; the knees, which are perfectly rounded;
and the beautiful shanks, which are broad and as pale-white as lotus petals. (24)

One should meditate on the fingers as being adorned with moon-like nails, and likewise on the ornaments and garments; one should remember the rows of necklaces, the line of teeth, and the heart as the mind. (25)
One should contemplate the meditative cultivation, the qualities, all sovereign powers, and the activity;
for indeed, it is through such contemplation of the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa that this occurs. ||26||
O King, eternal peace will surely arise; of this there is no doubt.
Then one should meditate upon that Lord Hari, namely Śrī Kṛṣṇa and likewise Rādhikā.
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, Brahmā and Sarasvatī, as well as Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, Śiva and Durgā Pārvatī. (28)
One should meditate upon Gaṅgā, Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, Vṛndā, and Tulasī;
there, in that which transcends the imperishable, one should likewise meditate upon the Vyūhas and the Vibhavas.
One should remember the images, the portions, the parts, the manifestations, and the divine glories within Hari;
one should remember Him as residing in milk, situated on white ground, dwelling in snow, and as being within oneself.
One should indeed meditate upon that Janārdana Viṣṇu, who has entered all bodies;
one should always behold that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in both man and woman. ||3.1||
In truth, whether in heaven, on earth, in the sky, in the netherworld, or in the ether of the heart;
in a son, a wife, an animal, a beloved, or among the class of insentient things—(32)
Whether it be visible or invisible, pleasant or unpleasant, acceptable or a thing to be avoided—one should indeed meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the cowherd boy. ||33||
It is divine, cherished by Kambharā, situated near Aśvapaṭṭasara, eternally meditated upon by Lomaśa, and worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others. 34.
I bow to the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Prabhā, Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, and Pārvatī; to the Lord of Jayā and the husband of Lalitā.

The Lord of liberation, the Lord of incarnations, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Protector, and the cause of the birth and other states of the universe. ||36||
One should meditate upon that Lord, whose beloved form resides within the lotus of the heart, who is served by the Siddhas, and who is the treasure-house of the wealth of knowledge and bliss. (37)
With single-minded devotion, a man or a woman should meditate upon their husband as the Lord, the Supreme Master who is served at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā. 38.
One should constantly meditate upon Him, remember Him, chant His name, bow down to Him, and likewise serve Him;
one should worship Him, adore His lotus feet, and drink the nectar held therein. 39.
One should swallow one's faith, which brings about fragrance and other such qualities;
one should perform circumambulation and praise, and offer a lamp and food offerings.
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering and practice the surrender of all one's possessions;
thus, the self must always be surrendered and offered unto Hari. 41.
Desire, anger, pleasure, affection, greed, delusion, and the like; as well as compassion, charity, courtesy, self-restraint, and the entire circle of faults. (42)
One should offer everything to him and cast it therein without interruption.
By that means, just as a mineral is purified in fire, so too is a human being purified. ||43||
Abandoning even the fruit of Indradyumna, one should always perform service (dāsya) to Hari;
may I attain divinity through service to the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 44.
He obtained long life, a body equal to that of Brahmā,
liberation while living, as well as sovereign powers, supernatural accomplishments, and the perfection of dispassion.

I attained contentment, the destruction of craving, and freedom from illusion; likewise, I attained freedom from the taints of illusion and the like, as well as the state of being devoid of all veils. ||46||
Having burnt away the afflictions and the latencies of karma, I move about like Hari;
indeed, by means of yoga, one crosses the ocean of waters just as one crosses a block of wood with a clod of earth. 47.
Through union with Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Lomaśa, the destroyer of all taints,
remains here liberated from Brahmā, the destroyer of the duration of the kalpas.
He who effortlessly creates, as a mere play, this entire universe—countless and extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—which serves as the support for all things moving and stationary; ||49||
Brahmā, Śiva, Śeṣa, Dharma, the Sun, Gaṇeśvara,
the assembly of great sages, and the Lord of the Gods meditate upon Yama day and night.
The Vedas praise Him, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the universe;
Prakṛti praises Him with joy, and Sarasvatī praises Him in fear. (51)
He whom the six-faced one, the four-faced one, and the five-faced one praise— that Hari—
whom the thousand-faced, the Veda-faced, and the fire-faced ones also laud.
[He meditated upon] the Lord, the Supreme Self, the Brahman which is higher than the highest, consisting of its own will, effortless, devoid of qualities, and stainless. ||53||
He is the eternally pervasive light, whose very form is the grace bestowed upon devotees;
he is eternal bliss, eternal, and possesses an eternally imperishable form. ||54||
Worship eternally the Guru, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as your husband;
that Blessed One has descended here for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth and other afflictions. (55)
The Lord, through his illusory power (māyā), assumes the guise of a cowherd boy and is the beloved;
he alone is the protector, the nourisher, and the destroyer—worship him always. 56.
O Lord of the Earth, worship Him alone as your father, mother, the bestower of knowledge and mantras, your true guru, and your husband—Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (57)
O Indradyumna, understand from me this knowledge which is higher than the highest;
abandon everything that causes obstruction and attain supreme joy in Hari. (58)
What is a kingdom? What is fame? What is one’s own village, and what is another?
Who is whose son? Who is whose father? Whose is a mother, and from where does she come? (59)
Beings come and go through saṃsāra solely by virtue of their own performed actions;
according to their karma, a living being is born in various different states.
By the power of karma, someone may be born from a Brahmin woman, a king’s wife, a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra woman; or even among animals, birds, or trees. (6.1)
They were joyful in the sensory objects bestowed by Nārāyaṇa,
yet they were despondent at the abandonment of the body and at the separation from their kinsman.
All that was done by means of illusion; the girl, the bride, and the dispassionate woman—these indeed were the different states of one and the same woman. (63)
The severance of offspring, land, wealth, and so forth is worse than death for the fool;
it happens constantly to the fool, but never to the wise man.
Be a devotee of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, a performer of sacrifices for Him, one who has Him as your supreme goal, a worshiper of the Kṛṣṇa-mantra, and one intent on the service of Kṛṣṇa. (65)
Out of fear of whom this wind blows and the sun shines eternally;
out of fear of whom the moon and Mahendra shine, and who rains at the change of time.
Fire burns and death indeed moves among living beings;
yet the tree, by the power of time, bears both flowers and fruits.
The wind has space as its support; water and the rest have the wind as their support;
the tortoise is the support of the water, and Ananta is indeed the support of that.
Within the infinite coils of Śeṣa are the cosmic eggs and the mountains;
there the water is motionless, and from that [support] the earth rests upon the water. (69)

The Great Virāṭ is the support of the seven heavens, the foundation of the earth, the wheel of light, and the abode of the planets; he is the source of all cosmic eggs endowed with their eightfold coverings.
The support for that is indeed Bhūman, Mahāviṣṇu, and Sadāśiva;
his support is Vaikuṇṭha, and Goloka is its refuge.
The supreme, auspicious abode of the imperishable, which is the support of Goloka, is the world of Brahmā;
it is higher than the highest, that most excellent and ultimate realm.
Divine, it is all-pervading and indeed devoid of boundaries;
therein indeed are all abodes, while its three-quarters are the immortal in heaven.
One foot of His consists of all beings; beyond that, nothing exists.
Residing there is Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the cowherd boy. (74)
O King, worship Hari, the delighter of Kambharā and the Lord of the Imperishable;
for He is that very Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, in the supreme abode.
The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) abides in the midst of infinite liberated souls;
likewise, the Imperishable Person (Akṣarapūruṣa) abides in the imperishable realm (akṣara-dhāman).
Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are in Goloka; the Lord Śrīpati is in Vaikuṇṭha;
he is in the form of Śiva in the world of Śiva; and in Satyaloka, he is considered to be Brahmā and Hari.
Among the radiant, he is indeed the sun; among the purifiers, likewise the fire;
among liquids, he is Hari (water); and among the senses, he is the mind.
He is the wind among those who move swiftly; he is indeed Yama among those who wield the rod of punishment;
he is Time among those who reckon, and he is the unchanging among all letters.
He is the Sāman among the Sāmans, he is Indra among the gods, and he is the scorcher among kings;
he is Īśāna among the lords of the quarters, and indeed, he is Kubera among the wealthy.
Salutations to Him who is the all-pervading; He indeed is the witness, and He alone is the witness.
Among luminous things He is gold, and among riches He is the jewel. (81)
Among jewels, Kaustubha is the foremost; Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself is the Lord;
likewise, among those worthy of worship, the Śālagrāma is supreme, and among leaves, that Tulasī is so. (82)
Among flowers he is Pārijāta; among sacred fords he is Puṣkara;
among Vaiṣṇavas he is Kumāra; and among the lords of yogis he is Gaṇādhipa. ||83||
He is Skanda among generals, for he is indeed the foremost of archers;
he is the Moon among the stars, for he is indeed Rāma among the wielders of weapons. (84)
Among months he is Mārgaśīrṣa; he is the spring, the best of sacrifices;
among the lords of kings he is Rāma, and among incarnations he is Nārāyaṇa. ||85||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed the Sunday among the days of the week for the blessed; He is the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) among the lunar dates; and He is the Earth among those who possess forgiveness. 86.
He is indeed the mother of offspring, for he is nectar among things to be consumed;
he is said to be clarified butter among products of the cow, and he is the wish-fulfilling tree among trees.
He is Surabhi among the wish-fulfilling cows, Gaṅgā among rivers, Hari among the learned, and he is the form of speech among words, as well as the Praṇava among mantras. (88)
Among all forms of knowledge, he is the supreme knowledge; among grains, he is the grain itself.
Among fruit-bearing trees, he is the Ashvattha; among teachers, he is Kṛṣṇa, the giver of mantras. (89)
He is Kaśyapa among the lords of progeny, and he is indeed Garuḍa among the birds;
he is Ananta among the serpents, and he is indeed the king among men.
Among the Brahman-sages he is Bhrigu; among the divine sages, Nārada;
among the royal sages, Janaka; and among the great sages, Śuka.
Citraratha is the chief of the Gandharvas, and Kapila is that of the Siddhas;
Lomaśa is the chief of the long-lived, and he indeed is the teacher of the wise.
He is Śukra among the best of poets, and he is indeed Śani among the planets;
he is Viśvakarman among artisans, and he is indeed the king of beasts among animals. (93)
Among vehicles he is the vehicle of Śiva; among elephants, he is Airāvata.
Among meters, he is the Gāyatrī; and among scriptures, he is the Veda itself. (94)
Among aquatic beings he is Varuṇa; among Apsarases he is indeed Kṛṣṇa;
among reservoirs of water he is the ocean; and among mountains he is Sumeru. (95)
Among those possessing jewels, Himādri is foremost;
among the natures of goddesses, Rādhikā; and among women, Kṛṣṇa and Śatarūpā.
Among the peaceful he is Kṛṣṇa; among those dear to him he is Sāvitrī; among those of virtuous character he is Suśīlā;
among the Daityas he is Prahlāda; and among the most powerful he is Bali. (97)
The venerable sage Nārāyaṇa is the foremost among the wise and those practicing celibacy;
he is Hanumān among the monkeys, and he is Nara himself among heroes. He is Droṇa among the daughters of the Nāgas and among the Vasus.
To those filled with desire he assumes a form of passion; indeed, he is Rambhā among the lustful women.
He is Goloka, the abode of all worlds and the imperishable realm of all abodes;
He is Vaikuṇṭha, the Lord whose dwelling is Śrī Rāmā.
He is peace within the group of mother-letters; he is indeed delight among beautiful women;
he is dharma within the assembly of witnesses; and he is the twilight within the days.
Among the gods he is Indra; among the Rākṣasas he is Vibhīṣaṇa; he himself is Hari;
among the Rudras he is Kālāgnirudra; and among the Bhairavas he is Saṃhāra.
Among conch shells, he is Pāñcajanya; in the body, he is the head;
and in his own narrations, he is the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Among the Manus he is Svāyaṃbhuva; among the learned he is Vyāsa Mādhava; among the wives of the ancestors he is Svadhā; and among the beloved wives of the fires he is Svāhā.

Among sacrifices, He is the Rājasūya; among the wives of the sacrificers, He is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); among those possessing policy, He is the eloquent minister; and among narrators, He is indeed Hari. 105.
Among those skilled in weapons and missiles, he is Paraśurāma; among divine powers, he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī; and indeed, among vows, he is that very vow. (106)

Among givers he is Indradyumna; among grasses he is Dūrvā; even among plants he is that [Dūrvā]; among blades of grass he is Darbha; and among those devoted to truth and vows, he is Truth itself. (1.07)
In vessels of oil he is but a son; in the circle of enemies, he is that very disease;
in services, he is mere servitude; and among boons, he is the supreme Śrī Hari.
Among the stages of life, he is the householder; among the discerning, he is renunciation.
He is the Sudarśana discus among weapons; he is the skill of those who offer auspicious blessings.
Among sovereign powers, he possesses great knowledge and detachment from pleasures;
among pleasant words, he speaks sweetly; and among gifts, he gives himself away.
In the accumulations, he is indeed the performance of dharma-works and the honoring of ritual acts;
in austere penances, O Kṛṣṇa, he is the fruit which is liberation itself.
Among women, he is constant devotion; among men, he is valor itself;
among the eight supernatural powers, he is the power of irresistible will (prākāmya); and among cities, he is Kāśī, O Kṛṣṇa.
Among cities, he is indeed the city of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
among regions, he is the Vaiṣṇava-kṣetra of Virāṭ; and likewise, among refuges, he is that very one.
Among subtle things, it is the atom; among medicinal herbs and the like, it is the elixir; for physicians, it is the two sons of Aśvinī; and for those who cause destruction, it is despair. 1.14.
Among those who know mantras he is Dhanvantari; among sweet things he is indeed hunger;
among musical modes he is Meghamallāra; and among the attendants he is Śrīdāmā. 1.15.
Among domestic animals he is the cow; among trees he is indeed the sandalwood;
among all that is pure he is the Vaiṣṇava; for he is indeed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (116)
He exists in trees in the form of sprouts, and he indeed exists in all objects; Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is always present within all living beings.
Just as fruits exist in the tree and the sprout exists within the fruit as its seed, so too does He exist as the form of all causes; indeed, there is no other cause whatsoever.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of All, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), is he;
those of wicked intellect, having fallen into the delusion of His Māyā, do not know Him. 11.9.
He is the very self of all beings, indeed the Lord of all embodied creatures, though he is perceived by one of evil intellect who is seized by darkness and deceived by fate.
O King, worship that Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Light;
and by worshipping the Lord of Pārvatī as well, you shall attain both heaven and liberation.
Whoever recites or hears this yoga of manifestation, which brings about both knowledge and discernment, for them Śrī Hari shall become present.
This Mañjulā is the Mañjuṣā (the beautiful casket) of the sages, steadfast in their minds;
she is the Haṃsā (swan) of the Paramahaṃsas, the mental power of the virtuous Hari.
By practicing this, the yogi becomes possessed of the Dharmamegha samādhi;
he becomes filled with the bliss of awakening to the realization and command of all supernatural powers. || 1.24 ||

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty of the Lord and Other Matters, Consisting of Wisdom, Higher Knowledge, and Spiritual Power, as Spoken by Lomaśa to Indradyumna," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, Lakṣmī, and then that great sage Lomaśa bestowed upon Indradyumna the knowledge that had been obscured by the illusory wind.
Lomaśa said: O King, listen to an account that occurred in the past.
Once, Nārada traveled from the world of Satyaloka to the glorious Badarī forest.
In the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, he was then at Viśālā to behold Nārāyaṇa and Nara; he was the son of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu.
While performing austerities and chanting the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
the sage Śrī Nārada beheld him who was named Priyavrata.
The king went near him and bowed with reverence;
the king, having performed many great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Resorting to the virtuous dharma of renunciation, he joyfully bowed to Nārada,
who blazed with the splendor of the sun, by rising from his seat.
He offered water for the feet, a seat, excellent food offerings, and jujube fruits;
then he inquired after his welfare and asked about his conduct in the world.
"O Blessed One, Nārada, tell me of anything wonderful that has been seen or even heard in this age known as Kali-yuga."
Nārada said: Listen to this wonderful and marvelous thing that I have seen;
O Indra among kings, yesterday I went to Śvetadvīpa.
There, having seen a lake of milk adorned with blooming lotuses,
as well as a beautiful, large-eyed maiden on its bank—
O King of kings, having seen that large-eyed maiden, I was struck with wonder and then questioned her, who spoke so sweetly.
"Who are you, noble lady? How are you? Or what business do you have here?
O beautiful one, whose every limb is lovely, tell me that which must be done, O fair one. (1.2)
When she had been addressed by me in this way, she gazed at me with unblinking eyes and remained silent for a moment; meanwhile, my supreme knowledge [arose].
All the Vedas, the Śāstras, and likewise the Saṃhitās have been forgotten; as have all the Yogas, the Śikṣās, the principles of Dharma and Nyāya, the arts, and so forth. (14)
O King, as soon as they all saw it, my daughter was carried away in an instant;
thereupon, I myself was overcome with amazement and agitated by anxiety and grief. (15)
Having gone to her for refuge, I beheld her again with my heart;
at that moment, a divine man was seen within her body.
In the heart of that man also was another, and on his chest yet another,
glorious one with blood-red eyes, resembling twelve suns.
Having seen it thus, three men who had entered the body of the maiden vanished in an instant; I no longer beheld them, and only the maiden remained.
Then I asked that goddess:
"O blessed lady, tell me how my Vedas were lost; explain the cause of their disappearance."
The maiden said: "O Nārada, I am the mother of the Vedas;
I am Sāvitrī, the wife of Brahmā, and your own mother, O Nārada. (1.522.20)
"Having come to me, you have neither honored nor saluted me;
because you do not recognize me, therefore the Vedas have been destroyed by you. (21)
Furthermore, for that twice-born man who does not know the Sāvitrī and the Gāyatrī,
knowledge of the Vedas shall never arise.
Upon the destruction of the mother, there would be the destruction of those sons who serve their mother;
for those sons are devoted to their mother, and they cannot exist anywhere without their mother.
The Vedas do not remain in their repositories; therefore, they have been lost to you.
They no longer perform the worship of their mothers, nor do they even acknowledge their mother.
Those who do not bow to their mother would indeed be fools and dull-witted;
for they neither recognize their mother nor serve her. (25)
Those who are devoid of blessings become dull-witted and characterized by darkness (tamas);
they are those by whom the mother's suffering was caused and she was not nourished. (26)
By that [action], they have been made to bear the burden of the womb and have shown contempt for their mothers;
thus they are deprived of consciousness, as well as insane, impoverished, and likewise suffering. (27)
Sons become anxious, beset by obstacles, and afflicted with disease;
therefore, a mother is indeed ten times more worthy of honor than a father by her son. (28)
When one goes anywhere for the sake of some business, if the mother calls out from behind, that task shall be accomplished successfully; therefore, the mother is most venerable.
The father is the provider of the seed; she who nourished him for nine months, having endured hardship while giving birth, protects him for five years.
She constantly washes away the urine, excrement, and other impurities of the infant;
therefore, the mother who carries the child upon her hip is a hundred times more [beneficial] than that. (3.1)
She who nourishes the belly, the hips, and the heart is always most worthy of honor; such a mother should be served by those who desire what is auspicious. (32)
Then Nārada, having risen and recognized her as his mother, bowed down, honored her, and asked: "Who are these three persons? (33)
The mother said: "He who was seen by me, beautiful and radiant in every limb, is indeed this Veda named Ṛgveda, Nārāyaṇa himself. (34)
Having become fire, he quickly burns away all sins immediately upon being uttered;
this very one, O son, was seen by you within his heart. (35)
That Brahmā of great power exists in the form of the Yajurveda;
and upon his chest is seated he who is pure and radiant.
The Sāmaveda is a great devotee of Bhagavān; that Śaṅkara, when remembered, quickly destroys sins like the sun. (37)
These three great Vedas and likewise those three gods, O son, are present here in this lake consisting of knowledge in my presence. (38)
Having bathed, receive the Vedas and other scriptures, and likewise attain omniscience;
once you have performed the bath in the lake of the Vedas, you will remember your previous birth.
Having spoken thus, my mother then vanished from sight;
I, having performed my ablutions there, obtained [the merit] born of a thousand births.
Having attained knowledge, I have indeed witnessed a marvel here;
I shall relate to you one of my births from a former existence. (41)
In a previous kalpa, you were a king on earth named Bāhudhana,
in the southern, western regions, in Siṃhāraṇya, and in Raivata.
At that time, I was there on the bank of the river Śatruñjitā as a Brahmin named Śāradā, well-versed in the Vedas and their branches of knowledge.
He had a large retinue of servants and possessed abundant grain, wealth, and other assets;
moreover, he was endowed with knowledge and was supremely intelligent. ||44||
Then I reflected in solitude: "What shall I do with this?
Having entrusted all these dualities to my sons, I shall depart. (45)
Having resolved upon austerity and having investigated the elixir of life, Hari is pleased by devotion in the form of service, and the ancestors by the performance of śrāddha rites. (46)
Gods [are won] by sacrifices, people by gifts, women by desires, and an enemy by destruction;
therefore, I have departed from my home toward the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having gone there, where Lomaśa indeed eternally shines upon the bank of the lake, I [saw] Viṣṇu, the ancient Puruṣottama. ||48||
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, was propitiated by me with supreme devotion;
consequently, the Blessed Lord, being pleased, appeared before my very eyes. (49)
Then Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was praised by me in this manner:
"The Supreme among the supreme, the immortal, the ancient, the Lord, the Puruṣa. (1.522.50)
I bow to the peerless Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the supreme master, the controller Hari, who possesses fierce splendor and is most heroic.
I praise you, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the Master Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the son of Kambharā-Lakṣmī, the youthful Gopāla. ||52||
[He is] the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padmā, Prabhā, Padmāvatī,
Pārvatī, Māṇikī, Gaṅgā, Lalitā, and Manasā.
I bow to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the virtuous;
may the renowned Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be my refuge. (54)
He is the Lord of Pradhāna, the Lord of the Abode, the Lord of the Imperishable, and the husband of Satī;
he has a thousand heads, infinite eyes, and possesses infinite arms, thighs, and feet.
He who resides in the milk, resides in the nectar, and dwells in Kuṅkumavāpikā;
he who is the three ages, resides in the three Vedas, and who possesses a white body in the Kṛta age.
Then he became red, then yellow, and again black;
he who exists in many forms and who created the brahmins from his mouth.
I bow to that God who, from his two arms, created the Kṣatriyas in many ways; from his thighs, the Vaiśyas; and from his feet, the Śūdras—He who possesses a universal body.
He holds the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, banner, and trident;
he is adorned with the svastika, golden lines, the śrīvatsa mark, and a necklace.
"May you always be my refuge; may you indeed be the giver of liberation to me"—thus was the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa praised by me.
"Choose a boon," he said repeatedly; I replied, "I desire liberation.
Then my chosen deity said to me, "O sage, you must worship Prakṛti. (61)
By my command, activity leads only to liberation, there is no doubt;
but without my command, cessation will certainly lead to bondage.
Therefore, go for another kalpa; though born this very day, you are indeed [as ancient as] the evening.
"Nāra" is said to mean water, and likewise "nāra" is called knowledge. (63)
He who bestows upon you Viṣṇu, who resides within the self as Nara—you shall indeed always have this name rightly celebrated. (64)
Having been addressed thus, O King, he bowed to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and to the great sage Lomaśa, and then came to your house.
Honored by you and requested for my release, I too said: "Worship Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as your husband and lord. (66)
O King, perform the service of Hari Nārāyaṇa himself;
you have abandoned the kingdom and have gone forth with me.
When we both reached the world of Brahmā, night had become day;
and then the day was created once again by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
There I was born as Nārada; O King, you were remembered by me, and thinking, "This is indeed that very Priyavrata," I have come to see you. (69)
"O King, since I have attained this state of greatness by meditating upon Nārāyaṇa,
therefore you too, O Indra among kings, become devoted to Viṣṇu."
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki— these are the ten.
Those forms of Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Viṣṇu are bestowers of auspiciousness;
they are beautiful stairways for those who desire to obtain a vision of them. (72)
I myself beheld that supreme form of theirs in a former kalpa, at that time, there in the temple of Kumkumavapika.
And here, O beautiful ones, are the two forms of him himself, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, established in the vow of celibacy for the sake of the welfare of the world. (74)
The first form of His is Earth, which sustains and nourishes all things;
the second form is Water; and the third is the radiant energy of Fire. (75)
The fourth is the life-force form, Vāyu; the fifth is that called Vyoman (Space);
the mind, the self, and the inner self—these are the eight forms of Hari.
"Indeed, this entire world is pervaded by Nārāyaṇa.
Thus was that great devotee of the Lord addressed by Nārada.
Having recited the supreme Brahman, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa, as taught by the Self-born One, he—
his mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa— attained the highest liberation.
In this manner, Lomaśa related everything to King Indradyumna—the knowledge centered upon Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (79)
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, the highly fortunate king was indeed delighted;
and he spoke again to Lomaśa, O Sage, regarding nectar that rests within his own self.
"Considering the disciple to be a worthy vessel, cause him to drink the nectar of Brahman.
When this was said, Lomaśa then imparted that knowledge of Brahman to him. (81)

The Vedic, that which is declared in the Sāmaveda, and likewise the profound Ārṣa [tradition], should be grasped by one possessing the eye of knowledge; it is the stable [teaching] that brings light to the heart. 82.
For meditators, there is that supreme Brahman of the Upaniṣads which is to be realized;
having heard it, one who is still stained by latent impressions becomes fit for absorption into Brahman. ||83||
The knot of the heart is severed, and likewise doubt is pierced;
the state of darkness dissolves away, and the riches of happiness increase. (84)
All karmas—whether dry or moist, even those that are firm—are exhausted by that knowledge through which the inner eye, enriched with sovereign power, shines forth. (85)

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Nārada’s Diminution of Knowledge regarding Sāvitrī in Śvetadvīpa, His Subsequent Acquisition of Knowledge of the Vedas and Other Scriptures through Sāvitrī, Its Narration to Priyavrata at Badarī, the Liberation of Priyavrata, and the Fruit of Knowing the Abodes and Incarnations of the Lord," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, during the dialogue between Lomaśa and Indradyumna concerning the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having become single-minded and having established the Supreme Lord within his own self,
[the sage] spoke to the king that supreme knowledge as it was told by Lomaśa.
Listen, having abandoned all other external activities that lead to liberation;
relying upon which, all the sages dwelt in the presence of Brahmā.
Lomaśa said to the king: "Om!
Having remembered and meditated upon my inner self as it has been described, I shall speak; listen to me."
Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Brahman, whose form both shines and does not shine;
to the Brahman-Savitṛ, who is clothed in the Imperishable Brahman and other [manifestations], and who possesses three powers.
He who is established as the divine form in the divine city of Brahman,
the inner controller within both the formless and the formed— that indeed is the Supreme.
The wise ones perceived the Puruṣa within this [body], whose form is excellent, who is beyond comprehension,
whose face is lovely, whose eyes are like those of a monkey, and who is the Supreme Person dwelling within the ages and the planets.
He who shines all around with the crimson luster of the tips of his fingers,
he whom these wise ones here recognize as the one who strikes down the heart and confounds the intellect.
The Brahman-cows perceived him as the Lord, possessing the luster of the moon and the sun,
with a nose like a sesame flower, radiant in human form, and full of splendor.
They entered that golden-haired one, whose vision is unimpeded, who is situated within them on all sides,
who resembles a youth, and who consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Indeed, they worshiped the vessels of Brahmā as the source of supreme excellence;
it was the sixteen-petaled lotus within the heart, resembling the splendor of the supreme Sun.
In his right foot, there are eight artistic designs (kalās), such as the triangle, the svastika, and so forth;
while in his other foot, there are [forms] such as the sky, the half-moon, and the fish.
For this one is the controller of all; beautiful in form, he lies upon every form as it is being formed.
Though existing in a thousand ways, he is likewise without end.
Possessing a form equal [to all], he is manifested in the imperishable world. || 12 ||
All living beings are indeed lords, and moreover, they are liberated;
the root of Brahman is the imperishable, beyond the qualities (guṇātīta),
having attained whose bliss they become blissful.
This very one is the supreme self, the ground of innate bliss. || 13 ||
All living beings are indeed lords, yet they are liberated through the root of Brahman, which is imperishable and transcends the qualities;
having attained its sovereignty, they become masters.
This indeed is the Supreme Self, the ground of innate sovereignty. || 14 ||
All living beings are indeed lords, and moreover, liberated;
they are the root of Brahman, the imperishable which transcends the qualities (guṇas).
Having obtained knowledge of that, the wise become enlightened.
This very one is the supreme Self, the ground of innate consciousness. || 15 ||
All living beings are lords, and moreover, they are liberated;
the imperishable Brahman, which transcends the qualities, is their root.
Having attained its existence, they become truly existent.
This very one is the innate ground of reality, the supreme self. || 16 ||
All living beings are indeed Ishvaras, and furthermore, they are liberated;
the root of Brahman is the imperishable, beyond the gunas,
having attained satisfaction in which they themselves become satisfied.
This very one is the supreme Self, the ground of innate satisfaction. || 17 ||
Like a servant for a wrathful master, I shall do service to the impetuous god, being free from sin.
The noble god, though himself without thought, has made me mindful; the more wise seer impels the skillful man toward wealth. 18.
May the smoke-crested flames of the peaceful one, who possesses the fortune of his dwelling, bring us lordship.
May we, through these invocations, overcome the sin of the ungrasping thief who employs deceitful snares, by means of our own lordly powers. 19.
Those apertures are turned away from the Supreme Self; though their essence is non-different, they appear as distinct objects of expression due to the movement of devotion.
Yet they captivate the knower of That, for they possess the singular power of aesthetic relish (*rasa*), while That itself remains non-different from them.
It is the hearing of the ear, the mind of the mind,
the speech of speech, and indeed the sight of the eye; it is the skin of the skin— such are its powers.
Or is it that of the liberated one, of space, or of Brahman? ||21||
Then, its nature is knowledge and its nature is mind; the experience of knowledge is that very mind.
That itself is intellect, that itself is modesty, and that itself is desire.
Intelligence, likewise desire, intellect, and action. || 22 ||
Even when filled with the mark of the *puṃs* (the male organ), pleasure is not concealed; even when to be enjoyed according to one's will, women are not [defined] by form alone.
Even though that [pleasure] is graspable, there is no injury from the knowledge of the void; and even in the union of separation, there is no contradiction of reality. ||23||
Because it is not born of a mother, there is no group of six sheaths; because it is not a sheath of food, there is no distinction between the built and the unbuilt.
Breath is its own power, for that which is breathless [has no such power].
Space, too, has a nature that is unobstructed. || 24 ||
For one who does not consume food, there is no urination and so forth;
from that, there is no guru and the like, and how indeed could there be sleep?
For one who is eternally serene, how could there be any lack of serenity?
Because of the singular nature of being the most beloved, there is no dependence on another's will. ||25||
Those with golden hair and nails like gold, with teeth as white as jasmine— such beings do not partake in yoga;
they are of the singular form of consciousness, whose very nature is delight.
They always shine forth as one in him. ||26||
Even in the past, this mover was swifter than thought; the wise did not overtake it before the time of its arrival.
Being most excellent among the wise, it surpasses others in its swiftness.
The Lord abides both in the unmanifested and in the manifested. ||27||
In its vicinity there is no fear whatsoever,
nor is there anything else there that is unprecedented;
having crossed both the states of the individual soul and the illusory power of the Lord.
Having transcended the smoky stage, he rejoices together with those who are united with him. ||28||
Having known that adorable Lord, who is difficult to be heard of even by many,
whom many do not understand even while hearing— Him who is the Knower of all that is to be governed.
Having realized that, he attains ultimate peace. ||29||
That ancient God, difficult to perceive, entered into the hidden, placed within the cave, and dwelling in the abyss— [one perceives Him] through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self.
Having understood this, the wise man abandons both merit and sin.
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, lighter than the lightest, and heavier than the heaviest—
him, free from action, one who has shaken off all evil beholds.
His being was completely filled by the grace of Hari. ||3 1 ||
That Supreme Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
he alone whom this Self chooses is able to attain Him, and for him the Supreme Self reveals His own form. 32.
Neither white nor black, free from passion, that is the controller, eternal, boundless,
beginningless, the supreme Brahman, the fixed Hari.
Having realized that, one is liberated from the jaws of death. || 33 ||
He exists as Brahman, as the liberated, as the Lord, as the Vasus, as the Unmanifest, as the individual soul, and as the effect;
nevertheless, the inner self is not stained, for it possesses the power of being unstained and acts as a mere reflection.
Having mastery as his companion, he is the inner self of all beings; he unfolds the seed, the primary matter (pradhāna), which possesses manifold forms.
Those who perceive him within themselves are liberated; for them there is eternal peace, but not for others. (35)

He is the eternal among the eternals, the consciousness of the conscious, the one who ordains the destinies of the many; those who perceive Him abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others. (36)
Before that [Self], the sun does not shine; neither does the moon, nor do the lightnings, much less this fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. That is the Reality. ||37||
Out of fear of Him, the sun shines in this world of Aśvattha, and fire and wind also blow;
even the lords sustain the cosmic egg out of fear of Him. Those who know Him go to that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (38)

The wise person who realizes that beloved deity—who is free from darkness, radiant, the embodiment of grace, shining with virtue, and whose nature is eternal consciousness—attains omniscience like Him through His grace. (39)

The liberated perceive Him who is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, devoid of eyes or ears, and without hands or feet; eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and the painless source of all effects. 1.523.40.
As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web],
as plants arise from the earth,
and as hair and body-hair grow from a living man; so does [the Self] manifest.
In this way, the universe arises here from the Supreme Lord. ||41||
The Supreme Brahman alone is this immortal reality in the east; the Supreme Brahman is in the west, in the south, and in the north;
the all-pervading Brahman is below and above as well. Thus is the nature of Brahman.
This entire universe is pervaded by the Supreme Brahman. ||42||
It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other senses, nor by austerity or ritual action;
rather, one whose being is purified through the clarity of knowledge beholds it while meditating.
That divine form is vast and of inconceivable nature;
it shines forth as subtler than the subtle.
It is far, yet far beyond; it is here, and yet near at hand.
While they were looking right here, it was placed within the cave.
That Supreme Self is attained through truth, austerity, knowledge of the Great Self, and constant celibacy;
for He is indeed pure and of divine form within His own essential nature.
That which ascetics, whose defects have been exhausted, behold. ||45||
When the seer beholds the golden-hued Creator, the Puruṣa who is the further shore of Brahman,
then the knower, having abandoned both white and black, [attains liberation].
One who is free from ignorance attains equality with Kṛṣṇa. ||46||
The embodied soul, though eternally immersed in the body,
becomes deluded and falls into grief when perceivable through illusion;
yet, when he beholds his own Self as all-pervading, [he is liberated].
And then the self is born free from sorrow. ||47||
Those two, O Sumitrā, resort to a single tree; they encourage one another in their respective tasks.
One, being impatient, eats the sweet fruit with greed, while the other, being patient and well-satisfied, gives it away. (48)
Just as rivers reach the state of the ocean after casting off their distinct designations and forms,
so too does one who is devoid of the known, the designation, and the form [attain liberation].
One goes beyond the perishable to the divine Person. ||49||
He who knows the Supreme Brahman becomes Brahman himself; he does not return to wander, dragged by karma.
Just as one abandons heat when it causes distress, so too, when the knots of the heart are severed, one is abandoned for the sake of immortality.

And he who here has attained eternal awakening, shining within this body in the cave of the heart—he, residing therein, is the creator of the universe and the destroyer of all; distinct from these, he dwells in the divine realm.
The wise know it, and we too know it; for in the absence of this knowledge, a great fall would have occurred.
Through the realization of that very [reality], the wise became immortal, while others indeed fell into suffering born of ignorance.
Thus one should know the greatness of the Supreme Self;
for it has neither increase through actions nor diminution.
He alone is the knower of the path who shall go to that abode.
By taking refuge in that, one is not defiled by evil karmas. ||5.3||
Everything that exists within the imperishable Brahman is likewise attached to the multitude of liberated souls;
indeed, all that has entered into the Lords is that very same [Brahman].
Likewise, others [are] in the state of having become living beings. ||54||
That which exists in the Imperishable (akṣara) becomes indeed that alone;
likewise, it is truly in the variegated (śabala) and the stainless (nirañjana),
in the golden one called the Great Viṣṇu, and in Viṣṇu.
And even while Rudra was reigning as Virāja. ||55||
He shines here upon the seven levels of the eightfold manifestations beginning with *prakṛti*;
here on this earth, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa reigns.
The Lord, knowing him to be immortal, said: "Go to Vraja."
For from that which is characterized by subtle consciousness and matter, that which is characterized by gross consciousness and matter is indeed produced,
because of the non-difference between the material cause and its effect.
All reality is indeed the one supreme Brahman alone. ||57||
A certain power of that Supreme Self, who descends in fullness, receives the name "Vyūha"; that same power, becoming diminished in degree, is the "Vibhava" incarnation.
It consists of forms such as the primary [state] of full manifestation, immersion, and the secondary.
Through union with this or that, one attains its essential nature; for in that state, one enters into a condition of being both merged and unmerged.
By the worship of the Supreme Self, they attain the Supreme Lord and reach supreme liberation; therefore, that is the truth.
The support of liberation, the pervasive consciousness of the Supreme Brahman, the imperishable,
the support of all, the body of the Supreme Brahman— the abode wherein He resides.
That very same imperishable abode of Brahman, consisting of the splendor of Hari, exists;
for that state is indeed attained through the Veda, austerity, and the practice of celibacy.
The body of Hari is both bodiless and embodied, both manifest and unmanifest;
it is pure, eternal, and the illuminator of Māyā and the rest.
The Supreme Reality exists as the Self, which dwells in truth, consciousness, and bliss, transcends birth, death, and old age, and is united with Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 6.3.
Worship Hari, the eternal overseer, who is non-different from the radiant splendor of the Supreme Brahman and who dwells beyond the further shore of the quality of passion (rajas).
Even above the supreme golden casket, there is the partless, radiant light of lights; worship Hari, the presiding lord therein. 65.
Just as the individual hairs on a cow's body possess non-differentiated self-power,
so too there is neither division nor abandonment [of parts], for there is a single essence, like that of the Supreme Lord.
Worship Śrī Hari, who resides there, whose omniscience depends on the remainder;
worship Hari there, who is composed of light and has entered the Supreme Brahman. ||67||
O King, worship Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who dwells there in that eternal realm where the liberated ones, free from beginning and eternal, reside. 6.8
Thus, having worshipped Him who dwells in the abode of syllables, who resides in the supreme abode, and who is Supreme, many have attained the state of equanimity; therefore, worship Him always.
He who is the bridge of all dharmas, whose ground is the imperishable Brahman—knowing Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to be situated there, worship Him always. (1.523.70)
He who is devoid of reverence for this [teaching] and is destitute of devotion and service—being impure and entangled in the cycle of worldly existence—he shall not attain Him. ||71||
He who possesses direct experience of that Nārāyaṇa attains His abode, and from there he is not born again. ||72||
He whose strength is devotion and whose knowledge likewise provides nourishment, having mounted the chariot of service to the guru, attains the abode of Śrī Hari. (73)
The Lords are superior to living beings, and the Imperishable is superior to the Lords;
having known that which is more beloved than the Imperishable, one shall attain that abode. //74//
The entire instruction culminates in the severing of the knot of the heart;
having attained the knot of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, go to the supreme state. (75)
"O others, whoever exists in you, in me, and in others—worship him with reverence;
for he who perceives him through differentiation falls into the snares of death. (76)
Having known that [Self] within with the heart and the inner eye as devoid of manifoldness,
and having slain death produced by manifold states of being, go to the supreme state.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations to Him!
O King, if you constantly recite this mantra, He will lead you to the further shore. (78)
For one whose body is falling away, no further bondage remains. For you, who are thus unbound and liberated, what remains here?
"Rooted above and with branches spreading below is this great tree, the Aśvattha.
Abandoning it, go to Hari—the imperishable Brahman, the immortal—so that you may behold Him."
Worship that Śrī Hari, out of fear of whom all splendors shine forth according to their laws, and by whom the lords have attained their lordship. 81.
Abandoning the desires residing in your heart, take refuge here in Kṛṣṇa;
enjoy the nectar of supreme bliss from Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||82||
For those in whom truth, austerity, celibacy, and service are firmly established, there exists the world of Brahmā—those in whom there is neither crookedness nor falsehood. (83)
O King, there are two kinds of knowledge in every respect: the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).
By the higher [knowledge], O Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa is attained in the imperishable state.
All other words besides those, by which Brahman is not attained, belong to those who indeed always utter speech that is most dear to the Supreme Self. (85)
He who knows the Supreme Brahman, serves it, and worships it, attains the meritorious state of Brahmā and enters into the service of the glorious Supreme Self. (86)
In the intermediate state between waking and dreaming, which possesses the supreme glory of the three states,
he enjoys all desires mingled with Brahman.
Know that food, life-breath, mind, knowledge, and bliss are He;
worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as the Self and the Inner Self. (88)
O King, by what joy is one filled through service to the son of Kambharā? One is enriched by cows through service to the young cowherds. (89)
Go to that bliss of Hari, whom neither speech nor mind can even make an object; from Him, you shall have no fear whatsoever.
From knowledge, sacrifices arise and ritual actions also come into being;
when offered to the glorious Kṛṣṇa, they result in supreme satisfaction. 9.1
He who knows the supreme Brahman and does not falter because of that, having cast off the evil of illusion (māyā), enjoys the delights of Brahman. ||92||
He indeed draws toward himself the virtuous one who speaks of Kṛṣṇa as virtuous, who meditates upon Him as virtuous,
and likewise serves Him as virtuous— the state of the virtuous.
For he, having created that very [universe], entered into it; he is higher than the high.
Just as truth is [perceived] through untruth, by him [all] is understood as "truth" alone. (94)
Through him, the unmanifest state and the well-performed [merit] are understood;
he, by means of the Imperishable (akṣara) and the Puruṣa, brought forth many cosmic eggs.
By union with that Supreme Self, one should understand that truth and merit reside within them, just as they do in the Imperishable; having known this, one shall attain liberation. ||96||
O King, in ancient times the Blessed One was indeed all that exists; from him, the entire reality, whose true nature is existence, was manifested.
He is the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa), the bestower of all flavors.
Having obtained its flavor, they become blissful. ||97||
By his bliss indeed the worlds become free from fear; that state where neither mind nor speech reaches—worship that Keśava. 98.
From him these beings are born, and by that Lord they live;
in him alone they dissolve—go to that eternal dissolution.
The Supreme Self, of divine form, was to be meditated upon in the house in ancient times; having fashioned a second [image], He dwelt there—worship Him.
All that is stationary and all that moves shines with wisdom as its eye;
worship Mādhava, who dwells within that wisdom and is its very eye. 101.
Worship with faith and austerity the peaceful, all-pervading Brahman— the supreme Ka, Kha, and Hari— the divine, unswerving leader who shines with splendor.
Worship Hari, who dwells within the divine, whose inner self is the essence of the bright fortnight,
who resides in the months of the northern solstice, and who abides within the year.
Worship Him who resides within the sun, whose inner self is the moon,
who bestows the light of lightning, and who dwells within the waters as Varuṇa.
The inner Indra is situated within Prajāpati, residing in Virāj;
it is the heart of Rudra, abiding in Viṣṇu, and established in Mahāviṣṇu.
Worship Him who abides in the stainless, who is endowed with diversity, and who is the absolute;
having become one who has reached the imperishable Brahman, always worship that Supreme Person.
One should meditate upon the Lord Hari, the bestower of the fruits of all gifts, who abides in the smoky night,
who dwells within the dark fortnight, and who moves during the southern solstice.
O King, always worship Him who dwells within the year, who dwells in the ancestors, who moves through the sky,
who dwells in the moon, and who resides in the protector of creatures.
Worship Śrī Hari, who dwells in the wind, who resides in the clouds, who abides in the mist, who exists within the seed, who takes the form of all effects, and who is all-pervading. 109.
Worship Hari among the Brahmins and others who are mines of delightful qualities;
worship Hari among the cows and others who are mines of objects worthy of compassion.
This god is one whose evil has been destroyed, free from old age and death;
he is devoid of sorrow, exempt from hunger and thirst, and the ordainer of true desires. (111)
Worship that Lord who is of your own nature, equal to you, and like unto you;
through His form you shall attain perfection, so worship Him accordingly.
Worship Him who is of such a nature—Him who, by His own form, is eternally playing, dancing, chanting, gladdening [the world], and remembering [all beings]. 11.3.
Without his devotee he finds no delight; therefore, he fashioned him as a second [self]. Always worship him who is pervaded by you, residing within your very heart.
Therefore, O King, this very Self must be seen by you with the eye situated in the heart;
it must be heard with the ear situated in the heart, and it must be reflected upon with divine luster.
One should determine his nature with the intellect and never abandon him;
thus, behold the eternal Kṛṣṇa with the state of being his very self. 1.16
All beings are established in Him; worship Him. Worship Him who is in the earth, in water, in fire, in air, and in space. 1.17
Worship Keśava, whose bodies these are, and who dwells within the body; worship Keśava, who is the Self, the Reality, and the Archetype. 1.18
Since all joys are equal and since all living beings are made joyful by Him, worship Nārāyaṇa, who is the fulfillment of all desires, the Great Bliss, and the Perfect One. 1.19
Abandoning desires, establish Hari within your heart with devotion; O King, recognize Him as truly present, go to Him for refuge, and worship Him.
There is nothing unattained by you here that remains to be attained;
this very supreme Brahma-knowledge, which bestows liberation, has been taught to you.
Then this king, being fully satisfied, beheld within his own self Janārdana, the supreme divine Person, the Highest of Men.
The array of conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, trident, and so forth;
Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Padmā, Pārvatī, and Māṇikīśvara.
And having beheld that Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in his heart— He who is served by all the female attendants as well as by the male associates— 1.24.
By His will, and through the grace of Lomaśa and the power of supreme knowledge, he beheld that Lord of Śrī even outside [the body].
A divine and exceedingly beautiful celestial chariot descended from the sky,
consecrated by a messenger of the gods at the command of Brahmā.
The divine messenger said: "Come, come, O King, to this celestial chariot!
I shall truly lead you to the world of the illustrious Parameṣṭhin."
And Indradyumna said to him: "I have no need for truth;
I shall certainly go to the feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
"By the grace of Lomaśa, [you shall attain] the supreme abode beyond the syllable.
Having been addressed thus, that messenger of the gods departed for the world of Brahmā.
Indradyumna ceased [his questioning] in the presence of Lomaśa;
and Lomaśa gave him an auspicious seat of grass on the shore of the lake.
Near the Kadamba tree, at the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
the king bathed, meditated upon Hari, and worshipped Nārāyaṇa.
Having honored Lomaśa and bowed to the sages in that hermitage,
he offered fruits and other provisions to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having offered [the food] there to his guru, he ate and drank water;
then, remembering Hari, he obtained a blissful yogic sleep during the night.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Remembrance of the Self through the Upaniṣadic Supreme Knowledge of Brahman as instructed by Sage Lomaśa to Indradyumna," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to the auspicious story of Lomaśa.
