Having risen in the morning and performed his daily rites, the king [set out] toward his preceptor.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he went for the purpose of beholding Him; joined by his preceptor with blessings, he questioned the sage Lomaśa. || 2 ||
O Blessed One, you are the giver of liberation, transcendent beyond illusion and having conquered the senses;
just as you abide in your own abode, so too do you appear here before our very eyes.
Tell me, O Lord: in the abode of the Blessed One there is no time; therefore, what is it that, being momentary in nature, regulates the various modes of eternal service? || 4 ||
"How is the daily ritual practice performed by the devotees?"—having been asked this, O King, Lomaśa spoke to the monarch. (5)
By the rays of the form of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, which are endowed with beautiful luster and spread forth in various forms, the [six] periods beginning with dawn exist at all times.
Those who know it perceive Him through His rays in the morning, at midday, and in the evening;
and there, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa accepts their service.
Sleep is a state of dissolution within the form; waking is service to the servant.
Day is the manifestation of white light, and twilight is the manifestation of red light.
Upon seeing His form, dark as a cloud, there is stability [in the heart] and the realization that it is night;
likewise, even in Goloka, all activities are carried out by the rays of Kṛṣṇa.

Likewise, even in Vaikuṇṭha, there are those who are overwhelmed by the splendor of Nārāyaṇa; and in the supreme abode of Akṣara, they are overwhelmed by the radiance of the Supreme Brahman and other such lights.
Thus, O Indradyumna, this which was told to you has been heard from those very liberated ones who have attained that state; what else do you wish to ask?
Then, O Lakṣmī, Indradyumna questioned the sage Lomaśa: "Does Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa desire to manifest here in this sacred field? (12)
At that time, does he remain within his mother’s womb or not? Is his body composed of the material elements, or is it of a different nature altogether? (1.3)
"Sever the doubt that has arisen in me and show compassion for this worldly matter.
Lomaśa replied, "O royal sage, [listen] regarding Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul... (14)
Whenever there is a manifestation of Nārāyaṇa’s various incarnations and so forth during the process of creation, it occurs according to the womb [of his mother]. || 15 ||
Hari always commands the wind situated within the womb:
"You must remain within the womb of the belly together with the water for this long."
Just as a pregnant woman is indeed visible from the outside,
so you should make her reach the state of having her womb distended, in whatever time it takes.
In whatever place and of whatever kind a specific time is required, having demonstrated that for so long, there is also the further development of the embryo. (18)
And at the time of birth, the emergence of the wind and water from the womb must be shown there according to worldly custom. || 1.9 ||
At that time, remaining there, I shall see it unobserved by others,
just as the form of an infant born from the womb is seen.
Only a mere appearance must be made for those who are immersed in the waters of the womb;
for those whose eyes are veiled by illusion, there is no access to me here.
Those with divine vision perceive my subtle, divine creation;
those with gross vision perceive it as a child born from a womb. ||22||
In this very way, those born from improper origins (ayonija) are indeed liberated;
for that [liberating] knowledge does not reside in the mother and father, since they are merely fond of pleasure.
In my birth, their appearance occurred in the very manner of Kāmadeva; yet for us two who were free from desire, that divine vision of me truly happened in an instant.
Therefore, O Vāyu, there is no entry into a womb for me, nor any reliance upon the elements;
nor is there dwelling in a fetal chamber, nor indeed any emergence from the birth canal.
I have no state of childhood, nor indeed do I have both birth and death;
for my body is not composed of the elements, yet show it to be so.
Thus does the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa command;
O King, in accordance with that, Vāyu displays his creative power.
For that Hari who is eternally satisfied, food and such worldly things do not exist at all; yet his devotees offer them with sincere devotion. (28)
Whatever object of enjoyment is dear to oneself and pleasing to the mind, that should be offered to Him before being consumed; this is the eternal law. (29)
Thus, service performed through devotion bestows satisfaction upon Him who is eternally satisfied;
for in ancient times, a boon was granted to Lakṣmī by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"Regarding what has been offered there, how can it ever become deficient?
Hari said: 'It is consumed by me; it shall increase and never go to waste. (31)
In whatever manner I consume it, in that very way it increases;
the insentient attains sentience and reaches a divine state. (32)
Having attained clarity, it then reaches full bloom;
it becomes ever new, imbued with aesthetic flavor, and bestowing auspiciousness. (33)
Those with divine vision perceive [this], while those with external vision do not;
this, O King, has been told as the means for increasing the food offering (naivedya).
O King, for those things offered to Kṛṣṇa in this manner, there is no decrease anywhere; on the contrary, everything increases. What else do you wish to hear? 35.
Then Indradyumna asked Lomaśa, the true guru of Hari:
"Why is it that even during the summer season, when the sun has reached its zenith," [you remain thus?].
"Why indeed do you not build a beautiful house for the purpose of dwelling?
Lomaśa said to that king, "I am short-lived in every respect. (37)
For whose sake should a dwelling be built, since life is impermanent?
If life were eternal and long-lasting, one might resort to a home. (38)
The king said: "It is heard that you are long-lived among all;
therefore, I have come here with the desire to behold you. (39)
Lomaśa then said: "Listen, O King, I shall tell you that:
with the arrival of every kalpa, a single hair of mine perishes. (1.524.40)
"In the absence of hair on my chest, my destruction will come to pass;
three hundred and sixty-five thousand [years] have passed for me. (41)
O King, eons have indeed passed there before my eyes, the Creator’s vision;
from my navel up to my throat, O King, hairs still remain upon me.
Those indeed amount to three hundred and fifty-six thousand;
and there are additionally three hundred and sixty-five thousand. (43)
Having dwelt for that many kalpas within the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), thereafter I shall go to the supreme world; indeed, what use have I for a home?
Behold here on my body, below the knee,
a space one finger-breadth wide that has become hairless and remains so for as long as an eon, rivaling [the perfection of] the kalpa.
Life is certainly not permanent; it is known even from the falling out of a hair.
For that reason, O Lord of the Earth, I do not build a house.
The king said: "O Sage, what action was performed by you in the past? What kind of austerity or gift was given, by which such a long life as this has been obtained? (47)
Lomaśa then said: "Listen, O King, for a long time to my story.
In a former creation, I was a Śūdra afflicted by poverty. (48)
Performing service at that time, I went to the Badarī forest;
emaciated by hunger and afflicted by thirst, I beheld Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person. (49)
Having offered water and lotus flowers and performed the ritual worship,
he then completed the pūjā and set out upon the path of the mountain.
Then, having met death from cold and hunger in the house of a brahmin, I became one who remembers my past lives; therefore, I maintain silence in every way.
"My father, filled with great joy, gave me the name Īśāna;
even when urged by others, I did not speak anything at all. (52)
Having attained supreme detachment upon seeing the condition of worldly existence, my father employed these words as a medicine for the sake of illumination. (53)
Therefore, laughter arises within me toward those people who have performed mantras, even as I dwell with a spirit of devotion in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ. (54)
Adopting the practice of gathering grains and living upon the bare necessities of life, I worship the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with a concentrated mind.
With oranges, jujubes, vegetables, cucumbers, fruits, and leaves, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa then became manifest before my eyes. (56)
He said, “I am well-pleased; choose a boon, O observer of noble vows.
Thereupon, I requested: “Make me free from old age and death. (57)
Kṛṣṇa said: "Indeed, immortality cannot belong to anyone in the mortal world;
therefore, set a limit for your life, and I shall grant that to you. (58)
Then Hari was addressed: "In every kalpa, let there be the falling out of my body hair from the navel down to the throat. (59)
"Let my lifespan be exactly one hundred and ten years, during which time this piercing [of the heart] shall dissolve; thereafter, I shall go to your abode."
"So be it," Hari said, and then he vanished from sight.
From that time forward, right here near Kuṅkumavāpikā, [the place became sacred].
I dwell in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara for such a duration; my long life is the fruit of my service to Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (62)
Thousands of dissolutions of the earths have been witnessed here during my life;
at the time of dissolution, I go to Vaikuṇṭha, which is situated upon the waters.
Furthermore, at the end of the period of the veil of fire, during the re-creation,
I shall come to the earth and dwell in the hermitage of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Likewise, the Brahmin who is faithful to his wife, and the devoted wife who is dear to him—those two shall live long, provided they do not pluck out each other's hair. (65)
Likewise, Śrī Kambharā and Lakṣmī, Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa,
and the two Brahmins— these six became long-lived, having caused their respective hair and sins to fall away.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, the Lord of Akṣara, is born as their young son in their home at every creation and in every kalpa.
I worship that very Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa at all times;
having observed their lifespan, pride no longer exists within me. (68)
I worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; you too, worship that Hari.
For the world, and for the devotee of Hari, nothing desired is difficult to attain. (69)
"Thus, O Indradyumna, has my history been told to you;
you have become renowned in the world, so go now to the imperishable abode of Hari."
Then Indradyumna spoke regarding the liberation from the curse for all—
the release of the tortoise, the owl, the vulture, the sage, the crane, and Mārkaṇḍeya.
"Tell me, O learned one, when will this come to pass? You are omniscient, just like Hari.
Then Lomaśa replied: "When [one worships] Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa... (72)
And they shall all worship [him] preceded by the reception of the mantra;
then, indeed, liberation will occur here in this sacred field, there is no doubt. (73)
Indradyumna, however, repeatedly remembered them all as those who had been his benefactors;
and they, possessing the memory of their former births and able to assume any form at will, arrived there.
Having bowed down, they worshipped Lomaśa and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
they honored Kambharā-Lakṣmī while worshipping Gopālakṛṣṇa.
On the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the sage Lomaśa offered a welcome and indeed bestowed the mantra of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord!
Thus they chanted as they remained there in the sinless hermitage of Lomaśa. (77)
Having bathed here at Aśvapaṭṭasara and gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā,
they drank the water and chanted mantras day and night.
Through the compassion of Lomaśa, their latent impressions (vāsanā) dissolved;
by the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they became liberated.
The sage Kacchapa was in the region of Kaccha at Lake Nārāyaṇa;
the sage Ghūka was in the sacred field of Śrī Hāṭakeśa on the bank of the Nāga river.
Gṛdhra-ṛṣi [resides] on the glorious Raivata mountain at the site of Dattātreya’s penance;
Bakara-ṛṣi [resides] in the field of the glorious Somanātha near the ocean. 8–1.
Mārkaṇḍeya and others dwell in the forest on the ground that is dark as a palm tree;
they are divine, long-lived, and always able to assume any form at will.
They will exist in every kalpa for the sake of the welfare of the world;
all of them come to Raivata on the full moon of Kārttika every year.
For the purpose of circumambulating the gods and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
I, Lomaśa, shall indeed go there for five days.
Uttering the noble name "Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," they indeed traverse the mountain;
the merit of their treading upon the earth [is as follows].
He would be born; indeed, I say that I am Lomaśa.
Then Hari himself was pleased by the devotion of King Indradyumna, through his supreme faith and by the grace of Lomaśa.
He bestowed upon his heart a supreme, divine vision free from all obscuration;
he beheld the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa within his heart.
Having placed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) upon Lomaśa and having merged his own self into the Supreme Self, he desires to depart by way of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). ||88||
Then, a celestial chariot arrived, adorned with divine syllables and resplendent like millions upon millions of suns; the king ascended it. (89)
Having bowed to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he went to the imperishable abode of Brahmā;
Lomaśa performed the ritual water-offerings and other rites for him according to the prescribed rules.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you the account of the origin of the name Lomaśa, arising from the shedding of body hair, and the narrative of the long-lived Ṛṣi Lomaśa. 91.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Familiarity with the Knowledge of Time in the Abode of the Lord within the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Section of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Divinity in Taking Birth, the Fulfillment in the Naivedya Offering, the Previous History of Lomaśa, and the Long-term Residence in Saurāṣṭra and Other Places by Mārkaṇḍeya and Other Long-lived Sages. || 524 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, a king renowned by the name Aśvaśiras arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa in the sacred field of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
The highly effulgent Kapila arrived for the purpose of seeing him;
Aśvaśiras then questioned that sage Kapila regarding his doubt.
"Is liberation attained through action or through knowledge? Speak the definitive conclusion.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the auspicious conclusion which the sage Kapila declared. (3)
Out of a desire for the welfare of householders engaged in action, I shall proclaim that whatever deed an embodied being performs, whether it be good or evil.
Having surrendered everything to Nārāyaṇa, one is not tainted even while acting;
listen, O Brahmin, to the account of Saṃyamana, who was born in the lineage of Atri.
Devoted to asceticism, he went to the Dharmāraṇya forest in the morning to bathe in the Bhāgīrathī river; there he saw a herd of deer standing.
A hunter named Niṣṭhuraka, greedy and equipped with a bow,
arrived at the bank desiring to kill, having strung it with an arrow.
Seeing that bow, the brahmin restrained the hunter who was devoted to the hunt, saying: "O gentle one, do not commit this slaughter of living beings."
Having heard this, the hunter laughed and said to that best of sages:
"Indeed, I do not harm living beings; I do not kill them under any circumstances. (9)
But this Supreme Self plays with the elements through His own Māyā;
His Māyā is indeed birth, nourishment, and death in their proper sequence.
For we are indeed merely occasional instruments for living beings there;
O Brahmā, the sense of ego must never be cultivated by those seeking liberation.
If one engages in this solely for the sake of maintaining the journey of life, one is not defiled;
however, he in whom egoism persists does not attain the state of a true sage.
"O twice-born one, having abandoned my ego, I shall catch a single deer. Having heard this, that lord of brahmins forbade the hunter.
Violence is evil in every respect; never commit such an act.
There are fruits, roots, leaves, and water. (14)
Use grains and vegetable leaves for your sustenance;
if you can maintain your journey without violence, do not harm living beings in vain.
"The thought 'I must not act with egoism' dwells in your speech, but not in your own self; for you are a devourer of deer for the sake of your own interest. (16)
Everyone offers instruction on the avoidance of pride,
yet they themselves do not abandon pride, each separately in speech and in mind.
They say one thing, they do another, they deceive others with one thing, and they live by another; though skilled in their own interests, having attained their personal ends, they remain so.
They indeed become distant after having destroyed their enemies. || 18 ||
The hunter said: "O Sage, I am not a deceiver seeking my own self-interest.
Conduct an examination of me in this matter; it shall indeed become evident before your very eyes. (19)
"Make a net of clods of earth and bring fire beneath it;
let a great heap of dry wood burn there intensely."
When the brahmin had done so, the fire indeed blazed up intensely;
flames issued forth through the windows and by the thousands through the lattice-work.
When that iron net then shone like fire, red with blood,
the hunter, having resorted to his own yogic power, [cast off] his body.
He assumed the form of fire, possessing a mass of heat like the sun;
yet the fire in front of him became devoid of its brilliance.
Rising up, that hunter sat down upon the net;
just as fire is not burned by fire itself, so it was with him.
The hunter was indeed not burned by the fire produced from the wood;
likewise, the self-restrained Brahmin and others were filled with wonder. (25)
They asked, "Who are you? Tell us! He replied, "I am the consumer of oblations (Agni).
I am self-existent; there is no violence on my part, for embodied beings are cooked within me."
Abandoning even the intellect, I act according to my own true nature;
my ego has been destroyed through austerity joined with knowledge. (27)
And when the ego-sense has perished, one is no longer stained by actions;
the ego-sense is the root, and the sense of "mine" is called its trunk. (28)
Attachment, aversion, pride, greed, and delusion are its branches; actions are its leaves, and tasting is its constant sap. (29)
The flower is called "initiation," and the fruit is likewise sweet happiness;
however, that which is unpleasant becomes suffering, which embodied beings always experience. ||1.525.30||
"Pour water at the base of the fire, from which place the flames are emerging.
Being thus addressed, the Brahmin quickly [placed] a jar full of water there.
When the fire suddenly cast itself down and was extinguished upon the ground,
all its flames were destroyed on every side due to the destruction of their very root.
The hunter said to that brahmin: "This is indeed a manifest illustration:
when the root is destroyed, the destruction of the entire tree follows. (33)
If pride, which is the root [of bondage], has been destroyed for those who have performed their actions, then one is never stained by either sin or merit. (34)
O best of beings, in this [body] the fire blazes with many branches;
yet when the root is destroyed, it is extinguished, and so am I, always possessed of karma. (35)
The self, having taken recourse to the body and assumed its physical nature, is possessed by hunger and thirst; it engages in activity by eating and drinking. (36)
Performing all actions while abandoning pride, which is the cause of attachment, and being united with the inner self, one who acts does not come to grief. ||37||
Then the hunter said to the brahmin, "O best of the twice-born, touch a clod of earth.
The clod was hot and burning; it was recognized and then released by the brahmin. (38)
Then that hunter touched him, yet no burning sensation arose;
the hunter then said to him, "The refinements [of the body] arise from egoism. (39)
Just as the impressions produced by fire in a clod of earth act as burners,
so long as these impressions persist in the person, they are burned in every way.
As long as such formative impressions of conceit persist within embodied beings, so long are they stained by merit and demerit; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, pride and the formative predispositions (saṃskāras) should be abandoned through austerity, as well as through devotion to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, yoga, and the practice of meditation. ||42||
"One who possesses devotion that offers everything is not stained by actions.
When this was said, O Brahmin, [a voice] from the sky above the hunter spoke.
A shower of flowers fell slightly upon the brahmin;
then the hunter killed that one deer at that time as well.
The Brahmin said, "Where is the one in the form of a deer going? Show me!
The hunter then conjured a celestial chariot born of the heavenly realm.
Then that best of brahmins beheld great celestial chariots, moving at will, filled with many jewels, and most excellent.
Among them, the brahmin saw Niṣṭhuraka, who was greedy, present among all of them, and capable of assuming any form at will. 47.
And having beheld a deer that had attained multiple bodies through yoga, perfected by the contemplation of non-duality, possessing a divine form, and being of the nature of a god; ||48||
Upon seeing this, the Brahmin Saṃyamana was filled with joy;
others there as well became free from the egoism of identifying with the body. 49.
Thus it should be understood that even while performing actions characteristic of one's own nature,
there is a state of non-attachment, free from the taint of sin or merit.
Such a one never creates for himself any bondage whatsoever,
just as the divine Nārāyaṇa is untainted and a mere substance.

Whether performing, receiving, causing others to perform, or causing others to receive—being free from attachment—it not only leads to the attainment of its own state, but renders that [action] devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). //52//
Likewise, the Self, being devoid of illusion (māyā), neither acts nor is it stained;
even that which is obtained, enjoyed, or insentient matter, it renders as truly divine. //53//
Having realized that [the Self] is indeed unstained, free from bondage, and established in liberation,
the self-controlled Brahmin departed for his own hermitage.
And Kapila spoke thus again to King Aśvaśiras:
"Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too [should worship] the Lord, the God Nārāyaṇa. (55)
Worshiping the Lord within your very own self, that is, within your own body, behold:
you will quickly become untainted, just as the hunter did in the past.
Having heard the words of Kapila, that auspicious King Aśvaśiras understood that liberation for those engaged in action comes through action dedicated to Kṛṣṇa.
Then, at that very moment, the great sage Jaigīṣavya,
whose lifespan lasts for fifty kalpas, arrived there at Lomaśa’s auspicious hermitage.
Then those sages offered mutual greetings to one another and engaged in auspicious conversation concerning the worlds of heaven and other realms. (59)
After all the sages had taken their seats, Aśvaśiras bowed to Kapila and, having prostrated before him, questioned him in the midst of them all.
"How may one propitiate the supreme god Hari Nārāyaṇa?
Kapila said, "O King, indeed, the Nārāyaṇas are infinite. (61)
"O King, it is indeed through the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa that these things come to pass. Who is this teacher, Nārāyaṇa, who is being spoken of by you? (62)
"O King, we two are indeed Nārāyaṇas, standing here before your very eyes.
Having heard this, Aśvaśiras spoke to those two brahmins.
"In former times, I heard in the sacred scriptures that Jaigīṣavya and Kapila were auspicious;
you two are Brahmins who have attained perfection and whose sins have been consumed by austerity. (64)
"How is it that you two say these words to me, 'We are Nārāyaṇas,' while [bearing] the conch, discus, mace, lotus, bow, and the svastika-banner? (65)
Clad in yellow garments, the Lord of Lakṣmī, whose vehicle is Garuḍa—Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman—who on earth is his equal? (66)
Having heard the king’s words, those two brahmins, accomplished yogins, laughed and exclaimed, "Behold Nārāyaṇa! (67)
Having spoken thus, that Kapila himself became Viṣṇu,
and Jaigīṣavya instantly became Garuḍa.
The king, struck with wonder upon seeing Hari together with Garuḍa, bowed and said:
"O brahmins, let there be peace; I shall not question this Nārāyaṇa."
But since Brahmā was born from the midst of the navel-lotus,
I declare this Nārāyaṇa to be the father of Brahmā.
And having heard this, Kapila became Padmanābha there;
Jaigīṣavya became Brahmā, stationed upon the navel-lotus.
From the forehead of Brahmā, indeed, Rudra emerged with blood-red eyes;
then the King, without further deliberation, spoke again to those two twice-born ones.
The all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, the soul of all, cannot be seen;
yet this illusion born of yogic perfection has been shown to you two by me, O practitioners of yoga.
But the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign who is the self of all, cannot be seen;
therefore, at that time, he was [seen] there by Kapila and Jaigīṣavya.
All forms consisting of the essence of both [the self and the other] have been shown by you:
bedbugs, mosquitoes, lice, bees, serpents, and birds. (75)
Horses, cows, elephants, lions, tigers, jackals, and deer; as well as other animals, insects, and likewise those both domestic and wild. (76)
"Animals, humans, trees, creepers, and all other beings—having seen that multitude of living creatures, the king was filled with wonder. (77)
He understood the greatness of Jaigīṣavya and Kapila;
with devotion, he asked those two sages, "O best of the twice-born, what is this? (78)
The two twice-born ones said to the king: "O King, remember what was asked by you;
how may one worship the supreme Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa? (79)
For the sake of your propitiation, Hari has indeed been revealed to you visibly;
and I, Kapila, who am Nārāyaṇa, appear here visibly as well.
Worship me if you have faith; for I am indeed directly present before you.
All the qualities of the Omniscient One exist in me in part. (81)
Therefore, everything has been obtained by me through devotion to you;
for that Lord Nārāyaṇa is omniscient and capable of assuming any form at will.
It is far beyond even Padmanābha and Mahāviṣṇu, and it exists beyond Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha in the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāman). ||83||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines among the liberated souls;
that gentle one is indeed found here by humans somewhere according to his own will. 84.
This Lomaśa attained that supreme Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, here in the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasara. (85)
"We two have come to this auspicious hermitage for the purpose of seeing him, the infallible one who descends through all incarnations. (86)
He indeed is the Supreme Self, the Lord of the universe, residing within all bodies;
He dwells within one’s own body and is perceived through one's own devotion. ||87||
For this reason, O King of kings, the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa has been shown to you, so that you may have conviction in both of us. 88.
Thus, the omnipresent deity dwells even within your body;
for he indeed abides in all subjects, in servants, and even among ministers.
O King, all animals, including swarms of insects and the like, are composed of Viṣṇu;
one should indeed maintain a firm conviction that Hari is everything.
There is no other being like Him who dwells within all beings; therefore, one should serve that God who resides within with the realization of "I am He. 91.
This path of worship, which bestows supreme liberation, has been shown to you. Worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa with a completely devoted heart. (92)

That Supreme Lord is easily attained through offerings of worship such as incense and the like, through food offerings, lamp-offerings, and so forth, as well as through meditation and the devotion of a servant. 93.
That Lord Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Supreme Self,
exists in many ways through various forms as the powerful master who accomplishes all tasks.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, the Dwarf, Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and likewise Kalki and others. (95)
Thus have been described his manifestations, beginning with Kapila;
as well as the virtuous men, the perfected ones, the virtuous women, and the true yogis.
Indeed, they serve as stairways for those who desire to attain his vision;
yet even the gods do not behold that which is his supreme form.
He indeed fulfills all contemplation through his essential nature as ourselves and others;
therefore, this entire world is pervaded by Nārāyaṇa. 98.
And worship that Acyuta, O beloved, who abides as you desire;
for in ancient times, Bṛhaspati spoke thus to Raibhya, the son of Brahmā.
O Raibhya, listen, O King Vasu; hear with respect concerning King Vasu by name in the interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa. 1.525.100.
Whatever action a person performs, whether good or evil,
by dedicating it all to Nārāyaṇa, he is not tainted even while acting.
And that glorious Nārāyaṇa resides within all living beings;
worship that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within. 102.
Thereafter, those two always took refuge in Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
they attained liberation in the supreme abode, characterized by eternal service.
Thus all this, the word of Kapila which bestows the goal of human life, has been told;
and King Aśvaśiras [addressed] his eldest son named Sthūlaśiras.
Having consecrated his own son in the kingdom and having bowed repeatedly to his gurus,
he went to the distant forest known as Naimiṣa, where he [sought] the Lord Hari.
He propitiated Hari through austerity, and Hari himself became manifest before him;
he led his own devotee to the imperishable abode by means of a celestial chariot.
Thus has been told everything regarding the liberation of the horse's head,
once the ritual action has indeed been offered to the Lord of Lords by one endowed with knowledge.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Knowledge by Kapila upon King Aśvaśiras, the Demonstration of Liberation through Action Consisting of Total Surrender by means of the Examples of the Ascetic, the Harsh Brahmin, and the Hunter, and the Exposition of the Many Manifestations of Kapila and Jaigīṣavya," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the former account of Vasu and how it came to pass;
thereafter, I shall relate the wonder concerning Raibhya as well.
The King of Kashmir himself was a great devotee of Vasu;
he had taken refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 2 ||
"Oṃ, salutations; salutations to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa"—this mantra he received from Nārāyaṇa in his old age.
Every year, O King, that monarch comes to Bādarī out of devotion, for the sake of serving and beholding Nārāyaṇa.
He always wears a beautiful garland of *tulasī* around his neck,
and he also always keeps a rosary in his hand for the purpose of recitation.
Knowing that his own existence lasts but a moment, and that the world is likewise, he realizes that all composite things fashioned within this cycle of existence bring only sorrow and fear. (6)
Wind, earth, space, water, and fire—the body of all embodied beings is composed of these five elements. || 7 ||
It is a false delusion, artificial, and endowed with illusion like a dream;
who is whose son there, what woman belongs to whom, and likewise, who is whose husband?
Everything is fashioned by actions; indeed, this world arises from the bondage of karma.
Pleasure, pain, fear, and sorrow accrue upon the union with a body.
Through one's own actions, one undergoes birth among humans, animals, gods, trees, insects, living beings, birds, and even as grass. (1.526.10)
One continues to wander again and again as long as there is no dissolution of karma;
the four ages—Satya, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—are indeed thus.
A fourth part of a *nimeṣa* is a *truṭi*; two of those are a *lava*.
Two *lavas* are declared to be a *yava*, and fifteen of those are a *kāṣṭhā*.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are said to be one *kalā*, and thirty *kalās* are considered one *kṣaṇa*.
Sixty *kṣaṇas* are said to be one *pala*, and sixty of those are one *nāḍikā*.
Two nāḍīs constitute a muhūrta; thirty muhūrtas make up day and night;
a month consists of thirty days and nights, and two months are considered one season (ṛtu). || 14 ||
Three seasons constitute an ayana, and two ayanas constitute a year; indeed, it is by this very measure that the years for human beings here have been established.
The Kṛtayuga is determined to consist of seventeen lakhs and twenty-eight thousand solar years. (16)
Those [mantras] numbering four thousand eight hundred are considered to be multiplied by three hundred and sixty when the Kṛta age is taken into account. || 17 ||
There indeed the Blessed One himself was born with a white complexion;
the people were liberated from sin, patient, self-controlled, and masters of their senses. (18)
Long-lived and immersed in austerity, free from desire, anger, and other such passions,
the progenitors never experience the birth of a son nor the sight of death anywhere.
Then the Tretā Yuga shall consist of twelve hundred thousand and ninety-six thousand solar years; this is the determination made by the gods.
Indeed, those [moments] numbering three thousand six hundred are multiplied by three hundred and sixty in the triad of ages (yuga). ||21||
Then, with one foot of sin remaining, he enters the fierce Dharma;
thereafter, the illustrious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa attains the state of blood-redness. ||22||
Then, through their sinful portions, people become mutually competitive;
for the sake of heaven, they perform various acts of charity and sacrifice in order to reach the celestial realm.
Some are born there with very short lifespans, even due to rivalry;
yet, while the father is still present, the death of the sons does not indeed occur.
Lust, anger, and the like may arise there or not;
at that time, that field has been sown once for all and is most excellent. (25)
The Vaiśyas, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, indeed accept [the offerings] seven times;
all the cows are praised as jars, and the buffaloes are fourfold. ||26||
At that time, human beings were capable of both cursing and bestowing grace;
there were no thieves or rogues, and all people were devoted to dharma. 27.
Then, in due order, the third age, Dvāpara, occurs;
in that age, two quarters of evil and two quarters of dharma remain established.
And that [period] is proclaimed as eight hundred thousand solar years;
at that time, a yuga consists of sixty-four thousand additional years. (29)
Indeed, those numbered at two thousand four hundred are multiplied by three hundred and sixty in the pair of ages (dvika-yuga). 1.526.30.
Lust, anger, pride, greed, hypocrisy, and envy—these six are born there, and jealousy is the seventh. (3.1)
Then, accompanied by them all, they indeed became mutually opposed;
yet some truly became peaceful, self-controlled, and masters of their senses.
Then the Kali Yuga is said to have begun, which is the refuge of all defects;
therein, virtue stands on only one foot, while evil is established upon three.
The Lord is white in the Kṛta age, red-colored in the Tretā,
blue in the Dvāpara, and indeed black like a bee in the Kali age.
The duration of the Kali age is declared to be four hundred and thirty-two thousand solar years. (35)
Indeed, those [periods] numbering one thousand two hundred, when multiplied by three hundred and sixty, are considered to be the duration of the Kali age. (36)
One, two, three, four, and ten thousand years respectively are the durations of the Kali, Dvāpara, Tretā, and Kṛta ages. (37)
The human [ages] are two, four, six, and eight hundred years respectively;
when these are combined, they total two thousand years. (38)
A cycle of four yugas for human beings consists of twelve thousand solar years;
furthermore, it should be understood as consisting of three million four hundred and thirty thousand [solar days].
The four yugas indeed consist of more than twenty thousand years;
for it is held that at the time of creation, the exhaustion of lifespan caused by the end of a yuga also occurs.
In the Kali age, men form friendships with those who possess wealth in their homes as well as charming women. (41)

Sons are intent solely on their own interests, and beloved wives are intent on interests other than their own; moreover, a daughter-in-law regards her mother-in-law as mere property, provided that she herself does not fall into decline. (42)
"I would possess a house and sovereignty; everyone desires that very thing.
Then the clouds will hold little water, and the earth will yield little grain. (43)
In the Kali age, those who are virtuous become rogues and mockers, and even teachers [act likewise];
then cows yield little milk, and there is no ghee to be found in that milk.
At that time, O Brahmins, all will be eaters of everything; the kings will be merciless, and everyone will be intent on acts of theft; the earth will have lost its youth. ||45||
The auspicious times have passed, and dreadful times have arrived;
within four years, a girl shall become pregnant. (46)
If one dies at fifteen years of age or less, death itself will surely occur;
and at the end of the Kali age, people will be only a span (vitasti) in height.
At the end of the ten-year lifespan, the home will be a hole within the earth;
at that time, clothing will indeed consist of nothing more than a mere covering for the private parts.
All castes will become of a single color, mutually intermingled;
they will become barbarians of wicked conduct, devoid of righteous deeds and duties.
Likewise, Manu and Mahendra enjoy a long life for seventy-one cycles of four yugas, again and again.
The maximum lifespan is proclaimed to be equal to that of Manu and Mahendra;
the passing of fourteen Indras is said to constitute one day of Brahmā. (51)
Thus, the night and the day are limited;
indeed, a kalpa is the measure for Brahmā, whose maximum lifespan is ordained as one hundred years.
By means of these four kinds of measures—solar, civil, lunar, and sidereal—time passes for all beings upon the circle of the earth. (53)
Three hundred and sixty-five days constitute a human year; that same period, minus five, is the solar (sāvana) year.
The lunar year is diminished by eleven, while that born of the asterisms is diminished by thirty;
thus, cold, heat, and rain are produced according to the human year.
Sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, marriages, festivals, and so forth, indeed take place according to the Sāvana [lunar] reckoning among all castes on this earth. (56)

Indeed, all transactions such as those concerning the lazy (kusīda) and others, as well as those that have already arisen, are governed by the lunar month alone, including the intercalary month. //57//
By the measure of the constellations, the stars are distinguished;
likewise are the gods, humans, Daityas, and others always upon the earth. (58)
This world thus proceeds, is born, and dies;
therein, one who is shrouded by the bondage of illusion does not indeed reach the further shore. //59//
Therefore, I must always worship, honor, and meditate upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, without interruption. ||1.526.60||
Time devours all beings, whether in a moment, a year, or an eon;
with his hand placed upon my crest, Time now desires to swallow me. (61)
Thus, endowed with such awakening and devoted to piety,
King Vasu protected his own kingdom with the approval of Dharma.
He performed many great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, offering his actions to Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of gods. (63)
He pleased him by serving in many ways as a slave;
then, after a long time, Vasu, through the practice of detachment, [attained realization].
Having reached the end of the pair consisting of the desire for royal power and enjoyment,
he [installed] his own son Vivasvat, who was the most excellent among a hundred brothers.
Having consecrated Puṣkara in his own kingdom,
he went to where the lotus-eyed Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent.
That King Vasu of Kaśmīra, remembering Hari there with devotion, beheld Him in a divine body, having been accomplished through his fierce austerities.
He praised the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the sovereign inner controller of all: "Salutations be unto You; O Lotus-eyed One, salutations unto You! (68)
O Viśvamūrti, abode of all splendor, Kṛṣṇa, salutations to You!
To Viṣṇu, the refuge, the protector, the victorious, who dwells in the sky. (69)
I bow to you, the child Gopālakṛṣṇa, who holds the discus in hand;
O Acyuta, I perceive nothing else whatsoever apart from you.
While he was speaking thus, a personified being indeed emerged from his body— dark blue in hue, dense and fierce, and terrifying.
The red-eyed and short-bodied one said, "O King, what shall I do?
Vasu questioned that evil-formed being: "Tell me here, who are you? (72)
"O sinless one, he who is indeed of sinful form said, 'I shall become your sin';
yet I am not merely sin, O blameless one, I am a *pāpapreta* (a ghost of sin) belonging to you. (73)
Listen, O King; formerly in the Kali age, you were a king in the southern region. Once, you arrived at Janasthāna for the purpose of hunting. ||74||
There, by you with a staff, the sage wearing the guise of a deer was struck on Mount Prasravaṇa and quickly died. (75)
Thinking that deer to be slain, just as you desired to seize it, you beheld instead a man in the form of a deer. (76)
And you have indeed fallen into great fear because of the murder of a human being;
for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa who was a ghost is most terrible. (77)
"O King, I, as the grasping spirit of Brahmā, have dwelt within your body;
today I have come to torment you and devour your frame. (78)
O King, the enjoyments of sovereignty were seen and experienced by me within your body;
your fresh blood was drunk and your flesh was constantly eaten. (79)
And you, O best of kings, by virtue of the power of your kingdom, do not appear at all emaciated,
owing to your abundance of food, drink, and other luxuries.
Then, O King, you reflected upon an expiation for that sin;
you observed the pure Dvādaśī of Śrī Hari.
Other vows were likewise performed with the thought, "May Nārāyaṇa be pleased with me," and gifts of cows were given again and again.
Then, in your own home in the southern region, you will become ill with a pain in the abdomen and die; your wife, a virtuous woman named Nārāyaṇī, [will remain].
And he placed the nectar from the feet of Śrī Viṣṇu into your mouth;
however, at that moment of death, you remembered and meditated upon your wife. (84)
Because of that, you were born again for one kalpa in Viṣṇupura as a youth possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā), since you were indeed deprived of liberation.
I remained there with you, dwelling indeed within your very body,
and until the end of the eon, I enjoyed all true pleasures while residing in you.
In that kalpa, you indeed enjoyed heaven in many ways;
and because of your merit, O King, I myself remained in heaven through my own splendor.
Furthermore, I remained in the form of a king for many years;
then, even when the conception of day had ceased and the conception of night had passed, [I remained]. (88)
Now, O lord of men, at the time of the original creation in the Satya Yuga, you were born, O great king, in the house of King Sumanas. (89)
"I dwell within your body hairs until this very day, O sovereign of the land of Kaśmīra, enjoying ever-new and fresh [pleasures]."
Even though you have performed many various sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
I was not captivated by them because they were devoid of the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
And now, in Viśālā, devotion has been shown by you toward Hari; here, with a humble disposition and with your whole being, a hymn of praise has been offered. (92)
By the power of your devotion to the lotus-eyed wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and by the offering of your entire self, Hari himself has been propitiated. (93)
The Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa dispatched his servants;
behold them now stationed in celestial chariots in the great sky. 94.
Thus, struck by these mallets of Viṣṇu’s attendants, I have gone to destruction and have fallen even from your pores. (95)
By the power of your devotion, having cast off my bodily hairs, I have been born anew as a single being in the form of a hunter in your presence. (96)
O King, having heard this hymn of praise to the Blessed One and out of devotion for you, I was freed from my great sin even by the touch of the staff of Viṣṇu’s attendant. (97)
"I am liberated from the state of a preta, and I possess a righteous mind.
Therefore, O King, [protect] your own friend who has taken refuge in you and is now without support. (98)
"Give me, your devotee, that which bestows happiness; grant me a boon and show me mercy.
Having heard this, Vasu also granted a auspicious boon to the hunter.
"Listen, hunter; I have been reminded by you of my previous birth.
Therefore, by my grace, you shall henceforth become a Dharma-hunter."
Having spoken thus, that king ascended an excellent celestial chariot to the realm of Akṣara, indeed, to the supreme Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Accompanied by his attendants, he went forth; thereafter, he became an attendant of Hari.
Then, performing righteous deeds, he indeed became Dharmavyādha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this supreme account of Vasu has been told;
whoever reads or hears it shall obtain the fruit of bathing at a sacred ford.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Vasu of Kashmir’s Previous Birth as a Deer, the Departure of the Sin of Brahmin-Slaughter through the Power of Devotion, and Vasu’s Subsequent Liberation," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the life-story of Raibhya, which grants liberation from the body.
Then Raibhya, whose wealth was his austerity, went himself to the meritorious Gayā.
There, propitiating his ancestors with supreme devotion by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas),
he performed a very great and intense penance that is exceedingly difficult to practice.
While that wise Raibhya was performing that intense austerity,
a great yogi, exceedingly radiant, arrived seated upon a celestial chariot.
In a pure celestial chariot, radiant like the sun and as fine as a mote of dust,
there dwells a resplendent person of the size of an atom.
He said, "O Raibhya of noble vows, what is the purpose for which you are practicing penance?
Having spoken thus, that man indeed appeared in the space between heaven and earth.
Indeed, a celestial chariot was produced that pervaded both heaven and earth,
wherein infinite sages were seen by the wise son of Indra.
He beheld a celestial chariot pervading the world of Viṣṇu;
then Raibhya, overcome with wonder, spoke with affection.
He asked that great yogi, "Who are you? Tell me.
The boy, whose life was but five years remaining, spoke to Raibhya.
"I am younger than Rudra, the mind-born son of Brahmā;
I am Sanatkumāra by name, and I dwell in Janaloka."
"Your father has indeed been satisfied by your ritual acts for his ancestral gratification and the like;
I have come into your presence solely to offer words of praise."
"You are blessed at all times, my child, the enhancer of the lineage of Brahmā;
by relying upon the Vedas, O sinless one, you always gratify the ancestors. (11)

Sons who provide satisfaction to their ancestors through mantras, vows, recitations, fire-offerings, and the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā are true sons; others are merely those born of impurity (sūtaka).
Listen, O Raibhya: in ancient times there was indeed a king named Viśāla;
being wise, he questioned the best of the twice-born for the sake of obtaining a son. (13)
The Brahmins said: "Having gone to Gayā, satisfy your ancestors with devotion through gifts of food, water, funeral cakes (piṇḍas), the gift of cows, and other forms of charity."
"Surely a son shall be born to you who will be a giver of happiness and a lord of the earth; he will be the ruler of Viśālānagara. Having said this, Viśāla then departed. (15)
While he was performing the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) to the ancestors at Gayā under the Maghā asterism,
three men appeared there in the sky.
Having seen the white, the red, and the third, which was black in color,
he bowed to them and said, "Please accept these fine lumps."
"Why is this being ignored by you? Tell me, for my curiosity is great.
Then Śita said to them, "Sons, I am your father."
By name, conduct, deed, and lineage, he is Śveta;
yet this father of mine is red and a cruel slayer.
His father was Kṛṣṇavarṇa by name, both by his occupation and his deeds;
indeed, many sages were formerly slain by Kṛṣṇavarṇa.
These two, having died, have entered for a long time the hell known as Avīci;
I, through my merits, have attained the throne of Śakra, which is so difficult to obtain. (21)
By you, the funeral cakes were offered at Gayā according to the prescribed rites with mantras;
therefore, these two have been drawn out from hell and brought here, well-established.
"O good son, may you offer this water given by you with the thought: 'I gratify the fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers. (23)
Therefore, our simultaneous union has occurred here in your presence;
we accept the offering of the funeral cakes and water, and we are entirely satisfied. (24)
"By the power of this sacred ford, I shall go to the world of the ancestors, there is no doubt;
for by the offering of funeral cakes here, these two, your grandfathers," [will attain that state].
Even in an evil state of existence, they both became purified and possessed of merit;
such is the power of sacred fords that even the son of a slayer of a Brahmin [was saved].
"By offering the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to his father, one may effect his deliverance once again.
For this reason, O King, I am your white father. (27)
I shall tell you something more, by which indeed our liberation may be attained;
listen to this knowledge concerning worldly existence, by which you will go to liberation. (28)
And having always risen in the morning and discarded the garments worn at night,
one should [visualize] the beloved deity in the heart-lotus and likewise the Guru in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having reflected with the mind upon all the morning duties, perform them completely;
during bathing, purification, and every ritual act, remember Hari again and again.
Having placed the Supreme Lord upon a clean cloth,
worship Him in a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, an image, or even in water.
Worship him in a cow, in a brahmin, and especially in your gurus;
worship him also in a water-pot, in an eight-petaled lotus, and in a vessel anointed with sandalwood paste.
O virtuous lady, worship the Lord of Śrī both at the Śālagrāma stone and within your mind; offer the sixteen articles of worship and perform devotional service repeatedly.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Rādhā, Gaṅgā, and Tulasī;
Nārāyaṇa, the Unborn, Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, Vināyaka, and the Guru.
Always worship with affection the guest, the sun, and the sacrificial fire;
worship the parents, the Brahmin, the virtuous man, and the sun with devotion. (35)
I shall describe to you that which is invisible; it is not beautiful to behold anywhere.
A wise person should not look upon excrement, for it is the very embodiment of the seeds of disease.
The urine and the seed of disease, as well as the cause of hell—the male organ and the womb, which bestow sin, suffering, illness, and poverty. (37)
One should not look upon the private parts of a woman, which are the cause of destruction;
and one should avoid excessive indulgence, which is the cause of diseases. (38)
At the time of sunset, one should not look at the sun or the moon, as that is a cause of disease;
nor should one gaze at the moon when it is partially risen, for that is a cause of affliction.
Seeing the sun and the moon reflected in water, a man may fall into grief; likewise, he who observes the sleeping place, the food, and the movements of another person [becomes sorrowful]. (1.527.40)
One should not do anything with a sinner, for it is a cause of total destruction;
[this occurs] from conversation, from touching the body, and from sharing a bed, a seat, or food.
Sins committed by others certainly transfer to a manifest person;
therefore, one should not go near predatory animals, as that is a cause of suffering. (42)
One should not associate with a wicked person, for it is a cause of sorrow; likewise, one should avoid associating with those who are hostile toward Brāhmaṇas, cows, Vaiṣṇavas, and the virtuous. 43.
One should not commit violence or cause harm toward the gods, the demigods, the brahmins, chaste women, or even the virtuous, for such acts are the cause of total destruction. 44.
One should not take away wealth, property, or riches, for that is a cause of ruin;
rather, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) quickly, otherwise it becomes a cause of destruction. 45.
By committing violence against living beings, the destruction of one's lineage will certainly occur;
he who does not bow to the deity or the guru shall partake in sin and go to hell. 46.
That foolish woman of wicked conduct who does not perceive her own husband as the form of Hari, shall fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell after being subjected to threats.
From verbal abuse one becomes a crow; from violence one becomes a pig;
through anger one becomes a snake, and through arrogance one becomes a donkey. (48)
The female dog [was saved] even by a harsh word, and the blind woman by the mere sight of the poison;
but the devoted wife would certainly go to Vaikuṇṭha together with her husband. 49.
Śiva, Durgā, Gaṇapati, Sūrya, and a Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa;
the father, the mother, the son, a virtuous wife, the preceptor, and the husband.
Having reviled a helpless sister or daughter, one shall go to hell;
however, those who consume the water of the Śālagrāma and the remnants of Kṛṣṇa’s offerings [attain liberation]. (51)
Those virtuous ones purify a hundred men and the earth at a sacred ford;
however, one who partakes of food through the grace of Viṣṇu obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice.
A blazing Śiva-liṅga, a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, as well as an image, a sacrificial thread, gold, and even a conch shell—these too [should not be touched]. (53)
Having cast a diamond, as well as a pearl, cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter,
and the water from a Śālagrāma stone upon the ground, one shall go to the nether regions.
He was poor, wretched, afflicted with leprosy, deprived of his lineage, and without a wife; he was landless, childless, bereft of kinsmen, and despised. ||55||
The evil-minded person who abandons these on the ground shall, in due course, become blind, lame, dwarfish, crippled, or even deprived of a limb. (56)
Having fashioned a linga from clay, ashes, balls of cow dung, or likewise from sand and other materials,
and having worshipped it even once, one shall dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas.
And listen as I describe the merit found in the sight of true brahmins, sacred fords, Vaiṣṇavas, and likewise virtuous people. (58)
Likewise, there is the supreme vision of the deities, of one's parents, and of one's husband; as well as the vision of the Sun, of virtuous women, of ascetics, and of celibate students. (59)
For renunciants, for cows, for fire, for the guru, for an elephant, for a horse, for a lion, for a cuckoo, and also for a wagtail and a parrot; 1.527.60.
Of swans, peacocks, blue jays, and conch-birds;
of cows accompanied by their calves, of *aśvattha* trees, and likewise of jewels. (6.1)
And for women who have sons, for those traveling to sacred pilgrimage sites,
and for lamps, gold, pearls, and diamonds— (62)
The sight of rubies, tulasī, and white flowers is considered meritorious, destructive of sin, and a bestower of auspiciousness. (63)
Fruits, white grains, clarified butter, curd, and honey;
a full water-pot, parched grain, sugar, a mirror, and water. ||64||
Upon seeing a garland of white flowers, a person shall attain merit; as shall one who sees gorocana, camphor, silver, or a lake. (65)
A flower garden, a blossoming [tree], the new moon in its bright phase, nectar, sandalwood, the rising of a deity, a temple, and a banner; ||66||
Musk, saffron, Devakhāta, the Vaṭa tree, and Dundubhi;
the banner, the divine pitcher, and likewise the fragrant breeze.
A conch shell, mother-of-pearl, coral, silver, crystal, kuśa grass,
copper, clay from the Gaṅgā, an image of Viṣṇu, a book, a gem, and unbroken grains of rice.
An ascetic, a learned man, the ocean, the black antelope, a sacrifice, a great festival, milk, cow urine, and likewise cow dung. (69)
The time of twilight, a cow’s footprint, a cow-pen, ground where grain has ripened,
a beautiful lotus pond, a dark-complexioned maiden, one well-dressed, and a virtuous woman.
Having seen the fragrant hand, the perfumes, and the consecrated food (siddhānna), one obtains merit and victory;
and he who, having offered rice-balls (piṇḍas) at the foot of Viṣṇu, worships Viṣṇu [attains the same].
It effects the liberation from rebirth for one's ancestors as well as for oneself.
This has been told to you, O King, which brings joy and increases merit. (72)
Thus, by the power of merit, his intellect becomes perfectly pure, and likewise, devotion toward his ancestors increases within his heart. (73)
Having instructed Viśāla, Śita said: "Always worship Kṛṣṇa;
give him the merit of the Ekādaśī fasts and the vows of the month of Kārtika. (74)
Grant the fruit of the worship of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for our liberation;
grant the merit of the unbroken Mātrikā for our liberation as well. (75)
Thus addressed, that king named Viśāla gave his merit in this manner;
taking water in his hand, he indeed released it upon the surface of the earth. (76)
At that moment, the attendants of Viṣṇu arrived, seated upon celestial chariots, chanting the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (77)
The four Vaiṣṇavas there spoke and said to the celestial chariot:
"Let them ascend to Vaikuṇṭha, and let the attendants come as well. (78)
Having been addressed thus, they departed for their own abode at that very moment along with the attendants.
For this reason, O Raibhya, you are called blessed by me.
To visit Gayā once and to offer the funeral cakes once is difficult to achieve; yet you remain here constantly and perpetually.
O Lord Raibhya, what more can be said of this merit of yours, by which Nārāyaṇa himself was seen face to face with the mace in his hand? (81)
Having spoken thus, the eternal sage vanished on the spot;
Raibhya then offered praise to Hari with a voice faltering with love.
I take refuge in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who was white in the Kṛta age, ruddy in the Tretā age, blue in the Dvāpara age, and resembles a bee in the Kali age. (83)
He who exists in the supreme imperishable abode, in Goloka and in Vaikuṇṭha—that Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dwells also within my heart. (84)
I bow to you today and take refuge in you, the omnipresent Supreme Lord dwelling within the body of the hairy one (Lomaśa), for the sake of crossing over the ocean of worldly existence. 85.
Matsya and the others, as well as Makha and the rest, are existent; they are the manifestations of your own limbs.
Therefore, even now, make me likewise adorned by the circle of the Siddhas. (86)
Thus praised, Viṣṇu then appeared in beautiful form,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, seated upon Garuḍa, and traversing the sky.
Raibhya said, "I am pleased; come with me.
Mounting Garuḍa, Raibhya went to where Sanaka and the others were.
Having gone there and bowed to them, O Lakṣmī, he went with Hari to Vaikuṇṭha in his divine body into the presence of your beloved.
Whoever reads or even hears this account of Raibhya as well as that of Viṣṇu, the wielder of the mace, shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of King Viśāla’s Liberation through Devotion to Hari, Raibhya’s Liberation through Knowledge of Reality and Devotion, and Raibhya’s Vision of Sanatkumāra along with His Instruction at Gayā," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, O best of sages! Once, the sage Āvaṭya, having performed a circumambulation of Mount Raivata in the month of Kārttika, [proceeded further]. || 1 ||
Then he dwelt for three months in the hermitage of Lomaśa,
on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, at the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
On the night of Śivarātri, he worshipped Lomaśeśvara;
and when it was the Brāhma-muhūrta of the morning, he fell asleep for a moment.
There, the sage named Āvaṭya had a dream;
he then traveled by means of a divine vehicle to Satyaloka, which is beyond that world.
He went to the world of Viṣṇu, the world of Mahāviṣṇu, and to Kailāsa;
from there, he proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha by means of an aerial vehicle.
Afterwards, he went to Goloka;
he went to the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāma), and he went to the supreme abode, the infinite, higher than the highest.
Having gone to the most excellent world of Brahmā, he beheld the divine and glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Liberated and the Imperishable.
To that Śrī Hari, who is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and is saluted by the liberated souls, he stood before him and spoke to Yāvaṭya.
"Tell me, what have you observed everywhere in the worlds?
Āvaṭya replied: "O Blessed One, that which is indeed seen here—"
Such a sovereign empire of bliss has not been seen anywhere—
not in Akṣara, nor in Goloka, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor even in Amṛta.
Yet on that level of truth, no mere portion of pleasure exists for you;
rather, you possess a pleasure of a different kind, which bestows eternal bliss and perfect contentment.
In Akṣara, there is an abundance of liberated souls; Rādhikā and others reside in Goloka, Śrī, Ramā, and others in Vaikuṇṭha, and the gods and other deities abide in Satyaloka.
What then can be said of other places? Indeed, all the realms of enjoyment—including Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Kailāsa, and the imperishable abode—are likewise [transient].
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, these four stages of yours have indeed been made eternal by you for the sake of the delight of your devotees. (14)
But to those devotees who desire service according to their wishes,
you grant satisfaction in the state of servitude through love, affection, and grace.
The bliss of the Self in Your form is distinguished in the supreme abode;
the bliss of service in the imperishable abode is distinguished beyond all others. (16)
The bliss of service is found in Goloka, the bliss of friendship in Vikuṇṭha, and the bliss of worship in Satyaloka; each is distinguished according to its appropriate place. || 17 ||
"O Blessed One, elsewhere the bliss of sense objects is distinguished by being mixed with afflictions; but here, I have seen that very same bliss within the abode of the Imperishable. (18)
And I beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Akṣara; in Goloka, you, O Rādhikā, saw Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as the Lord.
In Vaikuṇṭha, you were seen as Lakṣmīśa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
and on Kailāsa, you were beheld as one filled with the bliss of dispassion.
You alone are the yogi, the wise one, and the ascetic; you are Śiva’s consort and Hari himself. In Satyaloka, you are indeed Sāvitrīśvara.
This very same golden person that I beheld in the sun is you,
appearing as the young cowherd Kṛṣṇa on earth and in the Kuṅkumavāpī pond.
O Lord, you, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the son of Kambharā-Lakṣmī, reside there in the hermitage of Lomaśa; you dwell in that very temple. 23.
In some places he saw Rādhā, in some Lakṣmī, and in some the virtuous Pārvatī;
in some places the goddess Māṇikī, in some Prabhā, and in some Ramā. ||24||
In some places he saw Padmā, Jayā, Lalitā, Haṃsā, and Mañjulā;
as well as Padmāvatī, Satī, Vṛndā, Tulasī, and Sarasvatī. ||25||
In one place I behold Śivā by my side, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti); elsewhere, I see Devikā, Muktā, Campā, Haimī, and Śāntikā.
In some places, O Kṛṣṇa, I behold you as a virtuous yogin, a wise and eternal being; yet even after seeing these forms of yours, I do not reach the further shore.
Today my birth has become fruitful, since I have reached the further shore of liberation;
for your vision is not obtained even through the merit of many kalpas.
"By your grace, O Lord of Śrī, I have today obtained the sight of you.
As he was saying this, Avatya’s sleep vanished at that very moment. (29)
He beheld Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa smiling before him;
having prostrated, the sage said, "O Lord, a dream has been seen by me."
"Tell me now what the fruit of that would be for me; what eternal fruit might I obtain?
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa said: "O Āvaṭya, listen to the fruit of that."
"Your liberation will soon come to pass through the proximity of Lomaśa and by the power of this sacred field, Aśvapaṭṭasara. (32)
O Sage, by virtue of the merit of the Śivarātri vow and by your arrival here, please accept the mantra; may you both be intent upon our liberation.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; salutations!
Accept this garland of tulasī, and accept this necklace for your neck. (34)
"Tell me whatever else you desire, and I shall grant it to you here; of this there is no doubt.
Then Āvaṭya said: "Grant me liberation in the supreme, imperishable state. (35)
"Tell me here the knowledge of dreams for the sake of the welfare of the entire world.
"So be it," said the Lord Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (36)
O beloved, listen to that knowledge regarding dreams which Āvaṭya then spoke:
"The sight of a good dream is meritorious, provided one does not speak of it to a low person. (37)
Having abandoned Kāśyapa, the unfortunate, the base, the enemy, the ignorant, and the woman—both by night and by day—he speaks of the Brahmin as being truly wise. (38)
Having spoken of the deity in a temple, or of the Aśvattha, Tulasī, and Vaṭa trees, the merit is double; but if it remains unproclaimed, it is fourfold. (39)
Upon seeing such auspicious dreams, the wise man obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā;
he shall obtain wealth, riches, a wife, land, and a son.
One obtains liberation, supreme sovereignty, and everything desired;
however, a dream occurring in the first watch of the night yields its fruit within one year. (41)
In the second [month], a dream occurring within eight months; in the third, within three months; and in the fourth, within half a month, such a dream yields its own specific fruit.
A dream is fruitful even when seen at dawn within ten days;
however, a dream seen in the morning is fruitful if one is awakened at that very moment.
A man afflicted by anxiety or disease sees a dream;
all that is seen is fruitless, and a dream seen during the day is likewise fruitless.
One who is dull-witted, oppressed by urine and excrement, agitated by fear, naked, or with disheveled hair shall not obtain the fruit arising from dreams. (45)
Furthermore, one who falls asleep again after a dream does not obtain its fruit;
and for him who recounts a dream during the night, no fruit arises.
Having spoken [the name] of the Kāśyapa lineage, a person incurs misfortune;
he goes from one miserable state to another miserable state, and in a low birth, he encounters disease. (47)
One encounters fear at night, and a fool incurs quarrels;
there shall be loss of wealth through a woman, and danger from thieves at night. (48)
In sleep one experiences sorrow, whereas in the wise man there is the desired fruit;
O Kāśyapa, such a dream must never be disclosed by an intelligent person. 49.
Climbing upon cows, horses, mountains, palaces, elephants,
and trees in a dream is proclaimed to bestow wealth.
If one sees eating, weeping, or the playing of a lute,
or if one receives [these] in a dream, one should touch ground rich in crops.
If one is pierced by a weapon or missile, or likewise by a wound infested with maggots, or even smeared with feces or blood in a dream, such a person shall become wealthy. ||52||
Indeed, even in a dream, having sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached brings about the loss of one's wife;
being drenched in urine, one may drink semen and even enter hell.
If one enters a city that appears red, or drinks nectar from the ocean, he shall receive auspicious news and obtain abundant wealth. (54)
An elephant, a king, gold, a bull, and even a cow;
a lamp, food, fruit, a flower, a maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, and a banner. (55)
Having seen a family, one obtains fame and abundant prosperity; likewise, seeing a brāhmaṇa with a full water-pot, fire, flowers, betel, or a house [brings the same]. (56)
Upon seeing white grain, an actor, or a courtesan, one shall obtain prosperity;
and upon seeing the milk or ghee of cows, one shall acquire wealth and the riches of merit.
Having eaten milk-rice on a lotus leaf, as well as curd, milk, ghee, honey, sweet food, and the svastika dish, one will certainly become a king. ||58||
If a man eats the flesh of birds or humans, he obtains great wealth, auspicious news, and his desired fruit. (59)
Having obtained a parasol, a sword, and sandals, one goes forth with grain;
he who crosses water in a dream certainly becomes preeminent.
Seeing a tree bearing fruit, one will certainly obtain wealth;
a man bitten by a snake shall likewise become a possessor of riches. (6.1)
Upon seeing the sun and the moon in a dream, one's illness perishes;
by seeing a mare, a hen, or a female crane, a person shall obtain a wife.
He who, bound by fetters in a dream, obtains a firm standing and a son, and likewise eats from a lotus leaf on a riverbank or from a lotus cup; ||63||
If one sees curd-rice or milk-porridge in a dream, he shall become a king; of this there is no doubt.
If one sees a leech, a scorpion, or a snake in a dream, [he shall likewise attain sovereignty].
One obtains wealth, a son, victory, and firm standing, even if one is afflicted by horned animals, fanged beasts, boars, or monkeys. 65.
If one wears a crown on the head in a dream, one will become a king, or else obtain vast wealth or a preeminent position. (66)
Upon seeing fish, meat, pearls, conch shells, sandalwood, diamonds, crystal, and silver, one shall obtain abundant wealth.
Having eaten meat, blood, and gold, one shall obtain wealth;
having seen an image and a Śiva-liṅga, one shall obtain wealth and victory. (68)
Having seen a wood-apple tree bearing fruit and a mango tree in bloom, one shall obtain wealth;
having beheld a blazing fire, one shall obtain wealth, intelligence, and prosperity.
By seeing the *āmalaka* and the *kamala*, one shall become wealthy; so too by honoring the deities, the twice-born, cows, ancestors, the virtuous, and the preceptor. (1.528.70)
A wife, a husband, a king, a virtuous woman, or daughters devoted to their husbands—whatever such a person gives of his own in a dream, that object will certainly be obtained. (71)
Whomever women wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents, embrace in a dream, for him there is prosperity and happiness in every respect. (72)
He who embraces in a dream a woman wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents will experience auspiciousness.
All white [substances] are praised, except for ash, bone, and cotton; black [substances] are defective, except for those between elephants, horses, cows, Brahmins, and deities. (74)
O Brahmins, he whose house a divine woman, adorned with ornaments of jewels and smiling, enters, certainly attains what is dear to him. (75)
In the dream, the Brahmin was a god and the Brahmin woman was a divine maiden;
she was a celibate student, contented, smiling, and devoted to her husband. (76)
And he to whom it grants its fruit shall have a son, for whom virtuous Brahmins bestow auspicious blessings in a dream. (77)
Whatever they say, that object shall belong to him, as shall its sovereignty;
indeed, for him whose house a satisfied Brahmin visits.
Prosperity comes to him, as well as extensive fame and happiness;
at every step he finds joy, and he shall obtain honor and respect. (79)
But if, even by chance in a dream, he obtains a fragrant [garland],
there shall be gain of land for him, and his wife shall also be devoted to her husband.
If an elephant were to take something with its trunk and place it upon one's head,
that person would obtain a kingdom, as well as the rank of a teacher and the status of a preceptor.
That person whom a Brahmin, being well-pleased, embraces in a dream,
shall become endowed with fortune and fully prosperous, having bathed in sacred fords.
If a twice-born man, laughing, gives a flower to someone in a dream, that person shall become victorious, wealthy, famous, and happy. (83)
Having beheld sacred fords and houses of jewels and celestial palaces in a dream, he who has bathed at those fords shall indeed become wealthy and victorious. (84)
If someone gives a full jar to another in a dream, the recipient shall obtain a son as well as inexhaustible wealth. (85)
Whosever home a beautiful courtesan visits, taking with her a *kuḍava* or an *āḍhaka* measure [of grain], that person shall obtain abundant prosperity. (86)
If a divine woman, having gone to one's house, should void excrement,
there shall be gain of wealth for him, and even poverty shall depart.
To whosever house a Brāhmaṇa comes together with his wife—whether it be Śambhu with Pārvatī or Nārāyaṇa with Lakṣmī—[that house becomes sanctified]. ||88||
To him to whom a virtuous man, a virtuous woman, a guru, or a guru’s wife gives grain, a handful of flowers, or gold in a dream, prosperity indeed comes from every direction. (89)
To whomever a Brāhmaṇa offers a pearl necklace, a garland of flowers, or sandalwood paste,
in that person’s home Lakṣmī and Śrī abide, facing every direction.
If one obtains yellow orpiment, a banner, turmeric, a stalk of sugarcane,
or cooked food in a dream, his prosperity shall be all-encompassing.
Whether it be a Brahmin or a Brahmin woman who places an umbrella, flowers, or white grain upon someone's head, that person shall certainly become a king. (92)
One who, standing upon a chariot in a dream, adorned with white garlands and ointments, eats curds and milk-preparations—he indeed shall become a king. (93)
Whether it be a Brahmin or Brahmins who, in a dream, give him nectar, ghee, or curd, along with vessels of gold and the like—he too shall certainly become a king. (94)
And a young girl eight years of age, adorned with jewel ornaments—he whose [dream] she favors in a dream shall become a wise poet. (95)
If she gives him a book, he shall indeed become a lord among scholars;
if she teaches him like a mother, he shall become a scholar of universal renown.
The Brahmin who causes him to study shall become like Bṛhaspati himself;
he who obtains a book in a dream shall become a renowned scholar. (97)
In a dream, the Brahmin gives an image along with a mantra to someone;
by that, he becomes accomplished in the mantra, virtuous, and wealthy. (98)
A Brahmin, having received the blessing of a Brahmin, shall become a wise king and wealthy;
when a Brahmin is satisfied, he bestows upon people the earth filled with crops and grain. (99)
He who gives [a gift] in a dream shall certainly become a lord of the earth;
in a dream, a Brahmin may place him upon a chariot and show him heaven and other realms.
May he be long-lived, a long-enduring lord of wealth;
and may the Brahmin, being well-pleased, bestow his daughter upon such a Brahmin.
In dreams, he shall always become a lord of the earth, exceedingly wealthy;
and having beheld in a dream a lake, the ocean, a river, and a stream.
By seeing a white snake or a white mountain, one shall obtain prosperity;
whoever sees a dead person in a dream shall become long-lived.
Just as a healthy person feels upon seeing one who is ill, or a happy person upon seeing one who is miserable, so too does she feel when a celestial woman declares, "You shall be my lord. (104)
Having seen her in a dream, he awakens and certainly becomes a king;
having seen Kālikā in a dream and received a crystal rosary.
He shall obtain the rainbow, the thunderbolt of Śakra, and a firm foundation;
moreover, whatever Brahmin says to him in a dream, "Become my servant," that shall come to pass.
Having attained service to Hari and devotion, he becomes a true Vaiṣṇava;
even in a dream, the Brahmin beholds Hari, Śambhu, Brahmā, Kamalā, and Śivā.
She is Śuklā, the mother of the gods, Jāhnavī, or Sarasvatī;
she is Gopālikā, Satī, Sādhvī, Kanyakā, and Pativratā. (108)
She is seen to be very serene and bestowing blessings;
the king who beholds her shall become equal to a god, as shall the most excellent preceptor.
Thus has the fruit arising from the good dream been told to you here, O Āvaṭya;
having seen me, Nārāyaṇa, in a dream, one shall attain liberation.
Āvaṭya said: "O Blessed One, ten kalpas have passed for me;
through the power of Lomaśa, the fruit of your yoga has been realized. (111)
"Having approached, I shall today go to your eternal abode," having said this, he [attained] the refuge of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa with a divine body.
Having ascended the divine vehicle, he went to the abode of the Imperishable;
O Lakṣmī, by hearing or reciting this, a person shall become liberated while living.

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Sage named Āvaṭya attained liberation after hearing Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa declare the fruits of auspicious dreams following the sage’s vision of many divine abodes in his dream," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe those whose very sight is a sin—a source of evil dreams, a seed of wickedness, and a cause of obstacles alone. || 1 ||
One who kills a cow, one who kills a Brahmin, one who is ungrateful, as well as one who is crooked,
one who slays the gods, one who slays his father or mother, a sinner, and a betrayer of trust— [these are the ones he avoids].
One who gives false testimony, one who likewise deceives a guest, one who steals the property of gods or Brahmins, and also one who seizes land; || 3 ||
[He cursed] the destroyer of the Aśvattha tree, the destroyer of Vṛndā, the reviler of the gods,
the hater of holy men, the envious one, the one of improper conduct, and Devala.
One whose nose has been cut off, one devoid of devotion to her husband, an unchaste woman,
a widow, one who is angry, a wicked person, one burdened by debt, and one born of an adulterer.
Upon seeing a thief, a liar, or the moon or sun eclipsed by Rāhu,
one should perform a ritual bath and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
In the month of Bhādrapada, whether during the bright or dark fortnight, the moon that has set is not visible;
moreover, the moon that has risen on the fourth lunar day should never be looked upon.
If the moon looks at him out of desire, he gives that observer the stain of stealing Tārā, which is exceedingly difficult to bear. (8)
If a person unintentionally sees [impurity], he should drink water purified by mantra:
*Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all blemish.* 9.
