Then one should drink that well-purified water with this mantra: "To the remover of the moon's stain, the proclaimer of the purity of the stars. 1.529.10.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"Why is the sun, when seized by Rāhu, not to be looked upon, and likewise the moon?
O abode of the ocean of compassion, dispel this doubt of mine. (11)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Once, filled with great curiosity and accompanied by Reṇukā, the delighted Jamadagni went to the bank of the Narmadā.
And in a secluded place during the day, he engaged in sexual enjoyment with his wife;
it was according to her wish, not by his own desire, for the sake of her satisfaction.
Then Sūrya, the witness of dharma and knower of righteousness, spoke to the sage:
"You yourself are the knower and the performer of dharma; you are the great-grandson of Brahmā."
How indeed can one who is a great ascetic, full of splendor, a celibate student, and firm in his vows, abandon dharma by engaging with a woman during the day? (15)
"And I am the witness of those who follow dharma; therefore, I speak this to you.
Having said this to Sūrya, the copper-eyed one, overcome by a measure of anger, spoke further.
For the most powerful, there is no fault, just as fire consumes everything;
how was it that you embraced Saṃjñā, who is Vaḍavā, even during the day?
Through him, the two Aśvinī sons were born from the nostrils;
for a young woman who is consumed by desire, if she so wishes, he grants her union.
"May the fire of her passion be extinguished"—this was the great bull-like virtue of her husband.
"Who are you, a preacher of dharma to me? Go back to your own place! || 1.9 ||
"Today, in this secluded place, you have thwarted my desire;
by my curse, O evil-sighted one, you shall become invisible like Rāhu eclipsed by the sun."
"Because you have become arrogant through your own splendor, your radiance shall be destroyed;
covered by clouds, with diminished luster, become thus invisible even to the wicked. (21)
Thus cursed, Ravi said to the brahmin, that bull among sages:
"Forgive me; I am a pure Vaiṣṇava; perform your own duty."
"Just as you have cursed me, so shall you be cursed by me;
O lord of the twice-born, you shall be defeated by a kṣatriya. (23)
Your death shall come by the weapon of a Kṣatriya;
Jamadagni said to Ravi, "You shall be struck down by Śambhu."
There, the Creator of the Universe himself brought about the removal of the curse.
O Jamadagni, even though you have committed a killing, a place among the sages in heaven shall be yours;
may your life be long, and may you be peaceful and happy.
Then, on a certain day at dawn, Brahmā said to Sūrya:
"Even though you are currently covered by clouds, you shall soon become visible and be released. (27)
And in years of deficiency or excess, you shall be seized by Rāhu;
likewise when the sun is at its setting, when it is shrouded by clouds, or even when it stands at midday in the water. (28)
And at the time when the sun has half-risen, you will become visible to sinners;
otherwise, you will be visible to the meritorious at all times. ||29||
"You were defeated by Śambhu in the battle with Mālin and Sumālin;
you have returned to the excellent heaven, and you shall attain victory—do not grieve."
He spoke again to Jamadagni: "O son, even at the time of your death, Nārāyaṇa shall become your son through his own portion."
"By his valor as well, your fame shall be eternal.
Having said this and dismissed them both, Brahmā returned to Satyaloka.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the disappearance of the Sun been described at that time;
and on the fourth day of the month of Bhādrapada, the Moon carried off Tārā out of lust.
That devoted wife Tārā, though free from desire, cursed him in anger:
"Since you have touched the wife of your preceptor today, therefore on that very day... (34)
For you will become an object of evil sight for all, a source of reproach;
eclipsed by Rāhu and swallowed by the clouds, you shall become visible as something inauspicious.
Having said, "Become stained," she spoke thus to Kāma:
"You shall be reduced to ashes by some radiant being. (36)
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, it has been explained that from that time onward, the moon remains visible to evil eyes on that lunar day; such is the cause of its being visible to evil eyes.
I shall tell you of the bad dream that indeed yields evil fruit:
if one laughs with joy in a dream, or if one sees a wedding. (38)
Dancing, singing, and desired pleasures—his downfall is certain—if his teeth ache while he is walking about and he sees [them] moving. ||39||
There shall be loss of wealth for him, as well as bodily suffering,
from whose house a maiden departs taking a water-pot.
Or if one's own wife, filled with anger, departs from her home;
in such a dream, there will be the destruction of fortune and even poverty for the dreamer. (41)
But he who, having been anointed with oil, should travel toward the southern direction while mounted upon a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo—for him death is certain; of this there is no doubt.
If in a dream one sees a *japā* flower, an *aśoka*, a *karavīra*, salt, or oil on the ear, misfortune will surely befall him. (43)
Upon seeing a naked woman, a black woman, one with a severed nose, a female servant, or a widow, or upon seeing cowrie shells or palm fruits, one will experience grief. (44)
If one sees an angry Brahmin or a wrathful Brahmin woman in a dream,
there will be misfortune as well as the departure of Lakṣmī.
Upon seeing wild forest flowers, red flowers, a blossoming palāśa tree, or cotton and white cloth, one shall experience sorrow. ||46||
If one sees in a dream a woman singing and laughing, dressed in black garments, or a dark-skinned widow, one shall meet with death. ||47||
Where the deities dance, sing, and laugh; where they clap their hands and run—there indeed death shall occur. ||48||
If one sees vomit, urine, or feces, or a physician, silver, or gold—
either in person or in a dream— the observer shall live for ten days.
A woman dressed in black garments, wearing black garlands, and adorned with black ointments and the like— whoever she embraces, for him death shall certainly come to pass.
He who wears a garland of bones—whether from a stillborn calf, a shaven head, or from a deer or a human—will certainly meet with misfortune. (51)
If a man ascends alone a chariot yoked with donkeys and camels, death will watch over him even while he remains there for ten days. (52)
But if he is massaged with clarified butter, milk, honey, or even buttermilk and molasses, his pain will become extreme. (53)
If one embraces in a dream someone dressed in red garments, wearing red garlands, and adorned with red unguents and the like, that person will certainly fall ill.
Having seen fallen nails and hair, as well as an ash-covered funeral pyre that appears like extinguished embers, one certainly meets with death. (55)
Seeing a cremation ground, dry wood, a clod of earth, dry grass, something black, a horse, and a *śamī* tree, he became a partaker of extreme suffering. (56)
Upon seeing a sandal, a wooden plank, something red, a garland of flowers, something terrifying,
or a bean, lentil, or mung bean, one immediately becomes wounded.
One who sees a bracelet, a lizard, a crow, a bear, a monkey, or a cow, as well as pus or bodily filth in a dream, will become afflicted with disease. (58)

One who has broken vessels, one who is wounded, a Śūdra, one suffering from trickling leprosy, a sick person, one wearing red garments, one with matted hair, a pig, a buffalo, or a donkey—[these should not be looked upon]. (59)
Having seen a most terrible darkness, a corpse, a living being, or a source of fear, as well as a female organ or a male organ in a dream, one shall meet with calamity.
Upon seeing one of deformed appearance or a barbarian, as well as terrifying messengers of Yama with nooses and weapons in their hands, one will meet death swiftly. (61)
If, in a dream, a Brahmin, a Brahmin woman, a young son, or a young daughter laments out of anger, the one who sees this shall encounter suffering.
Upon seeing a black flower, a garland of such flowers, a crop, one bearing weapons or missiles,
or a barbarian of deformed appearance, one shall meet with death.
Having seen a corpse that has lost its life-breath and is dead, one shall meet with death;
indeed, for one who wears a fish or similar [amulets], the death of his brother shall occur.
Upon seeing musical instruments, dancing, singing, a singer dressed in red garments, or a mṛdaṅga drum being played, one shall experience sorrow. (65)
Or if one sees a severed headless trunk, deformed, with hair disheveled, quickly performing a dance, one shall meet with death. ||66||
Whether he is dead or she is dead, or if a terrifying black barbarian embraces him in a dream, or he himself embraces her; ||67||
Seeing one's own corpse in such a manner, one should quickly contemplate death;
likewise for one whose teeth are shattered and whose hair falls out.
For him, there shall be loss of wealth and bodily affliction at every step;
likewise, horned and fanged creatures shall harass him in his dreams.
The children, the men, the household members,
and his other servants— all of them shall have cause for fear from the royal court.
Upon seeing a tree being cut down, a falling object, a shower of stones, chaff, a razor, red embers, or a shower of ashes, one shall experience suffering. ||71||
Seeing a house collapsing, or a mountain, or a terrifying comet, or even a man with a broken shoulder, a person shall become distressed. (72)
If one falls to the ground from a tree, a mountain, a chariot, a house, a cow, an elephant, a horse, or from the sky in a dream, his misfortune is certain. (73)
They fall headlong into pits filled with ashes and charcoal, and into alkaline pits and powders; for them, death is certain. (74)
If a wicked person forcibly seizes a parasol or even a turban from a kinsman, there will be the destruction of his father, or of his teacher, or of the king. (75)
But from whosever house the fragrant earth departs, terrified along with the sun, from that house Lakṣmī and the proud Earth herself depart. (76)
He who is bound by the noose of Yama and led away by the messengers of Yama, or by barbarians, thieves, or others, has death close at hand. (77)
Whether it be an astrologer, a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa woman, a virtuous teacher, or a holy man, if they become angry and utter a curse, a calamity will surely befall that person. (78)
Enemies, such as cocks, crows, and hostile bears, fall upon his body when they approach; for his death is indeed certain. (79)
If in a dream buffaloes, bears, camels, boars, and donkeys run toward someone while enraged, that person will certainly fall ill.
Whoever offers oblations of red sandalwood wood smeared with clarified butter,
accompanied by a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, by that act peace is ordained.

If something undesirable should appear to oneself in a dream, that which causes it to be undesirable would become desirable [for the one who desires its cessation], and that which causes it to be desirable would become undesirable. (82)
By chanting the names of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, one shall attain freedom from sin;
at that time, an evil dream will no longer be capable of yielding its fruit.
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Śrī Hari; Śiva;
Śrī, Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, Jānakī, Prabhā, and Pārvatī. ||84||
In Japan, even twelve bad dreams result in auspicious fruits.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, salutation and svāhā to you, Durgā, the destroyer of suffering. ||85||
Having recited the mantra ten times, an evil dream becomes auspicious;
through one hundred lakhs of recitations, it becomes perfected and bestows the desired accomplishment. (86)
One should recite "Oṃ, obeisance to Mṛtyuñjaya, svāhā" one hundred thousand times;
even upon seeing death in a dream, the reciter shall become a centenarian. (87)
Having turned toward the northeast, one should reveal the dream to a wise, pure brahmin, or to a guru, a deity, or a divine being; thus it shall be fruitful. (88)

One should disclose one's dream to an Ashvattha tree, to an accountant, to a Brahmin, to the seats of the ancestors and the gods, to a noble woman, to a devotee of Vishnu, to a friend, or to one's husband. ||89||
O Kāśyapa, one should not describe a dream to one who is in a miserable state, who is lowly, who reviles gods, virtuous men, and brahmins, nor to one who is foolish, dull-witted, ignorant, or cruel.
Thus has this been told, O Lakṣmī, for the benefit of the worlds;
it brings merit, fame, and long life through both recitation and hearing. (91)

Thus ends the five hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Curse Occurring When the Sun and Moon Are Occasionally Invisible, and the Description of Evil Dreams, Their Consequences, and Their Aversion," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
For the sake of my benefit, tell me of the vows and duties of various human beings, so that the arising of liberation may occur.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Non-violence is the highest of all; it is a vow that bestows merit upon everyone.
Giving that which brings satisfaction to oneself is considered the supreme bestower of merit.
In whatever way possible, one should give happiness and satisfaction to living beings, through body, mind, speech, action, and material things. (3)
Blessings are obtained, as well as spiritual welfare, liberation, and prosperity;
likewise, bathing, meditation, my worship, the offering of food, and service [are attained]. (4)
People should always perform acts of helping others and practice contentment;
such a person, eating what is granted by the grace of Viṣṇu, becomes liberated while living. ||5||
Having received the Viṣṇu-mantra and having performed service to the guru,
and having meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, one shall attain the state of liberation.
The constant worship and nourishment of one's gurus must be performed;
indeed, among all those worthy of reverence, one's own father is the greatest guru.

The mother is a hundred times more venerable than the father; the deity is a hundred times more venerable than the mother; the teacher who imparts the mantra is four times more venerable than the deity; indeed, the teacher who bestows liberation is the most venerable of all.
The Guru who bestows both knowledge and liberation is a hundred times superior to one who merely grants liberation;
the Guru is the manifest Lord of lords, the Guru is the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
To that preceptor of the Veda, the liquor is offered during the formal instruction;
for one's own preceptor is Janārdana himself, the embodied one who is the direct enjoyer.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru himself is Śiva;
indeed, all the gods dwell perpetually and joyfully within the venerable Guru.
When the guru is pleased, Hari is pleased; by him the deities are satisfied.
The Vaiṣṇava guru is Nārāyaṇa himself, who brings about the attainment of Śrī Hari.
A Brāhmaṇa who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is eternally a guru, equal to the gods;
by drinking the water from his feet, living beings are indeed purified from sin.
One who eats the food granted by the grace of Viṣṇu makes the earth pure;
at the end, he rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha together with Hari as his attendant.
Then its support must be prepared, and the mantra should be received from that as well;
by the mere reception of the mantra, one becomes liberated while living. || 15 ||
That pure person, whose actions are directed toward the station of Viṣṇu and whose intentions are dedicated to Him, could effortlessly uplift even a thousand men. (16)
That very Śrī Hari alone is to be known; no one is dearer to me than He.
One should never receive a mantra from anyone who is impoverished or devoid of devotion.
Flesh must be understood by me as being entirely devoid of the nature of an offering;
even if it were equal to nectar, it is proclaimed to be unfit for consumption. (18)
Indeed, in former times, the Dharma-fowler, having recognized that the twice-born Mātaṅga was pure, gave his daughter to him,
for she was truly the son of Mataṅga.
"Great good fortune will come to my daughter in the house of Pavitra";
having reflected thus, she was given away, yet on one day, once again—
The mother-in-law said this to her daughter-in-law: "O daughter of a hunter, O child of a killer, you who are impure and quarrelsome, do you know what constitutes a righteous deed? (21)
Having heard this, the maiden went toward her father;
meanwhile, her mother-in-law said to me again and again, "O daughter of the hunter! (22)
The hunter went to his son-in-law's house and spoke words of auspicious greeting;
the mother-in-law provided him with food, though it was not first offered to the gods. (23)
There, neither the worship of the gods nor the purification of food was observed; the Vaiśvadeva offering was not performed at all, nor was any guest honored in that manner. (24)
Water was not even strained, nor was clarified butter offered into the fire;
no sacred utterance (vyāhṛti) was recited there, and indeed, no ritual bathing was observed in the house.
Indeed, he did not even provide a morsel of food for the cows or for the gathering of spirits;
nor did he perform the glorification of the gods, nor likewise the salutation of the Sun. (26)
Seeing that in her father-in-law’s house the rites for the gods and ancestors had not been performed by them at all, the girl's father, while seated for the meal, [spoke]. (Verse 7)
Standing there, he said: "I must certainly not accept this, because the food of one who does not offer it to the gods is declared to be mere flesh. (28)
And water is equal to the nectar of the Goddess Vāruṇī only when it is apart from the nectar of the Lord’s feet;
therefore, O Lord, I must not consume this food of yours. (29)
Since I gave away my daughter, knowing it to be a virtuous abode,
she was indeed bestowed for the sake of liberation, and certainly not for the sake of sin.
That food at which there is no twilight prayer, recitation, meditation, worship of the deity, or offering— whether it be grain or meat— is equal to liquor and water.
"Unknowingly, I have cast my daughter directly into hell;
yet, through the food offered to the deity, there is always purity for me from your house. (32)
"Without first offering to the gods, I never eat at all;
as for what was said regarding my being the daughter of a hunter, those words of yours are not true. (33)
One who is devoid of offerings to Hari is truly called a hunter by the truth;
therefore, you, Mataṅga, are considered a hunter, being bereft of the duties of a Brahmin. (34)
Even if I am a hunter by birth, I am not so in deed;
you, however, are always like a great hunter by your actions alone. (35)
"I will not send my daughter back to your home until you have returned," having said this, the Vaiṣṇava hunter, the king of devotees, went to his own home.
Having offered everything—including food, water, and so forth—to Kṛṣṇa, he ate it;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, whatever is offered to Me by people of all castes shall become auspicious. (37)
Divine food that grants liberation—such as water, leaves, petals, and the like—is always fit to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas; it should be sacrificial (haviṣya) and free from meat.
Through the renunciation of material things, one becomes radiant like the sun;
however, one who consumes food without first making an offering becomes a consumer of liquor and meat.
One should always perform the *śrāddha* rite and indeed offer water to the ancestors and deities;
likewise for one's mother, father, guru, wife, disciple, son, sister, and daughter.

Those who are without protectors, those belonging to the paternal lineage, those who must be constantly supported, and those dear to their elders—for by supporting them, Kṛṣṇa, the inner self, is truly pleased. (41)
"Whatever exists belongs entirely to Kṛṣṇa; I am not the doer of actions.
One should constantly reflect in this way through deed, mind, and speech. (42)
Every action performed as an act of total surrender shall be the severing of past karma;

Drinking milk from an iron vessel, as well as cow's products, cooked food, items from a frying pan and the like, jaggery, honey, and coconut water [are likewise forbidden]. 44.
One should not eat any fruit or root in an iron vessel, nor food that has been burnt, nor that which is excessively hot, nor that which is leavings, nor likewise that which is stale. (45)

That which causes intoxication, that which arises from the injury of living beings, and whatever is the inedible property of another; coconut water kept in a bronze vessel, and honey kept in a copper vessel. (46)
And cow-products placed in a copper vessel—all types of liquor except for clarified butter—as well as milk with salt, honey-mixed [substances], oil, jaggery, and clarified butter. (47)
One should not consume water left over from drinking in the month of Māgha, radish in Bhādrapada, curd, or juices passed from hand to hand. 48.
One should not consume camphor placed in a silver vessel that has been touched by roasted food.
Of the predatory beasts, the female boars, the female yaks, and the forest-dwellers.
Likewise, the milk of does, female monkeys, and female bears, as well as that of mares, female camels, female elephants, female donkeys, and female gavayas.
One should never consume the milk and other products of geṇḍī and citrakī; likewise, one should avoid unstrained milk, water, buttermilk, oil, ghee, and so forth. (51)
Furthermore, whatever is not offered to Hari and whatever is unfit to be eaten—
including honey mixed with ants, cow's products, molasses, and liquids [of impure origin]— is likewise forbidden.

That which is eaten by birds, that which is eaten by insects, pure cooked fruits and the like, that which is eaten by crows, and even all substances that are considered inedible—[all these may be consumed]. (53)
Food cooked in ghee, food cooked in oil, food cooked solely by fire, food cooked by the sun, or food ripened by time—such food shall be pure if it is fit for consumption. //54//
One should discard all impure water and food;
for the consumption of forbidden food, one should perform purification through the vow of reciting the name of Kṛṣṇa.
But as for action that is auspicious or inauspicious, there is no destruction of it without experience;
indeed, an evil deed never perishes through a good deed.
Good deeds are not destroyed by even an evil action;
rather, through merit, the power of sin becomes diminished. (57)
Merit arises by force, and in some cases, sin arises from one another;
however, when there is the disposition of offering everything to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, no new object of experience is produced.
Heaven is attained through good deeds alone, and hell through evil deeds;
liberation is not achieved by ritual action, but rather through service unto me. (59)
Whatever action is offered as an oblation into the fire of knowledge is reduced to ashes;
whatever is offered into me, that shall grant the fruit of liberation.
Listen to how the birth of people arises from sin;
I shall describe that birth which occurs following the punishment of Yama. 6.1.
The killer of a cow becomes a venomous serpent, and the cow itself becomes a Cāṇḍāla;
the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, having become a worm in excrement, subsequently becomes a Mleccha and then blind.
One who kills a woman shall be seized by consumption (yakṣman) and will become utterly destitute;
one who kills a fetus shall subsequently become a dog and likewise a horse.
A killer of humans becomes a lordly elephant, and from there he becomes a Kirāta;
he becomes a cock if he kills a dog, and a cat if he kills a cat. (64)
One who kills a snake becomes a snake, and one who kills an elephant or even a horse [becomes such];
one who commits the slaughter of small creatures is born as a small creature. (65)
The Śālmali tree becomes a destroyer of Aśvattha trees, and from that [karma], one becomes a Śūdra again;
so too does one who gives false testimony, an ungrateful person, and one who is exceedingly ungrateful.
One who betrays trust and slays a friend becomes a vulture again and again;
having become a pig and then a beast of prey, he is thereafter born as a Śūdra.
One who steals clothing, one who steals cattle, or a stealer of silver and pearls, having become a crane, shall thereafter become a Śūdra and then a leper. (68)
One who steals a treasury, one who steals fruit, or one who steals wealth becomes a Yakṣa;
having become a blue jay, he shall thereafter become a Śūdra.
One who steals cooked food becomes a musk deer;
a stealer of grain shall become a miser; but a stealer of gold shall suffer from leprosy.
One who dies in a state of anger becomes a donkey, a crab, a snake, or a crow;
a thief of iron is born into a lineage-less state, while a thief of ink becomes a cuckoo.
One who steals collyrium shall become a parrot; one who steals sweets shall become a worm.
One who hates Brahmins and one who hates his guru shall become a worm in the head.
One who steals blood-substances will be afflicted with blood-related disorders;
one devoid of proper conduct becomes a barbarian, and a violent person becomes lame. (73)
One who is full of egoism becomes earless; one who reviles the scriptures becomes deaf;
one who steals words becomes mute; and one who is violent becomes hairless.
One who speaks falsely will be devoid of a beard; one who utters wicked speech will be toothless; one who steals the truth will be tongueless; and a thief of books will become dull-witted. (75)
One who seizes a horse becomes a thief of horses, and is born again as a horse; furthermore, he becomes a small pony. One who steals an elephant becomes an elephant. (76)
One who steals a goat becomes a goat; one who obstructs a gift becomes a barbarian (mleccha);
and one who eats sweets alone becomes a fly or an ant.
A person who steals oil becomes an oil-presser; one who steals liquids becomes a turmeric-seller; and one who gives false medicine becomes a snake-catcher. (78)
A harlot shall become a lizard, a jackal, or likewise a female bear;
one who destroys a pond becomes a species of aquatic creature, a tortoise, or a fish. (79)
One who steals variegated garments shall become a peacock in forests and such places;
and one who steals a vessel of fire shall become a kāraṇḍava bird for a long time.
A thief of the images of the gods shall indeed become blind again and again;
one who destroys the worship of the ancestors and the gods shall become a jackal that feeds on corpses.
One who hates the guru shall become poor; one who betrays the gods shall be a hypocrite;
and one who extinguishes a lamp shall become a firefly in forest after forest. (82)
A stealer of a cow becomes a pigeon; a stealer of a garland becomes a bird;
a stealer of grain becomes a *caraka* (a type of wild animal); and a stealer of meat becomes an elephant. (83)
The frog, moreover, shall repeatedly cause suffering to the learned;
the mongoose shall be a hater of poetry, and after that, the lizard. (84)
One who sells a daughter shall indeed become a hunter again and again;
being devoid of dharma, he becomes a beast, and after that, an oil-presser.
One who speaks false slanders becomes a washerman and is also mute;
one who performs malevolent magic becomes a violent being and is also a hungry ghost (preta). ||86||
A false speaker, an astrologer, a monkey, and also a rogue—thus, O Lakṣmī, has the primary fruit born of karmic ripening been described. (87)
For one who has attachment toward desirable enjoyments and aversion toward the opposite, there will be birth again and again, born from the ripening of karma. (88)
He whose passion and hatred have departed, whose intellect is not defiled, and who has abandoned both merit and demerit, is not bound by action. ||89||
Having realized that the senses do not function toward their own objects, the one who performs the offering within the Self alone is not bound by actions. (1.530.90)
He who does not conceive the thought, "I am a woman" or "I am a man," but is always immersed in the true nature of the self—for him, karma does not cling. (91)

For one for whom suffering and happiness, and happiness and suffering, have both attained a state of equality, and who has destroyed the perception of other-nature, action does not defile them. //92//
Having himself become the very form of Brahman, if he acts solely for the sake of Brahman and remains engaged in me, the Imperishable, he shall attain liberation. ||93||
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the bondage of karma been described by me;
by reading or hearing this, the cutting away of karma shall occur. (94)

Thus ends the five hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Man in the Kṛta-yuga Lineage of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, the Becoming Hunters of Those Who Eat the Non-Consecrated Food of Hari under the Disguise of the Hunter’s Daughter, the Specification of Forbidden Foods, and the Demonstration of Birth and Other Consequences Arising from the Ripening of Karma Consisting of Sinful Fruits. ||530||

All the sages, including Lomaśa, Nārada, and others,

then the Blessed Lord Sanatkumāra spoke to those sages.
"May it be well with you, O sages; may your desired fruit of asceticism be ever-present.
In the case of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, inquiries after welfare are fruitless. (18)
Now all is well; it is indeed the time for the vision of the Supreme Self, who has manifested precisely for the purpose of relieving the burden of the earth.

The bodies of living beings who have performed actions arise from drops of blood;

In that forest of eternal bliss, a greeting of well-being is spoken:
"O you who rely on red virility, your body shall indeed never exist. (25)
By the mere act of bestowing grace upon your devotees, you are seen in a divine form; by taking refuge in you, the welfare of all living beings shall be secured at all times. (26)
Since by the touch of whom devotees attain a divine state such as yours,
you are blessed, O Blessed One, and worthy of honor even by the entire world.
"You are the Lord of all lords; there is nothing beyond you in the universe.
Having reflected thus, he bowed again and worshipped him with devotion.
To Śrīpati, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the sustainer of the imperishable realm (Akṣara),
Brahmā arrived in the meantime together with Sāvitrī.
Śambhu went with Pārvatī, and Dharma went with Mūrti;

Then Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa rose up suddenly with devotion,
and having offered the madhuparka and other gifts, he performed a most excellent reception.
Then all the sages bowed down to the gods, and the gods,
in turn, paid homage to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama.
Then, seated upon his throne in the assembly, Sanatkumāra said:
"The supreme abode has been seen by me, but Puruṣottama has not been seen. (34)
The abode and the syllable have been observed, yet the Lord of the Syllable has not been seen;
Goloka has indeed been seen by me, but the Lord of Rādhikā has not been seen. (35)
Then Vaikuṇṭha was seen, but the Lord of Śrī-Ramā was not seen;
then the Ocean of Milk was seen, yet Hari himself was not there.
Exhausted and dejected, he bathed on the shore of the Ocean of Milk;
there, upon that vast expanse, he beheld a tortoise many yojanas in size.
When I said to him, "You are fortunate," he replied to me, "I am not fortunate; rather, the Ocean of Milk is fortunate, for in it dwell beings such as I. (38)
Then I offered words of praise to the ocean;
the sea said to me, "I am not a worthy recipient of such praise. (39)
The earth, the sustainer of the world, is indeed worthy of praise,
wherein the seven oceans eternally reside within the span of a mere finger's breadth.
Then I offered praise to the Earth, and the Earth said to me: "I am not a worthy recipient of this praise. (41)
But Śeṣa Ananta is the worthy recipient of my praise, for he is my seat, upon whose hood infinite cosmic eggs reside like a tiny atom. (42)
Then I offered infinite thanks to Ananta;
Ananta said to me, "I am not a worthy recipient of this praise. (43)
The tortoise is indeed worthy of praise, my great refuge, upon whose back countless beings like me and Śeṣa dwell. (44)
Then I offered words of praise to the tortoise;
the tortoise said to me, "I am not a fit recipient for such praise. (45)
"O Sage, the earth and the waters where I dwell are indeed the ground for my praise;
for in the waters there are crores of tortoises like me. (46)
Then I offered words of praise to the great waters;
but the waters said to me, "O Sage, we are not worthy of praise. (47)
The recipient of my thanks was the one of great splendor who took refuge in the water;
therefore, I offered my gratitude to that embodiment of great majesty. (48)
And Mahātejas said to me, "The wind indeed possesses great merit;
it is fitting that I should endow the wind with words of praise. (49)
"Indeed, it is there that infinite circles of creation pass through;
and Vāyu said to me, 'O Lord, I am not worthy of praise.'"
Indeed, the recipient of this praise is the vast expanse of space;
I have offered this stream of thanks to the sky, and the sky has spoken to me. (51)
I am not blessed, for I am the inert sky, subject to birth and destruction;
rather, it is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) that is the true recipient of praise, since it is my very self.
In every creation, both origination and destruction arise;
I am but a single portion of Him, within whom reside Brahmā, Hara, and Hari. (53)
Those who dwell upon the ground of Vairāja’s hair grow for a hundred years;
from that state, I repeatedly offered my gratitude to the space of consciousness.
And the space of consciousness said to me: "I am not the vessel for the fortunate;
the state of being a vessel for the fortunate lies in the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (55)
He is united with the Lord of Syllables, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, the Sovereign Lord who ordains all incarnations. (56)
To the Lord of All, who is boundless and from whom everything proceeds;
from a single ray of whose hair there arise infinite spaces of consciousness (cidākāśa). //57//
Indeed, from whose rays the multitude of the sky of consciousness—wherein the abode of Goloka and other realms shine forth in every place—manifests itself. 58.
O Sanatkumāra, bestow upon me the state of blessedness in the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is Tāmranābha and the like; I take refuge in Him, the most blessed of all. (59)
Where the liberated ones dwell, from whence millions of incarnations arise,
and from whence the manifestations beginning with Vāsudeva come forth.
From whom dharma arises, from whom the Vedas arise, and wherein the state of the Inner Controller (antaryāmitā) resides;
he who is all-pervading and immanent, the omniscient and omnipotent one. ||6.1||
From whom the sacrifices and the ritual sections [of the Vedas] arise, and from whom the worldly activity of souls proceeds;
wherein in the end there is cessation, and from whom the fruit of action comes to be. (62)
O Sage, he who bestows the fruit, who is the cause of karma, the beginning of all, and the agent of all, should be addressed with words of praise; no other is the locus of such praise.
Having been addressed thus, I went by the power of yoga to the other world, situated beyond the imperishable realm, in order to see [him] and to offer words of praise. (64)
He is the cause of all causes; desiring to behold Him in His own abode, I am there, surrounded by the divine splendors of the liberated ones.
I was not at all able to see him, who possesses a divine form, even though he was present;
yet it is possible to go there through yoga, and it is possible to see him through his grace.
Not seeing him, he questioned the group of liberated souls as to where the Blessed One was;
having learned that he was shining resplendent near the auspicious Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, [he went there].
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpī, adorned with the hermitage of Lomaśa,
and in the home of the goddess Kambharā-Lakṣmī, within the temple of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.

Having understood this, I have come here for the purpose of seeing him who shines forth here, and to offer my words of praise.
The child, the son of Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa, is endowed with the fortune of Śrī Kambharā;

Therefore, salutations indeed to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;

Salutations to You for the destruction of the many asuras and for the protection of Your devotees;

Blessed is this Kuṅkumavāpī; blessed is this sage Lomaśa;

Blessed are these sages; blessed are the trees and plants;

You are seen as the object of all; indeed, You are attained by the wise.
Today our birth has become fruitful, and our merit is now free from bounds.

And here, for us, the four aims of human life have been realized; that refuge which is the state attained is now directly perceived and fit for service. (86)

it bestows strength and wisdom, and it destroys birth and death. (94)
It bestows upon men wealth, sons, beloved ones, and the prosperity of sovereignty;
it removes grief and suffering for whoever recites or hears it. (95)
The suffering person is released from bondage; the frightened one shall indeed be freed from fear;
the sick person is liberated from disease, and the poor man shall become wealthy. (96)
O Lakṣmī, a person seized by bandits, beset by enemies, or surrounded by predatory beasts, indeed attains well-being through this hymn. (97)
The blessed Sanatkumāra gave it to Śrī Lomaśa,
and Lomaśa, in turn, gave that which is the cause of liberation to other sages.
This should be given in every way to a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, to a servant-devotee, and to the wise seeker of liberation. 99.
This hymn bestows merit equal to a thousand horse-sacrifices, to circumambulating the entire earth, and to bathing in all the sacred fords.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Majesty and Other Qualities of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Who is Worthy of Praise, as Told in Succession by Sanatkumāra—who had arrived at the Lomaśa Hermitage in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā on the anniversary of the Jayantī festival of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to offer thanks and blessings—to the assembly of sages" in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of the sage Gauramukha.
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Supratīka, who was preeminent in strength.
He had two wives, Vidyutprabhā and Kāntimatī;
being childless, he gratified them with service at Citrakūṭa.
From him, Durvāsas granted a boon: "Become possessed of a virtuous son.
Thus, King [Vidyutprabha] obtained a son named Durjaya through Vidyutprabhā.
In Kāntimatī, he obtained a second son named Sudyumna;
thereafter, the king bestowed the kingdom of Vārāṇasī upon Durjaya.
He himself, however, went to Mount Citrakūṭa for the sake of penance;
the lord Durjaya, for his part, reflected upon the expansion of his kingdom.
Accompanied by an army of thirty akṣauhiṇīs, he conquered the northern direction— namely Kiṃpuruṣa, Harivarṣa, Romāvrata, and Kuru.
Having conquered Bhadrāśva and the region around Mount Meru, he went forth to conquer heaven;
as soon as he had ascended Mount Meru and was proceeding, [the gods obstructed him]. || 7 ||
Nārada spoke of Durjaya’s victory to the king of the gods;
Indra, taking up his army, set out for battle.
Defeated by the invincible trident of Śaṅkara,
Indra fell under his control, and all the gods likewise came under his sway.
Durjaya, having bypassed the world-protectors, went directly to the earth;
there he then encountered two asuras named Vidyut and Suvidyut.
Having arrived, both spoke to Durjaya: "Listen, O King!
Without conquering the world-protectors (Lokapālas), there can never be happiness."
"We two shall surely conquer them; grant us heaven as well.
Having said "Om," he gave the sovereignty of heaven to those two excellent friends.
Hetu and Prahetu, the two sons of Svāyambhuva Manu, who possessed vast armies and retinues, gave their two daughters in marriage.
Hetukanyā was Sukeśī, while Miśrakeśī was born of Praheta;
having obtained both of those who were difficult to conquer, he departed for his own kingdom.
Sukeśī’s son was named Prabhava, and Miśrakeśī’s son was Sudarśana; these two sons of Durjaya were possessed of great strength and prowess. (15)
Thus, King Vardhamāna once went to the Himālaya mountains with his army into the forests for the purpose of hunting.
He who then had his capital in the city of Hastināpura spent the summer season in the forests with his vast army. || 17 ||
Having stationed that army of five akṣauhiṇīs in the forest, he maintained a force numbering twenty-five [akṣauhiṇīs] in the city of Hāstinapura. || 18 ||
Then Durjaya, while wandering in the forest of the snowy regions,
saw in a wilderness area a sage named Gauramukha.
It was frequented by many sages and was the foremost abode of the great Bhāgavatas;
there, indeed, the great ṛṣis taught the Vedas to the young boys.
The sages were teaching sections of the Vedas to the maidens;
Durjaya indeed went to the circle of hermitages for the purpose of seeing them.
Then the sage Gauramukha offered a welcome to the king and provided food for him and his followers according to his ability.
"I shall do so; let the draft animals be released well throughout the forest.
The king, pleased by that devotion, remained right near the hermitage.
The sage, having remembered the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in his mind, quickly caused an army of five akṣauhiṇīs to encamp there.
Having reflected, "What food should be given to him by me?
he entered the waters of the Gaṅgā and praised the illustrious Narāyaṇa.
Salutations to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of the imperishable realm (Akṣaradhāman)!
Salutations to you, whose form is primordial, and who holds a lute with two arms! 26.
Salutations to the Lord of Lakṣmī, who bears the conch and the discus;
salutations to You, the divine bestower of all, the protector of devotees, and the upholder of wealth. || 27 ||
Salutations to you who abide here within the five elements, and salutations to you who reside in the heart;
salutations to you who fill all things and are imperishable. ||28||
Salutations to you who uphold the vow of Brahman and who reside upon Śeṣa in the ocean;
salutations to you, from whom all this has arisen and who are the giver of everything at all times. ||29||
From you come sacrifice, as well as offerings to the gods and ancestors, food, and water;
indeed, your entire body consists of these—therefore, offer this food to Him.
"O Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, this king here is indeed invincible;
he has arrived as a guest, so O Mādhava, grant him hospitality. (3.1)
"And I am your servant; provide a store of food and other necessities, for whatever I touch with my hand and whatever I behold with my eye," [he said]. (32)
Whether it be wood or grass-root, each of those four kinds of food;
likewise, drinkable water, sweet milk, curd, ghee, and so forth. ||33||
May all that which has been meditated upon by my mind be accomplished for me;
indeed, O Acyuta, let there be hospitality through your very power alone.
Thus praised, the gracious-souled Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, endowed with splendor and seated upon Garuḍa, appeared visibly in his presence. 35.
Seeing Hari holding a conch, a discus, a bow, a thunderbolt, a banner, and a trident, that sage bowed to him and, with palms joined in reverence, then spoke: ||36||
Now, this king, together with his army and vehicles, having taken his meal in my hermitage, shall depart for his own home tomorrow. (37)
Act accordingly, O Great King, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Master! ||38||
Thus addressed, Śrī Hari formerly granted him purity of mind;
thereafter, he gave him a divine cintāmaṇi jewel of great luster.
Having given that [gift], Kṛṣṇa vanished; and that sage Gauramukha, having touched the jewel, meditated upon a lofty, great palace.
The house, indeed, was a hundred stories high, shaped like a peak of the Himalayas,
pervaded by the rays of the moon, and furnished with objects of gold and silver.
By the power of Viṣṇu’s jewel, the brāhmaṇa constructed thousands, lakhs upon lakhs, and indeed all kinds of such dwellings in every direction.
Likewise, there were ramparts at the edge, with gardens attached to them,
abounding with cuckoos, swans, cranes, saras birds, and peacocks.
And there were [forests] filled with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *nāgakesara* trees, as well as various trees, creepers, shrubs, and flowers, frequented by many birds. ||44||
There were elephant stables for the elephants, horse pens for the horses, and sheds for camels, gayals, and bulls. (45)
By means of his resolve, he fashioned and prepared a collection of foods:
eatables, chewables, lickables, suckables, and drinks with sugar.
He provided food and drink, as well as vegetables and condiments, along with vessels of gold and silver, and various kinds of fruits. (47)
Having done this, that brahmin spoke to the king of great splendor:
"Let all the troops [enter] houses marked with their respective names. (48)
May they enter there happily and dwell there with joy;
[a city] ten yojanas in width and thirty yojanas in length.
The armies entered the divine city, which shone like the sun;
the king, however, entered his own palace, which was as lofty as a mountain.
Then Gauramukha, taking the jewel, said to the king:
"For the sake of bathing and dining, [send] servants as well as courtesans. (51)
Having addressed him and touched the jewel, he sent him forth and said:
"By its power, there shall arise male and female servants in nine different states. (52)
Then, while that king was looking on, women emerged—possessing delicate complexions and unguents, divine, and in the prime of youth. (53)
With beautiful cheeks, lovely-limbed forms, fine hair-ends, and beautiful eyes,
and possessing the luster of the color of golden campaka flowers, there were likewise hundreds of thousands of such youths.
Beautiful, having entered their youth, and resembling gods, some set out carrying golden vessels. (55)
In this manner, all the maidens and boys, as well as the servants,
prepared the cooked food for the sake of the king and his army.
Some performed the dressing of her garments, while others bathed her; some massaged her feet, and others prepared the bedding. ||57||
Others gave betel leaves and likewise offered sweet water;
others fanned them, while still others performed songs.
The servants indeed performed service for the people according to their needs,
and various kinds of musical instruments were played there in great abundance.
While that king was immersed, other women danced;
thus, having bathed with such divine attendants, the mighty king—
The army also ate various kinds of food according to the prescribed rites;
for the honoring of the servants was performed just as that of the king. (6.1)
The king of sages performed the most excellent honor for his elephants, horses, and other animals, as well as for his own male and female servants. 62.
Then the night arrived, endowed with the splendor of the moon;
and delightful visions were displayed by the sage.
The dances of women and great festivals were displayed,
as well as the auspicious wrestling matches of the athletes.
Divine songs and excellent musical instruments were played,
and those who delight in the melodies of the Gandharvas displayed their jeweled anklets.
Explanations, pleasing tales, and even jokes were composed; there were also gambling matches, magic tricks, and performances by actors and dancers.
And other types of visual bonds were displayed at midnight;
then, upon their couches made of jewels and gold, [the women lay down]. (67)
On soft surfaces strewn with flowers, the women performed their service;
and the king was served by celestial maidens upon an excellent couch.
Thus, through the power of that sage Maṇi, who was so well-disposed,
the king and his armies then slept happily and joyfully.
For the purpose of the morning rising rites, various musical instruments were played everywhere by the maidens along with singers.
Having bathed, drunk water, and partaken of food, the king,
together with his army, proceeded in haste for the worship of Gauramukha.
He arrived at the leaf-hut where the sage Maṇi resided;
then the maidens, the servants, and all the dwellings [followed].
The household utensils and all food and drink completely vanished; in an instant, that entire place became a forest.
Filled with wonder upon seeing that, the king reflected again and again: "How is it that this jewel has come to me? (74)
Thinking, "I shall take this wish-fulfilling gem from him," he bowed and, having gone outside the hermitage, spoke to the minister: (75)
"Go to the sage Virocana and indeed make a request for the jewel.
Having approached that ṛṣi, he prepared to ask for the jewel. (76)
"The king is a vessel for jewels; let a gem be given to him.
When the minister had spoken thus, Gauramukha, filled with anger, said:
"A king should always be the giver, while the recipient should be a Brahmin;
yet you, being a king yourself, how is it that you beg like a wretched man? (78)
"You are unworthy; you are not a fit vessel for the jewel. Do not make this request—[you who think] the three worlds, including heaven and even the underworld, are under your control. (79)
"Even though there is Mount Meru and the oceans of jewels, alas, there is still poverty!
You harbor an unjust desire for the wealth of a Brahmin. (1.532.80)
For the ignorant man who remains unsatisfied, all objects of sense may be present in his home;
nevertheless, that sinful man does not attain peace due to his craving.
"Speak thus to King Durjaya himself, who is of evil conduct:
'Go quickly, before some obstacle arises for you. (82)
The messenger went to the king and spoke as was appropriate;
the king, in anger, said to the vassal named Nīla, "Go, do not delay! (83)
"Having taken the Brahmin’s jewel, come quickly to my side!
Nīla then went very swiftly as he was entering the cave of the jewel. 84.
From that jewel there emerged by the millions warriors with weapons in their hands, some on chariots, others with banners, all bearing swords and shields. (85)
Equipped with bows, quivers, arrows, spears, and short clubs, there were fifteen akṣauhiṇīs and fifteen leaders. ||86||
By name they were Suprabha, Dīptitejas, Śubhadarśana, Sukānti, Sundara, Sunda, Pradyumna, Sumanas, and Śubha. ||87||
Suśīla, Sukhada, Śambhu, Sudānta, Soma,
and Suraśmi— all these formidable warriors engaged in battle.
Likewise, spears, tridents, swords, and bows, as well as maces, thunderbolts, and javelins of the great warriors fell [upon him]. (89)
Chariot stood encircling chariot, and likewise elephant against elephant;
horse rushed against horse, and foot-soldier indeed against foot-soldier.
While that battle continued unceasingly, a river arose there from blood;
the king’s minister, unconscious, was slain in the fray along with his army. 91.
Durjaya himself fought there with those born of jewels;
indeed, the slaughter of the remaining army appeared total.
Then, a great clamor was heard from Hetṛ and Praheta as they fought;
fifteen fierce armies were his allies in that battle.
Fifteen leaders were dispatched to the front of the battle;
hear now their names—those who did not rise again and perished. (94)
Praghasa, Vighasa, Saghasa, Aśaniprabha, Vidyutprabha, Sughoṣa, Pronmattākṣa, and Pratardana.
Agnidanta, Agnitejas, Bāhu, Śakra, Virodhaka, Bhīmakarman, and Vipracitti—these were the Daityas with supreme weapons. (96)
Mahāmāyā fought with those preeminent warriors armed with jewels;
and those fifteen akṣauhiṇīs of the Daityas were indeed slain.
Meanwhile, Hetu and Prahetu advanced with ten million troops;
likewise, Vidyut and Suvidyut were both asuras who had become lords of heaven.
Hearing that they had come to Himavat with thirty akṣauhiṇīs to provide assistance in battle, the earth trembled. 99.
There, the river Raktavāhā flowed swiftly toward the ocean;
then Gauramukha beheld the infinite army of the Rākṣasas.
He remembered the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master and Lord of Maṇipati.
Then Śrī Hari, clad in yellow garments and seated upon His bird-vehicle (Garuḍa), appeared before him. 101.
Having approached him, he said, "Tell me, what task must I perform here?
The sage replied, "O Blessed One, slay this invincible king."
Having heard this regarding the Daityas, the slayer of Daityas released his discus;
that discus, equal to ten million suns, reduced the invincible foe to ashes.
"Neither the armies nor the rākṣasas shall remain; not even one will be left here.
In a mere twinkling of an eye, this race of Dānavas has been slain," he said.
Therefore, this forest shall be known by the name Araṇya;
it will truly become the dwelling place of the seers (ṛṣis). || 1.05 ||
And I am the Sacrificial Person (Yajñapuruṣa) here in this forest retreat; these fifteen leaders are always to be worshipped by name. (106)
"In the Kṛta Yuga, these kings shall arise in succession from this jewel.
Having spoken thus and taken the jewel, the god vanished.
The twice-born one also remained in his own hermitage, filled with supreme joy;
and all the armies likewise attained absorption into Śrī Viṣṇu.
Durjaya became absorbed in Śrī Hari there through yoga;
the armies, struck down by the discus, went to heaven by virtue of that yoga.
Thus, O beloved, the portions of Nārāyaṇa born from the jewel have been described;
by reading or hearing this, there shall be liberation as well as heaven.
Then the brahmin Gauramukha, desiring to propitiate Hari for the sake of destroying the misfortunes caused by battle, went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa.
In Saurāṣṭra, on the Raivata ground, having bathed in the pool named Dāmodara, in the Nārāyaṇa lake, and in the ocean joined by the Gomatī river; || 112 ||
He went to the Sarasvatī in the east and to Aśvapaṭṭasara,
to the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, and to the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa.
There arrived the king of sages, the great seer Mārkaṇḍeya;
having first bowed to Lomaśa, he then paid homage to Mārkaṇḍeya.
To the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the giver of the jewel, who is present before one's very eyes, the son of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa; (1.15)
The sage Gauramukha indeed considered himself to have accomplished his purpose.
Om, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord. 1.16.
Reciting this mantra, he questioned the god Mārkaṇḍeya for the sake of liberating the deceased and for the destruction of evil deeds.
"Instruct me, O holy one, as to what I should perform here.
And Mārkaṇḍeya said to him: "Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is Hari. (1.18)
The Lord who exists here as the primordial source of all the gods—worship that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Śrī, directly before your eyes. 1.19.
By that, there shall indeed be liberation for all and the destruction of all evils in this sacred field; therefore, perform the śrāddha rites here.
Thus addressed, that sage performed śrāddha rites out of a desire for liberation;
he himself brought about the deliverance of those who had died in battle.
By means of their celestial chariots, they all went to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self.
This Gauramukha was, in a previous birth, Bhṛgu himself.
Then this son born of his lineage, the lord of sages Mārkaṇḍeya,
awakened his father once again through the performance of a Śrāddha ceremony.
Then Gauramukha, having understood that there and performed the libation (tarpaṇa), remembered all his past births; and having remembered them, he [focused] upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having surrendered his entire being, he went to the abode named Akṣara; he attained dissolution in the Lord of All, who is designated as "the state beyond rebirth."

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Durjaya’s Sovereignty over the Three Worlds, the Welcome with the Jewel Offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa at Gauramukha’s Hermitage, the Battle for the Cintāmaṇi, the Destruction of Durjaya and Others, Gauramukha’s Arrival at Prabhāsa, and His Liberation," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the discourse concerning the supreme self (adhyātma) that arose from the dispute among the gods—
the knowledge which the Blessed Lord Varāha formerly spoke to the Earth.
A king named Suprabha was born from a wish-fulfilling gem;
his second name, Prajāpāla, was indeed meaningful.
Once, he went with joy to see the sages at their hermitages,
where there dwelt a sage named Mahātapa who possessed a lifespan of an entire kalpa.
Performing penance without food, he recited the eternal Brahman;
there, where trees, creepers, shrubs, grasses, and birds [dwelt], || 4 ||
Even beasts, wild animals, and reptiles exist as seekers of liberation;
free from passion and hatred, they abide in austerity like sages.
Beholding those great ascetics, that protector of subjects entered their hermitage with joy; and upon seeing the sage, he rejoiced.
He bowed with supreme devotion and joyfully prostrated himself like a staff upon seeing that sage seated on a mat of kusha grass at that time.
The king quickly forgot his mind, which was composed of illusion and pervaded the world;
through the presence of the sage, he made his mind intent upon dharma.
Seeing that king, the sage performed the rites of hospitality for a guest, [inquiring] about his desire to know the self and likewise his acquisition of the means to liberation.
"An offering seat, a welcome, a drink, food, and kind words"—
then the humble king questioned that peaceful sage.
O Blessed One, please declare to me, who am bowed before you, that which must be done by men desiring victory who are submerged in the suffering of saṃsāra, so that it may bring them happiness. (11)
Having heard that, O King, Mahātapa said: "Listen to me;
it is a firm, stable, and solid boat for those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra."
One should serve the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama);
likewise, worship, gifts, sacrifices, meditation, and total self-surrender [should be performed]. (13)
And this servitude is indeed considered these divine stairways; taking hold of their ladder-like devotion, perform your ascent.
"You will undoubtedly go even to the further shore of the ocean beyond;
however, the king asked: 'How indeed should worship be performed for that Hari? (15)
The sage said: "The worship of Hari should be performed as I shall tell you;
it may be done before an image made of metal and other materials, or before a śālagrāma, or else before Śiva. (16)
One should meditate upon Janārdana within virtuous people, virtuous women, cows, the guru, one's master, parents, a devoted wife, and the sun.
One should meditate upon Puruṣottama in the fire, in a Brahmin, in a young girl, in a child, in one who is helpless and without refuge, in a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), and in the Tulasī plant.

One should meditate on the mind within the heart, and likewise upon the self within the senses and the body; one should meditate on the Self within the deities and worship the Lord of Śrī accordingly.
In this way, Kṛṣṇa is pleased with both men and women;
all these who have arisen are indeed the very body of Hari.
Agni, as well as the Aśvins, Gaurī, Gaṇeśa, and the serpent;
Kārttikeya, as well as the Ādityas, the Mothers, and the Durgās. || 21 ||
The quarters of space, Kubera, Viṣṇu, Yama, Rudra, Śaśin, and likewise the Pitṛs—these were born from the form of Nārāyaṇa. (22)
These indeed are worthy of worship, for they are endowed with Nārāyaṇa;
they truly become the very forms arising from Nārāyaṇa.
The king said: "Where must those beautiful forms be obtained by me, so that I may indeed worship them with excellent offerings and sensory enjoyments? (24)
The sage said: "Listen, O King; for their forms are of two kinds. Those that are divine and of the nature of gods do not become perceptible. (25)
The Ādityas dwell here within his body as its very range of perception;
they indeed always exist as the forms of the constituent parts of reality (tattva). ||26||
Once, they each individually became filled with pride on all sides, thinking:
"I am worthy; I am the best; I am always the one to be worshipped in this body. (27)
"And there is no one else here in this body who is equal to me.
Thus, indeed, a dispute arose among those principles. (28)
But for the sake of reaching a decision regarding them as they were disputing,
the blessed Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the Sovereign, spoke to them with logical reasoning.
"O King, that without which this [universe] would not exist for you is indeed the greatest.
When this was said, O King, Vahni (Fire) rose up first.
He said: "I am the Great One; worship me, take refuge in me.
Indeed, the body would surely meet its destruction if it were deprived of me. (3.1)
Having spoken thus, the digestive fire Vaiśvānara departed;
having left the body, he dwelt elsewhere for exactly one year.
But even after he had departed, that body did not decay;
then it was truly known by the fire that I am not the most excellent one after all. (33)
Then the two Aśvins, manifest in bodily form and consisting of the nature of prāṇa and apāna, spoke thus in the assembly of the gods: "We two are the foremost. (34)
Having spoken thus, they abandoned their bodies and remained somewhere;
for even without those bodies, they remained as if they were still there for the duration of a year.
And by means of *kumbhaka*, they indeed became perfectly steady and free from the movement of breath;
then knowledge arose in them both, since they were the most excellent of sailors. (36)
Then Speech spoke: "Gaurī, my preeminence prevails.
Having spoken thus, that auspicious goddess emerged from the field.
Even without her, that field remained deficient in speech;
by that silence, she realized: "I am not the most excellent, since [the field] is silent. (38)
Then Gaṇapati, known as Ākāśa, spoke these words:
"Without me, no body whatsoever can remain stable for even a year. (39)
Having uttered "I am great," he too emerged from the body;
though thus separated, he did not cause this body to perish.
Even that which is called destruction does not disintegrate without it;
devoid of its cavities, it remains established exactly as before. (41)
Through that, there arose in him the realization regarding space: "Since I am not the most excellent, [so too are] all the elements, including the gross elements and the rest. (42)
Saying, "The maintenance of this body bereft of us is impossible;
we are the most excellent," the vital breaths (śarīrajas) abandoned the body. ||43||
Even a field abandoned by those [cultivators] is still protected by the person;
it is not destroyed, but rather becomes withered, even though it was once endowed with consciousness.
"Indeed, because of him, knowledge of the elements has arisen; we are not superior.
Seeing him, Skanda, who possessed a nature of egoism, spoke. (45)
Even the very arising of the body is not admitted without me;
therefore, I am the most excellent, and there is no other equal to me. (46)
Having spoken thus, he departed from the body and stood apart;
for a year, the body remained as if abandoned by him.
Neither decayed nor dead, he remained peaceful as before; through that, knowledge arose in him: "Since [he is thus], I am not the most excellent. (48)
Then Cakṣurbhānu, becoming enraged, spoke in haste:
"Without me, this field does not function for even a single moment. (49)
Having spoken thus, that [body] departed; yet the body did not perish.
And having returned, he beheld that frame standing just as it was before.
From that, there arose in him the knowledge: "Since I am not the most excellent, therefore the mothers are merely the subtle elements of the defects such as desire. (51)
And the sense objects, beginning with sound, declared: "We are indeed the most excellent;
there is no existence of a body apart from us. (52)
Having spoken thus, the group of Mothers then went outside for a year;
yet his body did not decay at all, remaining exactly as it was before.
"Knowledge arose among the Mothers, yet for that reason we did not attain preeminence.
Then Durgā, who is the root-illusion (mūlamāyā) consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), spoke in anger: 54.
"Without me, there is no prosperity for him; therefore, I am superior in every respect.
