so too are Lomaśa, Nārasiṃha, Sanaka and the others, who possess long life. (95)
Mārkaṇḍeya, Pañcaśikha, Voḍhu, Āsuri, as well as Dattātreya, Hanumān, Gaṇeśa, and Vyāsa—[these are the sages]. (96)
Jāmbavān, Kapila, and others who dwell in that sacred field—by their power, living beings are liberated even from residing in the midst of it. ||97||
Ten thousand arbudas and three koṭis [of sages] always dwell in Saurāṣṭra, their forms invisible.
O virtuous lady, it is possible to describe the qualities of Mount Meru and even the drops of the oceans, but not those of the divine sacred field of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa here. 99.
"His virtues cannot be fully described even in hundreds of millions of years," Śaṅkara said to the Goddess, and then he became silent.
O Lakṣmī, having thus heard of the supreme and meritorious sacred field of my husband Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Pārvatī remembered Hari.
And remaining constantly established in meditation, she remembers with devotion the field of Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which bestows supreme liberation. 102.
Through hearing, reciting, remembering, or even bowing down to this,
the sacred field bestows enjoyment and liberation, as well as prosperity upon living beings.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Kuṅkumavāpī Tīrtha-Kṣetra in Saurāṣṭra, as Narrated by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī," within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī; then the goddess Pārvatī, remembering the words of Hari from her dream, praised and made a request to her husband Śaṅkara.
The Lord of Life, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Blessed One himself, said:
"O Mother, why indeed do you never come to my sacred field?"
"O beloved, I was addressed in this very manner by the Blessed One in a dream:
'I wish to see that sacred field adorned by Gopāleśvara. (3)
I desire to see that place where the glorious Lord Viṣṇu, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, resides together with millions of liberated souls and others.
That tantra which is indeed the wheel of the world, and that tantra which is the wheel of dissolution—
wherever that God resides, I wish to see that place.
For wherever that Kṛṣṇa resides, under whose authority the protection of the worlds proceeds, I desire to see that place.
I wish to see that place where he is supported by that region, by whom all the great elements are sustained within his body.
Because [he appeared as] the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, Kapila, Hari, Vāsudeva, and likewise Pṛthu; || 8 ||
Dattātreya, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, the Lord Vāmana,
Paraśurāma, Yajñanārāyaṇa, and the Kumāras.
Sanaka and the others, as well as Rāma, Hayagrīva, and Nārada;
Vyāsa, Buddha, and likewise Kalki, Haṃsa, and Mohinī.
For these incarnations of Viṣṇu are born as protectors of the world;
I wish to see that place where he shines. || 1 ||
Rādhā, Ramā, Satī, Lakṣmī, Padmā, Padmāvatī, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Lalitā, Kṛṣṇā, Jayā, Māṇikī, and Tulasī. (12)
Vṛndā, Śrī, Kamalā, Sītā, Rukmiṇī, Draupadī, Śivā, Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Haṃsā, Śāradā, Mañjulā, and Rati. || 13 ||
Mūrti, Mānasā, Sandhyā, Gāyatrī, Mūlaprakṛti, Sāvitrī, Devikā, Mukti, Śānti, and Bhakti are her feminine forms.
Since they were born from her as the mothers of the worlds and are bestowers of happiness, I desire to see that place where she shines. (15)
The Blessed One is indeed the foundation for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
I wish to behold that place of his, which is the site of both dissolution and renewed creation.
I desire to see that place where the god Sahasrakramaṇa, who possesses a thousand rays of knowledge, resides with his thousand necks.
That ancestral home which was produced from the navel through mere conceptualization, and that Lord, the husband of Śivā, who was born from a drop of dharma on the forehead; || 18 ||
He from whose heart Lakṣmīpati himself was indeed born, he too was born from whom; he is his great-great-grandfather.
O Śambhu, I desire to behold that place where You shine resplendent,
having made Your bed upon the ocean of milk while seated on the couch of Śeṣa.
I desire to behold the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, from whom he [the manifest form] arose, and who is the one who causes even Him to descend. ||21||

He indeed delights, in accordance with their respective natures, with those who consume oblations, those who consume raw flesh, those who consume worldly existence, those who consume the immortal nectar, and likewise those who do not eat at all.
I wish to see that Lord in the form of a child as seen in my dream, who is the Supreme Lord and the refuge of both three and four [worlds]. (23)
I desire to see that Lord, the five and the sixteen,
upon whom the splendors, the austerities, and the offerings depend.
O Śambhu, I desire to see quickly that Supreme Lord, the most beloved of the beloved, in whom ritual acts, renunciation, and self-surrender find their refuge. (25)
Thus addressed, Lord Śaṅkara, beholding the devotion of the woman,
spoke sweetly to the Goddess while remembering Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
O blessed one, O honorable one, always worthy of worship, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, and devoted to your husband—I rejoice upon hearing your words, which are nourished by the water of devotion. (27)
I am blessed, for in my home is a wife who is firm in her vows toward Nārāyaṇa, devoted to her chosen deity, and dedicated to the salvation of the world. (28)
O Queen, there is no one in all the worlds as fortunate as I, since my wife has been delighted by the service of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (29)
O virtuous lady, I too have a desire to see that place;
since much time has passed, I shall indeed go there once again with you.
"O beloved, may your good fortune increase, since you have pleased my mind;
we shall travel by way of the sky with many offerings of worship. (3.1)
We shall perform the ritual worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa according to the injunctions during the month of Kārttika; we shall indeed remain there in that beautiful place. (32)
"We shall observe Śivarātri there indeed on Raivatācala;
then, on the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day, we shall bathe at Somanātha. (33)
And we two shall perform the Śrāvaṇa rite at Kṛṣṇapattana on the Gomatī river;
having observed the Navarātra at Camatkāra, we shall go to Kailāsa itself.
"O Great Goddess, we shall come; tell us likewise of Nandīśvara, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya, and the circle of Yoginīs. (35)
Also the mandala of the Durgās, the eleven Rudras, Gaṅgā, Vīrabhadra, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍa as well. (36)
Śṛṅgin, Bhṛṅgin, Rīṭin, Kirīṭin, and Īśāna;
as well as Agni, Maṅgala, Candra, Kāla, and Bhairava. (37)
Tell me likewise of Durvāsas, as well as of Lābha, Toṣa, and the Siddhis;
and of Ṛddhi, Hanumān, and my other servants.
"O Goddess, tell your attendants as well: 'Let all those who are eager for the journey depart, taking with them the necessary equipment for their mounts. (39)
Having thus received this command from Śaṅkara, the virtuous Pārvatī,
being well-pleased, rose up and proclaimed it in every way.
Let them quickly prepare for a successful journey to the region of Saurāṣṭra, where Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), resides. ||41||
Somanātha, Vāmana, Bhaveśa, and Gopikāpati are there;
all those who travel through the sky must go there for the sake of pilgrimage. 42.
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and the sage Lomaśa. ||43||
Having seen, honored, and served our mother Kambharālakṣmī and our father Gopālakṛṣṇa, we shall go having fulfilled our purpose.
Thus, those inhabitants of Kailāsa, endowed with many jewels and other riches,
joyfully performed a pilgrimage on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
For the drums were beaten and cries of victory were proclaimed;
they all set out through the sky and arrived within the space of a single ghaṭikā. 46.
Adorned in the sky by the mounts of millions of goddesses,
Mahādeva, followed by them, spoke at every stage along the way.
I am this Kedāranātha, and likewise I am Dakṣeśvara; this is Arbuda, this is Puṣkara, and this is a field of the Siddhas.
And my sacred field Raṇeśvara has come here to Saurāṣṭra;
this is Mahāviṣṇu as Sāleśa, and this is the great river Bhadrā. 49.
This is the river Śatruñjitā and the Dhūnikā of Gorakṣa;
and this is the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, which forms the western and northern boundary.
In Madhyadvīpa is the temple where the Kuṅkumavāpikā is located;
this is the supreme abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
To the south, within this expanse of trees, lies the hermitage of Lomaśa;
likewise, this vast tiger-infested forest is seen stretching far and wide.
"To the west of this Raivata mountain lies another [range] five yojanas further away";
having spoken thus, Śaṅkara and his attendants, together with Pārvatī and her retinue, [departed]. ||13||
Handfuls of fresh flowers mixed with liquid sandalwood were offered from the path of the sky upon the seven-storied palace.
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is most victorious!"—with these words and sounds, all directions were filled on every side. (55)
Then Lomaśa, Kambharā-lakṣmī, Gopāla-kṛṣṇa,
and the sages, beholding those who had ascended upwards, followed after them in the sky.
Then shouts of "Victory!", "Homage!", and "Blessed! arose;
having gathered together, they descended upon the western region of Setumāṇḍala.
That region in the western direction became known by the name Teru;
and having gone to the east, they indeed performed a circumambulation of the Setu.
That region then became radiant; because they had previously departed through the path of the immortals, that place became known as Amarabhūmikā.
Through the sounding of the drum, the earth became filled with the roar of drums;
and having gone to the mouth of the tiger-infested forest by way of the bridge, those deities [proceeded].
Then, having arrived at the southwestern bridge,
they proceeded with eagerness to the pond-island and the seven-storied temple.
Lomaśa and the other sages offered a welcome and auspicious honor to Śambhu, the God of gods, and performed a most excellent worship of Satī.
They offered seats, water for honor, and fruits;
then they went to see Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who was staying within the palace.
There shines the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, endowed with hundreds of long-lived beings and worshipped by millions of liberated souls. 64.
Adorned with his incarnations and attended by the gods,
the Lord was worshipped by them on the night of the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
He is praised by countless consorts such as Rādhā and Ramā,
and extolled by Śaṅkara and others through Vedic mantras and the sixteen [great hymns].
Then Kṛṣṇa was consecrated with the lustration rite (nīrājita) and adorned again and again;
Pārvatī applied a mark of musk along with saffron upon his forehead.
Then Śambhu applied an auspicious tilaka, beautiful with unbroken grains of rice, and Pārvatī subsequently applied a lovely tilaka made of sandalwood paste.
The cheek of Hari, filled with the loveliness of ten million Cupids,
was repeatedly marked with fresh saffron as if it were adorned with a moon.
Seeing the enchanting Kṛṣṇa, the Queen of the Gods was filled with delight;
she presented him with various offerings, including jewels and gold.
Having prostrated like a staff, they conversed with one another;
[there was] the child Gopālanandana, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (71)
After the worship was concluded, the Supreme Lord himself rose quickly from his seat and bowed at the feet of Śambhu and Pārvatī.
Having washed his feet according to the rite of hospitality, Lomaśa drank water;
and with a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he prepared for the encampment of the armies.
He constructed a great circular city, Āraivata,
within an area of twenty-five yojanas on the earth.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself personally provided them all with food, drink, shelter, and other necessities, and served them all.
And the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, his eyes filled with tears, said to Śambhu:
"I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose; my home has been sanctified by you. (76)
And you have granted me the foremost place among all those worthy of veneration—these other lords who have come to my hermitage. (77)
Blessed is this bright earth as far as the cosmic egg shall endure;
for that long it shall be known as purifying and in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha). ||78||
The great Lakṣmī, known as Kambharā, spoke auspiciously to Pārvatī: "O Satī, what more need be said to the Mother of the World? I have been purified by you. (79)
My young son was raised by you, who dispel all suffering; O virtuous lady, she who could not be seen even through ascetic penances has been seen by me today.
The merit of all previous births has indeed been recalled here;
welcome in every way, O daughter of Himavat, O daughter of Śambhu, bestow peace! 81.
"O Bringer of Peace, I, together with my maidservant, shall perform service for you.
Having spoken thus, Kambharālakṣmī then began massaging his feet.
In the manner of a guest of Pārvatī,
he performed services such as attending to her needs upon most divine couches that surpassed even those of Kailāsa.
Those deities, beginning with Śaṅkara, attained splendor through offerings of food, excellent drinks, and betel leaves given with devotion. ||5||
All the people of Kṛṣṇa gave [gifts], they received them, and may you be happy;
Śaṅkara and the others indeed slept, as did Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa at that time. 85.
She said to her mother Pārvatī, "O virtuous lady, my words have been honored;
Ramā and my other wives offer you a warm welcome. (86)
"This is my [consort] named Pārvatī; this is her companion Prabhā; this is my beloved Māṇikī; this is the devoted Lakṣmī;
this is Rādhā; this is Lalitā; this is Jayā; and this is Kamalā."
This is Padminī, this is Bhārgavī, and this is the liberated Devikā. ||88||
This is the Campēyā, this is the Hemabhēyā, and this is the Śānteyā; this is the Vājinī, this is the Mauktikeyā, this is the Mañjuleyā, and this is the Guṇavatī Haṃsā. ||89||
In this way, thousands of others exist;
let these indeed perform service for you here, while I go to my own abode.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa went to his palace and slept soundly; in the morning, various musical instruments were sounded.
Divine instruments were sounded and the people awoke;
for this is the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārtika, the Jayantī of my Śrī Hari. (92)
Then, after performing their daily rites, Śaṅkara and the others became ready and resplendent before the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (93)
In the morning, the deities headed by Śiva and Indra, as well as the sages and seers, came to the temple to perform worship and consecration. (94)
The Pitṛs, Kaśyapas, and other Brāhmaṇas and humans, as well as the liberated goddesses, celestial maidens, and serpent-maidens, [attained this state]. (95)
Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Guhyakas, Sādhyas, Kimpuruṣas, and others; virtuous wives devoted to their husbands, women observing the vow of Brahman, and women perfected through yoga. ||96||
The mothers, the forest goddesses, the rivers, the cities, and the cows—these are the streams of milk, the streams of curd, and the clarified butters. (97)
Having gathered honey-syrups, sugar-candies, and waters from sacred fords, they brought golden jars filled with fruits and unbroken grains of rice.
Having performed the rites of the water-procession and other ceremonies while singing songs upon their heads,
they arrived at the divine and beautiful palace presided over by Sarvanātha.
Garlands of flowers, sandalwood, musk, and likewise unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as the essence of flower-nectar and fragrant oils.
Taking fragrant substances that were soft to the touch and those which caused a red hue,
they approached Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having put on his auspicious golden garment, sat upon an excellent golden throne on the shore of the lake.
Then, by the grace of the gods, Bṛhaspati and the others caused him to perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and gave him water for sipping (ācamana).
Having offered the *argha* and performed the ritual bath with water, thereafter,
a beautiful-looking bath with milk was caused to be performed in a vessel of milk.
Then the clouds released water via the path of the sky;
the cowherd women, the goddesses, and others showered thick curds upon Kṛṣṇa.
The gods released clarified butter and the forest deities released honey;
Earth and the other elements bestowed upon him a brilliant bath of sugar-candy.
The oceans, rivers, excellent holy fords,
and waters from other sources then performed an auspicious consecration for him with sandalwood oil.
Having performed anointing and massaging, and having bathed him, the gods gave him divine garments; and the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) gave him ornaments.
Likewise, others gave all kinds of excellent garments; others gave crowns, earrings, necklaces, rings, chains, and so forth. (109)
Having held up a parasol and black fly-whisks,
the deities joyfully performed the lustration ceremony with the principal Vedic hymns and other sacred recitations.
Having offered flowers as a gesture of apology, they placed food before him;
the Blessed One ate, drank, and gave [gifts] to those who had assembled.
Since the food served in a golden vessel becomes inexhaustible and multiplied ten millionfold,
the great sages, headed by Gālava, then fed them.
In the evening, they performed dances, songs, and hymns of praise;
and Hari bestowed various kinds of gifts beyond counting.
At night, they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered oblations into the sacrificial fire;
having concluded the festival, the lords went to sleep.
All tens of millions of couples have become peaceful and entered into yogic sleep;
by reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the fruit of that pilgrimage.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how, after learning [the truth] from Śaṅkara while he was absorbed in meditation, Śaṅkara—desiring to go to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī together with his attendants, Pārvatī, Śakti, Satī, Devadevī, Tīrtha, Divyeśvara, and all the other embodied manifestations—performed the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa on the Jayantī day of the eighth lunar tithi of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, on the morning of the ninth day, the sounds of musical instruments arose;
the gods and others woke up, bathed, and put on their garments.
For the sake of beholding the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
they arrived and worshipped the son of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, as well as the sage Śrī Lomaśa and Patnīvrata and others, performed for them a most Vedic worship.
The sages dwelling there performed worship at the descent-sites;
thus, millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) were produced here within this lake.
Lomaśa performed the worship of Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Brahmā;
however, the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa practiced the worship of Śambhu alone.
Śambhu said: "I always dwell in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, I shall become famous here by the name Gopāleśvara."
Satī said: "I, Kambharā Kamaleśvarī, who am always worshipped by Kambharā and Kamalā, shall dwell by the side of Śaṅkara."
"I shall become renowned in a divine form by my own will;
Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya shall be my sons along with me. (8)
The Blessed One and I shall successively be known by the names Śukaśuṇḍha and Satī;
I shall be contented and devoted to the life of celibacy.
"And I shall be known by the name Santoṣadurgā before the Lord.
Thus did Nandi, Vīrabhadra, and the other Gaṇas always [speak].
They shall dwell by the name of each [deity] before the temple of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
then follows the worship of Viṣṇu and Brahmā together with their consorts.
The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa performed [the rites] for them with devotion according to the prescribed rules;
there, they also took up residence with their divine bodies.
Indeed, those holy places (tīrthas) of the gods became tens of millions in number;
likewise, there were hosts of deities and others, as well as trees, rivers, and creepers.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others who were descendants of Kaśyapa and possessed divine vision,
having assumed celestial bodies, indeed made their dwellings in the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
In the field of Saurāṣṭra, entirely by the command of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
I then dwelt wherever my heart was inclined.
Then, having partaken of food and drink, those gods and goddesses bowed and departed joyfully for their own city.
Thus indeed did the deities dwell there for four months;
what fortune of this earth shall I describe, which has never been nor will ever be? (17)
Then, King Dattātreya constantly read the stories of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā in their proper sequence.
The goddesses and the deities, as well as the beings of the fourteen worlds—both the insentient and the sentient—constantly listened with supreme devotion. (19)
Possessing their senses, and residing in the celestial city until the month of Māgha,
they all went to Mount Raivataka on Śivarātri.
The blessed Dattātreya, however, made a firm dwelling upon the peak;
Ambā, Bhava, and Viṣṇu likewise took up their respective abodes. (21)
The Gaṇas, gods, and goddesses took up residence there on Mount Raivata as they pleased, having performed the Śivarātri vow.
Then they went to Somanātha, the supreme field, and to Prabhāsa;
by them, the auspicious Akṣayatṛtīyā was indeed established there at Prabhāsa.
Pārvatī said: "O Blessed One, why is this sacred field (kṣetra) called by the name Prabhāsa? Tell me the true meaning of it. (24)
Śambhu said: "Listen, O beloved; that which shines forth through my yoga is indeed the supreme Prabhāsa, renowned by the name Vetra. (25)
The moon's radiance was mine alone by virtue of my boon; because it shines forth when its waning has passed, it is therefore celebrated as "Prabhāsa. (26)
Prabhā, the daughter of the Sun and beloved of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, formerly dwelt there on earth in the form of a beautiful mortal maiden. (27)
Having attained the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa through ascetic penance, Prabhā obtained her seat there; therefore, it is celebrated as Prabhāsa.
Where the gods obtained their splendor through fierce austerities,
that place which shines forth first exists among all sacred fords.
Where Śrī and Bhāratī cast the Vāḍava fire into the ocean, that place,
shining brightly at that time, became known as Prabhāsa.
That ninth part of Saurāṣṭra which shines upon the earth is called Prabhāsa by virtue of its fame; it is "Prabhā," meaning splendor, and it bestows that knowledge. ||31||
The sublime splendor that resided in the mouths of the sages became the Veda-essence;
that sacred field is indeed Prabhāsa, beloved by the Brāhmaṇas.
Since the sun is directly perceived there in its true form as it arises from the Arka tree, therefore it is called Prabhāsa, as declared by the gods.
In ancient times, the splendor of the sun was unbearable; Viśvakarman, having ground the sun on a whetstone, rendered its brilliance manageable.
He divided the splendors severed by the saw for the purpose of weapons;
and the armaments were fashioned from those splendors by Viśvakarman.
Nevertheless, a remnant of that splendor remains here near the ocean;
that which was gradually established there has become the tranquil Prabhāsaka. (36)
The sixteenth part of the sun’s splendor became present in his orb; that energy of his which consisted of the *Ṛgveda* was made stable at Prabhāsa. (37)
The sky was brought to full nourishment by the splendor consisting of the Yajus,
and heaven was made to flourish by the splendor of Viśvakarman consisting of the Sāmans.
The discus fashioned by another belongs to Viṣṇu, the trident to Hara,
the palanquin to Dhanada, and likewise the staff to the Lord of the Dead.
Likewise, the spear of Kārttikeya, the mace of Hanumān, the sword of the Goddess, and the noose of Mahākāla; ||1.536.40||
Likewise, the Pāśupata and the Nārāyaṇa weapon were created from a portion [of himself], and other weapons as well were indeed fashioned according to their respective requirements. (41)
Thus, O Goddess, the great field Prabhāsa, situated near the ocean, possesses the splendor of the sun; it is my own dwelling place. 42.
To the south of Māheśvarī and [to the north] of Nyaṅkumatī is the mountain Kṛtasmara,
which extends for twelve yojanas and is radiant on all sides.
There, Sūrya attained the state of the Arka tree through his lineage and progeny;
whoever worships the Arka tree, his leprosy shall perish. 44.
From Someśvara, in the southeast corner, I am established as Siddheśvara;
here, by the perfected Jaigīṣavya, penance was performed for a thousand years.
"O Daughter of the Mountain, having performed this, I have been established as Siddheśvara;
there the Vālakhilyas indeed attained supreme perfection through their asceticism. (46)
O Holy One, beginning from Kṛtasmara up to Arkasthala,
the eight Siddhis dwell there, devoted to my service.
Brāhmī and Hiraṇyā are indeed the two rivers born of Brahmā;
likewise, there are Maṅkīśarṣi and the mothers beginning with Sunandā. ||48||

Having thus regained the memory of my former births along with my wife, I indeed worship Rudreśvara, who is situated here at Kedāra and has been adored since ancient times.
Therefore, the Rudreśvara Tīrtha bestows sovereignty through worship;
it grants dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as peace and happiness.
And that independent woman who had been her worshipper was reborn as the captivating celestial nymph named Rambhā in heaven.
In this way, the Kedārarudreśa Tīrtha is established there;
thereafter, one should worship Hara, known as Śvetaketvīśvara, at that place.
In ancient times, King Śvetaketu performed supreme austerity here and attained liberation; there, Śambhu became known as Śvetaketvīśvara.
Then one should go to Ādityeśvara, Hara situated in the east;
for it was there that Śambhu, from his own eye, [emitted fire] for the destruction of Tripura. (23)
He shed tears out of anger and became Maṅgala (Mars);
because he was worshipped there by him, Hara became known as Bhaumeśvara.
Thus, O beloved, the sacred ford of the nine planets exists there;
it consists of those three powers of Nārāyaṇa which are knowledge, action, and will.
Maṅgalā, Viśālā, and Catvarā are always situated there;
among them, the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) at Prabhāsa bestows peace. ||26||
Likewise, O Viṣṇu, in ancient times, Viśālākṣī was born at that holy site of Prabhāsa for the purpose of destroying the Daityas in battle. (27)
O Lakṣmī, in a former age, I indeed went together with you to Lakṣmītīrtha as well as to the sacred site of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (28)
In that excellent field of Soma, there exists the auspicious Kāmatīrtha and Ratitīrtha, which bestow liberation upon being seen; these two are located in Prabhāsa.
The Gaurītīrtha and the iṣātīrtha shine forth as destroyers of sin.
In ancient times, Nārada once performed the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice there.
That Nāradakratu-tīrtha is situated in Prabhāsa;
formerly, the sage Gautama also came there for the purpose of pilgrimage.
He performed penance for four months; it is called the Gautama Tīrtha.
In the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was indeed a great Daitya named Meghavāhana.
Having himself ascended the two sandals, that Ādinārāyaṇa became possessed of a massive body, a yojana in length and breadth.
He slew that great Daitya; this place is called Pādukātīrtha.
The Daitya was struck by the sandal (pādukā) when it was merely tapped upon his chest.
Seated upon my sandals, I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa myself, abide at the Somaka Tīrtha as the bestower of liberation and the destroyer of demons. (35)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you the majesty of Viṣṇu as the presiding deity;
now, there are indeed the sacred fords (tīrthas) of the eleven Rudras located there.
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, Raivata, Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Sureśvara; ||37||
The vital airs are Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna;
and [the five subsidiary winds] are Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkala, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya. ||38||
And including Ātman, those eleven Rudras were born in succession;
having been formless, they assumed form at that sacred site in Prabhāsa. (39)
Nandin also performed penance directed toward Hara, the Conqueror of Death;
that Nandi-tīrtha exists there, bestowing great merit.
In former times, having become cows, the Earth arrived there for the sake of visiting sacred sites;
the virtuous one bathed Someśa with a stream of milk.
Then, having bathed there, she dissolved; that very spot became Gotīrtha, which, through its connection with Pṛthivī, became beloved by the earth and a destroyer of the affliction of sin.
Now, previously there was a man-eating Rākṣasa named Virāva in the ocean;
he was slain there by Viṣṇu with the Sudarśana [discus].
This very place, situated in the west, is the site where the Virā river disappears;
it is a most beautiful sacred ford (tīrtha) purified by the discus of Viṣṇu.
I, Cakrapāṇi, am to be worshipped there in Virāvalīnaka;
my worshipper shall surely go to the supreme abode, of this there is no doubt. (45)
Then the twelve suns, for the sake of beholding Viṣṇu,
first go to Prabhāsa and thereafter to Aśvapaṭṭasāra.
They go to the sacred field to behold Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
[there dwell] Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Pūṣan, Maitra, Indra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman.
Vivasvat, Aṃśumān, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya— these twelve indeed—
at the time of the end of their respective months, having bathed, go to Prabhāsa.
Viṣṇu indeed bathes in the month of Caitra, and likewise Aryaman in Vaiśākha;
then Vivasvat in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and Aṃśumān in Āṣāḍha.
Parjanya bathes in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise Varuṇa in Bhādrapada;
Indra in the month of Āśvayuja, and Dhātṛ bathes in Kārttika.
Likewise, Mitra proceeds in Mārgaśīrṣa, and Pūṣan in Pauṣa;
Bhaga does so in Māgha, and Tvaṣṭṛ bathes there in Phālguna.
Having performed austerities at the end of their respective months and having bathed, these indeed depart;
thus exists the auspicious Ādityasthala Tīrtha in Prabhāsa. 52.
Then, during the festival of Somanātha, Brahmā, eight years of age, arrived at the installation ceremony; there he took his seat in the eastern direction.
That is declared to be the Brahmatīrtha, which destroys sins through bathing;
having placed the eight-year-old Brahmā upon a beautiful chariot, [one should proceed].
On the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, one should certainly cause a procession to be conducted for Somanātha, accompanied by Sāvitrī. ||55||
One should worship with a spirit of devotion using the sixteen and other ritual offerings;
one should by all means draw the chariot of that Four-faced One.
Desiring the welfare of the kingdom, one should again establish [the deity] in his temple with instrumental music and dances, and should arrange for a chariot procession.
O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you where the Grandfather (Brahmā) resides on the surface of the earth during creation, whether in this kalpa or in another kalpa.
In due time, one should also remember that place which bestows happiness;
at Puṣkara is the best of gods, and at Gayā is the great-grandfather. (59)
Vedagarbha is in Kānyakubja, Caturmukha in Bhṛgukaccha,
Sṛṣṭikartā in Kauberī, and Bṛhaspati in Nandigrāma.
At Prabhāsa he was eight years old and indeed beloved by the gods; at Kāśī he was a master of the four Vedas; at Dvārakā he was Vaidiśa; and at Bhuvanā he was the lord of the world.
In Pauṇḍraka he is Puṇḍarīkākṣa; in Hastināpura he is Pītākṣa;
in Jayantī he is named Vijaya; and in Jagannātha he is Jayantaka. (62)
In Vādyadeśa he is Padmahasta; in Tamolū he is Tamopaha;
in Ahicchatra he is Janānanda; and in Kāñcī he is indeed Janapriya and Aja.
In Karṇāṭaka he is indeed Brahmā; at Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the lord of sages;
at Śrīkaṇṭha, he is named Śrīnivāsa; and at Kāmarūpa, he is Śubhākara. ||64||
In Uḍḍīśā he is Devakṛta, likewise in Jālandhara;
in Mallikā he is Viṣṇu, while in Mahendra and other places he is Bhārgava.
The elder Brahmā resides in Gohasta; the Grandfather [Brahmā] is in Ujjayinī;
Mahādeva is in Kauśāmbī; and Arkapitāmaha is in Sāketa. ||66||
At Citrakūṭa he is Virañci; at Vandhyā, Viśvasṛṭ in the form of Varāha;
at Haridvāra, Sureśa; and on the Himādri mountain, Haṃsavāhana. ||67||
In Haihikā he has the Veda in his hand; on Arbuda Mountain he holds a lotus;
in Vṛndāvana he has lotus-like eyes; and in Naimiṣa he holds kuśa grass in his hand. ||68||
This Sucandra grazes in the pasture of Gopa on the bank of the Yamunā;
Padmabhū is on the bank of the Gaṅgā, and Jalodbhava is in Janasthāna. (69)
In the south is Setupāla, and in the north is Haṃsavāhana;
Brahmā makes his residence at Arbuda, and Nārada is the lord of Utkala.
On the shore of Aśvapaṭṭasara is Parameṣṭhin Pitāmaha;
at Prayāga is Yajurnātha; and at Raivatācala is Svayaṃbhū.
In Kaccha he was Nārāyaṇamadhur; in Brahmavāha, Asupriya; in Aṅkulaka, Brahmagarbha; and in Vidarbhā, Dvijapriya.
The sage Nārāyaṇa is at Gomanta; Indraprastha is difficult to approach;
Sudarśana is at Pampā; and Rāṣṭravardhana is at Surūpa. (73)
In Virajā, Mahārūpa is the presiding deity;
on Samasthala, Kelanādhyakṣa; and on Supīṭha, Jaladeśvara is located at Kadambe. ||74||
On Kailāsa he was Devagaṅgādhr̥t; on Śrīśaila, Trinetradhṛk;
at Tryambaka, Tripurāri; and likewise at Naimiṣa, Cakradhṛk.
Śūra was at Śṛṅgaveradhura, Virūpaka in Nandipurī,
Gotameśa at Svacchapāda, and Mālava in the city of Hāstinapura.
In Vācikṣetra he is Dvijeśa; likewise, in Svarge he is Diveśvara; in Bhūtikā he is Pureśa; and in Candrā he is Haṃsavāhana. ||77||
Gāruḍa Brahmā is in Campā; Mahāyakṣa is in Mahodaya; Suyajña is in Pūjāraṇya; and Vṛṣātmaka is in Dharmāraṇya. ||78||
In the eastern region, he is white-colored, born from a lotus at night;
in the Devadāru forest he is Keśin, and in his motherland he is Vināyaka. ||79||
In Alakā, he is the Lord of the Lord of Wealth; on Trikuṭa, he is the Unborn King of Yogins; in Pātāla, he is Brahmā, the source of the Nāgas; and at Kovidāra, he is the Creator of the Yugas.
In Strīrājya he is Suratādhyakṣa; on Mount Paurṇa he is Prabhogadhṛk;
on Śālmalī he is Takṣakeśa; and in Ambiṣṭhā he is Sudarśaka. ||8 1 ||
In Naravīthī he was Mahāvīra; in the wilderness he was the destroyer of difficulties;
in Padmāvatī he was Padmagraha; and in the sky he assumed the form of a deer.
In the ocean is Meghavāha, and in battles he is always Kṣārabhū;
in the wheels he is Mūlabīja, and likewise Guru is on the forehead.
In Satyaloka he is indeed the great-grandfather (Prapitāmaha) upon the darbha grass;
in sacrifices he is the preeminent Brahmin; in Vairāja he is the lotus-born (Brahmā);
on Meru he is in the form of the goat (Aja); and in Pitṛloka he is the father (Pitṛ).
In Camatkārapura he was Chinnaśiras; in Kuru, Vājapa;
among the Bhāgyadevas, Vedhas; and in Sṛṣṭikūṭaka, Vidhātṛ.
In the scriptures, the Supreme Lord Brahmā exists as the progenitor in the process of creation, possessing one hundred and eight forms according to the ritual injunctions.
At Prabhāsa, one should worship that Supreme Lord in the form of a child;
the fruit of this worship shall be equal to that of worshipping one hundred and eight world-creators.
If the asterism Āgneya (Kṛttikā) should ever occur on the full moon day of Kārttika,
or if the asterism Prājāpatya (Rohiṇī) should occur, that lunar day is merit-bestowing.
When the sun is in Viśākhā and the moon is in Kṛttikā, that conjunction is named Padmaka; it must indeed be performed at Prabhāsa. (89)
Now listen further, O Lakṣmī: in ancient times, Dakṣa gave ten daughters to Dharma; among them, one was named Viśvā.
From Dharma, Mahāviśvā gave birth to eight sons:
Āyu, Bhava, Sāman, Dhara, Nala, and Anila. (91)
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa were the eight Vasus, sons of Vṛṣa;
among them, the seventh was born as Prabhāsa through the desire for a son.
When that supreme hundred-year penance had reached its end, dawn arrived;
Somanātha, being well-pleased, granted him a son, Devala.
The great god Mahādeva, who bestows sons, is called Pratyūṣeśvara because he was worshipped there by Pratyūṣaka with that liṅga.
Then Anila also propitiated Śaṅkara at that very place,
and He granted him a son renowned as Manojava.
Thus Śaṅkara attained renown as Anileśvara;
likewise, by Prabhāsa, the Liṅga was established as Prabhāseśvara.
Bṛhaspati’s sister was Bhuvanā, who was his beloved wife;
from her, through Prabhāsa, the powerful Viśvakarman was born as their son.
That Mahādeva indeed became known by the name Prabhāseśvara;
he was established by Prabhāsa during the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
On the thirteenth day, during Śivarātri, that place indeed became a supreme sacred ford (tīrtha). Then, in that location, there was a great sacred ford named Vāmanasvāmī. 99.
Having bound Bali and having made him beg for his entire kingdom,
that place where the first foot was set down by Bali and Khātaka is the most excellent sacred site (tīrtha).
There exists a place near the ocean known as Viṣṇutīrtha,
where in ancient times the demon Śaṅkha was slain by Viṣṇu on its shore.
Through the yoga of Hari, Śaṅkhatīrtha exists, which causes the sound of trumpeting;
and there also exists the Śaiva Tīrtha known as Vīrabhadreśvara.
Then once, the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself,
accompanied by many gopīs, went to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Then, at the supreme sacred field of Prabhāsa on Mount Raivataka,
[he installed] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇeśa and Gopīśvara as the second.
Because Bāṇa was established there, that excellent tīrtha became known as Śubhra.
Then, on one occasion, those sixteen Candrakalās arrived.
Having bathed at Prabhāsa, they established Kāleśvara as a supreme sacred site;
[the goddesses] Lambinī, Candrikā, Kāntā, Kūṭā, Śāntā, and Mahodayā.
Bhīṣaṇī, Nandinī, Suparṇā, Vimalākṣayā,
Śubhadā, Śobhanā, Puṇyā, Haṃsā, and Sītā are the Kalās in sequence.
Kalāditya was installed, and Sūrya also performed his pilgrimage to the sacred site.
Then, on one occasion, the sixty-four Yoginīs gathered there.
From the very mountain of the Yoginīs to the west of Raivataka,
they established that very Lord as the Sovereign of the Yoginīs (Yoginīśvara).
O Lakṣmī, listen indeed to their names, those who are dear to Śaṅkara:
first is the principal Mahālakṣmī, then Nandā and Kṣemakarī.
Śivadūtī, Mahābhadrā, Bhrāmarī, Candramaṇḍalā, Revatī, Harasiddhi, Durgā, and Viṣamalocanā. || 111 ||
She is the innate, the born of the family, the hunchbacked, the illusory, the Śāmbhavī, and the active;
she is the primordial, all-pervading, pure, honored through contemplation, and transcending the mind. 1.12.
She is knowledge and ignorance, the great illusion (Mahāmāyā), the central channel (Suṣumṇā), and the all-auspicious one (Sarvamaṅgalā).
She is the Great Goddess whose essence is the syllable Om, the mother of the meaning of the Vedas, and the auspicious Śivā. || 11.3 ||
She is the initiation into the Purāṇas and the Ānvīkṣikī philosophy; she is Cāmuṇḍā, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she is Brāhmī, the bestower of peace, Gaurī, the friend of Brahman, and the one dear to the Brāhmaṇas.
Bhadrā, Bhagavatī, Kṛṣṇā, she who is garlanded with planets and constellations; Tripurā, Tvaritā, Nityā, Sāṃkhyā, Kuṇḍalinī, and Dhruvā. (115)
She is auspicious, beautiful, eternal, partless, and the supreme digit;
she is the Yoginī whose true nature is Yoga, attainable through Yoga, and dwelling in the cave of the heart.
Kātyāyanī, Umā, Śarvā, and Aparṇā—these were the wives of Hara;
likewise, in other ages, there were others who became his beloveds through the power of their worship.
Yoginīs, beloved of Śaṅkara, are also born here by the tens of millions;
this is the most excellent holy site (tīrtha) of these [goddesses] in the vicinity of Somanātha.
It proceeds for the purpose of destroying evil, being ever purifying and bestowing happiness;
therefore, the worship of these [goddesses] should always be performed by people on the Aṣṭakā days.
Those established in sattvic devotion attain the state of divinity; this auspicious [work], through both recitation and hearing, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 1.538.1–20.
The majesty of Somatīrtha and of Prabhāsa has been recounted before you,
just as it was told by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī at Prabhāsa.

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, wherein many famous holy places (*tīrthas*) are described, and Brahmā is depicted as being distinct in various locations; furthermore, the eight Vasus, the Sūryas, the Rudras, and the sixty-four Yoginīs are recounted.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī! I shall likewise describe to you other holy places (tīrthas) which were indeed spoken by Mahādeva to Mahādevī at that time.
The auspicious tīrtha of Vāmadeva Sāvarṇi, as well as that of Aghora and Kapila, is located in Prabhāsa.
Likewise, the forest known as Śrīmukha shines with splendor,
where Vaiṣṇava yogins and perfected beings (siddhas) always dwell.
Where the Sun-god Bhāsaka was established by Sagara in the city,
that Sāgarāditya Tīrtha is located at Prabhāsaka.
In former times, the daughter of an outcaste was a young woman named Akṣamālā;
in her previous birth, she had been a Śūdra woman who, while in her menses, [approached] Śaṅkara.
Because of that fault, the maiden became an outcaste;
however, she was accepted by Vasiṣṭha through the power of his asceticism when she was offered by Janaka.
Long ago, for many years, the god did not send rain; at that time, those people living in the snowy land begged an outcaste for food.
Then Vasiṣṭha, having considered the duty in times of distress, gave food together with his daughter to that outcaste, speaking to him as follows.
One who seizes [a being] for the sake of protecting his own life is not defiled by sin;
Ajīgarta, being famished, approached to kill his own son. (9)
In ancient times, Bhāradvāja, afflicted by hunger, accepted cows;
for in ancient times, Viśvāmitra also, indeed, approached a cow while tormented by hunger.
Having said this, that Vasiṣṭhaka took hold of that rosary;
and having eaten food, they arrived at Prabhāsa in the vicinity of the ocean.
Akṣamālā performed austerities, and she gave birth to Arundhatī;
by her, Śaṅkara was then installed as Akṣamālikeśa.
Now, the auspicious Siddhalakṣmītīrtha is indeed located there, and likewise the Tīrtha established by Mahākālī shines forth as well. (13)
The auspicious river named Puṣkarāvartakā, which bestows lotuses,
flows at the holy site of Prabhāsa, granting the attainment of a good rebirth.
Now, there was a certain scribe named Mitra on the surface of the earth;
he had a son named Citra, and likewise a daughter named Citrā. (156)
After the death of their parents, those two boys then went to Prabhāsa;
there they praised the Sun with austerity for many days.
The Sun became pleased with Citra and said, "Choose a boon.
He chose maturity and brilliance in all undertakings.
"So be it," said Ravi, and Dharmarāja likewise agreed;
having ascertained his supreme well-being, he appointed him as his own scribe.
And there, Sūrya also became renowned as Citrāditya;
and Citrā became the wife of Dharmarāja as the fruit of her ascetic penance.
There, that goddess shines forth as Citreśvarī;
and a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) has also arisen there, auspicious and a remover of the defects of disease.
Now, the goddess Śītalā, the destroyer of suffering, resides here;
for the sake of pacifying eruptive boils, one should make peacocks dance there.
There shall also be the pacification of boils and scabies for children.
Camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and flowers as well. ||2||
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one should offer an oblation of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa) and present a garland made of bilva leaves; thus diseases are destroyed from afar.
This very place is called Śītalātīrtha, which bestows happiness upon children and others;
that Citrā who was the wife of Yama is the excellent river Citrapathā.
Born in her second form at the site of Prabhāsaka, that very place is declared to be a sacred ford (tīrtha) for the purpose of pacifying sins and afflictions. || 25 ||
Likewise, there exists at Prabhāsa the sacred ford (tīrtha) created by Dharmarāja;
indeed, there is a pool (kuṇḍa) fashioned by Brahmā which restores one’s physical form.
There exists the sacred site (tīrtha) created by Nārada, which is illuminated by celestial light;
and there is the great sacred site of the sacrificial pit (yajñakuṇḍa), established by the gods beginning with Brahmā.
Indeed, on the banks of the Hiraṇyā, the giving of gold and other such acts bestow merit;
likewise, there is the Vainateya Tīrtha, which wards off the fear of serpents.
The great tirtha of Raivataka belongs to the son of the Sun;
by worshipping that horse [statue] there, one's misfortune perishes at sunrise. ||29||
The sacred ford created by Svargavaidya, also known as Sāvitrītīrtha,
which arises through ascetic penance, is indeed located at Prabhāsa.
Likewise, the Tīrtha known as Talasvāmī, endowed with hot water, exists in Siṃhāraṇya; it is purifying, auspicious, and bestows heaven.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to what occurred there in the past in the Siṃhāraṇya forest:
there was a Dānava named Mahendra who, by the power of his asceticism, [attained great strength]. (32)
Having conquered the gods, he requested a combat from Śaṅkara;
first, that destroyer of the cosmic egg fought with Śaṅkara.
Then, from Śiva’s body, many flames burst forth out of anger;
in their midst, Tala was scorched and fled into the depths of the forest.
Then Śiva, having gone to Someśvara, remained firmly established there;
he oppressed Mahendra and bound the lords of the quarters.
Then Tala, overcome with wonder, performed a dance of joy;
by his dancing, all things, both stationary and moving, trembled. (36)
All the mountains were shaken and the salt ocean was agitated;
at that time, the three worlds became utterly distressed, and the sage Lomaśa [spoke].
Having arrived at Prabhāsa, he said to Śaṅkara, "Protect us!
O Lord of Gods, destroy Tala; do not delay, act quickly! (38)
Rudra said: "Tala, who stands equal to my son, is not to be slain by me;
however, [he may be killed] in the beautiful Uṣṇavana forest, near the Taptodaka lake."
Durvāsā is present there; O gods and others, pray to him, for Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is in Guptaprayāgaka.
On Mount Śatruñjaya, at the lake known as Aśvapaṭṭa, the Blessed One himself resides in the great field of Saurāṣṭra. ||41||
Being praised with devotion by Durvāsas, Lomaśa, and others,
and being entreated by the gods, he will destroy Tala.
In age after age, the Lord remains in the tiger forest of his former realm;
again and again, he slays the demon Tala who has entered the lion forest.
Thus addressed, Lomaśa went from the vicinity of the hot springs,
brought Durvāsas before the divine Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having gone to his own abode, which is purifying, he spoke to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, a fierce Rākṣasa exists who is indeed incapable of being slain by Hara. (45)
Having gone there with His discus, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa must destroy him who brings suffering to gods and humans. (46)
Seeing Tala in the tiger forest, he indeed released the Sudarśana discus;
Tala then fled toward the lion forest and the cave of hot waters.
There, the Daitya was split in two by the discus and died;
he was honored by Durvāsas and worshipped by Mārkaṇḍeya. ||48||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa gave him the name Talasvāmī;
Talasvāmī is a great sacred site (tīrtha) that takes refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
There are also three eternal, inexhaustible pits of hot water,
which wash away sins and likewise bestow heaven and liberation.
Therein is found the sacred ford of Sāvitrī, a place of ascetic penance;
furthermore, there is another sacred ford known as Bhūtamātṛka.
And there are dwellings for hosts of *bhūtas* and *pretas* there as well;
one should worship the Mother of *bhūtas*, the dispeller of fear, there.
O Lakṣmī, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga within the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, she was a virtuous woman (*satī*).
Having married Śaṅkara, she indeed took her delight in the forest. ||53||
Then Śaṅkara became gratified by his amorous passion for Pārvatī;
meanwhile, Pārvatī performed her ablutions there in the grove of Kailāsa.
Merely by Pārvatī’s bathing, the Mothers—auspicious, formidable, innumerable, and devoid of fixed forms—emerged from the mire of the water. 55.
They were dark-complexioned, with terrifying faces, tawny eyes, and disheveled hair;
they were adorned with garlands of skulls and had severed heads fixed upon their half-bodies.
They bear skull-bowls and khaṭvāṅga staffs, as well as garlands of severed heads;
they wear garments of tiger-skin and have girdles of tinkling bells.
Filling the sky with the sounds of ḍimas and ḍamarukas and the cries of citkāra, ten crores [of beings] were well-born there, for indeed four were the heroines. ||58||
Raktakarṇī, Mahājihvā, Kṣayā, and Pāpakāriṇī—many Brahma-rākṣasas are born in their lineage. (59)
They mostly dwell upon those Śleṣmāntaka trees;
tall and fickle, they dance and laugh.
Even though they dwell in every forest among fierce, thorny trees,
Śaṅkara nevertheless performed his ablutions with the mud from that water.
Innumerable beings were born, hideous and terrifying;
two principal men appeared, exactly like them in form and ornamentation.
They became bearers of skull-topped staffs and khaṭvāṅgas, draped in skins,
followed by many most terrifying spirits.
With faces like those of lions, tigers, and other beasts, and with terrifying voices and actions, those two, overcome by hunger, repeatedly called out "Śivā! Śiva! to her and him.
Then Śambhu said to the two of them, "Food, food!
and added, "By the touch of your hands, let flesh, blood, and so forth arise. (65)
Both eating at night and wandering about share in the fault of sleeping during the day;
protect the worlds like sons and always uphold the Dharma.
When this was said, those two hosts, served by the leaders of the Bhūtas and Mātṛs,
became united in an instant as brothers-in-arms.
Indeed, because of our purity, we are always born as if defiled;
therefore, clothing must be given to these two far away on the western land. (68)
"May he be born in Saurāṣṭra, in the forest of Siṃhāraṇya near Somanātha, in that land of lions, tigers, and beasts. (69)
Where there are thorny trees and harsh battlefields,
and where clusters of blossoms are indeed painted upon walls and other surfaces.
Where there is a remarried wife, an anthill, and likewise a *śamī* tree;
where there are five men in a house, or where there are three women. (71)
Or wherever there is a lineage, there you shall dwell in their homes—in dark pits in the earth, in deep caverns filled with wealth. (72)
"One goat, two donkeys, three cows, five buffaloes, six horses, or seven elephants—this indeed shall be your dwelling in his house. (73)
In whichever house there is a spade, a box for gifts, or vessels such as cooking pots, there alone is that which is worn out. (74)
Scattered here and there, there is no order even regarding purity;
women sit upon the pestle, the mortar, and the threshold. (75)
Where there is excrement and urine, where there is filthy filth, and where grains, both cooked and uncooked, are trodden upon in the house; (76)
Indeed, you must not dwell in that house where the scriptures are transgressed, nor in a house where there is a human bone, nor likewise where there is a *sevatī* creeper. (77)
Where Rohita, Jaṭī, Agastya, Bandhujīvaka, Karṇikā, and indeed Sthalapadma grow; || 78 ||
And where Mallikā’s palace stands, there indeed shall be your dwelling;
and where there are palm trees, tamāla trees, bhallāva trees, and citron trees. (79)
The Bakula, the grove of plantains, the Kadamba, or even the Khadira;
likewise the Nyagrodha, the Aśvattha, the Āmra, the Udumbara, and the Panasa.
There is an Aśoka tree and an Oḍra tree, which is the dwelling place of spirits; there is no worship of the gods, nor is there any recitation of mantras and the like. (8.1)
That place where devotion to Kṛṣṇa does not exist is indeed the dwelling of worldly beings;
those mortals who have foul faces and wear soiled garments [dwell there]. ||82||
Householders with stained teeth are always a dwelling place for malevolent spirits;
in that house where there is no lamp, and in that neighborhood where there is no person [to offer it], [spirits reside]. 83.
In that place, there shall certainly be the dwelling of spirits and the like, along with foul-smelling reeds and such, where men and women live deprived of bathing. (84)
May the people who consume liquor and meat always be worthy of your dwelling—at the crossroads, in the cow-pens, at the front of village gates, and in the cremation grounds. (85)
In places where dead children have died, at a shrine, under a tree, on a bare rock, in a latrine, or in a hollow of a reed—there is always the dwelling of spirits. (86)
In the body of a mantra-practitioner, in that which has been consecrated by mantra, and likewise in the ear,
as well as in the object of the mantra and the body, there occurs the dwelling of the spirits.
Sudden death occurs on the ground by a pond, in the wind, on impure ground, and where spirits always dwell. (88)
On the new moon day, on the fourteenth day, and likewise in the months of Vaiśākha and Kārttika, may they never dwell in the houses of those who offer oblations and worship. 89.
O Nārāyaṇa! O Hari! O Kṛṣṇa! O Śiva! O Lord of Rādhā!
O Viṣṇu! O Śrīmat-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! O Lord of Śrī-Kamalā! || 1.539.90 ||
O Lord of Light, O Consort of Mahālakṣmī, O Lord of Śrīmāṇikī, O Lord of Pārvatī, O Lord of Padyā, O Supreme Lord of the Abode of Liberation! 91.
May they never dwell where there is worship of the Lord Hari in forms such as Akṣareśa, nor where there is the worship of the gods. 92.
Where there is purity as well as righteousness, where there is no quarrel, and where indeed there is no impurity—there let them surely dwell. 93.
Where there may be internal purity, let the element not remain there;
where there is the power of worship, the mother of the elements truly does not exist there.
During the fifteen days of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
the worship of Bhūtamātṛ should be performed with consecrated waters.
One should worship the neck with sprinklings, water-sprinkles, and vermilion, as well as with flowers and incense; and one should offer the oblation (bali) as is appropriate.
O Prajāpati, he who eats black food such as mung beans (māṣa) is indeed satisfied by him;
neither Śākinīs, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas remain in his house.
The spirits and other malevolent beings do not cause affliction, and the lineage prospers in happiness.
One should feed [the deity] with milk-porridge, *kṛsara*, *pūya*, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
By this, one shall obtain abundance of sons and cattle, as well as physical health;
then, having washed the wall on the eleventh and ninth lunar days.
One should cause the faces of the Mothers, the Caṇḍikās, and likewise the Rākṣasīs, to be painted with various colors and red collyrium.
One should likewise have the faces of the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and śākinīs depicted there, endowed with various gestures and expressions.
On the new moon day, one should worship those [deities] at night, provided with a lamp,
having placed them upon one's own head, accompanied by friends and well-wishers.
One should perform the wandering of a hero at the edge of a village or at the edge of a cremation ground;
he becomes a powerful practitioner, a lamp for all beings.
One should constantly wave a lamp at night in the village or at the cremation ground;
on the fifteenth day, one should perform the great festival of Bhūtamātṛ.
One should worship him, feed him, bow down, and after asking for forgiveness, go home;
thus, for one who performs the worship in this manner, no obstacle from spirits arises. 105.
Then, from the body of that Bhūtamātṛ, fifty million Piśācas were born from drops of sweat; they were all terrifying.
Their veins were prominent, they were emaciated, bearded, and clothed in skins;
they wore mortars as ornaments, carried winnowing baskets as parasols, and possessed harsh voices.
With their hands as their only bowls and their heads as their only ornaments, they are hungry and misshapen;
from their hair, which is ablaze with nails, they spit out glowing coals. 108.
With mouths gaped wide as far as their ears, long eyebrows, and thick noses;
with hands and feet on their backs, they crawled upon their backs and moved upon their rumps.
Abiding in the maternity chamber with dejected faces, they cried out;
when they requested food for Śambhu, Śambhu then granted them a boon.
Invisibility among the people, as well as the power to assume any form at will;
wandering during both twilights and sitting in ruined houses. (111)
The houses of those who follow improper conduct were shattered, as were the temples, the royal roads, the side streets, the crossroads, and the altars. || 11.2 ||
And likewise, he saw stones, the corners [of buildings], the exits of the streets, sacred trees and the like, as well as peaks and lofty elevations. (11.3)
And Hara assigned places for the residence of the Piśācas,
as well as for those people who were unrighteous and likewise addicted to liquor and meat.
Hara also gave them dwellings filled with excrement and urine;
a wise person should offer a bali-oblation for the destruction of their obstacles.
One should offer cakes, green gram, and *kṛśara* mixed with honey and sesame powder;
one should give boiled rice with liquor, as well as rice with sesame and rice with jaggery.
Black garments, smoke, and likewise flowers—
by providing these, they remain satisfied and always remove obstacles.
Thus, by Hara, the Mothers of the spirits and the Piśācas,
accompanied by all their hosts of sons, were sent to Prabhāsa.
A forest of lions, extending for a hundred yojanas, was indeed granted as a dwelling place,
where food would always be found for them by the western ocean.
Having abandoned Kailāsa, they arrived at Siṃhāraṇya,
and coming back again toward the subjects, they indeed caused disturbances.
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa released the Sudarśana [discus] there in the forest to slay them; they fled into the sky.
The Bhūtas, Piśācas, and others, as well as the Mātṛs, went to the western region;
those dark-complexioned Piśācas went beyond the ocean.
Those of ugly form made their dwelling there in an uninhabited region;
from them were born millions of humans who could indeed assume any form at will.
But those gods who were struck down by the discus then became defiled;
dwelling in the forest of lions, they assumed other bodies.
The disciples of you, Śambhu Somanātha, are indeed like excellent sons;
they dwell in Siṃhāraṇya as daughters, sons, and disciples. 125.
O Lakṣmī, on the mountains and in the forests surrounding the pool of hot water,
there are always tamasic deities for the sake of those who are tamasic.

They indeed become like sacred fords (tīrtha) through their inherent nature, virtues, and spiritual cultivation; yet among them, there is that great, dark (tāmasa) ford located in the Siṃhāraṇya forest.
It was the dwelling place of the Bhūtamātṛs, the Piśācas, and the Bhūtas;
indeed, the various classes of beings there were being crushed and utterly destroyed by his discus.
"Those born in the western land are like Piśācas";
thus was it told by Śambhu to the Goddess at Prabhāsa.
O Lakṣmī, I have related to you this account concerning Kailāsa under the guise of a pilgrimage to Somaka; for I was formerly your servant.
It was for the purpose of destroying Tala; likewise, hear another purifying [account].
From reciting or hearing this, the destruction of sin arises. (131)

Thus ends the five hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Part of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," concerning the description of the multitude of holy sites (*tīrtha*) in Prabhāsa-kṣetra: the account of Arundhatī’s previous birth, the narrative of Citrā’s previous life, the holy site of Śītalā, the narrative of Talasvāmī-tīrtha, the narrative of Bhūtamātṛ-tīrtha, the dwelling places of the spirits (*bhūta*), and the residence of those suffering in parched lands and similar regions. || 539 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to what Śambhu spoke by way of reply to the Goddess at the sacred ford; I shall relate it to you in due order.
The Puṣpadanteśvara Tīrtha as well as the Māṇḍavya Tīrtha—
these two are indeed the abodes of Tapas, belonging to Māṇḍavya and Puṣpadanta.
One should visit these five Prabhāsas on the principal bank of the Prabhāsa.
In the south is Prabhāsa, and in the west is Prabhāsaka;
in the north is Prabhāsa, and in the east likewise is Prabhāsa.
Yama, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Mahendra are situated on all sides.
And from that, indeed, a fourfold radiance shines forth;
for there exists the Jāmadagnyeśvara Tīrtha,
as well as the great Kṛtasmara Tīrtha, which is of the very nature of a mountain.
Having burnt Smara and created him again, Hara united him with Pārvatī.
Where Kāma was restored to life by Śaṅkara in ancient times—that mountain, known as Kṛtasmara, should be understood as being inhabited by Śaṅkara. || 7 ||
And there is the Kāmakuṇḍa there, where indeed Kāma resides;
having bathed there on the thirteenth lunar day, one becomes fortunate and handsome.
The meritorious Sārasvata Tīrtha, by which the Somakas live, as well as all other auspicious Tīrthas at the confluence of the ocean, [are there]. (9)
A meritorious person obtains [the merit of] Vaiśākha conjoined with the moon there;
what then is the use of millions of other festival days, even if they are new-moon days joined with the moon?
The bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, the karṇikāra, the mālatī, as well as the dhattūra, the campaka, the aśoka, the śrīphala, and unbroken grains (akṣata). || 11 ||
One should offer sugar, sandalwood, sweets, and a bracelet at the confluence;
and by men, Hari and Hara should indeed be meditated upon at the Sarasvatī.
To him, that excellent worship—bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation—should be offered;
there, the bones of the deceased body should be cast for the sake of final release.
As long as a human's bone remains in the waters of the Sarasvatī, for that many thousands of years he dwells in the heavenly world. || 14 ||
The Sarasvatī, which has arisen as a ladder to heaven and resides at Prabhāsa,
bestows the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice through the mere sight of her and by sipping her water.
There, the ancestors, being well-satisfied by one who is faithful, attain liberation;
and there, fifteen renowned muhūrtas of the day are known.
In the morning there are three muhūrtas; Saṅgava consists of three muhūrtas; midday consists of three muhūrtas; and likewise, the afternoon consists of three muhūrtas. (17)
One should know that the evening consists of three muhūrtas;
the performer of a śrāddha should not perform the śrāddha during that time, for the evening is the hour belonging to the rākṣasas.
The eighth muhūrta of the day is known as the time of *kutu-pa*;
that midday, consisting of the *kutu-pa* period, bestows infinite fruit. (1.9)
Because it is evil and contemptible, from what [source] does its protection and preservation come?
That is designated as the *kutupa*; the *kutupas* are eightfold in form.
Midday, a ball, a vessel, silver, cow's ghee, as well as darbha grass, sesame seeds, a cow, a daughter's son, and those who are Kutupas—these are [auspicious]. (21)
The four muhūrtas following the Kutupa muhūrta,
as well as the fifth muhūrta, are considered to be the abode of Svadhā.
Kuśa grass and black sesame seeds originated from the body of Viṣṇu;
therefore, those staying on dry land should offer a handful of water with sesame seeds along with darbha grass.
Three things are purifying at a funeral feast (śrāddha): a daughter’s son, the *kutu* vessel, and sesame seeds.
A daughter’s son is a ball; he is indeed like a horned animal upon the forehead.
The vessel belonging to that horn is known as the dauhitra;
it is the ghee that would be produced from the milk of a milch cow together with her calf. || 25 ||
Therefore, he is declared to be a *dauhitra* (daughter's son) in rites for the gods and the ancestors;
indeed, the son of a daughter is the most excellent for being fed at a *śrāddha*.
The tips of *darbha* grass are said to belong to the gods, while those with sesame seeds and fire belong to the ancestors; however, those *darbhas* which hang down are remembered as *kutapas*.
The ancestors and the gods are satisfied by wealth acquired through righteous means;
those born as outcastes such as Puṣkasas and others are satisfied by wealth acquired through unrighteous means. (28)
Those born as Piśācas are satisfied by food thrown upon the ground,
and those born of low wombs are satisfied even by the water used for bathing and washing clothes.
Those who have attained the state of deities become satisfied by drops of fragrant water;
and those born of the lower realms are satisfied by the particles of food removed from the funeral cakes.
Those born of animal wombs are satisfied merely by eating and sipping water;
likewise, brahmins at a śrāddha, a learned scholar, a yogi, and one versed in the Sāmaveda and Vedic lore [are satisfied]. (31)

One who has performed the Triṇāciketa rite, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn, one learned in the six Vedāṅgas, a daughter's son, a son-in-law, and likewise a sister's son are considered most excellent.
My maternal uncle was devoted to the practice of the five fires and dedicated to asceticism; likewise were my mother’s father, as well as my disciples, relations, and kinsmen. (33)

One who knows the meaning of the Vedas, a teacher, a student of sacred knowledge, one who bestows a thousand gifts, and one who is long-lived—these should be known as virtuous men and purifiers. || 34 ||
O Lotus-born One, a man should especially not bypass his sister's son, nor even his circle of kinsmen, even if they are fools. (35)
One should offer water, one should offer fruit, and one should offer rice-balls and milk-rice;
one should offer sweetmeats and sugar, and one should always offer whatever is most desired.
The acquisition of substances, vessels, and so forth would indeed grant satisfaction;
one should bestow them on auspicious days, as well as during regular and occasional rites. (37)
One should certainly give [the offering] on the determined day every year;
one should by all means give it on the new moon day (amāvāsya), so that the deceased may surely attain [the reward]. ||30||
Likewise, one should give great gifts at the abode of Nārāyaṇa;
[the area should be] as far as the ground remains moist from the water, or to the extent of four cubits.
In that regard, Nārāyaṇa is the master; he is said to have no other abode.
Cows, gold, silver, jewels, and Sarasvatī [are his]. (1.540.40)
Sesame, a maiden, an elephant, a horse, a bed, clothing, as well as land, grain, milk, an umbrella, and a house—these are the sixteen gifts. (41)
Truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, contentment, steadfastness, straightforwardness, knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and generosity—this is praised as the worthy recipient. 42.
Even a single cow should be given to one who delights in the path [of dharma], who is peaceful, who is distressed, and who maintains the sacred fires;
for such a gift bestows liberation upon a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya). //43//
A cow, a house, a refuge, and women should not be given to many;
yet there were auspicious palaces made of gold, resplendent with silver and jewels. (44)
The givers of cows go wherever the most excellent Apsarases dwell;
the giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years. (45)
Having thus visited the Sārasvata Tīrtha, one should proceed to the Mārkaṇḍeya Tīrtha,
where the sage remains for the sake of asceticism throughout the long duration of the Yugas.
From there, one should go to that place considered the site for the destruction of the Kṛṣṇa clan,
which bestows the abode of Goloka, is divine, and is the courtyard for the assembly of the first age.
O Lakṣmī, listen now to those ill omens that arose when the battlefield was formed, which portended their destruction. ||48||
Time itself is seen wandering through their very houses as a terrifying, hideous, shaven-headed man, dark and tawny-brown in hue. (49)
He has a broom for his great banner, a hibiscus flower as his crest-ornament,
a chameleon for his necklace, and crows for his ornaments.
Having inspected the houses of the Kṛṣṇas, he was not seen again once he had departed;
at night, the young women saw the hair of the sleeping men.
With their bracelets and armlets shattered, they beg for bribes on all sides;
and in the houses, the female jackal cries out constantly, "Menā! Cī-cī! Kū-cī! (52)
Harsh and rough winds blew, carrying pebbles,
and at that time the goats indeed imitated the howling of jackals.
Pale birds with red feet, impelled by Time, as well as pigeons and lice, indeed roam about within the houses. (54)
Asses were born from cows, and stallions from mules;
cats were born from bitches, and mice from mongooses.
Wives deceived their husbands, and likewise, men deceived their wives.
The blazing fire revolves toward the left. || 56 ||
Emitting his own rays separately— blue, red, and madder-colored—
the sun is constantly reversed at both its rising and setting.
He was seen repeatedly by the people surrounded by headless trunks (kabandhas),
amidst great seats, prepared, excellent food, and extreme splendor.
As it was being recited, worms were seen in the dining hall,
and the constellations were seen striking one another.
In front of the unoffered deity, the braying of donkeys was heard;
the thirteenth lunar day was seized by Rāhu, which always brings about destruction.
A dark woman with white teeth, having entered the city at night,
steals the hearts of the women and runs toward the city.
Cocks let out terrifying cries upon the field of battle;
there were those of ugly form with two heads, fierce and possessing four arms.
From the wombs of women were born Rākṣasas and Guhyakas,
as well as ornaments, umbrellas, banners, and armor.
They were seen being carried away by terrifying rākṣasas; having thus recognized these ill omens that had arisen, Mādhava [reflected].
Taking his kinsmen with him, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the inner apartments and armed with iron clubs, then proceeded to Prabhāsa, which abounds in Soma.
Their own clans were destroyed through mutual desire to kill one another;
that site of Kṛṣṇa’s nirvāṇa is declared to be the supreme sacred ford.
Even the grasses growing from the joints of the airaka trees became, by way of reversal,
like pestles and indeed like swords at that time.
O Dear One, wherever all that has been gathered upon the ground becomes dissolved within that earth extending for two *gavyūtis*,
there one should undertake the journey, which bestows great dispassion.
From there, one should go to the river Hiraṇyā and bathe, which bestows great merit;
from there, one should go to the field of Ruru, where the goddess Kumārikā resides.
For the sake of destroying that demon, she was born from the splendor of the gods;
she remains there, established as the maiden Pārvatī.
One should worship, perform prostrations, and offer auspicious betel-leaves;
then one should go to Ṛṣitīrtha, where in ancient times the great sages [dwelt].
The lords indeed made their residence there for four months for the sake of the sacrificial session (satra),
where the eternal lineage of the Trinetra-matsyas dwells.
Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, Viśvāmitra, Bṛhaspati, Saṃvarta, Cyavana, Raibhya, Durvāsas, Kaśyapa, and Manu. ||73||
Mārkaṇḍeya, Jamadagni, Uśanas, Kaṇva and Gālava, Nārada and Parvata, as well as Bharadvāja and Bhāguri; ||74||
Medhātithi, Yavakrīta, and other auspicious Vaiṣṇavas were present when King Vṛṣādarbhi then engaged in the sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
He said, "O bulls among sages, accept from me this gift:
mung beans, black gram, rice, as well as jewels and gold. (76)
Then the sages said: "We do not accept gifts;
we certainly do not accept royal wealth, which is fraught with great faults. (77)
A butcher is equal to ten slaughterhouses; a liquor-distiller is equal to ten butchers;
a prostitute is equal to ten liquor-distillers; and a king is equal to ten prostitutes. (78)
The king’s gift is so terrible that it cannot be digested;
O King, let it be given to others, and may you be well in every way. (79)
Having heard this, the king went to his own home and subsequently had secret Udumbara fruits filled with gold made for the purpose of giving them as gifts.
The ministers scattered [the fruits] where those sages were standing;
then Aṅgiras said, "O sages, do not indeed take these fruits."
Indeed, there are secret gifts for King Vṛṣādarbhi;
the accumulation of wealth is the destroyer of the accumulation of merit through austerity. (82)
No one who possesses accumulated wealth is seen to be free from calamity;
for those whose nature is to refrain from accepting gifts, their spiritual luster increases constantly.
When possessionlessness and kingship were weighed together on a scale, possessionlessness proved superior even to kingship and even to wealth. (84)
For wealth can take the form of misfortune, causing one to fall away from the highest good;
it brings about sorrow and delusion as well—one who is happy should abandon it from afar. (85)
Even thinking "this is for the sake of the Dharma," one should certainly not engage in attachment to material things;
for it is better not to touch mud at all than to wash it off. (86)
The hair of one who grows old decays; the teeth of one who grows old decay;
the eyes and ears also decay; but craving alone does not decay. (87)
That thirst for wealth is boundless, always bestowing suffering, and is full of unrighteousness; therefore, one should always distance oneself from it. (88)
Those who are discontented perish through the perils of greed for wealth;
indeed, a contented mind alone is a treasure-trove of happiness in all circumstances. (89)
Just as for one whose feet are covered by shoes, the earth is as if entirely shrouded in leather;
for those satisfied by the nectar of contentment, there is peace and infinite happiness.
For the greedy, destruction comes through craving; whence can there be peace, whence can there be happiness?
The desire of one who yearns for objects of desire is never at all fulfilled. (91)
Then another desire pierces him even more deeply, like an arrow;
for desire is never quenched by enjoyment.
On the contrary, when nourished, it increases like a fire fed with ghee;
a greedy creature desiring objects of pleasure finds no happiness. (93)
Even if a king enjoys the earth together with its four oceans, he is still not one who has achieved his purpose, nor does he ever become free from craving. (94)
For those who do not accept [offerings], the worlds bestow eternal bliss;
even without asceticism, their asceticism becomes manifold, by the hundreds of thousands.
The thread of the continuum is craving; residing in the body, it dries up the blood. Like a Rākṣasī, it is difficult to abandon; even as one ages, it does not age. (96)
Craving is a disease that ends one's life; one should abandon it, for then one is always happy.
Craving for the world, craving for wealth, and craving for a son are all merely desires. (97)
"These thirsts devour living beings; O Great Lords, let us fear them.
Therefore, let there always be only udumbara fruits for the king. (98)
Having spoken thus, and having abandoned the udumbara fruits containing gold within them,
those ascetics devoted to the Supreme Lord performed the sacrificial session with composed minds.
O beloved Lakṣmī, their meritorious holy site, the Tāraka-tīrtha, is located at Prabhāsa; it must be visited, for it bestows liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and fortieth chapter, titled “The Description of the Four Prabhāsa Tīrthas in the Kṛta-yuga Lineage, the Sārasvata Tīrtha among hundreds of holy sites, the Kutupa-period and other times, the matters concerning daughters’ sons and others, the Mārkaṇḍa Tīrtha and the Tīrtha for the destruction of Kṛṣṇa’s lineage, ill-omened signs at the start of battle, the hidden gold-filled Udumbara trees created by Vṛṣādarbhi, Aṅgiras’s refusal of gifts, and various other Tīrthas,” in the first section on the Kṛta-yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. ||540||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of Nanda-tīrtha as it was told by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī; I shall relate it to you. Indeed, there was once a devotee of the Lord named Nanda. (1)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord;
obeisance!"—this mantra was indeed received by that king from Vasiṣṭha.
For he was a great devotee, solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
there was neither famine nor disease, nor untimely death for men.
There were no thieves, no deceit, and no fear of drought or similar calamities;
while that lord of kings ruled, the subjects were always happy.
A celestial chariot was indeed granted to him by Viṣṇu himself out of satisfaction;
seated upon that excellent chariot, he wandered through all the worlds.
Once, while wandering upon the earth, he went to Lake Mānasa,
which is frequented by gods and others, and is perfumed with the fragrance of lotuses.
There he saw an auspicious, white lotus in full bloom, joined with divine water, providing coolness and satisfaction.
There he also beheld that most excellent of persons, standing the size of a thumb; and having seen him, he said to his charioteer, "Go indeed to the water."
This lotus which is seen here, resplendent with a man adorned with necklaces of jewels and wearing yellow garments and the like. (9)
"Bring this lotus, which is presided over in its center by a beautiful divine being with two arms, quickly into my presence."
"I shall bear [this] upon my head and I shall have fulfilled my purpose.
Having been addressed thus, the charioteer descended from the celestial chariot.
Supported by the wind, he descended through the sky toward the lotus pond;
as soon as he had extended his hand while remaining with his head downward, [he reached it].
He went to seize that lotus situated on its stalk by means of the sky alone;
as soon as he touched it, smoke was produced from it. || 13 ||
In that sky filled with darkness, the charioteer died;
and Nanda, in the midst of the celestial chariot, became black in color.
Devoid of strength and vigor, and bereft of intelligence and power,
he became like one insane, with a face that was withered and parched.
Seeing his body resembling a lump of soot, the king grieved.
"What is this that has happened to me? My charioteer is dead! (16)
"This anger has arisen in someone; may Vasiṣṭha protect me!
As soon as this was said, the preceptor Vasiṣṭha arrived there.
And having arrived at the vehicle by the power of yoga, he said to the king:
"Do not fear; go, O Indra among kings! May there indeed be well-being and peace for you. (18)
Upon seeing Vasiṣṭha, the king became free from sorrow;
having offered his salutations, he spoke to him like one who is distressed.
"O Blessed One, this transformation of my body has occurred for me;
