by the power of Kamala, my charioteer has been lost. (1.541.20)
"Tell me, O Brahmin, what is this? Grant him deliverance indeed!
Vasiṣṭha replied, "O Indra among kings, in this Mānasa lake," ||21||
This lotus, born from Brahmā and belonging to the lotus species,
arose indeed from the navel of Nārāyaṇa when Brahmā was born;
that very lotus, together with its stalk, is called "Padma."
But a lotus of that same species is here in this Mānasa lake. ||23||
In the form of the lineage, the Blessed One indeed protects the succession; for within his noble progeny, the Unborn One always resides like a lotus. (24)
There, Brahmā, resembling the size of a thumb, shines resplendent;
for as many lotuses as are there, they are indeed born from his lineage.
Indeed, that many [lotuses] are consecrated by Brahmā;
for other embodied beings, being devoid of merit, do not see them. ||26||
Those of great merit who are destined for liberation behold this lotus;
by the mere sight of it, all the deities shall be seen. ||27||
This indeed is seen by blessed people who are devotees of Brahman and the world; for it is precisely that which has been seen by you, the great devotees of the Lord.
But upon merely seeing this and having touched the water, one is liberated from all sorrow and shall attain the state of nirvāṇa. ||29||
O Indra among kings, your charioteer likewise beheld a lotus and touched its water and stalk; by that much alone, he attained liberation.
I come daily from the path of the sky for the sake of seeing you;
I do not touch the water, but rather having bowed to that Father, the Unborn.
"I am going back to my own place, Puṣkara and Arbuda mountain;
but since you are a great Vaiṣṇava, you have indeed seen it."
And your lotus is endowed with merit and is indeed eternal;
O King, because you have not touched its water, you live and flourish. (33)
But, O Lord of Kings, the desire arose in you to take the lotus;
by that fault, blackness has come upon you, and you have become blue in color. (34)
The gods, sages, and seers constantly long for it, thinking:
"When shall we behold that lotus of Brahmā in the Mānasa lake? (35)
And we shall attain the supreme Brahman, reaching which there is no returning;
for such is that lotus, distinguished by its splendor, which he desired to take away. (36)
Indeed, you incurred the fault of theft while acting in ignorance;
therefore, O King, [worship] Nārāyaṇa, who resides within the lotus and is endowed with creative power.
Go to the sacred field of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa in Somaka and worship Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa together with Brahmā at Prabhāsa.
"O ascetic, having fashioned a golden lotus, propitiate her;
then you will be released from the fault of your dark complexion—of this there is no doubt. (39)
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, King Nanda went to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having bathed there and bowed to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and Lomaśa,
he went to Raivatādri, and after bowing to Vāmana, he proceeded to Prabhāsa.
There, indeed, having placed a golden image of the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa seated upon a lotus and accompanied by Brahmā; 42.
He worshipped [him] with various services day and night,
and performed austerities preceded by the propitiation of the Blessed One.
He worshipped according to the prescribed rite the five deities: Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇapati, Pārvatī, and Divākara (the Sun), as well as Śrī Hari.
On the beautiful bank of the Māheśvarī, he established a place for penance;
and having observed his asceticism as well as his devotion, the deities likewise [acted]. (45)
Then Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and Lakṣmī granted him their vision;
being pleased, they said, "We are gratified; choose a boon as you desire. (46)
The king said: "A devotee of Hari does not desire anything of this world;
grant me liberation, grant me the company of the virtuous, and grant me the eternal abode. (47)
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, smiling, said:
"O King, that was indeed already determined by me for your sake."
"For me, your devotee, there shall be no obstruction either in eating or in liberation.
And I am pleased with you, O King; your blackness was born from the fault of the lotus. (49)
O you who have been born, let your existence go to dissolution; becoming one of divine body with the complexion of a fine campaka flower, worship me, the Supreme Person.
"Whosoever comes here and worships me, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as well as Brahmā, the five gods, and the sun and other deities," ||51||
And he shall be free from disease in this world, and at the end he shall go to the supreme goal.
Having thus granted the boon and having assumed a golden form,
Hari established that supreme holy site there and then vanished.
Having bathed at Nandīghaṭṭa, a man shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||53||
Having likewise visited Nandatīrtha, one shall not return to mortal existence;
and beside Nandatīrtha is the excellent site known as Tritakūpa.
A purifying sacred ford exists; it should be visited for the sake of attaining merit.
Formerly, in the region of Saurāṣṭra, there was a Brahmin named Ātreya.
He had three sons—Ekata, Dvita, and Trita;
Trita was endowed with all virtues, while the two elder brothers were fools. (56)
When his father had gone to heaven, Trita indeed took up the burden;
the thought arose in him: "How shall I perform the sacrifice? (87)
Having invited the best of the twice-born who were established in the sacrificial rites,
he departed on a journey for the sake of obtaining materials for the sacrifice.
Having taken his two elder brothers, Trita set out for the sake of the cows;
accompanied by his brothers, he went from house to house throughout the villages. (59)
In various places he received supreme honor and very abundant cows; likewise, he obtained plentiful wealth and vast herds of cattle.
Having taken [the cows], he returns home accompanied by his two brothers;
Trita goes in front of the cattle, while those two brothers follow behind.
Then, seeing that wealth of cattle brought for the purpose of extensive giving, the minds of the two elder brothers became exceedingly sinful due to their great greed. (6.2)
Those two evil-minded brothers said to one another:
"Trita is skilled in sacrifices and likewise skilled in the Vedas."
"He is honored and worshiped by all, while we two are fools and useless;
moreover, Trita will give away this entire wealth of cattle as a gift. (64)
"We shall have nothing at all; rather, whatever wealth belongs to our father, from that too we must give when the sacrifice takes place. (65)
At the sacrifice, people will give many worlds and even vast amounts of wealth;
all of those belong to Trita, not even a single cowrie shell to the two of us.
Therefore, since we two are destitute of wealth while Trita alone is wealthy,
for that reason the killing of Trita is appropriate.
Having reflected thus, the two elder brothers called out to Trita as he went further and further ahead,
like two seekers of water upon seeing a well.
"We shall drink water; come here, O Trita!
Having heard this, Trita arrived and was indeed thrown into the well by the two of them.
Then those two, who had acted out of greed, having led away the wealth of cattle and taken abundant goods, set out for their own home with joyful minds.
And having fallen into the well, the Brahmin reflected in his mind:
"Brahmins were invited for the sake of a sacrifice, yet no sacrifice was performed by me. (7.1)
Therefore, since that which is destined to happen has already occurred, I shall perform a mental sacrifice here at this well;
as long as I live, I shall offer water and likewise my own mind.
Having reflected thus and having repeatedly recited the hymns,
he performed an oblation with water and with mud using his joined palms.
As he gave with faith, the deities became even more satisfied;
they approached the Brahmin and said, "O sage, we have been fully gratified. (74)
"We are pleased with your mental dispositions; tell us what you desire and we shall grant it.
Trita replied, "Indeed, a sacrifice of intention (bhāvayajña) has been performed here by me. (75)
"O Lords of Gods, go to my house and perform that material sacrifice for me; grant me well-being and deliverance from this well. (76)
Having been addressed thus, the gods led the Brahmin out from the water;
having gone home and performed a sacrifice, he was honored by his two brothers.
Having given various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), Trita went again to the well;
remembering Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he performed extensive penance.
He went to the eternal abode of Śrī Hari by means of a divine vehicle;
that well is Tritakūpa, a purifying deity-tīrtha. ||79||
Liberation comes from drinking its water, and even from remembering it;
by hearing or reciting it, a person attains Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus, in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*: the liberation of King Nanda’s charioteer who had gone to Lake Mānasa to seize a Brahma-lotus; the fruit of King Nanda’s mental sin of intending to seize it, which was his dark complexion; the attainment of a fair complexion through bathing at the *Nandī-tīrtha*; and the story of the Brahmin Trita, whose two brothers cast him into a well, where he was rescued by the deities during a water-sacrifice (*jalayajña*), and his subsequent liberation through ascetic practice—this is the *Trita-tīrtha*.
Thus ends the five hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of [the aforementioned topics]."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to this auspicious and highly meritorious account of a former birth,
which destroys sin upon hearing and bestows supreme liberation through its retention.
I am indeed pleased by devotion, by faith, and likewise by service;
through the attitude of servitude and by love, I become the fulfiller of the desires of my devotees.
O Goddess, I am to be accomplished through spiritual disposition, not by wealth nor by recitations;
indeed, for my sake, there should never be any physical hardship for my devotees.
A person whose mind is fixed on me should practice non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and celibacy through deed, thought, and word.
One should practice eating once a day, eating only at night, fasting, and so forth;
as well as the chanting of my names, the remembrance of the virtuous, and refraining from censure.
O Rame, one should indeed perform worship for my great satisfaction.
In ancient times, there was a son of Brahmā known by the name Āruṇi.
That best of the twice-born went to the forest for the sake of some austerity;
he performed severe penance, devoted entirely to fasting.
On the delightful bank of the Nāga river, he built a dwelling for you;
once, having gone to the river to bathe, he stood on the bank after his bath.
There he saw a hunter approaching, equipped with bow and arrows;
that hunter had come to kill the twice-born one out of a desire for his bark garment.
The sage, perceiving with his divine eye that the hunter was in agony,
grieved in his heart, thinking, "Alas, this hunter has committed many sins."
"Alas, the sin committed by my own hand shall become even greater for him;
indeed, when will there ever be deliverance for such a perpetrator of evil? (11)
"Therefore, let him take up the bark garments even without having killed a twice-born man. Thinking thus, as many bark garments as were offered were indeed accepted by him.
Meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the Brahmin remained silent;
seeing that sage Suvrata, a brahmin who had internalized Hari within himself.
The hunter's mind there indeed became compassionate, peaceful-hearted, and averter of the sins of others, having truly abandoned its cruelty.
In another moment, he who was endowed with sattva and dharma turned back;
the hunter, casting aside his bow and arrows, spoke these words. (15)
"O Brahmin, I came here desiring to kill you;
now, because of seeing you here, my intent to harm has vanished. (16)
"O best of the twice-born, many Brahmins and women have indeed been killed by me, a sinner; what destination shall I attain, for I am a slayer of Brahmins? (17)
Now I desire to perform penance in your presence;
you ought to show me favor by granting me instruction and other such gifts.
Although addressed in this manner, that Brahmin did not offer a reply,
because sin is transmitted through conversation with a sinner.
Although not told, that seeker of dharma, the hunter, remained right there;
like the brahmin, the hunter performed austerities beneath a tree.
Then once, a certain lion arrived at the riverbank;
being hungry, he saw that brahmin and desired to devour him.
Just as the lion was about to seize the brahmin on the bank,
the hunter swiftly destroyed the lion with volleys of arrows.
The sage, having said, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master," became submerged in water and sat beneath the water. ||23||
Upon hearing the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the lion died;
having become free from sin, he then arose as a divine person. ||24||
Upon merely hearing it, he gave up his life-breaths and thereafter attained a divine body;
he said, "I am going to that place where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides."
"O best of the twice-born, by your grace I am cleansed of sin and shall attain liberation.
Having heard this, the brahmin, who had been staying within the water, emerged outside. (26)
He then asked that lion-man, "Tell me, who indeed are you?
The lion-man said to the brahmin, "I was formerly a follower of the Vedas. (27)
Known as Dīrghabāhu, he was devoted to the performance of rituals; "I know every requirement for sacrificial rites, and therefore I have no need for others. (28)
I know the Vedas, and I discern what is auspicious and what is inauspicious;
I have no need for Brahmins—what indeed are these Brahmins? (29)
When I spoke thus, all the brahmins, filled with anger, uttered an invincible curse: "You shall become a cruel lion! (1.542.30)
Your knowledge and your memory shall be utterly destroyed;
however, at the time of death, you will indeed hear the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||31||
"Then, O beast, your liberation will indeed come to pass in the presence of Āruṇi, when food arrives at the sixth mealtime by your own chance. (32)
Whatever species of animals, humans, or birds shall remain in your presence, you, having received a blow from their arrows while your life-breaths are at your throat, [shall be slain]. (33)
When you hear of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa from the mouth of a brāhmaṇa, then liberation will indeed be yours; there is no doubt about this. ||34||
Even the name of Viṣṇu, though uttered by another's mouth, was heard by me;
thus, even though I had committed an offense, the brāhmaṇa became the bestower of liberation upon me.
By the mere sight of whom Acyuta became manifest to his perception—he who, moreover, accepts Śrī Narāyaṇa with his own mouth. (36)
At the time of the departure of the vital breath, one certainly becomes liberated;
this is the truth, the truth, and again the truth—so it is said, raising up one's arm.
The Brahmins are the moving gods, and Puruṣottama resides therein;
through the union with the Brahmin Aruṇa, I go to the eternal state.
Having spoken thus and having worshipped Āruṇi, Brahmā departed for the imperishable state.
Then Āruṇi, with a gracious heart, spoke to the hunter.
"O son of noble vows, since I have been protected by you from the lion who desired to seize me, I am pleased with you; choose a boon."
The hunter said: "This indeed is a boon that you speak to me;
for your satisfaction with me as your son—what other boon could be greater than this? (41)
"Therefore, tell me what I shall do with this boon; instruct me.
The sage said: "O hunter, I have been entreated by you, who are seeking the fruits of asceticism."
I said nothing at that time because you were possessed by sin; now, through my ascetic power and protection, your sins shall be removed. (43)
Thus, by my very sight and by the hearing of the name "Kṛṣṇa," your sins have been destroyed;
you are now pure in body—of this there is no doubt.
"O virtuous one, perform penance; in this way you will attain liberation.
The hunter said: "The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has been described by you. (45)
"O Guru, how can that which is attained by those like me, who are devoted to evil, be reached?
The sage said, addressing him: 'One should perform the complete dedication.'"
He attains that supreme state through devotion, through vows, and through ritual action;
knowing this, perform every vow with devotion to Him. 47.
One should not consume what has not been offered as an oblation, nor should one ever speak untruth;
one should always perform the recitation of His name and likewise practice meditation upon Hari.
"O hunter, this vow has been prescribed by me; act accordingly.
Remain right here, engaged in ascetic penance, for as long as you desire. (49)
Having spoken thus, the sage again entered into the water;
the hunter, remembering his teacher, performed austerities while abstaining from all food.
At times of hunger, he ate withered leaves here and there;
then, little by little, he gradually gave up even the eating of leaves.
Without food, he performed penance, mindful of his guru with unwearied devotion;
while he was thus engaged in asceticism, the sage Durvāsas approached him.
He beheld that very hunter, whose body was withered yet who possessed life,
endowed with the splendor of austerity, and with his heart fixed upon Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having recognized him as a seer, that hunter bowed his head to the sage and said to him:
"O Blessed One, I have attained my purpose through the sight of you. (54)
"Now you have arrived as my guest; you are a deity to me. Having prepared with withered leaves and such, I shall gratify this best of the twice-born. (55)
Durvāsas, wishing to test the excellence of his penance, spoke these words loudly to him, who was purified by his pure disposition and had conquered his senses: ||56||
"Let sweet and well-prepared food made from barley, wheat, and rice be given to me, who am afflicted by hunger and have come here for your sake. (57)
Having been told, "This man is to be eaten by you," he fell into deep reflection:
"How can such a thing be brought here, and how could it possibly come about for me? (58)
As he was thinking thus and remembering Nārāyaṇa,
by the grace of his guru, an auspicious vessel fell from the sky.
He took that golden vessel, endowed with supernatural power, in his hand;
having taken it, he said to the sage, "Wait a moment, O Rishi."
"Please remain right here while I go for alms; during that time, O Guru, you should show me your favor. (61)
Having spoken thus, he, carrying his alms-bowl,
went to beg for alms not far from the city, which was adorned with trees, creepers, and other vegetation.
As he proceeded there, the creepers of the trees along the path moved toward him, and all manner of beautiful things appeared before him as he went.
From the trees emerged maidens with golden vessels in their hands,
as well as beautiful forest goddesses bearing auspicious cooked foods.
Condiments, drinks, things to be sucked, and foods to be eaten; edible items, beautiful things to be licked, and honeyed, delicious flavors. (65)
Milk products mixed with ghee, milk-rice with sugar, and various side dishes that were bitter, sweet, and sour; 66.
Those forest deities gave exactly fifty-six kinds [of fruits];
and he, considering himself to have achieved his purpose, then returned once more to the hermitage.
He approached the sage and said, "Alms have been obtained according to my desire;
O Brahmin, wash your feet and sit upon this auspicious seat. (68)
"Accept this alms-food and make me a vessel of merit.
Thus addressed, that sage, desiring to test the power of his asceticism once more, [acted]. (69)
He said to that devoted hunter, "I have no vessel for water;
I am unable to go to the river, and you likewise possess no vessel."
"How might there be a washing of my feet, O hunter?
Having been addressed thus, he, who was devoted to the hunter, again became lost in thought. (71)
Having remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as well as his guru,
he then sought refuge in that serpent-river.
Bowing down, he said: "O river, you are my refuge;
I am a hunter, I am a doer of evil deeds, and I am a slayer of a Brahmin, O best of rivers. (73)
Nevertheless, protect me here, your devotee who has come to you for refuge;
I know nothing of the deity, nor the mantra, nor likewise the ritual worship. (74)
"Having meditated upon the feet of my preceptor Āruṇi, I indeed behold what is auspicious;
O Goddess, best among rivers, show your grace to me, your devotee. (75)
"O River, come near to the sage for the purpose of washing his feet.
Having been addressed thus, the Naga-river took the form of a flow of water. 76.
He arrived at the place where Durvāsas stood, having taken refuge under a tree;
seeing that great marvel, Durvāsas was filled with wonder.
Having washed his hands and feet, the sage, being exceedingly pleased, ate the alms-food with faith; likewise, having sipped water for purification, he laughed repeatedly. (78)

To that hunter, whose body was withered and who had become weak from hunger, he granted this boon: "The Vedas, indeed, along with their auxiliary limbs and the methods of word-analysis, shall belong to you. (79)
"May all the Brahma-vidyās indeed become manifest to you;
and you shall become a preeminent sage (ṛṣi) by the name Satyatapas."
The hunter said, "How can I, a Śūdra, be one who has studied the Vedas?
The sage replied, "Your sinful body has certainly departed. (81)
A second body, consisting of austerity, now exists for you;
previously existing ignorance has gone to its destruction, and now knowledge has arrived. (82)
Thus you are of pure body; I tell you this as the truth:
by initiation, by austerity, and by devotion, the body indeed undergoes transformation. (83)
Therefore, the study of the Vedas and so forth will now appear to you as being in their former state—devoid of true knowledge and designated as unrighteousness (adharma). //84//
Your hunter's body has passed away; now indeed a second one, purified by devotion and endowed with the vows of dharma and other virtues, has been attained. (85)
That entity which previously existed within you as you were killing living beings—that body known as sin, designated by the name "evil," has indeed departed from you. (86)
Now, your second body, consisting of the nature of dharma, is established as one characterized by auspiciousness, virtuous conduct, austerity, straightforwardness, and devotion. (87)
The hunter said to the sage: "How indeed can Nārāyaṇa be propitiated by a yogin who possesses no means of practice and has renounced all possessions? (88)
Durvāsas said: "One should perform worship with the mind in every way;
neither wealth, nor lineage, nor prosperity is required therein. (89)
By such devotion, Janārdana, the Blessed One, is eternally pleased;
for having bathed and meditated upon Hari daily with mental offerings, he is ever satisfied.

One should worship, meditate upon, perform the lustration rite (nīrājana), and likewise ask for forgiveness; one should offer handfuls of flowers, water, and the arghya offering, and should also offer mental worship.
One should perform the offering of oneself, for by that Janārdana is pleased;
the Supreme Lord is attained by both the wealthy and the destitute alike. ||92||
He is not pleased even by millions of excellent gifts if they are devoid of devotion;
yet, with devotion, he is well-pleased even with the gift of a single leaf. (93)
He is satisfied even with water, sandalwood, or merely flowers;
indeed, by the very nature of Trita, he is honored even with mud. (94)
Indeed, all the gods were satisfied by water alone; this is a well-known illustration.
The Blessed Lord Hari was satisfied by the mere chanting of Prahlāda.
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was pleased by the offering of their hearts from the gopīs;
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was satisfied by the service of Lakṣmī. ||96||
Śaṅkara himself was personally pleased with Aparṇā, that is, Pārvatī;
and the Blessed Lord was likewise pleased with Ambarīṣa because of his devotion and his worship.
Thus, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the sovereign of Akṣara, becomes pleased through devotional sentiment; Acyuta is not pleased without such sentiment. 98.
The deities, the gurus, the virtuous, the ancestors, Dharma, and the Lord—liberation is their fruit; this is indeed conceived as being accessible through faith. (99)
Devotion, service, worldly interaction, acquisition, meeting, wealth, success, and happiness—this group of eight is to be accomplished through action. 1.542.100.
Mantra, vidyā, quarrel, singing, recitation, invocation, instruction, and explanatory discourse—these eight are accomplished by means of speech. (101)
Homes, beautiful women, obedient sons, land,
fame, honor, a husband, and attendants— this group of eight is to be accomplished through merit.
Peace, contentment, detachment, the highest good, merit, liberation, cessation, and assistance—this eightfold group is to be accomplished through knowledge. 103.
In ancient times, the Earth said: "The Lord in the form of a boar shall give me, the earth submerged in water, to Nārāyaṇa with devotion. (104)
Nevertheless, I shall be pleased, because I am indeed the essence within the earth;
for I have been remembered by you, O Goddess, and likewise worshipped with water.
"Having assumed the form of a boar, I have come for the sake of protecting you;
thus, with a mind filled with such devotion, one should go to me for refuge. (106)
I am entirely pleased with him and, being under his control, I grant him liberation;
so too for whoever performs worship with devotion at dawn on the twelfth lunar day.
"I shall grant him the eternal world of Brahmā,
O Earth," having said this, he lifted the earth from the waters with his snout.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Śambhu spoke to Pārvatī at Prabhāsaka;
by reading or hearing this, the fruit of the world of Brahmā shall be attained. 109.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Lion in the Presence of Āruṇi; the Protection of the Brāhmaṇa and the Ascetic Practice Performed by the Hunter; the Curse upon the Vedic Dīrghabāhu to become a lion due to his contempt for the Brāhmaṇas; the River Nāgamatī coming to wash the feet of Āruṇi at the request of the penitent hunter; the purification of the hunter and his becoming the Ṛṣi named Satyatapas; and the instruction on knowledge given by Durvāsas," in the first section, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 542 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how Pārvatī indeed questioned Śaṅkara regarding the lords of the lunar days (tithis) at Prabhāsa; I shall relate that to you.
O Lakṣmī, I shall now explain to you the deities and other attributes of the lunar days (tithis), beginning with the one which Brahmā assigned at the commencement of creation.
Brahmā set his mind upon performing the act of creation at Puṣkara;
when he attained nothing at all, then anger arose within him.
From his forehead, a drop of sweat in the form of anger indeed trickled down; having fallen as one born of fire, he was hungry and begged for food.
Furthermore, it is said that the oblation was consumed by Brahmā within his stomach during the sacrifice;
thus, the food offered by Purā, consisting of minerals from the earth and other elements, is to be eaten in three ways.
The fire is indeed threefold: the sacrificial (havanīya), the digestive (jāṭhara), and that which arises from the unmanifest (ākaraja).
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, Viśvarūṭ divided that first [fire].
That first lunar day (tithi) is offered to him, and the worship and other rites for the Fire-god must indeed be performed on the first day (pratipad) during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Then Saṃjñā, the wife of Sūrya, being unable to endure his brilliance,
assumed the form of Aśvinī and went to the city of Haimottara in ancient times.
The Sun, in the form of a horse, obtained union with her;
from this, the two Aśvins were born—the Prāṇa and Apāna breaths, the most excellent of physicians.
And in that same birth, in former times, Brahmā bestowed upon those two this lunar day (tithi) for worship and other rites, which destroys disease and affliction.
Then Brahmā, having brought forth Speech in the form of Gaurī,
gave her to Śaṅkara through the rite of marriage on the third lunar day.
That lunar day was indeed bestowed upon Gaurī, increasing her good fortune and other virtues;
then, from Gaurī, Gaṇeśa became her son, whose nature is identical to that of his mother.
On the fourth lunar day, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself became Gaṇanāyaka;
for the purpose of worshipping him, the Caturthikā was offered to him.
Then, when the boon for the consumption of the sons of Kadrū— the Nāgas— by Garuḍa was obtained, Brahmā therefore provided for their protection.
The Nāgas made a request, and Brahmā likewise granted them protection;
he ordained worship on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, which became known as Nāgapañcamī.
There, being satisfied by milk and sesame seeds, they do not bite humans at all.
Now, indeed, Kārtikasvāmī was born on the sixth lunar day in the house of Satī.
To him, whose nature is the ego (ahaṃkāra), the sixth lunar day was offered;
then, in the first age, the eye named Āditya was produced.
Having performed the offering of his own splendor for the sake of attaining the splendor of the world, Śrī Narāyaṇa established him in the sky on the seventh lunar day. 18.
That seventh lunar day was granted to him by Parameṣṭhin;
it had previously been given by the gods for the sake of destroying the Daitya named Andhaka.
The eight goddesses who have been proclaimed as the Mothers were indeed created:
Sound, Touch, Form, Taste, Smell, and then Desire.
Likewise, egoism, delusion, and the formless ones became embodied forms:
desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. (21)
In former times, slander and envy became their embodied forms;
know that Kāma is Yogeśvarī, and likewise, Krodha is Māheśvarī.
Know that greed is Vaiṣṇavī, and intoxication is indeed Brahmāṇī;
know that delusion is Svāyaṃbhavī, and envy is born from Kaumārī.
Know that backbiting, Yamadaṇḍī, and envy are the Mothers;
these, born within the house of the body, become consumers of blood. (24)
And from all that blood of Andhaka which was shed,
other Andhakas, born of that blood, then arose by the tens of millions.
Indeed, the eighth [digit] was given by the Creator to those very [deities] who had been lost;
there they are to be worshipped, and those auspicious ones provide protection day after day. (26)
Then, for the sake of destroying the staff of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son,
Durgā was manifested by the Creator from her own body as a mere illusory form.
That mental daughter, armed with weapons and possessing eight excellent arms,
seated upon a lion, then slew that Vetrāsura.
Residing in the Himalayas, her manifestation occurs on the ninth lunar day (Navamī);
Brahmā bestowed that Navamī upon her for the purpose of worship and other rites.
Then, in the past, all the principles indeed made an exceedingly earnest request to the Creator for a wonderful refuge of their own.
Then, however, ten maidens were produced by Brahmā from the region of his ear; they are the quarters, namely the East and likewise the South.
The western, northern, upward, and downward directions—these six are primary; together with the directions of Īśāna, Agni, Nairṛti, and Vāyu, they constitute the ten. (32)
To those whose nature was that of effects, he assigned space as their function;
and to those whose nature was space, lords were assigned. (33)
The eastern direction to Indra, the southern to Yama, the northern to Kubera, the western to Varuṇa, and the upward direction to Brahmā himself. (34)
One should offer the southern [quarter] to the Serpent, the northeastern to Īśa, the southeastern to Agni,
the southwestern to Nirṛti, and likewise the northwestern to Vāyu.
And Brahmā gave the tenth lunar day to them for worship;
then, on the eleventh day, the Lord created Kubera.
From Vāyu, known as Dhanañjaya, he received that lunar day;
and by the splendors of Nārāyaṇa, one daughter was indeed born.
That vow of the eleven senses is considered Ekādaśī;
indeed, he was born on the twelfth day from the supreme Nārāyaṇa. (38)
Padmanābha, who is the form of Manu, is Viṣṇu incarnate, the nourisher;
to him Harikṛṣṇa gave the Dvādaśī that bestows liberation. 39.
Now, indeed, Dharma was born from the chest of Brahmā;
at the beginning of the Yuga, he was truly four-footed and white in color.
It is proclaimed as being endowed with the fourfold set of substance, quality, action, and genus;
and it is remembered in the Veda as having three peaks, consisting of the Saṃhitā, Pada, and Krama recensions.
Likewise, he has two heads in the form of the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and end, and possesses seven hands;
these are: generosity, compassion, self-restraint, righteousness, wealth, desire, and liberation. (42)
Then, bound by the three [factors] beginning with the Udgātṛ, it is established as the Hand;
indeed, the Brāhmaṇa is formed there, consisting of four feet and six ritual acts. 43.
The Tretā age is the Kṣatriya there, consisting of three parts, yet it is merely secondary;
the Dvāpara age is indeed the Vaiśya here, consisting of two parts, and is even more secondary. ||44||
In that [age], Kali is a Śūdra, and Dharma is established there with only a single quarter; that Dharma was oppressed at its very inception by the Kṣatriya with one foot.
Tārā, the devoted wife of Bṛhaspati, was carried off by Candra;
because of that violation of dharma, he entered the most terrible forest.
In the fourteen worlds, the Dharma indeed fell into decline;
at that time, both the Asuras and the Suras were shrouded in unrighteousness.
Desiring to seize the homes of others, as well as the wealth and property of others' wives, they then wandered through the mansions of others, having become devoid of all restraint. 48.
They fought and seized one another's property;
Brahmā, perceiving this destruction, spoke of eternal Dharma.
Without you, however, the entire world will go to destruction;
let the moon abandon Tārā, but let Dharma abide in every way.
The earth is protected by you alone, and indeed the three worlds are protected by you alone; Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—all are protected by you.
There is nothing in the world, whether stationary or moving, that exists apart from you;
for if it were devoid of you, the world would instantly perish.

You are the Self of all beings; for those who are virtuous, you possess the nature of pure goodness (sattva); for those characterized by passion, you are passion (rajas); and for those characterized by darkness, you consist of darkness (tamas).
Deprived of you, all these gods have indeed entered upon a wrong path;
O son, restrain those who are deluded from the wrong path, for you are their supreme refuge. (54)
Thus praised, Vṛṣa looked with peaceful eyes at the deities and the others;
as soon as they were seen by him, their minds became fixed upon dharma.
In an instant, even the righteous Asuras were freed from their delusion;
they all became endowed with Dharma, as did all the Ṛtus.
Trees, creepers, men, women, sentient beings, and insentient things—all were endowed with their own specific duties, as were cold, heat, and the rest. (57)
In this way, the thirteenth lunar day was assigned to Dharma;
because Dharma was protected there, it is remembered as Dharmāraṇya.
Having thus instructed Brahmā in his duty, he then departed for Satyaloka, the foremost station of creation; and so the world became established in well-being.
Then he indeed became King Yama in embodied form;
thereafter, Rudra was born from the forehead of Brahmā.
On the fourteenth lunar day, a share of the sacrifice was also offered to him at the gate of Hara during Dakṣa’s sacrifice by the ṛṣis and munis.
That lunar day, known as Śivarātri, was entirely dedicated to Rudra;
Dakṣa was the father-in-law of Dharma, and he had a hundred daughters.
And for the sake of the great increase of creation, she gave them separately to the gods;
she gave Satī to Śaṅkara and gave ten to Dharma.
Faith, intelligence, fortitude, form, forbearance, modesty, purity, memory, power, and sacred learning—Nārāyaṇa became manifest within these forms. (64)
Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Nara—these four are born from devotion to the Form (Mūrti).
Kāmadeva has two wives, namely Rati and Prīti. (65)
Then he gave Svāhā to Agni and Svadhā to the ancestors;
furthermore, he gave the twenty-seven daughters, the lunar mansions, to the Lord of Night (the Moon).
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣyā, Āśleṣā, and likewise Maghā. ||67||
Pūrvāphālgunī, Uttarāphālgunī, Hastinī, as well as Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūlikā. ||68||
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhikā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapada, and likewise Uttarabhādrapada; ||69||
Revatī and Rohiṇī became the wives of Candra;
furthermore, Dakṣa gave thirteen auspicious daughters to Kaśyapa.
Aditi and Diti, Danu, Kāṣṭhā, Irāvatī, Vinatā, Kadrū, Siṃhikā, and Suprabhā likewise. (71)
Envy, deceit, violence, and ruin—these five were indeed offered to Varuṇa; [the goddesses] Gauḍī, Vastrā, and Vārtikā.
Sādhvī and Sumālikā—these are remembered as the daughters of Varuṇa;
and Bhadrā and Madirā, these five, he gave to Kubera. (73)
Vidyā, Dhanyā, and Dhanā—these ten were the daughters of Kubera; and to Rudra were born those [other] ten maidens, namely Jayā and Vijayā, as well as [the others]. (74)
Irāvatī, Madhucchandā, Supriyā, Janakā, Kāntā, Subhadrā, Dharmālī, and Śubhā are the wives of Rudra. ||75||
Dakṣa gave those twelve daughters to the Ādityas:
Prabhāvatī, Subhadrā, Vimalā, Nirmalā, and Vṛtā. (76)
Tīvrā, Dakṣā, Hmaruṇā, Vidyā, Dvārapālinī,
Varvasā, and Prabhā— these are the wives of Sūrya.
Dakṣa gave eight daughters to the Viśvedevas:
Yoganidrā, Vibhūti, Śiṃśapā, Śaramā, and Guhā. (78)
Mālā, Vaṃśā, and Jyotsnā are the wives of the Viśvedevas;
and from the two sons of Aśvinī were born Suveṣā and Bhūṣaṇā. (79)
Dakṣa gave one daughter, Śvāsā, to Vāyu, Sāvitrī to Brahmā, and Lakṣmī to Viṣṇu; thus he gave those hundred daughters.
In this manner, at the beginning of creation and in the [first] age, the giving away of a daughter took place;
through that, the custom of bestowing a daughter became established among all.
By them, the entire world, including all things stationary and moving, was completely filled.
Then indeed, in ancient times, all the Pitṛs [issued] from the mouth of Brahmā.
Arising in the form of smoke, with faces turned upward and moving upwards,
the New Moon (Amāvāsyā) was indeed offered to the ancestors in the first age.
And the full-moon night was offered to the Moon, the storehouse of all digits, by the Creator, who was born from the mind of Brahmā as the cool-rayed deity. (84)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the dedication of the lunar days has been described to you;
likewise, here are the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava) and the auspicious Dhanatrayodaśī.
O Lakṣmī, you have been entirely entrusted to Śarada;
furthermore, there is the conjunction of the Mūla asterism and likewise that of Śravaṇa. (86)
It was dedicated by me to Sarasvatī for the purpose of her worship by Hari;
thus are the various days [of the week] named according to their respective origins. (87)
In the first age, these were originally bestowed by me upon the seven gods;
by worshipping them therein, their power is obtained in every respect. (88)
Indeed, the deities bestow wealth, happiness, and equal sovereignty;
likewise, they bring about the pacification of obstacles and the destruction of poverty. (89)
The destruction of mental and physical ailments and other benefits arise from the worship of the deity;
thus, O Lakṣmī, it should always be done toward the God, whether in an image or on every lunar day.
I myself, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, dwell here;
I am well-pleased by their disposition, devotion, service, and in every way.
I, who am compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, shall bring about their welfare;
by hearing and reciting this, eternal fruit is obtained. (92)
Furthermore, the fruit arising from the worship of the respective deities of each lunar day shall be attained;
thus did Śambhu himself declare at Prabhāsa on the occasion of Śivarātri. (93)
O Lakṣmī, all this has been related by me to you as it was told to Pārvatī;
indeed, among all deities, one should especially meditate upon one's chosen deity. 94.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Descriptive Account with Causes of the Fifteen Lunar Days and Their Respective Deities," in the first section, the *Kṛtayugasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lotus-born one, to other sacred fords (tīrthas) spoken of by Śaṅkara;
the two rivers, the Nyaṅkumatī and the Devikā, bestow liberation.
In ancient times, fifty sons of the sage Saṃvarta,
seeking deer and clad in deer skins, always dwelt in a lion forest.
And there were ascetics, free from passion, who, urged by their ancestors for the sake of penance,
subsisted on grass, leaves, and other such things in the holy field of Prabhāsa.
Constantly devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya) and performing the ritual bath three times a day and other such rites, [they recite]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; obeisance! (4)
While they were chanting the name of Govinda, the trees became dwellings for those below;
then, on one occasion, King Vīradhanvan arrived at Prabhāsa.
When he saw those deer in the forest and pierced them with his arrows, those Brahmins died; indeed, the resulting sin of killing (brahmahatyā) arose, bringing great suffering to the king.
Then the king, overcome with anxiety, went to the hermitage of Devarāta;
having confessed his brahmin-murder, he wept, being exceedingly distressed.
That compassionate sage Devarāta spoke to the king:
"Do not weep; go to the vicinity where the Devikā river flows."
Perform penance on its bank and then commence a sacrifice;
by performing expiatory rites, O King, you will become pure.
Having heard this and bowed to him, he went to that river Devikā;
taking Devarāta with him, he performed a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.
He respectfully fed thousands of Brahmins,
worshipped the gods, and gratified the ancestors.
Then, during the conclusion of the sacrifice, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa gratified the mendicants with sweet foods and gifts.
And the sage Lomaśa, having become two deer, went there;
having reached the pavilion altar, they fearlessly took up the sacrificial smoke.
Both of them repeatedly drew him toward them there with their sense of smell;
the king, perceiving them to be gods, rose up and prostrated at their feet.
Then, as those two sneezed, the king was covered with mucus from their nasal secretions; thereupon, the king attained purity.
Then, from the body of the king, maidens of entirely black complexion emerged;
they fell into the sacrificial pit and blazed forth.
"What is this? What is this?"—such was the clamor that arose then;
those two deer, having assumed human form, became men. (17)
Lomaśa, possessing a divine body, and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa also spoke to that king, O monarch: "We have been gratified by you through this sacrifice."
"Behold, through our compassion here, the sins of Brahman-slaughter have been consumed;
you are purified in the field of Devikā by my devotion and the word of your preceptor. (19)
"Rule the kingdom with these; do not again commit such purposeless violence.
This is the time for the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (1.544.20)
"Observe the vow in the form of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika; worship me.
By doing so, you will surely proceed upon the path to liberation—of this there is no doubt. (21)
He performed the Jayantī-kālika vow exactly as prescribed;
Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, appeared before him again and again.
At the time of death, that king went by celestial chariot through the air from the Kuṅkumavāpikā field to heaven, to the world of Indra.
Indra, taking his offering of honor, approached him with a gesture of rising;
meanwhile, the attendants of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa remained seated in their celestial chariot.
The lords said to the king as he was making an effort to rise:
"O King, you must certainly not rise to greet us here. (25)
The gods possess less merit than you, while you increase in merit;
one endowed with great merit is master over one who possesses little merit. (26)
If one performs a formal rising in greeting toward someone of very little merit, then that small amount of merit will perish; therefore, do not practice such rising. 27.
In this way, whichever guardians of the directions had assembled for the sake of honoring him, each of them, having offered worship to this king with their own small bulls, [departed]. (28)
They each went to their own abodes, for the king had not yet arisen;
thus did that king attain liberation, reaching as far as the world of truth (Satyaloka).
In this world free from rebirth and devoid of burning dissolution,
he still remains even today upon the waters, being praised by the gods.
In the second form, he attained eternal bliss in Vaikuṇṭha;
when the Lord of Sacrifice is pleased, what indeed is difficult to obtain, even that which is most excellent? ||3 1||
In this very life, the Lord of Ramā bestows good fortune, long life, health, and prosperity, as well as the supreme liberation so difficult to attain. 32.
Thus the king attained liberation on the auspicious bank of the Devikā at the sacred ford (tīrtha) created by Devarāta, which is essentially Yajñanārāyaṇa.
Likewise, the Mṛgatīrtha exists there at Devikā;
having bathed, meditated, and remembered Hari, one shall certainly attain liberation. (34)
Formerly, on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, Śiva spoke to Pārvatī:
"The sage Cyavana, accompanied by his wife, [arrived] with a desire for the holy ford. (34)
He stayed for one year at Nyaṅkumatī, having arrived there on foot;
for one year at Somanātha, and for one year in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having spent one year on Mount Raivata and another year on Mount Arbuda,
and thus having visited these excellent holy places, he went to Badarikāśrama.
Then Śrī Pārvatī asked: "Who was his virtuous wife?
Śambhu replied: "Listen, O virtuous lady, to the noble story of Cyavana as well. (38)
Once, while established in ascetic penance on the eastern bank of the Hiraṇyā,
he performed a hymn of praise to the Sun consisting of one hundred and eight verses.
Then the Sun, being pleased, arrived in his presence and said to that ṛṣi, "Tell me, what boon shall I grant you?"
Cyavana said: "O Supreme Lord, you are the eye of the worlds, present in one hundred and eight forms within one hundred and eight places."
Dwell in embodied form in Saurāṣṭra within great temples;
King Hiraṇyasiṃha shall construct auspicious abodes for you.
"Reside here in Saurāṣṭra on all sides for the sake of protecting the world.
"So be it," the Sun replied, having performed one hundred and eight [circumambulations]. (43)
And Ravi remained among the forms (rūpas) in Saurāṣṭra according to his pleasure;
O Goddess, I shall tell you those names exactly as they are. 44.
Oṃ! Sūrya, Aryaman, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, Arka, Savitṛ, Ravi, Gabhastimat, Āditya, Dhātṛ, Āditya, and Prabhākara. ||45||
The Sun of the Earth, the Sun of the Forest, the Sun of Radiance, the Lord of the Sky, the Sun of Vital Breath, the Moon-Sun, the Guru-Sun, and the Maker of Day. ||46||
Śukrārka, Aṅgārakāditya, Indrārka, Bodhabhāskara, Dīpāṃśu, Vivasvān, Śucyarka, and Carabhāskara. ||47||
Brahmāditya, Raudrārka, Viṣṇu, Skandārka, Śravaṇārka, Yamārka, Vaidyutārka, and Divaspati; ||48||
Vaiśvānarārka, Agnyarka, Indhanāditya, Īśvara, Dharmāditya, Vedārka, Vācārka, and Kṛtabhāpati. ||49||
Tretāditya, Dvāparārka, Turyāditya, Kalīśvara,
Kalāditya, Kāṣṭhārka, and also Muhūrtāditya.
Cakrāditya, Vatsarārka, Tigmaraśmi, Vibhāvasu, Puruṣārka, Hiraṇyārka, Yogāditya, and Sadīśvara. ||51||
The Sun of the World, the Sun of Creatures, the Sun of the Universe, the Dispeller of Darkness;
the Sun of Varuṇa, the Sun of the Ocean, the Sun of the Clouds, and the Radiant One. ||52||
Bhūtārka, Nirmalārka, Lolārka, Tigmadīdhiti, Kuṣṭhaha-āditya, Īśārka, Bhānu, and also Kāmārka. ||53||
Jayāditya, Bhadrārka, Raivatādityakāntimān, Saṃjñeśa, Suvarṇārka, Śatruñjidarka, and Ādidṛk. (54)
Kapilāṃśu, Aṃśumālin, Kaṅkāditya, Bhāspati, Vanāditya, Saptāśva, Āruṇārka, and Triviṣṭapa. ||55||
Nārāyaṇa, Haritāśva, Sandhyeśa, the Lord Bhagavat, Prabha, Grahāditya, Cāmareśa, Kaṃthaḍeśa, and Karādhipa. ||56||
O Sun of the Vedas, O Sun of Surāṣṭra, O Solar King, O Lord of the virtuous,
O Jewel of the Sky, O Savitṛ, O Ordainer, O Disposer, O Arka— to you, salutations!
Thus, indeed, in Saurāṣṭra they dwell separately;
for these suns reside there for the sake of protecting the world—that sacred site which purifies the world. (58)
On the beautiful bank of the Hiraṇyā lies a place honored by the Kṣatriyas;
whoever recites [this] at sunrise shall obtain a multitude of excellent sons. (59)
One obtains recollection of past births, intelligence, health, and heaven;
as well as gold, elephants, a kingdom, beautiful women, and divine riches.
Thus, by virtue of his power to pass away at will, Sūryanārāyaṇa himself resided in Surāṣṭra in one hundred and eight forms.
Even at Cyavana’s hermitage, on the auspicious bank of the Hiraṇyā,
there exists a sacred ford (tīrtha) that brings about the welfare of the world.
Cyavana’s virtuous wife was the daughter of Śaryāti;
once, after some time had passed, the sage performed austerities in the forest.
Bhagu’s son, Cyavana, remained steadfast upon the earth for a long time;
O Goddess, after a great length of time, he became completely covered by ants.
Completely covered on all sides by lumps of earth and creepers,
and concealed by an anthill, he remained as if established in ascetic penance.
Then, after some time, a king named Śaryāti arrived in the forest where the auspicious hermitage of the sage was located.
The king’s daughter, named Sukanyā, surrounded by her companions,
while wandering about, came upon the anthill of Cyavana.
While gathering beautiful flowers, she saw the two eyes of a seer in an anthill; filled with wonder, she thought, "What is this? and pierced it with a thorn. (68)
Blood issued from the openings of her eyes; she was struck with fear by the wrath of the sage, as well as that of King Śaryāti and his army. (69)
When his excrement and urine were obstructed, the king was greatly distressed.
The maiden said, "O father, it is indeed because of me that the sage has been offended."
The king said to the sage, "You ought to forgive the maiden.
Cyavana replied, "Give me the maiden; indeed, I shall forgive the offense."
Then the king gave away his daughter, and the sage was indeed appeased;
the army became healthy once more, and the maiden attended upon the sage.
The two lords, the physicians of the gods, approached the aged sage and said to Sukanyā, "You are beautiful, yet not suited for an old man. (73)
"Therefore, abandoning Cyavana, choose one of us two.
The maiden replied: "A husband may be a god, whether he be old or even emaciated. (74)
"O physicians of the gods, make my husband young and powerful.
Those two physicians made that great sage resemble themselves.
"The three forms are indeed identical; they have not arisen as separate entities at all.
Thus the maiden reflected: "Who, then, among these is truly my husband? (76)
Through her devotion to her husband and her inner composure, she recognized her own lord; taking him by the hand, the virtuous woman fell at his feet. (77)
The two physicians were struck with wonder, thinking, "She is indeed truly devoted to her husband.
Those two physicians then spoke to Cyavana there regarding sacrifices in every respect.
"O Bhārgava, act in such a way that we two may also have shares;
let the sage grant shares in the sacrifice to those two best of physicians. (79)
Then once, Śaryāti came there to that hermitage to behold the supreme happiness of his daughter, and he saw the maiden.
The king questioned that maiden as she was serving a youth:
"Who is this being served, O maiden? Is there someone else? This is my confusion. (81)
The maiden said: "O father, I have a husband, the illustrious sage Cyavana;
through the union with the sons of Aśvinī, youth has been regained by my lord. (82)
Having heard this, the king became pleased and said to the sage, "I shall perform service for you; tell me, O sage, what it is. The sage replied, "Perform a sacrifice. (83)
Thereupon, being exceedingly delighted, Śaryāti made preparations for the sake of the sacrifice, and the descendant of Bhṛgu officiated as the priest.
Then Cyavana made the two excellent physicians partakers [of the sacrifice];
Indra, however, restrained him, saying, "For these two are not worthy of a share. (85)
These two physicians were censurable both by their profession and by their birth;
yet the sage, disregarding Indra, assigned shares to the pair of healers.
Indra seized his thunderbolt to slay the sage and raised his hand;
the sage paralyzed him, and Mahendra fell for refuge.
Afterwards, he gave them their share, and the paralysis subsided;
thus did the powerful Brahmin [behave] on the auspicious bank of the Hiraṇyā. 88.
Having built a hut, he performed severe penance for one year together with his wife Sukanyā at Prabhāsa in Saurāṣṭra.
Indeed, the Vaikhānasa sages also dwell in that hermitage;
one should perform that pilgrimage with devotion, for it bestows the perfection of capability and sovereignty.
It is the supreme bestower of wealth, sons, daughters, health, and prosperity;
by reciting or hearing it, one is liberated from all sins. (91)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī this most purifying story concerning Śaryāti and Cyavana.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Sūryatīrtha and Cyavanatīrtha, along with their Legends and the One Hundred and Eight Names," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛtayuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning the rivers Nyaṅkumatī and Devikā and the Devarāta-tīrtha.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; Śaṅkara spoke these purifying words to Pārvatī. I shall now describe to you the account of the holy fords (tīrthas) beginning with Agastya.
On the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, there was a divine and supreme hermitage of Agastya;
in the former Kṛta age, he performed penance there for the duration of a year.
Once, the sage Agastya went toward the southern direction with the desire to visit sacred fords; there, he subdued Vātāpi.
His elder brother, named Ilvala, was filled with deceit;
he lived in the city of Maṇimatī, while Vātāpi remained right there [with him].
Having heard of Agastya’s miraculous power, he went toward him and said:
"O Blessed One, grant me a son equal to Mahendra."
Agastya did not wish to give that Asura his son;
thereupon, the Asura became enraged at that Brahmin who was rich in ascetic merit.
While Agastya was on his pilgrimage,
Vātāpi appeared in the form of a fruit— a perfectly ripe kāliṅga— along the way.
The third was Kāmarūpa, and Atāpi had the auspicious Parṇagraha;
it became a beautiful hermitage of sages, complete with an altar.
And Ilvala always provided hospitality to those who arrived at his enclosure, with gifts such as fruit and food.
While the traveler, a guest who eats only fruit,
was eating his fruit and drinking water, the Asura Ilvala arrived there.
He summoned Vātāpi, who was within his belly and had become excellent fruit, saying, "O Vātāpi, come out! Hearing this, [Vātāpi] went into the belly.
Indeed, the living being, having burst through the belly, emerged at that very moment;
then those three brothers, filled with joy, gathered around that deceased person.
They were constantly devouring [beings] and thus perpetrating violence against the sages;
for it was along that very path that Agastya had indeed departed.
Ātāpi became a leaf-hut, while Vātāpi indeed became its fruit;
then Ilvala joyfully addressed that Agastya as his guest.
"O Sage, my fortune is blessed; please accept this fruit-offering.
Indeed, service rendered to a guest brings about supreme liberation. (15)
Agastya said to him, "So be it," and sat down within the house; Ilvala then divided that fruit into two parts and further into four.
He caused Agastya to be fed and summoned his younger brother again;
however, receiving no reply, the sage cooked for him.
Having whirled his hand about in his belly, he then produced a belch;
at that, Ilvala was seized with fear and fled from that spot.
They quickly made their escape, and Ātāpi also fled;
yet the sage reduced them both to ashes at that very moment with a mere glance of wrath.
Then Agastya, wandering through various holy places to perform purification of his body,
arrived here and settled on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī.
He performed penance for exactly one year at this very Agastya-tīrtha;
it was prescribed for the sake of purifying the body, and it is supremely sanctifying and bestows heaven. 21.
Now, in former times, there was a king, a lord of men named Nṛga;
once he went to Prabhāsa for the purpose of a pilgrimage.
Accompanied by only a few servants, he rested on the road in a forest of trees within a lion-infested wilderness; there, during the night, he obtained auspicious and pleasant sleep.
Having discovered this, hundreds of mountain-born thieves, equipped with weapons,
surrounded him on all sides in order to seize his gold and other wealth.
The king's guards were few, while the thieves numbered more than a hundred;
what could be done? To lose one's life for the sake of wealth is not preferable. (25)
Having reflected thus, Nṛga said: "Let them take this abundant wealth;
a wise man should protect himself with riches, wives, and likewise with integrity. (26)
"Although I am a king and these wicked men deserve to be punished by me, nevertheless, I have no army at all that would be sufficient [to subdue them] in the forest. (27)
Since the king has no concern for the loss of his life or the destruction of his vital breaths, my only worry is the loss that my pilgrimage—which brings about liberation—will not take place. (28)
Having given wealth and performed the departure rites, I shall then set out once more;
and having sought them all out, I will destroy them on the field of battle. (29)
While Nṛga was thus reflecting and giving orders to his servants to give wealth to the thieves, [the thief] emerged from the body of the king.
A certain woman, armed and filled with exceeding rage,
effortlessly slew all those thieves in battle with her weapons.
Once the king had recovered his health, he paid homage to that Prarakṣaṇī;
she, however, quickly entered the king's body once again. (32)
Then, at dawn, the king set out on the road toward Prabhāsaka;
he saw the seer Vāmadeva performing austerities on the bank of the Devikā.
Having rested for a moment at midday, he questioned his most venerable preceptor, Vāmadeva: "Who is this maiden born of Śarīra? (34)
Vāmadeva, having entered into meditative absorption and recognized his own ancestor, spoke to that meritorious king: "In a former life, you were Śūdraka."
The eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa was observed by you as a fast, as was the twelfth; that merit now rests within you. (36)
That maiden was indeed of the nature of merit, embodying two lunar days;
she was the maiden Ekādaśī, and the twelfth lunar day was Heti.
By those two, the thieves who were your enemies have been slain; such is the power of your vow at the sacred ford.
For in this way, the merit performed here today surely proceeds to the next world.
A friend, merit, and that which resides within oneself—these always exist together with joy.
Therefore, in human existence, one should perform pilgrimages, observe vows, and practice charity. (39)
Having been told this, Nṛga understood everything and became joyful;
bowing to the sage Vāmadeva and honoring him, he presented him with gifts.
That sacred ford of Vāmadeva is also celebrated as that of the deer;
it is located in Saurāṣṭra within the field of Somaka, and it bestows protection as well as liberation.
Having thoroughly worshipped Somanātha, he then went to his own palace.
Now, there was a twice-born man named Devaśarman, born at the Prabhāsa-tīrtha. 42.
He made his dwelling on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī; being destitute, he abandoned the village for the sake of wealth and committed theft. (43)
He had a son named Duḥsaha, who was indeed a thief;
addicted to vices, he lived in a dilapidated temple in the forest. (44)
Having then lit a lamp for the deity, he committed theft;
severely beaten by the people, he died in the temple of Śiva.
In the region of Gāndhāra, there was a king known by the name Durmukha;
he was a fool who oppressed his subjects and was excluded from righteous conduct. ||46||
Through the consecration of the temple of Śiva, he indeed became a devotee of Śiva;
he always [worshipped] Śiva with flower garlands, incense, food offerings, perfumes, and other such items. (47)
That descendant of Pṛthu also honors other gods with offerings of lamps, wherever he goes on his journey through the divine hermitages. (48)
He always offered lamps in temples;
once, while wandering among the sacred pilgrimage sites on Mount Raivata, he did so as well.
While traveling on the road toward Somanātha in the Siṃhāraṇya forest,
he met his death on the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī due to the power of time.
And by the fruit of his offering of lamps and his worship, that Durmukha became the son of Viśravas, Kubera, the king of the Yakṣas. (51)
Then Kubera, remembering his former birth, went to Prabhāsa,
where he had previously died on the bank of the Yamunā.
Having installed Śambhu there, he indeed constructed a temple at that sacred site,
naming it Kuberaśaṅkara after his own name.
Having performed [the rites] there, he, with a pure mind, offered praise to Śiva;
and Śaṅkara granted three boons to Kubera.
Friendship, sovereignty over wealth, and the guardianship of the quarters among the celestial dwellers—whosoever goes there and worships the Lord of Kubera with devotion [shall attain these]. (55)
In his house, the goddess Lakṣmī shall dwell for seven generations.
Now, during the Svārociṣa interval, there was a fisherman who killed fish. ||56||
Having taken the net, wet with water, from the shore of the ocean to the temple of Śiva, that net made of cords was fastened to the staff of the banner. (57)
And he stationed it so that the banner of the net could be seen, like a net for the drying up of water; thus, for a day, there was the "Net-banner. (58)
By that merit, in another birth, that fisherman became a king named Kratudhvaja in the field of Kunkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra.
He became a powerful king, always residing in the hermitage of Lomaśa,
constantly chanting "Oṃ Namaḥ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇāya."
By the grace of Śaṅkara, he became a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu;
remembering his former births, he offered [worship] at Somanātha in Prabhāsa.
Then, every year, he gave away a large, very long white banner;
for ten thousand years, that king ruled his kingdom.
In the middle of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake was the temple of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
when it had fallen into ruin, the king caused it to be renovated like Mount Śṛṅgavat.
Then, by means of a divine celestial chariot, he went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha;
by reciting or hearing this, the state of liberation becomes certain.
Likewise, there exists at Prabhāsa a beautiful sacred field containing a temple, where the delightful river Ṛṣitoyā flows and where the deities have gathered. (65)
Requested by the sages during a time of drought at a sacrificial session,
and [propitiated] by many sacrifices, the thirsty ones caused a most beautiful rain to fall.
Due to the assembly of the lineages of deities and sages, this excellent river known as Ṛṣikulyā is indeed a purifying sacred ford (tīrtha). ||67||
The sages who formerly dwelt in the tiger-infested forest once went to Satyaloka to behold Brahmā. (68)
They praised Brahmā, who was born from the lotus, with various hymns of praise.
Satisfied, Brahmā said to them all: "Choose whatever you desire in your hearts."
Then those sages said: "Whatever rite is performed, such as bathing or the twilight prayers, with ocean water bestows infinite merit."
In providing water for drinking and in honoring guests and so forth, we always have earth and water from wells and other sources wherever we reside. (71)
Therefore, O Brahmin, you must send rivers toward the earth;
for their waters are sweet and suitable for ritual acts at Prabhāsaka.
O Grandfather, act in such a way that we may obtain it;
O Grandfather, grant us a sacred river for our consecration.
Then Brahmā, having reflected upon what ought to be done,
looked about and summoned the rivers Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī.
Likewise, the Candrabhāgā, the Revā, the Sarayū, and the Gaṇḍakī; the Tāpī, the Godāvarī, the Śiprā, the Kāverī, and the Devikā. ||75||
The Carmaṇvatī, the Māhendrī, the Bhadrā, and likewise the Śatrujit—
indeed, all of them stood before Brahmā in embodied form.
Then Brahmā fixed his gaze upon the water-pot;
and perceiving his intention, they entered that water-pot.
Those excellent rivers, existing in the form of water within the jars, were indeed given by those sages to be led toward the earth.
Then that auspicious river named Ṛṣitoyā, which embodies all rivers, arose in Saurāṣṭra as the river known by the name Ṛṣitoyā.
In the Devadāru forest, where water had formerly been deposited from their water-pots by the sages, that river came into being.
For she was brought to the ocean and increased by her good fortune and other virtues;
then, at the Mūla-caṇḍīśa-tīrtha, she faced toward the east.
O Lakṣmī, that beautiful [narrative], which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, was indeed told by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī; it has been recounted by me to you in brief.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description with Narratives of Agastya’s Hermitage, the Destruction of Ātāpī, Vātāpī, and Ilvala, the Tīrthas of Vāmadeva, Nṛga, and Kubera, the Liberation of Kratudhvaja, and the Tīrthas of Devakula, Ṛṣitoyā, and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate the divine account of King Viśāla as it occurred in the past,
which Śaṅkara told to Pārvatī.
Formerly, there was a very powerful king named Viśāla in the city of Kāśī;
having been deprived of his kingdom by his kinsmen, he went to Mount Gandhamādana.
Having reached the auspicious Badarī in that valley, that best of kings performed penance while worshipping Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Once, the two ancient and most excellent sages,
the divine Nara and Nārāyaṇa, sons of Dharma, arrived there while dwelling in the Himālayas.
Seeing that auspicious king staying at Badarī, performing intense penance and meditating upon Janārdana, who is the supreme Brahman and the very form of Viṣṇu; || 5 ||
O King, seeing him whose impurities were destroyed, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, said: "Choose the boon you desire, O giver of boons."
The king said: "Who are you two? I do not know; how can I grant a boon? To whom shall I give a boon that I am able to bestow upon those who are unknown to me? (7)
"O brāhmaṇas, I shall worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world; from him alone, and no other, shall I receive a boon. (8)
When this was said, the two of them replied: "Whom do you seek to propitiate as your lord?
Or what boon do you choose? Tell us out of curiosity. (9)
Thus addressed, the king spoke to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, "I worship you constantly. Then the two of them spoke again: |||1.546.10||
"By the grace of that very god, we have obtained this boon;
therefore, accept a boon yourself—tell us, what dwells in your heart? (11)
Grant me this boon: may I possess the capacity to worship the Lord of Sacrifice with various sacrifices and diverse sacrificial fees. 1.2.
Then, having indeed shown his elder brother Nārāyaṇa to the king, Nara said: "Listen, O King, to the eternal [truth]."
"This elder brother of mine, the guide of the worlds, dwells at Badarikāśrama performing austerities together with me. (14)
This one was formerly a fish, and thereafter he became a tortoise;
he then became a boar, and after that he became Narasiṃha.
Then Vāmana was born, followed by Paraśurāma;
then Rāma, Buddha, and Kṛṣṇa, and after that, indeed, this Kalki. (16)
This very Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is without beginning and higher than the highest,
shines forth at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpī on the land of Saurāṣṭra.
He is this very Nārāyaṇa, the manifest Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of Ramā,
the Lord of Śrī, the Beloved of Kamalā, and the Sovereign Lord of Pārvatī.
Kṛṣṇa is the Lord of Rādhā, the Lord of Prabhā, and the Lord of Māṇikī; he is the Lord of devotees, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of the virtuous, and the Supreme Person.
O King, one should worship the Fish for the attainment of knowledge of the Vedas;
O King, one should worship the Tortoise for the nourishment of physical strength.
O King, one should worship the Boar-form for the attainment of sovereignty over the earth and other such goals;
one should worship Narasiṃha for the destruction of the enemies that are sins. (21)
One should worship Vāmana for the attainment of universal sovereignty;
one should worship Paraśurāma for the destruction of cruel enemies.
One should always worship Rāmāditya for the increase of dharma;
one should worship the virtuous Buddha for the attainment of self-knowledge. (23)
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, the beloved, for the attainment of Goloka and other realms;
O King, one should worship Kalki for the removal of passion, hatred, and the like.
One should worship the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and His Consort for the sake of imperishable liberation, and for the abundant attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (25)
Having spoken thus to him, the man said: "O King, always perform the vow arising from the day of Hari, as well as the fast on the Ekādaśī."
"Observe a fast on the twelfth day and become capable of performing the sacrifice.
Having said this, the two departed for Badarī, and the king followed after them.
He performed his vow according to the prescribed rites and indeed regained his power;
then Viṣṇu, being pleased, bestowed the Sudarśana discus upon him.
Having taken back that which was offered, he returned once more to his own kingdom;
and having conquered his enemies, that king became a universal monarch (cakravartin). ||29||
And by him, in former times, a place for penance was established on the Himalayas;
there indeed was a city built by the sage, abounding in leaf-huts.
For the sake of the ascetics, that king indeed established that Badarī, known by his own name as Viśālā, in the form of a hermitage.
Named after King Viśāla, that auspicious city became known as Viśālā;
it was the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa and provided a pleasant dwelling for the sages. 32.
Having made that the supreme sacred ford there, he goes to the supreme abode;
having remained in his kingdom again and again in that birth, this king— || 33 ||
Having worshipped Hari with various sacrifices, he made Him well-pleased;
then, on one occasion, he went to Arbuda-puṣkara for the sake of visiting holy places.
Then indeed [he visited] Lomaśakṣetra and Raivatācala;
having reached Prabhāsakṣetra and beheld Somanātha. ||35||
Having gone to Guptaprayāga, he indeed performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice;
then, having bowed to Lomaśa in the sacred field of Śrīkuṅkumavāpī, [he departed].
Then, having abandoned his kingdom, he departed from worldly existence and went to Badarī;
having attained Nārāyaṇa through devotion, he went to the supreme abode of Hari. (37)
By this king, a sacrifice was performed at Guptaprayāgaka;
that place indeed exists as a supreme, excellent, and liberating tīrtha. (38)
Listen also to another king, by whose name an excellent tīrtha was established at the bank of the Bhadrikā in the place called Jayantī; it is known as Bhadreśvara. (39)
In the Kṛta Yuga, there was a king named Bhadrāśva, a sovereign among devotees;
after his name, the region became known by the name Bhadrāśva.
Once, the most excellent Agastya, having come to his house, said:
"I shall dwell in your home for seven nights."
The king, bowing his head to him, said, "Please remain.
He had a wife named Kāntimatī who was devoted to her husband. (42)
Her splendor became equal to the luster of the moon upon the earth;
moreover, the king had five hundred other wives as well.
By the power of her asceticism, those [other women] perform tasks like female slaves;
moreover, she is a highly fortunate wife, radiant and supreme among all. (44)
And out of fear of her, her co-wives constantly performed service for her;
then Agastya saw that auspicious woman, endowed with beauty and splendor.
Seeing the king there to be greedy and devoid of devotion to Hari, and seeing Kāntimatī to be lacking in devotion, the sage spoke. ||46||
On the first day, seeing him gazing at the face of his beloved, Agastya, filled with great joy, exclaimed: "Excellent! Excellent, O Lord of the World! (47)
On the second day as well, having likewise beheld the queen and the king, [he cried]:
"Alas, this world of moving and non-moving beings has been robbed! Alas, it has been robbed! (48)
Thus Agastya spoke, shaking his head while the king was listening;
and on the third day, seeing both the king and the queen, he said out of grief: (49)
"Alas, the fools do not know the Supreme Lord, the Giver,
who, being pleased with the king in a single day alone, bestowed [all this] upon him."
On the fourth day, raising his hands, he spoke again:
"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of the World! Women and Śūdras—excellent, excellent! (51)
"Excellent, O twice-born ones! Excellent, O kings! Excellent, O Vaiśyas, again and again!
Excellent, O Bhadras! Excellent, O you! Excellent, O Agastya; excellent indeed is yours! (52)
"Excellent, Prahlāda! Excellent, you! Dhruva, excellent, you of great vows! Having spoken thus, Agastya danced exultantly in the presence of the king.
Having seen him in such a state, the best of kings, accompanied by his wife, asked:
"O Brahmin, what is the cause of this joy, that he dances here in this manner? (54)
Moreover, O learned one, with a mind full of supreme bliss,
Agastya spoke thus to Bhadrāśva and the queen.
"Alas! You are a foolish king and this beloved wife of yours is foolish;
all your ministers are fools, and alas, your priests are fools as well! (56)
O King, your entire realm appears to be filled with folly;
those who do not understand my opinion find it simple and self-evident. (57)
When this had been said, the king spoke again with palms joined in reverence:
"O Brahmin, we do not understand the meaning you have expressed, which is so full of profound intent. (58)
"O great sage, if you are inclined to show favor, then investigate [this matter].
Thereupon, Agastya related the account of his previous birth exactly as it had occurred.
In the city of Nagara-pattana, there was indeed a Vaiśya named Haradatta;
you were his servant, a man of the Śūdra caste who was exceedingly devoted to him.
This queen, your wife, was formerly a servant of a Vaiśya;
that Vaiśya, remaining self-restrained, stood on the twelfth day of the month of Aśvayuj.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord!
Having gone to the abode of Viṣṇu while chanting His names, one should worship Hari with flowers, incense, and other offerings. (62)
He indeed worships constantly and practices meditation for a long time,
having appointed you two as guardians within the temple.
Having set aside two lamps for the purpose of lighting [the others],
that Vaiśya then indeed went to his own home, while you two remained in the house of Hari.
Having performed daily the sweeping, the offering of water, the placing of flowers and *tulasī*, and the honoring of those who have arrived before Hari; 65.
Day and night,
you two remained there, having relit them once more, indeed protecting the lamps from being extinguished.
By that merit, your sins shall dissolve along with your lifespan;
then, when the night has turned to dawn, you two— ||67||
By the grace of Śrī Hari, they cast off their Śūdra bodies and passed away;
thereafter, O King, your birth took place in the house of Priyavrata.
This very Kāntimatī, who has come along with you, was your wife;
she was the flame of even another's lamp that had been lit in Hari’s house. (69)
This excellent kingdom has been acquired by you both through the grace of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who was propitiated by your service, devotion, and spirit of servitude.
Furthermore, the merit of one who lights lamps before Viṣṇu with his own wealth cannot be calculated. (71)
Sweeping, smearing [with cow dung], washing, cleaning the vessels, massaging the feet, washing the clothes, and likewise offering praise; ||72||

The restoration of dilapidated [shrines], worship, the offering of flowers and tulasī, the presentation of food offerings, water, leaves, fruits, and the waving of lamps, and so forth—[these are the duties]. (73)
One should daily perform the anointing with sandalwood, unbroken rice, saffron, and fragrant juices; it is impossible to describe the limit of that person's merit.
Therefore, O King, remembering your own merit as well as that performed in the past, I indeed exclaimed with joy: "Excellent! Excellent, O Lord of the World! (75)
The merit that is obtained in the Kṛta age by [one] year is obtained in the Tretā age by six months;
in the Dvāpara age by three months; and in the Kali age, that same merit is obtained in a single day.
Uttering "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya" and worshiping Kṛṣṇa with devotion, a person obtains the fruit of all [such acts]. (77)
Even though this is so, when the Kali age has arrived in this world,
people will indeed not worship Kṛṣṇa, as they did in the Dvāpara or even the Tretā ages.
They have been robbed by their own actions and are utterly deceived;
and you, O King, are likewise always devoted to this very beloved. (79)
"You do not remember the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa here;
having observed all this, I spoke thus on another day."

Alas, it is stolen! Alas, it is stolen! This entire world of moving and non-moving beings has been stolen; indeed, this world of moving and non-moving beings has been robbed and deceived by the wife of Śrī Hari. (81)
People do not worship Hari, the best of persons and the giver of prosperity;
rather, they seek great fruit even from the excellence of another's lamp. (82)
Even though the kingdom has been obtained, they do not chant the name of Śrī Hari;
neither the king nor the queen even remembers Narayana.
Even upon my arrival, these two will not worship the Supreme Person;
for indeed, through the company of the virtuous, even those who are everywhere non-devotees may [become so] for a moment. (84)
Fools never perform devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
even when there is a favorable opportunity, those devoid of devotion are indeed deluded—of this there is no doubt. (85)
"It appears to me that the king is foolish and his queen is even more foolish;
therefore, on the third day, having seen you both, I spoke thus. (86)
"Alas, the fools do not know Govinda, the Supreme Lord;
all this happiness as well is the fruit of the lamp-offering to Hari. (87)
