O King, by raising my hands on the fourth day, I obtained the fruit of a single day: a most excellent kingdom. (88)
"Having deliberated, this has been proclaimed to you both: all devotees are indeed virtuous, as are the twice-born, the kings, and those who are Vaiṣṇavas, by the Blessed One. (89)
They worship with various sacrifices; therefore, they are remembered as the virtuous.
Those who do not worship the Lord of Gods, even though the means for prosperity are available, [are not so].
Therefore, even one who is destitute is superior if he indeed worships Keśava;
for although I dwell in the forest, I am destitute and without family. ||91||
Nevertheless, I am indeed virtuous when compared with those possessed of worldly prosperity, for I never forget that Supreme Person. (92)
"O virtuous one, 'Agastya,' I said to him with certainty;
that woman is blessed, and that Śūdra is considered even more blessed. (93)
One should always perform service in every way toward one's master, who is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa;
and toward one's beloved husband, for Hari indeed resides eternally within him, even when he is out of sight.
Whatever action one performs with this understanding becomes a virtuous deed offered to Kṛṣṇa;
blessed is that woman, and likewise the Śūdra who is devoted to the service of the twice-born.
Indeed, those two perform that devotion to Hari by the command of the twice-born;
for those who are endowed with devotion to Hari are declared to be both twice-born and virtuous sages.
Those kings are said to be virtuous who constantly worship Hari;
having adopted a demoniac disposition, Prahlāda [worshipped] Puruṣottama.
Having abandoned everything else, he knows nothing other than that; therefore, he is called "Sādhu.
And Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, was indeed still a child. (98)
Having propitiated Viṣṇu in the forest, he attained the most exalted station;
therefore, O best of kings, I have declared that Dhruva was a virtuous man. (99)
O King, everything becomes auspicious when Śrī Kṛṣṇa is remembered in the heart;
it remains inauspicious only so long as Śrī Kṛṣṇa has been forgotten.
O King, you have attained supreme sovereignty, yet you have forgotten Viṣṇu;
therefore, worship here Govinda, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
Having been addressed thus, the couple bowed and, remembering the fruit born of their previous births,
took refuge in Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of fruits.
O Lakṣmī, liberation may also be attained by whoever hears this;
that which Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī has been related by me to you. (103)
Bhadrāśva went to Prabhāsa for the purpose of a pilgrimage to sacred sites;
there, in Saurāṣṭra, on the auspicious western bank of the Bhadrā river, he stayed.
In the city named Jayantā, there is the holy site (tīrtha) established by Śaṅkara;
it is called Bhadreśvara, and merely hearing its name destroys all sin.
Furthermore, the king granted him there the hermitage of Agastya,
which consists of asceticism and is frequented by Brahmanical sages, situated on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Viśālātīrtha established by King Viśāla, the Bhadreṣṭha-tīrtha established by King Bhadrāśva, and the Instruction of Agastya," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to what Agastya then told the auspicious King Bhadrāśva regarding self-knowledge; I shall relate to you that which grants liberation to the world.
Indeed, that was spoken by Śaṅkara to Satyā in Prabhāsa in ancient times;
Bhadrāśva then questioned Agastya regarding the boon that grants liberation.
"O one of great wisdom, tell me that knowledge by which I may indeed attain liberation.
Agastya said to the king: "Without a guru, there is truly no path."
The Guru is Brahmā himself, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and Nārāyaṇa;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman, the manifest Lord Hari.
By propitiating him, the embodied being first becomes fit for liberation;
indeed, his own self-gratification arises precisely through his blessings.
One should observe the vow, perform worship, and seek propitiation again and again;
furthermore, the bestower of knowledge and mantras shall deliver one from the ocean of worldly existence. || 6 ||
One should give food to the guru; this is called the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
One should perform the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and worship Hari, the Lord of Yogins.
To whoever should impart the secret doctrine of Hari along with the Sumantra [text],
one should give him everything one possesses, including what is dear, such as the offering of oneself.
The fruit of that which is given to him is many millions of times greater:
happiness, sovereignty, great bliss, heaven, and eternal liberation.
But if a teacher is present, that person of base intellect who would resort to and worship another does not obtain the fruit; indeed, what is given to him is rendered fruitless.
One should first cause the preceptor to receive [the gift] with effort, and afterwards cause another to receive it;
for whether he is ignorant or learned, the preceptor alone is Janārdana.
Whether situated on the path or not on the path, the Guru alone is the supreme refuge.
But he who, having approached a Guru, subsequently behaves contrary to him— || 12 ||
That lowest of men, who is a vessel for offenses against the guru, shall be miserable;
since Nārāyaṇa dwells within the guru, one becomes happy by propitiating him. 13.
The image is indeed Nārāyaṇa himself; consciousness is the preceptor alone.
It remains awake, bathes, puts on garments, and applies sandalwood paste.
He accepts the saffron and other fragrant substances offered by people, as well as flowers, leaves, fruits, water, food, and betel-leaf. (15)
He accepts the water, ornaments, collyrium, and so forth offered by the people, as well as the seat, the mount, the vehicle, the couch, the sandals, and the like. (16)
He accepts the water, the auspicious substances, and so forth offered by people; likewise, he accepts their mental disposition, love, devotion, service, and whatever else has been offered.
He accepts the massaging of his feet, drink, friendship, laughter, cheerfulness, prostrations, and service to his body, all offered by people. (18)
The compassionate one indeed takes upon himself the suffering of his disciple and even wards it off;
he constantly provides assistance and bestows knowledge that grants peace. 19.
He indeed burns away evil and bestows abundant merit;
the Guru alone is Janārdana himself, who gives everything of his own.
The guru alone is the husband, the son, the chaste, virtuous, and devoted wife;
likewise, the father, the mother, and the wife—the guru indeed is everything.
The Guru alone is the protector, the nourisher, the savior, the awakener, and the one who leads to the abode of Hari; indeed, the Guru is Hari himself.
A brother is to be honored with a single-fold degree; a father ten times more than that;
a mother is to be honored a hundredfold; and a teacher a thousandfold.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, possesses boundless qualities;
he is the Lord of Akṣara, the glorious Blessed One, Puruṣottama. || 24 ||
In this way, one should always worship the Guru who is indeed manifest before one's eyes;
for through divine yoga, the Guru is the very divine form of Hari himself. (25)
He who brings about the divine nature of the disciple is indeed the Divine Hari;
thinking thus, O King, one should always meditate upon and worship the Guru. (26)
A disciple should seek out a preceptor who is a supreme vessel that bestows ultimate welfare;
having heard the words of his own preceptor, Bhadrāśva rejoiced within himself.
Having attained everything, the Guru considered himself to have reached perfection; yet, for the sake of awakening the worlds, he bowed down and questioned him once again.
"O Guru, everything that was to be attained has been attained by me; nothing remains.
Nevertheless, speak to me of the dharmas of liberation which bring benefit to the world. (29)
O Blessed One, by what action is the cycle of existence severed? Or, having done what, do they not grieve upon being reborn in embodied or formless states? (1.547.30)
"And by doing what does a human being become composed of the Supreme Brahman?
Having heard these words of the king, Agastya spoke with great joy.
Listen, O King, to this divine narrative concerning those situated far and near, arising from the distinction between the visible and the invisible; be composed in mind.
In the past, as well as in the present and the future, there was a kingdom that was boundless and limitless, where neither the sun nor the moon shone. (33)
There was neither night nor day, nor were there directions or the earth;
there was no sky and no gods, for such was that divine sovereignty. || 34 ||
There, King Muktapāla, the sovereign whose life is eternal, protected the divine liberated souls who were beyond all numbering. (39)
The subjects honored him by offering their entire being;
indeed, the king provides everything, including the sweet food of his subjects. (36)
There was neither cold nor heat, and those beings were endowed with supernatural powers;
they were free from sleep, possessed eternal bliss, were perpetually satisfied, and devoid of desire.
All their intentions were fulfilled and they were overflowing with royal joy;
indeed, all the subjects lived under that very universal monarch. 38.

Where there is no other fragmented kingdom and fourfold socialism, there is the state of sharing the same world (sālokya) for all liberated souls, and the state of equal power (sārṣṭitā) for all embodied beings. ||39||
There is identity of form with all principles and union with all yogis,
whether in eating, sexual pleasure, traveling, riding, imagining, or in delight.
There is equality in knowledge, devotion, and perception, as well as in the benefits derived;
such is that great kingdom where there is only truth and no falsehood. (41)
Where there is no court of justice, there is no authority over wrongdoing; where there is indeed no theft, mental distress, or conduct characterized by enmity. (42)
Where there is no impurity, where there is no decay, and where there is no excellence—how could there be hatred or passion? (43)
Such is the entire essence of sovereignty, manifest as if held in the palm of one's hand;
yet it is also something seen from afar, heard from afar, and even contemplated from afar.
Everything is directly his own domain, and that means of accomplishment is indeed born of himself;
for that kingdom is the consecration of his subjects, who are themselves purifiers. ||45||
Indeed, even the mere passage of those who are impure does not occur there;
whatever is the boundary of the impure, beyond that, it is not to be accepted. ||46||
Untrodden forests extend all around;
that king, the protector of himself, went forth to roam in the forest. (47)
The forests, the oceans, the mountains, and the cultivated lands—those which exist on the lower slopes of the great divine kingdom. ||48||
That kingdom had indeed been given previously to a maidservant and to a servant;
desiring to see it out of compassion, the king went to the western shore. ||49||
Above is the eternal shore of the ocean whose further limit is infinite;
there, upon island after island within the ocean of worldly existence, dwell the fishermen.
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, and pride—these five, along with the eight trees that rain down desires, exist there. (51)
Dharma and adharma, as well as knowledge and ignorance as the fourth;
sovereignty and lack of sovereignty, passion and dispassion—these are they. (52)
Where the river named Manovahā flows constantly across, the five principal leaders also wandered below and above. 53.
Sound, touch, as well as form, taste, and smell by name—these exist always as one, the primary and principal, known as prāṇa. (54)
There dwells one woman who, like a queen, possesses superior power;
she, named Buddhi, O King of Kings, always serves him with threefold qualities. (55)
That woman constantly and firmly protects Mahendra upon her own breast;
she is like a hundred thousand moons and equal to a thousand suns.
Her lower [nature] has three transformations: laughter, wonder, and ferocity;
her color is also threefold: white, red, and consisting of darkness (tamomaya).
A young woman is always delightful, like a fresh [flower] remaining on its stalk;
yet without a man, she withers, becomes silent, and is as if dead. (58)
Upon seeing that divine person approaching the edge of the bank, she,
though lifeless and insentient, became as if possessed of hope and restored to consciousness.
The king also, gazing upon her again and again with sheer compassion,
entered the ocean, the forest, and her fields.
When the king had entered, the subjects residing in Strīrājya,
including the chief officials and others, then assembled and came together to welcome him.
Some, bowing down, brought water, vessels, seats, and so forth;
having fallen into a state of unity through fear, they presented these offerings in an instant.
Although the king was then surrounded by those fishermen who were devoid of righteousness,
as well as by desire and the other [afflictions], he nevertheless did not yield his heart to them.
Then this king, perceiving them to be arrogant and desiring to bring them under his control,
reflected upon one son of his mind as a leader.

As long as she remained childless, despite her longing for offspring, so that all these [beings] might be dependent upon her and yet not exist [as she desired], that woman remained without children. (65)
She entreated the king, "Make me pregnant with a son," and the king replied, "So be it. The woman then gave birth to her own son.
He was a person of three colors—white, red, and black—and being identical in all respects, as soon as he was born, he said: "Give me a name indeed! (67)
Thereupon, the king gave his son the principal name "Mahān" (The Great One);
by that, the king became pleased, and the son likewise [pleased] the monarch at that time.
He assailed him with speed, yet the exceedingly powerful king did not succumb to that assault;
therefore, out of a desire for a son, he [remained firm].
He praised that king, and by him a son similar to himself was granted;
he too became threefold, and the Great One said to him, "I am indeed He."
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), known by the name "I am" (asmīti), is like a father;
having thus obtained a son and a grandson, the woman is exceedingly joyful. ||71||
Then, by that power, the woman obstructed the king;
yet when he, being most powerful, was not restrained,
she again considered her own strength and the army to be inferior.
And she chose five other sons, the children of Ahaṅkāra. ||73||
The king gave those five boys, who were composed of his own essence;
and they all, having arrived and gathered together, besieged the king.
Nevertheless, the king was neither bound nor indeed liberated;
then that woman chose fifteen boys. (75)
"So be it," the king said, and he gave them the ten sense organs;
they also gave him the five vital breaths, and having come together, they besieged the king.
Nevertheless, he was not restrained; therefore, they went to another refuge.
Then, having surrounded Mahendra while he remained in his own kingdom, they stood there.
Indra is the Self, and Mahendra is that very one who was indeed obstructed by the Dasyus;
for all those Dasyus have become united as one with Indra.
Then they suddenly rose up there to kill, bind, or crush the king; yet even so, he remained bound indeed. (79)
Then, as the king desired to depart, leaving everyone behind,
at that moment all of them, including Indra, became as if dead.
Furthermore, he was entreated by all of them for the sake of living beings,
so that they might be gathered together in their own mandala and always remain with him.
Then the compassionate Lord, the master who establishes divine sovereignty,
made him his follower, like one bound, to carry out his work in his own place.
She gave birth to a man who was in accordance with his past actions—
golden-hued, untainted, and established in the application of the king’s commands.
By a woman with great pride, it was desired through lust and other passions;
it was honored by sounds and the like, by hearing and the like, and by the vital breaths and so forth. ||84||
Having produced them, he gave them to those [beings], while he himself remained obstructed and enveloped;
he is both the knot of the insentient and sentient, and that golden man.
He produced similar children, as numerous as the hairs on his body;
they were exceedingly beautiful Vairājas, yet they too were thereafter overwhelmed by thirst.
They created from their navel regions a few innumerable children;
to each of them was given a great thirst that impels them toward action. (87)
The creative impulse (vāsanā) that impels the performance of ritual action is not bestowed by another;
through both of these, Brahmā rejoices and generates further progeny. (88)
Having given all of this—his entire family, which was supremely capable of performing his duties—to his wife, that king departed for his own divine realm. (89)
All the auspicious families had indeed vanished;
with them vanished, O King, Indra became truly without refuge.
Obstructed by sin and conditioned by the sequence of his latent impressions, he wept;
then the compassionate king provided him with a comfortable shelter for that purpose.
Then that lord of the earth indeed gave ether, air, fire, water, and earth; he restored their manifest forms to those that had been dissolved. 92.
These five, which have attained a state of unity through their functional activity, are interconnected;
they are the supports and the objects of focus for Mahendra. (93)
Then those [elements], having indeed become sluggish and then arisen once more, returned to their own functions and remained established therein. //94//
Mahendra, surrounded by Dasyus, ruled his kingdom in the auspicious city of nine gates; he governed it himself in that manner. ||95||
Mahendra and the others wandered about, utterly distressed by their confusion regarding the directions;
then they said to that king, "Give us a guide."
Having heard their supreme prayer, the king gave his daughter Subodhinī to the one named Mahendra, just as the divine king of heaven [gave Sītā] to Rāma.
Mahendra was seen together with her and became happy;
they all dwelt in that auspicious abode as if they were formless. (98)
In the city with nine gates, which has a single pillar, extends in all directions, is crowded with thousands of rivers, and is the locus of all activities. (99)
But seeing his friend Mahendra alone— whirling about, bewildered, as if lost, and standing there— he, the king, [beheld him].
Having indicated the expressive words, he taught the auspicious Vedas;
at that time, he also indeed instructed them in the observances (niyamas) and the restraints (yamās).
By that means his delusion was indeed destroyed, and he remembered the king once more;
however, being bound by fetters, he was unable to escape.
Then, O King, he immediately desired weapons from the gods;
the monarch gave him an unimpeded weapon, the excellent *vajra*.
Then Mahendra, having severed his bonds, went to the king’s palace;
in an instant, he became endowed with eternal happiness and bliss.
All these Mahendras, according to their past karma,
become kings of the cities of bodies within the ocean of existence.
And by means of the twenty-four thieves, those situated in the middle are bound—
through service, through intellect, through devotion, through servitude, and through yoga.
Having pierced through both the bonds and [the body] with any one of the weapons,
he goes to a divine royal kingdom where there is no further bondage.
O King, this discourse has arrived; it resides within the domain of all, being identical in your body, in my body, and in the bodies of all living beings.
Having abandoned the kingdom of illusion, one should take refuge in the divine sovereign;
by that means, attaining the state of liberation, one enjoys eternal bliss. 109.
"Having abandoned the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*), one should attain the state of cessation (*nivṛtta*).
O Lakṣmī, this is what Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī, as I have related it.
And Agastya spoke to King Bhadrāśva:
"This very king, having attained unsurpassed knowledge in Saurāṣṭra... (11.1)
Having propitiated Nārāyaṇa there with devotion, he left the realm of Indra and went to his own kingdom. || 11.2 ||
He went to the divine state of liberation, which is the very form of the King;
whoever recites or even hears this shall obtain the relinquishing of the self.

One shall attain the further shore of existence, the ultimate shore where the ocean of illusion ceases through the destruction of latent impressions—the ancient, great friend; of this there is no doubt. (1.14)
O beloved, for one who possesses desire, wealth, sons, offspring, and likewise prosperity,
as well as constant health and the knowledge of reality, shall arise from hearing this.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Agastya as the Teacher of Self-Knowledge Bestowed upon King Bhadrāśva," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. ||547||

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of a most excellent and auspicious tīrtha in the eastern part of Prabhāsa, as told by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī, which effects the liberation of living beings.
There exists Guptaprayāga, and likewise the deity Mādhava;
indeed, the goddesses Jāhnavī, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī are also present there.
Furthermore, other holy sites also reside at that Prayāga,
and likewise, Śṛgāleśvara Tīrtha is situated in its vicinity.
The confluence of the three rivers is a supremely auspicious sacred site;
likewise, there are the auspicious Brahmakuṇḍa, Viṣṇukuṇḍa, and Rudrakuṇḍa.
Emerging from the middle of the pit, the Gaṅgā flows well toward the Yamunā;
between these two, the Sarasvatī remains hidden in a subtle form.
One who performs a bath here in the month of Māgha obtains the fruit born of bathing at Prayāga, equal to the fruit of the King of Tīrthas; there is no doubt in this matter. || 6 ||
Indeed, the Mothers and the Rakṣikas dwell at that sacred bathing place;
one should worship those Mothers for the destruction of fear from spirits and other such beings.
A bull should be given there for the attainment of the fruit of the pilgrimage;
moreover, the person who, having bathed in Viṣṇukuṇḍa, worships Mādhava [shall obtain that fruit].
He, however, shall go to Vaikuṇṭha, where Lord Hari himself resides;
this holy field named Śṛgāleśvara extends for half a krośa.
Those killed by cattle, those killed by twice-born brahmins, those killed by fanged beasts, those who commit suicide, and those who die from snake bites— [these go to the realm of Yama].
Those who die on their beds and are devoid of purity—for them, one should indeed perform a śrāddha here;
by that, they shall be liberated and freed from suffering and grief. (11)
There, the holy site of Siddheśvara was established by the gods in ancient times;
through its worship, one obtains the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* as well as prosperity.
From there, one should go to the Nāradāditya tīrtha, the abode of the Sun;
for once, in the course of a pilgrimage across the earth, [Nārada] arrived there.
But when Nārada arrived, due to the transition of the sun's movement,
a laxity came over his body as if it were caused by old age.
Therefore, the sage has no enthusiasm to go to the truthful heaven,
since he has attained deformity and is deprived of youth and the like.
"How can one dwell in this world which is real [only] by way of being of a different nature and so forth?"—
as he was reflecting thus, the Sun appeared before him in person.
Speak, Nārada, what anxiety has arisen in your mind?
For there are many others who wander about in the mortal world as well. (17)
Whether they be lords, gods, sages, or even yogis,
they too are pervaded by my activities and certainly undergo decay.
Just like mortals, they too, by the power of time, are swallowed up by human beings; they become old in every respect, just as men do.
Speak! You appear to be sixteen years of age and as if you have come from the realm of Satyaloka; yet today you were born upon this earth and are already seized by old age.
"Do not worry, O Brahmin; being young, you shall wander about.
The power of the rays [of the sun] shall not prevail over you. (2.1)
Thus addressed, Nārada, who was sixteen years old and very firm, became as he had been before; and the sun then vanished from sight.
Then, at that place, Nārada installed the Sun-god named Nāradāditya and established a purifying sacred site (tīrtha).
The man who beholds it on a Sunday falling on the seventh lunar day shall have no fear of disease, by the grace of Ravi, the sun, the jewel of the heavens. (24)
There exists another sacred site there, which is the refuge of Aparanārāyaṇa;
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, one should worship according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Viṣṇu, the lotus-eyed one, whose essence is Nārāyaṇa;
furthermore, the auspicious holy site of Gaṅgā is indeed situated there to the northeast.
Where there dwell three-eyed fish marked with the sign of Rudra—listen now to the arrival of the Gaṅgā at that place and to the three-eyed nature of those fish. (27)
When Rudra, being naked, once wandered among the circles of sages in the hermitages for the sake of alms, he was then [treated] by them... 28.
Indeed, Maheśvara was cursed by those enraged sages who did not know [the truth]:
"You shall wander in the world like an elephant, devoid of shame like a beast. (29)
"Therefore, O Śaṅkara, become an elephant dwelling in the forest. Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara immediately became an elephant and entered the forest.
There, Bhṛgu, having perceived Śaṅkara through his yogic vision and seeing the entire world devoid of joy, spoke to the supreme sages.
But this Śaṅkara had also become one in the form of an elephant;
thinking that a great offense had been committed against Śaṅkara, [he reflected]. (32)
Meditating, they made an intense request at the Prabhāsaka field,
specifically at the place named Śṛgāla where Guptaprayāgaka is located.
Then all those who were devoted to austerity and possessed of the power of asceticism arrived there:
Bhṛgu, Atri, as well as Manki, Kaśyapa, and Kaṇva.
Gautama, Kauśika, and Kuśika of great asceticism;
Jātūkarṇya, Vasiṣṭha, Satyatapas, and Parāśara. ||35||
Śāṇḍilya, Pulastya, Vatsa, and Sāvasti;
also Śūkara, Bharadvāja, Bhārgava, and Dīrghatāpasa. (36)
These and many other sages, such as Agastya and others,
having performed penance and meditated upon Hara, became absorbed in Him at that time.
Then Śambhu indeed appeared before them in person;
he spoke for the purpose of granting boons, and they chose their own desired gifts. ||38||
"O Lord of Gods, if you are pleased, bring the Gaṅgā here first;
having performed my ablution there and worshipped you thereafter," (39)
"Out of ignorance you have harmed us; from this we shall attain purification.
For with both our eyes, we did not recognize you as Śaṅkara."
Therefore, the offense committed against you would not be as it is for us;
O Śambhu, grant us a third divine eye, just like yours. 41.
May there be direct perception of Hari, Hara, and others who uphold the means of valid knowledge;
likewise, O Śaṅkara, grant me the inner eye for such acquaintance. 42.
Śambhu said, "So be it; you shall indeed be the purifiers of purifiers, and may you always possess three eyes. And here is Gaṅgā, who has arrived. (43)
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara quickly departed from that place;
and by the grace of Śaṅkara, the sages were liberated from sin. 44.
In that sacred field, they performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice for eight days;
the Brāhmaṇas, the deities, other holy places, and the forest deities were present. ||45||
They gathered at his sacrifice; having eaten the food produced by the grace of Nārāyaṇa, other living beings indeed attained supreme satisfaction.
All creatures born of water and born of land were satisfied there at that auspicious sacrifice; the fish spoke to all the sages, "Just as fishermen indeed are to us... (47)
"Those who desire to kill us would not do so; therefore, let a blessing be granted to us.
Then the sages said, "May you indeed possess three eyes! (48)
And may this third divine eye, which grants the power of far-sight—this very form of Śaṅkara—be ever present for you. 49.
And those auspicious three-eyed fish belonging to Śaṅkara were pointed out by the sages to the fishermen: "These must never be killed."
The reason for his having three eyes has likewise been declared in the Gaṅgāgamana;
having arrived at that pool and bathed there, one should look for fish. (51)
One should give chickpeas and other such items to them, and offer gold to a Brahmin;
by giving cows, clothing, and sesame seeds, one will certainly become three-eyed.
Having bathed in the waters of the Ṛṣitoyā and likewise in the pool of hot water (Taptodaka), one should worship Śaṅkara there; he shall become the lord of the world.
There resides the four-faced Vināyaka of great power;
by worshipping him on a Monday, a person shall obtain their desired wishes. (54)
From there, one should go to the supreme holy site of Hari, known as Gopālasvāmin,
which pacifies the flood of all sins and destroys the mass of poverty.
One should worship Bakulasvāmin Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
from there, one should go to Uttarārka, which destroys all diseases.
On that shore of the ocean, there is indeed the Ṛṣitīrtha;
there, sages are always seen in the form of stones. (57)
Then one should go to Maruddevī, who was formerly worshipped by the Maruts;
thereafter, one should go to Kṣemāditya, situated in the midst of the Śabara settlement.
From there, one should go to Mahādevī Śubhrā Kaṇṭakaśodhinī;
on the bank of the Ṛṣitoyā, the great sages performed sacrifices in ancient times. (59)
The sky was completely enveloped by the smoke arising from the sacrificial offerings and the *agnihotra* fires;
having smelled it, the Daityas emerged from the midst of the ocean and arrived there.
Deceitful, with massive bodies, dark-complexioned, and pot-bellied;
with long eyebrows, beards, and tips of the nose, they have red eyes and red hair. ||61||
And they created disturbances for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice;
seeing them, the sages fled, overcome with fear.
Some, filled with joy, quickly entered the wife's hall (patnīśālā),
having placed the sacrificial materials for the Agnihotra according to the mantras.
They offered oblations into the well-kindled fire for the sake of destroying the Rākṣasas;
as soon as the offering was made, a spear appeared that struck terror into the worlds.
Holding a sword, a spear, a trident, a scimitar, and a shield in her hands, she was most brilliantly radiant;
by her, all those Daityas were then slain. 65.
All the sages praised her, and she, being pleased, spoke to them:
"Choose a boon, O sages; I shall grant you here whatever you desire."
The sages chose you as the purifier of the thorns of the gods;
dwell here in this place named Kaṇṭakaśodhinī and protect us. (67)
"So be it," she said, remaining right there;
one should then worship her, who brings about welfare, on either the eighth or the ninth lunar day.
No fear shall arise for him from Rākṣasas or Piśācas;
he shall attain success in sacrifice as well as the fruit arising from the ritual.
From there, one should go to the holy site named Unnata situated in the northern region;
there, one should worship Brahmeśvara as well as Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa.
Formerly, on the banks of the Ṛṣitoyā, Brāhmaṇas performed most intense penance; because of that, Nārāyaṇa went there having become a mendicant. (71)
Then Śambhu, having become a bull, wandered in the presence of the sages;
there Nārāyaṇa was seen by Hara as one who perceives the three periods of time.
Upon merely being seen, Śaṅkara, who bore the form of a bull, ceased his movement;
there, Śambhu became established in the form of a liṅga as Caṇḍikeśvara.
O Lakṣmī, I am Nārāyaṇa; having been earnestly entreated by them at that time for the sake of protection from the Asuras, I then made this declaration.
"Build here a city of great splendor for our residence;
let the twice-born perform the agnihotra sacrifices and worship the deities at all times. (75)
Let sacrifices be performed with various rites, and let worship also be carried out;
let hospitality be practiced constantly, and let my devotion remain unwavering. (76)
"And by my grace, liberation will come to you in the end.
Then those sages, weakened by hunger and thirst, said: ||77||
"O Great King, what can we do here with this city, desiring as we do your devotion? Grant us liberation and always provide us protection. (78)
Hari said, "I shall always provide protection for you.
He then called to mind Viśvakarman, and Viśvakarman arrived.
And there, Śambhu, as Caṇḍīśvara, took possession of that quadrangular land,
eight yojanas in extent, for the purpose of establishing a city.
To the east is the glorious Śaṅkara, to the west is the Nyaṅkumatī, to the north is the Svarṇanandā, and to the south it extends to the limit of the ocean. 81.
In the center, Hari had a supreme, elevated city built as a field for the protection of the fire,
for the sake of providing a dwelling for those brahmins.
There, the Nyūṣus, who were devoted to the performance of oblations and sacrifices, remained, as did the exalted Vighnarāja, for the purpose of protection. 83.
Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa established [the image] in the presence of Śaṃsu;
it was worshipped as Dhanada, the granter of sons and wealth at all times. (84)
He will grant both desires and liberation, there is no doubt;
[one should worship] Gaṇeśa, Śaṅkara, and the illustrious Narāyaṇa in the rite of consecrating the site (vāstu). ||85||
The gods worshipped Viśvakarman, the groups of Mothers, and the Brahmins;
they also worshipped the water-pot (kalaśa), and then Śambhu arrived.
Kalaśeśa indeed became manifest before the water-pot;
and at the spot where they performed worship, Sthaleśvara came into being. (87)
In the month of Māgha, there was a festival of worship throughout the entire city;
thereafter, that city became known as Unnata, a place of pilgrimage for Brahmins.
The Viśvakarmeśvara Liṅga is also worshipped in that very place;
thereafter, Brahmā, in the form of a child, resided there at the site called Unnata.
On Mount Raivata, Vāmana exists as a child; at Prabhāsa, Hara exists as a child;
and on Mount Unnata, Aja exists in the form of a child—these three are equal.
In the form of a child, there is no illusion, nor deceit, nor latent impression;
indeed, the form of a child bestows liberation, and is worthy of worship, delightful, and free from affliction.
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, and the like, O you who possess the form of a child—these are utterly rootless; they have never arisen and do not exist at all from birth. (92)
Furthermore, from attachment or from mental impressions (saṃskāra), faults arise;
therefore, truthfulness, religious observance, and non-violence toward even a child must always be maintained there. (93)
Non-stealing prevails there, as does conduct like that of a Brahmin; likewise, non-possessiveness and trust in what is taught by one's mother [exist]. (94)
Freedom from passion, contentment with whatever fills the belly, purity within oneself, freedom from hatred, and the state of having one's intellect nourished by austerity; 95.
The chapter on knowledge, the lordly state, and all that pertains to the nature of worldly existence which leads toward the pursuit of sense objects—all these indeed exist within the child. (96)
That [essence] does not exist in that child; therefore, Viṣṇu is indeed the child.
Even the serpent, thinking it to be a child, crept upon the child. (97)
And one who possesses such childlike innocence, being fearless, proceeds on his way;
he always regards the offspring of anyone whatsoever with compassion. (98)
Likewise, all living beings born from every kind of womb gaze upon him with love;
it is that very nature of Nārāyaṇa which is recognized in the child. 99.
In ancient times, Dhruva, Prahlāda, Sanaka and the others, as well as Śuka, attained liberation after worshipping the Child-form of Kṛṣṇa.
Whether in youth or in old age, in a man, a woman, or a neuter, if there is a state of childhood, there is likewise no transmission of defects. (101)
He too is worshipped like a god, because that child is free from fault;
for both childhood and old age are devoid of defects.
There is equality between the two in their stainlessness, for both are places of purity;
indeed, children bow to the moon, and mothers look upon the child. 103.
Fools marry a young girl, and those without lineage take a child;
yet there is the power belonging to Nārāyaṇa, which is pure and born of creation.

One who possesses that [nature] is designated as a "child" (bāla); therefore, Nārāyaṇa is a child. Because people offer gifts of knowledge, gifts of food, and assistance to children, the child is thus praised.

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is always the very form of Brahman for the child (*bāla*). Therefore, the child who practices celibacy possesses authority over the world of Brahman and bestows both Brahman and liberation (*mokṣa*), just as Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa does.
By worshipping the gentle Gaurī Bālikā,
one obtains the fruit of both the worship of Pārvatī and the worship of Lakṣmī.
The youthful goddesses, ever free from passion, dwell in heaven;
they are Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, and the maiden Lakṣmī.
Its Lord is eternally a child—Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa, and likewise Hara;
yet the worlds, through their own conditioned states of being, imagine Him to be in the full bloom of youth.
Like their own [nature], the Daityas, being themselves defiled, seize those who are free from defects, always pure, and even divine— though appearing distorted in form and exceedingly non-divine.
If they possess defects, how can there be liberation; if they are free from defects, how can there be latent impressions?
Therefore, the gods are free from defects and always bestow liberation upon the ignorant.
The children are eternal, forever liberated, and they shine in the abode of Brahman;
they are eternally youthful, divine, and thus praised as boys. (11.3)
Having spoken thus to Pārvatī regarding Unnatādika and the other [sites], Śambhu said:
"O Lakṣmī, I have also described to you this holy ford (tīrtha) which grants liberation through the mere hearing [of its name]."

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Holy Places such as Guptaprayāga-tīrtha, Śṛgāleśvara-kṣetra, Aparanārāyaṇa-tīrtha, Trinetra-tīrtha, Unnatanagara, and Sthāneśvara, along with the Explanation of the Essential Meaning for the Youth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta-yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; thereafter Śambhu spoke to Pārvatī, and I shall relate that which bestows liberation and prosperity at the Unnata-maṇḍala pilgrimage site.
Durgāditya is an auspicious holy site, as is the excellent Vināyaka-tīrtha,
where in ancient times Vināyaka assumed the form of an elephant.
The great Mahākāleśvara Tīrtha bestows all forms of protection;
it is a supreme Tīrtha of great prosperity, situated within the waters of the Ṛṣitoyā.
At the holy site named Talasvāmin, the guardian of the field, Kālameghaka, resides;
he dwells at Siṃhāṇya for the purpose of protecting the forest.
On the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī, there is indeed the beautiful Śaṅkhāvarta Tīrtha;
to the south of the abode of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the excellent Goṣpada.
And at that sacred ford (tīrtha), which is protected by the serpent Ananta, who is the coiled body of Viṣṇu,
one who bathes and performs a śrāddha ceremony shall deliver twenty-one generations.
One shall personally attain liberation for one's family and reach the auspicious heaven;
at every step, the pilgrim shall become a possessor of the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Viṣṇu himself declared that it is also called Guptagayā;
by the offering of fragrance one obtains scent and the like, and from the offering of flowers comes good fortune.
Through the gift of incense, one attains sovereignty; through the gift of lamps, one attains radiance.
Through the gift of a banner, there is the destruction of sins; through a pilgrimage, one becomes a partaker of the world of Brahmā.
Listen now to what occurred of old at that great holy ford known as Goṣpada:
there was a son of the King of Aṅga named Vena, a lord of subjects.
Indeed, due to the fault of his maternal grandfather, that son of Kālakanyā became evil-minded, turning his back on the true dharma. || 11 ||
He indeed established the stability ordained by the Vedas and the Shastras;
for this thought arose in him when destruction was imminent. (12)
I am always to be praised and worshipped with all sacrifices;
sacrifices are to be offered unto me, and into me alone is the oblation to be poured. || 1.3 ||
Then those sages said to him, "O King, do not indeed commit unrighteousness!
Vena replied, "Both righteousness and unrighteousness have been created by me. (14)
"Gentlemen, how should I show honor? To whom indeed should I listen?
Who else on earth is my equal in heroism, learning, austerity, and truth? (15)
When he spoke thus, the sages were indeed unable to pacify him;
consequently, becoming exceedingly enraged, they struck that one of great strength.
Having struck him with an Atharvan mantra, they churned his left arm and produced the Niṣādas, who were black in complexion.
Then those great seers again took the right hand of Vena, [seizing] the Tumbaras, the Khasas, the Vaindhyas, the Dhīvaras, and those born from the sin of Vena.
And from that churning, Pṛthu was born, resembling the sun;
he held a bow, a banner, a trident, a fish, and a discus in his hands.
The external world, consisting of signs, lines, swords, and paths,
as well as rivers, streams, oceans, mountains, and so forth, arose from that.
Accompanied by their jewels, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the gods, the sages, humans, and trees approached that Pṛthu for his consecration. (21)
All beings, both stationary and moving, sprinkled that lord of men;
by Pṛthu, all those subjects were made to rejoice through the paths of dharma.
The earth yields crops without being ploughed; foods are accomplished by mere thought; all cows are milk-yielding wish-fulfillers; and in every leaf-cup there is honey. (23)
Thus, the Magadhas, the Sūtas, and the Bandins there sang the praises of the majestic Pṛthu,
having reflected upon what was destined to come to pass.
Having personally understood all future events, Pṛthu himself took up his bow in that manner and began to crush the earth.
Having become a cow, the Earth sought refuge with him;
for the sake of the world's welfare, she was milked by the king for many kinds of milk.
Having attained the status of Pṛthu’s daughter, she became the Earth, known as Prathā;
and Pṛthu indeed performed a sacrifice in order to secure a good destiny for Vena.
And then Nārada said: "Vena has now become a barbarian (mleccha);
indeed, due to his former sins, his birth is in the desert region."
"To uplift him, undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords; liberation will come to pass.
Pṛthu went to the regions of Maru and brought his father home. (29)
From there he went to Kurukṣetra and to a holy site (tīrtha) there belonging to the Mlecchas;
he bathed according to the prescribed rite, yet even so, his sin remained.
And Tīrtha said: "This Vena is permeated by tens of millions of prior sins;
his heaps of sin cannot be washed away. (31)
He, being utterly enveloped by terrible and great sins,
will become purified upon reaching the sacred ford of Prabhāsa.
There, the holy Sarasvatī flows with five streams;
of these, the fifth stream is called the Nyaṅkumatī. (33)
On its bank stands a sacred ford (tīrtha) known by the name Goṣpada;
there lies the Pretaśilā, which bestows liberation upon the departed spirits.
Where formerly twenty-eight crores of hungry ghosts were liberated,
and where Nandinī, the wish-fulfilling cow, once set foot here in ancient times.
For the sake of liberating the pretas, she remained there; that place is indeed like a mere cow’s footprint.
She said: "O pretas, my footstep always destroys sin and grants liberation. (36)
Whatever person comes here and performs a ritual bath and a śrāddha ceremony, their fruit shall be complete, seven times that of Gayā. ||37||
Having spoken thus and having brought about the liberation of the preta, she quickly vanished;
and there at that cow's footprint, the pretas also attained liberation.
Then Pṛthu went there to Goṣpada accompanied by the Mlecchas;
placing the Brāhmaṇas in front, he proceeded to the bank of the Nyaṅkumatī.
Having observed that the footprint of the Preta-śilā was situated in the Goṣpada field,
he constructed sacrificial pits, altars, and pavilions for the successful completion of the sacrifice.
There, a sacrifice was commenced according to the prescribed rites with abundant sacrificial fees;
his ancestors appeared before him in person, radiant as blazing fire.
And being satisfied, they said: "We are satisfied; we are contented and destined for heaven.
O King, you are blessed and meritorious, but we three are even more blessed. (42)
When the ancestors had spoken thus, the barbarian Vena immediately cast off his barbarian body and became possessed of a divine body.
Freed from sin, he said, "I am going to the abode of the thirty gods.
Go; enjoy your kingdom in happiness. You have fulfilled the duty toward a son. (44)
Having heard this, Pṛthu rejoiced exceedingly and bowed to them;
he gladdened those brāhmaṇas with gifts of gold, land, and wealth.
Then, having performed his pilgrimage to Guptaprayāga as well as Someśvara,
and having circumambulated Mount Raivata, he proceeded from there to Bhadreśvara.
Having visited the holy site of Kuṃkumavāpikā, the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, and the hermitage of Lomaśa, and having worshipped the goddess Kambharāramā; 47.
Having seen Gopālakṛṣṇa and having worshipped that supreme person—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama—[he remained there]. ||48||
Having bathed at the Siddhakṣetra Yamī, Pṛthu returned to his own abode;
he was indeed the Lord, the Blessed One, who is a portion of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (49)
Like Vena, Pṛthu attained eternal liberation at the end;
this narrative, contained within the Saṃhitā, should be heard at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony.
From there, one should go to the auspicious and supreme holy site of Nārāyaṇagṛha;
to the south of Goṣpada, on the shore of the ocean, Keśava resides.
In some places he was Janārdana, and in others Madhusūdana;
in some places he was Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and in others Nārāyaṇa himself.
Having utterly destroyed the great asuras, he indeed finds rest there at Kuberatīrtha,
Bālārka, and also at Bālārkeśvara.
This place of Ambikā destroys all sins;
from there, one should go to the auspicious Jāleśvara on the bank of the Devikā.
Listen, O venerable one, to this divine and ancient history concerning the dialogue between Nābhāga and Āpastamba, the treasure-house of asceticism.
The sage Āpastamba, formerly dwelling naked in the water,
performed severe penance like a fish at the holy site of Prabhāsa.
His body, which resembled gold, became covered with moss;
meanwhile, fishermen seeking to catch fish were [struggling] with their nets in the midst of the water. (57)
By the turn of fate, they seized that sage along with the fish,
having beheld him as a great seer, a human son of Brahmā.
Thinking, "We have committed an offense," they bowed to him with their very heads and said:
"O Compassionate One, you ought to forgive this fault born of ignorance. (59)
"Show service to the fishermen; be gracious, O observer of noble vows.
That sage, endowed with forgiveness, spoke thus to the distressed fishermen.
A great slaughter of these aquatic fish has been committed;
therefore, the fishermen must unite and carry out the protection of the fish.
Since we dwell together in the water, fish are indeed like my own kin;
yet they all act for their own sake—for the sake of others is truly difficult to find.
If even the minds of the wise are intent solely upon their own self-interest, then what distinction would there be between them and the ignorant, O skillful ones? (63)
If even the wise, established in the yoga of meditation, abandon [the world], then where will ignorant beings in this world find happiness? (64)
If a powerful person abandons the weak when they have encountered the same suffering, what power is that which nourishes only one's own interest? That is called useless and it is called sin. (65)
And one who is capable should indeed ward off the sufferings of others according to his strength;
such a destroyer of the suffering of others is said to be a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
The ancients declare that he who, despite possessing the capacity, does not effect the destruction of the suffering of others, commits a sin more evil than any other sin. (67)
There may be a means before me, but without releasing the fish, I do not wish to eat, just as [I feel] for those fish every day. (68)
"Let the fishermen eat me along with the fish as they please;
or let them abandon those fish together with me, all gathered here."
And into those fish from whose bodies the life-force has departed,
I shall enter by means of yoga and restore them to life through my ascetic powers and the gift of life.
Whatever merit I possess, may it go to those who are miserable;
and whatever evil they have committed, may all of that come to me. (71)
And whatever suffering belongs to the fishermen, may I now experience that as well;
having entered within all sentient beings, may I become the partaker of all their sufferings. (72)
It is my opinion that he in whom no compassion arises upon seeing the blind, the wretched, the maimed, the helpless, and likewise the diseased, is a demon. (73)
He who, though capable, does not protect living beings who have fallen into danger to their lives and are overwhelmed by fear, incurs sin himself. (74)
The happiness that arises for those who help others in their distress is such that neither heaven nor even liberation is worth even a sixteenth part of it.
Therefore, having abandoned these inferior ones who are terrified and deeply distressed,
I shall not depart even a single step from this place.
And this very thing has been declared by the seer to the fishermen:
"If I abandon the protection of the fish, there will be no protection for me. (77)
If I am to be protected, let the fishermen release the fish quickly;
or else, if there is grief for me in their abandonment, then let them abandon the fish. (78)
If it should then occur to you, "Let the king give us the price," then you would possess wealth and become partakers of the fruit of your efforts. (79)
"I shall remain together with the fish and free from bondage.
Having heard all this, it was reported by the fishermen to Nābhāga.
And Nābhāga went to that place where the fish were within the water-vessel;
there the king, having duly honored that god-like sage, [honored him]. (81)
"O Blessed One, speak; what shall I do at your command?
Thus addressed, the compassionate Āpastamba quickly spoke to the king: 82.
To these fishermen, who live in misery and are overcome by great toil, grant the wages for their labor, whatever you deem appropriate for me. (83)
Nābhāga said: "I shall give a hundred thousand gold coins with gems to the fishermen here, if their price is equal to yours. (84)
The sage said: "O King, I am not to be restrained by you with hundreds of thousands;
rather, let a truly fitting price be paid for me here. (85)
The king said, "Let ten million [gold pieces] indeed be given to the Niṣādas.
The sage replied, "O King, I am not to be restrained by you even with ten millions. (86)
"Let a fitting price be given; deliberate upon this with the Brahmins.
The king said, "Indeed, let half of the kingdom be bestowed upon the Niṣādas. (87)
The sage said: "Indeed, my entire kingdom is not its equal;
let a fitting price be given. Reflect upon this together with the other sages. (88)
Having heard those words of the great sages, Nābhāga became despondent;
in the meantime, Lomaśa of great asceticism arrived there.
From the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, Āpastamba arrived;
having learned of this wondrous event, he spoke to Nābhāga.
"Do not fall into despair, O King; there is no gold as the price for the sage.
However, Brahmins and cows were created by the Self-born One himself as divine beings. (91)
Since they both originate from that very same divine reality, they are indeed divine;
let the price for this divine [cow] be given—the price of the divine, which is a cow. (92)
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and spoke to the sage who was in the net:
"Arise, arise, O Blessed One! I have purchased you, O Sage, for a cow. (93)
The sage said: "O King, I have indeed been properly purchased by you with a cow;
for me, the price is two cows, which are supremely pure and holy. (94)
Cows should always be circumambulated and worshipped;
for they are divine abodes of auspiciousness, created indeed by the Self-born One himself. 95.
The dwellings and houses of Brahmins, as well as temples of the deities, are purified by cow dung; what, then, could be greater than this? 96.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter—these five purifiers of cows sanctify the entire world. (97)
May cows always be before me, and may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart and at my head, and may I dwell in the midst of cows. (98)
By him who gives daily fodder to cows, the sacred fires have been properly offered, the ancestors have been gratified, and the gods have been worshipped. (99)
The daughter of Surabhi, the goddess worshipped by the world, who abides in the station of Viṣṇu—may she accept all this which has been given by me; it has been given by me. 1.549.100.
By protecting calves and cows, by scratching them when they itch,
and also by protecting those who are exhausted or afflicted, a person is glorified in heaven.
Cows are proclaimed to be present in the beginning, outside, in the middle, and at the end; they always protect for the gods the milk, clarified butter, and nectar. || 10.2 ||
Therefore, cows should always be given as gifts and constantly honored;
they are fashioned like a staircase for the attainment of heaven. 103.
Having heard these words of the sage, the Niṣādas also, quickly recognizing the greatness of the cow, bowed to Āpastamba and said: [104]
Conversation, sight, touch, as well as praise and remembrance—
these are indeed always purifying for holy men and yogis.
For we have been purified by that Nābhāga; therefore, we shall indeed honor this pair of auspicious cows which you have accepted as our own.
You have been liberated, as have the fish, and the two cows have been liberated;
we too have been liberated, and Nābhāga has been liberated through the company of the virtuous.
"You are worthy of worship, as are the fish, and the two cows are worthy of worship;
we too are worthy of worship, and Nābhāga is worthy of worship because of this auspicious meeting. (108)
The sage said: "I have set the price at two cows for myself alone;
furthermore, I am pleased because of Lomaśa's instruction."
"I form this pure resolve: may the fish come to life.
By the gift of two cows, the fish shall attain life."
Therefore, O God, give a pair of cows to a high-souled Brahmin;
by that means the fish shall subsist, and you shall be free from fault.
Then, having heard that, the fishermen offered those two cows right there to the sage Āpastamba, having acquired them through blameless means.
The delighted sage said to them, "Behold the school of fish;
indeed, by the gift of two cows, life has been restored once again."
When this was said, the fish that were still alive went into the waters of the ocean;
as for those fish that had been mutilated and those that had already been cut up, they likewise departed.
For their sake of liberation, the seer Āpastamba spoke these words again:
"I accept this cow from you on account of your merit."
"O Niṣādas, go to heaven together with the fish and the sinless ones,
having produced joy for living beings even by means of a censurable deed."
Even if I should reach hell, I shall see it as heaven itself,
because of whatever merit I have performed through the actions of my mind, speech, and body.
"By that very act, may all those afflicted by suffering go to a fortunate rebirth;
then, through his grace, let the Niṣādas, along with the fish," || 1.18 ||
Seeing them gone to heaven, Nābhāga said:
"The virtuous, who are like the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites, should be served by those seeking their own welfare;
even a moment's attendance upon them here shall not be fruitless."
One should share a seat with the virtuous and engage in noble conversation with the virtuous.
One should conduct oneself according to the behavior of the virtuous and should not perform even the slightest act with the wicked.
It was solely through association with the virtuous that the fishermen attained the state of fish-eaters.
They reached heaven as if they were performers of the horse sacrifice;
there were the sage Āpastamba and the great sage Lomaśa.
The sage gratified the king with various desired boons and respectfully caused him to make the formal resolve for the sacrifice.
When he had said, "So be it," Āpastamba praised him with affection:
"O Indra among kings, you are truly blessed; your mind abides in righteousness. (124)
"You accept the command of a Brahmin; indeed, your family is blessed!"—yet kings, being generally possessed by pride, do not accept it at all. (125)
The words of the Brahmins, whose intellects were struck by constant calamities, were:
"For kings, birth is certain, delusion is certain, and hell is certain. (1.26)
Those who highly esteem your kingdom will pass away along with their kinsmen; however, the wise perceive sovereignty and such things as being like hell.
"Thus establishing the next world and their own eternal goal,
the two high-souled ones, having spoken thus, departed each to his own hermitage."
Nābhāga also, having received the boon, departed for his own city;
he duly performed an auspicious sacrifice on the bank of the Śatruñjita river.
Having worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Kamalā, he finally departed for the supreme, imperishable state of Brahman.
Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara were installed by the sage at the site of Jālasthala;
thus, that sacred field became renowned in ancient times as Jāleśvara.
There, on the bank of the Devikā, were Nābhāga, Matsyajīvin, Āpastamba, Lomaśa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa. || 132 ||
Merely being remembered, they grant liberation, because by them one goes to liberation;
such is the account of what occurred on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
If people perform ancestral rites (śrāddha), pilgrimages, or the gift of cows there,
they shall obtain enjoyment and liberation as desired, both in this world and in the hereafter.
O Lakṣmī, I have told you this as Śambhu spoke it to Satī;
by reading or even by hearing it, it shall bestow both heaven and liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Stories of Durgāditya, Goṣpada, Vena, King Śuddhi, Muktinārāyaṇa, Gṛhajāleśvara Tīrtha, Nābhāga, and the Sage Āpastamba," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which Śambhu then spoke to Pārvatī;
I shall also tell you of that best of holy places, which bestows heaven and other rewards.
In ancient times, there was a sage named Tuṇḍi on the bank of the Devikā;
there was a single well there which, through the power of the sage's yoga, became a bestower of liberation.
Fierce tigers fell there for the purpose of drinking water;
they were all killed by the sage, yet restored to life by the power of his asceticism.
Then, by the mere utterance of the syllable "Hūṃ," the water in the well was filled;
it flowed over the bank, which was truly marvelous.
There, he established the deity Tuṇḍīśvara as a sacred site (tīrtha);
having made that auspicious tīrtha, he then went to Āśāpura, the abode of Gaṇeśvara.
Having offered the sacrificial food (naivedya), one should give a gift of gold;
then one should go to the auspicious Kāpila Tīrtha, which removes all sins.
While Kapila was going toward Raivata, he stayed there for a year;
at that place, the river Kapilā manifested itself in the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha).
If Tuesday should fall on the sixth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada),
and that sixth occurs under the asterism Rohiṇī during the Vyatīpāta yoga, that sixth is considered Kapilā.
On the sixth lunar day at the confluence of the Kapilā,
one who is composed in mind should bathe in the Kapilā and worship Lord Viṣṇu as Śrīkapila, situated upon the solar orb.
One should pray, "May Kapilā and Viṣṇu in the form of Kapila protect me";
and by giving a tawny cow (kapilā-gau), one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
Then one should visit the supreme purifying holy site of Hāṭakeśa;
from there, one should go to the hermitage of Agastya, which has been frequented for a year.
In ancient times, the Kālakeyas, Daityas who dwelt within the ocean,
would repeatedly descend upon the earth at night and [attack] sleeping Brahmins and others.
Having learned that those Kalakeyas were harmful, they devoured them;
then Agastya went there toward the shore of the ocean.

Standing on the bank, he performed penance according to the rules for the duration of one year; having observed a fast at night on the fourth day of the month of Phālguna, he [continued his practice]. (14)
On the fifth day, having eaten sesame paste, he performed a fire sacrifice (homa).
In this manner, after taking only one meal throughout four months, he then [proceeded]. || 15 ||
Remaining without food, he undertook this supreme vow free from obstacles;
after a year had passed, that king of sages contemplated the protection of the world.
"Behold this marvel, O gods: the sea with its fish, crocodiles, and other creatures! I shall drink it up with my joined palms and dry up the great ocean. (17)
Having spoken thus, and having remembered Hari and placed Brahmā within himself,
he took a mouthful of water from the entire ocean, the lord of rivers.
The Kālakeyas were destroyed, and the waters were boiled;
thereafter, by the rains from the clouds, the oceans became full of water once again.
Thus, whoever comes here and worships me, together with Lopāmudrā, at this beautiful hermitage of Agastya— a sacred ford that destroys all sins— [shall attain the highest goal].
Hāṭakeśa has been brought by me; one should worship him according to the prescribed rite.
During the northern solstice, a mortal shall obtain the fruit of giving a hundred thousand cows. ||21||
There, King Bhadrāśva, desiring a vision of Agastya, arrived,
paid his respects, and inquired after his welfare.
"O knower of Dharma, if you have learned or even seen anything wonderful, tell it to me; then I shall go to Prabhāsa. (23)
Agastya spoke that story concerning Śvetadvīpa to the king:
"The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Master, is of wondrous form. (24)
Puruṣottama shines upon the bank of the Kuṅkumavāpikā;
many various wonders have been seen there. ||25||
This very Nārāyaṇa always lies down even in Śvetadvīpa;
and Nārada, having seen Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in Surāṣṭra... [26]
After seeing Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī Rādhikā, in Mathurā,
the sage then went to the Himālaya mountains and beheld Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa.
There he beheld Śvetadvīpa and those persons of uniform appearance,
possessing fierce luster, bearing conchs, discs, maces, and lotuses.
[He saw] youths who were similar, of similar appearance, and possessing similar excellence of qualities; they were endowed with beauty, well-proportioned, and captivating.
"This is Viṣṇu, this is Viṣṇu, this is the eternal Viṣṇu"—seeing them, the thought occurred to him: "Which among these is the Lord Viṣṇu? (1.550.30)

To whom else, indeed, shall I bow after him? For when one who is inferior fails to worship the first among those worthy of worship, he commits a transgression against the worship of the venerable. (3.1)
"There will be a loss of life, fame, and knowledge, and great transgression will ensue.
As he was thinking thus, his mind [was fixed] upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
My anxious thought has arisen in vain: how shall I propitiate him?
By what means may I know that supreme Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and what shall I do? (33)
Having reflected thus, he meditated upon that god, the Supreme Lord;
being thus meditated upon by him, the son of Kaṃbhara attained great satisfaction.
Nārāyaṇa, appearing in person and being well-pleased, said:
"Choose a boon; may prosperity be yours! My form has been beheld by you. (35)

"Those who come here in this world [possessing] the fourfold [attainments] beginning with 'form-similarity' (sārūpya)—they obtain these very [attainments] right here; tell me, what shall I give to you? (36)
Nārada said: "Tell me how that attainment may be mine.
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke to him the Puruṣasūkta itself.
O Sage, those people who, relying on that [teaching] where the Puruṣa with a thousand heads was described by me, shall perceive me as Nārāyaṇa. (38)
Those people who, by means of the path described in the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, constantly engage in the study of this Saṃhitā, shall attain me. (39)
Those devotees who shall worship me will certainly attain [their goal];
they will go to my sacred field and behold me.
Those who shall perform service to the virtuous will certainly attain me; indeed, my name has been established as distinct for the chanting of all. 41.
Even without ritual worship, people will certainly attain me through devotion to my name;
O Sage, all knowledge shall surely be revealed to you. (42)
O sage, all knowledge born of discernment shall belong to you, both that which is worthy of my vision and that which is worthy of liberation from vision. 43.
Having spoken thus to those Viṣṇus who were like him, the Blessed One departed;
and Nārada likewise went away, for he did not recognize that Lord.
Perceiving the invisibility of Viṣṇu and that all Viṣṇus are equal,
Nārada bowed down toward that very direction and departed for heaven.
While departing for Surāṣṭra, where I indeed dwell as Agastya,
he arrived there, stayed for a moment, and then departed for the city of Vaihāyasa.
That place, Nāradatīrtha, is indeed auspicious and bestows knowledge;
having bowed to the sage, Bhadrāśva also departed toward Prabhāsa.
Thus, having known Nārāyaṇa as residing on the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), and then as residing in Viśālā, in Yamunā, and situated at Kuṅkumavāpikā; ||48||
Having realized the form that is beyond the imperishable, one indeed attains liberation;
remembering Viṣṇu, reciting the Vedas, giving gifts, and sacrificing to Hari. (49)
A devotee who pleases the virtuous and the saintly attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
A holy place (tīrtha) consisting of saints and consisting of saintly women is supreme and bestows final release.
From there, one should go to the Bhīmanātha-tīrtha, which wards off fear;
then one should behold Suparṇeśī, as well as Suparṇa and Narāyaṇa.
From there, one should go to Kaubereśī, and then to the excellent tirtha of Bhalla;
at the Bhalla-tirtha, Viṣṇu always resides together with the Gaṅgā.
For the Gaṅgā is indeed a purifying Vaiṣṇava field, being the personified [form of Viṣṇu];
by means of the lute, the eternal Viṣṇu Kṛṣṇa was [pleased] by the Niṣāda. ||53||
Having fixed an arrow upon his bow, he was struck and became a resident of Goloka;
Vallaka, too, mistaking it for a deer, [struck] what was situated on the trunk of a Plakṣa tree.
Having struck Viṣṇu with a broad-headed arrow, he went and beheld Mādhava;
then, dejected, he offered praise and obtained his favor.
The fisherman went right there to Goloka along with Viṣṇu;
for that place is called Bhallakṣetra, where Hari was pierced in the sole of his foot.
It bestows liberation, grants heaven, is most excellent, and effects the piercing of birth and death;
from there, one should go toward Raivata, north of the Hiraṇyā river.
The supreme pilgrimage site of Kauśika, and then that which consists of Vastrāpatha; likewise Dāmodara, Raivataka, Bhava, and Indreśvara. 58.
Cakrodyāna, Revatītīrthaka, and Vāsiṣṭhaka-āśrama—O Lakṣmī, hear now the sin-destroying narrative of this land. (59)
There was a king named Gaja; together with his wife, that monarch went for the purpose of performing ablutions in the waters of the Gaṅgā and dwelt there.
Once, a sage named Bhadra came before him;
the elephant said to him, "O sage, grant me the knowledge for the sake of liberation. (61)
Bhadra said: "The Self itself is the holy ford that purifies all;
there dwells Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the most excellent among all holy fords. (62)
His knowledge, which takes the form of mindfulness, is here called supreme knowledge;
all other knowledge is merely intellectual, O King, and serves only as a burden to the intellect.
Those for whom sacred fords are merely full of water and gods are made of stone and clay do not see that Supreme, by which they perceive [the Self] as residing within themselves.
There are many sacred fords and holy shrines, as well as oceans and rivers with meritorious waters that are pure. (65)
And among the knowledge of those sacred fords, the knowledge of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Narāyaṇa, is considered the highest of the high. (66)
Matsya, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Kūrma, Hari,
Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Śrī Puruṣottama.
Hari, Śrī Kapila, Dattātreya, Buddha, and Paraśurāma; Vāsudeva, Pṛthu, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, and the Kumāras.
And Nārada, Kratu, Aśvagrīva, Vyāsa, Janārdana,
Mohaka, Rājarāja, Kalkaghna, and Pumsuttama.
To Nara, the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Master of Śvetadvīpa,
Padmanābha resting upon Śeṣa, and the Lord of the Universe stationed on the battlefield— [he bowed].
By remembering his names and dwellings, one shall attain liberation;
as well as the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the auspicious river Godāvarī. (71)
The Śatadru, as well as the Vindhyā, the Payodhā, and the Varadā;
the Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, and the Gaṇḍakī, which destroys fierce sins. (72)
The Candrabhāgā, the Vipāśā, the Śoṇā, and likewise the Brahmasutā—these and many other rivers, as well as the mountains such as Himāśraya and others. ||73||
Indeed, by the mere utterance of their names, evil is destroyed—
those of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and likewise of the Mānasa lake.
By the mere remembrance of the Nārāyaṇa lake, the Puṣkara lake, and the Indradyumna lake, one shall be liberated. //75//
By staying at Kānyakubja during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one indeed attains heaven;
likewise by staying at Arbuda on the full moon of Pauṣa, and at the Gayāsutīrtha on the full moon of Māgha.
On the full moon of Phālguna he dwells on the back of the Himalayas, and on the full moon of Caitra he resides at Prabhāsa;
on the full moon of Aśvinī he stays at Kuṅkumavāpī, and on the full moon of Vaiśākha at Avantikā.
On the full moon of Jyeṣṭha at Trikūpaka, on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa at the eastern ocean, on the full moon of Bhādrapada at the Sārasvata lake, and on the full moon of Kārttika at Raivatācala.
Likewise, on the island of Kāpila, at Śālagrāma on the earth,
during the Dīpotsava festival, and in Cāndrabhāga, one should perform ancestral rites (śrāddha), ritual bathing, and the recitation of mantras (japa).
In Goloka, the imperishable abode, Vaikuṇṭha, or Kailāsa,
the residence of those who observe vows and frequent sacred fords shall be according to their devotion.
Among months, Kārttika is the most excellent; in Kārttika, the Bhīṣmapañcaka;
and even therein, O King, the twelfth day is the best for Dāmodara when one is in water.
In the vicinity of Somanātha, there is the great mountain Udayānta;
on its western side, the great Raivata mountain is remembered to be located. 82.
And there a beautiful river flows, the Suvarṇarekhikā;
there the minerals are red, white, blue, and variegated. (83)
There are stones shaped like elephants, resembling golden ochre;
and there are trees, creepers, and shrubs produced from gold.
There, in the river named Svarṇalekhā, there is the pool of Nārāyaṇa, as well as the pool of Dāmodara, and also that of Rādhā and others. (85)
Having bathed there and drunk the water, embodied beings indeed attain liberation,
as did the powerful Hariścandra, Śibi, and Nahuṣa.
Indeed, great gifts were offered by Nala on Mount Raivata;
they have gone to the eternal and painless abode of Viṣṇu. 87.
Having heard these auspicious words, O lord of men, the elephant arrived at the sacred ford of Raivata and Prabhāsa. 88.
Having given manifold gifts and having offered oblations into the sacrificial fire,
he stood with his feet upward and, with his face turned downward, drank the smoke.
Others who had come with him were likewise performing penance;
there, a vow was undertaken by all, that Dāmodara should be meditated upon on the mountain.
By whomsoever the two syllables "Ha-ri" are uttered even once, the girdle has been fastened by him for the journey toward liberation. (9.1)
While that king remained there together with the sages,
thousands of celestial chariots indeed arrived at that very place.
In them, the goddesses headed by Ramā, the attendants of Nārāyaṇa, and other liberated souls became manifest by the hundreds and thousands. ||93||
Together with all his followers and his wife, that king ascended the celestial chariot and went to that supreme, imperishable state.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!"—thus was this mantra proclaimed throughout all the celestial chariots. (95)
A shower of flowers fell from the sky by which the inhabitants of heaven and other celestial realms, traveling in their liberated aerial chariots along the path, came to behold him. (96)
Having taken their places before King Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord,
they gazed upon him and paid homage to the lords.
Thus, having pierced through the worlds of the Pitṛs and the Munis beyond the cosmic egg,
they all went to the state of liberation after establishing the Raivata Tīrtha.
Śaṅkara spoke such a discourse concerning the sacred field to Pārvatī; O Lakṣmī, this auspicious account which brings about liberation has been told by me to you as well. 99.
From reading or hearing this narrative, there is the destruction of sin;
one shall attain heaven, truth, Vaikuṇṭha, and the supreme, imperishable abode.
Having heard this and gladdened by such devotion, one should offer praise;
being freed from all sins, one shall proceed toward the Supreme Brahman. || 101 ||
O Lakṣmī, what purity of Saurāṣṭra can be described by me?
It is the very jewel-form of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself.
There is a land known as Saurāṣṭra, which bestows liberation at every step;
there, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa has always resided from time immemorial.
In the west is the god Vāmana, in the south is Somanātha;
in the north is the city of Camatkāra and the auspicious Dvārikā.
Śatruñjitā, Svarṇarekhā, Bhadrā, Uṣṇā, Hiraṇyakā,
Devanadī, and Nyaṅkumatī— these auspicious rivers bestow liberation.
Therein are Raivata, Śatruñjaya, Varāṭaka,
Śālamāla, Navanīta, and other preeminent mountains.
For there dwell great sages who are indeed the very forms of the Blessed One,
and there reside goddesses who are like Lakṣmī herself, truthful and imperishable.
Even the moon becomes momentarily paralyzed upon beholding her face;
such are the divine goddesses, and the children are like the sun. (108)
Where those established in virtuous conduct dwell, there Nārāyaṇa himself resides in person,
as do the gopīs of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, in that Saurāṣṭra where hundreds of thousands of devotees and servants dwell, the entire land is permeated by Brahman; it is to me like Vaikuṇṭha itself.
Thus, all this has been told to you exactly as spoken by Śaṅkara;
both the reciters and the listeners, as well as the people who hear it, shall become liberated.

Thus ends the five hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description with Narratives of Tuṇḍīśvara, Kapilātīrtha, Agastya, Nārada, the Marvels of Bhīmanāthatīrtha, the Hallakṣetra, Raivatatīrtha, and the Liberation of King Gaja," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī: "O Lakṣmī, my dear, I shall tell you of whatever other holy places (tīrthas) exist in Saurāṣṭra; listen to me."
The auspicious Unnabilla-tīrtha, the Śāmbhava Gṛhātmaka,
and Gaṅgeśvara shine beautifully to the west of Raivata.
And you, O Śobhanā, having taken [the image] from the great holy site of Yakṣeśvarī in the city of Vāmana in the ancient and great field of Vastrāpatha. || 3 ||
Afflicted by grief for his son, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha went to the bank of the river Svarṇarekhā to perform austerities.
In the northeast corner of the city, in the waters of the Svarṇarekhā river,
that great holy place (tīrtha) belonging to Vasiṣṭha exists, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the vicinity of Kṛtasmara at Makhatīrtha lies Balikhāta;
there exists the Nāthatīrtha, which bestows liberation and grants peace to the world.
To the northwest of Vastrāpatha, there is a divine lake surrounded by Apsarases;
there the gods sport and bathe.
Jālīgahanaśambhu, the goddess Triśūlinī, and the one named Heramba, Gaṇeśa, all reside at this sacred ford (tīrtha). || 8 ||
There, in the western ocean, is the port city of Makarālaya;
there is also the city named Kundana, and Maṇibhadra, which is a source of auspiciousness.
Śrīdāmapura is preeminent, and Dvārakā-kṣetra is most excellent;
thus, numerous sacred sites dwell upon the shore of the ocean.
Having spoken thus to Pārvatī, the supreme goddess, Mahādeva performed the Prābhāsika sacrifice when the month of Śrāvaṇa had arrived.
Accompanied by hosts of crores, he went toward the city of Dvārakā;
the lords Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the other deities of the holy places paid him due honor.
Having spent a month in the black-soiled land, they went to Camatkārapura;
there, the sixty-eight goddesses were worshipped by Hara.
During the Navarātra vow, having obtained Śrī Śaṅkara as their husband,
they all became immersed in the vast expanse of happiness, which is the ocean whose self is the bliss of Brahman.
And in the month of Āśvina, they all went to Mount Arbuda,
where Puṣkara, situated in the sky, shines eternally.
The second is on a mountain peak, and the third is situated on the surface of the earth,
where the beautiful hermitages of the great sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, are located.
On the mountain, there were auspicious sands shimmering with various hues, and trees, creepers, and shrubs that appeared like ascetics. || 17 ||
There are indeed delightful forests as well as celestial gardens, the grounds for sacrifices, and the altars of ascetics. (18)
There are excellent dwellings for virtuous women, as well as hermitages for holy men,
and auspicious abodes for Brāhmaṇas and Vaiṣṇavas.
The sacred fords of Sarasvatī, the purifying rivers,
