the clouds dwelling upon mountain peaks, and the winds mingled with fragrances— [all these were present].
Where there are dwellings for millions of divine cows,
and where the circles of yogis and those with perfected lives reside.
Śiva and the others made their dwelling there on the Puṣkara peak;
likewise, the great sages such as Vasiṣṭha took up residence at the sacred fords beginning with Puṣkara.
Brahmā and the other deities likewise paid homage to Śaṅkara,
offering water, flowers, fruits, the arghya oblation, food offerings, and various services.
The gods offered worship to the illustrious Supreme Lord, the husband of Pārvatī;
and Vasiṣṭha performed an especially distinguished worship in his own abode.
Then they took complete rest on Arbuda Mountain, the domain of Śaṅkara.
This Arbuda, possessing a divine form, has rendered great honor.
Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī while seated on his throne during the night:
"Listen to this divine narrative, which destroys both sin and suffering. (26)
Gautama was indeed a venerable, blessed, and great sage among sages;
having made his dwelling on Śataśṛṅga, he performed penance. || 27 ||
His wife Ahalyā was also an ascetic who discoursed on the Veda;
residing in the Daṇḍaka forest, she was always a servant to Gautama. That beautiful woman constantly performed the worship of guests.
Once, when a drought occurred, there was no food on earth. || 29 ||
The Brahmins deliberated, "Where will the meal be provided?
Gautama is capable; he always honors guests."
Thinking, "We shall go to that house," they arrived from all sides;
and Gautama, having beheld that, [approached] Brahmā, the Great-Grandfather.
Brahmā, being present before his eyes, remembered many things and said, "Choose a boon. Gautama replied, "On this earth, let there be water, wheat, grains, barley, awns, and so forth. (32)
Beginning in the morning, let them be produced; at midday, let that be the lineage of their particles.

"May they always accept this cooked food of ours—the auspicious Vaiśvadeva offering, the Śrāddha, and the oblation presented to the deities—as well as hospitality for guests and Brahmins; may it be so for me. (34)
Having heard this, Brahmā said, "So be it," and departed from there.
Every morning, fresh grain was produced and it ripened;
likewise, food was provided daily for the meal of thousands of Brahmins. || 39-40 ||
In this manner, for a full year, she fed the Brahmins;
by the power of her devotion to her husband, Ahalyā performed service for him.
Every morning, she would constantly resolve to attend to her beloved’s feet.
Having bowed and prostrated, having washed [the feet] at the big toe, and having offered the *argha* water, [she said]:
"If I am indeed the wife of my lord, devoted to my lord, and faithful to my husband, then let a hundred thousand vessels be produced here perpetually. (38-39)
Let male and female slaves, servants, cows yielding flavorful milk, and all kinds of food and drink be prepared; let the Fire-god himself consume them.
"May the gods be my attendants in Daṇḍaka";
having thus made this firm resolve constantly and having established great kitchens, [he proceeded].
Having cooked fresh grains of rice and performed the offering to the Viśvedevas,
he scattered morsels for the cows and portions for all living beings, and offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors.
He daily fed one hundred thousand brahmins, and even more;
then, at the end of that year, there was a bountiful rain upon the earth.
"Food is produced in all lands everywhere;
the Brahmins said, 'We shall indeed go to other countries.'"
Then Gautama said to them, "O gods on earth, dwell right here.
Then those Brahmins replied, "O sage, we are independent. (45)
"Food has been given by you, and we have always been protected by you;
for he whose food one eats, his body indeed remains under his supreme control. (86)
"His word must be honored in every way, yet our desire to depart is firm.
Having said this, they reflected upon a wonderful pretext for going. 47.
A certain Brahmin named Rodhana, having performed *prāṇāyāma*,
entered into the inner heart of Gautama through self-restraint.
Furthermore, another beautiful cow was created there by means of illusion;
she went [to the stall], and Gautama likewise went to the shed where fodder was provided. (49)
Gautama also remained there, firmly established in breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Gaurī went to the leaf-hut, and Gautama, having seen her, [arose].
"By entering within the obstruction, the cow (gauḥ) becomes restrained by the vital breath (prāṇa);
thus he uttered [the mantra], and the cow became restrained by the vital breath. (5.1)
Then the brahmins, having fallen down and fainted, repeatedly said:
"Gautama is indeed a killer of cows; the gods on earth must not remain in his hermitage. (52)
Gautama repeatedly praised those venerable Brahmins with hymns:
"She is not dead; she is merely in a swoon. How might this fainting fit be dispelled? (53)
"I shall perform an expiation here; let not the Brahmins depart from my house.
Having been addressed thus, the Brahmins said: "There is no expiation for one who lives [in sin]. (54)
Or, if he has fainted, it should be performed so that he may indeed be freed from his fainting;
having brought water from the Ganges, sprinkle this earth with it. (55)
"Indeed, she will quickly fall into a swoon; let us go to another part of the forest.
Having said this, all the brahmins departed from the Daṇḍaka region.
Gautama traveled by way of the sky toward the illustrious Śaṅkara;
formerly, Śaṅkara had offered him a welcome there on Kailāsa.
Gautama, having bowed to Hara, begged for the water of the Gaṅgā;
then Śaṅkara, plucking out a portion of his own matted hair, gave it to him.
Having placed that body along with its limbs upon the head of a cow,
Gautama led it there and drenched it with the water produced from that [act].
Gaurī was born with a healthy heart and free from fainting while staying in the hermitage;
indeed, by the boon of the gift of a cow, she became the Gaṅgā known as Gautamī.
Known as Godāvarī, she dwelt in the Daṇḍaka forest;
then the sage Gautama spoke to those Brahmins who had fled:
"May you all become practitioners of deceit and mere semblances of dharma in another age. (61)
Fierce, with skulls attached [to their heads], and revilers of those who give food—
such being the case, this miraculous account of the power of that Gautama has been told regarding the region of Godāvara.
At that holy ford of the Godāvarī, Gautama had a virtuous disciple named Uttaṅka; having studied as many Vedas as there were,
he made a request to his teacher in order to give him the fee.
Then the guru’s wife said:
"The queen Madayanti of Saudāsa always wears a necklace of jewels upon her breast; you must bring it here—give it to me. (65–66)
Thus addressed by the preceptor’s wife, he then set out in haste and arrived at the house of Sudāsa; there the Brahmin saw Sudāsa, who had assumed the form of a tiger,
approaching to devour him.
The Brahmin said, "Eat me as you wish immediately after that."
"A guest has arrived; give me the necklace of jewels.
Having offered it to my guru, I shall bestow upon you the desired sacrificial fee."
The king said, "O Brahmin, let a boon be requested from my queen.
Thus addressed, the protector of the earth (the Brahmin) made a request of the queen regarding the garland.
The queen said, "Bring me indeed a token of recognition from the king.
Having gone quickly, he requested a token of recognition from the monarch. (71)
And Saudāsa spoke these words: "What is that token by which it may be known, without which there is no happy rebirth, and by which one goes to a miserable state? (72)
"Go and speak thus to that virtuous woman; upon hearing you, she will give the garland.
She gave this garland of divine and excellent luster to the Brahmin.
Then the Asura spoke there, standing near the battlefield:
Having come from the Atala hell, he desires a beautiful garland for me. (74)
The immortal Asura named Ajāmṛta caused that subterranean realm to be excavated;
he settled his own followers, the Rākṣasas, within the womb of the earth.
Indeed, it was by him that an exceedingly long cavity was created within the earth.
"One should not take back what one has brought in the same manner as one gave it; rather, depart after providing protection.
Having been told this, Utanka took the necklace of gems and, upon returning, gave the diamond necklace to his teacher’s wife.
He asked his guru about the auspicious meaning of the speech, and he replied:
"The twice-born, being propitiated with gifts, will grant you the supreme state. (78)
"The twice-born are never satisfied with him; his is always a miserable state.
Having understood this meaning, the Brahmin then rejoiced.
Having received the blessings of his venerable preceptor,
the great sage Uttaṅka went to the beautiful holy site of Puṣkara, his own abode.
Here there is the Uttaṅka-tīrtha, which destroys sin and suffering;
furthermore, this long and extensive cave was created by the Asuras.
Once, on that occasion, Vasiṣṭha’s wish-fulfilling cow fell [from heaven].
Thereupon, by means of his own yogic power, Vasiṣṭha [summoned] his own sacrificial cow.
From that time forward, he caused [the demon] to be expelled outside and constantly considered how to fill the cavity with the great mountain.
Vasiṣṭha indeed went swiftly to the Himalaya through the air;
he entreated that son [of Himavat] for the purpose of filling the cavity.
Vasiṣṭha gave him a son named Nandivardhana and led him away;
he established him in a cave under the name Nandivardhana.
And because it was supported there by the Naga Arbuda in its proper manner,
it thereafter became famous by the name Arbuda Mountain.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, Parvata arrived from whence he had come, and Vasiṣṭha also brought many sacred bathing places (tīrthas). ||87||
On its peak is the Nāga-tīrtha and likewise the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; there also is the dwelling of Śaṅkara, and having bathed there in the mountain stream— (88)
Wealth, prosperity, happiness, heaven, sons, fortune, and so forth are also obtained;
even a barren woman, having bathed, will surely become possessed of sons—of this there is no doubt. (89)
The ancestors will perform the śrāddha ceremony there in every way;
they shall attain liberation from heaven, and the performer as well shall go to liberation.
And Vasiṣṭha summoned the Gautamī and the Sarasvatī,
the Gaṅgā and the Mandākinī, as well as Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Mountain, to that place.
A certain Brāhmaṇī named Gautamī, distressed by childlessness,
being virtuous, came to the sacred ford called Āgatīrtha on Mount Arbuda.
Then she thought, "Fie upon me, who am bereft of a son!
While lost in such thoughts, she entered the Nāgatīrtha to bathe.
As soon as she had bathed and emerged from that water,
she became pregnant immediately, even without union with her husband.
And she, being filled with faith, then heard an incorporeal voice saying:
"Whoever stays here in the midst of the water, whatever he desires in his heart [shall be granted]. (95)
Whether it be a woman or even a man, one obtains that which has been thought of;
for you, however, having stayed here in these waters, a desire for a son was formed in your heart. (96)
"Therefore, a son shall be born to you, endowed with a [divine] embryo," having heard this voice from the sky spoken by the messenger of the gods. || 97 ||
Seeing her pregnant even without her husband, she spoke these words:
"Aha! This power of the holy ford appears unprecedented to me. (98)
Wherein a fetus is conceived in women without semen and menses, she went from there to her home and gave birth to an excellent son. (99)
The desires of those who bathe here at this sacred ford are surely fulfilled;
there is no doubt, for it is just like that Gautamī.
The Gomatī was brought to this pool by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
having bathed there, one attains the supreme heaven—of this there is no doubt. || 101 ||
Listen, O Goddess, to a marvel that occurred in the presence of Macaleśvara:
there was a parrot who had built a nest and used to perform circumambulations [of the Lord]. (10.2)
Flying up again and again, he would rest in his nest over and over;
and in time, having died, that king indeed became one named Veṇu.
Having remembered his existence as a parrot, that king became one who remembers his past births;
having reached Acaleśvara, he then performed a circumambulation.
He did nothing else at all; he simply performed the circumambulation. But Nārada and the other sages, seeing the king in such a state, [were amazed].
They asked: "How is the circumambulation alone to be performed? Why do you not offer the food offering, fruits, flowers, and so forth? Please tell us. (106)
The bamboo spoke: "In former times, I was a parrot dwelling here, performing circumambulations day and night around the deity stationed there."
By His grace and through the power of that merit, I have now become one who remembers my past lives;
remembering that great virtue, I perform the circumambulation of the deity.
"For the sake of attaining infinite merit, I am indeed performing this circumambulation.
Having heard this from the king, the seers exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (10.9).
Then, after a long time, through devotion to Hara, the king [recited]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to the Lord. (110)

Having received this mantra from Hara with devotion, he went to Vaikuṇṭha. O Lakṣmī, I have thus related to you this account as spoken by Śambhu to Satī. Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Departure of Śaṅkara and Others to Dvārakā, Camatkārapura, and Arbuda Mountain; the Account of Gautama; the Account of Saudāsa and Uttaṅka; the Greatness of Nāgatīrtha; the Liberation of King Veṇu; and the Account of the Bringing of Arbuda," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī; having heard that Śaṅkara had arrived at Arbuda Mountain, Agastya came from the south for the purpose of seeing him.
Having bowed to Śambhu and worshipped him, Agastya, seated comfortably on an auspicious seat and honored by Śambhu, then questioned Śaṅkara.
"O Lord, tell me how I may attain long life in this world.
Śambhu replied, "Worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men."
Indeed, even while residing in Saurāṣṭra as the Lord of Ramā at Kāmbharī,
divine status never arises for anyone anywhere without devotion to Hari.
Without divine power, one does not become long-lived;
the decay of time and such never touches one who possesses divinity. (5)
Without divine yoga, the state of divinity never occurs at any time;
the divine one is Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, the Lord who brings all beings into existence.
And when He has entered that body, it shall possess divine qualities in particular;
for those perfections (siddhis) abide where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
I am indeed Śaṅkara, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other inhabitants of heaven;
we are divine through a portion of Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, worship Nārāyaṇa.
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; salutations!
Recite the great mantra daily and always perform meditation upon Hari. (9)
Offer oblations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, with the mantra "Svāhā.
Being pleased, He will surely grant you divine splendor according to your desire.
Thus addressed, the king of sages, Agastya, performed meditation, worship,
salutation, and the constant remembrance of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he then resided at Aśvapaṭṭaka;
then once, that king of sages went to Kāśī for the sake of visiting holy places.
Having traveled through the sky to the Himavat mountain, he proceeded to Lake Mānasa;
there, the bull among sages beheld a divine tortoise in the lake.
He beheld most divine lotuses made of gold;
and a divine, auspicious lotus offered by Kacchapa as a welcome gift.
Meanwhile, that king of sages, possessing divine vision,
flew up there, bowed to the tortoise, and then departed for the place surrounded by the Avilā river.
On a plateau situated at the side of Meru, he beheld a magnificent lake;
on its shore, he saw a certain beautiful and great hut.
There, a certain ascetic was seen by him, lax in his fasts, with only skin and bones remaining, and clothed in rags and bark garments. (17)
And when asked by that great-souled one for the sake of understanding, "Who are you?", he replied to Agastya: "Stay, stay, O twice-born one! (18)
"O Brahmin, please accept this hospitality; please enter my dwelling.
Having heard this, Agastya entered that leaf-hut.
Then he beheld a radiant man, a Brahmin who was like the Lord himself,
seated upon an auspicious seat on the ground, chanting the eternal Brahman.
Placing a rosary upon his hand and applying a tilaka mark upon his forehead, he recited:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! (21)
While he was thus performing the fire-sacrifice, having obtained a jewel for each [offering],
he recited the supreme Pauruṣa Sūkta at the end of each rosary.
Such was that man who indeed recited the Lakṣmīsūkta;
and after the hymn, five maidens emerged from a pit within that wall.
Then one woman brought forth a golden throne;
a second performed the washing of his feet with a water-vessel;
and a third, holding a fan, provided air for the sage.
Holding the fourth and fifth [mudrās], they stand on either side with chowries.
Again, repeatedly reciting the Śrīsūkta, that ascetic performed the fire-oblation (homa) within the hut; meanwhile, hundreds of auspicious maidens appeared.
There, golden-pitcher-handed beings were born by the side of a lake,
which was swiftly created right there through a rite of oblation dedicated to Varuṇa.
Having brought water, they approached and bathed him;
they wiped him with a cloth and then gave him ornaments.
They gave him garments, performed worship, and offered excellent food offerings.
Then they gave him water and vanished in an instant.
Thereupon, Agastya, beholding this marvel, entered into meditation;
while his eyes were thus closed, he [beheld] himself on Mount Meru.
Standing upon the high peak, he beholds his own self by means of his own self;
likewise, he sees the seven oceans as well as the principal mountain ranges.
Seated upon Mount Meru, he beheld the earth consisting of seven islands;
having seen everything, the sage returned and once again entered into meditation.
He beheld Bhuvarloka, as well as Svarga, Jana, and Satya;
and remaining there, he indeed beheld the assembly hall of Brahmā and Vaikuṇṭha.
There he saw the four-armed Puruṣa, Janārdana.
And as soon as he opens his eyes and looks outside, for that duration—
Neither Mount Meru, nor the celestial cottage, nor even Lake Mānasa exists; yet Kāśikā is not non-existent either. (35)
Then, on the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, in the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa,
Agastya beheld himself within his own leaf-hut.
From that time forward, Agastya’s divinity in this world, his extreme longevity, and his superhuman powers of sovereignty became manifest. (37)
Thinking thus, "When shall I again reach that auspicious region where I was born? he set out for the Himālaya mountains to behold Śambhu.
He goes again and again to see Nara-Nārāyaṇa and to see Nārāyaṇa; he also goes repeatedly to Śvetadvīpa and Satyaloka.
Nevertheless, even so, he never obtains a vision of Him.
Thus did Śaṅkara speak to Pārvatī at that very moment. Then Agasti arrived once more at that Arbuda mountain for the purpose of seeing him;
having bowed to and prostrated before Śambhu, he then spoke what he wished to inquire about.
O Blessed One, please tell me the vow, the austerity, or the dharma that will lead to the attainment of that divine world which was previously seen by me. (42)
Having heard that, Śaṅkara said: "O Lakṣmī, listen to what I tell you:
without worshipping Hari with devotion, the attainment of those worlds will certainly not occur.
When Hari is worshipped, all the worlds will indeed be in the palm of one's hand. || 43 ||
The deity who is worshipped as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in sacrifice, from whom this entire world has arisen,
and in whom all things together with the gods are eternally dissolved—
he is the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, higher than the highest. || 44–45 ||

The glorious Lord of syllables, the perfect Śrī Puruṣottama, he who is the most complete—He alone is to be worshipped always by people, whether they possess desires or are free from them; for He is indeed the Lord who grants all goals. 46.
In the beginning, that very Puruṣottama became fourfold in nature:
in Goloka he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa; in Vaikuṇṭha he is Nārāyaṇa; in the unmanifest (Avyākṛta) he is Vāsudeva; and in the golden realm he is Nara-Nārāyaṇa. || 47-48 ||
Furthermore, this Śrī Puruṣottama became fourfold:
Viṣṇu in the realm beyond Satyaloka, and Viṣṇu in the Ocean of Milk;
likewise, Viṣṇu in Śvetadvīpa, and Viṣṇu Ādityaka in heaven.
Furthermore, that Blessed One manifested himself threefold:
as Sadāśiva, Mahāviṣṇu, and eternal Mahākāla.
Again, that Blessed One manifested himself threefold.
Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and the eternal Saṃkarṣaṇa—
again, that Blessed One manifested himself in three forms:
Brahmā as the rājasa form, and Viṣṇu as the sāttvika form.
And the form of Rudra is tāmasa, the cause of creation, nourishment, and destruction. || 53 ||
For the Blessed One is indeed one alone; in every kalpa he is born, and in every creation within the spheres, he assumes innumerable forms. ||54||
He who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā; he who is Brahmā is Maheśvara. Whether these be four or three, the reality is indeed one and eternal.
Bestowing liberation through its supreme form and prosperity through its active form, the Self becomes purified by means of *sattva* through the power of Śrī Nārāyaṇa. (56)
Indeed, a living being is liberated through purity; purity has its refuge in Nārāyaṇa. And the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa manifests himself in the form of sacrifice.
In the Kṛta age, the pure Nārāyaṇa is worshipped in his subtle form;
in the Tretā age, in the form of sacrifice; and in the Dvāpara age, through sacred narratives and ritual honors.
Even through many deeds performed with hypocrisy, one is honored;
and if one worships these who bear forms with a mind of hatred, [the result is still attained]. (59)
If one perceives through the intellect a sense of duality, there is indeed no liberation for him anywhere;
but he who, having known the One, worships it, shall be liberated—of this there is no doubt.

If, having made a distinction, one should worship the One alone and never hate the Supreme, then for such a person devoted to the vow of fidelity to the Lord, liberation will surely occur; of this there is no doubt.
If a person creates division and worships one while censuring another,
everything belonging to him shall be lost and he shall fall into a miserable state.
O Agastya, listen further to this ancient account as I relate it.
At the beginning of creation, the devotees of Hari indeed became the inhabitants of the created world.
Having worshipped Śrī Puruṣottama, all of them became established in the Dharma and partakers of liberation, as if they were omniscient ones, indeed standing upon the fourteenth stage.
They gradually attained liberation; then Brahmā remembered the Lord Hari, and the all-pervading Śrī Hari indeed manifested himself.
He said, "Tell me, what is to be done? Then Brahmā spoke to Hari:
"O God of gods, all people are now established on the path to liberation."
How indeed will creation come to be? And who would dwell in the heavens and other such realms?
Among these worlds of hell, in whose mind would there be a desire to dwell? (67)
Thus addressed, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa then said to him:
"Many ages will pass until they come to me in due course."
In the final age, high-minded men will become rare;
I shall quickly create this delusion which will bewilder everyone.
And Rudra repeatedly assumes many forms characterized by tamas,
such as Bhairava and others, while Pārvatī likewise assumes other supreme forms.
For the sake of destroying the Daityas, he will assume terrible forms;
indeed, embodied beings, deluded and greedy for liquor, meat, and such things, [will be overcome]. (71)
Relying upon those [false doctrines], beings deprived of the path to existence will go astray;
likewise, out of delusion born of darkness (tamas), they will abandon the Veda.
At that time, those who are devoted to hatred will resort to and practice tantras that are purely characterized by darkness (tāmasa) and abound in violence, according to their own whims. //73//
"There will indeed be no liberation for those who go to hell.
Then Brahmā said to him, "Utter words of delusion. (74)
Indeed, whatever [teachings] people in the world rely upon to become subject to rebirth—
from that time forward, O Agastya,
I have also composed Tantras characterized by darkness (tāmasa), which are dear to those possessed of desire.
The world, for the most part established in them, takes delight in these;
it flows indeed through the cycle of existence, repeatedly in death and birth. In the Kali age, people will for the most part take refuge with human beings.
Thinking of them to be the Supreme Self, they will revile Śiva and the other deities;
by that sin, they shall all certainly go to the hells.
Being themselves deluded, they will deceive their gurus and other men.
And by censures and passions, by hatreds, and by the defilements of the ego-sense "I. ||79||
Through constant deceit, theft, and betrayal of trust for the sake of their own interests,
those teachers will, by that sin, go to many hells;
in the worlds, these people who are teachers will be held in contempt like dogs.
By the power of that [merit], the paths of Yama and the realms of Yama shall be abandoned in Kāśī. ||8 1 ||
Therefore, O Agastya, this world has been filled by me in many ways through desire-driven action, yet liberation exists here and there.
O brahmin-sage, he who thus knows the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa—
The Supreme Brahman, who is the Self of all, as well as ourselves and many others. ||83||
Neither delusion in its primary form nor in its secondary aspects afflicts him;
behold, O Agastya, my supreme and eternal form. (84)
When the sage Agastya had spoken thus, he beheld Śaṅkara;
there he saw Brahmā within him, and within Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa;
and within Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the beginningless Puruṣottama.
Having seen him thus—possessing a blazing, radiant complexion and as beautiful as ten million Kāmadevas—the Brahmin Agastya praised the Supreme Lord:
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, you are Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman. (86–87)
In the sense of "entering into" (viśapraveśane), the verbal root [viś] takes the suffix *snup*, from which [the name] Viṣṇu is derived;
he is the all-pervading Supreme Lord among all the gods.
At times you are Brahmā, at times Rudra; you alone are the one higher than the highest.

Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Śambhu, Brahmā, and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—by these names the supreme, eternal Brahman is proclaimed. There is no difference among the incarnations within the one who incarnates. || 1.552.90 ||
Those who meditate upon this otherwise are to be known as followers of the nature of the Kali age;
those revilers, sinful men, go to a terrible hell.
Indeed, such will be the schismatics in the Kali Yuga.
Deluded deceivers in the world, mockers of the assembly of the wise, they will say:
"We are truly knowledgeable; we know the Supreme Lord. Others, who contemplate incarnations and the like, do not know that reality. || 92-93 ||
Thus, for these revilers who were hostile toward the incarnations of Hari,
the sacred fields of Dharmarāja were indeed established within the city.
Therefore, those who outwardly observe vows but are inwardly dark, disparaging, treacherous, and contemptuous, will certainly go to hell. (95)
In the past, I was created by Brahmā and told, "Create indeed progeny.
At that time, being incapable of discernment, I was submerged in the water.
There I beheld a divine, noble being, the size of a thumb,
a youth resembling a dark cloud, with eyes like lotuses.
I asked him, "Who are you? How were you born? Please tell me.
He said to me, "I am indeed you; I am Brahmā, I am Viṣṇu, and I am he."
I am the eternal god Nārāyaṇa, reclining upon the waters;
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa within my own abode.
"May you have divine vision here; behold me with effort, O Hara!
When he was addressed thus by him, I looked at him.
First, that Lord was seen by me in the supreme, divine, imperishable abode;
he was likewise beheld in Goloka and in Vikuṇṭha.
Mahāviṣṇu was seen in the water, and Virāṭ in his cosmic form was also beheld;
a lotus was seen at his navel, and Brahmā was observed therein.
I saw him by his side, and upon seeing him, I was filled with joy; remembering his qualities through my asceticism, I praised the illustrious Supreme Lord. || 103 ||
Thus did Śaṅkara speak to Agastya on Arbuda Mountain;
that speech which bestows liberation has been recounted by me here to you, O Lakṣmī.
From reciting and hearing this, liberation occurs in the supreme, imperishable state;
for those with desires, there shall be the prosperity of the home, wealth, sons, and so forth.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Agastya’s Attainment of Divinity and Longevity in the First Kṛta-yuga Lineage, the Marvel of Rudra on Arbuda Mountain, and the Continued Existence in the Stream of Saṃsāra for Humans of the Non-Satya Ages who Engage in Mutual Hostility toward the Three Deities," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how Śambhu then offered praise to Nārāyaṇa; I shall tell you exactly what he spoke.
Oṃ, salutations to the one who dwells in the imperishable, who shines in the supreme abode;
salutations be to you, the Supreme Lord, the Lord of the universe, and the Lord of the liberated.
Salutations again and again to you, the pure one, whose form is the primordial source and who is infinite;
salutations to him whose own nature is all forms, who possesses a thousand arms. || 3 ||
Salutation to the Creator endowed with a thousand rays, whose actions are pure, who dwells within the vast body, and who removes the afflictions of the universe. 4.
Salutations again and again to Śambhu, whose form is like a thousand suns;
salutations again and again to You, the wielder of the discus, the abode of all knowledge. || 5 ||
Salutations to You, Kṛṣṇa, who are eternally praised by all the gods;
to the beginningless Lord of the Earth, the infallible one who dwells upon Śeṣa.
Salutations always to you, the Lord of the Maruts, the Lord of all;
salutations to you, the Lord of the waters, the Lord of the earth, and the Eye of the Universe. || 7 ||
Salutations to you, the moon, the sun, and the Lord of the Universe;
salutations to you whose nature is inconceivable and whose form is nectar.
Salutation to You, who illumines the quarters of space and whose heart is the sky;
salutation to the one who leads to Nārāyaṇa, who faces in every direction.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the remover of the distress of the gods, who possesses innumerable faces;
salutation to the Great Lord, the ancient one, from whom the world is produced.
You are worshipped by some among millions as those who tread the path of truth;
you alone are beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), beyond the unmanifest (akṣara), and supreme.
He is the foremost among the knowers, omniscient, and possessed of a vast form; yet he is also of subtle nature, for the qualities derived from primordial matter (prakṛti) do not dwell within him.
He who is not an object of speech, yet is the object of the speech of his devotees;
and he who is not overcome by karma, yet constantly performs creation.
Though devoid of senses, You are worshipped by Indra and others who possess senses; and though this worldly existence is essence-less, You alone are its true essence. || 14 ||
Even such a four-armed one might be surpassed by those who sacrifice;
we do not know the supreme form, we know only that which comes within the range of our vision.
We know you as the embodiment of the incarnations; through them, we attain refuge.
Even the Lotus-born One does not know your true form, nor do I.
I know the ancient Seer, the Lord, through my purified asceticism;
I and the goddesses beginning with Padmā have been born from the All-pervading One again and again. || 17 ||
By me, who am but a child, and by others as well, you are not fully awakened to what you truly are.

We find satisfaction through prostration, and the followers of the Vedas are gratified by hymns of praise. (18) If, through your grace, an intellect arising from the discernment of previous lives should be attained, then by that means there would be auspiciousness leading to the further shore of Brahman. (19)

Subtle and yet becoming manifest, you have today become the very ground of my vision; you have been seen, and I have accomplished my purpose—you have become easily attained to me today by my good fortune.
I am born, O Viṣṇu; I am prostrate like a staff at your feet.
Accept the praise of this devotee, especially so, O Janārdana.
"O Brahmā, indeed create the creation; you have carried out my command.
Grant me that omniscience which pertains to all the earth, and I shall create through service. (22)
"You abide in my heart; salutations to you! I am outside; I bow to you!
For you, who are omnipresent, there is no distinction here from me."
Having understood this public praise as well as the internal verbal [prayer], O Blessed One, purify me who am afraid; contemplate that "I am yours. (24)
Thus praised by Rudra of immeasurable splendor, the divine Lord Viṣṇu, being well-pleased, said: "Choose whatever boon you desire."
Rudra said: "O Janārdana, grant me the knowledge of creation eternally;
protect me in every way therein, and after that, [grant me] the knowledge of dissolution. (26)
Having assumed human form for the performance of divine tasks, I shall worship you alone; may you always grant me protection.
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord said: "O Rudra, always be a possessor of knowledge;
may the ancient wisdom of creation be ever with you.
Indeed, may you possess a state of being worshipped throughout all the worlds that is even greater than mine."
Having spoken thus, Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa vanished from sight.
"I worship that god Nārāyaṇa, who is higher than the highest.
Thus this Lord Hari is all-pervading and the creator of all beings.
In former times he became a granter of boons to me; by him I am the most excellent among the gods."
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a god superior to Nārāyaṇa.
O best of beings, I have told you all this secret of the Vedas and the Purāṇas, by which the all-pervading Lord, who consists of everything, is realized.
Thus did Śaṅkara speak to Agastya, the bull among sages;
and Agastya, having heard that supreme knowledge, returned to his own hermitage.
Then Śambhu said to Pārvatī, "Listen, O beautiful lady."
My great Gaṇa Bhadrakarṇa slew Namuci, the best of the Daityas;
in that very place, there exists my beautiful and bliss-bestowing Tīrtha known as Bhadrakarṇahrada on Mount Arbuda.
Likewise, there is the supreme sacred site named Kedārakuṇḍa, which bestows excellent liberation;
there, the great king Ajapāla reigned in the city of Vaideha.
In a previous birth, this man was a Śūdra who once worshipped Śaṅkara with a lotus; by that merit, he has become a king.
Born in the city of Videha, he possessed the memory of his past lives; remembering his birth, he came to Mount Arbuda and established the Kedāra Tīrtha.
Brahmā, having taken all the holy fords with him, arrived at Arbuda.
At that time, Kedāra-tīrtha arrived in another form;
Kedāraka exists in three places: on Himācala, at Prabhāsa, and at Arbuda.
A sage named Maṅkaṇaka was dwelling on the bank of the Sarasvatī.
That virtuous soul performed austerities until there was no longer any redness in his body;
realizing, "I have attained perfection," he then began to dance.
As he was dancing there in this manner, the principles beginning with earth, as well as all things mobile and immobile, danced along with his dancing. (42)
Then the gods said to Hara: "O Mahādeva, quickly stop this dancing, lest there be a destruction of all beings. (43)
Śambhu, having arrived there, asked, "Why do you dance, and how so?
Maṅkaṇaka then replied, "O Brahmin, look at this physical body."
"Since my bile and blood have been destroyed by my asceticism, I rejoice out of joy.
When he had spoken thus, Mahādeva said, "Behold, Maṅkaṇaka! (45)
"I shall strike my thumb here with my forefinger; behold my ascetic power!
Having said this, he struck his thumb, and white ash emerged.
Having seen that, the brahmin was struck with wonder and became free from pride;
falling to the ground on his knees, he praised the ascetic Hara.
Lift me up, O Mahādeva; reveal your eternal form.
Here is the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī. 48.
The great tirtha of Maṅkaṇaka shall remain eternally established; for one who bathes here, the fruit shall be heaven, and in the end, liberation. ||49||
Śambhu said, "Let it be so; let there indeed be a holy place here named after you.
Having spoken thus, I then vanished from that spot.
Now, there exists another preeminent sacred site called Koṭīśvara,
where in ancient times Hara assumed many forms in a single moment.
That great holy place, which destroys sin and suffering, was established for the purpose of being seen and for giving gifts to Brahmins who are seekers of travel.
At Arbuda, there exists the supreme, purifying Rūpatīrtha.
Formerly, there was a certain Ābhīrī woman who was deformed and had a distorted face. (53)
Once, having come to a mountain torrent to fetch fruit,
she entered the water and became transformed into one of divine form.
With lotus-like eyes and beautiful hair, she was a young woman of sixteen years;
seeing her, the gods and humans were then filled with wonder. (55)
Once, Indra arrived at that forest at Puṣkara and beheld a divine, incomparable goddess who was like a celestial nymph.
The god, having become a human, asked her about her lineage and other details;
she told him of his own status as Indra, and he in turn spoke to that mistress of the gods.
"O Thousand-eyed One, lead me along with yourself to the abode of the gods.
Indra then led her to Amarāvatī by means of his own celestial chariot.
He made that auspicious Apsaras known by the name Vapu;
thus, indeed, exists the Vapu-tīrtha, possessed of such power.
There, to the east, there is a cave and a tilaka tree;
the water emerging from the opening has indeed been touched by that tilaka.
A barren woman who drinks [this water] shall become possessed of sons, and her disease shall perish.
In ancient times, Aditi performed supreme penance for a long duration at Rūpatīrtha.
While Indra was deprived of his kingdom and Bali was established as the lord of the realm,
Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the Asuras, was born from her through penance in a dwarf form.
Thus, her place of penance is declared to be Rūpatīrtha;
furthermore, the Āmbarīṣatīrtha is situated on Mount Arbuda.
Ambarīṣa performed austerities for many thousands of years;
and Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of Indra, [mounted] upon Garuḍa and the elephant.
Having arrived, he stood there and said, "O King, choose a boon.
The king replied, "I do not desire any boon from you other than Viṣṇu."
"You are not able to grant me liberation; go back to heaven as you came," he said, and having spoken thus, he meditated within himself upon Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
At that moment Indra became Viṣṇu and the elephant also assumed the form of Garuḍa;
then he said, "I am pleased with your devotion; O King, tell me the boon you desire."
The king, having opened his eyes, looked once more;
beholding Nārāyaṇa, he attained great joy and spoke.
"O Supreme Lord, tell me the means for crossing over saṃsāra. Hari said: "O King, having abandoned sleep in the morning, [you must listen]."
While I am still in my youth, I must repeatedly practice meditation upon her form;
thereafter, she shall perform the remembrance, the chanting, and the proclamation of her names.
At the time of bathing and other such rites, you should remember my form;
my worship should be performed within the heart or in images and the like.

Bathing with sandalwood paste, flowers, and the like; clothing and ornaments; food and the drinking of water; the waving of lights (nīrājana); and hymns of praise and so forth—[these are the services]. (72)
An offering of a handful of flowers should also be given to me, as well as the ritual dismissal:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (73)
The Vaiśvadeva and other offerings should indeed be offered into the sacrificial fire, which is the mouth of the virtuous;
you should also give what is sweet and pleasing, as well as worship to the cows and so forth. (74)
I must always perform devotion [to Him], and [call out] "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa";
everything—sons, wife, wealth, and so forth—must be offered to Kṛṣṇa. (79)
And the self must be offered with love as the means for liberation from that [bondage].
Listen always to my stories here; touch me, the Supreme Person.
Behold my divine image; eat the nectars produced from my grace;
accept the fragrance of my form, and perform a massage of my hands. (77)
Perform circumambulation of me with your feet and offer praise to me with your speech;
O King, accept my joy and that of my form in every way.
Always abandon that which is contrary to me and mixed with the vital air;
hold me eternally within the life-force, and direct my mind toward that which is mine.
Always grant me your thought, your decision, and your honor;
make everything consist of the bliss of Brahman, the essence of Brahman, and the nature of all the Vedas.
Wherever you may dwell—whether together with others or alone—[may it be so].
In every such state I am well-established; behold me in every respect.
"O King, while I remain present, maintain a gentle disposition toward everyone;
this which I have declared to you is the supreme and most effective means for your liberation. (82)
Thus addressed by that powerful Viṣṇu, the king stood up;
thereafter, the monarch established his supreme state of being absorbed in Him. 83.
He constantly worshipped him with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
then, after a long time, that king [attained his goal] in the abode of Hari.
Together with his sons, wife, and kinsmen, he engaged in excellent worship;
for the Blessed One was indeed always present there in that hermitage.
Having thus attained supreme devotion by which he reached the imperishable abode,
[he visited] that supreme holy site, the place of Ambarīṣa’s penance.
And on Arbuda there exists a beautiful place that bestows liberation and removes sin;
whoever worships Hṛṣīkeśa there on Arbuda with devotion, [attains the highest goal].
O beloved, by the grace of Śrī Hari, he goes to the realm of Viṣṇu,
where this Lord was propitiated by Ambarīṣa.
Nārāyaṇa shines forth in the form of Hṛṣīkeśa;
on the eleventh day, one should perform a vigil in the presence of Hṛṣīkeśa.
One who beholds him shall obtain the fruit of a *kapilā* cow;
and he who worships Hṛṣīkeśa there for four months [attains the same].
He goes indeed to the supreme Brahman, the highest abode; of this there is no doubt.
He alone, indeed, performs the merit of all holy places throughout the worlds.
Another beholds Hṛṣīkeśa with equanimity; it is held that the fruit for both is the same.
One person bestows all gifts upon worthy recipients. (9.2)
Another beholds Hṛṣīkeśa with equanimity; this is considered equal to the fruit [of the former].
One might give a thousand maidens in marriage at a sacred ford. (93)
Another beholds Hṛṣīkeśa equally; the fruit of that is considered to be the same.
One may behold Hari within the body, while another beholds Hari in the water.
For one who is fasting during the Cāturmāsya period, the merit of that is ten thousand times ten thousandfold;
indeed, a vision of Viṣṇu is equal to the gift of a thousand cows.
Indeed, the vision of Viṣṇu is equal to sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma;
one should cast off the body on the Himālaya and always speak of the knowledge of Brahman. (96)
Another beholds Hṛṣīkeśa equally; that is considered his fruit. One who undertakes a fast unto death likewise beholds Viṣṇu.
Another person, being composed during the Cāturmāsya period, should perform the Śrāddha at Gayā;
indeed, the sight of Hṛṣīkeśa is equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who performs penance for a thousand years becomes liberated by the mere sight [of him];
likewise, the vision of Hṛṣīkeśa is attained even through the study of the Vedas.
It increases merit, bestows heaven, and grants liberation.
What is the use of saying more here? Listen in brief, O beloved.
Everything exists on one side, while the vision of Hari exists on the other;
therefore, with every effort, one should remain in the presence of Hari.
On one side is Hṛṣīkeśa, and on the other side is Karṇikeśvara;
those who die between them go to Vaikuṇṭha into the presence of Hari.
He who offers even a single flower to Hṛṣīkeśa with devotion shall be endowed with all prosperity in this world and in the next.
The fruit of cleansing that place is proclaimed to be liberation for him who raises a banner during either the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight.
His sins are destroyed, and he goes to the imperishable abode of Hari;
he who performs worship with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and feeds Lord Hari. 105.
Or else, one should cause a gift of land to be given, or again, have a temple constructed;
in the eternal abode, one shall immediately attain liberation. || 106 ||
Thus did Śaṅkara speak to Pārvatī on Mount Arbuda. O Lakṣmī, I have thus declared to you the majesty arising from the sacred fords (tīrthas). 107.
By reading and hearing this, a person shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one who has desires will certainly become wealthy and possessed of sons and prosperity.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Praise of Nārāyaṇa by Śaṅkara on Arbuda Mountain in the Lineage of the Kṛta Yuga in the First Part of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā," wherein the Bhadrakarṇahrada Tīrtha, the Maṅkaṇaka Tīrtha at Kedārakuṇḍa, the Koṭīśvara Tīrtha, Rūpa Tīrtha, Ambarīṣa Tīrtha, and Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha are described along with their respective narratives.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; Hara spoke to Pārvatī concerning the circle of holy places (tīrthamaṇḍala):
"Viśvāvasu, devoted to Śiva, performed penance and attained perfection. || 1 ||
Śambhu was pleased with that king and appeared before him;
"Choose a boon," he said, and from Hara he chose spiritual perfection (siddhi).
That *liṅga*, Siddheśvara, manifested in the form of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*);
and Śukreśvara, established by Śukra, is likewise called a *tīrtha*.
Having performed difficult penance here, Śukra obtained from the venerable Śaṅkara the Sañjīvanī,
Mṛtyuñjayā, and Sandhāyinī vidyās.
There is a purifying and auspicious waterfall of water there;
having bathed in that pool, a person shall cast off the fear of untimely death.
From there, one should go to the most purifying place of asceticism of the Vālakhilyas;
by bathing in the pool there, a person shall assume a divine form.
There, a Kirāta woman, though ill-favored and overcome by thirst, went to drink the water upon seeing that excellent water fit for bathing. (7)
Having bathed, as she was going outside, she then became a divine goddess;
her husband, seeing her, asked, "Who are you, O beautiful one? (8)
"My wife has come here to this pool in her desire for water;
if you have seen her, who is dark-complexioned, then speak, O Devikā! (9)
She said to her own beloved: "I am indeed your beloved;
by the power of bathing at Kuṇḍa, I have become a celestial maiden."
"O Master, bathe here in this pool; you shall become equal to a god.
Thus addressed, he performed his ablutions, and at that moment, his sins were indeed destroyed.
Having abandoned her body and met her death, the devoted wife likewise bathed again, cast off her form, and [ascended] by means of a brilliantly radiant celestial chariot.
Adored by celestial maidens, the beautiful woman, together with her husband,
paid homage to that auspicious holy site and departed for the third heaven.
Where the Kirātī woman named Maṇikarṇā attained liberation,
that is considered to be the Māṇikarṇeśvara pool, the Liṅga, and the Tīrtha.
The Vālakhilyas always reside there at the auspicious time of Kutupa;
bathing there during a solar eclipse bestows the merit of Kurukṣetra.
Whatever merit is obtained through the remembrance [of this place] during bathing is attained here; of this there is no doubt.
Now, another is the Paṅgutīrtha, established by the Brahmin Paṅgu.
Once, in the lineage of Cyavana, a brahmin named Paṅgu arrived very slowly at Arbuda by chance, having joined a caravan. ||17||
Having reached a certain mountain stream, he performed most severe penance,
devoted to the worship of Śiva, subsisting on air alone, and engaged in the rites of fire-offerings and silent recitation.
Mahādeva, being pleased with him, appeared there in person;
on the fourteenth day of the bright half of Caitra, Hara granted him a boon.
By means of which [pilgrimage], having abandoned the state of being lame, he became possessed of a divine body;
and that man attained liberation after bowing at Paṅgutīrtha—this indeed is its significance.
Where Śambhu, accompanied by Umā, shines near a mountain torrent;
having bathed and drunk the water there, one attains liberation through the grace of Śambhu.
Now, in former times, King Citrāṅgada was devoted to sinful deeds;
he went to the forest near the Arbuda lake for the purpose of hunting. ||22||
Having bathed there in that lake, he went to drink water;
suddenly the king was seized by a crocodile and even devoured.
And Yamarāja spoke to Cchraṣṭapucchra and the others on that Arbudamattīrthaka ground. ||24||
"He has indeed died in this holy lake; he is certainly not deserving of punishment.
Let him go to heaven for twenty-one thousand yugas. (25)
Since he died at that very place where I formerly performed austerities, any person who bathes in that sacred ford will certainly attain heaven. (26)
That place is indeed declared to be Yamatīrtha, which grants liberation to Citrāṅgada;
from there, one should go to the Puṇḍroda Tīrtha, which destroys all sins.
In former times, a brahmin named Puṇḍrodaka, having established himself in detachment, arrived at the delightful Arbuda waterfall with the desire to die. ||28||
At that very same time, however, Sarasvatī herself was standing on that same secluded path,
engaged in the diversion of playing the lute.
The goddess said to the brahmin, "Tell me, what is it that you desire?
He replied, "I have no intelligence; I have been insulted by my teachers."
Sarasvatī, my mother, does not dwell upon the tip of my tongue; therefore, I wish to die right here, so that what is most beneficial may come to pass. (31)
The mother said: "By my grace, may your speech always be most excellent;
may the sciences born from the Vedas and other sources, adorned with logic, protect you. (32)
"From this day forward, you shall be eloquent in this world;
this auspicious sacred ford (tīrtha) of Sarasvatī shall be known by the name Puṇḍrodā."
"The wise man who performs his ablutions on the thirteenth day shall become perfected.
Having spoken thus, that goddess vanished right there.
For Puṇḍrodaka, having become omniscient, departed for heaven at the end;
from there one should go to Nala-tīrtha, where Śrīmātā shines resplendent. ||25||
Formerly, on that peak named Nala, there was a most terrible Dānava named Bāṣkali; for his destruction, Pārvatī [manifested].
The virtuous Śrīmātā was born in embodied form for the welfare of the worlds;
she seized Bāṣkali alive and rendered him free from death.
Having bowed to the great peak of the mountain, that Mother of the World herself sat upon it and dwells there as the protector of the world. (38)
When those two auspicious divine sandals have been placed there by her, whoever beholds them does not see cyclic existence again. (39)
Oppressed by the weight of my sandals, Bāṣkali, the foremost of the Daityas,
shall not go anywhere outside this place, nor shall he ascend upwards.
On the fourteenth night of the month of Caitra, my worship of the sandals must be performed there in the cave; I shall dwell there in the form of an atom.
"Those inhabitants of Kailāsa who shall perform a sacred ablution here will [attain their goal], of this there is no doubt"; having spoken thus, she vanished from sight. (42)
From there, one should go to the virtuous Vindhyācalī, who destroys the destruction of Śumbha;
by the command of Śiva, she shines upon Arbuda in a divine form. 43.
Having reached the interior of a cave, in a secluded and inaccessible place,
he who beholds her with devotion shall obtain everything desired.
Now, in former times, penance was indeed performed by the brahmin Maṅki;
formerly, that very foolish brahmin [saw] a beautiful buffalo on a mountain. (45)
He protected the milch cow as well as the other female buffaloes;
and having sold them, he acquired land and two bulls. (46)
While the two bulls were yoked to the pole at some point, a camel arrived;
having sniffed them, it thrust its neck through the hole in the wooden pole.
Then that camel, filled with fear, had the leather thong fastened around his neck;
indeed, at that time, the pair of oxen was hanging from his neck.
Because of that, the two bulls ran away and died from exhaustion;
then Maṅki, having attained detachment, [resided] at a waterfall on Mount Arbuda.
Resorting to severe austerity and chanting the name of Hari,
that Maṅki of Piṇḍāraka beheld Śaṅkara standing before him.
He praised him in that manner and attained liberation by the will of Śaṅkara;
because of Maṅki’s [attainment of] Piṇḍāraka, this place is therefore called Piṇḍāraka. || 51 ||
One should bathe at the famous Piṇḍāraka Tīrtha on the eighth lunar day;
there, by giving gifts of cows and buffaloes, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then one should go to the auspicious pilgrimage site of Raktābandha on Mount Arbuda.
Formerly, there was a king named Indrasena who possessed great strength. (53)
His wife was Sunandā, who was devoted to her husband;
the king went to the battlefield to fight and returned having conquered his enemies. (54)
He dispatched a messenger to the queen with this test:
"Go and say to Sunandā, 'Indrasena has been slain in battle.
Having heard this, observe her very facial expression and see what kind of reaction she makes."
If one should make an effort toward death, [the body] must be protected with great care.
Thus addressed, the messenger departed and reported exactly what had been said.
Upon hearing this, Sunandā quickly restrained her own life-breaths and gave them up,
thereby removing from the king the sin of slaughter that had arisen from the test of jesting.
The king's body became exceedingly heavy and sluggish. ||58||
Having returned home and perceiving that [his son] was devoid of luster, discolored, and bereft of serenity, the king lamented; then,
for the sake of expiating the murder of a woman, he departed for a sacred ford (tīrtha).
At Prāpti on Mount Arbuda, there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) called Raktānubandha.
Having bathed there and emerged, as soon as he looked at himself,
the shadow resulting from the murder of a woman that had clung to him was no longer seen.
He was born handsome and powerful, with an increase in his vital energy;
having performed penance at that sacred ford, he cast off his body through the power of yoga.
Having ascended a divine vehicle, he went swiftly to Kailāsa;
there, he effects the deliverance of those beings who are devoted to him.
Therefore, that sacred ford (tīrtha) shall always be renowned by the name Raktoddhāraka;
one should perform the auspicious Vināyaka rite at that ford for the pacification of obstacles.
Thereafter, one should go to the Pārśveśvara Tīrtha, which destroys all sins.
Devala had a wife named Pārthā, who was devoted to her husband. (65)
She performed penance there for the sake of destroying her barrenness;
she beheld Śambhu and indeed obtained the boon of a son.
Then, by virtue of a boon from Śaṅkara, she obtained a hundred sons at that place where there was pure water flowing from a mountain cave.
By performing the rites at this sacred ford (tīrtha), one shall obtain a wife, sons, and other blessings;
therefore, one who desires liberation should visit the Māmuñca lake-tīrtha. 68.
In ancient times, the sage Mudgala performed most rigorous penance there, constantly chanting: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (69)
Arbuda performed the three daily ablutions and became cleansed of all impurity;
then a messenger of the gods arrived to lead him to the great heaven.
Seated in his celestial chariot, he said to the sage, "Mount this; let us go to heaven.
I have been sent by Indra; come quickly, do not delay. (71)
Mudgala questioned him regarding the virtues and defects of heaven;
having heard [the answer], I shall consider whether the auspicious heaven is suitable for me to go to.
The messenger said, "O sage, heaven is attained by one's own merits.
The sage replied, "O follower, explain to me that fruit according to its true meaning."
"It is my firm resolve in my heart that I shall not go with them without having heard [the truth].
I shall perform abundant austerity and I shall worship Nārāyaṇa. (74)
The messenger said: "All virtues and youthfulness are equal in every respect;
so too are the delightful celestial groves of the gods, such as Nandana and others. (75)
There were enjoyments like no other, always providing satisfaction and happiness;
there was neither hunger nor thirst, nor laziness, nor even sleepiness. (76)
The goddesses, beautiful, uniform in form, and ever-fit for enjoyment, repeatedly cause the Gandharvas to constantly hear songs and the sounds of musical instruments. (77)
In their homes, beautiful women delight them with song, dance, and laughter;
no diseases afflict their bodies, and they possess nourishment born of nectar.
Vital energy (vīrya) is the full reality within the body, of which no diminution exists;
its food is indeed nectar, produced in manifold ways according to one's own will. (179)
There is no combination of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth among the deities;
there is no foul odor or the like, and their form is established by a single means of valid cognition.
There is no aging or decay of the skin, nor is there any impurity;
they possess divine vision, divine enjoyments, and divine garments. (81)
Indeed, the gods and other beings move through the path of the sky, as do countless celestial chariots, gems, jewels, and diamonds. (82)
All the lamps in the palace were divine, full of splendor, and produced by nature; every chamber was pervaded by a light equal to the radiance of the moon. 83.
Thousands of male and female servants who provide delicious drinks and grant all desires; moving at will, enjoying pleasures at will, they are mental creations of forms produced by the mind. (84)
Having a supreme lifespan lasting for a thousand yugas or even longer than that,
he enjoys heaven in accordance with his merit as one possessing a body of enjoyment.
As long as one's merit lasts, so long will one avoid falling;
such are the benefits that accrue, for service is not undertaken merely for the sake of the belly.
No new merit whatsoever is produced in heaven;
therefore, upon the exhaustion of their merit, the fall of the celestial dwellers occurs. (87)
This indeed is the great fault: falling is truly terrifying.
O Brahmin, this world is the land of action (karmabhūmi), while heaven is considered the land of enjoyment (bhogabhūmi). ||88||
Whatever supreme merit is performed here is enjoyed there;
yet when the power of the Dānavas arises, the Dānavas sometimes seize it. (89)
Indeed, by force they seized his house, his wife, and all his possessions;
this was the very corruption, as were the women enjoyed by others.
Likewise, having seen those possessing the power of merit multiplied ten-millionfold, one who possesses great wealth but little merit may even feel remorse. (9.1)
And those by whom abundant merit has been performed do not suffer even slight misery;
for that which is not bestowed upon mortals is never obtained in heaven. (92)
That suffering is said to be great for a human being, according to their prior karma.
All this regarding heaven, consisting of both virtues and defects, has been explained to you. (93)
"Come quickly, O sage, and tell me here what you desire.
Having heard this and reflected upon it all, Mudgala spoke like a mortal: [94]
Just as it is here, so it is there: wealth, wife, home, and the like are vessels for affliction, and likewise there is the fear of falling. (95)
"O messenger, there is always a loss of merit for me and no increase whatsoever; therefore, I have no need at all for that heaven. (96)
"By my command, you must clearly speak these words to the King of the Gods:
'May my offense be forgiven; I have no longing for heaven. (97)
I shall perform that action by which there will indeed be no falling;
I shall attain those worlds that are forever free from fear. ||98||
Having heard this, that messenger, who was indifferent to heaven, went quickly to Mahendra and spoke to him at length concerning Mudgala.
Having heard this, Śakra said to him: "Bring that sage by force;
for merit intended for the enjoyment of heaven will not go to waste until it has been experienced."
Having heard this, the messenger went to the place where Mudgala was staying;
having observed Mudgala’s conduct, Śīla entered the water through the power of yoga.
That messenger became motionless like a block of wood at the sage’s glance;
then Indra, the lord of the gods, being remembered by the messenger, arrived there.
Standing in the sky with a thunderbolt in his hand, he sought to carry off the sage;
but Mudgala paralyzed that Indra with a mere glance.
Then Śakra offered praise and, his enthusiasm broken, said: "Release me!
O Sage, whether you remain in heaven or in the mortal world, release me!"
Mudgala said: "O Lord of the Gods, your sight is difficult to obtain.
Go to heaven with your messengers; O sinless one, I shall remain right here."
"I shall worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and go to the imperishable abode.
"Release me," you said; thus the holy place is named Māṃmuñca. 1.06.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, let this lake always be renowned by your name; for those people who bathe here in this pool on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, [shall attain their desires].
"They shall satisfy the ancestors and indeed attain liberation.
Having heard this, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) took the messenger and departed for heaven.
Mudgala also remained there, meditating upon the Supreme Brahman;
having contemplated the imperishable Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he departed.
Thus Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī on Mount Arbuda, O Lakṣmī;
that which I have related to you is indeed the bestower of liberation and the purifier of the world.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Siddhatīrtha, Śukratīrtha, Maṇikarṇatīrtha, Paṅgutīrtha, Yamatīrtha, Puṇḍrodatīrtha, Śrīmātṛtīrtha, Vindhyācalītīrtha, Maṅkitīrtha, Piṇḍārakatīrtha, Raktoddhāratīrtha, Pārthātīrtha, Mudgalatīrtha, and Māmuñcatīrtha, along with their respective narratives, as well as the determination of the merits and defects of heaven," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, Lakṣmī; then Śambhu spoke to Pārvatī on Arbuda:
"I shall indeed tell you of other holy fords (tīrthas) that destroy all sins."
There lies the Caṇḍikā-tīrtha, where Caṇḍī, the destroyer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, was installed by the Brahmins and worshipped with Vedic mantras.
On Mount Arbuda, there exists an auspicious bathing pool of the Gaṅgā on the peak,
where the Gaṅgā meets with Śaṅkara once every year.
Furthermore, O Arbuda, through the granting of boons, there is assistance in one's service;
and there, the Śaiva holy site known as Acaleśvara is situated. || 4 ||
In that place where formerly a man of evil conduct, his body emaciated by leprosy,
had come for alms, he there obtained a gift of barley meal.
Having placed it in a small jar, while he was sleeping there at night, as soon as a moment passed,
a dog approached and devoured the barley meal.
Other dogs, having gathered together, engaged in a fight with the dog; hearing this, he became wide awake and saw that [other] dogs were eating the barley meal.
Then, having drunk only water and bathed near the tree, he fell asleep; and then, in the morning, he became wide awake.
He beheld himself resembling a god or a gandharva, and he recognized the power resulting from bathing in water, drinking, and other such acts.
Then, after some time, by the power of destiny, he met his death;
thereupon, he was born in the house of the lord of Vidarbha with the memory of his former life.
He was indeed the best of kings named Bhīma, the father of Damayantī;
he obtained a kingdom as the fruit of giving barley-meal to a dog. (11)
Having gone there, he indeed gave the barley-meal every day;
Gālava and the others asked him, "How is it that you give this meal?"
"Why are gifts of elephants, horses, and chariots not being given by you?
He then related the wonderful fruit of his previous birth.
Since I obtained this kingdom through the power of the gift of flour,
it is indeed fitting that my flour was eaten by dogs at that very sacred ford.
Then, having bathed and drunk that merit-bestowing water, I became a king whose sins were exhausted; I now perform the gift of barley-meal (saktu).
"Having understood that through this gift of barley-meal my fruit shall be eternal, I indeed give these barley-meals with devotion at this sacred site endowed with liberation. (16)
Having heard this, all those sages were filled with supreme wonder;
"Excellent! Excellent, O King! they said again and again. (17)
By reading this, or even by hearing it, a king shall obtain eternal happiness both in this world and in the hereafter. || 18 ||
On Mount Arbuda, there exists a sacred ford (tīrtha) that delivers one's entire lineage;
formerly, however, there was a man named Aprastuta who was devoted to sinful deeds.
The king, devoid of hospitality and lacking in the gift of knowledge,
accumulates wealth whether by righteous or unrighteous means.
Then, having reached old age and being exhorted by other elders, he said:
"O King, perform righteous deeds; at the time of death and thereafter, it will be auspicious. (21)
The king said: "Dharma is power, and it has been practiced by me;
wealth, kingdom, wife, home, and much else besides have been acquired. (22)
"There is no dharma higher than this, for there is nothing superior to that which grants satisfaction to the senses.
Having spoken thus, they observed silence and departed each to their own abode. (23)
Then, at the end, his ancestors, being distressed, spoke thus to him:
"In the past, we were of pure conduct and devoted to the dharma of giving. (24)
Having gone to heaven by means of their merits, they have today been struck down by you, a wicked son;
for you have become a bad son, devoid of righteous deeds.
Therefore, having performed some meritorious deed, deliver us all;
O evil-souled one, by your actions we have fallen into hell. (26)
"Ten will go to hell, and you too shall be among those destined for it.
Upon hearing this, the king fell into extreme distress and spoke to his wife.
Having heard this, his wife said, "Lift up your ancestors with auspicious deeds.
The king, having summoned the brahmins, performed the Pitṛmedha sacrifice.
He likewise undertook a pilgrimage to Mount Arbuda;
having arrived there, he performed a bath at the Kulasantāraṇa tirtha.
He offered handfuls of water while remembering his ancestors, beginning with his father and grandfather;
his ancestors were liberated from the terrible hell and became exceedingly joyful.
Then, seated in celestial chariots and adorned with divine garlands and garments, they all said to him:
"O son, we have all now been delivered by you."
"Since, O son, your family has been delivered by you at this sacred ford, therefore this ford shall be known by the name Kulasaṃtāraṇa (The Deliverer of the Family). ||32||
"Come, entrust the burden of the earth to your son Vasu and go to heaven"—having heard this proposal regarding his own office being transferred to his son, [he replied: 33.
Having given [the gift] and ascended the celestial chariot of the ancestors, he went to heaven.
O beloved, this power of the sacred ford has been described by me to you.
From there, one should go to the supreme holy site consisting of the hermitage of Paraśurāma,
where he performed austerities and obtained divine weapons from Śaṅkara.
Known as Rāmatīrtha, it destroys sin and suffering;
having bathed there in the lake of water, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (36)
From there, one should go to the most beautiful sacred site called Brahmapada;
in ancient times, it was requested by the Brahmins, "O Brahmā, grant us that object which bestows liberation."
Brahmā said: "I shall indeed grant my own station to him who worships me;
there shall be liberation for people through the service of his lotus feet. (38)
May all the sages and even the gods touch my foot when the full moon day of the month of Kārtika arrives; they shall worship it then. (39)
With water, fruits, flowers, perfumes, food, and ointments,
they shall go— without a doubt— to my world, which is very difficult to attain.
Having worshipped the station of the Grandfather (Brahmā), which indeed bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
there exists, O beloved, the primary Puṣkara in its threefold form.
This was always desired by the Lotus-born and was performed by Brahmā in ancient times;
indeed, Vasiṣṭha and other sages performed a sacrificial session (sattra) in the past.
Brahmā indeed arrived there at that sacrifice from Satyaloka;
however, for the sake of the three junctions of the day, he must go back to Satyaloka again and again. ||43||
After Brahmā and the sages had deliberated upon its lightness,
Puṣkara was brought from Satyaloka to Mount Arbuda.
While the sacrificial session was being held on Mount Arbuda, twilight fell for them;
at that time, other lotuses also arrived there upon the earth.
The supreme Puṣkara is in the sky, the middle one is upon the peak,
and the third is indeed a lake upon the earth.
Those who perform their ablutions with devotion on the full moon day of Kārtika shall attain eternal worlds, including those such as heaven that bestow all enjoyments. (47)
There, to the north, is the Sāvitrī-kuṇḍa, which indeed destroys sins;
there is also a beautiful image of Brahmā, which grants liberation upon being seen. (48)
In former times, Dhundhumāra was a devotee of Śrī Śaṅkara;
by him was established Umāmaheśvara, the destroyer of worldly existence. 49.
Having fully worshipped that deity, one should perform the consecration ceremony (*nirmitta*) at Arbuda Mountain,
where indeed King Nimi performed it in his old age.
Then Lomaśa also arrived there together with many sages;
the Brahmayajña was performed there and the Viṣṇuyāga was conducted.
The Rudrayāga was performed and the narrative of the Saṃhitā was told;
during that great festival, all [the inhabitants] belonging to Jambūdvīpa also [assembled]. 52.
The sacred fords (tīrthas) gathered there at that reservoir of water for the sake of the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha);
thus Jambūtīrtha was born, and likewise the tree [was established] as a sign of proof.
There, a divine Jambū tree suddenly appeared;
Nimi then performed his ablutions there, which embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having become divine and like a god, he went to heaven with his very body;
O Pārvatī, all this is the majesty of Arbuda for you. 55.
O beloved, this place of mine has been described as bestowing merit;
Arbuda itself is a sacred ford (tīrtha), and within it are millions of other sacred fords.

O Pārvatī, by virtue of their qualities, actions, and other attributes, they dwell there and will continue to dwell there; and indeed, through association with them and with faith, I too shall dwell there.
"O beloved, I have indeed visited many sacred fords through you;
I am truly blessed, for my wife is devoted to the gods and possesses devotion toward the Supreme Lord. (58)
She was zealous in performing religious duties, full of faith in meritorious acts, exceedingly gracious toward guests, and possessed of auspicious devotion in serving the virtuous. (59)
She was exceedingly swift in her own duties, always full of love for knowledge,
intent upon her reputation as if it were her own goal, and devoted to the practice of recitation.
Endowed with austerity, purity, and other virtues, devoted to burnt offerings and sacrifices,
regarding her husband as a god and the ancestors as gods, she likewise protects those dependent upon her.
I am the servant of Nārāyaṇa, who has become the self of all beings, and who bestows honor upon cows, the earth, Brahmins, the virtuous, and chaste women.
In patience she is equal to the earth; in dispassion, she is like a tree;
in virtuous conduct, she is equal to Brahmā; and in service, she is a vessel of affection.
Benevolent toward companions like a pillar, ever self-sacrificing in giving, and a helper in the next world—blessed is his life as a householder. (64)
He alone is called virtuous here whose wife is devoted to her husband;
he who has no such wife is not virtuous, but is a sinner.
He whose wife speaks harshly, casts a cruel glance, makes her face full of anger, and does not even grant him her heart; ||66||
Fie upon his life in this world, and indeed hell is his lot,
in whose house there is no merit and no service to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
There is no enthusiasm for food, no beautiful clothing and such, no speech full of affection, and no loving glance. ||68||
Whether it be a man or a woman, the birth of one who lacks such a virtuous beloved is in vain; I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, for I have such a faithful wife as this.
"By you, who are dispassionate, I am always blessed, even while being with one who is passionate;
others, having encountered agitation caused by women, go instead to the depths of the forest. (1.555.70)
The kind of success that might be achieved by them through dwelling in the forest is not such as could be attained even by a householder through the favor of a woman. (7.1)
For the weak, the protectorless, the ignorant, and likewise for the sick;
for the poor, the hungry, the thirsty, and those who are destitute.
For those yogis who are without support, yet exist as true beings within the world, their blessings bear fruit here swiftly, for they are indeed bestowers of accomplishment. //73//
Where the divine and delightful goddesses rejoice for householders, there reside fortune and prosperity; for the righteous, there is heaven and liberation.
Wherein every kind of peace and cessation exists perpetually, there liberation surely occurs; blessed am I, such a householder! (75)
That householder who, day and night, constantly strives only to acquire wealth, does not know how to protect his wife and family; he is merely a carrier of burdens. //76//
Food, clothing, wealth, travel, festivals, and so forth—all that wealth of his is indeed useless, for it is consumed by his very sighs. //77//
That wealth which is not to be enjoyed by the gods, nor by householders, nor by family members, nor by one's own kin, is equal to mere clay.
The husband who was not pleased, whose smiling face was no longer seen, nor heard the word "pleased" rich with love, nor seen his affectionate eyes; ||79||
There is no one with an equal heart, nor anyone endowed with such devotion;
he bestows no favor, nor does he act out of necessity.
He neither takes pleasure nor causes others to take pleasure, nor does he practice meditation;
he neither invites [others] with sweet words nor indeed acts [thus] from his heart. (81)
One should not feed him sweet food, nor should one give him sweet drink;
one should never mix honey with him, for he does not truly mingle even in solitude. (82)

One should not touch [a woman] for the sake of pleasure, nor should one even remember her in a pure place; one should not inquire about the state of a householder's wife, nor should one delight the mind [with such thoughts]. (83)
Of what use is such a husband in this world? His birth upon earth is in vain.
Therefore, O Goddess, you must protect me, even though I am established in detachment. (84)
"By you alone shall my state as a householder be made manifest in every way;
for by you, having previously performed penance, the value of my person has been increased. (85)
By you, having burned the body of Satī, my divinity was enhanced;
likewise, by slaying the Daityas, your preeminence as my lord was manifested. (86)
O Goddess, by giving me the two sons Gaṇa and Skanda, you have made me worthy of worship;
through you alone, O Goddess, I have attained the state of a householder in heaven and liberation even in the forest.
"O Goddess, by you alone have the holy places been established on earth today;
we shall now go to our own Kailāsa—tell me, what more remains? (88)
"O daughter of Himavat, tell me whatever pleases you; I shall fulfill your desire.
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, became silent. (89)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the Arbuda Tīrtha has been described to you;
it removes the heat of sin, grants liberation, and is supremely conducive to peace.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Origins and Legends of Caṇḍikā-tīrtha, Jāhnavī-kuṇḍa, Acaleśvara, Bhīma-tīrtha, Kulasantāraṇa-tīrtha, Paraśurāma-tīrtha, Brahma-pada-tīrtha, Tripuṣkara, Sāvitrī-kuṇḍa, and Nimita-tīrtha on Arbuda Mountain, along with Śiva’s Praise of Satī," in the first section concerning the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; having visited the holy sites on Arbuda, Śaṅkara and the others traveled through the sky in celestial chariots, beholding the surface of the earth and other regions.
And Satī, having seen the beautiful Ṛkṣaparvata, bowed to Śaṅkara and asked: "What mountain is this that shines forth? || 2 ||
Śambhu said: "This great mountain named Ṛkṣa stands here, where indeed dwell the sages, ascetics, and forest-dwellers."
"I dwell here in this Ṛkṣaka mountain together with you, known by the name Oṃkāra.
Upon hearing this, Pārvatī spoke again to Śambhu on that spot of earth: || 4 ||
Tell me, how many mountains from the Himalayas down to the ocean have you as their refuge, and how many rivers? (5)
Śambhu said: "Listen, O daughter of Himavat; here are the seven principal mountain ranges:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and Ṛkṣaparvata."
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these indeed are the principal mountain ranges;
others, however, are Mandara, Śāra, Kailāsa, and likewise Dardura.
Maināka, Vaidyuta, Vāraṇdhama, Pāṇḍuraka, Tuṅgaprastha, Kṛṣṇagiri, Jayanta, and Ṛṣyamūka; || 8 ||
Airāvata, Gomanta, Citrakūṭa, Śrīparvata, Cakorakūṭa, Śrīśaila, Śatruñjita, and Kṛtasmara. || 9 ||
