The Raivata mountain, Baradāda, Śāla, Mālā,
and others also exist as purifying sacred sites, auspicious lands that grant liberation.
"The great Himācala, possessing ten thousand peaks, stands as your father;
hear now of those rivers which have issued forth from him, who are your sisters. (11)
The Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Śatadru, Vitastā, and Sarasvatī; the Vipāśā, Candrabhāgā, Sarayū, and likewise the Yamunā. || 12 ||
The Irāvatī, the Devikā, the Kuhū, the Gomatī, the Bāhudā, the Dhūtapāpā, the Dṛṣadvatī, the Niścīrā, and likewise the Kauśikī. || 13 ||
The Cakṣuṣmatī, Gaṇḍakī, Lohitā, and Brahmaputraka—those merit-purifying rivers flowed toward the ocean according to their natural incline. || 14 ||
And listen also, O beautiful one, to those originating from the Pāriyātra mountains:
the Vedasmṛti, the Vedavatī, the Sindhuparṇā, and the Carmaṇvatī. || 15 ||
Candranābhā, Rohipārā, Nāśadā, Ācāranāmikā,
Vedatrayī, Vidiśā, and Vapantī— these are the rivers that flow into the ocean.
Listen now to the auspicious and purifying rivers born from the bears:
the Śoṇa, the Jyotīrathā, the Narmadā, and likewise the Surasā. || 17 ||
The Mandākinī, the Daśārṇā, the Tamasā, and likewise the Pippalā;
the Citrakūṭā, the Karatoyā, the Citrotpallā, and the Piśācikā. || 18 ||
Viśālā, Vaṃjukā, Vāluvāhinī, Virajā,
Śuktimatī, Paṅkinī, and Rātrī— these were the daughters of Ṛkṣa.
And hear now of those that arise from the foot of the Vindhya mountains, which destroy all sins:
the auspicious Tāpī, the Payoṣṇī, the Maṇijālā, and the Kumudvatī.
The Veṇṇā, the Pāśā, the Vaitaraṇī, the Śīghrā, the Antyā, the Girā, as well as the Durgā, the Toyā, the Vaidipālā, and those born from the Vindhya mountain.
Now hear also of the rivers flowing to the ocean that arise from the foothills of the Sahya mountains:
the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇā, Veṇī, and Vañjulā.
The Tuṅgabhadrā, the Suprayogā, and the Bāhyakāverī are remembered [as such];
as are the rivers born from the Malaya mountain, the Tāmraparṇī and the Utpalāvatī. (23)
Puṣpāvatī, Śatamālā, and these rivers flowing to the ocean; Mahendratanayā, Triyāmā, and likewise Ikṣulā. (24)
The rivers are Ṛṣikulyā, Trivindālā, Vaṃśavarā, Mūlinī, Śuktimatī, Palāśinī, and Lūtāsī. (25)
The Ṛṣikā and the Mandagāmā, as well as those flowing to the ocean—these are the greatest rivers, as are the Gomatī and the Bhadrikā. (26)
The Ojasvatī, Svarṇarekhā, Nāganadī, and Devikā; the Sābhramatī, Hiraṇyā, Nyaṅkumatī, and Śatruñjitā. ||27||
Manoramā, Candrakalā, Nārāyaṇī, and Māheśvarī—these and others indeed become destroyers of sin and bestowers of liberation. ||28||
Having heard this, Satī then spoke further to Śambhu:
"O Lord, tell me, among these [energies], where do you abide in embodied form? (29)
Śambhu said: "I abide in the Revā in the form of a Liṅga;
it is my established doctrine that all the servants of Narmadā are Śaṅkaras."
Pārvatī said: "A desire arises in me to see the banks of the Narmadā;
show me the Revā, for it is from there that she emerged. (3.1)
"O Śiva, show me everything where she has entered into the ocean.
"So be it," Hara said, and he then descended into the constellation Ṛkṣa.
Accompanied by Pārvatī and likewise by tens of millions of his own attendants,
Śambhu descended right there at the spot from which the Revā had issued forth.
On Mount Ṛkṣa, they all stayed overnight, bathed, and rested;
they drank water and took their meals, and then they proceeded toward Pārvatī.
In the midst of the assembly of the Gaṇas, he questioned Śaṅkara:
"Tell me truly about the origin of the Revā as well as its sacred fords (tīrthas).
Śaṅkara then proclaimed the descent of the Narmadā.
Listen, O daughter of Himavat, in former times there was a great Daitya named Hiraṇyakaśipu.
He oppressed the gods and others; the gods went to Nārāyaṇa and informed Viṣṇu of the most terrible suffering caused by the Daityas. (37)
Viṣṇu, in the form of Nṛsiṃha, slew the lord of the Dānavas;
thereafter, at the request of the gods, this [mantra] was taken from the abode of Hari for the sake of purification.
From Vaikuṇṭha, the purifying form of Revā, possessing a divine nature,
descended— she who is a divine maidservant and a devoted attendant of Nārāyaṇa.
Having herself become the form of water, she arrived together with the gods;
indeed, she remained in the celestial realm of heaven for many years.
Then there was a king on earth named Hiraṇyatejas;
born of the Lunar dynasty, he once went to the forest for the sake of ascetic penance.
At the command of the Brahmins, he went forth and performed intense penance for the sake of pleasing Mahādeva and for the welfare of embodied beings. 42.
Then, for the purpose of bringing [the image] to the earth of the Narmadā, that lord of men,
the king, beheld Mahādeva face to face.
He chose as his boon the auspicious descent of the Narmadā upon the earth, so that there might be the deliverance of all embodied beings. (44)
Śambhu said, "Let it be so; you have deliberated correctly.
He then remembered Narmadā, and she indeed appeared before Śaṅkara.
Śambhu said: "Go to the earth, O Revā, for the sake of liberation;
there, become the bestower of welfare upon people and the destroyer of sins. (46)
Revā said, "O Śaṅkara, being without support, where shall I stay?
Śambhu replied, "There stands a mountain named Udayācala. (47)
"He is capable of supporting you; therefore, descend upon his peak, my dear. Thereupon, Narmadā descended slowly from heaven.
Hiraṇyatejas then gratified the ancestors, beginning with his father and grandfather, with water; he indeed offered them water libations with sesame seeds.
All the ancestors were uplifted and went to heaven and liberation;
thus, this place is purified at every step by the waters of the Narmadā.
This very Narmadā is now being described, she who flows through seven kalpas;
those regions, those mountains, those villages, and even those hermitages are meritorious. 5.1.
Where the Narmadā, the best of rivers, flows for seven kalpas, there the merit of the Sarasvatī is attained in three days, and that of the Yamunā in seven days. (52)
The Gaṅgā purifies instantly, while the Narmadā purifies by mere sight;
and those trees on the banks of the Revā that have fallen with the passage of time [attain the same merit]. (53)
Touched by the waters of the Narmadā—whether at any confluence of the Revā or even upon its banks—they attain the supreme goal. (54)

Bathing, giving gifts, chanting, burnt offerings, self-study of scripture, worship of the ancestors, devotion to the deity, the great initiation, the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), and the relinquishing of the body. ||55||
Whatever [merit] there may be for human beings that yields infinite fruit,
that is bestowed as the fruit of a horse-sacrifice at the Mūlatīrtha on the Narmadā.
By bathing at the Revā-tīrtha, one shall uplift a hundred future generations and a hundred past generations of one's family, along with oneself. (57)
By the giver of land here, the attainment of a kingdom is surely obtained;
as is [the merit] from drinking the water of the Narmadā, bathing in it, and beholding it. 58.
Moreover, there is indeed a fruit greater than that of a hundred *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts for one who remembers the holy Narmadā in the morning; such a person shall attain liberation.
And that [goddess] who was situated on the mountain of sunrise, he brought back down to the earth;
he was the royal sage named Purūravas, who was born in the Lunar dynasty.
He made Candrapurī a great empire over which he was sovereign;
his subjects were free from affliction and devoid of poverty.
The people were long-lived, and the cows yielded all desires;
both men and women were adorned in garments of silk and fine cloth.
From tree to tree flowed streams of nectar, and the earth was rich with crops;
when the kingdom had been thus established by the king, everything indeed became filled with success.
During that solar eclipse, he gave away in abundance as gifts elephants, horses, cattle, houses, gold, silver, and jewels. (64)
The king also gratified the ancestors with offerings to the gods and the manes;
hear now of that wonder which occurred when the ancestors appeared before the king.
The ancestors are seen drinking water with great difficulty, their throats, palates, and lips parched by hunger, and they are defiled by the mud and water. (66)
Seeing them by the hundreds and thousands, naked and clad in soiled garments, King Purūravas bowed to his ancestors and spoke.
Who are you, with such deformed appearances, like hungry ghosts (preta) and spirits (bhūta), who are famished? Tell me so that there may be liberation from this state of being a preta.
The ancestors, however, said to the king: "We are indeed your forefathers;
this field is currently devoid of truth and abandoned by righteous deeds. (69)
"Indeed, there is no liberation without a sacred ford (tīrtha), and such a ford exists on these lands.
Having said this, they departed toward the southern direction, and the king likewise at that very moment.
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his son, he went to the Udaya mountain,
subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, and devoted himself to the worship of Śiva.
He offered supreme devotion, and Maheśvara, pleased by it,
became manifest before him and said to that king, "O King, choose a boon."
The king chose the glorious river Narmadā, which flows for seven kalpas, and said:
"For the sake of delivering my ancestors, please cause her to descend upon the earth. (73)
The river Narmadā was summoned by Śambhu for the sake of pleasing his devotees;
she had mounted the seat of a crocodile and was adorned with divine ornaments. (74)
A radiant young maiden, born from the body of Nārāyaṇa, endowed with every auspicious fortune and beautiful with dark locks of hair. (75)
Having arrived and bowed to Śaṅkara, she asked, "How indeed have you remembered me?
Śiva said, "Indeed, for your sake, [I have composed] fourteen thousand [verses]."
King Hiraṇyataijasa performed austerities for twelve years;
O King, you too must indeed go to Ṛkṣādri out of devotion for the sake of liberating your father.
"Deliver all my ancestors, who have the forms of pretas and dwell in hell!
Having spoken thus, Revā departed for the Ṛkṣādri mountain by way of the sky.
Śambhu gave her that foremost and very firm Ṛkṣaparvata;
Revā, falling from the sky, descended upon the mountain.
That royal sage Purūravas then spoke thus to Narmadā:
"O Goddess, you have bestowed a favor upon me for the sake of the deliverance of my ancestors."
Then, having bathed there in the river, the king thoroughly gratified the gods with libations;
he likewise satisfied the ancestors by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and other offerings.
All have been rescued from hell and established on the path of the gods—
those who are worms, insects, moths, and the like, as well as birds and those born from eggs.
And this incarnation occurred again in the first kalpa, during the Kṛta Yuga;
thus was she, the virtuous one born from the left side of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 83.
The maiden, the goddess Śrī Narmadā, was brought to heaven by the gods;
from heaven, she was led to Mount Udayaśikhara by Hiraṇyatejas.
And Purūravas led [the river] from the mountain of sunrise to the mountain of the stars;
having reached that region of the earth, she became the purifying one who flows to the ocean. 85.
Through bathing, immersion, drinking, remembering, and even chanting [the name], every terrible sin born of many lifetimes is utterly destroyed. (86)
Then, when the first Kali age had arrived, at the end of five thousand solar years, all the rivers likewise went back to heaven once again.
When the Kṛta age had arrived, the powerful King Purukutsa performed austerities once again for the purpose of bringing down the Narmadā. (88)
Being pleased, I granted him a boon;
thereupon, being remembered by him, Revā arrived on earth at my command.
She descended upon the lovely Paryaṅka mountain into a thicket of bamboo;
emerging from the couch with great speed, she flowed toward the western quarter and entered the ocean.
Having made Purukutsa her husband, she was raised from a curse by him;
thus purified, she exists in the world as a staircase to heaven. (91)
Even those in the world who delight in unrighteousness, if they die on the Narmadā,
they too attain the state of Rudra through contact with the waters of the Revā.
There, at the root of the bamboo, stands the god Vaiṇyeśvara;
that is indeed the primordial and supreme holy site (tīrtha), which destroys sin and suffering. (93)
To the north of Revodgama lies the excellent city of Anantapura;
it consists of the hermitages of sages and is divine, eternally bestowing liberation. (94)
In ancient times, there was always the supreme, purifying hermitage of Vyāsa at that place;
it exists as a supreme Śaiva field, an eternal and auspicious holy site (tīrtha). 95.
And where Mādhava, named Utpalāvarta, resides—there Viṣṇu, possessing a thousand heads, dwells upon that purifying ground. 96.
The sacred field of Hari along the Narmadā is proclaimed to extend for one krośa;
on the northern bank of the Revā is the supreme Kapilātīrtha. (97)
The Tripurī Tīrtha is located here, where Śaṅkara dwells assuming that very form;
it extends for a distance of two krośas and is auspicious, bestowing the heavenly realm. 98.
Having utterly destroyed Tripura, Hara rested for a moment at that purifying holy site, which bestows heaven and liberation merely by bathing there. 99.
Thus Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī, whose companion is the Narmadā:
"O Lakṣmī, that which was previously spoken by me is indeed desired by your mind. (1.556.10)

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of King Purūravas’s Deliverance of His Ancestors through the Descent of Revā," within the historical accounts of Veṇutīrtha, Anantapuratīrtha, and others, concerning the descent of Narmadā from the world of Brahmā to the Eastern Mountain (Udayācala), thence to Ṛkṣādri, and finally her appearance upon the surface of the earth, in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; thereafter Śambhu spoke this purifying narrative to Pārvatī, which I shall relate to you concerning the Kṛta Yuga in that primordial kalpa.
There was a king named Manu, of the solar dynasty and possessed of great strength;
at that time, his city Sāketa was the preeminent one on earth.
Because she could not be slain by the Dānavas, she became known by the name Avadhyā;
it was richly protected by seven walls and possessed seven circular moats.
Extending ten yojanas along the course of the Sarayū river,
he ruled over the earth divided into nine regions, remaining devoted to the vow of having only one beloved wife.
Once, that great king addressed Vasiṣṭha:
"A sacrifice must be performed by me in a remote forest region. (5)
"Show me such a purifying place as you please.
Having heard that, Vasiṣṭha also took the consent of the brahmins.
"In the forest on Mount Ṛkṣa, from which the Revā flows,
perform the sacrifice there, O King"— thus he gave the command in the past.
Having gone there, he performed the great horse-sacrifice (hayamedha);
that lord of the earth bestowed land, cattle, gold, and jewels at the sacrifice.
Devoted to sacrifice, the king had a pavilion constructed on the bank of the Revā, extending for ten yojanas, for the purpose of the sacrificial rites.
Having summoned all the deities, including Indra,
the subduer of Pāka, he gratified them with offerings of water for the feet (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), honey-mixtures (madhuparka), and seats (viṣṭara).
He gratified the Brahmins and the virtuous with food and other offerings,
as well as with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and various ornaments for the neck.
Whether gathered in dining halls or even in rows, birds and other fowl, or insects wandering in the forest— 12.
All those who had wallowed in the remnants of the sacrifice became golden;
thus was that great sacrifice brought to completion on the bank of the Narmadā.
Praised at the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), the wealthy river attained satisfaction from the king:
"You have become a staircase to heaven for the ancestors, bringing about their liberation. (14)
O destroyer of the sins of all worlds, O most venerable mother, O great virtuous one, O dispeller of the heat of sin, lead me to heaven! 15.
Having heard the hymn of King Manu, that illustrious goddess,
seated upon her crocodile-throne, was pleased and then replied to the king.
Richly adorned with all ornaments, her face resembling the luster of the moon, she appeared in the form of a maiden and, filled with laughter, said: "Choose a boon desired in your heart. (17)

The king said: "O virtuous one, you are always in this world the form of a sacred ford (tīrtha) that delivers others; therefore, O auspicious lady, deliver us here at this holy site, the ground of sacrifice."
"May rivers that carry you across dwell likewise in my kingdom for eternal ages, for the sake of the welfare of the subjects. (19)
And come with me in another form, O Narmadā;
dwell together with me on the Sarayū in the city of Sāketa.
Saying "So be it," Revā departed for him in another form;
she then dwelt in the city of Sāketa at the Revā-kuṇḍa.
On the sacrificial ground is a great holy site, the place of sacrifice at Ṛkṣaka;
by bathing there, embodied beings endowed with merit go to heaven.
Now the Blessed Viṣṇu resides at the most purifying Brahmakuṇḍa;
having bathed here where the Revā flows northward, one shall attain liberation.
Beyond that lies Haṃsatīrtha, where the swans departed for heaven;
and further ahead is Siddhatīrtha, where the perfected ascetics dwell.
Then follows the auspicious confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the waters of the Revā;
in ancient times, the sage Mataṅga summoned both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
Then, at the very dawn, for the sake of the ablutions of the great sages,
the personified Gaṅgā and Yamunā arrived at the water.
The auspicious holy ford (tīrtha) consisting of the triple confluence (Trisaṅgama) became the form of water;
then there was the beautiful Yogatīrtha, as well as the supreme Ṛkṣeśvara.
There exists a sacred ford named Āpsarasa, which wards off curses.
Formerly, in the assembly of Indra, the Apsarases performed a dance. (28)
Kāma himself, assuming a supreme form, arrived there;
seeing him then, the dancers were struck with wonder and became infatuated. (29)
They forgot the rules of rhythm, song, and melody, as well as the sequences of dance;
then Indra became greatly enraged and cursed those dancers.
Campakā, Sīmapranāmā, Keśinī, and Bhāminī; Kaumudī, Suprabhā, as well as Utpalā, Mahodayā, and Asimā. ||3.1||
The world-protectors and the lords shine here in this assembly;
they have attained their prowess through negligence, like a dance performed upon one's own limbs. (32)
Then let them go to the womb of a Niṣāda; for that training is indeed sufficient.
Then, having bathed repeatedly in the Narmadā during the Kumbha conjunction, ||33||
On the third day of the month of Māgha, remaining without food and without water,
you shall worship Gaurī and Śambhu, and you will regain heaven once more.
Thus addressed, those Niṣāda women likewise acted; having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, they attained liberation at that very sacred ford known as Apsaras.
Then, at that supreme holy ford where the Anadī river meets the Revā,
he bathed and worshipped Keśava.
Having shaken off all sins, one goes to the supreme abode of Śrī Hari;
thereafter, the holy site named Gāñjālabheda, which grants liberation, should be visited.
In the lunar dynasty there was a king renowned as Devānīka;
his son was the universal monarch (cakravartin) known by the name Harikeśa. (38)
His supreme capital was Kanyāpura;
there, on the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā, he performed many sacrifices.
Harikeśa gave a gift of one hundred thousand milch cows during a solar eclipse, and he gave a thousand gold coins to each Brahmin.
Then, for the sake of Vijaya’s mastery of Vedic knowledge, he again convened a great assembly of Brahmins there. (41)
To whoever might be victorious there, [this] cow with a single calf shall be given—she who yields milk, enriched with ornaments of gold and beautifully adorned with a necklace of diamonds. (42)
Having resolved that it must be given, the king indeed posed this question:
"In this conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun, what is the fruit of bathing at Prayāga? (43)
Is bathing born of *prārabdha* (the momentum of past actions), or does it occur even without *prārabdha*?
What indeed is the primary cause, and what might be the instrumental factor? ||44||
The ground of Prayāga is not present here, nor is there contact with that soil; how then could the fruit born of it arise? Without a cause, there can be no production. (45)
When this question was posed by the king, some of the learned sages then said that it was merely an explanatory statement (arthavāda) intended to convey praise.
Others say that without the ground of Prayāga, that fruit is not attained;
and others then say that the fruit is equal to that of Prayāga.
Others have declared that bathing is equal to bathing at Prayāga;
others say it is the bathing born of *prārabdha* karma, while still others say it occurs even in the absence of *prārabdha*.
Through diligent effort, bathing indeed becomes meritorious even without [external] means;
however, the primary cause therein is the desire for liberation or the desire for enjoyment. (49)
Desire is the primary cause, whatever it may be;
the caravan leader also acts as its stimulator.
The motivating inquiry, however, arises repeatedly from the scripture;
yet, the cause for application to the scripture is always considered to be the grace of the guru. (51)
Such would be the causes, possessing distinct forms;
thus has this debate proceeded, yet it has not been resolved by anyone. (52)
But the primary cause therein is that which resides in the heart, bestowing merit;
it has been forgotten that the Supreme Brahman Himself is the giver of the fruit. (53)
Consequently, no one then won the golden cow;
and even though the dispute proceeded for the sake of victory, no decision was reached. ||54||
And during the dispute among the Brahmins, there was a certain priest there named Raudrāyaṇa, a knower of the Atharva-mantras who acted as the challenger.
Even though a dispute arose, he did not obtain victory at all;
enraged, the king had him cast into the fire at that very moment.
By the king performing a fire sacrifice with fierce and highly potent mantras while ignorant [of the proper rites],
the [deity] became as brilliant as the fire at the end of an eon.
Fire rose from that sacrificial pit, terrifying with its garlands of flames;
by it the pavilion was indeed consumed, as were the men situated within the pavilion.
Likewise, another [body] has been reduced to ashes, along with the various objects that constituted the causal complex.
Regarding this, the king said: "For me, there is atonement for the elephants who have been burnt. (59)
"O Brahmins, let it be given in such a way that I may practice it; I shall perform it.
Then the Brahmins said, "Go indeed to Kalpagrāma."
"The sages, Bhṛgu and the others, should be questioned by you regarding the means of atonement there.
Having been addressed thus, the king went on foot to Sukalpa.
Having bowed down to the great sages, he indeed engaged them in conversation;
then he reported the terrible sin of slaughter committed during the sacrifice.
Having heard that, the sages said: "O King, recite the Gāyatrī one million times;
go from sacred ford to sacred ford until you reach the sixty-eighth."
Bestow gifts of cattle and gold, and likewise perform ten thousand fire-offerings;
give to virtuous Brahmins sacrificial fees of hundreds and thousands.
In this way, there shall be liberation from sin; perform pilgrimages to sacred fords with devotion.
For those who have died and been consumed by fire, the carrying away of their bones [is prescribed]. 65.
O King, perform [this] on the Narmadā; by that, liberation will be attained.
Through contact with the waters of the Narmadā, one attains the state of a deity in heaven.
By the offering of water with sesame seeds, their liberation will certainly be attained;
and on the beautiful bank of the Narmadā, they performed an auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
"Furthermore, practice that by which liberation will become possible.
Thus addressed, that royal sage [proceeded] once more toward the illustrious Narmadā.
He went to the sacrifice and performed a libation there on that auspicious bank;
the stream emerged there and entered the Narmadā. ||69||
He became renowned as Gāñjāli at the confluence of the Narmadā;
there, the ancestors who had been cremated by Harikeśa were restored to life.
Having all been delivered there, they were satisfied and then said to the king:
"O highly fortunate one, by your grace we have attained the state of gods. (71)
"Mounted upon the divine vehicle, we shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having heard this, King Harikeśa was filled with supreme joy. (72)
Having bowed to Revā, who remains steadfast for seven kalpas, he then offered this praise:
"Salutations to you, O best of rivers, who dwell for seven kalpas! (73)
Having bathed in you, O Great Goddess, people everywhere attain liberation;
by your grace, liberation from the ocean of worldly existence has been achieved.
"O victorious, compassionate Goddess! [Save] the ancestors who have been consumed by fire!
Hearing those words, Narmadā became a maiden in embodied form. (75)
"Choose a boon," she said to the king; then the king chose a boon:
"O virtuous one, O purifier, if you are a granter of boons to me, make me pure. (76)
Through bathing, immersion, drinking, remembering, and even chanting [the name], may the sin committed during seven lifetimes perish instantly. (77)
Revā said, "So be it," and then she vanished;
and Harikeśa, the universal monarch, having bowed again toward that direction, [departed].
Mounting a swift vehicle, he went to the city of Sāketa;
that auspicious Narmadā tīrtha destroys the sin of killing and bestows liberation.
And Harikeśa and Gāñjāla, which destroy the sin of killing;
they are auspicious, bestowing wealth, fame, long life, enjoyment, and liberation.
Now, in the southern direction, there is a sacred ford named Vālukaśāṅkara, where the confluence of the Kanyā and the Narmadā occurred, which indeed bestows liberation. ||81||
And further ahead, the sacred site named Pūrṇamanoratha is described;
formerly, Harivarmā was the sovereign of the city of Virāṭa.
He performed a sacrifice there and bestowed a hundred thousand cows;
the gods were well-satisfied there, and the Brahmins and the virtuous were honored.
Furthermore, there is another excellent sacred site, the confluence of the Revā and the Matsya, where the waters are pure and always bestow liberation through drinking and bathing. 84.
On the northern bank of the Revā, beyond the confluence with the Kapilā,
lies Narmadāpura, where there are brahmins who are ascetics.
Indeed, millions [of such sites] shine forth near the hermitage of Jamadagni;
there, Jamadagni performed most fierce ascetic penance dedicated to Śaṅkara. 86.
Śiva appeared before him in person and said to him, "Choose a boon.
The sage chose the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), and she arrived there from Goloka.
For the sake of righteous deeds, auspicious purposes, the worship of Śiva, the excellent libations, rites for the ancestors, and rites for the gods, cows are always most meritorious. (88)
And from the wish-fulfilling cow,
Jamadagni obtained all his desires in the form of dharma, as well as the granting of prosperity and the granting of heaven.
That twice-born one of great fame constantly fed thousands of sages; at that time, the earth was pervaded by the renown of Jamadagni because of his cows.
The daughter of the Daitya named Vipracitti was Māhiṣmatī;
after her name, he constructed the city of Māhiṣmatī. (91)
In whose presence Jamadagni had indeed dwelt in the great forest,
she went through the sky with her female companions to visit Mount Mandara.
There she saw an ascetic who was glowing with heat and known by the name Asva;
having seen that delightful hermitage, the beautiful woman began to reflect. (93)
Having terrified him, I myself remain here in this hermitage;
she too, assuming any form at will, dwells among those who live in the forest.
Having gone into the presence of the sages while assuming the form of a buffalo, she was indeed cursed by the sages to remain as a buffalo for a hundred years. (95)
"Having obtained Mahiṣa as a son, you shall then become well again.
Having been cursed thus, she departed for the excellent Narmadā-tīrtha. 96.
There, the great ascetic Sindhudvīpa performed severe penance;
indeed, his virility spilled onto the surface of a stone slab.
Then that queen drank that fragrant water mixed with water;
subsequently, she gave birth to a firm son born from the seed of the Brahmin. 98.
Because the great power Nārāyaṇī, who is Śāṅkarī, slew the cruel asura named Mahiṣa, she thereafter made Māhiṣmatī her own [abode].
Having gone to the city of Māhiṣmatī near the hermitage of Jamadagni,
she died in due time and, by the power of the sage, attained heaven.
That most beautiful Tīrtha of Jamadagni, Māhiṣmata, and Viśokairaṇḍikā is considered the third purifier. (101)
The fourth is Narmadā; at their confluence lies the Kapilā stone, a most meritorious sacred site (tīrtha) where, by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), [great rewards are obtained].
The ancestors attain liberation, having been delivered by Paraśurāma.
This has been told to you, O Lakṣmī, as it was spoken by Satyaśiva in the past. (103)
By hearing and chanting this, the state of divinity is attained in heaven;
even liberation and worldly enjoyment are obtained in the auspicious hermitage of Jamadagnya.

Thus, in the first section on the lineage of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, the five hundred and fifty-seventh chapter—titled "The Description of the Sacred Sites with Their Origins," including Manu’s Sacrificial Tīrtha on Mount Ṛkṣa, Viṣṇu-Brahma Kuṇḍa, Haṃsa Tīrtha, Trisaṃgama Yoga Tīrtha, Āpsarasa Tīrtha, the Confluence of Dattātreya, Gāṃjālabheda Tīrtha, Vāluka, Pūrṇamanoratha Tīrtha, the Confluence of Kanyā and Narmadā, Matsyāsaṃgama, Narmadāpura, Jāmadagnya Tīrtha, and others—is concluded. || 557 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to what was spoken by Mahādeva to Pārvatī;
I shall describe to you another sacred ford (tīrtha) located on the Narmadā.
Likewise, the confluence of the Matsyā and the Tāpyā bestows liberation.
Formerly, there was a celestial sage named Kalahaṃsa who was devoted to meditation. || 2 ||
Having established a delightful hermitage there, he performed most rigorous penance;
subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he remained standing on one foot.
While he was devoted to the meditation on Śiva, the King of the Gods himself, fearing his ascetic power, arrived in the guise of a brahmin to deceive him. || 4 ||
He said, "O Kalahaṃsa, for what purpose do you perform penance?
The sage replied, "And how is it, O Indra, that you mock me, a twice-born brahmin? (5)
I know you to be Turāṣāṭ; I do not desire the kingdom of Indra.
I am propitiating Śambhu; rule the kingdom as you wish.
Indra said, "O Brahmin, choose a boon; you shall behold Śaṅkara.
Then Kalahaṃsa replied, "I choose no other boon."
"If you are able, grant me this: may I always possess devotion toward Śambhu. "So be it," said the Lord of the Gods, and having spoken, he departed for heaven.
Then Śaṅkara himself quickly arrived there laughing; Kalahaṃsa prostrated before him and began to offer praise. || 9 ||
Salutations to you, O Mahādeva, endowed with compassion for your devotees; salutations be to you! Salutations to Śiva, the bestower of desired boons upon his devotees; salutations to you!
Salutations to you, the deliverer of those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence;
salutations to you, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, the foremost among the Vaiṣṇavas. || 11 ||
Oṃ, salutations to you who are the very self of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;

O King, a tenth part of that resides in you, and from that comes this drought. (92)
Therefore, O King, punish them and cause them to undergo the obstruction of their ascetic power;
furthermore, perform a great sacrifice in the sacred field of the Narmadā.
By that [act], rain will surely fall everywhere; of this there is no doubt.
You shall be released from the fault of sin and attain the kingdom and heaven. (94)
Having heard this, the king gave orders to his servants for the preparation of the necessary materials, so that the sacrifice might proceed within seven nights. (95)
The king, the subjects, the ministers, and the princes;
the sages, the ascetics, the brahmins, the queens, the gods, and the lords of the gods. ||96||
Invited there to the bank of the Revā, they arrived;
he then bestowed gold coins numbering in the hundreds of millions.
The king made gifts of ten million cows, elephants, horses, and so forth;
there were great pillars made of gold, and even the sacrificial ladles and other implements were of gold. (98)
In that region, there existed foods and drinks of unprecedented flavors, endowed with divine essences;
then Viṣṇu himself arrived there in person. ||99||
Rudra, Agni himself, Brahmā, and their respective goddesses arrived;
the sacrifice was completed in its entirety with the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the waters of the Narmadā.
They all performed [the rites], and a great rain fell upon the circle of the earth;
the gods and others were honored by the king, and the Brahmins were fully gratified. ||101||
Such was that auspicious Narmadā tirtha, fit for sacrifice and of great magnitude.
O ascetics, they were thus restrained from their austerities by the king.
And because those who were Cāṇḍālas performed penance, rain occurred;
having thus completed the sacrifice, they went each to his own abode.
From that time on, that sacred ford is indeed called Yajñatīrtha;
thus did Śaṅkara speak to Pārvatī concerning the circle of sacred fords.
And I have declared to you, O Lakṣmī, that which destroys sin and suffering.
Through both reciting and hearing [this], the water of the Narmadā bestows liberation.

Thus ends the five hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Miraculous Description of Śāṇḍilyākalpa-tīrtha, Rantideva-tīrtha, Harikeśa-tīrtha, Ambarīṣa-tīrtha, Bilvāmraka-tīrtha, Sālaṅkāyana-tīrtha, and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to those other holy places which were described by Śambhu to Pārvatī; I shall recount them to you in brief.
Formerly, at Camatkārapura on the bank of the Nāga river, there lived a certain sage named Aruṇi;
at that time, a hunter arrived there.
Through the yoga of the sage, Vyādha became pure-minded and practiced asceticism;
having attained the status of a twice-born by his actions, he indeed became known by the name Satyatapas.
But Satyatapas, having been joined with a blessing by Durvāsas,
went to the confluence of the Kubjā and the Narmadā for the purpose of bathing.
Having bathed and drunk the water, he, endowed with merit, went to the Himalaya mountain,
to the northern foot of the Himavat on the bank of the river Puṣpabhadrā.
Having occupied a variegated stone slab in the vicinity of a noble banyan tree,
he performed penance there as well, while devotedly worshipping Śrī Narāyaṇa.
Once, it is said, he was cutting firewood with an axe;
then, he cut off one of his fingers, specifically the left index finger.
The ash and powder fell away, leaving neither flesh nor blood;
by that act, his finger was restored as it had been before.
This marvel was witnessed by a single Kinnara who was traveling through the sky;
from there, that Kinnara went to heaven.
Having gone to the assembly of Indra, an unprecedented marvel was recounted—
namely, that wonder shown by the ascetic which was witnessed by me.
On the bank of the Puṣpabhadrā river lived an ascetic named Satyatapas;
his body was withered by penance, and only ashes remained upon his frame.
Having heard that, Śukra immediately spoke to his younger brother Viṣṇu:
"Come, O Viṣṇu, let us go to the excellent side of the Himavat."
"In that regard, a wonderful and unprecedented account was indeed told to me by the Kinnara.
Having been addressed thus, Viṣṇu then assumed the form of a boar.
The hunter and Indra likewise went toward that sage;
Viṣṇu, in the form of a boar, stood within the range of the sage's vision.
Having become visible, he became invisible again, and then he was seen once more;
meanwhile, Indra stood in the forest with bow in hand, holding sharp arrows.
Having arrived, he spoke to this sage Satyatapas:
"O Blessed One, have you seen here that vast and great boar?"
"O great sage, I shall kill him for the sake of supporting my servants.
Upon hearing this, the sage was struck with alarm and reflected on it instantly.
If I show him that boar, he will kill it;
otherwise, there is no doubt that his family will perish from hunger. (18)
In either case, sin will surely be mine; of this there is no doubt.
For the boar has indeed sought refuge in my hermitage for the sake of protection.
For the hunter, having approached me and seen that I am a speaker of truth, [realized]: "The fault in speaking untruth is supreme—the betrayal of trust. (1.560.20)
"Indeed, the injury or defilement of either one brings fear in every way.
This being the case, what more can be said? Then, reflecting thus upon Hari, [he remained silent]. (21)
At that moment, he quickly attained fortitude and steadfastness in the witness;
and in an instant, his noble intellect became protective in nature. ||22||
The eye sees but does not speak; the tongue speaks but does not see. One sees and another speaks; there is no single common function for the two. (23)
"The seer is mute and the speaker is blind; who could provide an answer? Speak!
Having heard this, Indra and Viṣṇu were highly pleased in an instant.
Revealing their true forms, they both spoke these words:
"Speak; we are pleased with you here, so choose one supreme boon."
Having heard that, Satyatapas, his heart filled with joy, said:
"There is no other boon on earth for me greater than the sight of Viṣṇu. (26)
By this, my purpose is fulfilled, for a sight of you is difficult to obtain;
nevertheless, those who are here at the edge of the Vaṭa tree by the waters of the Puṣpabhadrā— 27.
Having bathed, meditated, and remembered Hari, may they dwell there for one month;
may their sins be destroyed, and may you also grant them liberation. (28)
Having said "So be it," those two gods granted him the boon and remained for that very long time, stationed in their celestial chariot upon the path of the sky.
His preceptor Cāruṇi arrived and was seen there;
Durvāsas also arrived, for they had both been summoned by Satya at that time.
Having been honored by Satyatapas, they recognized him as a disciple who had achieved his purpose,
perfected through austerity, and standing before them with his sins consumed by penance.
Āruṇi said: "You have attained perfection; you have become Brahman in every respect.
Now, the time for your liberation is considered to have arrived along with the Self."
"Arise, my son, and come with me to the celestial chariot, together with Nārāyaṇa, Indra, and Durvāsas. (33)
"We shall go to the Narmadā tīrtha and the supreme, auspicious Kubjāmraka.
Having spoken thus, Āruṇi, Ātreya, and Satyatapas—the three of them—[departed].
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, they ascended a beautiful celestial chariot;
and by the desire of his devotees, Nārāyaṇa and even Indra [ascended] the Nārmada.
Having reached the sacred ford worthy of sacrifice and bathed there, they then went to heaven;
thereafter, Satyatapas attained liberation and the supreme state.
Other long-lived beings indeed departed for their respective abodes,
while Durvāsas and the others went to Kailāsa and other such eternal realms.
Now I shall proclaim another sacred ford in the waters of the Narmadā;
for there shines the sacred ford known as Maṇḍapeśvara.
Having bathed there and cast off his body, the king shall undoubtedly dwell in the city of the Vidyādharas for ten thousand years. (39)
Once, King Ajāpāla went to visit the two mind-born sons of Brahmā, Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭa, who were dwelling in the forest.
Having bowed down, the lord of Avadhyā asked the sages in sweet tones:
"Indeed, for the sake of delivering my ancestors, what gift should be given by me here? (41)
"Which sages will accept [the gift]? Let them come into my presence.
Then, with the exception of two—Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭa—[all came]. ||42||
Then others accepted the gifts bestowed by the king:
ten thousand elephants adorned with bells and ornaments. (43)
The king gave wealth to the brahmins and likewise constructed monasteries made of gold;
he then performed three circumambulations of Mount Kalañjara.
Having paid homage to all the sages, he departed toward his own city;
when that protector of the earth had gone, the sages were deluded by wealth. ||45||
Having attained supreme happiness through royal wealth, those kings fell from their asceticism and became indeed attached to sensual enjoyments. 46.
And having died through the exhaustion of their merit—with the exception of Bādara and Śākaṭa—the acceptance of gifts from a king is terrible, fierce, sinful, and fraught with fear. (47)
"Indeed, who would be capable of enduring [this] except for one whose nature is Brahman?
Having become overcome by lust and anger, those Brāhmaṇas then died. (48)
They have entered the womb of dogs and been born as eaters of impurity, because they resided among Brahmins engaged in the acceptance of gifts. (49)
Due to the fault of their association, Bādara and Śākaṭa were born with the faces of dogs;
seeing their dog-like countenances, the two of them reflected:
Thinking, "Indeed, through the fault of association, sin has attached itself to me from accepting a gift from the king," they both went truthfully to the Supreme Lord (Brahmā). (51)
Having saluted him, they spoke with distorted faces regarding their situation;
and having heard it, Brahmā declared that atonement should take place in the waters of the Narmadā.
"Purity shall be attained through bathing; let them go to Maṇḍapeśvara.
Having heard the words of Pitāmaha, Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭa [departed]. (53)
Then, accompanied by the sages, they both went to the Narmadā;
having bathed there and drunk its water, those sinless ones were freed from their sins.
Thus they went to heaven by means of divine vehicles; that is the most excellent tīrtha.
Merely by hearing of it or by reciting its name, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
From there, one should go to the supreme sacred site known as Śvetakiṃśuka;
at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Dantivanikā, one should perform an ablution. (56)
Then one should visit the auspicious Tīrtha known as Kapiśilā;
thereafter, one should proceed to the Śaśabhī-Narmadā-yoga Tīrtha.
From there, one should go to Rājatīrtha, which was frequented by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
in ancient times, having crossed the Narmadā, Rāma departed for the interior of the forest.
From there, one should go to the most auspicious Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha;
from there, one should go to Pipīlikoddhāra Tīrtha, which bestows liberation.
Then one should go to the auspicious confluence of the Vandhyā and Revā;
thereafter, one should go to the excellent Śuklatīrtha, which bestows heaven and liberation.
By bathing at the confluence of the Rāśabhī and the Narmadā, liberation shall certainly be attained.
In a former age, the royal sage Havirdhāna was capable [of this].
Ātreyi had a son named Harikeśa, and Agniputrī had a son named Sutejas; [these two were born] according to the rite of marriage.
Then she, named Sutejas, was given to Havirdhāna;
and the royal sage Havirdhāna, having learned that her season had arrived, went to her.
Once, however, a youth named Harikeśaka arrived there;
out of desire,
he took her hand within the sacrificial fire-chamber, acting according to the dictates of passion.
Harikeśa took his pleasure with her according to his desire.
And he beheld the pair [of Maruts] in the *havirdhāna* shed engaged in sexual union;
his face became dejected, for a Brahmin is indeed inviolable.
"Moreover, his wife is indeed not to be slain, for she belongs to the female species.
Having reflected thus, Havirdhāna spoke slowly to the Brahmin: 67.
Having approached his mother, the wife of his teacher, a sister, or likewise a daughter, a man shall enter the fire; thereby he becomes pure.
Having gone to the teacher and the teacher’s son, a woman would ascend the funeral pyre;
for you two are not capable of doing so. (69)
"O Brahmin, become a donkey with great luster; and you, O daughter, become a female donkey.
Thus, for a hundred years, you two shall be born as donkeys in the forest."
Once, those two, remembering their former births, went to the hermitage of Agastya and asked about a penance and a vow for the sake of ending the curse.
Agastya said, "Go indeed toward the Havirdhāna [hermitage]. Then those two went with respect to the Havirdhāna hermitage.
Having asked for forgiveness, they both then bowed at his feet; and Havirdhāna said to them, "Go indeed to the bank of the Narmadā."
Having bathed and drunk her water, with your sins destroyed by her asceticism, you two shall attain supreme liberation, which is the fruit of human birth. (74)
Thus addressed, they went to the Narmadā and practiced austerities;
having purified themselves, they abandoned their donkey births and became divine beings.
Mounted upon a celestial vehicle (yāna) and adorned with all ornaments,
the two went to heaven and dwelt there for seventy yugas.
Then, at the end, those two went to the glorious abode of Nārāyaṇa;
there is the sacred ford (tīrtha) Harikeśa, which is full of splendor and grants liberation.
At the confluence of the Revā and the Gardabhī lies the Havirdhāneśvara Liṅga,
which is supremely meritorious and destroys sins through its mere sight.
From there, one should go to the Karamarda Tīrtha, which bestows supreme merit.
King Kuśadhvaja arrived at the hermitage of Maitreya on the beautiful bank of the Narmadā; there, with sincere devotion,
he performed a śrāddha ceremony and bestowed ten times ten thousand cows as a gift.
Having fed those brahmins at the śrāddha ceremony with cows that had their calves, were golden-hued, and adorned with bells and ornaments,
that best of kings then departed for his own home, while the brahmins remained there.
Once, when those Rākṣasas had come into the forest to devour the cows,
some of the cows entered the Vārāṇasī reservoir and others then went to heaven;
thereupon, the Rākṣasas rushed toward the Brahmins in that place to eat them.
The brāhmaṇas remembered Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among persons;
Lakṣmīpati, the Lord of Light; Pārvatīśa, Narāyaṇa;
Māṇikīśa, Haṃseśa, and Mañjuleśa, who dwells within the heart.
Just then Viṣṇu arrived, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
With his discus, he destroyed the Rākṣasas like ripe karamarda fruits;
he protected the Brāhmaṇas, and the cows returned there once more.
Śambhu, as Karamardeśvara, emerged from the discus of Viṣṇu;
the sacred site of Karamardeśvara is considered the supreme provider of protection. (87)
Then, after some time, Viṣṇu, having caused the brahmins and the cows to ascend a celestial chariot, led them to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of liberation.
Having bathed there, they go to heaven; and once deceased, they are not subject to rebirth.
"From hearing and even from chanting [this], the fruit of a thousand cows shall be obtained.
Thus Śambhu spoke to Pārvatī; and this has been declared by me before you, O Lakṣmī, as the holy place (tīrtha) of the discus of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of Histories Including the Liberation of Satyatapas, the Disciple of Āruṇi; Maṇḍapeśvara Tīrtha; the Cessation of the Dog-Face Condition of Bādarāyaṇa and Śākaṭāyana; the Confluence of the Narmadā and Dantivani; the Account of the Donkey at the Narmadā Tīrtha; and Karamarda Tīrtha," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; Śaṅkara spoke of a holy place to Pārvatī.
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you that well-known Jvāleśvara.
Then Śaṅkara struck Tripura, the son of Bali, with a shaft, and [discharged] a weapon endowed with garlands of flames.
When the rain of the Kalpa-cow fell, the flames were then extinguished;
that place is indeed called Jvāleśvara, which destroys sinful demons.
Then, the supreme holy site known as Revācarusaṅga shines forth;
formerly, in the sacred field of Naimiṣāraṇya, there was an auspicious city.
Beyond this is the river named Hiraṇyavegā, which is filled with golden seven-storied mansions and accompanied by a city.
And the king named Hiraṇyabāhu indeed desired to perform a sacrifice;
he questioned all the sages in Naimiṣa regarding the sacrificial ground.
They, however, said: "Puṣkara is a great field fit for sacrifice;
whatever is offered or sacrificed there becomes ten million times more meritorious. || 7 ||
The king said, "Let my auspicious sacrifice be performed at Puṣkara.
Thereupon, the royal sage departed for Puṣkara, having gathered all the necessary materials.
There were ten million cows and one hundred and fifty thousand horses;
fifty-two thousand lordly elephants and ten thousand chariots.
The gems, rubies, jewels, garments,
and ornaments were indeed beyond counting, just like the wealth of Kubera.
Eatables, foods, and drinks were served day and night;
consequently, the sacrifice was inaugurated there, where the Creator of the Universe was invited.
At that time, Śukra alone was summoned by the Brahmins, for no other gods were invited;
what need is there for other gods, since everything is accomplished by these two?
Neither Viṣṇu nor the Ādityas, neither the Moon nor Varuṇa; neither Rudra nor the Maruts, nor others belonging to the quarters, nor the world-protectors [are able to protect him]. || 1.3 ||
When the sacrifice had commenced, the asuras— thorns to the gods— who were intent on searching for flaws in the ritual, arrived there to create obstacles.
In every way, the Dānavas, Daityas, Bhūtas, Vetālas, and Rākṣasas drank the Soma, the constituent part of the sacrifice, and they devoured the Brahmins. || 15 ||
The fire was extinguished, the sacrificial post destroyed, and the pavilion demolished;
Brahmā, Śakra, and the other deities beheld this sudden destruction.
Thereupon, having become invisible from that place filled with obstacles,
Hiraṇyabāhu then became enraged toward the Brāhmaṇas.

Indeed, at the sacrifice, the Brahmins, who were like beggars, fled from my sacrifice and abandoned it because they were intent on their own self-interest, having failed to invite the gods, the elders. || 18 ||
Then the Daityas, having gathered their provisions, departed for their homes;
the king, reflecting, thought, "This is not the moment for my personal prowess."
Neither for the sake of anger nor for the sake of war, even when the assembly of gods and others is enraged,
do I go alone, having mounted my horse together with my wife.
Where neither the Ādityas, nor Viṣṇu, nor Rudra, nor the Moon,
nor likewise the other guardians of the quarters are present, how can the sacrifice be successfully accomplished?
The Brahmins are greedy and desire everything; they are not protectors, but rather destroyers born of the root of greed and devoid of power. (22)
If truth exists for me, let the Brahma-rākṣasas become senseless in this thorny, waterless place! (23)
Having heard the curse, the king was indeed cursed from afar by the brahmins:
"O lowest of kṣatriyas, you have failed to protect the sacrifice. (24)
"Become indeed a donkey, a bringer of curses upon sinless Brahmins!
For twelve years in the forest, they became donkey-demons. (25)
Then, after some time had passed in the forest, the divine sage, the seer Nārada, arrived; he saw them as well as Khara and the other Rākṣasas.
Kharo bowed to the divine sage and asked about the cause of liberation;
Nārada then spoke of the excellent water of the Narmadā.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Revā and the Ācarukā, you shall attain liberation;
even the Brāhmaṇas and the Rākṣasas, having bathed there, shall go to salvation.
Having been addressed thus, they went to the Revā at the confluence of the Revā and the Caruka;
having bathed there due to the union with the waters of the Narmadā, they all attained liberation. (29)
Mounted upon the Brahma-vehicle and being praised by bards,
they went to the divine world of Brahmā through the confluence with the waters of the Narmadā.
Where Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Sūrya, and Nārāyaṇa reside, there is Śrī, as well as victory, and eternal enjoyment and liberation. ||31||
Wherever devotion to the guru exists— just as toward the Lord, so toward the guru—
the desires of that person are fulfilled by the power of Hari, who is identical with the guru.
By hearing, chanting, remembering, or even serving this [mantra], and by bowing to it or wearing it, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. //33//
Now, the most excellent holy site is called Amarakaṇṭaka;
from that point onward, the entire best of mountains is remembered as most meritorious. (34)
Indeed, as far as the great river Revā, known by four names, flows together, to the north lies the great, purifying Yajñaparvata mountain. 35.
In ancient times, the Sautrāmaṇi sacrifice was lost there by the Self-born One;
it was indeed at that very place that Maghavan formerly performed the horse-sacrifice.
Dadhīci and the gods performed great sacrifices in that very place;
it extends as far as the confluence of the river and as far as the Sacrificial Mountain (Yajñaparvata).
Indeed, the entire Rajas-tirtha exists as a purifier that bestows liberation;
it is where, in ancient times, the sage Suparṇa, the son of Brahmā, resided.
The learned Puruhūta, an expert in all the scriptures, made his residence at Saṅgama; his wife was Dharmapatnī, a devoted wife faithful to her husband. (39)
On one occasion, however, having propitiated her own husband, she spoke these words:
"O great sage, please unite with me at the proper time when I am in my season. (1.561.40)
May he be born as a son to me, one who purifies his entire lineage;
for through a son, one conquers the worlds, and the ancestors and deities are satisfied. ||41||
"There is no destination for one who has no son; therefore, you have given birth to a son.
Then the Brāhmaṇa said, "But, my dear, the new moon day was omitted [in the calculation]. (42)
"One should not form an attachment here, which would be an obstacle even for the ancestors.
For a thousand divine years, I have performed difficult austerities. (43)
O beloved, I shall strive for you to conceive a child so that such a destruction does not occur on another day; do not grieve. (44)
Thus addressed, his wife then spoke to the sage Suparṇaka:
"Behold here, at the Narmadā tīrtha, how one is freed from sin merely by bathing. (45)
Having become liberated even as a Cāṇḍāla, he went to heaven by means of a celestial chariot;
for him, no austerity was performed, no oblation offered, no mantra recited, and no restraints were observed. (46)
He did not know the religious observances, yet he went to heaven; he performed no vow at all, nor did he observe the rules regarding the menstrual period. ||47||
Even though he did not observe the days of religious vows, he nevertheless went to heaven;
O Sage, such is the supreme majesty of this sacred ford.
By the mere act of bathing, the destruction of all sins occurs in every way;
therefore, O treasure-house of compassion, enjoy my offerings here and accept me. (49)
In some cases, the wife’s word must be honored so that dharma is not violated—specifically when the wife has bathed after her menses and when the husband’s desire is powerful. (1.561.5) 0.
In that situation, the word of the wife must necessarily be honored;
indeed, a son will certainly be born then through the offering of the seasonal rite (ṛtudāna). ||51||
In that regard, one should abandon religious vows, as well as sacred festivals and celebrations;
for when time is wasted through lack of enthusiasm, even a pregnancy does not yield offspring.
When a thousand years had passed without any attachment indeed in such a place, Dharma [spoke], for nothing else was dearer than his wife’s words. (53)
In this there is no denial, nor contradiction, nor any fault to be found;
for how much is the mere grass and such in a great forest fire? (54)
How small is a blade of poisonous grass in oceans of nectar?
How small is the darkness within a house at the hour of the midday sun? (55)
O Lord, how much time remains until the day of Amāvasyā at Puṇyaparvata?
Therefore, O Protector, favor me this very day with a state of supreme love.
"Whatever sin might arise from taking [a gift] improperly, that same demerit indeed results from not accepting it.
Having been told this, the husband there took his wife according to his desire. (57)

He gave the embryo to his son, and that son was born resembling the sun. Then, those ancestors who had attained satisfaction by eating at the *amā-śrāddha* arrived during the night and, laughing, spoke as follows: [58]
Today, quickly perform the expiation for the bestowal of the embryo.
Having bathed again in the Narmadā, perform the fire-oblation and the recitation once more. We are satisfied and pleased for the sake of establishing a connection with progeny.
And because you were entreated by your wife,
you took that purifying water from the Narmadā, which destroys all sins, for the sake of obtaining a son.

The sin arising from the killing of a Brahmin, the killing of a child, or the killing of an elder or a woman; the sin born of the failure of religious vows and the like; and that produced by sexual misconduct and other such acts. (62)
"By merely bathing in the Revā, [all sins] are destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, his ancestors departed with contented minds. (63)
Stricken by the despair of childlessness, they lived on with their hope centered in the womb;
then, after some time, two *suparṇas* arrived there together with their wife.
Standing in a radiant celestial chariot, he went to the supreme city of Brahmā;
there, at that most excellent confluence, Suparṇa attained both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now, indeed, to the west of the Nīlagangā and to the north of the Narmadā,
there is a most beautiful sacred site named Vyatīpāteśvara.
Sāvitrī performed penance there, and so there exists the Sāvitrī-kuṇḍa. King Indradyumna, desiring to perform a sacrifice,
then questioned the great sages residing in Dharmāraṇya.
And Mārkaṇḍa and others called that the most excellent Narmadā-kṣetra. ||68||
The king then issued a proclamation for the subjects to go to the Revā river,
along with three hundred thousand cows that yield milk and are accompanied by their calves.
And there were one hundred and twenty-five thousand horses with black ears,
as well as ten thousand elephants adorned with bells and ornaments.
There were four thousand vehicles that travel at will,
a hundred thousand camels, and a hundred thousand gems and rubies.
Garments purified by fire, vessels made of gold, various kinds of foods, edibles, and diverse drinks; ||72||
Having gathered a hundred thousand laborers, as well as sesame seeds, darbha grass, and other items, the king, together with the brahmins, ascended a celestial chariot.
Filled with supreme joy, the king, accompanied by his harem and retinue, went to Dharmāraṇya, where that river Narmadā flows.
The delightful Yātrādri mountain stands there, adorned with lapis lazuli gems;
likewise, Oṃkāreśa Śambhu shines forth with great splendor. (79)
In the vicinity of Oṃkāra, the Revākoṭi Tīrtha shines resplendent;
whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, performed as a rite, or practiced as austerity here becomes indeed infinite. (76)
At all times and in all undertakings, the Narmadā bestows ten million-fold merit;
for a distance of thirty yojanas, she provides sacrificial posts and pavilions.
That king caused various sacrificial pits to be constructed;
the resounding roar of the Vedic chants touched both heaven and earth.
The fire became smokeless and accepted the offering of clarified butter;
it then summoned Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara.
There are eleven Rudras there, as well as twelve Ādityas;
likewise the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Maruts, and the Vasus.
The world-protectors, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains with their excellent trees, the guardians of the quarters, the guardians of beings, the sacred fords, and likewise the ancestors. ||81||
Siddhas, kinnaras, gandharvas, nāgas, rākṣasas, guhyakas,
vidyādharas, and cāraṇas also refreshed themselves there at that sacrificial festival.
Rivers flowing with ghee and milk appeared, with curds and milk-rice for their mud;
there were drinking waters and flavorful drinks everywhere. (83)
The gods, the sages, and the fourfold host of living beings were satisfied with various kinds of foods and drinks, as well as with desirable vehicles and other such things. (84)
Thus, when the sacrifice was completed, the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) took place in the waters of the Narmadā;
there was satisfaction from the sacrificial fees for all who were entitled to a share of the sacrifice.
The king himself worshipped Oṃkāreśa with gold and jewels, with gems such as rubies, emeralds, and diamonds, and with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood. (86)
Having worshipped Hara and Hari with various kinds of perfumes and flowers, with banners, umbrellas, and celestial chariots, as well as with yak-tail whisks and fans.
He praised the giver of liberation: "Oṃkāra, salutations again and again to you!
Then, Rudra himself appeared in personified form in his presence.
He said, "Choose a boon," and Indradyumna replied to him:
"Make your dwelling always in this valley on the mountain of sacrifice. (89)
Indeed, there shall be liberation even for the deceased, even for sinners,
for him who encircles the mountain with a single thread on a sacred festival day.
By him the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, was encompassed;
through that merit, his liberation here shall be the state of Brahman. || 91 ||
"So be it," Hara said, and vanished right there;
Brahmā then spoke to the king for the purpose of granting the boon.
The King said, "O Brahmin, become here indeed the bearer of the form of the Liṅga.
Having replied, "So be it," Brahmā disappeared from that place.
The king, having prostrated himself with all eight limbs, praised Viṣṇu—
Keśava, Mādhava, Viṣṇu, Govinda, and Madhusūdana.
Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Śrīdhara, Trivikrama,
Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, Śrīhari— the son of Kambharā.
The Lord of Rādhā, the protector of cowherd boys, the Lord of Śrī, the Sovereign of Ramā, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. ||96||
I bow to Mañjuleśa, the Lord of Pārvatī, the Lord of Prabhā, the husband of Māṇikī, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and the Lord of Haṃsā and Jayā. ||97||
I bow down to the Lord of the World, the Lord of the Universe, the Lord of Śrī, who is adorned with the conch, the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, and a garland of forest flowers. 98.
O Lord of the syllables, O Lord of the liberated, O Lord of Lalitā, salutations be unto you!
O Lord of incarnations, O Lord of gods, O Lord of the manifestations, salutations be unto you! (99)
O Lord of lords, Lord of Māyā, Lord of Durgā, Master of the Ganges!

Salutations to You, the primordial Lord, the peaceful one, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha;

salutations to you who are the form of Hiraṇyagarbha and whose abode is immortality.
Salutation to you who are the embryo of all, to Kṛṣṇa, and to your inner self;
salutation to you in the form of the effect—the creator, the preserver, and the destroyer.
Salutation to you who take the form of all the guardians of the quarters, whose very self is the protector of the world;
salutation to you, the triple deity, whose nature is half-female and half-male.
Salutations to You, the treasure-house of infinite bliss, the abode of Brahman;
salutations again and again to You, the bestower of the fruits of karma, who dwells within.
Salutations again and again to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self who made his dwelling in Saurāṣṭra, the beloved of ten million gopīs, and the bestower of happiness.

Homage to You, the abode of inconceivable qualities; homage to You, whose body is divine.
Homage to You, the bestower of boundless sovereignty; homage to You, who possess a visible form. 1.14
Salutations to you whose form is invisible yet visible, and who are eternal knowledge;

Salutations to you who have assumed the form of the five fires and who abide in your vow;

"O Viṣṇu, take my hand, as a bridegroom takes the hand of his wife;
grant me residence at your feet, O Keśava, for I choose no other. (121)
Having heard that supreme hymn of praise, Viṣṇu was pleased and said to the king:
"Choose a boon, O King; choose whatever boon resides in your heart."
"I grant it to you, have no doubt; the success of your sacrifice shall be achieved.
Then Indradyumna spoke in the presence of Oṃkāranātha.
O Kṛṣṇa, always make your residence upon the Vaidūrya mountain,
so that liberation may come to those who have arrived there through your worship.
Through seeing you, through saluting you, through serving you, and through immersing oneself in you—
even by the relinquishing of life— embodied beings shall attain your state.
By the gift of food to the ancestors, may they indeed go to the station of Viṣṇu;
even insects, moths, and the like, may they attain the supreme goal here.
"So be it," Hari said, and he descended there;
all the sacred fords (tīrthas) as well were established there within the lotus-feet of Nārāyaṇa.
And they descended to the sacred fords on the Narmadā, the land of sacrifice;
indeed, at the confluence of the Nīlagangā, there are those that truly bestow liberation.
The king praised Revā, saying, "Become possessed of seven streams," and he thus made this request; she too then became one with seven flows.
The river Revā, which bestows liberation and embodies all sacred fords, has appeared;
here, every gift given, oblation offered, prayer recited, and austerity performed becomes inexhaustible.
Having thus performed the sacrifice by the Narmadā,
Indradyumna indeed paid homage to Viṣṇu, the gods, and Oṃkāra, and then went home.
The gods and others, as well as humans and others, being satisfied by the sacrifice, went to their homes.
By hearing or reciting this, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī: "O beloved, liberation shall be attained here;
O Lakṣmī, I have described to you this supreme Tīrtha which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.33)

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Jāleśvara Tīrtha, the Liberation of King Hiraṇyabāhu from the State of a Donkey, Revā-Caru-Sambheda Tīrtha, Amarakaṇṭaka Tīrtha, Yajñaparvata, the Story of Suparṇa, Oṃkāra Tīrtha, and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the purifying story proclaimed by Śambhu to Pārvatī on Mount Ṛkṣaka; I shall now relate that tale which destroys all sins.
King Vasudāna, the sovereign of the entire earth, became the protector of those who could not be slain;
he worshipped Mādhava with a thousand horse-sacrifices.
All those subjects lived for more than one hundred and twenty-five thousand years;
at that time, there were indeed deceitful Daityas on the southern bank of the Revā.
Ketumālin, Suketu, Sumukha, and Dundubhi likewise became creators of obstacles to dharma and disruptors of sacrifices. || 4 ||
At that time, no one desired to perform sacrifices at Amarakaṇṭaka;
then the mighty king went to the Revā river to perform a sacrifice.
Accompanied by learned Brahmins and officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas,
he [gave] five hundred thousand cows that yielded milk along with their calves.
One hundred and twenty-five thousand horses, ten thousand elephants, as well as jewels such as gems and rubies, and wealth consisting of gold and silver; || 7 ||
Taking various kinds of food and drink, clarified butter, rice, and sesame seeds,
as well as pavilions and sacrificial posts, that king [proceeded].
Having gone there, he purified the ground and constructed pavilions;
he established the altars, the sacrificial pits, and the sacred fire.
He offered clarified butter and oblations, and gratified Mādhava;
he satisfied the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and the brahmins with food.
At that time, the host of asuras arrived for the purpose of creating obstacles by means of offerings such as sacrificial fees, as well as by means of living creatures, grains, grass, and the like.
Struck and put to flight by the king with the discharge of divine weapons,
that sacrifice, which bestows wealth, proceeded thus without obstacle.
The earth became drenched with the waters of the final purificatory bath (āvabhṛthya) and appeared as if fashioned of gold;
meanwhile, the beasts and birds that had been wallowing in the mud were left disheveled.
By the power of their merit,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara simultaneously became golden-hued there by means of streams of water.
Having been worshipped, that water became unified as a flowing stream;
likewise, the bathing water for all the gods was prepared by the sages. (15)
At that time, even the flow of that [river] merged there at the spring,
and the streams of the urine of hundreds of thousands of cows gathered together there.
There were streams of the remnants of various foods and drinks, as well as cascades of milk and clarified butter; there were also flows of milk that had become the byproduct of sacrificial offerings.
Those streams, consisting of rivers, merged into the sacrificial pit;
indeed, there was a purifying river named Kapilā with variegated waters.
This is that very region, Rudrāvarta, where he joined the Narmadā;
having beheld its wonderful waters, that river was frequented by celestial sages and seers.
Having been named "Kapila" after the satisfaction of Dakṣiṇā,
they indeed granted a boon to the king at the confluence of the Kapilā.
They shall bathe in the Narmadā and behold Maheśvara and Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa here; through divine means, they shall attain the supreme state.
Even the insects and others who were to die there shall go [to that state];
having thus granted this supreme boon, they all departed for their own abodes.
Vasudāna, having performed a sacrifice, arrived at Avadhyā;
by hearing of him and by chanting his name, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. (23)
Then there was King Viśravas, possessed of great strength,
who was the son of Arundhatī, the daughter of Dakṣa.
In the course of a pilgrimage to sacred sites, the king went to Amarakaṇṭaka; when he had bathed and was established in meditation on the bank of the Narmadā, [the following occurred]. (25)
Then, at midday, he beholds two suns that have gone to the eastern quarter from the solar disc in the west, and two [more] toward the southern direction. (26)
Two [suns] were below in Pātāla and likewise two suns of fierce form above;
then the fire of the Saṃvartaka eon blazed forth in the sky.
Fierce and terrible winds blew, causing great agitation;
there was a burning of the quarters, an earthquake, and the falling of dreadful meteors.
At that time, the king, who had been lying upon the earth, awoke from his meditation;
afflicted by thirst and tormented by burning heat, he went to the Narmadā to drink water.
But as he went along, there was indeed no water at all;
the flow had vanished, and he found no water anywhere. (1.562.30)
"Without water, my death today is certain," he thought;
then he indeed remembered the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (31)
He then remembered Oṃkāranātha and immediately beheld a blossoming kalpavṛkṣa tree, laden with fruit, richly adorned with leaves, and possessing beautiful branches.
Having seen that and reached the cool shade, the king became steady;
his body became as if immortal, and his thirst and fever subsided.
Then, his hope for life arose; and the king beheld a divine man of blazing splendor lying in the shade.
And on the side of the Kubhā, four [streams] stand full of water;
having bowed to him, the king stood there and beheld him in the form of Viṣṇu.
He beheld the second person, the three-eyed Śiva, as he slept;
at that moment, the king likewise beheld other gods, deities, and sages.
Then he saw a woman who was distressed and drenched in blood,
with her hair disheveled, holding a young girl upon her hip.
She spoke to the king: "O King, drink my breast-milk and abandon your thirst;
I am the goddess Earth, and this child is indeed the unborn creator of the universe."
This maiden is Narmadā; these jars are the oceans;
this banyan tree is the Kalpa-vṛkṣa; and we all shall remain steadfast for a long time.
"Imperishable and remaining for an entire kalpa, drink this water with devotion!
Having said this, she vanished; then the king beheld the Narmadā.
Having drunk the water along with its essence, Viśravas attained full satisfaction;
then, having performed his ablutions at the holy site, he returned once more to his own city, Mathurā.
Such an eternal sacred ford exists in the waters of the Narmadā;
by hearing of it and by chanting its praises, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā and to the west of the Kapilā, there is the beautiful city of Viṣṇu; that sacred site (tīrtha) bestows liberation and is auspicious.
The Daityas were previously destroyed by Viṣṇu, and after that, having arrived there, a beautiful and auspicious city was built by Viṣṇu. 44.
To the west, however, lies the Kapilā and the Nīlagangā;
between them are Cakratīrtha, Vāmana, and Yugandhara. 45.
There is the sacred ford named Sudarśana, also known as Daityasūdana;
likewise, there are Viṣṇvāvarta, Śivāvarta, and Lakṣmyāvarta.
By bathing and giving gifts there, one indeed enjoys infinite fruit;
that sacred field of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be one krośa in extent. ||47||
There, the ancestors are satisfied by the faithful and attain liberation;
whatever chanting or austerity is performed there becomes entirely inexhaustible. 48.
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in conjunction with the asterism Śravaṇa is meritorious, and the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) with Rohiṇī is auspicious;
by fasting thereon, a devoted person is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whoever observes a fast during either the month of Kārtika or Vaiśākha shall obtain there the fruit of ten crore fasts.
But that woman who is devoted to her husband and is indeed devoted to Nārāyaṇa should worship Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa there. ||5 1||
To her, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa grants eternal good fortune in his celestial abode, equal to that of Lakṣmī and filled with bliss. ||52||
At this sacred ford, out of respect for those who frequent holy sites, Dharmarāja himself comes to receive the offering of water (argha), bearing a body composed of the splendor of Dharma.
Standing before the devoted wives, he bows at their feet;
having beheld the world of Viṣṇu, he then returns.
Then, when Dharmarāja had returned to Satya, the ascetics—
the ṛṣis who were the mind-born sons of Brahmā— indeed questioned him.
And for what reason did Dharmarāja himself go forth, walking upon the path of Dharma? Laughing, he spoke these most wonderful words to them. (56)

The splendor of women devoted to their husbands, the splendor of those who fast for a month, and the splendor of the deities themselves—indeed, he personally possesses all these in a preeminent degree. (57)
I went for the purpose of seeing [him], but my servants were unable to remain in their presence; therefore, even though I had gone, I departed again.
Thus, O Goddess of Devas, the purifying Nārāyaṇasthala, which always bestows liberation, exists there; it grants liberation even by being heard.
The river Carukā flows forth, extending from the hermitage of Śākalya at Yajñaparvata as far as the bank of the Narmadā.
There, the Dāruvana forest is celebrated by all the gods;
in ancient times, Śakra performed a sacrifice there with Bṛhaspati as his domestic priest.
The Vyāghreśvara Liṅga, which destroys all sins, is situated there.
In ancient times, there was a most righteous king named Babhru.
And a Vaiṣṇava residing in Puṇḍravardhana reflected thus when the anniversary of his father's death arrived, at the time for performing the Śrāddha rite for a Vaiṣṇava.
That king did not find a Brahmin who would eat food at a *śrāddha* ceremony;
having reflected on this, he cast the cooked food intended for the Brahmins' meal into the water.
Then the Rigveda, embodied in form, spoke these words to the king:
"Go, O King, and entreat the auspicious Brahmin Bharadvāja."
Having heard that, the king went to the supreme hermitage of Bhāradvāja;
having saluted and paid homage to the sage, he spoke what was in his mind.
"O Great Sage, this is the time for the ancestral rites (śrāddha) for my forefathers;
you should act in such a way that I may feed the brahmins. (67)
Having heard those words of his, Bhāradvāja spoke these words to the thousands of great sages who were contented and whose vital energy was drawn upward.
If you are capable of feeding the foremost of those with hair like swans, then perform the śrāddha as you wish; we shall certainly feed them as well.
One should give a throne made of gold, as well as grain and wealth;
likewise, one should give a divine cow of honey and similarly a cow of milk.
A cow made of curd, a cow made of ghee, and likewise a cow made of sugar; a cow made of jaggery, a cow made of cloth, and also indeed a cow made of grain.
A water-cow, a gold-cow, a cow made of two grains,
a cotton-cow, and likewise a tawny cow with her calf— these are all types of cows.
"Give me a loincloth and also a garment purified by fire.
Having heard the words of Bhāradvāja, the king accepted them. (73)
Having gone home, he reported everything to his wife with devotion:
"I shall prepare meat and perform the ancestral rites. (74)
He gratified those ancestors with pure sacrificial meat alone;
but seeing that meat, the sages were enraged and then spoke. (75)
Having consumed what is unfit for consumption, a twice-born man should enter a fire of dried cow-dung;
by your attachment to meat, you have brought about the destruction of your very roots.
Babhru said: "I have performed what was declared in the Vedas, and not otherwise:
the Gomedha, the Hayamedha, and likewise the Naramedha. (77)
"A sacrifice for Kṣatriyas shall be performed by me according to the Dharma.
Having heard those words of the king, Bhāradvāja spoke this:
O King, you have invited Brahmins for the feeding of the ancestors;
yet these Brahmins are Vaiṣṇavas, and they are not eager even to look upon meat. (79)
Therefore, since you have indeed not acted appropriately here at this śrāddha ceremony, become a meat-eater through this sin; you shall be a tiger, and your beloved wife a tigress.
"You two shall wander upon the earth in the forest for a thousand years.
Having heard this, the king's wife named Sudharmā spoke these words:
