Since my husband, who follows the dharma of a Kshatriya, has been cursed by you, I too am a devoted wife, faultless, and likewise most righteous. (82)
Then I also bestowed a terrible curse upon the Brahmins:
"You shall indeed become most horrific Brahmarākṣasas. (83)
In a waterless desert region, they were exceedingly distressed by thirst and hunger;
then Bhāradvāja quickly went to Brahmā himself.
There he reported everything, including the cause of the curse;
and Brahmā spoke of the karma prescribed by the Vedas as well as that determined by one's birth.
If it were not honored by the world, one should never perform it;
for that which is declared in the Vedas, honored by the world, and even agreeable to the heart—[that alone should be done]. (86)
That task shall indeed grant happiness, for happiness is not found by following only one path.
Let that which has arisen be born; I speak of deliverance, my son. (87)
"Let the royal sage in the form of a tiger, the queen, the brahmins, and the rākṣasas proceed to the bank of the Narmadā toward the sage Mārkaṇḍeya. (88)
Thus addressed, Bhāradvāja, the king of sages, having led the brahmins away, went from the tiger and tigress to those Rākṣasas and then to the sage Mārkaṇḍa. (89)
They praised him with supreme affection and spoke of the cause of the curse;
for the sake of liberation, they entreated that sage as if he were their father.
"You are our father and our teacher; you are Hari, the Sustainer, and Śiva himself.
Lift us up from this terrible sin and from this horrific womb of birth. (9.1)
Then Mārkaṇḍeya said: "There is indeed the hermitage of Śākalya to the west of Vaidūrya, where many sacrifices were performed."
And those born there on that holy ground shall go to Maheśvara;
remaining steadfast in their vows, they shall also worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Let them remain constantly devoted to recitation and meditation, performing even fierce austerities, subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits; let it be so. (94)
"Devoted to bathing in the Narmadā and intent upon the worship of the gods, may you all quickly become liberated from the curse. (95)
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
May they chant this syllabic mantra and quickly attain [their goal]. ||96||
Having been addressed thus, they went there; they performed recitation again and again, bathed in the waters of the Narmadā, drank [the water], and practiced supreme austerity.
And within a month, at that very place, the Lord Hari, accompanied by divine Lakṣmī, arrived seated upon his celestial vehicle for the purpose of destroying the curse. ||98||
At the confluence of the Vyāghra and Revā rivers, the Blessed One himself liberated the Brahmins from their curse,
and likewise released the tiger and tigress from the curse.
The king and the queen went to their own supreme abode, and the brahmins later returned to their own homes; and in the course of time, they too departed.
Having attained the supreme abode of Viṣṇu through the power of the mantra, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice merely by hearing or chanting this. 101.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Historical Exposition of the Kapilā-Reva Confluence, Viśravas Tīrtha, Viṣṇupurī, Cakratīrtha, Dāruvana, and Vyāghreśa Tīrthas," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me how honey, cows, and other such gifts should be given;
what is the merit therein, what is the procedure, and how much should the gift of a cow be? (1)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you. In ancient times there was a great king, renowned as Vinītāśva, a lord who performed many sacrifices.
He commenced the Sarvamedha sacrifice; by means of it, cows, elephants, wealth, all gold, and palatial dwellings were given to the Brahmins.
At that time, he did not give food or water, considering them to be too little;
then, having died on the bank of the Gaṅgā, he went to heaven in due course of time.
His body was cast by the twice-born into a deep pit in the earth;
having recognized it as the meritorious clay of the Gaṅgā, it was indeed placed within the ground.
Then this king, though dwelling in a celestial chariot in heaven, being hungry and thirsty, came to the earth for the sake of food.
Having dug up his own corpse there, he devoured it;
at that time, the king’s priest, named Hotṛ, saw him.
He asked him who was devouring his own body, "What indeed are you doing?
The king replied, "No food presents itself for me in heaven."
"Tell me, what is the reason for this? Having heard this, the Hotṛ spoke to him; the Hotṛ said: "Previously, you gave gifts of water and food."

Thinking it to be very little, one does not perform [meritorious acts], and thus nectar is not attained; for whatever is performed or given here on this earth of karma is obtained [in the hereafter]. 1.563.10.
What has not been given does not remain; therefore, give water and food.
Give an auspicious sesame-cow and, O best of men, a water-cow.
Bestow a cow of ghee, a cow of juice, and a cow of curd;
likewise, a cow of milk, a cow of honey, and even a cow of sugar.
Indeed, bestow the cow of food, the cow of rice, and the golden cow;
and likewise, bestow the cow of cloth and the tawny cow along with her calf.
In this way, bestow other gifts as well and obtain their fruit;
through the gift of food, you shall dwell in heaven, free from hunger.
O lord of men, listen now to the ritual procedure for the sesame-cow;
in this context, one *prastha* is proclaimed to consist of four *kuḍavas*.
The cow should be made with sixteen [parts] and the calf with four;
its nose should consist of fragrant substances and its auspicious tongue of molasses.
Its tail consists of thread, its pair of garments is white,
its two eyes are made of pearls, its teeth are made of fruit, and its blanket is woolen.
She has a dewlap-like neck and breasts made of fresh butter;
she possesses a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, adorned with ornaments of bells.
A beautiful cow made of bell-metal, with a fourth-part calf, accompanied by a black antelope skin and all kinds of gems, and bringing joy. || 19 ||
One should cause the offering of mantra-worship combined with all medicinal herbs, [with the prayer]:
"May food be produced for me, as well as other drinks and all flavors. (1.563.20)
Fulfill everything for us, O sesame-cow; salutations be unto you!
I bestow you, together with sugar, upon this embodiment of a Brahmin. (21)
Thus, the best of Brahmins should accept what has been given according to the prescribed rite: the tail in his hand, as well as water, flowers, and even rice grains.
Having taken the fragrance and touched his eyes, he should offer it to the cows;
having prepared a mandala with cow dung, the donor should give [the offering] according to the prescribed rite.
Having performed a circumambulation and a prostration, one should give it to a twice-born man, saying:
"I am a twice-born man; with great devotion, I accept this for the sake of my family. (24)
"O Goddess, O sesame-cow, enjoy the objects of desire; salutations be unto you!
Grant to the donor all kinds of food—both hard and soft—as well as drinks and other things wherever he may be. (25)
"In this manner, the cow should be given by him; through it, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are attained.
The Hotṛ priest said: "In that case, give the water-cow according to the prescribed ritual. (26)
One should smear an area of ground the size of a cow's hide with cow dung;
there, one should worship that jar filled with water using unbroken rice grains and other offerings. ||27||
Having fashioned that cow and adorned it with garlands of *dūrvā* grass,
one should provide it with the five jewels as well as the seven types of grain.
One should place wheat, rice, barley, chickpeas, as well as black gram, mung beans, and millet; these are the seven grains (saptadhānya). || 29 ||
One should place a vessel of ghee, a vessel of curd, a vessel of honey, and sugar in the four directions, and likewise a golden vessel in its mouth.
One should fashion the two eyes from pearls, the two horns from sandalwood,
the back from copper, the udder from bell-metal, and the hair from *darbha* grass.
Upon hearing [the sound] of the copper plate, one should likewise offer a tail made of thread;
upon a blanket, a garland of flowers; and for one with molasses in its mouth, oyster-shells for teeth.
Having made the tongue out of sugar and the breasts out of fresh butter, and likewise having fashioned the stalks of the sugarcane, adorned with perfumes and flowers. (33)
Having placed it upon a black antelope skin and covered it with a cloth,
one should worship it with perfumes and flowers and offer it facing the east.

O Indra among kings, it should be given to a virtuous Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas, who maintains the sacred fires, who is advanced in asceticism, and who is a worthy recipient supporting a family.
O King, the man who gives, the one who sees, the one who hears, and the brahmin who accepts [the gift], are all liberated from every sin. (36)
The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a father, the killer of a cow, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—freed from all these sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. ||37||
One should fashion an auspicious calf for the water-cow within a water-pot;
the giver of the water-cow should subsist only on water for one day.
The righteous recipient should also remain there for three nights with water,
where rivers flow with milk and whose mud consists of honey and milk-rice.
Wherever the song of the Apsarases resounds, there go those who offer water;
or else, being liberated from sin, they attain union with Viṣṇu.
Then, having filled a jar with the juice of sugarcane, he should indeed give a "juice-cow" (rasadhenu), worshipping it as before, and likewise its calf.
Having fashioned [the image] with a fourth part [of the materials], provided with seven grains of rice,
equipped with all necessary utensils, and accompanied by vessels of sesame seeds and so forth.
Both the giver and the receiver, by eating at the same time, obtain the fruit of drinking the Soma; even for one who merely witnesses it, the fruit is likewise.
He shall cause ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself as the twenty-first to attain the supreme state; from heaven, he does not return again.
And give it away, O Great King; thus you shall attain the supreme state, having likewise fashioned a cow of molasses together with its calf and a bronze milking vessel.
Her two horns were made of gold, her teeth were set with jewels and pearls,
her neck was composed of gems, and likewise her nose was made of fragrance.
Its two horns were made of aguru wood, its back likewise of copper, and its tail of silk; it was adorned with all kinds of ornaments. ||47||
Having covered [the cow] with sugarcane for its feet, silver for its hooves, a woolen blanket, and silk thread, and having adorned it with silk thread, bells, and chowries; ||48||
The observer of the vow, having adorned with fruits a cow whose ears are decorated with auspicious leaves and whose udders are like fresh butter, should give her to a Brahmin with devotion. (49)
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, and having offered an umbrella and sandals, you have been given as a jaggery-cow; may you be the bestower of all prosperity.
"O mother, because of this gift, please grant me food to eat and drink—whatever was performed by word, whatever was done by deed, and whatever was conceived by the mind. (51)

May the deceitful deception of weights and the deception of measures, which are said to be for the sake of seizing a maiden’s wealth, come to destruction; may the cow made of molasses be offered to the twice-born.
By the gift of a cow made of molasses, one obtains complete good fortune for ten, twelve thousand, and ten and eight births. (53)
For him, sorrow, suffering, and misfortune never arise anywhere;
therefore, give this sugar-cow weighing four bhāras.

Having worshipped the cow, adorned with ornaments and accompanied by her calf, according to the previous procedure, the observer of the vow should place the cow facing east and set the calf to her north.
Having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) into his hand, one should present him with a cow enriched with sandalwood paste, perfumes, and flowers; and one should not look at his face.
A Brāhmaṇa who subsists on sugar for one day and dwells there for three days shall be born with all his desires fulfilled; of this there is no doubt. ||57||
I shall now describe the honey-cow, which destroys all sins;
having fashioned a cow made of honey, complete with sixteen full jars. (58)
With a fourth part likewise, one should fashion a cow-calf, endowed with the previously mentioned limbs and provided with the seven grains. (59)
Having seen the abundance of materials and Brahmins accompanied by four vessels of sesame seeds and honored with flowers, one should bestow that [gift].
May the ancestors and the gods be pleased; salutations be unto you, O Honey-Cow!
O Goddess, I accept you for the sake of my family; salutations be unto you.
Having given a gift, one should spend the day with milk-rice and honey;
those who give cows go to the place where rivers flow with honey.
By the gift of a honey-cow, one leads ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself as the twenty-first to union with Viṣṇu.
I shall now describe to you the milk-cow; listen to it and offer it.
On a patch of ground smeared with cow dung, upon kusha grass and a deerskin, [place her]. (64)
Having drawn a red line all around, one should place an auspicious jar filled with milk;
likewise, a jar called "Vatsa," as well as all the previously mentioned limbs [of the ritual diagram]. (65)
Having placed various items and vessels of grain and sesame seeds in the cardinal directions,
one should indeed give a worshipped milch-cow to a brahmin.
Those who behold it being given also go to the supreme goal;
for sixty thousand years, moreover, he is honored in the world of Indra.
Accompanied by his father and others, he shall go to the abode of Brahmā;
from there, assuming the form of Viṣṇu, he proceeds to the supreme realm.
A beautiful curd-cow, consisting of a jar of curd, should be given, accompanied by seven kinds of grain, provided with a calf, and likewise adorned. (69)
Having worshipped and adorned it, the observer of the vow should give it to a Brāhmaṇa;
the observer of the vow should take but one meal a day, and the twice-born should remain thus for three days.
By that gift of curd, the donor goes to the highest world even when requested;
one should give an auspicious cow made of fresh butter together with ten thousand calves.
As before, one should offer to a Brāhmaṇa [the image] which is rich in all splendors, fashioned with all its limbs complete, worshipped, and provided with grain.
Formerly, during the churning of the ocean by all the gods and asuras,
this auspicious, divine nectar was produced, which is like fresh butter.
O butter, you are the nourishment of all beings; salutations be to you!
I shall now describe the gift of the salt-cow, which should be given by one desiring auspiciousness. (74)
A cow weighing sixteen prasthas, with a calf that is one-fourth its size,
adorned with all ornaments and provided with the previously mentioned limbs.
In the event of affliction from planets or constellations, one should cause this to be given to a Brāhmaṇa:
"O Brahmin, accept this which has the form of Rudra; salutations be unto you. (76)
"O Goddess in the form of Rudra, fulfill my desire; salutations be unto you!
For three nights, the observer of the vow shall be a Brahmin who eats salt. (77)
Now, one should give a cotton-cow, which bestows happiness and peace, during fierce afflictions by the planets, upon bad dreams, or at the sight of an ill omen. (78)
One should give [the cow] well-nourished as before at sacred sites (āyatana), prepared with exactly four bhāras and accompanied by a calf. (79)
One should indeed offer her, fully worshipped along with all her requisites and all her limbs;
"O Great Goddess, grant protection both here and in the hereafter! Salutations unto you! (1.563.80)
A grain-cow and likewise an auspicious rice-cow should be given;
having fashioned their limbs as before, one should then worship them.
Having circumambulated the lamp, [one should say]: "May Madhusūdana be pleased!
O cow consisting of all prosperity, who takes the form of grain, salutations be unto you! (82)
Having recited this, one should present that cow to a Brāhmaṇa;
for as long as the entire earth exists, O King, so long do wealth and jewels [belong to him]. (83)
The merit of that is even greater than the fruit of a rice-cow gift;
it increases good fortune, longevity, and health in this world. (84)
At the end, he goes to the abode of Hari by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun;
now, therefore, I shall fully describe the most excellent Kapilā cow.
By the giving of which a person goes to the eternal world of Brahmā, one should give a cow together with its calf according to the previously mentioned procedure. (86)
O King, the head and neck of a tawny cow are adorned with all ornaments and decorated with every kind of jewel; they are, indeed, all sacred fords (tīrthas). 87.
Whoever bows down in the morning to the water from the head of a tawny cow becomes truly meritorious, having burned away the sins of thirty lifetimes. ||88||
One should perform circumambulation at dawn, which bestows the merit of circumambulating the entire earth;
a single act of circumambulation burns away the sins arising from ten lifetimes. (89)
One who has bathed with the urine of a Kapila cow is considered as one who has bathed at all sacred fords;
indeed, the gift of a Kapila cow is said to be equal to the gift of a thousand cows.
As long as a tawny cow smells the ashes of the deceased,
for that long the preta is filled with great merit and becomes a dweller in heaven.
Scratching the itch of cows is equivalent to the protection afforded by gifting a hundred cows;
providing grass, water, and the like is considered to yield the fruit of a cow-sacrifice (gomedha). 12.
One was golden-brown, the second was pale yellowish-brown, the third had red eyes, and the fourth was dark brown like molasses. ||93||
The fifth should be multicolored; the sixth is white and tawny;
the seventh has white and tawny eyes; and the eighth is black and tawny.
The ninth is to be known as Pāṭalā, the tenth as Pucchapiṅgalā, and the eleventh as Kṣuraśvetā; among these, the latter is considered the most excellent. (95)
For the Kapilā cow was indeed created by Brahmā in ancient times, having extracted all the vital energies for the sake of the Agnihotra, for the sake of sacrifice, and for the sake of the gods. 96.
Among all gifts, this gift is supreme; for among treasures, it is indeed inexhaustible.
The twice-born must offer the Agnihotra oblations both morning and evening.
Through the ghee, curd, milk, and clarified butter of a tawny cow,
the rites such as the honoring of guests are fulfilled here, and the sacrificial bricks are offered.
Agnihotra sacrifices are performed with various mantras by those who know the Veda;
she who is tawny and has reddish-brown eyes bestows all happiness. 99.
The cow that bestows success and wisdom, endowed with all auspicious characteristics— every such cow, when given at the confluence of two rivers, truly delivers [the donor] from all [sins].
She has fire for her tail, fire for her mouth, fire for her hair, and the radiance of fire;
likewise, she is known by the names Agnāyī, Śvetakhurā, and Suvarṇā. || 101 ||
One should wait for a cow that is about to give birth in order to present her as a gift,
while the face of the calf being born is still visible at the birth canal.
That earth should be known as such only so long as she does not release her embryo;
indeed, that cow who has half-given birth to her calf must be given to a Vaiṣṇava.
For as many millions of years as there are hairs on a cow together with her calf, for that long do they dwell in the world of Brahmā.
Having placed gold in the hand of the Brahmin,
and likewise having placed water in his hand, one should cause him to recite the words "the tail" and then bestow the gift.
By that [act], the earth—clothed by the ocean, adorned with mountains and villages, and filled with jewels—is indeed given; of this there is no doubt.
The donor goes with his ancestors to the supreme station called Viṣṇu;
and he who gives a cow with two faces attains the cessation of all sins.
On that day, one should subsist on milk-rice or water,
and one should indeed give excellent wealth, avoiding any stinginess regarding one's means.
I take this [vessel] which has openings on both sides; may there indeed be peace in both places. I give it for the sake of the increase of the lineage; always be a bringer of well-being.
I accept you, O cow, especially for the sake of my family;
may there be constant auspiciousness for me, O divine mother—salutations be unto you!
May there always be well-being for me; salutations to you who possess the form of Viṣṇu!
Oṃ, may Heaven grant you the earth; may you yourself accept it as well. (11.1)
"Oṃ! Who has given this to whom? This Brahman has given this to Brahman.
Having spoken thus according to the rule, one should duly honor the Brahmin together with a cow. || 11.2 ||
One should bow to that cow, follow her, and lead her to her home;
by such a gift, there is no doubt that the gift of the entire earth has been made. || 113 ||
If one recites this at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, the ancestors partake of it with devotion;
by reciting it on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), the forefathers remain satisfied for a hundred years.
Furthermore, the sin committed by the listener over a year is destroyed from afar on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha and on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
On the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, or specifically on the twelfth day,
or at any time as appropriate, one should offer gifts to the venerable Guru.
Indeed, those worlds contained within the belly of the cosmic egg were given by him;
or else, O King, you are being excessively tormented by hunger and thirst.
Tell me of the lineage of that person who would give such a gift,
especially of foods, waters, and juices.
"You should give cows; by that means, heaven shall be your food.
Having spoken thus to him, the Hotṛ departed for the hermitage of Badarī.
Then King Vinītāśva, intending to recount his own lineage,
proceeded to describe the acts of charity and other virtues performed by his ancestors.
By that means the king attained liberation in the eternal state of Brahman;
likewise, O Lakṣmī, this story was told by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī.
Since I have correctly proclaimed this to you here, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
the fruit of reciting or hearing it is equal to the merit of giving a cow.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of King Vinītāśva Performing the Hearing of the Rules for the Gift of the Twelve Rasas and Other Dhenu-offerings, Including the Kapila Cow," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the words spoken by Śaṅkara on the bank of the Narmadā,
between Kapilā and Amarā, in the midst of the Narmadā-omkāra.
"Wherever people may roam, there are indeed ten million sacred fords;
O auspicious lady, they are born as kings in the city of the Vidyādharas. (2)
Whatever gold, even the measure of a single *guñjā* seed, is given at Koṭitīrtha,
its value cannot be calculated until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*).
He who wraps the Sacrificial Mountain with thread on the sacred festival days is honored in the heavenly world for thousands of pairs of yugas.
A woman who possesses sons and is united with her husband should wear that [thread],
whether it be made of silk, woven silk, or highly radiant cotton.
And he who should make [the sacred thread] of nine strands, or of ten, twelve, eighteen, or even twenty-four strands; || 6 ||
One should tie a thread around a banyan tree, and there shall be the clearing of debts;
or whoever should wrap it with the syllable *Oṃ*, he indeed finds Kailāsa.
The thread-sacrifice shall then become fruitful;
one should thereafter feed ascetics, he who would otherwise wander the mountain of Śiva with physical hardship.
"Śaṅkara declared that for him there shall be the fruit of a sacrifice at every step;
indeed, the river Sarasvatī herself assumed the form of a female elephant."
He comes to bathe at Koṭitīrtha, and having bathed there,
he proceeds as far as the confluence of the Kāverī with the ocean.
In the meantime, indeed ten million holy sites (tīrthas) reside along the Narmadā,
while one million are situated between the Kāverī and the Paryaṅka mountain.
Having reached the great hermitage of Jamadagni on the Narmadā, one proceeds to Śrīkaṇṭha and Nīlakaṇṭha at Kanyātīrtha. ||12||
The Sūryapiṅgala-liṅga and the temple of Nārāyaṇa, as well as Lakṣmītīrtha and Satītīrtha, exist there as destroyers of sin. (13)
The meritorious mountain Amarakaṇṭaka is indeed the bestower of liberation;
by merely bathing in the Kāverī, people attain the supreme goal. 14.
That river which, indeed, became known by the name Kauberī due to the ascetic penance of Kubera, is celebrated as Kāverī, the river that effects the liberation of one's ancestors. 15.
With thousands of various mouths, Kāverī is considered a savior;
Narmadā is on the southern bank, at the Vindhya mountain during the Vārāha [kalpa]. (16)
The Payoṣṇī has emerged, the daughter of Candra, cool and exceedingly purifying;
born from the body of Varāha, she is the Somagaṅgā and the savior. ||17||
Having bathed there with devotion, a person shall indeed not be subject to rebirth;
at that confluence of the Payoṣṇī, there is the region known as Somāvarta. ||18||
There, it is impossible to calculate the number of those who bathe and give gifts;
the confluence of the Tāpī and Payoṣṇī is superior to Kurukṣetra by a hundredfold. (19)
Where the glorious Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, shines forth as the bestower of fruits— that is celebrated as the highly praised sacred field of Viṣṇu.
By offering a lamp on the full moon day of Kārttika, one becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) king;
and having pierced through the Revā, the river named Caṇḍavegā has issued forth.
Having bathed there, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are destroyed;
the great god Caṇḍeśvara dwells there as the destroyer of evil.
In former times, there was a king of the Lunar dynasty named Candrasena who was a doer of evil;
he was devoted to the wives of others, a thief, and a drinker of intoxicants. (23)
The virtuous Saudāminī by name, endowed with beauty, youth, and other such qualities, was the wife of Śāṇḍilya, who resided in the Naimiṣa forest. 24.
Candrasena beheld her wearing matted hair and bark garments;
he said to her, "Become my wife and enjoy abundant pleasures."
Having heard this, Saudāminī said, "O King, ask my husband, Śāṇḍilya. The king, utterly infatuated by her, questioned Śāṇḍilya.
If you give me your wife, who is now in the prime of her youth, today,
I shall give you as her price wealth by the hundreds of thousands.
The sage said: "O King, women are indeed rooted in deceit in every respect; no one is truly dear to them. Do as you wish. (28)
Then the king, blinded by lust, seized that virtuous woman by the hand;
she, however, spoke to the king in anger: "Today I am in my courses. (29)
"By my touch on this very day, you shall become a Caṇḍāla;
moreover, on the first day, you are considered equal to a Caṇḍāla woman when drenched in menstrual flow."
Although addressed thus, he forcibly touched her again with his own hand;
at that very moment, the king, who was terrifying to all, attained the state of a caṇḍāla.
In an instant, he became devoid of complexion and color, turning black;
and the king, having abandoned that virtuous woman, departed toward his own city.
And the inhabitants of Avadhī spoke among themselves, overcome with wonder: "How has the prince gone to the forest and attained the state of a caṇḍāla? (33)
Vasiṣṭha, however, said to the king, "Go back toward her indeed;
go and beg for forgiveness, and everything will become peaceful. (34)
Having bowed to that sage and having again bowed to the earth, the king departed;
and he repeatedly begged for forgiveness, while at that time the couple spoke as follows.
O King, proceed quickly to the confluence of the Caṇḍavegā;
having bathed there and worshipped Hari as Caṇḍeśvara, you will indeed attain [your goal]. (36)
Having heard that there was liberation from sin, the king went to the river Caṇḍavegā; having bathed there at Rekhā, he [worshipped] Hara and Hari.
He worshipped with supreme devotion and became free from sin;
in the end, he was also liberated through the power of Caṇḍavega.
Having ascended the divine vehicle, he went to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha;
through hearing and chanting as well, even terrible sin is destroyed. (39)
Then, on another day, there is another supreme holy site at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī and the Narmadā;
and there exists the Eraṇḍīśvara Liṅga, which destroys all sins.
Having anointed [the image] with saffron, one should worship it with fragrant flowers;
such a person rejoices in the presence of Śiva for a thousand divine years. 41.
In a former kalpa, Bhadra and Rudra were two Gandharvas;
having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, they went to the city of the Vidyādharas. 42.
Having likewise established Bhadreśvara and Rudreśvara, they departed for heaven;
thereafter, at one time, the sage Durvāsas, the king of sages, [arrived] for the sake of the satisfaction of his ancestors.
He wandered to all the sacred fords (tīrthas) and then arrived at Gayā;
there he offered funeral cakes (piṇḍas), as well as water, fruits, and flavorful juices.
He offered kuśa grass and sesame seeds there, but at that time the ancestors were not seen by the sage; then the sage himself spoke to the other sages.
"I have heard here that the ancestors take the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) with their hands;
today, however, O Lord, I do not see them, and thus my pilgrimage to sacred sites is fruitless. (46)
Having heard that, the sages said: "O Sage, one must wait for the day of the new moon;
on the new moon day, the ancestors receive the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) prepared for them. (47)
Indeed, Durvāsas remained there with faith until the time of the new-moon sacrifice;
nevertheless, he offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), yet the ancestors did not appear. ||48||
Then, having assumed physical forms, Durvāsas once again spoke to the sage named Eraṇḍa who was performing penance there.
"There can be no fulfillment of your purpose here; come indeed with me.
Having said this, he took the sage Eraṇḍa along and went to the Narmadā river.
Having arrived at Amarakaṇṭaka on the bank of the Ākāśagaṅgā, he stood there.
There he remembered his ancestors, and Brahmā himself arrived.
Then, having accepted the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered right there, he became satisfied;
Brahmā himself gave water, being satiated by the waters of the Narmadā.
Then the sage Durvāsas, having offered his wealth to Brahmā,
likewise held Eraṇḍaka upon his head.
The water from Brahmā’s water-pot fell to the earth from the top of an eranda tree, and its stream entered the waters of the Narmadā. ||54||
On the new moon day falling on a Monday, at the confluence of the Eraṇḍa and Revā rivers,
a great festival occurred at the sacred ford, which brings about the supreme liberation of one's ancestors.
Brahmā, being pleased, granted a boon on the banks of the Eraṇḍikā:
"The ancestors, remaining invisible, shall attain eternal satisfaction on the new-moon day. (56)
And even at Gayā, those who are invisible shall attain eternal satisfaction— those who are devoted to Viṣṇu, who are pure, and who observe the vow of Brahman.
The parents will always come within the range of vision of those sinless men who possess pure hearts; it shall never be otherwise. (58)
In this very way, the Araṇḍikā-tīrtha indeed became a confluence of the Revā;
by hearing of or glorifying it, there shall be the upliftment of those who visit the tīrtha of the ancestors.
Then there is another supreme tirtha belonging to the Revā and the Viśalyā,
where Bharata performed a sacrifice and [the arrows] became free from their shafts (viśalyakā).
The two rivers that had arisen entered the waters of the Narmadā;
indeed, the Asuras who were creators of obstacles fought with Bharata.
At that time, many asuras were destroyed by Bharata with his arrows,
for the sake of relieving the pain from the arrows of Bharata’s own warriors.
From the base of the sacrificial post, a river named Viśalyā emerged, which draws out all thorns;
having bathed there, Bharata and the others [performed] the sacrifice for Nārāyaṇa with horses.
They became free from pain and free from arrows, entirely sinless;
because of that, the two rivers are celebrated as Śalyā and Viśalyā.
That confluence, consisting of two currents, is struck together at the Narmadā;
this sacred ford on the bank of the Narmadā is supremely meritorious and purifying. (65)
When the Svāyambhuva Manvantara had arrived and the Kṛta Yuga of that first Kalpa had begun,
the gods, defeated by the Dānavas, took refuge on the banks of the Narmadā.
Those gods, together with Brahmā, sought refuge in the Lord;
then Bṛhaspati spoke to Brahmā, the Supreme Creator.
"Perform a most fierce sacrifice that will bring about the destruction of the Dānavas.
In the meantime, the gods went to the bank of the Narmadā.
Then, having pierced through the earth, a most brilliantly radiant Liṅga rose up;
it uttered the syllable *Oṃ* there and proclaimed the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
That mountain which has arisen from the mountain is called the Mountain of Oṃkāra;
then Śambhu, appearing in person, spoke these words to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"Perform a most fierce sacrifice that will bring about the destruction of the Daityas.
Thereupon, Brahmā performed a sacrifice for the peace of the gods.
Thus, broken by fear of him, they went to the netherworld (rasātala);
but by the power of the syllable Oṃ, the gods became fearless. (79)
Having worshipped Oṃkāra Śaṅkara, the gods and others went to heaven;
the great Liṅga, which endures until the end of the Kalpa, shines upon the mountain peak.
The five Brahmās have five faces and are endowed with nine powers;
the western face, Sadyojāta, resembles a conch, a kunda flower, and the moon.
From which the Ṛgveda emerged, Brahmā is the presiding deity there;
to the north is Vāmadeva, yellow-hued and most enchanting. (75)
Know that it originates from the Yajurveda; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity there.
Aghora, who has the luster of the color of clouds, is situated in the southern direction.
Know that which arises from the Sāmaveda to have the Sun as its deity and Time as its presiding power;
it should be known as Tatpuruṣa, resembling the reddish hue of saffron. (77)
The Atharvaveda has emerged as the fourth; there, the waters are the presiding deities (adhidevatās).
His face is that of Īśāna, five-colored and of great body.
The presiding deity there is Soma, whose music is established by the Vedas;
the sixth is named Sadāśiva, who is partless and free from all affliction.
Thus has this entire description of the syllable Om been told to you.
One should worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the form of Oṃkāra; one shall attain liberation.
One should provide the materials for the temple and the implements for worship;
one should cause the restoration of what is dilapidated and so forth, as well as the flagstaff, the bell, and other such items.
One should give garments, ornaments, mṛdaṅgas, and so forth to the embodiment of Oṃkāra;
one should offer gardens, groves, fields, and the like to him. (82)
It is impossible to calculate the measure of the fruit of that gift here;
the donor obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation—of this there is no doubt. ||83||
King Dhundhumāra, a worshiper of the gods and guests,
went to the Vindhya mountain and entered the forest of the Revā there.
He beheld a white-colored boar roaring;
just as he strove to slay it, at that very moment the boar also [attacked him]. (85)
Then he entered the water at Koṭitīrtha;
as he was thus entering, the king also followed behind him.
In that moment, Kroḍa’s body became divine and he ascended a celestial chariot;
seeing him in such a state, the king asked for the reason.
The divine Varāha, assuming a celestial form, said to the mountain:
"I am indeed a follower of Śambhu, known by the name Aṅgada, a skilled singer. (88)
Having seen Urvaśī and Rambhā as well, I became deluded by lust;
uttering the speech of a boar, I became entirely composed of amorous play. (89)
Seeing me, Nandin cursed me, saying, "Become a wild boar.
Being propitiated by me, Nandin granted a boon regarding the end of the curse.
By beholding Dhundhumāra and by resorting to Koṭitīrtha,
you shall abandon the womb of a pig and come to Kailāsa.
Having spoken thus and uttered the blessing "May it be well with you," the Gaṇa departed;
then the king sat down there upon the stone slab for a moment.
The king’s horse drank water from the Narmadā;
at that moment, it too became divine and stood in the sky, situated within a celestial chariot.
Having become a twice-born, he said to the king: "In former times, I was Gālava, a Brahman-sage in the Kuru field, [born] from the acceptance of the gift of horses. (94)
Having been consumed by attaining the body of Vāji through the yoga of Revā, I have attained liberation;
indeed, I am going to the true world of Brahmā, my own abode. 95.
O King, in the past, I accepted a gift from King Dumatsena.
It has been grasped due to the power of causes; listen, and I shall explain it to you.
The king of Madhyadeśa, having taken elephants, horses, chariots, and the like, as well as gold, jewels, garments, ornaments, and so forth, during the eclipse of the sun (97).
He arrived at Kurukṣetra in every way to offer gifts;
however, O Brahmins, having reflected upon the king’s terrible acceptance [of those gifts], [they hesitated].
Then the king did not accept [the advice], and he censured the Brahmins, saying:
"This place is unfit for Brahmins; it is devoid of sacred knowledge and unsuitable for officiating at sacrifices. (99)
"All the power of Brahmā was dormant; no worthy recipient of the gift was to be found.
Having heard the king's words, I manifested my power."
"I am Gālava; give me a gift, for I have the strength to accept it.
Then the king gave me various objects suitable for a kingdom. (101)
"I was born equal to a king, endowed with the enjoyments of sovereignty;
then the king departed, and I abandoned the *agnihotra* and other such rites. (102)
Having wandered among many pleasures, I died and became your horse;
now, having been released by the waters of the Revā, I am free—may prosperity be yours.
Having spoken thus, Gālava departed for his own true abode;
the king reflected, "Where indeed shall I go without the horse? (104)
Then a three-eyed young woman appeared before him in person and said to him:
"I am the river named Kapilā, whose waters flow within the Narmadā. (105)
And you, O King, having bathed here in my pool, drink this water;
having ruled your kingdom, go to heaven together with your harem and retinue. 106.
"O observer of noble vows, whatever desire you contemplate, that very thing you shall obtain.
Having spoken thus, that river Kapilā vanished from sight. (107)
Having prostrated before her, the king departed for his own city;
by hearing of her and by chanting her praises, one is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
Thus indeed was the greatness of the sacred ford (tīrtha) described by Śaṅkara to Śivā; that same supreme bestower of liberation has been told to you, O Lakṣmī. (109)

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wrapping of the Thread at Koṭitīrtha, the Piṅgala Liṅga of the Sun, the Abode of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Confluences of the Kāverī, Payoṣṇī, Somagaṅgā, and Caṇḍavegā, the Liberation of Candrasena from his Cāṇḍāla state, the Confluence of the Eraṇḍī, the Confluence of the Śalyā and Viśalyā, the Liberation of Dhundhumāra from his Boar-form, and the Liberation of Gālava from his Bird-form," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
By what various rites should a person perform actions,
so that even a householder may attain worldly enjoyment and liberation, thereby achieving success?

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, I shall tell you everything: even a householder who is devoted to his duties may attain the meaningfulness of his birth, even if he is possessed by desire, greed, and other such passions.

Having established the mind in Me, free from the notions of "mine" and "I," and always holding Me as the primary reality, one should be intent on forgiveness toward both the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer.
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and vegetables, and observing milk-vows and the like, [one should avoid] the sixth, the eighth, the new moon day, and the fourteenth of both fortnights. (4)
On days of religious observance, during festival times, on the twelfth lunar day, and at the time of ancestral rites or worship,
one should not engage in sexual intercourse, even when prompted by such specific occasions.
One should perform everything while remembering me;
indeed, if one acts for my sake, that person of firm vows should perform the rite through the application of yoga within me.
With a purified soul, endowed with dharma, and devoted to me with affection,
he experiences neither decay nor old age, nor delusion, passion, or envy.
He who creates an obstacle for me goes to the world of Yama;
yet, having performed my worship throughout his life, he is glorified in my abode.
Having heard this, Lakṣmī again questioned Puruṣottama:
"At what time is your worship to be performed, and how should it be done? Tell me in this matter. (9)
O Lord of Gods, what kind of ritual action is performed by you from time to time?
How is your installation here performed, as well as your invocation and dismissal?
O Hari, tell me what kind of incense and lamp you accept;
how do you receive the water for the feet, the vessel, and even the unguent? (11)
"O Blessed One, how do you accept seats, beds, vehicles, and roots, tubers, and fruits? And of what kind is the auspicious offering presented to you? (12)

What kind of action is appropriate in autumn? What kind of action is appropriate in the cool season? What kind of action is appropriate in spring? And what kind of action do you consider appropriate in summer? (1.3)
What rite should be performed during the rainy season, and what kind of practice should one undertake at its end? What flowers and fruits are to be enjoyed there? (14)
What is the authoritative measure for the image according to you, and what kind of installation is considered appropriate?
What should be its size, and what is the nature of the fast associated with it? (15)
Why do you take up yellow, red, or pale-pink garments? What kind of clothing is beneficial for them, and what form of dress is approved by you? (16)
In which substances do you consider the madhuparka to be mixed? What is the merit of giving the madhuparka, and what are its qualities like? (17)
To which worlds do those who consume the madhuparka go?
What should be the measure of the madhuparka and other offerings to be given previously? (18)
Which vegetables, grains, and even drinks are dear to you? By what ritual procedure is the offering for your consumption presented? (19)
Having worshipped you during the vow, so that there may be no transgression,
one should conduct oneself accordingly both in the worship and likewise in the touching.
What rites should one perform when eating the food of your devotee? How should the offering be presented to you, and what kind of vessel is prescribed? (21)
And who in this world enjoy that supreme, purifying grace of yours?
Those devotees who eat but once a day and worship Keśava. (22)
Those who dwell among your devotees constantly remember you;
O Lord, what is the destiny of those who practice devotion to you? (23)
Those who are devoted to the Kṛcchra and Sāntapana penances, or who subsist on air during their vows, touch upon the color black; what destination do they attain? (24)
And those devotees who abstain from pungent food and salt, who are intent on their duties, and who observe the vow of subsisting only on milk—what destination do they attain? (25)
Devoted to the service of cows, subsisting on a collection of cow's milk and other such products, and intent on the practice of gleaning, what kind of destination do these devotees attain? (26)
And those who live by begging, yet rely on the dharma of householders, being ever devoted to Mādhava—what destination do they attain? (27)
O Lord, what destination do those people attain who, having practiced the five-fire austerity, give up their lives in your sacred fields and holy fords? (28)
Those who died in the five fires, as well as those who died by leaping from a precipice, those who slept upon a bed of thorns, and those who remained lying in the open sky; ||29||
O Keśava, what destination do those who lie in the cow-pasture and remain on the path of devotion attain when they behold You?
They subsist on vegetables, on grain-husks, on cow-products, and on barley; they consume parched flour and worship you without interruption. (3.1)
Or even those followers who, intent on drinking milk, go to your abode carrying a lamp upon their heads—what destination do they attain? (32)
Holding a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, or even a piece of wood upon their heads, they perform service unto you; what destination do those followers attain? (33)
Having undertaken the vow of eating stones, those people constantly resort to it; they subsist on leaves and are devoted to performing circumambulations.
Those who practice their own dharma, who are devoted to serving virtuous women and holy men, and who crawl on their knees—those who go to your sacred field (kṣetra). ||35||
And as for those who go to your abode even by bowing down like a staff—what will be their destination, O God, in your world? (36)
Those who, having placed you upon your back, maintain a lamp for you, or even those who proceed with their faces turned downwards, go to your abode. (37)
O Nārāyaṇa, tell me: what is the perfected destiny for those who, having abandoned their sons, wives, and homes, have come to you for refuge? (38)
And when the life-force has departed, you are worshipped with the honey-mixture (madhuparka) in the burning fire, in the flowing water, and in the body which rests upon the earth. ||39||
Having attained perfect knowledge through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, what destination do they reach—
those who have offered their bodies to Your field and have resorted to the path of renunciation?
Constantly devoted to your name, [she recites] "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" and "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, Svāhā. (41)
And as for those men and women who are entirely devoted to the recitation of mantras and intent upon your Dharma—what kind of destiny is considered for them? (42)
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, those who are slain by weapons in battle chant Your names; what indeed will be their destination because of that proclamation of Your name? 43.
O Mādhava, what destination do those attain who, though meeting sudden death or even dying through possession, remain devoted to the remembrance of you?
I am established as your disciple and your servant through devotion;
indeed, I have spoken thus to you for the sake of bringing happiness to all the world.
This secret, joined with the Dharma and endowed with devotion to you, you ought to speak out after reflecting upon it for the sake of the world's welfare. (43)
Those men who are without women, and those women who are without men, have never attained satisfaction of desire; they are solely devoted to you.

And those people who die in this world unsatisfied, still possessing desires for objects of enjoyment—what destination do they attain? What of those who have renounced, such as widows and others? (48)

And what destination do women and men go to—those who have not attained the enjoyment of their desires, those who meet with death while still children, and those women who are devoted to servitude? (49)
They are devoted to your initiation and always subsist on alms from you;
they are intent upon your male and female devotees, and they have the power to fulfill their desires at will.
Devoted solely to love for those who are the objects of their affection, these Vaiṣṇavas—both men and women—do not go elsewhere. (51)
Out of a desire to attain you, they never long for anything else in their hearts;
such are the great devotees who offer up their very selves. (52)
O Mādhava, tell me what destination they attain—those who were teachers, kings of the world, householders, and enveloped in enjoyments. (53)
And what destination do those followers go who are submerged in sense objects?
Even though this is a supreme secret, tell me that out of affection for me. (54)
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
the Lord who is devoted to his own dharma, spoke those duties to Lakṣmī.
O Lakṣmī, listen to that which you ask, which brings happiness:
my devotees do not indeed suffer distress in any way whatsoever due to my conduct. (56)
I am not satisfied by a thousand gifts, nor even by a hundred sacrifices;
nor am I pleased by wealth, but I am pleased by love alone.
O Mādhavī, I am always pleased with him who worships me while fixing his mind upon me; my devotee is free from many faults. (58)
Those women and men devoted to me who worship me with devotion—at midnight, in the darkness, at midday, or in the afternoon—[attain my state]. (59)
My mind, established upon my form, does not attend to anything else; my life-breaths are attached to my body, and my hair is intent on me alone. (1.565.60)
They were thirsty for me, they dwelt with me, they were devoted to my body;
they partook of my betel-rolls and they kissed me.
They slept by my side, intent on ascending with me;
through the meditation of contact with my body, they maintained the concentration that brings liberation. ||62||
Devoted solely to action within me, they perceive only me;
having attained their goal and recognizing my qualities, they remain firmly established in devotion to me.
These people dwell in my world; they stay by my side and have taken refuge in me.
Those men and women who follow me find delight upon my bed. (64)
O my beloved Lakṣmī, I am not attained by very little;
for one who performs worship for but a moment, I, Nārāyaṇa, am difficult to reach. 65.
O Mādhavī, they perform my rites, behold me, and are established in devotion to me—even those who are likewise intent upon their own self-interest. (66)
O beloved, having observed a fast on the twelfth lunar day and being devoted with supreme faith, I grant them worlds such as heaven for the sake of their enjoyment.
In the morning, one should offer a handful of water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) to the Sun;
saying "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa," one should gaze at the Sun in the sky.
As many subtle drops as fall from the water held in one's cupped hands,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
Those people who worship me on the twelfth lunar day with white flowers, who incense me with fragrant incenses, and who remember me, having placed me within their hearts; ||1.565.70||
"Salutations be to Viṣṇu; accept this, O Blessed One, and may you be pleased with me.
Salutations be to you; accept this food and may you be pleased; drink this water. (71)
Thus, one should worship me with love and listen to my scriptures;
such a person shall indeed go to my world and be born as four-armed.
Śyāmāka, wheat, mung beans, śāli rice, barley, as well as nīvāra and kaṅguka—this food of munis is always characterized by sattva. (73)
Having offered me the food oblation, one who is devoted to me should eat;
whatever actions one performs, one should do them being intent on devotion to me. (74)
Devoted to the six duties and free from the sense of "I" and "mine," having abandoned both gain and loss, he subsists on alms with his senses conquered. (75)
He is devoted to his duty, free from backbiting, impartial in accordance with the scriptures, and does not possess the immature mindset of the elderly or the childish. ||76||
The Brahmin, having likewise become such, goes to me, the supreme imperishable;
having attained my very form, he enjoys pleasures together with me.
A Kṣatriya who is heroic in generosity, established in accordance with Dharma, skilled in sacrifices, pure, and devoted to my rites. (78)
He is free from the egoism of "mine" and "I," recognizes merit, remains impartial, speaks little, possesses great knowledge, is without malice, and avoids the censurable. (79)
Skilled in rising to greet others and other such virtues, always dear to the devotees of the Lord, and free from backbiting and deceit—he who remembers me constantly. (1.565.80)
And he who constantly worships me goes to my abode;
even a Vaiśya, established in devotion to me, remains intent upon his daily duties. ||81||
Equanimous toward gain and loss, peaceful, and free from the delusions of "mine" and "I," he approaches his wife only during her fertile period and is always affectionate toward his devotees. (82)
To him who constantly honors his guru and is devoted to my worship, I am never lost, and he is never lost to me. (83)
The Śūdra, having become my servant, performs his work as a slave;
the husband and wife are devoted to me and dedicated to my service. (84)
Both were devotees of the Lord, devoted to me, established in their duties, knowing the proper place and time, and free from passion and darkness. (85)
They were empty of the notions of "I" and "mine," adorned with faith and discipline, pure in soul, free from greed and delusion, and devoted to honoring guests. (86)
Constantly intent on prostrations and devoted to my service, they worshiped me alone and beheld the vision of the God. ||87||
Constantly devoted to meditation and filled with a sense of servitude toward me, a Śūdra or a Śūdrī should likewise perform my work. ||88||
Having abandoned thousands of sages, I worship my devotee, the Śūdra;
having renounced gain and loss, and having cast aside delusion and desire. (89)
He who constantly contemplates me as being eternally free from cold and heat, and neither in the bitter nor the pungent, nor in the sweet, the sour, the alkaline, nor the astringent; || 1.565.90 ||
Occasionally feeling a longing for savory foods—whether to be licked, sucked, chewed, or drunk—he should support his wife, son, and family while remaining solely devoted to me. (91)
Always devoted to fortitude and faith, loathing other activities,
he is forever free from the latent impressions of childhood, youth, and old age.
Having very few enjoyments, he maintains only what is necessary for the sustenance of his body;
he is compassionate toward all sentient beings and likewise intent on rising to greet them. ||93||
Maintaining especially the vow of silence, he always worships me;
the observer of the vow eats only after others have been fed and given food. (94)
Moreover, devoted to the performance of his duties, Manaścara remained by my side;
at the proper time, having voided urine and excrement, he was intent upon bathing. (95)
Always devoted to my service regarding flowers, incense, and perfumes, he subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits, and ate a meal of barley and parched grain. ||96||
At the sixth time, at the ninth time, and at the tenth fortnight—thus, for my sake, one undergoes these actions throughout seven births. (97)
For my sake, they have renounced all worldly ties and are solely devoted to renunciation;
these virtuous women, delighting in renunciation, live their lives for the purpose of serving me. (98)
Even practitioners of yoga always behold those men and women who possess great initiation at the break of dawn. (99)
Whoever performs their duties according to the method thus described,
him I indeed protect at my side, just as I do you, my beloved.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Dwelling in the Abode of Śrī Hari and Other Matters," following Lakṣmī’s questions regarding the actions of all [beings] through their Mahābhāgavata rites, and the subsequent performance of those actions characterized by both action and renunciation, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the procedure for all the questions you have asked—such as how and when worship should be performed; I shall now relate the method.
My worship should be performed with the sixteen secondary substances at dawn during the Brāhma-muhūrta, as well as at midday and in the evening. || 2 ||

One should perform the ceremonial bathing, the offering of food, the circumambulation with lamps, the decoration and so forth, as well as the drinking of water, the offering of betel leaf, and the presentation of handfuls of flowers.
During the cold season, one should offer blankets and the like, as well as warm water and so forth,
along with delicious foods that provide strength and nourishment.
O beloved, during the rainy season, food that is neither hot nor cold, as well as water and clothing,
along with nourishing meals, should then be given to me.
And during the time of the heat, cool and fragrant water,
fine garments and the like, as well as cooked food, edibles, fruits, and so forth, should be given.
And at that time, the ritual installation (sthāpana) should be recited: "Come, O Lord, O Beloved;
having taken your seat upon a throne of gold and other precious materials, accept my worship."
"Come, O Blessed One, O Lord, O Nārāyaṇa, O Master, O Sovereign!
Having accepted this worship, you must go to your own abode, and not otherwise."
O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Master, accept this incense, prepared from the powder of wood and other materials, and mixed with fragrant juices. 9.
O Supreme Lord, accept this ghee lamp which possesses cooling qualities;
with devotion, I offer this ghee lamp and sandalwood incense.
I offer a lamp of sesame oil and incense of guggulu;
or else, at the proper time, I take up the fragrant essence of flowers.
Having collected waters from sacred fords, my feet should be washed according to the season; I accept this purification of my feet.
The ceremonial bathing with the waters of sacred fords, and the massaging with curd, milk, clarified butter, honey, sugar, and oil.
A cleansing powder that is unctuous, white, and pacifying should be applied;
and an ointment should likewise be given to my body, especially where it is suitable. (14)
O beloved, I always accept with devotion sandalwood, the essence of flowers, and ointments such as Viṣṇutaila when offered by my devotees.
I shall accept the golden lion-throne and other items, as well as the woolen seat; and having sat upon the wooden plank, I shall undergo the consecration.
O Lakṣmī, I accept with devotion that which is given by a man or a woman upon a wide, soft, and beautiful couch or a delightful cushioned seat covered with a rug. (17)
It was joined with two sides, provided with two cheeks, endowed with two eyes,
adorned with a pillow, and furnished with a covering against gadflies.
I always sleep upon a lotus adorned with a hidden thread;
my vehicle is yoked with swans, horses, and graced by elephants and the like.
I carry either Garuḍa, whose form is fashioned of gold, who travels through the sky and is most great, or Māṇikī, or a divine chariot.
I accept bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth that are fragrant and flavorful, ripe and produced in their proper season, with a spirit of devotion. (21)
In a golden vessel, which is a vessel of love, the auspicious, consecrated [food] was offered—
just as one’s own [is offered] in the autumn, and just as one’s own [is offered] in the winter.
Just as it pleases him in spring, just as it pleases him in summer, and just as it pleases him in the rainy season and at the end of the rains. (23)
That which is to be enjoyed, worn, drunk, chewed, as well as clothing, ornaments, water, vehicles, mounts, and the like, wind, swings, forests, and so forth—[all these are perceived]. (24)
A dwelling, a bed, water, a couch, a female attendant, and so forth—all such things should be provided for me; they must be given in this manner and not otherwise. (25)
O beloved, just as it is done for the body, so too must the offering be made for the deity;
an image measuring more than six finger-breadths is considered auspicious.
It should not be recommended to be longer than sixty-four finger-breadths;
the foundation in the temple and the arrangement of the eyes should be equal.
The ground level for the eye-line should be four-fifths higher than the door; it is my opinion that the installation of the image should be done in such a manner. 28.
O beloved, having placed gold, jewels, and other precious materials beneath the image within the interior of the lion-throne,
the image of Śrī Hari should be installed there in the sanctum.
The Lord should be placed on the right, while on the left are Śrī Rādhikā, Śivā,
Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, Haṃsā, Prabhā, Pārvatī, and Mañjulā.
Jayā, Lalitā, Śāntā, Sarasvatī with her mind, Durgā, Gaṅgā, Kamalā, Sāvitrī, and likewise Virajā. ||3.1||
Any other [line] desired by the devotee that is dear to Śrī Hari may also be established;
it should indeed be sloping toward the ears, according to what is beautiful to behold. (32)
On the previous day, it should be the *nakta* (nocturnal) rite; *nakta* occurs prior to sunset. On the second day, the consumption [of food] should not take place by day or night.
The fasting from leaves, flowers, fruits, food, and so forth is what is traditionally known as *upoṣaṇa*.
Taking a single meal, subsisting on fruit, or subsisting on water does not constitute a violation. ||34||
In the spring, white garments; in Phālguna, saffron flowers;
likewise in Āṣāḍha, safflower-dyed ones; and in Āśvina, golden-colored ones. (35)

O beloved, at festivals and other occasions they are multicolored, but at all times they are of a single color; moreover, O dear one, I wear them adorned with the splendor of gold, silver, and the like.
It is held that all clothing, except for that dyed with mercury (lohātāra), brings about welfare;
red cloth is considered to bring prosperity, and yellow cloth is considered to bestow fortune.
White is considered to be the producer of knowledge and eternally variegated as the bestower of enjoyment;
blue is strictly forbidden here and should never be worn at any time.
Madhuparka is considered to consist of jaggery and clarified butter, or sugar and clarified butter,
or likewise sugar mixed with milk, or pieces of sugar-candy and curd.
That which brings peace to the digestive fire within the house when one has consumed a drink sweetened with honey or any other sweet beverage is considered *madhuparka*. (1.566.40)
The mango juice and so forth, ghee, and sugar—these three, along with sweet fruit and sweets, mixed together, constitute the madhuparka. ||41||
"Give me what is appropriate for me, something cool that brings me benefit;
by the offering of madhuparka, there shall be prosperity both here and in heaven. (42)
For the donor who constantly gives the merit of food, drink, and so forth, there appear in his house streams of ghee, streams of honey, and streams of curd. (43)
Rivers of milk, rivers of curd, and rivers of water come into being;
wherever those streams exist in the world, there go those who bestow honey.
As much honey as is required to pacify the stomach should be given—sweet and satisfying—by which the eternal worlds are attained. 45.
All these indeed become givers of nectar and givers of essence to the donor;
likewise, vegetables such as the pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa) and others are entirely of the nature of sattva.
Eggplants, gillikā and other such milky plants, as well as tāndūla and other leaves, and the petals of mustard and similar flowers; ||47||
O beloved, I am fond of cucumbers, bottle gourds, and long peppers, as well as those gentle tubers and roots that exist. (48)
Śrīkhaṇḍa, milk-pudding (pāyasa), and other auspicious boiled items, as well as kvathikā, rājikā, rāddha, and āranāla—these too [should be offered]. 49.
Garmarī, maricika, tiktaka, karavīra, and mangoes—
such delightful things as these are always dear to me.
"Enjoy at your pleasure this sweet and desired food, served slowly and in abundance, which bestows tranquility;
O Lord Keśava, eat the cooked foods and other delicacies according to your liking. (51)
In this manner he should feed me and fan me with a breeze;
then, out of love, the devotee should serve food into my bowl once again. (52)
In this manner, one should always feed [the deity], having placed me upon a golden seat;
having filled a golden vessel with water, [one should offer it] into a vessel such as a golden bowl.
Having served everything with love, he should give water to drink,
offer auspicious betel leaf, and perform a massage of the feet.
May it be so that they do not commit any offense against my worship;
may no one with an impure body ever touch me without having first bathed. (55)
One should not approach me while staying in the temple like a mute;
indeed, a mute person must not awaken me without the sounding of bells and other instruments.
One should never awaken me at an improper time or without restraint; nor should one cause me to keep watch for the sake of a merchant, a common person, or a king. (57)
One should never worship for one's own sake, nor should one ever show one's back; nor should one sneeze, engage in dispute, or abandon the bounds of propriety. (58)
One should not go to my temple while wearing unwashed clothes, nor after touching an impure object without having washed one's hands. 59.
"He shall not touch me, nor shall he touch my belongings;
having scratched himself, he shall never touch me. (1.566.60)
One should certainly not harbor even an evil intention while in my house;
during my worship, one should not eat oneself, nor drink even water and the like.
One should not worship like a mute person without my shouting;
furthermore, one must cast away my remaining garlands and materials with one's hand.
One should not touch new objects without having first washed them; nor should one discharge phlegm, flatulence, or similar waste within the temple. (63)
If one should void urine or the like, one must bathe and then touch me;
while engaged in my worship, one must not be intent on any other activity. (64)
One should not become dejected in mind, nor should one consume foul-smelling things;
one should not drink impure substances, nor should one be intent on violence. ||65||
One should not forcibly compel me to accept gifts such as clothing or ornaments;
rather, one should act in a manner that is favorable to me, just as it would be for oneself in regard to cold, heat, and other conditions.
One should perform the washing of the face, the rubbing with oil, and the application of sandalwood paste as is appropriate, and not excessively, so that it does not cause distress.
When it is cold, let him not perform my worship with fire to an excessive degree;
he should always effect an exchange for me regarding the wearing of garments. (68)
One should indeed change the ornaments worn on the body;
one should not utter insults, nor speak in disparagement of others, nor engage in vulgar conversation. (69)
One should not sleep naked in the middle of the temple, nor should one remain naked in the temple;
one should not sit with me on the back while facing toward the faces of people.
One should not enter the interior of the temple without first washing one's feet;
nor should one touch the *ārātrika* lamp or the ritual lamp without having used water for purification. (71)
Let the washing of my hands not touch me at all, nor any vessel;
let no one else enter, nor any woman, into the interior of the temple. (72)
One whose mouth or hands are soiled with food remnants should never enter the temple;
nor should one enter after having removed garlands, flowers, and the like, except at the specific moment of their removal.
Even if he were a lord of the earth, he should not give it to another person;
rather, having removed it on the preceding day, he should protect it and then give it. (74)
Or, having placed it in his hand, he should grant a temporary favor;
however, he must never raise the curtain again in the middle, nor should he let it fall in the midst while standing before the spectators. (75)
Having filled the conch with water and indeed lit a beautiful lamp, and having taken a cloth suitable for wiping and a vessel filled with fragrant substances; //76//
Having struck the bell, one should then perform the circumambulation with lamps;
at my time, when I am in the form of a naked image, one must never open the door.
When putting on clothes, ornaments, and so forth, one should perform the closing of the door;
one should indeed remove dust, dirt, and swarms of insects at every moment.
One should never open the temple doors at night after retiring for the night, nor before morning, nor during the midday period, unless there is an emergency.
Likewise, one should not open it even at midday, for there would be hardship within;
at the time of eating, one should utter the proclamation of the meal accompanied by musical instruments.
The unconditioned, the impure, that which lacks sattva such as the sky and so forth, ornaments such as necklaces and the like, and even food—[these are all considered] stainless. (81)
One should neither hold nor offer water or other weapons and such; nor should one cultivate a mental conception regarding mountains or the forms of minerals. 82.
I exist as the divine in every way, all-pervading and the inner self;
omniscient and abiding in all things, I behold [the world] while established within forms.
Indeed, one-pointedness of mind must be diligently protected during worship, especially regarding the activities of all the sense faculties toward my image. (84)
Sweet and pleasing food should be given to my devotee at his meal;
just as I am treated with great honor, so should my people be treated. (85)
O beloved, I eat there especially delicious food;
it is an excellent meal consisting of wheat, *kaṅku*, barley, and other grains. (86)
For my sake, having prepared auspicious cooked food, it must indeed be offered;
a new vessel made of gold or other metals must indeed be given to me. (87)
My devotees, the followers of the Bhāgavata, have become worthy recipients of my compassion;
adorned with garlands of Tulasī, they are fit to partake of my grace. 88.
Men and women who are initiated and joined with the great mantra, as well as those devotees who offer themselves, are worthy of consuming the food offering (naivedya). ||89||
For those residents among my exclusive devotees who are practitioners of the yoga of devotion,
their destination in my world is equal to mine, in the form of the Four-Armed One.
If people who perform ascetic vows such as the *kṛcchra* desire worldly enjoyments, they go to the great heaven, even to the world of Vairāja. (91)
Those who observe vows, abstaining from pungent and salty foods, and are devoted to my rites,
go indeed to Satyaloka, even if they always desire worldly enjoyments.
If my devotees, who are devoted to the service of cows, are great bhāgavatas, then those people go to my eternal abode, Goloka. 93.
Devotees who are intent on the practice of gleaning, free from attachment, and devoted solely to their daily journey, go indeed to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (94)
Those householders who subsist on alms, who are devoted to me, and who are virtuous,
go to my eternal abode— the imperishable, immortal, and undecaying.
Whoever is deprived of life in my house, or in the field near it, or in my temple or shrine, goes to my imperishable state. (96)
My devotees who perform the austerity of fire, being full of longing, indeed go to heaven;
those ascetics likewise go to the world of the Sun and to the abode of Indra.
Those who subsist on vegetables and the like, being solely devoted to me, go to my world called Amṛta; of this there is no doubt. (98)
Those who are devoted to the offering of lamps, those who are intent on austerity and have taken refuge in me, and those who give leaves, flowers, and so forth—they go to my supreme state. (99)
Those who are most righteous and devoted to the service of the virtuous indeed come to my abode;
my devotees, traveling on their knees, go to the supreme imperishable realm.
Even those who sleep on their backs and such attain the supreme divine state;
by renouncing everything, my virtuous ones indeed become of my own nature.
Wherever my body may be situated, those who fix their minds upon me go by their own selves to my world, the station resorted to by Rādhā and Lakṣmī.
Those who renounce, as well as followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, indeed become four-armed Viṣṇus; they are liberated and assume my own form—of this there is no doubt.
Men and women who perform the recitation of "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya" go to my supreme abode, which is beyond the imperishable (Akṣara). 104.
Even those who have been slain by weapons, if they are devoted to me with full devotion,
indeed become my eternal attendants in the imperishable abode.
If those who dwell within my heart should meet with sudden death, they attain the supreme goal by remembering me for even a single moment. (106)
Neither the groups of men nor the women who follow me depart unsatisfied;
they go to the worlds of the lords, served by ten million maidens.
Those intent on initiation go to the supreme abode and attain the state of the Great Self;
even householders, though rich in the enjoyment of desires, attain the transcendent state if they are devotees.
In the worlds, those free from feverish distress— whether they be renunciants, widows, and the like, or devotees desiring their heart's wishes— are [liberated] through Māyā and Pradhāna.
They are born in the abode as forms of Viṣṇu and forms of Ramā;
they enjoy happiness for millions of kalpas in Vikuṇṭha.
Men and women who are devoted to me with affection and great longing shall indeed become my wives, having attained eternal liberation.
Even those who were spiritual teachers and householders have become forms of Kṛṣṇa;
they enjoy all pleasures in Goloka, rejoicing in eternal bliss.
Thus, O sinless Lakṣmī, that which was asked by you has been told by me;
by reading or hearing this, one shall indeed attain the state of Śaṅkara.
One will undoubtedly attain the state of either Brahmā or Viṣṇu;
furthermore, O Pārvatī, I shall also relate what was told by Śaṅkara to her.
That which was asked by the bear at the root of the Narmadā brings auspiciousness;
for devotees, both suffering and happiness are merely conceptualizations of the mind alone.
Indeed, for the sake of the enjoyment of my devotees at the end [of time], I have created countless abodes, such as Goloka and others within the Imperishable Realm (akṣara), which are full of bliss.
My pairs of male and female devotees, who are solely intent on devotion to me,
remain among these by my will for as long as their enjoyment does not cease.
Indeed, upon the cessation of the pleasures of enjoyment and satisfaction in the imperishable abode,
those couples truly become intent upon my own essential nature.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Resolution Regarding the Destiny of Devotees and Other Matters," concerning the various questions posed by Śrī Lakṣmī, within the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how people indeed experience miseries without devotion;
likewise, I shall describe their happiness in every way through my yoga.
Perplexed by manifold thoughts, enveloped by the ego-sense "I am," with senses unsubdued and still longing for desires—what indeed could be more painful than that? (2)
Dissatisfied and excessively greedy, he causes agitation and affliction;
with his heart dragged by latent impressions (vāsanā), what indeed could be more miserable than that? (3)
One whose self is unpurified, devoid of dharma, and bereft of compassion and charity, is likewise deprived of fortune and enjoyment; what indeed could be more miserable than that? (4)
Disease, delusion, old age, and exhaustion; being armed with weapons, deceiving others, and inflicting suffering upon others—if these exist, what indeed could be more miserable than that? (5)
If one is devoid of the act of worshipping me, shuns the service of the virtuous, and becomes a source of affliction in his own home—what indeed could be more painful than that? (6)
"There is no god, nor indeed is there dharma; the next world does not exist, and one does not believe in rebirth—what indeed could be more miserable than that? (7)
What indeed could be more painful than this: that a person, despite having the means and proper hospitality, does not seek refuge in me? (8)
What indeed could be more painful than for one who does not take refuge in me—one who eats all things, sells all goods, and is devoid of humility? (9)
If one eats even before one's own kin, without first giving to a guest who has arrived or a visitor,
and thus creates a division in the cooking— what indeed could be more miserable than that?
One who torments others, is never content, is dull-witted, and is a reviler of the gods—being devoid of merit at the very root of decline, what indeed could be more miserable than that? (11)
Indeed, having failed to attain one's own welfare and having failed to burn away evil deeds, what could be more painful than falling under the power of the time of death? 12.
Even while possessing a kingdom, when one has fallen helplessly into the hands of the messengers of Yama, one undergoes the suffering of a messenger; what indeed could be more painful than that? (13)
Leaving behind elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, armies, and circles of servants, one departs helplessly; what indeed could be more painful than that? (14)
Some eat intoxicants, some eat rice, ghee, and the like;
some eat dry food, and others even eat tubers and fruits. (15)
Some enjoy beds covered with excellent cloths and well-adorned, while others sleep upon blades of grass; thus they do not bring themselves under their own control.
Death is common to all; it does not abandon one person and spare another.
Knowing this, they do not resort to me—what indeed could be more painful than that? (17)

One is seen to be handsome, while another is deformed and hunchbacked; one possesses virtues, while another is devoid of them; yet all share the same equality in the mere nourishment of their bellies.
One is learned yet like a mute, and another is not at all; indeed, no one here is eternal.
Having known me, he does not worship me—what indeed could be more painful than that?
Some miserly people remain deprived of enjoyments even while possessing wealth;
yet a generous person, despite being in poverty, is intent upon great expenditure. || 1.567.20 ||
