Even so, at the end of the year, the house of both is empty;
what is the fruit of that wealthy man, and what is the fruit of the poor man? (21)
In the absence of charity, sacrifice, and other such merits, what indeed could be more painful than that?
At that time, a person becomes possessed of two wives or even many wives. (22)
And whenever he was dissatisfied with one and praised another, that one woman there would always be ill-fated and intent on cursing him. (23)
Wealth brings the taint of curses and causes destruction in the next world;
knowing this, he still serves me—what indeed could be more painful than that? (24)
Those born into noble families and provided with all means of accomplishment yet commit sinful deeds—what indeed could be more miserable than that? (25)
Having attained human consciousness endowed with all forms of knowledge, they do not take refuge in me alone; what indeed could be more painful than that? (26)
Having performed extensive deeds while being solely intent on his own self-interest,
he falls into perverted views and is born for the sake of suffering.
Suffering is that which is contrary to one's own will; happiness is conformity to one's own will.
And for the self, the supreme suffering is the lack of eternal bliss. (28)
Indeed, that eternal happiness which is described as attainable by a human being after death through [right] action—if that is not obtained, then birth is in vain. (29)
While living, he is joined with suffering; even when dead, he partakes in suffering again.
His birth has passed in vain; what indeed could be more miserable than that? 1.567.300.
Having worshipped me and offered a distinguished oblation of food, he then eats the remaining meal; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (31)
Those who approach me at the three times of day, behold my image, and offer me devotion with love—what indeed could be more blissful than that? (32)
Having divided the food among the deities, guests, mortals, and cows, the master of the house eats afterwards, after [those] who have taken refuge [with him]. (33)
Deprived of hope, they do not depart; satisfied, they go away because of his giving.
For one who conducts himself in this manner, what indeed could be more blissful than that? (34)
That single day which occurs month after month and is called the new moon (amāvāsya), on which the ancestors are satisfied—what indeed could be more blissful than that? (35)
And for one who gives milk-rice to virtuous people at the beginning of a meal and so forth, with a face whose expression remains unchanged—what indeed could be more blissful than that? (36)
Even among many wives, he whose mind does not waver bestows equal happiness upon them all; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (37)
One whose inner self is pure should observe the vow of non-violence, abandoning anger;
upon seeing a beautiful form, an object of enjoyment, or the like, he does not fixate his gaze upon it. (38)
With a peaceful soul, free from desire and free from delusion in every respect, he looks upon gold as if it were a clod of earth; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (39)
And if one's life departs while engaged in worship, if death occurs for the sake of the deity, what indeed could be more blissful than that? (1.567.40)
One should never do what is contemptible, but should certainly strive for one's own liberation;
being content whether gain or loss occurs, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
For women, the husband is always their vow personified;
she who conducts herself in accordance with her husband is a devoted wife (pativratā). ||42||
Likewise, a devoted wife is the very embodiment of her husband's vow;
by pleasing his wife, a husband lives as a bestower of happiness. (43)
If a husband and wife are full of love for one another, what indeed could be more blissful than that? So too is the person who is both wealthy and possessed of disciplined conduct. (44)
If one were to have their senses restrained, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
For such a person endures insults and remains ever dejected in times of calamity.
What indeed could be more blissful than this:
that water is available for free and food is obtained through begging? (46)
There is no anxiety regarding the protection of wealth; what indeed could be more blissful than this—a body free from disease and a digestive fire that blazes brightly? (47)
It indeed cooks both the ripe and the unripe; what, then, could be more blissful than that?
It does not distress with excessive cold, nor does it overwhelm with heat. (48)
What indeed could be more blissful than making one's dwelling in a tree sheltered from the wind?
One's true kin are all people everywhere, and the Supreme Lord is the ultimate support. (49)
What indeed could be more blissful than the constant contemplation of Śrī Hari,
for whom the home belongs to another, who dwells in a cave-like abode, and who is free from all affliction?
His nourishment is like that of a cuckoo, his feeding like that of a parrot, and his devotion is innate;
what indeed could be more blissful than that? (51)
Whether with desire or without desire, for one who has made my abode his home, what indeed could be more blissful than to be separated from life? (52)
What happiness indeed could there be greater than for one who looks upon their mother, father, wife, teacher, deity, and children as if they were a god? (53)
Peace, knowledge, discernment, freedom from agitation, discrimination, fortitude, stability, and desirelessness—what indeed could be more blissful than that? (54)
The wise devotee of the Lord, pure and stainless, should worship Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the gods, and prostrate himself on the ground like a staff. 55.
Placing his joined palms upon his head, he should say to Hari, "Be gracious";
he should daily ask Hari for forgiveness—what indeed could bring greater happiness than that? (56)
He should give me an ointment, or he should provide a massage with oil;
he should anoint my entire body and even my head with ghee. (57)
Likewise, for as many drops of oil as there are in that which is being poured out,
for so many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
Then the person attains the blissful worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds;
thereafter, he finds Me, the Supreme Person, who am designated as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
And let him give me an ointment for rubbing the body, by which my limbs may be purified;
namely, *pippalikā*, *madhuka*, *aśvaparṇa*, and *karkaṭa*.
The auspicious powder of these [ingredients] brings comfort to my limbs;
having thus performed the dry massage (udvartana), one should rub [the body] very gently.
A devotee should, in every way, cleanse my hands with his own hand;
thereafter, [he should apply] an *āmalaka* fruit and excellent fragrant powder.
Having massaged all my limbs, that one of firm vows performed a cleansing with either alkaline substances, oils, perfumes, or medicinal pills. (63)
One should cause me, who bring happiness, to be bathed with streams of water;
thereafter, one should offer fragrance, as well as the essence of flowers and so forth.
One should cause offerings of garlands and handfuls of flowers that are fit for ritual action to be presented;
thereafter, one should offer me incense mixed with fragrant substances. (65)
Afterwards, he should give me a garment—either white or yellow linen;
then, having given me ornaments, he should prepare a seat for me.
Afterwards, having given food, one should then consume the *prasāda*;
thereafter, one should give me water, excellent betel-leaf, and my bedding and so forth. (67)
In this manner, one should offer devotion to me and perform the massaging of my feet;
one should delight me with stories and conversation, and likewise make me laugh and laugh oneself.
It would bring me joy; what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Whether a male or female devotee, one who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa should perform the offering of all one's possessions.
And Kṛṣṇa indeed bestows all that fruit upon him in Goloka;
when such a gain beyond liberation is attained, what indeed could be more blissful than that?
He served Kṛṣṇa like Rādhā, Nārāyaṇa like Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara like Pārvatī, and the Lord Bhāskara like Prabhāvatī. (71)
He serves his Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, like a ruby in His abode; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (72)
O beloved, those who indeed worship me according to this ritual procedure shall attain supreme, eternal perfection, having reached my own abode. 73.
O lady of beautiful hips, I alone am the eternal one among all beings;
I am established below, above, across, in the corners, and overhead. (74)
I am in the man, the woman, and the maiden; in the widow and in one overcome by old age; in the body and in the embodied soul; in the child, the youth, and the one dwelling in the womb.
Whoever should know me thus, worshipping me with total devotion, for him there is victory in saṃsāra; what indeed could be more blissful than that? (76)
Listen, O daughter of the ocean, to that by which one indeed does not enter the womb:
even after performing extensive deeds, one does not praise oneself. (77)
He performs all actions with a truly pure inner self;
endowed with sovereignty, he becomes capable of bestowing grace and other such powers. //78//
Established in the dark dharma, he discerns what ought and ought not to be done, and likewise endures cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, and thirst. (79)
Possessing black wealth, free from laziness, truthful in speech, and without malice,
he was constantly devoted to celibacy and likewise intent upon his own wife.
He was of truthful conduct, pure in soul, and always dear to the Blessed One;
he shared his wealth with others, possessed discernment, and was devoted to the virtuous and deeply affectionate toward them.
Speaking kindly to devotees and solely intent upon my service—he who is such a devotee of mine does not go to a base womb. (82)
He who does not desire heaven and the like, who abstains from violence toward living beings, and who acts for the welfare of all creatures, goes to my world. ||83||
Endowed with equanimity toward all things, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
he remained patient and self-controlled even while in his youth, delighting in what is auspicious.
When harm is done by another, he does not take it to heart at all;
rather, he remembers my service and speaks the truth regarding me. (85)
He who has turned away from falsehood and is firmly resolved upon truth,
who always abides in the excellence of silence, and who does not cast aspersions even behind one's back— (86)
One who desires offspring should approach his wife during her fertile period, not out of lust;
such people as these are auspicious and devoted to me. (87)
They do not go to dwell in a womb; rather, they go to dwell in my refuge.
One should act with firm resolve by oneself, having designated me as the witness. (88)
One should not engage in the doctrines of others, one should avoid deceit and dishonesty, and, established on my path of Dharma, one should not disparage religious acts. 89.
If one endowed with these qualities performs service unto me, he attains me alone; what indeed could be more blissful than that?
Furthermore, O Lotus-born one, I shall speak of another matter; listen to me, my beloved, by which means men cross the ocean of the cycle of existence within the womb. 9.1.

Those who have conquered their senses and subdued their anger, who are free from greed and delusion, who always act for their own spiritual benefit, and who are dear to the gods, guests, and gurus; ||92||
Those who constantly worship Kapilā, as well as those who perform pilgrimages to sacred fords, those who honor virtuous men and women, and those who show respect to the elderly; ||93||
He who protects the helpless, who does not create discord, and who makes no distinction among all his sons; ||94||
He who, seeing his own guru enraged, should appease him there;
who should worship a Kapila cow with devotion; and who should protect a chaste wife—[he is liberated]. ||95||
One should not step over fire with one's feet, nor should one urinate in water at any time;
one should always be devoted to the guru, possessed of knowledge, and not a chatterer. ||96||
Whoever, endowed with such righteousness, practices toward me, shall indeed not enter a womb; he goes instead to my world. ||97||
He who, having eaten the food of another, does not disparage it, and who has been constantly devoted to me since his childhood; (98)
Content with whatever comes his way, honoring his mother and father, he is a giver and an enjoyer according to justice, independent, and ever-restrained. (99)
Established in the vow of lifelong celibacy (kaumāra-vrata), he should not perform improper actions;
he should be endowed with compassion for all beings and possessed of the quality of goodness (sattva).
One who, through wisdom, is utterly free from desire and always lacks longing for the affairs of others—such a devotee, my disciple, goes to my world. (101)
O lady of excellent hips, this secret is difficult even for the gods to attain;
you are celebrated by me as my disciple, my servant, my devotee, and my wife.
Thus, on that Ṛkṣaparvata mountain, Śaṅkara formerly spoke to Pārvatī regarding my devotion and the sacred power of the Narmadā.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the State of Happiness, the State of Suffering, the Worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Fruit of Offering All Actions and So Forth, and the Absence of Rebirth," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to my supreme thought regarding those devoted to me;
even if one should become grey with dust at my sacred ford.
Nevertheless, I shall indeed bestow a great kingdom upon the deceased at the former sacred ford named Kokā, which is the site of the Boar incarnation.
A certain greedy man, intent on violence, went to the Kokamaṇḍala region;
seeing a fish there in the water, he caught it with a hook.
From his hand, however, a powerful fish quickly escaped;
then the hawk, seeing it, swiftly seized it with its talons.
Even though he had flown up, he was utterly powerless to carry such a great burden;
consequently, deprived of his feet, the fish fell into Kokāmukha.
Touched by the dust, he died and became a pure prince;
then, in the course of time, the wife of that very same hunter—
Taking the pieces of flesh upon her head, she indeed proceeded there on foot;
then a certain female lizard, agitated by the sight of the meat, arrived there to seize it.
Struck by an arrow by the hunter's wife, she fell down dead;
however, through her resorting to the dust of the holy site (tīrtha), she was born as the daughter of the king in Candrapura.
Even a young woman despises an excellent man and does not desire him;
she despises all men, even those who are gentle and handsome.
Then, as time passed, a relationship between the two arose through marriage;
and thus the couple remained, constantly upholding their religious duties.
At midday, a headache arose for her husband that was extremely painful;
despite thousands of physicians' medicines, that suffering did not cease at all. || 11 ||
Once, his beloved wife said this to her husband:
"O Lord, what indeed is this pain that does not subside despite medical treatments? (1-2)
Being questioned again and again, the husband spoke to his beloved:
"Relinquish this human state and remember your former birth."
If you have the desire to know, then receive the command of my aged parents to go toward the holy site of Kokāmukha.
"Having gone there, I shall speak; do not be deluded, O beautiful lady.
Then the daughter-in-law propitiated her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
He said that they wished to go to Kokāmukha for the sake of visiting the sacred ford;
however, due to the gravity of his current duties, he did not forbid them in any way.
Until today, I have never asked for anything from you two at any time; therefore, I now ask you both before you: you ought to grant it to me.
For this son of yours is always afflicted by a headache;
at midday, he indeed becomes as if dead, being exceedingly tormented. || 18 ||
"Without Kokāmukha, our suffering will not cease;
we wish to go quickly to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. (19)
Having heard these words of his daughter-in-law, the king spoke these auspicious words:
"O son, accept jewels, male and female servants, chariots, and other possessions."
O son, perform meritorious works with these objects worthy of gift and abundant wealth; O daughter, protect your husband with ease. (21)
King Śakra gave permission to the couple along with the merchants and others;
having gone there, they likewise worshipped Hari at Kokāmukha.
Having seen the gods and bathed in the water, they then gave gifts;
the night passed away, and in the morning the couple bathed.
Having bowed his head to Viṣṇu, the Lord showed his wife,
within the clay, the bones of a fish from a previous birth.
"These are indeed my bones produced from a former body;
formerly, I was a fish wandering among the flocks of birds in the water. (25)
I, a water-dweller, was seized by a hunter with a hook;
having escaped from his hand, I fell there upon the ground by force.
At that time, I was pierced by the talons of a hawk greedy for meat;
carried along the path of the sky, I indeed fell here from it.
And from that excessive blow, a pain arose in my head;
I alone perceive it and remember this intense sensation. (28)
"Because of that, my suffering is not pacified; indeed, it arises intensely at midday.
Having heard this, his wife also spoke of her own previous birth. (29)
And I remember my previous birth as Cillī; at that time, overcome by hunger and thirst, I was sitting upon a tree, searching for food in its midst.
Then a certain hunter, having killed deer at that tree together with his beloved,
arrived and placed the meat on the ground.
At that moment, I pierced the lump of flesh with my claws, which were like thunderbolts;
the hunter saw me there and struck me with an arrow.
And he cast me down to the ground; having fallen, I reached the state of death.
By the power of this sacred field, I have been born as your beloved, O King.
I remember all of this: whose bones these are, and which remain for me as well—how they have crumbled away until only a small portion is left.
Then, having resolved that a religious act leading to liberation must be performed there in the world of Viṣṇu which brings happiness, they both [proceeded]. (35)
They performed acts of veneration and the like, and gave gifts of wealth, jewels, and so forth;
filled with supreme joy, they bestowed their own remaining possessions upon the worthy recipients.
Remaining there, O lady of excellent hips, while established in my service,
they abandoned their bodies at that place and went to Śvetadvīpa.
Wearing white garments and adorned with divine ornaments,
they possess divine forms and are always my devoted Bhāgavatas.
Radiant and handsome, with an auspicious appearance like that of gold,
they had four arms and were graced by power, just like Lakṣmī and Viṣṇu.
Seeing their amazement, that attendant became devoted to my service and remained established in my work;
casting off his human state, he has come to my world.
The radiant one arrived there from every direction, having come into my presence. ||41||
O Lakṣmī, my female devotees indeed become identical in form to you;
they are radiant with splendor and adorned with the quality of pure sattva.
All were full of fresh youth, possessed the fragrance of blue lotuses,
had the beautiful hue of campaka flowers, were liberated, and were all devoted to their vows.
By my grace, O fair-hipped one, they shall all be filled with eternal youth,
possessed of perpetual bliss, and endowed with every supernatural power.
This is righteousness, fame, power, and great glory;
it is the supreme deed among deeds and the greatest austerity among austerities. (45)
It is the supreme among all discourses, the highest of all compositions, and the ultimate dharma among all virtues—that which is my taking refuge. (46)
Having taken refuge in my Dharma, having placed the dust upon his head, and having partaken of my grace, he is glorified in my world. ||47||
Having drunk the water from my feet and bathed in the waters of my sacred fords, and having repeatedly observed the conduct of me, a saintly one; 48.
Having always performed service to the virtuous and having repeatedly performed the worship of the Bhāgavatas, he also heard the Saṃhitā known as the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya. ||49||
People attain supreme liberation, just as Cilli and Matsya did in ancient times;
by remembering this even at the time of death, one shall be released from bondage.
O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you specifically of the auspicious times:
the month of Kumuda (Mārgaśīrṣa), Mārgaśīrṣa itself, Vaiśākha, and likewise Śrāvaṇa.
These months are vessels for my supreme joy, and they are for my worship;
specifically, on the twelfth day of the month of Kārtika, with fresh grains and fresh flowers.
One should worship with nine waters; that [practice] of mine conduces to the world [of liberation], when the time of the arrival of clouds has passed and the clear autumn has arrived. (53)
When the sky had become clear and the lunar orb was stainless,
at a time that was neither too cold nor too hot, and resounded with the cries of swans.
On that auspicious twelfth day of the month of Kumuda, which is filled with the fragrance of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and lotuses; ||55||
Whoever worships me on that day, performs my vow,
and observes the Prabodhinī fast, attains the supreme goal.
Even in the cool season, he who performs my worship on the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa with fresh flowers attains the supreme goal.
Just as the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and Vaiśākha are dear to me,
so too am I to be worshipped with flowers and other offerings during the day of the vow.
He who offers me worship shall remain in my world for nine thousand and nine hundred years.
The gift of even a single leaf of incense yields this great fruit during the month of Kaumuda as well as Mārgaśīrṣa.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha,
having become devoted to the practice of eating but a single meal, [one should worship] her adorned with a forest garland.
Whoever places ornaments of flowers and fragrant blossoms here, by him worship shall have been performed for twelve years. (62)
One should offer fragrant *śāla* flowers along with sandalwood during the month of *kaumuda*; likewise, one should offer auspicious blue lotuses and sandalwood during the month of *mārgaśīrṣa*.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should offer me land-lotuses, cool water with sugar, and sugarcane juice;
this bestows peace as well as nourishment.
But he who gives [this] while being solely devoted to me attains Vaikuṇṭha for a thousand divine years, and thereafter, even beyond that.
He goes to my supreme state; for him there is no end to merit.
For him there is neither birth nor death, neither sickness, nor hunger, nor thirst. (66)
A worshipper of mine shall attain such a supreme world on the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
One should worship me with beautiful vernal flowers with a pure heart—those that are white, pale, fragrant, and very lovely. (68)
He does not go to saṃsāra; he goes to my world, [offering] auspicious and fresh śāla flowers on the full moon day of Vaiśākha. 69.
Having given [these gifts] to me and to my devotees, a person is prepared for liberation,
after having worshipped the followers of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata and placed me before them.
A man or a woman should worship with supreme affection and pure devotion;
the sages praise him with mantras, and the devoted women praise him with hymns from their hearts. (71)
The Gandharvas and Apsarases, along with the inhabitants of the divine realms, also praise the Ancient One, the Supreme Person, with songs, dances, and instrumental music.
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas—all of them praise me, the god Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (73)
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of Maruts praise the Lord of the gods even at the dissolution of the ages.
The earth, the wind, the Viśvedevas, the fire, and the planets such as the sun—all these together praise this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). ||75||
Brahmā himself, Soma, Śakra, Agni, and Cit-ākāśa praise Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Great Lord of the World. 76.
Nārada and Parvata, as well as Asita, the sage Devala, Pulaha, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras—these too [were there]. (77)
These and many others, Mitrāvasu and Parāvasu, indeed praise me, the Lord of Ramā, the supreme teacher of yogins. (78)
The inhabitants of Satyaloka, who dwell in the support sustained by the eight enclosures—the Vairājas and the Īśvaras as well—worship me indeed, O Mādhavī. (79)
The Pitṛs, beginning with Aryaman, those belonging to Yama known as Śravaṇas,
and the years called Kāla, constantly offer praise to me.
All the ṛṣis and munis, the guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds, the treasures, the Kṛttikās, the cardinal points, the bodiless god of love, and likewise the Manus. ||81||
All the *kalās*, all the lunar days (*tithis*), and even the *tattvas* praise me; all the constellations, all the gods, the qualities (*guṇas*), and the castes (*varṇas*) worship me. 82.
All enjoyments and those who enjoy them, the yoginīs and hosts of apsarases, as well as sacred fords, streams, rivers, channels, and springs; ||83||
The Vālakhilyas, Piśācas, and other beings, Pretas, all the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Caṇḍikās, Vetālas, and Vināyakas praise me. (84)
The ḍākinīs, śākinīs, and likewise kṛtyās attend upon me;
as do those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those sprouting from the earth. (85)
Human beings, as well as those born of water and those born of land—embodied beings dwelling in the various stages of life (āśramas)—constantly praise me when they are in a state of suffering. (86)
The household deities, the village deities, the deities of forests, jungles, and so forth;
the forests, mountains, and the like; as well as the ponds and flowing streams. (87)
Both natural ponds and excavated pools, even the oceans, praise me;
the dwellings and village settlements, being conscious, indeed worship me.
Those engaged in karma, having made their dwelling in the realm of Yama, repeatedly remember me, the Lord of Compassion, for deliverance from suffering. (89)
Those in distress constantly praise me; sometimes those desiring knowledge do so as well, just as one who seeks wealth praises until his purpose is accomplished.
The charioteers, bards, panegyrists, heralds, and wandering minstrels always remember, praise, and worship him with the marrow of their bones. (91)
All those who offer praise, storytellers, and even those with matted hair worship me;
likewise, those who administer justice, rulers, thieves, and plunderers as well. (92)

Whether they be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), goodness (sāttvika), or passion (rājasa), the Bhaṭṭas, those skilled in the Gandharva [Veda], the Kinnaras, and those seeking the goals of human existence—all praise me. (93)
Sādhyās, Sādhvīs, as well as Satīs and Brahmacāriṇīs—even Ābhicāriṇīs—praise me and worship me. 94.
Nāgas, serpents, uragas, reptiles, wild animals, and the like—all indeed resort to me while abiding in their own respective dharma. //95//
I bestow upon them fruits according to their state, indeed in accordance with their karma;
yet those who are liberated constantly resort to me, having granted me a dwelling place within their hearts. 96.
To those devotees I give my heart, just as they are mine;
likewise, O Lakṣmī, all living beings are eternally and certainly woven into me. 97.
They do not remain at all without me; they tremble indeed without me;
they do not attain illumination at all without me, who am situated within the heart. (98)
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord; I am the Great King of the Kāmbharas, the sovereign over all embodied beings. 99.
My speech indeed illumines the hearts of all;
by my power, the senses perform their functions of perception.
Through my lineage, saṃsāra proceeds, dissolves, and persists;
for the sake of my service, all this is a ground of bliss.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, who is higher than the highest, should always be served with excellent offerings produced in all seasons,
as well as with mental palaces.
For the sake of uplifting them, I remain awake and do not even sleep; for I have no sleep on account of my devotees, nor any indifference toward those who have taken refuge in me.
Neither laziness for the sake of one's own comfort, nor a physical form devoid of love;
knowing this, those who worship, praise, and remember me—|| 104 ||
O beloved daughter of the ocean, those very men and women are indeed destined for liberation—those who recite, those who listen, and those who seek to contemplate [this teaching]. (105)
If all the burdens of worldly existence were to reach the supreme state,
that would be the fruit of all sacrifices for those who follow my word.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Dust of Viṣṇu’s Holy Places in the First Section on the Continuation of the Kṛta Yuga; the Liberation of Those from Śvetadvīpa; the Fruit of Performing Worship of the Lord on the Twelfth Days of the Months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, and Others; and the Attainment of the Lord through Praise and Other Acts Performed by All Beings and Living Creatures," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, Śambhu, the supreme devotee of Viṣṇu,
spoke to Pārvatī concerning my greatness arising from the holy places and other sources.
Candradvīpa, Prabhāsatu, and Tāmraparṇeya; Gabhastimān, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, and Gandharva as well. || 2 ||
Vāruṇa and Kaumārikeya—these indeed are the regions of Narmadā;
they are sprinkled with the waters of the Narmadā and are those who drink that water.
Through the connection with merit, embodied beings go to heaven and even to liberation;
living beings experience the auspicious and inauspicious fruits of their own actions.
For the sake of the highest good, austerity, fire-offerings, charity, meditation, worship,
compassion, and bathing in the Narmadā should be performed for the attainment of auspiciousness.
I shall relate an ancient narrative exactly as it occurred:
in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a royal sage named Kuvalayāśva.
Indeed, many thousands of various kinds of gifts were given by that king with devotion at all the sacred fords.
King Kuvalayāśva, devoted to the practice of charity and righteousness, performed sacrifices, with the sole exception of those performed on the Narmadā.
Indeed, at the conjunction of Rāhu and the Sun, he went to Kurukṣetra with one hundred thousand horses and ten thousand elephants.
Endowed with supreme faith, he gave gold, rubies, gems, and various garments to the Brahmins during the eclipse.
O King, having scattered all the remaining material at that sacred site, handful by handful at every spot like tiny pebbles, he performed his ritual bath.
Then, at the time of dawn, he went to his own kingdom and worshipped Hari;
thus King Mucukunda, a devotee of Viṣṇu who had conquered his senses, [attained his goal].
He was the lord of the Daityas, and he went to the Lord of Oṃkāra on the Narmadā, to the Vaidūryasiddha mountain, during a solar eclipse.
He resided at Koṭitīrtha at the confluence of the Narmadā and Kapilā,
where he possessed one hundred thousand milch cows as well as ten thousand horses.
A thousand elephants and a thousand chariots,
as well as a thousand desirable vehicles adorned with golden garlands.
Then, having performed the ritual bath as was appropriate, he bestowed wealth, grain, fine garments, and various kinds of jewels upon the brahmins.
He gave a gift of ten thousand [cows] to Oṃkāranātha;
whatever desire anyone wished for, he granted that very thing to him. || 17 ||
Having done this, he returned once more to his own abode at that supreme holy site.
Then, after some time, by the power of their respective merits, the two kings—
Having attained heaven, they were served by Apsarases and became like Indra;
indeed, Mucukunda’s chariot always travels upward in the celestial realm.
Kuvalayāśva’s vehicle, however, always travels beneath it;
both were reported by messengers to the wise Dharmarāja.
The royal sage Kuvalayāśva and the mighty Mucukunda—both of these, seated in celestial chariots, arrived from another world. (21)
The vehicle of Mucukunda rose up so high that it remained thousands of yojanas above, higher and higher still.
The vehicle of the Lord of the Unslayable (Yama) proceeded toward the lower region;
having heard this, Dharmarāja also questioned Citragupta.
"Which of the two kings should I honor with offerings such as the arghya? Tell me," [the king] asked.
Having observed the power of merit belonging to both, Citragupta replied: || 24 ||
First, he worshipped Mucukunda through the power of the Revā;
he also questioned the Seven Sages, and they spoke to him just as Citragupta had.
Having approached Mucukunda, honor him with water for the feet and the guest-offering;
the lord of the Dānavas is most meritorious and is to be worshipped with a gift of Kapila cow's milk.
Thus addressed, Dharmarāja approached the lord of the Dānavas;
then, having joined his palms in reverence, he stood before the vehicle.
"O Lord of Daityas, it is well with you today; you are endowed with all virtues.
By this gift upon the earth, you have conquered the three worlds. (28)
At the end of Oṃkāra-dakṣiṇa, at the confluence with the Mūrti river, on the bank of Saptakalpa-vaha, the measure of merit is beyond reckoning. ||29||
Having spoken thus and having offered worship, Mucukunda showed him the path to Viṣṇu’s world of Vaikuṇṭha and departed.
Then, having approached King Kuvalayāśva himself, Dharmarāja spoke: "I indeed offer you a welcome."
The king said: "There is indeed constant enmity between the gods and the dānavas;
since you are a god, why did you previously worship a daitya? (32)
"O Dharmarāja, how is it that you have performed everything in reverse? Having abandoned me, that lord of the Dānavas was honored by you with water for the feet and the arghya offering."
Yama said: "I have duties remaining that must be performed according to one's karma.
Cast off your despondency, O Indra among kings; the course of karma is profound."
The merit on the banks of the Narmadā is indeed superior to that of Kurukṣetra; no other holy sites, even including Kalpagayā, are worth even a sixteenth part of it at any time.
"I shall indeed act as the witness of the deeds of all according to what is right.
Then that king, filled with wonder, quickly bowed down to Yama, the Lord of Death.

Then, when full, it ascends to the eternal realm of Viṣṇu;
such indeed is the supreme, merit-bestowing Narmada Tīrtha. 38.
O beloved Kamalā, she bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation and washes away sins;
even sinful people attain liberation by bathing in the waters of the Revā. (39)
By the dharma of Viṣṇu, the ocean of worldly existence, so difficult to cross, is traversed;
yet people, being attached and deluded, indeed proceed toward extreme sin.
They do not know themselves, nor Kṛṣṇa, nor indeed the gods;
they do not hear of the supreme good, just as one does not see with the eyes when they are present [but not used]. ||41||
Traveling slowly on the same path, they stumble at every step;
even those souls released from Yama do not realize it, despite being awakened. 42.
Those men suffer in vain under the sway of various passions and greed, even after seeing before their very eyes the miserable pit of the womb, which awakens one to terror. (43)
They do not understand the path to liberation; for them, the Revā grants release.
All beings who have become pretas are under the jurisdiction of the realm of Yama. ||44||
Śiva said: "Listen, O Mountain; I shall relate to you an ancient narrative.
This ancient narrative concerning Narmadā was indeed told by the Sun. (45)
For the sake of his own son, Yama, who was intent on crossing over the world,

Indeed, through bathing, immersion, drinking, as well as acts of giving and so forth, she bestows a divine abode, liberation, heaven, and supreme welfare. 47.

By uttering "Narmadā, Narmadā," a sinner does not see the realm of Yama;

[There are] Vaidūryaparvata, Ṛkṣa, and likewise Āmarakaṇṭaka.

Those who give gifts of food, gifts of water, and all kinds of household requisites,
as well as gifts of palaces and gardens, go to liberation.
Indeed, the devotees of the Blessed One do not go to the realm of Yama;
this world must be examined, for it always exists as a mixture of both. (515)
Honor is accompanied by dishonor; union with the beloved occurs during separation; youth is seized by old age; and happiness is beset by suffering. (56)
With bodies worn out by strength and grey hair, they [no longer possess] that youthfulness of men and women which is so dear to one another. (57)
That very same body, when seized by old age, is no longer dear to either of them;
likewise, they regard themselves as something unprecedented, endowed with such frailty. (58)
Who else would be more senseless than that man who, though overcome by old age and surrounded by kinsmen such as wife and sons, does not become dispassionate upon seeing this? (59)
Due to his lack of power, he is treated with contempt by ill-behaved servants; one joined with old age cannot pursue virtue, wealth, pleasure, or liberation. (1.569.60)
Therefore, being capable of accomplishing it, one should practice Dharma quickly;
for the imbalance of wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth, constitutes the entire circle of diseases.
It indeed remains constantly in the body, repeatedly causing much suffering;
since these sufferings are to be known by one's own self, what is there to be known by others? (62)
O, one hundred and one deaths constantly occur;
among them, one is of the nature of time, while the remainder are known as adventitious.
Time, though peaceful, wears away the body at every moment;
for adventitious factors indeed erode the essential principles at every moment.
Adventitious conditions of death do not indeed kill one absolutely;
they are driven away by remedial means such as medicines and their counterparts. //65//
Timely death, whose nature consists of moments and so forth, and which is of the essence of Mahākāla,
cannot be pacified by means of recitation, fire-offerings, gifts, or medicinal remedies.
Untimely death of the body arises from poison, liquor, and the like; for all beings, it also arises from falling into water, falling into fire, and so forth. ||67||
He brings about the destruction of insects through rain and the like by means of floods of water;
this man is ever-knowing and constantly fears untimely death.
Various painful diseases, as well as creatures such as serpents, horned animals, and malevolent spells, are the doors of death for embodied beings. (69)
Even Dhanvantari himself cannot restore to health a living being who is afflicted by time, even if that being is beset by diseases, serpents, and other such dangers. (1.569.70)
Neither medicine, nor austerity, nor charity, nor friends, nor kinsmen are able to protect a traveler seized by time. (71)
There is no suffering equal to death; there is no enemy equal to death;
there is no time equal to death for embodied beings who imagine themselves secure in happiness. (72)
Death cuts asunder everything—virtuous wives, sons, friends, and the pleasures of sovereignty and royal power—even when it is being resisted with great force. (73)
"O son, this meaningful discourse on the King of Dharma has been told to you by me;
in the end, all of it will result in eating at the proper time in every respect. (74)
Therefore, with every effort, one should follow the path of Nārāyaṇī;
for Revā removes all suffering and destroys all sorrow. (75)
Whatever desires one may long for, the Revā bestows them all;
knowledge, meditation, and study—these indeed constitute the service of the Revā. (76)
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, truth, O Lakṣmī, and the service of water—these, even by the thousands, such as the *brahmakūrca* rite, are not equal to the waters of the Revā. (77)
A gift of cows given there indeed bestows the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
In ancient times, King Śaśānka resided on the banks of the Narmadā.

and he gave a cow that had recently calved to a high-souled Brahmin.

as long as both feet of the calf were visible and its face remained within the womb.

To that extent, the earth with its mountains, forests, and groves is to be understood as a cow, having horns of gold, hooves of silver, accompanied by her calf, and possessing a bell-metal milking vessel. (8.1)
Accompanied by a bath in the Narmadā, along with kuśa grass and sesame seeds, [one should offer] the moon at Koṭitīrtha, situated between the syllable Om and the Immortal (A). ||82||
He indeed assigned these, numbering one thousand, to the Brāhmaṇas;
by the merit of that gift, that king [resides] in heaven by means of a divine vehicle.
Then the celestial drums resounded in the sky as King Hariścandra ascended the vehicle at that very moment.
Having given a thousand cows at Kurukṣetra, he arrived by means of a vehicle,
with a golden parasol held over him and being fanned with chowries.
Hariścandra was situated a thousand yojanas below;
having seen this downward state, he quickly went to the Unborn One.
With a dejected face, he asked his grandfather the reason:
"I have indeed bestowed an infinite gift upon the field of the Kauravas. (87)
By Śaśāṅka, however, an infinite gift was given at the Revā;
