"Because of this, I, Hariścandra, who was formerly situated in a lowly state, have now become elevated.
Having heard this, Brahmā said to Hariścandra: "Do not give way to grief. (89)
O King, in former times, during a solar eclipse at Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, Śaśāṅka performed many thousands of sacrifices.
Formerly, I weighed all other holy fords on one side and Amarakaṇṭaka on the other; the Lord of the Immortals was found to be superior.
"If one desires the supreme state, let the goddess who flows through the Kalpa be served.
Then Hariścandra, having bowed down, departed for Amarakaṇṭaka.
Then, on the bank of the Narmadā, he gave away wealth, riches, and cows;
subsequently, through the rise of his merit, a celestial chariot indeed ascended upward for him.
Then, having attained contentment and ruled the kingdom for a long time,
he went to Vaikuṇṭha itself by the power of the Narmadā.
Although he gave many gifts even to the Kaurava,
the fruit of those was not at all equal to that of Nārmada.
Thus indeed is the Narmadā tīrtha, the supreme bestower of all prosperity,
granting both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and endowed with ten million other holy sites.
All of this was indeed narrated by Śaṅkara to Śivā;
O Mahālakṣmī, that fruit of the Narmadā has been told by me to you. 97.
O Lakṣmī, the person who hears this obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows;
by reciting, hearing, or remembering it, one indeed obtains such a fruit.

Thus ends the five hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Disparity between the Vimānas of Kuvalayāśva and Mucukunda, the Disparity between the Vimānas of Hariścandra and Śaśāṅka, and the Excellence of the Greatness of Narmadā and Marakaṇṭaka," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I have indeed heard the meritorious majesty of Narmadā and that which arises from Koṭitīrtha at Amarēśvara, which is a thousand times greater than Kurukṣetra. (1)
O Lord, how was it that you previously fashioned this through illusion?
In some cases merit is equal when an action is performed, while in others it is deficient or likewise excessive.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Everything is obtainable through my grace; the Narmadā flows through seven kalpas, as do the gods, sages, and virtuous beings of those seven kalpas."
By virtue of my incarnations, Narmadā is superior to all;
and at the time of universal dissolution, Revā remains eternally by my side in the Ocean of Milk.
Devoted to serving my feet, that beautiful woman remains;
through my yoga, my supreme and divine illusion (māyā) comes into being.
Listen to how I have fashioned this entire world consisting of illusion;
having created it, I enter into it, and by my yoga, it remains as my own.
Listen: Rudra, Indra, and even the Grandfather (Brahmā) do not know me;
for it was by me alone, as Nārāyaṇa, that these lords of the gods were created.
O beautiful one, all places become sacred through my dwelling;
when the rain-god pours down rain upon a land, that land is filled with water.
The sky becomes devoid of water, for Māyā takes the form of my creative power;
yet in an instant, the sky is seen once again completely covered with waters.
"The rain has fallen again and the place is empty; this was a deception created by me.
But all the water is purifying, O beautiful lady, because of my dwelling within it."
That which is specifically intended is indeed especially purifying,
just as the water of mountain torrents, when resorted to by the virtuous, is purifying.
Then, it becomes even more purifying when frequented by the gods;
when frequented by me, it becomes most purifying.
Why was that [place] not resorted to by me repeatedly, even in every kalpa? There, on the Ocean of Milk, I served Revā, and because of that, I became equal to her.
She is the purifier of purifiers, the most auspicious of auspicious things;
she is the supreme bestower of liberation among all givers of liberation, for she is indeed my own Māyā.
That the moon wanes in one fortnight and waxes again in the next,
and that it is not seen at all on the new-moon day— this is an illusion created by me.
"O beautiful one, in the winter the water in the well becomes warm, and in the summer it becomes cool; this is an illusion created by me. (16)
And the Sun always travels by a single path and not otherwise;
he eternally rises in the east and sets in the west. (17)
O beautiful one, through the variety of its arrangements, this illusion of mine attains depth, softness, and coolness below, and thereafter heat above.
Semen and blood are produced separately within the body;
through their union a fetus comes to be, and never otherwise.
It arises from that which is of its own kind, and it is not born from that which is of a different kind;
for having entered the womb, the living being experiences pleasure and pain.
Without a body, there is indeed neither suffering nor happiness for the self anywhere;
having been born, one forgets the womb—this is an illusion created by me.
According to his karma, a living being continues to live even when his body has perished;
according to his karma, death occurs even while he remains within the body. (22)
When the embryo, a mixture of semen and blood, is the size of a jujube fruit, there arise the fingers, the two feet, the two arms, the head, and likewise the waist. (23)
Likewise, the back and the belly, the teeth, the lips, and the nose; the two ears, the eyes, the two skull-bones, the forehead, and the tongue. (24)
Through my illusory power (māyā), these beings come into being and are born from that;
by that very power, what has been eaten and what has been drunk is digested by fire.
"Yet urine flows from below; this is an illusion created by me.
Sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and others likewise [are such]. (26)

The elements beginning with the gross elements (bhūta), those beginning with the mind (mānasa), those beginning with the vital breaths (prāṇa), and even the constituent tissues (dhātu)—all these indeed proceed from the principle of food; this is the illusion (māyā) created by me.
Even after thousands of years have passed in all seasons, he remains for a long time; he does not even perceive a new season, nor even one that is favorable to his well-being.
One does not know objects such as food and so forth in their true nature;
O beautiful one, why and of what kind would my gain be? This is a mere illusion for me. (29)
The celestial waters created by me, which take visible form from the invisible,
become terrestrial rivers that appear with abundant water.
In summer they all wither away, and then that wheel is just as it was before; they arise and wither again—this is a magical illusion that recurs every year.
Space is indeed of the nature of emptiness, and wind is also a mover;
yet, upon reaching the Himalaya, it even becomes cold-natured.
The snow, which is solid by nature, melts very gradually from the mountain peak;
having reached the earth, it becomes the Gaṅgā, which brings happiness to the land. (33)
The clouds draw up water from the salt ocean and rain it down sweet upon the world; this transformation of the liquid was performed by me. (34)
In some places that water is considered to have a bitter form, and in others it is sweet;
it arises with diverse qualities—this, O Padmaja, is my māyā.
"O herb, I deposit my virility, which destroys disease, into you;
or, while the herb is being given, becoming Time (Kāla), I take it away. (36)
The embryo, the infant, the youth, the aged, and the decrepit one devoid of strength;
the seed, the sprout, the leaf, the stalk, the stem, and the flower. ||37||
From a seed comes fruit, sap, and satisfaction, and from one seed, thousands of seeds;
yet sometimes a seed is fruitless—this is the illusion (māyā) created by me, O beloved.
The men and women created by me possess hundreds of sons;
yet I have no son—this is my illusion, O Lotus-born One.
From a single body alone, millions of living beings are born:
insects on the head, lice in the hair, bedbugs and other vermin in the clothes.
In the pores of the skin there are insects, as well as lice and the like arising from sweat;
and when the limbs are cut, worms also emerge from within the flesh. (41)
Just as minute insects indeed arise within urine and in reeds and the like, so too are embryos produced from semen born in the form of offspring. (42)
Indeed, from one and the same body, diverse creations are born;
for all sons are one's own children, since they have been produced from oneself. (43)
But for worms and the like, who are dissimilar, no affection exists;
embodied beings feel affection only for a son who is similar to themselves. (44)
I have deposited this illusion among all living beings:
hostility toward one creature and excessive attachment toward another, such as a son. (45)
Some sons drink blood like insects, while others drink everything;
they drink the mother's blood in the womb, and likewise drink milk from her lap. 46.
In childhood, they drink wealth; in youth, they drink prosperity;
in the state of mental distraction, they drink peace; and at death, they even drink their own life-breath.
In this way, O beautiful lady, this affection for all is but an illusion of mine;
there may be affection of a man for a woman, and affection of a woman for a man. (48)
Neither in women nor in men is there such an illusion as this of mine;
it exists in water, on earth, in taste, in the body, in rain, and in the seed that is consumed. (49)
Therein I release nectar; it is perceived as such when there is hunger. When there is no hunger, that same thing becomes poison; this, O beautiful one, is my māyā.
The world understands it thus: "Garuda carries Acyuta";
however, I, remaining within, carry Garuda as I proceed. (51)
All the worlds know that the gods are eternally consumers of sacrifices;
however, I shall sacrifice to the dwellers of heaven by means of the form of a sacrifice myself.
All the worlds know that the Guru bestows initiation;
however, I abide as initiation itself within the Guru through my illusory power (māyā).
All the worlds know that Varuṇa protects the ocean;
however, standing within Varuṇa, I always protect the oceans.
All the worlds know that Kubera is the guardian of wealth;
however, I, in the form of wealth, protect his status as Kubera. (55)
All the worlds know that Vṛtra was slain by Śakra;
however, it was I who, abiding within Śakra through my illusory power (māyā), destroyed Vṛtra.
Thus do people know that the great Sun is Nārāyaṇa;
however, it is I who, having entered the Sun, illuminate [the world] according to my capacity. (57)
Stability has been granted by me to Dhruva, and likewise impartiality to Meru;
I am in the form of the submarine fire within the ocean, and in the form of the wind within the clouds.
Water remains in the sky, yet people do not see it at all;
even the gods do not know where the nectar of immortality resides.
The medicine created by Māyā remains entirely within the forest;
I shall certainly bestow my power there, which always effects the destruction of disease.
For the world understands thus: "The king protects the subjects";
however, it is I who, having entered the king, protect my own subjects.
In the act of creation I take the form of evening; at night I possess the nature of dissolution; and in the morning, through Māyā alone, I become the very essence of the cosmic embryo.
The Sun ripens everything through his power of illusion (māyā), for I am established within the Sun;
Fire ripens everything through his power of illusion, for I am established within Fire.
I am the one possessing the form of the sun; having brought about the dissolution at the time of universal destruction and having withdrawn the world, I illuminate the sphere.
Even while I lay upon Śeṣa, Śeṣa himself was lying there by my power of illusion (māyā).
Behold the strength of my illusion: you always exist in the form of a woman.
"O Lakṣmī, tell me this: why are you not born in male form?
This is my Māyā, O Lakṣmī; it is your activity that manifests in female form. (66)
Within my male form, there exists the activity of Māyā; it is mine. From the midst of the waters, I create Prajāpati, Hara, and Viṣṇu.
They too do not know me, being deluded by my māyā;
in a former kalpa, I was a sage and brahmin named Somaśarman.
Though he was devoted, being covered by my illusory power (māyā), he did not recognize his own supreme [nature].
O large-eyed one, this Māyā of mine is Rohiṇī, who causes the hair to stand on end.
In some cases, even a yogi is bound by the fickleness of the senses;
Somaśarman, emaciated by my illusory power, indeed attained womanhood.
There was no such deed of his, nor was any offense committed;
yet, despite being intent on my propitiation, he obtained birth as a Niṣāda. (71)
O Lakṣmī, she constantly meditated upon my enchanting form;
then, after a long time, I was pleased by her acts of devotion.
Through my constant austerities, I have also become manifest before him.
He said to me, "I am pleased; for the sake of a boon, I shall grant you whatever you desire. (73)
Jewels, gold, and cows, as well as a sovereign empire free from thorns;
or else, you may desire heaven, where there is happiness and beautiful women. (74)
Wealth, vehicles, mounts, armies, and all manner of riches; golden vessels, palatial mansions, and radiant objects made of gold. (75)
"O twice-born one, tell me: I shall bestow upon you inexhaustible vessels, various kinds of nectar, and divine, sovereign enjoyments. (76)
"I grant you a boon, O Brahmin, whatever is intended by your mind.
Having heard my words, the Brahmin bowed and spoke to me softly: (77)
If you, O Lord, are not provoked to anger, I shall request a boon:
whatever has been spoken by you, O God, all that must be granted to me by you. (78)
"O Lakṣmī, although he was thus a devoted devotee, he entreated me with intense longing.
I said to him: 'O sinless one, why indeed do you ask for all this? (79)
The binding of my devotee causes me distress;
therefore, desiring to behold that wonder, I wish to see my own Māyā.
He spoke these sweet words to me, which were tinged with passion though they proclaimed dispassion:
"I do not desire gold, nor cows, nor jewels, nor a kingdom, nor heaven, nor beautiful women. (81)
O Blessed One, I desire sovereignty that is imperishable, a vessel of immortality, and vehicles for transport; O Lord, I do not desire divine status.
Likewise, I do not desire even a single one out of thousands of heavens;
yet, if such is my desire, how is it that you sport with me? (83)
O Lord of Gods, for the sake of illustration, I choose to see but a small portion;
indeed, Māyā appears as real, yet it is called false by the great seers. (84)
"What kind of thing is this to be understood? Show me its meaning through an illustration.
Having heard his words, I spoke there to him: ||85||
"O Brahmin, what use have they for my illusory power? Practice devotion and obtain happiness;
even the gods do not know it, being utterly deluded by my māyā. (86)
But you do not understand at all, even though you have fallen into illusion;
for you desire to investigate what is unworthy, even though you have already accomplished your purpose. (87)
"And how can you wish for grief while remaining one whose task is yet unaccomplished?
Though addressed thus, that deluded one, through his illusory power, spoke to me.
If you are pleased with me, O Kṛṣṇa, because of my devotion or my austerity,
show me a small portion of your illusory power (māyā), so that I may know it as it truly is.
"I shall indeed not be bound again to the entire wheel of saṃsāra.
Then I said to him, "Go to the place of Kubjāmraka."
The bank of the Gaṅgā is most divine; there you shall obtain everything.
Having heard my words and having circumambulated me, depart from here.
Desirous of performing his morning rites, he went to the holy site of Kubjāmraka;
there he took up his patched garment, his bamboo staff, his water-vessel, and his tunic.
Having placed his provisions on the bank and bowed to the Gaṅgā again and again,
he then took water upon his head and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having drunk water and remembered me, he entered the waters to bathe;
meanwhile, by my power of illusion, the brahmin vanished from sight within the water.
On the side, he entered the womb of a woman in a Niṣāda dwelling;
there, afflicted by the pains of the womb, he reflected in his heart: ||95||
"Alas, what a calamity I have encountered as the result of some evil deed, that I must dwell within the womb of a Niṣāda woman, which is like a hell! (96)
Fie on my asceticism! Fie on my ritual action! Fie on its fruit! And fie on this life, since I remain here within the womb of a Niṣāda, filled with urine! (97)
In this foul-smelling, unbearable place, which carries forth wind, bile, phlegm, and dust—what is the use of speaking here, and what indeed is the use of weeping for that which is lost? (98)
Desiring to test his illusory power, he was led into a field of urine;
"Where is Viṣṇu? Where am I? And where indeed is that water of the Gaṅgā? ||99||
Where is this womb of the Niṣāda woman, and where is this pool of urine?
Having emerged from the cycle of existence within the womb, I shall thereafter attain peace.
As he was reflecting thus, a period of nine months passed as if it were a single moment;
when the tenth month was complete, he emerged from the womb.
As he was falling to the ground, his thought concerning the fetus was lost;
then that girl was born as the daughter of a Niṣāda.
All her status as a Brahmin was forgotten by her, deluded as she was by that illusion;
then, having been married by her father, she became a young woman beloved by a fisherman.
The maiden gave birth to six sons and seven daughters at intervals of two years each;
she ate both what is fit and unfit to eat, and drank both what is fit and unfit to drink.
Having caused the killing of hares and other animals, she even makes a meal of their flesh;
she knows not what ought or ought not to be done, nor does she discern what should or should not be spoken.
Because she was shrouded by a net of illusion, she did not know who was approachable or unapproachable;
at the age of fifty, she was impelled by me within her heart.
Taking a water-pot for the purpose of washing a garment smeared with oil,
she went to bathe right there where her previous clothes had been placed.
Having set down her garments on the bank and placed her water-jar upon the shore, she,
tormented by the heat of perspiration, desired to bathe her head.
He entered the Gaṅgā to bathe; at that moment, that Brahmin named Somaśarman was born and remembered his former history.
Having come outside to the bank,
they saw at the hour of midday those garments, staffs, and water-pots which had been placed there at the time of morning.
Right there at his side, a woman was holding a jar made of human excrement;
seeing this, he experienced a great wonder at that very hour of midday.
That Brahmin, having previously discarded his fisherman’s clothes and other items,
then took up the discarded garment of a washerman and wore it out of shame.
Then, sitting down upon the sand, he grieved intensely as he remembered:
"What blameworthy and most painful deed have I committed through my sinful actions? (11.3)
Because I fell away from right conduct and reached such a state,
I indeed became a Niṣāda woman, for I did not distinguish between what was fit to be eaten and what was unfit.
I have not killed any living beings dwelling in water or on land;
yet I have distinguished between what is drinkable and undrinkable, and I have committed sexual intercourse with women who should not be approached.
Indeed, what was fit to be said and what was not fit to be said was not observed; acts such as theft were repeatedly committed, and even sons and daughters were begotten by me upon a Niṣāda woman.
In my house there dwell children who are still dependent on breast-milk;
they await your arrival, for I have indeed become a man here. (1.17)
"What is to be done? What indeed is not to be done? I do not cross over this delusion of Māyā;
overwhelmed by grief for my offspring, I have fallen into a state of confused recollection. (1.18)
Having become a brahmin, he sat there in silence, filled with great shame;
in the meantime, the Niṣādas and the boys were likewise there.
Because she had been gone for a long time, they went there to search for her;
they sought their wife and their mother, who were weeping.
And the Niṣāda, accompanied by his children, questioned that Brahmin:
"O twice-born one, have you seen my wife here, who came to bathe? (121)
Her young daughters wept piteously in the house,
even without breast milk and in the midst of their meals.
"O Brahmins, do you not see other men and women [coming] to fetch water for me and likewise to wash my clothes? (123)
And if you should tell me here that she came to bathe, and that she arrived carrying a water-pot in her hand and was seen by me; || 1.24 ||
But having received no reply, he wept again at that time;
people saw that brahmin holding a staff and a water-pot.
Not seeing that woman, how could they give an answer?
Bhīla, tormented by grief, looked at the water-jar, the cloth, and so forth. (1.26)
Not seeing his own wife, he lamented piteously:
"Could she have been seized by some crocodile while she was bathing?"
Nor have I ever spoken anything unpleasant to you regarding your duties, even in a dream; such has never been said before, nor could self-destruction possibly occur.
But she may have been devoured by a cruel piśāca or a rākṣasa, or perhaps she has been forcibly carried away to another land by someone. || 1.29 ||
"What evil deed did I commit in the past that brings such bitter fruit,
by which my wife has met her end before me due to a short lifespan?"
"Come here, my blessed and beloved wife, you who follow my heart!
Behold these boys and girls who are likewise weeping from hunger. (131)
"Surely you will know that I am both hungry and thirsty;
O Fate, if you hear me here, give me my beloved in accordance with dharma."
While the Niṣāda was thus lamenting here and there, the Brahmin spoke to him with shame: "Go, Niṣāda; she is not here."
Since she has gone according to her karma and will not return in any way, protect those children; go, why do you distress yourself in vain?
Out of compassion, I shall tell you how she became dear to you;
by the mere act of bathing, the sage was restored to his former state through my power of illusion.
The Niṣāda said to that Brahmin: "How indeed did you attain womanhood, and how did you also attain manhood? Tell this to me who asks."
The Brahmin said: "At that time, Hari was directly perceived by me through devotion; he invited me to choose a boon, and I too then chose what was desired. (1.37)
"O Lord, show me your illusory power; what might it be like?
Then I was told by him, "Go to the waters at Kubjāmraka."
Having said, "There you shall see him," he vanished.
Then I, the Niṣāda girl, arrived and bathed in the Gaṅgā.
"Then your wife became one born from the womb of a Niṣāda woman;
today, having bathed, you have been born again as a Brāhmaṇa, just as before."
Upon hearing this, that Niṣāda and the children vanished;
but I remained there in that form, O Lakṣmī, manifesting through my power of illusion.
At midday, the brahmins arrived to bathe and said to Somaśarman: "How is it that today the forenoon has been spent on the bank? (142)
And how is it that you remain here from morning until midday?
O beloved, at the half-day mark, you have displayed the illusion of being fifty years old.
Then, having revealed myself, I said to him regarding his past deeds:
"In another existence, you did not offer salutations to virtuous devotees. (144)
Due to that sin, such an enjoyment as this has come to you under the guise of Māyā;
go, O Brahmin, to the supreme abode, Śvetadvīpa, and be happy.
Then the Brahmin went to his abode and Nārāyaṇa vanished;
O Lakṣmī, this Māyātīrtha exists on earth as a bestower of liberation.
"From hearing and chanting this, indeed, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall arise;
so Śaṅkara spoke to Pārvatī long ago at the sacred site of Narmadā. (147)

Thus ends the five hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Creation of Illusion, Somaśarman the Brahmin’s Transformation into a Niṣāda Woman upon Seeing the Illusion, His Becoming the Mother of Twelve Children, His Return to Brahminhood and Liberation through Immersion in Water, and the Greatness of Māyātīrtha," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga Cycle, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the supreme moving pilgrimage site (jaṅgama-tīrtha).
Those who are pure devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) are truly my own forms.
Those virtuous ones who pay homage to them, indeed pay homage to me alone;
I am known here by them, O Kamalā, there is no doubt in this.
Those twice-born ones and others who desire to see me and are devoted to me—these pure Bhāgavatas are always worthy of worship and should be visited by men. (3)
Especially on earth, I abide in the form of virtuous twice-born men;
therefore, those who serve such virtuous ones are my devotees, without a doubt.
Whoever should desire for me, once I have attained supreme liberation here,
that he too may become single-minded and thus satisfy my devotees.
One should always satisfy me, as well as virtuous men and women,
through service, obedience, and the giving of desired gifts.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate to you a story from a former kalpa, just as it happened:
there was a great ṛṣi named Raibhya who lived at the bottom of the water.
Devoted solely to my propitiation and established in the practice of liberation,
he was a yogi who had conquered his senses, an ascetic of divine form.
For ten thousand years he remained with his arms raised upward;
for a thousand years he subsisted on water, and for as long again he subsisted on moss.
Then, having abandoned his dwelling on land, he lived in the water for ten thousand years;
indeed, I was propitiated by that sage with supreme devotion.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
Reciting this mantra and meditating upon me, he remains standing in the midst of the water. (11)
Delighted by that, I went into the presence of Raibhya to the waters;
I went directly to the Gaṅgā, where the water had been made dry by me.
Rai-bhya rose and approached a mango tree on the bank;
at that moment, even that large mango tree assumed a hunched form.
Just as a tree stands like an umbrella, sheltering a sage,
so too did I become hunchbacked and go beneath the mango tree.
Indeed, that holy place on the Gaṅgā known on earth as Kubjāmraka is so called because, upon seeing me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, arrived in person. || 15 ||
Falling to the ground on his knees, he praised me, the Lord of Ramā;
and having offered salutations, he stood before me, my ancient devotee.
Being compassionate toward him, I invited him to choose a boon;
he then said, "O Lord, please remain here forever as my dwelling."
May devotion to You, the Lord, always abide within me at this very spot;
O All-pervading One, devotion to any other never pleases me.
I shall worship you eternally, and by my good fortune, I shall behold you even here;
indeed, I shall dwell together with you, established as if in the imperishable.
"O Upendra, if you are pleased with me, let this boon be granted: 'May I truly receive a dwelling there. "The boon has been granted by me. 1.571.20.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am subject to the power of devotion, and I am a devotee; yet I am the sovereign of devotion toward me.
There is, however, no difference between us two, just as there is always none between Śrī and the Lord of Śrī.
"In that auspicious Kubjāmraka, O beautiful one, my abode is pleasing to me;
there I dwell, O lovely lady, under the name Puṇḍarīkākṣa. (22)
In my dwelling, a great and most wonderful marvel occurred in the past: a female serpent remained fearlessly amidst the heap of my discarded flower offerings.
While she was consuming perfumes, garlands, and offerings at her pleasure, a mongoose once arrived from another place. (24)
By him that female serpent was seen; then their battle took place at midday on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha in my temple.
The mongoose was bitten by the serpent, and the female serpent was also bitten by the mongoose;
both then met their death through those severe wounds. (26)
Vyālī was born in Prāgjyotiṣa as the wrathful daughter of a king;
meanwhile, Nakula was born as the son of the lord of Kosala, together with Saruṭ.
And both of them, endowed with their former impressions, grew up;
and that girl, upon seeing Nakula, would immediately rush forward to kill him.
Seeing a female serpent, the prince suddenly rushed to kill it;
yet, by the power of destiny and according to their former bond, the two were united in marriage. (29)
And love arose between the two of them like that of a bird and its wooden perch;
in this manner, seventy-seven years passed for them.
Once, while they were staying together in a park on a grassy spot, the prince saw a female serpent and rushed toward her to kill it. ||3.1||
Although she was being earnestly restrained by her wife, the serpent killed her while she was still alive;
then that queen, overcome with rage, experienced great sorrow in her heart.
And at that very moment, by the turn of fate, a mongoose indeed emerged from the hole and set out before the princess. (33)
Seeing that handsome mongoose,
the princess struck him with a staff out of anger, even though she was restrained by the king.
Seeing Nakula slain— his auspicious royal ornament—
the enraged prince spoke to the princess.
A husband is always to be honored by women; yet you, O cruel one, have transgressed against me—who am beautiful, beloved by kings, auspicious, and a harbinger of good fortune. (36)
"Why was Nakula killed by me, even though I was being restrained?
Hearing these words of her husband, the princess replied: [37]
Since the female serpent killed [the mongoose] even though she was repeatedly forbidden, therefore I too have killed the mongoose, the slayer of snakes. (38)
And the prince, rebuking her with these reasoned words, said to her:
"O wife, it is because of the bite of a serpent of virulent venom that people die. (39)
Therefore, this wicked man who acted for my harm and was arrogant with poison has been slain by me;
for a king is declared to be a protector of his subjects, and I punish those who stand on the path of unrighteousness.
Those who indeed harm virtuous men who are free from offense, and those who also harm women, must be punished according to the dharma of kings. ||41||
"It was indeed by me that the duty of a king had to be performed; therefore, she was killed by me.
Tell me, what offense did Nakula commit against you here? (42)
Handsome, auspicious, and fit even for the palaces of kings, and skilled even at dice—why has this very mongoose been killed by you? (43)
"Since you have taken your life even while being restrained by me, therefore you are no longer my wife, nor am I established as your husband. (44)
"Moreover, for what reason do I not kill you, since women are always inviolable?
Having said this, the king left her there in the garden and went home. (45)
Thus, having taken up anger, the two became devoid of affection; then that news spread from ear to ear among the subjects. (46)
Upon hearing this, the parents of the prince, the two lords of Kosala,
being aged, summoned their daughter-in-law and son to their presence.
Then, seeing his daughter-in-law and son, the father spoke these words:
"Son, where has your affection gone? What indeed is the cause of this? (48)
"You two have always been very affectionate; how is it that you now act so contrary?
My son, you are skillful; you ought not to abandon this most virtuous woman. (49)
Never before has she spoken anything unpleasant, nor has she done anything that was not dear to you; always skillful in pleasing you, it is not fitting for you to abandon her.
The duty of the household, the duty of kingship, and indeed the lineage-dharma and the sacrificial dharma always proceed from women alone. (51)
Having heard these words of his father, the prince replied:
"O father, there is no fault whatsoever to be found in my daughter-in-law anywhere. (52)
"Why did she strike Nakula before me even though I was restraining her?
Therefore, my anger arose and she was rebuked by me. (53)
"Your wife is not mine, nor am I indeed your husband.
Having heard these words of his son, the king then listened to the daughter-in-law. (54)
Having prostrated with her head, O King, that female serpent, though free from fault, spoke these words in fear. (55)
Though I tried to dissuade him, the prince killed her;
thereupon, consumed by anger, I remained standing, observing a vow of silence. ||56||
Just then, I saw Nakula and struck him out of anger;
though he was being restrained by the prince, he struck me again with a staff. ||57||
"Because we were vying with one another, Nakula was indeed killed by me.
O King, act with justice in this matter; inflict punishment, and I shall accept it. (58)
Having heard the words of the bride and the son, the king spoke these skillful words:
"For what reason have you two, though being animals, come to this separation? (59)
But since Nakula has been killed, my son, what is the cause of your anger?
Since the princess has been killed by a female serpent, why do you give way to wrath? (1.571.60)
"Why do you pointlessly accept such great ruin for the sake of a minor cause?
Having heard these auspicious words of his father, the young boy, who remembered his former births, [replied]. (61)
For he replied to his father: "The former nature prevails;
all beings follow their innate disposition; there is no way to restrain this. (62)
"Even for a very slight cause, enmity from a previous birth manifests.
Having heard these words of his son, the father then spoke to his son: (63)
"Speak, my son, according to the truth, regarding the cause of this interruption in our affection;
let that which occurred in a previous birth for both of us here be told."
If good sons do not conceal that which was asked by their father in secret, or if these sons do not speak the truth, even when it is indeed true; (65)
Those who, when asked by their father, speak either falsely or untruthfully regarding what is auspicious or inauspicious, indeed fall into the Raurava hell of heated sand.
"They attain a divine state, that state which belongs to those who speak the truth.
Having heard these words, the son spoke respectfully to his father: (67)
And having gone to that holy ford called Kubjāmraka, O lord of the earth,
it must be kept strictly secret, for it is a cause for the destruction of one's joy.
Then the king said, "So be it," and the queen said the same.
Thereupon, the king summoned his ministers and elders and spoke to them.
"Let us go to the auspicious holy site of Kubjāmraka;
let its accomplishment be swiftly achieved, and let the elephants and horses be harnessed."
Elephants, horses, cattle, vehicles, and so forth; kārṣāpaṇa coins, cows, gold, jewels, garments, and various kinds of food as well—71.
Then the king spoke to his son, appropriate to the time and place:
"O son, how can we depart, abandoning the kingdom which is now empty? (72)
The eldest son said to the younger one, "Give that back to him.
The king said, "If it were so, there would be a violation of dharma. (73)
"How should it be given to the youngest son while the elder son is still present?
The elder brother said, "Father, I give my consent; give the earth to him. (74)
In this matter, there shall be no loss of dharma, nor indeed will my existence cease;
I shall not return home again after having gone to Kubjāmraka. //75//
Considering these words to be true, he said, "Give the younger one indeed.
Upon hearing this, the king consecrated the youngest son in the kingdom.
The king went to the sacred ford together with the group of women from his inner apartments and others;
then, having performed the rites for the ford, he gave away gifts in abundance.
Food, clothing, gold, cows, elephants, horses, and houses [were given].
Then, when the night had passed, the eldest son, together with his daughter-in-law, [set out].
Having bathed and performed the rites of the sacred ford, having bowed repeatedly to his gurus, having circumambulated his father, and having saluted his mother; ||79||
Having gone to the Nirmālyakūṭa, which was certainly near the temple, he said to his father: "I was Nakula in my previous life. (1.571.80)
My residence was here in a grove of plantain trees;
for right here in my vicinity, I beheld a female serpent with venomous fangs.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at dawn, as the two of us were fighting due to our innate enmity, biting each other fiercely— 82.
At the same time, death occurred at the excellent holy site of Kubjāmraka, at Devāśraya; by that merit, I became your son. (83)
"This serpent of yours was formerly the daughter of the King of Prāgjyotiṣa;
thus, due to the impressions of her previous birth, she [felt affection] for both the serpent and the mongoose. (84)
Hostility has arisen between us two, and that is the cause of our separation;
now, O Great King, the full span of our lives has come to its end. (85)
"Indeed, at this sacred ford (tīrtha), by means of clear speech, we shall go to Vaikuṇṭha.
Having spoken thus and bowed to Hari, the lotus-eyed one, those two departed.
And likewise, having abandoned their bodies in an instant, the parents and the ministers became divine,
both bearing four arms, and [ascended] in a celestial chariot.
The two went indeed to Śvetadvīpa, traveling in the vehicle of Viṣṇu’s attendants;
the king and the others were filled with wonder, as was the devoted king himself at that time.
Afflicted by grief for his son, he performed a vow of asceticism;
in a very short time, he indeed accomplished the supreme perfection of an ascetic.
Having cast off his body along with his wife, he went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha,
the divine and supreme abode where Lord Janārdana resides.
Through my supreme grace and by the power of his asceticism, he performed devotion to me there and went to my imperishable state. ||91||
Having performed meritorious deeds for that retinue as well,
he too attained supreme perfection at Kubjāmraka and went to my abode.
Thus, O lotus-eyed one, the holy ford of Kubjāmraka was caused to flourish by Raibhya; it is rich with the dwellings of [divine] inhabitants and grants liberation to princes. 93.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; salutations to the Lord!
Having performed the auspicious bath while reciting [the mantra], as well as the drinking and the consecration [of the water]. (94)
Whether a woman or even a man, by beholding me and my form and washing away all sins, one attains the supreme goal. (95)
The supreme mantra already mentioned should always be recited by those of all four castes;
it is the primary object for all rites, and the deity here is Kāmbhareya.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Rādhā and Prabhā, the Master of Pārvatī and Māṇikī, is the Lord Lakṣmī Nārāyaṇa. (97)
Mañjuleśa, Haṃseśa, Saguṇeśa, Svayaṃprabhu, Dayānātha, Śāntinātha, and Campāhaimījayāpati. ||98||

Having worshipped him who is the greatest splendor among splendors and the greatest austerity among those who practice austerity, one shall become liberated in the presence of the Lord of Goloka. (99)
O Lakṣmī, that man who, having risen at dawn, recites this, is then filled with eternal happiness like Kṛṣṇa.
He shall deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants born of his own lineage;
indeed, he who recites this while giving up his life-breaths [attains the same]. || 10.1 ||
He shall become four-armed and established among the worlds;
even by merely hearing this, one shall be liberated—thus Śambhu spoke to Satī at that time.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of Raibhya’s Marvel, and the Liberation of Nakula and the Serpent after their Birth into Royal Families due to Mutual Enmity, by Returning to the Site of Their Previous Birth," within the section on the Greatness of Devotion at Kubjāmraka-Haridvāra, in the first book, the *Kṛtayuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the account of the great holy place Kubjāmraka, which grants liberation;
it is situated on the Narmadā at the confluence of the Kubjā and the Revā.
Established as permanent for seven kalpas, Śaṅkara declared this to Pārvatī while staying on the Ṛkṣaparvata during her pilgrimage.
Now, listen as I describe other holy sites as well:
to the west of Māhiṣmatī is indeed a sacred site that destroys all grief.
In that place known as Aśokavanikā, adorned by the hermitage of Mātaṅga,
a devoted wife should worship Gaurī on the third lunar day.
A maiden shall obtain a husband desired by her, endowed with wealth, beauty, and strength;
here, the celestial sage named Mātaṅga performed difficult penance.
In his previous birth, he was indeed a Niṣāda who always possessed the memory of his former lives,
due to his meeting with great sages at that place which destroys all evil.
Through his service to the Narmadā, he became preeminent in the knowledge of the Dharma, free from passion, awakened, and indeed possessed of merit. || 7 ||
And even that outcaste, filled with world-weariness, wearing matted hair and garments of bark,
dwelt in the Aśoka grove, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits.
For a thousand years, he indeed performed most rigorous penance;
and as he was thus performing penance, [flames] issued forth from the tips of his matted locks.
Yakṣiṇīs of dark complexion, radiant and adorned,
eighty-one thousand in number, bathed in the waters of the Narmadā.
Merely by bathing, they attained the worlds of the yakṣas with excellent vehicles;
even one devoid of mantras and yantras, simply by chanting "Obeisance to Śiva" (namaḥ śivāya).
He became a possessor of supernatural powers (siddhi), and Śaṅkara appeared before him.
Śaṅkara said to his devotee: "Choose a boon that you desire; I am Śaṅkara."
Mātaṅga said: "Let this sacred ford (tīrtha) become famous by my name;
for those of sinful birth—the Cāṇḍālas, the Śvapacas, and the leather-workers—" || 13 ||
Having come here, these pure ones shall surely attain liberation;
likewise, by bowing to the Mātaṅgeśvara Liṅga, they shall obtain emancipation.
"Grant this boon here, if I am indeed devoted to you.
Having heard that, Śaṅkara then replied, "So be it."
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations!
O Mātaṅga, by chanting this, supreme Vaiṣṇava liberation shall indeed be yours. (16)
There is no doubt that for those who follow your lineage, through the application of this mantra, liberation in Vaikuṇṭha shall come to pass. (17)
"Give me the mantra spoken by me and make all [others] Vaiṣṇavas as well.
Having said this, Śaṅkara thereafter vanished from sight. 18.
Mataṅga bestowed the mantra upon embodied beings of his own caste;
in ancient times, he indeed dispatched many Cāṇḍālas who were devotees of Viṣṇu.
In the month of Caitra, having ascended Goloka, the abode of Śrī Hari, and his own desire-yielding vehicle, he indeed attained supreme and auspicious liberation.
This Aśoka grove is called Mātaṅgatīrtha;
by the gift of sesame paste and the like, and by the offering of parched grain flour (saktu) for libations, [one attains merit]. 21.
The ancestors attain liberation by drinking the water; of this there is no doubt.
Right there, on the southern side, is the holy site named Mṛgavana.
Having bathed there, one should worship Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
fasting on the eleventh day, one should honor the Supreme Lord.
A devoted wife should worship her husband as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
by the power of bathing and giving gifts, she attains the Vaiṣṇava world.
In former times, there was a certain hunter who was ill-behaved and merciless;
carrying his bow, he slaughtered deer there, tormented by thirst. (25)
Having taken refuge for a moment under the shade of a tree in the absence of water, he fell asleep; immediately thereafter, a fire born from the friction of the forest trees broke out.
Having risen, he burned the forest filled with hunters and deer;
then, within a month, the rains fell, turning everything into ashes and fragments of bone.
Having gone to the Narmadā, they were all carried away by the flood of rain;
through their union with the Narmadā, those deer became Gāndharvas and ten million gods. (28)
That hunter indeed became a king upon the earth, and other living beings as well [attained the same state] through contact with the waters of the Narmadā. ||29||
The Yakṣas and other deities remained as gods for ten thousand years;
having enjoyed heaven, they likewise became the singers of this king.
Whether against his will or by his own volition, he who gives up his life on the Narmadā attains the state of Viṣṇu by means of the very vehicle of Viṣṇu.
He rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu for a thousand divine years;
the confluence of Aṅgārāvarta bestows the merit of giving a thousand cows.
And the god Aṅgāreśvara resides there at the confluence;
by merely bathing there, a man shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
On the fourth lunar day, under the auspicious influence of Mars, one should fashion an auspicious golden figure and wrap it in red cloth as well as ghee.
One should give a secret gift to a Brāhmaṇa and bestow a Maṅgalapurūṣa;
by the power of such giving and pilgrimage, one shall become a sharer of half the throne of Śakra.
In ancient times, there was indeed a great king named Yuvanāśva in Kosala;
he was a universal monarch in the Kṛta age, devoted to all duties. (36)
Having saluted Vasiṣṭha, he spoke to his priest:
"In what place, at what sacred ford, in what region, or in what temple of the gods, should one perform a sacrifice? (37)
Vasiṣṭha said to him: "The supreme sacred site of Naimiṣa is fruitful, and the horse sacrifice performed there is superior by millions upon millions of times."
It was spoken by Matsya and Viṣṇu, and likewise declared by Sūrya;
O Yuvanāśva, son of Manu, that which is worthy of sacrifice has been declared to you.
Having heard the words of his preceptor, the king commanded his ministers:
"Taking the requisites for the sacrifice, come here with all haste."
An announcement was made throughout the world and the gods were summoned to the sacrifice:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods (Indra), Skanda, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa.
Śambhu, the Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, the guardians of the quarters, and all the world-protectors; ||42||
Indeed, there were ten million cows accompanied by gold and jewels,
as well as one hundred thousand excellent horses and thirty thousand noble elephants.
Jewels, rubies, pearls, and infinite gold, as well as various kinds of goods and all sorts of foods to be eaten and consumed in every way. ||44||
Accompanied by all the sacrificial materials and whatever else there was, the king [set out] with various thousands of vehicles and thousands of diverse musical instruments. ||45||
Making the heavens resound with the great sound of the Vedas and with songs,
he entered the sacred site of Naimiṣa, where there is a vision of Lord Hari.
Then, having beheld the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the king gave one hundred thousand pieces of gold to ten thousand distressed people.
Having bathed, he gave away immeasurable silver ornaments;
indeed, having uttered "Oṃ namo viṣṇave," he placed water and darbha grass [upon them].
Having made his resolve, that king caused a sacrificial enclosure to be constructed using a golden vessel; he prepared a piece of land ten *kośas* in extent, filled with sacrificial stakes.
And he caused pavilions to be constructed, beautifully adorned with golden sacrificial posts,
along with altars and sacrificial pits, including the principal pit.
Then the sacrifice was concluded by the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha;
all the deities were delighted and indeed uttered cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Having completed the sacrifice, the king, together with his harem and retinue,
mounted his vehicle and departed from the Naimiṣa forest.
Then a certain monkey approached and repeatedly said to the king:
"Stop, stop! Listen, O King; you are possessed of false pride. (53)
I do not consider there to be any great fruit for you in the performance of sacrifices,
as was the case formerly during the sacrifice of King Satyadharma, the lord of the immortals.
Except for my face, everything from my throat downward became the color of gold;
all our children there likewise became golden.

At the confluence of the Kapilā and the Narmadā, through the power of the sacrificial waters—by bathing, immersing oneself, drinking, and even by wallowing in the mud of the sacrifice—[one attains merit]. //56//
The fourfold collection of beings has reached the world of the Gandharvas;
meanwhile, I was distracted during your sacrifice at Naimiṣa.
My body, smeared with mud, was washed with the water of sacrifice;
yet no fruit accrued to me, nor did my body turn to gold. (58)
Every sacrifice performed by you while under the sway of egoism is useless;
ten thousand cows, as well as infinite wealth and grain, have been given by you. (59)
Gold and silver were likewise given, yet all was in vain;
this I have told you, O King, for your sacrifice was not of such a nature.
Just as it happened for King Satyadharma on the bank of the Narmadā—may it be well with you; I shall now depart for the Narmadā, the bestower of the form of gold.
Having heard of your sacrifice, I indeed came to the Naimiṣa forest;
now, having become hopeless, I am departing, for no golden vessel has been given to me.
Having heard the words of the monkey, Yuvanāśva then said:
"Who are you, appearing in the form of a monkey? Tell me, O treasure-house of blessings! (63)
The monkey named Kadamba, the son of Jābāli, a knower of the Self who remembered his former births, having attained the state of a monkey due to stealing fruit, spoke.
O King, all the sacred fords were visited by me in this attire;
yet not even the slightest benefit was obtained by me at those holy sites. (65)
Only in the sacred field of the Narmadā, during that supreme sacrifice of truth and dharma,
my entire body became golden, with the exception of my face.
Having heard the words of the monkey, the king went once more to Naimiṣa to see that glorious Supreme Lord, the primordial God, the all-pervading Hari.
With supreme joy, he praised the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, a sacrifice has been successfully performed by me in the sacred field of Naimiṣa. (68)
At the end of this [speech], one who had assumed the form of a monkey made himself heard:
"I have gained nothing from your sacrifice; therefore, your sacrifice is in vain. (69)
He desires for himself a golden face, the highest of rites;
act in such a way that his face may indeed become golden.
Having heard this, the Blessed Lord, residing within the image, said to King Yuvana:
"Satyadharma will perform a sacrifice again on the Narmadā."
In that regard, his face will undoubtedly become golden;
therefore, O King, go to this monkey and proceed to the city of Kosala.
Having heard this, the king bowed to Hari at Naimiṣa and returned to his city;
the monkey, however, went again to the confluence of the Revā and the Kapilā.
Having gone there, he recounted the narrative of Satyadharma known as Naimiṣa;
and Satyadharma, having heard that, accepted the words of Hari as authoritative.
The monkey performed the sacrifice again after the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha),
repeatedly plunging his own face into the mud.
Then, having cast off the body of the monkey, he was born with a body made of gold and his entire face was golden.
Honored by the sound of celestial drums and by hosts of apsarases,
he departed for Vaikuṇṭha itself in a vehicle drawn by swans.
At that sacrifice, even beasts of prey and other creatures went to heaven after eating a mere morsel;
thus indeed does the Narmadā tīrtha prevail as the most supreme of all.
"From hearing and reciting this, the fruit of a thousand cows shall be obtained;
O Lakṣmī, this has been declared by me to Pārvatī, Śaṅkara. (79)
But he who performs a sacrifice on the bank of the Narmadā with his own wealth,
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having fashioned a golden *dhātrī* tree, one should bestow it upon a Brāhmaṇa;
by resorting to the banks of the Narmadā, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. ||81||
He who gives a living cow adorned with gold and jewels,
as well as a cow made of ghee, a cow made of molasses, or even a cow made of sugar— (82)
At the confluence of the Revā and Kapilā, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
now hear another story as well, which destroys both sin and suffering.
The son of Mitrāyu was the family priest of the royal seer Vīraṇa;
by him was established a sanctuary for Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
It was constructed on the bank of the Narmadā, adorned with a celestial pinnacle;
by the merit of that sanctuary and through the power of the Narmadā. (85)
Maitreya indeed rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu as a four-armed being;
meanwhile, this King Vīraṇa heard [the news] from a messenger of the gods.
O King, your preceptor has gone to Hari’s Vaikuṇṭha, having made even heaven seem low; how is it that you will not indeed go there to behold him? (87)
Having heard those words of the divine messenger, he asked, "How is the way [to heaven]?
Then the divine messenger said, "Perform a sacrifice on the Narmadā."
On the beautiful bank, having gratified Hari Kṛṣṇa, you shall depart;
Vīraṇa also performed an excellent Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
The gods arrived there, as did Maitreya and Nārāyaṇa;
the King also gratified all the Mothers, including Lakṣmī and the others.
Then, having performed the ritual bath at Avamṛthaka and having given sacrificial fees,
Vīraṇa became divine, a true Vaiṣṇava, and ascended in a celestial vehicle.
Being fanned by four-armed maidens, he was exceedingly beautiful;
bearing four arms, he repeatedly cried out, "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! ||92||
Honored with a welcome by the gods and his attendants along the way, he went to Viṣṇu’s supreme abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which bestows eternal peace. 93.
The royal sage Rantideva, having performed sacrifices at the Narmadā,
offered bilva and mango fruits to the Supreme Lord.
Having gratified Hari and the gods at that sacred site of Bilvāmraka,
and having received the command of Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, [he departed].
Having taken along some of his Vaiṣṇava devotees,
he went with his family and kinsmen to the shore at the edge of Hari’s abode.
In ancient times, the royal sage named Dadhīci, the king of Avanti,
went to the bank of the Narmadā and gave his own back to Indra.
Then, out of devotion, he went to the abode of Nārāyaṇa with that bone of his spine—the bone from which weapons were produced by which the gods indeed conquered the great asuras. 98.
O beloved, by bathing at Bilvāmra on the conjunction of the new moon and Monday,
people attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the power of the Narmadā field.
All the gods shall attain supreme perfection at Bilvāmra;
and the reciters and lay disciples as well shall go to the highest state.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Mātaṅga Hermitage in the Aśoka Grove, Aṅgāreśvara, the Golden Form of Nakula at the Sacrifice of Satyadharma, the Liberation of Vīraṇa, and Other Matters," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Mahālakṣmī, to this supreme account spoken by Śaṅkara concerning Suvarṇadvīpa Tīrtha, situated in the midst of the waters of the Narmadā.
In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, the great sage Hārīta indeed performed austerities there before the dark-complexioned Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Likewise, a beautiful vision arises for those ascetics who are practitioners of yoga.
Now, on the northern bank of the Revā, there is a mountain named Paryaṅka.
There, Viṣṇu himself, Mādhava, who removes all sins, resides;
that sacred field of Hari is proclaimed to be one *krośa* in extent.
Those who bathe there, even if they have died, attain the supreme goal. And on the southern side of the Narmadā is the excellent hermitage of Māṇḍavya.
In ancient times, Vibhāṇḍaka, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and others dwelt there;
likewise Viśoka, Narmadāsaṅga, and Śaṅkara Aśokeśvara.
There, at the confluence of the Narmadā and the Vindhya, lie the two beautiful rivers Nimnagā;
at that junction, goddesses who bestow liberation reside.
Harṣasiddhā, Sāvitrī, Aditi the mother of the gods, Devayānī, Brahmatanvī, Rohiṇī, and Kambharāyaṇī; || 8 ||

Dayā, Jayā, Lalitā, Mauktikī, Hemacampikā,

At the confluence, in the field of the Aśoka grove, a boon was granted to Gaurī on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina by her who is observant of vows.
Likewise, a woman who is childless, barren, unfortunate, or abandoned by her husband,

In the beginning, when [the lineage] was established, there was King Ravi, the lord of Kāñcīpura,

The king, together with his priest Śāṇḍilya, approached the Brahmin Agastya, the son of Mitrāvaruṇa;

The king said, "By the sight of you, my sin has indeed departed."
"Today my birth, my kingdom, and even my very life have become fruitful. In what place shall I perform a sacrifice so that the rite may reach its successful completion? (18)
"The gods obtain inexhaustible satisfaction, and there shall be liberation for the ancestors;

The Aśoka grove is renowned as a sacrificial ground honored by the gods;

Having taken King Agastya with him, he went to the Ashoka grove on the southern bank of the Revā, where there was a sacrificial altar and a pavilion.

Brahmadṛśya and Lomaśa, who was staying at Kuṅkumavāpikā, as well as the gods and other Brāhmaṇas, departed; then the sacrifice was commenced.

He said: "There is no place for me here; neither Vaivasvata exists here, nor Nārada, nor Parvata; neither Time nor Death is found here. (25)
"Since Citragupta is likewise not present, how was the sacrifice commenced?
Then Ravi and Candra, having bowed to Durvāsas, spoke these words. (26)
Who among even the hosts of gods and asuras is capable of creating an obstacle for me, by the grace of the Lord Aśokeśvara on the Narmadā? (27)
The sacrifice has been completed by me; you who are worthy of worship have assembled at this sacrifice.
May you also accept my honor as well as the sacrificial fees.
"I give to you, there is no doubt—Durvāsas, Nārada, and the others;

The great sages, Nārada and others, arrived there and were presented;

O Padmaja, hear now what was requested by Durvāsas once again:
"Formerly, due to the curse of Pārvatī, those residing in Pāṭalīputra... (3.1)
"Cursed indeed, these Brāhmaṇas have become dogs and are wandering upon the earth;

"By the power of my gift and through the grace of the great sages,

Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

one should never look toward the southern city.
Thereafter, one should go to Śuklatīrtha, the supreme site containing all holy waters;
by it, the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were made white.

Indra, having bathed Śambhu, worshipped him with bilva leaves.
There, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was worshipped by the guardians of the quarters;
[he went] to the meritorious hermitage of Kaśyapa, where there was a circle of ten thousand sages.

for that sacred site embodies all holy places and indeed embodies all the gods.
Where in former times the Lord of Sacrifice was worshipped by the Grandfather (Brahmā) in sacrifice,
all sins are destroyed by frequenting that land.
But for those who have died there due to no other recourse, that Śuklatīrtha grants liberation.
There was a righteous king named Yayāti who became a universal emperor (cakravartin).

Where there was no place for Hari, nor likewise any place for Śambhu,
the Daitya Jaṭāsura, seeing that vulnerability, then approached.
The sacrifice was destroyed by the Asuras, and the sacrificial posts were cast down;

One hundred and eight gods emerged in the form of deer;
then, remembering Hari and Hara, the king seized the weapon.
He slew the Dānavas in battle when the gods had again summoned him;
and by the grace of Hara and Viṣṇu, the sacrifice was set in motion once more.
There, by Hari and Śambhu appearing in person with their own splendor,
the entire world was turned white, like the imperishable Goloka.
Though entreated with a boon by Yayāti, Hara and Hari said:
"O Lords, remain right here forever in your divine forms."
From that time forward, those two, Śveta and Dīpyamāna, remain as Hara and Hari at the Śuklaka Tīrtha, bringing about the welfare of their devotees.

By the power of Śuklatīrtha, all those men shall go to their respective abodes; whatever desires they may cherish, those very desires they shall attain.
Yayāti, having had a magnificent palace built there and having installed the two deities within it, returned to his own kingdom.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!

O beloved, from there one should go to Śrī Śaṅkara, known by the name Meghanāda, where Viṣṇu, having been praised by Nābhāga, became manifest before his eyes.
In former times, indeed, the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa, while wandering this earth,

"Know me as Mandodarī by name; accept my auspicious welcome.
Rāvaṇa then said, "I am a king; give her to me here."
Then, according to the prescribed rites, Maya gave his daughter to him; Rāvaṇa then went to his own island of Siṃhala, where she gave birth to a son.
As soon as he was born, a sound issued from the boy’s throat;

Meghanāda became a devotee of Śaṅkara just as his father had been;

That body was emaciated by austerities such as fasting and the like;
then once, Meghanāda indeed went to Mount Kailāsa.

"I must inform my husband of my son's death tomorrow morning.

"Having bathed him, we shall perform the water-offering funeral rites.

indeed, go on foot, for you have come together with those who travel on others' feet.
O King, for one who arrives on foot, liberation here is certain;
therefore, O ruler, proceed on foot from your own city once again. (79)
"Then liberation shall indeed be yours; take this merit and go, O friend!
Having heard this, King Dharmasena then returned home once more.
On the thirteenth day, traveling on foot, he arrived at the Narmadā;
having bathed there at dawn on the fourteenth day, he beheld Sārikeśa.
Having directly beheld Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and remembering Hari,
he ascended a celestial chariot and went to the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Now, at the confluence of the Candrabhāgā and the Narmadā, there is a sacred ford;
here, Candreśvara, who is Sadāśiva, shines eternally.
Formerly, at midday, an excellent deer was killed by a hunter at the Hāriṇa-tīrtha on the bank of the Narmadā. (84)
Having fallen down, though his life-force had departed, he assumed a divine body;
by means of a celestial chariot, he went to the world of Brahmā.
Having seen this, the hunter became filled with world-weariness; having made the resolve to die, he immersed himself there in the water.
At that very moment, he, possessing a divine body, went to Gandharvapura;
this is indeed the Hariṇeśvara Liṅga, as well as Lubdheśvara. ||87||
There is also the holy site of Bāṇeśvara, and likewise Dhanurīśvara;
and Rameśvara is the fifth holy site, for it indeed bestows liberation. ||88||
There, with devotion, one should offer eight flowers to the God:
those born in water, as well as those that are lunar, fiery, windy, and earthly. (89)
The fruit of the forest tree (vānaspatya), that which belongs to Prajāpati (prājāpatya), and likewise the auspicious flower (śivapuṣpa) as the eighth;
water-born (vārija), water itself (salila), and the gentle (saumya) milk mixed with honey should be known [as the offerings]. ||1.574.90||
Incense, lamps, and the like belong to Agni; sandalwood and the like belong to Vāyu;
bulbs, roots, and the like belong to the Earth; and fruits and the like belong to the Vanaspati. ||91||
The Prājāpatya vow consists of auspicious food and the like; the flower of Śiva is spiritual service (upāsana).
Non-violence is the first flower, and the restraint of the senses is the second. ||92||
The third, however, is the flower of compassion; the fourth is the remembrance of Hari;
the fifth is service to the true guru; and the sixth is indeed the worship of the ancestors. (93)
The seventh is service to the Master, and the eighth is taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
by these indeed is the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa attained.
Rādhā is indeed the first flower; Lakṣmī is the second flower;
Pārvatī is the third flower; and Prabhā is the fourth flower. ||95||
The fifth is the Māṇikī flower, and the sixth is the Jayā flower;
Lalitā is the seventh flower, and Mañjulā is the eighth flower. ||96||
"These are indeed my own forms as flowers, residing within the blossoms;
without them, O Lotus-born One, I never take up flowers anywhere. (97)
The *haṃsa* and the *saguṇa* are flowers; the *campā* is a beautiful flower.
Compassion (*dayā*) is a flower, and the *devikā* is a perfect flower; the *muktā* is a beautiful flower. (98)
Even if there were sixteen thousand among the sixteen types of offerings, they would indeed enter into a single fraction of mine; therefore, I accept them all at once.
"I always accept worship through the object which is my own essential nature.
Having thus become one with Viṣṇu, he who worships shall attain the supreme goal.
Having indeed visited the Hariṇa-tīrtha, one should then proceed to the Bhārgava-tīrtha,
the supreme and most excellent of holy places, where the inhabitants of Kailāsa reside.
When the gods, having slain the demon Andhaka, arrived together with Śaṅkara at the Narmadā to bathe for the sake of visiting the sacred ford (tīrtha), [the following occurred].
Having diligently crossed to the northern and southern banks,
and having gone to the mountain named Bhṛgu on the southern bank, || 103 ||
Hara pierced it with his trident; by that piercing, Rasātala was split open.
From Pātāla, Gaṅgā indeed emerged, known by the name Bhogavatī.
There, a sacred ford (tīrtha) arose known as Śūlabheda;
there, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva themselves always reside.
Where the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī,
having assumed divine forms, are united and established at Śūlabheda.
Cakratīrtha is a supreme sacred ford that always exists there;
it is a sacred ford consisting of all other sacred fords, the highest and superior to all sacred fords.
The merit of Bhṛgutīrtha is superior to all merit, the supreme destroyer of all suffering; it is the most excellent and highest place where indeed Lakṣmī, the daughter of Bhṛgu, resides.
In ancient times, she was given to Viṣṇu by Bhṛgu according to the rites of marriage;
that sacred site is called Bhṛgutīrtha, for it is equal to Vaikuṇṭha.
The gift of a maiden and the worship of Śrī Hari must indeed be performed at that place;
by hearing or reading this, one obtains the fruit of giving and worship.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Tīrthas Beginning with Sahasrayajña, Tīrthaśukla, Dvīpeśvara, Meghanāda, Dāruvana, Karañjeśvara, Jīvana, the Confluence of the Viśvarūpā and the Revā, Candrāvatī, the Confluence of the Narmadā, Hariṇeśvara, Śūlabheda, Bhṛgukṣetra, and Others," in the first section concerning the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"O Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, please show me mercy and tell me: what kind of gift for a daughter (kanyādāna) ought to be given in the presence of my father?"
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
One should perform the excellent marriage of a daughter according to one's own wealth;
however, he who has no wealth at all should have his daughter beautifully adorned [with whatever he can afford].
Having touched a tulasī leaf with garments and other items in the presence of the fire,
the maiden should be given away in the presence of water and in the presence of Brahmins within the pavilion.
Having taken the garland of choice, the maiden should choose that groom;
if she has the inclination, she should provide food and other gifts according to her ability for the auspicious occasion.
Having obtained what is suitable, pleasing, and excellent, one should give it away without selling;
for selling it after acquiring wealth constitutes a great sin.
Having approached her, that supreme *tāraka* [mantra] should be imparted;
having summoned her, that middling *tāraka* should be imparted.
And she must be given by force; that is indeed the lowest form of gift.
She should be given like a maidservant; [otherwise] it is as fruitless as giving a common slave-girl.

While the giving away of the daughter is taking place, the women of the household should perform the chanting of the glories of Śrī Hari in that pavilion resounding with the noise of musical instruments.
Once that gift has been bestowed, the husband and wife should perform worship and behold Hari; thereafter, they may enter their own home.
They should daily perform worship and other rites in the morning with excellent materials;
they should perform them with the most sublime offerings and never commit an offense.
For those who commit offenses against worship, only sin arises.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, as I describe the faults along with their corresponding expiations. (11)
My devotee should always be intent upon my rites;
having set aside even a small portion of his house as a temple for the deity, he should worship me there.
Having installed the image as desired, one should worship it with baths, garments, pure sandalwood paste,
leaves, flowers, water, food offerings, incense, lamps, and ritual presentations.
One who is devoted to me should constantly worship [the deity], having offered circumambulations, lights, hymns of praise, prostrations, and formal dismissal, while remaining absorbed in meditation.
One should listen to the discourse, perform its recitation, and provide instruction; one should engage in dancing and instrumental music, and celebrate a most enchanting festival.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to my eternal dharma in its true essence;
even the gods who are masters of yoga and knowers of Sāṃkhya do not know this.
Without initiation into the Bhāgavata path, my worship is fruitless;
among hundreds of thousands, only someone rare attains initiation that brings me joy. (17)
Having made his mind peaceful within himself, he should approach the guru;
honoring his command, he should request: "O Guru, please instruct me. (18)
One should collect the materials for initiation and other requisites as shown by the Guru:
parched grain, honey, kusha grass, clarified butter, and also what is called nectar.
Milk, curd, cow urine, and cow dung mixed with fine sugar,
as well as a sacred thread, sandalwood paste, saffron, and unbroken grains.
Flowers, tulasī, incense, a lamp, food offerings, fruit, water, a garland, a necklace, a black antelope skin, and a sacred thread. ||21||
A staff, a water-pot, a lower garment, an upper robe, a jar, sesame seeds, sandals, a vessel for the guest-offering (arghya), a cooking pot, rice grains, and a ladle. ||22||
Barley, grains with molasses, fruits, and various foods—edibles, chewables, meals, drinks, and all things suitable for ritual action—in every respect. (23)
Whatever seeds there may be, and various kinds of jewels; glass vessels, jars, mango bowls, and cords. ||24||

The well-formed leaves of the *aśoka* tree, as well as a bench for the cloth, the threefold vessel for water for rinsing the mouth, and the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) and other implements for the fire-oblation (*homa*). ||25||
All the wood for the fire-oblation (homa) consists of Pippala, Udumbara,
Khadira, Bilva, Apāmārga, and also Arka wood.
One should collect the following pieces of wood: āmalaka, tulasī, sandalwood, vaṭa, as well as śāla and madhuka. ||27||
Having bathed and being endowed with auspiciousness, the Brāhmaṇa should construct a very beautiful altar, square in shape and sixteen cubits on all sides.
There, one should construct a Sarvatobhadra mandala using grains;
in its center, a new water-pot adorned with flowers and sprouts [should be placed]. (29)
One should place vessels made of gold, silver, or copper within a receptacle filled with jewels;
and upon that, one should duly set down a bowl filled with sesame seeds.
One should worship me, the Supreme Brahman, as well as the Guru, with excellent materials;
indeed, one should place consecrated substances upon the center of the altar.
O beautiful one, one should place four water-pots at the four sides, filled with water, provided with fresh leaves, and adorned with fruits. (32)
Having touched those [images] which are adorned with mango trees and enveloped on all sides with white cloths,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya) in the dwelling, in the pavilion, or in the presence of the Guru.
The disciple, facing north,
should receive the supreme Bhāgavata mantra from the guru who faces east, taking it into his left ear.
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge. Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! ||35||
The Guru should cause all women and men to hear these two mantras;
for the mantra is indeed a limb of initiation, and it is Hari who consists of knowledge. (36)
This disciple has become a devotee through the power of the mantra;
seeing these devotees, one should rise to greet them. (37)
Just as I am indeed worthy of honor, so too are the devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas). For one who is himself a pure devotee, upon seeing other devotees, [should show them respect]. (38)
He did not rise to greet me, and for that reason I was insulted;
furthermore, he who gives his daughter to a devotee should not send her away again. (3.9)
By him the eight classes of ancestors have been harmed; of this there is no doubt—for he is a pitiless man who harms his wife, his dear friend, and his virtuous spouse.
And even though he possesses a virtuous wife who is the very goddess of the household, an embodiment of Lakṣmī and a devotee of Viṣṇu,
he shall never again obtain a woman due to that very same sin.
Those who cause suffering to women always become miserable themselves.
[The trees] Bilva, Udumbara, Tulasī, Śakha, and likewise Āmraka—[these are auspicious]. 42.
The Aśoka, the Bakula, the Āmalakī, and likewise the Karṇikāra—
these trees of the gods are fit for ritual use and must not be cut down at their roots.
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, one who has been initiated must indeed avoid what is unfit to be eaten;
likewise, he must avoid what is unfit to be drunk, as well as censure and violence. 44.
Slander, theft, and seduction must be avoided, while the honoring of guests must be performed; sexual intercourse should be abandoned in every way, and celibacy is its restraint. ||45||
One must also strive diligently to maintain service to one's guru, even when seeing the good fortune, wealth, and prosperity of others. (46)
Seeing one's own poverty, one should never feel agitation;
thus indeed one should observe the rules and serve one's mother and father. (47)
One should always perform the worship of Śrī Hari with regularity;
then, one should place two leaves of the udumbara tree upon the altar. 48.
Then, having placed the water vessel and the razor, one should invoke me:
"Come here, O Blessed One, and be present in this image and upon this altar. (49)
Accept this water for honor and this water for the feet; thereafter, one should have the auspicious shaving performed beside the pavilion, so that the sins of the body hair may depart.
Having undergone a shave—leaving only the topknot, free of hair and devoid of blood—and having bathed, he should put on a clean, washed garment. (51)
Having likewise adjusted his upper garment, he should pay homage to the Guru and Hari;
and having kindled the god of fire with the oblation-vessel in the flame, [he should proceed].
Having performed the fire-oblation seven times with ghee mixed with honey, parched grain, black sesame seeds, and so forth, and twenty times with rice and sesame; ||53||
Then, having performed three circumambulations of the Lord, the devotee of the Blessed One, and the Guru, one should say: "I bow to you, Vahni, whose nature is Truth. (54)
Then, clasping the feet of the Guru, one should pray to the true Guru:
"By the grace of the Guru-deity, initiation has been obtained spontaneously. (55)
"May the Guru forgive whatever slight I have committed against him";
to the disciple who has spoken thus, he should give the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). //56//
Likewise, one should give a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) as a vessel for water for the sake of purification;
and one should also offer sandalwood paste, fragrance, and Vaiṣṇava oil to Viṣṇu.
The disciple should likewise offer the madhuparka as it comes in the sequence of worship;
he should then present garments, ornaments, and a garland of flowers to Nārāyaṇa.
Then the guru should place a tulasī garland around the neck of the disciple,
and likewise apply a forehead mark (tilaka) together with a crescent moon upon his forehead.
One should give him a name associated with Nārāyaṇa, endowed with the status of an Ācārya, or one associated with service; likewise, he should adopt the appropriate attire.
One should give gifts according to the individual and also according to one's own capacity;
and having bowed to the sacrificial fire, the deity, the guru, and the Vaiṣṇavas, [one should proceed].
Having given them a sacrificial fee, food, and clothing, he should go home;
the Brahmin should prepare a seat made from the skin of the black antelope.
This Brāhmaṇa should always carry a staff made of Palāśa wood;
the Kṣatriya, however, having laid down his weapons, undergoes initiation according to the prescribed injunctions.
One should take even a goat-skin, and especially a Plakṣa staff;
and having caused an altar twelve cubits in size to be constructed as before, [one should proceed].
During the initiation, one should receive all other auspicious matters from the guru; one should observe the restraints, thinking, "I shall not touch a weapon that causes harm. (65)
Then, having received the Bhāgavata initiation according to the previously stated procedure,
one should feed all pure Bhāgavatas and present them with gifts.
Then the Vaiśya, having brought all the necessary materials, should have an auspicious altar ten cubits in size constructed and should smear it with cow dung.
He should wear a goat-skin and likewise carry a staff made of udumbara wood;
everything else should be performed as before, and he shall become initiated.
Having performed salutations to the gods and to the foremost among the devotees of Bhagavān,
one should give food to the virtuous and ask for forgiveness for any offenses.
Even a Śūdra may receive the auspicious initiation of the Bhāgavata;
indeed, all the purificatory rites and materials have already been described by me.
One should arrange those [offerings] upon the altar; the altar should be provided with eight corners.
There, one should perform the rite according to the prescribed rule and worship Hari as before.
The skin should be that of a blue goat, and his staff should indeed belong to Viṣṇu;
having thus received initiation, a Śūdra may become a Bhāgavata.
One should indeed feed Vaiṣṇava sages and virtuous women according to one's wealth;
