and for all four castes, an umbrella should be given to the teacher who knows the Vedas.
The Guru should cause a white umbrella to be given for a Brāhmaṇa, a red one for a Kṣatriya, a yellow one for a Vaiśya, and likewise a blue one for a Śūdra. (74)
O Lakṣmī, I shall indeed tell you here what must be performed by those who are initiated:
O beloved, I am to be meditated upon in every way within the cow-faced [form] with a garland. (75)
The counting, the manual, the rosary, and the Tulasī—this is the initiation known as Gaṇāntikā, which consists of the seed-syllables that are the limbs of initiation. (76)
She should perform service for me so that my initiation may bear great fruit;
having made her secret and close to her virtues, the best of the wise should meditate upon me. (77)
In the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Vaiśākha, during the bright fortnight,
one should remain without food on the eleventh day and [take a meal] only in the morning on the twelfth day.
If one should indeed undertake initiation, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
One should give me an auspicious comb for the purpose of grooming my hair. (79)
One should offer collyrium and a mirror, and likewise offer a garland; one who is impure from eating should not touch the garland, for it should be placed in the open air.
My devotee should perform the twilight devotion (sandhyā), which consists essentially of meditation;
having fixed his meditation for a muhūrta, he should repeatedly recite my mantra. (81)
One should place a lamp before me, which increases the mass of splendor;
likewise, one should apply a crescent-marked tilaka upon my forehead.
One should offer fragrant incense and recite this verse:
"O Keśava, your limbs are fragrant by their very nature. (83)
Having perfumed that house with this auspicious incense,
one should offer a lamp made of ghee, which is auspicious and a deliverer of the ancestors.
A vessel made of gold, silver, or bronze is praised for me;
having abandoned all of those here, indeed, copper pleases me. (85)
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the truth from me as to why Tāmra is dear to me;
formerly, O lotus-petal-eyed one, there was a great Asura named Guḍākeśa.
Taking up the form of copper, he remained intent upon my worship alone for fourteen thousand years, perfectly steadfast.
Filled with joy, I went to his Tāmra hermitage;
seeing me, he who possessed four arms bowed down to me repeatedly. (88)
"I have said this to you; I am pleased, so ask for the boon desired in your heart.
Then Guḍākeśa spoke with a pure inner self: [89]
"May my devotion to you remain firm throughout thousands of births;
O Mādhava, I desire my death by the discus released by you."
O Lord, this fat, flesh, and so forth from me, who have been struck by the discus—this shall become copper, which is auspicious and a means of purification. (91)
"O Lord, let there be supreme satisfaction for you with this copper vessel offered to you.
"So be it," he said to me, [to last] as long as the world endures. (92)
"As long as you possess the nature of copper, you shall be worthy of me;
therefore, whatever is abundant that is given to me in a copper vessel [is acceptable]. (93)
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, when the sun was at its zenith, I fashioned that copper vessel, which is both auspicious and purifying. (94)
Desiring death by the discus while performing auspicious deeds for my sake, he thought, "When shall I become established in Viṣṇu? (95)
Having then performed worship of me, he prayed to me:
"O Lord, release, release the discus which possesses a brilliance equal to fire! (96)
"Let my body be quickly led forth, having had its limbs cut off on all sides;
struck by my discus, he has come before me, the Supreme Lord. (97)
Copper is its flesh and blood; I have explained it thus.
One should provide the offering of copper for the presentation of worship, food, and so forth. 98.
For every grain of boiled rice [offered], he shall obtain the fruit born of a hundred horse-sacrifices;
for that many thousands of divine years, he shall dwell in my abode. 99.
He rejoices there and then goes to the supreme abode, the highest state;
having thus fed me in a vessel of copper or gold.
And having offered betel-leaf, one should perform the dismissal;
thus indeed should my devotee, once initiated, perform the worship. (101)
"O beloved Lakṣmī, this was spoken by Śambhu as eternally true;
by hearing it or even by reciting it, one shall go to my abode. (102)
A man, a woman, or anyone else, having received initiation according to the prescribed rite, should worship me; for by that, one attains liberation for oneself and indeed the fruit of birth.
Thus, in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā,

[is described] the giving away of a daughter in marriage, the ritual procedure for initiation into the Bhāgavata path, and how, following the destruction of the Asura named Guḍākeśa by the discus, his fat, blood, and other substances were transformed into copper ore.
The five hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ceti and Other [Sacred Sites]."
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
O Lord, having heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa your auspicious initiation and having gained an understanding of your majesty, I have become pure.
Oh, how great is the majesty of the Lord, which brings happiness to the four castes!
It has indeed been realized through the granting of initiation, as well as for the sake of his devotees. (2)
I ask: regarding transgressions, what is the fruit and what is the remedy?
O Janārdana, tell me the means of purification for those devoted to your worship.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall proclaim the purification of offenses;
having become pure and a devotee of the Lord, one should be intent upon my worship.
O Lord of Creatures, even if fallen into distress, the king who eats food accumulated through sin shall dwell in hell because of that sin.
The king proceeds by performing actions characterized by darkness and passion;
his food is cruel, censurable, and a great burden of sin.
One should not eat the food of a king, for it leads to hell; however, that which is fit to be eaten may be consumed by men who are devotees of the Lord.
But having set me aside, O Lakṣmī, and having offered everything to me, if he accepts [the gift] after giving away wealth and grain in abundance; || 8 ||
The remnants of my grace have been established by the devoted followers of the Bhagavat;
for one who eats them, no stain of sin whatsoever arises.
O Lotus-born One, for my devotee who eats food that has not been offered with faith or is the king's food, purification shall indeed come through the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If one touches me after bathing without having chewed a tooth-stick and without having cleansed the mouth, he shall have foul-smelling breath.
O Lakṣmī, due to my offense, that devotee may become devoid of merit;
such a man becomes a sinner, possessed of phlegm, bile, and impurities.
Since his mouth is always foul-smelling with pus and blood, he draws in pure air and exhales it as a foul odor. (1.3)
Therefore, an offense against him arises from being too close to my image;
purification shall come through the use of a tooth-stick and the application of fragrant substances. (14)
When such an offense has occurred, one who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa should sleep in the open air for two days and perform intense worship of me. || 15 ||
One should perform a recitation of a hundred garlands [of mantras]; no fault shall be found. For if one has engaged in sexual intercourse and remains unwashed, he is indeed as one who is dead.
And as a ripening of that offense, he shall fall into the hell named Lāla;
for a human being, the supreme duty consists of ritual bathing, meditation, and worship. (17)
One who does not bathe, being laden with feces and urine, shall fall into the hell named Mala;
for him, an expiation must be performed with a mind endowed with devotion.
Or one should eat barley-gruel or oil-cake for three days, and fast on the fourth; by that, the purification of the devotee is accomplished. (19)
Furthermore, he who, having touched a corpse and gone to the cremation ground, does not bathe at all—
his ancestors fall because he is impure, and he too shall surely fall.
Having become jackals in a cremation ground, they become eaters of corpses;
for that, an expiation must be performed by my devotee directly. (21)
Eating only once a day for one day, and likewise fasting for one day, and then drinking the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one becomes pure; of this there is no doubt. ||22||
That pitiless man who touches me after touching a woman in her menses—
by that sin, even a devotee goes to the realm of Yama filled with dust.
From that, one is born blind, poor, and devoid of intelligence;
for the purification of that offense, there is indeed only one remedy: fasting. 24.
Having slept in the open air, bathed while still wearing his clothes, and consumed the products of the cow (gavya), that person devoted to my ritual practice is liberated from impurity. ||25||
O Lakṣmī, he who touches a corpse and remains within my sacred fields,
yet does not bathe and continues to touch me, shall attain birth as a Cāṇḍāla.
Thereafter he is born blind; he may become a frog, a fly, a *ṭiṭṭibha* bird, a mosquito, a lizard, or even a donkey. (27)
Even a cat or a monkey, if it has committed an offense, is born as such a devotee, intent on my ritual service, for the sake of purification. (28)
Thereafter, one should subsist on a single meal for fifteen days and consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); thus, one is purified from the offense. ||29||
When [the wind] touches me, it releases the downward-moving air (apānavāyu);
by that defect, flies and likewise mice are born.
Or he may be born as a dog or a tortoise; thereafter he becomes a human being.
Therefore, he should observe three nights of fasting at night; by that, he is purified.
One devoted to devotion should perform a hundred recitations of the *mālā-mantra* and bathe;
for he who voids excrement along with wind and the bodily humors [is purified]. (32)
Whether he is engaged in my worship or intent on other activities of mine,
he shall thereafter fall into the Yāmya Purīṣa hell because of that.
O Lakṣmī, a man who is devoted to my ritual duties is born;
therefore, an expiation must be performed, namely lying down upon the water. (34)
One should also lie upon the bare ground for one day;
by performing the recitation of the *mālā-mantra* one hundred times, one is liberated from the offense. (35)
Even if one has bathed, if he proceeds along dusty paths and approaches me without having washed his feet and so forth, [he is not fit]. (36)
"He too would be impure and sinful, a doer of what is displeasing to me;
therefore, I certainly do not accept the perfume and garland offered by him. Having washed my feet as well as my hands with that [water],"
Having sipped water according to the rule and being thus purified, one should touch me. Having likewise performed the removal of impurities, one should apply clay seven times;
having applied it to the organ, one should likewise apply it to the two hands.
Then one should wipe the feet five times and thereafter cleanse the vessel;
having performed seven mouthfuls of rinsing water (gaṇḍūṣa), one should then perform the bath.
O beloved, my devotee indeed becomes pure as a worshiper in this way, and not otherwise.
If one who holds a portion of incense in his hand should touch me, he would incur a fault;
having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and sipping water (ācamana), he should wash his hands.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, purity is attained, and no offense occurs.
But that man who, though devoted to me, is possessed by anger and touches my limbs, shall then become a partaker of sin.
By that sin he shall become a chameleon, and thereafter he shall become a hawk.
Through anger one becomes a worm, and through wrathful intent one becomes black in color.
One should not perform my worship with anger, nor with greed, nor with haste; for when performed according to the prescribed rite, it bestows liberation.
Having bathed, one should prepare a hundred garlands; by this, the purification of anger is considered achieved.
However, that fool on earth who worships me with unsuitable flowers—even if he is a devotee of the Lord—is thereafter born as a monkey.
Whether it be a cat, a bull, a goat, or a village cock,
or even a buffalo, may he become the giver of flowers to me— [that which does not please me].
And for the sake of its purification, he shall indeed eat but one meal for seven days.
He shall be liberated from all sins and find his place in my world,
even if he approaches me clothed in garments stained with blood,
or if he approaches me wearing clothes covered in the menstrual flow of a woman in her courses.
By that fault, one would be born as a dog-eater (outcaste); of this there is no doubt.
For one month he should eat only once a day and recite the mantra ten thousand times;
on the final day, however, he should observe a fast, and thus he becomes purified.
He who touches me in the darkness without a lamp incurs that fault;
he shall suffer the birth of blindness, and I shall prescribe the atonement for him:
[he must observe] a single meal for five days while keeping his eyes covered.
One should also make a hundred garlands and recite [the mantra]; then one becomes purified. ||53||
Black clothing must never be worn during my worship under any circumstances;
by that fault, one shall thereafter become either a mongoose or a tortoise. (54)
Or it may be a pigeon; I shall tell you the expiation:
one should eat only once a day for seven days and offer a hundred garlands.
Then there shall be purification for him, and he shall attain my world—[the one] who performs my rites even with unwashed clothing. (56)
Whether it be an elephant, or likewise a camel, a horse, a jackal, or even a deer;
therefore, purification must be performed with great effort. (57)
One should observe a single fast and recite the mantra a hundred times with a rosary;
furthermore, one should give the leavings from a dog's meal if it pertains to my ritual.
He too shall become a dog, a jackal, or even an owl;
purification must be performed for three days by one who subsists on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
In the fourth [period], one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise observe a fast;
thus the offense shall indeed be destroyed, and one shall attain my world.
In the illumination of a lamp, the finger may become blackened with soot;
it should be diligently washed away along with the scent of the burnt wick. (61)
If one touches me while my hands are unwashed, it would be an offense against me;
by that, one might become afflicted with leprosy or other diseases; therefore, one should wash one's hands. ||62||
When an offense has occurred, one should perform the recitation of the Śatamālā mantra while observing a fast;
by that means, purification occurs and one becomes fit for ritual action.
Any person who, having gone to a cremation ground, touches me without having bathed,
is reborn as a jackal, a vulture, or a piśāca.
Then one should fast for one day and recite the mantra a thousand times;
by that, purification occurs, and not otherwise merely by bathing.
Śrī Lakṣmī said:
"If the cremation ground is impure, how is it that Śambhu, the supreme devotee of the Lord, dwells there as your devotee, as if he were a partaker of its defects?"
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall relate to you an ancient account concerning Śambhu;
there is indeed no cremation ground that is pure, for it is always considered impure. (67)
For some reason, Śambhu chose to take up residence there;
yet he did not always regard that dwelling as being of the nature of a penance.
Although Śaṅkara is my great and supreme devotee,
I do not accept his worship and other offerings because he dwells in the cremation ground.
"After the performance of atonement, I accept everything, and never otherwise;
even as Śaṅkara destroyed the three cities and likewise the Asura."
Then, because of that sin, Śaṅkara— having been defiled by it— lost his sovereignty, along with the children, the elderly, and the women residing in Tripura.
His power of yoga was destroyed and his power of illusion was lost;
with a pale face, he became unable even to move.
He became as if dead from the curses delivered by the Asura women;
his consciousness was lost, his knowledge destroyed, and his joy vanished, though he remained possessed of his strength.
Then, having entered that state and beheld Śaṅkara, I said to him:
"Do not grieve; I shall indeed swiftly bring about your welfare."
Then, Śaṅkara was seen by me with divine vision;
at that moment, the power of Rudra once again became manifest.
"I have come for the sake of destroying your sin," I said.
Hearing this, Hara, his eyes burning with the heat of my transgression, spoke to me.
O Viṣṇu, by your grace the demon Tripuraka has been slain;
the Dānavas there have been killed, and those who were pregnant have been struck down. (77)
Children and the elderly were slain, and the three cities were burnt;
by the power of that sin, I am unable to move.
"O Viṣṇu, my sovereignty and power are lost, and my knowledge, self, and true strength have perished; what should be done by me now, who am in such a sinful state? (79)
"O Viṣṇu, tell me in truth the purification for this sin. To Rudra, who was thus entreating me, I spoke:
"Carrying a garland of skulls, dwell on earth as one defiled.
Śambhu asked me, "What is proclaimed to be this state of being defiled? (81)
I have indeed said that a cemetery is impure and called putrid;
dwelling in a cemetery is here proclaimed to be the state of being defiled. (82)
O Śaṅkara, taking up those skull-bowls, sport right there;
dwell for a hundred years together with your servants, such as the bhūtas and pretas.
For that long, no external worship of mine should ever be performed;
mental worship must be practiced, and there shall be no transgression. (84)
"When a full hundred years have passed, go to the hermitage of Gautama;
through the grace of the sage Gautama, you shall become free from sin. (85)
Then, through the destruction of your sins, perform purification of the body;
for one year, O purifier, undertake the vow of subsisting only on milk. (86)
Or else, you shall perform the excellent monthly vow known as Brahmakūrca;
thus purified, you will become worthy of worship. (87)
Henceforth, you must never dwell in a cremation ground with a corpse, if you desire my status as worthy of worship and the virtue of a Vaiṣṇava. (88)
Having thus granted the boon to Rudra, I vanished right there;
and Rudra, too, wandered for a hundred years in a cremation ground.
But having performed his purificatory rites and being devoted to my command,
Rudra went to the hermitage of Gautama when a hundred years had passed.
Then Gautama proclaimed this instruction to him:
"O Rudra, always maintain a twofold form according to the power of ritual action. (91)
All your sin has departed here; you are indeed pure, a great Vaiṣṇava.
Always maintain this sattvic form of a great bhāgavata.
Always remain on Kailāsa and be devoted to your devotees with a pure, sattvic nature; furthermore, assume a second form as Bhairava, consisting of your own shadow.
It is to be venerated by ghosts, spirits, and demons, and it is impure;
it is fit for dwelling in cremation grounds and is always the refuge of those characterized by darkness (tamas). ||94||
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara then again assumed two forms;
[one] standing in the cremation ground [said], "He is neither my devotee nor a Vaiṣṇava. (95)
"For my devotee residing on Kailāsa is indeed worthy of worship, the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this been told; [that] cremation ground is always perfectly pure.
Dwelling in cremation grounds, they are indeed impure and certainly not clean in that place of corpses;
afterwards, they are accompanied by Rudra’s attendants, such as the Bhūtas and others who are characterized by tamas.
Kailāsa is indeed described as the cremation ground of Śaṅkara;
however, in reality, there is no such thing as a cremation ground that is dear to Śaṅkara. (98)
O Lakṣmī, a cemetery is certainly not dear to anyone;
how then could it be dear to the gods, who are engaged in virtuous deeds? (99)
Thus the truth has been told to you; now I shall declare the expiation to you:
one should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while fasting for a single day.
A bath with one's clothes on and a meal consisting of *tulasī* leaves must be undertaken;
by that, one is liberated from sin and becomes worthy of performing my rites. (101)
One who commits the act of drinking liquor becomes fallen from his body;
his purification occurs in every way through the Brahmakūrca vow. 102.
Otherwise, he would become an owl, and indeed he becomes a worm once again.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe the Brahmakūrca vow, which brings about purification. 103.
A person who maintains the body should perform that [practice] for a month or a fortnight,
using milk, āmalaka, ginger, and also palāśa leaves.
One should boil sugar and *tulasī* leaves and drink it during the day, so that the ulcer may heal and not undergo further deterioration. (105)
One should not eat anything else nor drink water for the sake of peace;
this is the Brahmakūrca vow, observed either for a fortnight or for a month.
Whichever purifying leaves of trees there may be, one should boil them and drink [the decoction] daily; among these, the leaves of the Palāśa tree are certainly recommended. 107.
Or one may drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) every fortnight or every month;
that is equal to the Brahmakūrca penance and is a purifier of all sins.
This, however, makes the body free from impurities and bestows liberation when death occurs;
it is a purgative and a decoction for the purpose of purifying the bodily elements.
That which is performed with devotion to Brahman is indeed ordained for the sake of liberation;
that which is made into an expiation shall indeed be the washing away of sin.
If it is for the purpose of destroying disease, it shall bring about the purification of the bodily constituents;
however, if it is not digested anywhere, that indeed leads to death. (111)
A man who commits an offense against me shall become a pig that eats onions, vegetables, leaves, and the like; or he shall become a dog, or even a jackal. 1.12.
Having performed the Brahmakūrca vow, one should perform a hundred recitations of the Mālā-mantra;
by that, his purification shall be achieved, and he shall become worthy of performing my rites.
He who touches me with another's garment, even if it has been washed, attains birth as a deer and shall have only one foot. || 1.14 ||
In the month of Māgha, one should remain in the water for exactly two praharas;
by that, purification is attained, and if one recites the Śatamālā, one becomes stainless.
He who, drawn by sensual cravings, eats for himself without first offering new grain to me, becomes a partaker of sin; therefore, he must observe a fast.
Even by reciting the *mālā* mantra a hundred times, that man is purified;
yet he who offers me incense without first offering perfumes and garlands [is not]. 1.17.
He becomes a Yātudhāna; therefore, he must perform a fast. Furthermore, by reciting the mantra over a hundred offerings of parched grain (māla), that Vaiṣṇava is indeed purified.
But he who approaches me wearing sandals on his feet shall be born as a leather-worker, and thereafter become a dog and a pig.
O Lotus-born One, my devotee should observe the fortnightly fast and the practice of eating only once a day for a hundred times; by that, his purification shall be achieved.
But he who indeed awakens me without the sound of bells and other instruments becomes deaf because of that; therefore, a fast (samupoṣaṇa) must be observed.
Even one who has eaten a great deal of food and is overwhelmed by indigestion is purified if he is my devotee and performs a hundred recitations of the *mālā-mantra*. (122)
One who returns from a meal without having rinsed his mouth, or approaches while still unwashed, is indeed reborn as a monkey, a jackal, a dog, or a goat. (123)
One should fast for three days and perform one hundred rounds of the rosary;
whoever performs the expiation according to this procedure [shall be purified].
He shall not be tainted by sin; he goes to my world, whoever, being a devotee of the Lord, recites this daily upon rising at dawn.
Whether one recites it or even hears it, such a person goes to my world;
for what was spoken by Śambhu is true, O Padmaja, and thus have I told it to you.
It is the greatest health among all forms of health, the supreme liberation among all liberations,
the highest purification among all purifications, and the state of being a worthy vessel among all states of clarity.
I have declared that the supreme austerity among all austerities consists of devotion to me;
it must be practiced by my devotee, and there is no need for hesitation regarding the Rākṣasas.
This has been proclaimed by me here for the sake of those seeking liberation, for yogis, for virtuous women, for the righteous, and for those endowed with devotion to me. 1.29
O Lakṣmī, this purification has not been spoken by me for the sake of atheists whose hearts are seized by latent impressions and who are addicted to the poison of the womb.

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offenses Against the Worship of the Blessed Lord in the Kṛta Yuga Era of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, including their purification or the attainment of other bodies and wombs, and the explanation of Śaṅkara’s fondness for cremation grounds and his dwelling in non-cremation grounds," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, to how, following the death of the jackal and the vulture,
there was the attainment of a kingdom and liberation through the occasion of touching a sacred ford.
That princess, who had died against her will at a sacred ford,
became a female jackal with large eyes, yet still possessed of the sixty-four arts.
Having died there, that vulture likewise became a king. Oh, how great is the power of the sacred ford! Even two animals have attained divinity.
In the land of Haima, there was a king of Kāmpilya named Brahmadatta;
his son, Somadatta, having reflected upon the purpose of the śrāddha rite, [acted accordingly].
At that time, having gone into the forest for the sake of his ancestors, desiring game, he did not find anything there; instead, he beheld a female jackal.
Pierced by that arrow, she reached the waters of the Gaṅgā;
having quickly drunk water on the bank at the sacred ford, she released her life-breaths.
At that moment, the prince saw a vulture perched upon a banyan tree;
the royal youth struck down the vulture with an arrow.
Even he, having fallen by the water's edge, attained merit;
then Somadatta, taking the two of them, went home.
The vulture was the handsome son of the King of Kaliṅga;
likewise, that female jackal was born as the daughter of the King of Kāñcī.
Through the power of their respective sacred sites, a union occurred between the two of them spontaneously;
having married, they spent their time happily, full of great affection for one another.
Pervaded by love for one another, they never endured separation at any time.
Then, on one occasion, the wife, filled with affection, spoke to her husband.
"O beloved, you must grant me permission to observe a single vow;
out of affection for me, if it is dear to you, you ought to grant me your consent here."
Truth is the root of all beings, and Viṣṇu is established in truth;
the kingdom always has truth as its root, and the vow prospers through truth.
Thus addressed, the husband said: "Request it, my dear;
perform whatever you desire, and I shall provide you with the highest assistance."
Having heard her husband's words, she spoke to him with confidence:
"I, being in such a state, wish to sleep alone at midday. (15)
So that no one—neither my father-in-law, nor my mother-in-law, nor my husband, nor any other person—might see me even for a very short time at all. (16)
"He shall not see me while I am asleep; this is my vow for a moment. Having heard this, the prince said "Certainly" to his wife. (17)
He gave her an independent palace where no person at all would see her, nor would anyone see the woman of great vows upon her bed.
Having indeed made such an agreement, that prince lived accordingly;
he enjoyed and ruled over that kingdom bestowed by his father.
He had five sons; he bestowed the kingdom upon the eldest, and then he himself, like his wife, took up a vow.
He sleeps alone where no person sees him;
indeed, seventy-seven years have passed for him since then.
In his seventy-eighth year, that lord of men,
while the sun was at its zenith, remained in solitude, contemplating that very same matter.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, his mind was set upon the longing desire to see his beloved. (23)
Who is to be worshipped? What is her vow? She sleeps here in a secluded place;
for one who has fallen asleep, no vow whatsoever is accomplished, O performer of great merit. (24)
No one has created this dharma; it is simply a vow to be observed while sleeping.
Having indeed enjoyed sensual pleasures, and having eaten meat with rice, [one should observe this]. (25)
Betel, silken garments and the like, ornaments, garlands, all things such as cosmetics for adornment, and fragrant perfumes. ||26||
"Why should there be a vow here? Since she performs a vow while asleep, she must certainly be seen; what kind of vow does she practice? (27)
She may become angry when she sees [the fault], yet even so she will surely remain angry; or rather, let her go wherever she pleases once she has departed in anger.
Or if there should be some loss, let it be so;
nevertheless, for one who reflects in this manner, the sun has reached the sky. (29)
Then, having bathed according to the prescribed rite and being clothed in two linen garments,
he dismissed all his attendants from his presence.
"Today I must remain in my vow; no one should come home, neither man nor woman, nor even to the gate of the royal palace."
"If anyone should come here, he shall become my victim.
Having thus issued this command, the king went into his palace.
He remained hidden beneath the couch of the queen by means of coverings;
then, at the time of midday, the queen came to that seat.
Afflicted by pain and tormented by a headache, she wept there, thinking: "What did I do in the past, the fruit of which is this nature of suffering? (34)
Even my husband does not know that I am afflicted with pain upon his own head;
what should be done? Where should I go? Indeed, I must surely die.
"Does your husband not ask here what vow you have and of what kind it is?
I must tell him; otherwise, there will be no end. (36)
If I speak, my death will occur; if it is not spoken, it will cause destruction. If it is not told, constant suffering must be endured, for it does not cease. (37)
Therefore, I must go to that place together with my husband, so that I may relate there how I have fallen into this suffering. (38)
Having heard these affectionate words, the king rose from there,
embraced his beautiful wife with both arms, and spoke to her with fortitude.
"What is this that you say, O blessed lady, regarding your own afflicted self?
There are many physicians who will eliminate your suffering. (1.577.40)
Previously, under the pretext of a vow, you well concealed this knowledge, O blessed lady, because of which you are indeed suffering, oppressed by pain in your head. (41)
"O blessed lady, you who speak thus while being tormented by sorrow—having gone to that place where I was born previously, I shall speak to my husband. (42)
"O auspicious lady, tell me what that place is, if you find the journey pleasing;
you must certainly go there with me and obtain happiness. (43)
"What is this that you conceal, O Goddess, before your husband, you who are devoted to your husband?
The husband is dharma, the husband is fame, and the husband alone is one's own beloved. (44)
"Even that which is to be hidden must be told to one's husband; this is the duty proclaimed for a devoted wife.
Having been told this, she said to her husband: "In this matter, speaking would lead to destruction."
Therefore, O Lord, you should not speak that which causes you pain;
for you always abide in happiness, you are a great king and handsome. (46)
"Many wives resembling me reside in your inner apartments;
enjoy happiness, O Great King, without abandoning me alone. (47)
"I am going to my own place; therefore, death for me is certain.
You shine like a god, O King; you ought not to question me about that. (48)
You are my god, my manifest teacher, my eternal husband, my sacrifice; you are virtue, wealth, pleasure, fame, and heaven, O giver of honor. (49)
"When asked by me, you must speak what is beneficial, true, real, and pleasing to you;
this is the eternal duty of all women devoted to their husbands."
A husband should not be subjected to uncertainty by a wife who dwells in comfort;
having ascertained this, you ought not to ask me about my suffering here. (51)
The husband said: "Listen, O blessed lady, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
a woman who has been questioned by her husband must certainly speak."
Virtuous women do not conceal their secrets whether they are guarded or unguarded;
however, she who conceals what is guarded from her husband is certainly no virtuous wife.
The wife spoke these meaningful words, consistent with dharma, to the king:
"The king is a god, the king is a preceptor; it is recited that the king is Soma. (54)
"One should not speak untruth before a king; let us go to the place of the boar.
There, at that sacred ford, I shall tell you [all]; show me special favor. (55)
Saying "So be it," the king then commanded his ministers to go to the Saukarava Tīrtha, which flows toward the Badarikāśrama hermitage.
There were hundreds of thousands of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as tens of thousands of milch cows;
likewise, there was wealth, grain, jewels, ornaments, and garments.
Having taken his wife along for the sake of giving gifts, and accompanied by his aged progeny,
he went to the sacred ford known as Gaṅgātīrtha and resided there for six months.
Then, having performed the rites for the sacred ford, the couple, endowed with self-restraint, fasted for three nights and gave gifts of all kinds.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Hari, who was adorned with ornaments,
the virtuous and beloved wife stood before Lord Hari there and spoke to her husband.
"Come, come, O Lord; let us go and see that which was intended in secret.
Previously, I was a female jackal, established in the womb of an animal. (61)
"Long ago, he was pierced in the head by Somadatta with an arrow;
through that fault of his, this pain has now settled upon my own head. (62)
Your birth was in the royal family of Kāñcī; your beloved was given to you by your father.
By the power of my sacred field, this very success has been attained for me; salutations be unto you! (63)
Having heard this, the king also remembered his former birth:
"O illustrious lady, I was a vulture here at this banyan tree, wandering in the forest. (64)
"Pierced by Somadatta and dying here through the merit of this sacred site, I have been born as the king of the Kaliṅgas, my dear, and am now your husband. (65)
Behold the excellent fruit of the field even through an undesired death;
for they were the best among the devotees of the Lord and likewise dear to Nārāyaṇa.
The citizens and country-folk who had gathered there by the thousands were all filled with wonder and performed worship to Hari.
Having abandoned their own bodies, the king and queen became possessed of divine forms; with four arms, they ascended a celestial chariot and went to the world of Brahmā.
Those two, worthy of worship by the gods, departed; the kettledrums resounded in the sky, and the subjects who had followed them also left, abandoning all worldly attachments.
Right there they met their death through the grace of Nārāyaṇa;
and all of them, possessing four arms, went joyfully to the world of Brahmā.
All the male attendants hold conchs, maces, lotuses, and jewels; the women are endowed with four arms and possessed of all enjoyments. ||71||
The female attendants rejoice in the world of Brahmā in the abode of Hari;
thus, by the power of the sacred ford, they have attained eternal liberation.
Whatever merit was performed in previous lives, whether it be very little or much, that indeed bears fruit at some time, by which one comes to a sacred pilgrimage site. (73)
Even if it should arise in only a small measure, it leads to greatness for one who recites this, O fair-browed one, or hears it, or causes others to hear it. (74)
By that, my worship would have been performed for twelve years;
O Lakṣmī, Śambhu spoke this truth to me in the past, and it has now been told by me to you. (75)

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Jackal and the Vulture in Rājagṛha Following Their Death through the Greatness of the Vārāha Tīrtha, and the Narration of Liberation and the Causes of Head Diseases," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another narrative concerning sacred fords that destroys sins;
I shall relate to you that which was spoken by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī on Mount Ṛkṣaka.
In my sacred field, within my temple and in my very presence, while I am singing, playing sacred instruments, dancing, and likewise remaining awake; || 2 ||
Whatever fruit belongs to the giver of a cow, the giver of food, and the giver of water;
[to] the one who cleanses, the one who anoints, and the one who offers perfumes and flowers. || 3 ||

Whatever fruit belongs to the giver of incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings, as well as whatever fruit belongs to the performer of recitation, sacrifice, and other rites in this world; || 4 ||
I shall tell you that which pertains even to the world beyond;
listen. Formerly, there was a Khañjarīṭa bird on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having eaten many insects, he was indeed severely afflicted by indigestion;
he fell into the Ganges there and met his death in the water.
By that merit, he was born as a well-proportioned son in the house of a Vaiśya who was the master of more than ten million [coins] and possessed great abundance of wealth and jewels.
He constantly performs worship before the deity in my temple;
the merit born from a single act of kīrtana destroys the sins of seven lifetimes. (8)
Thinking thus, he performed singing in the presence of Kṛṣṇa;
when twelve years had passed, he spoke joyfully to his parents.
"If you would do what is pleasing to me, let one boon be granted to me;
I must by no means be restrained by my father or mother."
"Having undertaken the vow of truth, I am setting out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Upon hearing this, his parents were pleased and said, "Speak what you desire. (11)
There are thirty thousand cows, all indeed yielding auspicious milk;
if the gift pleases you here, give it without hesitation.
"Let wealth consisting of hundreds of millions be given away in charity;
O son, bestow riches, grain, and jewels without restraint."
"O bridegroom, marry these beautiful maidens according to the prescribed rites;
since you desire to perform sacrifices, worship the god Janārdana with them."
"O son, you may now do everything according to your own desire, whether you wish to satisfy virtuous men until they are satiated with food. (15)
"O son, go together with me for the sake of a pilgrimage to sacred sites;
indeed, O son, you have thought of an auspicious sacred site, the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa. (16)
Today, O son, your mother’s breasts have been made meaningful by you;
they come and go again, and others who have passed away continue to pass away.
It is observed that what is destroyed in one moment comes into being again and perishes once more;
therefore, devotion to Hari, the sacred ford, must indeed be practiced by good sons.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, recur in birth after birth; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong? (1.9)
Therefore, O son, by this auspicious deed today you have delivered our ancestors; we too are blessed by having such an excellent son.
But tell me, if there is some specific secret or mystery, do you possess dispassion or perhaps an indifference toward the household life? (21)
"O dear son, if it is already hidden, there is no need to guard it further from your parents.
Having heard these words of the two, the son bowed and spoke auspiciously.
"There, at the sacred ford in the presence of Śrī Hari, I shall speak.
To that son, the couple then replied, "So be it."
Having resolved to depart, they went toward Saukarava,
taking with them whatever little remained in the house that had been dedicated to Nārāyaṇa.
On the twelfth day of Vaiśākha, having arrived at the sacred pilgrimage site,
they bathed, satisfied Viṣṇu with offerings, and gave abundant gifts.
Then, six months having passed for them whose hearts were fixed on the auspicious moment of Kṛṣṇa’s birth,
they remained engaged in their vow on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika, in the month of Kaumuda.
On the twelfth day, the son was questioned by his parents regarding the Smāraka;
touching their feet, the son addressed his parents. (27)
"In former times, I was indeed a Khañjarīṭa bird on this very spot;
having died here from indigestion, by that merit you have become my son. (28)
I have been born endowed with devotion and the memory of my former births; therefore, I bow to you both.
Now that this secret has been revealed, my life reaches its fulfillment. (29)
"I shall go to the abode of the Blessed One; such is the fruit for me who sings this.
Having said this, he drank water and bowed at the feet of his father.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
Singing thus, he assumed a divine body. ||3 1||
With four arms and supported by his attendants in a celestial chariot,
he was liberated and went to the imperishable abode that transcends material nature.
Then the mother, the father, and others, having seen that unsurpassed wonder, they too, as well as all those who had gathered there, offered supreme devotion. (33)
And in a very short time, all those yogins there attained liberation for me in that abode, becoming fragrant like blue lotuses.
They rejoice according to their true nature through the grace of my Kṣetrajña;
thus, for me who am singing in this way, liberation comes, O sinless one.
Listen to the truth from me regarding the fruit obtained by one who smears:
one should smear my temple with a mixture of clay and cow dung. (36)
For as many footprints as he places there while plastering,
for that many thousands of divine years he rejoices in heaven.
If the king should remain possessed of desire for a thousand divine years,
established in devotion, he subsequently goes to my abode.
Whether near or far, if one goes and fetches cow dung, for as many steps as he takes, for that many thousands of years [he dwells in heaven]. (39)
And he who leads cows to pasture is honored in the heavenly world;
thereafter, he becomes a king for ten thousand years.
Having always practiced devotion to me, he indeed goes to my abode at the end;
for he who offers water during the application of unguents or during bathing [attains this]. ||41||
Indeed, for as many drops of water as there are therein, for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world. 42.
Having been a king for that many thousands of years, he thereafter propitiates me through his virtues; being my devotee, he goes to my abode.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever performs the sweeping of the temple—for as many particles of dust as fly up from the ground while being swept—[so many years shall they dwell in heaven]. (44)
For that many hundreds of years he is quickly honored in the heavenly world;
for that many hundreds of years thereafter, having become a king here on earth, [he remains]. ||45||
Through devotion to me, those who are intent on my service and engage in singing reach my abode, becoming one with my own nature. ||46||
For every single syllable [of this mantra], my worshiper—who is endowed with the virtue of serving all and worships me constantly—rejoices in heaven for a thousand years. (47)
Then he shall become a king on earth, a Vaiṣṇava together with other Vaiṣṇavas, constantly singing my glory, endowed with supreme devotion. (48)
By my grace, at the end of his life, he goes to my abode.
Indeed, there was once a certain Cāṇḍāla who lived in the forest in the presence of my own form.
He used to sing songs constantly, and once, having come from afar,
he was quickly seized by a rākṣasa in order to devour him.
He said to the Rākṣasa: "Eat me thoroughly with a song as the accompaniment;
however, release me for a moment now so that I may perform a meritorious vow. (5.1)
Indeed, for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, this song is sung by me;
I shall keep a vigil at night; come to me in the morning after you have eaten. (52)
If I do not return again, I shall go to the destination of those who do not bathe, of killers of Brahmins, of drinkers of liquor, of thieves, and of eaters of flesh. (53)
"I shall follow the path of those who travel through the air, provided that I do not return again.
Having heard this, he was released by the Rākṣasa, along with the song and the watch of the night.
Then, at dawn, the Caṇḍāla acted;
Hari, having become a Brahmin, arrived and said, "Do not go toward the Rākṣasa."
"There is indeed no fault in abandoning the truth for the sake of one's life.
Hearing this, the dog-cooker said: "Truth is my firmly established vow. (56)
The entire world has truth as its root, for the Self is established in truth.
I shall not act falsely; go, O Brahmin, salutations be unto you.
Having spoken thus, the outcaste went to where that rākṣasa was and said:
"Eat me quickly, and you shall swiftly obtain my release. (58)
The Rakṣasa said: "I am pleased; you have upheld the foundation of truth.
For you have protected that which is called Brahman—the steadfastness in truth—since it has been preserved by you. (59)
I do not wish to devour you; instead, give me the fruit born of my song, so that through it, I may attain liberation along with you, O one of noble devotion.
Then the fruit of the song was given by the Caṇḍāla to the Rākṣasa;
abandoning his body, the Rākṣasa went to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha. (61)
Even a Caṇḍāla who was a devotee of Hari went to the divine abode by means of a celestial vehicle;
having become four-armed there, he served the Supreme Lord.
Thus indeed, the merit of this song bestows heaven, liberation, and more; my very act of chanting destroys sin and brings about divine perfection. (63)
I shall declare the merit that arises for one who plays a musical instrument:
for every single note, he is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred years. (64)
Thereafter, he becomes a king for ten thousand years;
then, my devotee goes to my supreme and transcendent abode.
For one who dances in my presence, the abode of Lakṣmī is indeed certain;
whether it be a man or a woman, I grant him or her whatever is desired.
In my abode, the dancer is indeed liberated as four-armed;
for in that very abode, I grant him the dance of eternal bliss.
In the presence of me, who am awake, and of my form, I bestow upon you supreme divine omniscience and direct realization, just as I possess them.
To the giver of a cow, I grant my Goloka, the realm of liberation;
to the giver of food, I grant the nectar of immortality, heaven, and an inexhaustible meal.
To the giver of water, I grant the world of immortality which bestows inexhaustible satisfaction;
and to the giver of fragrance and flowers, I grant that which is a divine body.
For the sake of attaining bliss, the Lord, filled with enjoyments, sports with millions of sovereign goddesses, who are eternal and fulfill all desires regarding the principles of reality. //71//
From the giver of incense, a sweet fragrance arises like that from my own form;
from the giver of lamps, there always arises a divine eye like that of the sun.
Having first enjoyed the pleasures of heaven and other realms, he becomes liberated and goes to my abode;
I bestow upon him Vaikuṇṭha as the fruit of that food offering.

He who always offers me food offerings (naivedya) shall eternally enjoy the kingdom of Brahmā; and he who performs japa, sacrifice, and other rites shall attain the great status of a sovereign emperor.
I bestow upon the earth, and from that, heaven; beyond that, even the station of Vairāja, and thereafter, I grant liberation.
To those with desires, I grant in every way worlds that fulfill their wishes;
and to those without desires, I grant my own eternal abode.
Whether for men or even for women, I shall indeed grant whatever they desire;
I bestow upon them even the state of a god or a goddess in heaven and other realms.
I bestow lordship or even the state of being a sovereign goddess upon the Vairāja and other classes; and I likewise bring about liberation, the status of a liberated one, or whatever else is desired.
I grant him his desired state of being Brāhmī and even Brahmanhood;
I also grant him his desired state of being Kṛṣṇā and even Kṛṣṇahood. ||79||
Whether it be her state as Nārāyaṇī or even her state as Nārāyaṇa; whether it be the state of being an incarnation or the state of being the one who incarnates. || 1.578.80 ||
According to my devotion, according to my service, and according to my merit, I grant [this];
for the status of Supreme Lord belongs to me alone, and not to anyone else.
Thus, I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
from the imperishable abode, I, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), abide in my own supreme realm.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that which you desired to know has been told by me;
it was previously narrated by Śambhu while he was staying at the holy sites of Satya.
From reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall likewise arise;
I grant my eternal service, which is difficult for even devotees to attain. (84)

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Khañjarīṭa Bird while Singing, and the Description of the Attainment of Fruits for One Who Plays Instruments, Dances, Remains Awake, Gives Food, Water, or Land, Cleanses, Smears with Unction, Offers Fragrances, Flowers, and so forth, Presents Incense, Lamps, and Fine Offerings, and Performs Japa, Sacrifice, and other rites," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you what the fruit of Ravitīrtha is;
Śambhu, being requested by Pārvatī, spoke thus in the presence of Satī.
Once in ancient times, the sages headed by Yājñavalkya, who were renowned for their observance of vows, arrived at Ādityeśa on the banks of the Narmadā.
Having entered the forest abounding in flowers and fruits, all the sages beheld at the edge of the woods a radiant woman clad in red garments.
She is adorned with beautiful red garlands, anointed with red sandalwood paste,
draped in red ornaments, holding the moon in her hand, and inspiring fear.
Near her was one who was black in color, aged, and merciless;
he had a massive body, a noose in his hand, tawny eyes, and a long tongue.
With piercing eyes and exceedingly enraged, they were of a terrifying form;
the sages beheld those two evildoers and questioned them.
"Who are you two, deformed ones, standing at this sacred ford in the form of sinners?
They, Jarā and Haṃkā, the daughters of Kāla, then spoke to the brahmins.
"I am Yama myself, the eternal dispenser of punishment to sinners;
you, O Brahmins who practice righteousness, practice dharma on the banks of the Narmadā."
"O Vaiṣṇavas, enter the holy site of Kaccha and remain there in peace;
we two shall not harass those who are servants of the Narmadā."
"Here we shall send those who revile the Narmadā to the abode of Yama.
Hearing these words there on the banks of the Narmadā, they quickly [departed].
In that auspicious place, which bestows liberation and was inhabited by Bhṛgu, they made their residence;
meanwhile, five other men were seen there by the great sages.
Those men, endowed with great strength, were devoted to ritual bathing and the worship of the gods;
they reported to the brahmins that they had indeed bathed in the sacred fords of the earth.
That sin of ours has not been destroyed, for it was not destroyed by bathing here;
moreover, one among us previously defiled the wife of our preceptor. (13)
By the second [act], gold was indeed seized from Mitra in the past;
by the third, a terrible and fearsome brahmin-murder was committed. (14)
By the fourth [brother], the sin of drinking intoxicating liquor was committed;
by the fifth, the slaughter of cows was performed—these were they, and now we are here.
Having bathed in the Narmadā at Bhṛgukṣetra, pure and stainless,
they bowed to Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Bhārgavī.
Having performed circumambulation with devotion and having given up their lives, they went to heaven;
at that time, they were seen by the Brahmins at Ravitīrtha, traveling in celestial chariots.
At that time, they were not obstructed by Yama or Kālaputrī;
on the contrary, both repeatedly offered salutations from their hearts.
Now I shall describe another to you, the Tīrtha of Tvag-astyeshvara;
likewise, the second is the Ānandeśvara Tīrtha. || 19 ||
Likewise, the third holy site, Līneśvara, also exists there.
Once, a Dānava named Kālabāṣpa performed a difficult penance.
In the beginning, during the Kṛta Yuga, he performed penance in the waters of the Revā;
Śaṅkara, being pleased, appeared before him in person and spoke.
"Choose a boon as you desire; I shall grant it," he said.
Then that Dānava chose [this]: "O Maheśvara, grant this to me here."
"Whosoever I place my hand upon the head shall meet his death;
Śambhu has declared that whatever you desire shall come to pass exactly so. (23)
Having heard these words, the Daitya rushed toward Śambhu himself, saying:
"I shall place my hand upon your head; that statement of yours is not true."
Rudra fled because of that and went to Keśava for refuge;
having informed Keśava, Śambhu submerged himself there in the water.
To destroy the suffering of his devotees, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa assumed a female form and came directly before the Daitya. ||26||
Seeing a beautiful young maiden, radiant as the moon, in a secluded place, the Dānava, overwhelmed by delusion, began to embrace her.
"Be my wife," Keśava then said; she replied, "If you consider me your wife, then let there be proof for me. (28)
"Perform a dance with me; if you conquer, I shall indeed become your lover.
"So be it," said the Dānava, and he engaged thoroughly in the dance.
Then, raising his two hands to his head with a peacock feather, the Blessed One performed a dance; the Dānava did likewise.
Slowly joining his hands, he touched his own head;
that Dānava was reduced to ashes at that very moment due to his delusion regarding the dance.
Śaṅkara, having recognized that, emerged from the water;
after bowing to Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he became steady. ||32||
That sacred ford on the Narmadā is indeed called Līneśvara;
and the Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇeśa is that supreme Vaiṣṇava tīrtha.
Having performed this, the Blessed One and Hara also departed from sight;
by bathing there, a mortal obtains worldly enjoyment, liberation, and likewise prosperity.
On the southern bank of the Narmadā is the Gopālakeśvara Tīrtha;
there, Kāmadhenu performed penance for the sake of obtaining a son.
While she was meditating upon Maheśvara, the God of gods, with supreme devotion,
the Lord of the World, Maheśvara, was pleased with that Kapilā.
Indeed, Śaṅkara himself emerged from the middle of Kapilā’s body and said, "I am pleased; choose a boon as you desire. (37)
Surabhi said, "Give me a son endowed with divine qualities.
Hara replied, "So be it," and Dharma became her son. (38)
This bull, whose nature is four-footed, is indeed the protector of the world;
he is Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gopālas, as proclaimed by Surabhi. (39)
At that sacred ford, on the full moon day of either the month of Kārtika or Vaiśākha,
one should perform the rite of releasing a bull for the pleasure of Śaṅkara.
For as many hairs as there are on all the limbs of the bull,
for that many thousands of years one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Then, if he is a great devotee of the Lord, he shall go to the world of Brahmā;
or if he becomes a king on earth, he shall attain liberation once again.
Then there is the beautiful and supreme sacred site named Parāśara,
where indeed Parāśara formerly performed severe penance.
Mahālakṣmī, being pleased with him, granted a boon for the sake of a son;
Parāśara obtained a most excellent son who was a portion of Nārāyaṇa.
Then there is the auspicious Bhīmeśvara, which indeed destroys fear;
likewise, there is the Nāradeśa tīrtha, where yoga is attained.
Nārada indeed performed penance, keeping Śambhu within his heart;
Śambhu appeared before him in person and bestowed upon him supreme perfection in yoga.
From there, one should go to the Hanumadīśvara Tīrtha, which brings happiness;
it was there that the king named Sahasrārjuna defeated Rāvaṇa. ||47||
The great lord, the son of Jamadagni, conquered Kārtavīrya;
and the great lord, the son of Daśaratha, conquered the son of Jamadagni.
Having recovered Sītā from the son of Daśaratha through his previous merit, he brought about the slaughter of that Rāvaṇa who had carried her away. (49)
And Rāma’s devotee Hanumān, the best of monkeys,
was his [servant] after the burning of Laṅkā, solely for the purpose of pacifying the sin of slaughter.
Having arrived at Bhṛgukṣetra on the Narmadā, he became established there;
that supreme sacred site (tīrtha) is remembered by the name Hanūmadīśvara. ||51||
Listen to a marvel, O Lakṣmī; formerly there occurred a supreme event there.
On the surface of the earth, there was a royal sage named Suparṇa. (52)
His son Śatabāhu became a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu;
while wandering about, he once went by chance to the Vindhya mountain.
Having seen this young man and the tawny-colored brahmin alone in the forest, he asked: "How is it that you remain here, wandering about with a book? (54)
A Brahmin arrived from Kanyakubja in this forest;
he had been sent by the princess, desiring an excellent bridegroom. (55)
There was a king named Śikhaṇḍin who, being childless, performed austerities;
he obtained a daughter and now desires her marriage. (56)
In former times, on the bank of the Narmadā, that maiden said to her father:
"I was once a peahen there, accompanied by a peacock. (57)
Once, when a hunter arrived there, I was repeatedly struck by him with arrows;
along with my master, I was felled and then died.
Having severed my head and having cooked my body in fire,
he ate half of it and indeed cast the other half into the water.
By the power of that merit from the Narmadā, I have been born in your house as a princess, beautiful in body and adorned with a topknot.
"O father, remembering my past lives, I recall this merit-bestowing place;
send a Brahmin there to the site of Hanumadīśvara. (61)
Beneath a banyan tree with three branches and tawny leaves, there is indeed a tawny-colored rock;
my leaves were my bones there at that time.
Those [bones] that are scattered upon the rocky peaks and those that have become decayed must by all means be cast into the waters of the Narmadā. ||63||
"By that [merit], may my liberation indeed be attained with Nārāyaṇa as my husband.
By this command of the king, I, a twice-born, have come here seeking him.
"I have arrived; I shall read what is written, for that is the place.
Having said this, he reached that place and obtained the bones exactly as they were.
The Brahmin cast her into the water, and at that moment the maiden died;
Śatabāhu, right there, remembered his own state as a peacock.
He indeed lamented there at that sacred ford, and at that very moment he died;
then a divine vehicle arrived, and he remained situated upon it.
She went to that place where the princess had died;
she too, having assumed a divine form, became a goddess and ascended a celestial chariot.
He then ascended that vehicle and proceeded to the Narmadā;
at that moment, the brahmin remembered his own former birth as a hunter.
Having drunk the water of the Narmadā at that sacred ford, he died there;
assuming a divine bodily form, he ascended a celestial vehicle.
And those three, having bowed to the illustrious Hanumān, went to heaven;
such was the power of the Narmadā at the Hanumān-tīrtha.
O Lakṣmī, the bestower of heaven and liberation, the destroyer of sin and suffering—these three are indeed the peahen, the peacock, and the hunter. (72)
Having drunk the water of the Revā, they thereafter attained liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this meritorious narrative spoken by Hara been told. (73)
This divine [text], which is being heard by Pārvatī, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation through its recitation or even its mere hearing; it wards off the delusions of saṃsāra. (74)

Thus ends the five hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Sacred Fords along with Their Narratives, including Ādityeśa Tīrtha, Līneśvara Tīrtha, Gopāleśvara Tīrtha, Parāśara Tīrtha, Hanumadīśvara Tīrtha, and Others," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In Bhṛgukṣetra, at Somatīrtha, a wonder occurred in ancient times.
There was a king named Śambara, and his son was Trilocana.
Kaṇṭha, the son of Trilocana, became devoted to sinful deeds.
As he was wandering in the forest, a herd of deer was seen by him.
Having struck them with arrows, that twice-born one who had assumed the form of a deer was himself killed by that sinful act consisting of the murder of a Brahmin.
Wandering over the earth, Kaṇṭha reached the confluence of the Narmadā and the Āgasā;
there, having bathed in the waters of the Revā, the deer-eater (Mṛgādana) drank the water.
Having taken shelter in the shade of a tree, he slept; then, after a short while, he worshipped Someśvara Bāṇa there with water and other offerings.
Just then, a certain Brahmin arrived while traveling on the road;
a woman wearing red garments spoke to him on the path, "O twice-born one! (6)
"My husband stays at Somatīrtha; speak to him with anger:
'Your wife, for your sake, stands by the banyan tree and gazes upon you. (7)
Thus addressed, that Brahmin reached his throat and said:
"I saw her standing at the banyan tree, terrifying, with a noose in her hand."
"Your wife said to you: 'Send your husband here to me.
That beautiful woman stands at a distance, half a krośa from the place of our meeting."
Kaṇṭha dispatched his own servant to the place where she was staying;
having gone there, the servant asked her, "Who are you, and why do you remain here? (1.580.10)
The woman said: "O you who bear the burden of a Brahmin’s murder, I, born as a deer, await the slayer of deer here; for that purpose was my birth."
The teacher is the ruler of those who possess self-control; the king is the ruler of the wicked;
but for those whose sins are concealed in this world, Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the ruler.
"Within half a krośa on this bank at the confluence with the Narmadā serpent, the sin of killing a Brahmin cannot remain; therefore, I indeed abide here."
"Go, and quickly send my husband who has been dispatched by me.
The servant came and spoke those very same words to the king. || 14 ||
The king immediately fell into grief and collapsed upon the surface of the earth;
he said, "I shall give up my life right here at this confluence."
"Let fire and even abundant fuel be brought quickly!
At that very moment, all was brought by the servants to King Saṃgama.
Having bathed, kindled the fire, and bowed to Śrī Somanātha,
he performed three circumambulations and placed Janārdana within his heart.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! Reciting this while meditating upon the four-armed Viṣṇu, the Lord of Śrī, he entered. (18)
While he was remembering Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, saying, "Grant me a good rebirth," there appeared a divine celestial chariot attended by the attendants of Viṣṇu.
Having seen that miracle which had arrived, even the servants certainly made a firm resolve for liberation and entered the fire.
Having assumed divine forms and residing in celestial chariots, those foremost attendants went to the divine abode of Hari, which is adorned by Lakṣmī and Māṇikya.
It was graced by Prabhā and Pārvatī, attended by Haṃsā and Mañjulikā, and worshipped by Campā, Dayā, Ramā, Haimī, and Muktādevī. 22.

Those who have gone to the abode of Brahmā serve Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; during the occasion of Somatīrtha, gifts should be given with devotion. His ancestors are satisfied, and his lineage attains liberation. (23)
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the violator of the teacher's bed, and the slayer of an embryo—all these are purified there; of this there is no doubt. ||24||
Thereafter, one should go to the holy ford known as Ṛṇamocana, [to be freed] from the debts incurred here by oneself—whether divine, ancestral, or human. (25)
Having bathed at that spot, one is liberated, and as a god, one rejoices in heaven.
Furthermore, on the northern bank is the most excellent Vaiṣṇava tīrtha known as Vāra.
In ancient times, Viṣṇu was indeed present here under the name Jalaśāyin;
formerly, there was a Daitya named Nalamegha who caused great distress to the gods.
The gods went to Hari and spoke to Mādhava for the destruction of the Daityas;
the Blessed One, mounted upon Garuḍa and taking his discus, arrived.
Nalamēghasakhā’s son, Dhundhumāra, went forth for battle;
he was slain by Viṣṇu in a valley of the Himālayas. 29.
Then, greatly enraged, Nalamegha approached Hari;
he fought there in many ways with Viṣṇu and was slain by him.
Then, with his Sudarśana discus, he beheld that abode;
within a great cave, divine maidens were being guarded by the Daitya.
Having repeatedly slain many people—including humans, goddesses, gandharvas, and even those of the mountains—numbering fourteen thousand; ||32||
There Viṣṇu beheld the Daitya’s beloved wife;
she was named Maṅgalādevī, and she wept most intensely and repeatedly. (33)
Having heard of the slaying of the Daityas, the devoted women chose Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa as their husband,
and all the maidens chose the Lord of Śrīmāṇikī.
Then Viṣṇu brought those [images] of the Lord of Letters, the Lord of the virtuous, who were mounted upon Garuḍa, and bathed them in the Narmadā.
Having established a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), the Lord himself, in his form as the one who reclines upon the waters,
accepted all those [offerings] for a moment on his bed at the Narmadā.
Then, from Kuṅkumavāpī, the Blessed One, seated upon Garuḍa,
arrived at his own abode together with all his wives.
And Lomaśa brought all of them and presented them;
they remain constantly by the side of Viṣṇu, both in his celestial abode and upon the earth.
Those who listen to this Vaiṣṇava narrative shall be liberated at the Aśvapaṭṭasara tīrtha and in the temples dear to Hari. (39)
They are indeed blessed in the world of men, meritorious and most virtuous,
for whom there is a direct union with Kṛṣṇa upon this earth.
Those men and women who are born there become truly divine, whether they be stationary or moving;
by bathing in that divine water which has its source in Brahman, they become divine.
Then one should visit the supreme, purifying holy site known as Candrāditya.
Formerly, there were two Dānavas named Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa on the banks of the Narmadā. (42)
There, having performed their austerities, the two of them meditated upon the Sun;
Sūrya, being well-pleased, then said: "Choose an excellent boon."
"Invincible to all the gods, choose a boon; grant it to us.
"So be it," the Sun replied; thus was the Sun established by the two of them.
Having also visited Candra and the Candrāditya tīrtha,
one should then go to Vyāsatīrtha and worship the image of Vyāsa.
One should worship Siddhaśambhu and honor Dvīpeśvara;
likewise, one should worship the Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara Tīrtha and Saṃkarṣaṇeśvara.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa shines forth together with Rādhā and Balarāma.
From there, one should go to the purifying holy site named Eraṇḍī;
for it was here that Atri’s wife, the beautiful Anasūyā, was indeed childless.
She performed penance there on the bank of the Revā at the confluence of the Eraṇḍī;
when a hundred years had passed for her, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Pitāmaha [appeared].
And having arrived, they granted her a boon for the sake of sons equal to themselves;
her sons were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, who are equal to Atri.
Candradatta and Durvāsas—these three were born to them;
that sacred ford (tīrtha) is the pacifier of the torments of sin and the bestower of liberation for one's sons.
From there one should go to Dhūmapāta, and from there to Sāgarasaṃgama;
there the Lord of Rivers constantly offers an oblation to the Revā.
The Narmadā said: "O people, having bathed there at my confluence, you shall offer libations to the ancestors; I shall [deliver] their seven generations."
I shall deliver my devotees and liberate them from distress;
indeed, I repeatedly offer jests, laughter, and the like unto the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
"I delight Hari eternally, being absorbed in him upon my lap;
moreover, I grant liberation to men and women"—thus says the Narmadā. (54)
Thus, that supreme goddess Narmadā exists as the bestower of liberation;
O Lakṣmī, such is the excellent majesty of your friend Narmadā. (55)
O Satī, this was spoken by Śambhu on the Ṛkṣādri mountain;
having heard it with devotion, all people go to my abode. (56)
Having heard this from Śaṅkara, Satī ascended an excellent celestial chariot;
she was attended by millions [of attendants] and accompanied by Śaṅkara. ||57||
Filled with joy, she went to perform ablutions at the sacred fords (tīrthas) recommended by the Teacher;
having traveled as far as the ocean, Śailī worshipped the deities of those holy sites.
Afterwards, the virtuous lady herself gave gifts of ten million jewels and other riches;
then, meeting Bhārgavī at Bhṛgukaccha, she traveled by way of the sky.
The virtuous beloved, with the permission of Śaṅkara, departed for Kailāsa;
she also bestowed the waters of the sacred fords upon the inhabitants of Kailāsa.
Thus was this journey undertaken by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
for the sake of purifying the worlds, since he himself is of the nature of Brahman.
The highly fortunate devotee Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
the bestower of welfare upon all, dwells on Kailāsa, the golden mountain.
It is situated to my east, where I am performing penance,
having resorted to the Badarī tree for the passage of many years.
With each single fruit alone of the jujube tree, I subsist there;
for ten crores, ten years, and ten arbudas [of years] I remain in that place.
While established in austerity, ten other lotuses of the tenth stage appeared;
even the gods do not see me there, so how indeed could mortals? (65)
Established in austerity, I behold them all assembled together;
and by my very will, they please me with hymns of praise.
They behold the holy Śrī Badarī-āśrama standing before them at that very moment, wherever their devotee may be situated and whatever task they have to perform.
He goes indeed to the abode of Viṣṇu, served by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others;
my devotee, intent on yoga, shall partake in the fruit of liberation.
"Whoever understands me as the Lord at the sacred fords (tīrthas) shall be liberated.
Having heard these words of Nārāyaṇa, Lakṣmī then spoke.
"O Keśava, having shown affection toward me, even though I am a servant, listen to what I have to say;
O Janārdana, I shall speak to you with gentle and virtuous nature."
Women possess little vital strength; women are fields of enjoyment; they are always possessed of impurity and are devoid of righteous conduct. (71)
Dependent on others, subject to their husbands, and under the control of their offspring, women are always impure in matters such as the washing away of feces and urine. (72)
If you are impure, how could there be worship and so forth for you? Tell me that. And if you are in your menses, how could there be worship for you? Tell me that as well. (73)
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "O sinless one, you have asked well;
this bestows happiness upon devoted women as well as liberation. (74)
To those intent on washing their children's clothes, to those devoted to washing their own garments, to those dedicated to serving their husbands, and to those who were in their menses; (75)
For those who are occupied with rites such as the purification of the impurity of the house and other consecrations, true purity is certainly not observed to be constant. //76//
Indeed, for the sake of those women who are my devotees, I have declared myself to be the embodiment of mind; I dwell within the mind.
Women were created by Brahmā in the beginning as pure by their very nature;
since they are indeed entirely pure, they must certainly not be violated. (78)
Even when there are causes for impurity and even when impure acts have been committed, women indeed become pure simply by bathing. ||79||
Or rather, let my sight of you, whose form is so wonderfully variegated, always remain at a distance for as long as the four-day period of the menses lasts.
"Only this must be done, and nothing else; yet if you should perform another mental act, by that I am thoroughly pleased, O noble one devoted to the rescue [of others]. (81)
O beautiful one, whether in a state of purity or impurity, one who is devoted to me should always perform their daily duties by fixing the mind upon me. 82.
She is not stained by fault because she acts for my benefit;
listen further, Lakṣmī, for I am eternally pure and the Lord. (83)
And worldly impurity never touches me here at any time;
for through my yoga, even all impurities attain divinity.
However, for the sake of preserving proper conduct, I have performed purification and other rites;
[in truth], there are neither men nor women, nor are there those who are male or female.
Having restrained the senses and having caused the mind to enter into Me, they become purified through the yoga of surrender unto Me; of this there is no doubt. (86)
By whomsoever—whether a man, a eunuch, or a woman—in whatever state they may be, their mind is always fixed upon my image through discernment; [by them, this fruit is attained]. (87)
He indeed becomes pure and should perform the worship and other rites himself;
he may perform the worship independently in a forest or in a secluded place.
One should perform worship alone; I do not consider that a fault.
For the mind, the intellect, the consciousness, and the self of embodied beings are all dependent upon the Self. (89)
Even if men unite with me through true love, they do not indeed cling to me,
provided that their heart, mind, and intellect are equally established in me alone.
Whatever action one performs, like a lotus leaf in water, one is not smeared by contact; this is due to equanimity alone, and not otherwise.
Even those devotees who, day and night, perform here a mixture of ritual actions, they too attain supreme perfection if their mind is fixed upon me. ||92||
Whether waking or sleeping, hearing or seeing, whoever contemplates me within their mind—what fear can there be for one whose mind is fixed on me? (93)
Whether it be a Cāṇḍāla of evil conduct or even a Brāhmaṇa of such a nature, I praise one whose mind is fixed on me, but never one whose mind is elsewhere. (94)
Worshipping me, the source of all dharmas, and being refined by knowledge, they have surrendered their minds to me and are devoted solely to my worship. (95)
Those who perform service to me and keep me within their hearts—even if they sleep, eat, enjoy themselves, or even indulge in desire—[they are never separated from me]. 96.
Whether they proceed or return, all those dear to me, O Lakṣmī, are so because their minds are tranquil and they have fixed their resolve upon me alone. 97.
For the destruction of the mind is the liberation from the world and from saṃsāra;
therefore, having fixed their minds upon me, let women always touch me. 98.
He who, with his mind fixed on Me and filled with love, constantly worships Me, reaches My supreme presence and attains My own nature. (99)
On the fifth day of her menses, she becomes pure through the ritual gift of the season (*ṛtudāna*). For the sake of purification and for the sake of obtaining a son, the *ṛtudāna* must be given.
"I have observed celibacy by approaching my wife only during her fertile period;
even while remaining thus, if one should go [to her], there would be no fruitlessness of that [act] during the season. (10.1)
This rule regarding sexual union does not apply to those who are dispassionate;
for those with desire, union during the fertile period is praised.
O beautiful lady, a great devotee of the Lord, protecting his purity as prescribed,
should perform service to me with the spirit of servitude.
Those men and women who serve me with devotion, even in the state of a maidservant, are my dear ones; they dwell eternally within my heart. (104)
If the fault of my menstrual flow were unknown, then my touch and so forth might be permissible;
however, having bathed myself and even having caused me to bathe on the fifth day, [the impurity remains].
Or if another should bathe me or recite my hundred-name hymn while I am in my menses,
O Blessed Lord, one should then pray for forgiveness from the earth.
"Forgive this touch committed by one who was unaware, O Mine of Compassion!
Having spoken thus, she should bow to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; then she becomes purified. 107.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, neither a woman nor even a man is corrupted;
therefore, those dear to me perform their duties according to the rule.
O auspicious lady, every day let men and women who follow my will perform the festive rites for my service.
I shall certainly lead them to my own supreme and highest world—
thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives.
They revolve like a wheel because they do not know me out of delusion;
the world is shrouded by ignorance and brought under control by delusion. 111.
Bound by many attachments, he does not recognize me;
the mother indeed goes elsewhere, and the father goes elsewhere.
Sons go elsewhere, and the wife goes elsewhere;
one is born in one's own place, arising from the accumulation of one's own respective karma.
O Lakṣmī, people who are deluded regarding knowledge exist in this world bewildered;
considering even a short duration to be supreme, they are bound by that which is perishable.
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, those who possess this Vedic knowledge centered on Me, which is of My own nature, shall not dwell together with Me in My physical form.
Having entrusted one's own self to me, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this.
That person who, having risen at dawn, should hear this daily—1.16.
One attains abundant success that leads to my world;
