Then those two Vaiṣṇavas exchanged mutual greetings of well-being and welcomed one another, praising each other’s birth as being truly fruitful.
Then the King of Oḍhra said to him: "Hari resides on the shore of the southern ocean, on Mount Nīla, in a forest devoid of the movement of people."
On the second day, that mountain was covered by a whirlwind of sand;
Rauhiṇakuṇḍa was covered, and Nīlamādhava was covered as well. ||8 1 ||
Even the houses of the Śabaras have been shattered and destroyed;
this wrath has arisen from reflection, not from any offense whatsoever. (82)
"The kingdom is yours; I shall carry out your command.
Welcome! I shall send food and other provisions with my people. (83)
Having spoken thus and received blessings, the Lord of Uḍra remained silent;
Indradyumna then said to Nārada, "May your arrival not be in vain. (84)
"If I do not obtain a vision of Lord Nīvyādhava, I shall undertake a fast here and die for the sake of his liberation. (85)
Then Nārada said to him: "The Blessed One does not make the desire of a Vaiṣṇava fruitless;
you shall behold that sovereign lord of the earth. (86)
Maintain your fortitude; know, O friend, that the Blessed One is independent.
Yet, being solely subject to devotion, He will come under your control through your devotion. (87)
"You are indeed a Vaiṣṇava, the fifth person (puruṣa) born from the Lotus-born One;
even the Grandfather (Brahmā) has appointed me to this task for you."
"I shall tell you everything in the vicinity of the Blue Mountain.
Having heard this, the king was delighted and considered his good fortune to have increased. (89)
When my grandfather indeed granted me as his companion,
he then gave the command for all of us to go to the Blue Mountain (Nīlaśaila).
And the lord of the Oḍhra country sat upon the vehicle together with the king; they all departed by way of the sky, leaving the great river behind.
Then, in an instant, they reached the sacred field of Ekāmravana,
leaving behind the river Gandhavahā and the Lord Hara known as Koṭiliṅgeśvara.
Seeing Nārada accompanied by the sound of worshipful musical instruments,
he looked at Āraṇyaka and questioned him, for he [mistook him for] Mādhava.
"Has the Supreme Lord, who dwells upon the peak of the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), arrived?
The sage replied, "That Blue Mountain is located three yojanas away."
Indeed, this abode of Śaṅkara, consisting of the Lord of ten million Liṅgas, is Śambhu himself;
formerly, being afraid, he came here for refuge to the illustrious Hari. 95.
Having married Pārvatī, the Lord made her dwell in a golden abode;
when much time had passed, he spoke auspiciously to Menakā regarding Pārvatī.
"O daughter, your husband is devoid of qualities and lacks even a house door;
how long will he dwell in my home without a residence?
O little daughter, you do not shine at all without ornaments and prosperity."
"Speak, so that you may build a palace and dwell separately in your own abode. (98)
Having been addressed thus, Pārvatī, with a humble mind, said to Śaṅkara:
"O Blessed One, dwelling for a long time in the house of one's father-in-law is indeed disadvantageous."
Living under the control of others is like exile;
therefore, it causes suffering even to those as small as bees, as well as to the great.
Thus addressed, Śaṅkara quickly established Kāśī as his dwelling on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, which flows toward the eastern ocean. || 101 ||
In his own city of Vārāṇasī, which measured five krośas, Paśupati took delight with her for a long time within a pavilion of jewels. (102)
Then King Divodāsa, having indeed invited all the gods, dismissed them and ruled the kingdom among the Vaiṣṇavas. || 103 ||
Having established ten million liṅgas, Śambhu departed for Kailāsa;
subsequently, many kings arose on the land of Vārāṇasī.
Even the one named Kāśīrāja was a devotee of Śaṅkara;
through penance, he obtained from Śaṅkara a boon that was previously impossible.
"O subduer of enemies, you shall conquer Kaṃsa, the stealer of [my] joy, in battle;
for your sake, I shall then fight with Viṣṇu by every means."
Knowing that boon, Śrī Hari dispatched his Sudarśana discus in battle toward the slaying of the King of Kāśī; and so that discus was sent forth.
Having severed the head of the King of Kāśī, he completely burnt the city down.
Hearing that, Śambhu became enraged and [discharged] the Pāśupata weapon at Hari.
The Lord Hari rendered that [weapon] fruitless and released it;
then, overcome by fear, Śaṅkara praised Hari.
"O Lord Hari, forgive today the offense of your devotee;
O Master, I have been created as one of tamasic nature—protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Then the discus withdrew from Śaṅkara, and Kṛṣṇa became that [discus].
With a serene countenance and accompanied by Lakṣmī, Hari spoke laughingly:
"O Śambhu, how is it that after all this time, such evil intent has arisen? For what reason have you come forward to fight with me, a mere worm among kings? (111–112)
"Even if my discus, consecrated with mantras of wrath, were to destroy you and Brahmā, I shall show mercy to my devotee; go, O my devotee, to Śrī Puruṣottama.
If you indeed desire to sport for a long time together with Satyā, then [go there]."
There, in that stainless maṇḍala, it was ten yojanas in extent.
Starting from the Citrotpalā river as far as the southern ocean, the excellent Nīla mountain stands there; therein, I am established in fourfold form.
To the north of that is a great forest resembling a sapphire;
it is called Ekāmra, and there you may make your fearless dwelling.
"O Supreme among Men, you alone must protect my field.
Having been thus commanded, Śambhu departed and indeed took up residence there.
This is that Koṭiliṅgeśvara who was established by Brahmā;
having heard this, the king descended from his celestial chariot toward Hara.
He worshipped according to the prescribed rites and gave abundant gifts;
having bathed there at Bindu-tīrtha, he also fully worshipped Śrīśa.
He stood there and meditated upon that Śambhu; then Śambhu himself spoke to him:
"O Indradyumna, there is no great devotee on earth like you."
"Even though your desire is difficult to accomplish, it shall be swiftly fulfilled;
for Nārada has been commanded by the Self-born One himself to take on a body once again. (121)
Therefore, prepare a foundation for it, preceded by a horse sacrifice;
for Hari, whose body is like a blue gem, has now indeed become invisible.
In that place, establish the sacred field of Śrī Narasiṃha in my presence;
let the king certainly perform worship with a thousand horse-sacrifices.
At its end, show this king the Kalpa-nyagrodha tree;
from that tree, which is the very form of Brahmā, [arose] four auspicious images.
The son of Viśvakarman will strive and establish it when a thousand years have passed, due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā.
Indradyumna will behold Hari directly in bodily form—
the divine Nārāyaṇa— standing there having assumed a wooden body.
"O Nārada, worship this king; he is a master to those who worship Hari.
Having spoken thus, Śambhu vanished, and the king became one whose pride was humbled.
The king proceeded ahead and reached the site of Kapoteśa;
seeing that it was suitable for the encampment of his army, he caused the troops to settle there.
And having worshipped Bilveśvara, Kapoteśa, and Nārada.
He asked them: "How were Bilveśvara and Kapotaka born?
Tell us the story that grants supreme peace and brings about the attainment of Śrīpati."

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Decision to Depart for Jagannātha after Hearing the Account of Indradyumna as Narrated by Vidyāpati, the Arrival of Nārada, the Departure, the Visit to the Lord of Utkala on the Banks of the Citrotpalā, and the Worship of Koṭiliṅgeśa in the Forest of Ekāmraka," in the first section, the Kṛtayuga-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; Nārada spoke this auspicious narrative to that king.
I shall relate to you the story of Bilveśa and Kapoteśvara.
In ancient times, that place was Kuśasthalī, covered with sharp blades of kuśa grass;
there Śambhu performed austerities with the desire, "May I become worthy of worship. (2)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! Reciting this, he propitiated Hari, the Supreme Person. || 3 ||
Though he possessed eight forms, the twice-born one became as subtle as a pigeon;
having attained the status of Kapoteśvara, he came to be highly honored there.
Those who worship him go to Puruṣottama, the Lord of Śrī.
Now, once upon a time, the Dānavas were devouring many people.
Having indeed come from Pātāla, Śrī Nīlamādhava filled that opening there with a bilva fruit within it.
Having cast down the tree, he established Śaṅkara;
by that act, the obstruction caused by the Dānava became known there as Bileśvara.
Through the worship of that [deity], Śaṅkara attained it, and one goes to the supreme state.
Then the king traveled by means of a celestial chariot to Śrī Puruṣottama.
Then there occurred an ill omen, as well as a throbbing of his left eye and hand;
the king questioned Nārada regarding the cause of these inauspicious signs.
Nārada said: "In the third [period], covered with sand in the evening, the deity Nīlamādhava was seen here, having descended upon the earth."
Upon hearing this, the king was instantly overwhelmed with grief;
he said to his domestic priest, "Go and consecrate my son."
I shall dwell here in Mālava for the duration of another age;
I will not sustain my life nor will I behold Hari when that time comes.
"Having taken refuge in this sacred field, I shall make the remainder of my life fruitful.
To the king who was speaking thus, Nārada spoke with composure: 13.
"The illusory power (māyā) of Hari is indeed such; do not fall into delusion regarding it.
Brahmā himself said to me, "Go toward Indradyumna."
"Jagannātha is departing and will not see Mādhava;
no grief should be felt for this. Thus should that king be addressed. (15)
For his sake, having propitiated the Supreme Self, the Puruṣottama,
I shall lead him from Śvetadvīpa at the conclusion of the thousand-year great sacrifice.
Indradyumna, performing a thousand horse-sacrifices for Hari—
let him remain there until the end, for he shall behold my wooden body.
This descent of Hari shall again attain renown through him;
formerly, Hari existed as the Jewel-Form (Maṇimūrti), established in fourfold ways.
Having assumed a body of divine wood, he will descend again in four forms.
Come, O King, let us behold the sovereignty of Vālukā and the other directions.
On the Blue Mountain dwells the Lord Nṛsiṃha, the destroyer of obstacles;
let us behold that most formidable one, and he will effect the destruction of our impediments.
And having seen the Nīlamādhava mountain, we shall indeed go to that Kapoteśa site,
where there is a hall a thousand years old.
Having performed the horse sacrifice, worship Śrī Puruṣottama;
there, at that sacrifice, worship the image of Nṛsiṃha constantly. (22)
"By whom the destruction of obstacles shall occur, he will accomplish what you desire.
Having been told this, Indradyumna bowed toward that direction and proceeded forward. (23)
Then, having learned of the mountain’s summit through his association with Nārada,
he remained there in the form of a divine lion beneath a black aloe-wood tree.
With his mouth wide open, fearsome fangs bared, and his tawny mane disheveled,
the Lord Hari tore open the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu with his claws.
Hari is tawny-hued, with a quivering tongue, bearing the conch and the discus;
he is adorned with a crown and diadem, and is terrifying with his wide-open eyes. ||26||
Having seen him, the king and all the subjects paid homage to that lord of monkeys;
then they proceeded to the auspicious site of Nīlamaṇi Mādhava.
A banyan tree of vast extent, as high as a mountain peak,
filled with sand, which was the very self of Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, bowing down and repeatedly remembering the Lord, Nārada showed him that place where the God resides, covered by golden sands. 29.
To the west of the root of the banyan tree and to the north of Nṛsiṃha, O King,
stood Mādhava, the Lord who bears four forms.
To favor you alone, another image of Mādhava will manifest here once more, established by the citizens in the city. (3.1)
She too bestows liberation; what need is there to speak of her who was established by Brahmā?
Her manifestation and disappearance occur age after age.
"The Abode of Compassion remains here for the sake of favoring his devotees"—
having been shown this place, Indradyumna bowed down to it.
Having meditated upon him who dwells within the womb of the earth, he praised him with supreme affection:
"O Blessed One, all means indeed lead to the vision of you. (34)
Upon seeing you, the millions of layers of latent impressions are shattered.
O Lord, you alone are my refuge; show favor to me, who am wretched.
O Lord, I see you with the eye of a leather-worker; that is my purpose.
As he was speaking thus, a voice from the sky addressed that king.
"Do not fall into anxiety, O protector of the earth; I shall come within the range of your sight.
Do that which Nārada spoke in the words of Brahmā. || 37 ||
Then Nārada said to that faithful king:
"The gods come to the aid of those who are resolute in their virtuous endeavors. (38)
Therefore, O King, go right there into the presence of Nīlakaṇṭha;
I shall install Nṛsiṃha, and you should perform a sacrifice before him.
To the south of Nīlakaṇṭha, at a distance of a hundred bows, there stands a sandalwood tree; to its west lies a beautiful plot of ground.
It shall become a divine field equal to a thousand horse-sacrifices;
there, the son of Viśvakarman will construct a palace.
"Go; I shall remain right here for five days, propitiating this divine lion, Śrī Puruṣottama, in person. (42)
"O King, having installed the image within the replica [of the temple] and endowed it with life-force, senses, and mind, I shall indeed lead it there, into the presence of the sandalwood tree."
"A sacrifice performed in his presence would yield an extraordinary result.
Having been told this, the king went there, while the sage remained absorbed in meditation.
Just then, the son of the divine architect appeared in human form.
Then Viśvakarman, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, arrived there in great haste.
On the fourth day, he quickly completed the magnificent western-facing palace of Narasiṃha, which was most excellent and beautiful.
Then, at the clear dawn, Nārada, together with hosts of gods, goddesses, dances, musical instruments, and shouts of victory,
[beheld her] seated in a celestial chariot, beautifully adorned and decorated with jewels and gems.
Adorned with garlands and smeared with fragrant unguents, she was beautified by a halo of radiance. || 48 ||
Having taken up the beautiful image of Narasiṃha, whose vital breaths were firmly established and which was attended by goddesses, he stood before it.
The king and others prostrated before him and established her in the temple;
Indradyumna, together with Dharā and Ramā, offered him great praise.
O Lord, show me such compassion that at the conclusion of a thousand horse-sacrifices, I may behold you in your divine form with my physical eyes. 51.
O Lord of Sacrifice, just as this thousand sacrifices of mine may be completed without obstacle through Your grace, so may Your presence remain with me.
Having praised [her] thus, he ceased and performed the lustration ceremony (ārātrika). On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, conjoined with the Svātī asterism—|| 53 ||
Established in that field, one who worships the Divine Lion (Divyasiṃha) with a great sage shall obtain the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 54 ||
One should worship with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), or with milk, or with coconut juice, along with offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa) and hibiscus flowers (japā). ||55||
Being satisfied by all ritual offerings, one shall attain the abode of Nṛsiṃha;
[this occurs] on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha, on a Saturday, under the Svāti asterism.
One should worship that first incarnation of Nṛhari during the twilight hour.
Then, the gods, sages, and Vaiṣṇavas arrived at the sacrifice. ||57||

The ancestors, the gods on earth (brahmins) skilled in the Vedas, sacrifices, and other rites, as well as those who are kings in the three worlds, the Siddhas, the Vidyādharas, and so forth—[all these were present]. || 58 ||
The Kinnaras, the celestial Gandharvas, the Cāraṇas, and those who are Vaiṣṇavas arrived at the pavilion on the ground two yojanas away.
An altar was constructed within one *krośa*, and in its center, a spacious sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) was made;
O Brahmins, it extended for two *krośas*, and those fit for the sacrifice were stationed there.
In the midst of the kings, gods, and sages, he first honored the Lord of Śacī along with his domestic priest, providing them with all manner of opulences.
Then he worshipped the Siddhas, the gods, the great sages, the kings who were devotees of Viṣṇu, and the Brahmins and others, saying, "May they be pleased."
O Mahendra, grant me your permission; I shall worship the Lord of Sacrifice with a thousand horse-sacrifices until they reach completion.
"Stay for now with the thirty gods, seated in the midst of the assembly;
I perform this sacrifice for the sake of attaining Nīlamādhava, not for the attainment of the status of Indra. (64)
"Furthermore, when Kṛṣṇa is revealed, there will be welfare for you as well.
Having heard this, the gods then said, "We are in agreement with you. (65)
"O Indra among kings, perform your sacrifice with ease for Vaikuṇṭha, who is affectionate toward his devotees;
meanwhile, we ourselves shall worship Hari here in human form."
Then, at the commencement of the sacrifice, having invited the ancestors and the Brahmins, he, together with his wife, approached and worshipped the Blessed One.
Having performed the recitation of auspicious blessings by pure brahmins, as well as the rites for a holy day and prosperity, he chose them as his officiating priests; they too accepted the king.
Having initiated him along with his wife, he then brought the blazing Āhavanīya fire onto the altar and released the consecrated horse.
Then that consecrated king, remaining silent and seated in the sacrificial hall upon a skin of the ruru deer, gave instructions for the sake of the meal.
He caused all kinds of foods to be served—whatever foods exist throughout the fourteen worlds. (71)
He indeed caused to be given various items worthy of sacrifice, characterized by purity (sāttvika):
wish-fulfilling cows, kalpa-trees, and cintāmaṇi jewels in every respect.
The wish-fulfilling creepers and the supernatural powers (siddhis) fashion whatever is desired; Lakṣmī herself resides there, bestowing all prosperity and excellent enjoyments. (73)
At that sacrifice, nothing desired was lacking;
the splendors were then equal to those of the fourteen worlds.
Just as it was for the Vairājas, so too did they exist through the majesty of their lord;
therein were the ritual actions, the mantras, the objects, the sequences, and the vowels. (75)
In that state, things were indeed as they truly were, for there was no longer any obstruction to one's actions;
thus the sacrifice proceeded until, at last, there was only the narration of Hari.
The sciences of Brahman, praised by the virtuous as being true, proceed;
now the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* is brought forth. (77)
The gods, headed by Agni, being satisfied, did not even remember Amarāvatī;
all the inhabitants of Pātāla were likewise constantly satiated by those foods.
And all those embodied conscious beings, having been satisfied by their respective foods and drinks, no longer desired to return to their own homes.
Thus was the sacrifice of King Indradyumna commenced; indeed, in the sacred field of Puruṣottama, it was unprecedented and brought satisfaction to the three worlds.
By the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā), that lord of the earth attained, one by one in succession, [the remaining] ninety-nine established positions for the propitiation of Jagadīśa.
A king who performs a thousand horse-sacrifices shall attain divinity;
this applies to the seventh night prior to the Soma-consecration.
During the fourth watch of the night, the king saw in a dream Śvetadvīpa itself, situated in the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
There, in that divine pavilion, he beheld the glorious Supreme Lord seated upon an excellent lion-throne, bearing the conch, the discus, and other [emblems]. (84)
He was cloud-colored, wearing a forest garland, graced with loveliness,
the abode of the glory of beauty, and adorned with all divine ornaments.
On the right side stands Śeṣa, the infinite one, white in color, by whom a canopy is formed like a parasol with his thousand hoods. 86.
Wearing earrings and blue garments, with four arms equipped with a plow and other implements, he is adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and rings. ||87||

Then he indeed beheld Bhadrā Lakṣmī standing on his right side, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness and holding a lotus, possessing the luster of saffron and beautiful eyes. 88.
Her form was a wondrous sight that served as a model for the assembly of young women in the three worlds;
she sat in the lotus posture, richly endowed with qualities such as beauty, and was exquisitely adorned.
And he saw his grandfather before him with palms joined in reverence,
and on his left side stood the discus, adorned with various jewels.
Seeing him being praised by Sanaka and other great sages,
he emerged from his dream and repeatedly offered salutations.
He considered his thousand sacrifices to have borne fruit and his own purpose to be accomplished;
he recounted before Nārada how it had been experienced like a dream.
Nārada declared that as the fruit of this, one shall behold Hari directly within ten days; therefore, perform the sacrifice to completion according to the prescribed rules.
Then the Soma-pressing for the king’s horse-sacrifice commenced;
all gifts were bestowed, for the sacrificial session became like a wish-fulfilling creeper.
In the midst of that [place], on the southern bank of the ground near Bilveśvara, there was a great pool constructed for performing the avabhṛtha bath. ||95||
The appointed servants, seeing the banyan tree there, reported with agitation to the king: "A great tree has been seen on the bank. (96)
Its roots are in the ocean waters, while its branches reach as far as the bathing-houses;
marked with the conch and the discus, it exists everywhere, radiant like the sun. (97)
The celestial tree Sugandha, Viṣṇu having arrived in disguise, spoke with a smile: "Let the final oblation be offered. (98)
In a dream you saw Viṣṇu, and likewise the banyan tree was seen by your followers;
having completed the purificatory bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice, they held a festival on the bank.
"Place the Lord of Sacrifice, who is in the form of a tree, here upon the great altar. Having deliberated thus, King [Pṛthu] and Nārada went to the tree.
Having seen a tree with four branches emerging from the water like one with four arms, men pulled it out and both of them worshipped it.
Accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments, as well as Vedic mantras and the like,
they led the tree— adorned with garlands and perfumes— to the great sacrificial altar.
The king worshipped [the deity] upon the altar with thousands of ritual offerings;
then the monarch asked Nārada, "By whom was the image made, and how should it be fashioned?"
At that moment, an auspicious voice from the sky resounded there:
"Let the great altar be covered with trees and beautiful cloths."
For fifteen days, he himself will become the image;
Nārāyaṇa himself will be present there, assuming the form of an old carpenter.
That aged man has indeed arrived, weapon in hand and skilled in the arts;
having entered within him, let them diligently secure the door.
Let them make loud noises outside until the event takes place;
for once the sound of the event is heard, it brings about deafness and blindness.
One who destroys the lineage and one who destroys the kingdom—
one should never allow such a person to enter within, nor should one ever look upon them.

If anyone other than the appointed official should look [at the king's property], there shall indeed be great fear for both the king and the kingdom; furthermore, the seer shall suffer blindness of both eyes.
Therefore, you must not look upon him until his transformation is complete;
for once the god himself has emerged at the conclusion of the rite, he will speak with you.
Having said, "I shall construct it," the carpenter then vanished;
Nārāyaṇa was no longer seen on the altar, nor within the wood, nor beneath the cloth.
The king protected the sacrificial altar on all sides with guards,
and he attended to it exactly as the goddess of speech had instructed.

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Story of Bilveśa and Kapoteśa, the King’s Ill Omens, the Vision of the Divine Nṛsiṃha and Others, the Construction of the Sacrificial Pavilion at Kapoteśa-sthalī, and the Covering of the Altar with the Banyan Tree as Proclaimed by the Celestial Voice at the Conclusion of the Valedictory Bath," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then, O Lakṣmī, listen to how the manifestation of the forms occurred as it happened;
thus, as day after day passed, a divine fragrance was perceived.
There was a rain of pārijāta flowers, difficult for mortals to obtain,
as well as the sounds of divine music and beautiful songs.
There were droplets of white water and drops of sandalwood paste;
these became the ichor from the lordly elephants, such as Airāvata and others. (3)
He was worshipped from the path of the sky by hosts of invisible deities;
the gods paid him homage, and divine signs appeared.
When the fifteenth day arrived, he himself became fully manifest;
seated upon a divine throne, he was seen upon the altar.
The fourfold form consists of Jagannātha, Bala, Bhadrā, and Sudarśana;
indeed, this quartet is complete with all ornaments and splendors.
And this auspicious one is Lakṣmī herself, the embodiment of all consciousness;
you were my beloved, O dear one, and no distinction between us is ever appropriate.
"You cannot bear to let me go for even a moment while I have descended in this playful form;
thus indeed were four forms manifested by him. (8)
Then, O King, a voice from the sky arose on that stage:
"Fashion Viṣṇu as blue, Bala as white, and the discus as red; paint them vividly."
And she was auspicious, rosy-hued, and adorned with various ornaments;
indeed, no one other than the painter himself could behold her.
They should be carefully concealed with the bark of the *paṭa* tree;
they must be consecrated every year by releasing them from their previous consecration.
The divine, ancient form was accompanied by the application of bark-cloth;
however, upon the removal of that bark-cloth application, there occurred famine as well as death.
Indeed, there would be the destruction of the continuity [of the lineage], and those obstructions should not be seen;
yet, through negligence, they may be perceived by men as causes of fear.
Therefore, they should be viewed as variegated and adorned with many ornaments,
located on the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), one hundred cubits to the northwest of the Kalpa tree.
And to the north of Nṛsiṃha, he built a palace one thousand cubits high, richly adorned with pinnacles, most divine, very firm, and extensive.
Having had [the image] made and installed, enshrine these [mantras] therein:
Nīlamādhavasevākṛt, Śabara, the supreme Vaiṣṇava.
In former times, Viśvāvasu was a friend of yours when you had a family priest;
yet such was the case even with the offspring of Śabara, who had no family priest.
"And let him be appointed to the worship during all festivals and other occasions.
Having heard this voice from the sky, the king [took] the cloth for the covering.
Having lifted those forms for a moment, he beheld them as beautiful full [liṅgas], seated upon jeweled lion-thrones, pervaded by splendor, and perfectly circular.
He saw Kṛṣṇa, dark-complexioned and seated upon a lotus, and by his side, Balarāma, who was blue and white;
between them stood Bhadrā, auspicious and beautiful, amidst the vast circle of their hoods.
For a moment, everyone saw her standing on Viṣṇu’s left side and the Sudarśana discus in Kṛṣṇa’s hand; then she was covered again by the cloth.
Then everyone bowed down, and Citraśilpī prepared the pigments and other materials;
thereafter, he performed the worship according to Vedic rites with sacred hymns. ||22||
The king indeed worshipped Kṛṣṇa with the Pauruṣa Sūkta,
Bhadrā with the Lakṣmī Sūkta, and Bala with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, in Saudarśanī, Sudarśana caused various gifts to be bestowed;
he gave away tens of millions of cows as part of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) and distributed vast wealth.
From the connection with the earth being dug up by their hooves, a most purifying pit was formed;
and being further moistened by the water of their ichor, that very place became the sacred site known as Indrasaras.
It became the deliverer of Tāraka and the rescuer of his ancestors through the offering of water;
likewise, it bestows heaven through bathing and similarly grants the abode of Vaikuṇṭha through drinking.
The lake created by Indradyumna is renowned as the supreme among holy places; it bestows prosperity through giving, liberation through dwelling there, and even through death. (27)
Then the king began the construction of the palace;
and when the temple was completed, it was provided with a golden pinnacle.
Then, at an auspicious time and moment, the king, having worshipped the brahmins and the deities,
had them pronounce blessings for his welfare and the success of the rite.

Having offered the *arghya* water, requested the Lord of the World for the land to remain as a site for the palace for a long time, honored the artisans, and performed the *vāstuyāga* sacrifice, [he established the foundation].
Having held a great festival, he performed worship, gave gifts, and provided food;
then the king spoke in the assembly concerning the wealth that had been acquired by me.
I give all this for the sake of the temple of Jagannātha, for my own liberation;
for this body is the field wherein the omnipresent Lord dwells as the ego-sense. (32)
Through service to him, may the prosperity of my kingdom bear fruit for me in his own station;
for this Viṣṇu, whose body is wood, is the bestower of happiness and the kinsman of the abode.
Then, coming from behind Mūrti, a brahmin named Acyuta, resplendent with a halo of light, spoke in private: ||34||
The supreme abode, the abode of the Imperishable, the abode of nectar, the unmanifest, as well as Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the Ocean of Milk, and Śvetadvīpa. ||35||
If one desires to go to Badarī or other abodes,
then one must remain here in this divine field of Śrī Puruṣottama.

He desires to behold the supreme Brahman, the imperishable Brahman, and the liberated Brahman, as well as their divine manifestations (vyūhas), their powers (vibhavas), and their partial incarnations (aṃśas). ||37||
They must behold the form of Puruṣottama, as well as the worlds of Īśa, Satyaloka, Vairāja, and those known as Svarga. (38)
If one desires to enjoy the human, celestial, and subterranean realms, then they must perform giving, ritual bathing, and worship of this [Liṅga] here. (39)
If one desires to attain all sovereign powers, all branches of knowledge, all arts, as well as virtues, capability, existence, and so forth— 40.
Therefore, let this Śrī Jagannātha be served with offerings as long as possible;
this wooden Brahman bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (41)
In this abode of the glorious Puruṣottama, which bestows liberation as pure being, consciousness, and bliss even by mere sight, there is not the slightest distinction whatsoever. 42.
Therefore, O King, dwell here and accomplish liberation;
you are the most learned and devoted, so worship Him along with His limbs and subordinate parts. 43.

Leaves, flowers, water, roots, grains, clothing, and excellent sandalwood—even a tiny amount of water offered to the Lord of the World, who possesses the qualities of a lotus, becomes [meritorious]. (44)
Lakṣmī is my mother and the bestower of prosperity; she will grant enjoyments to her devotee.
To the giver, I shall give everything; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. 45.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin then vanished from the form of Hari;
for everyone, Hari became the object of a divine wonder.
Remaining within his physical form, he shed tears out of love;
Nārada attained steadfastness in the *mudrā* of meditation characteristic of the Naimiṣa forest. 47.
While performing it, he became momentarily dazed by samādhi and immersed in love;
at that very instant, bliss overflowed there as if in Goloka. ||48||
"Today my task is complete," having said this, Nārada spoke to him:
"O King, remain here after honoring him; I shall go to the Grandfather (Brahmā). (49)
"O protector of the earth, therefore build a palace with great wealth;
having installed an image of Nṛsiṃha, you shall be liberated—be happy."
"I shall inform Brahmā of what has been done and [report] you as his servant.
And Indradyumna said to him, "Dwell here together with me. (51)
"Having caused a temple to be built, we two shall go to our grandfather;
we will make our request to him, and he himself will surely come. (52)
"He will perform a great festival for the Blessed One here in this temple. Then Nārada and the king both agreed, saying, "So be it. (53)
Desiring to depart quickly, he set about the work of the temple;
he then employed thousands of the finest artisans there, and the expenditure of wealth, amounting to many millions, cannot even be calculated. (54)
Then, through the king’s faith, devotion, and virtuous disposition, even the Goddess Śrī became pleased and rendered her assistance in building the temple. (55)
Having performed the ritual installation of the embryo according to the rules and having placed a copper [image],
one should fix a fine plaque at the side to ward off obstacles such as the fall of lightning.
And he commanded his most excellent ministers for the purpose of leveling the peak,
so that the summit might be made like a mountain peak, reaching unto the sky.
Hearing the auspicious divine verses concerning the celestial realm, the king thought:
"What could be difficult for a sovereign to attain when he has Nārada as his companion? (58)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and likewise Lakṣmī—what inferiority could there be here?
Such a temple as this is being built has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again.
"Indeed, such an upward-moving being does not exist upon the earth or in any other place," hearing this, the Nameless One spoke thus to Nārada.
O King, that which has been earned through pilgrimages, mantras, recitations, gifts, sacrifices with abundant fees, vows, Vedic studies, and austerities— [6.1]
O Indra among kings, it was not possible for that which had come into your hand through devotion;
therefore, do not grieve further while your yoga of devotion is so abundant.
If he goes into the presence of the Lord, desiring to see the Grandfather (Brahmā),
He too will instruct him in those various pilgrimages and great festivals.
And at the time that temple is consecrated by the Self-Existent One, the Blessed One himself will grant you a boon.
I too shall come then, together with the seven sages;
then we two shall go there to the stainless world of Brahmā.
Having spoken thus, King Nārada bowed to Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma,
and Satī, and requested permission to depart for the world of Brahmā.
Both Nārada, through the yoga of devotion, and Indradyumna, the devotee of Viṣṇu, traveled toward Brahmā by means of a divine celestial chariot.
By the grace of Hari, they conquered the fourteen worlds;
meanwhile, the king also reflected for a moment upon his journey to the world of Brahmā.
A hundred yugas pass upon the earth; what then will become of this temple?
When I return, that which was built by me shall go to destruction.
"How shall I attain fulfillment by observing a firm foundation?"—to the king who was thus absorbed in thought, Nārada said: "Do not grieve."
Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is the maker of the length of time;
He is also the bestower of brevity, and He will even make a moment subtle.
In the time of the worlds Satya and Bhū, the Lord, having established equality for your sake by his own will,
shall perform his own task.
In whatever task the Lord Four-faced (Brahmā) is an assistant,
no obstacle caused by time or by material circumstances arises therein.
"Behold before you this mass of splendors, delightful like ten million moons;
know that it has arrived from the abode of Brahmā. (74)
Behold this city of Brahmā; behold its most beautiful assembly hall.
Beyond that, indeed, Vaikuṇṭha rests upon the waters.
Beyond that is the Vairāja abode, and beyond that is the immortal realm; further still is Paravaiṣṇava-vaikuṇṭha, and even beyond that is Goloka.
Beyond that is the imperishable abode; beyond that is the supreme state.
There exists the abode of Puruṣottama, than which there is indeed nothing else higher. (77)
Speaking thus about Indradyumna, Nārada’s celestial chariot reached the northern gate of the assembly hall of Brahmā and came to a halt.
Seeing the king and Nārada, the gatekeeper bowed;
and having received the command of Brahmā, he ushered them both into the assembly hall.
Bowing from afar to Brahmā, who was accompanied by Sāvitrī and Śāradā, the king stood still for a moment; then Brahmā called out to the monarch.
"Come, O King, welcome to you! You are truly the beloved of the Blessed One; by the power of Nārada, you have arrived here at this inaccessible place. (8.1)
"Accept this ambrosial food and drink this sweet-tasting nectar.
Tell me, what is the heart-pleasing reason for your arrival? (82)
Thus addressed, the king said: "By your grace, a temple has been built;
please come there and install Mādhava. (83)
O Father, O Grandfather, if you come and install Śrī Jagannātha, may your grace toward me become fruitful. (84)
"Be gracious to me and do this, for you alone are the Lord of the World.
Thus praised, Brahmā then spoke to the king with respect: 85.
"O King, you have indeed built a palace for the residence of the Blessed One;
yet at this time, neither do you possess a kingdom, O King, nor do you have any progeny. (86)
O King, since you arrived here on earth, a vast period of time has passed—more than a Manvantara, and a hundred Yugas have gone by. (87)
Even your lineage has been severed, and millions of kings have passed away;
yet, O King, in the divine field known as Śrī Puruṣottama— ||88||
The power of time’s decay and Time itself, by my command, shall be withdrawn by Śrī Kṛṣṇa until the temple is completed. (89)
There, the moments, the regions, and their inhabitants are equal to those of Satyaloka;
indeed, by my command at the direction of Hari, they exist there exactly as they are.
The Lord Śrī has placed the jewel of his crown in the sky as the sun;
leading one toward divine splendor, it creates a day equal to Satyaloka.
Therefore, O Great King, go immediately after me;
I am indeed coming for the sake of establishing [the site], so prepare the appropriate requisites. (92)
O King, in the former age, Janārdana, having assumed a body of sapphire stone, did not leave the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
"Now my second *parārdha* has arrived;
this Lord in the form of wood shall remain for the duration of my life once more. (94)
The hairs on the body of Kṛṣṇa residing in Śvetadvīpa became the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas);
from among them, a banyan tree was brought for the purpose of the wooden image.
That true personage, who rose up spontaneously from the waters of the ocean, was previously entreated by me for the sake of destroying this terrible cycle of worldly existence. (96)
And Janārdana, whose body was as firm as wood, having heard these words of Brahmā with manifold devotion, prostrated himself before the Grandfather.
By means of the celestial chariot, Nārada arrived on earth;
seeing that beautiful, divine, and full palace, he rejoiced. ||98||
He prostrated like a staff upon the ground and bowed to Śrī Nṛsiṃha;
and the king, who was himself Brahmā the Grandfather, spoke to the artisans and others. 99.
While he was coming with the gods for the rite of consecration for this [image],
the treasure-lotus (padmanidhi), impelled by Brahmā, arrived there.
The king performed a welcome reception, offering hospitality, honor, and the like;
Nārada, for his part, drew up a list of all his possessions on a written inventory.
For the purpose of the consecration, he quickly gave [the wealth] to Padmanidhi,
who likewise caused the auspicious preparation of excellent materials to be carried out.
In that same manner, he quickly caused a golden hall to be constructed, as well as a city extending for many yojanas, along with a pavilion and a sacrificial pit.
And he caused three supreme golden chariots to be made;
one was a sixteen-wheeled chariot for Viṣṇu, bearing the banner of Garuḍa.
For Padmadhvaja, the boon was Subhadrā and twelve discuses;
and for Bala, fourteen discuses and a mirror-banner.
Alternatively, the most excellent Śīradhvaja, the possessor of the plow (Balarāma), should be depicted;
a stainless mirror is always held in the palm of his hand. 106.
Because it stands upon a palm tree, that tree is marked by the palm;
indeed, the chariot of the Wielder of the Discus is sixteen cubits in width.
Balabhadra has fourteen wives, while Subhadrā has twelve;
however, that god (Kṛṣṇa) must not be wedded, since he stands upon a chariot that has no fixed foundation.
Whether in a palace, a pavilion, or even in a city, that [act] would be fruitless;
therefore, the king quickly caused the installation of the chariot to be performed.
Having constructed a very beautiful hall in the north-eastern direction of the chariot,
and having built a pavilion in its center, one should prepare a pure altar there.
One should have a square enclosure built, measuring four cubits on each side and likewise one cubit in height,
during the first part of the night at an auspicious moment, starting from the north.
Having proclaimed "Svasti," one should then perform the ritual sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa);
thereafter, one should offer oblations (bali) to the thirty-two deities according to the prescribed rule.
In the morning, one should cause a water-pot to be placed upon a mandala marked with a svastika on the sacrificial altar,
filled with the decoction of five trees, auspicious waters, and sprouts.
One should fill [the vessel] with collections of jewels, perfumes, and medicinal herbs, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one should worship it, encircle it with cloth, and invoke that Lord Hari.
One should worship him according to the prescribed rite, and likewise offer sacrificial fuel in the northwest;
then, having consecrated the clarified butter and the sacrificial porridge (caru) with mantras, one should perform eight thousand oblations.
Then one should cause the chariot to reach the point of impact with the pitcher and set it on fire;
having placed the wind-god upon the banner, one should perfume and fumigate it.
Having worshipped Garuḍa and offered prayers, one should place that pitcher upon the front of the chariot;
one should sprinkle it and bathe the chariot while it is atop Garuḍa.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should give abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
one should feed the people and thereafter worship Balaratha.
With the twelve-syllable mantra and the Lakṣmīsūkta, one should pray to the lotus— the chariot of Śrī— which has arisen from the navel of Kṛṣṇa and serves as the seat.
"You have been born for the sake of awakening the gods; remain steadfast!"—thus one should raise the lotus-bannered [image] upward and then bow down to it.
When the chariot was thus established, he placed all the gods upon it,
as well as men, women, elephants, horses, bulls, and so forth.
Those chariots should be led through the village and paraded around the temple;
standing upon the chariot, the most excellent Bali offering should be presented by the best of Brahmins.
O gods—Ādityas, Vasus, and Grahas; Maruts, Aśvins, Rudras, Suparṇas, Pannagas, and others—may you accept this offering! (1.23)
May the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, the Rathadevas, the Vināyakas,
the guardians of the quarters, the guardians of the worlds, and the Ṛṣis bestow well-being.
May these beings act without obstruction; may there be no impediments.
May the Daityas, the hosts of spirits, and others become gentle and satisfied. (1.25)
Then, one should move those chariots slowly with Vedic hymns;
hear now, O Lakṣmī, of the portents that occur there which bring about loss. 3 || 126 ||
If the pole breaks, there is fear for the twice-born; if the axle breaks, there is the destruction of the kṣatriyas;
if the balance-beam breaks, there is the ruin of the vaiśyas; and likewise, if the yoke-pin breaks, there is the destruction of the śūdras.
If the yoke breaks, there will be drought; if the pedestal breaks, there is danger for the subjects;
if the wheel breaks, another kingdom arises; and if the banner falls, there is a foreign monarch.
If the image breaks, death occurs; if it falls over, there is a calamity in the country;
and if the chariot becomes face-down, there is the destruction of all the local inhabitants.
When [the child] is thus born, one should perform the bali-offering and the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma);
one should prepare the fire for the chariot in the north-eastern direction.
One should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) that have roots and tips intact, using clarified butter, honey, and ghee;
one should offer the sacrifice for a broken limb while reciting words of peace (*śānti*) and words of well-being (*svasti*).
May there be well-being for the devotees; may there be well-being for men and women as well;
may there be well-being for the cows and cattle, and indeed may there be well-being for the entire world.
May there be peace, may there be auspiciousness, and may there be well-being for us from every side.
O Lord, Master, Sovereign of the World, grant us protection and peace. (133)
"Thus, O Lakṣmī, one should cause the rites of pacification, the worship of the planets, and so forth to be performed;
at that time, all of this was caused to be done for the king by the sage Nārada."

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Completion of the Four Images, Their Worship, the Construction of the Temple for the Icons, the Departure of Indradyumna and Nārada toward Brahmā, the Arrival of Padmanidhi for the Consecration, the Manufacture of the Chariots, the Worship, the Flagstaff and Other Details, the Results of Obstacles in the Chariot, and the Performance of Peace-Rites," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. || 587 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, when Indradyumna indeed departed for Satyaloka,
King Khaṇḍeśa was appointed to oversee the matter.
The protector of the earth named Gāla was the lord of Utkala and Ilā;
he is indeed called the king of Oḍhra, and by him [was established] the image of Mādhava.
It was installed for a short time for the purpose of constant viewing; and having removed that image as well as the excellent lion-thrones, (verse 3).
The king caused them to be constructed in the central area of the palace; then King Indradyuti adorned them with great splendor.
At that moment, a beautiful celestial chariot of Brahmā was seen in the sky;
it was drawn by swans, adorned with Sāvitrī and others, and endowed with splendor.
And Brahmā descended from there, accompanied by the waters of the Gaṅgā;
at that time, shouts of "Victory!", cries of joy, and words of "Salutation! arose.
Then, out of a desire to see the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds,
there was a great commotion as they vied with one another, each thinking "I first, I first."
They honored Brahmā with parched grain, flowers, and unbroken rice;
Brahmā, having approached Kṛṣṇa’s chariot, bowed down and beheld him.
Then he went behind Balaratha and Bhadrāratha;
he bowed down, praised them, and honored them with divine articles.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Śeṣa, and to Lakṣmī; salutations indeed to the Discus.
Salutations again and again to the non-duality of Viṣṇu, Rāma, and Subhadrā.
"Salutation to the destroyer of ignorance, whose self is the Sudarśana [disc].
Having thus prostrated and turned away, he followed the path directed by Nārada.
He approached to behold the palace situated on the Blue Mountain;
seeing the temple, the pavilion, the altar, and the hall, he was indeed filled with joy.
Seated himself upon the Brahmāsana in that grove, the Unborn One (Aja) sat there; the gods, sages, and Brahmins likewise took their seats in the pavilion.
Then, by the command of Brahmā, the officiating priests and others took their respective places;
thereafter, Bhāradvāja began to perform the rites for peace and prosperity.
Then the king performed worship for the inhabitants of the three worlds,
as well as for the body of the Blessed One and his beautiful temple.
Having erected the great banner on high, Bharadvāja requested the Grandfather for the preservation of his life-breaths.
Having performed the rites for auspiciousness, Brahmā, accompanied by the ṛṣis and the Brahmin priests, proceeded on chariots amidst the sounds of musical instruments and shouts of victory.
Having offered praise, the devotees of the Lord (Bhāgavatas) brought Him down from the chariot by way of the staircase and slowly led Him into the vicinity of the temple.
While these cotton-padded couches were being spread, a rain of flowers fell repeatedly:
"Victory to you, O Lord of the worlds! Victory, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (1.9)
"Victory to Saṃkarṣaṇa, O auspicious one! Victory! Grant us happiness!"—with such proclamations they brought him to the pavilion at the gate of the palace.

Having caused [the deity] to dwell [there], for the sake of consecration, [he should perform it] before a mirror-mandala with consecrated jars filled with water collected from sacred bathing places (tīrtha).
The king performed the consecration of Śrī and Puruṣa with two hymns;
then he [honored] the gods, who were adorned and graced with perfumes and garlands.
The Brahmins then consecrated those lords seated upon the lion-thrones;
Brahmā, his gaze cast downward, anointed their eyes with a small stick.
He performed their ritual installation according to the rules, adorning them with divine ornaments;
he meditated upon those divine forms as being present in bodily form and fully conscious.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony for them, he prayed with devotion:
"O you who are the foundation of the entire world, remain steadfast here within this image. (25)
When you are established, we and the gods are also established;
having assumed a divine form, dwell here permanently in this palace.
"By your command I shall set forth; may they be fulfilled through your grace.
Having said this, he touched his heart and muttered the infallible mantra.
He presented enjoyments, fed embodied beings,
caused gifts to be given, and he granted exemptions.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, in conjunction with the Puṣya asterism,
the installation was performed by the preceptor Brahmā Parameṣṭhin.
And whatever merit is performed on that day— bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth,
as well as austerity, vows, and worship— all of it shall attain imperishability.
Having gone there on that day, they behold Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Bhadrīkā, and Sudarśana; liberated, they go to my abode.
Then, on that day of Lakṣmī, in the evening, the Lord Nṛsiṃha was seen in the form of Kṛṣṇa by everyone, a sight most wonderful.
Then, in another moment, a fish was seen, and likewise a tortoise;
in another moment a boar was seen, and a swan was also seen.
Hayagrīva was seen, and Kapila was also seen;
Hari was seen, and Vāsudeva was also seen.
Pṛthu was seen there, and Dattātreya was also seen;
later Ṛṣabha was seen, and then Vāmana was also seen.
Then Paraśurāma was seen, followed by Yajñanārāyaṇa;
then Rāmāditya appeared, as well as the Kumāras, Sanaka and the others.
Nārada was seen, and the king of kings was also seen;
then Vyāsa, Buddha, and thereafter Svāmī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa appeared once more.
There Vairāja was seen, as were Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa;
and these, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, were also seen from moment to moment.
Then everyone was filled with great wonder and understood that all the incarnations of Hari originate from Puruṣottama. ||39||
From Him alone they are born, appearing according to the devotion [of their devotees];
for the kings and others were indeed filled with joy upon seeing Hari in such a manner.
Doubts regarding the relationship between the source and its manifestations have come to an end, for the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is the root itself, manifesting in all forms. ||41||
In whatever manner and by whomever [the deity] is propitiated, in that same manner it bestows its fruit upon him;
for whatever the extent of one's faith, so great shall be one's accomplishment.
Then Brahmā, with a faltering voice, made this petition to the Lord of the World:
"O Blessed One, throughout the thousands of births of Indradyumna..."
While you were practicing devotion here in former times, many ages have passed;
today, by your will, I have obtained the fruit of that devotion in this birth.
The king desires to worship you through the yoga of devotion;
grant him this instruction and ordain for him vows and festivals. (85)
Thus requested by Brahmā, Hari, whose form was that of wood, laughed and said:
"O Indradyumna, I am pleased with your exceedingly profound devotion. (46)
"I grant you a boon, O King: may your devotion to me remain steadfast, since you have constructed this temple for me, having renounced millions of wealth. (47)
"O Indra among kings, even upon its destruction, I shall never abandon this;
with this wooden body, I shall remain here for a supreme aeon. (48)
The second [rite] belongs to the Lotus-born [Brahmā], and it is performed until that [time] is completed;
then, those who [offer] me water from the well situated to the north of the Nyagrodha tree—
Those who bathe the auspicious Rāma shall attain my world;
and whoever beholds me while I am situated for bathing shall go to the supreme station.
On the fourteenth day, the twice-born should draw up water with golden jars;
on the morning of the Jyeṣṭhā constellation, they should place me, Rāma, upon a couch, while Bhadrā is placed in the pavilion.
Having placed [the image] in the northeast and bathed it, one should lead it back;
he who beholds me as I proceed facing south shall be liberated.
Then, O King, having kept me away for fifteen days, one should never look upon me, whether I am deformed or beautiful. (53)
Having offered this Jyeṣṭha-bath and performed [the rite], one shall be released from bondage.
Now, on the fifth day of Māgha, or on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra— (54)
One should perform the Guṇḍicā procession, for it indeed bestows liberation and happiness;
even the second day of Āṣāḍha, when conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, bestows liberation. (55)
O King, even in the absence of the constellation Ṛkṣa, a festival procession should be held by me on that lunar day;
on that day, having placed Rāma, myself, and Bhadrakā upon the chariot. (56)
The place where I was born is the site known as the Guṇḍicā-maṇḍapa,
where an altar for a thousand horse-sacrifices was constructed by you.
"Therefore, a journey must be undertaken to my place on earth;
for nine days I shall go to the Indradyumna lake. (58)
After that, I shall indeed go again to my own temple;
then, for the observer, there shall be at every step the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. ||59||
My rising, my sleeping, my turning upon my side,
my covering myself with a garment, and even the great festival of the Puṣya-bath.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, one should engage in play and hold a grand festival on a swing;
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the rite of fulfillment.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship me with *damanaka* flowers;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should smear me with sandalwood paste.
"O Indradyumna, these festivals must always be celebrated by you, for they grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation, since they are my favor and face-to-face presence. (63)
"O Brahman, go to Satyaloka; let the gods go to heaven, and let the king remain here.
I shall stay here until the completion of my full lifespan as Brahmā. (64)
Having been addressed thus, they all departed; Kṛṣṇa became manifest in his true form, Brahmā went toward Satyaloka, and afterwards the king held great festivities.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe the auspicious Jyeṣṭha-bath;
having performed the formal vow (saṃkalpa) on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one should remain restrained in speech.
On the morning of the eleventh day, he should then go to the Mārkaṇḍeya-avaṭa;
having sipped water, bowed to Śaṅkara, and bathed at the two testicles of the Bull (Vṛṣa).
Having touched the Liṅga with his thumb and the Śakti with his fist,
and having worshipped them, he should then proceed to the flawless Nārāyaṇa.
One should bow to the Nyagrodha tree and perform circumambulation, then pay homage;
thereafter, one should bow to Garuḍa and enter the temple of Kṛṣṇa.
Having circumambulated him three times, one should worship him and behold him;
and having presented offerings and obtained the permission of Ugrasena, [one should depart].
One should go to the ocean to bathe by way of the path to the gate of heaven;
having sipped water (ācamana) while facing east, one should draw a maṇḍala and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should firmly bind the armor:
"May Govinda protect me in the east; may the lotus-eyed one protect me in the south. (72)
May Pradyumna protect [me] in the west, and likewise Hṛṣīkeśa in the north;
may Narasiṃha be in the southeast, and Madhusūdana in the southwest.
May Śrīdhara protect [me] in the northwest, and Gadādhara in the northeast;
may Trivikrama protect above, and he who bears the form of the Boar protect below. (74)
May the Lord Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, protect me everywhere; may Janārdana, seated upon Garuḍa, protect my mind, and may he protect my intellect and ego.
"May the glorious Lord, the Master of Light, always protect my senses.
Having thus donned the armor, [one should worship] with the sixteen primary offerings and so forth.
There, in the mandala, one should worship the illustrious Lord Puruṣottama;
for the sake of internal purification, one should sip water, and externally, one should sprinkle darbha-grass water.
One should bathe three times in the ocean, whereby the destruction of all sins occurs;
having put on a garment, one should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) or a drop (binduka) and worship Hari.
In the mandala, one should invoke Śrīdhara and offer him a seat;
likewise, one should provide water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, and a bath.
Garments, a sacred thread, ornaments, fragrant unguents,
flower garlands, incense, a lamp, and sweet food and drink.

One should perform the offering of betel, the waving of lights (ārātrika), circumambulation, hymns of praise and so forth, the asking for forgiveness for offenses, and the ritual dismissal; this is the sequential worship.
Meditation, charity, austerity, recitation of mantras, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods—
all these, when performed for the King of Sindhu, shall become multiplied millions upon millions of times.
Having bowed to the ocean and the temple, one should go to the lake of Indradyumna;
having prayed to Narasiṃha there, one should bathe according to the prescribed rite.
Then, facing westward, one should go and worship Nṛsiṃha;
having performed the ritual bathing in the ocean, one should behold Puruṣottama. (84)
One should perform the Pañcatīrthī in this manner; one will certainly attain liberation.
On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, when the moon and Jupiter are in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, [one should do so]. (85)
Then one should visit the sacred fords and the holy field of Śrī Puruṣottama, and perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow known as Jyeṣṭhapañcaka. ||86||
One should worship Kṛṣṇa, Bala, Nṛsiṃha, Bhadrā, and Cakra;
one should worship Nīlamādhava, Garuḍa, and Puruṣottama. (87)
On the tenth day, one should worship Mādhava in a golden pitcher;
on the eleventh day, Nārāyaṇa; and on the twelfth day, Yajñasūkara.
Having worshipped Pradyumna on the thirteenth day, Nṛhari on the fourteenth, and all the gods on the full moon day according to the prescribed rite, ||89||
One should daily, or on the full moon day, offer milk-rice as a food offering;
one should present sweet foods, excellent soups, fruits, and the like.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations in the fire-sacrifice (homa) and feed virtuous people;
one should also make gifts of cows, and thus one shall become a partaker of desired fruits. ||91||
Thus, by performing the pilgrimage and other rites, one will certainly attain liberation;
O Lakṣmī, by reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the fruit of that pilgrimage. 92.

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Brahmā, the Consecration of the Life-Force (Prāṇapratiṣṭhā) of Jagannātha and Others, the Vision of the Incarnations within His Own Form, Festivals, the Chariot Procession, the Fruits of the Chariot Procession, the Five Holy Sites (Pañcatīrthī), and the Ritual for Them," in the first section on the continuity of the Kṛta Yuga of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī; I shall describe to you the great festival of Mahāvedī.
On the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, one should choose a brāhmaṇa.
One should also select a carpenter for the forest sacrifice;
having gone to a place in the midst of trees in the forest, [one should offer] one hundred and eight oblations into the fire.
Having offered clarified butter as an oblation even at the foot of the tree and having presented a bali-offering to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapa),
the twice-born man should then cut a small portion at the foot of the tree, after which the carpenter [should proceed].
Having taken wood, one should construct a chariot and worship Gaṇeśa;
the chariot of Hari should be twenty-two cubits in height and have four doors.
It is joined with sixteen wheels and adorned with the Garuda-banner;
for Śeṣa it has fourteen spokes, and for Bhadrā it has twelve spokes.
Having thus caused them to be made with all their limbs, one should cause them to be polished;
one should strengthen them with fine cloths and adorn them with excellent jewels.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, at the break of dawn, one should worship Hari;
thereafter, one should conduct the procession toward the Guṇḍikā pavilion.
One should celebrate a festival with royal honors and a hundred thousand men;
there is no greater means for attaining Viṣṇu than this.
One should establish [the offerings] during the four-month period and present the food offerings in Kārtika;
one should partake of the grace of Viṣṇu, which is sanctified by Śrī.
The food offered as oblation to the Lord of the Universe and the water of the Ganges—these two are equal;
even if touched by a dog or a Cāṇḍāla, that divine water and food remain pure.
Twelve processions indeed should be performed for the Lord of the World, which bestow liberation;
on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, there is the procession for the construction of the chariot.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should perform the pilgrimage to the five sacred sites (pañcatīrthī) by traveling on foot;
indeed, in Jyeṣṭha, the chariot procession (rathayātrā) should be conducted to Guṇḍikā.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the fourth [observance] is the procession to the temple;
in Āṣāḍha, the procession for the couch should be performed; thus there are four months.
In the month of Bhādrapada, there is the pilgrimage consisting of the circumambulation of Pārśvanātha in the form of worship;
in the month of Kārttika, there is the pilgrimage of awakening in the nature of a great festival.
On the road, there is the procession for the winter garments and the wearing of woolen clothes and the like;
in the month of Pauṣa, there is the auspicious Puṣya-bath procession, which consists of the Tapas-snāna (ascetic bath).
In the month of Pauṣa, the northern journey of the Sun is considered meritorious;
and in Māgha, the spring procession is considered to consist of worship and festivals.
In the month of Phālguna, during the Puṣpa-dolā festival, or else in Śrāvaṇa, such great festivals should be performed for the Lord of the World, which bestow liberation. || 17 ||
In the divine city of Jagannātha, no distinction of caste exists; nor should any distinction between men and women be made there in any way whatsoever. (18)
All those who were seen with four arms appear now with two;
all my liberated ones dwell there, bestowing heaps of merit. || 19 ||
Everything of mine is pleasing, divine, and free from defect;
even Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha have been established by me upon this earth.
By the grace, majesty, and favor of me, the Lord of the Universe, women are Lakṣmīs and men are Nārāyaṇas; this is my view. (21)
There, no food, drink, clothing, or other such things are found to be impure;
for by the power of Ekādaśī, she has brought even the consumption of food under her control. (22)
By my grace, eating food offered by others is not a defect but rather an ornament;
service to the virtuous, service to the guru, and service to me here grant liberation. (23)
By me, through the pastimes with the cowherd girls, a vision is constantly granted;
it is a divine play, capable of assuming any form at will, which destroys the nature of doubt. 24.
Bestowing a mass of the bliss of liberation upon those whose nature is divine, embodied beings attain divinity by thus realizing it within their own selves. (25)
I am the Lord of the Gopīs, renowned in Vṛndāvana at Kuṅkumavāpikā, in Puruṣottama-kṣetra, and in Durgā-bhūmi.
To whomever I may be gracious, nothing else remains for him;
indeed, I am the giver of bliss, according to how and by whom I am sought from me.
O Lakṣmī, in this field that bestows liberation, the installation of the Lord of the Universe grants liberation;
even seeing Him, touching Him, or remembering Him from afar grants liberation. (28)
This first and most excellent section of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, titled "The Division on the Lineage" (*Santāna-khaṇḍa*), has been narrated by me to you. (29)
In this opening section, there is the flowing toward Hari by Nārada in Vaikuṇṭha;
the liberation through merging for the liberated ones and others; and the possession of form within the supreme Imperishable.
The creation of Goloka was for the sake of Rādhā by Kṛṣṇa in his form as Kṛṣṇa; and the creation of Vaikuṇṭha was for the sake of Lakṣmī by the Lord of the Imperishable (Akṣareśvara). ||3 1 ||
Starting from Vāsudeva, there is the creation ending with Parameṣṭhin;
thereafter follows the manifoldness of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. (32)
And the divine nature of the indeterminate Badarikāśrama was beheld by Brahmā through his intellect within the body of Nārāyaṇa. (3.3)

The dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding their greatness, the [bestowal of] armor and other [protective gear], and the glorification of the manifestation of the Liṅga of Śambhu, which consists of the splendor of Brahman. 34.
Upon seeing the end of the linga, both Brahmā and the ketaki flower became liars;
they have always attained a state of unworthiness, whereas Viṣṇu has attained worthiness.
The production of minute eggs occurs within the coverings;
thereafter follows the calculation of time, beginning with the moment (kṣaṇa) and extending up to the great aeon (mahākāla). 36.
And by Brahmā were created the mental [sons], beginning with Guṇa, Ajñāna, and Adharma;
likewise, there was the creation of Dharma, Rudra, and Kṛtānta, as well as the dissolution of Rudra.
The manifestation of the Sāttvika Rudra, Rudrāṇī, and their male and female attendants;
the peaceful creation of Sanaka and others; and likewise, the revelation of the Vedas. ||38||
The majesty of the virtuous consists in the creation of divine songs and the like;
likewise, it is the creation of the maidens who are the Upaniṣads and the propagation of knowledge. (39)
It is the expansion of the Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī mantras dear to Brahmā,
and the creation of the worshipful offerings through devotion to Ekādaśī, Jayantī, and other sacred occasions.
The propitiation of Mahālakṣmī and Rāmārādhā, the creation of Satī, Gaṅgā, and others;
and the divine marks and qualities of virtuous women and celestial nymphs. ||41||
Then follows the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa in human form, marked by both male and female characteristics, as well as the birth and power of the devoted wife. 42.
Saffron, unbroken rice, betel, coconut juice, and so forth, as well as red ochre and other minerals, are prescribed exactly as they are found in nature. (43)
The origin of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), the creation of Kāmadeva and others, the birth of Pativratā and the twice-born, and the greatness of service to the ancestors. ||44||

The greatness of one devoted to his wife, the state of having a son bound by debt, the predominance [of the father's qualities] during conception and the rite of impregnation, as well as that arising from time, place, and other factors. ||45||
The rite of impregnation (*niṣeka*) is the vow that removes the defect of menstrual blood;
on the first day of Brahmā, however, it is the dismissal of the Brahmins. (46)
In Satyaloka, the mental creation of the Ṛṣis is revealed; likewise, the generation of the Pitṛs occurs in Maharloka, Janaloka, and Tapoloka. ||47||
Food and other offerings to be given to the ancestors, as well as the sacrificial trees and so forth;
the origin of the Sun, gold and other treasures, and likewise the birth of the Moon. ||48||
Due to his partiality for Rohiṇī, the Moon suffered the affliction of waning;
however, by the installation of Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra, he was freed from that decline. (49)
Gods, humans, spirits, Daityas, Dānavas, and moving beings—
just as they were created, so too have the accomplishments of the ages, years, and other such cycles arisen.

The loss of supernatural powers, cities and the like, medicinal herbs, the castes and stages of life, and so forth; as well as the fourfold division of the universal form and the taking [of the sacrificial victim]—these are the [manifestations]. ||51||
The making of the vajra from Dadhyañc’s bones, the slaying of Vṛtra, the horse sacrifice, the incarnation as Varāha, and likewise the descent of Pṛthu. (52)
The movement of mating pairs, dreaming, and likewise the granting of death;
the signs of a universal monarch (cakravartin), violence, and the swift falling of birds. 5.3.
The nature of the Dvāpara age, the arrival of Nārada at Raivata, the summary of the principles, the opening of the subterranean cavity, and the filling of that cavity of the earth. (54)
The lunar nature of Raivata is the very essence of the jewel;
the penance of Khadvaṅga at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake has been described. (55)
The holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā-tīrtha, the manifestation of Gopālakṛṣṇaka, and the appearance of Kambharā Mahālakṣmī have been described. (56)
The birth of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; the origin of Barhiṣan and Aṅgada; and the placing of a dead snake around the neck of the sage who was firm in his vow. 57.
By the curse of the sage’s son, there was also the "Bite of the Deceiver," as well as the king's fast unto death and the suspension of the story. (58)
The meditation on the form [of Dhanvantari], the arrival of Dhanvantari on the bank of the Vratadā river,
his protection during the snake sacrifice (sarpasatra), and also the marriage of Sūrya.
Then follows the assumption of two forms by Saṃjñā, the wife of Sūrya, and subsequently the birth of Śrāddhadeva, Yama, and Yamī.
Thereafter follows the origin of Chāyā, Aśvinī, Vaidya, and others;
then the description of the southern path, the Purāṇas, and the description of the hells. ||6 1||
The fruit of the karma of hell-beings, as well as the marks of birth and so forth,
the physical and divine signs, and the signs of prosperity for women.

The funeral rites for the dead, the affliction caused by a *preta*, the warding off of that [affliction], the state of being a *preta*, food offered to *pretas* and so forth, birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). ||63||

The fruit of giving is the unity of the individual body and the cosmic egg; [it involves] the rites of impregnation and birth, the destinies of the deceased through acts such as offerings, and the means for liberation. 64.
Also the Nārāyaṇa-bali, the story of Dhanvantari, the birth of Soma, the abduction of the preceptor’s wife, and the birth of Budha. 65.
The account of Divodāsa, including Dhanvantari’s three births;
Śambhu’s abandonment of Vārāṇasī, and the obstacles encountered by Divodāsa. (66)
The conduct of the Yoginī, the Sun, the Creator, and the illustrious Gaṇeśa in a dream;
Viṣṇu’s instigation of atheism and the destruction of the king’s majesty. (67)
The seven-day recitation of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, the consecration of Viśveśvara, and the increase of the king’s devotion. ||68||
In the assembly of Indra, there was the insult of his preceptor Durvāsas, as well as the insult to the garland; this led to the decline of Śrī’s fortune and the churning of the ocean. (69)
The origin of the jewels for the sake of the nectar, the deception of the Daityas, and thereafter the battle between the gods and the asuras, followed by the application of the mantra to Pārvatī.
The vow for the sake of a son, the vision of Kṛṣṇa, the birth of Kārttikeya, and his appointment as the commander-in-chief of the gods' army. ||71||
The destruction of the demon Tāraka, also known as the narrative of Tāraka;
the journey of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of alms, and also the birth of Gaṇeśa. ||72||
The destruction of the head, the restoration of Gaja’s head, and worship—these are the results of Saturn's aspect upon Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya. (73)
Also, the circumambulation of the earth, the marriage at Mallikārjuna, the manifestation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and the service to one's parents. (74)
The acceptance of Vaiṣṇava initiation from Śambhu, even if it is already accepted;
the merit of marking with the heated discus (taptacakrāṅkana); the meanings of the mantras; and the sectarian marks (tilakas). (75)
The names of the abodes and a description of the abode of the Supreme Brahman;
likewise, a description of the Imperishable (Akṣara) and a description of Goloka. ||76||
The description of the abodes such as the gate-towers (gopura) and the noble ladies;
the narration of Mahāvaikuṇṭha and the description of the sevenfold manifestations (saptavyūha) and so forth. ||77||
There is a description of the male and female servants, the mansions, and the attendants;
and a description of the second Vaikuṇṭha situated upon the waters. (78)
The third is the description of Śvetadvīpa along with its glories;
likewise, the fourth is the description of Vaikuṇṭha situated in the Ocean of Milk. ||79||
Likewise, the prevention of Śambhu’s apprehension regarding his smearing with ashes;
the birth of the demon Hayagrīva; and the incarnation as a fish.
The supporting of the boat, the destruction of Hiraṇyākṣa by the Boar, and the expulsion of both Jaya and Vijaya from Vaikuṇṭha. (81)
Then follows the re-establishment of the earth in its proper place by Vārāha,
the penance of Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the granting of a boon by Rudra.
Then there was the enmity of Prahlāda, followed by the manifestation of Nṛhari;
then the destruction of Hiraṇyakaśipu and the protection of Prahlāda. ||83||
On Mount Raivata, there is the majesty of Vāmana, the circumambulation, the sacrifice of Maya-rāja, and various sacred fords (tīrthas). 84.
Also [the account of] Aditi’s performance of austerities, the birth of Vāmana, his request at Bali’s sacrifice, and the granting of the three worlds to Indra. (85)
The milk-vow, the story of Mṛgīkuṇḍa, and the birds;
the ritual for sacred sites (tīrtha), various vows, and the narrative of Indreśvara. ||86||
The greatness of Śivarātri and other [festivals], as well as the Mandara and other Āgamas; the visiting of many sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) and the worship of Mahālakṣmī. ||87||
The origin of misfortune and those places where it dwells,
as well as the fact that Hari resides on the twelfth day and the worship of the abode of Lakṣmī.
The birth of Revatī and her marriage with Durdama, as well as the birth of Revata again in the house of Kṛtavāk, [are told]. (89)
Furthermore, the birth and marriage of Revatī with Balarāma,
as well as the fruits of performing śrāddha and other rites at the Dāmodarakuṇḍa tīrtha, [are described].
In this [chapter], there is the manifestation of all the abodes for the brahmin devoted to his wife,
as well as the commencement of the Śrāddha rite by the two Nārāyaṇas.
The holy sites of Vastrāpatha, the origin of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, and the manifestation of Hari as Mohinī for the sake of destroying the demons Madhu and Kaiṭabha. (92)
The manifestation of Kātyāyanī for the purpose of destroying the demon Mahiṣāsura, and her birth from the seed of Brahmā as previously described by the great sages, [have been told]. (93)
The birth of Satī, the birth of Dakṣa, and again the birth of Nārada; the birth of Śumbha and Niśumbha, and the births of Kālī and Cāmuṇḍikā. (94)
The destruction of Raktabīja and the others, as well as the emergence of the army of the Goddess; the slaying of Śumbha and his followers, and the festival marking the manifestation of Satī. (95)
The manifold birth of the hosts of cowherds and cowherdesses, the various origins of the goddesses, the emergence from the forehead of Śambhu’s enemy, and the performance of penance by Satī; 96.
The marriage, the birth of the Vālakhilyas and others, and even that of the Creator; the construction of the city on Kailāsa, and Śiva’s self-surrender.
At Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the curses of the twice-born became true, resulting in his destruction;
Vīrabhadra brought about the ruin of the sacrifice, and Dakṣa indeed performed penance. 98.
Śambhu’s wearing of ashes and bones, the birth of Pārvatī, and these three daughters of the Pitṛs—Menā, Dhanyā, and Kalāvatī. (99)
Their daughters were Śivā, Sitā, and Rādhā, the beloved of Hari;
there was also the festival of Kālī’s mantra and the description of Pārvatī’s virtues.
Then follows the penance of Pārvatī, the origin of Maṅgala,
and likewise the manifestation of Śambhu in the form of a bull within the cow of Goloka.
