From the virility of Brahmā came Brahmavīrya and also Brahmasaras;
and from the virility of Śambhu, through the medium of Vāyu, Hanumān emerged.
Śanaiścara, Pannati, Kāmadāha, Varas, Gaurītapaḥ, Śaṅkaradarśana, and Gṛhagati. 103.

The dancing of Śambhu, the reviling of Śiva, the determination of the auspicious moment for the marriage, the auspiciousness, the beauty of the pavilion, the letter, and the procession of the bridegroom. (104)
The cessation of Menā’s grief, the honoring of the bridegroom as well, the worship of the family deity, and the arrival of Śiva at the pavilion. || 105 ||
Then followed the marriage of Kālikā, after which Gaurī was born; then the falling of the Liṅga and the manifestation of the twelve Jyotirliṅgas. || 106 ||
The greatness of the worship of the Guru and other topics, the origin of the Sandhyā and the Pitṛs, the birth of Nārada from gold, and likewise his status as the son of a Gandharva. 107.
Death and the gift of life, the state of being a Vaiṣṇava and likewise death, the rebirth of Nārada, and the sage’s journey to Kailāsa. (108)
The knowledge of Brahman from Śaṅkara, the sage’s journey to Badarī, and the holy sites of Mārkaṇḍeya which are the cause of his long life. 109.
The holy sites beginning with Pañcaśilā, as well as Somakuṇḍa and others,
and the auspicious tirthas such as the place of Urvaśī’s birth.
The marriage of Nārada, as well as the description of the lineage of Agni, the enumeration of the progeny of Kaśyapa, and the description of the beginnings of the Kalpas. || 111 ||
The religious practices of the Kali age, then the description of the countries of Ānarta, Saurāṣṭra, and others;
the description of Dvārakā and the description of the Gomatī river and other sites;
the narrative of King Nṛga, and the stationing of Durvāsas upon the chariot.
The greatness of Gopītaṭāka and the holy sites such as Brahmakuṇḍa. (11.3)
The destruction of the Daitya Kuśādi, the sites of the principal queens,
the worship of Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the liberation of Somaśarman’s ancestors.
The Śaṅkhapiṇḍāraka Tīrtha, the confluence of the Godāvarī, the destruction of sins by Vajralepa, and the narrative of Māyānanda. 1.15.
The Trispṛśaikādaśī, as well as the destruction of the Daitya Uraṇa and other such [observances],
the Unmīlanī, the Pakṣavardhā, and the vows of others as well.
And likewise, there are the accounts of Svarṇāṅgada, Vaiśvānara, Luṃbhaka, Ketumān, Kapilā, and the two Gāndharvas.
The victory of Paraśurāma, the story of Dhātrī, the story of Medhāvin, the story of the two Lalitas, and the proclamation of the rescue of Varūtha and other deeds. || 1.18 ||
The liberation of Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, as well as the release of the locusts;
the narrative of Kratu, the narrative of Hemamālin, and the ordeal of Vāmana.
The great accomplishment of the Śrāvaṇas, the attainment of desires through Rati,
the narrative of Purūravas, and then the story of Hariścandra.
The account of Māndhātṛ, the penance of a Śūdra, and the destruction of Dharma;
likewise, the story of Candrasena and the narrative of Vedaśiras. (121)
The story of Indrasena and Candrabhāgā, the liberation of the Caṇḍāla, the Kṛcchra penances, and the increase of Śākaṭāyana’s prosperity. || 1.22 ||
The transition to the state called Akṣara occurs through the Puṇḍarīka and Kumudvatī [observances],
as well as through the Udyāpana rite and many other Pratipad-vratas.
The vows of the second, third, and fourth [days], as well as the vows of the fifth, the sixth, and those which are the vows of the seventh; 124.
Also the vows of the eighth, ninth, and tenth [lunar days],
as well as the vows of the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth.
The vows of the fourteenth, the full moon, and the new moon;
the swing-vow (dolāvrata), the chariot procession (rathayātrā), the month of Dhanus, and the spring season (vasantaka). || 1.26 ||
The transit of the sun, the Holi festival, the flower swing, the autumnal festival, the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow, and the narrative of Sumati.
The vow known as Haripañcaka, the various Vāra-vratas, the narrative of Rukmāṅgada, and that which is called Viddha, performed by Mohinī; || 1.28 ||
Then follows the lamentation of Yama and the birth of Mohinī; [then] Rukmāṅgada’s becoming her husband and the speech that caused the breaking of his vow. (129)
Then follows the offering of the head and other acts by his son named Dharmāṅgada;
afterwards, the cremation of Mohinī, and also her attainment of the state of a Viddhā-tithi.
Following that, [it describes] the greatness of the vow and the gift during the month of Puruṣottama at Badarī, as well as the exclusion of the intercalary month (malamāsa) from that occasion. (131)
The syllable, the abode, the goal, the Supreme Person, and the immeasurable—this is the fruit of the third arcā; the vow of the fourth [arcā] was established by Ramā. 1.32.
Śāradā indeed became the wife of Śrī Hari by virtue of the Pañcamī vow; Menā became the mother of the fortunate Umā, and the Īśvaras [attained their lordship] through the Ṣaṣṭhī vow. 123.
Śambhu, Rāma, and Kṛṣṇa, the supreme lords, became his sons-in-law; these sovereign masters became the husbands of Pārvatī, Sītā, and Rādhā.
Through the Saptamī vow, Śrī Gaṇeśvara attained success and wisdom,
as well as his husband, who is indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Goloka.
Due to the observance of the Aṣṭamī vow, there is always a residence for him in the presence of the gods, amidst an ensemble of musical instruments such as bells, conchs, and drums. 136.
Through the vow of the ninth day (Navamī), there is the worship of fire and gold;
through the vow of the tenth day (Daśamī), there is always the descent of Hari upon the earth.
Through the Ekādaśī vow, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were born from Mūrti;
through the Dvādaśī vow, Sāvitrī indeed obtained Brahmā.
Through the observance of the Trayodaśī vow, Jayā, Lalitā, and Pārvatī joyfully obtained the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa as their husband.
From the vow of the fourteenth day, Lakṣmī and Māṇikī obtained as their husband the Lord Ādya Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmin.
From the Pūrṇā-vrata, Narāyaṇa is the husband of both the beloved and the auspicious woman;
from the vow on the first lunar day (pratipad) of the other fortnight, he becomes the thousand-eyed one.
For by the vow of the second [lunar day], King Sarvahuta attained the auspicious Vairāja state of Īśvara; thus she is called Ṛtambharā. 142.
In the [first] birth, the two deities were Parameṣṭhin and Gāyatrī;
from the vow in the third [birth], they were Brahmā and Savitṛ, as well as Nṛpati.
Bhūriśṛṅgā and her wife became known as Sūrya;
by performing the Caturthī vow, Samit became the king of Pīyūṣa.
By performing the Pañcamī vow and likewise giving gifts of wealth, King Vasudāna became possessed of twenty-seven wives along with the Moon.
And his wife, Rādhyā, became golden;
both were formerly born on Mount Devayava through the practice of the Ṣaṣṭhī-vow.
Together with their two wives, they attained the station of Mahendra in heaven;
indeed, by performing the Saptamī vow, Sandhyā became Arundhatī.
Twofold twilight has arisen; it is the course of desire in youth, resulting from the performance of the eighth-day vow in the virtuous household of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama was born as the son of Kambharā Lakṣmī in the palace of King Śatamakha, due to his performance of the Navamī vow.
From Dyudharṇā were born Rāmāditya and Narāditya;
and from Vikuṇṭhā, by virtue of her performance of the Daśamī vow, [the sons] were born in their true form.
In former times, there were six forms of Śrī and four Vaikuṇṭhas;
even by means of the Ekādaśī vow, the ant attained the state of the ten Pracetas.
The daughter of the tree became his wife, resplendent with a body like that of Brahmā;
through the performance of the Dvādaśī vow, Jyeṣṭhā became the beloved of Hari in three forms.
By the vow of the thirteenth day, Sudughā became beloved by five husbands;
through the vow of the fourteenth day, Dṛḍhadhanvan indeed attained liberation.
Through the performance of the Amāyā vow, there is the liberation of the miserly and other such benefits;
furthermore, one obtains a lawful wife, her sons, and [the vision of] Brahmā and the others who perceive Brahman.
Through the fulfillment of their vows, they became those who behold Hari;
this occurred in the narrative of Jālandhara, following Vṛndā’s curse upon Rādhikā.
You are the daughter of Kālanemi, and Jālandhara was born from you;
Hari, having defeated the gods, dwelt in the house of Jālandhara.
Jālandhara went to Kailāsa to take Pārvatī;
[the story of] the breaking of Vṛndā’s devotion and the destruction of Jālandhara. 157.
Vṛndā gave a curse to Dharmadeva, while Vṛndā herself became Tulasī.
Lakṣmī attained the form of Tulasī, as did the rivers beginning with Gaṅgā.
Padmāvatī became Tulasī, and Sītā was born from Kuśadhvaja.
Sudāmā became Śaṅkhacūḍa, and there was a battle between him and Śambhu.
The breaking of a Tulasī stone and Viṣṇu in the form of a Śāla stone;
likewise, the greatness of worshipping Tulasī and Viṣṇu, as well as their marriage.
Then follow the accounts of the Gaṇḍakī, Viṣṇu, and Sālaṅkāyana, as well as the Cakraka; thereafter, indeed, are the holy sites at Śālagrāma and in the field of Hari and Hara.
The Ruru-Ṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha, as well as Lohārgala and others; the majesty of Mathurā-kṣetra, and the ancient incarnation of Kṛṣṇa. (162)
The birth of Niṣāda as a king, the liberation of the Rākṣasa, the various holy fords beginning with Bhāṇḍīra, and the traversing of the forests. 163.
Then follows the destruction of the Brahmin’s sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa and other such sins through the Kapilā cow;
thereafter, the divinity of the Vārāha form, and then the installation ceremony and so forth.
The prevention of the state of being a *rākṣasa* through the bath at the Viśrāma-ghāṭa, as well as the liberation of the *ḍākinīs* and others, was performed by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (165)
Subhadra’s attainment of a son, the Gaukarṇa Tīrtha, and the divinity of the trees, creepers, and other features in the Kuṅkumavāpikā garden. 166.
The liberation of Śuka, the release of the preta through Gokarṇa, the deliverance of the Pāñcāla twice-born, and the destruction of passion for one's sister. || 167 ||
The washing away of the sins born of agitation was performed by the women of Kṛṣṇa at Dhruvatīrtha; formerly, the liberation of ten million ancestors was made into a slave [of their merit]. 168.
Nimi performed a śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules for the sake of satisfying his sons; at that śrāddha, he recounted the story of Medhātithi and manifested the ancestors.
The discourse on Naciketas, the description of the ramparts of the city of Yama,
the vision of the denizens of hell, and the fanning of the emergence of karmic fruits.
Regarding the greatness of a devoted wife, there is the story of Janaka’s wife who, in ancient times, became possessed of all prosperity; such is the narrative concerning devotion to a husband. (171)
Service to cows is service to the virtuous; through Sāvitrī, one gains the vision of the Vedas. Saramā, the protector of the cattle, consumed the Daityas by means of a curse. ||172||
Sāvitrī became the daughter in the house of Aśvapati through her ascetic penance; [this section contains] the narration of the fruits of actions and the restoration of Satyavān to life. (173)
The marriage of Padmā with Pippalāda, the curse of Dharma, the divine narrative of Mahālakṣmī, and the transformation of Nahuṣa into a serpent. 174.
Likewise, Ahalyā’s union with the lord of the Kāśis, Sītā’s dwelling in Rāma’s forest, and the destruction of Rāvaṇa and the others [are described]. (175)
The praise of the instruction on wifely devotion by Rādhikā;
also the story of the house-lizard and the narrative of Kāṣṭhilā. || 176 ||
The description of the duties of women, the protection of the forest by Hariṇī, the divine story of Reṇukā, and likewise the story of Bhārgava; || 177 ||
The marriage of Bhārgavī with Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
the story of the sage Cyavana and his marriage to Sukanyā. || 178 ||
The story of Māṇḍavya Kauśika, the rising of the sun and so forth, the marriage of Madālasā, and the instruction of his sons. || 179 ||
The self-knowledge of Alarka, his discipleship under Dattātreya,
the birth of Padminī, and likewise her marriage to Nārāyaṇa.
On Mount Veṅkaṭa is the temple of Vārāha built by Toṇḍamāna, [dedicated to] the slayer of Ṛkṣaviśvāsa and [the protector of] Dharmagupta and others. 181.
The liberation of Sumati, Bhadra, and Rāmānuja; the Jābāli-tīrtha and Tumburu-tīrtha; and the worship of Vyāsa and other rites. 182.
The prevention of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the arrival at Suvarṇamukharī, the origin of Vārāha, the penance of Āñjanī, and the paralysis of the wings [of the mountain]. (183)
The stupor of Mahendra and the others, as well as the restoration of their consciousness;
the birth of Jayantī and Devayānī, and likewise the story of Śukra, has been narrated. (184)
The restoration of Nārada to life was brought about by Mālāvatī;
likewise, the wonders of Vīrā and Prabhāvatī were proclaimed. (185)
Yama and the others were cursed and turned into stone by Śakti’s wife;
[the text then describes] the birth of Ambarīṣa and the liberation of Śrīmatī.
It is the abode of poverty, hunger, strife, and the like;
it is the exposition of the religious duty of giving away female slaves, servants, and women for sale. (187)
Devotion to the husband was maintained by the serpent-lady toward the child Kṛṣṇa Hari;
and there arose Lakṣmī and others, as well as Satyabhāmā and countless other wives. || 188 ||
In ancient times, there was the vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, as well as the penance of the illustrious Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopāla Kṛṣṇa. 189.
Then indeed the duties of the four yugas were fully described;
a new heaven was established by Triveṇī in the house of Bharadvāja.
Likewise, there is the liberation of Śabarī and Pampā through union with Rāma, as well as the marvel of Citralekhā at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. (191)
The quarrel with the Rākṣasī and the subsequent supreme liberation;
the story of Viṣṇudāsa, the Cola king, and his birth as Kaikeyī. 1.92.
The liberation of the maidens of Gokula, the union of the cowherd women with Kṛṣṇa, and the deliverance of Vīrabāhu and Kāntimatī after three births. 1.93.
The turning away from their husbands by Kālindī, Uddhava, and others;
the expedition of King Dānaka; and the liberation of the denizens of hell.
By hearing the narrative of the *Saṃhitā*, one is liberated from the state of being a *piśāca*;
by Hemantā’s devotion to her husband, she attained a kingdom and was set free.
Then follows the doghood of Patidveṣṭrī and her subsequent attainment of the state of Urvaśī; thereafter, the liberation of Alambuṣā from Vidhūma is fully described.
The warding off of Vetāla-hood from Sudarśa the Vidyādhara; the wonder of Jaratkāru’s wife; and the manifestation of Sumitrā’s power. 1.97.
Lakṣmī, the daughter of Puṇyanidhi, became a servant who increased the fortune, grace, and other blessings of Dharmadeva as he performed austerities.

The status of being the family deity (*kuladevī*) of the *gāndharva* [sages], the lineage of the Brahmins (*vipragotra*), the liberation of women, and the divine nature of trees such as the *tulasī*—[these are established]. (1.99)
In the *Suyajña-rājasūya*, there is the discernment of the ungrateful,
as well as the departure of Suyajña and his wife to Goloka.
The abduction of Tārā, the protection of Candra, the awakening to Dharma, and King Daśārha’s fitness for receiving the mantra of Kṛṣṇa. ||201||
His wife, who was pregnant, was submerged in water and brought back to life;
and the son, who was dressed as a girl, became a daughter. (202)
Through a meritorious vow, the couple obtained a son as Gaṇeśa;
furthermore, by means of ashes, the Śabara husband and wife were restored to life. (203)
Through her devotion to Kṛṣṇa, Śāradā caused the union of Kṛṣṇa and his wife; Śiva and Acyuta brought about the liberation of the courtesan.
Then follows the rescue of Bandulā, the expansion of the Vindhya mountain, Lopāmudrā’s devotion to her husband, and thereafter the pilgrimage to Kāśī and other such events. (205)
The destruction of Jamadagni, the virtuous devotion of Reṇukā, the chastity of Manoramā, and the slaying of Sahasrārjuna. (206)
Gaṇeśa’s possession of a single tusk, the protection of Gṛhapati, Suśīlā’s attainment of a kingdom, and her liberation through devotion to her husband. (207)
Even though there are many excellent signs of purity among women, Draupadī’s wearing of used clothes, her eating of leftover food, and her arrival [at the assembly] are such [signs]. (208)
The conversation between Kadrū and Vinatā concerning the horse of the Sun, as well as Vinatā’s state of servitude, was brought to an end by Garuḍa. (209)
Likewise, Līlāvatī attained liberation; Dhūtapāpā, devoted to her husband, obtained Dharma-deva as her spouse; and Kalāvatī was filled with wonder. ||1.589.21||
Through union with Kṛṣṇa, Gāndharvī went to the abode of Goloka;
through union with Kṛṣṇa, the wives of the seven ṛṣis attained divinity. (21.1)
Named Surasā, she attained good fortune through devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
and Maṇḍūkī, through devotion to Śiva, became a Gandharvī.
A pair of pigeons attained eternal liberation through devotion;
Yama [attained] the status of Dharmarāja, and Paulomī [attained] the status of being Indra’s wife. 21.3.
The birth of a son for King Abhijit, his liberation to Goloka, the marriage of Durvāsas and Kadalī, and the Kadalī tree. || 214 ||
From Ambarīṣa, he obtained fearlessness; from Vāraṇa, the service of a devotee;
and from the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the acquisition of a wife skilled in the sixty-four arts. (215)
In Kāśī, there was the wonder of Vyāsa and likewise the majesty of Pārvatī;
Agniśarman and Vālmīki also became liberated from there. (216)
In Avantī, there was even mental dejection in Lakṣmaṇa;
yet the wives of the sages, though touched by fire, were indeed purified by the Pañcamī vow.
The auspicious account of Vyāsa’s birth from Narmadā, his devotion to his wife, and so forth; and how the three gods attained the state of being sons through Anasūyā’s perfection of asceticism. (218)
The liberation of Puruhūta, the slaying of Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and the destruction of Indra’s pride—all these were performed by Lomaśa. (21.9)
The shattering of Dhanvantari’s pride, the liberation of Aṣṭāvakra, the transformation of Kalaśa into a tiger, and his subsequent liberation through the power of the cow; 1.589.220.
The liberation of Śarmavatī and the deliverance of the leper Brahmin;
Mādhavī’s becoming the wife of Kṛṣṇa, and the wonder of Śāṇḍilī. || 221 ||
There is also the worship of sandals for the mother, the elder sister, and the daughter;
likewise when the elder brother has been consecrated to the kingdom, or during a drought and a fire. (222)
The fire for the meat-offering performed by Viśvāmitra vanished;
there were also the curses upon the elephant, the fish, and others, as well as the miracle of the goat-herd. ||23||
The obstruction of Rohiṇī by Śani for Daśaratha, and the sixty-eight holy sites offered by Damayantī. 224.
The Brahmins accepted the gift and descended from the sky;
such was the marvel of Bhadrikā, the story of Karṇotpalā. 225.
The wonder of Yājñavalkya, the story of the personified dwelling, the marvel of the full moon, and the enchantment of the long pond. ||226||
Through Phalavatī, the state of being a Yoginī was attained by the son of Vyāsa;
through Tilottamā, the five-facedness of Śambhu is said to have arisen. (227)
Then, through the ascetic power of Viśvāmitra, his status as a Brahmarṣi was attained;
likewise, the origin of the Sābhramatī river and the birth of Pippalāda occurred. 228.
The auspicious Pañcapiṇḍikātmagaurīvrata bestows good fortune;
likewise, at the sacrifice in Hāṭakeśvara, the status of a Brahmin was attained by Gāyatrī. ||229||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa arrived there, as did the Rākṣasa Viśvāvasu,
the assembly of the sixty-eight Mothers, and the family deities.
The liberation of the princess and the brahmin’s daughter through the power of Kṛṣṇa;
the divine play, the serpent-river, and the liberation of the brahmin’s daughter. (231)

Brahmā was cursed by Mohinī; though pure, he was born as a eunuch in the waters of the Nāganadī, and his liberation occurred through initiation by Hiṅgulāja. Likewise, the pride of Śambhu was destroyed, and Andhaka was slain by Hara.
Also the story of Indradyumna at Lomaśa’s hermitage; the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; Nārada’s knowledge of the Vedas;
the divine birth and the ancient origin of Lomaśa’s Brahma-lore. ||233–234||
The knowledge of Kapila, his lack of rebirth in a single form;
Vasu’s becoming a Dharma-fowler and the liberation of Raibhya of Vaiśāla;
the miracle of Āvaṭya and the description of the fruits of dreams and so forth. || 235 ||
The disappearance of the sun and moon along with its cause, the outbreak of disease,
and the greatness of Jayantī as proclaimed by Sanatkumāra; furthermore, the battle between Durjaya and Gauramukha for the sake of the jewel (236–237).
The knowledge of Vedānta was also declared by Mahātapa,
and the preeminence of Kuṅkumavāpikā was proclaimed by Śambhu to Pārvatī;
furthermore, there is the arrival of the inhabitants of Kailāsa on the Jayantī day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
At Raivata, Somanātha, Talaśyāma, and Prabhāsaka;
at Uṣṇagrāma, the holy sites (tīrthas) of Siṃhamukti are likewise proclaimed;
and at Nyaṅkumatī, Devikā, and Rāṣṭraka, there are the holy sites of the Sun.
And Cyavana, Agasti, Vaiśālabhadra, Aśvatīrthaka, as well as Guptaprayāga, Unnata, Bhīmanātha, and others. 241.
Dvārikā, Camatkārapura, and Arbuda as well;
the divine presence of Agastya, the Maṅkaṇaka-tīrtha, and other sites on Arbuda. (242)
The Narmadā, the Ṛkṣaka mountain, the various holy sites such as Kanyābheda, the confluence of the Matsyā and the Tāpī, and likewise other confluences as well. || 243 ||
The holy sites of Bilva, Āmraka, and others; the liberation of Satyatapas;
as well as Amarakaṇṭaka, Jāleśvara, Oṃkāra, and so forth. (244)
The gift of the cow, the liberation of Candrasena, the release of Gālava, the confluence of the Eraṇḍī, and the description of the liberation of Dhundhumāra and others. ||245||
The states of happiness, suffering, and so forth; the praise of Kārtika and other months;
and the praise of the Narmadā river through examples such as Mucukunda. ||246||
The birth of the brahmin named Somaśarman from a Niṣāda woman through illusion; the wonder of Raibhya; and the transformation of Nakula into gold. (247)
Yajñatīrtha, Śuklatīrtha, Bhṛgukṣetra, and others; initiation into the Bhāgavata path; and the copper-colored complexion of Guḍākeśa and Asura. 248.
The offenses against worship and their pacification; the story of the jackal and the vulture; the liberation of the wagtail; and the fruits for one who serves [the teacher]. ||249||
The destruction of Nalamegha, the confluence of the oceans, and other such events,
as well as the sacred narrative of the Nīla mountain in the holy field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
The divine nature of the banyan tree, the liberation of the brahmin and the kṣatriya, and the direct vision of Indradyumna and his journey to the city. ||25.1||
The narrative concerning Bilveśa and others, the completion of the sacrificial bath (avabhṛtha) and other rites, the consecration of the images, and the construction of the temple. ||25 2||

In that regard, there is the arrival of Brahmā, the establishment [of the deity], the construction of the chariot, as well as the manifestation of incarnations and so forth, and processions, festivals, and the like. ||25.3||

The stories belonging to the lineage of those who have performed worship and other rites for the speaker of the text have been told in brief; as well as other secondary and intermediate narratives. (254)
For there exist numerous narratives and sub-narratives that, by their very nature, bestow dharma, artha, kāma, and even liberation. (255)
Indeed, there exist [cities] concealed by former kalpas, upakalpas, and so forth, belonging to sages worthy of honor, ascetics, and likewise to kings. ||256||
And for maidens, children, women, and devoted wives; for holy men, trees, creepers, sacred fords, and likewise rivers. ||257||
Indeed, various narratives concerning gods and others, as well as beasts, birds, and rākṣasas, have been recounted incidentally in the course of the discussion. ||258||
The endeavors of the gods for the destruction of the asuras have been described, as well as the divine stories of the liberation of sinners through the grace of the gods. (259)
Many such [stories] have been told here, both those pertaining to the Vedas and others of that kind; they shall be fully understood by the recitation of these chapters. (1.589.26)
The wonders of the accounts of the sacred fords (tīrtha) and the intermediate instructions will be understood in their entirety through the examination of their respective sections. ||26.1||
The number of waves in the ocean cannot be counted; likewise, the enumeration of the subjects within this compendium is beyond the power of calculation. (262)
Thus has been told this chapter on the sequence for one who has established a lineage, for the sake of easy understanding in the search for the excellent path of those various stories. (263)
By reciting, remembering, and hearing the meanings of the discourses, one shall partake in the fruit of the Saṃhitā; and likewise by the study of the Krama and Adhyāya arrangements.
The fruit of all sacred fords arises for him; the fruit of all sacrifices arises;
the fruit of all gifts and the fruit of liberation arise for him. ||265||
Whoever should perform the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) of this section within a month, for him there arises the fruit born of a thousand horse-sacrifices. ||266||
The fruit of all sacred fords shall be attained, and the fruit of all gifts shall come to pass; in every leaf, the yoga of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is described herein. (267)
By hearing this, yogins shall obtain merit born of yoga;
through this [work], the self of the listeners becomes established in the state of Brahman. (268)
What discourse could there possibly be for a speaker in that place? The speaker himself is Nārāyaṇa;
the listener there is Lakṣmī herself; and this Veda is born from the Sāman.
There are divine melodies here, indeed words in every chapter;
whoever utters them, I lead him to the supreme abode.
Just as you, Lakṣmī, are dear to me, so too is this Saṃhitā dear;
having had it transcribed, it should be preserved in one's home, for it bestows both worldly prosperity and liberation. (271)
I am divine, you are of divine form, and this Saṃhitā of mine is divine;
for it stands as the highest of all, being equal to no other scripture.
In your second form, as the essence of the Saṃhitā, you are mine;
you are to be heard with attentive mind in the pavilion adorned with archways.
She should be established upon a golden lion-throne, adorned with golden garments and the like,
and constantly worshipped with sandalwood, flowers, fruits, grains, wealth, and other offerings.

She should be worshipped with the sounds of musical instruments such as the *ārātri*, with incense, lamps, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and so forth; with the fragrances of saffron and aloe-wood, and with shouts of "Victory! (jaya).
Then one should worship Vyāsa, the beloved of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the very form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, with wealth, food, garments, and ornaments. (276)
One should satisfy him with abundant offerings of milk, ghee, sugar, and so forth;
for there is no speaker inferior to me, and at that time, my entrance there [is assured].
The words of blessing originating from the seat of Vyāsa are fruitful;
by drinking the water from his feet, heaps of sins are destroyed. (278)
By obtaining a garland of its flowers, one shall attain the prosperity of Mahendra;
by the mere sight of it, one gains the fruit born from seeing Kṛṣṇa. (279)
By the mere touch of it, one obtains the fruit born from touching Kṛṣṇa;
by the gain of serving it, one obtains the fruit of serving Kṛṣṇa. ||1.589.280||
Through divine yoga, a man or even a woman may become divine;
having performed this [practice], people will speak of it as the root of all things. (28.1)
The Vyāsas shall indeed compose treatises expanded upon this foundation;
for within them lie the ancient hearts of all things. 282.
To that great soul, the venerable Ācārya Śrī Kṛṣṇasvāmin Svarūpa, who dwells upon the seat of Vyāsa and is indeed the creator of its illumination; 283.
The king should bestow cows, horses, elephants, villages, and wealth; others as well should give according to their means whatever brings satisfaction. (284)
The merit arising from the gift of the entire universe (brahmāṇḍa) shall be obtained through the worship of the reciter.
Indeed, gardens, groves, palaces, as well as groups of male and female servants suitable for royal service, should be given to the reciter. (285)
Whatever is most dear to oneself should be given to Vyāsa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
for he has established a lineage and performs his duties at the proper time. (286)
Filled with true dharmas, he is distinguished by all dharmas; having adorned him in many ways upon the elephant vehicle and upon its head. (287)
Having honored him with yak-tail whisks, parasols, and other insignia, and having celebrated with great festivities consisting of songs, hymns, dances, instrumental music, and Vedic praises; ||288||
By the thousands, among people in villages, towns, cities, and houses; in royal capitals, in the palaces of kings, and in the private residences of merchants. (289)
He should be especially honored with the *nidhana* sections joined with the *bhāva*,
as well as by young maidens with water-pots filled with water, leaves, and fruits.
Having greeted him with a welcome and honored him with fragrant substances such as saffron, he—who is auspicious by nature—should be saluted for the sake of obtaining the boon of good fortune. (291)
By other people, together with their wives, for the sake of obtaining their own desired happiness and so forth;
by men, for the sake of wives, children, and the like; and by women, for the increase of their good fortune. (292)
For the sake of increasing the wealth of knowledge and for the attainment of health, prosperity, and so forth,
the Khaṇḍa containing the Sāntānika [mantra] should be worshipped with abundant offerings.
Then, having touched betel nut, wealth, and gold that belongs to oneself, it should be kept in one's own treasury so that it may result in the increase of wealth. (294)
Indeed, all ritual means (*sādhana*) are not equal to this;
having worshipped this peerless [image] and having carried it in procession through the excellent city, [one attains success]. (295)
The most devoted practitioners should establish [the soul] entirely and permanently in the supreme abode, the imperishable abode, the immortal, and the highest Goloka. (296)
One who desires Vaikuṇṭha, Śvetadvīpa, or the abode of Śrī shall attain them; or one may desire heaven, the kingdom of Mahendra, or even the station of Brahmā (Pārameṣṭhya). ||297||
Whether one desires the sovereignty of Vairāja or the kingdom of the Nāgas, one shall obtain it;
for I am of divine form, having manifested as the embodiment of the lineage. (298)
This [work], consisting of five hundred and ninety chapters and fifty-five thousand verses that are the very form of Keśava,
should indeed be understood as my head, for it is situated above the throat.
O Lakṣmī, my Brahmarandhra exists, and yours is here within it.
He is the pinnacle of good fortune and merit, and is in every way the source of all auspiciousness;
whoever worships you and me together shall certainly attain all their goals. (301)

Thus ends the five hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Festival for the Construction of the Mahāvedī (Altar), the Twelve Processions, the Specification of Narratives Told in the Kṛta Age Lineage, and the Majesty of the Worship of the Speaker of the Text and Others," in the first section on the Kṛta Yuga lineage of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Beyond this, O Lakṣmī, my chest exists upon your own chest;
for there resides the divine Tretā-santānaka [Tīrtha].
In the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I narrated those auspicious stories to Rādhā in Goloka during the expansion of the Tretā age. || 2 ||
In a former age, my incarnation took place together with you in Surāṣṭra on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, during its first half. However,
in Saurāṣṭra, they always recognize that [period] as the dark fortnight of Āśvina.
In the time of the first half [of that age], all of that was overturned, O my beloved.

May those who have performed their duties toward the gods, those who have protected, those who have offered devotion, those who have done what is dear, those who have established righteousness, those who have perfected the self, and those who dwell in the consecrated sanctuary, protect us. (5)

May those who are true to truth, whose goddesses are truth, who are devoted to the vow of truth, who are virtuous women, who are sustained by the inner self of truth, and who are dedicated to truth—may they protect us. (6)
He who is beyond the gaze [of the senses], who has attained a swift motion following his own self-rush, and who,
possessing the mark of *lakṣma* and assuming the designation "yuk," became twofold as Nārāyaṇa.
I am that very person who, having gone to the Ganges, became a human being and was born as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the lord of speech and the master of the Rāma-lakṣmī;
yet, though I know this, let those [words] which are well-sustained by devotion go to my own utter failure.
The Nārāyaṇas, who are full of Brahman and possess divine bodies; Śrī and the Śris;
the Īśas and the Īśanikas—the manifestation of the principles (tattva) consisting of gods, sages, ancestors, and asuras.

May these hosts of *tali* spirits, who manifest as shrines and non-shrines and exist even among the animal realm, be for the sake of my entire lineage in the rite of self-surrender (*madarpaṇa*), so that there may be mutual prosperity upon the earth. (8)

Those who are born of the Kāśyapa lineage, as well as others who have come into the touch of my hand, and those who have entered my heart— these are the objects of the blessings of me, a virtuous man.
She who, having fully endowed me with her own virtues through total self-surrender as a sacrificer,
has reached the realm of Brahman— may I lead those born of her lineage to liberation in the Imperishable.

Some worship me with collections of sacrifices; others constantly with service and the like; still others with constant remembrance; and those other than them with total surrender and self-restraints.

Red in color, pierced by my arrows of passion, and enraged with anger, O beloved, may those who dwell upon the bull [Śiva]—delighted by you—be immersed in me, the divine and eternal state, through their virtues.
Now, O Lakṣmī, bring about peace; I shall relate further stories abounding in virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, and culminating in truth. 11.
While you exist— knower of the ordinances of truth, upholder of the vow of truth,
and the very lineage of truth— it is in you that truth here reaches its fulfillment.
I am the first Vyāsa, Śvetavyāsa; I take refuge in Hari, the support of all Vyāsas, and I offer this unbroken lineage beginning with the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Hari, whose very nature is that of the Lord, is directly perceptible for the welfare of human beings;
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is eternally manifest, is truly victorious here in this world. 14.
May Śrī Hari, who is all-pervasive and whose form is manifest, be victorious forever amidst the body, the senses, the internal organ, the self, the qualities, and actions. 15.
Indeed, there are fifty-five thousand, five hundred, and twenty-seven verses in the first section. (16)

Thus ends the five hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Introduction to the Tretā Age Lineage, the Benedictions, and the Hymn," within the first section, the Kṛtayuga Lineage, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Thus ends the first section, the *Kṛtasantāna-khaṇḍa*, in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*. May this be offered unto Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī. He who was the Observer (*Īkṣaṇaka*) entered into His own dissolution, which is the creation in the form of manifestation. The Self-possessed One (*Ātmavān*), the Inner Controller (*Antaryāmī*), having assumed the designation "Yuk"—the name of the Couple (*Yugala*)—and bearing the title "Lord of Lakṣmī" (*Lakṣmapadharaḥ*), He also bears the name "Lord of Rādhā" (*Śrāyaṇaḥ*).

The Lord of Lakṣmī, the Consort of Rādhā, the Lord of Lakṣmī; when my speech is imbued with devotion, He is Kṛṣṇa, the Supporter of Kṛṣṇa, and Nārāyaṇa. Having entered the cow (the Vedic word), He alone am I for those people who bear devotion; I attain victory through their cries of "Victory! Victory! May those devotees obtain from me a double victory, a twofold triumph.
Śrī Rādhikā said: Oṃ, obeisances unto the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the ruler of the imperishable realm. 1.
Salutations to the one who is the lineage of the Tretā age, the true father, the beloved of Rādhā, the yogi, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the possessor of glory, and the bearer of the Māṇikya jewel. || 2 ||
Salutations to the one who is his own lord, whose locks are beautiful, who dwells within the self,
the sovereign of Īśā and Pāravatī, the embodiment of all qualities.
Salutations again and again to the one whose nature is the light of the swan, who is endowed with power, sovereignty, and other attributes, and who is manifest in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Repeated salutations to the inner controller, the sovereign lord of all abodes;
salutations to You, the giver of heaven, liberation, and other blessings; salutations to Śrī Hari.
Salutations to the Lord of the Imperishable, who possesses the majesty of qualities consisting of infinite and equal sovereignty, and who is served by innumerable liberated souls.
Salutations to that Lord Śrī Svāmī, who, though one, is seen as many— manifesting as Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and others, and in the forms of Īśa, Īśānī, and so forth.
Salutations to the presiding deity of the supreme knowledge, who reclines upon the beloved of Brahmā, the Lord of the Gītā-Upaniṣads, and the Lord of Jayantī. || 8 ||
Salutations again and again to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is beloved of Ekādaśī, who is cherished by worship, who is the Lord of Mahālakṣmī, and who is the Lord of devotion.
Salutations again and again to the Lord of Muktīśā, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Gaṅgā;
salutations to You, the Lord of Rukmiṇī and the sovereign of devoted wives.
You are the lord of the wish-fulfilling cow, you are the sovereign of the earth, and you are the lord of Rati;
you are the lord of prosperity and the lord of Saṃjñā—may he grant welfare to those who serve him.
O beloved of Kamalā, Lord of the Goddesses, Consort of Mohinī, Bestower of Siddhis!
O Lord of Urvaśī, Lord of Buddhi, Lord of Pārvatī—grant me peace! 1-2.
O Lord of initiation, O Master of divine play, O Lord of Nārāyaṇī, O Sovereign!
O Beloved of Virajā, O Blessed One, O Lord of Vṛndā, grant me peace! 13.
O beloved of Sarasvatī, O beloved of Svarṇarekhā, O Lord of Sitā! O Devikeśvara, O you who sport with Tulasī, grant me peace. 14.
O Lord of the Night, you are the Sovereign of Form, the Lord of Victory;
may you, the Lord of Gomatī and the Lord of Pearls, be the bestower of gold.
O Lord of the beloved friend, O Lord of the Godāvarī, O Lord of Kapilā!
O Lord of the Earth, O Lord of Svarṇagaurī, be the bestower of everything.
O Lord Laliteśvara, O Raṃbheśa, O Sovereign of Kumudvatī, O Lord Śītalādhipati, O Beloved of Umā, grant us perpetual well-being! 17.
O Hemanteśvara, Nandeśa, Śāntisvāmin, Kalāpati, Nandinīnātha, Durgeśa, and Vijayeśa, grant us peace! 18.
Lord of the twilight, lover of musk, sovereign of the fortunate, boon-granter to Sāvitrī, you who mount the swing and partake of the fragrance of flowers. 19.
O Lord presiding over Savitrī, O Sovereign of Citralekhā, homage be to you!
O Brahmā, presiding over the full moon, O Beloved of Śāradā, O Mādhava!
O Lord of Mañjarī, beloved of the circle of Yoginīs, grant me peace!
O Lord of the Beloved, Lord of the Auspicious, Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, Consort of Aruṇā! ||21||
O Lord of Joṣṭrī, O Lord of Śabarī, O Lord of Pampā, O Lord of Gālavī,
O Lord of Yājñasenī, O Lord of the Earth— may victory be yours!
O Keśava, protector of Padmāvatī, you who are easily milked like a cow;
O Acyuta, best of lotuses, you who took the hand of Bhārgavī. 23.
O Lord of Śrīmatī, O Consort of Jaratkārvī, O Sovereign of Līlāvatī!
O Life-giver of Kalāvatī, O Lord of Kadalī—may victory be yours! 24.
O Lord of Kāntimatī, O Lord of Kālindī, O Lord of Revā, O Master;
O Lord of Vardhinī, O Lord of Sumitrā, O Lord of Puṇyanaidheyikā! || 25 ||
O Lord of Bandula, O Lord of Suśīlā, O Lord of Mānasa, O Janārdana!
O Śarmavatīśvara, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Mādhavī—salutations be unto you!
O Lord of Karṇotpalā, O Lord of Dīrghikā, O Lord of Akṣamālikā, O Lord of Udumbarī, O Sovereign of Ṛtambharā—may victory be yours! 27.
O Lord of Badarī, O Lord of Kubjā, O Lord of Haimī, O Consort of Maṅgalā!
O Lord of Mahāvedī, O Lord of Kṛṣṇā, I meditate upon You within my heart. 28.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: He who exists in the divine, imperishable abode, truly divine and well-served by infinite liberated souls;
Shining in the imperishable abode, he descended here upon the earth. ||29||
Indeed, He whose name is Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa and the Supreme Lord,
who dwells in Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha along with [His associates].
Indeed, when contemplated in the heart during the morning worship.
Thus, by means of his compassionate acts, he was born here upon the surface of the earth in the region of Surāṣṭra, in the pool named Kuṅkuma,
in the home of the virtuous Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī.
He attained the state of being the son of Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa. ||3 1 ||
Since I, though the most perfect, ancient Kṛṣṇa, became the husband of Rādhā,
and since [He] indeed became the husband of Lakṣmī;
The high-souled lord of the abode of Vaikuṇṭha. ||3 2||
From whom even the dwelling on Kailāsa arose, from whom even the abode of nectar arose;
from whom even the Unmanifest Lord arose, and from whom even Hiraṇyagarbha arose. ||3 3 ||
Śrī Badrikeśa is also born from him, as is Kṣīrodavāsī,
and Narāyaṇa, the lord of the abode known as Śveta.
From whom indeed was the Lord of Kamalā born. ||34||
O Rādhā, since even the lords of countless abodes become [servants] of Hari,
the God who is the Self, one should chant the praises of His qualities.
I speak of the Supreme Lord, O Rādhā. ||36||
You have praised Śrī Puruṣottama, who is higher than the highest, the cause of all causes,
the Lord of all incarnations, and the Ancient One.
I remember that Lord Śrī Puruṣottama. ||36||
I shall always [worship] the feet of those two hundred and sixty principal celestial women of the Supreme Lord, as described by you.
I bow to their Lord; salutations, salutations! ||37||
Having appeared before me, you were gazed upon by me together with the Supreme Lord,
and indeed Goloka, my own abode, was granted to you for your residence.
O Rādhā, salutations to you for the sake of this sport. || 38 ||
After that, he by whom Nārāyaṇa was made well-united with Lakṣmī and beheld,
was granted the abode known as Vaikuṇṭha.
Salutation to that Supreme Self, the Bestower. ||39||
Furthermore, when he beheld Satī once again, having assumed the form of Śambhu,
he bestowed upon her that abode known as Kailāsa.
Salutation to the giver of shelter, the upholder of virtues. 2.1.40.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, O Beloved, O Ocean of Mercy, O Supreme Lord, O Eternal One!
You who are known as the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, higher than the highest. (41)
Where the Upholder of Dharma indeed descended upon the earth, served by his attendants who were adorned with virtues, sovereignty, opulence, and beloved consorts. 42.
Tell me of His form, His qualities, His appearance, and even His sovereignty; likewise, tell of all His divine sports (līlās) which bestow liberation and grant the welfare of the world.
Remaining in Goloka itself, I desire to hear about that Lord,
where our birth shall take place upon the surface of the earth.
I wish to hear about that Brahmāṇḍa, that world, and that supreme, purifying place, together with all its daughters; please speak of it. 45.
The narrative of the wives of that Śrī Hari—who are his very forms, who serve him, and who are manifestations of his own nature—is for the liberation of embodied beings. 46.
He who perceives his own form does not perceive the root at all; he perceives nothing whatsoever. Therefore, O beloved, tell me about that.
"I am Māyā by nature, bearing half of your body;
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me of that Supreme Person who rests upon you. (48)
Every morning, I behold that Supreme Lord within your form—dwelling within your heart, smiling, and surpassing all. (49)
O Kṛṣṇa, tell me of that Supreme Person, white in hue, who draws my mind away from you—an ocean of beauty and form. (2.1.50)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, I shall describe Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), into whose very form millions of Kṛṣṇas like me are indeed absorbed. 5.1.
He in whose form millions of Nārāyaṇas are dissolved—such is the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Parameśvara. ||52||
For from his single hair-pore indeed arise the primordial oceans and earths,
and from his form emerge innumerable incarnations.
Infinite designations of manifestations remain merged in Hari, as do infinite worlds that abide within His sovereignty. (54)
O Rādhikā, within whose splendor the abodes such as Goloka always reside, having been brought together by Him with equal force.
O Rādhā, how can I describe that form which is directly witnessed by the eyes, from a single ray of which all manifestations arise? (56)
If even one person from his abode should come here by chance,
the entire world of Goloka would have its splendor eclipsed by me.
His one graceful wife—whether Jayā, Muktamāṇikī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, or Pārvatī—has arrived in your presence. (58)
"By his splendor, you shall be struck down by my wives' splendor;
he is such a one among all forms, possessing a form that surpasses every form. (59)
O Rādhikā, how can I describe this? It is beyond the reach of the eye and not within the range of speech—the very gem of whose crown has manifested from His own body.
He alone is capable of bestowing splendor upon all luminous beings;
I constantly meditate upon that beginningless, infallible Kṛṣṇa.
And others, residing in their respective abodes, indeed meditate upon that Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Svāmī, the Supreme Person. 62.
O Rādhā, I meditate upon Him, the ocean of great bliss, the cause of all incarnations, and the one higher than the highest. (63)
In the corner of whose single eye, in the side-glance, and in the center of the lips,
all aesthetic flavors, all desires, and all joys reside;
in whose belly, O Supreme Goddess, dwell the abodes of the Great Lords.
The arrays, manifestations, and penetrations dwell as the bases of happiness. ||65||
His qualities are indeed limitless and abide in the state beyond all comparison;
they exist in embodied form within his physical form, in the heart and other parts.
I meditate upon that Hari, whose fingernails are the creation, within whose nails resides the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), and from whose hands the lords of the world emerge.
O Rādhā, always meditate upon Him alone as the beloved even more beloved than your own lover;
He who is my beloved is indeed your beloved, the Blessed Lord, your husband. 68.
Having meditated upon Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, become a bestower of good fortune;
having served that Supreme Lord, become a possessor of unbroken prosperity.
Having worshipped and served him, become wise regarding your own true nature;
you are the imperishable abode of his mouth, while I am the supreme abode, the Self.
His dwelling is always with me; he was seen by you within me.
He alone resides in my heart, and I dwell within your heart.
O Rādhā, if you are the eternal desire residing within the hearts of all,
then you are indeed said to be composed of everything, and I too am composed of you.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is composed of mind and is beginningless, is thus described;
the one reality, the Supreme Brahman, is established in this twofold manner. (73)
Established in three ways, or four, or even infinitely, it is woven by that Divine Thread and does not exceed it. //74//
For him there is no separate existence, since he is the inner self;
yet, when distinct from the supreme abode, he is the sovereign of all.
Knowing this, one should worship and meditate upon that Supreme Lord—the Blessed One among the blessed, and the Divinity of divinities—and thereby attain him. (76)
The great sovereignty of the lords, who descends through incarnations;
the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, the protector, and the very Self of all selves. (77)
He is the creator among creators, the protector among protectors, the destroyer among destroyers, and the very object of meditation for those who meditate. (78)
The supreme goal to be attained by those seeking attainment, the consciousness of all forms of knowledge, the source of all lords, and the abode of compassion for the merciful. ||79||
He is the serene Lord of the serene, the stainless Lord of the stainless,
the pure Lord of the pure, and the divine Lord of the divine.
The supreme pilgrimage site among all sites, the highest dharma among all dharmas, the ultimate peace among all peaceful states, and the source of joy among all joys. (81)
The foremost of festivals among festivals, the most beloved among things dear, the most beautiful among lovely things, and the auspicious abode for those rich in love. (82)
Of all things to be upheld, it is the supreme object to be upheld; of the virtuous, the most excellent of the virtuous;
of ornaments, the foremost ornament; and of perfections, the highest perfection. (82)
It is the supreme morality among moralities, the highest vow among those who observe vows; it is the ultimate goal among goals, and the most cherished among all that is desired. (84)
One should contemplate the supreme truth among truths, the reality among the real, the foremost of the imperishable, and the preeminent essence among essences. (86)
The supreme essence of the Vedas, the highest of all recitations, the most excellent recipient for gifts, and the ultimate of all fire-offerings—[is this]. (86)
He is the supreme austerity among those who practice austerity, the highest sacrifice among sacrifices,
the great-grandfather of the ancestors, and the radiant Vedic wisdom of the sages.
One should worship the illustrious Puruṣottama, the most transparent essence among the pure;
the supreme Rādhā among those named Rādhā; and the highest prosperity among the prosperous. || 88 ||
One should worship Him, the imperishable substance of all riches, the eternal abode of houses,
the everlasting support of pillars, and the seed of all seeds.
He is the inexhaustible boat among boats, the inexhaustible mine among mines;
he is the fierce strength among strengths and the supreme eye among eyes.
One should always remember the Lord, the knower of all, the celibate practitioner, who is the supreme state of meditations, the pervader, and the unifier. 91.
The supreme vigor among all forms of vigor, the cultivation of all powers, the attractor of all things that attract, the sovereign lord;
the giver of refuge among those worthy of refuge, and the most patient among the patient.

One should always worship Śrī Hari, who is the very essence of fortitude and invincible heroism, as well as the supreme measure among those who are steadfast, heroic, and unassailable; He is the mother of all mothers who give birth, and the nourisher of all who sustain. || 93-94 ||
I always worship that dissolution of dissolutions, the supreme sheath of sheaths, and the self-restraint of the self-controlled, O Rādhikā—
from whom Mahākāla was born, the ordainer of all limitations. || 95 ||
For from him, through his divine play, Prakṛti and Puruṣa were indeed produced;
and because the name Mahāpuruṣa first proceeded from him, he is Vāsudeva, since he arises from dwelling [in all]. || 96-97 ||
I bow to him, my lord, who is Aniruddha because he is the progenitor, Pradyumna because he bestows nourishment, and Saṃkarṣaṇa because he draws [the world] toward himself. || 98 ||
All beings are indeed his foot, subject to Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the entire creation is like a flower in the hand of that Saṃkarṣaṇa, whose body extends beyond the creation by virtue of his grace. (99)
Indeed, the entire creation shines forth from him like the tip of a mace and its sheath.
I worship that Supreme Lord and Master of all, O Rādhikā, whose servant’s servant is even Gadādhara (Lord Viṣṇu).
By reading this, by hearing it, by remembering it, or even by speaking of it, one shall become a resident of the supreme abode; therefore, O Rādhikā, always worship Him.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Universal Sovereignty of the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, I shall describe Māṇikīśvara, which bestows peace;
for where I am, there you are, and from you comes the golden Person.
From that, Mahāviṣṇu was born, and from him Virāṭ was produced;
from Virāṭ, eight cosmic eggs endowed with the eightfold creative power were brought forth.
From the navel region of Vairāja, a stalk joined with the Creator of the Universe emerged there in the water, and the cosmic egg was entrusted to Brahmā.
One *aṇḍaka* measures fifty *koṭi*s of *yojana*s;
it is joined with a pedestal (*pīṭha*), consists of gold, is pervaded by splendor, and is a beautiful abode on the outside.
Then, by means of yoga, Brahmā fashioned the intermediate worlds,
numbering fourteen, situated one above the other.
In the center, the great mountain Meru serves as the supporting pillar;
Brahmā himself fashioned it, for it is considered the foundation upon which all other supports rest.
Just as the spinal column exists in the body, so does Mount Meru reign within the cosmic egg;
and from the body of Vairāja, the water that was produced there came forth.
From his navel, however, a lotus was born; there, Brahmā, together with his egg, developed for a full thousand divine years.
And when the water produced from himself had become his disciple, Vairāja remained for a thousand years;
for it was from that golden [egg] that Vairāja himself was born.
That golden sheath also split in two from the middle;
those two parts of the *kūrca* were born and remained in the great waters.
Just as a young bird, once fully developed with all its limbs matured,
breaks through the eggshell and emerges from it, so too does the Virāj emerge from that [embryo].
Having cast it into the water, he sleeps there while remaining present;
at that time, the two parts of the eggshell that were situated in the water become the two whiskers.
Having been cooked in water for many thousands of years while rotting,
two asuras were then produced from those two tufts of hair that had been boiled in water.
One was named Hiraṇyakūrca and the other was called Hiraṇyaṇḍa;
they possessed bodies equal to silver, yet their stature exceeded that of the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa).
Hungry, endowed with great strength and vigor, equipped with maces and armor, and firm,
they roared with loud cries, whirling their respective maces.
Churning the waters and splitting their own thighs,
they roared at all the directions and terrified even the great lords.
Then, laughing and emitting loud bursts of laughter,
they sportively looked all around at the foods there in the ocean.
And seeing their own reflections in the water and other surfaces as they ran about, they mistook them for food; thus, when it could not be obtained, they fell into despair.
Even after searching, they did not find any food produced from water;
then they approached to devour the sleeping Vairāja.
Then this Vairāja was supported by one at the head,
while he was supported by another at the feet in the midst of the water.
Then, having lifted them up from that place, both were prepared to depart;
but Vairāja beheld those two great asuras who resembled himself.
Both of those dark beings, invincible and intent on devouring him,
remembered his own progenitor, Mahāviṣṇu, the worthy refuge.
Oppressed by those two who were emaciating him, Vairāja praised them with supreme devotion; then, indeed, he struck them with maces and discuses.
He struck them with great force using his palms and fists;
nevertheless, disregarding that, they both seized him within the water.
Then, being under the control of another, that Vairāja, having become one-pointed in mind, meditated solely for the sake of his own protection upon his own father.
The lotus of Brahmā, its stalk, and the entire cosmic egg were all submerged in water there,
as if at the time of universal dissolution.
Brahmā, having fallen into fear, remembered the Supreme Lord, his own great-grandfather Mahāviṣṇu, who is golden-hued, for the sake of protection.
"O Blessed One, who are these two Daityas who bring about the destruction of the great rains?
Protect, protect us, O Mahāviṣṇu! Quickly destroy them both! (28)
Thus was Mahāviṣṇu, bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, sword, and spear, repeatedly remembered by Virāja and even by Brahmā.
Accompanied by iron arrows, mallets, tridents, and *śataghnī* weapons,
the Lord mounted a divine vehicle and approached the presence of the Daitya.
From those two fragments, two firm beings were produced by him;
desiring to slay their son, Vairāja, who was reclining upon the waters.
A sound was produced by that powerful Viṣṇu;
having pervaded the worlds of Īśa, that resonance filled Goloka.
Then he who awakens the battle completely pervaded Vaikuṇṭha and the unmanifest abode (avyākṛta-dhāma) on all sides,
as well as the abode known as Amṛta.
O King, the powerful Saṃkarṣaṇa, hearing that sound and realizing it was a battle, meditated for a moment for the sake of protecting the universe. || 34 ||
For the protection of Vairāja, Mahāviṣṇu, and Brahmā, he—possessing a divine body and equipped with a divine mace—went forth as soon as he was remembered. (35)
In that [waters], Mahāviṣṇu, Virāṭ, and even the two Daityas remained;
there Mahāviṣṇu [is] the protector of creation and the destroyer of the wicked-souled.
Having prostrated, he offered praise and requested protection;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa assumed a terrifying form.
At that time, he possessed ten thousand arms,
and his topknots extended upward, pervading the entire realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Ten thousand of his feet sank into the great waters;
even below the tortoise, there are millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) in the midst.
Those stones and weapons became like balls for him;
having hurled them with his hands, they struck against one another like cosmic eggs.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others indeed fought with the two Asuras;
many cosmic eggs were destroyed as they hurled them at one another.
Being struck by maces, those [eggs] then shattered like powder;
and the Daityas likewise took up those very eggs.
They both hurled their firm maces at Mahāviṣṇu and Saṃkarṣaṇa;
but Saṃkarṣaṇa struck them down as well with his own mace.
Thus a terrible battle took place between those two in the path of the sky;
then, having leaped up, Mahāviṣṇu struck Hiraṇyakūrca on the forehead.
Struck on the head by Hiraṇyāṇḍa, he fell into a swoon;
struck with a mace, Saṃkarṣaṇa was filled with rage.
In his rage, he struck Hiraṇyāṇḍa with his mace upon the surface of his golden egg-shell;
Hiraṇyāṇḍa fell unconscious for a moment, but then rose again.
And as soon as he had become composed, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa struck Hiraṇyakūrcaka in the chest with his mace.
His heart was indeed shattered and he died from that single mace-blow;
then Hiraṇyāṇḍa struck Mahāviṣṇu on the head.
Mahāviṣṇu, having leaped up, struck Hiraṇyāṇḍa;
he, having leaped up, fled with Saṃkarṣaṇa upon his back.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa struck that asura with his mace;
the asura also then struck him back with his mace.
Accepting that blow,
he let out a loud roar and whirled his mace in the sky until it resembled the ten-fold universe.
Mahāviṣṇu hurled that [gada] which had been released by hand with the intent to kill Saṃkarṣaṇa, and he struck that gada in its midsection with his own gada.
That mace shattered there in the water and indeed broke into a hundred pieces;
yet Sankarshana, still holding the mace, rushed toward the asura.
The Asura, for his own protection, seized the great cosmic egg consisting of fifty-six stars and hurled it toward Karṣaṇa.
At that time, that [object] belonging to Saṃkarṣaṇa was reduced to powder by the mace;
thereafter, running forward, he seized another great egg.
Struck by the mace of Mahāviṣṇu, it shattered into a hundred pieces;
thereafter, he ran with that third egg in his hand.
Having seized it, he quickly hurled it into the heart of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
though it struck his heart, it pierced through and was indeed reduced to powder.
Then the lord god Saṃkarṣaṇa, enraged, desired to kill with his mace that destroyer of creation who was indeed breathing there. ||58||
Saṃkarṣaṇa pursued the Daitya’s back in the great waters,
while the Daitya also fled, clutching the cosmic egg that was nearby.
That which is situated upon the Brahmā-stalk, together with its covering, Mount Meru, and the shell of the cosmic egg, all of which abide within the lotus along with Brahmā; ||2.2.60||
Having seized the entire earth out of fear of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
he fled through the path of the sky, and Saṃkarṣaṇa then pursued him.
Then the Asura entered the depths of the great waters;
and Saṃkarṣaṇa, following closely behind him, likewise entered the water.
And while the great asura was being seized by Saṃkarṣaṇa by the hair,
he then assumed a subtle form within the vast waters.
Indeed, out of fear and from the exhaustion of battle, being deprived of assistance,
he entered the eightfold enclosure and went into the interior of the cosmic egg.
There, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the master who assumes a subtle form,
having taken Brahmā with him, arrived in a mere moment.
He established Brahmā in Satyaloka, on the highest plane;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa assumed a fierce form as a matter of sport.
Then Mahāviṣṇu indeed assumed a subtle form of Viṣṇu;
and those three [gods] who dwell within the cosmic egg were likewise there.
They searched for the Asura who had become invisible on Mount Meru;
Hiraṇyāṇḍa, having assumed the form of an egg, was stationed upon the waist of Meru.
Even though he was being sought, Viṣṇu could not be seen by the body at that time; Viṣṇu then employed his yogic power and beheld him with his form concealed.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa-Rudra, assuming a subtle atomic form, took hold of the great hermitage which was situated in a hidden part of Merukaṭyā and was filled with fear.
Then, by means of the yoga-weapon, he entered the flank of Mount Meru and seized that great Daitya, who was living in concealment.
There, by means of his illusory power (māyā), the asura quickly became massive;
then, he emerged from the hand of that trident-bearing Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Having circumambulated Meru, he fled;
Saṃkarṣaṇa also pursued him from behind with great speed.
Thinking that Mount Meru was his refuge, the Asura wandered like a wheel;
indeed, he performed one hundred and more such revolutions.
Then, being utterly exhausted and desiring death,
Saṃkarṣaṇa turned around and was struck by Mudgala.
And Saṃkarṣaṇa also hurled his mace, released from his hand, in order to strike the golden egg;
meanwhile, the Daitya indeed [struck] with force.
Grasping the Saṃkarṣaṇī mace, she struck Saṃkarṣaṇa;
then she fled toward Mount Meru and wandered about in fear.
Saṃkarṣaṇa followed behind him wherever he ran;
grasping his mace, Saṃkarṣaṇa struck him on the back as well.
As they were thus rushing forward, an earthquake of Mount Meru occurred, as did a tremor of the earth,
the seven worlds, the heavens, and even the nether regions.
Making the earth tremble with his footsteps, the clashing of his mace, and his roars,
Saṃkarṣaṇa took that mace and fled.
Saṃkarṣaṇa took up the golden club of Mahāviṣṇu;
with their clubs, the two of them fought each other upon the slope of Mount Meru. 8.1.
From the striking of the two clubs, Meru, the king of mountains, was shaken;
all the sides of Meru were agitated on every side. (82)
An earthquake, a shaking of Mount Meru, and a trembling of its peaks occurred;
for when the striking of Meru’s waist proceeds fruitlessly, [such portents arise]. (83)
Then a fragment of Meru’s waist repeatedly breaks apart;
thus, through this state of disintegration, fire arises there from friction.
The forest fire of the world, having arisen, blazed indeed unto the heavens;
its rays were streams of flames produced from the impact of the mace. ||85||
Then, as far as the rim of the cosmic egg extended all around,
it, along with the celestial chariots of the gods, blazed up on every side.
Mahāviṣṇu extinguished the fire with nectar, and a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among all the inhabitants of the worlds.
Then, by the blows of the mace, fragments from the sides of Meru fell separately into the sky on all sides, struck and dislodged.
Some are eighty thousand yojanas long, some ten thousand yojanas;
others are twenty thousand yojanas, and others twice that. (89)
The segments are twenty-five thousand, thirty thousand, forty thousand, and likewise others in yojanas. (2.2.90)
Some then became sixty thousand yojanas in length,
while others were fifty thousand yojanas long.
Indeed, those eighty-four thousand [peaks] became elongated;
thus the black-colored mountains were split apart all around Meru. 92.
In the lower region of the heavenly world, some fragments fly up into the atmosphere; some remain in the water, while others indeed exist in the wind.
By means of attraction, indeed, all were drawn upward according to their respective positions;
then all the planets became like stars, and likewise the comets.
On the southern side of Meru, he struck the great asura Hiraṇyāṇḍa;
it then fell upon his chest, his side, and his head.
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa struck him with his mace,
hitting him repeatedly with various blows from that mace which was as heavy as the vital breath itself.
The southern portion of the earth split apart and flowed downward from Meru; it is a region measuring one hundred thousand *krośas*, filled with salt waters. (97)
Wherein there are Haima, Māhendra, Urala, and Āmrakācala;
also the king of mountains Abrikta, and other mountains as well that are present. 98.
By means of the yoga of constant attraction, situated beneath that in the atmosphere are the Uttarakurus, the Kimpuruṣas, and the Pradeśakas. (99)
Likewise, there are regions named Nara in the southern salt water;
and in that western part, there are indeed the regions called Āvṛktas.
The islands situated in the midst of the salt ocean are ten thousand yojanas [in extent];
others are one thousand yojanas; and still others are thousands more, but very small.
Those three southern regions are equal in extent to Meru in their fullness;
the salt-water ocean extends for sixty thousand krośas.
Measuring forty thousand *krośas* across its terrestrial portion,
the planet thus came to be one hundred thousand *krośas* in extent within the intermediate space.
There, due to the alternating succession of water and land over time,
the central oceanic regions were repeatedly overturned by the force of time.
Water becomes land, or water on land; a forest becomes a house, or a house a forest.
Thus, indeed, through the passage of time, such transformations arise upon the earth.
In the midst of the continents, oceans arise through the conjunction of time;
the water and the food-like [earth], resembling the navel of Brahmā, subsequently separates them individually.
The Siṃhāraṇya [region] is submerged in water and is separated from the unopened [area]; Śukla Kurus is submerged in water, as is Uttara Kinnarīyaka. 107.
He divides the land of Kiṃpuruṣa into the regions of Rāśanī and Jāpanī;
in the middle are the low-lying excavated lands and the intermediate districts.
In this world, within the golden terrestrial sphere, they distinguish [the regions] where Nara and Nārāyaṇa shine upon the Himālaya mountain, O beloved.
Therefore, O Rādhā, in this land of Cānarta, which is like a jewel to me, in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in Saurāṣṭra, there is Puruṣottama.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, the boy Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd, manifested as the source of the auspicious Lakṣmī Kambharā. || 11 1 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Lord;
go there, O beloved Rādhā, and become Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇī.
By serving Him who gave you away and to whom you belong, you shall obtain happiness.
Furthermore, by his permission, you shall go again to my abode, Goloka.
The golden egg, having perished on Mount Meru by the hand of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
that golden earth indeed came forth from within the middle of the egg.
And the one named Hiraṇyakūrca died in the water outside the Lokāloka mountain; from his body, the earth there became golden.
Thus, O Rādhā, this ancient narrative of the earth has been told to you for the sake of conviction and for the purpose of providing knowledge regarding the cosmic egg.
It was there, in that sphere which is the abode of Nara-Nārāyaṇa, that the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, manifested himself.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Two Asuras, Hiraṇyakūrca and Hiraṇyāṇḍa—born from the tuft of hair on the Cosmic Egg—and the Presentation by Śrī Kṛṣṇa of Himself to Rādhikā, Occurring within the Extensive Genealogy of the Lord of the Imperishable Supreme Abode in the Second Section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. || 2 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, I shall relate divine and captivating stories filled with the bliss of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 1.
Having created countless worlds of the lords and even millions of Vairāja realms, the illustrious Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign, [remained]. (2)
There are always crores of Bhūmans and also crores of Sadāśivas;
indeed, the number of Brahmāṇḍas is truly neither found nor even conceivable.
The gods, Daityas, and Rākṣasas; the Munis, Ṛṣis, virtuous men, and virtuous women;
the suns, moons, planets, Nāgas, mountains, rivers, and reptiles. || 4 ||
He [perceived] the stationary and moving worlds, the protectors of the worlds,
the abodes, the guardians of the abodes, the lords of the abodes, and the inhabitants of the abodes.
Although the Inner Controller of the Supreme Brahman has created everything— including the lords of the cosmic eggs, their protectors, and their dwelling places— he remains therein.
The Lord exists in every way, yet he remains beyond the range of vision;
as long as he does not manifest to them, so long does peace not arise.
Having reflected thus upon the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa...
These lords, the gods, indeed prayed for incarnations in their own abodes,
in the worlds, and even upon their respective lands,
so that they might behold the glorious Puruṣottama directly. Then, Śrī Puruṣottama [responded].

Even while abiding in the supreme abode, he was entreated by those dwelling in the imperishable realm; having become the sovereign of the imperishable, the two-armed Lord of the Imperishable sat upon the great lion-throne named Akṣara, manifesting in a second form.
He abides in the imperishable abode, worshipped by the Imperishable One.

The Lord of the Imperishable (Akṣarādhipa) accepts the worship, food offerings, and so forth performed by those who abide in the Imperishable and are liberated, following their meditative cultivation.
That Blessed One, possessing a divine form, shines in the imperishable abode by means of His own second form, through the desire to dwell in the imperishable.
For the sake of bestowing bliss upon his devotees and out of a desire to show grace to those who are liberated,
Puruṣottama shines forth among both the imperishable and the liberated.
Then, O Rādhā, that blessed Lord, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, was requested by me there; by my will, he shines in Goloka.
I worship the eternal Śrī Nārāyaṇa constantly;
O Rādhā, behold His eternal form in my temple. (16)
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā!
Thus I perform my recitation and I remember Puruṣottama. (17)
For my sake, for your sake, for the sake of the cowherd women, for the sake of the cowherds, and for the sake of my own abode, the Supreme Person has assumed a third form. || 18 ||
Indeed, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa resides here for the purpose of receiving the worship of his devotees who dwell in Goloka.
The Supreme Lord shines forth for the purpose of granting His vision;
He is the illustrious Blessed One Himself, assuming a fourth form. 2.3.20
In Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣottama shines, worshipped by Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; he was requested by Nārāyaṇa for the sake of worship.
He becomes a resident of that abode, bestowing bliss along with [the Lord] in the abode of Matsya, the abode of Kūrma, and the abode of Vārāha. ||22||
This very [liṅga], being worshipped, shines by itself even in the abode of Kapila, in the unmanifest abode of Hari, and in the abode of Vāsudeva. 23.
It shines in the house of Saṃkarṣaṇa, in the house of Pradyumna,
and also in the house of Aniruddha, the city of the Great Puruṣa.
In the abode of Mahākāla, in the realm of Māyā, in the dwelling of Sadāśiva, in the common abode of Viṣṇu, and likewise in the abode of Mahāviṣṇu; ||25||
He shines even in the house of Prakṛti-Puruṣa,
and he also shines in the abode of Pradhāna-Puruṣa, as well as in the splendor of the Infinite (Bhūman).
Thus, in the abode of Mahāviṣṇu, within the Vairāja-dhāma,
this Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa shines forth, having been entreated by those various beings.
That Hari exists, honored, saluted, and served by them in the worlds and the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. ||28||
Śrī Hari himself shines even upon Vaikuṇṭha, which is above the waters;
that Blessed Lord was entreated by the sages as well as by the ancestors.
The two-armed Lord shines among them, both in the worlds and in their homes;
He is the Master who is repeatedly entreated by the gods, including Indra and the others.
Likewise, he shines in the abode of Pṛthu, in the abode of Dattātreya,
in the abode of Haṃsa, in the abode of Nṛsiṃha, and in the abode of Ṛṣabha.
It shines in the abode of Vāmana, in the temple of Paraśurāma, in the temple of Yajña, in the temple of Rāma, and in the temple of Sanatkumāra. ||32||
In the world of Nārada, he shines in the hermitage of Hayagrīva;
and in the capital city of the king of kings, the Lord reigns resplendent.
It shines in the abode of Vyāsa, in the abode of Buddha, and in the abode of Īśa; it resides in the city of Varuṇa, in the abode of Kubera, and in the abode of Indra.
He shines in the abode of Yama, in the world of Nirṛti, in the realm of Anila,
in the world of Vahni, in the residence of Sūrya, and in the world of Candra.
Likewise, in the abode of Dhruva, in the residence of Śukra, in the residence of Maṅgala, in the residence of Budha, in the refuge of Bṛhaspati, and in the orb of Śani; ||36||
There, propitiated by the planets, entreated by the lunar mansions, and saluted by the stars, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent. (37)
Throughout all my islands, as well as those islands in the ocean.
And among the light-worlds, the worlds, the atmosphere, and those who dwell in the sky; ||38||
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shines even among those dwelling in the mountains,
in sacred bathing places filled with water, and even in earthly homes.
The Lord was repeatedly requested by the local residents at the shrines and sanctuaries,
and was constantly invited to their homes for the purpose of worship and for the sake of being seen.
The Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa Hari makes his dwelling in various places, abodes, residences, cities, regions, and lands. 41.
The great king appeared in embodied form, two-armed and exceedingly beautiful;
though he had reached the bloom of youth, he maintained the state of a youthful adolescent. ||42||
Becoming exactly as they are devoted, he shines forth as the bestower of bliss, both among kings in the worlds and likewise in abodes such as heaven. 43.
In the hermitages of the Vasus, in the spheres of the Ādityas, in the hermitages of the Rudras, and in the abode of the Aśvinīkumāras; (44)
In the abode of Dhanvantari, in the ocean, and also in the Milk Ocean;
on Śvetadvīpa, at Badarī, on Mount Māhendra, and on Mount Raivata. ||45||
That glorious Lord, Puruṣottama, always remains with two arms in divine fields, in forests, in woods, and even in groves.
Requested by his devotees, he has descended and shines forth even in Pātāla, in the world of Sutala, among the Nāgas, and even among the Asuras. (47)
He dwells in Atala, Vitala, Talātala, Rasātala, and Mahātala; even there, he shines resplendent, being entreated by the inhabitants of those realms.
In Bhuvarloka, Hari-Kṛṣṇa is [honored] by the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Supported by yakṣas, rākṣasas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and vināyakas,
as well as by others such as creepers, trees, shrubs, and grasses,
this Supreme Self, Hari, shines resplendent in that house, being entreated by them all. (2.3.50)
In the remaining houses—those of Kamaṭha, the Dānava, and the Daitya—the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shines, worshipped within those two dwellings. (51)
O Rādhā, the Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent in the homes of His devotees and within the hearts of His devotees. 52.
In the palaces of the pearl-necklaced women, in the dwellings of the female servants as well, in the kingdoms of the sovereign ladies, and in the residences of the goddesses; ||53||
In the palaces of devoted wives, in the hermitages of virtuous women,
in the dwellings of householders, and even in the caves of beautiful women.
It shines in the hermitages and homes of virtuous yogins,
in the hearts of maidens, and even in the dwellings of yoginīs.
The beloved husband shines resplendent in the dwellings of his mothers, in the pavilions of his friends, and upon the beds of his wives. (56)
Requested for residence in each respective world, the Lord Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, [remained] out of consideration for their desire. (57)
In order to fulfill their desires, the Supreme Lord appeared with two arms, assuming a form, character, and qualities that accorded with the aspirations of his devotees. (58)
The divine Lord, the illustrious Mahāprabhu, shines forth bearing a celestial form;
he is worshipped by all and he is propitiated by all. 59.
Everyone remembers him in the morning; everyone always worships him; and everyone entrusts to him everything that they themselves desire. (2.3.60)
Therefore, everyone desires the perfection of miraculous power and majesty;
without him, no one else's exertion can be effective.
That very [principle] is traditionally held to be present in both adversity and prosperity;
for in every creation, lords, gods, and humans are born. (62)
