During the great calamity, they prayed for the protection of the cosmic eggs;
then, for the sake of destroying their distress, he was born there.
Sometimes, out of compassion, He becomes dependent upon His devotees in the world;
for compassion is the primary cause that grants His own yoga to living beings. (64)
Through compassion, he goes to, shines upon, and becomes manifest before embodied beings;
having thus shown compassion toward all the universes, he is the Supreme Person. 65.
At the beginning of creation, he appears resembling the entire universe,
appearing sometimes in a divine form, sometimes in a ṛṣi-like form, and sometimes in a human lineage.
In some places he assumes a form at will as he moves among animals; in some places he is on land, in water, in heaven, in a shrine, in a forest, in a house, or in the expanse of the sky.
Whether in a celestial abode or in battle, he is born according to his will;
he dwells therein for the sake of his purpose, in accordance with the devotion of his devotees.
O Rādhā, where the Yamunā is, where the Gaṅgā flows, where Mount Raivata is, and where the hermitage of Nara-Nārāyaṇa is located. ||69||
Wherein the three fragments formerly resided in the split globe,
there this Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Hari, has appeared out of compassion.
In the field of Kuṃkumavāpikā and at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
he took birth in the first age in the house of Gopāla Kaṃbharā.
I was born in the house of Vasudeva, and you were born in the house of Vṛṣabhānu-kalā. ||72||
The terrestrial globe and the fragmented globes, measuring one hundred thousand *krośas* in extent, were indeed sanctified by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (73)
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the first fortnight, on the eighth day of the dark half,
the Lord Hari was born there upon the bed of Kaṃbhārī.
For the purpose of providing all forms of protection, for the attainment of all auspiciousness, and for the sake of bestowing blessings and purifying embodied beings, [I shall perform this]. (75)
When Hari, the Lord, desired to go there out of compassion,
he dispatched his own attendant Ānarta to the earth.
And he commanded me specifically for the purpose of giving him the jewel;
therefore, I presented the jewel to that high-souled Ānarta.
By him, the western region of Saurāṣṭra was made divine on earth;
there, I, Kṛṣṇa, a twice-born man devoted to his wife, was sent at that time.
Mahālakṣmī was sent forth, as was Mahāviṣṇu;
and you, O Rādhā, became the very embodiment of Mahālakṣmī. ||79||
She is a devoted wife, highly fortunate, and one who has practiced austerities for many years;
and I am Gopālakṛṣṇa by name, likewise devoted to my wife.
There, O beloved, a divine brahmin who was a promoter of the Vedas and Shastras was born;
at that time, I bestowed my seed upon Kambharā for you.
Then Kambharā bore that divine embryo, which was merely the filling of the womb and visible only as its dwelling place. 82.
In that age, creation indeed arose from mere volition; what need is there to speak of dwelling in a womb? This description by me is merely according to the conventional way of speaking. (83)
O beautiful one, Hari, who had been meditated upon there, arrived;
he took up residence in the heart of the father and within the womb of the mother. 84.
The Child granted his vision, just as one receives a blessing upon birth;
there a radiant bed appeared, and the quarters of the sky became resplendent. (85)
The principal incarnations, having assembled, respectfully rained down flowers, sandalwood, and parched grain. (86)
Then the female friends residing in every abode arrived there;
with eyes closed in ecstasy, they sang songs while being sung to by pairs of sweet-voiced singers.
The goddesses and the maidens of creation, all having arrived there, honored the Lord of the Goddesses, the Master of Brahman, the Sovereign who is the Fullness. ||88||
Having beheld the face of Hari, they, with hearts full of joy, repeatedly offered blessings to that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (89)
The lords, the world-protectors, the liberated ones, the lords of the gods, and the gods,
as well as the Apsarases from the lake of Brahmā, all arrived.
Having paid homage to the Lord, O beloved, the celestial musicians, the divine Gandharvas, the Cāraṇas, and the hosts of Kinnarīs performed a dance with great devotion. 9.1.
The Vidyādharīs arrived, as did the Gopīs and others who were liberated;
they played musical instruments and rejoiced upon beholding that Lord.
The Mānavī women, who dwell upon the earth, arrived having performed auspicious rites;
upon seeing him, they addressed that Supreme Person with gentle words. (93)
Nāginīs and other goddesses born from animal and human wombs, as well as others—both divine and non-divine—who dwell in grass and other such places, have all assembled together. (94)
Beholding their beloved, the supreme lover in the form of a child, the great Lord, they all attained bliss and honored him with uninjured [flowers]. (95)
The festival of that inquiry was magnificent and radiant everywhere;
it became renowned throughout the entire universe and in other creations as well. (96)
The Supreme Lords (Parameṣṭhins) possess infinite heads, a hundred thousand heads, ten million heads, and even hundreds, tens of thousands, and thousands of heads and so forth.
Likewise, the Viṣṇus and the Rudras, along with their wives by the millions, came to Kuṅkumavāpikā to behold the Lord. 98.
Having granted them his vision and bestowed blessings upon them, the Blessed Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa then departed happily. 99.
He indeed revealed himself to the people, abiding in the supreme imperishable abode,
possessing a divine form, situated in the highest realm, two-armed, and most excellent.
He whose nature is ten million Kṛṣṇas, who consists of ten million Nārāyaṇas, who has the form of ten million Vairājas, and who is a thousand Mahāviṣṇus. || 101 ||
He manifested before the lords a charming youth with two arms, endowed with infinite power, capability, and virtues.
And having thus displayed his divine form to Rādhā, he again showed his childhood form; the great lords (the gods) then worshipped him.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Omnipresence of Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa in All Creations through His Embodied Form and His Manifestation by Grace in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in Saurāṣṭra," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā; a very great festival has taken place there in the house of Kambharā, as well as in the homes of those residing in Saurāṣṭra.

Having learned [of this], the guardians of the universe, the world-protectors, Śiva and the others, as well as humans, gods, and goddesses, [arrived] by way of the sky in their celestial chariots. || 2 ||
All the sky-dwellers arrived for the purpose of seeing [him],
and the sky became covered with celestial, radiant aerial chariots.
In the house of Kambharā, there occurred a rain of flowers, a shower of sandalwood paste,
and indeed a rain of unbroken grains for those who had gone to the divine abode.
Then drops of divine saffron fell from the sky,
and shouts of "Victory!", sounds of musical instruments, and songs arose in the air.
Just as there is Goloka, or another Vaikuṇṭha,
or yet another unmanifest realm, or a second imperishable abode.
Likewise, the sacred field named Kuṅkumavāpī became equal to the realm of Kāma;
there, incarnations of Īśvara and the gods offered hymns of praise.
Having bowed down and performed the highest act of worship, they offered their oblations, saying:
"From whom we have arisen, and by whose sovereign power we enjoy our lordship. (8)
We bow to that Supreme Lord, who is to be governed by us at all times;
whose nature is both real and transcendent, and who dwells within all abodes.
Out of compassion for the protection of the world, we pay homage to the Lord, the possessor of Dharma, the supreme among the supreme, the child, the son of Kambharā-Lakṣmī. 2.4.10.
To you whose sovereign splendors have no end, who have manifested by contracting your own essence out of compassion—we bow to you, the Lord. (11)
We praise that Supreme Person, who bestows liberation upon all worlds, who grants the abode of light to those endowed with merit, and who grants heaven to those possessed of passion. 1.2.

Under the influence of compassion, you abide with an equal vision toward the Daitya, the Deva, the Rākṣasa, the human, and the Piśāca; toward the Nāga, the mountain, the sage, the woman, the animals, the tree, and the grass— as well as toward the Cāṇḍāla.
We pay homage to you, that best of men, whose father is the same as ours. || 14 ||
In future ages, other fields and sacred fords will indeed exist on earth;
nevertheless, they shall not truly be equal to this one.
Furthermore, the incarnations beginning with the Fish (Matsya) shall indeed come into being;
having reached this sacred field, they will dwell in your presence.
Wherever the Supreme Lord, the cause of the incarnations, resides, that sacred field shall forever be worthy of veneration among all abodes. || 17 ||
Indeed, this egg is more auspicious than all other eggs,
since within this fragment you shine as the indivisible, perfect Lord.
Even a sovereign, if deprived of your grace, is considered most wretched;
but one endowed with your grace, though lowly, acts like a king.
Without Your lotus feet, even divine ground is defiled;
but with Your lotus feet, even dark ground is radiant.
Blessed is this Lakṣmī Kambharā; blessed is Gopāla Kṛṣṇa;
blessed is the land of Surāṣṭra; and blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā. ||21||
Blessed is the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake; blessed are those trees and creepers;
blessed indeed are the men and women here, and even the insects and winged creatures. ||22||
To those women and those men who possess eternal union with Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—Victory to You, O Lord! Victory to You today! Victory, O God! Salutations be unto You! 23.
Having thus praised the Lord, O Rādhikā, they all observed silence;
then the Blessed Lord, smiling, [looked upon] those gods, goddesses, and others.
"Choose a boon," said the Blessed One, the abode of compassion.
Vakra, having prostrated before him, [requested] birth in Kuṅkumavāpikā. (25)
In the region of Kṣetra, in Surāṣṭra, where those two lotus-feet [of the Lord] reside,
the goddesses dwelling in Dhāma-dhāma likewise chose such a boon.
Taking birth as maidens, we dwell by your side;
and crores and arbuds of them have obtained [their births] in Saurāṣṭra and other regions.
And likewise, O gods, the Kumāras then became manifest;
the deities were born by mere volition in every single house. (28)
All those trees and creepers are indeed infinite goddesses;
likewise, the cows, bulls, and others—the elephants and horses—are as well. (29)
The deer and sacrificial animals then attained divine bodies;
the wish-fulfilling trees, creepers, and pillars likewise came to be.
There were always millions of wish-fulfilling gems and cows of plenty,
as well as swans, cranes, ruddy geese, cuckoos, parrots, and peacocks.
In Kuṅkumavāpikā, the deities assumed those very forms;
there were ascetics, sages, others, the seasons, and other virtuous beings.
There, among the trees and other surroundings, auspicious omens appeared on all sides;
and rivers, streams, and sacred fords took up their residence in that vicinity.
The principles (tattvas), both manifest and unmanifest, having assumed the forms of insects and moths on the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa, made their dwelling there. 34.
Gandharvas, other singers, goddesses, and daughters of the Nāgas, possessing divine bodies, joyfully took up residence there in the water. (35)
That region, Svarṇasthala, filled with jewels, attained a divine state;
indeed, whatever jewels exist in the ocean or in places such as heaven were found there.

Whatever riches belong to the gods on mountains such as Meru and even in their hermitages, and whatever prosperities belong to the Siddhas and the splendors belonging to the lords of the earth; || 37 ||
All of them arrived at the saffron pond at the feet of Hari, located to the east of Raivataka mountain and to the west of Śatruñjaya. (38)
To the south of the Bhadrā river, the supreme abode known as Kuṅkumavāpikā-kṣetra shines forth, extending fifty krośas in circumference. (39)
There, the Supreme Lord Hari shines with the playful behaviors of a child;
Brahmā arrived there, and he was presented by Śrī Hari.
And on the very first day of his own birth,
he bestowed the station of Parameṣṭhin upon Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the world, and Vaikuṇṭha above the waters.
Likewise, Śvetadvīpa was offered to Nārāyaṇa,
and Kṣīroda was offered by him to Śeṣanārāyaṇa.
At that time, Śrī Hari entrusted the kingdom of the ancestors to Aryaman;
he, in turn, bestowed upon Sanatkumāra the supreme status of a seer.
Then the status of a celestial sage (devarṣi) was granted to Nārada from his mind, and the position of Indra over the kingdom in heaven was given to Indra. 44.
By him, the station of Yama was surrendered to Dharmarāja,
the state of possessing great wealth to Kubera, and the domain of Varuṇa to Varuṇa.
The guardianship of the directions was likewise bestowed upon Vāyu, Agni, Īśāna, and Nirṛti; and the realm of light was given to Sūrya.
To Soma, [he granted] lordship over the medicinal herbs as well as sovereignty over the constellations;
to Meru, the kingship of the mountains; and to the ocean, the kingship of the rivers. (47)
The supreme sovereignty over the principles (tattvas) is established within each respective principle;
thus has this order been ordained in the world by that Supreme Self. 48.
Seated upon the jeweled throne, the Lord offered them crowns;
and they, having accepted those sovereign commands, honored Hari.
This arrangement, which sustains the world, was indeed established prior to my birth at midday;
it was composed in ancient times by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 2.4.50.
Then, on account of his birth and for the sake of the kingdom,
his father and the gods bestowed countless gifts.
Rudra, the creator of destruction, having attained his divine station, bestowed gifts;
Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa likewise gave away gifts consisting of tens of millions of cows.
He bestowed jewels, golden vessels, and gems;
indeed, he gave away beautiful and glorious mansions as gifts. (53)
He bestowed golden-colored vehicles equipped with canopies—divine aerial chariots as well as those drawn by elephants and horses. (54)
With joy, he gave daughters in marriage to the Brahmins, as well as wealth,
various kinds of food, and excellent, purified ghee.
She gave sugar, divine garments, ornaments adorned with diamonds,
bodily unguents, and Viṣṇu-oil and other such preparations.
Finger-rings, divine bracelets, beds, couches, and bark garments;
water-jars, cooking pots, water-vessels, and coverlets.
He gave divine vessels for worship, inexhaustible vessels,
suitable draft-oxen as vehicles, and heaps of food.
With joy he gave kalpavṛkṣa trees, kalpakalpa trees, and kalpavallī creepers;
he gave cintāmaṇi jewels, male and female servants, attendants, and laborers.
She gave golden lotuses, moonstones, and glowing gems,
as well as illuminating lamps and small golden caskets.
He indeed gave countless seats made of gold, silver, and thread, along with excellent cushions, mats, woolen blankets, jackets, and other such items.
He gave foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as drinks that were like nectar and inexhaustible;
he also gave pavilions with canopies and golden carts.
He gave camels, goats, sheep, horses, and gayals;
he also bestowed water-vessels that travel within the ocean.
He gave rosaries made of cow-horns, deer skins,
various types of seats, woolen blankets, and water-pots.
He also provided time-measuring instruments, poison-destroying gems,
body-ornamentation elixirs, and protective coverings against stings.
He gave instruments for fixed observation and magnets;
then he gave female buffaloes, yaks, cows, and black antelopes.
He gave all the household utensils suitable for domestic use;
he gave all the sacrificial vessels to the Brahmins, and he gave the Veda itself.
Then, with joy, he gave divine vessels for liberation and forms of the gods, as well as gifts of fearlessness and tokens of contentment.
He gave beautiful sacred threads, far-sighted instruments, devices for hearing from a distance, and cooling pearl necklaces. (69)
Then he gave away countless sun-stones and magnets;
he gave away wish-fulfilling gems, gems that provide all enjoyments, and gems that possess the power of destruction.
He gave flower-arrows, graceful charms, fruits, leaves, perfumes,
rain-clouds, mountain-daṇḍas, and wondrous liquors.
He bestowed divine mantras that have attained perfection and can assume any form at will;
he granted the wonders of the *Kalpajāla*, which possess the power of Brahma’s creative resolve.
She gave brilliant and auspicious Śāradā-kanyās (wisdom-maidens) to the Brahmins—
those suitable for Brahmins and those suitable for sages.
Then he gave to the Kṣatriyas those things which nourish the duties of the warrior class:
sound-engines, wind-engines, and likewise magical pills.
Then he gave all the implements suitable for Vaiśyas,
as well as those appropriate for servants and fixed for the various classes.
Whatever things were desired, those very things he gave at that time;
on that great festival, there was nothing whatsoever that he could not give away.

Whether it be born of *siddhi*, born of yoga, divine, arisen from the mind, or born of reality; whether it be elemental, consisting of the subtle elements (*mātrikā*), intellectual, born of mantra, or born of the self. (77)
Whatever was desired or sought by anyone at any time, that has indeed been granted by me as inexhaustible; for it is truly inexhaustible. (78)
Thinking, "May the thread of all world-dwellers attain inexhaustibility," he gave that which increases prosperity and bestows prosperity. (79)
She gave beautiful *kalpa*-dolls that grant all desires,
and she indeed gave *kalpa*-finger-rings set with jewels.
Thus, on the day of the birth of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa bestowed gifts throughout the night.
And Kambharā Mahālakṣmī indeed gave gifts from her heart:
garments, combs, mirrors, and bodices. (82)
Water-pipes and small garments, saffron and lac-dye, fragrant oils, bracelets, and chains; ||83||
For women, maidens, and young girls, he gave bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and *natthīs*, *cibukas*, and *bindvikās*. (84)
Moon-shaped earrings, necklaces, bracelets, and anklets, as well as silken garments and substances that bring good fortune; ||85||
Various kinds of foods and toys for children, as well as children’s seats, swings, hammocks, and cradles. ||86||
He gave small stools, low couches, and large beds, as well as wooden bowls, soft cotton cloths, and garments for young maidens. (87)
Water-pots, ewers, wooden troughs, jars, small vessels,
bowls, ladles, sacrificial spoons, cooking pots, and various other types of utensils.
And the virtuous woman gave him ornaments for his forearms bound with networks of tiny bells, as well as beautiful ornaments made of ivory. (89)
At that time, he gave fields, gardens, villages, groves, and forests, as well as crops of the finest grain and delicious foods.
Sindūra, parched grain, threads, as well as golden cīpiṭa ornaments, golden necklaces set with jewels, and garlands adorned with diamonds. ||9 1 ||
And armlets, crowns, crests, and turbans;
copper boxes, cymbals, and fly-whisks and fans. ||92||
He then gave blankets, balls of cotton, protective cords, and so forth;
he also gave milk, curd, clarified butter, ghee, sweets, and mixed delicacies. (93)
Having prepared the drinks and the foods for tasting, she took fragrant substances;
she gave ground rice, unbroken grains of śāli, and parched barley.
He gave wheat, mung beans, black gram, and other pulses;
he gave barley, rice, chickpeas, broken grains, and horse gram. ||95||
Then he gave molasses, honey, sesame seeds, and offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka);
he then gave fresh butter, ghee from a cow’s first milk, and milk-rice porridge.
Whatever came to his mind at that time, he gave that very thing as a gift;
the gods, Daityas, sages, and humans were filled with wonder. (97)
The lords and the guardians of the world, having seen this, were filled with wonder;
he gave him golden juice-vines and medicinal herbs such as the *sandhinī*. (98)
Having taken divine creepers and pills made from divine seeds and other ingredients— all those pills that grant the power to assume any form at will— they obtained women.
They rejoiced exceedingly and the masters bestowed their blessings; a great festival arose, accompanied by the offering of food and expressions of joy. (2.4.100)
The inhabitants of the fourteen worlds, having beheld Śrī Hari, presented offerings and accepted gifts from him. (101)
Having eaten and drunk together, and having attained eternal satisfaction,
they took with them the gifts and honors they had received and went to their own worlds at evening.
Then, following birth, the cutting of the umbilical cord and other rites were performed;
Mahāmāyā herself acted as the wife of the Great Puruṣa.
Bathing, purificatory rites, purification, and even the tending of the sacred fire—
all these were performed within the inner lying-in chamber just as they are for the gods in the world of men.
Janaka also made him fit for bathing and other rites;
though he had become like a child, the Blessed One slept in yogic slumber (yoganidrā).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnations of the Supreme Lord, the Arrival of the Lords, World-Guardians, and Subjects, and Various Gifts, on the Birthday of the Supreme Lord," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā; the mental service of the Supreme Lord is the goddess known by the name Ṣaṣṭhī, who is considered the protector of children. (1)
She, being ever present, acts in a divine form;
she resembles Rādhikā in beauty and Lakṣmī in nurturing.
She was like Pārvatī in her love, like Ramā in her beauty,
like Kamalā in her touch, and indeed like a mother in her affection.
Equal to Dhanvantari in medical treatment, she serves Hari;
and for one who remains in a state of childhood and is powerless, [she acts as a protector].

Like one who is powerless, his protection from the reality of the elements and so forth— protecting him from obstacles consisting of both the formed and the formless— is performed by the goddess Ṣaṣṭhikā.
For one who is free from obstacles, whence could there be an obstacle? Nevertheless, that virtuous woman, being of mental nature, imitates worldly custom by the will of the Blessed One.
On the sixth day, he had the worship of the Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī performed by Brahmins,
and his father indeed had the protective rite (rakṣā) performed by the sage Lomaśa.
And Gopālakṛṣṇa gave gifts of food, gold, and sacrificial fees, all occasioned by the sake of Parakṛṣṇa.
The Brahmin also caused the worship of the planets, the worship of the gods, the worship of the brahmins,
and likewise the worship of the Mothers to be performed.
The brahmins from Saurāṣṭra, having eaten that which grants infinite satisfaction,
bestowed blessings upon the boy and, having received wealth, performed sacrifices for him.
They celebrated a festival on the auspicious day of the sixteenth and the thirteenth;
at night, the goddesses performed a dance in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
The Blessed One, possessing a divine form and having assumed the state of youth,
watched the dancing, service, singing, and so forth, indeed smiling.
Then, when the night had passed, he became a child at dawn;
though ever-awake, he slept upon his mother’s very bed.
The sixth [mother] protected her beloved lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
during the day, the mother gratified her son with the drinking of milk.
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, he caused [the Lord] to sleep upon his side on a celestial,
enchanting golden couch, radiant as the moon.
The sixth mother remained awake for the sake of protection while the [other] mothers slept in slumber;
then, during the night, the Daityas dwelling in the netherworld arrived. (16)
Assuming forms at will, those divine goddesses took the form of young maidens and went to delight the boy.
Those Daityas who had gone to Pātāla were awakened to the form of the Blessed One by the Daityas who had arrived at and departed from the birth festival.
Then, filled with fear, they indeed informed him through their counsel:
"O lords of the Daityas, all of you, know that there is a great lord upon the earth."
And he who, abiding in the supreme state, is the cause for all incarnations, took birth upon the earth for the sake of dwelling there forever. (2.5.20)
Indeed, for the sake of destroying our power, that Hari will strive at every opportune time and will assume incarnations again and again. (21)
And the destruction of our family will come about through his guise;
he will provide protection for the gods and bring about the destruction of the Daityas upon the earth and other realms. (22)
That alone is the root cause and the cause for the manifestation of all things;
upon its destruction, there would be the destruction of those who are eternally opposed to the Daityas. 23.
When the root is destroyed, how can there be branches? Therefore, one should cut away the root.
As long as this [tree] exists merely as a sprout, so long should the cutting take place. ||24||
Disease, the enemy, and fire must indeed be destroyed while they are still small;
once they have taken root, these three destroyers become difficult to overcome. (25)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the cause of our enemies; indeed, our enemies are the incarnations of that Supreme Person. 26.
And this Supreme Lord is the root of all incarnations; in every kalpa, he indeed becomes the cause of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. 27.
Upon its destruction, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Paraśurāma, Hayagrīva, Vāmana, Vāsudeva, and others likewise [emerge]. (28)
They will never cease to exist; therefore, he must certainly be slain.
Even if his power is unfailing, he must be killed even if he is not slain [now]. (29)
Nevertheless, some auspicious fruit may arise for those who have exerted effort;
thinking thus, one should likewise apply effort to kill him. (2.5.30)
"May the host of Daityas neither be born nor perish"—having thus formed this resolve, Kalmaṣa and Kajjala likewise [remained]. (3.1)
Kaccara, Mala, Kardama, Kledana, as well as Mehana, Chikkana, Kṣuvana, and Pardana; ||32||
Lālana, Haṅgana, Ṣṭhīvana, Meṣana, Mardana, Nodana, Kampana, and Sphurjatha; ||33||
Khañjana, Śoṇaghoṇa, Kudarśa, Kucelaka, Khātanāsa, Durgajaṅgha, Araṇyaroman, and Darīśrava; ||34||
With his hand joined to his mountain-like thumb, and likewise with the interior of the netherworld [as his abode], these and other great Daityas consulted with one another. (35)
Where Mount Raivata stood behind them, they emerged through that opening,
bearing weapons in their hands, full of enthusiasm and intoxicated by the desire for battle.
In the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, they were as if fearless despite being afraid;
though bound by the power of Pātāla, they employed weapons, arrows, and sorcery.
Densely crowded with armies created by the magic spells of the Daityas,
they dwelt in the western forest of Aśvapaṭṭasara.
And having assembled in secret, they repeatedly sought to kill the child,
watching for vulnerabilities during the night of the fourteenth day.
Some assumed the form of cuckoos, others took on the appearance of owls;
some attained the form of jackals, and others the form of cranes.
Others took the form of female ospreys, while others had the forms of cats;
likewise, some had the forms of serpents, and others had the forms of those with terrifying roars. ||41||
Some had the appearance of variegated leaves, others assumed the forms of parrots;
some took the forms of mongooses and the like, while others likewise possessed the forms of deer.
Taking the forms of cats, house-lizards, gadflies, and mosquitoes, they arrived there;
yet the Blessed One, the beginningless and most excellent Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama), remained present.
Even those who dwell in concealment within the dwelling of the mother of the newborn know them too; it is Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who knows them. 44.
The sixth [consciousness] produces sleep like that of a child, and it also knows those [beings]:
gadflies, mosquitoes, lizards, and so forth, as well as cats, serpents, and dogs. (45)
And there, on that very night, they were struck down by the will of Nārāyaṇa;
though they were dead, they remained truly dead through the prowess of Manasā. (46)
Furthermore, the owls, cuckoos, jackals, cranes, and others who had come through the sky to slay Hari were also driven away on the sixth day.
Others, seeing that they had perished, took their corpses that very night and went to that forest where their dwelling place was.
In the morning, having seen those blood-born marks in the maternity chamber,
he purified them on the day of the Dīpotsava festival at dawn.
Gopāla, Kṛṣṇaka, and the others caused the recitation of peace-mantras; then they fell into grief, having lost their friends and family members. 2.5.50.
On the night of the festival of lamps, armed men arrived in secret, yet they were unable to kill the illustrious Lord due to their own fury. ||51||
They led away that goddess Manasā, the slayer of the sixty;
she too [led away] her beloved Mahākānta, her husband Śrīpumuttama.
As she was being led away there by the great asuras, she muttered prayers within her heart;
then the Lord, abiding within her own self, bestowed protection upon her.
On the sixth day, the Blessed One released the sovereignty of the great black fire, which burns and reduces everything to ashes; by it, they were consumed.
Having abandoned that goddess, they all fled far away;
then, indeed, from her own body, the goddess's army was manifested.
Likewise, there was an army of a hundred thousand maidens traveling in celestial chariots;
an army of a hundred thousand mounted on swans, and ten million mounted on tigers.
The abode of lions has one arbuda [of attendants], while that of the śarabha has ten thousand;
it is adorned with weapons such as spears, javelins, and nooses, as well as various mechanical engines.
In order to slay the Asuras, these maidens of fierce prowess then engaged in battle with divine weapons, their limbs remaining unhurt.
By them, many lords of the Daityas were slain there in that great forest;
some were thrown into a chasm while others, the foremost among the Daityas, died on the spot. (59)
Holding blades of grass in their mouths, they bowed down to the great and virtuous Ṣaṣṭhī;
having truly sought refuge in her, they were not killed at that time.
With their minds bowed in devotion, they proceeded through that forest;
meanwhile, those goddesses were praised there repeatedly by the crores.
On the sixth day, those who bring victory and are worthy of being chosen for Hari were all brought and presented by her to Bālakṛṣṇa.
Addressed by their lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, with the words "Choose a boon," they stood with faces turned toward the shore of the lake.
"Grant us residence, service, liberation, a sacred ford by name, and a husband," they said;
then Hari replied to those maidens, "So be it. (64)
Every day they made their dwelling in the sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā;
the Blessed Lord gave them the beautiful name Dīpāvalī.
He fashioned for himself a form composed of divine splendor suitable for his own nature,
and having created two-fold divine forms for them as well, he remained in his abode.
He sent others away and protected [the rest] at the hermitage of Lomaśa;
there, the sage Lomaśa, having bowed down with great compassion, spoke to Hari.
"By your will, these goddesses shall become your wives;
let them remain in my hermitage in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā."
In the hermitage of Lomaśa, they dwelt with great joy;
there, in that hermitage, they celebrated the Festival of Lights, which was equal to heaven.
Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Ūrja, they indeed celebrated a great festival there in every house at the very break of dawn with new grains.
Having prepared various kinds of cooked foods for the one of divine form, the ladies of the household offered them and performed instrumental music and dance. (71)
They ate prasāda and celebrated a great festival at night;
they indeed worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then, while they were all asleep at night, Ṣaṣṭhī protected the boy;
meanwhile, the Daityas arrived once more to kill Hari.
Then, having been routed there once again by the power of Hari,
all of them took the Daitya Sūtaka and went to their own abode.
Śrī Rādhikā said: Who indeed was this demon Sūtaka, and where did he appear?
What happened after that, O Kṛṣṇa? Tell me, for I have great curiosity. (75)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, this Sūtaka is a great Daitya born of the lineage of Asuras; hear how he was born and where he dwells by virtue of a boon.
Formerly, when there was a battle between Hiraṇyakuñca and Saṃkarṣaṇa,
the lotus of Brahmā repeatedly [fell] there.
At that time, the unborn Lord was indeed shaken by that asura;
trembling, he became afraid from the heart of Brahmā.
The son named Kampa was the first, the second was named Bhaya;
the third was named Sveda, and the fourth was named Śoka. ||79||
The fifth is called "distraught," while the sixth is "wailing" (hāhākāra).
The seventh is "unsupported," and the eighth is likewise "dependent on another."
Having gathered together, these lords spoke to Brahmā:
"O Father, how have we come to be born from you here in this ocean? (81)
"Tell us what must be done here; we shall quickly perform it accordingly.
Then Brahmā said to his sons regarding the great asura Brahmakūrca: 82.
"Run forth for the sake of his destruction, for he has become devoid of fortitude. Thus commanded, the sons then went quickly to the great asura.
Then, indeed, from Saṃkarṣaṇa, that [demon] met his death by the club; Brahmakūrca danced upon his body and its impurities.
And from his sense organs, which had issued forth due to the power of Māra’s agitation, there arose a man known as Janman, born from the emission of his virility. (85)
From his urine and semen was born a man named Sūtaka;
from the discharge of his waste matter was born a man named Nidhana. ||86||
From his piteous wailing, there arose in the water the one named Garjana;
and from his groaning, there then arose the man named Durgandha.
From her womb was then born an inauspicious son named Rakta;
then there arose one called Śava who was filthy, and from that, one named Pūya.
These undesirable elements became arrogant asuras,
whereas his auspicious elements then became gold.
These sons born of Asura, indeed filled with fear, bowed down to and praised the venerable Mahāsaṃkarṣaṇa, the refuge of all. || 2.5.90 ||
Protect, protect us, O Great Hero, O powerful one who effects the destruction of all!
We are your sons by Gadā; grant us the gift of life. (91)
Then Saṃkarṣaṇa granted them a promise of safety,
providing excellent clothing, dwellings, and food to those who requested them.
Saṃkarṣaṇa granted ten days for birth;
let the period of impurity (sūtaka) remain in the house of that woman who gives birth. ||93||
He gave her a maternity hut for her dwelling because of the blood, the foul odor, and the pus;
for birth is indeed blood, foul odor, and pus. (94)
They always dwell together with the mother in the womb;
then, after ten days have passed, they depart through the birth canal toward the ocean.
Thus, birth-impurities and other such things are demonic and bringers of suffering; this one called "birth-impurity" occurred at that time in the house of Kambharā. (96)
He indeed resided there for ten days according to worldly custom;
then others arrived, namely the one named Nidhana, Śava, and likewise Malinaka. (97)
Then they requested a place to stay, food, and other necessities;
and Saṃkarṣaṇa then gave all of them over to Death.
And at that time, for Kālaputra, wherever those [beings] may be—death, destruction, the corpse, death itself, impurity, and likewise birth-taint (sūtaka)—[all these are present]. 99.
These remain right there where the command for the time [of death] was given;
therefore, all these asuras are givers of fear and givers of suffering.
Then other sons of Brahmā, such as Kampā and others, also went at that time to where Death had arrived; for they had previously gone there.
When a corpse has arisen, they dwell there and then depart from that place;
thus have these sons been described to you as those who bring about the state of death.
Then, the person named Śrāddha was also created there by Brahmā;
he took up residence in the family where his own death had occurred.
Formerly, Nimi performed a śrāddha for the destruction of his own son, Ātreya; from that śrāddha, he became firmly established in the world.
Thus, O Rādhā, this asura named Sūtaka has been described to you;
he dwells in the maternity home together with his brothers.
On the tenth day, the Daityas forcibly took that newborn, who was staying in the house of Kṛṣṇa, to their own camp.
For the sake of destroying Śrī Hari, those fierce-born ones took counsel and gave the order to Sūtaka: "Bring the boy here quickly! (1.07)
"Having led that Lord Śrī Hari away, we shall enter Pātāla;
right there we shall kill him and cause him to be destroyed by our own hands."
"Otherwise, O best of Sūtas, we shall surely kill you!
Go quickly, perform your task, and bring the boy here tonight. (109)
"You must provide assistance to the Daityas; this is your duty.
Thus addressed, that Sūtaka returned to the lying-in chamber.
When midnight had passed, her circle of female companions fell asleep,
and Ṣaṣṭhī also there attained yogic sleep for a moment.
However, by the will of the beginningless Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
that Sūtaka seized Śrī Hari from His place on the bed during the period of ritual impurity.
In the darkness, they led him to the camp inhabited by the Daityas;
the Daityas rejoiced in many ways and raised shouts of "kilakila."
Having raised their entire camp, they went to Pātāla in an instant to slay Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Then the great messenger named Śrāvaṇa— the omniscient, all-pervading, and far-seeing one— led him to the slaughter-house of Yama, the Lord of Death.
"I have come to inform Śeṣanārāyaṇa of this, O Lord of lords, O Lord of the world, O Support of the universe, O Keśava! (1.16)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was harassed by the Daityas;
the child was taken to the Ghātakī hut in Pātāla.
"Protect, protect, O Great King, the cause of all causes!
Thus was the Lord, reclining upon Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk, entreated.
In an instant, he arrived swiftly at Pātāla with his chariot drawn by the power of his discus;
then the majestic one blew his conch shell with great force.
Then, by the sounds made by the blowing conch shell,
the women of the Daityas miscarried their fetuses, and their ears were split asunder.
Then all the Nāgas, together with Śeṣa, assembled and set out for battle; equipped with their weapons, they marched forth to wage war against the Daityas.
Then the Daityas also abandoned the child and came forward to fight;
Sūtaka, devoted to the child and overcome by compassion, protected him.
Before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa were Lakṣmī, Sudarśana,
Garuḍa, Nanda and Sunanda as attendants, Pārvatī, and Prabhā.
Rādhā, Ramā, Māṇikyā, Mañjū, Haṃsā, and others; likewise Saguṇā, Lalitā, Muktā, Jayā, Haimī, and Devikā. (124)
Dayā, Campā, Mauktikā, Śānti, Śāntā, and Manu,
as well as the other friends who were liberated, heard the sounding of the conch.
They arrived there in Pātāla, where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was;
Sūtaka became like a wretched man because he had committed an offense.
But he protected him while remaining concealed, for he was indeed a devotee of Hari;
he brought him away by force out of fear of the Daityas, and not of his own free will.
Therefore, this [world] was protected there by that Supreme Person with ease;
such was the will of Hari—who indeed is capable of restraining it? (1.28)
He related how the abduction had been carried out with the tail during the period of birth-impurity, and how everything was well protected; by this, Lakṣmī and the others were satisfied.
Then they offered him their thanks and placed him affectionately on their laps;
at that time, during another moment of the night, they indeed served him.
A terrifying battle took place between the Daityas and Śeṣanātha;
the Daityas were pierced by the discus and rendered incapable of rising again or being reborn.
"Those who have died have all gone together with the magician;
they have reached the city of King Yama, while all the survivors have fled. (132)
And Sūtaka, having led Hari along with Lakṣmī and the others, went to where the Lord Viṣṇu, the Master Nārāyaṇa, who is dear to Śeṣa, resides. || 13.2 ||
Śeṣanātha gave the young Lord to Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Viṣṇu; having bowed down, he departed for Kṣīroda, as did Ramā and the others.
Together with the birth-impurity, they went to the lying-in chamber;
meanwhile, at dawn, the roosters began to crow.
Having abandoned their sleep, they woke to find the child Hari asleep;
then his mother and the others awakened that Supreme Lord.
They do not know at all the deeds of Kṛṣṇa performed during the night, because Lakṣmī had informed them of everything regarding the conduct of the birth-impurity.
Then the father indeed had the peace-chapters recited;
the members of the household considered their son to have been born anew.
On the eleventh day at dawn, the Blessed One granted a boon to Sūtakā Bhakta, saying: "Indeed, you shall obtain divine worship."
On the eleventh day, indeed, the people will satisfy you with devotion through special divine offerings, such as baths, drinks, and excellent food.
"You shall become my divine narrator in the form of a Sūta;
wherever I am, there your dwelling shall be, though you appear in another form."
Your dwelling shall be among all living beings, of this there is no doubt;
from this day forward, your demonic nature will go to its destruction.
Thus addressed, Sūtaka also became a devotee under the power of Hari;
though he had attained the status of a charioteer, he was a bestower of liberation by reciting sacred verses.
Thus, O Rādhā, has been told how this wonder of Hari arose;
now I shall tell you of the naming ceremony that took place on the tenth day.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Protection by Ṣaṣṭhī in His Child Form, the Abduction of the Child by the Daityas through the Medium of Sūtaka-puruṣa in Pātāla, the Origin of Sūtaka and Others, the Protection by Śeṣanārāyaṇa, and the Devotion and Status of Sūtaka," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. || 5 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to the account of Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. When the eleventh day arrived, the great sages headed by Lomaśa [approached]. || 1 ||
Virtuous people devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, who were observant of vows and religious rites, arrived at the house of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa when summoned by their father. || 2 ||
They performed the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rites;
they also performed the first worship of the planets and the adoration of the deities.
The lords performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and the worship of Īśa and the others with devotion;
they also performed the worship of the Mothers and the worship of the sages.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, when the moon was situated in the constellation Mithuna, he was born;
therefore, his name was indeed Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He who has neither beginning nor end is therefore Anādinārāyaṇa; he is this very one who, as the Lord of incarnations, is called the Incarnator.
Because he removes all suffering, he is called Hari;
because he draws away (destroys) miseries, he is Kṛṣṇa; and because he resides within men, he is Narāyaṇa. || 5 ||
Since he does not abide in Nara, he is also called Nārāyaṇa;
and since he is the lord of the Imperishable, he is said to be beyond the Imperishable.
He is the supreme among men and is called Puruṣottama;
he is always declared to be the highest of persons, the Pumuttama.
Because of its vastness, its all-pervasiveness, and its transcendence in every respect, he who is the beloved of Kṛṣṇa is designated as the Supreme Brahman (Parabrahman). 2.6.10.
Because he is always endowed with splendor, he is himself the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
he is the lord of lords and is called the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). || 1 1 ||
He is the Lord of Māyās and is called the husband Mādhava;
since he is the master of all souls, he is Svāminārāyaṇa.
Likewise, there was always the preceptor Ghanaśyāma, as well as Chatraśāli;
and the Lord Jayārama, the husband of Lalitā and Māṇikyā, the Lord of Lakṣmī;
and the husband of Prabhā, Pāravatī, Mañju, Haṃsā, and Saguṇikā.
He shall become the supreme lord of one hundred and twelve excellent queen-consorts, and the husband of many other millions and billions of women.
In his hand, the bow, fish, banner, and the svastika shine resplendently;
likewise, the thunderbolt, arrow, trident, and the peak [of Mount Meru] are upon his feet.
The lines of the sixteen auspicious marks are clearly visible;
on his forehead, the golden line of the tilaka shines brilliantly. (16)
In the corners of his eyes there are red lines that cause total infatuation;
likewise, his eyes extend to the ends of his ears, and his face is as radiant as ten million moons.
His lips are naturally red, and there is a sesame-like mole on his throat;
moreover, a clockwise curl of hair is present upon his chest. (18)
And there is the auspicious golden Lakṣmī-rekhā, the streak of jewels, and a golden necklace without thread; these reside upon his heart.
His nails are like the moon, while the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet resemble the interior of a lotus, and they possess four wheels.
The auspicious conch-mark, which is the own-sign of Hari, is present upon him;
moreover, a mark of a wound exists at the base of his left thigh.
Upon his left thigh, above the knee, there is also a white moon;
for it is indeed the indicator of his lordship over ten million wives. (22)
On his hips, in the region below the navel, there exists the female organ;
thus he is Ardhanārīśvara, possessing the forms of both husband and wife.
Moreover, the arms of this Lord extend down to his knees;
indeed, there are three prominent circles upon each of his feet.
Indeed, in the middle of the right thigh there is the sign of a chariot;
Garuḍa stands there, and from that line Narāyaṇa is indicated. ||25||
This Supreme Lord does not indeed possess a thousand arms;
rather, there is a black sesame seed upon his *liṅga* and on its side.
Then that powerful one [placed] many [seeds] at the root of his left thigh;
and he had four testicles: two on the sides and two situated below.
Then he, the powerful one who satisfies ten million women and is unswerving, has a jar-like line above the navel upon his belly. 28.
There exists a line like that on a jar which obstructs the breath;
by means of it, one becomes a king among yogis, capable of assuming many forms. (29)
Even in darkness, his eyes shine like the sun;
therefore, that Supreme Lord remains a seer of the divine.
The tip of his tongue is red, and the tip of his penis is also red;
the tips of his fingers are naturally red as well. (3.1)
Then he shall become a king of kings, a supreme lord;
the hairs on his body will be golden-colored, fine, and delicate. (32)
They shine like flashes of lightning appearing in the darkness;
then that Blessed One, Puruṣottama, abiding in the supreme abode, [manifests].
Furthermore, the whiteness of his teeth is so marvelous and bestows such luster during laughter and other expressions that he is therefore called Narāyaṇa. (34)
Behold, both hands at the base of the arms of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa shine forth as divine, consisting of golden lines; therefore, he is Nārāyaṇa. ||35||
A brilliant triple-fold line extends from his navel to his waist;
his forehead is prominent, his eyes are long, and there is a slight curvature at the tip of his nose.
His teeth are equal and complete in number;
and his breath is always fragrant like the pārijātaka flower. (37)
In the physical form, it manifests as breath; it is also called *kaisara* and *vāsa*.
In the sweat, it appears as coolness, whiteness, purity, and fragrance. (38)
Even in its excrement and so forth, there is not even the slightest foul odor;
moreover, there is brilliance within its inner parts, and redness throughout the belly. (39)
There is blackness in the middle of the body hairs and blackness at the roots;
the channels (nāḍikās) are curved, and they are likewise dark red or tawny.
His vital points are white, his loveliness is captivating, and his tenderness is like that of a land-lotus. (41)
Speech is the Veda, song, and the autumnal tones and sounds;
and this Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord, is the treasury of all knowledge. 42.
His names are indeed infinite, and his qualities are likewise beyond counting;
his sovereign powers are also infinite and truly devoid of all calculation.
This beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shall always attain renown on earth in every way through the sages and the Saṃhitās. 44.
Through many narratives, as well as through billions of accounts of his wives,
numerous incarnations, and likewise through marvelous deeds.
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa, the best of sages, ceased;
and the other sages then likewise bestowed auspicious blessings upon him.
The maidens also, full of longing, waited upon their beloved;
then their father caused the name of Acyuta to be heard.
The excellent musicians played musical instruments, the singers sang songs, and the female dancers performed dances accompanied by rhythmic clapping. 48.
Then the goddesses of all the worlds honored him with blessings and delighted him exceedingly during the great festival of Kṛṣṇa’s name.
The subjects and the people ate their fill of foods,
and then the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa gave away gifts.
The lords worshipped the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and presented Him with offerings worthy of the celestial abode. (51)
Having performed such various rites, Lomaśa and the others went to their homes;
all the gods went to their respective abodes, and the people returned to their own places.
Listen here, O Rādhikā: at this great festival of the Name, a great asura who dwelt in the tiger-infested forest arrived to see the Lord. (53)
The asura named Sāṇa had made his abode in a mountain cave;
at that time, even those mountains where Sāṇa dwelt were likewise [afflicted].
In that way, the mountains of Sāṇa then attained their renown;
for this Sāṇa was produced from the city of Hiraṇyāṇḍa as he urinated.
At the time of the Asura's death, in the presence of Saṃkarṣaṇa,
he beheld Balarāma, the one who effects withdrawal, as the cause of the destruction.
Overcome with fear, he offered praise and sought refuge;
then Saṃkarṣaṇa granted him the gift of life.
Indeed, seeing the earth divided into fragments and desolate,
Sāṇa then came to Samaraṇyaka to make his dwelling there.
And seeing the vast forest with its dense trees extending for a hundred yojanas, he beheld there on the earth for a distance of a hundred krośas mountains as high as mountains themselves. ||59||
The Asura Sāṇa made his dwelling there, free from fear;
and he arrived there on the day of the naming ceremony.
In that house where the beginningless Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa truly resides, a demon indeed came in the form of a brāhmaṇa and, having arrived, received food.
Having brought various sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he went to the cave of Mount Aṇa;
on the twelfth day, an extremely dark-minded thought arose within him.
He remembered his paternal enmity toward Māra and that boy;
having ascertained that Mādhava was Nārāyaṇa in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
O Rādhā, having taken up missiles and weapons and being fully armored, the asura has arrived to destroy Kṛṣṇa, his enemy who appears in the form of a child.
For during the day, having become a Brahmin, he lived in the form of a guest;
searching for a way to seize him, he did not find any opening during the day.
Those maidens, six young girls, having come together, delighted, gladdened, and took delight in their beloved Acyuta without ceasing. (66)
At night, they departed from him and went to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
then, having found a great opportunity, the asura assumed the form of a tiger.
When half the night had passed, he of cruel form, cruel deeds, cruel eyes, and a cruel cry became intent on devouring the child for a moment.
Having arrived at the maternity chamber, he let out a roar;
other roars were likewise made, and then the forest was made to tremble.
The entire earth trembled and the worlds, overwhelmed, fell into terror;
the mother was distraught and afraid, and the father likewise succumbed to fear.
Out of fear of the tiger, the people there hid even within their houses;
at that time, there was only the sound of "Alas! Alas! cries coming from the place where Kṛṣṇa’s bed lay.
"Aha! A tiger, the very form of death, has come from the forest for the child!
Thus did the people cry out, "May the gods and goddesses protect the Lord! (72)
"May the protectors guard the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
Thus the mother spoke there repeatedly with cries of lamentation. (73)
Then the tiger, having leapt up, offered himself as a bed for the mother who had recently given birth;
meanwhile, that beast of prey strove, desiring to seize the infant with his paw. (74)
At that moment, Kṛṣṇa appeared there as a young boy accompanied by Sudarśana;
seeing this, his mother fell into a swoon, believing her son had been carried off by a tiger.
Indeed, the supreme Sudarśana discus, blazing with great luster and pervaded by fire, was released from the middle of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa’s finger.
Then that [discus], endowed with a thousand revolving spokes and surpassing a hundred suns,
became fiercely intense as it sought to slay Vyāghra.
Then, out of fear of death, the tiger leaped from the house to the outside,
fell down, and fled into the forest, eager to save his life.
The wheel became stuck in his back and burned him again and again;
touching his back here and there, it cut it into pieces.
Being struck down, that tiger leaped with great speed;
then, distressed and miserable, he cried out with a voice full of fear.
Having traveled only a *krośa* toward the southern direction, he was struck down by Sudarśana, along with his army and his body that had assumed the form of a tiger. (8.1)
That sacred site, Vyāghrahaṇa, was established by Sudarśana;
it is renowned as being to the south of the Aśvasarovara lake and the Kuṅkumavāpī.
When Sāṇa was destroyed, his body, a yojana in height, then blazed up;
by that very merit, it was indeed reduced to ashes by the Sudarśana fire.
Having emerged from that, he then became four-armed;
indeed, he was a divine attendant, devoted, purified in soul, and freed from sin. (84)
Uttering "Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa" from his mouth, he, being under the control of Sudarśana, rushed swiftly toward Anādi-Kṛṣṇa. (85)
Then, having dissolved into the Lord, he departed through the sky;
thereafter, those liberated souls of the Imperishable One, seated in celestial chariots, arrived to lead him away.
Then, from the form of Kṛṣṇa, he arrived at the field of Śrī Hari;
having emerged, he went to the eternal, imperishable abode along with Aṇa.
Then the Sudarśana [cakra], having become tranquil, merged into Kṛṣṇa’s finger;
and Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also slept happily. (88)
Then at dawn, others such as Mātṛ and the rest, as well as lords like Lomaśa and others, having entered into yogic sleep, performed rites for the pacification of obstacles.
Hearing that the asura Vyāghra had been slain, ordinary people concluded that he was a lord; they made the child their god and offered him worship. (2.6.90)
Upon hearing this, all the maidens wept with intense distress;
yet, hearing of the protective force, they rejoiced and came forward.
They gazed upon their beloved with profound affection,
bestowed auspicious blessings, and regarded him as if he were newly arrived.
The father performed fire oblations and recitations for the sake of pacifying the obstacle;
he gratified the virtuous and others with food, drink, and excellent wealth. (93)
The virtuous woman gave gifts of clothing, ornaments, and other items to the maidens; she also gave fodder to the cows and abundant sweet foods. (94)
He gave small portions of flour and other food to the tiny creatures such as ants;
having thus brought about peace, he delighted Mādhava.
O Rādhā, thus have been described the mother, the father, the other groups, and the assembly of young girls— this being the prowess of Bālakṛṣṇa.
Through both reciting and hearing it, it bestows supreme liberation and heaven;
it grants sons, wealth, and prosperity, and is the destroyer of disease. (97)
It is delightful, removing the obstacles of grief, providing protection and bringing happiness;
it removes the sorrow of women, is auspicious, and increases good fortune. (98)
This supreme purifier, the life-story of Kṛṣṇa which ensures freedom from widowhood, should be constantly heard with reverence by those who desire prosperity. 99.
Within six months, the supernatural powers (siddhis) attend upon the listener—
the divine qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as celestial prosperities.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Naming Ceremony of the Supreme Lord, the Destruction and Pacification of the Asura Sāṇa who had assumed the form of a tiger and desired to kill Hari," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhā, listen to the wonderful marvel of the Beloved of Kṛṣṇa that occurred on the twelfth day upon the swing.
On the day of the naming ceremony, the deity Gopālakṛṣṇaka had an auspicious swing made of sandalwood for the sake of his son.
And there he prepared a soft bed for lying down,
furnished with the finest essence of gems, pearls, diamonds, and other precious things.
It was enriched with the splendor of golden mirrors, adorned with various paintings and ornaments,
beautified by golden peacocks, parrots, and other birds, and possessed excellent quadrangular courtyards.
She is established in the form of the four Garuḍas and in the four swan-faces;
she is suspended from a diamond thread and rests upon a pearl staff.
[She resides] upon four divine creepers of flowers pleasant to the touch,
sheltered by a canopy in the center that radiates moonbeams.

By means of the natural flow of the wind, she produced a charming melody on her flute; though there was no physical drawing of the air, the movement of the notes was sustained by the will of the child.

In some places it was in the sky, in some on the ground; in some places it touched the lowlands of the earth, and in others it rose upwards; in some places it was white, and in others it had the appearance of gold.
In some places she moves with oscillation, and in others she is naturally steady;
she is endowed with the power of subjugating desire (kāmāvasāyitā) and possessed of the perfection of attainment (prāptisiddhi).
Having summoned Viśvakarman, the father indeed had such an auspicious swing, adorned with various ornaments, constructed.
On the day of the naming ceremony, at an auspicious moment, they placed their son Hari upon a swing;
they carried the lordly child with his head toward the east.
He caused that supreme being to rest upon the decorated swing;
then the gods arrived, bringing new swings as well.
O Rādhā, you went there for the sake of the repose of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, to his supreme swing born of Goloka.
Having brought a divine, highly precious, and most excellent celestial chariot,
Lakṣmī also arrived there with her auspicious swing born of Vaikuṇṭha.
The divine, supreme swing, exceedingly beautiful, which is rich with the reality of divine manifestations, stable in the path of the sky, and likewise the consort of the Imperishable. || 15 ||
Then the goddesses, the wives of Mahāviṣṇu and Vairāja, took up forms resembling divine thrones and gave them [to him].
The wives of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, truly possessing divine splendor, gave various swings to Bālakṛṣṇa; those women indeed presented them. || 17 ||
They may be quadrangular, circular, or fashioned in the shape of a lotus;
likewise, those shaped like a fish, a tortoise, or a conch are auspicious. (18)
There were elephant-shaped beds, horse-shaped ones, couches, and small stools;
there were also swing-shaped beds, those with a single pillar, those with two pillars, and those with many legs. || 19 ||
The pedestals were made of wheels, lotuses, wood, gold, silver, and other metals;
they were also made of moonstone, ruby, and pearl.
Śacī arrived there [and saw her] bound with a single chain,
auspicious, remaining in the intermediate space as a support for the attraction of the Pole Star (Dhruva).
Having brought forth that supreme [image] made of the essence of adamant,
he gave it to Kambharādevī, fragrant as the pārijāta flower.
Tārā, Rohiṇī, Menā, Siddhi, Vasundharā, and Satī— each flowing with nectar, auspicious, and moving like celestial chariots.
And they brought various swings that were enchanting to Kṛṣṇa—some fashioned from divine materials and others produced by divine resolve. ||24||
In each and every region, indeed, the celestial realm of Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the imperishable abode (Akṣara-dhāma) are seen within the circle of the earth. 25.
Wherever there is a single jewel, there the earth is seen together with its oceans and forests, as well as Mount Meru and the other mountains. (26)
In one jewel then the sun shone, in another jewel the moon;
in one it blazed as fire, and in another the sky was beheld.
In one place Satyaloka and the assembly hall of Brahmā are seen;
in another place, however, a multitude of cowherd girls is beheld within a jewel.
In some places, a vast circle of the rāsa dance is seen there;
and in other places, the seven oceans are beheld within a single jewel.
Thus, other forest regions are seen within the jewel,
and within that jewel, the great and radiant Nandana grove is also beheld.
O beloved, in other jewels the netherworlds are seen;
in some, the Ocean of Milk, and in others, the realm of the Nāgas.
Celestial chariots, all the abodes of the gods, and so forth, are seen;
in some places, more than one hundred and twelve excellent [chariots] are observed.
The circle of the seven sages, the pole star, and the planets and so forth, which are devoted to their own service for the wives of the Lord of the Supreme Abode; 33.
Marvels are seen within certain diamonds;
indeed, in some, pure gardens are clearly visible.
Thus, taking swings endowed with divine splendor,
the women arrived and presented them for the sake of Bālakṛṣṇa alone.
Cāraṇa women, Gandharva maidens, and Kinnara girls also arrived,
intent on dancing and singing, for the purpose of offering a swing to Kṛṣṇa.
The cowherd women gave her blankets, and the wives of the cowherds gave her small couches;
even the daughters of men gave her little rocking-horses. (37)
Endowed with golden rays, resounding with networks of tiny bells, producing the sound of desired musical tones, they were fashioned by the knotting of fine fabrics.
Having thus obtained [them], that mother became truly delighted;
and Kṛṣṇa simultaneously established his abode within all of them.
Hari, assuming as many forms as there were those swings,
himself took the form of a child and rocked them while laughing repeatedly.
Seeing this marvel, the women, overwhelmed by great wonder, fixed their beloved Kṛṣṇa in their hearts and meditated upon the form of their lord and husband. 41.
This glorious Lord is the sovereign of syllables, without beginning;
he is the fulfiller of all desires—what wonder indeed is there in this? 42.
Then, having beheld that radiant Hari, the Supreme Brahman,
who was their own protector, those women, their hearts overflowing with love, [gazed upon] the Lord.
While they were swinging and catching Hari in order to delight him,
the jewel fixed upon the swing assumed many forms.
And upon each swing, as soon as he beholds the Lord composed of many forms, that very reflection shall become [his own]. ||45||
Kṛṣṇa, the performer of wonders, was not even within her grasp;
then, having reached a state of despondency, my beloved remained as if insentient. (46)
Thus, on all the swings, they were bewildered because they could not grasp Hari, who assumed many forms; they wondered, "How is it that Kṛṣṇa cannot be caught? (47)
Then Lalitā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, Pārvatī, Jayā, and Māṇikyā—the eternal yoginīs—were there for the sake of providing proof to them. 48.
He said to them all, "Listen, sisters, to the truth regarding Ādhava;
if you wish to accept it, we shall state the proof of Hari. (49)
In his right hand are the fish, the trident, the bow, and the banner;
these should be on the right side of the image, while on the left side they should be on the reflected image.
Do not touch the reflection with your left hand that bears a mark;
grasp that Śrī Hari with your right hand that bears a mark, for He is the Truth.
Having been addressed thus, they held him up in that manner, lifted up the Supreme Lord,
and laughing and making him laugh, they seated the Beloved of Śrī upon their hips.
Having kissed her lord Kṛṣṇa— the beloved child— again and again,
she repeatedly rocked him back and forth, holding him like a swing between the palms of her hands.
Lifting him up, they took hold of him and, intent upon that, they delighted him;
thus, having attained great joy, they made Hari participate in the swing.
Then the Lord, having withdrawn those various forms, became a single form once more;
and those swings that had become empty were born from them as his grace-born attendants.
Kambharāśrī returned all [the items] according to the rules of restitution;
however, one [item], which was in the form of the syllable *preṃkhā*, was kept by Gopāla Kṛṣṇa. (56)
A beautiful swing made of sandalwood and another of fine wood were left behind, fashioned by Bālayuktā;
they were divine, most purifying, and took the form of graceful arches. (57)
Having taken the maiden, the goddesses of the northeast were filled with joy;
then one [of them] went to the abode of the Daitya Talu, who dwelt in the Siṃhāraṇya forest.
Then the daughter, the maiden named Talajā, who dwells on Mount Tala,
having heard of the festival, arrived there after assuming two forms.
She was alone, in the form of a maiden like Indra’s daughter,
richly endowed with the beauty of every limb and sporting in divine form.
Adorned with all ornaments and wearing golden garments and the like,
she was mounted upon a divine elephant and seated beside a divine young woman.
And he fashioned a second form called Dolā, adorned with many diamonds,
joined with many variegated ornaments, and featuring many jewels and excellent pearls.
Adorned with countless garlands, necklaces, and flocks of birds,
two lamps exist in the intermediate space, moving upward.
Supported by that [wind], the swing moved through the supportless sky, its motion produced by the heat of the lamp, with a divine silk ball as its pendulum. (64)
And of such a kind, shaped like a lotus flower, perfectly round, with a well-arranged comfortable bed in its center, soft, and white as milk. (65)
Having descended from the palm tree toward the surface of the earth,
that swing, which moves through the sky, was slowly brought down by the movement of her hands.
Although she was brought down to the ground, she nevertheless remained in the air at a height of one cubit above the earth; she did not touch the ground.
Seeing such an auspicious swing, the celestial women then were bewildered with joy and praised it again and again. (68)
Having fashioned an image of Hari and worshipped it with saffron and unbroken grains of rice,
Talājā, standing in the presence of Kambharā, placed it upon the swing.
Filled with the impurity of her mind, she slowly lifted Hari, who was asleep on a sandalwood swing, and placed him upon her own swing;
she then dispatched him with her palm to kill her enemy, Kṛṣṇa.
Assuming such a form, those wicked women slowly [approached] the boy who was seated upon the swing.
Lifting her up, she quickly fled through the path of the sky into the atmosphere;
she went eight yojanas away to her own hermitage in the forest.
And then this doe was recognized as being intent on killing [her].
In the depths of that lake, that Lord became four-armed. ||73||
And assuming a second form as a child, he resorted to the sandalwood swing located at Kuṅkumavāpikā and remained there, showing himself to the world.
There the goddesses delighted the Supreme Lord upon a swing;
for since no sorrow could befall them during the festival of the swing, He acted accordingly.
Though bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, He assumed the form of a child.
That exceedingly radiant Blessed One caused the Rākṣasī to laugh.
Then, seeing Hari who resembled the moon with his various jests, gestures, and the shaking of his body, that Rākṣasī was utterly bewildered.
"This child with such tender limbs was brought by me to be killed;
how can I kill him when he is so perfectly suited for being made to play?
Indeed, he must not be killed, but must certainly be made to play."
My master will grow up to become a firm young man. ||79||
Having thought thus, she [attended] to him constantly in that beautiful, secluded bed with fruits, excellent honey, juices, milk, and other such things.
He nourished her right there and always protected her;
even as a child, he constantly acted in such a way that she might be delighted. (8.1)
At that time, her resolve to belong to Kṛṣṇa became a source of merit for her;
considering his own devotee thus purified by that, Mādhava, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
brought about the destruction of the sinner's sins through her service.
She constantly accepted service and repeatedly drank the milk of love. Thus eight days passed; Tala waited for his daughter, who had not returned from the forest to his hermitage.
He realized that she was either dead, or staying in the house of Kṛṣṇa,
or else she had been overpowered and carried off by some other powerful man.
Thinking, "I shall search," he abandoned his hermitage and went from forest to forest;
whenever he saw a tree, a peak, a valley, or a mountain, he would proceed further. (86)
He saw the footprints of a woman at the entrance of the cave;
he called out to her by name, and upon hearing him, she was overcome with fear.
"Because I have brought her here for the purpose of killing her, and because she is being protected [by you], my father will fall into a rage and kill me along with this child. (88)
Thus, overcome with fear yet established in silence, she, having sought refuge with her whole being, praised the beloved four-armed Kṛṣṇa. (89)
Protect, protect me, O Hari, my beloved, Supreme Lord, Keśava!
My mind is fixed upon you; my father will kill me.
Having thus praised that boy and placed him upon her breast, the beautiful woman then shed tears; meanwhile, the youth Kṛṣṇa became firm.
Strengthened for the purpose of destroying the Dānavas, he indeed became one who held the discus;
as soon as Talajā beheld him, she kissed her husband for a moment.
The Blessed One, however, having granted Kṣaṇānanda and bestowed upon him divine power, merged him into his own body and assumed a dark form. 93.
He came out from the cave to where Tala was standing;
and Tala, armed with his mace, became apprehensive for his life.
There Hari blew his conch, and Tala fled in fear;
he hid himself within the depths of the earth, while Hari remained there.
Having abandoned that place himself, Hari, accompanied by the maiden, came regularly to Kuṅkumavāpikā at the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having assumed two forms as maidens at that very moment,
he sent one of his beloveds back to his own abode by means of a swan-vehicle.
In the second [birth], he was born as Kanyakārūpa, known by the name Lāja;
and in the hermitage of Lomaśa, he lived together with other maidens.
Having been offered to Kṛṣṇa, she, possessing a divine form, became the puffed rice (lājā) which is auspicious in nature within every act of worship. 99.
The celestial women constantly honor Śrī Hari with parched grain;
thus, that swing of *talājā* likewise took on the form of *lājā*.
Likewise, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, she always remains in the form of a swing;
in the form of a maiden, she is the wife of Kṛṣṇa, residing among the Kumārikās and others. (101)
Likewise, possessing a divine form, she shines resplendent in the supreme abode;
through her union with Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, she assumes fourfold forms.
Lājā, Preṅkhā, and Kanyakā remained devoted to the service of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; they were beautiful women who possessed liberated forms. 103.

Just as water from a street drain attains the state of being Ganges water through contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā, so too does a demoness attain liberation through union with the beginningless Kṛṣṇa. 104.
O Rādhā, what great wonder is there here that I tell you of Hari?
She who is like you shall indeed become the wife of Hari through marriage.
Then the Blessed Lord, assuming the form of a child once more, appeared before the mother and the boy, and then became absorbed within them.
This was told to the great seer Lomaśa;
and by Lomaśa, it was told to his two parents and to the deity.
When eight days had passed, the wonder was known by all;
they considered it a great marvel and performed recitations for peace.
Then, the gods and goddesses who had arrived for the festival were fed, saluted,
honored with gifts, and sent back to their own homes in peace.
On the thirteenth day, having gone home after eight days had passed,
and having recognized Kṛṣṇa’s majesty and his supreme, wondrous power, [he returned].
Through that lineage, those gods and goddesses rejoiced within;
they bowed and remembered Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa in their hearts. (111)
Thus, O Rādhā, has this great and auspicious festival of the swing been described;
and its wonder has also been told, which grants liberation to both the listener and the speaker. 112.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Miracles of Liberation and Other Wonders," concerning the daughter of Tala, the Rākṣasī Talājārā, who, though she had approached with deceit during the festival of Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa’s mounting of the swing in the second section on the Tretā Age of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, was nonetheless enchanted by Hari.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O fortunate Rādhā, listen to this narrative concerning the Supreme Person; after the festival of the swing, the supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa— || 1 ||
Thinking that Bālakṛṣṇa was stealing his daughter, the Rākṣasa named Tālaka became greatly enraged in many ways toward him in Kambharā’s house.
The affliction of this supreme being is not for his own sake; rather, the affliction belongs to the demon.
Therefore, let those who are situated there enter the cave by way of the opening and slay him. || 3 ||
Those Rākṣasas of their own kind were enlightened and consulted together,
joyfully resolving to destroy Kṛṣṇa at the Kuṅkumavāpī in Saurāṣṭra.
And having heard all that had occurred, beginning with the seizing of the skin,
they returned with the skin and settled in Siṃhāraṇya.
Wandering through the villages at night, intent on searching for vulnerabilities,
they were constantly striving to have Hari killed.
They approach in concealment, but failing to find even a moment's opportunity,
they depart hopeless, having become afraid of the Lord’s discus.
In this manner, the first month of Bālakṛṣṇa’s birth passed;
then, on the very first day of the second month from his birth, [the following occurred].
Then the mother, the father, and Lomaśa desired to make the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama drink divine milk; at that time, Hari [acted].
On the ninth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having risen early in the morning,
he would play and laugh upon a swing, manifesting his grace;
and his mother was exceedingly delighted to feed milk to Hari.
He milked the cow named Maṅgalāgaurī, who was a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadughā).
Having made the cow's milk lukewarm, mixed with sugar, held in a conch shell,
strained through a cloth, and still slightly warm, he caused Hari to drink it from that conch.
Knowing that the festival of milk had begun, the auspicious cows— capable of assuming forms at will, endowed with divine characteristics, and possessing speech like that of human women—
spoke to their mother: "Please let the Lord of Cows drink our milk."
Having heard the request for a thousand cows, the mother then said regarding those cows:
"How could this child be worthy of drinking all the milk?
All of that would be unwholesome; what indeed shall I do? Tell me! || 14-15 ||
The cows said: "What such misfortune could be ours?
We are your cows, yet we have not attained the service of Hari.
Even as the Mother heard the prayer of the cows, [she spoke].
Then, a hundred thousand cows arrived from Goloka via the path of the sky; likewise, millions of cows came from Akṣara, from Vaikuṇṭha, from the unmanifest heaven,
and also from the Vṛṣa forest on earth.
By the will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they arrived:
some traveling in celestial chariots through the sky, others moving through the intermediate space;
some staying upon the water, and others on the earth—they all stood there and bowed joyfully to Hari.
They caused milk to flow, and from that, a river of milk arose;
like the milk in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, it was mixed with the water. That became the Dugdhātīrtha (Milk Tirtha), which destroys both sin and suffering.
Having understood the desire of the cows, Hari spoke to his mother at that very moment:
"O Mother, tell them all: 'My son shall drink milk.
The cows offered praise to him and said, 'Drink our milk, O Acyuta!'"
"O Universal Soul, the essence of the interior of the cosmic egg, grant us success!
(23) Then, having accepted their prayer with grace, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa manifested indeed in ten million forms. (24)
That child, however, remained like one who milks a cow;
having reached the udder of each cow, which yielded its natural flow of milk as well as milk exceedingly sweet with affection, Hari took it into his own mouth. (25)
He drank water to his heart's content and caused the cows to suckle their milk.
He gave [the fruit] pleasingly to the gods, the maidens, and likewise to the ancestors;
thereafter, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa became one in form.
Then those cows entreated Kṛṣṇa, their true lord:
"O Protector, always protect us; indeed, we wish to serve before you. (28)
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, smiling, said, "So be it";
then the God assumed two forms for the sake of the cows.
One was in the form of a cow and the second was in the form of a maiden;
the Lord Hari protected those maidens in the presence of Lomaśa.
All the cows, possessing divine bodies, indeed departed for their respective abodes;
beholding this great festival, the gods and goddesses were filled with wonder.
