Provided with vessels made of gold and other materials, filled with camphor and other fragrances, and adorned with every kind of ornament, they were intended for the worship of the ancient deities. || 3 ||
On the day of the new moon, all of them, overflowing with love, arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa in celestial chariots filled with divine splendors.
Having first bowed to Lomaśa and their supreme father, the Guru,
they then remembered Hari there— namely Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Just then, Bālakṛṣṇa arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa, moved by compassion, in order to accept the offerings and worship presented by the maiden.
Seeing the radiant, enchanting youth Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa approaching, the daughters of the Pitṛs rose up quickly.
They approached with great joy, bowed, and honored him with parched grain, unbroken rice, and other offerings; they celebrated him exceedingly and fell at the feet of Hari.
And having addressed one another with mutual inquiries of welfare and health,
the thousand maidens placed flower garlands around his neck.
Placing the dust of his feet upon their heads, they placed his form within their minds; they placed his beauty before their eyes and fixed their affection within their hearts.

Then, having gathered together for the purpose of offering, they themselves established [the site] and arrived at that most excellent Satyaloka hermitage, which was filled with celestial lakes and maidens.
At first, there appeared a divine palanquin, like a celestial chariot, mounted upon swans;
it was adorned with a hundred moons and beautified by a golden framework.
It flowed with nectar on all sides and was endowed with fragrant cascades.
It was swaying of its own accord, enchanting with the sounds of song.
It moved according to one's desire, adorned with pillars of conscious beings,
resplendent with jeweled staircases, and flanked by crystal sides.
And the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa ascended that palanquin, which was adorned with soft, magnificent, and exquisite cotton and silk cloths.
At that time, the splendor of Hari became a hundredfold greater than that of the lion-throne.
Then, with the help of Apsarases and maidens, two very soft sandals [were prepared].
They were made soft for the sake of Makha and Malla by lightning, moonlight, and stars,
and were adorned by Bharata with continuous streams of gold and silver.
When those two beautiful sandals, resembling Indra’s cow (Kāmadhenu), were placed at the feet of Hari,
they departed according to their will, performing acts of steadfastness as they pleased.
And when the sandals were worn by Kṛṣṇa with great joy,
a vast and divine splendor was manifested from them.
Then, that [parasol], resembling ten million moons, pervaded the ends of the quarters;
subsequently, the daughters of Āryamā and the other suns offered it as a canopy.
Richly adorned with golden waistbands and garments, joined with silver tinkling bells,
it possessed a radiant and brilliant golden pitcher with a jeweled handle.
Adorned with clusters of silk and variegated with the brilliance of the sun,
a footstool was then presented by the daughters of Kubera.
Inlaid with soft gold, fashioned from sandalwood trees, it is beautifully adorned with lion legs and endowed with eight corners. ||23||
Transparent like a lotus petal, cool, and endowed with splendor; it was polished on its sides like a mirror and adorned with the moon in its center. ||24||
There, Śrīpati, the Supreme Person and Lord, set his feet down;
then the daughters of the mountain [offered] two chowries made from white yak-tail hair.
And two staffs made of jewels and gold were offered to Kṛṣṇa for his satisfaction;
then a golden cane was offered by the daughters of Indra.
His neck was as beautiful as a conch shell, shining like the summit of Mount Meru;
his chest was adorned with various bracelets, and his auspicious belly was marked by folds like creeping vines.
Bound with a yellow cloth at its edge and possessing the remaining hoods,
it was adorned on all sides in the middle with pearls, diamonds, and gems.
And then the daughters of Dharmarāja presented the sacrificial ladle, which was made of gold, with its tip possessing the power of destruction and its base the power of life. (29)
She possesses the power of meditative concentration and is endowed with the face of the embodiment of Dharma;
she is joined by the assembly of Yama in the center and surrounded by hosts of messengers at the periphery. ||2.18.30||
Then, with fans having jeweled handles, bound with golden bands and edged with silk, the daughters of Vāyu [fanned him]. (3.1)
Upon the casting of a golden cloth, which is endowed with both the sun and the moon, circular, bound with radiant jewels, and naturally resonant— 32.
Then the Ṛtukanyakās presented to Kṛṣṇa clusters for his crest-ornaments,
a ball of flowers, necklaces, and garlands filled with fragrances.
Then the daughters of Viśvakarman gave him a radiant crown— unfading, of divine form, sweet, pleasing, and fragrant.
Ornaments made of gold, garlands,
rings, waist-bands, finger-rings, and girdles.
They gave to Nārāyaṇa bracelets, armlets, chains, anklets, small bells, and various neck-ornaments. (36)
Then the daughters of Drūka gave him garments with devotion:
a protective undergarment, a washed lower garment, an upper robe, and a head-cloth.
They gave him a shoulder-cloth, a loincloth joined with gold thread, a wrap,
a handkerchief, a silk cloth, and a fine garment.
Then the daughters of the Śravaṇa Pitṛs, known as the Śrāvaṇīs, also gave auspicious golden jars filled with water to Śrī Hari. (39)
Then the daughters of Saṃvatsara Pitṛ gave to Hari cooked rice-filled pastries, milk-rice, vegetables, and various foods.
The daughters of Kāla gave him a divine wheel of fearlessness in his hand,
and the daughters of Agni and the Pitṛs gave him many vessels.
He also gave large pots, small bowls, water-jars, and *tāpalīnikās*,
as well as ladles and water-vessels made of gold, silver, and other metals.
Then the daughters of the ancestors of the deceased gave betel leaves,
and the daughter of the ancestors of the one born from a mine gave auspicious articles.
And they placed various liquid substances arising from mineral transformations and possessing beautiful colors,
as well as other offerings suitable for the ancestors, before Hari.
The Vārkṣyas gave caṭanyā and other foods mixed with bitter, sour, and pungent flavors;
thus, on the new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, all the ancestors [worship] the Lord Hari.
They worshipped him exceedingly with their own extraordinary articles;
they gratified him exceedingly by feeding him again and again. ||46||
Rice-milk and other foods, various kinds of fruits, and sweet cold drinks that are delicious and flavorful. ||47||

and fragrances, juices, and sandalwood pastes, which she offered to Hari. (78–79)
The divine zodiac sign of Libra, the beautiful one named Tulā,
dwells and moves within market streets, shops, marketplaces, cities, roads, houses, and other locations occupied by wealthy merchants. (2.19.80)
She too, for the sake of her beloved Kṛṣṇa, conducted that divine festival;
there she provided an abundance of food and delicacies, free from any deficiency,
and she established a divine scale upon which what was placed remained truly inexhaustible.
She gave him wealth—gold, silver, coins, and nooses—and having brought many riches from the abode of Kubera, she then bestowed them upon him. ||83||

And that which is the intense female scorpion (vṛścikī), the zodiac sign, in a chasm, on the surface of the earth, in an anthill, in dried cow dung, in a fissure, on dry ground, and likewise within the interior of the earth; ||84||
He dwells and moves within stone and the like, in skin, flesh, and so forth;
in the walls of houses, in forests, fields, wildernesses, refuse heaps, and even in a minute particle. ||85||
And that celestial maiden, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, brought forth from the mountains juices from stones, juices from trees, as well as tubers from the earth and radishes. (86)
He bestowed upon him juices produced from battle and juices produced from the earth known as "saline," as well as pungent,
sour, and sweet juices, and even poisonous juices.
The sign of Sagittarius is a divine maiden who assumes the form of a horse;
she is equipped with a bow and arrows, and is the most excellent among those skilled in heroic missiles and weapons. (88)
He stands or moves upon an elephant, a chariot, a horse, a vehicle, a celestial chariot, on the ground, in a cart, or in a palanquin. ||89||
Various vehicles for those respective places— elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth—
as well as divine celestial chariots accompanied by heavenly gardens.
During the festival, he indeed gave new celestial chariots adorned with swans, horses, elephants, and other [beasts] to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The zodiac sign named Makara is a divine maiden with the face of a deer;
she dwells in rivers, the ocean, great lakes, and similar bodies of water.
He moved likewise through the pits, the moats surrounding the gods' dwellings, and other such places;
he offered to Hari the various jewels produced in those respective locations. ||93||
Known as Kuṃbhikārāśi, she dwells upon the shoulders of men;
in the form of an empty jar and in the guise of a maiden, she resides in the houses of vintners.
She lived and moved about in gambling houses and halls;
and then she gave crores of golden jars to Hari.
The pair of Pisces, full of love, travels to the oceans of sacred fords; they dwell in holy pilgrimage sites and in the abodes of gods and Brahmins. (96)
The divine Mīnī, who was the daughter of Kanyā, arrived and presented to Hari all the vessels for worship as well as the most excellent materials for worship.
He joyfully bestowed sixteen offerings upon Hari.
Thus, at that time, the twelve-fold Sun-god presented a multitude of divine maidens. || 98 ||
Having extracted the essences from the very depths of the earth,
Viśvakarman, as soon as he was summoned, arrived at the marvelous pavilion and offered them to Śrī Hari.
And he constructed the Śatabhauma palace, which contained within it sacred fields, reached to the ends of the quarters,
possessed courtyards for the sky and for vehicles, and was beautifully adorned with gardens.

The assembly hall of Dharma, the assembly hall of Indra, and also the assembly hall of Bṛhaspati; the assembly hall of Śukra, the assembly hall of Brahmā, and the assembly halls of Viṣṇu and Śiva. || 101 ||
At that time, in that very pavilion,
there were divine thrones and golden banners where they had entered into absorption.
One hundred golden jars were set out,
and there was a mountain with a thousand peaks that was naturally radiant like the sun.
Resplendent with a mass of luster shining like the innate moon, possessing the beauty of millions of lightning-lamps, and adorned by ten million stars; || 104 ||
Adorned with ponds, wells, tanks, and other means for domestic enjoyment, it was resplendent with divine articles such as food, drink, and fragrant unguents. || 105 ||
Adorned with divine ornaments, garlands, and the like, with walls of divine rubies,
and well-furnished with necklaces and other jewelry made of divine pearls and gems.
With its many gopuras and enclosures, it was eternal and fixed like a thousand poles;
in its center was a great divine altar, naturally possessing sacrificial clarified butter as its fuel.
It was adorned with rows of pillars numbering in the hundreds of thousands, tens of millions, and hundreds of billions,
and was graced by all the gods, sages, and seers— the auspicious protectors of the worlds.
The area constructed above the pillar contains divine parrots and peacocks,
as well as divine houses for eating and so forth, provided with divine hearing, sight, and other such faculties.
By means of divine gardens, monasteries, and the like, as well as divine food, dwellings, and so forth.
And he was resplendent with excellent courtesans who possessed divine qualities for bathing.
Moving through the sky, going wherever he desires, adorned by tens of millions of billions of maidens,
it was filled with divine spectacles and served as a divine arena for the wrestling match.
He possesses divine knowledge of the Gandharva arts and is delighted by divine drama;
he is adorned with divine instrumental music, speech, song, and the sound of musical instruments.
Resembling an elephant, a lion, and other such beings, and adorned by all the gods—
indeed, there is nothing whatsoever in the Egg of Brahmā, in the world of Īśvara, or in the celestial abode that does not exist there.
Indeed, that [defect] does not exist there in the pavilion constructed by Viśvakarman,
nor in the creation of living beings, nor in the creation of the Lord, nor in the supreme realm of Brahmā's creation.
Whatever is renowned as existing has been fashioned here in this pavilion;
Viśvakarman performed the craftsmanship, and Brahmā performed the ritual arrangement.
Vāsudeva made manifest the forms of objects endowed with visibility;
he then brought about the manifestation of those forms from the imperishable Brahman.
O Rādhikā, you are Mahāmāyā; you yourself removed all deficiency, while Lakṣmī established fullness and Jayā brought about victory.
Thus, on the evening of the seventh day, the pavilion became magnificent;
once the Eternal Abode had arrived, night was no longer seen there.
Nidrā resides at Kuṅkumavāpī; Ānandinī has gone one krośa from the field of Mahābrāhmī; and Śakti is situated in Saurāṣṭra.
The rising of the sun was previously perceived merely by the sight of its orb; the arrival of night was indicated merely by the blackness of the horizons. || 2.19.1–20 ||
The departure of the rays to the ends of the quarters was certain from the mass of radiance, and the sunrise itself was inferred solely by the arrival of the Bālakhilyas. (121)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dispatching of Invitation Letters to All Worlds, the Presentation of Offerings by the Astrologers, and the Construction of the Great Pavilion," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the celebration of the commencement of the second year of the Lord Bāla-Kṛṣṇa on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When such a pavilion had been constructed there by hundreds of thousands of artisans (*kuñjala-kṣaka*),...
It was beautiful, adorned with patterns of vermilion, svastikas, and creeping vines.
In this auspicious rite, adorned with curds, goads, parched grain, fried rice, and pillars,
there stands a proclamation of verses placed amidst cymbals on all sides.
Upon which were placed the names of the principal deities,
and upon whose various banners were depicted their respective primary vehicles.
In the sky, amidst the encircling necks of the guardians of those respective gate-towers,
there was the delighting of the minds [of the people] by means of the names of those respective principal deities.
O you whose staff is encircled by a garment as beautiful as the seven colors, and whose circle of pillars is draped with divine golden cloths! (5)
O Fire-eyed One, on that ground made beautiful by the tops of pillars with images of divine goddesses,
there was land in the water and water on the land in both places.
It shone like a lake adorned with chowries like reeds,
and was as clear as liquid mercury on all sides, with streaks of lightning appearing everywhere.
In the middle of the upper stories, within a circular courtyard adorned with a *rāsa*-maṇḍala,
there was a doorway of exquisite beauty whose origin was unknown.
In which the paintings of dramatic performances on screens of lightning delight the audience with new sights,
and which is beautifully variegated by the wonders of the divine hosts descending in their military arrays.
In that place filled with the playful grace of millions of dark-hued beloveds, abounding in every prosperity, where desires are fulfilled at will, and which is a cavern of longing; 2.20.10.
And when the truth regarding the objects of desire was present, in that pavilion of true resolve on the morning of the eighth day, the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa appeared.
He sprinkled the ground with cool waters scented with sandalwood and other perfumes,
and made it fragrant with various kinds of aromatic incense.
He had various mandalas made with pigments— svastikas, sarvatobhadras, circles, and wheels.
He adorned those auspicious [sites] with unbroken grains, flowers, saffron, curd, and sprouts,
and he likewise decorated the gate-towers with arched portals.
With leaves from mango, *aśoka*, and other trees, and with the leaf-sheaths of plantain trunks; with fruit-bearing plantain trunks and branch-tips laden with fruit. (15)
He also adorned the garden paths with flowering clusters and hoisted banners that resounded with sounds announcing the festival.
He also had banners fastened everywhere in the pavilion,
as well as divine glass and other mechanical contrivances, along with electric lamps and the like.
It illuminated the pavilion and its surroundings perfectly on all sides; in every pillar of that exceedingly beautiful pavilion, the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) were present.
Taking forms that fulfill desires and merits, they fulfilled his wish:
the Dhruva-mechanism, the Kāla-mechanism, and the exceedingly great Vedha-mechanism.
Television sets and long-distance hearing devices, as well as projection machines, were present in every place and every home. (2.20.20)
And in the divine pavilion there were pillars and woven hangings,
as well as very long woolen carpets that resembled green meadows.
There were seats of grass and mats, lion-thrones, altars, elephant-seats, swan-mouthed [pedestals], and crossroads shaped like Garuda's face. ||22||
There were golden sands and the like, as well as seats inlaid with jewels;
there were also various kinds of swings and long couches on all sides. (23)
There are many valuable items, such as sandals and mattresses, enriched with gold, jewels, and gems, which shine brilliantly on all sides. (24)
There were earthen fields there, adorned with cotton and *tulasī* trees;
and various species of flowers, such as the *anagha*, *śārṅga*, and others, had grown there.
Auspicious Campaka and other trees stand in the pavilion;
the ground of golden sand shines indeed on all sides. (26)
Soft as young maidens, thin and exceedingly delicate;
the sacrificial enclosures, the broken streets, and the pathways were circumambulated clockwise.
In that pavilion, the pathways were beautified by sprouts, creepers, and the like,
and there were couches and platforms serving as seats for the spectators.
And all around, extending upwards and further upwards, there were indeed aerial vehicles belonging to the servants, cāraṇas, and bhaṭṭas, as well as to the soldiers, panegyrists, and bards.
The high seats of the learned brahmins, the wise women, the poets, the eloquent, and the singers shone like streaks of lightning. (2.20.30)
Then, within the interior of that [hall], rows of seats for humans, extending over a great width on all sides, shone like moonlight. ||3 1 ||
Then the yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas who dwell within, as well as the kūṣmāṇḍas, vaināyakas, vetālas, and kinnaras [were summoned]. ||32||
Then there were Kimpuruṣas, Vidyādharas, and hosts of Yoginīs;
they stood within, possessing divine bodies, resplendent with crowns and bracelets.
Gods, goddesses, guardians of the gods, lords of the gods, and followers of the Suras were present;
likewise, quadrangles and pavements were established at every spot. (34)
There stand the foremost of the gods and the lords of the earth, possessing four feet, eight feet, and likewise sixteen feet. (35)
Then there were lion-thrones with parasols having many hoods,
made of gold and exceedingly divine, presided over by their ancestors.
Then there were sages within [the assembly], reciters, contemplators of Brahman, chanters of the Vedas, and likewise reciters of the Lakṣmī-saṃhitā. || 37 ||
There were also chapters from the Saṃhitās of Rudra and Brahmā, as well as some readers of the Saṃhitā of Agastya. (38)
Then the great sages stood upon woolen seats laid out with cloth strips; thereafter, they sat upon a pedestal beneath the inner pavilion.
Those who dwell in Satyaloka as well as those who reside in Vairāja were devoted to celibacy and dedicated to the chanting of the Brahman.
And those most learned in the Veda became the officiating priests devoted to the sacrificial rites—
the Brahmā, the Hotṛ, the Udgātṛ, and the Adhvaryu, in their respective order.

There were chanters of the Sāmaveda, others who sang songs, as well as practitioners of mantras; there were those skilled in their respective duties, such as the Bhārgavas and others, accompanied by their Śaktis.

The sacrificial vessels, the ritual oblations, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other such implements, as well as the liquids, the wood fit for sacrifice, and the rice and other grains—all these became abundant. (43)
At that time, clarified butter and various kinds of sacrificial offerings were prepared in their entirety;
the sacrificial pit was vast, and the deity of the sacrifice was Vaiṣṇava.
And there the Vaiṣṇava fire, the Āhavanīya, shines forth;
and preceded by the recitation of auspicious blessings, the sacrificial rite proceeds. (45)
His mother was the illustrious Kambharā Lakṣmī and his father was Gopālakṛṣṇa; they both shone there in the place of the patron (yajamāna) in the presence of Lomaśa. 46.
There, Lomaśa performed the worship of Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rites, and thereafter the fire-oblation (havana) was commenced.
To the south of that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), auspicious beings liberated from the syllables (akṣara-muktas) reside;
on one side are those liberated in Goloka, and on the other side dwell the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. 48.
Then there were others dwelling in Vaikuṇṭha, those residing in Kṣīroda and Śveta, as well as those staying in Badarī, those on Kailāsa, and likewise those who had gone to other abodes.
On the right side stand those who are devoted to the perfect Brahman;
upon the altar is the Supreme Brahman himself, Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Lord Himself shines forth as a youth, assuming the form of a young boy. 51.
Although, according to worldly custom, he remains in his second year of wandering,
nevertheless the Supreme Lord shines forth, enriched by the form of his divine abode.
On the altar, upon a beautiful lion-throne in a celestial chariot, the Blessed Lord himself was present;
by his side were Rādhikā and I, Kṛṣṇa, your beloved. (53)
Śrīpati dwells at my side; by his side is Nṛnārāyaṇa;
by his side is Śvetavāsī, and likewise Kṣīravāsī thereafter.
Bhūmā and the others, Vāsudeva and the others, and thereafter Kapila and the others, sit upon the altar-thrones and in the celestial palaces (vimānas). //55//
His wives and daughters, as well as his attendants carrying staffs,
those holding parasols, and the chamberlains, stand all around him.
And musical instruments were sounded behind the altar, while ten million goddesses shone resplendent upon their thrones, some with attendants and others without.
Those who are fond of the great festival of Kṛṣṇa sing beautiful songs, divine and enchanting, which contain within them the eternal pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. 58.
A human being is indeed born there, and the lords and others are satisfied—the gods, the ancestors, all the incarnations, and the millions of liberated ones. ||59||
All of them indeed accept, under the guise of fire, the ever-fresh sacrificial offerings presented by the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Various kinds of milk-rice, as well as fruits, flowers,
and honey, and even grains and coconuts, are offered repeatedly.
Then, when the expiation has been performed and likewise the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is offered,
the assembly rises there in the pavilion and offers divine, excellent essences as oblations.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā, the planets, Gaṇapati, the Mothers, the water-pot, the guardians of the directions, and the lords of the deities; ||63||
Whichever [deities] were established there, consisting of their respective abodes,
they were worshipped in embodied form as participants in the oblation.
Having personally witnessed the oblation, they then receive it through the mouths of the fires;
satisfaction has arisen, the sacrificial rite is completed along with the sacrificial fees.
Satiated by the giving of infinite sacrificial fees, those Brahmanical deities then prepared to perform the worship of the primordial child Kṛṣṇa.
The incarnations, as well as the liberated ones, the Brahman-sages, and the great sages,
along with those dwelling in their respective worlds, set forth bearing gifts.
Musical instruments and trumpets, as well as those that produce high and pure tones—drums, kettledrums, and the like, along with water-organ pipes—were sounded. (68)
Stringed instruments, drums, conchs, bells, and likewise small cymbals, lutes, kettledrums, horns, and flutes were sounded. (69)
Then the lutes, flutes, drums, and cymbals were played, producing sweet sounds such as had never been heard before.
Then the twice-born began to employ the accents of the Vedic mantras,
and streams of blessings flowed toward Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Hari-Kṛṣṇa was sprinkled with the waters of the ocean-tīrthas,
with the waters of the Brahma-lake, and with the waters of the Gaṅgā, Virajā, and Yamunā.
Then, by the waters of the Sarasvatī, Svarṇarekhā, and Gaṇḍakī,
the youthful Kṛṣṇa shone, exalted by their splendors.
Upon his head shines a crown like ten million suns,
encircled by ten million moons, and resplendent with the Dharma of the Kali age.
Adorned with a divine peacock-feather ornament, he wore golden earrings in his ears, set with precious gems. (75)
The two beautiful earrings of Bālakṛṣṇa shine upon his ears,
and his head is adorned with a mass of matted hair fashioned with oil.
The forehead is adorned with an upright mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) made of kaisara,
while the moon [on the forehead] is auspiciously marked with sandalwood and saffron.
Likewise, the shining collyrium in her two eyes shone brightly,
while the application of sandalwood paste was marked by long, dangling streaks.
His forehead shines with beautiful lines formed by central dots;
on his right cheek, a subtle, pale dot extends far toward the eyebrow.
There is a mole on his chin and a mole on his neck;
endowed with splendor, he shines, and his cheeks are auspiciously rounded.
Having attained the state of lotuses, with eyes filled with love, they shine most charmingly with lines like red coral. 8.1.

The corners [of the eyes] extend as far as the ears; the ears are equal and capable of hearing from afar; the neck is like a conch-shell, the nape is well-formed, and the lips are red and enchanting. (82)
Resembling bows with their curved forms and endowed with sprouting shoots, those two seeds of Rati shine forth, drawing the heart of Hari toward them. (83)
With well-developed shoulders and full arms, adorned with graceful forearms,
they possess broad palms and are beautified by the three joints of their fingers.
Unstained by red lac, marked with fine crescent moons, and adorned with wheels, fish, bows, tridents, svastikas, and vajras; 85.
Adorned with the lines of longevity upon the ring finger, they are ever as clear as a mirror and capable of reflecting [the world]. (86)
His arms, with hair growing upwards, possess delicate joints and lovely fingers; turned toward his sides, they are pale white like the autumn moon.
His two sides were the abodes of desire, and his chest was beautiful, with the Śrīvatsa mark residing upon it;
his waist shone with lovely, right-turning curls of hair.
Adorned with the finest gems shimmering with golden lines, it shines with two strings of wish-fulfilling jewels that appear like necklaces without threads.
Her two breasts shine with the beauty of two dark blue pupils,
and are likewise adorned by a cluster of golden-hued body hairs.
The garden of her body-hair, which proclaims the virtue of her lack of deceit, shines forth;
and between the two lotuses, at their junction, there is a long golden line.
The line of hair on his hips, appearing like the beauty entering a painting, shines as if it were the water of a water-pot descending into his deep navel. 92.

The male organ is brilliantly radiant, adorned on the left with the beauty of sesame seeds; the two thighs possess the splendor of the interior of a plantain tree marked by the moon, and are covered with fine hairs.
With the nature of gold at their extremities, the two [eyes] shine as they move toward the imperishable;
they possess the beautiful hue of campaka flowers, are well-nourished, filled with vigor, and auspicious. (94)
Extending from the heels to the calves, and likewise upwards along the backs of the thighs, the lines of body hair appeared distinct upon the hips and reached as far as the buttocks. (99)
Two beautiful pathways to Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha exist, descending two finger-breadths below the root of his left thigh. (96)
And there is a mark of a wound from a stake, more than a finger-breadth in size, on the upper part of the left knee, a pale-colored spot upon the thigh. 97.
The sign is the lotus, the abode of Śrī, an eight-petaled lotus; it exists, rich in great splendor, as the manifest refuge of Kamalā. 98.
The two jewels Akṣaya and Vīrya are external and rest upon the bull;
the other two are hidden within, situated on the sides of the liṅga. (99)
Her navel-well shines, resplendent with its three-fold folds;
her hips are as white as the moon, soft as fresh butter.
The elephant, resplendent with hide resembling a golden girdle,
manifests with its back as a temple and its front as the abode of desire.
The shanks are rounded and globular, golden-hued, and adorned with hair;
on the side of the right shank, near the ankle, there is a black spot.
Likewise, on the right arm there shines a dot with three circles;
on the soles of the feet, which touch the lotus, there is the form of a tortoise.
It is endowed with upward lines, marked by the peaks of palaces and mountains,
and adorned with lotuses, finials, vajras, barley-ears, and other such symbols.
Adorned with sixteen, thirty-two, and eight auspicious marks and lines,
beautiful with soft fingers graced by moon-like nails, and altogether auspicious.
Resembling a white lotus, gentle, worshipped by ten million gods, touched by ten million maidens, and the abode of ten million sovereignties. || 106 ||
Victorious are the two feet of Hari, reddened by the glow of anklets, necklaces, and saffron-dyed garments, as they rest upon a golden pedestal.
His auspicious waist, marked by a golden girdle, shines forth;
his body is adorned with ornaments such as necklaces, rings, and finger-rings.
On the conch-mark between the middle fingers, there are eight wheels;
and on the palm of the left hand, there is also a large upward-pointing line.
It hangs from the base of the middle fingers down to the wrist;
its form is adorned with garlands of flower clusters and beautiful balls.
Adorned with golden ornaments, jewels, gems, and strings of pearls, as well as with various decorations of erotic charm, he shines forth most beautifully.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was resplendent in the midst of the assembly hall within the pavilion, seated upon an elephant-throne during his own great festival.
Śrī, Ramā, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Padmā— though possessing distinct forms,
all these shine forth united within the beloved Hari.
Such is this Blessed One, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person;
O Rādhikā, on his annual birthday, the All-pervading Lord shines forth in glory.
In the beautiful, supremely splendid, and delightful pavilion, which increases the splendor of the world, Hari shines resplendent in the center.
Sprinkled with fragrant Brahma-jala waters by the great sages,
Kṛṣṇa remained there all alone as a mere child among all embodied beings.
He was the object of the eyes and of the minds as well as of the hearts;
he alone existed both within and without, just as in the transcendent state of Brahman.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Splendor of the Great Pavilion, the Seating Arrangements for the Assembly, and the Description of the Adornments and Attire of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how He shines in the supreme abode;
Hari, the incarnation of the Supreme Soul, became manifest in that very form. || 1 ||
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is more than a hundred million times superior to Kṛṣṇa;
He is enriched with forms corresponding to His own form, possessing a true nature that transcends all.
He alone is the object of the eyes for all living beings;
He alone is the object of the mind, the ego, and the intellect, as well as the object of the Self.
Bearing a divine form, like a youth slightly less than sixteen years of age,
he was radiant and exceedingly brilliant, his garments glowing like a blazing fire.
His waist was adorned with a beautiful golden-colored loincloth, richly decorated with golden bells and ornaments,
as well as a white silk lower garment and a golden sash.
An excellent cloth, yellow like gold and covered with rows of stars, was placed upon his hips; likewise, a highly lustrous upper garment rested upon his shoulder.
A crown rests upon the head of this Śrī Paramātman;
it is permeated by every fragrance and endowed with divine scent.
He sat down in that auspicious pavilion, which was suitable for him and lofty;
there, upon the great altar, were excellent slabs of sandalwood.
There were four auspicious golden jars with firm feet;
each one indeed weighed as much as a thousand wrestlers.
The Gāruḍī, Nārasiṃhī, Śārabhī, and likewise the Kācchapī—these Śaktis, adorned with power, shine upon his feet. (2.21.10)
There, sixty-year-old elephants, adorned with four girth-bands and mounted by four mahouts, look magnificent as they stand tall, reaching toward the sky.
Wearing all kinds of ornaments and garments, those of golden complexion shine forth;
they have white bellies, white trunks, and white tusks, resembling the color of milk.
Upon the backs of elephants stood four auspicious golden lions, adorned with ornaments; those maned beasts, along with their trunks, reached toward the sky.
Upon the backs of the four lions, a great tortoise shines,
green in color and possessing a long, circular shell.
Behind him is the Śakti Māṇikī, whose form is divine;
richly adorned with all kinds of ornaments, she sits upon his back with her spine aligned. 15.
Upon its back was an auspicious, golden-colored, soft covering;
there lay a silken quilt, silver-hued and variegated in color.
With excellent and beautiful celestial cushions placed at her sides and back,
adorned with sacrificial blankets and rugs, that auspicious couch was seven steps wide.
Above is a parasol formed by the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa,
auspiciously bestowing divine splendor with its eyes of celestial diamonds.
There, the great king, the sovereign over the kings of kings, sat down upon a couch after placing his feet upon a footstool.
I am Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa stands at both sides;
accompanied by two chowries, the Imperishable (Akṣara) stands at the tips of His feet.
Lomaśa stood at the side of the tree with a vessel for worship in his hand,
while his mother and father sat down near Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
While this was happening, tens of millions of divine celestial chariots belonging to the gods were present in the sky at that time, stationed in pairs, in order to witness [the event].
For the purpose of worship, a beautiful and lofty ladder, consisting of a succession of steps, was constructed to ascend from the surface of the ground. ||23||
On the ground level, however, seven steps were made for the banners;
then there were two elephant trunks hanging down, which touched the banners.
Reaching down to serve as a support for the stairs, it stood like the pole of a ladder;
and from the tips of the trunks up to the frontal globes, reddish ornaments were fashioned.
The steps were bound with chains and made very firm;
right there at the two frontal globes (kumbha-sthala), a resting chamber was constructed.
Above that, two beautiful staircases were constructed for the two tusked elephants, whose trunks shone like staffs. ||27||
Then that ladder was made as far as the lion’s head;
a four-sided platform was placed upon the lion’s head, supported by a base shaped like a tortoise.
Two auspicious swans are situated at the sides of the tortoise's neck, and between their two arms, another ladder has been fashioned. (29)
With her face touching that of Māṇikī, she has two Garuḍas at her sides;
with their wings spread wide, they carry peacock-feather whisks upon the backs of swans.
Just as one touches the steps of a staircase one by one,
so indeed are the wings attached along the sides of the *māṇikī* and reaching up to the crest (*picchaka*).
Having taken his place upon a divine, vast, elevated, and beautiful throne, the Lord is worshipped there with offerings by the gods and others.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is worshipped by all;
yet neither has His seat been heard of nor seen before, O Lord of Śrī. (33)
There, Śrī Kambharā first arrived to honor him as he shone with the splendor of a sovereign king of kings. (34)
Holding a golden vessel in his hand, [he should fill it] with saffron, unbroken rice, sandalwood, musk,
bir-bir powder, and tulasī buds.
It was filled with colored powders (gulāl), sprouts, parched grain (lājā), flower garlands, ornaments,
fruits, water, sugar and other sweets, and the essence of fragrant scents.
Then, at that moment, Lomaśa spoke words of blessing:
"Oṃ, may there be well-being for Bālakṛṣṇa; may those who are liberated move about in peace. (37)
May he grant the imperishable Brahman, well-being, and long life as well!
Om! May Śrī Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa extend well-being to you. (38)
May Vāsudeva and the other lords grant well-being; may the incarnations of the lords of gods, such as Śaṅkara and others, grant well-being.
May the ṛṣis, the ancestors, the Siddhas, the holy men, and the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga [grant well-being].
May the gods and men grant well-being to the child Hari.
May all the holy fords, the Ādityas, and the Rudras grant well-being;
may the Vasus, the Nidhis, and the Vaidyas indeed bestow auspiciousness upon Hari. (41)
May the truthful ones, the virtuous maidens, and women devoted to their husbands,
as well as the deities dwelling in the forest, grant well-being to Hari. May the trees, the creepers, the celestial singers (cāraṇas), the kinnaras, and the others bring forth auspiciousness.
May the attendants, the servants, the rivers, and the streams indeed grant well-being to Hari. ||43||
May the Yakṣas, Ṛkṣas, Gandharvas, Māgadhas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Aśvakas, Vidyādharas, and Sādhyas indeed grant well-being to Hari. 44.
Mountains, mines, sacrificial posts, pits, battlefields, and forests;
the netherworlds, serpents, daityas, dānavas, and likewise asuras. ||45||
Rākṣasas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, pretas, and likewise piśācas;
mātṛs and kṛtyakās as well—those who dwell in the water and those who dwell on land. (46)
May the forest-dwellers and those who dwell in the world grant well-being to Hari;
may the sacred shrines, the mantras, the divine bodies, and the manifestations such as weapons and missiles do the same. (47)
Boys and groups of girls, the elderly, Brahmins, those born from a womb, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, those born from sprouts, and whoever else upholds well-being; ||48||
May Vināyaka, Gaṇeśa and the others, Hanumān, Garuḍa, and the attendants headed by Nanda, bring about the well-being of Hari. 49.
Rādhā, Ramā, Lalitā, Padmā, Jayā, Sarasvatī, Māṇikī, Śrī, Kamalā, Pārvatī, Prabhā, and Rati. (2.21.50)
Śāradā, Virajā, Gaṅgā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Narmadā, Sāvitrī, Mañjulā, Haṃsā, Amṛtā, Durgā, and Maṅgalā. ||51||
May the twelve beloved goddesses with their attributes grant a hundred blessings;
as do the other sixteen thousand, who possess the powers of millions, billions, and trillions.
May the sun, the moon, the planets, and so forth, bring well-being indeed to Hari;
may the principles (tattvas), the elements born of beings, and the states of existence—māyā and that which stands beyond māyā—be auspicious.
May the divine ornaments of Hari—the practitioners of yoga established in celibacy, who are the embodiments of the Vairāja qualities—grant well-being. 54.
May the various forms of the erotic sentiment, as well as musical notes and songs, and divine instruments, always bring auspiciousness to Śrī Hari. (55)
May Saṃkarṣaṇa, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Dharmarāja, and Dharmadeva—endowed with devotion—grant you well-being from Hari. (56)
May Janaka Kambharāsvāmī, the inner self and supreme self of Hari, grant well-being; may he grant well-being to himself. (57)
May Muktā, Campā, Jayā, Haimī, Ramā, Śāntā, Vrajā, Dayā, Bhānu, Dīpāvalī, and Ūrjā indeed bestow well-being upon Hari. (58)
Oṃ! May there always be perfect peace, long life free from all calamities, health, eternal happiness, and indeed the permanence of Hari. (59)
Thus Lomaśa, having consecrated him with auspicious words and with water and other substances,
as well as with barley sprouts and flowers, applied an auspicious tilaka and a crescent mark.
The mother caused him to perform worship with all its constituent rites;
the mother, the destroyer of sorrow, repeatedly placed sweet food in his mouth and offered water in her joined palms.
The mother bestowed upon his head words of blessing.
"May you indeed possess eternal life; become the Lord and Master of all.
Having said this, he placed a garland of divine flowers, fashioned like a kalpa-tree, around his neck.
Having scattered unbroken grains (akṣata) upon his head, she performed the lustration rite (nīrājana);
then, having offered a handful of flowers and bowed down, the mother returned to her own seat.
The father performed worship in this manner: "May you be well, my son;
may you be the one who joins the thread of the lineage, endowed with eternal life. (64)
Then Śrī Lomaśa, joyfully worshipping the Lord of Devas with all ritual offerings and mantras, bestowed auspicious blessings.
Through intellect, qualities, discernment, the self, devotion, and knowledge;
and through dharma and the most excellent yogic powers, may you attain eternal prosperity.
Through your divine lifespan, conduct, splendor, and strength,
and through your compassion and dispassion, may you become the eternal source of prosperity.
Through service to your mother and father, as well as through devotion to the venerable Guru, may you become one who protects those who seek refuge and attain eternal prosperity. (68)
Constantly devoted to the path of Brahman, fulfilling the desires of the mind,
possessing an even vision, a most excellent merchant, dedicated to the dharma of giving,
and a bestower of contentment upon all— may you be one whose prosperity is eternal. 69.
Thus, Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the delighter of children, was honored with blessings by Lomaśa and showered with parched grain.
Then, the opportunity for worship was granted to others;
the beloved wives of Śrī Hari, having gone to the supreme abode, were there for the sake of worship. ||71||
With the perfections of divine ritual means— namely, perfumes, sandalwood water,
jewel necklaces, beautiful garlands, and likewise flowers accompanied by the heart-mantra.
Then they performed worship and offered the *ārātrika* rite that dispels suffering;
and having placed their joined palms upon their heads, they also offered water for washing the feet.
Having drunk [the nectar], offered gifts, and applied the saffron of grace, she repeatedly touched her throat with love and gazed upon her beloved, who was dearer than life. (74)
Then Akṣara and the others departed from there in their own celestial chariots;
likewise, those liberated souls residing in Akṣara and other liberated beings also worshipped the Lord.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa accompanied by Rādhikā, and Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Śrī, as well as all the inhabitants of Goloka and the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha. ||76||
The liberated ones (muktas) reside in the four Vaikuṇṭhas, in the realms of Amṛta and Avyākṛta, in other abodes, as well as in the various manifestations (vyūhas). //77//
The incarnations and lords, headed by Sadāśiva, are equal to Mahāviṣṇu; they are Puruṣas in whom Māyā is predominant.
The Vairājas, the lords of the Brahmas and gods, the Munis, the Ṛṣis,
the Pitṛs, and millions of deities— all these dwellers of the Bhuvarloka.
Led by Bṛhaspati and led by Śukrācārya,
as well as rivers, streams, humans, mountains, trees, creepers, and so forth.
Stumps, sacred fords, shrines, men, bards and panegyrists, grass, those who dwell in battlefields, as well as beasts and birds—[all these were present]. (8.1)
The Nāgas, the best of Gandharvas, the Saurāṣṭras, the inhabitants of the earth, those from the sea, those who travel through the sky, and crores and arbuds of maidens [were there]. 82.
Likewise, all the world-protectors, the sovereign lords of the quarters, the kings, the divine kings, and the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas among the dwellers of heaven; 83.
They all honored Bālakṛṣṇa, the supreme among men, exceedingly; they applied the sectarian mark (tilaka) and the crescent moon (candraka), and they presented him with offerings. 84.
"May you be eternal and may your life be long"—thus they repeatedly offered blessings;
and all the goddesses of the entire universe assembled together like ten million wicks of a lamp. (85)
They performed the ārārtrika rite for Hari, revolving [the lamp] one hundred and one times;
then they offered handfuls of flowers and subsequently drank the water from His feet.
Having offered salutations with joined palms to the Destroyer of Suffering, they departed for their own celestial chariots;
thus indeed was the worship and the pronouncement of blessings concluded.
Then Lomaśa offered words of complete hospitality, saying:
"Śrī Harikṛṣṇa himself bestows a most auspicious welcome upon you. (88)
"By the blessing of you, the illustrious and all-honored ones, may I too attain eternal prosperity"—thus does Hari pray. (89)
"I have become one who has fulfilled his purpose; Bālakṛṣṇa is your son. Furthermore, I am to be beheld again every year and at every sacred observance. (2.21.90)
At every festival, he should be joined with excellent auspicious blessings;
here I am, a young son indeed, saluting him with reverence. 9.1.
O lords, any offense committed by me, my father,
the great seer Lomaśa, or even my mother, regarding the rites of hospitality and the like, must indeed be forgiven.
Having said this, Lomaśa spoke: "An auspicious moment for a meal is at hand;
the meal will come to your dwellings. (93)
"And the avoidance of the assembly shall result in victory; may you be victorious!
When this was said, Kṛṣṇa rose up, and the assembly likewise rose at that moment.
They returned to their own dwellings, taking with them food appropriate for each,
as well as various kinds of drink and maidens numbering in the hundreds of millions.
Assuming various forms, they became female servants and led them to their dwellings;
having gratified them with communal feasts and beds for rest, [they settled them there]. (96)
They offered service and performed excellent worship after midday;
then, having received leave, they departed for their own abodes with eager anticipation.
Then the father gave this triad as a reward to Viśvakarman:
the Kalpahāra, the Kalpasūtra, and the Kalpavallī. || 98 ||
He gave gifts to the other attendants,
and to Lomaśa he gave Kalpakanyā, born from the eternal thread.
He bestowed the supreme grace of Hari upon all those who were about to depart;
thereafter, he indeed caused the dismantling of the pavilion to be carried out.
But as for all those objects that remained there, they were given away on all sides to the destitute mendicants. || 101 ||
And to the dancing Apsarases, he gave the finest cosmetics,
necklaces, ornaments, and priceless items such as those from the Kalpa tree.
And the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, having concluded the evening festival,
attained supreme peace at night, the Blessed One who had assumed the form of a child.
Lomaśa sat upon a swing in accordance with worldly custom;
the maidens also went to Lomaśa’s hermitage.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this divine great festival of Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa was indeed celebrated at the beginning of His second year.
On this day, it increases all auspicious fortune and likewise bestows liberation upon those who remember it, recite it, and listen to it with devotion.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Seat in the Pavilion during the Grand Festival at the Beginning of the Second Year of the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, and the Narration of All the Performed Worship, Benedictions, and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, once in the past, there was a great treasure-house of austerities,
the best of sages named Cyavana, the lord of the Bhṛgus, who possessed immense ascetic power.
While visiting sacred fords, he went to Pātāla of his own accord by chance;
from there he reached Rasātala, where he beheld something beautiful.
He entered that great city of the Dānavas;
being honored on all sides by the daughters of the Nāgas, he moved about within that city.
Beholding that Cyavana, the lord of the Rasātala realm named Prahlāda performed the highest worship for the son of Bhṛgu, according to his merit.
They both inquired after each other's well-being and freedom from illness;
then, having bowed to the seated sage, Prahlāda addressed Bhārgava.
Today, by the sight of you, I have attained the fulfillment of my purpose;
for the sight of the virtuous removes sin, bestows merit, and is auspicious.
Virtuous ones such as you deliver worlds like mine;
out of compassion, they wander about for the sake of rescuing sinners.
O holy one, since you have come here intent on my rescue,
I, who dwell in the midst of Daityas and Dānavas, have been purified, O sage.
Dwell here, practice righteousness, perform sacrifices, and recite prayers and the like;
this kingdom is yours alone, and I shall serve you like a slave.
The sage said: "O devotee, it is indeed fitting for you, since you are a Vaiṣṇava;
while you, the lord of devotees and worshiper of gods and brāhmaṇas, are ruling. (2.22.10)
Kings always perform sacrifices on the earth according to the prescribed rites;
and Brāhmaṇas and others practice austerity, dharma, and undertake pilgrimages to sacred fords.
The gods exist and are free from anxiety, and the righteous laws prevail among the subjects;
O Daitya, while you remain established in the kingdom, the Dharma remains established in its excellence.
Whether in the netherworld, on earth, or in heaven, my state is the same;
wherever there is a devotee, O King, all that place is considered by me to be heaven.
"Indeed, for the sake of fulfilling your wish, I shall remain here during the northern course [of the sun];
thereafter, I shall certainly go to see the youthful Lord."
Then Prahlāda said: "Even though this has been heard by me from the mouths of the Daityas—that Hari, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, is there—" (15)
The boy shines as a sovereign upon the earth; nevertheless, tell me further:
who is he, how does he exist, and what is the nature of that Puruṣottama, the sanctifier?
I desire to see this Supreme Person who is without beginning;
tell me of His wonders, and tell me of His other holy places.
Which are the most excellent sacred sites on earth, which are in the sky, and which might be in the netherworld? Tell me this as well.
I shall go on a pilgrimage to perform the vision of the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (19)
For at that time, Cyavana spoke to Prahlāda, the foremost among devotees:
"In Saurāṣṭra is the supreme holy place, the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake."
On earth is Naimiṣāraṇya, in the intermediate space is Puṣkara;
in Rasātala is Cakratīrtha, and in Pātāla is Hāṭakeśvara.
On the mountain is the Badarī-tīrtha, in the forest is the Nārasiṃhaka;
in the water is the one reclining on the Ocean of Milk, and in heaven, on Mount Meru, is the abode of Hari.
"Thus there are sacred fords that purify even sinners.
O Rādhikā, having heard these words of Bhārgava, the king of the Daityas—
Desiring to go to the sacred fords (tīrthas), he spoke thus to the Dānavas:
"Arise! We shall go to bathe at the sacred fords on earth."
"We shall behold the Supreme Self, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Having spoken thus, the Dānavas, Daityas, Āsurās, and likewise the Rākṣasas [set forth]. (25)
They made an incomparable effort and emerged from the subterranean realm (rasātala);
together with Cyavana, they went to Śrī Hāṭakeśvara.
Having performed the ritual bathing, worship, and other rites according to the prescribed rules for the venerable Lord Hāṭakeśa,
they emerged from the subterranean realm (pātāla) through fissures in the earth and arrived at the surface in Saurāṣṭra.
Filled with joy, they performed their ablutions at the Kuṃkumavāpikā field, at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, and in front of the hermitage of Lomaśa.
That Cyavana and that Prahlāda, together with all the Daityas,
[worshipped] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in his form as a child.
He beheld that which was endowed with all manifestations, frequented by liberated maidens and others, and enchanting to all; he worshipped it and meditated upon it.
Then, having bowed to the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī and Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, and having worshipped Lomaśa, he went to the Puṣkara lake. ||3 1||
Having bathed in the Sarasvatī, he went to Dharmāraṇya;
after visiting the excellent holy sites of Meru, he then proceeded to Śrī Badarī.
There, Nara and Nārāyaṇa performed supreme austerity,
their minds intent on penance and bearing the weight of their uplifted matted locks.
He beheld the two stainless gods, sages of exceedingly gentle and steady form, wearing black antelope skins; he worshipped them with profound devotion.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā at the Śāla tree in the vicinity of the Naimiṣa forest,
that very lord of the Daityas went there and saw those two once again.
Those two best of men were ascetics dwelling in a residence made of *śāla* trees;
and at their sides were two divine bows endowed with auspicious marks.
He also took the Śārṅga and Ājagava bows, as well as two inexhaustible great quivers,
and a great-branched Śāla tree covered with arrows and weapons.
He saw other arrows stuck in his mouth, piercing one another;
then he beheld those arrows of wondrous form, serving as sacred thread-bands for the serpents.
Seeing this incomparable sight, the Daitya became enraged at the appearance of two forms;
seeing those two ascetics armed with weapons, he considered them to be hypocrites.
Pervaded by pride in his own strength, he said to the two Supreme Persons:
"Why have you begun this hypocrisy that destroys righteousness?"
"Where is asceticism, where is the mass of matted hair, and where are these two excellent weapons?
Then Nara said to the Daitya: "What anxiety do you have regarding what is done by another?"
Whatever one who possesses the necessary capacity may do, that is fitting for him;
we two are indeed ascetics, protectors, and slayers of demons. (42)
"O Lord of Daityas, do both; do not harbor pride.
Then the Lord of Diti said to them: "What power do you two have here?"
"While I, the protector of dharma and destroyer of the Daityas, remain present, the lord of the Daityas said to Nara: 'Power has been acquired by both of us.'"
No one would be able to conquer Nara and Nārāyaṇa in battle, for they are the supreme lords whose very selves are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa. 45.
Then, out of pride, Prahlāda made a vow before them:
"By whatever means possible, I shall conquer Nara and Nārāyaṇa in battle. (46)
Then Cyavana said to him: "Do not speak thus regarding Śrī Hari;
for this Blessed One can never be conquered by you through any means of destruction."
The Daitya said: "That vow which was uttered by me shall not be otherwise;
I will certainly make every effort and shall surely conquer those two. (48)
Having spoken thus and bowed to Cyavana, he strung his bow, drew it,
let out a roar, and struck the sound of the bowstring against the palm of his hand.
Having stationed his own forces in a compact formation, he prepared for battle in the forest;
then Nara, having bent the Ājagava bow, [discharged] arrows.
The bull among the Daityas released those [arrows] at him and cut them down with his own shafts;
then, seeing that his arrows had been severed by the Daitya at that very moment, Nara—
He also discharged great arrows, one after another, which were the destroyers of the Daityas;
the son of Diti struck Nara with one, Nara with two, and the Asura with three and four.
Nara released five; the son of Diti released six arrows capable of destruction;
Nara released seven; the son of Diti released eight; and Nara released three and six.
Then the Daitya [discharged] ten arrows and the man eleven; the Daitya [discharged] sixteen, the man thirty-two, and the Daitya sixty shafts.
The Daitya released a hundred men, and again two hundred;
the Daitya created three hundred men and six hundred more.
That man brought a thousand [arrows], and the Daitya brought more than a thousand;
thus, out of pride, the two of them discharged countless arrows at one another. (56)
With showers of countless arrows, Nara covered the surface of the earth;
yet the Daitya, with his own innumerable shafts, cut them down despite great effort. (57)
Then the man and the Dānava fought with excellent weapons accompanied by mantras:
Nara [discharged] the fire-weapon, the Daitya the water-weapon, and the wind-weapon and the mountain-weapon.
The Nāga missile, the Gāruḍa missile, the Dhūma missile, the Taijasa missile, the Nārī missile, the Nara missile, the Ṣaṇḍha missile, and the Yauvana missile. ||59||
Thus they both hurled [missiles] at one another with the intent to kill;
that best of Daityas discharged the most terrifying Brahmāstra.
At that very moment, Nara released the supreme Nārāyaṇa weapon;
once those two had been neutralized, Prahlāda was overcome with rage.
Seizing his mace, he swiftly leaped down from his excellent chariot;
and Nārāyaṇa, seeing him approaching with the mace, [prepared for battle].
Placing Nara behind him, he moved forward to fight;
the Daitya, having whirled his mace with speed, struck Kṛṣṇa on the head. (63)
From the two eyes of the struck Hari, much water fell;
the mace also, shattered into a hundred pieces, fell to the earth in fragments.
The Daitya, quickly mounting his chariot, took up his bow and released sharp,
bee-like arrows that possessed the luster of half-moons.
Hari pierced those [arrows] and struck the Dānava with his own shafts;
the Dānava, too, pierced Hari with stone-tipped arrows.
Thus, out of rage, they pierced each other in their vital organs;
at that time, the gods and embodied beings in the sky were desirous of witnessing it.
A gathering occurred in the sky, and drums of great sound resounded;
likewise, a rain of flowers fell upon those two bodies.
Then, having thus attained such power, both the Daitya and Nārāyaṇa bound the sky with showers of exceedingly sharp arrows.
Covering all directions, they fought most fiercely;
but Nārāyaṇa pierced that Daitya in his vital organs with arrows.
The Daitya pierced Narayana in the heart, the arms, and the face;
Nārāyaṇa, with a crescent-shaped arrow, severed the Daitya’s bow.
The Dānava, having strung another bow, rained arrows upon Hari;
Hari, having cut those [arrows], overwhelmed the Daitya with his own shafts.
Then, with a razor-edged arrow, he cut down another bow;
he likewise cut down the third, the fourth, and the fifth bow.
Then the Daitya seized a firm iron club and whirled it;
as he did so, the Blessed One cut it apart with his arrows.
Prahlāda whirled his mallet and hurled it at Nārāyaṇa;
when Hari cut that mallet with ten iron arrows, [the demon acted again].
The Daitya, bound by the noose, quickly rushed toward Śrī Hari;
Hari, however, cut the noose into many pieces with his arrow.
Taking up a spear as long as seven palm trees, the Daitya hurled it at Mādhava;
and Hari cut it to pieces with razor-headed arrows.
And the Daitya hurled a mountain peak at Mādhava;
Hari, however, tore it apart with his spear upon the chest of the Dānava.
Then the Dānava hurled a spear, equal in force to a *śakti*, with great speed;
O Rādhā, his heart pierced through, he fell down in the midst of the chariot.
Perceiving him to be unconscious, the charioteer bore him away from the battlefield;
meanwhile, the asura Nārāyaṇa regained his senses and rested.
Taking up his very firm bow, he returned once more to fight;
then, seeing him at evening, Hari spoke to the great asura.
"Go, O Lord of Daityas; we shall fight tomorrow morning. Perform your daily rites.
Having been addressed thus, he bowed and departed for Naimiṣa, and performed his daily rituals.
Thus, on that day, the great battle proceeded incessantly;
even at night, during the time of rest, the Dānava continued to reflect.
"How shall I conquer that heroic, deceitful lord who is so difficult to subdue?
Then the Dānava fought with him for many years.
And when he had not conquered the unconquerable Hari at the end of those thousand years, the Dānava approached Nārāyaṇa and spoke these words: ||85||
"For what reason, O Lord of the gods, am I unable to conquer you, the sovereign who is to be attained? Tell me the cause of this. (86)
And Nārāyaṇa said to him: "I am invincible by gods and asuras, even by all kinds of forces consisting of millions of missiles, weapons, and the like. (87)
Then Prahlāda said: "If he is indeed invincible and unconquerable, then my vow to conquer him here would become false."
"O Lord, how could I live, having been known as one who has failed in his vow?
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, in your presence I shall renounce my life. (89)
Having spoken thus, Hari sat before him, chanting the eternal Brahman; then the compassionate Lord spoke to his supreme devotee, who was filled with faith.
"Go; you shall conquer me through devotion, never by means of battle.
Then Prahlāda said, "The three worlds have already been conquered by me. (9.1)
But you have not been conquered, because you are the protector of the world;
for the sake of setting the Dharma in motion, you have undertaken the practice of asceticism. ||92||
O Lord of Gods, I shall practice supreme devotion to conquer you—the auspicious bestower of victory—through service, worship, attendance, and other such acts. 93.
I shall engage in such a battle that you may suffer defeat;
indeed, that battle so vowed will bear fruit for me.
"From now on, I shall indeed employ my weapon, which consists of devotion, toward Kṛṣṇa.
Having said this, that best of Daityas [spoke] to Andhaka, the son of Hiraṇyākṣa.
Having summoned him, the observer of vows, being delighted, said:
"O Andhaka, you must protect both the Daityas and the Dānavas as well. (96)
"Accept this kingdom surrendered by me and protect it;
I, meanwhile, shall strive through battle, asceticism, devotion, and likewise through worship. (97)
"I shall conquer Śrī Hari, the Lord of gods, the deceitful master!
Having spoken thus, the demon Andhaka seized the supreme kingdom.
Prahlāda went to the holy hermitage of Hari at Badarikāśrama,
where those two lords reside in the field of Naimiṣa and at Śālagrāma.
Beholding those two gods, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
he joined his palms in reverence and paid homage at their feet.
And Nārāyaṇa said to him: "O great Asura, why have you bowed down here without having conquered me? Tell me what you desire."
Prahlāda said: "O Blessed One, what man is capable of conquering you?
What man is superior to you? You alone are the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)."
You alone, resplendent with ascetic power, bear the mass of matted hair and the bow;
yogis contemplate you, and the wise offer you worship. 103.
The *snātaka* students chant your name; the performers of sacrifice worship you;
beautiful women delight in you; and devoted wives honor you. (104)
Those who possess sensory perception perceive you alone as the Supreme Lord;
you are the immortal Hṛṣīkeśa, the wielder of the discus, and the upholder of the earth.
You alone are the Great Fish, you are Hayashiras, and you are the one in the form of a tortoise; you are the Boar, you are the Lion, you are Brahma, the Lord of Shri, and the husband of Sati.
You are Kubera, Varuṇa, and you are Samīra, Bhāskara, and Śaśin;
you have become the self of all beings—O Mādhava, who shall conquer you?
"If you have come here to practice devotion, then submit yourself to devotion with all your heart.
Having said this, he prostrated once more at his feet.
And Nārāyaṇa said to him, "O sinless one, I am well-pleased with you;
for today I have been conquered by you through your undivided devotion."
"A defeated man pays a fine to his conqueror;
for the sake of that fine, I shall grant you whatever boon you desire."
Prahlāda said: "May my physical, mental, and vocal sins—whatever was committed by me while fighting—go to destruction. (111)
Whatever thought may arise in my mind, O Viṣṇu, let it be centered on you;
let it be intensely devoted to the worship of the gods, focused on you, and dedicated solely to you.
"May my supreme delight always be in your lotus feet.
Nārāyaṇa said to him, "So be it for you forever."
Furthermore, by my grace, O lord of devotees, you shall forever be imperishable, immutable, undecaying, and even immortal.
From here go to the supreme and most excellent Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā where Puruṣottama resides.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the glorious Supreme Lord;
having seen Him, having meditated upon that Śrī Hari, and having placed that Lord within his heart. (116)
Having received the great mantra from Lomaśa, Pāvana then said:
"Go, O tiger among devotees, to your own abode, intent on your religious duties."
Commanding all the Daityas, protect the kingdom eternally;
practice deceit and exercise authority in a manner consistent with your own kind.
No bondage of karma shall accrue to you, O Mṛtyu;
become the instructor of what is beneficial and the preceptor of the Daityas and Dānavas.
Having been addressed thus, he bowed to Hari, the divine Nara, and asked for his forgiveness;
then, accompanied by Cyavana, he went to Lomaśa’s hermitage in Saurāṣṭra.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, he beheld Puruṣottama;
having performed his bath in the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he worshipped Keśava.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; obeisance!
Having received the mantra and stayed for only a month, he departed for his home. (122)
He ruled over the city named Aśmaka and the subterranean realm of Rasātala;
he was seen and honored by the Dānavas, including Andhaka and others.
Worshipping the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he practiced the ninefold devotion, including meditation, ritual service, and other such acts.
Thus it has been told, O Rādhā, that Janārdana is won over by devotion;
yet even by a demon, through supreme devotion, the Supreme Lord was conquered.
In the second year, during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Daitya Cyavana resided at that great tīrtha called Cyāvana on the southern bank of the Hari.
The Aśvapaṭṭasara lake is indeed called Prāhlādika;
it is said that Prahlāda taught that mantra to the Daityas and Danujas.
Those lords who had descended to the netherworld also became devotees;
they worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa day and night.
Thus has this been told to you, O Rādhā; it is the destroyer of all sins,
the supreme means of accomplishment, the eternal and firm deliverer of the Daityas,
the bestower of victory, peace, prosperity, and everlasting joy.
"Bestowing the feet of Hari through study and hearing, it is the supreme giver of liberation.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Prahlāda’s Return to Earth from Rasātala for the Purpose of Pilgrimage by Means of Cyavana’s Yoga, His Battle with Nara-Nārāyaṇa, the Defeat of Nārāyaṇa through Devotion, and the Arrival of Prahlāda and Cyavana at the Hermitage of Lomaśa," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then those Dānavas, O Rādhikā, desired to see Kṛṣṇa immediately—
that child who is indeed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Instructed by Prahlāda, they desire to practice that devotion by whose majesty this lord of the Daityas conquered the Lord Hari.
Listen, O Rādhā, to that story of how those lords of the Dānavas,
having come together, became devotees of Hari and were engaged in his worship.
Those belonging to the lineage of Andhaka, those born in the lineage of Prahlāda,
and those born in the lineages of Kujambha, Jambha, and Śaṅkukarṇa.
There were also those born of the lineage of Maya and Dundubhi, as well as Śambara;
and the Dānavas and others born of the lineage of Ayaḥśaṅku and Vṛtra.
They remembered the brahmin Cyavana, the guide who showed the path to Prahlāda;
and Cyavana quickly appeared before them.
Having been saluted, honored, and questioned regarding his welfare,
Sukeśin, the eldest son of Vidyutkeśin, spoke to him.
I wish to question you; this doubt resides within my heart: what is the highest good in the next world, and what indeed is it in this one, O best of the twice-born? (8)
"By what means would one become worthy of honor among the virtuous, and by what does one increase in happiness?"—
thus were the Daityas, born of a noble lineage, questioned by Cyavana at that time.

Having reflected, he spoke for the sake of the highest good in this world and the next: "Merit is the highest good, as is dharma; it is beneficial in every way, both here and in the hereafter. (2.23.10)
One who relies upon the Dharma is worthy of honor among the virtuous and shall always be happy;
for one's own Dharma is right conduct, which brings peace to oneself and others and is a source of happiness. (11)
Bestowing peace upon one’s own self and always granting merit and happiness, the supreme duty for human beings consists of rites such as sacrifices and the like.
By what acquired do men become happy both in this world and the next: the study of sacred texts, the knowledge of reality, and likewise the worship of Viṣṇu? (13)
The protection of the gods' offerings, the acceptance of worship, the guardianship of subjects, and so forth—by means of that which was acquired [through these], they enjoy happiness. (14)
The Daityas possess great strength of arm, warfare, and even the art of salutation;
through that which has been acquired by him, their policy, devotion, and surrender have become sources of happiness.
The perfected ones possess the perfection of yoga, self-study, contemplation on Brahman, devotion, worship, and peace; by means of that which has been acquired, they are happy.
For the Gandharvas, there is song and dance, instrumental music, and speech that flows with sweetness;
and through the service of the great ones performed by means of that which was earned, you shall find happiness. (17)
The auspicious knowledge, discernment, manly effort, and intellect of the Vidyādharas, as well as their constant devotion to Nārāyaṇī—by that which they have earned, you shall be happy. (18)

Through that merit he acquired, you have attained skill in the solar devotion of the Kinnaras, in the Gandharva arts such as singing, and in the expression of humor and other sentiments; by this, you are happy.
The artisans’ skill in their craft, their contemplation of Nārāyaṇa, and their devotion to helping others—by means of that merit they have earned, you shall find happiness. (2.23.20)
The restraint of the senses and the faculties, freedom from pride, and constant devotion to the Supreme Lord—by means of that which you have earned through these, you shall attain happiness. (2.1)
The sages possess virtue, truthfulness, recitation, knowledge, forbearance, compassion, and a stainless inner heart; by means of that which they have acquired, they are happy. (22)
For those who are renounced, virtuous, and noble, service to their husband consists of offering him to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and remaining free from worldly attachment. 23.
Devotion to Hari should always be practiced; by that which is earned, your happinesses [shall arise].
The preservation of wealth, the enjoyment of it, its giving away, and service for the sake of others—[these are the uses of wealth]. (24)
By that which was earned by him, the Guhyakas obtained happiness;
for their devotion was aroused, yet the greed of Rākṣasas lies in seizing the property of others. (25)
Or rather, through devotion to Hari, your pleasures shall be acquired by that very devotion;
for lack of discernment, impurity, and untruthfulness are the characteristics of demons.
Through that which was earned by you, there were the pleasures of eating food, alms, and delicacies;
through that which was earned by you, there were the pleasures of being served by others among the animals. ||27||
Thus have been described these sixteen meritorious dharmas that grant liberation;
those established in dharma are always happy according to their respective castes. (28)
Among all dharmas, these are supreme and common to all:
the vehicle of the ford-makers, worship of the Lord, service to others, and austerity. (29)
Non-violence, contentment, and the chanting of Hari’s name as obtained through right conduct—whatever embodied beings may rely upon these virtues, [they shall attain the supreme goal]. (2.23.30)
Those who take refuge in Brahman certainly attain eternal liberation;
those who walk the path of righteousness are happy, while those whose sins have not been removed are miserable.
Having heard these words of Cyavana, the Daityas, seeking happiness and desiring his welfare,
took refuge at the feet of Prahlāda and considered him their true sanctuary for spiritual well-being.
And they asked Cyavana about the most excellent of all supreme holy places;
then Cyavana told them of the holy place Śrī Hāṭakeśvara.
The supreme sacred site of Badarīvana, Śrī Puruṣottama, the holy field of Śrī Gaṇḍakītīrtha, as well as Māthura and Puṣkara. ||34||
There lies Aśvapaṭṭasara, the most excellent among the best of holy places (tīrthas),
as well as the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Saurāṣṭra is the most excellent in every respect, graced by the Supreme Lord;
there dwells the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the form of a child. (36)
The Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, the most excellent of persons, the sovereign master of all abodes, and the cause of all causes, dwells there. (37)
He is the Lord who brings about all descents, the true master of all prosperity and other blessings;
he is the bestower of all liberation and supernatural powers, and the abode of impartial compassion toward all. ||38||
That sacred ford is the most excellent among all sacred fords;
having performed one's desired rites there and attained [the goal], one rejoices in all states of peace. (39)
Having heard this from Cyavana, the Daityas, desiring to visit sacred fords,
then took Cyavana with them and went to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
The Daityas and Dānavas, as well as their wives, sons, and others, joyfully went to the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā for the sake of visiting the holy site. ||41||
Through the occasion of Cyavana’s discourse and by the instruction of Prahlāda and others, they have come to behold the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||42||
Having descended from the sky to the hermitage of Lomaśa, those Dānavas, together with their families, bowed down before Lomaśa along with Cyavana.
Having observed the supreme devotion of the Dānavas, the sage Lomaśa,
together with Cyavana, offered them a most cordial welcome.
He offered the madhuparka, a seat, and other items, as well as water for drinking;
he provided delightful dwellings fashioned like those produced by the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa).
And from the city named Aśmaka, [he brought] more than a hundred most beautiful, highly prosperous palaces,
rich in all things and resembling the moon in luster.
Abounding in baths, food, and beds, adorned with assembly halls and pavilions, pervaded by gardens and groves, and possessing cool, pleasant, and delightful breezes. ||47||
The sage gave [them] those who were delighted by the fragrant perfumes of sandalwood, agallochum, and musk, who were provided with all necessary requisites, and who were devoted to service. 48.
Cyavana became very pleased because of Lomaśa’s state of distress; he then spoke to the Daityas and Dānavas: "The sages are without possessions. (49)
Free from partiality and the like, devoid of passion and hatred, intent on the welfare of all living beings, and tranquil, they indeed liberate people from sin. (2.23.50)
He in whom an equal disposition toward both enemy and friend is observed—he alone should be known as the giver of liberation, the most excellent and purifying sacred ford. 51.
By the grace of Lomaśa and by the water, all the masses of terrible sins born of your previous births shall indeed come to an end.
Therefore, serve the brahmin Śrīlomaśa with joyful hearts;
dwell here for some time and earn the instruction [of the Dharma]. (53)
Compared to stationary sacred sites (*tīrtha*), a moving one is a swift purifier;
virtuous people (*sādhu*) are the supreme sacred site, destroying sin through their very touch. (54)
Through prostration, service, massaging the feet, and pleasing them,
as well as by giving desired objects, they deliver even the sinful.
Service to the virtuous burns away even the greatest of great sins;
indeed, the virtuous are to be fed, honored, and beheld. ||56||
For the virtuous are indeed to be touched, bowed to, and gratified;
for the virtuous are indeed to be served by the offering of everything one possesses. ||57||
Meeting with anyone is easy, but meeting with the virtuous is difficult;
therefore, one must indeed please the virtuous through body, mind, and speech. (58)
Devoted to the culmination of meditation, treasuries of merit, radiant with austerity, intent upon the Supreme Brahman, dedicated to the welfare of their disciples, they were beloved. (59)
Being givers of all that is auspicious, they should be served for one's own liberation;
for [through them] one attains the state of a Dānava, the state of a Daitya, the state of a human, or the sovereignty of the gods.
It is certainly not eternal for the selves, for that [suffering] arises from the birth of the body and so forth;
indeed, upon the dissolution of the body, everything adventitious perishes. (61)
"This family and so forth are mine; this kingdom is mine; these are my kinsmen, sons, wife, and husband"—all such [notions] are false, produced by egoism. (62)
When the seed consisting of the ego-sense has departed, the latent impression will also depart;
and when the storehouse of karma is destroyed, where is there room for the state of a demon, and where for the state of a disciple? (63)
The Self, however, possesses its etymological designation through association with a illusory body:
since he was born from Diti, he is called a Daitya; and since he was born from Danu, he is called a Dānava. (64)
