He who is unborn and conscious is said to be "born" by virtue of being born [into] a body;
yet the Self is certainly not the body that is born, and therefore the Self does not participate in names.
In whatever place one is born, there alone one's offspring is produced;
however, attachment here is like a crucible, arising through the power of "mine-ness" within illusion.
Therefore, you are not inhabitants of the netherworld or the subterranean depths;
nor are you Daityas, nor are you truly heroes, because all of that is merely a portion of the body.
And by the yoga of the virtuous, the virtuous were born here at this lake;
having bathed and drunk the water here, the dust-particles of Lomaśa [became] living beings.
"You are purified by this connection with the sacred ford; receive the supreme mantra, honor this guru, and thereafter worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (69)
"We shall go indeed for the sake of seeing him; you will certainly attain the highest good.
Thus addressed, ten thousand Dānavas and Daityas [prepared to depart].
Having bathed at the Aśvapaṭṭasara tīrtha and having bowed to the sage Lomaśa, they venerated the site of Prāhlādika with great respect.
Having drunk the water used for washing the feet, they bowed to that sage Lomaśa and respectfully worshipped him with sandalwood paste, flowers, and garlands.
And they received the great mantra, which is purifying and bestows all happiness:
*Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā*. (73)
Having taken him up and reciting the mantra, those Vaiṣṇavas likewise [placed] a Tulasī garland on his neck and a forehead mark with a drop (bindu) upon his brow. (74)
Taking up the excellent food—consisting of what is to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked—they stood in rows, having received that which was offered by Lomaśa. (75)
In the hermitage of Lomaśa, they took sweet drinks and betel;
Cyavana too, having performed his twilight prayers, ate with joy. (76)
Then they all went to their own dwellings to obtain rest;
thereafter, at evening, they all indeed took up their offerings.
Desiring a vision of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
they went to the seven-storied palace of Śrī Kambharā Lakṣmī.
There, the Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa shines upon a swing,
and the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa holds his son by the hand.
Having arrived, he sat down appropriately upon the lion-throne;
both Lomaśa and Cyavana were there, accompanied by their disciples and hosts of Daityas.
And when they had arrived, their father himself offered them seats and then personally extended a welcome and hospitality to the Daityas as well. (81)
Having been offered seats, those Daityas, overwhelmed by their prostration,
considered themselves to have fulfilled their purpose upon seeing Lord Hari.
For a moment, they attained steadiness; with steady eyes and stable dispositions, they gazed at the Lord with supreme wonder.
Having gazed for a moment at Bālakṛṣṇa, who then appeared in the form of a youth—
possessing a supreme, radiant beauty that was perfectly suited to his divine form— (84)
There, upon the image, [he should worship] Prahlāda, and after him Śukrācārya;
then Kaśyapa, Diti, Dānu, and the patriarch Dakṣa. ||85||
And Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu, his grandfathers;
likewise Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu with four arms. (86)
Then there is the form of Vairāja and the fourteen worlds;
therein is Rasātala, and therein the supreme city of Aśmaka.
There, they all quickly beheld their own dwellings, their own family members, and their own forms. 88.
There, five thousand maidens of purified souls chose the youthful Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa as their husband. 89.
They beheld him thus; then Hari, having appeared in the form of a child, again assumed the form of a youth there.
Having beheld this, they were overwhelmed by supreme wonder;
they worshipped Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe. 91.
They first offered gifts and water for washing the feet;
then all those Daityas and Dānavas, as well as their wives, drank [the water]. 92.
Their daughters, numbering five thousand and possessing divine forms, were then transfixed by Śrī Hari; absorbed in meditation, they remained steadfast.
Thereafter, they chose Kṛṣṇa as their husband according to their own desire.
O Lord of the World, grant devotion to Your lotus feet. 94.
"Grant us liberation and grant eternal happiness, O Lord of the World!
"So be it for you," replied Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (95)
"A place has been granted, and devotion, liberation, and likewise happiness have been bestowed.
When he had spoken thus, those women of divine form indeed became so at that very moment. (96)
Those wives, numbering five thousand, quickly became the feet of Hari;
having obtained their lord, the master Hari, they stood there holding his feet.
They remained in the hermitage of Lomaśa, for they were protected by the beloved of Śrī;
then both Lomaśa and Cyavana, having worshipped Śrī Hari, [departed]. (98)
By the command of Śrī Hari, those maidens joyfully protected their own hermitage;
they were then established among the thousands of maidens on Mount Arbuda. By the grace of Śrī Hari, ten thousand Daityas quickly [arrived].
Desiring to go to Vaikuṇṭha, they chose that abode there;
and Hari, having endowed them with divine forms, led them to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then the Lord presented all those gifts which he had previously given to the maidens.
Śrī Hari himself gave suitable gifts to the two sages;
then, assuming the form of a child, he arrived at Dattela. Cyavana, having bowed to Lomaśa, offered auspicious blessings to the maidens.
Having given [these gifts], he went on a pilgrimage to the supreme Puṣkara forest.
Prahlāda, indeed, lived for a long time and eventually departed for the netherworld (rasātala).
Thus, O Rādhikā, is the account of that Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe.

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, during the second year, this exceedingly divine narrative became known; through its recitation and hearing, it bestows supreme liberation, as well as prosperity, longevity, and the granting of sons, grandsons, and wealth. (105)
"Since Hari is won over by compassion, he bestows unbroken prosperity.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Ten Thousand Daityas and Dānavas Residing in Rasātala and Other Regions, and the Choosing of Bālakṛṣṇa by the Five Thousand Maidens," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, at the beginning of his third year,
his father performed a great festival according to the prescribed rites, even more excellent than that of his second year.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he performed the saṃskāra of the tonsure ceremony,
having first performed an auspicious bath and the worship of the Mothers and other rites.
One should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha, the recitation of the Svasti-mantras, and the fire-oblation (homa) in the Sabhya-fire;
then, having set out the vessels, one should place them on the ground to the south of the fire.
Then, having placed twenty-one auspicious bunches of *darbha* grass, and having placed red cow-dung and other materials on the left side of the fire; || 4 ||
Thereafter, his father placed the cooked kṛśara-rice in a vessel;
having performed the *vyāhṛti*-oblations and other rites, he took up an iron razor.
Having first performed the shaving of the small tufts of hair situated on the southern and northern parts,
the father then gradually performed the shaving of the hair within the womb.
He had his son's hair cut by a barber, leaving a tuft on the crown;
he gave gifts such as cows and fed the Brahmins and yogis.
He gratified the inhabitants of the fourteen worlds;
he honored Lomaśa and fed the maidens.
On that day, he fed virtuous men, virtuous women, and guests;
he caused morsels of food for cows and flour-cakes along with grains to be given to all living beings.
In this way, he indeed performed the tonsure ceremony (*caula-saṃskāra*), which destroys all evil;
for although Śrī Hari is the destroyer of sin, how could there be any sin [in him]?
Nevertheless, for the sake of protecting the world and for the preservation of the Vedic path,
his father indeed performed that auspicious and appropriate consecration ceremony.
Having heard that, Rādhā then questioned Kṛṣṇa with humility: "May there indeed be welfare for the boys and the girls. (1.2)
For those whose hearts are pure, not overly agitated, and like a clear mirror, who enjoy moving at will, eating at will, and dwelling as they please; || 13 ||
"What indeed is that sin of theirs which is destroyed by the *caula* ceremony?
O Rādhikā, listen as Śrī Kṛṣṇa speaks of the transgression of children. (14)
Indeed, sins committed in previous lives follow one even from another birth;
whether from heaven or from hell, it is the residue of karma that follows him.

That very dwelling of the self which occurs in the womb, in the receptacle of urine, within the element characterized by fire and subject to falling, and accompanied by passion— that indeed arises from sin.
There, the arising of the body is produced by merit and demerit;
and dwelling in water during a fainting spell results only in demerit. (17)
Birth is indeed a great suffering, as is dependence on others due to one's sins;
even the act of living, such as drinking milk and so forth, arises from merit and demerit. (18)
Contact with feces, urine, and the like, as well as being bitten by insects and such, muteness, and incapacity arise solely from sin. (19)
Indeed, these very sins committed by him in the past manifest themselves at the time of birth, providing nothing but suffering in every way.
O beloved, those who possess no sin indeed have that Self like Rudra;
such a wise one is mind-born, equal to Sanaka and others, and not born from a womb.
Now, the removal of impurity arises through refinement alone;
for one whose body is unrefined, purification must be achieved through its very nature. ||22||
Indeed, the sins of previous births, along with impurity, grow upon the head in the form of black-colored hairs. (23)
The hair of the womb is the root of sin; its destruction brings about the destruction of sin.
Therefore, the rite of tonsure (caula) is indeed prescribed for children.
Because sin is dissolved by it, that tonsure is known as *caula*.
Now hear another thing, O Rādhā: indeed, the hair has been cut. (25)
There is a reason why matted locks grow with such speed;
indeed, the roots are the cause even in the case of new hair. (26)
Furthermore, by means of the rite known as *śukla*, that matted hair (*jaṭā*) shall come to be;
therefore, the matted hair or the top-knot (*śikhā*), according to the *Śuklasaṃhitā*, must always be protected.
And just as the fool indeed grows, so too does merit, demerit, or mixed karma arise through his actions. (28)
In this matter, it is declared that [the property] up to five years is indeed to be enjoyed by the father;
beyond five years, it is to be enjoyed by oneself, for it settles upon one's own hair.
Therefore, hair and body hair indeed become the stains of sin;
all these are merely useless cleansers of filth for the father of refuse.
Therefore, one should especially perform the shaving of the head at a sacred ford (tīrtha);
that cutting of the hair should be understood as the removal of sin.
In this manner, having shaved [the hair] on the third year,
they should thereafter shave it as desired all around, except for the *brahmarandhra*.
Or rather, let these meritorious matted locks—refined, beautiful, and faultless—be preserved;
for as long as those black locks of yours are visible to people, [so long shall you be honored]. (33)
Sensual objects cause embodied beings to commit sins only so long as they are not like the aged, whose white hairs reach to their ears; for such elders are indeed not defiled by them.
Therefore, for one who is old, there is no longer any traditional injunction regarding merit and demerit;
all of that is specifically declared to apply to one in the middle stage of life. (35)
Thus, O Rādhikā, the purifying *caula* sacrament was performed.
Rādhikā said: "O Blessed One, the accumulation of sins from my previous births—" [36]
"How does the child staying in the womb remain upon the body hairs?
O Rādhā, listen; Śrī Kṛṣṇa said, 'I shall tell you that.'"
In ancient times, there was a person named Adharma who arose from the back of Brahmā;
he was joined with his wife Hiṃsā, and from them was born their son Pāpa.
Devoted to his parents yet sinful, he did not leave his mother and father alone for even a moment, remaining close to them at all times and in every condition.
Where there is unrighteousness and violence, there the wicked prevail;
where there is neither unrighteousness nor violence, there the wicked do not exist. (2.24.40)
But for those souls who are situated in the womb, unripened, inactive, powerless, devoid of qualities, and enveloped by the membrane, there is no sin in causing them harm. ||41||
How indeed should one dwell there with evil committed in the past?
For if one abandons the sinner, the evil is not expiated without resentment. (42)
Then it goes far away; where could it stay without a support?
What is produced by one does not remain elsewhere, yet it departs. (43)
Whatever has been performed by someone remains entirely within that very person;
its destruction occurs after the experience [of its result], as is determined by its full extent. //44//
According to this principle, the son named Pāpa informed his father that while the child was in the womb, there was neither unrighteousness nor any act of violence.
"How can I remain there in that state without those two?
Having reflected thus, he spoke to his son, who was unrighteousness and known by the name Pāpa: 46.
"Son, come with me; I shall petition the Grandfather.
Whatever he may grant you for the sake of a dwelling, there you shall reside. (47)
Having spoken thus and taken that son with him, Adharma went to Aja;
and having paid obeisance to his father, he sat down before him. (48)
Brahmā questioned that son, who was accompanied by his own son, regarding the *Āgamakṛti*:
"Tell me quickly, how and for what purpose have you come here with your son? (49)
Adharma said, "O Blessed One, this son of yours is named Pāpa;
wherever there is violence, there I am always intent on dwelling. (2.24.50)
But for those living beings residing in the womb, both [of these] do not exist;
tell me now, how can they remain there due to their previous sins? (5.1)
Having reflected thus, Brahmā spoke accordingly to the one within the womb:
"By my command, you must indeed remain in the form of hair, which is of a sinful nature."
Then the wicked one, remaining in his own abode, attained supreme satisfaction,
even though he remained there for three years without his parents.
Then Brahmā, for the sake of destroying sin, produced through his own volition sixteen purifying sons who are the very rites of consecration (saṃskāras).
And therein, the sacrament of the tonsure (caula), which consists of the hair and destroys sins, was ordained;
likewise, other rites that destroy evil were performed.
Thus, O Rādhikā, for the sake of protecting the creation,
that which was performed by Brahmā in accordance with the previous creation has been described.
In that very same manner, for the sake of instructing the worlds, Hari’s father also performed the auspicious sacrament known as *caula*. (57)
If, however, there was astonishment there, then I shall tell you:
it was something never seen nor heard before by those who came earlier or even earlier still. (58)
O Rādhā, when I arrived there at that time, I saw those very hairs which had been removed from the head by the barber. (59)
When they were all cast into the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
then thousands of divine, auspicious, four-armed Nārāyaṇas appeared.
They bear the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus; they are adorned with frowning brows, wear golden earrings, are clothed in fire-like garments, and are attended by Lakṣmī.
Mounted upon the sons of Vinatā, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns,
the Blessed Ones shone forth, adorned with the Kaustubha gem and marked with the tilaka.
Then, at that time, they all appeared equal and similar;
first with eight arms, and from that very state, with sixteen arms.
Thereafter, Nārāyaṇas with thirty-two arms, then with a hundred thousand arms, and thousands of others in divine forms were seen. (64)
Thus, that mass of a hundred thousand head-hairs, which is indeed of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, was seen at that time; those hairs were short and possessed four arms.
Then there were seen long-necked Nārāyaṇas with eight arms;
beyond them were those with even longer hair who possessed sixteen arms.
Then his hair became extremely long, and indeed he had thirty-two arms;
thus his hair grew longer and longer, and he came to have hundreds of arms.
And thousands of Nārāyaṇas with a thousand arms were seen;
and those Śrīs who were with them were likewise seen with such arms.
Those pairs, numbering one hundred thousand, praised the Supreme Lord:
"O you whose hair is Nārāyaṇa, we are situated within your form. (69)
You are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
you are the source of innumerable incarnations, higher than the highest.
We remain merged within your form by your will;
and at the proper times, we emerge as the protectors of the universe. (71)
And we shall remain as your blessed servants for as long as your command endures; yet at your will, O Kṛṣṇa, we shall indeed undergo our own dissolution.
We worship you, we bow to you, and we carry out your command;
for we, O Kṛṣṇa, though born separately, are your very form, O Lord. (73)
"O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Imperishable! Give us instruction as to where we must go and where we must dwell; we shall act accordingly. (74)
And as for those other multitudes of hairs upon your form,
they too are indeed beginningless and liberated, whether they be innate or adventitious.
The liberated ones, the liberated women, the Brahmas, and the attendants of Brahma—those divine qualities that dwell in Your form, O Hari, belong to them as well. (76)
All the Viṣṇus are served by the maidservants of Lakṣmī;
and those ornaments which are upon your form are your own powers (śaktis).
By the command of Rādhā and Ramā, Lakṣmī, Pārvatī, Lalitā, Prabhā, Māṇikī, Mañjulā, and others indeed dwell there in the form of divine love. 78.
Those pearls, which are the very nature of ornaments, are indeed distinct from other pearls;
and Vāsudeva and the others are the very essence of your adornment.

O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, there exist manifestations such as Nakhā and others who are lords of lords; they are non-different from you, being merely distinct designations for your incarnations whose specific powers are not established separately. (2.24.80)
All of them dwell within you, hidden in the form of your own body;
we are your very nature as hair, yet we have become separate by your will.
Having received the *caula* sacrament, they have assumed their incarnate forms;
therefore, grant us permission to dwell [here], and we shall do so accordingly. (82)
Thus spoke the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
having been entreated for the sake of his command, he was pleased with them in his own presence.
And having summoned the *tilakas*— drops of saffron filaments—
and having applied them upon their foreheads, the Lord of Syllables spoke.
You are my incarnations and bearers of my auspicious sovereignty;
understand that multitudes of cosmic eggs are constantly produced by me.
"O venerable Narāyaṇas, by my command, go now to those who have produced Golakas today—those who possess but a single portion of the [Vedic] marks. (86)
Likewise, you went to the fourteen egg-worlds as four-armed ones;
likewise, you went to the twenty-eight terrestrial globes as eight-armed ones. (87)
Go to the fifty-six egg-stages with sixteen arms;
go to the one hundred and eight earth-stages with thirty-two arms. ||88||
Go to the Pañcaśata-taraṇḍaka with a hundred or more arms; go to the Sahasrabhūmikaṇḍaka with a thousand arms. (89)
In each individual egg, only one person such as myself is authorized here;
likewise, a new and fresh Brahmāṇḍa proceeds forth one by one.
Behold, whatever egg is seen by whichever eye of your own hand, that very thing shall enter it through the power of my yoga. 91.
Having been addressed thus, those forms of the illustrious Nārāyaṇa bowed and departed;
observing their respective cosmic eggs, they rested for as long as their lifespan lasted.
When they had all departed, Lomaśa said to Keśava:
"Show me those very cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) within which they reside."
Having heard this and smiling, Hari then touched Lomaśa on the eyes with his finger and water; he immediately became divine.
With divine vision, he beheld these incarnations and the *golaka*s;
overcome by supreme wonder, he indeed realized their majesty.
Then, he performed the ritual exemption from the sacrament known as *caula* (the tonsure ceremony) for the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, according to the prescribed rite.
Having given many gifts, Hari returned to his palace;
seeing the marvel, his father and mother attained great joy. (97)
Lomaśa, accompanied by a group of maidens, went to the hermitage;
thus, O Rādhā, has been described the activity of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa. 98.
It is inaccessible in every way to worldly beings and is to be realized through divine grace;
by reading it or even hearing it, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 99.
It bestows cattle and sons, grants grain and wealth, destroys sin,
grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa, and likewise grants the state of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sins in the Hairs Regarding the *Caula* Initiation of Lord Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, and the Description of the Hairs as Being the Form of Nārāyaṇa," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhā, to the purifying story of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
it took place in the third year, on the first lunar day (pratipad) of the month of Phālguna.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, Gopālakṛṣṇa celebrated the great festival of the flower-swing in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī.
When spring arrived there, the *kiṃśuka* trees, glowing with the brilliance of fire, shone constantly even though they were leafless, beautifying the surface of the earth.
O beloved, the lion of spring has arrived, having torn apart the elephant named Śiśira with his claws, as it were, by means of the blossoms of the Palāśa tree.
Then the ponds laughed constantly with their teeth-like lotus stalks,
and the forests of flowering *karṇikāra* trees shone brilliantly.
The red Aśoka groves, suddenly ablaze with blossoms, shine forth;
swarms of bees, turning the thickets golden-brown, gleam within the dense forest.
The cane trees on the riverbanks shine with clusters of blossoms;
O slender Rādhikā, you have the red Aśoka tree for hands and the Kiṃśuka tree for feet.
Dark-complexioned, she holds blue *aśoka* flowers; her face is like a blooming lotus, her eyes are like blue water-lilies, and her breasts are like *bilva* fruits of medium size. (8)
Her teeth are like blossoming kunda flowers;
she is adorned with hands like flower-clusters; her lower lip is like the bandhujīva; and her fresh sprouts are like the white sinduvāra.
Divine, with the voice of the male cuckoo, auspiciously clad in *kaṅkola* garments,
she possessed the beauty of a peacock’s plumage and the sound of cranes for her anklets;
the lovely *prāgvaṃśa* hall was her girdle, and her gait was like that of an intoxicated swan.
She was adorned with a line of body hair that resembled a cluster of *putrajīva* flowers.
The splendor of spring has arrived at the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa;
the lotuses, whose eyes are the waters, gaze with affection. 1.2.
The waves, with their hands of water, repeatedly call out to those who bathe;
the thundering of the water expresses laughter and joy. (13)
The parrots moving about his side announce the arrival of the rainy season,
and breezes carrying cool droplets draw the mind toward it.
The water-fowls invite even the sky, rich with stars;
and the Rohiṇa fish, submerged in the water, remind one of virtuous men.
In this world, the cry of the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird creates a desire for bathing in children, while the excellent dance of the peacock even brings them delight. (16)
When the youth of spring had arrived, the cuckoos on the flowering branches seemed to repeatedly call out to Hari with their warbling, as if inviting him to bathe.
Having thus beheld that forest, so serene and in full bloom, all the brahmins stood upon the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Then, by the thousands, young boys, girls,
and women went forth with eager minds to celebrate the festival of the flower-swing.
And having fastened pleasant swings upon the branches of the Kadamba trees, young boys, girls, maidens, and others swing back and forth.
And likewise, having filled jars and other vessels with filaments of the palāśa tree—yellow, red, green, and brown—in various colors. (21)
In the springtime, men and women took delight on the bridge with splashes of dust,
splashes of water, splashes of color, and sprays of gulāla powder.
On the bank of the lake, they took delight with saffron and red powders,
seizing one another in the morning and forcibly throwing each other down.
Eagerly, they repeatedly sprinkle themselves with the water from the Gargarī stage and smear their faces and other parts of the body with the sacred clay of the lake. (24)
Some sprinkle streams of water upon their heads with mechanical devices, while others dance, holding clusters of flowers to their ears. (25)
Some, filled with joy, sing the songs of Kṛṣṇa;
others wash their soiled bodies and their garments.
Shaking their heads, they brush away the hair grey with dust;
they wipe the dust from their eyes and enter the waters of the lake.
People cross over by various means of transport, they bathe together in the waters, and men and women wash garments dyed with colors. (28)
Young boys and girls delight in the groves of flower-clusters;
men and women delight in their own groups and shower [offerings]. (29)
Having played musical instruments, they also worshiped Vasanta,
having fashioned a golden image adorned with yellow garments.
Adorned with red flowers, wearing a crown together with earrings,
equipped with a girdle and anklets, and beautifully dressed in a bodice— thus she is most radiant.
Having attained the state of youth, she was captivating with her side-long glances;
seated upon a flower-chariot, gentle, and with a crest made of flower-clusters.

Her ears were adorned with clusters and bunches of flowers, and she was anointed with fragrant unguents; her shoulders shone with a mass of matted hair, and she was resplendent with a golden parasol. ||33||
She has a sun-gem at the edge of her garment and a moon as her upper cloth; she is adorned with a crown beautified by diamonds, gems, and fine pearls.
She has flowers as her crest-ornament, flowers at her waist, and is adorned with floral coverings;
she is richly decorated with garlands of *kadamba* flowers and a forehead-mark of *cāmpeya*.

Her forearms were like *karṇikāra* flowers, her arms were as beautiful as *pālāśa* leaves, she was adorned with clusters of *japā* flowers, and her beard-like hair was like blue water-lilies (*aindīvāra*).
Her eyes were like variegated flowers, she was radiant with jasmine-like teeth,
endowed with a nose as beautiful as a sesame flower, and her cheeks were adorned like kadamba blossoms.
Her forehead was richly adorned with plantain flowers, her thighs were like plantain trunks, her hips possessed the grace of a kālāra lotus, and her navel was beautiful with its golden luster.
Her shanks were like the trunks of elephants, her soles were marked with lotuses,
her nails had the subtle form of the moon, and she was pale-complexioned with a gentle smile.
All human beings worshipped the image of Vasantadeva with beautiful flowers, saffron and other pigments, as well as with ears of grain and fine śigru plants.
With saffron, bilva powder, gulāla, and pure celestial substances;
with flower clusters, red leaves, and various kinds of fruits. ||41||
They worshipped Śrī Vasantaka with milk-preparations and very liquid offerings; having also bathed Śrī Vasantaka with various melodies (rāgas), they honored him. 42.
They honored Vasanta, the lord of the flower-buds, with springtime garments and other ornaments, with floral scarves, and with garlands of flowers. (43)
The Lord of the flower-clusters and sprouts, the Sovereign of the shoots, the Master, the Lord of flowers, the Lord of the stalks, and the Season; 44.
On the bank of the lake, they worshipped Śādvaleśa, the beautiful youth, as well as other beloveds of Spring: the cuckoo and the female swan. 45.
The sixteen beloved wives worshipped Sārasī, Sumanā, Menā, Māyūrikā, Bhāsikā, Śukī, and Gāruḍī.
All those maidens were the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, beautiful with various colors, possessing a golden luster, and faces filled with the brilliance of the moon. ||47||
Some wear white garments, some yellowish-brown, some wear green robes; some are clad in brownish-red garments, and likewise others wear variegated clothes.
Some wore garments of golden luster, others wore brownish-red robes; some were clad in blue, some in white, and others were distinguished by their variegated attire. ||49||
Adorned with silken garments and wearing white raiment,
the women of spring, radiant with the splendor of their ornaments, paid their respects.
They worshipped him with sandalwood, agallochum, musk, saffron, unbroken grains, and water,
as well as with milk-puddings and other offerings, and with betel leaves.
Then the Blessed Lord, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of a youth, appeared there on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having established the season named Śrīvasanta upon a swing, accompanied by sixteen Āryās,
he worshipped it with various ritual offerings.
Then Vasantaka performed the nightly lamp-offering there;
accompanied by his sixteen wives, he indeed became manifest at that time.
And, possessing the form described above, he spoke to the worshipful Lord, the beloved and enchanting Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 55.
O Supreme Lord, adopting worldly custom, you, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), perform worship for me and grant to yourself the state of being worshipped by all the gods and others. (56)
Today I have become purified, along with my wife, as your servant;
I desire to worship you, so please sit upon this excellent seat. (57)
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Vasantasena, together with her beloved, descended from her own seat,
stood upon the ground, and [addressed] her lord, Puruṣottama.
Having placed [the image] upon a swing, Ṛtu, together with all his wives, worshipped it with devotion using the sixteen articles of worship. (59)
There she worshipped Śrī Hari, who had assumed the form of a youth;
having beheld Puruṣottama, whose every limb was perfectly proportioned to his beauty.
All those people, Vāsantī and the others,
as well as all the women of the spring season, were utterly bewildered by Your divine form, O Lord.
The sages and the wives of the sages were bewildered by the Supreme Lord;
thus for a moment they became motionless, stunned, and filled with bliss.
Then, by the side-long glance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which was filled with laughter and serenity,
they immediately thereafter regained awareness of their own selves.
They praised Śrī Hari, the beloved Supreme Lord who grants all desires:
"You alone exist as the Blessed One, the Lord of the lords of all worlds. (64)
O Lord, You who are endowed with all sovereignty, the manifest Supreme Person from time immemorial,
grant me Your feet forever so that I may serve them.
"Without you, everything indeed exists as fruitless and devoid of happiness";
having spoken thus, the people and women fell at the feet of Hari.
Hari said, "So be it; it shall happen thus, there is no doubt.
Thereafter, Keśava again displayed a miracle.
In the body of spring, the Lord’s own pervasive form is manifest; Śrī Hari himself is seen by all the beautiful women of spring. 68.
In the spring, when Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was the Lord, Master, and Protector, Kalikā and the others became infatuated upon seeing him as their husband and lord. (69)
These sixteen beloved ones chose this very youth, the Supreme Person; they purified him and praised him again and again.
They offered garlands and then fashioned the crescent moon;
Hari, perceiving in his mind their well-cultivated desire for self-surrender, [accepted it].
"So be it," said the Lord Hari, assuming the form of a youth;
and then the glorious Lord performed [the marriage] of the sixteen maidens.
Each of the two forms, however, is both divine and non-divine;
that which is non-divine, being equal to a deity, is indeed the sixteenth form. (73)
Then he gave to Vasantā that divine form of sixteen aspects, which was the beautiful form of the maidens; he concealed it within his own beloved wife.
There, in that hermitage among millions of maidens, he gave [himself] to Lomaśa for the sake of his residence;
thereafter, Kṛṣṇa assumed the form of a child.
While his mother went to the shore of a lake to bathe Hari, who was covered in paint,
a great demon staying in the water assumed the form of a fish.
The serpent, measuring thirty cubits in length, seized the child Kṛṣṇa;
thereupon the mother became overwhelmed with distress, fearing the loss of her son.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
Who was that great fish, the king of demons, who came there, O Kṛṣṇa, and stood ready to devour the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa? (78)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The great Daitya Sālamāla, born from the hair and skin of Hiraṇyakaśipu,
lived in the forest of Sālemāla, causing terror to the world.
In the eastern region of Saurāṣṭra, there was a great asura who fed on forest fare;
he was seven palm trees in height and one palm tree in width, resembling a mountain peak.
Bearing a mace and a club, and dancing while remembering his enmity toward his father, he then became like a dark cloud in the middle of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. ||8 1 ||
Then that Daitya, assuming a form at will and possessing thirty arms and eyes,
seized with his tail the boy who was bathing on the bank.
And standing on the beautiful, heart-stealing staircase by his mother's side, the child, an ocean of compassion, recognized that it was appropriate for the subduing of the demon. (83)
As he arrived swiftly to slay him and lead him to the bottom of the water, Bālakṛṣṇa then became twofold: a boy and a crocodile.
Having quickly become a boy, he stood upon the steps at the edge of the lake;
then, having become a crocodile in the midst of the water, he was fifty cubits in height.
In order to swallow the great fish, he indeed quickly turned onto his back;
out of fear of death, the fish fled across the surface of the water. (86)
Abandoning his form as a fish, that great Daitya Sālemāla became a man holding a mace and seized that fish. ||87||
The crocodile killed [the other] with speed, while that crocodile entered the water;
however, the man bearing the mace became seven palm trees tall.
A great battle took place there between Sālamāla and Nārāyaṇa, both exceedingly powerful, fought with maces. (89)
The mace, struck forcefully by Sāla upon the head of Hari, shattered into a hundred pieces; for Hari was as firm as a thunderbolt at that time.
The great lord struck that Daitya with his very mace;
struck upon the chest, he quickly fell down unconscious.
Rising again, he forcefully hurled his own mallet;
however, it was shattered against Hari's club by the blow of his fist.
Weaponless and wearing a garland of *sāla* flowers, he leapt into the sky like a mountain peak;
seizing the tip of Mudgala's spear, he brought it down upon Hari. (93)
And the Blessed One struck the mallet with his own club;
the Great Lord released the Sudarśana [discus] in order to destroy it. || 94 ||
Equal to a hundred suns, filled with garlands of blazing flames, and whirling rapidly, it fell upon the head of Śāla and severed his head. (95)
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there, and all the gods were filled with joy:
"This Sālemāla, who was as large as a krośa in body, is dead. (96)
He fell upon the earth, destroying trees and shaking the ground;
his soul attained liberation through union with the discus of Hari. (97)
By means of a most divine celestial chariot, Sālaka reached Vaikuṇṭha;
however, Garuḍa [took] his body from the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Seizing him by his feet, she carried him away and released him from the path of the sky upon the mountain Yaśodānottara, in the forest named Sālemāla.
There, those foremost of Daityas who had been born together with him,
as well as even his hundred wives, fell into the deepest grief.
Seeing their beloved fallen from the sky, they wept bitterly; then, in accordance with his caste, they performed the funeral rites for him.
Five hundred Daityas, one hundred wives,
and even a thousand sons found no happiness, being consumed by grief.
They all constantly contemplated how to dispel that enmity;
then, the Blessed One, having become a boy, appeared here in the vicinity of Aśvapaṭṭa.
Having celebrated the festival of the flower-swing, she returned home with her parents;
meanwhile, by his command, the maidens went to the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
Then the sages and their wives departed for their respective abodes;
and Hari’s father tied a protective cord (*rakṣāsūtra*) made of *caurṇaka* grass upon his hand.
Thus, during the festival of the swing, O Rādhikā, the Supreme Soul Nārāyaṇa displayed his miraculous power and destroyed the demon.
Whether by reciting or even by hearing it, a man, a woman, a maiden, a child, an ascetic, or even a youth shall obtain all auspicious fortune.
O beloved Rādhā, mistress of the shoreless ocean, by hearing with devotion that story of Hari— who is attainable through grace— one shall reach the supreme abode.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Blossoming of Spring, the Festival of the Flower Swing, and the Destruction by Hari of the Asura Sālamālā—who had assumed the form of a *timiṅgila* fish and arrived for the purpose of [attacking] Hari"—in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O daughter of Vṛṣabhānu, listen to another marvelous deed of Hari arising from His third year, which bestows happiness; I shall relate it. (1)
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, all the Brāhmaṇas residing at Kuṅkumavāpikā gathered on the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake for the sacrificial festival of the Brahma-thread.
Nine thousand sages, including Lomaśa and others, holding darbha grass, assembled at the Brahma-thread for the sake of purification through the sacraments.

Together with their vessels and accompanied by offerings for the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) and so forth, they performed the purification of the body through ablutions with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, as well as the libations to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa).
They also performed the worship of the gods and the offering of oblations;
they put on bright new sacred threads (yajñopavītas). || 5 ||
For that reason, they performed a great festival on the bank for Mahārudra and the daily Viṣṇu-sacrifice, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and dancing.
Through the teachings and narrations of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
the cooks [gathered] on the shore of the lake beneath a banyan tree in the kitchen.
Powdered sweets, pearl-like laddukas, pūrikās, apūpas, and milk-rice (pāyasa);
śrīkhaṇḍa, kvathikā, phullavaṭī, and various side dishes served on platters.
Likewise, there were soups and boiled rice, as well as sweet and bitter liquids; mustard-based curries, pickles, and fried cakes.
They caused food to be cooked in great abundance for the sake of tens of millions and hundreds of billions of brahmins;
there were mountains of cooked rice and lakes of ghee and milk.
Rivers of buttermilk and lakes of milk-rice were created and fashioned by the great sages, who were themselves like wish-fulfilling trees.
While the midday oblation was being performed there in the sacrificial fire,
an army consisting of the sons of the Daityas arrived from the sky.
That distance from the sacrificial ground was indeed only one krośa;
having heard their lamentation, the sage Lomaśa [listened].
And he quickly beheld with his divine vision the Dānavas,
together with the Dānavī women, holding weapons and missiles and bound in fetters.
But for the sake of avenging Sālemāla, those extremely cruel ones had assembled and stood ready, desiring to fight. || 15 ||
"This is the region of our enemy, and this indeed is the black palace; here is Lomaśa, the foremost of the twice-born. Let them strike them down and let them kill them! || 16 ||
"Our lord father has been killed by this Bālakṛṣṇa;
let them crush Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as his parents and Lomaśa! (17)
Let this village of hermitages and even the trees of these brahmins be split, cut down, set ablaze, and destroyed in an instant. || 18 ||
A thousand Sāla-sons, servants, female slaves, and kinsmen of Sālamāla fell down upon the bank of the lake. (19)
And others— maidens, wives of the Daityas, children, the elderly, and those in the prime of youth— descend with speed along the path of the sky.
And while they had not yet reached the sacrificial ground,
Lomaśa paralyzed them in the sky with Atharvanic spells.
At that very moment, he paralyzed those standing on the bank and at its side,
as well as the cooked foods and the sacrifice, so that they would not fall into ruin.
Having done so, Lomaśa indeed remembered the Lord, the Master of Śrī;
and Bālakṛṣṇa, appearing as a youth, arrived at the sacrifice in an instant.
Honored by the brahmins and worshipped, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Sudarśana and requested by them along with Garuḍa, set out to repel the army of the Daityas.
Having quickly bowed to the sages, the wielder of the conch, discus,
and mace swiftly mounted Garuḍa and departed for the path of the sky.
Having gone into the presence of the army, Hari himself blew his conch;
meanwhile, Lomaśa countered it with Atharvan mantras.
The conscious army fell upon Śrī Hari to fight;
with his mace, Śrī Hari crushed the army on all sides.
Then Garuḍa struck him in many ways with his two wings, his talons, and his beak, and cast him down upon the ground.
He caused the remainder to flee and protected the women;
then the Daityas, being put to flight, seized rocks and trees.
Turning back, they struck Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person;
thereupon, the Blessed One himself released the Sudarśana discus.
He cut down all those asuras born of the Salva lineage;
their splendors, having returned to Hari, came to rest within him.
Their wives and daughters, all standing at Vaṃśavaṭa, praised the Supreme Lord, and he granted them a boon.
O Kṛṣṇa, grant liberation to these Daityas and likewise to us;
protect us, protect us, O ocean of mercy! Grant us your refuge.
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, seated upon the glorious Garuḍa,
burned away their sins with the splendor of His discus.
Having fashioned bodies beyond compare and assuming divine forms, those women joyfully sought refuge in the Blessed One, who, being their protector, granted them his own protection. (35)
The Supreme Lord directed them to stay in the hermitage of Lomaśa;
Lomaśa, having sprinkled them with water and bathed them in the waters, [dismissed them]. (36)
Having performed purification with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) thereafter, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (37)
Having given them the mantra, a garland of tulasī, the tilaka, and other rites,
he initiated them all and made them Vaiṣṇavas.
Then he fed five hundred and one hundred women,
and he also sent the mothers and the maidens back to the hermitage.
Then the sages, headed by Lomaśa, having performed the ritual procedures of the sacrifice,
donned their sacrificial threads, and completed the final oblation.
The lords fed the maidens by the millions to their hearts' content;
likewise, they fed the householders and the guests. 41.
And they gave excellent gifts of various kinds:
cattle, fields, forests, jewels, garments, ornaments, and houses. ||42||
Having given vehicles with their furnishings, as well as draft animals, food, and water— having thus bestowed these gifts and completed the sacrificial rites.
Speaking of this supreme wonder, they went to their respective homes with joy;
and Gopālaka-kṛṣṇa also then departed together with Bāla-kṛṣṇa.
The bird went to his own abode, and from there he proceeded to Vaikuṇṭha;
meanwhile, Lomaśa and the others, filled with joy, returned to their own hermitages. 45.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, all those foremost demons of Sālemāla were slain by Śrī Hari, and they went to Vaikuṇṭha itself.
The maidens staying in Lomaśa’s hermitage chose Hari as their husband;
so too did his mothers and those wives of the Daityas who had entered the state of widowhood.
They questioned Lomaśa, the bull among sages, regarding their own welfare:
"O learned one, by what action here might there be prosperity for us in both worlds? (48)
In that same way, O eminent sage, Lomaśa then showed compassion toward the wives of the Daityas and toward their daughters in every respect. (49)
He spoke of those dharmas that always bring about the highest good and bestow prosperity:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, generosity, forbearance, self-restraint, and compassion.
Humility, purity, austerity, celibacy, auspicious speech, and service to the virtuous—these bestow the supreme good. ||51||
This Dharma, protected by men and women, constitutes a thirteenth part;
it bestows worldly happiness as well as eternal spiritual welfare.
Devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, tending the sacred fire, ritual bathing, subsisting on alms, service to the guru, and bringing about the guru’s satisfaction. ||53||
For it bestows both worldly happiness and eternal spiritual welfare;
one should dwell constantly in the house of the guru, as well as with his wife and his sons and so forth.
Regarding them as gods and likewise regarding them as goddesses, she should always worship them;
and by serving them free from pride, she certainly conquers death. (55)
By cultivating the self, she who virtuously and with devotion properly gratifies the ancestors, the gods, and guests, certainly conquers death. (56)
Good conduct must always be protected by Daityas, gods, and humans alike;
for one devoid of good conduct, there is no well-being here or in the hereafter. (57)
In this world, sacrifice, charity, and austerity always lead to prosperity;
yet for one devoid of right conduct, even these become entirely fruitless. (58)
For a woman of evil conduct does not find joy either in this world or the next;
therefore, one should always exert effort in virtuous conduct, for that is the destroyer of misfortune. (59)
For the tree of virtuous conduct exists within the body of a woman;
it descends even into the body of her offspring, bringing them happiness.
Dharma is the root of that tree; Artha is its well-developed branches;
Kāma is its beautiful flowers; and Mokṣa is its fruit endowed with flavor.
This practice, when cultivated by a noble woman, brings auspiciousness both in this world and the next.
At the first *muhūrta* of the Brahma-hour, she should wake up and remember Hari;
she should also utter the morning benedictions to the gods, the sages, and the virtuous women.
Śaṅkara, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, spoke these supreme auspicious words.
Listen as I relate that morning auspiciousness which, when recited by a mortal at dawn, liberates one from the bondage of sin. (64)
By hearing, remembering, and reciting this, one is liberated from all sins;
many have attained liberation through the chanting of this auspicious hymn.

May the Lord Kṛṣṇa—the Supreme Controller, who is unborn, beginningless, transcendent to the imperishable, and the source of all incarnations—and likewise the liberated souls existing throughout countless creations, grant me a truly auspicious dawn that bears the fruit of liberation. 66.
Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Rādhā and served by countless cowherds and beautiful gopīs, resides within the lotus of the heart;
likewise are Lakṣmī, Ramāpati, and his foremost attendants.
May they bring about for me an auspicious dawn that bears the fruit of liberation. ||67||
The supreme lords accompanied by Śrī Vāsudeva, the various Nārāyaṇas residing in diverse abodes, the liberated ones,
and those possessing the splendor of rubies, coral, and lotuses.
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation. ||68||
Hiraṇyagarbha, Hari, Śaṅkara, Sūrya, and Candra;
the Son of Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), Guru, Śukra, and Dharma;
the Sages, Śani, the Pitṛs, Īśa, Gaṇeśvara, and [the rest].
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation. ||69||
Raibhya, Gautama, Pulastya, Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Lomaśa, Gālava, and others;
Vasiṣṭha, Bhārgava, Ribhu, Cyavana, and the rest.
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation for me.
The illustrious attendants— Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatkumāra, as well as Saurabha, Piṅgala, Sanātana, Nārada, and others;
Indra and the other guardians of the quarters, along with millions of gods.
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation for me. ||7 1 ||

The seven musical notes, the surfaces of the earth, the extremely subtle elements, the gross aggregates of principles, the mountains and oceans, the sacred fords, the best of rivers, and devoted wives— [all these are manifestations of her].
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation. ||72||
Rukmāṅgada, Dhruva, Suyajña, Kapila, Puṇḍarīka, Prahlāda, Sūta, Śatadhanu, Suvarcaka, Ambarīṣa,
Śrīkṛṣṇavallabha, Divodāsa, Śuka, and others.
May my auspicious dawn bring about the fruit of liberation. ||73||
Thus, at dawn, one should hear, recite, or remember this supreme purifier with devotion; then a true auspicious morning shall surely come to pass—of this there is no doubt. (74)
Having remembered Hari, performed purification of the body, and bathed according to the prescribed rules,
one should likewise perform the libation (tarpaṇa), the twilight prayers (sandhyā), and the worship of Śrī Hari.
She should apply a forehead mark (tilaka) and a crescent-shaped mark (candraka), and also perform the worship of the gods;
she should bow to the sun and pay homage to her parents and her husband. (76)
Having bowed to the Guru, having bowed to the virtuous woman, and having bowed to the cow, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
In the morning, one should look upon curd, dūrvā grass, clarified butter, and a cow with her calf.
A water-pot, a bull, gold, a svastika, honey, cow dung, unbroken grains, parched rice, earth, and Brahmin maidens; ||78||
White flowers, grain, fire, sandalwood, the arka plant, the aśvattha tree, a virtuous person, a mirror, and an image of Hari; ||79||
One should honor a guest with sincere devotion and cultivate the company of the virtuous;
one should certainly not perform an oil massage on Sunday, nor consume milk on Tuesday.
On a Wednesday, one should not approach a woman; nor should one approach one's wife on a sacred festival day (parvan).
One should never sleep with the head pointing north, nor with the head pointing west.
One should perform a circumambulation— bestowing merit like that of a bull— around a temple, a sacred tree, a learned man, a crossroads, and an elder teacher.
One should never wear a garment that has been worn by another or is soiled;
one should bathe daily, especially at the commencement of a planetary transit, and perform offerings to the gods and acts of charity.
One should dwell among the virtuous, but not among the wicked; one should dwell in holy places, and never among people who harbor enmity or are devoid of dharma.

Those who have recently given birth, eunuchs, cats, mice, and cocks; outcasts, those who have cast off their sacred thread, the naked, Cāṇḍālas, and those who are most base—these are not to be fed. 85.
A Brahmin woman and a Brahmin who are both unchaste are called "birth-impure" (sūtika); the food of those two is censured. (86)
He who does not offer oblations at the proper time, who does not bathe, and who does not give gifts—
deprived of the worship of ancestors and gods, he is proclaimed a eunuch.
He who mutters prayers, performs austerities, and even studies for the sake of hypocrisy, and who does not strive for the sake of the next world, is proclaimed to be a cat. (88)
When wealth exists, he neither eats, nor gives, nor offers oblations; they call him a rat, and his food must not be eaten by one who follows the Dharma. (89)
He who, being a member of an assembly, resorts to partiality, they call a cock; his food and water are greatly despised. (2.26.90)
One who abandons his own duty and adopts the duty of another is considered fallen;
as are those who abandon the gods, the ancestors, and their guru, and those who cause harm to cows, Brahmins, and women. 9.1
That food which has been cast away, or which is defiled by sin, should not be eaten;
nor [the food] of those families in which there is no Veda, no sacred discourse, and no religious observance.
They are declared to be naked; their food is defiled by ritual impurity. They are those who do not give to those afflicted by hunger, and who forbid the giver from giving. (93)
That lowest of men, a Cāṇḍāla, who abandons one who has come for refuge—one must not eat his food; otherwise, one becomes a partaker in his fault. (94)

Furthermore, whatever action one performs such that one’s own self does not feel any sense of loathing in any way—that should be done without hesitation, for it will be the supreme bestower of welfare. (95)
For a virtuous woman who possesses such conduct, whether she dwells at home or in the forest, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa will surely be attained; of this there is no doubt. (96)
Sleeping on the ground, celibacy, self-realization through austerities, the renunciation of all attachments, and constant remembrance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (97)
The total surrender to Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Guru who is the inner self of all—by performing this, one is never stained by actions born of the body. (98)
"O ladies, you must by all means serve Hari, the eternal Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, in his form as a child; supreme liberation will then come to pass. (99)
And for that woman by whom self-surrender has been performed here, supreme liberation occurs in her abode; of this there is no doubt. (2.26.10)

Whether in sleep or wakefulness, in the dream state or the waking state, whether in the gross or the subtle, within the heart or in the rajasic, tamasic, or sattvic states—let them remember Mādhava. (101)
Let them propitiate that Lord Hari with their own selves, with their senses, with their bodies, through service, with their internal organs, and through their actions. 102.
Thus addressed, they received the name-mantra from Lomaśa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. (103)
Thus they recited this [mantra] day and night without weariness;
having done so for a hundred years, they attained divinity by virtue of their constant chanting.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, appearing as a child, arrived traveling in a celestial chariot,
accompanied by a hundred such chariots.
Mādhava caused them to ascend the foremost of celestial chariots and led them to the supreme abode,
which is indeed higher than even the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Then those maidens, having received that instruction from their preceptor Lomaśa, considered the boy Kṛṣṇa to be their own husband.
At that time, thousands of virtuous women remained right there among the maidens;
by reciting or even hearing [this], one shall obtain Bālakṛṣṇa. 108.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of the Daityas of the Sāla and Mālava Lineages at the Festival of the Sacrificial Thread on the Shore of the Lake on the Full Moon Day of Śrāvaṇa, Their Battle with the Lord, Their Destruction, and the Mokṣadharma taught by Lomaśa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; indeed, the gods, the Daityas, the millions of Dānavas, humans, sages, and the virtuous are all equal sons of Hari.
O Rādhikā, no one whatsoever is either disliked or liked by Him;
the devotee is dear, but the non-devotee is not, for Mādhava is fond of devotion.
O beloved, neither asuras, nor gods, nor daityas, nor humans are distinct from the Self;
rather, daityas, gods, asuras, and humans arise from their own natures born of the [three] qualities.
Intrinsic natures arise and pass away, following the force of purpose;
that purpose is happiness, and it follows the particularity of one's body and birth.
The body is considered to be of three kinds: female, male, and neuter;
and it is also [divided] as child, youth, and old man, or as householder, renunciant, and one observing vows in the forest.
Action conforms to the body, and desire follows the body;
one plays in childhood, attains tranquility in old age, but the youth does not [attain it].
Every woman is dependent on a man, while a man is constrained by his own independence; a Brahmin is a beggar, whereas the Kshatriya is always powerful through force.
In the dog and such, endurance is constant; in the serpent, it is not found at all.
In the tree there is service to others, and in the monkey, there is only self-interest. (8)
Compassion resides in the virtuous, pride in the wealthy, humility in the wretched,
affectionate devotion toward one's mother, and cruelty toward the enemy.
Cruelty is found in a thief; deliberation before acting in one possessed of learning;
modesty among the ranks of young women; and freedom from fault in a child. (2.27.10)
Nakedness indicates freedom from passion, while wearing new clothes indicates the presence of passion;
the Self exists like the sky, and the body is like the twilight, day, or night. 1.11.
The impulses of its qualities come and go according to necessity;
that illusion consists of those qualities, it is insentient, composed of karma, and eternal.
She is not attached to the self, nor is the self born therein;
there is a distinct path for each between the eternally bound and the utterly liberated.
O Rādhikā, knowing this, a person is never corrupted;
for when there is ignorance, both passion and hatred arise, which are the two defects.
From passion arises an activity that is intense with latent impressions and firm;
from hatred, one either desists or engages in something exceedingly cruel. (15)
They carry what is undesirable, concealed by what is desired, and possess an asuric disposition;
these very ones, having bodies like Daityas, depart from the Supreme Self.
When those gods become divine beings, they approach [the state of divinity] through non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses. || 17 ||
Generosity, compassion, patience, celibacy, freedom from pride, virtue, truthfulness, sweet speech, and constant delight in purposeful action. (18)
The practice of virtuous conduct bestows the status of divinity.
In ancient times, a Daitya named Sukeśin went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Having heard these thirteen auspicious teachings from the great seer Lomaśa, he questioned him further regarding the dharmas; thereafter, he departed for his own city.
Having summoned all the Rākṣasas, he spoke these righteous words:
"O Asuras, you must always protect the great dharmas beginning with non-violence. (21)
"Therefore, I command you all: let this be done without hesitation.
Then, at the word of Sukeśin, all the night-stalkers [acted].
With joyful minds, we performed the rite for thirteen parts;
thereafter, those night-stalkers attained even greater prosperity.
Possessing great prosperity through palaces, groves, fields, gardens, and vehicles, they were endowed with sons, grandsons, and wealth, and were indeed filled with happiness. ||24||
The city of the night-stalkers in the sky became filled with splendor,
such that there was no longer any need for the light of the sun or the moon.
Then, by the splendor of those high-souled Rākṣasas,
neither the sun, nor the stars, nor the moon were able to move.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the power of Dharma possesses such intense splendor that,
because of it, the city of the night-stalkers became illuminated throughout the three worlds.
By day it was like the sun, and by night it was indeed like the moon;
there, no regard for the splendor of the sun or the moon was found. (28)
On the contrary, because of the majesty of its splendor, day always prevails upon the earth and among all the planets by means of that very city alone. (29)
The movement of the sun in the sky is not perceived; likewise, the movement of the moon in the firmament is not known at all—how then could the movement of anything else be known? (2.27.30)
But Kauśika and the other night-stalkers were bewildered without the night;
having fallen into distress as householders, they were deprived of the duties of women [which depend] upon the night.
Then some reasoned: "Surely at night she was deeply distressed, for a beloved wife, a virtuous and devoted companion, cannot endure separation from her husband. (32)
For while her beloved was away in a foreign land, she, distressed by the pain of separation,
performed such austerities that she obstructed the setting of the sun.
The sight of her beloved was a union; the night did not pass for them in that way, as the sacrificers remained with their officiating priests in the fire-chambers during the ritual.
O Rādhikā, even at night they continued their ritual activities;
the great devotees of the Lord performed the worship of Viṣṇu with devotion. (35)
Other beings worship the Sun, others the Moon, and others Brahmā or Hara, thinking [of them as such] both by day and by night. (36)
The discerning, however, know the rising of the sun by the blooming lotuses, and the rising of the moon by the blossoming night-lilies. (37)
When the city of the night-stalkers had thus been brought under their power by the bulls,
the Sun, unable to endure that, devised a means to thwart it.
Then he was beheld by Bhānu with eyes inflamed by wrath.
Then Sukeśī, together with his village, blazed up in the sky.
The Sun quickly released his own solar disc at him;
that disc indeed shattered the city of that night-stalker.
Falling from the sky along with Keśin and the Rākṣasas,
Sukeśī cried out loudly, "Obeisance to Śambhu!
Then, hearing that cry of distress on Kailāsa, the Lord Śaṅkara—
Having perceived through meditation that the city of Bhakta had been struck down by Sūrya,
Śambhu, filled with wrath, gazed at Sūrya with his third eye.
Sūrya, fallen from the sky, plummeted to the surface of the earth.
From the place where the Lord of Yogis reclines up to the vision of Keśava—
from Prayāga as far as Keśava— the auspicious surface of the earth is vast.
This is the meritorious field of Hari, the city named Vārāṇasī; he fell within the space between this [city] and the Varaṇā river. 45.
Then the Sun, having scorched her for a moment, plunged into this lake;
thereafter, plunging into the Varaṇā and the Gaṅgā, he became known by the name Lolārka.
Then that Sun-god begged the Earth for forgiveness;
Hara, taking the Sun in his hand, placed him upon the chariot.
He also established Sukeśin as the lord of the city in heaven like a god;
for even a powerful Rākṣasa is born through righteousness in this manner.
Śambhu became his ally, and Sūrya obtained the fruit of his wrath;
thus indeed did Lomaśa bestow auspicious bulls upon the daughters of the Daityas.
He spoke of those things that bring about the highest good, and they questioned him again with reverence:
"O Lord, O Sovereign Guru, tell us: whose worship is it, and how should it be performed? (2.27.50)
Lomaśa said to them: "Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, sleeps upon the body of the serpent from the morning of the eleventh day of the month of Āṣāḍha."
Having made a couch of the coils of the serpent Śeṣa and having worshipped Keśava,
one should cause the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa to rest for a moment.
On the thirteenth day, Kāma himself sleeps upon his auspicious bed,
which is fashioned with the fragrant blossoms of Kadamba trees.
At that time, there, Kāma—the lord of delight and passion—should be worshipped especially with beautiful amorous gestures; he is the bestower of happiness within the form of Kṛṣṇa. (54)
Then, on the fourteenth day, the yakṣas sleep peacefully and coolly upon a couch fashioned from golden lotuses, provided with comfortable pillows. (55)
The Lord of Yakṣas, accompanied by Yakṣas and joined by Maṇibhadra and others,
should be worshipped with food, drink, and other offerings, and especially gratified.
On the full moon day, the Lord of Umā sleeps upon a bed of his own skin,
having bound up his mass of matted hair with another animal hide.
And there Śambhu is to be worshipped with dhattūra flowers and other excellent offerings;
thereafter, the Sun enters the zodiac sign of Cancer.
Therefore, for the immortals, the night becomes the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
Then, O beloved, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, Brahmā [arises] from the one made of blue lotuses.
On the second day, Viśvakarman sleeps upon his bed with the desire to contemplate the welfare of the worlds; on the third day, however, it is Pārvatī.
Vināyaka sleeps on the fourth day, and Dharmarāja also on the fifth;
Skanda sleeps on the sixth, and the Lord Ravi on the seventh.
Likewise, on the eighth day Kātyāyanī sleeps, on the ninth Kamalālayā,
and on the tenth the lords of serpents sleep, subsisting only on air.
On the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, the Sādhyas and the gods sleep;
on that respective lunar day, a virtuous woman should perform the worship of those deities.
Therefore, being observant of her vows, she should follow you for every kind of welfare;
for on the second lunar day, Viśvakarman Prajāpati sleeps.
When Hari is joined with Lakṣmī, his image should be fashioned;
he should be made of gold, four-armed, and marked with the Śrīvatsa.
On a bed that is level in its beauty and provided with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship Kṛṣṇa and place excellent fruits upon it.
Having thus offered fragrant substances, one should pray to the glorious Hari:
"O Lord, just as you shine with Śrī on the Aśūnyaśayana day... (67)
And likewise, may your bed never be empty; may it always be mine, and may your bed, joined with Lakṣmī, never be empty at any time. (68)
"In the same way, may my household life not be empty;
may Lakṣmīdhara be gracious"—having uttered this, one should perform the vow. (69)
During the four-month period, one should eat food free from oil and alkaline substances, having addressed a twice-born man with the words, "May Lakṣmīdhara be pleased with me. (2.27.70)
The observer of the vow should bestow as a gift fruit, gold, clothing, a bed, and a cow;
by that merit of the vow-observer, he rejoices happily in the state of a householder. (71)
The Sun, having reached the month of Āṣāḍha, becomes oriented toward Gemini;
from that point onward, he indeed shines until he is situated in Scorpio.
O Rādhikā, during that period between the two Cāturmāsya festivals, the gods awaken one after another there for those seeking the vow of enlightenment.
When the sun is situated in Libra, Lord Hari Kṛṣṇa awakens;
his worship should be performed with great gifts, offerings, and other rites. (74)
Thereupon, Kāmadeva awakens there; one should worship him. On the second day, however, there is a golden image of Lakṣmīdhara. (75)
A bed equipped with a coverlet, according to one's own means, should be given here as part of this vow; by this, there shall be no separation between husband and wife.
Now, the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada is considered Kālāṣṭamī;
on this day, when conjoined with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, Śaṅkara sleeps within the Liṅga.
One should bathe [the deity] with cow urine or even with water, and likewise perform an ablution for Śiva;
thereafter, one should worship him with flowers of the dhattūra plant and with sandalwood paste.
One should offer incense made from saffron resin, as well as food offerings of honey and clarified butter, while reciting the invocation:
"May Virūpākṣa be pleased with me. (79)
In the month of Āśvina, one should bathe [the deity] or perform the ritual bath oneself; then, worship with cow dung, offer lotuses, incense made from the resin of the Sarja tree, and honey-sweets.
One should feed [the Brahmins] and pray, "May Hiraṇyākṣa be pleased with me.
In the month of Kārtika, one should perform a bath with milk and worship with karavīra flowers.
One should offer incense made from the resin of the *śrīvāsa* tree and an offering of honeyed milk-porridge, while reciting, "May Sthāṇu be pleased"; then the gift of silver should be given.

In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform a bath with curd, offer cooked rice with honey as the food offering, and use the resin of the Śrīvṛkṣa as incense; one should pray: "May Śarva be pleased. (83)
In the month of Pauṣa, one should perform the ritual bath with sacrificial offerings (havis), worship with bilva fruits and other fruits,
use the resin of the madhuka tree as incense, and offer honeyed parched grain (madhusaktuka) as the food offering (naivedya).
One should offer a ring while making this petition: "May Tryambaka be pleased.
In the month of Māgha, one should perform a bath with water infused with *kuśa* grass and worship Śiva with white water-lilies (*kumuda*).
The incense is the resin of the kadamba tree, and the food offering is rice mixed with sesame seeds;
one should pray, "May Mahādeva be pleased with me," followed by the salutation *namaḥ*. (86)
Thus, this six-month vow always bestows good fortune;
furthermore, one should perform a bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the month of Phālguna.
One should worship with *kunda* flowers and incense with sandalwood;
one should offer as an oblation rice mixed with jaggery and ghee in a copper vessel.
Having said, "May Rudra be pleased with me," one should cause a pair of garments to be given.
In the month of Caitra, there should be a bath with water from the Udumbara tree and worship with Mandāra flowers. (89)
One should offer incense made from guggulu and present sweetmeats;
may the Lord of the Nāgas be pleased with me through this gift of a deer skin.

In the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform a bath with fragrant flowers and worship with clouds and blossoms; the incense should be the resin of the Sarja tree, and the food offering should consist of ghee along with fruit. 9.1.
"May the Slayer of Śālā be pleased"—with these words, one should perform the offering of a water-pot;
likewise, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, there is bathing with *āmalaka* fruits and worship with *arka* flowers. (92)
May he who destroys the eyes of Bhaga be pleased with me through the eating of curd and barley meal, the gift of an umbrella and sandals, and the offering of sandalwood incense. 93.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should perform a bath with bilva fruits and worship with golden flowers;
one should fumigate with jasmine and offer cakes as the supreme food offering.
May the Destroyer of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice be pleased by this gift of barley-grains and the like;
in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform a bath with *bhṛṅgarāja* and worship the auspicious *rudrākṣa*.
May Gaṅgādhara be pleased with me through the offering of agallochum incense, sacrificial food, curd, and sweetmeats, as well as the gift of gold, cows, and clothing. 96.
With these six months, worship bestows the fulfillment of vows;
then, when the year is complete, one should perform the breaking of the fast on the ninth day.
One should always observe the fast on the eighth day of the dark fortnight for twelve months;
thereafter, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to the words of Maheśvara.
Through this meritorious vow, a husband and wife obtain inexhaustible happiness; it accomplishes virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation—just so, and not otherwise. (99)
Since the lotus emerged from the navel of Prajāpati during the month of Āśvina, a lotus should be offered in the worship of Brahmā; it increases his delight.
The *kadamba* tree is in the heart of Kāma, the *vaṭa* tree in the hand of Yakṣa, the *dhattūra* in the heart of Śiva, and from the center of Brahmā indeed comes the *khadira*.
From the middle of Viśvakarman’s body, the Kaṇṭakī tree was born;
from the palm of Girijā’s hand, a cluster of Kunda flowers was produced.
The Sinduvāraka tree situated in the pitcher of Gaṇādhipa shines resplendently;
on the right side of Yama, the Pālāśa tree indeed grew forth.
To the south and north of Yama is the black Udumbara tree;
for Skanda it is the Bandhujīva, and for Ravi it is the Aśvattha. 104.
The Śamī tree was born from Kātyāyanī; the Bilva appeared in the hand of Lakṣmī; the reed-cluster (śarastamba) arose from the mouth of a serpent, and the Dūrvā grass from the back of Vāsuki.
And Candana was born in the heart of Sādhya, O Rādhikā;
this story belongs to another aeon, having come into being at the very beginning of creation.
Through their worship, the satisfaction of those gods becomes supreme;
and when they are propitiated, they bestow virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Narrative of Sukeśī, the Aśūnyaśayana Vow, the Auspicious Puṇyaka Vow and Others, the Sleeping of the Gods on Different Lunar Days, and Their Worship," within the section on the Religious Instruction for Daitya Women in the second part, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, in this manner the sage Lomaśa indeed instructed the daughters of the Daityas in the virtues and various religious observances.
And they performed the practices of the bull (the bull-vow), as well as the observance of vows,
the vow of the unempty bed, and the Cāturmāsya vows.
They performed the meritorious Śivakālāṣṭamī vow for a year, served the venerable Guru, and took refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 3 ||
Having become pure-bodied and pure-souled as well,
they [ascended] to the imperishable abode by means of celestial chariots driven by the foremost attendants.
Having gone and seen him, those maidens of divine form arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa; there they all worshipped Lomaśa, the preceptor of Hari.
Having realized the full majesty of Bālakṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
they took refuge in that supreme, beloved Lord Harikṛṣṇa as their husband and sovereign.
Thus, when the third year had passed and a very great festival was held at the commencement of the fourth year, the grand festival of his birth was celebrated.
Then his father fed millions of living beings and caused gifts consisting of jewels and gold to be distributed.
In that regard, O Rādhā, there was one marvel; listen as I tell it to you:
from the netherworld (pātāla) there emerged a serpent’s body with a human head.
With his hands joined in añjali at the height of a palm tree, the nāga named Svastika, weeping and deeply distressed, stood near Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (2.28.10)
Crying out, "Save me! Save me!", he arrived, his household now empty;
meanwhile, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa sat upon the elephant-throne.
Having arrived there, he repeatedly fell at the feet of Śrī Hari and said:
"O Blessed One, protect me, a serpent who has come to you for refuge!"
"Without you, no protector exists for me in the three worlds.
Śrī Hari said, "What sorrow has come upon you? Describe it. (13)
While everyone was listening and the festival had arrived, the Naga described his own suffering born of battle in Pātāla, just as it had occurred.
O Blessed One, in the netherworld dwell Nāgas of many species;
those who possess the lineage of Śeṣa become kings. (15)
Those born of Vāsuki become his ministers,
while those of Takṣaka’s lineage indeed become the honored Nāgas of the royal court.
I am a Brahmin of the Svastika lineage, devoted to the service of my gurus;
you Dhṛtarāṣṭras are Kṣatriyas of the Karkoṭaka race, devoted to the duties of warriors.
Those of the lineage of Kuhaka are indeed merchants, while those of the lineage of Suṣeṇa are cultivators of vegetables and the like. || 18 ||
Those who have been exiled to dwell in the forest are indeed the guardians of the wilderness;
they are always the *kārburakas* who perform servitude within the circle of kings.
Black-colored nāgas become enjoyers of the lordship of armies, while spotted nāgas become makers of gardens. (2.28.20)
The Ambarīṣas, the Sūtakāryakaras, the Vāhanarakṣins, the Godhūmīyas, the Nāgas, the Cāraṇas, and the Vaṃśabodhakas. ||21||
These wise brahmins of the Bhadrajātīya naga lineage recite the sections of discourse and instruct the children.
Those of the Kumuda class become enjoyers of pleasures who fall into a state of dependence;
those of the Piśaṅga class invariably become servants performing the work of cooks.
The Keśīyas are skilled in dramatic performance; the Śailūṣas are dancers;
the Āmṛtikas are singers; and the Ḍāṇḍikas are honored by the elders. ||24||
Those born under Bhūphalā are creators of gardens; those born under Śuka seek out stories;
and those of the Kapardajāti class are always purifiers of the village.
Thus, there are many others with various names who dwell there;
their king today is the great one named Kāraṇḍava.
He has a minister named Sumadhu who resides in the region of Sarpamaṇḍala;
he is honorable, worshipful, wise, and possesses great strength and prowess.
One who acts unjustly does so even for his own sake alone, whereas one who performs what is beneficial for others acts for the sake of others;
he is a benefactor of the subjects and one who honors those who have come for refuge. (28)
Therefore, the subjects honor him properly, just as they would a king;
meanwhile, the King held a great festival there for the trident-bearing Lord Hāṭakeśvara.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, he performs worship with bilva leaves and other offerings,
and he gives gifts accompanied by sacrificial fees for the satisfaction of the twice-born.
In this year, the minister Sumadhu summoned Brāhmaṇas there for the recitation of the Śatarudrīya for that king.
There were thousands there—reciters, readers, worshippers, and performers of fire-sacrifices; among them, I was a reciter.
I have one hundred sons and likewise twenty daughters; and by the power of the minister's grace, they all became scholars there. (33)
Maidens and the daughters of Brahmins constantly come and go; they arrive for the purpose of worshipping Hāṭakeśa and depart after having beheld him.
I have twenty daughters, beautiful and having reached the prime of youth;
they were all born from a single womb and all possess the beauty of Urvaśī.
Beheld by Sumadhu, they were beautiful in every limb;
in form they possessed the hue of the campaka flower, with long eyes equal to the beauty of Śrī. (36)
They had tawny eyes, halos of radiance surrounding their heads, bodies visible from every side, and were endowed with nails like jewels of splendor.
All of them could assume any form at will, possessed slender waists and beautiful hair;
they wore garments of fire, had lovely necks, and were filled with sweetness.
