Beholding me, Sumadhu saw all those pure brahmin maidens, their bodies filled with fragrance, possessing the characteristics of lotus-like women. 39.
Having summoned them, he said: "Give me twenty maidens;
these are suitable for me and worthy of a king—grant them to me. (2.28.40)
O Lord, having reflected upon that, I then said to the excellent minister:
"If they should desire my daughter, I shall certainly give her; of this there is no doubt. (41)
"Whatever is desired by their minds as a duty must always be performed by me.
Then I questioned them all, and their mother was also informed.
"You are indeed worthy of choosing a boon; tell us, which boon do you desire?
They replied, "O Father, O Mother, we have heard [of it] on the surface of the human world. (43)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of all and the Sovereign, dwells in the home of Śrī Kambharā as a young cowherd boy. 44.
And his form, following upon his beauty, is exceedingly captivating;
for we have heard from our friends that he is indeed such in every respect. (45)
The Blessed One, Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, is worthy of you as a bridegroom;
and other daughters of the Nāgas [are also] that Supreme Lord. (46)
By the thousands, they desire to make a husband through marriage;
therefore, we [desire] none other than Śeṣapati, Śrīpati, and Śrīdhara. 47.
"We do not wish to choose anyone else if you desire our welfare.
Thus was Svastika, their father, addressed by the maidens, as was I.
Then the king told the minister his intention regarding the maiden;
the chief minister replied, "The daughter is angry with me; daughters are dependent on their fathers and are not independent."
"Give [it] to me; I speak thus so that you shall obtain all happiness. Otherwise, suffering will be yours here, and your entire wealth will be taken away. (2.28.50)
Or else, I shall carry off your daughters by the rākṣasa rite;
then let your daughters follow me out of humility. (51)
"Tell me, if they do not wish to give [their daughters], I shall take them tomorrow on an auspicious day.
Having spoken thus, I later addressed those maidens of mine once again.
I told them all that, yet they did not believe it;
therefore, O King, I went to the monarch and reported it to him.
The king, being partial to that side, told me of the gain:
"Give those maidens to that minister; may you be happy. (54)
"I have heard that the king has certainly not granted his approval;
having heard all of this, I have reported it again to the maidens. (55)
They replied with a solemn vow: "We choose the Lord Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa in the form of a child. (56)
Otherwise, dear father, we must likewise resort to death;
I have reported this matter in every respect to my circle of kinsmen. (57)
Likewise, his kinsmen also gave their approval, saying, "So be it.
Hostility toward the king and his people is not the path to the highest good. (58)
"Therefore, a daughter should indeed be given to the minister as a means to destroy obstacles.
Then I told all of this to my wife, and she [responded].
She said to me, "O Lord, she must certainly not be given by you to a minister who has leprosy;
whatever may happen, she must not be given to one with leprosy. (2.28.60)
I asked, "My dear, how is it that you know he is a leper?
My beloved replied, "There is a maidservant of his named Karaṇṭikā."
She was a servant and handmaid of Sumadhu,
performing service for him such as massaging his feet, bathing him, and anointing him with oil.
She constantly attends upon that excellent minister and gazes at him in secret;
within the hidden parts of his body, cases of red leprosy (raktakuṣṭha) reside.
In her rambling talk about the news of the disease, she described the minister’s leprosy;
therefore, no daughter should be given to that leprous minister.
Having spoken thus, she ceased, overcome by the sorrow of her impending fate;
I, Svastika, am seized with grief, for a reversal of fortune is about to occur.
If that hardship has come about through destiny, it must be endured;
for the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign, is indeed Destiny itself. (66)
"And since this Hāṭakeśa has arisen from him, may he protect [us].
Having reflected thus, I indeed accepted the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). //67//
Even though he had gone home, he found no sleep; neither his wives nor his daughters could console him.
Then, at dawn, the ministers and soldiers arrived there.
"Since all twenty maidens have been desired by the minister,
let them indeed mount divine chariots for the sake of marriage with the minister."
"Thus, by the king's command and the minister's word, we, the king's officers, speak [this]; otherwise, out of persistence, we would have taken you away."
Since their daughters, fathers, mothers, sons, and humble folk were there, they wept and then became intent on fighting once more. ||7 1 ||
There, during the assault in battle, we were all captured by the soldiers;
our daughters were bound with ropes and our sons were taken away and imprisoned. (72)
"I have been liberated along with my wife during the month of Bhādrapada;
however, those maidens do not wish to choose husbands, as they remain confined within the prison. (73)
"Save us indeed, O Blessed One! Sent by our wife, we have come here;
for your sake, O Keśava, deliver those whose lives are dedicated to you. (74)
Thus addressed, Bālakṛṣṇa, laughing, granted him freedom from fear and called to mind Garuḍa and the terrifying Sudarśana.
Both of them arrived instantly, their gait equal to ten million suns;
being commanded, they departed, taking that very Svastika with them.
"Where those serpents dwell, having established their kingdom in Pātāla, Garuḍa said to the king: 'Let the King of Serpents act with justice. (77)
O King, the minister has committed a violation of dharma by forcibly abducting maidens;
indeed, give the daughters of brahmins to Svastika.
Everything must be accomplished through conciliation, even that enmity which is most difficult to end, by means of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa here on this earth. (79)
Sent by Nārāyaṇa, I, Garuḍa, the devourer of serpents, have come here;
indeed, he gave me the Sudarśana weapon.
"If you do not release the maiden, then fight with me!
Thus addressed, King Kāraṇḍava blazed with rage.
Having summoned his minister, he became intent upon war;
so too did the remaining Vāsukis, Takṣakas, and Kuhakas.
The Dhṛtarāṣṭras, Suṣeṇas, Hāritas, Karburas and others, as well as the Kṛṣṇas, Puṇḍarīkas, Ambarīṣas, and Bhadrakas. ||83||
The Kumudas, the Piśaṅgas, the Keśīyas, and likewise the Amṛtas;
the Śailūṣas, the Kapardas, the Bhūphālas, the Ḍāṇḍikas, and the Śukas. ||84||
At these words of the king, all these others, taking their armies, arrived for the sake of battle, intent on engaging in combat with weapons, missiles, and arms. (85)
Having realized then that the bird was small and the discus possessed little power,
Śrī Garuḍa thereupon remembered the Supreme Lord.
Then he assumed a vast form that pervaded the ends of the quarters;
with his two wings, he covered all the netherworlds with their plumage.
With his body he filled the sky, and with his two feet the surface of the netherworld;
then, with his beak, his claws, and his wings, he brought about destruction.
The king swiftly seized with his beak and devoured those elephants who were about to begin the battle and were striking with their weapons, along with their drivers.
His armies were slaughtered by that bird with its sharp beak;
likewise, hundreds of thousands were slain by its sharp talons and wings.
Others fled to the far shore of the ocean of milk;
they reported the remainder of the battle, known as Ananta.
Śeṣa arrived there and saw Garuḍa in that state;
beholding Sudarśana as well, he paid homage with supreme devotion.
He tried to restrain the serpents from fighting, yet when they did not desist, Garuḍa released his discus in the battle.
The netherworld blazed up, as did all the families of serpents;
there was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! and a massive commotion ensued at that time.
Śeṣa praised that discus and Garuḍa with great devotion;
the discus was pacified by Garuḍa for the sake of Śeṣa’s satisfaction.
Having entrusted the sovereignty of Pātāla to Anantaśeṣa,
and having likewise assigned the office of minister to Svastika, Garuḍa then departed.
He liberated the sons and daughters of Svastika from their bonds;
Śeṣa, Svastika, Garuḍa, and Cakra remembered the Lord.
To that beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa who exists in the form of a child, the Blessed Lord Hari then assumed the form of a youth. 98.
Having mounted the divine elephant, he went to Pātāla;
then those devotees of Kṛṣṇa indeed offered him a welcome.
There, Hari performed the consecration for his sovereignty over Pātāla upon the skull of Ananta-Śeṣa; it was done in every respect.
The minister Svastika also joyfully offered twenty of his own daughters to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Then, having taken Cakra and Garuḍa, and having taken the maidens who were mounted on elephants,
the illustrious Lord quickly went to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Through the power of yoga, he arrived at the Kuṅkumavāpikā field;
having bathed the maidens in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, [he departed].
He commanded that sage to remain in Lomaśa’s hermitage;
likewise, Māla gave the mantras to those two, and Lomaśa [gave them] in the hermitage.
Having received his command, Garuḍa protected [the child] and went to Vaikuṇṭha;
Hari’s discus became quiescent in his hand, and the girls remained thus in the hermitage.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the illustrious Lord, a treasury of divine and excellent qualities, performed a miracle at the beginning of His fourth year. Then,
in that Pātāla, Śeṣa’s wife Sunandinī—
In the month of Kārttika, he indeed remembered Bālakṛṣṇa in order to behold him.
Śrī Hari, knowing her mind, went there assuming the form of a youth;
having been worshipped by her, he gave his own mantra to her.
"Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
She gave him the rosary and the forehead mark, and she herself worshipped Hari with devotion.
There were ten thousand daughters of the deceased serpents;
to them Manu gave Sunandinī, and he gave Mālā and the others.
All of them became the most excellent Vaiṣṇavīs, beloved of Hari;
all those auspicious ones arrived upon the earth together with Śrī Hari.
Indeed, they were presented by Ananta, seated in celestial vehicles and accompanied by gifts.
And they were protected by the Supreme Soul in the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Blessed are those women, O Rādhā, who have been offered to Kṛṣṇa;
for in them the Supreme Brahman Himself, the bestower of perfect liberation, will take delight.

If that which is declared as "everything must be given" is indeed taken by him, such that nothing remains to be given, and if that which is declared as "that which is to be attained" is likewise grasped by him; (1.14)
What gain in this world could be greater than this, if Hari is pleased by one's body?
For by reciting or hearing this, the Lord becomes the bestower of bliss.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation from Suffering of the Naga Svastika of Pātāla—Minister to the King of Pātāla—and the Bringing of the Naga Maidens to the Hermitage of Lomaśa," occurring on the occasion of the Lord’s festival marking the beginning of his fourth year, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; in the fourth year, during the month of Māgha, they undertook the vow of bathing in the waters of the Aśvasaras lake.
Brahmins, sages, maidens, and others dwelling there bathe in the lake beginning from the hour of Brahmā (brāhmamuhūrta). || 2 ||
Five or six young boys and girls were constantly plunging into the water;
suddenly, they were no longer seen by those performing their ablutions who remained within the water.
Even by the people standing on the shore, no cause whatsoever is perceived; yet the people imagine there that there are predatory crocodiles.
Others say that crocodiles have gathered here,
while others merely conjecture that there are resident piśācas.
"Indeed, these murderous Rākṣasas are devouring these children;
what could be the cause of this, for it is not known through direct perception? (6)
At that time, there was lamentation everywhere throughout the land of Saurāṣṭra;
the waters of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara were swallowing five or six living beings at a time.
One must not perform ritual bathing there, because children die;
for by some means, children are carried away in the waters of the Aśvasaras lake.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
Who indeed was this child-killer who was there in the water at that time? Tell me the reason for his existence, and what had happened to the children? (9)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, I shall tell you all of that in brief.
In the western region of Ārakta, there was a king named Śāvadīnaka.

The self that exists in the corpse is the "corpse-self" (śāva); it remains right there in a wretched state through the functioning of ignorance, and thus it possesses the designation "wretched corpse-self" (śāvadīna).
He had a hundred wives, yet no son was born;
indeed, he had a thousand daughters, but not even a single son.
Then, overcome with grief, the king questioned his own guru, the ascetic:
"How may a son be born? Tell me now the cause for this."
The guru, who was even more wretched than the ascetic, reflected for a moment and said to him:
"A son is born from the bond of debt and out of a desire to discharge that debt."
If death occurs in this world for one whose debt has not been discharged,
his son, bull, or horse shall remain in his house to pay that debt.
Due to the bondage of karma, he is born as a camel, a goat, or even a donkey;
or else, the debtor may become the son of the creditor.
Having taken the wealth previously given, one goes to death free from debt;
for you, O King, have never before been a debtor to anyone. (17)
Therefore, you had no creditor who gave you wealth;
that debt does not exist for you at all, so how could there be a son born to you here? (18)
Freedom from debt is in every way the best, desired, and bestows liberation;
nevertheless, if you have a desire for a son, perform worship.
When Mahākālī, who is compassionate toward the distressed, is worshipped with an offering,
she will grant you a son who is a sovereign emperor and long-lived.
By offering a sacrifice of a child to Śāvadīnā Mahākālī, the attainment of a child occurs there; this sacrifice is declared to be the most excellent. || 21 ||
If a boy who possesses auspicious marks is less than five years of age when he is given to a Śāvinī woman,
then she too will burn her son.
The king said: "How and with what characteristics is the boy to be offered? Tell me those characteristics by which my son may become a sovereign ruler of the whole earth. (23)
The ascetic Yati-dīna said: "Listen, O King, I shall tell you that:
he in whose hand there is a fish-line, together with a bow, a string, and arrows. (24)
A banner, a trident, a svastika, a wheel, or a barley grain may appear;
or one whose foot has three ankle-bones, or who bears the markings of a palace.
If there is a single line on the forehead, or a dark mole on the neck, and if the form of the face has the luster of a campaka flower with the corners of the eyes extending like petals; 26.
That which shines as a line in the form of a doll upon the hips, or that which is a white lotus on the left thigh—[these are auspicious marks]. (27)
That boy indeed should be offered as a sacrificial gift (bali) to Mahākālī according to the prescribed ritual;
by that means, you shall have a son who will be a great emperor and a mighty king.
Having heard this from the ascetic Dīna, King Śāvadīna, distressed in turn,
appointed Siddhas and Yoginīs for the purpose of searching for such children.
Siddhas and ascetics traveling through the sky, who examine the lines on the palms, roamed upon the earth wearing blue garments for the sake of obtaining the child.
Those fools perceive lines, as well as luminaries, planets, and so forth;
at that time, O beloved, ascetics were wandering through all the regions.
Thereupon, one named Kāsadīna went to Saurāṣṭra;
he arrived at the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and reached the hermitage of Lomaśa.
[He found] the child possessing the aforementioned characteristics, named Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
He too, having heard from Lomaśa, [then spoke] to the son of Kambharā.
Beholding him endowed with auspicious marks, possessed of all the lines [of a great man], and auspicious,
he went swiftly through the sky toward the king in the region of Ārakta.
He said: "In the region of Saurāṣṭra, there exists a boy named Bālaka in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; he is the son of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. (35)
Having heard this, the king then gave five villages to his own favorite ascetic,
and furthermore, he then gave five other ascetics who were experts in the art of illusion.
He dispatched [the image] to Saurāṣṭra, to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake,
where in the month of Māgha people devoted to bathing bathe in the auspicious water.
There, those ascetics, who were constantly beyond the range of sight, wandered upon the bank, intent on making efforts to seize that child. (38)
They constantly submerge five or six children in water and quickly lead them to the presence of the king of the earth in a place where there is no blood. (39)
The king’s servants, who bestow happiness, protect those who are living;
thus do the ascetics act day and night on the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa.
Indeed, those ignorant ones take away many children for the sake of profit from a child who possesses [auspicious] lines; they are all unacquainted with the significance of the lines. (41)
But a wretched ascetic indeed performs the inspection of the lines;
as long as that line is not seen, he does not release [the thread]. (42)
The children there are being carried away while cries of "Alas! Alas! resound;
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is bathing within the house. 43.
He heard that the destruction of Bāla had occurred and that no one among the ascetics had been able to seize him;
thereupon, that Blessed One, together with his mother, forcibly departed from the house.
Having departed, she went to bathe in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
while the mother was bathing on the bank, the boy remained nearby. 45.
Desiring to seize him, the ascetic quickly approached there invisibly;
assuming the form of a water-man, he took hold of the boy.
Bearing two forms, the fool fell into his hands;
with his second form, he took pleasure in the presence of his mother. ||47||
"Look, look! Here is my mother; here is the formidable water-demon;
look at me, who am repeatedly taking hold of the child and looking back [at him]. (48)
"Look, look! Another boy, taking me with him, is going toward the surface of the water; see how he, along with the child, is entering the vast expanse of water. (49)
Measuring three *tālas* in height, with a luster like the moon and tawny hair upon his head;
he shone with eyes like those of a lion, and his pupils were tawny.
All the fingers of both arms are as long as cords;
and the two arms hang down like branches, thick and sturdy like elephant trunks.
His face was like that of a monkey, endowed with a red beard;
four fangs were visible on his sides, and his mane appeared formidable.
Its horn, shaped like a goad, is situated above its skull;
it has two tails on its shoulders and two tails at its hips.
He possesses four cords that are exceedingly long;
moreover, he suffers from chronic diseases of the heart and the back. ||54||
There are webbed membranes between his fingers and toes;
moreover, there is a mole upon his navel that shines like a lamp. (55)
The toes and feet are webbed and indeed long;
there is a furrow on the belly, and the face resembles that of a young elephant. (56)
One who has feet on his hands, hands on his feet, lacks breasts, lacks ears, and is covered in hair is a bringer of fear. (57)
Making the sound "ciṃciṃhuk, ciṃciṃ," he went beneath the surface of the water;
behold him here, resembling a demon, as he seizes the boys. (58)
Let all people see him and let them kill him;
for one who kills and harms should be swiftly destroyed by every possible means. (59)
Having spoken thus, Hari, who was in their hands, emerged from the water;
and the people there, both men and women, gathered together,
were overcome with terror and lamented for the many children.
Remembering the children who had been carried away, he devised a means to kill them:
a *śataghnī* weapon was placed on the bank, along with artificial child-dummies. When he came to the water’s edge to carry those dummies away, [he was struck]. || 6.1–6.2 ||
They reached the conclusion that he must be destroyed by means of a *śataghnī* weapon;
then, assuming the form of the wind, he unleashed a violent storm.
With great speed, Siddhadīna seized the *śataghnī* weapons as well as the mechanical dolls;
terrified, the people returned to their respective homes during the day. (64)
The mechanical dolls and the *śataghnī* weapons were all destroyed;
indeed, the people, struck with wonder, sought refuge with Lomaśa. (65)
"O best of sages, what must be done to destroy this water-demon?
This wicked-souled one carries off children; he is a terrifying destruction. (66)
Having heard this, Lomaśa reflected for a moment in his heart and said:
"These five ascetics who have arrived are indeed from the region of Cāra."
Possessors of the great vidyā of Indra’s net and capable of assuming many forms, these Mlecchas, performing Mleccha rites, have arrived here by the command of the Mleccha king. (68)
The Asuras, the Kārmaṇakas, the harmful, and the merciless—
Kṛṣṇa himself will bring about their destruction.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa knows that state,
since the manifestation of Śrī Hari was for the purpose of destroying the demons.
"He himself will provide the remedy for the Rākṣasas.
Having spoken thus, Lomaśa then called Bālakṛṣṇa to mind.
The Lord Hari, assuming the form of a youth, arrived laughing, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing his discus; he then spoke to Lomaśa and the others.
"How did I remember [this]? Tell me quickly!
Then Lomaśa and the others, having bowed, spoke of the affliction caused by Bālā and the rest. (73)
Having heard everything regarding the presence of the Rākṣasas in the lake in the form of water-demons, Hari spoke to the one who bore a fish, a trident, and a bow.
And they, remaining in the water, search for the boy Sadhvaja;
they also strive on my behalf in the worship of Śāva, Dīna, and Aprapūjana.
The boy, bearing a fish, a trident, and a bow upon his banner, must be offered as a sacrificial gift;
and by such an offering of a victim, the king shall indeed obtain a son of that same kind.
I did not come into their hands for that very reason;
thus they employ them in the abduction of children, and I am instructing them.
Having spoken thus, the Lord, appearing as a boy, went to the shore of Lake Aśvasaras; meanwhile, a water-manusya assumed a human form and seized Kṛṣṇa.
And while thousands of people were looking on in the world, O Rādhikā, then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from everyone there upon the bank of the lake.
Hari, possessing a divine form and his discus, entered the water;
he was seized by that asura and fought with him within the depths of the water.
With his discus, the Blessed One severed its four binding ropes, as well as its head, horns, and the forearms of its hands and feet.
In the time it takes to clap three times, Kṛṣṇa bound him with ropes and brought him out from the water alive.
Seeing that white water-man, who was three *tāla* units in height, the people were struck with great wonder and fell into a state of amazement. ||83||
Then four other ascetics who were staying there in the water also emerged outside in the forms of aquatic beings. ||84||
They entreated him most fervently for the sake of protecting their lives;
they sang, "The children have not been killed at all; they are all alive. (85)
"We shall certainly bring [him] here; however, grant us the gift of life.
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the sovereign Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, [replied]. (86)
The Lord granted them the gift of life and spoke to them again:
"Come with me through the sky, traveling upon Garuḍa."
Hearing those words of Kṛṣṇa, the Mlecchas, who were like water-demons, [realized] where these children were—indeed, they had been protected by him. 88.
Carrying Hari through the sky, they went to a region that was glowing red, with crimson-colored soil, red waters, and a circle of red-complexioned men. (89)
Where everything was mostly dyed red, including the ground-cover; where the great king was as wretched as a corpse, and the teacher was as wretched as an ascetic. (2.29.90)
Where Mahākālī Śāvadīnā resided in the king’s abode,
there Kṛṣṇa and those ascetics went, being well-honored by the king.
There, fifty children were shown, happy and free from distress;
indeed, the king and others beheld the beautiful Bālakṛṣṇa.
Having learned from the perfected ones (siddhas) of that supreme and auspicious wonder, the wives and daughters of kings [worshipped] Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person. 93.
Then, having massaged him with superior oils and fragrant powders, they bathed him thoroughly with very warm water.
Seeing him with limbs proportioned to his form, bearing a fish, a trident, and a bow, and holding a banner in his hand, they were both bewildered and delighted. (95)
"Aha! This man is worthy of the sacrifice; by good fortune he has arrived here.
Thus did the women quickly inform the king. (96)
The king, having reflected quickly, indeed laughed and gave the command to his soldiers and generals to seize him and place him in prison. 97.
Those maidens, captivated by his form, did not desire the death of Hari;
rather, as queens, they desired Hari there for the sake of obtaining a son as an offering.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇa, assuming the form of a child, was seized by the soldiers;
musical instruments were sounded, and the king considered his purpose fulfilled.
And Sudarśana and Garuḍa, having become two boys with beautiful faces,
joined together among the children and gave them courage as their protectors.
Then Kṛṣṇa was placed in prison by the soldiers and bound in shackles;
at that time, a thousand maidens fell into a state of swoon.
They joyfully undertook the Śāvadīnāmahākālī vow, thinking:
"If this boy is released, he shall then become our husband. (102)
"We shall observe the vow for one month consisting solely of milk, and we shall perform the worship of Śāva and the others day and night. (103)
Today we shall abandon sweet honey, wine, and the like;
we shall instead fashion five garlands from the corpses of women such as Devikā.
In this manner, they accepted that rule as a protector of the children;
then, at night, while the subjects, the king, the soldiers, and others were fast asleep, || 105 ||
The Lord Śrī Hari, who displays the divine play of the world while sleeping in bondage,
exists in his own abode in a second form.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, Hari, the source of all bliss,
relates news concerning the region of Ārakta to the venerable sage Lomaśa.
Everyone heard it and marveled at it as something produced from a distant land;
thus the night passed away and dawn broke.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Śrī Hari’s Journey There for the Purpose of Releasing the Bound Children Intended as Sacrificial Offerings to the Goddess Śāvadīnākālī by the King of Āraktadeśa for the Sake of a Son, and the Infatuation of the Thousand Maidens with Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to the account of what occurred there upon my arrival in the morning; I shall relate that which happened concerning you, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (1)
King Śāvadīna proclaimed among his subjects:
"A boy endowed with auspicious marks has arrived for the purpose of being offered as a sacrifice for the sake of a son. (2)
His hand is marked with lines depicting the fish-bannered god's bow, the trident, the discus, and other symbols;
and on the full moon day of Māgha, an offering of oblations shall take place.
For fifteen days during this bright fortnight,
beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), there shall be the constant worship of the Goddess.

Those who desire a son and those who seek their goals should always perform a great festival. Tomorrow, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, they should take the child to the temple in the morning.
"I, the King, shall go before the Queen together with my preceptor; and the preceptor shall establish the innocence of the innocent boy before the Queen. (6)
Then, by means of barbarian rites, the offering of liquor, and the preparation of *surā*,
that child— a devotee of the Goddess— will act according to the prescribed ritual.
He is born in the form of a god, and his service is always performed by people.
With foods, services, garments, waters, drinks, and massages. || 8 ||
All human beings should engage in the play of riding vehicles;
by this, the Great Goddess will become pleased during the worship of the Child.
Therefore, the sacrificial animal is to be honored with gifts, respect, worship, and the like.
Thus proclaimed by the king, it spread instantly among the subjects.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight at dawn, the lord of the earth, having bathed and being resplendent with his army,
went joyfully to the temple of the Goddess, taking the child upon his lap.
The Guru, by means of Mleccha mantras, made the boy a sacrificial animal for the Goddess;
he was consecrated and worshipped, and a great festival was celebrated.
Upon seeing Śrī Puruṣottama, the great goddess Śāvadīnā was overcome with shame; she quickly moved far away from his form.
The goddess grieved deeply, thinking, "He desires to slay them all;
however, the duty toward Kṛṣṇa must be fulfilled. || 14 ||
Having reflected thus, she did not desire to do anything at all without [her husband's] command;
so the Goddess remained silent until the worship was concluded. (15)
Then, during the great festival, the king bestowed many gifts;
at that time, even Bālakṛṣṇa became subject to another's will, as if dependent on him.
By his own will, he became an ordinary child like any other infant;
at night, he was guarded solely by the eyes of the Goddess, which served as a palace for him.
With a gracious heart, he should be there together with boys and girls;
likewise, he should be served by everyone with all forms of hospitality.
When midnight had passed, everyone fell asleep; then the auspicious Mahākālī, the virtuous consort of Śrī Hari, remained wakeful in his presence. 19.
Having become a maiden, the servant arrived trembling;
placing her head at [her master's] feet, she shed tears with her tongue.
Having wiped the feet of Hari, she said, "Forgive me";
she bowed repeatedly and likewise entreated Hari for his command.
"These kings and others, who are guilty of offenses against their lords and yet greedy for sons, must all be slain by me; give me your command, and I shall do it. (22)
His guru was Yatidīna, his king was Śāvadīna,
and he was Kāsadīna, who traveled along the lakes and marshes of Saurāṣṭra.
O Lord, those Mlecchas and the perfected ascetics must be slain by me;
likewise, any others who stand as their allies must indeed be killed by me here.
"Om," said Hari, the supreme among men, to that Śāvakālī;
he gave her a sword, a spear, a javelin, an axe, and even a noose.
A staff, a thunderbolt, a shield, a sword, a mallet, a mace, a trident,
a goad, a pestle, a discus, and likewise a bow with an arrow.
Then, holding a conch shell as well among those eighteen weapons in her hands,
she entered the king’s palace in the morning, filled with wrath.
Standing upon a lion, fierce in form, with eyes of fire and overflowing with poison,
she seized the king by the hair and cut off his head with her sword.
Having split the Guru in two with the trident, and having thereafter slain Kāsa along with the Siddhas and Mlecchas who provided him assistance, [he prevails]. (29)
Having slain the wardens of the prison, he liberated the children;
indeed, a great cry of lamentation arose among the people of the inner apartments.
They declared that she was the family deity (kuladevī) worthy of royal worship; when she became enraged, she destroyed the king, his preceptor, the ascetics, and others as well. (31)
Indeed, the sin resulting from the killing of children has fallen upon the king;
therefore, children must never be harmed by people. ||32||
For those who cause fear in children, total destruction shall occur in this world;
indeed, children must not even mentally destroy innocent flowers.
Those children are the dwellings of the Lord; they are never to be burned at any time.
They are free from defects such as bodily impurities and possess the true nature of Brahman and the virtuous. 34.
Indeed, children are to be honored, delighted, and satisfied;
food should always be given to them, along with the gift of fearlessness. (35)
A refuge must be granted to them, but the fear of death must not be granted;
for they are like unripe fruit, their livelihood dependent upon others. (36)
Those who are the support of one's mother and father must never be killed;
for in that case, death itself arises as the fruit of causing distress to children. (37)
The lowest of men, who terrifies the foolish and robs them, and the king who destroys righteousness, swiftly reaps the fruit of death. (38)
Then, seated upon the back of Keśarin, she went to the children's houses where those young boys remained during their confinement in prison. (39)
Where Garuḍa, the discus, and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa abide,
there this virtuous woman has suddenly gone, assuming the form of battle.
Having abandoned her cruelty, she became an exceedingly gentle and auspicious two-armed maiden; smiling, the girl said to those boys, "Look toward me! (41)
Beheld by the children, she too appeared in the form of each of their own mothers;
seizing them instantly by the neck, the boys indeed took delight in her lap.
Attaining extreme joy, they considered their own protection secured;
then she bowed to Bālakṛṣṇa and begged for forgiveness.
The Sovereign Lady gave milk and fruits to all the children;
the infants ate them and thus became happy.
Then the subjects indeed performed the funeral procession for the king;
all the widowed queens approached the queen and wailed aloud. (45)
All those maidens wept, as did the women of the elders and others;
the Goddess, having emerged from the image, was born in the form of a maiden. (46)
Having appeared in person before them all, she spoke these sweet words:
"O noble ones, do not grieve; the king has obtained his own due reward. (47)
"The king is intent on killing him whose wife I am;
my beloved Lord is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (48)
Janārdana, who bears the fish, the banner, the bow, the trident, and the discus,
indeed assumes the form of a child while remaining here within the prison.
"My husband was made my sacrificial animal by the king, even though he was my son;
as the fruit of that act, death has been bestowed by me upon that great sinner. (2.30.50)
A great blessing brought about by Hari shall come to you all;
praise the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa for the sake of liberation. 5.1.
Having been addressed thus, O Rādhikā, they all went toward Nārāyaṇa and praised him with supreme devotion for the sake of liberation from sin. (52)
Hari revealed his own form, which goes to the abode, to them;
and by his side was his beloved Satī, Lakṣmī in her true form, who is compassionate toward the wretched.
He likewise showed him Garuḍa, Bālaka, and the Sudarśana discus;
thereafter, he indeed showed him the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
The sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, as well as the hermitage of Lomaśa, and the ten million Arbudas and Añjakanyās, [attained] divine status belonging to the Supreme Lord. 55.
Having seen this supreme marvel, the mothers and the maidens were filled with wonder;
they quickly entreated him, saying, "Become our husband. (56)
Then Kṛṣṇa granted a boon to all of them according to their desire;
he said to Garuḍa, "We shall go to the glorious Badarikāvana."
Then Hari, mounted upon Garuḍa, took Sudarśana with him and called to mind his divine vehicle, which was a league in length and radiant.
Indeed, that golden celestial chariot, situated in its own abode, quickly arrived along with its attendants, as did all the women and maidens.
Having seated Mahākālī, who was formerly Śāvadīnā, and himself having placed the royal crown upon the devotee Jallāuddīnaka in the morning, Śrī Hari [departed].
Having offered the third [oblation] and traveled through the sky to Badarikāśrama,
he bathed in the Gaṅgā and performed the purification of his body.
He caused all of them to drink the nectar of Śrī Hari’s feet;
then, having performed the worship of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Hari [departed].
And he went to Kurukṣetra, which is ten krośas in extent,
supremely purifying, most excellent, and situated at the foot of the Himālaya mountain.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
When and by whom was Kurukṣetra created? Tell me that in detail;
how indeed is it purifying, and why is it always considered most excellent? (64)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In the beginning of the Kṛta age, there was a very powerful king named Ṛkṣa, born of the Lunar dynasty; from Ṛkṣa, Saṃvaraṇa was born.
He, however, was consecrated in his own kingdom by his father while still a child;
even in his childhood, he was devoted to righteousness and remained ever a devotee of mine.
His family priest was Vasiṣṭha, the son of Varuṇa;
that noble-minded sage taught him the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
On a day that was not a forbidden day for study, the king went forth to behold the forests; he entered the vast and delightful Vaibhrāja grove. 68.
He entered the Dvaitavana forest, where two furious bulls had gone;
then he beheld the edge of the wood covered with blooming red lotuses.
There he beheld the maidens of the gods,
and in their midst he saw Tapatī, the daughter of the Sun, who surpassed them all in excellence.
There, his mind fixed upon her, the lordly king set out toward Mount Meru;
yet he remained at the beautiful city of Pratiṣṭhāna, dwelling there while constantly remembering her.
When he had not returned home,
the family priest learned that he was staying on Mount Meru, his mind fixed upon Tapatī.
Having ascended, Vasiṣṭha proceeded toward the solar orb;
the Sun bowed to him, and he in turn bowed to and worshipped the Sun.
The sage asked the reason for his arrival and said to Sūrya:
"O Lord of Gods, O one of great luster, I have come to make a request of you. (74)
"You ought to give Tāpī for the sake of Saṃvaraṇa.
Having been thus asked, Sūrya gave Tāpī, and he (Saṃvaraṇa) rejoiced.
The sage returned after taking the kingdom, and Samvaraṇa also arrived;
seeing him, Tāpī desired him, and she was bestowed upon him by the great sage.
In due time, a son named Kuru was born to her;
at the age of sixteen, he married the daughter of King Sudāman.
Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to one named Kīrti, the king entered the forest;
together with his wife Saudāmnī, he indeed performed austerities in the Dvaitavana forest.
There he beheld the goddess Sarasvatī, who has a lion’s tongue,
the mother of Sudarśana, the daughter of Brahmā, and the one born from the Plakṣa tree.
Having bathed there and drunk the water, he approached the Brahmavedī;
that northern area is called the Brahmavedī, the sacrificial ground.
The central altar is the Brahma-vedi, which is called Prayāgarāja;
the eastern altar is the Gayā-vedi, while Virajā is indeed the southern one.
The western altar is Puṣkarā, adorned with three sacrificial pits;
Syamantapañcaka is the place of Dharma, serving as the northern altar.
Extending five yojanas all around on every side,
that royal seer considered it a sacred field yielding great fruit.
Having constructed a lake and built a leaf-hut, he took up residence there;
likewise, having fashioned a plough from the bull of Rudra and the buffalo of Yama.
Having arranged for a plowman, he himself prepared to plow;
as he was plowing, Mahendra arrived and asked him the reason for his action.
"O King, what is this act of Kārṣeya that you are intent on performing here?
The king replied: "Austerity, truth, purity, charity, compassion, and forgiveness. (86)
"Yoga and virtuous conduct—these eight are found herein. Thus Indra spoke, O King: 'May your desire be fulfilled! (87)
When Indra had departed, that king plowed incessantly;
he made the land, exceeding seven krośas, furrowed by the plow.
Then, O Rādhikā, having become a brāhmaṇa, I went into the presence of the king and asked:
"O King, how indeed is this suffering being endured by you? (89)
"Then the Great Eightfold Dharma was fully explained to me by the king. Thereupon, O King, I asked him: 'Where does its seed reside? (2.30.90)
He said, "Indeed, there is the seed of my mind within this body of mine.
I said to him, "Extract that seed from your body and give it to me. (9.1)
"I shall indeed sow the garden; you yourself must plow with the plough.
Thereupon, the king extended his right arm. (92)
By my discus, he was cut there into a thousand pieces;
likewise, his left arm, feet, and waist were split in two.
Those seeds grew in all directions, exceeding ten million in number;
then he gave me his head, and because of that, I was pleased with him. (94)
When he replied, "I am the giver of boons," the Kuru then requested a boon:
"Let this field of dharma, which has been ploughed by me, belong to you. (95)
For those who have bathed and for those who have died, there is indeed the fruit of great merit here;
likewise, fasting, giving, bathing, recitation, and worship [yield great results]. (96)
O Lord, may all [acts] such as the *homa* sacrifice become inexhaustible here;
likewise, may you, together with the gods, Brahmā, and Śambhu, [be present]. (97)
"Reside here, O lotus-eyed one, in this place marked by my name.
When he had spoken thus, I then said to him, "So be it. (18)
And so, may you once again possess a divine body and be well;
at the end of this long period, you shall attain dissolution into my own person.
And your fame shall be eternal through my support;
here you shall perform sacrifices by the thousands as the officiating priest.
The protectors of the field are the yakṣa Candra, the nāga Vāsuki,
the vidyādhara Śaṅkukarṇa, and likewise the rākṣasa Sukeśa.
I give you here eight thousand powerful archers, including Ajāvaṇa the king and Mahādeva the fire-priest.
In the midst of Kurujāṅgala is the great lake Pṛthūdaka,
and there also flows the auspicious, purifying river Sarasvatī.
Between the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī rivers, in Kurujāṅgala,
lies the auspicious Brahma-saras, a sacred bathing place extending half a yojana in every direction.
This was the first altar of Brahmā; from that, the Rāmahrada is remembered.
Beyond that, Kurukṣetra is proclaimed, for it is indeed the purifying Field of Dharma.
Whatever distance exists between Tarantuka and Arantuka, and whatever distance indeed exists from the five lakes of Rāma; || 106 ||
That vast Kurukṣetra, known as Samantapañcaka, was there;
into it, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa arrived through the sky.
O Rādhikā, having bathed the women at the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, and the Brahmasaras lake, he traveled by vehicle for but a moment.
He went to the Lomaśa hermitage in the region of Aśvapaṭṭasara;
there were boys, girls, women, the Goddess, Garuḍa, and Hari.
They descended there to the earth, and cries of "Victory! then arose;
musical instruments were sounded, and the conch of the Goddess was also blown.
The sages, headed by Lomaśa, and the subjects quickly arrived;
the brahmins and others, having addressed him, performed auspicious rites.
Having bathed in the lake and partaken of all kinds of foods, they refreshed themselves in the garden, weary from the fatigue of their journey.
A festival of victory was celebrated at night, and the destruction of the king was proclaimed;
then the children were entrusted by Hari to their own fathers.
All the young women were presented by Lomaśa for the purpose of guarding the hermitage and also for the purpose of imparting sacred mantras.
And Lomaśa gave to the pure women the mantra and garlands:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. || 1 15 ||
By the spiritual luster of Brahmā, they became divine forms of Vaiṣṇavīs;
and by the power of Kṛṣṇa’s grace, those Mothers performed worship.
Possessing divine bodies and traveling in celestial chariots, they went indeed to Vaikuṇṭha;
there, by the will of Śrī Hari, those maidens remained forever.
Thus, the children were protected and the barbarians were likewise destroyed;
by reading and hearing this, the fruits of heaven and liberation shall be attained.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Performance of the Animal Sacrifice for the Goddess by the King, the Destruction of the King and Others by the Goddess, the Return to Badarī, Kurukṣetra, and Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Entrusting of the Children to Their Fathers, and the Liberation of the Mothers," in the second section, the Tretā Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Goddess Rādhikā; the compassionate Kālikā took up her divine residence on the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, sheltered by a banyan tree.
The beloved eighteen-armed consort of Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is mounted upon a lion, indeed performs the protection of the field. || 2 ||
Possessing a divine form, she always protects young maidens;
by the will of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, she is seen visibly by people.
That holy place, the Kālikā-tīrtha, is situated at Aśvasaras,
on the western bridge there, in the vicinity of the constructed temple.
And at the conclusion of the Māgha bath, the subjects, the brahmins, and the maidens worshipped the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa most exceedingly.
A great festival indeed took place, for it was divine and bestows liberation;
then that news spread everywhere with the speed of the wind.
People come from afar to behold the man walking upon the water;
seeing it again and again, they consider it the great wonder of Śrī Hari’s power.
Then, sprinkled with water by Hari,
that man of the waters attained a divine form, with hands, feet, and all his limbs restored.
He praised Śrī Hari and prayed for perpetual service at His feet;
Śrī Hari then appointed him as the guardian of the sacred field (kṣetrapāla) right there by the lake.
"Your lineage shall spread everywhere, both mental and physical;
that creation will consist of water-beings," he said to him.
Then he cast his inert body into the midst of the water;
thereupon, one hundred divine male and female water-beings (Jalanaras and Jalaris) came into existence.
Then the people beheld Mahākālī and proceeded on their way;
they spoke of the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
They worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord;
and many attain liberation through the majesty of the Lord of Śrī.
Since Hari, the beloved Lord, had arrived there at that hermitage, those maidens observed the milk-vow (payovrata), for they had already honored him with that purpose in mind.
O Rādhikā, for the sake of nourishing the vow, the wish-fulfilling cows then constantly yield milk, while the maidens perform the vow.
In the morning, they bathe Śrī Hari with pure milk;
afterwards, having bathed the Lord with water, they honor him with garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
They delight the body of the Lord with their devotion, perfume it with excellent unguents, massage it, and please him with beautiful songs. || 17 ||
They cause laughter with their great sweetness, they please with their beautiful dances;
they gladden with pleasant touches and satisfy with excellent food. || 18 ||
They praise and indeed magnify [Kṛṣṇa] with lustration rites and petitions for forgiveness;
thus, those who observe the vow of Kṛṣṇa drink only milk.
Having observed the vow for a full month, they offered it unto Kṛṣṇa;
and having performed the ceremonies of giving gifts, fire-offerings, festivals, and the concluding rite (udyāpana), they brought it to completion.
They remained right there and joined Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama),
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who is the master of their very lives.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
How did Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman and the purifying Lord, accept the daughters of barbarian rākṣasas, who were born from a base nature? (22)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhā, I shall tell you my divine story.
Long ago, I was manifested as a partial expansion (svāṃśa) by the Supreme Brahman.
At that time, I made Rādhā, who was a portion of Him, my wife;
she does not obstruct His majesty, for such is indeed the nature of radiant beings.
By the Supreme Brahman, the four-armed Nārāyaṇa was created;
and Lakṣmī, who arose from the Supreme Brahman, was made his beloved by him. ||25||
Pride does not trouble one who has descended as Nārāyaṇa;
by Brahmā, his own lineage member Sāvitrī was married to him.
Gāyatrī, born of the lineage of Brahmā, was made his beloved daughter;
likewise, Sarasvatī was honored as his daughter and accepted as his wife. ||27||
The daughters of Dakṣa, born of noble lineage, were all married to the sons and grandsons of Brahmā’s son. (28)
In ancient times, Kaśyapa made those born as animals his own beloveds; Danu and Diti—these two were the Rākṣasa women who were the wives of Kaśyapa.
Arundhatī and Śvapacī were married by Vasiṣṭha;
Kālī, Bhairavī, and Durgā are the Tāmasī forms beloved by Śaṅkara.
Vṛndā and Tulasī were the two wives of the Daitya married to Viṣṇu;
from the hair of his body the Mlecchas were born, and they are remembered as the lineages of the cows.
The Blessed One is capable of purifying everyone at that very moment;
in his presence, there is no sense of caste, nor high status, nor low status. (32)
For the Blessed One is to be realized through meditative cultivation; when cultivated, he himself cultivates [the practitioner].
He is everything for him, in everything, because he is indeed of the nature of that very thing. //33//
The enjoyer of all, the creator of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of lords—by his command, Brahmā formerly created pairs [of beings]. (34)
That pair, consisting of a brother and a sister, became a thousand;
from that, creation indeed occurs in the Kṛta Yuga, and there is no fault in this.
At that time, there was no custom of giving daughters to others;
then, for the sake of ensuring the continuity of the lineage for those who were without daughters, [the following occurred]. (36)
The giving away of the daughter was to be performed by bestowing her upon another;
the rule was that the daughter must be given away into a different lineage. Thus was the subsequent injunction.

A girl should be given in marriage to one who is not a sapinda and belongs to the same caste; such is the rule that has been established. In this way, indeed, all obtain a daughter who continues their lineage. (38)
Certain dharmas existed in the past at the very beginning of creation; other dharmas prevailed during the Kṛta age, while yet other righteous paths were followed at the start of the Tretā age.
In the Kali age, O beloved, those who were unrighteous then became righteous; yet all those who practice the dharma of the Kali age are not considered righteous by virtue of that dharma.
Due to the differentiation of their splendor, beings with differing natures prevail in age after age;
therefore, there is no fault in Kṛṣṇa, for his action is indeed dharma itself. ||41||
That supreme tradition established by Him always governs the entire world;
yet that tradition is never able to govern Kṛṣṇa Himself. ||42||
The ritual practice of Kṛṣṇa is the great mother of the sacred tradition (āmnāya);
therefore, all the rituals of Kṛṣṇa have the nature of the self and the tradition. 43.
Neither that lust, nor that anger, nor sexual misconduct, nor violence, nor that theft, nor that confusion exists which has been performed by Kṛṣṇa. (44)
Divine passion as well as divine anger, divine sexual indulgence, and likewise divine violence, theft, and promiscuity—all these were always performed by Kṛṣṇa. (45)
Rādhā is divine, Rati is divine, and the state of enjoying divine opulence is divine;
everything there consists of the Supreme Brahman, and thus there is no fault. 46.
Where there is a mass of light, darkness is not found there;
for darkness is said to be a defect, and it cannot exist among those who possess brilliance. (47)
Those dominated by darkness perceive faults through their limited vision;
yet, through the vision of Brahman, those very same things indeed become ornaments.

Whatever affection one has for a wife, a son, a daughter, or one's father and other kin—if that very same affection is directed toward the virtuous, it bestows liberation, free from all worldly qualities. (49)
In the presence of virtuous women, faults are reduced to ashes through yoga;
indeed, by union with Hari, the virtuous attain divine states and become saintly women.
O Rādhā, just as your sons, though they may be like salt water, are in every way purifying, taking the form of sacred pilgrimage sites, and indeed possessing divine forms. 5.1.
Just as the linga is indeed the root of desire and of the nature of defects within the worlds,
it is nevertheless worshipped like Brahmā through the yoga of Śaṅkara.
Even stones and other materials are worshipped as images through their union with Brahman;
therefore, O Rādhā, everything belonging to my lineage should be worshipped by you.
O beloved, through union with Kṛṣṇa, even the barbarian attains purity;
indeed, through union with Brahman, the *bhaga* is seen within the sacrificial pit.
In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, an image of Aśvaliṅga is given into the hand of the wife;
O beloved, in every case, purification is brought about through union with Brahman.
Therefore, one should not entertain doubt as to how the daughters of Mlecchas can be dear;
for whatever is dear to Śrī Hari is indeed pure, without a doubt. (56)
Now, however, I shall proclaim this true nature of dharma; learn it from me, as it was perceived in former times by the high-souled sages who were knowers of dharma.
O lady of lovely countenance and sweet smile, it is said that in former times women were unconfined; they moved about according to their own will and lived independently. 58.
O fortunate one, O lady of excellent hips, no unrighteousness occurred when they transgressed against their husbands from their youth; for that was indeed the law in ancient times.
And even the creatures born of animal wombs always conform to that very ancient law,
following the seasonal ordinances.
This dharma, seen through valid means of knowledge, is honored by the great seers;
it prevails in the northern regions and among the Kurus as well. (61)
This dharma, characterized by having many husbands, is the beloved of the mountain-dwelling subjects;
it exists even among goddesses in heaven and other realms, for that indeed is dharma.
Even among female slaves, that very same dharma prevails everywhere;
indeed, that eternal dharma is attained through favor toward women.
Now, listen also to how a boundary was once established by Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, out of anger. (64)
It is said that in former times, in the presence of Śvetaketu’s father, a certain Brahmin took his mother by the hand and said, "Let us go. (65)
Then the son of the seer, impelled by indignation, became enraged upon seeing his mother being forcibly led away before his father. (66)
Seeing his son enraged, the father said to Śvetaketu:
"Do not give way to anger, my son; this is the eternal dharma. (67)
For on this earth, women of all castes are indeed unrestrained;
just as cows remain with their respective owners, so do young women with their husbands. (68)
But Śvetaketu could not tolerate that practice in any way;
he established this boundary between men and women on earth. (69)
Listen, O dear Rādhikā: from this day forward, the sin of a woman who commits adultery with her husband shall apply only among humans and not to others. 2.31.70.
For one who violates a wife who has observed lifelong chastity from her youth, there will arise a terrible suffering equal to the murder of a fetus. (71)
For a devoted wife, this alone shall constitute a sin on earth:
whether she is appointed by her husband or even for the sake of obtaining a son. (72)
And he shall not do so; for that very thing will happen to him by Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, who is indeed righteous.
Therefore, that very dharma has been established as a fixed boundary:
at every season, a husband must certainly not be disregarded by his wife. (74)
It is said that in all other remaining times, a woman deserves independence;
for instance, Saudāsa appointed his own wife to the task of procreating a son.
Madayantī went to her guru, the sage Vasiṣṭha;
from him she obtained a son, renowned by the name Aśmaka.
In ancient times, there was a wise sage known as Utathya;
he had a wife named Mamatā, who was highly esteemed by him.
The younger brother of Utathya, the highly effulgent Bṛhaspati, became the priest of the gods and took Mamata as his wife.
Mamatā, however, spoke to her husband’s younger brother, the best among speakers:
"O younger brother-in-law, I am pregnant by your brother. (79)
"Your seed is never in vain, yet there can be no conception from it within the wombs of these two.
Although addressed thus, he was indeed unable to restrain his desire.
Then, as he was emitting his semen, he sported with her;
while still within the womb, the son of Utathya addressed him: "There is no such possibility here. (8.1)
"There is no room for both; you ought not to cause suffering.
But Bṛhaspati, without even hearing those words of the one staying in the womb, [departed].
He indeed discharged his semen; that semen, struck by the feet of the child who was still in the womb, fell upon the earth. Thereupon, Bṛhaspati became enraged.
He cursed the fetus, saying, "O fool, you shall enter into long-lasting darkness.
He was indeed born as the sage Dīrghatamas, blind from birth. (84)
But the wise one then obtained a wife named Pradveṣī;
he begot sons such as Gautama and others who were practitioners of austerity. ||85||
Like a bull, Dīrghatamas engaged in sexual intercourse in public,
right in the presence of people, thereby destroying all social boundaries.
The sages shunned him, for he had indeed transgressed the bounds of propriety;
he, full of hatred, did not serve him, and then the sage spoke to her.
"O wife, tell me why you do not serve me at all; state the reason.
But the wife spoke with hostility to her husband: "A husband is so called because he supports (bharana). (88)

Moreover, the title of "husband" comes from the act of protecting, yet both of these qualities are absent in you; on the contrary, I, along with my son, am the one who suffers the hardship of supporting you. (89)
"And since I have become powerless, I shall take another husband;
do as you wish, O best of Brahmins, for I am going to another person."
Dīrghatamas said: "From this day forward, I shall establish this boundary in the world:
for a woman, there is but one husband who is her sole refuge as long as she lives. (9.1)
Whether her husband is dead or alive, she shall not obtain another man;
for it is ordained that if she obtains another, she becomes an outcaste.
Hearing this, she became enraged and said to her sons regarding their father:
"Throw this blind man, who speaks unpleasantly, into the boat! (93)
The sons, having bound their father, cast him into a boat on the Gaṅgā; and he, floating with the current, was carried along by the flow.
When the boat, having fallen into the current, reached a distant land, there was a single blind man on board who was engaged in the recitation of the names of Śrīśa. 95.
King Bali indeed saw him, seized him, and led him away;
recognizing the sage as one fit for his household, he who desired a son employed him with his wife. (96)
That queen Sudēṣṇā did not accept the sage;
instead, she then sent her own nurse’s daughter to that old man. 97.
In her, the sage begot eleven sons, Kākṣīvat and the others; thereafter, Sudeṣṇā indeed took a liking to him.
From him were born five princes by Sudeṣṇā; those sons of his were Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Puṇḍra, and Suhma, all of whom were powerful.
Their lands shall be known by those very names;
thus was the lineage of Bali formerly proclaimed by the great seer.
Parāśara united with Matsyagandhā, the daughter of a fisherman;
such was the dharma of former times—what need is there to speak of Nārāyaṇa?
Everything is the object of enjoyment for Nārāyaṇa, and everything is the body of Nārāyaṇa;
everything is the form of Nārāyaṇa’s wives, and the husband is Nārāyaṇa.
Do not harbor any doubt regarding Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Rādhā;
he who bestows offspring through Māyā bestows offspring even within that which is composed of Māyā.
He alone is the Supreme Lord—the creator, the protector, and the destroyer;
for he may indeed always take all the maidens, as that is ever appropriate for him.
Through reading and hearing this, the reality of Dharma that existed of old shall be known; doubt shall dissolve, and one shall become a partaker of merit. (105)

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Milk-Vow of Maidens, the Boundaries Established by Śvetaketu Regarding Ancient Dharma, Aśmaka Born of Vasiṣṭha’s Son upon the Wife of Saudāsa, Utathya’s Wife Touched by Bṛhaspati, and Dīrghatamas Procreating Sons through the Slave-Woman and Queen of Bali, and the Subsequent Establishment of Moral Limits," in the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa himself performed the worship of the planets and other deities when obstacles arose during the month of Māgha.
In the month of Phālguna, he caused the Viṣṇu-sacrifice to be performed by the Brahmins for the sake of pacifying obstacles in the sacred field and also for the sake of pacifying the planets.
He then gave away innumerable gifts so that the welfare and security of the children living in Saurāṣṭra might become auspicious.
The father indeed caused worship to be performed for the various gods, as well as for his mother and others; likewise, he had the best offerings and oblations presented.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
"O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, who are those grahas and bālagrahas that afflict children here? What are the forms of these grahas? Tell me this. (5)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In ancient times, Skanda became the son of Rudra, born from his seed,
as well as of Pārvatī, Vahni, Gaṅgā, and Darbhaka.
Then Skanda became the son of the six wives of the sages;
he was born as the commander-in-chief of the gods, and thereafter Lakṣmī took refuge in him.
Skanda was graced by Śrī on the fifth day; therefore, it is remembered as Śrīpañcamī.
Since he attained his purpose on the sixth, that great lunar day is known as Ṣaṣṭhī.
Then the six goddesses, the wives of the seven seers, approached Mahāsena, who was endowed with splendor and had been appointed as the commander-in-chief of the divine army.
Abandoned by the sages, they spoke to their son Kārtika:
"O son, we have been abandoned by our husbands for a trivial reason."
"It was indeed proclaimed by us in accordance with the Veda that you were born [of us];
because of that fault we have been abandoned. Therefore, you ought to save us. (1.1)
"Having fallen from our station in heaven, we have indeed been censured by the sages;
therefore, by your grace, please ensure that our stay in heaven becomes imperishable. (12)
"We desire you as our son; having done this, become free from debt.
At that time, the high-minded Mahendra spoke thus to Skanda.
The sister named Abhijit, who is younger than Rohiṇī, has gone to the forest to perform penance; she desires the status of being the elder for the sake of asceticism.
That place remains empty; O Skanda, fill that spot! Indeed, fulfill the completion of the number of constellations with the Kṛttikās.
Skanda appointed those six mothers in the form of the Kṛttikās;
thus that constellation named Kṛttikā shines with Agni as its presiding deity.
"Now, if it be asked how it is that the six Kṛttikās are considered there to have seven heads, listen; I shall explain the reason for that."
Vinatā also said to Skanda, "Include me there as well";
Skanda then granted her that seventh auspicious station.
Thus, that constellation Kṛttikā is considered to have seven heads.
Then those Kṛttikās spoke again to Skanda according to their desire: ||| 19 ||
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Nārāyaṇī,
Gāyatrī, Durgikā, and Māyā— these are the seven Mothers.
Those [categories] which were previously postulated for the world since beginningless time—our position would be that those very same [categories] do not exist for them. (2.1)
"O Kārtika, we would have been worthy of worship by the world, for they themselves were not worthy of worship;
since, by speaking thus, they caused our separation from the sages. (22)
We desire that the offspring of these mothers, who have the ancestors as their deities, may always be providers of enjoyment for us, just like the sages. (23)
Skanda said: "Let these indeed become the wives of Candra;
protect them, as well as our other sons who are always like our own children. (24)
Then the Kṛttikās said, "O son, we shall do so;
however, the offspring will be young men sixteen years of age. (25)
"And grant us mortals the power to enjoy [the offerings] through various forms of progeny.
Skanda said, "Let it be so; may you all be endowed with happiness. (26)
I, however, shall give you my own fierce and imperishable self;
united with that supreme [self], may you indeed dwell happily in heaven.
Having spoken thus, Kārtika produced from his body a person with the brilliance of fire in the form of a planet, and gave him to them for the attainment of happiness.
Having taken that being of fierce form, they went to the lunar realm;
those who know the truth call that graha "Skandāpasmāra."
Vinatā is said to be the most terrible bird-graha;
they call Pūtanā a Rākṣasī, and one should know her as the Pūtanā-graha.
The night-stalker (niśācarī) of terrible form and painful nature, the Piśācī of fierce appearance, is called Śītapūtanā. ||3.1||
That one of terrible appearance carries away the embryos of human women;
they call her Aditi, and Raivata is said to be her graha.
That most terrible great planet indeed afflicts children;
they call Diti, the mother of the Daityas, Mukhamandika.
She was exceedingly delighted by the flesh of porpoises and was difficult to approach;
and there were boys and girls who had been born from Skanda.
All those great planets, who consume the fetus and perform cruel deeds, [affect] the sons, the wives, the daughters, and the men [of the family]. (35)
Those performers of terrible deeds seize the children as they are being born;
however, there exists Surabhi, the mother of cows, in the abode of the gods.
Then, having ascended that bird, she eats the children on the ground together with him;
for she who is the mother of dogs is the goddess named Saramā, O Rādhikā. (37)
She always takes up the embryos of human women;
she who is the mother of trees is known as Karañjanilayā.
But Saikā is the bestower of boons, a protector, and compassionate toward all beings;
men who desire sons worship her at the Karañja tree. (39)
Moreover, other mothers and spirits who delight in meat and honey constantly remain in the lying-in chamber by day and by night. (2.32.40)
Then Kadrū, assuming a subtle form, enters the pregnant woman;
there she consumes that fetus, and [the mother] gives birth to one equal to a Nāga. ||41||
She is the mother of the Gandharvas, and having taken the embryo, she departs;
therefore, a human woman is seen by people with her pregnancy dissolved.
The mother of the Apsarases, however, remained holding her embryo; when such a thing occurred, people said, "The embryo has perished. (43)
The maiden of the Blood Ocean, who is known as the nurse of Skanda,
is worshipped by people under the name Lohitāyanī at the Kadamba tree.
As Rudra is among men, so is that noble lady among women;
she, the noble mother of Kumāra, is worshipped separately for the sake of fulfilling desires.
All these great grahas are indeed devourers of children;
for they are inauspicious for infants until they reach sixteen years of age. 46.
Furthermore, those who are the groups of Mothers and those who are the groups of male Grahas—all these are to be known in the world as Skandha-grahas, the givers of suffering. (47)
Their pacification must be performed through bathing, incense, and collyrium;
furthermore, there should be offerings of bali-oblations and especially worship to Skanda.
Thus worshipped, they all bestow longevity, vigor, and strength.
Now, those planetary spirits (grahas) that affect men after the sixteenth year— ||49||
Listen, O Rādhā, I speak to them; for they are considered to be devotees of Maheśvara.
That man who beholds the gods, whether he be awake or even lying down— 2.32.50.
Then he quickly goes mad; they know that to be possession by a deity.
And the man who, whether sitting or lying down, sees his ancestors [is possessed by them]. (51)
Then he quickly goes mad; this is known as the Pitṛ-graha.
He who insults the Siddhas is cursed with anger by the virtuous. ||52||
He who quickly becomes insane is known as one possessed by a Siddha-graha;
he also smells fragrances and even tastes flavors. (53)
He quickly becomes utterly deranged; he should be known as a Rākṣasa-graha.
And when divine Gandharvas enter that beloved man, [he is likewise possessed].
He quickly becomes insane; that is indeed a Gāndharva possession, which Piśācas constantly mount upon a man. (55)
That person quickly goes mad; he is indeed possessed by a piśāca spirit.
And when the time comes, yakṣas enter that man.
He quickly becomes insane; he should be known as one possessed by a yakṣa-graha.
The disorder, the seizure, the mental derangement, and the terrifying fear—[all these arise]. (57)
One indeed desires to play, another likewise desires to eat, and yet another desires sexual union; such is this threefold seizure (graha). //58//
These afflictions remain as seizing spirits for men until they enter old age;
beyond this point, fever becomes like a seizing spirit for embodied beings.
The planetary spirits always avoid one who has restrained his senses, who is devoted, pure, free from pride and sloth, and who is a believer and full of faith. (2.32.60)
Malevolent planets do not afflict those who are devoted, virtuous, saintly, and of disciplined conduct.
Then Skanda said to Svāhā, "You are indeed my dear daughter."
"O son, grant me a permanent dwelling to reside with Agni.
Skanda replied: "The sacrificial offerings for the gods and the ancestors have been praised by the twice-born with mantras."
"May there always be 'svāhā' when one offers oblations into the fire; may your dwelling always be with you.
Wherever there is no home and no sacrifice, there you shall dwell in the form of a planet. (63)
"You shall become [the goddess] Pañcakhādinī in the Pañcaka; of this there is no doubt.
Having been addressed thus by Vahni, Svāhā dwells there eternally with him.
Thus have those planets been described as being destructive in some instances and others;
therefore, they must indeed be worshipped, for when satisfied, they are known to bestow happiness. ||65||
On the eighth day of the month of Phālguna, Gopālakṛṣṇa caused that worship to be performed with mantras and the offering of various oblations.
With milk-rice, fried cakes, vegetables, and parched grains,
he devoutly gratified all the planetary deities with offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
Then Skanda, having done so, [commanded] Vinatā, Pūtanā and others,
the daughters of Diti and Aditi, the Piśācīs, Surabhi, and Śakuni.
Saramā, Kadrukī, and the mothers of the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
Dhātrī, Raktāyanī, as well as the gods, ancestors, Siddhas, and Grahas. ||69||
The Paiśācas, Rakṣasas, Gāndharvas, Yakṣas, Kāmas, Jvaras,
and the Svāhās— these are other lineages, and they constitute twenty-six groups.
And they descended visibly through the sky into the lake,
assuming gentle forms, at the place where this worship was being performed.
Having received worship, offerings, milk-preparations, and so forth in every way,
they were satisfied and praised Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord.
O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, we are planets that perform wicked deeds; for we were created exactly so, we shall not reach the end of our sins. (73)
Grant your grace so that we may cross the ocean of illusion;
indeed, always forgive the offenses committed by us in our wicked states of mind. 74.
Where Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa is, there is no oppression by us;
we never enter this sacred field for the purpose of causing harm. (75)
O Kṛṣṇa, by granting the nectar of Your feet, make us pure;
You are the God who is the seizer of the planets, their controller, and the Supreme Lord. (76)
Grant us residence at your feet, ever purifying those who are auspicious;
we have sought refuge in your lap—accept us as your own servants. (77)
Having thus entreated him, they then fell at the feet of Śrī Hari;
they were then duly consecrated with water by Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Sprinkled, purified, and satiated by the drinking of water, and touched and fed, they all then attained a divine state. ||79||
They were resplendent with divine forms, just like the attendants of Hari;
then, on the shore of the lake, Hari spoke to them in his celestial form.
May the gods always dwell right here, free from fear, free from disease, devoid of affliction, and ever bestowing prosperity. (8.1)
"Here on this southern bank, there shall be a famous pilgrimage site known as Grahatīrtha;
and those people who always worship your images here [shall obtain great merit]. (82)
"Indeed, let not the sons born of their lineage who reside in other lands be oppressed by you, even though you yourselves have gone to other lands. (83)
Then, let them wander this earth in their second forms and perform their appointed planetary duties as required. (84)
The sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā extends for ten yojanas;
leaving it aside, they may indeed commit their assault elsewhere when there is an opportunity.
Even there, let them not commit an assault upon my devotees,
nor let them commit an assault upon those who possess the vows of Brahmanical conduct.

Let them not commit an assault against the virtuous, the chaste, the Brahmins, those most devoted to the Veda, nor against those who perform penance, observe vows, and engage in meritorious deeds. (87)
They must by no means at all commit any assault or oppression against those who serve cows, gods, and virtuous people, nor against pure yogis or householders who are devoted to the Lord. ||88||
Let them practice the subjugation of atheists, revilers, and backbiters;
let them practice that toward the violent, the envious, and the wicked;
and let them practice the subjugation of those who do not honor the gods, the ancestors, or the sacred fires.
May they repeatedly inflict humiliation upon thieves, drunkards, those who cause suffering to others, the wicked, and those devoid of dharma; likewise,
upon the unjust, those who consume the deposits of others, and the divisive.
"May you ladies show defiance toward those who oppose virtuous deeds!
This field of Kuṅkumavāpikā is supremely divine and blissful;
it is equal to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself and is free from both merit and sin. (92-93)
This place, consisting of the offering to Brahman, is the ground of liberation and my own abode; let those whose true nature is liberated dwell there in my refuge.
My guru Lomaśa will bestow the mantra upon you here.
"Having reached that mantra, let the Vaiṣṇava planets remain there.
Thus addressed, all those planets—both auspicious and inauspicious—became twofold in form through Kṛṣṇa’s resolve; for those who were shadow-selves became sources of unhappiness.
Those divine beings in their original forms went to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Lomaśa bestowed upon them the mantra dedicated to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (97)
He placed a garland of tulasī upon their necks and gave them excellent sectarian marks (puṇḍraka).
Having thus become Vaiṣṇavas, they remained on the bank of Lake Aśva; then, as shadow-selves, they departed for whatever other desired lands they wished to go.
Thus did the Blessed One bring peace to all the seizing spirits;
they grant happiness to devotees and are always liberating and auspicious.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this divine marvel has been described;
whoever hears or recites it shall attain liberation with ease. (10.1)
There shall be abundant wealth, grain, cattle, birds, and riches;
and sons, grandsons, daughters, and their offspring shall remain free from disease.
They will become equal to the gods, overflowing with all bliss;
free from everything, free from duality, they will be the very embodiments of heaven.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifest Appearance of the Child-Spirits and Others upon their Worship, and the Description of Their Names, Forms, and Other Attributes," in the second section, the Tretā Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada in my fourth year, I performed [my birth rites]; now I shall relate to you the life-story of Śrī Harikṛṣṇa.
The noble ladies of Kuṅkumavāpikā and millions of maidens likewise observed the vow of Ṛṣipañcamī and performed the worship of the sages.

While she remained in her state of menstruation, they all thereafter performed worship and gave gifts as auxiliary parts of the vow, in order to eliminate the taint of contact and its associated impurity.
On the sixth day, they performed the Gaurī-vrata, having invoked her and worshipped her;
on the seventh day, they fed her with offerings of milk-rice and other foods.
On the eighth day, they indeed worshipped Gaurī with *dūrvā* grass;
they performed the worship of eight-year-old girls in the form of Gaurī.
With sandalwood and other unguents, saffron and the like, fragrant unbroken grains (akṣata) and so forth, with various erotic delights, garments, ornaments, and decorations; || 6 ||
With fruits, flowers, sweet foods, drinks, betel leaves,
and the offering of desired objects, they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites.
Then they performed songs and dances; subsequently, all the women and maidens went to Lake Aśvasaras in order to perform the ritual dismissal of Gaurī.
An earthen image of Gaurī,
adorned with every ornament and rich in all the splendor of finery, was placed upon the shoulder of a divine lion.
Carried in a divine palanquin, fanned with chowries and shaded by a parasol,
the women sing as they thus carry the image of Śrī Gaurī.
The sounds of musical instruments arose, signaling the festival;
and thousands of men and women went there as spectators. || 1 1 ||
And at the end, Kambharāśrī, the mother of Hari, went together with the cowherd women to the northern bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa to behold Gaurī.
Taking the boy Hari with them during the festival of Gaurī’s dismissal,
the women went to the riverbank and, full of eagerness, installed Gaurī there.
Then, having placed [the image] upon the ship, they performed worship and offered prayers:
