"May Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be like Śaṅkara unto us. (14)
"May he become as lovely and beloved as you yourself; be gracious to us.
Having thus prayed, they then offered a handful of flowers.
Amidst the sounds of musical instruments, they performed the ritual immersion in the water;
then, the cries of "Victory! from the women reached the very gates of heaven.
They gladdened the gods, the ancestors, and the best of sages;
when the dismissal of Gaurī had been performed, a miracle then occurred.
A certain very well-nourished tiger, as tall as a banyan tree,
suddenly arrived there where the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa was.
Widening his eyes and opening his mouth, emitting his scent, pricking up his ears and wagging his tail, he shook his hair and his hide. (19)
Displaying his anger and scratching the earth with the tips of his front hooves,
he quickly leaped up to seize the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
All men and women became paralyzed and motionless out of fear;
at that time, the sky was filled with thundering and began to tremble.
The trees shook, and for a moment the wind became motionless.
The earth became filled with trembling and hearts shook.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose when the tiger then sprang up;
people, their forms appearing like deer, fled in all directions.
Then the mother, Kambharā Lakṣmī, said, "May Gaurī protect [him]," and the other maidens there then made a vow:
"When the beloved of Kṛṣṇa has been protected here, we shall perform worship at the onset of night."
Furthermore, with all ritual offerings to Gaurī and Durgā as well,
they made this very vow; they indeed chanted the praises of Śrī Narāyaṇa,
and stood covering their eyes with both hands, unable to look upon him.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
Who was that great tiger? Why did he arrive in the evening?
For, leaving aside all others, he was indeed intent on seizing that child. (27)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: There was a Mleccha named Rakta, born in the land of Rakta, who was the younger brother of Śavadīna; he was a Rākṣasa who desired to avenge his brother’s enmity.
Assuming any form at will, he moves through the sky and even through water;
though dwelling in the forest, he sometimes acts like a tiger.
Among humans he acts as a human, and among birds he acts as a bird;
for such a person is indeed defiled, possessing a defiled intention.
When his brother was [bound] by the illustrious Hari at Cāraktadeśaka—
Slain then, he went to the ocean and became a wanderer abroad.
In an open place, far removed from the bank of the river Nāvilā,
one should purchase earth from a gold mine and other such sites.
Having taken golden clay, he returned to his own home;
there he heard of the death of his elder brother and the abduction of his daughters.

The death of the guru, a calamity, the loss of the kingdom to the power of enemies, and the reversal of the child’s festival—these also bring misfortune during the offering festival (balyutsava). || 34 ||

Beholding that entire carnage, the Guru— possessing the power to travel through the sky, appearing like a deity, and renowned as an ascetic— was filled with rage and grieved deeply for the kingdom, the army, and the queen.
When capable [remedies] exist, the writing on the forehead is not more powerful than destruction;
even when there is a capable brother and abundant wealth protected by the ocean. (36)
If the country is occupied by soldiers, there is destruction; thus one grieves, thinking it will happen even within the home.
Even a person born in a foreign land, though unaccompanied by an army, arrives and strikes. (37)
Having utterly destroyed that unscarred bird, the act of abducting the maiden from her mother is indeed a cause for lamentation.
Alas! Having heard this, neither my death nor my valor increases.
What is the use of such a futile life for an embodied being who has been thus humiliated? (39)
"I shall slay that enemy and bring back my daughters;
or else I shall give up my life—fie on this strength which is but useless strength! (40)
Having reflected thus, he abandoned the golden ship, his home, and so forth,
taking with him his own people who had assumed many forms as ascetics.
He went to Saurāṣṭra to slay the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. || 42 ||
And he beheld the vast and auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa;
he looked everywhere repeatedly for an opening to strike him down.
He constantly roams through thickets and dwells even among the trees;
accompanied by his retinue, he indeed wanders through the sacred field assuming many forms.
There, in various places, some of them act like crows perched upon the trees.
Likewise, others act like vultures and behave like wolves near the lake. 45.
Others acted like parrots, while yet others acted like cows; some acted like bulls, and even some acted like cats. (46)
Some act like mosquitoes, repeatedly seeking out a flaw to find an opportunity to kill the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (47)
Some act like fish in the water, while others behave like children;
still others assume the form of virgins and become their companions.
Even though they acted in this way, they could find no vulnerability to kill Kṛṣṇa;
then, becoming utterly despondent, they [attacked] the King’s younger brother with fury.
They said: "Indeed, no flaw can be found even in hundreds of years;
therefore, he must be slain by force, so that whatever will be, let it be. ||50||
Having thus made this agreement, those hundred heroes went to the shore of the lake and, having assembled, said: "We shall kill that slayer of kings."
They should gradually manifest one by one in the form of tigers;
first, indeed, they should enter among women in the forms of young maidens.
Thus, at that time, during the twilight, one hundred maidens of cruel disposition entered among the other maidens, intending to kill the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa.
Seeing Nārāyaṇa among the women,
the king’s younger brother himself considered him an easy target to kill, as he was alone and without a protector.
For the purpose of avenging his enmity, that first demon became a tiger;
as soon as the asura leaped up and went to seize the boy Kṛṣṇa,
Janārdana himself became a śarabha there.
Hari seized that younger brother of the king, who was distressed by the creeper and had assumed the form of a tiger;
grasping him by the throat, Hari swiftly slew the asura.
There, shouts of "Victory! arose for Hari, accompanied by a rain of flowers.
The gods brought about the destruction of suffering, and the women bowed their heads; Mahākālī appeared as a girl, wretched and pale, while Gaurī took on her true form.
Having approached him on foot himself, he bowed down to him;
but at that time, the Blessed One became like a child among women as before.
A tiger, having given birth to cubs there, died on that spot;
thus, that sacred bathing place known as Śārabha was born there at Aśvasaras.
Where Kṛṣṇa had bathed after slaying that asura at that time,
the goddess Mahākālī, acting as his servant, then praised Kṛṣṇa.
"I have understood, O Blessed One, that this obstacle which has arisen was not known by the Guardian of the Field; how and why indeed did this happen? (62)
Śrī Hari said, "O fortunate one, my will was such:
'This wicked one must be slain by me so that the virtuous woman does not find out.'"
I acted in such a way so that the Kṣetrapāla might not know;
thus, that entry was not noticed by you, the Kṣetrapāla.
Now behold these hundred very young maidens;
those Asuras who are their companions have indeed assumed disguised forms.
"They have come here in succession to kill me;
now that this leader has been slain by the tiger, they are terrified and have hidden themselves."
When the goddess and the guardian of the field saw the maidens, they turned into tigers;
and those who had gathered among the tigers likewise became tigers.
Then the goddesses and the maidens simultaneously rushed toward Hari to kill him, having made the firm resolve: "Either we must die, or he must be slain. (68)
Then Kṛṣṇa quickly blew his terrifying war-conch;
and Siṃha, the vehicle of the Goddess, arrived instantly.
The roars of tigers there were world-shattering;
indeed, the entire tiger-infested forest was filled with those cries.
The planets trembled, the trees shook, and the earth and the lake likewise quaked;
even the lion let out a roar, and froth fell upon the ground.
And from the roar, masses of foam flew up into the sky;
from them, indeed, five hundred lions were born in an instant.
Seeing the lions, some of the *balivyāghras* (offering-tigers) then became lions.
Then, indeed, a terrifying battle took place there among the lions.
And with his mouth and claws, he slaughtered both the lion and the army;
much pulling out of entrails and sucking at throats took place. (74)
"A woman must certainly not be killed"—this was their solemn vow of dharma.
Thus, even though lions fell in battle, those who were artificial ones were slain.
But the enemies who rely on the mane, being at the very root, are slain;
though they may be fewer in number, once dead, they are dead in every respect. (76)
And then, O Goddess, those lions born from the dead increased once more;
even the Blessed One, Nṛsiṃha, came to witness the battle of the lions.
Roaring toward the celestial realm from that place, the sons of Siṃha fought in the sky, leaping from *krośa* to *krośa*. 78.
The Blessed Lord, stationed in the sky, beheld him and roared;
the lion of the Goddess went forth and offered a welcome in the firmament.
Then the lions born from Siṃha slew the remaining asuras; all of them fell lifeless, having been killed by the hundred lions before Hari.
Then, by the grace of Lord Hari in the form of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, they—becoming one with Him and rendered sinless through their union with that sacred field—attained dissolution therein. (8.1)
Both the artificial and the natural [images] perished there at Narasiṃhaka;
they then attained dissolution and went to the abode together with Nṛsiṃha.
To those others who were born from the lion of the goddess, as well as the remaining ones born from the foam,
Śrī Hari gave the forest situated to the south for their residence.
That place became a lion-forest, always consisting of a dwelling for lions;
Hari granted that their lineage should remain unshakable.
He then gave a boon, as well as forest food and a herd of deer;
thereafter, the tiger who had been emaciated by the creeper died.
Those who were destroyers in the form of lions were indeed born as tigers;
even when struck down and killed, they did not die, for the Lord Nārāyaṇa was their protector. ||86||
To those who praised him, he granted the gift of life, health, and freedom from disease;
he gave them a forest for their dwelling, which indeed became a tiger-forest.
The lineages of tigers suited for the forest were indeed mixed with lions;
thus Hari established them both in the tiger-forest and the lion-forest. (88)
And having received the boon in Saurāṣṭra, they dwell perpetually in the forest;
those tigers are the Asuras and Mlecchas, while the lions are indeed the Devas.
Thus they dwell in Saurāṣṭra and in the southern forests.
On the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭa, there occurred a great battle between lions and tigers;
it was there that Narasiṃha descended from the sky. That place is proclaimed as the purifying Great Tīrtha of Lions and Tigers (Siṃhavyāghramahātīrtha).
At the onset of night following the battle, an excellent rain fell;
the surface of the earth attained clarity, and everyone went to their respective homes. (92)
Then those maidens performed a vow, worship,
and a night vigil for Durgā and Gaurī for the purpose of Kṛṣṇa’s protection.
At the end of the night, having worshipped Durgā and Gaurī and having asked for forgiveness, they [cast the images] into the water.
Then they performed the dismissal ceremony for Durgā and Gaurī, and thereafter for Hari.
They all went for the purpose of seeing [him] and considered their task accomplished;
then, having given gifts and duly honored their preceptor Lomaśa, [they departed]. || 95 ||
Having honored their parents, they then indeed broke their fast;
Kālī went to her own abode, and the lion also vanished from sight.
O Rādhikā, Saurāṣṭra then became healthy and free from fear;
this is the miraculous power of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. || 97 ||
For one by whom this is heard and recited, supreme welfare shall arise;
moreover, there shall be prosperity in this world, born from the continuity of one's lineage.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship and Dismissal of Gaurī, and the Destruction of the Vyāghrāsura named Vallīdīna along with a hundred demons assuming the forms of tigers and lions," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O highly wise Rādhikā, to this wonderful account of the fifth year of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self of all selves.
When the fifth year had arrived, the father duly celebrated the Lord’s birth festival,
performing the worship of all the gods according to the prescribed rites.
He arranged a gathering of Gandharvas for the singing,
and he had a pavilion constructed adorned with golden garments.
Viśvakarman himself fashioned there the deities, who were adorned with every visible beauty and possessed the splendor of many puppets.
Both Māyā and Śambara also rendered him assistance;
they produced the appearance of land upon water and of water upon land, as well as the appearance of earth upon the ocean.
Just as one might see an assembly hall on a wall, women in a gathering, or gardens in the corners of a canopy in the sky.
Seeing a staircase on a royal road or by rivers; seeing a gateway at a long enclosure or an enclosure within a gateway. || 7 ||
Thus, even though they were masters of science, they became bewildered upon looking about; and without a guide to show the way, they were unable to proceed. (8)
In entering, departing, standing, sitting, and looking about,
the members of the assembly— save for the spectators— had their movements rendered sluggish.
Having seated Bālakṛṣṇa upon a beautiful, divine throne within such a pavilion as this, the supreme lords performed his worship.
The celestial beings presented them; and having accepted them, the father, exceedingly joyful at his son’s festival, bestowed auspicious gifts upon them. || 11 ||
Having performed worship in this manner, the men remained seated in the assembly hall;
then the goddesses arrived there for the purpose of worshipping Hari.
With saffron, unbroken rice, perfumes, and so forth, as well as with flowers, darbha grass, and the like, and also with various sprouts, fresh grains, and other such items. || 13 ||
They worshipped him with garments, ornaments, decorations, and other beautiful objects, as well as with lustration rites that dispel all suffering.
The women of the city presented offerings and placed vessels of food before him; they set down sugar, fruits, and seeds, as well as various juices.
Then the inhabitants of the city worshipped the Supreme Lord;
the maidens also worshipped him, and the twice-born offered their blessings.
Ascetics, sages, and other virtuous, chaste women devoted to their husbands offered blessings to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. || 17 ||
Then, following the worship, the singers remained there, as did the musicians, born of both divine and human lineages. || 18 ||
Hāhā, Hūhū, Nārada, Parvata, Citradarśana,
Sudarśana, Tumburu, Viśvāvasu, and Parāvasu.
Meghasvana, Tāranāda, Dharaṇidhra, Anugālava, Vaṃśadhara, Taraṇika, Jalaghoṣa, and Vaiṇika.
Āmramañju, Calaṃbuṣa, Rāṃbheya, and Śaṅkhakarṭaka—these are the celestial Gandharvas, led by Cūḍavarman. ||21||
Those staying within the pavilion at that festival indeed performed singing, accompanied by musical instruments and adorned with rhythm, measure, scale, and modulation.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased with them, gave them garlands of diamonds and pearls; thereafter, the Gandharvas arrived at the assembly hall of the humans.
Citraratha, Pratola, Sāraṅga, Maṇirañjaka, Tāmareru, Tānasainya, Jagannātha, and Harītaka. || 20 ||
Bāṣpavarṣin, Dhūmramedhas, Śaśakunda, and Kapardaka—
these and other Gandharvas performed singing and instrumental music.
To them Hari gave delightful and diverse rewards:
ornaments of gold and silver, as well as golden coins and garments.
Then the Gāndharvas of the Dānavas and Daityas arrived at the assembly hall:
Kambukīrti, Gālavāda, Nassvana, and Bhujaghoṣaṇa.
Khātadhvaja, Golabhūpa, and these others performed a song of praise;
to them Hari gave garlands of pearls, gems, and corals.
Then the nāgas, cāraṇas, sūtas, māgadhas, and bards;
the brahmabhaṭṭas, vidyādharas, kinnaras, and kiṃpuruṣas—[all approached]. (29)
Accompanied by their poetic compositions, they arrived swiftly at the assembly;
they displayed the excellence of their respective works before the gathering.
They praised the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa exceedingly;
their father, being purified, gave them appropriate gifts of clothing.
The female dancers and singers performed songs, dances, and rhythmic movements for the pleasure of Hari; Hari, being pleased, bestowed wealth upon them.
Ornaments, vessels for decoration, various articles, divine garlands and garments, and rewards suitable for women. || 33 ||
Thus were the supplicants satisfied there at the festival of birth;
when they had all departed, the inhabitants of the abode were released.
The inhabitants of Akṣara, Amṛta, Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha,
and other realms offered their blessings to Him, their beloved Supreme Soul.
Śrī Harikṛṣṇa rose repeatedly from his seat and, taking them all at once onto his chest, embraced them many times over.
Assuming many forms, Kṛṣṇa took the flower garlands, the sandalwood paste, the unbroken grains of rice, and the moon-like [marks], as well as the worship performed all around by them.
Having given them a pleasing gift, he granted them leave from the assembly;
at the conclusion of their dismissal from the assembly, their father provided them with a meal.
He gave various kinds of drinks, as well as betel-leaf and gifts of satisfaction;
having celebrated that festival, everyone returned to their own homes.
Thus, when the great festival had taken place, there was a mighty cry of victory.
May the child Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be victorious in all worlds.
Thus, such words were heard everywhere on earth:
"The illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa is present here as a great lord of charity."
Transcending the mere requests of those who seek, he bestows whatever is desired:
food, drink, nourishment, wealth, clothing, and vehicles.
"Whatever desired object a seeker takes from the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa"—such was the fame that arose and spread among the people throughout the world. 43.
Having heard this on the Himalaya mountain, Dālbhya, Baka, Gavāyana,

Thus spoke the illustrious Hari; Hara and the others always resided there, for the illustrious Hari dwells in Śambhu’s palace, having constructed that very palace.
Thus, the divine Śaṅkara performed a supreme, celestial festival of dance in order to please Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Hari;
and the Blessed Lord, the Soul of All, likewise acted then to please Śambhu.
Having become a spectator, he remained there, stationed upon the stage of the performance.
Hari fulfilled the desire of his devotee Śambhu,
O Rādhikā, for Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is subservient to his devotees.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Naṭanāṭya Tīrtha and Other Matters," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning how the Lord was pleased by the various supernatural dances performed by the Kailāsa-based troupe of Ardhanārīśvara at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī; how He humbled the pride of Śaṅkara and became the bestower of liberation.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now I shall tell you another marvel of Hari; listen.
In his fifth year, during the month of Māgha, having observed the strength of his preceptor, || 1 ||
Having gone before Śrī Lomaśa, the father duly performed the auspicious commencement of Bālakṛṣṇa's education with him.
He worshipped Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, Sarasvatī, and the Vedas;
having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, he offered oblations of clarified butter.
He fed the brahmins and performed gifts of cows;
then Sarasvatī herself, being pleased, truly appeared before him in person.
Abounding in the beauty of the peacock posture and holding a lute in her hand,
she is worshipped by fourteen maidens of learning who possess her very form.
Adorned with the splendor of all ornaments, garments, and decorations,
Śāradā worshipped Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
When Bālakṛṣṇa had attained the state of invisibility, his beloved [Rādhā] likewise vanished;
thereafter, her friends were the Śrutis and the Smṛtis.
Narratives, poems, the power of logic, sections, philosophical inquiries, meditative concentrations, solitude, and likewise discourses; || 8 ||
The mantra-based, the tantra-based, the machine-based, and likewise the elemental;
as well as the arts, the calculations, the ritual placements, and the rites.
She is the formulation of elixirs, the art of warfare, and the power of illusion;
she consists of the Jyotis, Rk, Sāman, Atharvan, and Yajus Vedas.
The verbal, the metrical, the etymological, the astrological, the epistolary, as well as the oceanic, the aerial, the dream-based, the delusive, and the ornithological. || 1.1 ||

The bodily, the mental, the pertaining to living beings, the pertaining to gods, the life-restoring, the pertaining to transformation, the pertaining to the seasons, and likewise the pertaining to the elements. || 12 ||
She consists of the science of medicine, she is divine, she is both destructive and nourishing;
she is the artisan, the ground-cloth, the purifier of reality, and the one who follows the path of the mine.
Vaidyatī, Bahubhavanī, Sīvanī, Garbhavedinī, Drāviṇī, Mūrchinī, and others were the maidens who were these vidyās. || 14 ||
Young maidens, possessing a white luster and the hue of campaka flowers, entered into Kṛṣṇa following Sarasvatī, appearing as her very images. 15.
In this way, the boy then obtained his learning through the medium of his guru;
nevertheless, he practiced the writing of letters according to the worldly custom. (16)
He likewise practiced the repetition of syllables and words;
he was seen by people as a treasury of the sciences of the Vedas, the Shastras, and so forth. (17)
Then all those maidens serve him only from the outside; yet, remaining invisible, they always serve him within as well.
Having appeared, they remain and serve that very beloved;
those friends of Śāradā chose Śrī Narāyaṇa as their lord.
Those auspicious goddesses always dwelt in embodied form in the hermitage of Lomaśa, serving the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇabāla, the Supreme Lord, the Master, and the Sovereign.
By the very command of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the boy would daily go to his teacher for the purpose of practicing the most beautiful branches of knowledge. ||1||
Every morning, Lomaśa taught him meaningful lessons;
Kṛṣṇa grasped them like an ordinary person, and his teacher was exceedingly pleased.
He accepted the service of the maiden and thereafter went to his own home. Then, on one occasion, the preceptor of the gods arrived at the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Bālakṛṣṇa bowed to Bṛhaspati, who is praised by the gods;
at that time, Bṛhaspati indeed [did so] for the purpose of testing the intelligence of Hari.
In the very presence of Lomaśa, he asked a question consistent with logic:
"Tell me, what would be the value of a bhāra of gold measured by guñjās? (25)
The fool said: "If it were stable, it would be worth only a single *guñjā* seed;
if it were eternal, it would not be subject to manifold buying and selling. (26)
However many instances of ownership are transferred therein,
the object— whether distinct or differentiated— bestows exactly that manyfold merit.
For as long as it remains in one's possession—whether for a hundred thousand years or ten million years—the value shall increase by that same factor; therefore, its price is infinite.
That very gold, even when it is merely a *guñjā* seed in weight, undergoes transformation;
whatever new object is purchased with it will appear ever more new and fresh. ||29||
"O Teacher, in this way that gold is measured as being of infinite value.
Having heard this reply, the teacher was pleased with that logician.
The Omniscient One joined her with blessings: "Become all-knowing and all-seeing;
may your childhood, lasting until the end of the fifth year, be full and grant you nourishment. (31)
May your childhood, lasting until the end of the tenth year, be endowed with the dawning of knowledge;
and may your youth, up to the fifteenth year, be devoted to great prosperity.
Beyond that, may your youth be filled with infinite bliss;
may you possess eternal life and the nature of the Sanātana.
Having thus bestowed these blessings and received the worship then performed, he,
about to depart for Varāṭaka, questioned Śrī Hari, the great Asura.
And he saw him standing on the shore of the western ocean, performing supreme austerity,
speaking the truth, practicing non-violence, and established in the vow of non-stealing.
Devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), free from all possessions, possessed of purity, contented, and always delighted in the private recitation of the Vedas (svādhyāya). || 36 ||
Desiring the kingdom of Saurāṣṭra, which was supreme and dedicated to Brahman,
[he fought] against the son of the Asura Sālamālā, who was born from the ocean and possessed great strength.
"O Blessed One, here in Saurāṣṭra, on the shore of the western ocean, Varāṭaka, the son of Sāla, performs fierce penance for the sake of obtaining a kingdom. (38)
In summer he practices the penance of the five fires; in winter he stands in water;
likewise during the rains he remains motionless, subsisting continuously on air alone.
Placing his head on the ground and his feet in the sky, that great asura remained there day and night uttering "Oṃ," for the sake of sovereignty.
"Indra, having recognized this austerity, sent me; therefore I am departing.
I shall instruct him in such a way that he turns away from his penance. "Instruct me in that manner so that there may be a cessation of it."
You are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord. ||42||
"You are the protector of the gods and the subduer of the Daityas;
therefore, act in such a way that this Devaśūla does not attain sovereignty. (43)
"O Blessed One, instruct me; having gone, I shall do exactly as you say.
Upon hearing this, the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa spoke.
"And I desire that the obstruction of the Daitya's asceticism may come to pass;
O Guru, the Daitya should be restrained through conciliation, employing an awakening appropriate for him. (45)
I shall speak of the duties of the Daityas, as well as their knowledge, rituals, and so forth;
indeed, let instruction be granted by you in the form of a Brāhmaṇa.
For the most part, the Daityas, Āsurās, and Dānavas, being gratifiers of the senses, abide by acting according to their own whims, relying upon the doctrine that the body is the self. 47.
For the Daityas, however, dharma consists in the acquisition of wealth through battle, as well as seizing by force and bringing [the spoils] under one's own control. (48)
Valor is the duty of the Daityas, while austerity is the duty of those free from passion;
therefore, having caused him to fall away from that austerity, instruct him in the duties pertaining to the body. 49.
And by prioritizing hostility toward the dharma of the gods, atheism, the voidness of sin,
and violence, instruct the lowest of the Daityas.
Perception is indeed the only means of valid knowledge; there is no world beyond.
The fruit of asceticism is always trivial—understand it thus. (5.1)
"Tell him that Īśvara is partial and acts for the benefit of the gods, yet he has become hostile toward the Daitya by assuming deceit. (52)
"Even when granting boons, even in sovereignty, and even at the end, the destroyer of the Daityas and the Supreme Lord must indeed be slain by the Daitya; so instruct him. (53)
Thus instructed by his preceptor Bṛhaspati himself,
he bowed to Kṛṣṇa, held him in his heart, and paid obeisance to Lomaśa.
The great sage descended from the sky, having assumed the form of a brahmin, and went to the Daitya Varāṭaka, who was stationed on the shore of the western ocean. (55)
Blazing with splendor, yet gentle and endowed with serenity,
the Daitya Bhūmika— whose feet reached the sky— became absorbed in meditation.
The Brahmin gazed for a moment, enduring the hardship born of his faith; then he spoke softly to him: "O Varāṭaka, look at me."
I have come from the sky for the sake of fulfilling your desire;
look upon me, choose a boon—blessings be upon you—and tell me now what you wish.
Everything depends upon you who are powerful; behold me, a twice-born.
What use have you for this [creature], which brings only most terrible suffering? (59)
For that which is indeed unattainable by force must be accomplished through asceticism;
but that which is attainable by force must be acquired by force alone by one whose nature is strength.
Having been addressed thus, he looked at the twice-born man and bowed mentally;
he said, "Tell me everything, and grant me the boon as desired."
Then, O Rādhikā, Vṛhaspati enlightened him, saying:
"Tell me, what do you desire? How indeed can this suffering be endured? (62)
"I have come to grant a boon; I am the eternal Brāhmaṇa.
Hearing this, Varaṭaka said, "Welcome indeed to you, O twice-born one! (63)
"For the sake of sovereignty, I am performing this most formidable austerity;
command me as I exert myself, and grant me such a boon. (64)
"Listen, O Daitya, you are powerful," Bṛhaspati said upon hearing [the request], "so that I may obtain the kingdom of Saurāṣṭra which bestows happiness. (65)
"How indeed do you endure this painful asceticism? For dharma belongs to those free from passion;
for kings, however, dharma is battle; while for the weak, dharma is austerity. (66)
O powerful one, abandon asceticism and employ valor;
for the desires of the strong are indeed accomplished through exertion.
By asceticism for those who are weak, by dharma for those who perform sacrifices, by the army for kings, and by knowledge for the learned. (68)
By weeping for the sake of children, by deluding women,
and by serving those whose livelihoods are dependent on others through hardships and the like.
"By fasting unto death for the sake of the subjects, and by the very destruction of the enemies, the success of our foes will indeed be achieved. (2.36.70)
Having thus observed everything, you, being strong, must exert yourself;
abandon the thought that there might be some other donor for my asceticism. (7.1)
Having indeed been the best among the strong, that you now endure hardship in vain;
your body would become devoid of strength and would no longer be fit for enjoyment. ||72||
One who enjoys what is given by another is not praised in every respect;
for the collection of sense-faculties quickly succumbs to weakness when afflicted by hunger. (73)
Old age arises quickly, or else even destruction occurs;
therefore, casting aside hunger, do indeed nourish the body.
Nourishment alone is the supreme dharma; here, enjoyment is truly the supreme liberation.
Joy is the expansion of happiness; indeed, heaven is traditionally said to belong to those who live [righteously]. || 75 ||
A day that passes devoid of enjoyment, or one where life has departed, is indeed useless;
for when the body perishes, how can there be happiness? That which has vanished brings no benefit. || 76 ||
A result imagined merely by words does not persist beyond death;
since this [result] was not seen by the one person, how could it be seen by another? (77)
In this case, food is eaten even when it is appropriate; how then could it not be eaten when it is inappropriate?
A fool seeks to avoid the primary [meal] at the time of an eclipse. (78)
Disregarding his own body, senses, and life, that evil-souled person who endures suffering for the sake of his own pleasure is indeed called a self-destroyer. (79)
The destruction of happiness is the destruction of the self, which leads to hell and the experience of suffering;
therefore, abandoning hell, turn back from the destruction of your own self.
By whom was this ascetic cord, consisting of self-inflicted injury, taken up by you here—this useless storehouse of infamy arising from the agitation caused by sin? (81)
That which is conjoined with the body of an embodied being should be considered as truly real;
however, that which is devoid of conjunction with the body is entirely unreal. (82)
Indeed, the festivals of passion and the enjoyments exist only while the body exists;
the absence of such enjoyment is penance, which arises naturally in those who are aged. (8.3)
Fortune is attained through strength, and the earth is acquired through war;
a woman is won by good fortune, while prosperity is considered to arise from exertion. (84)
Life begins at birth and ends with death; no one has ever seen a rebirth. Therefore, abandon your asceticism and go toward happiness. (85)
At birth one is called a living being (jīva), and at death one is said to be liberated (mokṣa).
Between these two states, heaven is considered happiness, and the body is regarded as the locus of the self (ātman). 86.
O eternal servant of the Asuras, various sense objects are to be enjoyed there;
a day passed without such enjoyment is indeed a cause for regret.
That which has gone is indeed gone; it will never return again.
That gift which was given while not being enjoyed is lost; it is one's own fruitlessness. (88)
That which bestows one's own happiness is fruitful only when it grants happiness to oneself;
if one does not exert effort oneself, who else will grant it? (8–9)
Therefore arise from this suffering and exert yourself, O Varāṭaka;
for merit is considered to be action that bestows happiness and consists of enjoyment. (2.36.90)
Perform actions that grant happiness; do not perform asceticism that grants suffering.
A morsel does not enter the mouth of one who is fast asleep of its own accord. 91.
For one who exerts effort, wealth and other benefits inevitably come into their hands;
there is no giver of fruit, nor is there any supreme lord. ||92||
There is no one other than yourself; whom else do you wait for?
Abandon this entire magical illusion and don your formidable armor! 93.
Accompanied by a vast army, bring the earth under your control; for who is one's own and who is a stranger? That which is to be enjoyed is considered one's own. (94)
A wise person should acquire by force that which is otherwise unenjoyable;
those factors which are conducive to prosperity are considered in reality to be dharma.
In that regard, those who are hostile should be avoided with great effort;
having won over those favorable ones, O best of Daityas, acquire the kingdom. (96)
"Enjoy the highest happiness, O best of beings, and make the Daityas happy as well;
if my words please you, O Daitya, consider subduing them. (97)
Having joined Śukrācārya and others, and having gained strength, conquer Īśa and the rest; practice the bull-like conduct of the Dānavas.
Worship is false, meditation is false, and even self-restraint is indeed false;
the vow is false, sin is false, and whatever is not beneficial to oneself is false. (99)
The Lord is false, reliance is false; everything is false once one has died, it is all false.
Hope is false and fruitless; indeed, speech that is meaningless is false.
Strength without valor is in vain; valor without wisdom is in vain; wisdom that bears the fruit of suffering is in vain; and everything is in vain in one who is impotent. 10.1
If you are indeed a man, do not follow falsehood;
accomplish what must be achieved with effort quickly, and do not make my words vain.
Even ants and insects, relying on the proper season, exert themselves; gathering grains by force, they consume them when afflicted by the cold.
Just as lions, having attained valor and seized wild elephants and other prey, enjoy their fat with strength, so too should you enjoy the earth. 104.
Land, a woman, and prosperity are not obtained without effort; fame, purity, goodness, and ascetic merit are not obtained without austerity. (105)
The reality of this is not established by any other means;
having reflected upon it as you wish, O bull among Dānavas, do as you please. (106)
Leaving Lake Mānasa, swans go with great effort toward the ocean;
there they obtain their food, pearls, and they pass away.
Even crows, when roused by effort, obtain food that has been left overnight;
yet those who remain idle in their nests do not obtain it, just like lazy men.
Farmers, by exerting themselves, obtain the fruit produced from their crops;
for neither food, nor kingdom, nor the fulfillment of desires can be obtained without austerity.
Ghee held in the mouth indeed bestows nourishment through its sweet flavor;
yet ghee cast into the fire provides no satisfaction, having turned to ashes.
Why indeed do you offer up your youth, vigor, and strength in vain?
What fruit will you obtain there, performing penance upon this barren soil?
Therefore, arise and rely upon the consciousness granted by me;
accept the dharma of the best of givers and abandon that of the sick.
O Rādhikā, having been addressed thus by his preceptor, the Dānava reflected for a moment, abandoned his austerity, and said, "I am fulfilled. (113)
"Since I have been awakened to the Truth that stands as an obstacle to all hope, grant me a boon; show me such compassion that I may become a king. (114)
"So be it," the Guru said; the Dānava abandoned his penance, while the Brahmin Bṛhaspati was satisfied, having obtained the true fruit of his restraint in asceticism.
Accompanied by the Dānavas, he said: "Commence the effort to bring the earth under your own control from this very place, so that the kingdom may be yours."
May there be well-being for all, and may you have everything according to your desire;
by virtue of my boon, you shall possess the status of a mountain king.
Having spoken thus and taken the offerings, the brahmin departed toward heaven;
Varāṭaka, for his part, gathered the lords of the Daityas and held a council.

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Acquisition of All Sciences upon the Commencement of His Education, the Examination of His Intelligence, Bṛhaspati’s Instruction on Diligence to the Daitya Varāṭaka, and the Daitya’s Abandonment of Austerity," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Then, O Rādhā, the Daitya spoke to the greatest of the Daityas—
Pāvadurga, Makhkhana, Saiṃhikeya, and Coṭila.
And I shall maintain confidence in these chief warriors of great strength:
Airaka, Thūraka, Nīmba, Eraka, and likewise Barbura. (2)
Śālmali, jhimpaṭa, kūrci, karkaśa, and likewise gṛñjaka, tamālaka, garlic (laśuna), onion (palāṇḍu), and bhaṅgikī.
Ahiphena, mahājihma, vatsanāga, phenaka,
hīraka, and viṣakanda— these are indeed the foremost among the poisons of the Daityas.
For the sake of obtaining the kingdom of Saurāṣṭra and for the purpose of war, he spoke to Karka,
Kṛkalāsa, Śillaka, and likewise Godhaka.
The powerful Varāṭaka spoke of Ghorakhāda, Vṛka, Dvīpa, Śītadhāra, and the leaders,
for the sake of the mantras and for the sake of battle.
A certain Brahmin, however, said to me: "Asceticism is a most difficult and great thing;
it is the duty of those who possess nothing, and especially of those who are weak. (7)
War is indeed the duty of those who possess strength, since it is through this that one may obtain a kingdom;
therefore, [the conquest] of the Saurāṣṭra regions was carried out so as to bring them under one's own control.
"O best of Daityas, act quickly so that it may be so for us;
indeed, there is no land without battle, and truly, there is no victory without a host."
Prosperity does not come without effort; indeed, the acquisition of wealth through the exertion of a group brings happiness.
Therefore, we must forcibly seize these riches.
"Then everyone said, 'The kingdom of the land of Saurāṣṭra shall likewise be free from thorns; Om, so be it! May victory be yours! (11)
Then, starting from the western ocean,
those asuras began to harass the inhabitants of the villages and carried off their household wealth.
Indeed, a thousand villages near the western ocean,
as well as the northern land, were forcibly brought under their control by the Daityas.
King Khaṭvāṅga, the sovereign of all the earth, heard that the Khāḍika region had been brought under their control and was mostly occupied by those asuras.

Having understood that [the king's duty] consists of the protection of subjects, the removal of misfortune, the honoring of Brahmins, and the establishment of the kingdom, the lord of kings [acted accordingly]. || 15 ||
He dispatched a vast army through the path of the sky;
having formed a circular array, his soldiers engaged in battle.
Then the Daityas also fought with them in the sky,
using missiles, weapons, arrows, spears, bhallas, tomara-lances, and śaktis.
With spears, arrows, excellent swords, blades, mallets and the like,
with iron clubs, maces, fire-balls, and subterranean tunnels.
In the sky, there were spheres of water, spheres of poison, tears and vapors, poisonous winds, fires of venom, cold rain, and showers of lightning.
With violent winds, smoky gusts, showers of stones, and clouds of dust,
they created many illusions for one another.
Then the armies fought with those employing illusions, with artificial puppets made of air, and with artificial vehicles and warriors. 21.
The other asuras and many embodied men there were destroyed;
when those asuras were defeated, they became hopeless.
Desiring to enter the ocean, they ran hither and thither;
however, Khaṭvāṅgada’s armies were likewise surrounding them on all sides.
Having constructed ramparts on all sides upon the earth, in the sky, and in the water,
they were unable to go out from that region.
Then those Daityas, being deluded and intent on the desire for life,
[entered] the divine, vast, and unfathomable Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
Having deliberated and rushed forward, they entered the depths of that water;
then, for the sake of protection, they praised the Supreme Lord with their minds. (26)
To the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the son of Kambharā, the illustrious Gopāla Kṛṣṇa Bālaka. ||27||
To Hari, the Lord, the treasure-trove of compassion, the refuge, the Consort of Śrī, who has manifested in this world for the sake of its upliftment. (28)
O Lord of the Day, ocean of mercy, O Master who removes suffering!
You who protect those who have come for refuge, grant us the gift of life. (29)
"The armies of Khaṭvāṅgada are indeed destroying us on all sides;
O Lord, protect us who have sought refuge in you, even though we are the perpetrators of offenses. (2.37.30)
Relying upon the dharma of war as well as the dharma of force,
and following the customs of the Daityas and Dānavas, they have exerted themselves to attain sovereignty.
If there has been any offense against you right here, O Keśava, protect us!
Be patient, O ocean of mercy; instruct us and mete out the punishment.
When the demons, standing in the midst of the water, offered this praise,
Bālakṛṣṇa then blew his conch shell upon the field of battle.
He became ten millionfold in form there—in the sky, on the earth, and even in the water;
and upon seeing him right there, the armies instantly became devoid of pride.
Then the army commanders took refuge with him through the sky;
and Hari commanded them: "Those who have come for refuge must not be slain."
"O soldiers, I shall indeed seize these men alive and deliver them;
I will certainly inflict punishment according to their offenses. Let there be peace. (36)
"May these auspicious ones accept a welcome, as well as hospitality, food, and drink, from Lomaśa here, their preceptor and best of yogis. (37)
Thus addressed, they quickly made arrangements for the army; and, honored by Lomaśa with food and other provisions, they acted according to his command. (38)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
By the bestowal of this mantra, those soldiers were indeed made Vaiṣṇavas. || 39 ||
Then, in their presence, in the auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa,
the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa himself summoned the Daityas at night.
O Rādhikā, Hari indeed inflicted punishment upon them according to their offenses;
therein, he turned the Daitya Varāṭaka into a mountain as his punishment.
On the western shore of the ocean, however, there is a mountain named Varāḍa, which was frequented by Śrī Harṣadevī and Bṛhaspati. 42.
By virtue of the granting of that boon, this mountain was born as Bhūbhṛt;
Hari also [resides] on Pāvadurga, and indeed on the mountain Pāvadurga.
He fashioned that [image] in the form of a staff in the direction east of Saurāṣṭra,
and he also fashioned the mountain named Makhkhana, known by the name Makhkhana.
He fashioned the mountain Saiṃheyaka, Siṃhādri, and also the mountain Coṭila; he created Coṭīlaka, Dhāreya, and the one in the form of a stream (Dhārarūpin);
and indeed the mountain named Viśvasana, which is Viśvāmitra.
The Blessed Lord established their holiness through their residence at that sacred ford (tīrtha).
The auspicious fruit of taking refuge in Śrī Nārāyaṇa was attained there,
where indeed virtuous and pure sages dwell or reside.
Then they shall attain liberation at the end of the kalpa together with Brahmā;
and likewise for those other Daityas who were warriors.
I shall describe here the Daṇḍa; O Rādhikā, it arises from the earth. Airaka, however, is indeed a leafy stalk found in the ocean. || 49 ||
Having performed this, he granted a boon: "The attainment of Kṛṣṇa will occur somewhere.
Furthermore, he gave them a dwelling made of pillars within the ocean.
He also fashioned upon the earth a *thūṭaka* with thorns and provided with handles, resembling a rampart;
it served as a protection and even ensured long life. || 51 ||
He protected that bitter nimba tree in the royal courtyard, as well as the barbara tree, covered in thorns, which served as a tooth-stick tree. || 52 ||
At sacred fords such as those by rivers and mountains, he established a beautiful shelter;
on a mountain in the forest, he made a *śālmali* tree— which was adorned with soft fruits—
his bed and gave it to him along with its fruit.
It is made of cotton everywhere; indeed, that brings happiness to the merchants. ||54||
Then he indeed made a bundle of straw richly provided with splinters;
for those who possess long brooms are truly of great service. ||55||
In the forest, the Blessed One made the *kūrci* plant into a thorny creeper;
the Lord also fashioned the extremely pungent *karkaṭa* into the form of a creeper.
The Lord fashioned *gṛñjaka* and *tamāla* for the purpose of smoking;
he fashioned garlic (*laśuna*) and onion (*palāṇḍu*) in the form of bulbs.
He also created opium (*ahiphena*), *mahājihma*, hemp (*bhaṅgā*), and *vatsanābha*.
Kṛṣṇa fashioned the Viṣarūpa weapon, and he fashioned the Aphenaka and the Kṣāraka.
He fashioned diamonds from minerals, yet made them poisonous;
he fashioned pebbles as poison-tubers, and created a root within the earth that was destructive.
He assigned the chameleon, the lizard, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, and reptiles;
as well as the fierce-eater, the wolf, the hyena, and the sharp-fanged beasts.
Nārāyaṇa settled all those Asuras individually in the forest,
on the ground, in the water, in trees, and within walls.
For all these Asuras, whose lineages had expanded and increased,
were indeed rendered fit for liberation by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow through their connection with sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrtha).
Thereupon, peace and well-being arose among the subjects.
Bṛhaspati went to Mahendra, and Varāṭaka spoke to him:
"The ascetic has been driven away and has now instilled in him the intent for war;
he has waged war for the sake of the kingdom, for he has indeed been reduced to the state of a mountain. ||63-64||
Other Daityas as well were firmly restrained by the staff;
having heard this, he then attained peace, and Saurāṣṭra became happy.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the auspicious sovereignty of the Lord has been described to you;
by association with the holy places of the virtuous, they shall indeed attain liberation.
Now I shall tell you another account that purifies the sinful.
O Rādhikā, listen to [the account] of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa:
the Mlecchas of the Ḍaphphara caste, having followed the forest path and traveled by sea routes, settled in Surāṣṭra. ||67-68||
They were wicked, of evil conduct, eaters of the flesh of animals, as well as eaters of birds and fish; they were devoid of the duties toward their wives and husbands.

Having entered upon the mode of life of beasts, they subsist upon the wealth of others; they are constant performers of theft and are forever devoid of charity, righteousness, and other virtues. ||2.37.70||
They dwell anywhere at all, stealing food from the fields of others; they carry missiles and weapons, and they raise dogs and other cruel animals. (71)
Constantly devoted to the nature of hunters, dwelling forever in the forest, they were wicked men—
plunderers, slayers, and robbers of all, who moved with cruel conduct.
They will be drivers of carts, camels, and donkeys, filling their bellies at the expense of others' fortune; they will be destroyers of crops and oppressors of those who perform agricultural labor.
A thousand Mānavas appeared in person, terrifying like the messengers of Yama;
they were drinkers of intoxicants and destroyers of human kinfolk wherever they went. ||74||
Merciless, full of deceit, and revilers of the gods, the religious duties, and other such things, the inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra oppressed everyone on all sides. (75)
A cry of "Alas! Alas! arose throughout the land, in every direction and intermediate quarter, caused by them;
and the people were tormented by them at their own Śvapaṭṭa-sarovara lake.
They came before Hari—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama—to pray for their own protection. (77)
They reported their own suffering, born from that [poison], which was all-consuming.
Having heard this, the Blessed One said, "I shall provide a remedy for it. (78)
Having spoken thus, he called to mind his own discus, Sudarśana,
as well as the guardians of that sacred field and Kālī, the destroyer of the Mlecchas.
Then Hari remembered the army of Ardhanārīśvara, adorned with all manner of weapons and missiles, as well as the divine Garuḍa and the elephant. 2.37.80.
They arrived very quickly and bowed at the feet of Hari;
they informed him for the purpose of receiving his command, and Śrī Hari spoke to them.
The Mlecchas of the Daphphara race are afflicting Surāṣṭra;
they plunder wealth, food, and all agricultural goods in every way. (82)
Furthermore, those tools for cultivation that are situated in the forest—such as creepers and the like—which cut down trees, shrubs, climbing plants, and so forth; ||83||
They plunder groves rich in flowers and fruits, as well as vegetables and tubers;
they graze their own cattle upon the leaves, grain, and other crops. (84)
They carry off the ears and stalks of the ripened grain from the field's harvest;
in some places they kill men, and they carry away the herds of bulls and cattle.
Indeed, those sinful ones kill deer, hares, and other such animals;
they even forcibly seize and bind the subjects and lead them away somewhere. ||86||
They afflict men, women, and children among the subjects;
indeed, they exist here by the thousands in the forest to the north of this place.
Let them go forth in all directions against those who have committed offenses and inflict punishment upon them such that they will not act in this way again; or else, let them slay them on all sides.
Thus addressed, the personified Sudarśana discus and Kālikā, as well as the Ardhanārīśvara army and Garuḍa, became his servants. ||89||
Having assembled, they then departed swiftly to subdue the Dikparas;
and those Dikparas, beholding these instructors, prepared to slay them.
With darts, lances, and crescent-headed arrows, with maces, clubs, and swords,
and also with bandhūka-like shafts, discuses, and other weapons, they waged war.
Then the army of Ardhanārīśvara struck them down with spears,
javelins, arrows, and the like, as well as with clubs, staffs, swords, and mallets.
He fought with the Daphpharas using arrows, shafts, projectiles, stones, pellets, and the like, as well as spears and various types of nooses.
A most terrible battle took place, a struggle for very life;
on both sides, the night passed away into eternal sleep. ||94||
Then, having beheld the Sudarśana discus, which was self-luminous,
the fire-discus itself became manifest and the army of Ḍaphpharas fell upon it.
He swiftly severed the heads from the headless trunks; having split each one in two at the neck where it was caught, he moved on.
Many of them were indeed slain by the drum-beats, while others fled;
they then sought refuge in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||9 7||
Since the protection of those who have sought refuge must be ensured by a sovereign, the survivors were not killed; instead, they were banished to the far reaches of the land. (98)
Five hundred lived and went forth, not to any other place;
however, due to their own committed sins, they were destroyed by a storm at sea.
The Mleccha tribes with uplifted hoods met their death by drowning in the water;
through the majesty of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the people of Saurāṣṭra dwell in happiness.
All afflictions have vanished, and the subjects have taken refuge in happiness;
Sudarśana and the others, having accomplished their task, remain in the presence of Śrī Hari.
Those divine beings who had been crushed in battle, having themselves become possessed of life, also arrived and paid homage; thereafter, they merged into the physical form.
The army of Ardhanārīśvara vanished on the shore of the lake.
A cry of victory arose on earth for Hari’s weapons as well.
Thus, O Rādhikā, this auspicious life-story of Bālakṛṣṇa has been told to you; by hearing or reciting it, one attains heaven and liberation. (104)

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Defeat and Punishment of the Army of the Asura named Varāṭaka and the Destruction of the Mlecchas of the Ḍaphphara Tribe," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; indeed, in the fifth year, in the month of Vaiśākha, during the bright fortnight on the full-moon day, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa [appeared]. || 1 ||
In the evening, accompanied by her companions, she went to the eastern part of the Brahmavāṭikā garden, where the breeze was fragrant with the scent of kunda flowers;
there she wandered here and there, played, and moved about with the children.
Generally, at the approach of evening,
the Supreme Lord would see the *makāyī* and *jārikā* plants grown in his garden, with their leaves as green as turmeric and beautiful with clusters of *ḍoḍikā* flowers.
Taking those *ḍoḍikā* fruits and pouring them into the fire,
he then ate the seeds of the *ḍoḍikās* together with the children.
Then, by the side, mango fruits were also ripened by the winds.
Having gathered what has fallen [on the ground], he eats it together with his companions.
All the children, filled with joy, were eating oranges, mangoes, grapes, dates, and figs in the garden. || 7 ||
Then, at that time, three wicked rākṣasas arrived there;
they assumed the forms of children and began to eat together with him.
There they looked on, ate, carried [loads], and even drove [them];
they ran, leaped, laughed, and caused others to laugh.
Desiring to kill Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who was in the form of a calf and so forth—
Indeed, there was a single Rākṣasa there who had assumed the form of a cart.
Having made his dwelling beneath a Plakṣa tree in the garden, he,
overcome by intense passion, sought a way to destroy Bālakṛṣṇa.
A second Rākṣasa there assumed the form of a boar, right before that field where the boys were playing. || 12 ||
Having gone there, he pulled out a tooth and showed it, displaying a fierce woodworm;
shaking his tail and letting forth his own roar. (13)
Then, running with extreme speed, he came to kill them;
seeing that terrifying being and looking toward the cart, those children [fled].
Filled with fear, they ran swiftly toward the Plakṣa tree;
having quickly reached the cart, they indeed cried out in haste. || 15 ||
Then, as they mounted the vehicle that moved along the path from the wheel to the pole,
Kṛṣṇa quickly called to mind the black-maned lion.
The vehicle of Kālyā Śrīkṣetrapālinī was indeed a lion;
divine and powerful, it arrived there swiftly, making the quarters resound. || 17 ||
Having roared all around and bowed down to those standing in their wagons,
the boar leaped up and forcibly seized that Rākṣasa.
Then the boar also fought with the lion by means of his strength;
thereafter, roaring repeatedly, he assumed the form of a lion in an instant. (19)
Making all the directions resound and filling them with his roar, he fought fiercely;
what strength can there be in this artificial lion? It is merely a fabrication, a falsehood.
Then Kālisiṃha suddenly and effortlessly seized him by the throat,
and with his sharp claws, he tore at his waist and his belly.
Having been struck down and killed on all sides, he cried out and died in an instant;
thereafter, his very self attained non-difference from the lion of the illustrious Kālikā. || 22 ||
Then, at that moment, perceiving that Śakaṭa was without support and that all the boys were under his control, he indeed rose up into the sky.
Then, having become a sky-walker, he went swiftly through the path of the atmosphere to destroy the fools and cast them down to the earth.
Meanwhile, Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa increased his own weight;
by that excessive burden, the cart sank down toward the surface of the earth. || 25 ||
Kṛṣṇa caused them to descend so that the children might not perish;
having descended, the boys took refuge at the foot of a Plakṣa tree.
Then Bālakṛṣṇa, having placed his left foot on the ground from the base of the Triveṇī while it hung down from the carriage, then [placed] his right foot.
Having placed it upon the Triveṇī and supported it with both hands,
just as he was striving to descend, at that very moment—
The great demon named Śakaṭa, like a wedge,
had grown within his belly like a stake in order to kill Kṛṣṇa, beneath the triple-confluence of the rivers.
Then the boys indeed saw a very sharp, long trident-stake with a keen edge hanging down toward Hari. (2.38.30)
Those children said to Hari, but Bālakṛṣṇa, too, did not descend out of playfulness,
as long as he protected his own belly.
While his left foot was hanging down near the root of his thigh,
a sharp spike was forcibly driven into him by means of a cart.
Then, O Rādhikā, a stream of blood flowed from between her thighs;
at that moment, Bālakṛṣṇa quickly leaped up onto the carriage.
Then, recognizing the great asura to be wicked, she climbed back up;
and in order to slay him, she again assumed a weightiness like that of a mountain.
By that weight, the cart was bent and indeed broken; it fell, and this blind well was filled, while the camel and the driver were tormented. (35)
Under the weight of the invisible mountain, the cart was reduced to powder;
all the boys were amazed, as was the demon, who was slain yet remained alive.
That splendor issued forth from the cart and vanished into Bālakṛṣṇa;
then, seeing the cart thus destroyed and the boar likewise perished, [he was amazed].
The third Rākṣasa, appearing in the form of a child, inspired terror;
yet, perceiving that death was near, he reflected upon the passing of Hari.
"How indeed should this child be struck by me here?
Without the form of a mountain, there can be no destruction of this child. (3.9)
"Therefore, I shall indeed become a mountain; thus I will fall swiftly.
Having thus resolved, he suddenly ascended the path of the sky.
There he became like a mountain;
just as he was about to fall, Kṛṣṇa impelled his own Garuḍa with great speed.
And Garuḍa, possessing a divine form, flying through the sky with great radiance,
seized that mountain with effort using his two feet.
Then Hari, having prepared his own Sudarśana discus— most formidable,
adorned with garlands of flames, and capable of burning mountains— [hurled it].
The great mountain, situated at the lower part of the earth, was swiftly released by him and reduced to ashes by a circular fire resembling the flames of lightning.
That ash, through contact with fire on the ground and aided by the wind,
flew up again and again and fell scattered upon various parts of the earth.
She became white clay, pale upon the surface of the earth;
and Garuḍa, having attained subtlety, became a cool discus.
When he returned to his own place, Kṛṣṇa and the girls became free from ailment;
they became unhindered and happy upon the thigh of Bālakṛṣṇa.
And as for the blood that had flowed out, it then vanished into the earth of its own accord.
And the juice of the leaves of a medicinal herb was administered to bring about the cessation of his pain. ||48||
Then peace was quickly attained; however, the mark of Śaṅku was always preserved in its wounded form for the sake of the meditative practice of those engaged in meditation. (49)
O Rādhikā, that auspicious mark upon the thigh of Bālakṛṣṇa is always present on His form; it is as great as an eye for the purpose of meditation.
Having seen that eternal mark produced from the left thigh, which manifests the state of Ardhanārīśvara, the maidens and goddesses worshipped it.
The Earth performed worship of this sign with sandalwood and other offerings;
thereafter, the sages, headed by Lomaśa, took up the sign in meditation.
The children went home in the evening; Kālī, attended by lions and other beasts, proceeded to her own place on the northern ground, where there was a lake.
Having heard from the children that the Rākṣasa had been slain,
Kālikā’s father and all the others were amazed, and they then performed rites for the pacification of obstacles.
Those men went to various places where those Rākṣasas had died and saw a boar, powdered earth from a cart, and white ash.
In amazement, they all beheld a boar with a body one *krośa* long;
a cart-load of powder clinging for a *krośa*, and white ash extending for two *yojanas*. (26)
The child Kṛṣṇa possesses great power, by whom these three great asuras have been destroyed; these slayers are themselves the killers of children.
The destruction of these embodied fools has been rightly accomplished;
our sons have been protected, and may these children always prosper. (58)
Having spoken these words of blessing, they, being delighted, took refuge in the Lord.
Rādhikā said: "O Blessed One, who were those three rākṣasas? (59)
"Those who came here and contemplated the destruction of Hari—O Queen of the Night, listen as Śrī Kṛṣṇa speaks of that merit-purifying account. (2.38.60)
As Brahmā, born from the egg, was previously contemplating creation, there arose a supreme and delightful discourse on dharma concerning the offense against the gods;
from him were born the Vālakhilyas, mind-born and of pure form.
And there were eighty-eight thousand who remained chaste throughout their lives.
There, a sage named Vanaspati became the most excellent of all;
this occurred as that Creator, desiring progeny, was reflecting once again.
A thousand sages were born as householders subject to the law of emission;
they lived with their wives in the forest, yet their minds remained possessed by passion, hatred, and other such afflictions.
There, a sage named Nabhaspati was a preeminent householder;
yet, as he reflected further, he became deluded by passion.
The Vālakhilyas were born again, numbering sixty thousand;
they were all accompanied by their wives and devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas.
With hearts possessed by desire, anger, and other passions, though devoted to ritual bathing and worship,
they dwelt in the great forest in the vicinity of Mount Kailāsa.
Emaciated, with veins prominently visible, devoted to vows and fasting, they were ascetics who had practiced penance for a thousand years;
among them was a sage named Saraspati, the most excellent in his observances.
He was devoted to the duties of a householder and intent upon sacrifice and the private recitation of sacred texts.
Even as he was striving to propitiate them, Śaṅkara was not at all pleased;
then the goddess Śrī Pārvatī, moved by compassion, spoke to Śaṅkara.
O Śambhu, bring about the destruction of their afflictions; show me mercy. (7.1)
"How is it that success is not granted even after a thousand years have passed for those householders performing austerities, whose bodies consist only of dry sinews and bones?
Having heard that, Śaṅkara spoke of the profound course of Dharma.
O Goddess, you do not know at all that they are free from desire. ||73||
"Nor are they free from anger; they are merely deluded ascetics.
They do not understand the Dharma, and therefore no fruit is granted.
Satī asked, "How can these people be so corrupted by desire, anger, and the like?"
"O Śambhu, show that to me, for my curiosity is indeed great.
Śambhu said, "Stay here while I am present and behold the spectacle;
I shall go among the hermitages of those performing penance with my mischievous conduct."
Having spoken thus, Śaṅkara became naked, divested of his garments;
he was a youth, beautiful in every limb, richly perfumed with a forest garland,
carrying an alms-bowl, and went from hermitage to hermitage saying, "Give me alms."
Seeing him arrived at the hermitage, the women of those who discourse on Brahman [welcomed him].
Seeing him naked, they were bewildered by his nature as a true king; taking roots, fruits, and alms-food, they approached him and said, "Please accept these. (79)
Śambhu, stretching out his alms-bowl with great respect, said:
"Give me alms; may there be auspiciousness for you, O you who are fond of penance! (2.38.80)
Laughing repeatedly, making gestures, and manifesting his sexual arousal, he captivated their minds; they became afflicted with passion.
The women said: "Who is this whose vow and dharma you are practicing?
You are charming with your nakedness and mendicant's garb; you are a truly fortunate beggar! (82)
"Come, let us perform service for you and massage you in our home," they said; Śiva replied, "This is indeed my secret vow. (83)
"My vow must not be disclosed here; you all go to your own homes," he said.
The women replied, "Come to our houses, for you are a delight. (84)
Having spoken thus, they, full of desire, seized him with their sprout-like hands:
one on his hand, another on his neck, another on his knees, and another on his chin.
[The demon] seized them by the hair, at the waist, on the feet, and on the sides and back;
thus he tormented Śambhu and likewise agitated the women. (86)
Seeing him absorbed in meditation, those ascetics abandoned their austerities and fled, shouting, "Kill him!", brandishing wood, stones, and sticks. (87)
There, three hairs struck Śambhu on his body;
then the great ṛṣi Vanaspati, taking up a piece of wood, acted with haste.
Then Nabhaspati quickly took up a stone,
while Saraspati swiftly seized a hoe for the clod.
The lords struck down that erect phallus of Śambhu as it stood awake;
others likewise struck it from the sides of the waist with blades of darbha grass and with sticks.
When the linga had fallen, Śambhu vanished;
having reached Satī, Śaṅkara then remained there, invisible.
The Liṅga, leaping up again and again, indeed caused agitation to the world;
the entire cosmic egg having fallen into turmoil, the illustrious Śambhu became distressed.
Seeing them devoid of their male organs, Satī cursed those brahmins:
"May the lord of the forest become wood, and the lord of the sky become stone. (93)
"O Sarasvatī, let these merciless ones indeed assume the form of teeth!
For you have committed an exceedingly cruel offense against my husband. (94)
"Therefore, you Rākṣasas shall be deprived of your own characteristic marks.
Thus were those three principal sages cursed immediately. 95.
In that forest interior, there was a *sarja* tree, a lord of the woods;
though he was a *rākṣasa*, he possessed the form of wood while being able to assume any form at will.
At that time in the Dāruvana forest, Nabhaspati became a mountain;
the Rākṣasa, assuming any form at will, even took the form of a black stone.
Then Saraspati was born as a boar joined with teeth;
he was a Rakshasa devoid of a male organ, yet indeed capable of assuming any form at will.
Three of those *rākṣasa*s were born within the forest of *dāru* trees; others, the cursed *vālakhilya*s, became clusters of blossoms upon the water. 99.
Though they were rootless Nirgranthas, flourishing with nothing more than their bark garments, they became signless and dwelt in the water, staying upon the surface of the water.
All those Vālakhilyas, who subsist on nothing but water, live along the Brahmaputra, the Nanda, and other rivers; they are like clusters of flowers, not eating anything other than the earth.
At the time of the curse, submerged in suffering, they praised Satī in their minds, saying:
"Please act in such a way that our deliverance may come to pass. (102)
We do not know the true nature of the great-souled Śaṅkara;
therefore, let an end to our curse be ordained for us, for we have committed no offense.
The wives of the sages wept and praised their mother Satī;
then Satī spoke, [for she was] the supreme lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In Saurāṣṭra, in the western region, is the Lord, the son of Kambharāśrī,
the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord Hari.
"By his yoga, his deliverance will come about;
that Lord will bring about the complete rescue of the sages.
Having spoken thus, she, being deeply distressed, vanished from sight.
Then those sons of sages and others who were free from fault,
as well as other sages, spectators, Brahmins, and the like who were present there,
beheld that great upheaval which portended the dissolution of the universe.
There, the gods and others remembered Brahmā and sought refuge in Brahmā; they entreated him for the pacification of the fire from the liṅga.
And they were enlightened by Brahmā through various divine attributes—
[him] who is radiant, established in Brahman, the eternal embodiment of Brahman.
Having recognized you as one who follows worldly ways and is bound by the dharmas of desire, they have committed an offense against you; therefore, this great agitation has arisen. (111)
"He shall attain peace through the practice of worshipping the Liṅga, and not otherwise.
Alas! Those sages are deluded, having fallen under the sway of anger. (112)
That Brahman which is eternally present and stainless within the body and the self is accumulated even by one of pure heart through austerity or ritual action. (113)
For purity is indeed the expulsion of states such as desire and anger;
therefore, the wise man should purify that mind by means of the practice of the yoga of knowledge.
A person attains purity when his mind is indeed thoroughly purified;
for even the seers, though established in their hermitages, were overcome by anger and desire.
For those overcome by desire and anger, sacrifice, charity, bull-vows, austerity, religious observances, penance, fortitude, and meditation—all shall go to fruitlessness. (116)
Therefore, let them go to that place, having abandoned desire and anger,
and let them worship that god Śaṅkara, who fulfills all desires.
"By worshipping the Liṅga, peace shall surely follow. Having been told this, they all departed and worshipped the Liṅga with devotion.
Adhering to its place as it was, Śaṅkara became possessed of that liṅga;
and wherever this fell, there the jyotirliṅgas were born.
"Divided into twelve ways, that divine [path] indeed bestows liberation.
Thus, O Rādhikā, the entire world attained peace.
Then those three sages also became rākṣasas born of a curse.
Then, remembering their past lives, they came to Saurāṣṭra for the sake of their own liberation.
The Lord of the Forest, in the form of wood, was born as the essence of the chariot;
the Lord of the Sky, in the form of stone, was born as the mountain. || 122 ||
Bṛhaspati became a boar with tusks;
through the yoga of Hari-Kṛṣṇa, they were then liberated from the curse.
The divine sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, praised Hari again and again for the sake of uplifting all the remaining sages.
Then the Blessed Lord said: "Let them go there as well;
having arrived at the Dāruvana forest, I shall deliver them from their curse."
Having mounted Garuḍa, the Blessed Lord Bālakṛṣṇa,
Hari himself, rescued the Vālakhilyas who had taken the form of a pillar.
O Rādhikā, all those born in the forest of Dāru performed austerities;
consequently, they all became peaceful and took on the forms of sages.
The Vālakhilyas, who belong to that lineage, become pillars within the waters;
Hari, having raised them up and received their worship with reverence, [proceeds].
Accompanied by Garuḍa, he came to his own sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī;
O Rādhā, by reciting or hearing this, the sin of the curse is pacified.

It is a marvel that even when the state of a rākṣasa has arrived, liberation occurs through a spirit of aversion toward those endowed with devotion; for such indeed is the power of divine illusion (devamāyā). 2.38.130.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled “The Description of the Disturbance in the Garden Caused by the Great Sages Vanaspati, Nabhaspati, and Saraspati, who had attained the state of Rākṣasas due to Satī’s curse; the Liberation from the Curse by the Lord; and the Wandering of Nagna-Śaṅkara through the Hermitages of Ascetics, His Offense against the Sages, the Falling of the Liṅga, and the Causes of the Curse,” in the second section, the Tretā-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to this knowledge by which neither austerity nor anything else remains;
formerly, when the terrible single ocean existed and all moving and non-moving beings had perished.
There was a single great egg, containing the seed of all beings,
produced from Mahāviṣṇu, within which Virāṭ shines forth.
Having split the egg, the Blessed One brought forth the Vairāja outside;
from the Vairāja emerged the three-fold gods: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. || 3 ||
Then Brahmā, endowed with *sattva*, beheld the world as empty;
thereafter, through his *rājasa* nature, he indeed undertook worldly activity.
He remembered the divine Darśaka, Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond the senses, the Lord who transcends the qualities (guṇas), the all-pervading Supreme Person. || 5 ||
He by whom all this is pervaded, who is designated as the stable and conscious— whosoever knows that Great Soul, he certainly knows everything.
He who knows that Supreme Self—the Puruṣa who transcends the qualities (guṇas), the eternal Supreme Brahman—he knows everything; he is a knower of liberation.
What need have they for all the sacred fords or hermitages, whose infinite mind is established in the Self alone? (8)
The self is a river whose bathing-ghats are virtuous conduct, whose water is truth, and which is endowed with tranquility;
one who bathes therein becomes pure and meritorious, for the self is not purified by mere water.
The highest duty for a person is to abide in the bliss of self-awakening;
that alone is to be known by the virtuous, upon the attainment of which all desire ceases. (2.39.10)
For one who has attained union with Brahman, there exists no wealth superior to this:
equanimity, truthfulness, virtuous conduct, straightforwardness, and likewise renunciation. (11)
Upon attaining that [knowledge], one certainly reaches the supreme Brahman; of this there is no doubt.
O Rādhā, by knowing Him, the Lord, one shall obtain the fruit of dharma.
He who is established as all-pervading and eternal within this body, the life-force—
he is the beginningless Śrīpati, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, higher than the highest.
That glorious young cowherd boy, the son of Kambharāśrī,
exists as Bālakṛṣṇa in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
"O beloved, when the fifth year is complete, we shall go to see him.
Having been addressed thus, the goddess Rādhikā, full of enthusiasm, prepared her radiant attire.
He held that beautiful and auspicious vessel, rich in every splendor, filled with gold and rubies,
and inlaid with pearls, diamonds, and precious gems.
Having assumed various amorous ornaments mixed with the essence of fragrances, augmented by dots, leaf-patterns, body-paints, red lac, and collyrium. (17)
Adorned with garments of thread, strings, chains, rings, and ornaments, she was beautified by the weight of her braided hair, which bore clusters of flowers made of gold dust.
Holding in her hands a vessel containing articles for the worship of Śanaktaka,
she adorned her husband Kṛṣṇa, making him exceedingly beautiful, refined, and auspicious.
He quickly caused the celestial chariot and the bull-vehicle to be driven forth,
with vessels filled with fruits, flowers, delicious foods, and nectar.
Kṛṣṇa himself was the charioteer, and Śrī Rādhā herself was the chariot-rider;
having traversed the worlds of the lords beyond the glorious realm of Goloka, they proceeded.
Transcending the expanse beginning with Brahmā, Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa descended from the sky to the land of Surāṣṭra upon the earth, specifically to Kuṅkumavāpikā.
On the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, in the courtyard of the temple of Bālakṛṣṇa,
that splendor first pervaded the entire universe at the front of Śrīkṛṣṇa’s chariot.
The sun and moon were not visible, having been overwhelmed by her splendor;
the earth and the directions were greatly intensified by the radiance of Rādhā.
Lomaśa’s hermitage also became like the world of the moon;
and all the maidens there, endowed with forms even more beautiful than Rādhā,
shone when they beheld Rādhikā, appearing as if each were a hundred Rādhās plus one.
But upon seeing those maidens, Rādhā became free from pride. || 26 ||
At that moment, her pride in her physical beauty vanished instantly;
looking toward Kṛṣṇa, she spoke to Bālakṛṣṇa.
"Oh, O Lord, you have indeed made my personal manifestation successful, since I have obtained the vision of this Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa! (28)
At the commencement of the sixth year, on the morning of the eighth lunar day,
Rādhikā worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa with various offerings.
Rādhikā bathed the child with the milk of Goloka;
she performed his consecration with the waters of all sacred fords and other holy sites.
Having worshipped with the essences of the juices of sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and other liquids,
he adorned her with ornaments, garments, and decorations.
Then he performed the *ārārtrika* rite, beautiful with peacock feathers,
and placed a crown upon the head of Bālakṛṣṇa.
She placed the flute in his hand, placed her right arm around his neck,
and having made him smile, she gave him a beautiful tilaka-mark along with a moon-ornament and auspicious unbroken grains.
Placing her forehead [to the ground], Rādhikā performed the rite of *nīrājana*;
having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), she prostrated herself in salutation.
