He bestowed blessings, saying, "O beloved of Kāntā, may you be as beloved as Kāntā herself," while Rādhā, joining her palms in salutation, raised them from her head in a gesture difficult to endure.
And he gave food brought from Goloka, such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like,
as well as balls of milk, ice-cream, and pūrikās made from the essence of milk.
He gave sweet, divine, and excellent curd; he did not give anything else that was not desired by him.
Having fed him, he then gave him delightful and auspicious betel-leaf.
Then, having thus offered worship, Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself ceased; thereafter, he respectfully worshipped that Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
A turban, a yellow garment, a tunic adorned with golden stars,
a helmet, a sword, and two auspicious flower-earrings.
She placed a garland of *pārijātaka* flowers around the child's neck,
and likewise gave him two soft, golden sandals.
He gave him a beautiful parasol with lovely whisks, a girdle, and earrings;
as well as a jewel of the finest Kaustubha type and a necklace of pearls. (41)
He gave to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa a flute of soft sound,
as well as a staff consisting of spiritual perfection, and an excellent lion-throne.
Having thus honored the young lord, Kṛṣṇa offered this praise:
"O witness of all, salutations to you, the cause of all incarnations! (43)
O Supreme Person, O Lord of the Liberated, O Abode of the Supreme, salutations be unto You, from whom the present, the past, and the future proceed in every way. (44)
It shines forth as endowed with harmony, gentle, well-ordered, and following the proper sequence;
yet you, the ruler, are beyond such connection—to that Divine Being, salutations to You! ||45||
Infinite are your powers here, manifesting in the forms of Kṛṣṇa and Nṛsiṃha;
you whose nature is Rādhā, Ramā, and Śrī—I bow to that Supreme Lord. 46.
I am my own abode, Goloka, as well as Nārāyaṇa and Ramā;
I am Śrī, Vaikuṇṭha, and the immortal state from which the true station proceeds.
Before me is the imperishable abode, which is eternally embodied and serves as my servant.
The lords and incarnations are adorned by His portions and qualities. ||48||

The celestial armies, the guardians of the gods, the world-protectors, and the great sages, as well as the deities presiding over sacrifices, are each embodied forms of a single portion of his qualities. (49)
I bow to that Supreme Lord who exists here in this world;
O Inner Self, O Infinite Self, O Self of my own self, salutations, salutations unto You! 2.39.50.
O Supreme Self, witness of the world, infinite Lord, homage be to you!
O Omniscient One, supreme preceptor, object of knowledge and knower, homage be to you! ||5 1||
O Primordial God, difficult to propitiate, O Supreme Lord, salutations to You! O Great Master of Yoga, O Holy One, O Compassionate One, salutations again and again to You! ||52||
O Supreme Light, O Vaṣaṭkāra, O Svāhākāra, homage be to you!
O All-Seeing One, whose nature is the fire of universal dissolution and the moon, homage be to you!
Obeisance to you, Mahārājika, Siddhārcya, Hiraṇyavāha!
O Mañjukeśin, Bālakeśin, Dayādeśin, may there be homage to you! ||54||
O All-pervading One, O Sacrificer, O Lord of Sacrifice, you who have compassion for your devotees, salutations to you!
Be gracious, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; salutations again and again to you. (55)
Having spoken thus, the divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā bowed to the Lord and went into the presence of Śrī Kambharā within the world. 56.
Having bowed to her and likewise having bowed to the illustrious Rūpālākṛṣṇa,
and having received the welcome he offered, [the sage] praised the festival for his son.
Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā departed for Goloka by means of a celestial chariot;
then Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā, arrived from Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, for the sake of worshipping Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord Vāsudeva and Bhūman arrived, mounted upon Garuḍa and filled with joy.
Mahāviṣṇu, as well as Nārāyaṇa and Nara, arrived;
Śeṣanārāyaṇa, as well as Matsya and Kūrma, also arrived.
Vārāha, Kapila, Hari, and Pṛthu arrived;
likewise Dattātreya, Haṃsa, and Nṛsiṃha arrived. (61)
Ṛṣabha, Vāmana, and Paraśurāma arrived;
Yajña, Rāma, the Kumāras, and Hayagrīva also arrived. (62)
Nārada and the king of kings, the supreme lords, arrived;
they sang, "Victory to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!"
They performed the consecration with the five nectars and the [five] ambrosias using the child’s thumb;
afterwards, they performed the sprinkling with darbha-grass water and ambrosias.
With devotion, they reverently worshipped the sandalwood and unbroken grains upon his forehead; they applied a tilaka enriched with saffron and offered fragrant substances.
They placed flower garlands around his neck, crowns, and floral wreaths; they offered tulasī leaves, ornaments, and chowries.
They presented a celestial parasol, sandals, and various garments;
they performed the lustration ceremony with camphor and other substances, along with lighted wicks.
All the incarnations offered incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, nectar-like rice, fruits, water, and betel leaves.
And those women residing in that abode likewise presented many offerings originating from their respective worlds for the sake of worship. (69)
They arrived with many excellent articles and worshipped the Lord;
having thus honored Him, they departed for their own abodes.
Then the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and the seers,
as well as human beings beginning with the brahmins, indeed came for the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he rested here and there along the paths of the sky near the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and the temple of Kṛṣṇa.
They arrived and honored him with various offerings and gifts;
they delighted Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, exceedingly.
Then there were other lands, mountains, rivers, lakes, oceans, sacred fords, celestial trees, creepers, and flower clusters. ||74||
The forest goddesses, the shrubs, and various other elements also arrived for the sake of worshipping Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and performed acts of veneration. ||75||
Then the yakṣas, guhyakas, cāraṇas, and likewise the kiṃpuruṣas, as well as the bhāṭas, kinnaras, gandharvas, and celestial women [arrived]. (76)
The Māgadhas, bards, heralds, Vidyādharas, Pannagas, and others arrived for the sake of worship at the festival of the illustrious Bālakṛṣṇa. (77)
The dancers performed their dances as they offered worship to you;
excellent musical instruments were played, and the singers sang at that time. (78)
Storytellers recounted that story, actors performed their dances,
sacrificers performed the sacrifice, and the virtuous performed their recitations.
The noble elders gave blessings, and the venerable Gopālakṛṣṇa as well as the sage Lomaśa then offered auspicious benedictions. (2.39.80)
Likewise, other sages and the daughters of Brahmā who were present there performed the worship of Śrī Hari and joined him with their blessings.
Then the father gratified all those great men from every side with excellent foods such as milk-porridge and sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
And after having fed all those who had arrived,
Hari thereafter caused gifts to be given to the brahmins, the female slaves, and the servants.
And to the worthy recipients, according to their needs and as each mendicant requested, he gave gems, gold, silver, sweet food, and even garments. (84)
He gave rings, ornaments, vessels, and wealth as much as they desired, repeatedly, to all who had arrived.
Then, when they had all departed for their respective abodes and homes, Lomaśa, accompanied by the maiden, joyfully returned to his own hermitage.
Then other brahmins and others from the region of Kuṅkumavāpī arrived and, out of love, worshipped the Supreme Lord Hari, the Master. 87.
Afterwards, they went to their respective homes, and a great wonder indeed occurred;
listen, O Rādhikā, for a certain couple arrived there. (88)
The woman was the color of collyrium, and the man’s body was covered with leprosy;
having bowed to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he said, "O Child! (89).
"O Kṛṣṇa, perform the removal of the sins of these two fallen ones who have lost their lineage.
Although Hari already knew this, he questioned those two, whose minds were dejected.
"Who are you two? Tell me, what sin was committed, and how did this pain come about?
The man replied, "I was a Brahmin, Devāyana by name. (91)
In Gaurjara and in the illustrious city of Pattana, here is my beloved;
we both are devoted to the worship of the gods and dedicated to our daily religious duties. (92)
Afflicted by the cold and intent on worship without bathing, they both became [so];
consequently, due to that fault, their lifespan came to its end. (93)
They both died suddenly from fever and were born together in the house of a dog-cooker; then, in that very same city, they were married once again.
O destroyer of sins, having learned through the power of a dream that Kuṣṭhika and Kṛṣṇa were suffering and possessed memories of their past births, [he realized], "You are Nārāyaṇa, O Mādhava. (95)
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, having shaken off our sins, grant us liberation!
O Protector, today is the day for you to bestow release upon those who are bound. 96.
Having heard from the world that you exist as the remover of the sins of sinners, we have indeed come on foot to seek refuge in you. (97)
Having heard this, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to compassion, the ocean of mercy, and the destroyer of sins, spoke to those two, O Rādhikā. (98)
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and drunk its water,
and having then performed a circumambulation, drink the nectar of [my] feet.
"Having become pure, you two shall go to the world of Brahmā, O you who are beyond human measure.
Having heard this, they then acted exactly as they were told.
Instantly assuming divine bodies and mounting celestial chariots, they attained the fruit of hundreds of thousands and millions of sacrifices and ascended to heaven. (101)
Starting from Śrīpattana and ending at Kuṅkumavāpikā, for as many steps as there were, he indeed obtained the fruit of a sacrifice. || 102 ||
Such is the fruit obtained even by approaching holy men who are beloved of Śrī; how much more so, then, in the presence of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa? 103.
O Rādhikā, Śrī Hari is to be served, and His saintly devotees are also to be served;
likewise, a holy ford, a sacred field, and a vow that bestow the fruit of ten million sacrifices are to be served.
"At every step, the fruit of performing an Ashvamedha sacrifice arises.
Having spoken thus, those two were liberated by Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
On the auspicious festival day of the eighth lunar tithi at the commencement of the sixth year,
through both recitation and hearing [this], liberation and ultimate release shall likewise occur.

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Festival and Worship Performed by the Gods, Humans, and Others for the Divine Manifestation of Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa on the Eighth Day of the Lord’s Sixth Year in the Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, as well as the Liberation from the Birth of a Cāṇḍāla of the Brāhmaṇa Devāyana and his Wife. || 39 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, regarding that Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa there, you shall dwell in the presence of the Lord.
On the western bank of the lake, at the site where the bridge was raised,
they established Dattātreyatīrtha as the supreme sacred ford, as well as Vārāhatīrtha.
Kūrmatīrtha, Matsyatīrtha, Kapilatīrtha, Haritīrtha, Pṛthutīrtha, and likewise that named Vāsudevatīrtha. || 3 ||
Haṃsatīrtha, Dattātreyatīrtha, Nṛsiṃhatīrtha, the Tīrtha known as Ṛṣabha, and the Tīrtha named Yogeśvara; || 4 ||
Then there is the Vāmana-tīrtha, the auspicious Paraśurāma-tīrtha,
the Yajña-tīrtha, the Rāma-tīrtha, and the tīrtha named Hayaśiras.
The Sanatkumāra-tīrtha, the tīrtha known as Nārada,
the Vyāsa-tīrtha, the Kṛṣṇa-tīrtha, and likewise the supreme Buddha-tīrtha.
The Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha, the Viṣṇu-tīrtha, the Śrīpuruṣottama-tīrtha,
the tīrtha created by Mahāviṣṇu, and the one named after Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
There is the Ardhanārīśvara Tīrtha and the supremely auspicious Lakṣmī Tīrtha,
where both Rādhikā and I have bathed together with you.
Rādhātīrtha and Kṛṣṇatīrtha are located at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake;
they destroy the heat of sin, bestow liberation, and grant residence in the divine abode.
Thus were these sacred fords born there, O Rādhikā;
then, in the sixth month of Mārgaśīrṣa, they remained in the Mahākāla forest.
The sages and the heretics indeed arrived at the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭakṣetra;
[there were] Samīraṇa, Pavamāna, Santāraṇa, and Barbura.
Voḍhu, Ghanabheda, Dyuviśrāma, Paṅkila, Nīlakaṇṭha, Alarka, Puṇḍarīka, and Kalāyana. || 12 ||
Vītihotra, Camasa, Parṇakutsa, Aśvapāṭala, Bhāllaveya, Ūrjavrata, and also Āśvalāyana. ||13||
Pārṣṇirada, Sumantu, Aśokākṣa, Abhayākṣaka, Brahāstamba, Kūpyavāla, and Cetanabrahman—these too [are names]. || 14 ||
The goddesses are Śrī, Kamalā, Pṛthvī, Rāṇikā, Amaraputrikā, Dhanyeśvarī, Satīśā, Devānikī, and Kṛṣṇikā. || 15 ||
The Pampā, Nārāyaṇī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Gaṇḍakī, Kuśā, Sarasvatī, Hiraṇyā, Svarṇarekhā, and Gomatī. || 16 ||
Then, on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Gautamī creepers and trees, being composed in mind, nourished the principles as well. (17)
In the morning, the deities bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
having returned home, they bowed to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then they bowed to Lomaśa Ṛṣi, and the maidens also bowed to them;
everyone was fed, honored, saluted, and likewise worshipped.
The western shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake is adorned with kunda flowers;
it is devoid of groves and thickets, possessing the grandeur of a vast expanse.
Devoted to their daily rites, they went at midday to that place, which was enriched by groves of *pārijāta* trees and made charming by fragrant trees.
There, on a delightful and shaded patch of ground near the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa, beautified by guṇḍraka, dāḍima, and tintiḍī trees; 22.
They took supreme rest; at evening, the sage Urvajavrata recited a discourse from the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Kālajit, Pañcaśikha, Lomaśa, Āsuri, Jamadagni, Hanumān, and likewise Jāmbavat; ||24||
Vibhīṣaṇa, Vyāsa, Prahlāda, Bali, Ṛbhu,
Gālava, Kṛpa, and others who possessed a lifespan of a hundred kalpas.
Living for seven kalpas and living for ten thousand kalpas,
they sat in the assembly, intent on hearing the discourse.
There, the Lord Kambharānanda, accompanied by his parents,
sat upon the central throne and shone resplendently in the midst of those who were knowers of Brahman.
The gods, the celestial beings, along with the Gandharvas, the Vidyādharas, and humans, together with the hosts of goddesses, listened to the auspicious narrative. ||28||
And the great sage Ūrjavrata, the lord who possessed a lifespan of a hundred thousand kalpas, proclaimed the primordial auspiciousness of the perceptible Hari. ||29||
When there was neither the single imperishable syllable, nor even the abode of the cows,
nor even Vaikuṇṭha, that state of immortality;
When even the abodes did not exist,
and when the creation of the individual soul, the Lord, and so forth did not yet exist, he who was then present— [He is that.]
May He, who is beginningless and possesses the beautiful form of the child Hari-Kṛṣṇa, be mine; salutations to Him, the Foundation. 2.40.30.

May the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be the object of my speech—the Lord who is served in His own abode by liberated souls, and elsewhere by His other forms, His potencies, His manifested qualities, and His unborn opulences, all seeking Him; who, though delighting in two ways, is perceived here as one, like a child. (3.1)
If the Inner Self is present here within this discourse of the sages, then this child of Kambharā— who appears like a mere mortal—
is one whose play is free from clamor and who bears the weight of the entire universe within his belly.
May He, residing in the abode of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, make people's efforts fruitful. ||32||
May this delightful Kuṅkumī tank on earth be victorious,
as well as the foremost lake that removes the sins of the world and the Aśvapaṭṭa;
may the venerable sage Lomaśa, the best among the virtuous, be triumphant.
And may the Lakṣmī-saṃhitā, the bestower of liberation, be victorious. ||33||
May that very Supreme Brahman, Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa, who is sung of here as being at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, bestow auspiciousness.
The elder brother is the Blessed One, and the sister is the virtuous Santuṣṭā;
then there is the wise younger brother Śuka, as well as Śrīvallabha.
May his mother, Kambharālakṣmī, his father, Gopālakṛṣṇaka, and his one hundred and twelve wives, together with their children, be victorious! 36.
The disciple Svayamprakāśa was the foremost among the circle of disciples;
there were other groups of ten million disciples, and [wives] numbering in the tens of billions and trillions. ||37||
Lomaśa, the preeminent teacher, and other sages who know Hari—we, who belong to the lineage of Brahmā, bow down to them; they are the moving [deities] worshipped by those seeking sacred fords. (38)
May Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person, who is both manifest and unmanifest, the child who is beyond the great non-child, grant us our desired welfare. (39)
May Lakṣmīśa, Māṇikīśa, Pārvatīśa, Prabhāpati, and the beloved of Śrī Rādhā and Rukmiṇī grant auspiciousness forever. 2.40.40.
May the sages know him as the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest, Kṛṣṇa, the Master, the Supreme Controller, who is without beginning or end. 41.
For by him, in the past, the Vedas were likewise recovered from the ocean;
and in the past, the goddess Earth was likewise lifted up with the tip of his tusk.
Indeed, by him the remainder was held upon his back;
by him Nārāyaṇa himself was held upon his own couch. (43)
By him, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya was bestowed for the sake of self-illumination;
by him, in ancient times, knowledge was bestowed upon Brahmā by the illustrious Hari. ||44||
The Daityas were also destroyed by Vāsudeva, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
this very Hari, whose nature is the military array (vyūha), established the places for their birth and protection.
The earth was protected by him, and indeed he became the king of kings;
likewise, penance was performed by him, and thus he formerly became the swan. (46)
This very lion was once the slayer of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
now, devoted to virtuous conduct and intent on compassion, he has become a forest-dweller.
The one of short stature was Bhūmihartā, and he was indeed Mahendrānuja;
here the protectors were wounded by this wise man with a blow from a rib-stick. 48.
He is indeed the drinker of clarified butter in the fire, and he is also the bestower of the union with rain;
for he shall lead the Daityas dwelling in the southern region to the realm of Yama.
He who was formerly the son of Brahmā, the most excellent of the virtuous, appearing in the form of a child—
that very same best of men now exists here in the guise of a youth.
This very person is the great sage Vīṇāmagna, the distributor of Vedic knowledge, Rādhākānta, the one served by Satī, and indeed the ocean of awakening. 51.
He is the master, the beloved, the husband, the protector, the guardian, the progenitor, the father, the king, the witness, and the inner self; this child is esteemed by the sages. (52)
Worship with devotion and sincerity Him who is the giver of the eternal abode;
for I take refuge in that Supreme Lord, the unborn one who is dear to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Salutations to that Supreme Brahman, the Great Soul, the Lord of the entire universe, who is served by gods, lords of daityas, liberated souls, and others.
Salutations to the one who is all-seeing, whose self pervades everything, and who is the inner controller;
whom those who chant the Gāyatrī praise, and whom those who have offered themselves worship.
Salutations to that playful Lord, in whom all cause and effect, action and means, as well as the deity and the assembly, are contained. 56.
Homage to the peaceful one, the supreme lord, who holds the conch, the discus, the banner, and the lotus;
homage also to the wielder of the trident, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the wielder of the spear. ||57||
Salutations to you, the source of well-being, the one possessing the fish-banner; salutations to the all-powerful one.
Let there be salutation to the incomparable one who bears the banner of his own true form. 58.
Homage to you who are delightful in manifold ways, and homage to you who are most skillful!
Homage to you, the proclaimer of Sāṃkhya, and homage to you, the proclaimer of Yoga! (59)
Salutations to you, the proclaimer of the Vedas; salutations again and again to you, the proclaimer of logic.
Salutations to you, the proclaimer of liberation; and salutations to the bestower of instruction.
Salutations to the speaker of inquiry, salutations to the bestower of immortality;
salutations to the one with a golden body, salutations to the one with the luster of a campaka flower.
Homage to the mantra worthy of praise, who dwells within the bodies of all beings;
homage to the Hotṛ priest, who abides in virtuous vows and possesses a transcendent form.
Homage to you, O Long-eyed One, the bestower of all desires;
homage to you, the eye within the sky and the eye of all. (63)
Salutations to you who are distinguished by both difference and non-difference;
salutations to you, the transcendent one, whose nature is like shadow and sunlight, and who is peaceful being.
Salutations to Brahmā, who delights in his share of the sacrifice and possesses a single form;
to him who protects the daughter of Pañcāla and who causes the daughter of Bhaga to flow. ||65||
Salutations to the Lord of Anaraṇya’s daughter, salutations to the Lord of Nārāyaṇī;
salutations to You, the giver of food, the Lord of food, whose very self is the treasury.
Homage to you who belong to a lineage suited for the childish, who sport with the playful charms of a child; homage to you, the Child, the Elder, and the one with beautiful hair! ||67||
Salutations to you who are pleased by the six rites, and to you who possess a thousand ornaments;
salutations to you, the refuge of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Homage to you, the refuge of infinite qualities, sovereignty, and majesty;
homage to you, who possess the splendor of clouds and the radiance of the moon, sun, and stars! (69)
You are food and the eater of food; you are the purifying fire that consumes the cooked;
you are water and likewise satisfaction; you are happiness and bliss—salutations to You.
The womb-born, the egg-born, the sweat-born, and the sprout-born—all have been created by you;
indeed, O Lord of Incarnations, you alone are the fourfold multitude of beings. (7.1)
You alone are indeed the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of this world of moving and unmoving beings;
the wise call you Brahman, the supreme goal of those who know Brahman.
The supreme light of the mind, you are the light even of lights;
the exponents of Brahman call you the Haṃsa, the Tree, and the Honey-bee. (73)
The sages likewise declare you to be the performer of sacrifices, the bestower of fruits, and the one who delights in them;
you are eternally recited through the hymns of praise by the collections of Vedas and Upaniṣads.
Men, women, the stationary and the moving, and even animals—you alone exist as Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of the Universe. (75)
You alone are the masses of clouds, the lightning, the thunderbolt, and the roar;
you are the year, the seasons, the month, and even half a month.
The ages, the moments, the units of time, the lunar mansions, and likewise the planets—
you are the one who bears the spear, the mace, the discus, the sword, the thunderbolt, and the bow.
You are the cutter, the breaker, the striker, the thinker, the leader, and the eternal one;
you are the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the trees, the lakes, and the expanses of the earth.

Creeper-vines, grasses, medicinal herbs, and climbing plants; domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds; the undertaking of various actions and qualities; time; and the emergence of flowers and fruits. ||79||
The middle, the seed, the sprout, the leaf, the stalk, and the joint; the stem, the flower, and the fruit, as well as the sap and the fragrance—you alone are all these. (2.40.80)
O Supreme Lord, you alone are the ground of all that is crushed, sweet, and desirable;
you are the purity of purities and the auspiciousness of auspicious things. 8.1.
Among all risings, you alone are the foremost rising; you are the supreme goal.
You are the breaths, the winking of eyes, the yawning, the sneezing, and likewise the impact [of the senses]. (82)
You are the teacher and awakener of Brahmā, Kāla, Yama, and Agni; you are the fourth age, the four Vedas, and the promoter of the fourfold sacrificial office.
He is the leader of the four stages of life and likewise the creator of the four social orders;
he is the master craftsman, the calculator, the mother, and the initiator of all arts and crafts. 84.
Svāhā, svadhā, vaṣaṭkāra, salutation, as well as praise, prayer, and that which is prayed for—you alone are all these; homage, homage to you! (85)
You are the one of hidden vows, the one of secret austerity, the deliverer, and the sustainer of the earth;
you are the creator, the ordainer, and the uniter—to you alone, salutations again and again.
You alone are Brahmā, Śambhu, as well as Viṣṇu, Virāṭ, and Bhūman;
you are austerity, truth, celibacy, uprightness, and contentment. ||87||
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; you alone are the creation of the individual soul and the creation of the Lord;
you are the creation of Brahmā, the Truth, the initiation, the subduer, and Janārdana. (88)
You alone are the beloved, the dear one, the husband, the lord, and Nārāyaṇa;
you are also the point (bindu), the resonance (nāda), the sound (dhvani), Brahman, the reflective awareness (vimarśa), and the manifest word (sphoṭa). ||89||
You alone are Paśyantī, Parā, Madhyamā, and the distinguished Vāk;
you are the cow, the earth, the devotee of Brahmā, the virtuous woman, and the devoted servant.
You alone are everything that is subject to control; apart from you, there is nothing, indeed nothing at all—not even the moon, fire, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, or the maladies of old age.
O Janārdana, you are mental anxieties, physical ailments, peace, and the medicine;
you are the drinker of Soma, sweetness, the Lord of the Maruts, and the Lord of the universe.
O Lord of the World, you alone are Amṛtāśī and Kuṅkumeśa;
you are Akṣateśa and Gaṇeśa, and you are Mukteśa, the Supreme Lord.
You drink poison, fire, Soma, milk, and fresh butter;
you drink clarified butter and honey; you are the consumer of all things, O Grandfather. (94)
You alone are the golden-seeded one, the most excellent of persons;
you are both woman and man, and you are the third state, devoid of the two [other] conditions.
Though you transcend the three states of being, you manifest within those three states;
as the creator of the universe, you are the child, the youth, and the elder with gnarled teeth. ||96||
The moon and the sun are your two eyes; Sarasvatī is your tongue; day and night are your two winks; and the self is your dwelling place.
Neither Brahmā, nor Śiva, nor Viṣṇu, nor those ancient sages, O child, are capable of knowing [her] greatness according to its true nature. (98)
Surrounding tens of millions and hundreds of billions of liberated lords of men, you abide; you alone exist both within and without.
Beyond the great darkness, even beyond the Imperishable, you, the Supreme Lord, ever shine in the highest abode; it is you who are present here in embodied form.
Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who are sleepless, who have conquered their vital breaths, who abide in purity, and who dwell in Brahman, perceive as the Supreme while practicing yoga.
Those subtle forms which are impossible to be shown—
salutations again and again to all those forms of yours here.
The Blessed One, compassionate toward his devotees, dwells forever among his devotees;
he whose hair is the clouds, whose channels are the rivers, and whose belly is the great oceans.
Salutations to you who were lying upon the golden waters and performing ascetic penance; salutations to those persons the size of a thumb, whether conscious beings or stationary and moving things.
Those who [dwell] in rivers, in oceans, on mountains, and in caves;
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in the depths of dense forests.
At crossroads, on carriage roads, at squares, and in assembly halls;
in elephant, horse, and chariot stables, and in ruined gardens and dwellings. || 106 ||
Those who are also in the five elements, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, in the moon, in the sun, in Satyaloka, and in the fourfold realm known as Vaikuṇṭha; || 107 ||
Those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala) and those who have gone beyond that—
O Keśava, they are your devotees, your servants, and your attendants.
O Mādhava, your male devotees are true servants, and your female devotees are your handmaidens;
salutations to them, salutations to them, and salutations to both, O Acyuta! (109)
To those for whom there is no number, no measure, and no form—
those innumerable hosts of liberated ones, let there be salutation to them forever.
Be gracious, O you who possess the form of a child; reveal your own true nature.
Let our hearts be fixed on you alone—may this be the fruit of your sacred teachings.
Thus praised by Rādhikā at the commencement of the narration, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, granted her His own vision. || 11 2 ||
Indeed, each single hair-pore of Him is filled with the radiance of ten million divine suns;
all incarnations reside within His form, and all abodes of light are contained therein.
All the lords, sages, gods, millions of humans,
and the Daityas who form the armor of the universe move within a single hair of his.
Those who are liberated from the millions [of bonds], those who possess millions of beauties, and the great lords who protect the millions—
all shine within her womb, and in whom all splendors reside.
In that [reality] all dissolutions and all creations indeed reside;
therein all classes of selves shine forth through divine vision. (116)
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself revealed his own form— supreme, divine, embodied, and beautiful in its youthful splendor.
Having smiled and inquired after his welfare, he bestowed divine vision upon him;
then all the sages and others, having looked on, became intent on listening.
They beheld the Lord in the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā;
seeing Him, who was never seen before and was heart-stealing, they placed Hari within their hearts.
Having thus demonstrated this, he again offered a rebuttal;
just as a child behaves here, so once more did he become like a child.
Having seen it thus and considering themselves to have accomplished their purpose, those foremost of sages attained supreme bliss, as if they were eternally established in nirvāṇa.
Thus, having directly realized the Supreme Lord as the vessel of the Saṃhitā,
they then constantly listen to the nectar of His discourse.

Thus, for three months, that most auspicious Pārāyaṇa took place in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā; at that time, O Rādhikā, it granted liberation. At the conclusion of the narrative, having performed the Phālgunī festival, all the holy places were established in every way.
And the sages, each by their own name, took up residence right there.
This very place is celebrated as Saṃhitātīrtha and Koṭitīrtha;
it is also known as Ṛṣitīrtha, Kathātīrtha, and Divyatīrtha.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Divine Vision, the Hymns of the Sages, and the Holy Places Originating from the Dwellings of the Sages," occurring in the context of hearing the narrative of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā* performed by the sages during the *Ūrja-vrata* in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, within the second section, the *Tretā-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the supreme, divine, purifying, and wondrous narrative of that very Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
There was a righteous king named Kanthādharabhakta;
he indeed exercised his rule over Saurāṣṭra, his own kingdom.
For that powerful king, the lord of Koṭīnārā, was a devotee of Śambhu and a worshiper of Sthāṇu while dwelling in the Siṃha forest.
Having propitiated Śambhu through austerity, he obtained the Kāladaṇḍa;
wherever that staff is present, the noose of Yama does not exist.
Likewise, the messenger of Yama and Time (Kāla) turn back upon seeing the staff;
O King, [he who worships] Śaṅkara with a thousand lotuses daily becomes a sovereign ruler.
Having performed worship at dawn, one should recite the hundred-fold mantra while standing on one foot:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Kālakāla, to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Śambhu. (6)
"O Death, O Yama, grant me the state of fearlessness.
Thus he constantly recites this mantra as he repeats it.
Then, with a single recitation, he offers one hundred and eight oblations;
in the afternoon, he eats cooked vegetables that have been de-seeded.
He accepts only what is necessary for the maintenance of his body, always sleeping on the ground at night;
even though he possesses youth, he never desires a woman.
While the majestic king was conducting himself in this manner,
there was no theft, fear, disease, or adultery within his kingdom.
One should avoid liquor, meat, and forbidden foods, and offer oblations while serving the progenitors;
on the thirteenth lunar day and on both [the new and full moon days], one should resort to Somatīrtha.
Likewise, the auspicious sight of Bhavanātha and his worship, the bath in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, and the sight of Lomaśa. (12)
Thinking thus, "I shall perform a pilgrimage," he then returns home;
he [offers] the water from his pilgrimage to the millions of women and the common people.
And for the sake of the welfare of his subjects, he indeed provides sweet food to the people every month on the full moon day. (14)
He gives water to all, from children to the elderly, even to the beasts and birds,
as well as to the fish, insects, winged creatures, and trees.
Thus, for one devoted to the Dharma, both the kingdom and the subjects are free from fear;
even when he himself has gone elsewhere, no fear exists within the kingdom.
There was no untimely death, nor likewise any fear of fire;
yet, when time had passed in this manner, he conceived a desire for Puṣkara.
He went there to establish a sacred ford (tīrtha), and a month passed while he was there;
the king then propitiated Vasiṣṭha with excellent service.
"May you live long," he said; "So be it," the king replied.
Having attained supreme longevity and having also obtained infinite welfare, [he remained]. (19)
Having bestowed gifts at the sacred fords, bathed, and worshipped the Creator (Brahmā),
the king then bathed in the Sarasvatī and worshipped the Siddhas.
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he quickly returned to his own home;
on the way, he saw in a dream a son of a Brahmin being led away.
Thinking, "I shall protect [him]," a certain dark-complexioned man, having deliberated, ran with haste toward him in order to rescue him. (22)
His sleep then dissolved, and he perceived that nothing remained;
filled with apprehension, he quickly returned toward the kingdom. ||23||
Upon reaching the village boundary, every dream became true,
because it was within the kingdom of this brahmin, the village priest.
When his son reached death at the end of his lifespan while the father was still alive, he was seized by the messengers of Yama and led to the realm of Yama in an instant. (25)
At that very moment, the king returned from his expedition;
having learned of the weeping and lamentation, the king indeed fell into great sorrow.
Having fully understood the news and realized that death was immortal,
and having taken up the auspicious staff, he consoled that twice-born man.
The performer of the sacrifice followed behind with his son who was dead, desiring to bring back the brahmin;
wherever he went carrying the staff, there a path appeared for him.
Since his movement extends across the earth, water, fire, air, ether, and darkness, as well as among the planets and throughout the fourteen worlds, together with his rod of punishment; ||29||
Without the staff, he would have had no way to reach the surface of the earth;
by means of Śiva’s staff, this king traveled through the sky to the abode of Yama.
When the body of the young man was indeed restrained by the messenger of Yama,
he, touched by the King's staff, fell far away toward the realm of Yama.
Having fallen down and then risen up again, overcome with fear and following the path of Yama, he ran toward King Yama and reported his own defeat. (32)
"O Lord, a certain being possessing a human body has arrived from the city of Yama;
he was traveling with his staff, but I have restrained him with great speed."
Nevertheless, he was not at all obstructed; he struck me with his staff, and I was so utterly defeated that I felt as if I had been struck by a thunderbolt.
Falling to the ground and then rising, O Lord Yama, I approach you here to report that event: who is this person, and for what reason has he come? (35)
"I do not know, O Great King; consider therein as you wish.
Thus addressed by the messenger of Yama, Dharmarāja then [spoke] to his follower.
He summoned the one named Death and commanded him to banish [the king].
Death went and swiftly seized the king by the hand.
"Go," he said to the king, "if indeed death is not yours here.
Upon hearing this, the king applied the rod of punishment against Death. (38)
Mṛtyu leaped down onto the ground and fled quickly;
he reported the man’s strength to Yamarāja.
Then, at that very moment, Yama dispatched Mahākāla, saying:
"Who is this, and from where has he come? Bring him before me."
Thus addressed, Kāla himself approached his presence and, having bowed, said:
"Who are you here? Dharmarāja desires to know."
The king said: "I am the lord of Koṭīnāra in Saurāṣṭra, and I have come here to see the young Brahmin. (42)
"But where does he dwell, and how was he brought here by the messenger of Yama?
It is with this desire to know, O giver of honor, that I have come here. (43)
Kāla said: "Come, report this to Yamarāja;
he will give you the reply, for I am indeed not the one fit for that task."
Having spoken thus and led the king along with him toward King Yama, Kāla announced his arrival; and King Yama, for his part, brought him before himself.
Having offered a welcome, the king asked the reason for his arrival; he bowed to Dharma and spoke to the young Brahmin. (46)
"I have come to search for him; where is that young brahmin?
His father is weeping most piteously on account of his son. (47)
He has only one son, and likewise, death befell him;
indeed, it was for the sake of removing that grief of the Brahmin that I spoke thus.
"O King of Dharma, I wish to take that child back and give him to him;
meanwhile, let that corpse remain guarded until I have gone to him. (49)
"Therefore, give back the son of the twice-born; fulfill my request.
Then Yama spoke quickly to the messenger standing there and to Yama himself:
"Summon Citragupta along with his records for the sake of the Brāhmaṇas. Thus summoned, Citragupta arrived there together with the records.
"Behold how much lifespan this young Brahmin shall have!
Citragupta replied, "His full lifespan is complete; he has died because it has reached its end. (52)
Upon the departure of his body, he shall not have even the slightest remnant of enjoyment or lifespan;
and King Yama, having heard that, informed the king.
O King, his life-force has no power to remain in that body or to experience it;
this man is as good as dead, for you shall not obtain [the fruit], and here the logic of karma prevails. (54)
Whatever was done, by whomsoever, of what kind, to whom, for whom, from whence, where, and for what purpose—all that shall be exactly so and not otherwise. (55)
The king asked: "What evil deed was committed by this boy, by which a messenger of Yama has indeed become his life-breath? (56)
Then Citragupta, at the command of King Yama, said:
"This man was a brahmin and a constant worshiper of the deity. (57)
Indeed, while in the temple of Vāsudeva during the cold season, he raised the deity without having bathed; and by that very sin, his [condition was brought about].
The world of Yama is certain; without punishment, one is not purified.
There is no merit for the sake of humans, nor is there any further life. (59)
"O Indra among kings, how will you take [him] away without the brahmin boy's life-force?
The king said: 'I shall give him my own new life-force.'"
"Through the blessing of Vasiṣṭha, long life was obtained at Puṣkara; from that, I grant him ten thousand years of human life. (61)
Having spoken thus, he released water from his hand and granted him life;
Citragupta then recorded for him a lifespan of ten thousand years.
The two Dharmarājas gave him a child who was to live for ten thousand years;
then he asked the king, "From where did you obtain this strength? (63)
That Yama, Death, and likewise Time—who are invincible—have arrived here through the air in human form and have been overcome by you; [this is truly wonderful]. (64)
"Tell me, by what power was this supreme sovereignty obtained?
Having heard this, the king then replied, "By the power of Śaṅkara."
The power has been attained by the King of Dharma, by whom I have been seen here;
and even though I am but a child, this has been obtained through the compassion of the great ones. (66)
Then the King of Dharma said, "O Lord of the Earth, give me my staff.
The king replied, "Indeed, within this staff resides the entirety of my essential truth."
"O Bull, if my staff were broken, I would have no power to travel through the air;
therefore, I will not give up the staff, for it belongs to Sāṃkarṣaṇa. (68)
She remains there as the destroyer of time; what then can be said of anyone else?
If I were to apply my staff against you, your destruction would be certain. (69)
Having spoken thus to Dharmarāja, the king extended his hand to join that staff; at that moment, the bull fell into a state of agitation.
Even his throne shook, and Dharma bowed down before that king;
for true strength is the strength of the gods and long-standing virtue, not mere physical force.
Then the King of Dharma thought thus and consoled the monarch:
"Do not act this way, O Indra among kings; you are worthy of honor, for you have been sent by the gods. (72)
"By the grace of Kālakāla, everything is in your hand;
therefore, O Indra among kings, I give to you my daughter Hṛddhakāyinī. (73)
Having seen you— a beautiful woman whose every limb is blossoming with youth and whose body is radiant— desiring her, take her as your beloved.
Having spoken thus and having ascertained his strength, the king gave him that maiden Hṛḍḍakāyinī, who was to be his wife, as well as the Brahmin boy. (71)
Having traveled through the air by means of a vehicle dedicated to Dharma,
he arrived at the city named Koṭīnāra in Saurāṣṭra.
The celestial chariot, resplendent like the sun and full of magnificence, slowly descended from the sky near the house of that very brahmin.
Accompanied by celestial women, beautifully adorned with divine furnishings,
it is perfumed by various sovereign powers, supernatural attainments, and the like, and is fearless of Yama.
Seeing Satī as the wife of the brahmin and likewise the young boy, the people joyfully raised shouts of "Victory! and cries of exultation toward the king.
The king gave his son to that brahmin and prostrated before him;
he then became known there by the name of the sage Vṛṣaparvan.
Vṛṣaparvan rose up and entered the dead body;
the brahmins were pleased with the subjects and bestowed their blessings upon him. ||81||
The son of the Brahmin remained intoxicated and did not bow again and again to his elders, nor even to his parents or the king;
the king, however, performed a sacrifice.
Having placed his own queen Yamaputrī at the forefront as Hṛddhakāyinī,
the king performed fire-offerings (homa), gave gifts, bestowed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and provided meals.
Seeing whatever was given, the king blazed up within; he was possessed by darkness, filled with pride and malice, and devoted solely to his own self-interest. (84)
Excessively greedy for her own splendor and opposed to helping others, she causes the king to suffer during acts of giving, feasting, and fire-offerings. 82.
Again and again he said: "O King, do not cause expenditure;
you abide as the supreme Brahman, and you are indeed Nārāyaṇa himself. (86)
You are Viṣṇu, you are Śiva, you are Brahmā, and you are indeed Prajāpati;
you are the enjoyer, you are the creator, you are Agni, and you are the Lord of Heaven. ||87||
You are the vessel, you are the supreme teacher, you are the sacrifice, and you are the ultimate refuge;
you are the Lord of Svāhā and the Lord of Svadhā, and you are the ground of the Vaṣaṭ-call. 88.
You are the Hotṛ priest, you are the sacrificer; what other god is superior to you?
Therefore, O Lord, you alone are known as the supreme reality of all. (89)
Right here, you shall see the Lord himself, traveling in a celestial chariot like yourself,
the husband of Yamarāja’s daughter, his sovereignty fully increased.
And having abandoned [all else], who in this world is to be worshipped as Maheśvara?
Therefore, you must know you yourself to be the supreme reality, the Lord of Sacrifice. 9.1
You are capable of slaying Time and likewise slaying Death;
you exist as the Lord, able to restore the dead to life.
Neither Indra, Varuṇa, Pavana, Kubera, Agni, nor Nirṛti—nor any of the guardians of the quarters or the protectors of the world—are there any like you, O beloved. (93)
Everything in this world is under your control; whom else, then, do you worship?
Abandon sacrifice as well as giving, and renounce your concern for the world beyond. (94)
Devote yourself to your own true happiness; know that it is indeed granted by me through service.
Merit consists in serving one's own Self, while sin consists in afflicting one's own Self. (95)
Know that the sweet words of one's own beloved are different from those that are bitter and destructive;
having understood this, rule your supreme kingdom, which is sustained by your own mind. (96)
Thus that Hṛḍḍakāyinī constantly spoke to Rādhikā;
and he too, due to the fault of her association, gradually fell into atheism.
In lying down, eating, traveling, touch, holding the breath, looking, and acting—when he stands by one's side, his excellence exerts its influence. (98)
In living together, in conversation, in study, in kissing, in eating the food of the learned, and in [eating] human [flesh], sin is transmitted among people. (99)

When holding one's breath while above, when wearing a garment that has been held [by another], and when drinking water that has been offered, the intellect proceeds multiplied by those respective factors. (2.41.10)

Through association with hunger, the fluctuating intellect becomes cruel; through association with enemies, it becomes ruined; and through association with a beloved, it becomes an object of enjoyment. (101)

Through association with the virtuous, the mind always attains a state of goodness; through association with the Teacher, it attains humility; and through association with servants, it attains the nature of a master. 102.
Thus indeed, O Rādhikā, the king’s mind completely turned;
it became intent solely upon his own self-interest, just as Hṛṅkukāyinī had said.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of King Kaṇṭhādharas Attainment of Kālayaṣṭi through Devotion to Śaṅkara in the Tretā Age, His Longevity through Service at Puṣkara and the Blessing of Vasiṣṭha, The Bringing Back of the Brahmin’s Son who had gone to the City of Yama, The Granting of His Own Life-span, His Marriage to Hṛṅkukāyinī, the Daughter of King Yama, and the Occurrence of Atheism in that Connection," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the *Tretā-sattva-khaṇḍa*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; King Kanthādhara was indeed constantly devoted to women, and due to that association with women, he became an atheist intent only on his own self-interest.
The evil-minded one, a reviler of the Vedas, caused it to be proclaimed throughout the city:
"Nothing should ever be given, no sacrifice should be performed, and no oblation should ever be offered."
"I alone am indeed to be saluted here; I am always to be honored by you. Protected by me, you shall dwell in happiness as subjects. (3)
There is no other god for you to take as your ultimate refuge than I;
to me alone should be given the oblation, the sacrificial offering, the gift, and the priestly fee.
"I am the king, I am the guardian of the world, and I alone am the protector of the subjects; I alone am the giver, the sustainer, and the ordainer of all creatures. (5)
I alone am the giver of life, the giver of grain, and the giver of wealth;
I alone am the bestower of happiness, the wielder of the rod of punishment, and the provider of protection.
Fire itself resides within my mouth; what is to be given must be offered there, not elsewhere.
My hands are the vessels and my head is the sacrificial ground; it is only there that giving is appropriate.
One should give gifts, but not beg; for according to the principles of policy, one must give.
[The gifts include] garments, livestock, cattle, buffaloes, goats, sheep, and so forth.
All my wealth is to be bestowed; furthermore, for the sake of my subjects, it shall be employed during times of famine and the like for the purpose of bringing happiness to the people.
Having heard these words, the brahmins— seers of Brahman, advanced in progeny, learned, guided by the Vedas, and most excellent in wisdom— [spoke].
Having come together in great harmony for the sake of the king's instruction, they prostrated before the king and, being duly honored, spoke these words: ||| 1 ||1||
The Śruti is the authority for dharma; from it the sacrifice is established.
Without sacrifices, the gods who bestow grain do not remain satisfied in heaven.
When the gods are displeased, famine arises;
O King, there will be the destruction of the people and even the upheaval of the country. (13)
Therefore, O King, the pacification of elemental spirits and the pacification of planetary influences must always be performed,
as well as the gratification of the gods and the gratification of the ancestors through great sacrifices.
Sacrifice must never be obstructed, for the ritual is rooted in the Vedas;
the gods, who bestow happiness, are always to be gratified through the mouth of the fire. (15)
Although addressed in this way, King Kaṇṭhādhara did not believe it at all;
he censured the Vedas in many ways, saying they were intent on deception.
The Brahmins are intent on their own self-interest; these masses of Vedas were fabricated by rogues.
And the twice-born, greedy for sweet food, have made the sacrificial fire their deity.
Having cast something into the fire, they themselves eat sweet foods;
they themselves take for themselves the sacrificial fees, wealth, vessels, cows, horses, and elephants.
They grasp at it by means of that sign; therefore, they are indeed intent upon their own self-interest.
There is no deity residing in a physical form, nor does he eat, nor does anything please him.
The Brahmin was a manifest god; whatever pleased him, he would provide—whether it be sweet food or sweet water—by invoking the deity as the instrumental cause.
The Brahmin enjoys ornaments, flower garlands, and fragrances;
he receives the gift of a cow, the drinking of milk, the gift of a bed, and the offering of a house. (21)
The Brahmin who enjoys everything intended for the deity in the garden—including the vehicle, beautiful vessels, the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the mount—[incurs sin]. (22)
The Brahmin enjoys soft bedding, all manner of objects for enjoyment, savory juices, fruits, and the finest cooked foods. (23)
The twice-born worshipper enjoys male and female slaves as well as servants;
therefore, Brahmins intent on their own self-interest eat while designating it as a sacrifice.
Therefore, one should certainly not sacrifice, nor should one give at all;
such is the firm command of my queen, the lady of Ḍr̥ḍhakāyī. (25)
"Whoever transgresses this shall be subject to my punishment"—
thus did the king have drums beaten everywhere throughout the kingdom.
From that time forth, sacrifices for the worship of the gods ceased;
there was famine, and by that, the subjects were afflicted with suffering. (27)
The powerful forcibly seize the property of the weak,
and the king, being addicted to sensual pleasures, does not perform his duty of protection.
Then, indeed, the kingdom became utterly overturned by the force of time;
the staff of Śambhu, which bestows success, vanished from the king and disappeared. (29)
Then the king grieved greatly, thinking, "My life is indeed lost, and my sovereignty has vanished due to this insult from the gods. (2.42.30)
The subjects, enraged for the sake of grain, besieged the courtyard of the king;
having taken the grain, they then departed with wealth such as cattle and other goods.
The prosperity of the kingdom perished, and the subjects became exceedingly impoverished;
then there were Kanthadhara and his wife, Hṛḍḍakāyinī.
Both, overcome with extreme grief, fled to the forest out of fear;
and between them was a son, barely a year old and exceedingly tender.
The Brahmins escorted him to their own abode for his protection,
along with a celestial chariot, a divine staff, and divine implements.
When they had departed for their own abode, the kingdom then became empty;
indeed, when a mass of merit increases, one's powers and prosperity increase as well. (35)
When merit is destroyed, even the gods perish; what need is there to mention this king?
O Rādhikā, that king met his end in the forest.
Having abandoned food and water, even though she was dead,
Hṛḍḍakāyinī and those two atheists attained birth as Mlecchas on the shore of the ocean.
By the turn of fate, those two were born nearby as partakers of suffering;
the prince named Raṇaṅgama reached the age of twelve. (38)
Having learned of his father’s conduct from the words of the Brahmins while wearing the sacred thread,
he reflected repeatedly upon his father’s evil fate even in the forest.
Having completed his studies in the sciences, he became the bearer of the burden of the kingdom;
for they considered him supremely qualified and devoted to the performance of righteous duties.
The Brahmins consecrated him as king, the protector of the earth;
thereafter, he delighted his subjects by protecting them according to dharma.
The righteous-souled one performed a sacrifice and instituted the worship of the gods;
then, standing in the midst of the Brahmins, he prostrated himself before them and spoke.
"O twice-born ones, my father and likewise my mother were the ones who caused the interruption of the sacrifice; they have died in the forest—how am I to perform their funeral rites? (43)
"Announce [this] thus in the presence of the Brahmins," he said;
and he, shining with splendor, was named Svayaṃprakāśa (Self-Luminous). ||44||
The disciple of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, traveling through the sky while proceeding toward Somakṣetra, descended at Koṭīnāra.
Seeing those brahmins, he suddenly went out to meet them;
having offered them seats and prostrated before him, they questioned him.
We are blessed to have encountered the sight of the Great Sage at this very moment;
your conduct is for the sake of destroying the suffering of the world and for the sake of their ultimate welfare. (47)
O Blessed One, you know the auspicious and inauspicious of the entire world;
you are the very heart of Kṛṣṇa himself, his direct disciple. ||48||
The father of this king was a wicked soul, a reviler of gods and brahmins;
devoid of his own duty, he took refuge in the forest together with his wife.
"One who has met death in the forest—where does he abide, or what is the fate of one of evil deeds?
How might he attain liberation? Speak, for this boy is asking you. (2.42.50)
Indeed, on the shore of the western ocean, there dwells a king together with his queen;
born among the Mlecchas, he is afflicted with consumption and leprosy. ||52||
And his rescue must be accomplished by this son in every way;
for he alone is called a "son" in the world who protects his fathers from fear. (53)
"Let this son go there, taking the Mleccha along with his wife to the Aśvapaṭṭasara holy site, which is presided over by Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (54)
Then, let him make his body pure with the water of a sacred ford;
thereafter, freed from sin, he shall attain liberation along with his beloved—of this there is no doubt.
Having heard the words of Svayamprakāśa, the brahmins and the subjects said to Kumāra, who was on the battlefield, "Go toward him! ||56||
Accompanied by the Brahmins and a limited number of attendants, the prince set out for the shore of the ocean where his father was staying.
Having gone to that western region, which was a refuge for Mlecchas, filled with trees,
and abounding in places called Makarālayas, he searched for it with his servants.
The servants saw him as one afflicted with leprosy and consumption;
they saw that Hṛḍḍakini as well, possessed of leprosy and suffering from consumption.
Both were possessors of the memory of their past lives and were awaiting their son;
having heard that Uddhāraka had arrived, they were then exceedingly joyful.
The Mleccha and the Mlecchī, filled with eagerness, quickly arrived together with their servants to the place where the prince, the warrior, was staying.
And seeing that [child], they wept again and again for his rescue;
they entreated him there and remained in his presence.
Seeing them thus afflicted with leprosy and likewise possessed by consumption, the son, himself tormented by great grief, spoke these words: ||63||
"Taking your command, O parents, I shall go;
I will perform the pilgrimage to the Aśvapaṭṭasara Tīrtha for you both, free from ailment. (64)
Then, having gone before his father’s kinsmen, the king said this:
"Alas, O Mlecchas! I bow to you; here are these two lepers."
For the sake of medical treatment, I shall also take Kṣaya to my own home; there I will make these two free from disease, if it is your wish. (66)
"So be it," said all the Mlecchas to that prince who was supremely compassionate;
with all their limbs bowed in prostration, they said, "Do as you know best."
Then, having brought men equipped with a palanquin,
the king seated his two paternal ancestors upon it.
The king, his attendants, and the brahmins set out early in the morning and proceeded with haste; in the evening, they arrived at Aśvapaṭṭasara.
Although the sage was self-effulgent, he went to the Aśvapaṭṭa hermitage;
the king and the others, however, established themselves in their own place near the banyan tree.
And on the western shore of this lake, in the region of the wind-quarter,
they all took excellent rest at night upon that sacred ground.
Then, as the king and the brahmins were prepared to bathe them in the lake at dawn, the wind spoke these words from the sky: ||72||
O King, do not act rashly; protect this sacred ford with great effort.
These two are enveloped by every kind of terrible sin. (73)
These two sinners, who revile the Vedas, are enemies of the gods and destroyers of sacrifices;
they are the ruiners of Dharma, and for them, there is no end to their sin. (74)
If these two fall into the lake, the lake will become dry;
having bathed in this great holy site, these two fierce ones will cause its destruction.
"Therefore, do not immerse these two in the water on the shore of the lake.
Having heard these words from the sky, he was overcome with great sorrow. (76)
Afflicted by grief, O Lord, he spoke toward the voice from the sky:
"If these two are such terrible sinners, they are certainly not worthy of bathing at all. (77)
"I shall perform an expiation for the sake of those two; speak, O Lord!
Then Vāyu, the gods, and the sacred fords from all sides [spoke]. 78.
And having observed the king, they all spoke these words:
"Having bathed repeatedly in the sacred fords situated at Aśvasaras... (79)
Bathe yourself repeatedly with the waters from jars at sacred fords until their sins have been completely wiped away.
For a person who nourishes their own interests and corrupts the gods, purification is never produced anywhere by bathing even once. 8.1
Therefore, having bathed with devotion at these sacred fords (tīrthas) dedicated to these two, sprinkle them repeatedly with water; they will become purified. (82)
Having heard these words and having established a hermitage there,
he then bathed repeatedly at various sacred fords and filled a water-pot with water.
And day after day, having performed his ablutions at sacred fords,
the king constantly consecrated his two parents with the water of those fords.
Thus, having been consecrated again and again with the waters of all the sacred fords (tīrthas),
they were further purified by their son through the greatness of the Aśvatīrtha.
When they have become free from sin, then the holy fords tell the king:
"These two are supremely pure; cause them to bathe in the lake. (86)
Thus addressed, the king, having entered the waters of the Vaiśākha month while on the battlefield, instantly became self-restrained and endowed with divine bodies. (87)
The barbarian state vanished and divine splendor increased;
Kanthadhara, seated in a celestial chariot together with his wife, became a deity. (88)
Seated in his celestial chariot and filled with great joy, he praised the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, with supreme devotion.
O Supreme Brahman, embodiment of compassion and grace for the upliftment of others, O Lord,
two sinners have been delivered by your disciple, the sage.
O Hari, you have delivered us both through your son, and you have also delivered us yourself;
we, who were wicked, have been rescued by the waters of those devoted to the service of others.
We have been delivered from the terrible darkness born of the power of ignorance by the Brahmins;
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, we have been rescued from hell by taking refuge in you. 92.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Lord, who dwells within the heart and who is established everywhere;
salutations to You, whose nature is self-luminous and who is the soul of all sacred fords. ||93||
Salutation to the God who is the refuge, and to Him who bestows welfare upon the lives of the sinful;
salutation to You, the Child Kṛṣṇa, who grants liberation to those who take shelter. 94.
By your majesty alone, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas, as well as the wicked daityas, dānavas, and those of the asuras and tamas nature, truly cross over [their obstacles]. (95)
They were possessed of illusory tendencies, full of pride and arrogance, lecherous, eaters of flesh, thieves, and drinkers of intoxicants. ||96||
Even those who cause the intermixture of castes and those who commit the murder of cows or women cross over [to liberation] through your majesty, O treasure-house of compassion and grace. (97)
"O Lord, we two have been delivered; let us go to your immortal abode.
Having spoken thus and prostrated themselves, they said, "O son, may it be well with you. (98)
Having bestowed their blessings, they both departed for the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Om, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! (99)
Having received this mantra from Lomaśa and a garland of tulasī,
they became supreme Vaiṣṇavas and went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
The non-Buddhist ascetics and householders attained supreme wonder, for by merely bathing here, eternal liberation was indeed achieved. (101)
This is the supreme compassion of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
O Rādhikā, the desire of Hari is powerful, and his mercy is mighty.
There, at Kanthādhra, Hṛddhakāyinī became liberated;
that supreme holy site, Kanthādhra, attained renown upon the surface of the earth. (103)
Then that goddess Hṛṇḍakāyinī assumed two forms;
her shadow-form went to her own father, King Yama.
By the command of King Yama, she assumed the form of hiccup;
the Yoginī established her fixed residence among all living beings.
In her second form, being divine and dwelling within the heart, she went upon the path of liberation together with her divine husband. 106.
She too, following the path of her father, attained the state of liberation;
yet, through residual impression (vāsanā), she became a shadow-form in the guise of a hiccup.

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Kanthādharas’ Atheism through his Union with his Wife Hṛḍḍakāyinī in the Second Tretā Cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Loss of His Sovereignty due to the Cessation of Vedic Rites and other Duties, His Death in the Forest and Rebirth as a Mleccha, and His Liberation by his Son Raṇaṅgama at the Aśvapaṭṭa-saras Tīrtha. || 42 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen to this most purifying account of a devotee;
thereafter, this king, Raṇaṅgama, [performed] here at this holy ford (tīrtha) daily.
He duly performed the post-mortem rites, the ancestral *śrāddha*, and the libations;
he also fed the Brahmins, the virtuous men, the virtuous women, and the maidens.
To children, sages, gods, mendicants, and likewise to servants,
he gave various gifts of gold and silver with devotion.
He quickly received from Lomaśa the supreme Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (4)
He performed his vow according to the rules and duly observed the rites for visiting sacred fords;
he took up a garland of *tulasī* and the image of the Supreme Lord.
Then he sent Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
there he dwelt with great affection along with the Brahmins, servants, and others.
He indeed sought the company of the virtuous day and night;
and remembering his ancestors there, he desired to perform a sacrifice.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
Who is this king? In whose lineage was he born, and who were his ancestors?
How did he perform the sacrifice, when, and where? Tell me this. (8)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Ṛkṣa was the son of Candra; he lived for a hundred million years and was a knower of dharma and yoga.
His son was Saṃvaraṇa, who became a sovereign ruler of the earth.
He married Tapatī, the daughter of the Sun and a virtuous maiden;
from those two, after some time, was born the dispassionate King Kuru.
For this kingdom of the ancestors was indeed given by his father to his elder brothers;
therefore, having received his own share and gone to the Dvaitavana forest, he engaged in auspicious agriculture.
Having indeed made Viṣṇu present at the sacrifice through the supreme and most excellent vision of Brahman by means of the plow, he departed for the world of liberation.
The auspicious younger brother of Kuru, named Kaṇṭhādharas,
who was also the son of Saṃvaraṇa, received the portion of Surāṣṭra.
Having obtained a small kingdom merely for the sake of livelihood,
he resided in the city of Koṭināra in the Siṃha forest.
In this way, that descendant of the Lunar dynasty, his son Raṇaṅgama,
being devoted to sacred pilgrimage sites, remembered his ancestors at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
And he gratified Brahmā, Marīci, Kaśyapa, Candra, Ṛkṣaka,
Saṃvaraṇa, and Kanthādhra with offerings of sesame seeds and water.
He likewise gratified Sāvitrī, Kalā, Aditi, Rohiṇī,
Ghaṭikā, Tapatī, and Hikkā with water mixed with sesame seeds.
On the western bank of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, the exceedingly righteous King Raṇaṅgama desired to perform a sacrifice. || 18 ||
In the sixth year of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
during the Cāturmāsya period, he desires to perform a great Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
He quickly brought all the necessary materials from his own kingdom;
he prepared kusha grass and various kinds of sacrificial fuel.
He constructed a magnificent main pavilion and several other beautiful canopies.
He had leaf-huts suitable for dwelling constructed by artisans.
The sacrificial pits, the altars, the platforms, the seats, the excellent sacrificial vessels, and the supreme vessel made of udumbara wood. ||22||
He quickly had silken garments and fine clothes prepared; he also established juice-houses, cooking-sheds, and dining-halls among the trees and other structures.
He established auspicious drinking halls, water-stations,
cow-sheds, horse-stables, wives’ quarters, and places for religious observances.
He caused [the rites] to be performed according to the prescribed rule and had unbroken grains brought:
wheat, barley, rice, sesame seeds, fruits, and sugar.
All sacrificial substances, whatever dye-stuffs there may be, the most excellent articles for worship, and likewise abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 26 ||
All the implements for recitation and chanting, as well as the garments, the ritual jars, the colored cloths, and likewise the five kinds of leaves; ||27||
He had vessels of clarified butter, the sacrificial oblation for the gods,
and the ritual receptacles prepared according to the prescribed rule, accompanied by auspicious benedictions.

One should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), purification, sprinkling with water, and so forth; likewise, one hundred and eight or even a thousand Brāhmaṇas [should be fed].
The Yājñeyas, as well as others beginning with Brahmā, took their positions; likewise the Hotṛ, Udgātṛ, Pratyudgātṛ, those skilled in the Sāman, and those conversant with the Yantras.
The Āhartṛ, the Pratihartṛ, the sacrificers, the reciters, the readers, those engaged in the contemplation of Brahman, and likewise those who perform the duties of the subordinate priests. ||3.1||
Furnished with deer-horns and other implements, the sacrificial rites proceeded in the various pavilions;
the fire, the consumer of oblations, was duly established.
Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, was worshipped before him together with his twenty-four incarnations. (33)
Brahmā, Muktā, Rādhikā and others, as well as the other wives of Viṣṇu—Pārvatī, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, Satī, Kamalā, and so forth. (34)
Haṃsā, Paramahaṃsā, Saguṇā, Mañjulā, and Priyā;
the Mothers who are worshipped, as well as Śambhu, the gods, and Gaṇādhipa. ||35||
The celibate sages, other attendants, as well as the Śaktis, the princesses, Durgā and the others, the planetary deities, the gods, and the guardians of the fields; ||36||
The guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, the supernatural powers, the hosts of yoginīs, and the virtuous classes of ancestors were established within the divine mandala. (37)
The creation of Brahmā, the creation of Īśa, and the creation of the Jīva—the latter is most excellent;
she who is worshipped there in the pavilion and desires a share of the sacrifice. (38)
Those who were characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), as well as those who spoke like the servants of the gods,
were honored here by Lomaśa during the great festival of Viṣṇu’s sacrifice.
The sacrificer was Raṇaṅgama, and the preceptor was indeed the sage Lomaśa;
the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was the foremost deity of the sacrifice.
Everything there was perfectly accomplished during that four-month sacrifice performed day after day; this ritual, from beginning to end, was constant and complete according to the prescribed rules.
The commencement of this [rite] should take place in the month of Āṣāḍha, and its completion in Kārttika;
there, one should perform daily fire-offerings and feed ten thousand Brahmins.
For others, there is no end at all to the feeding of ten million maidens and so forth, nor to the constant giving of garments and the feeding of ten million children and so forth. (43)
There were thousands of streams of ghee, streams of curd, and streams of milk;
there were streams of savory juices and streams of honey, possessing the splendor of offerings such as the *madhuparka*.
There, sweet drinks and the finest delicacies are served in food in countless quantities; thus, embodied beings become fully satisfied. (45)
The Lord Fire, eternally embodied, himself consumes the oblation with his two hands;
self-luminous, he offers it back with a stream of clarified butter.
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Fire-god, receives [the offerings] in his lotus-face;
thus, those whose essence is sacrifice attain supreme satisfaction in the most excellent of rituals. 47.
Tens of millions of gifts were constantly bestowed by Raṇaṅgama;
thus, while this sacrifice was being performed perpetually, the inhabitants of the three worlds [were amazed].
The gods constantly come and go for the purpose of beholding him and for the purpose of offering oblations;
they worship Hari perpetually with thousands of lotuses. 49.
There, Kambharā Lakṣmī and Gopālakṛṣṇaka shine forth as the parents who provide the materials for worship. (2.43.50)
And since the two of them are also the providers of the sacrificial materials, what deficiency could there possibly be?
Furthermore, the great seer, devoted to his wife, is present here as the presiding authority over all. (5.1)
"In that regard, what deficiency could there be when all honors are provided with food and drink?
Thus, O Rādhikā, the sacrifice proceeded day after day.
Rain falls constantly, and the various crops rejoice;
indeed, a sacrifice has been performed by the son for the sake of Kanthādhara.
"Without even his patched cloak, my son gave away everything in charity while going forth to battle;
may Kṛṣṇa be pleased with him. Having said this, he gave it into the hands of a worthy recipient.

The gods, having descended from heaven and smelled the smoke of the clarified butter, assumed the forms of boars and spoke to one another in divine speech: 55. "The gods, having descended from heaven and indeed smelled the smoke of the clarified butter, assumed the forms of boars and spoke to one another in divine speech."

Blessed is he who goes to battle in this world, blessed is even one who wears a patched garment, and blessed are the elders such as Candra and others, in whose lineage there is such an expansion of sacrifice. (56)
In that sacrifice where the twentieth syllable is elided and nasalized,
everything is given away there— save for a loincloth and a patched garment.
In whatever sacrifice the goddess Kṣudhā has indeed met with defeat, there Tṛpti is victorious; truly blessed is the sage Lomaśa.
Blessed is the brahmin devoted to his wife, and blessed is the self-effulgent one, for whom the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa acts as a helper. (59)
The gods must always reside here during the four-month period by all means;
constant coming and going will not be permitted, as such effort would be in vain. (2.43.60)
A sacred place of merit is difficult to find, and likewise, association with the virtuous is difficult to find;
constant worship is difficult to attain, and refuge in Hari is difficult to obtain.
Merit and renown are difficult to attain, and hearing this narrative is difficult to find;
likewise, the constant sight of dear friends is always hard to obtain.
Devotion to Śrī Hari is difficult to attain; the nectar of his feet is difficult to attain;
and likewise, the constant consumption of his grace is difficult to attain. (63)
Everything that is difficult to attain has become easily accessible; blessed is Kuṅkumavāpikā, and blessed is the holy ford of Aśvasaras where this sacrifice is being performed.
O gods, there is no lake like this Brahmasaras, nor indeed any lake like this Puṣkara, which grants satisfaction to the three worlds and is in the direct presence of the Lord of Śrī.
The Mānasa lake is not like this; nor is the Nārāyaṇa lake like this;
nor even the Pampā lake is like this, where the Supreme Lord does not dwell.
Indeed, all trees and creepers here dwell as liberated beings;
indeed, all stalks, shrubs, and those consisting of grass dwell as liberated beings.
Beasts, birds, aquatic creatures, species of insects,
terrestrial beings, worms, and mosquitoes— all indeed dwell liberated.
Blessed is the dust of this land, whose touch destroys sin;
and blessed is the water of this lake, of which even a single drop bestows liberation.
"We are blessed partakers of the sacrifice, for whom this supreme gain has come;
may he who has gone to the battlefield be blessed, and may this divine body be restored."
May he be endowed with divine accomplishment, may he be laden with divine prosperity, and may this warrior in battle attain the state of a god. (71)
Thus addressed with these blessings, that king of devotees indeed set out for the battlefield; at that moment, a magnificent divine chariot appeared, having arrived for his sake.
It grants all desires, is joined with the wish-fulfilling creeper, is filled with bliss,
remains ever-present for constant service, and is offered by Indra along with its charioteer.
It was provided with male and female slaves and servants, accompanied by pools of edible nectar, illuminated, and furnished with all kinds of beds and articles for enjoyment. ||74||
Thus, by the great grace of the gods, King Raṇaṅgama obtained an imperishable celestial chariot that always bestows inexhaustible objects.
Having made a formal resolve, he constantly gave gifts amounting to billions and trillions;
and having summoned Viśvakarman, as well as Śambara and Maya, [he commanded them].
He caused to be built at that holy site, near the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
a ten-thousand-pillared seven-storied temple for the gods on all sides.
He caused the gods to shine like heaven and likewise established them there;
and for the sake of worship, he indeed gave gifts of houses to the Brahmins.
Then he gave a wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpavallī*) to each of the Brahmins;
everything that is desirable and fit for enjoyment bears fruit upon that creeper eternally. (79)
At that time, there was indeed no need here for fields, nor for crops, nor even for cattle; neither for grain, nor for chaff, nor for fat.
Although his kingdom was small, that king then enjoyed the most stainless lunar luster and fame throughout the world, such as that of a sovereign emperor.
O Rādhikā, for my devotee there is nothing whatsoever that remains unfulfilled;
to him who gives me his all, I give everything.
Thus, while the sacrifice was being performed and tens of thousands of temples were being constructed,
Raṇaṅgama then departed for heaven.
When the auspicious seventh year of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa had arrived, he celebrated the birth festival of Hari on the eighth day.
There, he seated the Lord Anādi-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon a jeweled throne and worshipped him with various divine offerings and other honors. (85)
He fed hundreds of thousands of Brahmins and even children;
he worshipped the gods and had songs sung. ||86||
The king performed various auspicious rites with devotion; he indeed honored the virtuous sages, the holy women, and the chaste ladies. (87)
He caused gifts to be given: gold, silver, and diamonds;
clothing, ornaments, cows, buffaloes, elephants, horses, chariots, and servants.
Then, during the night, Lomaśa recited a delightful discourse from the second section of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā.
At the conclusion of their conversation, ten million maidens performed the worship of their beloved;
then, in the night, Hari himself, assuming ten million forms, engaged in the Rāsa dance of love.
