The Supreme Lord Hari himself, together with ten million beloveds, sported in an expansive garden of land-lotuses. 9.1.
Then, having brought joy to her circle of friends, she offered her defense;
and at dawn, the king performed the sacrificial oblation as was his custom.
And for the gods who had arrived to celebrate the birth festival, the king performed service in many ways and then granted them leave to depart.
And on the full moon day of Kārttika, after the sacrificial oblations,
the king granted a remission for this sacrifice and bestowed the ritual fees.
He gave various gifts many times over, including ornaments of jewels, diamonds, rubies, gold, and silver, as well as clothing, food, vehicles, draft animals, and so forth.
He performed the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the lake together with the sages;
likewise, the incarnations were liberated, as were the other lords.
The gods, the ancestors, mortals, and all beings, both stationary and moving,
departed at the conclusion of the sacrifice to their respective abodes with eager anticipation.
Worshipping the eternal King Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
he was seated upon a divine vehicle together with the brāhmaṇas and his attendants.
[He beheld] the sages, Kṛṣṇa, his father, his mother, the gods, and the celestial abodes.
Having bowed down to the sacred fords, the trees, and the creepers, he departed for his home.
Honored by the people, he entered his own city called Koṭīnārā and rested in his own residence.
Then a yakṣa named Citramāla heard of that king—
powerful, deeply devoted, illustrious, and in the full bloom of youth.
He arrived at Saurāṣṭra and the Cāśvapaṭṭa lake;
he beheld the sacrificial grounds of the king and the splendor of the palaces (102),
having recognized them as being built by the king and having understood their supreme majesty.
He went to the battlefield to give his own daughter, Kṛtamālā, [in marriage]. || 103 ||
And by Raṇaṅgama, the city was renewed with wish-fulfilling trees;
the preeminent Yakṣa beheld the city as if it were the city of the gods.
He descended from the celestial chariot to the king's residence from the sky;
he gave the maiden, as well as female and male servants, to Raṇaṅgama.
The king performed the taking of her hand according to the marriage rites;
the son-in-law of the eminent Yakṣa shone upon the earth like a god.
Having bestowed his daughter, the Yakṣa departed for the city of Kubera.
"O Rādhikā, the listener and the speaker of this [account] shall partake in both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(107) Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fame Gained in Battle, the Seventh Birth Festival of the Lord, the Marriage of Raṇaṅgama with the Yakṣa Maiden, the Attainment of the Celestial Vehicle, and Other Matters," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; thereafter, the king, having attained spiritual perfection, established a great city named Somavelā. || 1 ||
There were ten thousand golden palaces,
as many silver palaces, and thousands of jeweled palaces;
there were diverse gardens and groves filled with lotuses and cranes.
He caused it to be made in many ways and caused the deities to dwell therein.
Then, he gave a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī) to each individual temple there,
as well as to the yakṣas, kimpuruṣas, bards, celestial singers, and the gods of the earth.
He settled millions of men who were like unto gods;
having thus constructed the twelve-gated city named Somavelā.
To the western part of the city, from Soma-tīrtha, is a charming place;
there, moreover, is the golden temple of the illustrious Somanātha.
Having demolished the old one, he indeed caused a great new structure to be built—
a gateway (gopura) seven stories high and rising to the height of a thousand cubits.
There, the god Somanātha, fifty cubits in width and resembling a mountain peak, shines resplendent, stationed in the sky and supported by it.
There shines a bell adorned with golden chains,
audible for ten yojanas and weighing a hundred bhāras.
He who is to be awakened by a hundred measures was proclaimed by means of a mere machine;
his pinnacle-vase was golden and consisted of seven parts.
It was fifty cubits in height, radiant like the sun;
its banner-pole was fifty cubits long, and its staff was one hundred cubits.
Where clouds rest continuously during the four-month rainy season,
and where a man standing there appears like a swan.
There he employed the Brahmins in the performance of worship with offerings; and that king, in particular, established a great sacrificial session of food (annasatra).
Where there were ten thousand women and likewise ten thousand men,
and fifty thousand boys as well as girls.
Thus, by the power of the merit of his sacrifices, King Raṇegama constantly partook of foods mixed with sweets and ghee. || 15 ||
By virtue of the majesty of his worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
he indeed became like a world-protector on earth and traveled in a celestial chariot.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, he indeed set out toward the southern direction in order to survey the region beyond the ocean by means of his aerial vehicle.
The mighty one went ahead to see the eternal Dakṣiṇā,
as well as the food and drink, the host of servants, the attire, and likewise the Kalpalatā.
Taking the ritual implements with him, he traveled through the sky by means of a celestial chariot;
having gazed upon the Siṃhāraṇya forest, he proceeded from Saurāṣṭra to the southern region.
Having traversed a region of a hundred yojanas, the king proceeded further ahead and beheld the ocean situated in the southern direction.
There he beheld the most beautiful island of lac-dipped lamps;
then, proceeding further through the sky, he saw Māladvīpa.
Having seen him, he traveled through the sky to his own desired island;
having beheld that auspicious place, he then saw the one named Muraśeṣa all around.
And he beheld the island where Murāsura had been;
and he arrived through the sky by way of the battlefield to engage in combat.
Having fashioned a formidable noose from the Vāruṇa kalpavallī,
the king bound the Daitya and then cast him into the ocean.
Just as someone accompanied by his life-breath might go to his own abode,
so then the king went forward to Kurujaṭa on the island.
Then, from there, Mānava saw Jaṭāyū all around him;
he proceeded ahead in his celestial chariot and beheld the island of Antarabījaka,
which is composed of coolness, where the people indeed have the faces of crocodiles.
And they were mostly seen by that king living in the water. ||27||
Then he traveled by means of a celestial chariot through the sky toward the southern direction;
there he beheld the earth, white and perfectly circular.
It possesses water-bearing channels covered with moss, beautiful and radiant;
there the earth consists of water, and embodied beings are white and luminous. (29)
All those who eat raw fish, who dwell in water upon the mountains, men and women alike, are shaped like fish and are always tolerant of water and mud. (2.44.30)
Drinking cool water, eating sugar-water,
and consuming moss and aquatic plants, they manage to survive.
There they dwell in houses constructed of water and stone,
possessing a radiance equal to the cool moon, and partaking of nectar produced from the waters.
Seeing such people, he beheld the southern pole star;
first [he saw] the land of Kārakī, and then he turned to look further.
From his position in the celestial chariot, the king beheld that circular earth.
The entire earth was made of silver and devoid of trees. ||34||
Where clouds are always present and the heat of the sun is not found, there are oceanic stones and minerals consisting of hailstones. (35)
Taste is indeed desired as nectar; it is watery and arises from hailstones.
Water consists of moss, water-weeds, aquatic leaves, and creepers. (36)
They are white in color with white fruits, resembling fragments of the moon;
their edible water-plants grow there, and their houses are made of water-stones.
The salty brine of the ocean becomes sweet sugar for waters;
even water-stones and tubers become edible foods for those humans through their happiness. (38)
Having observed all this, as well as the abode of Varuṇa, [he beheld] the place situated at the central point of the southern celestial sphere. (39)
Having looked [back], the king returned once more to the shore of the battlefield;
there he reached the region of Kampa, and then the city of Kaṭisara.
Having looked all around and subsequently at that region inhabited by Rākṣasas,
he went forward and beheld a place, a dwelling for maidens.
Then he saw before him the region of Kāṇākṣa;
and further ahead, he beheld that excellent land of Sagrīva.
Then he beheld a region free from mountains, consisting of water and rocks;
and he indeed saw that place where the enemy had gone, a region devoid of foes.
Then, having observed a region empty of summer and a region of foul odors,
he beheld the circular path of Saturn immediately after the fixed point (dhruvabindu).
Thus, as soon as he beholds that subterranean dwelling— cool and providing a mere refuge from the cold— he turns back from it.
At that moment, O Rādhikā, a certain man, resembling a white mountain, arrived from within the depths of the earth, traveling through the path of the sky. 46.

Possessing infinite vigor, he dwells within the interior of the cosmic egg; he is a householder with a family, white in complexion, clad in white garments, and endowed with the radiance of white light. ||47||
With white beard and white complexion, he held a mace made of white stone;
upon his head rested the clouds, and at his feet were the white mountains. (48)
That which has white moss upon its hips, thunder in its mouth, and whose sound proceeds pervading the southern pole; ||49||
His gait possesses the speed of lightning, his breath causes the ocean to tremble,
and his boisterous laughter returns after pervading the ends of the quarters.
And seeing him, Raṇaṅgama was seized by fear for a moment;
at that very instant, the white person called out to Raṇaṅgama.
"Come, come, O divine god, you who dwell in the sky! What fear indeed can you have of me, since you are supported by the wish-fulfilling creeper? (52)
Since the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa resides in your heart, you, such a great devotee, shine forth with power upon this earth. (53)

You are blessed, O King, for you have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord; though you are a mere mortal, by virtue of the vision of the Lord as your protector, you shine like a god yourself, for you have reached the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
Come, purify my own home, which is always perfumed by the excellent fragrance of the earth;
he who is constantly worshipped by me is indeed to be worshipped by you as well.
On the field of battle, the Lord of Lords was propitiated.
For I am a person born of the noble lineage of Śeṣa, dwelling here in the womb under the name of Lakṣmaṇa;
[I shall behold] the child Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa.
Together with all my kinsmen, I worship [him] eternally. ||56||
"Accept this unsurpassed hospitality prepared by me, and likewise grant me your vision.
I shall present these offerings worthy of worship; you ought to give them to Bālakṛṣṇa as well. (57)
Salutations, salutations to you, O devotee of my Lord; salutations, salutations to you, O knower of the Supreme Self.
Salutations, salutations to you, O devotee of the Supreme Lord; let there be salutations to you, the performer of great sacrifices. ||58||
Thus, O Rādhikā, having been well-honored by that Lakṣmaṇa and having gained confidence through his words, the warrior became steadfast on the field of battle.
Then Śrī Lakṣmaṇa assumed there the form of a human being—
gentle, handsome, inspiring confidence to his devotee, and adorned with a sectarian mark (tilaka).
Raṇaṅgama, with supreme devotion and intense emotion, bowed down with great affection to that Vaiṣṇava who was chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa while holding tulasī.
And Lakṣmaṇa said: "Behold here, for the sake of my confidence, the Lord Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa shining within my heart. (62)
In the midst of the battle, Raṇaṅgama beheld the Supreme Lord within his heart—
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, seated upon a lake of horses.
The Lord of Rādhā, the Master of Light, the Lord of Pāravatī, the most beautiful one,
the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of the Swan, and the glorious Joy of the Cowherds.
The Lord endowed with attributes, cherished by Kambharā, who delights his devotees, and adorned with divine bracelets, a crown, rings, and necklaces. (65)
He possessed a form of exquisite beauty, surpassing the splendor of ten million Cupids;
radiant and abiding in a gentle smile, he gazed upon the field of battle.
Having thus beheld his beloved Mādhava within his own heart,
the great devotee Raṇaṅgama regained his confidence once more.
Then, taking Lakṣmaṇa by the hand, he quickly caused him— who was a nāga in the form of a human being— to ascend the celestial chariot.
By that path shown by him, his own celestial chariot was driven until it reached Pṛthvīguptabindu, which lay beneath water, stones, and earth.
Near the mouth of the southern fixed celestial sphere,
there is a great opening through which one may indeed go into the interior of the earth.
It was circular, measuring one yojana, well-guarded by white serpents, with cool stone steps and protected by cool ramparts. ||71||
Following the path indicated by Lakṣmaṇa, the celestial chariot entered the interior of the cave in an instant, where shouts of victory then arose.
With the great roars of the gatekeepers, within the womb of the earth and in the intermediate space, amidst the brilliance of lightning-jewels and the radiant splendor of moonlight; 73.
Increased by maidens with parched grain offerings and honored with flowers and jewels,
the celestial chariot traveled through the intermediate space and descended upon the earth.
There indeed the earth is delightful, white, black, and pale;
and there are various medicinal herbs and trees beautifully adorned with fruit.
The abundance of the crops was seen to be golden-hued;
likewise, the rivers, streams, groves, and ponds were filled with water. (76)
Wells filled with nectar were beheld by him as he proceeded to the battlefield;
likewise, white and pale cows, as well as winged beings moving through the sky, were seen.
Others, assuming forms at will, were then like milch-cows yielding milk;
men and women were all beheld adorned with ornaments.
Resplendent like the moon, adorned with necklaces of jewels, cool as the moon, they all have eyes resembling lotus petals. ||79||
Handsome, with tawny eyes and red nails, lips, and palms;
all were clad in pure white garments, firm, and subsisted on white food.
Just as he beheld all these manifestations here on this portion of the earth, so too did that king behold them there. ||8.1||
The palaces were white in color, as were all the necessary implements; there were well-governed cities, mountains, and watery lands. (82)
Seeing that all the humans were white, he was filled with wonder;
then Lakṣmaṇa [steered] that celestial chariot toward the great city.
Where many gardens rich in flowers were shaken, and on all sides there were mansions and palaces resembling mountains. (84)
There, on that elevated portion of the ground, adorned with inner walls, was the palace of King Lakṣmaṇa, which resembled a mountain. (85)
Adorned with the marks of the name Lakṣmaṇa and graced by a banner in the sky,
that palace of a hundred stories shines forth as it was seen by Raṇaṃgama.
Then, O Rādhikā, the aerial chariot was brought down here into the garden courtyard by Lakṣmaṇa; indeed, musical instruments were played according to royal custom.
Victory shouts arose from the army protectors, and the capital, equal to heaven itself, was beheld by him as he proceeded to the field of battle. (88)
Having beheld a superhuman creation within the interior of the earth, Raṇaṅgama was struck with supreme wonder and rejoiced. (89)
Then Lakṣmaṇa led him into the assembly hall, the theater of battle,
where there were indeed one hundred queens and two thousand maidens.
Five thousand princes indeed attend upon Lakṣmaṇa;
seated by Lakṣmaṇa in the midst of the assembly on a sacred throne. ||91||
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa was installed in the temple of the gods;
the Blessed Hari was revealed in the form of a golden image. 92.
Then, for the sake of entering the field of battle, he offered him the highest *arghya* and *madhuparka*,
as well as the drink of immortality (*amṛta-pāna*) and excellent flower garlands and other gifts.
Then, by his command, one maiden took a flower garland and seated him there upon the auspicious throne. (94)
Having arrived, she beheld him, the auspicious refuge who had gone to the battlefield;
for the sake of a welcome, she placed a crescent-shaped mark of saffron and unbroken rice grains upon his forehead. (95)
She placed a flower garland upon his neck and took his hand;
she made a bouquet of fragrant flowers and prepared a fragrant unguent.
Seeing that youth, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu, red-complexioned, firm, and handsome, that maiden named Mālinī, overflowing with the vigor of youth, [was struck with wonder]. (97)
He was deluded in mind and considered the best [suitors] to be suitable;
then Lakṣmaṇa, having understood this, gave her to him who was going to battle.
Having obtained a devoted husband, she too rejoiced in her heart in every way;
then he spoke the mantra of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa to her. (99)
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Then Lakṣmaṇārya again joyfully [prostrated] before Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
With great affection, he remembered his own home, considering himself blessed;
at that moment, the Blessed Lord, the primordial Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, appeared there.
Having understood the true nature of his devotion, he became manifest before him,
appearing in the form of a divine youth and a treasury of all beauty.
Simultaneously, he appeared manifest in the assembly hall, resplendent with a brilliance exceeding that of a thousand suns, his every limb corresponding perfectly to his form.
Suddenly they all rose and bowed to the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
their eyes overwhelmed by his splendor, they stood for a moment like those deprived of sensation.
Having quickly offered his seat for the sake of the purity of his splendor, the Lord Hari accepted the worship performed by the noble Lakṣmaṇa with divine objects.
At that very moment, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, smiling joyfully, accepted the offered food, sweetmeats, water, and betel leaf.
Having said, "May it be well," and wishing for your welfare, prosperity, and eternal fortune, he quickly vanished while thousands of maidens were speaking [those words]. (1.07)
Seeing that Lord Hari, the innocent maidens chose him as their husband in their minds;
their father, knowing this intention, mentally offered them to Hari.
Then, on account of a pilgrimage,
that noble Lakṣmaṇa set out for the journey together with the princes, the maidens, and his mothers.
Having taken ten million jewels, gold, silver, and wealth,
as well as gems, rubies, and pearls, he boarded the aerial chariot Raṇaṅgama.
Having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, he comfortably ascended [the chariot],
which was a yojana long, expansive, and capable of moving at will by mere thought.
And Raṇaṅgama ascended the assembly hall,
which was highly meritorious and where the Blessed Lord himself resides, as it was suitable for his exit through the portal of the earth.
Having bowed down to the supreme Tīrtha, he became directly manifest; quickly departing from the region through the sky, he emerged from Bhūdvāra and reached Antārkivartula.
Having crossed that region of water and stones into the atmosphere,
that aerial chariot moved swiftly for a long distance over the ocean.
O Rādhikā, just as the sun arrives or the moon departs,
illuminating the quarters of the sky, they are beheld by those dwelling on land and in water.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Welcome by Lakṣmaṇārya to the Lord who, having traveled by celestial chariot from Raṇaṅgama to behold the Southern Dhruva, entered a subterranean opening in the middle of the circular Antarikṣa region, and the Departure of King Lakṣmaṇa along with his family for the journey to that chariot," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, that celestial chariot has departed toward the northern direction above the ocean, causing the entire circle of the wind to tremble.
Upon seeing that [being] resembling the moon, the oceanic waters were then agitated; in just a moment, however, that island consisting of Kurujaṭa appeared. (Re)
Having crossed over, he arrived at the island named Rūpyāyana;
likewise, he attacked the island situated nearby called Muraśeṣa.
But having heard this, the Daitya named Mātrāgaskara,
who was like a mountain, stood facing him together with his own mace.
Enraged and possessing the appearance of a barbarian, with the ocean reaching only to his waist,
he was the son of the Rākṣasī Mājjāmbikā, a devourer of timiṅgila fish.
Śrī Rādhikā said: How did this great Rākṣasa become an offender against his mother? What offense was committed by him against my mother? Tell me, O Mādhava. (6)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
In Saurāṣṭra, there was a virtuous servant of the Rākṣasī Talajā, known by the name Ajā; she was auspicious and capable of assuming any form at will.
She lived in the forest, dwelling in the wilderness; she provided food for the animals and gathered fruit, being beautiful and in the full bloom of youth.
Once, having gone into the great forest for the sake of food,
her course led by chance to the western Soma-tīrtha.
For there, seeing those beautiful and pure ascetics, she,
assuming a human form, approached them and joined with the ascetics.
One day he stayed there and heard a purifying discourse;
in that discourse, the spiritual reality concerning Rādhikā was revealed.
The Supreme Lord, the Supreme Soul, who is served by liberated beings with divine [forms] in the supreme abode, is the protector of both the insentient and the sentient. (12)
He is the treasury of all bliss and the vessel for the abundance of all happiness;
through the worship of Him by the name Nārāyaṇa, happiness shall arise.
He, indeed, is always pleased by devotion to the name Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, one should constantly and incessantly chant "Nārāyaṇa."
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Lord, you who are to be constantly glorified;
O Master of my life, O Giver of happiness, be the bestower of all prosperity. (15)
Thus properly distributed, it grants all that is desired:
women, happiness, great good fortune, sovereignty, grain, wealth, and so forth. (16)
They obtain a glorious and excellent husband, as well as sons, grandsons, and so forth; of this there is no doubt, nor do they fail to attain celestial chariots for their transport. (17)
The entire world is under his control, and he shines as a sovereign emperor;
for his kingdom indeed extends throughout the three worlds, and one who takes refuge in him shall be happy.
A wise man who desires the supreme heaven, endowed with the enjoyment of all desires, must perform service unto him.
By virtue of her support, supreme and constant good fortune increases;
even an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate, and even a maidservant may become a queen. (2.45.20)
By whom the earth was fashioned, and likewise by whom the water was created;
by whom fire exists, and by whom the wind was produced. ||21||
By him bodies were fashioned for them, by whom the self was sustained within those forms,
and by whom fruits of trees were produced here for their enjoyment.
By whom foods, sugar, milk, and flavors were created;
by whom the beautiful woman was made, and by whom indeed the man was fashioned. (23)
By whom the sense-faculties were created for the purpose of experience by embodied beings, by whom intelligence was bestowed, and by whom deliberation was fashioned. || 24 ||
By whom sleep and rest were brought to an end, by whom day and night [were transcended], by whom hunger and thirst were satisfied, and by whom Sarasvatī was made manifest. (25)
By him affection was made his son and daughter, and prosperity his wealth;
by him heaven was created, as were the earth, the stars, the sun, and the moon. ||26||
If one should worship Him by whom the oceans, the seasons, the clouds, and gold were created, He, the Supreme Lord, becomes gracious toward him. (27)
He constantly bestows and grants sovereignty, wealth, beloved ones, and happiness;
those seeking liberation worship this Lord of Śrī in many ways, again and again. (28)
Even those desiring worldly enjoyment worship this beloved Lord for their own sake;
yet, affection for Nārāyaṇa arises only through many births, like flowers [blooming] after many seasons.
The gods shall be full of moisture, while the other rākṣasas will be fond of wine and meat, intent on violence, and destroyers of others.
These people do not become happy, nor are they excessively lowly in causing suffering to others;
for there is no such thing as a "demon" (rākṣasa) or even a "god" (deva), other than one's own self.
Even though he is pure, that god is called a Rākṣasa by virtue of his karma;
the female body is always withered, a source of suffering, and subject to the control of others.
By taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the beautiful woman crosses over sin and suffering;
however, she should never commit a sinful act for the sake of nourishing her belly.
Indeed, this birth for the sake of liberation is not obtained again and again; how, then, could the sinful, animal-like activity be inferred there? (34)
Even if the self is sinful, from the moment it takes refuge in the Supreme Lord, from that very moment it becomes virtuous. || 35 ||
By hearing this discourse, his resolve shall become auspicious;
from that, through association with the virtuous, there shall arise the desire for knowledge that bestows liberation. (36)
Thereupon, his divine qualities of the nature of sattva indeed arise;
[he performs] righteous deeds, meritorious deeds, and auspicious deeds for the sake of others. (37)
From one's own nature, glory and fame arise and increase;
peace grows evermore, and the line of fortune shines forth. (38)
Benefiting others, generosity, truthfulness, and non-violence are the vows;
good conduct, contentment, purity, austerity, and service to the elderly [are the virtues]. (39)
Hearing of the Inner Controller, non-stealing, and likewise freedom from censure—
these indeed shall be his virtues, impelled by the lines of destiny.
Through them, prosperity, wealth, grain, home, field, excellent vehicles, family, sons, grandsons, and so forth—all this proceeds toward heaven. (41)
Eternal and supreme happiness is born in this world and in the next;
therefore, having obtained a human body, one should not become a Rākṣasa.
Through his actions, he subsequently becomes a Rākṣasa even in his body;
such a Rākṣasa in body and action is never liberated at any time. (43)
Even a Rākṣasa should abandon acts of violence augmented by injustice;
through that, his purity gradually arises, leading him toward the state of goodness (sattva). 44.
The body is purified by a sacred ford, and likewise by the company of the virtuous;
the inner self is purified by austerity, and the soul is thoroughly purified by its qualities. (45)
Having abandoned the demonic nature within his body and even in his mind, he will quickly become confident; thereafter, even his very self becomes purified.
Though eternally pure, he abandons the snare of association with the wicked and becomes purified;
by that means he subsequently becomes divine and indeed proceeds upon the path to liberation.
Therefore, having burned away one's sins, one should take refuge in the Guru;
through reliance upon the Guru, the attainment of Hari becomes constant. 48.
Therefore, whether a man or a woman, having abandoned sin, should take refuge in the Lord;
for [sin] committed over ten lifetimes indeed bestows a human body.
Indeed, the sin committed over a hundred lifetimes brings about a female body;
again there is sin, again rebirth, and for a woman, truly, there is the agony of hell.

Constantly burdened with excrement and urine, her function was always the discharge of excrement and urine; she possessed offspring that were excrement and urine, and she was menstruating with the very root of filth. ||51||
The womb is the receptacle for excrement and urine; it is a pit for excrement, urine, and the like.

How can one be liberated from sin if she does not worship the Lord?
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa must always be worshipped. (53)
As soon as knowledge has been received from the guru, one should take refuge in that very guru;

That which has been done while under the influence of passion becomes past once knowledge has arisen; thereafter, it leads only to dispassion. Having abandoned what is to be lamented, one should take refuge in the auspicious. //55//
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā!
He who constantly recites this mantra is never subject to sin. (56)
He who wears a garland of tulasī is liberated from all sins;
he who serves the best of holy men is always destined for liberation.
He who worships Śrī Hari attains eternal bliss;
one should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and even now what belongs to this very moment.
One should not let time pass by without discerning what task remains to be done;

That is true gain which is made when the time is right for the sake of one's own welfare;

Thus, at all times— midday, evening, and at every moment of the night—
human beings and others die and are born again and again, like the sparrows.
While still living, they behold in the womb the destruction arising from death;
or the destruction occurring in the month of birth, or total ruin within a year.
In childhood it meets with destruction; in youth, dissolution; in adolescence and manhood, decay;
and in old age, in solitude, it perishes. Once destroyed, nothing whatsoever remains.
When [the body] is lost, how could there be spiritual welfare? One should achieve it while still alive—[attaining] the cessation of birth, death, and a life free from mortality. (64)
May the highly fortunate ones acquire [the fruit of] time and abandon death;

People are intent solely on their own self-interest and act as obstacles to the next world; having displayed false affection, they are always destroyers of one's welfare.

A brother should offer light for Hari; a purified son should deliver [his ancestors];

If these qualities do not exist in them, then those who perceive such affection are seeing falsely; in this world, every kind of relationship results ultimately in deception. (69)
Having understood that everything is thus false and likewise yields undesirable results, and having reflected upon this, one should take refuge in Hari and worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (2.45.70)
By serving Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, with one’s body, mind, speech, actions, and affection, one shall attain the ultimate goal. 7.1.
O Rādhā, having heard this and other such stories, Mānājārā, desiring liberation, thereafter took refuge in Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. ||72||
Having established Somanātha as a supreme sacred site (tīrtha), she then became a devotee;

Having thus received this mantra, she then departed for her own abode. ||74||
And she constantly performs the service of a maidservant to Talājā;

She wandered about fearlessly, constantly chanting the name [of the Lord].

The ocean-dwelling Rākṣasa named Jhañjhīvara led King Murālaya to a place two thousand krośas away from the abode of Murā in the southwest.

at that time, the kingdom of Mura alone remained small, spanning only three islands. ||78||
Then King Sākṣīvara, along with his subjects, led that unborn one from his own kingdom toward the western shore of the earth’s ocean amidst great festivities. ||79||
A son was born to her, a Daitya who attained full youth at the very moment of his birth;
he could travel at will and move through the sky, and he possessed knowledge of illusions, houses, and other such things.
He brings about the destruction of all, hates everyone, increases the suffering of the world, and is constantly a source of anxiety; he shows no respect for the words of his mother or father. (8.1)
The abductor of another's daughter resorted to his own rakshasa nature;
he was a stealer of others' wealth, delighting in battle and constantly engaged in war.
Once, he forcibly brought the daughter of the Naga king from the waters of the ocean and made her his own wife. 83.
Living on land while dwelling in water indeed gave rise to disease;
she was seized by illness, weakened, overcome by fever, and afflicted with consumption.
Thus, while she was not taking pleasure [in the act], he killed her like a sacrificial animal;
at that time, she raised a cry of reproach and her mother wailed aloud.
Hearing this, Mīja arrived with a heart full of compassion;
she instructed her own son, saying, "O son, do not commit violence. (86)
A weak woman has no strength, especially one who is ill;
she is beaten while powerless, and that will bring you no good fortune. (87)
Deceiving the husband by the wife, likewise striking him out of anger, and forcibly engaging in sexual enjoyment, destroy the husband's longevity. (88)
O son, one must never go [to another man] when a woman is pregnant, ill, exhausted, menstruating, or devoid of blood.
In departing prematurely, there is loss and certainly no gain at all;
since one's wife is one's own limb and one's very self, how could a wise man cause her pain? (2.45.90)
Practice non-violence and purity; protect compassion for the sake of happiness indeed.
Abide in truth and non-stealing; remain steadfast in your vow for the sake of happiness indeed.
Proceed toward virtue, moral conduct, contentment, observance of rules, and self-restraint;
become a devotee of the Supreme Lord, be full of faith, and renounce the objects of the senses.
When the self is obscured by sins, then it has attained the state of a rākṣasa;
O son, the state of being a rākṣasa is clearly defined as causing suffering to others and to oneself. (93)
The consumption of liquor and meat is forbidden by worldly ethics; it is merely for the protection of the self.
Ethics consist of eating pure food and conducting oneself with the satisfaction of others. 94.
For that vow and the practice of peace are indeed what bestow divinity;
therefore, my son, become divine and do not resort to the qualities of the asuras.
Once the body has died, there will never again be the attainment of auspiciousness;
therefore, accomplish that by which there may be welfare in the next world. (96)
Worship Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who is without beginning and who resides within one's own self;
for I have heard His story in the past, and because of that, I am always happy. (97)
"O son, I am fully endowed with the prosperity and abundance of sovereignty; you, having performed your duties through statesmanship, should increase your eternal merit. (98)
Thus commanded by his mother, the evil-minded Rākṣasa took up a staff in anger and struck her as well.
Thus, the mother is constantly beaten by her son; likewise, the wife is repeatedly struck, being regarded as an enemy. (2.45.100)
Indeed, sugar-water does not impart sweetness to a neem tree;
even a well-spoken instruction turns to turbidity when placed in an unworthy vessel.
The mother of the Water-Daughter (Lakṣmī) always takes her side;
therefore, the Rākṣasa constantly strikes his own mother.
Then, although he was awakened by Janaka, he did not accept his instruction; instead, he prepared to strike Janaka.
On one occasion, that man devoid of merit bound his mother and wife very firmly with two ropes and threw them into the ocean.
Then the self-effulgent Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, being remembered by Mātṛ,
arrived there quickly and protected her two hands.
Having rescued both his mother and his daughter-in-law, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa took his devotees upon his own Garuḍa and delivered them back to their home.
Just then, Jhañjhīvara, who had gone to another country, returned;
having seen and heard the news, he fell into unbearable anger.
Then, having summoned his brother Muraśeṣa, he brought him there;
the brother went to inform the son in order to awaken him.
He behaved with such misconduct toward his brother;
thereupon Muraśeṣa, Jhaṃjhīvara, and their followers became enraged.
Considering him wicked and deserving of death, they prepared to kill him, thinking:
"This man is a traitor to his mother, a villain, and one who harbors hatred toward his father and others."
Fleeing from the fear of death, he ran into the midst of the waters of the ocean;
there, indeed, his enemies assailed that son-in-law.
All the people living on the island, being cruel, wicked,
and unjust, cast him upon the island and, out of rage, slaughtered him like an animal.
Gathering together with their fathers and others, those fierce beings struck the Daitya;
yet, out of compassion, those people there on the island abandoned him.
Having been exiled there, he, who was named Mātrāgaskara, humbly took up residence on the island where he lived.
He too, though powerful, by means of great force and through unrighteousness, failed to establish his own kingdom; therefore, he became an island in the midst of the ocean.
He became famous in the world by the very name Mātrāgaskara;
indeed, the kingdom of Jhaṃjhīvāra came to be known by the name Jhaṃjhīvāra. || 116 ||
And Māñjā, along with her daughter-in-law, was protected by Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
that devotee attained fame through the power of Nārāyaṇa. || 1.17 ||
From that time on, she became famous by the name Māñjāmbikā,
and the royal territory was likewise named Māñjāmbikā after her.
A temple exists there by her name, and the Goddess shines forth therein;
Daityas, Mlecchas, Rākṣasas, and Dānavas worship her.
Thus has been described, O Rādhā, the deed of this transgressor against his mother;
this Daitya, a violator of his mother, [ascended] his celestial chariot for the field of battle.
Accompanied by the noble family of Lakṣmaṇa, he obstructed [the path] in the sky;
having let out a loud laugh again and again, he prepared to fight.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Evil Conduct of the Rākṣasa Mātrāgaskara, who obstructed [the path] by beating his own sister, mother, and others, as well as the Protection of Māṃjāmbikā along with her daughter-in-law, who had been cast into the ocean, by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; I shall tell you what happened afterwards.
At that time, he who had committed an offense against his mother paralyzed the celestial chariot in the sky.
Standing in the presence of the noble Lakṣmaṇa, who was ready for battle,
he intended to conquer those two with his mace and bring their celestial chariot under his own control.
Intoxicated with pride, he uttered many roars;
by him the clouds were made to fall, and the waters of the ocean were agitated.
Even those situated at a distance of a thousand yojanas felt fear;
the earth trembled, and the wind caused the celestial chariot to shake.
Then the maidens and the youths were seized with terror for a moment;
but then this mighty devotee of the Lord, Raṇaṅgama, [appeared]. || 5 ||
He consoled them all and remembered Bālakṛṣṇa;
immediately thereafter, Hari appeared there upon the celestial chariot.
"Engage in battle; victory shall be yours," he said, and then he vanished.
At that moment, all those traveling in celestial chariots were filled with great courage.
Then the asura spoke again: "O sky-faring bird of the celestial chariot, either give me battle, or take your chariot and go to your own home."
The warrior said to him, "O hero, I grant you battle;
I shall give you a wrestling match, a mace-duel, and an arrow-duel."
"I shall grant you a battle with weapons, a battle with spells, or a battle of life and death.
Having said "Om," that Rākṣasa [struck] him, who was advancing to the fray, with his mace.
Then, leaping up from the battlefield and striking the mace with his feet, the warrior rushed forward and struck him with great force as he stood in his celestial chariot.
Then, as it was falling downward, he caught that mace with his two arms;
having seized that mace weighing a hundred bhāras, the king, who moves through the battlefield, [stood firm]. || 12 ||
Having become like a great mountain in the sky, he struck him in the heart;
then the Rākṣasa, leaping up from the path of the sky, [caught] her as she was falling.
Just as he was about to seize it with his hand on the field of battle,
another mace, weighing a hundred bhāras and endowed with fire, was hurled at him.
Having struck him on the top of his shoulder, she broke his neck and collarbone;
then, becoming enraged, he became a great mountain weighing a thousand *bhāras*.
Grasping his mace, he hurled it with great velocity at Raṇaga;
but Raṇaga, having become a massive mountain weighing a thousand bhāras, [received it].
And in another moment, the powerful one seized a mace produced from the Kalpavallī creeper and shattered it into a hundred pieces as it was falling upon him.
Then Mātrāgaskara, beholding this wonder, was filled with amazement;
enraged, he rushed toward the one who had gone to battle and seized him with his two arms.
And Raṇaga assumed a massive form four times [his usual size];
he then seized the neck of the Rākṣasa with his two arms like a noose.
Then the Rākṣasa, having assumed a subtle form, also withdrew;
for a moment, he remained fearlessly stationed in the sky above the battlefield.
At that moment, the Daitya, seizing a great spear from the path of the sky,
hurled it, blazing with fire, at the head of Raṇaṅgama.
Then Raṇaṅgama quickly drew back his own spear, which was capable of pulling out iron,
and hurled it into the belly of the asura.
Then, having pierced the intestines, it became firmly lodged there;
the powerful Asura [pierced] his split belly with chains and other weapons.
Having bound [his opponent] and discharged his power (śakti), he fell into a swoon for a moment;
then, remaining in the sky itself, he [discharged] a long arrow with the mantra of lightning.
Having consecrated it with mantras, he dispatched it to the battlefield to destroy [the enemy];
[the opponent], having gone to the battle, sent forth a thunderbolt born from the Kalpalatā.
Having destroyed the arrow, it entered the heart of the Daitya;
the Daitya fell from the sky into the waters of the ocean, having lost consciousness. ||26||
The ocean reached up to his waist as he was overcome by fainting;
then, having regained some coolness, he subsequently recovered from his swoon.
With his face bowed down in shame, he reproached himself;
then, indeed, he conjured up a terrible Rākṣasa illusion.
Then the Daitya, having become a thousandfold, struck the army on the battlefield from all sides with arrows, clubs, and mallets.
With maces, clubs, spears, javelins, stones, and the like; with pikes, swords, and weapons of many forms.
Then, by the power of the Kalpalatā, he vanished from the midst of the battlefield in an instant and appeared standing at the front of the celestial chariot.
Then the Daitya, overcome with rage, abandoned his position on the battlefield and,
in order to seize [her], stretched out his hands toward the celestial chariot.
Indeed, his two hands were burned by the fire arising from the Kalpalatā;
with his hands thus scorched, the asura was unable to seize the vehicle.
But the haughty one was unable to seize even his weapons;
the mountain became Jvālāmukha, overwhelmed by a forest fire.
Nevertheless, he indeed set his mind upon burning the battlefield;
yet the Kalpalatā, raining down nectar, protected the warrior on the field of battle and his celestial chariot.
And he protected himself and those situated in the celestial chariot with streams of nectar;
even as the Asura blazed there, the chariot was not burned at all. (36)
For his own protection, Lakṣmaṇa recited benedictory prayers—those meritorious rites of auspiciousness that are the most excellent of all blessings. ||37||
Oṃ! May Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, grant us well-being.
May Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Brahmā—the Infallible One—grant us well-being. (38)
May Śaṅkara, joined by Śivā, grant us well-being;
as well as the Lords, the Guardians of the World, the Planets, and the Great Sages. (39)
May the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the hosts of Sādhyas and Maruts, the fires, the suns,
the Yakṣas, the Vasus, and the Kinnaras and others grant you well-being.
The Nāgas, Suparṇas, rivers, lakes, and likewise the oceans;
the Sudarśana discus, the mantras, and the weapons of Hari; ||41||
May the devotees and the ancestors, the liberated souls, and the powers such as Rādhā and Ramā, as well as the radiant elements beginning with fire, bestow well-being upon you. (42)
May there be well-being for those with two feet and also for those with four;
may there be well-being for us from those with many feet, and may there be freedom from illness for those who have no feet. 43.
May there be well-being for the celestial chariot, and may there be well-being for him who mounts it;
may there be auspiciousness for the inhabitants of the celestial realms, and may there also be well-being and prosperity. (44)
May there be well-being from those with flaming mouths and also from those with illusory flames;
likewise, may the Inner Self grant us well-being from the Asuras. (45)
Thus, at that place, Lakṣmaṇa remembered Hari, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, who bestows well-being and auspiciousness. (46)
Bālakṛṣṇa appeared visibly on Mount Analaparvata, smiling and saying,
"May there be peace, coolness, and freedom from disease for your celestial chariot."
For the sake of reducing the Asura to ashes, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa commanded his own attendant, a personification of great splendor.
That person of great splendor forcibly set ablaze the Dānava Jvālāmukha, just as fire consumes a moth.
The Blessed One himself protected the celestial chariot along with the food;
he then reduced the Daitya to ashes within a great fire of flames.
At that time, the region of ashes belonging to the Daitya named Mātrāgaskara on that island extended for ten yojanas.
Thus, having destroyed the Daitya Surāṣṭraka with their celestial chariot, Śrīhari, Lakṣmaṇa, Āryaraṇaṅgama, and the others returned. 52.
Having beheld the Aśvapaṭṭa lake in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, as well as Lomaśa and the city resembling heaven; ||53||
Accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, they descended from the sky to the earth with ease;
having first bowed to Lomaśa, they went to the cowherd’s dwelling.
There, they were honored with joy by their father Bālakṛṣṇa and also by their mother Kambharā; being well-worshiped, they attained great delight.
Then Lakṣmaṇa and the others were offered seats, provided with lodging, given food and rest, and engaged in conversation until they had learned all the news.
They came to Kambharā’s house with offerings to worship the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. 57.
By his will, the infant Hari shone upon the lion-throne;
first, his two feet, which grant happiness, were bathed with waters of nectar.
All those maidens of divine form worshipped Śrī Hari;
and by the command of Lakṣmaṇa, they partook of the nectar of His feet. 59.
Garlands of flowers, necklaces of jewels, as well as strings of pearls;
crowns, earrings, swords, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, and diamonds.
They presented bracelets, waist-bands, ornaments, and garments;
they also offered fruits, drinks of nectar, vessels, and saffron.
They gave various articles to that Bālakṛṣṇa;
likewise, they performed the ārārtrika rite, circumambulated him, and offered salutations.
Placing their feet upon their chests, they attained supreme peace;
thus, having fully honored the Lord of Śrī, the maidens held him within their hearts.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved, entered into their hearts;
and Mādhava drew away the hearts of them all toward Himself.
Having understood the disposition of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa toward his beloved Kṛṣṇa,
he gave those women to Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He gave her a dowry consisting of many jewels and other riches, and she attained the fulfillment of her purpose;
thereafter, all the princes performed worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Then the noble Lakṣmaṇa performed worship dedicated to the Supreme Lord;
Raṇaṅgama and Mālinī likewise performed the worship of Hari.
Then they performed the worship of the auspicious Lakṣmī Kambharā;
they performed the divine adoration of the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa.
They went to the brahmin Śrī Lomaśa and performed his worship;
Bālakṛṣṇa gave the girls to Lomaśa for protection.
Lomaśa protected the wives of Kṛṣṇa, who were devoted to Viṣṇu, in his own hermitage;
thus they all attained fulfillment in the presence of Hari.
They experienced exceeding joy through the hospitality of food and drink;
then, at dawn on the full moon of Māgha, they performed the ritual for the sacred ford.
He gave divine gifts, including gold, jewels, and garments;
then, having granted an exemption, Lakṣmaṇa returned to his own kingdom.
And then Raṇaṅgama desired to go; Lomaśa said to him: "This great yogi even gives [this] to the Kumāras."
"O King, cause the mantra that grants liberation to be bestowed upon them in his presence.
Thereupon, the noble Lakṣmaṇa caused the mantra to be given to his sons.
Lomaśa, having remembered Śrī Hari, [addressed] the five hundred youths:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! (75)
Having fully prepared them, purified by mantras, and adorned with garlands of *tulasī*,
he bestowed upon them divine knowledge that brings about the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Sons, listen: this world is considered to be born from the bondage of karma;
service to the virtuous is auspicious action, and the worship of Śrī Hari is auspicious.
The highest good for oneself is auspicious and supreme; the destruction of craving is the ultimate happiness.
The strength of the body, senses, and so forth is considered to be what gives rise to latent impressions (vāsanā). //78//
When knowledge is predominant, that which consists of restraint arises as secondary;
for yogis, such restraint brings about the burning away of latent impressions (vāsanās). //79//
The strength of her body and senses becomes of no consequence;
the body is female, yet the life-force dwelling within it becomes a man as well. (2.46.80)
The living soul (jīva) experiences the body, and its enjoyment consists in the perception of pleasure and pain;
therefore, the soul must in every way be understood as being of the nature of Brahman. 8.1
And the taking of refuge in the Supreme Brahman is considered that which brings about his state of being Brahman;
for here, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself abides as the Supreme Brahman. (82)
Union with Him has now arisen for you; nothing further remains to be done.
For it is only through the merits accumulated over ten million births that this Kṛṣṇa is attained. (83)
Through association with the virtuous here, the attainment of that [state] arises swiftly;
for this king, Raṇaṅgama, is a friend of yours in the form of a holy man. (84)

therefore, O sinless ones, cultivate devotion toward this Nārāyaṇa.
O sinless ones, practice therein that state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya) which consists of the total surrender of all things;
for without direct perception, the goals of human life cannot be accomplished here. 86.
The supreme goal of human life has been accomplished for you through the yoga of direct perception—those whose devotion to Kṛṣṇa is supreme, and who regard the Guru as they do Kṛṣṇa himself. (87)
For them, all goals of human endeavor are indeed accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, those knowers of Brahman depart for the supreme state.
Complete surrender, trust, magnanimity, devotion, mindfulness, and affection for one's own [teacher]—these six bestow the Supreme Brahman. (89)
Peace, faith, freedom from craving, absence of agitation, fearless abiding, and independence—these six bestow great bliss. (2.46.90)
Saluting the elders, service, enthusiasm, the nature of duty to be performed, resorting to justice, freedom from possessiveness, and gentleness. (9.1)
These six, in every respect, increase the merit of people in the world:
enduring all forms of pain and abandoning the conceit of a body. (92)
Not seeking after fame and the like, practicing non-possessiveness, being free from longing for anything whatsoever, and the total abandonment of passionate activity. ||93||
These six, in every way, increase liberation while living in this world: the constant vision of the gods, as well as the vision of discernment; ||94||
The vision of the focal point, likewise the vision of the insignificant, the vision of the unobstructed, and the vision of the vision itself. (95)

These six are the givers of liberation and likewise the bestowers of victory; they are those without desire, those without self-interest, those with interest in their own selves, and those who act for the sake of others. (96)
Those who have not lost their virtuous conduct, those who are wise, and those six who are indeed free from darkness—namely, those who grasp only virtues and those who bestow only virtues. (97)
Those who practice with a vision of qualities engage others in those very qualities;
and those who rejoice in the knowledge of reality remain indifferent toward what is other than the qualities.
These six, being stainless,
exist within bodies as the states of the embryo, childhood, youth, old age, and likewise death.
Those for whom the state of being a ghost is equal [to other states] are liberated, though devoid of qualities.
He whose body, home, wealth, field, ornaments, clothing, and food—
these six— are treated like guests, indeed has his feet established in the Imperishable.
A woman [is considered] a son; a father, a mother, a daughter, a female slave, cattle, and so forth [are likewise]. || 101 ||
Those men who have acted here for the sake of the virtuous and for the sake of the Lord possess two feet within the Lord’s abode of imperishable syllables.
Whatever is dear to oneself for one's own sake, that indeed one should give for the sake of the virtuous;
he who gives life, he who gives a husband, and he who gives a beloved wife, partakes in liberation. (103)
One may give away wealth for one’s own sake; one may give away a beloved wife for one’s own sake;
one may give away a kingdom for one’s own sake; but for the sake of liberation, one should surrender everything.
Thus instructed by Lomaśa, the princes regained their sight;
endowed with divine knowledge, they prostrated before Lomaśa.
Having bowed down to all her sisters and addressed them with words full of affection,
she ascended the celestial chariot together with her father and the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa.
They joyfully went to the city of Koṭīnāra, which belongs to Rāṇaṅgama,
and likewise visited the holy site of Someśvara with great devotion.
Having accepted the worship offered on the field of battle,
they all traveled together by celestial chariot through the path of the sky to the orb of the setting sun.
Having caused them to enter the womb of the earth and having secured that kingdom,
the warrior returned once more to his own city of Koṭīnāra by means of a celestial chariot.
Thus, O Rādhā, has been described the conduct of the devotees of the Lord,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is most excellent, and brings auspiciousness to both the listener and the speaker.

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Raṇaṅgama and Mātrāgaskara, the Victory of Raṇaṅgama, the Arrival at Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Worship of the Lord, and the Offering of Two Thousand Maidens by Lakṣmaṇa," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to how Lomaśa truly instructed the two thousand maidens who were dear to Lord Hari. || 1 ||
Wealth is momentary, the mind is momentary, and the life of even a hero is momentary;
even volitions are momentary, but the Lord Hari is eternal.
The self is said to be his home, and Hari resides within that very self;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the Lord of the house, the protector, and indeed the master.
Water was created, and from that came the embryo (kalala), then the stage of the karkandhu fruit, then the peśī, then the puttala, and finally, by him, the body with fully formed limbs was fashioned.
O sons, childhood and youth were created by him alone;
likewise, old age, separation, and death were created by him.
Indeed, one who has entered the realm of the measurable should take refuge in the Mother of all created things;
then, through union with the immeasurable, the self itself becomes immeasurable.
O sons, he who dwells within your hearts and shines forth there is seen as immeasurable, yet like something measurable, just as to a child.
He indeed is to be served, He indeed is to be worshipped, and He indeed is to be meditated upon incessantly;
He who has been attained is the very goal to be attained, and nothing remains to be attained.
One should strive to attain eternal liberation by means of this impermanent body;
and one should propitiate the beloved Kṛṣṇa through these transient actions.
Vow is Kṛṣṇa, chanting is Kṛṣṇa; one should perform charity for Kṛṣṇa.
Austerity is service to Hari alone; restraint and discipline are directed toward Hari. (2.47.10)
The sacrifice is the offering of everything to Kṛṣṇa; it is indeed that eternal wealth.
Samādhi is the state of relishing Kṛṣṇa; yoga is union with Kṛṣṇa. || 11 ||
Worshiping Him, conversing with Him, chanting His praises, reciting His qualities, beholding Him directly, touching Him, and uniting with Him—[these are the means]. (12)
Following his will is considered both restraint and the giver of liberation;
his favor, O sons, is eternal merit and nothing else. (13)
One should indeed perform the hearing and the reflection upon Hari;
one should perform the ritual sleep there and always the ritual awakening for Hari.
That in which yogis delight is indeed Rāma; for those who are weary, this is true rest (virāma), while any other rest is meaningless. 15.
O beautiful daughters, here Hari eternally relishes the aesthetic flavor (rasa) for the sake of those who possess such taste; apart from that, any other tasting is utterly meaningless.
In the fifth year, she should in every way be treated as a daughter;
in the tenth year, she should in every way be treated as a female disciple.
Then, within fourteen years, they shall become maidens;
thereafter, they shall become wives to the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In this regard, O sons, listen to the true meaning of being a daughter and a disciple, as well as the appropriate state of being a maiden and the meaningful state of being a wife. (19)
She is celebrated here as "Putrī" because she protects one from the hell named Pūya;
she is a disciple who removes remaining sins, for she indeed removes the sin from the head.
After five years, the sin committed by her is transferred to the heads of her parents; however, that which occurred prior to her fifth year does not belong to them. (2.1)
The thread, myself as Gāyatrī, and the gift—that girl who [bestows these] is called Kumārikā.
She who provides the thread (the sacred thread), Gāyatrī, and the knowledge born of reality is proclaimed as Kumārikā. (22)
She is said to be one who has "bathed after knowledge," and she alone is said to be a "brahmacāriṇī. 23.
She who leads the husband into the womb as the very self of the embryo is the wife;
she who is led [to him] by the duty of a husband is the beloved wife. 24.
Listen also to the names of the hells, which indeed cause such terror for a childless couple regarding their state of existence. (25)
That suffering and even that first hell dissolve upon having offspring;
likewise, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and the libation of water for the ancestors [are fulfilled]. (26)
Everything performed for the sake of those without offspring arises lukewarm;
that suffering, to be experienced by the ancestors, is called the second hell. (27)
But when the ancestors have offspring, that suffering of theirs indeed dissolves;
for in a childless household, there are neither sacred rites nor festivals. (28)
The first sixteen [days] do not arise, nor are the deities satisfied;
the days beginning with the sixth are not worshipped, and there are no offerings. (29)
This suffering of the deities, which obstructs merit, is declared to be the third hell; it ceases upon having offspring. (2.47.30)
For one who is childless, prosperity is devoid of lineage and heirs;
fortune, stripped of trust, is joyless and lacks all enthusiasm. (3.1)
This fourth hell, which obstructs the fortune of wealth and happiness, is said to cease upon the birth of offspring.
In a house without offspring, there is neither a son-in-law nor likewise a daughter-in-law;
there is no marriage pavilion, no ruby pillar, and no circumambulation of the sacred fire.
The Gārhapatya fire, the deity of that limb, would surely not be pleased;
indeed, this suffering of sacrifice obstructs the expansion of one's lineage.
This is declared to be the fifth hell, which ceases upon having offspring.
In a house where there is no offspring, there is not even the slightest fruit of the law of desire.
There is no fruit from the seasonal rites, nor is there any fruit from gifts given during the fertile period;
the destruction of the seed is fruitless and becomes a producer of sin.
Sin brings about suffering and obstructs the goals of human life;
that is declared to be the sixth hell, which ceases upon having offspring.
Furthermore, guests do not find satisfaction in a house that is childless.
In the morning, men do not see the face of one who is childless. ||38||
Those who possess sons do not desire to dwell on the outskirts where there are no children;
for this is indeed a human misery that obstructs the respect of the people. (39)
The seventh hell has been described; it ceases upon having offspring. A childless couple, though beloved by each other, are as utterly contemptible as two ghosts.
Even while living, those two are as good as dead; no distinction exists here for those whose funeral rites (aurdhvadaihika) are performed by the hand of another at the time of death. ||41||
That which does not lead to rebirth and which obstructs the path to the realm of hungry ghosts is declared to be the eighth hell; it ceases upon the attainment of offspring.
Understand that these faults exist in a house without offspring:
the entry of others there and the service of sinners. (43)
Harshness consists in the useless acquisition of wealth through the practice of charity and other such dharmas;
it is a state of constant discontent that brings about the destruction of existence and prosperity. (44)
The falling away from one's own duties, killing, fear, even eating only sweet foods, as well as false accusations and the like; 45.
Cultivating another man's wife, greed, as well as covetousness, censuring those who have sons, and transgressing against the disciplined; ||46||
The destruction of the conduct of the learned, the abolition of virtuous rites and the like, the absence of purificatory sacraments, and rejoicing at the ruin of others. (47)
The loss of virtue, wealth, and pleasure; the remoteness from liberation;
and the state of being a threat to all—this is declared to lead to hell. (48)
Constantly surrounded by these hells named after men, a person who is childless indeed experiences those terrible hells. (49)
Offspring utterly destroys the terrible hell;
for this reason, heaven is considered to consist of sons and daughters.
The disciple and the female disciple indeed remove sins;
for example, one should become a disciple, a slave, a servant, or an attendant to those who are disciplined. ||5 1 ||
Or else, whether she be a disciple, a friend, a maidservant, a servant, or likewise an attendant; and he who assists those who are disciplined or venerable teachers—both of them [attain this]. (52)
Service to the gods, service to the ancestors, service to the sages, and even service to guests—these are all interrupted in times of calamity, except for service rendered to a disciple. (53)
That obstacle is said to be caused by the evildoer; therefore, the disciple should indeed deliver [the teacher].
But for one who is not a householder and is devoid of a disciple... (54)
Indeed, in this world, no undertakings whatsoever succeed; for that leads to hell.
[Yet] knowledge, the arts, skill, mantra, and the eternal way remain. 95.
Instruction, as well as the sequence, the method, the lineage, and even the commonality of nature—all that dissolves without a disciple. (56)
The destruction of that [knowledge] is said to lead to hell; it is averted by being under the guidance of a teacher. A disciple is joined with wisdom, but a son is joined with the inheritance. (57)
A wife who performs half the work is the destroyer of hell;
without a wife, there is no standing anywhere, even in respected homes and such.
There is no trust, no refuge, and no peace; for that is indeed hell.
There is no fire-oblation or the like, nor is there purification; that sin leads eternally to hell. (59)
In this world there is no success whatsoever, nor indeed in the next; that hell which is visible everywhere ceases upon becoming her co-wife.
Ignorance is declared to be hell; it is the lack of knowledge regarding all that is to be given.
However, among those who observe celibacy from their youth, it perishes through the possession of true knowledge.
This saṃsāra has been fashioned in such a way that, without assistance,
no task whatsoever can be accomplished here, whether among the social classes (varṇas) or even within the stages of life (āśramas).
For lack of assistance leads to hell, since it causes the failure of one's purpose;
whereas with assistance, it leads to heaven, since it brings about the accomplishment of one's purpose.
For in times of many tasks, a son is a helper; in times of many tasks, a disciple is a helper; and in times of many tasks, a wife is a helper who provides protection from hell. (64)
Whatever various kinds of evil there may be—whether physical, verbal, or mental, whether born of one's own nature, or committed without assistance—[all that I confess]. (65)
All that [merit] goes to waste through sons, disciples, beloved ones, and so forth;
therefore, a wise person should indeed appoint both a son and a disciple.
The heirs and the six types of kinsmen, as well as the six classes of progeny, have been proclaimed.
Thus, three disciples and three wives are proclaimed;
likewise, three husbands are mentioned as being bound by their respective actions.
Listen now to the daughters here; I shall describe them to you in brief. (67–68)
The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the given son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the son received—these six are heirs and kinsmen. (69)
While these six exist, there is the discharge of debts, the maintenance of the family estate, and the performance of religious rites;
the renown of the lineage, sustenance within the clan, social standing, and the expansion of the family line.
Among them, the legitimate son (aurasa), born of one’s own self, is like a reflection of one’s own soul.
And he who is begotten by another man on the wife with the [husband's] permission is the *kṣetraja* son. ||7.1||
He who is given by his mother and father is indeed proclaimed as the *dattaka* (given son).

He who considers the son of a friend or others to be his own son is the *kṛtrima* (artificially adopted son). But he whose birth in the house is not known by anyone is the *gūḍhaja* (secret-born son). ||72||
For that which is brought from the outside is indeed said to be "brought. || 73 ||

The son of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son received with a bride (sahoḍha), the purchased son (krīta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the self-given son (svayaṃdatta), and the son born of a woman of a lower caste (nimnavarṇaja)—these are merely bearers of names.
The son born of an unmarried girl is a kānīna; one conceived while pregnant and delivered after marriage is a sahoḍhaja.
One who is acquired for a price is indeed a purchased husband; one who is taken from another wife is a *punarbhava*. || 75 ||
A girl who, though already given to one man, is given again to another, is called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); the son born of her is a *paunarbhava*.

One who arrives of his own accord during a famine or similar crisis, or one who has been abandoned in the forest by himself, or one who has reached the forest without a protector, is declared to be a *svayamdatta* (self-given) slave. || 77 ||

A man of the highest caste born from a woman of a lower caste, or one of a lower caste [born] from a woman of a higher caste—among these, there is no mention whatsoever of debts, funeral offerings, or matters pertaining to lineage. (78)
The three types of disciples, the initiated, the servant, and the laborer—these are the heirs therein, as is whoever has made their livelihood their own. (79)

Wives are of three kinds: those married according to the law, those remarried, and those kept in secret; in legal proceedings, they are respectively considered superior, middling, and inferior. (2.47.80)
The husband, the married paramour, and likewise the paramour who has attained [the wife]—these are, respectively, the superior, the middling, and the inferior in legal proceedings. (8.1)
Instruction and the sacrificial thread should be given to them alone;
furthermore, the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) should be performed in order to eliminate their childlessness.
Just as heirs and kinsmen are of such a nature, so too are those related through kinship;
and just as sons born of unmarried women and others are of such a nature, so too are daughters. ||83||
Just as there are three types of male disciples, so too there are three types of female disciples; and within that context, there is also a practice that is superior, middling, and inferior. (84)
For here, by virtue of the mantra, you ladies become my female disciples;
likewise, the wives and daughters-in-law of the disciples also become vessels of knowledge. (85)
Therefore, knowledge consisting of the inheritance must be bestowed by me;
indeed, the inheritance must be received from the Guru by millions of disciples. ||86||
Knowledge, liberation, as well as devotion, service, worship of the gods and so forth, self-yoga, attainment of Hari, merit, and the visiting of sacred fords; ||87||
Thus, these shares of inheritance indeed purify the circle of disciples;
now I shall further describe the Sudarśana with its sixteen spokes.
Having known that which is the Sudarśana, the Supreme Brahman, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself, nothing further remains to be known. (89)
"The supreme beloved, who dwells within your hearts and yet exists outside, is the ultimate;
I shall now describe to you that supreme yoga whose essence is the Beloved, to be practiced within your own bodies. (2.47.90)
"Let the most excellent maidens come, let them take water in their hands, and let them all receive the mantra of Kṛṣṇakānta from my mouth. (9.1)
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā.
Thus did those Rādhikās receive the mantra from the mouth of Lomaśa. 92.
And for that purpose, he then spoke of the sixteen-petalled yoga:
"The syllable Om resides in the hair; this is the illustrious Puruṣottama. (93)
The syllable *na* is at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and Nārāyaṇa himself is the Lord;
the syllable *ma* has entered the mouth, and Maṇikyāpati is the Sovereign.
The syllable Śrī resides in the eyes as Śrīpati, the Lord of Kamalā;
the syllable Kṛ is indeed Kṛṣṇa himself, established in the position of the nape of the neck (kṛkāṭikā).
The syllable *ṣṇa* resides in the heart; this Lord is Bālakṛṣṇa.
The syllable *ma* exists in the navel, consisting of the essence of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. (96)
The letter *ra* exists in the places of the body hairs as the Lord of Rādhikā;
the letter *ya* exists on the seat of the womb as He who reclines in the waters of yoga. 97.
Indeed, the syllable *ṇa* resides in the circle of the channels for the best of men;
the syllable *ya* resides as Hari in the mind, bestowing the intended meaning through subtle gestures. (98)
The letter *pa* resides in the two feet; it is the Lord, the master of Pāravatī.
The letter *ta* is situated in the *piḍikā*; it is the Lord himself, the beloved of Prabhā. (99)
The letter *ya* resides at my knees; he is the Lord, the Sovereign of Sovereignty.
With his own form, the beautiful-souled one shines resplendent throughout all my limbs. (2.47.100)
The syllable *hā* is the very self of the *haṃsa*; it attained the sacrificial offering (*homam*) in service.
I am indeed the fifteenth [digit] of the Lord with qualities (*saguṇeśa*), while the sixteenth is the digit (*kalā*).
The possessor of all arts, Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the lord of all arts, is my protector; having realized this supreme truth, he is not subject to rebirth.
In this way, O Rādhā, those maidens received the garlands of mantras;
they chanted them, worshipped their beloved husband, who is none other than the Supreme Lord himself.
But those men and women who, having realized this supreme truth, worship Śrī Narāyaṇa— who shines forth visibly within their own bodies— [attain the highest goal].
They will undoubtedly attain the supreme state at the end;

by reading and hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained. Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Instruction Given by Lomaśa to the Maidens of Lakṣmaṇa in the Form of Sons, Disciples, Wives, and Others," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to this beautiful and wondrous tale concerning the worship of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa in the month of Caitra; I shall relate it to you. (1)
The daughters of the Grandfather (Brahmā) are eternally youthful, established in their vows, ever devoted to celibacy, and reciters of the Sāmaveda. || 2 ||
Endowed with forms like the sun, the three maidens Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā became young girls upon the earth by the command of the Creator.
Those women, possessing the speed of thought, arrived with the desire to visit the sacred ford;
for they had previously heard from the mouth of Nārada in Satyaloka.
On earth, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Kamalā, shines forth;
He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī Pārvatī. || 5 ||
Then, desiring to know, they questioned Nārada:
"Of what qualities does that Blessed One possess, of whom you are so intent on praising?"
Then Nārada indeed said: "O sisters, he is truly the Blessed One;
he is the father of our father, Vairāja, and the father of his father."
Mahāviṣṇu is his father; he who is the Pradhānapuruṣa is his father;
the Lord of Prakṛti is his father; and Śrī Hari himself is his father.
That boy is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
on earth, he is the son of Śrī Kambharā and the joy of Gopāla.
This world, along with the world of the ancestors (Svarga), and beyond that the terrestrial region; beyond that is the covering of water, and beyond that [is the covering of wind].
Beyond that shines Vaikuṇṭha, considered to be a mass of supreme splendor;
and there are the worlds named Vairāja, where the one called Vairāja resides.
Therefore, the Lord shines as that which is the station of Mahāvaiṣṇava;
Mahāviṣṇu resides there, for it is indeed the primary abode.
Therein lies that which is designated as "unmanifest" (avyākṛta), where the Infinite (bhūman) shines forth;
that indeed is the lower Vaikuṇṭha, which is the abode of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Then, in the world of Prakṛti-sāttvika, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, shines forth here in the supreme abode of Goloka within the unmanifest.
Beyond that is the imperishable abode where Brahman shines forth,
accompanied by infinite liberated souls and resplendent with divine sovereignty.
Beyond that is declared the supreme, vast, and auspicious abode of Hari;
it is eternal, enriched with all splendors, and the great, highest of all abodes.
Established in His supreme abode is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Śrī Nārāyaṇa;
He who is the Lord Himself, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (17)
For from him indeed arise the manifestations such as Vāsudeva and others, as well as the incarnations, the lords, the gods, and the best of sages. (18)
He whose infinite powers are Rādhā, Ramā, Prabhā, Śrī, Lakṣmī, Pāravatī, Haṃsā, Kṛṣṇā, Vṛndā, Jayā, and others. (19)
And there were one hundred and twelve excellent attendants; moreover, those four—Prabhā, Pāravatī, Rādhā, and Lakṣmī—were by her side.
Those [energies] are eternally non-different from His own form and reside within His heart;
Lakṣmī is situated upon His chest in the form of a line. 21.
A black radiance, appearing as a halo of splendor, is situated on his face;
on his left thigh is Pārvatī, whose nature is marked by the lotus.
In this manner, other parts of the body also exist; those others, numbering in the tens of millions and billions, are all located within the pores of the skin. (23)
The goddesses, established within his form, devotedly worship that husband, who is a treasure-trove of all loveliness, beauty, bliss, and good fortune. (24)
Ten million billion maidens dwelling in the realm of Brahmā serve him;
fourteen thousand Nālamedhyas also serve him.
Ten million Dīpāvalyas, sixty thousand Tatkanyakās, Talājā, Daityakanyā, and Gokanyā likewise worship him. (26)
The first hundred [of his daughters] worship that Supreme Lord;
a maiden named Krodhanikā also worships that Narāyaṇa. || 27 ||
Caves and maidens by the millions also attend upon him;
likewise, the Brahmaputrī, the Sūcī, and Vanadeva number in the hundreds of thousands. (28)
A hundred thousand Rākṣasa maidens attend upon him as their husband;
likewise, five or six thousand belonging to the Kaṅka and Tālīya tribes do so as well. (29)
The Apsaras of the Brahma-lake, the Devakoṭikas, the daughters of Aryaman, and likewise the daughters of Kubera; ||2.48.30||
The daughters of Indra, the daughters of Yama, and thousands of daughters of Vāyu;
the daughters of the Seasons, the daughters of Viśvakarman, and the daughters of the Trees. ||3 1||
And five thousand daughters of the Daityas and Dānavas worship that Supreme Lord, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 32.
Likewise, the sixteen wives of Vasanta attend upon him,
and five hundred maidens of the Sāla and Māla tribes also attend upon him.
Ten thousand Naga maidens, a thousand girls from Śāva-dīna, and thousands of maidens who were fierce sorceresses; ||34||
Sixty maidens and fourteen young girls, whose nature is knowledge (vidyā), are the daughters of Agni, the daughters of the Śravaṇas, and the offspring of Saṃvatsara. ||35||
Daughters born of trees and those born of minerals worship that Supreme Lord;
and two thousand maidens worship him for Lakṣmaṇa.
The Lord of Yogis, who possesses innumerable forms, is the eternal youthful Master;
through union with Him comes liberation and the generation of an ocean of bliss. (37)
Since it exists at all times and those seeking liberation worship it, I go there every morning to behold it. (38)
