"I shall sing of his virtues; Sarasvatī sings of him. Thus addressed by Nārada, these three sisters indeed [spoke]. 39.
With their minds fixed upon that goal, they departed by celestial chariot from Satya and followed the path of the Mandākinī toward the Himālaya.
Having seen and worshipped the Lord of Śrī-Badarī, they descended to Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, Arbuda, and likewise to the Sarasvatī. ||41||
Having seen Mount Catuṣṭila and Lake Aśvapaṭṭa,
they arrived by means of their celestial chariot, longing for a vision of Kṛṣṇa.
From the path of the sky, those beautiful women beheld the radiant earth at the moment of moonrise on the evening of the full moon of Caitra. 43.
And through the sky, I beheld that field of the Kuṅkumavāpī as if it were another sun shining brilliantly, and there was not even the slightest bit of darkness.
Then they reflected upon that field of Puruṣottama;
and they beheld a lake and a vast city.
In the center, however, they beheld an excellent golden palace, circular like the sun, appearing as if it were proclaiming itself to be the orb of the sun. ||46||
He saw various wonderful gardens made of celestial flowers,
delightful divine mansions, and thousands of hermitages of sages.
The divine deities and the forest goddesses also beheld the hermitages of the incarnations as well as the temples of the Lord.
They beheld the divine and auspicious hermitage of Lomaśa, radiant as the moon, filled with celestial medicinal herbs, and inhabited by maidens. (49)
And they beheld the Tīrthasetu all around from the sky;
having performed four circumambulations of that sacred field, they [proceeded].
Having beheld Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa’s abode, which resembled the sun, they uttered cries of "Victory! and showered flowers. ||51||
The cry of "Victory! from the goddesses pervaded the sky on all sides;
hearing those sounds mingled with shouts of victory, the people looked up into the sky.
The celestial chariot was pervaded by moonlight like that of the moon, yet in form it resembled a lotus;
it brought joy to the eyes and was richly endowed with exquisite fragrance. (53)
Resplendent and variegated, beautified by primary and secondary colors, it entered within and became visible to the eye— a beautiful form resting upon the maiden.
It was prosperous, enriched with divine objects, adorned with garments and archways,
provided with golden jars, possessing three peaks, and endowed with three thrones.
And the humans and others, having attained a state of supreme wonder, beheld the celestial chariot above the temple of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (56)
And while it remained steady in the sky, three young maidens there heard the sounds arising from the lustration rites (nīrājana) produced on all sides.
At that time, absorbed in those countless supreme hymns of praise which produced manifold resonant sounds,
they attained the highest peace.
Then, having learned that those devoted daughters of Brahmā were enamored [of him],
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself appeared in his youthful form within a celestial chariot.
He bestowed upon them the bliss born of divine vision, the supreme joy of touch,
and for a moment, the great happiness arising from their embrace.
There Śrī Hari brought down the celestial chariot to his own abode;
he then became invisible in that vehicle and entered the golden palace.
Those maidens descended from the celestial chariot into Kṛṣṇa’s palace;
they stood for a moment upon the moon-chamber (candraśālā) near the chariot.
Taking up celestial, radiant objects from their aerial chariots,
they placed them upon the moon-chambered roof, awaiting the arrival of the one who grants their desires.
She also knew the male and female servants, as well as the protocol for descending [from the palace],
and the porters and attendants who were to admit her into the interior.
Meanwhile, Śrī Kambharāsuta’s daughter named Santoṣā stood in the moon-chamber together with her friend Suśīlā. (65)
Together with his sister Amṛtā, he went to the divine maidens who possessed bodies of light and were situated in the moon-chambers of his brother, the Blessed One.
Having seen them, they quickly welcomed them with pleasant words:
"Come, O highly fortunate ones, toward Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. (67)
"The mother and the father also shine in the seventh state.
Thus addressed, they were Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā. (68)
Floral garlands, sandalwood, camphor, as well as unbroken grains (akṣata),
saffron, the essence of fragrance, and the finest filaments.
Jeweled necklaces, jeweled ornaments, a crown, and likewise earrings;
divine betel, divine fruits, and ointments as well.
And divine, beautiful collyrium; the most excellent oil of Brahmā;
the essence of fragrant waters; and garments purified by fire.
He gave necklaces of excellent gems and diamonds, golden vessels,
mirrors of divine appearance, and celestial powders for perfuming.
And [he offered] divine food offerings consisting of sweet, cooked foods and drinks, nectar-like substances that are the essence of milk, and countless seeds and fruits. ||73||
Furthermore, having taken up divine vessels filled with excellent drinks, as well as divine beds and coverings, and garments fit for the divine; ||74||
Holding their bowls in their hands, they descended slowly by way of the auspicious staircases down to the ground below.
In front was the maiden Santoṣā; in the middle were three goat-maidens;
and behind were Amṛtā, the wife of her brother, and Suśīlikā.
Having descended from one level onto a vast expanse of ground,
they entered the seventh level where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
Likewise, their virtuous mother, the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī, shone forth;
they bowed down to their mother and also paid homage to Bālakṛṣṇa. (78)
When divine seats had been provided, they sat down as was appropriate;
and they were addressed by their mother regarding auspiciousness and well-being. (79)
They spoke of their purpose, their birth in relation to their mother, and their entire background, saying, "We are the daughters of Brahmā."
Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and the maiden named Piṅgalā, by the instruction of their own brother Nārada, [became his disciples]. (8.1)
Having recognized this glorious son as the beginningless Supreme Lord, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa himself—the youthful, beloved, and infallible one—[he realized him to be so]. (82)
We have come here to see you; we are blessed by the sight of you today.
Today our birth has become fruitful, and our maidenhood has also become fruitful.
Your status as a goddess is likewise fulfilled, O Mother, through this vision of you.
Having spoken thus, he questioned Amṛtā, Santoṣā, and Suśīlikā.
Those esteemed ones performed worship of Keśava, Bālakṛṣṇa;
first, they worshipped Kṛṣṇa’s feet with water from the Gaṅgā. ||89||
They placed the nectar of the feet of Śrīkānta upon their mouths and heads;
thereafter, they applied a drop of sandalwood paste and other marks on the foreheads of Hari.
They applied fragrant ointments and gave them scented water;
they also gave them sandalwood paste, collyrium, saffron, and other such items.
They gave flower garlands, jewel necklaces, various types of crowns, as well as bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments of splendor.
They placed garments, beds, fruits, foods, and drinks, as well as offerings such as yak-tail whisks, before him. (89)
They also offered sacrificial foods (naivedya) and various sweet drinks;
they presented betel leaves and then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
They performed circumambulations and placed a great garland around her neck—an eternal signifier of their innermost feelings. (9.1)
Having accepted the worship offered by the beloved women with his hand, Kṛṣṇa, who understands their inner feelings, touched their hands, making them aware of what was to come.
Smiling and gazing repeatedly at their faces,
O Rādhā, they rejoiced greatly because of the attainment of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Then, likewise, they offered those unfading flower garlands around the necks of their mother, as well as Santosha and Amrita. (94)
They were bowed down before her, fed, and given rest; they were also given water to drink, laid to sleep, and had their feet massaged upon the couches. (95)
Attended by their female friends and maidservants, they slept;
and having risen in the morning, they bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having performed the supreme rite for the sacred ford and having gone to the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa, [he recited]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (97)

Having taken up the mantra, the rosary, and the tulasī, and having beheld a circle of maidens numbering in the millions and billions, they were filled with joy through their state of devotion to the worshipful one.
Having bowed, they quickly returned again toward Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved;
having obtained his sight, those women, who were under Kṛṣṇa's sway, were satisfied again and again. 99.
As if insatiable, they gazed upon their lord and master while holding him within their hearts;
having been accepted by Śrī Kṛṣṇa with his own heart, they returned toward their own homes.
When they did not wish to go, Narayana said:
"Having again received my father's command, return here with all haste. (101)
"I shall fulfill your hearts' desires; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, they offered all their possessions before Hari.
Having rendered the celestial mansion empty of objects and having worshipped Gopālakṛṣṇa,
one should then bow down and, after the meal, receive his command.
Having propitiated Śrī Hari, their beloved, and having bowed again and again to Rādhā,
they obtained the fruit and flowers born of His grace and ascended a celestial chariot.
Having repeatedly bowed to Aśvapaṭṭasara and Kuṅkumavāpikā,
and having bowed to the temple of Kāntadeva, he traveled through the sky by means of a celestial vehicle.
Having uttered cries of victory again and again, he vanished in an instant;
by reciting or hearing this, one becomes possessed of the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa. 106.

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Three Daughters of Brahmā—Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā—arrived by means of a celestial chariot, recognized the Lord as their husband, worshipped him, and departed," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O beloved, why was it that Suṣumṇā and the others, though accepted by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, were not commanded to stay in the hermitage of Lomaśa? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Seventy-two thousand other daughters of the Creator,
who are his mind-born offspring, also desire Kṛṣṇa as their beloved, the Supreme Lord."
They dwelt in Satyaloka and awaited with devotion the arrival of the three elder sisters, who would come upon seeing Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
We shall go there together with them to behold Him;
we shall serve Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beginningless Mādhava.
Thus, while they were waiting specifically for their arrival, those women have not been detained; indeed, they are now staying in the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa.
Sent by Brahmā, Kṛṣṇa will protect them once again;
then, by means of their own celestial chariot, they [depart] toward the western and southern directions.
And they beheld, by way of the sky, the ocean as well as the islands and excellent regions, desiring to circumambulate [the earth] from the north.
Traveling through the sky in their fearless vehicle, they repeatedly turned back and beheld a vast, exceedingly great region that was not yet covered by clouds.
Then, having seen the great island of Āra-bīja and the battlefield before him, and having seen the ocean of blood and the river Nārāyaṇī upon the earth; || 9 ||
And having seen the Rudrabāṣpa lake on the southern side,
as well as the excellent lake known as Vijñaturīya, he beheld them.
Having seen Tuṅgānīkasaras, as well as Nyāsasaras, Liṅgarasādri, and the Drākṣābīja mountain; || 1 ||
Having seen the Kālahari battle, as well as the Umāśambhu mountain, having seen the Karmāṅgī river, and likewise the Karmaghna mountain; || 12 ||
Then, having seen the Caṇḍasara lake and beheld the river Naṣṭajarā,
he indeed observed the battlefield known as Saharihara.
Having seen Mount Ataleṣṭa and Mount Tanmukha, as well as Mount Trirāśi and Mount Līlābījaraṇa; || 14 ||
Śrī Ramā, having seen the battle, and having beheld the kingdom of Turu, and having seen the ocean of Kaśyapa’s lineage and the Coral Mountain; || 15 ||
And in the west, having beheld Mount Kukkeśa and the blue ocean, as well as the river Nīparā and the mountain Kārpaṇthāyana. || 16 ||
Having seen the river Dīnayūpā and Mount Ailaparvata, as well as the mountain Īpīnāsana and the island Śāradīdvīpa. || 17 ||
Having beheld Mount Madhyavādhi and his own father’s mountain,
and having seen the rivers and the regions situated in the midst of the ocean, he [spoke].
And having seen the Lukvārā river, the Senā river, and the Khāḍikā;
as well as the region of Jarāmauna and the region of Bālayama.
Having likewise beheld the island of Īṅga, the island of Āya, and Khāḍikā,
he then saw Koṭadvīpa, Svedadvīpa, and beyond that, Phenadvīpa.
Then, having observed the groups of flour-like [substances], as well as the mountains, the earth, the earth of the nectar of Ālīśa, and the islands such as Divonada, etc. (2.1).
Having surveyed the islands of Khāḍikā, they went to the land of Vikturīya;
then, having crossed the Khāḍī river, they entered the Northern Kurus.
Among them were the Mahābṛhat lake, the great Sulva-named lake, the Ayābāṣka lake, and the Vinipāgacchaka lake. ||23||
The Haṭṭāsana, the Ocean, and also the Dviphenadvīpa;
the Earth beginning with Lambodara, and the lake situated directly above it. (24)
Having crossed the region of Santaluyī and the region of Aṭalānta, and having passed beyond the Mākṣika mine and beheld the island of Kyubā; ||25||
Having surveyed the Varṇadvīpas, he then looked for the Grīvas;
seeing the Āmārjunā river and a region of peaceful groves, [he proceeded]. (26)
Having beheld the earth as vast as Brahmā’s lāṅgala, they gazed upon the regions of their enemies;
and while surveying those territories, they looked out toward the two continents of Krauñca and Śāka.

Having observed the Grāhāma, the Cārakoṭa, and the circle ending with Antārkika, and having observed the regions of water and stone, as well as the point of the secret cavity of the earth (bhūguhyabinduka).
Turning back and passing beyond the Tirodeva mountain, they beheld the Paṭṭoga,
Cīllikā, Perukā, Pṛthvī, Pannāmnī, and likewise Nirjharā.
Having beheld Mount Mākṣika and the surface of the earth, and having observed the Nimnapūrṇa, Mount Kīṭa, Mount Roki, and Mount Ilāsana; || 2.49.30 ||
Beholding the Raṅgila mountain and the ground covered with fine silk cloths,
and having crossed the ocean that leaps twice over, he gazed upon the bird of desire.
Then, having seen the river Kālīmā, the Yāmā, the Bīnā, the regions of Tandrā, the river Yāneśī, and the river Obī; 32.
Having beheld Mount Urala and having observed the island of Nāvadvīpa, and having seen the islands of Phiyojāna and Āsanadvīpa with their flourishing populations. ||33||
And having beheld the great mountain Skandanābha, the White Ocean, the river Valgā of the goddesses, and the mountains known as the Valgās; (34)
Having seen Lake Urala and likewise Lake Bālakṛṣṇa,
and having seen the regions of Śveta and Rakta, he reached Sāvari-araṇya.
Having seen the land of Kimpuruṣa and the lake Dvikala, and having observed the mountain Prabhālunā and the mountain Stenāvāsa; ||36||
Having beheld the Akṣoda ocean, [he saw] the regions for drinking water and so forth;
having beheld the Piśaṅga ocean, he likewise saw the mountain Akṣigam.
Then, having beheld the mountain Āpatāyika, the mountain Triyānāsana, and the mountain Kunalīna, the cowherd women [proceeded]. || 38 ||
Having beheld Mount Kārukora, the radiant Cipiṅga region,
the river Śikṣāṅga, and the river Śikṣāṅgikā, [he proceeded].
Having seen the islands of Phullipāna and the Vāraṇīyaka islands, having beheld the Navagīti island, and having surveyed the islands born of the ocean; 2.49.40.
They beheld from the sky the earth known as Uṣṇālayā,
and then they looked upon the Cāṭa region, Divādi, and the mountains.
Having seen Okadvīpa and Navajīvadvīpa situated within the ocean,
and having seen the island of Trāsamāna at the abode of the camels, [they saw] the river Murā.
The Turunadī, the Aitanadī, Mount Mekadāneya, Mount Maśakagrīva, the Mahāraṇa forest, and likewise the Vana forest. ||43||
And having seen five lakes, Mount Dārāliṅga, Bālādri, Hemaśālādri, and the regions of Ārṇahemapradeśa; 44.
Having seen as far as Sumātra and the land of Malaya,
he then [saw] the islands of Annada, the Śyāma regions, and the river Mikāṅganā.
Having seen the river Īrāvatī, Mount Cārākarṇa, the lands of Brahmā, the forest named Sundara, and the great river Hutalinī; ||46||
The Gaṅgā and the Brahmaputrā, as well as the Khāsī mountains, the great mountain Patatkārya, and the regions of the Himālayas. 47.
Having seen Lake Mānasa and the region of Śrī, as well as Trivartana;
having seen the Indukuśa river and Mount Kṛpālupa. ||48||
Having seen Tharaṇa, Kaccha, and Lake Sābharaka, and having seen Mount Āravallī and the land of Narmadā; ||49||
Having seen the mountain named Saptapuṭa, the great river Tapatī, Mahābaleśvara, and likewise the Malaya mountain; ||2.49.50||
Having beheld the Sahya mountain and the southern regions,
and having sighted the island named Siṃhala situated in the ocean, they turned back.
The river Kāverī, the Kṛṣṇā, the great river Godāvarī,
the sacred field of Jagannāthapura, and also Kapilāśrama.
Having beheld Vaṅga, Aṅga, Vihāra, Bhūtānīpala, as well as Gaṇḍakī, Kurukṣetra, and Gaṅgādvāra, they [proceeded]. (53)
O Rādhikā, having gone to Badarī, they dwelt there happily through the night,
performing service to Nārāyaṇa and worshipping that Lord.
Having beheld Gaurīśṛṅga, Śivaśṛṅga, and likewise the celestial river (Svardhunī),
he traveled from the heavenly realm (Svarloka) to Satyaloka along the path of the celestial Gaṅgā.
Overflowing with great bliss, they went to the side of the glorious Brahmā;
then Iḍā, Suṣumṇā, and Piṅgalā likewise paid homage to their father.
Overwhelmed with great joy, they described the procedure for the pilgrimage as it was performed—the nectar of the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (57)
They offered garlands of flowers and chanted mantras again and again;
they also spoke to one another regarding the kindness shown by Nārada.
And having heard the news, seventy-two thousand other maidens likewise arrived to learn the account. (59)
Then, for the purpose of welcoming him, they arrived in the presence of Brahmā:
the illustrious Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, Viśvodarā, and Kuhū.
Alambuṣā, Gāndhārī, Śaṅkhinī, Payasvinī, Sarasvatī, Vāruṇī, Tejasvinī, and Raktinī. ||6.1||
The *purītat*, the *vīryavāhā*, the *prāṇavāhā*, and likewise the *ardrikā*—these and others, numbering seventy-two thousand, are present there. (6.2)
The sixteen divine maidens, each less than sixteen years of age, repeatedly offered a warm welcome with affection to the three women. (63)
They drank the water from the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and,
filled with reverence, accepted the flowers from His garland of grace.
They heard all the news concerning Śrī Hari, centered upon his form and beauty,
which was full of wonder, as well as that of the city itself.
They also heard that at the hermitage of Lomaśa and at the abode of Bālakṛṣṇa, there was the service of crores and billions of maidens.
The daughters of Brahmā, headed by Yaśasvinī, beheld the supreme beauty and auspiciousness of the three sisters. 67.
They reflected intensely upon that supreme good fortune of Kṛṣṇa, both the divine one bestowed by the beloved Kṛṣṇa and likewise the worldly one.
They considered it their own misfortune that the vision did not arise;
having gone for the sake of a vision, they did not obtain one at all—how indeed could there be a vision? (69)
Indeed, by my father’s command, I must certainly go to see Acyuta—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Supreme Lord. (2.49.70)
Thinking thus, they spoke eagerly to their father: "O Father, please arrange for us to have an audience with him, just as you did before. (71)
"We shall worship that very Lord of lords, the Supreme Person.
When this was said to Brahmā by them, Brahmā rejoiced in his mind.
What other supreme gain could there be beyond this, that Hari should become one's son-in-law?
Blessed are those maidens in the world; thus their maidenhood is made fruitful. (73)
Blessed is the father, blessed is the mother, and blessed is the family;
blessed are Bhṛgu, the Ocean, Kedāra, and Anaraṇyaka. (74)
Sūrya is none other than Nārāyaṇa, whose daughters are the wives of Kṛṣṇa;
blessed will be those people in the world who have such auspicious sons. (75)
They shall become the wives of Kṛṣṇa, like Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and others,
through devotion, knowledge, austerity, renunciation, and the performance of sacrifices and other rites.

If that which is to be attained through hardships, or through yogic practices, or likewise through charity and other such means, or even by serving the virtuous, can instead be obtained through affection; [then it is truly gained]. (77)
If the Supreme Person should meet with one through delusion, or even through youth, or through latent impressions, or desire, or through beauty, or the force of the senses; (78)
That delusion, youth, desire, latent impressions, form, and the sense faculties—all these are to be understood as being of the nature of phenomena (dharmas); even lust and anger consist of that. (79)
In Kṛṣṇa, desire as well as greed and delusion always bring about liberation;
and liberation is eternal bliss, and that resides in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Whether something blameworthy or praiseworthy has been done for the sake of pleasing Kṛṣṇa, all of that should indeed be understood as venerable; for it is purifying and salvific. (81)
"O daughters, I am indeed always blessed and fortunate, since I shall bestow gifts upon Kṛṣṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who is the most worthy recipient. (82)
"What is Kṛṣṇa’s will? Having known it, I shall grant what is auspicious.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā himself called to mind the sage Nārada.
In an instant, he appeared there, and having prostrated, he stood upon his seat.
Brahmā said: "Wherever your three sisters [are], there is Nārāyaṇa."
Having worshipped Suṣumṇā and the others, they gathered here once again;
meanwhile, these other maidens were eager to go there to see them.
"Therefore, they exist there and must be brought by you in celestial chariots;
when the proper time arrives, I shall give these maidens to Kṛṣṇa. (86)
Seventy-two thousand auspicious channels, such as Yaśasvinī and others, which are like the essence of a lake, desire to behold Keśava. (87)
Take this Great Vehicle, which has ten levels, a thousand peaks, moves at will, and is one yojana long and circular. (88)
Establish here the creepers of desire, the trees of desire, the wish-fulfilling gems that bestow wealth, and the nectar that provides desired food and other such things. (89)
In this place, there are indeed armories, barracks, dining halls,
as well as council chambers and collections of medicinal herbs and other such things.

In this place there are alchemy laboratories, clothing workshops, and likewise protective sanctuaries; here there are hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers, divine energies, handmaidens, and servants. (91)
Furthermore, these many weapons, the four Vedas,
and the ritual applications such as those for death— all these indeed exist here in embodied form.
For the purpose of destroying Indra’s net, for the purpose of destroying illusion,
and for the purpose of destroying the Daityas and Dānavas, there exist here embodiments of mantra.
"Ultimately, even I myself—Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Nārāyaṇa—dwell here in person as conscious beings, embodied in our respective forms. (94)
"Take this celestial chariot, which is indestructible, indivisible, untarnishable, imperishable, unburnable, and eternal. (95)
O Sage, O son, he himself is accompanied by the seventy-two thousand channels, including Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā, which are like young maidens. (96)
Go indeed to the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa who dwells upon the earth, bringing various offerings and your beloved daughters of divine splendor. (97)
Take with you on this journey auspicious items such as ornaments, necklaces, and decorations that do not cause harm, and bestow happiness upon the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Thus addressed, Nārada there entreated Sanatkumāra—the virtuous-formed, the embodiment of Brahman, the protector, and possessed of spiritual luster. (99)
Likewise, Brahmā requested Rudra and Dharmarāja for protection;
he then bestowed Rudra and Dharma upon Sanatkumāra.
The maidens, richly adorned with every kind of ornament, ascended the vehicle laden with divine objects and uttered cries of "Victory! (jaya).
Auspicious omens occurred there again and again at the start of the journey;
then Sāvitrī called out from behind as they departed.
Then he said, "Daughters, go with heedfulness; take provisions for the journey and garlands," and he gave them this most excellent auspicious gift.
Then Devaśivā, with a melodious voice, proclaimed victory from the left;
even Devahārīta himself stood before her with his face turned away.
As the vehicle was moving along, the lute fell from Nārada’s hand;
that indeed became an inauspicious omen, for it broke into two pieces.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Thus spoke Nārada for the sake of pacifying inauspiciousness. 1.06.
That celestial chariot descended from Satyaloka toward the earth in an instant, following the Lokāloka mountain in the western direction.
Having found a moment's rest upon the golden ground,
he fixed his direction facing east from the path of the sky.
Gradually they arrive; the maidens see the lands spread upon the earth, the oceans, and various regions, and they rejoice with one another.
Thus, O Rādhikā, those demons of cruel mind beheld that vehicle, which had arrived above the cloudless sky and was as radiant as the sun.

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Suṣumṇā and Others Viewing the Sections of the Earth by Means of a Celestial Vehicle and Then Departing for Satyaloka, as Well as the Seventy-two Thousand Maidens Setting Out through the Sky in a Celestial Vehicle for the Sake of Śrī Hari," in the second section, the Tretā-saṃtāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, listen to this divine wonder of Hari,
as well as the fruit that resulted for those seated in the vehicle when the lute was broken.
Those Mlecchas born of the Rākṣasa species who dwell in uncultivated regions—
whether they be forest-dwellers, village-dwellers, or inhabitants of forests and mountains— (2) |||
Standing at a distance of a thousand yojanas, they then gazed upon that celestial chariot in the sky,
which was equal to a hundred suns and possessed a radiant canopy.
With splendors surpassing the brilliance of the sun, he emitted ten times more rays into the sky by his power— rays that were neither hot nor cold, but endurable.
They were beautiful to behold and pleasant to touch, filled with the weight of exquisite fragrance;
they produced joy, bestowed peace, and were wondrously radiant.
O Rādhā, whatever has been offered by Brahmā for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—what indeed could be lacking there? Yet in that celestial chariot, one may become like a human being.
There were streams of ghee, milk, and curd, as well as excellent lakes of nectar-water;
there were also pills made from the finest essences of sandalwood paste, powders, and other such substances.
There, upon the eternal wish-fulfilling trees, there are always found supreme betel rolls, the essence of which consists of the finest fragrance of the quintessence of flavors.
The jewel-islands, worthy of being seen, radiant with many colors and the like,
are heart-captivating for maidens with the hue of golden campaka flowers.
With archways, gateways, groves, and other such features of golden hue, they shone with verdant lawns amidst delightful gardens fit for habitation.
There, auspicious plateaus shine like the surface of the moon;
the maidens have the form of celestial chariots, and their beauty is like moonlight.
Indeed, all forms of light are likewise produced from a lamp and form;
and the forms of jewels, gems, and so forth, are also distinct from one another.
Each one attained a state of mutual excellence, and the most excellent among them shone forth.
Whose minds among the people would not have become restless with rivalry,
drawn away by such divine rays?
And with divine maidens, as well as with divine riches.
Incited by them, the Mlecchas and Daityas dwelling in Abhravāsa,
wielding illusions and mantras, obstructed that celestial chariot in the sky.
Carrying hope and carrying gain, conceiving themselves as desirable and impetuous, these fierce [passions] fall without reflection even into that which brings suffering ending only with life.
Seeing the fire, moths fall into it with the desire, "We shall seize it," for the sake of its form and enjoyment; yet they are consumed by its extreme brilliance.
Even those who are unworthy vessels exert great effort toward abundant fruit;
having cast themselves into what cannot be reached by their power, they meet with death.
Those Asuras, the Kālasīdas and Mlecchas, considering their own strength to be superior,
quickly and angrily donned their armor and came to the battlefield.
Raktavārdhi, Raudrabāṣpa, Vijñaturīyaka, Tuṅgānīka, Nyāsasāra, Liṅgarasa, and Atidāruṇa; ||2.50.20||
Dhvākṣabīja, Mūśalāmba, Karmāṅga, Karmahā, Caṇḍasāra, Naṣṭajara, Sahāra, and Cātaleṣṭaka. ||21||
Tuṅgamukha, Trirāśi, Līlābīja, Bhayaṃkara, Phalgubīja, Gambikāya, Senāgola, and Sphuṭārdana. ||22||
Jīvala, Kedaṇḍa, Kumeru, Sthānali, as well as Tumbāsura, Līnāpa, Cāli, Viṣṭa, and Kimūṣaka; ||23||
Tūnāya, as well as Bāla, Rukvāsana, Māvura, Bāṅgivali, Dinolūka, Kuvaṃśaja, and Kurenṛka—[these were the sons]. ||24||
Dhodhasāda, Bahava, Ambikāsa, Śirvama, Deṣala, Kakrala, Ījyāpāta, and Nabījaka. ||25||
Sudāna, Sumāli, Kāṇiman, Trigoṇika, Rudraśiras, Triṣvāla, Pilipa, and Namākuva. ||26||
Dinameras, Aṅgulādas, Phenagas, Kāmanārunis, Nimnajharas, Lālavāras, Hrīyoḍhas, and Mārakarkaśas. ||27||
Alijīra, Roṇḍega, Śāhuda, Phakarāṇaka, Pārṣṇi, Kṛkāṭaka, Piṇḍanala, and Randhrapramoṣaka; ||28||
Bhujaha, Jatruśamana, Lāmaka, Mūrdhabhāmaka, Prakoṣṭhaka, Pṛṣṭhavaṃśa, and likewise Nitambaveṇuka. ||29||
Āsavāpa, Amīṣapa, Kukkuṭāśa, and Kṛkāśaka—these were powerful beings who traveled through the sky by means of their illusory power (māyā). ||2.50.30||
Indeed, all of them, with the speed of lightning, equipped themselves and arrived at the battlefield;
there, King Jumāsamlā sent the messenger Raktavārdhika.
And he dispatched his own messenger to the front of the celestial chariot to speak;
the king said: "O Raktaka, go to the front of the chariot and announce [this]."
"Let there be a celestial chariot for us here, and let our women become maidens;
let men situated in the chariot go to heaven, and let there indeed be happiness elsewhere. (33)
Otherwise, however, we shall simply seize the maidens by force; we shall also slay you. Therefore, do whatever you wish in this matter.
The messenger, having bowed and gone to the front of the celestial chariot, spoke those very same words.
Nārada said to that messenger: "Tell the Asura king this on my behalf. (35)
And those maidens who are here are indeed the daughters of Brahmā;
you, moreover, are born of the lineage of Kaśyapa, the grandson of Brahmā. (36)
The Daitya Hiraṇyacakṣus had sons: Sukālika, Añjana, Kālamegha, Jāsuśeṣa, and Malīnasa. ||37||
Hāvuka, Bhāvuka, Dāuka, and likewise Dhāvuka;
Kvāśmaka, Ajamāla, Saireya, and more than a hundred others [are the names of the trees]. (38)
When the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa had been slain by Viṣṇu in his boar incarnation,
they fled in terror from him, obstructed on all sides by mountains of battle.
Having arrived at this region pervaded by them, you have made your dwelling here;
indeed, you who belong to their lineage have become those whose bull has departed.
My kinsmen and those born of my lineage follow the conduct of barbarians and are unrefined;
I am here, as are Nārada and the sage Sanat. ||41||
Likewise, the King of Dharma shines here as the wielder of the staff;
and here shines Rudra, the supreme Lord who effects the dissolution of the worlds. ||42||
In former times, it is said, Rudra— the god Hara— was propitiated in the forest by the childless Hiraṇyākṣa for the sake of obtaining a son.
By his prowess, your grandfather became possessed of offspring;
let them not obstruct that Rudra, nor let them obstruct Yama, the lord of the dead.
All those mothers shall indeed become your daughters;
for without conquering Yama and Rudra, your desire is truly difficult to attain.
He who could cross the ocean with his two arms, cast the sun to the earth, or even uproot Mount Meru—he might conquer Yama and Śaṅkara. (46)
O King, have you not heard how in former times the Asura Cāndhaka, infatuated by his desire for Pārvatī, met his destruction along with all the Daityas? (47)
Mahiṣa, as well as Jambha and Kujambha, met their destruction;
likewise, Śaṅkhacūḍa and Jālandhara also met their destruction.
Bhasma, Mura, and others likewise perished, slain by delusion;
in ancient times, King Daṇḍa was ruined, being infatuated with desire for another's wife.
Having indulged in passion for the daughter of Śukra, he met his destruction along with his kingdom;
listen, O messenger, and having heard this, report it to the lord of men.
Daṇḍa was a great king, possessing abundant forces and vehicles;
protected by Śukra, that monarch performed various sacrifices.
Śukra was his priest at the sacrifice again and again;
once, Śukra went to Pātāla, being summoned by the Daityas.
Śukra had a daughter named Arajā who lived in his house;
she dwelt alone in a leaf-hut, tending the sacrificial fire.
The king, having come to the house made of leaves to see him,
bowed to the fire and beheld a single, beautiful maiden.
Upon seeing her, the king, tormented by desire,
did not bow to that daughter of his guru, who was radiant with full youth, at that very moment.
When he arrived, that maiden, whose wealth was her asceticism, rose up to meet him and, honoring him with brotherly affection, gave him a beautiful garland. (56)
Then the king said to her: "O young girl, gladden me here, who am tormented by the fire of desire, with the water of your embrace. (57)
She then said to him: "In that case, my father would surely burn you and me—he who is capable of reviving the gods and even slaying them. (58)
"O King, since you are my brother by dharma as a disciple of my father, you ought not to harbor such a thought in your mind in private. (59)
He said, "O timid one, Śukra will consume me in due time;
but today it is the fire of passion that burns me here—quench it!"
She said to King Daṇḍa, "Wait for a moment;
entreat that very preceptor, and he will grant it to you without a doubt. (61)
Daṇḍa said: "Delay for me is not at all appropriate;
indeed, at every single moment, a succession of obstacles is found everywhere. (62)
Virajā said: "O lord of men, I am not able to give myself away;
for women are especially lacking in independence regarding the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. (63)
What can I say to you, O King, who thus follow such a wrong path—regarding your kingdom, your realm, your family, yourself, and whatever else is yours? (64)
"Everything associated with you shall go to destruction through the curse of Śukra.
Do not do this, O King; do not cast yourself into the fire, for this is certainly not in accordance with dharma."
The king said: "If you do not agree, I shall indeed consume you by force, having placed the sacrificial fire of Arajā in my own hand upon the king."
"Go away, O evil-souled one, you whose mind has fallen from [virtue]!
Having spoken thus, she abandoned the leaf-hut and indeed went outside.
As she ran, he seized her and pressed her against his chest;
with his mind and self afflicted by lust, the dull-witted man violated her.
Having caused her to fall from her virtuous conduct, he went out and returned home;
that young girl Arajā, though free from passion, was now overwhelmed by passion, having been drenched by his semen.
Then, having departed from the hermitage, she stood outside with her face cast down,
thinking of her father and weeping again and again.
Without bathing or eating, she remained there, taking refuge under a tree;
at the end of three hours, her father Śukra arrived at the hermitage.
He beheld his own daughter, resembling the twilight and covered in menstrual blood;
he asked, "Daughter, by whom have you been violated, or how indeed has this come to pass? (72)
"Where has that wicked sinner gone who is destroying the maiden? Weeping out of shame, she spoke to her father regarding the one born of a spy. (73)
Though repeatedly forbidden by the king with punishment as he approached, I, helpless and weeping, was forcibly brought to such a state. (74)
Having heard this and having touched water for purification, the pure Śukra cursed him: "Since by that disrespect you have shown neither regard for my command nor for my dignity... (75)
Having disregarded those of virtuous conduct, they have been made subject to the law of death;
therefore, along with your kingdom, army, servants, and mounts, [you too shall face the same fate]. (76)
"Within seventy nights, let the ashes and the staff, along with their attendants, become [manifest];
then Śukra spoke to his daughter, who was of pure conduct and an ascetic.
"When the month has ended and your menstrual period has arrived, you shall become pure;
until then, my daughter, perform penance as you wish and as is appropriate for you. (78)
"O daughter, there is indeed no fault in you; you shall not conceive a fetus.
Drink the warm five-products-of-the-cow (pañcagavya), and do not fear, my little daughter. (79)
Then King Daṇḍa, along with his kingdom, army,
and mounts, was reduced to ashes by the curse within seven nights, O Asura.
Thus the formidable Daṇḍaka forest became a field of ashes;
such is the fate of those people who violate the wives of others. ||81||
All those, along with their kingdoms, armies, and vehicles, will be reduced to ashes;
for those who are virtuous in character, disciplined, and established on the path of justice are indeed fearless. ||82||
Those who forcibly violate the wives of others have no fear either in this world or the next;
the sun is endowed with dharma, and the brahmin is dharma personified, devoted to his wife.
Agastya, Manu, Svayaṃprakāśa, and other lords of sages—resplendent, capable of granting boons and releasing from curses, and honored by the gods. (84)
Those who abide in unrighteousness, such as Candra, Indra, and Andhaka, became miserable; therefore, dharma must not be abandoned, for dharma is indeed the supreme refuge. ||85||
Deliverance is the supreme dharma, whereas falling occurs through misconduct;
therefore, the pursuit of another's wife must always be forcibly abandoned. (86)
But those who lead others' wives [astray] are led by terrible great sins; those who are intent on the wives of others for the sake of another are always considered worthy of hell. (87)
Therefore, the wives of others should indeed be avoided from afar by the wise; those whose wisdom is destroyed by the wives of others do not attain prosperity.
"Listen, O messenger, I shall relate another story in brief.
Having said this, Nārada recounted an ancient, divine tale. (89)
The virtuous daughter of Viśvakarman was named Citrāṅgadā;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, like Kamalā or a lotus-lake.
She went to the Naimiṣa forest to bathe accompanied by her friends;
while she was bathing, Suratha, the son of Sudeva, saw her. 9.1.
She too became filled with desire and wished to give herself;
her friends said to her, "O girl, this is certainly not appropriate. (92)
In this matter of giving yourself away to another, you have no independence;
for the father may give away his son, since the son remains under the father's authority. (93)
"It is not fitting for you to offer yourself here personally to the king.
In the meantime, King Suratha was tormented by desire.
He said to her: "O intoxicating-eyed one, O charming girl, you seem to bewilder me;
therefore, you ought to lay me down upon the bed of your breast. (95)
Then, tormented by desire and repeatedly entreated by the king, she, though being restrained by her friends, surrendered herself by her own will. (96)
Because she had given herself away out of her own independence, and because she had disregarded both her father and her son, the father cursed her as she departed according to her will. (97)
Since you have abandoned the Dharma out of a desire for wealth and surrendered yourself to that foolish king, therefore your marriage shall not take place. (98)
Deprived of marriage, you shall by no means obtain happiness from a husband;
nor shall you receive the fruit of sons, nor shall you attain union with a spouse. (99)
As soon as the curse was uttered, the Sarasvatī swept away the king,
who had failed to achieve his purpose, for thirteen yojanas.
When the king had departed, she too, her desire unfulfilled, fell into a swoon there; then her friends [revived] her with water.
Having become chilled, they were extremely distressed within a moment; nearly dead, their enthusiasm destroyed, they slowly regained consciousness. (102)
Not seeing the king, she then fled with great speed;
she fell into the Sarasvatī, being overwhelmed by its waves.
She went out into the great forest, which was teeming with lions and tigers;
there a Guhyaka saw her and led her to the banks of the illustrious Yamunā.
There, having eaten, she cast it into the water in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
emerging with her head bowed, she remained standing at midday.
A certain ascetic named Ṛtudhvaja saw her and said to her:
"Daughter, whose daughter are you, and how have you come here? (106)
Then she indeed related the entire account exactly as it had happened;
having heard it, the sage became enraged at her father, the best of artisans.
"O Tvaṣṭṛ, since you, a sinner, have joined her—who was worthy of being given—to one who is not her husband, therefore become a monkey! (108)
Thus, due to the curse, Viśvakarman instantly became a human being;
because of the cause of that curse, he fell from the peak of Mount Meru to the surface of the earth.
Wandering the earth, he came to Śrīkaṇṭha, the son of Ṛtadhvaja, and entreated him: "The most terrible curse given to me—let it be revoked. (2.50.11)
"Recognize me as Tvaṣṭṛ, the father of Citrāṅgadā;
indeed, even sinful deeds were committed by me in the form of a monkey."
"May they come to an end for me; have mercy, O Ṛtudhvaja!
Then Ṛtudhvaja said, "There shall be an end to the curse."
Having procreated a son of great strength upon Ghṛtācī,
he then beheld the gentle Ghṛtācī and became filled with desire for her.
Desiring a child, she too conceived on the bank of the Godāvarī;
and when the time had come, she gave birth to a powerful son, Nala.
The monkey, having abandoned his monkey-form, became Viśvakarmā in an instant;
Citrāṅgadā went to the holy site of Saptagodāvara.
Because she was always immersed in the worship of Hāṭakeśvara,
that monkey then became Viśvakarman there.
The daughter had come to know all such suffering caused by independence;
then Viśvakarman spoke again there to King Suratha.
Having summoned him, he gave his own daughter Citrāṅgadā to him;
thereafter, she became happy, having endured a hundred years of hardship.
Therefore, O messenger, great messenger, you who possess excellent intelligence, report to King Jumāsmeḷa what has been spoken by me in the midst of the red ocean. 1.19.
Go home with everything as it truly is according to the prescribed rite and dwell there in happiness;
yet, without conquering the celestial chariot, you shall certainly not obtain the maiden.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Abrikta Blocking the Sarvakāma-Vimāna with His Generals, the Messenger’s Speech, Nārada’s Reply, and the Narratives of Śukra, Araja, Daṇḍa, Viśvakarman, Citrāṅgada, and Asuraratha," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; the great asura Raktavārddhi, acting as a messenger, went toward King Jumādagni of the Abhīkta region.
He indeed caused it all to be heard in its entirety, step by step as it was told;
yet that evil-minded one did not heed it, impelled as he was by his impending destruction.
Enraged and having equipped himself with all his armor, the exceedingly powerful one himself took up his mace and stood in the sky in front of the aerial chariot.
At the outset, he let out a roar that made both heaven and earth resound;
shaking the wind even more violently, he uttered these words appropriate for the time.
"Who is this leader of your celestial chariot? Stand before me!
Abandoning the chariot, go far away if you wish to live. (5)
If you desire to live, then do as I say:
let all these maidens here be given to us immediately.
Who is this Rudra, or Dharmarāja, or Sanatkumāra? Who are these mendicants who have come here for the purpose of destroying my life? (7)
Having indeed become ascetics, they all resorted to the enjoyment of celestial chariots;
yet, lusting after throngs of maidens, they followed a course of deceitful conduct.

Those who stand as intermediaries between the unenjoyable and the enjoyable, who awaken others to the bait of sin, and whose lineage is broken—such a woman shall become the wife of mendicants and dwell in their homes. || 9 ||
The wives of the Mlecchas who abide by dharma may be distinct from the milk;
indeed, we shall take these maidens as our wives, though they are distinct from the field.
Hiraṇyākṣa indeed had one hundred wives, and from among them thousands of daughters and thousands of sons were born. || 11 ||
Born from the seed of Hiraṇyākṣa,
they were then milked separately and subsequently married to one another.
Indeed, those born of the same mother do not become husband and wife;
however, those born of the same father from different wombs may be married. || 13 ||
This has always been considered the custom of those born in our lineage:
whether they be daughters of Brahmā or others, those not born of a mother are indeed dear to us.
Nārada said, "Only by conquering him will you obtain it; therefore, do what is beneficial.
Having heard that, the lord of the Dānavas, his eyes blazing with anger, [prepared] to follow.
He commanded the servant to strike the war-drum for battle;
the servant, moreover, struck the drum with great force.
She let out terrifying cries like a mad female donkey;
and hearing that sound, the great asuras, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, [rushed forward].
The aforementioned army commanders, eager for battle and fully armored, quickly arrived at the battlefield with elephants, camels, horses, and chariots. 18.
With vehicles, small chariots, and various weapons,
they fought with battle arrays surrounding the celestial chariot in the sky and on all sides of the earth.
Eagerly, they quickly obstructed him and roared;
then Rudra remembered Agni and also Nandin.
Having arrived quickly, both of them said, "Give us your command.
Hara then spoke to Agni: "O Fire, having constructed a brilliant rampart... (21)
"Protect the vehicle in the sky, which consists of flames of fire; remain firm!
Having been thus addressed, Vahni protected the celestial chariot on all sides.
And Rudra said to Nandin, "Quickly summon the Gaṇas here!
Having touched water for purification, Nandin called to mind the leaders of the Gaṇas.
Thousands upon thousands of hosts and lords of hosts, belonging to the lineage of Rudra and adorned with various weapons and missiles, arrived there by the tens of thousands.
Sixty-six hundred six-faced ones arrived, and six thousand lords of the Gaṇas with elephant faces came together. (25)
Then other hosts with black faces, fighting with swords as their weapons,
naked and resembling collyrium in hue, arrived by the tens of lakhs.
Śambhu quickly gave the command to the Kālānanas to fight;
they had four eyes, four arms, and their chests were marked with the Śrīvatsa. (27)
Twenty-one lakhs of Vaiṣṇava hosts arrived there, mounted on birds, firm, and bearing discs and spears.
Four-faced Brahmās, numbering one million, who were experts in missiles, weapons, and other sciences, arrived by way of the sky. (29)
Then a most terrible battle broke out on all sides;
the extremely fearsome women with faces like Time (Kālānanās) slaughtered those of the Mleccha race.
Being broken by the powerful leaders of the Gaṇas, those Daityas and Dānavas,
with mallets and clubs in their hands, set out to slay the Gaṇas.
Then, the gods—including Indra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha—as well as Sūrya, Candra, Varuṇa, and others, being summoned to mind, arrived in the sky, desiring to behold [the scene]. (32)
Then those black-faced ones slaughtered the army of the Dānavas;
indeed, the fourfold force consisting of the Mleccha tribes was utterly crushed.
The Mlecchas [attacked] with bearded darts, great globes, and small balls; with hissing weapons, thunderbolt-strikes, earth-pipes, and spears. ||34||
With swords, scimitars, shields, and the like, as well as with crescent-headed arrows,
spears, darts, and iron clubs, they furiously struck those whose faces were like Time itself.
With black-faced [missiles], moon-arrows, iron balls, clusters of fire,
arrows, *tūpakas*, and *dhūṣkṛtis*— in every way.
Then they struck Kālānalas with slings and many mechanical weapons; the Kālānanās, having fallen and leaped up again with speed through the paths of the sky, [attacked them].
They placed nooses around the necks of the Mlecchas and set fire to their beards;
meanwhile, those hundred thousand elite soldiers were destroyed and fled at that time.
They sounded their trumpets to summon the new army;
furthermore, there were ten lakhs of asura troops from that place.
Then, celestial vehicles indeed arrived from all sides there;
having filled the globes again and again with powders from the burning of wood.
Then they indeed hurled [their weapons] at ten million hosts of Brahmās;
at that time, the hosts of Brahmās struck the Dānavas with lightning-arrows.
The Dānavas also struck those who were devoted to Brahmā with mountains, trees, water, stones, and even by means of gusts of wind.
Those Dānavas fell upon the battlefield, their lives departed;
struck by lightning bolts, they went to their death with their vital breaths gone everywhere. ||43||
They have cocks' crests upon their heads, are adorned with conch-shell chains, wear garments of fierce tiger-skins, and have blue cloth wrapped around their waists. ||44||
Ten lakhs of those clad in yellow garments died;
then, seeing the destruction of his great army, the lord of the Dānavas—
The king indeed caused the sounding of kettledrums that roared through the sky,
like the cries of cranes amidst lightning flashes, for the arrival of an army of ten million.
That sound pervaded the great sky as far as the four oceans;
by the force of the wind, it surrounded the army of the Abriktadeśa on all sides. ||47||
Gathered together in the Middle Country, they indeed spread out in all directions;
from the mechanical device of Vijaya’s chariot came long-reaching sounds of victory.
Upon hearing this, the gods rejoiced, while the Mlecchas fell into great terror;
for the armies of the gods were indeed roaming all around them there.
At that moment, subtle beings, resting upon the top of the celestial chariot by means of powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*),
were like millions of locusts emerging from the sky.
Likewise, the Daityas from all directions rushed toward the celestial chariot, [crying], "Let them kill, let them destroy, let them devour those who ride in the chariot! (51)
Let them seize and take away the maidens and their wealth;
let them perish, let them destroy, and let them utterly annihilate the deities.
Let the soldiers facing them cut, pierce, and obstruct [the path] of him whose divine maiden has fallen into his hands. (53)
"All that shall belong to the victor; this is certain.
Thus did those crores of great asuras roar. (54)
With various weapons known as yantramāras and those that discharge bullets,
they struck the chariot from all sides, even though it was protected by fire.
Having reached the region of fire, the pills run forth;
having assumed the form of liquid mercury, they blaze like clarified butter. (56)
The Daityas did not understand that at all;
they only perceived it as a shower of pellets for the purpose of destroying the celestial chariots. ||57||
Some kill them with spike-machines, while others do so with *śataghnī* weapons;
they strike them down with terror-inducing machines and cast them into the three-fold crushing pits.
Thus, until the end of the fourth watch,
those Daityas reduced Māra alone to powder, having observed that his celestial chariot was shattered and its wooden framework destroyed.
The small stones were destroyed, and the fire consumed everything;
yet the celestial chariot remained perfectly steady and unbroken, staying in the sky.
Then there was an army of twenty-one lakhs of Vaiṣṇavas,
beautifully adorned with discuses, nooses, maces, spears, clubs, and other weapons.
By the command of Rudra, twenty-one hundred thousand Sudarśana discs descended upon the millions of the Daitya army.
Then, those [missiles] discharged out of anger indeed became unimpeded;
for that single army of the Daityas was split in two, even though it numbered ten million.
He placed wheels upon the necks of some, and on the shoulders, hips, backs, thighs, hands, knees, and likewise on the forearms of others.
They rendered lifeless the two [feet], which were divided in two— halved at the middle of the feet, one on the right and one on the left, and the other on the left and the other on the right.
Those [demons], numbering ten million—a single army—fell from the sky to the earth;
yet they met their destruction just as locusts do when they enter the ocean.
Then the king, overcome with grief, fell into a swoon for a moment,
remembering the many slain women who were now left without a protector.
"Among those who come to fight, not even a single one returns from the battle-storm with his life; thus he is distressed. (68)
Then, regaining consciousness after a moment, he said to his army commanders:
"One must not retreat from battle; the duty of a king would otherwise be violated. (69)
Whether there be victory or defeat, death or life,
I shall not consider retreating from the battle here as an acceptable course.
Then he summoned another army numbering ten million;
even during the night, there was no cessation of the battle at all.
Wearing tiger skins, these heroes were protected by iron guards;
they possessed machines that emitted fire and lightning, and they traveled through the sky in celestial vehicles.
Indeed, those warriors, numbering in the tens of millions and seven *tāla* trees in height,
arrived there on all sides where the celestial chariot was located.
They indeed fled to destroy the celestial chariot in its presence;
however, being protected by the blazing fire, they retreated.
Then they realized their own great incapacity:
"Even birds fly in the sky, and we too are just like them. (75)
"Since we are not able to endure even slightly the burning caused by fire, how shall we achieve victory?"—thus they fell into doubt. (76)
Nevertheless, thinking, "The king's command must be obeyed by soldiers in every way," they [flew] their aerial chariot from afar with balls of lightning.
Aiming at them, they struck down those who were fleeing like balls of fire;
indeed, it was a second marvel to behold from atop the celestial chariot.
Standing above, they rained down globes that cause destruction;
those globes, too, flowed and blazed in the sky.
The celestial chariot was always protected by Vahni himself and remained uninjured;
yet, he then sought to slay those lords of the six thousand hosts.
The gods, possessing elephant trunks, carry nooses, spears, and bows; they are enriched with javelins, darts, and followers, and hold kusha grass and vajras consecrated with mantras. ||8 1||
And Rudra dispatched them; in an instant they rose up above them, traveled swiftly through the atmosphere, and struck with weapons and iron balls.
Then, being struck on all sides by the lords of the Gaṇas, the Daityas—numbering ten million Mlecchas and Daityas—fell into the fire; they were truly unable to withstand them.
They were able to run, but they fell into the fire that was protecting it;
by the mere act of falling, they then became known as ashes even in the sky.
"Reduced to nothing but their names, they did not even return to see the king; thus did those ten million warriors meet their destruction there once again. (85)
They were devoured by Mahānala before they could even reach the state of being mere skeletons;
alas, the hope of the arrogant is powerful, yet it brings about their own destruction.
She was indeed the daughter of Time, as if the elder sister of old age;
and when the total destruction was known, the king abandoned his fortitude.
From that place, as soon as he desired to go to his own abode,
there appeared a general, Raktavārdhi, and another besides.
Both Raudra and Vāṣpa spoke to the king for a moment:
"The king must not go, he must not go! Having turned back from battle, as long as the army still exists and as long as there is strength on our sides. (89)
And as long as there is strength in my arms and the army commanders remain unhurt.
"As long as that is so, you must not go from the battlefield to home by any means.
Then we shall fight and conquer the daughters of Yana. (9.1)
Having spoken thus, those fierce ones caused the battle trumpets to resound,
as well as many fierce lightning-instruments and lightning-pipes.
They sounded their instruments exceedingly to awaken the troops and mounts;
hearing them, the army, numbering ten crores, gathered all around.
All gathered together there in an instant, in the Middle Country,
from the mountain Karmaghna all the way to the Caṇḍasara lake,
as far as the river Karmāṅgā, and as far as the Śvetanarāyaṇī.
Extending as far as Mount Trirāśi and providing shelter for ten koṭis of warriors,
that terrain then became a vast field of battle,
reaching from Lake Tuṅgānīka to Lake Nyāsasara. ||95-96||
Formerly, an army of ten million was indeed reduced to ashes in the sky;
and before that, Kālahari had [reduced] the Āsā mountain to ashes. 97.
On the bank of the river Vijñaturīya, ten lakhs [of beings] were slain; previously to that, and to the west of the Drākṣābīja mountain. 98.
O Rādhikā, on the bank of the Vāla river, one hundred thousand Daityas were indeed slain;
thus these ten crores of warriors, who possessed weapons created by lightning, [were destroyed]. 99.
Even those who were experts in the mantras of fire arrived there intending to bring about destruction;
they fought with fire-engines, lightning-balls, and various weapons.
By the god of fire, all those artificial puppets created by means of mantras were reduced to ashes in the sky near his celestial chariot.
Then they dispatched radiant celestial chariots,
wherein were great spheres of lightning as well as mechanical puppets.
There were mechanical horses, mechanical draft-animals, and copper-made mechanical chariots;
likewise, there were weapons for the machines made of lightning and copper.
By means of those practices performed by them, these ten crores of soldiers fought fearlessly, positioned within each successive rampart of fire.
Having leaped over the fire, they then went there in their celestial chariots;
at that moment, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and Śambhu stood up as Vāḍava.
He said to Anala, "O best of beings, go and reduce them to ashes;
let there arise a submarine fire resembling that of the time of universal dissolution. (106)
Spreading his crests in all directions, he assumed the form of ten million [heads],
licking up all those warriors as well as the puppets.
By his mere touch, he reduced ten crores of soldiers to ashes in an instant,
appearing like Jvālāmukha in the sky, or like a mountain, or like the sun among the planets.
Just as a vast mass of fire, resembling the cosmic egg, met its destruction,
so too did that which was visible become invisible.
Ten koṭis of soldiers there were consumed by the submarine fire (vāḍavavahni); and, desiring to save their lives, they fled from that place.
Then, for the sake of suppressing them, he bound the mighty Kārttikeya with six thousand five hundred serpent-nooses.
And they did not emerge there; having been reduced to ashes, they ceased to exist—those who had neither bones nor hair, nor heads nor veins.

O Rādhikā, in that conflagration, it is said that nothing at all remained—neither what was approachable nor what was obtainable; thus were the warriors, who prided themselves on their heroism, utterly destroyed.
Then, O Rādhā, at dawn, those who had assumed illusory forms again approached by means of mantras,
well-prepared to fight at the king's command.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of how the Mlecchas of Yodhinagara and eleven crores and eleven lakhs perished by means of the Brahma-vimāna in the land of Abrikta," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, to this: upon the destruction of ten crores of asuras, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! indeed arose among the families of the demons.
Then, even in their own lands, an invincible fear arose, [thinking]:
"Our king is indeed devoid of righteousness and has seized power by abandoning justice. (2)
The ignorant man invites the destruction of his country, kingdom, and family;
for both wealth and sovereignty are indeed the grounds for the pride of embodied beings.
Pride born of justice brings happiness, whereas that born of injustice leads to destruction;
oh, what a kind of wonder is the power of the Lord's illusion (māyā), by which this occurs!
Even though his wealth was bounded by the lotus [of the earth], and his kingdom extended to the ends of the ocean, and even though the king was ignorant and his beloved wives were virtuous; (5)
The power, strength, and sovereignty of one who is greedy for another's wife, wealth, and prosperity increase; yet in reality, these are considered to be like an enemy.
If those such as power and the like are to be understood as enemies that cause suffering, then pride is the messenger of Death and exists as the son of Wealth. (7)
Bala has a disciple named Dattaka, who possesses wealth, strength, and a retinue;
indeed, wherever these—wealth, strength, and a retinue—are present, [there he dwells]. (8)
In that situation, outbursts of pride arise for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose at the right time;
through such pride, a person thinks, "I shall conquer everyone. (9)
Time quickly observes the transience of even the most arrogant in a single moment;
injustice, lurking by the side of pride, incites human beings.
Then, for the theft of another's wife or property, or for their subsequent loss, he performs oblations;
and [he satisfies] the dog by means of food and other offerings given by those residing in his own carriage or house.
Though satisfied, he wanders along another street out of pride due to his craving;
thereupon, he is torn apart on all sides by other dogs with their fierce teeth.
A buffalo, having found satisfaction with grass and other fodder in fields, lands, and the like, yet through thirst and pride desires to roam the forest. (13)
In the forest, one is torn apart by lions; for indeed, thirst and pride bring about destruction.
Blinded by pride and devoid of stars, one does not perceive the crossing at all. (14)
Overcome by intoxication, he will cast himself alone into the current;
submerged there, he will quickly die at the hands of bees—of this there is no doubt. || 15 ||
Food, clothing, shade, and water are indeed the enjoyments of embodied beings; for the maintenance of life depends upon them, and if they proceed from happiness, [so does life]. (16)
How could a wise person, deluded by falsehood, engage in futile exertion?
Wealth is momentary, the mind is momentary, the home is transient, and so are kinsmen. (17)
Realizing that sovereignty and life are but momentary, while detachment from the body is likewise momentary, one should strive for the supreme good and not fall downward.
A fall occurs due to pride, craving, the desire for enjoyment, and undertaking tasks beyond one's capacity; therefore, one should abandon these through contentment.
O Rādhikā, many have perished, others will perish, and even those currently existing are perishing;
yet the earth did not perish along with them.
Wealth, prosperity, home, wife, husband, son, and family—there is no real bond; rather, the bond consists of the latent impressions (vāsanā) toward them.
That [suffering] persists eternally for the enjoyer who is unpeaceful and devoid of dispassion;
passion and unrest arise and increase in one who lacks knowledge. (22)
Wherever the void of knowledge shines eternally,
there the enumeration of desire, anger, and the rest arrives and dwells, filling it completely.
Lust, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, and pride—all these are brothers who devour even the master of the house. (24)
O Rādhikā, what indeed can be said regarding the consumption of others?
Vultures peck at all the lumps of flesh there with their beaks.
They pierce and carry off powerful vultures along with their flesh;
these Piṇḍikās have been fashioned by the God to be equal in all worlds.
And those who are sufficient for themselves have been granted by Your Majesty for the sake of attaining contentment;
those who remain discontented therein perish like moths in a fire. (27)
For those who have renounced impure food, this auspicious reflection arises, which yields the fruit of peace; for those dominated by tamas, such talk does not even exist.
For the asuras, daityas, mlecchas, and dānavas are indeed dominated by darkness;
resorting to a tamasic disposition, they cause agitation to the stable world.
Offered as oblations into the fire of anxiety, they summon Death;
for that which is called "the kingdom of Rādhikā" is where one reigns through righteousness (dharma). 2.52.30.
The subjects of that king are always peaceful and happy through food, wealth, and other necessities;
no calamities of war exist in his land, and the clouds rain down excellent water.
Abstention from harm is said to be non-violence itself, and its fruit is considered to be happiness; war should be waged for the sake of protection, and not for the purpose of attacking others.
War that relies on others and war that causes destruction are both ruinous;
yet dharma, artha, and kāma—these goals of human life grant liberation if they are pursued as true ends for man.
If those who do not find contentment with their wife or their husband were not hell-beings, then they would not be in hell; rather, they remain in their own homes. (34)

Those who are never content with their wife, house, field, wealth, prosperity, or cattle should be considered nothing other than hell-beings, constantly scorched by the heat of their own desires. (35)
Though you have food and clothing obtained as they may come, sufficient to sustain the body, you find no contentment; you remain submerged in the Vaitaraṇī river of craving.
Even while they live, there is no hope for peace; once dead, what peace will come? For those whose thirst increases with every taste and touch, how can there be tranquility? (37)
Indeed, hell manifests itself within the bodies of those [sinners];
it swiftly casts them into the pair of shackles known as desire and thirst.
The thirst of greed swiftly casts one into the stream called exertion;
the thirst of delusion swiftly casts one into the exile called acquisition. (39)
The thirst for anger casts a living being into the affliction called dispute; the thirst for pride casts an embodied being into the affliction of "I-ness" and "mine-ness. (2.52.40)
For humans, insects, and moths, sense objects are in every way the same;
yet those who are submerged in excessive exertion for their sake surely go to their destruction.
Having approached the king, the female messenger desires her own victory;
messengers and female messengers should be understood as being equal, whether they possess bodies or are bodiless. 42.
They desire their own victory, but the defeat of the king;
the fool, being deluded, does not understand these invitations to his own end. 43.
The merchant indeed knows the supreme profit derived from lending at interest;
yet the rogue knows only the principal wealth, never what must be repaid. (44)
Furthermore, one should not take less than the principal or the interest;
nor should one proclaim a failure to pay after having repeatedly received [the loan]. (45)
In this way, the deceitful merchant always triumphs while the honest one is subjugated;
indeed, the deceitful enjoy the preeminence, and the honest merchant is made to serve the deceitful. (46)
One who is hanging falls indeed; how can there be falling for one who is not hanging?
One who is running falls indeed; how can there be falling for one who is seated? (47)
The warrior perishes while fighting after having enjoyed pleasures that are like falsehoods;
one who is submerged may lose his life, but one who is crossing over does not lose his life.
One should reflect: "How small indeed is that for which one fights, or for which one drowns, or for which one falls! (49)
In this way, O beloved, separation must be practiced by the king or by the subjects;
for even King Kroḍa exists as the sovereign over his own body, senses, and kingdom. (2.52.50)
All these, from insects upward, are considered kings by virtue of their own actions;
yet humans remain in their homes, disregarding those very insects. (51)
Spiders make their dwellings on the walls and webs in the corners;
ruddy geese make their nests in the hollows beneath the pipes in the walls. (52)
Mice dwell in the conduits of the house, and insects live upon the ground;
crows and pigeons also reside above, in the height of the house. (53)
Whose house indeed is this to be known, which is enjoyed equally by all?
Yet they all consider themselves to be the masters of the house by force. (54)
Indeed, they all become utterly bewildered when their home is destroyed;
for whatever one's degree of possessiveness, such is the sorrow that belongs to him. (55)
Of one who is devoid of the sense of "I" and "mine," who dwells in the houses of others, who lives in a mouse-hole, and who is a persistent serpent. ||56||
Even upon the destruction of his home, no portion of grief arises in him, just as in a serpent;
if the king knows this, why indeed would he bring about his own destruction? (27)
Having manifested a pretext, one might think that the duty of a king is false;
O Rādhikā, everything is indeed considered false in every respect, for it brings only suffering.
One who possesses true knowledge should avoid falsehood and embrace truth;
one should not fight for the sake of destruction, but should fight for the sake of the eternal.
Even beasts fight for the sake of sense-objects and for the sake of their bodies;
therefore, the battle of the ignorant against the wise for that same purpose would be equal.
If those who possess knowledge, having attained that knowledge, still fight for the sake of sense-objects, then that knowledge is indeed like husks—devoid of grain and fruitless. (61)
Whether it be a king, or a subject, or a god, or even a human—because poison enters [into] him, he is the "object" (*viṣaya*); therein, the self (*ātman*) becomes like poison (*viṣāyate*).
They are called "objects" (*viṣaya*) because they bind; those which bind the mind to themselves, the self (*ātman*), when dependent upon such a mind, is designated as the "subject" (*viṣayin*). (63)
In ancient times, Citraketu had ten million wives;
nevertheless, by pouring thirst upon enjoyment, he did not attain satisfaction even in the end.
My wives, numbering in the hundreds of billions, could not endure separation from me; and for their sake, I incessantly bestowed enjoyments in forms as numerous as those very billions.
Even while I was thus bestowing that treasury of all-encompassing bliss,
I realized that they were never satisfied, due to their involvement with worldly agitation.
Yayāti was not satisfied; he chose youth from his son.
Nahuṣa also was not satisfied; he set his mind upon Paulomī.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, established in austerity, always lie there contented;
as do Dattātreya, Kapila, Lomaśa, Sanaka, and the others.
Ever-satisfied, she does not desire even the slightest assistance from the senses;
being truly content, she always desires no one other than Śambhu. (69)
The saintly, the virtuous, and those who are ever-contented with Hari become enchanted by Him, and no others;
for if that very body for whose sake the embodied soul strives should perish, what then? (2.52.70)
What kind of effort is that which has been described as being like a young scorpion, by which this king shines, even if his kingdom perishes? (71)
What kind of kingdom was ruled by him? Like sparks of fire upon cotton, even the divine stars fall; yet they constantly watch with their eyes. ||72||
Those who stand upon the branches do not see the fall of their own roots;
by one [the root] that which was to be given has been made distant, and by the other [the branch] that which was to be gathered has been held before them.
The desired is little and the undesired is much; thus this [result] will come in two ways:
by one who has cast the debt far away, and by one who has placed it right before him. (74)
But the vast desired fruit shall come to him of its own accord before her.
O Rādhikā, once Viśvāvasu [offered] three hundred maidens; 75)
He arrived to offer [the gift] to the sage Svayaṃprakāśa;
with supreme affection, he bowed to that best of sages, who was radiant like the sun. (76)
Having received a welcome, Viśvāvasu spoke what was on his mind:
"O Sage, you are a great yogi who assumes manifold forms. (77)
Likewise, he remains with his vital energy drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), a follower of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, these hundreds of daughters of his are truly suitable for you. (78)
Accept them, if you deem it to be for their supreme welfare;
for those possessed of splendor, indulgence, protection, and the like are not difficult to bear. (79)
The Self-luminous One said to him: "That which is in your mind is indeed true;
however, the welfare of the maiden must be secured, for this is the duty of fathers."
It should always be given to a worthy person who desires it;
however, giving it to one who does not desire it results in suffering for the maiden. (8.1)
I have no desire for maidens; give them to another great sage.
I am the Self, free from dualities, while the body is a burden of excessive dualities. (82)
In the morning, in the evening, at midday, and during the middle watch and so forth—one should [avoid] urine, feces, as well as saliva, phlegm, and even sweat. (83)
Spitting, sneezing, the movement of wind, urination, and so forth—by manifesting these suddenly, it indeed makes me subject to its own power. (84)
I always perform service for him in order to purify myself;
I offer him rest in order to alleviate his fatigue. (85)

In traveling, eating, drinking, performing fire-offerings (homa), reciting mantras (japa), or likewise sitting; whether in a lateral position, standing, or being bent over, or during walking and so forth—86.
Having undergone great exertion, the Guru becomes constantly weary;
there is no further time for me to remain for the sake of his pacification. (87)
O King of Gandharvas, for the sake of the three hundred maidens, why should I not, having found the opportunity, please those who seek happiness through service and other such means? (88)
I am indeed unable to perform service here for even a single body;
how then could I possibly manage the service of three hundred and one bodies? (89)
Therefore, O sinless one, I must not act, nor must you act;
that Brahman is to be understood as incomplete when there is a seeking of pleasure from anything else.
That Brahman which is fullness—the fullness of the bliss of the Self—is to be realized;
it is for the sake of attaining that [Brahman] that people engage in the pursuit of pleasure from others. (91)
Even the finest pearls from the ocean perish in the midst [of the sea];
therefore, Viśvāvasu gave three hundred maidens to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. 92.
Then, with devotion, he offered [it] to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the stainless Kṛṣṇa, the supreme among persons. 93.
Śrīpati Kṛṣṇa gave them all to the abode of Lomaśa;
and by his command, the divine Lomaśa protected them. 94.
Therefore, those endowed with knowledge do not become attached to the forms of affliction;
O Rādhikā, wealth, wife, beauty, sovereignty, and the like are all forms of affliction. (95)
But for that king named Jumāsena, who was attached to it, total ruin arose; he awaits only another moment.
When shall I seize a celestial chariot? When shall I touch young maidens? When, having ascended a celestial chariot, shall I bring even the earth under my control? (97)
Thus her craving became manifold; though he grew old, it did not age. Having become a young woman, she drew the king toward secret counsel. (98)
And then the king repeatedly commanded the commanders of his army for the purpose of investigating the destruction of the aerial chariot or its subjugation. 99.
The bugle, signaling the command, quickly resounded;
and the commanders of the army, having been thus appointed, arrived swiftly.
The vehicle must either be destroyed or brought under control;
let them devise means for that, as well as protectors and fire-destroyers. (10.1)
This final battle must be fought for one's welfare or misfortune;
whether we exist or do not exist, there is no need for fear here, O fishermen.
Having been addressed thus, the eighty-two brave asuras, headed by Raktavārdhi, who had not been slain in battle, took counsel together.
From a distance, the mounts of the army and those who watched the combatants of the army—
adorned with the insignia of the general’s office— then began to deliberate.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Knowledge of Discrimination and Non-discrimination Performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rādhikā," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to the counsel of the asuras;
Jumāsēmlā himself, the king, [summoned] the leaders of the hosts, such as Raktavārḍhya and others.
With a voice filled with grief and mental anguish, he spoke of the eighty-two armies that had gone forth in every way to do battle. || 2 ||
Everything has utterly perished; not even a single one returns.
Neither a corpse is seen, nor indeed is anything seen but mere ashes. (3)
On all sides of the celestial chariot was such a fierce and unapproachable fire;
by it the chariot was protected, while everything else was reduced to ashes.
Regarding our celestial chariot, even our mechanical balls and puppets are unable to move;
indeed, the warriors are reduced to ashes in the fire.
