Therefore, what should be done here so that the celestial chariot is destroyed, and those inhabitants of the chariots dwelling in their vimānas are likewise destroyed? (6)
Having reflected upon that, O Raktavārddhi, you must speak to me;
let those whose influence arises from fierce tears speak here according to what is right.
Then, having bowed to the king, they spoke words filled with many arguments for the sake of war, saying, "Indeed, destruction is seen as the result."
Some say that, having conjured a great illusion of the asuras,
they should thereafter extinguish the great fire with a great rain.
"Let them destroy that celestial chariot in an instant with a rain of rocks!
Others said, "We shall surely bring down a great rain, even of massive mountains. (2.53.10)
If they should render them rigid by means of those great illusions, then what would happen? Therefore, let another expedient be sought. (11)
Then a certain man of fierce resolve spoke these new words:
"Let us assume the form of the wind and go to that place."
By which means and in what manner that celestial chariot shall depart from here in an instant,
it will do so while we remain in the midst of those who have the form of wind.
Meanwhile, by violent and fierce whirlwinds in the form of gales,
the celestial chariot shall indeed be cast away and suddenly meet its destruction.
Having separated and divided all the limbs of the maidens and so forth,
and having broken them down limb by limb, we shall reduce everything to dissolution.
Then the Vijñaturīyaka spoke further to him:
"This is indeed appropriate; nevertheless, this Maheśvara remains seated upon his celestial chariot."
If he should swallow us all in a single breath like Agastya, then consider what our fate would be. (17)
Then Ataleṣṭaka also said: "Wherever the vehicle goes, let it assume the form of that region and possess its beauty. (18)
Seeing the beautiful land in the midst of the ocean and considering it his own territory, he will then joyfully make his descent out of confidence.
In that regard, we too must become like them, acting as their desired objects;
after sleeping at night, our dissolution shall take place.
After that, the commander-in-chief Nyāyasāra spoke:
"Even though everything had been created, the gods were deprived of sleep. (21)

"If they do not fall asleep, what indeed will be our remedy? Then the Daitya Rudraśiras spoke words full of reason: 22. "If they do not fall asleep, what indeed will be our remedy? Then the Daitya Rudraśiras spoke words full of reason.
In every way, one must seek refuge; there are deities worthy of being taken as refuge.
And those who have faith become protectors when a practitioner has come for shelter. (23)
They grant boons even without deliberation;
therefore, their refuge should be accepted and cultivated by their disciples. (24)
The mantras of that [deity] and the initiations bestowed by him should be received by householders;
the formal invitation should be offered for the sake of purifying the home. (25)
We must go from house to house and perform worship;
having set down our celestial chariot upon the earth, we shall offer supreme and auspicious service.
One should act with the devotion of a servant so that they may gain their trust;
then, having entered within, one should exercise power over time like poison. (27)
Then, however, the battle took place simultaneously with maidens and youths, and at the same time with the old, the children, and the young men.
Furthermore, whatever must be done here, let those who are the leaders of the forces,
having become bearers of celestial chariots, bring about destruction from there.
Alternatively, those who are considered the foremost among the gods and the authors of the mantras must first be slain; thereafter, the task will be accomplished.
At this time called Vijaya, by means of weapons that inspire confidence, an army must indeed be raised there; it will bring us victory over the enemy.
Having thus placed these words, which grant victory, within their hearts, all—the king, the army commanders, and the rest—reflected, "So be it. (32)
And all others who were authorized raised a banner that signified taking refuge, which appeared in the sky as the emptiness of weapons. (33)
Those of deceitful intent awakened him excessively and prostrated on the ground;
then Nārada said to Śambhu, "What is this excellent [state]? (34)
Having accepted their defeat, they granted you victory;
Śambhu said: "Those who are asuras from their very conception are never truly gods. || 35 ||
Indeed, these [gods] bow for the sake of the purpose of the covenant solely for the accomplishment of their own task;
however, the protection of those who have sought refuge is the supreme duty. (36)
We must provide protection, whereas in the opposite case, punishment is required;
this is the virtuous duty of beings, while that of Rākṣasas is characterized by darkness.
When they have not yet arrived, the tamasic ones fall under one's power; but once they have arrived, even enemies cut away one's wings, like a rat gnawing at the wing of a swan perched upon it. 38.
By his very nature, this disciple is a Rākṣasa who devours like Vātāpi;
when the time arrives, he will quickly become as fierce as a venomous serpent. (39)
Therefore, a teacher who possesses knowledge and consciousness must act with care; for one who is one-eyed, he may become two-eyed, and for one who has two eyes, he may become three-eyed. (2.53.40)
One should be doubly deceitful toward the deceitful and doubly virtuous toward the virtuous;
therefore, one must not place excessive trust even in a deceitful disciple.
At some point he might practice deception, like a snake raised on milk;
even if they have gone to you for refuge, there is still deception in that case as well. (42)
Even a lion would seek refuge at the stroke of a thunderbolt;
even a barbarian would become a disciple for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose. (43)
In ancient times, Indra became a disciple for the purpose of destroying Diti’s womb;
servants become disciples as well for the sake of accomplishing their master’s objectives. (44)
The crane remains still for the sake of the fish; the cat for the sake of the mouse;
the tiger remains silent for the sake of the deer; but when the opportunity arises, these slayers strike.
A thief stays with one like a servant for the sake of accomplishing his own purpose;
a wanton woman resorts to a householder like a wife for the sake of achieving her own ends. (46)
A mouse, indeed, for the sake of biting, touches a limb even after hissing;
and a crow, out of a desire for flesh, pecks gently at a bull with its beak. (47)
Even in a fearsome region, the hunter remains like a wretched man for the sake of deer;
though cruel, he endures even words that pierce his vital organs like one who is mute. (48)
Even a king endures loss arising from gambling, even when it is not his desire;
even a hero, while bound in fetters, endures insults from his equals. (49)
Even a pure woman endures the impurity of her menses and childbirth;
indeed, this impurity must be endured by us for a fortnight. (2.53.50)
Having made the Mlecchas his disciples, he acted so that his purpose might be fulfilled for their ultimate welfare; thus, one must remain mindful of them here and stay vigilant regarding them. (51)
When sprinkling with fire occurs, a fire certainly arises even while one is sleeping;
likewise, these Mleccha-fires are such that one must not sleep among them—enough said! (52)
"You must remain vigilant; do not bring about our defeat.
Having heard these words of Hara, Sanatkumāra spoke.
Whatever Hara says is indeed appropriate, for everything exists [within him];
for one of inferior luster perishes, but there is no destruction of those who possess splendor. (54)
Dharma said: "For we are the refuge and the warders-off of evil;
those who have come for shelter must be protected, according to their fitness. (55)
The elephant-keepers and lion-keepers were vigilant even toward those under their control;
likewise, Dharmarāja and Janarāja were vigilant even toward those under their control.
Just as elephant-keepers and cooks remain vigilant even toward those under their control, so too should one be vigilant toward those who are submissive and toward those who are being cooked. 57.
Having thus reached a unanimous agreement, Nārada said to them:
"Tell me, have you come under their control? Have you fallen under their sway? (58)
They said, "We shall come under your control; do as you wish.
Then Nārada spoke to them, who were indeed devoid of weapons, regarding the celestial chariot.
"It shall remain here in the sky; tell me, what kind of thing is desired?
The king said, "But let the celestial chariot touch the surface of the earth."
"We shall become your servants here, worthy of initiation and your eternal attendants.
When this was said by Rudra, the celestial chariot descended.
The king, as well as his servants, the leaders of the army and others, the throngs of women, and the masses of subjects from all sides, bowed down. ||6.2||
Having arrived there to see them, they all prostrated themselves;
then Rudra, having touched them with his trident, made them pure.
Sanatkumāra performed the sprinkling with water,
and Nārada offered the water contained in the vessel of Brahmā to them.
They drank [the water] for the sake of purification and repeatedly begged for forgiveness;
Yamarāja himself, through his hosts of messengers, [returned] their weapons.
Then, in an instant, he brought all those things under his own control;
thereafter, those asuras requested initiation from him.
Then Nārada first gave them the initiation mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (67)
Afterward, he gave this mantra and presented garlands of *tulasī*;
having made his own dependents [ready], he desired to go to Lake Āśva.
Then those Asuras, in order to make their own home pure and to make the regions and sacred fields (kṣetras) pure on all sides, [proceeded]. (69)
Requested by them to ensure a good rebirth for the deceased, the celestial sage Nārada and others, as well as Śrī Sanaka and his brothers, replied, "So be it. (2.53.70)
Having stationed their own protective soldiers, the lords of the Gaṇas and others, as well as fires, Yamas, and Kārtikeyas within the celestial chariot, the great sages [departed].
They went to their very homes on vehicles for the sake of purification;
first, however, the king led them to his own great palace. (72)
In the capital city named Mahādāna, he honored Nimbakaṭu, Cālogama, Śāvānna, and Aladāmaka. (73)
Āmeda, Yugānta, Nīrabīja, Kaṅguka, Tuṅgānīka, Pratāraka, Supāla, and Vīrakesara. (74)
In this manner, they respectfully led the principal figures of those other kingdoms and fragmented territories to their respective cities. ||75||
Those who were the commanders of the armies led them to various mansions and gave them fruits ripened by milk as well as meals.
They gave many other jewels, as well as male and female servants;
yet they became interwoven and entangled, shrouded in deceit.
Then they carried him by vehicle a great distance of a thousand yojanas,
as far as the city of Murārka, which lies on the opposite shore of the Araṇa river.
Nārada, Śaṅkara, Sanatkumāra,
and likewise Yamarāja and his messengers went to the city of Murāri.
Then King Jumaśemla and twenty army commanders went to the city of Murārka, while the Dānavas remained behind.
Then, in an instant, those army commanders stationed in their celestial chariots, along with fresh hosts of Rākṣasas consisting of both men and women, arrived swiftly. ||81||
Calamities were set in motion, causing the destruction of the celestial chariots;
indeed, artificial iron balls were cast therein for the purpose of destruction.
In some celestial chariot, fire was set ablaze;
moreover, a rain of stone mountains and a violent storm were manifested. (83)
In that very moment, the theft of the objects was accomplished;
then, a battle broke out in the celestial chariot with the hosts of Gaṇas, gods, and others. 84.
Then the Rudras and others, as well as the sons of the Kalpalatās, and millions of hosts of great strength, manifested themselves there. (85)
The Gaṇas, along with the Kārtikas, Rudras, Gaṇanāthas, and Vināyakas, being greatly enraged, began to slaughter that army of Dānavas. ||86||
Ten thousand Rudras, born from the wish-fulfilling tree,
struck down the army of the Dānavas, and the Dānavas met their destruction.
Śrī Gaṇeśvara, having struck Phalgubīja, the lord of the Dānavas, on the head with his mace, crushed him and rendered him lifeless. 88.
With his spear, Kārtikeya took the life of Gambika, and Gaṇapati rendered Senāgola breathless with his axe. ||89||
And one Rudra, with his encircling noose, struck Sphuṭārdaṇa and deprived him of life;
another Rudra, with his trident, instantly slew Keḍaṇḍa and Jīvala.
In that same manner, another Rudraka made Kumeru a Vipra;
and Vighnarāja struck Tumbāsura and Sthānalinga with his spear.
With their hearts pierced and deprived of life, the two were slain; their vital fluids dissolved, Vīrabhadra, that leader of the Gaṇas, struck the enemies on all sides with his mace.
He reduced to powder the mouse that had entered the grain, as well as the *tūnī*, the *abāla*, the *ruk*, the *āsana*, and the *māvura* [fevers]. (93)
And Bhadraka reduced each [of them] to powder with a single mace,
while Kālabhairava-Rudra did so with his staff that was like a thunderbolt slab.
He caused Bāṅgiva, Liṅdin, Ulūka, Kuvaṃśaja, and Kurenṛka—who were situated within the vehicles—to be cremated by the fire produced from his staff. 95.
Seeing the exceedingly fierce Rudras, the messengers of Yama fled in terror; beholding them, the Rudras pursued them as they fled upward.
Diving down and springing up, they seized all of them by the heads;
the Yama-messengers, who were like mountains, struck them from the sky with maces.
With mountain peaks, mallets, heavy wheels, and thunderbolts, all the thousands of assailants were killed with a loud crashing sound. 98.
Not even one remained; they all fell into the lake.
Śailādi, taking up his spear, struck Ambikā on the head.
Together with Nandin and the fire, he struck Deṣala, Kakrala, Ījyāpāta, and Nabījaka in many ways with his weapons.
Other Rudras, resembling mountains and bearing tridents of the fire of universal dissolution,
struck Sumālin and Sudānaka with fiery tridents.
He hurled at the three [Rudras] the Rudraśiras, Pilipa, and Namākūva;
desiring to protect Svar, Rudraśiras merged into the Rudras. || 102 ||
"I am your devotee and I have sought refuge; I have not committed even the slightest offense," he said there to the Gaṇas, and so the Gaṇas then protected him.
With terrifying fire-spears, they deprived all others of their lives;
even Dinamegha became a devotee of the Rudras and committed no offense.
Then the compassionate Rudras among the Rudra-host protected him;
thereafter, the twenty-four leaders began from one finger-breadth [and so on].
Having abandoned both the celestial chariot and the battle on all sides,
she constructed a protective barrier in the form of a wall through many skillful means.
Likewise, by means of extensive sorcery and illusions, they produced vast multitudes of false armies moving through the sky.
Equipped with weapons, missiles, and mantras, and possessing many similar forms,
they fought most fiercely against the Rudras on all sides.
With water, stones, trees, fire, and mountains; likewise with elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and celestial palaces (vimānas). || 109 ||
Then all the Rudras, ten thousand in number, went outside from their celestial chariots and [attacked] with their very counteracting illusions.
They destroyed the demoniac illusion by means of weapons, missiles, and mantras;
they countered the lightning-weapons with lightnings and the cloud-weapons with winds.
And those lords, with clouds and other means, warded off the weapons of the others;
then the attendants of Yama arose from the wish-fulfilling creepers, trees, and jewels.
Indeed, they were equal to Hiraṇyakaśipu and even stronger than he;
they let out loud bursts of laughter, and by them the entire universe was filled.
Having heard those sounds, which were like the roar arising from the kettledrums of the universe,
King Jumāsemlākhyu and his army commanders likewise [listened].
And the sages, headed by Nārada, having learned of that fierce battle,
arrived there in their celestial chariots within a mere moment.
But even after seeing the great army of the Daityas destroyed by the fire of Māyā,
others who were masters of illusions and sorcery continued to fight alongside the Rudras.
There, Śambhu assumed his own body, which was like the cosmic egg;
with the masses of matted locks on his head, he bound the army of the Daityas.
The entire army became illusory, merging into Jaṭā’s matted locks;
the other army, however, was struck with supreme terror from perceiving her majesty.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Daityas' Deceptive Seeking of Refuge, the Departure of Śaṅkara and Others toward Their Capital City, the Welcome Reception, and the Battle in the Airship from Behind," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. || 53 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā, at that moment there were hundreds of thousands of demon women who were skilled in battle, following along the path of the sky.
Flying up again and again, those cruel ones, armed with weapons,
entered from all sides onto the seventh level where the maidens were.
Seventy-two thousand women, whose minds were fixed on Kṛṣṇa,
cried out upon seeing the Rākṣasīs who were as radiant as collyrium.
Some were equipped with swords and spears, some held daggers at the tips of their hands; others carried tridents, scimitars, javelins, and mallets. || 4 ||
Some were accompanied by Sītās, others by Upās; some possessed clubs, and others were joined with stones;
they had wide-open eyes, red tongues, and visible fangs, inspiring great terror.
"Cut! Pierce! they cry out; "Eat! Chew! they shout. "Burn! Blaze! Destroy them all! Grind them to powder! (6)
Crying out, "Crush him! Abandon him!", those women, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle, with disheveled hair and armed with weapons, rushed toward him from all sides.
Just as they were setting out in their celestial chariot to kill him,
they touched the wish-fulfilling creepers and trees there, such as the Suṣumṇā.
He repeatedly formed this resolve: "Let the armies of magical spells (kṛtyā) arise on all sides for the sake of destroying the wives of the Daityas."
From those creepers there emerged thousands upon tens of thousands of extremely fierce Kṛtyās, whose eyes were like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Some followed the sky, some were subtle and short, while others were massive like mountains;
having searched for each one individually, they engaged in hand-to-hand combat with various weapons.
Then a various battle of blows and counter-blows took place among them;
seizing and repeatedly grappling with those female Daityas known as Kṛtyās, they were crushed.
They were broken, crushed, split apart, and even destroyed;
they were urinated upon in their faces and torn asunder in their hearts.
Their breasts were pierced and their vital organs tormented by arrows;
they were hacked to pieces, reduced to ashes, and slain by flames of fire.
Indeed, ten lakhs of women who had been destroyed by magical spells remembered Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, their beloved Lord. || 15 ||
Immediately that great lord, mounted upon Garuḍa, arrived;
having come at the commencement of the battle, he indeed appeared before their very eyes.
The Lord abides in the celestial chariot and he abides within hearts;
standing invisible at the commencement of battle, he beholds the conflict.
Seeing the Lord arrived before their very eyes, the maidens were filled with great agitation; overcome by the weight of their love, they worshipped him, prostrated themselves, and embraced him. 18.
Hari sits upon his lion-throne in the midst of the circle of maidens;
likewise, he shines within the circles of Śrī, Śaṅkara, and the others as well. (19)
Worshipped by Śaṅkara and others, by the Gaṇas and others, and by the sages,
the Lord sat upon a beautiful, excellent, worthy, and radiant throne.
Nārada related the account of the battle and,
with human-like grace, also gave an introduction to the king.
Then the king wept profusely and begged for forgiveness;
likewise, those who were leaders of his army and those who had gone far away remained with him.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, granted them freedom from fear.
The king and the others beheld [the universe] within the belly of the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The worlds, the oceans, and the nether regions; all things stationary and moving;
as well as the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the hosts of Viśvedevas. ||24||
Yakṣas and kimpuruṣas, as well as hosts of gandharvas and apsarases;
sages and human-sādhyas, and beasts, insects, and ants. ||5||
Reptiles, trees, shrubs, fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs;
those dwelling in water and those dwelling on land; those with unblinking eyes and even those with blinking eyes. ||26||
Both the unmanifest and the manifest—bipeds and quadrupeds, as well as Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and Uragas. ||27||
He also [beheld] the coverings of the cosmic egg, the Īśvaras, the Parameśvaras, the liberated souls, the dwellers of liberation, and the consorts such as Lakṣmī and others. ||28||
He also saw the attendants of Śrī Hari and other forms of Hari;
the king [beheld] his own country, his kingdom, his celestial chariot, and his army.
He beheld everything at that time and became bowed down with devotion;
remembering his own inner dispositions and those past deeds, he spoke as well.
Oh! Nārāyaṇa is truly the Supreme Self, higher than the highest;
yet his devotees were not recognized by me, who am greedy for worldly existence. 3.1
I have always committed sins and even great crimes;
wherever there might be destruction for them, I have committed evil even there. (32)
O Lord of Gods, O Mādhava, how and when can there be liberation from the sin that is like a diamond-paste? There would be none at all; therefore, deliver me from this evil! 33.
This is the very nature of the Daityas: they are infatuated with women and also consume liquor and meat; therefore, deliver us, O Mādhava! (34)
Indeed, by means of this human body acquired through ten million merits, liberation itself is attained here through the power of *prapatti*. (35)
O Mādhava, through the command for battle, I have attained that very surrender;
though I committed sin in the fight, the fruit has become merit for me. (36)
Today, in my lands, amidst the battle where embodied beings have been struck down, there shall be for me the yoga of those who perform rescues and the vision of the Blessed Ones. (37)
May the Blessed One himself, having wandered forth, perform this very deliverance;
I choose service to you as my deliverance, and I choose nothing else.
Having spoken thus, Jumārsemlānareśvara ceased;
then the venerable Sanatkumāra instructed him further.
O lord of men, may whatever evil deed you have committed, whether physical or mental, as well as whatever ill-conceived thought you have harbored— may such a disposition of yours, O Dānava, depart.
May your true devotion to the Supreme Lord remain ever firm;
you are now liberated from the state of being a demon—worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. 41.

Listen, O King: that which is eternal is what must be accomplished, never that which is transient. Prosperity should always be understood as unstable; therefore, one should achieve that which is everlasting through it. 42.
In ancient times, the Lord, being pleased, commanded Lakṣmī to assume four forms; she, too, became fourfold in form.
And another [goddess] wears white garments, is adorned with white garlands and unguents, is mounted upon a white elephant, is rich in goodness (sattva), and possesses a white form. ||44||
Another, wearing red garments, adorned with red garlands and unguents, mounted upon a red horse, and possessing a red body—that indeed is the Rajasic one. 45.
Clad in yellow garments, yellow in complexion, and adorned with yellow garlands and unguents,
she is mounted upon a golden chariot and has resorted to the quality of tamas.
Clad in blue garments, wearing blue garlands, possessing the luster of blue perfumes and bees, and mounted upon a blue bull—she is Miśrā, whose nature consists of the three guṇas. 47.
White, she stands facing Candra and the Sāttvika creators;
red, she attends upon Indra, the Rājasa Manu, and the kings. 48.
The yellow [light] went to the Prajāpatis and the very righteous Vaiśyas;
the blue, however, went to the Dānavas, Daityas, Śūdras, Rākṣasas, and others. ||49||
The Brahmins and others received Sarasvatī, who was white in complexion,
as well as the sacrifice, the mantras, the rites of worship, and all auspicious divine activities.
The Kṣatriyas embraced the red Jayalakṣmī, who is of the nature of Rajas; the Vaiśyas accepted her from all sides as she is of the nature of their own livelihood. 5.1.
The Śūdras took Nīlā, the goddess of service in the form of a maidservant;
thus was Lakṣmī divided as long as fortune endures.
The essential natures of these are the imperishable treasures (nidhis):
the Vedas, the Kathānakas and other narratives, the Saṃhitās, and the virtuous practices of the Śāstras. (53)
The sixty-four arts are white; the great treasure Padma resides there, along with jewels, gold, silver, elephants, horses, chariots, and ornaments. (54)
Weapons, missiles, and other such objects are known as the red lotus treasure; likewise, cows, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, gold, garments, and lands [are also included]. (55)
Herbs and animals are known as the Mahānīla treasure;
the service of all species is eternally established [therein]. (5–6)
Pervaded by pleasure and pain, she is remembered as the blue conch, the treasure (nidhi).
By these [energies], all those who take refuge in her—whether humans or others—are claimed as her own.
I shall describe to you their forms for the sake of awakening:
they are endowed with the splendor of beings, gentle, and observers of truth, purity, and other virtues. (58)
They are handsome, performers of righteous deeds, and givers of delight upon being seen;
they have long eyes and long arms, and are endowed with laughter, contentment, and other such qualities.
With unimpaired bodies and unbroken households,
with uninterrupted supplies of food and drink, they possess stainless and undiminished fame.
They were endowed with truthfulness and purity, delighted in the festivals of giving strength, and possessed faith, generosity, stainlessness, and a commitment to helping others.
O King, people who dwell near the Great Lotus become fortunate;
they are performers of sacrifices, blessed, proud, adorned with garlands, and givers of many sacrificial fees.
Possessing great enjoyments, many forms, and exercising sovereignty over many kings, they shine with the splendor of all their equipment and possess exceeding fame. ||63||
To the extent that they possess objects such as kingdoms and fields, they are happy; they are honored, bestowing honor, joyful, well-nourished, and long-lived. (64)
People with intoxicating eyes, brows arched with pride, bearded, with hair as long as a year's growth,
with red nails and red complexions, remain stationed there, resorting to lotuses.

They were joined with both truth and falsehood; they performed acts of charity, sought refuge, and offered sacrifices; they were endowed with both justice and injustice, yet they brought satisfaction to all.
The people there are devoted to the practice of giving; they possess neither excessive beauty nor fine clothing, nor are they particularly handsome.
Their bodies are coarse, their middles are well-nourished, and they dwell among those who are deep blue-black in hue.
They are atheists, devoid of purity, wretched, and deprived of enjoyments;
they are speakers of theft and falsehood, inflicters of suffering upon others, and deceitful. ||68||
Those who are intent solely on their own self-interest are black, ugly in form, devoid of noble qualities, scentless, of evil nature, and have formed friendships with flies. (69)
O King, people who wear garlands and reside in Śaṅkha—whether they be men, women, or eunuchs—while that [tithi] is current, [attain their goals]. (2.54.70)
And others—modesty, fame, splendor, as well as radiance, progress, forbearance, prosperity, knowledge, statesmanship, compassion, and intelligence—take refuge in him. (7.1)
Revelation, tradition, strength, fame, fortitude, tranquility, action, and accomplishment—
along with nourishment and contentment, as well as others— live as dependents upon the primary Śrī.
O King, that prosperity is dependent on a line; for as long as the line remains, so does prosperity.
Upon the disappearance of the line, all forms of prosperity depart. (73)
All forms of fortune arrive according to the ordinances of past karma;
O Lord of Daityas, those joys and sorrows must indeed be endured. (74)
For the sake of sons, friends, and wife, and for the sake of sovereignty, enjoyments, and wealth, no despondency should ever enter the wise man regarding either gain or loss. (75)
Seeing the arrival of calamities, the self-controlled one should not become despondent;
and having obtained vast prosperity, he should not become elated. (76)
They are not deluded by the loss of wealth, nor do they become corrupted by the arrival of wealth;
they alone are called steadfast, wise, and the best of men. (77)
Moreover, O mighty-armed one, listen to this other beneficial and highly significant counsel:
go for refuge to that Puruṣottama, the protector who is worthy of being sought as a refuge.
Those who take refuge in Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among persons, cross over the ocean of worldly existence; they are indeed honored by hundreds of their own lineages.
O best of Dānavas, fix your mind on him and become devoted to him in every way;
that very Nārāyaṇa will provide for your ultimate welfare.
Offer here, unto Mādhava, all actions—both auspicious and inauspicious—that have arisen from passion and hatred. (8.1)
For indeed, karma that has not been experienced does not perish even after the passing of ten million eons;
yet if it is offered to Nārāyaṇa, it must be exhausted and nothing remains to be experienced.
Just as a thief undergoes punishment according to his offense of theft and so forth, if the king were gracious, he would not impose any punishment at all. (83)
The glorious Lord here forgives everything done by those sinful ones who cling to life, yet He forbids them from doing it again. 84.
Having recognized the committed sins, Kṛṣṇa inflicts punishment in every way; however, if he is pleased, he does not inflict punishment at all. (85)
One should forgive everything done by him and forbid him from doing it again;
furthermore, his favor must be won even through various means. (86)
Whatever one might say while the perceptible is present, that one should practice;
for here exists the glorious, perceptible Supreme Person. (87)
"Come, go for refuge to Him; do whatever He says.
Having spoken thus to the Mleccha king, the sage Sanatkumāra—
The king led him to the feet of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and said, "O ocean of compassion, deliver him as you desire. (89)
I am a sinner, I am one of evil deeds, I am evil-natured, and I am born of evil;
O Abode of Compassion, uplift me, who have associated with the wicked.
Smiling, the illustrious Hari said: "You have become entirely pure;
through the direct association with the virtuous, you have been liberated from your demonic nature."
You—servants, generals, men, and women—all shall become purified through my virtuous union; of this there is no doubt. (92)
Your country, its cities, its lakes as well as its rivers, its mountains and its battlefields—all are sanctified through association with the virtuous. (93)
Having spoken thus, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa ceased;
and Nārada, having bowed to Hari, took the Kalpalatā creeper in his hand.
He wandered repeatedly through the seven-storied palaces,
engaging in combat here and there as if amidst refuse.
Having quickly envisioned everything—that which was broken, shattered, bent, overturned, or turned upside down—he had it all properly restored exactly as it was. ||96||
Having sprinkled water for purification over all the grounds,
he approached the presence of Hari and stood there, bowing with joy.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle Fought by the Daitya Women in the Vimāna of the Second Tretā Lineage within the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā; the Destruction of the Daityas and Others Created by the Kalpavallī as Kṛtyās; the Vision of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; the King’s Prayer; and the Instruction," in the seventh level of the Vimāna. || 54 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; at that time the king entreated the Supreme Lord:
"Grant mercy and act in such a way that those who have died may attain liberation."
Having arrived by means of his celestial chariot at every place where battle took place,
O Keśava, roam through those very sites of pilgrimage.
And may the worlds of the future become vessels for liberation;
O Lord, thus show supreme compassion toward sinners that delivers them. (3)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said:
"O King, blessed is your pure intellect that has now been activated;
I shall make this entire region, in every respect, a place in the form of a sacred pilgrimage site (tīrtha)."
"These rivers are the daughters of Brahmā; through their union with Daityas, they have attained the state of Daityas.
Though purifying, they shall indeed be purified by me today."
As soon as these words were spoken, the rivers, lakes, and mountains likewise arrived in embodied form to entreat the Lord.
They said, "O Lord, ocean of compassion, purify us on all sides!
Hari replied, "So be it; I shall indeed purify you quickly."
Then, having worshipped those rivers and wishing to see the daughters of Brahmā—
who were indeed his own sisters— he ascended to the upper level of a celestial chariot to behold them.
Having gathered there, they departed after repeatedly taking leave of and speaking with them;
and then, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa suddenly vanished from sight.
He traveled by means of a celestial chariot to visit the purifying holy places (tīrthas),
in order to uplift his deceased soul by performing circumambulations in due order.
First, Śrī Hari went there by means of his celestial chariot, and thereafter he proceeded to the auspicious Caṇḍanadī river from the battlefield in order to purify it.
Likewise, having bathed in the Caṇḍanadī and at the Caṇḍasaras, Hari,
all those traveling in celestial chariots, as well as men and women, [attained] the highest state.
Having established a sacred bathing site (tīrtha), they then went to Mount Trirāśi;
and having performed a circumambulation of the mountain and bathed in the waters and other [sacred sites], they departed.
Having made that mountain a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should bathe in the second Dhodha at Nārāyaṇī,
and having bathed in the third Dhodha, one should bathe in the fourth Dhodha.
Having bathed at Dhodha on the fifth day, and having bathed at Dhodha thereafter, and having bathed at the confluence of Anta and Vaira on the sixth Dhodhaka; || 12 ||
Having bathed in the Tūyāna lake at the confluence of the two Nārāyaṇīs, who possess white and blue forms respectively, the Lord established sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having bathed in the ponds known as Ābāla and others, he performed the gift of liberation;
thereafter, he constructed four more ponds of pure water.
Having summoned those various deceased spirits among all who had died in the great battle at the aforementioned excellent sacred sites, the Lord effected their liberation.
By means of divine vehicles, they all indeed went to the eternal heaven,
where Hari— the ocean of boundless compassion and the bestower of liberation— resides.
In that regard, which destiny is dependent on karma and which arises from compassion?
Then, having touched the river on the earth, [he reached] the lake of Rudra’s tears.
Having bathed in the Mārkaṇḍeya-dhoddhi, in the Ālāvarta lake, in the Antāvarta pond, and having bathed in the Kimuṣa lake; ||21||
Having bathed in the Vijñatūrīya lake, as well as in the Nyājāsarovara, the Tuṅgānīka pond, and the Rukvasarovara; || 22 ||
Then, having bathed at Raphijyā, he immersed himself in Rovuṃmā;
after bathing in Nyājāsarovara, he then went to Śivāsarovara. ||23||
Then, having bathed in the Jāmbū river and in the Baṅgavyālī lake,
and having bathed in the Māvūra lake, he then performed the Kaṅgū bath.
In each of those places, the Lord, the abode of compassion, liberated the hungry ghosts who had met their end there; likewise, he established them as sacred pilgrimage sites.
Then the Blessed Lord Hari went to Dinolūka-taḍāga,
having learned from Vijñaturīya-dhodhi that [the deity] was on the bank of the Kubaṅgikā.
Having bathed in that lake, he immersed himself in the Limpā river;
then, having bathed in the Bāla river, he went to the mountain Dakṣiṇāvarga.
Having ascended high above by means of the celestial chariot, he went across the ocean of artisans;
then, descending from the chariot, they all bathed in the sea.
Then, having mounted their vehicles, they went to the Orañjā river;
there they bathed and [retrieved] the asuras who had died in battle, even those who had perished at the places previously mentioned.
Then the illustrious Lord Kālahari liberated her from that ordeal;
having bathed at Kunayanā, he immersed himself in the Kurenṛkī river.
Having gone and bathed at the water-reservoir called Sthānala, which is born of a low lineage, and having bathed at the confluence of the great river Karmāṅgī, [he attained success]. 31.
Having bathed in the Limpā lake and likewise in the Tumbā lake, and having bathed in the waters of Āruva-mī at the lower regions of Sthānalya; 32.
Having bathed at Karmāṅgī and likewise at Uveṇī, and at the confluence of those two;
having bathed at the confluence of the ocean, there is the liberation of ten million pretas.
There, Śrī Hari, the bestower of eternal welfare, performed [these rites] for the deceased;
having established those holy places (tīrthas), he then departed for Āgīvyā.
Having made the mountain Karmaghna a sacred ford on the bank of the Venajā,
one should bathe at its confluence, where old age is destroyed upon arrival.
Having bathed in the Keḍaṇḍā river, likewise in the Caṇḍa lake, in the Phegavipīna lake, and at the confluence of rivers; ||36||
Having bathed in the Gambhīrā, the Sphuṭā, the Senā, the Gola, and the Sarit, as well as in the Phalgubīja, Hari indeed crossed over the battlefield.
Having bathed in the Raṇasarovara lake and visited Mount Ataleṣṭa,
he performed ablutions in the five lakes of Alajāli.
Having gone to Mount Tanmukha, and then to Mount Trirāśi,
and having gone to Līlābījaraṇa, one should indeed perform ablutions at the sacred fords (tīrthas) in the water.
Then, having bathed in the ocean in the center of the earth, in the sea belonging to Nārāyaṇa, and having bathed at the confluences of the oceans, first at Dhodhasāraka; 2.55.40.
Having seen the churning of the nine seeds and having bathed in the ocean of blood,
one should make all those waters pure.
He crossed rivers, streams, lakes, ponds, canals, regions, battlefields, mountains, great rivers, and water-channels. ||42||
The villages, cities, and houses situated in those respective regions, as well as royal capitals, water-stations, forest settlements, and lands; 43.
Having purified and sanctified [the place], the glorious Nārāyaṇa, together with ten million attendants, personal associates, goddesses, and holy men, [remained there]. ||44||
Having wandered on land together with Dharmarāja, Skanda, Śambhu, Vināyaka, and others, and having performed the rite for the liberation of the deceased spirits (preta-uddhāra), [he returned]. ||45||
Having made that vast, unbroken region a sacred site (tīrtha), he rendered the ten-thousand-krośa extent of land exceedingly pure.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, said to King Emḷān:
"O King, the desire you cherished here has indeed become fruitful."
"And now we are going to the Aśvasarovara on Mount Raivata.
Having heard this, the king said, "O Blessed One, I desire eternal liberation. (48)
If one does not find liberation even while meeting a giver of liberation, then saṃsāra will certainly remain fixed upon his head. (49)
I have enjoyed a vast kingdom for ten hundred thousand years;
before me, the Daityas lived for ten million years.

"O Blessed Lord, these women have never traveled with anyone else, nor will they ever travel with anyone other than me, even for the sake of the earth's prosperity or its subjects; therefore, O Lord, [grant me this]. (51)
Having shown compassion by upholding the Kurus, I shall attain that eternal state;
my family will be purified, and my earth will be sanctified.
All subjects were purified, and likewise the departed spirits were uplifted;
even the rivers and other sacred fords were rendered holy.
"I am going with my wife to your eternal abode;
therefore, O Lord of Life, show me that grace which arises from your favor. (54)
Moreover, I have these one thousand maidens, all sixteen years of age and possessed of beautiful limbs; become their bridegroom, O you who are accessible to friends.
I have other sons; do with them as you wish. And regarding my family members and servants, O Kṛṣṇa, do as you please. (56)
Having heard these most devotional words, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa said to the king, "O Indra among kings, your sins and merits have both departed. (57)
"You are worthy of liberation; I shall grant you liberation in a mere moment.
When he had spoken thus, the wise man [beheld] his own daughters at that very instant. (58)
Taking water in his hand and offering it into the hand of the Lord of Śrī, he said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, I give these thousand maidens to you as your wives. (59)
"May my lineage be endowed with all auspiciousness and be happy," having said this, she gave him a divine dowry of ten billion [gold pieces].
Gold, silver, nets of pearls, diamonds, and gems;
divine ornaments and garments, as well as vehicles and mounts.
He gave male and female servants by the thousands;
he also gave elephants, horses, camels, gayals, cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, having taken the maidens and their dowry onto the celestial chariot, spoke to the king.
O King, receive here the nectar of the feet from the illustrious Nārada;
let your three hundred queens receive the nectar of his feet.
"Let your sons take the family's nectar from [your] feet.
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, they indeed accepted the nectar from his feet.
They joyfully drank that water which had washed the feet of Śrī Hari;
instantly, they all entered into meditative absorption (samādhi), their channels merged into Brahman.
At that time, by the will of Kṛṣṇa, all of these became twofold;
those Maruts and gods became shadow-forms in the world of the gods.
Others, having appeared in divine celestial chariots and assuming divine forms,
then departed for the abode of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then these maidens prepared his grave-pit; having caused the earth to be settled, they likewise performed the subsequent rites and so forth.
And having caused everything to be performed according to the rules as was appropriate, Kṛṣṇa,
on the sixth day at the confluence of the two rivers, the Nīlā and the Śvetanarāyaṇī, [performed the rites].
Having completed everything according to the prescribed rites, the Lord then divided the two kingdoms at Adanākhāta on the bank [of the river], starting from the city of Jīmūti.
In the west is the port of Embāga, containing the Tūnāya water-vessel;
it is at the source of the river called Uṣṇāṅgī and to the west of Mount Karmāṅga.
Having shown and marked the boundary of this very region from its center all the way to the ocean, [he defined] both the southern and the northern limits.
Keśava bestowed the southern [portion] upon Rudraśiras, the yogi of devotion,
who was a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
And likewise, Keśava, Nārāyaṇa himself, gave the northern kingdom to his own devotee named Dinameṛa.
The two powerful generals, named Rudraśiras and Dinanemi, remained indifferent in battle; they were both devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
When the kingdom had been bestowed upon those two, Hari himself then consecrated them; he made them like unto gods and presented them with crowns.
And then, in the southern great kingdom, the capital was established;
it became renowned as Rudraśirā, situated on the fourth side known to the wise. //78//
In the eastern [quarter], it is ten yojanas long and exceedingly beautiful;
likewise, in the northern section, it was fashioned by Dinamere.
And the capital city, situated on the western ground near Caṇḍasaras, is named Dinamerā and extends for ten yojanas. (2.55.80)
Having constructed a temple for Him there, one thousand bow-lengths in height, [he installed] the supreme image of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (8.1)
The auspicious Kānakī was established by him together with Hara;
she was also honored by Sanat, Nārada, and Dharmadeva. ||82||
In this manner, Rudraśiras also had a beautiful temple constructed, one thousand bow-lengths in height, resembling the peak of a mountain. ||83||
The supreme form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa was [worshipped] by Sanat, Śambhu, Dharmadeva, and Nārada. 84.
A very beautiful golden vessel was placed and set there;
thus Kṛṣṇa himself gave it to the two devotees in the capital city. (85)
Having accepted the divine worship offered by the devotees, Puruṣottama bestowed all auspicious blessings and ascended his celestial chariot.
Honored by the group of maidens and by the throngs of male and female servants, he gave [gifts] to the two kings and their male and female servants, and indeed made them Vaiṣṇavas. (87)
Seventy-two thousand daughters of Brahmā, one thousand daughters of kings, as well as his own attendants and the servants of the gods—[he gave them all]. (88)
Taking everything with him, he went through the sky toward the east; then, having crossed the Red Ocean in the eastern quarter, Hari [proceeded]. (89)
From the path of the sky, he beheld the great land of Ārabīja;
there, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself spoke to Dharmarāja.
Behold, O King, that great Daitya who, having forcibly become a king in these regions, rules over a vast empire as a follower of the Dānavas. (9.1)
Raktabīja, the powerful destroyer of the world, whose seed is blood, dwells in the northern region of the great desert of Vālukā. 92.
Having established the city of Badhīrāyana, he dwells there fearlessly on the beautiful Śrīnāyi mountain, whose caves are greatly adorned. 93.
It was covered with vine-palaces, crowded with intoxicated beings,
and served as a refuge for fragrant breezes due to its various flowers.
Having seen that delightful place, Raktabīja and other Dānavas and the like—ten thousand in number, who indeed dwell there as the seeds of destruction—[remained]. 95.
O Yama, their vast kingdom indeed extends as far as the river Ūrdhvaretasī, and they follow the customs of the Mlecchas.
That Daitya was indeed an enemy of the gods, as were the Dānavas and others;
those Asuras destroyed the hermitage of the sage Bakadāna there. (97)
That sage remains there, having gone toward the river Tāyigrāsana and staying beneath the water, performing severe penance. || 98 ||
Having first bowed down to him, then destroy the asuras;
and having taken along the messengers of Yama as well as those of Rudra, set forth! 99.
Having either destroyed or driven all of them away to the subterranean realm (rasātala),
the King of Dharma restored the hermitage of the sages to a state free from fear.
Your messenger, named Arava by name, is devoted to the practice of silence and is skilled in yoga; entrust the kingdom to him.
Having spoken thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa placed a necklace around the neck of Yamarāja and likewise gave him a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā) for his army.
Having received the command, Yama, together with his army, traveled through the path of the sky and quickly went toward that Dānava, having diligently bypassed the battlefield.
The primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself,
arrived at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpī, at the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
Victory drums resounded swiftly, and cries of victory then arose;
indeed, the kingdom of Aśvapaṭṭasara became filled with the abundance of Brahmanic bliss.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, having wandered through uninhabited regions in the second Tretā cycle of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, established sacred fords (tīrthas), performed the liberation of the deceased, divided the kingdom into two parts and gave them to two devotees, and brought about the final emancipation of the royal family. || 55 ||
Śrī Rādhikā said: O Lord, who was that king named Jumāsena in former times?
And who were his generals, under whom Kṛṣṇa found refuge? || 1 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, listen with supreme attention to that ancient story, divinely ordained and destructive of sins, which was told by me.
The son of Svāyaṃbhuva was named Manu Priyavrata;
he had a son named Savana, who was renowned throughout the three worlds.
And he, being childless, having met his end, went to the realm of the departed;
there his wife Suvedā wept, overwhelmed with grief.
Having firmly resolved, she did not allow her husband’s corpse to be cremated;
crying out "O Lord! O Protector! many times, she lamented like one who was herself without a protector.
To her, a voice from the sky said: "Do not weep; abandon your grief.
If you possess affection for him and your great vow is indeed true," (6)
Then, having mounted her bull and entered the fire along with her husband, Satī, having heard those words from Suveda, gave him this reply: || 7 ||
"O Lord, I do not grieve for myself, unfortunate as I am and seeking only my own welfare;
rather, I grieve for this sonless man who is indeed deprived of any [auspicious] state. (8)

For one who has no son, there is no destination [in the hereafter], nor is there any rescue even from hell; nor does he have even the desire for ancestral rites (śrāddha). Therefore, his fall into Raurava is certain.
But for a beloved man who is childless, even his beloved wife is likewise without refuge and destined for the Raurava hell; therefore, one should desire a son.
"I grieve for the sake of attaining my highest good; O Lord, O Master, grant me that welfare.
Then a voice from the sky said: "O Queen, do not weep; do not grieve."
"You shall have seven sons as your lords, of this there is no doubt;
ascend the fire quickly, have faith, and be a virtuous wife."
The queen said: "Without a body, how indeed will my sons become human beings for me and likewise for my lord? Tell me now."
Then a voice from the sky spoke: "O beautiful one, by your truth, even as these two bodies are being consumed by fire, they shall become new again."
In another moment, you will become divine in mind and essence;
the embryo bestowed upon you by the king will take the form of a deity.
Through the power of your husband’s element, excellent sons will be born to you.
Thus addressed, she, relying upon truth and dharma, [regarded] that body of her husband.
She gave [the body] to be placed upon the wood, and then she herself went toward the funeral pyre;
having reached the fire, she meditated in her heart upon her husband and her sons.
Having entered the fire, the virtuous woman attained a divine body;
the king, endowed with celestial splendor, arose together with his wife.
Accompanied by the daughter of Sunābha, he then soared into the sky;
meanwhile, a divine, perfectly circular celestial chariot was seen in the atmosphere by everyone.
There, that queen suddenly became menstruating;
such was this great marvel, for as was her thought, so was her course. (2.56.20)
Even though it is among those with divine bodies and among goddesses born from fire, the temporary phenomenon of menstruation is certainly not appropriate there, for it lasts but a moment.

Nevertheless, due to the connection with latent impressions (vāsanā), by the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), and through the benediction of a voice from the sky, she became as if menstruating. (22)
And there, the celestial chariot remained fixed in the sky for five nights;
though it desired to go, it was unable to ascend to heaven.
Beheld by all, the moon was seen shining brightly in the sky;
everyone wondered, "How indeed does this go to heaven and not remain here? (24)
The sky above became covered with clouds, yet he remained hovering over the clouds; he did not go any higher than that. ||25||
The king, accompanied by his wife, remained in the sky for five days;
on the sixth day, desiring a son, he gave a gift to his wife during her fertile period.
However, by fate, there were indeed no sons in the fortune of the queen;
the seed did not remain stable in her womb, and for that reason it fell from the sky.
O Rādhikā, after the descent of the semen, the king, together with his queen-consort,
went by means of a celestial chariot to the world of Brahmā.
Where the semen fell upon the ground in the circle of Ṛjīva’s dwelling,
it split into seven parts like a brilliant water bubble.
One large grain fell swiftly to the ground from those [elephants],
while the other six grains were driven by the wind, each splitting into seven pieces.
Furthermore, there are seven for each, making three hundred minus six;
those particles are indeed the color of fire, like a shower of silver.
Are these like stars shimmering with the rays of the sun, or are they jewels, or perhaps drops of nectar? (32)
Thinking thus, the wives of the sages ran with their own hands to seize the grains;
but just as they reached the edge of the falling [fire], those [grains] became like fire itself.
Drawn along by the course of destiny, they have entered into bodies and become invisible;
indeed, they are like droplets of water that vanish along with one's breath.
At that time, even the great Kaṇa, producing the illusion of a jewel,
became intent on quickly seizing Sumadā as she was departing.
Nalinī, Citrā, Viśālā, Haritā, and Anilā—these and others likewise became pregnant with embryos thereafter. (36)
Those wives of the ascetics became bereft of Brahmanic luster;
the sages, having recognized their conduct and their loss of Brahmanic luster, [acted accordingly].
Having seen and recognized that they were pregnant with others' offspring, they abandoned them after only one year;
for all of them, being pregnant with others' children, left the Himālaya mountain.
They traveled through the sky to the western ocean to bring forth their sons;
having reached the river Nārāyaṇī, they arrived at an excellent, open plain.
Having settled there according to their convenience, subsisting on fruits, roots, and air,
the women there gave birth to sons at the same time.
And by the power of destiny, they all wept most terribly;
by the sound of their weeping, the entire world was filled. (41)
Then the Blessed Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, arrived there;
having approached, he said to the children, "Do not weep, O mighty ones! (42)
In the Maru country, from the act of impregnation in the sky, sons of the kṣatriya caste emerged from a kṣatriya woman, having entered her with the speed of the wind. 43.
Having been introduced to Brāhmaṇa women through contact with the Maruts,
you were completely abandoned by the Brāhmaṇas and indeed obtained birth here.
Thus, abandoned by your fathers and always harboring enmity toward them, you shall become filled with hostility toward Brahmins and Kṣatriyas here on this earth. (45)
Thus, indeed, through this state of enmity, although you are Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, having fallen into the impurity of hostility, you shall become Mlecchas and Daityas. 46.
Thus, you shall become unconditioned and empty of all transformations, like the hosts of Maruts in the sky through the emission of their seed. (47)
At times you sons of Diti shall become Daityas again;
and even as Daityas, you shall be restored to life by Mahendra again and again. 48.
"Even though you shall be cut down by the thunderbolt while in the womb, you will still become gods;
hear now the reason for that divinity, which I shall tell you. (49)
The eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself,
will come even to this land on account of the great war.
"By obtaining the water from his hands and by drinking the nectar of his feet, your purification will quickly come to pass here. (51)
And by that merit, you shall attain divinity;
indeed, you shall become renowned as the gods named Maruts.
Having spoken thus to those children, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds,
then [assigned] three hundred women to protect and nourish them.
There he gave a milch-cow born on his own back, produced from the very nature of a Mleccha; likewise, he presented three hundred servants.
They have black backs, possess cruel natures, are devoid of righteous deeds, and are bereft of the refinement of sacraments. ||55||
Then, having given those children to them who were established in the work of mere imagination,
those men, being fatherless, lived together with women who were likewise fatherless.
Having attained the status of husband and wife, you lived there happily;
from that time onwards, milk was consumed here in its various forms.
From that time forward, marriage with those who are not uterine siblings began to take place.
Thus Brahmā, having given the children to all of them, thereafter—
At the end of the period of birth-impurity, all the wives of the brahmins,
having become exceedingly pure and cleansed, were taken along by him and he went to the supreme Hemādri mountain.
Where those sages were, established in the vow of celibacy,
Brahmā descended from his foremost celestial chariot along the path of the sky.
Holding water-pots in their hands and uttering Vedic benedictions,
the sages and brahmins rose up upon seeing the Grandfather (Brahmā) submerged.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the earth, they gathered together and offered him a seat;
they performed worship as was fitting, and then Brahmā spoke to them.
O Brahmins, everything indeed comes to be by the will of the Supreme Lord;
both creation and dissolution, as well as sustenance, occur through the will of Hari.
The Lord, His knowledge, effort, and will, time, unseen destiny (adṛṣṭa), and one’s own karma—when these attain unity therein, then the effect comes to be. ||64||
O Brahmins, from the very essence of Savana, the son of Manu,
three hundred sons were born who became dear to you.
For all of them, with the exception of five, have been constantly protected by me;
yet they remain arrogant on the western land, devoid of your Dharma.
These women, pure by nature and purified by ritual acts, have been brought by me into your service with pure intentions. (67)
"They are staying in the celestial chariot; take these as your own!"—having been addressed thus, the Brahmins, upon hearing the names of their wives, were filled with joy. (68)
"Excellent, excellent! We shall do exactly so; we accept the Vedic revelation.
O Grandfather, bring forth the command issued from your own mouth. (69)
Having heard that celestial chariot descending from the sky toward the earth, Brahmā called out, "Come quickly! and his wives descended from it.
By the word of Brahmā, they all fell at the feet of their master;
and the master received them with affection, inquiring after their welfare.
Then they held a great festival, performing fire-sacrifices, feeding the people, and worshipping the gods; thereafter, they sent forth the Unborn One (Aja).
Brahmā, traveling in his celestial chariot, quickly departed for his own abode;
the wives of the sages, filled with the splendor of Brahman, shone forth exceedingly.
Thus, O Rādhikā, they were indeed born in the form of Daityas;
among them was one who was very powerful and named Jumāsamlā.
There was a king of all the unvanquished lands, powerful in every respect;
from birth he was a knower of war, a demon-like being burdened with the mastery of missiles and weapons. (75)
In the sky, during the conjunction with Venus, due to the arising of the touch of the winds,
he became a traveler of the heavens, equal to the wind and exceedingly powerful.
All those other fragments as well became sky-dwellers through their reliance on the Maruts; for they were all Daityas who had been the commanders of the king's army.
All were skilled in missiles and weapons, powerful, and followed the conduct of the Asuras;
then, by the force of time, offspring were produced by the millions.
If brothers and sisters who are not born of the same womb are united with one another according to the rules of marriage, then [it is permissible]. ||79||
For those mothers, the final vehicle was the very first;
because it was the final vehicle for the mothers, they are therefore called the Paścimamnarakas.
All these always take up the bull [dharma] in its entirety;
King Jumāsena was born in Sumādāyā. ||8 1||
Others, however, became army commanders who indeed bore many weapons;
yet they then died in battle along with their celestial chariots.
Having gone to heaven and then returning again to the earth of Mahāmara,
those gods were born as the sons of the sons of Ṛtadhvaja.
In the water there will be crocodiles due to the drinking of minerals from the belly;
on Mount Meru, the sons of Ṛtadhvaja will perform supreme austerity.
And Indra will send Pūtanā for the purpose of obstructing his asceticism;
and he shall see that Apsaras, beautiful and youthful, as she is bathing.
The ascetics will discharge [their semen] into the river Mandodavāhinī;
a crocodile will drink that fluid, and from it your sons, born of the water, shall arise.
The gods, following the path of the sky, will be known as the Maruts;
then, once again on earth, they shall possess bodies for the sake of the king.
A son named Jyotiṣmat was born to that husband from his lawful wife Suśroṇī, the daughter of the preceptor of the gods; they were indeed the Maruts.
There will be gods in the form of sons, dwelling in the sky;
thereafter, from the human Dantadhvaja performing austerities on earth, [they shall arise]. (89)
As he was performing the fire sacrifice into the flame, from every part of his own body,
sons were then born from the semen-portion of that fire.
Those gods will become the Maruts, wandering in the sky;
thereafter, they will again be born on earth in the house of King Ripujit. ||9 1||
For those Maruts shall indeed become gods as sons when Surati, the daughter of Sūrya, has died and been consumed by the fire upon the funeral pyre.
All the gods dwelling in the sky and the divine yogis [were present];
then, furthermore, because of the falling of the sage Maṅkaṇaka’s body, || 93 ||
Having seen the daughter of the Pitṛs, Tuṣitā, who was in the full bloom of youth,
bathing at the Saptasārasvata tīrtha, they shall become the hosts of Maruts.
O Rādhikā, at that time, all those Maruts, moving through the sky, shall become deities from the waters of the Sarasvatī.
Then again, those gods shall become the Maruts in the womb of Diti, the wife of Kaśyapa; they shall be struck by Indra’s thunderbolt.
Even the Daityas, born from the Daityas, through the very yoga of Hari, repeatedly become gods—clothed as gods, performing the work of gods, and possessing the nature of gods. (97)
So shall it be again and again in other creations as well;
thus, O Rādhā, has the origin of the Maruts been described to you here. 98.
Just as they possessed the nature of Asuras and the inherent character of gods,
so were these Marut deities then uplifted out of compassion.
By the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
indeed in a secluded place under the pretext of battle.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Marut Devas in the Form of Daityas, Their Subsequent Attainment of Divinity, the Narration of Their Previous Lives and Other Matters, and the Account of the Principal Daitya Abrikta," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Keśava, tell me the story of what the powerful Yamarāja did after he went there to the root of the *āra* tree. (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Having gone to the city of Yama, King Yama repeatedly caused the war-drum, which inspires enthusiasm for battle, and various other musical instruments to resound. || 2 ||
And the messengers sounded the war-drums again and again;
those sounds and echoes filled the sky and both heaven and earth.
Then, making the quarters resound repeatedly by way of the sky, Yama, the King of Death,
summoned the asuras who were stationed in various regions, forests, and mountains.
Having heard and even having seen them, those ten thousand warriors, filled with weapons and wonder, marched forth, with Raktabīja at their head.
Some travel through the sky, some through the water, and some by means of celestial chariots; some ride upon cocks, while others have elephants as their vehicles.
Some were mounted on donkeys, some had made their seats upon camels;
some stood upon the backs of gavayas, and some were seated upon rams and bulls.
Some were mounted on mules, some had horses as their vehicles;
others stood upon the backs of goats, and some were seated upon the backs of peacocks.
Some were borne by buffaloes, some rode upon the backs of rhinoceroses; others were mounted on crocodiles, and some were stationed in chariots drawn by jackals.
Likewise, others were borne by wolves, while still others rode upon boars; some stood upon the backs of screaming vultures, and others were entirely without mounts.
They were equipped with maces, swords, bows, and arrows;
they carried clubs, iron bludgeons, scimitars, daggers, and spears.
Equipped with javelins, armor, and spears, provided with balls, accompanied by whistling noisemakers and catapults, and possessing arrows, snares, and slings. || 12 ||
They carried staffs and firebrands, were ablaze with flashes like lightning, wielded nooses of illusion, and were equipped with slings and other weapons.
And other great warriors, archers equipped with nets of arrows, set forth from all sides upon hearing the sounds of battle from the Daityas. || 14 ||
The King of Death himself saw the Dānavas ready and set out for battle;
then the King of Death called them again by their names.
O Rakta! O Āra-bīja! O Marka! O Madānaka!
O Asīraka! O Pegan! O Adīna-parīmaka! || 16 ||
O Heḍemṛtyu, O Viharin, O Hasan Vaśarāsura!
O Irāka, O Damā Tuṣka, O Līlābīja Trirāśika! 17.
Either wage war or go to Pātāla, your own abode;
why do you endure such great suffering for the sake of the virtuous sage Baka-dālbhya?
"I shall swiftly grant you the fruit [of your labor] if you do not depart from here.
Thus addressed, those men of great pride, possessing immense strength and prowess, [remained]. (19)
Wicked men who consume liquor and meat, who eat fish and poultry, uttering harsh words and scattering showers of arrows. (2.57.20)
All those wicked men, resembling the messengers of Yama, approached undaunted;
but he of wondrous prowess, standing in his chariot, [faced] them as they arrived with nets of arrows.
O Rādhikā, Yama covered them with his own messengers;
having thus overwhelmed all those Dānavas with arrows, Yama [proceeded].
Yama slew the Pākāsuras with arrows having sharp points,
and likewise he destroyed all the other Daityas known by the name Dīna.
Then the great heroes among the Daityas also struck down the attendants of Yama with iron arrows, javelins, lightning-engines, spears, and other weapons.
With spears, slings, iron clubs, maces, and the like;
with balls, mountains, trees, peaks, stones, and so forth. ||25||
With elephants and horses, they struck down the servants of Yama;
and the messengers, as massive as mountains, crushed the Daityas while they were still breathing.
Raktabīja struck Śṛṅgavant, the messenger of Yama, on the thighs with his mace with extreme velocity,
and he roared again and again.
The messenger also, seizing that mace, struck Raktabīja on the head with great force, and the Daitya fell into a swoon.
And the follower of Yama, seizing a second mace of great weight,
whirled that heavy weapon in the sky and hurled it at Raktabīja.
At that moment, Raktaka indeed seized her as she approached in the sky and,
with ease, quickly hurled her toward Śṛṅgavat.
The messenger, seizing his own mace, pierced Raktaka in many ways with hundreds of arrows, as well as with razor-headed and feathered shafts.
There, the red *palāśa* tree shone like one covered in blossoms;
meanwhile, Raktabīja rose up and took his own weapon.
He hurled a spear adorned with a hundred bells at Śṛṅgaka, who was like Yama;
but Yama, the son of Śailapa, leaped swiftly into the sky and seized the spear.
Seizing him by the hand, he released him right onto the chest of Raktabīja;
and Śṛṅgavān, having crushed him with his mace, released it upon his head.
Since he was unable to restrain them when they arrived simultaneously, he protected himself with his great mace for as long as his power permitted. (35)
Like a mountain, it fell with extreme velocity into the aperture of Brahmā;
the skull split in two, and he fell to the earth from his head.
The Daityas indeed led the exceedingly powerful Raktabīja far away;
then Ārabīja released a spear at the foot of a mountain.
Śṛṅgavān seized that iron mace, which was adorned with a hundred bells and decorated with golden bands, and hurled it.
Śailapāda likewise released a great spear with great force;
he was struck on the head with the mace and likewise pierced in the chest by the spear.
Ārabīja died that night, crying out in agony within a moment;
then there were two other asuras, Marka and Madānaka.
Then both the messenger Śailapāda and Arkahanu rushed with great speed to destroy Śṛṅga as well. 41.
Grasping their maces, they rushed forward and made heaven and earth resound;
and in their presence, a duel with maces commenced between them.
Then cries of "Strike! arose, capable of destroying the very universe;
and the messenger Candrakarṇa also slew that Madānaka.
Then Arkahanu struck down the Daitya Marka with a spear,
while Śailapāda [struck him] with iron arrows, crescent-headed shafts, and stone-tipped arrows.
With extremely sharp razor-headed arrows, he pierced the Dānavas;
with great ease, he severed their arms and hands from the parts of their shoulders.
And he cut off Madanaka’s feet at the root of the thighs;
thus both Marka and Madanaka were born without hands or feet. (46)
Having abandoned those two at that time, the Yamas raised shouts of victory;
meanwhile, the great Daitya Asīraka was slain by the night-stalker Badhīraka.
The Daityas Pegan and Yamah, known as Agnimāla, fought indeed with iron arrows and rained down many shafts upon him. 48.
Then the sky was covered by showers of iron arrows,
released from the bows of the Daityas, numbering in the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions.
Then Agnimāla and Badhīra, the two messengers who move through the sky,
produced fire and swiftly set forth volleys of arrows like blazing flames.
The great mountain Bādhiraka, five yojanas in extent, fell upon Asīraka;
both were crushed to powder and died.
There, Adīnāsuraka, seizing a blazing tomara, swiftly struck Yama, who had a hideous face, in the chest from a distance. ||52||
Then the supreme Asura Parimaka, having attained a state of auspiciousness, fearlessly struck Yama with a blow to his vital channel (nāḍī).
Heḍamṛtyu indeed struck Yama, who has the fangs of Time,
forcefully upon his chest with a club resembling the peak of a great mountain.
Those three great asuras then flew up into the sky;
having soared upward with speed, those fierce beings began to slay the messengers.
Then these three messengers, along with six other mighty ones,
nine in all, met in the sky and struck the three asuras with arrows.
With maces, clubs, great staffs, and mountains,
those three fell down with their heads, necks, thighs, and chests shattered.
The Vyasa-s were born together, and they then shouted there as messengers;
then there were the Daitya Vihārī, Hasā, and the Asura Vaśarā.
Then, having united, those three— Sahāya, Rodana, Narmaka, and Adrimālaka— struck Lambanāsa, who was like Yama himself.
Then, seizing clubs, spears, and double-edged swords, they leaped into the sky;
darting up and down with the speed of the wind, they struck down the three Daityas.
Yama, whose nose was long, bound the wandering one with nooses;
he struck him with a mace and in an instant rendered him lifeless.
Rudana struck the head of the demon Vaśarāsura with his club;
he then forcefully hurled a trident right into his chest.
This army, pierced through the back, fled;
even Vaśara died, and Narmaka as well as Hasāna perished by my arrows. ||63||
Hasā was split at the throat, and Pāda died after being trampled;
then followed the battle between Ilāka and Adrimālayama.
There was a great battle between Damanaka and Mohapāśayama,
and also a battle between Tuṣka and Kālakarṇayama.
And by the crushing of the Daitya Līlābīja with his hand and by many weapons, it became terrifying and merciless.
The Daityas struck him with clubs, and the Yamas struck the Yamas with mallets;
yet the clubs and mallets were shattered against those [bodies] which were indeed like adamantine cement.
Then those fierce warriors fought in the sky with maces;
there, the maces were shattered by maces themselves.
Then, seizing their spears, they struck one another in great rage; grasping each other's spears, they broke them and hurled them into the sky.
Then the Dānavas struck them with mountain peaks;
the Yamas, however, effortlessly shattered those mountain peaks with their thunderbolts.
Then, for the sake of killing one another, they struck each other without any compassion, using arrows, bhallas, and many swift tridents.
Grasping and seizing their weapons, they struck one another repeatedly;
they all hurled [their arms] upon the ground and cut arrows with arrows.
Then, having cast aside their weapons, they struck one another like fools;
they fought fist-to-fist, and indeed crushed one another neck-to-neck.
Then there occurred a battle foot-to-foot and hair-to-hair;
and Adrimālaya, having struck Ilāka down upon the earth, [seized him]. (74)
Having cast down the Asura Mohapāśa upon the earth,
and having likewise struck down the Daitya Tuṣka from the sky to the ground, Kālakarṇi [prevailed].
And even while massaging his hands, he cast the *līlābīja* seed upon the ground;
then, with knees possessing strength equal to the wind, he crushed the Daityas against their chests.
Then those warriors, intoxicated by the fury of battle, repeatedly cried out and gave up their lives, reducing the bones of your chest to powder and fragments.
Wherever they were crushed upon the earth by the messengers, there,
due to the repeated blows from Yama’s agents, chasms a yojana in width appeared.
The rivers became flows of blood and the water turned red;
the earth then became crimson with the blood from the bodies of the mountain-like Daityas.
Indeed, O Rādhikā, a crimson radiance arose upon the field of battle;
then other eminent Daityas appeared, as well as the wretched Pāka and Trirāśika.
Alīthaka, Śirodhā, Piṇḍitāya, Vāyuja, Trithuka, Baṃsura, and Ūrdhvamīna are those situated at its tip. ||81||
Then they fought together with the Yamas, led by Bindumāla;
however, the pride-destroying Yama was [confronted] by that Bindumāla, who possessed great power.
Gaḍeḍa, Khañjana, Haḍeḍa, Bhaṣakānana, Śārdūla, Dhaḍaghāta, Kaṭakaṭa, and Dahanaśana. ||83||
In this manner and others like it, the lords struck down the Daityas of terrible pride;
lifting them up again and again, they dashed them against the earth.
They indeed split these Asuras in the middle of their thighs;
they indeed tore them asunder in two at the middle of their hips. ||85||
All those who had fallen into the hands of Yama indeed died;
others, from afar, fled toward Vaidiśā for the sake of their lives.
The army of the Daityas became wretched, its enthusiasm destroyed and its leader gone;
it was shattered, cut to pieces, and for the most part defeated on all sides.
Then the messengers of Yama blew their conchs, kettledrums, and bigūlakas;
yet all of them, freed from fatigue by Vijaya, were cheerful of countenance.
Dancing, laughing, and making others laugh, they became joyful;
and Raktabīja, seeing Vijaya thus approaching from the southern quarter, [acted]. (89)
Beholding his own defeat, he became bowed with shame for a moment;
then he checked the fleeing army with the sounds of battle-drums.
And with battle-signals and shouts, he restrained the army commanders;
mounting his elephant himself, he went to the front for the sake of combat.
Then the soldiers and the commanders of the army, filled with great rage, rushed forward;
in an instant, they surrounded Yamarāja in the sky from all sides with their celestial chariots.
They surrounded him for the sake of his destruction and seized Yamarāja,
just as ten million moths and ten million parrots seize a cage.
In that manner, the hosts of Dānavas instantly held Yama, the lord;
the celestial chariot was no longer visible at all, being then shrouded by the clouds of the Daityas.
Yamarāja himself, out of anger, released his staff of death (kāladaṇḍa).
From that staff, hundreds and thousands of other staffs were produced.
Any demon whom that staff touches is instantly destroyed by its contact.
Right there it turns to ashes, and not even a bone remains. || 96 ||
Thus, indeed, many thousands of Daityas were slain then in the sky;
scorched by the staff of Yama, they went to the abodes of Yama.
But those who desired to live, seeing their destruction in an instant,
all fled and went away, abandoning even Pātāla itself.
Taking their sons, grandsons, daughters, wives, cattle, and even birds,
as well as their own excellent and worthy wealth, they entered the netherworld (pātāla).
"O Rādhikā, even though Raktabīja has died, in the course of time he will indeed become a great Daitya named Dhundhu."
In another age, other Daityas will become his allies;
meanwhile, the sage Baka-dāna, having learned of the destruction of the Asuras, [will act].
Having emerged from the water, he approached Dharmarāja;
he offered him hospitality and likewise bestowed praise upon him.
When Dharmarāja requested a messenger for the sake of protection,
he gave his own messenger named Arava, as well as a female messenger named Aravī.
He gave him a hundred male servants and a hundred female servants for the sake of protection;
they and those women took up residence at the hermitage of Bakadāna.
In that age, ten thousand sons named Āravas were born from him,
and from them, ten thousand daughters were born, who were produced through union with female messengers (dūtīs).
From them, O Rādhikā, more than ten million offspring were born there;
thus indeed, Yama destroyed the Dānavas in that place.
Having bestowed the kingdom upon his own envoy and having ensured the protection of the sage,
he ascended a celestial chariot and departed for the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
King Yama, having become a Vaiṣṇava, dwelt in the presence of Kṛṣṇa with his second form and his Vaiṣṇava attendants.
