Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and having caused his servants to bathe as well,
he constructed a great palace and established a residence at that sacred site.
Rudra, together with the hosts of Rudras, and Nārada, along with Sanat,
each established their own dwellings by the command of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Seventy-two thousand maidens, having bathed in the house of Hari, bowed down to Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī; they were then honored and fed. || 11 1 ||
By the command of their beloved wife, they remained continuously in the hermitage of Lomaśa;
and the celestial chariot always remained there, accompanied by the dowry.
Seeing the divine abode of Hari in the garden of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa, which was like heaven itself, those maidens were filled with their former desires.
One in whose corner that celestial mansion might dissolve—
by reading or hearing this account, such a person shall become meritorious.
For him there shall be the destruction of obstacles and his impurity shall perish;
he shall have no fear from the messengers of Dharmarāja.

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the Ten Thousand Daityas beginning with Raktabīja by means of Yamarāja, the Granting of the Kingdom to the Messenger named Arava, the Protection of the Sage Bakadāna, and the Origin of the Arava Lineage," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.
Śrī Rādhikā said: O Kṛṣṇa, who was this demon Raktabīja in a previous birth?
How did he again become Dhundhu; who is he, and what will he do? (1)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā, to this auspicious and excellent narrative arising from a previous creation.
When the night of the past kalpa had passed, Nārāyaṇa became a great fish.
Having placed the boat upon his own horn in the water together with Satyavān,
he took seeds for the sake of protecting the world and also for the purpose of future creation.
Having taken hold of a boat, he moved about upon the surface of the frosty waters;
there, at dawn, a great fish born of the ocean emerged from the water.
Having arrived there to fight with Nārāyaṇa in the form of a fish,
he then engaged in battle, desiring to devour the seeds situated upon the boat.
Then the Sudarśana discus was held by Nārāyaṇa in the form of the Fish;
it was released upon the head of the Fish, and the Fish indeed split into two parts.
From his blood-drops, millions of fish were born in the water at that time from the ocean-fish as it was being torn apart by the discus.
Then, drops of blood flew from his body and fell into the boat;
they adhered to some of the seeds that were there, O King.
And when, at the very dawn, those ten thousand Rākṣasas known as Raktabījas were indeed thrown from the boat into the water, || 9 ||
But immediately, by their very nature, they were born there in the water as sons of fish, all of them dwellers in the ocean waters.
They searched for an island, a lofty and eternal dwelling;
meanwhile, the water that had been like frost became dry by morning.
There, the earth with its mountains was seen situated within the waters;
then the Blessed One, in his incarnation as a fish, [spoke to] King Satyavān.
Having commanded, "Sow the seeds upon the earth," he instantly vanished;
and the king likewise [disappeared] along with that treasure of seeds.
He cast [seeds] upon the earth, in water, in the sky, in the wind, and in fire;
having sown all the seeds, he indeed left the boat in the water.
Indeed, those very subtle seeds which had become attached to the wooden planks and the cracks in the boat— 15.
Indeed, the Rakshasas with blood-seeds rushed to devour them;
having boarded the boat, they then ate the fine seeds.
From eating that, boys known as Ārabījakas were born, and likewise girls of beautiful youth were born as Ārabījyas. (17)
When all of them had been born, even the boat vanished from sight;
so too did all those offspring of Raktabīja known as the Ārabījas.
Assuming various forms at will, dwelling in the sky, and remaining without support,
they flew up from the ocean and searched for places of residence upon the earth.
Wherever our dwelling may be, there let water be all around us, and surrounding that, let there be earth as well as forests and the like. ||2.58.20||
Battlefields, forests, men, seeds, flowers, and fruits, as well as various caves, should exist there on all sides. ||21||
Thinking that such a place on earth, along with its inhabitants, was entirely filled with the Raktabījas, we must dwell there. (22)
The true earth, consisting of islands and continents, was accepted by the Ārabījas;
in ancient times, there was a great king named Raktabīja, born from the seed of Matsya.
From that [union], a king was then born among those subjects;
from him arose the great Ārabīja, a king who acted as an adversary to the gods.
Having slain him, King Yama duly gave his kingdom to his own follower, Arava,
for the protection of the sages.
Raktabīja was slain in battle and went to the world of Yama;
there, the legitimate son of Kaśyapa experienced the fruits of his karma. ||26||
Born from the womb of Danu, he will be named Dhundhu;
having propitiated Brahmā through ascetic penance, he shall attain invincibility against the gods.
He will swiftly conquer heaven and himself become Śakra;
meanwhile, the kingdom of the Asuras will then be established in Triviṣṭapa.
Out of fear of him, the thirty gods will indeed go to the world of Brahmā;
and Dhundhu will say to the Daityas, "O Daityas, how indeed shall we [proceed]? (29)
"Let us go to Satyaloka to conquer the gods and others.
Having heard this, the Daityas will say, "Indeed, there is no access for us there. (2.58.30)
Beyond this lies the great world inhabited by hosts of great sages;
there, the Daityas burn women with their wrathful glances.
Beyond that is Janaloka, where the Janas, who are gods, dwell;
beyond that is Tapoloka, and beyond that Satyaloka, where those devoted to Brahman abide.
Upon hearing the sound of the Veda, the gods and others rejoice,
while the asuras and those who share their nature undergo contraction.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, do not resolve to go there;
the palace of Vairāja is agitated and difficult for the Dānavas to ascend.
Having heard their words, Dhundhu will speak to the Daityas,
desiring to go to the abode of Brahmā in order to conquer the lords.
By what karma and in what manner do the Dānavas go there?
How does Indra set forth, and how indeed do the gods proceed? (36)
"O Daityas, speak here to me and we shall do exactly as you say;
then Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, will explain the means of accomplishment. (37)
In ancient times, the thousand-eyed one performed one hundred and one sacrifices;
by means of those most excellent horse-sacrifices (vājimedha), he attained the state of Brahmāsada.
Then, having heard the words of Śukra, he will indeed perform sacrifices;
and having addressed Śukra, he will send the Daityas and Dānavas toward the earth.
Then that best of rivers, the Devikā, which bestows success, will flow there;
he shall perform sacrifices with the Bhārgavas, the disciples of Śukra.
At that time, Svarbhānu and others, as well as the Asura Agnidhūma, shall become the partakers of the sacrificial portions there as protectors of the horse.
Its fragrance will indeed pervade the earth and ascend to heaven;
having smelled it, the gods, becoming despondent, will address the Creator.
"By the power of destiny, they shall go to the Supreme Lord residing in the milk and shall offer their petition;
O Janārdana, let it be heard. (43)
The powerful lord of the asuras named Dhundhu dwells there, surrounded by his forces;
he is the sovereign of the three worlds, and no protector for us is to be found. (44)
Now, having adopted the counsel of Śukra, he is prepared even to conquer those dwelling in the world of Brahmā, and he performs hundreds of sacrifices.
He desires to ascend to the world of truth (satyaloka) and to conquer the Creator;
therefore, O Supreme Lord, consider this without delay. (46)
"Listen to the means for the destruction of the sacrifice by which we may be thoroughly at ease;
having heard it, the Blessed One will speak, and you must go to his abode. (47)
Having said, "I shall go to conquer him," he will depart;
the Blessed One, having become a dwarf (Vāmana), will bathe in the waters of the Devikā.
He will fall into the waters of the Devikā in the vicinity of the sacrifice;
sinking for a moment and then surfacing, he will perform various movements in the water.
Thinking that even those worthy of sacrifice would sink [in the waters], they will quickly go to rescue him,
and having rescued him, they will place him upon the shore.
The sacrificial priests of Dhundhu will question that dwarf Brāhmaṇa:
"Who are you? From where have you come? And what is your purpose? (5.1)
Then that brahmin will say: "I am suffering, deprived of my home;
my father’s name is Prabhāsa, and by lineage I am Vāruṇa. (52)
"My brother has gone to Netrabhāsa, and I myself have gone to Gati-bhāsa;
having abandoned our beautiful dwelling, our father has also died. (53)
At the end of the year, the elder brother said, "Let us divide our house.
He replied, "There is no share for you whatsoever. (54)
For those who are humpbacked, dwarfed, or lame; for the impotent, as well as for those with leprosy, the insane, and the blind, no share of the inheritance exists. (55)
Pleasant speech, residence in the home, food, clothing, and so forth—only this much is given to them; they are not heirs to the inheritance.
Then, after being expelled from that house with great difficulty, I heard of the sacrifice and arrived; having entered the water, I began to bathe. (57)
Since I have been submerged and do not know how I was brought down, who are you that have arrived here, showing such affection like kinsmen? (58)
Who is this who shines among you, resembling Śakra?
May you show compassion if a refuge can be found here. (59)
Having thus heard the words of Vāmana, the brahmins will speak to Dhundhuka for the sake of alms, and Dhundhu will give them what is excellent.
A magnificent residence, female slaves, various jewels,
all kinds of household utensils, male servants, cows, and vehicles.
"Even though there is gold, chariots, horses, and elephants, Vāmana will not accept these riches while he is preaching the dharma of the virtuous. (62)
Having renounced female and male slaves, servants, the house, jewels, and household furnishings, as well as three steps of land for a seat, he will indeed then attain perfection.
When Dhundhu shall grant me three paces of land, then,
assuming the form of Vairāja, I shall traverse this earth with a single step.
With the second [hand] Hari will seize the cauldron, and with the third the Dānava; he will then lead him down to Pātāla.
Having given his own kingdom to the gods, he will become invisible;
then, when Bali has grown powerful, he will seize his kingdom and reduce it to a mere trifle.
Then Dhundhu will also provide assistance to Andhaka;
a great battle between Andhaka and Śaṅkara will take place.
Then Śambhu, having cast Śukrācārya into his mouth and held him within his belly,
will subsequently expel him through his penis.
Taking the form of Śukra, he will become the son of Śambhu by the name of Śukra;
then Mahendra himself shall go forth to fight with Indhaka.
When he shall strike Andhaka, whirling the thunderbolt above his head,
the thunderbolt will be ground to powder right upon Andhaka’s own head.
Then the Fire-god will surely grant him a terrifying spear,
and likewise the gods and Gandharvas will give him an auspicious chariot.
Then the wife of the sage Śamīka will indeed place that child upon the ground as the earth trembles. (72)
At that time, there will be two boys together;
of those two, one indeed named Mātali shall go to Mahendra.
Then he will become his charioteer and provide assistance;
at that time, Rudra, Mahendra, and likewise the other deities together [will do so].
And Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, will slay Andhaka;
from above the forehead of Śaṅkara, drops [of sweat] shall fall due to the blow of the mace.
They will fall even upon the blood and become terrifying;
[they are] the King of Vidyās, the King of Rudras, Caṇḍa, and also Pracaṇḍa. (76)
Kapālin, Ekakapālin, as well as Lalitarājaka,
and Vighnarāja as the eighth— these Bhairavas then arose from that.
From the forehead-plate of Śambhu, one virtuous daughter shall be born, named Caṇḍikā, who dwells upon the Hiṅgulā mountain. (78)
Then, having slain Andhaka, Śaṅkara will make his own host of attendants named Bhṛṅgi; thereafter Dhundhu will be filled with fear.
He shall quickly go to Pātāla; thereafter, after an interval of time, Hari will again provide assistance to Bali.
"And with Sudarśana, he shall slay Dhundhu while he is still alive.
Thus, O Rādhā, has the narrative of Raktabīja been told. (8.1)
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how was the fish of the waters killed by Viṣṇu’s disc? Why did it not attain purity, since demons were born in its lineage? (82)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Rādhikā, the water-fish, severed by Viṣṇu’s discus,
was quickly freed from sin and attained the status of Mahendra in heaven.
He alone, born of that very resolve, became the Lord of the Devas;
then, for the sake of initiating the first age, he descended upon the earth.
In this world, there was a devotee of Viṣṇu renowned as Suvarṇāṅgada;
he was an exceedingly noble man and a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||85||
Then, O Rādhikā, he went to the supreme, divine abode of Kṛṣṇa.
Now, as for those such as Raktabīja and Ārabīja, and others likewise—
Since they all became destroyers of seeds at the beginning of creation, they fell into the state of Rākṣasas due to the curse of Satyavrata. ||87||
Those who destroy the primary seed and annihilate things that ought not to be destroyed are great sinners and extreme evildoers, because they bring about the destruction of the lineage. (88)
Having reflected thus, the king then cursed those obstructors:
"You shall indeed become Asuras who cause the destruction of seeds. (89)
Thus were they born as Asuras because of their demonic disposition;
for they were indeed Rākṣasas, devourers of the embryos and the fetal stages of birds.
Those who destroy the seed of cattle, who destroy passion and virility, and who destroy the sheaths of seeds—these are considered tamasic asuras. ||91||
But when the destruction of an unattainable seed occurs, a great sin arises;
first, [this happened] when the goddess Pārvatī was in union with Śaṅkara. 92.
At the moment when the seed was obtained, the gods created obstacles;
the virtuous beloved, with a distressed inner soul, uttered a curse. (93)
The gods are the destroyers of my desire for offspring, acting as such for the sake of achieving their own ends;
they are indeed the slayers at the sowing of the seed, since they have been born directed toward Hara. ||94||
"Because I have been made childless and barren by you, you too shall be childless, and your wives shall likewise be barren. (95)
"May they always remain childless," she cursed the gods;
therefore, O Rādhikā, this was indeed the first sin: the destruction of the seed. (96)
The destruction of a woman’s menses is indeed a sin greater than even that;
and the destruction of an embryo is declared to be a sin even more excessive than that. (97)
The sin of destroying a child is more grievous than all others;
the killing of two who have just been married is ten million times more sinful. (98)
The sin of killing one who is pregnant is more than ten billion times a hundred million sins;
indeed, killing while the pair [of parents] has not yet completed their union is equivalent to the destruction of creation itself.
Indeed, evil arises from that; therefore, those who destroy seeds do not attain liberation.
For this reason, the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) is considered to bestow both merit and liberation.
Where the seed is not destroyed but is protected by its very nature, the merit of that protection is great; indeed, even the act of giving is performed through dharma. (101)
"O Rādhikā, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva themselves have always proclaimed this great merit; thus has the cause for his state as a rākṣasa been explained. (102)
Kṛṣṇa himself does not come within the range of sight of those who destroy seeds;
the Lord has brought about their destruction through the agency of Yama. (103)
The gift of a wife during her fertile season is declared by the gods to be a source of great merit for householders;
likewise, the gift of a lineage is proclaimed as exceedingly meritorious for those who establish a family line.
Those without lineage do not rescue at all, nor do they cross over the ocean of saṃsāra;
but ancestors who possess a lineage, being satisfied, rescue [their descendants] from the sea. 105.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Asuras Raktabīja and Arabīja, the Birth of the Daitya Dhundhu, and the Sin Consisting of the Destruction of Seeds," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Rādhikā; now that Caitra has passed, hear the second account of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself, which bestows liberation.
There is a region renowned as Bhālladeśa, honored by the Vaiṣṇavas;
there is a famous city named Dhavala, an excellent provincial capital.
In that place, there lived a merchant named Godhana, who was engaged in the business of trade;
he was full of wealth, intelligent, and had reached the further shore of mastery in the arts. || 3 ||
Once, he prepared to go from his own kingdom to Saurāṣṭra,
accompanied by a vast caravan and laden with many goods and other merchandise.
As he was traveling at night, he encountered a band of thieves on a dry,
waterless stretch of ground where there was only a single fishing net.
Then that merchant, having had all his wealth stolen and being constantly afflicted by grief,
wandered here and there until he came into the vicinity of the Jālikā tree.
Seeing the net devoid of deer, birds, and insects,
he— enduring his hunger and thirst with a parched throat— approached the side of a tree.
He sat down and fell asleep; having rested, he became refreshed.
When he rose at midday, he beheld a ghost.
Surrounded by hundreds of pretas, being carried on a comfortable seat by pretas arriving from all sides toward the tree of Jālikā; || 9 ||
The King of the Pretas saw that merchant’s son, whose mind was steadfast, as he arrived at the very tree where the merchant’s son had been.
The deceased man offered a welcome, and the merchant did likewise;
having exchanged greetings concerning everyone's welfare, they saluted one another.
Then the merchant and the preta sat comfortably in the shade;
the lord of the pretas asked, "O merchant, from where have you come?"
Where is your dwelling, and where will you go from this place? And how have you come to take refuge in this desolate spot? (1.3)
Thus questioned, the merchant said: "Though I was once possessed of wealth, having been robbed of my riches by thieves in the forest, I now wander about in extreme misery."
But due to the merchant's distress, the preta became sorrowful for a moment;
he spoke to the merchant as if to his own kinsman, saying, "Do not grieve. (15)
Wealth will come again if you possess the power of fortune;
when fortune wanes, wealth perishes, but it returns upon its resurgence.
For this body that is subject to decay, no prosperity can arise through anxiety;
for the sun, both rising and setting occur perpetually.
The trees have become withered and yet have sprouted again;
likewise, there is brilliance in the moon for one fortnight, and the waning of its luster for the other.
In summer, the rivers run dry; in the rainy season, they are filled with water.
In some fields there is an abundance of crops, while in others there is a total lack of grain.
The eyes were dull and drowsy, yet at times they possessed the splendor of a lotus petal; and the sky was turbid at one time, while at another it was stainless and radiant.
A lamp burns at night but produces no light by day;
likewise, one may be a king in one place, a merchant-leader in another, or a servant in yet another. (21)
In one place he is the Teacher, in another the disciple; in some places he is free from the two extremes, and in others he is the glorious Lord of Lakṣmī, while in yet others he is devoid of fortune.
In childhood, all embodied beings are naturally free from possessions;
in youth, they are pervaded by craving; and in old age, they are devoid of power. (23)
They are born by the force of time and by their prior karma, because wealth was previously acquired from various sources in the form of debt. (24)
What is given to them does not indeed follow one as a debt later on;
they—the sons, grandsons, wives, and family members—are the givers. (25)
Kings, servants, and attendants indeed become bound by the fetters of the [four] castes;
or else, taking the form of thieves, they strike with violence. ||26||
Neither given away nor enjoyed, and though acquired in abundance, he increases it with effort and seeks its destruction. (27)
Wealth laughs at the lord of wealth; your status as lord of wealth is false, because you have not established that true existence through an exchange with one who is worthy. (28)
O merchant, death stands in close proximity; you must depart, leaving everything behind. Therefore, your lordship over wealth belongs to the wealth itself, and not to you.
Oh, how great is the power of greed! Even though he possesses wealth amounting to one hundred and seven crores, he still desires to accumulate more, even from what is found in his hair.
In its acquisition, there is supreme suffering arising from service and the like;
in its preservation as well, there is supreme suffering, for the tigress of anxiety leaps about.
Even in expenditure there is the suffering of loss; in enjoyment there is suffering and illness;
in pride there is the suffering of war and the like; and from wealth, death arises. (32)
Therefore, wealth that is not employed for the sake of Dharma is said to be suffering;
but when wealth is applied to Dharma, happiness arises from that Dharma and no suffering.
From the Dharma comes peace; through union with the Dharma comes the destruction of craving and solitude;
contentment with whatever is obtained, and conduct such as service to the gods. (34)
Within the family, there is a state of being like a sentient being, free from passion, hatred, and the like;
one is devoid of fear from thieves and other dangers, and even sleep occurs with ease. (35)
O merchant, such virtues as these bring happiness when one is poor; however, when one possesses wealth, they repeatedly give rise to the faults of suffering. (36)
In this regard, there is no great wonder, for [the cycle of] coming and going is like the waters of the ocean;
all wealth is indeed flickering, for fortune is always unstable. (37)
Life is also fickle; do not grieve over wealth.
By fortune everything will come about again, even for one who strives. 38.
Having spoken thus and summoned his servants, the deceased man said to them:
"Today this excellent merchant has arrived as a guest at our house. (39)
This dear friend of mine is venerable to me; he is my coeval and my countryman.
Seeing him, I feel as though I have seen my own kinsmen. (2.59.40)
"Today, indeed, incomparable joy has arisen within me upon his arrival.
Having said this, the preta recollected an excellent meal. (41)
Just then, a new, sturdy, and auspicious vessel arrived for him,
filled with sweet food as well as curd-rice.
Indeed, for the purpose of eating, there were vessels filled with leafy vegetables, soup, sour gruel, and so forth, as well as a new, sturdy pot filled with cold water. (43)
Then, seeing the water-pot and the cooking vessel, the Lord of the Dead said:
"Arise, O best of merchants! Wash your hands and your face."
Having spoken thus and offered water, the King of the Dead seated him upon a splendid throne; he then gave him sweet food, curd, and water.
The merchant ate rice, rice-gruel, and vegetables; he gave every kind of food to those who were hungry, into both vessels and onto leaves. (46)
The pretas ate the sweet food and delicacies with great respect, and they drank the water; thereafter, the Lord of the Pretas also consumed that which remained. ||47||
They ate and drank water, and thereafter they all became satisfied; the cooking pot, the water-vessel, and even the remaining food were entirely gone.
While the merchant was looking on, it suddenly vanished from sight;
having witnessed this wonderful marvel, the merchant indeed questioned [the sage]. (49)
"This vessel is full of food and this water-jar is filled;
tell me, O foremost of spirits, how did these come to be found here in the forest? (2.59.50)
Nevertheless, how is it that your servants are entirely emaciated, while you yourself are not at all well-nourished? Tell me, why is there such weakness? (91)
At that moment, a beautiful, new white garment arrived there;
it was then given with devotion by the preta to the merchant.
Seeing that wonder, [the merchant] asked, "From where has this garment come?
And the merchant questioned the ghost; the ghost spoke exactly as it had happened. (53)
"O merchant, in the past, in the city named Dhavala, I was a Brahmin named Prabhānātha; I was always a cook. (54)
I have a preeminent merchant, wealthy and a promoter of righteousness;
he is a devotee of Viṣṇu, a patron, my master, and a bestower of wealth. ||55||
This man named Dharmavardhana always commands me in matters of dharma, for the sake of dharma, to spend as much as he desires. (56)
He gives unhesitating commands for the sake of charity and for the sake of helping others;
yet I am a miser, greedy by nature, even though I possess abundant wealth. (57)
I give nothing to the gods, nor to the Brahmins, nor do I perform acts of charity; nor do I render any assistance to any living being who is destitute. (58)
I do not consider ascetics, holy men, or those devoted to dharma to be anything at all;
I do not even eat my fill, so what need is there to mention my greed for the property of others? (59)
For it is certain that the riches of one who lacks merit do not endure;
likewise, I did not possess such merit at that time, for I have not experienced [such fortune]. (2.59.60)
If, through negligence, I consume curd, milk, ghee, and so forth, or sweet food and sweet water, then grief arises. (6.1)
"Alas! Today I have indeed made an expenditure that is both useless and harmful;
sleep does not come to me at night as I am preoccupied with thoughts of my expenses. (62)
In the morning, whatever happens to me in any way whatsoever, I remain thus—so greedy and so excessively thirsty. (63)
When shall I pass my time, sustaining myself with meals of rice, sesame, oil-cakes, husks, vegetables, and other such coarse foods? (64)
Thus, although I possess wealth, no merit has been gained without giving;
a great length of time has passed for me, and now this solar eclipse has arrived. (65)
Likewise, when Śravaṇa-dvādaśī arrives in the month of Bhādrapada,
people go day after day to the Sābhramatī for the sake of the holy ford.
And I, having fasted on the eleventh day together with the merchant,
went to the Sābhramatī river to bathe from that very day of the eleventh.
I remained at that holy site until there was a solar eclipse;
during those days of Ekādaśī, that merchant gave away wealth by the millions.
Garments, excellent vessels, and cows—these were also given as gifts there by me according to my ability, having seen [the recipient] with great shame. (69)
A single new vessel made of dhauta was given to a Brahmin who knew the Vedas;
a new cooking pot, filled with food and full of sweets, was also offered.
Then, curd-rice with sour gruel and other items, as well as leafy vegetables, were offered; likewise, a water-vessel was given, and a wooden vehicle was also bestowed. (71)
At that time, an umbrella was indeed given to the brahmin for the sake of shade;
and the merchant's group of servants were employed by me for the sake of the brahmin. (72)
O best of merchants, only this much was offered by me at that time;
nothing else whatsoever was given by me, even throughout ten thousand years. (73)
Then, in the course of time, having met my death, I went to the state of a preta;
and these people, who had not given gifts themselves, lived instead upon the food provided by me. (74)
The servants of that merchant named Godhana have come under my control;
this wooden vehicle has been obtained, and those servants have been acquired by me. (75)
A cooking pot filled with delicious food was obtained;
this very thing, once given, returns day after day even at midday. (76)
As long as I do not eat food, it does not attain dissolution;
but when I have eaten and drunk, everything becomes dissolved.
"Because of the gift of the parasol, this tree has indeed been obtained by me eternally;
I dwell here for the sake of residence, and the pretas perform service for me. (78)
"All this that you have said regarding how giving brings about cessation [of suffering]—by that very sin, I formerly fell into the state of a preta. (79)
"Due to greed and craving, I, though a Brahmin, have fallen into the state of a preta;
for by the water and food given even once, I am sustained. (2.59.80)
Indeed, having given [alms] once every day, I always eat;
for one who constantly bestows gifts, heaven shall indeed become eternal.
Now, O merchant, I shall also act for your benefit in every way.
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake. ||82||
"O merchant, go quickly to that hermitage of Lomaśa, the abode of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa; perform your ritual bath and offer oblations there. (83)
"Perform the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) in my name;
by that gift of the rice-ball there, I shall instantly be released from the state of a preta. (84)
Being liberated, I shall attain the same world as those who bestow gifts;
for the auspicious eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) in the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada is meritorious. (85)
When conjoined with the asterisms of Budha and Śravaṇa, that [day] brings me supreme benefit;
or else, perform my śrāddha on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika.
On the day of the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, reflect that my liberation will certainly take place then. 87.
Having said this, he gave him gold, diamonds, and other such treasures;
then, placing that merchant upon his shoulder, he abandoned him in Surāṣṭra.
On the eleventh day of the month of Bhādrapada, he went to Aśvasarovara;
there, he performed the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased ancestors in their proper order.
Then he duly performed a great śrāddha for his kinsmen, followed by one for his ancestors, and likewise for himself, though without the use of sesame seeds.
The merchant performed the offering of funeral cakes for his kinsmen and others born of his lineage;
indeed, by means of the giving of śrāddhas and other rites, he liberated them all.
Then all those who were liberated from karma arrived in that presence, possessing divine forms and divine attire, and resplendent with a brilliance exceeding that of the sun. ||92||
There the merchant gave them water and a meal of sweet food;
then he led them, possessing divine bodies, to the hermitage of Lomaśa.
Then Lomaśa caused her to hear this Vaiṣṇava mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā. (94)
And he gave them garlands of *tulasī* and the nectar of his feet;
then the merchant departed, taking with him all those who had been liberated.
They all bowed down to the palace of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which was adorned with beautiful golden ornaments,
and worshipped Nārāyaṇa with great reverence.
Having drunk the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet, they became ten million liberated souls;
by the command of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, they ascended divine vehicles.
Then they went to that supreme, imperishable abode known as Goloka;
thereafter, O Rādhā, this merchant went to his own place.
In that city named Dhavala, he worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
having practiced the ninefold devotion, he eventually met his end.
Having become a god, and then a Gandharva and even a Guhyaka, he subsequently became King Virāṭ; for he was indeed a supreme devotee of the Lord.
He sent [him] to the primordial Supreme Brahman, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
at the end of his body, having praised Him again and again, he went to the abode of Hari.
Thus, O Rādhā, has been told how this miracle of Hari occurred,
whereby the pretas attained liberation upon seeing Him and assumed divine bodies.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Pretas through Śrāddha at Lake Aśvapaṭṭa on the Eleventh Day of Bhādrapada in the Tretā Age, and the Dialogue with the Preta-merchant," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhā, listen now to another wonder concerning Hari at that time. There was a righteous king named Udaya, who was a worshiper of the gods. || 1 ||
In the region of Aravalyadri, his sovereignty was most extensive;
and the auspicious city named Udaya served as his capital.
The king undertook a supreme vow: eating only once during the four months of the rainy season, daily giving gifts, feeding Brahmins and holy men, and tending to cows.
The offering of food and clothing to the destitute, children, and virtuous women;
likewise, wealth for the gift of knowledge and excellent riches for temples. (4)
One should always perform the *havana* in the morning and the ritual bath in the waters at night;
thus, while one is properly performing this vow throughout the month of Śrāvaṇa in every way, (5)
He had the desire to bathe for one month in the lake;
thus, during the month of Āṣāḍha, he went to the Dhīravīra lake.
Accompanied by a limited retinue, the king established his residence on the bank of a river within the hermitage of the sage Āryāyaṇa in the forest.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, having risen early every morning with haste,
he should bow down to Nārāyaṇa and meditate upon the infallible Śrī Viṣṇu.
Having bathed and worshipped Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Light, and having worshipped with devotion Rādheśvara, the Lord of Pārvatī; || 9 ||
Then he constantly performs worship of the sage Āryāyaṇa;
thereafter, he always goes forth specifically to behold the sacred fords (tīrthas).
Satītīrtha, Śambhutīrtha, and after that Cakratīrtha;
furthermore, Kṛṣṇatīrtha, Svāmitīrtha, and Mañjulātīrtha as well.
Then there is Sūryatīrtha, Indratīrtha, and beyond that Brahmatīrtha;
furthermore, Muktatīrtha, Ṛṣitīrtha, and Dharmatīrtha, which is a reservoir of water.
Having thus visited these and other sacred fords all around the lake,
and having circumambulated the lake while bestowing gifts of every kind, || 13 ||
Having given gold, silver, garments, various vessels,
and gifts of food and edibles, he then goes to his own abode.
Having done this, he then performs the fire sacrifice (homa) and the Vaiśvadeva rite;
[he honors] the Brahmins, the sages, virtuous and chaste women, holy men, children, and the helpless.
Having divided the food and fed the guests as well as his followers,
the king himself then ate after bowing down to the sage Ārṣyaśṛṅga.
Thus, by the power of his merit, whatever sins the king had committed in the past were completely consumed on all sides. (17)
Furthermore, a great heap of merit has been offered by him to Kṛṣṇa;
consequently, the favor of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa alone remains for him.
He considers nothing else to be as great a merit as clarity of mind;
thus Harikṛṣṇa became pleased, having entered the heart of the noble sage Ayanarṣi.
The sage said to the king: "O King, come into my presence;
receive the supreme mantra which the Lord Puruṣottama [taught]."
Then the king sat down before the sage; the sage [uttered]: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master, svāhā! (21)
Thus he imparted the mantra as well as a garland of tulasī;
thereafter, the sage Āryāyaṇa spoke the mantra to his followers as well.
Having received the mantra and bowed to the sage, the king, accompanied by his followers, went home;
there, on the bank of the river, he sat down in his own leaf-hut.
Just then, the youthful one arrived there, adorned with a flute in his hand, and attended by Rādhā, Prabhā, Lakṣmī, and Pāravatī. ||24||
The Blessed Lord himself, whose form is perfectly suited to every form, filled with joy, repeatedly laughed while making his beloved laugh, as he overflowed with aesthetic rapture. ||25||
Divine, surrounded by wives of divine form, he was adorned with a golden crown enriched with a crest of peacock feathers. || 26 ||
Wearing garments as pure as fire and resplendent with divine ornaments, his hands are marked with the fish-banner, the svastika, the bow, the trident, and other [symbols]. || 27 ||
A short distance from his side is the virtuous Lakṣmī-Śrī-Kambharā,
and a short distance on the other side is the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Other female and male servants likewise gathered there in the leaf-hut;
there, a blissful splendor shone forth, equal to millions upon millions of suns.
Beholding that beautiful form, the king stood motionless there;
his eyes closed, their rays obstructed by the splendor.
After opening it a moment later, as soon as he looked at Keśava, Kṛṣṇa became one with that form— Śrī Hari himself.
He showed him Saurāṣṭra, as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā,
Aśvapaṭṭasara, and likewise the hermitage of Śrī Lomaśa.
Likewise [he saw] the illustrious Kambharā-Lakṣmī, as well as Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa,
crores, arbuds, and hundreds of millions of maidens, and all the sacred fords (tīrthas) in every direction.
Having thus demonstrated this, the Blessed One caused everything to dissolve;
then, in an instant, he showed him his own two feet.
Pātāla is above that, and Rasātala is beyond that;
Mahātala is in the two shanks, and Talātala is in the two knees. (35)
Sutala is in the lower part of the earth, and Vitala is below the thighs;
Atala is at the base of the thighs; [he saw] the Daityas and Dānavas residing there.
He showed him the serpents, the nāgas, other living beings, as well as rivers, mountains, and the expanse of the earth, along with Śeṣa and the tortoise.
He placed the earth upon his hips and the Bhuvarloka upon his loins; beyond that, he placed Svargaloka at his navel and Maharloka in his abdomen, and Janaloka in his heart.
He showed him the world of austerity (tapoloka) in his mouth and the world of truth (satyaloka) on his forehead;
he also showed him the seven coverings within his skin.
Having thus displayed it, he then caused that form to vanish in an instant;
thereafter, he revealed to him his own Vaiṣṇava form.
To him who has a thousand heads, who is beautiful, and who possesses a thousand hands and feet,
he indeed showed that water at his two feet.
He meditated on fire, wind, and space, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, at his feet;
likewise, he meditated on Jala and Vaikuṇṭha at his shanks, and Mahāviṣṇu at his knees;
and Bhūmā at his thighs.
And the Pradhāna is at the root of the thighs, and likewise the Puruṣa is at the penis. ||43||
She showed Prakṛti on her hips and Vāsudeva at her navel;
she likewise showed Kālapuruṣa on her waist and Saṃkarṣaṇa at her side.
And on his side Keśava showed Pradyumna, while on his belly he showed Aniruddha;
in his two flanks Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, and on his chest the maidservants of Ananta,
as well as the powers such as Rādhā and Ramā.
And upon their necks were millions, billions, and hundreds of millions of pearls, which were portions of the very nature of Brahman.
He revealed the world of immortality in his mouth, the imperishable Brahman in his eyes, and a mass of splendors upon his forehead.
There, Hari revealed his own supreme abode at the *brahmarandhra* to Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī and the illustrious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa. 48.
There, the king beheld a divine lion-throne situated there, and likewise Hari seated upon it, being served by him. ||49||
Then once again, all of that became invisible,
except for him who remained in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā in the form of a child.
The king beheld his own glorious self, served by ten million embodied beings;
there, the monarch again saw himself standing nearby.
Then, seeing everything dissolved in an instant, the king was struck with wonder;
thereafter, in another moment, he beheld his own beautiful hut.
Having become composed and bowed to the quarters, he remained established in meditation and offered praise:
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrīnivāsa, the subduer of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti). (53)
Homage be to you, the unconquered god, the great-souled one;
homage be to you, the independent, the peaceful, the desireless. (54)
Salutations to the primordial God, who consists of all the gods;
salutations to You, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the seer and the original form. ||55||
Homage to you who are always manifest as the one without obstruction;
homage to you who are hidden, the light of the quarters, and the Lord of Qualities. ||56||
Homage to you who are inconceivable, immeasurable, and incomparable;
homage to you who are free from thought, primordial, and eternal. ||57||
Salutations to You, the Ancient One; salutations be to You who are devoid of qualities.
Salutations to the foundation of the universe; salutations to You who are established in Brahman.
Salutations again and again to Padmanābha, to Yoga, and to Govinda;
salutations be to You, the Lord of the Universe, who is known through Sāṃkhya. || 59 ||
Salutations to you, Hari, the protector of Śiva, Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to you, the Supreme Self, the giver of the immeasurable, whose strides are immeasurable.
Salutations again and again to You who are adorned with the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the mace, and the lotus;
salutations be to the Great Serpent, to the Lion, and to the Dweller in the Vedas.
Salutations to you, the great fish, the beloved, and the tortoise;
salutations to you, the dwarf, the long one, and the four-armed one.
Salutations again and again to the one praised by Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Gandharvas; salutations to Acyuta, who is all-pervading and who reclines upon the king of serpents.
Salutations again and again to the one who is milk-white, to the black one, and to the one with a golden luster;
salutations to you, the wearer of yellow garments and the destroyer of the Daityas and other foes.
Salutations to you, the imperishable, the lord of the imperishable, whose navel is a lotus;
salutations to you, the four-faced god, who possesses five faces.
Salutations to you, who dwell in the milk-ocean, who are glory, and who are beauty; to the giver of boons, the Lord of all, the beloved, and the sovereign of women.
Salutations to you, the most excellent one, the remover of obstacles, who are fond of devotion;
salutations to the one with lotus-like, long eyes, the one with a parrot-like nose, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Salutations again and again to you, the Lord of Yoga, the tree, the one with branches;
salutations again and again to you, the sage who is the path for the gods and the virtuous. ||68||
Salutations to you who appear in the form of the Enchantress (Mohinī) and who dwell within all living beings;
salutations to you as the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Śarabha. ||69||
I bow to the immutable one, the cause of all, the ancient Puruṣa, the beloved of Māyā, the beloved of Īśvara, and the beloved of all.
The Knower of the Field, the Lord of Time and Māyā, the Lord of the Vyūhas, the liberated soul, Vāsudeva, the beloved of Satī, the Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. ||7 1||
I bow down to that Kṛṣṇa, the delighter of Yaśodā, the young cowherd boy, who dwells in the supreme abode and is the most excellent of persons. 72.
I take refuge in Hari, whom the Brahman-sages call the eternal form of Brahman, the Lord of the Imperishable, and the Lord of Liberation. ||73||
I take refuge in the Lord, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, whose chest is streaked with white lotuses, who wears necklaces of three strands, and who is beautified by sixteen auspicious signs. 74.
In whom the universe resides and who is the universe itself; that in whom everything is established;
the source of all beings, the supreme Lord endowed with divine qualities. (75)
I take refuge in the supreme goal of the virtuous who are free from attachment,
in the Blessed One who dwells within the self, who dwells within women, the lotus-eyed one.
With devotion, I take refuge in the one worthy of refuge, who is compassionate toward his devotees, and who,
when the time of death has arrived, reveals his very self.
The Supreme Lord indeed leads His own devotee to His own abode;
I bow to that Supreme God, the Best of Persons, the bestower of liberation. (78)
Indeed, everything from the netherworld (pātāla) up to truth and the rest is contained within Him;
everything ending with Mahāmāyā is contained within that Janārdana.
I take refuge in that supreme Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, in whom infinite millions of abodes find their place within the Supreme Lord. 2.60.80.
O Lord, I do not know how to praise you as you truly exist;
I do not know your true nature, for I know you only from the outside. (8.1)
O Kṛṣṇa, that form consisting of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa which you have shown to me out of compassion is the fruit of my penance and the fruit of your grace. (82)
The abode was revealed, as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā;
Aśvapaṭṭasara was also shown, along with the hermitage of Lomaśa.
O Protector, I wish to see you again and again through service;
I desire your favor—thus, be the granter of my boon. (84)
Thus praised, the beginningless and glorious Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who bears the discus and the lotus, immediately manifested His presence. 85.
The lotus-eyed Lord, who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge, being full of joy,
spoke sweetly to that high-souled Udaya.
O King, I am pleased again and again by your hymn of praise;
and O King, through the connection with Āryāyaṇa, everything desired shall be yours.
"Before long, you shall have a dwelling in my field;
O King, I will lead you to my field by way of Varuṇa. (88)
"O King, through their yoga and my yoga, this shall become a sacred ford on the river; and those who recite this hymn, whether in a house or in the forest," (89)
Those people who, at this sacred site of the Dhīravīra lake, shall attain the supreme perfection whose very nature is the attainment of me.
Beasts, birds, insects, as well as trees, creepers, and the like, will drink the water and attain the purifying liberation. ||9.1||

Those who shall here offer, according to the prescribed rite, ancestral rites (śrāddha), gifts, recitation of mantras (japa), fire oblations (homa), libations (tarpaṇa), food, and water—for them there will be liberation. ||92||
Having spoken thus to the king, the Blessed One assumed an invisible state;
the king then chanted many times to the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He sang, he danced, he meditated, he laughed, and he wept;
he stood still, he served, he worshipped, and he gazed upon Him in whatever manner [He appeared]. (94)
He indeed dispatched his servants to his own city of Udayapattana,
and he commanded his son Nāgadeva to bestow the kingdom upon him.
There, the king, the best of devotees, conducted himself like a saintly person;
while he was sleeping at night on the eighth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the lord of clouds sent down rain.
The lakes, rivers, and wells took on the appearance of water like the ocean;
then, due to excessive rain, the leaf-huts were submerged within the waters. (97)
The people who had gone to their destruction, more than a hundred in number, were submerged in the water;
they remembered the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with extreme intensity. (98)
Immediately, O Rādhikā, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the ocean of mercy and the protector, took that eternal boat and departed. 99.
And assuming a thousand forms, wherever people— whether children, the elderly, and so forth, men, women, or even animals— were submerged in the water, [he rescued them].
He rescued them all; not even a single one met with death.
And the great sage Āryāyaṇa, who had entered into a state of meditative absorption while in the water, was also saved.
Having lifted it up, the Blessed One, the abode of compassion, held it upon a boat;
that boat was then placed by the Supreme Self upon the great river. 102.
Having rescued more than two hundred who were submerged therein, he protected them;
at that time, he also protected the animals and flocks of birds so that they might live.
The king and all the people, remaining alive, worshipped the glorious Narayana with undivided devotion; their boat remained upon the surface of the water.
O Rādhikā, she was indeed carried slowly upon the water, guided by Kṛṣṇa and protected by Kṛṣṇa; what cause for pain could there possibly be there? 105.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the King of Udayapura’s Vision of the Lord while staying on the bank of the Dhīravīra Lake during Cāturmāsya, His Being Submerged in Water due to Excessive Rainfall, and His Protection by the Lord via a Boat," in the second section (Tretā-santāna) of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O Rādhikā; our boat, accompanied by Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa, was occupied by two hundred men upon the waters of the earth.
The Blessed One carries her away with his former momentum and protects her;
and the waters that have gradually merged into the great river [flow on]. || 2 ||
At the confluence of the great river Bhramarā,
the boat was then on the verge of sinking in the water, but it was saved by Kṛṣṇa.
In Gurjara, that river was indeed long, deep, and terrifying;
driven by the force of its flood, it then traveled for a hundred krośas.
Then all those who had traveled by boat, having arrived not very far from the city called Lūnāpaṭa, were filled with great wonder. || 9 ||
Then they saw a forest ahead;
subsequently, due to the force of the current, the boat was carried away for a distance of fifty krośas.
The people traveling by boat beheld the great tīrtha of Devīkoṭa,
and beyond that, at a distance of fifty krośas, they saw Bhadrāyana.
Then, ahead of them, they reached the city of Kaṭhina, as well as the great pilgrimage site of Stambhapura and Kāvyatīrtha in its vicinity.
In the midst [of it], the great river, resembling the ocean, shone;
there, that boat, manned by people, moved upon the water where there was no ground.
Protected by Śrī Hari, that river Sābhramatī flows toward the ocean when its waters have merged with those of the unexcavated sea.
The boat, which had not yet reached the shore, crossed the confluence of the Dardurikā and the ocean and then reached a supreme island. || 11 ||
The vast [river] of the Lord of Śrī, supported by a thousand men through his power,
having crossed the Narmadā trench, reached the shore of Saurāṣṭra.
At the confluence of the Śatrujitā river with the ocean, she was made stable;
there, they all indeed partook of food and drink with great ease.
Then the boat, propelled by Kṛṣṇa, went first to Gopanātha,
and from there it proceeded further to Mādhuka and then to Jāphalita.
Then, having made the sky auspicious, he went to the city of Kṛṣṇāvatī;
from there he went to Somanātha, and after that also to Makarālaya.
Having seen the confluence of the Bhadrā and the ocean, he went to the city of Svarṇavatī;
then, entering Kacchākhāta, he arrived near Camatkārapura.
Then that boat, having assumed the form of a celestial chariot (vimāna), soared into the sky by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. 17.
She arrived swiftly through the sky at the Aśvapaṭṭa lake,
in a divine vehicle resembling the moon and radiant with the splendor of the sun.
Adorned with gold, worshipped by the gods, and protected by Kṛṣṇa,
it descended near the lake accompanied by two hundred people.
Shouts of "Victory! and cries of "Hail! arose there again and again;
the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā appeared full of enthusiasm.
The entire field was gazed upon,
and the golden temple was seen, along with the auspicious, lofty peak of the great devotee’s palace.
Kambharā’s splendor was seen, and Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa was seen;
likewise, the sage Lomaśa was seen and the city was beheld. 22.
And they descended from the celestial chariot accompanied by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, other devotees named Udaya, consisting of both women and men, also descended. (23)
Then the celestial chariot created by Kṛṣṇa vanished,
and Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa also disappeared along with his caravan.
Having seen his invisible form, they were struck with supreme wonder;
and all those pilgrims, having questioned the people again and again, [proceeded].
The gods went to where Bālakṛṣṇa was resplendent;
having all been granted a vision by this Kṛṣṇa, they were protected by him.
Remembering this, they were filled with joy and shed tears of love;
Bālakṛṣṇa then granted them a great abode worthy of their residence.
Provided with all necessary utensils and graced by male and female servants,
all the holy fords duly performed their rites around the Aśvasaras lake.
Then the Blessed Lord himself gave sweet foods and drinks—
edibles, chewables, lickables, suckables, and likewise various flavors.

The Blessed One, who is compassionate and affectionate toward his devotees, out of pity caused to be given powders for perfuming the mouth and other such substances that are to be rubbed upon the body. (2.61.30)
The Blessed One protected them all until the end of the four-month period,
and Lomaśa also gave them mantras and garlands of tulasī.
Having attained the divine Vaiṣṇava splendor in the presence of the Lord of Śrī,
they were beheld by Kṛṣṇa and became divine, endowed with divine qualities.
Having directly realized this Bālakṛṣṇa, the Great Lord,
who is the Supreme Brahman and the abode of bliss, they took refuge in that Supreme Controller.
Every day Lomaśa instructed them for the sake of liberation, saying:
"Listen to this beautiful and supreme means for attaining the highest good."
He whose body is everything and who exists within all—by praising him, one attains eternal protection from saṃsāra. (35)
Today I shall speak this hymn dedicated to Kṛṣṇa;
may Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord whose weapon is the discus, be present before me in the east. (36)
May Gadādhara Bālakṛṣṇa be with me always on the right;
may Śārṅgadhṛk Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa be with me forever on the west.
May Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, holding a sword, be ever present to my north;
may Hṛṣīkeśa be in the corners, and Janārdana in every center.
On earth may he be in the form of the Boar, and in the sky the Lord Narasimha;
and may the Sudarśana discus be exceedingly sharp as a razor’s edge on all sides.
May the mace, with its thousand edges raised aloft, strike down the hungry ghosts, the Rākṣasas who roam at night, the wolves, and the Piśācas.
The Śārṅga bow of Hari is for striking down the Kuṣmāṇḍas and others, as well as the Yakṣas, Daityas, Jṛmbhakas, cruel birds, and Vināyakas. (41)
By the sound of Viṣṇu’s conch, Śaṅkha shall slay the wicked serpents, as well as lions, tigers, śarabhas, venomous snakes, and other beasts. ||42||
May Viṣṇu’s lotus, through its fragrance, render my enemies gentle;
may it, by its remembrance, steal away their mental fluctuations, and by its strength and luster, take away their power and vigor. (43)
May he also pacify those who steal prosperity and enjoyments, those who take away auspicious marks, and those who seize one's wife, children, wealth, and home.
From the chanting of the names of Hari, may there be health for my senses, as well as health of intellect, health of mind, and health of body that brings happiness. (45)
May Hari be at my back, in front, on both sides, and in the corners;
may this Lord be in my crest-lock and in my nails; may Hari be the protection of my skin.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, svāhā!
Thus, O Rādhikā, did the sage Śrī Lomaśa [recite] this protective hymn (rakṣāstotra). 47.
Having first given [this] to all of them, he then related an illustration:
"In the past, in the city of Vaṭāsīna, there was a king named Krūrasiṃha. (48)
A betrayer of gods, brahmins, and virtuous women; a slanderer; the lowest of kṣatriyas; one who causes suffering to others; a base person who is by nature merciless. (49)
Deprived of the gift of Dharma and shunning the service of the virtuous,
he was indeed born at the end of his life as a fierce night-stalker in the forest.
Whichever animal, bird, or human he encountered in the forest, he would act with such cruelty as to think, "This one is to be eaten" or "This one is to be killed. (51)
Whatever animal or other creature he sees, that very one he seizes and, devoid of compassion, quickly devours as soon as it comes within the range of his arms. (52)
Thus, after a long period of time had passed, old age came upon that wicked man as he was wandering somewhere on the bank of the Narmadā.
While he was looking on, a brahmin ascetic named Jitaśravas, a sage devoted to yoga who had mastered his senses, arrived there.
Seeing him, the lord of the Rākṣasas ran swiftly to devour him;
meanwhile, the twice-born one quickly repeated the protective mantra again and again. (55)
Upon hearing this, the Rākṣasa immediately became paralyzed and rendered senseless;
overcome by the hymn of praise, he was unable either to advance or to retreat.
His fury having subsided, the Rākṣasa stood right there suddenly until the end of the day arrived for the twice-born man who was chanting his prayers.
Then, at the conclusion of his recitation, he beheld that night-stalker,
dejected, with his strength and vigor destroyed, fleeing in all directions, and deprived of his luster.
Filled with compassion, the brahmin repeatedly consoled the Daitya and asked him the reason for his state as a Rākṣasa and likewise for his arrival there.
The Rākṣasa related everything: his previous history, how he came to the abode of the Rākṣasas, and his arrival there for the purpose of devouring [them].
Despondent and deprived of happiness, he said to the brahmin, "Be gracious!
I have committed many sins and have killed many virtuous beings. (6.1)
He forcibly enjoyed many women, even widows,
and he brought about the great destruction of innocent beings.
Although I have always consumed liquor and meat in many ways, I desire liberation from that sin through your grace. (63)
Perform for me the practice of Dharma, which is sufficient to pacify that sin;
quickly perform that which brings about the destruction of this evil and bestows liberation.
Having heard the words of Niśāṭa, Jitaśravas said to him:
"Protection has been afforded to me here, and by me, you too have been purified. (65)
"O Rākṣasa, since you have developed the desire for liberation, go to Kuṅkumavāpikā, at the Aśva-sarovara lake in Saurāṣṭra, where Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides. (66)
Having bathed and gone to Śrī Lomaśa, pray to him in every way;
either Lomaśa or another brāhmaṇa will effect your deliverance.
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed through the path of the sky;
the rākṣasa arrived at the field of Kuṅkumavāpī and dwelt in a mango grove.
"How might I attain liberation in this state?"—with such thoughts, his mind became dejected;
and though he was tormented by hunger, he did not eat any living beings. (69)
Every tenth period of time he would devour a single creature;
having wandered through the tiger-infested forest, he would then go once more to the mango grove.
Once, while wandering in the forest during a great rainstorm, he became hungry;
there he saw a religious student (brahmacārin) who had come for the sake of obtaining fruit.
The Rākṣasa assailed the one named Brahmaprakāśa;
then, as a celibate student (brahmacārī), he addressed that Rākṣasa with conciliatory words (sāma).
"Tell me, forest-dweller, what is the reason for this assault upon me?
The Rākṣasa replied, "O friend, my mealtime occurs at the eighth watch."
"You have arrived here in this forest before me, who am hungry and fierce;
but that student spoke to him, saying, 'Listen to my auspicious words.'"
"O night-stalker, I am going to give fruits to my teacher;
having given them, I shall return, provided indeed that I am to be eaten by you. (75)
Therefore, wait for me right here for just a moment; once I have informed my teacher and return, you may eat.
Then the night-stalker said: "Go, but listen to what is for your benefit;
tell this to your teacher so that he may effect my liberation. ||77||
I shall certainly not devour you; for that purpose for which I have come is such that it would not be contrary to my preceptor’s will, nor would it be an obstruction to dharma. (78)
"O Brahmin, since even they did not take away my vow, likewise grant me liberation; for this is due to my very nature, and especially because of the defect of my birth. (79)
By means of a mind rich in sensual objects, evil karma was constantly accumulated;
from my childhood, my mind was not even slightly inclined toward dharma.
"Unrighteous deeds were indeed committed by me, especially on the banks of the Narmadā; having reached that state, O Brahmin, I have been sent here. (8.1)
I have come here with sincere intent, desiring to wash away my sins; since you have met me here, O sinless one, liberate me from my evil deeds.
Thus addressed, the brahmin said: "Through the power of your guru, I shall certainly effect your liberation by burning away all your sins. (83)
If fire has been worshipped according to the instructions of the preceptor,
or if the vows have been well-performed, let there be liberation for the Rākṣasa.
If I pay homage with reverence to my father, the god, and my teacher, as well as to my mother, Hari, may there be liberation for the Rākṣasa. (85)
If I do not cause my teacher Hari to be treated with disrespect by my mind, speech, or action, may there be liberation for the Rākṣasa.
Chant the name of the Lord of gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person;
Harikṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, and Janārdana. (87)
I bow down to the Lord of the World; may He, the Teacher of the moving and unmoving, the Master Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, grant me liberation. (88)
I bow to Hari, the lord of Lakṣmī, who holds the conch, the discus, and the Śārṅga bow, and who bears the banner; may he grant me liberation. (89)
I bow down to Dāmodara, the lotus-eyed one who reclines upon Śeṣa;
may Govinda grant me liberation.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa, to Nara, to the upholder of the earth, who dwells in the supreme abode; may he, the Lord of Light, grant me liberation.
I bow to the Lord of Śrī, whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the glorious husband of Pārvatī, the beloved of Ramā; may He grant me liberation. 92.
I have gone for refuge to Him whom the ascetics contemplate, who delights the Lord, and who is the embodiment of all objects of focus. (93)
I have gone for refuge to Him, the Lord of countless gopīs who is the Supreme Brahman, the son of Śrī Kambharā, the support of all, and the all-pervading. (94)
I have gone for refuge to that Supreme Self, who abides within the self, who possesses the power to wash away karma, and who is the destroyer of rebirth. ||95||
He creates and protects the Īśānas, gods, ṛṣis, ancestors, and human beings, as well as reptiles, trees, aquatic creatures, and those born from sweat. 96.
I have gone for refuge to him who bears the form of Brahmā, the source of the universe, the protector, the infallible one, and the youthful Gopālakṛṣṇa. ||97||
I have gone for refuge to Him who is the Lord of sacrifice, the Ender, the inner controller of all, and the Supreme Lord, than whom nothing else is higher. (98)
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dispel those auspicious and inauspicious deeds performed by me in other births. 99.
Whatever sin has been committed by me during the night, at dawn, at midday and the afternoon, and during the two twilights— may all of that be utterly destroyed.
Whatever painful karma has been committed by means of body, mind, or speech—whether while standing, walking, or indeed while lying down. || 10.1 ||
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, by one whose mind has wavered due to intoxication—may that [sin] quickly go to destruction through the chanting of the names of Bālakṛṣṇa. 102.
And that which arises from longing for another's wife or another's wealth, from malice, and from censuring the great-souled ones, which brings suffering to others; 103.
May whatever sin was committed through words that pierce the vital organs be destroyed;
likewise, [may it be destroyed] regarding what is eaten, drunk, chewed, sucked, and licked.
Whatever sin was committed by me in childhood, in youth, in my prime, in the decline of age, or in another birth—[may it all be destroyed]. (105)
May that [sin] immediately go to destruction through the chanting and glorification of "Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," by virtue of the majesty of the Bestower of Liberation. 106.
Salutations to Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā.
Salutations again and again to the child of the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa.
O Bhadra, I have thus narrated to you this [account] which destroys all sins. 108.
"O Rākṣasa, with this divine hymn, which bestows heaven and liberation and was uttered by your preceptor, you must propitiate Bālakṛṣṇa."
Every day, by means of this hymn, you should likewise remember Lomaśa,
your guru, as well as the Supreme Brahman, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama.
Having offered praise and established firm devotion, you shall then be liberated from sin;
for Hari, who is subservient to his devotees, removes all sins when praised with devotion.
Having heard this, the Rākṣasa said: "Lead me to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
show me my preceptor, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the bestower of liberation."
Thus addressed, the religious student gave that protective hymn to the cruel lion-demon; by means of it, he was freed from sin.
Having been born from that, he went together with that very same student;
then that Rākṣasa came to my hermitage, which is named Lomaśa.
Indeed, he was instantly freed from sin; having gone into the presence of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, he obtained a vision of Him and drank the nectar of His feet.
Having visited all the sacred fords, he indeed became possessed of a divine body;
mounting a celestial vehicle, he went to the imperishable abode.
You, Āryāyanā and the others, have been protected from the dissolution by water;
worship Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Having been delivered from death by him who will deliver us from saṃsāra,
we take refuge in that Savior, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person.
Having spoken thus and remembering Śrī Hari, Lomaśa remained silent;
and Āryā, Ayanodā, and the others attained supreme peace.

O Rādhikā, through the recitation and hearing of hymns, there shall be worldly enjoyment, the destruction of states of bondage, liberation, and peace; all this shall come to pass, of this there is no doubt. (2.61.120)

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord, having taken two hundred men submerged in water onto a boat, crossed the Stambha excavation via the Mahī river, circumambulated Somanātha, Svarṇapura, Camatkārapura, and other sites, and reached the field of Kuṅkumavāpī by means of his boat-vehicle; as well as the protective hymn instructed by Lomaśa, and the liberation of the Rākṣasa Krūrasiṃha through the attainment of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa by means of a Brāhmaṇa," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section, the Tretā-santāna.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Rādhikā, those two hundred men and women, having bowed down to and worshipped Śrī Lomaśa with devotion, became like ten million, a billion, and a hundred billion maidens.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇakāntā, they went to the auspicious dwelling place; there they took refuge in the glorious Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama). || 2 ||
O Lord of ten million maidens, O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Lord of the universe,
O Lord of all, protect forever those who have no other support and who have taken refuge in you.
Thus, having gathered together, they joyfully performed their worship, saying:
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Radiance! (4)
"O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī! O Lord of Mañju! O Lord of Śrī Pārvatī!
Thus did they, protected by the boat, cry out while beating their palms and whistling.
There they observed the Cāturmāsya vow, endowed with devotion to Kṛṣṇa;
then the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika arrived.
The festival for the manifestation of the chosen deity occurred in the eighth year;
it was celebrated by the gods, the lords, and the sages, and it greatly adorned heaven.
Beholding him, they were filled with joy and performed worship to Hari;
O Rādhikā, a supreme wonder then occurred—listen as I tell it to you.
The Blessed One, the king of kings, having been worshipped very early in the morning,
gave many gifts on the eighth year of his own birth.
He caused the Brahmins, virtuous men, and virtuous women, as well as girls, boys, maidens, the poor, the helpless, and young children to be fed.
Lame, one-eyed, deaf, maimed, blind, and likewise dull-witted,
as well as those with leprosy— all who had come from various regions to the sacred ford.
Seeing the embodied beings who were diseased and those who were crippled or deformed, such as the lame, the compassionate Blessed One himself spoke to them at midday after their meal.
May those with impaired bodies come, as well as the diseased and the suffering;
may those with missing limbs and even those with defective senses come as well. 13.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; on this festival of my birth, I grant you today an unprecedented gift that bestows happiness.
Having spoken thus and having placed a golden trough of sugar by his side,
he sat upon the elephant-throne in order to distribute the sugar.
The Khañja people also arrived, and having given them fine sugar,
Hari-Kṛṣṇa touched their share with his left hand.
Their lameness quickly vanished and they became possessed of full limbs;
then those who were one-eyed set out after giving them pebbles. (17)
He touched his eyes with his left hand for the sake of liberation from blindness;
at that moment, one-eyedness, blindness, and all defects of vision were instantly destroyed.
Indeed, their eyes were filled with a flood of full rays;
then the deaf arrived, and [the gods] gave them sugar-candy.
He touched their ears with his hand and called them by their names;
their deafness vanished and they regained the power of hearing.
Then, when they had arrived with their wounds healed, Narayana gave them sugar-candy upon their wrists,
forearms, and fingers.
He touched them with his hand and instantly removed their state of being maimed;
they became as if naturally endowed with hands, their minds filled with joy.
Then those who were dull-witted and senseless arrived in her presence;
sugar was given to them, and their bodies were indeed touched by her hand.
Likewise, by touching their heads, dullness, mental confusion,
diseases such as wind-disorders (vāta), and even sleeplessness were destroyed in an instant.
Then maidens arrived and lepers also arrived;
having given them sugar as well as the nectar of his feet, [he dismissed them].
Having sprinkled his limbs with water, he destroyed diseases and leprosy;
then there arrived birds and other creatures whose bodies were broken and mangled.
Having given them sugar-candy and touched them with his hand,
he mercifully destroyed their disease of the limbs at that very moment.
And by means of yoga, he quickly caused the broken part to heal;
thereafter, people suffering from leprosy came to the Supreme Lord.
Having given them sugar and the sprinkling of water, Hari himself indeed applied it to the areas affected by leprosy. ||29||
All their ailments vanished; in an instant, they attained whiteness and purity. Those meritorious ones became free from disease, serene, and radiant. (2.62.30)
Then those eunuchs said: "O Ocean of Compassion, O Śrī Puruṣottama, it was due to great sin that our state as eunuchs arose; you have now become [our refuge]. (3.1)

If [it is argued that] one who is capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise proceeds [to act], then for us who have attained the yoga of the Blessed One, there would be the state of having seeds (sabījatā). 32.
O Blessed One, what benefit would there be for you from seeing them, when Śrī Hari himself, having heard [of their devotion], simply gave them sugar-candies? (33)
Then he gave the command to bathe at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
all the eunuchs went there quickly, bathed, and then departed.
At that time, men who resembled humans in their masculinity, yet possessed the strength and qualities suitable for women,
became full of human characteristics and endowed with seed.
Women who resembled females in their female state were endowed with *rajas*;
those women possessing the marks of femininity became fully possessed by the abundance of *rajas*. (36)
Thus, indeed, out of compassion, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, by means of his own powers,
fashioned eunuchs, males, and females along with their constituent elements.
Seeing this, they were struck with wonder and attained supreme amazement;
that sacred bathing place where they bathed is called Ṣaṇḍhoddhāra.
Then all the women and men offered hymns of praise to Hari, their hearts full of love and the movements of their minds steady. ||39||
Salutations be to You who shine in the supreme abode as the Supreme Self;
salutations to the Teacher of countless virtuous, chaste, and noble liberated souls.
Homage to the Lord of Syllables, who bestows the instruction of the imperishable;
homage to the dweller in Goloka, who instructs the cowherds and cowherdesses. 41.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the cows; salutations to the husband of Śrī Rādhā.
Salutations to the dweller of Vaikuṇṭha; salutations to the husband of Śrī Ramā. ||42||
Salutation to the Lord of many Vaikuṇṭhas, the husband of Lakṣmī and Śrī;
salutation to the Master who possesses the qualities of the beautiful swan of the splendor of Śrī. ||43||
Salutations to the Lord of Vṛndā, Tulasī, Kamalā, and Pārvatī;
salutations be unto you, O Lord of the World, O Vāsudeva, salutations be unto you! ||44||
O Śrīnivāsa, salutations be unto you; O Viśvaksena, salutations be unto you.
O Garuḍadhvaja, Lord of the Gopīs, O Viṣṇu, O Vaikuṇṭha, salutations to you! (45)
O Supreme Person, Lord of Gods, Sovereign of All, homage be to You!
O Beloved of the Lotus-born, who are without beginning, beginning, middle, or end, homage be to You! 46.
O you who contain the creation within, salutations to you; O Śatruñjaya, let there be salutations to you!
Salutations to the one of golden form; salutations to you, Kālanetra. ||47||
O you of the great navel, O you of the great root, O abode of the root, homage be to you!
O abode of Dharma, O abode of the heart, O you of pure hearing, O you of wide renown! 48.
O Overseer of Dharma, Overseer of Subjects, Overseer of Time, homage be to you!
O Wielder of the Mace, Wielder of the Lotus, O you who are questioned by the Vedas, homage be to you! 49.
O Śrīdhara, O wearer of the forest garland, O Kṛṣṇa, salutations be unto you!
O Puruṣṭuta, O Great Kalpa, O Soul of All, salutations to you, O All-pervading Lord! 2.62.50.
O Supreme Lord, whose nature is time consisting of twelve parts, whose nature is the Sāman,
who consists of the sky and the sun, who consists of the moon, you who are most subtle— salutations be to you!
O blue-haired one, O Guḍākeśa, O great-haired one, homage be to you!
O lovely-haired one, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O all-haired one, homage be to you! ||52||
O White, Red, Yellow, Variegated, and Black One, salutations be unto you!
O Govinda, who brings joy to the lotus-dweller, salutations to you, the Swan! ||53||
Salutations to you, the eye of Dharma; salutations to you, the thousand-limbed one.
Salutations to you, whose form is the universe; salutations to you, whose form is the supreme abode. ||54||
Homage to you, the Nyagrodha, the Pippala, the one with great branches;
homage be to you, whose trunk, leaves, sprouts, creepers, and shoots [are all one]. (55)
You indeed are Viṣṇu, consisting of the Vedas, the omnipresent one who transcends the deities of the sacred fords;
you are the very embodiment of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; salutations to you, the enjoyer of the sacrificial portions. ||56||
O Supreme Brahman, salutations be unto you; O Word-Brahman, salutations be unto you.
You are knowledge, you are the object of knowledge; O Worthy of Veneration, salutations be unto you.
In women you are the very embodiment of speech, and in men you are the embodiment of compassion;
in sons you are the feeling of parental affection—we have come to you for refuge. (58)
"O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, grant us deliverance from saṃsāra!
Having spoken thus, the sage Āryāyaṇa then observed a vow of silence. (59)
With supreme affection, he praised the beloved of Śrī, the Supreme Person:
"I bow to the Fish; I bow to the Tortoise; I bow to the Horse-headed One."
I bow to Trivikrama, and I bow to the Lord Mādhava;
I bow to Īśāna, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Kumāriḷa.
I bow to Nārāyaṇa; I bow to him whose banner is Garuḍa;
I bow to Narasiṃha; and I bow to the protector of desires.
I pay homage to Śrī Nārāyaṇa, whose eyes resemble lotuses;
I pay homage to Him who possesses the banner, the discus, the lotus, the bow, the fish, and the beautiful trident.
I bow to Gopati, the son of Kambharā, the omnipresent Lord, the delight of the cowherds,
who holds a mace in his hand and resides at Aśvapaṭṭasara.
I bow to the Lord who is half-woman, who bestows happiness upon the multitude of women, who holds a lotus in his hand, and whose thighs are like lotuses. 65.
I bow to the one whose rays are like lotuses and who possesses a broad expanse of upward-pointing lines;
I bow to the one wearing a forest garland, whose hips resemble the goddess Lakṣmī.
I bow to the Lord of the Earth; I bow to the Lord of Śrī. O Lord of the helpless, salutations to You whether You are situated upon a boat or within a celestial chariot.
Salutations to you who abide in the heart, who abide in the play of devotion, and who abide in the protection of the wretched;
I bow to the Brahman of great splendor, the master of the three *Nāciketas* fires.
I bow to the destroyer of all diseases, who gratifies the sense of smell;
I bow to Rukmakavaca; I bow to Puruṣottama.
I bow to the Lord of the Forest, the Lord of Honey, and the Lord of Nectar;
I bow to Vāsudeva, the wielder of the discus, whose glory is his wealth.

I bow to the Lord of the Supreme, who has entered into all beings, who is peaceful, whose form is the Dharma, and who bestows liberation; I go for refuge to that Protector, the worthy object of refuge. 7.1.
Thus the illustrious sage Āryāyaṇa praised the Lord of Gods;
thereafter, at evening, the gods and men performed the ritual of dismissing the worship.
There, on the bank, the sage Āryāyaṇa always spoke to those men and women who had disembarked from the boat: "To Hari [you must go]. (73)
They prayed most fervently to behold their own lands;
at the end of the month of Kārtika, Hari there remembered his supreme vehicle.
A celestial chariot, endowed with divine qualities, arrived there;
having seated all of them within it, he traveled through the sky with speed in an instant.
The Blessed One reached the Dhīravīra lake on the slopes of Mount Aravallī, wherever his place of birth was located. //76//
