"We are blessed and honored that we have this assembly with him," having said this,
the glorious Nārada bowed down again and again.
Having placed jeweled garlands around the necks of the Lord Bālakṛṣṇa, Śuka, and Śrīvallabha, Nārada bowed down to them.
Looking again at the assembly, Nārada raised his hand and spoke with a long-drawn voice to all who were listening: || 111 ||
"Let the great ones hear the truth; I speak the truth:
in this world, incarnations of Kṛṣṇa shall appear by the thousands. (1.12)
But such a one as Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, is an incarnation who is at times the most excellent among the most excellent and the most perfect of all. 11.3.
Born today at the commencement [of his manifestation], he will never be born again;
others, being dark-complexioned, shall take refuge in his divine play with devotion.
From the feet up to the crest-lock,
there are thousands of marks of the Supreme Self upon every part of his body.
One hundred [beings] are in his feet, ten likewise in each of his shanks, twenty in his thighs, and five in his private organ.
There are thirty on his hips and twenty-five on his belly;
there are one hundred on his chest, and three hundred on his back and sides.
There are two hundred [marks] on the neck and the shoulders, one hundred on the face, three on the throat,
one hundred marks on the two hands, and likewise fifty on the two palms.
Ten on the forearms, twenty-five on the two eyes,
sixteen on the cheeks, five on the forehead, and likewise six on the two ears.
On his tongue and on his lips there were, respectively, ten and twenty lines;
on his nose were ten lines, and on his brow were six hundred.
There are twenty [hairs] in the hair, and four on the chin;
throughout the body hairs, there are heaps of the qualities of gold.

As many as are its qualities, its intrinsic natures, its lines, its speckles, its joints, its conjunctions, its configurations, its structures, and its excellent arrangement—[all these are present]. (122)
And it is not possible for me to describe each single limb;
here, every excellence that constitutes the nature of all things exists everywhere. (123)
Having taken portions from these fragments of the primary form, other forms will arise—other gods who are lords and supreme lords. (124)
"O you who are seated in this assembly, there is nothing more to be said by me as authority;
for you are incarnations, liberated souls, and supreme lords. (125)
Within the dwarf-form Viśvarūpa, however, between every two hairs, there stand millions of marks; they are not fit for counting.
Indeed, the nature of the three worlds resides within the form of the Blessed One;
for all the signs of universal creation exist within his very body.
Above the throat and in the head, the creation of the subtle is established;
below the throat and above the hands, the creation of the gross is situated.
Extending from below the waist down to the tips of the nails,
his body is marked with thousands of millions of lotuses.
Having spoken thus, Nārada ceased by the command of Sanaka;
and then the father presented gifts of gratification to Rādhikā.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Providing of Food to the Great Beings, the Subsequent Assembly Gathering, and the Instruction on the Supreme Knowledge Spoken by Nārada," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: Kubera, the Vasus, the wish-fulfilling trees, the earth, Lakṣmī, the treasures, and the cintāmaṇi jewels stand before Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
O Rādhikā, they indeed stood ready to bestow their rewards;
those born of divine opulence gave celestial garlands to the liberated souls.
Then, by the command of Kṛṣ� precious crowns and earrings from the incarnations themselves, and divine necklaces from the lords.
They indeed gave golden thrones to Brahmā and the others,
and they then presented inexhaustible vessels to the ancestors.
They gave sacrificial vessels and seats to the sages, and to the gods they gave suitable jewel necklaces, each according to their rank.
Then they gave [these things] to the Dānavas, the Asuras, and the Daityas as well;
they gave vehicles, mounts, ornaments, and wealth to human beings.
They gave jewels from the elephants, the nectar of food from the cattle,
and substances such as the juices of fruits and flowers from the birds.

He gave wealth appropriate to each— such as gold, silver, and so forth— to the Brahmins, and diamonds and such to the kings, according to their respective needs, along with both embodied and unembodied objects, as well as sentient and insentient things.
Then they gave garments, rags, and so forth to the virtuous men, and ornaments, clothes, and finery— which increase good fortune— to the virtuous women as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
They gave there until they were satisfied, yet the word "give more" was not spoken again;
and they gave in such a way that they were unable to carry away as much as they desired.
Whatever was desired by whomsoever was bestowed upon them there instantly;
the word "no" was never used, nor was the word "take" ever employed. (11)
In this manner, they gave abundant wealth as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and also as rewards (pāritoṣika) to those worthy recipients, such as the Brahmins and others.
They gave abundant wealth to the cooks and confectioners, and even to the laborers, gold and diamonds. (13)
They gave wealth to the bards, the wandering minstrels, and the artisans;
they gave wealth to the wrestlers, the dancers, and the female performers.

They gave necklaces, ornaments, garments, and other gifts to the female singers and maidservants; and they gave clothes, jewelry, and other items to the male servants, the helpless, and the destitute.
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, they gave ornaments, garments, wealth, and vessels of gold and silver to the daughters of the three worlds.
Whatever brings satisfaction to whomever, in whatever manner and by whatever means—that very thing should be given at that time; there is no hesitation whatsoever. (17)
And from virtuous women, from chaste ones, and likewise from those devoted to their husbands; and from widows, from elderly women, and even from mothers in every way. (18)
Then, by the command of Kṛṣṇa, they gave ornaments, garments, and wealth to their sisters, daughters, granddaughters, and the queens, each according to her rank.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself, saying "To those of great majesty," caused excellent rewards to be bestowed.
Indeed, Śrī Kaṃbharā bestowed ornaments of every kind, which were beyond price even through the likes of Kubera and Vasu, upon all the women.
Likewise, he gave golden necklaces of jewels, gems, and pearls;
and Gopāla gave objects made of gold to all the people.
Wealth, such as excellent jewels, necklaces, and so forth, is likewise powerful according to its specific requirements.
In this manner, Śrī Lomaśa then gave [the fruits] to all the great sages.
She from whom pills that grant one's desires arise moment by moment;
she is the sister of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa and his elder sister, Santuṣā. 24.
He gave auspicious marriage threads,
substances for dyeing, combs, golden ornaments, bodices, and likewise silken garments.
He gave her necklaces, colikās, and other ornaments, as well as natthis, baṃgiḍīs, girdles, bracelets, and rings that bestow contentment. (26)
Having thus bestowed gifts and rewards,
the father spoke words of favor to those assembled at the great festival.
Śrī Gopālakṛṣṇa said: "In the great festival of my son Kṛṣṇa’s sacred thread ceremony,
may there always be an increase in the splendor of you all who have assembled here."
I offer a welcome and give my thanks;
I speak here with humility regarding the deficient service rendered by me. (29)

One might think, "I am the Lord who is to be endured," considering that I am the object of forbearance for the liberated ones, for the incarnations, for the followers of Brahmā, and for those practicing celibacy. (30)
Of the lords and sovereign goddesses, of gods and divine women, of humans and human women, and of Daityas and Daitya women; ||3 1 ||
Of the nāgas and the wives of the nāgas, of those with inert or conscious bodies, of the guardians of the quarters, of kings, and of the ṛṣis and their wives. || 36 ||
Through your presence, the festive rites were magnified;
by your arrivals, I have been made a vessel for all glories. (33)
My son has been nourished by his own inherent splendors;
he must be understood once again, and my transgression must be forgiven. (34)
Having spoken thus, he repeatedly offered words of thanks to those who had performed the work;
together with his family, he requested their blessings. (35)
At that time, a cry of victory was raised by the assembly;
then Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa first [honored] Bālakṛṣṇa indeed. (36)
He came for the purpose of worship and honored him with divine offerings;
he presented a crown, cowherd attire, a flute, and wish-fulfilling gems. (37)
He gave away wish-fulfilling cows and worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings;
then Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa also worshipped Śrī Hari at that time.
The crown, earrings, conch, discus, mace, and likewise the lotus;
Garuḍa as his vehicle, and the divine garland of kaustubha gems. (39)
He gave [these] to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa and worshipped him with saffron and other offerings;
likewise did Vāsudeva and the other incarnations, the Lord of Prakṛti.
Pradhāneśa, as well as Bhūman, Mahāviṣṇu, Virāṭpuruṣa, and Sadāśiva, along with their respective Śaktis, arrived there with joy. ||41||
Having applied the *tilaka*, collyrium, and the *bindu* mark, and having indeed placed crowns, ear-ornaments, and necklaces made of pearls and gems; 42.
They gave them rings, girdles, and staffs,
as well as those divine weapons fashioned from their own respective abodes, which took the forms of swans, lions, and elephants.
And they gave the embodied child excellent seats;
likewise, the Īśvaras and the Seven Sages, stationed within the eight enclosures, [gave him gifts].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and other sages, practicing celibacy, [offered] garlands of gold and garlands of flowers, golden vessels, and sandals. 45.
They gave water-pots, jars, and numerous garments to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as fresh and ever-new divine wealth. 46.
The ancestors, sages, and gods likewise [offered] the parasol and the fly-whisks, as well as celestial chariots, vehicles, swans, male servants, and female servants. ||47||
A staff fashioned from gold, a mirror, parrots, and peahens;
various musical instruments, as well as jars of nectar.
And [he gave] wish-fulfilling creepers of desire and the like, as well as sun-stones and moon-stones,
and ornaments such as the attire of the lords of the directions, along with garlands of jewels.
The Daityas, Dānavas, and Asuras also gave divine riches and their own splendors to Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa. (2.68.50)
Then the Nāgas, Sarpas, and Bhogins gave jewels, rubies, pearls,
necklaces, and various excellent riches as gifts.
Then the oceans gave jewels and pearls;
the rivers and streams, such as the Varuṇā and others, also gave substances and essences.
The mountains and the mines also gave various kinds of jewels: gems, diamonds, pearls, and rubies.
Emeralds, sapphires, lapis lazuli, topazes,
karketanas, bhīṣmakas, pulakas, and those called rudhiras— ||54||
They gave him especially crystal, coral, and rows of lotuses;
the men indeed gave him beautiful garments of their own.
He also gave radiant blankets, as well as vessels, ornaments, and towels;
and likewise elephants, horses, bulls, cows, and female buffaloes.
The trees and creepers gave substances such as gold and silver to the child with devotion,
and they offered worship with garlands and other articles, providing sweet juices.
They gave couches, fine mats, straw mats, four-legged stools and the like,
as well as beds, lutes, carriages, and grinding stones.
They joyfully gave them hearth-stoves, threshing-floors, water-jars, brooms,
and secret chests for storing weapons.
Mortars, spinning-wheels, and priceless chests and baskets;
water-jars, milk-pails, and vessels for churning curds.
And Droṇa joyfully gave a vessel of curd, granaries, ear-rings, flour, a stone slab, a bell, and a sugarcane press. (61)
Swings, hammocks, small riding horses, four-legged couches,
silken garments, and even woolen clothes.
They gave garments of excellent quality adorned with gold, along with sugar and other sweets,
fruits, fruit-eaters, and likewise garlands of dried cardamom and other fragrant flowers.
Then they gave various kinds of cooling sandalwood;
indeed, they gave leaf-shields, body-armor, and helmets.
Bowls, pairs of vessels, pots, jars and the like, water-pitchers, various types of containers, and those vessels used for the *puṭapāka* method; ||65||
They provided water-sprinkling vessels, cooking pots, dining halls, spears,
shields, and even various weapons and missiles.
Then they gave away countless riches of gold and silver,
along with sandalwood, bīra, saffron, unbroken grains, and liquids mixed with gulāla.
With flowers, filaments, perfumes, and even musk;
with various camphors, dyes, coloring agents, and decorative leaf-patterns for necklaces. ||68||
And with sprouts and leaves of Tulasī, as well as Kunda and Ketaka flowers, Campakas, and fragrant oils, they worshipped the Lord, their Master. (69)
With one hundred and one supreme offerings, the deities and other incarnations,
as well as the lords, performed the lustration ceremony for Hari.
They joined him with blessings, circumambulated him, praised him, bowed down to him, and sat upon their seats. ||71||
Then, the compassionate Anādi-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa instantly granted him a vision of his own fundamental essential nature.
The members of the assembly beheld the supreme abode for the first time,
and they also saw there the pearls of men and the pearls of women who had been liberated.
They also beheld upon the head of the form of Bālakṛṣṇa the imperishable abode of Brahman, as well as liberated men and liberated women. (74)
They beheld thousands of incarnations of Hari upon his forehead;
Goloka in his right eye and Vaikuṇṭha in his left eye.
They beheld Amṛta and Nityakailāsa in their ears;
they beheld Mahāviṣṇu in the nose and Kāla upon the forehead. ||76||
At the two corners of the forehead, they beheld the Supreme Lord and the Lord of Nature; at the base of the nose, they saw the manifestations (vyūhas) beginning with Vāsudeva.
And those members of the assembly beheld the face of Vairāja in the center;
and upon his fangs, they saw the hundreds of faces of the Creator Brahmā.
And they beheld Rudras such as Śatanetra and others upon his teeth,
and Viṣṇus with thousands of hands and more stationed within the lines of his beard.
The members of the assembly beheld Mahāmāyā upon his upper lip and Pradhāna likewise upon his lower lip, while they saw Śrī Lakṣmī upon his chin.
In the hairs of Hanūmān, they beheld the lords of the eightfold māyā-enclosures;
and upon his two cheeks, they saw crores of the goddesses, the virtuous Satīs.
Indeed, at the roots of the hair is the world of Brahmā and the others;
in the middle of the hair are the heavens; and at the tips of the hair are the nether regions such as Atala.
Those members of the assembly saw human beings upon his head and back;
thus they beheld the entire creation, consisting of the nature of Brahmā and characterized by its causal essence. ||83||
They indeed beheld her as subtle, eternal, constant, and in the form of a seed; and then they saw her as the transformative [power] arisen from the creation of causes.
They again beheld the gross creation below the region of his throat;
in his throat was the Supreme Brahman, and in his heart was the Imperishable Brahman. (85)
They also beheld Goloka upon her breasts, Vaikuṇṭha on her right and left [sides], nectar on her shoulders, and eternal Kailāsa on her two shoulders. (86)
They beheld Mahāviṣṇu in the heart and Kāla in the throat;
and they beheld Pradhāneśa and Prakṛtīśa in the two armpits. ||87||
They beheld the manifestations beginning with Vāsudeva above the heart,
the Vairāja form below the heart, and the Vedhas (Brahmā) in the ribs.
One should place the Viṣṇus in the joints of the head, the Rudras in the joints of the back,
Mahāmāyā in the belly, and Pradhāna in the navel.
One should worship Śrī and Lakṣmī at the sides of the navel, the eight Āvṛtis on the hips,
the Īśvarīs below the hips, and likewise Satī at the base of the liṅga.
In their body hairs, they beheld Satyaloka and the other worlds, as well as the hidden lower realms beginning with Atala, and the oceans and mountains situated in those respective places. ||9.1||
Moreover, they likewise saw the remainder of the tortoise upon his hip, as well as a great mass of water within the channels of the suture and in the bodily constituents.
They beheld Kāmadeva at the tip of the liṅga, the Daityas and Dānavas in his two thighs, and the sages, ancestors, and gods within the pores of his hair. ||93||
And they beheld humans upon their knees, asuras upon the pair of their shanks,
and furthermore, they saw nagas, serpents, and others upon their feet.
Beholding again this form consisting of the three worlds and yet consisting of Bālakṛṣṇa— this great wonder— they realized their own cause.
Since all incarnations arise from this Supreme Person,
they reflected for a moment upon Bālakṛṣṇa.
Then, at the conclusion of the assembly, the sound of bells resounded;
accompanied by shouts of victory, the members of the assembly rose and departed for their own abodes.
Honored on all sides with sweet drinks and the like, betel leaves, and sweet speech, as well as with celestial chariots and other such honors, they were highly esteemed. 98.
Filled with happiness, they went to their own homes, regions, and foreign lands;
likewise, embodied beings, inert things, the principles, and qualities such as taste and the rest [departed]. 99.
Other groups, such as the servants and so forth, also went home after being honored;
thereafter, these sages and ancestors departed for heaven and other realms.
Then the supreme lords went to the worlds of Brahmā, the lords who dwell in Īśana; and the Daityas and Dānavas went to their own realms, such as Pātāla. || 101 ||
Mountains, trees, and creepers; rivers, sacred fords, and streams; lakes, fields, forests, and groves as well. 102.
Having bowed down again and again to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, they departed from the great pavilion, that magnificent palace constructed by Viśvakarman.
The Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa made his concluding remarks,
as did the venerable Sanatkumāra and Nārada, after bowing down.
Then the two maidens went to Badarī and to the hermitage of Lomaśa;
and thus, O Rādhikā, the festival of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) was most magnificent.
And upon completion in the eighth year, during the month of Vaiśākha, one shall partake in liberation through the recitation, hearing, and remembrance of this Supreme Self. 106.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Rewards upon the Great-souled Ones, the Worship of the Lord, the Presentation of Gifts, the Divine Vision, the Dispelling [of Doubts], and so forth," in the second section, the Tretā-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā.
Śrī Rādhikā said:
O Kṛṣṇa, how should Your service and worship be performed? By what form of adoration, O Kṛṣṇa, is Your pleasure fully aroused? (1)
What gifts should be given for your pleasure, O Hari?
What meritorious acts are praised as those which bring satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa? (2)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
All gifts are praised for the gratification of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
yet it is through worship performed with devotion that this Śrī Kṛṣṇa becomes fully satisfied.
Whatever one desires should indeed be offered to Kṛṣṇa for the sake of pleasing Him;
O beloved, every meritorious offering made therein brings satisfaction to Kṛṣṇa.
Those gifts which are given by the faithful and devoted, dedicated to the Lord of Śrī, never indeed undergo decay.
Those lunar days alone are most excellent where Kṛṣṇa is indeed attained; those days upon which service is rendered to the virtuous are [truly] auspicious, while all other lunar days are inferior.
When the virtuous are honored, the Supreme Lord is honored;
he who hates them is of base soul and goes to a low birth.
Whether it be a man or a woman who, being devoted to Kṛṣṇa, worships me with devotion, he or she is indeed my own body;
for I possess the body of a Vaiṣṇava.
The virtuous—whether they be wise or even ignorant—should not be held in contempt;
for they are my divine bodies, and therefore one should always worship them.
The virtuous should be satisfied through action, mind, or speech, by offering gifts, or even by service, food, or worship. (2.69.10)
Having risen early in the morning, remembered me, and bathed with auspicious substances, one should perform the worship of my form; for indeed, service to the virtuous is worship itself.
Devotion to me is indeed propitiation; servitude is always superior and more excellent.
Meditation upon me and upon the holy ones must be performed for the sake of liberation. (12)
O beloved, the massaging of the feet of the virtuous should always be performed;
for I reside within their senses, and their satisfaction is my own satisfaction.
They should indeed be worshipped with flowers endowed with fragrance and sap;
namely, the campaka, the kunda, the mango, the dhavala, and likewise the khadira.
Likewise, the śataghnī, the aśoka, the bakula, the karavīraka, the tilaka, the japā, the jātī, the yūthikā, and the padminī [should be planted]. || 15 ||
Kamalī, sthalapadmā, tulasī, kaumudī, sūryamukhī, cammilikā, pārijāta, and sukesara; || 16 ||
O Rādhikā, these flowers are the ketakī, the hāraśṛṅgāra, the kadamba, the devadāruka, the sarja tree, and the kalpavallī. 17.
In my worship, one should offer these things, with the exception of the *ketakī*:
the *bilva* leaf, the *śamī* leaf, the *bhṛṅga* leaf, and the *tulasī*.
The leaves of the *tamāla* and *mālatī* are highly recommended for my worship;
one should also honor me with the tender sprouts of creepers and *darbha* grass.
One should worship with coral, silk threads and the like, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass,
as well as with flower buds, sandalwood, saffron, *uśīra*, and filaments.
O beloved, I always satisfy you with the incense of fragrant woods;
and with barley, wheat, and rice, which have been consecrated by the oblation (havis).
Sesame, mung beans, and the like, as well as black gram and rice, are dear to me; likewise, the gifting of cows and the granting of land are purifying acts. (22)
O Rādhikā, gifts of clothing, food, and gold should be given for my pleasure;
in the month of Māgha, sesame seeds and fuel should be offered so that Hari may be pleased. 23.
In Phālguna, rice, clothing, deer-skins, and the like are recommended;
in Caitra, very fine garments, beds, and seats [are recommended]. (24)
In the month of Vaiśākha, fragrant and sweet-smelling substances should be given, along with water-pots, a cow, a palm-leaf fan, and excellent sandalwood. (25)
By him [who acts thus], a son, wealth, a wife, a daughter, and a cow shall be obtained;
he should constantly listen to the sacred narrative and worship Hari with devotion. (26)
Of that horse-sacrifice accompanied by sacrificial fees, and of the gift of gold, land, dogs, cattle, elephants, and chariots; || 27 ||
For one who listens to even a single verse of the story of Hari, whether woman or man, the merit of giving arises as supreme; of this there is no doubt. (28)
He is pure and meritorious in this world, for he has resorted to all sacred fords—
whether at the Gaṅgā, in the Naimiṣa forest, at Puṣkara, or likewise at Mānasa.
Whatever foremost merit is gained at Nārāyaṇa, Aśvapaṭṭa, Kokāmukha, and Prayāga during the month of Māgha, that shall be obtained from listening to this narrative. (2.69.30)

Whatever fruit results from the Rājasūya sacrifice, whatever great fruit exists in heaven, and whatever fruit exists in the world of mortals—all that shall arise from listening to this narrative. (31)

Whatever fruit is obtained from the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, whatever fruit arises from the gift of delicious food, and whatever fruit comes from the gift of jewels during an eclipse of the sun or moon; [all that is attained by this]. (32)
Whatever fruit comes from protecting one's kinsmen and the people during a famine, and whatever comes from guarding and protecting the gods, the sacred fires, the virtuous, and the brahmins; ||33||

Whatever fruit there may be from the duty of serving one's parents and parents-in-law, from serving a brother, from serving an elder, a child, or a cow, and whatever fruit may arise from such service—[all that is attained by him]. ||34||
O Rādhikā, the fruit of that shall be mine here through listening to this narrative:
a pair of sandals, an umbrella, salt, myrobalan, and so forth. (35)
O beloved, for my pleasure, one should give cool water, fine clothing, buttermilk, curd, shoes, and an umbrella during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, a fan, milk, sugar, garments, a vehicle, and mounts should be given for the sake of Rādhikā in the abode of Hari. (37)
O beloved, for my pleasure, one should always give all kinds of gifts throughout the month of Śrāvaṇa—food, clothing, utensils, flavors, and so forth, in every respect. (38)
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should offer milk-rice, salt, rice with jaggery, new grains, as well as honey and clarified butter for my pleasure. (39)
In the month of Āśvina, one should offer nine kinds of new grain, a bull, a horse, gold,
copper vessels, garments, lamps, and other such items.
In the month of Kārttika, [one should offer] gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth.
